## Volume Front Matter

### Series Title Page

## Complete Course of Patrology, or Universal Library

Complete, integral, uniform, convenient, economical, of all the holy Fathers, Doctors, and ecclesiastical writers who flourished from the apostolic age to the time of Innocent III; a chronological reprinting of all the monuments of Catholic tradition that have survived from the first twelve centuries of the Church, according to the most accurate editions, carefully collated with one another and with several manuscript codices, and corrected with the greatest diligence; continually illustrated by dissertations, commentaries, and variant readings; enlarged with all works discovered after the extensive editions produced during the last three centuries; furnished with particular analytical indexes following each volume and each author of any importance; adorned with chapters properly arranged within the text itself, as well as with headings distinguishing the upper margin of each page and indicating its subject matter; expanded by works both doubtful and apocryphal, and also by works possessing some authority with regard to ecclesiastical tradition; enriched with two general indexes: one of subjects, by consulting which whatever each Father has written on any topic may be seen at a glance; the other of Sacred Scripture, from which it is readily apparent to the reader which Fathers, and in which passages of their works, have commented on the individual texts of the individual books of Scripture.

The most accurate edition, and one easily preferable to all others if one considers the clarity of the type, the quality of the paper, the integrity of the text, the perfection of the correction, the variety and number of the reprinted works, the extremely convenient format of the volumes—consistently uniform throughout the entire work—the low price, and especially this collection, a single, methodical, and chronological compilation of six hundred fragments and minor works previously scattered here and there, but gathered for the first time in our library from works relating to every age, place, language, and form.

## Second Series

In which appear the Fathers, Doctors, and ecclesiastical writers of the Latin Church from Gregory the Great to Innocent III. Edited by J.-P. Migne, publisher of the Universal Library of the Clergy, or of complete courses in the several branches of ecclesiastical learning.

Patrology was printed in two editions: one Latin, the other Greek-Latin. The Latin edition, comprising 1,200 volumes, is sold for 1,000 francs; the Greek-Latin edition, comprising 1,300 volumes, for 800 francs. The purely Latin edition embraces all authors, both Western and Eastern; the latter, however, are provided in it only in Latin translation.

# In the Year of Our Lord 1107, Geoffroi, Abbot of Vendôme, Cardinal of Saint Prisca

[Col. 0009]

## Historical Notice

*(New Christian Gaul, vol. VIII, p. 1368)*

[Col. 0009A] Geoffroi I, whom Menagius asserts to have been the son of Henry, lord of Lion-d’Angers, the fourth-born son of Robert of Burgundy *(History of Sablé, p. 105)*, was certainly born among a distinguished and noble family of Anjou. He had Rainaldus Credo, lord of Credon, and Maurice, his son, as relatives; Hamerius the archdeacon and William the master were his tutors.

At an early age he entered the monastery of Vendôme as a monk. Not long afterward, while still a novice, young, and only a deacon, but mature in character, modest in appearance, physically robust, highly educated in letters, and adorned with every other virtue, he was proclaimed abbot after Berno’s resignation, on the twelfth day before the Kalends of September in the year 1093.

He was then inaugurated by Ivo, bishop of Chartres, on the ninth day before the Kalends of that same month, and presented him with a profession which later became the seed of a small dispute between them. In the first year of his ordination he went to Rome, where Urban II was hiding for fear of the party of Guibert. He bound the pontiff to himself by an immortal service, having abundantly supplied, fifteen days before Easter in the year 1094, the money with which the Lateran and the Crescentius Tower—now called the Castel Sant’Angelo—could be redeemed.

For this reason he was the first of all to kiss Urban’s foot on the pontifical throne after the restoration of the Lateran. Urban ordained him priest and also restored to him, together with the dignity of cardinal, the church of blessed Prisca, from which the monks of Vendôme had been violently expelled by the Guibertines.

Returning to Gaul, he was summoned that same year to Saumur on the Loire by Hugh, the legate, for the expiation of Fulk Rechin, count. Soon afterward, in the following year, he was called by Urban to the celebrated council held among the Auvergnats, and attended it. He would also have attended the Lateran Council of Paschal II and likewise the Roman Council of Calixtus II, by whom he was similarly summoned, had the brevity of time not prevented one journey and the severity of winter the other.

Urban loved him as a unique son for as long as he lived. In February 1096, Urban even stayed as a guest at Vendôme for eight days. He confirmed the monastery’s privileges, declared null and void the profession Geoffroi had made to Bishop Ivo, and consecrated the altar of the Holy Cross on the fourth day before the Kalends of March.

In the same year, the third of his ordination, Geoffroi subscribed the letter by which the duke of Aquitaine, acting on the pope’s mandate, restored the church of Saint George of Oléron to the monks of Vendôme, on the fourth day before the Ides of December. This restoration was confirmed at the Council of Saintes in 1097, which Geoffroi attended.

That same year he had a dispute with Geoffroi, count of Preuilly; Ivo, bishop of Chartres, settled it. In 1098 he received a bull from Urban II authorizing abbots to be blessed by any bishop, and providing that the church of the Holy Saviour at Angers should be united with the church of Saint Eutropius. In the same bull he confirmed the church of Saint Prisca, where, he states, he had seen the monks of Vendôme living religiously.

In 1101, summoned by the canons of Saint Maurice [Col. 0010A] to elect the bishop of Angers, he rejected Rainaldus of Martigné because the latter had been seized by the crowd against the wishes of the electors. Geoffroi was later reconciled with him.

Paschal II granted Geoffroi the mitre, dalmatic, sandals, and other insignia of cardinalitial dignity in 1102. In 1104 he settled with Alexander, abbot of Talmont, concerning half the offerings of the church of Saint Hilary of Château.

In 1107 he hosted Pope Paschal at Vendôme for eleven days. Around that time he entered into an association with the Cluniacs. Their abbot Hugh granted him, for as long as he lived, authority to govern the chapter, the table, and the entire Cluniac order in his absence; after his death, prayers were to be offered for him as for an abbot.

He also entered into an association with the nuns of Fontevrault in 1114. In 1115, a bull granted to Geoffroi by Paschal II confirmed the concord between the monks of Vendôme and those of Saint-Aubin, which had been sanctioned by Urban. In that year the count of Vendôme made satisfaction barefoot before the Lord’s altar.

In 1119 he obtained from Calixtus II a bull confirming his cardinalitial dignity and the church of Saint Prisca. That same year, when Calixtus was traveling from Poitiers to Tours and had been stripped naked at night by thieves, Geoffroi offered him a gray fur cloak and various other furs. He was also present at the dedication of the altar of the monastery of Ronceray, performed by the same pope in the same year.

In 1124 Count Fulk and his wife Aremburga offered him the waters and fisheries of the Mayenne River, from the wall of the city of Angers to the rock of Cancian.

About this time he congratulated Honorius on his election, but bodily illness prevented him from going to him. This illness had been contracted through excessive labor and repeated journeys to Rome: for the benefit of the Roman Church he had crossed the Alps twelve times and had been captured three times by its adversaries.

Around the year 1126, summoned by Humbald, legate of the Apostolic See, to the Council of Orléans, he refused to attend because the privileges of the Roman pontiffs forbade that the abbot of Vendôme, as a freeholder of Saint Peter, should be summoned to a council by a bishop or by any legate of the Apostolic See.

He attended the hearing concerning the church of Bellesme among the people of Le Mans in 1127. He obtained a bull from Honorius II in 1129. He attended the Council of Reims in 1131 and subscribed the judgment issued by the bishop of Aleth in favor of Marmoutier against the monks of Saint-Jacut.

Finally, while he had gone to Angers on behalf of the monastery of Aquaria, which had shortly before been burned, in order to rebuild it and provide the necessities for the brothers who lived there, he committed his body to the earth, while his spirit, as we believe, migrated to the heavenly realms, on the seventh day before the Kalends of April in the year 1132, as is read in the Chronicle of Vendôme.

In other respects, Geoffroi possessed a keen and vigorous intellect, especially exercised in sacred letters and the canons, as all his works testify. These materials have been collected from Sirmond, volume IV, except for the Commentary on the Psalms.

[Col. 0011]

## Literary Notice

*(Literary History of France, vol. XI, p. 180.)*

[Col. 0011A] 1. Geoffroi’s letters are divided into five classes. The first class contains thirty-one letters addressed to the popes Urban II, Paschal II, Calixtus II, and Honorius II, and to the legates of these sovereign pontiffs. Most were written by our author to implore the protection of the Holy See against those who attacked the privileges of his abbey and removed or retained its possessions. He bases his request on the fact that, by its foundation, the property of his monastery was a freehold of the Holy See.

This is indeed what most of the abbey’s documents state, as Father Sirmond observes in his note on the second letter. In this connection he reports the charter by which Geoffroi Martel, founder of the abbey, while transferring the county of Vendôme to Fulk, his sister’s son, excepted the abbey, declaring that it was a freehold and the patrimony of the Roman Church [Note: [Col. 0011D] “I offered it as an allod and patrimony to blessed Peter, prince of the apostles, and to his Roman Church, retaining only the defense of the place for myself and my successors, the princes of the Angevin land.”]. He reserved for himself and his successors only the defense and protection of this monastery. The origin of the counts of Vendôme is found in this charter.

In the third letter, Geoffroi complains to Pope Paschal about the countess of Vendôme, whom he does not name; about the bishop of Le Mans, who was retaining one of his religious; and about the bishop of Angers, who had authorized the establishment of a chapel in a parish of his diocese belonging to the abbey of Vendôme. This shows that the abbots claimed that chapels could not be built on lands under their jurisdiction without their consent. This agrees with the bull of Pope Lucius II in favor of the abbey of Cluny.

The fourth letter is addressed to Paschal II in the name of the entire community and the abbot, who complain in it of the vexations they suffer from the bishop of Chartres. In the seventh, Geoffroi urges Paschal II to revoke the treaty he had made with Henry V. After this pope had been taken by surprise and arrested in Rome by the emperor in 1111, he granted him investitures in order to save the city and Italy from the ruin that threatened them, and the prisoners from the death with which they were threatened.

Although the necessity and circumstances in which Paschal found himself seemed likely to excuse his action, it was nevertheless strongly condemned, especially by the abbot of Vendôme, who wrote to him about it with great force. After placing before his eyes the labors of the Apostles Saint Peter and Saint Paul, the zeal with which they preached the faith, the courage they displayed in shedding their blood in its defense, and the glory they enjoy in heaven, where they await successors who will not degenerate from their courage, he adds that the one who, sitting in their see, has renounced the glorious destiny of these saints by conduct opposed to theirs must rescind what he has done and repair his fault by weeping like another Peter [Note: [Col. 0011D] “He must himself undo what he has done, since by acting otherwise, while sitting in their see, he has deprived himself of their blessed lot, and, like another Peter, correct by weeping [Col. 0012D] what he has done.”].

“If weakness of the flesh has caused him to fall,” he says, “let the strength of the spirit raise him up,” and let him not be ashamed to correct himself: “let him not blush to make amends.”

Geoffroi then refutes what might be alleged on behalf of the pope, who feared for the lives of the prisoners held by the emperor if he refused the investitures. He maintains that the fault is inexcusable, and that attempting to excuse it only increases it. It must therefore, he says, be promptly repaired by renouncing the error, so that our spiritual mother, who seems about to breathe her last, may not die [Note: [Col. 0012D] “And since there is no doubt that this fault is wholly inexcusable, and that by excusing it one can increase it rather than diminish it, let it be corrected without delay by knowingly abandoning the error committed, lest our spiritual mother, who seems to be drawing her last breath, should die altogether.”].

Our author maintains that investiture is a heresy according to the tradition of the holy Fathers; that whoever approves it deserves to be cut off, ceases to be Catholic, and is a heretic. After several remarks as vigorous as those just reported against those who receive investiture from lay hands, he adds that he speaks in this way because, since the prophet allowed himself to be corrupted by Satan, it is necessary that the she-ass on which he was mounted rebuke his madness.

“And since in our own days we have seen Lucifer fall from heaven,” he says further, “let us not conceal his impiety, lest we fall with him into the abyss of despair.” He ends by saying that, if he has not said as much as he ought, this should be attributed to ignorance; and that if, on the contrary, he has said too much, he should be forgiven, because he did so only out of hatred for iniquity and love of equity. We do not believe that anyone can reproach Geoffroi with having fallen into the first fault.

The eighth letter, addressed to Paschal II, concerns a dispute he had with the abbot of Saint-Aubin of Angers. He speaks there of his attachment to the Holy See and of the effective signs he had given of it to Urban through the services he had rendered him.

In the ninth, addressed to the same pope, he justifies himself concerning certain accusations brought against him. This abbot was accused of communicating with the persecutor of the Church and with William, count of Poitiers, [Col. 0012C] who had been excommunicated several times. He asks the pope not to believe the false rumors spread against him by his enemies.

This places him under the necessity of saying things about his monastery that he would prefer to keep silent: namely, that it is the best-regulated monastery in France, and that he has rendered services to the Holy See. He hopes that, in view of this, Paschal will kindly restore him to possession of the church of Saint Prisca, which his predecessors Alexander II and Gregory VII had granted to the abbots of Vendôme.

In 1062 Alexander II had given Ordric, abbot of Vendôme, and his successors in perpetuity the church of Saint Prisca on the Aventine, together with the title of cardinal. Gregory VII had confirmed this privilege in 1079. The abbot of Vendôme was dispossessed of it during the schism of Guibert. Urban II restored it to him; but since the restitution made by that pope to Geoffroi may not have taken full effect, this abbot [Col. 0013A] pursued the matter with Paschal II, Urban’s successor, and finally obtained it from Calixtus II.

Honorius II confirmed in 1129 what his predecessor had done in Geoffroi’s favor. The successors of this abbot were later dispossessed of it again; Innocent III restored it to Hamelin, with some exception. From that time until the Council of Constance, the abbots of Vendôme remained in possession of the title of cardinal, which they have since lost, as well as the church of Saint Prisca.

The next four letters are addressed to Calixtus II, with whom Geoffroi had been connected by friendship before Calixtus was elevated to the see of Saint Peter. The fourteenth and fifteenth are addressed to Honorius II. In the latter he complains of the bishop of Angers, who was treating him badly; but he does so without departing from the charity that forbids lying and commands one to speak the truth, whether one is dealing with a friend or speaking about an enemy.

In the sixteenth, addressed to Peter, cardinal deacon and legate, he expresses his concern at his illness and offers him his services, asking him to turn to him as to a friend for anything he might need. He tells him that friendship is genuine only when it is demonstrated by services rendered to one another in time of need [Note: [Col. 0013] “Moreover, friendship is empty—indeed, it is no friendship at all—unless services are mutually rendered, especially in time of need.”].

The seventeenth is addressed to Richard, cardinal, bishop of Albano, legate of the Holy See. Geoffroi justifies himself against accusations brought against him by Radulph, archbishop of Tours.

The eighteenth is addressed to Conon, cardinal, bishop of Palestrina, legate of Paschal II.

In the nineteenth, addressed to Girard, bishop of Angoulême and legate of the Holy See, he implores his protection against the violence being exercised against his monastery.

In the twentieth, addressed to the same Girard, he expresses his astonishment that so prudent a prelate has advanced against him statements that he ought not even to have entertained, since they can be regarded only as calumnies invented by his enemies [Col. 0013C].

The following letters, through the twenty-seventh, are also addressed to Girard of Angoulême. The twenty-eighth is addressed to Hugh, archbishop and legate of the Holy See, who, according to Father Sirmond, was Hugh, archbishop of Lyon, who had been legate of Pope Urban II.

The twenty-ninth is written to Umbauld, archbishop of Lyon, who had invited him to a council. Geoffroi replies that, by virtue of a privilege granted by the popes to the abbots of Vendôme, he can neither attend, nor ought to attend, a council convened by a bishop or by a legate of the Holy See.

The final two letters of the first book are addressed, one to Radulph, archbishop of Tours, and the other to Renaud, archbishop of Reims—the same man who had been elected bishop of Angers in 1101 and whose election Geoffroi had opposed.

The second book contains thirty-two letters, nineteen of which are addressed to Ivo of Chartres and the remainder to Geoffroi, Ivo’s successor. Our author [Col. 0013D] there defends, with great firmness and respect, the privileges of his abbey against the bishop of Chartres, who, when giving him the blessing, had required of him a profession contrary to those privileges; this profession was annulled by Popes Urban II and Paschal II.

The authors of the New Christian Gaul *(vol. VIII, p. 1368)* say that this profession later became the cause of a small dispute between Ivo and Geoffroi: *quae dissidioli inter illos postea seminarium fuit*—“which afterward became the seed of a small disagreement between them.”

Nevertheless, it appears from Geoffroi’s letters and from those of Ivo of Chartres that the disagreement went quite far; the mutual recriminations of bishop and abbot prove this.

In the nineteenth letter, Geoffroi maintains that the anointing of the sick should not be repeated. He even condemns and labels as a serious error the practice of those who repeat it. He nevertheless wishes to know [Col. 0014A] Ivo’s opinion on the matter. Ivo replied in a way that confirmed the position of the abbot of Vendôme, relying on what Saint Augustine and Saint Ambrose say about public penance, which was not repeated.

“A frivolous argument,” says Father Sirmond *(Notes on Book II, Letter 19, and Letter 20, pp. 699–700).* It is true that public penance was not repeated; but this has no bearing on the anointing of the sick, which does not belong to public penance and, since it is not among the sacraments that imprint a character, may be repeated not only in different illnesses but also in the same illness, when, after some interval, the illness returns and the sick person again falls into new danger.

Father Sirmond might have noted another no less singular point: these two authors do not seem to have the same idea of extreme unction as that conveyed to us by our catechisms, which teach us that it is a sacrament instituted by Jesus Christ, like the others. Geoffroi, by contrast, seems not to regard extreme unction as a sacrament in the proper sense, and to believe that it was instituted by the Holy See: *cum ab apostolica sede sacramentum vocetur, secundum apostolicae sedis institutum, genus est sacramenti*—“since it is called a sacrament by the Apostolic See, according to the institution of the Apostolic See, it is a kind of sacrament.”

The reader may consult Letter 255 of Ivo of Chartres to Radulph, abbot, who was ill, in which he warns him not to repeat the anointing of the sick.

The following twelve letters of the second book, addressed to Geoffroi, Ivo’s successor in the see of Chartres, mostly have the same subject as the preceding letters.

In some of them—Letters 21, 22, 24, 26, and 32—our abbot appeals to the prelate against the vexations inflicted by the countess of Vendôme, the religious of Marmoutier, and others.

In others—Letters 27, 28, and 30—he defends the privileges and exemption of his monastery against the prelate himself:

“We are not therefore acephalous,” says the abbot of Vendôme in reply [Col. 0014C] to the reproaches of the bishop of Chartres in one of his letters (Letter 27). “We have Jesus Christ as our head, and after him the Roman pontiff. Our monastery has always had this head from its foundation, and, with God’s help, will have him until the end of the ages.”

However much zeal Geoffroi displayed in defending the privileges of his monastery, he always showed profound respect for the bishops against whom he defended them. He protests that he never wished to take anything away from the Church of Chartres; he merely wishes to preserve for the abbey of Vendôme possession of what was granted to it at its foundation, and he will return to the bishop of Chartres everything that the bishop had reserved for himself at that time in the abbey.

The third book of Geoffroi’s letters contains forty-three letters written to various bishops, especially to the bishops of Angers and Le Mans.

The first is written to Geoffroi, bishop of Angers, [Col. 0014D] who withdrew to Cluny in 1101.

In the second, addressed to Renaud of Martigné, Geoffroi’s successor, he urges him to defend the Church against the count of Anjou. He tells him that anyone who fears exile and death, and does anything contrary to equity out of fear of death or exile, is not a true bishop.

The following letters, through the tenth, are addressed to the same Renaud of Angers.

In the eighth, the abbot of Vendôme speaks of a monk of Saint-Nicolas who had answered the accusations brought against him by his abbot, using not the Latin language—for he was a layman and had not learned it—but his native language: *ad cujus objecta monachus, quia laicus est, non Latina, quam non didicit, lingua, sed materna respondet*—“to whose charges the monk, since he is a layman, replies not in Latin, which he has not learned, but in his mother tongue.”

This shows that, as early as the twelfth century, Latin was no longer the vernacular language and that laypeople had another language, which was called the mother tongue. This may also help explain why we have some sermons of Saint Bernard both in Latin and in French.

When the bishop of Angers ordered a monk of Saint-Nicolas named Savaric to return to his monastery, Geoffroi wrote to him about the matter (Letter 9). He praises the prelate’s good intention, but points out that a monk accused by his abbot ought not to be left under the accuser’s authority, and that this is contrary to the canons [Note: [Col. 0015D] “We declare this unprecedented, and it is found nowhere in the entire body of the canons: that anyone should be required to remain under the authority of one by whom he is accused of a crime.”].

When Renaud complained to Hamelin that Geoffroi had obstructed his election (Letter 11), our abbot again wrote him a letter on the subject. In it he told him frankly that he had been displeased by what was contrary to the rules and constitutions of the holy Fathers, and that he would not have been a servant of Jesus Christ but of the devil if he had not been distressed to see [Col. 0015B] the only door of the holy Church closed in order to open—by trampling underfoot the teaching of the Apostles and the holy Gospel—the door through which thieves and robbers enter the sheepfold.

Geoffroi adds that Renaud was wrong to make a personal crime of his opposition to what Renaud called his election, since everyone opposed it; it was less an election than a conspiracy of the people, in which no regard was paid to the holy rules.

He further reproaches him for having received investiture from the hands of a layman, and calls it heresy and simony. Our abbot maintains that there is no one who ought not and cannot rise up against so detestable an impiety; and that, if one does not possess the authority of a prelate, one possesses it in the capacity of a Christian [Note: [Col. 0015D] “There is no one who ought not, and who cannot, openly contradict it. For if he does not possess the authority of a prelate, he nevertheless possesses the voice of a Christian . . . . And if he should be vicious, or rendered infamous by any other crime, that is no reason why he should keep silent; for every sinner may defend the common faith of the Church—which he believes and confesses to be his own—and freely fight against its adversaries.”].

Even if one were guilty of some crime that rendered one infamous, that is no reason to remain silent, as is shown by the example of the good thief, because every sinner may defend the common faith of the Church, which he professes, against [Col. 0015C] those who attack it.

Renaud, to whom this letter is addressed, having been transferred to the see of Reims, Ulger was elected as his successor at Angers. Ulger renewed his predecessors’ dispute with the abbots of Vendôme concerning the redemption of altars, which Urban II condemned as a simoniacal pact at the Council of Clermont in 1095. This is the subject of Geoffroi’s twelfth letter, addressed to Ulger. The following seventeen letters are written to Hildebert, bishop of Le Mans. The thirteenth and fourteenth concern the irregular election of Renaud, bishop of Angers, which Hildebert had opposed. In the fifteenth, Geoffroi complains of the vexations inflicted by the countess of Vendôme. The sixteenth deals with the same subject, as do several others. The twenty-fourth, twenty-fifth, twenty-ninth, and thirtieth are written concerning a fugitive religious from the abbey of Vendôme whom the bishop [Col. 0015D] of Le Mans retained, although he had promised to return him to the abbot who was demanding him. In the twenty-sixth and twenty-seventh, he modestly reproaches Hildebert for having broken his word by failing to carry out the promise he had made him, because the clergy of Tours opposed it. Geoffroi regards [Col. 0016A] this opposition as an assault upon Hildebert’s dignity and an insult to the Church of Le Mans on the part of those clerics who, in contempt of all the rules, have risen above a bishop whom they are not even permitted to rebuke, except in the event that he should depart from the faith.

Our abbot adds that the archbishop of Tours himself, although superior to these clerics, would have had no right to prevent you from granting me the favor I was begging you to grant; and if he had wished to prevent you, you ought not to have obeyed him. One must indeed obey one’s superior, but not in everything he commands—only in those things commanded by God. For if superiors command something contrary to what God or the Fathers have prescribed, they lose the authority to command, and one must not obey them: the apostles teach us this by their example. They had certainly learned the rules of obedience [Col. 0016B] from a good Master, who had given them this instruction when speaking of the scribes and Pharisees: “Do and observe everything they tell you.” Yet when those same scribes and Pharisees later ordered them not to preach in the name of Jesus Christ, they wisely avoided falling into the trap of a false obedience, replying that one must obey God rather than human beings.

[Note: [Col. 0015D] “One must indeed obey a prelate, but not in everything he suggests, only in those things [Col. 0016D] that God commands. For if prelates command anything contrary to the ordinance of God or of the Fathers, they immediately lose the authority to command, and in that matter one must in no way obey them—this, clearly, following the example of the apostles. They themselves certainly received from the good Master the pattern of obedience, in which they were told concerning the scribes and Pharisees: ‘Whatever they tell you, observe and do’ (Matthew 23:3). But when they later heard those same men commanding them not to speak in the name of Jesus, they wisely avoided what had been deceitfully imposed upon them under the name of obedience, saying: ‘We must obey God rather than men’ (Acts 5:19).”]

The reader understands that what our author says—that superiors who command something contrary to what God and the Fathers have prescribed lose the authority to command—must not be taken literally. These words mean only that, in such a case, superiors have no authority to command what is contrary to the law of God, since they received their authority only to teach the truth and enforce God’s law. Thus, when they issue commands by which they depart from it, one must not obey them, *in illa re*—“in that matter”—although they otherwise retain [Col. 0016C] the authority they received for edification and not for destruction; an authority to which one is obliged to submit when those invested with it make legitimate use of it for the purpose for which they received it.

Among the letters that follow, seven are addressed to Ranulphe, bishop of Saintes, and to Pierre, his successor. Father Sirmond conjectures that the forty-second was written to Geoffroi of Chartres and the forty-third to Renauld of Angers, both of whom are designated only by the first letter of their names.

In the thirty-ninth, addressed to Pierre, bishop of Saintes, our abbot begs the prelate to prevent a duel between a cleric and a monk. He says that such a combat is forbidden by the laws and condemned by the sacred canons. In a curious note on this letter, the editor reports three examples of such combats. The first was between Haimeric, [Col. 0016D] viscount of Thouars, and Thierry, abbot of Saint-Aubin, concerning a levy demanded by the viscount and refused by the abbot as not being owed. The duel did not take place, because the viscount relaxed his demand.

In the second example, the combat took place in the presence of Hamelin, bishop of [Col. 0017A] Rennes, Count Conan, Robert of Vitré, who was then excommunicated, and others. The dispute was not decided by combat but was settled by agreement.

Finally, in the third example, the duel was fought between Étienne, the champion of the count of Angoulême, and a certain Guillaume, who was champion of a woman accused of sorcery. Étienne was victorious and went to give thanks to God at the tomb of Saint Eparchius, where he had spent the preceding night. Guillaume was carried from the field of battle with his body utterly broken by the blows he had received.

These duels, whose date Father Sirmond does not report, appear to be much later than Geoffroi’s time. Thus the zeal this abbot displayed against a practice so contrary to the law of God did not produce the effect one would have wished. Would to God that it had been so completely abolished that no trace of it remained in later centuries—or at least that none remained in our own.

[Col. 0017B] The fourth book contains fifty letters written to abbots or monks. The most remarkable is the forty-seventh, addressed to Robert of Arbrisselles, which has become famous because of the efforts made by certain disciples of the pious founder of Fontevraud to prove that it is not by the abbot of Vendôme. Their success has not been happy; but although they have not succeeded in proving that this letter is spurious, it has at least given them the opportunity to make themselves known in the republic of letters.

Father de la Mainferme, full of zeal for the honor of his holy patriarch, published a work entitled *Shield of the Emerging Order of Fontevraud*, whose principal purpose is to justify Robert against the reproaches Geoffroi makes against him, by attempting to prove that this letter is not by the abbot of Vendôme but by the heretic Roscelin.

It would have been easy for Father de la Mainferme to vindicate the memory of Blessed Robert and destroy all the false [Col. 0017C] rumors that gave rise to the letters of Geoffroi of Vendôme and Marbode of Rennes. Had the apologist of the founder of the Fontevraud order stopped there, he could have congratulated himself on achieving all the success he desired. But by going further and undertaking to prove that these letters were forged, he took on a useless task.

All the conjectures he adduces are far too weak even to cast doubt on the fact that this letter was written by the person whose name it bears. It is found among Geoffroi’s letters not only in the manuscript of La Couture at Le Mans, from which Father Sirmond published it, but also in two ancient manuscripts, one from the library of Christina, Queen of Sweden, and the other from the library of Santa Croce in Florence, both dating from Robert of Arbrisselles’ own time.

This is the judgment of Father Mabillon (*Mus. Ital.*, vol. I, pp. 54, 164), who saw and examined these manuscripts and mentions them in his account of his journey through Italy. Father Pagi [Col. 0017D] (*ad an. 1117*, no. 22) likewise states that he read Geoffroi’s letter in the manuscript of Santa Croce in Florence, a monastery of his order. Finally, the letter is also found in part in the Vendôme manuscript among Geoffroi’s letters.

The person who tore out the leaf containing the beginning of the letter spared the following leaf, leaving a continuation that betrays his false precaution and establishes the authenticity of the piece he wished to make disappear. What remains proves that it was formerly there and that, as in the printed edition, it constituted the forty-seventh letter of the fourth book.

We shall say nothing of the letter’s style, which is the same as that of the others, so that it is impossible not to recognize its author. [Col. 0018A] What is set against such convincing evidence? Frivolous conjectures, which leave that evidence intact in all its force without affecting it in the least.

Accordingly, the latest apologist for Robert, who published at Antwerp in 1701 a dissertation against what Bayle had said about him in his *Dictionary*, honestly admits that the letter in question is truly by Abbot Geoffroi and that it is found in the Vendôme manuscript.

In vain do Father de la Mainferme (*Clyp.*, vol. I, p. 7), the Bollandists (*ad diem XXV Feb.*, p. 600), and Father Dubois of the Oratory in his *History of Paris* (*DUB. ep. 11, c. 3, no. 5*), among others, attempt to pass it off as a work of the heretic Roscelin, who, according to Abelard’s testimony, published a letter full of calumnies against Robert of Arbrisselles.

These critics have misunderstood Abelard. Abelard does not say that Roscelin wrote one or two letters under another person’s name in order to disparage Robert of Arbrisselles; he says that Roscelin had written a letter against him and against Saint Anselm (*DUP. Bib.*, twelfth century, part II). That has no connection with Geoffroi’s letter.

Moreover, Roscelin’s writing against Robert was a genuine libel, according to the account given of it by the Parisian theologian who refuted the heretic’s errors (*Conc.*, vol. X, p. 487). That description does not fit the letter of the abbot of Vendôme, who, although prejudiced by the false rumors being spread publicly against Robert, nevertheless shows great respect for him in his letter and earnestly commends himself to Robert’s holy prayers: “And we earnestly beg you to make us sharers in your holy prayers.”

In short, Geoffroi of Vendôme’s letter can and should be regarded only as the letter of a friend to a friend, freely and charitably warning him about the unfavorable rumors circulating concerning him, so that he may correct himself if what is being said is true.

[Note: [Col. 0017D] “For this reason, venerable brother, we have set these matters before you: we have heard, as an evil report spreads, that you have done and are still doing such things. If they are true, we urge you, with the entrails of brotherly charity, not to defend them with any excuse but to correct them with all haste.”]

It does not even appear that he believed these rumors, for far from speaking affirmatively, he speaks only doubtfully.

[Note: [Col. 0018D] “If you are now doing this, or have at some time done it, you have discovered a new and unheard-of, but fruitless, kind of martyrdom.”]

Can such a letter be taken for a defamatory libel like Roscelin’s writing? We shall not dwell further on this critical question, which seems so clearly settled that it is astonishing that anyone could raise difficulties about it.

If any difficulties nevertheless remain, they will be entirely dispelled by two sound observations that D. Rivet made on this subject in the article on Roscelin. Father Pagi (*Ad an. 1117*, p. 400, col. 2) states that Father Sirmond, the editor of Geoffroi’s works, believed that this letter was spurious. Yet Father Sirmond placed it among the abbot’s letters without expressing any doubt that it was his. Father de la Mainferme even reproached him for doing so.

It is true that the Bollandists [Col. 0018D] (*ad diem XXV Febr.*) later claimed that Father Sirmond had repented of publishing it and intended to make a public declaration of this in a second edition. But Ménage, who was very close to Father Sirmond and had private conversations with him about this letter, assures us in his *History of Sablé* that Father Sirmond never had such an intention and never regretted publishing the letter.

The fifth book of Geoffroi’s letters contains twenty-eight letters. In the sixteenth, our author gives instruction on the necessity of confession to Guillaume, who had been his teacher. This Guillaume maintained that there were only four kinds of sins [Col. 0019A] that one was obliged to confess, and that God remits all the others without confession. He even appealed to a passage in the Venerable Bede (*lib. V Expos.*) to prove his opinion.

But the disciple, more enlightened and more capable than his teacher, teaches him the true meaning of Bede’s words and maintains that confession and penance are necessary for all crimes, and that nothing is more certain.

[Note: [Col. 0019D] “It is certain—nothing is more certain than this—that all sins or crimes require confession and penance.”]

The eighteenth letter contains a striking example of Geoffroi’s firmness and zeal for good order, which made him rise above all human respect. William, duke of Aquitaine, had asked him to send back a monk named Rainaud to an obedience from which Geoffroi had withdrawn him, and in which he was useful to the duke and necessary to the household. Geoffroi replied that, since this request was contrary to the Rule of Saint Benedict, he could not obey him.

As for the reasons the duke of Aquitaine alleged, [Col. 0019B] Geoffroi made clear to him that the soul of this religious, for which he himself would have to render an account on the day of judgment, ought to be dearer to him than all temporal interests. He concluded by asking him not to interfere in matters concerning the salvation of the souls entrusted to his care.

[Note: [Col. 0019D] “Do not meddle in the care of the souls entrusted to us.”]

The number of our author’s letters is 184, to which one more must be added—one of which Father Sirmond had no knowledge, addressed to the religious of Cluny. D. Mabillon published it in the third volume of his *Analecta* (p. 481), and it was later inserted into the collection of Father Sirmond’s works, in the third volume, which contains the works of the abbot of Vendôme (vol. III, preface, no. 3).

## 2. The Letters and Other Works of Geoffroi

[Col. 0019C] Geoffroi’s letters are followed by several short works in which he treats, with considerable order and clarity, various points of ecclesiastical doctrine and discipline.

The first treatise, *On the Body and Blood of Jesus Christ*, establishes in the clearest manner the real presence in the Eucharist.

“We first place bread and wine upon the altar,” he says, “but just as before the consecration there is nothing but bread and wine, so after the consecration nothing remains of the bread and wine except taste, appearance, and smell, and this because of human weakness and infirmity. For if the glorious flesh of Jesus Christ and his sacred blood appeared in their proper nature, human beings could not endure their splendor and would not have the merit of faith . . .

“Let us therefore firmly and without any doubt believe that what Christians receive upon the altar after the consecration is none other than what Truth itself declares when it says: ‘Receive; this is my body.’ It is that same, one, and true flesh which was conceived through the working of the Holy Spirit, born of the Virgin Mary, fastened to the cross, and raised by the omnipotence of his divinity, since he himself is God.

“The wicked receive it; but because they receive it badly, they become more wicked. The good who receive it, having charity in their hearts, become better.”

This treatise, despite its brevity, contains everything the Church teaches the faithful concerning the august mystery of our altars, and overturns all the heresies of the innovators of later centuries who have dared to attack it.

## 3. On the Ordination of Bishops and Lay Investiture

The second treatise, on the ordination of bishops and lay investiture, is addressed to Cardinal Peter of León. [Col. 0020A] Geoffroi teaches that election and consecration are as essential to making a bishop as the invocation of the Holy Spirit and water are to making a Christian. Thus election without consecration, or consecration without election, is insufficient for making someone a bishop.

When our author speaks of election, he intends a canonical election, which must precede consecration and is absolutely necessary. A bishop whose election is not canonical is a tree without roots which, although covered with leaves, cannot bear fruit. It is an injury to the Church and covers her with disgrace to give her ministers whose election is not canonical and to place persons without knowledge, piety, or morals in positions that belong to merit, learning, and virtue.

With regard to investiture given by the hand of laymen, Geoffroi refers to the first article of the council held by Gregory VII to learn what the Catholic Church teaches and has decided on this subject. He maintains that investiture—or rather, the opinion that [Col. 0020B] laymen can confer it—is a heresy like simony, and even worse than simony, because simony is ordinarily practiced in secret, whereas investiture is always public. He says that investiture was forbidden to laymen by Jesus Christ and by the apostles.

The reason the abbot of Vendôme calls the opinion that laymen can confer investiture a heresy is that he regarded investiture as a sacrament and even gives it that name. He claims that it is a sacred sign by which the bishop is distinguished from other men and established over the flock of Jesus Christ to care for it; thus he can receive investiture only from the hands of the one from whom he receives consecration.

Moreover, the heresy of investiture is also simony, since secular power would not be so jealous of this right if it did not find a temporal advantage in it, whether by extorting money or, what is even graver, by subjecting to itself [Col. 0020C] the person of the bishop.

Laymen must receive the sacraments from the hands of ecclesiastics, but they have no right to administer them to ecclesiastics. The ring and the staff are sacraments of the Church, just as salt, water, the holy oils, and chrism are, when they are given by those who possess the authority to give them and with the required ceremonies.

Accordingly, Geoffroi boldly declares that the person who receives investiture from a lay hand is not a member of the shepherd who gave his life for his sheep; rather, he is a thief, a robber, and a wolf who comes only to steal, plunder, and slaughter.

## 4. On Lay Investiture

The third short work, addressed to Pope Callixtus II, again treats lay investiture, which it attacks with the same arguments. Geoffroi urges the supreme pontiff to oppose it on every occasion.

## 5. On Secular and Ecclesiastical Investiture

In the fourth work, our author continues to discuss the same subject. He begins by saying [Col. 0020D] that emperors and kings must not take offense at what he says, nor claim, by virtue of custom, something that Truth itself, speaking through the mouths of its apostles, has declared not to belong to them.

Nevertheless, while maintaining that secular power cannot confer investiture by the ring and pastoral staff, Geoffroi admits that princes may give bishops investiture of the temporal goods possessed by the Church.

“Another kind of investiture,” he says, “makes the bishop; another makes the bishop subsist. The first derives from divine law; the second from human law. Remove divine law, and no bishop is created spiritually. Remove human law, and he loses the possessions by which he is sustained bodily. For the Church would possess no property unless kings gave it to her, and so forth.”

[Note: [Col. 0019D] “Certainly, one investiture makes the bishop complete; another feeds the bishop. The former is derived from divine law; the latter from human law. Take away divine law, and no bishop is created spiritually. Take away human law, and he loses the possessions by which he is physically sustained. For the Church would not have possessions unless they were given to her by kings, and so forth.”]

He confirms this with the authority of Saint Augustine (*Tractate VI on John*). He then adds:

“After the canonical election and consecration, kings may therefore give the bishop investiture of ecclesiastical goods and grant him their protection. It does not matter by what sign they do this: it harms neither the princes, nor the bishop, nor the Catholic faith. Jesus Christ willed that the spiritual sword and the temporal sword should be employed in the defense of the Church. If one blunts the other, that is against his will. This is what banishes justice from the state and peace from the Church; what causes scandals and schisms, and the loss of souls. This division between empire and priesthood places both in danger.”

Our author warns here that, in defending the liberty of the Church, one must act with great wisdom and prudence, [Col. 0021B] so as not to break the vessel whose rust one wishes to remove. On this subject he cites the celebrated passage of Saint Augustine—whom he calls “good and discerning”—in his letter to Parmenianus. There the holy doctor says that one must not excommunicate a person who has the multitude on his side, because it is better to spare one man than to cause a schism that would make several perish.

M. Fleuri says that this work is the first in which one observes the allegory of the two swords, signifying the two powers, spiritual and temporal, which later became so famous.

## 6. On Ecclesiastical Dispensations

The fourth short work is addressed, like the preceding one, to Pope Callixtus II and is related to the question of investitures. Geoffroi there establishes the rules that should be followed in the Church concerning dispensations.

“Dispensations must sometimes be granted in the Church,” he says, “not out of self-interest or favor, but through pious condescension, permitting something less perfect [Col. 0021C] for a time rather than placing the faith in danger, with the intention of restoring the rule at an appropriate time.”

This is how the blessed apostles Peter and Paul acted, so as not to scandalize the Jews. On various occasions they sometimes observed the legal ceremonies, although they were convinced of their uselessness. Their conduct in this was pious condescension, not deceptive dissimulation.

“One may also,” Geoffroi continues, “change by dispensation the customs of Churches and monasteries, but only in order to establish a greater good in place of a lesser one . . . Whoever dispenses otherwise in the Church contradicts reason and truth. Not only does he have no lamp burning, but he extinguishes that of others; he is not a true vicar of Jesus Christ but a blind man who leads other blind men.”

## 7. On the Properties of the Church

In the sixth work, also addressed to Callixtus II, Geoffroi discusses three properties specially attached to the Church. She must be Catholic, [Col. 0021D] free, and chaste.

As Catholic, she can neither be sold nor bought. As free, she must not be subjected to secular power. As chaste, she must not be corrupted by gifts. These three qualities are essential to the Church’s being the bride of Jesus Christ.

This good shepherd seeks a faithful bride and wants no unfaithful one; he unites himself to the free woman and rejects the slave; he loves a chaste bride and abhors one who is corrupt.

## 8. Allegorical Explanations of the Ark and the Tabernacle

The seventh short work contains allegorical explanations of the Ark of the Covenant and the tabernacle. It is addressed to two religious men named Hamelin and André, for whom Geoffroi had a particular affection. He addresses this brief writing to them for their consolation, and it contains very sound instruction concerning Christian and religious virtues.

## 9. The Effects of the Sacraments

In the eighth work, Geoffroi explains the effects [Col. 0022A] of baptism, confirmation, and the anointing of the sick in a Christian soul.

In baptism, one receives remission of sins through the power of the Holy Spirit. In confirmation, the Holy Spirit is invoked so that he may come to dwell in the habitation he has sanctified, defend it, and protect it. This sacrament is conferred by the bishop to signify that he gives the final perfection. It is received on the forehead because it is the perfect who openly profess the name of Jesus Christ.

Before receiving this anointing, before being confirmed by the Holy Spirit, the apostles were not perfect. They were timid; they did not bear the name of Jesus Christ upon their foreheads.

In the anointing of the sick, one receives remission of sins through the power of the Holy Spirit, so that the Lord’s mercy may not fail Christians either during life or at death.

Finally, in communion of the body and blood of [Col. 0022B] Jesus Christ, the Christian soul is healed of the sickness of its vices, restored to a state of eternal salvation, and made one body with Jesus Christ.

## 10. On the Repetition of the Sacraments

In the ninth work, Geoffroi treats the repetition of the sacraments. He repeats what he has already said elsewhere, as we have noted: that the anointing of the sick, being a sacrament, cannot be repeated.

He recognizes there that this sacrament, like all the others, comes from apostolic tradition. He then adds that it is forbidden to repeat any sacrament, which is plainly false. Did Geoffroi understand himself, when he knew perfectly well that penance, the Eucharist, and even marriage are received several times?

## 11. On the Profession of Abbots

The tenth work concerns the promises abbots made to bishops under the name of a profession when they received their blessing from them. Geoffroi calls this profession simony.

## 12. On Monastic Discipline

The eleventh is a rule of monastic discipline [Col. 0022C] prescribing how religious are to accuse themselves and defend themselves in chapter.

## 13. The Three Virtues of Pastors

In the twelfth work, he speaks of three virtues necessary to the pastors of the Church if they are to work effectively for the salvation of the souls entrusted to them and even provide for bodily needs. These virtues are justice, discernment, and foresight.

If one or another of these virtues is lacking in a pastor, he will accomplish no good. If he is equitable in his judgments but indiscreet in his commands, his indiscretion will destroy the good that might otherwise be expected from the equity of his judgments.

## 14. Dialogue Between God and the Sinner

The thirteenth work is a dialogue between God, who reproaches the sinner with his crimes and ingratitude, and the sinner, who, acknowledging his fault, implores the mercy of the one he has offended.

## 15. A Second Dialogue Between God and the Sinner

The fourteenth is also in the form of a dialogue. God urges the sinner to recognize his crimes and do penance for them. He sets before the sinner’s eyes the benefits with which he has overwhelmed him, the patience with which he has waited for him to return, and the goodness with which he has sought and recalled him when he was turning away.

The sinner confesses his crimes and begs the Lord not to allow him to perish, but to grant him the grace truly to recognize himself as a sinner and to satisfy God’s justice through worthy fruits of penance before he dies.

He asks God to inspire him with tender compassion for his brothers, so that he may rebuke them for their faults with gentleness and charity, and correct them without hatred or haughtiness.

## 16. The Sinner’s Lament

The fifteenth work is a confession and lamentation by the sinner, who deplores his condition by laying out all his miseries and recalling everything God has done for him.

After confessing his crimes and recognizing his inability to escape from them by his own power, he takes courage from the sight of God’s omnipotence and mercy, which do not permit a penitent sinner to despair of [Col. 0023A] salvation.

He hopes that by humbly confessing his misery and helplessness and firmly relying upon God’s omnipotence, he will obtain the pardon that the penitent Magdalene obtained through her tears.

## 17. A Prayer to Jesus Christ

A short prayer to Jesus Christ imploring his mercy.

## 18. A Prayer to the Virgin Mary

A prayer to the Blessed Virgin in the form of a hymn or prose composition.

## 19. Hymns on Mary Magdalene’s Penance

Three hymns or prose compositions on the penance of Magdalene, which appear to have been intended to form part of this saint’s office: at Vespers, Matins, and Lauds.

## 20. Sermons

Geoffroi’s short works are followed by eleven sermons: four on the birth of Jesus Christ; one on the Resurrection; one on the Ascension; one on the Purification; one for all the feasts of the Blessed Virgin—in which the preacher makes use of the *History of Theophilus* (see the article “MARBODE”); [Col. 0023B] one on Mary Magdalene, whom our author, like most other writers since Saint Gregory the Great, confuses with the sinful woman; one on the good thief; and one on the feast of Saint Benedict.

The last is less a sermon than a summary of the saint’s life. But the author gives a great eulogy of his Rule and regards it as much more perfect than anything that had preceded it in this genre.

## 21. The Final Treatise on Bishops and Investiture

Geoffroi’s final work is a treatise addressed to Cardinal Peter of León on the ordination of bishops and investiture.

Father Sirmond had initially intended to suppress it because the work appeared to him to be merely a repetition of what is said on this subject in the same author’s short works 2, 3, 4, 5, and 6. But after reflecting that this treatise was present in the two manuscripts of Geoffroi’s works, that it was also the one used by François Turrian, and that it contained substantial additions, he did not believe he should omit a work whose authorship by the abbot of Vendôme cannot be doubted.

## 22. Geoffroi’s Commentary on the Psalms

A large manuscript is preserved in the abbey of Saint-Germain-des-Prés containing a commentary on David’s first fifty psalms under the name of Geoffroi, abbot of Vendôme: *Goffridi abbatis Vindocinensis Expositio super L psalmos*—“Exposition on the Fifty Psalms by Geoffroi, Abbot of Vendôme” (*MONS., Bibl. bibl.*, p. 1126, no. 191).

This manuscript, which formerly belonged to the abbey of Vendôme, appears to be by the author. Its square script certainly dates from the beginning of the twelfth century. When this commentary is compared with Geoffroi’s other writings, certain expressions peculiar to him are found in it. Taken together, all these circumstances seem to establish that it is a work from this abbot’s pen.

The work is more an extended gloss than a formal commentary. The author offers various moral interpretations of certain words [Col. 0023D] without binding himself to a continuous explanation of the verses. This was the genius of the age.

He occasionally cites the Fathers, and Saint Augustine more often than the others. He also makes use of pagan authors, though very rarely. Terence, Horace, Juvenal, and Lucan are cited in it.

The explanation of the first psalm is preceded by a preface in which he begins by giving a definition of prophecy in general. It is, he says, divine inspiration: *Prophetia est divina inspiratio* (“Prophecy is divine inspiration”). He distinguishes three kinds of prophecy with respect to the present, the future, and the past. He further divides it into prophecy expressed through words, through vision or dream, and through action. The Psalter is a prophecy of the future expressed through words.

Following the method of the philosophers, he considers in this book: 1. the matter, the intention, and the end. [Col. 0024A] According to our commentator, two bodies constitute the matter of the Psalter: the first has Jesus Christ as its head, and the other the devil. These two bodies wage continual war against one another. The one whose head is Jesus Christ seeks the salvation of human beings; the other seeks only to destroy them.

2. The intention of the author of the psalms is to deliver the human race from three kinds of death represented in the Gospel by the death of the young girl resurrected in the house, by that of the young man being carried outside the city of Nain, and by that of Lazarus. The death of the young girl is an image of those who sin in thought; the death of the young man represents those who add evil action to thought; finally, Lazarus is the figure of hardened sinners who have grown old in crime. In connection with the resurrection of Lazarus, our author establishes with the greatest precision the necessity of confessing one’s sins to a priest. He is no less exact when he speaks of the Eucharist, original sin, the difference between the two covenants, the power and gratuitousness of grace, the good will that God gives through mercy, and so forth. [Col. 0024B]

3. The end of the author of the Psalter is to bring us to Jesus Christ, so that we may remain eternally in him. Geoffroi is convinced that David composed the psalms without giving them any titles or arrangement, and that Ezra gave them the titles they bear today and arranged them in the order in which we now see them. [Note: [Col. 0023D] “It should be known that the Prophet left the psalms disordered, without titles, and uncorrected; [Col. 0024D] the prophet and priest Ezra corrected, titled, and ordered them.”]

D. Mabillon, in his *Commentary on the Roman Order* (*Mus. ital.*, vol. II, p. 9), speaks of an ancient manuscript from the abbey of Vendôme, which he says belonged to Abbot Geoffroi and which the abbot may perhaps himself have brought from Rome during the time of Pope Urban II. Thus this ancient manuscript of the Roman Order—which, in D. Mabillon’s judgment, would be highly useful for correcting printed editions—may be regarded as a monument to Geoffroi’s zeal for the ceremonies of the Church. [Col. 0024C]

Abbot Geoffroi has always rightly been regarded as one of the lights of his age. The writings that we possess from him give a highly favorable impression of his ability. One readily recognizes in them that he was well versed in Scripture and the Fathers, and highly skilled in canon law. He possessed a firm and intrepid courage, free from human respect; he was zealous for the faith, good order, and discipline, and always ready to defend them against anyone who infringed upon them. The qualities of his heart corresponded in him to those of his mind, and his piety equaled or even surpassed his learning. He was beneficent, generous, a true friend, an enemy of vice, flattery, and dissimulation. By these qualities he won the esteem of popes, cardinals, princes and princesses, prelates, and all the great men of his age with whom he was in correspondence, as his letters show. Some of these letters are extremely forceful, including several addressed to popes and bishops. Such was the letter he wrote to Paschal II after the latter had granted investitures to the emperor Henry V. Such also were several other letters addressed to Renaud of Angers and Gérard of Angoulême. Yet this forcefulness should be regarded as the effect of his zeal and of the horror he felt toward everything that seemed contrary to equity, good order, and the holy rules. Geoffroi’s writings display more greatness of soul and nobility than elegance or refinement. Although their diction is not pure, it is natural, and the author expresses himself with a fluency that makes him pleasant to read, especially in his letters. [Col. 0024D]

[Col. 0025A] It is to the efforts of Jacques Sirmond that we owe the edition of the works of Geoffroi of Vendôme, which this Father published in 1610 from two manuscripts, one from the abbey of La Couture at Le Mans, the other from the abbey of the Trinity at Vendôme. The editor appended to the letters very important notes, which serve not only to identify the persons to whom they were written but also shed much light on the letters themselves by clarifying the matters treated in them. This edition appeared in 1610 in one octavo volume, in Paris, at the house of Jean Nivelle for Sébastien Cramoisy; it was included in the collection of Father Sirmond’s works printed at Paris and Venice. In the preface placed at the beginning of the third volume of this collection, there were added a letter from Abbot Geoffroi to the monks of Cluny and several facts concerning the abbot that had escaped Father Sirmond in the first edition or of which he had had no knowledge. [Col. 0025B]

The works of Geoffroi are also found in the second volume of the supplement to the Paris edition of the *Bibliotheca Patrum*, p. 487, and in the twenty-first volume of the Lyon edition. There are no other editions of Geoffroi’s works, apart from certain letters or individual writings printed separately in other collections. Thus Melchior Goldast had printed at Hanover in 1611 the treatise *On the Ordination of Bishops and the Investiture of Laymen*, following the *Apology of the Emperor Henry IV*. Even before Father Sirmond’s edition, François Juret had inserted substantial fragments of the treatise *On Ordination and Investiture* in his notes on the letters of Ivo of Chartres.

To leave Geoffroi’s article complete, we believe ourselves obliged to clear him of an unjust accusation made against him by two modern critics concerning a canon of the Council of Clermont in Auvergne. The authors of the *New Treatise on Diplomatics* have so thoroughly destroyed the calumnious charge brought against this illustrious abbot that it might seem unnecessary for us to undertake this task; but this is the appropriate place to do so. Let us begin by informing the reader of what occasioned the canon of the council held in 1095 at Clermont in Auvergne, so that he may understand the state of the question, which Geoffroi’s accusers appear neither of them to have understood. (See Sirmond, notes on epistle 12 to Ulger, book III; Fleury, *Ecclesiastical History*, vol. XIII, book LXIV, no. 29, p. 609.)

It is known that all churches are, by common law, under the authority and at the disposal of the bishops. Thus, when churches were offered to monasteries for them to possess, it was necessary to obtain the approval of the prelates. When granting them to monks, the prelates required that the monks pay them a fee or a certain sum of money at fixed times—that is, whenever the persons serving those churches changed. This fee was called *rachat* (“redemption”), by analogy with the redemption of fiefs when their lords changed; and it was called the redemption of altars, *redemptio altarium*, because a distinction was made between the church and the altar. The church meant the tithes and other fixed revenues, while the altars meant the offerings and incidental income that laypeople ordinarily left to those who served the church. The Council of Clermont condemned this redemption of an altar as detestable simony, while nevertheless preserving for the monasteries the altars or tithes that they had possessed for thirty years, subject to the annual census owed to the bishops—that is, as Fleury says, the former payment called the synodical or cathedral due.

After the Council of Clermont (Sirmond, ibid.), certain bishops, instead of the redemption of altars—which was paid only at intervals of several years—wanted to exact an annual tribute or fee. Among these were Ivo of Chartres and Ranulfe of Saintes, to whom Paschal II wrote on this subject. Ulger, bishop of Angers, wanted to do the same (book III, epistle 12) and claimed that the Council of Clermont had ordered the bishops to draw an annual tribute from the monks for the redemption of altars. The abbot of Vendôme opposed Ulger and wrote him a letter in which he said that he knew what had taken place at that council, since he had attended it; that the redemption of churches, ordinarily called altars, had there been condemned as simony by apostolic authority. He added that if the redemption of altars—which was paid after thirty years, forty years, and sometimes even sixty—had been regarded and condemned by the pope as genuine simony, the pope had not permitted bishops to exact an annual fee; otherwise he would have condemned a simony committed only once in a lifetime in order to substitute another committed every year. [Col. 0026A]

Baluze, in his notes on Gratian’s *Decree*, p. 499, was the first to seize upon this letter of Geoffroi in order to accuse him of rashness, claiming that he had removed this clause from the canon of the Council of Clermont: *salvo utique episcoporum censu annuo, quem ex eisdem altaribus habere soliti sunt* (“with the annual census of the bishops preserved, which they were accustomed to receive from those same altars”). It must be admitted that the designation “rashness” would not be too harsh if Geoffroi were truly guilty of the crime of which he is accused. But nothing is easier than proving his innocence and destroying the weak reasons on which Baluze relies.

It must first be observed that Baluze was young when he wrote his notes on Gratian and did not yet possess the learning that later made his name so famous in the republic of letters. This critic therefore supposed that there were two editions of the Council of Clermont: one general and common edition in which the clause in question appeared, and another peculiar to the abbey of Vendôme in which it had been removed. He based his system, first, on the cartulary of Vendôme, where, according to him, the canon concerning the redemption of altars had been transcribed and falsified at the same time; and, second, on the letter of Paschal II, truncated with respect to this essential clause. [Col. 0026C]

As for the alleged falsification of the canon of Clermont in the cartulary of Vendôme, Baluze had not seen this cartulary; he cites neither witness nor author who testifies in his favor. How, then, could he have asserted that the canon concerning the redemption of revenues had simultaneously been transcribed and falsified? Where did he learn this? Perhaps he concluded that Geoffroi had falsified this canon because Geoffroi sent a copy of it to the bishop of Angers. But, to speak in the words of the authors of the *New Treatise on Diplomatics*, even if Geoffroi had possessed neither conscience nor honor, would he have been so devoid of common sense as to defend his rights before a bishop by means of a falsification he had made in the canon of a council whose memory was still entirely recent? A thousand mouths would have risen against this manifest imposture. Baluze would therefore at least have had to produce a cartulary of Vendôme from which the clause favorable to the bishops had been removed in order to support so strange a claim. [Col. 0026D] But this he did not do, and no one ever will. In this matter we boldly challenge all critics.

As for the letter of Paschal II, in which Baluze claimed that the clause had been suppressed, we have in our possession what is needed to confound the accuser and utterly destroy the foundation of the accusation. D. Martène, while searching throughout France for materials for the *Gallia Christiana*, for his great collections, and for the edition of the letters of the popes, copied Paschal II’s letter from the cartulary of Vendôme with the most scrupulous accuracy. We have the letter before our eyes, and in it we read these words explicitly: *salvo utique episcoporum synodali censu* (“with the synodical census of the bishops preserved”). There it is, in the cartulary of Vendôme, the famous clause that Geoffroi is accused of having suppressed; and what deserves particular attention is that it removes the ambiguity of *annuo censu* (“annual census”) by substituting *synodali* (“synodical”). [Col. 0027A]

What now becomes of Baluze’s accusation and Simon’s tirade? An accusation of forgery against an abbot of the Order of Saint Benedict, however distinguished by his learning, uprightness, integrity, and piety, was too much to Simon’s taste—he was so well known for his outbursts—for him not to adopt it without examination.

“Could anything be more audacious,” he exclaims (*Critical Letters*, Basel edition, p. 134), “than the action of Geoffroi, abbot of Vendôme, who, in order to exempt his monks from a certain sum of money they paid to the bishops, called the redemption of altars, falsified the canon of the Council of Clermont in which this redemption was mentioned? . . . Geoffroi had removed from the canon of this Council of Clermont the clause *salvo utique*, and so forth.”

Geoffroi is sufficiently vindicated by what we have said against such an accusation. It remains only to determine whether this abbot claimed that the third canon of the Council of Clermont had deprived the bishops of their annual census from monastic parish churches. [Col. 0027B]

For a long time the bishops had been in possession of the right to levy upon these parish churches an annual census called synodical or cathedral (*New Treatise on Diplomatics*, p. 209). But in France this exaction was accompanied by another, condemned as simoniacal by a canon of the Council of Clermont. Whenever the parish priests or vicars responsible for serving the churches changed—especially when the churches passed from secular hands into those of regular clergy (Sirmond, notes on epistle 12, book III)—the bishops exacted a sum called the redemption of altars.

[Col. 0028A] Even after this abuse had been condemned, some people thought to increase their annual census by a sum equal to that which the canon had made them lose, distributing it over a certain number of years. But if the sum exacted whenever a priest changed was simoniacal, the distribution of it over several years was no less so. This is the abuse against which Geoffroi rose in his letter to Ulger, bishop of Angers. Pope Paschal II, the immediate successor of Urban II, had already declared himself against the same abuse in a letter to Ivo of Chartres and Ranulphe of Saintes. In that letter he described this false interpretation of the canon of the Council of Clermont as a device invented to disguise simony, and ordered them to carry out the council’s decree, even reminding them that they had attended it.

It is evident from this that Geoffroi, far from departing from what had been decided and regulated at Clermont, conformed to it according to the pope’s judgment; and that, on the contrary, the bishops who demanded an annual census from the monks despised and violated the decision of that council, [Col. 0028B] since Paschal set it against the prelates’ exaction. After this, can anyone think that Geoffroi falsified the canon of the Council of Clermont? If Baluze had made these reflections, he would never have brought such an accusation against an abbot as worthy of respect as Geoffroi of Vendôme. Let us go further: if he had understood the state of the question, which Father Sirmond explained so well in his notes on Geoffroi’s letter to Ulger, he would not have fallen into this excess. And it is surprising that, having had occasion to recognize and retract so great an error—especially when he published M. de Marca’s work, *On the Concord of the Priesthood and the Empire*—he did not render Abbot Geoffroi the justice he owed him.

[Col. 0027]

# To the Most Illustrious Prince, Caesar Bourbon, Duke of Vendôme, Viceroy of Armorican Brittany

At the time, most illustrious prince, when, through the generosity of your excellent father the king, you obtained letters patent for the principality of Vendôme, he thereby revealed, as I believe, not so much the indulgence he felt toward you as his singular foresight and benevolence toward the people of Vendôme themselves. His purpose was plainly that the rule of himself and his ancestors, which had been glorious and auspicious for them, should continue through you and your descendants; and that, under your leadership, the brilliant star of the house of Bourbon, beneath whose radiance they had flourished for so long, should shine upon them again as though newly risen.

Indeed, ever since Vendôme was transferred to Odo of Burgundy—if I do not go further back—through the dowry-gift of Adela, wife of Fulk Nerra, count of Anjou, it has always possessed outstanding princes, renowned for their achievements: the Fulks, Burchards, Geoffrois, Johns, Hughs, and others. Yet never did it have princes nobler or more illustrious in the glory of arms or piety than the Bourbons, so that they surpassed the others in every praise by as much as they preceded them in the prerogative of royal blood.

Hence it seems to have happened through a kind of divine plan that the dignity of Vendôme—once a portion of the royal inheritance, and having often changed its lords and passed through nearly every family of its counts—should finally find rest in this royal stock, glorious, honorable, and fortunate for it. For from John of Bourbon, count of La Marche, who was the great-grandfather of your great-grandfather, through whom the family of the counts of Vendôme was grafted into that of Bourbon, down to Henry IV, your father, the bravest and most merciful of kings, the lineage of the Bourbon princes of Vendôme runs in a direct and wholly unbroken succession. All of them were ennobled either by the highest offices held in France and the provinces they administered, by triumphal honors won through the defeat of enemies, or, finally, by kingdoms acquired abroad or inherited from their ancestors.

For this reason your people of Vendôme already perceive, with prophetic insight, which ancestral glories call you; what they ought to promise themselves from your father’s judgment of you; and what they ought to promise themselves for your descendants, who will be future dukes of Vendôme. As you found a new ducal line, you will also open a new path—such as your exceptional character promises—toward the immortal fame of your name.

But if our Geoffroi were to return to life, how greatly would he rejoice that light had been restored to him and to his works under your leadership! Or under whose auspices would he prefer them to emerge publicly rather than yours, under whose protection and patronage he himself would live if he were alive? They were, moreover, owed to you. For if the fruits follow the lord of the estate, who would not understand that whatever was once planted and born in the territory of Vendôme belongs to you alone, to whom the entire possession of Vendôme has been transferred by full and secure right?

He therefore now comes to you with greater confidence, the more just his act of homage, together with his introducer. Both ask the following: he asks that you cherish this offspring of his genius in his place, and that you be willing to confirm as lasting and perpetual the protection that the sworn counts of Vendôme once promised their monastery; I ask that you receive this slight token of duty with calm favor, as an encouragement to a wholly devoted spirit; and that, as heir to your father’s example, you protect the entire family of our order with the same benevolence and clemency in which you see him.

To Your Most Illustrious Highness.

Your most devoted servant,  
Jacques Sirmond, of the Society of Jesus.

[Col. 0029]

# To the Reader

[Col. 0029A] As you will rightly wonder, there is no mention anywhere of Geoffroi the abbot, either among the historians of those times or among those who, in our own age or in the memory of our fathers, have compiled catalogues of illustrious writers. To remedy this silence at least in part, we have assembled a brief biography from his own letters. We have then added several testimonies concerning him from writers of the same period, together with the eulogy of our own François Torrensis, whose diligent *polystoria*—his broad historical learning—did not overlook Geoffroi’s works, which seemed to have escaped everyone else.

In preparing this edition, moreover, we used two copies, both ancient and of good quality. Besides the copy from Le Mans, which we had already obtained from the monastery of Saint Peter of La Couture, another was supplied to us from its own monastery by the extensive and singular courtesy of D. Michael Sublet, abbot of Vendôme. To him we owe two brief works, numbers XIII and XVIII, which were missing from the other copy. [Col. 0030A]
