We separated the letters from the brief works and sermons. In both manuscripts everything had been mixed and confused together. But in the letters, since there were very few in the Vendôme manuscript, we followed the Le Mans manuscript. We also left the order untouched, except that several letters which had been read out of order—having apparently been written by Geoffroi after the first collection and scattered among other treatises and sermons—we placed in their proper locations alongside the others. We marked these letters with asterisks in the index, so that they too may be subject to your judgment.

For the sake of relieving weariness, we divided the entire body of both collections into five books. Readers commonly experience what happens to travelers, to whom, as Namatianus says:

> The intervals of the road seem to offer refreshment to the weary,
>
> when a stone inscribed with many miles marks them.

[Col. 0029]

# The Life of Geoffroi

[Col. 0029B] Geoffroi was born in Anjou. His family was especially distinguished and noble, as his second letter and others indicate, in which he calls Rainaud, lord of Credon, and Maurice, his son, his kinsmen. He was educated by Warnerius, archdeacon of Angers, and used William as his teacher, to whom he writes in book IV. In his early years he entered the monastery of Vendôme, which Count Geoffroi Martel had founded in the territory of Chartres only a few years earlier.

Not long afterward, while still a novice and a young man, and only a deacon, he was chosen as the fifth abbot of the same monastery after the death of Berno. Then, inaugurated by Ivo, bishop of Chartres, he went to Rome to Urban II, who was hiding for fear of the faction of Guibert. He bound the pontiff to himself by an immortal service, supplying abundant money with which the Lateran and the Crescentian Tower could be redeemed. For this reason he was the first of all to kiss Urban’s foot when Urban was restored to the papal seat together with the Lateran.

Urban also ordained him priest and restored to him, together with the dignity of cardinal, the church of Saint Prisca, from which the men of Vendôme had been violently expelled by the Guibertines. Returning to Gaul, he was summoned to Saumur on the Loire in that same year, 1094, by Hugh the legate, for the absolution of Fulk Rechin, count of Anjou. Then, in the following year, he was summoned by Urban and attended the famous council at Clermont in Auvergne. He would also have attended the Lateran council of Paschal II and likewise the Roman council of Callistus II, by whom he was similarly summoned, had the brevity of time not prevented the one journey and the severity of winter the other. [Col. 0031B]

As long as Urban lived, Geoffroi was dear to him as an only son. Geoffroi hosted Urban at Vendôme and later Paschal for eleven days. He was joined to Callistus by an old relationship and was his intimate friend, as their reciprocal letters demonstrate. The standing Geoffroi held with King Louis VI is further shown by the fact that the king selected him among the arbitrators in the dispute raised by the count of Anjou concerning the right of primogeniture and the seneschalship of France.

He governed his monastery with the greatest care and vigilance, so that, as he repeatedly declares, no monastery in all Gaul was considered more orderly at that time. Although he seemed harsh to some, he nevertheless writes that by nature he was more inclined toward indulgence. He increased the monastery’s revenues and external possessions so greatly that he left it twice as wealthy and prosperous as he had found it.

But, as is customary, he had to endure many troubles and disputes while defending its ancient rights and possessions against neighboring bishops, abbots, and other powerful men. His intellect was sharp and lively; exercised especially in sacred letters and the canons, it is attested throughout all his works, together with his singular piety. His freedom of speech is shown by even a single letter to Paschal concerning the investitures granted by him; his faith and devotion toward the Apostolic See—whose special sons the abbots of Vendôme are—are shown both by the immense expenditures he made for it and by the hardships of the journeys he undertook. In these journeys he crossed the Alps twelve times for the benefit of the Roman Church and was captured three times by its adversaries.

Nothing definite is known about his death. Letters written by Honorius II to Geoffroi in 1129 establish that he lived into the final years of Honorius’s pontificate.

[Col. 0031]

# Testimonies of Several Ancient Writers of the Same Period, and of One Modern Writer, Concerning Geoffroi, Abbot of Vendôme

## I. Letter of Hugh, Archbishop of Lyon and Legate of the Apostolic See, Concerning the Absolution of Fulk Rechin, Count of Anjou, at Which Geoffroi Was Present

[Col. 0031C]

Hugh, archbishop of Lyon and legate of the Apostolic See, to his most beloved brothers in Christ, the archbishops, bishops, abbots, and all the faithful of the holy Church of God: greeting.

We have judged it worthy to make known to the common notice of all the orthodox how, at the command of our lord Pope Urban, we undertook the obedience of going as far as the borders of Anjou on account of Fulk, count of Anjou, in order to absolve him from the bond of anathema with which he had long been bound because he had captured his brother Geoffroi in open war.

The count himself, however, did not avoid giving an account, making satisfaction, or submitting to judgment; rather, he was always ready to do so. And, as we learned from the report of reputable men, clerics and laymen, the aforesaid brother of his, at the time when he was captured, had been excommunicated by Cardinal Stephen, legate of the Roman See, on account of the many injuries he had inflicted upon the Church of Tours and upon the abbot of Saint Martin of the Greater Monastery. This same Fulk had received the principality of the county of Anjou from that legate, in the name of Saint Peter; and we learned through the truthful report of reputable men among his nobles that it had also been granted to him by his uncle Geoffroi. [Col. 0032C]

Having therefore accepted this legation, so that the force of apostolic obedience might be handled by us with greater authority, we took our venerable brother, the archbishop of Bourges, as a companion in this undertaking. Thus, having joined together, we deliberately approached the count’s brother, whom we had heard was being held captive. We found him so deranged, as everyone reported, that it seemed wholly useless and vain to entrust the government of the country to him, since by his folly he had made himself and everyone else useless to it. Indeed, he was so far gone that he did not wish to be freed from captivity even by our hands.

We therefore came to the monastery of Saint Florent. On the feast of the Nativity of Saint John the Baptist, in the presence of the religious bishops and abbots who had been invited and had come, we absolved Count Fulk, who was prepared either to make satisfaction or to give an account, by the unanimous vote and approval of all. We accepted from him guarantees that, if his brother recovered soundness of mind, he would, at the command of our lord pope or of us, either make peace with him or be ready to submit to judgment; and that he would not take a wife, without our counsel, since he was blamed for the number of wives he had had. We have judged it appropriate to lay before you the sequence of what was done.

The names of the religious men who were present are these:

Aldebert, venerable archbishop of Bourges;  
Ouveldus, bishop of Le Mans;  
William, abbot of Saint Florent;  
Bernard, abbot of the Greater Monastery;  
Bernard, abbot of Saints Sergius and Bacchus;  
Girard, abbot of Saint Aubin;  
Nualdus, abbot of Saint Nicholas;  
Baldric, abbot of Bourgueil;  
Geoffroi, abbot of Vendôme.

Done in the year 1094 from the Incarnation of the Lord, at the abbey of Saint Florent, on the feast day of Saint John the Baptist.

## II. Ivo, Bishop of Chartres (Epistle 40, to Geoffroi)

Ivo, humble minister of the Church of Chartres, to Geoffroi, abbot of the monastery of Vendôme, with affection, greeting.

See also Epistles 57, 92, 93, and 94.

## III. Hugh of Cleers, Angevin Knight, in His Commentary on the Right of Primogeniture and the Seneschalship of France

We have published this commentary in full after the notes.

King Louis asked Count Fulk to help him in this war. The count, however, replied that he owed him no service whatsoever. For the king was disinheriting him from the right of primogeniture and the seneschalship. Then King Louis sent word to the count through Amalric of Montfort, the count’s uncle, through Geoffroi, abbot of Vendôme, and through Ralph of Balgenci, promising that, on all these matters and other greater ones, he would make satisfaction to the count according to their counsel.

## IV. Letter of Pope Callistus II to Geoffroi, Abbot of Vendôme

[Col. 0034A]

Callistus, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his most beloved son in Christ, Geoffroi, abbot of Vendôme: greeting and apostolic blessing.

“And your devotion toward the Roman Church,” and so forth. See under Callistus II.

## V. François Torrensis, in His *Antapologeticus for the Residence of Pastors*

To say that the people once chose bishops, or that they can do so now, may pertain to the heresy concerning ecclesiastical investiture received from laymen, which the Roman synod condemned under Pope Gregory VII and branded by this name. Thus Geoffroi, abbot of Vendôme, an ancient authority and deeply learned in the Holy Scriptures, wrote in his book *On the Ordination of Bishops and the Investiture of Laymen*, addressed to Peter, surnamed Leo, cardinal of the Roman Church, and in his seventh letter to Pope Paschal concerning the agreement made with the German king.

# Works of Geoffroi, Abbot of Vendôme, Cardinal of Saint Prisca: Letters, Brief Works, and Sermons

Jacques Sirmond, priest of the Society of Jesus, first brought them to light and furnished the letters with notes, in the year 1610.

[Col. 0033]

# Letters of Geoffroi, Abbot of Vendôme, Cardinal of Saint Prisca

## Book One

### Letter One

[Col. 0033C]

To his dearest and venerable lord, Pope Urban: his Geoffroi sends reverence with the service of pure affection.

1. Desiring to visit Your Holiness, I had resolved to come to Rome; but the quartan fever that still torments me severely detained me against my will. And because I am eager, if God should someday grant me the ability, I shall not delay coming to you, desiring no ordinary satisfaction from the blessed sight of you. Meanwhile, sweetest Father, may your servant obtain from Your Piety, through your letters, both blessing and greeting.

I humbly ask that you command the Bishop of Saintes [Note: The Bishop of Saintes: Rannulf, to whom he writes about the same Eblon in Book III, Letter 31] not to absolve Eblon, who has always proved disobedient to you, on any pretext whatsoever, unless he first makes satisfaction to us for the invasion of our land and for the revenues that he unjustly held for four years.

Your goodness should in no way doubt the religious man who bears this letter, a lover of justice and truth and, as it seems, in every respect possessed of zeal for God. For he is the one who in our regions, almost as the first and greatest, never ceases to cry out with the Prophet: “Who will rise up for me against the wicked, or who will stand with me against the workers of iniquity?” (Psalm 93:16).

Kind Father, recently, while rereading the canons, I found a certain ruling that is inscribed to Pope Paschal [Note: To Pope Paschal: That name appears here for the first time. This canon is found in Ivo’s *Decretum*, Part II, chapter 84; the glossators of the Roman edition of Gratian’s Decretum, I, q. 1, *Quisquis*, also mention it, but attribute it to Paschal II, although they ought to have said “the first.” For that Paschal was the first, as this passage of Goffridus itself shows, since he is writing to Urban II, who preceded Paschal II.], in which it calls one who has been made a bishop while still a neophyte a heretic [Note: One made a bishop while still a neophyte: *Neophyte* here does not mean a newly converted Christian, in which sense the Apostle forbids a neophyte to become a bishop (1 Timothy 3), as does the Council of Nicaea in canon 2. Rather, it means a novice cleric, recently enrolled in the sacred order from the company of laymen, and still new—as I may use Gregory the Great’s words—in holy conduct. Gregory wished such men also to be called neophytes and to be excluded, together with the Simonians, by anathema from the episcopal rank. See Book IV, Letter 5, to Virgilius, and Book VII, Letter 112, to Syagrius and others. Although in the early centuries, because of the needs of the Church, not a few bishops of both kinds had been created, and some had succeeded brilliantly—for example Philogonius at Antioch, Nectarius at Constantinople, Ambrose at Milan, and our own Sidonius among the Arverni, among others—nevertheless, after the need had been removed, it was decided that the practice should be prohibited and that the ambition of men suddenly rushing toward sacred honors should be restrained. Indeed, the Second Synod of Auvergne, not yet published [Note: Later published in volume II of the *Councils of Gaul*, p. 389], following the Fifth of Orléans, had shortly before Gregory’s time prescribed a period of one year for neophytes in canon 9, in these words: “Let no one from among the laity be ordained bishop without a preceding period of one year’s conduct, so that within the space of a year he may be more fully instructed by learned and approved men in spiritual disciplines and rules.” Paschal followed Gregory’s opinion and words in his canon. But what is written in it—that Gregory calls these neophytes, if they become bishops, heretics—appears to be an interpolation, since it is nowhere found in Gregory. This may perhaps be why Goffridus is uncertain about that canon. Ivo, however, also calls the neophytes’ status heresy in Letter 149.]; and teaches and commands that a neophyte, just like a Simonian, must be separated from the holy Church.

But whether this ruling ought to be received among the canonical authorities, I do not sufficiently understand. What I understand still less from it, I desire to learn through Your Paternity’s instruction. May Your Majesty prosper.

## LETTER II

To his most beloved lord and venerable Pope Paschal, Goffridus, wholly his own, with the obedience owed in love.

I had prepared to come to you, excellent Father. Even if my tongue were silent, the very preparations that I had made would bear witness to how eagerly I desired to fulfill this wish. But while my willing desire to come was present, an unforeseen necessity was not lacking [Col. 0036A], and it completely obstructed my intention.

For in our region there are certain men sufficiently noble by birth [Note: Certain men sufficiently noble: The provosts of Olarion on the island of Saintes, where they exacted these customary dues. See Book III, Letter 38, and Book V, Letter 20], but very ignoble in conduct; related to me by flesh, but far removed from me in character and life. They are striving to extort from the property of the monastery, whose care I seem to exercise, although unworthy, certain perverse exactions or customary dues that their predecessors had long before imposed upon the property by violence.

Since I could not recall them from their impiety through ecclesiastical censure, I began to labor to see whether they might somehow be bent by the authority of the prince [Note: The authority of the prince: William, Duke of Aquitaine; see Book V, Letters 20 and 21. The monastery of Vendôme was indeed founded by Goffridus Martellus, Count of Anjou, and his wife Agnes; but Agnes had previously been married to William, Count of Aquitaine, son of William “Towhead.” From that marriage was born Guy, the grandfather of this William, the prince in question. Agnes, therefore, was his great-grandmother and the foundress. The protectors of the monastery of Vendôme were the Count of Poitiers together with the Counts of Anjou and Vendôme. Urban II, in a charter of 1098, states: “Moreover, we decree that the Counts of Anjou, Poitiers, and Vendôme shall always be protectors and helpers of that place, for the honor of the Apostolic See.”], whose predecessors had founded the monastery and had offered it, with its possessions, to blessed Peter as his patrimony and freehold [Col. 0034B], together with the property belonging to it [Col. 0037A] [Note: And they offered it as a freehold. In ancient times *allodium* meant a free estate subject to no one’s jurisdiction. Hence we still call an estate a freehold when it owes neither fealty nor payment; in this it differs from a fief, which owes fealty and lordship. Ivo of Chartres, Letter 168: “Count Rotrocus purchased that part of the estate which was a freehold, that is, which was held under free law; for the other part of the estate was not free, since it had been granted as a benefice.” To give as a freehold, therefore, is to transfer into one’s own right. To give as a fief is not the same, because ownership of the feudal estate remains with the superior lord; only its usufruct is granted to the vassal. Accordingly, what is a fief to the vassal is itself a freehold to the lord.

Even today several villages in France retain the ancient name *allodium*: because they were of free status, they were called *allodia* and *alodi*. For the people of Anjou still call *alodos* the lands that Countess Adela gave to Saint-Albino, and the Poitevin monastery of Saint Mary of the Freeholds is so called because it is situated in a village bearing that name.]

This is what holds me greatly in suspense. But as soon as the truth for which I labor has, by its grace, freed me from this uncertainty, I shall not delay visiting Your Holiness as is fitting.

Meanwhile, most pious Father, may your servant obtain from Your Paternity, through the saving sight of your letters, both greeting and joy. By their authority may we restrain the inhumanity—or rather the bestial savagery—of tyrants, which we shall scarcely, or never, be able to restrain by any other means.

### LETTER III

To his most beloved and venerable Father, Pope Paschal, Goffridus, unworthy minister of the monastery of Vendôme, with the obedience owed in love.

[Col. 0037B] The freehold of blessed Peter—namely, the monastery of Vendôme, whose affairs our humility is known to govern—is grievously battered in this world, as though in the middle of the sea, by a very severe storm.

It is no longer, as usual, ravaged by secular violence; but it is constantly harassed by the injuries and injustices of bishops, who ought to have been defenders of the Church. They themselves do us harm, and readily consent to the harms inflicted by others.

In the bishopric of Le Mans, the Countess of Vendôme [Note: The Countess of Vendôme: Her identity is uncertain; but the name of the church she had invaded is Saviniacus. See Book III, Letter 15], expelled from the county on account of her crimes, takes away from us a certain church, along with many other things. The bishop sees this and permits the robbery to go unpunished; although justice has often been sought, he does not exercise its rights.

He also detains with him, despite our protests, one of our fugitive monks [Note: One of our monks: John, who is frequently mentioned in the letters to Ildebert, bishop; see Book III], a mason [Col. 0037C]—though he does not possess the cement of charity by which he might be joined to Christ, the living stone—for the sake of his skill. There, with the bishop’s knowledge, he eats meat contrary to the monk’s profession and, wholly opposed to the holy Rule, works the destruction of his soul together with the dishonor of his body.

In the bishopric of Angers, we know that a church has been planted in one of our parishes, against our opposition [Note: A church in one of our parishes: It was an ancient and perpetual legal principle that a new church could not be built without the permission of the bishop in whose diocese it lay. The Council of Chalcedon, canon 4, states: “It has been decided that no one anywhere may build or establish a monastery or a house of prayer contrary to the judgment of the city’s bishop.” This right was so firmly established among our kings that they confirmed it both by their own law and by their example of obedience. See the *Capitularies*, Book V, chapter 182: “It has pleased us that chapels in our palace, or elsewhere, shall not be established without the permission of the bishop in whose parish they are.” What therefore belonged to bishops in this matter, abbots likewise claimed as their own in parishes under their authority. Such was the right of the Cluniacs by a privilege of Lucius II: “We prohibit anyone from presuming to build a church or chapel within the parishes belonging to the jurisdiction of the monastery of Cluny without the consent of the abbot of Cluny.” Rome, 1154.]. It was not planted by the heavenly Father, but by a certain layman who impressed it there through reckless power. We regard the bishop as the supporter of this act, although we ought to have had him as the avenger and corrector of so great an injury.

The Bishop of Saintes [Note: The Bishop of Saintes: The same Rannulf, from whom he complains that the island of Flaic, mentioned here, was once and again taken away from his monastery. See Book III, Letter 37], although our monastery had possessed it for thirty years and more without any protest, granted certain rivals of ours permission to receive it while we were absent—or rather, while we were unaware. Finally, when we appealed to the hearing of Your Holy Paternity, he heard us.

But may what was wholly unavailing with him prove beneficial with you, Father. Since it has been a long time, most loving lord, since we visited you [Col. 0038B], we humbly and earnestly beg that Your Sublimity, merciful to your servants, not be indignant with us for this. We delayed for no other reason than that we desired to have present before your just tribunal at least some, if not all, of those by whom we are unjustly oppressed.

Therefore, with all our heart, with all our soul, and with all our strength, we beseech Your Holiness that we may experience, according to our desire, the compassion of the Apostolic See, which is accustomed to come to the aid of all the oppressed; so that the storm we endure may at last cease its raging, and we, as is proper for monks, may enjoy the desired peace.

### LETTER IV

To the most blessed Pope Paschal, his dearest lord and Father, the entire congregation of the monastery of Vendôme [Col. 0038C], and their unworthy Father Goffridus, offer the obedience and submission owed with filial fear.

Exhausted by the injuries and persecutions that the Bishop of Chartres [Note: The Bishop of Chartres: Ivo, with whom he frequently argues about these troubles. See Book II. The letter was written in the name of the entire monastery, but dictated by Goffridus and carried to Rome to Paschal.] has raised against us and caused to be raised, we flee to the bosom of our mother, the holy Roman Church [Col. 0039A], thirsting for the breast of justice. For love and loyalty toward her, we have long endured the bishop’s manifold attacks.

We therefore flee to the Roman Church. While we desire to be gathered and nurtured beneath the wings of her motherhood, as is just, the aforesaid bishop strives to scatter us and drag us away, bound by the cords of tribulation. He despises the privileges of the holy Catholic and Apostolic See and, because the Roman Church, mother of all churches, cannot claim as her own those whom from the beginning of our foundation she has regarded as her own special sons and nourished with the milk of her affection [Note: Cannot claim them as her own: This was impossible because Bishop Theoderic, in his own name and that of his successors, had freed the monastery of Vendôme from the authority of the bishops of Chartres by a privilege, which we have published at the end of Goffridus’s works], attempts to extinguish us through detestable persecutions.

Therefore, Father of the best and most honorable life, we humbly implore your compassion: draw the sword of blessed Peter from its sheath, and correct the bishop and those who have obeyed him in our injuries in such a way that the others may fear, withdraw their hands from persecuting us, and, under the protection of Apostolic strength, may we possess the peace that befits monks.

Remember, most beloved Father, your venerable predecessors who went before you to the heavenly dwellings. Although their holy prudence, divided among many matters, may have been lesser in each individual case, nevertheless, in the affairs of our monastery—that is, in the patrimony of blessed Peter—it gathered itself together entirely, as it seemed.

Indeed, as their honorable letters truthfully testify—letters that we preserve as relics—they rendered manifold thanks to our benefactors and rebuked those who attacked us with the severest denunciations [Col. 0039C].

In those times we had peace and quiet, and it was possible to serve God without becoming entangled in worldly business. For if anyone planned to trouble us, he perished at the very place where the wicked thought had arisen.

But now we are battered by tribulations and wearied by injuries and persecutions; above all, we labor under those of the Bishop of Chartres. Yet, placing complete confidence in your goodness, most merciful Father, and in the integrity of your equity, we believe that we shall be freed from all these things.

Because of excessive delay, we have kept silent about the burdens by which the aforesaid bishop oppresses us and about the weight beneath which we groan. The lord abbot’s tongue will speak of everything better than a letter could report it.

### LETTER V

To the glorious and venerable Father in life, Lord Paschal, pontiff of the holy Catholic Roman Church, Brother Goffridus, called the sinful abbot of Vendôme, offers what a son owes to a father and a servant to a lord.

We received the letter of Your Holiness with the joy and reverence that we owed, and we wished to render it the obedience that was fitting. Whatever Your Beatitude had commanded us in your letter would certainly have been completed, had not the disobedience of Archembald, called the abbot of Saint-Albino [Note: Archembald, called the abbot: This matter is treated in the following letter], and of certain monks who favored him stood in the way.

Your holy and just command had been given; but those who love justice and holiness less than they should did absolutely nothing of all that you commanded [Col. 0040B]. It therefore falls to your discretion to correct what was done in disobedience, so that at least in this way everyone may recognize how grave it is to despise Apostolic commands.

For it is useful—indeed necessary—that so great a presumption on the part of monks not remain unpunished, lest, taking its beginning from the monks, the plague of disobedience dare raise its head in a higher rank.

This year, most beloved Father, I desired with all desire to come to you; but detained by illness and the manifold needs of our monastery, I could not come. But, God willing, I shall come to you as soon as I can, to see your blessed face and to recover the church of Saint Prisca [Note: The church of blessed Prisca: This too should be requested, as appears from Letter 9 of this book], or justice concerning the church, if this does not displease your goodness—which it certainly ought not to do.

### LETTER VI

To the most blessed Pope Paschal, his dearest lord and Father, Brother Goffridus, humble servant of the Holy Roman See, offers the obedience owed in love.

Know that Lord Paganus, the elected abbot of Saint-Albino [Note: Lord Paganus, the elected abbot of Saint-Albino: The old and distinguished monastery of Saint-Albino at Juliomagus, Angers, in which Archembald was created abbot after Gerard II in the year of Christ 1106. When Archembald had voluntarily resigned and Paganus had been substituted in his place, he soon changed his mind, desired the abbacy again, and obtained the annulment of Paganus’s election. Paschal sent Goffridus letters on Paganus’s behalf, concerning which see the preceding letter; but neither the papal letters nor the petitions presented to the legate and the Bishop of Angers [Col. 0040D] were of any help in preventing Archembald from retaining the abbacy], whom by a decree of your authority you commended to me, the least of your servants, has truly suffered many grievous wrongs.

First, his election was taken from him without judgment or hearing. Afterwards, Archembald was substituted in the place that Paganus had obtained by the election of his brethren, through envy.

In my presence, Archembald had already wholly resigned the abbacy in his chapter, into the hands of the Bishop of Angers, with the Rule of Saint Benedict [Note: With the Rule of Saint Benedict: That is, presenting the book of the Rule, he had resigned the abbacy. This derives from the ancient custom of those times, by which a staff, knife, or some similar object was used to ratify and confirm acts of resignation and investiture; sometimes, among monks, the book of the Rule of Saint Benedict was used. Various examples of this are preserved in the archive of Saint-Albino, such as the donation of Adelard of Château-Gontier, which we shall present in Book V, Letter 25. Likewise in another grant of Samson Passavant, a knight, in which, after enumerating what he had donated to the monastery at Courtchamp in the year 1138, he concludes: “Concerning this alms, therefore, I myself, Samson, with the Rule of Saint Benedict, with which I had received the benefice of the church from the aforesaid abbot and brothers, invested the aforesaid abbot and community; and I carried that same Rule onto the altar of blessed Albino as a perpetual memorial of its firmness.” Just as in these documents we read of the book of the Rule, so in other charters we read of a knife, staff, gloves placed into the hand and set upon the altar. Indeed, such memorials of the ancient custom still exist today in the same monastery of Saint-Albino and in many others: staffs, gloves, and other objects of investitures and transfers, inscribed with the titles of the acts they had marked.].

He had resigned it because, as he himself and the entire congregation publicly acknowledged with him, he could not bear so great a burden on account of his mental and physical weakness.

But when Paganus saw that, without being heard or summoned, he was treated as though condemned, he approached, in my hearing, the lord Bishop of Angers [Note: The Bishop of Angers: Rainaldus, to whom he writes in Book III] and the lord legate, the Bishop of Angoulême [Note: The legate of Angoulême: Gerard, concerning whom see Letter 19 of this book]. He sought justice and a hearing from them; but, just as both had been sought, both were denied him by both men.

King Solomon, however, and the evangelical Judge acted neither in this way nor taught the judges of the Church to act in this way. One of them did not disdain to hear the litigating prostitutes, but, carefully examining their cases, prudently settled them. The other wisely and mercifully freed a woman caught in adultery and accused before him.

Oppressed by these matters, which we have mentioned above, and by other grievous wrongs, the aforesaid brother appealed to the Holy Apostolic See, which is accustomed, with a mother’s compassion, to help all the oppressed; and he fled to it, as a son to his mother, seeking counsel and aid.

But neither his election nor his appeal to the Holy See—which once used to be effective—has yet been able to benefit him. And since it is not fitting for a son to remain silent about an injury to his mother, I can neither conceal nor ought I to conceal the injury done to the holy mother, the Roman Church, whose son I am, although unworthy.

Archembald and the monks who support his cause have so utterly despised everything that the Roman Church commanded them concerning Paganus [Col. 0041C] that they did absolutely nothing at all.

Yet it is useful and honorable to obey this universal mother of all Christians, and criminal not to obey her. She has always striven to preserve affection for those who obey and to repay disobedient people with punishment.

Therefore, most heartfelt Father, whatever sort of son he may be, your son humbly implores the compassion of a father: may the state of justice and the affection of charity flourish in our mother, the Roman Church, so that the poor innocent may not be oppressed, nor the proud rich person boast on any pretext.

But if the violence of the German king [Note: The violence of the German king: Henry IV, later emperor; this matter will be discussed shortly in the following letter] extorted from you something contrary to equity, and fear for the lives of your sons inclined your flesh, though not your soul, to this course, then, the less justice is recognized in that action, the more may it be carried out in other cases.

Most beloved Father in Christ, do not be excessively distressed if there was some wrongful action; do not let the king’s demand disturb the eye of your mind. Rather, as strongly as you can, now, after deliberation, uphold the rights of justice in other matters, so that what your humanity did for the king may be believed to have been done out of a father’s compassion for the lives of your sons.

## 11. LETTER VII

[Note: Letter 7: The subject of this letter was expressed in the index of the Le Mans manuscript as follows: “He reasonably demonstrates that the pact which he had made with the German king ought not to be kept.” The pact concerned the investitures of bishops and abbots, which Henry had extorted from Paschal by an armed force of soldiers after surrounding the city and capturing him by violence, on the third day before the Ides of April in the year 1111 [Col. 0042C]. Henry’s father had sought to obtain these investitures from Gregory and Urban, but they had never been swayed by threats, blandishments, or persecutions. Although necessity appeared to excuse Paschal’s action—since otherwise, as he himself argues in a letter to Guy of Vienne, the enslavement of the Church, the death of captives, and the destruction of the city and of Italy seemed imminent—it was nevertheless disapproved almost everywhere to such an extent that it nearly provoked an open schism. Thus prudent and resolute men, distressed by the violation of the Church’s rights—including our Goffridus and others whose letters survive—did not cease urging and pressing Paschal to revoke by public decree the pact that he had made unwillingly and himself voluntarily condemned. He did so the following year at the Lateran Synod, where he again abolished the investitures granted to Henry.]

To the most blessed Pope Paschal, his dearest lord and Father, Brother Goffridus, the least of the servants of the Apostolic See, offers the obedience that is according to God.

You know very well, best of Fathers, that Peter’s ship contained both Peter and Judas, and, as blessed Ambrose says [Note: [Col. 0042D] Blessed Ambrose says in Book IV on Luke, chapter 4: “This is that ship which, according to Matthew, is still tossed by the waves, while according to Luke it is filled with fish.” And later: “The one which has Peter is not troubled; the one which has Judas is troubled.”]: “As long as Judas was in it, it continually endured the storm; but after that son of perdition had been cast out, it enjoyed calm and quiet.”

Judas’s perversity indeed demanded that he raise a storm against the ship which carried both Peter and himself; but the faith and devotion of blessed Peter prevailed with the Lord, so that it would suffer neither collision nor sinking. And because in our own times another Judas, brought forth by the labor of the devil, is recognized as having been born against the holy Church, one who with every detestable presumption attempts to seize for himself the catholic faith, liberty, and her blessed chastity [Col. 0042C], it is greatly necessary that even now the faith of blessed Peter in his special see—which has never been accustomed to err—should be so vigorous that, above all, it may protect his holy Roman Church from collision and defend it from sinking, lest perhaps—God forbid!—with Satan triumphing, it succumb, intolerably overwhelmed by the waves of error. Then the whole multitude of believers might suffer and perish with him in Scylla and Charybdis, and blessed Peter might be believed to lie beneath the waves, though formerly he walked upon the waves.

We firmly believe, and do not err, that our Lord gave the primacy of the Church to two disciples, namely Peter and Paul. He made Peter chief of the catholic faith, and Paul chief of doctrine. He chose the one while he still remained bodily on earth, but the other while he was already dwelling in heaven. On earth, indeed, he chose Peter so that he might strengthen his Church by the power of his faith; afterward he chose Paul from heaven so that by his holy teaching he might adorn the Church already strengthened by faith.

These glorious triumphant men, preserving faith in the truth by their deeds rather than by their blood, preferred that one should obediently undergo the punishment of the cross, and the other carefully receive the sword with bowed neck; hence more milk issued than blood. They would not allow the power of faith and the liberty of the Church entrusted to them—which their good teacher and Lord had purchased by the shed blood of his most sacred body [Col. 0043B]—to be taken away.

These martyrs, of holy memory and venerable life, faithfully clinging to Christ their head, showed by their deeds more loudly than by their words how truly they were his members: they chose to die for him rather than to live against him. Crowned with their victorious blood, the holy Roman Church once triumphed over her enemies; in her teachers she has always desired to die for Christ and has refused to live for herself.

These holy men now rejoice with their Lord in heavenly dwellings. There, having obtained blessed immortality in place of temporal death, they await their successors—successors who will not be degenerate. If victory in suffering did not come to some of them, it was not denied by fear [Col. 0043C]; rather, the day of combat was lacking, not the passion itself. The earth rejoices in such patrons, and heaven exults. Because their blessed life merited a glorious death, the Christian people celebrate their holy festivals in great numbers and commend themselves with complete devotion to their Creator through their humble prayers.

To celebrate their festivals is therefore useful and religious; to commend oneself to their devout prayers is likewise useful and necessary. Whoever, while occupying their see, has deprived himself of their blessed lot by acting otherwise should himself undo what he has done and, like another Peter, correct it by weeping.

If the weakness of the flesh faltered for an hour through fear of death, let the integrity of the mind persevere in correcting the works of the flesh, and let it not be ashamed to amend them, attributing to the flesh—whether it wishes it or not, since it must die—the act which, having acquired immortality, it could have avoided [Col. 0043D]. But if he is proved to have done, or to have consented to those doing, things which Christ himself corrected, which blessed Peter abhorred, and which the sacred canons utterly condemn, out of fear of the death of his sons rather than of his own, so evident a wound cannot be covered by any disguise. For in this way a father could not show mercy to his sons, but only hinder their salvation.

No examples of the saints teach us to postpone the death which suddenly kills those destined to die, and to take away from those who will live forever the life prepared by God. For if Paul avoided death for a time, he did not thereby injure the faith in any respect, nor abandon the truth; rather, he is believed to have reserved himself for death instead of escaping it, so that afterward he might bear richer fruit. Hence it is truly recognized that it was neither justice nor mercy which counseled the removal from death of those who could immediately have been joined, for the benefit of the whole Church, to eternal life, but an instigation of Satan [Col. 0044A].

O how venerable, and how precious in the sight of the Lord, would have been the death—or rather, the life—of those to whom, if it had been granted from above, or permitted on earth, to suffer for the faith! Having overcome the Church’s heretical depravity, the holy Church would have continued, to the end of the age, to beget faithful sons for her spouse, who died and rose again for her; and thereafter the catholic faith could have been neither broken nor bent.

If it is objected that perhaps they would have suffered unwillingly, and that their suffering would therefore be considered fruitless because it would not have appeared voluntary, then again [AUG. ep. 61 to Dulcitius]: [Col. 0044B] “Punishment does not make a martyr, but the cause”; and that cause was suitable—indeed, exceedingly suitable—for it was the cause of the faith, than which none better could be found. For this cause, even if they could not have died otherwise, they ought to have died against their will; for even so they could not have been deprived of the martyr’s palm.

The innocent saints, who are read to have sought martyrdom neither by voice nor by will, are nevertheless not deprived of the martyr’s crown, because they endured it for the Lord. The holy Church confesses that these were not only martyrs but also the flowers of martyrs. Hence it must be firmly believed and in no way doubted that punishment by death inflicted on a person for Christ’s faith, even if he did not desire it because of the weakness of the flesh, yet did not deny it, wins for him the name and reward of a martyr [Col. 0044C].

But if the sons had been so degenerate that, although they had already drawn near the gate of paradise—not through the wickedness of the Teutonic king, but through the mercy of the Lord, who is accustomed to make good use of evil—they had wished, by denying the faith, to step backward, then the father’s steadfastness and reason ought rather to have shown favor to the spirit than to the flesh. He ought to have strengthened them in the holy faith by exhortation: if necessity pressed, he should be the first to succumb for the truth. And just as blessed Sixtus went before blessed Lawrence into eternal life, so he himself ought to have gone before them, lest through their imperfection the universal Church lose the charter of faith, chastity, and liberty which the Savior, dictated by his own mouth and sealed on the cross by his own hands, gave to all Christians as a pledge and guarantee of love.

And since there is no doubt that this guilt is wholly inexcusable, and that by excusing it one can increase it rather than diminish it, the error knowingly committed must be corrected without delay, lest our spiritual mother, who is drawing what seems to be her final breath, die altogether. The Church lives and flourishes by faith, chastity, and liberty; without them she languishes and is separated from life. For she is founded on faith, adorned with chastity, and protected by liberty.

But when she does not oppose lay investiture—which according to the traditions of the holy Fathers is proved to be heresy—but commands it; when she herself is corrupted by gifts; when she is subjected to secular power, faith, chastity, and liberty are taken from her all at once. And since she does not possess life, she is rightly believed to be dead [Col. 0044D].

To believe the author of this death, or even the Church’s last member, to be a pastor, although he may appear to be one [Col. 0045A], is an error. Whoever clings to this error will deserve to be cut off from the very root of life. If anyone thinks otherwise about these matters, he is not a catholic: let him be exposed, and by the proof of truth he will be shown to be a heretic.

A pastor is indeed to be tolerated, as the canons say, on account of reprehensible morals [Note: [Col. 0045D] “A pastor is indeed to be tolerated.” From the third letter of Anacletus, cited by Ivo, Decree, Part III, chapter 3.]; but if he has deviated from the faith, he is no longer a pastor but an adversary, to be detested by every merely catholic sinner. For according to the decrees of the holy Roman pontiffs, even a prostitute may defend the common faith of the Church, which she believes and confesses as her own. How much more, therefore, and how much more perfectly, is it fitting for a religious catholic to attack heretical depravity; and a Christian must not conceal the truth of Christian law in such a matter [Col. 0045B].

There are certain bishops whom neither clergy nor people elected, but whom a layperson alone invested. Against the statutes of the catholic Fathers, and especially against the truthful voice of blessed Pope Gregory VII, who died in exile in defense of this faith [Note: [Col. 0045D] “He died in exile.” At Salerno, compelled to yield to Emperor Henry, who had captured Rome. When Gregory VII fell into a fatal illness, Peter the Librarian records these words of his: “I loved justice and hated iniquity; therefore I die in exile.”], they conceal investiture and, if they can, deny that it is heresy, using words contrived for the purpose of seduction [Note: [Col. 0045D] “They deny that it is heresy.” He discusses this matter more fully in Book III, Letter 11, and in the shorter works.].

The faithful do not weigh these men on their deceitful scales; for the Spirit of God, by whom they are governed, guards them. These brothers—if only they could be catholic brothers—who have received or are receiving investiture from laymen, not from their consecrator and contrary to the keys of the Church, while attempting to defend any author of this crime, cover themselves under his defense [Col. 0045C], as though they had exposed and bared their shameful buttocks.

For when they falsely attempt to bury the chastity of God’s bride and to raise those buried in exceedingly filthy pollution, they make themselves still more clearly manifest. But since a heretic is not condemned by the testimony of another heretic in that kind of heresy in which they agree, it is not surprising that they utter such abominable things.

Against the man who believes and professes such things, King and prophet David shoots these words from the quiver of truth: “There is no God before his eyes; his ways are defiled at all times” (Psalm IX); and this also: “The words of his mouth are iniquity and deceit” (Psalm XXXV): “he refused to understand, so as to follow the things that belong to the faith.” A man of this sort desires to rule rather than to benefit, and to seek only what is his own, not what belongs to Jesus Christ (Philippians II); and he cares nothing if the sheep are driven over any kind of byway [Col. 0045D].

The milk and wool of the sheep are not enough for him; he devours their flesh and gnaws their bones. Yet he considers himself a shepherd of sheep, when he is rather their wolf. And rightly is he believed to be a wolf, not a shepherd of sheep, who does not feed them but feeds upon them [Col. 0046A].

We say these things because, when a prophet corrupted by Satan is recognized—one who is proved to have given counsel and consent to the destruction of the Christian people not only by word, like Balaam, but also in writing—it is greatly necessary that the she-ass on which he rides should speak and rebuke the prophet’s folly, since he has transgressed the sacred precepts of divine law and followed the madness of a sacrilegious king [Col. 0046A].

And since we unquestionably recognize Lucifer as having fallen from heaven in our own times, let us not cling to him by disguising his impiety on any pretext, lest we fall with him—God forbid!—into the pit of despair. If I have said less than I ought, let it be attributed to ignorance; if more, let it be forgiven, since it arose from hatred of iniquity and love of justice [Col. 0046B].

## LETTER VIII

To the most beloved Father and lord, the venerable Pope Paschal, Brother Goffridus, the least of the servants of the holy Roman Church, sends the obedience due with love.

It pleased Your Holiness, dearest Father, to summon Abbot of Saint-Albínus [Note: [Col. 0045D] “The Abbot of Saint-Albinus.” Archembaldus, of whom Letter 5 speaks. He was now being summoned to Rome with Goffridus, so that both might plead their case concerning the church of Saint John over the Loire. By the judgment of Urban II, the monks of Vendôme had been compelled to give it to the monks of Saint-Albinus in exchange for the church of Credon, which they were claiming. Goffridus, after becoming abbot, had conducted his case before Urban so successfully that Urban withdrew his judgment and later assigned the church of Saint John to the monastery of Vendôme among its other possessions. We have seen this done not only by Urban but also by Paschal, his successor, in a charter of the year 1103. Nevertheless, however the matter may have been settled, Urban’s decree ultimately prevailed, and the monks of Saint-Albinus still possess that church.] and, by a decree of Your Authority, to admonish him to render me justice in your presence by the feast of All Saints.

What he once did against the apostolic see, Your Beatitude knows better. Now, however, he dares not disobey you, since, if he did not come in response to this summons of yours, the Count of Anjou [Note: [Col. 0046D] “The Count of Anjou.” Fulk V of that name, the same man who later obtained the kingdom of Jerusalem; he is mentioned again in Letter 21 and Book XI, Letter 7.] would restore to our monastery the property which the monks of Saint-Albinus had taken away by underhand means [Col. 0046C].

I, however, detained until the appointed time by the unavoidable needs of our monastery, as I previously told the aforesaid abbot, shall not be able to come. But, if God grants me life and prosperity, I shall visit your blessed presence by the feast of Saint Clement, intending to receive justice from the abbot and the monks of Saint-Albinus [Col. 0046C], and to prove by many authorities of the holy Roman pontiffs that they deceived the lord Pope Urban of venerable memory.

Afterward, when he had seen our privileges, that same lord Pope declared that he had been deceived; and by the authority of his own privilege—which he had issued against us—he so retracted it that he confirmed without exception the church about which the dispute remains, and whatever his predecessors had established for our monastery [Col. 0046D].

Therefore, dearest Father, your discerning fatherhood is humbly entreated by one who is not an adopted but your own and special son [Note: [Col. 0047C] “Your special son.” Book III, Letter 34. Blessed Bernard, Letter 294 to Pope Eugenius: “We ask that the Abbot of Vendôme, who is especially yours, may himself also find special favor.”], not to let those who distrust justice benefit if they arrive before us.

The monastery of Saint-Albinus has never served, and will never serve, the Roman Church except for its own particular need. Our monastery, however, belongs to blessed Peter in such a way that from its very founders it was given to him as an allod and patrimony. From the beginning of our community, our predecessors have served the holy Roman Church exceedingly well; and, if one ought to boast—or rather, because one ought to boast in the Lord—none of them has served it better than I.

Therefore, without violating the truth, I declare that since I undertook the governance of the monastery, our poverty has spent thirteen thousand solidi of our coinage in the service of the Roman Church [Note: [Col. 0047C] “Thirteen thousand solidi.” Only twelve thousand are read in Letters 9 and 13 to Calixtus. Therefore this passage appears to contain an error.], solely out of love and not because of any need of my own [Col. 0047B].

I say this, God knows, not deceitfully reproaching anyone, but truly demonstrating our love toward the Roman Church, so that those who love the Roman Church may also love me and, together with me, raise a shield of defense against my adversaries.

Among the other services which my humility has rendered to the Roman Church in her need, I can and ought not to be silent about one, since it was especially famous. When it is heard, no one who loves the catholic faith will ever be able not to love me.

In the first year in which, by God’s will or permission, I received the name of abbot [Note: [Col. 0047C] “In the first year.” In the year of Christ 1094. From Berthold of Constance, who carefully followed Urban’s affairs [Col. 0048D], it is clear that at the beginning of this year the Tower of Crescentius was still in the power of the followers of Guibert. Goffridus records that shortly before the Easter holidays he recovered the tower together with the Lateran palace through his own efforts; it is certain that this occurred in precisely that year. Urban owed Goffridus the favor, and we owe him the memory of this outstanding deed. For unless he himself had revealed it, we would not know of it.], I heard that Pope Urban, of pious memory, was hiding in the house of John Fricapan [Note: [Col. 0047D] “In the house of John Fricapan.” This is the name of a very ancient and noble Roman family, now slightly altered; they are called Frangipani. Thus what Berthold writes in general—that Urban remained in Rome near Saint Mary the New in a very strong fortification—appears to be explained more precisely by Goffridus, who says that he was hiding in this John’s house.] and laboring manfully against the Guitbertist heresy [Col. 0047C] [Note: [Col. 0047D] “Against the Guitbertist heresy.” Against Guibert and his supporters. This is the man whom Emperor Henry, having imposed the name Clement III on him, created as a pseudo-pontiff against Gregory VII in the year 1083. From that time, both while Gregory lived and afterward against his successors Victor and Urban, he harassed them in various dreadful ways and kept them almost continually exiled from Rome. Thus, as Goffridus writes in the final letter, a catholic pope had not sat in the apostolic see for a very long interval. There were exactly eleven years from the beginning of Guibert’s schism to Urban’s recovery of the Lateran through Ferruchius’s surrender.].

Although our place was poor, I nevertheless came to Rome, wishing to share in his persecutions and labors and desiring, to the best of my ability, to relieve his poverty; and by God’s grace I did so. It would take too long to recount all the evils I suffered on the journey and in the city, having become in every respect the servant of our servants so that I would not be recognized.

Like another Nicodemus, I came by night to the lord pope in the house of the aforesaid John. There I found him stripped of almost all his temporal goods and heavily burdened by debts owed to others [Col. 0048A]. I stayed with him throughout Lent and, if it is permissible to proclaim the truth, supported his burdens as far as I could on the shoulders of charity.

Fifteen days before Easter, Ferruchius, whom Guibert had made guardian of the Lateran palace, spoke through intermediaries with the lord pope, asking him for money so that he might return the tower and that house to him. The lord pope therefore spoke with the bishops and cardinals who were with him and asked them for money; but because they were themselves oppressed at once by persecution and poverty, he was able to find only a small amount among them [Col. 0048B].

When I saw him not only sad but also weeping from excessive distress, I too began to weep. Weeping, I approached him and told him to make an agreement with Ferruchius without fear. There I spent gold and silver, coins, mules, and horses; and thus we obtained the Lateran and entered the palace.

There I was the first to kiss the lord pope’s foot, in the apostolic see where long before no catholic pope had sat.

## LETTER IX

To the most blessed Pope Paschal, Brother Goffridus, a humble son to his dearest father and a faithful servant to his good lord.

I saw your letter thirty-five days before the council [Note: [Col. 0048D] “Thirty-five days before the council.” The Lateran Council of the year 1112, discussed above in connection with Letter 7. Ivo of Chartres likewise used this excuse in Letter 150 for not going to the council: he received Pope Paschal’s letter summoning him only seven weeks—or, more precisely, forty-nine days—before the date fixed for the council.]. In it I heard what I would not have wished to hear, and what I did not deserve to hear by sinning.

For it reached your ears, through the report of I know not whom, that I was a participant with the persecutors of the Church and with the Count of Poitiers [Note: [Col. 0048D] “The Count of Poitiers.” William, mentioned in Letter 2, the last of that name and family, who is known to have been excommunicated repeatedly. The excommunication now at issue, however, is that which Gerard of Angoulême, the legate, and Peter, Bishop of Poitiers, imposed because of unlawful marriages contracted after the dismissal of a lawful wife, as William of Malmesbury recounts in Book V of his History. The monks of Vendôme possessed many rich estates in this prince’s territory, including the churches of Oléron and Surgères in the Saintonge, the church of Oloron, and others in Poitou.]; this, God knows, I never did, nor would I have wished your fatherhood to believe such a thing about me.

For this was sown by the enemy-man, and the spirit of deceit was in him [Col. 0049A]. Our monastery is known to possess in the Count of Poitiers’ land whatever it has that is best and by which we live almost entirely. Therefore I cannot avoid speaking with him from time to time; but I call upon the Holy Spirit as witness to my soul that this is done from necessity for our monastery, not from my own will.

Once, taking advantage of an opportunity, because our predecessor [Note: [Col. 0049B] “Our predecessor.” Shortly afterward: “Our predecessors.” Book V, Letter 21: “The rulers of our monastery who were before me.” There were exactly four abbots of Vendôme before Goffridus: Rainaldus, Odericus, David, and Berno, whom he means here. Count William had taken from Berno the obedience, or priory, of Saint George—which I believe is what is meant here—and Goffridus later restored it to him. Urban II wrote to Goffridus: “The church of Saint George on the island of Oléron, which Count William of Poitiers, compelled by our excommunication, returned free from every customary exaction, just as it had been delivered in your place by Count Geoffrey of Anjou and Countess Agnes.” The matter is discussed again in Book V, Letters 19 and 20. On the meaning of the term “obedience,” see Book IV, Letter 7.] could not or would not come to him, he took away from us a certain obedience, which I afterward had to redeem for twenty-five thousand solidi.

Yet in this matter, if I communicated with an excommunicated person, or shall communicate with him while he remains excommunicated, I must abstain from him; may God never grant me remission of that sin [Col. 0049B].

If anything else, bitter or otherwise, has been reported to you about me, believe firmly that it was deceitfully and spitefully invented. Therefore, if it is just, let a suitable time be appointed, and let those who shoot at me in secret be identified, so that I may know against whom I ought canonically to prepare myself, and perhaps say something about them, and so that we may be judged without mercy.

Attend to the truth, sweetest Father, not to the report of words. Certain people envy me, with a devilish envy. Because of their false slanders, I am compelled to proclaim openly the truth which I would have been quite willing to keep silent.

No one among the envious, then, will truly say that in all France there is a monastery better ordered than ours. In our time, by God’s grace, its devotion has grown more than the devotion of its founders had previously bestowed upon it; although I have never acquired a church, never a tithe belonging to another church, nor any ecclesiastical possession in the manner in which certain people do.

In the time of our predecessors, the Roman Church could scarcely receive from there even the due census—namely twelve solidi [Note: [Col. 0049C] “Namely twelve solidi.” He repeats the same amount in Letter 13 to Calixtus. The founders imposed this census on the Abbot of Vendôme as the allodary of the apostolic see. The foundation charter says: “The abbot, who is recognized as the allodary of blessed Peter, should endeavor each year to visit his mother, the Roman Church, either personally or through a legate; and if he does not show greater charity, he should at least not neglect to pay a census of twelve solidi for the provision of lamps before the venerable body of blessed Peter there.” Clement II, in the charter of confirmation: “For perpetual remembrance and recognition, we wish twelve solidi of your native coin to be paid annually to blessed Peter.” Formerly the Cluniacs paid ten solidi every fifth year in the name of protection. In the charter of Agapetus II: “Indeed, as recognition that the aforesaid monastery belongs to the apostolic see for protection and support, ten Vizeliac solidi are to be given every five years, and one pound of silver annually.” Paschal II to Abbot Altardus of Vézelay: “As an indication also of this liberty, let it pay each year to the apostolic see, whose jurisdiction it is recognized to be, one pound of silver”; and so with the other censuses.]. What I say is not boastfully but in thanksgiving: our poverty has spent more than twelve thousand solidi in the service of the Roman Church [Col. 0050B].

Within thirty-five days, most reverend lord, I could not prepare myself and come to you, being also burdened by bodily illness. I shall prepare our journey as soon as I can; and, if God grants me life and health, I shall see you at once as my dearest father, serve you diligently, and receive from you in mercy the church of Saint Prisca [Note: [Col. 0049D] “The church of blessed Prisca.” Alexander II was the first to grant the church of Saint Prisca, the title of a cardinal priest on the Aventine, to the abbots of Vendôme, together with cardinal dignity, as a privilege of dignity both illustrious and unusual. These are Alexander’s words in a letter to Abbot Odericus in the year 1062: “We also grant to all the abbots of this place the church of blessed Prisca with cardinal dignity, decreeing by the judgment of the Holy Spirit that from now on no ecclesiastical or secular person should presume for any reason to take away from them the aforesaid church of blessed Prisca or its dignity.” Gregory VII confirmed this benefit to Odericus in the year 1029. Later, when the Guibertine faction was dominant in the city, this church was taken from the monks of Vendôme because they opposed that faction, and was transferred to others [Col. 0050B]. Although Urban II returned its investiture to our Goffridus, as stated in Letter 16, it is nevertheless clear that they were again deprived of its possession, since Goffridus now claims it from Paschal and in Letter 13 testifies that Calixtus promised it to him. Eventually restored completely by Calixtus, he began to use the title of cardinal of Saint Prisca. Thus, writing to Calixtus himself, he calls himself so in Short Work 3. The charter of Calixtus, by which he restored Goffridus’s rights, will be presented in full at Letter 28 of Book II. Following his example ten years later was Honorius II, whose privilege, written at Rome on 9 Kalends of April in the year 1129, also survives. Yet this possession was neither sufficiently long-lasting nor entirely undisturbed for the monks of Vendôme. For whether they neglected the church’s repairs or some other cause was responsible, it was again taken from them and assigned by the pontiffs to other cardinals whom they created with the title of Saint Prisca. Finally, Innocent III restored the interrupted possession to Abbot Hamelin, the eighth after Goffridus, but with this exception: he and his successors, the abbots, were to retain forever their former cardinal dignity and its insignia together with the church of Saint Prisca. If, however, other cardinals of that title were ever created, those who administered the church of Saint Prisca for Vendôme were to obey them and pay them a fourth part of the revenues.

It will not be irrelevant to hear Innocent’s words, although they extend somewhat further. They are as follows: “Although our predecessors judged that the church of Saint Prisca, situated on the Aventine, with all its appurtenances and also with cardinal dignity, should be granted to your predecessors, as we have seen contained in their privileges, nevertheless, because after some time that church fell into ruin and desolation through their negligence and neglect, certain of our predecessors assigned it at various times to various cardinals whom they promoted to the title of that same church [Col. 0051C]. But wishing to show regard for your honor, by the customary benevolence of the apostolic see we grant that you and your successors shall nevertheless possess the dignity which your predecessors acquired by the grant of that church. By apostolic authority we perpetually confirm to you the use of sandals, tunic and dalmatic, mitre, and ring, as cardinal priests use them; and we restore the church of blessed Prisca itself to the monastery of Vendôme by special favor. This limitation is added: if we or our successors should happen to promote cardinal priests to its title, chiefly so that they may perform the customary office upon blessed Peter’s altar, as the holy Fathers wisely determined, then those to whom you have entrusted the care and administration of that church for the time being shall render due humble and devoted obedience to those cardinals [Col. 0051D]. Those cardinals, moreover, shall receive a fourth part of the revenues of that church; but you are to exercise diligent care over the church itself, lest through your negligence it again fall into ruin. For he deserves to lose a privilege who abuses the power entrusted to him.” Thus far Innocent.

As a result, thereafter there were two kinds of cardinals of Saint Prisca: ordinary cardinals, whom the pontiffs designated, and perpetual, as it were natural, cardinals outside the ordinary order—the abbots of Vendôme. The former possessed the office and function, the latter the title and dignity. Today they retain neither the church of Saint Prisca nor the dignity, although they still retained both at the time of the Council of Constance. [Col. 0052D] Such are the vicissitudes of affairs.], or, if you prefer, justice from the church [Col. 0051A].

It would be entirely worthy and just, if it seemed right to your discernment, that what was given to us by the authority of your holy predecessors—namely Alexander II and Gregory VII—and confirmed under their anathema, but was afterward taken away by the heretic Guibert because of our fidelity to the Roman Church, should be restored to us by the Roman Church, which is not accustomed to return evil for good.

For this is a repayment which God did not teach, nor did blessed Peter recognize. As for Guibert, I have taken excellent vengeance on him: after Pope Urban of blessed memory, and the foremost son of the holy Roman Church, Peter Leonis [Note: [Col. 0052D] “Peter Leonis.” In this age Peter Leonis was easily first among all Romans in wealth and power, the chief pillar and ornament of the Roman Church, not only under Urban but afterward under Paschal as well. As Dodechin and others write, he was the mediator and author of the peace with Henry; and likewise under Calixtus, as stated in Book V, Letter 3. He is the man whose tomb remains in the atrium of the basilica of Saint Paul on the Ostian Way, with an epitaph whose acrostic gives the name Peter Leonis.], Guibert took the Lateran palace away from him.

May the lord pope prosper and flourish; and may anyone who hates or deceives him be convicted, lest he perish.

## 24. LETTER X

To his dearest lord, the universal Pope Calixtus, Brother Goffridus, all that he is, all that he can do, and all that he understands and possesses.

First of all, your humble servant gives manifold thanks and expresses gratitude to your kindly fatherhood for all your benefits, dearest Father. Your affection commanded me, your servant, to wait within or near our abbey until I should see your messenger, prepared to come to you, because your holy and sincere intention was planning to make me dearer than dear and more familiar than familiar.

Dearest lord, I have obeyed your command: I waited, and I still await what was promised. If it has been prolonged through forgetfulness or some necessity [Col. 0051C], nevertheless I cannot be deprived of it on any pretext.

For there are especially three things which in no way permit me to despair of the promises of your free goodness: nobility of birth [Note: [Col. 0052D] “Nobility of birth.” For the father of Archbishop Guido of Vienne, who was called Calixtus II in his pontifical dignity, was Count William of Burgundy, a man distinguished by kinship derived from imperial and royal greatness, as I shall say with Suger in the Life of King Louis.], the truth-friendly character of apostolic dignity, and the bond of ancient affection.

Let my good lord therefore command me to come to him, as he promised and wrote that he would do for his servant, unworthy though I am. If he himself orders it, I am ready to come to him whenever and however he orders [Col. 0052A].

My humility has written these things to its most heartfelt lord; and if anything has been written insufficiently, when I am present I shall not remain silent. May our most kindly lord always prosper and flourish; and may every enemy of his either be converted or perish.

## LETTER XI

To his sweetest father and dearest lord, the universal Pope Calixtus, Brother Goffridus, a son to his father and a servant to his lord.

I shall speak to my lord, although I am not altogether a useful servant, but nevertheless a faithful one. I shall speak to my father, whom I have loved with all my heart, all my soul, and all my strength; and the proof of my love was once demonstrated in deed. I shall say nothing other than what Sacred Scripture has taught me to say.

In the case of Noah, the pious and just patriarch, neither Japheth, the lover of his father, deserved to forfeit his father’s blessing, nor Ham, the detractor of his father, deserved to receive it—especially that Ham who not only exposed his father’s nakedness, but also invented and publicized things that were not shameful in his father. Hence I have no doubt whatever—indeed, I confidently believe—that neither the judgment of justice, nor the laws of nature, nor the bond of ancient affection, nor the truth friendly to apostolic dignity, will allow me to be deprived any longer of the fatherly blessing promised to me.

For the merciful Father knows what he promised me, unworthy son though I am, and what he later conveyed to me in letters expressing apostolic truth. Let the good Father therefore act, lest the face of the son who has always loved the Father be put to shame by the Father’s unfulfilled promise; lest the man who has always hated both of them with wicked hatred boast that, through the insult inflicted upon the Father, he has obtained the Father’s favor, and rejoice at the son’s rejection.

Let the most merciful Father and lord call to mind, and keep fixed in his memory, how much I loved him before I knew him; how devotedly I served him before I had seen his beloved face. I am that man—I am that man—who honorably received, for love of him, the monk Armannus whom he had sent to Lord Pope Urban; and who, before the lord pope, who loved me as an only son, diligently pleaded his causes and completed his entire business as best I could. My conscience bears witness to this.

May my Father always prosper and flourish; and may every enemy of his either be converted or perish.

To his sweetest father and most beloved universal lord, Pope Callistus: Brother Goffridus offers what a son owes a father and a servant owes his lord.

## Letter XII

To the most beloved Father and lord, the universal Pope Callistus, his brother Goffridus offers whatever he is, whatever he can do, whatever he understands and possesses.

My sweetest Father, your affection commanded me to come to you, because your holy and sincere intention had resolved to make me, from dear to dearer and from familiar to more familiar, namely, to honor our person and to confer benefit upon our Church.

*Note: “Because from dear to dearer.” Above, in Letter 10, these are Callistus’s words in his letter to Goffridus, which we prefixed at the head of the work among the encomia.* Certainly, with God’s help, I shall come to my lord, ready to serve him and ready to receive from him what he promised me by word and in writing; nor shall I be ungrateful.

Meanwhile I humbly ask the merciful Father and lord to send to the bishop of Chartres a decree of his authority confirming the excommunication which that bishop himself, compelled by letters from the Apostolic See, pronounced against Nivelon and Archembald.

*Note: “To the bishop of Chartres.” Geoffrey, Ivo’s successor. Hence it is clear that the pontiff’s letters concerning the excommunication of Nivelon were sent to Geoffrey, similar to those which the monks of Vendôme preserve as having been written by Paschal to Ivo on the same matter.* They have inflicted very great losses and manifold injuries upon the monastery of Vendôme, the allod of blessed Peter and his patrimony, and they have not yet ceased to do so.

Let apostolic sincerity also strictly forbid the aforesaid bishop to presume to demand anything from us contrary to the privileges of the Roman Church. I have been told that Hugh, provost of the Church of Chartres, has come to you and that, as is said, he associates with the sacrilegious and excommunicated Nivelon and attempts to support him in the seizure of our possessions.

If your humble servant has ever deserved anything from your exaltedness, let that pious affection of your love toward me be felt by him; and do not accept his report, but await our truth instead, since, with the Holy Spirit going before me, you shall have me present shortly. If our humility has said anything insufficiently, the tongue of the bearer of these letters will supply it.

Let my Father recognize that these letters are indeed mine by this sign: I served the monk Armannus well at Rome for love of him.

*Note: “The monk Armannus.” Callistus, then archbishop of Vienne, had sent him to Pope Urban; see Letter XI.*

And when he was stripped by thieves during the night near Tours, I did not offer my Father merely half a garment, like Saint Martin, but a gray fur cloak and various furs—my Father, whom I have always loved and continue to love with excessive affection.

*Note: “When he was stripped by thieves during the night.” John VIII complains of a similar incident, when his horses were stolen by night at Chalon; Letter 97.*

May my lord and Father prosper and flourish; and may every enemy of his either be converted or perish.

## Letter XIII

To the sweetest Father and universal lord, Pope Callistus: Brother Goffridus offers what a son owes his father and a servant his lord.

The cleric whom I sent to you, dearest Father, returned to me eight days before Pentecost. On behalf of your goodness he announced to me that I should come to Rome with the count of Vendôme, who is going to Jerusalem, in order to receive the church of Saint Prisca.

*Note: “The count of Vendôme.” Unless I am mistaken, Goffridus Grisatunica, to whom Ivo writes in Letter 129. Two counts of Vendôme, both named Goffridus, undertook the expedition to Jerusalem with Abbot Goffridus. The first, Goffridus, son of Goffridus of Preuilly, was killed in that expedition at Ascalon in 1101, as William of Tyre, Book X, chapter 20, and Malmesbury, Book IV of *The Deeds of the Kings of England*, relate. The other is this Goffridus, surnamed Grisatunica, whose maternal lineage Ivo describes in the same letter. Having survived the sacred pilgrimage, he later died at the town of Saint-Gilles, leaving his son John as heir; Goffridus discusses him elsewhere.*

*Note: “The church of Saint Prisca.” This was discussed in the note to Letter 9, but we omitted to mention Abbot Odericus what we learned from another charter of Alexander II: that the monastery of Saint Prisca was then under the right and authority of the monks of Saint Paul, and that Hildebrand, archdeacon, administrator, and rector of the monastery of Saint Paul, obtained it on the condition that eleven, or at least eight, monks should be perpetually maintained there by the abbot of Vendôme from the revenue which Hildebrand, with the approval of the community of Saint Paul, assigned. Thus the monks of Vendôme thereafter served this church. Urban II wrote to our Goffridus: “The church of Saint Prisca, in which we ourselves saw the brothers of your monastery living religiously.” Among these was blessed Arnulfus, whom Alexander II later made bishop of Gap.*

Therefore I render to your most sweet fatherhood as many thanks and expressions of gratitude as I can. The presentation of present benefits is a kind of assurance of future ones. Accordingly, with God’s help, I shall come with that count, as you commanded, and sooner if I can; and I shall not keep silent about how many labors and fears, and how many dispersals of our property, I suffered last year in his presence, longing to see my most beloved Father and lord.

I trust—indeed, I confidently believe—that the humble servant and faithful son will yet greatly rejoice in his good lord, through whose kindness even his enemies obtain what they desire. I would certainly have come now, but I could not find a safe traveling party, and I feared the deadly heat of Italy. Christ indeed commands us to bear the cross, not to seek the grave.

And because I recognized that the church of Saint Prisca was insufficiently prepared, I thought it fitting to send this brother ahead to you, sweetest Father, so that he might prepare a place where we could live with some degree of propriety.

Attend to the truth, best Father, not to reports of words. Many envy us, but not with the envy of God; yet none of our rivals will truthfully say that, from sea to sea, there is a monastery better ordered than ours—one that in our time, by God’s grace, has grown more than the devotion of its founders had previously bestowed upon it.

Yet I have never acquired a church or any ecclesiastical possession by any device, nor accepted one from the hand of a layman. Would that others avoided this by following our example. In the time of our predecessors, the Roman Church could scarcely obtain from it even the census owed to her—namely, twelve solidi annually.
