I say this not from vainglory, but in thanksgiving: for the service of the Roman Church, not because of any need of ours but solely out of love, our poverty has spent before you and in your time more than twelve thousand solidi, worth one hundred marks of silver. From this, then, I desire that good be repaid to me for good—the repayment which Christ taught blessed Peter, and which blessed Peter, after him, teaches and commands us to maintain.

## Letter XIV

To his most beloved lord, the universal Pope Honorius: Brother Goffridus offers what a son owes his father and a servant his lord.

With very great longing I desired to come to you, best Father, and I had resolved to remain in the Roman Church not merely for an hour but for a stay. But bodily illness did not change my desire; it denied me its fulfillment.

I contracted this illness through excessive labor and repeated journeys to Rome—and I say this not from vainglory, but in thanksgiving—through service to the Roman Church, for which I was taken captive three times and crossed the Alps three or four times.

Moreover, in its service and because of its greatest need, during the time of Guitbertus, I expended my body and nearly everything I possessed. I am that man—I am that man—who, at Rome, fed on the bread of tribulation and drank the water of distress, and who endured many labors and fears for a long time with Pope Urban, of honorable memory, in the house of John Frangipane [reading uncertain].

What I did there for the fidelity of the Roman Church, and how I sowed all our resources, down to our last mount, for the acquisition of the Lateran palace, God and blessed Peter know, and the Romans of that time know as well.

At that same time I was ordained priest at Rome and received investiture in the church of Saint Prisca from the hand of Lord Pope Urban. Our predecessors had possessed it long before, but because they refused to obey Guitbertus, they had been expelled from it.

Although our age and infirmity now desire rest rather than labor, my spirit drawing me toward you, merciful Father, I shall undertake to come as soon as I can, though my mind itself greatly fears a foreign burial.

Meanwhile I send to my dearest Father the bearer of these presents, carrying some signs of our affection; his tongue will supply what the letter has said insufficiently.

*Note: “The bearer of these presents.” Paganus; see Letter 27.*

May the lord pope always prosper and flourish, and make us rejoice in his prosperity and affection.

## Letter XV

To the good lord and merciful Father, the universal Pope Honorius: the entire community of Vendôme offers what sons owe their father and servants their lord.

Following the Savior’s counsel, we knock at the door of your mercy; and, imitating the example of that Gospel woman, we humbly cry out after you, complaining of the injuries and vexations inflicted by the bishop of Angers.

*Note: “The bishop of Angers.” Ulgerus, against whom he complains of the same vexations in Book III, Letter 12. I infer that the archbishop of Tours was Hildebertus, and the bishop of Le Mans was Guido, Hildebertus’s successor in that see. The legate was Girardus; see Letter 19.*

Holy Father, you commanded him, out of reverence for blessed Peter and for you, to protect our monastery—which belongs especially and uniquely to the Roman Church—and to safeguard its property, permitting it to be disturbed by no injuries or annoyances. He received your letters, which had been sent to the archbishop of Tours and the bishop of Le Mans, as well as to himself, in the presence of your legate, the bishop of Angoulême; but he did not deign either to read them then or afterward return them to us, and thus we could not later show them to those to whom you had sent them.

Furthermore, he did not restrain the injuries of others, but intensified and continues to intensify them on his own part; and those whom he could, he encouraged by word and example to become plunderers of the world.

Our monastery, an allod of the Roman Church, for whose love and fear bishops and archbishops once rendered it honor and reverence, this lord has stripped of what it had held for a long time, without judgment or hearing, and he persists in his intention to strip it further.

Therefore we are not witnesses against Susanna; rather, we speak of the lord bishop with genuine charity, which teaches us not to speak falsely either of friend or enemy, and teaches us to profess the truth concerning both.

Since we have made a monastic profession, it is not fitting for us to revive a Philippic against a bishop.

*Note: “To revive a Philippic.” He speaks similarly in Book IV, Letter 12; Hildebertus likewise in Letter 33. You may expect an invective, and pale with apprehension you suspect that a Philippic is being revived.*

We do not say that he persecutes us with the tempest of his mind or crushes us by the weight of his greatness. Yet we do not know by what kind of holiness he does this, since we do not read of it as commanded in the Old Testament, nor promised in the New, and it is unquestionably contrary to the rules of the canons.

Our humility served the aforesaid bishop diligently in his need; but, with due reverence for him, we say that he has repaid us evil for good—the kind of repayment that God does not recognize.

Therefore, most merciful Father and lord, we implore you with all our heart to have us reinvested in what he stripped from us without judgment. If thereafter he wishes to bring a case against us, who belong especially to you, appoint between him and us a judge who will not be suspect to us, since we cannot come to you.

Certain people envy us with an evil envy, especially because we have been placed under the protection and defense of the Apostolic See. Our lord abbot, desiring to come to you, traveled as far as Vézelay, but remained there for several days, detained by a serious illness.

May the merciful Father and good lord prosper, be pleased with himself, and arrange that in his time we may enjoy the same peace that we had in the time of his predecessors.

## Letter XVI

To Peter, cardinal deacon of the holy Roman Church, most beloved lord and intimate friend: Brother Goffridus, the least of the servants of that Church, offers what he has, what he can do, and himself.

*Note: “Peter, cardinal deacon.” Of Saints Cosmas and Damian. I believe this was Peter Leo, the cardinal to whom Treatise 2 on the ordination of bishops is addressed. Created cardinal deacon by Paschal, he followed Gelasius into Gaul; this letter appears to have been sent to him when he fell ill there.*

We have heard of your illness, and with the affection of compassion and the innermost feelings of our whole soul we regard it as our own. We therefore ask—and in asking, humbly admonish your discerning affection—that if you need us or anything belonging to us, you do not hesitate in any way to let us know.

A friend ought not to be ashamed before a friend, except when he has offended him. Although there may sometimes be bodily dissimilarity between them, there must always be one image of their souls. Moreover, an amity is naked—indeed, no amity at all—if mutual services, especially in time of need, do not prove it.

Farewell, and write back whatever you wish.

## Letter XVII

To Richard, bishop of blessed life and venerable legate of the Apostolic See: Goffridus, the least of the servants of that See, offers affection and the service of affection.

From the report of the brother whom we sent to you with letters from the lord pope, we have learned that Radulfus, the so-called archbishop of Tours, complained about us in dishonorable words in your presence.

If this is so, we are greatly astonished, since we do not know on what grounds he could justly complain about us. Yet we neither can nor ought to be surprised if a man speaks dishonorably when, though nearly the whole world cries out and no one has yet exacted punishment, he commits many dishonorable and perverse acts.

Nevertheless, if it pleases your holiness, let him come with you to Vendôme, to the allod of blessed Peter, and let him bring with him the townsmen whom he hires for money; then let him carry out and receive whatever justice dictates.

## Letter XVIII

To Conon, bishop of praiseworthy life and legate of the holy Apostolic See: Brother Goffridus, allodial holder and servant of that See, offers affection and the complete service of affection.

*Note: “Conon the legate.” This bishop too was a cardinal, but of Palestrina; he was Paschal’s legate in 1115. In that year, as an old chronicle of Tours taught us together with Robert, monk of Saint Marianus, Conon’s legation held three councils in Gaul: the first at Reims, the second at Beauvais, and the third at Châlons. Several letters of Ivo to Conon the legate also survive.*

What liberty, immunity, or dignity the monastery of Vendôme—the allod and patrimony of blessed Peter—has possessed until now, and, with God’s protection, will possess to the end of the age, the holy authority of the most blessed apostles Peter and Paul, granted to that place through their venerable successors, will teach you better; and, as we believe, it will give you greater occasion to love us.

No one can fail to love us unless he does not love their irretractable authority. For this reason we send you transcribed certain privileges of our Church: we do not wish your goodness to remain unaware of the special—indeed, singular—dignity with which the holy Catholic Roman Church joined our place to herself from the very beginning of its foundation.

For whatever she has exalted and loved, we believe that you entirely love, and we have no doubt that you wish to honor it. Pope Urban, of excellent memory, and the present Pope Paschal, saw these and many other privileges in our Church, where they remained for eleven days through the grace of their affection; they read them with their own mouths and confirmed them by a decree of their authority.

*Note: “Eight pontiffs.” Benedict IX, Clement II, Victor II, Nicholas II, Alexander II, Gregory VII, Urban II, and Paschal II. We have seen letters from all of them concerning this prerogative of the monastery of Vendôme, except Benedict’s. Yet this concession is also mentioned in the letters of the founders, by whose direction and will this honor was granted by the Apostolic See to the abbot of Vendôme: that he should be subject to the pope alone.*

Thus, by the authority and confirmation of eight holy Catholic Roman pontiffs, our monastery flourished and remained at peace, and no person whatever except the pope alone was permitted to exercise any power or lordship over it, or to trouble its rulers on any pretext.

*Note: “No person whatever.” Neither bishops nor legates. Gregory VII wrote to Abbot Odericus: “Relying also upon this divine confidence, we prohibit by apostolic authority that anyone ever be permitted in the monastery of Vendôme, except the pope alone, to exercise any power or domination, or to excommunicate or impose an interdict.” See below, Book II, Letters 10 and 27.*

And this was entirely just, because from its very beginning it obtained this inviolable dignity from the Apostolic See through its venerable and religious founders.

With this great dignity granted by the successors of blessed Peter, our predecessors, none of them ever attended any council that had not been celebrated by the supreme Roman pontiff himself.

At those times, however, Hildebrand, archdeacon of the Roman Church and later pope, Girardus, bishop of Ostia, Stephen, Raimbaldus, and many other men of great authority, sent from the side of blessed Peter on legation, came into these regions. They loved our monastery, its liberty, and its dignity, and preserved them altogether undefiled.

*Note: “Hildebrand, archdeacon.” This was Gregory VII’s name and office before he was elected pope. He himself recalls the legation which he undertook in Gaul, sent by Victor II, in a conversation he held with Reginald, envoy of Archbishop Radulfus, as an old history in the archive of Saint Martin of Tours relates: “I remember,” he says, “that once, in the time of Pope Victor, I stayed at Tours during the days of Bartholomew, archbishop of that city, to examine the case of our brother B. I was honorably received by the clerics of Saint Martin whenever I wished, and I frequently shared in their communions.” During that legation he held two synods: one at Lyon against the Simoniacs, and another at Tours against Berengar.*

*Note: “Girardus, bishop of Ostia.” First legate of Alexander II and afterward of Gregory VII, who also testifies that he was at Tours in the conversation mentioned above, and records a synod convened by him in Gascony; Book I, Letter 16.*

*Note: “Stephen.” If the chronology is considered, he ought to be placed before Girardus. He first served as legate under Pope Nicholas II. Gregory VII says in the conversation: “Moreover, Stephen was sent to those same regions in the days of Nicholas II, pontiff of the Roman See, to exercise the apostolic office, a man of the greatest authority. He neither demanded a procession from the canons nor thought that one ought to be demanded—although, had he been so insolent, it could have been refused, since such a procession is never made except for the kings of France and for the apostles by the canons themselves. While he was there, they treated him honorably and bestowed upon him the greatest demonstrations of affection.” Gregory likewise, in Book VII, Letter 18, when he mentions both legates, names Stephen before Girardus. Stephen’s legation continued under Alexander II. He was the man who struck Count Goffridus the Bearded with anathema around the year 1068. Therefore, in my opinion, Girardus succeeded him.*

*Note: “Raimbaldus.” A subdeacon of the Roman Church and Girardus’s colleague in the legation; Gregory VII, Book I, Letter 6.*

We desired, and still desire, to come to you, whom we believe to be a most beloved lord and friend, and to serve you honorably. Our desire would indeed be fulfilled if bodily necessity and the perversity of certain men allowed it.

For there are certain enemies of our Church on the road, whose injuries we have already experienced even to the capture of our own bodies, because we do not wish to leave to them the possessions of blessed Peter entrusted to us. Even now they threaten us not merely with captivity but with death, taunting us with the death of the abbot of Vézelay, whom they say was beheaded without vengeance.

*Note: “The abbot of Vézelay.” See Letter 15. He went to Vézelay, a town of the Aedui in the diocese of Autun, where there was the noble monastery of Saint Mary Magdalene—“noble,” as Bernard calls it in Letter 150—founded by Count Gerard and his wife Berta in the time of Charles the Bald. Peter, abbot of Cluny, also discusses it in Book IV, Letter 28: “In our regions Vézelay, except for Cluny, permits no priory in the observances of our order to have a superior.” He said “of his order” because the monastery of Vézelay, although older, long stood under Cluniac discipline; it now has secular canons instead of monks. Letters of Paschal II survive, a passage from which we saw in Letter 9, written at Benevento in 1103 to Altardus, abbot of Vézelay—perhaps this very man, whose unpunished slaughter Goffridus relates.*

Therefore we humbly beseech your discernment either to obtain an escort for us or to indicate a safe place where we may meet you and disclose to your affection certain matters for the benefit of the lord pope.

## Letter XIX

To his most beloved lord and intimate friend Girardus, honorable bishop of Angoulême and vicar of the holy Roman See: Goffridus, allodial holder and servant of that See, offers affection and the service of affection.

*Note: “Girardus of Angoulême.” There were two bishops of Angoulême by this name within a short interval. The first attended the dedication of the church of Vendôme in 1040; but he undertook no legation whose memory survives. This is the fourth after him by lineage, a Norman who exercised almost continuous functions of the Apostolic See in Aquitaine, first under Paschal and the legitimate pontiffs after him, and afterward under the antipope Anacletus. According to Bernard, because he could not obtain a legation from Innocent, he defected to Anacletus through an ugly act of treachery. Two letters of Anacletus granting him the legation are found in the ecclesiastical annals; the miserable end of his life is described in the *Life of Saint Bernard*.*

We have taken care to make known to your holiness the pressures suffered by our monastery, the allod of blessed Peter and his patrimony; and we presume humbly to ask you to make them your own through the feeling of compassion.

This is indeed a great presumption, but it arises from your great goodness. Know, therefore, dearest Father, that Peter of Montaigu violently broke into one of our cemeteries and almost entirely destroyed two of our villages, carrying away all their goods.

Maurice Rotunardus, moreover, unjustly possesses one church and the land belonging to our church, which he took from us. Although he has often been admonished about this by the bishop of Le Mans and the bishop of Angers, he always scorns to return what he took.

*Note: “By the bishop of Le Mans and the bishop of Angers.” Hildebertus and Rainaldus.*

Therefore, seeking from the bosom of our mother, the holy Roman Church, the breast of justice with filial affection, we earnestly and humbly beseech your goodness to send the bishops mentioned above a decree of your authority, commanding them not to permit the monastery of Vendôme, the patrimony of blessed Peter, to be harassed or stripped of its possessions by their parishioners.

And because the venerable Roman pontiffs, by the irretractable authority of their privileges, have bound all our persecutors with the chains of excommunication—since they themselves cannot loose what those pontiffs have bound—let them hold Peter and Maurice, who have acted wickedly against us, excommunicated until, in accordance with canon law, they restore what they unjustly took from us.

## Letter XX

To Girardus the Norman, bishop of Angoulême and legate of the holy Roman See: Brother Goffridus, the Catholic servant of that See, offers not to sow discord, nor quickly to believe one who speaks lies.

I am astonished that you, a pontiff of such discernment, publicly uttered against me, although absent, things that ought never to have entered your heart, which should have been a treasury of truth and a seal of purity.

Those words, I think, were not first spoken by you; but wherever they originated, I do not doubt that they were devised enviously and maliciously. Just as it is true that true misery will follow the false blessedness of the Normans, so it is true that the things said against me were false.

*Note: “The false blessedness of the Normans.” I do not think this was said as though the Normans had some peculiar taste for false blessedness, but because Girardus was a Norman, he applied to the Normans what he often states in general terms: that true misery follows false blessedness; see Letter 30, Book II, Letter 3, and Book V, Letter 14.*

I am not so disturbed in mind, nor so ignorant of the holy Scriptures, that without cause I would have opened my mouth against one who owes his innocence to heaven alone—namely, against a spiritual father whom I ought to embrace in the arms of filial affection and venerate with pure truth, and from whose holy obedience I shall not be able to separate myself even in death.

If anyone thinks otherwise of me, he is foolish; nor does he strive to honor the lord pope, but to make public whatever he has done too little or too much. For whoever, against the purity of my mind, makes himself an advocate of disparaging the Father, let him come openly, and he will immediately find me a truthful corrector of his falsehood.

## Letter XXI

To Girardus, glorious bishop of Angoulême and legate of the Apostolic See: Brother Goffridus, abbot of Vendôme and faithful son of that See, offers the fruit of good works and the embrace of pure affection.

Since the holy Roman Church has exalted your humility—not indeed for your merits, but by grace alone—to such a degree that your little finger seems thicker than your Father’s back, as the lofty words you so often utter with great glory testify, you ought to obey her all the more faithfully: multiply friends with gentle speech, appease enemies, and proclaim her by deeds rather than words, lest her friends be scandalized by any wrongful action and her enemies be able to disparage her.

If you act, or have acted, otherwise, your exaltedness—whom our venerable lord pope, by his goodness, raised sufficiently high from a lowly station—repays him evil for good, namely, the repayment that God does not recognize.

*Note: “Our lord pope.” Paschal, who created him legate.*

We cannot and ought not conceal from you what we have heard, especially since, what is worse, the populace has composed a song about it, because it has become public knowledge.

We have heard, and we grieve, that Andrew of Vitré sold you his daughter in marriage, and that the son of the viscount of Maloleone purchased that marriage from you. The former gave you five hundred solidi as the price of the marriage; the latter, fifteen marks of silver.

The bishop of Poitiers, his archdeacon William, and certain others who were present will not deny this if they are unwilling to bury the truth.

*Note: “The bishop of Poitiers.” Peter, whose successor was William—perhaps the same William who was archdeacon here. The records of Saint Albinus show William, archdeacon of the Church of Poitiers, granting the monks of Mairon permission to establish an altar at Francavilla in the year 1100.*

You also purchased, for a thousand barbarian solidi, the abbot of Carrof—not regularly elected, but violently intruded, as is said.

*Note: “The abbot of Carrof.” At the dedication of Vendôme he is listed among the abbots who were present as Hugh of Saint-Sauveur, abbot of Carrof. This is the title of a monastery in the district of Poitou, founded in the time of Emperor Louis the Pious by Count Rotharius and his wife Euphrasia, as Theodulfus of Orléans states. It is called the monastery of Carrof in Fulbert’s Letter 117; and the calendar of Saint-Sergius of Angers shows that it was later restored and dedicated, in these words: “On the sixteenth day before the Kalends of July, the monastery of Carrof, of God and our Lord the Savior of the world, was dedicated in the year 1048 from his birth of the glorious Virgin.” If anyone happens to desire Theodulfus’s verses on the monastery of Carrof, they are these:

“Here is a place which the Gauls call by the name Carroph,

where the courtly gate of heaven lies open to the elect.

Here beneath the Savior’s name a church shines forth,

and the fair cloisters of the monastery stand.

Here, strong in the radiant pledge of saints, it gleams,

and there lives an eminent company of the faithful.

Finally Count Rotharius, mighty and illustrious hero,

with his wife Euphrasia, founded this work.

He adorns it with bright silver, gems, and gold,

and it abounds in books, vestments, and sacred things, etc.”

Carrof, therefore, is the name of a place, not of a man—as seems, surprisingly, to have persuaded writers of no mean age, who called it the monastery of Saint Carrof.*

*Note: “A thousand barbarian solidi.” Arab or Saracen coins, marked with barbarian signs. The same bishop Theodulfus writes in his *Paraenesis*:

“Here too he promises crystal and eastern gems,

if I should make another man possess the fields.

This man brings coins in heavy number, rich gold,

which the speech or writing of the Arabs engraves,

or which the Latin stylus impresses upon white silver, …”*
If, nevertheless, he acquires estates, fields, and houses. The use of coins of this kind, made of gold, was already widespread in Gaul at that time, when another royal dynasty of our kings held power—namely, after the establishment of the Saracen Arab empire in Spain. Hence, as I believe, that abundance of foreign gold flowed to us through commerce. Arab solidi are still being excavated in many parts of Gaul, as the distinguished Paulus Petavius, senator of the Paris court, taught us; to his information I also owe these verses of Theodulf.] You have caused [him] to be consecrated—or rather, if the truth be told, accursed—by an authority altogether too barbarous, against the will of his consecrator, while his clergy protested by every means available to them. A certain neighboring abbot of yours, who both witnessed the matter and took part in it, gave testimony, and many say that his testimony is true.

Furthermore, another abbot—whom I blush to name out of respect for the order—was caught in detestable bodily immorality and deposed from his abbatial authority, having himself confessed his crime. Without any prior judicial proceeding, and with no small sum of money assisting the matter, you restored him to his former rank, despite the opposition of the brothers of his congregation, in such a way that the mere collection of marks served as his purification from guilt. Abbot Bernerius of Bonneval [Note: [Col. 0063D] Bernerius, abbot of Bonneval. Several letters in Book IV are addressed to him.] attests to this; he condemns the crime, proclaiming it almost everywhere.

Abbot Fulco of Beania [Note: [Col. 0063D] Fulco, abbot of Beania. The monastery is in the diocese of Saintes; it is commonly called Saint-Étienne de Beania.] sought your letters so that justice might be done to him; your prudence refused them to him for so long that he finally bought them for one hundred solidi. But that man lost his money and could not obtain justice through you. He himself declares this, complaining that he lost both things at once.

What you did against the count of Anjou [Note: [Col. 0063D] The count of Anjou. Fulco V, concerning whom see Letter 8. He was at war with Henry, king of the English and duke of the Normans, in 1118, at the fortress of Alençon and at Sées; when the armies met, the count departed victorious.] should therefore have been suppressed in silence; but it could by no means be concealed, since it was publicized among many peoples. Some assert that you, like another Balaam, were corrupted by the money of the English king [Col. 0063B] and therefore pronounced an unjust sentence of excommunication against the aforesaid count. And although your excommunication could not retain its force even for a single day, it nevertheless brought shame upon the friends of the Roman Church and gave its enemies material for slander.

The sole remedy was that the lord pope wisely avoided confirming that excommunication, thereby silencing the mouths of the slanderers and erasing from the Apostolic See the disgrace that had been sown by you.

Among other matters, I ought to have kept one silent, if friendship did not permit a friend to warn his friend in advance. You reportedly promised the abbot of Angers [Note: [Col. 0063D] The abbot of Angers. Henry, to whom he writes in Book V.] that, if he gave you three hundred solidi of Poitevin males [Note: [Col. 0063D] Poitevin solidi males. In the Acts of Ademar, bishop of Angoulême: “When the bishop demanded one thousand Poitevin solidi from the provost as a composition, and he was unable to pay it, Iterius gave the bishop one thousand.” Poitevin males were coins of a particular type, like the strong Lyonnais coins mentioned in the testament of Guichard of Beaujeu, whose wife Sibyl declared in her charter of the year 1200 that she had bequeathed to the Church of Cluny, for her anniversary, ten pounds of strong Lyonnais coins annually.] you would depose Rainald Chesneili [Col. 0063C] [Note: [Col. 0064D] Rainald Obesnelli. Book III, Letter 39.]. Accordingly, you sent him transcripts of the charges by which he was to accuse that man. The abbot himself admits this and calls upon God as witness to his soul that he is speaking the truth.

We have brought these few matters, out of many, and these lesser matters, out of great ones, to your attention [42] out of affection—namely, so that, if the things circulated against your astuteness are true, the transgression of the past may become for you a safeguard for the future. For whoever uses the privilege of the Roman Church ought not to attack its sacred authority by perverse actions.

And since the Lord Christ conferred upon blessed Peter alone the power of binding what was to be bound and loosing what was to be loosed (Matthew 16:19), you ought not to usurp anything more, or anything different, on account of the legation entrusted to you. We thought it a new kind of presumption when, even in my presence and before laymen, you proclaimed that you possessed the power to depose bishops [Col. 0063D], because no apostolic legate is granted, on any grounds, what belongs to the dignity of the Roman pontiff alone.

But if matters are indeed as you are publicly reported to have proclaimed, you have made yourself another pope, and the voice of appeal to the Roman Church—until now freely available to anyone in his necessity—is denied. We, however, believed that your modest office consisted in holding a legation of the Apostolic See, not in being the Apostolic See; that you had received from the lord pope a share in the solicitude undertaken by other legates alone, not that you were exercising the fullness of power.

### 43 EPISTLE XXII

To the most beloved lord and intimate friend, Lord Girard, bishop of praiseworthy life and legate of the holy Roman See, Brother Goffridus, the least of the servants of that same See, sends eternal salvation from God, who is himself salvation, and from himself whatever is wise and powerful.

[Col. 0064B] First, I offer manifold thanks to your affection, which has remained toward me whole and inviolate. Next, I considered it appropriate to inform your fatherhood that, before the lord pope [Note: [Col. 0064D] The lord pope, Callistus II; see Letters 12 and 13.], on the very day when our legate reached him, through his good favor and the ill favor of my rivals, I obtained everything I wished.

I desire to enjoy your presence and have conversation with you. Deign to inform me, either verbally or by letter, where and when I may obtain what I ardently desire. This is necessary for the Church of God and useful to you.

### EPISTLE XXIII

To Lord Girard, bishop of honorable life and venerable legate of the holy Roman Church, Brother Goffridus, servant of your religious devotion, sends affection and the service of complete affection.

We have heard, most beloved lord, that the abbot of Saint Nicholas [Note: [Col. 0064D] The abbot of Saint Nicholas. Lambert, concerning whom see Book III, Letters 8 and 9.] abandoned his abbey into your hands, on the condition that he would not thereafter reclaim it except through your mercy, and also on the condition that that convent of Saint Nicholas should maintain firm peace and concord with him. The agreement concerning peace and concord that those monks made before you and through you lasted scarcely eight days, as he himself says and as we believe.

Therefore, most discerning Father, we earnestly and humbly beg you on his behalf that, in recovering the abbey which he abandoned on the advice of your will, the sweetness of your mercy may, for the love of God and of us, support him, and that he may obtain due justice against those monks who have neither kept nor are keeping the peace and concord promised to him. If you do this, know truly that you will in no way be able to accuse me of ingratitude.

He will not knock again at the door of the mercy of Angers [Note: [Col. 0065C] Of Angers. Of Bishop Rainald, concerning whose election, which he touches upon indirectly, see more in Book III, Letter 11.], because by experience he has already learned that mercy is lacking there. Whatever, however, was done concerning his promotion was accomplished not by the judgment of justice but solely by immense mercy. Farewell, and make your mercy known to us.

### EPISTLE XXIV

To Lord Girard, venerable bishop of Angoulême and praiseworthy legate of the holy Roman See, Brother Goffridus sends salvation from God and, from himself, the service of pure affection.

Let your affection know, dearest Father, that once and again we sent word concerning our brother, the bishop of Poitiers [Note: [Col. 0065C] The bishop of Poitiers. William, successor of Peter.], begging him to deign to escort us as far as you [Col. 0065B]. [45] He kindly received our request and promised that, on the Assumption of Blessed Mary, he would come in person to Fontevraud [Note: [Col. 0065C] To Fontevraud. See Letter 26 and Book IV, Letter 32.] and carefully carry out what we had asked.

We came, as he had directed, to the aforesaid place; but, finding neither him nor his messenger there, we withdrew from the place exhausted and in vain. We therefore beg, with all the humility we can offer, that it not be burdensome for you to receive the petition of a faithful servant and true friend, and to obtain from the aforesaid bishop a means by which we may travel to you. For we have resolved to do certain things on the advice of your holiness, which we do not wish to reveal either in writing or through another’s mouth.

### EPISTLE XXV

To Lord Girard, bishop of praiseworthy life and legate of the holy [Col. 0065C] See, Brother Goffridus, allodial holder and servant of that same See, sends from God the fruit of good works and from himself the service of pure affection.

You informed me through a brother whom I had sent to you for another matter—of which I was entirely unaware—[Col. 0066A] that, at the council which he is to celebrate in the middle of Lent, I should execute justice against the abbot of Batiacus [Note: [Col. 0065C] The abbot of Batiacus. In the region of Saintes. The Acts of Grimoard, bishop of Angoulême, state: “In his time, one of the nobles of Angoulême, Guadardus of Lorichis, built in the region of Saintes the monastery of Batiacus in honor of Saint Stephen the Protomartyr and made it tributary to the Roman Church. They now call it Bassac and de Bassac.”] concerning the church of Blessed Mary [Note: [Col. 0065D] Concerning the church of Blessed Mary. There were three churches on the island of Oléron belonging to Vendôme, which Gregory VII lists in these words to Oderic, abbot: “The church of Saint George on the island of Oléron, with a large part of that island; the church of Blessed Mary of the Castle of Oléron; the church of Saint Nicholas of Oléron.” Of these, the second was parish church, as Nicholas II testifies.], and the church of Blessed Nicholas, which our monastery is known to have possessed on Oléron for seventy years without canonical opposition.

I therefore inform you that at the appointed time I shall answer the aforesaid abbot according to what the holy Roman authority teaches and commands, unless I am prevented by a canonical impediment. In the meantime, if that lord abbot wishes, I offer him every form of justice, wherever I may be able to go under a safe-conduct.

But if neither of these alternatives pleases him, I desire and offer him the judgment of the lord pope, whose own property both the monastery of Vendôme and the things belonging to it are known to be. Whoever refuses to hear the equity of that judgment must fear lest he experience blessed Peter’s anger.

You should know that our monastery is the patrimony of blessed Peter and his allod [Note: [Col. 0065D] The patrimony and allod of blessed Peter. He often joins these two terms, and in reality they are connected. For what is an allod passes to the heir and becomes patrimony, which is not the case with fiefs or other benefices. Although nowadays in many places fiefs are hereditary, they do not possess this from the nature of the fief—which was customarily constituted in the person of the vassal—but from a particular pact and agreement. An allod, however, is always hereditary [Col. 0066C] property. Hence it is called patrimony and inheritance, insofar as it proceeds from another; it is the proper right and property possessed from the Lord. Thus these expressions are often connected: “in one’s own allod,” “from one’s own allod,” and others of that kind. Urban II, to Hugh, abbot of Cluny: “The monastery of the Most Holy Trinity at Marcigny, which you built on your own allod.” Our Letter II: “as his own patrimony and allod.”] and do not doubt in the least that the aforesaid churches have been secured in our name, by perpetual right and by the irrevocable authority of the Roman pontiffs.

As for what the abbot of Batiacus said—that I had obtained your letters on his behalf—know that he did not speak the word of truth. Rather, believe what I instructed you by letter concerning the servant who was supposed to bring your letters to us.

### EPISTLE XXVI

To Girard, bishop of praiseworthy life and legate of the holy Roman See, his lord and intimate friend, Brother Goffridus sends whatever may be requested and whatever may be salutary.

[Col. 0066C] Before your goodness, honorable Father, we complain with grief of heart and excessive anxiety of mind about Peter of Montcontour [Note: [Col. 0066C] Peter of Montcontour. Yet Robert, from the same family, had once adorned the monastery of Vendôme with his benefactions. Gregory VII: “The church of Saint Peter of Mont-Solet and whatever Robert of Montcontour gave to the monastery of Vendôme, and his son Bertrand granted.” Montcontour is a town of Poitou, made famous in our own time by a memorable battle.], who, within the bounds of your legation [Note: [Col. 0066D]

Within the bounds of your legation. Girard was not legate throughout all Gaul, but only in Aquitaine, as the Acts of the Lateran Synod of 1112 show. Nevertheless, to the legates of Aquitaine there was customarily assigned, in addition to the Aquitanian provinces, the third province of Lyon. Thus, in the case of Girard, many matters were handled that belonged to the diocese of the third Lyonnais province, as in Letters 6 and 23: the cases of the abbots of Saint-Aubin and Saint Nicholas before Hildebert, Letter 28, and the case of the abbot of Évron, the latter in the diocese of Le Mans and the former in that of Angers.

This is also clear from the letters of Amatus, bishop of Oléron, who was likewise legate in Aquitaine under Gregory VII, as Gregory himself bears witness in Book II, Letter 11. Writing to Ralph [Col. 0067C], archbishop of Tours, he orders him to come with his suffragans to the synod of Bordeaux, in these words. It is worth hearing his letter:

“Amatus, bishop of Oléron and, by the grace of God, legate of the holy Roman Church, sends greetings and every good thing in the Lord Jesus Christ to Ralph, venerable archbishop of Tours.

[Col. 0067D] ‘Let your charity know, dearest brother, that by the authority of Almighty God and with the consent of all the bishops, abbots, and princes belonging to our legation, we have decreed that a council shall be held at Bordeaux on the octave of Saint Michael. Therefore, with fraternal affection we admonish you by entreaty and command you by apostolic authority that, postponing all delay, you come to the aforesaid council with all your suffragans and with the privileges of your church, so that by your counsel and support the cause of God may be strengthened and, with God’s assent, the justice of your church—on account of which great and various disputes have hitherto arisen—may be restored. If God permits, on our return from Brittany we shall speak with you, so that, by the gift of Almighty God, we may salutarily arrange whatever ought to be settled concerning these and your other affairs.’”

From this, then, it is clear that the Aquitanian legation also encompassed the whole territory of the third Lyonnais province. [Col. 0068C] This is confirmed by what Abbot Bernard of Bonneval writes about this same Girard in Book XI of the Life of Saint Bernard, chapter 6: “He was ashamed to return to the first house, whose authority had been obeyed by the provinces of Tours, Bordeaux, and Auch, and by everything that stretches from the hills of the Iberians to the Loire and is enclosed by the Ocean.”]

—that is, in the bishopric of Poitiers—captured our brothers as they were returning from the monastery and violently took from them their horses and everything they possessed. We recovered part of their property through the count of Anjou [Note: [Col. 0068C] Through the count of Anjou. Fulco again; see the following letter.]; but that sacrilegious man still cruelly detains the rest. We are even more tormented by the injury inflicted upon the persons of the monks, and we humbly ask that your discernment avenge it in such a way that the robbers who hear of it may be afraid and withdraw their hands from such a crime.

We ardently desire to come to you, as we once informed you, but because of the numerous wars that have arisen in the bishopric of Poitiers, we dare neither come to you nor visit the places we possess in those regions. Moreover, we have learned through a true report that the female sex [Note: [Col. 0068D] The female sex. Ivo, Letter 28: “That sex is suspect and hostile to me, and at times is not sufficiently faithful even to friends.”], which we know to be hostile even to its friends, is hostile to us and lies in wait for us on the road.

Therefore we earnestly beg your affection to have us escorted to you by the bishop of Poitiers [Note: [Col. 0068D] The bishop of Poitiers. William.], or by anyone else, because we cannot safely proceed beyond Fontevraud. May the lord legate prosper and flourish, and, by the grace of his charity, enable us to travel to him and speak with him.

### EPISTLE XXVII

To the good lord and intimate friend, G., bishop of venerable life and legate of the Apostolic See, Brother Goffridus, his servant, sends whatever he can, whatever he knows, and whatever he is.

I inform your affection that I am sending Brother Paganus of Aleric to the lord pope [Note: [Col. 0068D] To the lord pope. Honorius II, as Letter 14 shows.], bearing to him certain tokens of our affection. If through him I can accomplish what I desire, I shall not go to Rome for the present; otherwise I am ready to go to Rome and visit the Roman Church in person, in which I was ordained priest by Pope Urban of blessed memory.

I offer manifold thanks and gratitude to your discernment, which once, twice, three times, indeed four times, commanded the bishop of Angers [Note: [Col. 0068D] The bishop of Angers. Ulger; see Letter 15 and Book CXI, Letter 12, where Urban’s decree is also discussed.] to restore what he had taken from our monastery and to obey the privileges of the Apostolic See. He not only despised both commands; he also complained about me to his priests in his synod because I had raised a complaint against him before your dignity.

He is attempting to annul the decree that the same lord Pope Urban established at the Council of Clermont against simony, which bishops once practiced under the name of vicars. The redemption of churches—which at that great council was called heretical depravity and condemned by the Apostolic See—although it had been exacted through vicars only once every several years, he now attempts to extort from our simplicity under the name of an annual census.

And because I and our brothers consider this a crime, we reject it; for that reason he has prohibited divine worship in our churches. The principal instigator and author of this crime is his archdeacon Richard [Note: [Col. 0068D] Richard, the archdeacon. Letter 31.]. And since neither of them ceases their persecutions, we cannot cease our outcries.

We therefore cry out to you: from you, who exercise the authority of the Apostolic See and who ought especially to defend blessed Peter’s allod, we ask counsel and help. And if you do not wish to act because we are your friends, then at least, because of our importunity, do what we ask.

We do not believe that you are unaware of what the count of Anjou wrote, asking your goodness to grant us justice. Farewell, and gladden us, your humble servants, by your constancy and the integrity of your justice.

### EPISTLE XXVIII

To Hugh, truly religious archbishop [Note: [Col. 0068D] Archbishop Hugh. He became archbishop of Lyon after serving as bishop of Die, and under Gregory VII he exercised a legation in Gaul in both offices. Later, as is clear from Ivo’s Letter 24 and others, he also did so under Urban II, whom Goffridus means here. The Angevin bishop Geoffrey of La Meuvane was elevated to that see in 1097. We have seen the letters of Hugh the legate in which he restored Fulco IV, count of Anjou, to communion with the Church at Saint-Florent, among Goffridus’s eulogies.] and vicar of the holy Roman See, his dearest lord and intimate friend, Goffridus, unworthy abbot of the monastery of Vendôme, sends reverence with affection.

I have heard that you sent your holiness letters from the lord pope, in which, as I have been told, it is said that I accused the bishop of Angers before him. If the lord pope says this, I can neither refute nor ought I to refute it; but, with due reverence to him, I say that I do not acknowledge myself to have been in any way an accuser of the aforesaid bishop, nor did I go to Rome in order to accuse him.

Other matters which I handled there make this more fully clear: with the lord pope adjuring me, and constrained by his adjuration, I could not conceal certain things about the bishop. Just as I was not permitted to keep these silent in the presence of the lord pope, so, if it pleases you, I shall not conceal them from you when the proper time comes.

### 50 EPISTLE XXIX

To the most beloved lord and intimate friend, Lord Um., archbishop of honorable life [Note: [Col. 0069C] Archbishop Umbaldo. He too was archbishop of Lyon, successor to John after Gauceran and fourth after Hugh; he was legate of Honorius II, as Letter 22 of Saint Bernard, written to Pope Honorius, shows. “To Umbaldo, archbishop of Lyon and legate of the Roman See.”], and legate of the Apostolic See, Brother Goffridus, allodial holder and servant of that same See, sends whatever he possesses, whatever he knows, and himself.

You sent, as I have heard, a monk to our monastery who, had he found me there, would have invited me to your council. I desire to come to you and to serve both you and your Church, which has greatly honored and served me. I shall carefully visit you at Orléans before the council, or after the council if the weakness of my body permits, on whatever day pleases you.

But I can neither come nor ought to come when summoned to the council of legates—which I say with due reverence to you. For let your affection know that the privileges of the Roman pontiffs—Victor, Nicholas, Alexander, Gregory, Urban, Paschal, and Callistus [Note: [Col. 0069D] Victor, Nicholas, and the others. The archive of Vendôme exhibits the privileges of all these men. Before them all there is also a diploma of Clement II concerning the same matter, providing that the abbot of Vendôme should not be compelled to attend any council that had not been celebrated by the Roman pontiff himself. Therefore it was unlawful for the legates to summon him. Alexander II to Oderic: “We also add that the abbot of Vendôme, who is known to be an allodial holder of blessed Peter, is in no way to be summoned to a council by a bishop or by any vicar of our See.” The other pontiffs later approved this by repeated enactments.]—have been confirmed under anathema and have forbidden that the abbot of Vendôme, the allodial holder of blessed Peter, be summoned to a council by a bishop or by any legate of the Apostolic [Col. 0069C] See, or compelled to come in any way. Farewell.

### 51 EPISTLE XXX

To Ralph, praiseworthy archbishop of Tours [Note: [Col. 0069D] Ralph, archbishop of Tours. Two men named Ralph succeeded one another in that see. The first was the son of Fulcred, to whom many letters of Gregory VII survive. The second, a native of Orléans, entered office under Urban II in 1094. It is to him that Goffridus writes here, as does Ivo of Chartres in Letter 235 [Col. 0070C]. Our author also writes about him in Book V, Letter 11.], Goffridus, humble servant of the monastery of Vendôme, sends love for what God loves and hatred for what he hates.

We have often complained to you about Arduino of Malliaco [Note: [Col. 0070C] Arduino of Malliaco. I do not know whether he was the brother of Jaquelin of Malliaco, whom the Acts of the Counts of Anjou report as having taken part, together with four brothers, in Fulco V’s expedition against King Henry, mentioned above [Col. 0070D]. Malliaco is a town in the region of Tours, toward Anjou.]. Because of the many wrongs that he had unjustly and violently inflicted upon our monastery, we understood that you had excommunicated him justly and reasonably. But we hear that he was absolved while impenitent, without prior satisfaction.

If it is believed that he could be absolved in this way, it is unclear what harm sin does and what benefit penance brings. For if true misery is denied to the impenitent, then surely false blessedness is promised to those who repent of their sins.

As we have said, that wicked man was accustomed to harass our monastery with much injury. You therefore admonished him to correct what he had done unjustly against us, and, because of you, he promised that he would do worse things to us; he fulfilled that promise with false truth, to your injury. For where did he preserve truth, when he harmed his neighbor and lost faith?

Therefore, venerable Father, we humbly beg that the wickedness of this perverse man be struck by the sword drawn from the sheath of your equity, so that he may restore what he unjustly took from us [Col. 0070B] and be compelled, even against his will, to acknowledge that in injuring you he has wounded even the pupil of the Savior’s eye.

If you act in this way, you will receive a worthy reward from God and the recompense due from us. [52] But if, out of fear or friendship, you spare an enemy of the Church of God, we cannot refrain from having recourse to the Apostolic See, where, necessity compelling us, it will not be possible for us to remain silent about the tribulations and hardships we endure in your bishopric with your consent.

### EPISTLE XXXI

To the most beloved lord and intimate friend, Lord R., archbishop of honorable life at Reims [Note: [Col. 0070D] R., archbishop of Reims. Rainald, formerly bishop of Angers, was transferred to Reims with the support of King Louis VI. Ulger was appointed in his place. The Brief Chronicle of Saint-Aubin states: “In the year 1124: The army from Montreuil. Rainald is elected archbishop of Reims. Pope Callistus died. In the year 1125: Bishop Ulger is ordained on the twelfth day before the Kalends of October.” The pope in this letter is therefore Honorius II, Callistus’s successor. The bishop of Angers is Ulger, and his archdeacon is Richard, mentioned in Letter 27. A few years earlier another Rainald of the same name had been archbishop of Reims, from the treasury of Saint-Martin; he was later the son of the countess of Greece. Ivo’s Letter 13 is addressed to him, and Anselm mentions him in the preface to his book On the Incarnation.], Brother Goffridus sends whatever he can, whatever he knows, and himself.

Good Father, I hunger and thirst to see you, and I desire to visit the lord pope with you. I humbly beg your beloved fatherhood that, if you are to travel as far as Rome by Easter, you deign to notify your servant of the day and place on which our humility may join your company.

Moreover, I and our congregation with me earnestly and diligently beg your kindness to deign either to admonish or to ask the bishop of Angers and his archdeacon R. not to attempt to disturb the grant of the churches that you kindly made to our monastery. If they despise the prayer or admonition of your holiness, they will indeed cause us hardship, but they will trouble their own peace; and the power and omnipotence of the blessed Trinity will nullify their efforts. Farewell, and write back whatever pleases you.

### BOOK II

### EPISTLE III

To Ivo, the bishop greatly worthy of honor, Goffridus, servant of the monastery of Vendôme, such as he is, sends the service owed by pure affection.

Concerning the brother [Note: [Col. 0072D] “Concerning the brother.” Named Daniel. For Ivo calls him this in Letter 82, to which Geoffrey here replies.], for whom you asked us, we certainly wish to act mercifully; but because we do not believe that an unregulated remission is mercy, we judge it useful—or rather necessary—for him to come to his monastery, be moved to repentance before the brethren, and thus deserve to obtain pardon for his transgression. Let him who once, at the devil’s prompting, did not dislike acting negligently now at last not dislike obeying according to the Rule. For your love, we would therefore pardon him whatever he has done wrong without requiring satisfaction; but we neither dare nor ought to promise a man true unhappiness and false blessedness. Let him therefore come to the monastery, as we have already said, and humbly confess that he has erred, so that [Col. 0073A] through true humility he may obtain pardon for his error, and may thereafter be able without difficulty to obtain whatever your holiness may wish to be done concerning him.

EPISTOLA IV.

To Ivo, bishop of revered life, Geoffrey, humble abbot of the monastery of Vendôme, the duty owed by a devoted son to a good father.

Since we have learned that everything must be done with counsel, it was good to consult your holiness about what we should do concerning the dignity of the order [Note: [Col. 0073C] “Concerning the dignity of the order.” In the earliest centuries monks were outside the clergy. Therefore, in canonical penalties they were punished not by deposition, as clerics were, but by excommunication together with laypeople. The Council of Chalcedon, canon 2: “And if he should be a cleric, let him be expelled from his own rank; but if a layman or a monk, let him be anathematized” (καὶ οὗτος εἰ μὲν κληρικὸς εἴη τοῦ οἰκείου ἐκπιπτέτω βαθμοῦ, εἰ δὲ λαϊκὸς ἢ μονάζων, ἀναθεματιζέσθω). Later they began to be initiated into the sacred orders. He therefore asks about clerical monks who, after apostasy, return to their monasteries: how are they to be received? Are they to remain in the dignity and rank of their former order, or rather are they to fall from it and be recalled to the condition of laypeople? Although the law of ecclesiastical censure was once severe toward clerics of every order in this matter, it was nevertheless sometimes applied more mildly, and an indulgence was granted according to the nature of the crime and the penance, as can be seen in what Gratian collected in Distinction 50. Ivo’s letter in reply to Geoffrey’s consultation about monks has perished.], concerning the brothers when they return. As for clerics, we speak of those who have both cast off the religious habit and, remaining for a long time in apostasy, mingled with illicit contaminations. We have heard and at the same time seen what the canons say about this; but because our Rule says little or nothing about such matters, we are uncertain what we ought to do concerning them according to the Rule.

EPISTOLA V.

To his lord and venerable father Ivo, bishop of true religion, Geoffrey, called abbot of the monastery of Vendôme, the duty owed by a son subject to his beloved father and by a faithful servant to his pious lord.

How purely and without any taint of malice the blessing of your charity made me abbot, though unworthy; and how diligently, and with complete truthfulness, your piety’s favor afterward often extended to me a helping hand in my necessities—I consider attentively. I would have judged myself an ungrateful and most useless servant if, whenever your will or the necessity of mutual charity required its service, I had not obeyed. Now also, since neither your will requires it nor necessity compels it, I freely offer myself for any service.

It has indeed been reported to me that you have now received a mandate from our lord the pope [Note: [Col. 0073D] “Our lord the pope.” Paschal II. It is unclear whether Ivo employed Geoffrey’s services. He says in Letter 147 that he once sent Bernard, abbot of Bonneval, as his legate to Paschal: “Therefore I have sent to you in my place Lord Bernard, abbot of the monastery of Bonneval, a man of good reputation,” and so forth.], by which you are to visit Rome, either in person or through your legate, by Christmas. If this is true, it displeases me not at all, since I desire to serve you. Indeed, I could wish that what your will has long denied me, necessity would at least now command. I do not say this because your greatness needs the help of my smallness, but because the affection I have for you, arising from the root of pure love, compels me to speak thus. Behold, I submit myself to your disposition, together with all my devotion; and if you order me to go to Rome on your behalf, something I have long desired, I do not refuse to obey. You may perhaps find someone better; but far be it that anyone should be found who would carry out your command more willingly! Before God, to whom it is impious to lie, my conscience bears witness that in this business of yours you will find no servant more faithful or more willing than I. Farewell, and, if it pleases you, write back to me concerning what you wish to be done.

58 EPISTOLA VI.

To his most beloved father Ivo, bishop of true religion, Geoffrey, unworthy minister of the monastery of Vendôme, with reverence joined to affection.

Since I find it written in the decrees of the Roman pontiffs that household members and relatives [Note: [Col. 0074C] “Household members and relatives.” This refers to what is found in Ivo, *Decree*, Part XVI, chapter 361: that kinship or relationship should in no way testify against outsiders. On this basis Ivo likewise makes the witnesses of the archbishop of Tours suspect before Paschal in Letter 108, since they were blood relatives and had been brought from his household. Alexander III also, in the chapter *On Witnesses*, rejects the witnesses of a certain nobleman of Fermo, whom he produced from his household in a divorce case. From this example, then, it is clear what Geoffrey is uncertain about: domestic witnesses are not to be admitted not only in capital cases but in other cases as well. Yet it is clear that they were sometimes admitted by privileges. For from a charter of King Philip the Fair we learn that, when a dispute had arisen between the abbot and convent of Saint-Denis and certain women of Lagny concerning their status, and witnesses brought against them were rejected because they belonged to the body of the Church of Saint-Denis, while the monks maintained that they possessed a royal privilege from Louis VI for this matter, the court, after the privilege had been read, declared that the witnesses were suitable in that case and that their testimony appeared valid. In the year 1287, in the month of June.], or those coming from one’s household, are not to be admitted as witnesses, we do not fully see whether this should be understood in all ecclesiastical cases—for nothing is excepted there—or only in criminal cases. We therefore humbly beg you, whom divine grace has specially set before the world as a light of knowledge, to teach us in writing, by the authority of your judgment, so that we may better understand what we grasp less fully from that source.

Although it would be useful, indeed necessary, for our smallness to ask your greatness many questions, we ask this one especially because the dean of a certain church in Angers is involved. He is violently attacking one of his fellow canons, saying that the man granted him his prebend, and that he has no testimony except from those who are his household members and come from his household. If what we promised you is delayed, do not be troubled, because its being delayed will not diminish it.

59 EPISTOLA VII.

To Ivo, bishop of praiseworthy life, his lord and also his friend, Geoffrey, servant of the monastery of Vendôme, sends affection and the service of affection.

I heard the letter you sent to the clerics and laypeople of Vendôme [Note: [Col. 0075C] “Your letter.” This letter of Ivo still exists.]; I would scarcely have believed it to be yours had I not seen your seal affixed to it. For the letter said that your faithful had reported to you that I had publicly uttered shameful and insulting words against you and your clerics.

In reply, subject to the truth, I categorically state that I have never said anything dishonorable or insulting about your person; rather, whatever good I could, I have proclaimed about you everywhere up to this very day. As for your clerics, since they sang badly to me, I neither can nor could dance well for them. I openly confess this much: I offered them no insulting words, except insofar as, feeling myself oppressed by their judgment, I appealed to the Roman Church, whose venerable privileges I saw them contemptuously rejecting, although the holy Roman Church had not deserved to receive such treatment from their greatness. For what they had bound wrongly, she released through the consideration of her piety; and if they repaid her evil for good, God certainly did not teach them this kind of recompense.

When they called me a man of bitter speech, I might perhaps have believed them if they had recognized more fully the sweetness of apostolic truth. As long as I see them ungrateful for its benefits, I shall also regard them as suspect in matters of truth. You asserted that I was subject to your Church, and I am in no way offended by this, because, although no person of whatever dignity or order may stand between the Roman pontiff and me, a sinner [Note: [Col. 0075D] “No intermediary person.” In the privilege of Victor II: “Therefore we confirm, and by the authority of the blessed apostles Peter and Paul specially strengthen this monastery, so that no person of whatever dignity or order may be regarded as an intermediary between the pontiff of the first and apostolic see and the abbot of the venerable place of Vendôme.” Nearly the same words occur in the charters of other pontiffs and in the records of the monastery’s foundation.], if the authority of the Roman pontiffs is preserved inviolate, I nevertheless declare myself subject to all the Churches, and indeed their useless servant.

But you called me your professed monk [Note: [Col. 0075D] “You called me your professed monk.” By ancient law all abbots were under the authority of bishops. The First Council of Orléans, canon 11: “For the humility of religion, abbots are to remain under the authority of bishops.” The Council of Chalcedon, canon 4: “It has been decreed that those monks in each city and region are to be subject to the bishop” (ἔδοξεν τοὺς καθ᾽ ἑκάστην πόλιν καὶ χώραν μονάζοντας ὑποτετάχθαι τῷ ἐπισκόπῳ). Therefore, before their consecration, abbots made to bishops a profession of subjection and obedience, in this form—or at least one very similar to it—which Honorius III says was customarily made by the Cistercians in the chapter *Lest the Church of God*, on simony: “I, N., abbot of the Cistercian order, promise that I shall perpetually maintain toward you, my lord bishop, and toward your canonically instituted successors, and toward the holy apostolic see, saving my order, the subjection, reverence, and obedience established by the holy Fathers according to the Rule of Saint Benedict.” Those who had been exempted from the authority of bishops by privileges of the apostolic see, as the monks of Vendôme had been, were not obliged to make that profession. Nevertheless, Bishop Ivo elicited it from Geoffrey, whom he therefore called his subject and professed monk. But, as he will say shortly, Urban disapproved Ivo’s action and annulled the profession extorted from Geoffrey. He repeats this again in Letter 11.]. It would have been much better if you had called me consecrated by you. And if you claimed a profession from me in exchange for consecration, and subjection to you as a freeholder of Saint Peter in exchange for the profession, you certainly did not bestow that consecration gratis. For that by which one man is made subject to another is not bestowed for free.

In that profession I accepted your advice with excessive simplicity. If anything was done otherwise, you did it knowingly, whereas I sinned through ignorance. But when our lord Pope Urban, of honorable memory [Note: [Col. 0076D] “But Pope Urban.” Urban’s privilege on this matter is inserted in Letter 27 of this book, addressed to Ivo’s successor as bishop, Geoffrey.], passed through our region, he heard from the brothers that I had made a profession to you. Calling me a deceived dove without understanding, and sharply rebuking me, he would truly have charged this to me as a crime had he not mercifully spared my ignorance and youth. What he said against you on this matter, respect for your order makes it better to leave unsaid than to speak. He therefore rendered null what I had committed unlawfully, and with the irreversible force of his privilege prohibited the abbot of our monastery from henceforth making a profession to any bishop. Following his authority, the present lord Pope Paschal likewise confirmed the matter again by his apostolic authority.

Furthermore, it was circulated in your letters to the laypeople that, if I did not come to you to make satisfaction, I would no longer have your assistance, and that if any evildoers plundered the property of our monastery, they would find you their helper rather than its defender. I do not believe that this was inserted in the letter on your behalf, since it is wholly contrary to Christian religion and is recognized as an incitement of Satan. Let friends and enemies alike firmly believe this: no one will receive from me such a payment that, in return for his assistance, I should subject our monastery—the freehold of Saint Peter—to him unlawfully.

Therefore, if your assistance is lacking in my necessities, I trust in the goodness of blessed Peter, because he himself will not be lacking to me. Since I desire to preserve faith with him, no bishop ought on that account to deny me assistance, or to usurp for himself, under any pretext, what belongs to him. I have neither given the Church of Vendôme to the holy Roman Church nor will I take it away. If I attempted this under any persuasion, I would sin against my own soul, nor could I accomplish it even through sin. I shall therefore preserve faith at all times with the Roman Church, to which I owe my entire self. For love and fidelity toward her I endure multiplied burdens with steadfast courage and integrity of heart, and if still greater burdens arise, I do not refuse to endure them for her.

I appealed to her in my afflictions, 62 and I still do not cease appealing. For if she now does not know how much I suffer for her, I know that, when she learns it, she will not deny assistance to one who asks; she who, ever overflowing with the bowels of mercy, has been accustomed to aid all the oppressed, and especially her own household.

Lord Ernald [Note: [Col. 0076D] “Lord Ernald.” He subscribes to Ivo’s letter containing the foundation charter of the canons of Saint John of Valiac, which is read among Ivo’s letters as no. 296: “The mark of Ernald, dean.” Apparently he was later made a monk from the clergy; then, abandoning the monastic purpose once more, he returned to his former rank. Ivo attests that he became a monk in Letter 262 to Pontius, abbot of Cluny: “I have sent you the collections of canons through Lord Ernald, now your monk, formerly our cleric.” Geoffrey silently indicates here that he did not persevere.], whom you call your dean, if it had pleased him to act according to justice, ought to have remained, as the little tuft of cloth on his head bears witness [Note: [Col. 0077D] “As the little tuft of cloth on his head bears witness.” A part of the monastic dress that he retained. As Clement V explains in *On the Status of Monks*, chapter 1, the *flocus* is the monks’ garment with long and ample sleeves. *Floculus* and *flocellus* mean a smaller *flocus*. Our people today, with a slight change of letters, call them the large and small *froc*. Those who had become monks from among the canons, if they returned to the canons, thereafter wore a cowl as a reminder, according to Urban II’s decree, Distinction 19, Question 3, *We command*.], in our lot rather than in yours [Note: [Col. 0077D] “Rather in our lot than in yours.” A monk rather than a cleric.]. Farewell, and do not act against the holy Roman Church, whose piety made you a bishop no less than your own religious standing did.

EPISTOLA VIII.

To his most beloved father Ivo, bishop of praiseworthy life, Geoffrey, humble servant of the monastery of Vendôme, sends reverence with the affection of pure love.

Concerning your archpriest Geoffrey Daniel [Note: [Col. 0077D] “Geoffrey Daniel.” Archpriest of Vendôme, whom he mentions again in Letters 9, 12, and 21, where he repeats the same complaints about him.], we sent two of our brothers to complain before your goodness. They, as we believe, conveyed both our outcry to your ears and, if anything had been done amiss by our household, offered you redress. You therefore instructed us that on the fourth day after the feast of All Saints, if you did not meanwhile come down to our region, we were to come to you, prepared both to do and to undergo whatever we ought. This was certainly an excellent command of yours, and therefore it was to be embraced no less with the arms of action than of devotion.

63 But, detained by certain obstacles that had already arisen—so it is said, through the contrivance of your archdeacon [Note: [Col. 0078C] “Your archdeacon.” The archdeacon of Vendôme, whom he also attacks without naming him and calls the glorious archlevite in Letter 17. I think he was called Raimbald. In Ivo’s letter by which he granted the church of Hauch to Marmoutier, dated 1114, the witnesses listed first are Raimbald, archdeacon of Vendôme, and Ansger, archdeacon of Blois. In the Church of Chartres, besides Urban the archdeacon, who is called “the great,” there are five archdeacons: of the Pays, Châteaudun, Pisciacum, Blois, Droue, and Vendôme.], before we sent our men to you—we are quite unable to observe it. Necessity alone prevents us from doing what both reason and will advise and command us to do. But when, with the grace of the Holy Spirit consoling us, we have been freed from the present necessity by which we are detained, we will come to you on whatever day you command and will do everything according to your counsel.

We nevertheless ask, with all the humility of which we are capable, that if you must come to Vendôme, you do not weary us with any persuasion into going to Chartres. Concerning Nivelon and his son Ursion [Note: [Col. 0078D] “Nivelon and his son Ursion.” They are discussed in Book I, Letter 12, and below in Letters 11, 13, 23, and 30. Letters of Paschal II to Ivo are preserved in the archives of Vendôme; in them he orders that both men be excluded from sacred communion because of the injuries and losses inflicted on the monastery of Vendôme.], and their men, we have often knocked at the ears of your piety with our complaints, and we still do not cease knocking, so that, if not out of friendship, at least because of our persistence, we may obtain the justice we seek. Farewell; and I earnestly beg you not to lose our service and affection through the incitement of those who, if they could, would often have incited me against you.

EPISTOLA IX.

[Col. 0078A]

To his lord and friend Ivo, honorable bishop of Chartres, Geoffrey, humble servant of the monastery of Vendôme, sends greetings with affection.

You instructed us that you neither grant nor ought to grant the delay we requested from you; for, as you say, we did not specify a certain day to you. In reply, subject to the truth, we state 64 that we could not possibly specify a certain day, because we did not know when the necessity by which we were detained would end.

You assert that you have excommunicated our servants. We are greatly surprised at this, since in our place no bishop [Note: [Col. 0078D] “No bishop except the Roman.” Book I, Letter 18, and below, Letter 27.], except the supreme Roman pontiff alone, is permitted to excommunicate or impose an interdict, or to exercise any authority or domination. We nevertheless shall diligently do whatever you command, saving the privilege of the apostolic see, against whose authority nothing ought to be demanded from us, nor ought we to obey. We neither can nor ought to diminish the excellence of the dignity that Christ our Lord conferred upon the Roman Church in blessed Peter; nor should anyone strive to diminish it.

Of the men whose names you wrote to us, we say that four of them are ours. Concerning these we shall willingly do what we ought on the fourth day after the Epiphany, although we could make many complaints against you, since you have not only denied us justice concerning our evildoers—a thing no other bishop is known ever to have done—but have also incited them against us by a decree of your authority.

If these things we communicate displease you, and you wish to oppress us by the weight of your greatness, or to burden us through someone else’s incitement or through your own will, we appeal to the Roman Church herself, for whose love we have long endured many burdens from you. With her we wish to endure adversity, and without her we refuse to possess prosperity. Therefore, if your assistance in our necessities, which you have long withheld from us, is lacking, we trust in the goodness of blessed Peter, because he himself will not be lacking to us. Since we wish to preserve faith with him, no bishop ought for that reason to deny us ecclesiastical justice, incite the savagery of secular men against us, or, under this pretext, usurp for himself what belongs properly to the holy Roman Church. From loyalty to her neither hunger, nor sword, nor nakedness, nor tribulation, nor distress, nor any persecution will be able to separate us, living or dead (Romans 8:35).

For if she now does not know how much we suffer for her, we know that, when she learns it, she will not deny assistance to those who ask; she who, ever overflowing with the bowels of mercy, has been accustomed to aid all the oppressed, and especially her own household.

We have often complained and continue to complain to you about your archpriest, and about Nivelon, his son Ursion, Buatmund, and their men. As yet we have been able to perceive neither justice nor even a spark of justice. Hence we see that the peace sworn by you is being observed less than it should be.

EPISTOLA X.

To Ivo, honored bishop of Chartres, Geoffrey, humble servant of the monastery of Vendôme, loving friends in God and enemies for God’s sake.

Although the injuries and vexations with which you have oppressed, and caused to be oppressed, both our monastery and us resound very frequently in the ears of the people, nevertheless, bound by the cords of the charity that God commands, we are compelled to love even one who does not love us. But you, who have inflicted the heavier troubles, we especially wish to love and diligently serve, if you are willing to temper the cups of bitterness that you have often offered us with the honey of love.

Indicate in your letters what kind of love it is by which you wish both to love us and to be served and loved by us, for we ardently desire your peace and affection. And if we perceive that you love us in truth, we refuse no service of yours by which we would not incur the indignation of our lord the pope or endanger our order.

EPISTOLA XI.

To Ivo, bishop of great renown, Geoffrey, humble servant of the monastery of Vendôme, acting prudently and simply in all things.

Our letter [Note: [Col. 0079D] “Our letter.” This is Letter 7 of this book. Ivo’s letter to which Geoffrey here replies, no. 195, begins: “I received your letter, which both caressed and pricked me: in some places it breathed the sweetness of honey, and in others it sprinkled the bitterness of gall.”], which, you said, breathed in some places the sweetness of honey and in others sprinkled the bitterness of gall [Col. 0080A], contained no bitterness at all according to our understanding, because it was full of the sweetness of charity.

You again asserted that the Roman Church had received from God no unjust authority. This is plainly so, and we neither can nor ought to fail to agree, since it is fruitless to struggle against so manifest a truth. For what madman would dare to believe or imagine that the good God ever gave anything unjustly, or that his holy Church received anything unjustly from him?

But if you believe, as you wrote to us, that the Lord conferred upon her the power of loosing what must be loosed and binding what must be bound, it is not surprising if she properly loosed what you wrongly bound.

The profession that you extorted from me [Note: [Col. 0079D] “The profession that you extorted from me.” This was stated in Letter 7 and will be repeated below in Letter 27.] when I was still young and a novice was in no way according to the Rule; to have made it was sinful, and to have accepted it irreligious. For if, in exchange for the blessing that you ought to have bestowed entirely for free, you exacted a profession, and in exchange for the profession subjection from the freeholder of blessed Peter [Note: [Col. 0079D] “From the freeholder of blessed Peter.” Above, Letter 7, *beneficiary*. Just as one who holds a lord’s fief is called his vassal, so one who holds an allod is called his freeholder. Yet these terms do not always correspond. The abbot of Vendôme cannot properly be called the freeholder of blessed Peter, because his monastery is the allod of the apostolic see; nor can he be called a vassal, because he does not hold the monastery by feudal right.], that profession was profane and therefore not to be maintained, since the subsequent blessing that you bestowed appears to have been rather a *navicular* blessing than one given freely [Note: [Col. 0080D] “Rather navicular than freely given.” He uses the same word in the same matter in Opusculum X, *navicularia*. The blessing is called *navicular*—not gratuitous but mercenary, and one for which payment is demanded—just as a shipmaster demands a fare and payment for transport. By a similar metaphor Ildebertus called it a *merchant’s reading* in Letter 1, describing sordid and ungenerous profit-seeking: “Hence it is that you pursue ostentatious furnishings with implacable hatred; that you reject a merchant’s reading; that you judge piety with sufficiency to be a great profit.”], since you are not ashamed to demand temporal payment for it, in violation of the Christian faith.

In that profession I accepted your advice with excessive simplicity. Yet whatever was wrongly done, you did knowingly, whereas I sinned through ignorance. But the apostolic sincerity, compassionate toward my ignorance and youth, mercifully forgave the guilt I incurred through the counsel of your impurity, and by the power of its authority prohibited any of our successors from thereafter falling into a pit of similar deception.
