If you wish to act against this, I do not avoid but appeal to that greater tribunal by which all Christendom is judged. Whoever despises hearing the judgment of its equity must fear that he may find blessed Peter angry.

EPISTOLA XII.

To his most beloved lord and father Ivo, bishop of praiseworthy life, Geoffrey, some sort of servant of the monastery of Vendôme, offers the service of true humility and the affection of pure love.

We have seen your well-formed and beautiful letters [Col. 0081A], which you sent to your archpriest Geoffrey [Note: [Col. 0081C] “Your archpriest Geoffrey.” Letter 8.] in order to secure justice for us, and we return thanks to your holiness—if not as many as we ought, at least as many as we can. For nothing else could be seen or understood in it except the expression of your great charity toward us.

All the priests of the castle of Vendôme saw the letter together with your archpriest, but with him—or rather through him—they refused to obey it, we do not know through what private counsels. Therefore, most beloved Father, we beseech your piety with whatever prayers we can offer, so that concerning what we have written to you truthfully, you may be as attentive with fatherly affection as that murderer of ecclesiastical justice [Col. 0081B], that enemy of the holy Church, may be enabled to recognize how serious it is not to obey just commands.

69 EPISTOLA XIII

To his honorable lord and intimate friend Ivo, bishop of religious life, Geoffrey, humble servant of the monastery of Vendôme, offers the blessedness promised by God to the saints and, from himself, pure and undivided affection.

We received your holy letter with joy and honor, but on the day that you specified in it we shall in no way be able to come to you, detained by the unavoidable necessity of our monastery, which also prevents us from remaining at the monastery at that time under any circumstances.

We cannot persuade our brothers to submit to judgment concerning the monastery’s possessions without our presence; and what is reasonably seen to be contrary to their will, we do not dare command them to do, lest they perhaps be scandalized. But when the necessity that unavoidably detains us has ended, we shall present ourselves diligently before the sight of your goodness, at a suitable place and time, ready to receive and do whatever we ought concerning Nivelon, whom neither respect for his order, nor the honor of the priesthood, nor the Savior’s coming has held back from a new kind of crime.

Meanwhile, most beloved Father, we ask with all the humility of which we are capable that, by your justice compelling them, we may deserve to be restored to the things that Nivelon and his men have violently taken from us and still cruelly retain. For, as you yourself know better, those who have been stripped of their own property [Col. 0082A] [Note: [Col. 0081C] “Stripped of their own property.” Below, Letter 29.] ought not be summoned to judgment until everything that has been taken from them has first been restored to their control. Farewell.

EPISTOLA XIV.

To his most beloved lord Ivo, venerable bishop of Chartres, and to the entire chapter of Saint Mary, Geoffrey, humble servant of the monastery of Vendôme, sends salvation from God and, from himself, the service of pure affection.

We have learned that this is the virtue of true justice: one ought not to help a friend by lying, nor to fail an enemy in the truth.

Concerning the deposition of Lord Geoffrey, formerly abbot of Blois [Note: [Col. 0081D] “Geoffrey, formerly abbot of Blois.” Of the monastery of Saint Laumer. Three letters of Ivo—Letters 164, 208, and 240—are addressed to him, after he had left the abbatial dignity and, from being abbot, had been restored as a hermit to his former solitude.], and concerning the promotion of Lord Maurice, who for a long time exercised unjust hostilities against us and lodged complaints of little profit [Note: [Col. 0081D] “Exercised hostility.” Evidently because of the controversy between the monks of Blois and those of Vendôme concerning the offerings of the parish of Huisse, discussed by Ivo in Letter 162.], we offer the testimony of truth, as we have seen and heard it [Note: [Col. 0081D] “The testimony of truth.” The reason Ivo sought this testimony can be understood from the three letters mentioned above, in which he explains that Geoffrey later regretted leaving the abbacy and therefore habitually disparaged and opposed his successor Maurice.].

We saw Lord Geoffrey, in the presence of Lord Bruno, then legate of the Roman Church [Note: [Col. 0081D] “Bruno, then legate.” Ivo, Letter 164, to Geoffrey of Blois: “You who, in the hands of the legate of the Roman Church, without anyone compelling you—indeed, while the legate himself advised against it—left the abbacy and gave the first voice in the election of that Maurice.” The legation of Bruno of Segni, a bishop in Campania in Italy, fell in the year of Christ 1106. In that year Buatmund the duke came to Gaul, as the *Chronicle of Saint-Aubin* records. Bruno the legate accompanied Buatmund at Paschal’s command. The sources are Peter the Deacon and Abbot Suger, who also mention the synod held by Bruno at Poitiers.], leave his abbacy, personally choose Lord Maurice as abbot, and place the elected man, whom he had led by his own hands to the position he himself had previously held. We saw this, and before God and human beings we publicly testify that it happened in this way.

But if something else was done secretly, we openly confess that we know absolutely nothing about it. For it could have happened that Lord Geoffrey pronounced one thing with his tongue while concealing another in his heart. Yet whatever was done at Blois in our presence concerning this matter, insofar as we were able to learn it, would not, as we believe, have harmed Lord Maurice, if nothing else had stood in the way.

EPISTOLA XV.

To his most beloved lord and friend Ivo, honorable bishop of Chartres, Geoffrey, humble servant of the monastery of Vendôme, condemning the faults of delinquent subjects by the judgment of the Holy Spirit in such a way that he may appear guiltless before the sight of the awe-inspiring Judge.

Most excellent Father, your clerics [Note: [Col. 0082D] “Your clerics.” The canons of Saint Mary of Chartres.], whom the humility of blessed Mary has made proud, have destroyed the steps of our house [Note: [Col. 0082D] “The steps of our house.” Letters of the pontiffs show that five churches were given to the men of Vendôme by Bishop Theodoric. In the privileges of confirmation, Clement II, and likewise Victor and Nicholas II, say: “The five churches that Theodoric, bishop of Chartres, gave to the monastery of Vendôme for the love of God and at the request of Count Geoffrey: namely, the church of Saint Biatus, the church of Saint John of Châteaudun, the church of Baigneaux, the church of Villarebla, and the church of Ancheric.” None of these, however, is close to Chartres. They must therefore be sought elsewhere.] not by the law of heaven or the judgment of the world, but in the customary storm of their minds.

We therefore humbly beseech your paternity to correct what your clerics are known to have done perversely, and to make them restore the steps of our house that they destroyed in the fury of a deranged spirit. And once we have been restored, according to the sacred canons, to possession of the property that we long held justly and that was unjustly taken from us, if they afterward complain about us, we do not refuse whatever a just judge and the divine law determine ought to be done.

Father of venerable life, the property of our monastery that is known to lie within your bishopric, and the monastery itself, offered to blessed Peter by its founders—if it were not burdensome to you—ought to be guarded and defended by you against all adversaries, as far as your capacity permits, both out of episcopal care and for love of blessed Peter, especially that property of the monastery [Col. 0083B] which you see situated almost beside the entrance to your gates.

# LETTER XVI

To my most beloved Father and lord, Ivo, bishop of praiseworthy life, Goffridus, humble servant of the monastery of Vendôme, offers pure affection of heart and the service of pure affection.

Best Father, we give thanks to your fatherhood because you caused the count of Vendôme [Note: The count of Vendôme: Goffridus, Book I, Letter 12.] to be summoned to account on our behalf; and because, although he had acted unjustly, he neglected to correct his conduct, you took away his castle and the banlieue of the castle [Note: The banlieue of the castle. Count Gauffridus, in the foundation charters enumerating what he had offered to the monastery of Vendôme, says: “In the castle of Vendôme, land for making a borough, together with seizure, theft, and arson, the vicaria and banlieue, and all customary dues.” Louis VI, in a privilege for the monastery of Saint-Denis in 1111: “Likewise we decree that whoever is within the banlieue of Saint-Denis, or within the boundaries established of old, is to be robbed by no one, nor are his goods to be plundered; but if he commits an offense outside, he is to be brought to justice only by the abbot or the monks.” *Banlieue* or *bannileuga* is the extent of land within whose boundaries the immunity or jurisdiction of a particular place ends. The word and its meaning are familiar in many parts of Gaul. Among our ancestors, *bannum* had several meanings. They called a public edict a *ban*, as well as a fine, confiscation of property, exile, and other matters connected with the highest judicial authority. The area to which that authority extended they called its circuit or boundary, in their language a *bannileuga*, either because it was defined, more or less, by the distance of a league, or perhaps because the name *leuga* or *leuwa* was used for any extent or tract of land. In a privilege of Charles the Bald for Saint-Denis, the banlieue is described as follows:

“We decree that the aforesaid place shall possess immunity.” And later: “For this immunity we judge that the very same boundaries should be imposed which are specified in the privilege of lord Dagobert, the most serene king, which that glorious king made concerning fugitives for the same monastery; that is, as far as the place where those traveling toward the same church enter the Tricenna bridge, and likewise as far as Montmartre, where that pre-eminent witness of the Lord faithfully completed his struggle, and similarly as far as the public road that leads to Luperus. Therefore we give this entire circuit to God and to his holy Denis, together with all judicial authority. That is, the *ban*, and every breach of it, and any other legal customs that there may be.”

From this description it is sufficiently clear that the banlieue of Saint-Denis extended beyond the space of one league. That they seem to have used *leuva* absolutely for an extent and measure is shown by another privilege of Charles the Great, by which he grants to the same monastery of Saint-Denis the villages of Faverolles and Noront, together with the Aquiline forest. He defines the leagues—that is, the areas and regions—of this forest by the following boundaries. I shall transcribe the whole passage, although it has been insufficiently corrected through the fault of the antiquaries:

“Moreover, together with the forest belonging to them, which is called Aquiline, with the foresters and the other boundaries marked out within it: namely, toward the district of Madrie, the *leuwa* reaches to the False Stone; then to the Priest’s Mountain, then to Condac as far as Cuculosa. The second *leuwa*, toward the district of Pinciacum, reaches to Codonaria, then to Vennes as far as Aureovalle, then to Levieias. The third *leuwa*, toward the Parisian district, reaches from Ulfanciaca to the Lord’s Field, then to the Field of Mulgevertus, then to Sarnecum as far as the cell of Saint Germanus, then by that road which leads to the old monastery. Toward the district of Étampes, the *leuwa* reaches to Rasbacium, then to Affrumenterila, then to Warancera. Toward the district of Chartres, the *leuwa* reaches to Putiola; from there to Putilitta, then to Hitlinvilla; from there to Wadastivilla and that pear orchard, then to the thicket that belonged to Stephanona. From there to Calmons; then to the road that leads to Helmoretum; from there to Longus Lucus and the Valley of Senona above Nivigella.”

Ivo used *leuga* simply in place of *banlieue* in Letters 101 and 259, where he says that this was the distance assigned from all the mills of the Beauvais league.]

you removed the divine office. He threatens to add worse evils to the existing ones; and, disobedient to you, he still violently persecutes us and our possessions. But because we have accepted this charge, that we should not seek human praise or fear their threats, with divine mercy protecting us and the censure of your authority supporting us, he will find us more steadfast in our hardships.

There is, however, one thing useful to us—indeed, very necessary—for which we humbly beg you, as sons beg a father: that the kind of piety by which the pastor of the Church, when necessity requires, must become impious for the Lord—for, as blessed Jerome says [Note: As blessed Jerome says: Letter 23 to Marcella, concerning the illness of Blaesilla.], it is a kind of piety to become impious for the Lord—may cause the zeal of your rectitude to extend against the count and against all his land. Specifically, you should exclude his entire county from the divine offices and bind him with the bonds of stricter justice, so that the whole people, who are not unaware of our injury and his wickedness, and to whom his iniquity is most displeasing, yet would not be displeased by greater justice, might seize this opportunity to cry out against him. Thus, since he does not voluntarily wish to desist from unjust action for the love of God, he would desist unwillingly through both the outcry and the fear of men.

For under how great a burden of his wickedness we groan, our humility would not remain silent if it were not tedious to recount each matter and wearisome to hear it; and perhaps our envoy’s tongue will state everything better than our letter could set it forth. You have permitted the bodies of the poor to be buried [Note: You have permitted the bodies of the poor to be buried. The interdict prohibits ecclesiastical burial. Innocent III excepts clerics, who nevertheless must obey the interdict, *c.* “Quod in te,” *De poenitentia et remissione*. That Ivo granted burial to the poor was an exceptional privilege.], which we can neither refuse nor dare refuse. But, with respect for your peace and reverence, we say that if they remained unburied for the sake of the Church’s justice, their souls would not therefore possess less glory. And because your holiness grants burial to the poor, now no one is excluded from burial under the name of the poor. Farewell.

# LETTER XVII

To my most beloved lord and Father, Ivo, bishop of venerable life, brother Goffridus offers every means of avenging disobedience and thus attaining eternal life.

Let your affection, dearest Father, know that in the castle of Vendôme [Note: In the castle of Vendôme. Vendôme, which is called both a castle and a fortified town by Goffridus, is a town of no obscure importance on the bank of the Loir, in the territory and diocese of Chartres. This is sufficient evidence to weaken the opinion that has spread among many today, namely, that Vendôme is mentioned by the geographer Ptolemy and called *Vindinum*. For Ptolemy places *Vindinum* (*Οὐΐνδινον*) not among the Carnutes but among the Aulerci Cenomani, and makes it their principal city. There can therefore be no doubt that it is none other than Cenomanum itself, the capital of the entire Cenomannian province; its name was adapted according to Gallic usage, even by Goffridus, Book III, Letter 16. The oldest mention of the castle of Vendôme that presently comes to mind occurs in the pact of the kings Guntram and Childebert, inserted in Book IX, chapter 20, of the history of Gregory of Tours.], those so-called regular canons of Saint George [Note: The regular canons of Saint George. They owe their origin to Countess Agnes, the very woman who founded the monastery of Vendôme with her husband Gauffridus. They are not much later, since the foundation charters bear the year 1048. They are no longer regular canons today.], solemnly celebrated a feast in the Church of Saint Peter, with its doors open, contrary to your interdict; and that other clerics of the same castle led a certain deceased townsman to burial in public processions, burying together with the dead man justice itself, as though it too had died. Concerning this burial of ecclesiastical justice, which is recognized as having been carried out in a spirit of defiance, and concerning vengeance for such a burial, our humility would have written something to your eminence if one monk were sufficient to accuse a multitude of clerics of disobedience, and if it did not seem presumptuous to teach a bishop of such discernment.

Let your affection nevertheless consider that, if so great an injury to justice is patiently endured, there is reason to fear that on this occasion the holy Church may lose a great deal of her position and suffer an intolerable loss of her dignity and order. Therefore, with filial affection, we beg your fatherhood to send us a decree of your authority, so that so destructive an act of presumption may by no means pass without punishment, and so that each transgressor may at least recognize how serious it is not to obey his bishop.

Concerning the lord archdeacon [Note: Concerning the lord archdeacon. Raimbaldus. See Letter 7 above.], whose virtues or vices we do not believe are unknown to your prudence, we do not dare write the truth to you, lest our truth generate his hatred toward us and cause one who acts badly to act worse. Certainly, if disordered leniency were piety or mercy, he would display it abundantly toward offenders who remain unrepentant; even when they do not knock, the door of his mercy stands open.

For which of the wealthy wishes to be buried contrary to your interdict and is not buried? Yet burial is denied to the poor, who bear no blame. Churches are opened to the powerful; the powerless, through whom what has been done wrongly cannot be corrected, are excluded from the churches. We know, on the testimony of the holy Gospel, and have no doubt whatever, that our gracious Lord Jesus gave blessed Peter the power to bind what was to be bound and to loose what was to be loosed (Matthew 16:19). But, differently from what the Lord gave, or blessed Peter received from him, your glorious archdeacon, teaching falsehood as though he were a prophet, binds what should be loosed and looses what should be bound.

Therefore take care, most beloved Father, lest your justice—which has already begun to perish in part—perish altogether, and lest what we truthfully entrust to you harm us.

# LETTER XVIII

To the honorable lord and intimate friend, lord Ivo, bishop of Chartres, brother Goffridus, servant of the monastery of Vendôme, offers whatever may be considered most salutary.

Concerning the condition of the lord pope [Note: Concerning the condition of the pope. Paschal II, to whom we saw Goffridus travel in Book I, Letter 4, apparently in the year 1112.], I truthfully announce to you that the lord pope possesses both Rome and the Roman Church with great peace and tranquility. I found the lord pope in Rome, and, among other matters, spoke with him about you. Whatever good I could and ought to say about your person, I did not keep silent before him, regardless of what others might have whispered.

After I had returned from there and had been received with great honor at Lyons by the lord primate of Lyons [Note: The lord primate of Lyons, John, successor to Hugh, whom it is surprising that those who have compiled catalogues of the bishops of Lyons have hitherto omitted. But the name and chronology of John, archbishop of Lyons, are confirmed by Letters 236 and 237 in Ivo, which are known to have been written in 1111. John therefore succeeded Hugh and governed the Church before Gaucerannus.], and by his entire Church, and had been carefully entertained for five days with all our company, I heard from that archbishop what I can neither conceal nor ought to conceal from your affection.

I heard, then, that the lord archbishop of Sens [Note: The lord of Sens: Daimbert, archbishop. He had more than one dispute with the archbishops of Lyons. The first was with Hugh the legate, when he delayed Hugh’s ordination, as Ivo’s Letter 60 reports. The second was with John, when John summoned him to the council of Anse outside the province, as appears in Daimbert’s own letter preserved by Ivo. The third, which Goffridus indicates here, was with the same John, but had arisen somewhat earlier from the longstanding controversy over primacy. For, as Ivo writes in Letter 51, disputes on this matter between the bishops of Sens and Lyons were frequent, even after Gregory VII’s rescript establishing that the four provinces of Lyons—Lyons, Rouen, Tours, and Sens—should obey the archbishop of Lyons as their primate; see Book VI, Letters 34 and following.], had made peace with him [Note: Had made peace with him. Concerning this peace, if I am not mistaken, John himself wrote to Daimbert: “You can remember that ever since you recovered the friendship and intimacy of the Church of Lyons, it has looked upon you with joy, received you with exultation, and honored you with as much affection as it could. Do not believe every spirit, brother. We once experienced that storm, but, by God’s favor, it subsided for a time, and by his doing it became calm.”], promised him every obedience as his primate, and that you had in no way shared in that peace. He also said that the letters which you composed in his name [Note: The letters which you composed in his name. That is, which you dictated in his name. Since Ivo was an associate and helper in all the controversies of his metropolitan, he had written letters in Daimbert’s name to Paschal, in which he attacked John as primate. When Daimbert made peace with John without Ivo’s knowledge, he denied that those letters had been written and sent to the pope at his command. This appears to be the true sense of this passage, although I see that another interpretation pleased a learned man in his observations on Ivo, Letter 67.] had not been written by his will or transmitted to the lord pope. Accordingly, he said that he had promptly informed the lord pope that he by no means believed those letters to have been his.

When I heard this, being concerned for you as for a most beloved lord and friend, I spoke with the lord primate and his clerics, who were opposing you in every way they could. By displaying the honor and distinction of your life and person, I most earnestly sought peace between you and them. Therefore I wish to confer with you whenever and wherever it pleases you, because I desire to disclose these matters, and certain others affecting your honor and, as I judge, your advantage, to your person alone.

If you want me to come, however, arrange a safe escort for me, because I still have—and rightly have—suspicions of the sacrilegious men who seized me as I was returning from your court when the lord was coming. Farewell, and write to me your wishes concerning these matters.

# LETTER XIX

To Ivo, bishop of the men of Chartres, brother Goffridus sends greetings from the Lord and, from himself, the service of due affection.

Just as we praise the customs of monks that agree with the Rule of blessed Benedict, so we cannot praise those which Saint Benedict neither teaches nor commands and which seem wholly at variance with reason. There are certain institutions among monks which reason in no way admits, which none of the holy Fathers discovered, but which the custom of foolish men established. Certain monks claim these for themselves as law in monasteries; and although Christ said, “I am the truth” (John 14:6), and did not say, “I am custom,” they nevertheless alter the law of truth for the sake of their custom.

To say nothing of other matters, they seem to us to err in no small degree in this: they think that the anointing of the sick [Note: The anointing of the sick. Goffridus and Ivo seem to have held in the following letter that no sacrament of the Church could be repeated, since, according to theological doctrine, only those sacraments which imprint a character—namely baptism, confirmation, and orders—cannot be repeated. It follows that, since extreme unction is not among them, it may be repeated, not only in different illnesses but even in the same illness whenever, after an interval, the disease returns so severely that a new danger to life arises.] ought to be repeated, although it is called a sacrament by the holy Catholic and apostolic See and no sacrament ought to be repeated.

Pope blessed Innocent [Note: Blessed Innocent. Letter to Decentius, bishop of Gubbio.] says that the sacrament of anointing is so great that it is thought in no way possible to grant it to penitents who are denied the other sacraments. Nevertheless, we wish to know what your eminence’s discernment thinks about this and what it teaches should be held. For although we have no doubt that these things are true both by reason and by authority, we nevertheless wish and ask that they be confirmed by a decree of your authority.

# LETTER XX [Note: Letter 20. This is Ivo’s letter, which is read in exactly the same words in Letter 255 to Ralph, abbot of Saint Fuscianus.]

Ivo, minister of the Church of Chartres, to Goffridus, abbot of Vendôme, sends greetings and affection.

I do not think that the anointing of the sick should be repeated because, as you yourself asserted, according to the institution of the apostolic See it is a kind of sacrament; and whoever repeats the sacraments of Christ and the Church does injury to those sacraments themselves. The anointing of the sick is a sacrament of public penance [Note: It is a sacrament of public penance. A futile argument. For how can the anointing of the sick be said to pertain to public penance, when it was formerly not ordinarily permitted to those doing public penance, as Pope Innocent taught? Thus what Augustine and Ambrose assert is certainly true: public penance is not to be repeated. But this has no bearing on the matter.], and Augustine and Ambrose testify that it, like baptism, is not to be repeated.

Augustine, in his Letter to Macedonius, says: “It has been cautiously and beneficially provided that the place of that most humble penance be granted once in the Church, lest the medicine become cheap and therefore less useful to the sick; for it is more salutary in proportion as it is less contemptible.”

Ambrose, in the second book *On Penance*, says: “As there is one baptism, so there is one penance, which nevertheless is performed publicly. For we ought to repent daily of sin; but this applies to lesser offenses, whereas that applies to graver ones.”

# LETTER XXI

To Goffridus, bishop of praiseworthy life [Note: Goffridus, bishop of Chartres. He was Ivo’s successor, a man distinguished by many praises for his life and achievements, especially in the Aquitanian legation which he undertook on behalf of Innocent II against Girardus of Angoulême and the other supporters of Anacletus. Concerning him, see Bernard himself, *Life of Saint Bernard*, Book II; Letters 47 and 55; Peter of Cluny, Letter 40; John of Salisbury, Book V; and chapter 15 of the *Polycraticus*.], his sweetest lord and intimate friend, brother Goffridus offers the service, as much and as great as he is able and understands, and the affection of pure love.

I complain before your goodness, venerable Father, about the countess of Vendôme [Note: The countess of Vendôme. Book I, Letter 3.], and our entire community complains with me. While I was in the district of Angers on the monastery’s business, she twice took from us land which our monastery had peacefully held; she also had the bark of trees, which our men had gathered for their customary uses, burned.

Moreover, the monks of the Greater Monastery [Note: The monks of the Greater Monastery. Below, Letter 26.], whom the humility of Saint Martin has made somewhat exalted, take from us by secular violence the tithe for which, in your presence, we offered them justice. Robert of Mount Laudatus—who is not praiseworthy—seized our plunder and received one hundred solidi for its redemption; having taken them wrongly, he spent them even more wickedly at Vendôme.

Which of these men has behaved better toward us cannot be known either by man or angel, since each of them has acted most wickedly against us. On account of all these matters, we humbly beg your affection to send a decree of your authority to the clerics of Vendôme, so that each of the persons mentioned above may be corrected in such a way that none of them rejoices in the wrongs they have committed against us.

By the grace of your goodness you instructed your archpriest [Note: Your archpriest. Goffridus Danielis; see Letter 8 above.] to assist us with ecclesiastical justice whenever necessary. He promises that he will do everything at your command, but of all that, he does absolutely nothing. Certainly, we know him to be ready and very attentive in matters belonging to the world, and he knows very cleverly how to divert another’s water to his own mill. In matters belonging to the justice of the Church we would praise him, but we do not wish to incur falsehood on his behalf.

# LETTER XXII

To his most beloved lord, lord Goffridus, bishop of Catholic life, brother Goffridus offers half his soul—and, if that is not enough, his whole soul and body.

Sweetest Father, we return to you many thanks for your many benefits, and especially for the depths of your affection, which we feel to be firm and unshaken toward us.

We have often complained, and continue to complain, about the monks of the Greater, as it is called, Monastery, whom the humility of Saint Martin has made proud and his poverty wealthy [Note: Whom the humility of Saint Martin has made. Thus the preceding letter speaks of the same monks; see Letter 15 concerning the canons of Saint Mary of Chartres.]; and in your presence, on the feast day of Saint Giles, we wish to obtain justice against them.

We do not dare come to Chartres because of that leper, William’s son, and because of the other enemies of our Church; nor do we dare come because of the troublesome crowd of laymen whom we have no doubt the aforesaid monks will have there. Nevertheless, we do not refuse to go and return at your pleasure, wherever or whenever you wish, under your safe conduct.

But let your honorable discernment so provide for your honor and our advantage that your most faithful friend may not suffer loss of his justice or incur disgrace to his person on any pretext. Farewell, and inform us by letter of what pleases you.

# LETTER XXIII

To his most beloved lord and sweetest friend, Goffridus, bishop of venerable life at Chartres, brother Goffridus sends salvation from God and, from himself, the service of pure affection.

Our littleness has heard something about your greatness which it could not hear without amazement. One of our brothers [Col. 0090B], as he told us, once came to you intending to make a complaint against Ursio, son of Nivelo. You scarcely deigned to hear half his complaint, but opposed to him the fact that your excommunicated persons were being received by our brothers. We believe that this was not devised by you but by someone else who, like one accusing Susanna, produced false testimony.

Far be it from the sincerity of our brothers that there should be so great an insult to Christ and so detestable a burial of ecclesiastical justice! They do not know how to bury the justice of God; but wherever they recognize it as dead, they try to raise it again by their prayers.

We complain, venerable Father of honorable life, about the aforesaid Ursio and about Paganus, the brother of Nivelo. One of them, namely Ursio, after many other evils that he has already done to us, took from us one thousand sheep and fourteen oxen. Paganus, however, burned by fire our mills which we had at Pisostum [Note: The mills which were at Pisostum. One mill at Pisostum is included among the mills that the founder gave to the monastery. The name belongs to a castle situated somewhat above Vendôme on the same bank of the Loir. It is also mentioned by Odo, bishop of Tusculum and legate, in a letter to the abbot of Vendôme in 1247.].

We have repeatedly complained to your goodness about the monks of the Greater Monastery, and we earnestly beg you to ensure that our complaint benefits us. Farewell.

# LETTER XXIV

To the good lord and intimate friend Goffridus, bishop of honorable life, brother Goffridus offers whatever God grants more salutary to a faithful soul.

You know very well, best Father, that I complained to your fatherhood about the countess of Vendôme. Still asking, I beg; and begging, I ask again for justice, so often sought, from that lady.

Through your goodness you instructed me that, between her and me, you had granted time either for litigation [Note: *Placitandi*. To dispute or litigate. Honorius II to Abbot Goffridus: “We forbid anyone to compel you or any of your successors to litigate concerning what that venerable place has held in possession for thirty years.” Likewise, in the litigation of the monks of Saint Albinus and Saint Sergius concerning Campiniacum in the year 1704, when the monks of Saint Sergius wished first to litigate over lesser matters and afterward over Campiniacum, the judges thought it unjust that the latter case should be heard, since the abbots had been summoned and had assembled for it.], or for making peace, until the feast of the blessed saint [Note: Time until the feast. A word frequent among writers of that age, by which they signified a respite and postponement of a lawsuit or other business. Goslenus, bishop of Chartres, to Suger, abbot of Saint-Denis, concerning the provost of Hienville: “When we asked for a respite, he refused to grant it, fearing that his profits would suffer if our case happened to come before you for examination. Therefore we appeal to your discernment on this matter, that you not submit the examination of this affair to anyone before yourself and order it postponed until it can be examined by you.” The very learned and diligent François Juret collected further examples in his notes on Ivo’s Letter 127. The word remains in the vernacular today. We say *sans respect*, “without respite,” meaning without interruption. From this they also formed the verb *respecter*, “to postpone.” Count Rodulfus of Vermandois to the same Suger: “The count of Angers postponed the meeting.” The same to the same: “If, then, it pleased you to conduct or postpone business at Paris, I would be very willing, and it would be good. For I do not know when I shall be able to come from court.”]

By the good grace of the Lord God, I have Christ’s peace and concord with every Christian, and I would very much like to have peace with that lady; but her peace is always discord. I either wish for peace through you as mediator, or I ask you as judge for justice.

By word and writing you forbade me, and rightly so, to conduct our case without your judgment. For it is wholly unjust and, as you yourself know better, entirely contrary to the sacred canons that an ecclesiastical case should be settled by a secular and foreign court [Note: Secular and foreign judgment. The first expression refers to *κοσμικὰ δικαστήρια*, secular or public tribunals; the second to foreign courts—that is, ecclesiastical courts, but those of a judge who is not one’s own, as when proceedings take place outside the province. Both are forbidden by the sacred laws. Ivo, Letter 125: “Although our judgment is foreign in your province, we nevertheless do not think our counsel foreign.”], and that what it is proper for you and your people to do should be conceded to others, even to ecclesiastical persons. If this could happen, your Church would suffer damage and lose much of her jurisdiction and honor. To give the glory of your Church to another is neither a form of holiness nor a part of religion.

You also know this well, most beloved: secular men, according to their custom, try to nullify the authority of the holy Church. When they are granted, even in a small matter, the opportunity to establish any custom against ecclesiastical rights, they thereafter strive to claim it for themselves at all times. Thus, whoever does this against his own Church stirs up a worldly quarrel; and when he later wishes to act otherwise, the secular storm does not permit it.

Our humility therefore earnestly asks your affection to come to our place—indeed, to your place—and let your discernment not hesitate to come at the appointed time to us, your servants of holiness. If you cannot or do not wish to come then, let another meeting between the countess and me be fixed by you, in a place safe for both her and me, where we may either make peace by your counsel or have our Church obtain justice by your judgment. Farewell.

# LETTER XXV

To his most beloved lord and Father Goffridus, bishop of Catholic life, brother Goffridus offers not to fear prison, exile, or death for Christ, nor to place anything contrary to these—on any pretext—before justice and truth.

We have heard of your adversity, which we truthfully make our own with all our heart. Since we do not rejoice in prosperity without you and wish to endure adversity with you, we earnestly and humbly beg you to inform us by letter if you need the service of our humility. Privately and publicly, we offer ourselves and what is ours to your will and your need.

Do not let it trouble you, sweetest Father, to accept in your need the service of our littleness—or rather, our greatness. In this matter, do not rely on your own judgment but on the sense of the Holy Spirit, who speaks through Solomon: “If you possess a friend, possess him in temptation” (Ecclesiasticus 6:7). A friend and a physician are proved in need.

Farewell; and if we have ever deserved well of you, do not spare us in your need.

# LETTER XXVI

To Goffridus, a Father of honorable life, pastor given by God to the Church of Chartres, brother Goffridus sends perpetual salvation from the Lord and, from himself, the service of due affection.

We have often complained and continue to complain about the monks of the Greater Monastery, who continually shoot at us with the arrows of plunder and secular violence.

The tithe which our brothers received from the first abbot of their monastery [Note: From the first abbot of their monastery. He was Raginaldus, a monk sent from the Greater Monastery to become abbot of Saint Nicholas of Angers, but appointed by Gauffridus Martellus of Vendôme. The matter is revealed by Count Fulk Nerra in the account in which he explains the origin of the monastery of Saint Nicholas, which he had founded. “After Abbot Baldricus,” he says, “had abandoned the monastery, secretly sought the wilderness, and finally returned to the Greater Monastery, he ended his life at the monastery of Tabennesi. After him, lord Abbot Albert restored the monk Raginaldus to his place. Before his blessing, however, he fled to my son Gauffridus and undertook the governance of the newly founded monastery of Vendôme without the permission of his abbot. After I saw that I had been deceived by two abbots, I became very angry and ordered the other monks to return quickly to their monastery. Then I asked lord Walter, abbot of Saint Albinus, to release lord Hildinus, the prior of that Church. He was ordained in the year 1033 from the Incarnation of the Lord, on the day of the Nativity of blessed Mary, which was the third year of King Henry, and he governed the monastery according to the rule.” I have transcribed this so that we may know in what year the monastery of Vendôme began to have an abbot. From this Raginaldus to Michael Subletus, who now presides over the monastery of Vendôme, there were thirty-seven abbots, whose succession is given in the following list.]

peacefully held, and from which, with you present, we offered them justice, they are taking it away from us, contrary to your prohibition, with swords and clubs—as though they had even brought Herodians along with them—and they are also taking another [portion] which previously they did not take. Thus they inflict upon us every evil within their power, and they think that what they do is permissible. You prohibited them by word and in writing, and prohibited their abbot as well, from taking that tithe any further, and you admonished them to come to your court, where they would obtain full justice.

[Note: Their abbot Odo; to him survives a letter of Hugh, abbot of Pontigny, and Bernard, abbot of Clairvaux, and another by our Goffridus, Book IV.]

 Yet they, equally contemptuous of your word and writing, strive more and more to harass us; they appear to be attacking your authority and disparaging you.

Accordingly, we humbly beseech your fatherhood to advance against them and set yourself as a wall before the house of Israel against the disobedient—something which you do not doubt is necessary for us and honorable for you. Yet we neither can nor ought to wonder if they act thus against us and against you as against dry wood, since they once blazed with sulfurous fire against green wood (Luke 23:31), that is, against their own shepherd, the archbishop of Tours, and did not afterward extinguish the sulfurous fire that had been badly kindled.

[Note: Against their own shepherd, the archbishop of Tours. The conflict between the monastery of Marmoutier and both its metropolitans named Radulf was grave and prolonged. An anonymous monk of the same monastery treats it at length; Juretus transcribes his lengthy account from an old manuscript in his note on Ivo’s Letter 108.]



Would that the merited death of the proud Saul, the leprosy of Miriam, Aaron’s sister, and the punishment of Judas, the perverse disciple, might deter them. Then, with the pride that is the mother and nurse of all iniquity—and especially of greed—dead within them, may they cease harassing the monastic brotherhood. May they neither persecute pontifical dignity as Judas did Christ, nor disparage the pontiff as Miriam did Moses. Farewell. May your justice be known to all people, and especially to us, who have the greater need of it.

**86. LETTER XXVII**

**To Lord Goffridus, the glorious bishop of the Church of Chartres, Brother Goffridus, an unworthy servant of the monastery of Vendôme, offers the service of his good custom and the affection of pure love.**

Your lord and ours, Pope Calixtus, wrote to you once and then a second time, ordering you to render us justice concerning those who were taking our property within your bishopric.

[Note: Pope Calixtus. Below, Letter 30.]

 We sought it from Hervé of Scales and from two priests, but we still cannot obtain it. We ask again that, in accordance with the pope’s command, you render us justice concerning the aforesaid men.

For we are prepared to come before you, at a suitable place and an appropriate time, to receive whatever is just, and to answer concerning our brothers against whom you are bringing a charge of sacrilege, to the extent that justice dictates and the authority of the Apostolic See permits. In this matter, however, we do not ask for nights, according to the customs of laymen, but for adjournments in accordance with the provisions of the canons.

[Note: “Not nights according to the customs of laymen.” Book LI, chapter 45, concerning the four lawful summonses: the first summons is after two nights; the second after fourteen nights; the third after twenty-one nights; the fourth after forty-two. See also IV, 83. After citizens and peasants have returned from any military expedition, the ban is revoked from that day for forty nights; this is called in the German language *scastlegi*, that is, “laying down of arms.” The Gauls formerly, as the very learned scholar observes from Caesar concerning the earlier passage, measured periods of time not by a number of days but of nights. Tacitus likewise wrote this of the Germans, and a trace of that ancient custom remains in our vernacular, when we sometimes express the present day as though saying not “today” but “this night.” Thus, in Goffridus’s time, when an adjournment was requested in legal proceedings, laymen asked for “nights,” while clerics asked for delays. Felix II, in his letter to the Egyptians: “When an accused person has come to judgment, if he wishes it and it is necessary, an adjournment, requested by him, is to be granted by the Fathers without impediment.”]

Do not judge personally. These are the Lord’s words: “No one rightly accepts another’s person in judgment unless he has first accepted his own.” Certainly, there is no more reason to retract what the Apostolic See grants concerning sacerdotal ornaments—than to retract the election of one who is made bishop without merit of life and without sacred orders.

[Note: “Concerning the granting of sacerdotal ornaments.” That is, episcopal ornaments. For the bishop is a priest of the first rank, and the presbyter of the second, according to Sidonius and others. Episcopal insignia are therefore the mitre, ring, sandals, and so forth. It was surely a bad practice for the Apostolic See to grant these to certain abbots, thereby making them resemble bishops. Nor was this matter once approved only by bishops, but by many others as well, including Saint Bernard in Letter 42 to Henry, archbishop of Sens, and Peter of Blois in Letter 90 to Abbot William. Yet it is incredible how widely this privilege eventually extended. The letters of Innocent III, addressed to the Vendôme community as cardinals, teach us that the right to the mitre and other insignia belonged to the Vendômois; see Book I, Letter 9. Furthermore, because bishops were offended that in councils and synods abbots possessing the right to the mitre were not distinguished from bishops, Clement IV established this distinction: in synods, exempt abbots are to wear gold mitres embroidered in the Phrygian manner, but without gems or gold or silver plates; non-exempt abbots are to wear simple, white, plain mitres. Elsewhere both groups may use whatever mitres the indulgences of the Apostolic See permit. Viterbo, the nineteenth day before the Kalends of September, in the second year.]

If anyone wishes to challenge what the Roman pontiff does, and dares to raise his voice against one who owes his innocence to heaven alone, let him also challenge the fact that the pontiff regarded him more with the eyes of mercy than with the judgment of justice.

[Note: “Than one who is without sacred orders.” Goffridus makes the same tacit objection to Goffridus of Chartres here that he makes concerning Rainaldus of Angers, who was elected before receiving sacred orders; see Book III, Letter 11. But he additionally indicates that Goffridus was of low birth and was created pope—“from nothing,” as he puts it—in Letter 30 of this book and Letter 42 of Book III.]

We are not acephalous,

[Note: “We are not acephalous.” The Council of Paris, in Ivo, Part VI, calls clerics who obey no bishop “acephalous,” that is, “without a head,” following the ancient custom of the Church. Their exemption was another head of the bishops’ longstanding complaint against abbots, for the bishops were displeased that abbots were not subjected to their authority. Hence they called them acephalous. Although that name may perhaps seem unjustly reproachful when applied to men who, like Goffridus, rely upon a privilege of the Apostolic See, it properly applies to those who claim and usurp liberty for themselves without authority. Concerning such men, I believe, and concerning the wicked custom they put forward, Innocent II wrote to King Henry of England: “It is expedient that, during your time, the wicked customs in the kingdom or duchy committed to you by divine appointment be cut away, and that, once the roots of vices have been severed, every good thing be planted through the zeal of your nobility, with the Lord’s cooperation. Otherwise abbots and the other clerics will be unable either to offer the Lord an acceptable service or to care for the salvation of their souls. Indeed, they are considered acephalous, that is, without a head, unless they are subjected with due humility to their bishops and prelates.” In another sense, Peter of Blois called monks acephalous when they have a superior who is sluggish and ineffective in his office.]

because we have Christ the Savior as our head, and after him, the Roman pontiff. Our monastery had this head at its beginning, and, with God’s help, it will have him until the end of the age.

You object to the profession.

[Note: “The profession that you object to.” See Letter 7 of this book. To Urban’s and Paschal’s decrees must be added the letter of Goffridus himself, bishop of Chartres, in which he testifies that, because of the prohibition contained in such documents, he waived the profession of Fromundus and Hubertus, the successors of Goffridus of Vendôme, when he consecrated them as abbots. The letter reads as follows:

“Goffridus, by the grace of God bishop of Chartres and legate of the Apostolic See, to Hubertus, by the same grace abbot of Vendôme, sends greeting and grace.

“After your venerable predecessor Goffridus had ended the course of his present life, as we believe, at God’s call, Fromundus, adorned with moral integrity and prudence, was elected abbot by the common consent of the chapter. When he was presented to us for blessing, we asked him for a profession, as we did from the other abbots of our diocese. He replied that he would under no circumstances make a profession, because the venerable pontiffs of the Apostolic See, Urban and Paschal, had forbidden under anathema that the abbot of Vendôme should make a profession for his blessing, or that anyone should receive one from him; and that, if the bishop of Chartres did not wish to bless him, he might receive a blessing from whatever bishop he wished. Having seen their privileges, and since we neither wished nor were able to resist them, we blessed him without a profession.

“After his death, we later blessed you as well, demanding no profession from you. Once you had received the blessing, you humbly asked us to give you our seal attesting that your blessing and that of your predecessor had been performed in this manner, and to prohibit by our authority any of our successors from demanding a profession from your successors. We therefore bear witness to the truth: your venerable predecessor Fromundus and you received a blessing from us in such a way that you made no profession to us or to our Church.

“Moreover, by God’s authority and ours, we prohibit our successors from demanding a profession from your successors, and your successors from making one to our successors. We also grant to the monastery over which, by God’s authority, you preside every dignity and liberty that our predecessor of blessed memory, Theodericus, granted to it. Whatever it currently possesses within our bishopric, whether in tithes, churches, or any other possessions, we confirm to it, as well as whatever it may acquire either by lawful purchase or by the donation of the faithful.

“And because that monastery is far removed from us, we grant to you and your successors that you may send your monks to whatever bishops you wish for ordination, asking those bishops to ordain them without hesitation and without fearing any offense from us or our successors. May the grace of God and of our Lord Jesus Christ be with all who preserve these provisions for that place. But may those who oppose them, unless they repent, perish eternally and remain in eternal death and damnation.”]

—know that it was completely invalidated by Pope Urban of holy memory, during the time of your predecessor, in these words:

“Urban, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to the venerable congregation of the monastery of Vendôme, greeting and apostolic blessing.

“It has been reported to us that the bishop of Chartres extorted a profession from our beloved son Goffridus, your abbot, at the consecration which he received from him. Since we have recognized that this was done contrary to the authority of the Roman Church, know that we have mercifully forgiven the abbot this fault, but we annul the profession itself so completely that it possesses no force whatsoever. Furthermore, so that henceforth the abbot of your monastery may not make a profession to the bishop, this has been confirmed by the privilege of our authority, and by these present letters we prohibit it.

“If anyone should hereafter attempt to act contrary to these provisions, let him be barred from the thresholds of the holy Church and remain excommunicated until he repents and makes satisfaction to the Roman Church.”

Given at Rome, on the eighth day before the Kalends of December.

**88** The lord Pope Paschal confirmed this same matter by his authority.

[Note: “Pope Paschal.” A copy of the privilege written at Rome on the second day before the Ides of March is preserved in the Vendôme archives.]

[Note: Concerning any monk of Vendôme. The monks of Vendôme preserve another, very similar decree of Urban, given at Rome on the eighth day before the Kalends of December. There is likewise another rescript of the same Urban to Bishops Ivo of Chartres and Ranulf of Saintes, in which, after other matters, the following is read: “For you were present at the Council of Clermont, where, while the bishops of Gaul sat with us, it was decreed—and by the authority of these present letters we confirm it—that bishops or archbishops are not to presume to exercise any authority over any of the monks of the monastery of Vendôme, or to dispose of any of the property of that place.” Given at Rome, on the second day before the Kalends of March.]

That no bishop may exercise any authority over any monk of Vendôme was likewise prohibited by Pope Urban of blessed memory himself, in the following manner:

“Urban, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to all the sons of the holy and apostolic Church, greeting and apostolic blessing.

“At the Council of Clermont, while the bishops of Gaul were seated with us, it was decreed—and afterward confirmed at Rome by the present decree—that no bishop or archbishop should presume to exercise any authority over any monk of the monastery of Vendôme.

“For that monastery and its brothers have been placed so specially under the protection of the Apostolic See and under Roman liberty that no human being whatsoever, except the Roman pontiff and their abbot, may claim any authority or dominion over them. If anyone knowingly presumes to violate these provisions, let him remain excommunicated unless he repents and makes satisfaction to the Roman Church.

“Given at Rome, on the second day before the Kalends of April.”

We have often offered you for inspection the privileges of the holy Roman Church by which our monastery is protected. But because your sublimity delayed seeing them, or did not wish to do so, we are sending your affection transcripts of certain of them, lest henceforth, as though out of ignorance, you raise your arms against the benevolence of the Apostolic See—which created both you and us, not through our merits but through its grace. Farewell always in the Lord.

**LETTER XXVIII**

**To the good lord and pious Father Goffridus, bishop of praiseworthy life, Brother Goffridus sends whatever may most beneficially be possessed or commanded.**

While you and we were together at Bonneval,

[Note: “At Bonneval.” Book IV, Letter 14.]

we were disturbed by the bitterness of our spirit. I did not wish to say in person what I am writing to you in your absence, lest I rightly keep you in suspense, since you had regarded me with suspicion without cause. My spirit had indeed been justly troubled, because I felt that evil was being repaid to me for good, hatred in return for my affection—a repayment which God neither recognizes nor teaches.

Whatever the sowers of discord may insinuate or mutter, this letter will speak not a report of gossip but the pure truth: namely, that I never sought anything from Pope Calixtus against you or against your Church, nor did he himself do anything against you or against your Church. A privilege was indeed supposed to be prepared for me at Étampes, and it was written there. But because certain provisions had been inserted in it that seemed beneficial neither to your Church nor necessary for our monastery, it remained where it had been written, without being sealed.

[Note: “Without being sealed.” Without a bull and seal. Archbishop Rathodus of Trier wrote in his formal letter: “We have decided to furnish this letter here and there with Greek letters, and to seal it with the ring of our Church.” Peter of Blois likewise used *bullare* of sealing, that is, affixing a seal. Hence the name *bullae* came to be applied to the charters of pontiffs and emperors, just as to the formal letters of ecclesiastical prelates, from the form or seal that was added; see elsewhere, if God wills, at Letter 8 of Book VI [Apollinaris Sidonius].]

Afterward, however, the privilege was made at Paris.

[Note: “It was made at Paris.” We shall transcribe this privilege of Calixtus in full, not only to confirm what Goffridus writes about it, but because it contains the principal prerogatives and immunities of the monastery of Vendôme and may therefore serve as a model for many others. This is its authentic copy:

**Privilege of Calixtus II, issued at Paris for the monastery of Vendôme**

“Calixtus, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved son Gaufridus, abbot of the monastery of Vendôme, and to his successors, who are to be regularly appointed in perpetuity.

“Since, by the authority and benevolence of the Apostolic See, we are debtors to all the sons of the holy Church, it is nevertheless fitting that we should show a more ardent zeal of charity toward those places and persons that adhere more specially and familiarly to the Roman Church. Therefore, beloved son in Christ, Gaufridus, abbot, we have rightly judged that your petitions should be granted, so that we might fortify by the privilege of the Apostolic See the monastery of Vendôme, over which, by God’s authority, you preside—the monastery that was offered to the Apostolic See by its very founders, Gaufridus, count of Anjou, and Agnes, countess of Poitou—in accordance with the example of our predecessors, Alexander, Urban, and Paschal, Roman pontiffs of holy memory.

“Therefore, just as those founders vowed, and as their charter records, we decree that this same monastery shall always remain free and released from every condition imposed by other persons, under the protection of the Apostolic See and under Roman liberty. In such a way, namely, that between the Roman pontiff and you and your successors there shall be no person of any dignity or order intervening. Nor shall the abbot of Vendôme be compelled in any way to attend a council at which the pope is not present.

“Furthermore, the church of Saint Prisca, situated on the Aventine Hill, which your predecessors are known to have possessed for a long time, with all its appurtenances, by the grant of the aforesaid lord Pope Alexander, we confirm to you and your successors with every dignity belonging to that church. By the judgment of the Holy Spirit we decree that henceforth no ecclesiastical or secular person presume, by any stratagem or pretext, to take from you or your successors the aforesaid church of Saint Prisca or the dignity of that church.

“If it should happen that a legate of the Roman Church visits the aforesaid monastery of Vendôme, let him be received there charitably, and, according to the resources of the place, let whatever is necessary for his bodily needs be carefully provided for him. But let the legate himself dare neither to arrange nor correct anything in that place on his own, nor presume to trouble the ruler of the place or the brothers under the pretext of his legation. If he should discover anything that ought to be corrected, he may report it to the pope.

“If anyone wishes to bring a claim against that place concerning any matter, let the abbot or the brothers in no way answer him before consulting the Roman pontiff, because whatever has been alienated or decided without judgment by us or by our successors will be invalid.

“As a sign of the liberty received from the Roman Church, you shall pay twelve solidi of the coinage of your homeland each year at the Lateran palace.

“If, therefore, in the future any ecclesiastical or secular person, knowingly aware of this page of our constitution, should rashly attempt to act against it, then, after being warned a second and third time, if he does not correct his offense by suitable satisfaction, let him lose the dignity of his power and honor, acknowledge himself liable before the divine judgment for the iniquity he has committed, be separated from the most sacred body and blood of God and our Lord Jesus Christ the Redeemer, and be subjected to strict vengeance at the final judgment.

“But let there be the peace of our Lord Jesus Christ for all who preserve these provisions for that place, so that both here they may receive the fruit of good action and before the strict Judge may find the rewards of eternal peace. Amen.

“I, Calixtus, bishop of the Catholic Church, have signed.

“Given at Paris by the hand of Chrysogonus, cardinal deacon and librarian of the holy Roman Church, on the eighth day before the Ides of October, in the thirteenth indiction, in the year 1119 of the Incarnation of the Lord, and in the first year of the pontificate of Lord Pope Calixtus II.”]

This privilege, in which the dignity and honor of our monastery are both recorded and confirmed, does not diminish the honor of your Church; rather, it increases it. This is evident to all who do not possess an envious eye and do not try to view well-accomplished affairs under an oblique star.

Far be it from the sincerity of my soul that I should present one thing readily on my tongue to a friend or enemy while holding another thing hidden in my heart. Believe this truthfully: the privilege itself contains no mention made against your Church or concerning anything taken from your Church. If the lord pope has granted us something of his own, and has not taken from you what belongs to you, we desire that you, our lord and intimate friend, rejoice at it. But if our enemies grieve and are saddened by it, we therefore can neither dissolve nor ought to dissolve what has been confirmed by apostolic authority and bound under anathema.

Farewell, and if I have spoken and acted well, bear witness to it. For I am not accustomed to act against myself, nor to bite my own tongue when I ought to speak.

**LETTER XXIX**

**To the good lord and his intimate friend, Goffridus, bishop of praiseworthy life, Brother Goffridus offers pure affection and the service of pure affection.**

The decrees of the holy Roman pontiffs teach us—namely, those of the great Leo,

[Note: “Namely, of Leo.” Relevant here is what appears in Letter 47 of his letter to the ecumenical synod, concerning the restoration of bishops expelled from their sees.]

Symmachus,

[Note: “Symmachus.” In the Fifth Roman Synod.]

Felix,

[Note: “Felix II,” whose canon comes from his letter to the bishops of Egypt, III, 3, 2: “For as long as he remains in the see.”]

Gregory,

[Note: “Gregory.” Gregory the Great, Book VIII, Letter 24, to Fortunatus, bishop of Naples.]

Hormisdas,

[Note: “Hormisdas.” His efforts on behalf of the restoration of the bishops Elias, Thomas, and Nicostratus are shown by Letters 56 and the several following letters, as well as Letter 72.]

Sixtus,

[Note: “Sixtus.” Xystus II, in his letter to the bishops of Spain.]

and Eusebius—

[Note: “Eusebius.” In his letter to the Egyptians and Alexandrians. Most of these decrees, as well as others of the same kind by pontiffs, may be found in Gratian’s Collections, II, 2, and III, 1 and 2, and in the Decretals, Book II, concerning the restoration of the dispossessed.]

—that no one who has been dispossessed of his property or expelled from his own see is to be judged in any matter or summoned to a council until everything taken from him has been restored to him in full; and that he is to possess it for as long a period as he is known to have been deprived of it.

If anyone says that a person who has been dispossessed may or must be summoned not to judgment concerning the case but to judgment concerning investiture, he is attempting to shake the keys of the holy Church and to violate the laws of the Catholic Church and of the Apostolic See, by which it is forbidden that anyone dispossessed be summoned to judgment or judged in any matter. Therefore, if one who has been dispossessed ought not to be judged in any matter, it is manifest—and no reasonable doubt can in any way be entertained on this point—that not only judgment concerning the case and concerning investiture is removed from the dispossessed person, but that no summons to judgment may be issued against him at all, since it would be pointless and empty to summon to judgment someone whom it is not permitted to judge in any respect.

Moreover, we who were present know that the lord Pope Urban, at the Council of Clermont, gave a definitive ruling on this matter, praised by all the bishops and abbots who were present: that whoever had been dispossessed without summons and judgment should likewise be invested without summons and judgment.

May my lord prosper and flourish, and may he be nourished by the truth of the holy Scriptures, so that he may not need another’s food, which often makes a hungry person even hungrier and satisfies no one.

**92. LETTER XXX**

**To Goffridus, venerable bishop, Brother Goffridus sends greeting and blessing.**
The laws of the Roman pontiffs you have expounded; yet your exposition appears to furnish more an opportunity for stripping the clothed than for restoring the stripped, since it attempts to defend the despoilers. Although I did not at all approve of it, I might perhaps have remained silent had I not seen and heard that it was expounded and upheld otherwise by the Apostolic See.

Our lord Pope Urban, of blessed memory, in a general council, not secretly but openly, adjudged that those who had been stripped without judgment and summons ought to be restored without judgment and summons, lest under the pretext of summons and judgment delay intervene, and through delay the stripping remain either prolonged or perpetual.

The Apostolic See therefore expounded these laws, since it gave them, and those who give laws ought rightly to be their interpreters. This is found both in the Old and in the New Testament. For Christ and Moses gave laws, and they expounded them. If others are called interpreters of the laws after them, they are to be accepted only insofar as they have understood nothing perverse or contrary to them.

By the same Spirit [Note: *By the same Spirit.* This is the sentence of Damasus, *Decretum* 25, q. 1: “Those who voluntarily violate the canons are judged gravely by the holy Fathers and by the Holy Spirit, by whose prompting and gift they were dictated.”], by whose inspiration the first law was given through Moses and the second through Christ, the holy Apostolic See gave the laws that we call canons [Note: *The Apostolic See gave the laws that we call canons.* “Ecclesiastical canons” (*κανόνες ἐκκλησιαστικοί*), that is, ecclesiastical rules, according to Athanasius in his letter *To the Orthodox*. What laws are properly in the civil state, that canons are in the Church. Hence they are often compared, as when it is said that “the canons hold the order of laws” (*τόξιν νόμων ἐπέχειν οἱ κανόνες*) and that “laws follow evil men” (*τοῖς κακοῖσιν οἱ νόμοι ἀκολουθεῖν*). Our author, *Opusculum* IV: “Although it is found neither in the laws nor in the canons”; and Book III, Letter 39: “The laws of the world permit it to be done by no reasoning, and the sacred canons altogether forbid it to be done.” Hence also the patriarch Photius entitled his work the *Nomocanon*, as being composed from laws and canons]. He also expounded them by that Spirit’s inspiration.

Therefore, if anyone thinks contrary to the Apostolic See in its exposition of the canons—the See that gave the laws of the canons—whoever he may be, he is not wise but foolish. And because he speaks by his own spirit, he is unquestionably recognized not as a worshiper or interpreter of divine law, but as its plotter and oppressor.

Formerly the Church of Chartres used to have cattle and sheep, or whatever ecclesiastical property had been seized, returned or restored [Note: *Returned or restored.* Ivo, Letter 275: “He shall return or restore the count of Nevers.” The terms are synonymous. For in legal language *recredere* means “to restore.” Hence *recredentia*, meaning a restitution of property or restored possession, is a familiar term in French courts] or immediately to exercise ecclesiastical vengeance upon the perpetrators of the robberies. Now, however, the Church of God is deprived of a possession held for fifty years without vengeance, and is summoned to judgment, although it is known to have been stripped without judgment and summons, or any form of protest.

Saint Eusebius [Note: *Saint Eusebius.* *Decretum* II, q. 2, in the Scriptures] did not teach this; his judgment requires no exposition by one less wise than he himself was, since he absolutely forbade the stripped person to be summoned to judgment. And the most blessed teacher and martyr Cyprian says that an evident matter ought not to be deferred by delay in counsel or by disputation. Pope Damasus [Note: *Pope Damasus.* Letter 4, to Stephen, chapter 5] ordered that what the stripped persons had previously possessed should first be restored to them in full, and that afterward they should answer.

He who admonished that what the stripped person had previously possessed should first be restored to him, and that afterward he should answer, did not permit the order in the Church to be reversed—namely, that the stripped person should first be summoned to judgment and restored only after judgment.

Likewise, from the African council: “If anyone has been stripped in his absence, whatever has been taken from him by any person whatsoever shall be restored without any delay.” He who prohibited every delay did not permit the stripped person to be summoned to judgment, since the summons to judgment itself cannot occur without delay.

I was indeed stripped in my absence; but it was not a private matter that kept me away—it was obedience to the lord pope. I could have brought forward many more judgments of the holy Fathers concerning those who have been stripped, had I not feared making the page too long. I shall nevertheless set forth and explain one point: namely, that ecclesiastical rigor can be altered by the malignity of hatred.

Indignation is very harsh and stubborn when it does not permit either the guilty person humbly to acknowledge his guilt or the innocent person reasonably to defend himself. This is done especially by those who grow proud through the humility of others and glory in domination rather than compassion.

Most dear Father and lord, through the sacrament of my first regeneration and through that of monastic profession I profess that I have put off the old man and put on the new; but I do not deny that afterward, following the traces of the old man, I offended the new. For, although I had been ordained a levite [Note: *Ordained a levite.* Goffridus was a deacon when he was made abbot; afterward he was consecrated abbot by Ivo, and then ordained priest at Rome by Urban], and thereafter—though not by instruction in wisdom—made an abbot and consecrated priest at Rome, in the holy and sacred order I was less concerned than I ought to have been for my own salvation and for that of others.

I confess myself wretched, utterly unhappy. Yet in this divine mercy preserved me: I was neither a secret nor a public purchaser of churches or ecclesiastical honors. I desire in no way to be torn from that tree; rather, I ardently desire to cultivate its root and to become one of its branches, however insignificant, since I know it was planted by the heavenly Father.

If that man is to be feared and avoided, as you rightly said, who deceives under the appearance of peace, then the one who loved through the truth of charity is greatly to be loved and honored. He not only displayed to the person whom he believed his friend whatever he possessed in his necessity, but also served him personally with great humility. He remembered the ecclesiastical assistance owed even to an enemy, and he ought not to have been silent about services rendered to himself with great devotion of affection.

It is safer to make known the benefits of others than one’s own, lest one receive in the present age the reward that ought to have been received in the future. A man who has watched well, and watches still so that he may watch better, ought to be admonished. For whoever is good must be admonished so that he may become better. Yet he who at some time watched well also fell asleep when he wished; and he who willingly gave assistance afterward, when he wished, delayed to give assistance.

For our monastery lost two hundred pounds [Note: *Two hundred pounds.* Book III, Letters 10 and 15], besides possessions and customary dues violently imposed upon our property, in your episcopate and during your tenure, when we complained to you before you. Afterward it could not recover anything worth sixty solidi.

Nor do I therefore think that you were pressed or compelled from elsewhere when the lord pope [Note: *If the lord pope.* I think this was Callistus. See Book I, Letter 12, where he asks Callistus for letters to the bishop of Chartres against Nivelon, and Book II, Letter 27, where he indicates that he wrote twice about the matter] laid before your reverence the injury done to the Apostolic See—an injury about which I ought not to have been silent and will not be silent, and which he himself could justly have avenged in person; and, if necessary, he will still avenge it with God’s help.

That man, I say, is exceedingly ungrateful toward the grace of the Roman Church if he pretends not to obey it, for whose sake the Church itself chose, as it were, to disregard the severity of justice and regarded him solely with the eyes of mercy. Nor does he faithfully keep the sworn oath of loyalty to the Roman pontiff who plots to take away his allodial property.

If the legate of the Apostolic See [Note: *If the legate of the Apostolic See.* Apparently Cono], as you wrote, ordered you not to render justice to us, he acted contrary to God’s constitution and the lord pope’s command, and turned his own arrow back upon himself when he prohibited obedience to the authority for which obedience is rendered. For when he issued a command against the authority by which he is permitted to command, he lost the authority to command.

Indeed, anyone who abuses the privilege he exercises deserves to lose the privilege [Note: *Deserves to lose the privilege.* Simplicius, Letter 6]. He truly abuses the authority granted to him who attempts, under the pretext of being the Roman pontiff’s legate, to act against the Roman pontiff; but while he raises his arms against the torrent, he wearies himself in vain.

And it went badly for the angel who wished to make himself equal to God; so it will go badly for the legate who desires to appear greater than the Roman pontiff himself. While he strives to become more than an apostolic man, he will become an apostate. And since, as it is said, a certain pride arose in him that needed to be restrained—so that he spoke perversely about the lord pope, our most dear Father, together with a certain bishop whom the Roman Church created from nothing—he ought to be rejected and detested by the Church of God, so that at least in this way he might recognize how grave it is to set one’s mouth against him who owes his innocence to heaven alone.

Your affection also knows what you owe to the master and what to the disciple. For according to the Savior’s testimony, “The disciple is not above his master” (Matthew 10:24), nor is an apostle greater than the one who sent him.

But if injury is inflicted upon me because of obedience to the lord pope, I rejoice and take no small delight in being injured for so great a lord. For him I am prepared not only to endure any injury whatsoever but even to carry the cross; and no one, living or dead, will ever be able to separate me from obedience and fidelity to him.

When, persuaded by your advice rather than led by my own will, he accepted with Nivelon not a case to be heard at Chartres but a hearing date concerning the restoration, I believed and still believe that the whole matter passed by because of you. For while I was still with you at Bonneval, you said that you could not bring me to Chartres at all, and therefore that it was useful, indeed necessary, for you to change the date and the place, as you did.

Afterward, through your dean Hugh [Note: *Your dean Hugh.* The successor of Ernald], you sent me word not to come to Chartres on the date fixed between Nivelon and me, because you could not be present there. Moreover, through our brothers Paganus and Gualterius, you indicated that you would come to our region by Rogationtide, where we could discuss the restoration safely and on a fixed day, and in the meantime you would ask Nivelon to restore us.

We did indeed await the appointed date, but saw neither you nor anyone on your behalf. Still stripped, and weighed down by the burden of repeated delays, we earnestly ask that we be restored and that the lord pope’s command be observed.

Otherwise, together with Naboth the Israelite and the people of Israel, we appeal to the advocate from heaven to come to our aid.

## Letter XXXI

To Goffridus, most beloved Father and lord, bishop of honorable life, Brother Goffridus sends both the affection and the effect of pure love.

I do not know whose suggestion or counsel led you to tell me repeatedly this year that I should not take from your church what it has and ought to have in our monastery. I have already told you, and I say again in this letter, that I neither can nor wish to take anything from your church. Rather, especially during your tenure, I desire with all my heart to love and honor it, if the malice of the envious permits it; if not more, then at least no less than any of our predecessors before me has done.

Whatever your church reserved for itself at the foundation of our monastery, or is afterward known to have possessed justly and according to rule, I do not dispute but grant; and as long as I live, whether the angels of discord wish it or not, I shall carefully observe it.

For it is unjust and impious to violate what we know was done by the just and pious disposition of your predecessors and the founders of our monastery, and was firmly established by them through the unshakable authority of the Apostolic See.
