I wished to show you at Angers the documents written to us by your predecessors, but you had no time to inspect them. For the commands and privileges have already been kept there for three years because of excessive waters, which so flooded and soaked our archives at Vendôme that part of our book that had been there was destroyed.

And since at present I may be unable to come to Vendôme, partly because of bodily illness and partly because of the needs of the monastery, I earnestly ask you to send Lord Bernard and Lord Rainard, or one of them, to us. I shall have him escorted from Vendôme to Angers and brought back to you, so that he may inspect our documents and, if you wish, bring copies back to you.

Again, if you ask for them when we come to Vendôme, we shall gladly show them to you. There, with God’s help, you will see what ought to restrain the importunate loquacity of our rivals, who by the windiness of their words attempt to raise a storm in the tranquil mind of good men.

## Letter XXXII

To the sweetest lord and chief among friends, Goffridus, bishop of venerable life, Brother Goffridus, called abbot, and the entire congregation of the monastery of Vendôme send whatever they can, whatever they understand, and themselves.

Your affection rightly—indeed most rightly—commanded that justice be done to us; but what was rightly commanded has not been rightly observed.

Theobald of Graville keeps at his table and in his service men who have been excommunicated, although he denied that they belonged to him. Many people know this, and perhaps your dean is not unaware of it.

In addition to these and many other injuries, Lord John, son of the count of Vendôme [Note: *Lord John, son of the count of Vendôme.* He is mentioned in Book I, Letter 13. He succeeded his father as count and waged war against Sulpitius, lord of Amboise, with whom Goffridus, John’s father, had previously fought; both conflicts ended unhappily, as an old author of the *History of Amboise* relates], together with certain vavassors [Note: *Vavassors.* Vassals. Among the letters of Suger: “To Lord G., abbot Suger, the mayor, the vavassors, and the whole community of Saint-Riquier.” What we now call nobles and inhabitants of a particular town. Obertus, Book II *On Fiefs*, title 10, calls them *valvasores* and explains that properly those are so called who hold a fief from the chief vassals; those who hold from the vavassors are called *valvasini*], knights from the castle of Vendôme, have so thoroughly plundered and devastated one of our excellent obediences that the monks who inhabited it and its cultivators must depart, and it must be reduced to solitude.

Your dean knows this. At our urging he spoke about it with the count. But the count did absolutely nothing useful to us. Therefore we humbly beseech your affection to correct what has been done against us and is daily being done most grievously, so that our wrongdoers, your parishioners, may restore what they have taken from us and thereafter permit us to remain in peace.

Good and pious lord, we can in no way continue to endure the many and great pressures, tribulations, and difficulties inflicted upon us by the people of Vendôme—some of which we described to you in the presence of the count and his men.

Among the other things their intolerable fury has done against us, they recently seized and bound the men of Saint Martin and Saint Launomar and brought them to one of our obediences [Note: *One of our obediences.* Book IV, Letter 7]. There they tortured them for as long as they pleased. They carried off what was in the house and turned the monks’ cloister into a prison for captives.

Compelled, therefore, by this excessive and unheard-of necessity, we must appeal to the lord pope. By his authority and counsel, we shall have to do one of two things: either change our location or obtain in our present place the peace that monks ought to have. One of these alternatives is urgently necessary, unless we are separated from one another and migrate to other monasteries.

## Book Three

### Letter I

To Goffridus, bishop of the Angevins [Note: *To Goffridus, bishop of the Angevins.* Son of Hugh of Meduana, who afterward abandoned the episcopate and became a Cluniac monk. The *Chronicle of Saint-Aubin*: “In the year 1093 Goffridus, son of Hugh of Meduana, was ordained on the eighth day before the Kalends of December. He remained in the episcopate scarcely seven years. For when many accused and complained before the pope that, at his command, a neophyte and almost illiterate man had been ordained, he abandoned the see at the instruction of that same Pope Urban and became a monk at Cluny. After his departure, Rainard was ordained bishop of Angers on the day before the Ides of January, in the year 1102”], his lord and friend, Goffridus, unworthy minister of the monastery of Vendôme, sends greetings.

I received your letter, which I would in no way have believed had I not seen it sealed with your seal. For it says that you have agreed to the election of Peter of Belloc [Note: *The election of Peter of Belloc.* There are many monasteries of this name in Gaul, so it may be doubted which abbot is meant here. I am inclined to think that it concerns the monastery of Lucay in the region of Tours, which Count Fulk Nerra, after returning from Jerusalem, built beyond the River Auger in honor of the Holy Sepulchre; there he also chose a place for his burial], and that therefore you must now consecrate him as abbot.

If this is so, you no longer need our humble counsel about it, since you already possess a matter completed. Nevertheless, if it pleases you and seems good to you to await me for this purpose, I shall come to you at the time you appoint, and I shall not at all conceal whatever better advice I am able to give you.

There is one thing, however, that I can neither conceal nor ought to conceal from you: he has had and still has communion with our excommunicate, William [Col. 0105C]. Because that man had taken away property belonging to our church and given it to his brother, I excommunicated him insofar as was lawful and as ecclesiastical censure required. Peter himself is not unaware of this.

Farewell, and do whatever you can, according to God, concerning his promotion.

### Letter II

To Rainard, bishop of Angers [Note: *To Rainard, bishop of Angers.* This Rainard, or Reginald of Martigné, son of Brientius, succeeded Goffridus of Meduana, as has just been said. Ivo addresses him in Letter 272, and Bishop Marbodus of Rennes in his Letter 80 to Hildebertus. That he was later transferred to the metropolitan see of Reims is shown by Book I, Letter 31, and by the calendar of Saint-Maurice of Angers: “On the nineteenth day before the Kalends of February, Rainard the Younger died, first our bishop and afterward archbishop of Reims; on his anniversary we must feed thirteen poor persons and ring the bells.” He is called “the Younger” to distinguish him from another Rainard, the sixth of that name], his lord and intimate friend, Goffridus, humble servant of the monastery of Vendôme, sends greetings and steadfastness in adversity.

If we firmly believe the sacred Scriptures, we know truly that a man is not a bishop if he fears exile, suffering, or death, or if he prefers their opposites to justice.

Therefore do not fail in defending the holy Church [Note: *In defending the holy Church.* Against the count of Angers, Letter 7]; do not incline the ear of your heart to the counsels of those who wish to live according to the flesh; do not withdraw your foot from the way of justice, lest you fall into Satan’s snare, where your soul may be captured, perish, and—God forbid—be tormented without end.

For this reason you must fear lest, because of the justice you have begun, you become contemptible in the sight of men; this will certainly happen if you falter. Through your failure, the Church of God, which is entrusted to you as chaste and free, will become a prostitute and a slave.

But if you act steadfastly, if you bring the justice you have rightly begun to the best conclusion, you will leave to your successors an example of every kind of strength and holiness. Glory and peace will be yours, and the chastity and freedom of the Church entrusted to your care will increase.

If anyone, out of love of money or for the sake of any other matter, suggests that you falter, say to him: “If anyone is for the Lord, let him join me” (Exodus 32:26). For those who hunger and thirst for money are by no means just before God; rather, those who love justice and hate iniquity will be satisfied.

I am that man, believe this most certainly, who by the feeling of compassion makes your anxieties and tribulations my own, and who wishes to resist with you the adversaries of the Church of God, even, if necessary, to the shedding of blood.

### Letter III

To Rainard, most excellent bishop, Goffridus, humble servant of the monastery of Vendôme, sends greetings with the feeling of pure affection.

Your archdeacon Hubertus [Note: *Your archdeacon Hubertus.* Mentioned in several letters of Book V], a man of venerable life, who loves you greatly and, as I think, does not hate me greatly, concerned for your honor and our advantage, whenever he hears of matters that ought to separate us from mutual charity, immediately transfers all the blame onto my soul, either personally or through his messengers. He reproaches me so severely that I can scarcely endure the blows of his words with patience.

Most recently, in these days, he pierced my entrails with the sword of his mouth so deeply that he left almost no health in them. He claims that someone—I do not know whether you or one of your people—told him that at the council I had spoken against your peace and safety, not openly indeed but secretly.

If you say this, I do not dare refute your words, because you are a bishop. But whoever else makes himself an advocate of this charge should come openly, and he will find me a truthful corrector of his falsehood.

As I said, I can neither speak nor ought to speak anything against your greatness. Yet I firmly maintain one point: in law it is regarded as criminal to accuse a friend without cause, especially one who knows how to honor those who love him very happily, and to whom it has always been shameful to whisper anything secretly about his rivals.

Farewell.

### Letter IV

To Rainard, great and glorious bishop, Goffridus, servant of the monastery of Vendôme, sends the affection of pure love.

A certain servant of our church, whom we had long removed from our service because of a sacrilege he had committed, posed to us, after we had departed from you, a question worthy of the most sinister wonder.

He spoke of two men, one of whom was said to be a monk and the other a bishop. The bishop came to the monk’s place and wished to lodge with him. The monk received him with joy and honor, and offered not only his possessions but also himself, with complete devotion, for the bishop’s service.

The monk would have wished the bishop to remain there longer, had the bishop consented. The bishop departed. As he left, the monk assigned one of his servants to accompany him, and the servant performed the office of serving him for as long as he wished.

The bishop began speaking with the servant and questioning him about the life of his innocent host—not approving it as was proper, but condemning it. With whatever words he could, he attempted to cover with crust the vessel full of charity.

When we heard this, we replied that this was a new kind of crime, and that in a deed of new wickedness it was necessary to seek the counsel of our elders. Therefore we especially wish to question you and desire to hear what your greatness thinks about this.

It seems to our humility that he was not truly a bishop who pursued the work of such depravity. Nor did he behave carefully toward his neighbor, after whose food he belched forth such wickedness.

### Letter V

To Rainard, distinguished bishop of Angers, Goffridus, whatever kind of servant of the monastery of Vendôme, sends the desire to love humility, patience, and kindness, and to hate whatever is contrary to them.

By the authoritative teaching of Scripture we have learned, most beloved prelate in Christ, that no Christian—and therefore even less the priest of the Lord—ought to return evil for evil or, on any pretext, avenge personal injuries.

Since, then, returning evil for evil and avenging one’s injury is dangerous, there can be no doubt that returning evil for good, or without cause inflicting injuries upon a neighbor who loves us, is highly destructive.

We have set these things forth, venerable man, so that if we have sinned in one of these matters—or, what is more serious, in both—we may not be ashamed to correct the sin that we ought usefully to have avoided.

By divine grace, more than by our merits, we have been placed over the Church of God. If, then, placed in such dignity, we sin by hating one another, we not only fail to illuminate our own lamps, but also extinguish the lamps of others by the evil example of our conduct.

And while we carry a beam in our own eye, we cannot examine the splinter in another’s. If at times we speak to people about the good things we know, they do not follow the words they hear, but imitate only the examples of wickedness they see.

Human frailty is more inclined to imitate evil. If it is destroyed by our conduct—God forbid!—the Lord will require its blood from us.

Therefore, most beloved, we must not act hatefully toward one another, for we ought to be more useful than powerful and to be exceedingly concerned about rendering an account of the souls entrusted to our care.

And since we have received the name and order of holiness, we ought to enlighten the blind, not blind those who see. While we pursue one another with hatred and the sword of the tongue—which is criminal sin—we leave darkness to the world in place of light, and incite the people, who are already excessively inclined to sin, as we have said, to sin still more, with danger to our souls.

Certainly, in small matters we provoke the Lord more gravely by our sins than the people do in great matters. For there is almost as much difference between the sin of a shepherd and the sin of the people as there was between the sin of the angel and that of the first-formed man.

Hence it was truly said that the person who enjoys greater honor sins with greater guilt, and that the loftiness of dignities makes the vices of sinners more grievous.

Let us therefore not be reluctant for one of us to humble himself before the other, because it is written: “The greater you are, humble yourself in all things” (Ecclesiasticus 3:20). And God, who deceives no one, promised that the one who humbles himself more would be exalted more.

If one of us desires to have victory over the other, let him seek the victory that is recognized as belonging to the devil. To conquer by humility, patience, and kindness is God’s victory; to prevail through pride, impatience, and malice is the devil’s victory.

Of these two, let us fear what condemns, and embrace with all our inmost being what crowns us. Let us return to charity, which covers a multitude of sins (1 Peter 4:8), despising whatever separates us from it; for without charity it is condemnable to possess the other virtues, and with charity it is pardonable not to possess the others.

## Letter VI

To Rainard, bishop of honorable life, Goffridus, unworthy minister of the monastery of Vendôme, sends himself as a devoted son to a loving father and a faithful servant to a good lord.

Let your goodness know, excellent Father, that your servants’ servant came to Angers on a mare. Nor did he disdain to come to Angers on a mare, since he knew that his Savior and the Savior of all had come to Jerusalem on a donkey.

He had little ability—or willingness—to come; but the beauty of your letter drew him, while neither the harshness of the season nor any personal necessity could hold him back.

He came, therefore, and he came very weary. What wonder? He repeatedly endured incessant floods of rain and the splashing of marshes reaching almost to his very eyes.

Farewell, and consider how great a rest such labor deserves—a labor which, as I suppose, you make your own through the feeling of compassion.

## Letter VII

To Rainard, bishop of praiseworthy life, most dear lord and intimate friend, Goffridus, humble servant of the monastery of Vendôme, sends the resolve to ascend diligently against the adversary and faithfully set himself as a wall for the house of Israel.

Most beloved Father, amid evil rumors we have heard that your count [Note: *Your count.* Fulk V, Book I, Letter 3] wishes again to subject the holy Church—redeemed from the devil’s servitude by the precious blood of God and our Lord Jesus Christ—to the yoke of servitude.

Despising the reverence for honorable princes that they once strove to maintain around the Lord’s temple in both the Old and the New Law, he attempts by new and execrable customs to take away from the mother who spiritually gave him birth the charter of freedom written and sealed by the Savior’s own hands.

Therefore, if this is so—indeed, because we groan that it is so—you must be warned and strengthened by the authority of Christian law to destroy his rash attempts, by which he persecutes the members of Christ, and to cut away with the file of canonical discernment whatever has grown excessively in him, the son, to the injury of the universal mother.

But if, God forbid, you should see the Lord’s free bride—whom he entrusted to your faith to be guarded, as he entrusted his mother to blessed John (John 19:27)—being made a slave, and remain silent, then, burying the rights of divine law and justice, you have completely killed her, whom you ought to have raised from the dead.

It does not befit any Christian flock, and even less the shepherd of a flock, to bury as though dead the law and justice of Christ, which give life to the dead. Rather, such a shepherd in particular must proclaim the truth of justice, not keep silent about God’s law, and strive to overcome by the judgment and truth of the Holy Spirit whatever he sees attacking the freedom of the holy Church.

We would have written much more to you about this matter, were it the abbot’s duty to provoke a prince, and were it not presumptuous for an abbot to instruct a pontiff. Yet provocation is not proved culpable, and that presumption is pardonable which arises from hatred of iniquity and love of justice.

Farewell.

## Letter VIII

To the most beloved lord and friend, Lord Rainard, venerable bishop of Angers, Goffridus, servant of the monastery of Vendôme, sends the resolve to act truthfully and simply in all things.

The slander which the abbot of Saint Nicholas [Note: [Col. 0109D] The abbot of Saint Nicholas. Lambert, who succeeded Natalis in 1096. The monk’s name, however, was Savaric, as appears in the following letter. The monastery of Saint Nicholas at Juliomagus was situated in the suburb of Angers; its founder, as was briefly noted in Letter 26 of Book II, was Fulk III, count. We also mentioned his commentary, in which he explains the monastery’s origin and begins his narrative with these words: “At this time certain kings and princes undertook to build churches in the name of Christ. And I, Fulk, count of Anjou, although one of the last and most negligent of men, resolved, in God’s name and that of the supreme bishop, to build a church overlooking the city of Angers, and in the year 1020 from the Lord’s Incarnation I had it consecrated by Hubert, bishop of the aforesaid city. Not long after its consecration, I appointed as abbot one of the monks of the monastery of Saint Martin of Tours, named Baldric, and I took care to enrich it from my own possessions for the support of the brothers and of the poor, etc.” After Fulk the founder, his son Geoffrey Martel and his successor Fulk IV greatly increased this monastery’s possessions. At the request of the latter and of Abbot Natalis, we read in the letters of Urban II, dated at Sabloil on the sixteenth day before the Kalends of March in the year 1096, that the church of Saint Nicholas was dedicated anew by Urban himself.] brought against one of his monks—absent indeed, but absent because he himself had caused his absence—we have heard. And because he brought against him charges of sacrilege and seduction, as well as of dissipating his monastery, we cannot fail to know the facts, since we were present. In answer to these accusations, the monk, because he is a layman, replies not in Latin, which he has not learned, but in his mother tongue. He says that he is guilty only of this: that he obeyed the abbot when the abbot ordered him to absent himself. In every other respect, just as he admits himself guilty in this one matter alone, so he does not shrink from showing himself innocent in your court, and from showing that he was seduced rather than a seducer.

If this is true—indeed, since we have already learned in part that it is true—the abbot could neither reasonably be angry with us nor justly complain about us for supporting the cause of truth. Since Christ is truth, if we wish to remain in Christ, we must remain in truth and, if necessary, fight for the truth even unto death. The fact that the aforesaid abbot admonishes the monk in question to return and tries to keep under his authority the man whom he publicly accused without cause is prohibited, not commanded, by canonical reason, and monastic religion does not require it. For far be it that monastic religion should be found contrary to canonical truth!

In the secret records of the most holy former Pope Felix [Note: [Col. 0110D] The former Pope Felix. Much of this is read in the letter of Felix II to the bishops of the Alexandrian synod, Question 3, “On Delays.” Some things also seem to allude to the letter of the first Felix to Paternus. But if Geoffrey means Felix II, why does he call him “former”? If he means the first Felix, why does he place the Council of Nicaea earlier than him? Perhaps he wrote “the later one.” Moreover, since the decree of the Council of Nicaea does not occur among the decrees that survive today, it is uncertain where he found it.] it is written—and it is nevertheless found to have been established much earlier in the Council of Nicaea—that if anyone is accused of a crime, he should not be held in any custody of detention, but should be allowed complete freedom in every respect: namely, to repel the schemes of his accusers, prepare his responses, and seek the assistance of friends, until either he is convicted as guilty or released as innocent. If anyone presumes to act otherwise, then, according to the institutions of the holy canons, his action will have no validity at all and will be entirely without force.

## LETTER IX

To Lord Rainald, bishop of praiseworthy life, most beloved lord and intimate friend, Geoffrey, humble servant of the monastery of Vendôme, sends greetings with the affection of pure love.

[Col. 0111B] You instructed, most beloved lord, through our brother Robert [Note: [Col. 0111D] Our brother Robert. To him he also writes in Book IV, Letter 28.] that Lord Savaric should return to Abbot Lambert. Although you say this with good intention, nevertheless, with due reverence for your fatherhood, we say that it is unusual and is found nowhere in the entire body of the canons: that anyone should have to remain under the authority of one by whom he is accused of a crime.

We do not presume to teach you, most beloved Father, from whom we can and wish to be taught better. And since we have learned that it pleases you that the aforesaid brother should do what you have commanded, he does not refuse to obey your will. But he asks your sweetness and piety for something that can appear quite just and canonical and that no canonical principle ought to deny him; and we ask it with him: namely, that by the command of your authority he may remain in his monastery in such a way that he is not oppressed by any kind of condemnation or detention until he has his accuser present and is granted a suitable place for his defense, where he may be able to repel the criminal charge brought against him.

If the aforesaid abbot says that he has been stripped of his possessions, he certainly does not lie. Would that he attacked, persecuted, and branded his despoiler as gravely as he could, for then he would be the first to fall into the pit he prepared for his neighbor! He stripped himself, for when he accused his subject before a superior person, he placed what was his under another’s authority.

If he again demands obedience from the man against whom he drew the sword from the sheath of deadly infamy in order to strike him down, that abbot is foolish or mad, and he imitates the perversity of the apostate angel, who suggests to human beings that they should obey him while he pursues them toward death. Excellent Father, it is not safe to obey an evil, crafty shepherd who has already taken from the execution of the obedience imposed upon a disciple an argument against the disciple by means of a criminal accusation. [Col. 0112A] For that cruelly crafty shepherd commanded the simple sheep to hide itself, as it were, among the bushes, so that, with no one protesting, he might devour it in the manner of a wolf.

The good evangelical shepherd is recorded to have carried the weary sheep, not cast it away (Luke 15:5); and the one he found condemned, he freed—he did not condemn one who was free.

Farewell. And may the judgment of equity, O Father of great discernment, prevail with you on our behalf; may the innocence of the deceived monk prevail; may the sincerity of our heart, by which we love you, prevail; and, if our humility has ever deserved anything good from you, may that prevail as well.

## LETTER X

To Rainald, bishop of Angers, whom Brother Geoffrey loves in God, with pure affection of that same love.

You told our prior and Lord Hamelin [Note: [Col. 0111D] Our prior and Lord Hamelin. He writes to both of them in Book IV.] that you had gone to Rome as the adversary of our adversaries. Moreover, you had arranged to give one hundred librates [Note: [Col. 0111D] One hundred librates. Book II, Letter 30, and Letter 15 of this book mention two hundred librates, evidently of land. In a charter of Saint Louis, king, from the year 1230: “To our beloved and faithful John of Valeriac, as an increase of the fief that he held, we gave one hundred librates of land.” This was in Auvergne, at Escurolles and Maesium Scholae. Ancient surveyors divided complete measures of land, after the model of the as or libra, into ounces and fractions of ounces, as may be seen in Columella, Book V, chapter 1. Varro, On Agriculture, Book I, chapter 10: “From this beginning, surveyors sometimes say that an ounce of land, or a sixth, or something else, is in the surplus, when they have reached the jugerum. It contains 288 scruples, the same amount as an as.” Thus what was done in parts was also done by some with the whole, so that they gave complete measures of land the name of libra or solid as. They therefore called a librate of land a complete jugerum of land, an arapennis, or something similar. From the same principle they also spoke of a solidate of land. In a charter of Seguin, bishop of Mâcon, from the year 1260: “Since William of Oblato, knight, held sixty solidates of land in fief from the church of Cluny, etc.”] to our church, because I had served you well. But afterward you changed the disposition of your good intention, because I had greatly offended against you.

I know the service; I do not know the sin. Nor is this surprising, since no such sin is found in the devil’s charter: God does not hate it, no soul is condemned for it, and no one does penance for it. Perhaps the fact that I served well and often is reckoned to me as a sin, and thus evil is repaid for good and hatred for my love. God certainly does not teach this repayment but forbids it, and whoever pursues it tries to surpass the devil in wickedness. For the devil seems to judge more justly than that man: the devil acts by repaying only evil for evil, whereas that man repays evil to us.

For my services I sought, and seek, no other reward than your affection. Some undeserving people quickly find it, while others, although they deserve it quite worthily, either never attain it or suddenly lose it. I say this, God knows, not with a bitter spirit. If it does not displease you that which ought least to displease you, let me be heard, and I shall prove what has been said by a true proposition.

## LETTER XI

To Rainald, prudent and exalted by wealth of many kinds, Brother Geoffrey, humble servant of the monastery of Vendôme, sends greetings and wishes that he carefully observe Christian law and hate no one because of an assertion of truth.

You told our brother Lord H. [Note: [Col. 0113B] Lord H., Hamelin, as in the preceding letter.] that I had opposed you in your election [Note: [Col. 0113B] In your election. Geoffrey will again discuss Rainald’s episcopal election, which he opposed on many grounds, in Book IV, Letter 9. Hildebert attacks the same election in three letters: Letter 9 to the archbishop of Tours, and Letters 12 and 13 to Rainald himself, whom he advises to renounce his uncanonical promotion. Marbod likewise discusses it in a letter to Rainald.]. Such was the way you chose to speak to your greatness; but it greatly displeased my littleness that I should know this to be contrary to the rules of the canons and the constitutions of the holy Fathers.

When I saw the one and unique door of the holy Church being closed, and another door being opened elsewhere, through which those who enter are thieves and robbers (John 10:1), I saw apostolic teaching violated and the holy Gospel utterly despised. Had this pleased me, I would not have been Christ’s servant but the devil’s. Yet, as I think, what can rather be imputed to your dean Stephen [Col. 0113B] and the persons who were present ought not to be imputed to me alone as a crime [Note: [Col. 0113C] Your dean Stephen. Letters 4 and 5 of Book V are addressed to him and others. Marbod and Hildebert also discuss him in the letters already mentioned. Since the words of both illuminate this entire passage, we shall append them. Hildebert writes in that letter as follows: “Your request, by which we are summoned to the consecration of your elected man, would easily find our agreement if reason supported it. But those who were present testify that the pontifical election was twisted toward a young man found below the sacred orders and the required age, who had not been elected by the clergy, by the seditious shouting of a disturbed crowd. The dean also asserts that the cantor, the archdeacons, and the greater part of the chapter protested as far as they were able and likewise withdrew their assent from such undertakings for good reason, presenting themselves there because of fear.” And again, Letter 12: “For the clergy did not elect you; popular threats thrust you in despite your resistance.” Thus far Hildebert. Marbod continues: “Nor, once I had escaped, did I cease to press my proposal, as I then thought, steadfastly, but as I now understand, obstinately; and to assert the grounds of your promotion against the best of the clergy, who for several reasons disapproved, without their assent, of an election made by the populace, since it was made below the required age, outside the orders, and amid a popular tumult, so that it was more fabricated than accomplished.” Concerning Stephen, a little later: “When this same Stephen, together with certain men whom you afterward made your friends—having, as is said, bargained for my deposition—was crying out against it, I, foolishly and imprudently, but led astray by your excessive favor, devoted myself. ‘Let this iniquity be upon me,’ I said.”].

Everyone opposed and rejected the election which you say was yours. Nor was this without reason; for, against their will and without their seeking it, you were seized by the populace, and what happened there was the work of a presumptuous and pernicious sedition. We neither can nor ought to remain silent about what we saw and heard.

In that action—or rather, in that conspiracy of the populace, which you regard as an election—the law was silent as though amid weapons; the divine voice had no place. There, levity and vanity claimed everything, where a certain actress and public woman, who noisily acclaimed you, was able to do more than the maturity of the people or clerical dignity.

Hence Hildebert [Note: [Col. 0113D] Hildebert. At this time archbishop of Tours; but when Rainald was elected, he was still bishop of Le Mans. See Letter 13 and those following.]—a religious man who was the first bishop in the province after the metropolitan [Note: [Col. 0113D] He was the first bishop in the province after the metropolitan. He was, of course, bishop of Le Mans. Among the bishops of the same province, the first was sometimes considered to be the one whose city held second place after the metropolitan city and was listed second after it in the provincial register. Fulbert uses this prerogative as an argument in his letter to Deodatus, bishop of Soissons: “But so that you may not deny the city or Church of Châlons its proper honor, you ought to remember that in the ancient description of the province of Belgica, that city holds second place after Rheims. Therefore, just as in Belgica II the city of Châlons is next to the metropolitan city of Rheims, so in the third province of Lyon the city of Le Mans is first after the metropolitan city of Tours. For this reason the bishop of Le Mans is the first bishop of that province.” In the same way, in Aquitania I the first bishop was the bishop of Clermont; in Aquitania II, the bishop of Poitiers; and so in the other provinces. In another sense, the first among the bishops of a province is said to be the one who precedes the others by seniority of honor; he was also customarily called the primate, as we learn from a letter of Pope Hilary. Thus he writes to the bishops of the province of Vienne and others: “From the one who is now permitted to preside over the Church of Narbonne, we have removed the power of ordaining bishops because of the wicked things that have been done. We have judged that this power should belong to our brother and fellow bishop Constantius, bishop of the Church of Uzès, because he is said to be first in seniority of honor; so that, if Bishop Herme should die while he is alive, this responsibility will fall to the man whom the episcopal order finds to be primate—that is, the oldest of the bishops of the province, who customarily sits and subscribes before the others in council,” according to the Council of Chalon, canon 6. But Saint Gregory, by a special privilege granted in favor of Syagrius, bishop of Autun, decreed in Book VII, Letter 112, that the bishop of that Church should hold first place in the province of Lyon I after the metropolitan; all the others should follow him, each according to the date and prerogative of his own ordination.] did not remain silent. Although summoned by his metropolitan [Note: [Col. 0114D] Summoned by his metropolitan. By Ralph, archbishop of Tours. This confirms what we noted shortly before: that Hildebert’s Letter 9, which bears no title, was written in reply to this Ralph, since Ralph had summoned him to Rainald’s consecration. Hildebert declines the summons and closes the letter with these words: “May the Father forgive me, because I shall spare my own soul; in vain, I say, will you await me, for you will lay on hands without me.”], he absented himself from your consecration and proclaimed, on the authority of apostolic and evangelical truth, that it was a curse rather than a consecration.

The good Maurilius [Note: [Col. 0114D] The good Maurilius. Life of Saint Maurilius, chapter 13.], whom you boast was your predecessor, was elected and consecrated when blessed Martin chose him and the Holy Spirit marked him out [Col. 0114B]. But you were created while the populace raged and canonical election was despised. The man who does not receive the lot of election and goodness that his good predecessor received boasts of that predecessor in vain. The goodness of another in no way assists one who remains in crime, and a bishop without canonical election [Note: [Col. 0114D] A bishop without canonical election. This entire passage on canonical election, and the following passage on lay investiture [Col. 0115D], are read word for word in the treatise addressed to Cardinal Peter of León, where both subjects are treated systematically.] is like a tree without a root.

A tree without roots, even if it has leaves, cannot bear fruit at all. Christ came to such a tree, and when he found no fruit there, he cursed it (Mark 11:13–14).

The entire ordination of a bishop consists in election alone and in consecration, provided that a proper election has preceded it. Christ first carried out these acts himself, and afterward his vicars. In the apostles they were carried out by Christ, since they were elected and consecrated by him; but for all others no one may perform them except Christ’s vicars. The clerics are Christ’s vicars in election, and bishops in consecration. All the rest may indeed request a bishop, but they may neither elect nor consecrate one.

Whoever, therefore, presumes in any other manner, as though under the name of a bishop, to claim the Church or ecclesiastical power for himself, no longer enters through the door but climbs in from elsewhere, so that he rightly should not be counted among bishops but numbered among thieves and robbers (John 10:1).

I must not be silent about the investiture that you received from the hand of a layman through the pastoral staff, nor speak of it without grief, since this was not done secretly but publicly, to the greater injury of the holy Church. Anyone who wishes to know what the catholic and apostolic Church has thought, taught, judged, and established concerning investiture should read the first chapter of the council held in the time of Pope Gregory VII. There he will find that all clerics who receive investiture from the hand of a layman were called heretics and therefore condemned and excommunicated.

Although one heresy is called investiture and another Simony, the heresy called investiture strikes more forcefully against the holy Church. For there the entire ecclesiastical order is first thrown into confusion, when what ought to be given to each person in the Church by his consecrator, with the prayers appropriate to the occasion, is first received from secular power.

The holy apostles not only forbade this; they also condemned, with the power entrusted to them by Christ, all those who obtain the Church through secular authority. And rightly, by the judgment of the Holy Spirit, the apostles resolved to condemn this heresy at the very beginning of the Church, since they foresaw that it would be born long afterward from the father of the devil.

Since, therefore, the Holy Spirit who spoke in the apostles entirely denied and forbade to a layman both investiture and every power of disposing ecclesiastical affairs, whoever receives investiture from a layman is now acting not merely against the apostles but against the Lord of the apostles; he exposes what is holy to dogs.

The investiture of which we speak is a sacrament—that is, a sacred sign—by which the prince of the Church, namely the bishop, is separated and distinguished from other men, and by which pastoral care over the Christian flock is entrusted to him [Col. 0116A]. He ought to receive this investiture from the one alone from whom he receives consecration. He must first be consecrated and then adorned, as the leader of the Church, with sacred insignia.

Anyone who thinks that this is permitted to any secular power is mistaken. If he tries to defend it, he desires to nullify the teaching of the apostles and the mind of the Holy Spirit; hence there is no doubt that he is a heretic.

Moreover, if it is rightly considered, this heresy of investiture is also proved by living and true reasoning to be the heresy of Simony. For what investiture is the secular power trying to claim, unless it is in order either to extort money or, more seriously, to make the bishop’s person subject to it in an improper manner? No layman, even if it were permitted to him, would desire to give a ring or staff with such intention unless, through these things—which are sacraments of the Church—he were eager for temporal profit.

Laymen may indeed receive the sacraments from the Church, but they may not give the Church’s sacraments. The ring and the staff, when they are given by those by whom they ought to be given, and at the time, place, and manner in which they ought to be given, are sacraments of the Church, just as salt, water, and certain other things are, without which the consecrations of human beings and churches cannot take place.

As we have said, a layman always claims for himself through investiture either money or, what is more serious, the person of a bishop or abbot. By this malignity, which is not so much human as diabolical, the catholic Church loses faith, freedom, and chastity, without which it cannot subsist in any way. The Church must always possess these three; if even one of them is lacking, it lies like a paralytic and has no power to bind or loose.

Whoever, therefore, presumes to assume the Church under the appearance of a shepherd becomes a paralytic polluted by heretical leprosy. I confidently declare that he is not a shepherd, nor any member of that Shepherd who laid down his life for his sheep (John 10:11). He is a thief, robber, and wolf, for he has come in order to steal, seize, and slaughter (ibid., 10).

Those who commit this detestable impiety are condemned, as are those who consent to it. One consents who keeps silent about it, who does not correct it, and who does not openly oppose it. No one is exempt from the duty and ability to oppose it openly. For even if someone lacks the authority of a prelate, he nevertheless possesses the voice of a Christian. Scripture says—and excludes no one—“Cursed is he who restrains the sword from blood” (Jeremiah 48:10), that is, who restrains his voice from rebuking sin.

Let him also remember that once a she-ass corrected a foolish prophet (Numbers 22:28). If he is vicious or has become infamous through any other crime, he should not for that reason remain silent, since every sinner may defend the common faith of the Church, which he believes and confesses to be his own, and may freely fight against its adversaries.

Those two men who were crucified with the Lord in his passion were entirely infamous, for they were public robbers. One of them deserved to hear that good and delightful word from our Savior—“Today you will be with me in paradise” (Luke 23:43)—not merely because he believed, but because he began to defend the truth of his faith against the other. Thus it is especially revealed in that robber that the defense of the faith merits paradise and being with Christ.

I have judged it worthwhile to recall to your eminence these few things from among many which you have perhaps consigned to oblivion, so that you may no longer be permitted to remain ignorant of where and how you took up the name of bishop. I remain silent about those matters which the lord pope knows and has forgiven, because it is not my task to reopen what he himself has done. For he knew that your life had not been approved in any way by religious discipline, that you were below the required age [Note: [Col. 0117C] That you were below the required age. Hildebert, Letter 9: “Found below the sacred orders and the required age.” The same writer, Letter 12: “There is an age which canonical rigor, because it fears for those who have been consecrated, excludes from those to be consecrated.” And shortly afterward: “In the highest priests a mature age is required, so that religion may fear no danger and dignity lose none of its reverence.”], and that you possessed no order at all [Note: [Col. 0117C] That you possessed no order at all. Hildebert, in the same Letter 12: “You lack the orders which we have recognized must be sought in those who are to be promoted.” And later: “Furthermore, whoever has not been found to belong to the sacred orders is forbidden by the canonical institutions of the Church to approach the supreme priesthood.” Ecclesiastical laws concerning the election of bishops require not merely orders but sacred orders, at least the diaconate. The Council of Arvernes, canon 5: “Let no layman, cleric, or mere subdeacon be elected to the episcopate.” Indeed, they considered only that man worthy of the highest rank who had long before been tested in each of the lower orders. Under this description our Sidonius commends John, bishop of Chalon, in Book IV, Letter 25, because he had served through each order, having occupied the rank of lector, deacon, and priest of the second order, that is, presbyter.].

At first you scorned to receive the orders, so that you might more freely exercise things that are in no way permitted for the salvation of the soul. Later you received all the orders, but without order, since you received them within eight days and not at the appointed times, because of your ambition for the episcopate. Thus it is proved by a true proposition that you received them out of love of temporal glory, not from love of Christ.

Whoever is not joined to the Church’s sacraments by the cement of charity indeed injures the Church, but is scattered like a mud wall. Although such a wall may be whitewashed for a time, those who had been sitting upon it are crushed by its sudden collapse.

From this comparison it is rightly concluded that whoever attains an ecclesiastical order, and especially the episcopate, to the injury of the holy Church first brings about his own destruction and then the death of the people. The Church suffers both injury and shame when canonical election perishes in the choice of a bishop, when what belongs only to one who has been properly ordained is given to one who is not properly ordered, and when one who has not been called by God is placed in authority but is violently thrust in by the populace.

Nothing is more serious in Christ’s sight than injury to the Church, whose sacraments those who perversely receive cannot share with Christ or make beneficial. No one can be with Christ and act against Christ, since he himself says: “Whoever is not with me is against me” (Luke 11:23). Whoever is not with Christ can benefit neither himself nor others, since he again declares: “Whoever does not gather with me scatters” (ibid.). And elsewhere he says: “Without me you can do nothing” (John 15:5).

For this reason I have written these things to your affection: while preserving our proper order, I have made peace with you; and I would not have preserved our order if I had kept this truth silent from you.

Farewell, and seek and love not what is yours but what belongs to Jesus Christ (Philippians 2:21).

## LETTER XII

To Lord Ulger, venerable bishop of Angers [Note: [Col. 0117D] Ulger. He succeeded Archbishop Rainald in the see of Angers, as was stated in the final letter of Book I; he governed that see for only twenty-three years, namely from 1125 to 1148. His work is an epitaph, composed in thirty elegiac verses, on the tomb of Marbod, bishop of Rennes, at Saint-Albin in Juliomagus. Saint Bernard’s Letter 200 was written to Ulger.], Brother Geoffrey, called abbot, sends greetings and affection in Christ.

I have been told that you brought a complaint against me in your synod [Note: [Col. 0118C] In your synod. Book I, Letter 27.]. But I wonder whether this is so, for I have offended your goodness in nothing. If you despoiled our monastery—Saint Peter’s freehold and patrimony—of possessions which it had long held peacefully and which had been confirmed to it by apostolic authority, I do not believe that I sin or have sinned in this matter.

If you did not wish to examine the privileges of the holy Roman pontiffs when they were presented to you for inspection, I neither can nor ought to be blamed for that. If the legate of the Roman Church [Note: [Col. 0118D] The legate of the Roman Church. Gerard, bishop of Angoulême, Letter 27.] ordered you to show due reverence to the privileges of the apostolic see and to restore what your eminence had taken from us, and if you observed neither instruction, our humility incurred no fault thereby.

You announced, it is said, to your priests and to the persons of your Church that the lord Pope Urban [Note: [Col. 0118D]

That the lord Pope Urban. The same letter. By common law all churches are subject to the ordination and authority of bishops: Council of Orléans I, canon 19; Council of Chalon, canon 10; and frequently elsewhere. Many people, however, used formerly to offer to monasteries churches founded by themselves or belonging to their own jurisdiction, so that these churches might be under the monasteries’ authority. Since this could not be done without the bishops’ consent, bishops sometimes granted churches to monks on the condition that at fixed intervals—namely, whenever the vicars or “persons,” as they were called, of those churches were changed—they would pay the bishops a fixed sum of money, which was called the redemption of altars. Urban prohibited this as wicked and Simoniacal in the Council of Arvernes. After the council, however, there were bishops who demanded annual payments in place of that redemption, which had occurred at intervals of many years. Among these were Ulger, bishop of Angers, in the present passage, and Ivo of Chartres and Rannulf of Saintes, whom Paschal II rebuked for this practice. The following letter of Paschal is preserved in the archives of Vendôme:

“Paschal, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to the venerable bishops Ivo of Chartres and Rannulf of Saintes, greetings and apostolic blessing.

“According to the sanctions of the holy canons, we believe that it is not unknown to you what punishment awaits members of the ecclesiastical order who despise the decrees of the apostolic see. You yourselves attended the Council of Arvernes, in which, with our predecessor Pope Urban of blessed memory presiding and the bishops of Gaul sitting with him, it was decreed that the altars which monasteries are known to have possessed for thirty years and under the redemption of vicars should henceforth remain securely with those monasteries, without any disturbance. But you attach duplicities inconsistent with this simplicity and try to extort the redemption of persons under changed names. It is fitting, however, that we oppose such tricks with the sincerity of apostolic truth. Therefore we command that that decree be observed fully and intact, and that you demand nothing further for those same altars. Indeed, what we command you, we also command all the other bishops of Gaul to observe with regard to the monasteries of their dioceses. Given at Rome, on the second day before the Ides of March.”

From this letter of Paschal and from Geoffrey’s words it is possible to understand what kind of synodal decree Urban issued concerning vicars, to which the end of the letter refers. Until now, however, it has not come to light.]

At the Council of Arvernus he had ordered that bishops receive an annual payment from monks for the redemption of altars. Your prudence knows very well that it is not right to preach the opposite of what is arranged with apostolic sincerity.

“Good lord, you were not present at that council; I was, and I know the truth of this matter. That redemption of churches which in the vernacular is called ‘altars,’ that blessed man called simoniacal wickedness and condemned it by apostolic authority. Yet that magical and simoniacal money was paid to bishops sometimes over thirty years, sometimes over forty, and sometimes even over sixty. But he who called the redemption of altars—which in most cases used to be made only once over many years through vicars—a heresy, and condemned it, taught that no annual payment should be extorted under the name of an annual census for the redemption of vicars, 124 or of altars; rather, he confirmed by the authority of the blessed apostles Peter and Paul that everything which abbots and monks had held in churches under the redemption of vicars should henceforth be possessed securely and without any exaction of money.

“For if, as has been said, money for altars was paid to bishops through vicars only once over many years, and that very payment has been proved by apostolic authority to be simony, what else is it to give bishops money every year for the vicars of altars than to practice, year by year under the name of a census, annual simony in exchange for the simony of many years? This is not the teaching of Christian faith, but a most wicked exaction that multiplies simony and violates the chastity of the holy Church.

“Therefore, money extorted for churches under the disguise of greed—which is called the redemption of altars—has been condemned by the Apostolic See. Whether it is extorted more rarely through vicars or more frequently for vicars, under whatever name or pretext, there can be no doubt that it is simoniacal wickedness; yet that form is the graver which is practiced more often. For this reason the Catholic Christian must especially avoid it, and the bishop must detest it above all, lest the last error become worse than the first.

“I have asked and warned you once, twice, and three times—indeed, repeatedly—and still, with the humility I ought to show and am able to show, I earnestly ask and warn you to let your greatness not delay returning what you have taken from us. Otherwise, since our brothers cannot endure your burdens any longer, they and we with them appeal to the Roman Church, although we have no doubt that you have often shown contempt for both it and its legates.

“And lest you doubt any further about the decree concerning vicars, we are sending you a transcript of it.

“Farewell.”

## Letter XIII

To Hildebert,[Col. 0120C] venerable bishop of the Cenomanni, Goffrid, an unworthy servant of the monastery of Vendôme, [Col. 0120B] neither turning to the right nor to the left, but keeping to the straight path.

**Note: Hildebert.** His letters and other short works survive. He succeeded Hoël in the see of Le Mans [Col. 0120D] in the year 1097. After relinquishing it, he later succeeded Gillebert at Tours in the year 1025, a man outstanding in the episcopate. Before him, as Ivo indicates in Letter 277, he had led a more relaxed life. Whoever obstinately denies that this letter was written about the Hildebert under discussion here, I think, would wish to be believed with his eyes closed. For what other election of a bishop of Le Mans occurred in Ivo’s time than that of Hildebert? We also know that he was raised from the rank of archdeacon—as Ivo notes—to the episcopal see. I do not argue this way in order to disparage the name of the learned man who held the contrary view, but because I judge that I owe it to Cardinal Baronius—whose memory is immortal—to strive, as far as I can, that what he said rightly and truly should be accepted as true.

If you seek those who belong to the Lord, so that they may be joined to you, behold, you have us ready. We also confess that we are sons of Abraham, and we desire to do his works. We do not fear to stand in battle on the Lord’s day and to set ourselves as a wall before the house of Israel, wherever the place shall be safe or suitable.

But we neither can nor ought to go to Tours, and we emphatically advise you against going there. For there all the agents of Rainald[Col. 0120D] will gather, ready to deal with you by fury and sedition rather than by reason.

**Note: All the agents of Rainald.** The elected bishop of Angers; see Letter 11.

That man also who summoned you there[Col. 0120D] thinks either that he can more easily overturn your justice there by the crowd’s untimely shouting, or bend you by entreaty or payment to consent to his folly—which God forbid!

You have begun well, since you have risen manfully on behalf of the liberty of the holy Church against its adversaries. By this you have made yourselves more dear to God and to the friends of God, and have spread the reputation of your name by no small amount. It will be a great honor for you in every respect if you act steadfastly, but a great disgrace if you fail.

Farewell; and believe truly that we shall be with you against Rainald and his supporters. Be so kind as to come on Friday as far as Château-du-Loir[Col. 0121C] or as far as Carcer,[Col. 0121D] so that there we may speak and confer with one another about this and other matters.

**Note: Château-du-Loir.** A town on the borders of Tours and Le Mans, but in the territory and diocese of the latter. The old history of Hildebert’s life calls it the Castle of the Lide; it relates that he withdrew there after the city was captured by Henry, king of the English [Col. 0121D]. “The Lide,” therefore, is the river which others call the Lidus or Ledus, as Sidonius does in his panegyric of Majorian.

**Note: As far as Carcer.** The name of a town mentioned in Letters 16 and 27 of this book.

## Letter XIV

To Hildebert, bishop of blessed life, his dearest lord and friend, Goffrid, an insignificant servant of the monastery of Vendôme: affection and the service of affection.

Since you did not consent to the unlawful election,[Col. 0121D] I give thanks for your goodness; and no one who loves God with a perfect heart refuses to do so with me.

**Note: The unlawful election.** That of Rainald of Angers, discussed in Letter 11.

Our reputation must in no way be diminished or harmed on account of the capture of the bishop of Rennes.[Col. 0121D] This was not done through me; nor did I know that he was to be captured by those who seized him. My enemies regard me as suspect in this matter, since they have always found me opposed to their wickedness. And because they cannot harm me by their deeds, they attempt and desire to do so by lying words. I call God as witness that I neither fear nor have ever feared their poisonous words; with Christ protecting me, whether they wish it or not, I shall be a source of fear to them as long as I live.

**Note: The capture of the bishop of Rennes.** Marbod; he was captured by the opposing party while imprudently favoring Rainald’s election. Thus he writes to Rainald, who later repaid Marbod with the worst kind of gratitude:

“For I suffered imprisonment and chains because of you, as I hurried to you when summoned at the beginning of that election of yours. This was brought about by the contrivance of that Stephen who now pleases you—as though fortune had then already foretold and forestalled it, so that I should desist from an ill-omened undertaking.”

Apart from Ulger, who wrote his epitaph, Rivallon, archdeacon of Rennes, expressed the outstanding virtues of this holy prelate in the following verses:

> He gave intelligence to make him wise, and a tongue eloquent;  
> A mind mindful, and vigilance attentive to the flock;  
> Long age made him an old man, grace of character a pleasant one;  
> Rank made him a bishop, and religion made him holy;  
> Sobriety made him sparing toward himself, generosity lavish  
> Toward the poor, and the rule of justice upright.  
> He was the Church’s foundation, bearing its burden; and at once  
> In gentleness an ox, in fierceness a lion.

For, as Ulger wrote in the epitaph:

> He was gentle toward the peaceful and stern toward the arrogant.

I nevertheless gladly do what you have commendably instructed me to do, and I shall never depart from your counsel. I neither can nor ought to doubt your affection.

## Letter XV

To Hildebert, bishop of the Cenomanni, Goffrid, unworthy minister of the monastery of Vendôme: to love justice and hate iniquity.

We have complained to you many times, and still complain, about the countess of Vendôme, who unjustly took from us the church of Savigny[Col. 0122D] and everything we possessed there, both movable and immovable, and has always held it by force. She seized our grain, which was kept in the chests in that church, after breaking open the chests themselves, and distributed it among the impious men who were with her.

**Note: The church of Savigny.** See Letter 21, “the church of Savigny.”

Your archpriest[Col. 0122D] told us, apparently on your behalf, to go to your court and submit to judgment concerning all these matters. We believed that this had been devised by him rather than commanded by you, since it does not seem just or canonical that anyone who has been stripped of his property should be judged before he has been restored to possession.

**Note: Your archpriest.** Peter, in the following letter.

We do not presume to teach you in this matter; rather, we have always desired to be taught by you. We would also gladly have come to your court if we could have obtained a safe-conduct, which we requested from the cleric mentioned above. For we endure many enemies—not because we wish to take away what belongs to them, but because we do not wish to grant them what we possess.

Ulric of Saint-Calais[Col. 0122D] and his knights have taken much of our property from us. We have therefore heard that you placed them under an interdict from divine worship. But how they were later released we do not know, because of what we lost we have recovered absolutely nothing.

**Note: Ulric of Saint-Calais.** Now the name of a family; elsewhere the name of the monastery of Anisole, as in the letters of Bishop Theodoric: “Ebrard, abbot of Saint-Calais.” It was also called the Castle or the town of Cajani. It formerly lay on the borders of Le Mans and Chartres, where Saint Carilefus founded a monastery at the river Anisola under King Childebert, leaving his name to the monastery, the castle, and the lords of the castle. Today it is called Saint-Calais.

We also say this truthfully, with due regard for your reverence: since, as we believe, God appointed you bishop, we have lost more than two hundred pounds’ worth in your episcopate, and since then we have obtained through your justice nothing worth twenty shillings. Yet we have committed this offense only by serving you and loving you. Perhaps this is how you know how to bless your friends. If so, you have discovered a new kind of blessedness. We have learned neither to bless you nor our friends with such a blessedness, nor do we wish to be blessed by you in this way.

Farewell; and recall to mind that “the wounds of a friend are better than the deceitful kisses of an enemy” (Proverbs 27:6).

## Letter XVI

[Col. 0122C]

To Hildebert, bishop of the Cenomanni, Goffrid, servant of the monastery of Vendôme: greetings.

The countess, just as you yourself commanded, offered us justice in your court, and still offers it. On this account it seemed to us that you were defending a large part of her injustice, since neither statement is true, except insofar as you assert that it is true.

For we have not yet seen or heard anyone from that countess’s side offering us justice. We know only that your archpriest Peter announced on your behalf that you would do us justice concerning her,[Col. 0123A] but he either did not know or did not wish to say where or when.

You are greatly surprised that we sought a safe-conduct; and certainly it would be greatly surprising if this could not rather be attributed to your weakness than to our fear. For who can fail to fear you while you are bishop in your episcopate? We have seen your parishioners avoid you out of fear and flee as though from enemies; it was shameful to see.

If you are surprised, you can certainly be surprised at this: that no one anywhere dares confidently promise security to anyone else. It was not our persons that we feared then, but our horses and servants. If any harm had befallen them, we would not have believed that we should receive more justice from you than we had received concerning our other property.

You commanded us to write to you precisely if you had failed us in any matter,[Col. 0123B] and you were ready to make good the deficiency. You spoke prudently in this, if you do not nullify your words by your deeds. But in what matters you have failed us, we cannot specify more accurately according to the truth of the case than by confessing: in everything about which we have repeatedly asked you until now.

For this reason we are astonished—and in our astonishment grieve—that you have forgotten the promise and intention which you made once and again in our chapter. You should not have allowed this, too, to fall so suddenly from your memory, since once you came to Vendôme to make a complaint before the count about Sigebrand;[Col. 0123D] and for your sake we stirred the count and countess to anger against us, by no means refusing to incur their hostility out of love for you.

**Note: Concerning Bishop Gratus.** It is surprising that Goffrid could have been unaware that Gratus was bishop of Carthage, since this could have been taught not only by the First Council of Carthage, over which he presided, but also by the Council of Sardica, to which he subscribed. But evidently, in the book of canons where he had seen the name of Bishop Gratus prefixed, the name of the city over which he presided was not read.

Then, for your sake, we offended the countess,[Col. 0123C] from whom—and because of whom—you have now, undeservedly, delayed justice for us, and still delay it.

We have heard mention made in the book of canons of Bishop Gratus, but we are completely ignorant of who he was. But who the ungrateful bishop is, or where he comes from, what his worth is, and how he lives, we cannot conceal, since he has revealed it himself.

If what we have said burdens you in any way, attribute it not to us but to yourself, since you were the first to pour out undisciplined words against us—not indeed from a judgment of equity, but from love of a woman.

My lord bishop, you should have remembered that we loved you greatly, served you greatly, and shall serve you greatly in the future. We sang well for you, insofar as we could, and waited for you to dance for us. But while we waited for you to give the dance in accordance with our song,[Col. 0123D] you directed against us certain bitter words written in ironic expression.[Col. 0124A]

Now we have come to know you truly as slow toward us, but swift and ready in deeds and words against us. Therefore, by the brotherhood that joins us, we ask you—and in asking, admonish you—to hasten to correct what you have shown less of justice and affection toward our monastery and your own.

It is neither necessary for us nor useful to you to be separated from the charity with which we have always loved you sincerely on account of the unjust case of the woman mentioned above. We have been and remain ready to receive justice from her in your court; and for this purpose we shall meet you at Mont-Aure,[Col. 0123D] or at Carcer,[Col. 0124D] or at Sées.[Col. 0124D]

**Note: At Mont-Aure.** That town lies below Vendôme, on the opposite bank of the Lide.

**Note: At Carcer.** Below Mont-Aure, on the left bank of the same river, not far from the Castle of the Lide and the borders of Tours, Carcer is a not insignificant fortress of the diocese of Le Mans. The Chronicle of Saint-Aubin relates that it was captured by Fulk VI in the year 1004:

> After not many days, when Count Fulk could not accomplish what he wished, he made peace with his son Geoffrey Martel; and in the following year they captured the fortress of Carcer together and burned the great and most noble fortress of Thouars.

Today it is called Chartré, which in the vernacular of our ancestors means Carcer. Thus, just as the people of Paris call the church of Saint-Denis de Chartra the place where that prison was, so the natives call the fortress Chartré, or Saint-Vincent de Chartré; for Goffrid, it is Carcer.

**Note: At Sées.** The name is still retained, together with the title of a county, in the territory of Le Mans, on the river Sarthe, which also flows past the chief city of the Cenomanni.

We neither can nor wish to go to Le Mans, because we fear burdening you, and because you once instructed us not to come to you with a crowd of servants. But believe me: it seemed less surprising to me that, in a place where no one can be safe, we sought a safe-conduct than it would have been surprising if we had crossed such long stretches of land without the company of servants.

We wished to carry out justice against Hilgot and Vulgrin, about whom you wrote to us, and we desire to receive the same from them.

Farewell. You should know beyond doubt that John the Mason,[Col. 0124D] our monk, whom you have with you, was excommunicated by us on account of his iniquity.

**Note: John the Mason.** Letter 25.

## Letter XVII

To Hildebert, bishop of good life, Goffrid, servant of the monastery of Vendôme: greetings.

We have heard and know that Hamelin of Mont-Aure,[Col. 0124D] excommunicated by you and by the legate[Col. 0124D] of the Roman Church for the wrongs he had done us, was absolved without any satisfaction being made to us.

**Note: Hamelin of Mont-Aure.** Here this is a family name, not a place of origin, as also in Book I, Letter 19: Peter of Mont-Aure, concerning Hamelin again in the following letter.

Therefore we earnestly beseech your goodness either to restore promptly what he took from us, or to subject him again to the excommunication which he appears unlawfully to have escaped, lest what is known to have been done against him by you and by the vicar of the Apostolic See be rendered void.

## Letter XVIII

To Hildebert, bishop of praiseworthy life, his beloved Father in Christ, Goffrid, the least of the servants of the monastery of Vendôme: always to live blessedly and not to believe every spirit.

You have learned, as you instructed us, that your cleric H. restored to himself the communion from which he had been barred because our brothers refused to receive justice from him. These brothers deny in truthful words that they did this for that reason, and affirm that neither justice nor security that justice would be done to them was offered.

Therefore, with due regard for your peace, we say that it distresses us that you have learned such things; it grieves us that you have sent such instructions; and it utterly troubles us that you have believed these clerics of yours in matters by which they both take away from us what is ours through their continued postponement and act wholly contrary to canonical rules.

For it is established, as you yourself know better, in the decrees of the Fathers[Col. 0125D] that ecclesiastical judges must take the greatest care not to pronounce sentence in the absence of the person whose case is being heard.

**Note: In the decrees of the Fathers.** Below, in Letter 33, these are the words attributed to Pope Zephyrinus, addressed to the bishops of Gaul, in *Decretum* III, question 9: “Let the judges of the Church beware lest, in the absence of the person whose case is being debated, they pronounce sentence, for it will be invalid.”

And just as punishment of condemnation does not immediately follow an accused person in his absence, so an excommunicated[Col. 0125B] or interdicted person ought not to obtain the remedy of absolution while the person who suffered his injury protests.[Col. 0125D]

**Note: While he protests.** That is, unless he has satisfied the opposing party. Thus, in Book I, Letter 30, he made a similar complaint to Radulf of Tours because he had absolved Harduin of Mailly without prior satisfaction. Ivo, Letter 38: “Those whom I cannot reconcile without satisfaction, I ought not to send into battle while excommunicated.”

Since these things are so, we are greatly surprised by what means H. is said to have been absolved, when our injuries against him still cry out and still make complaint. It is no less surprising if anyone attempts to absolve—or already holds as absolved—the man whom the Roman Church holds bound by the bond of excommunication.

Nor ought he lawfully to have been absolved, or granted a delay, under the name of justice, which he is said to have offered. For once someone has been expelled from the Church at the bishop’s command, he is not permitted to be reconciled by dispute or any other pretext, but only by satisfaction. You are not, as we believe, unaware that this was defined in this way by the Council of Toledo.

Let this suffice for the clerics, who, if they had truly feared God, would never have made his justice limp on both feet. But to your religious devotion, excellent prelate, we earnestly beseech you to put an end to our complaints and not delay any longer in restoring the justice that has been impaired by your clerics.

Farewell, and for the love of God come to the aid of us, your servants, lest, while justice is endangered, we lose everything in your diocese in this way.

## Letter XIX

To his lord and friend Hildebert, venerable bishop of the Cenomanni, Goffrid, servant of the monastery of Vendôme: reverence with affection.

Venerable prelate, when you and we were at Tours, you said that on one of the days of Easter week you would do us justice concerning the countess of Vendôme,[Col. 0125D] and you promised to inform us beforehand of the very day.

Since you either have not wished to do so or perhaps have consigned it to forgetfulness, we still beseech your affection for the justice we have long desired, diligently requesting the day for justice that you promised.

Farewell; and write back to us quickly and truthfully about your intention.

## Letter XX

To Hildebert, bishop of praiseworthy life, Goffrid, an insignificant servant of the monastery of Vendôme: greetings with the service of pure affection.

The graceful and beautiful letter of your prudence has reached us. Its music, like that of a cithara, has considerably soothed our mind, which—as you know—was troubled on account of our case; and with the hand of its gentleness it has wiped away the tears that had completely clouded our eyes.

Since at last you have begun to sing well for us, if you persevere to the end of the matter, you will find us to be dancers who are not ungrateful.

## Letter XXI

[Col. 0126B]

To Hildebert, prudent and simple bishop of the Cenomanni, Goffrid, servant of the monastery of Vendôme: greetings with the service of pure affection.

The countess of Vendôme, although she now says otherwise, returned to us in the presence of the cardinal the church of Savigny[Col. 0126D] and whatever she had taken from our monastery.

**Note: The church of Savigny.** He called it “the church of Savigny” in Letter 15, whose archpriest was Peter in Letter 16. In the records of Saint-Aubin there is also Durand, priest of Savigny, in the time of Helias, count of Le Mans—that is, in the time of our Goffrid. Savigny lies about seven leagues from the territory of Vendôme on the road to Le Mans.

Our humility would certainly not have refused to approve this if the testimony of the Roman Church had not preceded it; it is rash to add anything to that Church’s testimony, and criminal to contradict it.

Therefore you must beware, venerable prelate, lest a woman deceive your simplicity and compel you to act against the Roman Church, your mother. The female sex is very accustomed to deceive. For this sex, by its persuasion, deceived the first man, and by its questioning ensnared the apostle Peter. It drove the former to transgression and compelled the latter to denial.

Thus this sex, performing the office of a female doorkeeper, either excludes from life all whom it entices—as the Fathers did from Christ—or shuts them into death—as Eve did Adam in paradise.

We have written these things to your affection so that you may take from the downfall of others an example of better caution. But if ruin pleases you more than caution, and you wish to retract what the Roman Church has done, then, although unwilling and under great compulsion, we appeal to the Roman hearing, whose authority strengthens us.

## Letter XXII

[Col. 0126D]

To Hildebert, venerable bishop of the Cenomanni, Goffrid, called abbot of Vendôme: greetings and affection.

At the time you indicated, we shall appear before you, if meanwhile God grants us life and health. Yet it seems quite inappropriate to our lowliness that less credence should be given to the vicar of the Roman Church than to the words of a countess, and that a man of such authority should be regarded with suspicion because of the female sex.

## Letter XXIII

To his dearest lord and intimate friend Hildebert, bishop of venerable life, Goffrid, servant of the monastery of Vendôme: whatever service and love he can offer.

Since you were quite unable to do what you promised us, we regard you as excused before us, just as you requested. Nor can or ought we to accuse you before God, before whom, even if you have offended him in other matters, we excuse you in our prayers—not as much as we ought, perhaps, but as much as we can.

Still presuming upon your affection and humility, we again beseech you not to delay any longer, for any reason, fulfilling our petition and your promise. Come to Lavarzin,[Col. 0127C] as we desire, to do what you previously proposed, and notify us in which week of June you will celebrate the fasts.

**Note: Lavarzin.** The fortress of Lavarzin in the *Life of Hildebert*, whose homeland was Lavarzin, or, as it is called today, Lavardin, neighboring Mont-Aure on the opposite bank.

**Note: In which week of June.** From this it appears that before those times the summer fast had no fixed and definite place. This is indeed true. For in chapter 27 of the Council of Arvernus, among the materials collected by Lambert, bishop of Arras, it is decreed that the fast of spring should always take place in the first week of Lent, and the fast of summer during the week of Pentecost.

Bertold, in his appendix to Hermann, records that Bishop Gebhard, legate of the Apostolic See, established the same thing at a synod held at Constance in 1094. In my view he followed the example of Gregory VII, whom the *Micrologus* identifies as the first author of this decree.

How uncertain and unsettled the matter had previously been is shown by the Synod of Seligenstadt, which calls the fast of the Four Seasons an uncertain fast. There was indeed extraordinary variation among peoples and across periods.

To speak only of the summer fast in June: although it had become customary for most people to celebrate it in the second week of that month—as we read in an extract from the Synod of Mainz of 813, in Book V of the capitularies, chapter 86, and in the Synod of Rouen under Archbishop John in 1072—even in designating that week there was no uniform understanding or practice. Some began the reckoning on Wednesday, as the Synod of Seligenstadt prescribed; others on Saturday, as Berno, abbot of Reichenau, teaches.

There were also those who, whenever the second Saturday of June fell on the vigil of Pentecost, nevertheless observed the fast during that same week. Some preferred to anticipate it and move the fast back to the preceding week; others, by contrast, preferred to postpone it to the following week, which we follow today.

There was scarcely less diversity concerning the spring and winter fasts.
