Thus, although the matter was not great, it was important to remove this division from the Church and establish a common law for all, which we have said was enacted at the Synod of Arvernus. It did not immediately prevail everywhere. So difficult is it for most people to change ancient customs and rites, even for better ones.

For this reason Goffrid, treating the matter as still uncertain, asks Hildebert about it.

## Letter XXIV

To his beloved Father Hildebert, venerable bishop of the Cenomanni, Goffrid, humble servant of the monastery of Vendôme: greetings with affection.

You informed us that John the monk had returned from Jerusalem.[Col. 0127C]

**Note: John the monk.** The Mason; see the following letters, 29 and 30.

It would have been much better for him to have lived well in his own monastery. Not all who have seen the earthly Jerusalem, but those who have acted well, have deserved to possess the Jerusalem that is in heaven.

We would not have been displeased that he turned to you if he had first come to us, as he ought to have done. Your requesting, with our permission, that he live with you is not to care for his soul but to harm it. For he must first be reconciled by regular satisfaction to his monastery, from which he departed through disobedience, before he is worthy of communion with you or with any Catholic.

Let him therefore come to his monastery, confess that he acted less than perfectly, and receive from his imperfection not punishment but medicine. Thereafter, whatever your holiness asks of us, our humility will pursue.

Let him not fear to come; let him not tremble where there is no reason for fear.[Col. 0128A] It is our duty to heal the wounded, not to increase their wounds, because the supreme Shepherd is recorded as having carried the weary sheep, not cast it away. He had such compassion for its weakness that he would rather become weak himself than fail to heal its weakness with the remedy of mercy.

But if he does not obey when we earnestly call him, if he rejects the remedies of paternal affection offered and repeatedly extended to him, if he despises the bowels of maternal sweetness, we excommunicate him as a sacrilegious person until he makes regular satisfaction, insofar as the Rule itself teaches and commands.

## Letter XXV

[Col. 0128B]

To his dearest lord and friend Hildebert, honorable bishop of the Cenomanni, Goffrid, servant of the monastery of Vendôme and of its friends: greetings and affection.

You know with absolute certainty, and do not doubt in the least, that John the Mason is a monk of our Church and has repeatedly departed from that Church through disobedience. Nevertheless, against the fidelity of his profession and against our will, you have retained him for a long time and still retain him—apparently unconcerned for his salvation and forgetful of your promise.

For when you last spoke with us, you promised that you would promptly send him back to his monastery. Since he has not yet wished to come, neither sent by you nor permitted by his own wickedness, we admonish him now that he has already been warned, and by admonishing we ask him: let him who departed from us disobediently come to us by next Sunday, ready to obey according to the Rule and to be received mercifully.

If he delays for any reason, we excommunicate him until he repents, so that while alive he may receive no communion, and when dead he may receive no burial.

But to you, our dearest lord and friend, we send this supplication: since for a time we granted him to your request out of charity, let your prudence not withhold him from us any longer.

## Letter XXVI

To Hildebert, beloved Father and lord in Christ, bishop of the Cenomanni, Goffrid, humble servant of the monastery of Vendôme: to love truth and hate whatever is contrary to truth.

We have fully recognized the arrow that was sent against us, as though from Tours,[Col. 0129C] and from which quiver it came; for we are not ignorant of human schemes.

**Note: “The arrow which was, as it were, sent from Tours.”** The letter of the clerics of Tours to Hildebert, discussed in the following letter.

By no reasoning or authority could it have been prohibited to you that the good which, through the grace of affection, you had promised us nearly a hundred times should be denied to us. Authority was plainly lacking; but if you ever possessed it, your will has changed.

Your love of truth ought to have commended your promise, not allowed it to be obstructed by any deceitfulness. Nor ought we, nor can we, conceal from your goodness that it is hardly fitting for pontifical excellence to weary a friend without purpose and deceive a trusting man who had entrusted himself and all that belonged to him to your faith.

Farewell; and take care to correct what you have done less generously toward a friend—by “friend” I mean not just anyone, but one faithful to you in all things—and what you have done further against him through sinister counsel, just as you ought to have avoided it.

## Letter XXVII

To Hildebert, bishop of the Cenomanni, a man of honorable life, Goffrid, humble servant of the monastery of Vendôme: where there is no fear, not to fear, and by no persuasion to obey God less than human beings.

[Col. 0129C] You sent us the letters that the clerics of Tours sent to you [Note: [Col. 0129C] The clerics of Tours: of the metropolitan church of Saint Gatianus], in which, binding the dignity of your rank with the bonds of subjection, they ordered that you should not make a cemetery at the church of Saint Nicholas in the castle of Carcer [Note: [Col. 0129D] The church of Saint Nicholas: In the privileges of Innocent III and of John of the Castle of Carcer, three churches are numbered, which Hildebert is said to have granted to the monastery of Vendôme with the consent of the illustrious Goffridus of the Meduana. Guido, Bishop Hildebert’s successor, lists the same churches in his letters confirming to Abbot Fromundus all the churches that he possessed in the diocese of Le Mans. “The churches,” he says, “of Carcer—namely, the chapel of Saint Mary, the chapel of Saint Vincent, and the chapel of Saint Nicholas—we prohibit under perpetual anathema that any church or chapel be built within the banlieue of that castle without the permission of the chapter of Vendôme.”]. This whole undertaking is recognized as having been presumed upon to diminish your dignity and to injure the Church of Le Mans, because no rule of Scripture tolerates a bishop’s being subjected in anything to clerics.

With what, then, that fat of iniquity, did they presume to subject a bishop irregularly to themselves—one whom they ought not to have rebuked in anything, even if he had acted otherwise [Note: [Col. 0129D] “Even if he had acted otherwise”: *Aliter agere*, in Goffridus’s well-established usage, means to act badly and perversely, disgracefully and unbecomingly. He uses it in this sense in Book I, Letters 7; Book II, Letters 7 and 8; and in this book, Letter 41: “We ask that you correct what has been done otherwise”; Book IV, Letter 12. Likewise, Letter 47: “To do something otherwise is a mark of human perfection, and to refuse to correct what has been done otherwise is diabolical presumption”; and Book V, Letter 22. He had evidently read in Saint Benedict’s Rule, chapter 4: “Obey the abbot’s commands in everything, even if he himself—which God forbid!—acts otherwise.” The same words, but written about bishops, are read in Clement’s First Letter to James, in Rufinus’s translation.], unless he had dissented from the Catholic faith.

If their master, the archbishop [Note: [Col. 0130D] The archbishop: Radulfus, to whom Book I, Letter 30, is addressed] [141], had been present, no divine law could have prevented what we were rightly asking you to do; and if he had presumed to do so, it would not have been your duty to obey him in this matter. One must indeed obey a prelate, but not in everything that he proposes—only in those things that God commands. For if prelates command anything contrary to God’s or the Fathers’ constitution, they immediately lose the authority to command, and in that matter they must not be obeyed in any way, as the example of the apostles shows.

They certainly received from the Good Teacher a model of obedience. Concerning the scribes and Pharisees they were told: “Whatever they tell you, observe and do” (Matthew [Col. 0130B] 23:3). But when those same authorities commanded them not to speak in the name of Jesus, they later heard what had deceptively been imposed upon them under the name of obedience, and wisely avoided it, saying: “We must obey God rather than men” (Acts 5:29).

If it had pleased you to hold to this line of obedience, the fulfillment of your promise would certainly have consecrated its truth [Note: [Col. 0130D] “The fulfillment would have consecrated the promise”: In the preceding letter: “Yet the fulfillment of your promise in truth ought to have commended it,” that is, ought to have proved it. Promises are approved when they are carried out. Tertullian frequently plays upon this meaning of the word: *On Monogamy*: “But when the first crime, murder in the killing of a brother, was consecrated”; *On Repentance*: “From that moment he consecrated repentance in himself.” In the *Apology* he calls Nero “the consecrator of our condemnation,” that is, the first author of the persecution. For Tertullian, *dedicare* in these passages means to inaugurate or display something new. For Goffridus it means to carry out and complete, since new things are consecrated, and things are not ordinarily consecrated unless they have been completed.], and the archbishop would have had nothing reasonable to say against you on this account.

But if, contrary to the teaching of the apostles, than whom he is no better, he had wished to disturb your simplicity through anger, hatred, or any other storm of the mind, the testimonies of evangelical authority would have been available to you, and would have been hurled against him for his everlasting disgrace.

The letter that we sent you before this one [Note: [Col. 0130D] “The letter that we sent you”: Letter 26] disturbed your gentleness somewhat, as we have heard. We admit, therefore, that those who sent it regret having done so and that we were mistaken. But exhausted by excessive labor and driven by an immoderate storm of spirit, we were unable to steer the ship of our reason [142] against the assaults of so many resisting waves. Farewell, and complete by charity—which casts out fear (1 John 4:18)—the good thing that you abandoned through disordered fear.

## LETTER XXVIII

To his dearest lord and intimate friend Hildebert [Col. 0131A], a bishop of praiseworthy life, Brother Goffridus, humble servant of the monastery of Vendôme: affection and the service of all affection.

You know, dearest Father, that our monastery is the patrimony of blessed Peter and his allodial possession, and that its property and the things belonging to it, wherever they may be, are placed under the protection of the holy Roman Church. Therefore we humbly implore your kindly fatherhood, both for love of blessed Peter and out of regard for our humility, to do us justice concerning Peter of Caortia [Note: [Col. 0131D] Peter of Caortia: Book V, Letter 12. Hugo Caorcinus] and concerning the castle in which he lives. He shamefully knocked one of our monks from his horse, unjustly took one of our servants and two asses from him, and still violently detains them. Farewell.

## LETTER XXIX

[Col. 0131B]

To Lord Hildebert, bishop of honorable life, dearest lord and Father, Brother Goffridus, humble servant of the monastery of Vendôme: whatever may be usefully commanded and obtained.

Let your affection know, excellent Father, that we have repeatedly summoned John the Mason, our monk [143], who until today has remained with you by our permission, asking him to come back to us. He has repeatedly promised that he would come, but has not come, perhaps fearing that he would have to return.

Now, however, our humility asks your discretion to send him back—the man whom our affection commended to you for a time because of your need. If he does not come to us by Thursday, unless detained by serious bodily illness, let him know without doubt that we shall do to him what ought to be done to one who has abandoned the obedience of his own place and made void the fidelity of his profession.

## LETTER XXX

To all bishops, abbots, and all the sons of the holy Church, but especially to Lord Hildebert, discreet and venerable bishop of Le Mans, Brother Goffridus, humble servant of the monastery of Vendôme: to love what God loves and hate what he hates.

You should know that we have excommunicated John the Mason, a monk indeed [Note: [Col. 0131D] “John the Mason, a monk indeed”: This fugitive monk, repeatedly recalled by Goffridus without success, was being retained by Hildebert because of the usefulness of his craft, as Goffridus complained in Book I, Letter 3, to Paschal. It is likely that after his excommunication he was returned to the monastery and commended by some supplicatory letter, such as Letter 23 among Hildebert’s letters, which I would gladly insert here if the mark of the first character did not indicate that the monk for whom it intercedes had a different name [Col. 0132D].], but not one possessing the cement of charity, since he abandoned the obedience of his own place and made void the fidelity of his profession. Though repeatedly admonished and though we have waited for him a long time, he neglected—and still neglects—to correct what he had done wrong. Thus, insofar as the holy Rule teaches and commands, he has been separated from the body of the holy Church.

Therefore we humbly ask and beseech all Christians who believe in Christ, and who have not vowed to anyone outside the unity of the Catholic and apostolic Church [144], to abstain from the company of this excommunicated man, lest they be defiled and perish through participation in his foul and excessively filthy condition—which God forbid!

We earnestly supplicate the aforementioned honorable man, the bishop of Le Mans, not only to abstain from communion with that wicked man whom, for the need of his Church, we commended to him for a time, but also—as he has already promised that he would do—to make every effort to return to us the man entrusted to him.

## LETTER XXXI

To Ranulfus, bishop of blessed life [Note: [Col. 0132D] Bishop Ranulfus: Bishop of Saintes, successor of Boso. The beginning of his episcopate may be assigned, according to the old Chronicle of Vinetus, to the year 1083. He attended the Synod of Auvergne, as is shown by the letters of Urban and Paschal, which we printed in Book II, Letters 26 and 12. In the following year he received Urban, who was coming to Saintes, on the Ides of April], Goffridus, useless servant of the monastery of Vendôme, and the brothers entrusted to him, with affection offer reverence.

We know that it is sufficiently well known to you that, following your counsel and admonition, we made peace with Eblo and his wife [Note: [Col. 0132D] With Ebro: Book I, Letter 1]. We also know that you are by no means unaware of how this was done. We had you as mediator and at the same time advocate of this settlement, and we resolved that it should be made and confirmed through your hand, on this condition and with this intention: if anyone in the future should presume to violate what had been done in your presence, he would, by your authority, be regarded as excluded from the holy Church until he came to his senses. Ecclesiastical censure appears to contain this entire provision.

For the sacred canons state that anyone who attempts to overturn a matter justly settled in the presence of his bishop, after being warned once or twice, is to be excommunicated by that bishop if he refuses to amend—by the very bishop whose presence he has presumed to make void [145].

From this you can easily perceive what you ought to do against Jueta and Isembertus and their men. Eblo and his wife Jueta have now promised us in good faith, and have given hostages to you and to us concerning this matter, that their absent son Isembertus would consent to the peace that they themselves confirmed in your hand.

Because he delayed, and still delays, doing this, you withdrew the divine office from him and from his mother, as was worthy and just; and afterward you informed us by letter that we should have no doubt whatever about the justice that you had begun. We had already proclaimed this in many places to the praise of your dignity.

But since, according to an evil report, we have now heard that you have released Jueta, in whom the whole substance of the evil consists, if this is true, we both can and must be exceedingly astonished—especially since no one could have had greater confidence in your constancy and the integrity of your justice.

Farewell. We ask that you not delay supplementing what you have carried out less fully than justice required in our case. With God’s help, you will not be offering your assistance to ungrateful friends [Col. 0133A].

## LETTER XXXII

[146] To Ranulfus, bishop of honorable life, his dearest lord and intimate friend, Goffridus, servant of the monastery of Vendôme: greetings and reverence.

What Goffridus of Tauniac [Note: [Col. 0133D] Goffridus of Tauniac: There are two Tauniacs in Saintonge, distinguished by the names of the rivers flowing past them; one is called Tauniac of the Carantoni, the other Tauniac of the Vultonna] claims to have offered us as a settlement never pleased me, does not please me, and will never please me.

As for the fact that, following your counsel, he promises to satisfy us, we praise it highly. Yet you must fear that under this appearance of humility he may deceive your simplicity; we too are not a little afraid of this. We therefore ask your holiness, and in asking we admonish you, not to grant him a delay unless he has first made you fully certain that, by satisfying us, he will obey the lord pope’s decree.

## LETTER XXXIII

To Ranulfus, venerable bishop, Goffridus, allodial tenant of blessed Peter: to act prudently and simply in all things.

We received the letter sent by you. We would never have believed it to be yours if we had not seen it sealed with your seal. It states that you have begun to determine matters concerning our monastery’s possessions—that is, the allodial property of blessed Peter—and that, while we were absent, indeed unaware, you had assigned a day for judgment to certain unexpected adversaries of ours [147]. With all due respect, we say that this was neither just nor canonical.

In the decrees of the Roman pontiffs it is expressly commanded that ecclesiastical judges must not pronounce sentence in the absence of the person whose case is being contested [Note: [Col. 0133D] “In his absence”: See above, Letter 28].

If you object that you warned us through our brothers who were present, we answer, excellent prelate, no less humbly than truthfully, that it was neither your place to warn us in this way through them nor theirs—as they wisely avoided—to accept this warning from you.

Such a warning—as we do not believe you are ignorant—must be delivered not by those who are being accused, but by those who bring the accusation, or by other legates of the judge [Note: [Col. 0133D] “Such a warning”: A summons to judgment. Book II, Letter 29]. If the accused accepted a mission against themselves, they would carry with them the knife by which they were to be slaughtered. If anyone wishes to think otherwise, ecclesiastical authority will be lacking for him, and his will shall stand in place of reason.

We are greatly astonished at you, dearest Father. You have often seen and read the privileges of the Roman Church that we possess, and in reading them you found that all these matters for which our adversaries cry out against us have been indissolubly secured for our monastery by the bond of apostolic authority.

You also know that those privileges state—if you have not consigned it to oblivion—that whatever concerning our monastery’s possessions has been determined or alienated [Note: [Col. 0133D] “Determined or alienated”: The privilege of Gregory VII says: “If anyone wishes to bring a case against that place of blessed Peter concerning any possessions, neither the abbot nor the brothers shall answer him before consulting the Roman pontiff; for whatever shall have been determined or alienated without judgment of us or our successors shall be void.” The same appears in Urban II’s privilege of 1099 [Col. 0134D]—without the judgment and consent of the Roman pontiff shall remain void and empty; and anyone who attempts to determine such a matter shall be deprived of the dignity of his power and honor, with all hope of recovery removed [148].

Nevertheless, because we are your debtors in affection, we shall diligently present ourselves before your revered presence at a suitable time, there to receive justice concerning the adversaries mentioned above and to carry out whatever shall be required of us.

We shall inform you of the time and day through the brothers who come for the feast of the Holy Trinity, after taking counsel with them. If these arrangements displease you, though they ought not to displease you, we appeal to the hearing of the lord pope. Standing firm through his favor and authority, we fear no one whom we do not love.

Farewell in the Lord, holy Father.

## LETTER XXXIV

To Ranulfus, venerable bishop of the people of Saintes, his lord and intimate friend, Goffridus, allodial tenant of blessed Peter: to love equity and hate iniquity.

We have gladly accepted the date that you sent us, provided that in the meantime we are fully reinstated, as ecclesiastical law requires. For we read in the decrees of the Roman pontiffs that no one who has been stripped of his possessions ought to be summoned to a provincial or general synod [Note: [Col. 0134D] “No one to a synod”: Pope Eusebius, in his letter to the Alexandrians and Egyptians concerning bishops who had been dispossessed, says: “Know that they can be summoned neither to a provincial synod nor to a general one, nor judged in any matter, until everything taken from them has been restored by law to their authority.” Book II, Letter 29; Book IV, Letter 12] or judged in any matter.

If, contrary to this, anyone should attempt, with your consent, to strip us again of our investiture and possessions, we appeal to the hearing of the lord pope against both the consenting party and the presumption of the person attempting it [Col. 0134C], since we are his special sons.

Farewell. You ought, excellent prelate, to take care that you do not permit such things to occur, lest an intolerable burden arise for you—something we do not desire [149].

## LETTER XXXV

To Ranulfus, bishop of honorable life, Goffridus, his intimate friend: to act steadfastly in all things.

The judgment that you and we rendered together has greatly stirred the spirits of our rivals. I have been informed that their hoarse voice has reached the one who always walks along the crooked path [Col. 0134D]. By the truth of the holy canons, you both can and ought, through God’s grace, to silence their barking mouths, and to exercise with all your strength the censure of ecclesiastical discipline against those rebels, so that at least in this way they may learn how serious it is not to obey their bishop when he judges justly.

For the authority of the Council of Toledo [Note: [Col. 0134D] The Council of Toledo: Toledo IV, canon 48] restrains their importunate tongue when it says: “Whether paternal devotion or voluntary profession makes a man a cleric [Col. 0135A] or monk, whichever of these it may be, it will hold him bound.”

The Council condemns Michael—not the obedient archangel, I do not mean, but that disobedient cleric of Antioch [Note: [Col. 0135C] “Of Antioch”: Canon 5 says: “If any priest or deacon, despising his own bishop, separates himself from the Church, gathers people apart, and sets up an altar, and does not heed the bishop when warned, nor wish to agree or obey when summoned once and again, let him be condemned altogether and obtain no further remedy, since he cannot recover his dignity. If he persists in disturbing and troubling the Church, let him be suppressed by external authorities as a seditious person.” This is the complete canon against priests and deacons who secede from their bishops and erect separate altars for themselves. Goffridus—or perhaps someone before him—has abbreviated it in such a way that he seems to constrain all clerics who do not obey their bishops in every matter [Col. 0135D]] in these words:

“If anyone from the clergy despises his own bishop or refuses to obey him, let him be condemned altogether and obtain no further remedy. If he attempts to disturb or trouble the Church, let him be suppressed by external authorities as a seditious person.”

Again, against the archbishop [Note: [Col. 0135D] “Against the archbishop”: The archbishop of Bordeaux, metropolitan of Aquitaine II. At this time, I think, he was Arnaldus, successor of Amatus], who has already done much in your diocese without consulting you and is still attempting to do so, an arrow is directed from the quiver of Pope Julius [Note: [Col. 0135D] Pope Julius: Letter 1 to the Easterners on behalf of Athanasius, chapter 23] in these words:

“If any metropolitan bishop attempts to do anything in the province, except what pertains solely to his own diocese, without the counsel and consent of all the bishops of the province, he shall be exposed to the danger of his rank, and what he has done shall be considered void and empty” [150].

## LETTER XXXVI

To Ranulfus, bishop of Saintes, and Peter the archdeacon, his dearest lords and intimate friends, Goffridus, abbot, though unworthy: greetings and affection.

You should know that what the abbot of Saint John [Note: [Col. 0135D] The abbot of Saint John: The abbot of Angély, Book IV, Letter 3. The abbot of Saint John, Book V, Letter 19, which concerns this subject] and his fellow abbots testify—that the court hearing [Note: [Col. 0135D] “Court hearing”: Book III, chapter 83: “Let each count have his own court and administer justice.” They called a judgment, or an assembly held for the purpose of judgment, a *placitum*. Hence also *placitare*, Book III, Letter 24. But assemblies were held not only for judicial proceedings but for any kind of business, and the agreements and settlements of the matters for which they had assembled were called *placita*, such as the court hearing at Pavia of Charles the Bald in 877, “of the princes,” in Ivo, Letter 28. Flodoard, in his chronicle, under the year 853: “The king and Hugh held at Soissons, in mid-Lent, a court hearing of concord and peace.” A sale was likewise called a *placitum*, Book III, chapter 75. The Council of Tribur, chapter 9: “When the bishop, traveling around the diocese, has canonically appointed a court hearing and invited the people to it, and the count has appointed his own court hearing with the people on the same day and ordered them to come there by proclamation, let everyone postpone the count’s court hearing, and let the count himself and the people hasten after the bishop, knowing that they are not there to fight in seditious contention but to keep watch over the Catholic faith—not to gather a heap of money but gain for souls”] that we were to hold in your presence was postponed with my consent and advice until his return from Spain—is entirely contrary to the truth.

As for his promise to do us justice according to your judgment, your friend, whoever he may be, embraces it wholeheartedly, provided that his promise is confirmed by action.

At present, however, I cannot come to you as you instructed, being held by severe kidney pain and occupied by the unavoidable needs of our monastery. But when, by God’s gift, my bodily illness and our monastery’s necessity have passed, your holiness’s servant will present himself before your kindly presence at a suitable time. He will receive justice concerning the aforementioned abbot and diligently carry out whatever he owes.

If you reject these things, which you cannot reject canonically, I appeal to Rome. Supported by its authority, I fear no one’s injury [151].

## LETTER XXXVII

To Ranulfus, bishop of Saintes, Goffridus, servant of the monastery of Vendôme: not to be driven by every wind.

An evil report has reached us [Col. 0136B]: concerning the island of Flaici [Note: [Col. 0136C] The island of Flaici: It is not an island of sea or river, but land formerly reclaimed from the middle of marshes. Its site can still be seen not far from Surgères, whose church is its dependency. In Urban II’s privilege, issued at Rome in 1098: “The church of blessed Mary of Surgères, with the island of Flaici, which the knight Hugo, having wholly reclaimed it himself, left to the monastery of Vendôme through the hand of Ranulfus, bishop of Saintes” [Col. 0136D]], from which, while we were absent and appealing to the Roman hearing, you once dispossessed us, and afterward restored us by your judgment and that of your clerics, you now once again hold us dispossessed.

If this is true, we are exceedingly astonished. From where did you receive such great power that you can so lightly take away from us and confer upon whomever you wish the properties assigned to the Roman Church—properties concerning which no pontiff is permitted to remove or determine anything unless he incurs anathema?

We therefore admonish and beseech your exalted dignity, and in beseeching admonish you, to invest us still as your friends, in accordance with the cardinal’s command. Otherwise, against you, as against our persecutor and violator of the Roman privileges [Col. 0136C], we shall proclaim also what was done by you in the case of Haimericus of Rancone [Note: [Col. 0136D] Haimericus of Rancone: A distinguished family in earlier centuries. One Haimericus of Rancone, bearing this surname, subscribed among the nobles to the charter of the foundation of the monastery of Vendôme in 1040. Likewise, Gauffridus of Rancone was appointed by King Louis VII, duke of Aquitaine, over the region of Poitou; letters of his to Abbot Suger survive among Suger’s letters. An even earlier Haimericus of Rancone, and his bloody death, are mentioned by the old Chronicle of Ademar of Angoulême: “Haimericus, prince of Rancone, rising up against William, count of Angoulême, was stabbed to death by Goffridus, the count’s son”], without keeping silent about it.

Because Haimericus had done us many wrongs, he had been excommunicated by the lord pope and by you, and by God’s just judgment he was killed while under that excommunication. He was therefore rightly excluded from the cemetery.

Afterward, however, at the prayers of his wife and, as some say, after being corrupted by money, you communicated with the excommunicated man by absolving him—still excommunicated—from excommunication without satisfaction. In the presence of our brothers, through whom our injuries were reported in your hearing, and are still being reported, you yourself then committed his body to burial [152].

Yet, by the authority of the holy canons [Note: [Col. 0137C] The authority of the canons: Leo to Rusticus of Narbonne: “Those with whom we did not communicate while they were alive, we cannot communicate with when they are dead.” Innocent III to the archbishop of Nidaros, chapter 12, *On Burials*: “It has been established by the sacred canons that those with whom we did not communicate while alive, we must not communicate with when dead; and that those who had previously been cut off from ecclesiastical unity and were not reconciled to the Church at the point of death should be deprived of ecclesiastical burial.” Absolution can, however, be granted to the dead while under excommunication, followed by burial after absolution: *Canon A nobis*, *On the Sentence of Excommunication*], we firmly hold, without the slightest doubt, that we must not communicate with those with whom we do not communicate while they are alive, even when they are dead. Anyone who acts otherwise, if he is a layman, ought himself to be excommunicated; if he is a cleric, whatever his dignity or order, he ought to be completely degraded.

Farewell, and wisely consider what has been said.

## LETTER XXXVIII

To his dearest lord and intimate friend Peter, honorable bishop of the people of Saintes [Note: [Col. 0137C] Peter, bishop of Saintes: Successor of Ranulfus], Goffridus, humble servant of the monastery of Vendôme: a persistence in prayer with the devotion of pure affection.

Though absent in body but present in the devotion of our minds, venerable Father, we offer you thanks for the benefits that you so often bestow upon us. We recognize that the fire of your charity burns more ardently toward us insofar as your resolve is more steadfast against those who bring accusations against us.

Although we cannot repay you with thanks proportionate to your merits, we nevertheless presume greatly upon your goodness and humbly ask that you not find it burdensome to correct the injustices committed against us in your diocese.

William, provost of Oleron [Note: [Col. 0137C] William, provost of Oleron: He and his brother Haimericus are mentioned again in Book V, Letter 21. Oleron—or, as Sidonius says, Olarion—is an island in the Ocean of Saintonge. It was also mentioned in Book I, Letter 25. Pliny calls it Uliarius], and another man named Astho, wickedly and cruelly, have forcibly imposed upon our lands certain new exactions, entirely unknown in the time of our predecessors [153]. Our brothers, who endured their burdens, will tell you about them more effectively.

Although these things are true, we do not speak of them for this reason: it is more excusable to keep silent even about certain true matters than to exceed the bounds of truth through any sort of insinuation.

Prelate of praiseworthy life, do not overlook the seeds of evil on any pretext; but as soon as they begin to sprout, cut them out by the roots. For if shrubs are shaken as soon as they are planted, they cannot take root. If they are tolerated longer, however, they fix their roots more deeply; those that previously could be pulled out almost by hand and without difficulty will afterward never be eradicated without an axe, and scarcely even with one.

From this comparison it is easy to perceive that if the enemies of the holy Church are not resisted at the first assault, their wickedness grows while the ability to resist diminishes.

May our lord bishop prosper. We place complete confidence in his constancy and in the integrity of his justice.

## LETTER XXXIX

To his dearest lord and most intimate friend Peter, bishop of honorable life, Goffridus, humble servant of the monastery of Vendôme: salvation from God and the service of pure affection from him.

We have heard, dearest Father, that Rainaldus Chesnellus [Note: [Col. 0137D] Rainaldus Chesnellus: He is called Rainaldus Chesnelli in Book I, Letter 21], your cleric, took up a duel with Lord William [154], our monk [Col. 0138C] [Note: [Col. 0137D] “Took up a duel”: A single combat, by which disputed matters that could not be settled through ordinary judgment were resolved. In King Stephen of England’s charter to Hugh, archbishop of Rouen, concerning those who violate God’s truce and kill men during God’s truce, it is likewise decreed as my uncle Henry ordered it to be observed: if anyone wishes to prove by duel in God’s truce that someone is a killer, that duel shall take place in court. And later: if no one wishes to prove by duel that the killer violated God’s truce, then, summoned by the ministers of the Church, the killer shall purge himself according to the established law of judgment, either by water or by fire. This means the ordeal of hot or cold water, or of heated iron, for these were other forms of popular purgation.

This rite, received long ago into the Church from the ancient custom of the Franks and Germanic peoples—although the rulers of the Church protested against it—became so firmly established that only after the struggle of many centuries could its abolition scarcely be achieved.

To speak separately of the duel, the fight was conducted with a shield and club. Book IV, chapter 23: “Let them fight in the field with shields and clubs.” And chapter 29: “Let him be permitted to contend in the field against one of them with shield and club.” Although they fought with these weapons, however, the contest scarcely took place without blood, and at times not without slaughter. For this reason above all the Church prohibited single combat, as is taught in many places, for example by Ivo, Letter 247.

Thus King Stephen’s charter assigns the duel to the king’s court, while in the ecclesiastical forum the ordeal by water or fire is prescribed, because clerics were not only forbidden to engage in duels themselves but also forbidden to commit others to them. Nevertheless, through the fault of the times, both sides often violated this rule.

The two examples below bear witness to this. Since they illustrate the custom of ancient duels and also contain information about memorable events, they seemed worthy of being brought to light. The first is an example from the cartulary of Saint-Albans of Angers, showing a duel offered and accepted but not fought, in the dispute between Abbot Theodericus and the viscount of Thouars. It reads as follows:

**The dispute of Haimericus, viscount of Thouars, with Theodericus, abbot of Saint-Albans**

“Let it be known to all Christians, present and future, that Haimericus, viscount of Thouars, at the urging of his officials, demanded from Theodericus, abbot of Saint-Albans, who had recently assumed the burden of the abbacy, a certain unheard-of custom contrary to all religion: namely, for the change of abbots and the abbot’s relief, one horse worth one hundred solidi or one hundred solidi.

For it had been represented to him by those who hunted such profits that whenever a new abbot was appointed in the monastery of Saint-Albans, he was to pay the viscount the aforesaid levy for his appointment.

When this was reported to the abbot on the viscount’s behalf, he perceived that, if paid, it would harm both himself and his successors. He therefore refused to pay the custom, understanding that it was being demanded perversely.

As a result, he went to Thouars and approached the viscount, prepared either to prove through his representative, according to the monks’ law, by the ordeal of hot iron that this custom had never existed in the abbey of Saint-Albans, or to defend the matter with shield and staff according to secular law, and to prove that the custom was being unjustly demanded.

Which of these should take place was left to the viscount’s judgment. When he chose the duel rather than the other alternative, the abbot offered a man of Saint-Albans who would take the oath and give security for the oath by his arm.

Meanwhile the viscount’s leading men, recognizing how grievously this custom could injure every Christian profession, and especially the monastic order, and protesting to the viscount that he was acting against God, his saints, and his own soul, declared that it was unjust for a battle to be fought over so iniquitous a custom.

The viscount himself, a prudent and noble man of good character, though young, perceived that this fight endangered his soul, whichever combatant might win, since it might compel either his own man or the saint’s man to be killed. After taking counsel with his faithful men, for the soul of his father, who had died some time before and whose anniversary was being observed that very day, and also for his own salvation, which was daily at risk, and so that the abbot might grant him, his wife, and his brothers a share in the benefit of the community of Saint-Albans, he remitted the fight and remitted the custom. He ordered that a record of the matter be written so that no one thereafter might exact it within his jurisdiction or family.

He persuaded his brothers—namely Gauffridus and Rodulfus—and the knights who protested that this custom should be abolished from him forever—namely William and the provost Americus—to confirm this by their free authorization.

After the abbot had granted the fellowship of the benefit and the viscount had annulled the aforementioned custom, both parties departed in peace. These things were done at Thouars, in the court of the viscount Haimericus,” and so forth.

The second example is contained in a document of Saint Peter of Redon, in a letter of Bishop Hamelinus. It shows a duel that was joined but settled without a victory. It reads as follows:

**Letter of Hamelinus, bishop of Redon, concerning the dispute of Mainguenoius and Ivo, and the duel fought between them.**
I, Hamelin, by the grace of God bishop of Redon, commit to memory and hand down to the knowledge of my successors the conclusion of the dispute that took place in our presence between Mainguenoius, son of Evenus of Crotenay, and Ivo, late son of Hamelin, nephew of Galterius Groisnard. In the fourth year of my episcopate, this Ivo brought a claim before me concerning an inheritance which he asserted was his, and which Galterius, his uncle, and Hamelin, his father, had purchased from Bishop Maino and possessed peacefully during their lifetimes. After their deaths, Ivo himself and his brothers, compelled by poverty and their own isolation, while living in another parish, abandoned their inheritance into the hand of the bishop, free and unencumbered.

Now, however, he claimed that he was demanding back his inheritance, which Mainguenoius was unjustly possessing, having meanwhile received it from the bishop’s ministers, although none of his predecessors had previously possessed it. Summoned in response to this claim on the appointed day and at the appointed place, Mainguenoius gave the following answer:

“I possess neither your inheritance, nor your father’s, nor your grandfather’s [or, according to another reading, your great-grandfather’s], but my own inheritance, which my father, grandfather, and great-grandfather held and possessed peacefully in the time of Bishops Maino, Silvester, Marbod, and Rotald. They never lacked justice, nor were they ever dispossessed of this holding—and neither have I.”

To this Ivo replied:

“Neither you, Mainguenoius, nor your father, nor your grandfather, nor your great-grandfather ever possessed this land without our claim against it, nor were any of them ever invested with it.”

Judgment was then given that Mainguenoius should assert his account by oath. Ivo said that he would resist this oath. Accordingly, it was judged between them that there should be a duel. Both parties accepted it and approved the judgment.

When, on the appointed day, they had come to the field, and after the oaths had been made, the champions on both sides fought bravely and manfully in the bishop’s meadow beside the river Isola, in our presence and in that of Count Conan, Robert of Vitré—then excommunicated—Oliver of Dinan, Hamon of Guirchia, and many other nobles, as well as nearly the whole clergy and people of Redon. A settlement was then discussed, and it was agreed and approved that Mainguenoius should hold and possess his land in peace, and should give Ivo fifty solidi for expenses; Ivo would then entirely abandon his claim to that possession. This was done, and Ivo gave his pledge into the bishop’s hand that he would firmly and faithfully observe the terms of this peace settlement.

His brothers Rainaldus, Judicael, and Ruellonus Bodinardus likewise gave their pledges, as did Radulfus, Ivo’s father-in-law, and Robert ex Pallare. A place and deadline were also fixed for the fifty solidi to be returned to Ivo. On the appointed day, when Mainguenoius was present and Ivo, having been invited by us once, twice, and three times, refused to accept the money, I received it. I gave Mainguenoius security and promised him protection for all the days of my life and of the lives of my successors, the bishops. I also signed the written charter of the agreement with the episcopal seal, so that it might remain valid, firm, and undisturbed.”

But since we have advanced this far, let a third example of a duel be added, in which one of the champions is defeated and is described as drenched in his own blood, as we have mentioned. It is taken from an old History, or Deeds of the Counts and Bishops of Angoulême, where the account concerns Count William, son of Arnold, against whom a sorceress was said to have practiced harmful arts.

### The duel of Stephen on behalf of the Count of Angoulême, and William on behalf of the sorceress

“While the sorceress,” he says, “would not confess,” it was entrusted to the judgment of God that the truth hidden from view should be proved by the victory granted in a duel between two men fighting one another. After the oaths had therefore been made on the Monday of the first week of the Passion, they fought for a long time and with great violence outside the city, on an island of the Charente River: namely, Stephen, the count’s champion, and William, the defender of the sorceress, with clubs and shields. For the defender of the sorceress had himself been bewitched that day by certain enchanters and initiated with certain herbal potions.

But Stephen, trusting in the true judgment of the Lord alone, was victorious without injury to his body. The other, with his whole body battered and covered with an excessive amount of his own blood, stood defeated on his feet from the third hour until the ninth. When he could no longer move, he vomited out through his shield and club some of the magic substance he had tasted. Half alive, he was carried away in the hands of others and lay sick for a long time. His enchanters, meanwhile, standing at a distance and uttering certain incantations, immediately fled in terror.

Stephen, however, joyful and leaping for joy, ran at that very hour to give thanks to God at the tomb of Saint Eparchius, where he had kept an all-night vigil the previous night. He then returned on horseback to the city to refresh himself. The sorceress, tortured soon afterward by many torments without the count’s knowledge, still did not confess; but she was convicted by the testimony of three women who had taken part with her in the sorcery. Nevertheless, the count spared her and granted her life.”

, yet he had no witness on his side, nor on the side of the monk. Since the laws of the world allow this to be done in no way, and the sacred canons altogether forbid it, we humbly ask that what is recognized as having been presumed by ecclesiastical men in your episcopate against ecclesiastical regulations be annulled and corrected by your authority. Otherwise, perhaps, through a perverse custom, human iniquity may prevail over canonical equity, and thus—God forbid!—truth may be subjected to falsehood.

But if your Rainaldus attempts to brandish the keys of Holy Church and annul the decrees of the Roman pontiffs, which entirely prohibit single combat among ecclesiastical men, then against his inflated efforts we appeal to the humility of the Roman Church, which knows how to burst the swollen and restrain the proud.”

## LETTER XL

To my dearest lords and wholehearted friends, Lord Peter, venerable bishop of Saintes, and Lord Goscelin, his honorable archdeacon, Goffridus, their humble and faithful friend, sends greeting, service, and affection.

It has come to our attention that you have taken away from us the offerings connected with confessions in the church of Surgères.

[Note: “The offerings connected with confessions in the church of Surgères.” There was a similar dispute of the monks of Vendôme with the bishop of Angers, as was noted in connection with Letter 12. Before Innocent II, an agreement was reached between Bishop Ulgerius and Abbot Fromundus that the abbot would relinquish the baptismal offerings in the churches of the bishop of Angers, while the bishop would thereafter grant the abbot the offerings for churching after childbirth or for marriages, and others, as he had previously obtained them. Surgères retains its name as a castle in the diocese of Saintes. Concerning its church, Urban [wrote] to Abbot Gaufridus. The parish church of Saint Mary of Surgères, and all the churches contained within the boundaries of that same parish.]

If, while we were absent, you have therefore dispossessed us of what we held for thirty years without any bishop or archdeacon making a claim, and which was granted to us by permission of the Roman pontiffs, and if, against our will, you have transferred to our priest what belonged to us, then you have shown us neither affection nor even the appearance of affection. Or, if this is how you know how to bless your friends, you have discovered a new kind of blessedness and affection. If this had been done against us by other men, it would appear to be an act not of affection but of hatred.

If we seemed to have done you some harm, you ought first to have admonished us, so that, if there were fault, we might humbly acknowledge it, or, if there were none, reasonably defend ourselves. But if we were able to do you some good, and did so, we do not wish to receive a recompense which God does not acknowledge. Therefore, as our dearest lords and friends, we humbly ask you not to let us experience any evil from you, from whom we have always hoped for good. For because you are our wholehearted friends, we cannot patiently endure your burdensome treatment.

If you say that the person to whom the penitent confesses ought to have the offering connected with confession, you can likewise say that the offering of the altar should belong to the one who sings the Mass, and the offering for the dead to the one who buries the dead. In that case, let our minister take everything, leaving us none of the offerings in the churches where we serve day and night.

[Note: “The Church ought not to pay a tithe.” The bishop did not deny that the monks lawfully possessed the tithes; rather, he maintained that tithes were not owed by ecclesiastical persons. Goffridus cleverly refutes this.]

Out of reverence for your religious character, we do not say that this is unjust; but we entirely fail to understand how it is just. For the law of Moses did not command it, the prophets did not foretell it, the holy Gospel was silent about it, and the authors of the canons either did not wish to mention it or consigned it to oblivion. Farewell.

## LETTER XLI

To the honorable bishop P., Brother Goffridus, abbot of Vendôme, allodial holder of the Apostolic See and its servant, [sends this admonition:] not to do to others what he does not wish done to himself.

[Note: “To the honorable bishop P.” This was Peter himself, bishop of Saintes. The monastery of Vendôme also possessed tithes from saltworks, as is clear from its foundation charters, in the district of Poitiers at the Olonne. One might therefore wonder whether this letter was written to Peter, bishop of Poitiers, unless it were established that in the time of Calixtus it was not Peter who occupied the see of Poitiers but William, Peter’s successor.]

You received a decree of Lord Pope Calixtus in which you and certain other bishops were commanded to be defenders and helpers of the property of the monastery of Vendôme, as of property belonging personally to the Apostolic See. All the others obeyed the pope’s command not merely in word and speech, but in deed and truth. You, however, have heard enough about what has been taken from us in your episcopate and about how many and how great the injuries suffered by our brothers who live there have endured; yet either you did not wish to correct them, or you were entirely unable to do so.

Moreover, you are taking away from us the tithes of your saltworks, which our monastery—namely, the patrimony and allodial property of blessed Peter—is known to have possessed peacefully for sixty years. Therefore we ask your affection to correct what has been done otherwise, lest the man who was appointed our defender by apostolic command appear as our persecutor, and thus—God forbid!—the shepherd become a wolf, when he ought to have been a shepherd.

We have been told that you say the Church ought not to pay a tithe. This is true where one Church possesses nothing in the parish of another Church. But where a Church possesses some property in the parish of another Church, or anything that ought to be tithed, there that Church ought to pay a tithe to the other Church if it wishes to possess that property lawfully. Italy holds this principle; Gaul holds it. For there we know that Churches pay tithes to Churches, larger Churches to smaller, and smaller to larger, wherever one of them possesses property under the jurisdiction of the other.

We do this for Churches, and Churches do this for us. Your predecessors, men of good life and blessed memory, who went before you to the heavenly dwellings, did this as well: they returned the tithes which you now take from us without judgment and without a hearing. But perhaps those blessed men are thought to have been simpletons, because they possessed charity, avoided rapacity, and did not wish to oppress anyone by the burden of their greatness.

It is not fitting for Mother Church to usurp the rights or tithes of other Churches. For, as the Apostle Paul testifies, parents are to store up for their children (2 Cor. 12:14), not to take away what belongs to their children.

If, nevertheless, you are confident that you have some just claim concerning the aforesaid tithes, we offer you the judgment of the Roman pontiff, who alone is permitted to judge and define matters concerning our monastery’s possessions. And so that you may believe what we say to be true, and may not henceforth through ignorance incur the offense of the venerable Roman pontiffs against us, we send you copies of the privileges of Urban and Calixtus.

[Note: “The privileges of Urban and Calixtus.” We gave the complete decree of Urban on this matter, cited in Letter 33, in Book II, Letter 28.]

For your prudence knows that what is known to have been established or commanded by apostolic authority cannot be dissolved or disregarded without danger. Farewell, and while we pray, hear our prayer, if you do not wish your own peace to be disturbed.

## LETTER XLII

To his lord and wholehearted friend, the honorable bishop I., Brother Goffridus, least of abbots, sends affection and the service of affection.

[Note: “Bishop I.” I suspect this was Goffridus of Chartres, to whom he writes in Letter 30. The monk Paganus is also mentioned. They sometimes wrote Joffridus for Goffridus; thus the old manuscript represents our abbot in the letter to Honorius. This letter therefore belonged at the end of Book II.]

I cannot come to you tomorrow, the day after the beginning of the fast, because I am occupied by bodily necessity. When I have been freed from the necessity that holds me, I shall come to you at a suitable time, to recover justice from Paganus and his associates.

That Paganus, as is said, is demanding from you what was formerly forbidden by the holy apostles and is now forbidden by the decrees of the Apostolic See. As you yourself know better, every power to dispose of churches or ecclesiastical property is denied to laymen, even to religious laymen.

[Note: “Even to religious laymen.” From the third synod of Pope Symmachus, Book VI, chapter 294; Ivo, Part XVI, chapter 36; and Gratian, Part XVI, question 7.]

A cleric who attempts to obtain a church or ecclesiastical possession through a layperson is excommunicated according to Gregory VII, Urban, and Paschal II, and by those same authorities is also judged a heretic.

[Notes: “Gregory VII.” In the Roman synod, Letter 11 and Opusculum 2. “Urban.” In the synod of Clermont. “Paschal.” In the Lateran synod.]

Farewell; and may God promote you from one degree to the next for the benefit of his Church. In you, it is believed, what is read in the Gospel has been fulfilled: “He who humbles himself will be exalted” (Matt. 23:12). Until now we have believed your mind humble; we have heard humble speech; we have also seen a sufficiently humble garment. All these things you ought to increase, not diminish, lest there befall you—God forbid!—what follows: “He who exalts himself will be humbled” (ibid.).

What I have just said is indeed presumptuous, but it is presumed out of friendly presumption. You know my inmost feelings, and I know yours likewise. Mutual familiarity will produce contempt neither in you nor in me; rather, it will nourish assent to divine justice and a more devoted affection in God.

## LETTER XLIII

To his sweetest lord and wholehearted friend, Lord R., bishop of praiseworthy life, Brother Goffridus sends affection and the service of affection.

[Note: “The bishop.” Perhaps Rainaldus, bishop of Angers; indeed no one else occurs to whom it could more suitably be assigned. In this way it should be joined to the other letters written above to him.]

The council, as it is now called, will be held at Rome, not at Cremona, as we had heard.

[Note: “The council at Rome.” Held by Calixtus II in 1123. The Appendix to Sigebert says: “The council is held at Rome; peace between kingdom and priesthood is restored, and the right of episcopal investitures is wrested from, or renounced by, the emperor.” I think this is the same council to which Hildebertus had been summoned and concerning which he reflects on the grave difficulties of the journey in Letter 76: “Especially at this time we need your prayers, since we are being wearied by the journey to Rome, where the pope, having summoned the cardinals, bishops, and abbots from this side of the mountains, will celebrate a general council in the city. For us, who must travel there, winter is threatening: the Alps with snow, the waters with their rising, the emperor with his fetters, the city with seditions, and the palace with its demands.”]

My spirit is therefore greatly disturbed, because the pope’s will compels me to wish to go there, while the severity of the season and the distress of the longer journey dissuade me. These considerations would have had to be set aside for the will of so great a lord and master, if bodily illness permitted what is commanded to be done in any way. No sensible person has ever exposed himself to death unless with a certain hope of eternal reward. But if someone has brought upon himself a death that he ought to have avoided, he is not read to have found rest, but misery. Christ indeed commands us to carry the cross (Luke 14:24), not to seek burial. Farewell.

# BOOK FOUR

## LETTER I

To his dearest lord and most blessed Father, Hugh, most excellent of all abbots, Goffridus, the least of his sons, sends what a son owes a father and a servant his lord.

[Note: “To Hugh, most excellent of the abbots.” Hugh, fifth abbot of Cluny, was altogether an ornament of his age and a glory to his order. Ordericus Vitalis says of Robert, later abbot of Ouche, that he had gone to Cluny, where at that time Abbot Hugh presided over the monastic ranks as the special glory of monks in his generation. His praise was all the greater because his administration lasted so long: he presided for forty-three years. Urban II, who had been initiated by him into monastic life, showed how highly he regarded him in what he wrote to him at the very beginning of his pontificate, among other things: “To you, therefore, most holy, most reverend, and most beloved brother, a singular prerogative of affection is owed by us, both because of the ancient familiarity of the Apostolic See and because of the reverence due to the most noble religious life of yourself and your monastery. Moreover, there is another reason that makes us no less indebted to you and to your monastery: through you I received the rudiments of monastic religion, and in your monastery I was reborn through the second grace of the Holy Spirit.”]

Whatever health or honor your pure affection has conferred upon me, without any preceding or subsequent merit of mine, I often consider in my mind; yet I cannot discover what I might worthily repay for such great benefits. Nevertheless, I offer what I hold more dearly: myself, since by your goodness you have drawn my whole spirit to yourselves.

But the man whom your goodness wisely drew to itself and carefully subjected to itself, Abbot Henry, does not cease to attack me.

[Note: “Abbot Henry.” Henry of Angers, to whom Letter 3 is addressed. At this time the monastery of Angers was counted among those governed by the abbot of Cluny. So great was the reputation of the monks of Cluny in the early centuries that princes and bishops eagerly sought to incorporate ancient monasteries under their jurisdiction into their body and family. Among these, in Goffridus’s time, were eighteen abbeys which we have seen expressed in letters of Gelasius and Honorius II to Peter the Venerable: Saint Martial of Limoges; in Auvergne, Saint Austremonius of Mozac, Tiern, and Menat; in Poitou, the New Monastery, Saint Peter of Maillezais, and Saint Cyprian of Poitiers; in Quercy, Figeac and Saint Peter of Moissac; Saint Germanus of Auxerre; in Burgundy, Saint Mary of Vézelay; in Rouen, at Poteser; in the Tervan district, Saint Bertin and Saint Ulmar; in the Cambrai district, Hunold’s Court; in Saintonge, Saint John of Angers; in Nîmes, Saint Giles; and in Italy, Saint Benedict upon the Po. There were also several others afterward in which no abbot was elected without the consent of the abbot of Cluny. Thus the praise which Paschal attributes to the Cluniac order in writing to Hugh is not empty: “By the grace of almighty God, the kindness of the Apostolic See rejoices in your religious life, since, through the diligence of your care, with the Lord’s generosity, religion has been established throughout many parts of Gaul where it had not existed, and restored where it had failed.” Calixtus II also writes to Abbot Pontius that the monastery of Cluny was, in his time, a mirror of monastic religion and an example for Gaul.]

Before he had the abbacy and afterward, I said what good I could about him; I praised his name for the honor of the monastery of Cluny. Nor did I fear to incur the hostility of those over whom he presides, on his account. Yet he has repaid evil for good to me, his fellow brother, with a recompense which God does not acknowledge.

[Note: “A recompense which God does not acknowledge.” Marbodus of Redon to Rainaldus, bishop of Angers: “This is the recompense of the wicked, which the Lord does not know: that evil is repaid for good.” Our author uses the expression in Book I, Letter 15; Book II, Letters 17 and 28; and Book III, Letters 10 and 40.]

I do not know by what storm of mind he is driven, and without cause he attacks me, a servant of your holiness. He is trying, with considerable excess, to join to his own lands the land which our monastery is known to have possessed peacefully for thirty years and more in the time of his venerable predecessors, secured to it by apostolic authority, because it lies near his lands.

Taking this as an occasion, he exercises against me every device by which he can harm me, although he ought to have spared me, if not for brotherhood, at least for your fatherhood. Like another Saul, he pursues me as I flee like David; he is moved by no brotherly compassion toward me.

I can neither resist him nor ought I to do so, because I fear offending your gentleness. Since I do not dare in any way to rise against him, I humbly ask that your pious severity rise against him and deign to command him not to oppress me through your love rather than through the burden of his greatness. But if he complains about me, let your presence serve as judge of his complaint. I have always appealed to you, and I appeal still. I desire to submit to the judgment of your wisdom.

We are both your sons: he by profession of the mouth, but I—God knows, who knows hearts—by devotion of the heart. We therefore ought not to disagree with one another, but should seek together the honor and benefit of the monastery of Cluny: multiplying its friends, calming its enemies, and, if necessity requires, confronting them together.

Father of great discernment, restrain that lord abbot, lest he act otherwise—the man whom people say has long been a lover of discord, a sower of quarrels, and a disturber of peace. Let him not take your affection away from our brothers; let him not provoke them to anger without benefit; let him not give them occasion to proclaim against the place of Cluny, which I dare to call a second paradise.

[Note: “A second paradise.” Thus Fulbertus, Letter 71, to William, abbot of Dijon, complained that through his own fault he had been expelled from the paradise of your monastery. What these men praised of one or another monastery, others did not hesitate to proclaim of all properly ordered monasteries. Peter of Blois, Letter 13: “According to the judgment of my heart, if paradise exists in the present life, it is either in the cloister or in the schools.” But this passage recalls an old poem of this kind, by an author still uncertain, though, considering the times, by no means inelegant. I hope that those who delight in praise of the monastic life will not be displeased that it is inserted here, as we copied it from the manuscript of Saint Melanius of Redon.]

### Praise of the Monastic Life

Happy is the human flock that follows Christ’s teaching  
and, scorning wealth, retains nothing as its own.

Those whom the holy Rule restrains under one man’s authority,  
of whom each does nothing according to his own will;

whose hearts are one, whose will is undivided,  
whose dress and food are alike for all;

yet in such a way that each receives what he seems to need,  
as fragile age or weakness requires.

All luxury is absent; opportunity for sin is rare,  
since all fear the eyes of all.

The common law quickly requires faults to be disclosed,  
so that the punishment that follows may cut away the emerging vice.

They flee idleness; useful labor occupies everyone,  
lest harmful thoughts enter those who are sluggish.

Nothing is confused where everything is done in order;  
everything is cared for, and nothing is neglected.

There is order not only in life but also in speech.  
They distribute great things and small things equally.

No one speaks or keeps silence except as prescribed;  
each stands, sits, and walks according to his proper order.

They frequent the threshold of the church night and day,  
and by holy prayers help themselves and their own.

Why do I linger and try to unfold each detail in words?  
Whatever they do is a work of body or soul.

What of the fact that they live in such a way  
that the dwelling itself is sacred in its arrangement and number,  
and sufficient for itself?

The household structure displays a square form,  
with courts distinguished by four porticoes.

These are enclosed by three buildings, which bodily need requires,  
and by a fourth building, which is the house of the Lord.

They provide the monks with movement, life, and a place of standing,  
where they are contained like sheep in folds.

The first building keeps drink and food,  
from which the adjoining second building refreshes them.

The third warms limbs wearied by the day’s labor;  
the fourth continually resounds with God’s praises.

I pass over many things worthy of similar mention,  
but I shall say briefly: nothing is superfluous, and nothing is lacking.

I compare these nobles, this senate worthy of praise,  
small in outward appearance but excellent in conduct,

to ants, whose industrious little troop  
carries a burden greater than its body.

So that they may be able to lead a common life,  
they build small storehouses beneath the same roofs.

I compare them to divine bees, which in a small body  
carry mighty and noble spirits;

which store liquid honey in hexagonal cells  
and produce a wonderful work of usefulness;

which preserve discipline and household laws  
and are all refreshed together by their ingenious dwelling.

I compare them to the stars that make the upper court shine,  
which illuminate the dark air in the night,

which preserve through the ages the law once imposed upon them,  
and complete their accustomed courses and numbers.

I compare them to the heaven that solemnly revolves around all things;  
moreover, I compare them to angelic spirits,

who continually resound “Holy” with a threefold voice,  
while the monks on earth sing the same.

Thus the cherubim in heaven and the monks dwelling on earth  
offer one service to the one Lord.

[The preceding sentence continues:] I dare to call it a second paradise, so that he may have an occasion to proclaim it. Let him not, through his bitterness, cause to sprout again what was once cut away by the sweetness of your affection. Let him not separate our monastery from Cluny, the place of blessedness; let him not raise a scandal between you and our brothers.

I say nothing about myself, as though I ought to be scandalized; for even if everyone else is scandalized, I shall never be scandalized (Matt. 26:33). Farewell, my sweetest lord and Father.

## LETTER II

To the dearest Father, Lord Pontius, abbot of honorable life, Brother Goffridus, humble servant of the monastery of Vendôme and allodial holder of the Holy Roman See, sends pure affection and the service of pure affection.

[Note: “To Abbot Pontius.” Pontius of Cluny, Hugh’s successor, but very unlike him, as is shown by what Peter the Venerable and another Peter of Poitiers report about him.]

We have heard that one of our monks, named Peter Goscelin, has come to you, but we do not know with what intention.

[Note: “Peter Goscelin.” He had passed from the monks of Vendôme to those of Cluny. Goffridus demands him back and shows that he cannot be retained without his abbot’s consent. The first letter of Saint Bernard to his nephew Robert, who had fled from the Cistercians to the Cluniacs, concerns the same matter. In that letter, and in the work On Precept and Dispensation, where he also treats this question, there is much that agrees with Goffridus’s wording.]

If he did so to visit you or your community, then although it ought to have been done with our permission, we do not dare, out of reverence for you, to censure him. But if he acted with the intention of leaving the place where he received the habit of his second regeneration, we cannot approve it, since the Rule of Saint Benedict entirely contradicts this, and the authority of the holy Roman pontiffs, by which the patrimony of blessed Peter—namely, our monastery—is protected, forbids it under anathema.

Therefore, as your dearest lord and father, we humbly ask you to send our brother back to us in accordance with our humble petition, lest he appear to have made void the first faith of his monastic profession, and lest the bond of charity by which your venerable predecessor, a man of holy memory, Lord Hugh, carefully bound us to himself and to the monastery of Cluny be broken on this occasion—God forbid!

We tell you truthfully that if the aforesaid brother has acted against us, provided that he comes back to us, we forgive him everything and from the whole heart, out of love for you and for the soul of the glorious man Lord Hugh, who, although we were not worthy even to become his servants, made us his sons in charity.

But if he refuses to come to us and despises obedience, and, having violated the first profession he made with us, dares to profess elsewhere, neither will his first profession be pleasing to God nor his second. For the first did not await the fruit of the stability he had promised, while the second, having taken away from our Church the first offering of his monastic life, will constitute sacrilege.

If, however, the authority of some privilege permits you to retain without the permission of his abbot a monk from a known and regular monastery, the authority of that privilege struggles against the Rule of Saint Benedict and appears to contain something other than the privilege Christ the Lord gave to blessed Peter. For that privilege was granted by God to Peter so that he might loose what was to be loosed and bind what was to be bound, not so that it might provide men with an opportunity to lie or to commit perjury.

Since Saint Benedict binds with the chains of condemnation one whom blessed Peter does not absolve, we ought not to absolve him either. Although we do this with great reluctance and under compulsion, by the authority of the holy Rule and the authority of the holy canons, we excommunicate him until he repents, so that neither while alive may he receive holy communion nor, when dead, burial.

Moreover, we remind you of one thing which we do not believe your sincerity fails to know: every shepherd ought to preserve his own sheep, not seize those belonging to another. If he seizes another’s sheep, he follows the custom of a wolf, not of a shepherd.

If anyone again claims, by the authority of a privilege, that he can do such things, then by that same authority let him confess that he can gather what he did not sow; possess other men’s villages, castles, and cities; take sons from their fathers; and take wives from their husbands. What more? Let him confess that he can make every possession belonging to another his own.

Such a privilege contains a great deal of depravity and absolutely nothing of divine law. Its authority makes its own chief observers guilty and oppresses innocent neighbors. Whoever attempts by a privilege to act against the privilege Christ granted to Peter is proved to be like a prophet teaching falsehood. While Christian souls follow his voice, which proclaims false blessedness and true misery, they are endangered.

## LETTER III

To his dearest lord Hainricus, a man of venerable life, Goffridus, whatever kind of servant of the monastery of Vendôme he may be, sends the same salvation that he desires for himself.

[Note: “Hainricus.” Abbot of Angeriacum, to whom Ivo also writes in Letter 233. The people of Saintes formerly called Angeriacum a town on the Vultonne River; later, by a slight change of letters, it became Angeliacum, and Saint John of Angeliac, after the head of the Lord’s Forerunner had been brought there and a monastery founded by Pepin, king of Aquitaine, as an old account at the end of the works of Saint Cyprian relates. Ademar, a monk of Saint Martial, says: “Pepin, king of Aquitaine, son of the emperor Louis, by his father’s command, caused the monastery of Saint John at Angeriacum to be built.” It therefore retained its old designation together with the new, something that occurred in only a few cases; for elsewhere the earlier names fell completely silent. Thus Mons Indiciatus became Saint Flour among the Auvergnats; Centula, Saint Richarius among the Ambians; Segestrum, Saint Sequanus among the Lingones; Cessato, Saint Tiberius among the Septimanians; Catuliacum and Novigentum, Saint Denis and Saint Clodoaldus among the Parisians; and many others. The monastery of Angeriacum was later restored and enriched with revenues by Agnes, the foundress of Vendôme, and its new basilica was consecrated in 1058, under Abbot Goffridus, by the successor of Arnold, who had attended the dedication at Vendôme.]

What we recently established through mutual affection, the enemy afterward wished to obstruct in many ways. For, as I believe, he himself suggested to our brothers that they ought to resist those arrangements and not allow themselves to be bound by the bond of peace and affection established by us.

But the merciful God, who keeps even the evil one bound in the upper regions of Egypt, bound him with the reins of his power so tightly that whatever discord and dissension he had previously suggested to the brothers was unable to retain its force.

Therefore, through this letter I admonish your affection to come to our chapter on whichever day you wish, up to the next feast of blessed Mary, without any hesitation whatever, so that the peace and concord may be confirmed which, as is established, have been arranged by us and by you. For we are not the kind of people who have one thing ready on the tongue and another locked in the heart.

## LETTER IV

To Lord Hainricus, venerable abbot of Angers, lord and friend, Brother Goffridus asks from God the effect of pure truth and from himself the affection of true love.

I think that the expression we exchanged concerning God’s cause was, on your part, lip-service rather than heartfelt. Hence I regret that you used a less watchful word, and I understand that you possess a gladiatorial spirit.[^c0016-1] Nevertheless, God willing, I shall begin what I said, and, with his generosity, I shall complete what has been begun. Farewell; and if there are in you any organs of catholic piety, write back to me truthfully.

## LETTER V

To the most beloved Father and lord, Henry, abbot of honorable life, brother Goffridus sends greetings with affection.

Nearly two months have now passed since I sent our seal to you at Poitiers, as I had told you I would.[^c0016-2] And because you could by no means be found there, I would gladly have done it then; but I cannot do so until Lent. The opportunity to do what I had arranged to do with you has been taken away from me, but my willingness has not changed. For I have no money, wars are threatening, and the severity of the season forbids it. Farewell; and acknowledge what our brothers complain of: that in your abbey less regular, monastic kindness is shown to them. If you please, correct what has been done otherwise. I would have written to you about receiving guests, but I know that teaching Minerva is superfluous.

[^c0016-1]: **“A gladiatorial spirit.”** In Letter 1, concerning the same matter: “That abbot whom people say has long been a lover of discord, a sower of quarrels, and a disturber of peace.”

[^c0016-2]: **“I sent … to Poitiers.”** Flodoard, *Chronicle*, under the year 955: “Having set out for Aquitaine, he went to the city of Poitiers,” Book II, chapter 21. “I shall have him brought to Angers,” Peter of Blois, Letter 13. “Almost the whole of Orléans would dissolve into tears.” The writers of that period and of neighboring periods used *Aurelianis*, *Blesim*, and *Pictavim* in the singular. Yet when they indicated that something was in, or was being done in, those places, they used the plural: *Aurelianis*, *Blesis*, *Andegavis*. Fulbert, if indeed the text is to be read this way, in Letter 113 to King Robert: “But when I heard that you were going to hold a council at Orléans, a city devastated by fire, I marvel and tremble.” Our author, Letter 14: “We shall conduct business at Angers.” In the same way he commonly says *Turonum*, “from Tours,” and *Turono*, “at Tours,” as well as *Turonis esse*, “to be at Tours,” and *Turonis loqui*, “to speak at Tours.”

## LETTER VI

To John, abbot of venerable life,[^c0016-3] Goffridus, least of all abbots, sends the wish that he act mercifully in all things.

This brother, who returns to you out of necessity as well as willingness, as to his spiritual father, must be supported by great mercy. He has indeed sinned greatly; his tongue speaks sufficiently clearly of that. Therefore, if it pleases your piety, he seems more worthy of pardon than of punishment, and we ourselves join him in asking this of you.
