May, then, the humble and true confession of this penitent—as we believe it to be—have weight with your goodness. May our devout and charitable supplication on his behalf also have weight. Above all this, consider the compassionate reception owed by a pious father to a returning son, who, in a distant country, dissipated the portion of property he had received by living dissolutely (Luke 15).

[^c0016-3]: **“To John, abbot.”** Of Dol, as the index of the Le Mans Codex has taught us. Dol, or Bourg-Dol, is a distinguished monastery in Berry, founded by Ebbô the lord—not, as some have thought, under Charles the Bald, but while the Simplex was reigning—at approximately the same time as Cluny. There was also another monastery of Dol in Armorica, later converted into an episcopal see and then a cathedral seat; this is the Church of Dol mentioned by Ivo in Letter 176.

## LETTER VII

To the beloved Father in Christ, William, abbot of honorable life,[^c0016-4] Goffridus, humble servant of the monastery of Vendôme, never to forget the hospitality by which many have pleased God.

Because the evangelical command instructs us to care for the welfare of our neighbor as for our own, we neither can nor ought to conceal from you what we know to be contrary to the honor and good reputation of our monastery. When we were recently going to Saintonge, as we had previously told you we would, a sudden and terrifying storm of thunder and lightning arose. Greatly frightened by it, and severely exhausted by the reverberations of hail and the floods of rain, we judged it fitting to turn aside, for the sake of lodging, to your dependency at Pinu,[^c0016-5] which we encountered along the way.

There we found a monk, Garinus, cellarer of the house, most unworthy of a dependency—an inhuman man and a slave to avarice. When we first entered the house’s outer gate, he began to growl and to stare at us with a grim expression and sidelong eyes. Afterward he did not hesitate to utter undisciplined words, fearing neither God nor showing us, nor the Order, any reverence. With the cries produced in him by his deformed greed, he mocked us by calling us “lords”; that demoniac monk shouted:

“Where are you going in? The prior is away. We shall do nothing for you. We do not even have room in which your twelve horses might be placed.”[^c0016-6]

The place could sufficiently accommodate twenty horses, and still can. After we had endured these and many other words of expulsion from him for a long time, outwardly maintaining the appearance of patience, although something else was taking place in our hearts, and while reason was suppressing the flame of impatience, we said to him:

“Brother, do not be upset. You see that the rain is pressing upon us; the sun has already set; necessity urges us to seek lodging. We carry bread and wine, fish and cheese with us; we shall gladly buy whatever else we do not have.”

At last he gradually began to lay aside the ferocity of his expression, to raise his eyebrows somewhat, and to reveal the eyes he had previously kept almost closed. Then he deigned to speak to us; he was even willing to eat with us, though only after much urging. He offered us the bread and wine that he knew we possessed, and whose transport over a greater distance burdened the horses; but he utterly refused us the hay and grain that he had in abundance and that we urgently needed.

Farewell, and bind this disciple of Satan—who makes the Order, seasoned with charity, tasteless through his bitterness—with the bonds of monastic severity, so that he may do no further harm.

[^c0016-4]: **“To William, abbot.”** Of Saumur, that is, of Saint Florentius on the Loire; a man distinguished, according to the records of that monastery, both by birth and by religious character. He was the brother of the lord of Dol, who is said, for his sake, to have presented Saint Florentius with a richly furnished and revenue-producing dependency at Dol. William presided for forty-eight years, almost until the death of Paschal II.

[^c0016-5]: **“Your dependency at Pinu.”** That is, a priory, as appears somewhat farther below: “Where are you going in? The prior is away.” Churches, cells, and altars belonging to a monastery or to some greater church were called the “dependencies” (*obedientiae*) of that place because they were governed by its direction and command. Thus in Book I, Letter 9; Book II, Letter 32; and Book V, Letter 38. Fulbert, Letter 1: “The other two, namely Vivianus and Durandus, both provosts, pretending that they wished to go out to their dependencies.” The papal letters use the term frequently, as in Urban II: “Urban, bishop, to the archbishops and bishops in whose dioceses the priories and dependencies of the Church of Cluny exist.” Ulger, bishop of Angers, to Suger concerning the election of Robert, abbot of Bourgueil: “Indeed, the venerable and religious community of that place, who had gathered for the feast of that place even from the most distant dependencies, hastened to choose for themselves as father and shepherd one from the heart of their monastery, Robert, a great man.” Hence also *obedientiarii*, “superiors of dependencies,” as in the letters of Innocent II: “The priors and superiors of the dependencies of the Cluniac brothers.” In the county of Poitiers, besides this priory of Saint Florentius, the monastery of Saint Mary of Pinu, of the Cistercian Order, also bears the name Pinu.

[^c0016-6]: **“Your twelve horses.”** That Goffridus was accustomed to travel accompanied by a numerous cavalry is indicated by what he writes in Book I, Letter 8, to Paschal, and Book III, Letter 16, to Hildebert. Such, indeed, was then the splendor and wealth of the Church. Yet one would not call it excessive in Goffridus, unlike the conduct of another abbot rightly censured by Saint Bernard in the *Apology to William, Abbot*: “For—to say nothing of the rest—what appearance of humility is it to travel with so much pomp and cavalry, to be attended by the services of so many long-haired men, so that the multitude of one abbot is enough for two bishops? I lie if I have not seen an abbot lead forty horses, and more, in his retinue. He would allow thirty horses to one bishop; how few bishops today could maintain that many?”

## LETTER VIII

To the venerable lords and brothers William, abbot of Saint Florentius, and Bernard, abbot of Saint Sergius,[^c0016-7] Goffridus, servant of the servants of the monastery of Vendôme, sends the wish that they love God and the things of God with a perfect heart and hate with perfect hatred the things done against him in the world.

If we are bound to one another by the bond of true charity, and if, kindled by the fervor of the Holy Spirit, we have resolved to fight against that crooked and deceitful man whom you know,[^c0016-8] lest our souls perish with the people of God, then day by day we ought to be inflamed more and more by the fire of that same Holy Spirit.

We know, indeed, that the reward of eternal blessedness is not promised to everyone who begins well, but is granted only to those who persevere. For beginning something good, only to abandon it unfinished, is shown to be of little or no value. Even among secular people it seems worthy of great ridicule when someone begins something but does not bring it to completion. If this is so—or rather, because it is so—in worldly affairs, it is plainly evident what sort of people we ought to be in God’s affairs.

For if those who love the world and the things of the world are ashamed when their work is left unfinished, how much more ought we, who must love God and the things of God before and above all else, to be ashamed if we leave unfinished the work of his that we have begun?

Beloved, if we are now lukewarm or negligent in God’s work, and if, under the appearance of simplicity, we pretend not to resist the adversaries of his Church, we must fear that on the day of the great and exceedingly dreadful judgment we shall find him opposed to us, and that, when he rebukes us, we shall learn that we were deceived by foolish simplicity.

Then perhaps, to our disgrace—God forbid—he will uncover the scars of his wounds and say:

“O you deceived by false simplicity, I myself endured these things for you; and what return did you make to me, when you presumed to conceal the truth so that men might always be praised and venerated?”

We ought to fear these things greatly, lest the Lord bring them against us in his judgment. We already know that they have been announced in part through his ministers. For from the testimony of divine Scripture we have learned that, if we suppress the truth because of a person’s status, we deny Christ, who is the truth.

The Prophet also clearly shows that some deserve condemnation because of excessive simplicity, where they are said to be placed in hell like sheep (Psalm 48:15). He calls them “sheep” there not because of true innocence, but because of their dishonorable simplicity, by which they are unwilling or unable to resist evil; and he declares that they will perish without end.

Therefore, casting aside the veil of simplicity, let us speak the truth openly, saying with the Prophet:

“Who will rise up for us against the wicked, or who will stand with us against those who practice iniquity?” (Psalm 93:16).

Let us add the Apostle’s words:

“If God is for us, who can be against us?” (Romans 8:31).

We are, and ought to be, people who do not seek human praise and do not fear human reproach, because, according to the Apostle, those who are such cannot be servants of Christ. Hence the Prophet also says:

“Those who please men are confounded” (Psalm 52:6).

If we ask what we ought to do for God, or what we ought to suffer for his name, let us consider what he himself did and what he endured for us; then we shall understand more fully what we are to do for him.

We cannot recount everything that the Lord did and endured for us in the world, but let us firmly believe—and affirm by believing—that whatever he did and endured was entirely the mystery of our salvation.

Although he was God, he became man from a virgin mother. He endured reproaches, mockery, insults, tribulations, scourges, blows, and the spittle of unbelievers. He willed to be fastened to the cross with nails, crowned with thorns, fed with gall, given vinegar to drink, and wounded with a spear. By tasting death for a time, he broke the bonds of eternal death.

What else, brothers, did he teach us by doing these things, except to walk along the paths along which he himself first walked? Let us therefore walk in his paths and follow him, as he taught us to follow him continually. Whoever now refuses to follow him will undoubtedly follow the one whose punishment will have no end.

But how do we follow God and our Lord, and how do we walk in his paths, if we remain silent when we see the abomination standing in the holy place? The abomination seems to stand in a holy place when, in the holy Church, some abominable person dominates others without anyone contradicting him.

Whoever sees this and remains silent is said to be accursed by the Lord, for the Prophet says:

“Cursed is he who withholds his sword from blood” (Jeremiah 48:10), that is, who withholds his voice from rebuking sin.

If those who do not rebuke any evil deserve to be accursed by the Lord, how much heavier a curse do those incur who, by their silence, increase the abomination through which, without doubt, many are defiled? For the one who does not cut it off, insofar as he is able, greatly increases the abomination.

In our own time a new kind of abomination has certainly arisen. The son of perdition is already beginning to reign; what he once did as though in secret, he now openly performs as the mystery of iniquity.

Whoever lawfully fights against him will truly be crowned; and, becoming like another Enoch or Elijah, even if he does not thereby suffer martyrdom, he will nevertheless be glorified with the immortality of the martyrs.

And so that we may have stronger courage against the aforesaid wicked man, let us hear what Moses said when he saw certain members of the people of Israel inclined to sin:

“Whoever is for the Lord, let him join me; let him kill his brother, his friend, and his neighbor” (Exodus 32:26–27).

He kills his brother, friend, and neighbor who, when he finds things deserving punishment, does not spare even those whom he loves by kinship.

If, then, the one who is stirred by zeal for divine love against transgressors is called God’s own, surely the one who refuses to rebuke their wicked actions denies that he belongs to God.

From this it is easily understood what is owed by Christ’s faithful to that ambitious man whose name we have suppressed out of indignation. We do not know at all by what proper name he deserves to be called. From childhood, as rumor reports, we learned that he was excessively malicious, and we have come to know this ourselves in part.

And since we have heard that, to increase his iniquities, he relies against the holy Church upon the art of Simon Magus, it is extremely useful—indeed necessary—that we resist him to his face by the authority of Simon Peter.

If we do not resist him vigorously, as our office requires, let us have no doubt that we shall share the lot of that same Simon Magus, who first devised this kind of iniquity—God forbid.

For what does it profit us to pray? What does it profit us sometimes to fast? What does it profit us to refresh the poor, or to perform any other works of goodness, if we pretend not to drive the Simoniac heresy from our borders?

As blessed Gregory says, this heresy first entered the holy Church through deceitful fraud before all others, and, as though first and greatest, presumed to stain the Church’s chastity with exceedingly foul pollution.

Therefore, for God and on God’s account, we ask and entreat you: if you wish to have a share in Christ, labor with us with all your strength so that this savage plague, which has arisen in our region through the diabolical instigation of the often-mentioned minister of heretical depravity, may be utterly cut down—not with a sword of iron, but with the sword of the Holy Spirit—lest, while we remain silent, we sin against the Holy Spirit, a sin that will be forgiven neither in this age nor in the age to come (Matthew 12:32).

Farewell always in the Lord; again I say: Farewell. Let that contumacious man of whom we speak learn that by God’s power we can accomplish more than he can by the impious art of Simon Magus.

[^c0016-7]: **“Bernard, abbot of Saint Sergius.”** Saint Sergius was in the suburb of the city of Angers. In the letter of Hugh the legate, Bernard, abbot of Saints Sergius and Bacchus, is numbered among the abbots who were present at the absolution of Count Fulk. This monastery is sometimes called Saints Sergius and Bacchus, and sometimes Saints Sergius and Medard, as in the diploma of King Childebert III, to whose grandfather Clovis II the monks of Saint Sergius trace their origin.

[^c0016-8]: **“That crooked and deceitful man.”** Rainaldus, the elected bishop of Angers, whose name he suppresses here out of indignation, though he names him in the following letter. His election is discussed in Book III, Letter 21.

## LETTER IX

To William, abbot of Saint Florentius, and William, his faithful archdeacon,[^c0016-9] Goffridus, unworthy servant of the monastery of Vendôme, sends the wish that they despise the world’s prosperity and fear none of its adversities.

We ask and implore you by the truth, which is Christ, not to falter in any way in God’s cause, which you have undertaken against Rainaldus under the inspiration of the Holy Spirit.

If you do so, you have plainly denied Christ, who is the truth, and have made his Church—which ought to be entirely chaste and free—the concubine and handmaid of secular power, to the peril of your souls. Moreover, contrary to what we believe will happen, you will have become liars to all your friends and will rightly have incurred their enmity.

You need not fear, because, after God, you have many good helpers. Among them you may rightly count me and the abbot of Saint Sergius,[^c0016-10] who would rather be flayed alive than consent to so great an abomination.

Farewell; and do not fear losing temporal property on this account. The devil cannot take away as much as God is able to restore to you. Yet you will lose nothing through this cause, and you will receive a reward from God’s hand if you act steadfastly for his faith and name.

[^c0016-9]: **“William, the archdeacon.”** Of the Church of Angers, who, together with Stephen the dean, especially opposed Rainaldus’s election. Both afterward became his friends, having changed from his fiercest enemies into his friends; for this they are reproached in Marbod’s letter: “The malice of Angers is manifold; it has many Stephens and many Williams.”

[^c0016-10]: **“And the abbot of Saint Sergius.”** Bernard. Concerning this conspiracy of the abbots against Rainaldus, Hildebert writes to Rainaldus himself in Letter 11: “I have heard that religious abbots and men of unimpeachable reputation are standing against you, with whom it is all the more dangerous to contend because their reputation is purer, their cause more just, and their dignity greater.” Among them was also Benerius, abbot of Bonneval, mentioned in Letter 16.

## LETTER X

Goffridus, humble servant of the monastery of Vendôme, to his beloved Father in Christ, Archembaldus, abbot of Saint Albinus,[^c0016-11] sends the wish that he love the brothers entrusted to him and hate their vices.

From the testimony of divine authority we have learned that we ought to rejoice in our neighbor’s progress as in our own, and to grieve over his failure as over our own.

Therefore we are greatly distressed on account of one of your brothers, named Joscelinus, in whom we have recognized not merely that charity has been wounded, but that it has died.

Recently, when necessity compelled us to pass near Mairon,[^c0016-12] where he lives obedient to himself and not to God, we sent to ask him to receive us as guests in the house of blessed Albinus and in yours. The words he spoke in reply to those whom we had sent were certainly bad and altogether undisciplined, but his actions were much worse.

We did not wish to write to you everything that he, turning away from us, uttered against us, because it would be lengthy, and we do not wish in any respect to injure the truth, which is scarcely preserved unharmed in a long speech.

We hold this most firmly: he said that he would not receive us under any circumstances, and afterward he carried out that declaration in a manner lacking goodwill.

Writing these things to your affection about a servant of avarice, we ask not that an injury to ourselves, but that an injury to charity, be avenged.

[^c0016-11]: **“Archembaldus, abbot of Saint Albinus.”** Concerning him, the *Chronicle of Saint Albinus* records: “In the year 1106 Girardus, abbot of Saint Albinus, died on the fifth day before the Ides of January. He had been abbot for nine years. In the same year Archembaldus was appointed abbot on the eighth day before the Ides of February.”

[^c0016-12]: **“Near Mairon.”** Mairon was a very ancient possession of the monastery of Saint Albinus: the estate of Mairon in the county of Poitiers. Ancient records, given at Angers in the year of the Lord 966, in the fifteenth year of King Lothair, testify that part of it, usurped by the first counts of Anjou, was restored by Goffridus of the gray tunic, brother of Guido, abbot of that monastery. Mairon Castle is also mentioned in the *Chronicle of Saint Albinus*, where it concerns the war between Louis VII, king, and Count Goffridus in the year 1151: “The little monastery is destroyed. Mairon is restored to its former freedom. The king and count are reconciled. Count Goffridus dies.”

## LETTER XI

Goffridus, humble servant of the monastery of Vendôme, to his beloved brother in Christ, Archembaldus, abbot of Saint Albinus, sends the wish that he not conceal the sins of transgressors, but cut them out at the root as soon as they begin to arise.

We wrote to you complaining about your Joscelinus, and we waited—and still wait—for you to render manifest justice concerning him to God and to your Order. We have been unable to hear that you have done anything about this.

It is therefore clear either that our ears are deaf and unable to hear, or that your hands are contracted and you cannot open them at all to exercise the rights of justice. But by God’s grace we do not have deaf ears. Take care, then, that you do not have contracted hands.

If they have perhaps remained contracted or withered until now, let them no longer be anointed with olive oil, but with the oil of justice, so that they may be healed and quickly opened to restrain Joscelinus, who is swollen with destructive pride.

And because we know that his heart is filled with iniquity, while we believe yours to be full of charity, we ask you with all the affection of love to make your equity so vigorous against him that his iniquity may no longer be able to dominate the holy Order.

But if he should suggest to your goodness that we have a case against you,[^c0016-13] do not spare him on that account. Rather, consider how great are the entrails of charity.

For charity, as you well know, loves not only a friend; it also gives food and drink cheerfully to an enemy who is hungry and thirsty.

We, however, are not your enemies. Everything in you that God loves, we also love, and, if you please, we wish to serve you and yours with brotherly charity.

For whatever we may do concerning our complaints—which conceive labor and give birth to sorrow—we shall always, with God’s gift, preserve charity toward you intact, for charity is the bond of perfection.

This, I say, is that good—or rather, that best—virtue without which possessing the other virtues is condemnable, and with which lacking them is pardonable.

Farewell, and write back to us what you intend to do about the matters we have written to you.

[^c0016-13]: **“That we have a case against you.”** See Book I, Letter 8.

## LETTER XII

Brother Goffridus to Hamelinus, abbot of Saint Albinus,[^c0016-14] sends the wish that he love what God loves and hate what he hates.

It is unseemly for an ant to drag a wagon, and it is unseemly for a teacher of the Church to hold a lie in his hand. Rather, he must always attend to the truth, not to the report of words.

If Albericus denies that he was granted to us, and if Paganus, his son,[^c0016-15] professes that he was made a monk in our church under the title of your monastery, then both deny the truth by speaking falsely.

What Paganus reports to you, even if it were true—as it is clearly and truthfully known to be false—ought nevertheless first to have been investigated before your prudence received him, despite the protests of our monks.

For it is unjust and entirely contrary to the rules of the canons to strip one who is clothed without judgment. It displeases me greatly that you said he was not a fugitive. I had formerly believed your mouth to be a storehouse of sobriety and the seal of truth.

He certainly fled from our place, where he had become our monk, and, secretly fleeing after casting off the robe of his second regeneration, he broke into the cloister of blessed Clement.[^c0016-16] Thus he is recognized not only as a fugitive, but is also proved, by a true statement, to be sacrilegious.

If you offer us justice concerning him, do what is just; first put us in possession of him. For we do not believe that you are unaware that a dispossessed person ought to be summoned neither to a provincial nor to a general synod, and still less to any other legal proceeding.

Moreover, know that it is neither a form of true religion nor a sign of pure affection to revive a Philippic against a friend for the sake of Paganus’s friendship. Nor, if it had pleased your greatness, should the contention that used to exist between our monastery and yours—and that had been almost or entirely extinguished because of your affection—have been brought back to life for his sake.

As for what we did against Paganus, we continue to do it; and we shall not withdraw from him the sword drawn from the sheath of canonical justice until he has first made satisfaction.

If he understands that matters were previously handled otherwise, we shall nevertheless demonstrate, by the authority of the holy canons, that what was done was just and reasonable.

[^c0016-14]: **“Hamelinus, abbot of Saint Albinus.”** Later bishop of Rennes. Hamelinus succeeded Archembaldus in the administration of the monastery and was raised to the bishopric of Rennes in the year 1127. The *Chronicle of Saint Albinus* records for that year: “Hamelinus became bishop of Rennes on the Ides of May.” It records his death in the year 1141: “Hamelinus, bishop, died on the fourth day before the Nones of February.” He is the same man whose letter concerning trial by combat we cited in the preceding book, at Letter 39.

[^c0016-15]: **“Paganus, his son.”** He seems to be the same person mentioned in Book I, Letter 27: “I am sending Brother Paganus, Albericus’s son, to the lord pope”—a surname apparently formed from his father’s name, who is more properly called Albericus here. Therefore, I believe this reading should also be adopted in Book I.

[^c0016-16]: **“The cloister of blessed Clement.”** The priory of Cresson, concerning which see Letter 44.

## LETTER XIII

Goffridus, humble servant of the monastery of Vendôme, to Lord Walter, abbot of laudable life,[^c0016-17] sends greetings with devoted affection.

In the Rule of blessed Benedict, which we have professed, it is recognized as prohibited—and, what is more, by the authority of the holy Gospel—that one person should do to another what he does not wish done to himself (Luke 6:31).

Therefore, with the whole intention of our minds, we must take care that we never, on any pretext, do to others what we do not wish done to us. Otherwise, by tearing our profession of faith, we shall also be judged by God to be despisers of the evangelical tradition.

We have set this before you, venerable Father, because you have made a monk of a certain man, namely Garinus, son of Galandus,[^c0016-18] who, under the act of confession and the promise of his faith, had devoted himself and all his possessions to us, when he was suddenly afflicted by illness. You have accepted his property—indeed, our property, since it had previously been faithfully offered to our church.

If this was done knowingly—which God forbid—it is not hidden from us how contrary it is to Christian religion, and you are certain of it.

We therefore require this man from your affection, and we ask you not to delay returning to us both the man himself and all his possessions, lest the action of delay be charged against you as evidence of greed, and thus brotherly charity, which is the bond of perfection (Colossians 3:14), be wounded through you.

Farewell.

[^c0016-17]: **“Walter, abbot.”** Of Saint Sergius, the successor of Bernard, to whom Letter 8 was addressed. The records of Saint Sergius place Bernard’s death in the year 1102, on the eighth day before the Ides of April, and Walter’s in the year 1113, on the fifth day before the Ides of January.

[^c0016-18]: **“Garinus Galandus.”** The name is formed in the same way as Peter Goscelinus and Paganus Albericus.

## LETTER XIV

To Bernerius, abbot of honorable life,[^c0016-19] Goffridus, least of all abbots, sends salvation from God and the devotion of brotherly affection from himself.

I now need the service of your goodness, which you have often offered me, although I am unworthy of it. May the man whom charity has made a debtor by promising not be reluctant to discharge his debt by fulfilling his promises.

For on the day after the Ascension we are to conduct ecclesiastical business at Angers. We earnestly invite your prudent counsel and assistance and humbly ask that you not be absent from us in this present necessity.

If, however, you pretend not to hear our entreaty for any reason, you may indeed be called a friend—but one who does not remain in the time of necessity.

[^c0016-19]: **“Bernerius, abbot.”** Of Bonneval. This monastery belongs to the same diocese as Vendôme, namely Chartres, but lies in the district of Châteaudun. Bernerius was mentioned in Book I, Letter 21; elsewhere he is called a religious man of good reputation.

## LETTER XV

Goffridus, humble servant of the monastery of Vendôme, to his most beloved lord and most heartfelt friend, Bernerius, abbot of Bonneval, a truly religious man, sends the wish that he always love the blessed Trinity with a pure heart and, without any excuse, not be absent from its approaching feast.

The devotion owed to the celebration with us of the feast of the holy and undivided Trinity,[^c0016-20] which we have mentioned, compels you to come; and the affection of pure love that we hold toward you earnestly asks that, setting aside all other concerns, you not delay your coming in any way.

For it is a religious duty, and an increase of brotherly charity, to celebrate the feasts of God’s saints—and especially the feast of God himself—with devotion, and to fulfill with one’s whole heart the just desire of a neighbor who loves one.

Farewell, and in the matters about which we humbly ask, may it not be burdensome for you to obey God and us.

[^c0016-20]: **“The feast of the Trinity.”** This is the title of the monastery of Vendôme, as the letters of its founder Goffridus and of Bishop Theodoricus make clear. Urban II wrote: “To his beloved sons in Christ, Girardus, abbot of Saint Albinus of Angers, and Berno, abbot of the Holy Trinity of Vendôme.” The brief *Chronicle of Saint Albinus* records: “On the day before the Kalends of June, at Vendôme, the castle-monastery of the Holy Trinity was dedicated in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1040.” Goffridus himself mentions it in Book V, the final letter.

## LETTER XVI

Goffridus, useless servant of the monastery of Vendôme, to Bernerius, abbot of Bonneval, a man worthy of eternal remembrance, sends the wish that he abound in the valley of spiritual grain and sing an everlasting hymn to God.

Kindled, as I believe, by the fire of the Holy Spirit, and unable to restrain the spirit by which you are moved from rebuking Simoniac wickedness, you have stirred up many adversaries against yourself, among them especially one whose name I consider it unnecessary to mention, since it is not unknown even to the common people.[^c0016-21]

And if, because nature has denied it, the deaf do not hear that name and the mute do not utter it, it has nevertheless been indicated to them by gestures and signs from others.

Religious abbot, many people tell you that you are attempting in vain, by words, to extinguish the Simon Magus raised up in the Church in our own time, because no one can be found among men to correct him.

But, filled with prophetic longing, you cannot in any way be persuaded not always to seek someone who will rise with you against the abomination reigning in the holy Church, never ceasing faithfully to cry out with the Prophet:

“Who will rise up for me against the wicked, or who will stand with me against those who practice iniquity?” (Psalm 93:6).

Cry out, then, organ of God, trumpet of the Holy Spirit. Do not be silent, distinguished herald of truth, nor withdraw your voice from correcting heretical depravity. If you cannot drive from the temple by blows, as the Savior did, those who defile the chastity of the holy Church with exceedingly foul pollution, at least do not cease to do so by words, whatever the occasion.

Do not, holy man, do not believe those who assert that you speak without benefit because you cannot recall those against whom you speak from their crime. Those who say such things rebuke with you the holy John, the Lord’s forerunner.

For although he could not recall Herod from incest, he nevertheless did not remain silent about the truth, saying that it was in no way lawful for him to have his brother’s wife (Matthew 14:4).

Therefore, if the holy man deserved to be beheaded and crowned, then impious Herod, together with those who consented to him, deserved to suffer eternal torment.

It is much better, then, to rebuke with John than to consent to Herod by remaining silent about the truth.

Certainly, no Christian may silence the law of Christ, God and his Lord, nor conceal the truth on account of a person. For whoever conceals the truth because of a person seems to deny Christ, who is the truth.

Farewell, and may the impious Simoniacs recognize that, by the power of truth, you can accomplish more than they can by the perversity of Simon Magus.

[^c0016-21]: **“One whose name.”** Rainaldus, the elected bishop of Angers. See what we noted concerning him in Letter 9: Bernerius was among the abbots who jointly opposed Rainaldus’s election.

## LETTER XVII

Goffridus, humble servant of the monastery of Vendôme, to the venerable Abbot Bernerius, a truly religious man, half of his soul—or, if that is not enough, his whole soul.

Most beloved Father in Christ,

Desiring to know how you are, since I cannot be present in body, I have presumed by this letter to ask you, beloved of God and dear to men, how your community is disposed toward you; for I do not doubt that you are disposed most excellently toward it. I ask again about your bodily strength; for I considered it superfluous to ask about the virtues of your soul, because I believe that it progresses from day to day, with certain faith, since the long-standing practice of your goodness, aided by divine grace, completely strengthens and fortifies my judgment in this belief.

In asking how you are, it is not surprising that I am very anxious, for I rejoice and take great delight in your prosperity, while in your adversity I am deeply affected and saddened—although, in an adversity that tests a just man, one ought rather to rejoice, if the force of the love with which I have always loved you allowed the power of reason to prevail. Yet although this reason often knocks at the door of my mind, the door is not opened to its knocking; bound by the cords of your affection, it is not permitted to enter.

I can therefore love your prosperity, but I cannot in any way desire your adversity. Rather, making it my own through the feeling of compassion, I am ready to carry it with you on the shoulders of charity until death.

Farewell.

## LETTER XVIII

To the honorable Father and his intimate friend Bernerius, a man adorned with the teaching of wisdom and the merits of his life, Goffridus, humble servant of the monastery of Vendôme, offers himself wholly, with all that he can.

What I said to you, venerable Father, simply, just as I had heard it, your monks wickedly interpreted. I therefore inform you that I will gladly correct it, and that I will say nothing further from which your plotters—whom I believed to be your sons—might be able to trouble you.

I thought that I was speaking to simple men of good will; but in the presence of those enemies of religious simplicity, I shall place a guard upon my mouth. Their impurity, whether they wish it or not, will be able, as long as I live, to prove by clear indications how purely I love you. With you, if necessity requires, I rejoice to endure adversity; and apart from you I take no delight in possessing prosperity.

## LETTER XIX

To Bernerius, abbot of praiseworthy life, Brother Goffridus sends greeting and affection.

Know—though I tell you this privately—that, God willing, I intend for the present to go to Rome. But I have neither a mule nor a male donkey; and because I believe that you have what I do not, I humbly ask you to lend me both animals, or one, or, if you prefer, neither.

This does not mean that I love you any less because of your possessions; I love you for your own sake.

## LETTER XX

To his dearest friend Bernard, abbot of Saint Laumer, Goffridus, humble abbot of the monastery of Vendôme, sends greetings.

[Note: “To Bernard, abbot.” Of Saint Laumer—that is, of Blois, as he wrote in Book II, Letter 14. Ivo, Letter 172: “Maurice of Blois, abbot of the monastery of Saint Laumer.” Bernard, I think, was Maurice’s successor.]

We have taken care to send to you with our letter this brother, whom we have known to be familiar to you in part, so that you may receive him into your community for the salvation of his soul, if indeed you wish to receive him. For he was with us a long time, as you yourself know well, but he was unwilling to correct his conduct according to our desire. Thus, with good reason, either his malicious life may be blamed, or—God forbid—our ignorance or negligence.

## LETTER XXI

To the venerable brother and co-abbot Odo,

[Note: “To Odo, co-abbot.” Of Marmoutier. Such is our conjecture. Odo, a most religious man, is made by the records of that monastery the ninth abbot after the monks were restored to Marmoutier, and the successor of William. They record his day of death as the thirteenth day before the Kalends of July, and the place of his tomb as the right-hand portico of the church, beside Abbot Bernard, the predecessor of William. This is again Odo, abbot of Marmoutier, to whom there survives a letter of the abbots Hugh and Bernard, published after Ivo’s letters. It must therefore undoubtedly be addressed to Odo.]

his intimate friend, Brother Goffridus sends greeting and affection.

Through the evil rumor spreading everywhere, word has reached our ears that you intend to return to Jerusalem. It ought to be enough for you to have seen Jerusalem once; for if you had never seen it, neither would the devil’s slander have arisen against you, nor would you have needed God’s indulgence.

The faith of your monastic profession can in no way be observed by going to Jerusalem; rather, it would be violated. For just as going to Jerusalem has been prescribed for laymen, so it has been forbidden to monks by the Apostolic See. I know this myself, as one who was close to the lips of Pope Urban when he both ordered laymen to make pilgrimage by going to Jerusalem and prohibited that very pilgrimage to monks.

When Saint Benedict speaks of monks who are pilgrims, he means those who at that time renounced the world and professed themselves servants of the Lord, yet did not establish their stability anywhere by their profession. Those who profess themselves in a fixed place must remain where they professed, bear the Lord’s cross, and follow the Lord; they must not seek a burial place abroad.

Let us therefore not stray from the path of our profession under the pretext of a journey to Jerusalem, lest, while seeking a false blessedness, we find the true misery of both body and soul.

Because of your carnal love for your brother who is in Jerusalem—who may perhaps already be dead, or may die before you reach him—do not let your mind be drawn toward things forbidden, nor let care for your spiritual sons and the brothers whom you undertook to govern under the pledge of your faith be abandoned; you will also have to render an account of them to the Lord.

It is not the work of a faithful and good woman to expose her own offspring to pigs and, having once borne them while awake, crush them while asleep. By this art of Satan many who, in their first regeneration, renounced the devil, and in their second renounced both the devil and the world, and who had already entered the promised land under the guidance of the Holy Spirit, have returned in their hearts to Egypt. Disgusted with manna, they asked for pots of meat and other things contrary to the divine law.

They obtained food, then, but in that food they found nets by which they were captured, and a hook by which they were strangled. Such men may be compared to the faithless raven, the evil messenger, who out of desire for the corpse disregarded the command of the holy patriarch Noah. At first, like a dove, they received an olive branch with which they might return to the ark and remain in the ark; but from the windows of the ark, toward which they had already flown by the faith of baptism and monastic profession, they flew out, never to return.

I do not wish any man to be one of their number—much less the shepherd and guardian of the Lord’s flock—for fear that what God forbid might happen: that a shepherd should become a wolf, and a guardian a robber.

Farewell, and may it please you to retain what we have written in a good spirit.

## LETTER XXII

[Note: This letter is copied for the most part from Cyprian’s Letter 65 to Rogatianus.]

Brother Goffridus to his beloved fellow-brother Amblardus, abbot of Limoges,

[Note: “To Amblardus, abbot of Limoges.” In the charter of King Philip I concerning the transfer of the monastery of Mauziac to the Cluniac order, Ademar, abbot of Limoges—that is, of Saint Martial—is subscribed. Thus, at the dedication of the monastery of Vendôme, Abbot Odolricus calls the monastery of Limoges of Saint Martial—now containing secular canons instead of monks—and the monastery of Saint Martial one and the same, just as Floriacum and Saint Benedict’s, Miciacum and Saint Maximin’s, Segestrum and Saint Sequanus’s, Uticum and Saint Ebrulfus’s, Ricomagus and Saint Amabilis’s. One is the name of the dedication; the other is the name of the place in which they were founded. This is immediately understood in places that have only one monastery. In larger cities, however, which now flourish with many monasteries, the name should be understood of the oldest and, in its own time, unique monastery, as in the Council of Reims under Leo IX, where Oylardus, abbot of Châlons, is described as abbot of Saint Memmius; and in Ivo, Letter 216, “the abbot of Chartres,” that is, of Saint Peter.]

with affection: Love the brothers entrusted to you in such a way that you do not love their errors because they belong to you.

Having read your letter, in which you complained about your monk, we have recognized that, forgetful of ecclesiastical discipline, honor, office, and ministry, he presumed to provoke you with the barbs of his tongue.

The tongue, according to James, is indeed an unruly evil and a small member, but it sets a great forest ablaze, because it destroys the substance of soul and body. The tongue is a fire, and in it the whole of iniquity resides (James 3:5–8). The tongue is the sword by which our Creator and Redeemer is known to have been killed by the Jews. Christ’s death is attributed not only to those who killed Christ with a sword of iron, but also to those who killed him with the sword of the word. Christ himself, already placed upon the cross, prayed rather for those who pierced him with a sword of iron, not for those who killed him with the sword of the word.

If, therefore, the perversity of the tongue is not restrained, it is of little benefit if the other evils are corrected.

Regarding offenders of this kind, you have divine counsels and precepts in both the Old and the New Testament. The Lord God says in Deuteronomy:

> “And whoever acts presumptuously, refusing to obey the priest or the judge—whoever that man may be—shall die; and all the people, when they hear of it, shall fear and shall not act wickedly, lest they die” (Deut. 17:12–13).

And so that we may know that this word of God proceeded with his true and supreme majesty, for the honoring and avenging of priests who stand in his place—or fall from his place—when three ministers—Korah, Dathan, and Abiram—dared to act arrogantly against Aaron the priest, they were immediately swallowed up and devoured by the opening of the earth, and paid the penalty for their sacrilegious boldness. Nor were they alone: the other two hundred and fifty who had joined them in their audacity were consumed by a fire bursting forth from the Lord (Num. 16:1).

Thus it is proved by a sound argument that not only those who act arrogantly against the superiors of the Church, but also those who side with them, are condemned by God.

In the Book of Kings, when the priest Samuel was despised by the people, the Lord cried out and said: “They have not rejected you, but me” (1 Kings 8:7). To avenge this, he raised up Saul as king, who trampled and oppressed the proud people and afflicted them with various kinds of punishment, so that the despised priest might be vindicated by divine vengeance.

When holy David had secretly cut off the edge of the cloak of Saul, a most wicked king already deposed by God’s dispensation—an act signifying the slightest murmuring against a teacher—he arose with great contrition of heart. For in the sinful ruler he recognized the power of God, which he ought to have revered, and the authority that God grants neither more to just shepherds nor less to unjust ones.

Solomon, too, established in the Holy Spirit, teaches what priestly authority and power are when he says: “Fear God with all your soul, and sanctify his priests” (Sirach 7:32). And again: “Honor your God with all your soul, and honor his priests” (ibid., 33).

Remembering these commandments, blessed Paul, when he cursed a priest without knowing that he was a priest, and was told, “Do you insult God’s priest in this way?” (Acts 23:4), immediately acknowledged his fault. He asserted that he had incurred the offense through ignorance, saying: “I did not know, brothers, that he was the high priest. For it is written: ‘You shall not curse the ruler of your people’” (ibid., 5).

Elsewhere he says: “There is no authority except from God. And whoever resists authority resists God’s ordinance; and those who resist bring condemnation upon themselves” (Rom. 13:1–2).

Our Lord Jesus Christ himself, our king, judge, and teacher, preserved the honor of priests until the day of his Passion, although they had preserved neither the fear of God nor recognition of Christ. For when he had cleansed a leper, he said to him: “Go and show yourself to the priest” (Matt. 8:4; Luke 17:14).

With that humility by which he also taught us to be humble, he called a priest sacrilegious whom he knew to be sacrilegious. Likewise, when he had received a blow during the assault of his Passion and was told, “Is that how you answer the high priest?” he said nothing insulting against the person of the high priest, but rather preserved his innocence, saying: “If I have spoken wrongly, testify to the wrong; but if I have spoken rightly, why do you strike me?” (John 18:23).

He did all these things humbly and patiently so that we might have and follow the example of his humility and patience.

He teaches that the teachers of the Church must be honored lawfully and fully, even if they act otherwise than they ought, since God himself acts in this manner toward false teachers. Moreover, he subjected the holy apostles to the authority of the scribes and Pharisees, perverse and sacrilegious teachers, so that the apostles’ humility might be demonstrated, their merit increased, and the Christian people thereby learn to bear the yoke of a true priest even under a false priest.

Monks must remember that God instituted abbots, while abbots established monks. If we are able to dare anything against God, who makes abbots, then monks too may dare something against us, since they are the ones who make us.

Whatever the teachers of the Church may be, the Lord nevertheless says of them: “Whoever hears you hears me, and whoever despises you despises me” (Luke 10:16); and: “Whoever touches you touches the pupil of my eye” (Zech. 2:8).

To “touch” in this passage does not mean every kind of physical action, but detraction by tongue or heart committed by subjects against their superiors, with the devil speaking before them as their leader.

Mary, the sister of Aaron and a prophetess, when she spoke against Moses—although he himself had acted somewhat differently—was immediately covered with the mark of leprosy and cast outside the camp of the Lord (Num. 12). Likewise, Uzzah the Levite, when he saw the ark of the Lord tilting because the oxen stumbled and tried to raise it, was immediately struck by the angel of the Lord and died (2 Kings 6:6–7).

The ark signifies the superior of the Church, whom an inferior order is in no way permitted to rebuke.

It is useful and necessary, as blessed Eusebius says, that rulers be feared by their subjects and corrected by them, so that those who do not fear divine judgments may fear to sin through human dread.

[Note: Eusebius, the pope, to whom this saying is also attributed by Ivo, Decretum, Part V, chapter 252.]

He likewise asserts that those who pursue the life and conduct of teachers through detraction, even when those teachers appear blameworthy, are worse than those who seize the property and estates of others. Therefore they are rightly infamous and are expelled from the Church.

For God hates those who arm themselves against the Fathers with the swords of their tongues, or in any other way, so greatly that the attackers of the Fathers are marked with infamy throughout the whole world. Those whom God has reserved for his own judgment neither ought nor can be condemned by human examination.

And blessed Pope Gelasius says:

[Note: Blessed Pope Gelasius. The judgment attributed here to Gelasius is attributed to Pope Caius by Ivo, Part V, chapter 253. It is found in Eusebius’s letter to the Egyptians, and is therefore also cited by Gratian, Distinction II, question 7, under “The sheep.”]

> “The sheep entrusted to their shepherd ought not to rebuke him, unless he has deviated from the Catholic faith, nor can they accuse him in any way. For the deeds of shepherds must not be struck down by the sword of their mouths, although they may appear rightly subject to correction.”

And blessed Gregory writes in the *Moralia*:

[Note: Blessed Gregory in the *Moralia*. Book XXV, chapters 14 and 15; also in Adelbert the deacon, Book II, chapter 155 of the *Speculum*, which he excerpted from Gregory’s *Moralia*.]

> “Even when the life of teachers is rightly criticized, it is nevertheless necessary that it be endured and feared by their subjects.”

A subtle path of uprightness and humility must therefore be followed by subjects: the blameworthy actions of teachers should neither please them, nor should their minds withdraw from preserving reverence for their teachers.

This is well expressed by Noah in his drunkenness. When his nakedness had been exposed, his good sons came backward and covered his more shameful parts (Gen. 9:23). What else does it mean that the sons, approaching backward, covered their father’s shame by casting a cloak over their shoulders, except that good subjects are displeased by the evils of their superiors, yet conceal them from others?

If subjects neglect to restrain themselves from criticizing their rulers, they go so far as to criticize the Creator himself, by whose heavenly arrangement those rulers have been placed over them. For even if human actions appear unjust, the authority that comes from God will never be anything but just, although unjust men are often permitted to possess it because of the merits of their subjects.

Superiors must not tolerate the proud talk or presumption of their subjects. These things are, as the venerable teacher and martyr Cyprian writes, the origin of heretics and the efforts of schismatics who think evil, so that the proud may please the proud while despising their superior with arrogant swelling. Thus one departs from the Church; thus a profane altar is established outside the Church; thus rebellion is directed against the peace of Christ, his ordinance, and the unity of God. . . .

[Note: The venerable teacher and martyr Cyprian, Letter 65 to Rogatianus, concerning an insolent deacon.]

The monk about whom you wrote to me must therefore repent of his audacity, lest he himself become a demon; he must recognize the honor of God in a priest even when that priest acts otherwise, and must satisfy his superior with supplication of all his heart and body.

If he remains proud, exercise the authority of your office over him, so that, like a murderer, deposed from every rank, he may at least in this way recognize the rigor of ecclesiastical discipline. For if God did not spare proud angels, he has taught that proud men must not be spared.

Saint Clement, disciple and successor of blessed Peter, stated while sitting in council that there are three kinds of murderers and taught us that their punishment would be alike.

[Note: Saint Clement, Letter 1 to James, the brother of the Lord.]

Just as he called those who kill their brothers murderers, so he called those who slander them and those who hate them murderers. For whoever kills, whoever hates his brother, and whoever slanders him is a murderer, since detraction, even when mixed with truth, arises from hatred.

You should nevertheless prefer to overcome the injuries inflicted by those who hate through compassion and patience rather than avenge them by the permission and authority granted to you.

Farewell, and if what we have written to you is good, hold fast to it.

## LETTER XXIII

Goffridus, abbot of the monastery of Vendôme, to G., the venerable prior of La Charité, sends affectionate greetings.

[Note: G., prior of La Charité. Among the five principal priories of the Cluniac order, the leading place is held by the one that gave its name to La Charité in the Nivernais, on the Loire. A diploma of King Louis VI, issued at Orléans, shows the source of the Cluniacs’ possession in these words: “The priory of Blessed Mary of La Charité on the Loire, which Gaufridus, bishop of Auxerre, and William, count of Nevers, and Bernard of Chaillant, together with the other faithful of our kingdom, to whom that place of La Charité with its village and all its dependencies belonged entirely in spiritual and temporal matters, gave and granted to Hugh, abbot, and the monastery of Cluny and their successors, without retaining anything for themselves or their professed monks, to have, hold, and possess for all time.”]

We are sending to your goodness the bearer of this letter, so that, if you wish, you may receive him into your community for the salvation of his soul.

We neither dare commend this to you nor wish to condemn it. For he was with us a long time and continually refused to correct his evil conduct. But perhaps he will take care to do among you the good that he delayed doing among us for so long.

## LETTER XXIV

Goffridus, humble abbot of the monastery of Vendôme, to his beloved sons in Christ, Hamelinus,

[Note: Hamelinus. This letter, together with several following it, was written to the monks of Vendôme in Book III, Letters 10 and 11.]

and all the others: to despise the world’s prosperity and fear none of its adversities.

I rejoice greatly because of your steadfastness, which I do not doubt is pleasing to God and which I have learned has been approved by good men.

If you are troubled because you do not raise your voices by singing in the church, I tell you that God does not attend to the voice of the mouth but to that of the heart. Therefore, when we pray, there is no need for resounding words; but wherever we sacrifice, there we must also pray.

The Psalmist makes clear where the sacrifice must be offered when he says: “A sacrifice to God is a troubled spirit; a contrite and humbled heart God will not despise” (Ps. 50:19).

If anyone should attempt to oppose this statement, asserting that sacrifice must be offered upon the altar in the church, as is customary, what he says is certainly true. . . . But he must know that in the Church the altar signifies nothing other than the human heart.

Therefore, brothers, “what you say in your hearts, be moved to compunction in your chambers. Offer sacrifice, as we have said, hoping in the Lord” (Ps. 4:5–6); aided by his mercy, you will overcome the visible and invisible enemy.

Certainly, brothers, you are not fighting because you wish to take away or steal another’s property, but so that the Church, God’s bride, which ought to be entirely chaste and free, may not become the concubine and slave of worldliness. If this could happen—which God forbid—it ought to be called not so much the house of God as a den of thieves and a sewer of vices.

There is also another reason for your great security: you resist not by striking but by suffering; and you do this not so much for yourselves as for your successors. It is therefore clear that you follow the example of our Lord Jesus Christ, who endured death for others and, by suffering, conquered the enemy.

And just as we truly believe that the Lord Jesus, our head, conquered the devil, so we too will be able to overcome all our adversaries if we are his members.

Beloved, do not wonder that I delay coming to you, because I find that sex suspicious to me,

[Note: “I find that sex suspicious to me.” Book I, Letter 26.]

which I know is not to be trusted even by friends. This sex poisoned our first parent, slaughtered its own husband and father, handed Samson, the strongest of its enemies, over to his foes, and in a certain manner killed the Savior, since, unless its fault had demanded it, our Savior would not have needed to die for us.

Alas, how many it has already destroyed! It does not cease to destroy those whom it can still destroy. To speak briefly, this sex has brought a double death upon all who have perished, who are perishing, or who will perish until the end of the world. For if it had not sinned, and by sinning caused the first man to sin, man would not die in the body, nor would his soul perish eternally.

Woe to the sex in which there is neither fear nor shame, neither goodness nor friendship; a sex that can be feared more when loved than when hated.

With these words our letter is concluded. May the Lord Jesus Christ be your abbot and Father; may his good mother Mary be your mother. To God himself and our Lord, who, placed upon the cross for our sins, commended his most holy mother to blessed John, I commend your brotherhood, that in his mercy he may deign to grant you true charity, true obedience, and purity of heart and body; may he make you humble amid prosperity and secure amid adversity, and lead you to joys that will endure without end.

## LETTER XXV

Goffridus, servant of the servants of the monastery of Vendôme, to his beloved brothers in Christ: eternal blessing.

Know that the fact that I have not visited you for so long was not a matter of my will, but entirely of necessity. The illness that seized me while I was with you left me only four days after I departed from you; afterward it attacked me severely.

On the advice of our friends I therefore took a potion by which I ought to have cleansed my body, but by which I nearly cleansed myself of bodily life. By God’s grace, however, I recovered from that illness, and I shall return to you as soon as I can—you whom I have always loved and do love above all people.

## LETTER XXVI

To his beloved disciples in Christ, Ingelbaldus

[Note: Ingelbaldus. A monk of Vendôme. He was already porter before Goffridus became abbot, when he was sent together with Prior Frotmundus to Pope Urban concerning the dispute at Craon with the monks of Saint Alban.]

and all the others, Goffridus, their unworthy Father, sends greeting and blessing from God.

The calumnies that formerly arose against us in the regions of our native Anjou have, by divine assistance, been settled to our honor and advantage.

I have received a certain novice of honorable life and excellent learning; stripped of the rags of the world, I have clothed him in the regular habit.

Our lord prior is held by illness.

[Note: “Our lord prior.” An old manuscript reads *domnus*; likewise Book V, Letter 2: “to Lord Radulf.” In Goffridus, *domni* and *domini* are permanently distinguished when people are concerned: he prefixes *domni* to proper names, or to terms functioning as proper names, as *domnus* Hildebert, *domnus* Pagan, *domnus* Ernald, *domnus* Hamelin, and *domnus* bishop, abbot, prior, archdeacon. In other cases he uses *dominum* where it has the place of an adjective, as commonly in letter-headings: “To the lord and father,” “to the lord and friend.” There is, however, this exception: when speaking of the pope, for the sake of special honor he uses *dominum* for *domnum*, as “lord pope” and “lord Pope Urban,” whereas nearly all other writers say *domnum papam* and *domnum apostolicum*, reserving the name *dominus* for God alone.]

But what should I say about that blessed soul, which, if it were to depart from the world at the Lord’s summons, would, as I believe, never experience hell?

But alas for me! Wretched that I am! When the health of my flesh was flattering me, no recollection of my sins stung me; now at least an unexpected illness, which suddenly pressed upon me, ought to make me concerned about my evils.

Fearing an excessive loss of blood, I had a small amount removed. On the third day after the bloodletting, a disordered flow of the humors, violating the order of nature, poured from my body throughout the day and night. When God’s good mercy had restrained it, a fever, long familiar to me, immediately seized me, empty and exhausted as I was.

Therefore, not now as subjects, not now as disciples, but as lords and dearest friends, I beg you from the innermost affection of my heart: for the sake of charity, which is Christ, forgive me in heart and word whatever I have done wrong against you, and do not delay coming to the aid of my sick soul, since it is greatly in need.

The flesh—which ought to be a cause of boasting—is afflicted; but the soul must be aided by prayer, and we must grieve exceedingly if it is in danger.

## LETTER XXVII

Brother Goffridus, whatever kind of minister and humble servant of the monastery of Vendôme he may be, to his beloved sons and brothers, Hugh the prior and all the others: perpetual blessing from the Lord and pure, undivided affection from him.

Since the eye of our soul watches diligently over you, I humbly ask you to return to me the equivalent of the mutual affection with which I love you.

Therefore keep watch, praying for me, unworthy though I am, yet still your shepherd. I always hold you within the embrace of my memory and, from the breast of my own heart, give you the milk of paternal sweetness—absent in body but present in affection—as both drink and food for your souls.

By such drink and food the minds of faithful disciples are satisfied: by the sweetness and love of their shepherd.

I certainly feel deep compassion for your anxiety, which I do not doubt you experience because of my absence. My mind is often fed with the bread of tribulation and given to drink the water of distress.

Yet I have the greatest consolation: your dear affection, and the persecution of evil men, which you bear patiently. Truly, your genuine affection consoles me, since it prays to God day and night for the purification of my soul.

The curse of wicked men is greatly to be desired, while their blessing is to be feared to no small degree. For their curse creates blessedness, and their blessing acquires condemnation.

If I am not believed in this, let Christ at least be believed—he who does not lie and who speaks to his disciples, saying: “Woe when men bless you” (Matt. 5:11); and: “When men curse you, you are blessed” (Luke 6:26).

Christ promised his faithful, not occasional but continual, and not his unfaithful, oppression in this world. Thus it is proved by sound reason and Christ’s authority that whoever hates the oppression Christ promised does not receive the inheritance of a faithful son, but earns the prison of an unfaithful servant.

Nor does the one who hates the promise of the Christ who makes the promise love Christ the Promiser.

Let us therefore, brothers, love both Christ who makes the promise and his promise with all our heart, all our soul, and all our strength. If we wish to be his own, let us willingly offer ourselves to the oppression he promised his own, because it is little—or rather, nothing at all—to endure any oppression for so great a Lord, when we recognize the Lord himself as the reward of oppression.

Every oppression, tribulation, and distress must therefore be desired with intense longing wherever Christ is at stake. Christ is always at stake in the cause of his Church, in which he is absent from no person, whether just or sinful.

In this cause he tests the just, so that they may be justified still further; by it he examines the sinner, so that he may become just. For this cause he himself also took flesh and struggled to the point of death; and he conquered not by striking but by suffering.

Let us therefore no longer seek the praise of men, so that we may fear whatever oppression they bring, but let us firmly believe that Christ is with us in his cause. For him who redeemed us with his own blood, let us, if necessary, struggle even to the shedding of blood.

For he will reckon it to us as an almost—or entirely—unforgivable sin if we consider our blood more precious than his.

Farewell, and stand firm with him in the cause of God.

## LETTER XXVIII

Goffridus, abbot of the monastery of Vendôme, to his dearest brother Robert, sends greeting.

Abstinence, namely that you refresh yourself only three days [Col. 0170D] a week, would be sufficiently praiseworthy if it in some way appeared regular. For the Rule which you promised before God and his saints that you would observe commands that, if any of the brothers wishes to offer something to God, he should first show it to his abbot, so that it may be done with his will and counsel; but if he does otherwise, it will be counted as presumption, not as merit. You, however, undertook this abstinence without our consent. Hence I fear that it may be counted as vanity rather than salvation. 203 Therefore, brother, I admonish you to abandon, with our will and counsel, what you presumed upon by your own will, and to say with the Lord: “I have not come to do my own will” (John 6:38). Again, if you take pleasure in fasting, I praise you, provided that by fasting you eat [Note: [Col. 0171D] “I praise you, provided that by fasting you eat.” The same is the counsel of Saint Jerome, Letter 22 to Eustochium: “Let daily fasts be yours, and refreshment that flees satiety. It does no good to carry an empty stomach for two or three days if afterward it is equally overwhelmed, if the fast is balanced [Col. 0172D] by fullness,” and Letter 10 to Furia: “Moderate food and a belly that is always hungry are preferable to three-day fasts, and it is much better to take a little every day than enough only rarely.”], and by eating you abstain. For he eats by fasting and abstains by eating who eats every day in such a way that he never satisfies his stomach.

To abstain entirely on one day and then refresh oneself fully on the next does not seem sufficiently advisable. On the day when a person receives no food at all, he often grumbles; but on the other, when he has had the much-desired food in abundance, he scarcely observes moderation in eating, and once he has been filled he displays foolish joy. Therefore we recognize that it is highly useful, indeed necessary, for soul and body that the flesh be sustained daily with food and nevertheless restrained from vices. For one who lives in this way benefits in two respects, since he is both free from elation and does not refuse to perform the other good works.

For the attainment of eternal salvation, bodily abstinence alone is therefore insufficient unless the soul’s fast is also joined to it through abstinence from vices. And so, dearest one, discipline your body with fasts in such a way that you cleanse your mind of vices. This is spiritual fasting, through which, without doubt, one gains fellowship with the citizens above. He keeps this fast laudably whom no slander irritates, whom neither rage nor immoderate anger agitates, whom pride does not strip of the grace of God, whom the tongue does not stain with curses, whom resentment or grumbling does not torment. Farewell, and do not neglect to obey in this matter.

## LETTER XXIX

Goffridus, servant of the monastery of Vendôme, to his greatly beloved brother and son Rainaldus: fear God and love him with fear.

Your illness, which we make our own through compassionate affection, demands no more assistance for itself than our love desires to provide. But because nothing is hurried enough for a mind that longs, perhaps it has occurred to you that your recovery is either not cared for by us or has been consigned to oblivion. But that is not so, because we have sought everything that you told us was necessary for you; some things we have already found after seeking them, while others we have not yet been able to find. The physician on whom your entire hope of recovery depends came to us, intending to return to Tours and there prepare medicine that, as he says, will be entirely beneficial to you, and then to come to you with us. In the meantime he sends you an electuary very useful, indeed necessary, for your illness, which you should take every day while fasting, and after supper before you go to sleep.

## LETTER XXX

[Col. 0172A]

Brother Goffridus to the brothers and sons, R., the prior, and all the others: may everything necessary for the body and useful to the soul be multiplied for you by God the Father, the Lord Jesus Christ, and the Spirit, so that you may serve the Lord with good will and rejoice in him.

With tranquility, abundant peace, and every form of friendship, I long intensely to come to you; but matters necessary and beneficial to you hinder me. Therefore, with God’s help, I shall be released from them, and I shall see you as soon as I can. Although I may appear absent from you in body, believe firmly that I am always present to you in heart and in love; for you are my senses, my thought; you are my inward parts. To you I have given both, namely my body and my soul; for you I spend both daily, as faithfully as I can. Through you I commend both to the Lord God while living, and I shall commend them also when dying.

For the rest, brothers, think about and do what is good and holy, what belongs to good reputation, sound doctrine, and discipline, since God will repay you most generously, and so will I, according to my ability, whatever sort of shepherd of yours I may be. Farewell, and transcribe into your hearts what I have written for you on parchment, lest I regret having written such good things to you in vain—God forbid that you should be ungrateful!

206

## LETTER XXXI

Brother Goffridus to the brothers and sons, R., the prior, and all the others: fear God and observe his commandments.

[Col. 0172C]

I have said, and I say, that I delayed because of what I did for your need and benefit; but now, with the Holy Spirit going before me, I shall come to you, whom I have loved and shall love with the affection of pure love. If I find you as I desire to find you, may you find me as you desire to find me.

Preserve innocence, possess humility, love patience. These are what make the obedience of disciples praiseworthy and the minds of teachers tranquil. Though absent, I write this so that you may give me the opportunity to do for you what I can do better when I am present. If the brothers who acted otherwise than they ought have corrected themselves with suitable amendment, it pleases me greatly, and I give manifold thanks and gratitude to almighty God.

Our nature is dragged, even against its will, toward the punishment of faults, [Col. 0172D] and is swift toward pardon. A firm judgment ought indeed to exist in every ruler of souls, but when someone has sinned and repented, he should not be unwilling to change his decision. Would that the one who sinned might be led to repentance as quickly as our judgment concerning him were changed!

I understand that I have been sent for building up, not for destruction. I seek to trouble none of you, but I wish quiet for you all. But, I say, that man is insane and has an evil spirit who strives to provoke to anger the one from whom, after the Lord, it is permissible to hope for everything, and without whom nothing can be of benefit to him. Farewell.

## LETTER XXXII

Goffridus, abbot not by his own merits but by the grace of God, to his beloved sons R., the prior, and all the others: greeting and love.

The reason I was not with you at Easter was the illness of my body. A hump grew on my back, and because of it I had to be cut open. And although, amid the hands and tearful voices of the beloved women consecrated to God [Note: [Col. 0173C]

The nuns of Fontevraud. We encountered the bare name of Fontevraud in Book I, Letters 24 and 26. Here he names the nuns whose celebrated monastery at that place was founded by Robert of Arbrissel at the direction and under the authority of Peter, bishop of Poitiers, in whose diocese the place lies not far from the borders of Tours and Angers. Robert is the man to whom Letter 47 of this book is written.

The Tours Chronicle records its foundation in the year of Christ 1100 in these words: “In the year of the Lord 1100, the forty-fourth of Emperor Henry and the fortieth of King Philip, a council is held at Poitiers, and not long afterward the abbey of Fontevraud is built in the diocese of Poitiers.” It is remarkable [Col. 0173D] that Abbot Suger reports such a vast number of nuns at that place, writing—before fifty years had passed since the monastery’s foundation—that they had grown to nearly four or five thousand; but Suger’s letter deserves to be read in full because of its subject. Thus he writes to Pope Eugene III:

Letter of Abbot Suger to Eugene III on behalf of the nuns of Fontevraud.

“Most beloved lord and Father, by the grace of God supreme and universal pontiff, Eugene: Suger, abbot of blessed Denis, offers the fullness of obedience and service. On behalf of the sisters living at Fontevraud in a holy and acceptable religious observance, whom the bishop of Poitiers is harassing by demanding submission from them and refusing to bless their abbess, we appeal with every prayer we can to the greatness of your holy apostolate: as it belongs to your discretion to sustain the weakness of the weak by comforting them and to provide what is expedient for each person, may you condescend to the frailty of their sex, retain under your protection those who rely upon your authority, refuse to subject them to another, and grant them peace from this harassment. For your discretion knows that it is not expedient for their souls to leave the enclosure of their monastery or, on this or any other pretext, to join themselves to the world. You know, if it pleases your fatherliness, that the bishop mentioned above is accustomed to disturb those subject to him. May it therefore please your excellence to rescue them from these troubles and, so that they may serve God in peace, provide for them from the abundance of your mercy, cherish and protect them under the protection of the God of heaven and by your apostolic authority—as you would a place of such great religious devotion—which, when we were studying in those parts, we saw newly begun, and which we have heard and rejoice to learn has already grown, by God’s will, to nearly four or five thousand nuns.”]

of Fontevraud, with the razor writing its letters upon our flesh, and while our body was being greatly exhausted by illness and wound alike, neither the illness, nor the cruelty of the surgeon, nor the harshness of the salt immediately applied could make me forget you even for a moment [Col. 0173B]. Rather, the spirit of pure love with which I have always loved you, and love you, and shall love you, remained with you.

At last, with God’s merciful help, I recovered somewhat from my illness, and, carried partly by water and partly on horseback, I came to Angers. Farewell in the Lord at all times, asking God himself and our Lord to make me patient in illness and humble in prosperity, and to preserve both me and you in his love.

## LETTER XXXIII

Goffridus, abbot not by his own merits but by the grace of God, to his beloved sons R., the prior, and all the others: that blessing from God which he gave to his holy disciples.

For your pious prayers and tears, which you offered to the Lord God with filial devotion for me, although I am your unworthy shepherd, [Col. 0173C] I return manifold acts of thanks. The merciful and patient Lord, whose patience sustained me in my long sinning, in his mercy and through the intercession of your merits became the special physician of my illness and wound. Therefore I cannot in any way despair of recovery [Col. 0174A]. I shall come to you as soon as I can—to you whom I intensely desire to see and in whom, after God, I have placed the entire purpose of my soul. Farewell.

## LETTER XXXIV

Goffridus, servant of the servants of the monastery of Vendôme, to his beloved sons in Christ [Note: [Col. 0174D]

To Goffridus of Surgères. The list of letters in the Le Mans manuscript says that this was written to the brothers of Saintonge, and this is for the most part true. In the district of Saintonge there is the church of Surgères, mentioned in Book III, Letter 40, as well as the church of Puyravault, which Countess Agnes gave to the monastery of Vendôme with the approval of her son William, count of Poitiers. At Olonne on the Poitevin coast, the charter of foundation reads: “In the district of Poitiers, half of the churches of Olonne, with the tithes, saltworks, vineyards, and everything issuing from them.”], Goffridus of Surgères, Jordan of Puyravault, Rainaldus Cartaldus, and Hervé of Olonne: greeting.

We command you, and in commanding order you, not to delay coming to us at the next feast of the Holy Trinity and visiting your monastery as is fitting. Indeed, you ought to do this even without being invited. If any of you disobeys, unless detained by serious bodily illness, let him remain excluded from the thresholds of the holy Church until he has made satisfaction for his disobedience.

## LETTER XXXV

Goffridus, humble servant of the monastery of Vendôme, to his beloved sons in Christ, Jordan and Rainaldus Cartaldus: greeting and blessing.

If at times we burden you with our commands, you ought not for that reason to murmur against us or, God forbid, hate us, since we impose many things upon you out of the necessity of the monastery rather than from our own will. Obedience, however, claims this special power for itself: that the will of the one who commands, rather than merely that of the one commanded, should be fulfilled. Hence, giving the form of obedience in the Gospel, the Lord says: “I have not come to do my own will, but the will of him who sent me” (John 6:38).

It is therefore expedient for you, according to the Lord’s judgment, to obey another’s will and not follow your own. But if you consider carefully what great reward is promised you for this in the future, whatever you endure in the present for the Lord will be gentle and light for you. For you are promised life without old age, continual satisfaction without disgust, fellowship with the angels, and—what surpasses every good—to see God continually face to face.

And since we have begun to speak to your charity about obedience, under the name of that same obedience [page 210], and for the remission of all your sins, we command you to bring our fish—namely, the food of your brothers—as far as Angers. Farewell, if you have been obedient.

## LETTER XXXVI

Goffridus, who by the grace of God is what he is, to his beloved brothers in Christ, Hamelinus the prior [Note: [Col. 0175D]

Hamelinus the prior. Of Credon.
