Urban II to Goffridus: “The parish church of Saint Clement of Craon, and all the churches contained within the boundaries of the same parish.” For the castle of Craon and the church of Saint Clement in it, see Letter 44 and Book V, Letter 27.], and Briccius the cellarer: greeting.

I want you not to be unaware, but firmly to believe, that I shall come to Angers with a large retinue on the eve of the Ascension for the matter you know about, unless I am detained by bodily illness—which God forbid! I have taken care to announce this to you because I greatly desire to find you prepared to meet the expenses.

But if you object in words or with an outcry of heart that your poverty is quite unable to meet these demands, I am not compelled by any necessity to answer here. Truth commands, however, that you ought not to speak or think in this way, since, with Christ rich, you ought not fear poverty, and since what we possess can in no way fail you.

We would certainly rather spend honorably whatever we appear to possess at Craon than allow an undisciplined and foolish man violently to impose, without resistance, unjust and evil customs upon the property of the Church of God. Farewell, and place your confidence in the great mercy of Saint Clement, whom you serve, without the slightest hesitation concerning victory.

211

## LETTER XXXVII

Goffridus, humble servant of the monastery of Vendôme, to his beloved brother Hamelinus: obey in such a way that you may receive the fruit of obedience.

We sympathize as much as we can and ought, with heartfelt affection, with your illness, which, as you reported, grew worse and prevented you from coming to us, although it allowed you to return home. Yet we are greatly astonished at an illness that hindered you from coming to us but could not hinder you from returning.

Certainly, if you could not come as you were able to return, you ought to have sent someone through whom you could fulfill God’s and our ordinance [Col. 0175D]. Believe most firmly, and have no doubt whatever, dearest son in Christ, that a monk who knows obedience in words but does not perform the work of obedience appears to be a monk in words, but by his actions is denied to be a monk. Therefore his words deserve blows rather than grace. Farewell, and pursue the beautiful words of obedience through the beautiful work of obedience.

## LETTER XXXVIII

[Col. 0176A]

Goffridus, servant of the monastery of Vendôme, to his beloved brother Andreas [Note: [Col. 0175D] Andreas. A prior, as is clear from Letter 40, though it does not indicate of what place he was prior [Col. 0176D].]: do not consign the admonitions of salvation to oblivion.

Know that it has been reported to us about you that you rejected the common bread and wine of the refectory and ordered the cellarer to seek another bread and another wine for you. If this was said out of envy and not truth, do not doubt that the one who said it has acquired punishment for himself. But if it was done by you, correct wisely what you did.

For it is necessary, brother, that you moderate yourself in everything, lest, as though using unrestricted power, you do anything from which scandal or grumbling might rightly arise among the brothers whom we have entrusted to your love.

## LETTER XXXIX

Goffridus, humble servant of the monastery of Vendôme, to his beloved son in Christ Andreas [Col. 0176B]: minister prudently and simply in all things.

Toward the brothers whom we have entrusted to your care, you ought to be solicitous in such a way that, while you desire to save their souls, you do not neglect to provide care for their bodies. For one does not properly love the soul in a person who refuses to assist the body in its need. God created both, and in order to restore both he assumed both; he died in the flesh and again gave life to the soul, which it had lost through its sin.

Death did not proceed from the corruption of the flesh, as some think [Note: [Col. 0176D] “Not from the corruption of the flesh, as some think.” From Augustine, *The City of God*, Book XIV, chapter 3: “The corruption of the body, which weighs down the soul, is not the cause of the first sin but its punishment; nor did corruptible flesh make the sinful soul, but the sinful soul made the flesh corruptible.”]. Nor did the devil infect our flesh before he infected the soul. Hence one who believes correctly understands that corruptible flesh did not make the sinful soul, but the sinful soul made the flesh corruptible [Col. 0176C].

In saying these things to your fraternity, we do not mean that you should do or approve what pleasure desires in a disorderly way, but what necessity rightly compels. Farewell.

213

## LETTER XL

Goffridus, humble servant of the monastery of Vendôme, to his venerable brother Andreas: “I have not come to do my own will, but the will of him who sent me” (John 6:38)—retain this in your memory.

We have sent to you our beloved son Herbertus, whom we know to be prudent in secular affairs, and we command him to conduct wisely and with your counsel the matters that must be handled outside, charging him especially to love you with all his heart and diligently obey you as his prior.

You, however, should display toward him and the other brothers entrusted to your love such a character through pastoral care that the eternal Shepherd may find nothing lacking in them. If you show yourself solicitous, according to our admonition, for the souls entrusted to your keeping, believe most firmly and do not doubt at all that you cannot rightly complain of insufficient material resources. For God, through me, his unworthy servant, will supply your poverty [Col. 0177A], and you will receive from him an everlasting reward for a flock well cared for.

214

## LETTER XLI

Goffridus, humble servant of the monastery of Vendôme, to William and the other brothers living at Castellum [Note: [Col. 0177C]

William and the others at Castellum. The prior and monks. Letters of Honorius II and others use the plural, “the Church of Blessed Mary of Castellum,” which is how the village of Angers at the extreme end of their diocese, bordering the territory of Tours, is still commonly called. Thus the man called Goffridus’s prior of Castellum would by others be called the prior of Blessed Mary of Castellum.]: greeting.

Brother William, we told you to come to us as quickly as you could and to bring Bernard with you. You, however, did not do what we told you, but sent us a letter of your own choosing, in which you stated that Bernard could not come. To this we reply that, if he cannot come, he can be carried.

Therefore, by the authority of the holy Rule, we command you: within four days after seeing this letter, come to us, and, if Bernard cannot ride, have him brought [Col. 0177B]. But if you act otherwise, we condemn you to the mark of perpetual infamy, and we excommunicate Bernard in such a way that while alive he may receive no Communion and, when dead, may receive no burial.

## LETTER XLII

Goffridus, servant of the monastery of Vendôme, to William, prior of Castellum, and the brothers who are with him: observe the Rule and avoid the provocations of gluttony.

An entirely irreligious and disorderly report about you has reached our ears. For it has been said that, contrary to the Rule which you promised before God and his saints that you would observe, you solemnly and generally eat meat. Therefore, if this is so—or rather, since we believe that it is so—we deeply grieve over your intemperance, and by the authority of the Rule we prohibit you from doing this any longer [Col. 0177C].

Just as the eating of meat is granted to monks because of bodily illness, so it is denied to them for the pleasure of meat. Even if the sick abstained entirely from meat, they would not on that account violate the Rule. For in the Rule eating meat is not commanded to sick monks but permitted. But because we know that few or none possess the virtue of abstaining entirely from meat, when we allow someone to eat meat, a reasonable necessity must be considered, not a desire to nourish the appetite for flesh with flesh.

## LETTER XLIII

Goffridus, humble servant of the monastery of Vendôme, to his beloved son in Christ William and the brothers living with him at Castellum: obey God rather than men.

It has been reported to us that you tolerate such a great crowd of secular people—and, what is more dangerous, of women—with you that you can scarcely, or never, speak or meditate on the things of God. Where secular people are present disorderly and constantly, it is not thought that great iniquity will long be absent, especially in a place where the female sex is permitted to reside, through which even religious persons are regarded with suspicion.

Yet that sex, when good, none is better; when bad, none is worse. By this letter we admonish your goodness, dearest brothers, and in admonishing we ask that, if you have acted less cautiously up to now, you do not delay correcting it in any way, lest, God forbid, you acquire infamy for your order and thus, with justice dictating it, provoke us to anger against you. Farewell, and diligently observe what we command.

## LETTER XLIV

Goffridus, unworthy minister of the monastery of Vendôme, to his beloved brother in Christ Bernerius, prior of Craon [Note: [Col. 0177C]

Bernerius, prior of Craon. Craon is very well known, or, as French usage has modified the form, the castle of Craon, in the lower district of Angers, near the Armorican border. When Subardus, formerly lord of Craon, had given its neighboring church, dedicated to Saint Clement, to the monastery of Saint-Albini under fixed conditions, Guarinus, the son of Subardus, later reclaimed it as his own because the agreements had not been fulfilled, and installed clerics there in place of monks.

Afterward, however, Count Goffridus Martellus, having taken the lordship of Craon into his own hand and treasury, assigned the church of Saint Clement to the newly founded monastery of Vendôme, before granting the lordship of Craon to Robert the Burgundian. He himself attests this in the foundation charters of Vendôme in these words: “In the diocese of Angers, the church of Saint Clement at the castle of Craon, with everything belonging to it; this church, which had previously been given to blessed Peter, we retained as an exception when we gave the honor of Craon to Robert the Burgundian, our faithful man.”

From this arose the long and frequently disputed controversy between the monks of Saint-Albini and those of Vendôme over the church of Craon. It first came before Nicholas II, who adjudged it to the men of Vendôme, as his letter to Abbot Ordericus informs us: “At the castle,” he says, “of Craon, the parish church of Saint Clement, concerning which a dispute arose in our presence between the men of Vendôme and the monks of blessed Albini, was adjudged by the judgment of the Apostolic See to the monastery of Vendôme.”

It came again before Urban II, who settled the matter so that the church of Saint Clement would indeed remain with the men of Vendôme, but on condition that in its place they cede to the monastery of Saint-Albini whichever one they preferred of three designated churches. The church of Saint John above the Loire was selected and transferred to Saint-Albini.

A further controversy then arose over it through our Goffridus and the men of Vendôme, who judged themselves injured by Urban’s decision. Nevertheless, as was stated in Book I, Letter 8, Urban’s authority prevailed. The church of Saint John was left to the monks of Saint-Albini, in whose power it remains to this day, although, as I believe, Goffridus was still alive when Innocent II, in a letter to Frotmundus, Goffridus’s successor, no longer counted it among those churches which the monastery of Vendôme possessed in the diocese of Angers.

All this has been explained somewhat more fully here so that the causes of the controversy, which Goffridus mentions in several places, may be understood. We shall now produce from the archive of Saint-Albini Urban’s decree concerning this matter, since it may also be useful in other matters. This, then, is the text:

Decree of Urban II concerning the dispute at Craon between the monks of Saint-Albini and those of Vendôme.

Urban, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved sons in Christ Goffridus, abbot of Saint-Albini of Angers, and Berno, abbot of the Holy Trinity of Vendôme: greeting and apostolic blessing.

In the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1093, the fifth year of our pontificate, indiction 1, when I was in the province of Calabria at the monastery of Saint Mary called Matina, the monks of Saint-Albini—Girardus the prior, Milo, and Stephanus—lodged a complaint against the monks of the Holy Trinity of Vendôme, namely Frotmundus the prior and Ingelbaldus the porter, who were present. They alleged that the brothers of Vendôme were unjustly and forcibly retaining the church of Saint Clement of Craon, which the monks of Saint-Albini had lawfully acquired according to the custom of those times and possessed peacefully and without interruption for thirty years.

Although they tried to defend their case with their documents and arguments, the matter, thoroughly and at length debated on the first day of the complaint, could not be brought to any conclusion. On the second day it was likewise thoroughly discussed, but still brought to no conclusion.

On the third day, namely the twelfth day before the Kalends of December, when we were seated in the city of Anglone in Apulia, with religious and venerable bishops and cardinals or deacons of the holy Roman Church presiding, and with the noble Romans and the most illustrious counts of Apulia, Bohemond and William, also standing by, the matter was again investigated at length. At last, with God inspiring us, it became clearer toward which side justice inclined.

Since each side opposed us with its own allegations—on one side the agreement of the abbots, the confirmation of pontiffs and legates of the Roman Church; on the other, lawful entry and canonical possession for thirty years—we, who must weigh the cases of all the faithful in an even balance, chose, while providing for the benefit of both sides, to resolve the dispute through the equity of a suitable concord.

All who were present with us therefore approved this judgment. With the brothers of both monasteries mentioned above consenting and confirming their faith by promise in our hands, concord and peace were established between them in this manner: the monks of Vendôme shall, from among these three churches—Manitilium, Saint Saturninus, or Saint John above the Loire—give to the monastery of Saint-Albini whichever one the entire congregation of the Holy Trinity chooses, together with everything belonging to that church, movable and immovable, within and outside it, at present, within thirty days after they have returned home.

The brothers of Saint-Albini therefore renounced into our hands and those of the brothers of Vendôme every dispute and every charge arising from this matter. The men of Vendôme, for their part, returned one of the aforesaid churches into our hands, and through us invested the same monks with it.

By this present authority, therefore, we admonish and command your fraternity to keep and observe forever hereafter this agreement, arranged and established by us with the intention of peace and quiet, as ratified and unshaken. Whichever party does not accept the sentence of our decision or presumes to transgress it shall be subject both to the severity of the canons and to the penalty of a lawful settlement, namely one hundred pounds of gold, and shall entirely lose the case. Given at Taranto, on the eighth day before the Kalends of December.]

to love God and to fear him with love.

He does not properly keep faith with his profession who does not obey the Rule of blessed Benedict, which he promised under oath to keep [variant: *a se*, “by himself”] before God [Col. 0179A] and his saints. For, taught by the holy Rule, we have learned that a monk ought not to conceal from his abbot his own sins and those of others by which he is infected, but to reveal them.

You, however, concealed from us the sin of your superior [Note: [Col. 0180C]

Your superior. The superior of a monastery was the man whose responsibility for the household and domestic discipline came immediately after that of the abbot. Today he is called the cloister prior. Thus the abbot, or father, of the monastery is one thing, and the superior another. So in the monastery of Fondi, of which Saint Gregory speaks in *Dialogues* I: Honoratus was abbot, while Libertinus was superior; and at Soracte, concerning which he speaks in chapter 7, Nonnosus was superior, while another man was abbot, whom he writes was exceedingly harsh. The Greeks likewise distinguish between “the father and the superior of the monastery” (*πατέρα καὶ ἡγούμενον τῆς μονῆς*). From this passage it is clear that superiors existed not only under abbots but also under priors, namely in those priories which are called conventual; Craon is of this kind.]

—the sin which, by consenting to it, you made your own—not as something hidden but as something public, since it was committed publicly with public women and you concealed it from us. Hence it is most evident that by sinning and despising us you have injured both yourself and us.

Therefore by this letter we command you to destroy completely and without delay that little chamber in which that filthy and defiled man carried out his wicked act, and to expel him as an outsider from the cloister and from the court of blessed Clement [Note: [Col. 0180C]

“From the cloister and from the court of blessed Clement,” that is, from the monastery and the estate. Formerly they called estates *curtes*, but these were allods and properties held by free right. In the donation of Countess Adela, which she made to the monastery of Saint-Albini in 974: “Therefore I give him the estate given to me by my parents, situated in the district of Beauvais, which is called Undanis, with two churches, one built in honor of holy Mary, Mother of God, the other in honor of Saint Anianus.” Thus also the estate and church of Champigny, the estate of Mairon, the estate of Chiry, and others in the cartulary of the same monastery. The name *court* remains today in the names of many remote places in France, such as Bouvancourt in the district of Reims, Hunecourt in the district of Cambrai, and others.]

As long as you delay doing this, we want you to remain excluded from entry into the holy Church. Farewell.

217

## LETTER XLV

Brother Goffridus to Bernerius the prior: blessing from God and love from himself.

We have heard of your illness, dearest brother in Christ, and through the inward compassion of our heart have made it our own [Col. 0180A]. Since we know that you need counsel and assistance alike, we are sending you our beloved brother and son Gilbertus, who will carry out on your behalf the care of the entire household of blessed Clement and contradict none of your commands.

You, however, should moderate your commands toward him in such a way that whatever he does, he may do with the fear and love of God. Farewell.

## LETTER XLVI

Goffridus, servant of the monastery of Vendôme, to his beloved brothers, J., the prior, and all the others: blessing from the Lord God and love from himself.

You informed us that it had been told to you that Herbert, a priest from Saviniacum, was keeping a married woman, whose husband he had seriously wounded during the night because he would not loosen the reins of adulterous love toward his own wife. If these things that rumor has spread about the priest are true, the priest who did such things is exceedingly wicked. Yet it is not fitting for us, and according to the canons [Note: “According to the canons.” Gregory the Great, Book VIII, Letter 30, to Constantius, bishop of Milan: “It is sufficiently grave and improper that a definite sentence be given in a doubtful matter.” What follows is cited at one time from Victor’s letter to the Alexandrians, at another from Sixtus II, Letter 2, by Ivo, Part V, chapters 244 and 247; Gratian, XI, q. 5. Although true, it is from Augustine, *On Penance*, chapter 3.] no one is permitted to give a definite judgment in an uncertain matter. Even if these things are true, they are nevertheless not to be believed unless they have first been established according to canonical procedure, nor should the priest be stripped of his possessions or expelled from the Church until either he is proved guilty or he is acquitted as innocent. Nor are these matters to be investigated by us, but by his own bishop.

You wrote to us that the priest hates the people because of the truth that the people are saying about him. And I write to you that both things are true, because truth often produces hatred, and hatred often produces falsehood. Thus the priest may have hated the people because of the truth, and the people may have fallen into falsehood out of hatred against the priest. The people, brothers, must be led, not followed, and must not be admitted as accusers of clerics. There is truth in the proverb: “The one who leads the donkey must go before it.” The people are the donkey whom you ought to go before and lead, not follow.

## LETTER XLVII

[Col. 0181B]

Goffridus, humble servant of the monastery of Vendôme, to his much-beloved brother in Christ, Robert [Note: **To Brother Robert.** The catalogue of the Le Mans codex reads: “To Robert of Arbrissel, director of the nuns of Fontevrault,” whom he exhorted to conduct himself more discreetly toward the female sex. It calls him “director,” whereas others call him the founder. The *Chronicle of Saint-Albinus* records that in 1116 Robert of Arbrissel died on the fifth day before the Kalends of March. He was the founder of the monastery of Fontevrault.—Bollandus and Henschenius (*for February 24*, p. 606), Theophilus Raynaudus (*In the Triad of David’s Strong Men*, p. 46), Cardinal Joannes Bona, and others judged this letter to be spurious and clearly fabricated by the heretic Roscelin or some other wicked man, so incredible did they find what the letter relates about Robert of Arbrissel. Others, however, despite the criticism of such distinguished scholars, consider that judgment insufficiently supported by evidence—not because they think the things that these letters report to have been alleged against the most holy man are true, but because the new religious institute of nuns that he founded, and consequently the frequent conversations that he necessarily had with those women, gave wicked and malicious people an opportunity for slander. Everyone knows that the same thing happened even to the greatest and holiest men, Jerome and others, when they devoted special attention to instructing women in piety.

Robert of Arbrissel is certainly sufficiently cleared of every suspicion of wicked conduct by the countless and extraordinarily illustrious testimonies that numerous holy bishops, princes, and even supreme pontiffs gave concerning his virtue, piety, wisdom, and distinguished deeds. Paschal II called him “a man of great religion”; Robert of Torigni, “a man suited to winning souls”; and Blessed Peter, bishop of Poitiers, “an apostolic man, diligently devoted to the preaching of God’s word, who by the thunder of holy exhortation recalled many men and women from worldly luxury.” We omit other encomia of the same Robert, collected by others [Col. 0182C]. Certainly all the men of that age who were outstanding in virtue or learning both extolled Robert himself with great praises and warmly commended the religious family founded by him. Suger, abbot, a highly reliable witness, testifies in a letter to Pope Eugenius III that this community numbered five thousand sacred virgins already at its beginnings, while its founder and father was still alive; and Goffridus himself praises those nuns as beloved by God in one of his letters (Letter 32).

Who, then, would not perceive that Goffridus is in no way accusing or reproving Robert, but is freely and sincerely— as happens among friends—warning him about what malicious people were spreading? The very words of the letter sufficiently demonstrate this: “As it is said”; “as rumor spreads”; “you are said to be doing these things”; “we have heard, as an evil rumor circulates, that you have done such things” [Col. 0182D]. “You have climbed, as it were, a lofty mountain in the world, and for that reason have turned men’s tongues and eyes upon yourself.” And, something that must not be overlooked, at the conclusion of the letter he says: “Farewell, and we humbly ask you to make us participants in your holy prayers.” All this clearly shows how honorably Goffridus thought of Robert and how little weight he gave those sinister rumors, even when he was writing that letter.

These many clear testimonies, together with other compelling arguments, ought to have been sufficient to establish the holiness of Robert of Arbrissel for the learned man who some years ago defended this eminently just cause in a large commentary; certainly the author’s intention and diligence deserve praise. But it was surely neither fair nor necessary for dissolving a groundless accusation to bring the editor of Goffridus’s works, a man universally esteemed, into disrepute and harshly attack him for something he had never deserved. **The Venetian editor of Sirmond’s works.**]

—to observe the measure of discretion and to be content with the limits established by the Fathers.

Your affection, dearest brother, knows—and knows well—that to act otherwise is a mark of human imperfection, while refusing to correct what has been done otherwise is diabolical presumption. To do nothing beyond what ought to be done is angelic perfection, which our condition cannot possibly possess as long as we are here. Since, then, we do not possess the perfection of an angel, let us in no way possess the presumption of the devil.

We have set these matters before you, venerable brother, because we have heard through an evil and circulating rumor that you have done, and are still doing, such things [Col. 0181C]. If they are true, we urge you, with the inward feeling of genuine charity, not to defend them by any excuse but to correct them with all haste [Col. 0182A].

For we have heard that, concerning the female sex whom you have undertaken to govern, you make yourself so anxiously concerned in two ways, each wholly contrary to the other, that in both you completely exceed the bounds of discretion. You allow some of the women, it is said, to live with you in excessive familiarity; you speak private words to them very frequently, and you are not ashamed often to lie down at night with them and among them. Here you appear to yourself—as you claim—to be worthily carrying the cross of the Lord and Savior, since you attempt to extinguish the wrongly kindled fire of the flesh. If you are acting in this way, or have ever acted in this way, you have discovered a new and unheard-of, but fruitless, kind of martyrdom [Col. 0182B]. Certainly nothing undertaken contrary to reason can be useful or in any way fruitful. You have presumed against reason in no small degree if, on any pretext, you have slept with women whom you ought to have stolen from the world and won for the Lord.

Especially since Solomon forbade it, as the Holy Spirit thundered through him and in him: “Do not lie down with a woman, nor be constantly with her, nor gaze upon her, lest you be scandalized by her beauty and perish” (Ecclesiasticus 9:3–5). And again: “A woman captures precious souls; her conversation kindles a man’s heart like fire” (ibid., 9:11–12).

Never, brother, trust so greatly in your religious profession that you believe you cannot fall if you do not walk cautiously. The world is slippery, full of mire; no one has been able to stand firm in it for long. He has fallen suddenly and has risen only with difficulty, or never. You have indeed climbed, as it were, a lofty mountain in the world, and for that reason have turned men’s tongues and eyes upon yourself. Therefore, while standing on the mountain, take care that you do not fall and, through a martyrdom entirely unknown to the holy martyrs, leave a stain of disgrace upon the beginning of religious life.

Nor should you, by any action of yours, arouse scandal in the world, which almost entirely follows you. For your condemnation would become more severe through the downfall of many.

As rumor has spread, and as we said earlier, you often speak privately with some of the women and are tormented by sleeping with them as by a new kind of martyrdom. To them you always present yourself as cheerful in speech and lively in conduct, displaying every kind of kindness without observing any restraint. To others, however, whenever you speak with them, you always appear excessively harsh in speech and excessively severe in correction; you even torment them with hunger, thirst, and nakedness, abandoning all compassion [Col. 0183B]. If this is so, you offend grievously in both directions and transgress the entire measure of discretion. For toward the former you act too leniently, and toward the latter too harshly.

You have undertaken to govern a very difficult province, one that has very often dragged its ruler to death: “For from a woman sin had its beginning, and through her all die” (Ecclesiasticus 25:33). Therefore you must act so prudently and simply that toward women you may show yourself both a mother through the grace of compassion and a father through discipline; and those who possess less perfection should not possess less of your affection. One should not be loved by you more than another unless she is found to be better. According to the measure of merit or fault, extend the measure of correction or grace.

Let this, however, be fixed especially in your mind: the Lord says in the Gospel, “Blessed are the merciful, for they shall obtain mercy” (Matthew 5:7). The female sex is exceedingly fragile and delicate, and therefore it must be governed more by the sweetness of compassion than by excessive severity, lest it be overwhelmed by excessive sorrow (2 Corinthians 2:7), and lest the one who ought to govern it be thus outwitted by Satan.

A ruler is outwitted by Satan if, through excessive sorrow, those who could have been saved through leniency happen to perish. When we exhort your goodness here concerning compassion, we do not wish to take away from you the exercise of justice; we desire you to be both just and compassionate. Let your compassion reject unregulated leniency; let your justice always possess loving sympathy.

Farewell, and we humbly ask you to make us participants in your holy prayers.

## LETTER XLVIII

Goffridus, humble servant of the monastery of Vendôme, to the servants and handmaids of God, Herveus and Eva, enclosed [Note: **Herveus and Eva, enclosed.** The *inclusi* were a type of monk, but there were two classes. Some, having never experienced monastic discipline, immediately adopted this profession and, enclosed in cells generally situated near towns, imitated solitude; they were rather the shadows of monks than monks. The common people called them hermits and recluses. Their number was once considerable in Gaul, and these seem to have belonged to that group, to whom Goffridus is writing.

Others were genuine monks who, after leaving monasteries in which they had lived for some time with others, withdrew into solitary cells in pursuit of a more advanced progress. The Greeks also called them ἐγκλείσους, *enclosed*. Those to whom Theodore the Studite wrote more than once belonged to this class. Some elegant iambics of his also survive, entitled “To an Enclosed Person,” which I shall append:

### To an Enclosed Person (Greek)

An enclosed person is one who, dwelling outside the passions,  
Has shut his whole heart toward God,  
Shutting out thoughts that pursue error,  
Sending his mind [Codex Regius: “sending his own mind”] toward the contemplations above,  
Having prayer that burns demons,  
Maintaining a silence that initiates into the depths,  
An untroubled soul in the joy of hopes,  
And the rigor of manual work, toil, and hunger,  
An unceasing song, a contrite spirit.  
Thus revealing a vision fitting for angels,  
He shines his rays divinely upon those who behold him,  
Saying nothing useless for laughter,  
But only what may benefit the guest,  
And avoiding excessive long-windedness even in these matters.  
If you can attain these things, you are in a state of salvation.  
If not, return to a life shared with others,  
In which you may more abundantly make your ascetic struggles shine.

### To a Recluse (Latin version)

A recluse is one who, far from the passions,  
Has shut himself wholly into God in his heart,  
Reining in the wandering errors of the mind,  
And lifting his spirit toward heavenly concerns,  
Clinging to prayers that utterly burn demons,  
And to the silence through which hidden things are disclosed.  

Knowing no failing in hope and joy [Col. 0183D; Sirmond’s papers: “Not failing in hope, nor in the joy of death”],  
He disciplines his body with severe labor and hunger.  
With groaning spirit he continually sings hymns.  
Here, shining in visible countenance after the manner of an angel,  
He illumines the hearts of those who behold him with a divine torch  
[Col. 0184D; manuscript variant: “strikes them”].  

He is accustomed never to say anything empty merely for laughter,  
But only what those who hear may feel benefits them;  
Nor does he spread the sails of excessive speech.  
If you are able to attain these things, salvation is secure.  
If not, return at once to the communal life,  
Where you may further cultivate ascetic struggles. ]—

to bring your good beginnings to a better end.

The sacred writings, by exhorting us, teach us, and by teaching us exhort us; you have undertaken to obey them faithfully, so that we may continue to practice to the end what will make us worthy to rejoice without end. For it is beyond every misery to lose, for the sake of a temporal life full of pain and labor—which is certainly brief, and whose brevity is uncertain—the life that cannot be seen by the eye or comprehended by the silent thought of the mind; and yet to attain it is easier than to describe it.

There one lives without end, without pain or old age, without fear or danger; there is refreshment without satiety, requiring no assistance from food or drink. In that blessedness, to be refreshed means nothing other than to be satisfied by contemplation of the divine majesty. The holy angels behold it, and while beholding it always desire to behold it. None of the perfect will be absent from that blessed vision—those who in the world, for Christ’s name, despised both themselves and their possessions.

Let us therefore, dearest ones, while we have time, hasten through holy works toward it [Col. 0185A]. Whoever has seen it once will never be able to lose it again, despite the ambushes of any enemy. Certainly we must hasten while he calls us, confident of so great a reward, though uncertain of the day. Let the final necessity find us awake, for it often overtakes those who are sleeping.

We shall regret too late that we have acted wickedly, when, at the arrival of the final day, each person sees himself separated from his body, and when, as he closes his eyes at the end, everlasting night begins to grow dark and dreadful for him. Then, truly, our wickedness will cease; the vanity of the world will fade like a shadow; carnal pleasure will vanish like smoke. In their place only reproaches and crimes will remain, together with torments destined to last without end.

Oh, how miserable that soul will be when, immediately after leaving the body, the dreadful faces of the infernal ministers begin to insult and assail it [Col. 0185B]! As it bids its final farewell to human affairs, with death before it and life left behind, it will be dragged into that terrifying abyss, scarcely reachable even by the eyes. Alas, how great a joy it has lost, destined to receive so great a punishment!

What will its state of mind be when it receives its body again, to increase its eternal condemnation? On that day it will be presented before the King of the ages, to render an account of what it has done in the body. But because it will be unable to display any good deeds in comparison with its evils, it will be cut off from the very root of the holy Church and handed over to the fires of Gehenna, from which it can never escape, to be tormented forever.

Oh, how sad and mournful it will be to be separated from the sweet sight of the saints, and how terrible to be joined to the ranks of unclean spirits! Anyone who is joined to them would call himself blessed if, like any brute animal, he could die in soul and body [Col. 0185C]. But because that death has no end, a person there is always dying in such a way that he is always rising again; he rises for the purpose of perishing, yet does not cease altogether to exist by perishing. He is always dying, but never finds the end of death.

The misery of the condemned person will be increased especially by this: he will see God but will not possess him, and he will perish before the sight of his Redeemer. Woe to those who now refuse to fear what they will have to endure in the future; if they feared it now, they would never endure such things.

I say “to fear” not with just any fear, but with the fear produced by true faith, which proceeds from sincere charity. For charity produces fear and drives fear away. It produces fear, as Scripture says: “Blessed is the man who is always fearful” (Proverbs 28:14). It drives fear away, as the Apostle says: “He who is perfect in charity does not fear” (1 John 4:18). One of these fears is recognized as filial, the other as servile. The filial fear is offered with love and desire; the servile with disgust and hatred.

Perhaps someone will say: “Why do you threaten a person with so many and such great things from God? He will never destroy the one whom his grace created, whom, after he had been created and ruined by his own fault, he freed from the devil through ineffable love, paying a price for him.”

I regard such a person as not despairing, but as hoping beyond what he ought; unless he ceases to hope in this way before the end of his life, I have no doubt that he will perish [Col. 0186A]. For, as it seems to me, and as reason itself demands, our offenses are more serious before God in proportion as his benefits toward us prove greater.

There is also reason to fear that, in his judgment, he will bring forth against the vessels of iniquity that voice which bears witness to the precious marks of the glorious resurrection, and say: “Put your finger here and see my hands; and bring your hand and put it into my side” (John 20:27), “and recognize what I have endured for you and from you, human impiety.”

Let this be said against those who flatter themselves excessively concerning the promises of mercy and despise the force of justice. God is not such that he speaks truth in one matter and lies in another. Just as what he promises is certain, so what he threatens is also certain [Col. 0186B].

Therefore, dearest ones, confessing in belief and believing in confession that our God and Lord Jesus Christ is both compassionate and just, let us say with the Psalmist: “All the ways of the Lord are mercy and truth” (Psalm 24:20). The two ways of the Lord are the two advents of his Son. In the first he bestowed mercy; in the second he will bestow justice. And lest we perish then when justice dictates, let us now flee to him, who is more ready to grant pardon than a sinner is to turn to repentance, and more prompt to forgive than any human being is to sin.

I have said these things so that those who wish to convert may have hope and, having hope, may thoroughly repent. May his compassion deign to grant this—he who has so ordered the two lives that in the present age labors and sorrows should soon come to an end, while in the future age the joys of honors and rewards should remain without end.

## LETTER XLIX

Goffridus, unworthy servant of the monastery of Vendôme, to his friend Herveus the enclosed: perseverance in his holy purpose.

H., secretary of Blessed Mary [Note: **Secretary of Blessed Mary.** Of the Church of Chartres. See Book II, Letter 14, “The Chapter of Saint Mary,” and Letter 15.], if he wishes to become a monk, as you informed us, is not to be rejected. Therefore take care that he convert more quickly and abandon the world, which perhaps he is serving unlawfully.

As for the other man, who has recently become a priest and about whom you likewise informed us, if he appears to you to be of good character, take care to send him to us; and do not delay sending us any clerics of honorable life whom you may find [Col. 0186D]. We value honest poverty in men more than their proud riches. If they possess riches, they are not to be rejected, for they too have their proper place; nevertheless, we seek nothing in order to make monks. But if anything is offered, we accept it, because the Rule commands that it be accepted. For our order requires us to be people who devote ourselves not to temporal profits but to winning souls.

## LETTER L

Goffridus, useless servant of the monastery of Vendôme, to his beloved Herveus the enclosed, enclosed among stone walls [Col. 0187A] so that he may not be violated in any respect by the stony words of slanderers.

You informed us, dearest son in Christ, that one of our brothers had said that, by sending Britons to our monastery to become monks, you had disgraced our community; but you kept silent about the name of the brother who said this, for whatever reason. In reply to the babbling words of that faithless brother, we truthfully declare that our community is not disgraced by you and by those whom you sent us, but is suitably adorned.

We should nevertheless like to have that man who declares what is good to be evil brought before us, so that the truth might openly expose his falsehood. Certainly, excellent brother, the man who speaks so wickedly does not merely accuse you unjustly, but rather charges us with a crime [Col. 0188A]. For you did not associate anyone with us by force; we willingly received those whom you were able to take away from the world.

If anything in this action of ours and yours was done otherwise, then we sinned more, and you less. Let us, however, carry these sins together with unrepentant hearts in such a way that, God granting it, we may have no others. And if you and we have done anything out of charity, you should not be surprised if it displeases the man whose heart is full of iniquity.

For the sons of Babylon will always disagree with the sons of Jerusalem. Let your religious commitment also recognize this without doubt: no one can obtain Abel’s righteousness whom Cain’s wickedness does not attack.

Farewell, and recall these words to mind frequently.

## BOOK FIVE

[Col. 0187]

## LETTER I

[Col. 0187B]

Goffridus, humble servant of the monastery of Vendôme, to Walter, treasurer of laudable life [Note: **Walter the treasurer.** Of the Church of Blessed Martin of Tours; more will be said of him below in Letter 3.], and Goffridus of Alogia [Note: **Goffridus of Alogia.** Fulbert mentions the estate of Alogia, from which this Goffridus took his name, in Letter 23.], his intimate friends, affectionate greetings.

I have heard of your illness and, as my heart truly knows, have made it my own through compassion. I sent you a physician whom I greatly value; I would have sent myself even more willingly, if I had been needed. If you still wish to keep him—as I know you do not dislike doing so—I do not object. If you wish to send him back, that is also agreeable to me, and I need him, provided that you can return him without harm to your health.

May you always be well in the Lord; and since I love you as far as my humility permits, have no doubt of it [Col. 0187C].

## LETTER II

Goffridus, servant of the monastery of Vendôme, to Walter, treasurer of honorable life: himself and all that is his.

When we were recently speaking in your house at Tours about the overthrow of the adversaries of the Church of God [Col. 0188B], and were binding ourselves there before witnesses by the bonds of mutual affection, among the other things we discussed you urged me to make peace with Archbishop Ralph [Note: **With Archbishop Ralph.** Of Tours; he was discussed in Book I, Letter 30. He is also criticized in Letter 17 and in many places by Ivo, especially Letters 66 and 108.]. You said that this would be useful and very necessary in the matter you know.

Considering this again and again, I find your advice sound: we should always use wicked men for a good purpose, following the example of the Savior, who made the apostate Judas an instrument of our salvation. It is also an excellent strategy and a profound thought if one wicked man can be condemned through another wicked man.

I therefore want your prudence to speak wisely with him about this, and not to delay informing me quickly what comes of it.

## LETTER III

[Col. 0188C]

Goffridus to Walter, designated archbishop of Tours [Note: **Designated archbishop of Tours.** He was designated after the death of Archbishop Ralph in 1119, but did not take possession, being forced to yield to Gilbert, Ralph’s nephew, whom another part of the clergy had elected with divided votes [Col. 0187D]. We owe our knowledge of this matter to the old *History of the Affairs of Amboise*, which explains the entire dispute over the see of Tours and the devastation that followed, with Hugh, lord of Amboise, supporting Walter’s party and Archembald of Brais supporting Gilbert’s, since Archembald had married Gilbert’s sister. It finally describes the outcome of the controversy in these words:

“After the death of Ralph, one part of the clergy elected Gilbert, brother of Gilla, as pastor and administrator of the Church of Tours; the other part designated Walter, treasurer of Blessed Martin, a man noble by birth and thoroughly trained in good morals, as bishop of the holy mother Church of Tours. All the nobles of Tours throughout the diocese favored Walter the bishop, except Archembald of Brais. Hugh, who had then changed from friend to enemy of Archembald, fortified Bléré, placed soldiers and servants there, and destroyed by devastation whatever he found around Blais. He burned the archiepiscopal towns of Larchay and Vernon. In reply, Gilbert placed many soldiers and retainers at Brais, who laid waste almost the whole of Champagne as far as the River Cher, except Bléré.

“One day Archembald of Brais and his men, having crossed the River Cher, entered Hugh’s territory. When Hugh learned this, he gathered his forces that same night and at first light found them ravaging his land. Attacking them, he routed them and forced them to cross the Cher; after capturing many, he drove the rest as far as the River Indre. Archembald escaped by fleeing as far as Loches. Not long afterward Hugh again burned and destroyed all of Brais except the residence.

“Gilbert, accompanied by Alvered, archdeacon—a man almost unrivaled in prudence among the clerics of that city, distinguished in person, outstanding in every good quality, endowed with humility, adorned with patience, and divinely skilled in divine and human wisdom—through the indulgence of Lord King Louis, with all the people deliberating and supporting him, and with the suffragan bishops extending their hands at the command of the lord pope, took possession of the episcopal see in peace with the help of Almighty God. Gilbert then became Hugh’s closest friend instead of his enemy and was firmly reconciled with Archembald of Brais.”]

Brother Goffridus: himself and all that he can do.

I long, with the desire of my mind, to obey you; but what the strength of my mind eagerly desires, the weakness of my flesh greatly fears. From travelers recently arriving from there I have heard that the city of Rome is so disturbed that the lord pope [Note: **The lord pope.** Callixtus II. When he came from Gaul to Rome in 1120, the antipope Burdinus, having abandoned the city and driven out Peter Leonis, seized nearby Sutrium, a town of Etruria, apparently intending to defend himself there. Callixtus, however, after gathering forces to attack Sutrium, did not remain long in the city but went to Benevento to William, duke of Apulia. The following year he recovered Sutrium and confined Burdinus in the monastery of Cava. These events are recorded by Pandulf and other writers of that period.] is not there, and Sutrium has been taken from Peter Leonis.

The lord pope is staying near Benevento, but has no means of returning to Rome. If anyone is found traveling to him, his cloak is not taken from him [Note: **“His cloak is not taken from him.”** He is not stripped but killed. We read of merchants’ cloaks in Lupus, abbot of Ferrières, Letter 125; but the analogy confirms Goffridus’s reading. The word *cappa* seems to have been used in this sense, just as *cappae* denotes a type of cup, and *capulum* a handle or bier, from *capere*, “to take”; hence also *capella*.], but his life and limbs are immediately dealt with.

Therefore I must still hear your advice. If you wish to expose yourself to certain danger of death before your envoys return—which I can neither praise nor ought to praise—let me know. For my part, I dare not move without you; yet with you, and for your benefit, if I am well, I am ready to go both to prison and to death.

Farewell, and do not proclaim to anyone what I tell you privately.

## LETTER IV

Goffridus, humble servant of the monastery of Vendôme, to his beloved friends in Christ, Stephen the dean [Note: **Stephen the dean.** Of the Church of Saint Maurice at Angers, as was stated in Book III, Letter 11, when the election of Bishop Rainald was being discussed; that election is also discussed here and in the following letters.], Hubert the cantor, and Warnerius the archdeacon: the service of pure affection.

Because you summoned me, unworthy and sinful as I am, to the election of your bishop, I give you many thanks. I would have readily agreed to your summons if I had not feared undertaking, under this pretext, something I do not wish to mention. And since, as you requested, you cannot now have me present, I approve in my absence what you have done according to God.

## LETTER V

Goffridus, unworthy minister of the monastery of Vendôme, to Stephen the dean, Hubert the cantor, and Warnerius the archdeacon: greetings.

We now recognize that that deceitful man, whom his great falsehood makes suspect even when he speaks the truth, has truly been frustrated in his desire. Therefore we must unanimously give thanks to Almighty God, by whose gift of mercy this is evidently accomplished.

And because, through the clemency of that same God and our Lord Jesus Christ, we see our cause to be entirely in a prosperous condition, we must take the greatest care not to turn the prosperity that he has mercifully granted us into error. Often some people, placed in adversity, desire to serve God and seek him; but once they have attained prosperity, they refuse to obey the one whom they had previously seemed to love [Col. 0190A].

Therefore, just as, with his goodness assisting us, we were not broken in adversity, so let us not be elated in prosperity, lest prosperity, by flattering and seducing us, harm more seriously those whom adversity could not harm by frightening them.

May you always be well in the Lord, and do not in any way lose confidence in our assistance.

## LETTER VI

Goffridus, unworthy minister of the monastery of Vendôme, to the venerable precentor Hubert [Note: **To the precentor Hubert.** At one time he calls him cantor, at another precentor, as in the dedication at Vendôme. At Chartres, Arnulfus was archdeacon and precentor. Close to Hubert in rank and time was Stephen, likewise cantor and archdeacon of Angers, concerning whom the calendar of Saint Maurice says: “On the fifteenth day before the Kalends of November died Stephen, cantor and archdeacon, killed by enemies in the service of this Church, in the year of the Lord 1116.”]: to love what God loves and hate what he hates.

I am your friend—not just any friend, but one who will never be able to withdraw his heart from the love with which he began to love you. Yet, as it seems to me, you love me less than usual, and you care little or not at all that I love you. If either or both of these things are true, I would indeed wish that neither were so; nevertheless, I shall not love you less earnestly, since genuine charity compels me to love even one who does not love me. If you had some reason by which you could justly love me less, I certainly would not have excused the fault; but, by God’s grace, you have found nothing improperly done by me.

You object only that you see peace restored between me and the lord bishop of Redon [Col. 0190D] [Note: “The bishop of Redon”: Marbod, who initially supported Rainald’s election, for which he was also arrested, as stated in Book III, Letter 14. Later, when he began to oppose Rainald as an ingrate, this is shown by Marbod’s own letter among the letters of Hildebert, no. 80. Consequently, reconciliation with Goffrid—who had opposed Rainald’s election above all others—was then easy for him.]. From this no scandal arises for anyone who loves God, and you ought to rejoice if your heart could in any way bear it. For if avoiding hatred is rightly called a fault, then the devil, who constantly pursues it, is wrongly said to have been assigned to punishment. But that is not so, excellent cantor: no Christian, and therefore much less a priest, ought to exercise hatred toward a brother, or avenge personal injuries, but should forgive them wholeheartedly.

Injuries would not need to be forgiven if there were no sins for us to have remitted; but because we are people to whom forgiveness is owed, and who also owe forgiveness, it is absolutely necessary that we forgive others what they owe us, if we desire that what we owe should be forgiven us. [Col. 0190B]

Perhaps you now say that you are not displeased to see us, who were formerly at odds, finally reconciled; but because I did this without your advice, you count it against me as though it were a crime. Advice should indeed be sought, especially in doubtful matters; but in a matter so clear, we do not see that advice was necessary.

O cantor of venerable life! If you truly knew how much I love you, you would certainly trust our counsel and, having taken a draught, cleanse yourself of a certain humor greatly opposed to you, and thus avoid the illness that is to come. If you do not yet know this humor, nor the illness of this humor, go and consult physicians, and you will recognize what this humor is; nor will you be able any longer to doubt its illness. I mean physicians not those who restore bodily health for a time, but those who, if rightly understood, bestow everlasting life.

These physicians are the divine books. If they are firmly believed, the contrary humor is immediately recognized; the illness itself is then feared, and the medicine by which the humor can be healed and the illness avoided is also found. Although a contrary humor is born in a person through sin, it is certain—nothing is more certain—that it rules that person in excessive measure: the one who again raises Simon Magus, formerly destroyed by blessed Peter, against the holy Church [Col. 0190C] [Note: “Raises him again”: in Rainald.], or, once raised, neglects to destroy him on any occasion. This person will suddenly feel the illness produced by that contrary humor, because unless he comes to his senses through repentance before the end of his life, he will suffer endless pain for the iniquity he has committed. Farewell, and wisely attend to what I have said.

## EPISTLE VII

Goffridus, humble servant of the monastery of Vendôme, to his most beloved Hubert, archdeacon of praiseworthy life [Col. 0191D] [Note: “Hubert the archdeacon”: of Angers; in Book III, Letter 3, to Rainald, bishop: “your venerable archdeacon Hubert.” The catalogue of the Le Mans manuscript identifies him with Hubert the cantor, so that he was both archdeacon and cantor, which seems plausible.], from God the fulfillment of eternal blessing, and from himself the affection of genuine love.

Your friendship toward me acted beneficially for a long time; it neither failed nor suffered weariness. It sought me—indeed, it acquired me; it found me when sought, and, although I was unworthy, it gave itself to me. Once it began, it never ceased; whatever benefit or honor it was and is able to confer upon me, it neither withholds nor has delayed.

If anyone understands these words of mine as spoken flatteringly or ironically, we do not resist him with sophistical chatter; rather, he is proved to possess a warped understanding by the plain truth. For what more could a friend have done who so often offered himself and all that was his to me, and gave them to me even more often? Before God, to whom lying is nothing other than condemnation, I firmly assert that, if he shows himself to everyone as he has shown himself to me, he is more worthy of heaven than of the world. Yet he is considered greatly necessary in the world, because he is set before many as a pattern of life.

Here, while speaking, he keeps silence; and through honorable silence he also speaks. [Col. 0191C] His words are full of fairness and tranquility. He speaks through honorable silence because, while he is silent reasonably, he plainly shows by the serene voice of his silence how others ought to conduct themselves. He knows how to possess wisely the things of the world, and he does not cease simply to seek the things of God. Whenever he wishes to correct human conduct by speech, he can immediately find in himself what he should say and from what source he can instruct others better. For we may rightly call this man’s life both teaching and discipline.

May my beloved live—he to whom, although I speak while bodily absent, I nevertheless keep present in my mind and hold fixed in my heart. [Col. 0191D]

## EPISTLE VIII

Goffridus, servant of his friends at the monastery of Vendôme, to his most beloved Hubert: “not yet to depart, and always to be with Christ” [Col. 0192A].

Our brothers, recognizing the benefits you have bestowed upon them and bestow daily, humbly begged us not to be reluctant to convey to your charity, at least by letter on their behalf, the thanks that they are unable to express in words. But even if we had a thousand thousand limbs, and the joints of all those limbs were turned into individual tongues, we could not speak of the benefits you confer upon us, nor in any way repay your love with a thanksgiving worthy of it.

For what we ourselves are entirely unable to do, we implore with the affections of our hearts that God, who can do all things, may deign by his ineffable goodness to repay you. [Col. 0192B]

## EPISTLE IX

Goffridus, humble servant of the monastery of Vendôme, to Hubert, archdeacon of honorable life, his most intimate friend: to love enemies for God’s sake and fear none of their snares.

Dearest, if you wish to obtain Abel’s righteousness, do not consider it contrary to endure Cain’s wickedness. You cannot become another Joseph unless you have experienced the persecutions inflicted upon you by false brothers. I cannot praise the fact that, in the presence of the lord bishop [Col. 0192D] [Note: “The lord bishop”: Rainald of Angers.], you began to handle the matter you reported to me without our advice; and because I spare you, I do not wish to condemn it.

Nevertheless, weak and corrupt cases are commonly strengthened by the help and advice of friends; and provision is made for those that seem sound and firm, so that they cannot be weakened by the deceitfulness of rivals or corrupted in any respect. But you presumed so greatly upon the elevation of your understanding and upon the support of those who surpass me in age and knowledge that, in so important a matter, you had no need of the advice of our insignificance—which is especially yours.

Yet it often happens that inferiors come to the aid of superiors; and what the Lord has hidden from the wise and prudent, he is accustomed to reveal to little ones (Luke 10:21). In every necessity, call upon me, your little one, whose sincere eyes will take care that no one can weigh out a fraudulent measure against your simplicity, and that Neptune and Ethiopian, of whom you wrote to me, even if sunk into his own pit, will not be able to conceal himself. [Col. 0192C]

Farewell always in the Lord. I do not indeed demand that the day of your case be made known to me, but I desire it. [Col. 0192D]

## EPISTLE X

Goffridus, humble servant of the monastery of Vendôme, to his intimate friend Hubert, honorable archdeacon: not to follow the world as it rushes headlong, nor wish to be filled with its bitter sweetness.

Dearest, whoever follows this headlong thing cannot help being hurled headlong; and whoever is filled with its sweetness cannot help becoming embittered. Truly, he is hurled down gravely—indeed, very gravely—who follows the world along byways, deceived by love of it, and is not joined by the cement of charity to the way that Truth itself has taught.

That man also becomes exceedingly bitter to whom, while the present age flatters him with the sweetness of prosperity, it is turned into the bitterness of another’s vine; and because he did not wish to be grafted into the true vine, Christ, so as to become a branch, he is cut off by Christ in order to become a twig. [Col. 0193A]

Would that we could not only fail to be ignorant of the way which eternal life has taught us must be followed specially and uniquely, but also be unable not to accept it and be willing to keep it! That way is certainly this: not only to distribute to Christ’s poor what belongs to oneself, but also to deny oneself for Christ. [Col. 0193B]

To give the poor what is one’s own is a virtue of perfection. For even if we bestow all our possessions upon the poor, it cannot benefit us if we take ourselves away from God, whose we are. When God made the human being from the clay of the earth, the human being was made for this purpose: to possess with God in heaven riches that would endure without end, not to give riches that would quickly perish to the poor in this world.

Afterward, when humanity, desiring false blessedness and finding true misery, was broken and fell from the height of true blessedness, God, who had created it, had compassion on its misery, gathered up its fragments, fused them in the fire of charity, and restored what had been utterly shattered.

In this work of his immeasurable love, the merciful Lord sought not what the human being possessed, but what the human being was—not from his own necessity, but for humanity’s benefit. [Col. 0193C] God gave himself for humanity, becoming human for humanity; and when, from the wound in his side—or rather, from the vein of his sweetest charity—he poured out his own blood for humanity upon the cross, he acquired humanity by such a transaction, not humanity’s property.

Let the human being therefore give himself back, and not delay in giving himself back, to God. Let him believe that he was mercifully bought and redeemed by God’s precious blood, and let him not prefer himself to the one who redeemed him, but rather grant what that redeemer most greatly seeks. For it is unjust that a human being should take himself away from God, who acquired him at so great a price. [Col. 0193D]

Rather, diligently holding to the counsel of his Creator and Redeemer, let him leave all his possessions for love of him; and let him give himself, because, even if he has left everything, it will not benefit him in gaining eternal salvation unless, renouncing the world, he follows Christ, just as Christ taught that he must be followed. To follow Christ and the world at the same time is impossible.

Therefore, if we are not believed, let at least the one who does not lie be believed—the one who says in the Gospel: “No one can serve two masters” (Matthew 6:24), namely, God and the world.

Far be it from us to condemn acts of generosity performed for the poor! But we would give this advice to the rich of this age, if they were willing to heed us: let them make the bellies of the poor their granaries, so that the poor may not perish from hunger, nor the rich themselves from hoarding.

Certainly, feeding the poor is commendable; but making oneself poor for God is far more commendable. Many have fed the poor and left everything, but because they preserved themselves, they were found condemned to themselves. No one, however, has ever made himself poor for God and been unable to possess God.

Therefore, when Peter said in the Gospel that he and the other disciples had left everything and followed him, the Savior did not respond on the grounds that they had left everything, but on the grounds that they had followed him; and for this he promised them the reward of eternal recompense. The Lord would certainly not have done this if a person could possess God merely by abandoning possessions. Nevertheless, he did not reject leaving everything for his sake; rather, he approved what he knew to be the sure salvation of humanity.

And so we do not reject leaving everything for God and refreshing the poor, because it is good. But what is better, as Truth teaches, we approve; and we ask—and by asking, admonish—all, and especially our friends, to hold to the path of undoubted salvation. If this prayer or exhortation of ours is despised, we cannot rightly be blamed; but we ought to mourn and grieve greatly over those who are culpable for such contempt and seem less capable of reason than animals.

For animals willingly seek better pastures, carefully follow their shepherd to them, and, if they are perhaps led to less good ones, resist with whatever movements they can. Therefore, when a human being—whom the Lord, in forming him, made not only rational but also impressed with the seal of his image and likeness—sees animals, which the Creator of all creatures made irrational, providing for their own welfare and, for the sake of better usefulness, obeying their shepherd in heart and body, avoiding what is less good so that they may find what is better, then, if he does not allow himself to be led by the counsel or command of his God and Lord, let him at least be urged toward better things by the example of an animal. Let him leave transitory things, with which he himself will certainly pass away, so that he may deserve to find eternal things. [Col. 0194C]

Yet it is much better for a rational human being to be led by the counsel of God’s rational wisdom than to be stirred by the example of a senseless and irrational animal. Let him therefore be led by God’s counsel, making himself poor for love of God—who did not enrich us with the resources of reconciliation because he fed the poor, although that would have been good, but because he made himself poor for us.

For if the Lord had wished to become rich in the world, he would certainly have fought so that he would not be handed over to the Jews, as he himself says in the Gospel; nor could he have been crucified or died for us. And since human misery would have found no help elsewhere, the punishment of the wretched would have lacked an end.

If this is so—or rather, because it is truly believed to be so—after the Savior’s hanging, after the cup of gall, after the wound in his side, after receiving the grace of baptism, it is useful and necessary that sinful humanity, remembering that it has become estranged from its Creator by sinning, be reconciled to the Lord through voluntary poverty. For the just Lord is acknowledged to have reconciled sinful humanity to himself; hence the gate of paradise stands open to the poor, while the rich are excluded from it. [Col. 0194D]

## EPISTLE XI

Goffridus, unworthy servant of the monastery of Vendôme, to Guarnerius the archdeacon [Col. 0195A] [Note: “Guarnerius the archdeacon”: of Angers; to him, along with others, Letter 4 was addressed.], concerning what a true friend owes a friend.

If, in the judgment of justice, you have risen up on behalf of our affairs against Adelard of Château-Gontier [Col. 0195D] [Note: “Adelard of Château-Gontier”: we shall speak of Adelard in Letter 25, which was written to him. Château-Gontier, situated on the river Mayenne in the Angevin district at the old village of basilicas, had a distinguished founder, Fulk III, count; but it received its undistinguished name from Fulk’s villein, Gontier. The matter is related in the ancient charters of the monastery of Saint-Aubin concerning the fortified castle at Cour de Basilicas, to which Fulk himself subscribed in 1037. Their beginning is as follows: “In the year from the Incarnation of the Lord 1007, indiction 5, Goffridus Martellus was born. And his father Fulk, most noble count of Anjou, son of Goffridus, the most valiant count who was surnamed Grisia Gonella, fortified a castle above the river Mayenne, in the court called Basilicas, which he had exchanged many years earlier with Rainald, abbot, and the monks of Saint-Aubin, for a certain court called Undanisvilla, situated in the district of Beauvais; and he had handed it over to them to possess forever, securely and peacefully, with everything belonging to it. After fortifying the castle and defending it as well as he could, he called it Château-Gontier after one of his villeins.”], I can and ought to give you thanks.

But because, according to rumor, I had heard that you had acted otherwise, I wondered with sorrow, and in my wonder I sorrowed. Now, however, just as you have reported, you are exercising full justice against that tyrant on behalf of our possessions, which he unjustly took and still violently retains; nor have you ever delayed exercising it.

Therefore, if this is so, you have made yourself dearer to me and made me more indebted to you. If you continue to act in this way, know that you will find that you have rendered your service to a friend who is not ungrateful.

## EPISTLE XII

[Col. 0195B] Goffridus, whatever sort of servant of the monastery of Vendôme, to his most beloved fosterer and intimate friend Guarnerius: greetings and love.

It has reached our ears that Hugh Chaorcinus [Col. 0196D] [Note: “Hugh Chaorcinus”: from the castle of Caor, in the district of Le Mans; Peter of Caor is also mentioned in Book III, Letter 28, to Hildebert.] has taken the monastic habit at Craon. We ought therefore to rejoice, because the one who had long been dead in soul has been brought back to life by God’s raising him up.

But because you blaspheme what has been done in him, we ask that your goodness—which carefully nurtured me—entirely desist from such blasphemy for love of us, lest the one who existed in perversity for a long time become worse on this account. For medicine must be mixed for a wounded soul in such a way that it is not wounded further by excessive harshness of the medicine. [Col. 0196D]

## EPISTLE XIII

[Col. 0195C] Goffridus, servant of servants of the monastery of Vendôme, to Guarnerius the archdeacon: greetings.

When, in the letter you sent to your archpriest, you declared that I was a robber, you would have acted much better if you had instead claimed that you were a robber of souls and an importunate exactor of another’s money, and had thus recognized that you, whom you confess to be a shepherd, were a wolf.

For you ought first, my not-so-good brother, to have removed the beam from your own eye, so that you could recognize the speck in mine and shake off the dust by which it is burdened, in order to look clearly upon the stain in another’s limb. Since your hands are muddy, why do you strive to wipe away the dirt of others?

You called me a robber—which I certainly would have been, had I been able to snatch you, weighed down by greed and defiled by covetousness, from the lake of such misery and from the mire of filth (Psalm 39:3). You said that I was acting against a synodal decree, which I earnestly desire to obey, if it is established that it was enacted with apostolic discernment.

For no decree or council is read as valid unless it has been confirmed by apostolic authority; still less, therefore, is one valid that appears contrary to the privileges of that same authority. [Col. 0196A] Our monastery, the patrimony and allodial possession of blessed Peter, remains specially under the protection of the apostolic see; and the privileges of apostolic integrity, by a decree that shall endure forever, strengthen its right to possess everything it is known formerly to have held, without alienation or diminution of any kind, and condemn with perpetual anathema anyone who withdraws anything from it. [Col. 0196D]

[Note: “No council is valid”: the council of Pope Julius against the Easterners, in support of Athanasius. Nor is any council valid, or will ever be valid, unless it has been supported by his authority—that is, by the Roman Church—according to Gratian, 517, 10. 2.]

## EPISTLE XIV

Goffridus, humble servant of the monastery of Vendôme, to his most beloved fosterer Guarnerius the archdeacon: not to trust the deceiver of the world, nor cling longer to the world as it slips away.

To live religiously is honorable; to flee and abhor sins and crimes, which are the works of the devil, is useful—indeed, necessary; to love God with one’s whole heart is glorious.

Therefore, the person who hates his sins and crimes with perfect hatred lives religiously; and the one who is able to love God with his whole heart does so by despising the world and the things of the world, recalling the day of the final judgment before the eyes of his mind, praying constantly and saying with the Prophet: “Do not destroy my soul with the impious, nor my life with men of blood” (Psalm 25:9). And also: “Be for me a protecting God and a house of refuge, so that you may save me” (Psalm 30:3).

The world must first be abandoned, and then God must be prayed to, lest dwelling in the world impede the voice of the one who prays. For God does not approve but disapproves the prayer of the person who prays to God with his mouth while his heart thinks about the things of the world, just as he himself declares concerning certain people who seemed to speak well but savored earthly things in their hearts, saying: “This people honors me with their lips, but their heart is far from me” (Isaiah 29:13).

Certainly, those whose hearts are entangled in worldly business become far from God and perish. Hence the Psalmist says: “Those who distance themselves from you will perish; you have destroyed everyone who commits fornication away from you” (Psalm 72:27). Without doubt, the person who, departing from God, follows the fleeing world—though he never catches it—commits fornication away from God.

But whoever, as we have said, sets that final and greatly fearsome judgment before the face of his soul and considers with a pure intention what will happen there has nothing else left to do except, laying aside every other concern and driven by the weight of so great an examination, tremble with all his inward being; and, so that he may be able to find the just and exceedingly strict judge favorable to him in that hour, despise for love of him whatever can delight him temporarily here.

Who, I ask, could think perfectly about that day and love the present world, whose lovers will then be cast headlong without remedy or hope of remedy into the horrible pit of Gehenna, full of unbearable stench, unquenchable fire, an immortal worm (Mark 9:42–43), and other indescribable torments, where they will be tortured?

Whoever does not believe this before seeing it will suffer eternally when he begins to see what he could profitably have believed and avoided. [Col. 0197A]

Let us remember, dearest, while we may, that final and trembling hour, and set before the eyes of our memory that day on which there will indeed be repentance, but too late; perpetual groaning, but fruitless; unceasing tears, but sterile; continual mourning and weeping, but empty. Nor will any offering then be given by sinners for their sins.

Let us also consider how great will then be the reward of those who, as though they hated the sweet affections of relatives and the beloved faces of parents, fled from them, left the present age with its pleasures, and, in order to love God purely and without hindrance, either refused to possess riches altogether or despised those they possessed.

On that day, I say, after receiving their bodies and now secure in blessed immortality and indescribable glory, how happily they will appear before the Judge of the ages! And, as we have learned from the testimony of the holy Gospel, possessing twelve seats, they will judge with him (Matthew 19:28).

What wonder and exaltation there will then be, when each of them, by the merits that follow God’s gift of grace, is raised to the state of angels, and, lifted on high with the earthly body he once possessed, is enriched as a beloved son with God’s splendid inheritance!

I would have the desire to say much about this, but the immensity of such glory, such joy, and such blessedness forbids it; it surpasses even the tongues and understanding of the holy teachers. Human ability cannot fully explain how great is the reward God has prepared for those who love him in truth.

Let us love him, dearest, not only in word or with the tongue, but in deed and truth. Let us follow him, as he teaches that he must be followed—he who neither deceives nor is deceived—leaving the world for love of him, since the world deceives all the more when it flatters. [Col. 0197D]

Let us abandon that perverse and damnable habit which, while the devil attacks us, we have conceived in our worldly way of life as a monstrous offspring—or perhaps through some violence inflicted upon us—so that we may flee the death of the soul and return to the one who carefully created us in his image and likeness; from him we have often departed by sinning, and yet he still mercifully calls us, so that he may cleanse us, stained with the great dust of sins and crimes, and make us beautiful.

Let us return, dearest, to our most merciful Creator while we have time; let us always embrace him in the arms of our soul, and prefer his love to the world and its deceptive riches. Let us never, on any pretext, imitate that disobedient raven which, from greed for a stinking corpse, despised the command of the holy patriarch Noah.

Let us therefore heed the counsel of our Lord and Savior and, as he commands—he who deceives no one—renounce the world, whose false blessedness is followed by true misery, whose pleasure is brief and whose punishment for pleasure is everlasting.

Let us choose a poor life with humble and despised Lazarus rather than riches with the glorious and proud rich man. Poor Lazarus was received into Abraham’s bosom, to be glorified with the saints; the proud rich man was swallowed up by dreadful Tartarus, to be tormented with the impious. The former earned a blessed lot through poverty; the latter, everlasting death through riches. The former was exalted by his poverty; the latter was cast down by his riches.
