The rich man, having become utterly needy, was buried in hell (Luke 16:22) and condemned without end; Lazarus, placed in Abraham’s bosom (ibid.), rejoices with God, possessing the riches of paradise. Woe to riches, which not only perish but also cause their lover to perish! Blessed and secure is poverty, which enriches and raises up the person who patiently bears it.

Let no uncertain hope of riches flatter us on any occasion; rather, let us pursue voluntary poverty, so that it may make us participants in the riches of the one who wished to become poor on earth in order to enrich us by his poverty in heaven—Jesus Christ our Lord, to whom, with the Father and the Holy Spirit, be honor and glory forever and ever. Amen.

## EPISTLE XV

Goffridus, undeserving steward of the monastery of Vendôme, to G., venerable dean [Col. 0197D] [Note: “G., the dean”: Goffridus, as the catalogue of the Le Mans manuscript indicates. It does not state of which church he was dean; I suspect it was the church of Le Mans, the same person to whom Ivo’s Letter 52 survives.], his useful and truthful friend: to live happily and be blessed.

How purely and firmly you have loved us has been proved every time that our will or necessity summoned you to advocate our case. My mind confesses what my tongue speaks, and neither becomes ungrateful. My mind is therefore grateful in confession, and my tongue in speech; may God forbid that I should become ungrateful in action!

And because, as we said earlier, your love has until now been ready to serve us, let it not lose its excellent habit in our great anxiety. Your faithful friend, not indeed by merit but by grace, asks for it as his desire. [Col. 0198D]

For we have a case against our kinsman Maurice of Craon [Col. 0197D] [Note: “Maurice of Craon”: the son and successor of Rainald, lord of Craon, whom he also calls his kinsman in Letter 27. Maurice of Craon is specifically mentioned among the nobles who followed Fulk V, count, in the Norman war against King Henry. The Deeds of the Counts of Anjou say: “With him were Hugh of Matafelon, and his son Theobald, Fulk of Candé, Maurice of Craon, Peter of Camilliac, Jaquelin of Maillé with his four brothers, and so on.”], on the day after Palm Sunday. We ask you in many ways to assist us then.

If you are absent on any account, we shall grieve bitterly, since we shall have lost such a friend, one whom we possessed in our affection as second to no one. If we possessed him first in affection, we ought to possess him first in temptation, as it is written: “If you acquire a friend, acquire him in temptation” (Ecclesiasticus 6:7). Farewell.

## EPISTLE XVI

Goffridus, servant of the monastery of Vendôme, to Guillelmus [Col. 0199C] [Note: “Guillelmus”: the Le Mans catalogue says: “To Guillelmus, who had formerly been his teacher; in it he rebukes him for holding an incorrect view concerning the confession of sins.”], formerly his teacher: “Not to think more highly than one ought to think, but to think with sober judgment” (Romans 12:3).

All who are seen to live in sincere faith ought to labor with one accord in every place so that the truth of our faith may be instructed, not destroyed. Therefore, concerning the question proposed to us—which appears for the most part, indeed altogether, according to its interpretation, to conflict with the Catholic faith—we give a full account of the faith that must be followed, explaining how it ought not to be understood in the way you once understood it, or perhaps still understand it.

For, unless we are mistaken, you proposed that only four sins required confession, while the others were healed by the Lord without confession. You claim to have found this in Bede’s exposition of the Gospel [Col. 0199C] [Note: “Bede’s exposition of the Gospel”: the words of Bede against which Guillelmus stumbled occur in Book V of the Exposition on Luke, chapter 69. As Goffridus explains them, they have a clear and definite meaning.], where the ten lepers healed by the Lord are mentioned.

But we do not judge that this should be understood in that way at all; and according to the Christian faith, we neither can nor ought to understand it so. This statement must be carefully determined so that it may be understood profitably and the integrity of our faith preserved.

Those four sins—namely, pagan error, fraternal schism, heretical depravity, and Jewish perfidy—stain the chastity of the universal Church insofar as they prevail. Hence, whoever is polluted by these sins, or by even one of them, must confess not merely to the priest, as is done in other cases, but to the whole Church; and thus he must return to the unity of the Church whose faith he previously attacked.

For it is just that those who, through diabolical presumption, teach others unbelief should also strengthen them in the faith by public satisfaction, and that those who previously became an occasion and example of public destruction should become a model and example of public reconciliation.

Other vices, as you say, the Lord heals and corrects by himself. For although the Lord heals and corrects everything that is healed, he is said to heal and correct certain things by himself—namely, those that are privately revealed to him in confession, so that they may be healed.

I say “to him,” because confession made to a priest is known to be made chiefly to God. [Col. 0199D] [Note: “I say ‘to him,’ because confession is made to the one whose place [the priest] is known to occupy”: namely, confession is made principally to God through the priest. Leo the Great, in his letter to the bishops of Campania, says: “Let that confession suffice which is first offered to God and then also to the priest.” Sidonius likewise, Book IV, Letter 14. But Sidonius contains a notable passage concerning sacred confession, worthy of the more attentive consideration of the Guillelmuses of our age. He writes as bishop to Polemius, prefect of the Gauls, and distinguishes his own court—that is, the ecclesiastical—from the secular or praetorian court. “But if,” he says, “our humble profession seems worthy of contempt because, while Christ is to heal human affairs and lives, we open with a knife the foul ulcer of corrupt consciences—an ulcer which, in men of our order, though it may still stink somewhat of negligence, no longer swells with pride—I want you to know that it is not the same before a bishop as before the Judge of the world. For just as the person who does not conceal his own crimes from you is condemned, so among us the person who confesses the same things to God is absolved.”]

It is certain—nothing is more certain—that all sins or crimes require confession and penance; and although some of them seem to be punished through public penance, none require any other public confession except those that attempt to violate the common faith of the Church. [Col. 0200B]

## EPISTLE XVII

To the most illustrious duke of the Normans and most excellent king [Col. 0200C] [Note: “Henry, duke of the Normans and king”: son of King William the Great, youngest of all his children but the only one born in his father’s royal purple. After the death of his brother William Rufus in the year 1100, he occupied the kingdom while Robert, his other brother, was absent on the expedition to Jerusalem; precedence of age had assigned the kingdom to Robert. The Chronicle of Tours says: “In that same year William Rufus, king of England, went out hunting in a forest and was struck by an arrow shot by the knight Walter Tirel, who had aimed at a deer; he died and was buried at Winchester, and his younger brother Henry succeeded him.” Ivo the bishop congratulated him on his accession to his father’s throne in Letter 106. This is the king with whom, as we have already said, Fulk V, count, fought. Later he was joined to Fulk by a double marriage alliance: he married Matilda, Fulk’s daughter, to his son William, and gave his own daughter, also named Matilda, widow of the emperor Henry, as wife to Geoffrey, Fulk’s son; Henry II was born from this union.], Henry of the English, his most beloved lord and intimate friend, brother Goffridus, abbot of Vendôme, wishes him present prosperity always and happiness, and in the future to remain with the King of the English.

I informed your greatness, sweetest Father and lord, of our journey; and because I perceived that it was displeasing to you, I immediately changed my plan for the journey. Therefore, your servant—God is my witness—remains faithful to you, and in that fidelity I shall remain without interruption for as long as I live. When and how it pleases your excellence, I shall prove this by deeds according to my ability.

May my lord the king prosper and flourish. May almighty God defend him from every adversity and grant him what he rightly desires.

## EPISTLE XVIII
Guillelmo, duke of Aquitaine [Note: [Col. 0200D] Guillelmo, duke of Aquitaine. He was count of Poitiers, as in Book I, Letter 9, and in his own letters, which we shall produce at Letter 22; he was duke of Aquitaine and count of Gascony. To the county of Poitiers, which had been the most ancient possession of the counts of Poitiers—whose family this Guillelmus, as stated, brought to an end—there were later added, first through the benefit of marriage, the duchy of Aquitaine and then Gascony, that is, the county of old Julian Aquitaine on this side of the Garonne.] most illustrious, Goffridus, humble servant of the monastery of Vendôme [Col. 0201A], sends love of God and victory over enemies.

Just as it is fitting for you to seek from us whatever accords with the fear of God and the Rule of Saint Benedict, and for us willingly to obey you in this matter, so whatever is contrary to God and the holy Rule is neither fitting for you, given your dignity, to demand, nor is it right for us to obey you in it. For you and our other benefactors can place little confidence in the service that, though unworthy, we offer God daily in Masses, prayers, and the refreshment of the poor, once you have seen us violate the Rule according to which we made our profession—a Rule that must be observed by all.

You therefore asked us to send Rainaldus Quartaldus back to the obedience from which we removed him [Note: [Col. 0201D] Rainaldus Quartaldus. He is likewise called this in Letter 22, whereas in Book IV he is written Cartallo and Cartaldo. The name of the priory or obedience that this Rainaldus governed is suppressed. Ivo likewise, in Letter 163, replying to Goffridus’s consultation concerning another obedience, concealed its proper name. “Concerning that monk,” he says, “whom you bound by oath not to administer any longer the obedience that he had for some time usurped through disobedience, my advice is that he should no longer possess it, since this would be criminal for him and ruinous for the other brothers.”], because he was useful to you and very necessary to us. We believe what you say about his usefulness to you; but that he would have been necessary to us, if he had wished it, we do not doubt at all. And the more he recognized that he was useful to you and necessary to us, the more securely he practiced the disgrace of his body and the destruction of his soul. Therefore we ought not to have made temporal advantages more precious than the soul of our brother, for which without doubt we shall have to render an account on the day of judgment.

But for what faults we keep him with us for the salvation of his soul and body is neither yours to investigate nor ours to disclose further to you. When, however, we come for the present to your region, whatever you ask of us in accordance with God and our order [Col. 0201C], we shall willingly do. Farewell, and do not undertake to interfere in the care of the souls entrusted to us. We would rather lose whatever is temporal than consent to the ruin of any one of our brothers’ souls.

254. LETTER XIX

To Guillelmo, master of all knights and most noble duke of Aquitaine, Goffridus, servant of the monastery of Vendôme, sends in the present life victory over enemies and in the future everlasting glory.

Your prudence, excellent prince, ought to remember that we settled, for love of you, the complaints that we had against the abbot of Saint-Jean [Note: [Col. 0201D] The lord abbot of Saint-Jean: Henry of Saint-Jean-d’Angély. Relevant here are the things he wrote in Book III, Letter 36, to Ranulfus, bishop of Saintes, who is also discussed here. This letter is certainly later than that one, because in the meantime he had visited the bishop, yet still complains of the kidney pain that had prevented him from going to the bishop at that time.]—not that we granted any truce concerning our land [Col. 0202A], which he had violently invaded. Therefore we went to the bishop of Saintes, by whose judgment he claimed to have seized it, and there, through the mouth of that same bishop, we learned truthfully that no judgment concerning it had been rendered. Thus what he had unjustly presumed to do was declared invalid and void by the canonical judgment of the bishop and his clergy.

But you, duke of praiseworthy life, whom God honored in this world above others for the beauty of your body, so that he might make you, who are “beautiful in form beyond the sons of men” (Psalm 44:3), beautiful and great in heaven, do not in any way permit our monastery—which your parents honorably built in its own right and at their own expense—to be dishonored or diminished in its possessions. If you do this, you should fear that your parents may be informed of it by the holy angels [Col. 0202B], and that you may make their souls sad, when you ought rather to have made them rejoice.

255. If you once injured us in anything [Note: [Col. 0202D]

If we once injured you in anything. When he took the church of Oleron from Abbot Berno, Goffridus’s predecessor. This matter was discussed in Book I, Letter 9. It is worth hearing, however, the letter of Urban, by which Guillelmus, in obedience, restored the church, along with other matters that it recounts concerning him and his father. It is preserved in the Vendôme cartulary as follows:

Urban II to Guillelmus, duke of Aquitaine.

“Urban, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved son Guillelmus, count of the Poitevins: greeting and apostolic blessing. We have often admonished your character to imitate the devotion and prudence of your distinguished father. He cultivated the churches of his principality with the greatest devotion, enriched many of them from his own resources, and also built new ones from their foundations. We are astonished at you, for although you are powerful in other good pursuits, insofar as befits a knight, you are said to degenerate from your father’s integrity in this respect: that you disturb the rights of churches and strip those that he founded. It has come to us that you have taken from the monastery of Vendôme the church of Saint George, situated on the island of Oleron, together with a certain excellent estate. Therefore, dearest son, by this present letter we admonish you that, just as you love the grace of the holy apostles and of ourselves, you restore entirely to the monks of Vendôme that church and the other things that you have taken from them. For their possessions are alms given by your parents and the allod of the apostolic see. But if, within thirty days after seeing this letter, you disdain to fulfill what we command, know without doubt that you have incurred our indignation and have been struck by the anathema of the apostolic see. The monastery of Vendôme and the possessions belonging to it are known to have been strengthened by apostolic authority in such a way that, if anything belonging to them has been taken away or alienated by anyone, you should not doubt that he was excommunicated by our predecessors. And one whom those blessed men excommunicated we can neither absolve nor ought to absolve; rather, by the same authority, we confirm what they did. Given at Rome, on the second day before the Kalends of April.”]

if we have injured you in anything, we earnestly beseech the Lord God, with whatever prayers we can, to forgive you that offense by the gift of his mercy, to grant you a repentant heart for all that you have unlawfully committed, and to allow you to possess toward everyone—and especially toward us—the inward affections of pure charity.

Our desire to come to you, man revered throughout the world, would not have been delayed if illness of the kidneys, together with pain in the side, had not prevented it. Since necessity, not unwillingness, detains me, may your sublimity kindly accept the careful apology of your humble friend, indeed your servant. Farewell.

## LETTER XX

[Col. 0202C]

To the glorious and venerable Guillelmus, duke of Aquitaine, Goffridus, humble servant of the monastery of Vendôme, sends the fear of God and love joined with fear.

Being very concerned for your honor and advantage, excellent prince, I instruct you that, if you ought to send someone to Rome, as you once discussed with me, you should not delay any longer. I am prepared to give you whatever advice and assistance I can concerning this, and, for the enlargement of your kingdom, to undertake such a labor with only one or two of your clerics.

I can neither do nor ought to do this, however, nor ought you to demand it, without suitable remuneration. For the present I seek this remuneration: that you leave to God and to our house the customary dues or exactions [Col. 0203A] that your provosts have violently imposed upon our lands [Note: [Col. 0203D] Your provosts. Guillelmus, provost of Oleron, Haimericus, Asto, and others, concerning whom see Book I, Letter 2; Book III, Letter 38; and this very next letter.], although your religious predecessors, founders of our monastery, granted those lands to God and to our house without customary dues or any exaction, and that you make me fully secure that they will not be demanded again.

If this pleases you—as it certainly ought to please you—I do not refuse to obey in the aforesaid business, although it cannot be done without great expense from our resources and, still more, without the greatest labor and anxiety of our body. Farewell, and communicate to me by your letters, in a very familiar manner, whatever you decide concerning this.

## LETTER XXI

To the most illustrious duke of Aquitaine and incomparable knight, Guillelmus, dearest lord and intimate friend, Goffridus, humble servant of the monastery of Vendôme, sends the resolve to love what God loves and hate what he hates.

Duke of praiseworthy life, you commanded me to come to you, but you did not indicate the day or place where I might find you. Therefore I immediately sent a monk to your region to tell you that I would come to you wherever you yourself ordered. After waiting there for you for twelve days, and being unable to find you, he returned to me and reported that you had departed for Clermont [Note: [Col. 0203D] You had departed for Clermont. The chief city of the Auvergnats, which has changed its name from time to time. Its most ancient name was Nemossus, written by Strabo as Νεμωσσὸς, although he incorrectly places it on the Loire. From the altered and blended form Augustonemetum, after the time of Augustus, came the name then used according to the particular custom of each of the cities of Gaul, Arverni and the city of Arverna. Finally came Clermont—Clarus mons—from the name of the ancient citadel, when building began there after the fire under Pippin [Col. 0204C]. At this time the count of the Auvergnats was a feudal vassal of the duke of Aquitaine; Guillelmus therefore had many reasons for traveling to the Auvergnats.].

I am sending this brother to you again; through him let me know whether it pleases your greatness that my smallness should speak with you for the present, and where and when it will please you. I would have come to you more often [Col. 0203C] and spoken with you about your interests [Col. 0204A], if I could have found in you the favor and affection that our people are truly said to have found with your predecessors. Perhaps I deserved this by sinning against God; but God knows that I have never deserved anything from you except by serving and loving you.

Nevertheless, I long to speak with you, intending to bring before you a complaint concerning your provosts, Guillelmus namely and his brother Haimericus, who have almost entirely destroyed the possessions that your venerable predecessors, founders of our house, bestowed upon that same place as the price of the redemption of their souls. The administrators of our monastery who preceded me received those possessions, rich and prosperous, from the generous hand of your predecessors, who, as we believe, preceded you into the heavenly dwellings, and held them throughout their lives without hardship.

But I, who have labored and spent much on these possessions, found them poor; and through the evil favor of the aforesaid provosts I find them growing poorer day by day. Therefore, excellent prince, if I am not believed, let at least the alienation of the possessions and the poverty of the places be believed—things that can neither lie nor be concealed.

Farewell, duke greatly worthy of human praise; and may you be worthy of still greater divine praise!

258. LETTER XXII

Goffridus, humble abbot of the monastery of Vendôme, to his dearest lady Mathildis, countess of Poitiers [Note: [Col. 0204C]

Mathildis, countess of Poitiers. The wife of Guillelmus, the count to whom the preceding letters are addressed. We would have had to linger for a long time in investigating this Mathildis if an old charter of her husband Guillelmus had not opportunely come to our aid. She subscribed it concerning the altar of Saint Mary of Soulac, which, following his father’s example, he granted to the monastery of the Holy Cross at Bordeaux, from which it was copied, in the year 1096. It reads verbatim as follows:

Privilege of Guillelmus, duke of Aquitaine, for the monastery of the Holy Cross at Bordeaux.

“I, Willelmus, by the ordering of divine providence duke and count of Aquitaine and Gascony, wish it to be made known to all the faithful through this privilege of our authority [Col. 0204D] that the venerable man Fulco, abbot of the Holy Cross, asked us that, just as our illustrious father, of venerable memory, Willelmus, who was also called Goffridus, granted the altar of Saint Mary of Soulac, with all its appurtenances, in perpetual right to Arnaldus, abbot of the Holy Cross, and to his successors, by the judgment of the legates of the holy Roman Church—namely Amatus, bishop of Florence, and Hugo, bishop of Die, presiding at the council of Bordeaux, with Goscelinus, archbishop of Bordeaux, assisting, together with many other archbishops, bishops, and abbots—so we too would grant it; and that we would receive the place of the Holy Cross, together with the place of Saint Macarius, under our protection and defense. We most willingly gave our assent to this petition, and command Petrus, dean and archdeacon of the church of Bordeaux, to write all this, or to have it written, under witness, and to have it marked with the impression of our seal, etc.

“I, Mathildis, wife of the lord Guillelmus, duke of Aquitaine and count of Gascony, was present and gave my assent. I, Petrus, dean of the holy mother church of Bordeaux and archdeacon, subscribed; confirm this, O God. Eblo the archdeacon, Arnaldus Simon’s cantor, Andro, and many other canons of Saint Andrew were present. Hugo, brother of Count Guillelmus; Arnaldus of Blancafort; Willelmus the provost; Gumbaldus Austrini; and many other knights likewise. It was enacted and granted in the year 1096 of the Lord’s Incarnation, on the eighth day before the Kalends of April, epact 23, concurrent 2, indiction 4, under Pope Urban II and the lord Amatus, archbishop of Bordeaux. Given by the hand of the lord Count Guillelmus before the altar of Saint Andrew. To Fulco, co-abbot, on the eighth day before the Kalends of April; first grant in the tower of Aastellari, on the eleventh day before the Kalends of April.”]

, sends the fear of God and love joined with fear.

[Col. 0204C] Since the lord count, your husband, went to Jerusalem [Col. 0205A] [Note: [Col. 0205D] Your husband went to Jerusalem. In the second expedition to Palestine, which followed the first after a few years, in 1101, Guillelmus, count of the Poitevins, was leader and chief; with him were the other counts Stephen of Burgundy, Hugh of Vermandois, Stephen of Blois and Chartres, Goffridus of Vendôme, and Hugh, brother of Raymond, count of Toulouse. William of Malmesbury, Book IV of The Deeds of the Kings of the English, says that there were more than sixty thousand soldiers, besides many more infantry. William of Tyre discusses the same men in Book X, chapters 12 and 19, of his History of the Holy War.], we did not visit you, do not be surprised, we humbly ask, for we gave up doing so more from necessity than from willingness. Therefore, God willing, we shall come to you for the present and shall willingly serve your nobility in matters concerning the possessions of our church.

There is one thing, however, that we can neither conceal nor ought to conceal from you: we greatly fear that it is dangerous to your soul and contrary to our dearest lord and friend, your husband, if—God forbid—it has been done through you. There is, then, in your region a certain man, namely Rainaldus Quartaldus [Note: [Col. 0206C] Rainaldus, namely Quartaldus. See Letter 18.], who appears to be a monk in tonsure and habit, but is very far removed from a monk’s works and life. For, utterly scorning his profession and the Rule of Saint Benedict, trusting in you, as he himself asserts [Col. 0205B], he flees the commands of holy obedience and of his monastery and uses his own will as the law of the Rule, caring nothing for the ruin of his soul.

Therefore, as a beloved daughter of the holy Church, we implore you, and for fear of God and love of your husband—whom may God himself bring back to you safe and sound with every victory—we humbly beg you not, through your protection, to allow this man to lose his soul, since by his own iniquity he is already known to be separated from God.

Your excellence should know without doubt that this man, together with all who consent to him, has been excommunicated by the lord pope and by us, if he should ever again presume to be disobedient to us and to his monastery.”

## LETTER XXIII

[Col. 0205C] Goffridus, humble servant of the monastery of Vendôme, to his beloved daughter in Christ, Ermengardis, countess of Brittany [Note: [Col. 0206C] Ermengardis, countess of Brittany. Daughter of Fulco IV, count of Anjou, and sister of Fulco V, king. She married Alan Fergent, count of the Bretons, and bore Conan III, who was surnamed Conan of Ermengardis after his mother. The calendar of Saint Maurice at Angers records: “On the Kalends of June died Ermengardis, countess of Brittany, mother of Duke Conan and sister of Fulco, king of Jerusalem.” Of her the author of The Deeds of the Counts of Anjou says: “Fulco took several wives, including the daughter of Lancelin of Balgentiac, from whom was born the countess of Brittany, the woman who, after her husband’s death, practiced the monastic life in the church of Saint Anne at Jerusalem.” Thus she professed herself a nun after her husband’s death, but later, changing her counsel, returned to the world. Goffridus wrote this letter to her at that time, urging her to resume her former way of life. It seems that she eventually did so. For many years later Bernard wrote to Ermengardis as one devoted to God and a humble handmaid of Christ, in Letters 116 and 117.]—not to follow the world or take pleasure in its flower, since it quickly withers.

There is indeed one whom we ought to follow and in whose beauty we ought rather to delight: namely Jesus Christ our Lord, who loved us so greatly that for us he took on body and soul; and, so that we might not be condemned to everlasting death, he surrendered himself to death with immeasurable love.

His benefits, I say, if you had wished to consider them carefully, O creature for whom the author of life died, the tongues of flatterers would not have separated you from your Creator, nor joined you again to the world from which you had once withdrawn— the world in which you will find nothing except what is fatal. For true misery and false blessedness accompany the present world in such a way that whoever embraces it can scarcely, or perhaps never, possess God.

Farewell, and wisely consider what has been said.

260. LETTER XXIV

Goffridus, humble servant of the monastery of Vendôme, to his beloved daughter in Christ, Ermengardis, countess of praiseworthy life [Col. 0206B], sends the wish that she may act mercifully in this world so that in the next she may see and possess the merciful Lord.

I have learned something about you, royal daughter, which does not displease me and ought to displease no one, because it pleases God. As I have heard, you exercise the rights of justice in earthly government and establish peace in your homeland; you advance the interests of many, feed the hungry poor, offer drink to the thirsty, clothe the naked, and, surpassing the nobility of your birth by the nobility of your conduct, you appear to serve God rather than become entangled in worldly affairs.

I both can and ought to praise these holy works of justice and piety in you with joy. But there is another matter which, out of reverence for you, I do not presume to condemn, yet do not dare to approve. For while, through the gentleness of your charity [Col. 0206C], almost every sorrowful person who comes to you wipes away his tears, and scarcely anyone is permitted to leave your presence sad, and while the offering of your devotion very often opens the doors of many churches, it is neither especially astonishing nor a matter for pious wonder that you do not strive to honor with filial affection the church in which your venerable father [Note: [Col. 0206D]

The church in which your venerable father chose his burial. In the preceding letter Ermengardis’s father was said to have been Fulco IV, count of Anjou, who was called Rechin. Both chronicles of Saint Alban, the calendar of Saint Sergius, and the calendar of Saint Maurice record the day and year of his death in these words: “On the eighteenth day before the Kalends of May died Fulco, most beloved count of Anjou, nephew of Goffridus the elder Martel.” They do not give the place of burial.

That he was buried in the church of the priory of the Holy Trinity at Angers was noted from that church’s necrology by the distinguished Aegidius Menagius in his History of Sablé.]

chose his burial, the church that ought to have been honored by you even more, and, preserving the rights of nature, do not show through fitting benefits that you were his daughter, as you truly were.

In ancient times, both under the old law and under the new, there were religious princes worthy of all praise and remembrance who, knowing the places where their fathers’ bodies had been buried, always cherished them more dearly and devoted themselves wholeheartedly to adorning them with various kinds of ornament and enlarging them with possessions of many kinds.

We, whom that man of pious memory fathered neither in the flesh nor endowed with great wealth or any possession, love and honor the church in which he was buried for his sake; and, increasing the number of monks who offer God daily in that church the precious sacrifices—the prices, that is, of their souls—we have given them a large portion of the possessions of our abbey from which they may live [Col. 0207B].

We have written this special letter to you concerning your father, who died to the world—may he live to God!—because, unless you alone become heir to your father’s soul, no other heir begotten of his flesh can at present be found. When, mindful of your father’s salvation, you open the embrace of your charity to others, do not thereafter, on any pretext, keep it closed toward the place where your distinguished princely father lies bodily.

Farewell; and forgive me if I have spoken badly. If I have spoken well, heed me.

262. LETTER XXV

Goffridus, humble abbot of the monastery of Vendôme, to Adelardus of Château-Gontier [Note: [Col. 0207C]

Adelardus of Château-Gontier. From the letter of Fulco Nerra, whose beginning we quoted in Letter 11, it is clear that he gave the castle of Gontier, which he had fortified, to a certain Rainaldus, son of Ivo, whom he calls an excellent knight. Adelardus, heir of this Rainaldus after others, was lord of the castle, and this letter was written to him. An important memorial of him also survives in the ancient charters of the monastery of Saint-Aubin, by which he granted Saint-Aubin the tithe of his port. They are as follows:

Grant by Adelardus of Château-Gontier of the tithes that he offered to Saint-Aubin.

“Rainaldus, bishop of Angers, took care to commit to writing the gift that Adelardus, lord of Château-Gontier, made through our hand to Saint-Aubin from the tithe of the port of his castle. It was done in this manner:

“In the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1123, indiction 1, on the Kalends of March, Thursday, namely on the very day on which the most celebrated solemnity of Saint Aubin is observed, I came to the church of that same saint. At the request of Lord Hamelin, the abbot, and his monks, I entered their chapter with many distinguished persons, clerical and lay. There Adelardus, lord of Château-Gontier, came and placed in our hands, in the Book of the Rule, the tithe of the port of his castle from wine. A few days earlier, at his castle, with the consent of his wife Mathildis and his son Adelardus, he had re-enfeoffed Abbot Hamelin with it; then, on this occasion [Col. 0208C], he revested through us the aforesaid abbot and the monks of Saint-Aubin, and carried the Book of the Rule that he had placed in my hands onto the altar of that same saint.

“Because Adelardus was making this alms generously, the aforesaid abbot gave him, in the name of charity, twenty-six pounds of denarii and ten solidi, and five to his son. As a testimony to this grant, and for the authority and inviolable firmness of this matter, we decreed that the present page should be confirmed by our seal, the abbot’s seal, and the seal of Adelardus himself. Present were Petrus, abbot of Saint George; Daniel, abbot of Saint Mary of Évron; Ranulfus, abbot of Saint-Maur; and many others.”

[Col. 0208D] These charters show that Adelardus’s wife was Mathildis and his son Adelardus. Perhaps he is the one mentioned with his wife Melissendis in the calendar of Saint Maurice: “On the Nones of August died Adelardus, lord of Château-Gontier, for whom we must do as much as for one of our bishops. On the eighteenth day before the Kalends of September died Millissendis, wife of Adelardus, lord of Château-Gontier.”]

, sends equally the fear and love of the Lord.

You have done us many wrongs and have greatly provoked to anger, against us, the God whose servants we are, though unworthy. We bore with you patiently for a long time, hoping that you would eventually repent of such great wrongs. But because you did not fear to add certain new offenses, worse than those that came before, we ask you, as our dearest friend, to hasten to correct what you have unlawfully done against us and to release the quiet prey [Note: [Col. 0208D] Release the quiet prey. Letter 11.] that you seized.

If you refuse to heed our advice, you should fear that your entire land may be struck by such an interdict that thereafter it cannot be lifted without the permission of the apostolic see, whose allod the monastery of Vendôme is known to be. Moreover, in that same monastery and in all the churches belonging to the aforesaid place, every day before the most sacred body [Col. 0208B] and blood of our Lord Jesus Christ we shall make a public appeal concerning you, so that he who can do all things may deign, by the power of his right hand, to correct and restrain your violence—which we can neither restrain by human force nor ought to do—lest, because of this, your soul suffer everlasting fire in the future.

Farewell.

263. LETTER XXVI

Goffridus, abbot of the monastery of Vendôme, to Goffridus of Mayenne [Note: [Col. 0208D] Goffridus of Mayenne. Mayenne, a town of the county of Maine on the river of the same name, now bears the title of a duchy. The age of this Goffridus, whom our author indicates to have been advanced and burdened with years, suggests that he was the very man who fought for a long time for the freedom of the people of Maine against the Normans and their prince Guillelmus, as Ordericus Vitalis, among others, recounts. Ordericus calls Goffridus of Mayenne “the bravest of the men of Maine,” in Book IV of his Ecclesiastical History.], sends greeting.

In this present life you spent a long time acting wickedly, wise only in doing evil; but you could scarcely act well because you were unwilling. You did perform certain good works, but in comparison with your wrongs they are few or altogether nothing.

Therefore, as though you were already placed in your final hour, I advise you by admonishing you and admonish you by advising you: hasten, at least at the end, to correct the evil works that you have perpetrated over a long period, lest you die in soul together with the death of the body.

Know with complete certainty that the remainder of your life, which is short, must be preserved by living for God, your Creator and Redeemer, because whatever you have lived until now, you have lived wholly or almost wholly for the world. Anticipate your sins, then, lest they anticipate you. If, by an evil chance—God forbid!—you are overtaken by them, I truly believe that your punishment will have no end.

Each person anticipates his sins when, through repentance, he abandons the evils he has done and can still do. But a person is overtaken by his sins when, because the necessity of death presses upon him, he is no longer permitted to do evil.

Farewell, and heed our advice.

264. LETTER XXVII

Goffridus, servant of the friends of the monastery of Vendôme [Col. 0209B], to Rainaldus, his dearest kinsman [Note: [Col. 0209C] Rainaldus, his kinsman. The lord of Crèdon, as the following makes clear, and as the Cenomannian list confirms; he is the same man who founded the monastery at La Rota in the county of Anjou in 1096. His son Mauritius of Crèdon, whom Goffridus also called his kinsman, is mentioned in Letter 15. There were two families of lords of Crèdon in that century. The earlier was headed by Suhardus of Crèdon and his son Guarinus, who possessed Crèdon in the time of Count Fulco Nerra. The head of the later family was Robert the Burgundian, to whom Goffridus Martel, son of Fulco Nerra, granted again the castle of Crèdon, which he then held as his demesne in his own hand. Robert’s son and heir was Rainaldus of Crèdon; Mauritius was Rainaldus’s son. Abbot Goffridus was kinsman to both of them.], his friend and intimate companion, sends the wish that he may possess temporal things in such a way as not to lose eternal ones.

The pious scourges of divine mercy that came upon you this year ought to have greatly terrified your mind and recalled you more quickly from the things you did against God. For, as we believe, they were mercifully bestowed upon you by God so that, since in bodily health you delayed seeking God by your own will, you might at least hasten under the pressure of necessity, through fear, to make satisfaction for your unlawful works.

You also promised us this when we last spoke with you: that you would undertake the amendment of your life according to the counsel of God and of us. We do not know what works you have done or are doing since then; but if they are contrary to our most merciful Redeemer [Col. 0209C], we suffer no small grief on that account.

Would that, dearest friend, you might continually consider how great the sadness on the day of judgment, how great the tribulation, how great the misery, and how great beyond all other pains the pain will be for the person who will see God but will not possess him, and who will perish before the presence of his Redeemer [Col. 0210A]. No one who has chosen to serve the world rather than God has ever been able fully to contemplate this.

Perhaps now your own thought tells you, or those who flatter you tell you: “If our lord were to become a monk or die, all his land would immediately be scattered.” Know that those who speak in this way are not concerned for your soul. For your land and whatever you possess temporally must, whether you wish it or not, be left by you in the present.

But it will be very harmful to your soul if you do this from necessity and not from choice. Certainly, dearest friend, God, who permitted you to possess the lordship of Crèdon [Note: [Col. 0209D] The lordship of Crèdon. That is, dominion. Honor is commonly used for rule and dominion in the records of that age. We saw it in the passage from the Foundation of Vendôme in Book IV, Letter 44. Martel likewise says in the Foundation of Crèdon: “When I held the lordship of Crèdon in my own demesne, I gave that church to the Holy Trinity, before I had granted the lordship to Robert the Burgundian, my faithful man.” Thus “the lordship of Vendôme” means the county in the letters of that same Martel that we produced at Book I, Letter 2. “The lordship of Anjou” occurs in a letter of Fulco the Younger in 1096: “For the souls of my parents, namely my uncle Fulco and my paternal uncle Goffridus Martel, who raised me, through whom, after God, I hold this lordship.”], could, if he had wished, have given that lordship to Orhanda the one-eyed woman, whom I remember seeing at your court when I was a boy.

And the more you recognize that God has given you, the more indebted you are to him. He is very wretched, and does not truly believe in God, who allows the world to abandon him before he himself abandons the world.

We abandon the world before it abandons us when, voluntarily renouncing it, we hate for love of eternal life whatever filth or crime we have contracted from it. But the world seems to abandon us first when the final day finds us prostrate in our filth. Then the pitiable condition of the human being groans because he was unwilling to serve God when he can no longer repair the wickedness of the life he lived.

266. LETTER XXVIII

[Col. 0210C]

Goffridus, servant of the monastery of Vendôme, to his most beloved lord and intimate friend Radulfus:

[Note: [Col. 0209D] The Cenomannian list. To Radulfus of Beaugency, to whom Ivo also writes in Letter 248. Beaugency is a town in the region of Orléans on the Loire, made famous by the frequent assemblies of bishops [Col. 0210C] and princes held there. The Vendômois still possess there a noble church, concerning which Urban writes to Goffridus in these words: “The church of the Holy Sepulchre at Beaugency, which Raunarius, of blessed memory, bishop of Orléans, at the request of Lancelin, lord of that castle, granted to your predecessor Odericus to possess in perpetuity.” Lancelin of Beaugency was the father-in-law of Fulk Rechin, count, and the grandfather of Ermengard, Fulk’s daughter, of whom mention has been made. The son of that same Lancelin was, I think, Radulfus. Therefore, what is said in this letter about Radulfus’s father must be understood of Lancelin. William of Tyre numbers Radulfus among the principal commanders of the Jerusalemite army, Book I, chapter 17. We read that the same man, together with Amalric of Montfort and our abbot Goffridus, was sent as an envoy by King Louis VI [Col. 0210D] to Fulk, count of Anjou, in order to settle the dispute concerning the office of major or seneschal of France, which Fulk claimed had been granted by King Robert to his great-grandfather and his descendants by hereditary and perpetual right. Hugh of Clairy, an Angevin knight, himself also sent as an envoy to King Louis by Fulk for the same reason, recorded the matter for posterity. Accordingly, I shall append his complete account to these notes as a kind of conclusion, so that it may shed light on this affair, about which the most distinguished and highly learned John Tilius professed uncertainty in his collections, under the chapter “On the Great Master of France.” Of this account, which he begins with the words of Count Fulk, the following copy exists in the ancient manuscripts of Saint-Albin. (See below, under HUGH OF CLERIS, for the year 1120.—EDITOR OF THE PATROLOGY.)]

Radulfus, [Col. 0211A] so that through temporal goods he may pass on to the attainment of eternal ones.

We know that you love with all your heart our monastery, which has been established and consecrated in honor and under the name of the Holy Trinity. And we, with the full affection of our mind, beseech that same blessed Trinity—the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit—for whose love you do this, that it may guard your body and soul from every impediment in the present life, grant you everlasting life in the future, and, through its ineffable mercy and the glorious intercession of Blessed Mary ever-Virgin, absolve from every bond of sins and crimes the soul of your father, for whom we know you are greatly concerned; and may he be able to see and possess his God and Lord, who is the forgiveness of sins and the reward and recompense of his servants. [Col. 0211B]

You asked that the brother who has recently entered the order be released to his parents, after changing the religious habit, so that in this way they might recover their temporal loss. For love of you, he may indeed be released; but the religious habit cannot be changed without offense and the mark of infamy. If anyone objects that bishops and abbots have often gone to Rome after changing their habit, he must know that this was compelled by the obedience owed to the Lord Pope. For the necessity of the time, the Lord Pope issued a new command of obedience; in your request I hear, so to speak, a new sin of greed. Again, if you say that he has not yet made his profession, and has not yet received the monks’ blessing, believe firmly and acknowledge truly that no one can become a perfect monk or Christian without devotion of heart, whether by profession or by blessing. And wherever there is devotion of heart, there the holy blessing and the true profession cannot be absent. Therefore, if the customary profession, which is made visibly, and the blessing do not bind him, as you say, the devotion to religion that he still perseveres in does not permit him to be free from the world—especially since he had already made that profession willingly and received the blessing, had it not been delayed by us for their sake.

## NOTICE ON THE FOLLOWING LETTER

That Goffridus entered into a bond of confraternity and fellowship in suffrages with the Cluniacs is attested by a letter of Goffridus himself, published by the most distinguished John Mabillon in Volume III of the *Analecta*. We place it here so that this new edition of his works may not lack that writing of Goffridus.

## LETTER OF GOFFRIDUS TO THE CLUNIACS  
### For Entering into a Fellowship of Suffrages

[Col. 0211C]

I, Brother Goffridus, abbot—whatever sort of one—of the monastery of Vendôme, coming into the presence of Lord Hugh, venerable abbot of Cluny, asked him to grant me a share in the fellowship and confraternity of his whole house and of the entire flock entrusted to him by God, so that I, who placed little confidence in my own perfection, might be able through their suffrages to obtain eternal life.

He received this graciously and fulfilled it most willingly. By a general decree he determined that, for as long as I live, whenever I come to Cluny in his absence, I am to preside in his place over the chapter, the table, and the whole order; and that, when I depart from this light, prayers and almsgiving are to be performed for the repose of my soul in that place in every respect as for one of their professed abbots or monks, with the addition of a thirty-day series of Masses, together with the sending of brief notices and the recording of the rule.

## WORKS OF GOFFRIDUS, ABBOT OF VENDÔME, CARDINAL OF BLESSED PRISCA

### I. TREATISE ON THE BODY AND BLOOD OF THE LORD JESUS CHRIST

[Col. 0211D]

Brother Goffridus, a sinner and, in the present treatise, a Catholic writer, to all Christians: they should faithfully believe concerning the body and blood of the Lord, and should likewise see and possess Christ the Lord himself, whose body and blood they receive.

When the faithful piously ask what ought truthfully to be said and firmly believed concerning the body and blood of God and our Lord Jesus Christ, let it be said—by the gift of Christ God and our Lord—so that no doubt may remain in their hearts.

First, bread and wine are placed upon the altar; but just as before consecration they possess nothing besides the proper nature of bread and wine, so after consecration they retain no nature or substance of bread or wine, except as regards taste, appearance, and smell. This, however, is on account of human weakness and frailty. For if that most glorious flesh and that most sacred blood were to appear to human beings not under the appearance of bread and wine but in their own proper nature, people could not endure them because of their greatness. And if this could happen, there would be no merit of faith.

But if the holy apostles Peter, James, and John could not gaze upon the Lord, while he was still mortal and bearing corruptible flesh on earth, when he was transfigured, how could other people endure the immense glory of that body, now incorruptible and glorified? For the Lord did not show those holy disciples the nature of his divinity, as some suppose, but displayed the appearance of the flesh that was later to be glorified.

Therefore let us firmly believe and in no way doubt that what is received upon the altar after consecration by the Christian religion is nothing else and possesses nothing else than what Truth itself openly declares: “Take; this is my body” (Matthew 26:26). And concerning which body he was speaking, he himself explained when he said: “Which will be delivered up for you” (1 Corinthians 11:24). Likewise concerning the chalice: “This is my blood, which will be poured out for you for the remission of sins” (Matthew 26:28).

But if anyone believes that the Lord Jesus possessed flesh other than this, he is foolish; he is not a Catholic but a heretic.

Christ redeemed humanity by this flesh; by this flesh humanity killed Christ. Yet the soul and flesh of the human being were redeemed, and this human flesh was the price of redemption. This is that one and the same truly true flesh—not another—which, through the cooperation of the Holy Spirit, was conceived and born of the Virgin Mary and suffered on the cross, and which God himself, by the power of his divinity, raised from the dead on the third day.

Therefore no one should fear calling this flesh of Christ God, the only-begotten Son of God the Father, natural and proper, now made incorruptible and immortal; nor should anyone fear believing it when he calls it so, and receiving it through belief—not merely in the sacrament, which many wicked people also do, but even unto participation in the Spirit.

In this holy mystery, which is also called a sacrament—that is, a sacred sign—because one thing, namely Christ’s holy flesh, is present, while another thing, namely the appearance of bread, is seen, many perverse people receive that most blessed and life-giving flesh. But because the wicked approach wickedly, they become worse than they had previously been.

Others receive it unto participation in the Spirit, because those who receive it with charity—that is, with love of God and neighbor—participate with Christ unto the enlivening of the soul. And just as no one can receive the most holy body and blood of Christ without charity without becoming worse, so no one can receive it with charity without thereby becoming better.

Hence, if someone asks how bread can become Christ’s flesh and wine his blood, certainly, if the Lord had not created the things that exist, he perhaps could not change what had been created. But it was no lesser miracle to create everything from nothing than to transform certain things from among all created things into something better.

You who ask such questions, do not go astray. If you believe that God is omnipotent, you will be unable to doubt this in any way. For if you confess that he can do all things, you cannot deny that he can also do this, since it is something drawn from all things.

He who was able ineffably and truly to assume flesh from a Virgin mother while her virginity was wholly preserved, who, although immortal, died for us, and on the third day raised himself from death by the power of his dominion, converts the substance of bread and wine in consecration into the nature of his body.

### II. ON THE ORDINATION OF BISHOPS AND THE INVESTITURE OF LAYMEN

Goffridus, humble servant of the monastery of Vendôme, to his most beloved lord and intimate friend Peter of León, cardinal of the holy Roman Church: to love the Catholic faith with all his heart, and to oppose with all his strength those who contradict it.

Mindful of your request and my promise, I have delayed—if not as I ought, at least as I was able—to discharge what you asked of me and what I promised: namely, concerning the ordination of a bishop and the investiture of laymen.

First, we must believe firmly and in no way doubt that, just as baptism makes a Christian, so election and consecration make a bishop; and just as it is impossible to become a Christian without baptism, so it is impossible to create a bishop without election and consecration.

In the ordination of a bishop, election and consecration are both so necessary that consecration without election, and election without consecration, are by themselves insufficient to make a bishop. For just as water and the invocation of the Holy Spirit are necessary in baptism, and together make a Christian, so in ordaining a bishop election and consecration are joined by necessity, and together create a bishop.

And just as by water alone, or by the invocation of the Holy Spirit alone, neither baptism can take place nor can a person become a Christian, so by election alone or consecration alone no one can be ordained or made a bishop.

The sacrament of baptism, and of election and consecration of a bishop, is indeed great. But Christ commanded the former and performs it through others, while he accomplished the latter through himself. In the former, a human being is created spiritually and is called a Christian by Christ; in the latter, a lord and ruler of Christians is created—one who is not merely called a Christian by Christ but is also believed to act in Christ’s place.

It must be understood that here, and wherever the election of a bishop is discussed, a canonical and evangelical election is required: one who has been rightly elected must also be justly consecrated. Otherwise there is a kind of perverse deception in the Church and no small mockery of ecclesiastical dignity.

For whoever approaches as though he were to be consecrated without having been canonically elected departs accursed, and is falsely called a bishop—one who attempts to overturn the order of election and consecration that Christ himself first instituted.

For Christ himself first chose the apostles and consecrated them; he did not wish to consecrate them unless they had first been chosen. This holy sacrament—namely, the election and consecration of the apostles—Christ first performed as the first sacrament, through which the other sacraments were to be performed.

None of the apostles boldly sought the apostolate; none of them shamelessly offered himself to be chosen. Therefore the whole ordination of a bishop consists not in his own election and consecration, but in that of others, provided that a right election has preceded.

Christ himself first performed these acts, as has been said; afterward, his vicars did so. In the apostles they were performed by Christ, because they were chosen and consecrated by him. In all others they may be performed by no one except Christ’s vicars.

Christ’s vicars are the clergy in election and bishops in consecration. All others may indeed request a bishop, but they cannot elect or consecrate one.

Therefore whoever presumes in another manner, as though under the name of a pontiff, to claim the Church or ecclesiastical power for himself, no longer enters through the door but climbs in from elsewhere; he rightly must not be counted among bishops but numbered among thieves and robbers (John 10:1).

Such a man does not offer blessing to others but rather pestilence, and appears to inflict a wound rather than bring salvation; by such presumption he deserves the curse of God.

For a bishop without canonical election is like a tree without roots. A tree that has no root, even if it has leaves, is entirely unable to bear fruit. Christ approached such a tree, and when he found no fruit there, he cursed it (Mark 11:13–14).

He is especially cursed by God who desires, through his own ambition, to be joined to the sacraments of the Church rather than through the charity of Christ. And everyone who is not joined to the sacraments of the Church by the cement of charity does indeed injure the Church, but is scattered like a mud wall. Although such a wall may be whitewashed for a time, those who previously trusted in it are crushed by its sudden collapse.

From this comparison it is rightly inferred that whoever, to the injury of the holy Church, obtains ecclesiastical office—especially the pontificate—first brings about his own destruction and then the death of the people.

The Church likewise suffers injury and shame when, in choosing a pontiff, canonical election perishes, and what is owed to the merits of a good life, to the teaching of wisdom, and to sacred orders is imposed upon those for whom neither the merits of a good life, nor instruction in wisdom, nor sacred orders provide support.

Such men have an earthly—or rather, marshy—foundation, and therefore those who are built upon such a foundation collapse. Of them it is said in the Psalm: “You cast them down when they were raised up” (Psalm 72:18).

Nothing is more grievous in the sight of Christ than an injury to the Church, whose sacraments those who receive perversely can neither be with Christ nor be of benefit.

No one can be at once with Christ and act against Christ, since he himself says: “Whoever is not with me is against me” (Luke 11:23). Whoever is not with Christ can benefit neither himself nor others, since he again declares: “Whoever does not gather with me scatters” (ibid.), and elsewhere says: “Without me you can do nothing” (John 15:5).

There are some who think that everything is permitted to the Roman Church, and that by a certain dispensation it may act differently from what divine Scripture commands. Whoever thinks in this way is foolish. For after Peter, the Roman Church may not do what was not permitted to Peter.

Christ gave Peter the power to bind what was to be bound and to loose what was to be loosed (Matthew 16:19); he did not grant him the power to loose what was to be bound or bind what was to be loosed.

Even if Peter at some time acted otherwise, Paul, though a newcomer in conduct, was not afraid to resist him to his face (Galatians 2:11). Peter, willingly accepting the rebuke of his junior, carefully corrected what he had done beyond what was right.

Moreover, nothing may rightly be done that Christ refuted by his own example. He did not come to abolish the law but to fulfill it (Matthew 5:17).

Therefore the Roman Church ought not to abolish the law of the divine Scriptures but to preserve it; and it ought to use the power handed over to it by Christ not according to its own will but according to Christ’s tradition.

If the Roman pontiff is advised by his junior that he has at some time acted beyond what is right, he should correct himself justly, just as Peter accepted Paul’s admonition; and if he desires to imitate Peter, he too will accept it.

Concerning the investiture of laymen: if anyone wishes to know what the Catholic and Apostolic Church has thought, taught, judged, and decreed, let him read the first chapter of the council held in the time of Pope Gregory VII. There he will find that all clerics who receive investiture from the hand of a layman are called heretics and are therefore condemned and excommunicated.

Although one heresy is called the heresy of investiture and another Simoniacal heresy, the heresy concerning investiture strikes more forcefully against the holy Church. Simoniacal depravity is often practiced secretly; the heresy of investiture, however, is always conducted publicly.

There too the whole ecclesiastical order is first thrown into confusion, when what ought to be given to each person in the Church only by his consecrator, with the prayers appropriate to the occasion, is first received from secular power.

The holy apostles not only prohibited this; by the power given them by Christ they also condemned all those who obtain the Church through secular power.

And rightly, by the judgment of the Holy Spirit, the apostles resolved to condemn this heresy at the very beginning of the Church, since they foresaw that it would be born much later from the devil, its father.

Since, therefore, the Holy Spirit who spoke through the apostles entirely denied and prohibited to a layman both investiture and every power of disposing of Churches or ecclesiastical things, whoever receives investiture from a layman now exposes what is holy to dogs—not merely acting against the apostles but against the Lord of the apostles.

The investiture of which we speak is a sacrament—that is, a sacred sign—by which the prince of the Church, namely the bishop, is distinguished and recognized as separate from other human beings, and by which pastoral care over the Christian flock is entrusted to him.

He ought to receive this investiture only from the one from whom he receives consecration. He must first be consecrated, and afterward, like a king of the Church, be adorned with sacred insignia.

If anyone thinks that this is permitted to any secular power, he is mistaken. If he attempts to defend it, he desires to nullify the teaching of the apostles and the mind of the Holy Spirit; therefore there is no doubt that he is a heretic.

The investiture of laymen, then, which is performed by staff and ring, is rightly called heresy. For just as the heresy is called Simoniacal from Simon, so, from the one who invests and the one who is invested—because each of them in that action attempts both to handle the keys of the Church and to violate its one and unique door—it is rightly called the heresy of investiture.

Moreover, if it is rightly examined, this heresy of investiture is also shown by clear and true reasoning to be Simoniacal heresy. For what does the secular power attempt to claim for itself through investiture, except either to extort money by it or, what is more serious, to make the person of the pontiff improperly subject to itself?

There is no layman—not even if it were permitted to him—who would desire to give a ring or staff with such an intention unless, through these things that are sacraments of the Church, he were eager for temporal profits.

Laymen may indeed receive the sacraments from the Church, but they may not give any of the Church’s sacraments. The ring and staff, when they are given by those by whom they ought to be given, and at the time, place, and manner in which they ought to be given, are sacraments of the Church, just as salt and water, oil and chrism, and certain other things are, without which the consecrations of people and Churches cannot take place.

The layman always claims for himself through investiture, as we have said, either money or—what is more—the person of the bishop or abbot.

By this malignity, which is not so much human as diabolical, the Church loses Catholic faith, freedom, and chastity, without which it cannot exist in any way. The Church must always possess these three; if even one of them is lacking, it lies like a paralytic and possesses neither the power of binding nor of loosing.

Therefore whoever presumes to receive the investiture described above under the appearance of a shepherd becomes a paralytic, polluted by heretical leprosy.

I do not confidently call him a shepherd, nor any member of that Shepherd who laid down his life for his sheep (John 10:11); he is a thief, robber, and wolf. For he has come to steal, rob, and slaughter (ibid., 10:10).

Not only those who commit this detestable impiety but also those who consent to it are condemned. The one who remains silent about it consents; so does the one who does not correct it and the one who does not openly oppose it.

No one is exempt from the duty—and everyone is able—to oppose it openly. For if he does not have the authority of a prelate, he nevertheless has the voice of a Christian. Scripture says, making no exception: “Cursed is he who restrains his sword from blood” (Jeremiah 48:10)—that is, who restrains his voice from rebuking sin.

Let him also remember that the she-ass once corrected the foolish prophet (Numbers 22:28).

If he has been morally defective or made infamous by any other crime, he ought not for that reason to remain silent, since anyone may defend the common faith of the Church—which he believes and confesses to be his own—against its adversaries and fight freely on its behalf.

The two men who were crucified with the Lord in his Passion were altogether infamous, for they were public robbers. Yet one of them, not merely because he believed but because he began to defend the truth of his faith against the other, deserved to hear that good and delightful word from our Savior: “Today you will be with me in paradise” (Luke 23:43).

Thus, in that robber above all, it is made clear that a Catholic man, though stained with marks of infamy, deserves through the defense of the faith both paradise and to be with Christ.

### III. ON SIMONY AND THE INVESTITURE OF LAYMEN: WHY BOTH ARE CALLED HERESY

To Pope Calixtus, his good lord and intimate friend, Goffridus, abbot of Vendôme, cardinal of Blessed Prisca: as a son to his father and a servant to his lord.

Since both Simony and the investiture of laymen are called heresy, why each is heresy and rightly ought to be called heresy will be demonstrated sufficiently in this brief letter, so that there may henceforth be no doubt about it.

Believe most firmly, dearest Father, that nothing is properly called heresy except what attempts to separate the Son or the Holy Spirit from the unity of the Father, or asserts that one Person is less or greater than another.

Therefore Simon Magus was not merely a heretic but the first and worst of heretics. He not only thought that the Holy Spirit could be separated from equality with the Father but also presumptuously desired to become greater than the Holy Spirit by attempting to possess him.

For when he thought that he could possess the Holy Spirit with money, what else did he seek than to be considered greater than the Holy Spirit, since the possessor is greater than what is possessed?

Since, therefore, whoever attempts to assert that the Persons of the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit are unequal must be regarded as a heretic both by reason and by authority, much more must Simon Magus be called a heretic, since he attempted to subject the Holy Spirit, equal in all things to God the Father and the Son, to himself by money. Simony, which was invented by him and named after him, is therefore proved to be heresy.

But when a layman grants the investiture of Churches by staff and ring—things that are sacraments of the Church, like salt and water, oil and chrism, and certain others without which the consecrations of people and Churches cannot take place—he usurps for himself Christ’s right and power and in a certain manner proclaims himself higher than the Son of God.

For when those sacred sacraments of the Church are given where, to whom, and when they ought to be given, they are given by the Son of God through the consecrator, who is the minister of that action, just as the Holy Spirit was given for the remission of sins through Peter.

Hence God the Father speaks to John, saying: “Upon whom you see the Spirit descending, he is the one who baptizes” (John 1:33). When he said, “He is the one who baptizes,” he signified the whole by a part. For the Son of God accomplishes and bestows all the sacraments of the Church.

But when a layman presumes in this way against the Son of God, he swells with pride no less, if not more, than Simon Magus; and he too swells with pride when, in conferring the sacraments, he places himself before the Son of God.

And because he attempts not only to deprive the Son of God of equality with his Father but also appears by his impious action to declare himself superior to the Son of God, he too is rightly called a heretic, and his investiture is called heresy.

Farewell, and strive to oppose Simony and the investiture of laymen, setting aside every occasion and every dispensation.

### IV. ON THE INVESTITURE OF ECCLESIASTICAL POSSESSIONS, WHICH IS GRANTED TO KINGS

Let emperors and kings not be displeased by what we say, nor let them attempt by custom to claim for themselves what truth denies them.

Since the apostles prohibit laymen, even religious ones, from having any power to dispose of Churches or ecclesiastical things, it is evident that investiture is denied them by Truth itself—namely, by Christ, who spoke through the apostles.

That Christ spoke in the apostles the Apostle Paul asserts when he says: “Do you seek proof of the one who speaks in me—Christ?” (2 Corinthians 13:3).

Since Christ is Truth, as he himself said, “I am the truth” (John 14:6), and never said, “I am custom,” let the Christian follow Christ, and let the king follow the King of kings, namely Truth itself, not custom.

Although such investiture is found neither in laws nor in canons concerning ecclesiastical possessions, it is nevertheless granted to kings in order to avoid scandal and schism, so that neither they may perish because of it nor the holy Church suffer harm.

To receive investiture by staff and ring from anyone except one’s consecrator is clearly harmful, because no layman is permitted to give those sacraments of the Church, just as he is not permitted to consecrate a bishop.

Furthermore, things once given to the Church ought not to be given again by kings, nor can kings appropriately invest anyone with them. For to give to someone what he already has, and to invest someone with what he already possesses, is superfluous and futile; it does not, however, appear criminal.

There is one kind of investiture that perfects a bishop, and another that sustains a bishop. The former is derived from divine law, the latter from human law.

Remove divine law, and a bishop is not created spiritually. Remove human law, and he loses the possessions by which he is sustained bodily.

The Church would not have possessions unless they were given to it by kings, and unless it were invested by them—not with divine sacraments but with earthly possessions.

By divine law we exercise dominion over kings and emperors; yet, by that same law, because they belong to Christ the Lord, we owe them honor and reverence, as the Apostle says: “Honor the king” (1 Peter 2:17).

By human law we owe them only as much as we value the possessions with which the Church is known to have been enriched and endowed by them or by their parents.

Hence Blessed Augustine speaks as follows concerning John:

“Do not say, ‘What have I to do with the king?’ What have you to do with possession? For possessions are held by the rights of kings. If you say, ‘What have I to do with the king?’ then do not call the possessions yours, because you have renounced the very rights by which possessions are held.

“For according to the law of emperors you possess earthly things. Remove the laws of emperors: who would dare say, ‘That estate is mine,’ or ‘That servant is mine,’ or ‘That house is mine’?

“By what law do you defend estates—the divine or the human? We have divine law in the Scriptures, human law in the laws of kings.

“From what law does each person possess what he possesses—if not from human law? For by divine law: ‘The earth is the Lord’s and its fullness’ (Psalm 24:1). God made the poor and the rich from one clay, and one earth supports both rich and poor.

“Yet by human law you say, ‘This estate is mine; this house is mine; this servant is mine.’ Therefore by human law, by the law of emperors—why? Because God distributed those human laws through emperors and kings of the world to his Church.”

After canonical election and consecration, kings may therefore give a bishop, by royal investiture in ecclesiastical possessions, a grant, assistance, and protection without offense. Whatever sign may have been used for this will not harm the king, the pontiff, or the Catholic faith.

The good Lord and our teacher Christ willed that the spiritual sword and the material sword should both exist for the defense of the Church. If one is blunted by the other, this occurs against the will of the one who appointed them.

On this account justice is removed from the kingdom and peace from the Church; scandals and schisms are aroused, and the destruction of souls and bodies occurs together.

While kingdom and priesthood attack one another, each is endangered. When the king and the Roman pontiff rise against one another—one on behalf of the custom of the kingdom, the other on behalf of the freedom of the Church—the kingdom cannot obtain that custom and never will be able to obtain it, and the Church loses much of its freedom.

Moreover, the king is deprived both of sacred communion and of royal dignity; while the Roman pontiff, compelled by necessity, is made to serve many who ought to serve him. And the people, who ought to be taught by the pontiff and led by the king, follow the king and the pontiff.

Let the Church have peace and the kingdom justice. Let the king have his custom, but a good one—not the custom he wrongly demands, but the investiture described above.

Let the Church have its freedom, but let it take the greatest care lest, while drawing too much, it draw blood, and while trying to scrape rust from a vessel, it break the vessel itself.

This is the principal element of discretion: that no one should be deceived by Satan through any action of the Church.

A person is deceived by Satan when, under the appearance of justice, someone who could have been saved through indulgence happens to perish through excessive sorrow.

Moreover, the good and discerning Augustine says in his letter to Parmenianus that someone who has a stubborn multitude with him in an evil work should scarcely ever, or perhaps never, be excommunicated. For it seems more tolerable to spare one person lest the schism of many be sown in the Church.

And the most blessed teacher and martyr Cyprian says: “Schism must not be made, even if the one who departs does not remain in the same faith and in the same tradition.”

And Solomon says in Ecclesiastes: “Whoever cuts wood will be endangered by it, if the iron slips” (Ecclesiastes 10:9).

Likewise in Exodus: “It shall be eaten in one house; you shall not cast any of the flesh outside the house” (Exodus 12:46).

From these words it is inferred that one who has a multitude with him should not be excommunicated, lest, while we attempt to correct one person, the destruction of many result.

Jerome also writes this to Augustine, saying that, according to the prudent and honorable dispensation of the blessed apostles Peter and Paul, it is sometimes necessary to do what is rightly censured, lest scandal arise among the Christian people.

For fear of the Jews, lest they be scandalized, Paul, after his conversion, had Timothy circumcised and even practiced the ceremonies of the Jews; and Peter compelled some Gentiles to Judaize. Each holy apostle, pretending to observe the precepts of the old law, acted so that those who had become believers from among the Jews would not, after being scandalized, deny the knowledge of truth they had received.

The holy apostles did this out of merciful and pious compassion, not through deceptive pretense, although they had no doubt whatsoever that the law was not to be observed after the Gospel.

Here the men of most blessed life are understood not to have changed their judgment, but to have adapted, for a time and for the salvation of others, the position of their teaching.

If in the present matter I have said less or otherwise than I ought, let it be attributed to ignorance and mercifully forgiven. But if I have spoken well, let it be kindly received and carefully observed.

### V. TO POPE CALIXTUS: HOW DISPENSATIONS OUGHT TO BE MADE IN THE CHURCH
Dispensations must sometimes be made in the Church—not out of love of money or any other human favor, but with a devout and merciful intention. For then [Col. 0221C] a dispensation by the Church’s pastor is believed to be devoutly and mercifully made when something is temporarily done or permitted by him in a less perfect manner, not by his own will but because of the necessity of others, lest, specifically, the Christian faith itself be endangered in them. Thus a dispensation must be made by the Church in such a way that the truth of our faith is always taught; and if anything has been done or permitted otherwise for a time, it must be corrected at the appropriate moment.

The blessed apostles Peter and Paul used this discreet and holy dispensation because of fear of the Jews, lest they should be scandalized. For after his conversion Paul had Timothy circumcised and also observed the ceremonies of the Jews; and Peter compelled some Gentiles to Judaize. Each holy apostle pretended to observe the precepts of the old law, lest those who had become believers from the Jews, being scandalized, should deny the knowledge of the truth that they had received. The holy apostles did this out of merciful and devout compassion, not through deceitful pretense, although they had no doubt that the law was not to be observed after the Gospel. In this, the men of most blessed life are understood not indeed to have changed their purpose, but, for a time and for the salvation of others, to have modified the judgment of their teaching. For concerning this matter, both they and others acted differently, and afterward corrected both themselves and others.

Dispensations may also and should be made by which the customs of churches and monasteries are changed, but only when a lesser good is set aside so that what is better may be established. No evil, however, should be done or permitted [Col. 0222A] except in that sole necessity in which it is feared that the faith may be endangered, and even then it must afterward be corrected. For the Apostle Paul declares that those who do evil so that good may come are justly condemned. But if anyone makes dispensations in the Church otherwise, he contradicts reason and truth alike; he not only does not possess a burning lamp, but also extinguishes the burning lamps of others. Therefore he is not rightly called Christ’s vicar, but is himself a blind guide of the blind.
