## VI. THE THREE THINGS THAT THE CHURCH MUST ESPECIALLY POSSESS, TO THE SAME POPE

The Church must always be catholic, free, and chaste. Catholic, because it must neither be sold nor bought; free, because it must not be subjected to secular power; [Col. 0222B] chaste, because it must in no way be corrupted by gifts.

For when the Church is sold or bought, faith is emptied, because what was made incomparable by God is judged capable of being purchased by a human being. Moreover, the one who sells the Church imitates the covetous Judas; but the one who buys it follows Jewish avarice. Judas, certainly, sold Christ, who is the head of the Church, out of covetousness, and the Jews bought him out of avarice.

But when the Church is subjected to secular power, she who was previously mistress becomes a servant; and she loses the charter of liberty that Christ the Lord dictated on the cross and, as it were, wrote with his own hands in his blood. For Christ claimed this charter of liberty on the cross and gave it personally to his bride, the Church, so that she, being free, might make free men and children of God those whom sin [Col. 0222C] had made servants of the devil, and might make her own servants—those who served her diligently and humbly obeyed her like devoted sons obeying a good mother.

The Church’s chastity is likewise placed in complete danger when she herself is corrupted by gifts and, from being the chaste and virginal bride of the Lord, is truly recognized as having become, so to speak, a public woman. For this is characteristic of a prostitute: always to be reduced to a price.

These three things that we have mentioned the Church must properly and exclusively possess. If one of them is lacking, she is falsely called the bride of Christ; she lies like a paralytic, possessing neither the power of binding nor of loosing. For Christ, the good shepherd, seeks a faithful bride and rejects an unfaithful one; he joins himself to the free woman and casts away the servant; he loves the chaste and hates the corrupted.

## VII. 291 ON THE ARK OF THE COVENANT

Goffridus, humble servant of the monastery of Vendôme, to his beloved disciples in Christ, Hamelin and Andrew: may you bring good beginnings to a better conclusion.

Devoted to many and varied affairs of the world, I cannot speak or write to the brothers whom divine patience has entrusted to my imperfect direction as I ought. Yet it is right to wish rather to be of service than to preside; nor is it fitting for a pastor of the Church to be less concerned for the salvation of souls than for the administration of material affairs.

Therefore, although my mind according to its custom was occupied with other matters, I judged that I ought not to withhold from you, whom I especially love, certain things for your consolation and I considered it a religious duty not to remain silent [Col. 0223A]. And since I have resolved to console you, I cannot console or build you up more profitably than by endeavoring to reveal to your humility a few things from among the many that are recorded as having been done under the old law.

I considered it superfluous to discuss matters that are obvious and thoroughly familiar to everyone, because they produce weariness in hearers and make them culpable through contempt. Yet those things must be brought forth that you can understand and that can suitably be applied to your life.

Therefore, after the Hebrews’ departure from Egypt, after the crossing of the Red Sea, and after the destruction of the Egyptians, what the Lord commanded Moses for the benefit of his people must be heard attentively and retained in memory [Col. 0223B]. Moses accordingly tells the whole people that each person should contribute according to his means and make the tabernacle. That contribution was not to be made under any compulsion, but by spontaneous willingness. For God says to Moses that each person should offer, according to what seems good to his heart, those things necessary for constructing the tabernacle (Exod. XXV, 2).

At the outset I mentioned the Hebrews’ departure from Egypt, the crossing of the sea, and the destruction of the Egyptians; and because these matters are closed to some people, I judged it useful—indeed necessary—to unlock them. Although all these things truly happened, precious jewels of mysteries nevertheless lie hidden within them.

By Egypt, in which Pharaoh ruled like a lord, the present age is signified, whose prince is Satan [Col. 0223C]. The Hebrew, by whom the faithful people are represented, wisely avoids the wretched domination of this prince by departing—that is, by making progress—under the leadership of Moses. He renounces Egypt, that is, the present age, and embraces Christ, his lawgiver, in love by adhering to his commandments. He no longer listens to the voice of alien and evil spirits, but to Christ’s own voice, which says: “Whoever serves me must follow me” (John XII, 26).

The Red Sea, which was a protection to the Hebrews and brought destruction upon the Egyptians, is understood as the water of baptism or as penitence expressed through tears. It is called red because in baptism it is consecrated by Christ’s blood, and because in tearful penitence one sometimes reaches the blood of the eyes, and sometimes even [Col. 0223D] the mortification of the flesh.

In this sea, therefore, our Egyptian adversaries are drowned, because through baptism and through penitential tears our sins and crimes—which separate us from God—are put to death.

The tabernacle, from which I began chiefly to speak, we read to have been covered externally with skins and goats’ hair, but adorned internally with gold and silver, bronze and precious stones, and many other things, which it is not necessary now to discuss individually. In the tabernacle there was also a lampstand and an ark made of setim wood; and inside the ark, as we read, were contained the law, manna, and Aaron’s rod (Hebr. IX, 4).

The tabernacle signifies the Church, that is, the congregation of the righteous. The skins and goats’ hair with which it was covered externally [Col. 0224A] indicate the mortification of vices. Gold signifies faith; silver, confession. Bronze expresses fortitude; precious stones signify the precious words of eternal life. In the lampstand, the manifest activity of good intention is understood. The ark signifies memory; the setim wood, purity; and the law, God’s commandments. We call the manna the sweetness of devotion, but the rod the severity of discipline.

In his law the benign God commands us, for our benefit and not from any need of his own, to make a tabernacle for him—that is, a dwelling place of sanctification. Scripture indicates where this dwelling is to be made or constructed when it says: “Prepare your hearts for the Lord” (1 Sam. VII, 3). We prepare our hearts for the Lord when we present them to him as clean receptacles in which he can worthily dwell [Col. 0224B].

Nor does he wish these receptacles to be presented to him with any difficulty, but with complete devotional joy. The all-powerful Lord is most discerning. Like an unreasonable exactor, he does not demand from us what we do not have, nor does his command compel us to offer him what ought to be contrary to our heart.

We properly cover the tabernacle externally with skins and goats’ hair when we mortify our exterior and lower self—that is, our flesh—with its vices and desires, so that our heart, which is called God’s tabernacle, may not be corrupted by their enticements.

We adorn the tabernacle with gold if pure and complete faith is in our heart. Pure and complete faith is this: that we believe, without any hesitation but with complete love, that the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit are one God and Lord [Col. 0224C]. For although the Trinity exists in persons, there is one nature and one substance of the Godhead. And although the Father is one, the Son another, and the Holy Spirit another, the Father is not one thing, the Son another, and the Holy Spirit another; rather, the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit are, as we have said, three persons, and these three persons are one God, of one and only one nature, substance, and essence.

And lest, in the Trinity that created all creatures, for whom nothing is impossible, we imagine anything contrary to this faith, we also find in human creatures a likeness of what has been said. Among created things there are certain things that, although they are three and each [Col. 0224D] has its own individual person within itself, nevertheless possess one and the same nature and one and the same substance.

Let us come, then, to a spring and consider the stream of the spring; let us also see the water proceeding from both, which is called a pool. Behold: we find three persons—the spring, the stream, and the pool. Although there are three persons, there is nevertheless one water, and the water has one and the same nature and substance.

We offer silver for the beauty of the tabernacle when, through true and holy confession, we cleanse our souls from every contagion of sin and crime. But we must know where, to whom, and when that confession should be made.

Where? Not among heretics, as often happens, but in the catholic Church every Christian must confess [Col. 0225A].

To whom? Especially to his own pastor, provided that he is such a man as knows how to heal his own wounds and those of others by genuine charity, not to expose and publicize them through pride.

When? While bodily health remains, while each person still exercises his own power. People should not wait until the last day of their life in order to confess, because those who postpone confession until the end scarcely, or never, attain salvation. Of such people it is said in the psalm: “When God slew them, then they sought him” (Ps. LXXVII, 34).

We join bronze to the gold and silver in the tabernacle if we persevere, strong in faith and confession of Christ, until the end of this life. Faith and confession are much more precious when the strength of works accompanies them against every adversity.

In the structure [Col. 0225B] of the tabernacle we place and arrange precious stones when we propose and explain to one another the words of holy exhortation. In explaining, one person ought to show another where he was, where he is, where he is not, and where he will be.

Where he was: in paradise, in the place of blessedness, where purity and holiness abounded and where, unless the first man had sinned, he would have enjoyed perpetual immortality.

Where he is: in this world, under the yoke of harsh existence, where each day he lies in the pit of misery and in the mud of filth.

Where he is not: in that devotion of mind with which the blessed apostles, martyrs, confessors, and holy virgins loved our most kind God and Lord Jesus, and for love of him utterly despised the world [Col. 0225C] with all its blossom.

Where he will be: on that exceedingly dreadful day of judgment, when no one will dare to protect or defend another with carefully arranged words for speaking; when iniquity cannot be disguised by an arrangement of words; when no one will be permitted to excuse himself or conceal anything; when an accuser and a witness will proceed from conscience itself. There, to be accused once will mean nothing other than to be condemned eternally.

We fashion the lampstand for the honor of the tabernacle when, through manifest works of good intention, we show others examples of goodness.

We also place the ark in the tabernacle when we apply our memory to the things that belong to God. For this reason the ark is said to have been made from setim wood, which is incorruptible: our memory must not be a place of corruption [Col. 0225D] or any disgrace, but a treasury of complete purity and a seal of chastity.

The ark is also said to contain the law within itself because our mind and memory must constantly observe the divine commandments.

Manna and the rod are likewise contained in the ark. Our memory must contain devotion, by which the humble and gentle are fittingly entreated so that they may advance toward what is better, and also the severity of discipline, by which the proud and harsh must be corrected and rebuked.

Our correction or rebuke must not be made with anger and indignation, but with tranquillity. Although discipline may rage outwardly, the heart must always be full of charity.

It must nevertheless be understood that we may sometimes become angry and indignant with those who offend. But it must not again be consigned [Col. 0226A] to oblivion that our anger or indignation must not be the execution of vengeance, but rather the work of absolution. We ought to become angry and indignant for this purpose: to provoke those who offend to satisfaction, not to despair. For, as the Apostle says, we have not been sent for destruction but for edification (2 Cor. X, 8).

Therefore, brothers, let us do everything we do with just compassion and compassionate severity together, so that, while retaining all the other things said about the tabernacle, we may deserve to become a holy and immaculate tabernacle, by the grace of our Lord Jesus Christ, who, with the Father and the Holy Spirit, lives and reigns as God through ages of ages. Amen.

## VIII. WHAT BAPTISM, CONFIRMATION, THE ANOINTING OF THE SICK, AND THE RECEPTION OF CHRIST’S BODY AND BLOOD ACCOMPLISH IN THE CHRISTIAN SOUL

[Col. 0226B]

In baptism, forgiveness of sins is given through the Holy Spirit. In confirmation, the Holy Spirit is invited to come and inhabit, strengthen, and defend the very house that he has sanctified.

The apostles themselves also received the Holy Spirit after baptism, whom they had already received in baptism for the remission of sins. They received the Spirit again on the day of Pentecost, for the perfection of every virtue and of knowledge. Therefore this final confirmation is commanded to be administered by bishops, in imitation of complete perfection.

It is commanded to be performed on the forehead because it belongs to the perfect to bear the name of Christ always, not in secret but openly [Col. 0226C]. Before the apostles were anointed with this anointing and confirmed by the Holy Spirit, they were not yet perfect: they were still afraid and did not yet bear Christ’s name on their foreheads.

In the anointing of the sick, forgiveness of sins is again given through the Holy Spirit, so that the mercy of Christ may not be absent from Christians either in life or in death.

In the reception of the Lord’s body and blood, the Christian soul is healed from the wound of vices, restored to the state of eternal salvation, and made one body with Christ.

## IX. WHAT THE REPETITION OF A SACRAMENT IS

A sacrament is repeated when the same thing is given again [Col. 0226D], as though what was previously given were believed capable of being given afterward. For example, if someone who had been baptized were again immersed in baptismal waters with the intention of being released from original and other sins.

Otherwise a person is not rebaptized, even if he is submerged many times in baptismal waters. But when something is given for one purpose and then for another, the sacrament is not repeated; it is bestowed for an increase of virtue.

Although a person is anointed with chrism first on the crown of the head and afterward on the forehead, the sacrament of chrism is not thereby repeated, because, as we said above, it is done for one purpose and then for another. Baptism likewise is not repeated even if, after baptism, we are sprinkled many times with baptismal water.

The anointing of the sick is a great sacrament, and therefore it must in no way be repeated. For just as the Christian religion is believed to have received the other sacraments [Col. 0227A] through the apostles, so there is no doubt that it received this one also from apostolic tradition.

Every sacrament is prohibited from being repeated by the Holy Spirit through holy teachers, in whom he speaks, specifically so that the holy medicine might not become cheap and less effective; for it is all the more health-giving the less contemptible it is found to be.

## X. ON THE PROMISES THAT ABBOTS MAKE TO BISHOPS FOR THEIR CONSECRATION, UNDER THE NAME OF PROFESSION

Our God and Lord Jesus Christ warns and says in the Gospel: “You have received freely; give freely” (Matt. XVI, 8); and what he teaches in words he fulfilled in deed. For he created us freely and redeemed us by his mercy [Col. 0227B].

By his words, therefore, he warns us, and by his deeds he teaches that his gifts—namely, the sacraments of the holy Church—must both be received freely and given freely. For although the gifts of the Holy Spirit can be possessed, they cannot be purchased; and anyone who believes or proclaims by deed that what God made incomparable can be purchased by a human being is proved, by reason and authority, to be a heretic.

Simon Magus therefore became a heretic because he judged that he could possess God’s gift with money. No sacrament of the Church, which is a gift of the Holy Spirit—through which, in which, and by whom the divine mysteries are rightly celebrated, forgiveness of sins is given, and without whom no offering is sanctified—may be sold or bought.

Consecrations or blessings of churches and persons [Col. 0227C] must therefore be performed entirely free of charge, and nothing whatever should be demanded by any device for such an act, lest, while a false blessedness is sought, true misery be found.

There are certain bishops who demand from abbots, under the name of profession, something in exchange for their blessings; this is profoundly contrary to Christian profession. For since one profession is made in praise of God and another for the laying aside of sins, this profession does not praise God but diminishes him; it does not lay aside sins but adds to them.

Nor should it properly be called a profession of the holy faith, but an accursed promise, which attempts to brandish the keys of the Church and violate her one and singular door. This practice was discovered neither through truth nor authority, but through custom and human greed [Col. 0227D]. It attacks the holy Church in three forms of simony, since there simony is committed by the tongue, simony by the hand, and simony by service.

It is by the tongue when that promise is publicly recited; it is by the hand when the written document containing it is placed upon the altar; it is by service when the wickedly promised service of submission is observed.

The person who acts in this way may perhaps say: “I am not seeking money for the blessing.” Indeed, he demands something much greater, because he demands the person of a human being. Just as the soul is more than the body, so body and soul together—that is, the whole person—is much more than his money.

Divine law and manifest reason prove that a blessing is by no means given freely when it is preceded by that proscription of the abbot, by which he obtains what he desires [Col. 0228A]. For he would not make it if he did not suffer rejection.

Even what is good becomes harmful when it is promised wrongly or received improperly. The money that Simon Magus offered to Peter was indeed good, but because he offered it wrongly, he is proclaimed to have been condemned by Peter.

Therefore that blessing is neither evangelical nor canonical, but a “shipboard” (navicularia) blessing, as it is called; it is preceded or followed by a profession falsely so called. There, the Church’s first sacrament is sold and bought at the same time. For Christ himself first performed this sacrament: the consecration of the apostles.

Furthermore, it must be known and never forgotten that whoever buys a church imitates the Jews’ faithlessness, while whoever sells it imitates the traitor Judas. The Jews are known to have bought [Col. 0228B] Christ, who is the head of the Church, and there is no doubt that Judas sold him.

But whoever demands a gift for a divine mystery follows Gehazi, the disciple of Elisha, and inherits the leprosy of Naaman the Syrian.

Let bishops and abbots therefore beware—bishops and abbots who are called Christ’s vicars because they are believed to act in Christ’s place—lest, against the authority of Christ, who gives freely, and against the word of him who warns and commands that gifts be given freely, they follow greed or custom, by which the faith, liberty, and chastity of the Church are corrupted together.

A bishop certainly commits no small offense if he does not give freely; and an abbot likewise sins if he does not receive freely, because equal punishment binds together the one who acts and the one who complies; and the deed makes those whom it stains equal (Lucan, book V, 290).

## XI. ON THOSE WHO SHOUT DISORDERLY IN THE CHAPTER, AND ON THOSE WHO RESPOND DISORDERLY THERE

[Col. 0228C]

It often happens among monks that, through those who raise complaints against others in chapter and through those against whom the complaints are raised, disturbances of mind, bitter words, and disputes arise. This happens chiefly because those who are accused do not know how to respond, and those who accuse do not know how to accuse.

For although the accusers ought to make the fault known solely out of hatred of sin and love of their brother, they do not do so; instead, they threaten and rebuke. Those who are rebuked, although as Christians and monks they ought to imitate Christ’s patience—[Col. 0228D] Christ who did not open his mouth before the one who sheared him, and who is read not to have uttered insulting words against his impious and lying accusers during his passion, but to have answered patiently even the judge who judged him unjustly—are ashamed to do what Christ did. They forget Christ, his example, and the Christian name, as well as their own monastic profession, which is a sign of the greatest humility. Instead, they prepare proud and contentious words against those who speak about them, adding worse things to their former evils and calling upon accomplices like themselves as avengers of insults.

Therefore, with God as our authority, we wish to establish how and to whom our sons and brothers, when accused in chapter, should respond, and how those who accuse should make their accusations [Col. 0229A].

We therefore ordain and, in the name of holy obedience, command that each person make his brother’s fault known in chapter in such a way that he does not presume to threaten him or rebuke him.

The person who has been accused must not contend against his accuser with any words, but must answer humbly and truthfully to the abbot alone, or to his prior, concerning the matter of which he is accused.

Anyone who is accused may either humbly acknowledge his fault or, if he is in no way guilty, excuse himself—not boldly but patiently.

If anyone knowingly violates this ordinance, which has been made by God rather than by us for the peace and tranquility of the souls and bodies of our brothers, then, in addition to the present blows of the rods, he shall be given only bread and water for seven consecutive days, without indulgence.

## XII. THE THREE THINGS THAT MUST BE PRESENT IN PASTORS

[Col. 0229B]

Three things in particular must be present in pastors of the Church: namely, justice, discernment, and foresight.

Every steward of the Church ought therefore to be just in judgment, discerning in command, and provident in counsel. Through these three things especially, a pastor can benefit both the salvation of souls and the needs of bodies. But if one of them is lacking, the other two are either less useful or entirely useless.

For if a pastor judges justly but commands without discernment, that indiscreet command will itself destroy the just judgment. If he commands discerningly but judges unjustly, the unjust and iniquitous decision will corrupt the discerning command.

But if he both judges justly and commands discerningly, yet is in no way provident in counsel for souls, the rashness of unwise counsel will dissolve both the just judgment and the discerning command [Col. 0229C].

Therefore every pastor of the Church ought to possess truth in judgment, love in command, and diligence in counsel.

## XIII. GOD’S INVECTIVE AGAINST THE SINNER, AND THE SINNER’S CONFESSION AS HE PRAYS FOR MERCY

Wretched man, I made you from clay and raised you to my own image and likeness. +

It is so, Good One. I acknowledge that by your grace alone I was made immortal and eternal from sufficiently fragile material—if I had not sinned. +

Ungrateful for such great grace, you became a despiser [Col. 0229D] of obedience. +

It is as you assert, Holy One: I gave place to the author of my misery. +

For your sake, I—God and Lord—became flesh: for you, a slave of sin; and I became a perfect human being composed of a rational soul and flesh. +

What you confess, merciful Creator, I too confess; and this was done so that I, a sinner, would not perish. +

In addition to all this, I was born of a woman, captured, bound, scourged, subjected to many and various insults, and even killed, so that I might make you, who were a slave of the devil, a son of God. +

I truly believe, Kind One, what you say, but in confusion over my great and prolonged iniquity I can scarcely endure it. +

Many and many are my good deeds toward you; many and many are your evil deeds against me. +

In no way, Most High, can I deny that your words are true, because, just as you stated in a true declaration [Col. 0230A], many are your good deeds toward me, and many are my evil deeds against you. And what is the more grievous fault, I have never at any time made a pure confession that I am guilty, nor have I properly acknowledged my guilt. +

Without any preceding or subsequent merits of yours, I permitted you to become the guardian and pastor of my Church. +

I embrace these things, Compassionate and Merciful One, as true; but I confess both to your mercy and to your compassion that I was formerly and afterward remained a wretched sinner. I ought greatly to fear that from a shepherd I may have made myself a wolf, and from a guardian, a robber.

I do not conceal my misery, but seek your mercy, O God of almighty power and immeasurable grace. Therefore, by your grace through which I was made, and by your merciful compassion through which I was redeemed, have mercy on me, miserable and sinful as I am [Col. 0230B], and make me share in the blessedness of that thief to whom, as he hung upon the cross, you said: “Today you will be with me in paradise” (Luke XXIII, 43).

## XIV. ANOTHER INVECTIVE AGAINST THE SINNER, AND THE CONSOLATION OF THE PENITENT SINNER

Sinner, acknowledge your fault and do penance. With what presumption have you acted against your Creator and Redeemer? How lukewarmly and negligently have you lived for so long in the holy and sacred order!

Useless servant, recall God’s benefits and love him. Weigh your sins insofar as they can be weighed, and tremble.

Wretched minister of the holy Church, consider within yourself what the good Lord has done for you and what you have done: he has bestowed many good things upon you, and you have committed many evils. He himself did not teach you this repayment, nor ought you to have been taught it in such a way by another [Col. 0230C].

Debtor to God and deceiver of yourself, remember the promises that you so often made to the supreme Lord and did not keep well.

He waited for you for a long time with great patience, and you despised him; he called you, and calls you, and you were unwilling to return to him; he follows you as you flee, but does not pursue you because of your sins, and, so that you may return to him, he entreats you with paternal affection, saying: “I do not desire the death of the sinner, but only that he repent and obtain life” (Ezek. XXXIII, 11).

Repeater of sins, remember the final judgment, and how great will be the glory of the saints and the misery of the impious there, where no evil soul will find any good, nor any good soul any evil.

Vessel utterly shattered by sins, groan while you may, and while you are granted a respite [Col. 0230D], weep tearfully for everything that, corrupted by Satan, you have perpetrated against the kind God and Lord. Confessing your great misery, humbly seek his great mercy.

Sinful man, do not despair of your imperfection more than, by repenting, you dare to hope in the mercy of him who redeemed you with immeasurable love. Full of mercy, he seeks you in your misery and does not cast you away; almighty medicine does not reject you in your weakness.

The merciful one desires mercifully to assist the miserable, lest it justly befall the just one to condemn the miserable.

That good shepherd is read not to have cast away the weary and wounded sheep, but to have carried it; and not merely to have carried it, but to have preferred to die rather than that it should die.

These things reveal God’s mercy and compassion [Col. 0231A] and remove from the sinner the occasion for despair. For the Lord desires the sinner’s life, not death; he desires sin to perish, not the human being.

Therefore every sinner may hope for pardon from the Lord’s great compassion if he recognizes himself as a sinner and, having compassion on his neighbors, wishes to repent of his sin.

Behold, merciful Jesus, I am the one whom, not through my merits but by your grace alone, you either willed or permitted to become some kind of pastor of your Church; and although unworthy, you called me to the office of pastor. Do not allow me to perish. Instead, among the other gifts of your grace, grant that, truly acknowledging myself to be a sinner, I may make worthy satisfaction to you for my sins before I am taken from this present life.

And whenever I hear the sin of any of my brothers [Col. 0231B], let me not rebuke him proudly, but have compassion; and although I hate the sin, let me nevertheless love the sinner.

May I always have no small compassion for the sinner and measured correction toward sin. Far be it from me, out of hatred for guilt, to destroy the rights of nature! Human nature seeks indulgence for itself, not to be afflicted beyond measure; and because it quickly slips by itself, it must be raised up, not trampled down.

May God cause what belongs to the devil in a human being to perish, and preserve what is his own, lest it perish. Guilt is from the devil; the creature is from God.

Therefore may divine moderation temper his justice in me also, lest, while I seem to pursue guilt as though from love of justice, it should happen that the creature perishes. And if it should happen that I bind someone with the bonds of discipline, let me not oppress him by my own authority, but make him worthy of absolution [Col. 0231C].

May no one under my authority perish through excessive sorrow; rather, may all be able to be freed through indulgence.

May you deign to grant this, merciful and good Jesus, who reign and rule with the Father and the Holy Spirit through ages that shall endure without end. Amen.

## XV. THE LAMENT OF A CERTAIN SINNER ACCUSING AND JUDGING HIMSELF

[The supplied source ends here, with this heading incomplete.]

My wretched life does not terrify me as much as it ought to. For my soul, cast away from its faithful friend because of its filthy thoughts and subjected to a cruel enemy, abandoned the loving Shepherd and became prey to the wolf; and she who had previously been Christ’s bride reduced herself to slavery under Antichrist. Thus the adulteress bore sorrow and shame for God, but joy and victory for the devil.

O my soul, greatly sinful and greatly wretched! Why did you conceive such evil thoughts, by which you prudently and knowingly kindled the fire of lust, uncleanness, and greed, by which you also burned continually and beyond measure, and delivered yourself to be consumed forever in the fires of Gehenna? Had you not read—and in reading, heard; indeed, had you not read and understood—the Apostle saying: “Every fornicator, or unclean person, or covetous person has no inheritance in the kingdom of Christ and of God” (Ephesians 5:5)?

You certainly had material from which, if you had wished, you could have thought profitably: namely, God’s benefits and what you had done against him. You ought to have remembered and considered who it was who made you, what he did for you, what you did, and what sort of person you made yourself, so that either love of your Creator or fear of hell might make you cease from sin, and so that you might mourn in repentance what you had wickedly done, in order that, if you were not worthy of deserved rest, you might at least be free from punishment.

God and Lord himself is benevolent: by grace alone he made you when you did not exist—holy, that is, and immortal, if afterward you had not sinned by your own will. You died there, namely, where you withdrew from him by sinning. Yet, so that he might bind you to himself with bonds of greater love, although you had withdrawn from him and had been captured by the devil, he redeemed you—not by offering some ordinary price for your redemption, but by giving his own Son: like you in nature and in the truth of flesh and soul, yet utterly unlike you in the power and omnipotence of his deity.

And because the Son of God recognized that you had corrupted both yourself and the flesh associated with you, so that he might redeem both, he assumed both. Behold, for your sake God became man. For the maidservant, the Lord became a servant. For your sake the Creator became a creature, and the Redeemer himself became the price of your redemption.

O my unhappy soul, unworthy of rest and worthy of destruction, acknowledge, believe, and devoutly confess what God endured for you, wretched—indeed most wretched—as he took flesh! Conceived in the Virgin Mother, with the Holy Spirit accompanying and cooperating, and with that same Spirit guiding him, he came forth from the virginal womb, beautiful beyond the sons of men. A new man he entered the world, and there, for your sake, he suffered many injuries for a short time.

O wicked and cruel soul, when you were thinking proudly and filthily, where was the memory of the Lord’s passion and cross? Where was the crown of thorns fixed into the head of your Creator? Where was his beloved face, drenched with blood flowing from his wounded head? Where were the bonds with which the gentle and humble Savior was bound with such cruelty for your sake? Where were the blows of the palms? Where the strokes of rods, the blows of fists, and the spittle of the wicked Jews, which your meek Redeemer endured for you? Where was the cross imposed on him for his disgrace, on which he himself was crucified? Where were the places of the nails? Where the cup of gall? Where the side pierced by the lance?

You believe all these things and deny them; you confess them and disavow them. You believe with your heart and confess with your mouth, but by your conduct you deny and disavow them. Thus you have faith, but a dead faith. For faith without the love of God is dead. If you believe but do not love, you imitate the devil. The devil believes and confesses the Lord; but because he does not love him, he has no remedy—not even for a single moment—and his punishment has no end.

O shameless, filthy, wicked soul! Truly you have acted in this way. You did believe, and perhaps still believe, but you did not love God at all. If you had loved him, you would certainly have hated the devil; and, carefully observing the knowledge of truth you had received, you would have neither nullified your first faith nor your second.

For in baptism you had renounced the devil; in your monastic profession, both the devil and the world. But now neither your first profession nor your second will be pleasing to God, because you have committed both perjury and sacrilege: perjury, because you did not fulfill what you had sworn to God; sacrilege, because you took away from him to whom you had devoted yourself.

You exposed not only yourself but also the flesh that was your companion to the will and desire of the most shameful and foul corrupter, so that you made all the members of your body vessels of vice.

O proud and puffed-up soul, whose good works did you not despise? But your own works, which scarcely possessed any goodness, or almost none at all, you continually praised while admiring them. Though thousands upon thousands of times you had been corrupted either by thought alone or by thought together with action, you painted yourself as though with the colors of chastity; and though you were utterly unclean, you rejoiced to be called modest. And if at any time, confessing yourself guilty, you accused yourself, you desired to please the person hearing you rather than God, the one who made you.

Daughter of the devil, violator of the temple of the Holy Spirit, what shall I say of you—or rather, what can I say worthily against you—who have almost wholly, or entirely, taken yourself away from God and given yourself to the devil? Remember, captive, at what price you were redeemed; whose bride you were; how beautiful and holy you would always have remained with him, if you had been willing to keep faith with him.

Remember also from where and to where you fell. By God’s calling and election you had ascended even to heaven, and you fell into hell. O what a wretched lot you chose, following your most cruel condemner and abandoning the author of all goodness!

Your God, your Lord, your Creator and Redeemer, could give you nothing greater than himself, nor anything better. First, when he made you, he gave you himself. Later, when you had been lost through sin, he offered himself as the price of your redemption. You, certainly, sinned, and he himself made satisfaction for your sin.

O deeply ungrateful soul! You denied the benevolent Redeemer who died for you so that you would not perish, and you chose as your Lord the terrible enemy who killed him through the tongues of the Jews and the hands of the soldiers. In the holy font you had once extinguished him, and by the holiness of the order you had undertaken you had crushed him once extinguished; but by sinning you revived him for your perpetual punishment.

As long as you were with the good God and loving Lord, you were strong against the devil, and the devil was weak against you: you were sound, he infirm; you were mistress, he servant. But after you withdrew from him who created you by his goodness and redeemed you by the love of immeasurable charity, the spirit of fornication raised its head against you and immersed itself wholly within your entrails. There the worst fornicator, staining you with exceedingly foul pollution and entering you repeatedly with a multitude of demons, left behind his fetid tracks within you.

Thus, impregnated with the poison of lust, you conceived pain and gave birth to iniquity. Such couples produce a monstrous, horrible, shameful, unclean offspring.

Woe to you, wretched soul, who have become the maidservant of your most contemptible servant and the concubine of the worst fornicator! O you who have become utterly vile, where do you hope to go? What do you expect? To lie in filth is condemnable; to rise from filth is impossible for you.

Tell me, if you know: from whom can you obtain counsel, through whom assistance, to whom refuge? You cannot approach the saints, because you are bound; nor can you invoke them, because you are mute. And even if they should deign to speak to you, you would not hear them, because you are deaf.

What will you do? What remedy will you find? Many and very many are your sins and crimes. Yet God’s mercy is greater than all of them. God is omnipotent and compassionate; his omnipotence and mercy, which are boundless, do not allow anyone who repents to despair.

Acknowledge, therefore, your weakness. Confess that you have been condemned by your own iniquity; and if you cannot come on your own feet to the pool of saving water into which the Lord’s angel descended, approach at least with the steps of good will. If you cannot cry out or speak, you can still breathe and sigh.

Breathe at last, then, and sigh from the depths of your heart. Perhaps Christ will find you sighing—he who found a man who had been ill for thirty-eight years—and, taking pity on your weakness as he is accustomed to do in his compassion and goodness, will say to you: “Do you want to become well?” (John 5:6).

If you humbly confess your misery and helplessness, and firmly acknowledge and believe his omnipotence, then what he did for that man he will do for you; and what he did not refuse to Mary Magdalene when she repented and confessed her sins with tears, he will not refuse you. He who cleansed the humble leper will cleanse you of every leprosy of your sins and crimes. He will raise you, like a four-day-dead man already beginning to stink, from the sepulcher of misery and from the mire of filth; and Jesus Christ our Lord will command you to be released.

He is God of boundless compassion and omnipotence, and he lives and reigns with the Father and the Holy Spirit, forever and ever. Amen.

## XVI. PRAYER TO JESUS

[Col. 0234C]

Good and compassionate Jesus, Son of the living God and of David, I adore you, I praise you, I glorify you. To you, almighty God, my most compassionate Creator, supreme and true Priest, and to your most blessed mother Mary, ever-virgin, and to all your saints, I confess that I am exceedingly wretched and sinful, and such as you know me to be.

Just as I neither can nor could be justified by my merits, so I profess that by your great mercy I can be saved. Trusting in the greatness of that mercy, I have hoped in you. I could indeed despair, because I have lived otherwise than I ought; but your great compassion, which brought you down from heaven to earth so that I would not perish, does not allow me to despair.

Save, I beg you, gracious Jesus, your servant, because I have hoped in you. And all you who hope in him, pray for me, so that, even if I am not presently worthy of rest, I may at least, through his mercy, be found free from eternal punishment.

## XVII. PRAYER TO THE MOTHER OF THE LORD

O glorious Mary,

Noble offspring of Jesse,

Through whom death was condemned

And life restored;

Ever-precious Virgin,

More beautiful than all others;

Star of the sea, gate of heaven,

From whom light arose for the world;

Sacred temple of the Savior,

Refuge of the sinner,

Salvation of the world, death of sin,

Made the mother of the Son Most High.

You who have as your Son the King

Who gave the divine law:

You, mother, you, bride of God,

Have mercy on me, the guilty one.

From the valley of tears,

Burdened by the weight of sins,

I cry to you, loving Virgin:

Be my guide and my way.

Whoever you, blessed woman, rule,

Observes the commands of the law,

Loves God, believes in God,

And never departs from him.

Rule me, I beg you, wretched as I am,

Most holy among women,

So that, mindful of the divine law,

I may be ready to do the will of the great King.

May he, through his love,

Grant me chastity;

And, cleansed of every stain,

May I love him with a pure heart.

He whose being is eternal

Knows what I need;

He knows my weakness,

And may he heal it through his mercy.

This is my weakness:

Sin and iniquity;

The scar of my wound,

The hardening of my crime.

I languish from the sickness of sin;

I have no one to cure me.

Only the medicine of God

Can have mercy on me.

Sinning in heart, sinning in mouth,

I withdrew from the Creator;

But come to the aid of me, the guilty one,

His mother, the holy Virgin.

Make him whom you bore as your Son

Propitious toward me;

Pray for me to him,

And come to my aid without delay.

May he who assumed flesh from you

Hear your prayer;

He will deny you nothing,

Whom your breast nourished.

And to him whom, in his cradle,

You gave dear kisses,

Whatever you ask of him,

You will be able to obtain.

May God, the child born from you,

The Son given to us,

Cleanse me by his mercy

From every iniquity. Amen.

## XVIII. HYMN ON SAINT MARY MAGDALENE

### At Vespers

Mary, model of repentance,

Hope of pardon for the fallen,

Obtain that the author of goodness

May raise us up,

Already buried in sins.

Pray for our sins,

Justified sinner,

With that devotion of mind

With which you entreated

The eternal, living, true Lord.

Mary, the wave of Christ’s compassion

Watered you.

May he who washed and cleansed you

Wash us from our sins

By the grace of charity.

This weak woman came

To the physician, seeking a remedy;

She prostrates herself and does not speak,

But confesses through her tears:

Thus she conducts her case.

The physician, full of mercy,

Provides remedies.

The almighty medicine

Rejects no wounds,

But seeks the innermost heart.

She offers repentance;

He grants forgiveness.

Sevenfold clemency

Drives away seven demons

From the woman who has been converted.

May the devotion of the penitent,

The remission of sins,

Be granted to us by the Most High God,

Who is our redemption—

Praise, honor, and glory. Amen.

### At Matins

A certain woman named Mary,

Known by the surname Magdalene,

Seductively ensnared by demons,

Was exceedingly sinful.

She grew swollen with pride in her appearance

And shamefully succumbed;

Through the vice of a proud mind

Came the corruption of the flesh.

The crime of the mind is indeed more serious,

But that of the flesh more shameful;

She blushed more deeply

At what was more shameful,

And feared what was more serious.

The maidservant seeks the Lord;

The sick woman desires the physician.

She offered service;

He bestowed a remedy—

Miraculous power

And the grace of compassion—

By which, in this sinful woman,

He healed wound with wound.

Glory be to the highest Father,

Praise to his Only-Begotten,

Honor to the Holy Spirit,

To the Trinity, one God. Amen.

### At Lauds

The merciful God calls

Wretched women and wretched men—

Everyone—to repentance,

And promises pardon.

The one who rejects repentance

Alone is deprived of pardon.

Christ, author of mercy,

Have mercy on us.

Your boundless goodness

Gave Mary tears;

Through the river of tears

She restrained the flood of crimes.

She who had been subjected to demons

And devoted to vices

First obtained from you

Whatever she offered to you:

From you came contrition of heart,

The wiping with her hair,

The kissing of your feet,

And the pouring out of ointment.

Grant, compassionate Lord,

That we may do for our sins

All that she did

Through your total compassion,

Lest we perish.

To God the Father and the Son,

And to the Spirit, the Comforter,

Be honor, power, and glory

Throughout everlasting ages. Amen.

[Col. 0237]

## SERMONS OF GOFFRID, ABBOT OF VENDÔME, CARDINAL OF ST PRISCA

## SERMON I. ON THE NATIVITY OF THE LORD I

[Col. 0237B]

Today, dearly beloved, Mary, the venerable and universal queen of angels and human beings, a virgin who conceived him through the word of the angel, brought forth to the world, with her womb closed, the Savior who had been born. O nativity worthy of wonder, with its joy and faith!

Behold: a woman conceives without intercourse, becomes pregnant without burden, gives birth without pain. A holy virgin before childbirth, a holier virgin in childbirth, a most holy virgin after childbirth—she alone merited to receive at once the joy of motherhood and the glory of virginity. From her chaste womb God, having become man, came to us, not disdaining, in the bosom of the Virgin Mother, to seek with filial affection the blessed breasts by which he was lovingly nourished.

And let us, brothers, celebrating with devotion the nativity of God and man, rejoice, because this nativity of God and our Lord restored to human beings the remedy of life they had lost and brought new joy to heaven. The restoration of the human race was the death of sin, the confusion of the devil, and the despoiling of hell.

This ineffable nativity of God, beloved by angels and necessary for human beings, made man—first the devil’s servant through the sin of disobedience—free. It led him back to paradise, from which he had fallen, granting him no less glory than he had possessed before he sinned. The guilt of disobedience had power to cast man down, but the grace of the Lord’s nativity proved more powerful to raise him up.

The poisonous cunning of the ancient serpent had power to infect him, but the almighty medicine of the Savior who was born healed the infected man. The devil, enemy of God and man, proved to be the inventor of misery, but God was the maker of mercy. The devil made man miserable by his deceit; God, taking pity on the miserable man so that he would not remain in misery, showed mercy. He who had earlier justly condemned the sinning angel mercifully regarded the man whom the angel had seduced.

The angel sinned, and God condemned him eternally; man sinned, and God had such compassion for him that he deigned not only to become incarnate and be born for him, but also to die.

O wondrous and indescribable goodness of the Lord toward man! O severity exceedingly strict, yet entirely just, toward the angel of God! Thus the just and compassionate Lord acted with severity toward the angel and with the love of compassion toward man.

Both had fallen through sinning, but God, by the judgment of justice, assigned the angel to eternal punishment, while by the consideration of mercy he recalled man to glory. For by God’s provident and rational dispensation it came about that the one whose rank had been higher should suffer the more grievous fall; and because he had no other persuader or deceiver than himself, and bore no human flesh from which he might perhaps—though unjustly—derive an occasion for sin, but was the sole author of his own destruction through the iniquity of pride and of another’s guilt, since pride began in him, his punishment would have no end. Nor was it thereafter permitted him, for any reason, to hope for pardon, since he was and remains the inventor and author of such great wickedness.

Man, however, was inexcusable, because he sinned through disobedience and, when questioned, delayed confessing his fault; he deserved humiliation and ruin. He had previously known only blessedness in paradise, but when he saw that through sin he had been handed over to the devil and experienced various miseries in the world, compelled by excessive unhappiness he began to mourn the happiness he had lost, turning to tears.

The guilty man groaned under the burden of guilt, nor could he be washed from sin by his tears, because the magnitude of his sin surpassed the tears of that miserable man. But God, wishing to save the guilty man and condemn his guilt, descended, through the message of an angel and the coming of the Holy Spirit, into the Virgin’s womb; and there he assumed the flesh in which he would suffer for man.

O astonishing assumption, to be embraced with the arms of faith and love, through which the creature is united to the Creator, created nature to its Maker, and God becomes man for man, merciful for the miserable, the just one is condemned for the sinner, and the compassionate one for the impious!

O immeasurable compassion of divine goodness, through which the Son of God was born and appeared to the world! Although he was Lord of all, so that he might redeem his servant from death, the immortal assumed death. But because death could not rule blessed life, the Lord rose on the third day.

By his death our Savior raised up man who was dead in sin; rising from the dead, he not only restored paradise to him but also bestowed heaven.

The incarnation, therefore, of our Redeemer, his nativity, death, and resurrection were the work of our salvation and the destruction of the devil’s art. Moreover, by his incarnation the gracious Jesus set before us an example of humility. Born and appearing to the world and speaking with human beings, he instructed us by the teaching of his wisdom; by his death he taught us patience; by his resurrection he invited us to glory.

Therefore, dearly beloved brothers, let us love the things that are above, not those that are on earth; and let us follow our Redeemer by holy works toward the joys of eternal happiness, to which he himself went before us in our flesh and calls us while seated at the right hand of the Father.

Let us also believe with our whole heart that he intercedes for us with the Father, because unless we are protected by his most holy intercession and power, we cannot resist the devil, who, though cast down, has changed his strength but not lost it. Truly the Lord prays for us in the flesh that he assumed for us.

Nor is it surprising that, having wished to become man so that man would not perish, the compassionate Lord presents to his Father prayers of propitiation for man’s salvation. The gracious Lord, taken up into heaven, does not disdain to help on earth the man whom he wishes to cleanse from sin and to have reign with him in heaven. He embraces him with such great love that, if the demands of justice required him still to die for him, the bowels of his compassion would not fail him.

Man ought not to despair over his own fall, since God has compassion for him with such affection of love; nor should he again hope without fear, lest he take from the greatness of mercy an occasion for sinning. That man is exceedingly guilty—indeed, entirely guilty—who makes himself impious because of the Savior’s compassion and turns his loving benefit into an increase of iniquity.

He opposes the Christian faith and undermines compassion who, presuming upon God’s mercy, sins more securely or heaps up sins in the hope of later doing penance. For divine mercy and repentance, which is extended to us infirm people by that mercy as a medicine, are remedies against sinning, not incentives to sin.

With fear and love together, dearest brothers, let us admire and, in our admiration, understand the precious gifts of divine love and grace bestowed upon us; and let us renounce our sins with perfect hatred.

To renounce sins with perfect hatred means to love oneself as God made one and to hate the person one made oneself by sinning. Let us place before the eyes of our soul and hold firmly in our memory the admirable grace by which God created us before we existed; from how great misery and by how great a mercy of his we were afterward delivered. And let us love with all our inmost being him who today was born for us from his most holy and glorious virgin mother, Mary.

He loves us, though guilty, and hates our guilt. May Jesus Christ, God and our Lord, deign to cleanse us by the grace of his compassion. To him, with the Father and the Holy Spirit, be all honor and glory, throughout all ages of ages. Amen.

## SERMON II. ON THE NATIVITY OF THE LORD II

[Col. 0240B]

Today, dearly beloved, a special and singular work of our Redeemer has taken place, because he who was born from a mother without a father in the world, and who before the ages was born from the Father without a mother, came to us from heaven.

He was born from a virgin woman, the omnipotence of his deity transcending the order of nature and preserving the honor of his most honorable mother with the seal of chastity and virginity.

Now the wretched must not despair of pardon, if only they repent of their great offenses, since today Mercy is born in human flesh from a Virgin. Today medicine is given from heaven to the world, by which weak and sinful souls are healed, and human nature—condemned and disfigured by sin—is restored to its original condition.

Today a ray, far more splendid than a splendid star, went forth into the darkness; illuminating with great and wondrous brilliance the people dwelling there, honoring the creature and consuming guilt, it carried them forward to the glory of the heavenly homeland.

Considering these things carefully, dearly beloved brothers, concerning the omnipotence and compassion of our Savior, let us not despair more over our offenses than we presume upon his goodness in repentance. Presumption upon the Lord’s compassion is exceedingly fruitful when the soul is first accused and healed through repentance, sin is exposed and destroyed, and the one who had previously been a sinner is made just from being a sinner.

Such presumption softens the Judge; it does not provoke him. His intention is to free the man accused by the devil, the accuser, so that he does not perish. And if at times the compassionate Lord grows angry with us sinners in indignation, he does so in order to convert us through fear of his indignation; his anger or indignation becomes not the execution of vengeance but rather the absolution of our sins.

The Lord is truly good and benevolent in all things. His indignation displays the art of a compassionate and merciful justice, and his anger is the working of a mercy that rightly counsels.

Our most compassionate Redeemer possesses incomparable friendship and incomprehensible patience. He endures daily the man for whom he suffered death, though that man continues to sin; he waits a long time and promises him, if he returns to him, not only pardon but also a reward.

The Lord therefore forgives a sinning but repentant man—not because he sinned, but because he repented. If he had not sinned, he could never have repented of sin, and the Creator would have nothing to forgive his creature.

Is it therefore good for a man to sin if he repents? No, I say; but it is good for the one who has sinned to repent and not to sin again. Nor should we sin again so that God may forgive us—far from it. Rather, let us expose the sins we commit through confession, and cover them with repentance, so that he may no longer recognize them.

Sometimes, however, the good and compassionate Lord, to display his good will—which always clings to sinners with something like the affection of a loving father, so that he may not hand the erring over to punishment—when we, who do not even use good things well, turn our medicine into a wound, himself applies medicine to us from our wound.

We are wounded by our medicine when we grow proud of our abstinence or of any virtue of ours that ought to have been medicine for the soul. But the merciful and almighty God works medicine from our wound when, as we fall into lust—not because lust is more serious than pride, but because it appears more shameful—he humbles us; and thus in us he heals one wound by means of another.

This physician is truly true and full of compassionate tenderness. Entirely sympathizing with our weakness, he demands no price for providing health to us weak people. If only we desire to be healed by him, he promises a reward—namely, himself—and gives himself.

As we said above, the Creator of the heavens came today from the heavens, born from the Virgin Mother. He who pronounced the sentence of condemnation against proud and impenitent angels brought the remedy of absolution to the penitent.

Although, dearly beloved brothers, we ought to celebrate this most sacred day as an entirely festive occasion in praise of the Lord’s nativity, and although on so joyful a solemnity it is not fitting for a Christian, for whom Christ was born today, to be afflicted by temporal sadness or bodily grief, nevertheless, if it pleases you, as it certainly ought to, let us say something, however little, about repentance, without which no sacraments benefit sinners and no festivals are worthily celebrated by them.

Let us first say what repentance is, with what fruit it should be undertaken, at what time, and with what intention of mind.

Repentance is humble satisfaction for past sins and prudent concern for future sins to be avoided; it is the end and hatred of evil, and a certain beginning and love of good.

The fruit of repentance is great, useful, and equally necessary. For repentance, preceded by divine goodness, turns the sinner so that he becomes just; it makes the man conquered by the devil into the devil’s conqueror. It prevents God from remembering the sins of wanton youth, as well as the ignorances of childhood; it also restores the elderly who have been deceived by a long habit of sinning, though by the renewal of the mind rather than of the body.

Repentance, acting like a faithful doorkeeper, opens whenever it wishes the gate of paradise that is closed to sinners. Those whom it recognizes as repentant it admits inside; but the impenitent it allows to enter neither by prayer nor by payment, because they loved death, and so it excludes them entirely from life.

Repentance must be undertaken at the time when bodily health remains, while each person still has the use of his own power. We must not wait for the final day of our life to undertake repentance, because those who postpone repentance until the last day scarcely, or never, attain salvation.

What often happens to wretched people is that their life is spent in the pleasures of the flesh; but when pleasure itself is suddenly taken away, when the flesh is worn down by illness, when the soul is already being forced to depart, then, as though for living well, they seek the salvation they have lost—people to whom, in exchange for brief pleasure, eternal punishment is owed.

Of such people it is said in the Psalm: “When God was killing them, they sought him” (Psalm 77:84).

Certainly, a person will have begun to present his case far too late before the Judge who does everything justly when he has received from that Judge the sad and unchangeable sentence of his condemnation pronounced against him.

Therefore, while it is permitted and time for repentance is granted, it is not fitting for us to be idle or excessively secure. According to the merits of each person, after this life—which is brief, and whose brevity is uncertain—either everlasting happiness or misery destined to last without end is reserved for us.

Let us undertake repentance with this intention of mind: not to seek human praise from it, but to please God alone through the goodness of repentance. Those who repent cannot truly displease him, while sinners cannot in any way please him without repentance.

Let us mourn our past sins in such a way that, with the help of divine compassion, we commit no further sins for which we must mourn. Divine compassion desires to help if a repentant person does not delay confessing. It seeks to repair a broken vessel, not to shatter what has been damaged; and it patiently waits for the sinner to turn to God, so that God may turn toward the sinner.

It desires our groans, but temporal ones, so that it may forgive eternal ones. It demands from our eyes the tears of this brief time, so that it may pour out upon us the anointing of the Holy Spirit, which in the present wipes away every stain from us and in the future wipes every tear from our eyes.

Brothers, we must not despair of the Lord’s such great compassion. We must flee not from him but to him, for he is believed to be more willing to forgive than the devil was to suggest sin or man to commit it.

What we have said here about repentance should not have been passed over, since after baptism it alone remains to human beings as the medicine of sin.

We proposed to discuss the nativity of our God and Savior Jesus Christ. Although our life does not deserve it, although eloquence for speaking is lacking, and although our knowledge offers little or nothing at all in support, nevertheless, presuming more upon the Lord’s sweetest charity and his compassionate patience than despairing of our own imperfection, we shall continue as he himself may grant us to speak worthily of the things he often bestows upon the unworthy.

This solemnity, which Christian religion celebrates annually today, requires joy of mind rather than affliction of the flesh, because today we ought greatly to rejoice and be glad: the lost man has been found, and the one who had died has come back to life.

Today God became man and was born, suffering many injuries for us for a short time. When he was placed upon the cross by those for whom he had come, from his most sacred side, wounded by the lance, there flowed a stream of compassion rather than of blood.

O human wickedness, utterly powerless unless permitted by God, hear and understand what almighty God endured for you and from you. He was not bound to the cross by your accursed hands—hands that he had consecrated when he made you—but fastened with nails, so that you might constrain him with greater pain: him who had come to free you from eternal pains, and so that you might inflict a heavier vengeance upon him who had committed no fault.

You wickedly raged against him; yet in this he himself compassionately took pity on you. For that reason he endured the more grievous torments of your cruelty, so that he might show greater love to you, who hated him without cause, and through the memory of such an injurious passion might pierce your sinful soul with something like the nails of mercy, so that in this way he might recall you, the one who had gone astray, lest you perish.

The compassionate and benevolent God, when he declared on the cross that he thirsted and received the bitterness of gall from that faithless people, offered the sweetness of charity by praying for them. Nor did the humble steward of our salvation then thirst so much for a cup of wine or water as for the salvation of the people who were killing him.

O immeasurable benevolence of God and our Lord Jesus Christ toward sinners! O ineffable mercy! O indescribable mercy! O admirable patience!

For what greater benevolence, mercy, humility, or patience could be shown to sinners than that God himself should become the price of the man who despised him? Thus man sinned against God, and God made satisfaction for sin; man raged against God, and God showed favor to the one raging against him; the Lord of heaven and earth assumed the form of a servant; in that form the true bread hungered, the living fountain thirsted, the strongest power became weak, and immortal life died for its own killer.

Whatever good God displayed on earth, he did for man; and whatever evil he endured came from man and was for man.

What shall we think of these things, brothers? What shall we say? What shall we do, since God is toward us such that he cannot be better, while we are toward him such that we can scarcely be worse? Where shall we go? Where shall we flee? Or what counselor or helper can we unjust people have against God, the just Judge?

Absolutely none—except God himself.

Let us therefore ask counsel and help from him through love, humility, patience, and chastity, whose goodness and mercy are without number.

Would that each one of us would recognize himself as guilty in repentance as quickly as God would forgive his guilt! Would that we would turn to repentance as quickly as our compassionate Creator would be ready to change the sentence already determined against us!

The unchangeable sentence of the Creator is changed by the conversion and good conduct of the sinner; and to the one who had earlier been threatened with death because of his iniquity, once converted, he promises and grants everlasting life.

May our God and Lord Jesus Christ, who today deigned to be born for the salvation of the world, grant this to us through his sweetest charity, mercy, and goodness. He lives and reigns with the Father and the Holy Spirit, throughout all ages of ages. Amen.

# SERMON III. ON THE NATIVITY OF THE LORD III.

Christ the Son of God, dearest brothers, who in the Gospel teaches and commands us to believe that he was bodily born on this day, had also previously said through the prophet that he would be conceived in a virgin and born of a virgin, as is recognized in the following prophecy: “Behold, a virgin shall conceive and bear a son” (Isa. VII, 14). What the prophet long ago foretold as something that would happen concerning the incarnation and birth of God and our Lord Jesus Christ, we now recognize as having happened.

[Col. 0244B] For, according to the prophecy of that most holy prophet, a certain virgin was to conceive and bear a son; and this virgin was the good Mary. She conceived and bore not just anyone, nor the son of just anyone, but God and the Son of God. God with the Father, Son from the Father, one God with the Father, because they are of one substance, one essence, one divinity, one power, and one nature. He is Son from the Father because he is in the Father and is his wisdom from the Father. We rightly call the Father’s wisdom his Son because, just as any earthly king governs and orders his kingdoms through his wise son, so the heavenly Father created, orders, and governs all things through his wisdom.

He arranged that this dearest Son of his, consubstantial and coeternal with him, should become incarnate—that is, should assume humanity from her—and that this same man should mercifully die, so that by the death of the second man he might raise the first from the death of sin. Thus the heavenly and new Adam restored to life the earthly and old Adam, from whom he had departed.

This holy mercy—that is, the indescribable manifestation of divine compassion toward sinners—was accomplished by God the Father through the Son, with the cooperation of the Holy Spirit, from the virgin, in the virgin, and through the virgin, with the archangel announcing it. The Father commanded in love that the Son should become incarnate; the Son assumed flesh by his will; and the Holy Spirit sanctified in Mary the very flesh that the Son assumed.

And just as there are two commandments of love, so the Holy Spirit operated principally in two ways in the sanctification of the Virgin. The first operation of the Holy Spirit in the Virgin was the putting to death of all sins. The second was the holy preservation of her blessed virginity. This is what the angel said to Mary before the Son of God was conceived in her: “The Holy Spirit will come upon you, and the power of the Most High will overshadow you” (Luke I, 35).

The Holy Spirit came upon her because he cleansed her body and soul from every sin. The power of the Most High overshadowed her because it preserved her blessed virginity undefiled. She who was a holy virgin before childbirth became a holier virgin in childbirth, and a most holy virgin after childbirth.

The Holy Spirit and the power of the Most High are not two, but one, as Christ says to his disciples in the Gospel: “I will send the promise of my Father upon you”—namely, the Holy Spirit—“but remain in the city until you are clothed with power from on high” (Luke XXIV, 49), that is, until you are filled with the Holy Spirit.

The archangel Gabriel, sent by God, came to the virgin Mary, announcing to her the divine and human birth that would take place from her. Thus Christ assumed flesh from the Virgin, in the Virgin—not from sinful Adam, but from the source from which just Adam received his soul—and, proceeding through the virgin with flesh, appeared to the world as God and man.

The soul was given to Adam by God, as it is written in Genesis: “He breathed into his face the breath of life” (Gen. II, 7). And the Holy Spirit, who animated Adam’s flesh formed from the clay, also animated Christ’s flesh in his mother’s womb.

Therefore, from the source from which Adam had received his soul long before, and of the kind he had received it, Christ also received his—not of the kind Adam later made it by sinning. Other human beings, who are merely human, are born according to the law of human beings—that is, in sin, with the pain and corruption of their mothers. But the Son of God, who was God and man, was indeed born according to the law of humanity, but also, and more fully, according to the law of God.

Insofar as he was born of a woman, he was born according to the law of humanity; but he was born more fully according to the law of God, because he was without sin and without the pain and corruption of his mother. By being born of a woman he showed himself to be truly human; by being born without sin and of a virgin mother, he showed himself to be almighty God.

Nor should it be believed that it was impossible for him who can do all things both to create himself as man in his mother and from his mother, and to preserve his mother’s virginity.

[Col. 0245C] God, then, both could and willed to become man and to be born of a virgin, so that by becoming man he might show the reality of flesh, while by emerging from his mother’s womb with the seal of virginity unbroken he might display the omnipotence of his divinity.

Moreover, in the case of other human beings, their bodies are first formed in their mothers’ wombs, and afterward souls are breathed into the formed bodies, by which those bodies are given life. But the true flesh of the Son of God was not conceived in the virgin’s womb before he himself came into the Virgin; nor, after he assumed flesh, was a soul joined to that flesh. Rather, as soon as he came into the Virgin, he assumed the whole man at once—both soul and flesh.

Thus Augustine says: “When the Word of God was joined to a soul possessing a body, he assumed both soul and body at once.” And Leo the Great says: “The Son of God assumed soul and body at once in the Virgin.”

And blessed Gregory says: “The flesh of the Lord was not first conceived in the Virgin’s womb and afterward divinity came into the flesh; rather, as soon as the Word came into the womb, it became flesh and a perfect man, that is, complete in the reality of flesh and soul.”

In this wondrous manner, dearest brothers, “a child is born to us, and a son is given to us” (Isa. IX, 6). It is characteristic of a child not to harm anyone, to obey humbly, and quickly to forgive an injury done to him. The child Christ harmed no one, benefited everyone, was obedient to the Father even unto death, and forgave the injury of his death; indeed, he earnestly prayed even for those who killed him.

This child, brothers, was truly innocent, truly humble, truly patient, and deeply compassionate toward our weakness. He sought children who were small not in age but in wickedness—not, however, equal to himself, but like him. No one can be made equal to this child; yet, just as no one can be his equal, so no one, with his help, is incapable of imitating him in something by which he may be saved.

He was born for us, that is, for the sake of our salvation. For this reason he was born, that he might be a priest—and not merely a priest, but both priest and sacrifice. He is not a priest according to that by which he was born from the Father, but because of the flesh assumed from the Virgin Mother. He is a priest because of the victim he received from us and offered for us.

He also appeared to us for this purpose: to teach us first by the example of his innocence, humility, and patience, before he underwent death for us. He taught us a new life, which we should hold fast; he un taught our old life and forbade us to follow it, because a good death does not follow an evil life.

Christ, a little child born of his mother, is the exalted Son of God the Father, equal to him in every respect according to divinity. This merciful, humble, gentle, and kind one was given to us as the price of our redemption.

We were debtors of the devil, and because none of us could pay what was owed to him through the sin of the first man, we were held captive in his prison, bound by the harsh and dreadful laws of sin. But no one was able to free us from sin except the one who alone was without sin, the Son of God.

Like a wise physician who loves the sick person while hating the sickness, he assumed flesh and made medicine for our sin from his own flesh. He truly assumed flesh, and is rightly believed to have discovered the art of an immeasurable mercy: that the blessed life, which could not die, should die for the life of man.

Thus the prophet Isaiah says: “His name shall be called Emmanuel,” which means “God with us” (Isa. VII, 14). What is “God with us” except God who was to become man from us and for us?

What the prophet foretold as future, the evangelist John asserts has already happened, saying: “The Word became flesh and dwelt among us” (John I, 14). “The Word became flesh” means nothing other than that the Son of God became man. “He dwelt among us,” that is, in our flesh—our flesh, I say, according to the property of flesh, not according to the origin of sin.

For he assumed a holy soul in a holy and immaculate mother, and flesh—indeed, as has been said, the whole man—in the Virgin.

Christ, brothers, God and Lord of the angels, became not only man but also the servant of men in order to free man from the servitude of the devil. I say that the Son of God assumed the form of a servant, in which he served human beings unto death and unto the restoration of the heavenly life that they had lost by sinning.

The first man had sinned and was broken, having slipped from paradise. But the merciful God, taking pity on the wretched man, gathered up the fragments and fused them in the fire of love on the cross, making whole what had been broken.

Thus God-man willed that sinful humanity should share in his divine nobility and raised it to be heir of eternal blessedness.

[Col. 0247A] We must know and firmly believe that the nativity of Christ and his death benefit only those who follow him in love, as he taught that he should be followed. He makes these people not merely his members but his very inward parts; he strengthens them in goodness and guards them from evil.

Therefore it is said through the prophet: “He shall eat butter and honey, that he may know to reject evil and choose good” (Isa. VII, 15). Butter is pleasant and honey is sweet, and nothing is sweeter or more pleasant than love, on which the whole law and the prophets depend (Matt. XXII, 40).

Christ will eat this butter and honey: those who are pleasant and sweet, possessing his love, he will bring into his body—that is, as has been said, he will make them his members and inward parts. And rightly are those who possess love called the members and inward parts of Christ, because Christ meditates in them and works through them.

“ That he may know” means that he may cause them, in this way, to know how to reject evil—that is, to turn away from evil—and to choose good, persevering in the choice of good to the end, as he himself says in the Gospel: “The one who perseveres to the end will be saved” (Matt. X, 22).

With such butter and honey Christ especially nourished his most blessed mother. By this love of his and of her neighbor he sanctified her inward parts, from which he fashioned human members for himself. For he would never have assumed flesh from her had she not first been nourished by him with love.

But, filled with this grace of love, Mary first dedicated her virginity to God; hence she merited to have a son who was her Father and the Father of all.

This is certainly that good woman—or rather, the most blessed Mother of God—whom the Lord mentioned when he threatened the devil hidden in the form of a serpent in paradise: “I will put enmity between you and the woman, and between your seed and her seed; she shall crush your head” (Gen. III, 15).

Truly blessed Mary crushed the devil’s head, for she completely extinguished in herself his principal suggestion. The devil’s principal suggestion is the desire of mind and body. By desire of mind we understand every perverse thought, and by desire of the flesh every evil action.

But the good virgin Mary, the Lord’s mother, possessed neither of these. Filled with the Holy Spirit, she was equally holy in mind and body.
