The seed of blessed Mary is Christ, and the virtues of the soul that she brought forth in Christ. The seed of the devil is every vice. What enmity has been established between virtues and vices is sufficiently clear, because neither desires anything belonging to the other that is not contrary to it.

It is true, brothers—nothing is truer—that Mary once gave birth to Christ from virgin flesh, and that Christ spiritually gives birth to the Christian every day in baptism.

Therefore let us, who are called Christians from Christ and are Christians, believe with all our heart and confess that Christ, true God and true man, was born today from the Virgin Mother. With praises worthy of our faith, let us humbly and earnestly beseech him and his most blessed mother, the virgin Mary, that by his sweetest compassion and through the intercession of his sweetest mother he may cleanse our souls and bodies from every sin and enlighten them with virtues, so that we may worthily celebrate the feast of his most holy Nativity and may deserve to see and possess him who deigned to be born and die for us and rose again on the third day, God who lives and reigns with the Father and the Holy Spirit through all ages of ages. Amen.

# SERMON IV. ON THE NATIVITY OF THE LORD IV.

What happened today is wondrous, but it is to be wondered at with faith and devotion. Today, for our salvation, God was born of a woman; the Father of a daughter; the Lord of a handmaid; the Creator of a creature; the sun of a star.

Today he was born in time who was born before all ages, who made the ages and created all things from nothing: Christ, through whom God the Father created everything. He willed to be what man is, so that man might be able to become what Christ is. Man became what Christ is when Christ became man.

I say this according to the nature of the humanity he assumed, not according to the substance of his divinity. Man is in that respect what Christ is in which Christ assumed man. Man is not in that respect what Christ is in which Christ is the maker, but in that respect in which Christ is the thing made.

For Christ subsists in one person from three substances, namely divinity, flesh, and soul. Just as the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit are three persons, and the three persons have one substance, so the Word, flesh, and soul are three substances, and the three substances have one person, God and man.

Thus today, in one person and one man, true divinity was born, and in God there were a true soul and true flesh.

By this nativity, through the compassion of truth, the devil was stripped of the prey that he had captured by falsehood. The Creator raised up the creature that had fallen, and the destroyer lost the one he had destroyed.

Today a greater concord arose between God and man than had existed before the fall, and a graver discord arose between man and the devil. That most wicked rival is ashamed that he has been defeated, and unquestionably recognizes that the man whom he had conquered has been placed above the angels.

Today the enclosed garden proceeded from that gate, and into it and through it flowed the sealed fountain of which the prophet says: “There is a gate that shall not be opened in the house of the Lord; it is closed” (Ezek. XLIV, 1).

This gate of the temple, and the temple of the Lord, is the most blessed and incomparable virgin Mary, from whose womb the image of God the Father came to us.

How and why he came is shown when the angel revealed to Mary and Joseph the plan of the divine dispensation. To Mary he said: “The Holy Spirit will come upon you, Mary, and you will conceive the Son of God” (Luke I, 31). To Joseph he said: “Do not fear to take Mary your wife, for that which has been born in her is from the Holy Spirit. She will bear a son, and you shall call his name Jesus, for he will save his people from their sins” (Matt. I, 20–21).

Although the birth of our Savior was manifested to the holy angels and, through them, to people of good will, it was hidden from the devil and his idols. The idols of the devil are chiefly unbelieving and backsliding people, to whom, because of their unrepentant hearts, the mystery of the Lord’s conception and birth is unknown.

They are rightly called the devil’s idols because in them and through them he speaks and acts at the same time.

Holy Scripture rightly called our Savior a fountain because, through the water and blood flowing from his side, he washed the human race from the filth of sins, created the Church without wrinkle or stain (Eph. V, 27)—that is, without deformity or impurity—and chose her as his bride and temple.

This fountain is appropriately said to be sealed (Song IV, 12), because by the Father he was sanctified in all truth and holiness.

This abiding and unfailing fountain, by its dew—that is, by the outpouring of the Holy Spirit—watered the inward parts of glorious Mary. The fullness of divinity dwelling bodily in her (Col. II, 9) gave her his goodness (Ps. LXXXIV, 13), granting her a new and unique conception without parallel.

That most holy earth, namely the virgin Mary, gave its fruit (Ps. LXVI, 7). She conceived him in faith and love when the angel announced him, and with the gate of her womb closed she bore a son—God in man and man in God.

In this ineffable and inconceivable manner, “the Word became flesh” (John I, 14): God, the Son of God the Father, became the son of a virgin woman, born both naturally and by power.

Naturally, certainly, because Christ was born from that part of the body of the virgin Mary from which every human being is born from his mother. But he was born by power because, as has been said, the gate of that virgin’s womb remained closed, preserving in one respect the nature of humanity, while in the other the omnipotence of divinity surpassed human nature.

If anyone thinks or speaks otherwise about this, he must be avoided, not followed, because he follows a deviation. He un teaches the truth and teaches error. When he attempts to say things alien to what the Holy Spirit spoke through the mouths of his saints, he paints for himself, as it were, a new glory; and while pursuing false happiness, he attains true unhappiness.

I have said this because it is attributed to certain persons that they indeed proclaim the Lord’s mother a virgin both before and after childbirth, but acknowledge that the gate of her womb was opened in childbirth and immediately closed afterward—as though she were a virgin for one moment and lost her virginity for another.

It is insane to say this and profane to believe it. Whoever says or believes this contradicts the Holy Spirit. For he denies the truth that the Holy Spirit confesses through the prophet Ezekiel, saying: “There is a gate in the house of the Lord that is closed, and it shall not be opened” (Ezek. XLIV, 2).

But I firmly believe in the Holy Spirit, and without hesitation profess, that she was a virgin both for an instant and for all duration, before childbirth, in childbirth, and after childbirth; that she gave birth to God and man in one person; and that this occurred without the opening of the flesh and without corruption of body or soul.

In paradise this condition would indeed have existed had our first parents not sinned: they would have begotten and been begotten without corruption—that is, without injury to body or soul—but not without the opening of the flesh. For if there were no opening of the flesh, virginity would be preserved, and everyone would thus be born of a virgin.

But it could by no means happen that a man should be born of a virgin except that one who is God and man.

Therefore whoever thinks differently about this is foolish and tells what is completely alien to the truth. They are in error, and it does them no good to confess the Savior’s mother a virgin before and after childbirth while denying that she was a virgin in childbirth.

The holy virgin was a virgin before childbirth, a holier virgin in childbirth, and a most holy virgin after childbirth, because the greater the divine operation accomplished in her, the more holiness and reverence grew within her.

This is taught by the Catholic faith, and Christian doctrine abhors the contrary.

The gate of our Savior’s mother’s womb, therefore, was never open, but always closed and sealed. Through it God-man himself came forth, “like a bridegroom proceeding from the bridal chamber” (Ps. XVIII, 6).

The womb of the good and blessed virgin Mary is called a bridal chamber because in it divinity was joined to flesh and our flesh to divinity.

A woman’s womb is rightly called the gate of her belly, because through it a human being comes out and enters this world when he is born. In other women it opens as the child comes forth; but in the mother of the Lord alone, it is truly read and firmly believed to have remained closed both when he was born and before and afterward, as the prophet Ezekiel bears witness, saying: “There is a gate in the house of the Lord that is closed and shall not be opened” (Ezek. XLIV, 2).

This honorable and praiseworthy woman, Mary, a virgin worthy of God, is called the house of the Lord, in whom the eastern gate is said always to remain closed.

Mary is rightly called the house, that is, the temple of the Lord, because God himself dwelt in her both through the sanctification of the Spirit and through human conception.

Thus, while the proper nature of divinity was preserved, flesh was made in the virgin’s womb, and a perfect man in the reality of flesh and soul. Through the temple gate facing east—which neither opened of itself nor was opened by another—he proceeded from the virgin mother.

He came forth with the womb of his mother closed by the same power as if it had been open. Both things are wondrous: that God became man and that God-man was born of a virgin.

[Col. 0250D] If anyone considers that God became man, why does he doubt the birth from a virgin? It was not a lesser miracle for God to become man than for a virgin woman to give birth.

I shall speak briefly, so as not to weary the listener. I ask: from where, and by whom, were all things made? By whom they were made is known; from what they were made is unknown. God certainly made all things, but there was no material beforehand from which he might make them.

He had only the will to make them: “He spoke, and they were made; he commanded, and they were created” (Ps. XXXII, 9).

Behold, God created the universe without difficulty and without material. Could he not convert some of the things he made to other uses and use them as he wished and in the manner he wished? Certainly he could.

The Son of God is almighty, and in him and through him are all things. He was able to make whatever he wished, and in whatever manner he wished, according to his will.

And just as he entered to his disciples through closed doors (John XX, 26)—even though he entered through those closed doors, which had also been barred because of fear of the Jews—so he came forth through the gate of the blessed and virginal womb, closed and barred alike, and appeared to the world.

It was by one and the same omnipotence of divinity that he entered to his disciples through closed doors in his resurrection and came forth at his birth through the closed gate of his mother’s womb.

God willed to be conceived as man in a woman and to be born as man of a woman, so that by becoming man he might show the reality of flesh, while by being conceived as man in a virgin and born as man from a virgin he might show himself to be the omnipotent God who created all things from nothing.

Perhaps someone still asks how it could happen that God-man, having been made from a woman, should be born from her while her virginity was preserved.

You who inquire about this, do not doubt but firmly believe: if you truly believe that God is omnipotent, you cannot in any way doubt this. For if you confess that he can do all things, you cannot deny that he can do this, since it is one among all the things he can do.

God would not be omnipotent if he could not do whatever he wished.

Christ is therefore perfect God from God the Father and perfect man through the assumption of soul and flesh. Although God is one thing and man another, there is not one Son of God, God, and another son of the virgin, man.

The Son of God and the son of the virgin are one—not one thing, but one person: truly God and man, as was said above, consisting of three substances, namely Word, flesh, and soul.

This Only-Begotten of God the Father and firstborn of the virgin mother came into the world full of mercy and truth. He came mercifully; he came truly. He freed us from the power of Satan, and just as he had previously said through his prophets that he would come, we now know that he has come, having suffered for us, for a short time, no small injuries in this world.

From the day when the Father’s love and his own will sent Christ down to earth and he appeared to the world as man, the man for whose salvation he had come sought deceitfully to kill him and laid ambushes for him.

To summarize briefly: he endured many persecutions and insults from human beings and for human beings. But that merciful and compassionate God and Lord, desiring not vengeance upon men but their absolution, not only forgave his own injuries but also suffered the cross and death for those who had injured him.

Thus the true light and blessed life, God the Son of God, raised us wretched people—who by the right and gain of sin were in darkness and buried in death—through his mercy and compassion. The joys of light and the remedies of life that had first been given to us by him but had not been well preserved by us, he gave back to us.

Therefore, although we do not doubt that we were and are unworthy of his grace and mercy, let us nevertheless offer thanks and gratitude to our Creator and Redeemer, with the help of him without whom we can do nothing good.

On this day also let us believe with pure faith and confess with true love that God and man was born from the virgin Mary for our salvation. To him belong all honor and glory with his God the Father and the Holy Spirit through all ages of ages. Amen.

# SERMON V. ON THE RESURRECTION OF THE LORD.

Today, beloved, because we are celebrating the solemnities of the Lord’s Resurrection, it is religious to speak about so great a solemnity, and we consider it irreligious to remain silent. Let us therefore propose and explain, insofar as he grants it who knows all things, why the Lord rose neither on the first day, when he died for our salvation, nor on the second, but on the third day. We must also ask why, after his resurrection, he appeared only to the good and to a few, and for a short time, whereas before his resurrection he had appeared to many—both good and evil—and for a somewhat longer time. [Col. 0252B]

By raising himself, the blessed life, God, from death on the third day, he signified that our resurrection would take place on the third day—something he had foretold long beforehand through the prophet. The prophet Hosea, about to speak of our resurrection before our death and resurrection, urges us with pious and faithful exhortation, lest the just Judge find us unprepared, saying: “Come, and let us return to the Lord, for he has begun, and he will heal us; he will strike us, and he will cure us” (Hosea 6:2).

He says, “Come,” that is, “Keep to the way”; let us turn neither to the right nor to the left, but let each one of us return to the Lord through faith, confession, and repentance. Let us have faith, which through love works every good thing and especially hatred of sin. For faith without a good work, and especially without hatred of sin, is considered dead. [Col. 0252C]

Let us come to confession, through which the poison of the ancient serpent is vomited out, the sinner is released from sins, victory is produced for God, and shame for the devil. Let us do penance, through which divine mercy forgives us in such a way that the devil does not recognize us as sinners, nor does God acknowledge us as such. This is to return to the Lord after sin; whoever returns to him keeps to the way and does not follow a deviation.

The good Lord began to heal us when, in his great compassion, he freed us from the infirmity of eternal death. [Col. 0252D]

In the first human being, the devil made us both weak and wretched through sin. But God, the merciful and almighty physician, taking pity on our misery and infirmity, discovered an antidote—something that had not existed before and that was fitting for us wretched people both in name and in action—by which he might heal us. He himself baptized this greatest work of his charity, giving it the name “mercy,” and setting it against our misery and infirmity as a medicine. By this wholesome and saving medicine, therefore, he healed our souls and bodies. Through this incomparable and pre-eminent work of his love, he forgave us and bestowed very great gifts upon us. He forgave guilt and gave grace. He put our death to death and restored life. By this art of mercy he conquered the devil and shattered hell; he opened for us the gates of heaven and gave himself.

We have said that the almighty God, in his mercy, bestowed these great benefits upon us. With his help, we shall now say how he himself made mercy. [Col. 0253A]

With the whole Trinity at work, therefore, the Son of God was conceived as man in the Virgin’s womb and was born into the world from the Virgin Mother. The blessed Trinity—Father, Son, and Holy Spirit—is one God; the operation of the whole Trinity is one. The Father ordained this astonishing operation, wondrous to contemplate with love and faith, in charity. The Holy Spirit sanctified the Virgin, whom he had already begun to sanctify, far more completely, making her entirely most holy in soul and body. The Son, in that most holy Virgin, assumed the whole human being, that is, soul and flesh. For no part of her could be anything but most holy, since the fullness of divinity dwelt bodily in her. [Col. 0253B]

God, therefore, the Son of God, having assumed flesh and having suffered many insults for a short time, mounted the cross so that he might die for us. Although he had been unjustly judged by man, there we also recognize him as the judge of man, and as having been made priest and sacrifice for the name.

Truly placed upon the cross, the Lord was judging; already, by royal power, he was separating the sheep from the goats. There, with merciful compassion, he summoned to glory the one thief placed on his right, in whom the mystery of faith and confession had gone before; the other, placed on his left, he left in punishment by the sentence of justice.

At the hour of the day when the first human being became a thief, followed the thief-devil, was expelled from paradise, and lost life—that is, at the ninth hour—Christ suffered death and opened the gates of paradise to the thief.

He himself says in the Gospel: “No one has greater love than this, that someone lay down his life for his friends” (John 15:13). He said “no one,” but he himself, who is God and man, displayed far greater love: he laid down his life not only for friends but also for enemies, and he prayed to the Father on behalf of his enemies. [Col. 0253C]

Christ did not wish to possess the priesthood or kingship that sometimes makes a man proud. Rather, appointed by the Father as king and priest on the cross, on the altar of the cross—which he sanctified by the presence of his body—he offered himself as a sacrifice for our redemption. Thus the merciful king and just judge guided us to the heavenly kingdoms.

On that holy cross, blood and water came forth from the right side of Christ (John 19:34): blood, by which he might redeem us from the power of the devil; water, by which he might cleanse us from sins. Why did blood and water come forth from his side? So that, plainly, from the place from which guilt had proceeded, grace might also proceed. From Adam’s side woman was made, and she fed us with the food of sin. From Christ’s side grace flowed forth; it both removed sin and bestowed the remedy of life. [Col. 0253D]

Blood and water are said to have come forth from Christ’s right side rather than from his left. For by his left hand we understand his left side, namely, the assumption of human flesh; by his right side, which we understand through his right hand, we understand the divine majesty. Since no one could express this in any other way, it received this designation, that is, “right.” From that side, therefore, came both Christ’s incarnation and that blood and water and all the mysteries of the same incarnation—from the side from which every good thing proceeds.

For this reason also the righteous are to be placed on the right at the day of judgment: in Christ they understood the divine majesty, and with love they believed in his incarnation. Even if some of them, while not yet believing, killed Christ in the flesh, afterward, once they believed, they ate Christ’s flesh and drank the blood they had shed.

But the unrighteous will be on the left, because they neither tasted the sweetness of the divine majesty that is in Christ nor revered his incarnation. They always savored their own flesh, and therefore loved the left—that is, unrighteous—works, for which they will have perpetual hatred of their Creator. [Col. 0254A]

Blood and water certainly came forth from Christ’s side, but the evangelist does not say that both came forth simultaneously. If the water had come forth together with the blood, water could not at all have been distinguished by human beings within the blood. The blood therefore came forth before the water, and rightly so, because baptism and the forgiveness of sins follow the shedding of blood—that is, faith in the Lord’s Passion.

By this faith the patriarchs and prophets, and many others of both sexes, hoped for Christ the Redeemer who was to come. What we believe to have happened, they believed while awaiting it as something that would happen. Because they had already conceived faith in Christ, they were Christians, and they were redeemed. All who, after seeing the Savior, hoped for salvation concerning him among the dead were likewise freed from the punishments of hell.

We and those blessed predecessors of ours who went before us to the heavenly dwellings, because we inherited offense from our first parents, have been healed through the grace of the Redeemer, as though by certain ointments made from his blood, so that we who fell into death through the infidelity and transgression of others might rise again to life through the compassion and mercy of another—that is, of our Creator. [Col. 0254C]

The prophet says: “The Lord will strike us, and by striking he will heal us” (Deuteronomy 32:39). By these words he plainly shows that it is no light matter to repeat crimes that have once been redeemed by Christ’s Passion. I say that the person who kills again the soul redeemed from death by Christ’s Passion and blood will be guilty—indeed, guilty not of some insignificant matter, but of the blood of the Passion.

As we have said, our Redeemer and Lord first healed us from the transgression of our parents by his own blood. But he applied something like ointment to those wounds of ours, and we who had received the wound of sin from one source received the remedy for sin from another. Now, however, because we have sinned by our own will and in mature age, striking is necessary—that is, contrition of heart. If we wish to be healed, let us no longer seek olive oil or any other ointment, since the heated iron of severe penance is necessary to burn away the rust of our sins. [Col. 0254D]

After committing even one mortal sin, let no one ever consider confession or penance useful to him unless it is preceded by a troubled spirit and a contrite and humbled heart (Psalm 50:19 [51:17]). For where there is no true conversion of heart, full remission does not follow.

Therefore, according to the Savior’s example, each one of us must be inwardly shaken in spirit against the capital offense committed and disturb himself with a certain anxious concern, so that over his extinguished soul he may be able to offer heartfelt sighs and tearful lamentations, and thus, at least, may come back to life through God’s mercy.

When Christ came to raise Lazarus, who signifies a person buried in mortal sin, he wept, was deeply moved in spirit, and troubled himself (John 11:33–35), and said: “Lazarus, come outside” (ibid., 43). And we read that he was thus raised by the Lord. There, words did not precede tears; rather, tears preceded the Redeemer’s words. He did not first call Lazarus from the tomb, nor did Lazarus rise first, until Christ was deeply moved in spirit and troubled himself. [Col. 0255B]

Having done this, the merciful Redeemer and good teacher taught the sinner with what zeal, with what disposition of mind, with what bodily action, and with what inward shaking of the entrails he ought to do penance if he desires to be raised from the grave of sins.

Penance after sin is useful, indeed necessary, since we read that Christ raised the dead, but absolved no one who was dead in sins.

It should not be surprising, however, if one must act vigorously for sins committed knowingly and personally, since the punishment of another’s sin follows us—not only us, but also followed the holy apostles, even after baptism. Although we do not know who baptized them, by whom, where, or when, we nevertheless do not doubt that they were baptized, since we believe that the Savior himself was baptized.

Our Savior first wished to be baptized, and afterward said: “Unless someone is born again of water and the Holy Spirit, he will not enter the kingdom of heaven” (John 3:3). By word and example he taught his disciples this form of baptism; when they preached it to others, they had first observed it in themselves. It would not have been fitting, and it would have been less beneficial, if they taught others to be baptized while they themselves were not baptized. [Col. 0255C]

And therefore we believe both that they were baptized and that one was baptized by another, since at that time they alone had received from the Lord the power to baptize.

There was no way to alter what the Truth said: “Unless someone is born again of water and the Holy Spirit, he will not have the kingdom of heaven.” We can have no greater authority or better author in anything than the Truth itself. Therefore, by the declaration of true faith—or rather, by the voice of Truth itself—we prove that no one can or will be saved who has not been baptized.

Some receive baptism where the mysteries of baptism are celebrated visibly. Others, like the evangelical thief and the holy martyrs, although the mysteries of baptism were not visibly celebrated upon them, nevertheless received baptism through faith and will. For, as we truly read: “All who have the Spirit of God also receive his grace” (Romans 8:14).

That thief would certainly have received baptism visibly if he could have, because he was not saved by his suffering, or by any good work he might have done previously, but by faith in Christ and confession. He was not crucified for the name of Christ, nor is it believed that he suffered because he believed; rather, he believed while he was suffering. [Col. 0255D]

It is futile for anyone to become, as it were, a martyr for the name of Christ unless the faith of baptism has gone before in him.

How powerful, even without the visible sacrament of baptism, is what the apostle Paul says—“With the heart one believes unto righteousness, but with the mouth confession is made unto salvation” (Romans 10:10)—is made clear both in that thief and in the holy martyrs. But this is fulfilled invisibly when the circumstance of necessity does not permit the visible mysteries of baptism to be performed, not when there is contempt for religion.

For after the Truth once promulgated the aforesaid decree of baptism, crying out and saying, “Unless someone is born again of water and the Holy Spirit, he will not enter the kingdom of heaven,” if the thief, to whom the Truth itself said on the cross, “Today you will be with me in paradise” (Luke 23:43), or any of the martyrs could have had visible baptism and had despised it, the thief would have asked the Lord in vain, having spurned his command, and the martyr would have endured martyrdom without benefit. [Col. 0256A]

As has been said, good and evil alike have this: the punishment of their ancestral sin follows them. The punishment of sin is hunger, thirst, the suffering of labors and pains, being disfigured and dying in the body, and experiencing various miseries in the world. All these things arise from the sin of the first parent, although they can also be possessed without sin.

But it seems astonishing that, when God has forgiven our sin, the punishment of that already-forgiven sin still follows us. Could God not have forgiven us our sin in such a way that the punishment of sin would not follow us at all? He certainly could, but he did not wish to.

He could also have arranged in paradise that neither the devil would incite man to sin nor man would sin. But if he had not given man power over himself, and if he therefore had not sinned because he could not sin, he would have had neither a basis for being praised by God nor a basis for being rewarded.

The first human being could always have possessed the praise of his Creator and his great reward if, swollen with pride and corrupted by excessive love of his own wife, he had not risen up against his Creator. [Col. 0256D]

Contrary to what almost everyone says, Adam’s first sin was not that he ate what had been forbidden. Some elevation had already preceded this in him, an elevation arising from the greatness of the present and future blessedness and requiring restraint. Hence, by God’s just judgment, he was permitted to be tempted by the devil and to succumb to the tempter.

It had to be shown through the experience of punishment to a soul that was exalting itself and presuming too much upon its own virtue how badly a created nature fares if it withdraws from the good Creator.

By the same sword with which the evil angel killed himself in heaven, he killed man in paradise. That angel did not become swollen with pride only because of what he had already received from God, but as much because of what he would have received from him if he had been willing to submit humbly to him.

If, therefore, in those places of blessedness—or rather, in those very creatures in which the dignity of precedence had gone before—the depravity of pride was found, what would become of us, or what would remain for us to do, if in this world, so close to hell and so near to sins, we were never old but always healthy, always young, and made immortal? [Col. 0257A]

Certainly we would seek no other blessedness, nor would we even recognize the Creator himself. Instead, always exalted and proud, we would be ungrateful both for the Creator’s grace and for the Redeemer’s mercy.

For although the punishment of sin follows us, we are so puffed up and proud that our pride works the death of our soul daily—or rather, continually. Yet divine mercy wished us to be scourged and chastised by the punishment of sin for this reason: so that in this way, at least, we might recognize what we are through ourselves and what we have been made by God; hate what we have made ourselves; love him above all and before all; love ourselves as he made us; and give thanks to him who makes the punishment of sin a medicine for sinners.

That we rise again on the third day the prophet of God affirms, saying: “The Lord will revive us after two days, and on the third day he will raise us up” (Hosea 6:3).

The first day extended from Adam to Noah. From Noah the second day extends to the end of the world. The third day will be the second coming of Christ. On that third day Christ will raise our bodies by the omnipotence of his divinity, he who raised himself from his death on the third day. [Col. 0257B]

When the prophet says, “He will revive us after two days,” namely, on the third day, and on that same day “he will raise us up,” he shows the order of our resurrection. We shall rise in the order in which Christ rose, except that we shall not raise ourselves as he raised himself.

But just as Christ’s soul, once assumed by him and thereafter never separated from him, returned to the tomb on the third day and there gave life to its body, and thus Christ raised himself from the tomb, so our souls on the third day, at God’s command, will be joined to their bodies in the tombs, and thus, once given life, will immediately be raised from the tombs.

The bodies will first be given life by God—that is, they will be animated—before they are raised. This is clearly shown by the Lord’s raising of a man who had been dead for three days. He had been dead before the Lord came there and called him from the tomb, but as soon as he called the one who had been dead, he came out of the tomb alive. The Lord did not say to him, “Dead man,” but “Lazarus, come outside” (John 11:43). [Col. 0257D]

It is therefore clear that, in the tomb, he had already given life to the one whom he called forth alive. One word of the Lord there accomplished two miracles simultaneously: it restored life to the dead man in the tomb, and it brought the bound man outside the tomb.

After his resurrection, only the good and the few, and for a short time, saw Christ our God and Lord. For only the good will possess the glory of the future resurrection, and they will see without end their Creator and Redeemer, whose bodily presence they had for a short time after his resurrection. They will be few in comparison with the wicked. For, as he himself says in the Gospel: “Many are called, but few are chosen” (Matthew 20:16).

Before his resurrection, many—both good and evil—and for a somewhat longer time saw our Savior and had him present in the flesh. Since he had come for the sake of many, indeed of all who were to be saved, he was to be seen by all for a considerable span of time, so that they might be able to believe in him and be saved. Those who did not wish to believe, however, would have no excuse for their sin and would be condemned. [Col. 0258A]

Our Savior performed many works in this world, through which everyone could have believed in him if they had wished. But he did three things in particular and above all, which no one else will do or has done.

The first was that he was born of a virgin; the second, that he raised himself from death; the third, that, having assumed flesh from a virgin, he ascended into heaven, made King and Lord even in a human body, of the angels.

We said above that after Christ, the Son of God, assumed our soul, he loved it so greatly that thereafter he did not separate himself from it at all. For just as he assumed our flesh, so he assumed our soul in the blessed and glorious virgin Mary—but a soul such as Adam had before sin, not such as Adam made it by sinning. [Col. 0258B]

By this example he taught us not to hand over our soul—whom he loved so greatly that he died for it and did not separate himself from it even in the anguish of death—to our faithless servant and cruel enemy on any pretext, since that enemy strives to make it both adulterous and enslaved.

The death and Passion of the Son of God separated the flesh from the soul, but they could not separate the soul from the Word, that is, from the Son of God.

To commend the grace of his exceptional love for humanity, so that man might be able to be what Christ is, he wished to be what man is. Let us love with all the innermost affections of our soul him who joined us to himself with such great love. Let us humbly and earnestly beseech him who made himself a participant in our nature to make us participants in his glory. [Col. 0258C]

We have already once risen, through his grace and mercy, from the baptismal font without sin. May we rise again in that second resurrection, through the same grace and mercy, without any stain of sin. May we deserve both to see and to possess Jesus Christ himself, our Creator and Redeemer, who, one God with the Father and the Holy Spirit, lives and reigns throughout all ages of ages. Amen.

## SERMON VI. ON THE ASCENSION OF THE LORD

Today, beloved, man has ascended into heaven in God, and God in man. Christ, the Son of God and of the Virgin, left on earth the mother in whom he had assumed soul and flesh bodily, and, ascending into heaven, sought the Father: although he was one thing in the one and another in the other, he remained the same in both. He is different in the nature of divinity, but not different in the person of the assumed humanity. The form of God was clothed in the form of man—which is believed for our salvation—and he who was with the Father sought the Father in man.

But one is raised up by the other, and, received by a cloud, is placed at the Father’s right hand. Christ first foretold this venerable ascension to the apostles himself, and afterward Mary Magdalene announced it. When they saw him ascending into heaven and marveled together, the angels speaking to them confirmed them in faith and hope of the first and second resurrection. [Col. 0259A]

The first resurrection has already gone before in our Head, and is believed through true faith; the second will follow in the members, and is awaited in certain hope.

The mysteries of this wondrous divine and human ascension, to be marveled at in joy and love, are great. Neither man nor the angel from heaven could say so much about their greatness that, in comparison with their magnitude, it would not seem—and actually be—little.

Among other things, this is to be marveled at with great devotion: man, previously subjected to the devil through sin, has not only been freed from sin, but whatever he binds is known to be bound, and whatever he looses is known to be released.

Man had previously been made lower than an angel, but afterward, crowned with glory and honor, he was set over everything that God had made. [Col. 0259B]

Man, by his greatness, surpasses the angels, archangels, thrones, dominions, principalities, powers, virtues of heaven, cherubim, and seraphim; he commands them, and they obey him willingly.

Moreover, man, placed in heaven in the Son of God, at the seat of divine majesty, will come to judgment—not in that humility in which he was unjustly judged, but in that power in which he will justly judge.

It seems to have been a special mystery of the divine dispensation that, in the fact that the Son is less than the Father, man would be equal to the Son; and that from the beginning this special privilege would be reserved for man, so that he would become not only the judge of men but also of angels.

When man is said to be singularly destined to exercise this judicial power, the members are by no means separated from the Head. God, the Son of Man, as man, is the head of the Church; and the apostles in particular are called members of this Head. They will judge with him, as Christ declares in the Gospel (Matthew 19:28). [Col. 0259C]

Nor will the apostles alone judge with him, but also those who imitate the apostles in life and conduct.

This power was given by God the Father to the Son, by the Son to Peter, and in Peter to the Church. The Son received it in the form of man, in which he is less than the Father, not in the form of the Father, in which he is equal to the Father.

In the form of the Father, in which the Son is equal to the Father, he can be neither less nor greater; likewise, he can have neither less nor more than he has. In that form nothing is given to the Son, since in it he himself contains and possesses all things.

But the power of which we are speaking was received by the humanity from the divinity, as it is said in the Gospel: “Authority was given to Christ to exercise judgment, because he is the Son of man” (John 5:27). [Col. 0259D]

The power that Christ did not have from the fact that he is the Son of man, he received from elsewhere. From where? From above, certainly—from the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit.

Christ received power from the same source from which his blessed soul and flesh were made blessed. Christ the man was made blessed by Christ God, and power was given to him by Christ God.

Christ God is one thing and Christ man another, yet there are not two Christs; Christ is one, God and man. With power assumed in his humanity, Christ the man in Christ God, and Christ God in Christ man, binds, releases, and judges.

So closely are divinity and humanity united in the Son of God that, although they are not one thing, there is nevertheless one person of both, one work, one will, one power, one truth, one mercy, and one sentence of justice. Everywhere the operation of the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit is one and common; and by the disposition of the whole Trinity, judgment specially belongs to the form of man, which the Son alone assumed.

He himself asserts this in the Gospel, saying: “The Father judges no one, but has given all judgment to the Son” (John 5:22). [Col. 0260A]

When it is said elsewhere, “I judge no one” (John 8:15), this refers to what he had said to the Jews: “You judge according to the flesh” (ibid.), that is, carnally: “I judge no one carnally,” that is, unjustly, “as you do.”

Or, “I judge no one according to the flesh alone, as you judge, but also according to the intention of the heart.”

Or: “I judge no one”—he did not say, “I will judge no one,” but at the hour when he was saying these things, he was judging no one.

He came into this world to be truly judged and to judge, and sacred Scripture testifies that he will come again as judge. Where sacred Scripture testifies that he will come again as judge, it clearly shows that he has already been judge. Whatever is to be done a second time must plainly have been done once before.

Our good Maker and merciful Redeemer looked upon us wretched people with the gaze of mercy, but he acted against the devil with the sentence of justice. When he was unjustly judged to death on our behalf, what else was he doing than freeing us from eternal death by true judgment? [Col. 0260C]

When he was bound, what other work was he doing than loosing, by just judgment, the bonds of our sins?

Christ also judges his own in this age, when he tests them either by martyrdom, exile, or the persecution of false brothers. Hence the apostle Paul says: “When we are judged, we are chastened by the Lord, so that we may not be condemned with the world” (1 Corinthians 11:32).

Christ himself testified that he had come as judge when he said: “I judge as I hear, and my judgment is true” (John 5:30). And again: “For judgment I have come into this world” (John 9:39). And elsewhere: “The prince of this world has been judged” (John 16:11).

“I judge as I hear,” namely, from my Father in the flesh assumed; “thus I judge, and my judgment is true.” It is as though he said: “My judgment cannot fail to be true, because the Father, who grants me the power to judge, is truthful, and I who judge am Truth.”

He testifies that he came into this world for judgment, so that he might judge, not merely so that he might be judged. Hence it is added: “So that those who do not see may see, and those who see may become blind” (John 9:39). [Col. 0260D]

Those who did not see when Christ came—those who did not consider themselves to see, that is, did not consider themselves righteous, but confessed themselves sinners—were enlightened, because they received the light of life.

And those who did see, namely the scribes and Pharisees, who believed that they alone saw, that is, were righteous, and despised the others as though they were blind, were made blind, because they lost the light of truth, which they had present before them.

This was therefore accomplished, and is still accomplished daily, by Christ’s judgment: humble sinners are enlightened, and proud righteous people are blinded. Christ called this discernment, which he held and holds between the good and evil works of men, judgment.

Elsewhere it is said: “God did not send his Son into the world to judge the world, but so that the world might be saved through him” (John 3:17). This is altogether believed to be true; for what Truth speaks cannot fail to be true. Truly, the Son of God was not sent into the world by the Father to judge the world, since he came into the world for this purpose: that the world might be saved through him, if the world had wished it. [Col. 0261A]

But what Christ wished, the world did not wish. If the world had wished what Christ wished, he himself would not have said in the Gospel: “Jerusalem, Jerusalem, how often I wished to gather your children, as a hen gathers her chicks under her wings, and you were unwilling?” (Matthew 23:37).

If the world had wished what Christ wished, it could certainly have believed and been saved. It could not believe because it did not wish what Christ wished. And because it became unbelieving of its own accord, not by Christ’s will, we do not doubt that it was judged, since Christ says: “Whoever does not believe has already been judged” (John 3:18).

In this passage, by the name “world” the Jewish people are understood, to whom he himself spoke in particular and to whom he was sent especially.

Therefore, both the world and the prince of this world (John 16:11) have been judged, with Christ bearing witness. When he asserts that the prince of this world, the devil, has been judged, he clearly shows that he judged the devil, since the devil can be judged by no one except by him and through him. [Col. 0261C]

The devil was therefore judged by Christ when he lost those whom he had bound with the bonds of unbelief, after they had been converted through Christ’s preaching; when he mourned that he himself had been cast out of the hearts of men; and when he could hold no one who believed.

Even while fixed upon the cross, he exercised the rights of justice concerning those two crucified thieves, between whom he himself had been crucified: there he judged one of them for glory and assigned the other to punishment.

Standing fixed upon the cross by his own will, that true emperor triumphed over the proud enemy. Already, by divine power, the just Judge was judging; already he was separating the sheep from the goats; and he was signifying what he would do in the other judgment.

By reason and authority alike it is taught that he has already come as judge and is awaited as the judge who will come.

The Son humbled the divine majesty, which he possesses equally and as one with the Father and the Holy Spirit, when he assumed the form of a servant. In that form the Lord of all became the servant of men and served men unto death. [Col. 0262A]

He raised up this form, which he had assumed secondarily, and in it he will carry out that final and greatly fearful judgment, at which all the elements and even the powers of heaven will be shaken (Matthew 24:29).

The form of divinity, which is one and shared by the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit, neither appeared to the world nor will it appear in the judgment. But the form of man will be seen with great splendor and great power; in it the Son of God, and it in the Son of God, will judge.

This has plainly been arranged by a just and rational ordering: God will judge the world in the form in which he was judged by the world. Because the world saw him humble and, in its pride, despised him, it will see him exalted and will fear him. The form that was exalted on the cross for punishment, and in the ascension for glory, will be exalted in the judgment, and the proud will be humbled. [Col. 0262B]

Then what is said will be fulfilled most completely: “Whoever exalts himself will be humbled, and whoever humbles himself will be exalted” (Luke 18:14).

Because our Savior’s coming is the coming of God and man, it must be loved intensely; and because he has been judged and will judge, it must be feared greatly. Let us therefore fear the coming of God and man with love, and love it with fear, so that we may be able joyfully to see and possess as judge our Lord Jesus Christ, who, with one and the same glory and majesty as the Father and the Holy Spirit, lives and reigns as God throughout all ages of ages. Amen.

373 **SERMON VII. ON THE PURIFICATION OF HOLY MARY.**
This solemnity, which is celebrated today in honor of God and of his most holy mother, is rightly believed to be no lesser than the greater festivals of the year; this will be demonstrated by reason and truth. May God-man and the virgin mother grant that what has been promised for the praise and glory of both may be rendered through the help of both. For just as the days of the Lord’s Nativity and Epiphany are known to be celebrated by the Christian religion with the same devotion, so this day also ought to be celebrated. For just as that day belongs especially to him and to his mother, so this day belongs particularly to him and to that mother. [Col. 0262C]

The solemnity of that day is indeed great, on which Christ was born of the virgin mother and was baptized by John; and this day is equally great, on which he was offered to God the Father in the temple by that same Virgin and by the righteous Simeon. God the Father, before the ages, gave to the virgin mother the Son begotten from himself, so that he might become human in her; the virgin mother, having given birth in time to that very one from herself, offered him today as a human being to God the Father. Thus he remains a wondrous son both to God the Father and to the virgin mother. For it is greatly wondrous that, apart from the common creation of human beings, God has a human son, and a woman has a son who is God. This is plainly known to have taken place in Christ, [Col. 0262D] who is God and human being, and both are one, 374 and he is the son of both.

This only Son was offered by an only mother to the only Father: one to one; indeed, in the one Son all the faithful were offered. The Gospel testifies that this venerable day is the day of Mary’s purification according to the Law. The mother rightly observed the Law whose Son had both given the Law and come to fulfill in himself the Law that he had previously given to others. Yet that chaste girl had nothing, either in herself or concerning herself, from which she then needed to be purified. For the holy virgin was pure both in the conception and in the birth of her child; and therefore the child born from her did not open her womb, although he was born through the passage of that womb.

The gate of the belly of that virgin was her womb, of which the prophet Ezekiel speaks as follows: “There is a gate in the house of the Lord; it shall be closed and shall not be opened” (Ezek. XLIV, 2). [Col. 0263A] The house of the Lord is the good Mary, because he himself founded her, and became human in her (Ps. LXXXVI, 5). The gate of this house, as was said above, was the womb within the virgin’s body, through which, although it remained closed, God and human being went forth in one person. Its most blessed mother, although she was not unaware of who the one she had borne was—for the Law had not been imposed upon him but was subject to him—nevertheless offered her son in the temple according to the command of the Law.

She waited for the day of purification and concealed the divinity of her Son. For if Christ’s incarnation had been known to the devil, Christ would neither have died for us nor would our redemption have taken place. After a child was born, the Law commanded that a lamb, a pair of turtledoves, or two young pigeons be offered for her (Lev. XII, 6). [Col. 0263B] But if anyone happened to lack a lamb, he was to offer the other or both of these to the Lord for the offering of the child—namely, a pair of turtledoves or two young pigeons (ibid., 8). 375

In both Testaments—in the Law and in the Gospel—the Lord requires equality of mind and body. That equality is this: the good that is displayed outwardly by us must first be conceived in the mind. A good work ought not to be done with difficulty but with cheerfulness; nor ought we seek human praise for it, but await recompense from the Lord. In this way the sacrifice becomes pleasing to God, and the one who extends his hand to the poor in this manner makes himself pleasing to God.

The turtledove is a chaste bird which, rejecting numerous marriages, does not care for the blandishments of others but is content with one spouse alone. By it [Col. 0263C] the Catholic Church is signified: betrothed solely to one man, Christ the Bridegroom, she is not corrupted by gifts and, as it were, rejecting numerous marriages, avoids association with heretics.

According to the decree of the Law, two young pigeons are offered as a burnt offering. That there are two commends charity; that they are young signifies innocence; that they are said to be pigeons indicates unity. Charity is rightly commended by the two, because it contains the two commandments by which God and one’s neighbor are loved. In the young birds—that is, in the little ones—innocence is rightly signified, since by them an injury is not avenged but forgiven. In the dove, the unity of the Church is suitably figured, just as the Lord says: “My dove is one” (Song VI, 8). [Col. 0263D] 376

Moreover, the dove does not abandon but faithfully preserves the unity of those dwelling with it; and if the situation demands it, it fights bravely. Every faithful person will then be a dove if, with devout patience, he remains to the end in the unity of the Catholic Church and if he contends lawfully in defense of the faith.

“And behold, there was a man in Jerusalem, whose name was Simeon; and this man was righteous and devout, awaiting the consolation of Israel” (Luke II, 25). “Behold” signifies the feeling of one who desires, because nothing could come quickly enough for Simeon’s mind, which longed to see Christ. “And there was a man named Simeon in Jerusalem”—that is, in the vision of peace. In this vision of peace, everyone in whom the Holy Spirit dwells is certainly believed to be present; likewise, there is no doubt that everyone who does not have the Holy Spirit is far from it.

Thus, if anyone wishes to know why so many and such great blessings [Col. 0264A] mentioned in the present Gospel were bestowed upon the old man Simeon, let him learn from the interpretation of his name. For Simeon is interpreted as “hearing sadness,” and sadness signifies repentance. Simeon, in whom all penitents are represented, ceased through repentance to be a sinner and became righteous from being a sinner. He was concerned not only for himself but also for his neighbors, praying for them continually. He prayed for them and feared for them. For he knew that the same duty was owed for his neighbors as for himself, and that the reward was to be awaited both for himself and for his neighbors.

He was therefore rightly declared righteous and devout: devout because of the memory of past sins, the observance of the Law, the practice of faith, and his pious compassion for his neighbors; and it was rightly testified that the Holy Spirit was in him. 377 [Col. 0264B]

“And he had received an answer from the Holy Spirit that he would not see death before he had seen the Lord’s Christ” (ibid., 26). Just as we do not know where and when he received this answer, so we are certain of what he received, from whom he received it, and how he received it. For through faith and love, abundant prayer, continual supplication, and the affirmation of good works, he deserved this answer from the Holy Spirit and obtained the promise.

Every faithful soul spiritually receives this same promise from the Holy Spirit: that it will not see death unless it first sees the Savior. Simeon saw Christ in the flesh with bodily sight and had him bodily present. We, too, see him with the eyes of the mind and of faith, remaining and working in us through his sacraments. For unless each person, before the death [Col. 0264C] of the body, should behold and possess God by spiritual grace, he would be condemned to eternal death.

Simeon saw Christ the human being with the eyes of his body, and with heart and body he adored the majesty of God in the human being. We, for our part, see water with the eyes of the flesh in baptism; and in the water we discern Christ himself, present to the eyes of the soul, and in him the whole Trinity. For just as the whole Trinity was present at Christ’s baptism, so the whole Trinity is firmly believed to be present also in the baptism of the Christian. In it we not only see Christ but put him on.

“And he came in the Spirit into the temple” (ibid., 27). If it is asked in what spirit the righteous Simeon came into the temple, the answer is certainly: in the Holy Spirit, who, according to the evangelical truth, 378 was in him. Truly, [Col. 0264D] the Holy Spirit by whom Jesus was led into the desert was in Simeon; and Simeon came into the temple through his power.

“And when his parents brought in the child Jesus, to do for him according to the custom of the Law, he also received him in his arms” (ibid., 27–28). This indeed happened by the Lord’s just arrangement, so that the righteous man who for a long time had served Christ’s divinity with the devotion of his heart might now, as though placed at the end of his life, serve his body also with the service of his own body, and thus end his devout life with a death worthy of it.

“And he blessed God” (ibid., 28). By blessing God—that is, by giving him thanks—he deserved to be blessed by him. To bless God is to desire to be blessed by God and to give him thanks.

The blessed old man knew through the Holy Spirit, with whom he was filled, that through Christ’s incarnation [Col. 0265A] both original sin had been forgiven him and the guilt that he had contracted through himself. Therefore he rejoiced inwardly and was glad outwardly, saying: “Now you dismiss your servant, Lord, according to your word, in peace” (Luke II, 29).

He calls himself a servant and calls Christ Lord—a servant, certainly, of that Lord, and dismissed according to what he had promised him. The holy prophet is believed to have been both sent and dismissed. Where was he sent? From where was he dismissed? He was dismissed from the tribulation of the world, from the first transgression, and from personal offense, and was sent into peace. For no one can possess the peace that Simeon had unless he becomes alienated from this world and is released from the burden of sins.

“Because my eyes have seen your salvation” (ibid., 30). The one whom he saw as a human being with the eyes of his body, he believed in his heart and confessed with his voice to be the Savior of the world. 379 [Col. 0265B] Thus the intention of this venerable old man’s heart concerned his own righteousness, while the confession of his mouth concerned the salvation of his neighbors.

“Which you have prepared before the face of all peoples” (ibid., 31). This salvation of God, prepared—that is, set before all for salvation—was not seen by all peoples with bodily or spiritual eyes. But it is said to have been prepared before the face of all peoples because people from every nation believed in Christ, and those who believed beheld him with their eyes.

“A light for revelation to the Gentiles” (ibid., 32). By this light the Gentiles who, worshiping foreign gods, had hidden themselves from the face of the Creator were revealed; by this light those who had been lost were found. They were also enlightened by this light, because through this light they received the light [Col. 0265C] of faith.

Christ is the light. He not only enlightens the Gentiles but is the light of all who are enlightened, whether inwardly in the soul or outwardly in the body. Concerning this light the Prophet says: “Approach him, and be enlightened, and your faces shall not be confounded” (Ps. XXXIII, 6). For the things done in darkness are evil and worthy of shame. Hence the Lord says in the Gospel: “Everyone who does evil hates the light and does not come to the light, lest his evil works be revealed” (John III, 20).

The light prepared for the revelation of the Gentiles was also prepared for the glory of the people of the Jews (Luke II, 32). That people was greatly enlightened and is especially his own, because it was chosen before the other nations. From that people he chose patriarchs, prophets, and holy apostles, 380 [Col. 0265D] and from those who belonged to that people he made keepers of livestock, rulers of peoples, and lords. He gave this people the Law and the promises, and much else in every way, as the apostle Paul bears witness.

Beyond all the other things he had given them, he chose from them his mother, and from their flesh he assumed flesh. The flesh of all human beings is indeed one, made from one clay. Yet Christ willed to receive flesh more particularly from the people of Israel, for their greater glory, rather than from another nation. In this flesh his honorable Virgin Mother conceived and bore him, and, as the cause of salvation and an example of humility, offered him in the temple as a living and life-giving sacrifice, a fragrance of sweetness.

Truly the good Mary bore Christ, and in Christ she bore Christians. [Col. 0266A] She is therefore the mother of Christ and the mother of Christians. If she is the mother of Christ, she is certainly the mother of Christians; it is therefore clear that Christ and Christians are brothers. Christ is not only the brother of Christians but the father of all human beings, and especially of Christians.

We are indeed Christians; but by our will, wickedness, and manifold evil we have degenerated from such a great brotherhood and made ourselves unworthy of the inheritance of so great a Father. Therefore let us turn back to his mother, and through her to him, who in a devout and merciful dispensation willed his mother to be our mother, so that she might bring us help in our need.

And since we know our Redeemer to be most ready to forgive, and since we have his glorious mother as our help, if we are willing, we must not lie prostrate [Col. 0266B] in sins but rise again quickly. And because by our merits we can accomplish little—indeed, absolutely nothing—let us seek counsel elsewhere. Nothing remains for us to do except through the mercy of the Redeemer and the help of his mother.

Therefore, brothers, let us humbly confess that we are wretched and unhappy, and let us pray with fear joined to love to the good mother of the Lord, Mary the devout Virgin, that she not be indignant with us sinners, whom we have never honored as we ought but have provoked to anger by many injuries. Let her not remember the injuries; rather, let her be overcome by the love with which she bore us, and let her remain with us in the compassion of a mother, as though we had already been assigned to punishment for our sins.

Let the most merciful mother undertake our cause and conduct our business, and let her help us so that, raised from the death [Col. 0266C] of sins by her aid, she may lead us with the light of faith and wisdom into the temple of heavenly glory, and offer us to her Son. Let her place us at his feet and, in Jerusalem, which is the vision of peace, make us remain with the righteous Simeon through her holy prayers. May the Son of God and son of the Virgin, Jesus Christ our Lord, deign to grant us this. He, one God, lives and reigns with his Father and the Holy Spirit in one and equal glory and majesty, throughout all ages of ages. Amen.

## SERMON VIII. ON EVERY FESTIVAL OF THE BLESSED MARY, MOTHER OF THE LORD

We rightly celebrate this day as a festival, brothers, since we know it to have been consecrated to the honor of the glorious mother of the Lord, the most blessed [Col. 0266D] and incomparable Virgin Mary. For she alone conceived as a virgin, gave birth as a virgin, and after childbirth remained inviolate in mind and body as a virgin.

Just as a ray proceeds from a star, so the Son of God proceeded from Mary. The star is not corrupted when the ray proceeds from it, nor is the blessed mother violated when her Son is born. Certainly, the divine birth of this virgin brought her fertility and preserved her virginity. And just as he willed that one person—God himself and a human being—should truly come to be in her, so he willed that she herself should become one person, mother and virgin.

Let us therefore call this birth blessed—indeed, let us believe it with certain faith to be most blessed—the birth by which the singular and honorable Queen of Heaven, the Virgin Mary, brought forth Christ to the world, not through the merits of the world but through the grace of God. This virgin ineffably conceived and gave birth ineffably to the true Son of God, a true human being [Col. 0267A]; and in her conception and childbirth she received holiness and incorruption in far greater measure than she had possessed before.

If it is asked why this holy virgin so pleased the Son of God, the answer is: by the love and humility with which she first consecrated her virginity to the Lord. For divine Wisdom itself says: “I love those who love me” (Prov. VIII, 17). Truly the Wisdom of God loved Mary, and Mary loved—and loved greatly—the Wisdom of God, namely, God the Father’s Son.

Each loved the other, but God loved more greatly, since he both knew how and was able to love more greatly. He loved her above the blessed company of the apostles, angels, and archangels, and above all the powers and authorities of heaven.

To this most blessed virgin God [Col. 0267B] the Father sent the Son begotten from himself, so that the Son of God himself might also become the virgin’s son and bridegroom. The Father arranged this in love; the Son fulfilled it by his will; the Holy Spirit prepared and adorned the bridal chamber—that is, he cleansed the virgin’s womb from every corruption of sin and filled it with manifold holiness.

There, as in a royal hall, God, who had created all things beforehand, created himself in Mary. Let no one be surprised that we have called her son her bridegroom. The Father and bridegroom of this virgin is her Son: plainly the Father, because she was created by him; the Son, because he was born from her; and the bridegroom, because she was joined to him in love.

A wondrous marriage, but wondrous in faith and devotion: there the virgin became mother, virginity became wife, the Holy Spirit became husband, conception took place through the ear, the angel became the interpreter of conception, the seed [Col. 0267C] became Christ, and the Son of God became the virgin’s offspring.

In this most holy union, flesh did not carnally touch flesh; rather, God the Father poured his Wisdom into the virgin’s womb. Wisdom both assumed flesh in the Virgin Mother, preserved his most blessed mother incorrupt, and, proceeding through the virginal body, caused the Word whom Mary had conceived through the angelic word to appear as true God in a true human being.

Truly the true Son of God, Christ the Lord, assumed in a true virgin the whole human being, namely, soul and flesh. In this flesh the human being was born for the human being. In this flesh he redeemed humanity upon the cross. In this flesh the human being killed Christ. The human being was redeemed both in soul and in body, 384 [Col. 0267D] but this flesh of the Lord was the price of his redemption.

He gave this flesh, under the appearance of bread, to his disciples to eat at the supper that he held with them as his last supper before his Passion. Therefore he declared to them, saying: “This is my body” (Luke XXII, 19). And because he was speaking specifically of his own body, he added: “which will be delivered for you” (ibid.).

Let no one hesitate over the fact that Christ fed his disciples with his flesh, since this food must be understood as food for souls rather than for bodies. For if Christ’s flesh were not food for souls, Christ would never have given it to his disciples after bodily food. By the death of his flesh he redeemed his own; by that same flesh he also spiritually nourished the souls of his own.

God did what he willed, and he was able to do what he willed to do. Otherwise [Col. 0268A] God would not be almighty if he wished to do something that he could not do. The manner in which God did this need not be debated; faith is to be given, and that is sufficient. For these works of God are known by faith, not by sophistical contention.

He himself truly raised this flesh of his from the dead on the third day by the omnipotence of his divinity. In the sight of the apostles he raised it into heaven; in this flesh he will come to judgment with great power and majesty. The wicked will see God in this flesh—not in the humility in which he was unjustly judged for them and by them, but in the sublimity in which he will justly judge them for their crimes.

They will see, I say, him who loved them and whom they hated, namely, their Redeemer; and before the sight of their Redeemer they will perish. But the righteous, beyond anything that can be said or imagined, will rejoice at the good news, 385 [Col. 0268B] and will exult.

For they will hear the Son of God himself calling them and saying: “Come, blessed of my Father; receive the kingdom prepared for you from the foundation of the world” (Matt. XXV, 34). On that day, human beings who in this world are humble and obedient will enter that heavenly and exalted homeland, with their leader and head Christ, in great honor and exultation—an inheritance from which the proud and disobedient angels fell with great shame and confusion.

There human beings will see God face to face, as he is, and eternal life, salvation, and glory will be given to them; and this is God himself. But blessed Mary, the virgin mother and untouched bride, will there obtain, as the most devout one before her most devout Son, that none of those for [Col. 0268C] whom she has prayed even once should perish.

Nor is this surprising, because by her prayers she can save the whole world, if she so wills. Indeed, she would be most ready to pray for the whole world, and the whole world would be saved if it made itself worthy of her prayers. This most truthful Virgin can obtain through prayer from her almighty Son whatever she desires, as we have said; but she does not pray at all for those who always desire to sin. For those of this kind cannot please God in any way.

No saint dares to intercede for such people, nor do almsgiving, for the obtaining of eternal life, or sacrifices benefit them. Hence Paul the apostle, the chief teacher of Christian doctrine, says: “After receiving knowledge of the truth, no sacrifice for sins is left for us [Col. 0268D] who sin willingly” (Heb. X, 16). It is as though he were saying: No baptized person can reconcile God to himself after sin so long as he remains in the will to sin.

The other saints pray to the Lord God, and by praying obtain their requests. But the honorable Virgin Mary, if she is rightly believed to entreat him insofar as he is God and Lord, is nevertheless, insofar as he is human and born from her, believed in devout faith to obtain from him whatever she wishes, as though by a certain authority of a mother.

For if any saint obtains from God, the just judge, whatever is justly due to him, she who is the mother of the Judge and the mistress of all the saints will never be deprived of what belongs to her by right as a mother. This is the dignity of maternal right among sons who are exalted as lords: when their mothers ask them repeatedly, because they are lords, they sometimes also command them, because they are sons.

The good of nature that God gave to human beings, he who is the highest good, and from whom all good things proceed, will never deny to himself. And since this blessed Virgin, the Mother of the Lord, is read to have done this on earth, it should not unjustly be doubted that she would do it also in heaven.

When the wine ran out at the wedding in Cana of Galilee, the Mother of Jesus—namely, the Virgin Mary—said to Jesus, her Son: “They have no wine,” as though she were commanding him to make those who had no wine have some. 387 [Col. 0269A] This good mother commanded the deed out of devotion, and the good Son fulfilled it through devout obedience.

Let us hesitate at nothing in praising this virgin. For the one who praises the mother honors the Son; without praising her, it is impossible to please God, and with her praise no one can displease [Col. 0269B] him.

Let us therefore praise this most holy and wondrous virgin, because we cannot please the Son of the Virgin without praising his virgin mother. Let us love her as the dearest Mother of the Lord, whom he loves as his own flesh. He determined to approve and honor her praiseworthy virginity so greatly that he preferred that some should doubt his origin rather than the integrity of her virginity.

This is the sweetest mother, the Virgin Mary, who gave birth to the death of death, to human life, to the confusion of the devil, to the absolution of sins, and to the blessedness of all the righteous. A wondrous thing—but one to be wondered at with joy and faith! The human being born from this virgin is not only King of human beings but also Creator and Lord of angels and of all the heavenly powers.

This is she whom the angels [Col. 0269C] serve and the archangels attend; the entire army of the heavenly host also praises and venerates this virgin. After God alone, she holds primacy over all creatures.

O how venerable, how exalted is this most blessed mother, whose Son, although he is almighty God, has never been able to deny her anything! This virgin, so holy, so glorious, so honored, and so exalted by God, is so humble, so compassionate, so merciful and devout that, for the sake of a sinful soul already assigned to eternal punishments, she has opposed herself to the severity of the strict judge.

A certain Christian, Theophilus by name, as is truthfully related, had been driven to such despair by his misfortunes and deceived by a certain Jew that [Col. 0269D] he had denied Christ the Lord and his most holy Mother, renounced the Christian faith that he had received in baptism, worshiped the devil himself, and made him a written charter of this detestable deed, sealed with his own ring.

Afterward, however, touched by the mercy of divine compassion, he turned to the most merciful Mother of the Lord, Mary the most devout Virgin, to seek counsel and help. He rightly reflected that none of the saints, neither an angel nor any heavenly power, had as much power with God as his mother. He also considered that a son avenges an injury done to his mother more seriously than one done to himself, and that he would in no way leave it unavenged unless she first pleaded for the one who had injured her.

Thus he confessed to the glorious Virgin Mother, weeping bitterly, the bitterness of his sinful offense [Col. 0270A]; he struck his breast with blows, pleaded with continual groans, and entreated her constantly, more by the intention of his heart than by words.

But let us carefully hear what the Mother of mercy did. She consoles the sinner and, as though making his sin her own through compassion, takes up the sinner’s case in order to plead for him before the Judge. The merciful mother pleads for the wretched man before the merciful Son; mercy frees the wretched man from misery.

This sinner weeps, as we have said, but bitterly. The mother approaches, pleading for the sinful son; the Son looks upon the sinner; sin departs from the sinner. The Virgin powerfully commands the devil, the deceiver, to return the charter of the deceived man; the unwilling and ashamed accuser obeys. The man receives the charter through the Virgin’s hand [Col. 0270B], absolved; and, pouring forth abundant tears for joy, he offers to God and to his most blessed mother no small praises and manifold thanksgivings.

This is the praiseworthy and universal empress of angels and human beings, the most holy Virgin. Although she was created by the Creator of all, in her the Creator himself became a creature. She is the daughter of God, but also the incorrupt mother of God and of a human being.

After her Son, she is the chief refuge for sinners, to which they may flee after their fall; counsel, so that they may repent; and help, so that they may be converted and not perish. No wound of sin or crime is so serious that, if she wills, it cannot have her as its remedy. She desires confession and repentance for sins in human beings, so that she may have an opportunity to plead for them.

Therefore, humbly entreating this most excellent [Col. 0270C] and devout Mother of the Lord, Mary ever Virgin, let us not delay confessing what we have done badly for any reason, and through her supplications let us commend ourselves and all our actions to the Lord. Thus may we deserve to reach him who is justly angry with sinners but mercifully forgives penitents. May this be granted by him who for us became human from her, Christ our Lord, who with the Father and the Holy Spirit lives and reigns as God throughout all ages of ages. Amen.

## SERMON IX. ON THE FESTIVAL OF THE BLESSED MARY MAGDALENE.

We have heard, brothers, when the Gospel was read, [Col. 0270D] that a certain Pharisee asked the Lord to dine with him (Luke 7:36). Although the Lord, who knows all things, was not unaware of the Pharisee’s pride, nevertheless he entered the Pharisee’s house and reclined at table. From this we should thoughtfully consider how greatly God loves charity, since he does not reject even the appearance of charity. For the Pharisee was exceedingly proud and therefore could not possess charity. When, then, he invited the Lord to dine with him, he displayed not the virtue he did not possess, but the appearance of charity.

Meanwhile, a woman who was a sinner in that city, when she learned that the gracious Jesus had reclined in the Pharisee’s house, brought an alabaster flask of ointment. Standing behind him at the Lord’s feet, she humbly began to bathe his feet with her tears, to wipe them with the hair of her head, and to kiss them; [Col. 0271A] and then she did not cease anointing them with the ointment she had brought. There is no doubt that this sinful woman was Mary Magdalene. At first she had been a notorious sinner, but afterward she became a glorious preacher.

When she learned that the Savior was with the Pharisee—humility, that is, with pride—she chose rather to trust in the Savior’s compassion than to fear the Pharisee’s severity. Her fragile sex feared the Pharisee, a merciless and excessively harsh man who despised the woman, considered her alien to salvation, and utterly disdained to be touched by her. But God, the fountain of goodness and source of compassion, humble and seeking humble sinners, not to condemn them but to justify them, did not despise the sinful woman. He did not withdraw his feet from her, but surrendered them to her, and received her service with great gratitude.

When she first approached the Lord, let us listen attentively to what she did. She stood behind him at his feet and wept, because, although she presumed greatly upon the Lord’s mercy, the accusing consciousness of her sins pressed heavily upon her. Thus, while love gave this sinful woman hope and the memory of her sins inspired fear, she was almost uncertain what to do. The recollection and fear of her crimes held her back from approaching Christ more closely, while hope and love prevented her from remaining away from him any longer.
