At last, when fear had been harmoniously joined to good hope, both became guides for the sinful woman. Together they led her to the feet of the most gracious Savior, until she could hold them; there they happily commended her, laying her low in devotion. [Col. 0271C]

Blessed are such guides, who always lead to Christ! And blessed is the sinful woman who deserved to have such guidance! Let us recognize, beloved, that hope and fear are so necessary to one another that we should never believe one can benefit us without the other. Fear without hope is despair; hope without fear is foolish presumption.

Behold, the sinful woman holds the feet she had long desired to hold and pours her tears over them. [Col. 0271D] We do not read that she spoke there, but that she wept; nevertheless, we believe that she spoke most eloquently, through tears rather than words. For the speech of tears is exceedingly fruitful before the good God. While the woman kept silence with her mouth, the tear conducted her case; while her tongue was silent, the tear confessed more effectively and pleaded more becomingly.

It was fitting that the holy sinner, while she wept, remained silent, lest she perhaps say less than she had wickedly done. The prayers of tears are certainly much better than those of words. Someone who prays in words sometimes gives offense; a tear, however, scarcely knows how to offend. Words sometimes fail to express the whole matter; a tear always reveals the entire feeling of the mind. Therefore the woman no longer used the words by which she had deceived many and, in deceiving them, had greatly sinned. She did not wish to be believed less readily in confessing by means of the words she had been accustomed to use in sinning. For much human falsehood makes a person suspect even when speaking the truth.

Thus she preferred to conduct her case before the judge, from whom the secrets of the heart are not hidden, by means of weeping, and to erase through tears what she had done wrong with her voice. Certainly God himself, the fountain of mercies, had bestowed upon the sinful woman a fountain of tears. The fountain did not dry up of itself, because an unfailing natural spring watered it abundantly. [Col. 0272A]

With her hair she wiped the feet she had washed with her tears. In this she showed us an example of fortitude. For when, by humbly weeping, we wash away our sins and crimes, it is greatly necessary that thereafter, by the reasoning of the mind—which is our strength—we avoid not only crimes but also sins. Thus tears preach the extinction of sins not by word but by action; and the wiping with her hair indicates the exercise of fortitude, since afterward we must avoid sins.

Although hair may seem to be superfluous upon the head, it sometimes represents human strength. This is clearly shown in Samson, that man of extraordinary strength, whose greatest power is reported to have been in his hair. [Col. 0272B] Hence the Savior also says to his disciples: “All the hairs of your head are numbered” (Matthew 10:30). He does not mean that the hairs which are accustomed either to be cut and thrown away by the blade or to fall out and perish with the passing of time have been numbered. Rather, he called the virtues of the soul and the multitude of the senses that proceeded from the principal part of the mind, as from the head of the apostles, “the hairs of your head.” These hairs were indeed found in the Nazirites; with these cords, so to speak, they bound foreigners.

She kisses the feet she had washed with her tears and, as we have said, wiped with her hair. A kiss is the most intimate sign of peace and concord. Behold how great is the fruit of fortitude and tears: it establishes peace and concord between a deeply guilty servant woman and God, the most just judge.

Truly, I shall call this woman very guilty, but also very glorious. She is not glorious because of the same thing by which she is guilty—for she was very guilty when, by sinning, she despised the Lord—but she became very glorious when she loved him. When this woman anointed the Lord’s feet with the ointment she had brought with her, the fragrant medicine of her good action—an action she spread far and wide throughout the whole world—she healed and continues daily to heal not only her own wounds but also those of many sinners by soothing them. [Col. 0272C]

For who, hearing of Mary’s sins, could fail to hope for forgiveness, if he wishes to repent perfectly? It is impious to believe that someone should be assigned to eternal punishment who, after sinning, repents and keeps the Lord’s commandments.

This woman, I say, is read to have been possessed by seven demons; that is, she is said to have been filled with the whole multitude of vices. But when, with a contrite heart, she returns to the most merciful Lord—or rather, when she is mercifully drawn by him to himself—she is immediately cleansed from the filth of her sins and crimes. She who had previously been the possession of demons is entirely filled with the grace of the Holy Spirit. Thus, from a pitiable sinner she becomes a blessed disciple and thereafter diligently serves the Lord throughout her life.

Among the services this holy woman rendered him, although the whole world knows of them, I have considered it irreligious to pass over one in silence. When our Lord and Savior Jesus Christ was reclining with his disciples in the house of Simon, about to dine, this woman approached him. As she had fittingly been accustomed to do, she brought ointment and, with great devotion, poured it over his head—something the apostles themselves would never have presumed to do. [Col. 0273A]

O how blessed is the woman who, previously a humble sinner, anointed the Lord’s feet with fear of the Lord, and afterward, burning with love for her Creator no less than Peter himself, deserved to anoint his head! Peter denies him whom the woman proclaims, and by a mystical anointing she declares him to be the God of all.

This, I say, is that good woman who first came to the tomb with the devotion of pure love. This is truly the woman who there wept blessed tears. Christ, rising from the dead, first appeared to her; and she was the first to announce to the apostles that he had risen. [Col. 0273B]

She is an example of repentance and a hope of forgiveness for sinners. She does not permit even a sinner guilty of many crimes to despair, provided that he repents of his offenses and turns to the Lord with his heart.

Furthermore, she is not ignorant of human frailty, for which she continually implores divine compassion. Let us appeal especially to her, after the Lord and his most holy Mother, the wondrous and incomparable Virgin. Let us implore her with tears rather than words, so that she who, by the Lord’s favor, obtained forgiveness of her offenses through tears may, by her holy intercession, make her propitiator favorable to us sinners. Having received remission of our sins, may she admit us within the gate of paradise [Col. 0273C] and present us holy and immaculate before his divine presence.

She, as we have said, is especially to be invoked by us; she is to be humbly and frequently entreated to act as our patron. For by experience she learned what is most necessary for sinners: how human frailty falls by itself, how it rises through divine assistance, and she learned whatever lies within and whatever lies without.

Although still ignorant of the divine mystery, she had first fallen by sinning; but from her fall she rose stronger than she would have been had she never fallen through sin. For what bonds of sin would not be loosened by the outpouring of holy tears over the Savior’s feet? What wound of crime would not be healed by that anointing of the Redeemer’s head, celebrated with such devotion?

O [Col. 0273D] how pure and prudent was the intention of this penitent woman! Although the compassionate Lord had forgiven whatever she had done wrong, she thereafter pursued and, as it were, hated her own flesh. She chastised it with continual fasts, wearied it with long and constant prayer and vigils, and carefully subjected it to the law of the mind and reason. This was not because holy flesh resisted the spirit, but so that she might offer to her propitiator from her flesh not merely a daily sacrifice of praise, but a continual one.

O how venerable is this disciple of truth! After receiving from the Lord Jesus Christ absolution from all her sins, after his resurrection and ascension into heaven, and after the coming of the Holy Spirit, she avoided the hatred of the Jews, bade her homeland its final farewell, and joyfully accepted exile for the love of her Creator. [Col. 0274A]

She therefore departed from her own territory, constantly preaching the Lord Jesus Christ as the true God and bearing witness to the truth of his resurrection. She remained in this assertion of the truth until the end of her life.

This holy woman offered to those needing correction a lesson in correction, and to those already corrected an example of virtue. Her prayer is a remedy for sin, and her devout tongue has become the gatekeeper of heaven. She opens the gate to every truly penitent person; no sinner is excluded by her except one who, remaining impenitent, refuses to enter.

To this glorious woman, then, my brothers, let us commend our souls and bodies with complete attention and strength, so that through her aid and intercession we may be received within that gate of blessedness and may deserve to reach the one whom she herself has already happily reached, and to see and possess our Lord Jesus Christ, [Col. 0274B] who with the Father and the Holy Spirit lives and reigns as God throughout all ages of ages. Amen.

## SERMON X. ON THE THIEF SAVED ON THE CROSS

In the passion of our Savior, that thief who had been placed on the left, who flattered the Jews and reviled Christ, ended a bad life with a worse death and received what he deserved. Therefore it is vain labor and useless delay to speak at length about him. Let us speak instead about the other thief, about whom the subject is faithful and the cause salutary.

This man, who had been placed on the right, suffered not because he had believed in Christ, but believed while he was suffering. With bodily sight he saw Christ, a man crucified with nails on the cross, stretched out with his whole body; he saw in him the wounds of thorns, [Col. 0274C] the blood streaming from his limbs, and only the signs of affliction and death, as in a man about to die. But when faith had been conceived and born in him through the work of the Holy Spirit, he contemplated with angelic eyes the immortal and divine majesty of Christ. He admired, adored, praised, and confessed him.

From the cross he fought for the faith; he rebuked his blaspheming companion and condemned the unbelief of the Jews who were present. He neither flattered them nor feared them.

Wondrous is divine power! The cross, which had previously been carried for punishment, now supplies aid toward a reward; and the guilty man who was being condemned on the cross for his crime produces from his guilt an antidote by which he is healed, and from the cross brings about a mystery. Guilt is changed into repentance, and the destruction of death into eternal life.

This is indeed a blessed exchange, nor is the one that follows less so. A thief becomes a confessor, and a martyr emerges from a confessor. The torments that had begun in the thief now, through a new grace, receive the lot of a martyr’s crown and reward.

This blessed and wondrous man lacked no sacrament of salvation. For what Christ visibly performs in other Christians through his ministers, he invisibly performed in this man through himself. Thus, through Christ, he received baptism on the cross, together with the other sacraments of the faith. For unless he had been baptized by Christ and had become a wholly perfect Christian, Christ would certainly not have said to him: “Today you will be with me in paradise” (Luke 23:43). [Col. 0275A] For he had already said: “No one will enter the kingdom of heaven unless he has been born again of water and the Holy Spirit” (John 3:5).

Let us see how perfect this blessed man was made by God. He came to faith at the very time when Peter abandoned the faith; and what the apostle had lost, the thief found on the following day. At the voice of a servant girl, the first shepherd of the Church denied that he knew the one whom the thief publicly proclaimed. The man whom the chief of the apostolic election denied even knowing as a human being, the thief openly and devoutly confessed to be God.

The whole company of the blessed apostles, having abandoned the Lord, was disturbed and fled amid the fury of the Jews. The thief remained fearless among the raging Jews, asserted Christ’s innocence, and was not ashamed publicly to declare himself guilty, nor to confess his guilt.

Thus he asked Christ for forgiveness and prayed for mercy, saying: “Remember me, Lord, when you come into your kingdom” (Luke 23:42). Christ sympathizes with the man asking forgiveness and shows mercy to him who implores mercy. God crucified in a human being speaks thus to the thief crucified beside him: “Today you will be with me in paradise.”

This thief, placed on the cross, had already first received the confirmation which the apostles received through the Holy Spirit on the day of Pentecost. He neither feared Jewish faithlessness nor carried the name of Christ in secret. As a perfect Christian, a devout confessor, and a glorious martyr, he bore it openly.

The apostles had been called and chosen by Christ. They had often heard from him, privately and publicly, words of eternal life. They had seen him give sight to the blind, cleanse lepers, cast out demons, and raise the dead. They had also recognized in him many things that no one else could do except God alone. In his name they themselves did what he did.

But in his passion, which he had foretold to them, they were so disturbed that they neither recognized him nor remembered what they themselves had been through his power. [Col. 0275C]

The holy thief had previously known neither the faith nor holiness, since he had never received the beginning of a good life. In Christ’s death, however, he recognized the truth of the faith that Peter had learned in the presence of Christ’s bodily divinity and from Christ himself as his teacher.

A wondrous thing! Where the apostle laid down the faith, the thief received it. If this man had known Christ earlier, he would certainly have believed, and in that blessed assembly of the apostles he would not have been last who proved first in the kingdom and second to no one in faith.

Both things—the denial of the first chosen man during Christ’s passion and the venerable thief’s confession on the cross—came about according to the design of heavenly medicine. The chosen apostle was permitted to fall so that everyone might learn not to presume upon himself because of any perfection. The thief who had fallen was raised up so that no one might despair of his own imperfection, provided only that he repents and confesses worthily.

In the one, God chastises with the rod of justice; in the other, he supports with the staff of mercy. In the former he instills fear in the righteous, lest they fall into pride; in the latter he grants hope to sinners, lest they fall into despair.

Let us say briefly something that may truly be said about Peter and the thief. Peter was called and chosen by Christ; the thief was chosen but not called. Peter became an apostle and martyr; the thief became a confessor and martyr. In good works, virtues, miracles, labors, and the power of binding and loosing, Peter was far superior to the thief. If the thief was not greater than Peter in faith, nevertheless he was not inferior.

Both were exceedingly good, but in the matters we have mentioned the thief was inferior to Peter. Whoever of these two is less powerful before God obtains from him what he asks, requests, and desires.

Let us therefore diligently pray both to blessed Peter, chief and prince of the apostles, and to that glorious confessor and martyr named Dimas, so that by their prayers and merits before our good Creator and loving Redeemer they may obtain for us that he himself, at the end of our life, may guard our souls from the power of the devil. When he comes into his kingdom, into that royal and wondrous glory in which he will judge the living and the dead, may he deign to remember us and say to each of us: “Today you will be with me in paradise”—he who lives and reigns as the one God with the Father and the Holy Spirit throughout all ages of ages. Amen.

## 402 SERMON XI. ON THE FEAST OF BLESSED BENEDICT

Although, beloved brothers, we ought to celebrate the feasts of other saints with devout love, this holy solemnity of our most blessed Father Benedict demands from us, as though by a debt, special honor and devotion. For this glorious saint proved to be both the inventor and the author of our second regeneration.

The monastic way of life, I say, which he instituted, is rightly called a second regeneration and is also not unreasonably compared with episcopal confirmation. Through the observance of this life, past sins are erased, as in baptism, and the Christian is fortified against future sins, as in confirmation. By this blessed life those who had previously died through sinning in secular conduct are brought to life; and afterward, when the permission to sin is put to death by strict correction, the Christian soul is admirably fortified, since only the ability to do good is left to it.

Celebrating, therefore, the feast day of this most holy and honorable man with due reverence and special devotion, let us rejoice. We have no doubt that the angels, archangels, and all the orders of heaven rejoice in his blessed and friendly company and praise the Son of God with him.

Benedict received the blessed name “Benedict” from the grace of heavenly blessing, but the holy man did not prove ungrateful to grace. While he was still a boy, he rejected every childish pursuit. Retaining only humility, patience, and innocence in his devout heart, he abandoned worldly society and commended himself entirely to the Lord.

He therefore scorned the study of letters to which his parents had entrusted him, lest love of his parents or their riches alter his resolve for a better life. Fleeing from them as though he hated them, while he desired to gain Christ’s riches through a poor life, he judged worthless and almost impious what many others regard as dear and pious. [Col. 0277A]

Thus the servant of God was filled with divine inspiration. His still tender and delicate flesh was strengthened by the steadfastness of his mind and the vigor of his spirit. If violence was necessary, he did not hesitate to inflict it upon himself, so that, crucified, he might follow the crucified Lord.

Only his nurse followed this servant of the Lord. She had nursed him tenderly and he loved her with considerable affection. She was not inflamed with love of holiness, but desired, out of carnal affection, to serve him even against his will. The blessed man, however, wanted rather to serve God than to be served by a human being. There was piety in the hearts of both, but their intention was very different, although it appeared friendly: she planned to serve the flesh, while he intended to serve the spirit.

They went together like mother and son until they came to a place called Effide. There, for the love of Christ, a poor man received the poor man of Christ and his nurse as guests.

When his nurse had received from neighboring women a sieve in which she was to clean a small quantity of grain given to them for the love of God, she placed the vessel carelessly upon the table. It fell and broke so completely that it was found divided into two pieces. When she saw the sieve lent to her broken, and recognized that the people of that region were grasping and persistently demanding the return of what was theirs, while she had absolutely no means of repairing another person’s loss, she began to weep and fill the house where they had been received with tearful cries.

But when the devout and holy boy heard and saw his nurse crying and weeping, he made her anxiety his own through compassionate feeling. He took the two pieces of the broken sieve and, with tears, offered the sacrifice of prayer to the Lord with complete devotion of mind. When his prayer was finished, the sieve was found so sound and whole that it seemed never to have been broken. [Col. 0277C]

The devout soul received it with thanksgiving to almighty God; consoling his nurse with holy and humble words, he returned the sieve to her. Although she was astonished by the miracle, the sound sieve nevertheless greatly rejoiced her, since its being broken had caused her no small grief.

When the inhabitants of that place learned what had happened, not without great amazement, they hung the vessel above the doors of the church that had been built there in honor of blessed Peter, so that everyone, present and future, might recognize how perfect a service the faithful servant of the Lord, Benedict, had begun to render him.

Filled with the grace of the Holy Spirit, receiving human praise and blame with the same disposition, he secretly left his nurse and sought the seclusion of a deserted place, friendly to religious life. While he was traveling there, he met a monk named Romanus. After carefully questioning him, Benedict eventually disclosed to him, under the form of confession, the secret of his devout purpose.

When the monk Romanus learned of his soul’s devotion to Christ, he did not act as an envious detractor of another’s holiness. Rather, he proved a devout conciliator and helper. To the man whose virtue he had already conceived in his mind, he gave the religious habit.

Benedict, a worshiper of God and one who despised himself, reached a place called Sublacus. Among clefts in the rocks he withdrew into a very narrow cave. There, mortifying the desires of the flesh through the reasoning of the mind, he remained for three years unknown to everyone except the monk Romanus.

Romanus piously absented himself from the sight of his abbot, Adeodatus, at whatever times he could, and carried to Benedict the bread he withheld from his own body. He could not come to the aforementioned cave, which the servant of God possessed in place of a homeland, because the ascent was too difficult. But on a rock that rose above it he fastened a very long rope, to which he tied bread. He also attached a small bell, so that by the sound of the bell the holy man might know that Romanus had come to him with the bread.

But the devil, the enemy of God’s friends, threw a stone and broke the bell attached to the rope, in order both to extinguish the fire of charity in Romanus and to turn Benedict’s mind away from his good purpose, perhaps by compelling him through hunger. [Col. 0278B]

Nevertheless, the good Romanus did not abandon the work of charity he had begun.

Almighty God, the good Lord who rewards and mercifully pardons, had determined to repay the blessed man Benedict a hundredfold in this world. In Benedict’s heart and body the world and its flower had entirely withered from love of the heavenly homeland. God wished that, once the first promise had been fulfilled, Benedict might know with certainty that he would receive the second—namely, eternal life—as one who had perfectly despised worldly imperfection.

Therefore the Lord deigned to appear in a vision to a certain devout priest who was preparing food for himself on Easter Day. He earnestly addressed him, saying: “You have prepared delicate food for yourself, while my servant Benedict is being tormented by hunger.”

Although the priest did not know either the place or the servant of the Lord, he immediately arose and took with him whatever he had prepared to eat, intending to feed the man of God. Because he did not delay in obeying the divine admonition, he could not lack the Holy Spirit as the guide of his journey. With the Spirit going before him, he came to the place where the holy man was hiding in concealment.

Benedict, who desired to please God alone, was so removed not only from human knowledge but even from knowledge of what was happening in the world that he was completely unaware when Easter or any other solemnity was being celebrated.

After prayer and sweet conversation concerning eternal life, the priest who had come to him addressed the saint in this way: “Rise, and let us both eat together, because today the Easter solemnity is being celebrated.”

The man of God immediately replied: “I know that it is Easter, because my humility has deserved to see you.”

The honorable priest again affirmed: “Truly, today is the day of the Lord’s resurrection. You may not abstain on so glorious a feast. Therefore I have been sent by the Lord, so that I may give you the food I had prepared for myself.”

Thus they blessed the Lord and ate together. After they had finished their meal and holy conversation, the priest returned to the church he governed. God had wished to show through him an example of good living to human beings; the priest could neither conceal nor wished to conceal what had happened. [Col. 0279A]

When the report of Benedict’s holy way of life spread everywhere, his name became widely known throughout the world. A lamp placed upon a lampstand cannot remain hidden; so Benedict’s lamp, dispelling the darkness of human sins and illuminating people’s minds with the radiance of good action, turned them toward love of their Creator.

This man’s life was praiseworthy, and the deeds he accomplished in this world with the Lord’s cooperation are wondrous—indeed, astonishing to faith. For apart from the Rule of the Monks, in which every perfection of human beings is found and which he wrote under the dictation of the Holy Spirit, he himself lived no less perfectly than he taught.

He is truly recognized as an imitator of all the holy and venerable Fathers who have existed from the beginning of the world. It is believed without doubt that he performed either an equal work or one similar to the work they performed.

Therefore, in the second book of the Dialogues of Saint Gregory, that teacher of a praiseworthy life who wrote Benedict’s venerable life, he is rightly proclaimed to have possessed not merely the spirit of all the righteous, but to have been filled with the spirit of all the righteous. [Col. 0279B]

We must not remain silent, but must state truthfully why the monk Romanus was then permitted to perform any good work without the permission of his abbot, whereas monks are not permitted to do so now. This becomes sufficiently clear if time and the order of time are carefully considered.

There were abbots and institutions of abbots before Saint Benedict, just as Moses existed as a lawgiver before Christ. Moses brought a good and holy law to the Jewish people, but Christ brought a better one to the Christian people. Likewise, the holy men of that earlier time established rules for monks according to the grace given them by God. But our Father and lawgiver Benedict, just as he received greater grace from God, established a better law.

Whatever those men prescribed to be done, whether less or more, or permitted to be done, Benedict corrected after them. Thus monks are now forbidden to perform good works without the permission of their spiritual father, lest any of them follow his own will under the appearance of piety or of any good work.

Through this the nature and greatness of the virtue of obedience are especially revealed: subjects are commanded not only to avoid evil but also to abstain from certain good works. Since subjects bound by the cords of obedience do not do what seems good to them, it is necessary that those who govern them, for their part, point out the good works they are to perform.

The Lord first instituted this form of obedience for our first parents in paradise. Although he had permitted them all the other trees of paradise, he forbade one, so that they might recognize that they had above them a Lord and master whose will they were bound to obey. They did not sin because the fruit they ate was evil, but because they touched what was good against the Lord’s prohibition. [Col. 0280A]

Saint Benedict understood the virtue of obedience more fully than any abbot before him, whether those abbots had been unwilling to reveal it or had understood it less well.

Romanus is therefore rightly praised for his action, because at that time this and certain other things were permitted to monks that are now forbidden. There are, in fact, certain good things that may at first be permitted but later become unlawful.

The monks of that time were permitted such acts of humanity because they had not promised to abstain from them. But such things can in no way be permitted to monks today, since they have vowed and confirmed by the faith of their profession that they will do neither those nor any other good works without the will of their spiritual father. They have promised before God and his saints to keep this faith of their profession according to the Rule of Saint Benedict.

A woman may also marry if she wishes, because marriage is rightly permitted to her. But if she has vowed virginity and afterward marries, she will be held guilty. Marriage is nevertheless good, but virginity is better than marriage.

Thus every institution of the holy Fathers who preceded Benedict is indeed good, but that of the venerable Benedict is far superior. What the Fathers established before him was hard and harsh, like the law of Moses. The institution of the truly wise Benedict is holy, gentle, and light, and full of the mother of virtues, namely, discretion.

The decree of the ancient Fathers had, as it were, worshipers of the old law. But the devout and discerning Father Benedict, tempering their statutes like the authority of a harsh law, brought us forth as children of the new grace. Almost all those former things have passed away, as old things—or nearly all of them—and behold, through Saint Benedict they have become new.

Those earlier institutions also seemed to be, as it were, a shadow and figure of the future monastic life; but through the praiseworthy Father Benedict, with the Holy Spirit cooperating, the reality was revealed.

Yet, out of his great humility, Saint Benedict praises and admires the life and works of Saint Basil and of the Fathers who preceded him, either saying nothing about his own or speaking of it as though it were insignificant.

The good disciple imitated the excellent Master, who commanded silence when he was performing works that no one else could perform without him.

Indeed, those holy predecessors of ours who went before us to the heavenly dwelling places lived religiously and wrote religiously. But just as, after the three blessed evangelists—Matthew, Luke, and Mark—the fourth, the apostle John, wrote, and wrote better, so this blessed man, after the other Fathers, wrote the Rule of the Monks, by which, as by the cement of a sweeter charity, he joins us more closely to Christ the man, the living stone. [Col. 0280D]

Of him we may truly say, and must firmly believe, that he was sent to us by God like an apostle and an angel. For God sent him to us especially so that, through the example of his formed and beautiful life, he might shape us personally and uniquely, and so that through his teaching and wisdom he might announce to us familiarly the things that are good.

God also decreed that after him he should be the chief Father, shepherd, physician, and teacher of monks.

Let us therefore, beloved friends and brothers, humbly entreat this most blessed man with heart and voice, so that he may deign to be our Father, shepherd, physician, and teacher: may he nourish us with devoted fatherly care, feed our souls with the bread of virtues, heal the wounds of our sins and crimes, and, carefully instructed by his teaching, enable us to perform what is good and to deserve to reach him, [Col. 0282A] who is the giver and rewarder of good works, our God and Lord Jesus, who with the Father and the Holy Spirit lives and reigns throughout all ages of ages. Amen.

## [TREATISE ON THE ORDINATION OF BISHOPS AND ON LAY INVESTITURE]

## [Col. 0281]

### TO THE READER

As you see, I had almost decided to omit this little book, since it seemed to be nothing other than a repetition of several short works—that is, 2, 3, 4, 5, and 6—gathered together into one body.

Afterward, however, it occurred to me that it not only exists in both of our manuscripts, but was also present in the manuscript used by Brother Turrianus. Moreover, in this work the things said in those short works are repeated in such a way that some passages are at times added, removed, or interpolated. It is therefore impossible to doubt that Goffridus is also the author of this little book. Considering it wholly wrong to pass it over, we have therefore taken care to publish it at least here.

## [Col. 0281]

### GOFFRIDUS’S TREATISE ON THE ORDINATION OF BISHOPS AND ON LAY INVESTITURE

[Col. 0281B] Goffridus, humble servant of the monastery of Vendôme, sends to his intimate friend Peter Leo, cardinal of the Holy Roman Church, a wish that he may love the catholic faith with all his heart and attack with all his strength those who oppose it.

Not forgetting your request and my promise, I have tried, if not as I ought, at least as I was able, to fulfill what you asked of me and what I promised: namely, concerning the ordination of a bishop and the investiture of laymen.

First of all, we must firmly believe and in no way doubt that, just as baptism makes a Christian, so election and consecration make a bishop. And just as it is impossible for someone to become a Christian without baptism, so it is impossible for someone to be made a bishop without election and consecration. In the ordination of a bishop, election and consecration are so mutually necessary [Col. 0281C] that consecration without election, and election without consecration, cannot by themselves suffice to make a bishop. For just as in baptism water and the invocation of the Holy Spirit are necessary, and together make a Christian, so in the ordination of a bishop election and consecration are joined by necessity, and together create a bishop. And just as baptism cannot take place through water alone or through the invocation of the Holy Spirit alone, nor can a man be a Christian, so no one can be ordained or made a bishop by election alone or consecration alone.

Great indeed is the sacrament both of baptism and of the election and consecration of a bishop; but the former Christ commanded and performs through others, whereas the latter he accomplished through himself. In baptism a human being is created spiritually and is called a Christian through Christ; in this other sacrament, however, the lord and ruler [Col. 0281D] of Christians is created—one who is called a Christian by Christ not only in name, but is also believed to act in Christ’s place.

It must be understood, however, that here and wherever the election and consecration of a bishop are discussed, a canonical election and a free consecration must necessarily be meant: that is, one who is canonically elected must be freely [Col. 0282B] consecrated. Otherwise a kind of wicked pretense is created in the Church, and a considerable mockery of ecclesiastical dignity. Therefore, whoever approaches as though he were to be consecrated without having been canonically elected, or whoever has not been freely consecrated—even if a canonical election preceded—withdraws accursed.

For just as where there is no true conversion of heart complete remission does not follow, so where free consecration does not follow, even if a canonical election precedes, it is of no benefit, since neither one alone is sufficient to create a bishop. Nor is that consecration free which is preceded by an oath made without judgment and justice, since Blessed Jerome, commenting on Jeremiah, says that an oath must not be made where justice, truth, and judgment are not present together. If anything is presumed otherwise, it will not be an oath but perjury.

[Col. 0282C] Moreover, the Church ought properly to possess three distinctive qualities; if one of them is lacking, she lies like a paralytic and has no power either to bind or to loose. The Church must therefore be catholic, chaste, and free: catholic, because she must neither be sold nor bought; chaste, because she must in no way be corrupted by gifts; free, because she must not be subjected to secular power, nor may any sacrament be extorted by secular authority from her spouse on any pretext, since divine law altogether forbids this, and no sacrament may be demanded from a bishop except for the sole sake of the catholic faith.

Christ, truly the good shepherd, seeks a faithful bride and rejects an unfaithful one; he loves the chaste and hates the corrupted; he joins to himself the free and casts away the slave. He is therefore falsely called a bishop who attempts to abolish the order of election and consecration [Col. 0282D] that Christ himself first instituted. For he was the first both to elect the apostles and to consecrate them.

The entire ordination of a bishop therefore consists in election and consecration. As has been said, Christ first performed these through himself; afterward, his vicars did so. In the apostles, they were performed by Christ [Col. 0283A], because they were both elected and consecrated by him. In all others, however, no one else may perform them except Christ’s vicars. The clergy are Christ’s vicars in election, and bishops in consecration. All the rest may indeed request a bishop, but they cannot elect or consecrate one.

Christ first performed this holy sacrament—namely, the election and consecration of the apostles—in order that the remaining sacraments might be performed through it. If the sacrament that Christ, as has been said, first performed through himself is carried out otherwise than he taught, then reason does not show what force the other sacraments that follow can possess, and Christian faith does not know it.

Whoever, therefore, without a canonical election and free consecration, presumes under the title of bishop to claim a church [Col. 0283B] or ecclesiastical power for himself, no longer enters through the door but climbs in from elsewhere, so that he deserves not to be counted among bishops but to be numbered among thieves and robbers (John 10:1).

Such a man does not extend blessing to others, but rather appears to inflict plague and wound instead of salvation; by so great a presumption he merits God’s curse. For a bishop who lacks canonical election and free consecration is like a tree without a root. A tree without a root, even if it has leaves, cannot in any way bear fruit. Christ indeed approached such a tree, and when he found no fruit on it, he cursed it (Mark 11:21).

[Col. 0283C] It is above all the one who desires, out of his own greed rather than Christ’s love, to be joined to the Church’s sacraments who is cursed by God. Everyone who is not joined to the Church’s sacraments by the cement of charity does injury to the Church; but he is scattered like a mud wall which, although it can be whitewashed for a time, crushes those who previously trusted in it when it suddenly collapses.

From this comparison it is rightly concluded that one who attains an ecclesiastical rank, and especially the pontificate, to the injury of the holy Church first brings about his own destruction and then the death of the people. The Church suffers both injury and shame when, in the election of a bishop, canonical election and free consecration perish, and what is owed to the merits of a good life, to the teaching of wisdom, and to sacred orders [Col. 0283D] is, as it were, imposed upon those whom neither the merits of a good life, nor the teaching of wisdom, nor sacred orders support.

Such men have an earthly—indeed, marshy—foundation, and therefore those built upon such a foundation collapse [Col. 0284A]. For of them it is said in the Psalm: “You cast them down when they were lifted up” (Psalm 72:18).

Nothing is more grievous in Christ’s sight than injury to the Church, whose sacraments those who receive perversely can neither be with Christ nor benefit others. No one can be with Christ and act against Christ at the same time, since he himself says: “Whoever is not with me is against me” (Luke 11:23). Whoever is not with Christ can benefit neither himself nor others, since he again declares: “Whoever does not gather with me scatters” (ibid.). Elsewhere he says: “Without me you can do nothing” [Col. 0284B] (John 15:5).

There are some who think that everything is permitted to the Roman Church, and that, by some sort of dispensation, she may act otherwise than divine Scripture commands. Whoever thinks in this way is deceived. For after Peter, the Roman Church is by no means permitted to do what was not permitted to Peter. Christ gave Peter the power to bind what was to be bound and to loose what was to be loosed; he did not grant him the power to loose what was to be bound or to bind what was to be loosed.

Even if Peter at some time acted otherwise, Paul, although still a novice in the faith at his conversion, was not at all afraid to resist him to his face (Galatians 2:11). Peter, for his part, willingly accepting the rebuke of his junior, carefully corrected what he had done beyond what was right.

Moreover, there is no justification for doing what Christ did not teach by his example; for he came not to abolish the law [Col. 0284C] but to fulfill it (Matthew 5:18). Therefore the Roman Church must not abolish the law of the divine Scriptures, but preserve it, and must not use the power entrusted to her by Christ according to her own will, but according to Christ’s arrangement.

If something is suggested to the Roman pontiff even by his junior—namely, that if he has at some time done more than was right, he should correct it justly—then, just as Peter accepted Paul’s admonition, so he too will accept it if he desires to imitate Peter.

Against those who arm themselves against Christ’s ordinance, the good teacher and martyr Cyprian speaks, saying:

> Whatever is instituted by human action so as to violate Christ’s dispensation is adulterous, impious, and sacrilegious. Whoever acts in this way gives darkness instead of light, night instead of day, hunger instead of food, thirst instead of drink, poison instead of a remedy, and death instead of life.

The age of those who wished to corrupt the chaste Susanna was not venerable, nor is their authority to be imitated. Those who contrive to violate Christ’s truth and the virginity of his bride imitate their ancient wickedness. These are the ones who alter God’s ordinances and attempt to establish their own traditions. When the Lord’s teaching departs from them, the Lord’s grace also departs; and at some time the supreme Shepherd will avenge their actions, both with the force of an avenger and with the authority of a judge.

Dispensations in the Church must indeed be made, not out of love of money or any human favor, but with a pious and merciful intention. A dispensation is then believed to be made piously and mercifully by the Church’s shepherd when something is temporarily done or permitted by him in a less than perfect manner—not by his own will, but because of the necessity of others, lest the Christian faith itself be endangered in them.

[Col. 0284D] Thus a dispensation must be made by the Church [425] in such a way that the truth of our faith is strengthened; and if something has been done or permitted otherwise for the moment, it must be corrected at the appropriate time.

The blessed apostles Peter and Paul used this prudent and holy dispensation because of fear of the Jews, lest they be scandalized. For after his conversion Paul had Timothy circumcised and also observed Jewish ceremonies, while Peter compelled certain Gentiles to Judaize. Each holy apostle, pretending to observe the precepts of the old law, did so lest those who had become believers from among the Jews should, after being scandalized, deny the knowledge of the truth they had received.

The holy apostles did this out of merciful and pious compassion, not through deceitful pretense, although they had no doubt that the law was not to be observed after the Gospel. In this way it is understood that men of most blessed life did not change their decision, but temporarily adapted the judgment of their teaching for the salvation of others. For in regard to what they and others had done differently, they afterward corrected both themselves and others.

Dispensations can and ought also to be made by which the customs of churches and monasteries are altered, but only when a lesser good is set aside so that what is better may be established. Evil must never be done or permitted except in a necessity of such a kind that there is fear that the faith may be endangered, and even then it must afterward be corrected. For the Apostle Paul declares that the condemnation of those who do evil so that good may come is just.

If anyone makes dispensations in the Church otherwise, he contradicts reason and truth alike. He not only lacks a burning lamp, but also extinguishes the lamps of others. Therefore he is not rightly called Christ’s vicar, but is himself a blind guide of the blind.

Concerning the investiture of laymen, if anyone wishes to know what the catholic and apostolic Church has thought, taught, judged, and decreed, let him read the first chapter of that council [Note: [Col. 0285D] Concerning this, see also above, Epistle 11, Book III], which was held in the time of Pope Gregory VII. There he will find that all clerics who receive investiture from the hand of a layman were called heretics, and for that reason were condemned and excommunicated.

Although one heresy is called the heresy of investiture and another is called simony, the former strikes more forcefully against the holy Church. For simoniacal depravity is often practiced secretly, whereas the heresy of investiture is always carried out openly.

There, moreover, the entire ecclesiastical order is first thrown into confusion, when what ought to be given to each person in the Church only by his own consecrator, together with the prayers appropriate to the occasion, is first received from secular power.

The holy apostles not only forbade this, but also condemned with the power entrusted to them by Christ all those who obtain control of a church through secular power. And rightly, by the judgment of the Holy Spirit, the apostles resolved to condemn this heresy at the very beginning of the Church, since they foresaw that it would be born long afterward from the devil, their father.

Since, therefore, the Holy Spirit who spoke through the apostles has utterly denied and forbidden a layman both investiture and every power to dispose of churches or ecclesiastical property, whoever receives investiture from a layman now exposes what is holy to dogs—not merely against the apostles, but against the Lord of the apostles [Col. 0285D].

The investiture of which we speak is a sacrament, that is, a sacred sign, by which the ruler of the Church—namely, the bishop—is separated and distinguished from other men, and by which pastoral care over the Christian flock is entrusted to him. He ought to receive this investiture from the one alone from whom he also receives consecration.

He must first be consecrated and then, like a king of the Church, adorned with sacred insignia. Whoever thinks that this is permitted to any secular power is mistaken; and if he attempts to defend it, he desires to abolish the teaching of the apostles and the mind of the Holy Spirit. Hence there is no doubt that he is a heretic.

The investiture of laymen, therefore, which is performed through the staff and ring, is rightly called a heresy. For just as the heresy of simony is named after Simon, so this is rightly called the heresy of investiture after the one who invests and the one who is invested, since each of them, in that action, attempts both to manipulate the keys of the Church and to violate its one and unique door.

Moreover, if properly considered, this heresy of investiture is also demonstrably the heresy of simony, by a sound and truthful argument. For what reason does secular power attempt to claim investiture, except that by this means it may extort money or—what is more serious—make the person of the bishop subject to itself in an improper manner?

There is certainly no layman who, even if it were permitted to him, would desire to give the ring or staff with such an intention, unless through these things, which are sacraments of the Church, he were eagerly seeking temporal profit. Laymen may indeed receive sacraments from the Church, but they may not give any of the Church’s sacraments.

As we have said, a layman always claims for himself, through investiture, either money or—what is more—the person of the bishop or abbot. Through this malignity, which is not so much human as diabolical, the catholic Church loses faith, freedom, and chastity, without which she cannot exist in any way.

[Col. 0286C] Whoever, therefore, presumes to receive the investiture described above under the appearance of a shepherd becomes paralytic and polluted by heretical leprosy. I do not confidently call him a shepherd, nor any member of that Shepherd who laid down his life for his sheep; he is a thief, robber, and wolf. For he has come in order to steal, slaughter, and destroy (John 10:10).

Not only those who commit this detestable impiety but also those who consent to it are condemned. He consents who remains silent about it, who does not correct it, and who does not openly oppose it. No one is exempt from the duty—and everyone is able—to oppose it openly.

For if he lacks the authority of a prelate, he nevertheless has the voice of a Christian. Scripture says, and exempts no one: “Cursed is he who withholds his sword from blood” (Jeremiah 48:10), that is, who withholds his voice from rebuking sin.

Let him also remember the event in which a she-ass once corrected a foolish prophet (Numbers 22:28). If he is defective or infamous because of any other crime, he should not for that reason remain silent, since every sinner may defend the common faith of the Church—which he believes and confesses to be his own—and freely fight against its adversaries.

For the two men who were crucified with the Lord in his Passion were altogether infamous; they were public criminals. Yet one of them, not merely because he believed but because he began to defend the truth of his faith against the other, deserved to hear that good and pleasing word from our Savior: “Today you will be with me in paradise” (Luke 23:43).

Thus it is especially demonstrated in that criminal that a catholic man, even if previously stained by marks of infamy, may through the defense of the faith merit paradise and being with Christ.

And since we have mentioned simony, why it is a heresy, and why the investiture of laymen must rightly be called a heresy, will be discussed further with God’s help, so that no one may henceforth doubt the matter.

This also must not be left unsaid: just as some investiture by laymen is contrary to the faith, so some investiture by them can take place without harm to the faith.

You must believe, dearest brother, and hold firmly above all else that the principal heresy is that which attempts to separate the Son or the Holy Spirit from the unity of the Father, or asserts that one person is less or greater than another. There are indeed errors and divisions that are called heresies, in which people think perversely concerning the person of the Father, the Son, or the Holy Spirit, or concerning the whole Trinity together.

But it must be understood that the one who most especially and properly is called a heretic is he who appears with obstinate mind to attack the faith of Christ that he has received.

Thus Simon Magus, baptized by Saint Philip, was not merely a heretic but the first and worst of heretics. He not only thought that the Holy Spirit could be separated from the equality of the Father, but also presumptuously desired, by attempting it, to be greater than the Holy Spirit.

For when he thought that he could possess the Holy Spirit with money, what else did he desire except to be regarded as greater than the Holy Spirit, since the possessor is greater than what is possessed (Acts 8)?

Since, therefore, anyone who attempts to assert that the persons of the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit are unequal is to be regarded as a heretic both by reason and by authority, much more must Simon Magus be so regarded: he attempted with money to subject to himself the Holy Spirit, equal in all things to God the Father and the Son. Thus heresy is proved both in Simon and in simony, which was invented by him and named after him.

When a layman grants the investiture of churches through the staff and ring, which are sacraments of the Church, like salt and water, oil and chrism, and certain other things without which the consecrations of human beings and churches cannot take place, he usurps for himself Christ’s right and power and, in a certain sense, proclaims himself higher than the Son of God [Col. 0287D].

For when those sacraments of the Church are given where they ought to be given, to whom, when, and how they ought to be given, they are given through the minister of consecration by the Son of God, from whom all sacraments are made and by whom they are bestowed.

Hence God the Father speaks to John, saying: “Upon whomever you see the Spirit descending, he is the one who baptizes” (John 1:33). When he said, “he is the one who baptizes,” he signified the whole by a part. For the Son of God performs and bestows all the sacraments of the holy Church.

When a layman presumes in this way against the Son of God, he has become swollen with pride no less, if not more, than Simon Magus; and so too does the man become swollen with pride who, in the bestowal of the sacraments, places himself before the Son of God.

And since by his impious action he appears not only to attempt to deprive God the Son of the equality he has with his Father, but also to signify that he himself is superior to the Son of God, he too is rightly called a heretic, and his investiture is called a heresy.

Let emperors and kings not be displeased by what we say, and let them not attempt, by custom, to claim for themselves what truth denies them. Since every power to dispose of churches or ecclesiastical property is forbidden by the apostles even to religious laymen, it is clear that investiture is denied to them by truth itself—namely, by Christ, who spoke through the apostles.

That Christ spoke in the apostles is asserted by the Apostle Paul, who says: “Are you seeking proof that Christ is speaking in me?” (2 Corinthians 13:3).

Since Christ is truth, as he himself said, “I am the truth” (John 14:6), and since he never said, “I am custom,” let the Christian follow Christ; and let the king follow the King of kings, namely truth itself, not custom.

In the matter of ecclesiastical possessions, although such investiture is found neither in the laws nor in the canons, nevertheless, in order to avoid scandal and schism, let such an investiture be granted to kings that neither they perish because of it nor the holy Church suffer harm.

To receive investiture through the staff and ring from anyone except one’s own consecrator is clearly harmful, because no layman is permitted to give those sacraments of the Church, just as he is not permitted to consecrate a bishop.

Things that have once been given to the Church, kings neither ought nor can appropriately give again or invest someone with them. For to give someone what he already possesses, and to invest someone with what he already holds, is superfluous and vain, although it does not appear criminal.

There is, however, one investiture that perfects a bishop, and another that sustains a bishop. The former comes from divine law; the latter from human law. Remove divine law, and a bishop is not created spiritually; remove human law, and he loses the possessions by which he is sustained bodily.

The Church would not have possessions unless kings gave them to her; and by those kings she would be invested not with divine sacraments but with earthly possessions.

By divine law we rule over kings and emperors; nevertheless, by that same law, because they are the lords of Christ, we owe them honor and reverence, as the Apostle says: “Honor the king” [Col. 0288D] (1 Peter 2:17).

By human law, however, we owe them only as much as we value the possessions with which the Church is known to have been enriched and endowed by them or by their parents.

Hence Blessed Augustine speaks as follows concerning John (Tractate 6):

> Do not say: “What have I to do with the king?” What, then, have you to do with property? Possessions are held by the rights of kings. If you say, “What have I to do with the king?” then do not call the possessions yours, because you have renounced the rights by which possessions are held. According to the law of emperors you possess earthly things. Remove the laws of emperors: who dares say, “That estate is mine,” or “That slave is mine,” or “That house is mine”? By what law do you defend estates: divine or human? We have divine law in the Scriptures; human law in the laws of kings. By what right, then, does anyone possess what he possesses? Is it not by human law? For by divine law, “The earth is the Lord’s and its fullness” (Psalm 24:1). God made the poor and the rich from one clay, and one earth supports both rich and poor. Yet by human law you say: “This estate is mine; this house is mine; this slave is mine.” Therefore, by human law. Why by the law of emperors? Because God distributed those human laws to his Church through the emperors and kings of this world.

Kings can therefore, without offense, after canonical election and free consecration, grant a bishop, through royal investiture in ecclesiastical possessions, concession, assistance, and protection. Whatever sign may have been used to accomplish this, it will harm neither the king, nor the bishop, nor the catholic faith.

Our good Lord and teacher Christ willed that there be both a spiritual sword and a material one for the defense of the Church. If one is blunted by the other, this happens against his will.

On this account justice is taken away from the kingdom and peace from the Church; scandals and schisms are stirred up; and the ruin both of souls and of bodies follows. When kingdom and priesthood attack one another, both are endangered.

For when the king and the Roman pontiff rise up against each other—one on behalf of the custom of the kingdom, the other on behalf of the freedom of the Church—the kingdom cannot and will not be able to retain that custom, while the Church loses much of her freedom.

Moreover, the king is deprived both of the holy communion and of his royal dignity; while the Roman pontiff, compelled by necessity, is served by many who ought to have served the king. The one who ought to have been taught by the pontiff and guided by the king is followed by the king and pontiff alike.

Let the Church have peace and the kingdom justice. Let the king have his custom—but a good one, not the one he wrongly demands, but the investiture described above. Let the Church have her freedom; but let her take the greatest care lest, while squeezing too hard, she draw blood, and while attempting to scrape rust from a vessel, she break the vessel itself.

This is the principal element of discretion: that no ruler of the Church be ensnared by Satan through any action of his own. A ruler is ensnared by Satan when, under the appearance of justice, through excessive grief he brings about the ruin of someone who could have been saved by leniency.

Moreover, the good and discerning Augustine says in his letter to Parmenianus that one who has a stubborn multitude with him in an evil undertaking should scarcely ever, or perhaps never, be excommunicated. For it seems more tolerable to spare one person lest the schism of many be sown in the Church.

And the most blessed teacher and martyr Cyprian asserts, saying: “Schism must not be made, even if the one who departs does not remain in the same faith and the same tradition.”

Solomon likewise says in Ecclesiastes: “Whoever splits wood will be endangered by it if the iron slips” (Ecclesiastes 10:9). Again, in Exodus: “It shall be eaten in one house; you shall not cast any of the flesh outside the house” (Exodus 12:46).

From these words it is gathered that one who has a multitude with him must be tolerated by the Church, lest, while we attempt to correct one person, the destruction of many result.

Jerome also writes this to Augustine, saying that, in accordance with the prudent and honorable dispensation of the blessed apostles Peter and Paul, it is sometimes necessary to do what is rightly criticized, lest scandal arise among the Christian people.

If the person of an emperor or king—not, however, the land itself—must sometimes be spared in the interest of the highest justice, this is so lest the greatest evil increase as a result. The ministers of the Church must be strictly forbidden to obtain what is just through unjust means.

If I have said less or otherwise than I ought concerning the present subject, let it be attributed to ignorance and mercifully pardoned. But if I have spoken well, let it be received kindly and carefully observed.

## APPENDIX

[Col. 0289]

### PRIVILEGE OF THEODERIC, BISHOP OF CHARTRES, FOR THE MONASTERY OF VENDÔME, WRITTEN ON THE DAY OF ITS DEDICATION

[Note: [Col. 0289D] Concerning this, see the notes to Goffridus’s Epistle 4, Book I.]

[Col. 0289D] In the name of almighty God, the Father and the Son and the Holy Spirit. I, Theoderic, by the grace of God bishop of Chartres, make known to all the faithful of the holy Church that the illustrious Count Gaufridus and his venerable wife, Countess Agnes, built at their own expense, with our advice, a monastery dedicated to the holy and undivided Trinity in their castle called Vendôme; and, with the consent and grant of ourselves and our clergy, they offered it as a patrimony and freehold to Blessed Peter and his Roman Church, confidently trusting—not in vain—that by this means they would more easily attain the blessedness of the life to come through the prayers of Blessed Peter and more happily complete the present life.

When they had enriched it with the liberal munificence of their possessions and adorned it with a varied and manifold array of ornaments, they summoned us and many other bishops and abbots to the dedication of that venerable place. They asked us, so that the brothers who would serve God there according to the rule of Saint Benedict might remain more peacefully and without any disturbance, to remit, in the presence of the persons who had assembled for the dedication, whatever other churches pay in revenue or due subjection to our episcopal see [Col. 0290D] and, for the honor and love of the supreme Trinity and in response to their petition, to prohibit by our authority anyone from giving or granting to another abbey any church or ecclesiastical possession in the county of Vendôme, insofar as it belonged to our episcopate.

We therefore thought it just to confirm, with the approval of our clergy and in so great an assembly, what they had requested from the beginning of the monastery and what we had done. Accordingly, we have granted and do grant that the aforesaid monastery shall remain perpetually entirely free on our part and absolved from every subjection, retaining no power or lordship for ourselves or our successors over that place or its inhabitants, but granting them the counsel of fraternal charity and, in their need, the assistance of our authority.

We also grant to the same monastery whatever it possesses today within our episcopate and whatever it may justly acquire in the future. And we prohibit anyone from giving or granting to another monastery any church or any ecclesiastical possession in the county of Vendôme belonging to our diocese, except to the monastery of Vendôme.

So that this grant and guarantee of freedom may be believed more truly by future generations and preserved more firmly, we ordered this charter to be written, read aloud in the hearing of the gathered populace, and condemned by public excommunication all persons, both of the ecclesiastical and of the secular order, who oppose this act of ours, unless they should afterward produce worthy fruits of repentance.

We also placed this charter with our own hands upon the altar of the monastery of Vendôme, as a sign and testimony of perpetual freedom. The honorable persons among the bishops, abbots, and clergy were with us as guarantors and witnesses of this matter.

Arnulf, archbishop of Tours; Isembert, bishop of Poitiers; Gervasius, prelate of Le Mans; Hubert, bishop of Angers; Gerald, prelate of Angoulême; Amelinus, bishop of Albi.

# In the Year of the Lord 1108: Thiofridus, Abbot of Echternach

[Col. 0293]

## HISTORICAL NOTICE

*(Fabricius, Bibliotheca medii et infimi latini, vol. VI, p. 233.)*

[Col. 0293B] Thiofridus, abbot of Echternach, of the Order of Saint Benedict, died in the year 1110. He wrote a Life of Saint Willibrord, founder of his monastery and archbishop of Utrecht, published by Surius on 7 December. He also wrote *The Flowers of the Epitaph of the Saints*, Book IV, published at Luxembourg together with the *Life of Saint Willibrord* and notes by John Robert, S.J., in 1619, quarto. See Valerius Andreas, *Bibliotheca Belgica*, p. 832; Sweertius, *Athenae Belgicae*, p. 692.

Possevinus, following Eisengrein, attributes to him in volume II of the *Apparatus*, p. 469, books *On the Consummation of the Age* and *On the Last Day*.

[The *Life of Willibrord* published by Surius is entirely different from the one written by Thiofridus. For Surius published the one that Alcuin composed in prose. Thiofridus’s work was never published, as the writers of the *Literary History of France*, volume IX, p. 508, point out. The same abbot also composed another Life, namely that of Saint Irmina, abbess of Heresiensis in the diocese of Trier, which likewise has never appeared.

The short work *On the End of the World*, attributed by Possevinus to this Thiofridus, belongs to Theofridus, abbot of Carmeries; and it is certainly none other than the book *Micrologus on the Sixfold Fall of the World*, written by that same Thiofridus, as we learn from the same authors. [Col. 0293C] Mansi.]

[Col. 0294B] Two sermons by a certain abbot Thiofridus, *On the Relics of the Saints* and *On the Veneration of the Saints*, first published together with Berengosus at Cologne in 1555, octavo, and later included in the *Bibliothecae Patrum*, gave rise to learned controversy. Most scholars, with Cave, maintain that he was the eleventh-century abbot of Efternach mentioned above. The authors of the *Literary History of France*, however, vol. IV, p. 60, attribute these sermons to Thiofridus, who in the seventh century was first abbot of Menat in the diocese of Auvergne and later of Carmeri in the territory of Velay. Manuscripts of the sermons of Thiofridus the abbot are in the Vatican Library. Bern. de Montfaucon, *Bibliotheca bibliothecarum manuscriptorum*, p. 134. [Although those two sermons, known here to the Bibliographer, were attributed by the authors of the *Literary History of France* in vol. IV to this abbot Thiofridus, in volume IX, in their account of the *Life of Thiofridus, abbot of Efternach*, they attribute them to the same monk of Efternach, retracting their earlier opinion. See there the conjectures that led them to this conclusion. Moreover, this Thiofridus was abbot of Carmeri in the diocese of Velay. MANSI.]

[Col. 0293]

## LITERARY NOTICE

(*Literary History of France*, vol. IX, p. 505.)

[Col. 0293C] 1. The principal, and perhaps the first, work of Theofroi—because he calls it the first fruits of his labor—is a collection entitled *The Flowers of the Epitaph of the Saints*, which he undertook at the request of Abbot Régembert, his immediate predecessor (MAB. *An.*, bk. LXXI, no. 23). It is known that this abbot had an extraordinary veneration for the saints; this led him in 1059, with the consent of his community, to establish a feast on 19 December in honor of those whose relics were preserved at Epternach. The origin of this work may perhaps be assigned to that period. The author later dedicated it to Bruno, archbishop of Trier (BROW. *An. Trev.* I, XII, no. 9). Nothing could be more magnificent or more honorable to the patron, nor anything more modest and humble on the author’s part, than the inscription of this dedication, which deserves to be reproduced here for its singularity:

> To Bruno, the fruitful, beautiful, splendid, and fruit-bearing olive of the house of the Lord, archbishop of the holy see of Trier: Thiofridus, the dry wild olive-tree, *hēgoumenos* (abbot) of the monastery of Epternach.

The penultimate expression, which is Greek and means “leader” or “first in dignity,” shows that the author took pleasure in Greek expressions. This is reflected throughout the work and makes its style harsh and lacking in fluency. It nevertheless displays great learning for its time, together with eminent piety and considerable modesty.

The purpose of Theofroi in this work is to recount the wonders that God had performed, and was still performing, through the power of the relics of his saints—the power of their ashes, clothing, or other mortal remains, and even of the instruments of their sufferings. In undertaking to censure the luxury of his own time, which was disguised under a pretext of apparent devotion, Theofroi expresses himself as follows:

> “One must not imagine,” he says, “that the saints seek gold and silver; they seek only to make themselves favorable to those who use such things in a holy manner. They do not desire magnificent churches to be erected for them, in which one sees an ingenious arrangement of colonnades shining with gold, nor rich paneling, nor altars enriched with precious stones. They do not ask that costly vellum, such as purple vellum, be used to copy books, nor powdered gold to embellish the letters, nor precious stones to adorn the binding, while almost no regard is paid to the ministers of the altar, and the members of Jesus Christ are left to die naked at its door.”

This work is divided into four books. It was printed in Luxembourg in 1619 by Hubert Reulandt, in a quarto volume, through the care of Father Jean-Robert, a Jesuit, who enriched it with notes.

2. As early as 1555, two sermons or homilies were printed at Cologne under the name of a Theofroi described simply as an abbot. They later passed into the various collections bearing the title *Bibliotheca Patrum*. The position assigned to them by the editors of the latest of these collections, printed at Lyon—between the writings of Abbot Isaiah and those of St. Maximus the Confessor (*Bib. PP.*, vol. XII, pp. 417–419)—led us, when we were working on our eighth century (*Hist. lit. de la Fr.*, vol. IV, pp. 60–61), to think that these homilies might belong to St. Theofroi, who died in 732 as abbot of Carmeri, better known in common usage as St. Chaffre, in the diocese of Le Puy-en-Velay. We expressed ourselves at that time in accordance with this view. But when we noticed that the style bore the character of the eleventh century rather than that of the eighth, we took care to warn that there might be stronger reasons for attributing these two pieces to Theofroi, abbot of Epternach. After a fresh examination, we are now convinced of this. One need only compare these two homilies with the preceding work [Col. 0295C] to have no doubt that they are by the same author.

One of these homilies concerns the respect due to the relics of the saints, for several reasons that Theofroi develops in great detail, principally because of the power of miracles that God has attached to them. We have seen that this is one of the principal subjects of the preceding work. The other homily treats the veneration owed to the saints themselves and again touches upon the respect due to their relics. Theofroi delivered them orally, as appears from various passages of the text, and says that the place where he was speaking was rich in these holy remains. This corresponds perfectly to the abbey of Epternach, where the body of St. Willibrord, first bishop of Utrecht, was preserved, together with relics of St. Liutwin, bishop of Trier, of St. Irmina the abbess, and of still other saints. The homilies display much learning and sound doctrine on every religious subject touched upon by the author. He names only St. Gregory the Great, but it is clear that he was well versed in the writings of St. Ambrose, St. Augustine, and the other Fathers of the Church. The second homily is almost continuously an allusion to numerous passages of Holy Scripture. The style of both is more abrupt than that of the collection *The Flowers of the Epitaph of the Saints*. It is, however, filled with balanced sounds and verbal correspondences, a feature that clearly points to the eleventh century, when Abbot Theofroi was writing. Cardinal Bona (*Not. auct.*, p. 45) found sufficient beauty in it to describe it as a style of clear and polished eloquence, *nitidi eloquii*. At least, one does not perceive in it the author’s inclination toward Greek expressions. Barthius, attending only to the two principal characteristics of Theofroi’s writings—learning and piety—calls him *scriptor eruditus et piissimus* (“a learned and most pious writer”) (BARTH. *Adv.*, bk. XLII).

The title of a manuscript in the Vatican Library announces sermons under the name of Theofroi (MONTFAUC. *Bibl. bibl.*, p. 134). But since the place they occupy in that manuscript, between the opuscula of Abbot Isaiah and those of St. Maximus, is the same as that occupied in the *Bibliothecae Patrum* by the two homilies just discussed, this is sufficient to leave no doubt that the manuscript sermons are the same as the printed homilies.

3. Theofroi wrote a *Life of St. Willibrord*, patron, founder, and titular saint of the abbey of Epternach. The famous Alcuin had already written it in prose and verse before the end of the eighth century, as has been related in its proper place. This work, which might have seemed sufficient—especially since it was written by so accomplished a writer and nearly at the same time as the saint—did not prevent Abbot Theofroi, whether out of veneration or for some other reason, from undertaking a new work on the same subject. Thus, in imitation of Alcuin, he in turn composed a *Life of St. Willibrord* both in prose and in verse (MAB. *Act.*, vol. III, p. 630, [Col. 0296B] no. 3): the former divided into thirty-six chapters, the latter into four books. Mr. Cave (p. 559) says that the work was printed together with the *Flores epitaphii sanctorum*, and implies that it is also found in Surius under 7 November; nevertheless, there is no other work on St. Willibrord there than Alcuin’s prose life. Oudin (*Scri.*, vol. II, p. 949), who reproaches Cave for having passed over Abbot Theofroi—a reproach that is unfounded, as we see—nevertheless adopts his opinion concerning the supposed editions of the work of our learned abbot. So far, however, nothing of it has been printed except what Dom Mabillon published after Alcuin’s work, as an appendix or supplement (MAB. ib., pp. 629–630).

If this *Life* by Abbot Theofroi had been printed by Father Robert, the editor of the *Flores epitaphii*, as he promised in his preface, Father Brower, his fellow Jesuit, who drew extensively upon it for his *Antiquities and Annals of Trier*, would have used that edition—which, on the assumption in question, would have been known long before he wrote. Yet he never cites it except as a manuscript. The author gives a fairly detailed account of what happened at Antwerp and Walcheren during the journey he made there to restore peace among the peoples of that island. If the three verses that Father Brower copies in his account of this event are taken from the other, verse *Life of St. Willibrord*, and if all the rest are equally well sustained, they would do honor to the century that produced them.

4. Theofroi also left a prose *Life of St. Liutwin*, or Ludwin, bishop of Trier at the beginning of the seventh century. He dedicated it to Udo, archbishop of the same church from 1067 to 1078. The author therefore wrote it before he was raised to the dignity of abbot, and it appears from this that it was one of the earliest productions of his pen. But [Col. 0296D] what became of this work is now unknown. The learned Father Henschenius, followed on this point by Mr. Baillet (BOLL. 4 Mar., p. 314, no. 5; p. 319, no. 19; BAIL. 4 Mar., *tab. cr.*, no. 3), wished to transfer the credit for it to Nizon, whom others call Mizon, abbot of Mithlac. Nizon wrote a *Life of St. Basin*, another bishop of Trier before St. Liutwin, whose maternal uncle he was. To establish his claim, the first of these critics adduces a passage from Nizon’s work which, on closer examination, proves precisely the opposite.

Since the history of St. Ludwin is naturally connected with that of St. Basin, whose nephew, pupil, and successor he was, Nizon—who himself makes this observation—warns that he cannot undertake the life of one without saying something about the other (BOLL. ib., p. 319, no. 19). For this purpose he has recourse to the *Life of St. Ludwin*, which already existed; and after borrowing several details from it, even copying the original author’s words, he refers the reader for [Col. 0297A] the rest to the complete work. Far from Nizon saying here anything that even remotely suggests that the writing before him was his own, the manner in which he expresses himself leads one to judge exactly the contrary. Moreover, the Greek expressions found in what he extracted clearly reveal the writing style of the abbot of Epternach, to whom other monuments attribute this *Life of St. Ludwin*. In any case, when the industrious continuators of Bollandus bring it to light again, as there is reason to hope they will, it may provide still stronger evidence in support of what we have just established.

5. Theofroi also wrote a *Life of St. Irmina*, a virgin and abbess of Oeren, or Horren, in the city of Trier (MAB., *Act.* ib., p. 532, no. 2; CALMET, *Hist. de Lor.*, vol. IV, part I, p. 123). She is supposed to have been the daughter of King Dagobert—that is, Dagobert II, since she is said to have lived at the beginning of the eighth century. But no one tells us what became of this *Life*, any more than of that of St. Ludwin.

Possevinus (*App.*, vol. III, p. 287), confusing, on the authority of Eisingrenius, Theofroi, abbot of Epternach—whom he places only in 1145—with St. Theofroi, or Chaffre, abbot of Carmeri from the first years of the eighth century, attributes to him a treatise concerning the end of the world and the last day, together with several other works in prose and verse. But this treatise, announced under such a title, is nothing other than the little work on the course of the sixth age of the world, entitled *Micrologus*, etc., which was discussed in the article on St. Theofroi (*Hist. lit. de la Fr.*, ib., p. 61).
