It belongs to him, according to the testimony of the author of his *Life*, who was writing in the tenth century, and thus at least a hundred years before Theofroi of Epternach.

**The Four Books of the Flowers of the Epitaph of the Saints, by D. Thiofridus, Abbot and Lord of Epternach, Until Now Never Published.** A work filled with great piety, manifold learning, and truly floral abundance. John Roberti, priest of the Society of Jesus and doctor of sacred theology, transcribed, revised, divided, and illustrated it with notes from two manuscripts of the library of Epternach, that of St. Clement Willibrord. (Luxembourg, 1619, quarto.)

[Col. 0297]

## DEDICATORY PREFACE

To the most reverend Father in Christ, noble and most illustrious prelate, Lord Peter Richardot, licentiate in sacred theology, abbot and lord of the imperial monastery of St. Clement Willibrord at Epternach.

That wise man of Jerusalem, most illustrious prelate, Jesus son of Sirach, who renewed wisdom from his heart (Ecclus. 50:19), after he had written instruction in every kind of wisdom and discipline in the ecclesiastical book, nevertheless considered that he had done little unless, after everything else, he praised illustrious men (ch. 44:1) and our fathers in their generation. In this way he showed himself to be the wise man whom he had previously described (ch. 39:1 ff.), when he said: “The wise man will seek out the wisdom of all the ancients.” He gives an entirely just and weighty reason for this study (ch. 44:6), because those ancients were “men rich in virtue, devoted to the pursuit of beauty, and making peace in their houses.” But still weightier is what he adds (v. 13): “Their children, for their sake, remain forever.”

For what could be more just than for you to remember with grateful and honorable recollection those who, if they had not been what they were, would mean that you were not what you are? If I say that you imitate this Jesus, just as he himself imitated Jesus Christ, I shall attribute nothing to you except what the Apostle seriously and repeatedly demands of all who bear the Christian name (1 Cor. 4:16; 11:1; Phil. 3:17). I therefore prefer to say what properly concerns my subject, rather than imitate those who, whenever they write a preface or dedication, pursue every subject from every direction, even matters external to it, provided that they seem in any way to contribute to the praise of the person whom they address.

If I were to do this, your family would provide me with abundant material. Without speaking of the living, your two brothers, the great-hearted Francis and Anthony, commanders of infantry and cavalry, would immediately suggest themselves—men whom their country, their princes, their king, the faith, and God saw purpled with their own blood, falling in glorious death, one at Nieuwpoort, the other at Rheinberg. Another brother, John, would present himself: Arras, concerning the deeds and life of its bishop, set forth in a most illustrious position; Cambrai, of its archbishop; the Holy Council, of its senator; and the supreme pontiff, head of the Church, of the envoy sent to him on the gravest affairs—what would they not relate devoutly, almost as testimony?

Meanwhile another bishop of Arras, Francis, your paternal uncle, would thrust himself forward: a man piously delighted by the just praises of his nephews, but himself so illustrious that Burgundy, Belgium—the most serious theater of the world—the Council of Trent, and finally the whole world, through the many noble books he published, know him as distinguished not only in life. And when it comes to your father, the prelate Richardot—under this name alone, even if nothing else were added, all Europe knows him—how could I ever lack something to say, since he has supplied material to numerous writers who confess that they cannot sketch with the pen what he expressed through his life? Hence those ingenious and majestic summaries: “the Phoenix of Burgundy,” “another Parmenion,” “Leonidas,” “Zopyrus,” “Nestor,” “Aristides.”

If I had to speak of his deeds, I too would use a summary, merely indicating in a word that through his wisdom and diligence three most serious and destructive wars were brought to an end: two with two most powerful kings; the third, shall I say, with citizens or with the bitterest enemies?

And your maternal lineage, the illustrious family of Baillencourt—what honors would it suggest to me, what most distinguished deeds, whether at home or in military service? The heir of both lines in a long succession is Claudius de Baillencourt, commander of all the galleys and of the entire Maltese military force, your relation through marriage to the most illustrious prince, Lord Alof de Wignacourt, grand master of the Knights of Malta. He continues even now to serve the whole Christian commonwealth, proving himself worthy both of himself and of his ancestors.

But setting these matters aside, I prefer, as I said, to recall what properly concerns you. For I gladly hear the good poet:

> For lineage, ancestors, and deeds  
> That we ourselves have not performed,  
> I scarcely call our own.

Nor is it my intention to speak of everything concerning you—for that would be more suitable to a panegyric than to a brief letter—but only of one matter which, as I was beginning to say, is so closely connected with what I have in hand that I cannot omit it. I shall speak of it in such a way as to attribute it not so much to you—for your piety and religious modesty forbid this—as to God Almighty, from whom comes every good gift and every perfect gift (James 1:17).

I shall do as the divine Bernard professes to do. When he was about to praise something concerning his brothers, he said: “My mouth shall speak the praise of the Lord, not your praise.” Thus I too rightly speak the praise of that Lord who, just as he had willed the boy Maurus to be handed over by his father Eutychius to himself and to St. Benedict, so willed that you, while still almost an infant, should be consecrated to him, with the same St. Benedict and Vedastus as your patrons and educators. In their noble monastery you were brought up and instructed until manhood, as was fitting for you and for them, so that in this respect also you might imitate the man Maurus: as a child, you were like that child, with the will of both those saints. You were then entrusted to St. Willibrord, whose household at Epternach you were to govern.

How you have governed it I shall not say, lest I seem to have turned from the praise of the Lord to your own. But you may rightly praise with me that same Lord, who gave you such a mind and grace that you not only provided in every way for your children, but also raised up your fathers as though from the dead, so that from these men restored to life they might draw instruction and exhortations toward blessed life, while you sang to each of them that salutary verse:

> Learn virtue, boy, and true toil from these men;

or rather, the words of the more divine prophet:

> Ask your father, and he will declare it to you;  
> ask your elders, and they will tell you (Deut. 32:7).

Perhaps some inexperienced person will wonder what I mean by this raising of the dead. Does he not, in a certain sense, raise the dead who unexpectedly makes those who have kept so deep a silence for so many centuries speak—or rather, cry out?

Thiofridus had been silent, his monuments—most worthy of immortality—lying hidden in the narrow confines of a single library, and this for nearly five hundred and fifty years. Thiofridus, whose *Flowers*, scattered around the tombs of the saints, were themselves, so to speak, enclosed in the tomb of oblivion and unworthy ignorance, lay concealed, though they were most worthy of being brought to the nostrils of all the pious, since they are “the good odor of Christ unto God,” and “the odor of life unto life” for those who are being saved (2 Cor. 2:15–16).

If some filthy beetles are offended by this fragrance so sweet, there is nothing surprising in that: for even the good odor of Christ is to those who are perishing “the odor of death unto death” (v. 16).

You, most illustrious prelate, are bringing forth this fragrance, these *Flowers*, not content merely to enjoy them yourself unless—as you have learned without pretense—you share them with everyone without envy (Wis. 7:13). For this, the Christian world will owe you great thanks; but you will owe still greater thanks to God, who after so many years chose you above all others—although so many heirs of Thiofridus before you had remained as silent about him as he himself had been—to place this lamp, hidden under a bushel, upon a lampstand [Col. 0301] (Matt. 5:15), and to show that you took to heart the saying of the Wise Man: “Wisdom that is hidden, and treasure that is not seen—what profit is there in either?” (Ecclus. 20:32).

What wisdom is this? What treasure? The inscription speaks: *The Flowers of the Epitaph of the Saints*. These are not fading flowers, over which the prophet thunders a dreadful “Woe!” (Isa. 28:1). Rather, they are flowers that, like a rose planted beside streams of water, bear fruit; like Lebanon, possess a fragrance of sweetness; like a lily, give off perfume and flourish in grace (Ecclus. 39:17–19).

This fragrance, clearly, filled your perceptive nostrils and made you run after the scent of these Flowers. That was not enough for you. Lest the fragrance of the rose, Lebanon, and the lily seem of little usefulness—though exceedingly pleasing—Theofroi’s book blossomed for you like an early grape, and your heart rejoiced in it (Ecclus. 51:19). This joy carried you farther. You resolved to declare what fragrance these *Flowers* emitted, and in your eagerness to proclaim them you became, as it were, filled with frenzy (Ecclus. 39:16).

I say nothing to flatter your ears. I saw you so carried away in publishing these Flowers that you seemed truly to be borne along rather than acting of your own accord. It seemed to me that this early grape had intoxicated you with its fragrance. Thus you became like a drunken man, like one drenched with wine, “because of the presence of the words of the saints” (Jer. 23:9), which the Lord pours forth through Thiofridus’ mouth; you felt in your heart something like a burning fire, and you grew weak, unable to endure or contain it (Jer. 20:9). Therefore, with every gate thrown open, you are sending forth this fragrance, these Flowers, and making this treasure, hitherto hidden, publicly available.

This treasure, as though found on your own estate, rightly returns to you, although through your generosity it will belong to everyone. These Flowers, gathered from your garden, are offered chiefly to you—not smelling more sweetly, but shining somewhat more pleasantly. I do not ask you to judge favorably the little work I undertook with your approval. Your courtesy itself persuades me of this; I would wrong you if I offensively demanded what you willingly offer me.

That same courtesy will cause me to edit with greater eagerness the *Life of the great saint Willibrord*, written by the same flower-gatherer Thiofridus, and soon to publish it in print under your auspices as well. Through the same work it will become increasingly evident that the Lord, who gave you to bear the yoke from adolescence—indeed from childhood, as I said (Lam. 3:27)—also gave you to raise it above yourself.

I shall not be thought to take this improperly if I explain here that a person raises himself above himself when he raises his mind, thoughts, and cares toward knowing the life, virtues, deeds, and writings of his ancestors, and toward making them known to others also. Thus you raise yourself toward Thiofridus, who lived more than five centuries above you; toward Willibrord, who lived almost nine centuries ago.

Continue in this way, and do not cease to win the favor of the Catholic Church. Her children joined me in praying that you might one day be raised into heaven before their eyes, since you wished their deeds and achievements to be known on earth. May the Eternal One bring this about.

Luxembourg, 21 March, on the feast-day itself of St. Benedict, the great Father of monks, in the Christian year 1619.

Your most reverend and most illustrious Lordship’s servant in Christ,  
Johannes ROBERTI.

[Col. 0301]

## TO THE READER

[Col. 0301A] I scarcely see what I should say to you, friendly reader, that you could not yourself draw either from the preface to the most illustrious prelate, from the *Life of Thiofridus*, or from my notes. Nevertheless, accept these few remarks.

1. I could not provide a more accurate text than the one I give, being deprived of the assistance of better books. I nevertheless hope that nothing of any importance is present that cannot be understood without difficulty. In more obscure passages, the notes will help.

2. For your convenience, I placed the epigraphs of the individual chapters, in the author’s own words, at the beginning of each chapter, although he himself had placed them only at the beginning of the book.

[Col. 0302A] 3. Since I wanted the notes to be more readily available, I preferred to append them to the individual chapters rather than relegate them to the end of the work. I hope you will approve.

You now have these materials; farewell, and expect the remainder of Thiofridus from me. Indeed, if you can, help me by arranging for other works or letters of his to be brought to me from elsewhere. I shall see that you receive them with interest and gratitude.

But listen. One more word. If you are a Zealander or a Hollander, I commend this book to you, if only because of the noble history that you will find in the *Life of Thiofridus*, § 4.

[Col. 0301]

## AGAIN TO THE READER

As times now are, while I am preparing to publish the *Life of Thiofridus*, it occurs to me that there will be some who will say that he was not important enough for it to matter greatly who he was or what he did. But whoever thinks this may perhaps be one of those who greatly esteem the *Lives of the Romans and Greeks* written by Plutarch. Nor do I despise them. What of the *Lives of the Philosophers* in Diogenes Laërtius? What do they seem to be? Let them too have their due honor. What of the lives of poets published by Crinitus? Certainly some of them could have remained unknown without great loss. What of the *Icones* and *Lives of Calvin* and similar pests, which Beza—the pest himself, epidemic in character—spread by infecting the Christian world?

Yet I judge this man worthy who, while professing to celebrate the living illustrious for both learning and piety, through whose ministry true religion was chiefly restored, nevertheless, blinded concerning one of these illustrious heroes by the just judgment of a just God, wrote explicitly that he had spent almost his entire life at court, that worst of teachers of piety and honesty, and had not amended his insufficiently Christian morals even in extreme old age. This was Clément Marot. Behold from whom you are to seek the restoration of true religion! Let Beza, his equal, seek it from him. For my part, he shall certainly not have me as a rival.

I cannot endure even the thought of comparing our Thiofridus with such monsters. Indeed, I confidently declare that he is far preferable both to Plutarch’s Catos, to the Biantes of Laërtius, and to the Propertiuses of Crinitus.

This is my opinion; reader, I pray that it may be yours with me.

[Col. 0303]

## THE LIFE OF D. THIOFRIDUS, ABBOT AND LORD OF EFTERNACH

Collected diligently from his works by Father Johannes Roberti, priest of the Society of Jesus.

[Col. 0303B] Learned reader, I condemn my own undertaking: I am about to write a life which I must confess that I scarcely know at all. It would therefore be more correct to change the heading and rewrite it as: *Fragments of a Life*. And these fragments themselves are extremely few; but—and you should value this highly—they have been collected from Thiofridus himself, who alone knew best what should be written about him. If anyone can assist from another source—and so far I have sought help in vain—he will do me a kindness by supplying it; and I shall add what I can when possible. But enough of a preface for so brief a writing.

### § I. His Name

I do not approve those who alter his name and call him Theofridus, since he everywhere writes himself Thiofridus; or, with the Latin ending changed into the vernacular, Thifrid or Thiefrid. Book III of the poem *On the Life of St. Willibrord* says:

[Col. 0303C]

> The monk Thifrid came to the renowned mart.

I understand or approve even less the fact that some person—I do not know from where—called him Theodefridus.

Should anyone also think that he was called Vernatus on the basis of that verse in which he dedicates the *Life of St. Willibrord*, written by himself, to the saint:

> Thiefrid Vernatus, I dedicate this gift to you, Willibrord,  
> The offering of a poor talent.

Away with that! Without doubt it should be read: *Verna tuus*, “your servant.” He calls himself the servant of St. Willibrord, and in the thirty-sixth chapter of the same saint’s *Life*, which you will read below in this *Life*, he also calls himself the Lord’s little servant.

### § II. His Homeland

His name seemed to me to sound somewhat English or Frisian. But names easily migrate. I have nothing else to add [Col. 0303D] except an ingenuous confession of my ignorance.

### § III. The Course of His Life

Here again, little is clear to me. Accept the few things I have read or gathered. To say nothing of his life before he entered religious life and joined the community at Epternach, about which I have absolutely nothing to say, I infer from his age, discussed below in § 9, that he undertook this way of life when he was fairly young, almost a boy. After at least thirty-nine years of religious profession, he became abbot. See the same section. He lived twenty-eight years as abbot.

This is taught me by an annotation written in an ancient hand by some religious of Epternach at the end of Book IV of the *Flowers*. From it we learn other things about Thiofridus as well, and I therefore reproduce it here word for word. It reads as follows:

> Thiofridus, abbot of this monastery, an outstanding teacher, the author of this book, in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1078, on the thirteenth day before the Kalends of September, assumed the abbacy at Rome and governed it most vigorously for twenty-eight years. A man of subtle intelligence, he left behind very many monuments, in prose, in verse, and in various historical songs, in which he was wonderfully distinguished.

So much for the general course of his life. Let us now examine certain particulars.

### § IV. His Deeds

In addition to what the preceding annotation suggests, I have observed the following.

1. He succeeded Abbot Regimbert, after the latter had presided for thirty years. Thus says the Epternach manuscript entitled *The Golden Book*, p. 115.

2. While Regimbert was still alive, Thiofridus was his coadjutor, or designated successor. But after Regimbert’s death, when a certain rival appealed to the emperor against Thiofridus, Thiofridus in turn approached the pope, who at that time was Gregory VII. Before this entirely impartial judge he obtained his right, and thus, as the annotation says, assumed the abbacy at Rome. See Bertelius in the *History of Luxembourg* [Col. 0304D] and the manuscript catalogue of the abbots of Epternach.

3. He arranged for the rights and liberties of the monastery of Epternach to be confirmed by the Emperor Henry IV. After *The Golden Book* had included the imperial diploma, it concludes as follows on p. 101:

> These things were enacted in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1095, in the third indiction, in the fortieth year of the reign and the twelfth year of the empire of our lord, the Emperor Augustus Henry, through the efforts of Thiofridus, successor of the venerable lord Abbot Regimbert.

It adds:

> The suitable and most noble witnesses of this grant and confirmation are these: Henry the Palatine, etc.

Clearly, at that time it was considered so important to pursue the churches of God with benefactions that even emperors made this their sole concern, and the greatest princes considered it especially honorable either to be present as witnesses or to act in that capacity. We see how matters stand in this respect now. But it should not be left unmentioned that the very words just copied from *The Golden Book* were written by Thiofridus himself. For who else would call the deceased Regimbert “the venerable lord abbot,” while failing to honor Thiofridus, who was then seated at the helm of sacred government, with even a single title of honor?

[Col. 0305B] 4. He acquired the allod of Gichilingen near Born and Alstorff and assigned them for the use of the brethren. These are the words of the catalogue of the abbots of Epternach.

5. That Thiofridus was a great man, held in the highest esteem, is evident from the fact that Bruno, archbishop of Trier, not only regarded him as an intimate friend but also entrusted his soul to him, as you will read in the dedicatory letter of this work, the *Flowers*. I take this to mean that Thiofridus was Bruno’s confessor and spiritual adviser.

Bruno’s love and affection for Thiofridus continued until Thiofridus’ death, indeed until his burial. The catalogue of the abbots teaches this:

> In a good old age, he fell asleep in the Lord, and was buried in the presence of Bruno, archbishop of Trier.

This Bruno belonged through his father, Arnold, and his mother, Adelheid, to the illustrious families of the counts of Bretherm and Lauffens, as our Christophorus Browerus reports in his *Annals of Trier*, not yet published, under the year of Christ 1102. There, and afterward, he records other matters concerning Bruno’s virtues, especially his remarkable generosity; he also records his authority and supreme dignity, namely, that he obtained the office of vicedominus for the Emperor Henry and held the direction of affairs, and that during the greatest disturbances of the commonwealth he handled the reins of government skillfully and wisely. I have no doubt that in these matters as well he made use of the excellent and salutary counsel of our Thiofridus.

### 6. Among these fragments of Thiofrid’s works

Among these fragments of Thiofrid’s works, I would consider myself guilty of irreverence if I passed over his singular achievement, in which—if anywhere—there appears his prudence, his authority, and his sanctity. Moreover, it is a little jewel of history, such as one does not readily find elsewhere, since it is worthy of the highest remembrance. Thanks for publishing it will be owed to me—certainly they will be owed—by all other students of antiquity, but especially by the apple of Belgium’s eye, Antwerp, and the island of Walcheren, and on it the city of Middelburg. (Alas! Where now is that ancient Catholic piety of theirs?) But far greater thanks will be owed to the very reverend and most distinguished man, the Lord Peter Richardot, abbot and master of Echternach, who made available a copy of this narrative from the library of Saint Clement Willibrord. And still greater thanks are owed to Thiofrid himself, who performed such deeds in such a manner and handed them down in such a manner to pious posterity in writings destined for immortality.

I would therefore regard it as sacrilege either to alter even a word in his words or to allow anyone to withdraw credit from him. Accordingly, in the Life of Willibrord, which Thiofrid carefully composed in thirty-six chapters—and this Life, hitherto unpublished, will be provided for you, kindly reader who loves ancient piety, furnished with some notes of mine—after he had carefully explained in chapter 35 how the Walcheren people, severely harassed in war by Rupert the Younger, son of Baldwin, count of Flanders, had obtained, through the aid of Saint Willibrord, a noble and indeed miraculous victory, he treated in chapter 36 the civil war that subsequently arose among them. Here you have that chapter, with its heading.

### CHAPTER XXXVI.—On the arrival of Abbot Thiofrid on the island of Walcheren, and on the peace restored and confirmed there through delightful miracles

“After it had driven away dangers from foreign wars by its courage and by the grace of the Lord—namely, the island of Walcheren—it turned its weapons, as it were, into its own entrails; and, following the example of madmen, it sharpened the sword of its hands and limbs against its own civil blood, itself cutting itself. It burst into mutual destruction; and after the leading nobles of the island had been slain, it broke out into such great discord that no one had the freedom either to enter or to leave safely. From one people there arose two contending bodies, and the men of the same strongholds were divided into two hostile lines.

“In the several factions the fire of deadly hatred burned so fiercely that, without the display of arms, without a gathering of fellow tribesmen and retainers, they did not dare—not even on Good Friday, on which the supreme High Priest and Shepherd of the true tabernacle, essentially good, offering his life for his sheep, presented his blood, the priceless ransom of the world, as a sacrifice to the Lord the Father—to approach to kiss the Lord’s cross.

“At last, exhausted and broken after many funerals of their own people and various hardships, amid such an intensity of dangers they saw as their safest harbor of counsel the plan of summoning to themselves by a common embassy Thiofrid, the Christ-loving abbot of Echternach, so that, by the authority of the illustrious patron Willibrord, whose place he held, he might advise them in their ruined affairs and undertake, for the sake of reconciliation, to restore and settle the treaties of disturbed peace.

“They waited for him as he approached the harbor of Antwerp for two days, with sixteen long ships. But since necessity delayed him on the journey, and they were forced to return because of the demands of their general assembly, which was to take place on the third day, they entrusted the honor of his arrival and reception to his necessary attendants and friends, the magistrates of the emporium.

“Now all their crops had withered through the unseasonableness of the weather; they were watered by no moisture of dew or rain, but the harvests threatened to enter upon a barren year. And when the wind, filling the sails, drove the fleet onward, and the ships had reached the middle of the deep, they cried out with joyful devotion, though their minds were grieving, yet inflamed by a great ardor of faith:

“‘O Lord, O holy Willibrord, if you are coming to us, your special people, give an evident sign of your apostleship in the Lord; and before we are shut in by the deep harbor, make a fruitful rain descend and flow upon us.’

“No delay followed. Suddenly the left-hand thunderclap sounded, and the troubled waters testified that the wind had arisen. Now clouds, pressed together in the sky, thickened into rain; becoming dense, they poured down and drove away the losses caused by heat and drought. The Lord set apart a willing rain for his inheritance, and by this most evident sign of his mercy declared the spiritual arrival of his beloved servant.

“Immediately the sailors’ cry struck the heavens. With arms drawn back, they churned the waters into foam; the sea opened beneath the oars, and the waters shrieked under the ramming prows. All of them, singing a churchly rather than a nautical chant, joyfully sprang upon their own shores.

“Scarcely had they begun to approach their native walls when, far from the city, all the men of Antwerp came forward to meet the representative of the excellent bishop Willibrord, carrying the reliquaries of their saints, hammered with elaborate work in gold and silver. He was received with immense glory, like an angel of the Lord, like Christ Jesus. After restoring the dissenters to friendship and binding them together in the firmest peace, he was carried with honorable transport to the harbor facilities of Middelburg.

“At twilight, when his arrival became known, islanders of both sexes and every age filled the shores in a joyful gathering. They received him with the deepest devotion and magnificent honor, as though their common patron and Lord had come in the flesh himself, and they escorted him with hymnic cries into the prayer-house.

“On the following day, when bright daylight first drove the stars from the sky, they gathered in crowds at the joyful gates. In the presence of the Lord’s envoy, so that the existing order of affairs might be firmly established, they stood with the greatest discipline and reverence, contrary to barbarian custom. But he, governing their minds and soothing their hearts by his words, decided first to undertake and deal with lesser matters and to postpone until the next day the greater and harsher ones.

“While he was occupied with these matters and was taking counsel with them and with others whom he considered suitable, he saw close by a certain man from the poor, prostrate himself and embrace the feet of one of noble lineage and rank among the rich. At some time, through thoughtless insolence, he had inflicted upon this man an almost irremediable and deadly wound.

“Thiofrid rose and hurried to the place. Prostrating himself together with the prostrate man, he kissed his knees. He placed the staff of the excellent bishop upon the ground before the man, who was refusing and resisting with increasing obstinacy, and begged, urged, and implored him to grant pardon for the offense to the penitent.

“But that man’s adamantine heart and contemptuous spirit were softened by none of the remedies of sound teaching. Though all who stood around shouted out and detested such hardness, he felt no shame and gave no assent.

“Out of his mind, he departed in an outburst and returned home. There, immediately, he paid the penalty for his contempt and disobedience.” For he became possessed, terrified all who stood by as they watched him being struck, and brought the greatest grief and mourning upon the whole neighborhood and his household.

“His panting breast and distended belly were shaken by frequent and extremely violent throbbing; a sound could be heard as though some force within were driving the rib cage and stomach with hard levers. And what could be more cruel than such torture, what more bitter?

“Terrified by so great a punishment of divine vengeance, his dependents and kinsmen wearied Thiofrid with many entreaties and compelled him to go there as the Lord’s courier, so that they might rescue the captive from the bitterness of such suffering.

“He came, placed upon the possessed man’s belly his small reliquary, in which a little portion of the rib of the most merciful Father Willibrord was enclosed; and immediately the Devil, unable to bear the weight of such holiness, abandoned the vessel which he had seized to punish disobedience, leaving it to glorify the power of the supreme Maker.

“Great rejoicing arose, because salvation had come to that house, because a son of Abraham had been liberated and freed from the son of eternal death.

“Meanwhile, in the presence of the assembled and waiting people, another sign was made known, similar in cause but different in punishment. A certain man fell on his face before a rich man whom he himself had wounded long before and earnestly labored to make him favorable and reconciled to him.

“Ekehard, an excellent coenobite and the abbot’s interpreter, who before his conversion had been one of the most distinguished among the princes of that island, approached the man who was refusing and resisting. I repeat, he approached and pleaded with many and most humble entreaties and bendings of the knees that, for the sake of the Lord and Clement Willibrord, he should reconcile his spirit to the man seeking pardon, though by the law of nations he was estranged from him.

“But that wicked man, in youthful arrogance, scorned to listen. He sprang up, departed, and withdrew a short distance. Then, behold, divine vengeance came upon him.

“For just as his inner eyes had been deprived of their inner light, so his external eyes were suddenly deprived of their external light and darkened by the gloom of blindness. His iniquity had emerged as though from fat; he had swollen with the breath of pride without having been scourged; he had not feared to set his mouth against heaven. He was compelled to learn what it meant to be under the lash.

“He struck against things and was struck by them; groping, staggering, he turned this way and that, and, clothed in his confusion as though in a double cloak, he feared the approach and sight of men.

“At last his father ran up to him as he stumbled on offended feet, drenched entirely in a shower of tears. Rebuking the hardness of his heart, he took him by the outstretched hand and led him back to the place from which, angered by resentment, he had departed in reckless boldness.

“There he granted pardon to the man who begged him; he recovered the clarity of his sight and returned as many thanks as he could to the illuminator of all.

“On that day divine mercy displayed a beautiful spectacle to pious minds, and by instilling fear and the greatest terror into the proud laid the foundation of future peace and reconciliation.

“In the narrow space of time, four miracles were celebrated in two men. One, because of the guilt of having shown contempt, lost his reason in madness; for the benefit of many he came to his senses and recovered with sounder understanding. The other, seeing a speck in his brother’s eye while not seeing the beam in his own, stumbled into the obstacles of blindness; but, led by repentance, he was enlightened with a clearer light in both body and soul.

“On the following day, when the first lamp of day was illuminating the earth, the whole island, of one mind and with one judgment, assembled in groups like swarms of bees, so that in the presence of the representative of the excellent bishop and of his relics, the causes and quarrels of all might be examined and settled, and the old offenses and deadly hatreds of their feuds might be put to rest.

“They stood like stars in their stations and order, and with the most subtle investigation they sought the light and the counsels of prudence, because all her ways are beautiful and all her paths peaceful.

“Without delay, eternal Wisdom, which had proclaimed herself through the mouth of Solomon the Ididaean, saying, ‘I am present with the learned in their thoughts; counsel is mine, and equity; my is prudence and strength; through me lawgivers decree what is just’—by the grace of her hidden inspiration drew all their hearts into one and the same resolution: from the families of each side whose members had been killed, seven leaders nearest in blood were to be chosen.

“By the decree of these men and of the presiding lord, the archimandrite, with his companions, and after the most careful investigation, the firmest treaties of peace were to be arranged.

“Accordingly, in accordance with their common counsel and decree, after thirty pounds had first been paid in settlement of the blood-matter, according to the custom of the people, with a threefold compensation, they were made—whether they wished it or not, so that no disagreement might arise from past events—soldiers of the avengers of blood, for the eternal oblivion of discord.

“Without any human fear but by divine terror, men endowed with such beauty of form, such stature of body, and such greatness of strength and wisdom that anyone who did not know them would judge them chosen not from one people but from the whole world—men, I repeat, most distinguished in birth, reputation, and wealth—were compelled to submit and obey wards far beneath them. Unless they had been restrained by heavenly power, they would have preferred to gain death rather than endure what seemed a disgrace and an insult.

“This deserves to be noted and transmitted to posterity as a matter of supreme wonder: that a people so fierce, bold, and warlike, which could never be subdued by the sword, endured being bound and constrained by the reins of simple words. And, to say nothing of the decrees of the Lord’s courier, whatever his aforesaid interpreter ordered by his authority and by that of Saint Father Willibrord—as though it were ordered from his own mouth—no one at all dared to violate or transgress; no one delayed to obey. So great was the terror of the Lord that fell upon them all.

“Peace, both private and public, was thereafter restored by the merits of the excellent bishop Clement Willibrord, through the wonders he performed, as though he himself were bodily present in the assembly and directing it; and it was confirmed by the sacrament of an oath, not only on Walcheren but on every neighboring island. The earth poured forth golden crops in abundance from its full horn.

“During the two months in which the abbot, the little servant among the Lord’s servants, prolonged his stay there for the common good, no work and no activity was practiced there except joy, honor, and dancing; extraordinary rejoicing, feast days, banquets, and festivities.

“At last he returned to his homeland amid the magnificence of the highest honor; received with the great joy of his entire city, which poured out to meet him, he offered a sacrifice of due praise to the eternal Trinity.

“And since we have traversed an immense expanse and it is now time to release the horse’s foaming neck, let us bring this long work to an end, passing over a certain unusual miracle—namely, that in the basilica endowed with the blood of so great a Father, silver stolen from the cross could not be melted by the application of fire for three days; and when it was cut into equal parts, it split into the seed of three names, in a manner never seen by men to be made even; while the altar cloth could be cut neither with scissors, nor with a knife, nor finally with the sharpest sword.

“Passing over, I say, this sign so miraculous, let us impose an end upon our long work, so that at the end, which is without end, we may remain in Christ Jesus, our only Lord, offering him, according to the measure of our ability, manifold thanks for all that he has given us, and for the multitude of blessings which, through the renowned patronage of his most beloved Clement Willibrord, he has bestowed upon us according to his mercy and according to the multitude of his mercies. To him be praise, honor, unimaginable glory, and dominion throughout infinite ages. Amen.”

With this noble chapter our Thiofrid concludes the Life of Saint Clement Willibrord. If anything in it should appear somewhat obscure, the candid reader will find its explanation in the proper place—that is, in the Life of Saint Willibrord itself, which, with God and his holy servant favoring us, we shall publish not long afterward.

Moreover—something which perhaps I should more properly have placed before this chapter—I certainly must not remain silent about what my Thiofrid did not leave unsaid in the final part of chapter 35. After the miraculous victory over Count Rupert that I mentioned, Thiofrid says:

“The victorious phalanx, after the glory of so great a triumph, offered a victim of due praise to the Triumphator of all; and, renewing and confirming the vow by which it had previously bound itself, sent two standards of the defeated prince to the church of Echternach, there to be preserved as an everlasting memorial of the glorious victory granted to it through the merits of the magnificent bishop Clement Willibrord.”

Look upon these things, Walcheren Zeelanders, and neighboring Hollanders, and think of your ancestors.

### § V. Virtues and sanctity

Thiofrid was not a man who trumpeted his virtues or displayed his sanctity. Yet just as fragrance breaks forth from spices, however secretly they may be carried and carefully concealed, so virtue shines out even when one presses it down. This happened in the case of our author. To say nothing of his other virtues, his humility shines everywhere,

> like the moon among lesser fires.

This humility makes such a great man a dry wild olive tree and an abbot of the Echternach monastery of no consequence (Preface to the *Flowers*, at the beginning). It makes him earth, and unworthy of the Lord’s footstool (ibid.). Though God, heaven, and earth alike attest and applaud him with many and very great signs, though he is glorious through miracles and, so to speak, swims in their midst, it nevertheless makes him “the Lord’s little servant” (*Life of Saint Willibrord*, chapter 36). Finally, the same humility “denies that a pilot suitable for steering a ship through any stormy sea can even guide a skiff upon a lake” (*Prologue to the Life of Saint Liutwinus*).

His religion and his worship of God, the saints, and sacred relics are so well known from all these and his other books that they need no explanation in my words.

You will read of his charity and zeal for the public good when you read these words of his:

> “Excessive charity, which can do all things, hopes all things, and endures all things, drives us to hang our swelling sails upon the mast, uncoil the ropes, steer the rudder, and, with the Holy Spirit furthering our course, come to rest.”  
> (*Prologue to the Life of Saint Liutwinus.*)

You will discover the remaining virtues of this holy man for yourself in his writings, marvel at them, and—as I pray—imitate them.

I also assigned sanctity to this paragraph. I certainly know that sanctity consists in the grace of God and in the virtues. Thus, while speaking of the virtues, I may seem to have said enough about sanctity. But I wish to add some conspicuous signs of sanctity, such that anyone who saw them would immediately form an opinion of holiness.

Such are those which we placed shortly before from Thiofrid himself, performed on the island of Walcheren. Such is the fact that he perceived a certain divine fragrance from the relics of the saints, as you will learn from Book I, chapter 6, of the *Flowers*. There are other examples of the same kind, which you yourself will notice.

### § VI. Friends and contemporaries

To illuminate Thiofrid’s life, it is relevant to know with whom he associated familiarly. You have already heard about Archbishop Bruno, who entrusted his soul to Thiofrid. Regimbert, the abbot—a holy man—held such an opinion of Thiofrid’s sanctity, learning, and style that he considered him worthy to be entrusted with writing down what Regimbert himself had received from the Holy Spirit (Book IV of the *Flowers*, chapter 7).

He lived with Abbot Humbert, a man of the highest religious devotion, as Thiofrid himself says, and of sanctity, as the narrative indicates in Book I, chapter 6, of the *Flowers*.

Let us add that at this very time there lived throughout the Christian world many men renowned for the glory of sanctity and learning. It is permissible to believe that with some of them, at least, our Thiofrid had dealings either through conversation or through letters. Such men were Gregory VII, supreme pontiff; Lanfranc, archbishop of Canterbury; Hugh, archbishop of Grenoble; Saint Bruno, founder of the Carthusian institute; Ivo, bishop of Chartres; Saint Anselm, archbishop of Canterbury; Robert, founder of the Cistercians; and many others.

But without conjecture or controversy, it is certain that he was familiar with those great men of the monastery of Mettlach, concerning whom he reports in the *Life of Saint Liutwinus*, chapter 5:

> “Within our own memory, such bright lights of the world and such magnificent names of men shone there at Mettlach that the one considered least among them in rank was regarded as most worthy of the highest pinnacle of honor; and whatever church obtained one of them as its ruler would be illumined by the light of his teaching and virtues, just as the world is illumined by the sun’s radiance.”

Moreover, although Thiofrid enjoyed the circumstances and good fortune of so many other distinguished men, he also had adversaries and Momuses. Read the *Prologue to the Flowers* and the *Life of Saint Liutwinus*.

### § VII. Learning and style

Thiofrid possessed learning which, for those times, was very great and—what you will marvel at still more in a coenobite—extremely varied. He speaks almost continually in the language of Scripture, as Saint Bernard did after him. He borrows mystical meanings chiefly from Saint Gregory the Great, although he often employs meanings of his own invention, and very sharp ones at that. He frequently cites the other Fathers, especially Augustine.

He had carefully read both sacred and secular histories, and often employs them with great skill. One may marvel at his oratory and poetry, and at the force of both, in a man who, as I infer from good evidence, achieved everything by his own study, without a teacher and without formal instruction. You will also notice philosophy and the mathematical disciplines brought forward in their proper places with learning and gravity. What is more, as I note elsewhere, he employed scholastic theology before either its teachers or its name was heard among the learned.

He was not ignorant of the Greek and Hebrew languages, although, since he lacked practice, he does not appear to have mastered them perfectly.

As for his style, you can see what it is. He possesses an immense abundance of words and thoughts; his periods are rounded and driven into a circle as though by a compass. Yet they are generally too long and therefore obstructed, deceiving the reader who is beginning to doze. My notes, if I am not mistaken, will provide a remedy: in them we have briefly and clearly gathered the whole sense of his sentences.

He is frequent in allegories, antitheses, and allusions to Scripture, histories, and poets. His affectation of Greek expressions offends more delicate ears. You see that I am not acting as Thiofrid’s eulogist, since I also disclose his faults, although I willingly attribute them to his century and to the lack of a teacher.

### § VIII. Writings

The works which I have so far been able to see are these: the *Life of Saint Liutwinus*; the *Flowers of the Epitaphs of the Saints*; the *Life of Saint Willibrord* in prose, and the same work in heroic verse. Also a sermon for the feast of the same saint, and another sermon for the feast of Saint Wilgis, who was the father of Saint Willibrord.

That he wrote more is testified by the Annotation cited above by me in section 4, and by several fragments in Jodocus Coccius’s *Catholic Treasury*.

### § IX. Age

I think that he died at the age of one hundred, or close to it. To demonstrate this, consider the following.

He became abbot in the year 1078 and remained so for twenty-eight years; he therefore ceased to be abbot in 1106.

Yet he was alive in the year 1031, as is clear from Book I, chapter 6, of the *Flowers*, letter O.

You have seventy-five years.

Now that he was then not much younger than twenty-five is sufficiently indicated by the event narrated in that chapter.

Add that Bertelius and Miraeus write that Thiofrid died in the year of the Lord 1110.

If that is so, he handed over the abbacy to his successor Gerard four years before his death.

And thus, although in that chapter 6 he was only twenty-one years old, he nevertheless died a CENTENARIAN.

### THIOFRID’S VERSES ON HIS *FLOWERS*

I build pyramids and ciboria; I gather FLOWERS;

I scatter them over the tombs made sacred by the flesh of the saints.

I note bonds, crosses, grilles, saws, stones, and racks.

The life of the world and the salvation of so many are their sufferings.

### [THE FLOWERS OF THE EPITAPHS OF THE SAINTS]

## THE PREFACE TO THE BOOK OF THE *FLOWERS* BEGINS

**Note:** “Preface.” This first word reminds me to say once and for all that our Thiofrid has certain peculiarities in spelling, which some overly fussy person might call bad spelling instead. Yet in such matters one must defer to usage, concerning which Horace elegantly says:

> “In whose power are the judgment, the law, and the standard of speech.”

So, by the same right, I would say: of writing. And if anyone should protest more insistently, let him know that the origin of these forms plainly resists him; it was not my intention to claim authority for myself in another’s writing or to use knife and sponge according to my own will. Let Thiofrid’s age also appear in these matters.

Furthermore, other words occur which, although they seem to depart from the customary manner of writing, nevertheless have good—and indeed great—authors on their side; if no others, at least the poets. Such are *ammirari*, *optinere*, *abicere*, *disicere*, *adprime*, *amminiculum*, *inlecebrae*, *inlectus*, *flagrantia* for *fragrantia*, and *ortus* for *hortus*.

## INTO THE BOOK OF THE *FLOWERS*

**Note:** “Into the *Flowers*.” He rightly calls it this. Everything in this little work is flowery, and indeed consists of genuine flowers. To say nothing of the diction—which in that age you might call not merely flowery but jewelled—consider the matter itself.

You would admit that some little Greekling was being frivolous when, having gathered material from everywhere, even from the dregs, he called the epigrammatists’ collection an *anthology* (*anthologia*, ἀνθολογία); Apuleius’s books the *Floridia*; and the sayings gathered by Stobaeus from philosophers into commonplaces, the sentences which Suidas called an *anthologion* (ἀνθολόγιον).

These flowers and this flower-gatherer far surpass those and those works. Finally, what Carus falsely claimed about himself, Thiofrid, most beloved of God, may rightly and truly claim with pride:

> As bees in flower-bearing groves taste everything,  
> so we too graze upon all golden sayings.  
> *(Add: and deeds as well.)*  
> Always worthy of a golden and enduring life.

Read, and it would be astonishing if, enticed by the fragrance of the sweetness of these *Flowers*, you did not wish to become entirely a nose.

## OF THE EPITAPHS OF THE SAINTS

**Note:** “Of the *Flowers of the Epitaphs of the Saints*.” He had undertaken to adorn the tombs, monuments, and relics of the saints. This also reflects the custom of the early Christians, which persists even today, of scattering flowers over the monuments of the saints.

The Calvinists cry out that this is idolatry; we call their accusation blasphemy and impiety. Which side is more correct? Let Augustine judge—or rather, let God and his wonder-working hand judge. Let the bishop of Hippo himself tell it in his own words:

> “At the waters of Tibilis, when Bishop Projectus brought the relics of the most glorious martyr Stephen, a great crowd gathered and came forward to honor his memory. There a blind woman, when she was being led to the bishop who was carrying the sacred relics, prayed. She gave him the flowers she was carrying; she received them back; she brought them to her eyes, and immediately she saw. Those who were present were amazed. She went ahead rejoicing, making her way along the road and no longer seeking a guide for the road.”  
> (*The City of God*, Book XXII, chapter 8.)

I believe this to have been the thought of our Thiofrid himself, since he affirms it in Book IV, chapter 7, at the very beginning, and in the poem inscribed for the image at the threshold of the book, where he sings:

> Flowers  
> I scatter over the tombs made sacred by the flesh of the saints.

## OF THE EPITAPHS OF THE SAINTS

From a rich, beautiful, splendid, fruitful olive tree (Jeremiah 1:16) in the house of the Lord, to Bruno, archbishop of the holy see of Trier,

**Note:** “A fruitful olive tree.” Our author delights in allegories and in the mystical and accommodative meanings of Scripture, which he uses with great skill, as you will discover while reading. This address has its twin and counterpart in that of the *Life of Saint Willibrord*: “Cedars of Lebanon planted in the house of the Lord,” and so forth.

To a dry wild olive tree (Romans 2:17), the insignificant abbot of the monastery of Echternach,

**Note:** “A dry wild olive tree.” Again, in the preface to the *Life of Saint Willibrord*: “A wild olive grafted into an olive tree through rich mercy,” and so forth.

**Note:** “Of the Echternach monastery.” I know that the name is written both *Epternacum* and *Echternacum*. But when authors vary, why should I follow anyone other than the form presently in my hands?

**Note:** “Abbot.” He calls himself this again in the prose *Life of Saint Willibrord*, chapter 36, which is the last chapter, and in Book III of the poem. I think it is a Greek word, *hegoumenos* (ἡγούμενος), meaning leader, guide, or superior. The author’s delight in inserting Greek words into his text is evident throughout all his works. He especially uses those employed by sacred Scripture.

Thus, in Matthew (chapter 2), we read: *ek sou gar exeleusetai hegoumenos* (ἐκ σοῦ γὰρ ἐξελεύσεται ἡγούμενος), “From you a leader shall go forth.” And in Luke 22:26: *ho hegoumenos hōs ho diakonōn* (ὁ ἡγούμενος ὡς ὁ διακονῶν), “The one who is foremost as the one who serves.” And in Stephen (Acts 7:10): *katestēsen auton hēgoumenon ep’ Aigypton* (κατέστησεν αὐτὸν ἡγούμενον ἐπ’ Αἴγυπτον), “He appointed him ruler over Egypt.” In the same book (14:11): *hēgoumenos tou logou* (ἡγούμενος τοῦ λόγου), “leader of the word.” Finally, in chapter 15:22: *andras hēgoumenous en tois adelphois* (ἄνδρας ἡγουμένους ἐν τοῖς ἀδελφοῖς), “men who are foremost among the brothers.”

Thiofrid therefore signifies that he is an abbot and set over the others. Hence, in the cited passage of the poem, shortly afterward, as though explaining himself, he says:

> Thifrid, the remembered abbot, came into the emporium.

Nor, so far as I know, does he give this title anywhere else to anyone who does not possess some authority. Christophorus Browerus, our own scholar, likewise understood Thiofrid in this way. Joannes Dulmenius, a priest of our Society, testifies that he found the following note among the papers of our Christopher Browerus, of blessed memory. Some time after sending me letters about this matter and others, he was cut off by an untimely death; with him much learning and great hopes were lost.

While writing these things, I came upon the eighth synod and, in it, a letter of Ignatius, patriarch of Constantinople, to Pope Nicholas, containing these words: *hēgoumenōn te kai presbyterōn, kai heterōn monachōn plēthos apeiron* (ἡγουμένων τε καὶ πρεσβυτέρων, καὶ ἑτέρων μοναχῶν πλῆθος ἄπειρον), “of abbots and presbyters, and an innumerable multitude of other monks,” where *hēgoumenoi* plainly means the superiors of monks, or heads of monasteries. Otherwise he would not properly have said “of other monks.”

Thiofrid, abbot, asks for the incorruption of soul and body and the inward contemplation of the supreme good.

**Note:** “Of soul and body.” He frequently sprinkles his pages with these Greek words, more than with any others: *psychēs kai sōmatos* (ψυχῆς καὶ σώματος), “of soul and body.”

Before you, my lord, jewel and glory of bishops, had ascended the heights of the archiepiscopal dignity,

**Note:** “Archiepiscopal.” A word apparently coined by Thiofrid to express what belongs to an archbishop.

just as David’s soul was joined to Jonathan’s, so my soul, which is an irritant to your holy soul,

**Note:** “An irritant.” This expression frequently occurs in the prophet Ezekiel: “a house provoking,” referring to the people of Israel. It signifies one who is rebellious and obstinate against God. In a spirit of humility, our author professes himself to be such.

has been joined to it—both because of the most honorable courtesy and moderation of your character and because your kinsmen,

**Note:** “Your kinsmen.” Enough has been said about Bruno and his family in Thiofrid’s *Life*. Likewise about his familiarity with Thiofrid and the soul entrusted to him.

heroes of the highest nobility and dignity, have shown me esteem and goodwill. But from the time when, through the manifold grace of divine providence, you were enthroned and entrusted your soul more familiarly to me, the vilest little ash, as though I had some importance with the Lord, the flame of my intimate love for you burned more ardently in my meditation (Psalm 38:4), and I poured out toward you all the marrow and inward parts of my heart.

And I call Jesus, his saints, and his kingdom to witness: there is nothing false or feigned in my friendship; whatever there is, it is wholly true and wholly voluntary. Nor is it in order that I may cunningly entice your munificence into bestowing any benefits upon me and mine, but because of the excellence of your virtue, which has been proclaimed and recognized.

For nothing is more lovable than virtue, as Cicero, the king of orators, declares; nothing draws us more powerfully toward love, since because of virtue and goodness we in some way love even those whom we have never seen.

Therefore, …

[Note: [Col. 0315C] O refuge and protection. In brief notes on such a writer, it would be tedious and childish to collect every possible item, even from the grammarian’s register [Col. 0315D]. Therefore I omit here the remark that this verse is borrowed from Horace, right at his first entrance. I do note this: as I mentioned in the Life, Thiofridus, who lacked no branch of learning, also drew quite a few things from the poets, as you will discover for yourself when reading.]

O refuge and protection and my sweet glory, and the crown of all the clergy throughout the world, never forgetful of any honorable consideration: because of so great a fire of my love, kindled toward you, I consecrate to your name, as to an exalted Divinity, the first-fruits of my labor, the little book whose title is [Note: [Col. 0315D] The inscription of the title. The epigraph of Psalm 15 is: “The inscription of the title: to David himself.” Thiofridus, thoroughly versed in the divine writings, has words from them come to his mouth and pen without his intending it. You may observe the same thing in Saint Bernard.] “The Inscription of the Title: Flowers of the Epitaph of the Saints”; I have dedicated it to you, having [Note: [Col. 0315D] Four volumes—seven chapters. This writer enjoys extracting mysteries from numbers. He took this from the Fathers, whom you will often see wholly immersed in such matters—including the great Augustine. I record this lest some shallow critic think Thiofridus pursued the point frivolously. Concerning the number four, Philo says much in *On the Creation of the World* and *Life of Moses*, as does Origen in *Homily 1 on Ezekiel*; Augustine, Book II of *On Christian Doctrine*, chapter 16, and elsewhere frequently. Others likewise in other places. Concerning the number seven, Philo does so in *Allegories*, Book I, and *On the Creation of the World*; Ambrose in *On Noah*; Gregory in *On 1 Kings* and *Morals*, Book XXXV, chapter 7; and the others throughout.] divided it into four volumes for that reason, and prefixed seven chapters to each: because bodies compacted from the four elements, having been exhausted by pains and distress in the present life as though on the sixth day, keep sabbath and rest within the innermost recesses of the tomb on the seventh; and on the Lord’s Day, when the spirit comes from the four winds (Ezek. XVII, 9), they will rise again in the glory of incorruption.

Yet I am not unaware that this little work of mine has not everywhere been polished to the touchstone of worthy refinement, and that very much in it lies open to criticism, both in the composition of the words themselves and [Note: [Col. 0316C] In the truth of the matters. He says this, conscious of human weakness, in fear, not from knowledge. Otherwise, a diligent reader will find sound doctrine everywhere.] in the truth of the matters. I realize that this happened to me, first, because of the demands of my office; then because of the care of household affairs, although they are slight; next because of the frequent infirmity of my little body; and finally because of the countless—indeed numberless—troubles of the inner man, conceived [Note: [Col. 0316C] About new and unusual affairs. Thiofridus entered the abbacy in the year 1078 and held it until 1106, during a period of great disorder throughout the Church. There were several schisms. The most shameful was that in which Cardinal Benno, dissenting from the most holy pontiff Gregory VII, drew twelve other cardinals after him, like another Lucifer, as though they were stars. There was also the most disgraceful lapse of Berengar, the arch-heresiarch of the sacrament, repeated several times after his recantation. I believe these are the “new and unusual affairs” meant, especially since Emperor Henry was at that time disturbing both the empire and the Church, while careless or ambitious bishops shamefully adhered to him. See Baronius.] amid new and unusual affairs, which suddenly emerged in our days for the dispersal of all honorable arts [Col. 0316B]. No one is so hard-hearted that he could not be weighed down by an exceedingly heavy burden of sadness and grief.

Nor is it hidden from me that those who tear apart the books of Wisdom and the saints themselves will not spare me; rather, with immense bitterness of spirit, they will indignantly ask by what audacity I was emboldened to rush into so difficult a subject without fear; why I did not show reverence toward the sacred writings; why I did not fear treating them unworthily and wearing them down through the fault of my own intellect (Horace).

But I silently consider this with myself: scarcely any writer, or rather no writer, has ever trusted so much in his own authority that he did not need the defense of princes and wise men. Flaccus Horace rejoices in the protection of Maecenas; [Note: [Col. 0316D] Pollio loves Maro, Virgil. He took the words from Virgil himself:

“Pollio loves our Muse, although she is rustic.”]

Pollio loves Maro, Virgil, and the imperial protection of Augustus favors them both. The most charming of comic poets, Terence, would have incurred hatred instead of favor when the envy of his rivals was aroused, had not [Note: [Col. 0316D] Through the skillful arguments of Calliopius. Most copies of Terence add at the end of each comedy: “Calliopius revised this.” This actor customarily defended the poet, who was gravely accused by malicious persons, by means of arguments. See the prologues to the *Andria*, *Eunuchus*, *Heautontimorumenos*, *Adelphoe*, and the remaining plays. Thiofridus calls his arguments “skillful” chiefly, I think, to allude to the name Calliopius.] the prudence of Calliopius, through his skillful arguments, opposed his accusers.

Anicius Manlius Torquatus Boethius, a man distinguished by perfection in every art and by consular rank, [Col. 0317A] when he had transferred into Latin treasures [Note: [Col. 0317B] Into Latin treasures. In the Preface to his *Arithmetic*, addressed to the patrician Symmachus, Boethius says: “From the abundance of Greek letters we have gathered and brought together materials for the treasury of Roman speech.”] the [Note: [Col. 0317B] The theorems of the quadrivium. Again, Boethius, in the same work, chapter 1: The nobility of wisdom is traced, as it were, through a quadrivium. He makes the obscure statement clear immediately afterward in the same place: “Arithmetic’s integrity contemplates multitude, which exists in itself. Music’s harmonies discern that which exists in relation to something else. Geometry promises knowledge of immovable magnitude. The expertise of astronomical discipline claimed knowledge of movable magnitude.” A little farther on: “This, then, is that quadrivium by which those must travel who are led from the senses created together with us toward the more certain things of understanding by a more excellent mind.”] theorems of the quadrivium expressed in figures—approved and refined by the judgment of Pythagoras, in the opinion of all the leaders of ancient philosophy—nevertheless repeatedly and humbly begged in earnest prayer that this labor might be advanced by the ancestral favor of the patrician Symmachus.

And since men of such great renown distrusted the ability of their most illustrious labors to stand without the favor of the foremost, how much more am I, whom neither fortune nor learning commends, without hope or resource unless I obtain your protection?

If only by your protection—you who are heaven, the Lord’s seat (Isa. LXVI, 1); you who are the seal of the Lord’s likeness (Acts VII, 49); you who are perfect in the eminence of divine beauty and full of wisdom (Ezek. XXVIII, 12), and walk in the midst of fiery stones (ibid., 14)—if, I say, by your protection I, earth, unworthy of the Lord’s footstool (Isa. LXVI, 1), who lament with pitiable grief the hardships of my exile and cry out in my ecstasy, “I am cast away from before the sight of the Lord’s eyes” (Ps. XXX, 23), may rejoice in your assistance and [Col. 0318A] in [Note: [Col. 0318B] In the first metropolis of three-part Gaul. Caesar begins *The Gallic War*, Book I, as follows: “All Gaul is divided into three parts: one of which the Belgae inhabit, another the Aquitani, and the third those who in their own language are called Celts, in ours Gauls.” Pliny likewise says this in Book IV, chapter 17. Thiofridus accordingly recognizes Trier as the noble metropolis of Belgic Gaul.] the first metropolis of three-part Gaul, may I be protected by a defender foremost in nobility and religion. I have no fear at all of being harmed by the bite and criticism of barking envy, because when the ray of your splendid authority, like that of the sun itself, shines upon me, it will necessarily prevent the darkness of my ignorance from appearing.

Therefore place the finishing hand upon my work; and, in accordance with your benevolence toward me, cut away what is superfluous, fill what gapes open, correct what is erroneous, and, following the example of your predecessor, fosterer, and blood-relative, Udo, the archbishop of eternal memory, who strengthened by the examination of his testimony the life of Lwttwin, [Note: [Col. 0318B] Lwttwin. Concerning his Life, see Thiofridus’s *Life*, where his writings are discussed.] traced out by my inadequate pen [Note: [Col. 0318B] “Traced out.” He transferred this word from Greek and gave it a Latin form. Greek χαράττω—“I engrave, I write”; future χαράξω. It occurs again below.] (καράττω, future καράξω), receive what has been suitably said with cheerful spirit; and, transmitting it to posterity as a generous pledge of our friendship through the authority of your name, consecrate and insert it in the archives of the holy Church.

Farewell.

[Col. 0317] The Prologue ends.

## The Chapters Begin

[Col. 0317]

I. On the fact that the Lord our God, great in great things, works more gloriously in the smallest things.  
II. On the concord of spirit and flesh after their struggle, and the precedence of each in blessedness.  
III. That no substance of flesh is nobler than the flesh of the saints, and that it is more glorious even in corruption itself.  
IV. On the relics of the martyr Babylas, and on man’s power over the apostate angel.  
V. On the exceedingly sweet fragrance of the bodies of the saints, and on the mystical correspondence of the temple of God, the ark, and the altar.  
VI. On the dowry of the holy soul, and on the transfusion of fragrance into the lifeless body.  
VII. On the difference between the bodies of the dead sons of the old Adam and those of the new Adam.

The chapters end.

# Flowers of the Epitaph of the Saints  
## Book One

## Chapter One  
### On the Fact That the Lord Our God, Great in Great Things, Works More Gloriously in the Smallest Things

[Col. 0317B]

Since the Lord our God is great, and exceedingly worthy of praise, and there is no end to his greatness (Ps. CXLIV, 3), it is altogether difficult—indeed impossible—for a human being, earth and ashes (Ecclus. X, 9), to give glory to his praise in proportion to his greatness (Ps. LXV, 2). Yet because every creature is led by natural inclination to praise the name and magnificence of its Creator, and because only after the death of the flesh the exercise and jubilation of the saints, the inward contemplation of divine glory, and eternal praise are believed to exist, let us, a small though lowly portion of his creation and the work of his hands (Job XXXIV, 19), strive according to the measure of our weakness to praise and glorify him who is essentially and supremely worthy of praise and glorious forever (Dan. III, 56).

Let us confess with our own will and most ardent desire of mind the holy name of him toward whose praise nature draws us, and let us glory in his praise (Ps. CV, 47). With heart and mouth let us say to the Lord God, our Savior:

“How dreadful, how magnificent are your works, O Lord! Your thoughts have become exceedingly profound” (Ps. XCI, 6), because “how dreadful he is in his counsels above the children of men” (Ps. LXV, 5). And although he is great in great things, [Note: [Col. 0319B] Glorious in the smallest things. These words are the epigraph and a summary of the whole chapter. It is Thiofridus’s constant practice to place at the beginning of each chapter a clearly expressed sentence that contains the entire subject in a few words. Anyone who pays attention will easily notice that this first chapter is not merely the Preface of the whole work, but also contains briefly what is treated at greater length throughout all four books. Everything comes down to showing that God is wondrous not only in his saints but also in any of the saints’ possessions, even the smallest.

As for the matter itself, it also seems true in nature that there is more to admire in small things than in great ones. Scripture did not remain silent about this. “There are four things that are smallest on the earth,” says Proverbs XXX, 24, “and they are wiser than the wise.” It then names ants, rabbits, locusts, and lizards.

Nor did this escape the wise men of the age and the diligent investigators of nature, to say nothing of the Fathers inspired by God. Pliny, indeed, in Book XI, chapter 1, both shows himself an acute observer of these things and presents himself as an eloquent describer. “There remain,” he says, “animals of immense subtlety”—speaking of small creatures. Again, concerning the same creatures: “Nowhere else is the craftsmanship of nature’s works displayed more splendidly.” In the following chapter: “In great bodies, or at least in larger ones, the workshop was easy and the material compliant. In these creatures so small, and so seemingly insignificant, what reason, what power, what inextricable perfection! Where has it placed so many senses in a gnat? And there are other things smaller still to mention. But where in it has it extended sight? Where has it applied taste? Where has it inserted smell? Where, indeed, has it implanted that savage voice, enormous in proportion, which it possesses? With what subtlety has it attached its wings?” See more there and afterward concerning other tiny animals, especially bees and ants.

Let us conclude with his own words, with some justified indignation: “Yet we marvel at the tower-bearing shoulders of elephants, the necks of bulls, the savage leaps of tigers into the heights, the ravages of tigers, and the manes of lions, although nature is nowhere more wholly present than in the smallest things.”]

yet he works more gloriously wondrous things in the smallest.

For what is less than disintegrated ash? What is briefer than a transitory name, [Note: [Col. 0319D] For its being is to pass away. We pass away with the time in which we exist and by which, willingly or unwillingly, we are swept along, so that we are never the same; and we are taken away so that even in this form we do not remain long. Saint Augustine discusses time and its flow at length in several chapters of Book II of the *Confessions*.] whose being is to pass away?

But just as the incomprehensible and ineffable power of the divine majesty formed shapeless earth into a living soul (Gen. II, 7), so it gives the earth conformed to his human body, returned to earth and dust (Gen. III, 19), a more wondrous life in the dust through the life-giving Spirit (1 Cor. XV, 45). And he who created the universe of things from nothing deigns to manifest the power of his intransitive and eternal name in the name of dust, [Note: [Col. 0320B] Whose essence has no substantial nature. This is either hyperbole, since nothing can exist without essence; or he compares the essence of dust with the divine essence; or, as I am more inclined to think, he indicates that dust is considered nothing because it is not among those things that are accorded any account—not, I say, a human being, nor any other animal, nor a tree, nor a stone, and so forth.] whose essence has no substantial nature: before it is named, it is nothing; in being named, it is nothing; after it is named, when every sophistical exaggeration is removed, in itself it is nothing [Col. 0320A].

[Note: [Col. 0320C] “Nothing,” and transitory, among us, and so forth. The meaning is that God, through his benevolence and power, brings it about that something which otherwise was regarded as nothing is counted as something, and even as something great. Thus the Teacher of the Gentiles calls those things that are not as though they were (Rom. IV, 17). And the Master of life says: “All live to him” (Luke XX, 38). From this passage of Thiofridus, and from others, we gather that he was imbued not only with philosophy but also with what we call scholastic theology—not through the speech or books of teachers, which had not yet become common in that age, but through excellence of intellect and constancy of study. Therefore I have no hesitation in counting him among those who either discovered or illuminated that discipline.]

That which is nothing and transitory among us, whose being is from nothing and consists in passing, is, in the sight of him who alone is, intransitively and truly; and what is dead to our mortality is alive to his immortality; and what has being for us is established as nonbeing for him.

And so that his invisible things, his eternal power, and his divinity may be more deeply understood and perceived (Rom. I, 20), he exercises a more laborious power in those things which, having arisen from nothing, seem to have returned to nothing.

And when the saints, divine and heavenly creatures, after the rivers of Babylon over which they sat and wept while remembering Zion (Ps. CXXXVI, 1), [Note: [Col. 0320D] After the heavy torrent of the Chobar. At this river marvelous things were shown to Ezekiel, as he himself testifies in chapter I and elsewhere. The Chobar is generally held to be the Euphrates, according to the opinion of good and authoritative writers. Thiofridus calls it “heavy” because the Israelite captives lived beside it, as Ezekiel says in chapter I, 1, and more clearly in chapter III, 15. But why does he name this river among all the rivers of Babylon where they sat and wept? Is it because the name of this one is known while the others are not? Or because of the etymology of the name, which he customarily pursues? For Chobar, besides other meanings, signifies “now” in Ecclesiastes I, 10, insofar as it is used of past events: “It has already existed in the ages that were before us.” In this way it may be understood as sweeping us along in its extremely rapid course, just as Thiofridus asserts when he says that we are perpetually passing away. I would gladly hear the judgments of others.] have dwelt after the heavy torrent of the Chobar (Ezek. III, 15) in Jerusalem, the City of the Lord of hosts (Ps. XLVII, 9), and have acquired it as their inheritance, he adorns their earthly dwelling, dissolved (2 Cor. V, 1), together with all its appendages, both inward and outward, with such great glory that they are then rightly believed to exist only when, under the condition of mortality, they are judged to have returned to their origin and to be nothing.

Then the lowly wood is exalted, and the dry becomes green, when its root has grown old in the earth and its trunk has died in the dust (Job XIX, 8–9). For at the smell of water, through the glorification of the glorified Spirit, names completed with an infinite end, and olives withering [Col. 0321A] in the house of the Lord, put forth fruitful shoots [Note: [Col. 0321C] Shoots. A word used by Ovid and Persius, the latter of whom writes:

“Shoots of the old beech.”]

(Jer. XI, 16), the remnants of extinguished flesh [Note: [Col. 0321D] Remnants. This is Greek: λείμματα, “remnants,” from λείπω, “I leave behind.”]—and they produce a crown, as though when they were first planted and joined together (Job XIV, 9). They display their greenness in the expression of an astonishing work, which they possessed from the creation of the world in the foreknowledge of the Creator.

Finally, according to the immutable decree of divine providence—which has decreed, in an inconceivable and incomparable manner, to glorify both the souls and the bodies of the elect, together with everything pertaining to the nature and every need of the body—they accomplish marvelous and exceedingly astonishing things through the power and merit of his sanctified Spirit, and bear witness to his inestimable honor and magnificence in the inward contemplation of the supreme and uncircumscribed Spirit of God.

And although they wither and are nothing in themselves, they grow green and exist through him who [Note: [Col. 0321D] “Who reigned in himself.” Understand the spirit, or soul, of the human being, which subdued the flesh in order to raise it up. This mortification is what the Apostle speaks of in the same sense: “If by the Spirit you put to death the deeds of the flesh, you will live” (Rom. VIII, 13). This passage of the Apostle is well commented upon here by Thiofridus.] reigned in himself, who, after confirming the judgment of innate reason, corrected and restrained beneath himself wandering and irrational impulses.

All things that a rich and unwavering faith deserves are possible—indeed, they are possible through the one who was once their inhabitant and proclaimer, who in this life freed himself from the bonds of the body by the death that virtues bestow; who despised bodily allurements; who, stripping himself of the sweet snares of desire and all the remaining passions, crossed beyond the prison of the flesh and ascended almost free to his possession, the palace of heaven.

“Almost free,” I say, as one who has subdued the flesh and become its victor and lord, subject to it in nothing except the single function of giving it life and nourishment.

## Chapter Two  
### On the Concord of Spirit and Flesh after Their Struggle, and the Precedence of Each in Blessedness

And certainly, since the human being is composed of flesh and spirit, which oppose each other—for “the spirit desires against the flesh, and the flesh against the spirit” (Gal. V, 17)—after peace has been given through the Lord’s power (Ps. CXXI), and the deeds of the flesh have been put to death (Rom. VIII, 3), as great as their former discord was, so great a concord grows between them after their struggle. And in death, which is the soul’s separation from the body, it does not come to an end; rather, it is perfected. It does not fail but advances toward the increase of God.
