[Note: [Col. 0321D] The flesh becomes spiritual. Not because its nature is changed, but through obedience and imitation of the spirit, to whose command it adapts itself. Thus we call a horse almost a participant in reason when it proceeds eagerly and vigorously wherever the slightest sign of its mounted master indicates. With this meaning David says: “My heart and my flesh have rejoiced in the living God” (Ps. LXXXIII, 3).]

For when the flesh has been subjected to the authority of the spirit, it becomes, as it were, one with it; it follows its nature and becomes spiritual. Conversely, if the spirit degenerates, if it does not consider the precedence of its condition and dignity, if it is conquered by the flesh and reduced to servitude, it becomes fleshly. And just as the flesh feeds the dying worm, so the spirit feeds the worm that does not die (Isa. LXVI, 24; Mark IX, 43, 45, 47).

The spirit, moreover, glorified, glorifies its own flesh, which it afflicted and put to death through its desires; and through whose mortification it escaped death and merited the eternity of blessed life, it grants after the end not to end, and after corruption to be clothed with the glory of incorruption.

[Note: [Col. 0321D] To be clothed over with the glory of incorruption. He is referring to the Apostle’s statement: “This corruptible must put on incorruption” (1 Cor. XV, 53). Moreover, he took the verb “to be clothed over” from the Second Epistle to the Corinthians, chapter V, verse 4. I would not have noted this except to indicate at the same time that it is familiar to Thiofridus, when he brings something from Scripture, to draw it simultaneously from several passages. This shows that he is full of Scripture and overflowing with it on every side, so that it may be said of him: “He belches forth what he has drunk.”]

The flesh receives all rewards and all the joys of the spirit if it consents to the spirit; the spirit suffers all punishments and all the hardships of the flesh if it submits itself to the flesh, [Col. 0322B] if it does not pass through its impurities by an undefiled path [Note: [Col. 0322D] “If he does not pass through the impurities of the flesh by an undefiled path.” This is taken from the Church’s office for Saint Agnes.] if it does not extinguish its fiery furnace and [Note: [Col. 0322D] The burning pot. He frequently mixes allegories and mystical meanings into his writing. What is the pot in this passage? Let Saint Gregory the Great speak, whom our author read carefully and cites more than once. “The burning pot,” he says (*Morals*, Book XVIII, chapter 11), “is the human heart, boiling with the fires of worldly cares and the anxieties of desires. It is kindled from the face of the north, that is, it is inflamed by the devil’s suggestions. For he is accustomed to be called by the name of the north, since he said: ‘I will sit on the mount of assembly, on the sides of the north’” (Isa. XIV, 13). See more there and in Book XXXIII, chapter 41, of the same work.] the burning pot whose face is toward the face of the north (Jer. I, 13).

The flesh, taken from the earth but dead to earthly pleasures, ascends upward with the spirit; the spirit, taken from heaven but not inflamed by heavenly desires, indeed wholly given over to the flesh, descends downward with the flesh. And just as the latter, unhappily victorious, does not fail even amid punishments in the reprobate, but persists by continually failing and dies without dying, so the former, more unhappily conquered, while always living essentially, does not live; rather, by not dying it dies; by not failing, not persisting, it fails, persists, and is brought to an end forever, and exists without end.

O how unhappy is the human spirit if it is depressed and overwhelmed by the flesh, which is corrupted and weighs down the soul (Wis. IX, 15)! How happy is the flesh that does not resist but is subjected to the spirit! How happy is the human being who directs his heart toward the Lord, whose spirit the Lord draws to himself, so that he changes both his inward and outward life into conformity with the desire for him; so that nothing external now pleases the mind, nor anything internal the flesh—or, if it desires something, it strives to attain it—but all that the human being is burns inwardly in longing for him from whom he is, and outwardly restrains himself by subduing himself!

Truly happy is the flesh that wholly fails in this life, that no longer serves any of its own impulses, but over which the presiding spirit restrains all its flux; and with a kind of sword of its discipline kills everything in it that lived wrongly.

Without doubt, every human being is happy who, while living, returns to ashes; who does not forget his mortality; who dies to the flesh before the death of the flesh; whose inward parts are fed upon by the worm (Ps. XXI, 7), begotten from earth alone and pure—namely, from the undefiled Virgin.

[Note: [Col. 0323D] The worm from earth alone and pure. He indicates Christ, who called himself a worm in the psalm. This worm feeds upon our innermost being when we burn with love for him.]

Happy, I say, is the one who is no longer in the flesh but in the spirit; whose body is dead because of sin, while the spirit lives because of justification, and who awaits the redemption of his body (Rom. VIII, 10, 23).

And since in one human being there are two human beings, the inner and the outer, and the two are one, he is certainly happy in whom what is written comes to pass:

“If two of you agree about any matter whatever that they ask, it will be done for them by my Father; for where two or three are gathered in my name, there I am in the midst of them” (Matt. XVIII, 19).

For the supreme and inward blessedness of a human being journeying in the body is this: that in the midst of two who possess one agreement there is the mediator between God and human beings, the man Christ Jesus (1 Tim. II, 5), who is our peace, who made both one, and in his flesh destroyed the dividing wall of enmity, so that he might create the two in one human being, making peace, and reconcile both in one body to God through the cross, killing the enmity in himself, so that through both we might have access in one Spirit to the Father (Eph. II, 14–18).

And truly, except for the angels of light, nothing among created beings is happier than the human being who is not overcome by the flesh but rules over its desires, which wage war against the soul (1 Pet. II). Nor is anything, except the apostate spirits, more unhappy than the human being whose life is daily endangered and whose soul’s freedom is taken captive.

The victor will judge the angels (1 Cor. VI, 3); the vanquished, together with the sinning angels and those dragged away in the chains of hell, will be dragged down into Tartarus (2 Pet. II, 4), where their fire will not be extinguished, but they will be a spectacle unto satiety for all flesh (Isa. LXVI, 24).

The former will be equal to the holy angels; the latter will be lower and more wretched than the beasts. For, as a certain fellow initiate of eternal wisdom asserts, the beasts do not expect judgment, do not know torment, and have not been promised salvation after death [Col. 0323D] for themselves. But the human being’s joy in this life, although entangled in countless adverse circumstances, is nevertheless like a point and passes like a night vision (Job XX, 5, 8). And because here he sins through soul and flesh together, there he will endure punishment in soul and flesh alike, in the fire [Note: [Col. 0323D] The fire that is not kindled. He is speaking of the infernal fire. He says that it is not kindled, namely, by human effort and the piling up of wood. It is eternal without these things, by the will of God.] that is not kindled (Job XX, 26).

Here, the one whose weakness the Spirit helps (Rom. VIII, 26), whose hidden man of the heart is in the incorruptibility of a quiet and modest spirit and is rich in the sight of God (1 Pet. III, 4), proceeds to the place where life is.

And just as everything belonging to the reprobate descends into the deepest hell (Job XVII, 16; Jas. I, 14), drawn away and enticed by the allurements of the flesh, so that even the fact that they leave behind what is dead here does not free them from torment, so everything belonging to the one who is in the world yet outside the world ascends to the heaven of heavens, so that even what, being insensible in itself, he leaves behind on earth is not excluded from the inward grace of reward.

Rather, the flesh, which in all things was companion and participant in labor and mortification, is also a sharer in honor and glorification.

Therefore, if you look at the flesh of a condemned sinner, what is more abject than a human being, what more foul? If you look at his spirit, what is more pitiable, what more deserving of condemnation? If, likewise, you consider the flesh of a person of proven holiness, what on earth is nobler than it, what more wondrous? If you consider his spirit, what is more excellent, what more glorious?

## Chapter Three  
### That No Substance of Flesh Is Nobler Than the Flesh of the Saints, and That It Is More Glorious Even in Corruption Itself
Apart from the flesh of Christ, which is the price of the world, no substance of flesh is nobler than the flesh of the saints; and the more subject it is to the spirit, the freer it is, and the more glorious in the very dissolution of corruption. In birth it is born for labor and misery; in death it is born for rest and glory. For glory, I say, it is born, although what is conceived and brought forth from a worm is eaten by worms, and dust returns to dust: for that which in most saints appeared to differ in nothing from the flesh of sinners, was assigned to punishment, and was held in contempt, is distinguished in death by a great separation, as light from darkness; and it is recognized most clearly that one thing comes from nature, another from merits and grace. By nature it is putrescent; by merits and grace it remains incorruptible for a very long time, even contrary to nature, and the worm, hungry for it, is repelled by it. And although worms are human beings’ fellow citizens, they do not easily or immediately recognize as their own citizen the one who is a citizen of God and of the angels.

[Note: [Col. 0323D] “Citizen of God and of the angels.” This might seem an arrogant assertion, unless the Apostle had said even more boldly (Eph. II, 19): “You are fellow citizens with the saints and members of God’s household.” It is a great thing to be a citizen of God; but greater still to be a member of his household. Whenever, then, we glory, may we glory in the Lord.]

And he who drove away from himself the worms—that is, troublesome thoughts—does not possess the worms’ sweetness, nor is he greedily torn apart or devoured more eagerly, as though satisfying a hungry appetite.

[Note: [Col. 0324D] “The worm’s sweetness is not present.” Job, speaking of the impious (chapter XXIV, 20), says: “His sweetness is the worms.” Thiofridus freely uses those words in another sense, in the sense commonly called accommodative. After our Thiofridus, this manner of using Scripture became extremely common with Saint Bernard, so that at times he even seems to be making a pious joke.]

Sanctified flesh, by nature clothed in putrefaction and the filth of dust, sleeps in the dust (Job VII, 5, 21); by grace and merit, it keeps watch in a wondrous work, and raises from the dust him whose sweetness is the worm (Job XXIV, 20), and restores him to grace. And altogether it is a marvel: it feeds worms and heals human beings; it is putrefaction and removes putrefaction; it lies down and raises those who lie down; it is dissolved into nothing and is feared by the principalities and powers of this air. He who was the seal of likeness, full of wisdom and perfect in beauty, who lived in the delights of God’s paradise (Ezek. XXVIII, 12), and who was made so that he feared no one (Job XLI, 24), reveres dissolved ashes; and the king over all the sons of pride, who sees every high thing (ibid., 25), is tortured by a speck of ash. He who was created among the morning stars to praise the magnificence of the Creator (Job XXXVIII, 7) roars at the remembrance of dust and turns angelic harmony into the sound of brute animals. He feels dust ruling over him, who refused to have God rule over him (Luke XIX, 14), who wished to make himself equal to God. He confesses his wounds in the possessed; he is compelled to obey the ash, by whose wicked deception man, after the worm, is dissolved into dust. He whose being is from heaven alone is tormented by him whose being is also from earth. He dares not mutter before the ash, although he is the beginning of the ways of the Lord (Job XL, 14), he who dared to tempt the Lord his God. And although, by experience,

[Note: [Col. 0325B] “By experience.” He says that experience and examples show that demons shudder before sacred relics and, as he himself puts it, dare not mutter before the ash. This has prevailed throughout every age since the Son of God clothed himself in our mortality. It would require lengthy histories to encompass the matter; otherwise it would not be difficult to produce many examples of this kind. Let one or two suffice. Saint Ambrose, in his sermon on the saints Nazarius and Celsus, says: “Why should the faithful not honor that body which even demons revere—those who afflicted it in punishment but glorify it in the tomb?” Saint Jerome, writing against Vigilantius and expressing indignation that that impure heresiarch called the relics of the saints the most worthless dust, addresses the devil and says: “You have often been tortured by this most worthless dust.” The same author, to Marcella (Epistle 17, chapter 5), speaking of Christ’s tomb, says: “If we do not believe ourselves, let us at least believe the devil and his angels, who, whenever they are expelled from possessed bodies before it, tremble and roar as though standing before Christ’s tribunal, and too late grieve that they crucified the one whom they lament.” It is not surprising that this occurred at Christ’s tomb, when the same Jerome, and the most holy woman Paula, are heard giving similar testimony concerning a tomb far inferior to it—namely, those of Elisha, Obadiah, and John the Baptist. Concerning this, then, in Paula’s epitaph addressed to her daughter Eustochium the virgin: “There she was overwhelmed and trembled amid many wonders. For she saw demons roar under various tortures, and before the tombs of the saints human beings howl like wolves, bark with the voices of dogs, roar like lions, hiss like serpents, and bellow like bulls.”]

and by the authority of Scripture, this is evident,

[Note: [Col. 0325D] “From the authority of Scripture.” Let Luke relate it, and let Paul and his relics triumph: “God performed no ordinary miracles by the hand of Paul, so that handkerchiefs and aprons were even carried from his body to the sick, and diseases departed from them, and Τὰ πνεύματα τὰ πονηρὰ ἐξέρχεσθαι ἀπ’ αὐτῶν, ‘the wicked spirits went out from them’” (Acts XIX, 12). Let the wretched Calvinists blush.]

nevertheless, nevertheless, to relieve the reader’s weariness—for uniform discourse commonly produces it—let us bring forward in our own style a clear testimony from a threefold history.

## CHAPTER IV. On the relics of the martyr Babylas, and on the power of man over the apostate Angel.

Julian, the model of apostates, anxious about victory in the Parthian war that he was conducting, followed the footsteps of Ahaziah, the idolatrous king of Israel, who sent to consult Beelzebub, the god of Ekron (2 Kings I, 2), although according to the prophet the Lord God must be sought concerning the living and the dead (Isa. VIII, 19), and consulted the oracle of the Pythian Apollo at Daphne.

[Note: [Col. 0325D] “The Pythian Apollo at Daphne.” He calls Apollo “the Daphnean” because he was worshiped at Daphne. It was a place near Antioch. For the complete history, which Thiofridus says he is recounting in his own style, see Sozomen, Ecclesiastical History, book V, chapters 18–19; Rufinus, book I, chapter 36; Socrates, book III, chapter 18; and Theodoret, book III, chapter 16. Against the testimony of all these authors, and even of Saint Chrysostom in his work Against the Gentiles, the Magdeburg Centuriators monstrously lie (century IV, chapter 13), saying that the devil deliberately pretended to be hindered by the martyr in order to promote the translation and veneration of the relics.]

But when the oracle’s voice was withheld,

[Note: [Col. 0326B] “The prophetess of the temple at Cirrha.” Cirrha was a town in Phocis, famous for Apollo’s oracle. Hence Apollo himself was called “Cirrhaean.” Juvenal writes:

“And Mars’s spear, and the darts of the Cirrhaean prophet.”

Hence also Thiofridus calls the prophetesses “Cirrhaean Phoebades,” as Seneca does earlier in the Oedipus:

“Moving the prophetic mouth of the Cirrhaean prophetess.”

I believe he transferred the term from that passage.]

and the prophetess of the Cirrhaean temple

[Note: [Col. 0326C] “They might enjoy a cessation of judgment.” It is well known that *justitium* means a suspension, or especially a cessation, of the administration of justice. The author elegantly transfers the word to the sluggish silence of the oracles—a silence that, having come upon the whole world after Christ’s advent, the Christian Fathers admire with applause, while the poets resent and lament it. Let Prudentius speak for all in the *Apotheosis*:

“God clothed himself in human limbs;

the Delphic caverns fell silent, their lots condemned.

No tripod does the prophetic curtain cover.”]

were enjoying a cessation of judgment, and before the terrifying threshold the Phoebad, fearful, dared not stand,

[Note: [Col. 0326C] “The Phoebad, fearing to stand at the terrifying threshold.” Female priests were called Phoebades, dedicated to Phoebus and filled with frenzy. Maro describes one so that you seem to see her. *Aeneid* VI:

“But in the immense cavern, still unable to endure Phoebus,

the prophetess rages, if only she might cast the great god

from her breast: all the more he wears out

her frenzied mouth, subduing her savage heart,

shaping it by pressure.”

Thiofridus reports, not without mockery, that the Daphnean prophetess, who had been accustomed to fear such frenzies, was now utterly peaceful, since the oracle had ceased. Shortly afterward he says that she is driven by that frenzy, pressed by the Phoebean lash and goad. This is elegant and suited both to his talent and to his practice, for he likes poetic idioms in prose.]

then, in the very prophetic shrine, breathed upon him with a tranquil breast and was not pressed by the Phoebean lash and goad. At last, when the Delian god was asked the reason for so deep a silence, he gave this answer:

[Note: [Col. 0326D] “By the word of the Lord.” How does Apollo—that is, the evil demon—give an answer “by the word of the Lord”? It means, “at the Lord’s command,” as in: “At your word I will let down the net” (Luke V, 5). Even today the Church’s exorcisms compel demons to confess the truth.]

“By the word of the Lord”: the tomb of the distinguished martyr Babylas was nearby, and he was being crushed beneath the weight of such holiness; and he feared the proximity of so decomposed a body as much as spirits fear the presence of the Spirit who reigns with the God of gods.

When the emperor, confused by the privilege of so great a proclamation, ordered the martyr’s relics to be carried away by the Galilaeans—as he used to call our people out of hatred for the Christian name, almost as a term of abuse—the Church of God, black but beautiful, dark as the tents of Kedar and lovely as the curtains of Solomon (Song I, 4), assembled. Every age, every sex, and every condition of the ecclesiastical order came together, and the servants of the Lord led forth the ark with jubilation (2 Kings VI, 15). In gladness of heart, for six thousand paces, they sang in a loud voice:

“Let all those who worship graven images be put to shame” (Ps. XCVI, 7).

As they walked, there was something like the sound of a multitude, like the sound of armies (Ezek. I, 24); the earth resounded with their voices, and they interpreted prophetically for themselves:

“You shall go out in joy and be led forth in peace” (Isa. LV, 12).

They followed the dissolved ashes of the distinguished martyr as an army follows its commander. Love, which casts out fear (1 John IV, 18), expelled from them all fear of earthly rule; the cruelty of the profane prince had no power over their minds. For Christ’s name they thirsted for punishments sweeter than honey and the honeycomb (Ps. XVIII, 11). Dead bones were more precious and glorious to them than the glory of the whole world carried in a gleaming chariot.

But while the children of God shouted for joy (Job XXXVIII, 7) in the exultation of their hearts, the idolaters were covered with shame as with a double cloak (Ps. CVIII, 29), and wasted away in grief from contrition of spirit (Isa. LXV, 14). The joy of the children of men was utterly confounded (Joel I, 12), and, in vengeance for the betrayal of God’s athlete,

[Note: [Col. 0327D] “In vengeance for the betrayed athlete.” The meaning is that when the devil had betrayed Babylas and brought about his expulsion, the temple itself was immediately struck by lightning and burned. See the authors named above.]

the hinges of heaven were shaken (Isa. VI, 4); the ancient temple was consumed by heavenly fire; the gilded image of the Pythian god was shattered and materially reduced to ash and cinder (Job XXX, 19).

[Note: [Col. 0327D] “Materially.” In my judgment this means “in reality,” so that no one might think that it was regarded as ash and cinder merely in the Christians’ estimation; which, in any event, had already been true before.]

The betrayer of the martyr’s tomb became the author of his own disgrace; from the source of the most glorious witness of God’s glory, the disgrace of demonic falsehood was increased; and the price of betrayal was turned into punishment for the betrayer.

By a wondrous dispensation of God, it was arranged that a human being, even when stripped of the body, should possess and exercise authority over an angel; for the dominion of the angel over man was overthrown in the death of the mediator between God and human beings, the man Christ Jesus (1 Tim. II, 5). He who, by the privilege of his first condition, had been made superior to all created things was, by the irremediable ruin of his first transgression, reduced below everything. He whom no substance of weak flesh drew into guilt is ruled, even when that flesh is dead, by the flesh whose weakness became the cause of its own ruin and of the ruin of the soul that presided over it and gave it life. In turn, the flesh rules the one to whom, while subordinate, it had served. That which derives its being from earthly clay presides over him whose nature is heavenly and angelic; and whatever punishments the victor could inflict upon the vanquished, the redeemed, victorious and ruling flesh of the Lord compels the conquered one to pay.

And who can search out the unsearchable riches of the divine dispensation? Who can conceive or explain the depth of the Lord’s understanding? He makes an angel a worm; he reduces an angel below a worm and all the lowest things. From earth he makes heaven; from highest heaven he creates the lower abyss. What is above he places below, and what is below he sets above; and in his wisdom he weaves an inextricable labyrinth. It is therefore not at all surprising that Paul, the most eminent vessel of election, who was caught up to the third heaven and into paradise, and who marveled at the height of the divine mind, exclaimed through the Holy Spirit:

“O the depth of the riches and wisdom and knowledge of God! How unsearchable are his judgments and how inscrutable his ways!” (Rom. XI, 33).

He did not assume the substance or form of an angel, but came in the likeness of sinful flesh (Rom. VIII, 3); he took our clay and knew our formation, and, mindful that we are dust and that man is like grass (Ps. CII, 14–15), he himself became grass so that our flesh might not remain grass forever; he turned our grass into grain and gave himself to us as the living bread (John VI, 51–52), so that he might pass into our body, and we might become his body, bone of his bones and flesh of his flesh (Gen. II, 23).

In the poverty of his flesh he concealed all the treasures of wisdom and knowledge (Col. II, 3); and when he made us his members, he wondrously transferred the riches that he had brought with him also into the extinguished flesh and bones of the elect. Just as he himself is by nature the Son of God, so those who are led by the Spirit of God are by adoption the sons of God (Rom. VIII, 14). And just as his flesh did not see corruption (Acts II, 27, 31), so their flesh, naturally corruptible, does not lose the sanctification of its God over it.

## CHAPTER V. On the fragrance of the sweetest odor of the bodies of the saints, and on the mystical correspondence of the temple of God, the ark, and the altar.

[Note: [Col. 0328D] “It does not contain within itself.” He is speaking of the flesh of the saints, concerning which he spoke at the end of chapter IV.]

It does not contain within itself, nor emit from itself, the stench of corruption, but the odor of future incorruption; it does not smell foul but smells sweet; it does not infect the air but affects the noses and hearts of the faithful with the sweetness of a paradisiacal fragrance. It harms no one; rather, it benefits everyone’s salvation. It makes foul-smelling limbs cease to stink; it drives out weakness by weakness; it cures the corruption of body and soul consumed by the wound of sin, both by the pus of its own corruption and by the medicine of its spirit.

This excess of some disordered humor—which in the saints, whether gouty, arthritic, dropsical, or otherwise afflicted, often removed even the company and most agreeable attentiveness of close companions—

[Note: [Col. 0328D] “It removed even the company of the closest companions from him.” This happens not only to the lowly and children of the earth, but also to kings. The impious Antiochus is a witness: his army was burdened by his smell and stench, and no one could carry him because the stench was intolerable (2 Macc. IX, 9–10).]

after the soul’s departure attracts everyone, of whatever condition or nation, to glorify the generosity of the Author of its inner sweetness, and sends forth an exceedingly sweet fragrance from putrefaction.

The sweetness of the odor reveals the dignity and purity of the soul; the obscenity of the stench reveals the worthlessness and uncleanness of the flesh. In foul-smelling flesh, the foulnesses and vices of the flesh stink; in the fragrant soul, virtues and merits give off their fragrance.

Foul-smelling flesh is the court of the unclean spirit, which, after taking with it seven spirits more wicked than itself, entered the vacant and swept house (Matt. XII, 45). Once dissolved, it reveals what uncleanness the most shameful guests exercised within it. But holy flesh is the hall of the Holy Spirit and the golden couch (Song III, 10), on which the Son dined with the Father (Rev. III, 20), and for which there is a couch of cedarwood with a purple ascent (Song III, 10, 9). It plainly declares, through its wondrous odor, that he reclined within it with the greatest reverence, dignity, and modesty—he whose throat is most sweet and whose cheeks are like beds of spices (Song V, 16, 13).

But if someone should wish to gnaw at us with a Theonine tooth because we presume to assert that the flesh of the saints is the house of God, let him know that there is an outer sanctuary and an inner sanctuary (Heb. IX, 2–3). Let him know that the Apostle said, in the same spirit but with a very different meaning: “I know that good does not dwell in my flesh” (Rom. VII, 18); and likewise: “Do you not know that your bodies are a temple of the Holy Spirit?” (1 Cor. VI, 19).

The bodies as well as the spirits of God’s elect are certainly the temple of God, and blessed is the glory of the Lord from its place (Ezek. III, 12), where, in a spirit of humility and a contrite heart (Dan. III, 39), the children of God offer to God rich and marrow-filled burnt offerings—that is, works acceptable to God, wholly drenched in the tears of prayer. The smoke of incense rises from the angel’s hand upon the golden altar, which is before the Lord (Rev. VIII, 3–4).

In so great a sanctuary of the temple there is placed the ark of the covenant (1 Kings VI, 19), made from incorruptible *setim* wood, which hardens in fire but does not burn.

[Note: [Col. 0329D] “Setim wood.” A kind of white thorn, but one that grows to the size of a proper tree. See Jerome on Isaiah XLI. Some think it is the cedar itself.]

This signifies the flesh of our Redeemer, the green wood (Luke XXIII, 31), alone to be feared and adored by the cherubim and seraphim; alone, outside the condition of nature, incorruptible forever and after a brief passion durable and incorruptible,

[Note: [Col. 0329D] “After a brief passion.” He does not mean that Christ suffered little—far from it—but that he did not suffer for long, especially when compared with eternity.]

because alone, at the end of time, it was conceived and brought forth contrary to the natural condition and propagation of flesh.

It is, I say, within the Holy of Holies, the ark of the covenant, covered on every side with the purest gold (Heb. IX, 4), and covered by the mystical mercy seat: namely, the body of the Lord Christ, who is the author of the Old and New Testament. His blood is the key of paradise; he, who was made by the Father’s wisdom, is the propitiation for our sins (1 John II, 2). Gold from Ophir is not comparable to him (Job XXVIII, 15). To the one who conquers he gives hidden manna (Rev. II, 17), most sweet and most excellent, the gift of immortality and heavenly bread. He writes his laws not with ink but with the Spirit of the living God; not on tablets of stone but on tablets of human hearts (2 Cor. III, 3). The resurrection of his flesh on the third day was prefigured by Aaron’s rod (Num. XVII, 8), which, among the twelve rods, alone returned to flower and put forth leaves in the tribe of Levi, and bore the fruit which nature had not given it: a type of all our barrenness until the time of restoration, and, in the mystery of the body of the Lord, our true Priest, of one who after the barrenness of death bursts forth into the flower of resurrection.

[Note: [Col. 0329D] “In the tribe of Levi.” Thiofridus does not add this without purpose, but to indicate that he recognizes Christ’s flesh as taken not only from Judah, the royal tribe, but also from the priestly tribe. Saint Hilary, speaking of the holy evangelists Matthew and Luke (*Commentary on Matthew*, canon 1), says: “Each, in his respective portion, proved in the carnal birth of our Lord Jesus Christ, who is eternal King and Priest, the glory of both lines.” Saint Augustine likewise uses a similar method of proof (*On the Harmony of the Evangelists*, book II, chapter 1) and concludes: “It must be held most firmly that Christ’s flesh was propagated from both lines, namely, that of kings and that of priests.”]

And this mystical and saving ark is placed between two golden cherubim, made by hammering and extension (Exod. XXV, 18). Between the cherubim, I say, are understood holy souls and flesh in the fullness of divine knowledge and the sanctity and purity of charity, because through the mystery of human redemption body and soul are sanctified and shine with the purest gold, that is, with divine wisdom. They are beaten and extended through the arduous exercises of this life, so that both may be preserved blameless on the day of our Lord Jesus Christ (1 Thess. V, 23).

Since everything said tropologically of the head of the elect also corresponds mystically to their members, the souls and bodies of the saints are likewise the ark of the covenant, covered within and without with gold: within, they shine with divine knowledge; without, with the excellent harmony of their conduct. In them is placed the testimony (Exod. XXV, 16), that is, the abundance of all holy doctrine; and on either side the cherubim stand (ibid. 18), namely, the guardianship of angels, so that they may be protected within and without from the violence of the destroyer of Egypt (Exod. XII, 29).

And in so wondrous a temple of God there is a mystical altar (Exod. XXV and following): the most purified and spiritual heart. On it every holy person, priest in soul and body, continually nourishes the fire of twinfold charity (Lev. VI, 12 and following). And so that it may never be extinguished, each morning, at the rising of the sun of righteousness, when the darkness of the mind has been illuminated, he heaps up wood—both the examples of the Fathers and the Lord’s commandments—and places himself upon it as a burnt offering, while he burns away every vice within himself. From his inward richness, like the fat of a peace offering, he makes peace between himself and the Lord and gives forth from himself the sweetest odor. The flame of so great a fire never fails or diminishes; rather, even after this life’s “nail” [a corrupt reading; the note proposes *ignem*, “fire”], it increases more fervently and abundantly through inward contemplation.

[Note: [Col. 0331C] “After the end of this life.” This is how it stands in both manuscripts, and therefore I have not wished to alter it. Yet I have no doubt that no sound meaning can be extracted from it and that *ignem* (“fire”) should be read. For he was certainly speaking of the unfailing fire; since he interprets it as charity, it most fittingly agrees with the Apostle’s statement: “Charity never fails” (1 Cor. XIII, 8).]

In praise of so great a temple of God, Ezekiel, the mouth and instrument of the Holy Spirit, to whom the mystery of the whole spiritual building and of the doors closed in the house of the Lord was revealed in a mystical riddle, is told:

“Show the house to Israel, so that they may be ashamed of their iniquities, and let them measure the structure, so that they may be ashamed of all that they have done” (Ezek. XLIII, 10).

The temple of God is shown for the confusion of sin when the holiness of the body and soul of God’s elect is proposed as an example of virtue, to be carefully considered and profitably imitated. The more carefully it is examined, the more deeply the sinful soul is ashamed and confounded by all that it has done; and the more strictly it judges its faults in itself, the more profoundly it considers what it ought to admire.

It is indeed ashamed of itself when it recognizes that it cannot possibly be saved unless a little dust saves it through the merit of the sanctifying Spirit; when it sees that, while alive, it did not truly live, whereas extinguished ashes live more effectively after death—indeed, not so much live as reign and shine with the glory of miracles.

[Note: [Col. 0331C] “It is indeed ashamed of itself.” It recognizes that it cannot possibly be saved unless a little dust saves it through the merit of the sanctified Spirit. This must be read cautiously and understood soundly. A person can certainly be saved in another way; but the good God, who glorifies his saints in various ways, carries out his decree concerning the salvation of certain people only through the relics of the saints. Who, unless he is a Calvinist or otherwise a heretic, would deny that the salvation of many has been advanced by miracles witnessed at the tombs of martyrs and other saints? Saint Paul uses a similar expression (Acts XXVII, 31): “Unless these men remain in the ship, you cannot be saved.”]

Therefore it is no wonder that the dissolved temple of God—namely, the flesh of God’s elect, the ark of the covenant—surpasses all spices by the fragrance of its odor, since from it, through the Spirit dwelling within it, works of virtue rise like a little column of smoke from myrrh and incense (Song III, 6), namely, chastity and saving prayer; and like all the dust of the perfumer, who prepares and distinguishes the spices of good works, who descends into his garden to the beds of spices, so that he may pasture in the gardens and gather into the kingdom of his love lilies of extraordinary and everlasting whiteness (ibid., 1).

## CHAPTER VI. On the dowry of the holy soul and on the transfusion of fragrance into the lifeless body.

[Col. 0332A]

According to Ambrose, the dowry of the devout soul consists of the mystical and most sweet fragrances of myrrh, saffron, and aloe; and, possessing within itself the scent of the field that the Lord blessed (Gen. XXVII, 27),

[Note: [Col. 0331D] “According to Ambrose.” The reference is to Saint Luke XXIV, 1, where the holy women carry the spices they had prepared.]

it desires the south wind to blow, not the north wind (Song IV, 16), so that its gardens may be in bloom and their flowers not be stripped away.

[Note: [Col. 0331D] “It desires the south wind to blow, not the north.” These are the Bride’s words (Song IV, 16): “Arise, north wind, and come, south wind.” Here *surge* (τὸ *surge*) is a word of dismissal and expulsion, as though she said, “Give way; depart.” Why? Thiofridus briefly explains it here: “so that the flowers of his garden may bloom, not be beaten down.” Thus each wind has its own effect. But without doubt these words must be understood mystically. Therefore, with Saint Jerome (on Isaiah XIV), let us regard the north wind as the extinguishing of charity, and, with Saint Gregory (*Moralia*, book IX, chapter 9), the south wind as the fervor of the Holy Spirit, at whose coming the ancient enemy is driven out like the north wind.]

It invites the bridegroom into its garden to eat the fruit of its trees (Song V, 1), so that its spices may flow for him (Song IV, 16), and so that he may delight in the variety of its fruits and fragrances.

The bridegroom comes, gives kisses to the bride, dwells among her breasts, and hears amid the musical sounds of the wedding song:

[Note: [Col. 0332C] “Musical sounds.” In Greek, *krouō* (κρούω) means, among other things, “to strike musical instruments.” Hence *krouma* (κροῦμα) means the stroke itself. Thiofridus either read or formed *krousma* (κροῦσμα), which also means applause. I think he understood it in this way, as the very heading of the preface to the *Life of Saint Willibrord* seems to show:

“Prologue in a life of Willibrord worthy of musical applause.”

You may take it in the same sense here without impropriety.]

“Your breasts are more beautiful than wine, and the fragrance of your perfumes surpasses every spice” (Song IV, 10).

And when the king is on his couch, and the queen is there (Song I, 11), the perfect soul certainly stands at his right hand in a garment of gold, clothed in the variety of virtues (Ps. XLIV, 10). Its nard gives forth its fragrance (Song I, 11), and a fragrance of supreme sweetness vaporizes and fills the bridegroom’s and bride’s entire inner and outer chamber.

And just as the odor of a fragrant fruit, precious ointment, or spice is transferred to the hand of the one who touches it or to the covering of the one who wraps it, so from the golden couch of the true Solomon (Song III, 10)—that is, from the spirit of supreme holiness—the tabernacle of the body, joined and fastened together in proportions corresponding to its measurements,

[Note: [Col. 0332C] “In proportions corresponding to its measurements.” Proportions are the relations of dimensions—length, breadth, and height. The measurements of the Mosaic tabernacle are accurately described in Exodus XXVI, and various authors have explained them mystically in various ways. Briefly, take from Saint Gregory what fits the meaning of this passage: “The court is measured both in length and in breadth, because when a sinner is led to faith, it is necessary for his teacher to consider how much he is progressing, through his instruction, in the length of hope and the breadth of charity” (*Homily 19 on Ezekiel*). Nor should it trouble you that the discourse concerns the tabernacle of the body, for it is speaking of the body of the holy soul, so to speak, proportioned to it.]

receives that fragrance in greater measure. And when the inhabitant has departed, the house of flesh has remained empty, the flesh is turned into putrefaction, putrefaction is reduced to dust, and dust is dissolved into the elements, so that it is no longer visible to human eyes, nevertheless that fragrant force sweetens the sense of smell,

[Note: [Col. 0332D] “That fragrance sweetens the sense of smell.” Since Thiofridus himself, in this very chapter, gives examples of this fragrance, I may remain silent. Otherwise, an abundance of examples is readily available. Saint Hubert, apostle of the Ardennes, could stand in place of many: in the seventeenth year after his death he was found not merely intact, but also filled the noses and minds of those present with a heavenly fragrance. Our Dauroultius gives more examples in *Historical Catechism*, chapter III, title 57. Concerning Saint Hubert, see Baronius under the year 771.]

and there a human being is satisfied with a sweetness as great as that of incense, where he does not know what it is or what it had been.

Do not the chambers and wrappings of spices continue to smell fragrant even after the spices have been removed? But a very different breath of fragrance comes forth from the lifeless limbs of the saints than from spices, because it is an entirely different kind of sweetness: the Spirit, giving life and illumination to rational creation, subtly and substantially diffuses sweetness.

[Note: [Col. 0333C] “Substantially diffuses sweetness.” From the contrast with what he adds concerning an inseparable accident, Thiofridus seems to mean that one should not think that this kind of fragrance comes to the relics of the saints from elsewhere or from an accident, but that the substance itself has acquired it divinely through its merit. I admit that the passage is obscure, and that I must obtain light from elsewhere through grace.]

The other kind is something implanted accidentally, though inseparably, in insensible things created as fragrant objects and delights for rational beings, who by reason of mind, in holiness and righteousness, bear within themselves the image of their Creator, the author of all sweetness.

Aromatic odor affects the body but does not refresh the soul; it becomes a fault if someone abuses it for sensual pleasure. But the sweetness of the Spirit, transfused into the limbs of the saints, anoints the soul and body through its affection and, through the anointing of the Holy Spirit, pierces them with love for spiritual life.

The former generates disgust with itself; the latter, the more it satisfies, the more abundantly multiplies the thirst for its sweetness. This is an image of the thirst that is satisfied in the angels from the fountain of life and the torrent of delight (Ps. XXXV, 10, 9). It contains no weariness of satiety, because it satisfies the thirsty without any disgust and makes the satisfied thirst without any anxiety, so that it may refresh them.

The former fails with the passage of time; the latter increases. The former requires external assistance if it is not to fail; the latter, even in the very putrefaction whose nature is to stink, possesses the means to increase, contrary to nature, by giving off fragrance throughout all the days of the age.

And indeed I have abundant material in the sacred writings from which to select testimonies to so sweet and lasting a fragrance. But when the mind runs through each one, all the passages that are splendid and excellent in comparison with those surpassing all excellence always seem small and insufficiently luminous.

I could certainly mention the fragrance that, at the discovery of the most precious body of the thrice- and four-times-blessed Stephen, the protomartyr, after the passage of 382 years from the Lord’s Passion,

[Note: [Col. 0333C] “After the passage of 382 years from the Lord’s Passion.” Quite correctly. For if you add the years during which Christ lived this mortal life—namely, thirty-three—you arrive at the year 415 from his birth, in which year the relics of the great protomartyr were found by the presbyter Lucian, Gamaliel having revealed their location. See Baronius.]

so filled the nostrils and hearts of all who stood nearby that they seemed to be walking among roses and lilies in paradise, not in Chaphargamala.

[Note: [Col. 0333D] “Not in Chaphargamala.” This was the name of the village where the bodies of Saint Stephen and the others were found. Lucian the presbyter, their discoverer, begins the booklet he wrote about the matter as follows: “Lucian, in need of the mercy of God and the least of all human beings, presbyter of the Church of God which is in the village of Caphargamala, in the territory of Jerusalem, to the holy Church and to all the saints,” and so forth. If you ask what this name means and where it comes from, Gamaliel answers in that booklet, revealing himself and his companions to Lucian. Speaking of Saint Stephen’s body, he says: “I urged them and persuaded them to go secretly and carry his body in my carriage to my village, that is, Caphargamala, which means ‘the village of Gamaliel,’ twenty miles from the city,” and so forth. See the entire history, most worthy of reading, in Baronius under the year 415. As for the interpretation of the name, it is established that *copher*, or *caphar*, means “village.” An example is found in 1 Samuel VI, 18.]

I could also mention—passing over for the moment a notable miracle, which ought certainly to be judged far more excellent under grace than the cloud that appeared over the tabernacle of the covenant under the Law, both when the Lord was angry and when he was appeased (Num. XIV, 10; Exod. XXXIII, 9–10)—namely, what occurred after the lucid sun of the whole world,

[Note: [Col. 0334C] “The sun of the whole world.” Elsewhere too he calls Saint Willibrord a sun. He begins his metrical *Life* in this way:

“The Britons brought forth the sun of the fourfold cosmos.”]

[Col. 0334D] The sun of the whole world, Willibrord, who illumines the world with his light. ] After the setting of the flesh of Willibrord, the sun of the whole world, the first archbishop of the holy Church of Utrecht, an immense globe, like a dense cloud in the form of aromatic smoke, very often filled and covered the entire vestibule, [Note: [Col. 0334D] Where he suffered the eclipse of the light of this life. That this occurred at Utrecht, where the seat of his bishopric was, is attested, among others, by Saint Boniface in his letter to Pope Stephen. It is found in Baronius under the year of Christ 755.] [Col. 0334B] where he had undergone the eclipse of the light of this life, and he passed into the company and brightness of the heavenly lights; omitting, I say, the proclamation of so great a miracle, I could mention that [Note: [Col. 0334D] In the year 292 after his departure, and in the year 1031 of the incarnate Word. Saint Willibrord died in the year of Christ 739; add 292, and you will find Thiofrid’s calculation of the year of Christ 1031 to be entirely exact.] in the year 292 after the departure of that most glorious bishop from spiritual Sodom and Egypt, and in the year 1031 of the incarnate Word, when the translation was being arranged, [Note: [Col. 0334D] The translation was being arranged. Concerning this translation of Saint Willibrord, see the Life, chapter 34, and Book IV of the Poems.] on the fourteenth day before the Kalends of November, such a delight of extraordinary sweetness overflowed from his tomb that, when all those worthy of the divine gift had been infused and magnificently refreshed, the most devout abbot, named Humbert, [Note: [Col. 0334D] The abbot Humbert. He was abbot of Echternach for twenty-four years; Regimbert succeeded him and held the office for thirty years. Our Thiofrid then succeeded him. So it is recorded in the manuscript of that monastery called the Golden Book, p. 115.] having opened the sarcophagus slightly, thrust in his hand—not with presumptuous recklessness, but with the most ardent desire of his heart—to remove a little from the treasure of the most exalted sacred relics. Asked what he had perceived by sight and what by smell, he imitated Paul’s silence, full of cries, when he had returned to himself from the third heaven and from the loveliness of paradise, where he heard secret words that are not [Col. 0335A] permitted a human being to speak (2 Cor. 12:4). He did not disclose what he had perceived—not things equal in scale, but how great and astonishing they were—according to the order of what he had seen, but according to the magnitude of his testimony. Through what he was able to say, he suggested that we could easily infer [Note: [Col. 0335C] We can infer. He seems clearly to indicate that he was present at this translation. Concerning it, see the Life.] that the things he either could not or feared to express in words were exceedingly great.

“What you ask me to utter,” he said, “is ineffable to me. I plainly do not know the things you believe me to know. Neither my heart suffices to conceive them, nor my tongue to recount them.” I deliberately pass these things over. I do not state what men of the highest authority discovered and committed to memory through report and testimony. I am silent about what I myself, with God as my witness and confidant, perceived by smell [Note: [Col. 0335C] I perceived by smell myself. You will read about this also in Thiofrid’s Life.], from the ambulatory of our Church, where, although it is often foul with the stinking odor of sins, I was nevertheless flooded and refreshed by a saving fragrance breathing from an aromatic garden, which the fountain of living waters, that is, of spiritual gifts, flowing forcefully from Lebanon, watered from above (Song 4:15).

## CHAPTER VII. On the difference between the bodies of the deceased sons of the old Adam and those of the sons of the new Adam

But I confidently declare that, since God’s elect are the archisterium of eternal Wisdom, whose dwelling exhales fragrance like cinnamon and balsam (Sirach 24:21), and since they possess golden bowls full of incense, the mystery of abundant preaching and expansive charity (Rev. 5:8), the most equitable principle of divine equity is at work: those who, in corruptible flesh, obeying the apostolic statement that “corruption shall not possess incorruption” (1 Cor. 15:50), have chosen incorruptibility of spirit, should, contrary to the condition of the flesh, communicate to mortal senses the fragrance of the sweetest odor in which their souls incomparably delight in contemplating their Creator, when they have descended under mortal conditions into corruption (Job 33:24).

[Note: [Col. 0335C] Archisterium. This is a word invented by our author and frequently used on the model of μοναστήριον (*monastērion*) and φροντιστήριον (*phrontistērion*). He uses it for the chief place of a dwelling, without a palace, in which τὴν ἀρχήν—that is, primacy and rule—is chiefly displayed. For the most part he applies the term to great friends of God and uses it as a special expression of their praise. Sometimes, however, it signifies quite different things, as when below he mockingly applies it to the apostate Julian.]

They derive the weakness of corruption from the old Adam; but they have obtained a glory so much more excellent above the sons of Adam as the new differs from the old, the heavenly Adam from the earthly. What they received from the old descends into corruption (Col. 3:9); what they borrowed from the new knows only incorruption. And because they have put off the old person with his deeds and put on the new, who was created according to God (Eph. 4:24), by the grace of the new they possess and display, within the same corruption of flesh that they carry from the old, the incorruption of inward sweetness.

The corpses of those born from the old Adam and of the less perfect stink above all foul things. Even if the dead are rich and clothed in purple, [Note: [Col. 0335D] They are wrapped in waxed cloths. This was a kind of garment in which corpses were wrapped for burial. One may suppose it was linen or cotton, since wax was applied to thicken it. I do not recall reading this word elsewhere, except in John the Deacon, *Life of Blessed Gregory the Great*, Book II, chapter 42, in the story that our Thiofrid describes from it below, Book III, chapter 4, and in Gregory himself, Book II of the *Register*, Letter 30.] even if they are sewn into the hides of wild animals, nevertheless, unless they are enclosed with the greatest care in firmly sealed coffins, [Note: [Col. 0335D] *Libitinae*. *Feretrum* commonly signifies a bier. Here it is clearly used for a sarcophagus.] the living bodies of those near them either die from their stench or are afflicted with serious illness.

But the bodies of those reborn in the new Adam, walking in the newness of life and not straying from the path of perfection, bodies that will be conformed to the body of divine glory (Phil. 3:21) and will be spiritual in the glory of the resurrection, then, like perfumes—not so much whole as crushed—and like spices, which give off a pleasant fragrance when ground and scattered, by the grace of a more exalted and manifest divine miracle breathe upon human breasts an air of more fragrant odor. When, with the most precious pearl [Note: [Col. 0335D] A broken pearl. I think he alludes to Mark 14:3, “having broken the alabaster flask, she poured it out,” and so here too *pearl* should be understood as a vessel made from it. The figurative expression nevertheless requires us to understand the body, or flesh.] broken, [Note: [Col. 0336C] To its origin and former possession. Origen’s error was that souls existed before bodies and lay hidden—I do not know in what receptacles—until God sent them, one after another, into bodies. See Book I of *On First Principles*, chapter 7. The Platonists had already raved about this delusion long before. See, if you wish, Rodiginus, Book X, chapter 16. Far be it from us to think that our Thiofrid held this view or intended it here. This most learned man was not unaware of, nor did this most religious man neglect, the opinion of Pope Leo I, who condemned that error in writing against the Priscillianists, Letter 93. Thus Thiofrid teaches only that the soul has its origin from God, whose throne of majesty is in heaven, and not that it is transmitted through generation—a mistake of Tertullian’s that certain heretics have revived in our own age. His manner of speaking is also not far removed from that of the Wise Man: “The spirit returns to God, who gave it” (Eccles. 12:7). For “returns” seems almost to indicate that it was already there before it was given to the body. But the expression signifies only origin and the action of the Maker.] the soul, seasoned with the spices of virtue, has flown back to its origin and former possession.

For since the soul derives its origin from heaven and shares in that nature, while the substance of the flesh receives its material from the earth and preserves the quality and likeness of its own origin, it would indeed be less astonishing if, in the mutual and measured union of the two, that which is from heaven and whose citizenship is in heaven among human beings (Phil. 3:20), where the fragrance of perpetual sweetness naturally exists, exercised the force of its condition on earth, where the one nature is hindered by its entanglement with the other. On earth, I say, which the serpent eats (Gen. 3:14), which, condemned in the first-created man by a curse, was permitted to bring forth thorns and thistles—certainly pricks and incentives to vices (ibid., 17)—and which must necessarily be accompanied by intolerable stench according to its nature.

But this is worthy of incomparable wonder: in the separation of the two, when each has returned to the primacy of its own nature, that which was conceived from the unclean seed and stench of the earth (Job 14:4) exhales from itself an immeasurably sweet odor, as though it originated from the height of heaven rather than from an earthly dwelling, according to a heavenly nature rather than its own earthly one. It manifests and displays in itself not the dignity and condition of its productive material [Note: [Col. 0337B] Productive material. This appears to be a catachresis. He calls it “productive” because the body was compacted and produced from it.], but those of the life-giving soul.

And just as above, the soul is in the flesh yet outside the flesh, so the flesh is above the flesh: on earth, yet above, indeed outside, the earth. It follows not so much the nature from which it was taken as that by which it was given life and nourishment.

The earthly nature is changed into a heavenly one [Note: [Col. 0338B] The nature is changed. Not in substance, but in accident.]. Death no longer holds its rights perfectly over the flesh of the saints; rather, in the flesh of Christ, with death destroyed, the flesh lives more effectively even when dead. It does not know the stench of its mother, but preserves within itself the fragrance of its most fragrant spirit. And because it stinks from itself in conception, in birth, in nurture, and finally throughout the administration of the whole present life, at last, as a result of the preceding union of the two, it breathes forth from itself, in its dissolution, the fragrance of every sweetness, which it does not possess by its condition.

**The first book ends.**

# The Chapters of the Second Book Begin

[Col. 0337]

I. On the mausoleums of the saints, and why every precious stone and gold is their covering.  
II. That material gold, nor everything precious among transient things, can compare with such ashes.  
III. That the right of the holy soul pours the abundance of its holiness into all the ornaments and coverings of its dust.  
IV. That the citizens of the heavenly city indeed regard the monsters of avarice as worthless, but esteem highly the devotion of Christian faith.  
V. That even heavenly things are compared through the desirable things of the world.  
VI. That the poverty of the saints is illustrious, since after the death of the flesh it merits the riches of heaven and earth, and why they have *ciboria* and pyramids.  
VII. What should be thought about those pledges of God’s elect that are consumed by beasts and birds or submerged in rivers.

**The chapters of the second book end.**

# The Second Book Begins

## CHAPTER I. On the Mausoleums of the Saints, and Why Every Precious Stone and Gold Is Their Covering

[Col. 0337C]

Certainly the mausoleums of the saints are not sordid [Note: [Col. 0337C] The mausoleums of the saints. The greater the piety and religion of our ancestors, the more lavish was their generosity in adorning the holy relics and honoring them with carefully chosen ceremonies. Hence those mausoleums, many of which are still seen today, receptacles of the bodies of the saints. The Calvinist iconoclasts leveled many with the ground, and even dug them up from within the ground, moved no less by hatred of the saints than by love of gold and silver.], like the Pharisaic tombs that are whitewashed on the outside (Matt. 23:27), but even the death itself that is in them is precious (Ps. 115:15)—the supreme and irreparable punishment of the first transgression—vital and glorious. What is death in the less perfect, and destruction among earthly living creatures, is transition in them; what is the end of life in others is celebrated in them as a birthday.

[Note: [Col. 0337D] Birthday. Thus the ancient Church’s martyrologies call the day of the saints’ death, undoubtedly because, having died to us, they are born much more happily to God and to the company of the blessed. There was much pomp and vanity among the ancients on their birthdays. Martial writes:

“March’s Kalends are birthdays to me,  
A light more beautiful than all the Kalends.”

Why so? Because on that day a little human being, fashioned from mud and clay, was born. How much more beautiful is that eternal light which is precious in the sight of the Lord—not less the death than the life of his saints? How beautiful, I say, is the light of that city which the glory of God illuminates and whose lamp is the Lamb (Rev. 21:23)! Thus such a birthday, which Thiofrid mentions here, is rightly celebrated.]

Nothing at all in the corruption of their flesh is foul to the eyes of the mind; nothing is sordid. Rather, everything is so sweet, everything so honorable, and endowed with such divine power, that every soul devoted to God may rightly cry out in a voice of rejoicing and worthy wonder: “How beautiful are your tents, Jacob, and your tabernacles, Israel! Like wooded valleys, like gardens beside irrigated rivers, like tabernacles that the Lord has fixed” (Num. 24:5–6). And since the heavenly city of the King, itself set out in a square (Rev. 21:16), to which the entire company of the saints belongs, itself has streets paved with pure gold (ibid., 18), in which divinity walks eternally and takes delight, surely the pledges of God’s elect, who build upon Christ’s foundation with gold and precious stones, not with wood or straw (1 Cor. 3:12), whose wisdom and sincere purity of body and soul are understood in the most precious gold of metals, rightly receive boxes and cases constructed and adorned with gold and gems—that is, *ciboria* and pyramids.

[Note: [Col. 0339C] *Ciboria* and pyramids. I know that Horace is written as follows:

“Fill light *ciboria* with forgetfulness-bringing Massic wine …”

From this passage it is clear that *ciboria* denotes a kind of capacious drinking vessel. I know also that in the sacred furnishings of Christian churches a *ciborium* is a vessel in which the most holy body of Christ the Lord is placed and preserved. But here I think it is used in another and less usual sense, for a repository of sacred bodies—not for a small chest or sarcophagus, but for a larger chamber, chapel, or vault in which several sarcophagi could be placed. Aegidius of the Golden Valley, a monk, clearly uses it in this sense in his additions to Anselm the canon, in Floribert, chapter 30: “That bier,” he says, “has been placed in the *ciborium*, beside the body of blessed Lambert, even to the present day, with the other pledges of the saints.” Further below, concerning the body of Saint Madelberta: “It has been placed in the aforementioned *ciborium*, in which many other bodies of saints also rest.” Hence, in the verses placed at the beginning of this work, he says that not only pyramids but also *ciboria* are built, indicating that it was a type of building. What form that structure of the *ciborium* had, you will see elegantly described by our author below, in Book II, chapter 6.]

For, leaving aside the allegorical meaning, why, in the literal sense, should every precious stone and gold not be their covering (Ezek. 28:13), since they enter the grave in an abundance of virtues (Job 5:26), since they are “kings and counselors of the earth,” building solitudes for themselves (Job 3:14) through the pursuit of tranquil minds, and possessing the gold of wisdom and the silver of divine speech tested by fire (Ps. 12:7)?

[Note: [Col. 0339D] Kings and counselors of the earth. These are Job’s words. How our author calls the saints kings, he explains below in this same chapter.]

Indeed, God’s elect are lofty and eminent golden vessels, which are not reckoned against the eternal Wisdom (Job 28:18); they themselves are topaz from Ethiopia (Ps. 119:127); they themselves are pure gold from which that heavenly city, of which we have spoken above, was built (Rev. 21:18).

[Note: [Col. 0339D] The heavenly city. That is, the celestial city. The Greeks more commonly use οὐράνιος (*ouranios*).]

In praise of its construction and immeasurable adornment, the prophetic voice mystically promises through the Holy Spirit: “Behold, I will arrange your stones in order, and I will lay your foundations in sapphires; I will set jasper as your battlements, your gates in carved stones, and all your boundaries in precious stones” (Isa. 54:11–12). The solution to this veiled riddle is: “All your children shall be taught by the Lord” [Col. 0339C] (ibid., 13).

[Note: [Col. 0339D] The solution to the veiled riddle. What is said with such elaborate display and variety concerning stones, but obscurely and almost enigmatically, is explained, he says, when he adds: “All your children,” that is, these very children are the stones, as he explicitly states.]

For the renowned sons of Zion are clothed in the finest gold (Lam. 4:2); they are stones of wondrous size and highest value, mystically woven in four rows into the breastpiece of the high priest [Col. 0340A] (Exod. 39:8, 10), and through the variety of their names and colors they display, in a tropological manner, the distinct and desirable forms of every virtue.

[Note: [Col. 0340C] Mystically woven in four rows. Mystically and typologically—likewise, he says that something is done mystically and typologically—Thiofrid describes whatever in the Old Testament signified some mystery of the New Testament, or some sacred and spiritual reality; he also uses the terms for the mystery itself or the reality signified in that manner. If you observe this, you will easily understand many passages of this author. Thus here he wants the stones in the high priest’s breastpiece to have been a type of the distinguished and sacred variety of the virtues that would exist in the saints.]

They are also a royal priesthood (1 Pet. 2:8). And since, corresponding to the number of the eight beatitudes (Matt. 5:3–10), [Note: [Col. 0340C] The eight ornaments of the priests. These eight are described in Exodus 39 and fashioned at God’s command by Bezalel: the shoulder-piece, the breastpiece, the robe of the shoulder-piece, the linen tunic, the turban, the undergarments, the sash, and the plate of sacred veneration. The author does not seem to assign any force or mystery to the number eight here, but merely to indicate a variety of adornment. To discuss each of these would be endless and entirely unnecessary; let us retain only this point: that by this variety of ornaments the various qualities of holy minds are indicated. See, if you wish, those who wrote on Exodus, such as Origen, Homilies 9 and 13; Rupert, Book IV, chapter 23; Clement of Alexandria, Book V of the *Stromata*; and Jerome, *On the Priestly Garment*.]

there are in the Law eight things of immeasurable value and beauty, made from figured linen, purple, scarlet, fine linen, violet, gold, and the most precious gems (Exod. 39)—not so much garments as ornaments of the priests, and, with the whole structure of the world, a wondrous mystery scarcely expressible in human words concerning all the sacraments that must be administered in the Church through the priestly office—when the flesh, surrounded by weakness, is clothed with the majesty of so great an adornment while the soul is still a pilgrim away from the Lord (2 Cor. 5:6), [Col. 0340B] will it not, after enduring so many long labors, when clothed in the robe of immortality and crowned with glory, reign gloriously in the heavenly court, rightly deserve to have, whatever belongs to the earthly house of its dwelling (ibid., 1), these elaborate and artfully fashioned garments, of Minerva’s workmanship [Note: [Col. 0340D] The price of Minerva’s workmanship. I think *price* is used for a precious object. Since he is discussing garments fashioned by art, recalling the poetic fiction, he calls them Minerva’s workmanship, for Minerva presided over weaving.], and embossed work in admirable figures of cast metal, together with many kinds of gems of varied color, according to the devotion of the faithful, as the ornaments of its covering [Note: [Col. 0340D] *Redimicula*. He uses this word broadly for everything by which someone is adorned, such as a garment with which a person is clothed.]?

And why should their lowly remains not be clothed and wrapped in the highest beauty and glory, since they belong to the heavenly city and are not merely its leaders but its kings? God, the true and rightful supreme prince of kings, does not boast of them as the Babylonian king boasted of his own, saying, “Are not my princes at the same time kings?” (Isa. 10:9).

They are certainly kings, and they possess senatorial dignity. Their blessed eyes contemplate more closely in their heavenly home the King of the ages, who has written on his garment and on his thigh: “King of kings and Lord of lords” (Rev. 19:16), in his beauty; and they participate in the dance of eternal festivity, never to see an end to such celebration and joy.

And since every earthly king, on the greatest festivals, is adorned with the ornaments of the world, not like a human being but like another god, and since those who are in kings’ houses wear soft and exquisite garments (Matt. 11:8), why should the bones and ashes of the saints—before which kings themselves clothed in purple and princes bend and bow the knee—not be stored in mausoleums, cases, and wrappings elaborately fashioned at the greatest expense?

## CHAPTER II. That Material Gold Cannot Compare with Such Ashes, Nor Everything Precious among Transient Things

[Col. 0341B]

Indeed, just as mystical refined gold does not equal eternal Wisdom (Job 28:15), so material gold does not compare with such ashes, nor does anything that is precious among temporal things. For what is gold, and everything precious that comes from the earth, except clay with its color changed?

But there is a great difference between the nature of ashes and the gleam of gold [Note: [Col. 0341C] The gleam of gold. Thiofrid is steeped in the poets, and poetic language naturally comes to him. Virgil, *Aeneid* VI:

“Whence a varied gleam of gold flashed through the branches.”

Understand *gleam* as radiance.]: ashes are naturally squalid, while gold shines; the former gives pleasure spiritually, the latter carnally. Gold does not permit a person to travel safely among thieves; ashes bind sacrilegious persons and thieves with an invisible fetter and, together with their booty, make them stand motionless,
as the Marpesian crag stands. For the Dialogue of that most vigilant theological pope Gregory [Note: [Col. 0341C] Gregory’s Dialogue contains this. See Book III, chapter 22.] records that, before the most sacred ashes of a man of magnificent holiness [Note: [Col. 0341D] Of a man of magnificent holiness. St Gregory does not name him further; he merely says that he was a priest of the province of Valeria.], a thief who, especially at night, greedily coveted the darkness, having furtively stolen a ram from the sheepfolds near the tomb of that same elect of God [Note: [Col. 0341C] “Furtively.” The Greek is κλέπω, “I steal,” from which Plautus has *clepo*. Both forms mean “to steal.” Just as *furtim* (“furtively”) is formed from *fur*, so our author, with a certain liberal and not unusual license, formed *cleptim* from that word, with the same meaning.], stood alive, bound by invisible chains, with the dead lion—or rather the sleeping one—[Eccles. IX, 4]; nor, by any effort, could he struggle or wrench himself free, nor could he cast away the booty which he had been allowed to steal, to his own shame; until, after the morning office, the brothers who went out—the Lord’s sheep [Col. 0342A] [Note: [Col. 0341D] Brothers, the Lord’s sheep. Thiofridus enjoys such constructions in his prose, which grammarians call apposition. I believe, moreover, that he mentions the sheep here because the stolen ram was under discussion.]—found him being tormented, both by an avenging conscience and by divine examination [Note: [Col. 0341D] “Divine examination.” Understand examination by the application of torments, as in: “You have tested me by fire” (Ps. XVI, 3).]. Since it was uncertain whether he had come to offer something or to take something away, they were at last assured by his confession of guilt and by the clearest manifestation of divine punishment, and only with the greatest difficulty obtained by supplication that he who had come to lie in wait for their property might at least depart empty-handed and free.

Indeed, since it is written that everything consists of earth (Eccles. III, 20), the great ashes of the saints, gold, and everything in the world that is the object of the lust of the eyes (I John II, 16) differ not in substance but in appearance, not in the truth of nature [Note: [Col. 0341D] “Not in the truth of nature.” Understand this with respect to their material, as the reason added makes clear.] but in color. Yet a manly body and spirit are not enervated so much by this monster of avarice as the man whose spirit cleaves to the divine, unbounded Spirit is strengthened and enriched by that treasure of outstanding merit, with the riches of God’s supremely abundant grace.

A little dust is more precious than pure, refined gold, although the womb of earth is the origin of both. More precious, I say, because gold deceives and, with its deceptive color, flatters unhappy avarice; whereas the dust, without any deceptive embellishment, advances the world’s salvation through the sanctification of its spirit, with immense and well-deserved admiration from all. Gold, and whatever in material things dazzles the eyes of the flesh with its splendor, is regarded as being of lower value the more it is diminished by being divided, and the greater the loss suffered by the one who divides it.

But the electrum of so much dust [Note: [Col. 0341D] “The electrum of so much dust.” He elegantly joins two things that are most widely separated, just as when the saints call extreme poverty “the richest poverty,” and Origenes, concerning Mary Magdalene seeking from Christ, as though from a gardener, whether he had taken Him away, says that she “wisely did not know and wisely erred.” Origenes considered electrum a metal more precious than gold itself. Pliny says it is a mixture of gold and silver, with only one-fifth silver added. [Col. 0342D] Whatever the truth may be, it certainly possesses extraordinary brilliance, by which it undoubtedly surpasses gold. Hence it gave rise to the proverb: ἠλέκτρου διαφεγγέστερον, “more translucent than electrum.” Accordingly, the prophet Ezekiel sometimes compares it with fire (I, 27), I suppose because it vibrates in a similar manner; elsewhere (VIII, 2) he describes it as shining like the appearance of brilliance, as the vision of electrum.] is distributed more widely in the patronage of the churches of God [Note: [Col. 0342D] “In the patronage of the churches.” Let the Calvinists blush: while they trample underfoot the electrum of this dust, they show themselves to be auxiliaries of that serpent which, under the pressure of the curse, eats the dust of the earth. It was he who incited Julian, the enemy of God and religion, to remove the noble dust of the martyr Babylas far from the Daphne shrine. The Calvinist offspring of that apostate went much further, burning the most sacred relics of the saints. The practice of distributing the saints’ remains throughout the churches will be discussed below, Book III, chapter 4, and Book IV, chapter 5.], without any loss to the one distributing it; and therefore the price of reverence and honor is bestowed on it more lavishly, as is the remedy of salvation for suffering mortals.

Gold is extracted from the veins of the earth with the greatest labor; its dross is smelted to purity with the greatest sweat (Isa. I, 25), and only then, in the furnace, does it advance toward the brilliance of its nature, when it loses and casts off its impurities. Thus this treasure of such great value does indeed arise from earth, but it is removed from earth when, in the saints who are still fighting in the battle line, it is separated from earthly action together with the spirit that is in them, through the regard of divine mercy. Like gold passing through fire, it is tested and burned by the scorching of tribulation; and, cleansed from every stain of vice, it is forged from the crown of Melchom into the ornament of a diadem (II Kings XII, 30; I Chron. XX, 2) by David, truly strong of hand [Note: [Col. 0343D] “From the crown of Melchom.” He was the king of the Ammonites, from whose most precious diadem David fashioned a crown for himself—as though, in a certain sense, he had made something sacred from something profane. Thiofridus says that, if one considers their origin, the ashes and relics of the saints are profane, but that they are so consecrated by the holiness of the spirit that Christ, the true David, does not disdain them; indeed, they are like a crown of glory in the hand of the Lord and a royal diadem in the hand of their God (Isa. LXII, 3). I am not unaware that some prefer Melchom to have been a god, an idol, and that this crown belonged to it. But they do not persuade me. They seem to do violence to the clear words of Scripture: “He took the diadem of their king from his head” (II Kings XII, 30). I would almost dare to say that they also do violence to David’s piety, since he would surely have considered himself contaminated rather than adorned by wearing such a thing. The argument from the weight of a talent—125 Roman pounds—does not frighten those who have persuaded themselves, on sound grounds, that the talent did not contain even a twelfth of that weight; I agree with them. See Ludovicus ab Alcasar, *De ponderibus sacris*, proposition 22, § 3, letter G. Finally, why hesitate, not to say deny, that David could have worn that diadem, when Scripture says in such explicit words: “And it was placed upon David’s head”? That certainly excludes every quibble. [Note: [Col. 0343D] “Truly strong of hand, David.” He alludes to the etymology of the name David, which some interpret as “strong of hand.”].

The sanctification of so much dust liberates from the treasury of mammon of iniquity (Luke XVI, 9), and sanctifies for the Lord, through the commerce of its holiness, the gold, gems, and everything which, according to Ezekiel’s prophecy, the merchants of Aram and Eden and the traders of Sheba and Asshur have wrapped in many kinds of coverings—violet cloth, embroidered fabrics, and precious stores—and bound with the cords of sins, in the markets of the symbolic Tyre [Note: [Col. 0343D] “In the markets of the symbolic Tyre.” Tyre signifies the world, or the congregation of the ungodly. He says that human bodies—apparently exposed for sale in the world and somehow placed in the treasury or storehouse of iniquity—are freed from that disgrace by holy souls and their works and are carried into the sacred treasury of the Lord. These markets, which are nothing but buying and selling, resemble what Scripture says of Ahab: that he had sold himself to do evil in the sight of the Lord (III Kings XXI, 25).] (Ezek. XXVII, 23), so that, deposited in His treasuries (Josh. VI, 19), they may adorn the place of His rest and, in the worship of His mystical tabernacle and temple, shine with the value not so much of their own as of the far more excellent treasure stored within them.
