The gleam of gold and similar delights of the world, beautiful to behold, are darkened by the mixture and sprinkling of unsanctified dust, which overlays their apparent splendor and beauty; but, illuminated by sanctified dust, they do not so much adorn as become adorned, and they are made radiant with a more abundant brilliance. Hence they customarily darken carnal persons materially and enlighten them spiritually: by their own splendor they attract fleshly eyes, while by the merits and grace of what is stored within them they attract spiritual eyes.

By themselves they produce the deadly avarice of the flesh; but through the deposit enclosed within them [Note: [Col. 0344C] “Through the deposit enclosed within it.” He gracefully calls the sacred relics a deposit of gold or silver, in which they are enclosed as things to be guarded.], they arouse a living and saving avarice of the soul, since Augustine even calls the Lord avaricious [Note: [Col. 0344C] “Augustine also calls the Lord avaricious.” The passage is Augustine’s commentary on Psalm XCIX. The words are: “God is avaricious for our salvation.” This holy avarice is thirst, which tormented the Lord when He said, “I thirst.”]. For the holier anyone is, the more eager he is for such a great treasure; and although dead to the world, he does not love the world or the things that are in the world (I John II, 15), yet with the subtle judgment of his mind he considers that what it encloses or wraps is not of the world—since it is evident that it is above the world.

Is not the price of sanctified dust above the world, in which, through the merit of the glorified spirit, there is the salvation of the world? [Note: [Col. 0344D] “The salvation of the world.” Let the Calvinist gnash his teeth at this. But a prudent Catholic will easily grasp the sound meaning. Whoever wishes assistance should consult what was noted above, Book I, chapter 5.] It is in the world, yet outside the world; it is not of the world. But, according to what Christ said when reconciling the world in Himself to God the Father (II Cor. V, 19), and when He spoke to His apostles whom He had chosen through the Holy Spirit (Acts I, 2)—“You are not of the world, but I chose you out of the world” (John XV, 19)—that which was produced in the world and from the world is so chosen from the world that it is no longer of it, not by the prerogative of its own merit, not by its own nature, but by the gratuitous grace of God.

In gold and in all the spoils of Damascus, which is a type of the world [Note: [Col. 0344D] “The spoils of Damascus.” He alludes to Isaiah VIII, 3–4.], there are the presumption and glory of the world; but when they are chosen and set apart as coverings and ornaments for the dissolved dust of God’s elect, there is also in them the most evident power and glory of God. For just as the seventy men were infused and filled from the spirit of Moses the lawgiver (Num. XI, 25), without any diminution to him, as types of the lesser priests in the Church (Jerem. XXIX, 10), so, through the mystical number of seven decades—seventy years (Dan. IX, 2) [Note: [Col. 0344D] “The mystical number of seven decades.” Many have taught that the seventy years of captivity signify the period of this wretched life. Scripture agrees: “The days of our years are seventy years” (Ps. LXXXIX, 10). No Catholic doubts that complete holiness—the mystery which Thiofridus places in this number—is attained through observance of the Decalogue and the sevenfold grace of the Holy Spirit.]—throughout the whole period of the passing age, the beloved of God are infused and filled with the fullness of all graces from the holiness of the glorified Spirit. It is not so much their tested limbs as everything, whether within or without, with which their ashes are covered, as they return by natural dissolution and are restored to the origin of their nature.

## CHAPTER III. That the right of the holy soul pours the abundance of its holiness into all the ornaments and coverings of its dust

[Col. 0345A]

For just as the living and effective word of God, sharper than any two-edged sword, reaches mystically even to the division of soul and spirit, and of joints and marrow (Hebr. IV, 12), so the holy power of the soul, now reigning with God, wonderfully diffuses itself from the innermost parts to the outermost—both to what belongs to it while it is enclosed in the prison of the flesh and to what belongs to it after it has been transferred to citizenship in the heavenly Jerusalem. Whatever it wondrously effects through flesh and bones by the prevenient and interceding merits of the saints, it effects still more wondrously through dissolved dust, diffusing itself into everything, both exterior and interior, whatever the material or value of the ornaments and coverings of so great an ember may be.

And just as the soul itself is not seen in the body, yet works marvels through the body, so the treasure of precious dust, although it is neither seen nor touched, nevertheless transmits the abundance of its holiness—by which it is watered through the illustrious merits of its sanctified spirit from the fountain that flows from the house of the Lord and waters the torrent of thorns (Joel III, 18) [Note: [Col. 0345D] “Waters the torrent of thorns.” He says that this torrent is watered by the fountain of divine grace. St Jerome’s *Apology to Pammachius for his book Against Jovinianus*, near the end, sheds light on this otherwise none-too-clear passage: “The sealed fountain,” he says, “from which that river flows, according to Joel, which waters the torrent either of ropes or of thorns: of ropes, namely, of sins by which we were formerly bound; of thorns, which choke the seed of the master of the household.” For the benefit of Calvinists, let us note in passing that, in Jerome’s view, the river here is the perpetual outpouring of God’s grace, while the fountain is the most blessed Mother of God, the Virgin Mary, through whom all grace is conveyed to our souls.]—into everything in which it is hidden, within and without.

If the outer enclosure of this dust is touched by the steadfast hand of faith—whether it be a foil of gold or silver, a gem of whatever value, or any woven, wrought, cast, marble, or wooden material—it is as though what is hidden within were touched. Thus the power of the divine majesty works salvation in the midst of the earth (Ps. LXXIII, 12). In the glorification of the dust, it remembers His mercy (Luke I, 54); He manifests toward us the compassion of His condescension. Nor does He wish man to be unaware that, after the worm, he will become dust: that incomprehensible, inconceivable, ineffable sublimity of sublimities humbled and lowered itself even to the dust (Isa. XXVI, 5), and therefore covered the appearance of its inward beauty with the darkness of assumed dust.

Finally, He slept in the dust (Job VII, 21), so that sanctified dust, in the very sleep and decay of its corruption, might surpass the beauty of all things dissoluble into earth—not in the quality of corruptible substance, but in the prerogative of merit and the gratuitous gift of heavenly grace. He was beautiful beyond the sons of men (Ps. XLIV, 3), yet did not wish to possess beauty or comeliness (Isa. LIII, 2), but a face as though hidden and despised (ibid., 3). He wished to be a worm, born in the flesh without seed and not a man—indeed, in man more than man—the reproach of men and the outcast (Ps. XXI, 7), for the sake of dust, so that dust, most foul by nature and appearance, might be considered most beautiful through the grace and sanctification of its glorified spirit.

And just as, according to the distinguished defender of the Church, Jerome [Note: [Col. 0346D] “Defender.” The Septuagint interpreters frequently call God in the Psalms ὑπερασπιστής, “defender” or “protector,” as though He held a shield before us for our protection. For ἀσπίς is “shield.” Thiofridus, apparently neglecting the sign of aspiration, seems to use this word for any eminent or courtly man. Thus, in the prologue to the *Life of Saint Willibrord*, he calls Alcuin the *yperaspistes* of Charlemagne.], the perpetual Virgin Mary, from whom God Himself and man was born, is greater in merits—not in nature—than a virgin and a man, so this dust would be granted the privilege, not by nature but by grace, of being more than dust and the food of worms, through the immeasurable treasure of the world, weighed upon the scales of the cross, the world’s wondrous price.

He repaid the dust with an incomparable return; and just as His supreme and essential brightness and beauty was as hidden as it was manifest in the dust, so, through an incomprehensible reversal of things and a dissimilar likeness ordained beforehand, He arranged that the substantial decay and foulness of dust should be as hidden as it was revealed in the beauty of gold, of every most precious metal, of gems, and of elaborate clothing. It would not so much receive beauty as restore it; and gold would not be highly valued for the appearance that dazzles the eyes of avarice, but would be highly valued because of the dust.

He subjected all the glory and ornament of the world to the ornament and glory of dust, because He Himself, although the creator of dust, consented to be conceived, formed, and born from dust, after emptying Himself of the appearance of His majesty. I say this confidently: according to the essence of bodily substance, He became that from which dust was conceived and brought forth—dust from dust. God became man from dust for man’s sake; and He made men, to whom the word of God was addressed, gods from dust. And since He granted dust a share in His name and divinity, why should anything precious from the earth not be expended for its adornment, when He willed to make Himself its participant and companion, and willed His blood to be its price?

He in a certain way granted the glory of His flesh in common to sanctified dust, because whoever makes himself free from the vices of the flesh by cleaving to the Lord is one spirit with Him (I Cor. VI, 17), and is one flesh with His flesh. Therefore Christ Jesus nourishes His own flesh in man—not in just any man, but in one who is in the flesh and loves Him diligently, since He loves those who love Him (Prov. VIII, 17)—and, when He spoke with His most intimate conversational companion, the lawgiver Moses [Note: [Col. 0346D] “When He spoke to Moses.” Here Thiofridus suffered a human lapse, his memory wavering: he attributes to Moses what the prophet, by God’s command, later reproached the priest Eli for saying. The words are clear in the history of Kings; I find no such statement addressed to Moses. [Col. 0347C] The Greeks call this an ἀμάρτημα μνημονικόν, “a sin of memory” or lapse of memory.], said: “Whoever honors me, I will honor him” (I Kings II, 30).

He judged, by the unchangeable decree of His providence, that almost the same honor which was paid to His divinity and humanity should also be paid to the spirit, the flesh, and the dissolved ashes of the saints; and by the law of that same eternal decree He ordained it.

He redeemed dust not with corruptible gold from its vain way of life, but with His most precious blood (I Peter I, 18), which, according to the truth of the nature He assumed, had dust as the beginning of its veins. Therefore, foreseeing that a man living in the flesh could not, without nausea and bitter disgust, see and touch the putrefying corruption of a human body, He veiled His most holy body and blood with the customary and familiar covering of bread and wine, lest those receiving them should recoil at their rawness and bloodiness. In the same way He persuaded the minds of the children of the Church to wrap and enclose in gold and in the most precious materials used for objects of every kind the pledges of blessed flesh, dead in the Lord; lest, when they were presented to human eyes under the appearance of their own nature and offended them, they should be less honored than despised.

For these things ought not so much to be looked upon with bodily eyes as with spiritual eyes. While one considers the preciousness of the material in which they are enclosed or wrapped, one should weigh with the utmost subtlety not what they are by nature, but how excellent their merit is before God, with whom the spirits and souls of the righteous reign. From the fact that through gold, electrum, and similar substances the mud shines through with the radiance of virtues, it should be believed without hesitation that the saying is true: “The righteous will shine like the sun in the kingdom of their Father” (Matt. XIII, 43).

## CHAPTER IV [Note: [Col. 0347D] This chapter, as its heading announces, mocks the foolish wisdom of heretics, while responding learnedly and solidly to their foolish objection.] That the citizens of the heavenly city indeed hold the monsters of avarice in contempt, but esteem the devotion of Christian faith

But we, who are soft clay, who build Egyptian cities from clay and straw (Exod. I, 11–14), do not exalt gold and whatever is precious in metals, clothing, or gems with such great praises because we, whether proselytes [Note: [Col. 0347D] “We proselytes.” Out of humility he counts himself among proselytes rather than Israelites. He has in mind the innumerable mixed multitude that went out of Egypt with the children of Israel (Exod. XII, 38).] or true Israelites who went out with a strong hand (Exod. XIV, 8), consecrate the spoils of Egypt for the worship of God in His mystical tabernacle, and foolishly affirm that the souls of God’s elect take pleasure in these things, when, on account of their contempt for such objects, they themselves deserved to be transferred as tested gold into the treasury of the heavenly emperor.

The citizens of the heavenly city hold in contempt those monsters of avarice which are equivalent to idolatry; but they esteem the devotion of Christian faith. Following the example of the God of Israel, who preferred the typical sacrifices of the Israelite people to be offered to Him rather than to idols, they prefer to be honored by men as the most eminent of all, with the most precious things granted both for testing and for use. They prefer that their own possessions, which they leave from earth in the earth—pledges most vile in relation to the sublimity of their immortality, but most excellent in relation to the needs of our mortality—be covered and adorned with these things rather than that the storerooms of mammon of iniquity be packed full.

And they prefer that the sin which sits upon a talent of lead be increased and transported by two winged women—namely, the principal vices, pride and empty glory—into the broad valley of dreadful stench, the land of Shinar, carrying the prophetic vessel raised between heaven and earth (Zech. V, 7ff.) and placing it in the house built in Babylon, the summit of confusion [Note: [Col. 0347D] “The sin which sits upon a talent of lead.” He learnedly interprets that vision of Zechariah as referring to avarice. The earthly weight of lead and the vessel, made as though for storing plates of yellow metal, fit it beautifully. Origenes and St Gregory the Great certainly interpret this passage as referring to the same vice. Thiofridus rightly notes in particular that avarice dwells in the land of Shinar, a word whose origin signifies “the awakening of the sleeper.” Those who sleep less peacefully are more frequently and miserably awakened than those whom the most wicked Mammon, having reduced them to his power, presses under his dominion and restrains with chains and imprisonment.].

They do not covet gold, but allow themselves to be propitiated by those who distribute gold religiously. They do not covet buildings of prayer raised high, or the architraves of columns fashioned from gold, or ceilings glittering with riches, or altars repeatedly marked with emeralds. They do not seek to have parchment dyed purple, or gold melted into letters [Note: [Col. 0348C] “Gold melted into letters.” I have no doubt that Thiofridus is referring to those books which he and earlier generations saw written entirely in gold; several of this kind are still preserved by the pious diligence of later generations in illustrious churches and monasteries. At Bamberg I had the opportunity to see one donated by that rare—and, so to speak, paradoxical—pair of princely spouses, Henry and Cunigunde, founders of that church, with this inscription:

“Henry and Cunigunde bring forth these gifts to you, O God.”

Nor is Echternach lacking such furnishings. A very large volume of the four Gospels is still preserved there, written in liquid gold, with great splendor of images and titles. Its boards, which are externally provided as protection, are covered with gold plates, fashioned with elegant and ancient workmanship. Besides several images of saints, two figures in imperial attire are also visible. Beneath the one on the right is written, “OTTO REX”; beneath the other, “[THEOFPHANIU] IMP.” This must be Otto II, for he had Theophania as his wife, the daughter of the Byzantine emperor Nicephorus, whose brother was Blessed Gregory, abbot of Porz. See Molanus, *Natales Sanctorum Belgii*, 4 November. There is therefore no doubt that this codex was the gift of these rulers, and our Thiofridus consequently saw it, since they preceded him by a full hundred years. One may note in passing the piety and munificence of these most Christian rulers in this matter also, and the worship of the saints attested by so many proofs. The saints whose images I said were visible are, first, Willibrord—to whose honor this gift was chiefly presented—and then Saint Benedict; opposite them are Saint Boniface and Saint Ludger. They did not learn such practices in the school of the Calvinists, who, wherever they find such things, teach that they should be destroyed along with the dust. Moreover, they blaspheme the saints themselves, burn their holy relics, and scatter their ashes to the wind. This truly is to be “reformed” and to be reformers.].

Nor do they wish codices to be covered with gems, while Christ’s ministers receive little or no care and naked Christ dies before their doors. For, just as, according to Isaiah’s prophecy, the Medes do not seek silver and do not desire gold (Isa. XIII, 17), and just as, according to Solinus the natural historian, all the mortals who live in the town of Carbyla or Barbita—which lies 335 miles from Susa, the famous city of Persia—out of hatred for gold purchase this kind of metal and throw it into the depths of the earth, lest, polluted by its use, they corrupt justice through avarice [Note: [Col. 0349D] “In the town of Carbyla or Barbita.” There seems to be a corruption in the text. Solinus’s words are in chapter 56: “Babytace, a town of Persia. In it all mortals, out of hatred for gold, buy this kind of metal and cast it into the depths of the earth, lest, polluted by its use, they corrupt justice.” Pliny, Book VI, chapter 27, says: “In the northern channel of the Tigris is the town of Babytace,” and adds the same details as Solinus.], so many of the saints, lest they seem to commend and commend to the greedy minds of men a love of silver and gold, reject and shun precious ornaments as impediments to their most excellent holiness.

Thus, that the secure sufficiency for life of a poor and cramped household, and the gifts of God not yet understood through visible things (Rom. I, 20), may exist and be recognized as manifest, they do not deem themselves worthy to possess sanctuaries glittering with Eastern gems or mausoleums unviolated by any riches throughout the ages. They considered golden headbands, which are profits to the sons of the age, as dung (Phil. III, 8)—not as an insult to or prejudice against Christian devotion, which is most pleasing to the Holy of Holies, God, and to all the saints, but so that it might be plainly evident to carnal minds how detestable avarice is.

The head does not disagree with the members, nor the members with the head. Rather, just as God alone, according to the most orderly administration of His providence, knows how to provide medicine suited to human weakness, so now, as an antidote of frugality by which He may cure the disease of avarice, He rejects the material of the love of money; now He admits it into the sacrifice of righteousness, to prove that the devotion and offering of every faithful soul please Him.

Thus, among His elect, some, as a salutary example by which they may win others, regard all the ornament of the world as a loss to themselves; others deem themselves worthy of such honor for the increase of holy charity and orthodox devotion. For if the Lord of heaven and all the heavenly beings did not equally receive the outward gifts of the orthodox, Scripture would falsely say: “The redemption of a man’s soul is his own riches” (Prov. XIII, 8). But when the man who devotes himself to supporting the poor of the common people—among whose rags and bodily filth blazing lust holds sway, and who cannot possess eternal dwellings because they possess neither present nor future ones—redeems his soul with his own riches, how much more does that blessed man do so who understands the poor and needy (Ps. XL, 2), and shares both in the necessities of the saints and in worthy and fitting ornaments?

## CHAPTER V. That heavenly things too are compared through the desirable things of the world

[Col. 0350B]

Indeed, the poor in spirit (Matt. 5:3) are God’s elect and household, both those of heaven, whom the Spirit of God adorned, as with shining and [Note: [Col. 0350C] The mystical stars of the Pleiades and Arcturus. Thiofridus was greatly influenced by his reading of St. Gregory the Great, whom he habitually called “the most lucid theologian.” In his writing on Job, Gregory takes Arcturus to signify the Church, in which shines the Spirit’s sevenfold grace; the Pleiades, however, signify all the saints, who amid the darkness of the present life illuminate us with the light of that same grace, etc. See Job 9:9 and 38:31. See also St. Gregory, *Moralia* XXIX, chs. 28–29.] mystical stars, with the splendors of the virtues, of the Pleiades and Arcturus; and the ornaments of God’s dwelling. Therefore every orthodox person who, according to Aratus’ saying—confirmed by the testimony of Paul, the teacher of the nations (Acts 17:28), [Note: [Col. 0350D] “We are the offspring of God.” The half-line of Aratus quoted by St. Paul in Acts is: Τοῦ γὰρ καὶ γένος ἐσμέν, “For we are indeed his offspring.”] is the offspring of God, and thrice and four times blessed, [Note: [Col. 0350D] He deserves the cube of the eight beatitudes. It is well known in geometry that a cube is a figure equally square on every side, as we see in dice. In numbers, however, the term is used proportionally. To pass over other cubic numbers, such as 27 and 64, Boethius speaks briefly and clearly of eight (*De arithmetica* II, 25): “If you multiply two times two by two, the quantity eight increases, and this is the first cube.” Among the sacred interpreters, the cube was a symbol of the supreme Godhead. Thiofridus assigns as the supreme beatitude that which consists in the vision of that Godhead.] deserves the cube of the eight beatitudes, if he spends with the greatest devotion and eagerness of spirit whatever he can regard as precious in gold, silver, pearls, and various silk garments, on the expenses of the house of the Lord and the adornment of the glory of the children of God.

For unless heavenly things are compared through the desirable and delightful things of the world, [Col. 0350C] the Fathers of both the Old and the New Testament [Note: [Col. 0350D] The Fathers of both the Old and New Testaments. In the Old Testament, David and Solomon are well known; in the New, Constantine and Charlemagne. I do not pile up further examples, although Christian history teems with them.] would not have spent their resources with such vigilance of spirit on the house of God, the buildings of the saints, and the manifold adornments of divine worship. But when it had become clear to minds illumined by the supreme light of the Godhead that eternal dwelling places are also acquired from unrighteous mammon (Luke 16:9), [Col. 0351A] excellent men and women, under both the Law and grace, offered with the readiest minds the best of their temporal possessions—things that had come to them from divine generosity—as the heavenly city’s treasuries, according to the tropological vision of Ezekiel (Ezek. 45:5; 46:19). Whatever was necessary for the worship of both the material and spiritual tabernacle, for the temple of God, for the oratories of his elect, and for holy vestments, they offered most willingly (Exod. 35:21): bracelets, earrings, rings and armlets, violet, purple, twice-dyed scarlet, fine linen, goat hair, and reddened skins—typological gifts. Through their most orderly distribution, every golden vessel was set apart and consecrated among the Lord’s treasures (ibid., 22).

I could indeed, if I wished, make a digression; I could, I say, pursue in whatever style I might the great devotion with which Moses the lawgiver and the whole Israelite people adorned and erected the tabernacle of testimony during their journey (Exod. 36 ff.), the type of the Church journeying through the desert of this age toward the promised land. I could likewise describe with what immense solicitude of spirit David prepared the ten-stringed instrument of the Holy Spirit. [Note: [Col. 0351C] The beginning of the fourth age of the world. For Thiofridus, as for many other authors, the first age is reckoned from Adam to the Flood, the second to Abraham, and the third to David, who by this method of reckoning begins the fourth.] He was the beginning of the fourth age of the world and [Note: [Col. 0351C] The head of the second *tessareskaedecados*. When St. Matthew had described Christ’s genealogy, beginning with Abraham, he concluded (1:17): “Thus all the generations from Abraham to David are fourteen generations, and from David to the deportation to Babylon are fourteen generations,” etc. In Greek, γενεαί δεκατέσσαρες, which, with the order of composition changed, is also written τεσσαρέδεκα; with the conjunction added, τεσσαρες-καί-δεκα. From this Thiofridus formed the word *tessareskaedecados*, whose length and harsher sound might frighten the unlearned, especially those ignorant of Greek; for their benefit we have written this note.] the head of the second *tessareskaedecados* of the genealogy of the incarnate Word; and he prepared and described for his son Solomon the expenses of the house of the Lord (1 Chron. 12 and 28). With what care and subtlety of divine genius did Ididia, “beloved of God,” [Note: [Col. 0351D] Ididia, “beloved of God.” He took this from the history of the Kings (2 Kings 12:25), where we read of Solomon, newly born: “The Lord loved him. And he sent word through Nathan the prophet, and called his name Jedidiah, ‘beloved of the Lord.’” Hebrew: *Ididia*, in one word.] build and consecrate the temple to the name of the Lord (3 Kings 6; 2 Chron. 3 ff.), magnificently marked with mystical dimensions, mystical cherubim, lions, and oxen in relief—[Col. 0351C] a temple which, constructed in the homeland and royal city, is a sacrament of the royal and enduring structure founded upon the inviolable foundation that is Christ Jesus.

“Before evening should close Olympus,” [that is, before I could turn my eyes back through the annals and calendars and express in any eloquence] how great was the industry with which—what according to Jerome appeared difficult, indeed impossible, in human eyes, but in the eyes of the Lord was most easy and entirely possible—[Note: [Col. 0351D] Priestly and royal power. It was chiefly through the authority or accusations of these powers, among both Jews and many pagan peoples, that innocent martyrs were persecuted. Nothing is more frequently mentioned by ecclesiastical writers.] the priestly and royal power, which during the time of persecution destroyed the assemblies of the faithful, whose envy [Note: [Col. 0351D] The devouring flame consumed the divine books. Arnobius laments this tearfully in *Against the Gentiles* IV: “Why, indeed, did our writings deserve to be given to the flames?” This barbarity was practiced especially during the tenth persecution, that of Diocletian and Maximian. It began in the year 302. Some were found who handed over the sacred books, and for this reason were called *traditores*; Baronius discusses them extensively in that year and the following ones. How much better were those glorious confessors whose eternal epitaph is found in the Roman Martyrology for 2 January: “At Rome, the commemoration of many holy martyrs who, scorning the edict of the emperor Diocletian by which the sacred books were ordered to be handed over, preferred to give their bodies to executioners rather than the holy books to dogs.”] consumed the divine books in an insatiable flame, whose impious edict filled the islands and prisons with chained multitudes of confessors and martyrs, and whose obstinacy, as though by a decree of the senate, strove with all its might to extinguish the name of Christ—then, in turn, from the resources of the state, built the basilicas of the Churches and raised their lofty roofs; and not only [Note: [Col. 0352C] Coffered ceilings and roofs dazzling with golden splendor. Constantine alone accomplished so much in this field that it was difficult for writers to record it and long for us to read it. See the remarkable account in Eusebius, *Life of Constantine* III, 39 and many following chapters.] covered ceilings and roofs shining with golden splendor, but also clothed the very walls with slabs of varied marble and [Note: [Col. 0352C] The varied composition of the *lithostroton*. If one considers the composition of the word λιθόστρωτον, it means nothing more than “stone-paved,” so that any pavement might be called by that name. But common usage suggests something additionally ornamented and exceptional. Thus the place in Jerusalem in John 19:13; and so here in Thiofridus. An ancient poet describes it in verse that vies with the work itself:

> All fitted like little cubes  
> Within the pavement, and in mosaic pattern.

Our author says: “By a composition of many kinds.”] the varied composition of a *lithostroton*; and he consecrated in the library of the Holy Church sacred books gilded and dyed purple and embellished with a variety of gems.

Time would leave me before I could discuss fully from what height of majesty, according to the splendors of the age, the imperial magnificence of Augustus Constantine descended—and according to God ascended—when [Note: [Col. 0352D] Twelve baskets of sand upon his royal neck. This happened while he was still in the white garments of baptism, on the eighth day. See the most memorable account of the event in the *Acts of Pope Liberius*, in Baronius, under the year 324.] he carried twelve baskets of sand upon his royal neck, [Col. 0352C] [Note: [Col. 0352D] As a mystery of the perfection of the number twelve. The Fathers—Origen, Ambrose, Jerome, and others—say much about the number twelve. One passage from Augustine will suffice. Writing on John (Tractate 27), he holds that this number possesses a mystery in the apostles, since they were to proclaim the Trinity throughout the whole world, that is, to the four quarters of the world. Thus it pleased Christ that they should be three times four.] as a mystery of the perfection of twelve, the prince carried them to the thresholds of the chief apostles Peter and Paul.

It would also be easy to recount which supreme pontiffs of the Holy Roman See, endowed with the offices of various dignities and rich both in worldly goods and in God, built, renewed, and adorned with the greatest diligence, at both private and public expense, the oratories of the saints. But lest I be drawn far from the sequence of my subject by a lengthy digression, I pass over what the distinguished minds of noble writers have committed to the annals and to memory.

I shall take an example from a nearby time, showing how much it benefits the soul of every orthodox person brought forth from the prison of the flesh if, while in the flesh, he spends something of his resources on honor and reverence for the patronage of the saints. When Henry, of blessed memory, the second king of that name and the first of the emperors, [Note: [Col. 0353D] Emperor Henry I. Baronius makes him the second. But since the event itself is certain, it matters little in what order he is counted. This noble story is also related in the *Chronicle of Monte Cassino*. Thiofridus tells it in such a way that he seems to have wished to display a specimen of his eloquence.] was paying nature’s debt, [Col. 0353B] at the very hour when an eclipse was impending over the world of so bright a sun, a man distinguished by the privilege of the contemplative life offered God, in the prayer of his contrite spirit and broken and humbled heart, a sacrifice (Dan. 3:40). He saw an army of unclean spirits pass his cell with the greatest eagerness, gathered as though for immense and certain spoils. He recognized not the camp of God (Gen. 32:2), but the principalities and powers of this air (Col. 2:15; Eph. 2:2). At the unusual sight he first trembled, as a human being among humans; but afterward, as a man beyond ordinary humanity, armed with the armor of God (Eph. 6:11, 13), he questioned with careful inquiry the last of those passing by, whom he had summoned with commanding authority, asking the reason for such haste. And when he had forced the truth from the author of every falsehood, he commanded him, under a terrible adjuration by the divine name, to depart and return by the same route, whether the business for which they were hastening had been accomplished or not.

He obeyed without delay and,

> Equal to light winds and very like swift sleep [Eurus],  
> disappeared;

and soon returned, no different in appearance or gait, in the foul breath of Stygian stench, but truly and without hesitation appearing covered in pitch-black darkness. [Col. 0354A] [Note: [Col. 0353D] Vedius appeared. We know that Vejovis was a deity—or rather a wicked demon—intent on harming mortals. The ancients also called him Vedius.]

Defiling his most loathsome face with his claws and beating his breast with his fists, amid great wailing, he himself disclosed the outcome of what had happened, [Note: [Col. 0353D] Outside the order by will, not by nature. Thiofridus’ friend enjoys a play on words in the conjunction and collision of expressions. He is about to say in what order the wicked demon narrated what had happened; on that occasion he says that the demon was “outside the order,” as if to say: However much he is outside, or even contrary to, every order, nevertheless in narrating he maintained good order. That he is not by nature outside the order is easily persuaded to one who believes that those condemned spirits are creatures of God, and that there can be no doubt that God, who made all things in number, weight, and measure (Wis. 11:21), also made them in order. But that he is outside the order by will—what is more contrary to every order than to rebel against one’s creator and to wish by sacrilegious will to make oneself his equal? Thus they were deservedly cast down to the place where there is no order, but everlasting horror dwells (Job 10:22).] outside the order by will, not by nature, in this order:

“Alas! What shall I complain about our lot and injury? Everywhere we lose what is owed to us and what has already been assigned to us by the censure of the unchangeable decree. We, whose nature is subject to mutability, are always pressing our purpose with the obstinacy of a wholly fixed and never-changing perverse will. God’s judgment, unchangeable in itself, changes everywhere in our affairs; and while God, who governs the world by perpetual reason, remaining stable, gives all things movement [Note: [Col. 0354D] Boethius, *The Consolation of Philosophy* III, meter 9, Migne edition, p. 758:

> O You who govern the world by everlasting reason,  
> Sower of earth and heaven, who command time  
> To proceed from eternity, and, remaining stable, give all things motion. [EDIT.]]

he delights in being invoked, as though by a flattering Davidic prayer: ‘My protector, my God, my mercy’ (Ps. 143:2). Mercy triumphs over judgment (Jas. 2:13), and by some incomprehensible mode of divine reason truth and mercy thus meet one another, peace and justice thus kiss one another (Ps. 84:11), that, without changing, he may be changeable and relenting over evil (Joel 2:13), and may always be praised for justice and never reproached for injustice.

“But why do you command me to renew an unspeakable grief [Note: The words are from Virgil, *Aeneid* II, 3: “You command me to renew an unspeakable grief.”]—to unravel what [Note: The quotation is broken off in the source.] the mind shudders to remember and recoils from in grief? Why do you strike me with wound upon wound? (Job 16:15)

“We Tartarean brothers, the dreadful council [Virgil], men of such majesty, anticipating the death of our monarch by the imperial edict of our ruler, who broke the eternal silences of the silent kingdom and thundered in a terrifying voice, ‘Gather together and hurry to devour him’ (Jer. 12:9), gathered as though for a most necessary council, to determine how we might crush him from the land of the living.

“And nearly all the lords and princes of the shades assembled in one mass, and the phalanxes of the companies of Cocytus, as many as there are kinds and species of sins; [Note: [Col. 0354D] As many phalanxes of Cocytus’ companies as there are kinds and species of sins. Although there is no doubt that all infernal spirits drive everyone they can toward every crime, it is nevertheless also clear from confessions forced out of them by exorcisms that some of them urge particular vices more than others, openly and as though assigned that task in a special capacity. Scripture too has not been silent: it says that seven unclean men, the husbands of Sarah, were killed especially by the unclean demon Asmodeus (Tob. 3:8).] we hastened as though toward rich spoils, spoils due to our kingdoms. When we arrived at the appointed place in time to examine the sinful soul, we produced the tablets of the eternal decree and suspended two scales in balanced judgment. We weighed both everything honorable and pleasing to God that he had done from the toys of infancy to the hour of his final necessity, and everything that he had either publicly conducted without repentance, with royal arrogance and license, as though he were another god of the earth, or that he had

> [lacuna] rejoiced in vain theft,  
> postponed the expiation of her offenses until late death,

we weighed on the balance of the most exact and subtle examination.

“And because the weight of his good deeds, when placed on the scale, was found wanting (Dan. 5:26), his soul was handed over to us by judicial sentence and, as our companion to be dragged into the abyss of our damnation, we claimed it under our right.

“But while we rejoiced, as victors rejoice over captured spoil when they divide the plunder (Isa. 9:3), and were already dragging the condemned soul along the rough road, through the stages of the Tartarean descent, into the lodgings of death, behold, that scorched martyr, that distinguished victor, that man whose glorious and continual victory over us gave him the ominous name Laurence, came forth for the salvation of the earthly Christ who is yours, together with his everlasting Christ, and rushed upon us like a whirlwind to scatter us.

“And wishing to strike the head from the house of the wicked, he cursed not only his scepters but also the head of his warriors. And lest our exultation be like that of the one who devours the poor in secret (Hab. 3:13–14), he shouted in a terrifying voice behind the backs of the triumphant hosts, like the foreigners exulting at the captivity of the typological Samson (Judg. 16:23 ff.): ‘Return, transgressors of justice, to judgment’ (Isa. 46:8).

“What, then, could we powerless beings do? With what effort or audacity could we dare resist one by whom we had so often been defeated and so often expelled from the bodies we had possessed? It seemed intolerable to us that the princes of this air (Eph. 2:2) should not be allowed to use a sentence once justly determined, and that the Tartarean assemblies should be forced to accept a petition of a new law, something that even secular courts do not permit.

“For who, concerning one and the same matter, once examined with precise scrutiny and settled by the judgment of the judges and the common consent of all, is compelled without injury to undergo two trials? Nevertheless, whether we wished it or not, against right and law, retracing the road already traversed, we assembled where the seats of judgment were set (Ps. 121:5). And while we strove with our utmost efforts to assert the most equitable case of our party through every ingenious twist of propositions, through all the enthymemes of rhetoricians, and through every sophistical argument, that martyr of commanding authority—a certain golden vessel, a work embossed with marvelous figures, of extraordinary value and workmanship, adorned with handles—brought forth from the church of Mersburg; and with the ingenuity of all of us provoking wonder and contradiction, he placed it on the balance. And, oh, how dreadful, how enormous, how ill-omened was the weight by which the scale of our portion was forced downward! How great a mass was suddenly snatched from our jaws—the soul of so great a monarch of the Roman state, truly a rich victim of Orcus!

“And lest you think that I, the head of all falsehood, am also lying to your holiness in the rest of my account, have this same weight, cursed by the judgment of the whole Stygian army but blessed by a divine mystery, investigated through your messengers. And when you have found certain signs of my testimony, know that I am bound to you by an oath before the Lord [Note: [Col. 0355D] Not to act the part of an *aretalogus*. This is what the mountebank storytellers are called, those trifling performers who present comic and invented characters to the people in public theaters.], and that I am not acting the part of an *aretalogus*.

“For when the scale of our portion, hanging as though entirely empty, was weighed down by the unjust weight, and the other side was inclined, that ruinous golden mass, shaken loose, fell away; beneath its immense collapse, the highly wrought fastenings of its handles came undone, and, so that they might forever testify to our lawsuits, no human art and no material will ever be able to make them solid again.”

When the author of falsehood had finally been released by this forced confession of the truth, he vanished like smoke. The hermit, the chief priest of the Holy Spirit, rejoicing at the rescue of so great and noble a soul, sang to the Lord in the jubilation of his mind, in wonder at the inconceivable and incomprehensible divine mercy: “For he is good, for his mercy endures forever” (Ps. 135:1 ff.).

Without delay, after sending an embassy to Mersburg, he discovered a gift worthy of royal munificence—a cup, namely, [Col. 0356C] gilded and decorated with the most sought-after gems, [Note: [Col. 0355D] Exceedingly distinguished in workmanship. He uses a comparatively uncommon word for “noble” or “splendid.”] splendid in the most delicate workmanship and most precious, consecrated in the treasury of the victorious martyr Laurence by the devout generosity of the prince mentioned above. He found it irreparably ruined, its handles loosened and diminished; and then, finally, a brief narrative from his fellow initiate revealed the secret to him: a most useful example for all time to come, for the salutary and God-pleasing generosity of the rich, whatever their dignity or condition. [Note: [Col. 0356D] Most useful. This accords with Thiofridus’ style: he uses *utillimum* for *utilissimum*, “most useful,” just as one says *facillimum*, “very easy.”]

For if, [Note: [Col. 0356D] Under the color of gold, clay is given. “Let no one,” he says, “think that he is giving anything great when he gives gold; for gold is clay with its color changed.”] under the color of gold, clay is given, and if the most precious pearl, a soul born from heaven, is freed from the deepest pit of misery and from the mud of filth (Ps. 39:3), who would so wretchedly misuse deceitful and fleeting riches that, by spending them lavishly on the worship and adornment of God and his saints, he would not strive to become himself an ornament and a crown of glory in the hand of the Lord (Isa. 62:3), himself most precious rather than utterly worthless?

## CHAPTER VI. That the poverty of the saints is splendid: after the death of the flesh it merits the riches of heaven and earth, and why they have canopies and pyramids

But oh, how happy are those whose delights are wholly opposed to worldly pleasures—hunger, indeed, vigils, nakedness, tears, and limbs worn away by fasting; battering themselves upon bare earth and making their bodies enemies to ease and wantonness. These things are so recompensed by the reciprocal payment of divine grace that, for the covering and adornment of their little dust, the most precious riches of the whole world are spent; so that the ashes of those whose spirits, exiled in the prison of the flesh under mortal conditions, had been held in the greatest contempt may, after their departure—after Israel’s exodus from Egypt (Ps. 113:1), from the iron furnace (Deut. 4:20)—be served with the utmost devotion.

O what recompense for the world’s voluntary renunciation! O what a reversal of things! O by what and how great an exchange are human things traded for divine, earthly things for heavenly, the most worthless things for the most precious! O what splendid poverty, [Col. 0357B] which after the death of the flesh merits the riches of heaven and earth! O what remarkable nakedness, which, clothed in the robe of immortality, surpasses imperial cloaks! O what a most precious woven covering of thorns—the ancient *xerampeliae* of the servants of God—[Note: [Col. 0357D] The context plainly shows that *xerampeliae* is a kind of clothing, since he compares it with royal purples. The Greek name, derived from “dry vine,” means something like “dry-vine garment.” Suidas sheds light on the word: he calls ξηραμπέλινος χιτών a “dry-vine garment,” whose color is that of a dried vine; it is fitting that such a garment should be of the lowest value. This is confirmed by what immediately follows concerning the fringe of such *xerampeliae*.] with which even the purples of kings cannot be compared; whose thinnest fringe is stored in a gilded and jeweled box, and, honored, effects salvation both in the outward and inward person.

Those who in the flesh had either no garment at all or one of little value, once stripped of the flesh, rest in the Lord wrapped in silk and gold, and lay beneath their feet the purple robes and military cloaks of exalted emperors and commanders.

And how worthily, how fittingly, the kings of kings—truly poor in spirit—after dwelling with the inhabitants of Cedar [Note: [Col. 0357D] Cedar. The word signifies blackness and sadness, which suits this passage.], have golden and silver and most precious stone canopies and royal pyramids, [Note: [Col. 0357D] Canopies and pyramids. Here Thiofridus transfers much from arithmetic and geometry to spiritual interpretation. We have said something about this above.] which, after the likeness of Noah’s ark, grow broader below and narrow in height (Gen. 6:15), because the fiery power raised them beyond humanity—burning with the fire of the Holy Spirit and expanded in the inmost parts of Christ Jesus—through the breadth of God’s commandments, by the narrow and difficult-to-climb way of life (Matt. 7:14), to the height of unending glory.

For in the pyramid’s form the fiery power is signified; in the canopies, which derive their name from cubes, the cubic perfection of the soul is measured. A pyramid, rising from a four-sided base to the heights of its summit, signifies that the spirits and bodies of God’s elect, through the four kinds of virtues, have raised themselves to the simplicity of the indivisible and unbounded Monad and to the summits of heaven’s heavens; and that the ark, broad in carnal things but constricted by a certain narrowness in spiritual things, will be completed according to the measure of the mystical cubit (Gen. 6:16), when God will be all in all (1 Cor. 15:28), and they will have occupied and possessed the highest chambers.

This too mystically accords with the merits of the perfect: in arithmetic, just as the triangle is the first number among plane figures, so among solid figures the pyramid is the beginning of depth. Once its progression begins from triangles, it advances upward from all plane surfaces, and its sides are bounded only by triangles. For the elect of God, founded upon the unbreakable faith and first foundation of the everlasting Trinity and built above it from manifold virtues—civic and purgative—and from minds already purified and cleansed, grow and are consolidated from many-angled forms, according to the theorem of the perfect pyramid extended into the spaces of the higher summit, toward the apex of undivided and immutable unity. The angles themselves of the Church of God, joined and fitted to the angular cornerstone, are joined by equal sides to the unique faith, hope, and charity, and to the Father, Son, and Spirit, the Comforter, on the sides turned toward the northern cold.

In the conical form of the canopy, which is supported by the summit of its columns, it is tropologically suggested that the saints of God have mystically been made into a litter of wood from Lebanon by the true Solomon (Song 3:9), with silver columns (ibid. 10), and, heard in their tribulation, run in the breadth of God’s commandments (Ps. 117:5; 118:32); and that they are wholly smooth and wholly round.

So that nothing external might be able to hinder them by its roughness, they have deserved to gather the circle of holiness for eternity. And indeed all geometrical forms, whether triangular, quadrangular, or circular—which, because of the revolution of a single line, are most suitable to divinity and the most excellent of all, and with which the relics of the saints are marked—bear witness to their sanctity and magnificence and attract the beauty of every faithful soul to the adornments and delights of the virtues.

## CHAPTER VII. What should be thought about those relics of God’s elect that are consumed by beasts and birds or submerged in rivers
But what are we to think about those relics of God’s elect whose tombs are either the gullets of birds and beasts, or the deepest abysses of rivers and the sea, [Col. 0358D] or the narrow channels of sewers? Are they not of the same merit before God as those whose tombs are golden or silver, whose ornamentation taxes and exhausts quarrymen and cement-workers, skilled architects, goldsmiths, embroiderers, and [Note: [Col. 0358D] Plumarii, polymitarii. Exodus sometimes uses these two terms indiscriminately for the craftsman who decorates costly garments with varied and multicolored workmanship. At other times it seems to distinguish them so that the plumarius is the one who paints with a needle, and by that painting, through delicate craftsmanship, represents the colors of various birds; while the polymitarius performs much the same work, but in the very weaving of the garment. See our Cornelius a Lapide on Exodus.] jewel-workers [Col. 0359A] and tapestry-workers?

But we, following Jerome’s [Note: [Col. 0359B] According to Jerome’s statement. This is Jerome’s opinion in Book I Against Jovinianus, toward the middle.] statement concerning the protomartyr and first archdeacon Stephen, and [Note: [Col. 0359C] The toparchy of Timothy. He means the Ephesian Church, of which Timothy was bishop.] concerning Timothy’s province, dare no more place them beneath than above one another; for just as in an army there are commanders, tribunes, centurions, [Note: [Col. 0359C] Ferentarii. For Sallustius they are almost the same as light-armed troops, since they used stones and slings.] skirmishers and light infantry, and common soldiers and companies—and when battle has been joined, the names of rank cease to matter, and only courage is sought—so also in the Lord’s warfare, in which the battle is fought against invisible forces, rank and little displays of glory are not sought. Rather, under the true commander Christ, he is the more glorious who is not the nobler or wealthier, but the stronger and more victorious.

Nothing at all is taken away from the glory of the saints, however or wherever they are reduced to their origin. For if they are honored with earthly ornaments, they are not thereby more honored before God; nor, even if they are cast upon a dungheap, are they more despised. God does not seek material ornaments so much as spiritual ones.

And since He therefore fashioned the structure of the world as a sphere, [Note: [Col. 0359C] So that, with everything that revolves confined within it, nothing enters from outside and nothing withdraws beyond it, and so that it is covered by the heavens, which have no vessel. Thiofridus calls all created things “revolving,” since they are carried along together with the world’s structure itself and the succession of passing ages. He says that these are confined within the structure of the world and thus equally covered by heaven itself. It therefore matters little if another covering is added, nobler for some and baser for others.] so that, with everything that revolves confined within it, nothing enters and nothing departs, and so that it is covered by heaven, which has no urn, are those relics of theirs more highly regarded by Him which are stored where there are broad porticoes, where there are gilded ceilings, where [Note: [Col. 0359C] Houses clothed in the punishments of wretches and the labor of the condemned. It is well known that one form of punishment was to be condemned to the quarries and to the excavation of stone. Entire bands of martyrs were forced by tyrannical emperors to undergo that punishment. The one holy Clement, Roman pontiff, cast into exile by Trajan, found two thousand people in those hardships [Col. 0359D] and, as a good shepherd, joined himself to those innocent sheep.] houses are clothed in the punishments of wretches and the labor of the condemned; where basilicas have been built like palaces, so that the frail little body [Col. 0360A] of a human being may walk more proudly, and, as though anything could be more splendid than the world, may wish to look upon roofs rather than heaven?

They are not, I say, more highly regarded than those which, together with the type of the Lord Jonah (Jonah II, 1), are prey in the greedy jaws of fish, and, in allegorical interpretation, [Note: [Col. 0359D] They destroy the whale that is in the sea. The subject is the devil, whom our abbot asserts is overcome by the devout not only on land but also in the midst of the sea.] destroy the whale that is in the sea, and descend—or rather are cast—into the mire with Jeremiah, sanctified before he was born (Jer. I, 5; XXXVIII, 6)? No aspect of any place either increases or diminishes the merits of holiness, just as no degree of disgrace, however great, deprives a sacred place of holiness.

For the place of the Lord’s resurrection did not thereby become inglorious because, from the time of the emperor Aelius Hadrian until the reign of the emperor Constantine Augustus, [Note: [Col. 0359D] For approximately 180 years. In the eighteenth year of his reign—which was the year 137 of Christ—Emperor Hadrian, says Saint Paulinus in his eleventh letter, thinking that he would destroy the Christian faith by dishonoring the place, consecrated an image of Jupiter at the place of the Passion. If the 180 years mentioned by Thiofridus are added to these years of Christ, the year 317 emerges, around which time that disgrace was removed from places deserving every honor. Paulinus continues in the same passage: “This sacrilege of an earlier age remained almost until our own times, until Constantine, who deserved to be the foremost of Christian rulers not more by his own faith than by that of his mother Helena,” and so forth. See also Severus, Paulinus’s contemporary and almost kindred spirit, Book II of Ecclesiastical History.] for approximately 180 years it had been foul with the filth of Jupiter’s image and sacrificial blood. Nor is the place of the saving cross thereby more despised because a marble Venus was worshiped there; nor [Note: [Col. 0359D] A grove of Adonis overshadowed Bethlehem. I am certain that when Thiofridus wrote this, he had in mind—if not before his eyes—the letter of the holy Paulinus mentioned above. If you wish, compare this passage with the one from which, to make it more accessible, I shall not hesitate to transcribe a portion. I know that the pious and learned reader will be delighted by a most honorable pleasure. Paulinus writes as follows: “In Bethlehem, where the ox had recognized its owner and the ass the manger of its Lord, there the rulers of men, denying the Savior God, honored infamous human loves and deaths. Where the Chaldaeans, having been informed by a new star of the cradle of the eternal King, had worshiped with their riches, there the Romans consecrated barbarous lusts. Where shepherds, the night illuminated, had greeted the newborn Savior with a chorus of the angelic host and heavenly joy, there prostitutes, mingled with eunuchs, mourned the lover of Venus. Where the infancy of the newborn Savior had cried, there an infamous rite howled the lamentations of those who feigned grief for Venus with wanton mourning; and where the Virgin had given birth, adulterers were worshiped.” Thus far the bishop of Nola.] our Bethlehem, house of heavenly bread, the most august place in the whole world, where truth arose from the earth (Ps. LXXXIV, 12), is thereby more abject because a grove of Adonis overshadowed it; and in the cave where Christ the Lord once wailed as a little child, where the army of heaven stood around in place of midwives, [Note: [Col. 0360C] The most shameful Tahtmoz, Venus’s lover, was mourned. The prophet Ezekiel describes many abominations, both elsewhere and especially in chapter VIII, where, among other things, we read at verse 14: “And behold, there women sat mourning for Adonis.” In Hebrew—or rather Chaldean—“mourning for Thammuz.” This form, Tahtmoz, seems to have been produced by an unskilled scribe; nevertheless I have retained it in the text because both copies displayed it. Moreover, according to Saint Jerome, Thammuz among the Chaldaeans and Syrians is Adonis, that impure lover of Venus who was killed by a boar while hunting. See Ovid, Book X of the Metamorphoses; Macrobius, Book III of the Saturnalia; and Lucian, Book On the Syrian Goddess, where he describes that mourning graphically, in his customary manner. Some, moreover, think that the name was given to Adonis from the month of June, which is likewise called Thammuz by those peoples. Much more probably, however, the month was named after that impure lover, just as two Roman months, Quintilis and Sextilis, were called July and August after Roman rulers.] the most shameful Tahtmoz, Venus’s lover, was mourned.

And indeed nothing is more precious than the body of Christ the Lord, nor is any punishment lower than the cross’s gallows; but when that supreme and eternal Majesty did not shrink from the scandal of the cross, and, after the most glorious triumph of death, in the place where the price of the world was hung and the bond of human captivity was loosed, endured for so many years, with immeasurable patience, the disgrace of the Passion—more painful than every dishonor—namely, the foulest worship of idolatry, without moving earth and heaven alike (Hag. II, 22), and without, by a rift in the earth, as with Dathan and Abiram (Num. XVI, 31), plunging its idolatrous enemies into the abyss, it is plainly evident that the saints of God, whose place and dwelling are in peace, in Zion (Ps. LXXV, 3)—those who do not reach that place laid in gold or buried in incense—see the mockery and abasement of their own relics and regard it as of no account where or in what manner they are consumed, since by the irreparable loss of the first transgression this has been granted and assigned to the bellies of worms.

And it is undoubtedly true that human nature far surpasses angelic nature in dignity, and that human art and every degree of knowledge, however excellent in the most excellent things, cannot even be compared with angelic subtlety and wisdom. Yet the buildings constructed on earth by angelic hands through divine dispensation, as religiously believed, are conspicuous neither for worldly ornaments, nor architecture, nor mechanical art; rather, to human sight they are far inferior to human constructions, while they are in every respect more excellent than basilicas built up by the operation of divine power and adorned with gold and silver.

For the church of the archangel Michael on Mount Gargano is of a far humbler form, [Note: [Col. 0361D] The church of Michael the archangel on Mount Gargano. Discovered in the year of Christ 493. Sigebert and Baronius. Hence the feast of the Apparition is still celebrated throughout God’s Church on 8 May.] [Col. 0361C] and, amid the wave-tossed waters of the sea, the church of the distinguished Pope and martyr Clement, [Note: [Col. 0361D] The church of Pope and martyr Clement. See Baronius under the year of Christ 102.] constructed by an angelic mystery through an unheard-of miracle, [Note: [Col. 0361D] From the stone mass suspended from his neck. I do not know where our Thiofridus obtained this account. That it concerned an anchor is clear from the Acts.] was made from the stone mass suspended from his neck—whereas the typical house constructed by Solomon, wisest of men, was made of gold and silver, precious stones, cedar wood, and thyine wood.

Yet although the cloud of the shadowy Law filled that house as a type (II Chron. V, 13), how much more brilliant than the legal shadow are the truth and grace of evangelical light; and therefore how much richer, more frequent, and more evident in miracles is the magnificence of eternal divinity and angelic visitation!

What mind, then, can penetrate so great an abyss of divine dispensation? Who can weigh the manner in which He dispenses and orders all things with such perfect arrangement? “Eternal Wisdom is hidden from the eyes of all the living” (Job XXVIII, 21); “he made darkness his hiding place” (Ps. XVII, 12). And, according to the mystical conclusion of the bride’s epithalamium, “the Bridegroom is like a gazelle and a fawn of the deer” (Song II, 9); He flees above the heights of the clouds and frustrates the gaze of those who look upon Him.

Just as, by the incomprehensible establishment of His eternal decree, He humbles one and exalts another (Ps. LXXIV, 8), and gives these storehouses full, overflowing from one into another (Ps. CXLIII, 13), while denying others even the necessities of life, so by the equally inscrutable counsel of His providence He also dispenses the relics of the saints: some He stores amid all the finest material things, with the greatest glory; others He leaves to common burial and deprives of every human service and care. Yet in the court of the heavenly kingdom their spirits may hold equal or even higher precedence in excellence of dignity and inward intimacy.

Among the unburied—those whom river, or sun and storms, and the longer passage of days have dissolved and mingled with the earth, whose flesh has passed into fish, beasts, and birds—He has among them his most intimate friends, who are as much more visible and honored throughout heaven as they were despised on earth. The loss of burial He repays with an inconceivable and ineffable compensation of glory; and whatever honor is temporally lacking to dead flesh benefits the holy soul eternally, beyond all comparison in measure and manner—the soul that lives with the Holy of Holies and reigns more gloriously.

Therefore the sacred remains of the saints—both those without a name or the honor of due veneration and those whose adornment is served by all the most precious riches of the world—are to be honored and glorified with the utmost reverence; and, as the Lord’s vessels in which the gifts of sevenfold grace have been stored, they are to be embraced and admired, and, if permitted, touched and kissed with eyes and mouth.

Therefore, “let them kiss us with the kiss of his mouth” (Song I, 1), with the kiss of his inward love: all God’s elect, formed from dust, but raised above the common condition of dust by the glory and honor of holiness. Their sacred relics and the names written in the book of life and of the Lamb (Rev. XIII, 8) are not to be approached with presumptuous recklessness, but as Mary, once an impious sinner and now a devout intercessor for sinners, stood behind the Lord and cherished his feet with kisses, washed them with tears, and wiped them with her hair (Luke VII, 37–38). So let us kiss them and water them with a flowing fountain of tears; and [Note: [Col. 0361D] Let us wipe them with hair in the historical and allegorical sense. “In either way,” he says, “let hair be understood, whether, I say, in the literal and historical sense or the mystical sense, and let us use it to wipe the sacred relics.” Indeed, we seem to wipe with hair properly so called when our head, bowed to the ground in profound humility, rather than our foot—as the Wise Man teaches that honor should be shown to persons of understanding (Eccl. VI, 36)—wears away the steps of their doors. Nor is too much demanded of us by this prescription, since even kings and queens worship the Church with their faces lowered to the earth and lick the dust of her feet (Isa. XLIX, 23). What members of the Church, moreover, are nobler than those whose precious dust is the subject of our author here? In the allegorical sense, however, if we trust Saint Gregory (Book V of the Moralia, chapter 23) and other Fathers, hair signifies temporal goods—gold, silver, and gems—which Thiofridus teaches should be devoted to the adornment and honor of the holy relics.] [Col. 0363A] with hair, in the historical and allegorical sense, let us wipe them with the whole intention and application of our minds [Note: [Col. 0363C] Because they are clothed in the fleece of the spotless Lamb. He wishes the saints to be washed by us with a flowing fountain of tears in their relics, just as sheep and lambs are accustomed to be washed at particular times of the year.]: because, clothed in the fleece of the spotless Lamb, Christ, they are without blemish before the throne of God and the Lamb (Rev. XIV, 5).

They are “partakers of the divine nature” (II Pet. I, 4), and “light in the Lord” (Eph. V, 8); they walk along the road “where light is dispersed” (Job XXXVIII, 24). And while they are changed from temporal glory into eternal glory, as by the Spirit of the Lord (II Cor. III, 18), they illuminate their beloved ashes—humanity—with the rays of their inward splendor, illuminating the exterior human being whom, according to the most luminous theologian Gregory, they formerly bore outwardly as an aid to their inward intention and good works [Note: [Col. 0363C] Lamps among the thoughts of the wealthy. Saint Gregory discusses these at length in Book X of the Moralia, chapters 28 and following.].

Lamps, despised in the estimation of the rich who judge outward things carnally, yet prepared for the appointed time, bring forth their radiance and show how brightly they shine, when they pour into their dissolved ashes and corruption, from above, the light of glory which, imprisoned in the prison of the flesh, they did not possess. Day after day they contemplate God, who dwells in inaccessible light, with the most penetrating light of inward contemplation; and the Lamb who is in the midst of the throne illumines them with the full splendor of his majesty.

They are most luminous lamps, kindled by the true light that enlightens every human being; and according to the diversity of their merits, doctrine, and wisdom, they shine “like the brightness of the firmament” and “like stars for everlasting eternities,” through the incomparable and immeasurable splendor of the Sun of righteousness. He alone, in a mystical sense, can make the shining Pleiades [Note: [Col. 0363C] The Pleiades. He discusses these and Arcturus again above in this book, chapter 5.]—all the saints, [Col. 0363C] divided by time but not by proclamation, and endowed with different virtues—unite and join together in the radiance of one and the same intention; and He can separate, transform, and transfer the circle of Arcturus, the labors of the holy Church, into rest.

On the day of Midian—which is interpreted as “from judgment”—for the overthrow of his yoke, the burden upon his shoulders, and the scepter of his exactor, from the judgment of divine equity, under the true and unconquered leader Gideon, most valiant of men, who is strong and powerful in battle, mystically embracing all things through his divinity and assuming humanity within the womb of a perpetual virgin, [Note: [Col. 0363C] It is interpreted “going around in the womb.” The discussion concerns the name Gideon. Rupert of Tuitia gives the same derivation in Book I, chapter 2, on Numbers, and Book I, chapter 11, on Judges. One should not suppose that Thiofridus borrowed it from Rupert; although they were contemporaries, Rupert was somewhat younger. Nor do I assert that Thiofridus took it from him. Rather, both received it from Saint Gregory the Great, in whom it is found in Book XXX of the Moralia, chapter 32. It is entirely fitting that such men should retain their full authority and reverence, which we lesser persons owe them. But I confess that I cannot derive that etymology from the Hebrew root. I acknowledge, with all Hebraists, that *gadagh* means “to crush” or “to break,” from which Gideon would be “the crusher” or “the breaker.” But I nowhere find either “circuit” or “womb.” I await anyone who can explain it, and to whom I shall gladly owe this favor.] is interpreted as “going around in the womb.”

Marked with the *tau* (Ezek. IX, 4), the mystical sign of the cross, and with the mark of that same letter, registered under the number designated by the element [Note: [Col. 0363D] The number of the letter *tau* is three hundred. For the Hebrews express that number with the little letter that is last in their alphabet. Sacred history is found in the events of Judges. Several holy Fathers describe the most distinguished allegory. See, if you wish, Saint Augustine, Sermon 108 on the Seasons; Gregory, Book XXX of the Moralia, chapter 32; and Rupert, Book I, chapter 11 on Judges. Why he calls that number “designated” is unclear. It seems to me that, after saying that Gideon’s soldiers had been marked with *tau*, the mystical sign of the cross, he calls the character itself the “title,” by which they were titled or marked.] with which the perfect knowledge of the undivided Trinity is signified [Note: [Col. 0364D] By which the perfect knowledge of the undivided Trinity is signified. That the number one hundred signifies perfection is too well known to require explanation. Tripled, it gives honor to the Holy Trinity.], drawing streams of heavenly doctrine with knees upright (Judg. VII, 6), so that there might be no slackness of works among them, they offered their souls to danger in the battle against Midian, with a mode of combat unheard-of and unprecedented through the ages.

The stars, remaining in their order and course, fought against Midian (Judg. V, 20), and [Note: [Col. 0364D] The skins of the land of Midian were troubled by fear of judgment. A little earlier he said that Midian signifies “from judgment.” Here, playing pleasantly upon that etymology, he implies that the very name of the Midianites contains an omen of fear and trembling.] through fear of judgment and eternal punishments the skins of the land of Midian were troubled (Hab. III, 7). “The Lord fought among the strong” (Judg. V, 13), and “chose new wars” (ibid., 8).

Is it not new and altogether unusual to come into battle with trumpets, lamps, and jars (Judg. VII, 16)? The princes of Israel, so that the people of the Lord might obtain dominion, sounded the trumpets of evangelical preaching under their leader. They broke the jars when they exposed their bodies to be shattered by the swords and arrows of every adversity; and they shone with lamps when, after the dissolution of their bodies, they flashed forth in miracles.

“In a foreign land they sang the hymn from the songs of Zion” (Ps. CXXXVI, 3–4), with “trumpets of beaten metal” (Ps. XCVII, 6), battered by various sufferings, struck and afflicted by the blows of the hardest hammers, continuous, unceasing, and never sparing. I mean, worn down by the dread blows of that hammer, of which the truthful prophet testifies: “The hammer of the whole earth has been broken.” The Lord, the Ruler, according to the prophecy of Isaiah, noble and urbane in eloquence [Note: [Col. 0364D] The noble and urbane elegance of Isaiah. Thiofridus took this from Saint Jerome. In his Preface to Isaiah that doctor says: “It should be known of Isaiah that he is eloquent in his speech, a noble man, indeed, and of urbane eloquence, with nothing rustic mixed into his language.” I would suppose that in Thiofridus *eloquentiae* should be restored in place of *elegantiae*.], “broke the little flask in terror” [Col. 0365A] while, just as he glorified his shattered body through the glory of the resurrection, in the terror of the whole human race, so he caused the bodies of God’s elect, broken apart in the separation and dissolution of flesh and soul, to become a source of terror and wonder to all through the efficacy and glorification of miracles.

And “glory to God in the highest,” according to the saying of Job, who, in the Lord God grieving together with our sufferings, prefigured all those who are watered by the rains of the mountains and nourished by the streams of the teaching of the holy Fathers, yet do not possess the veil of perfect action. They embrace stones when, trusting in no virtue of their own works, they run to the intercession of the saints; and, weeping earnestly before their sacred bodies, with the utmost devotion and contrition of heart, they kiss the pavements, reliquaries, and mausoleums. They pray more urgently and abundantly that they may obtain pardon through the saints’ devout intercessions, nor are they frustrated in the hope and fulfillment of their prayer and intention.

The second book ends.

Here begin the chapter headings of the third book.

[Col. 0365]

I. On the grace and power of the names of the saints. II. On shadows. III. On rods and staffs. IV. On garments of every texture and kind. V. On liquids of water, wine, and oil, and on the tomb of Nicholas. VI. On the collective tomb (*polyandrium*) of John the fellow-initiate (*symmystes*). VII. On vessels and little beds.

The chapter headings of the third book end.

The third book begins.

[Col. 0365]

CHAPTER ONE. On the grace and power of the names of the saints.

[Col. 0365B]

But these things, spoken in part of the ways of the Lord (Job 26:14), may be demonstrated in all the external appendages of the most glorious bodies of the saints—more gloriously, and by miracles far surpassing them: first, in the most sacred names, which are intransitive in their transitive usage;

> [Note: [Col. 0365C–0366D] Intransitive in transitive names. The names pass away together with the sound itself, since they are indeed sounds. Yet they do not pass away with respect to memory, which is in blessing and remains. For their name lives from generation to generation (Sirach 44:14). It also remains in their effects, as he himself soon explains.]

then in the life-giving shadows of their bodies; in rods, staffs, haircloth garments, and clothing of every texture; in vessels and utensils; in various liquids of water, wine, and oil, touched and consecrated by their hands; and finally in all the kinds of instruments of torture devised and invented for their punishments—not so much by human as by demonic cruelty: chains, stocks, clubs, racks, crosses, and blows from stones. With these they were tested in the fiery furnace like gold (Wisdom 3:6); and after they had been released from this body of death (Romans 7:24), they flew forth freed from their bonds, as though from the torments of the Tartarean prison, to be inserted and woven into the immeasurable ornaments of the heavenly court.

For their names live forever, through the Word who was in the beginning, who was God with God (John 1:1), and who proclaims with the evangelical trumpet: “Heaven and earth will pass away, but my words will not pass away” (Luke 21:33). Through the Word, I say, the Wisdom of the eternal Father, whose speech—although it passes by its own nature without passing away, expressing immutable and abiding judgments—renders names intransitive in their very natural transitivity through participation in and communion with the immutable and intransitive nature, though they are not permanent by remaining.

They do not remain through the irrevocable flight of articulated speech; rather, they remain and flourish through the immutable and eternally abiding name of the Lord, which comes from afar (Isaiah 30:27), and by which he called his servants by another name (Isaiah 65:15), for the established salvation and well-being of all believers. By the decree of immutable eternal providence, while they pass through the mouths of those who invoke them in faith, they advance into the effect of healing and deliverance, without any mutability or transition in themselves; and, in passing, they do not pass away.

Through the immutable and abiding riches of God’s manifold grace, through the efficacy of assured healing and salvation, they do not pass away but rather remain. They exhibit a nature that is greatly different in the mutability of sound and the immutability of operation. The names named by the mouth of the Lord—new, fixed, and without transition before God, who promised his bride, the Church: “You shall be called by a new name, which the mouth of the Lord has named” (Isaiah 62:2)—are fixed and enduring without change unto eternity, and are held fast; for, remaining without mutability, the judgments of all healings and graces are decreed and obtained through them.

What could the names of those who reign with the King of kings not accomplish, when, by the simple words of God, the door of the heavenly kingdom is closed and opened even for those still journeying abroad [Col. 0367A] (John 20:22), when the sinful soul is bound and the soul desiring pardon is absolved?

> [Note: [Col. 0367C] Through the words of those who are absent … arranged on slips of paper, and so forth. Apart from the older miracles mentioned by Thiofridus, great miracles performed through fragments of letters written by holy men provide more recent confirmation of the truth of this claim, in the writings of our blessed Ignatius and Xavier, whose lives are in circulation.]
