Through the words of those absent—not uttered aloud, but arranged in written slips—as truthful writings testify, the afflictions of various illnesses are healed. And just as though the elements, the first seeds of things, understood letters, so, at the sacred writings of these men sent to them, rivers threatening a cataclysm, although angry as if confronting an impassable barrier, nevertheless obedient to their powerful words, leap back and settle again into their channels.

> [Note: [Col. 0367C–D] Rivers threatening a cataclysm. Water has also honored the saints and their prayers or relics in other ways. An example is Mary of Egypt, who walked upon water as upon solid ground, as Christ, Lord of the water, had once done, and Peter at his command; and Bessarion, who did the same, and by whose prayer the bitterness of the sea was changed into sweetness; and that Gregory Thaumaturgus who, after driving a stake into the shore, forbade the river Lycus, raging and threatening the inhabitants, to advance any farther. The example given by our author is more similar in the case of the cataclysm. See the earlier examples in the *Lives of the Fathers*, restored by our Rosweyde; the last in the *Life* published by Surius under 17 November.]

Since that which passes through their mouths is, in a certain sense, intransitive, much more so is the name that encloses and circumscribes their substances in its meaning. The voice that proceeds from their arteries drives out the venom of the ancient serpent; it brings blessing and cursing. And just as their words, once uttered, fly forth irrevocably and are never changed, so their names also extend without end. They are plainly written by the finger of God in the book of life and of the Lamb (Revelation 13:8); and just as everyone who calls upon the name of the Lord will be saved (Acts 2:21), so, in whatever distress of body and soul, anyone who is found troubled and anxious, if he recalls the name of God and turns over within himself that half-line of David’s song, “And honorable is their name before him” (Psalm 71:14), and honors and names it worthily with the innermost devotion of his heart, emerges safe and unharmed from his distress and from the anxieties of every impending loss, adversity, and danger.

The names of God’s elect, written in eternity, and called etymologically from *notamen* or *notio*—“marking” or “recognition”—make known to us, through their invocation and through the execution of saving aid by divine propitiation, the glory before the divine majesty and the efficacy of virtues that are unknown to us in the corruption of this mortality.

> [Note: [Col. 0367C–0368C] Names are said etymologically to derive from *notamen* or *notio*. He is playing on the word. “There is nothing surprising,” he says, “if the names of the saints make a virtue otherwise unknown become known, since the word *nomen* itself is said to derive from *notamen* or *notatio*.”]

For at the saving invocation of the saints’ names there are present the merits and presence of the most precious spirits. And just as the highest and uncircumscribed Spirit promises through the prophet—“You will call, and the Lord will answer; you will cry out, and he will say: Here I am” (Isaiah 58:9)—so the saints of God, when their names are invoked and they are called upon with perfect faith, cry out in response through the bestowal of sudden and inspired salvation: “Behold, we are helpers in times of need; in tribulation we are present” (Psalm 9:10).

And just as the mystery of the Lord’s body and blood, which is prepared daily through the ministry of priests under the appearance of bread and wine, truly and without any doubt for the faithful, represents that body of the Lord Christ which was crucified, pierced by the soldier’s lance, and put to death, and that blood which flowed with water from the pierced body of the Crucified One as the price of human redemption;

> [Note: [Col. 0368D] It represents that body of Christ. Beware the Calvinist impiety, from which Thiofridus is very far, as his words and manner of speaking plainly show. The word *repraesentat* does not merely denote an image or figure; in the sense frequently used by Latin writers of good standing, *repraesentare* means to exhibit or set forth a thing as actually present, as in Columella: “The steward will readily accomplish these things if he has always presented himself.”]

so the invocation of the sanctified names, without any ambiguity, discloses to those who merit it the whole reality and power of inward virtue, and the presence of the spirits reigning with the uncircumscribed Spirit. For when their names are pronounced in the devotion of faith, they themselves, before God and in that assembly of the heavenly senate, plead the causes of those who invoke them, so that through their merits mercy may triumph over judgment (James 2:13). Since they always stand before the divine countenance and never depart from it, in an inconceivable and ineffable manner of divine dispensation they display their presence in every distress and pressure to those who hope in them and cry out to them, through the efficacy of the much-desired and supremely necessary *boēmata* (βοημάτων, “cries for help”) in the greatest difficulty of affairs.

And just as, through the sign of the life-giving cross impressed upon the forehead of every believer, every assault of invisible enemies is driven away, and priestly and royal chrism, the oil of consecration, the mystery of baptism, and finally whatever in the Church must be consecrated for the benefit and salvation of believers are sanctified;

> [Note: [Col. 0368D] Priestly and royal chrism. It is well known that in God’s Church, from the earliest times, not only priests but also kings were accustomed to be anointed. Elizabeth, who claimed both dignities for herself in England, accepted anointing when the time required it. But after returning from the altar to her women’s quarters, she mocked it. How piously she did so is now well known.]

> [Note: [Col. 0368D] The oil of consecration. With this catechumens or the dying are anointed for the struggle against demons.]

so also through the invocation of the saints’ names. First the names are pronounced; then, with the cooperation of the holy spirits whose names they signify, divine and ecclesiastical ministries are carried out through the saving mystery of the cross.

And I do not know by what ineffable manner of divine providence the most precious cross and the names of the saints are so confederated—unless it is because they took up their cross and followed the Crucified One (Matthew 16:24), glorying in the Lord with Paul, that most eminent vessel of election: “The world is crucified to me, and I to the world” (Galatians 6:14).

While the Lord’s cross is named, the Lord works salvation in the midst of his earth (Psalm 73:12); likewise, while the intransitive names of the saints are named, every consecration of the Christian religion is confirmed, danger threatening from every side is avoided, the hostile phalanx is defeated, the harshness of the weather is moderated, the stormy sea is calmed, and health is restored to living and dead bodies.

Indeed, if I wished to prove and enumerate these claims by examples—whose names, invoked in dangers of rivers, dangers from robbers (2 Corinthians 11:26), dangers in prison, captivity, chains, and despair of safety and life, have suddenly made the presence of the saints’ spirits manifest through their answering—neither a hundred tongues, nor a hundred mouths, nor an iron voice would suffice me.

Yet let this be said confidently, without detracting from the grace of all the saints: their names are much more glorious than their bodies. For when the bodies fail through natural dissolution, the names seem to advance through the continual invocation of the faithful. When the bodies are most closely hidden in the narrow space of a single small tomb, the names are celebrated throughout the whole world, on land and sea, in the hearts and mouths of all.

For when countless thousands of people invoke and glorify the names of the saints with the greatest devotion, they do not know in what part of the world their most sacred relics are hidden. And when long distances across the earth prevent refuge in the relics themselves, through the invocation of these names every soul that, in faith without hesitation, needs and deserves whatever aid, obtains it in every distress.

They are one with the incarnate Word and with the infinite name of the Lord; therefore, just as that name is wholly everywhere and is supremely beneficial, so they are wholly present and abundantly beneficial whenever and wherever necessity requires, according to the faith of those who deserve their aid.

The relics cannot be carried everywhere, however nobly and worthily; but the names of the saints spontaneously present themselves everywhere to the contrite and afflicted soul in every necessity. The relics pass from place to place only when divided into fragments; the names enter the hearts and mouths of all, not piece by piece but whole. They fill the entire hearing and the entire mind. They do not deem the external eye worthy of admitting them for sight, but the interior eye. They are everywhere present to faith, while the bodies are far away.

There is absolutely nothing that faith cannot obtain through them; nothing that divine power cannot accomplish through them. While the precious bodies rest in peace, the souls of the saints, disturbed and summoned from the bosom of their eternal rest, are called forth through their names invoked with contrite hearts.

> [Note: [Col. 0369D] To a certain hierarch keeping vigil all night in prayer. This was Saint Servatius, bishop of Tongeren, who, while keeping vigil at Rome at the tomb of the apostles, received from the prince of the apostles himself the response here reported by Thiofridus. See Hariger, abbot of Lobbes, in the *Life of Saint Servatius*, in Chapeaville, vol. I, and Gregory of Tours, *History of the Franks*, book II, ch. 5.]

Accordingly, a certain hierarch of outstanding holiness, keeping an all-night vigil in prayer with watchful concern for the liberation of the Lord’s flock entrusted to him, finally received this answer in a friendly apostolic voice:

> “Why do you trouble us, most holy man? The elect of God certainly rest while their bodies are dissolved; they seem to be disturbed when they are invoked opportunely and importunately for help through their names. I say that they are disturbed—not because they suffer any loss of their rest, but because, just as the holy angels, although they always stand before God, are nevertheless said to be sent forth, so they, while enjoying eternal rest and contemplation of the divine countenance, are drawn forth by the invocation of their names to provide outward assistance.

> “And not only when they reign and rejoice in the heavenly palace, but also while they journey away from the Lord in this mortality (2 Corinthians 5:6), their holy names are more immediately present than their bodies in every temptation and danger.

> “The Holy One of holies, God, by his eternal providence, before the world was founded and adorned, immutably preordained and decreed that, in proportion as the relics of the elect and predestined could accomplish greater miracles through their spirits, their names should accomplish more glorious deeds, remain while not remaining, and be present everywhere while absent.”

> [Note: [Col. 0369D–0370D] The angels, although they always stand before God, are nevertheless said to be sent forth. They truly are sent forth, and Thiofridus does not deny this; he denies only that they are sent in such a way that they do not remain present. This standing before God is what the Lord of the angels means when he says that they always behold the face of the Father (Matthew 18:10).]

## CHAPTER II  
### On Shadows

Since the excellence of divine power gathers and accompanies everywhere such glory in names that pass without transition, it also pours that glory, in an abundant transfusion of mercy, into the shadows of bodies, and strikes the hearts of mortals with immense astonishment.

In former times the sick were placed in the streets so that, when the chief of the apostles came, or even any companion of his holiness, at least his shadow might overshadow one of them and they might be freed from their illnesses (Acts 5:15), so that God might be proclaimed more gloriously and wonderfully in his saints (Psalm 67:36).

And what is so glorious, what so miraculous, as that a shadow—which is not substantially part of the body—should drive every hostile sickness from the body? > [Note: [Col. 0370D–0371C] On the shadowy mountain. In that celebrated canticle (Habakkuk 3:3) it is written: “God will come from the South, and the Holy One from Mount Paran.” The Septuagint Greeks rendered it: *Ho hagios ex orous kataskious daseos* (Ὁ ἅγιος ἐξ ὄρους κατασκίους δασέος), that is, “The Holy One from a shadowy, dense mountain.” So too Saint Gregory, *Morals*, book XXXIII, ch. 1. This is the meaning of *Pharan*, whether derived from the root *Phara* or from *Pharah*, both of which mean “to bear fruit” or “to grow”; hence dense trees or thickets, and *to skieron* (τὸ σκιερόν), “the shady place.” Thiofridus, with Euthymius and Theophylact, interprets this shadowy mountain as the Virgin Mother.]

From the shadowy mountain came the mountain of strength (Deuteronomy 32:2; Habakkuk 3:3), whose mother the Holy Spirit overshadowed by his power (Luke 1:35). Under the shadow of his protection every holy soul rests, and to him the mother and bride, the Church, sings in the Song of Songs:

> “Under his shadow, whom I desired, I sat” (Song of Songs 2:3).

> [Note: [Col. 0371D] “Under his shadow, whom I desired, I sat.” He applies this allegorically to the Blessed Virgin. For in Latin the relative is masculine, as are the Greek and Hebrew pronouns and suffixes. I have said something briefly about this accommodated sense in the notes to the preface.]

> [Note: [Col. 0371C–D] The mountain of strength. He calls the Lord Christ by this name, as many Fathers call Christ a mountain. Certainly it cannot be denied that Christ is the stone cut from the mountain without hands, which became a great mountain and filled the whole earth (Daniel 2:34–35). Thiofridus not improperly calls him the mountain of strength: for how could strength be lacking in the one who is a stony mountain, indeed a mountain that is itself stone?]

After the guilt of the first transgression, Adam, the transgressor, alas, fled beneath the shadow of the fig tree; but there he was not so much protected as exposed, and he transferred all his posterity into the shadow of death.

> [Note: [Col. 0371D] “Beneath the shadow of the fig tree.” For they sewed fig leaves together and made themselves loincloths (Genesis 3:7).]

> [Note: [Col. 0371D] “He transferred them into the shadow of death.” He alludes to: “To enlighten those who sit in darkness and in the shadow of death” (Luke 1:79).]

But the propitiator and the second Adam of the mystical tabernacle of propitiation, who restored the transgressor Adam, shed the splendor of eternal light upon those dwelling in the region of the shadow of death (Isaiah 9:2; Matthew 4:16), so that the brightness of eternal truth might exclude the shadow, and that complete healing might accompany—not merely the bodies but also the shadows of bodies destined to be conformed to his glorified body (Philippians 3:21)—through the merits of glorified spirits.

And since, according to a certain teacher of practical philosophy, the accidental definition of a shadow is “air deprived of light,” so, by contrast, the shadows of bodies illumined by the radiance of the true sun, through their celibate and most luminous souls, would strip the aerial powers of all their dominion and illumine and remove the darkness of human misery.

> [Note: [Col. 0371D] “Through their celibate souls.” He elegantly calls them celibate because they are no longer joined or, as it were, wedded to the body. Above he likewise spoke of the separation of body and soul.]

The bridegroom dwells in shadow and darkness; there, when the shadows bend, he calls the bride to himself (Song of Songs 4:6). Therefore he rightly glorifies the shadow of the sons of his bride and grants to the imagined shadow a measure of healing grace equal to—indeed more glorious than—that granted to the touch of his holy hand.

And just as Jonah, the type of the Lord, rejoiced and delighted in the shade of the ivy (Jonah 4:6), which typologically signifies Judea, so the soul that, according to Jeremiah, is sorrowful because of its greatness and proceeds in anxiety and abasement (Baruch 2:18) is gladdened when protected by the defensive shadow of a sanctified body, and is healed by its remedy.

> [Note: [Col. 0372C] The ivy, which typologically signifies Judea. Thus Saint Augustine, *Epistle* 49, question 6.]

For shelter from the sun, some material object is placed in the way of its rays, so that its heat and brightness may be diverted and moderated for those sweating or suffering from sore eyes. In a dissimilar but analogous way, if material of spiritual and certain faith is interposed, then, through grace flowing from the highest *noy* (Νοῦ, “of mind”) into the holy soul, from the psyche into the body, and from the bodies into the shadow, the whole disorder of sickness is not merely moderated but entirely driven away and excluded.

> [Note: [Col. 0372C–D] “From the highest Nous.” An unskilled hand seems to have corrupted something here, which I do not venture to correct without the help of a better manuscript. The sense is that grace, by which illnesses are excluded, flows from the highest Mind—which is God—into the soul, from the soul into the body, and finally from the body into the shadow. If permitted, I would read *de summo Νῷ* (“from the highest Mind”). The expression is harsh.]

A shadow represents light and truth, while the act of overshadowing restores health through the holiness of a sanctified body.

## CHAPTER III  
### On Rods and Staffs

Since, through the shadows of bodies, the merits of the saints’ spirits accomplish all that the will of the supreme and uncircumscribed Spirit, who presides over all things, wills, it is evident that divine power accomplishes no lesser things—but rather greater ones—through objects consecrated by their use and the touch of their hands.

The almond rods, symbolically stripped of their bark before the Law and placed in the channels (Genesis 30:37–38), produced various kinds of offspring for the flocks. Although natural philosophers attribute this to natural causes, and ecclesiastical philosophers to the mystical meanings of sacred Scripture, we nevertheless believe that the event occurred chiefly because the Creator and Lord of all nature, moved by sympathy with the many and great labors of his patriarch, preordained that it should happen in this way.

For God, who, according to Zechariah’s prophecy, took two rods and called one “Beauty” (Zechariah 11:7)—plainly the beauty of the whole human race under Noah, when the world had been restored—and named the other “Cord,” namely the Israelite people, his special inheritance, himself both Creator and Shepherd, whose own sheep recognize his voice (John 10:14), fed the flock with an invincible dominion by an iron rod (Psalm 2:9). For the honor of his saints and the salvation of the faithful, he infused the power of his royal rod and his rod of guidance (Psalm 44:7) into sanctified rods.

> [Note: [Col. 0372D] “He took two rods for himself.” Saint Jerome explains these rods in his comments on Isaiah 54 and Zechariah 11.]

> [Note: [Col. 0372D] “A special cord of his inheritance.” He says this according to Scriptural usage, in which inheritance or possession is called a cord or rope. The reason for the expression derives from the Jewish custom of measuring fields with ropes whenever they were divided. Hence: “The cords have fallen for me in pleasant places” (Psalm 16:6), followed immediately by: “Indeed, my inheritance is pleasant to me.” Elsewhere the cord itself is called a cord of distribution. More relevant to this passage, these measurements and divisions were also made with poles, staffs, or rods. “You redeemed the rod of your inheritance,” says the same prophet (Psalm 74:2).]

It is known to nearly all learned readers of both Testaments how, in Egypt, the rod was changed into a serpent (Exodus 7:10); how it changed the river Nile into blood (Exodus 7:20); how, at Israel’s departure from Egypt, it divided the Red Sea (Exodus 14:21), a type of holy baptism; how, in the wilderness, it drew from the symbolic rock a stream of sweet-flowing water (Numbers 20:11) and restrained the murmuring of the thirsty people.

Nor is it unknown to learned minds that the glory of such a rod foreshadowed the proclamation of the Lord’s Passion. Thus Jesus Christ, the rock—for “the rock was Christ” (1 Corinthians 10:4)—struck twice, first by Jewish acclamation and then by military cruelty, brought forth from his side (John 19:34) the abundant and life-giving mystery of the whole Church, the ineffable adornment and dowry of that same bride.

And when David, the instrument of the Holy Spirit, sings, “Your rod and your staff, they themselves have comforted me” (Psalm 23:4), the rod of God—that is, God’s discipline—and the staff of God—that is, God’s support in every tribulation of body and spirit—have themselves comforted all God’s elect.

The rod and staff are so joined together that neither can the rod’s correction be effective without the staff’s support, nor can the staff’s support in every respect be beneficial without the rod’s correction. Therefore, with equal and fittingly excellent praise, the operation of divine power is glorified as having been infused into sanctified rods and likewise into the supports of staffs.

The rod under the Law drowned the pursuing enemies in the sea and delivered them to death (Exodus 14:27–28), and it carried the people, tested and instructed through forty years in the wilderness, across the pathless way of the sea.

At the beginning of grace, the staff of the chief of the apostolic order, buried for forty days, restored him to his former life and made him a future steward of the house of God for an equal number of years.

> [Note: [Col. 0373C] The staff of the chief of the apostolic order. Let us add this testimony, among so many others, in passing, in support of Saint Peter’s primacy. It comes from a man both highly learned and notably pious who flourished about 550 years ago.]

> [Note: [Col. 0373C–D] “Buried for forty days.” This was Saint Maternus, sent to Trier by the blessed apostle Peter with Saints Eucharius and Valerius. On the journey, he was suddenly taken from human affairs by a severe fever, as Abbot Hariger of Lobbes relates. See *On Maternus*, chapter 6. He adds that the companions returned to Saint Peter and, having received his staff, went on the fortieth day to the body of the dead Maternus; there, just as his shadow had healed every kind of disease, his staff recalled blessed Maternus from death.]

> [Note: [Col. 0373D–0374C] “For an equal number of years, to be the steward of the house of God.” For Saint Maternus was bishop for forty years. Harigerus states explicitly, in chapter 13: “Just as he had previously lain in the grave for forty days, so afterward he remained for the same number of years in priestly ministry.” In this whole remarkable story one may wonder at Baronius’s profound silence. I suppose he had not seen Harigerus, nor Aegidius of the Golden Valley, nor the Latin and French chronicles of the people of Liège, which Chapeaville read and cites and which agree with Harigerus. Yet Otto of Freising was readily available (*Chronicle* 3.15), a witness to the same truth in every respect, except that he gives thirty-three days instead of forty. I shall not omit to record the testimony of public report and of a tradition still prevailing in the midst of heresy. The learned B. Rhenanus, though corrupted by erroneous opinions, says of Saint Maternus’s death and restoration in *History of German Affairs*: “Nor do I think the report of this matter empty. At the village of Ehl, three miles from Sélestat”—Sélestat is a distinguished town in Alsace and Rhenanus’s birthplace—“a tomb is still shown in which he lay dead for some time; but shortly afterward he was restored to life, so that he might continue to instruct the people of Trier and Cologne.” He adds that, although he may doubt the chronology, he is sufficiently certain of the event itself. Before me, our Aegidius Bucherius cited this passage from Rhenanus in his *Historical Disputation*, chapter 2.]

Under the Law, as we have mentioned, a dry rod, putting forth new growth contrary to nature, produced fruit and a kernel within its shell (Numbers 17:8), prefiguring the most sweet Son of God in the flesh. Under grace, to testify to and commend chastity to later generations, the staff of a certain hermit is recorded to have put forth leaves and borne fruit after laying aside its dryness.

> [Note: [Col. 0374D] It is recorded that the staff of a certain hermit put forth leaves. This is recorded, without the hermit’s name, by Rufinus in *History of the Holy Fathers*, book 3, section 24, in the edition of our Rosweyde.]

And truly, for this reason the green wood dried up in the Passion, so that the dry wood (Luke 23:31), through the glorified Spirit of holy men, might become green again, recover the ordinances proper to its nature, fulfill its rights, restore bodies dried up in death to life, and drive away the afflictions of every illness.

## CHAPTER IV  
### On Garments of Every Texture and Kind

The same must be believed and held as certain, without any ambiguity, concerning sacred garments of every texture and kind, fitted to the limbs of the saints and far surpassing the purple garments of the rich woven with gold.

Under the Law, indeed, by means of the garment that fell when the prophet—the chariot and charioteer of Israel—was carried away in the fiery chariot, the Jordan lost the laws of its current (2 Kings 2:12) and conveyed the heir of the double Spirit over dry ground to the nearer bank.

Under grace, nothing has ever been discovered or found anywhere on earth more precious or more exalted—apart from the excellence of holiness—than the Lord’s garments. From touching their fringe, the flow of blood of the woman with the issue of blood was stopped (Matthew 9:20); and as many as touched them (Matthew 14:36), restored to soundness, saw death itself abolished and annihilated.

Of their division and casting of lots, the excellent psalmist David prophetically sang in the psalm whose mystical title is “For the morning reception,” or “For the hind of the morning”:

> “They divided my garments among themselves, and over my clothing they cast lots” (Psalm 22:19).

The Lord’s garment was divided into four parts as a type of the four-part Church, distributed equally and harmoniously through the four regions of the world. To foreshadow the unity of the parts, which is contained in the bond of perfection—the jewel of charity, which possesses the more excellent way and surpasses knowledge (Ephesians 3:19)—the lot, signifying the grace of God, was cast over the seamless tunic, woven from above throughout (John 19:24), mystically named from this wholeness by the Greek term for the Catholic Church.

> [Note: [Col. 0374D] The lot, by which God’s grace is signified. This is Augustine’s teaching in his commentary on Psalm 30. He adds that neither lot nor grace belongs to human choice but to the divine will. Hence the lots of the righteous are said to be in the hands of God.]

The seamless tunic, so that it might never be torn, came by the lot of divine grace to one man, because the charity of God, poured into our hearts through the Holy Spirit (Romans 5:5), gathered everyone into one.

But O how impious, how great and monstrous a crime it is that the impious heresy continually tears apart, rips, and destroys with the enormity of deadly hatred and schism the most holy garment that the soldiers of the governor reverenced enough not to tear!

No heart is sufficient to conceive, no tongue sufficient to recount, the abundance of holiness with which that seamless tunic is endowed. Through it the indivisible unity and charity—which is God—are prefigured; and beneath it the inconceivable and ineffable Majesty and Divinity clothed itself in flesh. Under it that most exalted sublimity, dreadful and worthy of adoration to thrones and dominions, tempered for itself every harshness of air and weather and turned it aside.

For just as, from the Lord’s incorruptible flesh, the grace of incorruption and sanctification was poured into all the flesh of the saints, so from his dispensational and mystical clothing an ineffable abundance of virtues was transferred into every kind of covering belonging to sanctified bodies.

O how precious are the threads of warp and woof from which the saving tunic was woven—the tunic warmed by the Lord’s flesh, which in turn warmed the Lord’s limbs through reciprocal relation! Beneath its seamless and mystical texture lies hidden the Wisdom of God, which is concealed from the eyes of all the living (Job 28:21).

This garment of such great renown, after whose pattern Joseph wore the ankle-length and many-colored robe (Gen. 37:3), and how greatly it ought to be embraced and honored with faith and reverence, the most vigilant diligence of Jewish perfidy has taught us. At last, the guardianship of so precious a treasure, handed down through legitimate successions, was eventually entrusted by hereditary right to a certain Simon, son of Jacob. This Jew, hard of neck, [Note: [Col. 0375D] In the time of the emperor Maurice. More precisely, in the eighth year of his reign, which was A.D. 593. Thus Baronius, following Sigebert.] enduring by his inborn stubbornness monstrous punishments for two weeks in order to keep silent, finally revealed that it had been hidden in the city of Zaphat, not far from Jerusalem, concealed in a marble chest.

Let anyone who recognizes himself as a clay vessel, fragile and breakable, consider, I beg, at what immense value it appeared to the human mind, for which he did not spare his own flesh, and for which he preferred to endure every kind of torment rather than see his people deprived and left without so great a treasure. But, good and gracious Jesus, what heart could conceive, what tongue could explain, how great must have been the jubilation then among the citizens of the heavenly homeland at the discovery of so great a treasure, and how great the exultation that arose among the sons of the Church? All the ages that had passed since the Lord’s Passion, as though unhappy ones, proclaimed themselves exceedingly happy because in them divine generosity had at last deigned to reveal so great a treasure, hidden for so long.

Men endowed with the highest honors and the highest virtues came together: Gregory, patriarch of Antioch; Thomas of Jerusalem; John of Constantinople; many other distinguished bishops; and people of various ages, sexes, and ranks, rejoicing over the indescribable gift of God (2 Cor. 9:15). And lest they be branded with the charge of rashness; lest the service of faith appear to be devotion no more than presumption; lest divine vengeance rage against them as it did against the men of Beth-shemesh (1 Sam. 6:19) and Uzzah the Levite (2 Sam. 6:7), they first purified and sanctified themselves by a three-day fast. Then they lifted the ark of the Lord amid rejoicing (2 Sam. 6:15). It was in no way heavy with the natural weight of marble, but, by divine power, exceedingly light, as though it had been constructed and assembled with the work and labor of an architect from acacia wood, like the ark of the covenant (Exod. 25:10). They accompanied it as though their saving garment had been put upon them and Christ the Lord were leading the way, and placed it in the famous city of Aelia, at the site of the Lord’s Anastasis, renowned for power and glory, where at every moment and instant of every hour the divine favor and propitiation, most immediately present for the salvation of all believers, is there.

This saving and seamless garment mystically covers the nakedness of all those whom the guilt of the first transgression stripped of the robe of immortality and overwhelmed with garments of skin (Gen. 3:21). If I had the leisure to unfold what garments, and the garments of which hidden elect of God, have shone with the splendor of astonishing holiness from the prison of the flesh, I would spend my effort on a lengthy and tedious train of discourse. Therefore, [Note: [Col. 0375D] I pass over the excellent brothers. He imitates Terence, who retained this Greek word. It indicates the two sons of Zebedee, whose cloth belonged to James and whose tunic belonged to John; Thiofridus mentions both here. See both stories in Ribadeneira’s Lives of each. But since not every author is readily available to everyone, receive somewhat more information about the cloth, which released the bonds of the bound Philetus. When James was devoting himself especially earnestly to the work of preaching, near the end of his life, two magicians, Hermogenes and Philetus, rose up against him together with the Jerusalem crowd, preparing to overwhelm the great son of thunder with the brutal lightning-bolts of magic. Hermogenes therefore sent Philetus as his disciple and ordered him both to defeat James in debate, make him contemptible to the multitude, and hand him over to the spirits of Tartarus for torment. But the outcome was very different. Philetus, who had unhappily sought victory, was happily defeated by James, both through divine arguments and through astonishing miracles performed openly before him. He voluntarily surrendered and, falling at the sacred feet, begged forgiveness. Enraged by this, Hermogenes, by magical arts, bound Philetus so tightly that he could not move from the spot at all. But the apostle, completely undaunted, merely sent a little cloth, and at once released the devilish bond.]

I pass over the excellent brothers, illustrious fellow-mystics of God, named by the mouth of the incarnate Word Boanerges, “Sons of Thunder” (Mark 3:17). The cloth of one of them released the bonds of the bound Philetus; the tunic of the other brought the benefits of former life and health to two condemned men who had been killed by drinking poison.

I think I should leave unmentioned what Augustine proclaims in a lofty voice: that the garments of certain people who had died, carried to the memorial [Col. 0376D] of the thrice-and-four-times-blessed protomartyr Stephen, [Note: [Col. 0376D] In memory of the blessed protomartyr Stephen. Everyone who has even barely greeted the sacred authors knows that “memorial” is used for a tomb or burial place. Concerning garments carried there, laid upon the dead, and restoring them, see St. Augustine, *The City of God*, book XXII, chapter 8.] received such grace of salvation that, when brought back and placed upon the lifeless limbs of the dead, as though they had belonged to the dead themselves, they restored their lost life and complete health.

I pass over the tunic of Paul the first hermit, [Note: [Col. 0377D] The tunic of Paul the first hermit. St. Jerome describes this distinctly in the Life of Paul.] which he himself wove from palm leaves in the form of baskets. On the solemn days of Easter and Pentecost, Antony, heir to his virtues, put it on as his most precious and celebrated adornment. Jerome, that crown among interpreters of divine Scripture, remembers it thus:

“If the Lord granted me adoption, I would much rather choose Paul’s tunic together with his merits than the purple robes of kings together with their kingdoms.”

I will not speak—indeed, I will remain silent—about how splendidly and how preciously the distinguished bishops Serapion and Athanasius, [Note: [Col. 0377D] Serapion and Athanasius. Athanasius himself honorably mentions these gifts from Antony in the history he wrote of him.] boasted that they had been enriched by gifts, when Antony, the special and principal courtier of the Holy Spirit, distributed to one a melote and the worn cloak laid over it, and to the other another melote that had emerged from the iron furnace, as a memorial of himself.

Passing over the galummate of the distinguished virgin and martyr Agatha [Note: [Col. 0377D] Agatha’s galummate. “I cover, I veil” is in Greek καλύπτω, whence κάλυμμα, “a veil.” Either Thiofridus took a cognate letter for the proper one, or it slipped in through a copyist’s error. It is not such a grave fault that it must be changed. I preferred to point it out.], that is, κάλυμμα, “a veil,” which whenever

> Aetna thunders nearby with terrifying ruins  
> and lifts globes of flame that lick the stars,  
> sometimes, torn away, the rocks and entrails of the mountain, spread out and held before it,  
> it raises, belching forth, and seethes from its deepest foundation—  
> amid so great a convulsion, it frees the people of Trinacria from the danger of fire and trembling. [Note: [Col. 0377D] The people of Trinacria. Sicily is so called from its three promontories: Pachynus, Lilybaeum, and Pelorus.]

For the advancement and glory of kings and emperors, I would like briefly to touch upon what and how great a merit [Note: [Col. 0378D] Gunderamnus. This holy king of Gaul is also called Guntheramnus and Guntramnus. For this story, and more about him, see Gregory of Tours, *History of the Franks*, book IX, chapter 21.] of the most powerful king Gunderamnus obtained before the divine Majesty, without his knowing it.

When the son of a certain poor woman was so afflicted by a quartan fever that all hope for his life had been abandoned, his mother, anxious with fear of bereavement but endowed with the faith of the aforementioned woman with the issue of blood in the Gospel, followed the footsteps of the most glorious king as he proceeded to church. Among the densely packed ranks of his attendants, she secretly bent toward his back and, by a pious and faithful theft, tore away a fringe of his royal garment. Having returned home with her wish fulfilled, she placed the medicinal thread in water and offered it to her half-dead son to drink. The healing liquid extinguished and drove away the fever that was leaving him breathless.

Who could conceive, who could adequately explain how wonderful and memorable is what happened in the time of the most illustrious theologian Gregory, to the praise and glory of divine magnificence? [Note: [Col. 0378D] In the holy Roman Church an ancient custom took root. Concerning this custom—namely, that garments which had touched the relics of the saints were regarded as relics—apart from this noble example approved by God through so distinguished a miracle, see Baronius under the years 519 and 560.]

In the holy Roman Church an ancient custom arose and became an unbreakable practice: consecrated *brandea*, [Note: [Col. 0378D] Consecrated *brandea*. What a *brandeum* is, I explained above, book I, chapter 7. Moreover, what Thiofridus relates here about St. Gregory the Great, you will find in his Life written by John the Deacon, book II, chapter 42.] requested by the faithful, were sent as relics of the saints and, once stored away with due honor, were themselves honored.

When the thrice-and-four-times-blessed Gregory had distributed such *brandea* to certain envoys from the West, enclosing one in each small box under the names of the martyrs requested and securing it with the apostolic seal, and had granted them permission to depart, they had traveled some distance. Then, employing obscure diligence, they wished to know for certain what kind and what sort of relics of the saints they were carrying. They rashly removed the pontifical seal and, finding pieces of cloth delivered as relics, lamented as though they had been deceived.

Without delay, returning to the city in great indignation, they broke into tears and insults against so great a bishop. Through the archdeacon of the Apostolic See, they sent word to the apostolic lord, who was celebrating the solemn Mass, with grave reproach: “Our lords abound in the most precious and beautiful cloaks and have no need of the worthless *brandea* of the Romans.”

But the most illustrious theologian received the *brandeum*, placed it upon the altar, and gave himself to prayer with all who were present. When he had been heard, he rose and ordered the incredulous envoys to stand closer. He pierced the cloth with a little knife, and—wonderful to relate—blood flowed copiously from each puncture, shaking the minds of all who were present with immense astonishment.

Struck with awe, they all prostrated themselves on the ground with the apostolic bishop and offered the sacrifice of the most intense prayer for as long as it took for all the holes in the *brandeum* to be restored by the power of the divine Majesty.

Indeed, in golden fringes (Ps. 44:14), the saints of God in the Church that has neither spot nor wrinkle (Eph. 5:27) proceeded into the Holy of Holies with bells (Sir. 45:10), clothed all around in varied garments (Ps. 44:14)—that is, with vocal ribbons of diverse virtues. Therefore, whatever belongs to their garments, of whatever warp and woof, by right and through the innate warmth of divine virtue, exudes salvation and the health of soul and body in return for their outstanding merits. In times of drought and flooding, when raised from their shrines and carried out amid litanies of the highest faith and devotion, they command the disturbances of the atmosphere and grant the Christian faithful who implore them now serene weather, now rain suited to their prayers. By the clearest signs it is shown how generous, merciful, beneficent, and marvelous God is in his saints.

Nor is it surprising that the inner and outer things of the saints are glorified with such magnificent virtues, since the Wisdom incarnate of the Father testifies concerning them: “All that is mine is yours, and what is yours is mine” (John 17:10). Nor, according to Augustine’s judgment, soaring higher than an eagle’s flight, is it permissible that any saint belong to anyone except him by whom they were created and sanctified; and consequently all that belongs to them must also belong to him to whom they themselves belong.

## CHAPTER V  
### On the liquids of water, wine, and oil, and on Nicholas’s tomb

Lest a rougher and more extended discourse produce weariness, I bring my silence to a close and suppress how many astonishing and delightful miracles divine favor has worked through the various liquids of water, wine, and oil consecrated by the blessing of the saints. But lest I give an opportunity for an adversary to reproach me by claiming that what I report cannot be proved by any authoritative testimony, I bring forward one such clear testimony concerning the liquid element of water that every doubt about all the others may be removed. For it is plainly evident what the demonstration of merit in serious matters is worth when the sanctification of this liquid has been so beneficial even in trifles.

In the marketplace town of Gaza, when a certain man was training horses for the Circus games and feared a suspected sorcerer, lest he should hinder them with some demonic curses, he took, despite the strong reluctance of Hilarion, the great leader of the Holy Spirit—since Hilarion considered it foolish to waste prayer on such trifles—[Note: [Col. 0379D] For the Circus games. Our abbot borrowed this charming little story from St. Jerome, who wrote the Life of the blessed Hilarion.] a clay cup filled with water, which Hilarion was accustomed to drink, and sprinkled the stable, the horses, his charioteers, and the barriers of the starting gates, without any hesitation in faith (James 1:6). [Note: [Col. 0379D] A clay cup. I restored the reading from St. Jerome himself, although both copies foolishly suggested “fertile.”]

No sooner had the appointed day arrived and the signal been given than these horses flew forward, while their opponents were impeded. The wheels beneath the latter’s chariot grew hot; they could scarcely see the backs of those who flew past them. The former, to the immense applause of everyone, won glorious victory; the latter were thrown aside, sluggish and inglorious.

For the water, seasoned with the honey of the holy man’s merits, emptied out the poison of every spell and magical art. Flowing inwardly from the abundance of the house of God, from the river of delight (Ps. 35:9), and hollowing out stones (Job 14:19), it softened the stony hearts of the pagans to the glory of God. [Note: [Col. 0379D] It softened the stony hearts of the pagans. For many, seeing that miracle, embraced the Christian name, condemning the impotence of their gods.]

And what wonder is it if divine mercy worked through the element over which the Holy Spirit (Gen. 1:2), before the adornment of the world, spread his divine power as a type of future baptism; through the element which the Word of the Father made flesh (John 1:14) chose as the beginning of his signs when he changed it into wine at Cana of Galilee (John 2:9); through the element which, for the redemption and cleansing of the human race, he poured from his side together with blood (John 19:34), as a nuptial gift and hereditary pledge of his Church? What, I ask, is so astonishing if through this element he glorified his saint, a man of supreme perfection, when, [Note: [Col. 0379D] In the dregs of our own age as well. Our Thiofridus often indicates that holy men lived in his own time, and even that he knew some of them personally. See the Life. But whom he specifically means here is unknown to me.] even amid the dregs of our own age, filthy water—water secretly sought and granted by chamberlains after the servants of God had washed their hands, to be thrown out together with the dirt—drives away various kinds of illness and grants the grace of health?

The holy men of God, from whose bellies rivers of living water flowed (John 7:38)—spiritual graces and streams of heavenly teaching—certainly did not drink the turbid water of Gihon in Egypt, [Note: [Col. 0380D] The turbid water of Gihon. What Jeremiah (2:18) called the water of Shihor, our translator rendered “turbid”; Vatablus and Pagninus rendered it “of the Nile”; the ancient Septuagint has γηῶν, “Gihon.” It is well known that the ancient Fathers often adhered to the Greek while omitting the Hebrew text. Our Thiofridus did the same several times. In this passage, however, he fully represented the Latin version and added “Gihon” from the Greek for purposes of explanation. There is no contradiction: the Hebrew *Shihor* is the river Nile, which the Greeks call Gihon, and its water is turbid—something the Latin translator especially wished to express.] but the clearest water of divine Scripture; nor did they muddy with their feet the rest of the water that the Lord’s sheep could have used (Ezek. 34:18). Therefore, water employed by them in whatever way obtained such efficacy from divine action.

And what person of little faith would ask what the anointing of sanctified oil can accomplish, or what wine can accomplish, which the priestly blessing in the word of the Lord changes into the Lord’s blood? Through the consecrated oil of mercy, the health of souls and bodies is restored; through wine, which both according to ordinary human use and in its mystical meaning gladdens the human heart (Ps. 103:15), the limbs of the sick are restored and the minds of the sorrowful are cheered.

To speak briefly about the liquid of oil, what is more marvelous in all Lycia than that oil flows from the precious marble tomb of the thrice-and-four-times-blessed Nicholas, bishop of Myra, and that by its anointing those smeared with it are freed from every adverse illness?

To human judgment it is certainly astonishing where this liquid comes from, since no tree exudes or drips it. No material olive tree springs from a root there; it spreads no branches, produces no shoots, and bears no fruit; yet, contrary to the laws of nature, oil overflows there as though pressed out in an oil press. From where, then, does oil pour forth there for the salvation of believers? Is there some vein of that land naturally rich and overflowing with this liquid? Or does it rather flow from the dead flesh of the distinguished bishop? But the nature of dead flesh is such that it produces from itself fetid decay and the stench of corruption rather than any liquid of sweetness. Nor is the soil of that city naturally endowed with such a rich vein that the explanation could reasonably be judged consistent with the truth.

For when a certain distinguished successor of the distinguished bishop had been expelled by civic dissension, the abundance of oil ceased to flow for so long, [Note: [Col. 0381D] It ceased to flow. John the Deacon reports this in the Life of St. Nicholas, which he compiled from Patriarch Methodius and published. It is rightly concluded from this that the oil flowed by divine power, without any natural agency. Thus, from the Breviary of the Church of Toledo, let us rightly sing of blessed Nicholas:

> Whose tomb bears oil,  
> unknown to olive-bearing mothers;  
> what nature did not produce,  
> marble gives birth to by sweating.]

until the expelled bishop, after suffering insult, was restored to his Church with immense honor and glory. For if it flowed by nature, it would not lose the course of its flow. But because Nicholas of outstanding holiness flourished like a palm tree (Ps. 91:13) and bore fruit like a fruitful olive tree in the house of the Lord (Ps. 51:10), by a miracle unheard of through the ages, through unheard-of generosity and benevolence of the Lord God who created all things from nothing, oil drips from the soil of this man of such great virtues, of whom it is proclaimed:

“For he was exceedingly compassionate, and he carried within him a pious interior of pity and mercy toward the afflicted.”

It drips not to the prejudice of material nature, but as the clearest proof of the overflowing and surpassing divine clemency toward his saints.

## CHAPTER VI  
### On the polyandrium of John the fellow-mystic

[Note: [Col. 0381D] The heading of this chapter is: “On the polyandrium of John the fellow-mystic.” He calls the apostle a fellow-mystic because many initiates belonged to the same fellowship. He calls the tomb of St. John a *polyandrium*—or rather *polyandrium*—by catachresis. For both scholarly usage and the origin of the word itself indicate a place filled with many tombs, such as a cemetery.]

Although I must employ the rhetorical figure of hysterology, [Note: [Col. 0382D] By the rhetorical figure of hysterology. He means that he is using an inverted order, saying later what ought to have been said earlier. This is what hysterology is. But why does he say this? I think it is because, after treating many other subjects that do not touch the bodies of the saints so closely, he is now treating the tomb, which is most intimate to them—or rather, in which their bodies are entirely enclosed.] and thus use a backward order, I nevertheless do not presume to pass over the mausoleum of the apostle and evangelist John, fixed in the reverberating focus of my mind, like an eagle flying toward the very rays of the eternal Sun.

What accords with the prerogative of his virginal chastity is that manna flows from his tomb instead of worms. He set before the world for eating, more clearly than all the fellow-mystics of God, the bread of angels, the Word in the beginning, God with God (John 1:1). Therefore, contrary to the condition of human nature, he deserved to be honored at the division of soul and body.

He alone among mortals, after the earth had been dug out and cast beyond the basilica’s doors, entered the polyandrium alive; and there, having preached to his people and offered the sacrifice of prayer, he fell asleep in the Lord as though resting most sweetly. [Note: [Col. 0382D] He entered the polyandrium alive. Concerning the paradoxical death of this beloved disciple, see Baronius under A.D. 101.]

Manna is Mary, the perpetual virgin, delicate and most sweet, from whom comes forth the worm who sings in the psalm, “I am a worm and not a man” (Ps. 21:7). [Note: [Col. 0382D] Mary sprinkled with oil and mixed with fine flour. Such sprinkling signifies an abundance of mercy, according to the authority of the blessed Gregory the Great (*Homily 12 on Ezekiel*), whom our Thiofridus willingly follows.] Mary, I say, sprinkled with oil and mixed with fine flour, commended to him by the heavenly Bread itself, possessing every delight and every taste of sweetness (Wis. 16:10), at the hour of the Lord’s Passion, the virgin received her into his keeping (John 19:27). From the firmament of his most pure heart, manna rained down as from heaven, small and as though pounded in a mortar (Exod. 16:4)—clearly the evangelical teaching, separated from all impurity of error through the inward wisdom of God. In his Apocalypse he promises the victor hidden manna (Rev. 2:17). Therefore, as the clearest testimony to his victory and bright, perpetual chastity, his virginal body was covered and hidden with manna.

What heart could be capable of conceiving how great is the expenditure of divine favor and grace even upon the least and most rejected of the elect? Nature, for which this sentence was prescribed—“You are dust, and to dust you shall return” (Gen. 3:19)—not only ascended into heaven but, even in the very dissolution of its corruption, shines more through divine glorification than it is soiled by the filth of decay.

Surely it should not be judged more marvelous that manna, whose taste was like flour mixed with honey (Exod. 16:31), fed the Israelite people through the revolutions of forty years (Deut. 8:3), than that, instead of the discharge of filth and the boiling forth of worms naturally flowing from putrefying flesh, a tomb should boil forth manna through John, the mystic master, down to the present day.

## CHAPTER VII  
### On vessels and little beds

If I were to overflow with eloquence more profusely than

> the greatest Roman authority in eloquence,  
> Tully, … whose often-added force of eloquence  
> strengthened a feeble cause … [Col. 0382C]

I would still not adequately express how astonishing the signs and prodigies are that the saints, the Lord’s vessels, have worked through vessels.

What abundance of speech would be available to me if I attempted in writing to pursue the oil jar and the vessel of flour through which Elijah, the herald of the coming Judge, was sustained in the presence of the widow of Sarepta until the day on which the Lord God gave rain upon the parched face of the earth after three years and six months? (1 Kings 17:16.)

No vein of talent is so rich that I could bring forth how great were the merits before God of his successor and heir of the twofold spirit, Elisha: by the tiniest quantity of oil, all the little jars of the widow—she who preceded as a type of the Church—both her own and those supplied by her neighbors, were filled to the brim, and the greed of the rapacious creditor was drowned (2 Kings 4:5).

I think it better to remain silent than to say too little about how the elect of God, the vials of the fragrances of the Lord’s altar, from the small woven vessels of their journey, made of wicker and of modest capacity, [Note: [Col. 0383B] They satisfied a very great multitude. Let two examples from the Lord suffice: Mark 6:41 and John 6:11, and Mark 8:6; and one from a servant—Elisha, that is—2 Kings 4:43. You will find others in the Lives of the Fathers and in other sacred histories.] satisfied a very great multitude, and how they cheered princes setting out against the enemies of the state for so long with a small but inexhaustible and continual abundance, the liquid of Lyaeus overflowing, until they won the palm of victory.

What shall I say about the little beds endowed with the glory of supreme holiness, which, for as many ages as the phoenix lives, are free from every kind of decay? Every one of their straws and splinters frees people from the most bitter toothache and from the deadly bitterness of fevers.

And concerning all their other utensils, while I strive for concise brevity, what more particular thing can I write about each? The same operation of divine power is distributed equally through all and in all.

They endured a most hostile and cruel world and conquered it, not by resisting but by dying. They were refined to purity in the furnace of tribulation through marvelous patience. Therefore, in so many miracles, such power follows them and all things belonging to their use.

Nevertheless, as Augustine declares in book XXII of *The City of God*, it cannot come within the knowledge of any mortal whether God himself works such wonders directly or through his ministers; whether he also accomplishes through the spirits of the saints, rejoicing in his majestic presence, some of the same things that he accomplishes through his ministries; whether he acts through human beings beyond themselves, still confined in the wearisome custody of the flesh; or through angels, whom he commands invisibly, incorporeally, and immutably; so that the things said to be done through the saints are done by them only as they pray and obtain them, and not also as they perform them—a matter known by reason to the eternal Divinity alone.

But by whatever incomprehensible means they are brought about, they bear witness to the glory of God and the merits of his elect.

*The third book ends.*

## The chapters of the fourth book begin

[Col. 0383]

I. On the wood of transgression.  
II. On the wood of restoration.  
III. On the Lord’s nails and the soldier’s lance.  
IV. That sanctification has been poured from the saving gibbet of the cross into every punishment of the saints.  
V. That nothing precious in the world can be compared with the crosses of Peter and Andrew, or with Paul’s chain.  
VI. On the stones of the protomartyr Stephen and Laurence’s gridiron.  
VII. How the author of this little book, attracted by desire, ventured to insert the hand of his small talent into this most difficult subject.

*The chapters of the fourth book end.*

# THE FOURTH BOOK BEGINS

[Col. 0383]

## CHAPTER I  
### On the wood of transgression

Now necessity compels me, as though amid rocks and reefs with shipwreck threatening, to turn the ship of my dictation and to keep watch lest it suddenly strike. For I am passing from difficult matters to the most difficult; from subjects that are especially useful and refreshing to human beings, and sweet, to those that are altogether contrary and most bitter to human weakness: to the various kinds of torment.

But may the breeze of the Holy Spirit blow, fill the sails, and carry me, among the spiritual passengers, if only at last, into the bosom of a tranquil harbor.

In the irremediable transgression of our first parent, bitterness was written against us with an adamantine stylus (Jer. 17:1), together with the document of death, rights, and laws; and all his posterity was filled and drunk with wormwood. And because the wood of transgression, beautiful and delightful to the sight (Gen. 3:6) and sweet to the taste, passed down through the throat of the first human being into his entrails and onward into all his descendants like a sharp sword, it inflicted an incurable wound. Therefore, alas, our eye dwells amid the greatest bitterness (Job 17:2).

The wood of transgression is the primary cause and the very effective cause both of eternal damnation and of every punishment and pain; it is the beginning and fuel of all sorrow and tribulation. From the place where the first destruction of humanity arose, innumerable kinds of punishments were devised by human cruelty. [Note: [Col. 0383D] Crosses and scourges were devised. An elegant and learned treatment of these and other instruments of punishment is found in Antonio Gallonio, a priest of the Congregation of the Oratory.]

From there were devised crosses, scourges tearing the skin, knotted staffs, stocks, [Col. 0384D] and clubs that kill. And because termites eat wood and decay consumes it, the hardest material of metals was forged into every kind of instrument of torture. It is forged day and night so that the forms of punishment may be durable, cruelty may consume bones and flesh, and no softness or hardness may be able to resist.

For in the fruit of that baneful tree, the sweetness presumed upon and desired, and the bitterness transmitted through the entrails of our first parent into all posterity, the belly of everyone was embittered (Rev. 10:10). And, by I know not what demonic invention, ever since then joy is despised, a sad exile is loved more than one’s homeland, and the cup of death is poured out and drained as though it were the delights of life.

Bitterness is a delight; sweetness is a source of disgust. Amid torments, the human being, a clay vessel and most fragile, exults with laughter and, with astonishing and wondrous joy, mocks the cruelty of his torturers.

War is desired more ardently than peace; if an external enemy is absent, one is sought at home. It is sweet to cruelty to see entrails spilled out and discolored with blood, and rivers driven toward a flood. It is pleasant to hear the gnashing of teeth and the groaning of those falling in death.

And a person, harboring anger against another person (Sir. 28:3), does not consider that he is surrounded by weakness (Heb. 5:2), nor attend to the fact that he is a vessel of clay. Even if he himself escaped when seized by cruel hands, he would immediately devise a punishment much more cruel.

As though over delicate foods and exquisite dishes, so he dwells upon and delights in the dreadful and harsh new inventions of punishments. He feeds and grows cheerful upon the greatest bitterness, although he was created for the sweetness of an inconceivable and ineffable delight, so that he would feel or know no bitterness of pain and sorrow at all, and think of nothing, see nothing, hear nothing except the jubilation and blessedness of eternal joy.

With the monstrous weight of so great a calamity and misery, the wood of desire has weighed down the neck of the entire human race in captivity. It has taught humanity not to desire what ought to be desired and to desire what ought not to be desired; it has accustomed humanity to seek evil instead of good and bitterness instead of sweetness.

## CHAPTER II  
### On the wood of restoration

But just as, in accordance with an unchangeable dispensation, it was arranged by the immutable decree of divine Providence that the irreparable damage of the first fall should be repaired by no other creature, visible or invisible, and that the human being—captured Leviathan, the human being (Job 40:20)—should not be released except through a human being similar in form but not in sin, so divine providence also ordained that all the bitterness of the wood of transgression should be driven out by the sweetness of the saving wood, and that the woodworm corrupted at its root should be removed, [Note: [Col. 0385D] The beam sanctified by its own weight. The cross is that beam. And what is its weight other than the burden with which the cross was loaded? No Christian is unaware that this was Christ. The noble hymn of the Church:]

“[It] bears a sweet burden.”] So that, sanctified by its own burden, it might expiate and sanctify [*termes*: uncertain reading in the supplied text]. For the guilt of the first transgression, which made the supreme and most shameful punishment consist in death, produced that universal pronouncement of the Law: “Cursed is everyone who hangs on a tree” (Deut. 21:23; Gal. 3:13). The same mystery was proposed by the restoring grace of human renewal: from the very source where humanity first earned unspeakable torments, there it was first wondrously restored (Col. 0386B) and freed from eternal sufferings; and from the place where, under the judgment of the Law, the general sentence of dreadful malediction was proclaimed, there, at the beginning of grace, through him who was made a curse for us (Gal. 3:13), the abundance of every blessing might flow forth and overflow.

What was once the most shameful and miserable punishment of death has now, through “the change of the right hand of the Most High” (Ps. 76:11), become supreme salvation, supreme sweetness, and the supreme remedy of life. For because the sweetest sweetness of life hung upon it, not only at the touch of its smallest splinter, but also at the invocation of its name and at the sign of its figure traced by the fingers of faith, the bitterest curse accumulated against the human race through the guile of the ancient serpent is dissolved and driven away; and a sweet-flowing blessing and consecration is poured into every creature (Col. 0386C).

What brought death through the transgression of the first Adam condemns, excludes, and puts death to death through the confession of the true faith of the second Adam.

[Note: What is the mystical washing of baptism without its mystery? He is speaking of the cross, concerning which the most illustrious martyr Cyprian, with the same understanding, says (*On the Baptism of Christ*): “The power of the cross accomplishes all the sacraments; without this sign nothing is holy, nor does any consecration attain its effect.”]

For what is the mystical washing of baptism without its mystery? What is the supreme consecration of chrism? What benefit is there in the anointing with sanctified oil? If the mystery of the life-giving wood does not approach the spiritual rock, the water of eternal refreshment and satiety does not flow forth (Num. 20:11). When those who had gone out from Egypt came to the waters of the Red Sea, saw Pharaoh perishing with his army, and, while Miriam led the singing—

[Note: “With the bodies’ tambourines.” For Origen (*Homily 6 on Exodus*), the tambourine made from the hide of dead animals signifies the mortification of the flesh. Catholics likewise know that, among the various forms of the cross—or mortification (Theophri[dus] calls it a “cross” in this passage)—there is also that by which the body is worn down with scourges and beaten like a tambourine. Such a tambourine-player was Saint Paul, who chastises, or “buffets” (*hypōpiazei*, ὑπωπιάζει), his body and makes it livid (1 Cor. 9:27). His meaning is that unless we are put to death with Christ, we will not live with him nor enjoy his sweetness—especially since water of eternal refreshment could not flow from Christ himself, whom he calls, with the Apostle, the spiritual Rock, unless the mystery of the cross were present. This is altogether Catholic doctrine, even if it might seem strange to someone. God certainly could have refreshed us without the passion of his Son; but he had decreed that it should occur only through the passion. Therefore, by divine decree, it could not happen otherwise. To understand this entire most elegant allegory, one should not hesitate to read attentively the passages of Exodus enclosed in parentheses.]

with the bodies’ tambourines resounding with the songs of the triumphant, the spring at Marah, though abundant in water (Exod. 14:15), does not lose the nature of its bitterness through any sweetness, nor does it refresh anyone, unless the priest who leads God’s people introduces the confession of the cross and the mysteries of the Lord’s passion.

Thus the life-giving wood of the saving cross expiated and emptied out the wood of the first transgression. And because upon it the saving Victim of the Father drank from the most bitter torrent (Ps. 109:7), he changed the bitterness of eternal damnation and destruction written against us (Job 13:26) into the sweetness of eternal salvation. If the mystery of the saving cross had not intervened, the whole human race could in no way have escaped Tartarus’ punishment. Destined for punishment before we were born, we have nevertheless been freed from punishment through punishment, by a far more excellent predestination of restoring grace. Through undeserved punishment we escaped the punishment we deserved; and what we had earned as everlasting destruction was transformed into the inconceivable remedy of eternal life.

On the cross, the death of the Son of God became the price paid for the deaths of all God’s children on earth. On the cross a great exchange took place, when the side of the mediator between God and human beings (1 Tim. 2:5) was pierced by the soldier’s lance (John 19:34). It paid out the purse of human redemption, and from it flowed the price of the whole world.

[Note: There, although his strength was hidden. For on the cross the weakness of the flesh appeared rather than the strength of the Godhead.]

There, although his strength was hidden, nevertheless “before his face went” (Hab. 3:4), and death was swallowed up in victory (1 Cor. 15:54). There all the faithful were purchased; all the martyrs were purchased in name and by their lavish blood, outstanding and unconquered witnesses of the Lord’s blood, the common price of the whole human race. There the aerial forces were defeated, overcome, and crushed.

This wood of life was mystically prefigured in the typological flood through Noah’s ark, which was three hundred cubits long (Gen. 6:15); that number is marked by the character *tau*.

[Note: It is marked by the character *tau*. Above, he discussed this same character and mystical number when speaking of Gideon’s soldiers. See Book II, chapter 7.]

It was also mystically prefigured in the crossed hands of the patriarch Jacob, when the right hand was placed over the head of Ephraim, the younger son, and the left was transferred to Manasseh, the elder, in the likeness of the cross (Gen. 48:14). Through the mystery of this, the greater people, who forgot the Lord their Creator (Deut. 32:18), serves the lesser (Gen. 25:23), who was made fruitful throughout the breadth of the world by abundant mercy (Ps. 91:11).

This was shown at Marah, when the bitterness of the Law was changed into spiritual sweetness (Exod. 15:25). This was shown at Rephidim, through the extension of the hands of Moses the lawgiver against Amalek (Exod. 17:11). This was prefigured at the torrent of the grape-cluster by the pole with which two men, figures of the two peoples, carried a grape with its branch (Num. 13:24), as a type of the Lord’s divinity and humanity.

This was shown at Salmona (Num. 33:41), the thirty-first encampment of the children of Israel, which is interpreted as “a little image.” There, by the wood on which the leader of God’s people raised up the bronze serpent as a mystery of the Lord’s death, the deadly bites of the fiery serpents were swallowed up and healed (Num. 21:9).

[Note: “A little image.” Saint Jerome gives this interpretation in his letter to Fabiola, concerning the forty-two encampments. He also explains its meaning in these words: “Hence, too, the little image, contemplating the passion of the true and express image of the Son of God, is preserved.” Christ himself clearly teaches this concerning the serpent, by which he was signified (John 3:14). But when Theophri[dus] calls Salmona the thirty-first encampment, unless the number is a copyist’s error, it is a lapse of the author’s memory. It is actually the thirty-fifth encampment; if Jerome had not written this, it would have been easy for us to count.]

This was likewise shown in the two pieces of wood belonging to the widow of Sarepta (3 Kings 17:12), a figure of Mother Church. It was prefigured by the wood through which the iron that had slipped from its handle and fallen for the prophet’s son was recovered (4 Kings 6:6). The prophet Elisha, heir to the twofold spirit of Elijah, raised it from the depths.

As a type of this saving wood, pastoral office, and condescension, the same prophet placed mouth to mouth and hand to hand with the lifeless son of the Shunammite widow (4 Kings 4:34), and restored him to his former life and health.

In praise of this saving wood, the Holy Spirit, through Ezekiel—whose name means “the strength of God”—wove this prophecy long before the mystery of the Incarnation:

“Pass through the midst of the city, through the midst of Jerusalem, and mark a *tau* upon the foreheads of the men who groan and grieve over all the abominations that are committed in its midst” (Ezek. 9:4).

And how blessed is the person who weighs and imitates the perfection of good works and the broadest charity in the breadth of the saving cross; perseverance to the end in its length; the highest end, to which all works performed well and steadfastly are referred, in its height; and all good things proceeding from the depth of divine grace, which cannot be comprehended or judged, at the boundary of its depth.

But, to say nothing of the life-giving cross itself, which, dedicated in the body of Christ and adorned from his limbs as though with pearls—

[Note: “Dedicated in the body of Christ.” These are the words of Saint Andrew the Apostle, yearning for the cross, as recorded by the priests and deacons of Achaea.]

and which, according to Augustine, was a tribunal—

[Note: According to Augustine, it was a tribunal. Augustine wrote this in *Tractate 31 on John*: “The cross itself, if you attend to it, was a tribunal.”]

on which, with the Judge established, one thief, who believed, was freed, while the other, who insulted him, was condemned, in a likeness of the future judgment; and he who was being judged was already threatening judgment—

to say nothing, I repeat, of that living wood, in whose praise

[Note: “The Sibyls.” Many authors have written much about the Sibyls, and different authors have offered different accounts. Among the ancients there is Varro, from whom several others drew their material. See Clement of Alexandria, Book I of the *Stromata*; Lactantius, Book I of the *Divine Institutes*, chapter 6, and *On the Wrath of God*, chapter 22; Saint Augustine, Book XVIII of *The City of God*, chapter 23; Suidas in his *Lexicon*, and others. Among more recent writers, Onuphrius in his own short work and Ludovicus Vives in his commentary on the Augustinian passage seem to have treated the subject more carefully. I omit much that is irrelevant. As for the number, the opinion of many is that there were ten. Theophri[dus], in his customary manner of speaking, rather clearly indicates that he follows Martianus Capella, who lists only two—the very ones our author names—except that, apparently through a copyist’s error, *Therophila* has been written instead of *Erophila* or *Herophila*, and *Marmensi* instead of *Marmesi*.]

a truthful prophecy was proclaimed by the Sibyl—not by the Trojan Therophila of Marmessus, but by the Erythraean Symmachina, daughter of Hippotensis—whose name is interpreted as meaning something like “counsel of God,” that is, “the judgment of God.”

“O thrice-blessed wood, upon which God himself was stretched out.”

[Note: “O thrice-blessed wood.” Others express the Greek verse in this Latin line:

“O happy wood, on which God himself hung.”]

At the sight of its figure—even if merely painted, sculpted, cast, or engraved in any material, or traced with the fingers upon the forehead and breast—all the aerial powers and the spiritual forces of wickedness in the heavens grow faint and vanish like smoke. When the sign of the cross is traced in the air with two fingers against them, the aerial princes fear it more than the inextinguishable fire boiling up from the flame-vomiting furnace of hell.

Although experience itself makes this well known by night and by day, nevertheless, in order to glorify more honorably the standard of the wondrous cross—the unique price and remedy of human salvation, transferred from punishment, and the safest barrier against the savage darts of enemies—let us refresh the mind of the wearied reader by gathering, as though fragrant flowers, testimonies from the paradise of sacred Scripture.

Let us begin, in a brief and accessible account, with the efficacy of the virtues possessed by the figure of so great a sign in any material. When Constantine the sole ruler—after Philip, the first of all the Roman emperors, had been regenerated by the waters of holy baptism for this one purpose: that the world might celebrate, under a Christian emperor, the thousandth anniversary of exalted and admirable Rome, in its foundation, name, fame, and dignity—

[Note: “Rome’s thousandth year.” When he says that this year was celebrated under a Christian emperor, he means Philip, not Constantine. Philip became a Christian in the year of Christ 249. Add 751 years from the foundation of Rome to Christ, and you will see a complete thousand. Yet it seems strange that he says Philip became a Christian solely so that the world might celebrate the thousandth anniversary of the city’s foundation under a Christian emperor. I think he asserts this because, during the four years in which Philip ruled as a Christian, he did nothing at all against the pagans and their superstition. Thus, according to Eutropius, he was enrolled among the gods by the pagans themselves, together with his son.]

Constantine, I say, the second Christian emperor in the catalogue of the Augusti, the thirty-fourth after Augustus—

[Note: “In the first year of the two-hundred-and-first Olympiad.” A monstrous chronological error, which I would rather attribute to the copyist than to the author. Seventy entire Olympiads—two hundred and eighty years—are missing. See Baronius under the year of Christ 306; from him and his sources, restore here: “in the first year of the two-hundred-and-seventy-first Olympiad.”]

having been appointed emperor in the first year of the two-hundred-and-first Olympiad, according to the *Tripartite History*, prepared to wage war against Maxentius, son of Herculius Maximianus. As a swelling and flooding sea of anxieties swept his mind, wavering in different directions, just as Cornelius the centurion, the most eminent vessel of election, before baptism saw an angel of light in a manifest vision at the ninth hour (Acts 10:3), so he, although not yet initiated into the divine mysteries, saw around midday, when the sun had already begun to decline, a sign of the most victorious cross formed from light in the sky.

While he was stunned by the marvel of so great a vision and turned over during the night what it might be and what it might signify, Christ the Lord appeared to him in sleep, in order to make him his own anointed one. With the same sign that had appeared in the sky by day, Christ commanded him to have an image of it produced with the utmost devotion, so that in every encounter of battle it might be the unconquered liberation of God’s army and the impregnable defeat of its enemies.

Without delay, the Augustus of blessed memory, as the sun’s rays rose, summoned men distinguished by virtue, noble in lineage, and accomplished in the priestly order, and consulted them about the doctrine of the Christian religion. Having been instructed by them that the divinely manifested sign was the trophy of every saving victory, he ordered the military sign called the *labarum*—which, among other standards, was customarily carried and worshiped before the emperor as the most precious and excellent in Roman military practice—
