[Note: “The military sign called the *labarum*.” The *labarum* and its appearance have been discussed by nearly every writer and are therefore well known. See Baronius under the year 312.]

to be forged and transformed by the most learned goldsmiths, from purest gold and most precious gems, into the standard of the life-giving cross. He then assigned this duty to the standard-bearers, ordering them to carry it in turn upon their shoulders before all the ranks and to be present with the phalanxes, especially those suffering most in battle.

When a certain man—who ought not to be called a soldier, since he carried a body without courage—was terrified by the enemy’s attack and handed the standard to another to carry, thinking that he was thereby looking after his own life and withdrawing from the battle, and wishing to evade the darts, he transferred the trophy of life from himself to another.

[Note: “He consigned him to life and himself to death.” This occurred in the year of Christ 317. The same is recorded by Baronius.]

For immediately, while fleeing from death, he fled into death and was pierced through and killed. But the bearer of the life-giving standard, though countless darts were hurled at him and turned back by divine power, remained unharmed and returned home victorious with the sign of victory.

Never afterward did anyone in battle die from a wound or suffer the calamity of captivity if he had been worthy to carry the labarum of that same saving cross.

In the palace of the Augustus Constantine of blessed memory, a certain chief official named Probianus, a man of the highest integrity and diligence, languished under an incurable attack of gout. No medicine of human skill could cure him, because, having been converted from paganism to Christianity, he refused to acknowledge the principal cause of all salvation, the power of the saving cross; and he refused to bend his stiff neck and knees before it—the cross through which, in the name of Jesus, every knee bends (Phil. 2:10).

[Note: “The first, a certain man named Probianus.” In the year of Christ 330.]

When he had long been worn down by the divine scourge and, as though already despairing that he could escape the necessity of the death threatening him, had himself carried to the edge of Mount Garganus, to an oratory venerated by angels and human beings, which, because of the frequent visitation and immediate help of the archangel Michael, is now called the Michaelium, divine power appeared there after a very abundant rain of tears and prolonged sighs, when the sick man had fallen asleep. It restored him to health and, rebuking his unbelief and hardness of heart, placed before his mind’s eyes the sign of the life-giving cross set upon the altar of that wondrous church.

It explained, with the clearest assertion of truth, that from the time when Christ, the salvation of the world, offered himself to God the Father upon the altar of the *stauros*—σταυρός, “cross”—as a living, holy, and immaculate victim for the sins of the whole world—

[Note: “On the altar, *stauros*.” The cross is called *stauros* (σταυρός) by the Greeks. Our author uses this word several times in the accusative.]

whatever has been done in any way for the welfare and salvation of the human race, whether by angels of light or by human beings outstanding in holiness, could in no way have been accomplished apart from the power of the cross, worshiped by thrones and dominions.

And would that the inspiration of divine power might not ulcerate the accomplices of the Berengarian heresy with gout, but might free them from a similar plague and danger of blasphemy through the antidote of inward counsel! For while they know more than they ought, they “become wise beyond measure” (Rom. 12:3), passing from the waters of snow into excessive heat (Job 24:19). Just as they do not believe that the bread and chalice upon the altar, the mystery of human reconciliation and faith, are truly the Lord’s body and blood—

[Note: “They do not believe that the bread and chalice upon the altar are truly the Lord’s body and blood.” He does not think that bread remains, as the Lutheran heretics do; rather, he calls “bread” what had been bread. Likewise, it is bread, but spiritual bread, which came down from heaven.]

so with equally ill-considered and profane boldness they try, by every sophistical subtlety of syllogisms and enthymemes, to persuade the minds of those amazed by their doctrines—

[Note: “That they should not bend their knees and pour out tears.” Let us learn this heresy of Berengarius from Theophri[dus]; I do not remember reading about it elsewhere. Here again we recognize the Calvinist spirit already breathing and inspiring.]

that they should not offer the due reverence and honor to any saving cross formed in the likeness of that cross upon which the salvation of angels and human beings hung.

For, saying that they were wise, they became fools (Rom. 1:22), since those who, terrified by the darkness of night, sleeplessness, and phantasms, protect themselves against dangers by making the character of the cross with their fingers upon their foreheads or in the air do not fear to detract from its unconquered power in any material by persuasive words of human wisdom (1 Cor. 2:4).

[Note: “Who in the darkness of night.” According to our author, the Berengarians, either persuaded by custom or compelled by necessity, sometimes used that saving sign, although elsewhere they wickedly taught that no honor should be given to it.]

They defend themselves with the sign of victory and try to dishonor the trophy of their salvation; and in this they imitate Julian the Apostate, the Devil’s arch-minister. For that most bitter enemy of Christ’s cross, when inflamed by ambition for imperial power, was admitted by a certain expert in magical arts into a prophetic sanctuary to consult the oracle. When spirits appeared to him as deceivers, he was compelled, according to their usual custom, by the magnitude of his terror and necessity to trace upon his forehead the sign of the *stauros*, hated by both them and himself yet most victorious.

When the hostile phalanx saw the figure of the Lord’s trophy, remembering its own defeat, it vanished. The Apostate, who was destined to be struck by lightning, grew pale, stunned by the horror of so great a vision, and departed unadvised and confused. Against all those marked upon the forehead with the character *tau* (Ezek. 9:4), he raised the singular standard of deadly hatred, and did not cease attacking them until, in the kingdom of the Persians, that singular wild beast, the destroyer of the Lord’s vineyard (Ps. 79:14), paid the penalty for his long devastation and, struck by a divinely inflicted wound, succumbed to eternal death.

[Note: “Struck by a divinely inflicted wound.” Since accounts of Julian’s pitiable death vary, the one I prefer is that he was killed by Mercury the martyr at God’s command. Damascenus recounts this in his first oration *On Images*. To strengthen the authority, he says not that it came from himself but from Helladius. Anyone wanting more may consult Baronius under the year of Christ 363.]

And, lest my excessive zeal in praising the life-giving cross produce weariness, I pass over the fact that Laurence, crowned with the laurel of his name, restored sight to the blind through the distinguished sign of the cross. I do not mention that Benedict, the most temperate organizer of monastic life, broke and expelled the cup of deadly poison by producing the same life-giving sign with his fingers in the air.

Nor will I relate how a certain fellow initiate of the Holy Spirit named Martyrius, when he marked with his hand a loaf baked beneath the ashes and covered with embers, that same bread gave an immense crackle, like a pot crackling in the fire; when baked, it displayed upon itself the inscription of that character, which had been written not by touch but by the merit of faith.

[Note: “Named Martyrius.” Read this elegant little story, expressed somewhat more fully and clearly in Saint Gregory the Great, *Dialogues* I.11, where he says that the remaining loaves were customarily signed with the cross; this one alone had been neglected, and the holy man, merely producing the sign in the air, marked it with the cross while it lay hidden beneath the ashes.]

So great and so numerous are the marks of praise belonging to the wondrous cross that they cannot be conceived or comprehended by the human heart, nor expressed in any way by the tongue. Therefore, because of my devotion to it, I fear that I may rightly be rebuked and branded with the charge of supreme presumption for wearing away, through the fault of a dull and barren intellect, so many praises of the restoration, salvation, and life of all the restored.

For what is more evident than the prerogative of so great a sign? What is more excellent than its power? The Lord’s cross is a scarlet ribbon (Song 4:3), to which the bride’s lips are compared in the *Song of Songs*—

[Note: “*Sirasirim*.” The Hebrews call the *Song of Songs* *Sir ha-shirim*. Our author, or his copyist, has made a single word of it.]

because every evangelical teaching, authenticated by the authority of the Lord’s passion, is smeared and endowed, as though with flowing blood. When harmful thoughts are stirred in the silent mind through the enemy’s intrusion, if, through regard for divine mercy, a medicinal band is impressed upon the wavering breast with the fingers—

[Note: “A medicinal band is impressed by the fingers.” He calls the cross impressed upon the breast a bandage by which its agitation may be stilled.]

whatever unlawful and impious matter is being contemplated is drawn out and cast away like deadly poison; and the luxuriant excess of thoughts, flowing chaotically like hair—

[Note: “The flowing and disorderly excess of thoughts is compressed.” He refers to what he said shortly before: that the Lord’s cross is a scarlet ribbon. Hair is restrained by a ribbon.]

is restrained, and a graceful and fitting order is restored to the mind of the soul, the head of its natural and divinely implanted beauty.

It rules every creature, and every nature of things rightly serves it. It displays the magnificence of its power in the four elements and in all things composed of them. When traced in the air with the fingers, it scatters and removes collisions of winds and flashes of lightning; when introduced into fire, it sanctifies it and makes it worthy of Paschal rejoicing—

[Note: “Makes it worthy of Paschal rejoicing.” This clearly refers to the ancient rite of the Church by which, on Holy Saturday, newly struck fire is blessed and the Paschal candle is lit from it. Let heretics blush, scarcely born the day before yesterday.]

it either extinguishes or drives away conflagration. When traced upon water, it effects the grace of regeneration and a transformation of nature—

[Note: “Effects a transformation of nature.” Since he is speaking here of baptism, no other transformation can be understood than a spiritual one. For although by nature we were “children of wrath” (Eph. 2:3), through baptism we have become children of God.]

and it restrains the flooding of rivers and the rising and mountainous surges of waves, forcing them down into their channels and, as though by an unbreakable barrier placed before them, enclosing and confining them within banks and shores.

Opposed to the unevenness of the earth, it makes barren fields fertile and refreshes them with abundant produce. Finally, it brings every disorder into order and either holds up, immovably at the moment of its fall, a mass of wood or stone that is about to collapse, binding and compressing it—

[Note: “A wooden mass about to fall.” See Sulpicius Severus, *Life of Saint Martin*, where Martin performed this act fearlessly, amid the astonishment and even the salvation of many of his companions, who were overcome with fear, although the danger seemed to threaten him alone. Concerning a mass of stone suspended by the power of the cross, see Saint Gregory the Great, *Dialogues* I.1.]

or casts it down without any danger and with the greatest wonder of those who watch.

Why should I delay any longer, or speak at greater length? All the kingdoms of heaven, earth, and hell are subject to the dominion of the life-giving cross, through him by whose bodily exchange they were restored: who made alive and raised again, by the wood of redemption, those made dead by the wood of transgression (Gen. 2:17); who extinguished and excluded through the tree of true obedience the death that arose and entered through the tree of disobedience; and who made the momentary suffering of assumed flesh the singular medicine, refreshment, and destruction of eternal sufferings.

## CHAPTER III. Concerning the Lord’s nails and the soldier’s lance

But what should be thought concerning the most precious nails driven through the Lord’s hands and feet into the holy cross? What concerning the soldier’s saving lance, which drew forth and produced from the side of the crucified Lord the mysteries of the Lord’s blood and of sacred Baptism?

O how excellent is the particular material of the Lord’s nails and of the saving lance, whose substance far surpasses gold, silver, and every metal! By it human beings, armed not through discord for mutual destruction but through inward harmony and peace of good will, have been joined in alliance with the angels.

O how holy, how precious, how sweet, how lovable and delightful is the material of iron from which the nails were driven into the Lord’s flesh, from which the saving lance was forged! Through it the flaming sword of paradise was removed (Gen. 3:24), and the weapons of the enemy failed forever (Ps. 9:7): namely, the darts of diverse errors by which the unhappy soul is slain as though by hostile swords. To refute these errors, bring their failure to an end, and destroy the cities of the principalities of this air (ibid.), the two-edged sword—hidden at its first coming in the sheath of humility—will be brandished at his second coming in the manifest splendor of his glory and the flashing terror of his appearance.

At that second coming, I say, according to the truthful prophecies of the distinguished prophets Amos and Zephaniah, all the sinners of the earth will die by the sword (Amos 9:10), and the Ethiopians of gloomy color will be killed (Zeph. 2:12) by the strict, bitter, and irrevocable sentence of the final judgment and examination.

In praise of these saving nails and of the Lord’s lance, the Holy Spirit long ago prophesied through the prophet Zechariah, his instrument: “They will look upon me whom they pierced” (Zech. 12:10; John 19:37); and shortly afterward: “Sword, awake against my shepherd” (Zech. 13:7).

And what material among all metals is more precious than that which the Father, through the Holy Spirit, commanded to awaken against his shepherd and strike the shepherd (ibid.), his only-begotten Son, the prince of all?

This sword of such great price, in the year 1098 from the generation of the Word—

[Note: “The year 1098.” Baronius places an encyclical letter concerning this discovery in the year 1100. But it is reasonable to believe that it was written two years after the discovery. For Theophri[dus]’s credibility in this matter must remain intact, since he was flourishing at that time.]

was found at Antioch by divine revelation in a marble chest and fixed to a standard. It struck down countless thousands of pagans and glorified the Christian phalanxes, previously afflicted by every hardship of siege and famine, with a joyful and bloodless victory.

And what is holier or more exalted than the nails of the crucified Lord? Indeed, just as the maker of all things, grieving over the ruin of the first-formed man, when he fell through the bite of the noxious fruit into the workshop of death, marked out beforehand the wood of redemption by which he would undo the damage of the wood of transgression—

[Note: “Grieving over the ruin of the first-formed man.” He has taken this passage from the famous hymn of the Church beginning:

“Sing, tongue, of the glorious  
battle of the struggle,”

whose author was Venantius Fortunatus, who lived in the year of Christ 570.]

so, by the most orderly arrangement of his providence, he preordained from the very beginnings of the world the material of the nails by which the hands of the redeemer of humanity would be stretched out in place of the hands of the transgressor, and the feet in place of the feet that, through the most cunning persuasion of the crafty serpent, had advanced irrevocably toward the forbidden branches of desire, so that those hands and feet might be fastened to the tree of the *stauros*.

[Note: “Irrevocably.” For fallen humanity could not retrace its step unless the cross and passion of Christ raised it up.]

## CHAPTER IV. That sanctification has been poured from the saving cross’s gibbet into every punishment of the saints

But, to descend gradually from the supreme height of the saving wood, concerning whose mystery the Bridegroom sings mystically in the Song of Love, “I said: I will climb the palm tree; I will take hold of its fruits” (Song 7:8), and again, “Under the apple tree I awakened you” (Song 8:5)—to descend, I say, from the height of so precious a wood into the garden of nuts, so that I may see the mystical apples of the valleys (Song 6:10), in whose figure the beloved woman sings to her beloved, “I will give you a cup of spiced wine and the juice of my pomegranates” (Song 8:2), I venture to assert, with faith preserved and confidence received through the Holy Spirit, that from the life-giving and saving gibbet of the cross—by which the sin of the first transgression was avenged and expiated and the bond of death was dissolved—salvation and sanctification have been poured into every punishment by which the saints and elect of God, crucifying their flesh with its vices and desires (Gal. 5:24), have deserved to become an acceptable and richly nourishing sacrifice to Jesus Christ crucified, a pleasing fragrance.

For the only-begotten Son of the Father, who, according to Paul, the chosen vessel, is the head of the body, the Church, and the beginning, the firstborn from the dead, making peace through the blood of his cross in all things, whether on earth or in heaven (Col. 1:18–20)—the only-begotten Son of the Father, I say, who forgave us all our offenses and erased the bond of the decree that stood against us and was wholly opposed to us, taking it out of the way and fastening it to the cross (Col. 2:14), poured the sweetest sweetness from its most bitter bitterness (Isa. 38:17) into all the most grievous forms of punishment suffered by the saints.

Through the illumination of the spirit, he transferred punishments of every degree and kind, endured by sanctified flesh, into the sweetest and most health-giving delights and remedies of body and soul. Thus, as though the order of nature had been changed and reversed, all the instruments of torment applied to the bodies of the elect are desired more eagerly than the most exquisite banquets and the richest pleasures of the whole world; and, for their acquisition and veneration, riches acquired with the greatest labor and danger and destined to perish in an instant are prodigally expended.

[Note: “Are prodigally expended.” All histories are full of this devotion and of this zeal for the holy relics. Take an example from chapter five, which now follows.]

## CHAPTER V. That nothing precious in the world can be compared with the crosses of Peter and Andrew, and with Paul’s chain

[Col. 0396B]

For what treasure, what precious stone, what garment of elaborate workmanship can be compared with the holy cross, and with the bonds of Peter, prince of the apostolic order, crucified with his feet inverted in incomparable humility? What wealth of the passing world can be set beside the cross of his brother Andrew, manly both in name and grace? What kind of exceptional metal can be equated with the chain of Paul, teacher and master of the nations, whose praise Gregory—the most lucid and vigilant interpreter and contemplator of religious theory—set down for the devout Empress Constantia, most ardent lover of that same *spermologus* (“seed-word gatherer”)?

[Note: “*Spermologi*.” The philosophers at Athens called the Apostle Paul thus; the old translator rendered it *seminiverbius* (“seed-word man”), Acts 17:18.]

[Note: “To Empress Constantina.” It should be corrected to “Constantia,” from the passage itself in Gregory, *Register*, Book II, Epistle 30.]

Gregory says:

> “Of the chains which the holy Paul himself wore around his neck and on his hands, from which many miracles are displayed among the people, I shall hasten to send you some portion, if indeed I can remove it by filing. For since many frequently seek a blessing from the same chains, so that they may receive a little of the filings, a priest stands by with a file, and when some ask for it, a little is struck off so quickly that there is no delay. But when others make the request, the file is drawn for a long time over the chains themselves, and yet it does not succeed in bringing out anything.”

[Col. 0396C]

What a splendid and excellent thing this is: through that distinguished apostle, the special instrument of the Paraclete, the proclamation of apostolic suffering, the merit of his magnificent spirit and body is made manifest! It is certainly worthy of the highest veneration and wonder that an iron file, devised and fashioned by subtle human art to strike off and abrade metal, while a priest of God, with the highest supplication and fitting reverence, stands beside that supremely chosen vessel, polished to the finest point, and with the ecclesiastical order, can strike off nothing except when, and as much as, and for those to whom the indulgence and overflowing kindness of apostolic favor grant it.

O how much more precious than refined gold is the apostolic chain, through which the iron hardness of the nations was bound, drawn toward the knowledge of the Lord God of Hosts, and made firm in the Catholic faith!

**CHAPTER VI. On the stones of the protomartyr Stephen and the griddle of Lawrence**

But what should be inferred from the stones of the torrent with which the protomartyr Stephen was overwhelmed for the crown of his name? What should be thought of the iron griddle upon which Lawrence was burned and, having received the most glorious laurel, acquired his name? The suffering of both has been turned into the remedy and consolation of the whole world, and by the merit of those who pray with inward heart and steadfast faith, it liberates bodies and souls from suffering.

The equal merit of both was distributed by an equal grace of divine dispensation into the unequal suffering of each; the instrument of dissimilar punishment became, through its benefit, alike for the world, and a great cause of rejoicing for angels and human beings. In each of these members of supreme beauty and holiness, Christ the Lord, the head of the elect, suffered: in the one, struck down by a mass of stone; in the other, placed upon burning coals, roasted as the paschal fish.

[Note: “The paschal fish.” He alludes to the fish placed upon the coals in John 21:19. Through it Thiofridus intends Christ, following several ancient Fathers, such as Augustine, *Tractate* 123 on John; Gregory, *Homily* 24; and likewise Jerome, Origen, and Tertullian.]

And therefore, just as he provided, arranged, and consecrated the cross of his saving passion, so also, from the most sacred chalice of his passion—from wine seasoned with “must of pomegranates” (Song of Songs 8:2)—he provided, arranged, and consecrated the suffering of both, which had been inebriated by that wine, for the salvation of all who merit it.

And who would not judge any fragment, however small, of the hard stones touched—and indeed stained, or rather consecrated—by the blood of the protomartyr Stephen to be of far greater value than, in the historical sense, the covering and ornament of the prince of Tyre (Ezek. 28:13), namely, the splendor of the twelve stones arranged under the Law in four rows upon the breastpiece of the high priest, mystically disposed so as to dazzle and blind the eyes of the covetous mind? (Exod. 39:8 ff.)

Those are indeed precious stones, instruments and incitements of joy-producing greed; these, truly taken from the torrent, are defenses and bulwarks against spiritual wickedness, and victorious arrows of David’s victory (1 Sam. 17:40). The brilliance of the former darkens the mind’s vision and arouses fraternal and friendly hearts to mutual slaughter; the hardness of the latter, with one mystical blow, overcomes the hostile Goliath, savage and strong, protected by terrifying weapons, and throws into confusion, puts to flight, tramples down, and destroys the entire camp of the Philistines—that is, of the opposing power (ibid., 49–53). Driving every discord from hostile hearts, it binds them with the tightest bonds of friendship and charity, and reconciles them to God, who gives peace upon peace.

Through this rain, as it were, of stones, hardness was shattered and the arid earth of hearts was drenched. And Saul, rushing forth in the morning with wolfish fury and devouring his prey (Gen. 49:27), once struck down, changed his name and his merit; then, raised up as Paul, the vessel of election, in the evening divided the spoils of evangelical preaching among all the nations.

[Note: “Saul, rushing in the morning with wolfish fury.” He took this from Augustine; do not be reluctant to read this elegant allegory there, *Sermon* 14, “On the Saints.”] Thrice beaten with rods and once stoned (2 Cor. 11:25), and having undergone every danger of human affliction by land and sea, in his most bitter old age he paid the penalty for having, as a rash young man, guarded the bundles of clothing; and, by returning them all, he cast through every hand of those who stoned him stones—innumerable living stones (1 Pet. 2:4), spiritual and precious—founded upon the foundation that is Christ Jesus, and carried and transferred them into the building of the heavenly court.

[Note: “He cast stones through every hand.” Augustine is the source of this passage; in the same work you may read this elegant allegory, *Sermon* 14, “On the Saints.”]

Plainly, the material of such stones is to be venerated and desired with the greatest devotion: it joined the protomartyr more intimately to Christ Jesus, the supreme cornerstone (1 Pet. 2:6), and through his distinguished examples and merits transferred countless thousands of martyrs—hewn stones destined to construct the wall of the heavenly Jerusalem, “which is built as a city” (Ps. 121:3), where neither axe nor hammer is heard (1 Kings 6:7)—into places appropriate to the merits of each. They had been trained by adversity and the discipline of truth and polished to the perfection of the finest finish, and they were arranged according to the most orderly disposition.

And what price does the roasted fish with honeycomb (Luke 24:42), the most exquisite paschal food of Christ the Lamb, possess in itself through the merit of the outstanding martyr Lawrence’s griddle? What, I ask, can anyone set beside it in material value? For that very griddle, concerning which the magnificent proclamation was made—“As far as Rome can be hidden, so far can Lawrence’s crown be hidden”—that griddle, I say, like gold smelted in fire, tested and purified sevenfold (Ps. 12:6), and by its immeasurable example provoking people of both sexes to its number, kindled by the flames of more ardent faith and charity, sent an incomparable and most precious treasure into the treasury of the King of kings and Lord of lords.

One exceedingly tiny fragment of so great an iron griddle certainly surpasses—indeed, incomparably surpasses—everything that is the delusion of the human mind in its insatiable desire for material pleasures.

And from where does this overflowing grace abound, from where does such glory pour forth, except from the inconceivable and ineffable munificence of the Creator’s *hyle* and *aplanes*?

[Note: “The Creator’s *hyle* and *aplanes*.” In Greek, *hyle* (ὕλη) means “matter”; *aplanes* (ἀπλανής) means the star-bearing heaven. See Macrobius, Book I of *The Dream of Scipio*, chapters 6 and 9.]

For he who works all things in all (1 Cor. 12:6), who mystically and tropologically compares the condition of human existence, through the mouth of grieving and lamenting Job, to ships carrying apples (Job 9:26)—since, when the natural goods born within them are restrained by the mystery of the most glorious cross, they carry apples, as it were, upon the wood—he, I say, poured into the elect, into whatever material suffering they may undergo, as we briefly indicated above, from the root of that most precious wood, the *stauros* of salvation, as though through a fruit-bearing trunk into its branches, the sap and fruit that are the price of human salvation. Thus, just as nothing in the nature of all things can be compared with so great a gallows, so nothing can be compared with the sufferings of those who, bearing the marks of Jesus in their bodies (Gal. 6:17), deserved, on the altar of passion, to be an acceptable sacrifice to the Lord God, and a rich and most pleasing burnt offering.

He himself became their way. He walked upon the sea (Matt. 14:25), to show that “there is a way in the sea” (Wis. 14:3), but one accessible to no one except him who travels in a ship, is carried upon wood—namely, the Lord’s cross. Just as, through the death of the only-begotten Son of God, the death of all God’s elect is precious (Ps. 116:15), so through his saving suffering all their sufferings have been made saving and consecrated for the honor and glory of God.

Just as, through the dipping of his most holy body in the Jordan (Matt. 3:16), he conveyed sanctification into all waters everywhere destined for baptism, so, through the fastening of that same body of his to the gallows of the cross, he transferred the salvation and redemption of souls and bodies into all the material sufferings of the saints.

And this faith, founded upon the rock that is Christ (1 Cor. 10:4), holds with complete certainty, without any hesitation, that all these praises which we have traced with the pen concerning the sufferings of a few of the most excellent nobles of heaven and earth can rightly and fittingly be applied to stocks, poles, brooms, scourges, racks, and, finally, to every kind of torture belonging to all the elect of God. Through the merits of those whom these instruments conveyed as peace offerings and marrow-filled, rich burnt offerings into the sanctuaries of the heavenly tabernacle and temple, they deserved to become saving remedies for every kind of human weakness.

[Note: “Stocks,” that is, wooden implements. On these instruments of torture, see Antonio Gallonio’s distinctive and elegant little book.]

**CHAPTER VII. How, enticed by desire, the author of this little book dared to apply his feeble hand to this most difficult subject**

But because, while gathering fragrant flowers with which to weave garlands and plucking the epitaphs of God’s elect, I have wandered on too long, I turn again to myself the distich of the Mantuan poet:

> You who gather flowers and strawberries growing on the ground,  
> Flee hence, O boys: a cold serpent lies hidden in the grass.

And lest, walking barefoot like Orpheus’s Eurydice, the physical sense and musical arrangement be endangered by the serpent’s bites, I intend to bring this long labor to an end.

Before, however, I sing with a joyful heart the *celeuma* of the expected shore, holding the tambourine with Mary (Exod. 15:20) and joining in the song of victory before the Israelite people, I must first briefly and most truthfully explain why and from what source I was so drawn and enticed by desire that I dared to apply my very feeble hand to a subject of the greatest difficulty, one which has scarcely been attempted even by the most eminent intellects of the age; and, trusting in the inspiration of the Creator of all spirits and of the Lord, the Holy Spirit Paraclete, presumed to hoist the sails and, with his benevolent charity and favor guiding the helm, entrust the ship of my mind to the pursuing waves of Malea.

[Note: “To the pursuing waves of Malea.” Malea is a promontory in Laconia, projecting far out into the sea and notorious for frequent shipwrecks, so that it gave rise to a proverb. Virgil, *Aeneid* V:

> … and the following waves of Malea.

Thiofridus is certainly referring to this passage.]

Therefore, Reginbertus, abbot of the sacred church of Echternach, the chief mystery of that same boundless Spirit, governed according to the etymology of his name

[Note: “Abbot Regimbertus.” This abbot immediately preceded our Thiofridus, as I have already noted on Book I, chapter 6.]

 with the highest excellence in the purpose and governance of holy religion—when he was often lifted by the very lofty flight of contemplation and balanced toward the heavens by the swift impulse of his mind, like an eagle—suddenly, weighed down by the fetter of human condition, flew downward from the heights and inclined and fixed that same inward gaze, which he was accustomed to direct toward the rays of the eternal sun, upon the sight of flesh indeed dead, but glorified through the merits of the soul that gives life; and he sought food in a sanctified corpse (Job 39:30).

As though after flight, the spiritual eagle sought the earth in order to consume flesh, coming, as it were, from the highest things to the lowest. He sought to consider and scrutinize, with the eager devotion of his soul and the perceptiveness of his exceedingly keen intellect, how precious is the death of the saints (Ps. 116:15), by which he desired to be refreshed and restored to life; and likewise how abundantly the riches and delights of divine power and activity overflow in their limbs, examined and resolved back into their origin, and in all their appendages, both substantial and accidental.

The true Israelite did not disdain to eat the mystical victims. Having mystically removed the victim’s skin and cut its limbs into pieces (Lev. 1:6), he ate, amid blessed labors happier than those of the blessed, the work of his hands (Ps. 128:2); and, abundantly refreshed by the food of inward nourishment, he belched forth a good word (Ps. 45:1) through the grace of the incarnate Word.

For everything inserted in the pages of this little book he conceived through the inspiration of the Spirit Paraclete and entrusted to me, the last of his followers and most unworthy of the dust of his feet, as certain seeds to be winnowed in the field of the mind and, after the winnowing fan of the most subtle examination, to be sown.

[Note: “Through the inspiration of the Holy Spirit.” From this, see how highly this work must be esteemed. There is no reason to regard this testimony of the excellent man concerning an excellent man as fiction, especially since we know him to have been an outstanding cultivator of humility.]

Through the wisdom poured more abundantly by the Lord God into the sanctuary of his soul, he considered and weighed that, as the end of the world approaches and sin increases, Leviathan (Job 21:33), the adversary of the human race, who will drag behind him every person living carnally and before him—before his entrance into the man of eternal perdition—draws countless people to destruction, though not all of them carnal, since some escape from his jaws through brief, and others through lengthy, labors of repentance, as the bracelet of divine mercy pierces his jaw (Job 40:21). He considered, I say, that destruction and eternal perdition press upon and threaten our ruin with an envy all the more bitter because they know more swiftly approaching the time when, brought out from the pit of the abyss (Rev. 20:3, 7), Leviathan will pour out every serpentine poison through a vast, foul, and deadly gaping mouth, so that, awake among the heap of the dead and seeing his graves all around him (Ezek. 32:22), he may rejoice and triumph in the countless number of the condemned and of those whom he has caused to perish along with himself.

He considered and observed how many weapons and protections of auxiliaries are needed against the aerial powers and phalanxes that wage an unceasing and unappeasable war against the soul. He reflected on how just and inescapable is the vengeance owed by the God of vengeance (Ps. 94:1) for our negligences, because no special thanksgiving, no fitting and deserved honor, is rendered in particular for the immense benefits of those whose individual daughters of the universal Church—of whom it is mystically sung in the *Song for the Beloved*, “Virgins shall be brought to the King after her” (Ps. 45:15)—although their names are unknown, are more familiarly governed and sustained by their merits and intercessions for the sake of the pledges entrusted to them.

Thus, pondering and trembling at the judgment of divine equity, and wishing, like the creature full of eyes before and behind (Rev. 4:6), to foresee and provide from afar what was most necessary for human need amid so many intolerable troubles—the intercession of God’s elect—in the year of the incarnate Word 1059, in the twelfth indiction, and in the fourth year of the reign of our lord Henry IV, king and third emperor, and in the ninth year of his own holy ordination,

[Note: “In the year of the incarnate Word 1059.” The year of Christ agrees correctly with the stated indiction and the emperor’s year. Baronius, however, holds that the Western Empire was then vacant for several years and recognizes Henry only as king.]

he shared the mystery of his counsel with the leaders of the small congregation entrusted to his care, men of the highest religion and prudence (Judith 2:2).

[Note: “Of the small congregation.” He uses *conciolae* as a novel form in place of *conciunculae*. He means the congregation itself.]

With the joyful consent and applause of all of them and of the entire holy community, he established and confirmed the decree of the Holy Spirit: that on the thirteenth day before the Kalends of December, on which night the distinguished pope Sergius of eminent merit was admonished by an angelic revelation

[Note: “The distinguished pope Sergius was admonished.” The same pontiff learned by divine revelation of the death of Saint Lambert the martyr and the succession of Saint Hubert, as I explain in this History.]

—to grant with the greatest readiness of spirit whatever in ecclesiastical ornaments and the patronage of the saints might please Willibrord, a man of outstanding holiness who would arrive in Rome four days later and be raised to the highest episcopal dignity—on that day, I say, throughout all succeeding ages, the evening and morning sacrifice should be offered with solemn and magnificent rite in the most celebrated commemoration and more intimate service of all those through whom such heavenly consolation and such an immeasurable and incomparable price of safety had then and afterward been provided and conveyed to that most sacred church.

He did not undertake so great a matter and so great a salvation through his own presumptuous devotion, as it were, but through the illumination and divine revelation of the Spirit Paraclete, as we have already indicated.

[Col. 0402B]

For while, during the period of his novitiate, the custody of the Church had been entrusted to him, as a man of the highest chastity and purity, after long watches of vigil, after offering the calves of his lips upon the altar of his heart, he was overcome by the weakness of human nature and fell asleep. Like the lawgiver Moses, who typologically represented the integrity of the *Theotokos* Mary—“the most beautiful rose” destined to arise from the thorns of the Israelite people and to give birth to “the lily of the valleys”—and who marveled at the bush as it seemed to burn and yet remain unconsumed (Exod. 3:2), so he too, with an equally typological significance, was deemed worthy to see a wondrous vision.

[Note: “Theoticos.” A corrupt form in place of Θεοτόκου, that is, “of the Mother of God.”]

For, raised up and taken away by the grace of the Holy Spirit, he saw in a vision of the Lord a flame gradually growing from the chamber of the sacred shrine in which the treasure of relics of inestimable value was stored in a more intimate and abundant manner; and he saw the flame, harmless to the touch and mystical,

[Note: “Fire harmless to the touch.” When Thiofridus wrote this, he had in mind these verses of Virgil, *Aeneid* II:

> Behold, a light flame was seen from the crown of Iulus  
> Pouring forth light, and a harmless fire  
> Gently licking his soft hair and feeding around his temples.

]

fly out through the ceiling and roof of the holy enclosure and reach the citadel of the heavenly palace, where all the souls of the elect, clothed in white robes (Rev. 7:9), reign most gloriously with the King of everlasting glory.

This man of exceptionally penetrating intellect saw it; the inward hearer of God’s words saw it. Having beheld the vision of the Almighty (Num. 24:4), with Daniel, the man of desires, he languished and was sick for days (Dan. 8:27)—not with bodily illness, but with holy longing. Astonished at the sight, he set his face toward the Lord God of heaven to pray and plead (Dan. 9:3), in the harshness of sackcloth and the frugality of a salutary and medicinal fast.

And the Lord God, the desire of the eternal hills (Gen. 49:26), granted him the desire of his soul and did not withhold from him the request of his lips (Ps. 21:3). Establishing him in his station and upon his feet through the entrance of the Holy Spirit into him (Dan. 8:18), he strengthened him. Then, having strengthened him, the essentially good Shepherd, who laid down his life for his sheep (John 10:15), entrusted his flock, in the mountains of Israel and in exceedingly rich pastures (Ezek. 34:14), to be fed by a good shepherd whose goodness was an accidental gift of his own.

Thus, from an outstanding guardian of the material Church’s goods and ornaments, he was chosen, seized, and transferred to the custody and governance of the spiritual Church. Made one spirit with the guardian of all spirits, of whom the prophetic mouth repeats:

> “Watchman, what of the night? Watchman, what of the night?” (Isa. 21:11)

he set before the eyes of his mind the example of that Samaritan (Luke 10:30 ff.) who, moved by mercy, pitied the human race as it descended from the heavenly Jerusalem, the vision of peace, into Jericho—the loss of inward light—and was wounded by robbers.

[Note: “In Jericho, the loss of inward light.” He refers to the name Jericho, which in Hebrew signifies “moon,” whose borrowed light is often diminished.]

Approaching through the mystery of his incarnation, he bound up its wounds with the hand of supreme tenderness and inward compassion; bearing its sins and paying their penalty in his body upon the wood (1 Pet. 2:24), he placed it upon his own beast and led it into an inn. There he entrusted to the innkeeper—namely, the apostolic order, endowed through the grace of the Spirit Paraclete and the illumination of heavenly medicine with excellent knowledge for this purpose—the two denarii inscribed with the character of the eternal King, that is, the two Testaments of the Law and the Gospel, or the two commandments of charity, to be expended with the utmost care for healing the wounded man’s wounds.

Our excellent Samaritan, the guardian of souls, the breath of our mouth, of whom we said, “Under your shadow we shall live among the nations” (Lam. 4:20), set before himself this model of such great mercy and compassion, to imitate it and transmit it to posterity by his example. He devised and supplied the most excellent remedy of heavenly medicine for healing the wounds of the Lord’s flock; and he provided and appointed so many holy watchers and guardians over the custody of his familiar Church as he judged should receive special honor and reverence for the pledges of God’s elect buried there.

Finally, imitating Boniface IV, fourth after the most watchful Gregory in the apostolic see—Boniface, who, after consecrating the Pantheon, proclaimed the most celebrated solemnity of All Saints—he granted and established that the festive day of special commemoration, as we stated above, should be celebrated with particular devotion and zeal throughout the whole succession of his holy congregation.

[Note: “The fourth Boniface, according to the most vigilant Gregory.” This was Boniface IV, who obtained the Pantheon from the emperor Phocas and consecrated it in honor of the Virgin Mother and the holy martyrs in the year of Christ 607. Thus Baronius, following Anastasius.]

He decreed that all those who throughout the circuit of the entire year were weighed down, bound by the cords of forgetful negligence, in the worthy and fitting services owed to their special holy patrons should, by redeeming the time (Eph. 5:16), be freed from the evil of the day (Matt. 6:34) through the multiplied patronage and intercessions of their most intimate advocates, and should be expiated by the one saving victim of one most celebrated festival; and that they might deserve to be enrolled and transferred into the senate of the heavenly court, where an unending festival is celebrated with inconceivable and ineffable rejoicing.

Therefore, considering the example of the supreme patriarch Abraham’s supreme humility, an inheritance for all who are blessed in his seed, in Christ our Lord—Abraham, I say, who rejoiced that he would see the day of his Lord, his seed, and saw it and rejoiced (John 8:56)—yet, after the inward revelation and contemplation of undivided unity and undivided Trinity, spoke with humble mouth and suppliant voice:

> “I shall speak to my Lord, although I am dust and ashes” (Gen. 18:27).

Let us return to ourselves; let us set ourselves before ourselves; let us look upon and contemplate our disgrace. Let us recognize that we are soft and utterly worthless clay, unclean ashes; and let us render due honor and service to the life-giving ashes of the saints and to everything whatsoever that pertains to them, whether substantially or accidentally.

And because from them the highest rejoicing arises, and upon them the salvation of the human race depends, let us pour out all the marrow of our hearts into their glory and praise, so that afterward, when we have become worms and been reduced to dust, through the continual and most devoted intercession of them all, we may deserve to pass from mortality to immortality and from corruption to incorruption—through the favor and provision of our propitiator, whose flesh, assumed from the incorrupt and undefiled flesh of the *Theotokos* for the redemption and restoration of our soul and flesh, did not see corruption (Acts 2:31); who, by abolishing enmity in his flesh (Eph. 2:14–16; 3:7) and erasing the bond of the ancient offense, established our flesh in himself, according to the working of his mighty power, at the right hand of the Father in the heavenly places, above every principality, authority, power, and dominion (Eph. 1:20–21).

**Praise be to God and to the Virgin Mother**

**Two Sermons of Thiofridus, Abbot**

(They are extant in the *Bibliotheca Patrum* of Lyon, volume XII, page 417, among the monuments of the eighth century. See the literary notice on Thiofridus above.)

**FIRST SERMON. ON THE RELICS OF THE SAINTS**

[Col. 0405A]

Let us praise the Lord, wondrous in his saints, but even more wondrous in their relics; for although he is great in great things, yet, glorious, he works wonders in the smallest. It is not enough for him to glorify the souls of the saints in the realm of eternal happiness unless he also glorifies their relics during this pilgrimage. Nor is it sufficient that he grant them the delights of immortality unless he also bestow upon them the riches of the whole world. For towns and castles, villages and cities—all of which great princes once possessed—are now possessed by the small quantity of the saints’ dust; an abundance of worldly goods lies subject to their relics. Their souls rejoice in the heavenly palace, while their relics are exalted in the world subject to them.

[Col. 0405B] They can never be buried so deeply in the earth’s bowels that, through the effects of miracles, they do not shine above the earth more brightly than the sun itself. He has given them to the peoples of the various provinces and cities for consolation, so that, while they are hard-pressed by the relentless attacks of visible and invisible enemies, they may be defended through their merit. For any king intending to defend the walls of a city, the more numerous and bolder he discovers the enemy forces to be, the stronger and more numerous are the soldiers’ breasts he sets against them in the fortifications. So too God, seeing the multitude of our enemies flying throughout the air and devising a manifold battle against the children of his adoption, mercifully provides for human misery; and, multiplying his patronages upon the sand, he guards and protects his city, that is, the Church.

[Col. 0405C] To each place, as also to this one of ours, he generously assigns great relics of the saints, so that, while they are honored worthily and more familiarly by the local inhabitants, those same inhabitants may be strengthened by their perpetual protection. Wherever on earth any part of them exists, they have the nature of lamps; and lamps, wherever they may be, cannot be hidden, but spread the radiance of their light far and wide. For no one lights a lamp and puts it in a hidden place, or under a bushel, but upon a lampstand, so that those who enter may see the light (Luke 11). The relics of the saints are lamps that have been lit; although the holy teachers also teach us to understand that the Lamp itself of the Holy of Holies was not hidden from believers, nor placed under a bushel—that is, enclosed within the measure of the Law and confined within the boundaries of the single nation of Judea.

[Col. 0405D] These lamps, I say, lit by that Lamp of eternal salvation, are not placed in a hidden place or under a bushel—

[Col. 0406A] that is, they are not placed without honor in some unsuitable or unknown location. They are nowhere permitted to remain concealed, but are openly set upon the lampstand, which is Christ and the Church, so that those who enter may see the light of faith and divine knowledge. They may see the light, I say, when they observe the relics of the saints flashing with miracles, and may understand how wondrous God is and how great is his compassion. But if the relics of the saints were hidden and were not illuminated by signs of their powers, what would rouse the hard and stony human heart to desire heavenly things? What would renew it from vices to virtues? What rewards could a person hope for if he did not see those whom he knew to have been most righteous in their life preserved in memory? And how could one who now scarcely advances toward the worship and love of God, who now scarcely shakes off the torpor of unbelief, be moved, while he sees the relics of God’s elect illuminated by the grace of miracles?

[Col. 0406B] Indeed, the edifice of the holy faith grew through miracles, and, when they ceased, declined among certain peoples. For unless the holy preachers shone forth through miracles, they would preach the word of life in vain. And although signs are not for believers but for unbelievers (1 Cor. 14), nevertheless the faith of believers is strengthened by signs, whether they have heard that such signs were performed by the holy Fathers or see them being performed before their own eyes through their relics. Truly, the relics of the saints, the lamps of the world, spread the radiance of their brightness farther, and, as we have said, the merits of those to whom they belong never allow them to lie neglected in obscurity.

O marvelous mercy of divine compassion! O ineffable condescension toward the relics of the saints! God is the Holy One of holies, and the assembly of the saints is God’s dwelling. Their relics are not of little but of the greatest value in his sight; he exalts them above all the adornment of the world. Indeed, no precious stone can compare with their excellence; rather, whatever is precious among created things is judged most worthless in comparison with them. They are the fortifications of lands, the tokens of eternal recompense, and proofs of divine greatness. For it is evident from unmistakable judgments how great God’s magnificence is, since the relics of the saints possess such glory.

[Col. 0406C] For if human things may be compared with divine things, if small things may be compared with great, whoever sees the servants of some temporal lord can discern in them how great the dignity of that lord himself is. If the servants are powerful and rich, he is believed to be richer and endowed with far greater power under whose dominion they stand. Thus one may discern how great divine majesty and greatness are, when it is seen that, by his freely given gift, such brightness and power have been granted to the relics of the saints.

[Col. 0406D] For, to use the eloquent words of the most illustrious Father Gregory, the sick come to their dry bones and are healed; the perjured come and are tormented by a demon; the possessed come and are freed; lepers come and are cleansed; the dead are carried there and are raised. To consider, from one example, what should be understood concerning all: through the bones of the prophet Elisha a dead man came back to life—blessed is God in all things. The bones of Elisha gave life to the dead man and released him from the danger of death. Therefore, after the death of the flesh, the saints of God live more fully, whose bones here live through so many miracles.

[Col. 0407A] Concerning these wondrous bones of the saints the truthful prophet says: “And your bones shall sprout like grass” (Isa. 66). Although the bones of the saints wither according to mortal condition, they nevertheless sprout like grass through the greenness of their virtues, although, as divine Scripture asserts, this will be fulfilled more perfectly in the general resurrection. In that well-ordered house of God, so vast as though belonging to a master of a household, the elect are believed to have been and to be vessels of honor (Rom. 9); therefore their relics are stored in vessels of gold and silver, in jeweled vessels, and in everything that is precious.

[Col. 0407B] And just as a holy altar is not sanctified by gold but sanctifies it, so also any vessel that contains within itself the treasure of holy relics does not give but receives the grace of healings; and when it is touched—as though what lies within were touched as well—it drives away many kinds of illnesses. The hostile phalanx of invisible beings cannot stand before them; it groans, recognizing itself confounded and defeated. He who boasted that he would set his throne upon the mountain of assembly, on the sides of the north, and make himself like the Most High (Isa. 14), is overcome by the dispersed dust of the saints and bound with fiery chains.

[Col. 0407C] Although this dust is dispersed and insignificant, it nevertheless rules the powers of this air. It is rightly honored by all mortals, small and great, because just as heat is inseparably implanted in the nature of fire, so holiness is established in them. If they were to lose the gift of holiness, they would likewise lose the name of saints. They possess holiness through an added gift, but they do not lose that same holiness, because immortality does not pass over into mortality.

O how magnified are the works of the Lord; exceedingly deep have the thoughts of our God become (Ps. 9). The relics of the saints are like precious spices and fragrant fruits: if anyone handles them, his hands receive their fragrance. They smell, I say, like lilies and precious spices, filling the nostrils of mortals with the sweetness of a marvelous scent. For God divided the light from the darkness by a great separation (Gen. 1)—that is, the devout from the impious, and the bones of the less perfect from the relics of the saints.

## SERMON II. ON THE VENERATION OF THE SAINTS

The Christian religion derives its name from Christ so that a Christian may always remember how the glory of so great a dignity is to be preserved, lest what the tongue proclaims in the name appear discordant with what is done in practice. But the virtue of holy charity, which once adorned the worship of faith in the Fathers, has declined in their children as the world grows old and sin increases; indeed, it has so dissipated in individuals that its trace can scarcely be recognized in its pastures.

[Col. 0408A] Foreseeing the dangers of this peril, the grace of our most merciful Redeemer displays the treasures of Holy Scripture and sets before us the examples of the saints, so that piety may always shine forth in action and the remedy of doctrine may never grow slack upon the tongue. Since, therefore, brothers, we have the examples of the saints as an utterly reliable antidote, may the virtue of holy charity be restored in us, so that through us God may worthily be praised in his saints.

Let us therefore praise the Lord in his saints, who is the glory and strength of the saints (Ps. 150), so that through his mercy we may be able to reach their fellowship. In the memory of the righteous, let us magnify the author of righteousness; in the merits of the saints, let us magnify the giver of holiness. For “the memory of the righteous shall be with praises” (Prov. 10), in which God and their Lord takes delight, so that through their intercession he may have mercy on our transgressions.

[Col. 0408B] Like the faithful Moses, they have been appointed mediators between us and God, so that we who are despised because of our own merits, like the Pharisee, may be justified through their justification, like the Publican (Luke 18). We believe that they have great power with God, since they placed nothing in this world before his love. Fulfilling in all things not their own will but that of the heavenly Father, they deserved, by the merit of Jesus, both to be called and to be his brothers and sisters (Matt. 12). No degenerate pride weakened the line of this kinship; rather, holy humility ennobled it through generations and generations.

[Col. 0408C] In the sight of God, brothers, the saints always displayed such meditation of heart that they could arrest the passing Son of David for the spiritual illumination of the mind. The holiness of their virtues did not fail; truth was not diminished upon their lips. A heavenly coal purified their lips (Isa. 6), and the Holy Spirit animated their words with the flame of its own ardor. They were not counted among sinners in the works of their hands (Ps. 9), for they showed every kindness to the least of the Lord, as faithful people.

With blessed Job, they were an eye to the blind and a foot to the lame (Job 29); in the burial of the dead they were found no inferior to Tobias (Tob. 12). Their prayer pierced the clouds (Ecclus. 35); through fasting and almsgiving it flew up to heaven and filled the bowls of the twenty-four elders (Rev. 5), becoming a fragrant offering before the throne of God’s majesty.

[Col. 0408D] The labor of life weighed down the corruption of the flesh; the purity of their actions purified the soul’s freedom. They lived as friends of piety, made a spectacle through works of piety to God and human beings (1 Cor. 4). They scattered these seeds of action upon the threshing-floor of the active life, so that they might fill the granary of the contemplative life in the vision of heavenly peace. They did not pour out the treasure of faith, which they possessed in earthen vessels, in worldly affairs, but placed it in the treasury of the heavenly King, where no loss lies hidden; for when the spirit had cast off the covering of flesh, it flew freely and unencumbered to heaven.

[Col. 0409A] The Church, which is seen in the passing course of the uncertain world, nourished sons proven in good works, whom the heavenly Bride, remaining above the stars, received. Coming out of Egypt—that is, from the darkness of sins—they came through the pillar of cloud into the promised land, which is the homeland for which they daily yearned while still held captive in the pilgrimage of this life. There is the dwelling toward which the desire of the faithful is directed, who carry God in their minds as long as they are held in the prison of the flesh.

O how happy the city where no captivity reigns! Whoever has hastened to it by the steps of virtue has ceased to be a captive forever. Its structure consists of living stones, which peace and concord have joined together, with the rejected stone made the head of the corner (Ps. 117). No storm of adversity can shake it, for its foundation (Rev. 21) has been laid upon an immovable rock.

[Col. 0409B] It needs no lamp for its light, for its brightness is that cornerstone, the rock of the foundation, the Lamb who takes away the sins of the world (John 1). He is also the bridegroom, who reigns in this tabernacle: God with human beings. Before his throne the spirits and souls of the righteous resound with song. He himself is their praise and exultation; he crowns them with joy, and through him those who have run well in the racecourse of this world are rewarded in heaven with a worthy prize.

They have nothing more to desire, where they behold God face to face, the one who brought them to the palm of victory, to which the King of Glory himself went before them. The dignity of their blessedness surpasses the measure of human understanding; indeed, it is what “has not entered into the heart of man, what God has prepared for them” (Isa. 64; 1 Cor. 2).

[Col. 0409C] Let the piety of the faithful therefore determine what veneration is especially owed to the bodies of the saints, whose spirits are honored by God with immeasurable glory. Let us celebrate their praise on earth with devotion proportionate to the greater merit we believe them to possess in heaven. What their souls can do with God is shown every day by the limbs of their lifeless bodies. Whatever nature denies, or unforeseen circumstance weakens in human beings, divine mercy restores at their tombs.

They illumine the blind, strengthen the steps of the lame, restore tongues, open ears, command demons, open prisons, loosen bonds, raise the fallen, correct the unjust, and love the just. These things are performed through the bodies of spirits who now stand in the divine presence.

[Col. 0409D] Is it surprising that those established in the glory of immortality can do such things, when they could do similar things while clothed in mortality? We read and believe, brothers, that God, wondrous in his saints, performed many works through the saints in this life (Ps. 67). Let us set aside flesh and bones and speak of lesser things, things inferior to flesh. We offer a few examples so that the faith of those who doubt may be strengthened by many.

Peter’s shadow healed all the sick who were placed in the streets (Acts 5). Paul’s handkerchiefs drove demons from possessed bodies (Acts 19); James’s cloth loosed Philetus.

[Col. 0410A] The forms of these bodies worked such powers of healing, so that the faith of believers might understand what the merit of the saints is like, and what their presence was capable of when their absence shone forth with such power. We would have many examples not only concerning the apostles but also concerning all the saints, if a lengthy discourse did not produce weariness.

What is surprising if the spiritual sons of Holy Mother Church possessed such great merit, when even the offspring of the carnal Synagogue shone with similar powers? In Egypt, Moses’ staff performed signs and wonders, and, under the appearance of baptism, divided the Red Sea (Exod. 14 [the printed citation reads “XLV”]). Elijah’s mantle doubled the spirit in Elisha, and that same garment divided the course of the Jordan (2 Kings 2).

[Col. 0410B] Under the Law and under grace God performed these miracles through the saints in the flesh, so that we might understand and faithfully hold what power their spirits possess with him.

Whatever relics of the saints we possess—whether in clothing, dust, or bones—let us guard them carefully and prudently, and let us offer whatever service we can especially to their veneration. They are worthy of honor among human beings, for they daily intercede for human salvation. Mindful of human weakness, the mercy of the Savior has bestowed this grace upon us: what we cannot obtain through our own merits as sinners, we may obtain through the patronage of the saints.

They are already secure concerning themselves, yet they are solicitous for our salvation; for their joy will not be complete as long as they see the exile of our pilgrimage, nor will their blessedness be perfect until the fullness of the entire Church has entered.

[Col. 0410C] Since it will be beautiful and joyful for us to dwell together in their fellowship (Ps. 129), the more we believe their prayer benefits us, the more devotedly let us offer veneration to their merits. Let us offer sacrifice to the Lord, so that, through the prayer of the saints, the smoke of incense may rise for us, presented to the divine presence by the hand of an angel (Rev. 8). Let us follow the footsteps of those who themselves followed the Lord. Let us walk along the path of righteousness so that we may reach the dwelling of the heavenly homeland.

Let us examine their perfect life, and correct what in our own is less well ordered, so that those whose imitators we are in our actions may be our helpers in our prayers. Let us leave everything with the apostles, so that we may freely follow the Lord’s footsteps. Let us join the martyrs in suffering, so that we may share with them in consolation.

[Col. 0410D] So that a thief may not break into our house (Luke 12), let our minds keep watch with the confessors. Let us adorn our lamps with the virgins, so that we may enter the wedding feast when the bridegroom comes, and so that the harshest declaration, “I do not know you” (Matt. 25)—which will be the confusion of the impious—may not terrify us; rather, may the blessing of the righteous gladden our hearts, through him who is life and resurrection, God of gods and Lord of lords, forever and ever. Amen.

[Col. 0411]

## FRAGMENTS OF THE DOUBLE LIFE OF ST. WILLIBRORD, WRITTEN BY THIOFRID, ABBOT OF ECHTERNACH

(Mabillon, *Acts of the Saints of the Order of St. Benedict*, Century III, part I, p. 629.)

### I. On the beginnings of the monastery of St. Willibrord

[Col. 0411A] Duke Pippin, of most excellent nobility, together with his wife Blitrude, who was likewise born of noble parentage, gave Blessed Willibrord the entire half of the fiscal estate of Echternach on the third day before the Ides of May, in the twelfth year of the most glorious King Childebert. This half had been conveyed to him by Theodard, son of Theothar, an outstanding duke. Irmina, however, daughter of King Dagobert (namely the second, as is thought), added the other half on the Kalends of December: she possessed it by hereditary right, together with all its appurtenances and adjacent lands, including the estate situated on the mountain in the district of Tulbiacum (at Zülpich, in the diocese of Cologne). Under a written deed, in the fourth year of King Dagobert, on the sixth day before the Nones of March, that same generous prince conveyed to him [Col. 0411B] an estate situated in the district of the Moselle people, called Suestra from the name of the river flowing past it, and acquired by the shrewd exertions of the excellent Blitrude from free men at the cost of money. Since the location of both places seemed pleasant to so wise an architect, and especially suitable and worthy for the pursuits of monastic life, he laid foundations in each and built a monastery; and on the mountains of Israel, in most fertile pastures, he assembled the Lord’s flock to be fed.

### II. On the translation of St. Willibrord, and on Frithelo, a count who became a monk

In the year 1031 from the birth of the Word, 292 years after the passing of that glorious Father, once the structure of the decayed chapel had been repaired, Abbot Himbert and the entire community resolved that, on the fourteenth day before the Kalends of November, after inviting the distinguished Poppo, archbishop of the holy see of Trier, and Henry, the glorious duke of Bavaria and defender, they would transfer his bones during the solemnities of the dedication to the place where they are today seen to rest with reverence and due honor. Monks distinguished in reputation and noble in their commitment to holy conduct were selected to seek out and excavate so precious a treasure. While, with the doors of the church locked, they were attempting to break through the pavement, one of them, named Thietmar, having forgotten that he had been deceived by a nocturnal apparition, felt his arms, as he was about to swing an axe, bound as if by divine power. Accordingly, astonished and anxious in mind, he was led by Provost Hubert into the inner sanctuary of a more private place [Col. 0412A] and was fatherly admonished to cleanse himself with the groans of a pure confession, if he were conscious of any crime. Since he hesitated and found that he had committed nothing new, he was ordered to go aside to the washing-place and carefully inspect his *sarabara* (that is, his garments). When he had done this and discovered his garments defiled, repentance entering his mind, he returned himself to the sacred work. After the earth had been removed and two crypts broken open, they found in a third the most sacred sarcophagus and a silken pall spread over it. Wonderful to relate: through so many centuries it had remained not merely uncorrupted, but beautiful and wholly intact, and to this day hangs as an ornament of God’s basilica—an evident testimony to the incorrupt life and merits of so great a bishop.

[Col. 0412B] Then Abbot Humbert came forward to distribute the relics [perhaps: to uncover them]; and, having raised the lid a little, he was granted sight of his beloved lord lying there in an uninjured cowl and hair-shirt, with almost his whole body intact, and exhaling such great fragrances as though he had been anointed with every ointment and spices were bubbling forth from his dead flesh in place of worms. He also put in his hand and, not without the greatest fear, drew out one of the holy man’s ribs. While the sarcophagus was carefully sealed and raised, and sacred vigils were being celebrated, a certain monk named Frithelo came up. Born of noble stock, he had laid aside the belt of worldly soldiery and, presenting before him two sons of outstanding promise, had submitted himself to the sweet yoke of the Lord’s service. He was wholly weakened in every joint, since his intestines had prolapsed and were hanging down at the boundary and edge of the privy. [Col. 0412C] Prostrate in deepest prayer, he offered sacrifice; rising, unknowingly he struck against the tomb, and without any delay, through that healing collision, his entrails returned to their place and he recovered his former health.

### III. On the same Frithelo, from Book IV of the metrical Life of St. Willibrord

While, renowned in warfare, he put on a soldier’s arms,

And, bearing standards, fiercely struck down enemies,

He fell from his horse and lay there, lamenting his prolapsed entrails.

[Note: [Col. 0411C] “To these times,” says Brower, “from whose Book II I have excerpted these passages, must be referred what Thiofrid wrote concerning another Frithelo, advocate of the monastery of Echternach. This man, possessing extensive holdings in the district of Beden, had shamefully harassed the possessions of St. Willibrord through himself and his men, and finally dared to provoke Adelbert, count of Namur, to war. But, routed in the first encounter, [Col. 0412D] he fled, to the great loss of his followers. The district of Beden was then plundered, and Frithelo was run through by a common soldier. His son-in-law Bertram, himself also an offender against the saint, lived out a miserable life.”]

[Col. 0413]

## RHYTHM ON ST. WILLIBRORD

(Dom Gerbert, *Writers on Music*, II, 121.)

[Col. 0413A]

On this present day

Let all the faithful everywhere

Celebrate Christ’s praises

With great rejoicing,

In veneration of the distinguished father,

Saint Willibrord.

A shining moon, descending from heaven, marked him out,

Which appeared to his mother in a heavenly vision.

Thus, like a most brilliant star,

He spread the ray of his radiance

Through the circuit of the world,

When by the splendor of the Word

He had driven from human hearts

The dark shadows of sin implanted there.

This the people of Britain and Ireland,

Together with all Frisia,

[Col. 0413B] This the Franks and Germans,

The peoples of Gaul, attest.

Nor did the renowned city of Romulus fail to know him,

Though powerful mistress of the world,

When the bishop, instructed by an angelic oracle,

[Col. 0414A] Consecrated him to the Lord.

Thereafter, kindled by fervor of faith,

He prudently broke the altars of demons.

A sword-stroke reached

His head, but did it no harm.

For water entrusted to his prayer

Thereafter gave drink to troops of many in a dry place.

Then he abundantly increased cups of wine;

He brought very many aids to the sick.

This true Israelite today

Escaped Egypt’s darkness,

Enriched with his neighbor’s spoils.

And coming faithfully with gain,

He deserved gladly to hear,

“Enter joyfully, well done.”

[Col. 0414B]

Come now, let us all devoutly ask him,

Singing and saying with mouth and heart:

“We who celebrate your feasts

With pious mind, O merciful one,

Mercifully help us always.”

## IN THE YEAR OF THE LORD 1107: PIBO, BISHOP OF TOUL

[Col. 0413]

## HISTORICAL NOTICE

(From the new edition of *Gallia Christiana*, vol. XIII, p. 991.)

[Col. 0413C] Pibo, or Poppo, was a Saxon by nation. His parents were noble by birth: his father Theotmar and his mother Duguerca, otherwise Udica. Under the master Anno, who later became archbishop of Cologne, he studied letters for six full years. He was first a canon in the church of Halberstadt, then at Mainz. Thereafter Emperor Henry IV honored him with the offices of almoner and chancellor. He came with that prince to Toul in the year 1070, at the very time when the election of a bishop was under discussion. Pibo’s full brother Bernard, a count, moved every influence with the emperor to have his brother advanced to episcopal rank. Indeed, when the canons learned the prince’s will, they unanimously elected Pibo bishop. The archbishop of Trier approved the election and, at the emperor’s request, consecrated the elect at Metz; [Col. 0414C] the bishops of Metz and Verdun assisted, accompanied the new bishop as far as Toul, and installed him in the episcopal see.

Ignorant of the language of the people of Toul, Pibo deeply lamented that he could not instruct the people entrusted to him in their native language. Yet, although already sixty years old, he applied himself so diligently to French that within less than a year he was able competently to teach his flock. In that same year, 1090, he confirmed to Abbot Adalbero of St. Benignus at Dijon the donations made by his predecessors. He received a letter from Pope Alexander II about the year 1072, in which the pontiff complained that Pibo wished to deprive the church of St. Maurice, situated at a place called Villa on the Blaise, of the same liberty which Pope Leo had granted to the people of Der: namely, that the monks living there should possess St. Maurice’s altar perpetually without any payment, except that the chaplain entrusted with care of the estate should pay a rent.

[Col. 0415A] In the same year Pibo granted many things to the monastery of St. Aper: namely, the altar of Blénod on the Moselle and the altar of Fains beyond the Meuse near the castle of Bar; he also confirmed everything which had been conveyed to that place by his predecessors or other donors. Moreover, in a synod he forbade any local lord to compel the monastery’s vassals to take up arms without the abbot’s consent, since only the abbot, or a monk designated by him, had the right to lead them into military service. On the fifth day before the Ides of October 1074, he settled a dispute concerning a portion of the estate of Bainville that had arisen between Wido, abbot of the same monastery of St. Aper, and the knight Odelric. At the request of that same Abbot Wido, in 1079 and the following year, [Col. 0415B] he approved all the properties conveyed to St. Aper by Burchard, Gauzlin, and Bruno. Together with Herman, bishop of Metz, at whose installation he was present in 1073, he was witness and arbiter of the agreement made on the third day before the Kalends of May of that year between Walo, abbot of St. Arnulf at Metz, and the abbess of Buxières. She was allowed to build a bridge over the river Meurthe, on condition that she pay the abbot an annual rent of twelve denarii. Pibo also issued letters in favor of the church of St. Deodatus.

In 1074 Pope Gregory VII appointed him, together with Udo, archbishop of Trier, and Herman, bishop of Metz, to urge Theodoric, bishop of Verdun, to lift the excommunication he had pronounced against the monks of St. Michael [Col. 0415C] because they had refused to attend a general supplication. Pibo granted a privilege to the monastery of St. Michael on the Meuse in 1076, the year in which a most serious charge was brought against him. A certain cleric, keeper of the church of Toul, lodged a complaint with the pope that the bishop had not only denied him a church dependent on the office of keeper, but had also suspended him from his functions. He further said that he had replied to the bishop that no obedience was owed him because he was guilty of simony. The keeper accused him of having sold archdeaconries, consecrations of churches, and the churches themselves; of living publicly with a concubine, whom he had joined to himself by an oath in the manner of laymen and by whom he had begotten a son; [Col. 0415D] and even of having purchased the bishopric for money. The cleric added that he and other canons had heard Pibo confess these crimes and say that he wished to do penance.

Burning with anger, Pibo was gravely enraged against the cleric and left the city. During his absence, knights entered the cloister and threatened the cleric. Fearing for his life and honor, he secretly left the city. When the bishop learned of the keeper’s flight, he exhausted and plundered all his resources and reduced him to utter poverty. The keeper therefore thought it proper to appeal to the supreme pontiff. On this matter the pope sent two letters to Udo of Trier and his suffragans, Theodoric of Verdun and Herman of Metz, instructing them to admonish the bishop to render the clerk due justice.

[Col. 0416A] “Then,” says the pontiff, “summon the clerics of Toul and bind them by true obedience—indeed, under accusation of anathema—so that they may disclose whatever they know concerning the bishop’s accession and life.
