Having thoroughly investigated the truth in every direction, do not in any way fail to notify us by your letters, in synod or before the synod which we are to hold in the first week of Lent, what is to be believed concerning this matter. But if the bishop, as we hope, should prove innocent of so many and such serious crimes, we shall, God inspiring us, see to it that the cleric, who has sinned rashly in coming before our tribunal, is corrected justly. If, however, the bishop cannot truthfully clear himself of the charges brought against him, it must in no way be tolerated by us or by you that a wolf should occupy the place of a shepherd.”

Meanwhile Pibo embraced the party of the schismatics and, shortly thereafter, was present at the assembly held by Emperor Henry IV at Worms. With many other bishops, under a pretext of false charges, he dared to judge that Hildebrand was not the supreme pontiff. Several bishops who attended the gathering, including Udo of Trier, Theodoric of Verdun, and Herman of Metz, lamented that they had fallen into so grave a fault. When Pope Gregory learned of this, he admonished them by letter to correct by fitting amendment the error they had committed through the attack of the schismatics: “so that,” says the pontiff, [Col. 0416B] “as your mother grieved at your transgression, so she may rejoice at your satisfaction.” He also instructed these bishops to admonish Pibo that henceforth he should not fail to do what had been enjoined upon him. “For,” this pope adds, “it would have been fitting that he should answer the accusations brought against him, rather than take up arms against the authority of the prince of the apostles in defense of his iniquities, and incite the king to presume against us that which has never been permitted, nor, God willing, ever will be permitted, to be done against any cleric. If he should despise the words of our exhortation, notify him that by the authority of Blessed Peter he is separated from communion in the body and blood of our Lord Jesus Christ.”

Pibo, however, renounced the schism about the year 1078 and returned into favor with the pope. The following year he attended, with the bishops of his province, the election of Egilbert of Trier; yet he refused to lay hands upon one elected not by canonical procedure but by royal authority. At that time he determined to clear himself of the accusations laid against him by the cleric of Verdun. On this matter there is a letter of Gregory VII to Herman of Metz, in which the pontiff says that, since Pibo could not, because of disturbances in the empire, assemble six bishops to attest his innocence, he permitted him to perform episcopal duties, provided that his innocence had first been established before four bishops. “If,” he continues, [Col. 0416D] “you ascertain beyond doubt that he is blameless, do not delay to offer him the helping hand of brotherhood.”

Nevertheless, I know not through what fickleness, Pibo returned to the side of the schismatics and, in the synod assembled at Utrecht by command of the emperor, where it was decreed that Gregory VII should be struck with anathema, attended in the year 1080; indeed, he himself had received from the emperor the responsibility of carrying this out. But, terrified by fear, he secretly withdrew by night with Theodoric of Verdun, lest he become a participant in so wicked a crime.

After this gathering, he is said to have gone to Rome to visit the pontiff, from whom he obtained not only absolution but also the authority to absolve schismatic prelates who returned to the bosom of the Church. Having fallen into the emperor’s displeasure in 1084 because he had not gone to Mainz for the consecration of Egilbert of Trier, he judged that he ought for a time to yield to the emperor’s anger. He therefore resolved to go to Jerusalem for religious reasons.

Before he departed, Countess Sophia desired that the chapel begun by Theodoric, duke of Lorraine and her grandfather, and completed by herself, should be consecrated at Asmantia. Hodierna, abbess of Saint Glodesindis in the city of Metz, intervened, induced by the argument that this chapel had been built in the territory of Saint Martin, which legally belonged to her chapter; but she finally consented on the condition that the countess pay a fixed rent to Saint Glodesindis. Then Sophia transferred this chapel, dedicated by Pibo in honor of Saint Mary, to Saint Michael on the Meuse, into the hands of Abbot Sigifrid.

Bishop Pibo granted the chapel its liberty, stating that this agreement had been confirmed in the year when he himself was about to go to Jerusalem, namely, in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1085, indiction VIII. He undertook the pilgrimage to Jerusalem with Conrad of Luxembourg and, on the journey, bound himself by a vow that, if he returned safely and unharmed to his homeland, he would profess the monastic life. After actually returning, he fulfilled this vow in the monastery of Saint Benignus at Dijon, to which, in the first year of his episcopate, he had confirmed by his letters the two altars granted by Udo.

After making his profession, he was desired by his diocesans and, by order of Pope Victor III, was compelled to resume the governance of his Church. To it he gave a portion of the True Cross, received as a gift from Constantinople and adorned with gold and jewels. In 1088 he approved the monks’ cell founded by Countess Sophia at Bar and placed under the monastery of Saint Michael in the diocese of Verdun.

In 1091 he gave his assent so that Lutulfus, the dean, might build a monastery in honor of Saint Leo, and he praised all the donations made to that place. In the same year he ordered a tower to be built in the cathedral church, in which he hung two bells and erected three altars. He gave his Church the great crown suspended between the choir and the altar, around which candles are lit. Add to this forty measures of wine, as well as a church which he granted on condition that his anniversary should be celebrated there every year.

He dedicated the church of Saint Chlodulf at Laium in 1092 and shortly afterward buried at Toul Beatrice, formerly the wife of Duke Berthold, who had died on the seventh day before the Kalends of November of that year. In 1093 Pibo and his fellow provincial bishops declared that they would no longer obey Egilbert, the metropolitan tainted by schism. To this period appears to belong Pope Urban II’s response to the many questions submitted by Pibo.

In 1094 he issued letters concerning the foundation of the priory of Saint Theobald of Amereville. In 1095 he honorably received Richer of Verdun, recently ordained by Hugh of Lyon and returning to his episcopal city. In that same year he attended the Council of Clermont, at which war was proclaimed against the Saracens for the recovery of the Holy Land; indeed, he would himself have taken the cross had he not been prevented by age and infirmities.

He consecrated very many churches in his diocese and approved the foundations of several abbeys and priories. In 1096 he granted the altar located at Commercy to Blessed Mary of Molesme, on condition that a rent of six denarii be paid.

A certain Ursus, a native of Benevento, after various pilgrimages, came to Lorraine and settled near Neufchâteau on Mount Sion, where he built an oratory in honor of the apostle Saint James and placed there the relics which he had brought with him. This oratory was consecrated by Pibo. A cell was afterward attached to the oratory, which Pibo, at Ursus’s request, granted to the monastery of Saint Mansuetus, so that monks might be placed there. He granted them the altar of Saint Germanus of Sion and, by letters issued in 1097 on the fourth day before the Kalends of March, decreed that all who would inhabit that mountain should come to this cell for baptism and burial and for all other assistance of soul and body.

In 1101, on the fifth day before the Ides of October, he consecrated the church of Port. At the request of Theomar, abbot of Saint Mansuetus, he ratified the gift of Drogo the steward and his wife Eve, who were buried in the church of Saint Mansuetus, in the year 1102, indiction X. At the same abbot’s request, he confirmed all the possessions of Saint Mansuetus in 1103, indiction XI.

In 1105 he subscribed letters concerning the foundation of a cell near the castle of Vallis-Coloris, on land assigned to the monastery of Molesme by Josfrid, a most noble prince. In 1107 he honorably received Richard, bishop of Albano and legate of the Apostolic See, and asked him to consecrate the recently restored church of Saint Mansuetus, as well as the church completed by Seher, abbot of Calmiciacum, for whose benefit, as the chronicle of Calmiciacum testifies, he had already done very many things.

In that same year he died in November: according to the necrology of Saint Mansuetus, on the eleventh day before the Kalends of December; according to the necrologies of Saint Vitonus and Saint Benignus of Dijon, on the ninth day before the Kalends; and according to the cathedral necrology, on the eighth day before the Kalends. He had presided over the Church of Toul for thirty-eight years. He was buried in the church of Toul, in the chapel of Saint Mary Magdalene. Many years later his bones were exhumed and buried with the bones of Reginald, bishop of Senlis, near the smaller gate through which one descends from the cathedral into the cloister.

[Col. 0419]

## DIPLOMAS OF PIBO

### I. Privilege for the monastery of Saint Aper  
*(Year 1072.)*

[Dom Calmet, *History of Lorraine*, vol. IV, Documents, p. 472.]

[Col. 0419A]

In the name of the holy and undivided Trinity, creator and governor of all things that eternally exist, Pibo, humble bishop of the holy Church of Toul by the grace of the divine disposition.

Whenever the mind of anyone is inspired to will what is good—especially the mind of one who is seen to possess more than others in this world—he ought to be vigilant that, through the things of earthly dominion, the mercy of God may be made favorable toward him. Yet upon us, pastors of the Church, a pious concern is imposed: that the Lord’s flock placed under our care may be fed by our foresight and supported, under temporal administration, by the twofold substance of life.

Therefore we wish it to be clearly known to all members of our Church, over which by God’s authority we preside, both to the faithful now living and to those who will follow long afterward, that when we came to the place of Saint Aper and piously considered the provision of food for the monks, we believed that it would greatly benefit us at the strict judgment of the future if we increased the things belonging to the nourishment of the brothers serving God there. Through this, our memorial would be established more securely in that place, and the prayer of God’s servants for the attainment of our salvation would never cease.

[Col. 0419C]

Moved by this consideration, and also stirred by the example of our predecessors, who from the possessions belonging to them gave certain things to the same place for the remedy of their souls, with the counsel of our faithful we have firmly granted to them, for the remedy of our soul and of those of our predecessors and successors, the two altars: namely, the altar of Bladenac on the Moselle in its entirety—although they have hitherto held one half of it from ancient times, just as they still retain one half of the church of that village—and the altar of the church of Fain beyond the Moselle, near the castle of Bar, under the same condition by which they had anciently held the other altars of the whole abbey.

That is, when the vicars die, to whom alone we entrust the care of souls by their election, they shall in no way be compelled to redeem those altars; they shall merely, as has been said, provide replacement vicars who shall receive the care of souls from our hand.

By our pontifical gift we also deliver to the place and brothers of Saint Aper, with the approval of our faithful, a certain woman named Peila, together with her two sons, including Gavalon, who have long belonged to our authority; and from our right we transfer them permanently to their right, so that, for the remedy of our soul and of those of our predecessors and successors, all their posterity may remain in the service of the brothers of the aforesaid place.

[Col. 0420A]

We also confirm to the same place everything contained in the privileges of our predecessors—namely, Gauzlin, Gerard, and Bruno of blessed memory—in the archive of that place, and which they still appear by God’s grace securely to retain. We likewise confirm what the same monastery acquired in the time of the aforesaid venerable Bruno, namely, the cell of Danguiliac with all its appurtenances, as is recorded in the charter of Walter, count of blessed memory, who gave the house of that cell to Saint Aper for the remedy of his soul.

Moreover, we confirm what the aforesaid monastery acquired in the time of our predecessor Udo at Baini-Villa from Holdierde and his son Odelric, as is contained in their charter.

We therefore strengthen all these things by this present pontifical charter, granting them to the aforesaid monastery to possess perpetually, so that by this act of piety the brothers may continually recall how earnestly they ought to supplicate almighty God on our behalf for our good will.

Finally, we ask, beseech, and implore the paternal benevolence of our successors that this offering of our generosity remain firm and ratified, just as they too will establish their own decrees to preserve it perpetually inviolate. Let them know beyond doubt that they will be rewarded for good will, just as they will be more severely punished by the creator of the world for presumption in altering what has been established for the remedy of souls.

So that this grant of our transfer may be held more firmly in future times and preserved perpetually unharmed, we have caused it to be confirmed by the hands of all our faithful, and have decreed that it endure by the authority of our office through successive ages.

I, Pibo, bishop of Toul by the grace of God, have signed.

Sign of Hugh, primicerius. Sign of Milo of Verdun, primicerius and archdeacon of this see. Sign of Lambert, chief archdeacon. Sign of Rudolph, archdeacon. Sign of Hugh, chief archdeacon. Sign of Lambert the younger, archdeacon. Sign of Alberic, archdeacon. Sign of Lutulfus, archdeacon. Sign of Hugh the younger, archdeacon. Sign of Theodoric, archdeacon. Sign of Frederick, count of this city. Sign of Haimon, count, and of his son Odelric. Sign of Everard, count, and of his sons Gilbert and Henry. Sign of Milo and of his brother Walter. Sign of Hugh and of his brother Warner. Sign of Henry, advocate. Sign of Lord Wido, abbot of the monastery of Saint Aper. Sign of Lord Vinbald, abbot of the monastery of Saint Mansuetus.

Given on the fourth day before the Ides of October in a plenary synod, in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1072, indiction X, while Henry IV was reigning as king of the Romans, in the seventeenth year of his reign, under Duke Theodoric.

I, Walter, chancellor, dean, and archdeacon, have examined, subscribed, and signed this.

### II. He settles the dispute between Valo, abbot of Saint Arnulf, and the abbess of Buxières concerning a bridge  
*(Year 1073.)*

[D. Calmet, ibid., p. 474, from the authentic charter of Buxières.]

[Col. 0421B]

In the name of the holy and undivided Trinity, Father, Son, and Holy Spirit, Pibo, bishop of the Leuci by the grace of God.

Since divine grace has deigned, not on account of our merits, to promote us to the pastoral office, we ought diligently to take care of the affairs of our Church, both small and great. Therefore let all posterity, both present and future, know that a dispute arose between two abbeys, namely Buxières, belonging to our Church, and Saint Arnulf of the Church of Metz, concerning a certain bridge which the abbess of Buxières had recently built on her own land, but within the ban and watercourse called the Meurthe, belonging to the abbey of Saint Arnulf.

To settle this dispute amicably, I and our brother, the venerable bishop Herimann of the Church of Metz, met with Duke Theodoric and the venerable Abbot Valo of the monastery of Saint Arnulf. There we arranged, through brotherly charity, that the aforesaid abbot would permit a bridge to be built there, on the condition that a public rent of twelve denarii be paid to him annually on the feast of Saint Remigius. On that day an agent of the abbot of Saint Arnulf was to be present on the bridge to receive the rent, from the first hour until the sixth; after that time the agent was to depart.

If, however, the agent of the abbess of Buxières paid the aforesaid rent at Laium cell by evening, it was to be accepted without penalty. But if he neglected to pay beyond nightfall, he was to pay it on the following day with the penalty. If the bridge were destroyed through neglect or by a threatening flood, and they were unwilling to restore it, the abbot of Saint Arnulf was to return to the former custom of his ban, and the abbess to the ancient practice concerning her ferryboats. She was also to uproot the piles of that bridge, lest they obstruct fishing or the boats of the abbot of Saint Arnulf.

[Col. 0422A]

So that this common settlement of ours might remain ratified and stable forever, we decreed that this charter be written, so that each abbey might possess one part of it as perpetual testimony confirming our settlement.

I, Pibo, bishop of the Church of Toul, have signed. Sign of Hugh, primicerius. Sign of Lambert, archdeacon. Sign of Hugh, archdeacon. Sign of Odelric, archdeacon. Also sign of Odelric, archdeacon. Sign of Count Frederick. Sign of Odelric, advocate of Nancy. Sign of Albert. Sign of Henry, advocate. Sign of Hugh, steward. Sign of Berenger, advocate.

I, Herimann, bishop of the Church of Metz by the grace of God, have approved this with the counsel of our faithful. Sign of Albero, primicerius. Sign of Richer, dean and archdeacon. Sign of Valo, abbot of Saint Arnulf. Sign of Gervald, archdeacon. Sign of John, treasurer. Sign of Folmar, count. Sign of Menzo, advocate. Sign of Chuno of Tincherey. Sign of Haimon. Sign of Everard of Asmantia. Sign of Alberic. Sign of Otto. Sign of Lambert. Sign of Dodo. Sign of Gerard.

Done publicly at Toul in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1073, indiction XI, on the third day before the Kalends of May, while Henry the younger was reigning as king of the Romans and Duke Theodoric was governing the duchy of the kingdom.

Given through the hands of Walter, chancellor and archdeacon, with the suitable witnesses written above attesting to it.

### III. Confirmation of the privileges of the priory of Asmantia  
*(Year 1076.)*

[Dom Calmet, ibid.]

[Col. 0422D]

In the name of the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit.

It is exceedingly useful and necessary for the rulers of churches to commend the arrangements of accomplished deeds most firmly to the memory of writing, for the knowledge of posterity. Let it therefore be known to all the sons and brothers of holy Mother Church that I, Pibo, bishop of Toul by the grace of God, at the request and through the favor of Countess Sophia, our beloved daughter, consecrated a certain church in honor of Blessed Mary, which she had built from its foundations.

But because the parishioners of Asmantia had formerly been subject to Saint Martin, as had those of the neighboring villages—namely Laium, Oemont [also, Eumont], Blanzey, and Sechamp—and because now those of Asmantia and of the aforesaid villages had for certain reasons been removed from such subjection, the aforesaid Countess Sophia, at the advice of her nobles, asked us to commit to writing what rights those serving the church of Blessed Mary had possessed or would possess, and for what reasons the parishioners of Asmantia had been removed from subjection to Saint Martin, so that no dispute or controversy might arise in the future.

Let everyone therefore know that the church of Blessed Mary, with its chapel in the castle, had been constituted so free from the lords and princes of the castle that it owed neither rent nor any other due to the Church of Toul. Nevertheless, when a cleric invested by the countess or her successors with the prebend of Blessed Mary came to Toul, he would receive the care of souls from our see and would make an oath of loyalty for the preservation of Christianity.

We faithfully write the reasons for which the parishioners of Asmantia had been removed from subjection to Saint Martin, as we learned them from the countess herself and her faithful. Duke Theodoric, the countess’s grandfather, who had succeeded Count Folmar in Asmantia by hereditary right, gave and granted half of the tithes of the church of Saint Martin under this agreement: that the priest of Saint Martin would give oil and chrism to the chaplain of Blessed Mary on Holy Saturday, and that in every synod and council he would in every respect excuse that chaplain on account of the said tithe.

My predecessor, Bishop Berthold of blessed memory, established, as a memorial of the former subjection, that two offerings should be brought to Saint Martin every year. And because the people of Asmantia had always been harsh and fierce, so that no archdeacon or dean dared enter their town for any reason, that same bishop also decreed that they should be summoned and go to Saint Martin for the synod.

Moreover, having been entreated by the gifts and prayers of Duke Theodoric, with the approval and consent of Berenger, the archdeacon of that castle, and with the concession of his chapter, he decreed in full synod—and judged that it should be observed thereafter—that the church of Saint Martin should no longer demand or receive from the church of Blessed Mary or from its parishioners any subjection, payment, or other exaction.

Therefore Countess Sophia, loving sufficiently the church of Blessed Mary, which, as we have said, had been dedicated by us and which she had made new out of the old, willingly granted that the church should possess two manses formerly given there as alms. As an increase of the alms, she likewise gave to the altar of Blessed Mary two other manses, together with two female servants and one male servant, under the same terms on which she herself held them, with the approval of her son, Count Theodoric. She also gave all the great and small tithes from the castle and town, namely from all demesne lands, rent-paying lands, arable lands, and cleared lands.

For the honor of Mary, the Mother of God, we therefore praise and confirm this gift. In the presence of many nobles and commoners, we acknowledge and praise the liberty of the church, recognized and approved before us, and we confirm it by anathema, so that it may be preserved forever through the impression of our seal.

Sign of Pibo, bishop. Sign of Alberic, abbot of Saint Mansuetus. Sign of Richard, abbot of Saint Aper. Sign of Hugh, primicerius. Sign of Riquin, archdeacon. Sign of Stephen, archdeacon. Sign of Dodo, dean. Sign of Theodoric, archdeacon and chancellor. Sign of Ibin, scabine. Sign of Count Theodoric. Sign of Count Rainard. Sign of Wiric of Belrain. Sign of Wiric of Danubre. Sign of Walter and Arnulf, brothers.

This was enacted at Toul in the major church, in the year from the Incarnation of 1076, indiction XIV, and in the tenth year of our ordination, while Henry III was emperor, while the Lord Jesus Christ reigns happily throughout the ages. Amen.

### IV. Charter for the church of Saint Deodatus  
*(Year 1076.)*

[Gallia Christiana XIII, Documents, p. 472.]

[Col. 0424B]

In the name of the holy and undivided Trinity, Father, Son, and Holy Spirit, Pibo, bishop of the holy Church of Toul by the grace of God, sends peace and the kingdom of Christ to all reborn in Christ.

The love of the future homeland, which burns exceedingly in the hearts of the children of God, wisely deliberates over the care and administration of the present Church. It fosters and embraces her all the more powerfully because it recognizes that what one longs for cannot be reached more happily by any other way.

We too, therefore, attending according to the measure of our office to the matters belonging to us, have likewise taken similar care of the church of Saint Deodatus, which is under our protection. We have granted forever for the prebend of the brothers the church on Mount Saint Remigius, which Duke Theodoric had long held through acts of seizure, but which, in the time of Reimbald, provost of the aforesaid church, was recovered by synodal judgment and canonical authority, with the lawful approval of the provost himself.

Because the preceding clause is textually corrupt, we translate its discernible sense: we transfer the altar of the acquired church to the brothers serving there, to be held perpetually in memory of my death every year, under the same right and with the same integrity with which we held it.

But because the enemies of charity begrudge charity, and the opposing party resists good institutions, we decree that whoever disturbs this decree, struck by our anathema, shall feel the anger of the just judgment.

We therefore confirm this present document by our authority, and have judged that it should also be strengthened by the testimony of our faithful.

Sign of Pibo, bishop. Sign of Ricuin, primicerius. Sign of Reimbald, archdeacon. Sign of Deodatus, provost. Sign of Stephen, archdeacon. Sign of Hugh, archdeacon. Sign of Gotbert, cantor. Sign of Albero, cantor. Sign of Thromar, abbot. Sign of Mansuetus. Sign of Widric, abbot. Sign of Aper. Sign of Bertric, abbot of the monastery of Medianum. Sign of Count Rainald. Sign of Varin, advocate. Sign of Letfrid. Sign of Henry of Saint Vedastus. Sign of Gilbert, steward.

### V. Letters concerning the church of Munz  
*(Year 1079.)*

[Baluz, *Capitularies*, vol. II, p. 1555, from the archive of Saint Mansuetus of Toul.]

[Col. 0425A]

In the name of the holy and undivided Trinity, Father, Son, and Holy Spirit. Pibo, bishop of the Leuci by the grace of God, sends perpetual greeting to all the sons of holy Church.

Since times, which always flow away and never remain in the same state, produce forgetfulness through the length of days, and disputes often arise through forgetfulness, actions are therefore commended to writing as a precaution and entrusted through writing to posterity. For what is committed to writing is easily retained.

Let it therefore be known to people of the present and future that the church of Munz was formerly a chapel of Blano, and that the people living in the same village of Munz customarily assembled three times a year at their mother church of Blano—namely, at Easter, Pentecost, and Christmas—and paid the priest of Blano the offerings owed there.

But because in our time the people of that village of Munz attempted to oppose this ancient custom, for two years they were placed under divine interdict by our pastoral justice and by the judgment of the holy Church of Toul, until they corrected their presumption by suitable satisfaction.

Compelled by this necessity, the people of Munz approached their lord, Duke Theodoric, in whose hand the aforesaid village then was, earnestly asking that through him they might be released from this sentence. Through the intervention of Duke Theodoric, we therefore granted the aforesaid people of Munz a baptistery and free burial, and decreed that thereafter they should not be compelled to go to Blano on the three solemnities already mentioned.

When this settlement reached the ears of Lord Theomar, who at that time presided over the Church of the most blessed Mansuetus, he opposed the arrangement by reasonable arguments, with the counsel of the wise men whom he had taken into his deliberations. He did so lest, if the aforesaid chapel should by permission of the deacon and archdeacon become a mother church and possess a baptistery and free burial, the people of the parish, together with their successors, should at some time provoke and trouble them concerning the roof of the church, which would have to be covered.

Therefore the lord duke, foreseeing the future loss to the Church of Saint Mansuetus and the disturbance which the aforesaid peasants might cause, by common agreement and at the request of Alberic the steward and the other people of Munz, in the presence and with the approval of the venerable Abbot Theomar, decreed that the people of Munz should repair the roof of the aforesaid church, whenever it was destroyed, together with the other interior furnishings—namely, vestments, chalice, missal, and [scarsal, perhaps a liturgical book or cloth; reading uncertain].

Thus the aforementioned Abbot Theomar, at the request and insistence of the aforesaid duke and of the many others who had assembled to petition him about this matter, granted their request and, from what belonged to his jurisdiction, contributed the offerings of the three festivals toward covering the church’s roof, except for the bread offerings of those same festivals.

And lest either our institution or that of the aforesaid abbot should ever be altered in any way by the calumny of posterity or the wickedness of slanderers, we ordered this charter to be written as a memorial. We also judged that it should be strengthened under threat of anathema by the impression of our own image and by the signs and testimonies of our faithful.

Sign of Pibo, bishop. Sign of Theomar, abbot. Sign of Duke Theodoric. Sign of Widric, abbot. Sign of Aper. Sign of Riguin, primicerius. Sign of Bruno, archdeacon and provost. Sign of Gengulf. Sign of Albero, chancellor. Sign of Oger, priest of the same chapel of Munz. Sign of Alberic, steward of the same village. Sign of Bencelin, knight and sub-advocate of the castle of Castenay. Sign of Humbert, knight of the same castle. Sign of Milo of Gondrecourt.

This was enacted in the year from the Incarnation of the Lord 1079, in the eleventh year of our ordination, while Henry III was emperor, Theodoric was duke of the Lotharingians, Rainard was count of Toul, and the Lord Jesus Christ reigned happily throughout the ages. Amen.

### VI. Letters concerning the cell of Asmantia  
*(Year 1085.)*

[Baluz, *Miscellanies* III, 58, edited by Mansi.]

Since certainties must be sought concerning uncertain matters, it is useful and necessary to commend them to posterity in writing.

I, therefore, Pibo, bishop of Toul, make known to my successors that a dispute had long existed between Countess Sophia and Hodierna, abbess of Saint Glodesindis, over whether the chapel under Asmantia should be consecrated, because it had been built in the territory of Saint Martin.

Sophia came to us many times so that we might offer our advice in this matter. Finally, after Bishop Herimann of Metz had been summoned, by his counsel and assistance we obtained from the abbess that, if the countess Sophia would grant her the rent-paying revenues which she held at Laium, and would kindly grant Aremfrid, Badin, and Lampizo together with the quarter-lands and forest of Eingiviler, the chapel might be consecrated with the approval of the abbess and chapter of Saint Glodesindis.

Abbot Alberic of Saint Mansuetus, Everard of Saint Aper, and our primicerius Hugh were present at this agreement. Afterward, in the presence of Herimann, bishop of Metz, and of Abbess Hodierna, Countess Sophia placed in the hand of the abbot of Saint Michael the gift of the cell and the gift of the chapel of the castle, together with the tithes of the arable lands, cleared lands, and demesne lands, and a tenth of all tithes which she might acquire from her own resources.

She therefore requested that a charter be made for her concerning the liberty of the cell. I had made it free, with the approval of our chapter, from every exaction. The vicar was to be free, serving both the cell and the chapel of the castle; he was also to swear fidelity to the abbot of Saint Michael concerning matters belonging to the abbot’s jurisdiction, and fidelity to the abbess concerning matters belonging to her. Sophia graciously consented to the appointment of the vicar by the abbot of Saint Michael and confirmed it in writing forever.

We willingly assented to her request, imposing our seal and ban. So that this might be held and known with greater certainty, we asked that this present charter be written with the signs of those who were present.

This agreement was confirmed in the year when I was about to go to Jerusalem, in the year from the Lord’s Incarnation 1805 [probably 1085; the text prints “1805”], indiction VIII, epact XXII, concurrent II, under Pope Gregory VII and King Henry III.

Sign of Pibo, bishop of Toul. Sign of Herimann, bishop of Metz. Sign of Alberic, abbot of Saint Mansuetus. Sign of Everard, abbot of Saint Aper. Sign of Hugh, primicerius.

These are the witnesses from the household: Maimbold, Bovo, Emyco, and Enzelin, through whose hands thirty pounds of Metz currency were delivered to Abbess Hodierna.

Moreover, the predecessors of the aforesaid Countess Sophia had given, within the suburb of the city, near the gate called Eckeard’s, a mansus to Saint Stephen the protomartyr, at Raimbald’s Corner; but it had been consigned to oblivion for a long time.

The gift was therefore renewed through our hand and confirmed by this present writing, so that the memory of her predecessors might be held more securely in our charter, especially for the liberty of the cell of Asmantia, which I had made free from every exaction.

### VII. Foundation of the monastery of Saint Leo of Toul  
*(Year 1091.)*

[Dom Calmet, *History of Lorraine*, IV, Documents, p. 489.]

In the name of the holy and undivided Trinity.

Instructed by the evangelical and apostolic Scriptures, pious kings, religious pontiffs, and other Christian princes, whose hearts have been enlarged by the breadth of charity and by the manifold possession of their goods, customarily build churches, gather communities of saints together, provide the necessary stipends, and enrich them with every sufficiency.

I, however, Lutulfus, a humble cleric and dean of the cloister of the Church of Toul, although supported by no possession of property, was nevertheless inspired to imitate so great a purpose. A certain magnanimity, daily urging me with good hope against my faintheartedness and continually reproving my timid spirit, encouraged me.

Let no prudent judge of this world, calculating the expense and method of the work, mock or despise my weakness in this matter, since God’s munificence, always the faithful companion of good will, brings my undertaking—because all things are possible to one who believes—to a successful completion.

As I stood between hope and anxieties, I explained this desire and concern of mine to Count Hugh, son of Count Henry, since I was well known to him. That faithful man of God, inwardly touched in his heart by the Spirit of God, answered me in these words: he would become the companion of my anxieties and the indefatigable, indeed principal, collaborator in the labor undertaken if I would dedicate there a monastery in honor of blessed Leo, pope and bishop of Toul, and build around it hospices for the poor.

Then, as long as he and his wife lived, daily prayer would be offered there for their safety and prosperity; when they had been gathered to their fathers, more earnest ecclesiastical remembrance would also be owed to their souls and those of their fathers, and the kindly provided refreshment of the poor would be beneficial. I, Lutulfus, gladly assented to this.

Therefore the count himself, his countess, and I, having reached a common agreement, approached the bishop of Toul, the venerable Pibo of blessed memory, a lover of God’s churches and one who rejoiced in and cooperated with every good undertaking.

When the holy priest heard the proposal, he piously admired the devotion of the secular man, stirred and strengthened his sincerely contrite mind by priestly exhortation, and promised that he too would greatly assist the undertaking, although at that time a great work was already in his hands, since he was building a tower before the principal oratory of the Protomartyr.

The same most pious Count Hugh held a great and ancient benefice from that venerable bishop. From this benefice he and the countess released from his hand a certain village called Martin-Mont, and, excluding the hereditary claim of all successors, restored it to the lordly hand of the bishop.

Likewise Gerard of Brescia, son of Walfrid, restored to the lordly hand of the bishop the heads of all persons of both sexes whom he had living in the same village and held from the bishop as a benefice.

The distinguished pontiff himself likewise released from his table, from his own provision, those inhabitants of the same village who belonged to him, so that the gift might be made complete. When the village had been restored with all its members and made demesne, the venerable Bishop Pibo, with the counsel and consent of the same counts, placed it upon the altar of Saint Stephen by a quiet and firm transfer, calling upon divine and human assistance.

Thus the same village, namely Martin-Mont, with its church and appurtenances, was to remain attached to the altar of Saint Stephen and, when the monastery had been built and a number of monks gathered, serve their needs.

He also added manses in the city, which belonged to the benefice of that village and paid a rent of two solidi.

Moreover, I, Lutulfus, acquired from Countess Recheza the church of Wandelin-Villa, with the full endowment of that church. She also gave one man, together with two quarters of a mansus, on the condition that he pay to the altar of our monastery the rent owed on his land to the ban, and that he should thus remain peacefully within the ban of the village.

Once these matters had been arranged, there was still lacking a mansus on which the church, hospices, and the attached shelters could be built. The most pious bishop himself, moved by his charity, immediately granted it; it was sufficiently long and broad not only for the buildings but also for supplying other needs most generously. Thus, once the church and suitable shelters had been built, I, Luctulfus, unmistakably perceived that God’s visitation and his aid presided over that place. Therefore, confidently relying on the benevolence of the Almighty, I approached with many entreaties certain holy men who, after selling their patrimonies and distributing the proceeds to the poor, were living religiously on Mount Rumberch; and, finally, having invited them by episcopal authority, I brought them to myself, so that they might lead an apostolic life—that is, the first-fruits of Christian religion—in our monastery also, just as previously on the mountain, under the rule and written constitution of Saint Augustine. For it seemed a salutary and fitting arrangement that one city should contain three more perfect members of the Christian religion: namely, canons possessing their own properties; monks, black-clad in the ranks under the rule of Saint Benedict; and white-clad Nazarenes leading an apostolic life, so that whoever wished to convert to the Lord might find in this one city whatever stricter form of religion pleased him.

Accordingly, these holy men, living perfectly in the tranquil sincerity of their purpose, attracted many secular people of both sexes to follow the poor Christ by the delightful fragrance of their holy way of life, and drew some of those whom they had attracted into their fellowship.

Among these, Peter, son of Dodo, gave himself and his vineyard; likewise Walter, son of Bererius, a young cleric; and, just as Peter had done, he gave himself together with vineyards and one mansus. Likewise Varnuldis, a virgin of Christ, surrendered herself to their provision and discipline, and gave several jugera of arable land and a vineyard at Scrupulas, which I later enlarged either by purchase or by exchange with her brother. Likewise, I bought a vineyard at Barromont from the cleric Trelino. At Focaucart I purchased, with my own money, an allod from a certain matron named Aia, in its entirety, just as she had possessed it by hereditary right from her ancestors. Officia, a girl and the sister of Hugo, gave vineyards and two jugera of land. Certain others, also fearing the Lord, freely gave several jugera here and there out of benevolence. I thought it tedious to enumerate them individually by donor and by place, lest I weary the synodal ears.

After these things, I, Luctulfus, seeing that the possessions of the holy men had multiplied and were still multiplying, and considering that among wicked customs the uprightness of the just, because of its innocence, is not sufficiently safe by itself without the protection of the great, wisely decided that the gifts written above, as well as those to be given in the future, should be confirmed by synodal authority under anathema, so that no rash person might dare to take any of them away. I also decided briefly to describe the immunity in which our congregation should live according to the rule of Saint Augustine: namely, that our canons, just as they have their own rule, different from that of others, should be permitted to live under episcopal obedience according to their private right, without the censure of others, whether canons or monks.

Let them choose their own prior for themselves and appoint him over themselves. Let them ask and receive from their bishop, through their prior, the care of souls. Let no primicerius, no dean, and no abbot presume to judge their offenses—which divine power forbid—unless their prior or the bishop does so, if disobedience or necessity summons him to it. On the festivals of the greater church or of other churches, let no one summon or compel them to processions or to the burials of the great outside their own precinct. Rather, let their life, being singular, remain enclosed in secluded tranquility.

I, Pibo, bishop of the Church of Toul, sitting in full synod, asked in the synodal assembly whether the canons of Saint Augustine who live in the monastery built outside the city walls by Brother Luctulfus would approve and request that the immunity of those canons described above be confirmed, or would protest should anyone infringe any of the gifts. When everyone had received what was promulgated above favorably and had requested its confirmation, I too, moved by my own spontaneous will, added from my own gift that they should perpetually possess this right which the bishop has over the altar of Wandelini-villa and over the altar of Martini-mons, except that they must pay the census.

Likewise, I granted them permission and authority to establish a burial ground in their own precinct, in which they might receive for burial, whether commoners or nobles, anyone who should request it; and, in receiving them, no abbot or priest should dare disturb or distress them on account of his adjoining territory. All these matters described and granted above, and those to be granted in the future through the devotion of the faithful, I, Pibo, bishop of Toul, both will and command to remain valid and unshaken; by episcopal authority, under anathema and by synodal judgment, I confirm that they are to be observed.

“May the Lord do this and add this” (2 Samuel 3:9), the entire assembly replied.

Sign of Pibo, bishop. Sign of Hugo, primicerius. Sign of Requinus, archdeacon. Sign of Albero, archdeacon. Sign of Stephen, archdeacon. Sign of Hugo, cantor, and of Stephen Rufus. Sign of Theoderic. Sign of Angeherus. Sign of Deodatus.

In the year from the Incarnation of the Lord 1091, indiction 15, on the sixth day before the Ides of October, the charter of this privilege was confirmed and signed by Lord Pibo, the venerable bishop, presiding in a full synod.

### VIII. Privilege for the Abbey of Saint Leo of Toul. (Year 1091)

[Dom Calmet, as cited above.]

[Col. 0431A]

In the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit. Pibo, by the grace of God humble bishop of the Leuci, to all the faithful of Christ, present and future: the grace of the Holy Spirit.

It is the duty of our office to provide for the faithful of Christ, especially those entrusted to us, not only spiritual but also temporal goods, and to procure for the sons of peace whatever pertains to their living a tranquil life. Therefore, rejoicing in the devotion and zeal of our son Luctulfus, dean of our Church, with which he labors in building a memorial of Blessed Leo IX, and wishing to join our hand to his hand in assisting him, we have diligently undertaken to set down how he and the church which he is building acquired the village of Martinimons, with God’s munificence lending its aid.

Indeed, the vigorous Count Hugo of Dasborc, venerable son of Henry, inwardly touched by divine inspiration and led by the sweetness of the noble lineage of Blessed Leo, from which he descended, with the consent of his wife and heirs, removed the aforesaid village from a certain great benefice which he held from us, released it from his hand, and restored it to our lordly hand, excluding every hereditary claim. He retained in his hand nothing of the gift, advocacy, or any right whatsoever. Gerard of Bricey, son of Valfrid, likewise restored to our lordly hand the heads of all persons of both sexes who lived in the same village and whom he held from us in benefice.

Rejoicing, therefore, in the devotion of these men, we too released from our provision all the people living in the same village who belonged to our table, restoring them in their entirety to the lordly domain. Accordingly, when this village had been restored with its members and had been brought into demesne, with the counsel and consent of the aforesaid men we freely restored it upon the altar of Blessed Leo, and under anathema confirmed it to that church for perpetual possession, for the provision of the brothers serving the Lord there.

We also placed upon the same altar of Blessed Leo, within the ban and jurisdiction of Maserias, a certain croft lying above that village among vineyards and meadows, free from every tithe and census, and a meadow lying between the public road and our meadow, for which four coins are paid to the wardens of the ban. Finally, we wish it to be known to those present and future that the boundaries, pastures, and woods of Maserias and Martinimons are entirely held in common, so that it is an injury and injustice if some presume to exclude others from any of these things. They and their animals may use them in common without damage. If damage should happen to occur, let it be restored through the fidelity of the people, and, as a matter of justice under our ban, let two coins be remitted, with no more being paid. We have granted and confirmed this right in all our villages and courts for the Church of Blessed Leo to possess.

Moreover, the practice and custom of marriages and betrothals are observed there as follows: if anyone from Maserias wishes to marry one of the women of Martinimons, he may do so without hindrance. The men of Martinimons likewise possess this right in the court of Maserias.

If, however, a betrothed woman from the furrows of Martinimons has been endowed, or if she has first spent the night in that village on the day of her betrothal, wherever she later lives, except in Maserias, she shall be liable to the census of Martinimons, and she and all her offspring shall pursue their lawsuits there. The same shall be done with women of Martinimons who are taken in marriage within the ban of Maserias.

We have therefore granted and confirmed by this present privilege that, in the villages and courts belonging to our jurisdiction, the Church of Blessed Leo may freely possess what has been granted in peace and freely receive what is to be granted through the devotion of the faithful. In all these matters, for the salvation of our soul, we have wished to relinquish all our rights to that church; and, so that no advocate or any of our officials may inflict trouble upon it or bring a malicious accusation out of greed, we forbid this by the authority of God and of ourselves, commanding it under anathema. Let none of them have any right in all these matters except from us, nor any power except through us. If, led by greed, anyone should inflict trouble upon the church on this account, bound by the bond of our anathema, he shall be guilty before divine justice.

Afterward, when that church had grown by God’s gift and had obtained an abbot, the abbot himself, named Scherus, honorable in life and conduct and prudent in counsel, considering the daily growth of human wickedness, taking precautions for the future, and recognizing that without the protection of some prince the same village could in no way remain secure by itself from the attacks of evildoers, followed our good counsel and that of religious men. When I, Duke Theoderic, Simon his young son, Gerard the duke’s brother and count, Renard count of Toul, and many other nobles, both clerical and lay, had gathered together at Châtenois for a certain matter, the abbot restored the village into the hand and custody of that duke—not as an advocacy—in the sight and hearing of us all. He granted the duke permission to receive each year in the same village seven and a half modii of wine for its custody; if there were less wine, or none at all, he stipulated that the duke should receive sixteen denarii per modius.

The duke, being pious and kind with regard to the salvation of his soul, accepted custody of the village. Because of the village’s poverty, it was established there that whomever the duke might wish to send on his behalf should have two services per year in that village, together with three or four companions, and should exact nothing more. He should not sit in court nor compel anyone to appear in court, unless perhaps the abbot or his provost requested that he do so to restrain someone rebellious against them. The duke, graciously assenting to this arrangement, affirmed it under oath of fidelity, promising that he would diligently provide for the custody of the village and faithfully observe the constitution prescribed above.

[Col. 0433A] If anyone from that village should happen to depart because of poverty or some other necessity and move elsewhere, wherever he might turn, no one except the abbot shall have any claim over him.

Lest the Church of Blessed Leo should suffer any trouble from anyone in the future concerning all these matters, or any dispute should arise, by this present writing we give testimony to all of them. We have wished it to be signed with the seal of our name and have confirmed it by pontifical authority. If anyone, led by pride or greed, should oppose these provisions and presume to exact more than has been established, we declare him excommunicated by divine and our own authority and subject him to the bond of anathema. We have also wished the names of the legitimate men who were present at these proceedings to be written below as testimony.

Sign of Pibo, bishop. Sign of Theoderic, duke. Sign of Gerard, count. Sign of Reinard, count of Toul. Sign of Hugo, primicerius. Sign of Luctulfus, dean. Sign of Riquinus, archdeacon. Sign of Wideric, knight of the castle of Noviler. Sign of Karlon of Fonteniac. Sign of Hodivat, knight of Deprées, and of many others.

In the year from the Incarnation of the Lord 1091, indiction 15, on the sixth day before the Ides of October, the charter of this privilege was confirmed and signed by Lord Pibo, the venerable bishop.

### IX. Foundation of the Priory of Saint Theobald. (Year 1094)

[Dom Calmet, *History of Lorraine* IV, Preface, 498.]

Pibo, by the grace of God unworthy bishop of the Church of Toul, to all, present and future: temporal salvation and enrichment with eternal gifts.

Since not all people have the same ability or desire to return to their homeland, but, as the Apostle says, “each has his own gift from God, one in this way, another in that way,” some, through the working of God’s mercy, stripped of the possession—or even the desire—of earthly things, enter boldly into combat while the adversary blocks the paths of men. Others, weighed down by the burden of those things they fear losing, come timidly to the contest and, what they despair of through awareness of their own weakness, they seek through the prayers of those who already reign with God and through the support of those who live spiritually here, so that they may not succumb or, if they fall, be shattered.

By a most just exchange, giving for their use some of what they must eventually leave behind, they trade perishable things for eternal ones in a fortunate commerce. Among these, Hugo and his brother Haymo jointly gave to Blessed Mansuetus and the brothers living in his monastery a certain part of the forest of Amerellivilla, separated from the whole by fixed boundaries. For all that lies between the merchants’ road and the old road that runs above the valley, as far as the bank of the river and as far as the little forest of Flaviniacum, their devotion, with the consent of their heirs, granted to the aforesaid monastery. They also obtained from the abbot who was then in office that a cell should be built there and monks established, who would continually pray to the Lord for their offenses and those of others.

For the necessary expenses of these monks, the younger brother Haymo, lying sick with a grave illness, granted to the aforesaid confessor whatever he possessed in Amerelli-villa, at Asmancium, and in the village called Saphez, as well as the allod of Sendruviler, together with the church’s dependent holdings in bondmen, cultivated and uncultivated lands. Renouncing the world in the same monastery, he received the monastic habit.

Afterward, the elder brother Hugo gave to the same cell his portion in the aforesaid villages, entirely as he possessed it. At the advice and urging of his wife, he also added certain things in the same Amerelli-villa: two quarteria, the resident tenants, their wives and children, together with half the village ban, jurisdiction, and every due. The whole cultivated and uncultivated land of Mizon, one fisherman in the water, the re-tithe of the gate and of the fish. At Monasteriolum, two quarteria with the resident tenants, their wives and children, and, in every use of the demesne labor, the entire tithe; the tithe of bread and wine; half of Crusillis. Likewise, at Helegia, two quarteria and the inhabitants with every due right. The entire allod of Senungis, in woods, fields, meadows, and all customary uses.

The following free men, competent to testify, were present at this gift: Drogo the younger of Bosanivilla, Widricus of Straena, Paulinus, Odelricus of Ferrières, Hugo of Buxières, and Hugo of Clermont.

And lest lack of temporal provisions make the brothers living in this cell less attentive to divine service or turn them entirely away from their purpose, the abbot of the aforesaid monastery, with the counsel of his faithful and brothers, added the following items under this condition: if, by some movement of divine providence, it should fall into destruction, everything assigned there should be restored in full to Blessed Mansuetus.

At Haleium, nine quarteria. At Avios, two quarteria. At Chalmont, two quarteria. At Novumvillare, two quarteria with resident tenants. At Petraevilla, two quarteria. At Huldeni Mons, one and a half quarteria. At Hulciolivilla, one and a half quarteria. At Domnumbasolum, whatever Drogo of Estraines gave to Saint Mansuetus in the same village, for his soul and those of his ancestors and for the provision of his son: namely, a stone house adjoining the wall of the church, and the people belonging to that allod. Albertus, and whatever he possessed in lands, meadows, woods, mills, and all customary uses. Herimannus of Saint Christopher gave to Blessed Mansuetus at Novumcastrum one quarterium in manses, small dwellings, cultivated and uncultivated lands, male and female servants.

Since a higher rank does not protect one from falling but sometimes causes a more serious fall, we who, with no merit of our own to support us, unworthily hold the place of Saint Mansuetus—so that, with him extending his hand, we may rise from the pit of misery and the mire of filth, and, with him protecting us, avoid whatever dangers threaten—we judged, with the counsel and encouragement of our clergy, that it would not be inappropriate to cut away something from our right for the benefit of this cell.

Finally, at the request of Lord Abbot Temarus, with the archdeacon and dean consenting, and with the canons of Saint Gengulf, together with their provost, also agreeing—for the cell lies within their parochial territory—we have freed from every subjection to that mother church the entire place marked out by fixed boundaries, together with the cell. We grant the entire tithe of every sort of thing within the boundaries described for the cell. We decree that all newcomers who have taken up residence in the aforesaid place, unless they belong to that parish, are wholly released from the yoke of the older church.

And so that no violent wickedness should ever dare to arise against these statutes, we bind with the bond of anathema all who remove anything from these gifts. So that with the passage of time none of these things may disappear from human memory or be enlarged, we confirm them by this writing. To confound and silence every envious and creeping judicial calumny, we strengthen this confirmation both by the well-known impression of our image and by the appended testimony of such men that it would be impious not to trust them.

Sign of Pibo, bishop. Sign of Temarus, abbot of Saint Mansuetus. Sign of Scherus, abbot of Saint Leo. Sign of Hugo, primicerius. Sign of Luctulfus, dean. Sign of Riquinus, archdeacon. Sign of Bruno, archdeacon and provost. Sign of Adelbero, archdeacon. Sign of Stephen, archdeacon. Sign of Hugo, archdeacon. Sign of Tecelinus, archdeacon. Sign of Adelbero, chancellor.

[Col. 0435D] These matters were indeed carried out at the see of Toul, in the major church, on the eighth day before the Kalends of March, at the beginning of the fasts, in the hearing of the clergy and an innumerable multitude of the people, in the year from the Incarnation of the Lord 1093, in the twenty-fourth year of our ordination, indiction 2, on Wednesday, with concurrent 5, lunar date 3, epact 1.

### X. Privilege for the Church of Saint Mary. (Year 1096)

[Dom Calmet, ibid., p. 502.]

In the name of the supreme and true God. Since, as a certain wise man says, it is beautiful to do good for the earthly commonwealth, it is clearly supremely beautiful and salutary for this to be done for the spiritual and divine court. Therefore, we wish it to be known to all the faithful of our diocese, present and future, that I, Pibo, by the grace of God bishop of the see of Toul, gave to the Church of Saint Mary, which is at Molehme (the Abbey of Molesme), the altar situated at Commarcey for the benefit of the monks serving God there. Since that monastery is not subject to us or to our church, we establish that, in addition to the census owed, they shall regularly pay our see, together with that census, six denarii.

Lest anyone henceforth claim that this gift or statute had not been made, or presume to violate it, we have taken care to strengthen it by the written record of this privilege, by the impression of our seal, and by the competent testimony of those subscribed below, both clerical and lay.

[Col. 0436B] Witnesses to the first gift: Sign of Riquinus, archdeacon. Sign of Gerard, count. Sign of Reinard, count. Sign of Odelricus, count of Brissey. Sign of Godbertus of Asperomont.

Witnesses to the renewed gift: Likewise, sign of Riquinus, archdeacon. Sign of Tasselinus, archdeacon. Sign of Stephen, archdeacon. Sign of Ramboldus, chancellor. Sign of John, dean. Sign of Bernard, priest. Sign of Edelricus of Rinnel. Sign of Henry, advocate of Toul. Sign of Sigiffridus and Hugo, officials, and of Godbertus, chamberlain.

[Col. 0436C] The gift was renewed in the year from the Incarnation of the Lord 1096, indiction 4, epact 24, concurrent 2, under Pope Urban, with Pibo as bishop, Henry IV as emperor, Theoderic as duke, and Reinard as count; while our Lord Jesus Christ reigns everywhere, to whom be honor, praise, and glory throughout all ages of ages. Amen.

### XI. Foundation of the Priory of Saint James at Château-Neuf for the Abbey of Saint Mansuetus of Toul. (Year 1097)

[Dom Calmet, as cited above, p. 509.]

To all worshipers of the Christian religion, Pibo, by the grace of God steward of the Church of Toul: greetings and the undivided love of simple truth.

The more strongly the duties of piety and good action diffuse far and wide the pleasing fragrance of an honorable reputation, and the more effectively bring about the desired enlivening of souls and, afterward, the restoration of bodies, the more earnestly the devoted affection of all the faithful ought to seek and embrace them. Therefore, we whom that supreme father of the household—may he have placed us as watchers in his house not for judgment—has appointed, ought in the race of this course to strive lawfully with such eagerness to surpass others, since, if we appear negligent not only concerning ourselves but also concerning all whom we have undertaken to govern and correct, he who entrusted them to us will at last, in anger, demand an account.

Having therefore heard and received the proclamation of apostolic preaching—that with God there is no respect of persons—we gladly received the prayers of a certain poor exile. At his request, with Abbot Grimbaldus intervening, to whose protection he had wholly commended himself and his possessions, we dedicated, with the counsel of our clergy, the church which he had built on Mount Sion.

This poor man, Ursus, a Beneventan by nationality, after examining the advantages of many places, chose the aforesaid mountain as suitable for his purpose and for his secluded way of life. He deposited there the relics of the holy apostle James, which he believed he had with him, and obtained permission to dwell there from those who held the place temporally as a benefice. But when, because of reverence for the relics and the novelty of the place, an innumerable crowd of people began to gather there, the same poor man was raised up by divine favor and strengthened by the very frequent visits and encouragement of those living around him. He built there a church as best he could. The place is thought to have been inhabited in former times and is still enclosed by a mound of stones, almost like a wall. He arranged with those in whose power it lay that, at the time of its dedication, it should be handed over, with our consent, to the church and to those serving the Lord in it. Through our hand he then gave it to Blessed Mansuetus for perpetual possession, so that monks might be established there.

Since, however, the brothers and inhabitants of the place, because of its dryness, had no necessary water within their own boundaries, the madness of those who owned the allod blocked access by force to a spring situated on the descent of the mountain, setting humanity aside. Corrected by divine inspiration on this account, namely Aidricus of Sionna, with his wife and sons, and Odelricus and Ahelinus, granted to the same cell the land in which the spring is situated, and in which a vineyard was later planted, together with whatever they possessed on the mountain.

Albricus of Haynolvilla also gave to this church, for the souls of his father Frambertius, his mother Dada, and his brother Theoderic, who are buried there, half of the entire estate which his father held in the village of Rossoil, with four manses and small dwellings, half a mill, two men, Herbertus and Seyardus, and a woman named Wigerda, and nearly two parts of the forest situated on the southern side of the same mountain.

Walter of Monh gave a quarterium of land and five enclosed manses, in which there are two springs greatly necessary for the use of the village. He also gave Tebaldus, with his wife and sons, together with his own holding, extending to sixty jugera. His brother Haymo added to this gift one quarterium and Richardus with his allod.

Furthermore, Lord Abbot Albricus gave this place whatever Count Haymo had given to Blessed Mansuetus in the same village, namely half the tithes, and Drogo with his holding, together with his wife and children. Count Humbert of Clermont gave the wife of Bernard, his son.

Gerard of Corcelles gave to Blessed James, in the village of Sionna, an enclosed mansus in which there is a mill called Atalenum, and whatever allod he possessed in the same village. In that village Hatto and his wife gave half a mansus and half a meadow producing four cartloads of hay, together with whatever allod they possessed on the mountain.

Hugo, formerly … [lacuna] … Camerarius gave in the same village seven enclosed manses and bondmen—Erundus, Benhelinus, and Bernardus, with their wives and children, and the remaining persons of both sexes—as well as the mansus in which there is a mill, and the lands and meadows belonging in their entirety to that mansus. His nephews, his two brothers, Albericus the knight and Hugo the priest, consented. He received from Abbot Thiemarus a price of one hundred solidi, and from the aforesaid Hugo a male servant and a female servant with their children, together with two enclosed manses, retained under this condition: the priest shall pay one denarius from them each year throughout his life; after his death, the remaining allod shall be restored in full. The same shall apply to the knight if he dies without a legitimate heir.

Widricus and Albricus of Paterniacum, with the consent of the same Hugo, gave outright in the same village whatever they possessed, and at Paterniacum the servant Hardenus. Rodulfus of Sorcey and his wife gave twelve jugera. Drogo, Rainerus, and Henricus, brothers, gave one quarterium in the village of Sionna. At Munli in Estraes they gave, for the present, half of their entire holding under this condition: if they should die without legitimate sons, the remaining portion should follow the first. In the same village, Henricus the priest gave one vineyard, and Malbertus whatever he possessed in that village.

The church of Bu was also added for the use of the brothers, through the administration of Lord Abbot Thiemarus; Walfridus gave it. The allod of Buris, given by Angilbertus. The allod of Lizeivilla, given to Saint Mansuetus by Morundus of Aquaso and Rodulfus of Germiney. The allod of Allinivilla, with male and female bondpeople, given by Widricus of Deusluwart. The allod of Lifou, given by Baldowinus. The allod of Sulz, given by Walterus. The allod of Seroltmont, given by Robertus and his wife for themselves and the souls of their brothers. At Marcey, one fourth of Widricus’s allod, which he gave with every customary use; he further added a male servant and a female servant with their children and holding. The allod given by Odelricus of Monh and his wife at Bunnecourt.

We, rejoicing in the temporal growth of this church and especially in the spiritual advancement of many, and looking ahead to the freedom and future peace of the brothers so that we might entirely cut away all anxiety from them, granted the altar of Saint Germanus of Sionna, with the consent and approval of Riquinus the archdeacon and Hugo the priest, who then held the altar, under this condition: as long as the priest lived, he should pay six denarii from it; after his death, the abbot should possess the church without dispute and administer it through his hand.

We also gave Warinus and his wife, received from Joffridus, whose benefice she belonged to. So that these matters, not erased by age but recalled to mind whenever necessary, might be summoned by human memory, we committed them to writing … [lacuna] … so that the rash wickedness of all detractors might be blunted by our authority. We sign them with the impression of our own image. If anyone attempts to diminish anything that this church has already acquired or may yet justly acquire, we command that he be removed from the entire Christian congregation and decree, with such rigor as we can and ought to exercise, that he be bound by the bond of anathema until a fitting satisfaction has been made. We strengthen this by the testimony of ourselves and of the reputable men who were present, subscribed below.

Sign of Pibo, bishop. Sign of Riquinus, archdeacon. Sign of Albero, chancellor. Sign of Herbertus, dean. Sign of Hugo, priest. Sign of Boso, priest. Sign of Desinus, priest, who also gave this church two meadows. Sign of Milo, from whose benefice the aforesaid mountain came. Sign of Odelricus of Brissey. Sign of Walter and Haymo, brothers. Sign of Cuono. Sign of Albricus. Sign of Hugo. Sign of Drogo. Sign of Lord Thiemarus, abbot of Saint Mansuetus. Sign of Widricus, abbot of Saint Aper. Sign of Hugo, primicerius. Sign of Liutulfus, dean. Sign of Albero. Sign of Stephen. Sign of Hugo. Sign of Thiebaldus, monk.

In the year from the Incarnation of the Lord 1097, indiction 5, epact 4, concurrent 3, lunar date 11, on the fourth day before the Ides of April, these things were happily completed at the see of Toul, in the major church, with the clergy and the entire multitude of the people hearing and witnessing them. Amen.

### XII. Foundation of the Priory of Landécourt. (Around the year 1100)

[Dom Calmet, ibid., col. 513.]

I, Pibo, by the grace of God unworthy minister of the Church of Toul, to all the sons of Holy Mother Church, present and future: perpetual greeting in Christ.

[Col. 0439D] All who administer pastoral office in the house of God ought to show the greatest diligence in building basilicas and enlarging and preserving their possessions; and if any layman should burn with the same desire, his efforts ought everywhere to be supported by their assistance. Therefore, we make known to your fraternity in Christ and commit to the memory of all of you that our most beloved friend, Lord Bencelinus, returning from Jerusalem, obtained from Lord Paschal, pope, through his prayers, the freedom of a certain church which on that day he had not yet built but had long before determined in his mind to build.

Returning to his own lands and enjoying favorable success, he revealed outwardly the desire with which he burned within: namely, he began to build the church and, as was fitting, honorably brought the work he had begun to completion. Having built and adorned it with the finest treasures, and having received it from us consecrated and dedicated in honor of the Mother of God, Saint Sigismund, glorious martyr of Christ, and Blessed Nicholas the confessor, he handed it over to God, to Saint Aper, and to those serving him. At present he has established brothers there to serve God, having assigned them an allowance by which they might be fed without anxiety.

Moved by his good intention, overcome by his requests, and because I received his son from the sacred font, with the counsel of my clergy, who appear to offer the sounder advice, and by the authority and command of my master, Lord Paschal, pope, and of our Lord Jesus Christ, I establish at the outset that this church, with all its appurtenances, shall be perpetually free, without census and without any custom, subject neither to the archdeacon nor to the dean, and answerable to no one at all except the Church of Saint Aper, of which it is free.

Moreover, by the authority I ought to exercise and for the reason I am able to give, I command that the monks who serve God there, whatever violence may be committed against them by anyone within their precinct or in the church itself, shall never cease from divine office except through the sole obedience owed to their abbot. Therefore, relying on the counsel of our most approved men, we bind by an indissoluble and perpetual bond of anathema anyone who, in whatever order or dignity he may be, wishes to take away the freedom of the aforesaid church.

To confirm knowledge of this matter, we have also summoned suitable witnesses, whose names we have thought worthy to inscribe below:

Riquinus, primicerius. Stephen, archdeacon. Hugo the Bald. Thiemarus, abbot of Saint Mansuetus. Berengerius, dean. Walfridus of Roseriis. Walter, his brother. Paganus of Saint Germanus. Sicchardus of Paurey. Theoderic of Jorcey. Richard of Episcopi-villare.

### XIII. Charter of Pibo, Bishop of Toul, concerning the Consecration of the Church of Porto. (Year 1101)

[Gal. Christ. XIII, 481.]

[Col. 0440D]

In the name of the holy and undivided Trinity, of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit, to all worshipers of the Christian faith: Pibo, by the grace of God bishop of the Church of Toul, sends greeting, that they may be united in the bond of peace and thus incorporated into Christ.

The fellowship of the citizens above, with all the advantages by which it abounds, defeats the eager efforts of human ingenuity to unfold them, since Scripture says: “What God has prepared for those who love him has not entered into the human heart.” The way to this fellowship, through the various degrees of the virtues, lies readily open to the devotion of the faithful, as the Truth bears witness when he says: “For my yoke is easy and my burden light.” Yet the virtue of charity, whose work is measured in love of one’s neighbor, enjoys, as though by a special privilege, the dignity of introducing one in a particular way.

Therefore, out of hope for that desirable fellowship and love of fraternal charity, we have recalled with no small grief the people of Porto, so often exposed to the violence of raiders and almost every misfortune. They are separated from the monastery by distance and by the considerable width of the river that frequently intervenes; consequently, they could neither be nourished by the sacred mysteries as was proper nor, in time of need, find refuge within the precinct. We therefore consecrated, with the advice of our clergy, the church which Abbot Henry, of pious memory, had permitted them to build, granting it the same liberty that the mother church of the village of Warengis has possessed from ancient times and still possesses—that is, exemption from the census and every exaction.

The provost bound them by oath under this arrangement: they were not, on account of the neighboring church, to consider themselves freer from the service of the brothers, nor were they to diminish their tithes or other revenues. Rather, although they lived within the precinct, they were to pay without resistance whatever they had been accustomed to pay according to ancient custom. If, because of some necessity, they wished to hear Mass there, the familiarity or service of the monastery’s vicar would intervene. Otherwise, if they gathered at the monastery as before, the provost would arrange how the divine service was to be conducted there. For no pastoral care pertains to that place; we have entrusted it to the disposition of the brothers like any other altar of the monastery.

The provost shall appoint a custodian there. If the devotion of the faithful should present anything to God and Saint Nicholas, he shall faithfully preserve it for the use of the brothers, except that he shall give the monastery’s vicar half of the offering that is presented by hand during Mass.

It also seems appropriate to make known to your affection that the aforesaid church of Warengisville has from ancient times possessed half of the tithes from nine *quartaria* at Delherimont, whoever may cultivate them. It also possesses, in the surrounding parishes, the whole tithe from all its *corvées*, and half at Ancingis. At the village itself, at Mannon’s court, and at Bellois, it possesses the whole tithe from its *corvées* and Ancingis, and half from the other lands belonging to the same church.

We have taken care to commit these matters to writing for remembrance, lest oblivion erase them through the decay of antiquity. But because, with the cooperation of mercy, we have undertaken this out of charitable affection, we have decided to confirm it by episcopal authority, under the bond of anathema and with the impression of our seal, so that none of our successors may presume to alter it. We have also added the testimony of reputable men, whose names are subscribed below.

The sign of Lord Pibo, bishop. The sign of Riquinus, primicerius. The sign of Bruno, cardinal archdeacon. The sign of Stephen, the same archdeacon. The sign of Raimbald, archdeacon. The sign of Hugh, archdeacon. The sign of Thizelin, archdeacon. The sign of Albero, chancellor. The sign of Albric, chaplain. The sign of Vidricus, abbot. The sign of Aper. The sign of Temarus, abbot. The sign of Mansuetus. The sign of Scherus, abbot. The sign of Leo. The sign of Odelricus, abbot. The sign of Michael. The sign of Hubinus, dean. The sign of Duke Theoderic. The sign of Gerard, his brother. The sign of Count Reinard. The sign of Odelricus of Brissei. The sign of Peter, his son. The sign of Morundus of Altirei. The sign of Theoderic of Hancei.

Done at Toul in the major church, in a full synod, on the fifth day before the Ides of October, in the year from the Incarnation of the Lord 1101, indiction IX, in the thirty-second year of our ordination, with Lord Adelon, provost of that place, taking part.

## XIV. Privilege for the Church of Saint Gengulf. (Year 1105.)

[Dom Calmet, *History of Lorraine*, IV, Documents, p. 513.]

In the name of the holy and undivided Trinity, of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit, to all the sons of holy Mother Church, both present and future: Pibo, by the grace of God bishop of the Leuci.

It ought to be the chief concern of all the faithful, and especially of bishops, that the churches whose protection the bishops have undertaken should remain unimpaired in their times. If possible, they ought to establish them during their own days in such a way that no adversity of a later age could tear them from the condition of their integrity. For the Truth says: “Where I am, there also my minister shall be” (Matthew 12:26). Those who recognize that they are God’s ministers in governing churches ought rightly to keep watch over this matter and faithfully administer the ministry of the blessed promise entrusted to them.

I, therefore, the great steward of the Church of Toul, recognizing myself as Christ’s minister and desiring already to become a participant in blessed hope, have watched over the Church entrusted to me as I could and insofar as I could. I have carefully considered both the safety of my see and that of the churches subject to it. Accordingly, the Church of Saint Gengulf, situated within the walls of our city, founded by my predecessors, Saint Gerard and Bishop Udo of pious memory, enriched with very many possessions and gifts, and made illustrious through a congregation of brothers serving the eternal King there—I too have embraced this church with a father’s affection and have always protected it with whatever patronage I could provide.

Since, moreover, many things have accrued to that church in my own time, some of them through me personally, I have decided, on the advice of venerable men, to record its possessions and privileges in the present charter. I have confirmed them all by my authority and with the consent of the entire clergy and people in the presence of a general synod.
