Let it therefore be known to all the faithful, present and future, that the Church of Saint Gengulf possesses by secure right and without any contradiction the following written properties:

All the land in the village of Boso’s Mount, with its dependencies and with the entire church of Saint George; the church of Travillon, the church of Marbagium, the church of Senois, with the chapel of Cheulaio; the church of Menoville, sixty-six and a half *mansi*, except the demesne land; at Pomponius, two vineyards; at Middle Village, four *sessi* and as much demesne land as suffices for the plowing of three plowmen, with seven *quartaria* and the ban over the demesne meadow, together with the remaining meadows and other dependencies; at Fagus, in Lersivallis, four vineyards, twenty *journals* of land, and two dwelling *mansi*; at Wandini-villa, four *mansi*, except the demesne land; at Hermoteseim, the vineyards given by B., provost of that place, and by his brother Count Albert; at Ameralli-villa, seven and a half *mansi*, with the church and all its appurtenances; at Banniolum, seven *mansi* and three *quartaria*, except the demesne lands, and the share that the brothers of Calmesiacum held there—for the church of Domno-Martino was given in exchange, along with what they appeared to possess at Hundinivilla; the estate of Cruceliae, with its church and four mills; and the estate called Saint Anianus, situated beside the gate of this city, with its church and mill, and everything belonging to both estates, with the full ban, persons of both sexes, woods, meadows, vineyards, cultivated and uncultivated lands, watercourses, outgoings and revenues.

Also, within the walls of this city, a *mansus* on which stand the house and cellar that Ascelinus gave for the salvation of his soul, with all his inheritance: namely, in Varneri’s plantation, two and a half rows of vines, and all the inheritance that Duorardus gave for his son. A vineyard *mansus* beside Saint Amantius; at Barro, one vineyard, which Romanus gave for his son; above the Moselle, beside Caldeniacum, one mill with a *sessus* and vineyard, which Renaldus, a canon there, gave; an oven with a *mansus* at the fountain of Saint Mansuetus, with one vineyard at Mardeau; on Barro Mountain, two vineyards; in Carravallis, four rows of vines; in Hatton’s Valley, six rows; at the summit of Barro, one vineyard; at Calvomons, eight rows; in Amantius’s meadow, eleven rows; between the vineyards, one row; at Gula, one vineyard; at Calcatoria, one vineyard, five rows, twenty-one purchased from Maria, and two others.

My predecessors, enriching the aforesaid church with these possessions, entrusted them to it so that it might be subject solely to the bishop, might never be granted as a benefice to anyone, and might receive as provost the man whom the common election—and specifically the demand of the sounder part—called for. They also established that the provost himself should hold the cardinal archdeaconry as the benefice of that provostship.

For we have learned that Provost Olderic and, second, Bruno, held that office in the same basilica. We have decided that Richuinus should succeed them as the third—not by hereditary right, so that this succession should or could pertain to his primiceriusship by the law of benefice or by any other reason, nor so that any other primicerius might claim succession in this matter, but solely because the brothers of the same church elected him, since they recognized that they had abundant counsel in his wisdom and considerable protection in his integrity.

My aforesaid predecessor, Bishop Udo, also established that the congregation of that monastery should come to our prepared seat on the days named below to celebrate the divine office: on the feast of Saint Stephen after the Nativity of the Lord, for the public Mass; on the day of his Invention, for Vespers; and on those days when the bishop of this see celebrates the full order, namely Maundy Thursday, Easter, and Pentecost, deacons and subdeacons shall be taken from that congregation, as necessity may require.

I, Pibo, have therefore received this most sacred institution with a kindly mind, and have confirmed by legitimate authority the aforesaid possessions and everything contained in the aforesaid privilege. I strike with the curse of anathema all who should presume to pervert or diminish anything in the matters stated above. So that all these things may remain firmer and undisturbed forever, I have confirmed them, with the advice of the entire clergy, by the impression of my seal, and strengthened them by the subscription of suitable witnesses.

I, Pibo, by the grace of God bishop of the Leuci, subscribe in approval and with the ring bearing the sign of our Church. The sign of Riquinus, primicerius and provost of the same church. The sign of Saint Stephen, archdeacon. The sign of Thiercelin, archdeacon. The sign of Hugh, archdeacon. The sign of Elberic, archdeacon. The sign of Rambald, archdeacon. The sign of Hugh the Younger, archdeacon. The sign of Gobert, archdeacon and thereafter canon. The sign of Lord Widricus, abbot of Saint Aper. The sign of Lord Thiemar, abbot of Saint Mansuetus. The sign of Lord Scherus, abbot of Saint Leo. The sign of Humbald, dean of the same place, and of the other canons, Theoderic and Gilbert. The sign of Count Renard and Warin, his son. The sign of Walter of Cominatus. The sign of Sigifrid, advocate. The sign of Henry of Saint Vedastus and Theoderic, his son. The sign of Renald, dapifer. The sign of Vileri. The sign of Wolfandus. The sign of Beretus. The sign of Promidus, and others.

Given and read aloud in the major church, in a full synod, on the eighth day before the Ides of June, in the year from the Incarnation of the Lord 1105, indiction XIV, and in the thirty-fifth year of our ordination.

[Col. 0445]

## Letter of Pibo to Pope Paschal

(See under Paschal, below.)

## Appendix

[Col. 0445]

## Deeds of the Bishops of Toul, edited by Professor Georg Waitz of Kiel

(*Monumenta Germaniae historica*, *Scriptores*, vol. VIII, p. 631.)

[Note.]

I do not see why we should doubt that the brief history of the bishops of Toul, extended to the year 1107, in which Bishop Pibo died, is owed to one and the same writer. The same method of narration and the same style of expression occur everywhere, and all the manuscripts known to us, except one mutilated copy, reach this year.

[Note: Compare Martene, *Thesaurus* III, p. 990; *Historia litteraria* IX, p. 390. The words in chapter 39, “Since we have learned that the deeds of the earlier bishops of this see have, as occasion offered, been written down, it seems unfitting to us that we should conceal the acts of venerable Udo under the bar of silence ...,” refer to the *Life of Bruno* and others.]

Those who attributed part of the work to Adso, Widricus, and other writers from Toul had before their eyes a history interpolated from their writings, as we shall see later. [Note: Calmet, *L. Probb.*, p. 83.] The author of the *Deeds*, who seems to have lived at the beginning of the twelfth century, was doubtless either a man of Toul or a monk or cleric there. He gathered into one brief sequence what had previously been written about the affairs of Toul and supplemented it as far as he could.

He partly copied Adso’s book *On the Life and Miracles of Saint Mansuetus* [Note: Chapters 2 and 3.], the *Lives of Saint Aper* [Note: Chapters 8 and 31.], of Saint Gerard by Widricus [Note: Chapters 31 and 34.], and of Saint Bruno by Wibertus [Note: Chapter 38.]; partly he referred readers to them. Perhaps he also had before him the *Life of Udo* [Note: Chapters 39 and following. For when Benoît cites a *Life of Udo* whose opening agrees word for word with the *Deeds*, he adds that a canon of Toul wrote it and used these words: “Accordingly, with Lord Riquinus, primicerius of this see, urging us to write out certain deeds of Udo …” These words do not occur in the *Deeds*, and since Riquinus was primicerius while Pibo was alive, that *Life* must have been written earlier.] and incorporated part of it into these *Deeds*.

Moreover, he relied chiefly everywhere on diplomas and charters, recording donations and foundations. When he lacked such sources, he seems to have followed a certain tradition. As a result, the history of the earlier bishops is quite uncertain and disfigured by serious errors [Note: Compare Benoît, p. 207; *Acta Sanctorum*, September I, p. 620.], while the chronology is especially confused, so that establishing a reliable order is extremely difficult. [Note: Calmet treated these matters with his customary carelessness; nevertheless, the author of volume XIII of *Gallia Christiana* follows him everywhere and almost copies him word for word.] For this reason, the author does not even seem to have possessed older catalogues.

Adso indeed cites the *Deeds of the earlier bishops of the city of the Leuci* [Note: *Acta Sanctorum*, September I, p. 664.], but these taught us almost nothing—whether they had been lost or were filled with the same errors. Certainly, concerning the first bishops, he merely copied Adso’s book, which is unworthy of credence. [Note: Nor, as I. Limpenus thought (*Acta Sanctorum*, September I, pp. 619–620), is this *Life* older than Adso.] Later too, whenever he could possess well-established information, in his eagerness for brevity he omitted many important matters, so that he merely skims over Pibo’s deeds and scarcely touches in a word on the disputes he had with the emperor Henry IV.

Martene published these authentic *Deeds of the Bishops of Toul* from the Camberon manuscript, *Thesaurus*, III, p. 991. Our Bethmann found the same manuscript, apparently, at The Hague, no. 274a, and compared it with the printed editions. I have made the following manuscript the basis of this edition:

1. A parchment book in quarto, written neatly and with sufficient accuracy in the thirteenth century. [Note: It also contains Pope Calixtus’s book on the translation of Saint James, Turpinus, and the *Life of Amelius and Amicus*.]

2. I have had put to our use a copy of the former Toul manuscript of Saint Mansuetus, which Martene saw and which Calmet had transcribed (*L. Probb.*, pp. 83–166), preserved at Nancy in the library of Monsieur Noël, a public notary. The parchment codex, written in quarto in the twelfth century, already consists of 134 folios and contains a text enlarged and interpolated in many places. It also includes the complete *Lives of Saint Mansuetus, Saint Aper, Saint Gerard,* and *Saint Bruno*. Consequently, it appears to present a collection of writings about Toul rather than the *Deeds* themselves. The book was already mutilated at the end in Martene’s time; it breaks off in *The Life of Bruno*, 1.12.

3. In the Royal Library at Paris, among Baluze’s collections, Arm. V, package 5, no. 2, there is preserved a copy of another manuscript of Saint Mansuetus. It agrees in many respects with no. 2, but sometimes alone preserves the true reading, and it does not insert those *Lives* in full. In their place, other material has been added, partly drawn from the same *Lives* and partly from elsewhere.

Nevertheless, I am not persuaded that this fuller text, rather than the shorter and genuine text of the author preserved in the Hague manuscript, is the original. We have often seen histories of this sort expanded in the same way; but why a scribe would have omitted these passages cannot be understood. In addition, we see that sources generally well known were used in these additions: the *Lives of Saint Gerard* and *Saint Bruno*, which the author of the *Deeds* expressly says he does not wish to copy. Perhaps, then, the additions found in the history of Udo were likewise inserted from the *Life* written at Riquinus’s command.

Supported by these materials, our edition presents a purer text, which I have attempted to illuminate with the necessary notes.

G. Waitz

## Appendix to Pibo: Here Begins the Catalogue of the Bishops of Toul, from Saint Mansuetus the Blessed Onward

[Note: Thus in manuscript 2; absent from manuscript 1.]

[Col. 0447]

Although the virtues and examples of all the saints rightly ought always to be recalled and commended to memory, according to the scriptural saying, “All peoples proclaim the wisdom of the saints, and the Church announces their praise” (Ecclesiasticus 44:15), nevertheless we ought more frequently to review the deeds of those whose relics we possess, or by whose patronage, through the Lord’s gift, we are governed.

Therefore, since we have decided to write, as the Lord grants, about the deeds of the bishops of the Leuci for the memory of posterity, it is fitting that we begin with the first father and bishop of that city, Saint Mansuetus.

### 2

The same venerable father, as we have learned from the account of our elders, was descended from a noble Scottish race. [Note: “Scottorum” in manuscript 2; “genere” (“race”) is absent in manuscript 2.] But by the providential mercy of God, which wonderfully foreordains and disposes all things, he was made an exile from his own borders so that he might become a settler in the heavenly region and make those who were exiles from the homeland of the heavenly kingdom fellow heirs of the citizens above.

It is therefore no wonder that the Lord and Savior of all, who wishes everyone to be saved and to come to the recognition of the truth, summoned such a teacher from the distant parts of the earth and sent him to sow the seeds of the divine word and illumine the blind hearts of the barbarians. He himself, descending from the heavenly dwelling places, graciously visited the human race, bound by original and actual sin.

At the time when the Roman Church shone through the preaching and apostleship of blessed Peter, chief of the apostles, blessed Mansuetus was brought there under Christ’s guidance and submitted himself to apostolic teaching. Instructed by him in the lessons of the Catholic faith and fully trained in knowledge of the divine words, he was consecrated by pontifical blessing and sent to the aforesaid city like a shining lamp to drive away the darkness of error.

How brightly he shone there in holiness of life and perseverance in preaching cannot be sufficiently told by a barren tongue. Not only did his abundant teaching of evangelical faith shine forth for overcoming the ferocity of the pagans, but he also deserved to be illuminated by such great grace of miracles that, through his prayers, he raised the son of the city’s ruler from death and restored him alive and unharmed.

Terrified by this miracle, the father bowed his neck to the devout faith of Christ. After every diabolical error had been expelled, he, together with his son and the entire multitude of pagans, deserved to be purified by Saint Mansuetus in the bath of baptism.

After all the superstitious and empty filth of idols had been cleansed, he built there a temple to the Lord in honor of his perpetual Virgin Mother and of Saint Stephen, the first martyr, as well as other churches throughout the surrounding region. Priests and deacons were appointed there, and the wondrous God was glorified in his saints down to the present day.

It is impossible to touch in writing upon everything that so great and remarkable a man accomplished while still in the body, or all that he taught, or the vast multitude of believers whom he begot in Christ through the Gospel, or how vigilantly he guarded the Lord’s flock entrusted to him, teaching it worthily and living holily.

We present only this brief summary, lest such a lamp, hidden under a measure through our unworthy silence, should fail to shine for all who are in the house of God. When he had completed the course of his admirable life and confirmed the Church in Christ, that glorious priest of the Lord left the shipwreck of the present age, seeking the harbor of perpetual rest, crowned by Christ forever.

His most holy body, buried not far from the aforesaid city, is kept in the church said to have been founded by him and dedicated in the name of the blessed apostle Peter. His presence there adorns it through his relics and illuminates it with innumerable miracles. Whoever approaches that place to ask for something in faith undoubtedly rejoices that the request has been granted.

Let us humbly beg his help, and may he, through his patronage and pastoral protection, guard us in the present from every adversity and, when the contest of this life is completed, bring us happily to the prize of our reward, through the merciful grace of our Redeemer, who appointed such a shepherd over his sheep. For with the coeternal Father and the Holy Spirit he possesses the Trinity of equal Godhead throughout endless ages. Amen.

[Note: At this point manuscript 2 inserted Adso’s *Life of Saint Mansuetus* (*Monumenta Sanctorum*, IV, p. 487).]

### 3

After the death of the aforesaid most holy bishop and excellent teacher, let us recall who succeeded him in the episcopal see.

First after him, Lord Amon (c. 400?) attained the dignity of the episcopal chair. [Note: This too is taken from Adso’s *Life of Saint Mansuetus*, book I, near the end.] He rests with his predecessor, the blessed Mansuetus, in the aforesaid church of Saint Peter, chief of the apostles. Through the merits of both of them—that is, Saint Mansuetus and the aforementioned blessed Amon—many afflicted by blindness, leprosy, fever, and other illnesses are restored to health.

Many kings and princes were accustomed to come to their patronage and enrich their place from their own resources. A crowd of visitors and an innumerable multitude of poor people gathered there, and the faithful had provided them with the means by which they could live. Hence, down to the present day, the place is called “the matricula of Lord Mansuetus and Lord Amon.”

### 4

After him, a remarkable man named Alcha attained the honor of the pontificate. [Note: “Alcna” in manuscript 3.] By the privilege of his personal name, he watched over the flock entrusted to him with diligent care. For *Alchos* means “white” in Aeolic, [Note: “d. a.” in manuscript 3.] in Latin usage, [Note: “Latiari” in manuscript 3.] because he himself, whitened by every adornment of virtue, led the sheep entrusted to him by words and examples to the pleasant pasture:

> The good shepherd enters the fold, preceded by a white fleece;  
> the Lamb, the sheep, and the whole flock of virgins enter, all shining white.

[Note: “Intra” for “intrat” in manuscript 3.]

### 5

When he had therefore been removed from the earthly calamity, Celsinus became bishop. [Note: “Became bishop” is absent from manuscript 3.] Raised to the greatest height by divine graces, he shone upon earth through works of heavenly virtue. Because he embraced the exalted Lord, high above all nations, with a faithful mind, he was therefore exalted by him in the horn of his people.

### 6

When the departure from this life to God had taken place (c. 470), Auspicius was ordained in the aforesaid see, [Note: “Aspicius” in manuscript 3; manuscript 2 corrects it to “Auspicius.”] a man distinguished for goodness and, while he lived, perceptive toward his own people through vigilant concern. For this reason he deserved eternal recompense from Christ and attained fellowship with the citizens above and with the chosen shepherds.

[Note: His metrical letter to Count Arbogast survives; Duchesne I, p. 844.]

### 7

Next came Ursus, who followed the footsteps of his predecessors so closely that he is believed to enjoy eternal glory with them.

[Note: “Since he imitated the ferocity of his own name against vices, he commendably followed the gentleness of the virtues,” added in manuscripts 2 and 3.]

### 8

After these events had passed, through the abundant mercy of almighty God, which so ordained matters and mercifully regarded that place, the most holy man and confessor of admirable life, Lord Aper, is recognized as having been carried to the height of the same pontificate (c. 500), as though seized rather than elected, according to what is read in his book of life.

Following the example of his first predecessor, Lord Mansuetus, he shone forth not only through abundance of teaching but also through the effectiveness of wondrous virtues. If anyone wishes to know about this, let him read through his book of life; there he will find everything in full. [Note: “Which is kept at the place of his tomb” is added in manuscripts 2 and 3.]

He held the episcopal see for seven years. The deposition of his most sacred body is celebrated on the seventeenth day before the Kalends of October in the suburb of the same city, in the church whose construction he himself began from the foundations.

According to the authoritative books, he is known to have lived in the time of the most cruel emperor Hadrian. [Note: In the *Life of Aper* apud Martene, *Thesaurus*, III, p. 1030, and *Acta Sanctorum*, September V, p. 87, it is said that Saint Aper approached Hadrian, who at that time was exercising the office of judge in the aforesaid city. Martene thought this had given rise to this entirely false opinion.] Hadrian decreed that all the judges under him throughout the world should be called by his name. In his fourth year blessed Aper was ordained bishop; in his eleventh he departed from the human condition.

[Note: At this point manuscript 2 inserted the *Life and Miracles of Saint Aper*.]

### 9

Leaving aside what we already know to have been written about him by others, let us insert the deeds and names of his successors, insofar as we know them.

Lord Albinus succeeded him, [Note: “Albauldus,” corrected by a later hand to “Albinus” in manuscript 2.] a remarkable man distinguished by every goodness. [Note: If we read “Albauldus,” he may perhaps be the same man who is called Alodius in the Council of Aureliacum of 549, *Councils*, ed. Harduin, II, 1449. Certainly this order of bishops deserves little confidence.] He fulfilled the desirable vow of his predecessor and rebuilt with careful skill the church that Saint Aper had begun.

There he gathered faithful men who would live according to the example of the apostles, and obtained from the supreme pontiffs and martyrs Stephen and Fabian an apostolic decree concerning the same monastery, as it is found in the most ancient *thomocartae*. [Note: Here the author is completely mistaken concerning the names of the supreme Stephen and Fabian, who lived long before Albinus. —Martene.]

### 10

After him, Trisoricus was raised to the episcopal chair. He too was no inferior to his predecessors. To the best of his ability, in the fervor of divine religion, he wisely fed the sheep entrusted to him with the nourishment of the divine word and led them to the heavenly halls by the exemplary model of virtues.

### 11

Then Dulcitius was ordained bishop by common will and by the equal counsel of the people and clergy. [Note: “Of the clergy and people” in manuscript 3; “consent” in manuscript 2.]

[Note: “Nor without reason: for together with the honeyed sweetness of his name there flowed an integrity of character, and, like the wisest bees, he gathered the honeycombs of devout religion in the hearts of his subjects,” added in manuscripts 2 and 3.]

### 12

After him came Praemon. [Note: “Bishop” is added in manuscripts 2 and 3.] Fortified by the help of God, he fought manfully against spiritual wickedness and earnestly warned the minds of his subjects to overcome Christ’s enemies.

Much remains omitted by us concerning how these aforesaid fathers lived in this see, with what religion and in what manner, and how they labored in God’s harvest—material that had long ago been neglected by earlier writers.

### 13

When the aforesaid Praemon had been taken from this light, Autmundus was ordained bishop. Through his gentle goodness, many people in his time who loved and sought God began to hate the world.

Among them were men of wondrous holiness, Pihentius [Note: “Pientius” in manuscripts 2 and 3.] and Agentius, as well as Saint Columba and very many others. Serving God together with the aforesaid Lord Autmundus, they came to rest in peace.

He cultivated the memory of Christ’s confessor Aper with devoted care. He increased his monastery in the practice of divine religion and, in his honor, wrote various texts and responsories for the remembrance of posterity.

### 14

Next, Eutulanus deserved to attain the summit of the pontificate (c. 600). [Note: “Eudula” in manuscript 3.] In his days the Lord began to enrich the place he held with landed possessions. Among them Luciacus was acquired there. [Note: “Lucianus,” corrected to “Lucicus” in manuscript 2.] [Note: Lucey, according to Benoît, whom I have followed in explaining these names.]

While he occupied the episcopal chair, a certain woman devoted to God and to the enlargement of God’s churches, named Praetoria, gave to the aforesaid see of Saint Mary, Mother of God and ever-virgin, and of Saint Stephen, the first martyr, the church of Saint Maximinus, the village of Videliacum, [Note: Villey (Villers)-Saint-Etienne, Villey-Le-Sec, Biqueley.] and another village called by the same name, as well as Buchuliacum, the abbey of Saint Pientius, and another place called Ardinio [Note: Andilli.] or Titiliacum, and Brueriacum. [Note: Bruley.] This is contained in her charter. [Note: “Charters” in manuscript 3.] [Note: The diploma of King Theodebert, by which he is said to have confirmed these grants (Benoît, p. 250), does not appear to survive.]

[Additional textual apparatus omitted above.]

[Note on the opening of the Catalogue: “rightly” (*merito*) is manuscript 3’s reading. Manuscripts 2 and 3 read, in reversed order, “by whose patronage, through the Lord’s gift, we are governed, or whose relics we possess.” Manuscript 1 reads *actu* for *actis* (“deeds”); manuscript 2 spells *Leuchorum* with a lower-case initial; manuscripts 2 and 3 add “namely Saint Mansuetus” after “first father and bishop of that city.”]

[Chapter 2, additional notes: Manuscripts 2 and 3 read “for he was” (*fuit enim*). The author here follows Adso’s fancifully composed *Life of Saint Mansuetus*. Manuscripts 2 and 3 read “in” for “to” in “come to the recognition”; manuscript 2 reads “also” for “and”; manuscript 2 has an erased or otherwise defective reading after *de* (“from”), apparently “de s. descen...”; manuscripts 2 and 3 omit “blessed Mansuetus”; manuscript 1 has *repellandas* for “to drive away”; manuscript 1 perhaps has *sterili* for “barren”; manuscripts 2 and 3 read “diabolical” for “of the devil”; manuscript 1 reads “purified” for “cleansed”; manuscripts 2 and 3 add “God” after “his Mother”; manuscript 2 reads “throughout the surrounding regions”; manuscript 3 reads “it is indeed” for “it is impossible”; manuscript 1 perhaps reads “these things” for “this”; manuscripts 2 and 3 read “for” for “when”; manuscripts 2 and 3 omit “and” in “and entrusted to him”; manuscript 3 omits “of the Lord”; manuscript 3 reads *irradat* for “illuminates”; manuscript 3 reads “whoever” for “who”; manuscript 3 reads “all” for “his sheep”; manuscripts 1 and 3 read “eternal” for “coeternal”; manuscript 3 omits “of ages” in “throughout endless ages.”]

[Chapter 3, additional notes: Manuscripts 2 and 3 read *principis apostolorum Petri* (“Peter, chief of the apostles”); manuscript 2 reads “and” for “and also” in “leprosy, fever, and other illnesses.”]

[Chapter 4, additional notes: Manuscript 1 reads *commissi* for “entrusted”; manuscripts 2 and 3 read “and” for “because”; manuscript 1 reads *nomine* for “in Latin usage.”]

[Chapter 5, additional notes: Manuscripts 1 and 2 read “earth” for “earthly”; manuscript 1 omits “calamity.”]

[Chapter 8, additional notes: Manuscript 3 places before “After these events” an addition which is printed elsewhere in its proper place: “All of whom, having imitated the ferocity of their own name against vices, nevertheless commendably followed the gentleness of the virtues.” Manuscript 2 corrects *predecessoris* to *praecessoris* (“predecessor”).]

[Chapter 9, additional note: Manuscript 2 reads “privilege” for “decree.”]

[Chapter 10, additional notes: Manuscript 2 repeatedly spells “chair” as *chathedra*; manuscript 3 reads *imitabili* for “exemplary.”]

[Chapter 11, additional note: In the addition of manuscripts 2 and 3, *prudentissimas* (“wisest,” feminine plural) is corrected to *prudentissima* (“most prudent,” neuter plural).]

[Chapter 13, additional note: Manuscript 2 omits “and” before Saint Columba.]

[Chapter 14, additional notes: Manuscripts 1 and 2 omit the words from “God” through “Mary” in “God’s churches ... Saint Mary”; manuscript 3 omits “and” after “as well as.”]

### 15.

After Lord Eutulanus [Note: [Col. 0451] *Eudulam* in witness 3, corrected to *Eutulanum* in witness 2.], an outstanding man of admirable holiness attained the height of pontifical honor, bearing no small care for the Lord’s flock [Note: [Col. 0451] *gerens dominici gregis* (“bearing the Lord’s flock”) is absent in witness 1.] [Col. 0451C] and beloved by everyone—kings and dukes in particular—as subsequent events proved, while the growth of his see demonstrates it even more clearly: Lord Teufridus [Col. 0452A] (c. 630) [Note: [Col. 0451] *Teutertous* in witness 3.].

Among his many works of piety [Note: [Col. 0451] Absent in witnesses 1 and 2.] he obtained from the most glorious King Dagobert, through the intervention of his revered mother, Queen Chimechildis [Note: [Col. 0451D] She was the mother of Dagobert II.], for the church over which the revered bishop presided, a villa called Bladenau [Note: [Col. 0451D] Blenod.] with its neighboring estates: namely, Cotanicurt in its entirety, Montis [Note: [Col. 0451D] Mont and Montenoy.] and Montenonis, Gaiacum [Note: [Col. 0451D] Galiaud or Gayaux?], and the mansus of Fredo.

The aforesaid bishop also acquired for the said see other estates, namely Bladenau [Note: [Col. 0451] *Blandenau* in witnesses 1 and 2.], situated overlooking the river Arufia: Venna with its church, the mansus of Medulfus, the *villare* of Gebenus, and many others, as is found in his charters [Note: [Col. 0451] From *et* through *repperitur* (“and … is found”) absent in witnesses 2 and 3; where these words are added: “and whatever appears to belong to the aforesaid places.” The same venerable bishop also endeavored to acquire from the same king other estates along the river Meuse: Traveron, Paterniacum [ [Col. 0452D] Pargney.], Campaniacum [ [Col. 0452D] Sampigny or Champugney. Calmet.], Biliniacum, Alonum, Huncilinimons, and whatever in Saviniacum and Lamnari-lannaricurt and Regniacum [*Reginacum* in witness 3.] appears to belong to the royal fisc.]

The aforementioned king also, through the intervention of the same revered bishop, gave to the aforesaid see of Toul, in the district of Bedinse beside the little river Vidus, a royal estate called Noviantum [ [Col. 0452D] “Known today by the name of Void.” Benoit.], together with the royal palace, the churches constructed there, and all ecclesiastical furnishings.

Indeed, at the prompting and inspiration of the Almighty’s mercy, that religious king, rich in generosity, for the enlargement of this bishopric and out of devotion to the same bishop, also granted an estate called Viskerium [ [Col. 0452D] Vicherei.], with its royal palace, churches, and everything adjoining that estate.

The same venerable bishop also obtained from King Sigibert, the son of the aforementioned most religious King Dagobert, the estates called Longus Campus, Vicricinum [*Vicritinum* in witness 3.], and as much land as he appears to possess in Framariaca [*Framarata* in witness 3.], as well as the estate of Rufiaca [ [Col. 0452D] Erufe.]—and Ribojaca [*Ribojacam*, added in a later hand in witness 2]—in its entirety, together with their dependencies.

All these possessions the oft-mentioned bishop deserved to acquire from the most pious King Dagobert, in their entirety and without any diminution, with the favor of the omnipotent mercy of God. [Note: The concluding sentence and the intervening material are absent in witnesses 2 and 3, where the additional material beginning “He also acquired …” appears.]

### 16.

Bishop Leudinus succeeded him in the order of pontifical dignity [Note: [Col. 0451D] Leuduinus, also called Bodo, bishop of Toul and brother of Salaberga, appears in the Life of this virgin, chapter 17.] (c. 660). He truly shone all around like the Lord’s lamp placed upon a lampstand, near and far, through the example of holy religion [Note: [Col. 0451] Witnesses 2 and 3 add: “Raised by the wings of a twofold charity to the vaults of heaven, he despised the world’s amusements and, enriched with heavenly riches …”].

### 17.

After him Eborinus became bishop [Note: [Col. 0452D] Brequigny, p. CCLXVII, considers false the charter of Numerianus, archbishop of Trier, in which Ebroinus (Eboricus) is called bishop, though he relies on several less substantial arguments.] (c. 665). In accordance with Jeremiah’s prophecy [“more ruddy than ancient ivory”; not added in witness 3], although, having lived in peace, he lacked the redness of martyrdom through the shedding of blood, nevertheless through his confession of holy faith he obtained the martyr’s lot by his vow and desire for martyrdom [Note: [Col. 0452D] In the year 680 Adeodatus, bishop of Toul, subscribed to the Roman council. *Councils*, ed. Harduin, III, p. 1131.].

### 18.

Ermenteus succeeded him as bishop. He was truly a good shepherd of souls, without the fear of a wicked hireling, feeding the flock of the heavenly King with the sweetness of celestial pasture and, according to his strength, rescuing it from the attacks of infernal wolves [Note: [Col. 0452D] Benoit, p. 271, citing some fragment of a Life unknown to me, reports that Ermenteus was ordained priest by Adeodatus and recovered from King Theodoric the estate of Ociacavilla, which Count Hildramnus had usurped.].

### 19.

Magnardus [Note: [Col. 0453] *Magnaldus* in witness 2.] succeeded him as bishop [Note: [Col. 0453C] Benoit, p. 272, reports the following from a catalogue of bishops: “Magnaldus added Gereon’s estate in the district of Sungent to the matricula of Saint Stephen; likewise he gave certain properties in the district of Vabrinc, namely the estate of Corniac.”].

He was great before God through the merits of his virtues and great among the people through the examples of his good deeds. The Almighty magnified him on earth through the episcopal office and crowned him in heaven with glory and honor.

His venerable body was buried [Note: [Col. 0453] Absent in witness 2.] in the cemetery of Saint Aper; it lies transferred on the left side beside the altar of Saint Christopher the Martyr.

After him Dodo became bishop [Note: [Col. 0453C] He is said to have consecrated the church of Lord Martin and acquired many possessions. Benoit, in the same place.] (c. 700). Clad in the breastplate of faith, covered with the helmet of holy hope, and wrapped in the wedding garment of charity, he fought manfully in the arduous struggle of this world [Note: [Col. 0453] *Labriosa* in witness 2.]; therefore, victorious [Note: [Col. 0453] *Victoriosius?* in witness 2.], he returned to the heavenly King, received into the celestial court.

### 20.

Then Garibaldus, son of Volfaudus [Note: [Col. 0453] *Volfaldus* in witness 3.] [Note: [Col. 0453C] He founded the monastery of Saint Michael. See *Chronicle of Saint Michael*, MGH SS IV, p. 79, and the charter of Wolfoldus in Calmet I, p. 264.], was unanimously chosen as a suitable bishop [Note: [Col. 0453] *Adonus* in witness 3.] (c. 710). He gave to the church over which he presided everything he possessed from his inheritance. He also acquired many other things, as is recorded in his charters [Note: [Col. 0453] The words from “He also acquired” through “is recorded” are absent in witnesses 2 and 3, where the following is added: “in the estate of Tranculfus and in Arusia [*Arusga* in witness 3], as well as in the estate of Ribodus. He also acquired for the same church which he governed, from the glorious King Childebert, through the intervention of Queen Ermenechildis, his wife, a small monastery dedicated in honor of Saint Peter, situated in a forest called Dervo [ [Col. 0454C] Montier-en-Der.], and the estates called Magniaca villa [ [Col. 0454C] Mogneville.] and Boneriacus, together with Copedonia [ [Col. 0454C] Couvonge.] on the river Saltus.”].

In his time also, Deodatus, a man of supreme holiness and formerly bishop of Nevers, renouncing the world, obtained from the aforesaid bishop a place in the Vosges forest in which to pursue the religious life [Note: [Col. 0453] This is plainly false.].

### 21.

Godus, a venerable man, succeeded him as bishop (c. 750?). During his time, because of the people’s crimes, the city of Leucha was consumed by fire. But that bishop obtained from King Pippin both immunity for his city and the recovery of the charters which the fire had destroyed for his church.

When he died, he ordered himself to be buried in a church belonging to one of his estates called Castellum; his tomb is still shown there today.

### 22.

When he had departed this life, Lord Bodo [Note: [Col. 0453C] Mabillon considers this Bodo to be the same as Baudinus—read Leudinus—the brother of Salaberga, abbess of Laon, who was also called Bodo. The author of this work seems to support his view when he says that Bodo was transferred from the cemetery of Saint Mansuetus to Laon; for no other reason for this translation appears likely than that he was Salaberga’s brother. Martène. Yet this cannot be so unless we suppose that the order of the bishops has been greatly disturbed.] became bishop [Note: [Col. 0453] Witnesses 2 and 3 add: “Bodo, who, abandoning the love of the world, turned to Christ, became a follower of the most religious life, and was a founder of churches and monasteries.”], whose praiseworthy life remains in every respect worthy of the memory of posterity [Note: [Col. 0453] Witness 3 lacks this phrase.]. Born in the district of Odern [ [Col. 0454C] Ornois in Lorraine.], the son of Bertoldus [*Bertauldus* in witness 3] and Bertildis, he was approved in conduct and way of life and deserved to become bishop of Toul [added in witnesses 2 and 3].

Among the other works of goodness which he continually performed, he built a monastery in honor of the most blessed Mother of God, Mary, and of blessed Peter, chief of the apostles [Note: [Col. 0453] “Of the most blessed Virgin Mary” in witness 1; “of the most blessed Virgin Mary” in witness 3. “Saint” replaces “blessed” in witness 2.], appointing there women consecrated to God [Note: [Col. 0453] Absent in witness 2.] to serve him. He placed his daughter, named Teutberga [Note: [Col. 0453] *Teuberga* in witness 1; *Zeutberga* in witness 2; *Temberga* in witness 3.], over them; in honor of his name the monastery is still called Bodo’s monastery [Note: [Col. 0454C] Bonmoutier.].

He left that place, together with everything he had been able to acquire there, to the church over which he presided as a possession by right. Thereafter [Note: [Col. 0453] *Inde* in witness 3.] he deserved to receive an apostolic privilege from the great teacher Gregory and his predecessor Agapetus [Note: [Col. 0454C] The author is mistaken here concerning the names of the Roman pontiffs Agapetus and Gregory the Great, who had died long before Bodo. Martène.].

He also gave to the same church, in the district of Odern, from his own property [Note: [Col. 0453] “From his properties” in witness 2.], the estates called Nasius [Note: [Col. 0453] *Nasyus* in witness 3.] and Nasitus [Note: [Col. 0453] *Nasytus* in witness 3.] [Note: [Col. 0454C] “Greater and lesser Nançois.” Benoit. “Nas and Nançoy.” Calmet.].

He likewise transferred to Saint Stephen the place called Stivajum [Note: [Col. 0453] *Stivanum* in witness 1.] [Note: [Col. 0454C] Estival.], which had been left to him by his parents. There he built a monastery in honor of blessed Peter the apostle on the river Murt [Note: [Col. 0454C] The Meurthe.], and gathered twelve canons [Note: [Col. 0453] *Canones* in witness 3.] there.

In the same way he transferred to the aforementioned see, in perpetuity and by right, the monastery of Offonis villa [Note: [Col. 0453] *Villa* in witness 3.] [Note: [Col. 0454C] Odonville-sur-la-Plaine, later destroyed, seems to have been situated near Badonviller, perhaps where the estate of Fonviller stood; see Calmet, p. 455. Since Saint Leodegarius died in 678, the brother of Salaberga could scarcely have dedicated a monastery to him.], which had been granted to him for the service of God by paternal right [Note: [Col. 0453] *Paterno* in witness 2.].

After carrying out these holy works, when the labor of the present age had been completed, he was buried in the cemetery of blessed [Note: [Col. 0453] In witness 2, certain words have been torn away.] Bishop Mansuetus. From there he was later transferred to the city of Laon [Note: [Col. 0453] *Lugdunum* in witness 3.] [Col. 0455A], where he is honored with extraordinary devotion by the faithful. The final day of his life was the third day before the Ides of September.

### 23.

Bishop Jacob [Note: [Col. 0455] *Aco*, corrected by a later hand to *Jacob*, in witness 2.], who occupied the episcopal chair after Lord Bodo [Note: [Col. 0455D] He subscribed to the Council of Compiègne in 765, *Councils*, ed. Harduin III, p. 2008, and to the Council of Attigny in 765, *Monumenta Germaniae Legum* I, p. 30.] (c. 756), obtained from the most pious King Pippin the abbey of Saint Deodatus [Note: [Col. 0455] “Most glorious” in witness 2.] [Note: [Col. 0455D] See the charter of Otto II in Benoit, p. XXIII.].

In his time [Note: [Col. 0455D] The author has again seriously confused the chronology. The same events are already related in the older Life of Saint Hildulf, in Belhomme, *History of the Median Monastery*, p. 56.] Saint Hildulf, archbishop of Trier [Note: [Col. 0455] *Hidulfus* in witness 1?], having abandoned the honor of the world [Note: [Col. 0455] “Having set it aside” in witnesses 2 and 3.], built the Median monastery in the Vosges forest, with the consent and assistance of the aforesaid bishop.

That same bishop Jacob of Christ, when he was dying [Note: [Col. 0455] “Dying” in witness 2; “died” in witness 3.], rests in the crypt [Note: [Col. 0455] *Scripta* in witness 1.] of the church of Saint Benignus the martyr at Dijon [Note: [Col. 0456D] See the *Chronicle of Saint Benignus of Dijon* in D’Achery, second edition, II, p. 370.], with an altar dedicated to Saint Mansuetus the confessor at his head.

### 24.

After him Lord Borno was bishop (c. 770) [Col. 0455B], a venerable and exceedingly religious man, so that everyone called him an apostolic man. While he presided over the see of Leucha [Note: [Col. 0455] *Leuchae* in witnesses 2 and 3.], that same city was finally [Note: [Col. 0455] “Again” in witness 3.] consumed by fire, its sins demanding it. But he obtained from King Charles the restoration of the charters burned by the fire [Note: [Col. 0455] “Consumed by fire” in witness 3.], and from the same king he acquired the abbey of Offonis villa.

He died in peace on the eleventh day before the Kalends of April.

### 25.

His successor was Bishop Wanincus [Note: [Col. 0455] *Wanicus*, corrected to *Wanincus* in witness 2; *Wannicus* in witness 3.] (c. 800), a man most zealous for the church of God. He always showed tireless care both in shaping the character of his subjects and in constructing the church’s adornments. Passing to a blessed end, he departed from this world on the seventh day before the Kalends of January [Note: [Col. 0455] “The seventh” in witness 3.]. He was buried in the cemetery of Saint Aper [Note: [Col. 0455] “The confessor” in witnesses 2 and 3.].

### 26.

Frotarius [Note: [Col. 0455] *Frotharius* in witness 2; *Frotuarius* in witness 3.], a most holy man, first abbot of the monastery [Note: [Col. 0455C] Absent in witness 1.] of Saint Aper, succeeded him as a suitable bishop [Note: [Col. 0455] *Ad onus* in witness 3.] (813). He exalted the aforesaid monastery both through the increase of divine religion and, to no small degree, through the augmentation of its external goods [Note: [Col. 0456D] See the charters of Frotarius in Calmet I, p. 301, and *Gallia Christiana* XIII, 447.].

He obtained from the emperors Louis [Note: [Col. 0455] *Leudovinus*, corrected in a later hand to *Ludovico* in witness 2.] and Lothair the immunity of the county and toll, the restoration of the charters that had been burned, and the forest with its ban which they call Ermundies.

He governed that church for thirty-five years. He was ordained on the eleventh day before the Kalends of April and was removed from the world on the eleventh day before the Kalends of June. His body is kept in the cemetery of Saint Aper, within the cloister, at the entrance to the monastery [Note: [Col. 0455] Witness 1 adds: “but afterward transferred beneath the altar of the Holy Cross”; witness 3: “Now it rests transferred behind the altar of the Holy Cross.”].

### 27.

Then Lord Arnulfus the bishop attained the episcopate [Col. 0456A] (847). Born in the district of Orléans [Note: [Col. 0455] *Aurelianensi* in witness 3.], the son of Alnaldus [Note: [Col. 0455] *Arnaldus* in witness 3.] and Flammola, he was a man conspicuous for holy and great [Note: [Col. 0455] “For great holiness”; “conspicuous for great holiness” in witnesses 2 and 3.] religion and most zealous in teaching the word of God. Like an immovable column, firmly holding the foundations—or rather supporting the summit—of the Church amid the trials of the wavering world [Note: [Col. 0455] “Wavering” in witness 1.], he could neither be lifted up by prosperity nor turned aside from the path of rectitude by adversity.

At the time when this revered bishop governed the church of Toul, there was a king named Lothair the Younger. He accomplished many things vigorously, since he was descended from royal stock; but, corrupted by the craft of the ancient enemy, he did not bring his good beginnings to a proper conclusion.

For although he took a wife named Zeutberga [Note: [Col. 0455] *Zeuberga* in witness 1; *Teutberga* in witness 3.], born, as was fitting, of the most illustrious lineage, he loved a certain concubine named Waldrada with a blind passion, to such a degree that, which was wicked, his lawful wife appeared to have been abandoned by him.

When many who at that time seemed endowed with pontifical honor heard of this, alas for the wickedness, they began to conceal it in silence, some through fear and others through unlawful affection [Note: [Col. 0455] Absent in witness 1.].

When the aforementioned strong champion and bishop, Lord Arnulfus [Note: [Col. 0455] Witnesses 2 and 3 add “of the Lord.”], learned of this, he preferred to be deprived of temporal and passing goods for Christ’s name and, if necessary, ultimately to suffer the danger of the present life rather than fail in the proper rectitude of a shepherd.

Therefore, repeatedly reproving the aforesaid king for this crime, when he was unable to recall him to the right path, he bound him with a pastoral sentence until he should come to his senses.

For this reason, through that king and his supporters in evil [Note: [Col. 0455] “Agents” in witness 1.], the venerable bishop and his church remained for a time completely deprived of their abbeys [Col. 0456C]. But, by God’s merciful favor, after the death of the mad king, the aforesaid church recovered part of the abbeys of which it had been deprived [Note: [Col. 0455] “Deprived” in witnesses 2 and 3.] and part of its other honor, both through him and through the venerable Arnaldus [Note: [Col. 0455] *Arnauldus* in witness 2.], his successor and nephew [Note: [Col. 0456D] See the charters of Louis the Stammerer in Bouquet IX, p. 398, and of King Arnulf in Bouquet IX, pp. 366 ff.].

In his time many free men from the estate of Ingolin and from Mauri villa submitted themselves to the church of Saint Stephen.

That venerable man occupied the episcopal see for twenty-five years. He departed from this valley [Note: [Col. 0455] “Vale” in witness 2.] of tears on the fifteenth day before the Kalends of December and was buried [Note: [Col. 0455] Absent in witness 1.] beside the body of Saint Aper, in the crypt of Saint Anianus [Note: [Col. 0455] *Amanus* in witness 3.] and the holy martyrs Cornelius and Cyprian; [Col. 0457A] he has now been transferred beside the altar of Saint Peter, chief of the apostles.

### 28.

After him Lord Arnaldus, bishop, with God’s favor, took up the church [Note: [Col. 0457D] See Flodoard, *History of Reims* III, 21.] (872). Following the footsteps of his aforementioned uncle the bishop, he governed it with pious moderation for twenty-three years.

Although he worked with no small zeal in the care of the flock and the advancement of the church entrusted to him, he was especially devoted to prayer and was generous in his care for the needy [Note: [Col. 0457] “Generous in the benefits of his hands” in witness 1.].

He acquired the church and four mansi in the estate of Frabodus [Note: [Col. 0457] *Fratbodus* in witness 3.], seven mansi from King Charles in Oscadus [Note: [Col. 0457] *Moscadus* in witness 3.], and six mansi in Waldinus villa, Cretenau, and Rusb [Note: [Col. 0457] *Rusp* in witness 3.].

He is therefore buried in the aforesaid crypt at Saint Aper. He departed from the troubles of this age [Note: [Col. 0457] “Of life” in witness 3.] on the Nones of December (5 December 894), and now [Col. 0457B] lies transferred beside the altar of Saint Peter, first of the apostles.

### 29.

After his death, ravenous wolves burst into the church [Note: [Col. 0457] “Into the same church” in witnesses 2 and 3.], like wolves into a sheepfold abandoned by its shepherd. Their bites inflicted no small devastation, and, although life might still have been hoped for, because sins obstructed the way, the entire city appeared to have been utterly destroyed by the conflagration of a fire.

But the Lord’s immeasurable mercy—he does not wish sinners to perish if they return to him with all their heart—grieved by the loss of his church and considering the injuries suffered by his flock [Note: [Col. 0457] “Of his flock” in witnesses 2 and 3.], and unwilling that it should be left wandering in the desert [Note: [Col. 0457] Absent in witness 3.], deigned to restore as shepherd to that city, sitting in sorrow, Lord Lugdelmus [Note: [Col. 0457] *Ludelmum* in witness 3.], a man of great intelligence (895).

How bravely he acted there against such a grievous and tearful devastation was revealed by the restoration itself of that church and city. For he not only restored the church to its former splendor as far as he was able, but also honorably strove to raise it to a greater and higher eminence. He enriched it, as far as he could, with the dignity of its clergy, with noble laymen, and with landed endowments.

He also acquired the small abbey of Saint Pientius, which the most faithful servant of God Pretoria had once given [Note: [Col. 0457] “Formerly” added in witness 3.], and the estate called Videliacus, which he transferred to the canons’ table [Note: [Col. 0457D] See his charter in Benoit, p. LX.], on the condition that Mass for all the faithful departed should be celebrated daily in his memory [Note: [Col. 0457] “Should be celebrated” in witness 2.].

He also obtained from King Louis the city’s mint and toll, together with the immunity of the county [Note: [Col. 0457] *Ludovinus* in witness 2.], and subjected the city’s market to his church [Col. 0457D] [Note: [Col. 0457] Witness 1 reads “gave it”; witness 3 reads “subjected it to his own church.”].

Furthermore, he acquired from Everelmus, the royal physician, four and a half mansi in Isciacum [Note: [Col. 0457D] Issey; compare the charter of Zwentibold in Bouquet IX, p. 378, and that of Charles the Simple, ibid., IX, p. 553.] with a church, as well as eight mansi in Bella villa [Note: [Col. 0458D] Rosières-en-Haye, Belleville, Meillery, Marbache.] and in Rauserias, Melaridum, and Merbachia [Note: [Col. 0457] *Mebarchia* in witnesses 1 and 2.], with a church.

He also obtained from King Arnulf the church of Gundulfi villa [Note: [Col. 0457] “The estate of Gundulfus” in witness 1.], and in the district of Liuvensis twenty mansi in the estates called Wandra, Savia [Note: [Col. 0457] *Cavia* in witness 3.], and Retines, together with the chapel of Arvia [Note: [Col. 0457] *Harvia* in witness 2.].

From King Zwentibold he obtained the forest belonging to the church of Saint Stephen, situated in Gundulfi villa [Note: [Col. 0457] *Guadulfivilla* in witness 3.], free from every ban, and obtained that the men of Saint Stephen should be free from guarding the forest of that estate.

If we were to write down his holiness and fortunate works in every detail, we would produce a very large book [Note: [Col. 0457] *Efficerem* in witness 3.].

Thus, after holding the episcopal government for ten years, he was struck in the eleventh year by a severe pain in the arm. As it grew worse and penetrated his vital organs, he exchanged the present life [Col. 0458B] for another and ordered himself to be buried in the city, to the amazement of many, since no one had done this before. He had previously chosen [Note: [Col. 0457] “Designated” in witness 3.] his burial at the monastery of Saint Aper in the suburb.

The passage of this blessed man from the world took place on the third day before the Ides of September. He was buried inside the church of his see, before the altar of Saint Martin.

### 30.

After his death (906), Lord Drogo, born of the noblest lineage, seized the chair of this see against the will of the kingdom’s leading men [Note: [Col. 0457] “Willing” corrected to “unwilling” in witness 3.] [Note: [Col. 0457] Witness 3 reads “the leading men of this kingdom.”], by force, by ability, and by the consent of the citizens; afterward, however, he governed nobly with everyone’s common consent.

Just as he was distinguished by the pride of his blood, so by his exceptional subtlety of mind he devoted himself on the one hand to public affairs and on the other to spiritual matters. Thus [Note: [Col. 0457] “Such a man” in witness 1.] he had made himself so capable in everyone’s eyes that he gained the love and veneration of all, difficult to loosen from him [Note: [Col. 0457] “Difficult” in witness 1.].

From his own property he gave this see the estate of Domnus Martinus with its church and assigned it for the support of the canons. He also recovered [Note: [Col. 0457] “He” corrected to “and he” in witness 2; “He” in witness 3.] from King Charles the abbey of Bodo, which had long before been taken away from his predecessors [Note: [Col. 0458D] See the charter in Bouquet IX, p. 515.].

By command of King Louis he held the abbey of Pauliniacum [Note: [Col. 0457] *Pauliniascensem* in witness 1.].

He also acquired from a certain soldier named Sigibert, in the estate of Bertricus, one mansus with a church; half of the church of Domnus Aper [Note: [Col. 0458D] Domèvre.]; a third part of the church of Saint Hilary [Note: [Col. 0457] *Hilarii* in witness 3.] in Vermensis; one mill with a fishery; and whatever he could possess in that estate. From King Charles he obtained the royal forest called Ermundies [Note: [Col. 0457] *Hermundies* in witness 3.].

In his time the savage plague of the Danes, joined to the fury of the Hungarians, burst out from the confines of its native habitation and, after devastating the borders of many regions, set Germany and Belgic Gaul ablaze [Col. 0458D].

Terrified by news of them, the monks of Saint Aper carried the venerable relics of their bishop into the city. Then, lest they be forcibly retained by the aforesaid bishop, they secretly carried them back and concealed them for many long years.

He therefore, devoted to divine religion, after wearing the priestly stole for seven years, was removed from human affairs on the fifth day before the Kalends of February and was buried within the city before the altar of blessed Peter the apostle.

### 31.

Lord Gauzlinus succeeded him as shepherd and lover of the flock (922) [Note: [Col. 0459D] This has been taken from the miracles of Saint Aper.], a thoroughly Catholic man [Note: [Col. 0459] “Thoroughly Catholic” in witness 2.] and a most devoted observer of monastic religion.

Born of noble Frankish blood, he was raised in the palace among the kingdom’s nobles. Soon to become a bishop, he surpassed many of his peers and contemporaries through the twofold gift of knowledge [Col. 0459B] [Note: [Col. 0459] “Shone forth” in witness 3.].

Raised to the pontifical stole by the prayers of all, he was ordained, with Christ’s favor, on the sixteenth day before the Kalends of April. By the kindness of his most merciful heart, the serenity of his very cheerful face, and the gentleness of his speech, he continually surpassed the sweetness of his lineage [Note: [Col. 0459] “Hoped for” in witness 3.], while devoting himself wholly to vigils and almsgiving.

To crown his good works, in the fourteenth year of his ordination, by God’s will he established at Saint Aper’s the rule of Saint Benedict, long sought and discovered far away, but unknown to all the inhabitants of this kingdom.

He built from the foundations the monastery of the holy Mother of God, Mary, at Buxeria [Note: [Col. 0459] “Of God” absent in witness 2.], established there a community of handmaids of God, and adorned it with possessions, estates, and ornaments.

Because of the merit of this deed, God revealed to his successor, Bishop Gerard, that Gauzlinus had been joined in heavenly glory to the martyr Apollinaris [Note: [Col. 0459D] From the *Life of Gerard*, chapter 17.]. I think it worthwhile to transmit to posterity the occasion of this glorious event, for remembrance [Note: [Col. 0459] “For recollection” in witness 3.].

### 32.

Finally, Hardradus [Note: [Col. 0459] *Varderadus* in witness 3, with N written over V.], the full brother of the aforementioned Bishop Gauzlinus [Note: [Col. 0459] Absent in witness 2, where *Gauzlini* appears.], a man exceedingly energetic in military pursuits and greatly beloved by all for the goodness of his character, was once engaged in hunting beside the river Meurthe [Note: [Col. 0459] *Exsistebat* in witness 1?].

It happened that his dogs pursued a fierce boar. Driven by their barking, the boar strove to escape the death that threatened it. It ran for a long time through trackless places [Note: [Col. 0459] *Discurrit* in witness 3.] and at last, fleeing, reached a mountain situated above the estate of Buxeria.

When it arrived there, it planted its feet beneath a thorny tree. Soon the pack of dogs followed, barking, but by divine power it held back their swift advance [Col. 0459D]. The beast stood fearlessly beneath the tree; the force of the barking animals stopped at a distance, mute and stupefied, and did not dare approach the vicinity of the thornbush [Note: [Col. 0459] “The neighborhood” in witness 3.].

The aforementioned soldier followed on horseback and was astonished that something so unusual had happened to him. Jumping down from his horse, he entered the thicket and saw a ruined altar with the buildings around it.

He therefore reverenced the divine event, allowed the beast to depart safely, and quickly returned home. He reported to his brother the bishop what had happened and what he had found.

The lord bishop then sent reliable messengers [Note: [Col. 0459] “There” added in witnesses 2 and 3.] and inquired of the elders how the matter had occurred. He learned from an ancient account that a church dedicated to the holy Mother of God had once been built there, but that, as age consumed it [Note: [Col. 0459] “Having consumed it” in witness 3.] and negligent neglect left it desolate, it had fallen into ruin.

They also affirmed that at night divine lights very often shone there and flooded the neighboring places with their brightness.

When the venerable bishop learned this, he was exceedingly glad [Note: [Col. 0459] Witnesses 2 and 3 add: “and, considering the plan, he deliberated on rebuilding the church.”].

Since the mountain belonged to the episcopal territory of Metz, he asked Bishop Theodoricus, who was also called Sixtus [Col. 0460B] [Col. 0460D] [Note: At that time Adelbero was bishop.], to give it to him in exchange [Note: [Col. 0459] *Concabium* in witness 2.]. In return he gave him the venerable staff of the apostle Saint Peter [Note: [Col. 0459] “Of the apostle Peter” in witnesses 2 and 3.], which blessed Mansuetus had brought with him from the city of Rome.

Having obtained the mountain, he rebuilt the church [Note: [Col. 0459] *Rexstruxit* in witness 1.] and established an altar upon the stump [Note: [Col. 0459] *Stipem* in witness 3.] of the aforesaid tree, in honor of blessed Mary.

Because the sick, afflicted with various illnesses, were healed there through the prayers of that same Mother of God, and because the vows of the common people frequently converged there, by divine inspiration he judged it fitting that the place should not remain without divine worship for longer.

He began to consider how, if they could be found by God’s gift, a community of holy women might be established in that same oratory, to serve the perpetual Virgin under the rule of Saint Benedict.

This undertaking, by divine mercy, deserved to be advanced. For, by God’s foreordination, he found certain holy women, like wandering sheep but nevertheless seeking the pastures of eternal life [Note: [Col. 0459] Absent in witnesses 1 and 2.], fervent in the love of God and desiring a secluded place in which to serve him.

Moved by compassion for them, and with the counsel of Lord Archemboldus, who presided over the monastery [Note: [Col. 0459] “Of Saint Aper” in witnesses 2 and 3.] of Saint Aper, and of the other faithful, he assigned the aforementioned cell to them as a dwelling. He appointed Rothildis abbess over them, so that she might govern their life [Note: [Col. 0459] *Proficiens*, corrected in a later hand to *praeficiens* in witness 2.].

And so that they might devote themselves more freely to spiritual matters there, he provided them with the means of living from the possessions of the bishopric: namely, the church in that same village of Buxeria, with its tithes and everything belonging to it, as well as the chapel of Porchera’s estate with all its tithes.

Thus, it is said, the monastery of Buxeria had its beginning [Note: [Col. 0459] Absent in witness 3.]; with God’s help it increases from day to day.

### 33

In the days of this venerable pontiff [Col. 0459: *autem gachlini* in manuscript 3], ancient prodigies were renewed to such an extent that, in the thirtieth year of his episcopate [Col. 0461D: *Annals of Hersfeld*, year 958; *Annals of Corvey*, year 959], crosses appeared on garments—crosses which, as we read in ecclesiastical history [Col. 0461D: *Tripartite Ecclesiastical History*, book V, end, Paris edition 1541, p. 412], the Almighty permits to appear to mortals in order to refute the unbelief of infidels. [Col. 0461: manuscript 3 reads “of his bishopric.”]

He acquired for the see over which he presided an estate at Boiacum [Col. 0461D: Bosc or Boucq] from Angelbert [Col. 0461: manuscript 1 perhaps reads *Angebert*], and from Fulmar a forest in the valley of Brieri. From King Otto he also obtained the abbey of Moyen-Moutier, on the condition that Duke Frederick should retain its advocacy during his lifetime, that the bishop should arrange the provision of the place, and that, after the duke’s death, the entire abbey should come to the bishop.

He also obtained the city’s toll and county by a charter of King Henry [Col. 0461: manuscript 1 and the text below read *Henry*; Col. 0461D: see the charter in Benoît, p. XVIII], and firmly possessed the abbey of Pauliacum, that of Derversem [Col. 0461: manuscript 1 reads *Deversem*, corrected to *Derversem* in manuscript 2], and the property of Offon’s village.

By an exchange he gave Bishop Archad of Langres the abbey of Varennes [Col. 0461: manuscript 1 reads *Verenne*]; in return, Archad gave the Bishop of Toul whatever he appeared to possess on Mount Boson [Col. 0461D: Bazonmont], at Ursacius’s village, and at Sejonz. [Col. 0461: manuscript 2 and 3 read “to the church.” Manuscript 2 reads *concabium* for *concambium*; manuscript 3 reads *Achardus* for *Archadus*.]

He also obtained from Count Rotger [Col. 0461: manuscript 1 reads *Roger*] the village of Amboldi [Col. 0461D: Ambleville] in the county of Ordon [Col. 0461: manuscript 3 reads *Ordernon*; Col. 0461D: Ornois]; and from Countess Eva the village of Angeriaca [Col. 0461: manuscript 3 reads *Angwiaca*; Col. 0461D: Aingerey] with its chapel, Molisiaca, the village called Girinvicinus [Col. 0461D: Girovoisin], Nordalli ford [Col. 0461: manuscript 2 reads *ualum*, corrected to *uabum*], a portion at Buchuliacum [Col. 0461: manuscript 3 reads *Buculiacum*], the village of Radaldus [Col. 0462D: perhaps Rainville near Soulosse-sur-le-Vair; *CALM*], the village of Sion, and the church situated in the village called Blaseius [Col. 0461: manuscript 3 reads “the church in the village called…”]; also a portion of the church in the village of Rameium [Col. 0461: manuscripts 2 and 3 read *Ramey*], which paid five shillings. From Angelrannus [Col. 0462A: manuscript 1 reads *Angelanno*] he obtained two manses in the village called Portus, and from Hano [Col. 0461: manuscript 3 reads *Hamone*] the church of Bladin’s village.

In the time of Emperor Otto, he proved with twelve free men against the abbess of Andelach that Bodo’s monastery was subject to the church of Saint Stephen. From that same emperor he obtained half the toll of Mont-Saint-Élophe [Col. 0462D: compare the charter of Otto II, year 974, in Benoît, p. XIX; this is Mont-Saint-Élophe near Soulosse].

Through the assistance of Count Eberhard [Col. 0461: manuscript 3 reads *Ebardus*], he also obtained from King Henry whatever that king possessed in Gundulf’s village [Col. 0462D: see the charter cited in Benoît, p. XVIII].

This blessed man, having once undertaken the purpose of good works, continually displayed to all an admirable courage. After many labors in the service of Christ, and after being tested by the Lord like another Job through a four-year illness [Col. 0461: manuscript 1 consistently reads *langor*], he departed to the heavenly dwellings in the forty-fourth year of his episcopate, on 7 September 962.

He was carried by clergy and people to the monastery of Buxeria [Col. 0461: manuscript 1 reads *Buxiensis*] and received, as he had ordered while alive, a most worthy burial among the choirs of virgins whom he had gathered there in considerable number under a stricter rule of life, a burial to be commemorated through long ages in the praises of God.

[Col. 0461: In manuscript 2 this passage is followed by the Life of Saint Gerard written by Widricus; in manuscript 3 the following excerpts from it are found.]

“The Almighty God, who consoles the flock of the inheritance of his Son through the blessing of shepherds, lest it be exposed to the snares and plunder of the devouring enemy, did not wish the church, deprived of the consolation of its ruler, to be tossed amid the waves of the world without a helmsman. He visited it and appointed the venerable bishop Gerard to preside over it.

“Before he knew how to call his father and mother, he was marked out as a bishop by a certain presage. Handed over to the schools, he was afterward endowed with the clerical dignity in the church of Saint Peter, prince of the apostles, at Cologne, and, as befitted his nobility, was nobly educated. Not long afterward, by the authority of the august Otto and through the agency also of his brother, the lord Bruno, archbishop of Cologne, he was elected by the unanimous acclamation of all and consecrated bishop of the city of Toul on 29 March [4 Kalends of April]. We shall refrain from saying more here about his wondrous works, since a book of his memorable virtues is preserved among us. He obtained a charter [lacuna] and usurped an abbey.” [Widricus, chapter 21.]

“Now the chief concern of this aforesaid bishop of God was the construction of churches for God, which he also adorned with a desirable gift, namely the relics of many saints. He repaired the basilica of his see from the foundations, together with the other churches attached to it. He also built, with suitable dignity, the church of the holy Mother of God beside the episcopal chamber and the workshops of his palace.

“He restored the abbey of Saint Mansuetus, the first bishop of this see, which had been almost destroyed, to a proper condition, and rebuilt its monastery from the foundations. He was also the first to construct the abbey of Saint Gengulf at the southern entrance of the city, and there established a community of nuns to serve God under the strict strength of the rule.

“The Lord revealed, through his merits, the long-hidden body of the blessed confessor of Christ, Aper; and he bought, at no small price from the people of Trecassin, the body of his sister, the most blessed virgin Apronia. Adorned with these and other exercises of holy labors, and made manifest among the people by very many signs of miracles, he governed the episcopate for thirty-one years and rendered up his spirit to heaven on 24 April [8 Kalends of May], with a glorious death.

“His venerable body, honorably buried in the middle of the choir of his see, shines forth through numerous miraculous powers, if true faith in the powerful requires it. His successor was Lord Stephen, and so forth.”

### 34

Meanwhile, when Lord Gauzlin, bishop of the see of Toul [Col. 0462D: this entire chapter is taken from Widricus’s Life of Gerard, chapter 3], had been removed from human affairs—he who, illustrious for the sanctity of his conduct, has, as we believe, been received in heaven into the fellowship of the angels—the people of Toul deeply lamented that they had been deprived of the consolation of so great a shepherd.

At that time the venerable Bruno was supreme bishop of the church of Cologne. He exercised imperial authority throughout Germany and the neighboring regions, since he was the brother of the august Otto the Great. The aforementioned prince himself happened then to be away, having gone to the Italian territories because of pressing affairs.

Therefore the sorrowful people of Toul, deprived of the counsel of their shepherd, sent envoys to the aforesaid archbishop Bruno. They humbly reported their desolation and urgently begged that aid be supplied to them, lest, like a wandering flock deprived of its shepherd, they should perish.

Moved by compassionate kindness of heart and grieving over their lamentation, and considering that the city itself bordered the kingdom of France but had most recently been joined to the Roman Empire, Bruno was troubled by the greatest anxiety of mind. He reflected on whom he could choose as a suitable bishop for that church according to the provisions of the canons: a man adorned with goodness of character seasoned by the salt of wisdom in the practice of divine religion, and trained in the study of secular learning.

But God, who always assists the good designs of the devout in bringing them to completion, did not permit his mind to be long agitated by waves of anxiety. By his counsel he inspired him to choose the venerable Gerard for this office, since it was clear that, by the gift of the heavenly Creator, Gerard was useful in every respect. [Col. 0463: manuscript 1 lacks *in bonis*; manuscript 1 perhaps reads *inspirante* for *inspiravit*.]

At that time this servant of God, hindered by the obedience of the cellarer, had been confined within the cloister for some minor transgression, bound by a lighter fault. There he was offering himself more earnestly as a holocaust of tears and prayers. Heavenly providence permitted him to be tested by this small affliction so that it might become evident to all what merit this distinguished man possessed in the sight of divine contemplation.

The religious bishop Bruno therefore summoned the leading clergy to himself, tearfully informed them of the death of his fellow bishop, Lord Gauzlin [Col. 0463: manuscript 1 perhaps reads *Gauzelin*], and confidentially sought their advice about whom he should substitute for him as a worthy successor.

At once the dean, a lover of divine religion and prudent in sound counsel, answered his questions as follows:

“If, my lord bishop, you deign to believe my very small word, I truthfully assert, on reliable testimony [Col. 0463: manuscript 1 perhaps reads *juridico*, “legal,” for *veridico*, “truthful”], that Brother Gerard is more suitable than any other for this dignity. I confidently testify that he is submissive in true humility, distinguished by ready obedience, and most certainly proved by long-suffering patience.”

He further reported Gerard’s long perseverance in penance and, by God’s will, quickly inclined the bishop’s mind to believe him.

Then the aforementioned dean snatched blessed Gerard away from his penitential life in the cloister, unexpectedly brought him to his own house, bathed him, clothed him in splendid garments from his own wardrobe, and, while Gerard wondered what novelty this signified, foretold that he was to be a bishop.

But the man of God, firmly established on the foundation of humility, resisted this appointment with all his strength. He preferred to return to the former leisure of penance rather than be weighed down by the burden of this laborious office.

Nevertheless, although he protested and resisted greatly, he was brought before the aforesaid archbishop and, under the command of obedience, was compelled to accept the episcopal dignity.

Thus, while the year of the Lord’s incarnation 963 was running, he was brought to the city of Toul. He was received by the assembled crowds of the people with hymns of praise and, as custom required, was enthroned in the episcopal seat.

Then there arose marvelous rejoicing among the gathered people. Everyone rejoiced at having obtained a shepherd, and the tears of all were wiped away by his new arrival. All declared that he had been given to them by divine providence, and they resoundingly applauded their assent to his appointment.

If anyone delights in hearing his deeds, let him read through the book of his life and acts, which is kept at his tomb; there he will find them fully recorded.

### 35

When he had entered upon the way of all flesh (994), Lord Stephen succeeded him. He was born of a noble Parisian lineage and came from the ancient family of the village of Lineri [Col. 0463D: Lunéville].

He was consecrated with episcopal anointing in the monastery of Metelahc [Col. 0463D: in the diocese of Trier] on 24 June [8 Kalends of July]. He held the office for only a short time, namely a year and a half [Col. 0463: manuscript 1 reads “years”], and died at Bodo’s monastery on 12 March (996) [4 Ides of March]. He was buried near the altar of blessed Peter, prince of the apostles, in the monastery of Moyen-Moutier [Col. 0463D: compare the *Chronicle of Moyen-Moutier*, *MGH SS* IV, p. 91].

### 36

But when this same city of Toul had been left without its ruler, God’s providence did not allow it to remain long in ruin. With the prayers of both orders of the faithful, through the favor of the divine majesty, and by the decree of the unconquered victor, namely the august Otto III [Col. 0463: manuscript 1 lacks *domni*, “lord”], Lord Bertoldus, born of the most noble Alemannic ancestry and distinguished in holy religion, was chosen through God’s providence and ordained bishop of this see on 11 October [5 Ides of October].

[Benoît observes on p. 341, citing a charter, that a certain Robert had been elected bishop before Berthold. Since I have not found the document published, I leave the matter uncertain.]

He imitated as far as possible the conduct and institutions of his predecessor, Lord Gerard. It cannot be adequately expressed how greatly he was distinguished by works of goodness and generosity for the adornment of his own see.

For he diligently instructed the clergy, embracing prudent men with familiar affection above all others [Col. 0463: manuscript 2 reads “more familiarly,” manuscript 3 “more familiarly still”], and relying on their counsel in every matter. He increased the city’s resources, adorned it with wisdom, and fortified it through prudent administration.

Who could explain in any reasonable speech how prudent and cautious he was in arranging all his affairs; how many and how great ornaments he acquired for his church; with what buildings he adorned the cloister of his clergy [Col. 0463: manuscript 3 reads “adorned,” rather than “built”]; or by what revenues he enlarged his see? Let us touch briefly on a few matters among the many, since no one could adequately pass through them all individually.

From Duke Theodoric he acquired the village of Askeim [Col. 0463: manuscript 1 reads *Askim*, manuscript 3 *Aschei*; Col. 0464D: Acreignes, Haracour, Manonville], the estate of Alraldus [Col. 0463: manuscript 3 reads *Adraldus*], and the village of Monoldus, giving in exchange the village of Vamplena and the other properties which Bishop Gerard had received from Duke Beatrice in return for Mount Bar [Col. 0465: manuscript 3 reads “the blessed Gerard”; *concambium*, “exchange,” is misspelled in manuscript 2].

From Hugh the cleric he obtained the church of Sorciacum [Col. 0465: manuscript 2 reads *Sortiacum*], the estate called Dominica via [Col. 0465: manuscript 3 reads “the estate of Nintauia”], the church called Castellum, the estate called Baddonviler [Col. 0465: manuscript 3 reads “of Baddonviler, together with the church”], the church and castle of Pauniacum [Col. 0465D: Pagny], the estate of Pauniaca village, a third part of the forest of Haseium [Col. 0465: manuscript 1 reads *Saseium*], the estate of Marceium, and Odelric’s portion in the villages of Wasleium, Longort, Laio, and Orcadis.

From the Emperor Henry he obtained the hunting ban over the River Meuse (1011), from the county of Saintois [Col. 0465D: *Segintensis comitatus*, Saintois] to Sorciacum [Col. 0465: manuscripts 1 and 2 read *Sortiacum*; manuscript 3 reads *impetravit*, “obtained,” instead of *reimpetravit*, “obtained again”; manuscript 2 misspells *imperatore*].

He also obtained again from the same emperor the restoration to his church of the village situated in Alsace [Col. 0465: manuscript 2 reads *Halsacium*] called Berchem [Col. 0465D: compare the *Chronicle of Moyen-Moutier*, *MGH SS* IV, p. 92], as well as the toll and jurisdiction of the mina [Col. 0465: manuscript 1 reads *Belchem*; manuscript 3 adds “and the market and ban in the same village, Berkem”].

He also acquired from Countess Emma the estate called Fontiniacum, and from the aforesaid emperor whatever he appeared to possess in Caulei village [Col. 0465: manuscript 3 reads *Taulei*].

He built a monastery in honor of the Holy Savior in the Vosges forest, enriched it most suitably with various ecclesiastical ornaments, and assigned from his acquisitions a subsistence for a community of twenty monks there.
