He built within his own see the church of blessed John the Baptist, called “at the Springs,” as well as the basilica of the venerable bishop Vedast, together with the church of the virgin Saint Genevieve (1018) [Col. 0465: manuscripts 2 and 3 add *autem*, “also,” after “in the Vosges forest”].

In the Vosges forest he rebuilt Bodo’s monastery and also the monastery of Saint Deodatus.

He polished the doors of his see with marvelous beauty, adorned the high altar beyond comparison with the radiance of gold and gems, and acquired countless kinds of vessels whose beauty and quantity could not be valued at any price [Col. 0465: manuscripts 2 and 3 add “there”; manuscript 1 reads *taxanda*, “to be valued,” rather than *texanda*].

Like a most prudent bee, he searched everywhere to discover how he might benefit the church of his see. When he learned how wicked and detestable men had injured his predecessor, Lord Gerard [Col. 0465: manuscript 1 lacks *domno*, “Lord”], he pursued them everywhere in vengeance for the holy church. He utterly destroyed their hiding places, where they had concealed themselves like savage beasts—namely, the castles of Reuvalt [Col. 0465: manuscript 2 reads “Renualt,” manuscript 3 “Mirowat”; Benoît, p. 346, likewise gives “Mirovalt”] and Pauniacum. He so annihilated their hateful offspring that it was no longer possible for any of them to multiply [Col. 0465: manuscript 1 reads *prosecutus*, “pursued,” corrected to *persecutus*, “persecuted”; manuscript 3 reads *omnemque*, “all,” instead of *omnem*].

After holding the episcopal dignity for twenty-two years, it is not easy to tell what benefit his desirable life brought or what loss his mourned death inflicted upon the present age [Col. 0465: manuscript 3 reads “upon us.”] Every tongue falls short in recounting his deeds; and his death, inconsolably lamented, caused a greater loss than, if one may say so, his life, desired by the whole world, would have supplied benefit.

Thus, on 25 August [8 Kalends of September], departing this human life with a blessed death, he so devastated his own see by his fall that all could truthfully proclaim concerning him: “Bertoldus, incomparable to all his successors.” [The Latin *cunctis succiduis sibi incomparabilis* literally refers to all who follow after him.]

He was buried in the middle of his episcopal church, leaving inconsolable mourning to our entire country.

### 37

Lord Herimannus succeeded him. He was born of noble Cologne ancestry and, as befits nobles, was exceptionally well educated in literary studies.

Consecrated with episcopal unction on 20 December [13 Kalends of January], he lived for seven years in the office entrusted to him by God [Col. 0465: manuscript 1 reads “in the office visible to him,” rather than “entrusted to him”].

He transferred the body of blessed Amon from the monastery of the glorious bishop Mansuetus [Col. 0465: manuscripts 2 and 3 add “bishop”] and placed it in the church of the episcopal see, where it is now honorably venerated.

Although he acquired no estates for his church, being overtaken by the brevity of time, he nevertheless adorned it with various ornaments as far as he could [Col. 0465: manuscript 2 reads “as far as he could do so.”] He gave the church of Saint Stephen a substantial quantity of gold, from which he had intended that a chalice of marvelous beauty should be made. He also gave silver crowns to each of the abbeys in his diocese, adding numerous and varied hangings [Col. 0465: manuscript 1 perhaps reads *diocesis*, “diocese”; manuscript 3 reads “adding them to them with a great variety of hangings.”]

He completed the castle of Rodortei [Col. 0466D: Rortey], begun by his predecessor, and built from the foundations the strong castle of Saint Martin, highly useful for guarding the neighboring estates.

He governed the church entrusted to him by God with such wise administration that he enjoyed complete peace from all the adversaries surrounding this see. None of his predecessors or successors governed this bishopric in such tranquility [Col. 0465: manuscript 1 reads “predecessor and successor”; manuscript 2 reads “this church.”]

Although he acquired nothing there by his own labor, nevertheless, with God’s grace supplying what was needed, he suffered no loss of what it possessed [Col. 0465: manuscript 3 reads “with God’s grace supplying what was needed.”]

Removed from this earthly mass on 1 April [Kalends of April], he was honorably buried at Saint Gereon in Cologne, in whose monastery he had been wisely nourished from childhood on the milk of divine and human wisdom [Col. 0465: manuscripts 2 and 3 read “sagaciously” rather than “wisely.”]

[Col. 0465: Manuscript 2 continues here with the Life of Bruno by Wibertus; manuscript 3 instead has the following.]

“The venerable Bruno, light of the world, succeeded him; he was afterward elected by the Lord as pope of the Roman see. We shall refrain from saying much here about his deeds, since we know that they have been fully described elsewhere.

“It has pleased us to insert only this: that he received the abbeys of Moyen-Moutier and Saint Deodatus as a gift from the glorious Emperor Conrad and left them securely in the possession of the holy see of Toul. Among the many things he bestowed upon his church, he also greatly enlarged the provision of the canons of Saint Stephen by returning to them the valley of Mumiri with its church and all its appurtenances, the village of Ranculfus and all its appurtenances, and also the church of Luciacum, in memory of his ordination, so that on that day a suitable meal might be provided for the brothers through the hands of the dean of the cloister of his see, together with alms for one hundred poor people.

“After he had been raised to the apostolic see, he did not forget his first see, namely the church of Toul. At Rome, in the synod at which he caused Saint Gerard to be enrolled among the saints, he consecrated the lord abbot of the monastery of Dervensis, dedicated to Saint Bertharius.

“The aforesaid abbey of Dervensis had long been subject to this see, namely from the time of Garibaldus, bishop of Toul and son of Volfadus, during whose episcopate that abbey was built; but Count Odo had held it by force and, after accepting a considerable price, had placed over the monastery a certain brother of that place named Milo. To suppress the subjection of the church of Toul, he compelled Roger, bishop of Châlons, to ordain him.

“While the most blessed pope was holding a synod at Reims, Milo, moved by repentance for having unjustly accepted ordination, made public satisfaction before the lord pope, returned the gift of the abbey, and went to Cluny, where he lived in good conduct.

“By the consent of the entire community, Lord Wandelgerus was substituted in his place [compare the *Miracles of Saint Bertharius*, chapter 12; Mabillon, *Acta Sanctorum*, II, p. 850: ‘This man—recorded in notes’]. To remove every opportunity for opposition, he asked Roger, bishop of Châlons, for his blessing; but Roger, finding pretexts, delayed his ordination.

“The aforementioned Wandelgerus then went to Rome to the lord pope, who was still governing the people of Toul, explained the whole matter in order, and implored his counsel and consolation. The lord pope therefore, with the counsel of the archbishops Helinard of Lyon, Hugh of Besançon, Mainard of Sens, and the other bishops who had attended the synod, ordained the aforesaid abbot. In memory of the event, he also decreed that he should be called by his former name, Bruno, and confirmed by his authority certain privileges concerning the property of that abbey. Since, and so forth.”

### 38

When Bishop Herimannus had entered upon the way of all flesh (1026), the venerable Bruno succeeded him. He later assumed the dignity of the apostolate in the city of Rome and took the name Leo IX.

Therefore, if any faithful person delights in hearing what and how much he accomplished in the episcopate of Toul, and how he conducted himself after becoming bishop in the city of Rome, let him read the book of his life and virtues kept in the church of Saint Aper; there he will find everything fully recorded. [Col. 0467: in manuscript 2 the middle portion of Bruno’s Life is missing.]

### 39

Since we have learned from written records, insofar as events permitted, the deeds of the former bishops of this see, it seems improper that we should conceal in the silence of oblivion the deeds of the venerable Udo [Col. 0467: manuscript 3 reads *Udonis*], who succeeded in this see the most holy pope Leo IX [Col. 0467: manuscript 3 reverses the order to “Pope Leo IX”]. Rather, we should entrust them to the memory of those who come after us, so that they may be preserved [Col. 0467: manuscript 3 reads “so that they may be handed down for knowledge to those who follow.”]

He was born of a most noble lineage of parents [Col. 0467: manuscript 3 reads “family” or “stock”] and was distinguished on both sides by royal descent. His father was named Count Riquinus [Col. 0467: manuscript 3 lacks “count”] and came from the region of the Reubarii; his mother, named Mathildis, traced her ancestry to Alemannia.

Both were endowed by their ancestors with revenues from estates and great wealth. They burned with zeal for divine religion and were not greatly inclined to set their hearts on arranging the honors of this world.

They therefore entrusted this boy, almost ten years old, to the glorious bishop Bruno of the see of Toul, so that he might be instructed in sacred letters and canonically attached to the venerable community of the house of Saint Stephen [Col. 0467: manuscript 1 perhaps reads *congregationis*, “of the community,” rather than *congregationi*, “to the community”; manuscript 3 lacks “canonically”].

Educated in good learning under Lord Walter, later dean of the aforesaid community [Col. 0467–0468: manuscript 3 reads “carefully instructed in learning”], and sufficiently instructed, he abandoned childish—and indeed youthful—trifles and devoted himself diligently to psalms and prayers.

Although his parents had assigned him more than enough support according to a proper measure [Col. 0467: manuscript 3 reads “according to what had been allotted”], he lived sparingly from it. Whatever remained to him from that income he distributed to the needy. With the simplicity of a dove he also pursued the prudence of the serpent.

[Col. 0467: Manuscript 3 adds: “Having therefore passed through the years of childhood and ascended the steps of adolescence at the fork of the Pythagorean letter Y, he diligently followed the right-hand path, and by the narrow way, advancing from virtue to virtue, he made lasting progress.”]

The glorious Bishop Bruno, seeing him rise so greatly in usefulness to the holy church, rejoiced in his inmost heart and considered how he might exalt him by some office. When Gebizo, the primicerius, had been removed from human affairs [Col. 0467: manuscript 3 adds “from human affairs”], Bruno promoted Udo to the dignity of that same primiceriatus, although Udo was then only just entering the threshold of adolescence and was still beardless.

[Col. 0467: Manuscript 3 adds: “Having been promoted to this office, he strove through the practice of virtue to surpass others, loved chastity above all things, and diligently admonished those subject to him to preserve it carefully; nevertheless, he did not wish in any way to despise those whom he saw to be weak in this matter.”]

### 40

He had vowed his virginity to the King of heaven, and to preserve it he entreated His majesty with tireless prayers.

[Col. 0467: Manuscript 3 adds: “Amid many commemorations of the saints, he invoked the name of his beloved lord, Saint John the Evangelist, asking that he, who was the adopted son of the virgin Mother, might be a favorable guardian and defender in winning the saint’s grace.”]

An evil tempter did not fail to oppose this holy will pleasing to God. By pressing upon him night and day [Col. 0467: manuscript 3 reads “by day”], he tried to draw him away from his holy purpose.

According to human frailty, Udo had inclined his mind to comply with the tempter’s evil suggestion [Col. 0467: manuscript 3 lacks “evil”]; and, unless the Lord had helped him [Col. 0467: manuscript 3 reads “had helped”], his soul would have come very near to dwelling in hell.

But, anticipated by divine grace, he fell into a prolonged illness, and the ancient enemy could not prevail in carrying out his wicked suggestion.

[Col. 0467: Manuscript 3 adds: “Thus, being held by a continuous illness lasting almost a year, he was already despaired of by all his familiar associates as though destined for death, and all present were discussing his funeral rites.”]

But so that Almighty God might show that He had sent this illness upon him for the purpose of correction, He deigned to admonish him in a dream through Saint John the Evangelist, so that he might repent of his perverse intention.

He said to him:

“Know, brother, that you suffer such things because you have decided to break the vow that you made to God. But if you wish to persevere faithfully in your promise, you will soon be granted the health you desire, and divine grace will support you in all your actions.”

[Col. 0469: Manuscript 3 adds: “Indeed, Saint John the Evangelist appeared to him in apostolic attire, whose appearance he recognized as though he had often seen it. The saint asked him why he had lain so long in illness. When he answered that he did not know, the saint seemed to reply to him with considerable friendliness.”]

When, in a dream, he promised with God’s assent that he would observe these things, it seemed to him that the saint gave him something like three prophetic inscriptions foretelling future events and placed them in his mouth to eat. He always retained their memory in his heart and did not wish to reveal them to any of his familiars until the end of his life. We shall recount their sequence later, when a suitable place arises.

He affirmed that this vision had appeared to him on the same night on which his venerable father, Lord Bishop Bruno, dreamed that the blessed apostle Peter, together with the protomartyr Stephen, led him honorably, vested with episcopal insignia, to the principal altar at Worms and gave him five golden chalices as a foretelling of events to come [Col. 0469D: see Wipertus’s *Life of Bruno*, II.1].

### 41

Not long afterward, the same glorious Bruno was promoted to the apostolic see at the aforesaid city of Worms (1049). He took the venerable Udo, of whom we are speaking, with him to Rome, together with certain of his familiars. Because Udo adhered to his service more diligently than the others in every respect [Col. 0469: manuscript 3 reads “because he adhered to his service more diligently than the others in every service”], Bruno bound him to himself in a closer friendship of intimacy [Col. 0469: manuscript 3 reads “bound him.”]

After nearly two years had elapsed (1050) [Col. 0469: manuscript 1 reads “after nearly two years had been completed”], the lord pope wished to revisit his ancient homeland and first see. Through the intervention of the same Udo, he restored to the community of the brothers of the church of Saint Stephen the church of Tranculfus’s village and the estate of Mundrivallis, and strengthened for those same canons a privilege of liberty supported by apostolic excommunication [Col. 0469D: compare the charter in Benoît, p. CXXVI].

Finally, when the lord pope saw him advancing from virtue to virtue in holy religion, he resolved, following the election of the clergy and people, to substitute him for himself in the office of bishop of this see (1051). He sent a legation to Henry III, ruler of the Roman Empire, and arranged to appoint Udo as his successor.

### 42

Having therefore obtained the honor of the episcopate, he began to be energetic in all matters that had to be undertaken, as though he had been carefully trained from early childhood in arranging such affairs [manuscript 1 reads “from the primicerius”].

They had reached Trier on 18 August [15 Kalends of September] for the blessing of his sacred ordination. There God graciously revealed to him the disposition of His mercy.

For, as is customary, when the book of the holy Gospels had been placed upon his shoulders, he recognized in a truthful oracle the exemplars of the three predictions mentioned above [Col. 0469: manuscript 3 reads “inscriptions”], which he had seen in dreams.

First, the following passage of divine speech was recited by the reader:

“Have you never read in the Scriptures: ‘The stone which the builders rejected, this has become the head of the corner’? This was done by the Lord, and it is marvelous in our eyes.” (Matthew 21:42.)

Then the second passage was spoken from the prologue of the Gospel of Luke:

“Serving the Lord without blame.”

The third was found in the same Evangelist, concerning Zechariah and Elizabeth:

“Walking in all the commandments of the Lord without complaint.” (Luke 1:6.) [Col. 0469: manuscript 3 reads “in all the commandments and justifications of the Lord, without…”]

Remembering that the exemplars of these words had long before been shown to him by the Lord [Col. 0469: manuscript 3 reads “by God”], he revolved them tirelessly in his mind, like a most prudent bee constantly gathering food from flowers.

Although some rejected him as though because of excessive simplicity, he nevertheless continually strove, according to human possibility, to be found before God’s eyes serving Him without blame and without complaint [Col. 0469: manuscript 3 reads “to find himself”].

### Source-associated textual apparatus (supplement)

The following readings are retained in their actual Latin form with their English force; *deest* means “is absent/omitted,” *add.* means “is added,” and *corr.* means “corrected.” They supplement the inline apparatus above.

**Chapter 33, Col. 0461.** MS 3: *episcopatus* (“bishopric/episcopate”); MS 3: *alodum* (“allod/independent estate”); MSS 1–2: *deest ab* (“*ab*, ‘from,’ is absent”); MS 3: *achardo* (the name-form “Achard”); MS 3: *ambodi* (the place-name form “Ambodi”); MS 3: *ordernensi* (the place-name form “Ordernensis”); MS 3: *angwiacam* (the place-name form “Angwiaca”); MS 2: *ualum corr. uabum* (“*ualum*, corrected to *uabum*”); MS 3: *buculiaco* (the place-name form “Buculiacum”); MS 3: *in villa quae dicitur* (“in the village which is called”); MS 2: *ramei*, MS 3: *ramey* (place-name spellings); MS 1: *angelanno*; MS 3: *hamone*; MS 3: *ebardi*.  MS 2–3: *Idem* (“the same”), rather than *Isdem*; MS 2: *concabium* (“exchange,” misspelled); MS 1: *deversem*, corrected in MS 2 to *derversem*; MS 1: *henrici* (“of Henry”), also below; MS 1: *uerennis*; MS 2: *archardus*, MS 3: *achardus*; MSS 2–3: *ecclesiae* (“of/to the church”); MS 1: *rogero*.

**Chapter 36, Cols. 0463–0465.** MS 3: *ornaverit* (“adorned”), rather than the printed wording; MS 1: *askim*, MS 3: *aschei*; MS 3: *adraldi*; MS 2: *concanbium* (misspelling of “exchange”); MS 3: *beatus* (“blessed”); MS 2: *sortiaco*; MS 3: *p. de Nintauia* (“the estate of Nintauia”); MS 3: *de baddonwiller d. cum ecclesia* (“of Baddonwiller, together with the church”); MS 1: *panniaco*, and below *panniaca*; MS 1: *saseio*; MS 3: *deest et* (“*et*, ‘and,’ is omitted”); MS 3: *seguitensi*; MSS 1–2: *sortiacum*; MS 3: *impetravit* (“obtained”); MS 2: *impetore* (misspelling of “emperor”); MS 3: *deest suae* (“*suae*, ‘his own,’ is omitted”); MS 2: *halsatio*; MS 3 adds *et mercatum et bannum in eadem villa Berkem* (“and the market and ban in the same village, Berkem”); MS 3: *taulei*; MSS 1–2: *deest in honore* (“*in honore*, ‘in honor of,’ is omitted”); MS 2?: *pren.* at *pernoscensque*, “and learning thoroughly,” apparently indicating the transposed spelling *prenoscensque*; At *persecutus*, “pursued,” MS 1 has the *pros-* spelling and MS 2 corrects it to *pers-* (apparatus *pros.*, *pers.*); MS 2: *renualt*, MS 3: *Mirowat*, while Benoît gives *Mirovalt*; MS 3: *omnemque* (“and all”); MS 3: *nobis contulerit*, “contributed to us” (apparatus *nobis c.*); MS 3: *sibi succidius*, a transposed and malformed reading for *succiduis sibi*, “those succeeding him”; MS 3: *agripinensium*, spelling of “of the people of Cologne”; MS 1: *visibili*, “visible,” for *sibi*, “to him”; MSS 2–3 add *praesulis* (“of the bishop”); MS 1: *deest domno* (“*domno*, ‘lord,’ is omitted”).

**Chapter 37, Col. 0465.** MS 3 omits the entire passage from *Is*, “He, although he acquired no estates,” through *gubernavit*, “governed this bishopric in such tranquility”; MS 2: *alio atramento pergit* (“it continues in different ink”). MS 2 transposes to *suo pro posse*, “according to his ability” (apparatus *suo p.*); MS 1 perhaps *diocesis*, “of the diocese”; MS 1 *rodotei*, the Rortey place-name; and MS 2 has *vocabulum erasum* (“a word erased”). MS 1 reads *praecessor ac successor* (“predecessor and successor”); MS 2 *hanc ecclesiam* (“this church”); MS 3 reads *qua sede*, “in which see,” and transposes *Dei suppeditante gratia*, “with God’s grace supplying [help]” (apparatus *q. sede*, *d. s.*); MSS 2–3 *sagaciter* (“wisely/shrewdly”).

**Chapter 39, Col. 0467.** MS 3: *priorum* (“of the former ones”), and MS 3: *deest successor* (“*successor* is omitted”); MS 3: *udonis*, “of Udo”; MS 3 transposes *noni papae*, “of the ninth pope [Leo]”; MS 3: *occultamus* (“we conceal”); MS 3 transposes *servanda tradamus*, “let us hand [them] down to be preserved” (apparatus *s. t.*); MS 3: *progenie parentum stirpe editus*, “born from the lineage/stock of his parents” (apparatus *progenie p. stirpe editus*, a redundant construction); MS 3: *deest comitis* (“the count-title is omitted”); MS 1 perhaps *congregationis* (“of the community”); MS 3: *deest canonice* (“canonically is omitted”); MS 3: *doctrina impense*, “thoroughly [educated] in learning”; MS 3 joins *a parentibus*, “from his parents,” as *apparentibus* (which by itself means “appearing”); MS 3: *directis* (“directed”).

**Chapters 40–41, Col. 0469.** MS 3: *interdiu* (“by day”); MS 3 omits *pravam*, “wicked,” qualifying the suggestion; MS 3: *adjuvasset* (“had helped”); MS 3: *Et* (“and”); MS 1 omits *cum*, “when”; MS 3 transposes *se haec*, “[promised] that he [would observe] these things” (apparatus *se h.*); MS 3 also omits *quasi*, “as if”; MS 3: *eadem* (“the same”); MS 3 transposes *apostolum Petrum*, “the apostle Peter” (apparatus *a. p.*); MS 3: *quique ei prae ceteris in omni servicio sollicitius adhaesit*, “who, more than the others, attended him more diligently in every service” (the apparatus abbreviates this as *quique ei p. c. in omni servicio sollicitius adh.*); MS 3: *connexuit* (“bound/connected”); MS 1: *exaucto*, literally “increased,” a malformed alternative to *exacto*, “elapsed,” of the nearly two years; MS 1: *primicerio* (“from/with the primicerius”); MS 3: *superscriptionum* (“inscriptions”); MS 3: *mandatis et justificationibus eum sine*, “commandments and ordinances … him … without [complaint]” (apparatus *m. et justificationibus eum sine*); *eum*, “him,” is syntactically disrupted in this supplied reading; MS 3: *deo* (“God”); MS 3: *inveniret* (“might find”).

43. He also strove, as far as he could, to imitate the customs of his predecessor, Lord Bertold [Note: *Beltodi* in 1.], in increasing the revenues and ornaments of his own church and see; and he did not fear to make the enemies of his country hostile to him in defense of the poor and of the churches [Note: “of himself” is added in 3.]. He also acquired from Count Haimon a certain church [Note: “of …” in 3.] for the service of the brothers of the congregation of Saint Stephen, and granted it to them in perpetuity so that it might be commemorated annually on the day of his ordination.

In destroying the castle of Vallicolor [Note: *Vallicolorum* in 3.; [Col. 0469D] Vaucouleur], in the annihilation of which his venerable predecessor Bruno had labored without end, he achieved through many kinds of entreaty and payment to the neighboring countrymen that he twice demolished it from its foundations with military arms [Note: *efficit* in 3.; *eum* in 1.]. He restored the monastery of Saint Gengulf, which had long been almost entirely ruined and had also been burned by fire, to a suitable condition; enlarging it with ecclesiastical ornaments, necessary resources, and buildings, he made the place fit for divine service and holy religion [Note: See the diploma of Udo in Benoît, p. LXXIV, and that of King Henry IV, 1065, ibid., p. XXIX.]. There, as we hope, heavenly service flourishes commendably according to canonical custom and, with Christ’s favor, will flourish forever.

He received the estate of Saint Anianus, situated with its appurtenances in the suburb of his city, from the abbot of Inden by an exchange authorized by the royal authority of the glorious Henry III, Roman emperor [Note: See the diploma in Benoît, p. XXVIII.]. In return he lawfully transferred certain properties granted to him by his parents under hereditary right [Note: See Udo’s charter, ibid., p. LXXIX.], where he had arranged, with divine grace supplying the means, to construct buildings suitable for the monks’ use, to gather there twenty-four brothers fervent in love of holy religion, and to provide from the revenues of his own inheritance, in which he abounded greatly [Note: *habitabat* in 3.], the expenses suitably necessary for them.

What the arrangement was of the properties assigned there by him is contained in the apostolic privilege of Pope Alexander, preserved in the treasury of the holy protomartyr Stephen [Note: *archarissimo* in 1.]. But, overtaken by death, he could not carry his desire through to completion; he left it to whichever of his successors God should grant both the will and the ability to bring it to fulfillment.

44. Thus, in his time, the city of Leucha, burdened by many adversities from neighboring countrymen [Note: *adversantibus* in 1.] and outsiders, did not so much grieve over the hardships that it endured while he lived as it wept because it had not been worthy to possess for long a man of such sagacity and fervor toward the welfare of his church. For, as we have already said, he left the castle of Vallicolor [Note: *vallicoloris* in 3.], which had grievously afflicted the church of Leucha for almost forty years [Note: *annos* in 3.], destroyed during his lifetime [Note: “to be destroyed” in 3.], although in the very year in which he departed this present life it was rebuilt through the treachery of certain men.

At his end he had all the enemies of his see either defeated or reconciled; whatever belonged to the episcopal provision, just as his predecessor Bishop Bertold had held it, he left firmly secured for his successor. Therefore, as heavenly will ordained, on the day before the Ides of July, in the year 1069, the eighteenth year of his ordination, he was taken from this light [Note: “was taken from this light” in 3.] and was honorably buried in the church of his see before the altar of Saint Blaise.

[Col. 0471C] 45. When Lord Udo had been removed from this life [Note: “bishop of Leucha” is added in 3.], the venerable Pibo soon succeeded to the same see, to be ordained [Note: *s. m.* in 3.]. He was born of parents who were not lowly: his father was Thietmar [Note: *Thiemaro* in 3.], his mother Dudicha, and he came from the land of the Saxons.

From his earliest age he was given over to the discipline of letters. Under the teacher Anno, later to become bishop of Cologne [Note: *Agrippinesium* in 1.], he passed through his schooling [Note: *transiens* in 1.] and shone preeminently in knowledge both of divine instruction and of worldly matters. Then, while still a young man, he became a canon in the church of Halberstadt [Note: the word is absent in 1.]. There, among his peers, he so far outstripped everyone in every path of prudence, with a modest exercise of courage [Note: *praecurrit* in 3.], that he gradually undertook all the offices of that church and performed them commendably. Indeed, he so wisely arranged all the church’s dignities except the pontificate that, being subsequently raised to the royal palace, he first became chaplain and afterward chancellor.

There, too, it became sufficiently evident to the princes of the kingdom how great he was.

46. Through the hidden disposition of the Almighty [Note: *dispensatione* in 3.], he was granted the episcopate and ordained to the church of Toul in 1070. Finding its building not merely unfinished but also ruined, he grieved deeply [Note: perhaps *cor doluit*, “his heart grieved,” in 1.], and even considered turning back. For what distressed his mind most severely [Note: *durius* in 3.] was that, groaning without interruption, he despaired of consolating the souls entrusted to him, since he entirely lacked the language in which he could teach the people [Note: *lingam* in 1.].

But divine power deigned to display a glorious miracle in him: although he was already sixty years old, he learned in a short time a previously unheard-of language [Note: “namely, French”; the note is by P.], by which he earnestly governed Christ’s people, teaching them intelligibly enough both to desist from evil and to accomplish every good work.

Moreover, how tireless he showed himself in God’s service; how constant he was during the nocturnal hours of the divine office [Note: “and during the daytime” is added in 3.]; how solemn he was at the celebration of the most holy mystery, with his heart sacrificed inwardly; how angelic he appeared in the sacred ordinations of the episcopate—this could scarcely be made known to future mortals, just as it cannot slip from the memory of those who saw it.

He was exceedingly merciful in almsgiving, most cheerful in receiving pilgrims and guests, a most compassionate visitor to prisoners and the sick, most just in defending widows and orphans, and, finally, he persevered with the greatest fervor in love of God and neighbor [Note: “Neither exalted by favorable circumstances nor cast down by adversity, but patiently bearing the insults inflicted upon him for Christ’s sake, he appeared lovable not only to acquaintances and friends but also to enemies” is added in 3.].

Thus filled with God’s grace, he supported with material aid, not merely with words of paternal consolation, all whom he observed in the clergy to be inferior either by birth or by lack of intelligence [Note: “But he educated noblemen splendidly, enriching them with the church’s resources or dignities” is added in 2.].

47. How richly he endowed the city, its suburb, and its other appurtenances, which had been almost deserted since the days of his predecessor [Note: “his predecessor” in 3.], is demonstrated by the buildings constructed in his time. Whenever war threatened the episcopal residence [Note: *episcopo* in 3.], he sold as many of his table’s provisions as possible [Note: *plurimum* in 3.] and purchased peace for the church from the tyrants attacking it on every side [Note: “If anyone should doubt the matters we have recalled in this account, let him turn the eyes of his mind toward the church of the protomartyr; he will not convict us of falsehood or flattery” is added in 3.].

At the very entrance of the aforesaid basilica of Saint Stephen, he built from the foundations a tower with two bells [Note: Benoît, p. 398, places this in 1091 and reports the following from a certain manuscript, perhaps the *Gestes*: “Pibo founded and constructed the tower of this church with two bells and dedicated it. Therefore every year, on the day after the translation of Saint Gerard, the entire community celebrated the offices in that tower from first vespers until second vespers. It should be known that from ancient times the young men of the church, including canons, gathered there on that day, and in the said tower drank and ate together; each brought his portion out of reverence for the festival and as a sign of brotherhood, and one person read at table.”].

Beneath it the same bishop rests honorably buried beside the altar of Saint Mary Magdalene [Col. 0473A]. In the central height of that same structure he also devoutly consecrated three altars: the middle one to the glorious Mother of God, Mary; the one on the right to all the apostles; and the third, on the left, to the holy martyrs. He placed upon them many reliquaries containing relics.

He also decorated the ceiling of the same monastery, gleaming with symbolic workmanship, and adorned with the most precious artistry and design the painting of the Lord’s majesty above the principal altar. Likewise, he ordered a silver crown, shining with golden variety, to be made; it hung down in the middle of the basilica with beautiful breadth [Note: *fabricari* in 3.]. He also increased the number of sacred vessels by adding a chalice of the purest gold, adorned with the most precious stones.

After constructing a wooden bell tower projecting above the highest ridge of the roof [Note: “of the church” in 3.], he covered it with sheets of lead; he likewise saw to it that the screen was covered with the same metal. Who could ever recall one by one the deeds of so great a bishop [Note: *rememorari* perhaps in 1.]?

Keeping constantly in mind what he had read—“Idleness is the enemy of the soul” [Note: absent in 1.]—he was never found idle, whether laboring to increase the church’s ornaments and rebuild its sacred buildings [Note: *desudando* in 3.] or attending to the public arrangements of his entire parish [Note: *barrochiae* in 1.].

48. But because the venerable Pibo could be bent neither by threats nor by flatteries of royal power from faith and obedience to the holy Roman see, amid the innumerable losses of so great a persecution, which he endured steadfastly, he restored to the church before the end of his life the estate belonging by right to the church of Toul, called Bercheim [Note: *Bertheim* in 3.], once famous for its dignity and frugality, which it had lost for many years through the king’s supporters, restoring it over a period of five years.

Finally, when the aforesaid shepherd saw that the imperial persecution was not diminishing at all [Note: *nequaquam* in 3.], but that certain bishops throughout the German kingdom who adhered to the king were being condemned for disobedience to the Roman see, he nevertheless did not waver in his steadfastness [Note: perhaps *tantum* in 1.]. Rather, moved by divine prompting and desiring, in repentance for his sins [Note: *poenitudinem* in 3.], to visit the place of the Lord’s Passion, he reached Jerusalem in 1085 with Count Conrad of Luxembourg [Col. 0474D] and many princes of the kingdom, God guiding him.

There, visiting all the most holy places of the Lord’s earthly life, not less contrite in body than in heart, he poured forth abundant floods of tears before the Lord’s tomb for the forgiveness of his offenses, devoting himself to very lengthy prayers. He also entreated the Lord for the souls entrusted to him. There, in the hearing of his companions, the suppliant bishop vowed that, if God ever granted him permission to return to his homeland [Note: perhaps *repatriari*, “to be restored to his homeland,” in 1.], he would immediately become a monk.

Returning, therefore, from Constantinople in 1087, he obtained from the most glorious emperor of the Greeks, who loved him greatly, a considerable portion of the Lord’s cross. Together with sacred reliquaries, precious dorsal hangings, and many gifts of another kind [Note: “also many” in 3.], he devoutly brought it to his church [Note: absent in 1.].

He therefore ordered a great cross to be skillfully made from the purest gold and shining gems. In it, a pearl of the life-giving wood, more precious than all riches, was suitably set for carrying, so that it might nevertheless appear clearly to the eyes of those looking upon it through the brilliance of the stone placed above it and bring both compunction and salvation to the hearts of the faithful [Note: *p. a.* in 3.].

What more? Afterward, having abandoned everything in the world, he was consecrated a monk; this, however, was done secretly in the monastery of Dijon.

[Col. 0474B] 49. When the people of Toul realized that they had been deprived of so great a patron, they mourned beyond comparison, but then received from heaven the soundest counsel they could. They approached the supreme shepherd of the Roman see through legates, disclosed to him the course of their desolation and what they desired, and persisted in tearful supplications before him until the most holy pope, in his piety, pardoning their petition, ordered that their own shepherd, whom they sought, be restored to them as he was—that is, as a monk—and indeed compelled this by apostolic authority.

Having received this favor of divine mercy, they rendered due praises to the Almighty and to the princes of the apostles, and joyfully approached the monastery of Dijon. With thanksgiving they received the most reverend Pibo as though returned from the dead. After he had been solemnly re-enthroned in the see of Leucha with much greater rejoicing than at first, the clergy together with the people, from the greatest to the least, served him with faithful obedience for as long as he lived [Note: *obsecunctur* in 1.]. And just as he remained a monk in genuine religion, so he remained a venerable bishop, Pibo beloved by both God and human beings, through diligent administration [Note: *permanxit* in 1.; “the beloved Bishop Pibo” is absent in 3.].

50. We have also judged that the following should not be passed over in silence: the often-mentioned father granted the church of Bue to his brothers, so that it might be solemnly commemorated on the day of his ordination while he lived, and no less after his present life had ended, on the annual day of his deposition [Note: *rememoranda* in 3.].

Likewise, for the three altars consecrated in the tower, that most kind father granted thirty solidi from his own revenues, namely from the toll, on these terms: every year, for the celebration of the dedication, ten solidi from this sum were to serve the brothers; the remaining twenty solidi were to go to whichever brother served there diligently and always supplied the nocturnal light, together with linen coverings, for the altars. He also granted to the service of the aforesaid canons half the wine called “from the bishop’s tavern,” whose total amounted to forty *modii* [Note: the words “he nevertheless granted no less” are absent in 1.].

He also acquired an allod at Geminold’s estate and donated it, sufficient for the lights, to Saint Mary Magdalene, beside whose altar he awaits the day of the final resurrection [Note: “By laboring over these and similar activities, this man of blessed memory adorned many years with a good fragrance until the completion of his life” is added in 3.].

Finally, commending to the supreme Shepherd the sheep entrusted to him, which he had long nourished in peace [Note: “once entrusted to him” in 3.; “to Christ” is added in 3.], the venerable Pibo, in the thirty-eighth year of his ordination, in the year of the Lord’s incarnation 1107, on the eighth day before the Kalends of December, rested in Christ with a blessed end, mature in old age [Note: “weary with ripe old age” in 3.].

## In the Year of the Lord 1107: Suavius, Abbot of Saint-Sever at the Head of Gascony

[Col. 0475]

### Historical Notice

*(Histoire littéraire de la France*, vol. IX, p. 328.)

Suave is known in history only from the time when he attained the dignity of abbot of Saint-Sever at the Head of Gascony, in the diocese of Aire. This occurred in 1092, when he succeeded Arnaud Destios. He appears to have been very zealous for the welfare of his monastery, and no less so for the place where it was situated. At first it was only a market town or village; but the generous abbot had enough courage to undertake its elevation to the status of a town and enough influence to succeed. Having obtained permission from William Sancho, duke of Gascony, and Urraca, his wife, to surround it with walls, he found the means to pay for the work. Once the project had been completed, he assembled the inhabitants and agreed with them upon the customs and usages that were thereafter to be inviolably observed, so that good order and uniform civic administration might be maintained.

Although Abbot Suave was attentive in reclaiming the property of his monastery, he was not inclined toward litigation. He demonstrated this by the care he took to settle the disputes between his house and the abbey of La Sauve-Majeure. To tighten the bonds of peace between them, he established a mutual fellowship of prayers.

Suave continued to govern his monastery on this basis until the thirteenth of February 1107, when he ended his days. He was fortunate in his successors: the first and the third successively became bishops of Agen before the middle of the twelfth century.

Two literary monuments remain from this abbot. The first is the collection of usages and customs just mentioned, which Dom Martène and Dom Durand brought out of obscurity. They comprise nineteen articles and form the code of laws according to which the town of Saint-Sever was henceforth to be governed. The collection goes into considerable detail and adopts proper measures to distinguish clearly the respective rights of the abbey on the one hand and of the citizens on the other.

The other monument of Abbot Suave is a letter, as forceful as it is respectful, to Pope Paschal II, asking him to do justice against a sentence delivered by his legates to the disadvantage of his monastery. The matter concerned the church of Notre-Dame de Solac, which the abbeys of Saint-Sever and Sainte-Croix of Bordeaux disputed, and which the legates Amat of Oloron and Hugh of Die had adjudged to the latter monastery, although rescripts of Popes Alexander II and Gregory VII confirmed possession of it to the abbey of Saint-Sever.

After Suave recovered these documents, which had been impossible to produce, he requested a retrial of the case; this is the subject of his letter to Pope Paschal. Although he had an interest in winning the pontiff’s favor, he did not seek to court him by giving him pompous titles, as so many others did on similar occasions. In the inscription of his letter the author simply calls him “bishop of Rome by the grace of God”; this is one of the features that make the letter especially remarkable.

[Col. 0477]

## Statutes of Suavius, Abbot, for the Town of Saint-Sever  
*(Around the year 1100.)*

[Martène, *Thesaurus Anecdotorum* I, 277, from the cartulary of the abbey of Saint-Sever.]

[Col. 0477A] Since human days are short and their memory fleeting, we have therefore judged that useful things, and things that may prove useful, ought to be committed to writing.

Let it be known to those present and to successors that Suavius, abbot of Saint-Sever, permitted and allowed the settlement that the most illustrious duke of Gascony and his wife Urraca had established in honor of Saint Peter and Saint Severus, at the insistence and request of the inhabitants of that same place, to be surrounded and fortified on every side, so that they might remain there more safely from the attacks and malice of men.

Nevertheless, before granting them his assent to the enclosing of the town, they agreed among themselves concerning the customs, usages, fines, and tolls to be received there; and, touching the most holy relics, the aforesaid inhabitants swore on behalf of themselves and their successors [Col. 0477B] that whatever was established would be observed inviolably. In like manner the aforesaid abbot affirmed that these provisions were to be observed forever.

1. First, therefore, it was established that the abbot would always close and fortify the gates of the town, and that at those gates, by reason of his lordship and the closing of the gates, he would collect tolls from those entering and leaving. The townsmen, however, would always close and fortify the rest of the town’s enclosure at the abbot’s discretion.

Likewise, the abbot retained for himself and his people, freely and without any servitude, two streets around the monastery, for walking about and building houses: one from the sand-pit to the moat, running straight from there to Gala; the other from the refectory [Col. 0477C] to the road that goes to Pontillum. He had already granted certain other spaces for building houses there and at that time freely granted them to the bishop of Aire and to certain other knights.

2. Furthermore, it was established that if anyone killed his neighbor, the killer and his property would be in the abbot’s power. Likewise, if anyone killed an outsider within the town’s boundary, he would be condemned to the same punishment, unless it were established that he had killed someone from the town or forced him to pay a ransom.

The same punishment as for homicide was to apply to thieves and to those who consented to them. If anyone, moved by arrogance or indignation, drew weapons against someone outside his own house, he was to pay six solidi to the abbot.

[Col. 0477D] 3. If he wounded anyone, he was likewise to pay the abbot six solidi for the wound; and for each kind of weapon, he was to pay the abbot six solidi. If the wound was a legitimate one in depth or length, he was to pay eighteen solidi to the wounded man; if it was not legitimate, he was to do for the injured party whatever judgment prescribed.

It was established that if one person beat another, he was to pay six solidi to the abbot and six to the beaten man, unless the latter struck him back; then each was to pay six solidi to the abbot.

It was also established that if anyone invaded his neighbor’s house, he was to pay six solidi to the abbot and likewise to the master of the house. If anyone seized a man within the town without permission or command of the abbot, unless he caught him stealing or found him with stolen goods, he was to pay the abbot 150 solidi for violating the town and return the captive to the abbot.

Likewise, if anyone broke the abbot’s ban or seal, whoever had imposed or placed it, he was to pay six solidi to the abbot. Similarly, whenever the abbot’s herald or messenger commanded or prohibited anything, everyone was to observe it; whoever did not observe it was to pay five solidi to the abbot.

4. It was also established that if the abbot sent for one of his townsmen and ordered him to come to him, he was to come without delay. If he began anything before coming, he was to pay six solidi to the abbot, unless the table had already been set for him to eat, or he had already begun to wash his head, or had cut his own garments, or was burdened by an illness that prevented him from coming, or someone had died in his house. Once these matters were completed, he was not to delay coming to him immediately.

It was likewise established that if the abbot or his people suffered an injury from anyone, and the offender refused to submit to judgment, and the abbot wished to ride against him because of the injury inflicted upon him, or to mobilize an army against him, the townsmen were to follow the abbot against the offenders at his command. If anyone was absent from the mounted expedition without the abbot’s permission, he was to pay six solidi to the abbot; if he remained away from the army, he was to pay six solidi to the abbot and restore to him the damage caused by his absence.

5. Moreover, after much deliberation and repeated consultation, they established concerning the market called Labere that whoever came to that market would come safely and without any impediment, unless he was a debtor, a surety, or a murderer.

It was also established that if anyone bought or sold anything outside the boundaries of the market, and it could be seized outside those boundaries, the market warden would retain the thing bought or sold.

6. Furthermore, if one person injured another at the market, he was to pay twenty denarii to the abbot or his messenger and make lawful satisfaction to the injured party.

The market and its protection lasted from Thursday afternoon until Sunday, until Prime had been celebrated. It was also established that if anyone went outside the town and on the road bought some merchandise being brought to the town, he was to receive the *lesda* from the seller and pay it to the abbot, or pay it from his own resources.

7. Likewise, it was established that if anyone went to the houses of peasants outside the town, bought wine or cider from them, and brought it to the town himself or through another person at his own risk, he would be free from the *lesda* whenever he sold it.

He enjoyed the same freedom if he sold oxen, cows, sheep, goats, or pigs, unless he sold them specifically in the slaughterhouse or at the established market. But if he bought grain or anything else and sold any part of that merchandise within a month and a day, he was to pay the *lesda* on the whole.

Outsiders, however, if they brought anything for sale to the town, whether they sold it immediately or later at the entrance to the gates, were to pay the *lesda*, or give the collector of the *lemna* security that they would not sell it.

8. It was also established that if a traveling merchant, in order to evade the toll, left the highway or, passing through the town, failed to pay the toll, then, if he could be caught, he would lose his merchandise; or he could settle the matter with the abbot.

[Col. 0479C] 9. It was also established that whoever had woolen cloth for sale in the town was to pay the abbot eight solidi annually.

10. It was likewise established concerning the fair that it would begin on the Thursday after Pentecost and last for eleven days, so that everyone who came to it would be safe, unless he was a murderer or had forced someone from the town to pay a ransom.

For as long as the fair lasted, all those under ban and all those whose goods had been pledged would be released. If anyone injured another at the fair, he was to pay the abbot twenty denarii as a penalty and do what was just for the complainant, unless he committed homicide there.

11. Furthermore, the aforesaid abbot granted the inhabitants of the town—not for sale, but for building houses, making fires, and other uses—two forests, one called Padoence and the other called Martini . . .

He retained the rest, namely the cultivated and uncultivated lands, just as they had been given and granted by the monastery’s founders to the most blessed martyr Severus and to Salvator, abbot of that place, as is written in our charters and privileges.

12. It was also established that if outsiders, for the purpose of selling, carried anything away on animals or carts, they were to pay the *lemna* when leaving through the gates. We say the same concerning tanners: they were required to pay the *lemna*.

13. It was established concerning the townsmen that when leaving they were not to pay the *lemna*, except on iron, salt, and fish. Nevertheless, for as long as the fair lasted, the aforesaid townsmen, like the other inhabitants, were to pay the *lemna*.

14. It was also established that if anyone possessed a false measure for buying or selling anything, he was to pay the abbot six solidi without mercy. But if neighbors complained about a false measure, the abbot was to receive six solidi for each complainant, and the falsifier was to restore the damage to the complainants.

15. Finally, seeing the scarcity of inhabitants and that the town could not easily be populated, so that it might be populated more quickly, the abbot declared and granted that if men from Saint-Sever wished to build houses there, they would be permitted to do so for twenty years.

After the twenty years had passed, if they wished to remain there and stayed there for a year and a day, ate their own bread, and acted without complaint from the abbot thereafter like townsmen, then—unless, by chance, their dependent holdings (*casalli*) later remained deserted—they were to cover, maintain, and serve those holdings through their sons or by themselves, even though they built in the town, and were to remain on them.

But if they were servants or hired men of the townsmen, the abbot might deal with them as with other men, according to whatever pleased him, and place them wherever he wished.

16. It was also established and firmly confirmed that if, once the town gates were closed, anyone entered it or left it by another route, unless to escape death, he would be judged and condemned as an invader of the town.

17. It was also established that if anyone from the town deprived another of one of his major limbs, he was to pay the abbot 150 solidi and reach an agreement with the injured man concerning the mutilated limb; concerning the mutilation of other limbs, the matter was to lie in the judgment of the judges.

18. It was also established that if anyone died without an heir, the abbot would succeed to all his property; and if anyone refused to make a testament concerning his possessions, he was to give half of them to the monastery for the sake of his soul.

[Col. 0480D] 19. As time went on, it was established that if the abbot always kept by him a legitimate measure for buying and selling grain, he was to receive from each seller a handful of grain for the measure.

Finally, it was established that if it became necessary to establish anything new, it should be established and preserved. Amen.

## In the Year of the Lord 1107: Folcard, Abbot of Lobbes

[Col. 0481]

### Historical Notice Concerning Folcard

*(Histoire littéraire de la France*, IX, 348.)

Folcard, abbot of Lobbes in the diocese of Cambrai, had succeeded Arnulf as early as 1094. At that time the monastery, formerly so illustrious, had been groaning for eighteen years under the oppression of the latter and of the false prior Oibald, who had reduced it to a deplorable condition. Monastic discipline suffered, as is almost always the case, from the scarcity of temporal goods.

Hospitality and almsgiving had almost been abolished because the funds intended for them had been dissipated. This provided a major opportunity for Folcard’s sagacity and zeal. He made such use of both that, during the thirteen years in which he governed the monastery as abbot, he succeeded in restoring something of its former splendor. He died with the reputation of an exact and zealous servant of God, devoted to good discipline and especially to the divine office.

A memoir of his survives concerning the condition in which his monastery then found itself. He presented it to Emperor Henry IV, and that prince did it justice by a diploma printed after it, as it appears in the *Chronicle of Lobbes* (*Spicilegium* VI, 601 4). Folcard’s memoir is important for the history of this abbey, especially with regard to the conduct of its former advocates. It is known that they were supposed to be defenders and protectors of monasteries, their temporal fathers and the guardians of their privileges; but this document shows that they had become the monasteries’ greatest plunderers.

The opening, which precedes the account of Lobbes’s miseries, and the conclusion are well composed. In them the author expresses his confidence that he will find at the prince’s tribunal the justice he did not hope to receive from his ministers. He also leaves evidence of his modesty and humility by describing himself as abbot in name only, *nomine, non merito*—“in name, not in merit.”

[Col. 0481]

## Letter XIV of Folcard, Abbot, to the Emperor Henry

*(Spicilegium VI, 601.)*

[Col. 0481A] To Henry, by the grace of God most excellent Roman emperor, Augustus: Folcard, abbot in name, not in merit, and the little flock of the monastery of Lobbes, send increase from heaven of victory and peace, for the salvation of the twofold human being.

King Solomon, once peaceful, dedicating the beginnings of his kingdom to the judgment of justice in a dispute between women, commended a memorable sentence concerning it to posterity, saying: “To practice mercy and judgment is more pleasing to the Lord than sacrifices.”

With confidence and hope in this declaration, that we may obtain mercy and judgment, I, Folcard, carrying with me the body of our patron—namely Saint Ursmar, the bishop—and the present community, boldly hastening as far as the royal throne—for justice nowhere occupies the imperial benches, since everyone seeks recompense and gifts—pray that, in your clemency, you patiently hear us and, in your justice, grant our request concerning our manifold affliction and poverty, the pitiable plundering of the estates, possessions, and resources of our holy mistress, the church of Lobbes, and the loss of her former freedom.

Our church, founded in the next-to-last corner of your kingdom and dedicated under the title of the Apostles Blessed Peter and Paul, has enjoyed for five hundred years the excellent liberty firmly granted to it by the former kings, both by royal authority and by the authority of the realm, together with the most generous abundance of estates and possessions. Since nearly all these have been taken from it, it cries out to you, as a widow, because nowhere else—unless truth and mercy meet before you, Caesar—do they encounter one another, nor do justice and peace in any way rush together in a kiss.

Such, then, were the ancient laws in the abbey of Lobbes, and they remained intact until Bishop Theoduinus. The castellan of Thuin, which borders us, ought to hold the entire prefecture of the castle from the abbey in his own hand, and he ought to tolerate no defenders or advocates except those who are hereditary by ancestral inheritance. Now, however, there are many advocates—or rather, plunderers—in the villages of Saint Peter: in some places five, in others four, in others three, and in some even seven. Besides the three principal general courts, whenever they wish they hold separate hearings there individually. They frequently exact “precarias”—or rather, robberies—which they ought not to receive at all: oats, fines, money, and nearly every kind of movable property, contrary to the will of the poor. They do this not by asking but by taking, and, lodging separately by night, they oppress the poor tenants in every possible way.

In the courts, apart from the *bincina* and *testeia*, an advocate ought to receive no more than three denarii, and in some places two. Now, if someone has been defeated without the advocate’s authority in a matter not belonging to the court of the *scabini* but under the ban, the advocate wishes to take a third denarius. This must in no way be done unless the person, having resisted completely, has been defeated by the advocate’s jurisdiction. In floggings, bloodshed, manumissions, permission to marry, and mortmain, the advocate ought to receive nothing unless the abbot’s minister has lodged a claim before him, and the advocate himself has redeemed it from that minister. Now, sometimes they seize and claim for themselves a third part, and sometimes all three parts.

The legitimate advocate ought to hold the entire household of the altar of Saint Peter in his hand. Now it is being divided among this person and that as benefices, and is being plundered and destroyed by the violence not of one man but of many. Wherever an advocate ought to receive a third denarius from pledges, the abbot’s minister and the advocate’s minister ought jointly to assess the pledge. Now the advocates separate themselves from this arrangement and, according to their own judgment, receive their laws in full.

Besides these matters that we have mentioned, certain men among them are so hostile to us that, unless each year we give them some gift of their choosing, they invade even the villages assigned to their protection on any pretext, and either take for themselves all the grain and the revenues that come to us from it, or violently hold them until they exact from unwilling people more than they had previously demanded.

As these evils among us have multiplied for thirty years, during these last two years the sword has reached even to the soul. While, amid the heat of tribulation, we seek the shade of rest that we have not yet found, we have encountered the sickle of destruction and the spear. We lament that the soldiery of the countess of Mons has brought these upon us: they have reduced the entire territory adjoining our jurisdiction to fire, plunder, captivity, and death. In all these things her fury has not turned away; her hand is still extended. Although she restrains the sword from bloodshed, justice has gone beyond the bounds of the earth.

In these days Eibertus, a noble young man, dying from a blow received in battle, while lying in his agony, made Saint Peter and Saint Ursmar his heirs, and left them all the possessions belonging to his legal right for the repose of his soul. After three years, when his body had been brought here, we lawfully entered upon all these things, or converted them to our possession, by legitimate right. But his cousin, Henry of Marbais, has not feared to oppose the holy man and us concerning that principal allod called Asgup, although unjustly. For this reason we implore the excellence or clemency of your dignity, that we may obtain the restraint of his excellence, which still resists us.

For the rest, lest you condemn our lengthy speeches, let this be the conclusion of our complaint: let there be peace through your power, and then there will be abundance in our towers, whose provisions fail even each year.

## Between the years 1100 and 1110: Adelgorius, or Adelgotus, Archbishop of Magdeburg

[Col. 0483]

## Letter of Adelgorius and others to the bishops of Saxony, Francia, Lotharingia, and all the faithful of Christ

They seek help against the pagans, who were slaughtering Christians with the utmost cruelty.

(Edited by Dom Martène, *Amplissima Collectio*, vol. I, col. 626, from the manuscript of Graffchat.)

[Col. 0483C] Adelgorius, by the grace of God archbishop of Magdeburg; Albuinus, bishop of Merseburg; Walerannus, bishop of Naumburg; Herewigus, bishop of Meissen; Hecil, bishop of Havelberg; Hartbrath, bishop of Brandenburg; Otto, count; Ludovicus and all the great and small men of eastern Saxony, send love, prayer, and greeting in the same faith to Reginhardus, venerable bishop of Halberstadt; Erkambertus, abbot of Corvey; Heinricus, bishop of Paderborn; N., bishop of Minden; Fridericus, archbishop of Cologne; N., bishop of Aachen; O., bishop of Liège; G., duke of Lotharingia; Ruotbertus, most glorious count of Flanders; Lambertus, archdeacon; Buricholdus, most prudent provost; and Tanchradus, distinguished philosopher; and to all the faithful of Christ—bishops, abbots, monks, hermits, recluses, provosts, canons, clerics, princes, soldiers, ministerials, retainers, and all great and small.

Oppressed for a very long time by the manifold oppressions and calamities of the pagans, we sigh for your mercy, so that you may help us bear the ruin of your mother Church together with us. The most savage heathen have risen against us and prevailed: men without mercy, who glory in the wickedness of their inhumanity, have profaned Christ’s churches with idolatry, demolished the altars, and perpetrated against us what the human mind recoils from hearing.

They repeatedly rush into our region, sparing no one. They carry off, slaughter, shed blood, and torment their victims with carefully devised tortures. Some they behead and sacrifice their heads to their demons. From some they remove the entrails, cut off their hands, and bind their feet. “Where is their God?” they say.

Some, lifted onto the gallows, they leave there to drag out a life more wretched than any death and to endure greater tortures, so that while still alive they see themselves killed by the cutting off of their individual limbs and, finally, with their bellies cut open, miserably disemboweled. They flay many alive; after removing the skin from their heads, they burst into Christian territory in this disguise and, pretending to be Christians, carry off plunder with impunity.

Whenever their fanatics wish to devote themselves to feasting, [Ferus?] in their words, they say: “Our Pripegala wants heads. Such sacrifices must be made.” Pripegala, as they say, is Priapus and the shameless Beelphegor. Then, after beheading Christians before the altars of their profanation and howling with horrifying voices, they say: “Let us celebrate days of rejoicing! Christ has been defeated; Pripegala, most victorious, has conquered!”

[Col. 0485D] Such afflictions we either endure or fear without interruption, because we continually lament that they advance and prosper exceedingly in everything. Therefore, dearest brothers—the bishops, clerics, and monks of all Saxony, Francia, Lotharingia, and Flanders—take an example from good men, and in this too become imitators of the Gauls. Cry out in the churches:

“Sanctify a fast, call an assembly, gather the people, proclaim this, and make it heard throughout all the boundaries of your jurisdiction. Sanctify war; rouse the strong. Rise, princes, against the enemies of Christ; take up your shields; gird yourselves, mighty sons, and come, all you warriors. Let the weak man say: ‘For I am strong, because the Lord is the strength of his people and the protector of the salvation of his anointed.’”

Break forth and come, all you lovers of Christ and of the Church, and prepare yourselves, like the Gauls, for the liberation of Jerusalem. Our Jerusalem, free from the beginning, has been made a slave by the cruelty of the heathen. Its walls have fallen because of our sins. But let this ruin be repaired under your hand, so that all its walls may be built of precious stones and the towers of Jerusalem with jewels. Let its streets be paved with pure gold, and, in the presence of Pripegala, amid the dreadful noise of the heathen, let a song of joy be sung in it. Instead of the sacrifice of the shedding of Christian blood, let the poor eat flesh and blood and be filled, so that you may praise the Lord, you who seek him, and so that your hearts may live forever and ever, and ‘alleluia, alleluia’ may never fail from your mouths.”

For this war the king of the Danes and the other neighboring princes offer their devoted hands together with their people. Our own king also, the author of this war, will be a most willing helper with all whom he can bring. Our assembly will be at Merseburg on the Saturday in Rogation Week, and we have suitable places wherever necessary in eastern Saxony.

Most holy fathers, monks, hermits, and recluses, you have chosen the better part with Mary. But because the present time demands it, you must now rise with Martha from the quiet of contemplation, since Mary is greatly necessary to your brothers, who are deeply troubled, together with Martha.

We speak to you—or rather, Christ speaks to you through us:

“Rise, hasten, my beloved, my dove, and come. The flowers of good works have appeared in the land of our princes; the time for pruning idolatry has come; the voice of the turtledove has been heard, because the chaste mother Church groans over the filth of idolatry. No one lights a lamp and puts it under a bushel, but on a lampstand, so that those who enter may see the light. Let your light shine before men, so that they may see your good works. Rise, therefore, bride of Christ, and come. Let your voice sound in the ears of Christ’s faithful, so that all may hasten to Christ’s war and come to the aid of Christ’s soldiers.”

These heathen are exceedingly wicked, but their land is excellent, rich in meat, honey, flour, [lacuna], birds, and, if cultivated, in the abundance of every product of the earth, so that no land could be compared with it. Thus say those who know it. Therefore, O Saxons, Franks, Lotharingians, and most renowned Flemings, conquerors of the world, here you may both save your souls and, if it pleases you, acquire an excellent land in which to dwell.

May he who led the Gauls, advancing from the farthest West, to triumph by the strength of his arm over their enemies in the most distant East, grant you the will and power to subjugate these neighboring and utterly inhuman heathen, and to prosper well in all things.

## Circa 1107: Theodoricus, abbot of Saint-Hubert of Andage

[Col. 0487]

## Letter to the people of Liège

(See the *Chronicle of Saint-Hubert of Andage*, *Patrologia*, vol. CLIV, col. 1428.)

## In the year of the Lord 1106: Hugo, archbishop of Lyon

[Col. 0487]

## Historical notice

(*Gallia Christiana nova*, IV, 97)

[Col. 0487A] Hugo was a man of the highest nobility, being descended from the line of the dukes of Burgundy. He was prior of Saint-Marcel of Chalon, or rather, as it appears, a monk; for, as our Mabillon observes, it is not likely that secular persons were priors of monks at that time. R. P. Pagi calls him chamberlain of Lyon, though I do not know on what basis. He was subsequently bishop of Die, legate of the Apostolic See, archbishop of Lyon, and cardinal.

We have already shown that he was raised to the see of Lyon before the year 1086, but in what definite year he assumed that office is difficult to say. Baronius and D. le Laboureur, in *Ruins of the Île-Barbe*, chapter 17, assign the year 1080; the brothers Sammarthani and our Mabillon assign 1082; D. de Lamure assigns the following year.

The first opinion is refuted by the fact that in the years 1080, 1081, and even 1082 he is everywhere consistently called bishop of Die. Thus Gregory VII, book VII, letter 12, dated 3 January, indiction III—that is, in the year 1080—writing to Manasses, archbishop of Reims, says: “We wish you to appear before our legate, namely the bishop of Die, at the council of Lyon.” And in the twentieth letter, dated 17 April, indiction III: “Let your fraternity know that we have confirmed by apostolic authority in the Roman synod the sentence of deposition pronounced by our legate, the bishop of Die, at the council of Lyon.” The same is found in book VIII, letters 17, 18, and 19.

The same is also shown in the *History of Saint Arnulf*. Theobaldus, bishop of Soissons, died in 1080. Ursio obtained the bishopric through the king’s favor, but when it was reported to Gregory that there was something blameworthy in him, Gregory sent letters to Hugo, bishop of Die and then legate in Gaul, instructing him to investigate his life. Hugo summoned a council at Meaux. When Ursio refused to appear before it [Note: *Acta SS. ord. Bened.*, saec. VI, part II, pp. 531 and 556.], he was deposed, and Arnulfus was elected bishop. After his election he came to Hugo of Die, by whom, it appears, he was consecrated at Die on the Sunday before Christmas, which fell on 19 December.

Thus, in Labbe’s collection of councils, Hugo, bishop of Die and legate of the Holy Roman Church, celebrated the council of Avignon in 1080. Thus also, in the charter of Walter’s election as bishop of Chalon, made in the year 1080 of the Incarnation of the only-begotten Word, among the supporters of that election is listed “Lord Gibuinus, distinguished archbishop of the sacred see of Lyon.” He was therefore alive and presiding at Lyon at that time; consequently our Hugo was bishop of Die.

Thus also in the *Chronicle of Saint Peter the Living at Sens*, by Clarius the monk, vol. II of the *Spicilegium*, p. 747:

“In the year 1082, on 19 October, Walter, bishop of Meaux, died. In the following week Hugo, bishop of Die and legate of the Roman Church, gathered a council in that same city and ordained Robert, abbot of the Church of Rebais, bishop there.”

A contemporary writer and familiar associate of our legate, Hugo of Flavigny, records Mabillon’s opinion in the *Chronicle of Verdun* in these words:

“When Gibuinus, archbishop of Lyon, had died at that time, and there was disagreement over the election of some person, Lord Hugo, bishop of Die, by the election of the clergy and people and by the authority and command of the Roman pontiff, was promoted to be archbishop of Lyon in the year of the Lord Jesus 1082.”

If, however, it is true that he held the see for twenty-three years, eight months, and seven days, as an ancient document of the church reported by Severtius states, and since it is certain that he died on 9 October 1106, he must have taken up the see in 1083, as de Mura will have to be explained.

Gregory’s letter 18 of book IX, which lacks a heading, appears to have been addressed to him. It says:

“You must take the greatest care that, in the great see of Lyon, the bishop’s ordination not be long delayed…. But if he cannot quickly be found, by apostolic authority we command you, when asked by your brothers and elected by the sons of that Church, to proceed without hesitation to govern the aforesaid Church of Lyon, confidently relying on heavenly assistance, imitating … Blessed Peter, who was transferred from the lesser Church of Antioch to the Roman Church.”

Gregory VII writes to him:

“To our beloved brother and fellow bishop H., archbishop of Lyon, greeting. The bearer of this letter has reported to us that your fraternity has forbidden him and his church to perform the office, because he failed to appear at the appointed place to resolve his dispute with the abbot of La Chaise-Dieu.”

Gregory orders Hugo to restore the ecclesiastical office to him and settle the dispute.

Anselm, bishop of Lucca, in the letter addressed to Pontius, abbot of Fraxinetum, before the year 1086, when Anselm died, orders that Lord Hugh, archbishop of Lyon, be greeted in his name:

“if, indeed, a reasonable necessity excuses him from the necessity of the whole world. For if, whether from fear, negligence, or a love of guilty repose, he delays visiting his mother, the Roman Church, and freeing her from the hand of death, he will be guilty before the judgment, unless he hastens to come without delay and strives to help in everything.”

Such was his reputation at that time, and such was the esteem Gregory held for him, that when the pope was near death and was asked, amid such great confusion of affairs, to designate a successor, he gave three choices, one of whom was Hugo, archbishop of Lyon.

But what Hugo did afterward greatly diminished his reputation. After Desiderius, abbot of Monte Cassino, had been elected, Hugo showed that he had suffered something human—or rather, that his mind had been embittered by envy and consumed by hatred—in a letter to Countess Matilda preserved by Hugo of Flavigny in the *Chronicle of Verdun*.

He wrote that the abbot of Monte Cassino had been elected pope before Hugo himself had arrived in Rome, and that Hugo, like the other brothers, had consented to his election out of regard for men rather than for God. But when he had met him at Monte Cassino, he claimed to have heard such unspeakable things from his mouth that he immediately recognized how intolerably they had offended God in electing him.

Desiderius had allegedly said that, unless Hugo had heard it from his own mouth, he would never have believed that he had given his allegiance to the man called King Henry, promising faithfully to help him obtain the crown of the Roman Empire; and that this same king had been led, by Desiderius’ own counsel and persuasion, to invade the lands of Blessed Peter.

He had further added, in the hearing of himself and his followers, that whoever was eventually elected pope would be excommunicated unless he declared Atto, the cardinal-elect of Milan—although publicly excommunicated by Pope Gregory, with Desiderius himself subscribing to the act, and having died without penance—to be blessed; and that Desiderius prayed that he might possess no other glory than that which he himself possessed.

Hugo added that he called H. … and B. … as witnesses to all these things: they had either heard them from Desiderius’ own mouth or said that they had heard them from trustworthy men whom they believed without hesitation. Finally, Desiderius had openly condemned and destroyed the decrees of his lord Pope Gregory and of other holy fathers. He had very often asserted that his election had been made not according to God but tumultuously.

Since all these matters proved him unworthy of the papacy, it seemed to Hugo and to others that, after the election repeatedly rejected by Desiderius had been returned to the Church, they should go to Capua under the pretext of designating a bishop, and there elect the Roman pontiff. Hugo said that he had in fact come there from Salerno with the abbot of Marseille, the archbishop of Aix, and others; but that the abbot of Monte Cassino had compelled his followers to force him, as it were, to assume the papacy.

Hugo, together with the bishop of Ostia, the monk Witmundus, and others, had opposed his elevation unless he cleared himself of certain accusations being spread against his reputation. Desiderius refused to do so and again rejected his election; thus the assembly was dissolved.

Meanwhile, by the consecration of Alfano as bishop of Salerno, Desiderius had won the duke over to his side. Supported by the duke’s favor and wearing the papal mantle, he had set out for Rome, without consulting the bishop of Ostia or Hugo and his followers, who were entirely unaware of the plan.

But the bishop of Ostia, who had until then resisted Desiderius, fearing that he would lose his rank if Desiderius were consecrated by someone else, had forgotten his purpose and his pledged word, been reconciled to the abbot, and shown him every mark of reverence as pope.

Hugo of Flavigny adds that such a great crime did not long remain unpunished. Victor, after being consecrated, was saying Mass at Saint Peter’s when, during the liturgy, he was struck down by the judgment of God. Although he recognized only later that he had erred, he deposed himself and, summoning the brothers from Monte Cassino who were present with him, ordered them to carry him there and bury him in the chapter house not as pope but as abbot.

The more horrifying these things are, the less credible they are. Certainly they appear contrary to the accounts of contemporary writers and entirely foreign to probability. Therefore they must be rejected as false, or at least as lies in most respects. Nevertheless, they were the seeds of the schism that Hugo raised together with Richard, abbot of Marseille; for this reason both were removed from communion at the council of Benevento in 1087.

Hugo tried to repel the disgrace of schism from himself in a letter written to the same Countess Matilda in 1088, after the election of Pope Urban. He says:

“Although we did disagree with certain bishops and cardinal-priests of the Holy Roman Church concerning the recovery of the election of the lord abbot of Monte Cassino, and although we publicly gave an account at Capua to some of them of why it seemed otherwise to us, nevertheless we wish you to know that we have been joined to them in unity, within the body of Holy Church, for the service of Blessed Peter by divine favor. We have neither departed nor, with God’s mercy, shall we depart forever; rather, we have resolved in every way to serve the advancement of the Apostolic See.”

In the same letter he complains about Hugh, abbot of Cluny, and the Cluniac monks, saying that they inflicted such great injuries upon him that he could not endure them. They avoided him as a schismatic, the author of schism, and an excommunicated man, citing certain letters of Pope Urban, whose authenticity he tried to cast into doubt, and so forth.
