If Urban was angered against him, he was soon appeased, and the dignity of legate of the Apostolic See was immediately restored to Hugo by Urban himself. In that same year, indeed, the synod approved the absolution at the point of death granted by two monks to Theodoricus, bishop of Verdun, who had stubbornly adhered to Emperor Henry. The synod was presided over by “Hugo, legate of the Apostolic See, formerly bishop of Die and then bishop of Lyon,” as stated in the *History of the Bishops of Verdun* written by Laurence of Liège.

Peter the Venerable gives the same testimony, book I of the *Miracles*, chapter 22, in these words:

“At that time, as it happened, the venerable Hugo was archbishop of the Church of Lyon. He was a man of great moral virtue and religious conduct, and had been appointed legate by Lord Pope Urban over almost all Gaul.”

This is also proved by the fact that in 1090, when Hugo was at Saumur, a dispute that had long been contested between the monks of Saint-Serge and Saint-Aubin of Angers was brought before him, “a man of distinguished virtue and primate of all Gaul,” as they say. He entrusted its determination to the bishops of the province.

In 1092, Poppo, a cleric of Trier, was elected bishop of Metz. Because Jarento, abbot of Dijon, feared that Poppo would be ordained by the bishop of Trier, who had been contaminated by communion with schismatics, Jarento escorted Hugo, archbishop of Lyon, with two of his suffragans, the bishops of Mâcon and Langres, “through battles and swords, when everything seemed to threaten death, all the way to Metz.” Poppo was consecrated by Hugo “in the first week of Lent.”

“In the following year Richerius came to Lyon for his consecration. After having purged himself by oath of simony, he was consecrated on the holy day of Easter.”

Thus writes Hugo of Flavigny. Laurence of Liège gives a different account in the *History of the Bishops of Verdun*. He says of Richerius:

“In the year of the Incarnation 1088, Richerius was elected bishop of Verdun. But because he had incurred the displeasure of the Roman Church, he remained for seven years without episcopal blessing, until Rodulfus, abbot of Saint-Viton, led him to Lyon in the year when Pope Urban celebrated a synod at Clermont. There the archbishop Hugo, after his renunciation of the Henryan party, consecrated him priest on Holy Saturday and bishop on the feast day. On his return he was received most honorably by his fellow bishops, Poppo of Metz and Pibo of Toul, and by the entire city.”

In 1093, when Lambert, the elected bishop of Arras, was being delayed by his metropolitan in receiving consecration, he set out for Rome. On the journey he was received by Hugo, “a burning and shining lamp in the house of the Lord, commendably honorable and honorably commendable, primate of Lyon and legate of the Apostolic See.” Hugo detained him at Lyon for six days because of the excessive flooding of the waters and the severity of winter, supplied him with everything necessary for his journey, and, when Lambert was returning from the journey, gave him a letter of recommendation to Robert, count of Flanders.

In 1094 the council of Autun was held, which Berthold, from the vernacular name Autun, calls the Ostian council. Our Hugo presided; thirty-two bishops and a very large number of abbots attended. Among other matters, the excommunication of Emperor Henry, the antipope Guibert, and Philip, king of France, who had rejected his wife Bertha and brought in Bertrada, was renewed.

A letter of Hugo survives in which he invites Lambert, bishop of Arras, to this synod. In the same year he also presided over another council at Autun, as well as over the assemblies at Brioude and Dol. That year he gave the church of Saint-Desiderius at Bressia to the monks of Cluny. On the feast of Saint John the Baptist, at the command of Urban II, he absolved Fulk, count of Anjou, in the monastery of Saint-Florentius from the excommunication with which he had been bound.

The letters of absolution are reproduced by Sirmond in the *Eulogy of Geoffrey of Vendôme* and in volume I of *Gallia Christiana*, p. 3.

About that time the prodigy described by Peter the Venerable in *On Miracles*, book I, chapter 22, occurred. When an immense flame was devastating everything in the convent of Marcigny, “the archbishop of the Church of Lyon happened to be there … He quickly entered the nuns’ cloister and urged them all with the greatest insistence to withdraw from the danger. When they utterly refused and firmly declared that they could die before violating their resolve, he said:

“‘By the authority of Blessed Peter and the Lord pope, and in obedience to your abbot, I command you to leave this place for the present …’

“To this a woman of great nobility replied: ‘Do not impose upon us what we are not permitted to do. Rather, just as you command us to flee from the fire, so command the fire, armed with the power of Christ, to flee from us.’

“Struck with wonder at the woman’s faith, and suddenly himself filled with faith, the archbishop said: ‘In the name of the Lord and by the power of this faith that has now spoken, depart, destructive fire, from the dwellings of the servants of God …’

“When these words had been spoken by the prelate, the immense flames were suddenly restrained by an invisible power. They could advance no farther and, without any human assistance and without a single drop of rain, extinguished themselves with incredible speed.”

Finally, in the same year, indiction II, Hugo gave Hugh of Cluny the altar of Reortorium with the church of Saint Paul within the fortification of that same castle, subject to an annual rent of five solidi, half of which was to be paid on the feast of Saint Martin and half on the Purification of the Blessed Virgin Mary. From the second Cluniac chartulary, fol. 212, charter 339.

In the year 1095, summoned to the synod at Piacenza in Lombardy, since he had not come and had not sent a legate on his behalf with a canonical excuse, he was suspended from office, says Berthold of Constance; [Col. 0493A] nevertheless, the pontiff’s displeasure did not last long, once full satisfaction had been given. In the same year, on 4 April, he set out for Saint James, attended by an honorable company of clergy and laity; and after lingering for three days at Le Puy, he was with the greatest difficulty torn away from them. He arrived at Saint James on the eve of Pentecost, and on the holy day publicly celebrated the solemn Mass at the saint’s altar, with the bishop, clergy, and an innumerable crowd standing by. The next day he returned, and entered Lyons on the third day before the Nativity of Saint John the Baptist. In the same year, but on an uncertain day, he subscribed King Philip I of France’s charter concerning the subjection of Maziac to the monastery of Cluny. He accompanied Pope Urban when he entered Gaul, came with him to Cluny, and consecrated the altar in the new basilica.

[Col. 0493B] He attended the Council of Auvergne, over which the Supreme Pontiff presided. There, having been chosen—together with the archbishop of Bourges—as arbiter of the dispute that had arisen between Hugh, abbot of Cluny, and Pontius, abbot of La Chaise-Dieu, concerning the cell of Boort, he settled it and assigned the cell to the Cluniacs on 1 December. We have seen above that Gregory VII confirmed to the archbishops of Lyons primacy over the four provinces of Lyons. At this synod Hugh complained to the archbishops of those provinces that, whenever an opportunity arose, they attempted to diminish that primacy, or rather not to acknowledge it. Therefore, at Urban’s command, all documents pertaining to it were read.

Then Richer, bishop of Sens, was summoned to court. Since he attempted to evade judgment by various delays and postponements, at last “with the approval and judgment of the entire synod [Col. 0493C] it was decreed that the archbishop of Sens owed subjection and obedience to the archbishop of Lyons as primate. To this sentence, they had promised on oath that they would humbly submit; and each of the suffragans of the Church of Sens professed this in his own voice. The same was additionally confirmed concerning the Church of Rouen. As for Tours, since it had already obeyed without resistance from earlier times, no question was now raised.”

Even then Richer did not yield. Urban, “with the whole council consenting,” prohibited him from using the pallium and from receiving the obedience of his suffragans until he himself obeyed. The sentence was repeated and again confirmed at the synods of Tours and Nîmes; but even so, Richer’s obstinacy could not be overcome. He complained about all these judgments to Ivo, from whom he received advice full of wisdom: namely, that he should meanwhile submit to the matter already judged, until, if authentic documents could ever be found, he might demonstrate the liberty of his Church.

The bishop of Sens rejected this advice, and thus compelled Ivo to withdraw from the reverence toward the Church of Sens that had been forbidden him by papal decree. Consequently, when Richer summoned him to the castle of Nanton for the ordination of Sancio, the elected bishop of Orléans, Ivo refused to obey the command, because of the primacy of the Church of Lyons, which Richer irrationally rejected. Richer himself, together with the other suffragans of the province, laid hands on Sancio.

What is more, because of his disobedience, the same case—brought forward by our Hugh—was reheard in the Council of Tours and likewise in that of Nîmes, and was decided in the same way, as is clear from another bull of Urban addressed to the archbishop of Lyons. Moved by none of this, Richer preferred to die under interdict rather than for a time diminish the dignity of his Church.

I am not unaware of what the adversaries of the primacy of Lyons reply: that Urban’s bull is false and spurious. But if this is admitted, all the monuments of antiquity collapse, for scarcely any of them rests on stronger testimony. D. de Marca published it from an ancient Lyons manuscript. Second, its *vidimus*, as they call it, was publicly drawn up by the Lyons judge in ecclesiastical matters in a solemn court in 1409, and he had it subscribed by four notaries—nothing more solemn could be found in such matters. Third, Martin V, in a diploma [Col. 0494B] issued at Geneva on 1 August, in the first year of his pontificate, A.D. 1418, cites both of Urban’s bulls. Fourth, in the manuscript canon VII of Cencius the chamberlain, one reads: “The primacy of the Church of Lyons was restored over the provinces of Lyons, Sens, and Rouen.” Baluze asserts that he saw these same words in a very ancient manuscript of the abbey of Aniane, in his notes to *On the Concord of the Priesthood and the Empire*, vol. II, p. 286.

Finally, all the matters contained in the bull are reported by Ivo, bishop of Chartres, who had attended the Council of Clermont, as is evident from what has already been said and from what will be said below. To set out everything relating to this controversy at once: after Richer, archbishop of Sens, had died, Daimbert was elected in his place. [Col. 0494C] Taking advantage of the opportunity, the bishop of Lyons forbade hands to be laid upon him before he had professed the obedience owed to the Church of Lyons, as Ivo’s sixtieth letter to him explains.

In that letter Ivo first states that he and his fellow provincial bishops had, at his command, “withheld their hands from the consecration of the elected archbishop of Sens.” Yet he says that he is astonished that the archbishop had ordered “the elected archbishop of Sens to be presented to him before his consecration, and to profess subjection and obedience by right of his primacy, although antiquity has hitherto instituted no such practice, either in the province of Sens or elsewhere, and custom has observed none.” He therefore begs him, if nothing contrary to the sacred canons is found in the matter, to permit him to be consecrated according to the ancient custom.

“If you yield to this petition of ours,” he says, “we shall earnestly persuade the consecrated man to show you, as his primate, the deference due to the primacy of the Church of Lyons, and to offer every proper reverence according to the traditions of the Fathers. If he refuses to yield to our persuasion, we nevertheless shall not depart from what the Apostolic See has commanded.”

The bishop of Lyons replied with a letter that may be found in Baluze’s *Miscellanea*, vol. VI, p. 426. Ivo himself also wrote his sixty-fifth letter to Urban: “Concerning the elected archbishop of Sens, whose consecration is being prevented by your legate, the archbishop of Lyons, because he does not profess obedience to him, before his consecration, by right of his primacy—let your fatherhood write back what we ought to do.”

[Col. 0495A] Urban was angered against Ivo and, as Ivo himself believed, at Hugh the legate’s instigation. Thus, in his sixty-seventh letter to that pontiff, he says that in one of his letters certain “words had sounded otherwise than he wished, especially concerning the primacy of Lyons”; and that, “according to the way he felt,” he had wanted Urban “to share in his bitterness.”

At last, when Daimbert accomplished nothing, he went to Rome and was consecrated by the pontiff subject to a condition. Later, however, he again went to Rome, both to pursue the case concerning the primacy and “for the common synodical summons.” In the presence of Hugh’s legates—Ismio, bishop of Die, Girin, dean, and others—and compelled by the Apostolic See’s judgment, he finally abandoned all evasion and professed in Urban’s hands that he acknowledged the primacy of the Church of Lyons [Col. 0495B] and would obey Hugh and his successors as primates. He further declared that, at the time fixed by the pontiff, he would come to Lyons and profess the same thing with his own mouth in the presence of the Church of Lyons.

That he kept his promises is clear from what Hugh’s successor wrote to him: “You may remember that, from the time you recovered the friendship and familiarity of the Church of Lyons, it saw you with joy, received you with exultation, and honored you with as much affection as it could.”

The same is attested by Goffridus, abbot of Vendôme, in Letter 18 of Book II: “When I had returned from Rome,” he says, “and had been honorably received at Lyons by the lord primate . . . I heard from the archbishop himself . . . that the lord of Sens had made peace with him and had promised him every obedience, as [Col. 0495C] his primate.”

In the year 1096 he accompanied Urban to Tours, where he attended the council celebrated by the pontiff. He subscribed to the settlement of the dispute between the monks of Cormery and the Church of Saint Martin of Tours; to the pope’s decision by which the churches of Sainte-Croix and Saint-Nicolas of Loudun were adjudged to the monastery of Tournus against the abbot of Saint-Florent; and finally to the consecration of the church of the Great Monastery.

In the same year, William, count of Forez, restored to Hugh the archbishop the Church of Saint Julian of Mondon, which the counts of Forez had held in fief from the Church of Saint Stephen of Lyons for many years. Hugh in turn gave it to Pontius, abbot of La Chaise-Dieu, [Col. 0495D] and confirmed this gift at Lyons in an assembly of the canons.

It is astonishing with what kindness, reverence, and munificence he received the exile Anselm into his household, and how closely bound the two men were by mutual friendship. This friendship had already begun before Anselm assumed the archiepiscopal insignia of Canterbury, as is evident from his Letters 11 and 17 of Book II.

Accordingly, when everything in England was troubled in 1095 because Anselm had declared that he recognized Urban as the legitimate pontiff, contrary to the king’s intentions, he wrote to our Hugh, asking his advice as to whether, amid such disturbances, it would not be better to resign the episcopate than to retain it without fruit (*Book III, Letter 34*).

The following year, when he had come to Gaul and had sent a messenger ahead to the archbishop before departing for Lyons, Hugh indicated through the more distinguished members of his household that he was consumed by a great desire to see him, and begged him to come to him as quickly as possible. When the holy man reached Lyons, it is beyond belief how reverently he was received.

In 1099, when he returned from Rome to Lyons, he was treated there not as a guest or stranger, but truly as a native and lord of the place. He exercised episcopal functions just as in his own Church, administered the sacraments, and enjoyed every right, even against his will. Hugh’s reverence for him was so great that, when Anselm celebrated Mass, Hugh served him in place of a suffragan, and wherever Anselm preached, Hugh sat at his feet.

Thus, in a letter to Hugh, archdeacon of Canterbury—the ninth in the *Spicilegium*, vol. IX—[Col. 0496B] in which Anselm relates how kindly he had been received everywhere by the bishops, he writes: “Among them, the venerable archbishop of Lyons rejoices at present to show me his munificence abundantly and honorably, and desires me always to remain with him, as long as I am an exile from our Church.”

In 1103, when the holy pontiff was again compelled to leave England, he returned from Rome to Lyons, where the archbishop received him, as usual, with the highest honor. He stayed with him for a full year and four months. Among Anselm’s letters there is a letter from Hugh to him, stating that Hugh had returned safely from Jerusalem and inviting him, if he were harassed by the king of the English, not to disdain to withdraw to him: “and to your house,” he says, “which was yours, and which is now yours, and which from day to day will always be more truly yours.”

But now let us return to Hugh’s annals.

In the year 1097 he consecrated Berard, archdeacon of Lyons, as bishop of Mâcon. He granted Hugh, a monk of Saint-Bénigne, to the people of Flavigny as abbot; and when Hugh had come to him, he sent him to Haganon, bishop of Autun, to be consecrated, with a letter to the bishop that Hugh himself reports in his chronicle. The dispute that the monks of Tournus had brought before the Roman See against the Cluniacs Urban referred to our pontiff, who immediately settled it.

In 1099 he accomplished something worthy of eternal remembrance by fostering the beginnings of the Cistercian monastery and order. [Col. 0496D] For when Saint Robert, abbot of Molesme, had decided, together with several monks, to observe the Rule of Saint Benedict without any mitigation, and was afraid of the authority of the bishop of Langres, by which he had already been recalled from Vivicus, he left Molesme with six companions and sought Lyons. There he explained his purpose and that of his companions to Hugh the archbishop and requested protection and support.

Hugh did not immediately consent. He ordered them to consult God and write back to him. They complied and indicated that they were firm in their purpose. He replied to them in the following manner [Note: [Col. 0495D] *Exordium magnum Cisterciense*, chap. 12]:

“Hugh, bishop of Lyons and legate of the Apostolic See, to Robert, abbot of Molesme, and the brothers with him who desire to serve God according to the Rule of Saint Benedict. Let it be known to all who rejoice in the progress of Holy Mother Church” etc.

See below among Hugh’s letters.

Nor did he do only this: he also commended the holiness of the Cistercian solitaries to Odo, duke of Burgundy, from whom they received many gifts. Meanwhile the monks of Molesme went to Rome and demanded with the greatest fervor that their abbot be restored to Molesme at the council.

Moved by their complaints, Urban wrote to Hugh in these words: “Compelled, we command your belovedness by this present letter, informing you that it would please us if, if possible, that abbot were brought back from the desert to the monastery.” If you cannot accomplish this, let it be your care both that those who inhabit the desert should be at peace and that those who are in the monastery should serve under regular discipline.”

After receiving this letter, Hugh convened a council. At his persuasion, he ordered—although unwillingly—that Robert return to Molesme, and he warned the bishop of Langres, by the council’s decree, to see that it was carried out.

In the same year, 1099, he called a provincial council at Pierre-Perçée and invited Daimbert of Sens to it. When this seemed contrary to law to Ivo, he wrote him mordant letters. In one of them he not only reproved this action, but also appears to criticize him for being too ready to decree excommunications and interdicts, without danger to himself but with great danger to others.

About this time Paschal, who had succeeded Urban, abandoned the custom of his predecessors. They had entrusted their authority in Gaul to Hugh or to another Gaul; Paschal instead sent legates from Italy, whose excesses wearied our countrymen, and whom they endured with difficulty.

Therefore Ivo of Chartres, in his own name and that of his colleagues, asked the pope to entrust the legation to someone from Cisalpine Gaul: “for this responsibility,” he says, “we know no one more suitable than the lord archbishop of Lyons, who has already served for a long time in the same office and who, as we know by experience, has benefited both the Roman Church and the churches beyond the Alps in a marvelous way.”

Nevertheless Paschal persisted in his purpose and sent John and Benedict. They called a council at Autun and held it at Valence in the year 1100, on 30 September. They invited Hugh to it, but he did not attend because he was ill, says the Chronicle of Verdun. He sent his legates, however; nor did his suffragans, the bishops of Langres and Chalon, attend, “being forbidden, as was said, by that same archbishop of Lyons,” says the same chronicle.

Indeed, he openly disapproved of what the legates had decreed against Norgaud, bishop of Autun, at this council and later at the Council of Poitiers, and in the end he acted so that the decree was annulled. His spirit was great and lofty, accustomed to command; he now considered it beneath his rank and dignity to be subjected and obedient to inferiors. And, apparently to avoid all such circumstances, he conceived the plan of traveling to Jerusalem. He sent legates to Rome [Col. 0498A] to consult the pope on the matter. Paschal consenting, and offering him the legation of the Apostolic See in Asia, he set out for Rome in the year 1101. There, using the considerable authority he possessed in the Roman curia, he arranged for Norgaud to be absolved.

[Note: [Col. 0497D] The date of this pilgrimage is inferred from a charter recording the donation of the Church of Blessed Mary of the Forum to the monastery of Savigny (De Mura, p. 392): “In the year in which Hugh, archbishop of Lyons, set out for Jerusalem . . . he held an assembly of his Church . . . to discuss the welfare of his Church and his journey; and this was on 13 March, the Wednesday of the first week of Lent. At this assembly he made this gift of the Church of the Forum to our community,” etc. For if 13 March was the Wednesday of the first week of Lent, Ash Wednesday fell on 6 March; and therefore Easter fell on 21 April, which agrees with the year 1101.]

Earlier, in the year 1100, always fostering the new foundation of Cîteaux, he gave letters of recommendation to Pope Paschal for John and Hildebod, sent by Alberic to Rome. In them he wrote: “Know that they are from a certain place called the New Monastery—for Cîteaux was then called this—where they have left the Church of Molesme with their abbot,” etc. See below among the letters. Nor was the archbishop’s request without effect, for the members of the new reform returned to their own house with a privilege from the Roman pontiff.

[Col. 0498B] Milo, cardinal and bishop of Palestrina, sent by Paschal to Gaul, held an assembly at Marseille, at which the rights and immunities of the Cluniacs were confirmed. These acts were drawn up at Marseille in the year 1103, in the presence of Berard, bishop of Mâcon, “who at that time, together with his bishopric, was exercising the authority of the lord Hugh, archbishop of Lyons.”

About the same time Bego, abbot of Conques, governed the monastery of Conques in Rouergue. Our Hugh granted him the churches of Sainte-Foy of Châtelet and Saint Victor, situated on the Loire, subject to an annual rent. De Mura gives the charter on p. 298.

King Guntram had given the village of Floriacum, in the county of Dijon, to the monastery of Saint-Marcel of Chalon. A monastic cell was later established there. Otto, duke of Burgundy, had usurped its serfs contrary to law, and his son Hugh retained them, [Col. 0498C] until the dignity of the priory of Saint-Marcel passed “to the venerable lord Hugh, archbishop of Lyons, nephew of Hugh.” On one occasion he received the duke as a guest at that village and asked him to free it from such servitude.

Duke Hugh consented and later drew up a charter concerning the matter “in the chamber of the abbot of Dijon, named Jarenton, and placed it in the hand of the venerable Hugh, the archbishop of Lyons named above . . . in the year from the Incarnation of the Lord 1104, indiction XII.”

In the same year he wrote to Daimbert of Sens, reproving him on many matters and summoning him to the Council of Troyes. In the following year, the same archbishop, Norgaud of Autun, and Walter, bishop of Chalon, confirmed to Hugh, abbot of Cluny, the monastery of Saint Mary Magdalene of Quadrella—that is, Charolais—and the churches of that district concerning which Leotbald of Dijon and his son of the same name were raising a dispute.

Finally, in the year 1106, when the canons of the cathedral church complained that he had given Hugh of Cluny the Church of Artenay, which had belonged to Saint Stephen from ancient times, he restored it to them and gave Cluny another church, called Saint-Germain, in exchange.

When a dispute had arisen between the monks of Saint-Bénigne and the clergy of Besançon over the churches of Salins, he settled it amicably: “Hugh, by the grace of God archbishop of Lyons and legate of the Apostolic See . . . Done publicly at Lyons, in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1106, on the day before the Kalends of April, Saturday in the Octave of Easter [Note: [Col. 0499C] *Collection relating to the history of Burgundy*, pp. 209–210].”

Shortly before his death he granted the Church of Saint-Treverius to Aimeric, abbot of La Chaise-Dieu. Paschal II attests this in a diploma by which he confirms to that monastery the monasteries and cells subject to it, including Saint-Treverius, which, he says, “the venerable Hugh, archbishop of Lyons,” had recently granted to it.

He ended his life in this same year, 1106, and indeed on 7 October, if the necrology of Saint-Bénigne is to be trusted, at Susa, in Segusio, at the foot of the Alps, while traveling by order of the pontiff to the Council of Guastalla. He was buried in the same city, in the abbey of Saint Just, as Hugh, abbot of Cluny, teaches in his letter to Anselm of Canterbury, writing as follows:

“Since we knew how great, by God’s will, the friendship between you and the lord Hugh, archbishop of Lyons, had been, we considered it fitting to inform you that his death is grievous to us and to all good men and irreparably lamentable, so that, through you and yours, you may strive to repay him, now dead, with the true affection that he showed while alive. For he died in peace on 7 October at Susa, while he was going to a council summoned by the Apostolic See, and was buried there with due honor in the abbey of Saint Just,” etc.

[Col. 0499C] Baldric, abbot of Bourgueil, wrote this epitaph for him [Note: [Col. 0500C] Duchesne, *History of France*, vol. IV, p. 258]:

[Col. 0500A]

Afterward bishop of Lyons, formerly Hugh of Die,  
A great son of the Roman Church.  
The Roman pope asked him to be his legate;  
Coming to the synod, alas, he fell dead.  
The man of Susa buried in this earth  
The cell of virtues, the hall of the divine heart.  
Justus rejoiced, a gracious host, at so great a guest,  
Whom the exalted God sent him as a companion.  
Mourn, Lyons: the solemn councils  
Died for you with the death of your father.

From an ancient monument Severt reports the following: “Hugh, archbishop of good and faithful memory, beneficially provided for that Church. He left nine copes with gold embroidery, four chasubles, six dalmatics,” etc.—that is, all and each of the ornaments required by a bishop when celebrating Mass [Col. 0500B] or conferring orders.

“Moreover, he adorned the wall of the church and five windows, built the high altar, constructed the episcopal chambers with part of the towers and the courtyards, decorated the episcopal chapel with paintings and a pavement, and left the storerooms of the house full.” He also gave very many books.

“He governed this Church of Lyons for twenty-three years, eight months, and seven days. At Saint Irenaeus he established canons living according to a regular rule, to whom he transferred for common use lands that had formerly belonged to that same saint and had been purchased from laymen at great cost,” etc.

In the first document, which Menestrier reports among the proofs of his *History of Lyons*, he is said to have given Saint Stephen—that is, the cathedral church—the Church of Sandrens with its dependencies, the Church of Saint Mary of Cherers, and those of Saint Stephen of Coisia, Saint Symphorian of Castello, Saint Martin of Pomey, and Saint Martin of Noailles.

[Col. 0499]

## Literary Notice

(*Literary History of France*, vol. IX, p. 315)

Almost all that remains of the works of Archbishop Hugh consists of simple letters, but they are valuable both for their great number and for the subjects they treat. Even these are only a portion of those that he had occasion to write and actually did write. This is suggested by the multitude of ecclesiastical affairs with which he was charged for more than twenty years, during which he exercised the functions of legate in France and Burgundy.

There can be no dispute that all the letters of a prelate who played so considerable a part in the government of the Church must have been interesting and deserved to be preserved for posterity. Yet it has also happened that those which escaped the shipwreck of the others are extremely scattered through foreign collections, where they are often virtually submerged. If someone should one day undertake to gather them together so that they might be read consecutively, in order to understand more fully what was then taking place in the Gallican Church, we should be pleased to shorten his labor by taking care to make them known and to indicate their chronology as far as possible.

The collection in which the greatest number are found is Baluze’s *Miscellanea*. He published three in the fifth volume and nine or ten others in the following one (Baluze, *Miscellanea*, vol. V, pp. 273–274). The first three are embedded in the acts concerning the restoration of the ancient episcopal see of Arras. Only the first, however, directly concerns that subject; the others were included because they are addressed to Lambert, the first bishop to occupy that see at that time.

This first letter is written to Robert, count of Flanders, instructing him to recognize the new bishop, who had come from Rome, where he had been consecrated, and to grant him his protection, chiefly so that he might reclaim the possessions alienated or taken from his bishopric. The letter was therefore written in 1094, after the metropolitan and the suffragan bishops of the province had themselves recognized Lambert as their colleague. This took place at a council held at Reims on 17 September of the same year. Dom d’Achery (*Spicilegium*, vol. V, p. 552) had already published this letter in the fifth volume of his *Spicilegium*.

In the second of the three letters, Hugh informs the same prelate of the death of a nun who had gone from Arras to Lyons, where she ended her days on 24 January, apparently in the following year, 1095; from this one may conjecture the date of the letter. It is written with profound sentiments of piety and faith in prayers for the dead.

The third is written on behalf of the person who had undertaken to deliver it to Bishop Lambert. Since this person had a dispute with the bishop of Amiens, who was then Gervin, and with Fulk, archdeacon of the same church, he had asked Hugh the legate to induce the bishop of Arras to have justice done to him. Hugh, charging him with this commission, instructed him, should the bishop refuse to carry it out, to ask Renaud, archbishop of Reims, on Hugh’s behalf to give judgment on the complaints of the bearer of the letter.

This letter seems to have been written in the same year as the preceding one. In both, the author, with humble modesty, calls himself a servant of the Church of Lyons, as he does in several others.

Among those contained in the sixth volume of the collection in question, four were written when Hugh was still only bishop of Die. The first is addressed to Raoul, archbishop of Tours, inviting him to a conference at which matters were to be discussed that would show whether this prelate was as devoted to the pope as he wished to appear. Hugh gives himself no other title than that of apocrisiary of the Holy Roman Church. The editor dates it to 1075; from this it may be seen that Hugh began then—namely, the year after he was ordained bishop of Die—to exercise the functions of legate in France.

The next three are addressed to the same archbishop, inviting him to as many councils, to which he was asked to bring the suffragans of his province. They are short, but say much in few words. The first especially contains a vivid description of the sorrowful condition to which the Church had then been reduced, a condition that ought to have stirred the zeal of good bishops. It was written immediately after the legate had concluded the first council he held at Anse, and it indicates to Raoul the council he was to hold at Dijon on 2 January of the following year, 1077.

By the second of the three, Hugh indicated another council at Clermont, in Auvergne, for 9 August of the same year; by the last, the council that was to assemble at Autun on 10 September thereafter. The legate wished the abbots and most learned clergy of the province of Tours, together with all the bishops, to attend it as well. These letters, moreover, are the only documents that provide the precise dates on which all these councils were held.

Next comes another work by our legate under the title of letters, but it is properly only a donation of the churches of Sainte-Foy of Châtelet and Saint Victor to the abbey of Conques in Rouergue. The donation was made by Hugh himself, then archbishop of Lyons, with the consent of his canons and under certain conditions set out in the undated instrument executed in the archiepiscopal residence.

Two other letters of our archbishop and legate follow: one to Hugh, newly ordained archbishop of Besançon, which shows that the person meant is Hugh of Burgundy; the other to Lambert, bishop of Arras (Mabillon, *Annales*, vol. V, appendix, p. 675, no. 2).

The purpose of the first, which was reprinted by Dom Mabillon, is to urge the first of these prelates to restore to the abbey of Saint-Bénigne of Dijon the Church of Notre-Dame of Salins, in accordance with what had been settled at the Council of Meaux. The archbishop of Besançon, his predecessor, had refused to attend that council, although he had been summoned to it. The author adds that the pope had confirmed the settlement and offers an extract from the pope’s letter as proof. This was doubtless Urban II, for Hugh was not ordained archbishop of Besançon until sometime in 1088. There is no other indication by which to discover the date of this letter from the legate.

In the following letter he invites the bishop of Arras to the Council of Autun, which he was to convene on 15 September and which was in fact held in 1094. To remove any difficulty that might have arisen from his metropolitan, the archbishop of Reims—who, by virtue of the privileges of his Church, did not believe himself bound to obey the orders of the legates of the Holy See—the author copies for him the pope’s decision on this matter.

Another letter of our archbishop had unfortunate consequences and for a time caused its author to quarrel with Ivo, bishop of Chartres, to whom it is addressed. It is the reply to Ivo’s sixtieth letter, in which Ivo, as first suffragan of the metropolitan see of Sens, had asked permission to ordain, at the beginning of Lent, Daimbert, who had been elected archbishop in place of Richer, who died toward the end of December 1096. The letter insists on the refusal that the legate had given him. Thus Ivo’s letter and Hugh’s reply belong to the beginning of the following year.

Hugh’s reason for refusing was that he wanted Daimbert first to acknowledge the right of primacy granted to the Church of Lyons. Ivo undertook to show him, by several authorities, that what he demanded of the newly elected archbishop had never been observed either in the province of Sens or anywhere else. He also reproached him with having reconciled, without his knowledge, the lords of Puiset, who had been excommunicated by the bishops of the same province for the plunder they had inflicted upon the lands of the Church of Chartres. Ivo’s letter is strong in argument, but somewhat vehement and insufficiently measured in its wording.

The legate was therefore offended by it. He replied by maintaining his refusal and attempting to show that it was justified by the disobedience of the clergy of Sens, from which the new archbishop had been taken. This is how he characterized that Church’s opposition to recognizing the primacy of the Church of Lyons.

As for the reconciliation of the lords of Puiset, which the bishop of Chartres treated as a kind of crime on Hugh’s part, the legate replied that it was pure slander and supplied proof of this. He ended his reply by asking God Himself to soften the agitation that Ivo had displayed against him without having deserved it.

Ivo’s letter clearly presupposes another letter from the legate in reply to the fifty-ninth letter of the same bishop. In that letter, which appears nowhere, Hugh clearly stated his refusal to grant permission for Daimbert’s consecration, suspended Ivo, and accused him of having received the investiture of the archbishopric from the king’s hand. This is not, moreover, the only letter of our archbishop to Ivo that has been lost. We possess eight letters addressed to him by that bishop, but only two of those written by the other in reply have survived.

There follows in Baluze’s collection, which serves us here as our guide, another letter from Hugh to Daïmbert himself, then ordained and exercising the functions of archbishop of Sens. Dom Martène, believing that it had not yet been printed when he found it in a manuscript of Saint-Victor in Paris, published it anew. The author, after expressing to Daïmbert his just astonishment that he had still received no reply to several other letters concerning the accusations brought against him by the abbots of his diocese, politely—but nevertheless making him feel the authority with which he was invested—orders him to attend the council he had announced at Troyes after the octave of Pentecost. The editors of the letter disagree about the date of this council. One maintains that it was held in 1104, while the other argues that it was not until the following year. If a council was in fact held at Troyes in either of those two years, it is certain that neither of them is meant here. The reason is conclusive: Hugh was still legate of the Holy See when he summoned this council, as is evident both from the power he possessed to convene it outside his province and from the title he assumes in the heading of his letter. But he ceased exercising those functions as early as August 1099, when Paschal II was raised to the supreme pontificate, as we have seen in his history. Nor can this council be understood as the one mentioned by Manassas I, archbishop of Reims, in his apology to our legate, since he had not yet attained the archbishopric of Lyon, nor Daïmbert that of Sens. We must therefore conclude that it was a council held—or at least announced—at Troyes in the penultimate or final year of Urban II’s pontificate, and otherwise unknown to us.

Baluze published in the same collection two deeds of donation: one from the year 1094 and the other from 1106, by which our archbishop transferred to the abbey of Cluny two or three churches named therein. These documents are not otherwise interesting, except insofar as they reveal the piety of the benefactor. This appears especially in the first, one of whose conditions is that the monks of the abbey should pray for the remission of the archbishop’s sins, for the welfare of the Church of Lyon, and for the salvation of all his canons and their parents. From the same document we learn two details that should not be omitted: first, that Hugh then had a nephew of the same name among the canons of his church; second, that it was a monk of Saint-Bénigne of Dijon, also named Hugh, who wrote the document in the chancellor’s absence, although this took place at Lyon.

Let us return to the subsequent letters of our archbishop and legate. Four of considerable length and great importance are found in the General Collection of Councils (vol. X, pp. 364–365). The first, in which the author describes himself as the very unworthy servant and priest of the church of Die, is addressed to Pope Gregory VII, to whom he reports everything that had taken place at the council of Autun, held in September 1077. It was not, however, written until the beginning of January of the following year. This is clear from the fact that Hugh mentions the council of Clermont, which preceded that of Autun by approximately a month, as having been held in the preceding year. Hugh postponed giving this account to the pope because he had entrusted a cleric from Paris, who enjoyed the pontiff’s confidence, with informing him orally when he should be in his presence; he was to go there shortly after the council, which he had attended, had ended. But the cleric had returned, and Hugh, receiving no news either from him or from the pope, decided to write the letter in question. It reveals the unappealing character of several French bishops who were accused, or even convicted, of various vices at the council of Autun. It is in the same letter that the legate Hugh gives Manassas II, later archbishop of Reims, and Saint Bruno those glorious testimonies that we have collected in their histories. At the end, the author announces to the pope the council he was to hold at Poitiers on 15 January. This is further evidence for the date we assign to the letter.

The council was held at the appointed time, and what took place there is the subject of the second letter in the collection containing the four that we are undertaking to discuss. Hugh, abbot of Flavigny, who took care to inform us of what he knew about the history of our legate, thought it appropriate to include this same letter in his chronicle. It fits perfectly there, since it is entirely historical. It gives a sad account of the opposition that the legate and those attached to him had to endure at this council, which was full of turmoil and violence, and where some came close to losing their lives. The archbishop of Tours and the bishop of Rennes, who were partly responsible, are portrayed in a manner that does them no credit. Hugh ends his letter by complaining that the guilty men whom he condemned in France ran to Rome, where, instead of being treated more harshly, as they deserved, they were shown mercy and consequently became still more insolent.

The third letter of our archbishop and legate among the four under discussion is also embedded in the chronicle of Hugh of Flavigny. It is addressed to Matilda, countess of Tuscany, the most zealous protector of the popes in that period, and was written in 1087, when Desiderius, abbot of Monte Cassino, elected pope as early as 1085, finally accepted that supreme dignity after resisting it for nearly two years. Until then Archbishop Hugh had hoped to be raised to it himself. But stung by seeing his expectations frustrated, he wrote this letter to oppose Desiderius’s ordination and to set out the alleged reasons that he believed he had for opposing it, although by his own admission he had consented to his election. These reasons, moreover, are almost all slanders with which he burdens the new pope, and some of them also fall upon Cardinal Odo, who himself became pope shortly afterward under the name Urban II. To be convinced of this, it is enough to know that almost everything the author asserts here is contradicted by the public history of the period. Thus, for the honor of the archbishop and legate, one could wish that his letter had been buried in eternal oblivion. Yet no man, however great, is without his weakness.

Finally, the fourth letter in the collection, which had already been published by Dom d’Achery, is also addressed to Countess Matilda and was written in 1088, immediately after the election of Urban II. The author begins it with a very fine eulogy of the princess, and speaks of Pope Gregory VII and Anselm, bishop of Lucca, who had died two years earlier, as two saints enjoying eternal glory. Hugh’s principal purpose, however, is to clear himself of the report that he had gone into schism with the Roman Church. He therefore protests that he had never separated himself from its communion and was very far from intending to do so in the future. He complains somewhat bitterly about Saint Hugh, abbot of Cluny, and the brothers of the monastery, because they were among those who regarded him as a schismatic and consequently insulted him. The irritation this caused led him, in the presence of the countess, to make something like a charge against the holy abbot: namely, that on Good Friday he had recited in the office the prayer for the emperor Henry IV, although the emperor had been excommunicated several times. The bearer of this letter was entrusted with several others that the archbishop was writing to Rome, and Hugh commends them to Matilda. This letter appears to have been the prelude to its author’s reconciliation with the Holy See.

Besides all these letters of the legate Hugh, two others belonging to him are found among the letters of Saint Anselm of Canterbury. They are the sixty-fourth and the one hundred twenty-fourth of the third book, where their order has been reversed. The second was actually written before the one that now stands first, and is out of place for another reason as well. It was assigned its present position because it was assumed to be the reply to the one hundred sixty-third letter, which immediately precedes it; in fact, it is the reply to the twenty-fourth letter of the same book, in which Saint Anselm consults his friend the archbishop about the perplexity that troubled him—namely, whether, in view of the reasons he sets out, he should resign the episcopate into which he had recently entered or remain in it. One need only read these two letters of Saint Anselm to be convinced of what we establish here.

Hugh persuades his friend to answer in the affirmative—that is, to retain his archbishopric—and offers him compelling reasons. Yet, in giving him this advice, he adds that he is acting against his own inclination, because by doing so he will be deprived of seeing the man who, after God, is his dearest consolation. This detail seems to imply that the two archbishops had already seen one another and knew each other in a way other than through letters. The letters they wrote to each other breathe a pious and tender union. In them they mutually give each other the title of holiness, which, as one can see, had not yet been reserved solely for the supreme pontiff.

Hugh’s other letter to Saint Anselm was written to inform him of his return from Palestine, where he had gone to visit the holy places, as was said above. It was therefore written during the course of 1103, before the longer stay Saint Anselm came to make at Lyon at the end of that same year, when he spent more than a full year there. In this letter our archbishop urges him, with extraordinary affection, to return and live in the archiepiscopal residence, which belonged entirely to him. This letter too is out of place. Saint Anselm replies to it in the eighteenth letter of his fourth book, where Hugh’s letter ought to have been placed immediately before the reply and thus made the seventeenth of that same book.

Of all the letters of our archbishop and legate to Saint Anselm, only the two just discussed are known to remain. We nevertheless have five from Saint Anselm to Hugh, without counting those that may have been lost, like Hugh’s letters, of which it is evident that at least three have suffered that fate.

The *Origins of the Order of Cîteaux*, printed by Father Labbe in 1657, provide us with three further letters from the archbishop of Lyon, who, taking an interest in the first foundation of this great order, wrote them on behalf of those who undertook it. From that editor’s collection these letters passed to the beginning of the library of Cîteaux, where the *Origins*, published as early as 1657, were reprinted in 1660 under the title *Exordium of the Abbey of Cîteaux*. The first of the three letters is also repeated in what is called the *Great Exordium of the Order of Cîteaux*, printed after the preceding work, and in the new *Gallia Christiana*, with a lacuna that is easy to fill. This letter is properly a permission granted to Saint Robert, abbot of Molesme, and to six of his monks, who are named in it, to leave that monastery, where, for several reasons they stated, they could not observe exactly the Rule of Saint Benedict, which they had embraced and hoped to follow elsewhere with greater perfection. They went expressly to Lyon to ask the legate for this permission, which he willingly granted both to them and to all who might be inspired to imitate them. This is expressly stated in the document he granted them; relying on it, they withdrew, twenty-one in number, to the desert of Cîteaux on 21 March 1098. This shows that the legate’s letters shortly preceded that date.

The second letter in the collection is addressed to Robert, bishop of Langres, in whose diocese the abbey of Molesme was situated, and was written during the first months of the following year. The author there details what had been settled at the assembly he had just held at Pierre-Encise with several bishops and abbots concerning the return of Abbot Robert to Molesme, where the pope, yielding to the importunities of the monks of that place, wished him to return. The letter is valuable for this point of history, which is nowhere else found in such detail. It further shows that the measures adopted for Robert’s departure from Cîteaux and return to Molesme were so prudent that none of the interested parties could lose any of their rights. A breviary is mentioned, the use of which began at that time, as we have observed elsewhere.

The third letter that follows in the indicated collections is written to Pope Paschal II. It was delivered to him, together with letters from the legates John and Benedict and from Walter, bishop of Châlons-sur-Saône, in whose diocese Cîteaux was then situated, by John and Ilbold, monks of that newly founded monastery. The purpose of all these letters was to induce the pontiff to extend his protection to the same monastery, whose abbot Alberic had just been elected. After his election, Alberic believed that he ought to undertake this démarche with the Holy See, and he had instructed his envoys to pass through Lyon and obtain the archbishop’s recommendation. On the strength of his letter and the other two, Paschal granted a bull in favor of the new monastery. In it, when speaking of our archbishop, he implies that Hugh was no longer his legate, as has been stated in his history. Hugh wrote this letter shortly before going to Rome himself, passing through there on his way to Palestine. What he says about the jealousy already conceived by other monks living near Cîteaux, when they saw the poor and penitential life of its first inhabitants, shows that this evil—which later had unfortunate consequences—had already begun at that time.

In the same volume of Father Labbe in which the three preceding letters were first printed, there is another by the same author, embedded in the chronicle of Hugh, abbot of Flavigny. It was written in 1097 and addressed to Haganon, bishop of Autun, on behalf of that abbot, whose memory it greatly honors. Having confirmed Hugh’s election in his capacity as legate, our archbishop sent him with this letter to Haganon, the diocesan bishop, to receive the abbatial blessing.

The author of the history of the abbey of Saint-Hubert in the Ardennes, who took care to incorporate into his work several original documents from the periods he had occasion to discuss, has given us another letter from our archbishop and legate. It is interesting and addressed to Pope Urban II, to inform him of what had taken place in the appointment and deposition of Robert, abbot of Saint-Remi of Reims, one of the historians of the First Crusade. The account is very fully detailed, and nothing is better suited to acquaint us with this event, which caused some stir at the time. The author of the letter, who describes himself in it as servant of the church of Lyon, as he does in almost all the other letters he wrote after his translation to that primatial see, says that he refused to consent to the election of another abbot in Robert’s place solely because Robert had appealed to the Holy See. Nevertheless, Archbishop Manassas II had asked him by letter to consent, and Hilgode, bishop of Soissons, Ponce, a canon of the cathedral of Reims, and Raoul, its provost, had come to ask him for the same favor. This letter was written in 1097, as appears from a rescript of Pope Urban, partly quoted in the archives of the abbey of Saint-Remi.

Another letter also belonging to Archbishop Hugh, which Jean-Baptiste Souchet took care to publish in his observations on the letters of Ivo of Chartres after extracting it from manuscripts. Hugh addresses it to that bishop, who at the death of Richer, his archbishop, was then governing the diocese of Sens. He orders him to enforce the interdict pronounced against Ursion, the king’s steward, and his accomplices, [Col. 0507] because Ursion had seized and imprisoned a man from the diocese of Évreux who was traveling on pilgrimage to Sainte-Marie-Madeleine of Vézelay and to Saint-Gilles in Languedoc. The letter is from the year 1096, as the date of Archbishop Richer’s death shows. From that time, at least, it was publicly believed that the relics of Saint Madeleine were at the abbey of Vézelay, which does not support the claim of the Provençals.

There is yet another letter by our archbishop, printed in various collections indicated in the margin. This one is circular, being addressed to all archbishops, bishops, abbots, and other faithful, to notify them of the sentence of absolution pronounced by the archbishop and legate, assisted by Aldebert of Bourges, Hoël of Le Mans, and several abbots, at the abbey of Saint-Florent of Saumur on the feast of Saint John the Baptist in 1094, in favor of Fulk Rechin, count of Anjou, who had long been excommunicated for the reasons detailed in the letter.

[Col. 0507]

# Letters and Privileges of Hugh, Archbishop of Lyon

## I. Letter of Hugh, bishop of Die, to Raoul, archbishop of Tours, concerning his legation. (Year 1075.)

[Baluze, *Miscellanea*, edited by Mansi, III, 53.]

[Col. 0507A]

To Raoul, venerable archbishop of the people of Tours, Hugh, apocrisiarius of the Holy Roman Church: the blessedness of eternal life.

Now you will show how highly your generosity esteems your mother, the holy Roman Church; whether you cleave to the apostolic lord from the heart; and with what love you embrace him. On his behalf I have certain matters to give and communicate to you, for which it is necessary that you come to me. Although I am the least of his faithful, he has nevertheless entrusted me, as his son and as a son of the Holy Roman Church, with his responsibilities in conducting ecclesiastical affairs. For this reason, with God’s help, your prudence must labor vigilantly and our modest knowledge must strive with the greatest diligence before I depart from you. I therefore admonish, entreat, and, by the authority entrusted to me, advise you not to delay speaking with me as soon as you can. Farewell.

## II. Another letter to the same, inviting him to the council of Dijon. (Year 1076.)

[The same source.]

Hugh, by the grace of God bishop of Die and legate of the Holy Apostolic See, to the archbishop of Tours: greetings.

We believe, dearest brother, that you are not at all unaware how many dangers the holy Church suffers among the Lord’s sheep, as iniquity increases, the charity of many grows cold, the number of those opposing the holy faith multiplies daily, and the pastoral order is found insufficiently attentive to the charge it has undertaken. But if the authority of the holy Fathers has labored with every effort so that the dignity of the Christian religion might always increase, we must keep the utmost watch lest, through our negligence, what their diligence increased should perish. We therefore notify your fraternity that we have held a council in the diocese of Lyon, at Anse, and, with God’s help, provided for certain ecclesiastical necessities. Because several matters arose that were very necessary for restoring the condition of the holy Church, we have resolved, with the counsel of the brothers sitting with us, to hold another council on 2 January at the fortress of Dijon in Burgundy. We order you to come to it and, on our behalf, invite your suffragans. Farewell.

## III. Another letter to the same, inviting him to the council of Auvergne. (Year 1077.)

[The same source.]

[Col. 0508B]

Hugh, by God’s favor bishop of Die and legate of the Roman Church, to Raoul, archbishop of Tours: greetings.

The harvest is indeed plentiful, but the laborers are few. Therefore we have even more cause for lamentation, we who seem to thresh on the Lord’s threshing floor. Since we see the Lord’s Church being torn apart on every side, we have summoned a synodal council at the city of Auvergne on 7 August. We have invited your fellow provincials and as many religious men from other regions as we could. We also call upon you, as a most faithful companion on the way of God and his helper, with affection and, by the authority granted to us, command you to come and to invite all your suffragans to come, without any excuse whatever. Farewell.

## IV. Another letter to the same, inviting him to the council of Autun. (Year 1077.)

[The same source.]

Hugh, by the grace of God bishop of Die and legate of the holy [Col. 0509A] Roman Church, to Raoul, archbishop of Tours: greetings.

I offer you countless thanks because you have always proved obedient and have not refused, according to your ability and knowledge, to assist the holy Church in her need. We therefore summon you, by apostolic authority, as someone greatly necessary to us—and also because of your own need—and through you your suffragan bishops, as well as your more useful clerics and abbots, and command you to come to the synod to be held in the city of Autun on 10 September.

## V. Deed of Hugh, archbishop of Lyon, concerning the church of Sainte-Foy of Castellet, given to the monastery of Conques.

[The same source.]

[Col. 0509B]

In the name of the holy and undivided Trinity. Let it be known to all the sons of the holy Church of God, present and future, that I, Hugh, by the grace of God archbishop of Lyon, give to God and to Saint Faith of Conques, and to Abbot Begon and his successors and to the brothers of that monastery, the church of Sainte-Foy of Castellet and the church of Saint Victor with their dependencies. The river Loire divides the aforesaid church. The gift is made subject to an annual rent of eight solidi, half of which shall be paid on the feast of Saint Martin and half on the Purification of Saint Mary, while synod dues and customary payments are retained according to the usage of the other churches, together with the obedience to be rendered both to us and to our successors and to our archpriests.

This donation was made at Lyon, in our episcopal residence, [Col. 0509C] with the counsel of our canons, Bladin the dean, Arbert the archdeacon, and Verin our chaplain. To ensure that this donation should remain firm, we have signed it below with our own seal and have delivered it to be confirmed by witnesses.

Sign of Bladin.  
Sign of Arbert.  
Sign of Verin Calvus.  
Sign of Verin, our chaplain.  
Sign of Rostagnus Ferlot.  
Sign of Fulcher.  
Sign of Verald.  
Sign of Ponce.

I, Hugh, wrote and subscribed this in the place of the chancellor.

## VI. To Gregory VII, Roman pontiff—Concerning the council of Autun. (Year 1077.)

[Mansi, *Councils*, vol. XX.]

See under Gregory VII, *Patrologia*, vol. CXLVIII.

## VII. To the same—Concerning the council of Poitiers. (Year 1078.)

[Mansi, *Councils*, vol. XX.]

[Col. 0509D]

To the lord Pope Gregory, blessed in merit, Hugh, humble priest of Die: greetings in the Lord God.

At the council which, by God’s grace, we held at Poitiers with some fruitful result, we encountered many dangers on the journey and many adversities in the city itself, both within the council and outside it. For behold, the king of the Franks, contrary to himself because he was contrary to the King of Heaven, first sent me a letter in which he confessed himself to the Lord, ardently desiring to be called my son, and with every glory and honor rendered the authority of our legation commendable. [Col. 0510A] Then he sent letters to the count and also to the bishops under his jurisdiction, adjuring them by every appeal and making them liable to the charge of offending his majesty and fidelity. Specifically, he warned the count that, if he allowed us anywhere within his power to hold gatherings and quasi-councils—for that is how he described them—he would be liable. He warned the bishops that they would be liable if they attended or supported our decrees, by which we sought to obscure the splendor of his crown and that of the princes of his kingdom.

Thus, emboldened by this adversity to insult us, the enemies of truth nearly dragged to the left those whom I had regarded and seen on the right, and I found that there was no one who recognized me. For behold, the archbishop of Tours, a plague and disgrace to the holy Church, and with him the bishop of Rennes, most arrogantly perverse, occupied almost the entire council. The bishop of Rennes was proved guilty because, without first having been ordained a cleric, he had been ordained a bishop. Beforehand, and afterward as well, the bishop of Angers had promised and given him the pallium, though the bishop of Rennes was unaware of it. Before his ordination, however, he confessed another matter: while still a knight, he had thrown an enemy knight from his horse, and a fellow knight of this bishop of Rennes stabbed the fallen man, who died from that unhorsing and wound. We, therefore, yielding to the prayers of many, left him—not yet deposed but suspended in the meantime, because he was useful to his Church—to be presented to and judged by your mercy.

The archbishop of Tours, on the other hand, was proved to have purchased the deanery before his episcopate, although according to the custom of his Church no one could hold it unless he was already a priest or was destined to become one. This archbishop of Tours, therefore, having been in no way canonically elected, could not obtain from the king the gift of the bishopric until his own nephew had acquired the aforesaid deanery by money. He was also accused of simony on another count, because he had promised a forest to a certain knight if the knight would help him obtain the bishopric. When the knight afterward reproached him for this, the bishop of Angers was present and gave us clear testimony to the fact in a loud voice.

It would take too long, Father, to enumerate the disturbances and conflicts that this archbishop of Tours brought upon us, their number and manner and place: at one time arguing for the bishop of Rennes without ever reasoning but always chattering; at another protesting on his own behalf, with all the loquacity [Col. 0510D] and shameless audacity of his clerics. For when they had almost bent the archbishop of Lyon to their defense, so that he either prayed for them or spoke against us, their servants broke down the church doors and entered armed with axes. In such great tumult they disrupted the council that they would have put Brother T. to death if the Lord had not crowned him with the shield of his good will.

Thus, leaving us in small numbers and disgraced, the archbishop of Tours and his suffragans withdrew in proud tumult, disorderly and uncanonically. The following day, when a council had been opened in the church of Saint Hilary, without any promised or preliminary satisfaction for the injury, that dragon again rose up like a roaring lion and could no longer be heard. But drawing the sword of the Spirit, which is the word of God, [Col. 0511A] we struck down his pride and, after issuing the decree in this matter, suspended him even from priestly office. Since he appealed to the Apostolic See, asserting that he would clear himself there of simony, we sent him to the Apostolic See and left him to be deposed by your judgment.

The abbot of the church of Bergues in Flanders was proved to be simoniacal and was deposed. The archbishop of Besançon did not appear before either the council of Autun or that of Poitiers, nor did he send a canonical excuse. We referred to your judgment the bishop of Beauvais, accused of simony and of having sold prebends after the decree had been issued. We did the same with the bishop of Noyon on account of his case. Likewise with the bishop of Amiens, the usurper, together with those who ordained him: the bishops of Laon, Soissons, and Senlis. We are also keeping silent about certain evils within our own body, because, with God’s help, when we come to you shortly we shall more conveniently tell you privately the names of those by whom they were inflicted.

As for the causes of the count of Angers, we heard them from his own mouth, as you ordered, and judged them almost reasonable. But, not daring to decide upon his absolution, we commit the determination of this matter to your holiness’s wisdom. If we have written anything inadequately to your holiness, your son Teuzo, our most faithful fellow worker in the Lord, will give you a fuller account of what we decided concerning the bishop of Thérouanne together with the bishop of Poitiers.

Therefore let your holiness take care that we are not longer reproached so shamefully because simoniacs and all kinds of criminals whom we have suspended, deposed, or even condemned willingly run to Rome, where, instead of experiencing greater rigor of justice, they carry away what amounts to mercy at their pleasure. Those who previously did not dare to sin even in small matters afterward practice the most skillful commerce with tyranny in the churches entrusted to them.

Pray, most holy pope, for me, the unworthy servant of your holiness.

## VIII. To Matilda, countess—Concerning the election, promotion, and consecration of Desiderius, abbot of Monte Cassino, as Roman pontiff under the name Victor III. (Year 1087.)

[Mansi, *Councils*, vol. XX.]

Hugh, servant of the holy Church of Lyon, to his most beloved sister in Christ, M., an overflowing grace of divine consolation.

How many and how great letters of the holy Roman Church, of blessed Anselm, whose memory we reverence, and of you—both your legations and your letters—compelled me to come to Rome, and how long I remained in the regions of Italy contrary to the purpose of my office, your prudence does not need to be told. You heard sufficiently, however, that the election of the abbot of Monte Cassino had been held before I came to Rome. Both I and my other brothers, sons of the holy Roman Church, gave our assent to it according to the weakness of the times, preferring human glory to God’s.

After we had stayed for some time in Rome, we reached Monte Cassino, where he himself had already gone. Under his guidance, and through conversations with his intimates, we necessarily discovered much more fully how intolerably we had offended God in his election—especially when he did not blush to recount boastfully in the ears of the bishops and cardinals his most wicked acts.

For who, unless he had heard it from his own mouth, would ever have believed that he had given his faith to the king called Henry, promising faithfully to assist him in obtaining the crown of the Roman Empire? Or whose accusation against such a man would have been accepted unless he himself, as though adding it to the height of his glory, had told us that the aforesaid king had never crossed into Rome to invade the lands of blessed Peter except at his counsel and persuasion?

Would anyone not seem delirious if he claimed that a Roman elect, after receiving absolution from the most blessed Pope Gregory, had been excommunicated—unless he himself had dared to proclaim in our common assembly that Cardinal Atto of Milan, elected by the aforesaid pope, had been publicly excommunicated while that same abbot subscribed to the act, and had died without penance? He even dared to call Atto blessed, and prayed that he himself might have a future glory nowhere other than in the glory in which Atto was.

In all these matters we call as witnesses our most beloved brothers, Cardinals H. and B., whom we suppose to be with you. They either heard these things themselves from his mouth or said that they had heard them from reliable men whom they unquestionably trusted.

How often he openly rejected by word the decrees of his lord, Pope Gregory, and of other holy Fathers, and afterward destroyed them by manifest deeds; in how many places and on what occasions he publicly repudiated his own election, declaring that it had been made tumultuously and not according to God, and asserting under terrible oath that he had never consented to it and would never consent to it; and which persons he said were suitable to be elected Roman pontiff when he returned the election to the Church—including one whom he named to you, namely Her. of Metz—since these matters are largely known to you and would exceed the proper limits of a letter, we omit writing them out in order.

Now, when at last, after so much labor uselessly expended, we seemed to be able to breathe again, we hoped shortly, supported by divine grace and by your counsel and assistance, to proceed freely with an election so often rejected and returned to the Church. On the pretext of electing R. as pontiff, the apostolic vicar of those regions therefore convened a council at Capua.

I, the abbot of Marseille, and the archbishop of Aix were staying at Salerno when we were invited by the bishop of Ostia, the prince of Salerno, and Concianus R., on behalf of the vicar and the Roman Church, to come and elect R. as pontiff by common counsel. We obeyed by going. The duke, too, youthful and deceived by certain stratagems of Prince Jordan, came there.

When we were preparing to discuss the matter at hand, the abbot began, through certain soft and theatrical refusals, to provoke his supporters—the bishops and the prince—to compel him. Once his trickery had been discovered, and when the aforesaid men were compelling him, as though against his will, to accept restoration, we, together with the bishop of Ostia, the monk Witmund, and certain others, took counsel about how we should oppose his craftiness.

When he was already prepared to resume the insignia of the pontificate and to turn upon himself once again an election that had been repeatedly rejected even in that assembly, we, following the counsel of those mentioned above and rejecting the man’s great fickleness and the mutability of his purpose, declared in the hearing of all that we would by no means give our assent unless, first, a canonical investigation were held into certain matters concerning his reputation and the dignity of so great an order that had come to our knowledge after his election.

Taking this badly, he publicly declared that he would neither submit to an investigation nor ever accept the election. Thus, after he had once again given us permission to elect whomever we wished, he shook his arms and began to withdraw from us. Then Witmund, on the advice of the bishop of Ostia, publicly exclaimed that an infamous person ought not to be elected or ordained Roman pontiff, since it was certainly established that he had incurred infamy by having endured the excommunication of Lord Pope Gregory for a full and continuous year, and even longer, without canonical penance.

The assembly was therefore dissolved. Since night was approaching, we departed, while the duke remained with him, retaining the bishop of Ostia along with the other Roman bishops and cardinals.

There the duke persisted for a long time in asking him to consecrate a certain Alfanus as bishop of Salerno. But because the bishop of Ostia objected, the abbot did not dare to fulfill the duke’s wish, since Alfanus had been convicted of the most obvious ambition. The duke, greatly angered, withdrew from them.

The abbot, therefore, deprived of the duke’s favor—for he despaired of aspiring to the Roman pontificate without him—sent a delegation to the duke deep in the night, while everyone was asleep. When the duke returned to the abbot, the abbot obtained the duke’s favor in order to become pope, and the duke obtained from the abbot what he sought: that Alfanus should be consecrated the following day, namely Palm Sunday. On the abbot’s command, they all replied that they would do this.

On that same day, after dinner, when the abbot, the duke, and the prince had risen from their midday sleep, and while the sun was declining toward the lower regions but wine was prevailing over the upper ones—alas, what grief!—the abbot, as the reward for that most wicked consecration, supported by the duke’s authority, put the pontifical mantle upon himself, without consulting the bishop of Ostia or us, who were entirely unaware of it.

When these things had occurred, the bishop of Ostia, who had in every respect acted well with us, saw that the abbot intended to go to Rome to be consecrated by the power of Prince Jordan. Perhaps fearing that he would be deprived of his dignity if another laid the first hand of consecration upon him, he turned on the day of battle. Forgetful of his purpose and of the pledge he had made to us—something shameful to relate—he made peace with the abbot and paid him every honor as though he were pope.

As for how and by what means he intends to go to Rome, the bearer of this letter and the pilgrims will be able to report to you more fully whatever they saw being arranged after they left us and passed through Capua, or learned from the reports of others.

After he had therefore been consecrated by the bishop of Ostia, while celebrating Masses at Saint Peter’s, he was struck down during the liturgy by the judgment of God. Although he recognized, belatedly, that he had gone astray, he deposed himself. Then he summoned the brothers from Monte Cassino who were with him and ordered them to carry him there, and to bury him in the chapter house not as pope but as abbot.

### IX. To the same. — On the same matters. (1088)

[MANSI, cited above.]

To Mathilda, most beloved sister in Christ and only daughter of blessed Peter, Hugh, servant of the holy Church of Lyon: greetings in sincere charity.

Although we know, venerable lady, that you understand and eagerly seek only what pertains to the honor of God and the apostolic see, we nevertheless cannot refrain from admonishing your piety about this, so that we may join the efforts of our humble station to your holy desires.

We know how, in a manly heart, you have conceived a flame of charity burning beyond the measure of women, and have become an example to all princes. When they learn that you, who abounded in temporal power and wealth, have spent everything for the name of the Lord and overcome the fury of the world and the power of darkness with the armor of faith, they will likewise be ashamed not to do so and will not hesitate to do so with ready devotion.

But amid these things, most beloved lady, you must often bring to mind that you should strive in every way to persevere to the end and complete your glorious beginnings with a more fortunate conclusion. For, as we recognize your prudence as taught by the Spirit, there is then certain confidence of salvation and rewards when perseverance in the holy purpose is extended to the end.

You have in this matter most faithful helpers and kindly advocates of your devotion before the Lord: namely, our most merciful Father, Pope of holy memory, and blessed A. [lacuna], bishop of Lucca. Just as, while they were still living, they instructed you in every form of piety and justice, so now, from that bosom of eternal rest into which we trust they have been received, they will commend the works of your charity by their merits and prayers, and inspire in the depths of your devotion the love of everlasting life with which they are ineffably filled.

Supported, therefore, by their patronage, devote yourselves with all your strength to advising the Roman Church, taking the greatest care that you consent to the election there of such a person in whom there may be both an end to so many labors and the salvation of souls, the confusion of enemies, and the restoration of apostolic dignity.

Although we have disagreed with certain bishops and cardinal priests of the holy Roman Church concerning the restoration of the election of the lord abbot of Monte Cassino, and although we openly gave some of them our reasons at Capua for why the matter appeared differently to us, we nevertheless want you to know that we have neither withdrawn from their unity, by which divine favor has joined us in the body of the holy Church to serve blessed Peter, nor will we ever withdraw from it, God having mercy. Rather, we are resolved in every way to serve the advancement of the apostolic see.

Furthermore, we inform your unanimity that the Cluniac monks have inflicted upon us such great transgressions and injuries that we are in no way able to bear them with equanimity.

Last year, before we set out for Rome, we had learned that the abbot had publicly celebrated on Good Friday the prayer that he had been accustomed to make for the emperor—a prayer that has now been interrupted because of the excommunication and deposition of Henry imposed by Lord Pope Gregory. When we called the same abbot to account for this, weakened by his conscience, he replied that he had said that prayer for any emperor.
