When, from the circumstances of the prayer, we pressed him that it referred specifically to the Roman Empire, since by the judgment of the apostolic see that office was then vacant, he fell silent, overcome by the truth; nevertheless, he did not amend his acknowledged error by the penance that was due.

After our return, when we attempted to resist the unrestrained invasion of his monks, he produced certain letters that he said had been sent to him by Pope Urban. They stated that he and his holy brothers should take care to abstain from communion with us and with Richard of Marseille. He used the alleged letters as a pretext for retaining our injuries.

Those letters, composed contrary to apostolic moderation and gravity, contained manifest falsehoods. They asserted that a full year had elapsed from the time of the election held concerning the abbot of Cassino until the council held at Capua, although it is true that in that interval a full year had not at all elapsed.

Among other things, they impudently lied in one respect: they claimed that we had voluntarily separated ourselves from communion with the Roman Church, whereas our conscience and the charity by which we are joined in the Lord bear witness that we not only did not avoid their communion but resisted everyone who urged us to do so.

After we had taken the advice of our confrères and fellow bishops, and a conference between the abbot and us had been arranged through their mediation, he understood that we would not reach agreement with him unless, once his fault had been recognized, he restored the aforesaid prayer. He refused to submit to judgment with us, using many pretexts. Nevertheless, through the efforts of the bishops who were present, our disagreement was somewhat moderated and, by means of a postponement, softened until the appointed time.

We have shared with your charity these matters concerning us, asking in return that, if anything concerning the service of our humility should please you, you assign it to us without hesitation, since we desire this most earnestly.

If, however, the bearers of this letter lack the opportunity or ability to go to Rome, we have the greatest confidence in your kindness and ask you to see that the letters we have entrusted to them for delivery to the bishops, sons of the holy Roman Church, and to the cardinal priests are sent promptly.

For the rest, we commend to your nobility our beloved brother Lord Rotger, cardinal subdeacon of the holy apostolic see, who says that he will soon come to Rome through you for the benefit of the holy Church. We ask you to assist him, for the grace of blessed Peter and for our sake, with safe conduct and in all other matters in which he may need the counsel of your kindness. Through him you will learn more fully about the matters concerning us.

### X. Letter of Hugh, archbishop of Lyon, to Hugh, archbishop of Besançon, on behalf of the monks of Saint-Bénigne of Dijon. (Around 1088)

[BALUZ. *Miscellanea*, ed. Luc. III, 56.]

[Col. 0516B]

Hugh, by the grace of God servant of the Church of Lyon, to his beloved brother in Christ Hugh, venerable archbishop of Besançon: greetings.

We inform your affection that the lord pope recently sent us a letter in which, among other matters, he commanded us to approach you and admonish you by his authority to restore to the abbot of Dijon the church of Saint Mary of Salins.

Concerning this complaint, as we remember, your predecessor was often summoned by us, together with the aforesaid abbot, to carry out justice, and at last was invited to the council of Meaux. Since he absented himself from that council without any canonical excuse, it was judged by the same council that the abbot should be invested there, or that the church should be deprived of divine worship until full justice had been done.

Therefore, bound by the aforesaid command, we admonish your affection by apostolic authority to invest the abbot with the aforesaid church, according to what was reasonably provided by the judgment of that council. From the sentence of the lord pope, which we append here in his very words, you will be able to understand how earnestly your prudence ought to attend to this. He writes to us as follows:

“Moreover, we command your vigor to approach the bishop of Besançon on our behalf and admonish him by our authority to restore the church of Saint Mary of Salins to the abbot of Dijon, and in addition the produce of the estates that they appropriated during the period of their retention.”

### XI. Letter of the same Hugh to Lambert, bishop of Arras, inviting him to the council of Autun. (1094)

[BALUZ., cited above.]

[Col. 0516D]

Hugh, archbishop of Lyon, legate of the apostolic see, to his venerable brother in Christ Lambert, bishop of Arras: greetings.

Your fraternal affection knows how, through frequent letters of Lord Pope Urban, I have been admonished and bound by obedience to convene a synod in Gaul, and how for a long time I refused to undertake that burden.

Since I neither wished nor ought to resist any longer, at last, with the counsel of the lord abbot of Cluny and of religious bishops and abbots, we designated that a council should be held at Autun on the Ides of October. By apostolic authority we invite your affection to it.

Although we believe that you are not unaware of what the lord pope has commanded us concerning our most beloved brother, the archbishop of Reims, or concerning the privilege that he received from the apostolic see, we have nevertheless sent you the pope’s own letter, in which, after some other matters, he admonished us concerning these things in the following words:

“While preserving the reverence due to the Church of Reims, in the privilege that we gave and established for our brother Rainald, archbishop, we determined that his case should be decided by no one other than the Roman pontiff, as the decrees of the canons have also established concerning the more important cases of the other bishops.

“This must be understood in such a way that no primate may presume to demand it as a special privilege of his own Church. When someone is subjected to the legate of the Roman pontiff, he is subjected to the one whose office is exercised through that legate.

“Therefore, through the diligence of your solicitude, summon the archbishop of Reims himself and the others who are ordinarily subject to your legation to the council, and labor fervently for the interests of the holy Church, putting aside all dissimulation.”

In accordance with these words of the lord pope, we invite your fraternity, together with your abbots, by apostolic authority to the council named above. We trust in your friendship, and we know that in so important a matter the counsel of a friend is useful and entirely necessary to us. We too, God willing, are ready to follow your counsels.

### XII. Hugh, archbishop of Lyon, to Robert, count of Flanders. — On behalf of the Supreme Pontiff, he asks him to receive and protect Lambert. (1094)

[*Spicilegium* V, § 2.]

Hugh, archbishop of Lyon, legate of the apostolic see, to Robert, count of the Flemings: greetings.

We commend to your excellence our venerable brother in Christ, the bishop of Arras. We ask you to protect him with your aid and assistance as a cardinal bishop, as one consecrated by the hands of blessed Peter. In the place of the lord pope, according to his command, we order you, for the remission of your sins, to do this.

Also extend to him the arm of your assistance for the restoration of the property of his Church, recognizing that through this obedience you will obtain apostolic favor and a reward from God.

### XIII. Charter of Hugh, archbishop of Lyon and legate of the apostolic see, concerning the absolution of Fulk, count of Anjou. (1094)

[*Gallia Christiana nova*, documents, vol. IV, p. 10.]

Hugh, archbishop of Lyon, legate of the apostolic see, to his most beloved brothers in Christ, the archbishops, bishops, abbots, and faithful of the holy Church of God: greetings.

We have judged it worthy to make known to all orthodox people how, at the command of our lord Pope Urban, we undertook the obedience of traveling to the borders of Anjou on the case of Fulk, count of Anjou, in order to absolve him from the bond of anathema with which he had long been bound because he had captured his brother Geoffrey in open warfare.

The count himself did not evade giving an account, making satisfaction, or submitting to judgment; indeed, he was always ready to do so. Yet, as we learned from the report of reputable clerics and laymen, his aforesaid brother, at the time when he was captured, had been excommunicated by Cardinal Stephen, legate of the Roman see, because of the many injuries he was inflicting upon the Church of Tours and the abbot of the monastery of Saint Martin the Great. The principality of the county of Anjou had also been granted to this Fulk by that same legate in the name of Saint Peter.

We learned from the truthful report of reputable noblemen that it had likewise been granted to him by his uncle Geoffrey.

Having therefore undertaken this legation, so that the force of apostolic obedience might be handled by us with greater authority, we associated with ourselves our venerable brother, the archbishop of Bourges, as a partner in this execution. Together we approached the count’s brother, whom we had heard was being held captive.

We found him so deranged, as everyone reported, that it seemed entirely useless and futile to entrust the government of his country to him—he who had become useless through his folly both to himself and to everyone else. Indeed, he was so far gone that he did not even wish to be rescued from captivity by our hands.

We therefore came to the monastery of Saint Florentius. On the feast of the Nativity of Saint John the Baptist, in the presence of religious men, bishops, and abbots who had come by invitation, we absolved Count Fulk by the unanimous vote and acclamation of all, since he was prepared either to make satisfaction or to give an account.

We accepted from him guarantees that, if his brother recovered soundness of mind, he would, at the command of our lord pope or of us, either make peace with him or be prepared to submit to judgment; and that he would not take a wife without our counsel, since he was blamed for having several.

We have judged it proper to disclose to you the sequence of what was done. The names of the religious men who were present are these:

Aldebert, archbishop of Bourges; Ouvellus, bishop of Le Mans; William, abbot of Saint Florentius; Bernard, abbot of Saints Sergius and Bacchus; Girard, abbot of Saint Albinus; Nuald, abbot of Saint Nicholas; Baldric, abbot of Bourgueil; and Geoffrey, abbot of Vendôme.

Done in the year from the Incarnation of the Lord 1094, at the abbey of Saint Florentius, on the feast of Saint John the Baptist.

### XIV. Hugh, archbishop of Lyon, gives the church of Saint Desiderius at Brescia to the Cluniacs. (1094)

[BALUZ. *Miscellanea*, ed. Luc. III, 59.]

In the name of the holy and undivided Trinity, Father, Son, and Holy Spirit.

Let all the sons of the holy Church of God, present and future, know that I, Hugh, by the grace of God archbishop of Lyon, give to God and to Saint Peter, and to our most reverend father in Christ, Lord Hugh, abbot of the Church of Cluny, and to his successors and to the brothers serving under their direction, the church of Saint Desiderius situated at Brescia, under an annual census of three solidi, with the *paratae* and synod dues retained according to the ancient custom of the other churches of our bishopric; and the chapel of Reortier, together with the church of Saint Paul situated within the fortification of that castle, with its appurtenances, under an annual census of five solidi, half of which shall be paid on the feast of Saint Martin and the other half on the Purification of Saint Mary.

Thus, without prejudice to the subjection owed to the holy Church of Lyon, I give these possessions to the Church of Cluny through the hand of our most beloved brother in Christ Seguine, the chamberlain of the aforesaid lord abbot, to be possessed in perpetuity, for the remedy of my soul, and so that the brothers of the Church of Cluny may pray to God for my transgressions, for the condition of the Church of Lyon, and also for the salvation of all our canons and relatives.

This donation was made at Lyon in the presence of Gerin, our chaplain; Hugh, our nephew; Godo, archpriest and canon; and Girard, archpriest. To ensure that this donation should remain firm, I confirmed it below with my own seal.

Done at Lyon in the year from the Incarnation of our Lord Jesus Christ 1094, indiction II, concurrent VI.

[Col. 0519C]

I, Hugh, monk of the Church of Dijon, wrote and subscribed this as vice-chancellor.

### XV. To Lambert, bishop of Arras. (1095)

[BALUZ., *Miscellanea*, ed. Luc. II, 139.]

Hugh, servant of the holy Church of Lyon, to his most reverend brother Lambert, bishop of Arras: greetings.

We take care to inform your affection that our sister in Christ Emma, who had lived enclosed among us for many days out of love for the name of Christ, departed from the present world to the heavenly realms, as we believe, on the ninth day before the Kalends of February.

But since the salvation or destruction of mortals is known to God alone, and no one is able to be justified before him by his own merit unless he is cleansed by divine mercy, we earnestly beseech your charity in advance that you assist her soul in your prayers and good works, so that you too may deserve to obtain the same reward from the same Creator and Redeemer, Jesus Christ.

She was a daughter of your Church, as she herself very often testified, and belonged to your fraternity. Farewell.

### XVI. To the same. (1095)

[Ibid.]

To the venerable brother Lambert, bishop of Arras, Hugh, servant of the Church of Lyon: greetings.

This brother, the bearer of this letter, has presented us with a complaint concerning our brother, the bishop of Amiens, and Fulk the archdeacon, our friend and familiar. He asks that we entrust his case to your fraternity.

We therefore charge your charity to approach the bishop of Amiens and the aforesaid archdeacon Fulk, and admonish them to render justice in your presence to the aforesaid brother concerning the matters of which he complains.

If they are unwilling to do so, ask our friend, the archbishop of Reims, on our behalf to compel them to carry out whatever is just for the brother in question.

### XVII. To Ivo, bishop of Chartres. (1096)

[*Works of Ivo*, note to Letter 153, p. 235.]

[Col. 0520B]

H., bishop of Lyon and legate of the apostolic see, to his reverend brother Ivo, bishop of Chartres: greetings.

Let your fraternity know that the complaint of our brother Gis., bishop of Évreux, has recently reached our ears concerning Urso, the king’s steward. During the days of Holy Lent, Urso seized one of the bishop’s parishioners, named Rotger, who was traveling for the sake of prayer to Saint Mary Magdalene of Vézelay and to Saint Giles.

You should know that not only during Lent but at every time, those who go on pilgrimage and travel for God ought to be safe from the attack of all enemies. Those who disturb them, as people who do not keep the fear of God before their eyes, ought to be punished with the severity of ecclesiastical discipline.

We have therefore placed under interdict all divine worship for Urso himself, for his entire household, and for all his accomplices in so great a sacrilege. By apostolic authority we command you—you whose parishioner he is said to be and who exercise the functions of the deceased archbishop of Sens—to enforce the same interdict.

Write to the clergy of Orléans, imposing upon them on our behalf and on yours that they likewise interdict divine worship for Vito (Latin *Vitoni*) and for his household and for his accomplices, until he allows the aforesaid Rotger to leave his captivity free, without any ransom, and restores to him what was taken away.

By the same apostolic authority we also interdict the celebration of divine worship wherever the captive is held, for as long as he remains there.

### XVIII. To the same. — A reply to Ivo’s Letter 60. (1097)

[BALUZ., *Miscellanea*, ed. Luc. III, 57.]

[Col. 0520D]

Hugh, bishop of the first see of Lyon, to his reverend brother Ivo, bishop of Chartres: greetings.

Among the other chapters whose accumulation you have used, as if by an indirect attack, in an attempt to stain our innocence—matters to which we shall respond in due time—we have decided for the present to answer your request concerning the final two.

We thought that we had not irrationally or contrary to the ancient rules of the Fathers forbidden both you and your suffragans to lay hands upon the elected man of Sens until he promised us obedience and due subjection and recognized the primacy of the Church of Lyon according to the apostolic sanctions of our lord Pope Urban and his predecessors.

We do not believe it has escaped your knowledge with what stubborn obstinacy—and obstinate contumacy—the clergy of Sens, from whose number that man is known to have been elected, have opposed and disobeyed the apostolic decrees and privileges concerning the primacy of Lyon. They compelled their deceased archbishop to persist in his disobedience until death.

Because of this disobedience, our lord Pope Urban suspended him from episcopal office and made you and your other suffragans promise obedience and subjection to us as your primate.

As Gregory testifies in the last book of the *Moralia*, disobedience is called the sin of divination, and refusal to obey is compared to the crime of idolatry. Obedience, however, possesses the merit of faith. Without it, anyone is proved an unbeliever, even if he appears to be faithful.

Accordingly, by this reasoning and authority of blessed Gregory, both the aforesaid man and the other clergy of Sens, by rejecting the primacy of the Church of Lyon and refusing so arrogantly and stubbornly to obey apostolic authority, and by compelling their bishop, as we have said, to persist in his disobedience until the end of his life—not merely by persuasion but also by violent pressure—are proved to be unbelievers and, as it were, idolaters, although they may appear faithful.

Let your discretion therefore consider whether an unbeliever or idolater can or ought canonically to be elected or consecrated bishop until he has repented of his unbelief or idolatry.

Consider also whether, if we are forbidden to prevent this by private laws and new traditions, as you say, we are attempting to remove the ancient traditions and customs concerning the consecration of a metropolitan—or whether in this matter you have accused us of straining out a gnat while swallowing a camel.

By the privilege of our legation we do not insist that the man in question, or any other elected person, be presented to us. Rather, according to apostolic tradition, we wish the election and the name of the elected person to be reported to us, so that, once we know it, we may approve it.

If, however, by the right of the primacy of the Church of Lyon, confirmed by its privileges and by the authority of our lord Pope Urban and his predecessors, we demand from the elected man of Sens the obedience and subjection owed to a primate before consecration, we do not understand this to mean that we are cutting away the traditions of the holy Fathers, or that we harm him if he makes the profession—as though by that profession he appeared to have purchased his consecration.

Episcopal dignity ought to be acquired through good merits and fruits arising from obedience, and in examining the person to be consecrated it is required that it be established before consecration whether he wishes to be obedient to the Roman Church.

Relying upon these reasons, we do not wish to alter what we commanded concerning him or concerning your fellow provincial bishops.

If you say that the lord pope has diminished or altered anything from the thoroughly proven tradition of the Fathers who preceded him, or has admitted some novelty; or if you wish to oppose, or decide that opposition must be offered to, his decree concerning the investiture of bishoprics or other ecclesiastical dignities—which kings formerly usurped through changes and still endeavor to usurp—you will see to it yourselves.

When you have seen or heard that this was promulgated so firmly not only now but also in the time of Pope Gregory of blessed memory, if you knew that anything needed to be added, removed, or temporarily suspended so that spiritual or temporal advantages might not be obstructed, you ought not to have concealed it as though lying in wait for an opportunity to rebuke us. Rather, like a good and prudent son, you ought to have suggested and communicated reverence for those men as for fathers.

We, however, seeing that this constitution is canonical and was made according to the ancient lawful customs of the holy Fathers, both wish to preserve it and command all over whom we exercise the office of legation to preserve it.

You said that we had restored the priests of Puisieux to communion without your knowledge and without the knowledge of your fellow bishops, although you and the Church of Chartres had deprived them of communion because of plunder committed against you and against the Church of Chartres.

Since you neither saw nor heard this, and since we did no such thing, you ought by no means to have made the accusation.

Nevertheless, returning good for evil and overlooking this insult or accusation, we sent a letter to the chaplains and clergy of Puisieux and prohibited divine worship from being celebrated there, except for the baptism of infants and the visitation of the sick.

Since you took our rebuke concerning the consecration of Sens more harshly than was just—as the outcome will prove by divine power—we beseech the mercy of almighty God to deign to temper the movement of your spirit against us, who are undeserving of it.

### XIX. To the archbishop of Sens, on behalf of the abbot of Saint-Pierre-le-Vif. (Before 1099)

[BALUZ., cited above.]

Hugh, servant of the Church of Lyon, legate of the apostolic see, to his venerable brother and fellow bishop Daimbert, metropolitan of Sens: greetings, and service to the Lord in fear.

On the complaints of certain abbots against you, we remember having written to you repeatedly; [Col. 0522D] but we are utterly astonished that we have made no progress with you and have received no reply whatsoever from your dignity. Certainly, if you were legate of the Roman Church, just as it would be salutary for you to obey us, so your magnificence ought, by virtue of our legation over you, to heed our humble authority. Behold, likewise, we report to you the complaints of our venerable brother, the abbot of Saint-Pierre-le-Vif. He complains that, under the pretext of a certain feeble priest who was demanding justice, you have caused one of his churches to cease divine worship; that burial was denied to a certain priest who, while he lived, had been marked by no fault and had made a good and prudent testament; and that even those who piously and dutifully buried him were forbidden communion with the Church. [Col. 0523A] We therefore command you, and earnestly admonish you as a brother, that, setting aside whatever justice you may claim, you preserve peace for the abbot and his churches, more beneficially absolve those whom you have excommunicated in this manner, and receive and render justice at the council which, with the Lord’s help, we shall celebrate at Troyes on the second day after the octave of Pentecost, concerning both your complaints and those of the same abbot. You ought indeed to fear that, if you act otherwise, you may both offend against the sacred canons and incur, to some degree, the indignation of the lord pope, from whose liberality that same abbot had very recently received a privilege, and that on this occasion as well you may appear to have despised our commands.

XX. To Haganon, bishop of Autun, on behalf of Hugh of Flavigny. (In the year 1097.)

[Col. 0523B]

See Patrologia, vol. CLX, col. 355, under Hugh of Flavigny.

XXI. To Pope Urban.—Concerning Robert, abbot of Saint-Remi of Reims. (The year 1197.)

See Patrologia, vol. XLC, col. 1432, in the Chronicle of Saint-Hubert of Andage.

XXII. Letter of Hugh the legate to Robert, abbot of Molesme, founder of the Cistercian order. (Between 1097 and 1098.)

[LABBE, Bibliotheca nova manuscriptorum, II, 640, in the Origins of Cîteaux]

[Col. 0523C]

HUGH, servant of the Church of Lyon and legate of the apostolic see, to ROBERT, abbot of Molesme, and to the brothers who with him desire to serve God according to the Rule of Saint Benedict.

Let it be known to all who rejoice in the advancement of holy Mother Church that you and certain of your sons, the brothers of the monastery of Molesme, appeared at Lyon in our presence and professed that you wished henceforth to adhere more strictly and more perfectly to the Rule of blessed Benedict, which until then you had observed lukewarmly and negligently in that same monastery. Since it is clear that, because of the many obstacles present in that place, you cannot fulfill this, we considered it beneficial for the welfare of both parties—that is, of those departing from there and of those remaining there—that you withdraw to another place which divine generosity might designate for you, [Col. 0523D] and that there you serve the Lord more beneficially and peacefully. Therefore, in the presence of Robert the abbot and of the brothers Alberic, Odo, John, Stephen, Letald, and Peter, and of all whom you shall decide to associate with you lawfully and by common counsel, we then advised you to preserve this holy purpose and now command you to persevere in it; and by apostolic authority, through the impression of our seal, we confirm it perpetually.

XXIII. Decree of Hugh the legate concerning the entire affair of Molesme and Cîteaux. (Between 1097 and 1098.)

[LABBE, cited above.]

HUGH, servant of the Church of Lyon, to his most beloved [Col. 0524A] brother ROBERT, bishop of Langres, greetings.

We have considered it necessary to inform your fraternity what we recently determined concerning the affair of the Church of Molesme at the conference held at the port of Anse. The monks of Molesme came before us there with your letters, showing the desolation and ruin of their house which they had suffered through the removal of Robert the abbot, and earnestly requesting that he be restored to them as their father. For they had no hope that peace and quiet could otherwise be restored to the Church of Molesme, or that the vigor of the monastic order could be brought back there to its former condition. Brother Geoffrey was also present before us, the man whom you had appointed abbot of that Church. He said that he would gladly yield his place to Robert as to his father, if it pleased us to return him to the Church of Molesme. After hearing the petition of yourself and of the monks of Molesme, and rereading the lord pope’s letters addressed to us concerning this affair, in which he committed the whole matter to our disposition and judgment, [Col. 0524B] we finally, yielding to the prayers of yourself and of the others, with the counsel of many religious men—both bishops and others who were present with us—decided to restore him to the Church of Molesme, on the following conditions: before returning there, he must come to Chalon and, into the hands of our brother the bishop of Chalon, to whom according to the custom of the other abbots he made his profession, return the staff and charge of the abbey; he must release and absolve from their profession and obedience the monks of the New Monastery who had made their profession to him as their abbot and promised him obedience; and thus he must receive from that bishop absolution from the profession which he made to him and to the Church of Chalon. [Col. 0524C] We have also granted permission for all those brothers of the New Monastery who followed him when he left the New Monastery to return with him to Molesme, on the condition that, by this decree, neither party presume to solicit or receive members of the other, except in accordance with what blessed Benedict commands concerning the reception of monks of the New Monastery. After he has done what was stated above, we return him to your affection, so that you may restore him as abbot to the Church of Molesme; yet if thereafter he should abandon that same Church with his customary fickleness, no one shall be appointed in his place while Abbot Geoffrey lives, without the consent of yourself, of us, and of Geoffrey himself. We command that all these provisions be valid by apostolic authority. [Col. 0524D] Concerning the chapel of the aforesaid abbot Robert and the other possessions which, when he left the Church of Molesme, he returned with himself and with them to the bishop of Chalon and to the New Monastery, we establish that all shall remain secure for the brothers of the New Monastery, except for one breviary, which they may retain until the feast of Saint John the Baptist in order to copy it, with the consent of the monks of Molesme. The following were present at this settlement: the bishops Nortgaud of Autun, Walter of Chalon, Beraud of Mâcon, and Pontius of Belley; and the abbots Peter of Tournus, Jacento of Dijon, and Gauceran of Ainay. Also Peter, the lord pope’s chamberlain, and many other honorable men of good reputation.

XXIV. Letter of Hugh of Lyon to Pope Paschal.—He commends the messengers of Alberic, first abbot of Cîteaux. (Between 1097 and 1098.)

[LABBE, cited above, p. 643.]

[Col. 0525A]

To the most reverend Father and his lord, PASCHAL the pope, HUGH, servant of the Church of Lyon, offers himself entirely.

These brothers, bearers of the present letter, were traveling to the height of your fatherly dignity and passed through our territory. Since they have a permanent residence within our province, namely in the diocese of Chalon, they asked that they be commended to your highness by a letter from our humility. Know, then, that they [Col. 0525B] come from a certain place called the New Monastery, to which they came to live after leaving the Church of Molesme with their abbot, because they had resolved to lead there, according to the Rule of Saint Benedict, a stricter and more secluded life. They had laid aside the customs of certain monasteries, judging their own weakness unequal to bearing so great a burden. For this reason the brothers of the Church of Molesme, and certain neighboring monks as well, do not cease harassing and disturbing them, thinking that they will be regarded as meaner and more contemptible in the world if these men, as singular and new monks, appear to live among them. [Col. 0525C] Therefore we humbly and confidently beseech your most greatly desired fatherhood to look kindly, as is your custom, upon these brothers, who place all their hope in you after God and therefore flee to the authority of your apostolate; and, by freeing them and their place from this harassment and disturbance, to fortify them with the privilege of your authority. They are Christ’s poor, preparing no defense against their rivals by wealth or power, but placing their hope solely in the mercy of our God.

XXV–XXVI. Hugh to Saint Anselm, archbishop of Canterbury.

(See among the letters of Saint Anselm, letters 64 and 124, book III, Patrologia, vol. CLIX.)

XXVII. Donation by Hugh, archbishop of Lyon, of the church of Saint-Germain. (The year 1106.)

[BALUZE, Miscellany III, 62.]

[Col. 0525D]

To the most reverend Father, lord HUGH, abbot of Cluny, and to the whole Cluniac congregation entrusted to him, HUGH, servant of the Church of Lyon, greetings.

We know that, at the request of lord P., the lord pope’s chamberlain, we formerly gave you and your Church the church of Artense. For this reason our sons, the canons of the Church of Lyon, were troubled and began earnestly to implore our clemency not to allow the aforesaid church of Artense, on any pretext, to be alienated and separated from the church of Saint-Stephen of Lyon, whose property it had been from ancient times. Moved by their cries and petitions, we promised the aforesaid lord P. that, in exchange for the Church of Artense, we would give you the church of Saint-Germain, which lies between the church of La Chapelle and the church of Marlieu. [Col. 0526A] Now fulfilling that promise, we grant you and the Church of Cluny the aforesaid church of Saint-Germain, to possess in perpetuity by right, retaining in it the synodal dues and another census which the late Archbishop Gibuin imposed upon it, as well as the episcopal obedience and reverence owed as in the other churches which we have granted to blessed Peter. Sign of Girin, dean. Sign of Teotard, chamberlain. Sign of Girin, chaplain. Sign of Gauceran, cantor. Sign of Arnold, master. Sign of Godon, canon and archpriest.

Done at Lyon in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1106, [Col. 0526B] indiction XIII.

XXVIII. Hugh, archbishop of Lyon, in the presence of the bishops of Grenoble, Die, and Langres, settles the dispute between the monks of Saint-Bénigne of Dijon and the clerics of Besançon concerning the churches of Salins. (The year 1106.)

[PÉRARD, Charters of Burgundy, p. 209.]

HUGH, archbishop of Lyon and legate of the holy apostolic see.

We wish it to be known to all the faithful that, in the time of Lord Pope Paschal II and at his command, we summoned the clerics of Besançon and Jarenton, abbot of Dijon, to Lyon in order to settle the controversy between them [Col. 0526C] concerning the church of Saint Mary of Salins. After hearing their actions and responses, it seemed to us and to the venerable bishops who were with us—namely Hugh of Grenoble, Irmion of Die, and Robert of Langres—that we should end their dispute by an amicable agreement rather than by a judicial sentence. It was therefore agreed between them that the monks of Dijon would, through our hand, entirely renounce and relinquish to those clerics all claims which they appeared to have, whether in writing or without writing, against the clerics of Besançon concerning the churches of Salins; and that the clerics of the Church of Besançon would possess all the churches of Salins in perpetuity, without any complaint from the Church of Dijon. The clerics, however, would grant the monks of Dijon permission, in a suitable place on the land of the Church of Dijon, to build at Salins a chapel seven measures in length, apart from the apse, suitable for one altar only, and four measures in width. [Col. 0526D] A cemetery of seven measures likewise on every side around the chapel would also be permitted, solely for burying monks; but they were not to bury other persons there. Nor were they to receive the parishioners of Salins, either living or dead. If any parishioner of Salins, lying on a sickbed, wished through fear of death to become a monk, they were not to receive him unless the priest of whose parish he was a member consented. The clerics also granted the monks the tithe of only one vineyard, which they would select from those which at that time the clerics held in demesne, preferably, and make known to the clerics, until the next Pentecost. [Col. 0527A] The abbot and his monks promised, through our hand, that both in these matters and in other matters pertaining to the diocese of Besançon, they would obey the Church of Besançon, without prejudice to their order, and would diligently observe the canonical bans and the excommunications of the archbishop and his ministers. We therefore decree and confirm by apostolic authority that this settlement shall remain inviolate on both sides. If anyone knowingly violates this settlement of ours, unless within forty days after admonition he repents and makes suitable satisfaction, by amicable settlement or competent judgment, to the person whom he has injured, let him be held guilty of offending apostolic majesty.

Done publicly at Lyon in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation [Col. 0527B] 1196 [sic], on the day before the Kalends of April, Holy Saturday. The witnesses to this settlement are: the signature of Hugh, bishop of Grenoble; the signature of Irmion, bishop of Die; the signature of the bishop of Langres; the signature of Rostan, archdeacon of Lyon; the signature of Theotard, chamberlain of Lyon; the signature of Jocerand, cantor of Lyon; the signature of Godon, canon and archpriest; the signature of Mainer, dean of Besançon; the signatures of Hugh, Stephen, William, archdeacon, Stephen the cantor, Hugh the archdeacon, Jarenton the abbot, Geoffrey the prior, Hugh the monk, another Hugh of Berth the monk, Odo the monk, and Evrard the monk.

XXIX. Charter of the donation of the church of Saint John of Bruilloles by Hugh, archbishop of the Church of Lyon, to the abbey of Savigny.

(DE LA MURE, Ecclesiastical History of Lyon, p. 390, from the Savigny cartulary, fol. 120.)

[Col. 0527C]

Archbishop Hugh of Lyon donated and confirmed to Saint-Martin of Savigny, to Lord Iterius, the second abbot, and to the monks serving God there, the church of Saint John of Bruilloles, in the presence of these witnesses: Girin Calvus, Girin the chaplain, Berard Ursel, Catard, Bostan, and Ferlo. William of Algeroles and his brother Pontius also gave to Saint-Martin, for themselves and their parents, the share which they possessed in this church, and gave it to the aforesaid abbot without any payment. [Col. 0528A] The remaining share, which the old man Artald claimed was his by hereditary right, he likewise gave in the chapter-house of Savigny before the abbot and the brothers. William of Malboson also gave and renounced without any reservation whatever he claimed in that church. Amblard, Theotyrinus Portatus, and Boso gave in full whatever they appeared to possess there. Whoever violates these donations or brings a claim against them, let him be anathema. Amen.

XXX. Charter of the donation by Archbishop Hugh of Lyon to the abbey of Savigny of the chapel of Saint Peter of Camopseto.

(DE LA MURE, cited above, from the cartulary of the same abbey, fol. 121.)

Lord Hugh, archbishop of Lyon, gave and confirmed to Saint-Martin of Savigny, to the second abbot Iterius, and to the monks serving God there, the church [Col. 0528B] of Saint Lawrence and the chapel of Saint Peter of Camopseto, with their tithes and appurtenances.

Sign of Wigo, the abbot, his brother; of Arbert, archdeacon; of Girin Calvus; of Girin, chaplain; of Bostan; and of Arbert, archpriest.

XXXI. Charter of the donation of the church of Bessennac to the abbey of Savigny by Hugh, archbishop of the Church of Lyon.

(DE LA MURE, cited above, from the cartulary of the abbey of Savigny.)

Hugh, archbishop of Lyon, inspired by God, [Col. 0528C] gave the church of Bessennac to Saint-Martin of Savigny, to the second abbot Iterius, and to the monks dwelling there. Wigo Longus, Amblard, and William, his brothers, held lordship over this church; for their own redemption and that of their parents, they gave and confirmed it in its entirety to Saint-Martin of Savigny without any payment, in the presence of Barnuin the archpriest and Hugh of Lasney. Stephen Nigellus gave to Saint-Martin, at his death, the share which he had received from his wife, in the presence of his sons William and Stephen, and also of Stephen Willencus and his brother Hugh.

IN THE YEAR OF THE LORD 1106, PETER ALPHONSE, A CHRISTIAN FROM A JEW

[Col. 0527]

HISTORICAL AND LITERARY NOTICE

(Bibliotheca Hispana vetus, by D. Antonio, III, 16)

[Col. 0527C] Moses, Hebrew by nation and religious affiliation, converted from it to Christianity in the year 1106, in the city of Huesca in the kingdom of Aragon, and was called PETER ALPHONSE [Col. 0528C] because, having been washed in the sacred font on the feast of the holy apostles Peter and Paul, he deserved to have as sponsor or godparent Alfonso, king of Aragon as well as of Castile and León, whose physician he was; [Col. 0529A] or, as he himself calls him, his spiritual father. The same man relates this most explicitly in the prologue to his Dialogue, of which we shall speak shortly. That the Alfonso whom we have indicated is the one of whom he speaks is proved against those who understand him to be Alfonso II of Aragon both by the chronology and by the title “emperor of Spain” which he gives him, since Alfonso II did not begin his reign before the sixty-third year of that same century. No less deserving of the censor’s rod is Peter Amboesius, who, in the preface to his Apology for Peter Abelard, calls this king Alfonso “the best of kings and a most learned mathematician,” confusing him with Alfonso X, king of Castile, son of Ferdinand the Saint, surnamed the Wise.

He also calls Huesca, the city in which he was baptized, the most illustrious city of that kingdom, an academy of Sertorius, and far more renowned for the birthplaces of the most holy martyrs Laurence and Vincent [Note: [Col. 0529C] What is reported thus far under this number seems to me to savor more of panegyric than of history; certainly it calls for correction. It is truly astonishing that such things should so easily have escaped our author, otherwise a critic of Cato-like severity.], from which place our Peter Alphonse perhaps came by birth [Note: [Col. 0529C] Lanuza believes this, History of Aragon.]. The author of the Great Belgian Chronicle, among the German historians edited by Pistorius, corruptly calls it Osta while recounting the events of the year 1101 [Col. 0529B]; and still more corruptly Vincent of Beauvais and Saint Antoninus of Florence, in whose works it is read as Hostia. Likewise Matthew Palmerius wrongly mentions our man in his Chronicle under the year 1068 [Note: [Col. 0529C] Together with him, Paul Langius in the Citizen Chronicle, also under this year.], although he had been born only six years earlier; for in the year 1106, when he was received into the bosom of the Church, he was, as he himself says, forty-four years old. What name, then, should be given to the gross error of those who assign Peter to the Dominican order of Preachers more than a century before Dominic, the most holy father of the Preachers, had founded his order? This error was inadvertently admitted by Andreas Schottus in the Bibliotheca Hispana and by Valerius Andreas Taxander in his Catalogue of Spanish Writers. He wrote, in order to vindicate his name from the slanders of his fellow Gentiles, who maliciously interpreted his passage to the camp of the Christians [Col. 0529C], with the utmost learning and erudition:

Dialogues—or rather a dialogue divided into twelve parts or titles—in which the impious opinions of the Jews are refuted by the clearest arguments both of natural and of heavenly philosophy, and certain more obscure passages of the prophets are explained. They were first published at Cologne from the Gymnicus press in 1536, in octavo, after having been diligently sought out by Hermann, count of Nuenar and provost of the Church of Strasbourg, a most learned man and a great friend of learned men, and finally discovered in the library of Corbie. This is a work which Moses the Jew and Peter the Christian—that is, the man he formerly was and the man he had now begun to be—carefully weave together. In it, the author says, “I first set forth the destruction of the credulity of all other nations; after that I concluded that the Christian law is superior to all; finally I set forth all the objections of every opponent of the Christian law, and, according to my ability, destroyed the objections I had set forth by reason and authority.” It also appeared in volume XII of the edition of the Library of the Fathers, and in the latest Lyon edition, volume XXI. A writer of the following century, Raymond Martini, a Dominican, praises both the man and the work in his Pugio fidei against Moors and Jews [Note: [Col. 0529C] Part III, distinction 3, chapter 4, p. 540 of the Paris edition of 1651.], asserting that before he became a Christian he had been a great rabbi among the Jews. Vincent, as we have said, of Beauvais [Note: [Col. 0529D] In the Historical Mirror, part II.], and Antoninus of Florence, and Matthew Palmerius [Note: [Col. 0529D] In the Chronicle under the year 1068.], as well as Alfonso de Spina, author of the Fortress of the Faith [Col. 0530B] [Note: [Col. 0529D] Book I, fols. 39 and 65, and book III, cols. 122, 128, 134, 137.], who calls him most wise and learned, the physician of the emperor Alfonso, and venerable; our Valerius the historian [Note: [Col. 0529D] Book VIII, title 6, chapter 9.], Alfonso Venerus [Note: [Col. 0529D] In the Handbook.], Jacobus Philippus Bergomensis [Note: [Col. 0529D] Supplement, book 12, fol. 210.], Paul Langius [Note: [Col. 0529D] In the Citizen Chronicle under the year 1068.], besides the more recent editors of libraries, Possevinus, Schottus, Miraeus, and the Spanish historians. The following work is also attributed to him by some [Note: [Col. 0529D] Bergomensis, cited above; Venerus, in the Handbook.]:

On Knowledge and Philosophy, book I. This is perhaps the same as the book On Discipline, so called by him [Note: [Col. 0529D] See below the notice prefixed to the book On Clerical Discipline. EDITOR OF THE PATROLOGIA.]. A very old manuscript copy of it is preserved in Vatican manuscript 4161; its beginning is: “Peter Alphonse, servant of Jesus Christ, compiler of this book, said: I give thanks to the Lord,” etc. And shortly afterward: “Prologue to the book of Peter Alphonse. May God be my help in this little work, who compelled me to compose this book and translate it into Latin. Since with me often,” etc. And a little farther on: “Therefore I composed this little book, partly from the proverbs of philosophers, and their Arabic admonitions, and fables, and customs; partly [Col. 0530C] from comparisons drawn from animals and birds,” etc. The beginning of the book is: “This philosopher, who in the Arabic language is called Edrich, said to his son,” etc. At the end is: “Here ends the book of Peter Alphonse, entitled Discipline, as stated in the preface.” The script is difficult to read because of the frequent abbreviations, and is contemporary with, or nearly contemporary with, the century in which the author lived. Labbe praises a manuscript of the Dialogues in the second part of his New Library of Manuscript Books, p. 26 [Note: [Col. 0529D] The work of Peter Alphonse, Dialogues against the Jews, is often found in the more celebrated manuscript libraries and bears various titles. In the Cotton Library, in Galba, codex XV, p. 68, col. 1: Judaism. In the Alnwick Library, Class IV, Division 6, p. 247, ascribed by Bosquier: On True Friendship. In the library of the king of France, vol. III, p. 252, codex 2213: On the Prophecies of the Old Testament. Not likewise [Col. 0530C] the Book on Knowledge and Philosophy, from which it is uncertain whether it is the work which Peter Alphonse himself called Discipline, and which Oudinus, Fabricius, and others entitled On Clerical Discipline. Our author is undecided. To me both seem to be the same work; for in the library of El Escorial, shelf q, pluteus 1, under no. 14, I found the following entry: “The work of Peter Aldefonsus, or Alphonse of Huesca, On Proverbs or Clerical Discipline.” At this point, in the catalogue of the manuscripts of that library (vol. III of the Latin manuscripts, p. 10, beginning), I added: “In three books: indeed in the Latin language, but of Hebrew or Arabic flavor.” Properly, therefore, the title On Proverbs is placed before the title Discipline; for its author says that the work was compiled from the proverbs of philosophers. It exists in the Royal Library of Turin, vol. II, codex DCCXXXVII, p. 236, with the same beginning as in our author: “Peter Aldefonsus said,” etc. It is also found at Oxford and Cambridge, in Oudinus, vol. II, p. 993, col. 1. He also reports that a Logic written by Peter Alphonse exists in the library of the king of France, codex 6279; yet I searched for it in vain under that number and in the indexes of volume IV of that library, and I think it is the Logic of Peter surnamed the Spaniard rather than of Peter Alphonse. Sanderus, cited by Fabricius, Bibliotheca media et infima, vol. V, p. 239, attributes to him: On Abundance in Speech for Every Subject. In the library of the king of France, vol. IV, p. 212, col. 1, codex 6184, I read the following as though it were contained in that codex: “7. Fragment from the book of Peter Alphonse against the Jews.” That fragment ends with these words: “But between what has already been said and what is to be said, I wish here to insert that metrical fable which I wrote elsewhere three years ago; when its figures and comparisons are fully and perfectly understood, they will disclose the characteristics of nations and orders, and the causes of the disturbances of the universal Church.” [Col. 0532C] [Col. 0531C] Immediately afterward there follows a poem about the allegorical peacock, that is, [lacuna], from which one may infer that the author of this poem was Peter Alphonse. Thus far.] 

[Col. 0531]

A SECOND NOTICE

(Prefixed to Peter Alphonse’s Clerical Discipline, first published in Paris in 1824 under the direction of D. Labouderie, vicar general of the Church of Avignon.)

[Col. 0531A] Pierre Alphonse, or d’Alphonse, formerly Rabbi Moses Sephardi, was born in 1062 at Huesca, in the kingdom of Aragon. He was raised in the Jewish religion, which was that of his fathers, and distinguished himself by knowledge in more than one field. At the age of forty-four, he embraced Christianity and was baptized in his native city by Stephen, who was its bishop, on the feast of Saint Peter in 1106 (1144 of the Spanish era). Hence he took the name Peter, to which he added that of Alphonse in honor of Alfonso VI, king of Castile and León, styled emperor, who was willing to be his godfather and gave him the position of physician at his court. His fellow believers slandered his action and represented it in the most unfavorable light: [Col. 0531B] some accused him of changing religion out of contempt for God and for his word; others, through ignorance of the law and the prophets; and still others, through vainglory, self-interest, and because he saw his nation plunged in disgrace and dishonor. To refute all these accusations and make known the true motives of his conduct, he composed a dialogue in twelve titles—or rather twelve dialogues between a Jew and a Christian—in which the Jew Moses, the name he bore before his baptism, raises the difficulties, and the Christian Peter Alphonse, the name he received at baptism, answers everything triumphantly. These dialogues were printed at Cologne in 1536, in octavo, under the title: “Dialogues most worthy to be read, in which the impious opinions of the Jews [Col. 0531C] are refuted … and certain more obscure passages of the prophets are explained.” They were included in the Great Library of the Fathers, volume XXI, pp. 172–221, Lyon edition. Mariana, General History of Spain; Ferreras, Chronological Historical Synopsis of Spain; Nicolas Antonio, Bibliotheca Hispana vetus; Vincent of Beauvais, Historical Mirror, book XXV, chapter 118; Bartolocci, Thomas Hyde, Casimir Houdin, Raymond Martini, Alfonso de Spina, Paul of Burgos, Possevin, Hermann Hardt, Noël Alexandre, and other writers speak of him with great praise. Indeed, these dialogues are very substantial and learned, although some weak [Col. 0532A] or peculiar arguments may be criticized. We think the reader will not be displeased to learn their outline.

TITLE I.—The Jews form a false conception of the Godhead; they distort his attributes. Peter Alphonse recounts curious facts in support of his arguments.

TITLE II.—The cause of the dispersion of the Jews is none other than the condemnation of Jesus, whom they overwhelmed with insults and represented as illegitimate. God preserves them among the nations only to perpetuate the memory of the dreadful deicide they committed.

TITLE III.—The Jews’ fantasies concerning the resurrection of the dead at the coming of the Messiah and concerning his intermediate reign, adopted by some Fathers of the [Col. 0532B] early centuries and by some moderns. There is much bad physics in it; one also observes a slight tendency to weaken the dogma of the general resurrection as Christians profess it.

TITLE IV.—The Jews observe only the smallest part of the law of Moses and consequently cannot be pleasing to God.

TITLE V.—Peter Alphonse develops the reasons that led him to embrace the law of the Christians in preference to that of the Arabs, among whom he had lived from childhood and whose language he knew perfectly.

TITLE VI.—After refuting Judaism and [Col. 0532C] Islam, Peter Alphonse proceeds to set forth the mysteries of the Christian religion. He first discusses the Holy Trinity, whose traces he discovers in the Old Testament, in the ineffable name of God [Note: [Col. 0532C] Col. 608], and in the manner in which the priests, descendants of Aaron, blessed the people [Note: [Col. 0532C] Col. 612].

TITLE VII.—The Virgin Mary conceived through the operation of the Holy Spirit, without having known a man, in accordance with the prophecy of Isaiah, chapter VII.

TITLE VIII.—The Word became flesh. Jesus Christ, God and man at once. A multitude of passages in support of these divine doctrines.

TITLE IX.—The Messiah came at the appointed time; everything the prophets announced [Col. 0533A] concerning him was fulfilled literally. There are some very substantial arguments here.

TITLE X.—The Messiah submitted to death of his own free will; he allowed the Jews to fasten him to the cross. In this dialogue Peter Alphonse treats several incidental questions: What is the devil? How did man fall under his power? Why did God deliver him from it? … etc.

TITLE XI.—The Messiah rose from the dead; he ascended into heaven, from which he will come to judge the living and the dead. More subtle than substantial.

TITLE XII.—The Christian law is not opposed to the Mosaic law; one is the fulfillment of the other. He offers some fairly ingenious correspondences between the rites of the Old Testament and the [Col. 0533B] events of the New [Note: [Col. 0533D] Col. 000].

What we have said thus far about Peter Alphonse is drawn from his own writings; the Spanish historians do not express themselves in every respect as he does. This may be judged from the two accounts which we are about to quote.

“Moreover,” says Mariana, “a certain Jew named Moses, a man of great learning who knew many languages, in the latter part of the reign of Don Alfonso, having abjured the superstition of his fathers, became a Christian. The king himself was his godfather at baptism, which was the reason he was called Peter Alphonse. He attacked in writing the sects of the Jews and the Moors, and through his diligence many members of both nations were brought back to the truth. This Jew’s conversion must have been famous and remarkable, since the historians of Aragon attribute it to Don Alfonso, king of Aragon. They say that at Huesca, on the twenty-ninth of June, he was baptized in the year 1106; that Don Stephen, bishop of that city, performed the ceremony, and that the godfather was the king himself of Aragon. In this dispute, we neither wish nor could we render judgment for either side; let each person follow for himself what seems more probable.” Mariana, General History of Spain, vol. I, p. 471.

“Don Alfonso, king of Aragon and Navarre,” says Ferreras, “being at Huesca in the month of June, a Hebrew named Moses, a man of profound learning who was established in that city, decided to embrace the Christian religion after having become fully convinced of his error by the Holy Scriptures. His decision soon came to the monarch’s knowledge, and, to express his joy, the king wished to honor him by holding him at the font. Thus the Jew received baptism in the cathedral of that city, administered to him by the bishop of the same Church, on the feast of the apostle Saint Peter. He left his former name to take that of Peter Alphonse, in honor of the saint and of the king, his godfather. He later wrote several very learned books against the Jews, entitled Dialogues, which are printed in [Col. 0534A] the Library of the Fathers.” General History of Spain, translated from the Spanish of Jean de Ferreras by d’Hermilly, vol. III, p. 299.

It is probable that Peter Alphonsi’s dialogues led some biographers to suspect that he had sought permission from the sovereign pontiff to enter into conference with two rabbis, named Samuel Abrabalia and Solomon Levita, in order to defend the interests of the Christian religion against them and demand an account from them of various passages in the Talmud. We nevertheless confess that we have no certainty on this matter, and that we are led to this conjecture by certain expressions of Wolf. *Bibliotheca Hebraea*, article 1824.

We have been unable to establish with any greater certainty [Col. 0534B] than that Rabbi Jacob ben Ruben wrote his work, entitled *Milchamoth Jehovah* [Note: [Col. 0533D]] (“The Wars of the Lord”), against the work of Peter Alphonsi, and that Rabbi Shem Tov ben Isaac ben Sprot of Tudela directed his *Even Bochen* [Note: [Col. 0533D]] (“Touchstone”) against it. In that work he introduces two interlocutors, one Jewish, under the name Ammejachèd [Note: [Col. 0534D]] (“unitarian”), and the other Christian, under the name Ammescalesc [Note: [Col. 0534D]] (“Trinitarian”); they discuss approximately the same subjects that Peter Alphonsi had treated, and end by conceding victory to the law of Moses. For while Wolf and Hardt take the affirmative position, the celebrated Abbé de Rossi declares in favor of the negative. See *Mss., cod. hebr.*, article 760; *Biblioth. Jud. antichrist.*, article 146, and elsewhere.

[Col. 0534C] The second work of Peter Alphonsi is the one that we are presenting to the public under the title *Disciplina Clericalis*, “Clerical Discipline,” because it makes the cleric well instructed; or, otherwise, *The Admonition*. The author compiled it partly from the proverbs and admonitory tales of the Arab philosophers, and from fables and verses, and partly from representations of beasts and birds.

The Latin text, still unpublished, was collated by M. Méon from seven manuscripts in the King’s Library and from several others belonging to foreign powers, though they had been held in France some years earlier. Rodríguez de Castro knew of only one copy in the library of the Escorial, *Escritores Rabinos españoles*, p. 20; Nicolas Antonio speaks only of the Vatican copy, and even then does not describe it accurately.

The French prose version was likewise unpublished. It evidently dates from the fifteenth century. M. Méon, whose opinion carries such great weight, believes that it is by Jean Miellot.

As for the French verse version, under the title *Chastoiement* or *Castoiement d’un père à son fils* (“A Father’s Admonition to His Son”), one had already appeared in 1760 in Barbazan’s *Fabliaux*. M. Méon, to whom we owe excellent editions of the poets of the eleventh, twelfth, thirteenth, fourteenth, and fifteenth centuries, published it [Col. 0535A] again in 1808, with considerable additions. The one that we publish in our *Mélanges* is entirely different; it is another work.

The peoples of the East possess several compilations resembling that of Peter Alphonsi, although greatly inferior to it. Among others are: *Pirke Aboth*(8)[Col. 0529D] *Lib.* VIII, title 6, chapter 9 (“Chapters of the Fathers”), collected by Rabbi Nathan of Babylon, who flourished in 121, and translated into all languages; *Mivchar Happeninim*(9)[Col. 0529D] *In Enchiridio* (“Choice of Precious Stones”), compiled in Arabic by Rabbi Jedaiah Bedersi around 1298, containing many sayings of the ancient Greek and Arab philosophers, translated into Hebrew by Judah ibn Tibbon (Soncino, 1484), and into Latin by Erbert (Frankfurt, 1630); *Proverbiorum arabicorum Centuriae duae* [Col. 0535B] (“Two Centuries of Arabic Proverbs”), by Abu Ubayd, translated into Latin by Scaliger and Thomas Erpenius (Leiden, 1614, quarto); *Apophthegmata Ebraeorum ac Arabum ex Aboth R. Nathan, Aristea, libro selectarum margaritarum, et aliis auctoribus selecta, latineque reddita, cum brevibus scholiis* (“Apophthegms of the Hebrews and Arabs, selected from the *Aboth* of Rabbi Nathan, Aristeas, the book of selected pearls, and other authors, and rendered into Latin with brief scholia”), by J. Drusius (Frankfurt, 1612, quarto).

We have found some of the fables of *The Admonition* in *The Thousand and One Nights*; we think it unnecessary to indicate them.

Peter Alphonsi is credited with: first, a *Logic*, which is said to have initially been translated into Hebrew and which is also claimed to have been translated into Greek long afterward by George Scholarius, known as Gennadius. Lambecius reports an extract from it (*Biblioth. Caes. Vindobon.*, vol. VIII, p. [Col. 0535C] 285):

> Διαλεκτική ἐστι τεχνη τεχνῶν, καὶ ἐπιστήμη ἐπιστημῶν etc.: “Dialectic is the art of arts, the science of sciences, providing a way to the principles of all dispositions”; [Col. 0536A] but it is entirely evident that Master Peter the Spaniard, author of this latter work, who, according to Lambecius, died in 1277, is not Peter Alphonsi, who flourished at the beginning of the preceding century.

Second, *De abundantia in sermonibus ad omnem materiam* (“On abundance in discourse for every subject”). See Fabricius, *Biblioth. mediae et infimae latinitatis*, book XV, vol. III, p. 239, who cites Sanderus, p. 205, and who improperly refers to Trithemius, *De scriptoribus ecclesiasticis*, p. 149, Cologne edition, 1546, quarto.

Third, *De scientia et philosophia* (“On Knowledge and Philosophy”). Wolf believes that this treatise is the same as the *Disciplina clericalis*; *Biblioth. Hebr.*, vol. I, p. 971. D. Joseph Rodríguez de Castro, *Escritores Rabinos españoles*, p. 20, likewise adopts this opinion, which Nicolas Antonio makes certain by citing several passages from the *Book of Knowledge and Philosophy* that occur in *Clerical Discipline*; *Biblioth. Hisp., vet.*, vol. II, pp. 7–8, Rome edition, 1696, folio.

Fourth, *De Pavone figurali* (“On the Figurative Peacock”). This short poem, directed against the vices of the Roman court and against mendicant religious orders, cannot be by Peter Alphonsi: it is later than the First Council of Lyon, held in 1245.

It would be ridiculous to prolong the enumeration of the works attributed to Peter Alphonsi and rightly denied to him by enlightened criticism. The time and place of his death are unknown; nevertheless, Casimir Oudin implies that this learned man died in 1110.

[Col. 0536C] J. LABOUDERIE, Vicar General of Avignon, etc.

[Col. 0535]

**THE DIALOGUES OF PETER ALPHONSI, A CHRISTIAN FROM JUDAISM**

In which the impious opinions of the Jews are refuted by the clearest arguments both of natural and celestial philosophy, and certain more obscure passages of the prophets are explained.

(*Biblioth. Patr. Lugdun.*, XXI, 172.)

**PREFACE OF PETER ALPHONSI**

[Col. 0535D] To the One and Eternal First, who lacks both beginning and end, the Almighty, Creator of all things, knowing all things and doing all that he wills, who placed rational and wise man above every animal, so that by these two virtues he might understand and pursue what is just and avoid what is contrary to salvation—to him be honor and glory, and may his wondrous name be blessed for ever and ever. Amen.

The compiler of the following work said: The Almighty inspired us with his Spirit and directed us to the path of the straight way, first removing the slight film from our eyes and afterward the heavy veil of our corrupted soul. [Col. 0537A] Then the barriers of the prophecies were opened to us, and their secrets were revealed, and we applied our mind to grasping their true meaning and devoted ourselves to explaining it. From this we discerned both what is to be understood in them and what is to be believed from them: namely, that there is one God in a Trinity of Persons, who neither precede one another in time nor are separated from one another by any division, whom Christians name the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit; and that blessed Mary, conceiving from the Holy Spirit and without intercourse with a man, bore Christ, generating an animated body that was to be the dwelling place of the incomprehensible Godhead.

Thus there is one Christ, perfect in three substances—namely, body, soul, and Godhead—and he is both God and man; and the Jews crucified him by his own arrangement and will, so that, just as he was the Creator, he might also become the Redeemer of the whole holy Church, that is, of the faithful who preceded and followed him. He died in the body and was buried, and on the third day rose from the dead; he also ascended into heaven and is there together with the Father, and he will come on the day of judgment to judge the living and the dead, as the prophets spoke and foretold would happen.

When, therefore, through the prompting of divine mercy I had reached so lofty a degree of this faith, I cast off the cloak of falsehood and was stripped of the tunic of iniquity. I was baptized at the see of the city of Huesca, in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit, and was purified by the hands of Stephen, the glorious and lawful bishop of that same city. At the hour of baptism, in addition to what has been stated above, [Col. 0537C] I believed in the blessed apostles and in the holy Catholic Church.

This took place in the year 1106 from the birth of the Lord, in the forty-fourth year of my age, in the month of July, on the feast day of the apostles [Col. 0538A] Peter and Paul. Therefore, out of veneration for and in memory of that apostle, I took the name Peter. My spiritual father was Alphonsus, the glorious emperor of Spain, who lifted me from the sacred font; therefore, adding his name to the name already mentioned, I took the name Peter Alphonsi.

When it became known to the Jews who had previously known me and had judged me skilled in the books of the prophets and the sayings of the teachers, and also somewhat knowledgeable in all the liberal arts, that I had accepted the law and faith of the Christians and had become one of them, some of them thought that I had done this only because I had cast away all sense of shame and had despised both God and the law. Others said that I had done it because I had not understood the words of the prophets and of the law as I ought. Others attributed it to vain glory and accused me of having done it for worldly honor, since I saw that the Christian people surpassed all others.

I therefore composed this little book so that everyone might know my intention and hear my reasoning. In it I first placed the destruction of the beliefs of all other peoples; afterward I concluded that the Christian law is superior to all. Finally, I set out all the objections of every opponent of the Christian law and, to the best of my ability, refuted them with reason and authority.

I divided the entire book into a dialogue so that the reader’s mind might become more ready to understand. In defending the arguments of the Christians, I used the name that I now bear, Christian; in refuting the arguments of the adversary, I used the name that I had before baptism, namely Moses. I also divided the book into twelve titles so that each reader might find more quickly in them whatever he seeks.

**HERE BEGINS THE DIALOGUE OF PETER, SURnamed ALPHONSI, A CHRISTIAN FROM JUDAISM, AND MOSES THE JEW**

[Col. 0537]

[Col. 0537D] **PETER.** From the earliest age of childhood, a certain most excellent friend named Moses had been attached to me. From our earliest years he had been my companion and fellow student. When news reached him that, having abandoned the law of my fathers, I had chosen the Christian faith, he left the place where he was staying and hurried to me. On his arrival he bore the face of an indignant man; he greeted me with reproaches, not as a friend but as though I were a stranger, and began as follows:

“Ah, Peter Alphonsi! A great deal of time has passed since I was eager to come to you, see you, speak with you, and remain with you; but until now my desire lacked fulfillment, whereas now, by the grace of God, I see you with a joyful countenance. I ask you now to disclose your intention to me and to explain the reason why you abandoned either the ancient law or chose a new one. For I know well that formerly you were highly skilled in the writings of the prophets and in the words of our teachers; from childhood you had been an expounder of the law above all your contemporaries. If there was an opponent, you held up the shield of defense before him; in the synagogues you exhorted the Jews never to depart from their faith, instructed those who shared your knowledge, and advanced the learned to greater learning. [Col. 0539A] Yet now, I do not know by what means, I see you changed and estranged from the path of uprightness, which, as it seems to me, has happened through error.”

I replied: “It is the custom of common and ignorant people that, if they see anyone doing anything contrary to their own practice, even though it remains right and entirely just, nevertheless in their estimation and judgment it incurs both the name and the blame of injustice. But you, who were nourished in the cradle of philosophy and suckled at the breasts of philosophy, with what face can you accuse me before you are able to prove whether what I have done is just or unjust?”

**MOSES.** Two contrary thoughts arise in my mind. First, I judge that you, being a prudent man, could not have departed from the law that you held unless you had truly recognized the one you adopted as better. Second, I regard the law that I hold and you have abandoned as the better one. Therefore I both judge what you did to be an error and do not know to which side I should give my assent. For this reason I ask you to remove from my mind the anxiety of this doubt, and let us both range through the field of alternate reasoning until I arrive at an investigation of this matter and am able to learn whether your action is just or unjust.

**PETER.** Human nature has this characteristic: when the mind is disturbed in any way, it lacks the eye of discernment for distinguishing truth from falsehood. Therefore, unless you remove all disturbance from your heart, so that, in the manner of wise men, we may praise what is just and reject without contention what is unjust, we shall never bring our work to an end, but shall throw words [Col. 0539C] into the air to no purpose.

**MOSES.** I willingly accept this agreement, and I ask you to accept the same agreement on your part.

**PETER.** I gladly consent.

**MOSES.** I ask you to grant this also, if it pleases you. If you bring forward any authority from the Scriptures, I ask that you do so according to the Hebrew truth. If you act otherwise, understand that I will not accept it. But if I bring forward anything according to what is found among us, then accept it as I wish you to, and do not in any way contradict what you recognize as true.

**PETER.** I certainly do not refuse this either; for I greatly desire to kill you with your own sword.

**MOSES.** Moreover, if something should arise at any time that appears foreign to the purpose of the laws, please do not be annoyed; when the appropriate opportunity requires it, strive to answer the questioner concerning the other arts. I also wish you to grant me permission sometimes to question, sometimes to answer, and sometimes even to oppose you by mutual reasoning, as the course of the discussion may allow.

**PETER.** I grant it. You may now ask whatever you wish to know, about any matter and with any intention.

**MOSES.** Do you acknowledge Moses, son of Amram, to have been a true prophet of the Israelite people and truly sent by God (Exod. III), and do you acknowledge that whatever he prophesied and declared in God’s name he faithfully announced and spoke?

**PETER.** I certainly acknowledge it.

**MOSES.** Do you also acknowledge that all the prophets after Moses came to confirm his law, and not to refute it in any respect?

**PETER.** I acknowledge this also.

**MOSES.** Nor do you deny that the law now held by the Jews, which they assert was written by Moses, remains in every respect just as Moses wrote it?

**PETER.** How could I deny it, especially since that same law, translated for us by teachers of old whose testimony we accept, in the very words of Moses and written down among us, is the same except in certain places where, although the words are changed, the meaning nevertheless remains the same?

**MOSES.** How, then, do I see you transgressing it and straying from its very paths?

**PETER.** It is not so. Rather, I now preserve its complete faith as I ought and proceed with a straight step along its most upright paths.

**MOSES.** Your words make it understood that from the words of the law and the prophets you derive the right meaning, whereas the Jews, worshipers of that same law, are estranged from its right intention and therefore, in your judgment, seem to understand it badly.

**PETER.** You have penetrated the meaning of my words correctly.

**MOSES.** Then make me understand in what respect you think the Jews have erred in explaining the law, while you understand it better.

**PETER.** I see that they attend only to the surface of the law and explain the letter not spiritually but carnally; hence they have been deceived by the greatest error.

**MOSES.** I do not sufficiently grasp what you mean by these words, and therefore I beg you to speak more clearly.

**PETER.** Do you not remember your teachers, who wrote your doctrine, upon which, according to you, your whole law depends? How they assert that God has a body and a form, and apply to his ineffable majesty things that cannot be established by any reason? Indeed, they have uttered concerning him statements that seem to be nothing other than the words of people joking in the schools of children or of women spinning in the streets.

Again, explaining the law according to the capacity of your understanding, you hope to escape captivity in a manner that cannot happen. Again, in your escape from captivity you hope for so unusual a miracle that he will raise your dead, who will begin once more to inhabit the earth as before. Again, while you are in captivity, I see you carrying out only the smallest part of all the precepts of the law, even according to your own explanation. Yet you believe that what you do pleases God and is acceptable to him, while you trust that he will in no way blame you for what you omit; and you seem to yourselves to have fulfilled everything. This plainly occupies the highest place among your errors. For there are many other errors into which unsound explanations of the law have thrown you.

**MOSES.** You attack our disgrace too profoundly and seek to overwhelm the Jewish people. The words are few and light, but in them lies a weighty and serious meaning. If we wish to bring the entire argument under a single judgment and comprehend many matters under one title, when we ought to clarify each separately, by mixing everything indiscriminately we introduce obscurity. Therefore, if it seems good to you, let us assign a separate title to each statement of our reasoning, so that, after each has been examined by alternate discussion, we may proceed in order to the next and thus bring our work to a fitting conclusion.

**PETER.** Let what you have well proposed be carried out, and let what you have fittingly advised be completed. After titles have been assigned to the individual statements, ask first about whatever you wish, since I am ready to answer.

**FIRST TITLE. He shows that the Jews understand the words of the prophets carnally and explain them falsely.**

[Col. 0541B]

**MOSES.** Let us establish the first title in this way: it will contain the arguments with which you attack us and our teachers, namely, that we attribute a body to God and ascribe to his nature things that the truth of reason rejects. Let us therefore examine this matter carefully until we arrive at its investigation by reason and argument.

**PETER.** I approve the proposal.

**MOSES.** First of all, then, I want you to show me where our teachers said that God has a body and a form, and how they spoke on this matter.

**PETER.** If you wish to know where it is written, it is in the first part of your doctrine, whose title is *Benedictions*. If, then, you wish to know how they said that God has a head and arms, and wears a small box (*pixida*) bound by a strap in his hair, with the knot of that strap fastened at the back of his head below the brain; and that inside the box are four scrolls containing the praises of the Jews; and that at the top of his left arm he wears another box, likewise bound with a strap, containing a writing with all the praises said to be written in the aforementioned four—do you acknowledge that all these things are written in the manner I have described in the place I mentioned?

**MOSES.** I cannot deny what is evident.

**PETER.** What authority do they have for this matter, I ask?

**MOSES.** For the box that he wears in his hair and for the knot of the strap, they draw their authority from the passage where the Lord says to Moses: “You shall see my hinder parts, for my face shall not be seen” (Exod. XXXIII). Moses then saw the knot of the strap. But the knot itself must belong to some box. For the one that he wears on his arm, authority is brought forward from Isaiah, who says: “The Lord has sworn by his right hand and by the arm of his strength” (Isa. LXII). By the arm of his strength he wishes the left arm to be understood, in which the power of that box is contained.

**PETER.** You have brought this back to my memory. I remember that I have already read this passage, but this authority gives you no protection. For although the law states that God said to Moses, “You shall see my hinder parts,” and although it is certain that God cannot lie, so that we do not doubt that the event occurred afterward even though Scripture is silent, nevertheless the law nowhere mentions that Moses saw anything in God’s hinder parts. How, then, do you say that he saw the knot of a strap—a thing scarcely capable of being said without laughter? Moreover, since “hinder parts” may more suitably mean not only the neck but any part of the body, you prove your assertion that he saw the neck not by reason or the authority of the law, but solely by your own will.

**MOSES.** Our teachers say that “hinder parts” ought to be understood as the neck.

**PETER.** Let me proceed according to the sequence of your foolish explanation, which lacks both the support of Scripture and the aid of reason. For, even if I grant that God has a neck—a thing that seems and is impious for a wise man to say—Moses might nevertheless have seen nothing of him except his neck. Or, if we imagine that he saw something else, he could have seen a cap or the knot of a strap, namely, that crown which you say the angel named Mitraton places on God’s head every day.

**MOSES.** Our teachers certainly maintain that what he saw was the knot of a strap. For that reason they assert that God showed Moses his neck, so that he might see the knot of the strap.
