**PETER.** Let us grant, for the destruction of your argument, that what you assert is so. Even if we suppose that Moses saw the knot of that crown, while he did not see God’s face in any way, how did this prove to him that God wore a box on the front of his head?

[Col. 0542C] **MOSES.** Because Moses saw the knotted strap, the teachers understood that the box bound by it was on God’s head.

**PETER.** This understanding is not entirely sound, if we say that God carries something. Nevertheless, that strap might have been fastened to a cymbal, some bell, a precious gem, or anything of that sort. Still, to remove from you every foolish answer, I shall grant that this is as you wish and say. But once this is granted, how, I ask, could Moses understand that scrolls were contained inside, much less know what was written on them? Yet what is most worthy of wonder above all this is that, as you believe, the only thing written on that scroll is the verses that Moses himself, dying long afterward, composed while teaching the Israelite people, praising it, and that after many years Solomon, worshiping God, composed a praise of it. There is no reason why it should be believed that this was written on God’s head.

**MOSES.** What Moses did not see with bodily eyes he learned through the revelation of the Holy Spirit. As for the writings on the scrolls, I confess that I have no explanation.

**PETER.** Glory to God. For a little while you lack an answer to your foolishness. Again, if we grant that Moses saw some of these things and learned some through the revelation of the Holy Spirit, since Moses himself nowhere left this in writing and no prophet after him disclosed it, how did the secret of so hidden a matter become known to your teachers?

[Col. 0543A] **MOSES.** Through the successors of the ancients it finally came to the knowledge of our teachers.

**PETER.** Since your argument flees to the refuge of so irrational a conclusion, you will be able to establish every lie for yourself through the succession of the ancients. Yet it is highly offensive that you attribute to your teachers something they perhaps do not want, since they themselves testify that they did not receive this from the report of the ancients through Moses, but that they themselves invented such interpretations in explaining the verses.

**MOSES.** I answered not with a sound argument, but by way of escape.

**PETER.** Let us therefore hold to the truth and avoid vanity, since at the beginning of our reasoning we both established this principle.

[Col. 0543B] **MOSES.** I consider that proper.

**PETER.** Tell me, please: do you know how much truth this account contains by reason, apart from the fact that, as we established earlier, it has no authority?

**MOSES.** I see that authority is destroyed in both respects. Now I require you to demonstrate it by the reasoning of nature.

**PETER.** You insist that God has a head, arms, and the entire form of a body. If this is so, then you must admit that God necessarily consists of dimensions of length and height. If he is enclosed by these three dimensions, he is therefore bounded by the six parts of a body; and that is incongruous, as will be shown in its proper place.

As for the strap that you say he has on his head, I put two alternatives before you. Your strap is either from him or from elsewhere. If it is from him, then God has already been divided from himself. But if it is from elsewhere, it is either the Creator or a creature. If it is the Creator, then there are two creators; if it is a creature, then some creature is greater than some part of the Creator, which is incongruous.

Again I ask: does he carry what he wears on his head or arm out of some necessity, or without necessity? If he carries it out of necessity, then the Creator needs a creature, which is another incongruity. Now you can plainly recognize that I have shown you by the reason you requested what a vile thing this strap is that you believe in.

**MOSES.** I understand.

[Col. 0543D] **PETER.** Again, your teachers assert in their book of doctrines that God is only in the west, confirming this by the authority of Ezra, who says: “The army of heaven supplicates you” (II Esdras IX). They explain this by saying that, when all the stars descend toward the west, then the army of heaven supplicates God; and since this supplication of the stars occurs in the west, they therefore assert that God is in the west. This, as I say, is their opinion. Although they are strangers to the name of God, if at least they recognized the form of the world, they would not entertain such unworthy thoughts about God.

**MOSES.** I wish you to show me, if it pleases you, how it can be inferred from this statement that they did not recognize the form of the world.

**PETER.** Because we call “east” only the place where a star first appears, and “west” only the place where it is withdrawn from our sight.

**MOSES.** Now I beg you to show me the definite place of east and west and to examine the knowledge of this matter precisely.

**PETER.** Since you have asked that this matter be shown to you precisely, you too ought to contemplate it with a discerning eye. Consider it in this way. Stand wherever you wish, and from that place draw a straight line toward the east. When it reaches a place beyond which your sight can extend no farther, understand that place to be the east for you. In the same way, if from the place where you stand you draw a straight line toward the west, when it reaches a place that sets a limit to your sight, establish that place for yourself as the west.

**MOSES.** Now I wish you to show me the hour of the true rising and the hour of the true setting.

**PETER.** When a star is rising, extend the aforementioned line as far as the star itself and fix the line at the center of the star, so that half of it appears above the earth and half remains hidden beneath it; call that moment the rising of the star. When the sun begins to rise above the earth in this manner, that hour is, among astronomers, the true rising of the day.

Likewise, when a star is setting, direct the aforesaid line toward that western region as far as the star and fix the end of the line at its center, so that half stands above the earth and half beneath it; call that moment the setting. When the sun sets in this manner, that hour is, among astronomers, the true setting of the day [Col. 0544C] and the beginning of night.

**MOSES.** From your reasoning the following conclusion follows: although the eastern part of the globe is the same for everyone, the place of the east is not the same for everyone. Likewise, although the western part is not the same for everyone, the hour of rising is not the same for us and the other peoples, nor is the hour of setting the same for us and the other peoples. Rather, according to the variation of the places of the earth in longitude, the place of the east and west and the hour of rising and setting vary.

**PETER.** I am pleased that you grasp the truth of the matter.

**MOSES.** Please speak still more clearly and demonstrate so subtle a matter by some comparison.

**PETER.** Let us therefore place the sun at the first degree of Aries and at the first point of that degree, and let us say that it has just begun to rise for the city of Aren, which is situated in the first of the seven climates of the earth. It has ninety degrees to the east and as many to the west, and it likewise has ninety degrees to the north pole and as many to the south. When, I say, the sun begins to rise for this city, what hour will it be for the city that is sixty degrees distant westward from the city of Aren?

**MOSES.** According to what I find written in the books of astrologers, two hours of the preceding night still remain.

**PETER.** When, then, the sun has set for the city of Aren, what hour will it be for the city mentioned above?

**MOSES.** Likewise, two hours of the day remain.

[Col. 0545A] **PETER.** But when the sun begins to rise for that city, what hour will it already be for the city of Aren?

**MOSES.** After two hours have elapsed, the third hour begins.

**PETER.** And when the sun has set for that city, what hour will it be for the city of Aren?

**MOSES.** Two hours of the night have now been completed.

**PETER.** If, then, you draw a straight line from the city of Aren and extend one end toward the east and the other toward the west, and in the same way draw a straight line from the other city, with one end extending toward the east and the other reaching toward the west, will the termini of the two lines, on either side, be able to coincide together?

**MOSES.** Not at all. The farther apart the cities are from one another, the farther apart will the ends of the lines be on either side—namely, by thirty degrees.

[Col. 0545B] **PETER.** Now it is perfectly clear to you that the places of the east and west and the hours of rising and setting are not the same for everyone but vary according to the different longitudes of the earth.

**MOSES.** At last I understand it well.

**PETER.** Again, when the sun rises for the city of Aren, if at that same hour in the other city we mentioned you extend a line from the east of that city to its west, which points of the sky will the summits of its two ends touch?

**MOSES.** The summit that turns toward the east will occupy the first point of the first degree of Pisces, while the one directed toward the west will strike the first point of the first degree of Virgo.

**PETER.** Again, when the sun is setting for the city of Aren, if in the other city we extend a line toward the sky at both ends in the manner described, which parts of the sky will each summit touch?

**MOSES.** The one extended toward the east will meet the first point of the first degree of Virgo; the one toward the west will meet the first point of the first degree of Pisces.

**PETER.** Again, when the sun is rising for that city, if at the city of Aren we draw lines extending toward its east and west up to the sky itself, which part of the sky will each summit touch?

**MOSES.** The one that touches the east will strike the first portion of the first degree of Taurus; the one that touches the west will meet the first point of the first degree of Scorpio.

**PETER.** But when the sun is setting for that city, if we draw the aforesaid line from the city of Aren in the stated manner toward the pivots of the sky, which parts of that same sky will each summit touch?

**MOSES.** The eastern summit will touch the beginning of the first degree of Scorpio, while the western summit will touch the beginning of the first degree of Taurus.

**PETER.** Now you can recognize that the degree of the sign that is in the east when the sun appears for the city of Aren is not the same as the degree that appears at the same hour for another city. Likewise, the degree that is in the west when the sun sets at Aren is not the same as the one that appears at the same hour for another city. And this occurs for all cities, according as one is distant from another in longitude.

**MOSES.** I understand everything clearly.

**PETER.** Nor is that part of the sky which today appears in the east at sunrise from any place on earth the same part that will appear tomorrow at the same hour in the same place on earth.

**MOSES.** This too is plainly evident.

**PETER.** This variation of the degrees in the sky occurs every day, just as the sun itself continually varies through those same degrees.

**MOSES.** I cannot deny what reason demonstrates.

PETRUS. Since it is necessarily established by reason that matters are as we have said, and since throughout the whole extent of the earth the places of east and west are not equal, nor are the hours of rising and setting the same, it necessarily follows that stars which set for some rise for others at that same hour. Nor is there in the entire sphere of heaven any fixed place of east and west; rather, it changes daily through various degrees. Much less, then, should one believe that a change of east and west occurs among the celestial creatures, for no obscurity ever intervenes among them, but the brightness of unfailing light shines eternally, as the prophet David says: “For darkness shall not be darkened by you, and night shall be illuminated like day; as its darkness is, so also is its light” (Psalm 38); and Daniel: “He,” he says, “reveals deep and hidden things, and knows what is established in darkness, and light is always with him” (Daniel 2). Since, moreover, no ascent or descent in heaven can be a local change, it is therefore most plainly evident to anyone that in heaven there is neither east nor west. Once this has been proved, the folly of those who say that God’s place is in the west, where the stars supplicate God, is obvious.

MOYSES. Although I cannot resist manifest arguments, I nevertheless wish, if it pleases you, to be shown how the lengths of cities distant from one another can be proved or determined, so that we may better understand the differences of the hours appearing over them at the same time.

PETRUS. Let us therefore place the sun at the first point of Aries. If a solar eclipse begins at the city of Aren, it will certainly be at the first point of the seventh hour; at that same hour the first degree of Cancer will be in the east of Aren itself. If you then wish to know at what hour the same eclipse begins in the other city mentioned above, by looking carefully you will find that it begins there at the first point of the fifth hour; at that very moment the first point of Gemini will appear in the east of that city. Hence it is indubitably clear that the two cities are thirty degrees apart in longitude. By this method astrologers determine how great the longitude between two cities is.

MOYSES. Drawing the veil of great blindness from my breast, you have poured into me the lamp of truth most brilliantly; may God therefore grant you a worthy reward in return. But since I remember your having said above that the city of Aren is situated in the middle of the hemisphere of heaven, so that it is equally distant from all parts, and that it lies in the first of the seven climates, I want you, by showing me the description of this location with the greatest clarity, to make me understand it as though I were standing in that same city. For when you say that Aren is situated in the middle of the earth, you seem to indicate that the surface of the earth is flat; but from the reasoning you gave earlier concerning east and west, you indicated that the earth has a spherical roundness. Everything round, however, lacks a beginning and an end; but wherever you seek a beginning or an endpoint, there without doubt you will also find the middle.

PETRUS. Consider, then, that Aren lies in such a place on the terrestrial sphere that it is equally distant from both the northern and southern poles, and that the two first points of Aries and Libra pass daily through its middle. Thus it will be ninety degrees from either pole, and Aren will lie, with respect to longitude, in the first part of the first climate.

MOYSES. From your words it can be gathered that the entire habitable part of the earth consists in only one region. I therefore wish to know which region that is.

PETRUS. From the middle of the earth toward the northern part.

MOYSES. I desire that you show this to me visibly in a geometrical figure, since I do not doubt that different peoples, on the evidence of their books, have held differing opinions about this matter. They also divide the earth into five zones: they say that the middle one, scorched by the sun’s heat, is therefore uninhabitable; they prove that the two outermost zones, being farthest from the sun, are likewise uninhabitable because of the immensity of the cold; but they assert that the two middle zones, tempered by the heat of the former and the cold of the latter, are the only habitable ones.

PETRUS. That opinion is contradicted by what sight demonstrates. For by sight we prove that Aren is situated in the middle of the earth, and that the beginning of Aries and of Libra proceeds above it in a straight line; and that the air there is so temperate that the periods of spring, summer, autumn, and winter are almost always equal there. Aromatic plants of beautiful color and honey-sweet taste grow there. The bodies of human beings there are neither excessively lean nor excessively fat, but are well formed through a balanced distribution of humors. The temperateness of the climate also renders human bodies harmonious with one another, as well as livestock, because they possess ineffable wisdom and natural justice. How, then, could anyone presume to say that the place over which the sun passes in a straight line is uninhabitable? Rather, the entire habitable extent of the earth exists as a continuous region from the aforesaid place to the northern globe. The ancients divided it into seven parts, which they called the seven climates, according to the number of the seven planets. The first of these lies on the central line, where the city of Aren was founded; the seventh occupies the extremity of the northern world, while the others contain the intervening space. No place is uninhabitable except where either the dryness of extensive sands together with scant water, or the roughness of mountains, prevents the plow from carrying its burdens. A figure placed before the eyes demonstrates all these things:

[Col. 0548A]

[Col. 0548B] The northern extremity, uninhabitable because of cold

MOYSES. By briefly but brilliantly demonstrating to me a matter hitherto unknown, you have satisfied my desire; I thank you. I therefore ask you to show me why either that part of the earth which lies beyond Aren toward the south is not inhabited, as this part which lies on this side toward the north is, so that Aren may be in the middle of the habitable region; or why the part beyond is not habitable while the part on this side toward the north is uninhabitable.

PETRUS. Because the center of the sun’s circle lies outside the center of the earth’s circle on the northern side. Thus, when the sun descends to the six signs of the southern region, which extend from Libra to Aries, it is then nearer to the earth; and by the proximity of its heat, scorching the earth, it renders all things unfruitful and completely sterile, and therefore that region is uninhabitable. From the first climate, therefore, as far as the north, a habitable region remains, divided into seven distinct climates. Whatever lies beyond the seventh climate, when the sun declines from there toward the six signs of the southern region, remains deprived of all heat and abounds in an excess of rain, clouds, and cold; consequently, it lacks the habitation of every living creature. How the center of the sun’s circle lies outside the center of the earth’s circle on the northern side, the diagram placed before the eyes clearly demonstrates:

[Col. 0548D]

[Col. 0549A] MOYSES. I thank you for demonstrating, by a brief but lucid argument, a matter hitherto unknown to me; and I see that you have sufficiently answered those who hold somewhat different opinions about the division of the earth.

PETRUS. Since, by God’s will, the present discussion has been completed, I am willing to return to the subject at hand.

MOYSES. I consider that appropriate.

PETRUS. In the third book of their doctrinal work, your teachers assert that God is in a place bounded on six sides, supporting this with the testimony of Daniel, who says: “As I was going out, behold, the prince of the Greeks entered” (Daniel 10). From this they infer that God is in a place where there is an entrance and an exit. If this is so, it is therefore clear that he exists in a place bounded on six sides. But if he is enclosed within a bounded place, then some place is empty of God. If that is so, how does he know what happens in another place where he is not, or how does he act in it?

MOYSES. He can indeed possess such wisdom and will that he both knows by wisdom what exists elsewhere and acts there by will.

PETRUS. I therefore want you to answer me whether that wisdom and will are in him and always with him, or outside him, and thus also without him. For if you say that they are in him and not outside him, the same consequence follows for them as for him: they will not be in every place. How, then, can he know what exists elsewhere or act there? But if you say that they are outside him and fill every place, then they are distinct from him. They know something that he does not know, and they act by themselves in a way he does not act. They, therefore, are the creators, and the world has no need of God.

MOYSES. They can indeed be in him and, by knowing and acting, radiate into every place, just as the sun, although it remains in one place, nevertheless spreads its rays everywhere, heating and illuminating.

PETRUS. If this is so, it follows that this wisdom and will do not exist equally everywhere. For whatever is spread out in this way does not have the same force at its extremity as at its source, which is wholly incompatible with God. Since you dare to impose a boundary upon God, would that you at least believed him to be simple and did not attribute bodily accidents to him!

MOYSES. How do you say that we should believe this?

[Col. 0549D] PETRUS. You say, indeed, that he becomes angry once each day, once in the day, bringing forward as evidence David, who says: “The Mighty One is angry every day” (Psalm 7). You also assert that he becomes angry at the first hour of the day, saying that the cause of this anger is that at that hour the kings of iniquity rise up, place diadems upon themselves, and worship the sun. Do you see how absurd this statement is, and how foolish are those who put it forward, since they have no understanding at all of the nature of anger? If they knew it, they would not hold this opinion about God.

MOYSES. What, then, do you consider anger to be?

PETRUS. Anger occurs when, after hearing something displeasing in speech, red bile—that is, gall—boils, spreads over the liver, and mingles with the blood. As a result, the human being grows hot and becomes pale in the face. This, however, belongs only to a thing composed of the four elements. God is not subject to such bodily configurations.

MOYSES. I cannot contradict the truth.

PETRUS. No less abhorrent is their claim that he becomes angry over something for which he cannot take revenge. For if he could, his anger would certainly cease. They further say that no one has ever known the exact point of the hour at which he becomes angry except Balaam son of Beor. In this statement, however, you contradict yourselves, since on the one hand Moses calls him a soothsayer (Numbers 22), and you also call him wicked; while on the other hand you imply that he was wiser than Moses, because he knew the precise point of the hour that had escaped Moses. And although this claim is made with great admiration, it becomes insignificant when compared with the greater folly of your assertion that a rooster, an irrational animal, knows the exact point of that hour every day. Do you concede that they said all these things in this way?

MOYSES. Even if I wished to deny it, I cannot.

PETRUS. Nor is it enough for them to say this about God: they also say that he weeps once each day, and that two tears issuing from his eyes fall into the great sea; they assert that this is the flash seen to fall from the stars at night. This reasoning, however, shows that God is composed of the four elements. For tears are produced only from an abundance of moisture descending from the head. If this is so, then the elements are God’s matter. Every matter, however, is prior to and simpler than its form. Therefore these things are prior to and simpler than God, which it is impious to believe. Accordingly, if God is such as you say he is, since he neither partakes of food nor drink and emits two tears from himself every day, he must diminish—unless perhaps he continually drinks from the waters that are above the heavens. From their words it can also be inferred that they do not know what that flash is.

MOYSES. I wish to know what you think that flash is.

PETRUS. A certain smoky vapor rises from the earth, exceedingly dry; it therefore passes through the region of the clouds and reaches a place where there is not much heat, because it is remote from the motion of the firmament. When it arrives there, and a great quantity of it has gathered in one place, it is gradually burned by the slight heat of that place; once burned, it vanishes. This is what we see moving rapidly through the air.

MOYSES. Since through you I continually grow more learned, I rightly give you uninterrupted thanks.

PETRUS. They also say that the weeping which they unworthily attribute to God is caused by the captivity of the Jews. Indeed, they assert that because of his grief he roars three times a day like a lion, and for that reason beats the heavens with his feet in the manner of those treading grapes in a winepress; that he also produces a certain murmuring sound like a dove; that each time he shakes his head and says in a voice of grief: “Alas for me, alas for me! Why have I reduced my house to a desert, burned my temple, and transferred my children among the nations? Alas for the father who transferred his children, and alas for the children who were transferred from their father’s table!” They also say that one of your teachers heard this voice in a certain noisy place. Furthermore, they say that he strikes his feet together like a woman in labor, claps his hands in the manner of one grieving, and that he prays daily that his mercy may be upon his anger and that he may go among his people in mercy. Tell me, O Moyses: when God prays, whom, I ask, does he worship? Himself or another? If another, the one whom he worships is more powerful than he. If he worships himself, either he is powerful enough to accomplish the thing for which he prays, or he is powerless. If he is powerless, he worships himself in vain; but if he is powerful, either he wishes what he prays for or he does not wish it. If he does not wish it, he prays for nothing. If he does wish it, there is no need to pray. You see, therefore, O Moyses, how entirely this people is alien to divine knowledge. But if it is true that God weeps for you, roars like a lion, beats the heavens with his feet, groans like a dove, shakes his head, and cries out in excessive grief, “Alas for me,” and moreover strikes his feet together in grief, claps his hands, and prays daily that he may have mercy on you, what prevents your captivity from being ended? Does this delay proceed from you or from him? For in this way you show him to be less powerful for accomplishing his own will, when you claim that, wishing to accomplish something but unable to do so, he weeps like a child. If, then, he is powerless now, say whether he will have power in the future or not. If he will ever have it, then both your grief and his will be without end, your prayer will be empty, and there will be no hope. But if he is going to acquire the power, either he has not yet had it but will possess it at a predetermined and fixed time, and when he has it he will free you from captivity; or he already had it but lost it through the intervention of certain accidents, and, once these have again been removed, he will recover it and lead you out of captivity. If he is to have it at a fixed time, you must still say what now prevents him from having it: whether you attribute this to the small number of his years, to weakness of his limbs, or to the obstacle of some matter from which he cannot defend himself. It is impious to believe this about God. For we read in the sacred Scriptures, in which you join us in placing faith, that God performed greater miracles in ancient times than freeing you from captivity would have been. For example, he struck Egypt with ten plagues (Exodus 7–8), then brought you out from there with a mighty hand and divided the Red Sea, into which he submerged Pharaoh with his army (Exodus 14); he fed you in the desert with manna and quail from heaven (Psalm 77; Exodus 16; Numbers 11); he also made the waters of the Jordan stand in one place like a mountain (Joshua 3); at Joshua’s prayers he made the sun and moon stand still (Joshua 10); in a single night he caused one hundred and eighty-five thousand of Sennacherib’s army to be killed (2 Kings 19; Sirach 48). In the days of Hezekiah he commanded the sun to turn back fifteen steps (2 Kings 20). He delivered Daniel from the lions’ den (Daniel 16), Hananiah, Mishael, and Azariah from the fire (Daniel 3), and delivered you from the captivity of Babylon (1 Esdras 7); and he performed many other miracles that it would take too long to enumerate. You cannot therefore say that he was not powerful in ancient days. But if, as is right, you grant that he was indeed powerful, yet say that through the intervention of other accidents he became powerless, and believe that after those accidents have departed he will recover his ability, you must necessarily admit one of two things: either those accidents existed from him and in him, as an illness, an accident affecting a human being, restrains the execution of his will until he recovers; or they were inflicted upon him by another, as captivity inflicted upon someone by a king deprives him of the power to exercise his will until it departs with the arrival of freedom. If you say that they existed from him and in him, then you say that God has a body susceptible to contraries, which is not fitting to believe about God. But if you say that they were inflicted upon him by another, you show that the one who inflicted them is more powerful than God, which is no less unacceptable. If you say that you yourselves are the cause of your captivity, as though it were better for you now to be in captivity than formerly in freedom, it is obvious to everyone that this is false, because captivity can never be compared with freedom. But if you delay your freedom for some other reason—namely, because he wishes to free you and you, through obstinacy, resist his will, so that because he cast you into captivity you, in opposition, wish to remain in captivity longer than he wishes—then he ought to satisfy your will and not continually burden himself with such great grief; or you ought to spare him and not cause him such sorrow. But this cannot stand at all, since you pray to him daily to rescue you from captivity. I therefore beg you, Moyses, to drive such a labyrinth of circumstantial arguments from my breast.

MOYSES. None of the things you have enumerated prevents our captivity. Rather, we confess that God always has been and is omnipotent; nor do we deny that we wish to escape captivity. But we say that God has appointed a fixed end for our captivity, and that until the time arrives which he has determined, sworn, and confirmed, we cannot possibly be freed.

PETRUS. In this statement you attribute ignorance to God, since you say that he determined and swore to something that afterward he regrets having sworn and confirmed. The sign of this is that he is continually afflicted on your behalf in so many ways; if he had foreseen it, he would not have determined it beforehand. According to you, therefore, he was foolish. Since this is established among you, you ought certainly to forgive him and not trouble him with continual prayers. For the more frequently you pray, the more you renew his grief; and the more, by ceasing from prayer, you refrain from disturbing him, the more you allow him to be consoled. But tell me, I beg you, O Moyses—tell me, I say—should anyone believe teachers of this kind and entrust himself to their treatises?

MOYSES. Since they confirm their statements by the authority of the prophets, why do you attack them so severely while saying nothing against the prophets? Do you not know that the prophets said that God has a head, eyes, nostrils, hands, arms, and all the features of a body? They themselves also said that he becomes angry every day, roars like a lion, and many other things that are confirmed by their authority.

PETRUS. The statements of the prophets are obscure and not sufficiently clear to everyone. For this reason, whenever we find in the prophets things which, if taken according to the letter, would cause us to stray from the path of reason, we interpret them allegorically, so as to bring them back to the path of correctness. Necessity compels us to act in this way, since otherwise the literal meaning cannot stand. Your teachers, however, did not understand God as they ought to have done; therefore, by explaining the prophets’ statements only on the surface, they went astray concerning him. This is why, and because of many similar matters, I said above that I understand the prophets’ statements as sound judgment requires.

[Col. 0553B] MOYSES. I now want you to show me a passage that must necessarily be understood allegorically because, if expounded according to the letter, it cannot stand, so that it may become clear that what you say is true.

PETRUS. I will show you what you ask. For Moses says to Pharaoh: “The locust will cover the eye of the whole earth” (Exodus 10). Does the earth, then, have an eye? Again, the same writer says concerning the sons of Korah: “The earth opened its mouth and swallowed them” (Numbers 16). Does the earth, then, have a mouth? Again, in the Book of Judges Gaal says to Zebul: “Behold, a people has descended from the navel of the earth” (Judges 9). But does the earth have a navel? Isaiah says again: “From the wing of the earth we have heard praises” (Isaiah 24). Does the earth have a wing? David also says: “The fields and all that is in them will rejoice” (Psalm 95). Again, the same writer says: “The rivers will clap their hands; the mountains will rejoice” (Psalm 98). Can fields rejoice, rivers have hands, or mountains exult? Solomon also says: “The birds of heaven will carry your word, and the one who has wings will announce the sentence” (Ecclesiastes 10). Can a bird speak a word, or can one who has wings announce anything? The prophet Habakkuk also says: “The stone will cry out from the wall, and the wood that is between the joints of the buildings will answer” (Habakkuk 2). Can a stone cry out, or can wood answer?

MOYSES. I confess that what you say is true, and that in many passages an allegorical meaning is necessary. Nevertheless, as for what the prophets said about God’s bodily features, if it is expounded according to the letter, I do not know why you have called it absurd.

PETRUS. The bodily accidents that you attribute to God correspond only to bodily substance and an imagined thing. It is improper to believe that God is such. Therefore, what has been said about God as though he were corporeal should not be expounded solely according to the letter. For if anyone holds this opinion, he stands opposed both to Scripture and to reason.

MOYSES. I want you to show why someone who understands it in this way is opposed to Scripture.

PETRUS. Because if we say that God has any image or likeness, we contradict many authoritative statements of the prophets. For Moses says to the children of Israel: “Guard your souls carefully. You did not see any likeness on the day when the Lord spoke to you at Horeb from the midst of the fire, lest, deceived, you make for yourselves a carved likeness or image of a man or woman, the likeness of any beast that is upon the earth, or of birds flying beneath the heavens, or of reptiles that move upon the earth, or of fish that dwell beneath in the waters” (Deuteronomy 4). After prohibiting them from likening God to bodies composed of parts, and fearing also that they might conform him to simple bodies, he added: “Lest, raising your eyes to heaven, you see the sun and moon and all the stars of heaven, and, deceived by error, worship and serve them, which the Lord God created for all the nations beneath heaven” (ibid.). Do not suppose that Moses, when giving this command to the people, feared that they would worship figures or images of the aforesaid bodies, since they did not doubt that these were creatures. Rather, he feared that they might believe God to possess the image of one of these things and therefore worship likenesses of this kind made in his place.

MOYSES. This is a very subtle argument, and it is not accessible to everyone’s understanding; therefore I still need some clearer examples.

PETRUS. The prophet Isaiah says: “To whom have you likened me and made me equal? says the Holy One” (Isaiah 40). And again: “To whom have you made God like, or what image will you set beside him?” (ibid.). And again: “To whom have you likened and made me equal and compared me, and made me like?” (ibid.). David’s words also prove that God is not local, and thereby indicate consequently that he is not corporeal. For he says: “Where shall I go from your spirit, and where shall I flee from your presence? If I ascend into heaven, you are there; if I descend into the underworld, you are present. If I take my wings at dawn and dwell at the ends of the sea, even there your hand will lead me, and your right hand will hold me” (Psalm 139). Solomon, holding the same opinion, says: “Must it then be thought that God truly dwells upon the earth? For if heaven and the heaven of heavens cannot contain you, how much less this house that I have built?” (2 Chronicles 2). And elsewhere: “In every place the eyes of the Lord contemplate the good and the wicked” (2 Chronicles 16). Jeremiah says: “Can a man hide himself in secret places, and I will not see him? says the Lord. Do I not fill heaven and earth? says the Lord” (Jeremiah 23). Now you can clearly perceive that if, while saying that God has a body and all the members of a body, we explain the Scriptures—which we wish to use as authority to prove this—only on the surface, we contradict all the testimonies mentioned above.

MOYSES. Since I see how contrary my understanding is to Scripture, I wish, in accordance with your promise, to hear how far it also deviates from reason.

PETRUS. As we are about to recline in the palace of great reason, let us spread the floor of that palace with certain flowers of argument, so that afterward we may sit there and reason more pleasantly. Those arguments will serve as steps for us toward proving that God exists and discovering what he is. First, we must prove that God exists, and afterward show that nothing is like him. For some people deny that God exists and assert that the world has existed eternally and without a Creator. Necessity therefore compels us first to demonstrate that God, who created the world, exists.

MOYSES. Why, when speaking about the Scriptures above, did you not do this, so as to demonstrate first that God exists?

PETRUS. Those who place faith in the Scriptures do not deny that God exists. Consequently, it was not necessary to prove this to believers in Scripture, but only to those who believe no writing.

MOYSES. Since you do not wish to prove through the Scriptures that God exists, and since he himself cannot be apprehended by any bodily sense, it greatly pleases me to hear by what philosophical reasoning this can be established.

[Col. 0555B] PETRUS. If I demonstrate that the world, together with everything in it, was created, I will necessarily conclude that God—the one who is interpreted as “Creator”—exists.

MOYSES. And how will you be able to prove this?

PETRUS. “To know” is spoken of in three ways. One thing is perceived by a bodily sense; another is known by necessary reasoning alone; a third is discovered through the likeness of other things. What is perceived by some sense cannot be proved by any other argument. Thus, someone blind from birth can distinguish differences of color in no other way than by hearing alone; yet hearing does not fully satisfy his mind, and the same applies to the other bodily senses. What is known by necessary reasoning is of the following kind: when we say that a body cannot move and stand still at the same moment; or when we say of nothing that it truly both is and is not. What is perceived through likeness is such that, if you hear a voice somewhere, you understand that something vocal is there, although you do not see it; or when you see smoke anywhere, you recognize that fire is there, even if you do not see it. Likewise, if we see a vessel that has been made, we know with certainty that some maker existed (Romans 1), even if we do not see him. Therefore, we must first prove that the world was created, so that it may be established that it had a Creator. And once we have proved the Creator of the world, we will consequently show by reason that the Creator himself has no likeness.

[Col. 0555D] MOYSES. It is fitting for me to bless you for your words, from which I believe I am receiving such great profit. Fulfill your promise, then, and spread the palace with the flowers of which you spoke.

PETRUS. In this all philosophers agree: the beginning of things is perfect wisdom, a splendid light, the substance of substances, the rationale of all things. After this comes the world of the universal soul, and after it matter. These two—the universal soul and matter—are simple, and are the first of all created things, the origin and cause of the entire composite reality. From them the firmament was made step by step, together with all the forms and images that it possesses.

MOYSES. From your words it is understood that the firmament, together with everything in it, is composite. Yet in many places I have found it written that whatever is below the circle of the moon is composite, while whatever is above it is simple.

PETRUS. In truth, the firmament, together with everything it contains, is composite; but in relation to the things beneath the circle of the moon it is called simple. This is the case with all things: something is called composite in relation to that from which it was made, but simple in relation to what is made from it. In the same way, whatever is above the moon is simple in relation to the things beneath the moon that were made from it; but in relation to matter it is composite, since it was made from matter.

MOYSES. I want to understand more clearly how the firmament, although it is one substance, can be called composite.

[Col. 0556B] PETRUS. Every body is composite, but every composite is either substantial or partitive. It is substantial when one substance is joined to another; it is partitive when the parts of one substance are joined together. A substance is joined together, for example, when a head is composed from bones, flesh, and veins joined together, or when a door is composed of wood and iron. Thus everything perfected through the conjunction of different substances is called a substantial composite. The composition of a partitive composite is more subtle. This is evident because every body, having length, breadth, and height, which is not joined to another body, is composed solely of the parts of its own substance—for example, when many parts of silver are joined until they produce something weighty and solid. This composite is simpler than the former. That alone is called simple in the fullest sense which is free from both kinds of composition. Since the firmament is a body consisting of three dimensions, it is truly composite.

MOYSES. I wish to know the reasoning by which every body consisting of length, breadth, and height is composite.

PETRUS. Every body whose nature is capable of motion in some direction moves in that direction only through its own nature. It is known that the direction toward which it moves by nature is its natural place. Since this is so, it is impossible for it to have any dimension extending toward another direction that is contrary to its natural place. If it is found to have a dimension extending in another direction, one of two things is the cause of this: either it is composite externally, as a wall joined by the superposition of stones; or internally, as the parts of a tree, emerging from within, spread themselves in this or that direction and acquire a certain dimension. From this it is understood that whatever has a dimension toward a direction contrary to the direction of its natural motion is composite. Therefore the firmament too, although it is one substance, is composite.

MOYSES. Reason has now thoroughly taught that the firmament, together with everything it possesses, is composite. But I do not know how the universal soul and matter can be found in it, or how they themselves are simple.

PETRUS. Once it has been proved that the firmament is composite, it necessarily follows that there is some matter of which it is composed, just as the matter of a bed is wood and the matter of a knife is iron. This matter must be simpler than the firmament, just as wood is simpler than a bed and iron than a knife. Since every matter is simpler than that which is made from it, and since it does not itself contain the form or image of its composite, it is clear that the matter of the firmament contains no bodily form in itself and is therefore entirely simple. But if we say that something composite exists in it, it is necessary that there be another matter from which that composite is made, and that this matter be simpler. If we then call that matter composite, we will admit that it has another, simpler matter, and so on to infinity. To avoid this, we must acknowledge that matter itself is simple. Thus it has been sufficiently proved that matter exists in the firmament and that matter itself is simple.

We shall find the soul in it as follows: the forms by which matter has been informed were not made solely for the completion of a body. Forms are spoken of in two ways. Some merely display the boundary of a body, such as triangularity, roundness, or any other figure. In a stone they serve no other purpose than to produce the shape of the body itself. Other forms both inform a body and, compelled by nature, appear to have been made suitable for some utility: the form of an ear for hearing, of an eye for seeing, and the individual forms of the other limbs, each suited to its function. Likewise, the form of a knife is for cutting, of a saw for sawing, and a rake is suitably formed for digging.

Since matter received within itself various new forms that it had never previously possessed, it is clear that it acquired them not from itself but through the conjunction of another thing that was both more excellent and simpler, which produced within itself various forms and images—especially since there was no necessity that such forms or images should be made in it. Rather, this was done by the desire of the soul, which wished to be mixed and joined with a thing with which it had never previously been mixed. Through this new mixture, matter was informed with new forms.

Since, therefore, according to the philosophers, the firmament together with everything it possesses is undoubtedly composite, it must be believed to have a beginning. For every composite has some beginning. In this way it is clear that the world was created. Every composite, moreover, must have a composer. Nothing can compose itself; likewise, everything created must have a creator, for nothing can create itself. Therefore the Creator of the world, who is called God, necessarily exists.

**MOSES.** The adversary could therefore insist, saying that this composer is the power of the universal soul—that power, namely, which is called nature. [Col. 0558A] This soul, he might say, joined to matter, composed the firmament and everything that is in it, and there is no other composer or creator of things.

**PETER.** What you say cannot stand. For since we see that the forms with which matter has been endowed are various and suited to various uses, it is clear that nature itself, through whose admixture and power the forms were made, cannot have been entirely unrestricted, but must in some way have been restricted. Yet this restricted nature must necessarily have some restrictor who is himself restricted by no one.

**MOSES.** I reply that the soul itself is this restrictor, since it restricted its own power as it wished.

**PETER.** Such works cannot belong to the soul, but to a maker of such a kind that he is perfect in wisdom in himself. [Col. 0558B] The soul, however, does not possess perfect wisdom.

**MOSES.** By what reasoning can you demonstrate that the soul does not possess perfect wisdom?

**PETER.** Because from the moment when the soul was joined to matter, and matter was incorporated into the soul, the soul has never afterward been free from alternating pains and pleasures. For no pleasure arises unless pain has preceded it: no one is ever delighted by drinking unless he has first suffered from thirst; no one is delighted by eating unless the pain of hunger has preceded it; nor does anyone delight in rest unless he has previously suffered from toil. And so it is with all the passions. But when reason strips itself of bodily contamination and contemplates itself in its purity, it judges that what feels nothing is better and more worthy than what is subject to the accidents of so many different passions. It is therefore clear that the soul does not possess perfect wisdom.

Another argument concerning the same matter may also be given: when the soul casts off reason, it immediately delights in lust, theft, murder, and other vices, which the wisdom of perfect reason detests. Hence again it is evident that the soul’s wisdom is imperfect. It has therefore been sufficiently proved, for those who do not believe the Scriptures, that there is another maker whose wisdom is perfect in itself, just as reason shows us that the works of the soul, without reason itself, are vicious and in a certain sense shameful. It follows, therefore, that the one through whom we received reason is not the soul but another, since it cannot happen that one who abhors or detests something should wish to make it. It follows also that the soul has imperfect wisdom, while the giver of reason has perfect wisdom.

And since reason operates in the soul, the giver of reason is necessarily the maker of the soul. Since this is so, and since the soul, as was proved above, formed all composite things in matter, it can be concluded without doubt that the one who gave reason made everything and exists as the cause of everything.

This, then, is the philosophical view concerning the soul. Philosophers say that the rational soul proceeds from the universal soul. The Jews, as you know, assert that all souls were created together at the beginning of the world, placed in one location, and that the day of judgment will not come until they have all been embodied; and that, once they have been embodied, the end of the world will immediately follow. Christians, however, maintain that new souls are created each day and infused into newly formed bodies in the womb. Whatever you choose to believe about the soul, nevertheless, without doubt—as has been said—the one who gave reason made everything and exists as the cause of everything.

This Creator, moreover, who possesses perfect wisdom, must be eternal and neither created nor new. For if he is believed to be either created or new, he must necessarily have another creator or renewer. Nothing can ever create or renew itself, and thus the number of creators or renewers would be without end. But if makers are without end, the thing made will never arrive at a definite limit. We must therefore believe that the first maker was neither created nor renewed, but necessarily eternal.

Furthermore, it is proper to believe that he is not composite but simple. For every composition is motion, and an activity of something simple. Again, what is prior cannot have a beginning; but every composition has some beginning. Therefore the first Creator is not composite.

Nor is he corporeal. For everything corporeal, as we discussed more fully above, is composite. Nor is he mobile. Everything that moves consists of parts; but whatever consists of parts is composite. What is first of all, however, is not composite. Therefore it is not mobile.

Again, every motion takes place in a body, whether it is rectilinear motion—as when someone leaves one place and occupies another—or circular motion, when something remaining in the same place, such as the firmament, revolves in a circle; or the motion of the parts of some thing toward one another, whether from the extremities toward the middle or from the middle toward the extremities, as occurs in the parts of the air; or the motion of a thing that remains in the same place but spreads here and there through successive stages of increase, as happens in the branches of trees, which gradually grow in every direction. None of these motions can take place except in a body. But it has been proved that what is first of all is not corporeal. Therefore it does not change and cannot perish.

Again, it neither grows by itself nor is increased by something else. Everything that receives increase or augmentation is undoubtedly composite; but we have shown above that what is first of all is not composite. Therefore it neither grows nor is augmented.

Nor does it diminish. For what diminishes perishes; but it has been proved that what is first of all does not perish. Therefore it does not diminish.

Again, it bears no likeness to any creature. Likeness is a quality; but what is first of all is subject to no quality, and therefore to no likeness.

Let us suppose, nevertheless, that it bears the likeness of some creature. It is evident that likeness makes one of two things equal to the other: for example, if two things are said to be alike in whiteness, the whiteness of one must be equal to the whiteness of the other; and the same applies to blackness and to everything else that establishes likeness between things. Therefore, if this were so, what is first of all would at the same time be first and last, and what is last would at the same time be last and first. How contradictory both of these are is obvious to everyone.

Again, since created matter has no form or image within itself, much less should God, the Creator of that nature, who is of a simpler and subtler nature, be thought to possess any likeness. Thus, fulfilling our promise, we have demonstrated, clearly, as I think, by reason that God has no likeness.

**MOSES.** I give thanks to God and to you, because I have come to know, without any obstacle of doubt, that the Creator of all is like no creature and has neither beginning nor end. It has also become clear from your words that God the Creator of all things is principally the root and foundation of everything; and secondarily, that the soul and matter exist, that God made the soul, and that the soul, made by God, operates in matter.

There is, however, one scruple that still troubles my mind, and I ask your acumen to unravel it. I have read in many books of philosophers that there were five things before the establishment of the world: God, who holds the origin of all things; then the soul and matter; and time and place. Since you have discussed the first three, I am greatly surprised that you have made no mention of the last two.

**PETER.** Because I judged that they had no bearing on the present discussion, and that it would be superfluous to speak about them.

**MOSES.** Although they may seem foreign to the discussion, I nevertheless wish to hear what you think about them, because the Catholic sages, whose faith you have embraced, have thought about these matters very differently from what the books of the ancient philosophers say. The Catholics testify that these things had a beginning, whereas the ancient philosophers testify that they are eternal.

**PETER.** Without doubt I give credence to those who have said that they existed from antiquity, not together with the world.

**MOSES.** I wish to know by reason how this can be established.

**PETER.** Place is spoken of in two ways. Sometimes it is spoken of as the cause of another thing, and sometimes in itself. It is called the place of another thing when something is inserted into a place, and that place is said to be the place of the thing while the thing remains in it; this is called a partial place. If the thing should depart from the place itself, the place loses what it previously possessed—namely, its relation—because it is no longer called the place of that thing.

Place in itself, which is called universal place, is any emptiness. We must not suppose that it exists because of the thing that is in it, since place must always precede the thing that is destined to be in it.

Concerning this place, Plato offers the following syllogism: “Everything that exists as a whole through another whole—if any part of that which is the cause of its existing is destroyed, then a part of that which exists through it is necessarily destroyed as well. But if a part of that which exists through another is destroyed, it is not nevertheless necessary that any part of that which is the cause of its existing should be destroyed.”

Since place is the cause of existence for the thing that is in it, it necessarily follows that no part of place is destroyed merely because some part of the thing existing in it is destroyed. Once this is granted, it follows also that place does not exist as the cause of something else.

For clarity, let us introduce the following comparison. Suppose we say that a mountain has been removed from some part of the world. The place in which it stood is not thereby diminished. It has lost its former name, because it can no longer be called the place of that mountain, but both the name and nature of universal place remain there.

Again, suppose you say that someone’s slave has died. Has his master therefore ceased to be his master because the slave has died? No; he has merely lost the name “master,” which he possessed in relation to that slave. It is therefore clear that when the thing located in some place is removed, the name of the partial place changes, but the substance of the place is not taken away.

Concerning time, he also says that it is a substance existing in itself, not an accident that subsists for the sake of something else. For example, if we suppose that a vessel containing water is used to mark the passing of individual hours, we must not judge that the vessel is the cause of time’s existence, but only that it is a sign for distinguishing time. Time would occur no differently even if that vessel did not exist.

In the same way, we must understand that the firmament is in no way the cause of time, but only its measure and sign. Time itself—simple, without a sign, measure, or any distinction—would exist just as the time of the hours of the day would remain undifferentiated if the vessel containing the marked water were absent.

Let us now briefly summarize everything. It has been proved that God is the maker of all things, as his works indicate to us, since they proceed from perfect wisdom; that the soul has both been made and is a maker, since it makes something in matter, although it is not corporeal; that time and place exist in themselves and are incorporeal, yet substantial; and that matter has indeed been made, but is not a maker.

**MOSES.** The clarity of manifest reason has driven the darkness of every doubt from my breast. I have learned that the world and everything in it were made, and are not eternal.

But something remains for you to complete your work: you must provide an argument against those who say that the world existed eternally—an argument that destroys their position. For they argue as follows: “What reason did the supreme Creator have for creating things so suddenly and recently, when he had not created them long before? For it is impious, they say, to believe of God that he either remembered something or suddenly saw something which he had once forgotten or had not seen.” I have previously found no answer to this question of theirs.

**PETER.** You should know that there are three roots of all actions. One action is something that ought to be done; another is something that ought not to be done; and another is simply good.

An action that ought to be done is one for which, if you perform it, you will receive thanks, but if you do not perform it, you will be blamed. An action that need not be done is one for which, if you perform it, you will be thanked; but if you do not perform it, you will nevertheless not be blamed.

The latter category is without both measure and time. For example, if someone gives alms today, one should not ask why he did not give them yesterday. Likewise, if he gives one coin, one should not investigate why he did not give two. And since the whole creation of the world is good—as Scripture also bears witness, saying, “God saw everything that he had made, and behold, it was very good” (Genesis 1)—there is no need to ask why he did not make these things earlier.

**MOSES.** I justly pray that God grant you a great reward, because you have answered so subtly the question raised by those who do not believe in the world’s creation against believers. Now I want you to explain what you said above: how everything was gradually made from the conjunction of soul and matter.

**PETER.** Philosophers say that when the soul had been joined and bound to matter, the first thing formed was the greater composite, the firmament, in which there are no stars and which causes all the circles to move.

After that the zodiacal circle was formed, in which twelve signs shine forth. Third, the circle of the stars was made; these always preserve their position and remain fixed in their places. Fourth, the circle of Saturn was established. Fifth, the sphere of Jupiter was established. Sixth, Mars’s sword claimed its place. Seventh, the circle of the Sun shines. Eighth, the globe of Venus possesses its place. Ninth, Mercury received his. The tenth place was assigned to the Moon below.

When all these circles and everything within them had been completed, that circular motion began which is called simple and perfect. That motion generated heat in matter; the heat spread through it, and matter received it. From this came the four elements: fire, air, water, and earth.

It is established that every motion which proceeds from something that moves, and every power of anything possessing power, has greater force and strength the nearer it is to the source from which it proceeds; and the farther it is from that source, the softer and weaker it becomes.

Since this is so, it is evident that the heat which proceeded from the motion of the firmament was much hotter and burning in the regions nearer to it, and became fire—dry and hot by nature.

But when that heat withdrew somewhat farther from the firmament, it lost some of its force, became moderately warm, and was weaker. It also moved here and there, and from this arose the nature of air, hot and moist. For as long as heat is strongest, it dries and burns. Once it becomes moderate, it causes a thing to soften and liquefy.

When it withdrew still farther from the firmament, its root being, as it were, at a distance, it lost its vigor. Its nature therefore remained cold, and it became liquid and heavy.

And since it withdrew still farther than before from the firmament, the nature of its coldness, because of the excessive distance, became stronger, denser, more frozen, and harder. It thus became dry and cold, and this is earth.

Once the nature of the elements had been completed in this way, that nature and the power of the firmament moved them to fulfill God’s will and command. When the power of the firmament had moved all things in this way toward one another, they were mixed and joined together, and from their very mixture other, smaller bodies were generated: inanimate things, living things, and animals.

Inanimate things include stones, metals, and other things contained within the earth that do not grow, such as quicksilver, sulfur, and the like. Living things include trees and grasses. Animals include irrational creatures, that is, beasts, and the rational creature, namely the human being, who was made after everything else.

Thus every creature began from the universal soul and proceeds step by step, passing from one thing into another, until it ends in the human being. The soul and matter, therefore, are simple and, through the ineffable providence of the supreme Creator ordering all things subject to them, are makers of everything beneath them.

Whatever is lower than these, obeying the will of the ruler above, possesses both the function of being made and of making. Each of them is made by what is above it and makes what is below it in this way.

Therefore the prophet David also sings of them, saying: “Bless the Lord, all his works, in every place of his dominion” (Psalm 102).

Although all these things are diverse, divine power nevertheless restrains them in such a way that they appear nowhere to be wholly in conflict or discordant with one another. David likewise testifies to this elsewhere, saying: “Let them praise the name of the Lord, for he spoke, and they were made; he commanded, and they were created. He established them for ever and ever; he gave a command, and it shall not pass away” (Psalm 148).

Each lower thing, in relation to what is above it, is called simple; but in relation to what is below it, it is called composite. The human body, however, which is lower than everything else, since there is nothing beneath it in relation to which it could be called simple, is rightly called wholly composite. Thus the human being was made from a completely simple creature—the soul—and from a body wholly composite.

God poured into him and illuminated him with the wisdom of his exalted nature, through which he could know and distinguish all things. The human form was therefore made better, more elegant, and superior in every respect than all the forms of animals. Hence it is not unjustly called the lesser world.

**MOSES.** You have demonstrated a difficult matter, obscure and unknown to many, in a brilliant and sufficiently clear discourse. From these words of yours I now plainly understand what Moses could have meant, philosophically, at the beginning of the book of Genesis. He says: “In the beginning God created heaven and earth” (Genesis 1)—that is, the universal soul and matter. He then enumerated all creatures in succession until he reached the human being, who was finally created on the sixth day after the succession of the days.

But another question arises among some who do not at all believe that God is the Creator of the world. It is this: “If all worldly things were not created by themselves, they say, but there is another Creator who created everything, and if he is, as you say, omnipotent, why did he not complete all these things in one day, rather than working little by little over so many days?” I do not know what should be answered to this.

**PETER.** Reason does not allow us to believe that, because one creature was created later than another, their supreme Creator was therefore less powerful. His inability was not involved in this; rather, one of the creatures was softer and another harder in receiving its creation and form.

For example, suppose you take a single mass in which iron, bronze, lead, tin, pitch, and wax have all been placed together, and suppose that you put this mass, mixed from all these substances, wholly into the fire at one and the same moment. Will everything liquefy at one and the same instant?

Certainly not. First the wax will melt, then the pitch, afterward the tin, next the lead, then the bronze, and finally the iron.

Do you attribute to the power of the fire the fact that some melt more quickly than others, or do you attribute it to their differing degrees of hardness?

**MOSES.** No one doubts that the power of the fire is the same toward all of them; the softer melt more quickly, while the harder melt more slowly.

**PETER.** In the same way, the passage of so many days in the creation of the world occurred for no other reason than that some of the creatures were slower in receiving their form.

**MOSES.** Once the error of doubt has been removed, I now see the light of truth.

**PETER.** This argument is sufficiently clear and sound for anyone, supported on every side by proof from argument and reason. Yet your teachers, while stubbornly attempting to resist us on certain points, are also found to contradict themselves.

**MOSES.** If you please, show me what this error is.

**PETER.** They say that when God established the firmament, he deliberately refused to complete it entirely and left unfinished the space of a great opening in the northern region. They assert that he did this so that, if someone should ever rise up, make himself equal to God, and say that he was God, God could oppose him with the completion of that space, saying: “If you are a god like me, close that place if you can—the place which I left open.”

But how obvious a lie this is escapes no one’s sight. For we always see the axis of the northern pole, at its greatest height, above us, and never hidden; and we see it whole, complete, and perfect. Do you perceive, then, how manifest this error is?

**MOSES.** I do perceive it, and I recognize that this statement is deprived of every force of reason.

**PETER.** Is not the lie they invented about Korah’s keys much more shameful and absurd?

**MOSES.** In what way do they appear to you to be lying?

**PETER.** They said—as you yourself know—that when Korah was passing through the wilderness with Moses and the children of Israel, he had three hundred camels loaded with nothing except the keys to his treasure. All these keys, they say, were made from strips of cowhide so that they could be carried more easily.

Let us calculate, then, if you please, O Moses, and see whether this can stand. Let us assume, at minimum, six keys to a pound, and that each camel carried at least six hundred pounds. A single camel would therefore carry three thousand six hundred keys. Thus the keys borne by three hundred camels would number 1,080,000.

But since every key is for at least one chest, there would undoubtedly be as many chests as keys. Let us therefore allow at least two chests to each camel, and there would be 540,000 camels carrying chests.

Moreover, according to the custom of the wealthy, who take greater care to guard their riches, at least two camels ought to have had one guard, who, preserving the treasures with the utmost diligence, would scarcely even sleep. There would therefore be 240,000 camel guards.

But from the book we have learned that Korah’s army, organized by houses, kinships, and families, numbered only 8,600 men.

No less ridiculous is the similar story they tell about the sons of Jacob carrying their father to the tomb. They say that the sons of Esau, likewise carrying their father to the tomb, met them with a large retinue. Since a great army was present on both sides, and each party wanted to claim the tomb for itself, they say that Dan’s son climbed a mountain and cut off a stone as large as the entire army of Esau might have been. He placed the mass on his head and brought it along so that, throwing it upon the enemy’s wedge, he might overthrow them all with a single blow.

But when he arrived and found that the two sides had already reached an agreement, he threw the mass he had brought into the sea. The sea’s waters, exceeding their bounds because of the size of the mass, overturned two cities by their overflowing. These, they say, were the cities that Pharaoh, king of Egypt, later ordered the children of Israel to build.

Does not this invention, I ask, rightly seem worthy of the greatest laughter? For when Jacob’s sons were still only twelve in number, there were already four hundred men of Esau’s tribe. Now that the number of Jacob’s sons had increased, how much greater must the number of Esau’s sons be thought to have been? Their multitude therefore had to be so great that it could resist both the sons of Jacob and the whole Egyptian people who had come with Joseph.

Tell me now which of these matters is more worthy of admiration: where he found such a large mountain; on what mountain there was a mass of such astonishing size; or how he could carry such a heavy stone on his head, so that he could overthrow so large a cohort?

No less astonishing is the monster-story they tell about Og, king of Bashan. Seeing the immense army of Israel—namely, 604,500 men twenty years old and above, not counting the women and children, who could not be counted—he placed a mass of unheard-of size upon his head and wished to overthrow the entire army with it.

But a very small bird, a hoopoe, settled beneath the mass and battered it with its beak for so long that it bored a large hole in it, proportionate to the head of that same king. The mass passed over his head and came to rest upon his shoulders.

With his head unharmed and his entire body uninjured, he might perhaps still have lifted it from his neck, had he not suddenly been hindered by the size of his enlarged teeth. For as soon as the stone descended onto his neck, his teeth suddenly grew so large that, when he wished to lift it again, he could not.

When Moses saw this—for you assert that his body was ten cubits high and assign the same length to his staff—he raised himself ten cubits above the ground in the manner of a leaping man, so that he might strike him somewhere on the body with his staff.

If, then, you calculate the ten cubits by which he was raised from the ground, the ten cubits of his body, and the other ten cubits to which his staff extended upward, you will find thirty cubits from the ground to the top of the staff. Yet although Moses had raised himself so high, the top of the staff with which he intended to strike him could reach no farther than the joint where the lower leg joins the foot, which is commonly called the ankle.

When he struck him there, he immediately fell and died. From this anyone can understand that from the sole of the foot which he kept fixed on the ground to the joint at which he was struck there were thirty cubits. From that point to the top of his body there were therefore no fewer than eight hundred cubits, while the head alone could easily have been ten cubits high. It follows that that bird bored through the mass itself for ten cubits.

When I consider how many astonishing things are involved in this feat, and what I should be more astonished by, I am amazed. Where could one find a stone so large, or how could he carry so great a weight? Or how could such a tiny bird penetrate so quickly a body of stone so immense, so hard, and so dense? By what means could his teeth grow so quickly? Or how are we to believe that he was of such immeasurable and unheard-of size, especially since the Law says that his iron bed was only nine cubits long (Deuteronomy 3)? And how could so enormous a man have fallen from such an easy wound?

Let me still disclose another ridiculous matter, in order to reveal even more clearly their stupidity. They say that Moses ascended into heaven to receive the Law, and that there he argued with the angels in the following manner. The angels, they say, said: “We will certainly not allow you to carry away this Law, which we know to be more necessary for us than for the children of Israel.”

Terrified by this extraordinary vision, Moses did not dare to answer anything. But when the Lord strengthened him so that he might answer confidently, and commanded him to do so, he said to the angels: “Since this Law contains instructions for governing bodies, I do not sufficiently understand what need you have of it, since you are creatures that are entirely spiritual.”

The angels, having nothing to say in reply, fell silent, defeated. You say that God laughed at Moses’ victory and rejoiced greatly, and that Moses afterward descended joyfully with the Law.

How many varieties of stupidity, I ask, are contained in this extravagance? How could Moses, weighed down by the mass of his body, ascend to the height of heaven? Or, if God wished to give the Law, how could the angels prohibit him?

Again, what is more foolish than to say that God exulted over the defeated angels and laughed in childish fashion? And if the angels, as you say, were so eager to retain that Law, why had they not asked God for it earlier? Or what benefit did it bring them to rage in dispute? They could have observed the Law together with the Jews, and there was no reason why they should have tried to prevent Moses from receiving it.

Another story that they themselves relate is no less ridiculous than all these. They say that the angel of death appeared to a certain man named Joshua, son of Levi, a teacher, and said to him: “Know that I have come to receive your soul, and that you must die.”

“Not at all,” he replied. “I will do what you command only after you have shown me paradise.”

The angel therefore took him upon his wings and led him to a place from which he could see paradise. But that cunning man slipped from his wings and allowed himself to fall into paradise.

The angel, distressed that he had been deceived, said with a most angry expression: “Come out, so that you may die.”

“Not at all,” he replied. “I will not come out.”

When the angel repeated the same words a second and third time with a great shout, and the man ignored his words, the angel became extremely agitated, went to God, and complained about what had happened.

God, however, asked him to return and command that man, in God’s name, to leave paradise. The angel therefore went to paradise and said: “God commands you to come out.”

The man swore and said: “By God, I will not come out.”

The angel returned to God and said: “He has firmly sworn that he will never leave that place.”

God then gave judgment and replied: “Review all the volumes of his life and deeds, and read them carefully. If you find that he has ever sworn and committed perjury, his oath now too will be of no value to him. But if you prove that he has never committed perjury, you need not fear on this occasion.”

The angel therefore carefully examined all the volumes and found that he had never committed perjury. He therefore left him alone, defeated. As you say, he remains unharmed and alive to the present day.

Consider, I ask, how many things worthy of laughter can be noted in this little story. What should we be more astonished by: the angel’s stupidity, because he did not recognize the man’s cunning trick beforehand; or the man, because, after hearing God’s command through the angel, he dared to swear against that very command; or should we say that God was powerless, since he could expel him from paradise only through a messenger; or should we attribute ignorance to God, because he could not otherwise know whether the man had committed perjury unless he ordered the books of his life to be reviewed?

Are not all these things utterly foolish? If we were to set down everything that your teachers have written resembling these stories, we too would fill many books with tales of nonsense, just as they have. We have introduced only a few examples so that their wisdom—or their stupidity—might be evident to all.

This, then, is what I told you above: the words of your teachers seem to be nothing other than the words of people joking in boys’ schools or of women spinning in the streets.
