But tell me, I beg you, O Moses: do you judge that the Law should be received from such men, or that their authority should be approved?

May divine mercy rescue you from their detestable teachings and counsels, just as it rescued me—not through my merits—and may it subject you together with me to its saving commands, so that it may enrich us both alike with its ineffable rewards.

**TITLE II. Treats of recognizing the cause of the present captivity of the Jews and how long it ought to last.**

**MOSES.** Since you have shown that whatever our teachers improperly attribute to the divine majesty cannot stand by the light of your invincible arguments, either by the authority of Scripture or by the force of reason, let us now, if you please, come to the second part of the matters proposed, in which you spoke about our captivity.

For you said—unless I have forgotten—that we should hope to escape captivity in a way in which we can by no means escape. I therefore ask whether you grant that we can escape in the way we believe, or in another way, or even in no way at all—which may it not be so.

**PETER.** I do not believe that you will be freed in the way you yourselves think, but I do not deny that you will escape in another way.

**MOSES.** I wish to hear why we cannot be freed in the way we say, and what the way of liberation is.

**PETER.** Since you have denied that Christ is the Son of God or that he came into the world for the redemption of the human race, and since you have refused to keep his commandments, you will not be able to escape from captivity. But if you believe both that he is the Son of God and that he has already come, and if you keep his commandments, you will immediately leave captivity.

[Col. 0568B] **MOSES.** What authority can you bring forward for such a statement?

**PETER.** First, I want you to state what was the cause of your captivity, so that, once we have learned it, we may also recognize more clearly the way of escape, following the practice of a wise physician, who first examines the illness in order to know what medicine is required.

**MOSES.** I approve what you have said.

**PETER.** First, I want you to tell me the cause of the Babylonian captivity, which lasted only seventy years, because once we have heard it, it will help us recognize the cause of this present captivity, which is so great.

**MOSES.** Very many sins were the cause of the earlier captivity, and it would take too long to enumerate them.

**PETER.** I grant that this was so, but I want to hear some of them from you.

**MOSES.** I will bring forward a few of those which are proved by prophetic authority: taking interest or accepting a gift in exchange for injustice; swearing a false oath; giving counterfeit money in buying and selling; giving false testimony; slandering one another; dishonoring parents, places of sanctification, and the Sabbath days; revealing the shame of one’s mother, sister, daughter, mother-in-law, or any forbidden woman; committing murders; worshiping idols; sacrificing to the stars; denying God; and killing God’s prophets, such as Uriah, Zechariah, and Isaiah.

There were also many other offenses which, as I said above, would take too long to enumerate. They increased to such an extent that God said to the prophet Jeremiah: “Go through the streets of Jerusalem, and see and consider; seek in its squares whether you can find a man who practices justice and seeks faithfulness, and I will be merciful to him” (Jeremiah 5).

Ezekiel likewise says: “I sought among them a man who would interpose a barrier and stand before me on their behalf, so that I would not destroy it, but I found none” (Ezekiel 22).

PETRUS. I rejoice and give thanks, because I recognize that you now perceive some spark of the truth. Tell me, then, if you know, what was the cause of this captivity, so long and so dreadful, which has now lasted one thousand and forty years.

MOYSES. These same sins, and others like them.

PETRUS. You can establish this explanation by no authority, because for three hundred years before Jerusalem was overthrown there was no prophet in Israel who foretold or wrote this; especially since your teachers say that the sole cause of the destruction of Jerusalem was that each person hated and envied the other without cause. Moreover, to demolish your argument they add that, after the Temple had been built, God delivered the chief of sin into their hands. With his hands and feet bound, they tore out one of his eyes; and from that day he no longer had the power to deceive people into homicide, idolatry, or the exposure of the shame of kinswomen. Therefore, not all the things that had been causes of the former captivity were also causes of the second captivity.

They also say that, while the Temple still stood, there were many men of good life who ought to have been prophets, had the time been suitable for prophecy. Many others performed extraordinary new miracles, as they say that John, son of Zachai, was a man of such holiness that, when he sat in his chair to read his books, God, in order to display the virtue of his merits, caused all the birds flying above him to be burned and fall to the ground.

They also assert another such miracle concerning another man, namely Hunni. In his time, they say, the land suffered from drought. He entered a circle made of stones and said to God: “I swear by your name, O God, that I will not leave this place unless rain descends upon the earth.” It therefore began to rain lightly; but when he asked for heavier rain, such a great downpour fell that it almost devastated the whole land. When he made a moderate request, however, a temperate rain descended, and the earth abounded in every good thing.

They also say concerning Hananiah, son of Dosa, that a voice came daily from Mount Horeb, bearing this testimony to his holiness: “Because of the goodness of Hananiah, son of Dosa, I govern the whole world; yet a little of the world is sufficient for him.” They assert another such miracle concerning him. Although he and his wife lived an extremely poor life for God, every Friday he ordered the oven to be heated, so that his neighbors and those living nearby would think that he abounded in food and lived well.

One day, then, when he had ordered the oven to be lit according to his customary practice, and one of the neighboring women had noticed why this was being done, she suddenly came to the oven, intending to expose their actions and bring shame upon both the man and the woman. When she came to the oven and looked inside, she saw it full of loaves, and she ran quickly to report this to the woman mentioned above. Thinking that the other woman had said this not truthfully but as an insult, she refused to believe her until she herself had verified it. She therefore went, looked, and found it to be as her neighbor had said. Returning joyfully to her husband, she told him in detail how God had changed the intention of the wicked woman into an honor.

He, judging it unworthy to take for his own use what God had done as a miracle, replied that he would taste nothing of it, and had it all distributed to the poor.

They further say that in those same times Nicodemus, son of Guirion, was a man of highly praiseworthy life. In his days such a great drought afflicted the land that those going to the Temple for the sake of prayer could find nothing to drink along the way. On the road there was a cistern belonging to a certain gentile prince. Nicodemus approached this prince and said: “If it pleases you, grant me your cistern for the use of the whole people; and on that day I will return the cistern with its water, or an equivalent price.”

Why say more? He obtained what he requested and relieved the people’s thirst. But when the creditor arrived on the appointed day to demand payment, and the cistern contained no water because of the excessive drought, Nicodemus, after pouring out a prayer to God, obtained rain from heaven over the whole land and returned the cistern full to its owner, just as he had received it.

But because, when that rain descended, the day was already declining toward evening, the prince said to Nicodemus: “I accept the water restored by your prayer; nevertheless, since the entire hour of the appointed day has passed, you must pay me the price you owe.” Nicodemus therefore prayed again, stopped the course of the sun, and, with the whole world illuminated by its light, escaped the creditor’s demand.

You also have it written concerning Akiba that whatever he asked of God, he obtained. The following is read concerning the greatness of his holiness. When Moses had gone up the mountain to receive the Law, and, with the Holy Spirit dictating, had foreseen all the times that would follow him and all the generations of the ages, and had seen among human beings Akiba, who would surpass the limits of human life and be endowed with great merits, he said to God: “Since there will be a man of such exemplary life, why, Lord, is it pleasing that you should administer your law to the peoples through me rather than through him?”

God replied: “Because the Law is necessary in the present world, whereas Akiba will come only after a long time.”

From this it is understood that Moses foresaw that the man about whom he said such things would be far better than himself.

These men, and others like them, were your superiors and judges. They commanded their inferiors to do good, and the others willingly obeyed their admonitions. If even one man like them had existed during the time of the former captivity, that captivity would never have occurred, as we showed above that God said through Jeremiah (Jer. V).

And what is more astonishing is that during the days when the best of these men flourished, the Jews themselves were taken captive after the Temple had been destroyed. Tell me, then, O Moses, what was the cause of this captivity, since the cause you mentioned above stands firm by no reasoning at all.

MOYSES. I have nothing else to say except that, while the Temple endured for a long time, many sins gradually increased along with it, as our teachers said—but with the offense multiplied.

PETRUS. As for your claim that the Temple continued for a long time, it actually endured only ten years longer than Solomon’s earlier Temple had endured. But your claim that sins were heaped upon sins is not accepted by reason. In the first captivity, sins were added to sins because wicked kings gave others an example of evil: they set God aside, worshiped idols, and compelled the people to do the same, as did Ahaziah, Ahaz, Manasseh, Amon, and Zedekiah (IV Kings I, XVI, XXI, and XXIV).

The rulers of the second period, however, were entirely different, because by living good lives they also compelled the people, through their example, to live well. By what reasoning, then, can it be shown that so many sins increased that captivity occurred on their account?

As for your claim that that captivity occurred because of the ill will they held toward one another, it rests on no anchor of sound reason. This sin was one part of those they had committed during the first captivity; yet they ought not to have been taken captive because of it unless other, greater sins had increased along with it. We do not know how to distinguish the quantity of greater and lesser crimes except according to the measure of the vengeance imposed by God. The punishment for this offense, however, is no more than forty lashes.

There are other crimes whose punishment is greater: when someone is ordered to be executed by beheading, killed by hanging from a noose, buried beneath stones, or even burned by fire. How, then, can it be true that the crime of ill will should be considered equal to greater crimes?

Furthermore, reason recoils from believing that this crime reigned to such an extent in those times, since the words of the prophet Haggai testify that, after the Temple had been built, God said: “The glory of this latter house shall be greater than that of the former, says the Lord of hosts, and in this place I will give peace” (Hag. II).

MOYSES. Since every avenue of my arguments has been blocked, please unlock for me, with the key of your solution, the door of this question.

PETRUS. Since you do not know the origin and cause of the captivity, you cannot answer why it was so harsh, cruel, and intolerable. In the first captivity, although they were led to Babylon like other captives, they endured no punishment beyond servitude. They cultivated fields, planted vineyards, and built houses; they lived securely with their wives and children.

In the second, however, they inflicted upon them so many and such great insults, so unheard-of, that nothing similar or equal has ever been seen or heard. They were killed, burned, and sold like captives; and the sale increased to such a degree that thirty captives were offered for one silver coin, yet no one was found to buy them, as Moses foretold when he said: “You shall be sold to your enemies as male and female slaves, and there shall be no one to buy you” (Deut. XXVIII).

Ships were also filled with them and released to wander across the sea without any oarsman or rudder, to their disgrace and degradation.

Moreover, after you had been cast down into this captivity, intolerable commands were issued against you: you were forbidden to read the Law or to teach it to your children. If anyone was found reading it or teaching it to his children, he was either burned or torn apart with the teeth of extremely sharp iron combs.

Furthermore, you were not permitted to celebrate either the Sabbath or Passover. If anyone was found doing so, he was punished most severely. In addition, you were forbidden to circumcise your sons according to your former custom, and so much time passed during which no one dared circumcise his son except secretly. Anyone found circumcising was subjected to the gravest punishments.

A particularly harsh edict was also promulgated against you: if one of you took a virgin girl as his wife, he first had to bring her to the provincial governor, so that the governor might sleep with her; only then could she return and marry a Jew. Because of this you were so crushed that no one wished to become betrothed to a virgin. Thus, throughout the succession of the ages, various commands of evil were issued against you, as is proved by the testimonies of your own books.

MOYSES. I concede without doubt every kind of evil, but for a long time now I have eagerly desired to hear the cause of such great tribulation.

PETRUS. Because you do not know the cause of the evils, you do not know why the captivity is so long. For behold, one thousand and forty years have already been completed in it, and you still have no written certainty about how long it must continue.

Yet civil justice requires that, once those who committed some crime have been punished or have died, their successors should be freed from captivity. This is what is written in the Law: the spies who had been sent to inspect the land of promise rebelled against God’s will; and, so that their sin would not remain unpunished, they stayed forty years in the wilderness, and during that period all those transgressors died (Num. XIII and XIV). After they had been punished by such a death, their sons, who were innocent of their fathers’ crime, entered the land promised to their fathers.

In the Babylonian migration, too, they remained for seventy years, until all those whose sins had caused the captivity had died; then their sons, who had earned nothing of it, were freed from the yoke.

In this captivity, however, which was brought about by Titus, innumerable generations have already passed, and it still has no end. This contradicts the statement that the Lord made to Moses: “Fathers shall not be put to death for their sons, nor sons for their fathers; each one shall die for his own sin” (Deut. XXIV).

Ezekiel likewise says: “As I live, says the Lord God, this proverb shall no longer be spoken as a proverb in the land of Judah. Behold, all souls are mine: as the soul of the father, so also the soul of the son is mine. The soul that sins shall itself die” (Ezek. XVIII).

MOYSES. Although the length of our captivity is contrary to these examples, it nevertheless agrees with other passages of the Law. In Exodus the Lord says: “I am the Lord your God, strong and jealous, visiting the iniquity of the fathers upon the children to the third and fourth generation, among those who hate me” (Exod. XX). Jeremiah’s words are also these: “Our fathers sinned and are no more, and we have borne their iniquities” (Lam. V).

PETRUS. The matter is otherwise than you say. If the prophet’s words were as you claim, they would contradict one another. Both passages, however, are reconciled in this way. The statement that sons will not bear the iniquity of their fathers (Ezek. XVII) is understood to mean that they will not bear it if they do not commit the iniquity of their fathers. The statement that sons bear the iniquity of their fathers (Exod. XX) means that they are said to bear it if they commit their fathers’ crimes.

MOYSES. What you say produces a reasonable and just interpretation for the wise. From your words, however, it is understood that all the generations of successors remain in their fathers’ captivity because they carry out, as far as they can, the deeds of their fathers. If they abandoned their fathers’ deeds, they would leave the captivity.

PETRUS. That is indeed my view.

MOYSES. Now, if you please, disclose the magnitude of so great a guilt.

PETRUS. Because you killed Christ, the Son of God, saying that he was a magician, born of a prostitute, and that he had led the entire nation into error. Your ancestors protested these and similar charges until they made the whole people partners in their perverse will. They brought a just man unjustly before a most unjust tribunal, crucified him, and killed him.

The magnitude of so great a guilt is therefore the cause of such a prolonged captivity. And so long as you remain in your fathers’ will and faith, you will certainly remain in the same affliction of condemnation.

MOYSES. Whether that man was the Son of God will have to be debated more fully later, because so great a question requires the vehicle of a very strong argument. For the moment, however, I want you to show in what way, and by what authority, you attempt to assert that the man of whom you speak became the cause of our tribulation.

PETRUS. What authority, please, do you demand from me in this matter, when you have already conceded that an entirely unprecedented sin was the cause of such an unheard-of affliction? Since you are wholly unable to demonstrate that sin in any way, the equity of judgment requires that you hear me; you should not ask how I can prove it, but refute it by whatever means you can, or concede what you are unable to deny.

Nevertheless, although I am not constrained by the strictness of judgment, I will produce not one but many authorities on this matter.

MOYSES. That is what I desire with all my heart.

PETRUS. You should know that, when forty years had elapsed after Christ’s death, the city of Jerusalem was destroyed by Titus. Likewise, forty years before its destruction, portents and signs were seen in it, clearly indicating that the destruction of the Temple and city was to come, as the books of your teaching testify.

For they say that, forty years before it was overthrown, the red wool attached to the horns of the goat did not become white according to its customary practice; and the lamp of the candelabrum that faced west was extinguished before its usual time. Moreover, the gates of the Temple, without anyone touching them, opened again of their own accord with a great crash.

When one of your teachers, named John, son of Zachai, had often seen them opening in this way, he was deeply disturbed and finally cried out: “Be quiet!” He added: “Temple, temple, I know for certain that your final burning will possess you, just as the prophet says: ‘Open your doors, O Lebanon, and let fire consume your cedars’” (Zech. XI).

Since these portents were seen forty years before the destruction, and the city was destroyed by Titus in the fortieth year after Christ’s death, it is clearly concluded that these signs began at the time of Christ’s death.

John, together with your other teachers, also understood that Christ’s death was the cause of your captivity. They did not say that it was the cause, but that the ill will and envy of men were the cause of the captivity; yet they concealed the true cause. The envy and malice of the Jews were the cause of Christ’s death, whereas Christ’s death was the cause of the captivity.

MOYSES. If it were certain that he was such a man as you say, and that his death was the cause of our tribulation, none of us would be worthy to live. Such a sin is greater than denying God. For the one who denies God merely alienates from himself the faith he had received; but the one who kills the Son of God, in addition to denying the invisible divinity, adds this further sin: he also removes from the faith of his mind a visible being whom he sees with bodily eyes, although what is seen ought to bring greater credibility to the mind than what is not seen.

Moreover, our fathers covered him with spittle, struck him with blows, subjected him to many and various insults, and innocently delivered him to death by crucifying him. Therefore, this crime was not unreasonably greater than the one they committed in the wilderness when they worshiped a golden calf in place of God.

At that time, we read, God wished to destroy Israel completely, unless Moses intervened on their behalf and turned away the Lord’s anger with abundant weeping, fasting, and prayer, afflicting himself for that same sin through forty days and forty nights of continuous fasting (Exod. XXXII). The Law bears witness, saying: “I fell down before the Lord as before, eating no bread and drinking no water for forty days, because of all your sins that you committed against the Lord. For I feared his anger and indignation, with which he was enraged against you and wished to destroy you” (Deut. IX).

If Moses’ prayer had not intervened, not one person of the whole people would have remained. Since they presumed to commit this other deed, which exceeds the measure of crimes—namely, to kill the Son of God—and since there was no one to intervene on their behalf, no one ought therefore to have lived.

You see, however, that this is not so. God permits us to live and shows each day how much he loves us, granting us favor in the sight of our enemies, enriching us with possessions, and exalting us with honors, just as he promised us through the mouth of the prophet Moses, saying: “Even when they are in the land of their enemies, I did not utterly reject them, nor did I despise them so that they would be consumed and I would invalidate my covenant with them. For I am the Lord their God” (Lev. XXVI).

PETRUS. You do not form a correct understanding of this matter. God does not allow the remnants of your people to live because he has any thought for their welfare, but only so that you may serve all the nations and be, in the eyes of everyone, a reproach, a byword, and a curse, as the giver of the Law promised you when he said: “You shall become a destruction, a proverb, and a byword among all the peoples to whom the Lord will bring you” (Deut. XVIII), and so that you may be a parable and proverb to the whole people, sought out by everyone in relation to one another.

What do you think is the reason why God subjected this nation, dispersed throughout the whole world, to perpetual servitude and condemned it to the punishment of so many evils? Another person will answer: “They came into these evils because of such a sin: they killed the Son of God solely out of envy.”

If, at the very time when the sin was committed by you, he had completely destroyed the entire Jewish race, then, after many ages had passed and the guilt had been erased by oblivion, no mortal would know of it; thus you would have avoided both the reproach of infamy and the danger of evils, as has happened to many nations and kings whose deeds have been erased by the antiquity of time.

There is another reason why God did not wish to destroy the Jewish people. He saw that some of your descendants would at some time believe in him and be saved; and therefore, for their sake, he did not wish to destroy your stock entirely, as Isaiah says: “As when a seed is found in a cluster and it is said, ‘Do not destroy it, for there is a blessing in it,’ so I will act for the sake of my servants, that I may not destroy the whole” (Isa. LXV).

The testimony of divine compassion toward you that you brought forward from the book of the Law as a promise made to Moses does not refer to the present captivity, but to the former Babylonian captivity, from which he was eventually going to lead you out.

MOYSES. By what authority do you prove that this promise refers only to the Babylonian captivity?

PETRUS. Because, in the passage where God made this promise to Moses, if you pay a little attention to what precedes it, you will find that the same Moses had first said: “Then the land shall enjoy its Sabbaths throughout all the days of its desolation. When you are in the land of your enemies, it shall keep Sabbath and rest during its Sabbaths” (Lev. XXVI).

Ezra confirms in the Book of Chronicles that this was fulfilled for those who were led into Babylon, saying among other things: “Israel was led away to Babylon and served the king and his sons until the land had celebrated its Sabbaths. For throughout all the days of its desolation it kept Sabbath” (II Chron. XXXVI). These words clearly show that he is speaking of the first captivity.

MOYSES. This authority is not sufficient for my doubt, because it does not show that we fell into this captivity because of that man.

PETRUS. What more evident testimony could you seek that you underwent this captivity because of Christ’s death than what you read in your own writings? For, at the very beginning of the captivity, a certain ruler of your land took ten of the best men of the entire Israelite people—namely, Hananiah, son of Terradion; Simeon, son of Gamaliel; Ishmael, son of Elisha; and Akiba, together with the others—and put them in prison, asking why they had sold the Just One.

“The Law,” he said, “determines that whoever sells a Jew shall be punished by the sentence of death. You, therefore, must die according to the judgment of the Law.”

“After the decree was spoken, he gave their bodies to varied deaths.”

For he did not subject them all to one punishment; rather, different kinds of death were assigned to each. One was burned by fire, another expired after being torn apart by the claws of an iron comb, and another was consumed by some other kind of death, as the book of your teaching recounts those deaths.

Your teachers, however, changing the name of the Just One for whom those men were punished, were entirely silent about Christ in this matter. They said that the ruler understood the Just One to be Joseph, son of Jacob, whom his brothers had sold into Egypt (Gen. XXXVII), and that, demanding his blood from them, he inflicted such punishments upon them on his account.

But it appears absurd to reason that he should demand from them what had happened at least fifteen hundred years earlier, especially since, in the period when Joseph was sold, there was no law by which that ruler could convict them of a capital offense.

MOYSES. Your arguments are not sufficient for me, because you do not confirm them by any authority; you invent them according to your own judgment, and they contain no necessity that could compel me to believe you. But I want you, if you can, to bring forward some authority from the prophets by which you may necessarily show that this captivity occurred because of that man, that he was Christ, and that there can be no certain end to our tribulation.

PETRUS. The prophet Isaiah says: “From the ends of the earth we have heard praises, the glory of the Just One” (Isa. XXIV). These words show that the praises of this Just One were heard throughout the world. We have never heard of the praises of any just man being so great that they reached to the ends of the earth.

Because he foresaw that this Just One would suffer tribulations without cause, he sympathizes with him in these words: “Woe is me! The transgressors have transgressed; they have transgressed with the transgression of transgressors” (Isa. XXIV).

For the prophet foresaw the tribulations they would bring upon the prophets who announced God’s coming beforehand, and he said: “The transgressors have transgressed.” But when he perceived that, not content with the members, they would also, filled with envy, oppress the head himself by whatever means they could and kill him according to the vulnerability of the body, he repeated the name of transgression, adding: “They have transgressed with the transgression of transgressors.”

But because he foresaw by the Spirit that they would be punished for this sin, he immediately added: “Terror and pit and snare are upon you, inhabitant of the earth” (ibid.).

Elsewhere, concerning the same people, he says: “For its iniquity will weigh it down; it will fall and will not rise again” (ibid.), where he entirely removed from you any fixed limit for escaping captivity.

The Lord also spoke similar words through the same prophet in another passage, saying: “Now go in, write this on a boxwood tablet, and carefully inscribe it in a book; and on the last day it shall be a testimony forever: For this is a rebellious people, lying sons, sons unwilling to hear the law of God, who say to the seers, ‘Do not see,’ and to those who look, ‘Do not look upon for us the things that are right. Remove the way from me; turn aside from me the path; let the Holy One of Israel cease from before our face’” (Isa. XXX).

Boxwood is hard and imperishable. He therefore commanded that this be written on boxwood and carefully engraved in a book so that it would endure forever and remain until the last day as a testimony and reproach of their unbelief. By saying “on the last day,” he also indicates that the error of the Jews would persist until the final day.

What should be written, and why, he indicates in a single verse when he says: “For this is a rebellious people, lying sons, sons unwilling to hear the law of God.” Which law of God did he mean? If the prophet had wished to speak of the law of God that he had given through Moses, he would not have said “unwilling to hear the law of God,” since they had already heard it frequently; he would certainly have said “unwilling to fulfill it.” Therefore, he meant the Law that Christ was going to give, and the prophet already foresaw that they would be unwilling to hear it.

When he added, “who say to the seers, ‘Do not see,’ and to those who look, ‘Do not look upon for us the things that are right. Remove the way from me; turn aside from me the path,’” he added this on account of John, son of Zachariah, the forerunner of Christ (John I), and the others who not only foretold that Christ would come but also pointed him out with their finger. He foresaw that the Jews would not believe them, but would speak such words.

What follows must not be passed over. They say: “Let the Holy One of Israel cease from before our face.” Who is this Holy One of Israel? Is God visible, so that they could say of him, “Let him cease from before our face”? Or can this be said of an invisible reality, that it should cease from a human face, when it cannot be seen by it?

If, then, you seek God who can be seen, you will find no one except Christ. He is one God with the Father (John X), and yet through his humanity he appeared visibly to the world (Tit. III).

After he had set forth so many of their transgressions, he introduced the vengeance for that sin, saying: “Because you rejected this word, and trusted in slander and tumult, and relied upon it, therefore this iniquity shall be for you like a breach falling down, and like a crack sought out in a high wall; for suddenly, when it is not expected, its collapse will come, and it will be shattered as a potter’s vessel is crushed with a most powerful crushing, so that not even a potsherd will be found among its fragments in which to carry a little ember from the fire or draw a little water from a pit” (Isa. XXX).

Christ is the Word of God (John I). Whoever therefore rejects Christ also rejects the Word, and conversely. Because they rejected the Word of God, they are therefore punished and condemned because they rejected Christ and placed their trust in the words of their teachers.

Consider how harsh the collapse destined to come upon them for this sin will be. “A sudden breach,” he says, will come upon them, and will therefore be more harmful; and it will come from a high wall, because anything is crushed more thoroughly at the bottom the higher the place from which it has fallen.

This collapse is also compared to a potter’s vessel shattered into fragments. It will be so complete, he says, that not even a potsherd will remain from its breaking. Every ordinary vessel that is broken can be repaired and fashioned into some useful object; but if a potsherd is broken, its pieces, through violent crushing, can serve no purpose. And the more a potsherd endures after being shattered, the more its fracture continually increases.

Since, then, their collapse is compared to such a potsherd—one that can neither take an ember from a fire nor draw water from a pit—it is clearly understood that your captivity has been brought to such a state of degradation that it will never return to its former freedom.

Because God wished to preserve your seed for the sake of those who would at some time believe in Christ and therefore be saved, the prophet, under the image of a blessed remnant, added this statement of grace: “As when a seed is found in a cluster and it is said, ‘Do not destroy it, for there is a blessing in it’” (Isa. LXV). In the same way he promised that he would not entirely scatter you when he said: “So I will act for the sake of my servants, that I may not destroy the whole” (ibid.).

He immediately explains why he made this promise, saying: “I will bring forth from Jacob a seed, and from Judah one who will possess my mountains; my chosen ones and my servants shall dwell there” (ibid.). By “mountains” he means the apostles, who, like lofty mountains, have been seen by the whole world, although in what follows he understands “the holy mountain,” expressed in the singular, as Christ. By “chosen ones” and “servants” he means various other saints, for whose future salvation you have been preserved.

Hear what sentence he next pronounces upon those who will not believe. “You,” he says, “who have forsaken the Lord, who have forgotten my holy mountain, who set a table for Fortune and pour libations upon it, I will number you for the sword, and you shall all fall in the slaughter, because I called and you did not answer; I spoke and you did not hear” (Isa. LXV).

Having rebuked their iniquity, he condemns them in this way, also praising his faithful and rebuking the unbelieving in these words: “Therefore thus says the Lord God: Behold, my servants shall eat, but you shall hunger; behold, my servants shall drink, but you shall thirst; behold, my servants shall rejoice, but you shall be put to shame; behold, my servants shall praise because of the exultation of their heart, but you shall cry because of the anguish of your heart, and because of the contrition of your spirit you shall howl; and you shall leave your name as an oath for my chosen ones” (ibid.).

And because, once all these evils had passed, no hope of escaping captivity could remain, he adds something else that removes every comfort of confidence from them. He says: “The Lord your God will kill you” (ibid.). One who is killed can in no way afterward be restored to what he was. Therefore those who remain in unbelief cannot be restored.

Having said this about the unbelieving, he next speaks of those who will believe: “And he will call his servants by another name” (ibid.). Since they will be servants of Christ, they will be called Christians by Christ (Acts XI).

What follows—“You shall leave your name as an oath for my chosen ones”—means as though he said: “My chosen ones will swear by your name,” just as Christians still swear today when they are asked to do something they do not wish to do: “May I be a Jew if I do it.”

The prophet Amos also clearly confirms the same thing, saying: “Hear this word that I take up over you as a lament, house of Israel: ‘The virgin Israel has fallen; she shall not rise again. She has been cast upon her own land; there is no one to raise her up’” (Amos V).

The same prophet says elsewhere: “The end has come upon my people Israel; I will not pass by them again” (Amos VIII). Both statements entirely remove from you the hope of escaping captivity.

He also confirms that this evil came upon you because of Christ, saying: “Thus says the Lord God: For three crimes of Israel, and for four, I will not revoke it, because he sold the Just One, and the poor man, for shoes” (Amos II).

In this passage he uses “four” for “the fourth”; saying “for four” has the same meaning as saying “for the fourth.” Solomon provides a similar statement. According to the testimony of the Hebrew books, he says: “There are three things too difficult for me, and four that I do not understand at all” (Prov. XXX). If you wish to understand “three” by itself and “four” by itself, there will be seven. Yet he counts only four things that he says he does not understand. Therefore, we must take “four” to mean “the fourth.” The same interpretation must be applied to this prophet.

He immediately identifies this fourth crime when he adds that “they sold the Just One for silver” (Amos II). It is fitting to understand this Just One as Christ.

MOYSES. Everything you have said up to this point would be suitable and worthy of praise, had you not introduced this authority, which stands on no rational foundation—especially since many objections can be raised against it. Many of the ancients before you have frequently brought forward this same verse as a testimony against the Jews, but they could not defend it by any sound reasoning.

I am particularly astonished that, as a prudent man, you have introduced so weak an argument, one resting on no foundation of strength, especially since you yourself know very well everything that can be said against it.

PETRUS. Since I have considered that all those before me are said to have introduced this authority against the Jews correctly, but failed to destroy the Jewish objections sufficiently or openly, I deliberately introduced the same authority at this point, so that you might make all the objections that can be made as effectively as possible, and then, with the roles reversed, undertake their destruction.

**MOYSES.** This may rightly be raised as the first objection: the prophet, after saying “for three transgressions,” immediately added, showing that Israel had committed those three sins; but the Christ whom you wish to understand here was killed not by Israel but by Judah.

**PETRUS.** Your objection presents no obstacle to me, since the books very frequently testify that Israel is used in place of Judah.

**MOYSES.** I do not doubt that matters are as you assert. But since he first mentioned Judah’s sin and then followed with Israel’s sin, it is sufficiently clear that Israel’s sin is different from Judah’s sin.  
[Col. 0579D]

**PETRUS.** Nor does this obstruct my reasoning. The sin committed by Judah alone he calls Judah’s sin; but what Judah and Israel committed together is called Israel’s sin.

**MOYSES.** Since the entire people of Israel, dispersed throughout all the lands, by no means inhabited the land of Jerusalem at that time, how could they have been held guilty of Christ’s death?

**PETRUS.** Do you deny that a large part of the sons of Benjamin and Levi was then in Jerusalem together with Judah?

**MOYSES.** Who would dare deny what is certain to everyone?

[Col. 0580A]

**PETRUS.** Therefore, by right, a part ought to bear the name of the whole. There is also another reason no less compelling: although the people of Israel were not bodily present at the death at that time, nevertheless, when they heard what their associates had done, they became partners in the guilt, their praisers and accomplices, and were made altogether participants in the will. Their will, therefore, must be reckoned as the deed.

**MOYSES.** And although I shall grant that matters are as you say, I do not see how what the book says happened “for the righteous man sold” can apply to Israel. For they are read as having bought the Christ of whom you speak, not as having sold him, and as having bought him only from Judas Iscariot (Matt. XXVI; Luke XXII; Mark IV).

**PETRUS.** Your objection rests upon no anchor of reason, because those who gave their consent and assistance so that Christ might be sold incurred the crime no less than if they themselves had sold him (Rom. I). For Solomon himself did not manufacture the idols; but because he gave his assent to his wives and concubines while they manufactured them, Scripture says that he manufactured them (III Kings XI).

**MOYSES.** Although I admit that you have spoken truly in the matters mentioned above, no necessity nevertheless compels me to grant that this righteous man must be understood as Christ, since Joseph ought to be understood in the sound sense: his brothers sold him for thirty pieces of silver (Gen. XXXVII).

**PETRUS.** If the prophet had wished Joseph to be understood, he would have said “for the righteous man,” not “for the fourth,” but rather “for the first” sin. For they committed that earlier offense on account of which they afterward suffered Pharaoh’s most grievous yoke (Exod. XII). But since, after completing their repentance, they have already been freed from the punishment, why should they again be charged with a sin that has been forgiven?  
[Col. 0580C]

**MOYSES.** Even if I cannot defend the claim that this was said about Joseph, I can nevertheless assert that it was said about some other righteous man.

**PETRUS.** It seems unworthy and unreasonable that, when the crime is so great that no forgiveness follows it, on account of which the divine judgment rages against Israel in its entirety, the person against whom it was committed should be concealed and left unknown—especially since this guilt is described in the Hebrew language by a term such as is applied to one who has denied God. A Jew’s sale, however, is not equal to a denial of God. But they sold such a man, and so great a man—namely Christ, the Son of God—that in guilt they are the equals of those who deny God.  
[Col. 0580D]

**MOYSES.** Show that there were four sins, all of which are plainly equal to denying God.

**PETRUS.** I do not know how to disclose what the book has left unsaid, but perhaps the first sin was committed when, in the wilderness, they worshiped a cast image of a calf in place of God (Exod. XXXII). By this act they plainly denied the true God; and because this sin was perpetrated by everyone, it was therefore common to all. The second was one in which they likewise denied God and all sinned together: namely, when Jeroboam fashioned similar calves and established that they should be worshiped by everyone (III Kings XII). The third was when they all, with one and the same will, killed God’s prophets and despised their words (II Chron. XXXVI). The fourth, greater and more serious than all the others, which is not even said to be pardonable, was when they unjustly sold Christ, the Son of God and a man wholly free from every contagion of sin (Isa. LIII; I Pet. II), and condemned him to an unjust death.

Behold, in this passage of Scripture which I brought against you, I have proved that everything you might object cannot stand with any force, and I have concluded that it reasonably applies to Christ. Since this passage and all the authorities cited above rest upon unshakable firmness, I consider it indubitably proved that this captivity of such long duration came about on account of Christ’s death and their malevolence.

Once it has been established that the captivity occurred because of Christ, it follows that you will not come out of it until you correct in yourselves the sin of your fathers—until you believe what they did not believe. When anyone’s mind has been cleansed from guilt, divine mercy immediately follows him. One of your own teachers also wished this to be expressed more subtly in hidden words, if only the hardness of your mind had allowed you to penetrate them. When he was asked when the Son of David would come, he said: “Today, if you will believe his words.” By these words he indicated that whoever, at any hour, obeys Christ’s commandments and believes in him, the Son of God immediately comes to him.

I believe it is also manifest and clear to you that everything I have proved by the testimony of your books is so. Therefore, brother, implore with me the mercy of that same Christ, so that, once every error of falsehood has been removed, he may pour into the eyes of your mind both the splendor of the true faith and the love of all goodness, and may repay right faith with a worthy reward in the future, so that through it you may come out of captivity. Amen.

## TITLE III. On refuting the foolish belief of the Jews concerning the resurrection of their dead, whom they believe will both rise again and inhabit the earth once more

**MOYSES.** As regards the present title—namely, what was the cause of our captivity of such great duration and by what means we might escape it—you have proved everything that needed to be drawn from the matter by arguments that are invincible and most evident. I do not see what further point about it should either be doubted or investigated. Therefore, so that we may pass to other matters, I desire that we proceed according to the order in which they were arranged above.

You said at the beginning of the book that we were mistaken because, after escaping from captivity, we believed that God would perform for us an unprecedented miracle: that the dead would be raised again and inhabit the earth once more. I beg you to explain why we seem to you to be mistaken in this belief.  
[Col. 0581D]

**PETRUS.** You yourselves assert that this miracle is beyond ordinary experience. Whatever occurs beyond custom ought not to be believed before it happens without authority or reason. I therefore judge it an error to believe what you cannot prove by any authority.

**MOYSES.** We can certainly prove this by many authorities. It is proved by the testimony of Moses, who says to the people of Israel: “See that I alone am, and that there is no other God besides me. I kill, and I make alive; I strike, and I heal” (Deut. XXXII).  
[Col. 0582A]

Since, then, God promises that he will kill and make alive, why does our faith concerning this matter seem to you worthy of rejection?

**PETRUS.** This authority departs from the path of reason. He says this to demonstrate his omnipotence, not because he himself is going to raise your dead.

**MOYSES.** From the day on which God promised that he would do this until the present day, do you grant that he has at some time performed these miracles?

**PETRUS.** Certainly, he did them all. When he wished, he struck Mary, the sister of the prophet Moses, Job, Hezekiah, Naaman, and many others; when he wished, he healed them (Num. XII; Job XII; IV Kings III; XX). Likewise, in a single night he killed all the firstborn of Egypt (Exod. XII), and within the space of one night he killed one hundred and eighty-five thousand in Sennacherib’s camp (IV Kings XIX). But, conversely, through Elijah he raised the widow’s son (III Kings XVII), and through Elisha he raised the son of the Shunammite woman (IV Kings IV).  
[Col. 0582B]

**MOYSES.** Since you believe that he has already performed these miracles, what prevents you from believing that he will at some time do the same again?

**PETRUS.** I do not deny that the Almighty can raise the dead (I Cor. XV), and I both confess and believe that all human beings will be raised by him on the day of judgment (John V; Matt. XXIV). But I do not believe what you add: namely, that they will inhabit the earth once more.

**MOYSES.** Nor should this seem contrary to faith, since the person raised by Elijah or Elisha afterward lived a long life, had a wife, fathered children, and fulfilled all the ordinary duties of human life.

**PETRUS.** It is true, and it could have happened either by a miracle or through the prayer of the holy man, because the body had not yet been dissolved. Nevertheless, we would not believe it at all if we did not have prophetic testimony concerning it.

Yet human faith is not accustomed easily to accept things that occur beyond ordinary experience unless they are confirmed by the authority of prophets, whose utterances enjoy the approval of all their hearers, and unless the prophets speak of those very things with complete clarity. No prophet, however, expressly declared this. Although your teachers have said it, no one among those who lived before Christ foretold it. Later followers, however, invented this error so that the Jewish people might persist in their unbelief.  
[Col. 0582D]

**MOYSES.** If you maintain that our teachers fabricated these things in order to mislead us, what will you answer concerning the prophets who did the same? Isaiah says: “Your dead shall live; my slain shall rise. Awake and praise, you who dwell in the dust” (Isa. XXVI).

**PETRUS.** These words in no way show that your dead are to be raised in order to inhabit the earth, because, if we attend carefully to what is said, we shall not find there a clear prediction of the resurrection of the dead. Otherwise the prophet would seem to contradict himself, since earlier he said: “The dead shall not live; the giants shall not rise” (ibid.).

What therefore differs from the course of nature and also introduces a contradiction into the prophet himself must by no means be interpreted according to each person’s preference in a sense contrary to nature, when it can be understood in another sound sense—unless necessary reason compels it to be taken otherwise.  
[Col. 0583A]

**MOYSES.** It is pleasing to hear in what other way the meaning of this verse can rightly be understood.

**PETRUS.** This statement can be understood in two ways: either it may be believed to have been spoken about the resurrection at the final judgment, or the name “resurrection” may signify escape from captivity. The latter meaning seems more relevant to the literal sense, since shortly before this the prophet had lamented the captivity and affliction of his people and immediately introduced the consolation of divine promise and mercy, saying: “The dead shall live,” and the rest.

Nor does he indicate that this escape will occur at some indefinite time, but after a short interval, when he says: “Go, my people, enter your chambers, shut your doors behind you; hide yourself for a little moment, until the indignation has passed away” (ibid.). These words appropriately refer to captivity.  
[Col. 0583B]

**MOYSES.** Will you be able to raise any objection to something similar in the words of Daniel? He says: “Many of those who sleep in the dust of the earth shall awake, some to everlasting life, and some to reproach, so that they may see continually” (Dan. XII).

**PETRUS.** This authority differs from your intention by so much the more as it is more clearly understood to have been spoken about the final judgment. In that resurrection they will go either into everlasting life or into everlasting reproach (John V; Matt. XXV).  
[Col. 0583C]

**MOYSES.** Can you find anything to say against the prophet Ezekiel? After he had raised many dead people by divine power, he also prophesied concerning these future events in the following words: “Thus says the Lord God: Behold, I will open your graves and bring you out into the land of Israel” (Ezek. XXXVII). And shortly afterward: “And I will cause you to rest upon your own soil” (ibid.). Behold, the prophet most plainly and unambiguously shows both that the dead will be raised and that they will inhabit their own lands.

**PETRUS.** We must first examine this, so that we may determine in what manner he raised them—namely, whether after their raising they fulfilled all the functions of the human body or not. For this too has become a matter of doubt for many.  
[Col. 0583D]

**MOYSES.** As our teachers testify, he caused them to rise not in a dream but while awake. And to make it still clearer that this is true, they maintain that all the dead whom he raised belonged to the tribe of Ephraim, and that they were said to have died in the region of the Philistines when the people departed from Egypt. This raising was a sign of the future one: just as all those people were raised by him, so all the rest are believed eventually to be raised.

**PETRUS.** How did he confer a true and perfect resurrection upon them, when he did not restore to them a rational soul?

**MOYSES.** How can you maintain that they did not receive a rational soul, when the same prophet, at God’s command, prophesies to the spirit in these words? “Thus says the Lord: Come from the four winds, O spirit, and breathe upon these slain, and let them live. And I prophesied as he had commanded me, and the spirit entered into them, and they lived and stood upon their feet, an exceedingly great army” (ibid.).

**PETRUS.** This spirit, which is commanded to come from the four winds, is by no means the rational soul, but that which is formed from the conjunction of the four elements.

**MOYSES.** From your words it is understood that the bodily spirit is one thing and the rational soul another; and if that is so, their operations too are different.

**PETRUS.** No wise person doubts that this is so.

**MOYSES.** I wish to hear the difference between the two.

[Col. 0584B]

**PETRUS.** The bodily spirit is a very light and subtle body, which is formed in the human body from the conjunction of the four elements. From that place it is spread through all the veins, gives the body life and breath, supplies the arteries with their continual pulse, and produces the natural movement of the human being. It is corrupted together with the body that it vivifies.

The rational soul, however, is a substance subsisting in itself, incorporeal, which by voluntary motion causes the body to move while itself remains unmoved. Even when the body to which it is attached has been corrupted, it remains incorruptible. Joined to the genus, it completes the species of the human being.

**MOYSES.** I remember that many before us have said that the rational soul is created from the conjunction of the four elements. When this conjunction is formed subtly, they said, containing no density in itself, they called the soul subtle; but if it contains some obscurity and thickness, they called the soul sluggish and dull, proving this by the following argument.

“We often see,” they say, “that from the combination of certain things such properties arise—colors, powers, and operations—which do not proceed from any one of those things when they are separately taken apart. Likewise, when fire, air, water, and earth are joined together, a rational soul is produced; yet if it is sought in each individual element, it is not found there in manifest form.”

**PETRUS.** If the rational soul is born from a body perfected through the conjunction of the four elements, then, when the strength of the body fails, the soul’s power ought to fail as well. But if the soul’s power fails when the body’s strength fails, then, when the dissolution of bodily vigor begins, the soul’s power must likewise dissolve. If this is granted, it follows that when the body is corrupted, the soul too is corrupted.  
[Col. 0584D]

**MOYSES.** The right order of consequence shows that this is what happens.

**PETRUS.** But the conclusion of the argument conflicts with the evidence of our eyes. It often happens that the more the body grows weak and approaches death, the more the soul grows strong. Thus, as sometimes happens with many sick people, the nearer a person is to death, the more he remembers than usual with a sharper keenness of mind, foresees everything, and dies at the very moment when the soul is flourishing most vigorously.

When the soul possesses such keenness, as I have said, all the functions of the failing body decline still further. Moreover, we find many old people who, when they have reached such an age that they possess no bodily strength, then excel in judgment and every form of wisdom.

From this, therefore, a clear argument is gathered: the rational soul does not proceed from a union of the elements, but, as we said above, is a substance subsisting in itself. For whatever exists as one in number, remains unchangeable in its own nature, and is receptive of contraries, is certainly a substance subsisting in itself.

Since, then, the soul is one in number—for example, the soul of Plato, of Socrates, or of any one human being—and is in no way changed in its own nature, but is receptive of good and evil, it necessarily follows that it is a substance subsisting in itself.

It is proved in the following way that it is not corporeal. Every quality of a body is subject to human senses. But the qualities of any thing that are subject to no bodily sense must not themselves be called corporeal. The qualities of the soul, however, are good and evil, and these are perceived by no bodily sense. Therefore the soul is not corporeal.

The same point is also proved by another argument. Every body is perceived by some bodily sense. But the soul is subject to no bodily sense. Therefore it is not corporeal.

This soul also is not corrupted when the body is corrupted. The corruption of a body occurs in three ways: either when something withers and dries up, as we see in trees and plants; or when it suffers a diminution of itself, as salt or hay does when it is moved from one place to another; or when it is dissolved, as a house is when it is destroyed, or a vessel when it is broken. None of these occurs except either in a body or in something that happens to a body. But the soul is neither a body nor grounded in a body. Therefore it is not corrupted in any of these ways.

Furthermore, this rational soul completes the species of the human being, since it is what makes a human being rational.  
[Col. 0585C]

**MOYSES.** I have clearly understood how the bodily spirit differs from the rational soul. But since philosophers say that there are three souls in human beings, I ask you to explain what they are.

**PETRUS.** The three souls they speak of are the vegetative soul, the animal soul, and the rational soul.

**MOYSES.** I ask you to describe the operations and functions of each of them.

**PETRUS.** I wish to ascend step by step from the lowest to the higher. The vegetative soul has two functions. It produces the growth of things and supplies bodies themselves with nourishment. It does both of these only through the four powers of nature: the appetitive, retentive, digestive, and expulsive powers.

This soul is found in all shrubs and plants growing from the earth, and in every species of animal. The functions of the animal soul are truly the senses of the body and movement from place to place. It is found only in animals, and this soul is joined to the bodily spirit as if by certain bonds.

The functions of the rational soul are to deliberate, to remember what has been deliberated, to distinguish, to establish something fixed and certain, to retain memory, to wish to investigate the causes of things, and, after investigating them, to arrive at the truth of the matter. This soul remains in no species of animal except the human being alone.  
[Col. 0586A]

**MOYSES.** I neither understand nor cease to wonder how these three souls have come together in one human being, while two are found in irrational animals and only the third is found in all things growing from the earth.

**PETRUS.** I have read in the books of certain philosophers that, when it pleased the Creator to bring forth the bodies of all living and growing things, he mixed the four elements together and tempered one of their qualities with its contrary. From that mixture the bodies mentioned above were produced.

From the tempering of the qualities there arose the four natures that we called powers above: the appetitive, retentive, digestive, and expulsive powers. Once such bodies had been produced, the vegetative soul adhered to all of them and exercised its functions in them—namely, growing, nourishing, and generating.

The animal soul was joined to the subtler bodies so that it could display its functions in them—namely, providing sensation and movement from place to place. But to that which was the subtlest, lightest, and most perfectly tempered of them, and most suitable for receiving reason, the rational soul joined itself and displayed there the functions we mentioned above.

Thus, according to God’s will and arrangement, these three souls came together in the human being, while only two came together in irrational animals.  
[Col. 0586C]

The third alone is found in trees and plants that grow from the earth.

**MOYSES.** You have kindly shown me what I did not know, but one matter remains that I ask to have explained. Since all bodies are composed of the four elements, I am greatly surprised that some should be lighter than others.

**PETRUS.** This results either from the difference in the quantities of the elements joined unequally in the creation of bodies, or from the difference in the tempering of their qualities. If you wish to know more fully about this, you will find it in the books of the philosophers. For the present, however, we have neither the time nor the place to explain such a matter; we ought rather to return to the subject before us.  
[Col. 0586D]

**MOYSES.** Up to this point you have treated philosophically enough the difference between the bodily spirit and the rational soul. But since the less learned do not penetrate the depths of subtle arguments with their simple minds, I ask you, if you can, to prove this same difference by the testimony of the Law or the prophets, so that, although the weight of profound arguments has not enlightened their minds, authority may at least make them believe.

**PETRUS.** At the beginning of the book of Genesis the prophet Moses says: “God formed man from the clay of the earth, and breathed into his face the breath of life, and man became a living soul” (Gen. II). By “the breath of life” he understood the bodily spirit, and by “a living soul,” the rational soul.  
[Col. 0587A]

**MOYSES.** We can understand “the breath of life” as the rational soul.

**PETRUS.** What you say cannot stand. In the same book, a little later, it is written: “All flesh that moved upon the earth perished, birds, living creatures, beasts and reptiles that creep upon the earth, all human beings, and all things in which there is the breath of life died upon the earth” (Gen. VII).

Behold: after enumerating birds, living creatures, beasts and reptiles, and human beings, he suddenly adds that all things in which there is the breath of life died. If he had wished the rational soul to be understood by “the breath of life,” then all creatures would already possess a rational soul. But since no creature except the human being has a rational soul, it is clear that “the breath of life” did not signify the rational soul. Solomon, likewise, the wisest of men, expressing the same view, says: “Who knows whether the spirit of the sons of Adam ascends upward, and whether the spirit of beasts descends downward?” (Eccles. III).

Behold: he says that the spirit of human beings ascends upward because it remains incorruptible after the body, but that the spirit of beasts, which is corrupted and perishes together with the body, descends downward.  
[Col. 0587B]

**MOYSES.** From every angle I have plainly understood that the rational soul is one thing and the bodily spirit another, and that the bodily spirit is formed from the conjunction of the four elements. I therefore recognize that the spirit which the prophet Ezekiel, at God’s command, ordered to come from the four regions of the world (Ezek. XXXVII) must be understood as the bodily spirit. And concerning the dead whom he raised, although many believe that they received a rational soul, I confess that I find no authority for this.

Nevertheless, whatever the manner in which that resurrection occurred, I both say and believe that it was a sign of the future resurrection—namely, that God will one day raise our dead so that they may inhabit the earth once more, just as the same prophet showed earlier when he said: “And you shall know that I am the Lord, when I open your graves and lead you out of your tombs, O my people, and give my spirit in you, and you shall live, and I shall cause you to rest upon your own soil” (ibid.).

**PETRUS.** This could certainly have been said about the resurrection of the dead on the day of judgment.  
[Col. 0587D]

**MOYSES.** If he intended it to be understood of that judgment, he ought not at the end of the sentence to have said, “I shall cause you to rest upon your own soil.” For then no one will be permitted to rest upon his own earth.

**PETRUS.** This rest can be understood in such a way that it signifies the soul’s resting in the body, which is not improperly expressed by the name “earth,” from which the body was taken. Scripture itself confirms this, since it frequently calls the body by the name “earth.” Moses says: “God formed man from the clay of the earth” (Gen. II).

Behold: although the human being is perfected through the conjunction of the four elements, he is said to have been made only from the earth, which is one element. This is not inappropriate, because the name “earth” signifies the body.

We can therefore understand the words “he will cause them to rest upon their own soil” to mean that the soul will return to the body, and both will be judged (I Cor. XIII; II Cor. III; I Thess. IV). This meaning can be soundly understood in the explanation of that prophecy, so that no passage of Scripture or argument of reason seems contrary to it.

Whatever can be understood in several ways in the obscure sayings of the prophets is not objectionable if someone explains it in a different but legitimate sense, provided that in explaining it he departs neither from the testimony of Scripture nor from the path of reason. But if someone’s interpretation is or appears to be foreign either to Scripture or to reason, it must rightly be judged to lack force.

Since, therefore, your explanation is found to be contrary both to Scripture and to reason, it must be rejected by the judgment of equity.  
[Col. 0588B]

**MOYSES.** It is pleasing to hear in what way my interpretation is contrary to Scripture.

**PETRUS.** The prophet David says this concerning the dead: “Their graves are their houses forever; their dwelling places are from generation to generation” (Ps. XLVIII). Again, concerning the same matter: “He will enter unto the generations of his fathers, and forever he will not see the light” (ibid.). Elsewhere: “Like the wounded who sleep in the graves, whom you remember no more, and they are cast away from your hand” (Ps. LXXXVII).

Job also, expressing the same view, says: “Remember that my life is wind, and my eye shall not return to see good things, nor shall the sight of man look upon me. Your eyes are upon me, and I shall not remain. As a cloud is consumed and passes away, so one who descends to the underworld shall not ascend; he shall not return any more to his house, and his place shall know him no more” (Job VII).

Again, elsewhere: “I shall go, and shall not return, to a land that is dark” (Job X). Again, the same man says: “When a man has fallen asleep, he shall not rise” (Job XIV).

Solomon too expresses a view consonant with these words, saying: “The living know that they will die, but the dead know nothing more, nor do they have any further reward, because their memory has been given over to oblivion. Love, hatred, and envy will perish together, and they have no share any longer in this age or in the work that is done under the sun” (Eccles. IX).

Behold: Solomon, the wisest of men, agrees with the authorities of the others that the dead are not to be raised in order to inhabit the earth; yet he declares that they will rise at some time when he says that they have no share in the things done under the sun—that is, in earthly things—thereby indicating that they will have a share in the things done above the sun—that is, in heavenly things.  
[Col. 0588D]

**MOYSES.** Half of the arguments or authorities you have introduced would be sufficient for any wise person. Nevertheless, since you have said that our interpretation is contrary both to Scripture and to reason, it remains for you to show in what respect it disagrees with reason.

**PETRUS.** Do you not believe that, when your dead rise at the coming of the Anointed One, Adam and Seth, Methuselah, Abraham, Isaac and Jacob, Moses and Aaron, the other patriarchs and prophets, and all the righteous who died before his coming will also rise together with them? Do you not believe that they will perform and endure all the functions of the human body, recall their former customs, inhabit the earth once more in the ancient manner, and that Aaron and his sons will offer sacrifice as before, while Moses clothes them in priestly garments?  
[Col. 0589A]

**MOYSES.** I cannot deny that our teachers have said all these things.

**PETRUS.** Who, I ask, will then be the greatest high priest?

**MOYSES.** Who could be greater than Aaron?

**PETRUS.** What, then, will become of Eleazar and the many others who were once all high priests? Will they be supreme at the same time, or will they be deprived of the dignity of that order?

If you say that, while Aaron is alive, they cannot exercise the high priesthood, what benefit will their resurrection bring them? Their rising will bring them more disgrace and inconvenience than honor and advantage. It would have been better for them to remain in death than to lead a life of misery—especially since by this arrangement the Law of Moses is also destroyed, for it commands that no one who has been raised to a higher rank may afterward be reduced to a lower one.

But if you grant that all will be equal in the order of the high priesthood, you take away Aaron’s honor, since no one among many equals can possess an outstanding honor. Moreover, many high priests require many temples. From this, therefore, another absurdity and another destruction of the Law follow, since it commands that there be neither more than one priest nor more than one temple.  
[Col. 0589B]

**MOYSES.** I have no argument that can obstruct your reasoning. For I see that we must either grant that we shall have a new law, or concede that the Law of Moses cannot stand in its entirety.

**PETRUS.** I rejoice that the light of truth is already entering your mind to some degree. Tell me, then: will you have several kings, or one?

**MOYSES.** We must certainly have one, as the prophet Ezekiel declares: “They shall all have one shepherd” (Ezek. XXXVII). For if there are several, since they will not be able to agree, they will destroy the peace of the kingdom.

**PETRUS.** You have begun to answer wisely. But can you say who that king will be?

**MOYSES.** The Anointed One, at whose coming we shall escape captivity and our dead shall be raised; rightly, he ought to govern the kingdom.

**PETRUS.** What you say could be correct if that Anointed One were both human and God. But if, as you believe, he is to be merely human, what then will Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob do? What will Moses and the other prophets do? Will they be subjected to his authority?

**MOYSES.** It ought not to seem surprising if they are subjected to his power. Samuel too was subject to Saul, Elijah to King Ahab, and Elisha and many other prophets to their kings.

**PETRUS.** The analogy with present circumstances does not apply. Although prophets who were by no means kings were subject to kings, it does not therefore follow, nor is it necessary, that a king who is also a prophet should be subject to some earthly king—such as Abraham, David, or Joshua, each of whom was both king and prophet. Moses too was king, prophet, and lawgiver of the entire people. The book of the Law bears witness to him in these words: “No prophet arose again in Israel like Moses, whom the Lord knew face to face, in all the signs and wonders that he sent through him” (Deut. XXXIV).

When such great men are raised and subjected to the authority of that Anointed One, would it not, I ask, have been better for them not to be raised? Moreover, two absurdities follow from this. If Moses is inferior to him, then Scripture lies; but if he is superior, the Anointed One is all the more dishonored.  
[Col. 0590A]

**MOYSES.** Let us therefore propose Moses himself as king.

[Col. 0590B]

**PETRUS.** What, then, will that Anointed One do? And what will Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob do, whom Moses himself, while he lived, held in such high regard (Exod. XXXII) that, whenever he implored something from God, he prayed that he would obtain it for love of them?

If you consider the matter carefully, you are in great difficulty. But I want you to say, if you know: will those dead who are then to be raised possess the nature and power to beget children?

**MOYSES.** I shall deny that they will beget children, so that I may hear what you will answer.

**PETRUS.** First answer whether nature will deny them the function of generation, or whether the command of the Law will prohibit it.

[Col. 0590C]

**MOYSES.** I answer that they will be restrained by the command of the Law.

**PETRUS.** Since the Law of Moses commands that children be begotten, you demonstrate that you will have a new law—which is contrary to your faith.

**MOYSES.** In turn I shall prove that generation is prevented in them by nature, not by the Law.

**PETRUS.** What you say cannot stand. The ear recoils from it, and the mind refuses to believe that there could be an animal whose nature makes it unable to generate unless, through some intervening circumstance, it loses its generative power.

If you say that nature itself will be new, you ought not to say that they will be raised, but that a new creature will come into being, similar to the first only in form and not in its entire nature. They will eat and drink, certainly, but they will not beget children.

**MOYSES.** Whatever we have said up to this point in our exchanged disputation, we have spoken not so much in defense of the truth as through the labyrinths of syllogisms. Our belief is that, just as they will possess the other functions of humanity, so too they will possess the nature of generation, to such an extent that we believe a woman will conceive every day and give birth every day.

**PETER.** What you say can scarcely be heard by human ears. For—to admit that what you say is true—that all will believe in the Anointed One and be resurrected: if they were to beget children every day, surely even if the earth were twice as large it could not contain them; or even if the sea became land, space would be so cramped [Col. 0591A] that they would have no fields to cultivate. Rather, because of the lack of land there would always be contention and quarrelling among them. Furthermore, when all are raised, will each man return to the wife he had, or will he have another, a new wife?

**MOSES.** Each man will certainly recover his own. For this will be the consummation of their joy.

**PETER.** That woman, then, who died after having had three or more husbands—which of them will she have at the resurrection? (Matt. XXII; Luke XX; Mark XII.) For if you answer that she will have the first, Moses’ law will be destroyed, since it says that after a second husband she must not return to her first husband. But if you answer that she will have someone other than the first, there is likewise a destruction of the law, since the same law commands that, while the first husband is alive and has not repudiated her, she cannot marry anyone else (Lev. XX). But see: when so many have been raised, and so many have been born after them, will each of these eventually die?

**MOSES.** From that time onward they will remain immortal.

**PETER.** Reason demonstrates that what you say cannot stand. For once a human being has eaten, drunk, and made use of procreation, he must be composed of the four elements. But whatever is composed in this way must also be subject to corruption. Therefore necessity concludes that they too, since they are composed in this way, must be subject to the corruption of death. Again, if they are immortal, they are no longer subject to the specific definition that now applies to a human being. For the definition of a human being is “a rational, mortal animal.” But this definition cannot be predicated of immortal human beings. Therefore neither can “human being” be predicated of them specifically. From this intermediate conclusion it follows correctly that those whom you call human beings are not human beings—which is absurd. Again, as we said above, the entire space of the earth would not suffice for their multitude if we assert that this enormous population is immortal, since we have said that they will continue to beget children without interruption; even if they were piled upon one another like stones, they could in no way be contained within a space twice the size of the earth.

**MOSES.** Since I cannot defend them as immortal, I will at least concede that they are mortal.

**PETER.** Since you concede that they will die, I want you to say whether that resurrection will be for punishment or [Col. 0591D] for a crown.

**MOSES.** That resurrection will be for glory and honor, so that the anointed may behold glory and sovereignty and possess perfect joy of body and heart.

**PETER.** Concerning the condition of the good in the interval before they rise, I want to hear what you think: will they remain in punishments or in repose until the time of the resurrection?

**MOSES.** It is absolutely certain that they will enjoy the blessedness of repose with God.

**PETER.** Since, as you assert, that is so, this resurrection will be for punishment rather than for a crown. For if they now rejoice in the gift of eternal life, why will they again be thrust into the prisons of bodies, where they will once more be tormented by hunger, thirst, wakefulness, and various and innumerable [Col. 0592A] sufferings? What is more, according to your view they will endure the fear and punishment of a second death. From all this it is sufficiently clear to anyone that this resurrection will take place for their disgrace rather than for their honor and glory.
