**MOSES.** Even if they now remain in repose and delights, from which they will return to the confinement of bodies, nevertheless such great exultation will be theirs at seeing the presence of the anointed one and rejoicing in his kingdom, at dwelling in Jerusalem as formerly and sacrificing in the temple according to the ancient rite, that the punishment of their bodies will be nothing to them, and the repose they now possess will afterward be regarded as insignificant.

**PETER.** What you say departs from the path of truth. No honor or glory of the present world can in any respect be compared with the delights and repose of eternal life, since no one can enjoy the delights of this world even for a single moment without labor and suffering. But the glory of that blessed life continues perpetually and without interruption, with no affliction intervening—especially since, as your teachers testify, all the honor and glory of this world are to the delights of that life as one is to sixty. Moreover, unless someone is entirely devoid of reason, it is evident to everyone that the joy of seeing God is incomparably greater than seeing such a person as you describe.

**MOSES.** Everything we have said up to now we said for the sake of reasoning and argument. This, however, is the certainty of our faith: that they will be raised, will eat and drink, and will possess both the nature and the use of procreation; and, after the course of a thousand years has elapsed, they will be transferred, without undergoing any death, into the kingdom of perpetual blessedness and immortality.

**PETER.** If you concede that they are immortal, you return to the original absurdity. Within a thousand years their population will multiply so greatly that they will in no way be able to fit within the circuit of the earth. Still less, therefore, will any space remain for cultivating fields. Moreover, the point we made above remains in question: the patriarchs, prophets, and all the righteous who were already shining in glory are again subjected to new punishments by being returned to their bodies. There is another point as well: everything that eats, drinks, and begets also experiences pleasure and sadness; it is beyond doubt that such a thing is composed of the four elements. But how can something composed of them and affected by those passions be transferred into that kingdom with those same affections, without change? But let us grant everything: what will you say about those who are to be born when the anointed one comes and afterward? Will you assert that they will die, or not?

**MOSES.** They will indeed die at the end of Christ’s kingdom.

**PETER.** What, then, will their parents do at their death? It would be better for them not to rise than to endure such grief at their children’s death.

**MOSES.** Let us therefore say that they will not die.

[Col. 0593A] **PETER.** Then Scripture lies when David says in the Psalm: “Who is the man who will live and not see death?” (Ps. LXXXVIII.) So, if you consider the matter from every side, the paths of reason and escape are closed to you. The resurrection of the dead cannot possibly occur in the manner you describe; for this reason we had already refuted it above by the testimony of the law. How, then, brother, can your soul, listening to stories of this kind, indulge them? Pray with me, therefore, for the Lord’s mercy, so that just as he has freed me, he may likewise release you from the error of this unbelief. Amen.

**TITLE IV. To show that the Jews observe only a small part of the whole law of Moses, and that even that small part is not pleasing to God.**

[Col. 0593B] **MOSES.** I rightly give thanks to the Illuminator of hearts, who, even if late, has driven from our mind the darkness of such great blindness. I also rightly return the greatest thanks to you, who by the light of the clearest and unconquerable arguments have removed from me this error of unbelief. Now, if it pleases you, continue in order what you began and disclose the next part of our propositions. For you said that we perform very little of the precepts of the law, and that even this little is not pleasing to God. I eagerly desire to hear why, or with what intention, you said this.

**PETER.** What I said—that you observe very little of the commandments of the law—requires no proof either from authority or from reason, since it is plainly evident; this can be demonstrated from the sacrifices themselves, which you do not celebrate at all. [Col. 0593C] For you sacrifice neither the victim of a lamb, as formerly, at the morning and evening hours, nor the holocausts of the new moons, Sabbaths, and ceremonies; nor do you offer the libations of bread, wine, and oil, which you have likewise abandoned (Num. XXVIII; Ps. LXXX); nor the daily arrangement of the table on which your fathers were accustomed always to set out the bread of the Presence on the seventh day (Exod. XXV).

The lamps prepared in the morning they also used to light in the evening, and at the same times they caused incense placed in censers to be burned in the temple. They likewise observed the ordinations and anointings of priests and the various changes of garments (Exod. XXX), as well as the many varieties involved in the taking of food and the rotation of ministries week by week, according to the precepts of the law (Lev. VIII). They also appointed the Levites chosen according to the law (Deut. XIV), and made them sing with musical instruments as Moses had instituted (Lev. III; Ps. LXXX). They redeemed the firstborn of human beings and of unclean animals at a price (Num. X), and offered upon the altar the first fruits of trees as food for the Lord (Exod. XIII), which were entrusted to the priests for food (Lev. XXIII). The fruit that remained on the trees during the third year yielded no useful benefit. In the fourth year all their fruit was consecrated to the praiseworthy Lord. They also offered the first fruits of their produce to the priests (Num. XVIII; Exod. XXXVI), and from two tithes they gave one to the Levites, while they carried the other to Jerusalem to be eaten in the holy place. The Levites also paid to those same priests a tenth of the tithe they received.

The seventh year was a Sabbath for the land, while the fiftieth was a jubilee (Lev. XXV). The law also subjected every manifestation of leprosy and every leprous lesion (Lev. XIII), the mark of a blemish on houses, the shining spots of erupting swellings, and discolorations changed into various kinds of colors to the judgment of the priests, so that it might be known when something was clean or unclean. The law likewise entrusted to the priests’ decision the case of one who suffered a seminal discharge and of a woman separated during her menstrual periods (Lev. XV), together with their purification sacrifices.

If anyone entered the tent of a dead person or touched the corpse of one who had been killed, or his bone or tomb, both he himself and all the vessels of the tent were unclean until they had been cleansed by being sprinkled with the ashes of a burned heifer (Deut. XIV). In addition, there are very many other precepts in the law (Lev. IV) that you have long since entirely neglected.

**MOSES.** We cannot rightly be reproached for failing to observe the precepts of the law, since we are exiles from our homeland and lack both the temple and the lawful institutions.

**PETER.** You have offered an invalid excuse. For if your sacrifices were acceptable to God, he would not have expelled you from the land in such a way that you could not perform what he had commanded.

**MOSES.** Far be it from us to say that he expelled us from our ancestral soil for the purpose of preventing us from obeying his precepts, since it would not be the work of a wise and just being to command something and afterward prohibit it from being done. Rather, let him demand from us an account of why we did not perform those things: because we sinned in his sight, he became angry with us and expelled us from the land where we cannot fulfill his precepts. Our inability therefore cannot be held against us until the time comes when we return to the land of our dwelling; then we will fulfill in action what the Lord commanded us, and our sacrifice will be acceptable to him, as the prophet Malachi testifies, saying: “And the sacrifice of Judah and Jerusalem will please God as in the days of old and as in ancient years” (Mal. III).

**PETER.** The testimony of this prophecy has no bearing on our present argument. For if you examine the preceding and following account, you will find that it was spoken of the sacrifices of the temple built in the time of Ezra (III Esdras VIII). Concerning your exile, however, I affirm what I said: he expelled you from the land so that you would not offer sacrifices, observe new moons or any festivals in the former manner, or wear away the thresholds of the temple. For when God commanded through Moses that sacrifices be made, he did so precisely so that those who rightly believed in him and loved him with all their mind might observe the precepts of his law with all the care and purity that was fitting—not so that, while practicing thefts, murders, robberies, and other vices, and sacrificing to idols as well, they might handle God’s law unworthily and, polluted by many contaminations, enter his holy temple unfit to offer sacrifice to God, as the prophet Jeremiah testifies, saying:

“Behold, you trust in lying words that will not profit you: to steal, to kill, to commit adultery, to swear falsely, to offer libations to the Baals, and to go after foreign gods whom you did not know. Then you came and stood before me in this house in which my name has been invoked, and you said, ‘We have been delivered,’ even though we had committed all these abominations” (Jer. VII).

Therefore God abominated your works and your victims, together with your songs, and expelled you from his temple and from the land, as the prophet Isaiah makes perfectly clear in these words:

“Of what use to me is the multitude of your victims, says the Lord? I am full; I do not want the holocausts of rams, the fat of fattened animals, or the blood of calves, lambs, and goats. When you come to appear before me, who has required these things from your hands, that you should walk in my courts? Do not offer sacrifice any longer in vain. Incense is an abomination to me. I will not endure your new moon, Sabbath, or other festivals. Your assemblies are wicked. Your new moons and solemnities my soul has hated; they have become burdensome to me. I am weary of enduring them.”

Jeremiah also confirms this, saying: “Why do you bring me frankincense from Sheba and sweet-smelling reed from a distant land? Your holocausts are not acceptable, and your victims have not pleased me” (Jer. VI). Elsewhere he says: “When they fast, I will not hear their prayers, and if they offer holocausts and victims, I will not accept them” (Jer. XIV). The prophet Amos likewise says: “I hate and have rejected your festivals, and I will not accept the odor of your assemblies. If you bring me holocausts and offerings, I will not accept them, and I will not regard the vows of your fattened animals. I will take away the tumult of your songs, and I will not hear the music of your lyre” (Amos V).

Malachi says again: “I have no pleasure in you, says the Lord of hosts, and I will not accept an offering from your hand” (Mal. I). And the Psalmist says: “You did not desire sacrifice and offering, but you fashioned ears for me” (Ps. XXXIX). Through the prophet Hosea he likewise says: “I will put an end to all her joy, her solemnity, her new moon, her Sabbath, and all her festivals” (Hos. II), and many other things that it would take too long to enumerate.

These are the principal and greatest precepts of your law, which, as prophetic authority and the age of the present times indicate, God by no means wishes to receive from your hand.

**MOSES.** We both say and believe that all the prophetic words you have introduced were foretold concerning the Babylonian captivity and were fulfilled in it. For after that captivity, God again looked upon us and accepted our sacrifices.

**PETER.** My excellent understanding agrees with your explanation. For when God led you out of captivity and restored you to the temple and your homeland, it is clear that he fulfilled the threats of the prophets, and, having forgiven your offenses, regarded your victims as acceptable. But when afterward you returned to your former crimes, you were again punished with your former penalties; and since the second captivity was greater and more severe than the first, it is equally clear that God’s indignation against you was greater in the second than in the first.

[Col. 0596A] **MOSES.** In this statement you show yourself inconsistent, since earlier you said that the people of that time were religious and just and faithfully observed the precepts of the law, whereas now you affirm that their works displeased God.

**PETER.** I do not deny that they observed the law worthily, according to the way the lawgiver Moses had received it from God and set it before them. But after Christ came—he who revealed the mysteries of the prophets and, removing the veil from the law, opened the spiritual meaning that had lain hidden (Luke XXIV)—from that time onward they ought to have observed the legal institutions not according to the letter that kills, but according to the life-giving spirit (II Cor. III), since the one who gave the law understood it better than the prophets who had been its hearers. Because they neglected to do this, [Col. 0596B] God refused to accept their ancient observances, just as he also prohibited them from practicing the ancient rites that they had practiced before receiving the law through Moses (Lev. XVIII): taking two sisters as wives at the same time, taking one’s paternal aunt as a wife, and eating every kind of animal (Deut. XIV). Before the law, those who did these and similar things were not held guilty; afterward, no one could do them without sin.

**MOSES.** I believe and judge that our law, as Moses gave it and as every generation of our fathers observed it from ancient times, must likewise be kept in every respect by us.

**PETER.** If the ancient observances of the law had been acceptable to the Lord while you were carrying them out, he would certainly not have expelled you from the temple and your homeland. But, to grant your words for the moment, I will show that you must be refuted by your own judgment, since, as I said, you observe only a few of the precepts of the law, and do not keep even those few in full as the law commands. For neither on your Sabbaths, nor on your solemnities, nor in your fasts do you have the victims or the other things that are necessary and prescribed.

The prayers that you pour out to the Lord in place of sacrifices do not rise to his ears so as to be heard. You cannot or dare not attribute this to my ill will, since your own teachers themselves testify that God has not accepted your prayers from the time when the temple was destroyed. The prophet Jeremiah also confirms this by his authority, saying: “When I cried out and pleaded, he shut out my prayer” [Col. 0596D] (Lam. III). And again: “You have set a cloud before yourself, so that prayer may not pass through” (Lam. III). Isaiah says: “When you stretch out your hands, I will turn my eyes away from you; and when you multiply your prayer, I will not hear” (Isa. I).

Moreover, according to the law of Moses, all of you are unclean. For there is no one among you who has not been polluted by contact with the dead (Num. XIX). This stain is not removed except by sprinkling with the ashes of a red heifer (Lev. XV); since you cannot presently possess such a heifer, you cannot be freed from uncleanness. All your women are likewise believed to be polluted by discharge, since the former priests are absent, and it was left to their judgment to distinguish between a woman polluted by menstruation and one polluted by a flow of blood, as well as to judge children born from pollution. [Col. 0597A] All your foods, too, are proved unclean by the judgment of the law.

Since, then, your entire nation is shown to be polluted, all the women polluted, and therefore all the children to suffer from pollution, while all your foods are unclean and your prayers do not reach the ears of God, and your works do not please him, how, I ask, can they have any assurance that they will either reach an end of their evils or possess any worth before God? I myself give due thanks to him because he has freed me from their error, and I devoutly pray that he may free you as well. Amen.

**TITLE V. On overthrowing the law of the Saracens and refuting the foolishness of their opinions.**

**MOSES.** Up to this point you have shown and proved by the clearest arguments how empty and inconsistent the faith of the Jewish people is in every respect, how irrational and ungrateful their service to God is, and why you have withdrawn from that faith; you have also shown me how great an error I have remained in until now. But since you have abandoned the faith of your fathers, I am surprised that you chose the faith of the Christians rather than that of the Saracens, with whom you have always associated and among whom you were brought up. For I would like, just as I did with the Hebrew sect, to raise against this sect every obstacle I can, so that you may offer an account by which it too can be overthrown, just as you did with ours.

For, as I said, you have always associated and been brought up with them, you have read their books, and you understand their language. Thus, since I am to assume their role, you ought to have chosen this faith above all others, which is plainly more respectable and more suitable than the rest. Their law is indeed broad, preserving many commandments concerning the delights of the present life; in this it is shown that divine love toward them was very great, and it likewise promises its worshipers ineffable joys.

If you seek the root of this law, you will find it founded upon the foundation of unshakable reason. A sign that God loved them and did not wish to burden them with many precepts, but spared them, is that he commanded them to pray only five times a day. Indeed, before they pray they always wash, with perfect cleanliness, their buttocks, penis, hands, arms, face, mouth, nostrils, ears, eyes, hair, and finally their feet. [Col. 0597D] Having done this, they proclaim aloud, confessing one God who has neither anyone or anything like him nor anyone equal to him, and that Mahometh is his prophet.

They also fast for an entire month each year. While fasting, they eat at night and abstain during the day, so that from the hour of the day when they can distinguish a black thread from a white one by sight until sunset, no one dares to eat, drink, or defile himself by intercourse with his wife. After sunset, until the dawn of the following day, they are always permitted to use food and drink and their own wives, as each person wishes. If, however, someone is weighed down by illness or is on a journey, for as long as the illness or journey lasts he may both eat and make use of whatever he wishes, provided that afterward, when possible, he makes up what he failed to complete because of the necessity of illness or travel.

Once each year, solely as an act of recognition, all are commanded to go to see the house of God—which is in Mecca—and worship there, wearing seamless garments, to circle around it, and, as the law prescribes, to cast stones backward between the thighs, for the stoning of the devil. They say that Adam built this house for the Lord after he had been exiled from paradise, and that it was a place of prayer for all his sons until Abraham came. Abraham, the faithful servant of God, strengthened and restored it, made vows to the Lord in it, and offered sacrifices there; after his death he left it to his son named Ishmael. It remained a house of prayer for him and all his sons through many generations, until Mahometh was born. At his birth, they claim, God promised it as an inheritance to him and to all his descendants.

Moreover, they are commanded to plunder, capture, kill, persecute in every way, and destroy God’s enemies and the enemies of their prophet, unless they are willing to repent and convert to their faith, or pay the tax imposed on them for servitude. They are also permitted to eat every kind of flesh except pork, blood, and carrion. They reject whatever has been consecrated in the name of anyone or anything other than God.

Apart from this, they are permitted to have four lawful wives at the same time and, whenever one is repudiated, always to take another, provided that they never exceed the number four. In repudiation this is also observed: it is permitted to repudiate a woman up to three times and then take her back again. It is likewise permitted to possess as many purchased and captive women as one wishes; one has free power to sell and buy the same women again, provided that, after once making one of them pregnant, she cannot be bound to another yoke of servitude.

They are further permitted to take wives from among their own kindred, so that the offspring of their blood may increase and the bond of friendship among them may grow stronger. Their judgments concerning the recovery of possessions are such as, as you know very well, exist among the Hebrews: the claimant must establish his case with witnesses, while the denier clears himself once by an oath. They accept no witnesses except highly suitable and approved persons whom they can believe without an oath.

In certain other matters as well they preserve the custom of the Mosaic law: whoever has shed human blood is punished with the same penalty (Gen. IX), and whoever is caught in adultery is stoned together with the adulteress (Lev. XX). Whoever commits fornication with any other woman is subjected to eighty lashes. The penalty imposed for theft is such that the thief endures eighty lashes the first and second times, loses a hand the third time, and a foot the fourth; and whoever has cut off a limb from another person redeems it at an appropriate price.

All these precepts were established by God so that, if there were excessive freedom to do anything whatsoever, the entire nation would quickly be ruined. They are always commanded to abstain from wine, since it is the fuel and breeding ground of every sin. These are the principal commandments of the law, since it would take too long to linger over each one.

Therefore God promised paradise—that is, a garden of delights watered by flowing streams, in which they will have everlasting dwellings—to those who believe in him and in his faithful prophet Mahometh and fulfill the commandments of his law. The shade of trees will protect them, and they will suffer neither cold nor heat. They will eat every kind of fruit and every kind of food. Whatever each person’s appetite suggests, he will immediately find before him. They will be clothed in silk garments of every color. They will recline in delights, and angels, serving as cupbearers, will walk among them with golden and silver vessels, offering milk in the golden vessels and wine in the silver ones, and saying: “Eat and drink in all joy; behold, what God promised you has been fulfilled.”

They will be joined to virgins whom neither human nor demonic touch has violated, and whose beauty surpasses the splendor of hyacinth and coral. These good things will be given to believers; for those who do not believe in God and his prophet Mahometh, there will be endless infernal punishment. However great the sins by which someone is bound, if on the day of his death he believes in God and Mahometh, he will be saved on the day of judgment through Mahometh’s intervention.

Since you have known these things and many others, too numerous to enumerate, from childhood, and since they are celebrated with the greatest honor by the entire Saracen people, why have you followed the Christian religion rather than the Muslim one, when you could have enjoyed greater happiness both in the present life and in the life to come?

**PETER.** Although the structure of your speech, possessing great elegance and sweetness, may succeed in winning as much favor among those who regard bodily pleasures as the highest good as it would if Mahometh himself were present, it is nevertheless astonishing that you should expect this of me and persist in trying to persuade me of something in which you believe I could not possibly be deceived. For you are certainly aware that I am not ignorant of who Mahometh was, how by cunning pretense he fashioned himself into a prophet, and who his adviser was in contriving this scheme. One thing, I think, remains uncertain to you: how empty I judge the doctrine they call Mahometh’s.

When you have heard my account of his life and character arranged in due order, you will easily be able to distinguish whether I know what is true about him or do not know it.

[Col. 0599D] **MOSES.** I eagerly await hearing that from you.

**PETER.** Mahometh, deprived of both parents, spent the years of his childhood under the protection of his uncle Panephus, at that time serving, together with the whole Arab people, the worship of idols, as he himself testifies in his Qur’an, saying that God told him: “You were an orphan, and I took you in; you were in error, and I guided you; you were poor, and I enriched you.”

After some years had passed, he became a hired servant of a certain very noble widow named Chadigiah. In a short time he so gained the favor of his mistress that, by right of marriage, he took possession of all her affairs and likewise became their master. Made from the poorest to the richest through her wealth, he broke out into such arrogance of mind that he promised himself the hope of ruling Arabia, if he did not fear his fellow tribesmen, since they would not regard him as king, being both his equals and his superiors.

Nevertheless, devising a means by which he might become king, he decided to pretend to be a prophet, relying on the cleverness of his eloquence, which he had acquired through the lightness of his wit among various nations while laboring at commerce. He also relied on the fact that at that time the greater part of the people were soldiers and farmers, and almost all of them idolaters, apart from certain people who held the law of Moses heretically according to the Samaritans, and others who were Christians—Nestorians and Jacobites.

The Jacobites are heretics, named after a certain Jacob. They preach circumcision and believe that Christ was not God but merely a just man conceived by the Holy Spirit and born of a virgin; they nevertheless do not believe that he was crucified or died. At that time there was also, in the region of Antioch, a certain archdeacon who was a friend of Mahometh and himself a Jacobite. He was summoned to the council and condemned. Grieved by the shame of this condemnation, he fled from the region and came to Mahometh.

Relying on this man’s counsel, Mahometh brought to completion what he had been thinking about but could not accomplish by himself. There were also two Jews from that Arabia whom we called heretics, named Abdias and Cahbalahabar. These men joined Mahometh and provided assistance for completing his folly. These three adapted Mahometh’s law, each according to his own heresy, and showed him how to say in God’s name things that both the heretical Jews and the heretical Christians living in Arabia believed to be true. Those who were unwilling to believe of their own accord nevertheless believed through force and fear of the sword.

We know of no other prophecy or miracles of his, as we do of Moses, Joshua, Samuel, Elijah, and Elisha, whom we have heard about and read of as having performed many miracles.

**MOSES.** We believe in many prophets whose miracles we do not read of, such as Jeremiah, Obadiah, Amos, Hosea, and others.

**PETER.** Miracles should not be sought in their case, just as they did not introduce any novelty into the law or in any way contradict the Mosaic teaching; and we know that some of what they foretold was fulfilled.

[Col. 0600D] **MOSES.** There is no doubt that the patriarchs Noah and Abraham gave new commandments divinely, such as those concerning sacrifices, the eating of meat, circumcision, and other rites. Why, then, did their descendants believe them without the illumination of miracles?

**PETER.** They are rightly believed because a prophet testifies concerning them—one whose testimony no one doubts, namely Moses. How, then, should Mahometh be received among the prophets, since he cannot be compared with any prophet with even a trace of probability?

**MOSES.** Why do you say that he was demonstrated to be a prophet by no probability, when you have often heard him clearly marked out by miracles? Did not a dumb animal, namely the ox called Doregele, proclaim him a prophet? Did not the moon, entering through both sleeves and emerging from his bosom restored, identify him as a wondrous prophet? Did not a sheep, whose udder he stroked, provide the entire crowd with an abundant draught of milk, thereby making him known? It was also wondrous that, when he called a fig tree to come to him, the tree did indeed come to him, and he ate its fruit; and the arm of a poisoned sheep that had been placed for him in a dish spoke with him and said: “Do not eat, because I am poisoned.”

PETRUS. The things you are pursuing are frivolous, and are not judged worthy of belief by all your people, especially since Muhammad himself reported nothing of the sort in his Qur’an; rather, he forbade anything about him that had not been written in the Qur’an to be believed entirely true. [Col. 0601B] “Many have lied about many things,” he says, “and, lest this happen to me, let only that concerning me be held true which is confirmed by the authority of the Qur’an.” And, wishing to show why he did not perform a miracle, he introduces the Lord speaking to him, saying: “The Lord said to me: I therefore do not permit you to perform miracles because I fear that, as with the other prophets, you might be contradicted in your miracles.” Thus, by his own testimony, he is shown to have performed no sign of power. By what other indications, then, is he proved to be a true prophet?

The signs of a true prophet are integrity of life, the performance of miracles, and the firm truth of everything he says. In Muhammad, goodness of life consisted in violence, by which he forcibly caused himself to be proclaimed a prophet of God; he delighted in theft and rapine, and burned with the fire of lust to such an extent that he was not ashamed to defile another man’s [Col. 0601C] marriage-bed through adultery, as though the Lord had commanded it, as is read concerning Zanab, the daughter of Las and wife of Zet. “The Lord,” he says, “commands you to dismiss your wife Zet.” After she had been dismissed, he immediately took her for himself. The disgrace of his wife Iassa more clearly revealed how empty his prophecy was: when she was caught in adultery, he falsely confirmed, through the testimony of many, that she had not been caught, because he did not wish to dismiss her, claiming that the message had come from Gabriel.

Concerning the power of this vice—lust, namely—it is reported that he praised God because it abounded in him forty times beyond the human measure, congratulating himself because the pleasant fragrance and beauty of women, granted by God, delighted him exceedingly. Enough has already been said about the miracles. As for the wars which he confessed to having undertaken at the Lord’s command and with victory promised to him, his teeth broken in battle, his face struck, and the many slain and fleeing among his followers testify to the truth. If, as you say, an angel of the Lord guarded him, these things would by no means have happened to him, just as we read of Elijah and Elisha (III Kings XIX), whom God always rescued from their enemies. Moreover, if he were such a man as he claims, victory would always have followed him, as it followed Moses, Joshua, and David, who, engaging in battles at the divine command, were always accompanied by victory (IV Kings VI; Exodus XVII; Joshua I). If he were also a true prophet, as you say, he would have known whether he was going to fare badly when he entered battle. How, then, after abandoning my law, do you say that I ought to follow his law rather than the Christian one?

[Col. 0602A] MOYSES. This argument certainly appears true to anyone who examines it clearly.

PETRUS. The fact that you said earlier that I had read their books, knew their language, and would always be brought up among the Saracens does not mean that I should therefore adopt their law.

MOYSES. Because I believed it to be good, I said that you ought to accept it.

PETRUS. You also said that the root of their law was built upon the unshakable foundation of reason. Therefore, let us range through the field of disputation, word against word and command against command, if we can find it well founded.

MOYSES. I agree.

PETRUS. When you say that Muhammad commands prayer five times a day, he did this because, following the advice of his teachers, he wished to make his law a mediator between the law of the Jews and that of the Christians—not through its own integrity, nor with God’s assistance. The Jews, according to the law, pray three times a day, while Christians pray seven times; but he established a midpoint between the two by praying neither three nor seven times, but five.

Your praise of his command that, before praying, they wash their hands, arms, and the other members of the body has nothing to do with prayer. What pertains to prayer is to be cleansed inwardly, not outwardly. The cleansing of the limbs through washing belonged to the worshipers of the star Venus, who, wishing to pray to it, adorned themselves in the manner of women. Because he became king through the sign of the star Venus, he therefore issued these commands.

You admit that, at the time of prayer, they proclaim it publicly in a loud voice. This is not appropriate to prayer, unless it is because he could impose no other new sign. You say that he commanded them to fast for an entire month, in order to restrain the vices of the flesh; this is the beginning of repentance. But tell me, please: what benefit is it to fast by day, to eat three or four times at night, to enjoy good meats and the finest foods, and to have intercourse with women? These things do not weaken the flesh; they strengthen it.

When you say that once a year they go to the house of God, which is in Mecca, for the sake of recognition, and pray there—at the house which they say was Adam’s and Abraham’s—they have no authority for this, but invent it as some sort of fiction. Before he preached the law, that house was full of idols. But if you, O Moses, knew what that house was like, what secret it contained, why Muhammad went there, and what the law commands them to do there, you would be greatly astonished at it.

[Col. 0602D] MOYSES. I ask you to explain what you are suggesting. Although I preach this law to you, I do not know why he commanded them to make that journey and to perform there the other things prescribed by the law.

PETRUS. I had intended to inform you briefly, but since you have now asked, I shall show it openly. The two sons of Lot, Ammon and Moab, honored this house, and two idols were worshiped there by them, one fashioned from a white stone and the other from a black stone. The name of the one made of black stone was Mercury; the name of the other was Chamos. The one made of black stone was built in honor of Saturn, and the one made of white stone in honor of Mars.

Twice a year their worshipers ascended to adore them: to Mars, when the sun enters the first degree of Aries, because the ram is the honor of Mars. At his departure, as was customary, stones were thrown. To Saturn, however, they went when the sun enters the first degree of Libra, because the scales are the honor of Saturn. That they burned incense naked and with shaven heads is still practiced in India to this day, as I have said.

The Arabs worshiped the idols together with Ammon and Moab. But when Muhammad came after a long interval, he could not abolish the ancient custom; instead, as though the practice had been somewhat changed, he allowed them to go around the house covered with unstitched coverings. Yet, so that he would not appear to command them to sacrifice to idols, he built an image of Saturn into the wall, in the corner of the house, so that its face would not be visible; only its back was placed on the outside.

The other idol, that of Mars, since it was sculpted on every side, was placed beneath the earth, and he put a stone over it. He commanded the people who gathered there to worship to kiss these stones and, with their heads bowed and shaven, to throw stones backward between their legs. Those who bow down uncover their backs, which is a sign of the former law. Tell me, then, Moses: with what intention did he command these things, unless it was the intention I have described?

MOYSES. I told you that I do not know his intention, because I have nowhere found it written. I do know one thing about the throwing of stones: they say that they do this to drive away demons. I saw it written in their books that a certain Bomar, one of Muhammad’s ten companions, began in the customary manner by kissing the stones. “I say to you, stones,” he said, [Col. 0603C] “that I know you can neither help nor harm; but because Muhammad did it, I follow his custom.”

PETRUS. What you said about driving away demons by throwing stones does not seem to follow logically, because that which is not perceived by any bodily sense can by no means easily be driven away. Demons are driven away by the divine name.

MOYSES. Since I have heard some people say that they have seen demons, heard them, and spoken with them, I am surprised that you say they cannot be perceived by the bodily senses.

PETRUS. Although an angel cannot be perceived by bodily sense, angels nevertheless become visible to those who walk according to God’s commandments. Similarly, the devil appears visibly to his friends.

[Col. 0603D] MOYSES. I would indeed like to know by what instruction or art I might see them or speak with them.

PETRUS. Why do you desire to know something that in no way concerns you?

MOYSES. Not so that I might practice such works, but I would like to possess the knowledge alone.

PETRUS. How can you wish to learn something that would increase your error?

MOYSES. You have corrected me well, thanks be to God; through your words I have learned the meaning.

PETRUS. Enough has now been said; let us return to our subject. Because Muhammad commanded that the adversaries of God should be plundered, taken captive, and killed until they were willing either to believe or to pay tribute, this does not belong to the works of God. Nor did he command any of the prophets to compel anyone to believe. He himself issued this command out of greed for money and in order to destroy his enemies.

As you know, this ought not to be done. Rather, if anyone wishes to convert another, he should do so not through violence but carefully and gently, as Muhammad himself testifies in his Qur’an, speaking in the person of the Lord and saying the same thing: “If the Lord your God wished it, the peoples of the whole world would believe. Why, then, do you compel them to believe?” For no one believes except by the will of God.

And elsewhere he says: “O peoples, the truth of God has now come to you. Whoever believes does so for himself; whoever goes astray does so for himself; and I am not your guardian.” He continues: “Follow what is revealed to you, and wait until God judges, for he is judge over all.”

Likewise, in the same book, he says: “The Lord your God, if he wished, would place everyone under one law without disagreement.” Elsewhere he pretends that God is speaking to him: “There must be no violence in religion; truth and justice have now appeared. Whoever wishes may believe of his own accord.”

Again, in the Qur’an: “O unbelievers, I do not worship what you worship, nor do you worship whom I worship; nor do I worship what you worship; for me is a law, and for you a discordant law.” And elsewhere he says: “Do not argue with the peoples of another religion except with gentle words.”

Why, then, did he command them to plunder, take captive, and compel peoples by force to believe, while admitting that all these things are the paths of God? Tell me, Moses: why do you command belief in a law that contradicts itself?

MOYSES. The book of the Qur’an is such that what comes later also destroys the earlier order.

[Col. 0604C] PETRUS. The Qur’an was not written by Muhammad’s own hand; for if he had done so, it would have been arranged in order. After his death, however, his companions, who had lived with him, each reporting, so to speak, his own reading, composed the Qur’an. Hence we do not know which order was earlier and which later.

Muhammad therefore commanded them to plunder, take captives, and kill peoples because the Arabs, who lived in the desert without knowledge of God, delighted in raiding—and especially so that they would believe in him.

MOYSES. I consider what you say to be true.

PETRUS. When you say that all flesh is permitted to them as food except the flesh of pigs, blood, and carrion, all flesh is permitted to us as well. We disagree only concerning the flesh of pigs. Muhammad did this so that we Christians would differ from his law in that respect.

As for what you said about wives—that it is permitted to take four and to take another after divorcing any one of them—this is prescribed by no valid principle. A man is commanded to take a wife only for the purpose of begetting children (Leviticus XVIII). But that they may have as many purchased and captive women as they wish is, as far as we are concerned, adultery, since a father has often purchased a woman violated by his son, and conversely a son or brother has purchased one corrupted by his father.

MOYSES. What you say is believed to be true. But since such disagreement existed among these commandments, why did Muhammad, who appears so wise, command these things to be done?

PETRUS. Muhammad loved women exceedingly and was excessively lustful; as he himself confessed, the power of forty men’s lust resided in him. And especially because the Arabs were very lustful, he satisfied their desires so that they would believe.

As for your statement that they were permitted to take wives from their own kin, this was customary among all peoples at that time, so that the bond of friendship might remain strong among them.

Regarding the judgments you mentioned earlier, in some matters they agree with the law of Moses, while in others they disagree; Muhammad made them so that his law would differ somewhat from the law of Moses.

They are commanded always to abstain from wine so that, perhaps, his companions, when drunk, might not reveal the downfall of the people.

What you preached about paradise must be set aside, since it cannot be established by reason. For when the soul has been separated from the body and the four elements have been separated from one another, [Col. 0605B] a person will not use these worldly things in the way he did before. We condemned this above in the third title, where we spoke about the resurrection of the dead. A wise person does not believe in such a paradise, nor is he deceived by such words.

The people of Muhammad’s time, without law or Scripture and ignorant of every good thing except warfare and the plow, desiring lust and devoted to gluttony, could easily be addressed with preaching suited to their wishes. For if he had acted otherwise, he would not have drawn them toward his law.

MOYSES. Without God’s assistance, such a great people would not have believed in him.

PETRUS. If he had accomplished everything with God’s assistance, he would not have been defeated so many times, nor would his teeth have been broken in battle, as we said above. Like other kings, he was defeated and at times he won.

After his death, however, all wished to depart from his law. He himself had said that on the third day his body would be carried up to heaven. But when they recognized him as a liar and saw that the corpse was rotting, the greater part of the people departed, leaving the body unburied.

A certain son of Abitharius, one of Muhammad’s ten companions, then obtained the kingdom after his death. He preached gently and craftily urged the peoples to believe, saying that they did not properly understand Muhammad’s words.

“Muhammad,” he said, “did not say that he would be lifted up to heaven before burial or in the sight of human beings. He said that, after the burial of his body, angels would carry him up to heaven while everyone was unaware. Therefore, because they did not bury him immediately, he began to rot, so that he might be buried at once.”

For this reason he kept the people for a while in their former error.

Two brothers who were Muhammad’s scribes, named Hazan and Hozain, severely afflicted their bodies with fasts and vigils and nearly reached the point of death. Their father often warned his sons not to weary their bodies through such prolonged mortification. When he saw that they were fools and had already come to death’s door through excessive labor, he revealed to them what had happened with Muhammad.

Once they learned from their father of Muhammad’s wickedness, they began to eat and drink wine, and, although they had previously persevered vigorously in his law, they eventually began to abandon it, though not entirely. Some part of the people followed them in this practice.

Thus, O Moses, we can recognize in every way that he was neither a true prophet nor were his words true. Although we pass over many things that we could say about him, let us introduce one matter that both you and we believe: namely, Christ, whom we equally believe to have died and been crucified. Muhammad denies this. For he himself says: “They did not kill Christ or crucify him, but it appeared so to them.”

You will find him to be a liar not only in this matter. Read again all the books and the words of the prophets, and in everything he said about them you will find that he lied. How, then, do you urge me to believe that liar, when you have found him deceitful in everything?

I beseech the mercy of almighty God to free me from his error and to bring to completion the law that I have begun to fulfill. Amen.

# TITLE VI. On the Trinity

MOYSES. Enough has been debated so far against our sect and the sect of the Saracens. You have refuted both, relying on reason as well as authority. Now explain what your faith is like, and distinguish the manner of your belief under separate headings.

PETRUS. At the beginning of my book I already explained to you the manner of my belief under headings. Now ask about each heading in the course of the same discussion, and, if you can, destroy what I have said.

MOYSES. I desire this, if I can. I shall therefore begin by asking about the first part of your belief: namely, how God is one and there are three persons, so that none of these is naturally prior to another in time, nor is one substantially separated from another—those whom Christians call the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit. Afterwards we shall debate the other parts of your belief until we have completed them all. Explain, then, first in a rational manner what these three persons are.

PETRUS. I wish to call the three persons substance, wisdom, and will. I call the first person substance because wisdom and will are in it and from it, while it is from no one, although all three persons are one substance.

MOYSES. Can these three be discovered by reason?

PETRUS. They can. For in the first part of my book we discussed substance sufficiently and firmly, establishing what it is, and we do not need to inquire further about it. But it remains to explain whether wisdom and will inhere in substance itself.

MOYSES. This is what I ask.

PETRUS. Since it is therefore established that substance truly exists, that it is the creator of all things, the beginning of things begun, and the maker of things made, it must possess wisdom and will, so that it may know what it wishes to make before it wishes to make it, and so that, before the work appears outwardly in its execution, it may first be formed in the mind by imagining it. This imagining is wisdom.

When it possesses wisdom in this way, it either acts or does not act. It does not act if it does not wish to. But if it acts, it both wishes and acts, and this is will. [Col. 0607A] Thus it appears from our manner of speaking that an action is preceded by wisdom and will. Therefore the Creator of the world could not create anything before wisdom and will existed in him.

MOYSES. It is true.

PETRUS. Therefore God is substance, wisdom, and will.

MOYSES. It is true. But you must still prove that this wisdom and will exist eternally in God and are inseparable from him, and that, as you believe, neither is earlier than he in time.

PETRUS. I shall prove it. Since it is established that God possesses wisdom and will, we must determine whether this wisdom and will, existing in him and not separated from him, are sometimes with him and sometimes not.

MOYSES. It is true that they are in him and are not separated from him, because otherwise God would be not wise after having been wise, and would be without will after having possessed will. For it cannot happen that, once they are in him, they are separated from him, except accidentally—and accident is not found in him.

PETRUS. May God bless you, because you have understood and conceded the truth well, and have shown that you possess a sound faith. But you must still inquire whether this wisdom and will are eternal or had a beginning.

MOYSES. Let us suppose for the moment that they had a beginning.

PETRUS. Then your statements contradict one another. [Col. 0607C] For you said that God cannot be not wise after having been wise, nor be without will after having had will. Then, since you supposed that they had a beginning, they were at some time in him and at some time were not.

MOYSES. This is not at all contrary to my assertion. Earlier I said that God cannot lack wisdom and will after he has possessed them. But when I conceded that they had a beginning, I did not contradict the possibility that he could possess what he had not possessed.

PETRUS. If they had a beginning, then either God created them, or they created themselves.

MOYSES. Without doubt God created them, because no thing creates itself.

[Col. 0607D] PETRUS. Therefore, if God created them when they had a beginning, the Creator himself needed another wisdom and will by which to create them. And, as has been said, an artisan must possess wisdom and will before he makes anything. Thus we proceed to infinity.

It is therefore necessary that wisdom and will exist eternally in God and be inseparable from him, and that God not be earlier than them in time. This is what we wish to explain.

MOYSES. It is true; it is right and useful for us to assent to the truth.

PETRUS. But it remains to say which of these two—wisdom and will—is called the Son, and which the Holy Spirit.

MOYSES. Since neither of them is prior to the other in time, and substance is not prior to them, can any of these three be prior to another in some order of speech?

PETRUS. It can, according to the order of names, not according to nature. Substance contains wisdom and will, and therefore is first. Wisdom is prior to will because, before the Creator wishes anything, he must know what he wishes.

According to this ordered arrangement of names, substance is prior to wisdom and will, and wisdom is prior to will. In the same way, the names are Father, Son, and Holy Spirit.

We have discussed this matter with you so crudely because you do not perceive subtler things, so that in this manner at least you might be able to understand something of it. If we were speaking about it with some Christian, we could debate it with him much more subtly.

MOYSES. Since you have shown by reason that God possesses wisdom and will, can it be found in the sequence of any authoritative book that the Creator himself used wisdom and will in the creation of the world?

PETRUS. Certainly. Concerning wisdom, Solomon says in Proverbs: “The Lord founded the earth by wisdom; he established the heavens by prudence” (Proverbs III). Concerning will, David says in the Psalm: “He has done everything whatsoever he willed” (Psalm CIII).

MOYSES. Why do you call the second person of your Trinity by this name, wisdom, when others call it the Word?

PETRUS. There is no contradiction here. The Word of God is his perfect wisdom, as the Psalmist also shows when he says: “By the word of the Lord the heavens were established” (Psalm XXXII). It is therefore clear that the wisdom of God and his Word are the same.

MOYSES. So far you have treated the explanation of the Trinity quite philosophically, but I would like at least one authority from Scripture to prove that there are multiple persons in God.

PETRUS. I shall prove it not by one authority but by several—not by hidden passages, but by clear and intelligible ones.

MOYSES. Then reveal them.

PETRUS. What could be clearer or more effective for proving this than an explanation of the names of God, such as Elohim and Adonai? For Elohim demonstrates plurality; its singular is Eloha.

When I say Elohai, it is as though I were saying “my gods,” indicating a plurality of gods but only one person speaking. When I say Elohemi, it is as though I were saying “our gods,” indicating the plurality both of the gods and of those who speak. If Elohi is said, however, it is as though one were saying “my God.” Yet this is found in no Hebrew Scripture: no human being is ever found to call God Elohi, although, according to the rules of the Hebrew language itself, it could be said.

MOYSES. In your Gospel, however, Christ is found to have called out Elohi from the cross (Mark XV; Matthew XXVII).

PETRUS. I know that this presents no contradiction for me. Christ was invoking God the Father, that is, one of the three persons—one person rather than another.

Similarly with the name Adon, meaning “Lord.” When we say Adon, it indicates singularity. When we say Adonai, it is as though we were saying “my lords,” indicating a plurality of lords while the speaker is singular. When I say Adonemi, it is as though I were saying “our lords,” indicating both many lords and many speakers. When I say Adoni, it is as though I were saying “my Lord,” indicating one Lord and one speaker.

A human being, however, is found to be called by this name only by another human being; God is never found to be called so. Since in the sacred Scriptures God is found to be called Eloha and Adon, which are interpreted in the singular as “God” or “Lord,” he is therefore one. Elsewhere he is again found to be called Elohim and Adonai, which signify plurality, and gods are thereby indicated. This appears contradictory. For either God will be one or he will be many.

There is no contradiction in God. When he called himself by a singular name, this certainly refers to one substance; when by a plural name, it refers to several persons. There is therefore one God in several persons.

MOYSES. That the names Elohim and Adonai signify plurality follows from the rules of the literary art. But that God called himself by these names, without being compelled by any rules, he did according to his own will; and his will ought to be subject to no rules.

PETRUS. It is indeed true that those names should not be subjected to rules—but only if they are proper names, not appellatives. These, however, are appellatives, and therefore are rightly subject to rules, as we explained above.

Thus, when they are expressed in the singular, they signify singularity; when in the plural, plurality. We find this in Genesis, where Lot called the angels Adonai (Genesis XIX), that is, “my lords,” because there were certainly two angels.

Elsewhere in the same book, Laban, rebuking Jacob, says: “Why have you stolen my Elohai?” (Genesis XXXI), that is, “my gods.” In the Psalms it is written: “I said, Elohimatem” (Psalm LXXXI), that is, “you are gods.” And the Lord, speaking through Moses to the Israelite people, says: “You shall not have Elohim Mermi” (Exodus XX), that is, “foreign gods.” The books of the prophets likewise abound sufficiently in similar testimonies.

MOYSES. Although it has been shown that Elohim and Adonai signify plurality, when they are spoken of God they signify singularity, as is shown by the action joined to them, which is expressed by a singular verb. For Scripture says of God “he made” and “he said” (Genesis I), or something similar, and does not say “they made” or “they said.”

PETRUS. This is my authority: the name of God is expressed in the plural, while the action is expressed in the singular. Hence it is clear that God is one in several persons.

Nevertheless, to cut off all your objections, I can show that both the name of God and the action itself are expressed in the plural. Although it has already been shown by many arguments that there is only one God, we cannot refer this to several gods. It must therefore refer to one God and several persons.

MOYSES. If you show this, then what you have proposed will have been most fully proved.

PETRUS. If, with God’s help, I show this to you, will you believe in one God and several persons?

MOYSES. I shall make no agreement with you concerning this matter; I merely wish to listen attentively.

PETRUS. I certainly know the hardness of your heart, but I shall nevertheless now show it to you. Perhaps through this you will remember some good thing.

In the Book of Samuel it is written that, when the Philistines saw the ark of the Lord coming against them, they said: “Elehem Elohim” (II Kings IV), that is, “These are the gods who struck Egypt with every plague in the desert.” Here both the name of God and the action are expressed in the plural.

MOYSES. I do not grant that you have proved what you proposed by this. These people said this while believing not in one god but in several, and they supposed that the gods of Israel were many, just as their own gods were.

PETRUS. Since you do not grant this, I shall now show you a similar statement in the books of the prophets. It is written in Genesis: “The Lord spoke to Jacob: Arise, go up to Bethel and dwell there, and make an altar to the God who appeared to you when you were fleeing from your brother” (Genesis XXXV). Here both the name of God and the action are expressed in the singular.

Then it is written in the same book that Jacob fulfilled the Lord’s command. It continues: “He built an altar there and called the name of the place the house of God. For God appeared to him there when he was fleeing from his brother.” Here, however, both “God” and “appeared” are expressed in the plural in Hebrew. For Elohim and Niglu occur there, and Niglu signifies “they appeared” in the plural. If he had wished to say “he appeared” in the singular, he would have written Nigla.

Likewise, in the Book of Samuel, David praises God and says: “What other nation is like your people Israel, one nation on earth, for whose sake God went to redeem it for himself as a people?” (II Kings VII.) Here too both “God” and “went” are plural in Hebrew. Elohim occurs here, along with Halcu, meaning “they went,” whose singular is Halac. “To redeem” and “for himself,” however, are singular.

Again, in Jeremiah it is read: “But the Lord God is true, the living God, and the everlasting king” (Jeremiah X). Here again both “God” and “living” are expressed in the plural in Hebrew.

Since, then, in Scripture the name and action of God are expressed sometimes in the singular and sometimes in the plural, it is clear in both respects that God is one and that there are several persons.

MOYSES. Since it has been shown from the names of God that there is one God in several persons, it remains to ask why there are only three persons, as you believe, and not two, four, or more.

PETRUS. We already demonstrated this above: namely, that there are three persons, when we treated the matter by reason. If you disagree, now that you have conceded from the names of God that there are several persons, say how many persons you wish to believe there are, and I shall weaken your arguments if I can.

MOYSES. I believe neither in two nor in three, nor in any number of persons. I asked this only in order to oppose your arguments.

PETRUS. The Trinity is indeed subtle, ineffable, and difficult to explain. The prophets spoke of it only obscurely and under a veil, until Christ came; he revealed it to the minds of the faithful, according to their capacity, as one God in three persons.

If, however, you consider the matter more subtly and examine that name of God which is explained in the secrets of secrets—I mean the name of three letters, although written with four figures, since one of them is doubled and written twice—you will see that the same name is both one and three. What is one refers to the unity of substance; what is three refers to the Trinity of persons.

That name consists of these four figures: [the four Hebrew figures are absent or illegible in the supplied text]. If you join only the first and second, namely [illegible Hebrew forms], it will be one name. Likewise, if you join the second and third, namely [illegible Hebrew forms], you will have another. Similarly, if you join only the third and fourth, namely [illegible Hebrew forms], you will find a third. Again, if you connect all of them together in order, there will be only one name, as is evident in the following geometrical figure.

[Col. 0611C]

[The geometrical figure is absent from the supplied text.]

Consider, then, O Moses, how secret, subtle, and ineffable this name is, and that it can be recognized only through the keen insight of the mind and profound investigation. Moses testifies to this when he says in Deuteronomy: “Know today and consider in your heart that the Lord himself is God in heaven above and on earth below, and there is no other” (Deuteronomy IV).

Where Latin has “Lord,” you will find the aforementioned name in Hebrew; where Latin has “God,” Hebrew writes Elohim, which signifies plurality. But, so that it might be clear that the same God is called both by a singular proper name and by a plural appellative, and so that they would not think there were several gods, he added: “and there is no other.”

When Moses said, “Know and consider in your heart” (Exodus XX), he truly suggests that the hidden subtlety of this name cannot be grasped by sight, hearing, or any bodily sense, but only by clear intellectual understanding and marvelous intelligence.

The Trinity can also be signified in many other things, such as the fringes which the Lord commanded the children of Israel through Moses to have on their garments, saying: “Speak to the children of Israel, and say to them that they should make fringes for themselves on the corners of their cloaks, placing in them violet cords; when they see them, they will remember all the commandments of the Lord” (Numbers XIX).

Those fringes consisted of four threads, but the threads were doubled; in their upper part they had three knots, and in their lower part two. The four threads signify the four seasons of the year; the doubling of the threads signifies days and nights, so that throughout the four seasons of the year, and by night as well as by day, they might remember God’s commandments.

[Col. 0612B] The three upper knots signify the Trinity of persons; the two lower ones signify the two Testaments, namely the law of Moses and the Gospel.

The Trinity is also indicated in the three blessings with which Aaron and his sons blessed the children of Israel at the Lord’s command, when he said to Moses: “Speak to Aaron and his sons: Thus you shall bless the children of Israel, and say to them: May the Lord bless you and keep you; may the Lord show his face to you and have mercy on you; may the Lord turn his countenance toward you and give you peace” (Numbers VI).

When a priest blessed someone with these blessings, he held both palms extended before his face. When he said “the Lord”—expressed in Hebrew by that threefold and single name mentioned above—he raised the first three fingers of each hand high and straight: the thumb, index finger, and middle finger. Having said the name of the Lord in this way, he lowered the fingers as before.

But tell me, O Moses, what could be allegorized more appropriately by the raising of three fingers than the excellence of the Trinity? If you know and can point out anything else to be noted concerning these matters, please explain it to me.

MOYSES. In truth, we have never noted either what you have said or anything else concerning these matters. Nor have our teachers said that anything should be noted.

PETRUS. What else can be signified by the prophet Isaiah’s statement than the Trinity of persons—namely, by the threefold voice of the angels praising God and saying: “Holy, holy, holy, Lord God of Sabaoth”? (Isa. VI.) Why do they say “holy” exactly three times, rather than once, twice, ten times, a hundred times, or some other number? If they wished to praise him briefly, why would they not say “holy” once? If at length, why would they not offer praise a hundred, a thousand, or an innumerable number of times?

MOYSES. We know no reason for that threefold voice in the angels’ praise except their own choice.

PETRUS. If you answer “We do not know” to each question I put forward, what else do you admit than that you are defeated and unable to offer opposition? David also bears witness to the Trinity of persons when he says: “Seek the Lord [and be strengthened, etc.] and his strength, and seek his face always” (Ps. CIV). For what does he mean by saying, “Seek the Lord and his strength, and seek his face,” except “Seek the Father, the Son, and the Spirit”? For who is understood by the Lord’s strength except his Son, and who by his face except the Holy Spirit? If you understand it otherwise, explain it.

These testimonies of the holy Scriptures concerning the Trinity of persons can therefore suffice for those who understand them. If I were to introduce all the testimonies I could bring to bear on this subject, not even a large book could contain them. Enough on this matter for now. If you have anything else to ask, do not delay.

## TITLE VII. How the Virgin Mary, conceiving from the Holy Spirit without intercourse with a man, gave birth.

[Col. 0613B]

MOYSES. Now I want you to explain concerning Mary how you believe that she gave birth without intercourse with a man (Luke I; Matt. I), and I shall oppose you if I can.

PETRUS. We certainly believe that, when the Holy Spirit came upon her and the power of the Most High overshadowed her, forces came together in her members, as God willed, and that in this way she conceived without intercourse with a man.

MOYSES. It is indeed a remarkable and difficult matter to understand how a son could be begotten from a mother without a carnal father. For in the customary generation of human beings we see that a human being cannot be generated except from the union of two corresponding natures, namely, a man and a woman.

[Col. 0613C]

PETRUS. Why does this generation seem remarkable and ineffable to you, when you have already heard of a similar one, which both you and we believe: namely, that Eve was created without a mother, from a father—that is, from Adam’s flesh? (Gen. II.)

MOYSES. That generation, like this one, could indeed have occurred by a miracle. But concerning that one we have an authority stating that it occurred—namely, Moses (Gen. II), whom no legitimate authority contradicts. Concerning this one, however, I think you will find no authority, unless you have heard one in the books of the prophets that you can produce.

PETRUS. I shall cite not one authority concerning such a matter, but many, since the prophets spoke beforehand in many places about the future birth of Christ.

[Col. 0613D]

MOYSES. If you accomplish what you claim, you will undoubtedly safeguard your faith.

PETRUS. First of all, then, recall what was said through Isaiah to Ahaz, king of Judah. When his enemies had come against him—namely, the king of Armenia and the king of Israel—Isaiah spoke to him as follows: “Do not fear, Ahaz,” he said, “for Jerusalem will not be destroyed, and do not doubt. Ask a sign for yourself from the Lord your God, either in the depths of hell below or in the heights above.” And Ahaz said: “I will not ask, and I will not tempt the Lord” (Isa. VII).

But when Isaiah realized that Ahaz had not spoken in good faith—in fact, that he neither feared nor loved God—he answered: “Hear, then, O house of David: Is it not enough for you to weary men, that you are also wearying my God? Therefore the Lord himself will give you a sign: Behold, a virgin will conceive and bear a son, and she will call his name Emmanuel” (Luke I; Matt. I). This prophecy was spoken concerning Christ and was repeated to blessed Mary through the angel.

MOYSES. How can it stand that what Isaiah announced to Ahaz was spoken, as you assert, concerning Christ and Mary, when, as you yourself know, many hundreds of years passed between Ahaz and Mary?

PETRUS. If you do not believe that it was spoken concerning Christ and Mary, concerning whom do you suppose it was uttered?

MOYSES. Surely concerning the wife of Ahaz and his son Hezekiah, who was born from her.

PETRUS. What you say is false, and you assert it either through ignorance or because you show neither reverence nor honor toward God, daring to lie about him and think wrongly of him. At the time when these words were spoken to Ahaz, he himself was already king, and his son Hezekiah had already completed nine years. On the first day of Ahaz’s reign he was twenty years old, and he reigned for sixteen years. His son Hezekiah, who succeeded him immediately in the kingdom, was twenty-five years old when he began to reign. Hezekiah was therefore nine years old when his father became king. Thus this prophecy of which we are speaking was spoken neither concerning the wife of Ahaz nor concerning his son Hezekiah.

MOYSES. I want you, then, to show and explain to me how this prophecy was spoken concerning Mary and her son.

PETRUS. I shall certainly find many things in the very words of the prophecy by which I can very easily prove that it was uttered not concerning Ahaz or his son, but concerning Mary and her son Christ. Although the prophet was speaking to Ahaz, the prophecy was not spoken only to him or only about his own time. For this reason it says: “Hear, O house of David” (Isa. VII), not “Hear, you, Ahaz.”

Again, when the prophet says, “The Lord himself will give you a sign,” because he added “himself,” it can be understood as though he were saying, “not another”; from this it may be understood that the Lord himself was to be the sign. The fact that he says “to you” in the plural, and not “to you” in the singular, also indicates that this was not spoken on account of Ahaz or to him alone.

Moreover, what follows—“Behold, a virgin will conceive and bear a son, and she will call his name Emmanuel”—plainly indicates that the prophet was not speaking of the wife of Ahaz or of her son. For he would not have called a married woman a virgin, nor would it have been any miracle or sign for a woman with a husband to conceive or perhaps to bear a son.

Furthermore, in the fact that the text says “she will call,” two things are to be noted: namely, that God wished the Son to be called by this name, and that a virgin would bear a child without a carnal father. For this reason he says “she will call,” as though he were saying, “she herself will call him,” and not the father. We also know that neither any son of Ahaz nor anyone else of that time was called by the name Emmanuel.

MOYSES. I am truly astonished at you, a man so skilled in our language, because you confuse the words in this way and distort the Scriptures. For, as you yourself know, the prophet did not use in Hebrew the word that in Latin means “virgin.” If he had wished to do so, he would certainly have used *bethula*. Instead, he used *halma*, which signifies only “girl.”

PETRUS. You are manifestly contradicting me unjustly, O Moyses, and you seem not to recognize either the usage or the nature of the Hebrew language. A woman, whether young or old, is a woman; as long as she is young, she is a virgin, but if she has been violated, she can be called *nahra*. But *halma* is used of no one unless she is both young and untouched.

As for what the prophet added concerning the child, saying, “He will eat butter and honey, so that he may know how to reject evil and choose good,” tell me, I ask you, O Moyses, what did he intend by that honey and butter? Did he intend to suggest some allegory, or did he simply mention honey and butter?

MOYSES. We understand it only literally: namely, that he will be wise and will have discernment between good and evil. Therefore, he says, he will eat honey and butter, which are sweet and good.

PETRUS. He should certainly not be regarded as wise because he will eat honey and butter. For although they are sweet, if they are not healthful, they are not good; and whoever eats what is neither healthful nor good—how will he be wise? If you understand the statement in another way, as is possible—namely, that “he will eat honey and butter” means that he will know how to reject evil and choose good through eating honey and butter, that is, that through eating honey and butter he will acquire knowledge of good and evil and thus be wise—if, I say, you understand it in this way, you do not seem wise to me. For where is it indicated in the nature of things that eating butter or honey confers wisdom? Certainly nowhere. It remains, therefore, that we understand it allegorically.

MOYSES. And what allegory can you understand there?

[Col. 0615D]

PETRUS. These two words can indeed signify the two laws: the Gospel and the law of Moses. For in many places in the prophets we find the words of the Lord compared with honey and milk (Pss. XVIII, CXVIII; Ezek. III).

MOYSES. What, then, is the meaning of what follows: “Before the child knows how to reject evil and choose good, the land that you detest will be abandoned by the presence of its two kings” (Isa. VII)? What, I ask, did the prophet intend by such words? These words seem to indicate that the child concerning whom the prophecy is made had been born at that time.

PETRUS. Do you wish, O Moyses, to understand the words of the prophets according to the ordinary order of human speech? That is entirely impossible. Their words are like a dream and, like the words of people suffering from an acute fever or delirious with another illness, are not connected in any order. In the same way, the words of the prophets are not spoken in continuous sequence, nor do they consider what they say earlier or later, except as the Holy Spirit reveals it to them.

Therefore these words must be connected in this way: “He will eat butter and honey, so that he may know how to reject evil and choose good,” because the words “before he eats” are understood: “he will know how to reject evil and choose good.” This is the Hebrew truth, and here the prophecy that was spoken on account of Ahaz’s unbelief to the house of David finally ends.

For what follows immediately—“The land will be abandoned,” and the rest—is said about something else, just as we find elsewhere. For we read in Exodus:

“Moses said to the Lord: ‘Who am I that I should go to Pharaoh and bring the children of Israel out of Egypt?’ He said to him: ‘I will be with you, and this will be the sign that I have sent you: When you have brought my people out of Egypt, you shall sacrifice to God on this mountain. When you have brought my people out of Egypt’” (Exod. III), etc.

The words “this will be the sign that I have sent you” seem to refer to what he said, “I will be with you,” but they do not. Once the people had been brought out of Egypt and Moses had sacrificed on that mountain, everyone already knew that Moses was both a prophet and sent by the Lord. Moses therefore began there, in the manner of a prophet, to say something other than what he had said earlier.

If you object and ask what that sign was, know that the sign was what he said: “I will be with you” (Isa. VIII).

MOYSES. If that is so, what is the meaning of what is read later: “Before the child knows how to call his father and his mother, the strength of Damascus will be taken away and the spoils of Samaria before the king of the Assyrians”? Are all these things not said about the same child—namely, the one who was also born before the destruction?

PETRUS. We do not understand everything to have been said concerning Christ. These things could therefore have been said not about him, but about the child who was born at that time, concerning whom the Lord said to the prophet: “Call his name: Hasten to seize the spoils; hasten to plunder” (Isa. VIII), or about some other child.

MOYSES. I shall show you that he calls that child Emmanuel and that he was born at that time. When the prophet was speaking about the coming of the king of Assyria upon the land of Judah, he said concerning him: “And he will spread out his wings, filling the breadth of your land, O Emmanuel” (Isa. VIII). Here he shows that Emmanuel already existed at the time of his coming.

PETRUS. This certainly does not prove that Emmanuel was born at that time. For this was not his name according to the flesh, but according to his divinity, according to which it is established that he was Emmanuel both at that time, and before, and afterward.

MOYSES. From these words of yours I now understand something that you did not say before. For you seem to imply that the child of whom you are speaking was to be God and man.

PETRUS. I unquestionably believe this, as I have also noted in my explanation of my faith, and I shall show it to you if you ever ask about it.

[Col. 0617A]

MOYSES. I am not asking about that at present. Rather, I want you first to answer whether you still have any authority from a prophet that that child, the son of Mary, was born from his mother without a carnal father.

PETRUS. I certainly do. For he says: “Drop down dew, O heavens, from above, and let the clouds rain the Just One; let the earth be opened and bring forth the Savior, and let justice arise together; and: I, the Lord, created him” (Isa. XLV).

By the words “Drop down dew, O heavens, from above, and let the clouds rain the Just One,” he signified that the Holy Spirit would descend from heaven. By what follows—“Let the earth be opened and bring forth the Savior”—we understand the body of the Virgin, who, when the Holy Spirit came upon her, was to conceive and bear the Savior.

But by the words “I, the Lord, created him,” it is also indicated that the Lord brought him forth without the aid of a carnal father (Ps. CIX). Therefore, against those who do not believe this, he added what follows: “Woe to him who contradicts his maker, a potsherd among the earthen potsherds; will the clay say to its potter, ‘What are you doing?’ and, ‘Your work is without hands’?
