And: ‘Woe to him who says to his father, “What are you begetting?” and to his mother, “What are you giving birth to?”’” (Isa. XLV).

For in this way he inveighs against those who doubt this and ask how God begot him, and who reproach blessed Mary because she gave birth without intercourse with a man. Again, speaking against unbelievers, the prophet says: “Will I, who make others give birth, myself not give birth? says the Lord. If I, who grant generation to others, shall be barren, says the Lord your God?” (Isa. LXVI.)

In this way it is shown that God begot him without a carnal father. I believe this is enough for those who understand: that that child was born from his mother without a carnal father.

## TITLE VIII. How the Word of God was incarnated in Christ’s body, and Christ was both man and God at the same time.

MOYSES. Up to this point you have argued sufficiently from authorities concerning the child’s generation, and reason sufficiently permits that it could have happened in this way. But it is far more marvelous to everyone how the Godhead, which is simple, could have been joined and united to a human body, which is composite. I therefore ask you to explain, as you promised, by what reasoning this could have happened.

PETRUS. No necessary reasoning was required for this to happen, since it was accomplished solely by God’s will and goodness (Titus III). If he himself had not wished it, he would not have united himself to human nature. Nevertheless, it is not asserted that it had to happen by any necessity. For just as the soul, which is simple, is joined to a composite body, and the two become one human being without any contradiction from reason, so also God could unite himself to man without any obstacle from reason.

MOYSES. I would also like to hear something else from you, if you please. Since you say and believe that the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit are one, tell me how you believe that the Son alone became incarnate, and not the Father or the Holy Spirit.

PETRUS. You, I think, certainly regard as marvelous and impossible what we do not believe to be marvelous. Although this cannot be demonstrated in the Godhead, since it is subtle and spiritual, we can nevertheless find something similar in corporeal things, through which you can recognize that matter as well. For example, in fire, which is a substance, brightness is always present together with heat. You will not find the substance of fire without brightness and heat, nor brightness together with heat without the substance of fire. Yet heat sometimes comes to us without brightness, and sometimes brightness without heat.

MOYSES. It is certainly true that brightness sometimes comes to us without heat. We can perceive this from a candle, whose brightness we see but whose heat we do not feel. But I do not see how heat can come to us without brightness.

PETRUS. I can show this very easily. If you take some metal and heat it so that you can use it to heat another body, when you bring yourself near it you will feel the heat but will not see the brightness.

MOYSES. From your words you now seem to believe that just as brightness sometimes comes without heat and heat comes without brightness, although they are not separated from fire, so the Son assumed flesh without the Father and the Holy Spirit, yet for that reason did not depart from them.

PETRUS. That is exactly what I believe, and you have understood correctly—if only you believed it. For Truth itself said: “I am in the Father, and the Father is in me” (John XIV); and again: “I and the Father are one” (John X, XVII).

MOYSES. I concede sufficiently that the Godhead could unite itself to man. Nevertheless, since it was not necessary for this to happen, why should we believe that it did happen?

PETRUS. We who do not believe that the prophets lied must, since they foretold that Christ would be both God and man, also believe that they truthfully said this.

MOYSES. I would like you now to show me where the prophets testify to this concerning him. For I especially desire to hear that from you.

PETRUS. We read in Genesis that the Lord said: “Let us make man in our image and likeness,” and elsewhere: “God created man in his image and likeness” (Gen. I). Tell me now, I ask you, what is this image or likeness of God? In what respect are the image of God and the image of man alike?

[Col. 0618D]

MOYSES. It is certainly good to acknowledge the truth, and I truthfully say that they are alike in no respect. For earlier it was shown both by reason and by authority, and we conceded, that God bears the likeness of no thing.

PETRUS. Then Scripture lies when it says that God created man according to his image and likeness.

MOYSES. Not at all.

PETRUS. To which of those two prophets, then, should we give credence: to the one who said that God bears the likeness of no thing, or to the one who said, “God created man,” and so forth? Which of them spoke truthfully?

MOYSES. Certainly neither of them should be said to have lied.

PETRUS. And how can two contradictory things exist in the same subject—namely, that God both has an image and does not have one?

MOYSES. This is what I want you to explain to me: how do you yourself understand these things?

PETRUS. This is indeed true: God, as we said earlier, bears the likeness of no thing, and we know that Moses truthfully said that God created human beings according to his image and likeness. For he himself was truthful in everything. But by the image of God of which Moses spoke, we must understand that image—that is, the human form—which the Son of God assumed when he became incarnate.

MOYSES. How can this stand, when at the time Adam was made he had not yet assumed that image which you believe God assumed?

PETRUS. Even if that image did not yet exist in actuality, it already existed in his providence and will. Since his will does not change, there is nothing preventing us, with regard to him, from believing that his image had always existed. We also find this elsewhere in the prophets (Num. II, III; Mal. III): they speak of a future event as though it were past. Thus Isaiah, speaking in the person of the Lord, says: “The day of vengeance is in my heart; the year of my recompense has come” (Isa. LXIV). The day or year had certainly not yet come, but because it was already in his heart, he said that it had already come.

MOYSES. Do you have any other authority by which you can show more clearly that that child had to be both God and man?

PETRUS. I certainly have many. Isaiah says concerning him: “For a child is born to us, and a son is given to us, and his name will be called Wonderful, Counselor, Mighty God, Father of the age to come, Prince of Peace” (Isa. IX). All these names belong only to the Godhead.

MOYSES. You understand Scripture incorrectly. For it should not be read as saying that the child will be called Wonderful or Counselor, and so forth, but rather: “He who is wonderful, who is counselor, who is mighty God, who is father of the age to come—he, I say, will call him Prince of Peace.” If this is so, of whom is it said that he will call him?

PETRUS. This causes me no difficulty, because God called himself by that name. The Hebrew language also readily permits this, as is found in the book of Numbers: “This is the law of consecration: When the days that he had determined by vow have been completed, he will bring him to the entrance of the tent of the covenant” (Num. VI). The same person is referred to by both “he will bring” and “him.”

Moreover, what the prophet says in the same passage—“His authority will be multiplied, and there will be no end of peace; he will sit upon the throne of David and over his kingdom, and to establish and strengthen it in judgment and righteousness, from now and forever” (Isa. IX)—all this, I say, shows that that child was destined to be both God and man. For whatever belongs to man will have an end, but God—and what belongs to him—remains forever (Ps. XVI).

Besides all this, you contradict me unjustly concerning the names mentioned above. For your teachers also said that Christ would have seven names, and they listed these same names. At the beginning of our disputation you did not make an agreement that you would contradict something unjustly.

MOYSES. I remember, and it is true, that our teachers said this.

PETRUS. I shall give you still another authority, if you wish, that that child was to be God and man. The same prophet says concerning him:

“A branch will go forth from the root of Jesse, and a flower will rise from his root, and the Spirit of the Lord will rest upon him: the spirit of wisdom and understanding, the spirit of counsel and fortitude, the spirit of knowledge and piety, and he will fill him with the spirit of the fear of the Lord. He will not judge according to the appearance of the eyes, nor rebuke according to the hearing of the ears, but he will judge the poor in righteousness and rebuke with equity on behalf of the meek of the earth. He will strike the earth with the rod of his mouth, and with the breath of his lips he will slay the wicked” (Isa. XI).

What he says—“He will not judge according to the appearance of the eyes,” and the rest that follows—certainly applies to no one except God alone. For a human being cannot judge anything justly except what he has seen or heard.

[Col. 0620C]

MOYSES. Part of the authority you have brought forward in support of your case actually obstructs the proof you are trying to establish. For it says there: “The Spirit of the Lord will rest upon him, the spirit of wisdom and understanding, the spirit of counsel and fortitude, the spirit of knowledge and piety, and he will fill him with the spirit of the fear of the Lord.” If he were to be God, he would surely be the giver of these things, not their recipient.

PETRUS. There is nothing in your objection. I told you at the beginning, in my explanation of my belief, that Christ himself consists of three substances: body, soul, and God. According to his Godhead, those seven names are attributed to him; according to his soul, he could receive the seven gifts mentioned above. For this soul, apart from being joined to the Godhead, was also in itself the most excellent of all souls.

MOYSES. Since, then, according to his Godhead he received seven names, and according to his soul those seven gifts, I want you to make clear what you attribute to him according to his body.

PETRUS. Although you put this forward somewhat mockingly, I shall nevertheless tell you, if you wish, what I attribute to him according to the flesh. Isaiah says:

“I will give in the wilderness the cedar, and the acacia, and the myrtle, and the olive tree; and I will place in the desert the fir, the pine, and the box tree together” (Isa. XLI).

By these seven trees the body of Christ is signified. For why would he speak of some wilderness, when such trees always inhabit the wilderness? By the wilderness, therefore, the world is understood, which at the time of Christ’s coming was empty of every good thing and desolate.

MOYSES. Since he signified his body by trees, why, I ask, did he not place fruitful and more precious trees in its representation?

PETRUS. He did this with considerable insight and reason. For just as those trees are always green and never lose their foliage, so the body of Christ always remains living, entire, and whole.

I also have another argument from authority to prove that man and God could be united. Isaiah says: “And they will say on that day: ‘Behold, this is our Lord. We have awaited him, and he will save us’” (Isa. XXV). We do not wish to explain this verse otherwise than your teachers explained it long ago. Through it they taught that a time would come when the world would see God and the people would point him out to one another with their fingers. But this could in no way happen unless someone became both bodily and God.

The prophet also says: “The voice of your watchmen: they have lifted up their voice; together they will praise, because they will see eye to eye when the Lord restores Zion” (Isa. LIV). This verse, I say, your teachers explained in the same way we have described, because of the words “they will see eye to eye.”

The prophet also stated something else by which the foregoing can be proved no less. He says: “And the glory of the Lord will be revealed, and all flesh together will see that the mouth of the Lord has spoken” (Isa. XL). A spiritual voice of a thing can indeed be heard, just as the children of Israel heard the voice of the Lord on Mount Sinai (Exod. XX). But you will not see the one speaking unless the thing is corporeal.

Again, Zachariah says: “On that day the Lord will protect the inhabitants of Jerusalem, and the one who stumbles on that day will be like David, and the house of David will be like God, and like the angel of God before them” (Zech. XII). By saying “the house of David will be like God,” he certainly intended it to be understood that one would be born from the house of David whom everyone would regard as God. By saying “like God,” rather than simply “God,” he indicates that the one who was to arise from the house of David would be in some respect less than God (John XIV). David also bears witness to this in a psalm when he says: “You made him a little lower than God [than the angels]” (Ps. VIII).

Micah likewise says: “And you, Bethlehem Ephrata, small among the thousands of Judah: from you a ruler will go forth for me, one who is to be ruler in Israel, and his origins are from the beginning, from the days of eternity” (Mic. V). The words “from you a ruler will go forth for me, one who is to be ruler in Israel” are spoken according to the body, according to which that prince was to come in time. But what follows—“his origins are from the beginning, from the days of eternity”—indicates the perpetuity of the Godhead. This he attributes to the Godhead, which, I think, does not belong to man.

David also says in a psalm: “Your throne, O God, is for ever and ever; the rod of uprightness is the rod of your kingdom. You have loved righteousness and hated wickedness; therefore God, your God, has anointed you with the oil of gladness above your companions” (Ps. XLIV). When he says this, he shows that the one to whom he speaks is both God and man. For when he says, “Your throne, O God, is for ever and ever; the rod of uprightness is the rod of your kingdom,” does he not plainly call him God? Then, when he says, “You have loved righteousness and hated wickedness; therefore God, your God, has anointed you with the oil of gladness above your companions,” we perceive that he is speaking to him as man. For God neither has a God nor companions.

David says elsewhere in a psalm: “O God, give your judgment to the king, and your righteousness to the king’s son” (Ps. LXXI), along with whatever else is in the psalm. Tell me now, who is this king’s son: Solomon, or Christ, who was to come from David himself and be called his son?

MOYSES. I do not wish to tire you over this. It was spoken concerning Christ, as our teachers taught.

[Col. 0622B]

PETRUS. Since you have conceded that the psalm concerns Christ, let us see whether the following things read in it were said of a mere human being:

“He will remain with the sun and before the moon, from generation to generation”; and: “May his name be blessed forever; his name endures before the sun”; and: “All kings will adore him; all nations will serve him” (Ps. LXXI).

Let us see, I say, whether all these things were said of a mere human being. Certainly not, but of God. It follows, therefore, that we must say that Christ is both man and God.

Moreover, because David knew through the revelation of the Holy Spirit that this was so, and foresaw the miracles he was to perform, he therefore brought the psalm to this conclusion: “Blessed is the Lord God of Israel, who alone does wonders; and blessed is the name of his majesty forever, and the whole earth will be filled with his majesty.”

Likewise, in the book of *Dabrejamin*, that is, “Words of Days,” the *Paralipomenon*, it is read that, when David was considering building a house for the Lord, the prophet Nathan spoke to him in the person of the Lord in these words:

“When your days are completed, so that you go to your fathers, I will raise up your seed after you, which will come from your sons, and I will establish his kingdom. He himself will build a house for me, and I will establish his throne forever. I will be a father to him, and he will be a son to me, and I will not take my mercy away from him as I took it away from the one who was before you; and I will establish him in my house and in my kingdom forever, and his throne will be most firm forever” (1 Chron. XVIII).

Tell me, I say, O Moyses, concerning whom was this prophecy spoken?

MOYSES. Concerning Solomon.

PETRUS. That cannot be so. For when it says, “When your days are completed, so that you go to your fathers”—that is, “when you have died”—“I will raise up your seed after you,” it is clear that this was not said concerning Solomon. Solomon was already king while his father was still alive. If he had wished to speak about Solomon, he certainly would not have said, “which will come from your sons,” but “which will come from you.”

What also follows—“I will establish him in my house and in my kingdom forever, and his throne will be most firm forever”—is plainly recognized as not having been said concerning Solomon. Solomon was not established in the house or kingdom of God, nor did his throne remain most firm forever. Since this applies to God alone, the one of whom this passage speaks was destined to be both man and God.

[Col. 0623A]

MOYSES. Since you understand all these things to have been spoken concerning Christ, what is meant by the statement: “He himself will build a house for me”? What was the house that Christ was to build?

PETRUS. By that house we certainly understand the holy Church, which Christ built upon the firm rock.

MOYSES. What, then, did Nathan answer David concerning the house that David said he wished to build for the Lord?

PETRUS. He answered what David himself reports when speaking of his son Solomon:

“The word of the Lord came to me, saying: ‘You have shed much blood and waged very many wars; you cannot build a house for my name, because you have shed so much blood before me. Behold, a son has been born to you; he will be a man of great peace, for I will give him rest from all his enemies round about. For he will be called Solomon, and I will give peace and quiet to Israel throughout all his days. He himself will build a house for my name, and he will be a son to me, and I will be a father to him; and I will establish the throne of his kingdom over Israel forever’” (1 Chron. XXII).

I concede that this was said concerning Solomon because of the words: “Behold, a son has been born to you,” and afterward, “He will be called Solomon.” David also attests this when speaking to the children of Israel concerning him in these words: “Of my sons—for the Lord has given me many sons—he chose Solomon, my son” (1 Chron. XXVIII).

This statement of David concerning Solomon is entirely different from the one Nathan spoke to David concerning Christ. Here we read: “A son has been born to you, and he will be called Solomon”; there, however: “I will raise up your seed after you, which will come from your sons,” and no name is assigned to him.

There also he says: “I will establish him in my house and in my kingdom forever, and his throne will be most firm forever.” Here, however, he says only: “I will establish his throne over Israel forever.” From this it is shown that, as long as the kingdom of Israel endured, a king from Solomon’s lineage would not fail, whereas the kingdom of Christ would always remain without end (Isa. IX; Luke I).

Moreover, Christ’s kingdom was promised without condition, whereas Solomon’s was promised conditionally. For concerning him we read in the book of Kings, where David speaks to his son Solomon as follows:

“May the Lord confirm his words, which he spoke to me, saying: ‘If your sons keep my law and walk before me in truth, with all their heart and with all their soul, a man will not be taken away from you from the throne of Israel’” (3 Kings II).

David himself also testifies that the prophecy we mentioned—“When your days are completed,” and so forth—was spoken concerning Christ. On hearing it and understanding it as we have explained, and also giving thanks to God for it, he said:

“Who am I, Lord God, and what is my house, that you have brought me this far? Yet even this seemed a small thing in your sight, O God, unless you also spoke concerning the house of your servant for a distant future, and saw me in the law of the exalted man of the Lord God” (2 Sam. VII).

By saying, “Who am I, Lord God, and what is my house, that you have brought me this far?” he spoke about himself and his son Solomon. But what he added afterward—“Yet even this seemed a small thing in your sight, unless you also spoke concerning the house of your servant for a distant future”—he truly said concerning Christ, whom he saw as destined to come from his house.

By saying, “And you saw me in the law of the exalted man of the Lord God,” since he also said this concerning Christ, he plainly indicates that the one who was to be exalted and to be man must also be God.

# TITLE IX. That Christ came at the time when the prophets had foretold that he would come, and that whatever they proclaimed about him was made manifest in him and in his works

**MOSES.** Since, then, you have shown by many authoritative passages that the one whom you call Christ would be human and could also be God, by what authority, I ask, can you show that he has already come, as you believe? Perhaps he has not yet come, but will come at the appointed time.

**PETER.** There are indeed many things, Moses, that clearly show that he has come. For the time at which the prophets foretold that he would come has already passed; and we know that he came at that time. Besides this, there are many other things that we have recognized in him, in his words, and in his works, just as the prophets foretold.

**MOSES.** First, I ask you to show me concerning the time: where and in what manner the prophets spoke about it, and how they defined its limit.

**PETER.** We certainly read that Jacob, speaking to his sons and calling each of them to himself, blessed them and said:

> The scepter shall not be taken away from Judah, nor a ruler from his loins, until he comes who is to be sent, and to him the nations shall gather (Gen. XLIX).

I will not explain this prophecy in any other way than your ancient teachers explained it. For they too said: “The scepter,” that is, the rod, “shall not be taken away from the kingdom of Judah, nor a ruler from his loins,” that is, from his descendants, “forever, until he comes who is to be sent,” that is, Christ, “whose is the kingdom, and to him the nations shall gather.” We know, moreover, that after Christ came, there was no longer either a king or a ruler from Judah. We must therefore believe that the time of Christ’s coming was determined here, and that the one who came at that time was, without any doubt, Christ.

Again, in the Book of Daniel, the angel spoke to Daniel in this way concerning the time of Christ’s coming:

> Seventy weeks have been determined for your people and for your holy city, so that transgression may be completed, sin may reach its end, iniquity may be blotted out, everlasting righteousness may be brought in, vision and prophecy may be fulfilled, and the Holy of Holies may be anointed. Know, therefore, and understand: From the going forth of the word that Jerusalem should be rebuilt, until Christ the ruler, there shall be seven weeks. And there shall be sixty-two weeks, and the street and the walls shall be rebuilt again in the distress of the times. And after the sixty-two weeks Christ shall be killed; the people, with the coming ruler, shall destroy the city and the sanctuary, and its end shall be desolation; and after the end of the war desolation has been decreed. He shall confirm the covenant with many for one week, and in the middle of the week sacrifice and offering shall cease, and in the temple there shall be the abomination of desolation, and desolation shall continue until the completion and the end (Dan. IX).

This prophecy, Moses, is certainly closed and difficult to understand. Many chronological limits are marked in it, yet all have been set forth to demonstrate Christ’s coming.

First, then, it must be understood that these weeks are weeks of years. When it says, “Seventy weeks have been determined for your people and for your holy city, so that transgression may be completed, sin may reach its end, iniquity may be blotted out, everlasting righteousness may be brought in, vision and prophecy may be fulfilled, and the Holy of Holies may be anointed,” by this, I say, it wished to indicate that seventy times seven—that is, four hundred and ninety years—had been appointed from the same year of the prophecy until the destruction of Jerusalem and the Temple, which was carried out by Titus, emperor of the Romans. Christ had already come by the time of that destruction; he was both the righteousness of the ages and the Holy of Holies, through whom all sin and iniquity were blotted out and every prophecy fulfilled.

All the remaining statements concern the division and determination of these four hundred and ninety years. Thus, by the words, “From the going forth of the word that Jerusalem should be rebuilt, until Christ the ruler, there shall be seven weeks,” it is indicated that from the day of this prophecy until Cyrus, ruler of the Persians—who is himself called “Christ” by God through Isaiah (Isa. XLV)—there were seven weeks of years, that is, fifty-nine years. It was by Cyrus’s decree that Jerusalem began to be rebuilt.

From the rebuilding of Jerusalem, and after the work had been completed, until Titus came against Jerusalem, there were four hundred and thirty-four years. This is what is meant by: “There shall be sixty-two weeks,” that is, four hundred and thirty-four years, “and the street and the walls shall be rebuilt again in the distress of the times; and after seven weeks Christ shall be killed”—that is, after the seventy weeks—and after Christ has been killed, “the people,” namely the Roman people, “with the coming ruler,” that is, with Titus, “shall destroy the city and the sanctuary; and its end shall be desolation, and after the end of the war desolation has been decreed.”

As for what follows, “He shall confirm the covenant with many for one week,” that one week was certainly seven years of siege. For the city was besieged by the Roman army for seven years, and during those seven years the people inside were so constrained and afflicted that they had no means by which they could offer sacrifice. This is what is meant by: “In the middle of the week,” that is, during the week, “sacrifice and offering shall cease, and in the temple there shall be the abomination of desolation.”

The further statement, “Desolation shall continue until the completion and the end,” indicates that that captivity and desolation would have no end. Thus seven weeks extend to Cyrus, sixty-two weeks from Cyrus to Titus, and one week of the siege: altogether, these are seventy weeks.

**MOSES.** Since you have established from the testimonies of the prophets the time of Christ’s coming—and, as you said, it has become sufficiently clear—I want you now to explain those other matters that were made manifest in him, in his works, and in his words, which, as you maintain, were foretold about him by the prophets.

**PETER.** We read in Deuteronomy that, when death was already approaching him, Moses spoke to the people of Israel in this way:

> The Lord your God will raise up for you a prophet from your nation and from your brothers, like me; you shall listen to him, as you asked of the Lord your God at Horeb, when the assembly was gathered and you said: “I will not hear again the voice of the Lord my God, nor will I see this great fire anymore, lest I die.” And the Lord said to me: “They have spoken well in everything. I will raise up for them a prophet from the midst of their brothers, like you, and I will put my words in his mouth, and he shall speak to them everything that I command him. Whoever will not listen to his words, which he will speak in my name, I myself will be his avenger” (Deut. XVIII).

Who is it, Moses, whom the Lord says will be raised up like Moses and commands to be heard?

**MOSES.** Surely this could be said of Joshua son of Nun, who arose after Moses and in his place.

**PETER.** It cannot possibly be about Joshua. Scripture speaks about him quite plainly, as we read in the Book of Numbers:

> Moses answered the Lord: “May the Lord, the God of the spirits of all flesh, provide a man who shall be over this multitude and who can go out and come in before them, and lead them out or bring them in, so that the people of the Lord may not be like sheep without a shepherd.” And the Lord said to him: “Take Joshua son of Nun, a man in whom is the Spirit of God, and lay your hand upon him. He shall stand before Eleazar the priest and the whole multitude; you shall give him commands in the sight of all, and a portion of your glory, and the whole assembly of the children of Israel shall hear him” (Num. XXVII).

Since Joshua is treated so openly here, why should that other prophecy, which is so obscure—namely, “The Lord your God will raise up for you a prophet,” and so forth—be understood of him? Moreover, the passage says, “You shall give him a portion of your glory,” as though it said, “not all your glory,” by which it is shown that he was not like Moses. At the end of Deuteronomy we read: “No prophet has arisen again in Israel like Moses” (Deut. XXXIV). By these statements, I say, it is indicated that the words “The Lord your God will raise up for you,” and so forth, were not spoken of Joshua, since the passage continues, “like you.”

The prophecy that says, “The Lord will raise up for you,” and so forth, also differs in another way from what was said about Joshua. In the former it is written, “Whoever will not listen to his words, I myself will be his avenger”; but concerning Joshua it is written: “Whoever contradicts your mouth and does not obey all the words that you command him shall be put to death.” It is therefore clear in every respect that that prophecy was not spoken about Joshua.

**MOSES.** About whom, then?

**PETER.** About Christ, who was like Moses, because, like Moses, he too gave a law.

**MOSES.** Now, then, show how you can apply every part of the prophecy to him.

**PETER.** This prophecy responds to the request of the children of Israel. For, as it is written (Exod. XX), they had asked at Mount Horeb not to hear the voice of the Lord visibly again, nor to see that great fire, lest they die. In response to this, the Lord says to Moses (Deut. XVIII): “I will raise up for them a prophet from the midst of their brothers, like you,” as though he were saying: “The one whom I will raise up will be from their Jewish lineage, and he will also be like you—that is, just as you gave the law, so he too will give it.” This is also indicated by the fact that he used the singular “prophet,” and used it in an eminent sense. For if he too were not going to give a law, he would surely have said, “I will raise up prophets,” not “a prophet.”

God raised up many prophets who announced his words, but none of them gave a law in the likeness of Moses except Christ. “And I will put my words in his mouth”: this means that because they cannot endure the force of my voice, I will speak to them through him under the veil of flesh. “He shall speak to them everything that I command him.” It is as though he said plainly: “He will say absolutely nothing beyond what I will wish and command.”

“Whoever will not listen to his words, which he will speak in my name, I myself will be his avenger”: that is, whoever refuses to obey his commands will not be killed or punished in any other bodily manner, but I myself, according to my will, will mercifully take vengeance upon him.

Since Christ was born from the Jewish lineage, became a lawgiver like Moses, and since the Word of God lay hidden under the veil of his flesh, and he taught nothing other than what God the Father commanded—as he himself testifies in the Gospel, saying, “The word that you have heard is not mine, but the Father’s who sent me” (John XII)—and since he himself did not wish anyone to be killed or punished bodily, but preached mercy in all things, nothing at all prevents the entire prophecy from having been spoken about him.

**MOSES.** One matter still remains, to which I want you to respond. Since Christ, as you believe, was both God and human, how did he call him a prophet?

**PETER.** You seem to think that “prophet” is merely the name of a human being; but that is not at all so. Rather, whoever declares what is going to happen in the future is called a prophet.

In Isaiah we read the following:

> Behold my servant; I have received him, my chosen one, in whom my soul is well pleased. I have given my spirit upon him; he shall bring forth judgment to the nations. He shall not cry out, nor exalt himself, nor shall his voice be heard outside. He shall not break the bruised reed, nor extinguish the smoking flax; in truth he shall bring forth judgment. He shall not fail or withdraw until he establishes judgment on the earth, and the islands shall await his law (Isa. XLII).

To whom, Moses, can we apply this prophecy better than to Christ? He was the servant of God and his chosen one, in whom God was well pleased. This was said about him according to the body. What follows, “I have given my spirit upon him,” was spoken according to the soul.

“He shall bring forth judgment,” that is, the law, “to the nations.” Christ brought forth—that is, explained and disclosed—the law that had been closed and covered, and that had existed only among the Jews; he drew out its marrow so that the nations too could receive it.

It follows: “He shall not cry out, nor exalt himself, nor shall his voice be heard outside.” We know that Christ was not loud, arrogant, or desirous of empty glory (John XIII; Matt. II); rather, he loved humility above all things.

“He shall not break the bruised reed, nor extinguish the smoking flax.” We know that a bruised reed can easily be broken, while smoking flax—that is, linen that has been burned but still retains smoke, or the trace of fire—can very easily be extinguished. But what can be understood better by the bruised reed or the almost extinguished flax than the frailty of the sinner, who has been crushed and almost extinguished in sin?

Christ did not break the bruised reed or extinguish the smoking flax, because he did not command sinners who were nearly dead in their sins to be killed. Instead, he mercifully endured them (Matt. III) and called them back to repentance (Matt. XI). The prophet also indicated this in what follows, when he added: “In truth he shall bring forth judgment.”

Truth and justice are the same thing. In the law of Moses there was judgment and a commandment that the sinner be killed. Christ brought judgment forth into truth and justice when he commanded that sinners not be killed but, as is more just, be sustained until they repented, saying: “I do not desire the death of the sinner, but rather that he be converted and live” (Ezek. XXXIII).

“He shall not fail or withdraw until he establishes judgment on the earth.” The prophet wished Christ’s death to be indicated by “failing,” and by “withdrawing,” his ascent into heaven. It is as though he said: “He will not die or depart from the earth—that is, ascend into heaven—until he sends the law upon the earth.”

Before Christ died according to the flesh or ascended into heaven to the Father, he established judgment on earth when he gave us the law, that is, the Gospel. He did not say, “He will not die,” but “He will not fail,” because Christ’s death was not truly death, but rather a kind of passage and departure. A human being who dies no longer lives. Christ, however, rose on the third day and now lives forever (John XIII), and “the islands shall await his law.”

By the islands we understand the nations. The nations awaited Christ’s law because they received it not from Christ himself but from his disciples, that is, from the apostles. For it was not he himself, but the apostles, who preached to the nations.

Again, in Isaiah:

> I am the Lord; I have called you in righteousness, and I have taken you by the hand, and preserved you, and given you as a covenant of the people, as a light to the nations, so that you might open the eyes of the blind, and bring out the bound from confinement, from the prison house those who sit in darkness. I am the Lord; this is my name. I will not give my glory to another, nor my praise to idols (Isa. XLII).

Isaiah also spoke this about Christ. The Lord called him from the womb of the Virgin in righteousness—that is, without sin and without the desire of the flesh. Christ was born in pure flesh from a holy and righteous Virgin (Luke I; Isa. VII).

“He took him by the hand”: this is a sign of protection and guardianship. He preserved him, just as he rescued him, still crying as an infant, from Herod’s hand, led him into Egypt, and brought him back (Matt. II); he repeatedly freed him from the hands of the Jews who wanted to stone and kill him (Luke IV; John VIII), and in his many other adversities he proved to be his guardian and protector.

The Lord gave him as a covenant to the people of Israel—that is, he gave him for this purpose: so that he might show the people of Israel the truth of the law. “And as a light to the nations” (John XVIII) the Lord gave him, because the nations, abandoning their error and expelling the darkness of their unbelief, were sprinkled with the light of Christ’s law.

He also sent him “to open the eyes of the blind, to bring out the bound from confinement, and from the prison house those who sit in darkness.” Christ opened the eyes of the blind when he disclosed the hearts of unbelievers and, removing the shadow of the law, showed the light. He brought the bound out of confinement because even to this day he frees and releases those who believe in him from every captivity. He also brought out from the prison house those sitting in darkness, because, descending to the underworld, he himself drew out those who were held in the dark prison of hell.

The Lord gave his glory and praise to no one other than Christ, because he never united his divinity to any other human being, nor bestowed such praise on anyone else.

Again, Isaiah:

> Seek the Lord while he may be found; call upon him while he is near. Let the impious abandon his way, and the wicked man his thoughts, and let him return to the Lord, and he will have mercy on him, and to our God, for he is abundant in forgiving. For my thoughts are not your thoughts, nor are my ways your ways, says the Lord. For as the heavens are exalted above the earth, so my ways are exalted above your ways and my thoughts above your thoughts. And as rain and snow descend from heaven and do not return there again, but water the earth, soak it, make it germinate, and give seed to the sower and bread to the eater, so shall my word be that goes forth from my mouth. It shall not return to me empty, but shall do whatever I have willed (Isa. LV).

Tell me, Moses, how do you explain this entire passage? When is the Lord found, and when is he not found? When is he near, and when is he far away?

**MOSES.** For God to be found and for him to be near are the same thing. He is near and is found by those who faithfully serve him.

**PETER.** The Lord actually wishes to be nearer and offers himself more readily to sinners and to those who seem far away than to the righteous and faithful who, as you say, are near. The prophet also testifies to this elsewhere, saying: “Peace, peace to him who is far away and to him who is near, says the Lord” (Isa. LVII).

For whom do we understand by one who is far from God, if not the sinner, and by one who is near, if not the righteous? The prophet mentioned first the one who is far away and afterward the one who is near, and thus showed that God is nearer to the sinner than to the righteous.

**MOSES.** We can also say that those ten days are near to God, which extend from the first day of the seventh month to the Day of Atonement; for this is what our teachers have said.

**PETER.** This too is wrong. For if God is near and can be found only during those ten days, then if at another time a sinner wishing to convert should seek God and not find him because he was far away, it would already be God’s fault, not the sinner’s, that he could not turn back to God.

**MOSES.** Our teachers also say something else: namely, that God was near and could be found as long as the Lord’s Temple stood; but after the Temple was destroyed, he withdrew and no longer wished to be found.

**PETER.** They were foolish in this matter also. For Moses says against this to the children of Israel that if at some time they provoked God to anger, so that he scattered them as captives among the nations, nevertheless, if at the very end they should return and seek him, they would undoubtedly find him (Exod. XXXIV; Deut. XXXII).

**MOSES.** Since you contradict both this and that, when and in what manner do you maintain that God is found or is near?

**PETER.** The Lord was found and was near when he assumed flesh from the holy Virgin and dwelt among us in person. It was then that the prophet commanded that he be sought and invoked, when he said, “Seek the Lord,” and so forth.

For, with the Holy Spirit revealing it, he foresaw that this would happen; therefore he added in what follows: “Let the impious abandon his way, and the wicked man his thoughts, and let him return to the Lord.” This means that they should not think wickedly about him or doubt that he was God because he had assumed flesh; rather, they should believe faithfully, for faith exists in thought alone (John XVII).

Human thought is certainly different from God’s thought. Hence it follows: “For my thoughts are not your thoughts, nor are my ways your ways, says the Lord,” as though he were saying: “Do not think that what you see and hear—that is, the Son without a human father—is contrary to custom. I think one way, and you another. You think only in bodily terms, whereas I think spiritually. I proceed one way, and you proceed another. You know no way except one that accords with ordinary practice, whereas I also know what is contrary to ordinary practice, and I can accomplish whatever I wish.”

This is what is meant by: “As the heavens are exalted above the earth,” and so forth.

As for what follows—“As rain and snow descend from heaven and do not return there again, but water the earth, soak it, make it germinate, and give seed to the sower and bread to the eater, so shall the word that goes forth from my mouth be; it shall not return to me empty, but shall do whatever I have willed”—he added this in order to show, through the likeness of visible things, what could not be seen so plainly in the subtlety of the divine nature.

He said: “Just as rain, when it descends from heaven, does not return again to heaven before it softens the earth and makes it fertile and fruitful, so my word that goes forth from my mouth”—that is, my Son, whom I will send into the world to take flesh—“will not return to me empty. Before he returns, he will accomplish whatever I will”: that is, he will assume flesh as I have determined, be scourged, die, rescue his own from the underworld, rise again, and open the law, which is closed to those who understand it imperfectly.

But if God wished it to be understood that he was speaking about his word, that is, about his speech, when he said, “My word that goes forth from my mouth,” he would certainly not have added, “It shall not return to me,” and so forth. For a word, that is, speech, does not return to the mouth after it has once gone forth from it. By this he therefore clearly showed that he spoke of the person of the Son when he said “my word.”

**MOSES.** Your words now suggest that snow and rain, after they are sent down from heaven, return again to heaven.

**PETER.** It is true.

**MOSES.** I would now like you to show me by what reasoning this can be proved.

**PETER.** You must first investigate where clouds and rains come from; then you will more easily discover what you are asking about.

**MOSES.** Please make that clear to me.

**PETER.** You must understand, Moses, that when the sun is positioned in a straight line over the sea and the land, a moist vapor rises from the sea, while a dry vapor rises from the land. Both ascend by the heat of the sun, just as water vapor rises through the heat of fire. When these two vapors rise, each mingling with the other, they form dense clouds from themselves.

When the clouds have grown to a height of about sixteen miles, they encounter cold air there, and therefore cannot pass any higher. Thus they fall back to the earth, and from them rains arise.

God made hollows in the mountains so that rains might be stored there as in a kind of treasury. He also made small openings at the lowest points of the mountain heights, through which the water gradually flows away—water that had been hidden and kept as though in a treasury. These are the springs from which all rivers arise.

The fish of the whole world are nourished by these rivers; meadows and vineyards are irrigated; the crops of human beings and the herds of animals are watered; villages are passed by them, as are great cities.

The proof of this is that when rain fails, springs and rivers dry up, as we find in the Third Book of Kings, where Elijah says: “After some time the torrent dried up, for it had not rained upon the earth” (III Kings XVII).

After rivers have flowed over the earth for a long time, they eventually reach the sea and merge with the waves of the ocean. Thus the vapor of the sea rises again, as we said above, and forms clouds from itself once more. There is no end to this rising and falling, nor has there ever been one since God ordered the world; nor will there be one as long as the Creator of all things wills it.

Solomon bears witness to this when he says in Ecclesiastes:

> All the rivers enter the sea, and the sea is not filled. To the place from which the rivers flow, they return, so that they may flow again (Eccl. I).

**MOSES.** You have brought forward many authorities from the books of the prophets and explained them according to your own will. But I would like you to show me at least one clear passage by which what you intend could plainly be proved.

**PETER.** The hardness of your heart and that of those like you is certainly not new. For you did not believe even when the prophets spoke plainly and without allegory to you. So it is no wonder if the words of my explanation seem deaf to you.

Nevertheless, to cut off all your opportunities for objection, I will now tell you one exceptionally clear passage from Isaiah himself. Isaiah says:

> Behold, my servant shall understand; he shall be exalted and lifted up, and shall be very high. Just as many were astonished at you, so his appearance shall be without glory among men, and his form among the children of men. He shall sprinkle many nations. Before him kings shall shut their mouths, because they shall see what was not told them, and contemplate what they had not heard. Who has believed our report (Rom. X), and to whom has the arm of the Lord been revealed? And he shall rise up like a young shoot before him, and like a root from thirsty ground. He has no appearance or beauty, and we saw him, and he had no aspect; we desired him despised, the last of men, a man of sorrows and acquainted with weakness. His face was as though hidden and despised, and therefore we did not esteem him. Truly he himself bore our infirmities and carried our pains. And we thought him as one stricken, smitten by God, and humbled. But he was wounded for our iniquities; he was crushed for our crimes. The discipline of our peace was upon him, and by his bruise we were healed. All we, like sheep, went astray; each turned to his own way, and the Lord placed upon him the iniquity of us all. He was compelled and afflicted, and did not open his mouth. He shall be led like a lamb to slaughter, and like a sheep before its shearer he shall be silent, and shall not open his mouth. From distress and judgment he was taken away. Who shall declare his generation? (Jer. XI; Acts VIII) For he was cut off from the land of the living. Because of the crime of my people he was stricken, and he gave his burial with the wicked and his death with the rich, although he had committed no iniquity, nor was there deceit in his mouth (I Pet. II). And the Lord willed to crush him and to make him weak. If he places his life as an offering for sin, he shall see offspring, and his time shall be prolonged, and the will of the Lord shall prosper in his hand. From the labor of his soul he shall see and be satisfied. By his knowledge he shall justify the just one for many, and he himself shall bear their iniquities. Therefore I will make him share in many things, and with the strong he shall divide the spoils, because he handed over his life to death and was counted among criminals; and he himself bore the sin of many and pleaded for transgressors (Isa. LII–LIII).

I have certainly labored greatly over this prophecy, Moses, more than over all the others, in order to introduce it according to the version current among you. In doing so I even abandoned the true translation of blessed Jerome. I did this in order to remove all your opportunities for objection.

Since we apply the prophecy to Christ, and you perhaps do not concede this, I would like you to say of whom you understand it to have been spoken.

**MOSES.** Some of our teachers certainly assert that it was spoken about Jeremiah, because he was scourged, beaten, and imprisoned (Jer. XI), and endured many other evils that would take too long to enumerate. According to others, however, we understand it of King Josiah, who, although he was a holy and righteous man, was killed for sins that were not his own but the people’s (IV Kings XXIII).

**PETER.** It cannot certainly be about either of them. For you will be unable to apply the whole prophecy to either one. If you understand it of Jeremiah, Jeremiah indeed endured scourging, imprisonment, and much affliction, but he was not killed; nor, when scourged, did he remain silent; nor did he bear our sins; nor will you be able to apply the rest of the prophecy to him. As for Josiah, you will find nothing in the prophecy that could have been said about him except that he was holy and was killed for the crime of the people.

**MOSES.** About whom, then, do you understand the prophecy to have been spoken, so that all its parts can be applied to him?

PETRUS. About Christ. For when he said, “Behold, my servant shall understand; he shall be exalted and lifted up, and shall be very high,” we know indeed that Christ was both God’s servant and of great understanding, and that he was more exalted and lifted up than all God’s servants. His works were also wondrous and astonishing, and he never concerned himself with glory. And this is what follows: “Just as many were astonished at you, so his appearance shall be without glory among men, and his form among the children of men.”

It continues: “This man shall sprinkle many nations.” The Lord Christ indeed showered the Israelite nation like a great rain, when he came among them as among his own people (John I), and displayed his works and mighty deeds to them. But he sprinkled many other nations because, not by the presence of his signs, but through hearing of them and their fame, he watered them from afar, as with a kind of dew, and rendered them all stupefied and silent with astonishment. Hence it says: “Kings shall close their mouths because of him, for they shall see what was not told them, and contemplate what they had not heard,” just as the Jews had been told and had heard about him.

The prophet himself, marveling at this, says: “Who has believed our report, and to whom has the arm of the Lord been revealed?” It is as though he said: “The things I foretell are so astonishing that scarcely anyone will judge them worthy of belief—namely, that the arm of the Lord is to be revealed,” that is, that his Son is to become incarnate and thus, through the flesh he assumed, to be visibly displayed to the world.

“And he shall ascend,” he says, “like a shoot before him, and like a root from thirsty ground.” We see, of course, that from thirsty ground—that is, from dry earth—neither a branch nor a root can grow without moisture. Moisture is, as it were, the male element of the soil. Christ, however, ascended like a root or shoot from dry earth before the Lord, when God the Father brought him forth from the flesh of the Virgin without intercourse with a man.

But what he added—“There is no appearance or beauty in him; we saw him, and he had no aspect; and we desired him despised and last among men”—he added to display his humility and his contempt for worldly pomp. “A man of sorrows,” he says. He truly was a man of sorrows, because neither in infancy, boyhood, nor youth was he free from the plots of evil-minded men or from toil. Thus he became a man of greater fame and wider renown, being known through suffering. By this suffering the prophet wished nothing other than the miseries and labors that Christ endured in the world according to the flesh to be understood.

It continues: “His face was as though hidden and despised, and therefore we did not regard him.” Christ’s face was as though hidden because the splendor of his divinity lay concealed beneath his flesh, and although he could have resisted those who attacked him, he did not wish to do so. Therefore he was despised and not regarded—that is, not valued.

“And truly he himself bore our infirmities, and he carried our sorrows,” when he himself endured the pains and punishments that were owed for our crimes. “And we thought him as one stricken, smitten by God, and humbled.” That is, we thought that the wound—that scourging and striking and that humiliation—had happened to him on his own account, but it had not.

And this is what he says: “But he was wounded for our iniquities; he was crushed for our crimes.” [Col. 0634B] “And the discipline of our peace was upon him”—that is, the discipline and correction that we would have had to endure in order to obtain peace, he himself endured for us, as the merciful and kind one. Hence it follows: “By his bruise we were healed,” namely, by the bruises of the scourges and wounds that he suffered for us.

It continues again: “We all wandered like sheep, and each turned aside to his own way.” Sheep are simple, extremely foolish, and wandering animals. We too, foolish like sheep, wandered because we did not know who or what he was; but each turned aside to his own way. This means that scarcely anyone believed his teaching, while each person retained his former way.

“And the Lord laid upon him the iniquity of us all”—that is, original sin, by which we are all ensnared; through him, that is, through the baptism that the Lord himself gave, he forgives and washes it away.

“He was compelled and afflicted, and he did not open his mouth; and like a lamb he shall be led to slaughter, and like a sheep before its shearer he shall be silent, and he shall not open his mouth.” None of this requires explanation; indeed, it is clear to everyone. For Christ, brought before Pilate, falsely accused, scourged, and struck even with blows on the face, remained silent. To Pilate himself, who questioned him repeatedly, he scarcely gave any answer.

But what follows—“From distress and judgment he was taken away”—is expressed by a hendiadys. For “from distress and judgment” means “from a narrow judgment.” We call a narrow judgment an unjust judgment. Christ, however, was taken away from a narrow judgment—that is, through a narrow and unjust judgment he was seized, although he had committed no wrong.

“Who shall declare his generation?” He certainly spoke of his divine generation, which is indescribable and ineffable, and thereby showed that he was destined to be God. Hence it also follows: “He was divided from the land of the living.”

“For the crime of my people he was struck”: this is the same as what he said above, “He himself was wounded for our iniquities; he was crushed for our crimes.”

“And he gave his burial with the wicked, and with the rich his death.” “With the wicked” and “with the rich” mean the same thing. For nearly all the rich of this world are wicked (Matthew XIX; Luke XVIII; 1 Timothy VI). Among the Jews it was customary for wicked people and those killed for some crime of their own to be buried outside the common fellowship of the others.

[Col. 0635A] And Christ was crucified and died with the wicked—that is, with the robbers—and was buried outside the common burial place, although he committed no iniquity and there was no deceit in his mouth. But the Lord willed it so, as it is written in what follows: “And the Lord willed to crush him and to afflict him,” that is, to make him suffer.

“If he sets his soul for sin, he shall see offspring,” and so forth. We certainly know that in ancient times Scripture called the sacrifice made for sin by the name of “sin.” Hence the prophet also says here: “If you set, Lord, your soul”—that is, Christ’s soul—“for sin,” that is, for the sacrifice for sin; in other words, if he is sacrificed for our sin, “he shall see offspring,” that is, a great offspring, and shall have many heirs (2 Corinthians V).

And through the sacrifice of his body and his death, Christ saw a great offspring and very many heirs; “the time was prolonged,” and the Lord’s will was fulfilled in him.

“From the labor of his soul he shall see, and he shall be satisfied.” It is as though he said: “His soul shall labor so greatly that, when he sees that labor and recognizes how immense it was, he shall be satisfied”—that is, it will seem excessive to him, just as even today one says, “I suffered so much evil and distress that I became sated with it.” Christ endured immense distresses and labors.

“By his knowledge he shall justify the just one for many.” This means that through his knowledge the Lord shall show to many that the one who is just is just. Christ was just, and the Lord showed to many that he was just.

But what follows—“And he himself shall bear their iniquities”—is the same as what he said above: “Truly he himself bore our infirmities, and he carried our sorrows.”

“Therefore,” says the Lord, “I shall make him share in many things, and with the strong he shall divide the spoils.” Christ shared in many things because many from many nations believed in him. He divided the spoils with the strong because, with the rulers of hell who had despoiled this world, he divided the plunder, as it were, and carried away his portion when he rescued from there those who had believed that he would come.

It continues: “Because he handed over his soul to death.” He repeats the reason why he shared in many things: namely, because in his immense compassion he consented to die for the redemption of the world.

It continues again: “And he was counted among the criminals.” As we said, Christ was counted among criminals because he was hanged with robbers.

“And he himself bore the sin of many,” not of all, because he saved not everyone but many.

It continues again: “And he shall pray for transgressors.” Christ prayed for transgressors when he prayed for those crucifying him, saying: “Father, forgive them, for they do not know what they are doing” (Luke XXIII).

Therefore, O Moses, since both the time and all the other things that the prophets foretold about Christ have become evident in the one whom we believe to have been Christ, as well as in his words and works, it is truly clear that he has already come, and you ought no longer to doubt this.

MOYSES. I understand well enough what you have said. But if this is so, why have all the other things written about Christ in the prophets not been fulfilled in this man whom you say has come? [Col. 0636A]

PETRUS. What things?

MOYSES. The same Isaiah says of Christ: “And he shall judge the nations, and rebuke many peoples; and they shall beat their swords into ploughshares and their spears into pruning hooks. Nation shall no longer lift up the sword against nation, nor shall they train for war any longer” (Isaiah II). These things have not yet been fulfilled, although they will undoubtedly be fulfilled after Christ’s advent. To this day, nations still wage war against one another.

PETRUS. You do not consider how what you say was spoken. For when the prophet said, “They shall beat their swords into ploughshares and their spears into pruning hooks, and nation shall not lift up the sword against nation, nor shall they train any longer for war,” he did not, I say, describe what the nations would do, but showed what Christ would command, just as Zechariah elsewhere says about him: “And he shall speak peace to the nations” (Zechariah IX). For just as here we understand that the statement refers to his commanding peace (John XIV), so also there. Since he himself commanded this, if it has not been fulfilled, the fault is not his.

MOYSES. Jeremiah says: “In those days”—that is, the days of Christ—“Judah shall be saved, and Israel shall dwell securely” (Jeremiah XXIII). But this too has not yet been fulfilled. It ought to have been fulfilled after the advent of that man whom you call Christ, if he were Christ. For Judah and Israel are still in misery and captivity.

[Col. 0636C] PETRUS. This promise was made only to those of Israel and Judah who were destined to believe. Therefore it was not fulfilled in unbelievers, just as, after the people of Israel had been led out of Egypt, certain people did not enter the promised land because they sinned and departed from the Lord’s commandments (Psalm XCIV; Numbers XIV). The Lord had promised this land to Moses, saying: “I have come down to deliver him from the hands of the Egyptians and to lead him from that land into a good and beautiful land” (Exodus III). Indeed, they all died in the wilderness.

MOYSES. Here is another matter that has not yet been fulfilled, which Isaiah prophesied would occur at Christ’s advent. For he says: “The wolf shall dwell with the lamb, and the leopard shall lie down with the kid; the calf, the lion, and the sheep shall dwell together, and a little child shall lead them. The calf and the bear shall feed; their young shall rest together, and the lion shall eat straw like an ox” (Isaiah XI; LXV).

PETRUS. O Moses, you understand this prophecy, as it is written, with the greatest foolishness if you take it literally.

MOYSES. Yes.

PETRUS. In this, the ignorance of your heart is exposed. For if, as you say, the wolf has no peace except with the lamb, the leopard except with the kid, and the lion except with the sheep and the calf, what benefit would such an alliance provide? The wolf would disturb the kid, the lion the lamb, and the leopard the sheep and the calf.

MOYSES. How, then, do you understand it?

PETRUS. By those beasts that live by plunder and flesh we understand wicked and rapacious people; by the other animals, however, we understand the gentle and simple. The prophet said that Christ would command these people to dwell together and have peace.

That he wished this to be understood of human beings the prophet indicates in what follows, when he adds: “For the earth is filled with the knowledge of the Lord” (Isaiah XI). He certainly did not say this on account of animals, which neither possess a rational soul nor can possess the knowledge of the Lord—that is, knowledge of the Lord.

But for the destruction of this interpretation of yours concerning the prophecy, your teachers said that there would be no difference between the present time and the time of Christ except that, in his time, you would escape all captivity and misery.

MOYSES. Here again is something from Isaiah that we do not yet know to have been fulfilled. He says: “The light of the moon shall be like the light of the sun, and the light of the sun shall be sevenfold, like the light of seven days, on the day when the Lord binds up the wound of his people” (Isaiah XXX).

PETRUS. There is no nation in the whole world more foolish than you, who think that God will increase the body or light of the moon or of the sun. If the sun, which is now as large as it is, were merely twice as large, it would certainly burn up the entire world—how much more if it were sevenfold! And if its light were seven times greater, it would blind our eyes with excessive brilliance. If the moon’s light were made equal to the sun’s brilliance, no one would ever rest again, for it would always be day.

By the increase, therefore, of lunar or solar light, the prophet wished the faith and glory of those who would believe in Christ to be understood. It is as though he said: “Their faith and glory shall be many times greater and more radiant than those of the present generation.”

That the prophet is not speaking of this visible moon or sun, but of the glory and splendor of Christian belief, he testifies in what follows, when he adds: “The sun shall no longer be your light by day, nor shall the brightness of the moon illuminate you; but the Lord shall be your everlasting light, and your God shall be your glory. Your sun shall no longer set, and your moon shall not wane, because the Lord shall be your everlasting light” (Isaiah LX).

For if he were speaking literally of the sun or moon, what he says—“The sun shall no longer be your light by day, nor shall the brightness of the moon illuminate you”—would contradict what he had said above, namely, that the light would be like the light of the sun and would be sevenfold.

It is therefore clear that the prophet is speaking here of the splendor and glory of the faith of the holy Church. This is also indicated by what follows: “But the Lord shall be your everlasting light, and your God shall be your glory.” It is as though he said: “You will no longer need the radiance of this light of your cruelty, which resembles that of the transient sun or moon; for the Lord will illuminate you eternally with the glory of his own light.”

And what follows—“Your sun shall no longer set, and your moon shall not wane”—if, I say, this were understood literally, so that the brilliance of the sun or moon were continuous, there would no longer be day or night, month or year, all of which result from the alternation of the sun and moon.

Therefore, not without reason do we understand this spiritually as having been said of the light and glory of our faith, which will neither diminish nor set.

MOYSES. What also is this that Isaiah says: “Then you shall see and abound, and your heart shall marvel and be enlarged, when the multitude of the sea has been turned toward you, the strength of the nations has come to you, an inundation of camels shall cover you, the dromedaries of Midian and Ephah; and all those from Sheba shall come, bringing gold and frankincense and proclaiming praise to the Lord” (Isaiah LX)? For these things too have not yet been completed.

[Col. 0638B] PETRUS. They were indeed completed during the time of the Second Temple, which Ezra built at Cyrus’s command, as the prophet Haggai bears witness when he says: “Thus says the Lord God of hosts: Yet a little while, and I will shake heaven and earth, the sea and the dry land. And I will shake all nations, and the desired things of all nations shall come, and I will fill this house with glory, says the Lord of hosts. Great shall be the glory of this latter house, more than that of the former, says the Lord of hosts. And in this place I will give peace, says the Lord of hosts” (Haggai XI).

Indeed, what Isaiah had said would come to pass, Haggai indicates was to be fulfilled in the Temple that had already begun to be rebuilt in his own time.

[Col. 0638C] MOYSES. It may indeed be as you say.

PETRUS. But tell me, O Moses, what does Haggai mean when he says, “Great shall be the glory of this latter house, more than that of the former”? In what respect was the glory of the latter house greater than that of the former, when the latter lacked those precious insignia that were present in the former? For the Lord’s ark was not in the second, nor did they use the breastpiece in it; nor did fire come down from heaven there to consume the holocausts; nor was there an anointed man or prophet at that time—and there were many other such things besides.

MOYSES. We know nothing about this except what we have heard from our teachers. They themselves said nothing else except that the second house remained for ten years longer than the first.

PETRUS. That is certainly no glory.

[Col. 0638D] MOYSES. Then Haggai undoubtedly lied.

PETRUS. Far be it from us. The glory of the latter house was greater than that of the former in this respect: Christ came while it was still standing, and his advent was more glorious than all those things mentioned above.

But, if you please, we can understand this much more subtly: namely, that “latter” and “former” were said of the same house, referring to its beginning and its end. For since Christ came near the end of it (Colossians II), and through him divinity itself dwelt in that house, its glory was indeed much greater at the end than at the beginning.

At Christ’s advent, everything that Isaiah says and Haggai confirms was fulfilled. For when he came, the multitude of the sea and of the earth was converted to him; heaven, earth, and the seas were shaken. I say “shaken” to mean that heaven and earth and their inhabitants rejoiced, and that from every direction various offerings were brought to Jerusalem in praise of Christ himself.

MOYSES. Why should I bring anything more against you, when you explain all my authorities according to your own will?

PETRUS. Truth has strong pillars on which it may rest.

TITLE X. That Christ was crucified and killed by the Jews of his own free will.

MOYSES. Peter, I wish us to return to the subject and ask you to answer me about other parts of your belief. Since you believe Christ to have been both man and God, why did he allow himself to be crucified and did not rescue himself from the hands of the Jews? How was the sovereignty of omnipotence diminished?

PETRUS. He could have defended and saved himself perfectly well if he had wished, but he willingly endured this for the salvation of his own people, although it was not pleasing to the flesh that came from the world. For the Word of God would never have assumed flesh for any other reason than to free from the devil’s captivity those who had believed and would believe in him (John I).

MOYSES. Many questions arise from this statement of yours. First, what the devil is; second, why man came under his power; third, why God freed human beings from his hand, since he allowed them to fall into it; fourth, why, when he wished them to be redeemed, he did not do this by his own power, but preferred to become incarnate and suffer.

PETRUS. Since you have raised several matters at once, and several matters cannot be answered fully at once, ask me about them individually, if you please, and I will answer what I think concerning each.

MOYSES. First of all, then, I wish to hear what the devil is.

PETRUS. The devil, O Moses, is indeed a subtle and spiritual being, and was once one of the good orders of angels. Two of the princes of that order are called Huza and Hazazel in Hebrew, but Haroth and Maroth in the Arabic language. This devil, weighed down by his sin and iniquity and made, as it were, somewhat heavier, fell from the highest heavens, descended somewhat lower, and his dwelling is here below the firmament.

MOYSES. It is certainly written among us that there are devils, and that two of their princes are called Huza and Hazazel. But I would gladly hear whether you can show, by some philosophical reasoning, that they exist and what they are.

PETRUS. First, then, you must know that the art called necromancy has nine parts. The first four treat of the four elements and of how we can operate physically within them; the remaining five concern how one can operate only through the invocation of evil spirits.

[Col. 0640A] Those evil spirits are called devils by human beings.

MOYSES. Perhaps these devils were never good angels, as you say, but were always wicked spirits.

PETRUS. That is certainly not true. For God made nothing except what was good, since Scripture, which is entirely truthful, says: “God saw everything that he had made, and it was very good” (Genesis I). But because they chose evil, they became wicked.

MOYSES. Since we know by experimental evidence and by the approval of our teachers that the devil exists, we should no longer doubt that they exist, nor do we need a lengthy discussion about such a question. Let us therefore leave this matter aside and inquire why man came under his power.

PETRUS. Since God created Adam in his own image and likeness (ibid.), and therefore made him excellent among creatures, he created him both composite and simple: composite so that he might inhabit this world, exercise power and dominion over it, and be capable of dissolution; simple so that, whenever it pleased the Creator, he might pass to the heavenly homeland of the angels without the death of the flesh.

Since, I say, God created him in this manner, the devil, who dwelt in this lower air near the earth, saw it, grew envious, and sought his condemnation as best he could. He even inspired his heart to transgress God’s command and eat from the forbidden fruit, so that he might fall from his dignity, just as the devil himself had fallen.

MOYSES. Before you say anything else, Peter, I want you to answer me: what do you mean by saying that Adam was made simple and composite? This seems contradictory. Moreover, when we were discussing the resurrection of the dead, you denied that any body could be both simple and composite.

There is another contradiction as well: you said that he was created capable of death, and yet in such a way that he could pass to the homeland of the angels without death. By the one statement he is shown to be mortal, by the other immortal.

PETRUS. You should know that all animals are composed of the four elements. They also vary according to the variation of those elements, which are joined unequally in their composition according to their qualities and quantities. From this arises the dissimilarity of the various species.

But since the heat of the elements from which they are composed conflicts with cold, moisture with dryness, emptiness with solidity, heaviness with lightness, and subtlety with dullness, and since all their remaining qualities are mutually opposed, everything composed from them is continually changing: it grows and diminishes, becomes hot and cold, and is affected in turn by the other accidents.

When these qualities, each tending toward the expulsion of the other, are so disposed that one grows slightly stronger and another slightly weaker, illness results. But if one becomes excessive and another declines so far that it cannot resist it even a little, their connections are dissolved, their components separated, their composites destroyed, and that dissolution is called death.

When God created Adam, however, he was pleased to create him in such a way that he could both die and not die. He therefore made him from the subtler elements, and from all of them in perfectly equal measure, so that their qualities would not possess any power to overcome one another. He was made in such a way that he could not die, and for this reason I called him simple and immortal.

In this way he was immortal, just as all other simple things are immortal. Certain animals provide a clear indication of this, since, being formed more equally than other animals from the elements, they undoubtedly live longer.

But because Adam was made from the four elements, and everything made from them is capable of dissolution, I called him mortal and composite.

MOYSES. I accept what you say. But since, as you assert, he could both die and not die, why did mortality overcome immortality, so that every human being has been mortal to this day?

PETRUS. This is what I intended to explain, and it is the reason why Adam came under the devil’s power. When the devil inspired him to transgress the obedience owed to the Creator, Adam thought about it. After he had thought, he chose; after he had chosen, he desired; after he had desired and acted, he sinned.

But after he sinned, he lost the quality he possessed—and thus immortality—and entirely assumed mortality, as is the nature of composite things. Henceforth this could not be separated from him, and he received the definition according to which he was called rational and mortal. Indeed, everyone descended from his seed possessed the same nature that he himself had.

For it is just that if something proceeds from another, it should receive a likeness of that other’s nature.

Adam’s soul, however, being of a subtler and stronger nature than the body, because it consented to that sin and did not resist when it could have done so, could no longer transcend the height of heaven, which belonged to its nature, when every soul that became joined to a body generated from that corruption departed from the body. Rather, it remained here in the lower air near the earth.

Because the soul came to this place as though from elsewhere, while the devil was its citizen, the devil therefore had power over it, and his desire was fulfilled. Since Adam’s sin was also twofold—spiritual and bodily—the spiritual sin consisted in choosing to believe and obey the devil rather than God, which pertains to the spirit; the bodily sin consisted in taking pleasure in the sweetness of the forbidden fruit, which pertains to the body. Therefore he suffered both the death of the flesh and the death of the soul—that is, a twofold punishment.

MOYSES. It seems to me that you have explained clearly and orderly enough how Adam, and consequently every human being, came under the devil’s power because of his sin. But I should like you, if you know, to reveal this also: by what physical process and in what manner did he lose, because of the transgression of the command, the balance that Adam had possessed in his constitution?

PETRUS. Know, then, that since Adam had been made equally from all the elements, he ought also to have had an equal tempering of his emotions: of anger and sadness, eating and drinking, and all the rest, none of which becomes excessive or deficient in a human being except through an excess or diminution of the qualities of the elements.

When the devil advised him to transgress the command of his Lord, and Adam thought about it, choosing to act, while his soul did not prevent him even though it could have done so, he began at that moment to sin and to depart from his balance. He lost that tempering and desired to eat what he did not need and what had even been forbidden him. Thus he gradually proceeded to the act, ate, and then completely lost his balance.
