If at the outset he had thought about it only to examine whether what he heard was good or evil, and had not chosen it, he would certainly neither have sinned nor lost his balance.

For example, when someone is neither excessively joyful nor excessively sad, but is balanced in both respects, if he hears a rumor of such a kind that he can, if he wishes, become angry or not become angry, but thinks about it in such a way that he takes offense at what he has heard, red bile, from which anger arises, is stirred in him by such thinking. He then grows hot and becomes angry; and the hotter he grows, the more the bile is stirred, until he becomes completely angry. Thus the moderation and tempering between sadness and joy that he previously possessed is destroyed.

But if he reflects on that rumor without being troubled by it, the bile is not stirred, the man does not grow hot or become angry, and that tempering does not depart from him.

MOYSES. We certainly believe that Adam sinned at the serpent’s counsel (Genesis III), and that through his sin every human being was condemned to death. Our teachers attest that there were many men who would never have died except for the serpent’s counsel and Adam’s sin. But we do not believe that the souls of the saints descended to hell after death. Therefore, if you have any authority for this, I ask you to show it to me.

PETRUS. I shall explain it briefly to you, but I will nevertheless produce several clear authorities concerning it. In Genesis it is written of Jacob that, when his daughters gathered around him to console him concerning his son Joseph, he refused consolation, saying: “For I shall go down mourning to my son in the underworld” (Genesis XXXVII).

MOYSES. Jacob certainly said this according to the body. By “the underworld” he intended the earth in which everyone is buried. It is as though he said: “When I die and am buried in the earth with my son, I shall mourn continually even in that very destruction.”

[Col. 0643A] PETRUS. What you say is not true. For he knew that his son had not been buried in the earth; rather, he thought that he had been devoured by some beast. Therefore he said this according to the soul: “For I shall go down mourning to my son in the underworld.” It is as though he said: “Because my son has died, I shall die and, mourning, go down to the underworld where his soul is, together with all the souls of the dead.”

David also testifies to this in a psalm when he says: “What man is there who shall live and not see death, and shall rescue his soul from the hand of the underworld?” (Psalm LXXXVIII.) By saying, “Who is the man who shall live and not see death?” he indicates that there is no human being who will not die. By saying, “and shall rescue his soul from the hand of the underworld,” he indicates that in his time no soul could be preserved from the hand of the underworld.

Hezekiah too, as we read in Isaiah, although he was a good and holy man—as he himself testifies in his prayer when he says, “I beg you, Lord; remember, I beseech you, how I have walked before you in truth and with a perfect heart, and have done what is good in your eyes” (2 Kings XX)—although, I say, he was holy, nevertheless showed that he would descend to the underworld when he says in what follows: “I said: In the middle of my days I shall go to the gates of the underworld” (Isaiah XXXVIII).

MOYSES. If it is as you say, then the souls of the patriarchs and prophets and all the other saints who died before the death of that one whom you call Christ dwelt in one place together with the souls of the wicked.

PETRUS. It is certainly true that all were in darkness and shadows, but they were not all in places of punishment or under torture, for each received recompense according to his merits. Nevertheless, all were in the underworld and under the devil’s power.

For no dead person, from Adam until Christ’s death, avoided the confines of the underworld. We perceive this from the words of Moses, who, when he urged the children of Israel to obey the Lord’s commandments and announced what rewards they would receive for doing so, never promised them anything concerning the blessedness of paradise. It was already known at that time to everyone that no one would enter there before Christ’s death.

MOYSES. I do not think Moses refrained from speaking about paradise for the reason you have stated. Rather, he recognized that he could urge them to obey God’s commandments more effectively either through those visible goods that they greatly desired or by deterring them from their iniquities through the present evils and labors they feared, than by predicting future punishments or a heavenly blessedness of which they had no knowledge.

PETRUS. That opinion of yours is misguided. For if he had spoken to them both of a twofold reward and of a twofold punishment, he would have urged them all the more both to flee evil and to embrace good.

Moreover, if you wish, I can show you, according to your own belief, that the souls of the saints were in the underworld and under the devil’s power before Christ’s death.

[Col. 0644A] MOYSES. I desire nothing except the truth.

PETRUS. First, then, I ask you: where were the souls of the saints, if you believe that they were not in the underworld?

MOYSES. They were certainly in heaven.

PETRUS. Answer me this also, please: have you ever read or heard how far upward the power of those who practice the art of necromancy can rise?

MOYSES. Only as far as the firmament.

PETRUS. And can it pass beyond that to any extent?

MOYSES. It is strange that you ask, since you have heard it said proverbially not only by the wise but also by old women: “You have as much power in this as the devil has in heaven.”

[Col. 0644B] PETRUS. Now, then, I want you to say how you believe the event recorded in the First Book of Kings (chapter XXVIII) occurred—namely, that Samuel was raised by a woman who possessed a pythonic spirit. Was it true or an apparition?

MOYSES. In many ways, indeed, it is shown to be true. First, because he plainly speaks from there, namely, how he had risen from the earth, what his appearance, age, and clothing had been, and how, on God’s behalf, he truthfully answered everything that Saul asked; and nothing of what he said was false. Second, because Saul knew himself to be in the woman’s power, in that she could summon Samuel; surely, he would not have asked for him to be summoned. Third, because our teachers assert that God forgave Saul his sin at his death, on the basis of Samuel’s own speech to Saul. For from his saying, “Tomorrow you and your sons shall be with me” (ibid.), they establish that Saul came with Samuel to a place of rest.

[Col. 0644C]

PETRUS. I do not wish to debate any longer whether it was true or false. But if it is as you assert, how could he have been summoned by necromantic art if he was in heaven? And if he was not in heaven, he was undoubtedly under the devil’s jurisdiction and resting in hell.

MOYSES. You have indeed laid a good trap for me and defeated me well, and up to this point it has been sufficiently shown how a human being came into the devil’s hand. It follows, then, that you explain why God brought him out from there, since He had allowed him to fall.

[Col. 0644D]

PETRUS. Since the human race was condemned through the serpent’s counsel and the sin of the first parent Adam—condemned, I say, and punished with the twofold death, as we have said—because there were many holy men who, through no sin of their own, had fallen into the devil’s snare, except for that ancient and almost already natural sin, the Creator of the human race, looking upon this, moved by pity and mercy, wished to free them from there.

MOYSES. And since, as you assert, He was moved by pity toward them, why did He allow them to be detained there for so long, namely until the time of the one whom you call Christ?

PETRUS. He did this not through any justice, but solely through His pity and simple goodness. And simple goodness, as we said at the beginning of our conversation, ought to have neither measure nor limit.

MOYSES. And why, as I said above, when He wished to redeem them, did He not do so by this power, but instead preferred to have His Word become incarnate and suffer?

PETRUS. The fact that He rescued them in this manner was surely the most perfect wisdom, as is found in His other ancient works. For when once, as you yourself know, He was preparing to lead His people Israel out of Egyptian captivity, and wished the evil spirit to kill the firstborn of the Egyptians while preserving His own people unharmed, He commanded them to sacrifice a lamb or kid in each household and to stain the doors of the houses (Exod. XII), so that when the evil spirit came, he would pass over the house marked with blood. But when He wished to protect them in this way, could He not have done so without this action?

MOYSES. Certainly He could.

PETRUS. Why, then, did He require such a means of liberation?

MOYSES. It is surely His wisdom to assign some cause to each thing by which He wishes to bring it to completion, just as through the sacrifice of a lamb or kid He wished to redeem them from that death. But we cannot grasp all the causes of things.

PETRUS. The mysteries of God are so deep and inscrutable that no one can penetrate them. Why, then, do you wonder, by questioning, that the Lord sent His Word to become incarnate and die for the redemption of humankind?

[Col. 0645C]

MOYSES. And why did He not redeem them from that sin of Adam by the sacrifice of any animal, just as it was commanded in the Law that some animal be sacrificed for sin (Lev. IV; Num. V)?

PETRUS. You are the most foolish of all! Where could He have found so many animals? For as many human beings as there had been from the beginning of the world and would be until its consummation, so many animals would necessarily have had to be sacrificed. Besides this, since that sin had occupied both body and soul, it could not rationally be erased except by a sacrifice that possessed both body and soul.

MOYSES. Since, then, He wished that sin to be redeemed by such a sacrifice, why could that sacrifice not have been made by some prophet or any other holy man, rather than His promising that His Word would take flesh and undergo death?

[Col. 0645D]

PETRUS. Because it would have been necessary for the man who was to die for the redemption of so great and serious a sin to be free from every fault. If he did not need to redeem his own sins by his death, such a person could not be found among those who were merely human. For the nature of the body does not permit it to avoid sin, as God testifies in Genesis, saying that the mind of man is continually inclined toward wickedness from youth (Gen. VIII). Solomon also says in Ecclesiastes: “There is no human being on earth who does good and does not sin” (Eccl. VII). It was therefore both reason and God’s wisdom that His Word should receive a human body and preserve it free from all contagion and sin, so that, being thus clean and pure from every fault, it might redeem that universal offense; and that, having been assumed by Him who is the origin of all things, it might erase the first sin of all. It was also so that, being born without a human father, it might remove the offense of the one who was made without a father. Moreover, it was so that God might rationally condemn on the day of judgment those who, after being freed from the devil’s snare through the death of His Son, would afterward fall back into it through their own iniquity.

MOYSES. Since you assert that the one whom you call Christ died willingly and spontaneously for the redemption of humankind, why do you condemn his killers and declare them guilty of sin, when they fulfilled his will so completely?

[Col. 0646B]

PETRUS. If they had acted with that intention—namely, to fulfill his will, and because of his death believed that they would come out from the devil’s power—they would undoubtedly have incurred no sin. But because they rejected him and killed him out of envy, they are therefore guilty of so great a crime, and they will not escape misery and tribulation either in the present age or in the future, so long as they persist in this wickedness. I shall show you by a parallel that they have been rightly condemned as guilty and deserving of punishment, and you yourself will judge it to be right.

MOYSES. When I have heard it, I shall judge it right if it is right.

PETRUS. A certain man had a ship, and he intended to burn it so that he might have its nails separately and make charcoal for himself from its wood. While he was considering this, one of his enemies came to the ship by night and, unaware of his intention, burned it out of hatred. When morning came, the man in question found, as he had wished, the nails of his ship on one side and charcoal on the other.

Here is another example. A certain man had a stone house. He wished to destroy it in order to build another structure from its stones. By chance, one of his enemies pulled it down one day so completely that not one stone remained upon another, and he did this not to fulfill the intention he did not know, but out of hatred. When the aforesaid man came to his house the next day, he found accomplished what he had been planning and wishing to do.

Since neither the man who burned the ship nor the one who pulled down the house had acted to fulfill the will of his enemy, but out of hatred and envy, what judgment will you pass on them?

MOYSES. I judge both that they are guilty and that they ought to be punished.

PETRUS. By the same reasoning, therefore, those who killed Christ out of the poison of hatred and envy, rather than to fulfill his will, are guilty and must be judged.

MOYSES. They would undoubtedly be guilty if they had acted in the manner you describe. But they did not act in that way; rather, they killed him after a just judgment.

PETRUS. And what fault did they charge him with, since they condemned him to death?

MOYSES. Because he was a magician, and by magical art led the children of Israel into error, and besides this called himself the Son of God.

PETRUS. It is not surprising if they said these and other lies about him, although he himself had come to redeem them. The prophet Hosea foretold this about them: “Woe to them, because they have departed from me. They shall be laid waste, because they have transgressed against me. I redeemed them, and they spoke lies against me” (Hos. VII).

Moreover, where could he have learned so much magical art that by it he changed water into wine (John II), restored five thousand men with five loaves (John VI), healed lepers (Luke XVIII) and dropsical persons (Luke XIV), gave the lame the ability to walk, the deaf the ability to hear, and the mute speech (Matt. IX), restored sight to the blind, and—greater than all these things—raised the dead (Mark VII; John XI; Luke VII), besides performing other miracles too numerous to recount?

MOYSES. Our teachers certainly say that he learned it in Egypt.

PETRUS. According to your own words, then, it is established that he was in Egypt at that time, since they themselves performed the same works.

MOYSES. It may be so.

PETRUS. Why, then, were their works neither spread abroad nor heard of, as his were? And why would the wise men of Egypt accept his teaching and law if they recognized him as a magician?

MOYSES. I certainly do not know how to answer you about this. For I have never heard that any of them believed in him, nor how or when they did so.

[Col. 0647C]

PETRUS. Let us set these matters aside for now and examine his individual works, to determine whether they were done by magical art, by some other natural art, or rather by the power of God.

MOYSES. You speak well. I also do not care greatly to investigate the lesser matters. For if you show that the greater works were done by the power of God, I shall have no doubt about the lesser ones.

PETRUS. You speak wisely. And, as you say, I agree. Ask first about each matter in turn.

MOYSES. First of all, I want an answer about how the lepers were cleansed (Matt. VIII; Luke XVII), and how the blind were given sight (Luke XVIII).

PETRUS. Know that leprosy cannot be cured in any way except either by medicine or by the power of God. If by medicine, it is purged either internally through potions or externally through ointments. But since no medicine was seen to be applied by him, and he cured them by a mere word and in an instant, it is clear that this was done by the power of God.

MOYSES. Do we not read that the magician Firminus cleansed a leper?

PETRUS. It is certainly false that he cured him. Rather, by his magical art he deceived human eyes and caused something that was not actually present to be seen. The proof of this is that after some time the sick man contracted the same illness again; and although outwardly he saw his skin clean, like that of others, nevertheless, as he himself said, he never ceased to feel the illness internally. Moreover, nowhere in the whole of necromantic literature does it say that a leper was ever truly cured through it. As for the blind—those born blind—natural science denies that medicine can give them sight. The magician Assitha likewise testifies that through necromancy sight is not truly restored to them.

MOYSES. It may be so. But what will you say about the dead, since that same Assitha asserts that a person can raise them and speak with them, and in his book shows the method by which this can be done; while, on the other hand, the Book of Kings states, as we said, how Samuel was raised through a woman who possessed a familiar spirit? (I Kings XXVIII.)

[Col. 0648B]

PETRUS. It is certainly true, as you say, that Assitha testifies to this. But in the raising of the dead there is a great difference between God’s work and what is done by magical art. Those raised by some magician cannot walk farther than the length of their own shadow; when they reach its end, they fall back dead upon the earth. Those, however, who are raised by God’s power drink and eat, walk wherever and as far as they wish, and live as other human beings for as long as God pleases—like those whom both Elisha and Elijah raised, and Christ as well (III Kings XVII; IV Kings IV; Luke VII).

MOYSES. Since it has been sufficiently shown up to this point that this man accomplished everything not by magical art but by the power of God, like the other prophets, I want you to explain why he dared to call himself not a prophet but the Son of God.

PETRUS. He did so because he truly was the Son of God. Since we demonstrated this earlier by many authoritative testimonies, when we were discussing that he was both God and man (John I), there is no further need to prove it. But if you wish, let us enter into a brief argument about it, and I shall show you by reasoning that when he called himself the Son of God (John XI), he spoke the truth.

MOYSES. I agree.

PETRUS. Can one who acts through the power of God do anything without God’s own will?

[Col. 0648D]

MOYSES. It seems necessary to me that whoever does something by God’s power can do it only by the will of that same God.

PETRUS. And does it not follow that one who acts by God’s power and according to His will is God’s friend and His faithful servant?

MOYSES. It certainly follows. For we find this by reading that the holy prophets who once performed miracles were beloved by God and faithful to Him—such as Moses, Elijah, and Elisha, and many others who performed numerous miracles during their lives (Exod. II, III; III Kings XVII and XVIII; Eccl. XLVIII; IV Kings II, IV, V, VI).

PETRUS. And it is necessary that one who is God’s friend and faithful to Him never say anything false about God or on God’s behalf.

MOYSES. It is true.

PETRUS. Since, then, as was proved above, Christ performed miracles through God’s power and will, and since it follows from this that he was God’s friend and faithful servant, it is undoubtedly concluded that he never spoke anything false about God or on His behalf. Since this is so, he therefore truly called himself the Son of God (John X).

MOYSES. What you have said is rational. But I am greatly astonished that, although at that time there were many men endowed with great understanding and wisdom, they did not perceive that he was such a person. And if they recognized it, why did they reject his faith and teaching, and knowingly incur the condemnation of their souls by crucifying him?

PETRUS. As we said earlier, they did this out of envy, because they feared that through him they would lose their dignity and reputation (John XI). We find something similar occurring in the time of Jeroboam, king of Israel. After Solomon’s death, his kingdom was divided into two, as Scripture testifies: his son Rehoboam obtained one part, while his servant Jeroboam obtained the other. Jeroboam, having taken counsel with his nobles, made two golden calves for the people to worship, lest, if they frequently went up to Jerusalem to pray and sacrifice, as was customary, they should perhaps remain there at some point, attach themselves to Rehoboam’s side, and thus Jeroboam lose his position. As the same Scripture teaches, it says:

“Jeroboam said in his heart: ‘Now the kingdom will return to the house of David. If this people goes up to offer sacrifices in the house of the Lord at Jerusalem, the heart of this people will turn to their lord Rehoboam, king of Judah; they will kill me and return to him.’ And having taken counsel, he made two golden calves and said to them: ‘You shall no longer go up to Jerusalem. Behold your gods, O Israel, who brought you out of the land of Egypt’” (III Kings XII).

Although Jeroboam himself and his nobles were endowed with great wisdom—first through Solomon, who had preceded them and, according to Scripture, had been wiser than all who came before or after him (III Kings IV), and also because great peace had existed in Solomon’s time, which provided an excellent opportunity for learning wisdom—it is plainly evident that, as we have said, they acted out of envy and fear of losing their kingdom.

You should therefore not be surprised if the teachers of the Law and the scribes killed Christ through the poison of envy, since they feared that through him they would lose their glory and dignity.

MOYSES. What you say is plausible. Nevertheless, I am still greatly astonished, although I have asked about the same matter elsewhere; I am astonished, I say, that although, according to what you say, he was powerful from God, he did not immediately avenge himself.

PETRUS. He did this through his great goodness and mercy. We learned this from his words while he hung on the cross, when he said: “Father, forgive them, for they do not know what they are doing” (Luke XXIII). By this he showed that he loved them very much, although they acted wickedly against him, as the prophet Zechariah testifies:

“And it shall be said to him: ‘What are these wounds in the midst of your hands?’ And he shall say: ‘With these I was wounded in the house of those who loved me’” (Zech. XIII).

But, O Moses, if it pleases God, a time will still come when the descendants of their fathers will acknowledge their wickedness, and, grieving and lamenting their sins, will mourn them; they will turn to the Lord and return to Him, as the prophet Zechariah says:

“And I will pour out upon the house of David and upon the inhabitants of Jerusalem a spirit of grace and supplication; and they shall look upon me whom they pierced, and they shall mourn for him with a mourning like that for an only son, and they shall grieve over him as one grieves over the death of a firstborn” (Zech. XII).

And may almighty God grant you, I ask, that you may be one of those who will turn back. Amen.

## TITLE XI. On Christ’s Resurrection and Ascension into Heaven

MOYSES. Up to this point it has been sufficiently shown concerning that man that he willingly undertook death for the redemption of the human race. Now, however, I wish to speak with you about the fact that, as you said in your exposition of your faith, he rose on the third day. And this could indeed have happened, since, as you say, the fullness of divinity dwelt in him (Col. II), and he restored the other dead to life, so that he could also raise himself. But I ask you whether, after he rose, he was God and man as before, or not.

PETRUS. I undoubtedly believe that he was so. For when his soul, separated from the body, descended to hell in order to rescue the good from there, divinity itself never departed from it. Therefore, when it returned to the body, divinity remained with it always; and for this reason he was then, is now, and will be forever both man and God.

MOYSES. I think it is sufficiently clear that you believe this, but one matter still remains about which I want you to answer me. Since he assumed flesh for no other reason than to rescue the sons of Adam from the devil’s yoke, after he had completed this, as you say, in accordance with his will, why did he again burden himself with the weight of the body?

PETRUS. Christ’s body was subtle and completely cleansed from every sin (Isa. LIII; I Pet. II). For it contracted no sin either from the first parent Adam or from itself; and since it was such, ought it to have died, when Adam himself died only because of sin, and when divinity also dwelt in Christ?

MOYSES. No.

PETRUS. Since, then, he suffered death for no fault he had committed, but solely for the salvation of his own people, ought he not rightly to have been raised?

MOYSES. The order of reason certainly requires this. But why did he hasten to be raised so quickly, rather than wait until the other good people who have died should be raised at the end of the world (I Cor. XV; Matt. XXV)?

PETRUS. Other dead people committed many sins in this world, and they also received death—the punishment for sin—because of Adam’s offense. Therefore they cannot be raised until God is pleased for them to be raised. He, however, had neither Adam’s sin nor any other sin, as we have said. Rather, he willingly died for our redemption on one day, and on the next descended to hell in order to lead the good out from there. Since he had already completed everything for which he had come, and, so to speak, had nothing further to do, he rightly rose on the third day.

Moreover, Enoch and Elijah, because they were holy and worthy men, as both we and you believe, are still alive (Gen. V; IV Kings II); and although they will die at the end of the world, they will nevertheless immediately rise again on account of their holiness. Since this is so, ought not Christ’s body, which was the holiest of all and completely free from sin, to have been raised immediately, when he wished it?

It was also necessary for him to be raised so that, just as by his death he descended to hell and freed the dead from the devil’s jurisdiction, so by his resurrection he might free those who were to come from the hand of that same devil. For when they hear that he has risen, they believe, and thus depart from his yoke.

MOYSES. What you have said is rational. But can you show by the authority of the prophets that he ought to have been raised?

PETRUS. I certainly can. David says in a psalm: “You shall add days to the days of the king; his years shall extend to the day of generation and generation” (Ps. LX). Of what king could this prophecy have been spoken except Christ? By “the days of the king,” the Prophet wished to indicate the fixed period during which Christ lived in the world before his passion. By the days that he said were to be added to the king’s days—days which he left without specification—he understood the time after Christ’s resurrection; and he signified that this time would have no end when he added, “his years to the day of generation and generation.”

It is also written in Isaiah: “Now I will arise, says the Lord; now I will be exalted; now I will be lifted up” (Isa. XXXIII). Here the Lord wished three things to be understood. When He says, “Now I will arise,” He speaks of the resurrection of His body from death. What follows, “Now I will be exalted,” He applied to His ascension into heaven. The third phrase, “Now I will be lifted up,” He added concerning the exaltation and glory of those who believe in Him.

MOYSES. Since you have mentioned the ascension, and I had already long intended to ask about it, I now ask you, if it pleases you, to tell me how you believe it happened. For reason forbids a heavy thing either to ascend above a light thing or to be supported by it.

PETRUS. My faith is certainly that he ascended into heaven. I also believe that the power of his omnipotence is so great that, however it happened, it was possible for it to happen as he wished. If I were discussing this with a faithful person, I would give no other answer. But because you are unbelieving and understand nothing except what is gross and can, as it were, be touched, I shall answer you somewhat more materially, because I wish you to believe something good through this.

MOYSES. I ask you to do so.

PETRUS. You know, then, that the goose and hen, the sparrow and lark, were all made from the four elements and have wings?

MOYSES. I certainly know this.

PETRUS. Tell me, then: why do the sparrow and lark rise so high by flying upward, while the goose and hen cannot do the same?

MOYSES. Because the former have small bodies and are therefore lighter, whereas the latter are larger and consequently heavier.

PETRUS. If lightness comes from size, why does the vulture or eagle, although it is larger than all these, rise higher than all of them by flying?

MOYSES. Because its body is composed more subtly from the elements.

PETRUS. And although it is light and subtle, what makes that body rise upward?

MOYSES. Without doubt, the spirit, without which it could not only not fly but could not move at all.

PETRUS. Since, then, Christ’s body after the resurrection was exceedingly light and subtle—for in death it had lost all heaviness and density, as is shown by the fact that afterward it required neither food nor drink—and since, I say, it was such, and had the spirit, that is, the soul, with it, and in addition had divinity, which, as Moses testifies, rules over and surpasses all the spirits of flesh, could it not ascend into heaven when it pleased?

Consider also Elijah, whose body acquired no subtlety through death, and yet rose on high in the presence of his disciple Elisha. How do you believe this happened rationally and according to natural science?

MOYSES. Elijah certainly fasted much and ate little; hence his body acquired such lightness and subtlety that it could rise as far as the air. There the angels also received him and carried him wherever God wished (IV Kings II, IV).

PETRUS. Since, then, Christ’s body was made subtle through death, and also because after the resurrection he neither ate nor drank out of any necessity, and since it contained within itself the fullness of divinity, which is above the angels, why could it not, as we have said, ascend into heaven?

There is also a rational proof that he ascended. If the Lord calls the place where Moses stood when He appeared to him in the bush holy because of His presence there for one hour, and on account of its holiness commands Moses to remove his sandals, saying, “Remove the sandal from your feet, for the place on which you stand is holy ground” (Exod. III), ought Christ’s body, in which the fullness of divinity dwelt not for a moment but perpetually, to have remained after the resurrection amid the filth of this world? No; for the just reason we have given, he left it and ascended upward into heaven.

MOYSES. You have proved this by a clear argument and introduced good parallels. But can some authoritative testimony concerning his ascension be found among the prophets?

PETRUS. It certainly can. In Genesis we read that the Lord spoke about this to Abraham, although secretly. For it is written:

“And He brought him outside and said to him: ‘Look up at the sky and count the stars, if you are able to count them.’ And He said: ‘So shall your seed be.’ And Abraham believed God, and it was reckoned to him as righteousness” (Gen. XV).

But tell me, O Moses, what does the statement “He brought him outside” mean? Why did He do this? Did Abraham not know inside as well as outside that he could not count the stars? Or could God, if He wished, not have said to him inside what He said outside?

Again, when He says, “So shall your seed be,” why did He not say, “I will make your seed like the stars of heaven; if anyone can count the stars of heaven, your seed also shall be counted,” just as elsewhere He says, “I will make your seed like the sand of the sea; if anyone can count the sand of the sea, your seed also shall be counted”?

MOYSES. In this matter I know nothing except that it pleased God to speak in this way.

PETRUS. I want you to understand the whole statement, and to know that Scripture did not place any word there rashly. The fact that it is written, “He brought him outside,” was done by the Lord for two reasons. First, to show him the place of heaven, which is indicated by the words “Look at the sky” (Gen. V). Second, to show the multitude of the stars; this is what is meant by “Count the stars, if you can count them.”

As for what follows, “So shall your seed be,” in Hebrew there is a word which in Latin is rendered both “here” and “thus,” because it signifies both place and likeness. If He had wished to use one signifying only place, He would undoubtedly have said *henna*; but if one rendered only as “thus,” He would have used *cacha*. By placing *co* there, He therefore wished both the place in which Abraham’s seed—Christ, namely, after his ascension—was to be, and the multitude of that seed, to be indicated.

MOYSES. I know that *co* in Hebrew is rendered *sic*—“thus”—in Latin, but I do not think that it ever signifies a place.

PETRUS. It certainly does. In Exodus we read concerning Moses that he saw an Egyptian striking one of his Hebrew brothers. “And when he had looked around, here and there, and had seen that no one was present, he concealed the slain Egyptian in the sand” (Exod. II). Wherever “here and there” occurs, you will find *co* and *co* in Hebrew.

But as confirmation of this interpretation, what follows in the same passage is: “Abraham believed God, and it was reckoned to him as righteousness” (Gen. XV). Why did Abraham believe God in this promise more than in the other promises made to him by God?

MOYSES. He believed in all of them, since he was never unbelieving.

PETRUS. And why does Scripture not say in each promise that he believed God, as it does here? Or, since he had always been believing, why did it remain silent about this in the other cases but not here?

MOYSES. I do not know, but that is what it says.

PETRUS. Have we not said above that Scripture did not place any word there rashly?

MOYSES. Then tell me why it said this.

PETRUS. Surely because that promise was contrary to ordinary experience and incredible—the promise that his seed would ascend into heaven. Therefore the words “Abraham believed God” are added to show his holiness. Since it would not have been surprising if he had doubted, but he nevertheless did not doubt and believed, it therefore follows: “and it was reckoned to him as righteousness.”

David also speaks in a psalm about Christ’s ascension, when he reports what the Lord promises concerning his seed:

“His seed shall endure forever, and his throne as the sun in my sight, and as the full moon forever, and as the faithful witness in heaven always” (Ps. LXXXVIII).

Was this promise made on account of anyone from David’s seed besides Christ, or concerning Christ alone?

MOYSES. Since I gain no advantage from contradicting you, I do not deny that it was truly made concerning Christ. For the proof is that the promise made by the Lord to David concerning his seed is always accompanied by a condition when it concerns someone other than Christ, as we find in the Third Book of Kings. When David’s days of death were already approaching, he admonished his son Solomon and said to him, “Be strong and be a man,” and immediately added the reason why he admonished him, saying:

“If your sons keep my way and walk before me in truth with all their heart and with all their soul, a man shall not be taken away from you from the throne of Israel” (III Kings II).

But the promise made to him concerning Christ, even if his sons should sin and therefore be punished, is nevertheless promised to be fulfilled, as it is read in the same psalm:

“But if his sons forsake my law and do not walk in my judgments; if they profane my ordinances and do not keep my commandments, I will visit their iniquities with a rod and their sins with blows. But I will not remove my mercy from him, nor will I make void what proceeds from my lips” (Ps. LXXXVIII).

PETRUS. You have spoken well and shown that you understand the Scriptures well, and you have offered no contradiction. But how will Christ remain forever unless he is God? How will his throne be like the sun or moon in the Lord’s sight, and he himself always a faithful witness in heaven, unless he is in heaven? The Psalmist therefore indicated that Christ would ascend into heaven. But, as we believe, no one could do this unless he were both God and man.

MOYSES. The order of the argument seems to me indeed to require this.

PETRUS. David also says elsewhere in a psalm concerning the same one:

“Rise, my glory; rise, psaltery and harp; I shall rise at dawn. Be exalted above the heavens, O God, and let your glory be over all the earth” (Ps. LVI).

Here David intimates Christ’s resurrection, his ascension, and certain other matters. The words “Rise, my glory” signify Christ’s resurrection, as though he were saying: “Christ, who is my glory, will rise from death.”

The words “Rise, psaltery and harp” he introduced on account of the joy and gladness that were to proceed from Christ’s resurrection. These are suitably signified by the psaltery and the harp, since such instruments are played in times of prosperity and joy. It is as though he were saying: “When Christ rises, every joy and gladness will rise with him.”

By the third phrase, “I shall rise at dawn”—where “at dawn” must be supplied—it is indicated that David himself was to be rescued from the darkness of hell when Christ rose. Here we understand “dawn” as light, just as in many passages we customarily understand by the word “evening” darkness and night. It is as though he were saying plainly: “When Christ rises, I too shall rise with him from the darkness, in glory and great light.”

The fourth statement, “Be exalted above the heavens, O God, and let your glory be over all the earth,” he added concerning Christ’s exaltation and ascension into heaven, from which ascension glory was to come to him throughout the whole world. It is as though he were saying: “You will be exalted above the heavens and will ascend, and from there glory will accumulate for you throughout the whole earth.”

But in saying “O God,” we necessarily understand him to be speaking of Christ, who was both man and God. For pure God, since He does not move from place to place, undoubtedly neither descends nor ascends nor is exalted.

MOYSES. I confess that what you have said about the ascension is sufficient. But in your exposition of your faith you also touched upon one further matter: namely, that he is to come on the day of judgment to judge the living and the dead. I do not ask for either proof or reasoning concerning this. For if, as you believe, he is both God and man, I readily grant that he is also the judge of the world. But do you have any authority from Scripture concerning this?

**PETER.** Certainly I have. For thus we read in the Book of Daniel: “I watched until thrones were set in place, and the Ancient of Days sat down” (Dan. VII). And afterward in the same passage: “The court sat, and the books were opened.” Then also in the same vision: “I watched,” he says, “in the vision of the night, and behold, one like a Son of Man was coming with the clouds of heaven; he came even to the Ancient of Days, and they presented him before him. And he gave him power, honor, and a kingdom, and all peoples, [Col. 0655D] tribes, and languages shall serve him. His power is an everlasting power that shall not be taken away, and his kingdom shall not be destroyed” (ibid.).

The Ancient of Days who sat is God the Father. By the statement, “The court sat, and the books were opened,” the judgment is signified that is to take place at the end of the world, in which the merits of each person will be examined as though they were written in books (Matt. XXV). He who was coming with the clouds of heaven is Christ, who is rightly called not simply “the Son of Man,” but “one like the Son of Man,” because he was born not of a carnal father and mother, but of a virgin and God the Father.

By the fact that, when the judgment had been prepared and the books opened, the Ancient of Days gave him power, honor, and a kingdom, and promised him the service of all peoples, tribes, and [Col. 0656A] languages, it is plainly shown that the judgment of all humanity was granted to him at the consummation of the world. By the statement that “his power is an everlasting power that shall not be taken away, and his kingdom shall not be destroyed”—which pertains only to divine kingship—and by what precedes, namely that “one like a Son of Man was coming,” it is undoubtedly indicated that the one to whom such judgment and kingdom were given is Christ, who, as we have said, was to be both God and man.

May the Lord grant you, my friend, that in that judgment you may be one of those who are to be placed on the right hand (ibid.). Amen.

## TITLE XII. That the law of the Christians is not contrary to the law of Moses

[Col. 0656B] **MOSES.** Up to this point we have argued sufficiently about each part of your cruelty. But at the beginning of the discussion you said one thing more: namely, that at the time of your baptism you believed the apostles. I ask that you answer me what you mean by this belief—whether you believe merely that they were good and holy men, or that what they preached was true, and that you also believe what they themselves believed.

**PETER.** I certainly believe both: that they were holy, that they preached the truth in every respect, and that I practice, insofar as I can, what they preached.

**MOSES.** You have now fallen into a snare from which you will not be able to escape. For when at the beginning I asked about the law of Moses, whether you observed it as it had been given by Moses—the law which seemed to me to have been transgressed by you—you replied that you fulfilled it, truly observed it, and walked with upright steps along its perfectly straight paths. The one whom you call Christ also preserved it in every respect, as he himself testifies when he says: “I have not come to abolish the law but to fulfill it” (Matt. V). But the apostles, whom you assert that you believed, dissolved it and commanded other things contrary to its precepts (Gal. IV). Therefore, when you say that you believe what they taught, you appear to believe one thing and its opposite.

[Col. 0656C] **PETER.** The apostles were truly disciples of Christ, and whatever they preached they certainly did through Christ; they did not abolish the law of Moses but fulfilled it.

**MOSES.** And how can we know that they preached it through Christ, when it is well known that they preached nothing until after his death?

[Col. 0656D] **PETER.** How could we doubt this, when we know that they preached nothing other than Christ and his commandments? The proof that they preached both him and his commandments is that, in order to spread faith in him, they went barefoot to various distant lands and, for confessing him, almost all of them endured thirst, hunger, nakedness, cold and heat alike, hardship and labor, scourging, and death. For how could they have endured these things for him while being opposed to or disobedient to his commandments?

[Col. 0657A] **MOSES.** If, as you say, the apostles did not disagree with Christ, nor Christ in any respect with the law of Moses, why then were the apostles opposed to Moses?

**PETER.** And in what respect will they be found to have been opposed to him?

**MOSES.** In every respect.

**PETER.** You have said far too much. They preached fasting, almsgiving, and mercy; they commanded that God be loved above all things and one’s neighbor as oneself; they too forbade murder, fornication, theft, false testimony, envy, and the other vices that reason rejects and Moses prohibits (Eph. V; Rom. VI). How, then, can you say that they were opposed to Moses in every respect?

**MOSES.** If they agreed with Moses in the matters mentioned above, why did they disagree with him in certain others?

[Col. 0657B] **PETER.** In which?

**MOSES.** First, the apostles set aside circumcision, which God commanded both to Abraham and to Moses, and which Christ also, whom you call Christ, received; indeed, they prohibited it from being performed (Gal. V).

**PETER.** We must first consider why that circumcision was commanded and for what purpose; then we shall better recognize whether what the apostles did was just or unjust.

**MOSES.** Agreed.

**PETER.** Tell me, then: what benefit do you believe that circumcision could bring, or why was it commanded to be performed on the eighth day? (Gen. XVII; Lev. XII.)

**MOSES.** As for the eighth day, I know no reason except that it was God’s will. But it brought this benefit: it was an occasion of salvation.

**PETER.** From your words, then, it follows that anyone circumcised on any day will be saved, and thus the command that it be done on the eighth day is pointless and without benefit. But I would also like to ask something else. Does that circumcision require something additional for salvation, or is it able by itself to confer salvation?

[Col. 0657C] **MOSES.** It certainly requires something additional, because for perfect salvation the law of Moses must be fulfilled in addition to circumcision. If you wish, you can hear how this is to be done. If someone has been circumcised and has faithfully observed the whole law, he will undoubtedly be saved. But if he has been circumcised and has presumed not to observe the law in certain matters, he will indeed suffer punishments for his transgression, but from there he will nevertheless pass over to salvation. If, however, he has kept the whole law but has not been circumcised, he will in no way be able to be saved, whatever punishments he may suffer.

[Col. 0657D] **PETER.** Where did this belief of yours come from, when God never promised this either to Abraham or to Moses, and no prophet ever said it?

**MOSES.** We understand it from the words that the Lord spoke to Abraham: “The male who is not circumcised in the flesh of his foreskin, that soul shall perish from his people” (Gen. XVII). By this, it is implied that whoever has been circumcised will not perish but will be saved.

[Col. 0658A] **PETER.** According to your explanation of this authority, the person who does not fast on the tenth day of the seventh month, even if he has been circumcised, will nevertheless have no salvation. For it is written in Leviticus: “Every soul that is not afflicted on that day shall perish from among its people” (Lev. XXIII). If he will perish for this reason, circumcision will certainly be of no value.

**MOSES.** Reason certainly seems to say so.

**PETER.** What, then, do you say about Adam, Seth, Enoch, Methuselah, Noah and his son Shem, and many others whom we believe were never circumcised and nevertheless were saved?

**MOSES.** They lived before circumcision was commanded, and therefore they could be saved without it.

**PETER.** And what will you say about Job and his companions, who lived after the commandment of circumcision, and although uncircumcised were nevertheless saved?

[Col. 0658B] **MOSES.** They were not of that people to whom the commandment of circumcision had been given.

**PETER.** What, then, made all those people mentioned above saved?

**MOSES.** I truly do not know, but I suppose it was their good faith and the sacrifices they used.

**PETER.** What, then, do you say about Ishmael, to whom circumcision was commanded but not the law, and whose descendants are circumcised to this day? Are they saved by that circumcision? But if you say they are, then circumcision alone confers salvation without the completion of the law of Moses. If you say they are not, you will contradict yourself, since above you said that circumcision is a cause of salvation.

[Col. 0658C] **MOSES.** What you say is reasonable.

**PETER.** What, again, will you judge concerning Jewish women, who cannot be circumcised and yet are believed to be saved?

**MOSES.** They are saved because they are born from circumcised men.

**PETER.** What, then, about Sarah and Rebecca, Rachel and Leah, and Moses’ wife Zipporah, who was a Midianite, and Ruth—all of whom, as we believe, are saved, and yet were not born of Jews? For if they were not going to be saved, their husbands, who were both holy men and prophets, would certainly not have taken them as wives or fathered children by them.

**MOSES.** I do not know how to give you an answer about this, for it has never been shown to me. But you, if you know, explain to me the benefit of circumcision.

[Col. 0658D] **PETER.** Circumcision was certainly given for this purpose: so that the people of the Lord might be distinguished from and recognized among the other nations. For the greater distinction of that people another commandment was also given, namely that no one should take a wife from another tribe (Num. XXXVI). This entire command was given because Christ was to come from the seed of Abraham, under the law of Moses, and from the tribe of Judah, so that when he came he could be recognized as the one he was, and so that no one might arise from another nation and claim to be Christ, thereby leaving the world in error.

We have two clear arguments that circumcision was commanded for the distinction of the people, not, as you said, for salvation. The first is that it was commanded to be performed on the eighth day and not before, because [Col. 0659A] before the eighth day the child is not separated from its mother, and there is no fear that it will be mixed with others. On the eighth day, when the woman is commanded to be cleansed and washed from that pollution, the child is circumcised before she does this, lest, after the mother has been removed, the child be exchanged or another child be mixed in (Lev. XII).

The second is that during the forty years in which the children of Israel lived in the desert, all those born there were not circumcised. But when they came to habitable land, so that they would not mingle with other nations, they were immediately commanded by the Lord through Joshua to be circumcised, as those who read the Book of Joshua itself find (Josh. V).

[Col. 0659B] As for your statement that circumcision is a cause of salvation, circumcision alone was certainly not the cause of it; rather, good faith, sacrifices, and righteous works were also involved, both after circumcision had been given and before it, as is clear in the case of Adam, Seth, Enoch, Methuselah, Noah and Shem, Job and his companions, and the Jewish women. All of these were saved without circumcision, through right faith and good works.

Moreover, none of the kinds of salvation mentioned above conferred salvation except upon those who, possessing understanding, believed in the coming of Christ and did not believe that they could be saved except through him. When Christ the Savior whom they were awaiting came, he wished to be circumcised in order to fulfill the law of Moses and also to make clear by this that he was to come from the seed of Abraham, under the law of Moses, and from the tribe of Judah, as we have said.

[Col. 0659C] When, therefore, everything for which circumcision had been given had been fulfilled, no one any longer needed circumcision, since there was no longer any need for a distinction of lineage (Col. III). For anyone who turns to the law of Christ, whatever his lineage or language, if he wishes only to be faithful, is equal to the other Christians.

Furthermore, after baptism came—which is the universal salvation of men and women—circumcision was no longer necessary for salvation. Since it has been demonstrated in every way that circumcision was not necessary after Christ’s coming, you can now clearly understand why the apostles did not command it to be performed.

**MOSES.** And if they did not command it, why did they also prohibit it from being performed?

[Col. 0659D] **PETER.** They did so in order that people would not suppose that circumcision, like baptism, conferred salvation, or that circumcision conferred salvation together with baptism, and thereby fall into the error of the Nestorians and Jacobites, who think that no one can be saved except through both. You yourselves do the same today: if someone from an outside nation wishes to convert to your law, you command that, if he is a man, he first be circumcised and afterward baptized; but if she is a woman, she is only to be baptized.

**MOSES.** Your words imply that we practiced baptism only after Christ’s coming, as though we had learned it from Christ himself.

**PETER.** If not from him, from whom, then, did you learn it?

[Col. 0660A] **MOSES.** From Moses.

**PETER.** That is false. We have two arguments for this. The first is that when the Lord gave Moses a command concerning foreigners, saying: “If any stranger wishes to enter your settlement and celebrate the Passover of the Lord, every male of his shall first be circumcised, and then he shall celebrate it properly, and he shall be like a native of the land” (Exod. XII), then, if baptism had been necessary at that time, he would have commanded it just as he commanded circumcision. Since he did not command it here—where, if what you say were true, he especially ought to have done so—and since Moses never mentions it anywhere else, you cannot in any way prove that you learned it from him.

[Col. 0660B] The other argument is that your teachers who lived before Christ never said anything about that baptism, thereby showing that you did not receive it from Moses. Those, however, who lived after Christ’s coming learned baptism from him, and, mixing it with circumcision, left the people in error.

**MOSES.** You have answered satisfactorily about circumcision. But what will you now say about the Sabbath day, which the Lord commanded through Moses to be observed in many places, and which he himself, speaking to the children of Israel from Mount Sinai, commanded to be observed? The commandment concerning its observance was written on stone tablets as follows: “Remember,” God said, “to sanctify the Sabbath day” (Exod. XX; Deut. V). He adds the reason in what follows, saying: “For in six days God made heaven and earth and the sea, and everything that is in them, and he rested on the seventh day. Therefore the Lord blessed the Sabbath day and sanctified it” (ibid.). Moreover, he commanded that the person who did not observe it be stoned (Num. XV). But the apostles rejected it and commanded that another day be observed.

[Col. 0660C] **PETER.** It is true that the Lord commanded that day to be observed, as you said, in memory of the beginning of the world, and he also made it a sign of another event that was to come.

**MOSES.** And what was that future event?

**PETER.** The coming of Christ, who completed all his works that he performed while living in the world on the sixth day—that is, Friday—when he accepted death for us. On the seventh day, that is, the Sabbath, he rested; [Col. 0660D] indeed, he also caused all who had died believing in him before his death to rest with him from the pains of hell. Once that event, of which the observance of the Sabbath was a sign, had been completed, it was no longer necessary to observe it.

**MOSES.** According to your words, if the observance of the Sabbath was a sign of the event you mention, then once that event had been completed it ought to have been observed all the more—both in memory of the beginning of the world and because of the saints’ rest from the pains of hell.

[Col. 0661A] **PETER.** The matter is not as you think. Your ancestors who lived before Christ’s coming observed the Sabbath both in memory, as has been said, of the beginning of the world and because they believed that on that same day they would rest through Christ from the pains of hell.

After Christ’s resurrection, however—which was the cause of Christian belief, and belief the cause of salvation—although all salvation proceeded from Christ’s death, it brought no benefit without belief; after Christ’s resurrection, I say, it was no longer necessary for all who believed in him to observe the Sabbath, but rather the Lord’s Day, namely the day of the resurrection, which became the cause of their salvation.

**MOSES.** And why did they not observe both: the Sabbath in memory of the world’s origin, and the other day in memory of their salvation?

[Col. 0661B] **PETER.** The Sabbath, which we said was observed in memory of the world’s origin, was certainly observed because of the creation of all things, which was completed then, as it is written: “And God completed on the seventh day his work that he had made, and rested from all the work that he had done” (Gen. I).

But because that same day was the beginning of the condemnation of souls—and this occurred through Adam, who sinned on the preceding day at evening, namely at the twelfth hour, and thus fell from glory into condemnation—after salvation for souls came through Christ’s resurrection, the day of condemnation ought no longer to be celebrated. Rather, the day that was the beginning of salvation should be celebrated.

I can also show you this by an example, if you wish. A certain king built a certain city, in which he founded costly buildings, planted shrubs and vineyards all around, and [Col. 0661C] led streams of water here and there through its middle. He also made it rich and overflowing with every delight. A king of another nation began to wage war against it. Consequently, whenever anyone came out of it, that enemy was ready and, lying in wait, seized him and thrust him into a dark prison.

The king who had founded the city promised its inhabitants that the time would come when he would resolve to free them from that enemy. He required from them no other tribute or repayment except that they celebrate with great honor the day on which the city had been completed—and also because on that same day he was going to free them from the enemy mentioned above. They celebrated it for a long time, as the king had commanded.

[Col. 0661D] After some time had passed, however, he took pity on them and, moved by compassion, decided to free them from that captivity in person. Therefore he sent his son. After he had defeated the enemy, the son released the captives from his hands. Once they had been freed from the enemy’s yoke, the king arranged the city in such a way that they no longer needed to fear being captured by that enemy.

Tell me, Moses: which day ought rather to have been celebrated—the day on which the city was completed, although its people fell into the hands of the enemy, or the day on which it was arranged so that they would no longer fear being captured by that enemy?

**MOSES.** Without doubt, the day on which it was so arranged.

[Col. 0662A] **PETER.** For the same reason we ought to celebrate the Lord’s Day, because of Christ’s resurrection, which, as we have said, was both the cause of belief and the principal cause of salvation. Those who died believing in Christ before his death were indeed saved when he died, but they first entered the darkness of hell. Those who believed after his resurrection are saved through his death and nevertheless did not experience Tartarus.

This, then, is why the apostles commanded that day to be observed with the greatest care, and not the Sabbath, although our Lord Christ observed it. He did so only in order to fulfill the law of Moses, and because the day of the resurrection, which he was to observe, had not yet come.

**MOSES.** And what will you say about the festival of Passover, which the Lord commanded to be observed, and at which a lamb was to be sacrificed and eaten with unleavened bread and bitter herbs (Exod. XII)? The apostles abandoned all this, commanded another festival, and established another order, while Christ—whom you call Christ—never wished during his lifetime to celebrate it in the manner the apostles commanded.

[Col. 0662B] **PETER.** First, Moses, we must carefully examine the rites and the reasons for the rites by which Passover was commanded to be celebrated in Egypt, and why afterward it was commanded a second time in the wilderness (Lev. XXIII; Num. XVIII). Once we have done this, we shall certainly see whether we ought to celebrate the Passover festival after Christ’s death or not.

**MOSES.** Agreed.

**PETER.** These, then, are its rites and religious observances. [Col. 0662C] On the tenth day of the month, a lamb or kid was commanded to be taken and kept until the fourteenth day. It was also commanded that it be male, young, and entirely free from disease. On the fourteenth day, between the two evenings, it was to be sacrificed by the entire assembly of the children of Israel; its blood was to be put on both doorposts and on the lintels of the houses, and this only in those houses in which it was to be eaten.

Its flesh was not to be eaten raw or boiled in water, but roasted only by fire. The whole animal, complete with its head, feet, and entrails, was commanded to be cooked by fire and eaten at night and in haste. Its bone was not to be broken. Thus it was to be eaten with unleavened bread and bitter herbs (Exod. XII).

[Col. 0662D] **MOSES.** It is exactly as you have said.

**PETER.** Tell me, then, for what reasons were these rites commanded?

**MOSES.** I do not know, but the Lord willed that it be done in this way. As for the blood, I know that it was commanded to be put on both doorposts of the houses and on the lintels so that, when the destroying angel came, he would pass over the house marked with that blood.

**PETER.** Have I not often told you above that no word ever came rashly from the Lord’s mouth?

**MOSES.** Then you tell me. Why were those rites commanded to be observed?

**PETER.** That Egyptian lamb and its rites were a figure and likeness of the Lamb of God who was to be sacrificed—that is, of Christ. For just as through that lamb the Lord’s faithful were saved from the hand of the angel who was killing bodies, so through Christ those who believed in him were to be redeemed from the devil, who condemned souls. That lamb was, as it were, announcing the one who was to come after it.

**MOSES.** You have answered satisfactorily about the lamb. But how will you apply the lamb’s rites mentioned above to Christ, whom you call the Lamb of God?

[Col. 0663A] **PETER.** Just as that lamb was commanded to be taken on the tenth day of the month and kept until the fourteenth day (Exod. XII), so, on the tenth day of the month—that is, on Monday—your teachers took counsel about arresting Christ (John XI).

On the preceding Lord’s Day Christ came to Jerusalem in order to celebrate the Passover there. The entire people received him with joy, great ceremony, and honor. Consequently, the envy and ill will of the teachers grew stronger, and on the following day they began taking counsel with one another about arresting and killing him (Matt. XXI; John XII; Mark XI; Luke XIX). That plan, however, remained hidden and concealed until the fourteenth day.

Just as that lamb was commanded to be male, young, and entirely free from disease, so Christ was male, young, and free from every disease—that is, from sin (1 Pet. II). [Col. 0663C] The reason why the victim was commanded to be taken from a sheep or goat, and not from a cow, although a cow is among the animals from which sacrifice was commanded under the law, was that a sheep or goat does not resist when it is captured, as a cow does. This was also a sign that Christ, when he was captured, did not resist or defend himself, although he could have done so.

The fact that it was commanded to be sacrificed by the whole assembly of the children of Israel, although the command concerned one individual lamb—for not everyone sacrificed one lamb, but each person sacrificed his own in his houses and families—signified that the entire multitude of the Jews killed Christ. Although not everyone was present, everyone nevertheless gave consent.

Since it was to be sacrificed on the fourteenth day and between the two evenings, we must determine what the two evenings of the day are. One is when the sun begins to descend from the midpoint of the heavens; the other is when it has completely set before night. Christ expired on the fourteenth day and between the two evenings of that same day, namely at the ninth hour, as you yourselves believe.

The two evenings can also be understood as your two captivities, namely that of Babylon and that of Titus. Christ died between the two evenings because he died after the Babylonian captivity and before the captivity under Titus.

[Col. 0663D] The fact that the blood of the lamb was commanded to be placed on both doorposts and on the lintels of the houses as a sign—that is, as a sign of the cross—signified the blood of Christ that was poured out on the cross. And just as the blood of that lamb, as we have said, protected the Lord’s faithful from bodily death, so the blood of Jesus Christ redeemed his faithful from the destruction of the soul (Rev. I).

[Col. 0664A] Moreover, just as that blood preserved no house except those in which the lamb was eaten, and therefore was commanded to be placed only on those houses, so the blood of Christ that was poured out on the cross saves no one except the person in whom the Lamb of God is eaten—namely, the one who eats the body of Christ.

Furthermore, just as the lamb was commanded to be eaten at night, so Christ was captured at night, so that he could not be liberated or defended by the people. Just as the lamb was neither raw nor boiled in water but roasted by fire, so Christ was condemned neither without judgment nor by a just judgment, but by an unjust one, just as meat roasted by fire is neither wholly raw nor properly cooked.

For the same reason it was commanded to be eaten in haste and with unleavened bread. Just as unleavened bread is not allowed to wait until the dough is fermented but is made hastily, so in Christ they did not wait for any justice in the judgment; rather, he was condemned hastily.

[Col. 0664B] The bitter herbs with which that lamb was commanded to be eaten signify that calamity and bitterness came from that unjust condemnation. The fact that it was commanded to be cooked whole, with its head, feet, and entrails, and that its bone was not to be broken after it had been eaten, indicates that no limb of Christ was cut off during his killing; rather, he was suspended with all his limbs. Nor did any of his bones decay after his death, nor did he undergo any other dissolution; instead, he rose again whole and entire.

You see, therefore, that, as has been stated, that Egyptian lamb and its rites were a figure and likeness of the Lamb of God—that is, of Christ. If we have left any rite unexplained, you will likewise be able to apply it to Christ if you investigate attentively.

[Col. 0664C] **MOSES.** Since, Peter, you have explained the Egyptian Passover in a way that is satisfactory, I want you to say, if you please, why Passover was commanded to be celebrated a second time in the wilderness (Lev. XXIII; Num. XXVIII).

**PETER.** It was done for no other reason or purpose than in memory of the Egyptian Passover and to announce the Passover in which Christ, the Lamb of God, was to be sacrificed. Christ also celebrated that Passover throughout his lifetime, both in order to fulfill the law of Moses (Matt. V) and because those rites had not yet been fulfilled.

[Col. 0664D] But after everything had been fulfilled through his death, it was no longer necessary to celebrate that Passover. Instead, there is the Passover that our apostles instituted for us. For it is right that we exchange the day of the salvation of souls, which is more worthy of honor, for the day of the salvation of bodies. When greater joy arrives, lesser joy withdraws; when the sun rises, the brightness of the stars disappears.

We must also abandon the memory of what came before for the memory of what follows, just as the Lord promised through the prophet Jeremiah: “Behold, the days are coming,” says the Lord, “when it shall no longer be said, ‘As the Lord lives, who brought up the children of Israel from the land of Egypt,’ but rather, ‘As the Lord lives, who brought up and led the children of Israel from the land of the north’” (Jer. XVI).

[Col. 0665A] **MOSES.** This promise will certainly be fulfilled when Christ comes.

**PETER.** It is true that it was to be fulfilled when Christ came. But since it has been proved that Christ has already come, the prophecy was fulfilled when he came. It is to be understood in this way: we must no longer remember that the Lord brought the children of Israel out of Egypt, but rather out of the land of the north—that is, out of hell—since the devil is understood by the north, and hell is his land and dwelling, as the prophet Joel says: “And him who is from the north I will drive far from you, and I will expel him into a dry and desolate land; his face toward the eastern sea and his rear toward the western sea; and his stench shall rise, and his decay shall rise, because he acted proudly” (Joel II).

I do not concern myself with explaining how we can understand the devil by the north, for your teachers have sufficiently explained this.

Moreover, how can you say that you celebrate Passover when you neither offer a sacrifice nor have an altar or a priest to offer it? [Col. 0665B] Do you think that you can fulfill Passover merely because you eat herbs and unleavened bread? You even sometimes change the day of Passover and postpone it until the following day, because you never celebrate it on Monday, Wednesday, or Friday. I want you to explain to me why you do this.

**MOSES.** I know no reason other than that our teachers ordained it in this way, especially Gamaliel.

**PETER.** And do you know why Gamaliel did this?

**MOSES.** No.

**PETER.** Gamaliel was a holy and faithful Christian man (Acts V). Since he knew that on Monday the Jews had taken counsel about how Christ might be condemned, that on Wednesday evidence was given for Christ’s betrayal, and that on Friday he was fastened to the cross—since, I say, he knew this and did not wish any joy to be expressed on those days, he therefore prohibited Passover from being celebrated on them (Exod. XII) and commanded that it be postponed until the following day. He did not wish to reveal this secret to everyone.

[Col. 0665C] **MOSES.** Since you have condemned the Passover festival, which precedes and surpasses all the others, and concerning which it is commanded that whoever does not celebrate it shall perish, it would now be pointless for us to argue about the lesser festivals, since you could condemn them much more easily.

As for the fast of the tenth day of the seventh month (Lev. XXIII), I ask you to answer me. The Lord commanded it to be observed for the expiation of our sins to such an extent that he said that the person who did not observe it would perish from his generation. Your apostles, however, set it aside.

[Col. 0665D] **PETER.** First I want you to tell me about that fast: is it by itself sufficient for anyone to destroy sins, or does a person also need repentance along with it?

**MOSES.** Certainly, without repentance there can be no expiation.

**PETER.** I also ask you: in what do you say the power of that expiation consists—in the day of fasting or in repentance?

**MOSES.** In both.

**PETER.** Answer this as well: if one person, having omitted the fast, repented and then died, while another died after fasting but without repenting, which of them ought rather to be saved?

[Col. 0666A] **MOSES.** Without doubt, the one who repented.

**PETER.** Then we can affirm that the power of that expiation consists in repentance, not in fasting, as Isaiah testifies when he says: “Is this the kind of fast that I have chosen? Loose the bonds of wickedness; undo the bundles that oppress” (Isa. LVIII).

**MOSES.** What purpose, then, does fasting serve?

**PETER.** It is certainly the beginning of every good thing. It is commanded both to weaken the human body and to restrain it from vices.

**MOSES.** According to your words, anyone who fasts and repents on any day will receive remission of sins.

**PETER.** That is true.

**MOSES.** Why, then, did God specifically command that day of fasting to be observed? (Lev. XXIII.)

[Col. 0666B] **PETER.** So that on the appointed day everyone would assemble and, fasting, practice repentance.

**MOSES.** And why did your apostles set all this aside?

**PETER.** Because Christ came and fulfilled the whole law, and fasted for forty days (Matt. IV; Luke IV; Mark I). Therefore the apostles—that is, his disciples—commanded forty days in place of one, because a fast of forty days is more effective than one day, and repentance for forty days is more beneficial than repentance for one day.

**MOSES.** You have answered satisfactorily about the fast. But what will you say about the sacrifices that the Lord commanded to be made from an ox, a goat, and a sheep, which your apostles omitted, commanding that sacrifice be made only from bread and wine?

[Col. 0666C] **PETER.** All the sacrifices that were commanded and ordained to be made under the law of Moses were nothing other than figures and representations of the principal sacrifice that was to come. They were also given so that the nations might become accustomed to sacrifices, and so that through them it might be understood that, just as these customary sacrifices cleanse sins, so the greatest sacrifice could erase the greatest sin.

But when Christ, the Holy One of Holies (Dan. IX), came as the principal sacrifice and was offered for our redemption, it was no longer necessary to make those ancient sacrifices. After Christ himself came, we use that sacrifice—namely, bread and wine—which the apostles ordained for us; indeed, Christ himself gave it (Matt. XXVI; Mark XIV; Luke XXII; 1 Cor. XI).

[Col. 0666D] This sacrifice resembles the sacrifice that Moses, when commanding it under the law, called the sacrifice of *toda*, that is, of praise (Exod. XXV; Lev. II, VII, XXIV; Num. XXVIII), and which he commanded to be made from bread and wine alone as a figure of ours.

[Col. 0667A] David, foreseeing that it was to come and rejecting all other things in comparison with it, says in the psalm: “Shall I eat the flesh of bulls, or drink the blood of goats? Offer to God a sacrifice of praise” (Ps. XLIX). By this he indicated that all the other sacrifices were to be set aside and that the sacrifice called the sacrifice of praise was to be offered.

This sacrifice of ours is indeed a sacrifice of praise. In performing it, we praise God for the benefit that he granted us by saving us through his Son Jesus.

## MOSES

And what will you say about those meats which Moses also prohibited from being eaten in the Law (Lev. XI), and which your Christ likewise did not eat, whereas the apostles not only did not prohibit their consumption, but themselves also ate them?

## PETER

Since everything that God made is good, as Scripture testifies, saying, “God saw everything that he had made, and behold, it was very good” (Gen. I); and since God said to Noah and his sons, “Everything that moves and lives shall be food for you; just as I gave you all green plants, so I give you all things” (Gen. IX); and since Abraham, Isaac, and the other patriarchs ate everything they wished until Moses, and Moses himself did so before he had received the Law [Col. 0667B]—why, then, were meats forbidden to be eaten in the Law?

## MOSES

Because at the beginning of the world human beings were still, as it were, savage and bestial, and could in no way be instructed so quickly to obey God’s commandments. God’s wisdom, perceiving this, did not wish to give them all the commandments at once, but gradually gave one to Adam—namely, that he should not presume to eat the fruit which he had forbidden (Gen. II); another to Noah—namely, not to eat flesh with its blood and not to commit murder (Gen. IX); and he commanded Abraham to offer sacrifices and to practice circumcision (Gen. XVII). But when Moses came, and God wished to unite the children of Israel with him and distinguish them from the other nations, he commanded them his precepts as seemed fitting, and forbade them to defile themselves with unclean meats [Col. 0667C], indeed giving them a sign of distinction between clean and unclean animals (Lev. XI).

## PETER

And this uncleanness that you have mentioned concerning meats—is it itself a body, or something that happens to the body?

## MOSES

Neither; rather, it is a certain spiritual thing that descends upon the body. Yet it attributes to the body neither increase nor diminution, but prohibits something which had never previously been prohibited to it. It joins itself to the body in four ways.

First, when it adheres to the body from the moment of its creation and never departs from it—just as it comes hereditarily from father and mother, as we see in the pig and in the other prohibited meats.

Second, when it is joined to something with which it had not previously been joined, but afterward is not separated from it, as is seen in the dead and in lepers [Col. 0667D].

Third, when, for some reason arising, it is applied to the body and afterward is separated for another practical reason, as those who touch a dead body are unclean until they are made clean by the sprinkling of ashes (Num. XIX).

Fourth, when for some reason it joins itself to the body but withdraws without any ritual action, as those who have handled some carcass remain defiled for the whole day but, when the sun has set, are clean without any purification (Lev. XI).

Since, therefore, those meats were unclean, they were also prohibited by Moses, namely, so that they would not make unclean those who ate them. They were also prohibited, as your teachers assert, so that they might not bring hardness into people’s hearts or dullness, preventing them from understanding.

[Col. 0668A] ## PETER

These two defects—uncleanness and hardness—formerly affected bodies and meats when they were still entangled in general sin and did not possess the fullness of the Holy Spirit. But when Christ came, cleansed the bodies of believers through baptism, and poured into them the fullness of the Holy Spirit, no kind of meat could thereafter defile or dull the human body. Your teachers also testify to this: they said that after Christ’s coming what was inedible was to be changed into something edible.

This same reasoning can be given concerning all uncleannesses. Moses also openly declares that meats would be released from prohibition after Christ’s coming, speaking to the people of Israel in these words:
