“When the Lord your God enlarges your boundaries, as he has spoken to you, and you wish to eat meat [Col. 0668B] because your soul desires it, but the place which the Lord your God chooses so that his name may be there is far away, you shall slaughter from your herds and flocks which you possess, as he has commanded you, and you shall eat in your towns as you please. Just as the gazelle and the stag are eaten, so you shall eat them; the clean and the unclean alike shall eat together” (Deut. XII).

Before Christ’s coming, the boundaries of Israel were narrow, because they did not even possess the whole land which the Lord promised them through Moses. But after Christ’s coming the Lord enlarged Israel’s boundaries, when the apostles preached the Law throughout the whole world. The place also which the Lord had chosen for his name to dwell there is now far away, because that ancient temple of the Lord has been destroyed.

Thus anyone may now eat any meat, whether clean or unclean, as he pleases, without transgression. What I have said so far, Moses, I have certainly said in order to satisfy your wish. If I wished to defend myself in another way, I would surely say that we possess a new Law, and that it is in no way contrary to the Law of Moses. For concerning the commandments of the Lord, one commandment is not contrary to another; rather, when the time appointed for one commandment has been completed, he gives another commandment as he sees fit.

We see this in the commandment concerning the eating of meat which the Lord gave to Noah (Gen. IX): after Moses came and the time of that commandment had been completed, he gave Moses another commandment concerning meats—namely, that they were to be prohibited (Lev. XI). When the time of this commandment, in turn, was completed with Christ’s coming, behold, that ancient commandment which had been given to Noah—namely, concerning the release of meats from prohibition—returned once more [Col. 0668D].

The Lord indeed promised through Moses himself that a prophet like Moses was to be raised up—namely, Christ—who would give a new Law, just as Moses did, as we said above (Deut. XVIII).

Isaiah likewise foretold the new Law which he foresaw was to come, in this manner:

“It shall be,” he says, “in the last days: the mountain of the house of the Lord shall be prepared on the top of the mountains, and it shall be raised above the hills; and all the nations shall flow toward it. Many peoples shall go and say: ‘Come, let us go up to the mountain of the Lord and to the house of the God of Jacob, and he shall teach us his ways, and we shall walk in his paths; for the Law shall go forth from Zion, and the word of the Lord from [Col. 0669A] Jerusalem’” (Isa. XI).

What, Moses, is this mountain of the Lord? If you wish to say that it is Mount Zion, on which the house of the Lord—that is, the temple—stood, reason certainly contradicts you. For it is not situated on the top of the mountains, since there are other hills around it higher than it; nor can it be said ever to be raised above the hills.

What, moreover, does he mean when he says, “Many peoples shall go and say: ‘Come, let us go up,’” and so forth, “and he shall teach us his ways, and we shall walk in his paths, for the Law shall go forth from Zion,” and so forth? What are those ways and paths of the Lord, or the Law that was to go forth from Zion, and the word that was to come from Jerusalem?

For he would not be speaking of the Law of Moses, which is known to everyone, when he says, “He shall teach us his ways.” Nor did that old Law go forth from Zion, but from Mount Horeb; nor did the word of the Lord which Moses proclaimed come from Jerusalem, but from Sinai [Col. 0669B] (Exod. XX; Deut. V).

The prophecy is therefore to be understood as follows. Without doubt, the holy Church is the house of the Lord. Kings are customarily compared with mountains, and prophets with hills. The mountain—that is, the King of the holy Church, namely Christ—is the one upon whom the Church itself has been built; he was prepared on the top of the mountains and raised above the hills, because he was exalted and honored above all kings and all prophets.

And rightly does the prophet say of the holy Church and Christ, “All the nations shall flow toward him”—that is, toward Christ—because many from all nations believed in him, saying: “Come, let us go up to the mountain of the Lord”—that is, to Christ, whom the Lord appointed king of all—and to the house [Col. 0669C] of the God of Jacob—that is, to the holy Church. “He shall teach us his ways”—that is, the teaching of his Law—“and we shall walk in his paths”—that is, in the observances of his Law, which is new, just as we call new routes “ways” and “paths.”

What follows—“For the Law shall go forth from Zion, and the word of the Lord from Jerusalem”—indicates that Christ’s Law was to go forth from Zion, and his word from Jerusalem. For in Zion the Holy Spirit came upon the apostles; his coming became the foundation of the Law, and the Law was given through him and preached by him. In Jerusalem, before anywhere else, both the apostles and Christ himself preached, and from there the preaching went forth throughout the whole world.

It is therefore clear that Isaiah prophesied concerning this new Law.

Jeremiah likewise speaks in this way concerning the new Law:

“Behold, the days are coming,” says the Lord, “when I shall make a new covenant with the house of Israel and with the house of Judah, not according to the covenant which I made with their fathers on the day when I took them by the hand to lead them out of the land of Egypt” (Jer. XXXI).

Where the Latin has *foedus novum* (“new covenant”), in Hebrew you will find *berith, hadasa*, which is interpreted as “new Law,” as Moses attests, who in many places calls the precepts of his Law *berith*. Jeremiah himself indicates that by “new covenant” he meant the new Law when he says: “Not according to the covenant which I made with their fathers on the day when I took them by the hand to lead them out of the land of Egypt.” For here he plainly speaks of the covenant—that is, of the Law which the Lord gave to Moses in the wilderness after the departure from Egypt.

[Col. 0670A] ## MOSES

We have debated long enough about our Law and yours and about their successive alternation. You have answered all my objections as you wished, and I have been able to explain nothing against you. But I have reserved one matter for you, as though in a treasury; when I bring it forward, I trust that you can be overcome without any defense, because you will find nothing that can be answered against it.

## PETER

And what is this matter of such great force and power, about which you are so confident and with which you threaten me so greatly?

## MOSES

It is certainly something that you do against God and all the prophets: namely, that in the forest you cut down a certain tree, and afterward seek out a woodworker who will cut it, carve it, shape it into the form of a human being, polish it, and paint it [Col. 0670B]; then you set up that image in your churches, in a particularly elevated place, and worship it.

Therefore Isaiah also, to rebuke and reproach you, says these words:

“The woodworker stretches out the measuring line; he forms it with the plane; he makes an image of a man, like a handsome human being dwelling in a house.” And later in the same passage:

“They do not reflect in their mind, nor understand, nor perceive, so as to say: ‘I burned half of it in the fire, and I baked bread over its coals; I baked meat and ate it, and from what remains shall I make an idol? Shall I fall down before a block of wood?’ Part of it is ashes. A foolish heart worships it, and it will not deliver his soul, nor will he say: ‘Perhaps there is a lie in my right hand’” (Isa. XLIV).

## PETER

The matter is not as you suppose. We neither make idols nor worship them. Rather, we make a cross [Col. 0670C] and place upon it the image of a human being; by the cross we signify the altar, and by the image the sacrifice which is upon the altar.

Just as animals were sacrificed upon the altar, so the Lamb of God was sacrificed upon the cross. And just as no concern was given to what became of the remains of the stones with which they built the altar, so we do not concern ourselves with what becomes of the remains of the cross or of the image placed upon it.

Moreover, just as Solomon and others fell prostrate before the altar but worshiped not it, rather God alone, so we, bending our knees before the cross, worship not that cross or the image placed upon it, but God the Father and his Son Jesus Christ.

## MOSES

What you say would indeed be reasonable if you possessed that cross upon which the Lamb of God was sacrificed [Col. 0670D]. But now you worship another cross, upon which that Lamb was never sacrificed.

## PETER

Certainly, we cannot possess that cross everywhere. Therefore it is neither strange nor wrong if we make other crosses in its likeness, so that those who did not see Christ’s cross may at least see others made in its likeness, and may remember and understand the sacrifice that was performed upon it, just as children do also.

The sons of Reuben likewise built an altar beyond the Jordan in the likeness of the altar at Jericho, so that their sons and wives, who could not cross over, might see it, solely as a testimony to and a means of knowing the other altar, as you can find written in the Book of Joshua (Josh. XXII).

[Col. 0671A] ## MOSES

God has certainly given you much wisdom and has enlightened you with abundant reason, since you possess such great understanding of Scripture that I cannot overcome you, indeed, that I have nothing with which to contradict you.

## PETER

Without doubt, the gift of the Holy Spirit was bestowed through the grace of baptism, which so illuminates our hearts that we do not presume to believe anything false. [Col. 0672A] If you too believed what we believe and had yourself baptized, you would possess the same illumination of the Holy Spirit, so that you would recognize what is true and reject what is false.

But now, because I have compassion for you, I implore God’s mercy: may he enlighten you with the fullness of his Spirit and grant you a better end than your beginning. Amen.

[Col. 0671]

# THE CLERICAL DISCIPLINE, BY PETER ALPHONSO

## [NOTE.]

According to the first edition, given at Paris in 1824 under the supervision of D. Labouderie, vicar general of the Church of Avignon, printed by Rignoux in duodecimo. It consists of two volumes or parts. The first presents, in a single view, the original text and a French translation, apparently from the beginning of the fifteenth century, entitled *La Discipline de Clergie*. It begins: “Pierre Alphonse, serf de Jhesus-Crist, qui fist cestui livre,” etc. It ends: “Cy fine Pierre Alphonse.”

The second part, entitled *Le chastoiement*, presents an old French translation of the same book, written in verse. It begins:

“Qui veut honor en siecle aveir  
Premereiment deit saveir,” etc.

Later appeared *Petri Alphonsi Disciplina clericalis*, edited by Fr. W. Val. Schmitt, Berlin, 1827, published by Theod. Chr. Fr. Enslin. We, omitting both translations, reproduce the Latin text.

[Col. 0671B] Peter Alphonsus, servant of Christ Jesus and composer of this book, said:

I give thanks to God, who is first, without beginning; from whom is the beginning of all good; the end without end; the completion of every good; the wise one who grants wisdom and reason to humanity; who has inspired us with his wisdom, enlightened us with the marvelous brightness of his reason, and enriched us with the manifold grace of his Holy Spirit.

Since God has deigned to clothe me, though a sinner, with manifold wisdom, I have been admonished by the same Spirit to compose this book for the benefit of many, so that the lamp entrusted to me may not lie hidden beneath a bushel. I beseech him to join a good end to the beginning of this little book [Col. 0671C] and to guard me, lest anything be said in it that displeases his will. Amen.

May God therefore be my help in this little work—God who compelled me to compose this book and translate it into Latin.

For when, by repeatedly reflecting within myself, I labored earnestly to understand every aspect of the reasons for the creation of humanity, I found that the human intellect had been appointed by the precepts of the Creator for this purpose: that, as long as a person remains in this world, he should devote himself to the holy exercise of philosophy, through which he may gain better and fuller knowledge of his Creator; should strive to live with measured self-restraint; should know how to guard himself against impending adversities; and should walk in this world along the path that leads him to the kingdom of heaven.

If he lives with knowledge of the aforementioned holy discipline, he has fulfilled the purpose for which he was created and ought to be called perfect. I also considered the frailty of the human constitution, which must be instructed briefly lest it become wearied [Col. 0671D]. Remembering its hardness as well, I saw that it must necessarily be softened and sweetened in some fashion, so that it may retain what it learns more easily; for it is forgetful and needs many things to make it remember what it has forgotten.

For this reason I assembled this little book partly from the proverbs of philosophers, their Arabic admonitions, fables, and verses, and partly from comparisons drawn from animals and birds. I also considered moderation, lest, if I wrote more than necessity required, what was written should be a burden rather than a help to the reader, and lest it should take away from readers and hearers the desire and opportunity to learn.

Let the knowledgeable, through what is contained here, remember what they have forgotten.

I have given this little book a name appropriate to its subject: **CLERICAL DISCIPLINE**. For it makes a cleric disciplined. I nevertheless resolved, as far as my understanding permits, to avoid allowing anything to be found in our treatise contrary to our belief or different from our faith. May almighty God, in whom I place my reliance, help me in this. Amen.

If anyone runs through this little work with a human and outward eye, and sees anything in it which human nature has insufficiently guarded against, I urge him to read it again and again with a more discerning eye; and finally I submit it for correction both to him and to all who are perfect in the Catholic faith. For the philosopher considers nothing in human actions to be perfect.

Enoch the philosopher, who in the Arabic language is called Edric, said to his son: “Let the fear of the Lord be your business, and profit will come to you without labor.”

A certain philosopher said: “Whoever fears God is feared by everyone; but whoever does not fear God fears everyone.”

Another philosopher said: “Whoever fears God loves him; whoever fears God obeys God.”

An Arab said in his verse: “You disobey God if you pretend to love God, and it is incredible: if you truly loved him, you would obey him; for whoever loves obeys.”

Socrates said to his disciples: “See that you are not obedient and disobedient to God at the same time.”

They said to him: “Explain to us what you mean.”

He replied: “Abandon hypocrisy. For hypocrisy is to pretend before human beings that one obeys God while secretly being disobedient.”

One of his disciples said to him: “Is there another kind of hypocrisy from which a person ought to beware?”

Socrates said: “There is a person who shows himself obedient to God openly but not secretly, so that everyone will regard him as holy and therefore honor him more. There is another, subtler than this one, who abandons this hypocrisy in order to serve a greater one.

When he fasts or gives alms and is asked whether he has done so, he replies, ‘God knows,’ or ‘No,’ so that he may be held in greater reverence and it may be said that he is not a hypocrite, since he does not wish his deed to be publicized among people.

I believe that there are few who do not share in some form of this hypocrisy. See, therefore, that you are not led astray by it and deprived of the reward for your labor. To prevent this, do everything with a pure intention, and do not seek to gain glory from it.”

Another philosopher said: “If you firmly imitate God, everything will prosper wherever you go.”

Balaam, who in the Arabic language is called Lucaman [Note: [Col. 0673D] Lockman], said to his son:

“My son, do not let an ant be wiser than you: it gathers in summer what it will live on in winter.

“My son, do not let a rooster be more watchful than you: it keeps watch in the morning while you sleep.

“My son, do not let a rooster be stronger than you: it does justice to its ten hens, while you cannot discipline even one wife [Col. 0673C].

“My son, do not let a dog appear nobler in heart than you: it does not forget those who have done it good, whereas you forget those who have done you good.

“My son, do not think it a small matter to have one enemy, or a great matter to have a thousand friends; I tell you this.”

# FIRST FABLE

An Arab who was about to die, having summoned his son, said: “Tell me, my son, how many friends did you acquire while you lived?”

The son replied: “I believe I acquired a hundred friends.”

The father said: “The philosopher said, ‘Do not praise a friend until you have tested him.’ I was born before you and have scarcely acquired half a friend; how, then, did you acquire a hundred? Go, therefore, and test them all, so that you may learn whether any person will be a perfect friend to you.”

The son said: “What do you advise?”

The father said: “Put a slaughtered calf, chopped into pieces, into a sack, so that the outside of the sack is stained with blood. When you come to a friend, say to him: ‘My dear friend, I have perhaps killed a man. I ask you to bury him secretly, for no one will suspect you, and thus you will be able to save me.’”

The son did as his father commanded.

The first friend to whom he went said: “Carry the dead man on your neck. Since you have done evil, suffer the punishment. You shall not enter my house.”

When he had done the same with each of them, they all gave the same answer. Returning to his father, he reported what he had done.

The father said: “What happened to you is what the philosopher said [Col. 0674A]: ‘There are many friends when they are counted, but few in time of need.’ Go to the half-friend I have, and see what he says to you.”

He went and said to this man what he had said to the others. The man replied: “Enter the house. This is not a secret that ought to be spread among the neighbors.”

He then sent away his wife with his entire household and dug a grave. When the other man saw that everything was ready, he explained the matter as it really was, giving thanks.

At last he reported to his father what he had done. The father said: “Of such a friend the philosopher said: ‘He is truly a friend who helps you when the world fails you.’”

The son said to his father: “Have you ever seen a man who gained a complete friend for himself?”

Then the father said: “I have not seen one, but I have heard of one.”

Then the son said: “Tell me about him, in case I might acquire such a friend.”

But the father—

# FABLE II

[Col. 0674B]

I was told about two merchants, one of whom was in Egypt and the other in Baghdad. They knew one another only by hearsay and sent through intermediaries for whatever they needed.

It happened that the one who was in Baghdad went on business to Egypt. When the Egyptian heard of his arrival, he went to meet him and welcomed him joyfully into his house. He served him in every way, as is the custom of friends, for eight days, and showed him all the kinds of singing and entertainment that he had in his house.

When the eight days had ended, the visitor fell ill. The host was deeply distressed on account of his friend and summoned all the Egyptian physicians to examine him. The physicians, having felt his pulse repeatedly and examined his urine again and again, recognized no illness in him. But since they recognized that this bodily illness was a passion of love, they understood what was happening.

Once he had realized this, the host came to him and asked whether there was some woman in his household whom he loved.

The sick man replied: “Show me all the women in your house, and if I see her among them, I will point her out to you.”

On hearing this, the host showed him the female singers and maidservants, but none of them pleased him. Afterward he showed him all his daughters; he rejected and disregarded these just as completely as the others.

The host had a certain noble young woman in his household whom he had long been raising so that he might take her as a wife. He showed her to him as well.

When the sick man saw her, he said: “I am dying because of her, and in her lies my life.”

On hearing this, the host gave the young woman in marriage to the sick man, together with everything that he was to receive with her; in addition, he gave him what he would have given the girl if he had taken her as his wife.

When this had been completed, the man took his wife and the things he had received with her, conducted his business, and returned to his homeland.

Afterward it happened that the Egyptian lost all his possessions in many different ways. Having become poor, he considered going to Baghdad to his friend there, so that his friend might take pity on him.

He set out on the journey naked and starving, and reached Baghdad in the silence of the night at an untimely hour. Shame prevented him from going to his friend’s house, lest, being unknown at such a time, he should perhaps be driven away. He entered a certain temple so that he might spend the night there.

But while he was anxious and turning many thoughts over in his mind, two men happened to meet near the temple in the city. One of them killed the other and secretly fled. Many citizens, running out because of the commotion, found the murdered man. Seeking to discover who had committed the homicide, they entered the temple, hoping to find the killer.

They found the Egyptian there. When they asked him who had killed the man, they heard him say: “I killed him.” For he wished to end his poverty at least by death.

He was therefore arrested and imprisoned. When morning came, he was brought before the judges, condemned to death, and led to the cross.

Many people came, as was customary. Among them was the friend on whose account he had gone to Baghdad. Looking at him more closely, the friend recognized that he was the man he had left in Egypt. Remembering the good things the Egyptian had done for him there, and considering that he could not repay him after his death, he resolved to undergo death in his place.

He therefore cried out in a loud voice: “Why have you condemned an innocent man, and where are you taking him? He does not deserve death. I killed the man!”

They then laid hands on him, bound him, and dragged him with them to the cross, while releasing the other from the punishment of death.

The actual murderer, observing this as he walked in the same crowd, said to himself: “I killed him, and this man is condemned. This innocent man is assigned to punishment, while I, the guilty one, enjoy freedom. What is the cause of this injustice? I do not know, unless it is God’s patience.

“Yet God, the just Judge, leaves no crime unpunished. Therefore, lest he later take vengeance on me more harshly, I shall confess myself guilty of this crime, and by releasing them from death I shall atone for the sin I committed.”

He threw himself into danger, saying: “I am the one who did it; release this innocent man.”

The judges, greatly astonished, bound him while releasing the other from death. Then, already doubting their judgment, they brought him, together with the others who had first been released, before the king. They reported everything to him in order, compelling even the king to hesitate.

After deliberation, the king pardoned them all for the entire crime with which they had charged themselves, on the condition that they reveal the causes of the charges laid against them. They explained the truth of the matter to him.

When all had been released by common agreement, the native of Baghdad who had resolved to die for his friend led the Egyptian into his house and, after honoring him in the customary manner, said: “If you agree to remain with me, everything we have shall rightly be held in common. But if you wish to return to your homeland, let us divide my possessions equally between us.”

The Egyptian, caught by the sweetness of his native land, accepted the portion of his entire wealth that the other had offered him, and so returned home.

When this had been told, the son said to his father: “A friend will scarcely be found.”

Another philosopher said: “On account of untested friends, take precautions once against enemies and a thousand times against friends, since perhaps a friend may at some time become an enemy; thus you will be better able to seek compensation for your loss.”

Again another philosopher said: “Beware of the counsel of the person from whom you seek advice, unless he has been proven faithful to you.”

Another said: “Advise your friend for his good as far as you can, even if he does not wish to believe you. It is right that you should advise him, although it is proper that one who has not sought counsel should not follow your advice” [Col. 0676A].

Another said: “Do not reveal your counsel to everyone. For whoever keeps your counsel in his heart is better able to choose according to his own right.”

Another said: “A hidden counsel is shut up as though in your prison; once revealed, it keeps you bound in its prison.”

Another said: “Do not associate with your enemies when you can find other companions. For they will mark the bad things you do, while they will avoid whatever good things there may be.”

A certain versifier said: “One of the greater adversities of this world for a free man is that necessity forces him to seek help from an enemy.”

Someone asked an Arab: “What greater adversity has befallen you in this world?”

The Arab replied: “Necessity compelled me to approach an enemy so that he might grant me what I wanted.”

Another said: “Do not associate with a flatterer; his companionship is a disgrace to you.”

Another said: “Do not glory in the praise of a flatterer; his praise is your blame, and his blame is praise.”

A certain philosopher, passing along a road, found another philosopher joking with a flatterer and said: “To attract what resembles oneself is the property of a magnet.”

The other replied: “I have never joined myself to him.”

The passer-by said: “Why, then, were you applauding him?”

The other replied: “I was not. But even an honest man, compelled by great necessity, sometimes has to approach a latrine.”

Another philosopher said: “My son, it is difficult to climb steep heights, but easy to descend from them.”

Another philosopher said: “The enmity of a wise man is better than the friendship of a fool.”

Another philosopher said: “Do not regard the friendship of a fool as a great thing, for it is not lasting.”

Another philosopher said: “For a wise man, a harsh life among the wise is sweeter than a pleasant life among fools.”

Another philosopher said: “There are two kinds of wisdom: one natural, the other acquired by art; neither can remain without the other.”

Another said: “Do not entrust wisdom to fools, for that would be injurious to them; nor deny it to the wise, for it belongs to them to impart it.”

Another said: “Gifts of this kind are diverse: to some is given possession of things, to others wisdom.”

A certain man, speaking to his son, said: “Which would you prefer to be given: wealth or wisdom?”

The son replied: “Either of these needs the other.”

There was an excellent and learned versifier, but poor and a beggar, who was always complaining to his friends about his poverty. He also composed verses about it expressing this meaning [Col. 0676D]:

“You who distribute portions, show why my share is lacking for me. You are not to blame, but tell me whom I should blame; for if my constellation is harsh toward me, it is undeniable that this too was done by you. But between me and it, you are both advocate and judge.

“You gave me wisdom without substance. Tell me, then, what can wisdom do without substance? Take part of the wisdom and give me part of the money. Do not allow me to lack what would bring me shame if I lacked it.”

Another philosopher said: “One person needs another in three ways. In the matter in which someone benefits from you, you are greater than him; in that in which you do not need him, you are his equal; but in that in which you need him, you are inferior.”

Another said: “Wisdom gives life to dead bodies through its brightness, just as dry earth grows green through the moisture of rain” [Col. 0677A].

Another said: “Wisdom is the brightness of the soul, while wealth is the brightness of the body.”

A disciple asked his teacher: “How should I conduct myself so that I may be counted among wise disciples?”

The teacher replied: “Keep silent until it is necessary for you to speak.”

Silence corrects a wicked tongue without being commanded. For the philosopher said: “Silence is a sign of wisdom, and talkativeness a sign of folly.”

Do not hasten to answer until the question has been completed. Do not attempt to resolve a question raised in an assembly when you have realized that someone there is wiser than you. Do not answer a question addressed to someone else, nor seek praise for something unknown to you.

For the philosopher says: “The testing proves to be a liar the person who seeks praise for something unknown to him.”

Another said: “Submit to the truth, whether spoken by you or put before you.”

Do not glory in your wise words; for, as the philosopher testifies, whoever glories in his own wise words is proved to be a fool [Col. 0677B].

Another said: “Whoever wishes prudently to seek a solution will understand prudently.”

Another said: “Whoever, out of shame, does not endure discipline for a short time will remain forever in the shame of folly.”

Another said: “Not everyone called wise is wise, but the one who learns and retains wisdom.”

Another said: “If a person has failed in learning, his nobility will profit him little. Nobility needs doctrine, and wisdom needs experience.”

# FABLE III

## THE ARAB

A certain prudent and witty versifier, but of ignoble birth, offered his verses to a certain king. The king, recognizing his wisdom, received him honorably.

Other versifiers, proud of their noble birth and accustomed to associating with the king, envied him and said: “My lord king, why do you exalt this man of such base lineage?”

The king replied: “The man whom you thought to disparage you have praised all the more.”

The man who had been disparaged added: “A rose born from thorns is by no means to be disparaged.”

The king then dismissed him with the greatest gifts and honors.

It happened that a certain versifier, born of noble lineage but poorly instructed, offered his verses to a king. The king accepted them, but despised them as badly composed and gave him nothing.

The versifier therefore said to the king: “If not for my verses, at least give me something on account of my noble birth.”

The king replied: “Who is your father?”

The versifier told him.

The king said: “The seed has degenerated in you.”

The versifier replied: “My king, rye often grows among wheat.”

The king then said: “You have proved yourself of lesser nobility than your father,” and dismissed him without recompense.

Another versifier likewise came to the king. His father was ignoble but his mother noble. He was certainly disordered and offered disordered verses.

His mother had a brother who was learned and distinguished for his wit. The king did not receive the versifier honorably, but asked whose son he was. The man presented his maternal uncle to him instead, whereupon the king burst into tremendous laughter.

His attendants asked him: “What is the cause of such great laughter?”

The king replied: “I had read a certain fable in a book, and now I see it before my eyes.”

They asked: “What fable is that?”

The king said: “A fox found a newly born mule in the pastures and, wondering, said: ‘Who are you?’ The mule said that it was a creature of God. The fox asked: ‘Do you have a father or mother?’ The mule replied: ‘My uncle is a noble horse.’

“Thus, just as the mule does not acknowledge the donkey as its father because it is a sluggish and deformed animal, so this man was ashamed to confess his own father, who was unknown because of his own dullness.”

The king nevertheless turned to the versifier and said: “I want you to tell me who your father is.”

The man told him.

The king then learned that his father was base and undisciplined, and said to his servants: “Let us give this man something from our possessions, for he is not degenerate.”

An Arab said to his father: “I am amazed that I have read that in former times noble, witty, and wise men were honored, whereas now only flatterers are honored.” To this the father replied: “[Col. 0678B] Do not be amazed, my son, for clerics honor clerics, the well-born honor the well-born, the witty honor the witty, and flatterers are revered by flatterers.”

The son said: “I have seen something else: clerics, because of their wisdom, are not honored; consequently they have become flatterers and have attained great honor.” Then the father said to him: “This has indeed happened through the lethargy of the times.”

To this the son replied: “Explain to me, dearest father, the true definition of nobility.” The father answered: “As Aristotle recalls in his letter composed for King Alexander, when Alexander asked him whom he should make his counselor from among men, Aristotle replied in a letter as follows: ‘Take,’ he said, ‘a man who is instructed in the seven liberal arts, educated in seven forms of practical skill, and trained in seven virtues; and I consider this perfect nobility.’”

The son said: “[Col. 0678C] This nobility has not appeared in my time. Rather, all the nobility I see consists of gold and silver, as a certain versifier says:

> Treasures glorify those private men whom nobility has not endowed,  
> and poverty oppresses another house endowed with nobility.

A certain versifier, speaking of the misfortunes of the world that overtake the noble, says:

> Tell those who despise us because of the adversities that befall us  
> that the world has made itself contrary to no one except the noble alone.  
> Do you not see that the sea carries off dung and straw,  
> while precious stones sink to the bottom?  
> Do you not see that there are stars in heaven whose number we do not know?  
> Yet none of them suffers an eclipse except the sun and the moon.”

The father said: “It is through the lethargy of the age that people judge wealth alone to be worthy of praise.” [Col. 0678D]

One of the disciples asked his master, saying: “Since there are seven arts, seven virtues, and seven practical skills, I should like you to enumerate them for me just as they are.”

The master said: “I shall enumerate them. These are the arts: dialectic, arithmetic, geometry, physics, music, and astronomy. As for the seventh, there are differing opinions among many about what it is. Philosophers who do not follow the prophets say that necromancy is the seventh. Some of those who believe in prophecy and philosophy do not want it to be a science that surpasses natural things or the elements of the world. Some who do not study philosophy assert that it is grammar.

“These are the virtues: riding, swimming, shooting with a bow, fighting with the cestus, bird-catching, playing chess, and composing verse. [Col. 0679A] The practical disciplines are these: not being gluttonous, a drunkard, lustful, wine-soaked, a liar, or greedy, and not having bad conduct.”

The disciple said: “At this time I think no one is of such a kind.”

A certain philosopher corrected his son: “Beware of lying, because it is sweeter than the flesh of birds, while it is easy for others to utter a lie; therefore telling the truth seems difficult.”

Another philosopher said: “If you fear saying something for which you will repent, it is better never to say it. Thus, in the shame of refusing, beware lest you bring upon yourself the necessity of lying, for it is more honorable to deny a matter than to postpone it with lengthy excuses.”

Another said: “If anyone is saved by a lie, he is saved much more by the truth.”

A certain man, accused and brought before the king as judge, denied the crime laid against him but was eventually convicted. The king said to him: “You will be punished twice: once for the crime committed, [Col. 0679B] and a second time for the crime denied.”

Another man, similarly accused, did not deny what he had committed. Those standing by said to the king that judgment should be imposed for the confessed crime.

“Not so,” said the king, “for the philosopher says: ‘For one who confesses his sin, reason requires that judgment be relaxed.’” Thus he was set free and departed from the king.

Socrates said: “Just as a lying man is not fit for companionship at the beginning, so he will be excluded from the kingdom of heaven.”

A certain philosopher said to his son: “Just as fire does not punish fire, so evil does not yield to evil; as water extinguishes fire, so anyone can destroy evil with good. Do not repay evil with evil, lest you become like the evil person; instead, return good, so that you may be better than the evil person.”

Another philosopher said: “Do not trust an evil person merely because you have escaped one danger, only to enter another; for you will not encounter it in such a way as to pass through it.”

[Col. 0679C] An Arab said to his son: “If you see someone weighed down by evil deeds, do not involve yourself, for whoever releases a hanging man will have it fall upon him.”

## FABLE IV

A man passing through a forest found a serpent stretched out and tied to stakes by shepherds. He immediately released it and took care to warm it. Once warmed, the serpent began to coil around the man who was tending it and finally constricted him tightly.

Then the man said: “What are you doing? Why are you repaying good with evil?”

The serpent replied: “I am acting according to my nature.”

“I did you good,” said the man, “and you repay me with evil?”

While they were arguing in this way, a fox was summoned among them as judge, and the whole matter was shown to it in the order in which it had occurred.

Then the fox said: “I do not know how to judge this case by hearing alone, unless I see with my own eyes how it first occurred between you.”

The serpent was tied up again as before.

“Now,” said the fox, “serpent, if you can escape, go away; and you, man, do not trouble yourself to release the serpent. Have you not read that whoever releases a hanging man will have it fall upon him?”

An Arab said to his son: “If you are burdened in some way and can easily free yourself, do not delay. For while you wait to be freed more easily, you will become more heavily burdened. And beware lest what happened to the hunchback and the versifier happen to you.”

“And what was that?” asked the son.

## FABLE V

A certain versifier composed verses and presented them to the king. The king praised his talent and ordered him to ask for a gift in return for his work. He asked for a gift of this sort: that the king make him doorkeeper of his city for one month, and that he receive one denarius from every hunchback, one from every scabby person, one from every one-eyed man, one from every person with impetigo, and one from every person with a hernia. The king granted this and confirmed it with his seal.

Having undertaken the office, the versifier sat at the gate and performed his duty. One day a well-dressed hunchback entered the gate with a staff. The versifier met him and demanded a denarius, but he refused to give it. When the versifier used force against him and lifted the hood from his head, he discovered that the hunchback was one-eyed. Thus he demanded two denarii from the man from whom he had earlier requested only one.

The man refused to give them and was detained. Having no help, he tried to flee, but when he was pulled back by his hood, he appeared with his head uncovered to be afflicted with scabies. The versifier immediately demanded three [Col. 0680B] denarii.

Seeing that the hunchback could defend himself neither by flight nor with assistance, he began to resist by force. As he defended himself with his arms bared, he appeared to have impetigo. The versifier demanded a fourth denarius.

When the man continued to defend himself, the versifier pulled off his cloak. As the man fell to the ground, the versifier discovered that he had a hernia and therefore extorted a fifth denarius.

Thus it happened that the man who had refused to give one denarius unwillingly gave five.

A philosopher said to his son: “My son, beware of passing through the seat of an evil people, for passing through it becomes the cause of staying, staying the occasion of sitting, and sitting the cause of action.”

## FABLE VI

It is said that two clerics left the city in the evening in order to go abroad. They came to a place where drunkards had gathered.

One of them said to his companion: “Let us turn aside by another road, for the philosopher says that one must not pass through the seat of an evil people.”

His companion replied: “Passing through it will do no harm, if nothing else happens.” As they passed by, they heard a song in the house. One of them stopped, held back by the sweetness of the singing.

His companion urged him to go on, but he refused. When his companion departed, he remained alone. Enticed by the song, he entered the house. Invited from every side, he sat down and drank with the others.

Then suddenly a herald, following a spy who was fleeing from the city, entered the drinking house behind him. When the spy was found in that house, he and all the others were arrested.

“This,” said the herald, “was the lodging of this spy. He left from here and returned here. You were all his accomplices and associates.”

They were all led to the gallows, and [Col. 0680D] the cleric, standing among them, proclaimed in a loud voice to everyone: “Whoever enjoys the companionship of an evil people undoubtedly earns the punishment of an undeserved death.”

It is told of two disciples that, as they were leaving a certain city, they came to a place where the very melodious voice of a woman could be heard. The words of the song were well composed, and the song itself, musically constructed, sounded extremely delightful and amorous.

One of them stopped, held back by the song. His companion said to him: “Let us turn aside,” and they turned away from that place, “because sometimes a bird is deceived by a song that leads it to death.”

Then one of them said again: “This voice is sweeter than the one that my master and I heard some time ago.”

“What was it like?” asked the other, “and how did you hear it?”

“It happened,” replied his companion, “that we had gone out from the city, and a very harsh voice was heard, with an unstructured song; the words sounded disordered, and whoever was singing repeated the same thing again and again. Yet he was held by his own harsh song as though it were delightful.

“Then my master said to me: ‘If it is true what people say—that the voice of an owl portends a man’s death—then without doubt this owl-like voice announces death to a man.’

“I replied: ‘I am amazed that, since the song is so dreadful, he takes such delight in it.’

“He said to me: ‘Do you not remember that philosopher who says: “A man takes delight in three things, and even if they are not good, he delights in his own voice, his own song, and his own son”?’”

After he had told this about himself and his master, they both departed from that place.

A certain philosopher said to his son: “Follow a scorpion, a lion, or a dragon, but do not follow an evil woman.”

Another philosopher said: “Pray to God to free you from the wicked disposition of women, and take care yourself that you are not deceived.”

For it is said of a philosopher that, while passing through a place where a bird-catcher had stretched out a net to deceive birds, he saw a little woman behaving wantonly with him. He said to her: “You who try to deceive birds, beware lest, having become a little bird, you be caught by this birdlime.”

A certain disciple said to his master: “I have read in the books of philosophers, where they command a man to guard himself against the disposition of a perverse woman, and Solomon gives the same warning in Proverbs [Note: [Col. 0681D] Chapter V, verse 8.]. But if you remember anything about her disposition, whether from stories or proverbs, I should like you to instruct me by recounting it.”

“I shall gladly do so for your sake,” he replied, “but I fear that if some people of simple mind, reading the verses that we write about women’s arts for their correction and for your instruction and that of others, should see how women, without their husbands’ knowledge, summon their lovers, embrace and kiss the men they have summoned, and satisfy in those men whatever their lust demands, they might believe that their wickedness rebounds upon us.”

The disciple said: “Do not fear this, master, because Solomon in the Book of Proverbs [Note: [Col. 0682D] V. 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, and elsewhere throughout.], as well as many wise men correcting their evil conduct, wrote such things and earned praise rather than blame for doing so. In the same way, write about them and show us what has been requested without hesitation.”

Then the master said:

## FABLE VII

A certain man went to harvest grapes. When his wife saw this, she understood that he would remain near the vineyard for a long time. She therefore sent a messenger to summon a friend and prepared a feast.

It happened, however, that the master was struck in the eye by a vine branch. He returned home quickly, unable to see anything with the injured eye, and, arriving at the door of his house, knocked.

When his wife realized this, she was extremely agitated. She hid the friend whom she had summoned in a secluded place and then ran to open the door for her husband. He entered, deeply distressed and in pain because of his eye, and ordered the room to be prepared and the bed made, so that he could rest there.

The wife feared that, when he entered the room, he would see the friend hiding there. She said to him: “Why are you hurrying so much to bed? First tell me what is wrong with you.”

He told her everything that had happened.

“Allow me,” she said, “dearest [Col. 0682A] husband, to strengthen your sound eye by medicinal skill and by a spell, so that nothing may happen to the sound eye as has now happened to the injured one. Your misfortune is shared by us.”

She placed her mouth against his sound eye and continued tending it until the friend departed from the place where he was hiding, unknown to her husband. At last she rose and said: “Now, dearest husband, be confident that what happened to the other eye will not happen similarly to this one. If you wish, you may now go down to bed.”

Then the disciple said to the master: “You have instructed me well, and what you have related about their arts is treasured by my eager mind. I would not exchange what I have learned from it even for the wealth of the Arabs. If you please, continue, and explain what we may be able to transfer into the higher sphere of public administration among those who are to come.”

“I shall do so,” he replied.

## FABLE VIII

It is said of a certain man who went abroad that he entrusted his wife to his mother-in-law. His wife, however, fell in love with another man and told her mother about it. The mother, moved on behalf of her daughter, favored the affair. She summoned the man and began to feast with him and her daughter.

While they were feasting, the husband arrived and knocked at the door. The woman rose, hid the lover, and then opened the door for her husband. After entering, he ordered a bed to be prepared for him, since he wished to rest and was tired.

The woman, disturbed, hesitated about what to do. Seeing this, her mother said: “Do not hurry, daughter, to prepare the bed until we show your husband the linen cloth that we have made.”

The old woman took out a linen cloth. As far as she could, she raised one of its corners and gave the other to her daughter to lift. Thus, with the cloth stretched out, the husband was deceived until the friend who had been hiding came out.

Then she said to her daughter: “Spread the linen cloth over your husband’s bed, for it has been prepared and woven by your hands and mine.”

The husband said to her: “And you, my lady, know how to prepare such linen?”

She replied: “My son, I have prepared many things of this kind.”

The disciple said in response: “I have heard something marvelous, but I should like you to instruct me further, because the more I consider their ingenuity, the more I am sharpened to guard myself.”

The master replied: “I shall tell you more, and in this way our examples will be sufficient for your instruction.”

The disciple said: “As you wish.”

## FABLE IX

“Once again,” he said, “it is reported that a certain man, setting out on a journey, entrusted his wife to his mother-in-law for safekeeping. The wife, however, brought in her lover.

While they were feasting, the husband arrived and knocked at the door. The wife rose and allowed her husband to enter. But the mother, remaining with her daughter’s lover and having no place where he could be hidden, first hesitated about what to do.

While the daughter was opening the door for her husband, the old woman seized a naked sword and gave it to the lover. She ordered him to stand before the doorway, at the entrance, when her daughter’s husband arrived, holding the drawn sword, and to answer nothing if he said anything to him.

He did as she had ordered. When the door was opened and the husband saw him standing there in this manner, he stopped.

‘Who are you?’ he asked.

When the man did not answer, the husband was first astonished and then became even more frightened.

The old woman answered from inside: ‘Dear son-in-law, be silent, lest someone hear you.’

He was even more amazed. ‘What is this, dear lady?’ he asked.

Then the woman said: ‘My good son, three men were pursuing this man. When we opened the door, we allowed him to enter with his sword, until those who wished to kill him had gone away. Because he feared that you were one of them, he was stunned and did not answer you.’

He said: ‘May you prosper, lady, for having freed this man from death in this way.’

He entered, summoned his wife’s lover, and made him sit with him. Having soothed him with pleasant conversation, he allowed him to leave around nightfall.

The disciple said: “You have told me marvelous things, but now I am even more amazed at their presumptuous boldness. Nevertheless, I want you to tell me more about their devices, if it is not burdensome. For the more you tell me, the greater will be your reward.”

To this the master replied: “Are these things not enough for you? I have told you three stories, and you still do not cease urging me on.”

The disciple said: “By saying ‘three,’ you greatly increase the number in recounting them, if only a few words have sounded. Tell me one thing that will fill my ears with lengthy speech, and that will be enough for me.”

The master said: “Beware lest what happened between a certain king and his storyteller happen between us.”

The disciple said: “What, dear master? What happened at last?”

## FABLE X

A certain king had a storyteller who was accustomed to tell him five stories every night. Eventually it happened that the king, troubled by certain cares, was completely unable to sleep, and asked to hear more stories than usual.

The storyteller told three additional stories, but they were short. The king asked for more. The storyteller absolutely refused, for he said that he had already told many, as it seemed to him.

To this the king replied: “You have already told very many, but they were extremely brief. I should like you to tell some tale that may be extended through many words, and then I shall allow you to sleep.”

The storyteller agreed and began:

“There was a certain peasant who had a thousand solidi. Setting out, he purchased two thousand sheep, six denarii each. It happened, when he was returning, that a great flood of waters rose. Since he could cross neither by a bridge nor by a ford, he went on anxiously, looking for some means by which he could transport his sheep.

“At last he found a tiny boat. Compelled by necessity, he put two sheep into it and crossed the water.”

After saying this, the storyteller fell asleep.

The king woke him and urged him to finish the story he had begun. The storyteller replied: “The wave is large, but the boat is tiny, and the flock of sheep is countless. Therefore allow the peasant mentioned above to transfer his sheep, and I shall bring the story I began to an end.”

In this way the storyteller pacified the king, who was eager to hear lengthy stories.

“But if you compel me to add still other stories to those already told, I shall try to free myself by relying on the example just mentioned.”

The disciple said: “It is said in ancient proverbs that the one who weeps for gifts does not suffer from the same contrition as the one who is burdened by pain in his own body. [Col. 0684A] Nor did the storyteller love his king as much as you love me. He wished to beguile him somewhat with his stories, but disclose the previously mentioned devices of women.”

The master said:

## FABLE XI

It is said that a certain nobleman by birth had a wife who was exceptionally chaste and beautiful. It happened that he wished to go to Rome out of devotion to prayer, but he did not wish to appoint any guardian for his wife other than herself, trusting sufficiently in her chaste conduct and the honor of her virtue.

The wife remained, living chastely and acting prudently in all things.

Eventually, compelled by necessity, she left her own house in order to visit a neighbor. After completing her business, she returned home. A young man saw her and began to love her with ardent passion. He sent many messengers to her, wishing to be loved by her as much as he loved her.

She rejected these messengers and utterly despised him. When the young man realized that he was held in such contempt, he became so grief-stricken that he was weighed down by the burden of a serious illness. Nevertheless, he often went to the place where he had seen the lady leave, hoping to meet her, but he could not accomplish this.

As he wept from grief, an old woman, adorned in the habit of a religious woman, came upon him and asked what cause was compelling him to suffer. The young man did not at all wish to reveal what was occupying his conscience.

The old woman said to him: “The longer someone delays revealing his illness to a physician, the more severely he is worn down by the disease.”

On hearing this, he related in order what had happened and disclosed his secret.

The old woman said: “With God’s help I shall find a remedy for what you have told me.” Leaving him, she returned home.

She forced a little dog that she kept with her to fast for two days. On the third day she gave the fasting animal bread prepared with mustard. When the dog tasted it, its eyes began to weep because of the bitterness.

Afterward the old woman went to the house of the chaste woman whom the young man had fallen in love with. Because of the great appearance of her religious devotion, the woman received her honorably. The little dog followed her.

When the woman saw the little dog weeping, she asked what was wrong with it and why it was crying.

The old woman answered: “Dear friend, do not ask what is wrong, for the pain is so great that I cannot speak of it.”

The woman pressed her still more to tell her. The old woman then said: “This little dog that you see was once my daughter, exceedingly chaste and beautiful. A certain young man fell in love with her, but she was so chaste that she utterly rejected him and refused his love. As a result, he became so grief-stricken that he was seized by a serious illness. For that fault, the daughter I mentioned was miserably transformed into a little dog.”

After saying this, the old woman burst into tears from excessive grief.

The woman said: “What am I to do, dear lady, since I am conscious of a similar sin? A young man loved me, but I despised him out of love of chastity, and the same thing has happened to him.”

The old woman replied: “I advise you, dear friend, to take pity on him as quickly as you can and do what he seeks, lest you too be changed into a dog in the same way. For if I had known of the love between the young man mentioned above and my daughter, my daughter would never have been changed into a dog.”

The chaste woman said: “I beg you to give me useful advice in this matter, lest I be deprived of my own form and become a little dog.”

The old woman replied: “For the love of God, for the remedy of my soul, and because I pity you, I shall gladly seek the young man mentioned above, and, if I can find him anywhere, I shall bring him back to you.”

The woman thanked her. Thus the old woman, through her artful words, gained credence. She brought back the young man whom she had promised to bring and joined the two of them together.

The disciples said to the master: “I have never heard anything so marvelous, and I think it was accomplished by the art of the devil.”

The master said: “Do not doubt it.”

The disciple said: “I hope that if someone is so wise that he always fears that he may be deceived by a woman’s art, perhaps he will be able to guard himself against her ingenuity.”

The master said: “I heard of a certain man who labored greatly to guard his wife, but it did him no good.”

The disciple said to the master: “Tell me what he did, so that I may know better how to guard the woman I marry, if I marry one.”

The master said:

## FABLE XII

There was a certain young man who devoted all his attention, all his understanding, and even all his time to learning every kind of female art. Having done this, he wished to take a wife.

First, however, he went to seek advice and approached the wisest man in that region. He asked how he could guard the woman he wished to marry.

When the wise man heard this, he gave him the following advice: He should build a house with high stone walls, place the woman inside it, give her enough food but no superfluous clothing, and construct the house so that it had nothing but a single door and a single window through which she could see, at such a height that no one could enter or leave through it.

The young man, having heard the wise man’s advice, did as he had ordered. Each morning, when the young man left the house, he secured the door, and he did the same when he entered. When he slept, he hid the key beneath his head.

He did this for a long time.

One day, while the young man was going to the marketplace, the woman, as she was accustomed to do, climbed up to the window and watched attentively those who were going and returning. On that day, while she stood at the window, she saw a handsome young man in body and face. At once she was inflamed with love for him and, as was said above, began to think, now that she was guarded, how and by what art she might speak with the young man she loved.

Being full of ingenuity and the art of deceit, she thought that she would steal her husband’s keys while he slept, and she did so.

She was accustomed to intoxicate her husband with wine every night, so that she could more safely go out to her lover and fulfill her desire. Her husband, however, having already been instructed by philosophical warnings that women’s actions are never without deceit, began to consider what his wife might be plotting through her frequent and daily drinking. To conceal his intention, he pretended to be drunk.

The woman, unaware of this, rose from bed during the night, went to the door of the house, opened it, and went out to her lover.

Her husband, however, quietly rose in the silence of the night, came to the door, closed it while it was open, secured it, climbed up to the window, and stood there until he saw his wife returning in her shift. When she returned home, she knocked at the door.

Her husband heard and saw her and, as though he did not know who she was, asked: “Who is it?”

She begged forgiveness for her fault and promised that she would never do such a thing again, but she accomplished nothing. The husband, angry, said that he would not permit her to enter but would expose her to her parents.

She cried out more and more loudly, saying that unless he reopened the door, she would jump into the well beside the house and thus end her life, and that he would then have to answer to her friends and relatives for her death.

Ignoring the threats of the woman of his house, he did not allow her to enter.

The woman, however, full of art and cunning, took a stone and threw it into the well, intending that when her husband heard the sound of the stone falling into the well, he would think that she had fallen into it. Having done this, the woman hid herself behind the well.

The simple and foolish man, hearing the sound of the stone falling into the well, immediately left the house and hurried to the well, believing that what he had heard—that the woman had fallen—was true.

The woman, seeing that the door of the house was open and not forgetting her skill, entered the house, secured the door, and climbed up to the window.

When he realized that he had been deceived, he said: “O deceitful woman, full of the devil’s art, let me enter, and believe that I shall forgive you whatever you have done to me outside.”

But she rebuked him and utterly denied him entrance to the house, even under oath, saying: “O seducer, I shall expose your behavior and your crime to your parents, because every night you are intent on sneaking away from me in this way and visiting prostitutes.”

And she did so.

When his parents heard this, believing it to be true, they rebuked him. Thus that woman, freed by her own art, shifted onto her husband the disgrace that she deserved. Guarding the woman did him no good; indeed, it harmed him.

For this additional misery also befell him: in the opinion of many people, he was believed to have deserved what he suffered. Consequently, driven from many good things, stripped of his dignities, and disgraced in reputation because of his wife’s evil speech, he endured the punishment for sexual wrongdoing.

The disciple said: “No one can guard himself against a woman’s ingenuity unless God guards him, and this story is a great warning against taking a wife.”

The master said: “You must not believe that all women are like this, because great goodness and chastity are found in many women. Know that good companionship can be found in a good woman. A good woman is a faithful guardian and a good household.

“Solomon, at the end of his Book of Proverbs, composed twenty-two verses in praise of the excellence and goodness of a good woman [Note: [Col. 0685D] Chapter XXXI, 10–31. [A long lacuna follows in the supplied text.]].”

The disciple replied: “You have comforted me well. But have you ever heard of a woman who tried to turn the ingenuity of her mind toward good?”

The master said: “I have heard of one.”

The disciple said: “Tell me about her, because the matter seems new to me.”

The master said:

## FABLE XIII

I was told that a certain Spaniard went to Mecca. While traveling, he reached Egypt. Wishing to enter and cross the desert land, he decided to leave his money in Egypt. Before doing so, he asked whether there was some trustworthy man in that region to whom he could entrust his money.

They showed him an old man renowned in that place for the virtue of his faithfulness. To him he entrusted a thousand talents of his property. He then went on his journey.

After completing his journey, he returned to the man to whom he had entrusted his money and asked him for what he had committed to his keeping. But the man, full of wickedness, said that he had never seen him before.

Thus deceived, he went to the respectable men of that region and reported to them how the man to whom he had entrusted his money had treated him. The man’s neighbors, hearing such things about him, refused to believe them and said that the matter was nothing.

[Col. 0687B] The man who had lost his money went every day to the house of the one who was unjustly withholding it. With flattering entreaties he begged him to return the money. When the deceiver heard this, he rebuked him, saying that he must not say anything of the sort about him or come to him again; if he did, he would deservedly suffer punishment.

Having heard the threats of the man who had deceived him, he began to return sadly. On the way he met an old woman dressed in the rags of a hermit. She supported her frail limbs with her staff and, as she went along praising God, placed stones on the road so that they would not injure the feet of passersby.

When she saw the weeping man, she recognized that he was a stranger. Moved by pity, she called him into a narrow side street and asked what had happened to him.

He related the matter in order.

After hearing his words, the woman said: “Friend, if what you have reported is true, I shall bring you help from that place.”

He replied: “How can you do this, handmaid of God?”

She answered: “Bring me a man from your own land whose words and deeds you can trust.”

He brought such a man.

Then she ordered the deceived man’s companion to buy ten chests, decorated with precious colors from foreign lands, bound with silver-plated iron, and fitted with good locks, and to bring them to her lodging. She ordered that they be filled with small stones.

He did as she had instructed.

When the woman saw that everything she had ordered was ready, she said: “Now find ten men who, going to the house of the man who deceived you, will carry the chests with me and your companion, one after another, advancing in a long procession.

“As soon as the first has arrived at the house of the man who deceived you and rests there, come and ask for your money. I trust in God so fully that your money will be returned to you.”

He did just as the old woman had ordered. She, not forgetting the plan she had begun, set out and came with the deceived man’s companion to the deceiver’s house.

She said: “A certain man from Spain lodged with me and wishes to go to Mecca. Before setting out, he wants to entrust the money he has kept in ten chests to someone, so that it may be guarded until he returns. I therefore beg you, for my sake, to guard it in your house. Since I have heard and know that you are a good and trustworthy man, I do not want anyone other than you to be entrusted with this money.”

While she was speaking, the first man carrying a chest arrived, while the others could be seen in the distance.

Meanwhile, the deceived man, not forgetting the old woman’s instructions, came after the first chest, just as she had ordered him.

The man who had hidden the money, full of wickedness and evil cunning, saw the arrival of the man whose money he had concealed. Fearing that, if the man asked for his money, the other man bringing his own money would not entrust it to him, he went toward him saying:

“O friend, where have you been, and where have you stayed so long? Come and take the money that has long been entrusted to my keeping. I have found it, and I am now weary of guarding it.”

The other man, delighted and rejoicing, received the money and gave thanks.

When the old woman saw that the man had his money, she rose and said: “My companion and I shall go to meet our chests and hurry them along. You wait until we return and guard well what we have already brought.”

The man, happy at heart because he had recovered what he had received, guarded it and, as best he could, awaited their arrival. Thus, through the old woman’s good ingenuity, the sum of money was restored to its owner.

The disciple said: “This was a marvelous and useful device. I do not think that any philosopher could have devised a subtler means by which a man could more easily recover his money.”

The master said: “A philosopher could readily have devised it through his natural ingenuity.”

The disciple said: “I readily believe that. But if you have stored some philosopher of this kind in the treasury of your heart, give him generously to me, your disciple, and I shall entrust him to faithful memory, so that one day I may be able to offer the most delicate nourishment to disciples raised on the milk of philosophy.”

The master said:

## FABLE XIV
It happened that a certain man had a son to whom, after his death, he left nothing except a house. The young man, with great bodily toil, could scarcely provide even what nature required [Col. 0688C], and yet he did not wish to sell his house, although driven by severe hunger. He had a very wealthy neighbor who wanted to buy the house in order to enlarge his own. But the young man was unwilling to sell it either for persuasion or for money. When the rich man discovered this, he began to consider by what schemes and devices he might take the house away from the young man; but the youth, as far as he was able, avoided his intimacy.

At last, grieved both because of the house and because he could not deceive the young man, the rich man came one day to him and said: “Young man, rent me a small part of your courtyard for a price, because I wish to store ten casks of oil beneath the ground there. They will cause you no harm, and you will receive from them [Col. 0688D] some means of sustaining your life.” The young man, compelled by necessity, agreed and gave him the keys of the house.

The youth then, as usual, sought his livelihood by serving free men generously. But the rich man, having received the keys, dug beneath the young man’s courtyard, hid five casks full of oil there and five half-full casks, and, having done this, summoned the young man. Giving him the keys of the house, he said: “Young man, I entrust my oil to you and place it in your keeping.” The simple young man, supposing all the casks to be full, accepted them into his custody.

After a long time, it happened that oil became expensive in that land. When the rich man heard this, he said to the young man: “My friend, come and help me dig up the oil that I entrusted to your keeping long ago, and you shall receive a reward for your labor and guardianship.” Having heard the request, the youth agreed to help the rich man as far as he was able, in return for payment.

The rich man, not forgetting his most wicked fraud, brought men to buy the oil. When they had arrived, they opened the ground and found five full casks and five half-full ones. Having perceived this, he summoned the young man and said: “My friend, because of your keeping I have lost my oil; moreover, you have fraudulently taken away what I entrusted to you. Therefore I want you to restore what is mine.” Having said this, he seized him and, whether he wished it or not, brought him before the court.

When Justice saw him, she accused him; but the young man did not know what he could say in reply. Nevertheless, he asked for a delay of one day, which Justice granted because it was fair. In that city there lived a certain philosopher surnamed “Aid of the Needy,” a good and religious man [Col. 0689B]. Having heard the praises of his goodness, the young man went to him and asked his advice, saying: “If what many people have told me about you in the ordinary course of conversation is true, bring me aid, for I am being unjustly accused.”

When the philosopher heard the young man’s plea, he asked whether he was being accused justly or unjustly. The young man firmly swore that he was being accused unjustly. Having learned the truth of the matter, the philosopher, moved by compassion, said: “With God’s help I will bring you aid. But just as you have obtained from Justice a postponement until tomorrow, do not fail to go to the hearing. I shall be ready to support your truth and harm their falsehood.”

The young man did what the philosopher had instructed him. In the morning, the philosopher came to Justice. When Justice saw him as a wise man and philosopher [Col. 0689C], she called him and had him sit beside her. Then Justice summoned the accusers and the accused and ordered them to recall their respective claims; and they did so. While they stood there, Justice told the philosopher that he should hear the case and then pronounce judgment.

The philosopher then said: “Justice, order the clear oil from the five full casks to be measured, and determine how much clear oil there is; likewise, do this with the five half-full casks, and determine how much clear oil was in them. Then have the thick oil from the five full casks measured, and determine how much thick oil they contain; likewise, have the five half-full casks measured, and determine how much thick oil was in them. If you find as much thick oil in the half-full casks [Col. 0689D] as in the full ones, know that the oil was stolen. But if in the half-full casks you find a proportion of thickness corresponding to what the clear oil present there would require—and you will likewise be able to find this in the full casks—know that the oil was not stolen.”

When Justice heard this, she confirmed the judgment. It was done accordingly, and in this way the young man escaped through the philosopher’s intelligence. When the proceedings had ended, the young man thanked the philosopher. Then the philosopher said to him: “Have you never heard that saying of the philosophers: ‘Do not buy a house before you have come to know the neighbor’?”

The young man replied: “We had the house first, before he settled beside us.”

The philosopher answered him: “Sell before you remain beside a bad neighbor.”

**Student:** “This judgment appears to belong to a philosopher, and it is truly by the grace of God. He was rightly called by the name ‘Aid of the Needy’ [Col. 0690A].”

Again the student said: “Although what I have already heard rests in my mind, it urges me on to hear more.”

The master said: “I shall gladly tell you,” and thus he began:

## FABLE XV

It was said that a certain rich man, going into the city, carried with him a purse containing a thousand talents and, in the same purse, a golden serpent with hyacinth-colored eyes. He lost all of it together.

A certain poor man, traveling along the road, found it and gave it to his wife, telling her how he had found it. When the woman heard this, she said: “Let us guard what God has given.”

On another day, a herald went along the road proclaiming: “Whoever has found such a sum shall return it, and without committing any sin shall receive one hundred talents from it.” When the finder of the sum heard this [Col. 0690B], he said to his wife: “Let us return the sum, and without sin we shall receive one hundred talents from it.”

The woman replied: “If God had wished him to possess this sum, he would not have lost it. Let us guard what God has given.”

The finder of the sum tried to have it returned, but she absolutely refused. Nevertheless, whether the woman wished it or not, her husband returned it and demanded what the herald had promised. But the rich man, full of wickedness, said: “You should know that one more serpent is still missing.”

He said this with evil intent, so that he would not give the poor man the promised talents. The poor man, however, said that he had found nothing more. But the people of that city, favoring the rich man, disparaging the poor man, and bearing an implacable hatred against the poor man’s fortune, summoned him before Justice.

The poor man, as stated above, said that he had found nothing more [Col. 0690C]. But while this sort of dispute between poor and rich passed from mouth to mouth, the reports eventually reached the ears of the king through the officials. As soon as he heard it, he ordered the rich man and the poor man, together with the money, to be brought before him.

When they had all been brought in, he summoned the philosopher called “Aid of the Needy,” together with other wise men, and ordered them to hear and unravel the words of both the accuser and the accused.

When the philosopher heard this, moved by compassion for the poor man, he said: “With God’s help I shall try to free you.”

The poor man replied: “God knows that I returned as much as I found.”

Then the philosopher said to the king: “If it pleases you to hear a proper judgment concerning this matter, I shall give it.”

The king, wishing him to judge, asked him to do so.

Then the philosopher said to the king: “This rich man is a very good man, and it is not credible that he should claim anything [Col. 0690D] that he had not lost. On the other hand, it seems credible to me that this poor man found nothing more than what he returned, because if he were a bad man, he would not have returned what he did return; rather, he would have concealed the whole of it.”

Then the king said: “What judgment do you give concerning this matter, philosopher?”

The philosopher replied: “King, take the sum and give the poor man one hundred talents from it. Preserve what remains until the person to whom the sum belongs comes to claim it, since this rich man is not the owner of this sum. Let this rich man go to the herald and have him proclaim a purse containing two serpents.”

The judgment pleased the king and everyone standing around him.

When the rich man who had lost the purse heard this, he said: “Good king, I tell you truthfully that this sum was mine. But because I wanted to deprive the poor man [Col. 0691A] of what the herald had promised, I said that one more serpent was still missing. Now, king, have mercy on me, and I shall give the poor man what the herald promised.”

Then the king returned the sum to the rich man, and the rich man gave the promised amount to the poor man. Thus the philosopher freed the poor man by his intelligence and ingenuity.

**Student:** “This appears to be the ingenuity of philosophy. In light of this example, it is no wonder that Solomon judged between the two women [Note: [Col. 0691] 3 Kings, chapter III, verse 27].”

The philosopher said: “Do not set out on a journey with anyone unless you have first come to know him. If someone unknown to you joins you on the road and investigates your journey, say that you intend to travel farther than you had planned. If he is carrying a spear, go to the right; if a sword, to the left.

“An Arab admonished his son, saying: ‘Follow the paths [Col. 0691B], even when they are longer than the side roads. Also, take a young woman as your wife even if she is elderly; and likewise, take your merchandise to great cities even if you think you will sell it there more cheaply.’”

To this the son replied:

## FABLE XVI

“What you said about the great roads is true. For one day, while my companions and I were traveling toward a city, with sunset approaching and while we were still far from the city, we saw a side path that, to those traveling by sight toward the city, seemed to promise a shortcut.
