“We found an old man and asked him about the route of that path. The old man said: ‘The side path leads closer to the city than the main road, and yet you will reach the city more quickly by the main road than by the side path.’

“When we heard this, we considered him a fool. We abandoned the main road [Col. 0691C] and turned onto the side path. Following it, we wandered to the right and left throughout the night and did not reach the city. But if we had proceeded along the main road, without a doubt we would have entered the city in the middle of the night.”

The father replied:

“This happened to us on another occasion when we were traveling by the main road toward a city. A river lay before us, which we had to cross somehow before entering the city. As we traveled, the road divided into two parts: one led to the city by a ford, the other by a bridge.

“At last we saw an old man and asked him which of the two roads led to the city first. The old man said: ‘The road by the ford is shorter by two miles than the road by the bridge [Col. 0691D], but you can nevertheless travel more quickly by the bridge.’

“Some of our companions mocked that old man just as you had mocked your old man earlier, and they set out by way of the ford. But some of them left their companions drowned behind; others lost their horses and baggage; still others, soaked by the river, mourned those who had been entirely lost. We and our old man, however, having crossed by the bridge, proceeded without hindrance and without any inconvenience. We found them still on the riverbank, lamenting their loss.

“While they were weeping and searching the depths of the river with rakes and a seine, the old man said: ‘If you had traveled with us by the bridge, this would not have happened.’

“They replied: ‘We did this because we did not want to delay the journey.’

“The old man answered [Col. 0692A]: ‘Now you have been delayed even more.’ Leaving them behind, we happily entered the city gates.

“There is a proverb that I have heard: ‘The long road that leads to paradise is more valuable than the short road to hell.’”

The Arab admonished his son:

“My son, if you are on the road with a companion, love him as yourself, and do not plan to deceive anyone, lest you too be deceived, as happened to two townsmen and a peasant.”

The son said: “Tell me, so that those who come after us may gain some benefit from it.”

## FABLE XVII

It was said that two townsmen and a peasant were traveling to Mecca for prayer. They agreed to share their food until they reached Mecca. Then their food ran out, so that nothing remained except enough flour to make only a small loaf.

When the townsmen saw this [Col. 0692B], they said to one another: “We have little bread, and our companion eats a great deal. Therefore, we must devise a plan by which we can take away his share of the bread and eat it alone.”

They then agreed to make and bake the bread and, while it was baking, to sleep; whoever among them saw the most marvelous dream would eat the bread alone. They proposed this artfully because they regarded the simple peasant as suitable for such a deception.

They made the bread and baked it, and then lay down to sleep. But the peasant, having perceived their trick, pulled out the half-baked bread while his companions slept, ate it, and lay down again.

One of the townsmen awoke as though terrified by a dream and called to his companion. The other townsman said to him [Col. 0692C]: “What is the matter?”

He replied: “I saw a marvelous dream. It seemed to me that two angels opened the gates of heaven, took me, and led me [Col. 0692D] before God.”

His companion said: “The dream you saw is marvelous. But I dreamed that two angels were leading me to hell, splitting open the earth as they took me down.”

The peasant heard all this and pretended to be asleep. But the deceived townsmen, wishing to deceive him and make him wake up, called to the peasant.

The peasant, craftily pretending to be terrified, answered: “Who are those calling me?”

They replied: “We are your companions.”

The peasant said: “Have you returned already?”

They answered: “Where did we go that we should have to return?”

The peasant replied: “Just now it seemed to me that two angels took one of you, opened the gates of heaven, and led him before God. Then two other angels took the other and, after opening the earth, led him into hell. When I saw this, I thought that no one would return, so I got up and ate the bread.”

“O son! This is what happens to those who want to deceive their companion: they are deceived by their own ingenuity.”

Then the son said: “It happened to them as the proverb says: ‘Whoever wanted everything lost everything.’

“This is the nature of the dog, which those men adopted: each wishes to take food from the other. But if they had followed the nature of the camel, they would have imitated a gentler nature. For such is the nature of the camel: when food is given to many at once, none of them eats until all eat together; and if one becomes ill and is unable to eat, the others will fast until he is removed [Col. 0693A].

“These townsmen, after wanting to assume an animal nature for themselves, ought to have claimed the nature of the gentlest animal; and deservedly they lost their food.

“Indeed, I wish that this had also happened to them, as I once heard from my master that it happened to the king’s tailor because of his apprentice, whose proper name was Nediu: they were beaten with sticks.”

The father replied: “Tell me, son, what you heard about how it happened to the apprentice, since such a story will refresh the spirit.”

The son replied:

## FABLE XVIII

“My master told me that a certain king had a tailor who cut garments suited to him at different times. The tailor had apprentice tailors [Col. 0693B], each of whom skillfully sewed whatever the master, the king’s tailor, cut.

“Among them was an apprentice named Nediu who surpassed his companions in the art of sewing. But when a feast day approached, the king summoned his tailor and ordered precious garments to be prepared for himself and his household.

“To ensure that this might be done quickly and without hindrance, he assigned one of his chamberlains, a eunuch whose office this was, as overseer of the tailors, and asked him to watch their crooked fingernails and supply them with whatever they sufficiently needed.

“But one day the servants gave the tailor and his companions hot bread and honey, together with other dishes, for them to eat. Those who were present began to eat.

“While they were dining, the eunuch said: ‘Why are you eating in Nediu’s absence and not waiting for him?’

“The master said [Col. 0693C]: ‘Because he would not eat honey even if he were present.’

“And they ate.

“Then Nediu came and said: ‘Why did you eat while I was absent and not reserve my portion?’

“The eunuch replied: ‘Your master said that you would not eat honey even if you were present.’

“Nediu kept silent and considered how he might repay his master for this.

“Having made his plan, Nediu secretly said to the eunuch in his master’s absence: ‘Sir, my master sometimes suffers a fit of frenzy, loses his senses, and indiscriminately beats and kills those standing around him.’

“The eunuch replied: ‘If I knew when this happened to him, I would bind him and restrain him with straps so that he could do nothing rash.’

“Nediu said: ‘When you see him looking this way and that, beating the ground with his hands, rising from his seat [Col. 0693D], and seizing with his hand the bench on which he sits, then know that he is insane; and unless you take precautions for yourself and your men, he will split your heads with a stick.’

“After saying this, Nediu secretly hid his master’s scissors the next day. The tailor, searching for the scissors and not finding them, began striking the ground with his hands, looking this way and that, rising from his seat, and moving the bench on which he had been sitting.

“When the eunuch saw this, he immediately called his attendants and ordered the tailor to be bound and beaten severely so that he would not beat anyone else.

“But the tailor shouted: ‘What wrong have I done, that you afflict me with such blows?’

“They answered him nothing, but beat him more harshly.

“When they finally grew tired of beating him, they released him, worn out with life. He drew breath, but after a long interval [Col. 0694A] asked the eunuch what wrong he had done.

“The eunuch replied: ‘Your apprentice Nediu told me that you sometimes went mad and would stop only when restrained with bonds and corrected by blows. That is why I bound you.’

“When he heard this, the tailor summoned his apprentice Nediu and said: ‘My friend, when did you ever know me to be insane?’

“The apprentice replied: ‘When did you ever know me not to eat honey?’

“When the eunuch and the others heard this, they laughed and judged that both men had deservedly suffered their punishments.”

To this the father said: “It deservedly happened to him, because if he had observed what Moses commanded—that he should love his brother as himself [Note: [Col. 0693D] Leviticus XIX, 18]—this would not have happened to him.”

He admonished his son, saying: “See that you do not lay any accusation upon your companion, whether servant or free, lest what happened to two jesters before the king happen to you also [Col. 0694B].”

To this the son said: “Please tell me, father.”

The father replied: “So be it.”

## FABLE XIX

A certain jester came to the king. The king summoned him and had him sit and eat with another jester. But the jester who had arrived first began to envy the newcomer, whom the king and all the courtiers preferred to him.

He considered how he might shame the newcomer so that he would at least flee. Thus, without the others knowing, the first jester secretly arranged the bones and placed them before his companion. When the meal was over, he cast the pile of bones before the king as an accusation against his companion and maliciously said: “My lord, my companion has eaten the covering from all these bones.”

The king looked at him with a grim expression.

The accused said to the king: “My lord [Col. 0694C], I did what human nature required: I ate the meat and left the bones. But my companion did what his own nature—that is, a canine nature—required, because he ate the meat and the bones.”

The philosopher said: “Honor one younger than yourself and give him of what is yours, just as you wish someone older than you to honor you and give you of what is his.”

Another said: “It is very shameful for a rich man to be miserly; for a man of moderate means, it is beautiful to be generous.”

The student said: “Write down for me the definition of the generous man, the miser, and the spendthrift.”

The father replied: “He who gives to those to whom it is proper to give, and withholds from those from whom it is proper to withhold, is generous. He who withholds from those from whom it is not proper to withhold is miserly. He who gives both to those to whom it is proper to give and to those to whom it is not proper to give is a spendthrift.”

Another said: “Do not associate yourself with a failing enterprise, and do not offer yourself to a growing one.”

Another said [Col. 0694D]: “A small happiness is worth more than a house full of gold and silver.”

Another said: “Seek useful things with great judgment, not with great speed.”

Another said: “Do not look upon one richer than yourself, lest you sin against him; look instead upon one poorer than yourself, and for this give thanks to God.”

Another said: “Do not deny God because of poverty; because of wealth, do not become proud.”

Another said: “Whoever desires many things wastes away from hunger for greater things.”

Another said: “If you wish in this world to possess only as much as nature requires, you ought not to gather much. But if you wish to satisfy your desire, then even if you gathered whatever wealth the whole world contains within its circuit, your thirst for possession would still burn.”

Another said: “He who spends his possessions sparingly retains them for a long time.”

Another said [Col. 0695A]: “He who wishes to leave the world should see to it that he retains nothing belonging to it, for this is as effective as trying to extinguish fire with straw.”

Another said: “He who gathers money labors greatly and wastes away through sleepless vigilance lest he lose it; in the end, he grieves when he loses what he had acquired.”

The student said to the master: “Do you praise the gathering of money?”

The master replied: “Yes: acquire it justly and spend it for good; do not bury it in a treasury.”

Another said: “Do not desire another’s possessions, and do not grieve over possessions that have been lost, since grief will recover nothing. Hence it is said:

## FABLE XX

A certain man had a small grove in which green grass grew beside flowing streams, and, because of the suitability of the place, birds gathered there, producing various songs with the melody of their voices.

One day, while resting from his labor in his orchard [Col. 0695B], he saw a little bird sitting in a tree and singing delightfully. When he saw it and heard its song, he captured it in a snare.

The bird said to him: “Why did you labor so much to capture me, or what profit did you hope to gain from my capture?”

The man replied: “I want only to hear your songs.”

The bird answered: “For no reason, since I shall sing neither for entreaty nor for payment.”

The man said: “If you do not sing, I shall go and eat you.”

The bird replied: “How will you eat me? If you eat me boiled in water, what value will such a small bird have? Moreover, my flesh will be tough. If I am roasted, I shall become much smaller. But if you let me go, you will obtain great benefit.”

The man replied: “What benefit?”

The bird said: “I shall show you three wise precepts that you will value more highly than the flesh of three calves.”

The man, confident in the promise, let the bird go.

The bird said to him [Col. 0695C]: “The first of the precepts is: Do not believe everything that is said. The second is: Always keep what is yours. The third is: Do not grieve over what is lost.”

Having said this, the little bird climbed into the tree and began to speak in a sweet song: “Blessed is the Lord, who has closed the sight of your eyes and taken away your wisdom; for if you had searched the folds of my intestines, you would have found a hyacinth weighing one ounce.”

When the man heard this, he began to weep and beat his breast with his palms, because he had trusted the bird’s words.

But the bird said to him: “You have quickly forgotten the meaning I told you. Did I not say to you, ‘Do not believe whatever is said to you’? How can you believe that there is in me a hyacinth weighing one ounce, when I myself do not weigh so much in total? And did I not tell you: ‘Do not grieve over lost things’ [Col. 0695D]? Why do you grieve over the hyacinth that is in me?”

Having said this, and having mocked the peasant, the bird flew away into the remote parts of the forest.

The philosopher admonished his disciple, saying: “Read whatever you find, but do not believe whatever you read.”

To this the disciple replied: “I believe that not everything found in books is true. For I have read something similar in the books and proverbs of philosophers: ‘There are many trees, but not all produce fruit; there are many fruits, but not all are edible.’”

An Arab admonished his son, saying: “My son, do not abandon present things for future ones, lest perhaps you lose both, as happened to the wolf because of the oxen promised by the peasant.”

## FABLE XXI

It was said concerning a plowman that his oxen [Col. 0696A] refused to proceed in a straight line. He said to them: “May wolves eat you!”

When a wolf heard this, he accepted the promise.

As the day declined and the peasant had already unyoked the oxen from the plow, the wolf came to him and said: “Give me the oxen you promised.”

The plowman replied: “I spoke the word, but I did not confirm it by an oath.”

The wolf answered: “I ought to have them because you granted them to me.”

At last they agreed to go to court. As they did so, they met a fox.

When they approached him, the fox said: “Where are you going?”

They told the fox what had happened. He said to them: “You are seeking another judge for no reason, since I shall give you a just judgment. But first permit me to speak privately with one of you and then with the other. If I can reconcile you without a trial, the sentence will remain concealed; otherwise, it shall be given publicly.”

They agreed.

The fox [Col. 0696B] first spoke with the plowman and said: “Give me one hen and another to my wife, and you shall keep the oxen.”

The plowman agreed.

Having done this, the fox spoke with the wolf and said: “Friend, listen. Given your merits, whatever eloquence I possess ought to work on your behalf. I have spoken so much with the peasant that, if you release his oxen entirely, he will give you a cheese made as large as a shield.”

The wolf agreed to this.

The fox said to him: “Allow the plowman to lead away his oxen, and I shall take you to the place where such cheeses are made, so that you may choose whichever one you wish from among the many.”

But the wolf, deceived by the cunning fox’s words, allowed the peasant to depart peacefully.

The fox, wandering here and there, led the wolf as far astray as he could. When dark night came, he led him to a deep well. Standing over the well [Col. 0696C], he showed him the shape of the half-full moon shining at the bottom and said: “Here is the cheese I promised you. Descend, if you wish, and eat it.”

The wolf replied: “Descend first, and if you cannot bring it up by yourself, I shall do what you urge me to do and help you.”

As he said this, they saw a rope hanging in the well, with a bucket tied to one end and another bucket at the other end of the rope. They hung in such a way that when one rose, the other descended.

As soon as the fox saw this, he entered one bucket, as though complying with the wolf’s request, and reached the bottom.

The wolf, delighted, said: “Why do you not bring me the cheese?”

The fox replied: “I cannot, because of its size. Enter the other bucket and come down, as you promised me.”

When the wolf entered the other bucket, the greater weight quickly carried it to the bottom [Col. 0696D], while the other bucket, containing the lighter fox, rose.

The little fox reached the mouth of the well, leapt out, and left the wolf in the well. Thus, because he abandoned the present for the future, the wolf deservedly lost both the oxen and the cheese.

The Arab admonished his son: “Do not trust every piece of advice you hear until it has been tested to determine whether it is useful, lest what happened to the thief who trusted the advice of the master of a certain house happen to you.”

To this the son said: “How did it happen to him, father?”

The father replied:

## FABLE XXII

I was told that a certain thief went to the house of a rich man with the intention of stealing. He climbed onto the roof, listened at a window through which smoke escaped, and tried to discover whether anyone inside was awake.

When the master of the house [Col. 0697A] realized this, he said softly to his wife: “Ask me in a loud voice where this great fortune I possess came from, and take great pains to learn the truth.”

Then she said in a loud voice: “My lord, where did you acquire such a great fortune, since you have never been a merchant?”

He replied: “Keep what God has given and do with it as you wish; do not investigate where so much money came to me from.”

But she, as she had been instructed, pressed him more and more to learn the truth.

Finally, as though compelled by his wife’s entreaties, the master said: “See that you reveal our secrets to no one: I was a thief.”

She replied: “It seems astonishing to me that you could acquire such a great fortune by theft, since we have never heard either a cry or any complaint arising from it.”

He replied: “A certain master of mine taught me [Col. 0697B] a spell that I would recite when I climbed onto the roof. When I came to the window, I would take a ray of moonlight in my hand and recite my spell seven times—namely, *saulem*—and thus I would descend without danger. Whatever valuable object I found in the house, I would take away by gnawing it loose. Having done this, I would return to the ray of moonlight and, after reciting the same spell seven times, would climb up with everything taken from the house and carry what I had stolen to my lodging. By such a device I possess this fortune.”

The woman said: “You did well to tell me such things, for if I should ever have a son, I shall teach him this spell so that he may not live in poverty.”

The master said: “Let me sleep, for I am weighed down by sleep and wish to rest.” And, to deceive the thief further, he began to snore as though asleep.

After hearing these words [Col. 0697C], the thief, delighted, recited the spell seven times, took a ray of moonlight in his hand, and, loosening his hands and feet, entered through the window into the house. He fell with a great noise, breaking his leg and arm, and groaned.

The master of the house, pretending not to know, said: “Who are you, who have fallen in this way?”

The thief replied: “I am that wretched thief who trusted your deceptive words.”

To this the son said: “Father, may you be blessed, because by means of this deceit you have taught me to avoid trusting advice.”

The philosopher said: “Beware of unleavened advice until it has fermented.”

Another said: “Do not trust the advice of one who urges you to deny another’s benefaction; he who denies it in the sight of one who sees everything accuses himself.”

Another said: “If you possess some good fortune [Col. 0697D], do not sin against it, since very often the greatest good is diminished or lost.”

The disciple said to the master: “The philosopher forbade denying a benefaction.”

To this the master replied: “He who denies a benefaction denies God; and he who does not obey the victorious king is disobedient to God.”

The disciple said: “Show me how this can be so.”

The master replied: “No benefaction proceeds from one creature to another unless it proceeds from God; therefore those who deny their benefactors also deny God.”

Another said: “Guard yourself against a king who is fierce like a lion and whose temper is as light as a child’s.”

Another said: “Whoever speaks evil of the king will die before his time.”

Another said: “God allows the reign of a king who sins in his own person to endure longer, if he is good and gentle toward his subjects, than he would allow the reign of a just king to endure in his own person if he were evil and cruel toward his subjects [Col. 0698A].”

Another said: “Maintain upright justice among people and they will love you. Do not hasten to repay anyone for good or evil, because a friend will wait for you longer, and an enemy will fear you longer.”

## FABLE XXIII

Plato related in his book *On Prophecies* that there was a certain old king in Greece who was cruel toward his subjects. A great war grew against him from many regions. Wishing to know its outcome, he summoned the philosophers of his entire realm and its neighboring lands. When they had assembled, he said:

“See that a great war is threatening me and you, which I believe has come upon you because of my sin. But if there is anything in me that ought to be censured, tell me, and I shall hasten to correct it according to your judgment.”

The philosophers replied [Col. 0698B]: “We know of no criminal fault in your body, nor do we know what is going to happen to us or to you. But three days’ journey from here lives a certain wise man named Marianus, who speaks through the Holy Spirit. Therefore send some of our philosophers to him. Through them he will reveal to you what is going to happen throughout your entire life.”

When this had been arranged, the king sent seven philosophers to him. After they had entered the place where he lived, they found that most of his great city had been deserted. As they sought lodging with Marianus, they were told that he and many of his fellow citizens had gone into the wilderness.

When they heard this, they went to him. As soon as the wise man saw them, he said:

“Come, come, ambassadors of a disobedient king. God entrusted various nations [Col. 0698C] to his keeping, but he has proved not a righteous governor of them, but a harsh one. God, who created him and his subjects from the same material, long endured his immoderate wickedness and warned him through many forms of correction so that he might be converted. But finally, for his harm and leading to his death, he stirred up merciless barbarian peoples against him.”

Having said this, the wise man fell silent. When the philosophers and everyone present heard this, they marveled.

On the third day, when the philosophers asked permission to return home, that venerable man, speaking with a philosophical spirit, said: “Return, for your lord is dead, and God has already placed there a new king who is a righteous governor and gentle toward his subjects.”

When the philosophers who had come heard this, three remaining with the wise man, the other four [Col. 0698D] returned home. They found everything true and established just as it had been told to them.

The Arab said to his son: “Do not remain in the city of a king whose expenses will exceed his revenues.”

## FABLE XXIV

It was said that, by the common agreement of his nobles, a certain king entrusted the reins of the entire kingdom to one of his retainers whom he had previously known to be prudent in secular affairs. He was to collect the revenues of the provinces and adjudicate their cases.

This man’s brother, a wealthy merchant of another kingdom, lived in a distant city. When he learned of his brother’s elevation, he set out with a suitably prepared retinue to visit him. At last he sent a messenger ahead, so that he would not arrive suddenly or unexpectedly, to inform his brother of his coming [Col. 0699A].

When he approached the city where his brother was staying, the brother, having heard of his arrival, went out to meet him and received him with a cheerful expression and considerable care.

After several days had passed, he chose a suitable time and place and reported to the king, among other things that he knew would please him, that his brother had arrived.

The king said to him: “If your brother agrees to remain with you in my kingdom, I grant that the guardianship of all my possessions shall be shared with him as with you. But if he refuses the work, I shall give him extensive estates in this city and remit the customary services and whatever he ought to perform for me. If, finally, moved by love of his native soil, he wishes to return home, give him an abundance of changes of clothing and whatever else he may need.”

When the brother heard the king’s words [Col. 0699B], he went to his brother and repeated in order everything the lord had promised.

His brother said: “If you want me to remain with you, show me how great the king’s revenues are.”

He showed him all of them.

Then the brother asked what expenses the king incurred, and the man explained them to him. He then calculated together with his brother that the expenses were as great as the revenues and said to him:

“My friend, I see that the king’s expenses are as great as his revenues. If war should arise against your king, or anything of that kind, from where will he provide soldiers, or where will he find money for them?”

His brother replied: “We shall acquire it by some plan.”

The other answered: “I fear that my own fortune may be part of that plan. Therefore, farewell, for I do not wish to remain any longer.”

Philosopher: A king is like fire: if you approach it too closely, you will be burned; if you withdraw entirely, you will grow cold. [Col. 0699C]

Son to father: If I believe the philosopher’s words, I shall never be familiar with a king.

Father: My son, pleasing a king is the height of prudence.

Son: Father, teach me how, if it should be necessary for me to serve a king, I may be able to please him as a prudent and well-instructed man.

Father: For instruction of this kind, many things would be necessary, which we do not now recall to mind; and perhaps, if they were prescribed to you while you are still young, they would become tedious. But we shall report a few of the many things which, if you observe them, will be useful.

The son replied: And since I desire to hear many things with attentive ears, I eagerly and earnestly demand what you have promised me.

Father: Whoever wishes to be familiar with a king must see with the full vision of his mind that, when he comes before the king, he can stand for a long time. He must never sit down until the king gives the order; he must not speak unless there is need; he must not remain with the king unless the king orders him to remain; and he must faithfully keep counsel. He should always be attentive to hear what the king says, so that the king does not have to repeat an order twice. Whatever the king commands, he should do. He must take care not to lie to the king, and thus he will be obedient to him; nor should he ever associate with a man whom the king hates. When he has done all these things, and many others besides, perhaps he will receive no great profit from the king.

Son: Nothing worse can happen to a man than to serve a king for a long time and acquire nothing good.

Father: This has already happened to many; and therefore the philosopher instructed that no one should remain too long in the service of a king.

Philosopher: “He who serves a king without fortune loses both this age and the next.” [Col. 0700A]

Son: O Father, why have you forgotten to say how a man ought to eat in the presence of a king?

Father: I did not forget to say it, because there is no difference between eating before a king and eating elsewhere.

Son: Tell me, then, how I ought to eat everywhere.

Father: When you have washed your hands in order to eat, touch nothing except your meal until you eat. Do not eat bread before another dish comes upon the table, lest you be called impatient; nor should you put so large a morsel into your mouth that crumbs fall here and there, lest you be called a glutton. Do not swallow a morsel before it has been thoroughly chewed in your mouth, lest you choke; and do not take a drink until your mouth is empty, lest you be called a drunkard. Do not speak while you have anything in your mouth, lest something pass from your throat into the inner windpipe and become the cause of your death. If you see a morsel that pleases you on a serving dish before your companion, do not take it, lest you be accused of disgraceful rusticity. After the meal, wash your hands, because this is medically sound and salutary; for this reason many people’s eyes grow worse when they rub them after meals without washing their hands. [Col. 0700B]

Son: If someone invites me to a meal, how shall I reply? Shall I accept immediately or not?

Father: Do as the authority of the Jews commands. [Note: [Col. 0699D] Talmud.] For it says: “If someone invites you to a meal, look at the status of the person inviting you. If he is an important person, accept immediately; otherwise, according to his standing, accept on the second or third invitation.” This is also related of Abraham. One day, while he was standing before his door, he saw three angels passing by in human form. He respectfully asked them to enter his house, wash their feet, partake of food, and refresh their weary limbs with sleep. Since he was an important person, they consented to his request. [Note: [Col. 0700D] Genesis XVIII.]

Young man to old man: When I am invited to a meal, should I eat little or much?

Old man: Much. For if the person who invited you is your friend, he will rejoice greatly; but if he is your enemy, he will be distressed.

When the boy heard this, he laughed. The old man said to him: I have remembered a saying I heard about Black Maimundus. An old man once asked him how much he could eat. Maimundus asked him: “At whose meal—mine or someone else’s?” The old man replied: “At yours.” Maimundus said: “As much as I possibly can.”

Old man: You are now remembering the words of a certain glutton, idler, fool, chatterer, and trifler; and whatever is said about him is found in him to an even greater degree.

Young man: I am very pleased to hear about him, because everything about him is ridiculous. If you retain in your mind anything about his sayings or deeds, tell it, and I shall regard it as a gift.

Old man.

## FABLE XXV

One night a master ordered his servant to shut the door. But the servant, overcome by laziness, could not get up, and therefore said that it had been shut. In the morning the master said to the servant: “Maimundus, open the door.”

The servant replied: “Master, I knew that you wanted it to be open today, and therefore I did not wish to shut it late yesterday.”

Only then did the master discover that the servant had left it open out of laziness, and he said: “Get up and do your work, for it is day and the sun is already high.”

The servant replied: “If the sun is already high, give me something to eat.”

The master said: “Wicked servant, do you want to eat at night?”

The servant replied: “If it is night, allow me to sleep.”

Again, at night, the master said to him: “Maimundus, get up and see whether it is raining or not.”

The servant called a dog that was lying outside the door. When the dog came, he felt its feet; finding them dry, he said to his master: “Master, it is not raining.”

Again, at night, the master asked him whether there was a fire in the house. He called a cat and tested whether it was warm or not; finding it cold, he said: “No.” [Col. 0701A]

Young man: I have heard about his laziness; now I wish to hear about his chatter.

Old man: It is said that his master was returning happily from the market because he had made a considerable profit. The servant Maimundus went out to meet his master. When the master saw him, he feared that, as was his custom, the servant would tell him some news, and he said: “Take care not to tell me any bad news.”

The servant replied: “Our little dog, Pipella, has died.”

The master asked: “How did she die?”

The servant replied: “Our mule was frightened and broke its halter. As it ran away, it suffocated the dog beneath its feet.”

The master asked: “What happened to the mule?”

The servant replied: “It fell into a well and died.”

“How was the mule frightened?”

“Your son fell from the upper room and died, and the mule was frightened by this.”

“What is his mother doing?”

“Overcome by grief at the death of her child, she died.”

“Who is guarding the house?”

“No one, because it has been turned to ashes, together with everything that was in it.”

“How was it burned?”

“On the same night that the mistress died, the maidservant who was watching over her forgot a candle in the bedroom, and so the entire house was burned.”

“Where is the maidservant?”

“She wanted to put out the fire, fell upon her head, and died.”

“How did you escape, since you are so lazy?”

“When I saw that the maidservant was dead, I fled.”

Then the master, greatly saddened, went to his neighbors, asking them to receive him and give him lodging in one of their houses. Meanwhile he met one of his friends. When the friend saw him grieving, he asked why he was so sad. The master recounted everything his servant had told him.

The friend, wishing to console the desolate man, recited these verses to him:

“Friend, do not be desolate, for often such grave floods of adversity befall a man that he wishes to end them even by a dishonorable death; and immediately such great benefits come to him that it is altogether sweet for him to remember his former adversities. But this immense fluctuation of human affairs is distinguished by the judgment of the Supreme Ruler, according to the varying order of merits.”

This is confirmed by the example of the prophet Job, whose spirit was not cast down by the loss of his possessions. [Note: [Col. 0701] Job I, 22.]

Have you not also heard what the philosopher said: “Who can possess anything stable in this age, since it is changeable?”

The Arab to his son: My son, whenever something adverse should happen to you, do not be excessively desolate or excessively grieved because of it, for this is a kind of denial of God. You must always praise God both for adversity and for prosperity. Many evils befall people in order that they may escape greater evils; and many things happen that end in good. Therefore you must praise God in everything and trust in him, as the versifier said:

“When you are in sadness, do not be anxious on account of it,  
but leave the hour to its appointed ordering;  
always hope for what is good to come,  
and thus you will forget your sorrows,  
because many evils occur that end in good.”

Philosopher: The goods of this age are mixed; for you will not eat honey without poison.

Another: Whatever exists in this age is changeable; and whatever good things are destined to come to you from them, even if you are weak, you will have them, while you will not be able, by your strength, to avoid evils.

Another: What gives the lazy man his desired attainments denies the swift man the things he wants to obtain.

Another: By its attractiveness the world disgraces itself, and the earth swallows and devours the person who desires it.

Another: The glory of the world ends as if in the blink of an eye, and frail care sees that it does not remain as it desires.

## FABLE XXVI

It is commonly said that Socrates, avoiding worldly tumult and longing for a rustic life, lived in a grove and inhabited half a barrel in place of a hut. Its bottom was turned toward the wind and rain, while the open part faced the pleasant sun. When the king’s hunters found him and saw him there, they mocked him for suffocating lice and began to deprive him of the pleasantness of the sun’s rays.

With a calm expression he said to them: “Do not presume to take away from me what you do not give me.”

Angered by this, they wanted to expel him from the shelter where he lived and lead him away from the road, so that the eyes of the passing king would not be offended by so base a person. When they could not do this, they threatened him, saying: “See to it that no evil befalls you through your insolent behavior, for our king and lord, with his household and nobles, will pass this way.”

But when the philosopher saw them barking at him, he said: “Your lord is not my lord; rather, he is the servant of my servant.”

When they heard this and looked at him with stepmotherly faces, some of them resolved to cut him to pieces. The less wicked among them decided to wait until they had heard the king’s judgment.

While they were quarreling in this way, the king arrived. He asked the cause of the dispute, and, when his servants reported it, learned what had been done and said. Wishing to discover whether the philosopher’s words had been invented, the king hurried to him and asked what he had said about him.

As he had said to the servants, the philosopher asserted that the king was the servant of his servant. The king kindly asked him to explain carefully the meaning of these words.

The philosopher, maintaining the dignity of his expression, gently replied: “My will is subject to me and serves me; I do not serve it. You, on the contrary, are subject to your will and serve it; it does not serve you. Therefore you are the servant of one who serves me.”

Then the king, lowering his gaze for a while, began: “As is clear from your words, you confess that power is nothing.”

The philosopher, withdrawing into the narrow chamber of his mind, replied: “You yourself know that ambition for mortal things has exercised too great a dominion over you, and that you desired opportunities for accomplishing deeds, lest your virtue, as you yourself admit, grow accustomed to remaining silent. But because of your desire for glory, you have done what was necessary to attain it, as the truth of the matter shows. Consider how slight it is and how entirely devoid of weight.

“Your past power, since it is now nothing, is not to be feared; nor is your future power, whose outcome is doubtful and uncertain. As for the present, it is clear that it is so small and so fleeting that it will be destroyed in the blink of an eye. For this reason it is not to be feared in any respect.”

Finally, having understood the philosopher’s words, the king said to his companions: “He is a servant of God. See that you do nothing troublesome or dishonorable to him.” [Col. 0703B]

Disciple to master: Since these things are so fleeting and slight, why do we prepare so much as though they were lasting?

Master: Because the end of life is uncertain.

Philosopher: “Work for the age to come as though you were about to die now, and for the present as though you were always going to live. For it is better that after your death your enemies should have what you sought than that during your life you should lack what your enemies might provide for you.” Therefore provide everything for yourself honorably, because the course of life is short.

Another: The world is like an unstable spring: its entrance is the mother’s womb, and its exit will be death.

Versifier:

“Death is an open gate, accessible to all earthly beings;  
but I ask what dwelling is to be possessed after it.”

There is a dwelling of delights for those who serve God, and there is another, with different punishments, for those who deserve them.

The Arab to his father: Father, how will I be able to gain the dwelling of delights and its glory?

Father: Place in it whatever you have that is best and most precious, so that it may be kept there; and when you arrive there, you will find it prepared for you.

Son: How can I send money ahead to a house whose door I do not know how to approach?

Father: Hear what the son of the king’s counsellor did after his father’s death.

Son: Father, tell me; I shall not evade obedience to your admonitions.

Father.

## FABLE XXVII

A certain king had a wise counsellor and intimate companion who, when he was finally summoned by the laws of nature, left behind a young heir, well-disciplined and courtly. To him he transferred his entire estate, which was large, together with his heaps of wealth, and then surrendered to death.

After this, the king summoned the boy to him. He admonished him not to grieve more than was fitting over his father’s death, confirmed by his testimony everything that the father had entrusted to him to administer, and further promised that, when his age required it, he would receive him in his father’s place.

After taking his leave, the cheerful young man returned home. The king forgot him, and the young man himself did not hurry to return to the king.

After a long interval of time, the people in the same region where the boy lived began to suffer such need that they were endangered by hunger and lacked food. Seeing this, the boy, being of good character, felt compassion in his heart. He emptied his granaries and distributed the contents to the poor; from his storehouse he brought out wine and meat, which he gave to the needy.

As the scarcity increased, his dwindling money was no longer sufficient for those in need. Then he gave his treasure for grain and did not delay in sustaining, as long as he could, the lives of those suffering from hunger or thirst; but even this did not suffice.

He did the same with his clothing and precious stones. Thus a year passed, during which he had already freed not a few people from the bonds of death. [Col. 0704A]

Now in the same region there was a certain notary of the aforementioned king who, touched by the stain of envy, begrudged the boy and secretly practiced grave hostility against him. He inflamed the king’s anger against the boy with these words:

“Lord, your mildness of character toward the son of your counsellor, whose father left him an immeasurable fortune, was, not to call it foolish, excessively indulgent. For now neither you nor he has any money, since this thoughtless man has squandered it all in excess.”

The king was angered by these words and sent for the boy. To him he said:

“Foolish son of a wise man, idle son of a skilful man, wasteful son of a generous man, why have you handed over to destruction the wealth wisely gathered and entrusted to you for safekeeping?”

At this the boy lowered his eyes to the ground, for he feared the ruler’s angry face, inflamed as it was by grim eyes. He said:

“Lord, if I may speak with your permission, I was not left to you by a wise father as a fool, as some think. My father gathered a treasure, placed the treasure where thieves could seize it, and left it to me in a place from which you could take it, or fire could burn it, or some accident could snatch it away.

“I, however, placed it where it would be faithfully preserved both for itself and for me.”

The king asked him what he had done with it.

The boy recounted what he had done and how he had done it.

When the young man’s skill had finally been discovered, the king first praised him before those standing around him and rewarded him, repaying the service of his father. From then on the boy acquired new and greater riches by profitable dealings. In this way the son of the king’s counsellor stored away what he possessed of value in the treasury of the dwelling of delights.

After hearing his father’s words, the son said: “This young man acted wisely and showed in himself a great indication of future goodness. He did as the philosopher instructed his son, saying: ‘My son, sell this age for the age to come, and you will gain both.’ And so it happened.”

Another, correcting his son, said: “My son, work for the age to come before death separates you from bodily labor.”

Another: “See that worldly delights do not deceive you, and that, ensnared by worldly deceptions, you do not forget the death that is to come, lest what happened to the thief entering the house of a rich man happen to you.”

The son said to him: “Tell me, father, what happened.”

Father:

## FABLE XXVIII

A thief entered the house of a rich man and found it filled with various treasures. Astonished, he carefully set about choosing among different things, selecting the more precious from among the precious. Since he spent time in choosing while leaving the less valuable things behind, day came before he had decided what he wanted to do.

The household guards, suddenly awakened, found the thief still choosing. They seized him, beat him with leather straps and clubs, and thrust him into the lowest part of the prison.

Finally, after hearing bitter stories and receiving the sentence that had already been pronounced against a confessed criminal, he underwent capital punishment. If he had foreseen that the day would come so soon, he would have taken precautions so that he would not be beaten with straps and clubs—or, what was more serious, so that he would not be deprived of his head.

Another philosopher said: “The riches of this age are transitory, like the dreams of a sleeping man. When he wakes, whatever he had is irrecoverably lost as soon as he opens his eyes,” as the proverb says. [Col. 0705A]

## FABLE XXIX

A shepherd once had a thousand sheep in a dream. A certain man, wishing to buy them at a high price in order to sell them more dearly, wanted to give two solidi for each one, just as it appeared to the dreaming shepherd. But the seller, in addition to the two solidi, demanded one denarius more for each sheep.

While they were arguing about the price, the dream vanished in this manner. But the seller, when he realized that it had been a dream, began to shout without opening his eyes:

“Give me twenty-five denarii for each one, and lead away as many as are with you.”

In this way the day that comes unexpectedly, and the end of life, overtake those who pursue the passing joys of the world and long to retain various things. Whether they wish it or not, they are deprived of everything they desired. [Col. 0705B]

The son again: Will we be able somehow to escape the bonds of death?

Father: Not at all, for its bite is incurable, and we shall not escape its bitter hands through medical arts.

Son: How, then, shall we endure it, so that it may not harm us too greatly?

Father: Do as the versifier says:

“What you cannot avoid, receive with steadfast mind;  
thus death, which was harsh to you, will be gentle.”

## FABLE XXX

It is said of a certain philosopher that, while passing through an ancient cemetery, he saw a marble slab placed over the ashes of a dead man. On it were inscribed verses expressing the words of the buried man speaking to passers-by in this manner:

“You who pass nearby and do not say, ‘Hail,’ stop;  
hold these words of mine in the ears of your heart.

I am what you will be; I myself was what you are,  
mocking bitter death while I was permitted,  
with peace assisting, to enjoy life.

But when death came, after I had been snatched  
from my friends and servants,  
my house, bereft of its parent,  
covered me with earth and mourned me as I lay.

Upon my ashes it bestowed its final gifts;  
then the earth gnawed away the brightness of my face,  
and all the great glory of my appearance fell away.

You could not recognize that I had been a man  
if I were now perhaps uncovered from the earth  
and brought again into view.

Therefore pray for me to God with a pure mind,  
that he may grant me to enjoy eternal peace;  
and whoever prays for me, let him bring about this one thing:  
that he may remain with me in the heavenly region.”

After reading these verses again and again, the philosopher abandoned worldly affairs and became a hermit. [Col. 0705D]

It is also related of Alexander that his tomb was made of gold and placed in an open courtyard accessible to everyone. Many philosophers gathered there, and one of them said:

“Alexander made a treasure from gold; now, conversely, gold makes a treasure from him.”

Another: “Yesterday the whole world was not enough for him; today four ordinary cubits are enough for him. Yesterday he commanded the people; today the people command him.”

Another: “Yesterday he was able to free many peoples from death; today he could not avoid even its arrows.”

Another: “Yesterday he led armies; today he is led by them and given to burial.”

Another: “Yesterday he pressed down upon the earth; today the earth itself presses upon him.”

Another: “Yesterday nations feared him; today they count him as worthless.”

Another: “Yesterday he had friends and enemies; today he has all people as equals.”

But it would be tedious to recall to memory what each of the twenty-two philosophers standing around him said about the most powerful king.

Again, the philosopher-hermit corrected his soul in this manner:

“My soul, know and understand what you are doing while power is in your hand, before you move from your place to the house where justice dwells and to the gate of judgment, where the laws record on a scroll everything that your hand has done in this age; where the angels, on the right and on the left, will uncover and report your purpose and whatever you have conceived.

“Your judgment will come before God. On one scale, whatever good you have done, and on another, whatever evil, will be revealed in one and the same examination. All your brothers and friends will not find your ransom; they will abandon and leave you.

“Therefore obtain redemption today, do good continually, and return to God before the day of summons comes. Do not say, ‘Tomorrow I shall return, and I shall not delay,’ because desire may hinder you while you postpone until tomorrow, or perhaps the final day may hold you back. Therefore remember the days of the world, the generations of ancient years, all of which have passed away.

“From this draw understanding: Where are the kings? Where are the princes? Where are the rich, who stored up treasures and became proud because of them? Now they are as those who never existed; now they have ended as those who never lived; now they are like a leaf that falls from a tree and does not return to it.

“Do not fear, my soul, do not fear. Let your fear not arise excessively from the adversities of this age. Fear the day of your judgment; dread the multitude of your sins; remember your Creator, who is your judge and witness.” [Col. 0706C]

Another hermit cried out through the streets: “Do not consign lasting things to oblivion in exchange for things that will have an end.”

Another: “Love your souls as much as your bodies, and you will perfect them.”

Another: “Do not forget the one who does not forget us, and serve the governor.”

Another: “Fear the Lord, because the fear of the Lord is the key to every good thing and the means of attaining glory.”

Concerning this Solomon says: “Fear God and observe his commandments, for this is the whole of man.” [Note: [Col. 0705] “And observe his commandments: for this is the whole of man. And so forth. Ecclesiastes XII, 13–14.]

“God will bring every deed into judgment, including every error, whether it is good or evil.” [Col. 0706D]

For this reason, therefore, we suppliantly beseech the immense omnipotence of God that, with your good works going before, after the strict day of judgment we may deserve to be placed at the right hand of his Son and to enjoy eternal rest with his faithful in the heavenly court; through our Lord Jesus Christ, to whom are honor and glory with the Father and the Holy Spirit, for ever and ever. Amen.

Here ends *The Clerical Discipline*, translated by Peter Alfonso from Arabic into Latin.

In the year of the Lord 1110. Walter of the Islands, Bishop of Maguelone, and Lietbert, Abbot of Saint-Ruf.

[Col. 0707]

## HISTORICAL NOTICE ON WALTER

(*Gallia Christiana nova*, vol. VI, p. 745.)

[Col. 0707A] Walter immediately succeeded Gothofredus. He was born at Insula, a town of Flanders, a man long trained through diligent study in divine learning and not ignorant of secular letters, outstanding in intelligence and distinguished in eloquence. In his own time he was highly esteemed for his learning and education.

This is that Walter whom Gariellus improperly separates from Walter, Bishop of Maguelone, mentioned by Trithemius. For Trithemius must be read as saying “Maguelonensem,” not “Magolensem”; this is proved by Walter’s own letter to Robert, provost of Insula, published by Mabillon, since the catalogue of bishops assigns no episcopate either to Magala in Palestine or to Magalis in Spain.

From this letter and another written by Bruno, Bishop of Segni, to Walter, found in volume XII of the *Spicilegium*, [Col. 0707B] p. 79, it appears that Walter devoted himself greatly to the sacred Scriptures while he was living at Insula. The poems of Verdala teach that he later served under Gothofredus before becoming bishop.

After the death of his master, the disciple succeeded him in 1103, or at least in 1104, as is clear from an ancient charter issued on 9 May 1125, which Walter counted as the twenty-second year of his episcopate, as we have said.

Having become bishop, he applied himself to restoring sacred buildings. He supported the partly ruined basilica of Maguelone; built from the foundations the tower of the Holy Sepulchre, the refectory, the dormitory, and a chamber; increased the church’s priestly furnishings; supplied it with gold, silver, and silk; and granted the churches of Saint Brice and Laureto to the canons.

He was chosen by Paschal II, together with ten other arbiters, to report on the dispute that had arisen between the abbots of Casade and Aniane concerning the monastery of Gordanics; the supreme pontiff suppressed this dispute at Valence in 1107.

He confirmed in 1110, indiction III, the church of Saint Martin of Lundres, granted to the monks of Gellone by the blessed Gothofredus of venerable memory, retaining for himself a fourth part of the tithes and of the offerings, and securing twelve Melgorian solidi for the canons, according to the Gellone archive.

At about the same time, William, lord of Montpellier, swore an oath of fidelity to Walter. In 1111 Eleazar of Castries granted him the church of Saint Martin of Cretio, a fourth part of the tithes of Saint Michael of Agusanica, and whatever he had previously granted to Gothofredus.

Walter attended the Council of Vienne in 1112. In the same year William of Fabrègues, through Walter, granted to the church of Saint Baudilius the hill on which the church stood and everything he possessed in the valley of Carrières.

Ato of Cornone paid half of the tithe of Saint Michael of Grimianica to the monks of Gellone through Walter on 11 May 1113. [Col. 0708A]

William, lord of Montpellier, while setting out against the pagans to conquer the island of Majorca, made his will in 1114 on the advice of the same bishop. To Walter and the church of Maguelone he bequeathed the entire town of Montpellier, which had anciently been the allod of Saint Peter’s church of Maguelone, the entire fief that he held from the bishop in the parish of Saint Firmin and Saint Dionysius of Montpelliéret, and other possessions.

Walter subscribed the will; William entrusted the copy to him for safekeeping. In the same year Peter Bernard, Bishop of Elne, summoned Walter so that together they might bring to an end the long-standing dispute between the monasteries of Cuxa and Arul concerning the church of Saint Peter of Turrilles.

At about the same time Pontius Raymond restored to Walter whatever he possessed in the church of Saint Stephen of Pinian. Ademar of Montarnald left him the church of Senteiranica; Peter of Salses mortgaged to him the church of Casa Vetere and a fief in Gigean for four Melgorian pounds.

He received the homage of William Ribaute, son of Dalmatius, and of Raymond of Castries for the castle of Gigean. Count Bernard and his wife Guillelma restored to him the cemetery and its site beside the church of Saint Romanus of Melgueil.

Eleazar of Monterotondo left the church of Saint Giles of Fisco to the community of the see of Maguelone for fifty Melgorian solidi, in Walter’s hands. [Col. 0708C]

He is listed among the bishops who consecrated the church of Cassian in 1115; Walter himself solemnly dedicated its altar to the holy apostles Peter and Paul, Andrew, James, and Saint Faith.

At the request of the bishops of Viviers and Avignon, he confirmed in 1116 the church of Saint Vincent of Junquières, already granted by his predecessor to Stephen, abbot of La Chaise-Dieu, and added the churches of Saint Peter of Portian and Caucon.

In 1118 he approved the construction of the church of Murs. He attended the Council of Toulouse, where he subscribed the judgment given by Calixtus II in favor of the monks of Aniane on 15 July 1119.

Gariellus assigns to the same year a building erected by William of Montpellier for the Templars in the suburb of Sonaria and the church of Blessed Mary of Lezès, now Saint John the Great, which was dedicated by Walter and later converted into a preceptory. But this learned man did not notice that the Templars did not penetrate into the West before 1128. [Col. 0709B]

Walter subscribed, together with many bishops, the bull issued by Calixtus II on 14 July 1120 for the monastery of Electa. He is mentioned in a charter of Raymond of Cornone and his wife Ricarda for the monastery of Gellone on 6 December 1121.

In the same year William, lord of Montpellier, dying, bequeathed all his silver vessels to the church of Maguelone.

In 1122 Walter attended a gathering held at Caslar in the diocese of Lodève, where, by his judgment, the dispute between the monks of Juncellus and Conques concerning the church of Casulas was brought to an end.

Since Walter could not reconcile William of Montpellier and the count of Melgueil, although he was endowed with great eloquence and gentleness, he wrote to Pope Calixtus II. In 1124 the pope induced Peter, Archbishop of Vienne; Hugh, Bishop of Grenoble; Hildegarius, Bishop of Tarragona; and Artaldus, Bishop of Carpentras, to settle these hostilities together with Walter.

The arbiters, therefore, chosen in the church of Saint Martin of Cretio, assembled on Saturday, 9 May 1125, in the twenty-second year of Walter’s episcopate. There they defined all the matters disputed between the count and the lord, and persuaded William to swear an oath of fidelity to Bernard.

Walter reported this settlement to Robert, provost of Insula, in a letter in which he called himself a legate of the Holy Roman Church—a title with which he may have been honored by the supreme pontiff so that he might preside over the judgment between the count and the lord.

Under this same title he excommunicated the monks of Casade, who had renewed their lawsuit against the Anianese concerning the church of Gordanics. At the urging of the same arbiters, William also rendered to Walter the oath of fidelity that he had previously refused, as is clear from the acts of the consuls cited by Gariellus.

About this time, what Walter had not yet been able to accomplish because he was occupied with the burdens of pastoral office and the legation, he finally fulfilled. He did not, as Trithemius says, write two books, but published the *Flowers of the Psalms*, collected by Lietbert, canon of Saint Peter at Insula and later abbot of Saint-Ruf, and sent them to Robert, his kinsman and provost of Insula, and to the other canons of that church.

Trithemius also attributes to him letters to various persons, not inelegantly written, and several other works.

Finally, when the abbot of Aniane refused to attend the synods of Maguelone, the matter was brought by the bishop before Honorius II, then seated in the chair of Saint Peter. The supreme pontiff commissioned the archdeacon and precentor of the church of Agde by a bull issued at the Lateran on 31 May, in the fifth year of his pontificate, in the year of Christ 1129.

When this was communicated through the legates, Peter, abbot of Aniane, promised obedience according to God to Bishop Walter before the altar of Saint Brice and yielded several churches. In turn, the bishop, with the consent of the canons, gave the church of Saint Mary of Roveto to the monastery of Aniane and exchanged other properties with the aforesaid abbot, as is recorded in an ancient instrument preserved by Gariellus. [Col. 0710B]

It is necessary to conclude that Walter died not long after this agreement had been reached. Raymond, his successor, was already presiding in August, as we shall soon see.

After his death, he was buried in the same place where his predecessor Gothofredus had been laid, as is established by the poems given below. From this Gariellus concludes that, toward the end of his life, Walter, an imitator of the piety of his predecessor bishops, went to Palestine, died there, and was buried on Mount Pilgrim in the same tomb as his predecessor.

But since the former claim is not established, and is questioned by some, as we have already said, the latter remains uncertain and exceeds all credibility because of the shortness and brevity of the available interval of time.

In the ancient necrology of the church of Maguelone one reads: “On the first Monday after the synod of Easter, the chapter is required to celebrate a Mass for the soul of Lord Walter, Bishop of Maguelone.”

His death is assigned to 5 December in the necrology preserved in the library of the Friars Preachers at Chambéry, where he is called a monk of Molesme, a detail that I have so far found nowhere else.

An old poem at Verdala also sang of Walter:

“Walter succeeds him, his son,  
a son in obedience, a son in office,  
learned and clever, famous and incisive in verse, [Note: [Col. 0709D] Perhaps misled by this passage, the very learned Pagi confuses our Walter with Walter of Châtillon, the celebrated poet who flourished in the thirteenth century. Others, however, read *percomis* (‘very courteous’).]  
great in counsel and great in eloquence,  
pure in body and severe in religion,  
intolerant of crime and compassionate toward the wretched.  
He increased the followers of the Rule and our honors;  
the treasury, the buildings, the reputation, and the house grew.  
Then, following the sad footprints of his master by an unhappy fate,  
he died and was placed where his father had previously been.”

[Col. 0711]

## HISTORICAL NOTICE ON LIETBERT

(*Fabricius, Bibliotheca medii et infimi latini*, IV, 271).

# Historical Notice on Lietbert

Lethbertus, or Lietbertus, an Augustinian canon of Lille, later abbot of Saint-Ruf near Valence in Narbonnese Gaul. He wrote explanations, or *Flowers of the Psalms*, which Galterus, bishop of Maguelone, afterward sent to Robert, provost of Lille, after Lietbert had collected them. Galterus, bishop of Maguelone, mentions manuscripts of the work, besides Oudinus, volume II, page 1081, and Sanderus, page 154. Galterus held the bishopric of Maguelone from 1108 to 1129. Pitseus is therefore mistaken when, following Bale, XIII, 32, he assigns this Lietbertus to the year 1210. [The authors of the *Histoire littéraire de la France*, volume IX, report and demonstrate that this learned man did not live beyond 1101, or at least 1114. For his other writings, see the same authors, page 577. MANSI.]

# Literary Notice

(*Histoire littéraire de la France*, volume IX, page 575.)

The writings of the pious and learned abbot Lietbert shared in the fame enjoyed by their author. A great many copies of them are found among the manuscripts of the libraries of France and England. Nevertheless, all bibliographers, up to and including Trithemius, omitted him from their catalogues. Jean Bale was the first to raise him to the rank of an ecclesiastical writer, and this honor was rightly due to him, if not for the number, at least for the merit, of his works.

## 1

There is by him a Commentary on the Psalms, entitled *The Flowers of the Psalms*, or, more properly, *The Flowers on the Psalter* [Note: [Col. 0711] Mabillon, *Analecta*, volume I, pages 289–290; Sanderus, *Bibliotheca Belgica*, manuscript section, volume I, page 97.]. Lietbert worked on it when he was still merely a canon of Lille, and seems to have completed it only after he became abbot. He gave it the title it bears because he had drawn it from the Fathers of the Church who had undertaken before him to explain the Psalms, especially Saint Augustine and Cassiodorus. The work is almost entirely moral, since the author’s principal aim was to collect whatever seemed most suitable for correcting the vices that were then disfiguring the face of the Church. The abundance of the material obliged him to divide it into two parts, although some copies are found divided into three.

When Lietbert left Lille, he took the work with him; evidently it was not yet finished. After his death—or even during his lifetime—Gautier, bishop of Maguelone, who knew the author personally and held him in extraordinary esteem, managed to obtain a copy. Some time later, when the duties of his legation had taken him to Lille, where he stayed for a while, Hescelin, a canon of the place who had heard about Lietbert’s Commentary, earnestly asked the bishop-leg

ate to let him read all or part of it. Since Gautier’s extensive responsibilities prevented him from immediately granting Hescelin’s request, Hescelin repeated his appeals until he obtained what he sought.

Bishop Gautier sent the work, together with a letter in his own name, to Robert, provost of Lille and his close relative, so that all Robert’s associates, and especially Hescelin, might read it whenever they wished. From that time onward copies of the Commentary multiplied greatly.

Copies are found, sometimes in two volumes, as the author himself divided it, and sometimes in three, in the libraries of England, the Netherlands, and, in still greater numbers, France [Note: [Col. 0711] Pitseus, *Scriptores Angliae*, page 275; Sanderus, same work, pages 97, 154, 238; Andreas, *Bibliotheca Belgica*, page 626; Oudinus, *Scriptores*, volume II, page 1081; Montfaucon, *Bibliotheca bibliothecarum*, page 1182; Le Long, *Bibliotheca sacra*, volume II, page 287. — The three-volume copy preserved in the Premonstratensian abbey of Braine, in the diocese of Soissons, is in the hand of John of Abbeville, a monk of that house who later became a cardinal, around 1210 (Hugo, *Annales Praemonstratenses*, volume I, part I, page 411).]. But the bishop Gautier’s letter, which ordinarily stands at the beginning and clearly indicates that the Commentary belongs to Lietbert, has sometimes caused the work to be credited to the bishop of Maguelone. It is in fact identified by his name in the King’s Library and in the libraries of the abbeys of Clairvaux and Pontigny.

This Commentary begins with the words: “Prophecy is divine inspiration.” Estienne Petringon, a learned theologian and skilled preacher of the Order of Saint Francis, who was bishop of Saint David’s at the beginning of the fifteenth century, made extensive use of it in his own time. One may consult the dissertation that M. de Villebrun, parish priest of Montpellier, published on the author of this Commentary; it appeared in the *Mercure français* for November 1739.

## 2

We have two letters by Lietbert, written when he was already abbot, one fairly lengthy and the other very short. The first [Note: [Col. 0711] Martène, *Anecdota*, volume I, pages 329–332.] is addressed to Otgier, provost or superior of a house called Ferran, otherwise unknown, and to his entire community. But the author intended it also to circulate generally, as the subject demanded; hence, in the address, he includes all who had embraced the order of regular canons. Lietbert aims to show that the more excellent this order is, the more perfection and holiness it requires of those who profess it. To demonstrate its excellence, he joins it to the priesthood, from which it was ordinarily inseparable. He first says that the order was prefigured by the priesthood of the ancient law, and that everything said about the clothing and ministry of the priests and Levites of that time is a figure of what regular canons ought to practice.

[Col. 0713] From there he proceeds to the New Law and adds that Jesus Christ himself prescribed their way of life, which was put into practice by his apostles and by the faithful of the primitive Church. The white garments in which Jesus Christ appeared at the Transfiguration, and the linen garment worn by Saint James, the brother of the Lord, foretold those of the regular canons. Saint Peter was the first to wear, in memory of the Passion of Jesus Christ, the same form of tonsure and crown that they themselves wore. As charity grew cold and persecutions increased, this order, which had flourished in the time of the apostles and the first faithful, fell into decline. But Pope Saint Urban, a martyr, caused it to revive through his decrees. Saint Augustine restored it through his Rule, and Saint Jerome and the other priests of the Church enhanced its worth in their writings. Here we see what the first regular canons thought concerning the origin of their order.

The other letter of our abbot was written to a secular cleric who had asked him to prescribe, in a few words, a way of life. Lietbert confines himself to urging him to avoid associating with women who were not among his closest female relatives. The entire letter turns on this point.

## 3

Besides the Commentary on the Psalms, Pitseus also attributes to Lietbert another work on Sacred Scripture in general. But since he does not copy its opening words, as he does in the case of the first work, he gives us to understand that he had not seen it.

Manuscript 1543 of the Vatican Library, among the manuscripts once belonging to the Queen of Sweden, presents an explanation of Saint Paul’s First Epistle to the Corinthians as far as chapter XI, under the name of a Lietbertus [Note: [Col. 0713] Le Long, *Bibliotheca*, page 824.]. But this interpreter is identified as “of Poitiers” (*Pictaviensis*), which prevents us from treating him as the same person as Lietbert, abbot of Saint-Ruf.

# Letter of Galterus, Bishop of Maguelone, to Robert, Provost of Lille, on the *Flowers of the Psalms* Collected by Lietbert

(Mabillon, *Analecta*, new edition, page 461.)

[Col. 0713A] Galterus, bishop of Maguelone and legate of the holy Roman Church, sends greetings in the Lord to his most beloved kinsman Robert, provost of Lille, and to all the canons of that same church.

When we were staying with you some time ago at Lille, your fellow canon Hescelin, among the other matters he discussed familiarly with us, began carefully to inquire about the *Flowers of the Psalms*, which he had heard had been extracted and gathered into one work by Lietbert of holy memory, formerly your canon and afterward abbot of Saint-Ruf. We replied that, insofar as we had understood from the writing itself—for we knew that blessed man’s religious character and intention—his purpose in this work had been to select from various sources and set down in two volumes only what seemed most necessary for the correction of morals in the Church of God. For he knew the great and extensive exposition on the Psalms published by blessed Augustine, as well as those of Cassiodorus and the other teachers of the Church of God. But because he was wholly inflamed by the fire of divine love, yearning for heavenly things and devoting himself entirely to the gaining of souls while setting temporal concerns completely aside, he directed all his study and ability toward acquiring as many souls as possible for almighty God, whether by writing or by speaking. An attentive reader can observe this in the same *Flowers*.

When your fellow canon had heard of this most blessed man’s diligence, and also of the usefulness of that reading, he began earnestly to press us with his requests, asking that, if he possessed any place in our friendship or any favor with us, he might receive through us all or part of the work, according to our promise. He frequently repeated that verse of the Psalm: “Remember your word to your servant, in which you have given me hope.”

But because from that time onward we were occupied with many and varied affairs through our pastoral responsibilities and the legation entrusted to us, we have so far been entirely unable to fulfill our desire and promise. Nevertheless, the charity with which we love you in God and for God does not allow us to forget this obligation. Therefore, in two volumes, just as those same *Flowers* were extracted and divided by that holy man, we send them not to any single person but to your entire Church, exhorting your brotherhood by this letter always to remember the life and learning of one who was formerly nurtured among you, and to read this work frequently and commit it to memory, keeping before your eyes and imitating the conduct of so great a man.

[Col. 0715A] Nor should you consider what or how much is offered to you by us, but from the abundance from which it is offered to you. God is my witness how I long for all of you in the inner affections of Jesus Christ. And this I ask: may almighty God deign, through a worthy fruit of repentance, to lead you to the pastures of eternal life. For we can never forget you. We wish and ask that whenever Lord Hescelin requests those same books for reading, he may always be permitted to have them, in accordance with his request and our promise.

By the preceding grace of God, through our labor and persistent efforts, peace has been restored among our princes, and our entire homeland rejoices because of it. Farewell, and always remember your friend.

[Note: [Col. 0715A] This letter, or preface, which we recovered from the library of the Belgian monastery of Dunes, confirms the opinion of Robert in the shorter *Gallia Christiana*, who judged that Galterus, bishop of Maguelone, was the same person as Galterus who published the *Flowers of the Psalms*. The San-Marthans in the fuller *Gallia Christiana*, and Peter Gabriel in his list of the bishops of Maguelone, therefore unjustly accuse Robert of error, since they insist on distinguishing two Galteruses. [Col. 0716A] Furthermore, this letter establishes that Galterus, bishop of Maguelone, held the dignity of apostolic legate, a fact that none of them noted. It also shows that he was a kinsman of Robert, provost of Lille, as he himself expressly acknowledges. Galterius held the see from 1103 to 1129, during the time of Saint Bernard, abbot of Clairvaux, who praises “Brother Hescelin” in Letter 98—no one else, I think, than the canon of Lille mentioned here by Galterus.]

# Charter of Galterus, Bishop of Maguelone, for the Monastery of Gellone

(*Gallia Christiana*, new edition, volume VI, instruments, column 275.)

[Col. 0715B] Record of the donation that Gotafridus, bishop of Maguelone, made to the monastery of Gellone. Accordingly, the bishop Gotafridus of blessed memory gave the church of Saint Martin of Lundras to the monastery of Gellone. Before making this donation, the same bishop retained for himself a fourth part of the tithes, offerings, and other revenues of that church, as the sacred canons prescribe. He gave this fourth part into the hands of Augerius the archdeacon and Rostagnus of Cavaierago, for the benefit of the brothers living according to the rule.

After Bishop Gotafridus died and Bishop Galterius was appointed in his place, the canons of Maguelone reached the following settlement with Abbot Peter: every year the monks of Gellone were to pay them one cow worth twelve solidi; and if they did not wish to give a cow, they were to pay twelve solidi in Melgueil currency. It was to remain at the monks’ discretion whether they paid a cow or twelve solidi. The monks were to render this due—a cow or twelve solidi—to the canons of Maguelone in the first or second week of the Advent of the Lord.

The bishop, however, retained for himself and his successors in the aforesaid church of Saint Martin the episcopal reverence, due obedience, and synods: namely, five solidi and ten denarii between the two synods, as well as lodgings for himself and his successors.

[Col. 0716B] This settlement was made by Bishop Galterius and Abbot Peter between the canons of Maguelone and the monks of Gellone at Montpellier, in the presence of the following canons of Maguelone: Peter the archdeacon, Deodatus the serf, Nicetius, Peter of Frizonicus, and William of Diae. With the abbot were Raimundus of Pradinas, called the prior, Raimundus of Baladuc, Seguinus the cleric, and William Belinus.

And I, Galterius, bishop of Maguelone, out of reverence for the holy place and love for Saint William the confessor, confirm the aforesaid church to Abbot Peter and his successors according to the settlement contained above, together with its tithes, first fruits, freehold lands, offerings, cemetery, and all rights belonging to the same church.

Executed in the year 1110 from the Incarnation of the Lord, indiction III.

# Letters of Lietbert, Abbot of Saint-Ruf

(Martène, *Anecdota*, volume I, pages 329–332, from the manuscript of Stamedium.)

## I. To Otgerius, Provost of the Ferranian Congregation  
### He commends the canonical order

[Col. 0715D]
