To Otgerius, venerable provost of the Ferranian congregation, [Col. 0716D] and to his holy community, and to all who live according to God in the canonical order, Lambertus [Note: [Col. 0715D] In the lists of the abbots of Saint-Ruf he is commonly called not Lambertus but Lietbertus.] humble servant of the church of Saint-Ruf [Note: [Col. 0716D] Saint-Ruf was the distinguished monastery of Regular Canons of the Order of Saint Augustine, the head of that order. It was founded by Benedict, bishop of Avignon, in 1038, not far from Avignon; it was subsequently transferred to a place near Valence and finally restored in the city of Valence itself.] sends greetings and grace in Jesus Christ, and [wishes you] steadfastly to observe the shining purity of the sacred order you have undertaken.

We give thanks to the Holy Spirit, through whose inspiration we know that you brothers possess zeal and devotion for the canonical order. For the holier the order, the greater should be the devotion and care of those laboring in this grace. The dignity of this order, namely the canonical and priestly order, is demonstrated in many ways by ancient and new figures and examples.

The Holy Spirit commends it in the Psalm, saying: “Moses and Aaron among his priests called upon the Lord, and he heard them” (Psalm XCVIII, 6). And again he led [lacuna], whether as a rule of discipline; he strikes Egypt, frees Israel, divides the Red Sea, turns waters into sweetness, and brings rivers out of the rock.

Through the priest God gives the law, instructs concerning the tabernacle, the ark, the vessels, the vestments, the rites of sacrifice, and all the other things belonging to the worship of God. The splendor of Moses’ face, the glory of Aaron’s garments and those of his sons, and what was said to Moses—“Make everything according to the model shown to you on the mountain” (Exodus X, 4)—commend this priestly dignity.

From these words it is gathered that the canonical and priestly rule is fashioned according to heavenly models themselves, and should be called divine rather than human. As a figure of our order, priests and Levites were commanded not to possess an inheritance among their brothers. “I,” says the Lord, “will be their inheritance.” They guard the sacred vessels, keep watch around the tabernacles, appease the anger of God, bear the sins of the people, and are appointed mediators between God and the people.

From these words it is clear that those who belong to this order, although human, ought to be above ordinary human beings. They rouse the people with trumpets; they flourish and bear fruit in Aaron’s iron rod, and they surpass the other orders. They carry the ark, divide the Jordan, occupy the land of promise, destroy Jericho, and crush barbarian peoples. All these things are spiritually prefigured in our order.

Our habit also was figured and consecrated there in many ways, in the garments of Aaron. Twisted byssus shines brilliantly; his sons gleam in linen garments in the service of God; their descendants wear the linen ephod. Therefore, when the priests shine with linen whiteness, together with the other materials, from the undergarments to the tiara, what is signified except the inviolable authority of our order and the radiant purity of chastity and honorable life?

What does the tunic of Samuel, who appointed kings, signify except our linen, ankle-length tunic, whose name is etymologically associated with purity of heart? We have observed the royal and priestly order; before the supreme King we shall stand.

Let us call to mind the man whom Ezekiel describes as clothed in linen, with a writer’s inkwell at his waist. Such power is attributed to him that, beginning at the sanctuary, he marks with the letter Tau those whom he judges worthy, while those whom he judges unworthy he does not fear to expose, without a mark, to the swords of six men. The sublimity of this power is attributed to those who, joining bodily chastity to purity of heart through discernment, gird the sword of the divine word most powerfully around their thigh, guard the bed of the true Solomon, and with pure eyes contemplate the King himself continually in his beauty.

After mentioning a few matters among many, let us come to the New Testament. It is clear that the Son of God and man consecrated in himself all the grades of the clerical order, and that he handed on to his apostles the rule by which we live. He gathers disciples and establishes a common life, saying: “Whoever does not renounce everything he possesses cannot be my disciple” (Luke XIV, 33).

The apostles handed this rule on to the primitive Church, as it is written in their Acts: “They were one heart and one soul in God, and they did not call anything their own, for everything was common among them” (Acts IV, 32). And what was written long before concerning this order of ours was fulfilled: “Behold, how good and how pleasant it is for brothers to dwell together in unity” (Psalm CXXXII, 1).

The first heard, “Behold, how good,” but they did not hear it alone. For this love and unity of brothers did not extend only as far as them; it descended also to their successors, even to the present day, so that we may now say: “Behold, how good and how pleasant it is for brothers to dwell together in unity.”

But to what are we like? Let the Psalm say: “Like the ointment on the head, which ran down upon the beard, the beard of Aaron” (ibid., 2). Our Aaron, our priest, is Christ. He offered himself for us as a sacrifice, rose again, ascended into heaven, and the Holy Spirit came from the head to the beard, from Christ to the disciples.

The beard signifies maturity and perfection. What descended to the edge of his garment passed down to the successors of the Church. For the Church followed—the Lord’s garment—and gave birth to monasteries. As I have said, they were filled with the Holy Spirit and commanded to preach to every creature; they drove out demons, healed the sick, raised the dead, celebrated the sacraments, released sins, and opened heaven.

Finally, let us return to commending the splendor of the garments and the habit. You heard that, when the Lord was transfigured on the mountain, his garments shone like snow. We also read that angels appeared in white garments. James, the brother of the Lord, bishop of bishops, always used linen garments. Peter was the first to wear this form of our tonsure and crown in memory of Christ’s Passion.

As I said, this order of ours first flourished in Christ, in the apostles, and in the primitive Church. But when charity grew cold and persecution pressed upon it, it afterward withered. Pope Urban, a martyr, then began to revive it through his decrees; blessed Augustine organized it through his rules; Saint Jerome commended it in his letters, as did the other holy men whom it would take too long to name.

Thus the servants of God, aroused by these examples, are now returning in many lands to the former school of this order of our Savior; already the regions are white for the harvest. Therefore, dearest brothers, we exhort you who have embraced so illustrious an order to watch with the greatest care, so that he who shines in body through order and habit may also shine in you through purity of mind and beauty of life; so that life may agree with the name and profession may be perceived in conduct.

For it is fitting that this should truly be said of you: “You are the light of the world; you are the salt of the earth.” Let your light therefore shine before people, so that they may see your good works and glorify your Father who is in heaven. Three things above all are commended by these words: order, life, and habit.

## II. To a Friend  
### He discourages clerics from frequent association with women

[Col. 0719B]

You asked me to explain briefly how clerics ought to live. For this reason many accursed adversaries lie in wait for me, because I do not keep silent about the truth.

The first temptations of clerics are frequent visits to women. This sex makes clerics blameworthy. What have you really to do with women, you who serve with the Lord at the altar? Everyone in public—the peasants, plowmen, and vine-dressers in the fields—will severely tear you apart every day if, contrary to the arrangement of faith, you insist on living with women. And because, as I suppose, you desire to be found beyond reproach, fortify yourself with a good testimony.

Were women present in the choir of the apostles? Prevent virgins who are not of your family from living with you, lest, while you enter secretly and alone, you stain your testimony. Married people are instructed in one way, and those who practice continence in another, to undertake ecclesiastical ministry.

The fellowship of women with clerics is commanded to be avoided in every way. Woman is a snare of the devil, a way of iniquity, a scorpion’s sting, and a harmful species. When straw comes near, it kindles fire; with flaming fire a woman strikes the conscience of the man who lives with her and burns up the foundations of the mountains.

I judge that, if women live with men, the devil’s substitute will not be lacking. By them the man is seized. [lacuna] Lust subdues iron minds. If someone binds fire in his bosom, will his garments not burn? Or if someone walks across burning coals, will he not burn his feet? Believe me: one who is joined to women’s visits cannot dwell with the Lord with an undivided heart.

But you say: “Whoever walks innocently walks confidently.” Well said and cleverly put; but one must have a good testimony.

# A.D. 1102–1126. Werner, Abbot of Saint Blaise in the Black Forest

# Notice

(Dom Gerbert, *History of the Black Forest*, 1793, quarto, volume I.)

Werner, abbot of Saint Blaise in the Black Forest, was distinguished no less by learning than by exceptional integrity of life, and he brought distinction to this age. The domestic records testify that he wrote very well on the mystery of the Most Holy Trinity, although none of that work has reached us [Note: [Col. 0719] The book *Deflorationum* that we reprint under his name from the Basel edition is attributed by Fabricius and by the Benedictine authors of *Gallia litteraria*—although they had not seen the volume—to a certain Warnerus the Englishman.].

Felix Faber speaks of him in his *History of the Swabians* as follows:

> “A holy and exceedingly religious man, noble by birth from Ellerbach, and much nobler in religion. Because this abbot nurtured deeply devout monks, he was asked by many virgins devoted to God to build a convent or cloister for them beside his monastery. Yielding to their prayers, he built a reclusory beside the convent, in which a community of virgins devoted to God was gathered for a long time, near the chapel of the Blessed Virgin Mary. That chapel still stands today in the cemetery where the aforesaid sisters were buried, among whom many are believed to have been holy. Werner died in the year of the Lord 1126, in the twenty-fourth year of his abbacy.”

# Books of Extracts or Excerpts

From the honey-flowing teaching of various Fathers, especially Augustine, Jerome, Ambrose, Gregory, Hilary, Chrysostom, Maximus, Origen, Remigius, Cassiodorus, Bede, Alcuin, and other orthodox teachers, concerning the seasonal Gospels throughout the course of the year, written by the reverend Father Lord Werner, abbot of the monastery of Saint Blaise the Martyr and Bishop in the Black Forest, of the Order of Saint Benedict, in the diocese of Constance, and arranged or composed into the following homiletical sermons.

(G)*

## Note

We have copied the title above exactly from the Basel edition of 1494, printed in Gothic type in two columns. It displays initial letters illuminated in red; the page numbers are absent. The volume is in a smaller folio format and consists of two parts bound together, although they had appeared separately.

Werner’s sermons conclude with a printer’s note, though the printer’s name has been suppressed: “Here ends the book of the *Deflorationes* of the Fathers, printed at Basel in the year of the Lord 1494.”

The first part contains a collection of sermons whose beginning is as follows:

> “Here begin very notable and highly formal sermons of Brother Soccus of the Cistercian Order, on the saints, so called because they have been most elegantly and exquisitely collected from *succus*, that is, from the marrow of Sacred Scripture.”

At the end one reads:

> “The sermons on the saints, honey-flowing little flowers of the holy doctor Bernard, adorned above all others in various ways, carefully prepared by the discerning man John [sic] of Grüningen in the illustrious city of Strasbourg, in the year 1484 from the birth of Christ, on the Ides of April. They end happily.”

# Prologue of Lord Werner, Abbot of the Monastery of Blessed Blaise the Bishop, of the Order of Saint Benedict in the Black Forest, in the Diocese of Constance, to the Books of Extracts from the Holy Fathers on the Seasonal Gospels throughout the Course of the Year, with Very Useful Sermons

[Col. 0725]

Because the days are evil and the time is approaching when people, as the Apostle says (Ephesians V), grow weary of sound doctrine and turn rather to fables than to things that contribute to their salvation, it seemed good to set these things down so that those who serve the doctrine of the word of God may have at hand what they should offer to their hearers.

But because, through the constant hearing of the word of God, the honey-flowing teaching of the Fathers has become greatly wearisome in the ears of modern people, and consequently the straight road by which one reaches the heavenly kingdom is now unknown to many, we have arranged a collection of various Fathers in the composition of sermons, so that the souls of those to be saved may be refreshed by them.

It is customary among mortals for foods repeatedly set before people to become distasteful to those to whom they are served. To prevent this from happening in sermons, we have written down an abundance of them, repeated often, so that when these are rejected because they are frequently recited, at least through another sermon, because of its rarity, the people of God may be encouraged by the teacher.

Moreover, it should be known that this book is entitled *Defloration*, that is, an excerpting of the Fathers, because it is arranged from the authoritative teaching of the Fathers—Gregory, Hilary, Augustine, Isidore, Jerome, Bede, Remigius, and others—who in modern times were Catholic and orthodox teachers.

[Col. 0725] Here ends the prologue.

Here begin the chapters of the first book of the *Deflorationes*, from the Advent of the Lord through the First Sunday after the octave of Pentecost.

## Chapter I

On the Fourth Sunday before the Nativity of the Lord. Exposition of the Gospel: “Behold, I send my angel, etc.” A sermon on the Advent of the Lord, the ages of this world, and the calculation of the years of this world, divided into three parts.

## Chapter II

On the Third Sunday. Exposition of the Gospel: “There will be signs in the sun and moon.” Also a sermon on the final time of Antichrist and the last tribulation. Also a narrative concerning Antichrist: his origin, his deeds, his persecution, and his end, divided into three parts.

## Chapter III

On the Second Sunday. Exposition of the Gospel: “When John heard in prison.” Also a sermon on the Advent of the Lord, divided into two parts.

Also another sermon on the Day of Judgment and the Advent of the Lord, divided into two parts.

## Chapter IV

On the First Sunday before the Nativity of the Lord. Exposition of the Gospel: “The Jews sent from Jerusalem.” Also concerning the time when people began to be bound by the command to receive baptism, and concerning the beginning of baptism. Also a sermon on the coming and the character of the Judge at the judgment, divided into two parts.

## Chapter V

At the vigil of the Nativity. A twofold exposition of the Gospel: “When she was betrothed.” Also a sermon on the betrothal of Saint Mary. Also a sermon on how one should understand what is written: “He was conceived by the Holy Spirit.”

## Chapter VI

On the Nativity of the Lord. Exposition of both Gospels: “A decree went out”; and: “The shepherds were speaking.” Also concerning the fact that the Son alone assumed flesh. Also a sermon on the flesh assumed by Christ, that is, how the Son of the Virgin could be assumed without sin from the mass of the human race fermented by sin. Also a sermon on the Nativity of the Lord, and another divided into two parts.

## Chapter VII

The First Sunday after the Nativity of the Lord. Exposition of the Gospel: “Jesus’ father and mother were there.” Also a sermon on the three silences. Also concerning the fact that the Word assumed flesh with punishment but without guilt, with mortality but without iniquity.

## Chapter VIII

On the octave of the Nativity of the Lord. Exposition of the Gospel: “When the eight days had been completed.” Also a sermon on the Lord’s octave, divided into two parts.

## Chapter IX

On the Epiphany of the Lord. Exposition of the Gospel: “When Jesus had been born.” Also a sermon on the Theophany, divided into two parts. Also on the Gospel: “When Jesus had been born.”

## Chapter X

The First Sunday after the Epiphany. Exposition of the Gospel: “When Jesus was twelve years old.” Also a sermon on the fact that the Word assumed, together with flesh, a rational soul; and on what that soul was like in wisdom, virtue, justice, and goodness. Also an exposition of the same Gospel: “When Jesus was twelve years old.”

## Chapter XI

The Second Sunday after the Epiphany. Exposition of the Gospel: “A wedding took place.” Also another exposition concerning the six water jars.

## Chapter XII

The Third Sunday. Exposition of the Gospel: “When Jesus had come down from the mountain.” Also a question whether the power of God and the will of God are equal. Also an exposition of the same Gospel: “When he had come down.”

## Chapter XIII

The Fourth Sunday. Exposition of the Gospel: “As Jesus was getting into the boat.” Also a sermon on the measure of love for God and neighbor, divided into two parts.

## Chapter XIV

[Col. 0727] The Fifth Sunday. Exposition of the Gospel: “I confess to you, Father, Lord of heaven.” Also a sermon on the words, “Come to me, all you who labor,” and on the seven capital vices and their works; also on the seven virtues and their works, divided into two parts.

## Chapter XV

On Septuagesima. Exposition of the Gospel: “The kingdom of heaven is like a householder.” Also a sermon on Septuagesima, Sexagesima, and Quinquagesima, and on why these Sundays are so called, divided into two parts.

## Chapter XVI

On Sexagesima. Exposition of the Gospel: “The sower went out to sow.” Also a sermon on the numbers seventy, sixty, fifty, and forty, divided into two parts.

## Chapter XVII

On Quinquagesima. Exposition of the Gospel: “Jesus took his twelve disciples.” Also a sermon on the fifteen degrees of charity. Also on fear and love, and on the four kinds of fear.

## Chapter XVIII

On Quadragesima. Exposition of the Gospel: “Jesus was led into the desert.” Also a sermon on diabolical temptation and the four temptations. Also a sermon on Quadragesima.

CAP. XIX. The Second Sunday in Lent. Exposition of the Gospel: “Jesus went out and withdrew into the region.” Also a sermon on the three kisses—of the feet, hands, and mouth—and on the upper and lower lip.

CAP. XX. The Third Sunday. Exposition of the Gospel: “Jesus was casting out a demon.” Also a sermon on sin and the confession of sin, divided into two parts.

CAP. XXI. Mid-Lent Sunday. Exposition of the Gospel: “Jesus went away across the Sea of Galilee.” Also a sermon on fish: the *staro*, the blind fish, the moray eel, the viper, the octopus, the crab, the land urchin, and the sea urchin.

CAP. XXII. Passion Sunday. Exposition of the Gospel: “Which of you will convict me of sin?” Also a sermon on the flesh that the Word assumed—what it was according to its capacity for suffering and its affections.

CAP. XXIII. Palm Sunday. Exposition of the Gospel: “When they had drawn near.” Also a sermon to be delivered on Palm Sunday.

CAP. XXIV. On the Lord’s Supper. Exposition of the Gospel: “Before the feast of Passover.” Also two sermons on the Lord’s Supper.

CAP. XXV. On the Preparation Day. Exposition of the Gospel: [Col. 0728] “Mary Magdalene.” Also a sermon on Easter Day concerning Christ’s resurrection, the two hells, and the nine punishments of hell; concerning souls at considerable length, their immortality, and the resurrection of bodies, divided into three parts.

CAP. XXVI. Exposition of the Gospel. Easter Monday.

CAP. XXVII. Exposition of the Gospel. Easter Tuesday.

CAP. XXVIII. On the Octave of Easter. Exposition of the Gospel: “When it was evening on that day.” Also a sermon on the Octave of Easter.

CAP. XXIX. The First Sunday after the Octave of Easter. Exposition of the Gospel: “I am the good shepherd.” Also a sermon on shepherds and those subject to them.

CAP. XXX. The Second Sunday. Exposition of the Gospel: “A little while, and you will no longer see me.” Also a sermon on the vision of God.

CAP. XXXI. The Third Sunday. Exposition of the Gospel: “I am going to him.” Also a sermon on the three days of the Passion, Resurrection, and Ascension.

CAP. XXXII. The Fourth Sunday. Exposition of the Gospel: “Amen, amen, I say to you: If you ask anything.” Also a sermon on the order of the resurrection—how, and what sort of bodies, will rise—divided into two parts.

CAP. XXXIII. On the Rogation Days. Exposition of the Gospel: “Which of you has a friend?” Also a sermon for the Rogation Days, divided into four parts.

CAP. XXXIV. On the Ascension. Exposition of the Gospel: “As they were reclining.” Also a sermon on the Ascension, divided into two parts.

CAP. XXXV. The Sunday after the Ascension. Exposition of the Gospel: “When the Paraclete comes.” Also a sermon on Christ’s ten descents to human beings and the soul’s eight ascents to God. Also on how earthly bodies remain in heaven.

CAP. XXXVI. On Pentecost Day. Exposition of the Gospel: “If anyone loves me.” Also a sermon for Pentecost Day, divided into four parts.

CAP. XXXVII. Pentecost Monday. Exposition of the Gospel: “For God so loved the world.”

CAP. XXXVIII. Pentecost Tuesday. Exposition of the Gospel: “Amen, amen, I say to you: Whoever does not enter.”

CAP. XXXIX. On the Octave of Pentecost. Exposition of the Gospel: “There was a man from among the Pharisees.” Also a sermon on what baptism is and on the institution of baptism.

[Col. 0727] Here end the expositions, or chapters, of the first book.

# THE CONFESSION OF THE CATHOLIC FAITH OF LORD WERNER, ABBOT

Taken from the third book of Ambrose, *On the Trinity*

[Col. 0727]

[Col. 0727A] The assertion of our faith is this: that we say there is one God, not two or three. He who separates the divinity of the Trinity declares that there are three gods. We, however, confess the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit to be one God, so that in the perfect Trinity there is both the fullness of divinity and the unity of power. For God is one. “God” is the name of magnificence, the name of power. If, then, there is one God, there is one name, one power, and one Trinity. Finally, he says: “Go, baptizing in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit” (Matt. XXVIII). In the name, therefore—not in the names—there is one name, where there is one divinity, one substance, and one majesty. This is the name in which all ought to be saved (Acts IV).

Likewise: “I and the Father are one” (John X). He said “one,” so that no distinction of power might be made. He added “are,” so that we might recognize the persons. For the Father himself is not the Son, but the Son is begotten from the Father: God from God, fullness from fullness. These, therefore, are not empty names, but indications of power: fullness of divinity in the Father and fullness in the Son—but not something discordant, nor something confused that is one, nor something multiple that is undifferentiated.

[Col. 0729A] How the Son is begotten from the Father it is impossible to know: the mind fails, the tongue is silent. It is beyond not only human beings and angels, but beyond the angels, beyond the cherubim, beyond the seraphim, beyond every understanding. We are commanded to believe; we are not permitted to investigate. Remove arguments where faith is sought.

We believe in one God, the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit: the Father because he has a Son, the Son because he has the Father, and the Spirit because he proceeds from the Father and the Son. The Father, therefore, is the source of the divinity: just as he was never not God, so he was never not Father. From the Father the Son was born, and from him and from the Son the Spirit proceeds. The Father is eternal because he has an eternal Son, whose eternal Father he is. The Son is eternal because he is co-eternal with the Father and the Holy Spirit. The Holy Spirit [Col. 0729B] is called eternal because he is co-eternal with the Father and the Son—not a Trinity confused in person, as Sabellius says, nor separated or divided in the nature of divinity, as Arius blasphemes, but one person is the Father, another the Son, and another the Holy Spirit; one in nature, God in Trinity: Father, Son, and Holy Spirit.

Likewise: It was not the Father who assumed flesh, nor the Holy Spirit, but the Son alone, so that he who was the Son of God in the divinity of the Father might himself become, among human beings, the son of a human being; and so that the name “Son” might not pass to another who was not a Son by birth. Thus the Son of God by divine birth became the Son of man: born according to the truth of nature, from God as the Son of God; according to the truth of nature, from a human being as the son of a human being. Thus the truth of the one begotten possessed the name “Son” by birth in both births—not by adoption or by designation—and he was true God, true human being, one Son.

[Col. 0729C] Likewise, therefore, there are not two Christs or two sons, but one Son, God and human being. For this reason we call him the Only-begotten, remaining in two substances, as the truth of his nature conferred them—not with the natures confused or mingled. For the Son assumed humanity in such a way that he who assumed and that which he assumed were one person in the Trinity. Nor was a quaternity made by the assumption of humanity. Rather, the Trinity remained, that ineffable assumption producing the truth of one person in God and in the human being. For we do not say that Christ is God alone, or a human being alone, but [Col. 0730A] true God born from God the Father and a true human being born from a human mother; nor does his humanity, being less than the Father, diminish anything of his divinity, which is equal to the Father.

This one, therefore, is both: one Christ, who according to his divinity said, “I and the Father are one” (John X), and according to his humanity, “The Father is greater than I” (John XIV). From the moment he began to be human, he began to be nothing other than the Son of God—and this the Only-begotten. Because of God the Word, through whom, when he had assumed it, flesh was made (John I), just as any human being is one person—namely, rational soul and flesh—so Christ is one person, Word and human being.

Christ Jesus is the Son of God, both God and human being: God because he is the Word of God; human being because, in the unity of the person, a rational soul and flesh were joined to the Word of God. And he who is the unique Son of God is also the son of man—that is, he himself is both from both, one Christ, one Son of God and likewise the son of man—not two sons, God and human being, but one Son.

Likewise, God assumed the human being, and the human being passed into God—not by a changeability of nature, but by God’s gracious condescension. Thus neither was God changed into human substance by assuming humanity, nor was the human being changed into divine substance by being glorified in God. Since a change or mutability of nature brings about either diminution or abolition, we believe that the Trinity is joined without confusion and distinguished without separation.

Likewise: Nothing created or servile is to be believed in the Trinity; nothing unequal, nothing equivalent to grace, nothing earlier, nothing later or lesser, nothing external or serving another, nothing invisible to itself, nothing visible to creatures, nothing differing in character or will, nothing transferred from the essence of the Trinity into the nature of creatures, nothing singular in function or incapable of being communicated to another, nothing confused—but everything perfect, because everything is from one, and one, yet not solitary.

Likewise: The Son is therefore *homoousios*—of one substance—with the Father in divinity; the Holy Spirit is *homoousios* with the Father and the Son; and the one Son is *homoousios* with God and the human being, remaining God in his humanity. Desirable to be seen by the angels in the glory of the Father, the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit are thus worshiped by the angels and every creature—not the human being because of God, or Christ together with God, but the human being in God and God in the human being.

# THE FIRST BOOK OF EXCERPTS BEGINS

[Col. 0729]

# THE FOURTH SUNDAY BEFORE THE NATIVITY OF THE LORD

[Col. 0729D] “The beginning of the Gospel of Jesus Christ, Son of David. As it is written in Isaiah the prophet: Behold, I send my angel before your face, who has prepared your way before you,” etc. (Mark I).

The Greek word *euangelion* means “good announcement” in Latin, and properly concerns the kingdom of God and the remission of sins. Hence it is said: “Repent and believe the Gospel, and the kingdom of heaven will draw near to you” (Mark I).

“Of Jesus Christ,” that is, of the anointed Savior. In Hebrew, Jesus; in Greek, *Soter* [σωτήρ]; in Latin, Savior. “Christ” means “anointed,” that is, he is called king and priest, since he is born from the lineage of King David and is foretold by the voices of prophets of the Levitical lineage.

It follows:

“Behold, I send my angel before your face, who will prepare your way before you.”

(REMIGIUS.) John is certainly more than a prophet, because he is called an angel not by nature but by the dignity of his office. Of him the Father speaks to the Son, as he says in Malachi: “Before your face”—that is, before your manifestation—“he will prepare the way,” that is, by preaching repentance and baptizing, he will make the hearts of those who hear you ready in advance.

All who are reckoned under the name of the priesthood are also called angels, as the prophet testifies when he says: “The lips of the priest guard knowledge, and they seek the law from his mouth, because he is the angel of the Lord of hosts” (Mal. II). Moreover, every believer who turns a neighbor away from wickedness and exhorts him to good, who announces to one wandering astray the eternal kingdom or punishment, plainly becomes an angel—that is, a messenger of the Lord—when he does these things.

Then it follows:

“This is he who was spoken of through Isaiah the prophet, saying: The voice of one crying in the wilderness: Prepare the way of the Lord; make his paths straight.”

(BEDA, on Mark.) John preached in this way: “This is he of whom the prophet Isaiah speaks: The voice of one crying,” etc. Just as the voice sounds first and understanding is conceived afterward, so John’s preaching went before, announcing Christ’s coming. Therefore John is called the voice of Christ—that is, of “the Word who was in the beginning with God” (John I)—which cries out through John to the deaf Jews, who are far removed through their sins and deserving of a cry of indignation.

To the Jews who harden their ears, the voice and cry arise in the wilderness because they are without the Spirit of God, without a prophet, without a king, and without a priest. What does Christ cry out through John? “Prepare the way of the Lord.” The way of the Lord, by which God descends to us and we ascend to him, is faith in repentance and love. The paths—that is, intentions—are straight if they are raised purely toward God. They become crooked if, for the sake of earthly things, we do what ought to be done for God.

*Phyris* in Greek means “vision of God” in Latin. Hence a prophet of God is one who sees from afar. Then he adds:

“John was in the wilderness, baptizing and preaching a baptism of repentance for the remission of sins.”

“John was in the wilderness,” and the rest. John is interpreted as “the grace of God.” The account begins with grace. Hence it follows: “Baptizing.” For through baptism grace is given, by which sins are freely forgiven. Therefore the Apostle says: “By grace you have been saved through faith; and this is not from yourselves, for it is the gift of God, not from works, so that no one may boast” (Eph. II).

“And preaching a baptism of repentance for the remission of sins.” What is completed through the Bridegroom is announced through the friend of the bridegroom. Hence catechumens—that is, those who have been instructed—begin through the priest and are anointed with chrism through the bishop. Now, however, the Bride is led in by the Bridegroom’s friend, and through the boy Isaac Rebecca is brought in, veiled in a white cloak.

“And the whole region of Judea and all the inhabitants of Jerusalem were going out to him, and they were baptized by him in the Jordan River, confessing their sins.”

John baptized not so that his own baptism might grant remission of sins, but so that it might run before Christ’s baptism, which remits sins. The difference between John’s baptism and Christ’s baptism is this: in John’s baptism, through immersion in water, only the sacrament was given. In Christ’s baptism, however, together with the sacrament the reality of the sacrament is also received.

John immersed sinners in water and imposed repentance on those confessing their sins. Christ baptized and forgives sins. John, while baptizing, preached that the one who was to come would baptize with the Spirit; Christ, baptizing for the remission of sins, pours in the Spirit. There human beings were baptized in the name of the one who was to come; here human beings are baptized in the name of the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit.

The sacrament, therefore, was the same in both cases as far as the outward form was concerned; but as far as its effect was concerned, it was not the same. There the sacrament alone was present, but remission of sins was not; here both the form of the sacrament and the power of the sacrament are present. In the same way, remission is granted for the forgiveness of sins.

People were baptized by John in the Jordan, which is interpreted as “descent,” descending from the pride of the old human being to the humility of confession and amendment.

“And John was clothed in camel’s hair, with a leather belt around his waist. His food was locusts and wild honey.”

For John, the wilderness is the place, and meditation is the activity. He proclaims repentance, through which there is a return from error, a withdrawal from crime, and, after the shame of vices, a declaration of the intention to cease.

He was clothed in hair, not wool, which is a garment of austerity, not luxury. The leather belt signifies the poor who are dead to the world; Elijah too was girded with it. A belt is made from the dried skins of animals. Hence John was girded around the waist to mortify luxury.

He ate locusts and wild honey because it is fitting for an inhabitant of the wilderness not to pursue riches but necessity. Our Peripatetics say that there is an herb called “wild honey” that abounds around the banks of the Jordan, whose peeled stalks provide marrow with the taste of honey. The locust, without doubt, is also an herb, and itself of excellent taste. Its nature is to transplant its annual fruit from place to place without anyone carrying it. Hence the Latins gave it this name, since both have the same name as an herb, with the same designation or meaning: *locusta*. Some say that John ate animals bearing this name, others herbs. For the Jews, locusts are animals permitted as food.

[Col. 0733A] Wild honey, however, is clearly an herb, as are the locusts, and there is an abundance of both in the desert. This is what concerns the locust and wild honey.

A cheap and rough garment of camel hair, or of any animal skins, signifies the contrite and humbled heart of the penitent. The girding of the belt admonishes us to be girded for every service of Christ’s will.

The locusts, creatures that flee and are chosen for food, represent us: previously, as though by certain leaps of the body, we were carried about, wandering in will, useless in deeds, querulous in words, and foreign to our proper dwelling. Now, however, we are the nourishment and satiety of the saints and prophets, chosen together with the wild honey, because we are to provide the sweetest food—not from the beehives of the Law, but from ourselves, as though from the trunks of the wild trees of paganism.

# SERMON ON THE ADVENT OF THE LORD

[Col. 0733]

[Col. 0733B] “Blessed are those servants whom, when he comes, the Lord finds watching” (Luke XII).

If any of you, beloved, expected your master to come to you at night, you would await his arrival with complete vigilance and hasten with the greatest eagerness to welcome him when he came, so as to commend yourselves to him through his great favor. Behold, our true Lord announces that he will come to us, his unworthy little servants; he declares blessed those who await his coming in wakefulness and go out to meet him.

Therefore, since we do not know the day or the hour when he will come, each of us ought to strive to remain watchful in good action, lest, coming late at night, or at midnight, or at cockcrow, or in the morning (Mark XIII), he find us unprepared.

The Lord comes late when he orders someone to depart from this life in old age. He comes at midnight when he calls someone in youth by an unexpected death. He comes at cockcrow when he orders someone to depart in adolescence. He arrives in the morning when he removes someone in childhood.

Blessed, therefore, are those whom he finds watching in faith and action, because they will feast with him at the eternal banquet. Exceedingly wretched, however, are those whom he finds surrendered to the sleep of sloth. For he will separate them from his chosen ones and place their portion with the hypocrites—that is, with the demons.

It should also be noted that the Lord is said to come not by day but at night (Matt. XXIV), because no one foreknows when he will come. For if the master of the house knew at what hour the thief would come, he would certainly keep watch and would not allow his house to be broken into or his possessions to be taken.

The house is our body; the master of the house is the soul; the thief is death. It comes at night when it presses upon a person unexpectedly. It finds the master asleep when it finds the soul sluggish in good works. It breaks into the house because it immediately kills the body. Once the master has been killed, it takes his goods because it tears the wretched soul away from the goods of eternal life and drags it off to be tormented in Tartarus.

Night is known to have twelve hours, which are divided into four watches, each watch being assigned three hours. Human life is compared with night because it is darkened by the shadows of ignorance. It is measured in twelve hours because the present life revolves through twelve months. It is divided into four watches because the year is measured by four seasons: spring, summer, autumn, and winter. Three hours are assigned to each watch because three months belong to each season. The four watches are also understood as the four ages, in which those who keep good watch will be rewarded with a heavenly prize.

[Col. 0734B] Concerning these watches the Lord says: “If he comes during the second watch, and if he comes during the third watch, blessed are those whom he finds watching.”

The first watch is childhood. Those who preserve innocence keep good watch in it. They immediately open to the Lord when he knocks, receiving death without fear, because they know that they will soon reign with Christ.

The second watch is adolescence. Those who do not defile themselves with the allurements of the flesh keep vigilant watch in it. They too gladly open the door to the Lord when he comes, because they hope to receive joys through death.

The third watch is youth. Those who are not overcome by the desires of the world, but exercise themselves in divine commandments, await the Lord vigilantly in it. They also meet the Lord eagerly, because they will soon reap in joy what they sowed in tears.

The fourth watch is old age. Those who persevere in good action to the end await the Lord by keeping watch in it. They welcome the long-desired Lord with rejoicing, because they immediately receive from him the denarius of life for their labor.

This is how we shall celebrate. The heavenly King came into the Babylon of this world to take the Church as his bride, entrusting her to servants for safekeeping; he himself went up to heaven to prepare the banquet. He commanded the servants: “Keep watch, so that at whatever hour he comes they may be ready to go out to meet him with lamps” (Matt. XXV).

He promised that he would come with great splendor and bring his bride into the prepared city. O exceedingly blessed are those who will then be ready to meet him! For they will enter with him into the wedding feast, into the joy of their Lord, and, appointed over all his goods, will rejoice forever.

Alas, how exceedingly wretched are those who are then found asleep in sins, because, once the door has been closed, they will be excluded from the eternal banquet. Therefore, beloved, since we do not know the hour of Christ’s coming—that is, the day of our death—let us all, young men and maidens together, the old with the young, keep watch in good works. Let us anticipate the face of the Lord in confession, so that at his Nativity we may worthily receive the sacrament of his body, and so that, when he comes a second time, we may appear with him in glory.

[Col. 0735] Here the sermon may be divided, if desired; and the same arrangement should be kept in the other places where a division has been made.

[Col. 0735A] The entire time of this age is compared with night; upon it comes the serene day of the age to come, illuminated by the Sun of justice. For just as the time of night, compared with the light of day, is darkened by dreadful gloom, so the light of all the days of this age, compared with the light of the coming day, is reckoned sheer dense obscurity.

Concerning the time or day of this age, it is said that at its beginning God created twenty-two works. On the first day he made seven works (Gen. I): namely, the formless matter, the angels, light, the higher heavens, earth, water, and air. On the second day, the firmament alone. On the third day, four: the seas, seeds, sown fields, and plantations. On the fourth day, three: the sun, moon, and stars. On the fifth day, three: fish, aquatic reptiles, and flying creatures. On the sixth day, four: wild beasts, cattle, reptiles of the earth, and the human being. Thus all twenty-two were made in six days.

There are also twenty-two generations from Adam to Jacob, from whose seed the people of Israel were born. There are twenty-two books of the Old Testament, ending with Esther, and twenty-two letters of the alphabet, from which the teaching of the divine Law is composed.

When, therefore, the twenty-two works had been completed in six days, God rested from them on the seventh day (Gen. II), because this world will be completed in six ages. The first of these ages is from Adam to Noah, which, according to Isidore, amounts to 2,252 years; the second, from the Flood to Abraham, amounts to 1,187 years; the third, from Abraham to David, amounts to 1,134 years; the fourth, from David to the Babylonian captivity, amounts to 1,609 years; the fifth, from the Babylonian captivity to Christ, amounts to 1,154 years.

From Christ’s birth until the time when Isidore wrote this, no certain number is available unless one calculates the years that elapsed up to the time of Heraclius, the devout ruler. In the fourth and fifth years of this ruler Sisibut, the Jews in Spain were baptized; at that time there were 1,836 years from the Lord’s birth, when the years of the earlier ages are included. This is the sixth age, which is now in progress until the day of judgment. The seventh will be the rest of the saints, which has no evening, because no limit closes it.

[Col. 0735D] In the first age, the human being was made in paradise like light (Gen. I) [AUGUSTINE, *On Genesis against the Manichaeans*]. In that age God divided the sons of light, as it were, from the sons of human beings, as from darkness; and the evening of this day is the Flood.

In the second age, something like a firmament was made between water and water: namely, that ark which floated, standing between the rains and the seas. Its evening is the confusion of languages.

In the third age, the one who separated his people from the nations was manifested through Abraham, distinguishing him like dry land from the waters, so that he might bring forth the shoot of herbs and trees—that is, saints and the fruit of Holy Scripture. The evening of this age was the sin of King Saul.

The fourth age began with David, when God set luminaries in heaven: David in the splendor of his kingdom, like the excellence of the sun; the moon, casting its shadow in hope, like the Synagogue; and its stars, its rulers. The evening of this age was the time when the people of God were led captive into Babylon.

In the fifth age, that is, in the Babylonian captivity, creatures were made as though in the waters, and birds of heaven, because at that time the Jews began to live among the nations as though in the sea; nor did they have a settled place, like flying birds. The evening of this day, as it were, is the multiplication of sins among the Jewish people, when they were so blinded that they could not even recognize the Lord Jesus.

The sixth age began with the advent of our Lord Jesus Christ. For just as on that sixth day the first Adam was made from the clay of the earth in the image [Col. 0736B] of God, so in this sixth age of the day the second Adam, that is, Christ, was born in the flesh from the Virgin Mary: the former in a living soul, the latter in a life-giving spirit.

And just as on that day a living soul was made, so in this age there are those who desire eternal life. And just as on that sixth day the earth produced the kinds of serpents and beasts, so in this sixth age of the world it generated the Church from the nations that desire eternal life.

And just as on that day male and female were created, so in this age of the world Christ and the Church were manifested. And just as on that day the human being was placed above cattle, serpents, and birds of heaven, so in this age Christ is placed above peoples and nations, so that they may be governed by him—whether, like cattle, they are devoted to carnal desire; whether, like serpents, they are darkened by earthly curiosity; or whether, like birds, they are characterized by pride.

And just as on that day the human being and the animals with him were fed with seed-bearing herbs, fruit-bearing trees, and green plants, so in this age the people themselves are spiritually fed with the nourishment of the Holy Scriptures and with divine law, to receive the fecundity of reasoning and discourse. These are like seed-bearing plants, partly for the usefulness of human conduct and life, partly for the vigor of faith, hope, and love unto eternal life, like green plants that do not wither in the heat of any tribulations. The carnal person—that is, the little one in Christ—is like God’s sheep, so that he may believe in the one whom he is not yet able to understand; nevertheless, they all have the same foods.

After this evening, morning will come, when the Lord himself comes in glory. Then they will rest with Christ from all their works. After such works, rest is to be hoped for on the seventh day, which has no evening.

O what glory belongs to the light of that seventh day, in which Christ is proclaimed in his own brightness, illuminated by the very Sun of the angels, whose beauty the sun and moon here admire! O what grace belongs to that day, which all the angels and all the saints will illuminate, each shining sevenfold more brightly than this sun!

And if this world is judged so beautiful, though it is illuminated by only one sun, what must be thought of that life which is illuminated by so many suns? But perhaps someone might say: “This sun provides great light because it shines with a large body; but what light can souls provide, even though they are most serene, when they are altogether small?”

Certainly, this sun is circumscribed by our eyes: its ray cannot pass through any body placed in its way; it is covered by clouds; at night it is wholly hidden from us. But angelic spirits and the souls of the saints are contained in no bodily place. They are believed to be circumscribed only by the incomprehensible and uncircumscribed God, and they are known to penetrate with the light of their brightness everything that stands in their way. Each of them, illuminated by the eternal Sun, shares its immense radiance with that day, and they delight in one another’s brightness.

# DIVISION OF THE SERMON

[Col. 0737B]

The heralds of all the prophets sang of the incomparable glory of this day, because this day is better than life lasting thousands of years.

The night of this age is divided, as it were, into four watches (Luke XII), because this world is distinguished by four intervals. The first watch was from Adam to Noah. In it, a few who were vigilant in goodness escaped danger; but the Flood drowned those oppressed by the sleep of wickedness.

The second watch existed from Noah to Moses. In it, those who kept good watch deserved to enjoy conversation with God; but those weighed down by the sleep of negligence were partly consumed by sulfur and fire, and partly swallowed by the Red Sea.

The third watch was from Moses to Christ. In it, cocks seemed to crow around midnight, when Moses through the Law and the prophets through their writings roused those who slept to the praise of God. Those who kept watch over the Lord’s commandments took possession of a land flowing with milk and honey; those devoted to the torpor of sloth perished in captivity and wars.

The fourth watch extended from Christ’s coming to the end of the world. In it the true morning star, Christ, appeared; through him it became clear that the dawn of the eternal day was present. In this watch, noble cocks—by their wings and voices—roused those sluggish in sleep, while the apostles and their followers urged all nations, by deeds and words, to awaken to the light of the true God.

In this watch the vigilant friends of the Bridegroom will rejoice; those wrapped in the sleep of error will be devoured by a stream of fire. Three hours are assigned to each of these watches [Col. 0737D], because in each of these periods the righteous are known to have possessed faith in the Holy Trinity.

The guardians of these four watches instructed us to keep watch, when they taught us the four principal virtues by words and examples. The observers of the first watch taught prudence; the sentinels of the second, courage; the guardians of the third, justice; and the combatants of the fourth instructed us in temperance.

And because they awaited Christ’s coming in these four watches, four Sundays concerning the Lord’s Advent are celebrated in the liturgy. And because the four regions of the world were to be cleansed through his second coming, the fourfold Church customarily celebrates his coming through four sets of offices.

In the dark night of this age, certain stars shone joyfully at various times and poured their light upon us. Although they could not then drive horror away from us, they pointed out the way for those proceeding toward the true Sun.

In the first watch Abel shone like a star: he taught us to die for justice when he himself, innocent, set.

After him others gleamed like stars in the night: Enos taught us to invoke God through piety; Enoch, to walk with God through purity; Lamech, through pious action, to hope for future rest.

In the second watch others shone like the stars of heaven: Noah showed us uprightness; Shem, modesty; Eber, steadfastness; Melchizedek, devotion; Abraham, faith; Lot, hospitality; Isaac, obedience; Jacob, endurance; and Joseph, chastity.

In the third watch various clusters of stars adorned the night with their rays. Moses instructed us in gentleness; Phinehas, zeal; Joshua, constancy; Job, patience; Gideon, confidence; Samuel, temperance; David, humility; Solomon, prudence; Hezekiah, supplications; Josiah, religious observance; Elijah, abstinence; Elisha, honor; Isaiah, holiness; and Jeremiah, sincerity.

The twelve prophets also shone like the Pleiades, teaching us concord. Ezekiel showed kindness; Daniel, faithfulness; the three youths, praise; Tobias, almsgiving; Esther, propriety; Judith, modesty; and the Maccabees, endurance, through their examples.

In the fourth watch, the star of the sea, the Virgin Mary, gleamed like a brilliant flame, showing by humility and chastity the way to the eternal Sun.

In this watch John the Baptist also shone like a planetary star, being the first to teach sinners repentance. In it too the true morning star, Christ, the glory of the stars and the light of the angels, shone forth. He established the radiance of the eternal day when he instructed us in love.

At the same time, shining stars scattered their flame-spitting radiance throughout the world, when the apostles instructed us in love, the martyrs in courage, confessors in sobriety, hermits in mortification, virgins in chastity, and widows in continence. All these shone like stars in this night and provided us a path to the eternal day.

[Col. 0738D] When this night has passed, the true Sun will shine in its unity. When the Son of God, the splendor of the Father, shines in his majesty for judgment, then he will remove the moon—that is, the Church—from darkness and illuminate it with eternal brightness; and he will transform all the stars into the glory of the sun.

Then he will reward the sentinels of these watches, when, passing from judgment, he will serve them eternal sweetness at the marriage feast of the Lamb. Therefore, beloved, let us live soberly, justly, and piously during this Advent of the Lord, so that at his second coming we may joyfully receive him and be able to reign with him forever, where eye has not seen and ear has not heard.

# THE THIRD SUNDAY BEFORE THE NATIVITY OF THE LORD

[Col. 0739]

[Col. 0739A] “And there will be signs in the sun and moon and stars, and on earth distress among nations because of the confusion caused by the roaring of the sea and the waves. People will faint from fear and expectation of what is coming upon the whole world,” and so forth (Luke XXI). A little earlier the Lord had foretold, saying: “Nation will rise against nation, and kingdom against kingdom, and there will be great earthquakes in various places, and pestilences, and famines” (ibid.); and, after inserting certain intervening material, he added this Gospel passage: “And there will be signs in the sun, and moon, and stars.”

(GREGORY.) Of all these things, some we plainly see already fulfilled, while we fear that others are near at hand. For we see nations rising against nations and their oppressions weighing upon the earth more in our own tribulations than we read of them in books. We hear from other parts of the world almost every day that earthquakes have overthrown countless cities [Col. 0739B]. But we have not yet clearly seen signs in the sun, moon, and stars. Nevertheless, because these things too are not far away, we infer it from the very alteration of the air. Indeed, before Italy was handed over to be struck by the sword of the nations, we saw fiery armies in the sky and the blood itself that was later poured out from the human race flashing in the heavens. The confusion of the sea and the waves has not yet newly arisen; but since so many things previously foretold have been fulfilled, there is no doubt that the few things remaining will follow as well, because the fulfillment of past events gives certainty concerning what follows.

We have said this so that your minds may awaken to the practice of caution, lest they grow sluggish through security or languish through ignorance [Col. 0739C], but so that fear may always urge them toward good works and concern may strengthen them. (BEDE.) The phrase “because of the confusion,” that is, “before the confusion,” means that the signs and the distress of the nations will come first. Then will follow the confusion caused by the roaring of the sea and the waves. The prophet Joel says: “The sun will be turned into darkness and the moon into blood, before the great and manifest day of the Lord comes” (Joel II).

As judgment presses upon the world, it is rightly thrown into confusion by the roaring of the sea and the waves; its inhabitants press upon one another, the earth is polluted, and the greatest lights of heaven are disturbed. For just as trees driven toward their fall usually give warning beforehand through the crash and movement they will make, so, as the end of the world approaches, the elements, as though afraid, tremble and totter. Nor is it surprising that people faint from fear, in whom this will be fulfilled: “The whole world will fight on his behalf against the senseless” (Wisdom V).

(GREGORY.) Everything that we received for the use of life, we have turned to the use of sin. But everything that we bent toward wickedness is turned against us for the use of punishment. We turned the tranquility of human peace to the use of empty security; we loved the pilgrimage of the earth as though it were the habitation of our homeland. We reduced the health of our bodies to the service of vices. We twisted the abundance of fertility, not toward the needs of the flesh, but toward the perversity of pleasure. We compelled the very serene caresses of the air to serve our love of earthly delight [Col. 0740A]. It is therefore just that all the things which had served us, all together subdued by our vices, should strike us all together, so that as many joys as we previously possessed unharmed in the world, so many torments we may afterward be forced to experience from it itself.

“And if those days had not been shortened, no flesh would be saved; but for the sake of the elect those days will be shortened.” The meaning is this: if God, who gives the strength to endure, had not by his own ordering shortened the power to persecute, few or none would be saved. He does not therefore say this so that times may be altered according to the ravings of certain people who fail to attend to what is written: “By your ordinance the day endures” (Psalm CXVIII), but so that the prolonged duration of wickedness may not shake the faith of believers. For the greater the future tribulation of Antichrist will be than all others, the more moderate it will be because of the brevity of its duration [Col. 0740B]. The Church will be attacked by Antichrist for three years and six months.

“Immediately after the tribulation of those days the sun will be darkened, and the moon will not give its light, and the stars will fall from heaven, and the powers of heaven will be shaken, and then the sign of the Son of Man will appear in heaven.” Understand “the sign” as the cross or the banner of victory. At the day of judgment everything will be dark, not because the light has diminished, but by comparison with the true light. Isaiah prophesied of this, saying: “The moon will be ashamed and the sun will be confounded, when the Lord of hosts reigns on Mount Zion and in Jerusalem and is glorified in the presence of his elders” (Isaiah XXIV).

After the day of judgment has been completed and the glory of the future life has begun to shine [Col. 0740C], then heaven will begin to be new and earth new. Then what the same prophet says elsewhere will come to pass: “Then the light of the moon will be like the light of the sun, and the light of the sun will be sevenfold, like the light of seven days” (Isaiah XXX).

(GREGORY.) Whom does the Lord call the powers of heaven except the angels, archangels, thrones, dominions, principalities, and powers, who will visibly appear to our eyes at his coming, so that then they may strictly demand from us what the invisible Creator now bears with equanimity?

(BEDE.) What wonder if human beings tremble when angelic powers tremble at the sight of judgment? Hence Job says: “The pillars of heaven tremble and are terrified at his command” (Job XXVI). What, then, do the boards do when the pillars tremble? What does a slender branch of the desert suffer when the cedar of paradise is shaken?

“And then he will send his angels with a trumpet and a loud voice, and they will gather his elect from the four winds, from the highest parts of the heavens to their boundaries.” The trumpet signifies the power to raise the dead; the loud voice signifies that no one will remain unraised and that all will be present at the judgment.

(BEDE, on Mark.) “From the four winds,” that is, from the four regions of the world: east, west, north, and south. And lest anyone suppose that they would not also be gathered from the regions lying between these, Mark added: “From the farthest part of the earth to the farthest part of heaven” (Mark XIII) [Col. 0741A], that is, from the remotest ends of the earth directly to its furthest boundaries, where, for those waiting far away, the circle of heaven appears to rest upon the earth. All, therefore, both elect and reprobate, will come to judgment.

Matthew says: “From the highest parts of the heavens to their boundaries” (Matthew XXIV), which signifies everyone who is beneath the curvature of heaven, as though beneath the horizon.

Alternatively: immediately after the tribulation of those days has begun, though not yet ended, the sun of righteousness will be darkened for cold hearts.

(AMBROSE.) Just as, according to the capacity of the one who sees, a ray of the worldly sun appears either paler or brighter, so, according to the devotion of the believer, spiritual light is poured into each person. The moon does not give light if, because the earth intervenes, the sun’s rays are shut out; so the Church will not give light when the vices of the flesh obstruct it, preventing it from borrowing radiance from the rays of divine light [Col. 0741B]. For in persecutions it is generally the love of this present life alone that shuts out the light of God.

“The stars will fall from heaven”: the same is true of the Church, because the seed of Abraham, to which the stars are compared, will be almost lacking.

(REMIGIUS.) “The powers of heaven will be shaken,” because certain very strong believers will be disturbed when the wicked rage beyond measure. Or the angels will be moved to the anger of vengeance; they are the ones who will be sent by the Son of Man with the trumpet. They are said to descend with the trumpet—that is, to bring war in the name of God—because the final trumpet signifies the last war against the evil spirits, who have often been defeated by the angels, as the apostle John says: “I saw Michael and his angels fighting in heaven against the dragon” (Revelation XII). It will be the final war, because then they will be sent into Gehenna.

At the time of the tribulation of Antichrist [Col. 0741C], the sign of the Son of Man will appear—in heaven, it is understood, and not on earth. The power of the cross will then be hidden on earth, but it will be most clearly manifested in heaven among the thousands of saints.

“Then all the tribes of the earth will mourn,” that is, they will do what deserves mourning, and what necessarily follows mourning. For they will do things worthy of mourning, and mourning will necessarily follow.

“And at last they will see the Son of Man coming in the clouds of heaven,” that is, in the saints, just as even now he does not cease to come, according to what he said: “From now on you will see the Son of Man seated at the right hand of the power of God and coming in the clouds of heaven.” But he will then come with great power and majesty because his greater power and majesty will appear to the saints, to whom he will give great strength so that they may not be overcome by so great a persecution [Col. 0741D].

“And he will send his angels,” that is, preachers; “with a trumpet,” that is, with manifestation. For in the Law trumpets are commanded to be made of beaten gold, bronze, and silver, so that they may resound with the sublime mysteries of doctrine.

“And they will gather his elect from the four parts of the world,” that is, from the whole earth. The steadfastness of the saints will certainly be great when it is heard that Antichrist has been killed by the breath of the Lord’s mouth and that all Israel has been converted to the faith.

“When these things begin to happen, look up and raise your heads, because your redemption is drawing near.”

(GREGORY.) When the plagues of the world multiply and the terror of judgment is displayed through the shaking of the powers, “raise your heads,” that is, make your hearts joyful. For while the world to which you are not friends is coming to an end, the redemption you sought through faith is drawing near [Col. 0742A]. In Holy Scripture “head” is often used for “mind,” because just as the limbs are governed by the head, so thoughts are ordered by the mind. To raise our heads, therefore, is to lift our minds toward the joys of our heavenly homeland.

Those who love God are commanded to rejoice and be glad at the end of the world, because they will soon find the one whom they love, while the one whom they did not love is passing away. Far be it from any believer who desires to see God to mourn at the world’s blows, since he knows that the world is being brought to an end by those very blows. For it is written: “Whoever wishes to be a friend of this world is made an enemy of God” (James IV). Whoever therefore does not rejoice as the end of the world approaches testifies that he is its friend and is thereby proved to be God’s enemy.

But may this be far from the hearts of the faithful! May it be far from those who believe by faith that another life exists and love it through their works. To mourn at the destruction of the world belongs to those who have planted the roots of their hearts in love of it, who do not seek the life to come, who suspect that neither that life nor any other exists. But we, who have learned the eternal joys of our heavenly homeland, ought to hasten toward it as quickly as possible. We should desire to depart sooner and reach it by a shorter road.

## Concerning the final time of Antichrist and the last tribulation

(AUGUSTINE, to Hesychius, in the letter *On the End of the World*.) We do not dare to calculate the times of the Savior’s coming, which is expected at the end, nor do we think that any prophet fixed a number of years concerning this matter. Rather, what the Lord himself said prevails: “No one can know the times which the Father has placed in his own power” (Acts I).

To calculate the times—that is, to know through chronological reckoning when the end of this age or the Lord’s coming will be—is, in my view, nothing other than wanting to know what he himself said no one can know (Matthew XXIV). The appropriate time for that event certainly had not yet arrived, because the Gospel had first to be preached throughout the whole world as a testimony to all nations. For the Savior’s statement on this subject is read with complete clarity: “This Gospel of the kingdom will be preached throughout the whole world as a testimony to all nations; then the end will come” (ibid.). “Then the end will come”—what does this mean except that it will not come before then? [Col. 0742D]

When it will come afterward is unknown to us; nevertheless, we certainly must not doubt that it will not come before that time. If, therefore, it is hidden when the whole world, flourishing and increasing through the Church, will be filled from sea to sea, then without doubt it is hidden when the end will be. For it will not come beforehand.

“Then the lawless one will be revealed,” that is, Antichrist, “whom the Lord Jesus will kill with the breath of his mouth” (II Thessalonians II).

Concerning the final tribulation, the same Augustine says in the book *The City of God*: “Then Satan will be released from his prison, and he will go out to deceive the nations that are in the four corners of the earth, Gog and Magog” (Revelation XX). We understand the interpretation of these names to be: Gog, “roof”; Magog, “from the roof,” as though they were the house and the one who comes forth from the house.

The nations, then, are those among whom we previously understood the devil to have been shut up, as though in an abyss; and he himself, in a certain manner, will raise and bring himself forth from them, so that they are the roof and he is the one from the roof.

We must consider why the devil is now bound. The devil’s binding means that he is not permitted to exercise all the temptation of which he is capable, whether by force or deceit, to compel people violently or fraudulently to his side, whether by coercion or deception. If this were permitted, then during so long a time, and amid the great weakness of many, he would overthrow and prevent from believing very many such people as God does not wish to suffer this; he would cast down the faithful and hinder them from believing. To prevent this, he has been bound.

Then he will be released, when the time will also be short. For it is read that he will rage with all his own strength and that of his followers for three years and six months, and those with whom he must wage war will be such that they cannot be conquered by the force of his assault and ambushes [Col. 0743B].

Satan will be released at the end of the age so that the city of God may see, with the great glory of its Redeemer, helper, and liberator, how powerful an adversary it has overcome.

Why he is released at the very end should be considered. As has been said, Satan will go out into open persecution and burst forth from the hiding places of hatred. This will be the final persecution, when judgment is about to arrive and the holy Church suffers throughout the whole world, while the entire faithful city of Christ is opposed by the entire city of the devil, however large each may be on earth.

Hence the Apostle says: “The love of many will grow cold, and iniquity will abound” (Matthew XXIV). Hence Daniel says: “There will be a time of tribulation such as has not been since a nation came into existence on earth until that time” (Daniel XII) [Col. 0743C].

This final persecution by Antichrist will last three years and six months. Christ will not come to judge the living and the dead unless his adversary Antichrist has first come to deceive those who are spiritually dead; the Lord Jesus will kill him with the breath of his mouth.

Then Elijah the Tishbite will also come, before the great and glorious day of the Lord comes. He will “turn the heart of the father to the son, and the heart of a man to his neighbor, lest, when he comes, he strike the earth utterly” (Malachi IV).

It is a very common belief in the speech and hearts of the faithful that through this great and wondrous prophet Elijah, the Jews will, at the end of time before judgment, have the Law explained to them and will believe in the true Christ—that is, in our Christ. He is rightly expected to come before the advent of the Savior as judge, and he is also rightly believed still to be alive. For he was carried away from human affairs in a fiery chariot, as Holy Scripture most clearly testifies (IV Kings II).

When he comes, therefore, he will explain spiritually the Law which the Jews now understand carnally. “He will turn the heart of the father to the son,” that is, the hearts of the fathers to the children. The hearts of the fathers will be turned to the children when the understanding of the fathers is brought to the understanding of the children, and the hearts of the children to their fathers when the children agree with what the fathers understood.

## Another account of Antichrist

Before the terrifying coming of our Redeemer, as has been stated, Antichrist will come. He will be born in great Babylon from a prostitute of the line of Dan [Col. 0744A]. But since you wish to know about him, first note why he is so called. He is called this because he will do everything contrary to Christ. Christ came humbly to raise up the humble and justify sinners; he, by contrast, will come proudly, cast down the humble, magnify sinners, exalt the ungodly, and teach the vices opposed to virtue.

He will destroy the evangelical Law, restore the worship of demons to the world, seek empty glory, and call himself the omnipotent God.

This Antichrist will therefore have many ministers of his wickedness. Some of them have already preceded him in the world, such as Antiochus, Nero, and Domitian. Even in our own time we know many to be antichrists (I John II). For every layman, cleric, or even monk who lives contrary to justice, attacks the rule of his order, and blasphemes what is good belongs to Antichrist and is a minister of Satan.

But let us now examine the beginning of Antichrist. I am not inventing what I say about him from my own opinion; rather, by reading the books carefully, I find everything written there. Thus, as our authorities say, Antichrist will be born from the Jewish people, from the tribe of Dan, according to the prophet who says: “Let Dan be a serpent on the way, a horned serpent on the path” (Genesis XLIX).

For like a serpent he will sit on the road and be on the path, so that he may strike those who walk along the path of righteousness and kill them with the poison of his wickedness. He will be born from the union of a male and a female, like other human beings—not, as some say, from a virgin alone—but he will be entirely generated in sin [Col. 0744C].

At the very beginning of his conception the devil will enter together with him into his mother’s womb; he will be nourished and protected there by the devil’s power, and the devil himself will always be with him.

Just as the Holy Spirit came upon the mother of our Lord, overshadowed her by his power, and filled her with divinity, so that she conceived through the Spirit and what was born would be divine and holy, so also the devil will descend into the mother of Antichrist and fill her completely, so that what is born will be wholly iniquitous, evil, and lost.

Hence he is also called “the son of perdition” (II Thessalonians II), because insofar as he can he will destroy the human race, and in the end he himself will be destroyed.

You have heard how he will be born; hear also the place where he is to be born. Just as the Lord chose Bethlehem for himself, so that there he might assume humanity for us and be born, so the devil knows a suitable place for that lost man called Antichrist, from which the root of all evils is to arise—namely, Babylon.

In this city, which was once a famous and glorious city of the nations and the capital of the Persian kingdom, Antichrist will be born. He is said to live in the cities of Bethsaida and Chorazin.

The Lord reproached these cities in the Gospel, saying: “Woe to you, Bethsaida! Woe to you, Chorazin!” (Luke X.)

Antichrist will have magicians, sorcerers, diviners, and enchanters [Col. 0745A]. Inspired by the devil, they will nourish and instruct him in every iniquity, falsehood, and wicked art. Evil spirits will be his guides, companions, and inseparable associates.

Then, coming to Jerusalem, he will slaughter through various tortures all the Christians whom he cannot convert to himself, and he will establish his seat in the holy temple. He will also restore to its former state the destroyed temple built by Solomon, circumcise himself, and falsely claim to be the Son of the Almighty.

He will subject the entire human race to himself in four ways, because he will rule the whole world. First, he will attract the nobles to himself through wealth, which will flow to him in abundance, because every hidden treasure will be known to him. He will first convert kings and princes to himself, and then convert others through them.

Second, he will subject the common people to himself through terror, because he will rage with the greatest savagery against the worshipers of God.

Third, he will win over the clergy through wisdom and incredible eloquence, because he knows all the arts and all the Scriptures by heart.

Fourth, he will deceive those who despise the world, such as monks, through signs and wonders.

He will destroy the places through which Christ the Lord walked and which he illumined. Then he will send messengers and preachers throughout the whole world. His preaching and power will extend from sea to sea, from east to west, and from north to south.

He will also perform many great, wondrous, and unheard-of signs. He will cause terrifying fires to descend from heaven; trees suddenly to flower and wither; the sea suddenly to be disturbed and calmed; natures to change into different forms; the courses and order of waters to be altered; the air to be stirred by winds and by disturbances of many kinds; and countless other astonishing things to occur. He will cause the dead to be raised in the sight of people, so that, if possible, even the elect may be led into error [Col. 0745C].

He will also cause the fire that seems to descend from heaven at his command to consume his adversaries before him, and the dead who have risen to bear witness on his behalf.

Will he truly raise the dead? Certainly not. Rather, through his magic the devil will enter the body of some condemned person, bring it forth, and speak through it, so that it appears to be alive.

He will rebuild ancient Jerusalem and command that he be worshiped there as God. When even those who are perfect and chosen by God see such great signs, they will doubt whether he is the Christ who is to come at the end of the world or not [Col. 0745D]. But, as has been said, all these miracles will be entirely false, produced through diabolical enchantments, although they will appear true to sinners and unbelievers.

## Division of the account

Antichrist will stir up persecutions against Christians and all the elect beneath the whole heaven. He will therefore rise against the faithful in three ways: through terror, miracles, and gifts. He will give an abundance of gold and silver to those who believe in him. Those whom he cannot deceive with gifts he will test through terror. Those whom he cannot overcome through terror he will test with signs and miracles. Those whom he cannot deceive even with signs he will kill a miserable death before everyone.
