“Then there will be such tribulation as has not been since the nations began to exist until that time. Then those who are in the field will flee to the mountains; and the one who is on the roof will not go down into the house to take anything from it” (Mark XIII) [Col. 0746A].

Then every faithful Christian who is found will either deny God or, if he remains in the faith, perish by the sword, by fire in a furnace, by serpents, by wild beasts, or by any other kind of torture.

This terrifying tribulation will last throughout the whole world for three years and six months. “Then the days will be shortened for the sake of the elect. For if the Lord had not shortened the days, no flesh would have been saved” (ibid.).

The time when Antichrist will come, or when the day of judgment will begin to appear, is described by the apostle Paul in the Epistle to the Thessalonians: “We beseech you by the coming of our Lord Jesus Christ.” He makes the matter clear where he says: “Unless the apostasy comes first and the man of sin and son of perdition is revealed” (II Thessalonians II) [Col. 0746B].

For we know that after the kingdom of the Greeks, and also after the kingdom of the Persians—each of which flourished in its own time with great glory and power—at last, after the other kingdoms, the Roman kingdom began. It was the strongest of all the preceding kingdoms, drew all kingdoms to itself, and held them under its domination; all nations served the Romans under tribute.

Therefore the apostle Paul says that Antichrist will not come into the world unless the apostasy comes first (II Thessalonians II), that is, unless all the kingdoms first depart from the Roman Empire to which they had previously been subject.

That time has not yet come. Although we see the Roman Empire destroyed for the most part, nevertheless, as long as the kings of the Franks endure—since they are to hold the Roman Empire—the dignity of the Roman kingdom will not wholly perish, because it will stand in its kings [Col. 0746C].

Some of our teachers say that one of the kings of the Franks will hold the Roman Empire in its entirety; he will be the greatest and last of all kings at the end of time. After he has governed his kingdom successfully, he will finally come to Jerusalem and lay down his scepter and crown on the Mount of Olives. This will be the end and completion of the Romans and of the Christian empire.

Immediately afterward, in accordance with the apostle Paul’s statement mentioned above, they say that Antichrist will appear. Then a certain man will be revealed (II Thessalonians II)—namely Antichrist—who, although he is human, will be the source of all sins, the son of perdition, that is, the son of the devil, not by nature but by imitation. For he will fulfill the devil’s will in every respect, and the fullness of diabolical power and every evil intention will dwell bodily in him; in him will be all the treasures of malice, wickedness, and iniquity.

“He who opposes,” that is, who is contrary to Christ and all his members; “and is exalted,” that is, raised up in pride, “above everything that is called God,” that is, above the elect or the gods of the nations—Jupiter, Apollo, and Mercury, whom the pagans consider gods. Antichrist will exalt himself above all these, because he will make himself greater and stronger than all of them.

And not only above them, but also “above everything that is worshiped,” that is, above the holy Trinity, which alone must be worshiped and adored by every creature [Col. 0747A]. He will exalt himself so far that he will sit in the temple of God, displaying himself as though he were God.

For, as we said above, having been born in the city of Babylon, he will come to Jerusalem, circumcise himself, and say to the Jews: “I am the Christ promised to you. I have come for your salvation, to gather and defend you who are scattered.”

Then all the Jews will flock to him, thinking that they are receiving Christ when they are receiving the devil.

But lest Antichrist come suddenly and unexpectedly and deceive the entire human race all at once, destroying it through his error, two great prophets, Enoch and Elijah, will be sent into the world before his appearance. They will fortify God’s faithful against Antichrist’s assault with divine weapons, instruct and strengthen the elect for battle, and preach for three years and six months.

At what age will those two come? At the age at which they were taken up.

Whatever children of Israel are found at that time, the prophets and teachers will convert them to the grace of faith and make the pressure of so great a storm bearable for the elect. Then what Scripture says will be fulfilled: “If the number of the children of Israel is like the sand of the sea, the remnant will be saved” (Romans VIII).

After they have completed their preaching over three years and six months, the persecution of Antichrist will immediately begin to blaze up. Antichrist will first take up his weapons against them and kill them, as it is written in Revelation: “And when they have finished,” it says, “the beast that rises from the abyss will make war against them, conquer them, and kill them” (Revelation XI) [Col. 0747C].

After these two have been killed, he will persecute the remaining faithful, either making them glorious martyrs or turning them into apostates. Whoever believes in him will receive the mark of his character on the forehead.

But we have now said enough about his beginning; let us say what his end will be.

## Division of the account

This Antichrist, son of the devil and craftsman of every wickedness, is called by three names in the three parts of the world—Asia, Africa, and Europe—and in three languages. In Hebrew, *Amoime*, that is, “I deny”; in Greek, *Antimosi*, that is, “contrary”; in Latin, *Titan*, that is, “sun” or “giant” [Col. 0747D].

For three years and six months, as stated above, he will afflict the whole world with a great persecution and surround the entire people of God with various punishments. After he has killed Enoch and Elijah and crowned the others who remain steadfast in the faith with martyrdom, at last the wrath of God will come upon him.

He will extend his tent on the Mount of Olives to attack the righteous, and there he will be found dead by a sudden death. As blessed Paul writes: “For the Lord Jesus will kill him with the breath of his mouth” (II Thessalonians II). Either the Lord Jesus will kill him by the power of his appearing, or the archangel Michael will kill him through the power of our Lord Jesus Christ; he will not be killed by the power of any angel or archangel.

The teachers also relate that, as we have already stated, Antichrist will be killed on the Mount of Olives in a tent, and on his throne, in the very place in which God ascended into heaven [Col. 0748A].

We must know, however, that after he has been killed the day of judgment will not come immediately (John III). Rather, as we read in the book of Daniel, the Lord will grant the elect forty days in which to do penance, since they had been deceived to some extent by Antichrist.

After they have done penance, no one knows how much time will pass until the Lord comes. It remains in God’s ordering: he will judge the age at that hour, although he fixed beforehand when the age was to be judged.

The judgment will take place in the valley of Jehoshaphat, as it is said. The valley of Jehoshaphat is called the valley of judgment. A valley is always beside a mountain. The valley here is the world; the mountain is heaven.

Judgment therefore takes place in the valley, that is, in this world—namely, in the air—where the righteous will be stationed at Christ’s right hand like sheep, while the wicked will be placed on his left like goats.

How are they placed on the right or left? On the right, that is, upward in glory; on the left, downward upon the earth. The righteous are lifted to the heights on the twin wings of love, as it is said: “The saints will take wings like eagles.” The wicked, weighed down by sins like lead, are thrust downward toward earthly things to which they had clung with all their heart.

Concerning the speed of this judgment, Augustine says to Consentius: “In an atom,” says the Apostle—that is, in a point of time which cannot be divided—“in the twinkling of an eye,” that is, with the utmost speed—“at the last trumpet,” that is, at the final sign which will be given so that these things may be accomplished.

“For the trumpet will sound,” he says, “and the dead will rise incorruptible, and we will be changed.” This change must undoubtedly be understood as being for the better, because everyone, both the righteous and the unrighteous, will rise [Col. 0748C].

But as the Lord says in the Gospel: “What he has done well will rise to the resurrection of life; what he has done badly, to the resurrection of judgment” (John V), calling judgment eternal punishment. As he says elsewhere: “Whoever does not believe,” he says, “has already been judged” (John III).

Therefore those who rise for judgment will not be changed into that incorruptibility which cannot suffer the corruption of pain. That belongs to the faithful and the saints. These others, however, will be burned in everlasting damnation, because “their fire will not be extinguished, and their worm will not die” [Col. 0748D].

Thus they will indeed rise incorrupt in the integrity of their limbs, but they will nevertheless be corrupted by the pain of punishments when they hear: “Go into the eternal fire prepared for the devil and his angels” (Matthew XXV)—from hearing this evil report the righteous will not be afraid.

## On the same subject

Just as the ray of our eye does not reach nearer things more quickly or farther things more slowly, but reaches both distances with equal speed, so, when the resurrection of the dead occurs “in the twinkling of an eye,” as the Apostle says, it is equally easy for the omnipotence of God and his ineffable will to raise recent corpses and bodies that have long since decayed.

## Again on the same subject

The judgment will be exceedingly swift at the Lord’s unexpected coming, though it had been thought exceedingly slow, because he will convict the consciences themselves, even if not by a lengthy speech. For, as it is written, “the interrogation of the wicked will be in their thoughts” (Wisdom I).

And the Apostle says: “Their thoughts accuse or even excuse them on the day when God will judge the hidden things of human beings according to my Gospel through Jesus Christ” (Romans II).

The Lord is also to be understood as a swift witness, since without delay he will recall to memory the grounds by which he will convict and punish the conscience [Col. 0750A].

In what form will the Lord appear there? To the elect, in the form in which he appeared on the mountain; to the reprobate, in the form in which he hung upon the cross.

Will the cross be there—that is, the wood on which the Lord suffered? Certainly not, but a light in the form of a cross, brighter than the sun.

At what hour will the judgment take place? At midnight, the hour when the angel devastated Egypt and the Lord despoiled hell. At that same hour he will free his elect from this world.

## THE SECOND SUNDAY BEFORE THE NATIVITY OF THE LORD

[Col. 0749]

[Col. 0749B] “When John heard in prison about the works of Christ, he sent two of his disciples and said to him: ‘Are you the one who is to come, or should we expect another?’” (Matthew XI.)

You are Jesus: tell me whether I should announce you to those in the underworld, where I am about to descend, or whether it is unfitting for you to taste death, since you are the Son of God?

(GREGORY, on Ezekiel.) The spirit of prophecy sometimes touches the soul of the prophet concerning the present and not the future, as when John says: “Behold the Lamb of God” (John I). But, about to die, he inquired through his disciples, saying: “Are you the one who is to come, or should we expect another?”

By this he showed that he knew the Redeemer had come, but doubted whether he would descend into hell by himself. Through such a lapse arising from piety and love, not from unbelief, even the saints did not believe that Christ would die [Col. 0749C]. Hence Peter, the chief of the faith, said: “Far be it from you, Lord; this shall not happen to you” (Matthew XVI).

John also sent his disciples to Christ to provide for their ignorance, so that, seeing the signs, they might believe. They were suffering scandal because they had heard Jesus being preferred to their teacher. This became clear when they said: “Rabbi, the one to whom you bore witness—behold, he is baptizing, and everyone is coming to him” (John III).

At that very hour he cured many of illnesses, wounds, and evil spirits, and bestowed sight on many blind people. And he answered them: “Go and report to John what you have seen and heard: the blind see, the lame walk, lepers are cleansed, the deaf hear, the dead rise, the poor are evangelized” (Luke [Col. 0749D] VII). These words refer to the scandal of the messengers, not to what was asked. He calls them “poor” either in spirit or in works, so that in the preacher there may be no distinction between the noble and the lowly, between the rich and the needy. “The poor are evangelized,” that is, they are drawn by the Gospel and converted to the faith. “And blessed is the one who is not scandalized in me.”

Here the Lord answers concerning the humility of his death. The faithful are blessed whose faith is shaken by nothing—not the cross, death, or burial. He rebukes the messengers of John, who did not believe that he was the Christ, for the scandal of their unbelief, and explains to John himself what he was asking: that God is the one who saves, and that the Lord’s exits are from death (Psalm LXVII). After seeing so many signs, anyone could have been moved not to scandal but to wonder. Yet the mind of unbelievers was deeply troubled when they saw the Lord die after so many miracles. Hence Paul: “But we preach Christ crucified: to the Jews indeed a scandal, but to the Gentiles foolishness” (1 Corinthians [Col. 0750B] I).

The Lord performed wonders, but then he did not disdain to die. And indeed, since it seems to many that John at least knew from the writings of the prophets that Christ would finally die, let us read the passage in that sense as well. Just as the Lord said to Lazarus, “Where has he been laid?”, so John questions Christ—not for himself at all, but for his disciples. The question may also be understood in this way: “Are you the one whom the Law foretold would come, or is another Christ to be expected?” The Lord answers by deeds rather than words. Certainly, the miracles that were seen give full testimony that he is the Son of God. Such things had been rare or nonexistent before the Gospel. Tobias alone received his sight, and this was the healing of an angel, not of a human being. Elijah raised a dead man, but he himself pleaded and wept. This one commanded. Elisha caused a leper to be cleansed, yet there the authority of the command did not prevail; rather, it was a figure of ministry. After the things mentioned above, he adds what concerns the cross, death, and burial, which is the fullness of faith. For no testimony is greater than that he offered his whole self for the world. By this alone the Lord is fully declared. Thus he was also declared by John: “Behold the Lamb of God; behold the one who takes away the sins of the world” (John I).

“Now, as they were departing, he began to speak to the crowds about John: ‘What did you go out into the desert to see?’” (Matthew XI.) “A reed shaken by the wind.” Because the surrounding crowd did not know the mystery of the question and supposed that John doubted concerning Christ, in order to make clear that John had asked not for himself but for his disciples, he says this in praise of John. By the reed he signifies a mind empty of the thought of God and wandering at the breath of unclean spirits. John did not possess such a mind, since he was neither lifted up by prosperity nor accustomed to bend before adversity. It continues:

“But what did you go out to see? A man dressed in soft clothing? Behold, those who are in costly clothing and luxury are in the houses of kings” (ibid.). (Jerome.) Thus the person led on by vainglory seeks profit, though he lives on locusts for his food and wears camel’s hair. Here it should be noted that a strict life and preaching ought to avoid the palaces of the soft, who frequent them dressed in softness and flattering—those who place cushions beneath their elbows, who caress the lives of sinners rather than prick them, so that in this way they may receive some honor. (Gregory, in a homily.) [Col. 0751A] “Let no one suppose that sin is absent from the pursuit of costly clothing.” Hence the apostle Peter says in his letter to women: “Not in costly clothing” (1 Peter I).

“But what did you go out to see? A prophet? Indeed, I tell you, and more than a prophet” (Matthew XI). In this respect John is more than a prophet: he pointed with his finger to the one whom the others had foretold would come. (Hilary.) Those two occurrences of *sed* (“but”) are read in place of *et* (“and”).

Mystically: The Law, joined to the sins of the people and enclosed in the breasts of sinners as in prisons devoid of light, was held captive, so that through it Christ could not be understood. (Ambrose.) Therefore he sends the disciples to contemplate the Gospel, so that they may receive its completion, because Christ is the fullness of the Law. And when the truth often seemed uncertain without deeds, the fullest faith is presented through the testimony of events. [Col. 0751B] (Gregory.) John was not dressed in soft clothing, because he did not indulge the lives of sinners with flatteries but rebuked them harshly. Hence Solomon: “The words of the wise are like goads, and like nails driven firmly” (Ecclesiastes XII).

“For this is the one about whom it is written: ‘Behold, I send my angel before your face, who will prepare your way before you’” (Matthew XI). (Gregory.) What is called *angelus* in Greek is called *nuntius* (“messenger”) in Latin. Rightly, therefore, the one sent to announce the heavenly Judge is called an angel, so that he may preserve in his name the dignity that he fulfills in his work: it is indeed a lofty name, provided that his life is not low. Accordingly, all who are reckoned under the name of the priesthood are called angels, as the prophet testifies when he says: “The lips of the priests shall guard knowledge, and they shall seek the Law from his mouth, because he is the angel of the Lord of hosts” (Malachi II).

But you too, if you wish, can earn the dignity of this lofty name. For each one of you, insofar as he is able and insofar as he has received the grace of heavenly inspiration, if he recalls his neighbor from wickedness, if he takes care to exhort him to do good, if he announces eternal kingdom or punishment to one who is in error, when he offers words of holy exhortation, certainly becomes an angel. And let no one say, “I am not capable of admonishing; I am not suited to exhort.” Offer whatever you can, lest, by wickedly preserving what you have received, you be required to render an account amid torments.

For we know that in the tabernacle not only bowls (*phialae*) but, at the Lord’s command, also cups (*cyathi*) were made (Exodus XX). [Col. 0752B] By the bowls, overflowing doctrine is signified; by the cups, a small and limited measure of knowledge. One person, full of the doctrine of truth, intoxicates the minds of his hearers. By saying this, he plainly offers a bowl. Another is able to explain what he understands. But because he communicates both, he plainly supplies a cup. Therefore, placed in God’s tabernacle—that is, in the holy Church—if you are not at all able to serve bowls through the wisdom of doctrine, give your neighbors cups of good speech to the extent that divine generosity enables you. And insofar as you judge yourselves to have advanced, strive to draw others along with you. Desire to have companions on the way of God.

## SERMON ON THE ADVENT OF THE LORD

[Col. 0751]

[Col. 0751C] “Say to the fainthearted: ‘Take courage. Behold, our God will come and save us. Then the eyes of the blind shall be opened, and the ears of the deaf shall be unstopped; and the lame shall leap like a stag, and the tongue of the mute shall be opened’” (Isaiah XXXV).

Before the Lord’s advent, dearest brothers, the entire human race was enveloped in such darkness that people neither knew God nor wished to hear his words; they neither did good works nor confessed their sins. Since they were held by many illnesses of the soul, it pleased the supreme physician to visit them and relieve them with his medicines. But the prophet Isaiah notes that they suffered especially from four illnesses: they were blind, deaf, lame, and mute. And since he wished to heal their diseases, so that the wretched might not despair, he wished to announce his advent to them and console them with his encouragements.

Do you wish to know who the messengers are? Isaiah and the other prophets. Hear, then, what consolation he entrusted to the messengers: “You are my ministers; say to the miserable peoples who lie in anguish and despair in their infirmities: ‘O fainthearted, take courage, because behold, our God will come. Behold, our medicine; behold, our salvation will come and will save us. He will heal those infirmities to which you are subject, because then the eyes of the blind shall be opened,’” [Col. 0752C] and so forth.

They were blind because they did not know God. They were deaf because they neglected God’s words; lame because they did not walk rightly through good works; mute because they kept silent about their sins. This deafness and blindness, and the other conditions that follow, took their beginning from the first man.

For Adam became deaf at the first command imposed on him by God. When it was said to him, “On whatever day you eat from the tree of the knowledge of good and evil, you shall surely die” (Genesis III), he appeared not to have heard the words “you shall surely die.” But since he did not observe the commandment, he was blind when he did not understand the words of the devil: “You shall be like gods” (ibid.). When he supposed, plainly, that he would become God, he already bore a blinded mind. The Lord afterward reproached him for this, saying: “Behold, Adam has become like one of us” (ibid.), [Col. 0752D] as though he were mockingly saying: “Behold Adam, who thought he would become God; now he finds himself wretched. ‘Having become like one of us,’ that is, having become God, made like the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit”—this was said ironically, as though he had found himself otherwise than he had thought.

Adam also limped, because when he began to walk, he walked with a crooked step, wounded by the sting of the poisonous serpent; and thus, by doing evil, he limped. The first sin that he is recorded to have committed was likewise this: to limp. A person ought to have two feet: love of God and love of neighbor. Whoever lacks one of these is lame.

Adam, therefore, limped because he loved his wife excessively when he turned away from the love of God. He did not love God, whose commandments he neglected. He placed the love of his wife above the love of God, since he obeyed his wife’s will more readily than God’s. (Augustine.) For after the woman had been deceived and had eaten from the forbidden tree, she gave some to him so that they might eat together. He did not wish to sadden her, believing that she might waste away without his support if she were separated from his affection, and that she might altogether perish through this disagreement—not conquered by the desire of the flesh, which she had not yet experienced, but by a certain friendly benevolence, through which it often happens that God is offended lest a human being become an enemy from being a friend.

Thus, in another way, he too was deceived; but by that serpent’s deception by which the woman was deceived, I believe that he could in no way have been deceived. (Augustine, *On the Literal Meaning of Genesis*, book I, chapter 27.) [Col. 0753B] “For she was first deceived through the serpent, and afterward the man through the woman. The devil, however, spoke in the serpent, using it as an instrument and moving its nature in the manner in which that serpent moves; and the serpent could be moved to produce the sounds of words and bodily signs by which the woman might understand the intention of the persuader.” Therefore the serpent did not understand the sounds of the words that came from it to the woman, since even human beings, whose nature is rational, do not know what they are saying when a demon speaks in them with that affliction for which an exorcist is required.

Adam, then, as we have already indicated, because he obeyed his wife’s persuasion more readily than God’s will, therefore limped. He was also mute in the confession of sin, because he not only did not confess his sin but even began to excuse his wrongdoing, saying: “The woman whom you gave me as a companion gave me from the tree, and I ate” (Genesis III). [Col. 0754B] When he says, “The woman whom you gave me as a companion,” he shifted the blame onto the woman, and in the words “whom you gave me” he also wished to defame God.

Here, if it pleases you, let the sermon be divided.

[Col. 0753B]

You have heard, brothers, how Adam became deaf, mute, blind, and lame. Before Christ came into the world, the human race was enveloped in these same vices. They were so blinded that they worshiped idols. Hence the Apostle: “They became futile in their thoughts, and their foolish heart was darkened. And because they did not approve of acknowledging God, God gave them over to a debased mind” (Romans I).

They were deaf, in accordance with what Isaiah says: “The heart of this people has grown fat, and they have heard with difficulty with their ears. They have closed their heart and their eyes, lest they ever see with their eyes and hear with their ears” (Isaiah VI). They limped by doing evil, according to the words, “All have turned aside,” and so forth. And again: “The sons of strangers lied to me,” and so forth (Psalm XVII). They became mute by keeping their sins silent, in accordance with what David says of himself: “Because I kept silent, my bones grew old” (Psalm XXXI).

All these things, dearest brothers, the heavenly physician healed. He illumined the blind when he opened human understanding so that people might understand the Scriptures, and he announced his Father to the world, in accordance with what he himself says: “Father, I have manifested your name to human beings” (John XVII). For he was previously in the world, and the world did not know him. This is the illumination for which David asks, saying: “Illumine my eyes, lest I ever sleep in death,” and so forth (Isaiah XII).

He opened ears when he cried out: “Whoever has ears to hear, let him hear” (Matthew XI). And the Gentile people had open ears when they willingly received his preaching, in accordance with what he himself says through David: “A people whom I did not know served me,” and so forth (Psalm XVI). These are the two things that the prophet promised when he said: “Then the eyes of the blind shall be opened, and the ears of the deaf shall be unstopped” (Isaiah XXXV). It continues:

“And the lame shall leap like a stag” (ibid.). They were lame, as we have said, because they did not walk rightly, since they were not occupied with good works. But he directed the steps of human beings [Col. 0754B] when he directed their hearts toward the way of the heavenly homeland. Hearts are directed when they turn neither to the right nor to the left. The right is the mercy of God; the left is despair. Hence Isaiah says: “This is the way; walk in it, turning neither to the right nor to the left” (Isaiah XXX).

Judas and the devil, who despaired, turned to the left. Origen too, by trusting excessively in God’s mercy and preaching that the devil would be saved and released after a thousand years, turned too far to the right. Therefore the middle path must be followed, so that people neither despair nor, trusting in mercy, sin freely.

A figure of this is found in the fact that when the ark of the covenant was brought back from the land of the Philistines to its place, two cows drew it on a cart along a straight road, and they did not turn either to the right or to the left (1 Samuel VI). The ark is the Church. The two cows are the preachers of Gentiles and Jews, who feed some with their milk and lead others to the Church. Therefore David says: “The Lord is well pleased with those who fear him, and with those who hope in his mercy” (Psalm CXLVI). He has set down both hope and fear. Hope without fear is presumption. Fear without hope is despair. Fear removes security in mercy, lest one cling too closely to the right.

Concerning this straight way John says: “Prepare the way of the Lord,” and so forth (Matthew IV). But on this straight way one must leap. Hence it is said: “And the lame shall leap like a stag.”

There are two kinds of stags. One kind, when it finds a serpent in the cave where it lies hidden and senses that it has been weighed down by illness, draws the serpents out of their caves with the breath of its nostrils; then, when they emerge, it strikes them on the neck by hurling them from side to side and kills them. Then, because of the swelling produced by the poison, it runs to the purest waters, vomits out the poison after drinking, and in this way loses its hair and casts off its antlers. This stag represents penitents. When they are inwardly constricted by the awareness of their sins, they fall upon the springs—that is, upon the teaching of the Scriptures. They also cast themselves out externally, since through penance they are separated from the body and blood of Christ until they are received again through the priest’s reconciliation.

Another kind of stag, if it finds a serpent, kills it; after its victory, it seeks the mountains, where it may find pasture. So too, when someone perceives that the devil has infused into himself or into others the poisons of evil persuasion, he should strive, by the Lord’s power, to kill him—that is, cast him away from himself—and should come to the mountain, that is, to Christ, seeking pasture lest he completely fail.

(Augustine.) Stags also, when they walk in their herd or when they swim to seek other regions of land, customarily place the burdens of their heads upon one another. One stag leads, and those that follow place their heads upon it; others then follow and place their heads upon those ahead of them, and so on until the herd is complete. The one that carried the weight of the heads at the front, when fatigued, returns to the rear, so that another may succeed it and carry what it had carried; and it restores its strength by laying down its head, just as the others had done. Thus, by carrying in turn what is heavy, they both complete the journey and do not abandon one another.

Therefore spiritual teachers are called stags or does, as is said through Jeremiah concerning teachers who carelessly abandon the children they have begotten: “The doe gave birth in the field and abandoned it” (Jeremiah XIV). The apostles, as teachers, while crossing the fleeting moments of this temporal existence as though they were certain rivers, in compassionate love place their burdens upon one another, [Col. 0755C] because with careful observance they keep what is written: “Bear one another’s burdens, and thus you will fulfill the law of Christ” (Galatians VI).

When a stag comes to thorny and muddy places, it leaps over them. Similarly, O sinner, if the love of riches confronts you—love that pricks through anxiety—or if the mud of lust or of some foul pleasure confronts you, leap over it in your mind. The stag abandons the valleys and climbs the mountains; so you too abandon earthly things and seek heavenly ones. Hence the Lord says through David: “He made my feet like those of stags,” and so forth (Psalm XVII).

An aging stag devours a serpent and then, because of the excessive heat, runs to a spring. After drinking from it, it sheds its old skin and its antlers and comes back to life. So you too, sinner, kill the serpents [Col. 0755D] and run to the spring—that is, to Christ—and put off the old man, that is, pride, so that you may say with David: “As the stag longs for the springs of water,” and so forth (Psalm XLI).

It continues: “And the tongue of the mute shall be opened.” When Christ cried out, “Do penance,” and so forth (Matthew IV), those who had previously been ashamed to confess their sins then repented and disclosed their sins in confession. Mary, who had previously been mute, cried out for pardon. The thief on the cross, who had previously kept silent about his sins, cried out for pardon. Behold, the mute woman spoke; and behold, the mute man spoke.

We have shown what benefit the first advent of the supreme physician brought to the world. The prophecy was fulfilled: the physician came and healed the sick. But since we have said some things about Christ’s first advent, it is fitting that we also say something about his second advent.

## DIVISION OF THE SERMON

The whole Church of God holds in confession and profession that Christ will come from heaven to judge the living and the dead, as blessed Augustine says. We call this the final day of divine judgment, that is, the last time. For how many days the coming judgment will last is uncertain.

Christ, the Son of God, when the end of the world has been completed, will come to judgment with all the saints in the form of the body in which he ascended into heaven. For when he comes from heaven to judgment, the powers of heaven will be shaken; and then the sign of the Son of Man will appear in heaven. Then all the tribes of the earth will mourn, and they will see the Son of Man coming on the clouds of heaven with great power; and he will send his angels with a trumpet and a great voice, and they will gather his elect from the four winds, from the highest heavens to their farthest boundaries (Matthew XXIV).

Fire will go before him, burning, and a mighty storm will surround him (Psalm XLIX), because the same one who once came secretly to be judged will then come openly to judge all. After all his saints have been gathered from heaven, he will descend and arrive exceedingly fearsome and dreadful on the day of his examination, when he is seen in the grace of majesty, with angels and archangels, thrones and dominions and the other powers, with heaven and earth also burning, and with all things shaken in terror at his service.

But it must be considered how Christ comes with his cross, in accordance with what was said: “And then the sign of the Son of Man will appear in heaven.” John Chrysostom defines this question as follows: “If they say, ‘Behold, Christ is in the storerooms; behold, he is in the wilderness,’ do not believe it” (Matthew XXIV).

This concerns the second manifestation of Christ’s glory. It is said because of false Christs and false prophets, and because of the Antichrist, so that no one, overtaken by error, may fall into a false Christ when the Antichrist will precede the advent of Christ the Savior. Therefore one must carefully beware lest anyone seeking the shepherd—that is, Christ—find the wolf, that is, the Antichrist. For this reason it is foretold there.

From this you may recognize the advent of the true shepherd: he gave this sign. For this was his will: that his first advent should take place secretly, while he sought what had been lost. His second advent, however, will not be so. Rather, he plainly says: “Just as lightning coming out from the east appears in the west, so will be the advent of the Son of Man” (ibid.). For he will suddenly appear to everyone, and no one will need to ask whether Christ is here or there. Just as, when lightning flashes, we do not need to inquire whether a flash has occurred, so, when the revelation of his presence shines forth, we will not need to ask whether Christ has come.

But the question is whether he will come with the cross. Let what follows be considered concerning this.

“Then,” he says, “when Christ comes, the sun will be darkened, and the moon will not give its light” (ibid.). For such will be the eminence of Christ’s splendor that even the brightest lights of heaven will be hidden before the brilliance of the divine light. Then the stars will fall, when the sign of the Son of Man appears in heaven.

Have you considered how great is the power of the sign, that is, of the cross? The sun will be darkened and the moon will not give its light; but the cross will shine. When the lights of heaven have been darkened and the stars have fallen away, it alone will radiate, so that you may say that the cross is brighter than the moon and the sun. Illumined by divine brilliance, it will surpass their splendor; and just as, when a king enters a city, an army goes before him carrying signs and royal banners and announcing the king’s entry by the appearance of an armed procession, so, when the Lord descends from heaven, an army of angels and archangels will precede him, carrying that sign and triumphal banner on exalted shoulders, and will announce the entrance of the divine heavenly King to those who tremble.

The same teacher also says: “But why will the cross appear then, and for what reason will the Lord come with it leading the way? The reason is clear: so that those who crucified the Lord of majesty may recognize the plan of their wickedness. Through this sign the senseless impiety of the Jews is refuted, because he will come bearing the very cross, according to the Gospel, since then all the tribes of the earth will mourn. And when they see their accuser—namely, the cross itself—and recognize too late that it reproves their sin, they will confess their impious blindness in vain.

## SUNDAY IMMEDIATELY BEFORE THE NATIVITY OF THE LORD

[Col. 0757]

[Col. 0757B] “The Jews sent priests and Levites from Jerusalem to him, that they might question him: ‘Who are you?’ And he confessed and did not deny; and he confessed: ‘I am not the Christ,’” etc. (John I). He confessed that he was not Christ; nor did he deny what he was, namely, that he was the forerunner, as what follows makes clear. Here John’s humility is commended. Since he earnestly sought humbly to acknowledge his own weakness, he deserved to attain God’s exaltation. Wonderful blindness of the Jews! Although they believed John to be Christ, they were unwilling to believe John himself when he testified that Christ was the Savior, approved by so many signs and powers.

“And they questioned him: ‘What then? Are you Elijah?’ And he said: ‘I am not.’ ‘Are you the prophet?’ And he answered: ‘No’” (ibid.). (Gregory.) The Lord had said to his disciples, “John himself is Elijah” (Matthew XI), because John was Elijah in spirit, not in person; this is why John says here that he is not Elijah. John denied that he was a prophet because he was more than a prophet, showing the one whom the others had foretold. Or because the messengers intended to ask whether he was Elijah and Elisha, in whom the figure of baptism had previously appeared, or some other of the ancient prophets.

“They therefore said to him: ‘Who are you, that we may give an answer to those who sent us?’ He said: ‘I am the voice of one crying in the wilderness: Prepare the way of the Lord, as Isaiah the prophet said’” (John I). John is the voice in which the Word resounds: the manifestation, prophecy, and lamp of the Word of God present in John, through whom he cries out, present in assumed flesh, to whom John bears testimony, according to the saying, “I have prepared a lamp for my Christ” (Psalm CXXXI). He makes straight the Lord’s way who humbly hears the word of truth. He makes straight the Lord’s way who prepares his life for his commandments. Hence: “If anyone loves me, he will keep my word” (John XIV).

“And those who had been sent were from the Pharisees. And they questioned him and said to him: ‘Why then do you baptize, if you are neither Christ nor Elijah nor the prophet?’” (John I). The Pharisees had heard from the prophets that Christ would come and baptize. Knowing also that the Jordan had prefigured baptism, and that Elijah and Elisha had crossed it dry-shod as a figure of baptism, they thought that these men too had now risen to baptize. Since John says that he is none of these, they ask by what authority he baptizes.

“John answered them, saying: ‘I indeed baptize you with water unto repentance; but he who is to come after me is mightier than I, whose sandals I am not worthy to carry. But one stands in your midst whom you do not know. He will baptize you in the Holy Spirit and fire’” (ibid.). (Augustine, Gregory.) As though he said: Let what I do not be imputed to presumption. I baptize with water unto repentance, that is, as a sign of repentance that cleanses souls; I wash bodies and establish the practice of baptizing, preparing the way for one mightier than I, whose sandals I am not worthy to carry. So great is his excellence, surpassing my littleness. But he whom I preach stands in your midst, and you do not know him because you do not make use of his humility. He will baptize in the Holy Spirit and fire, that is, both with the cleansing of sanctification and the testing of tribulation; or in the Holy Spirit, that is, in the fire which he came to cast upon the earth. (Bede.) The Holy Spirit is understood through fire, since it both kindles hearts with love and enlightens them with wisdom. Some explain it thus: in the Holy Spirit in the present life; in fire in the future. For as we are now reborn from water and the Holy Spirit for the remission of sins, so then, from the slight sins with which we die, we shall be cleansed through purgatorial fire, as through baptism. Hence the Apostle: “Fire will test what sort each person’s work is” (1 Corinthians III).

The Evangelist John wrote: “Whose sandal strap I am not worthy to untie” (John I), which pertains to a mystery. Among the ancients it was customary that, if someone did not wish to take as wife the woman who belonged to him, the person who by right of kinship was to betroth her to himself would untie his sandal. Christ, however, was the bridegroom of the Church, as John says: “He who has the bride is the bridegroom” (John III). Therefore John, who was thought to be Christ, rightly declares himself unworthy to untie the strap of his sandal. As though he said: I cannot uncover the Redeemer’s footsteps, because I do not claim for myself the bridegroom’s name. Or thus: sandals are made from dead animals. The Lord appeared, as it were, shod after he assumed flesh. No person has been able fully to investigate the mystery of this incarnation. The sandal strap is the binding of so great a mystery. Therefore John cannot fully untie the strap, because he is unable fully to investigate the mystery of the incarnation.

“His winnowing fan is in his hand. He will thoroughly cleanse his threshing floor, gather his wheat into the granary, but burn the chaff with unquenchable fire” (John I). The function of the winnowing fan is to distinguish fruitful things from unfruitful. Its being placed in the Lord’s hand indicates the judgment of his power: he stores the wheat, that is, the perfect fruits of believers, in granaries, while he burns the chaff, that is, the unfruitful vanity of human beings, with the fire of judgment. The winnowing fan represents the discrimination of the righteous judgment; the threshing floor represents the present Church. The cleansing of this threshing floor is even now taking place, when the wicked are cast out of the Church for manifest sins or, after death, are condemned by divine severity. There is a difference between chaff and tares: chaff proceeds from the seed of pure wheat, whereas tares are produced from a different origin. Thus chaff signifies those who are instructed in the mysteries of faith but differ from the elect through the frivolity of unbelief; tares signify those separated from the elect in deed and profession. These are not removed by this winnowing fan, since they have already been judged; only the chaff is winnowed.

“Exhorting them in many other ways as well, he proclaimed the Gospel to the people. These things took place in Bethany beyond the Jordan, where John was baptizing” (ibid.). Bethany is a village two miles from Aelia, on the side of the Mount of Olives, where the Savior raised Lazarus. Rightly the forerunner of our Lord is said to have baptized in Bethany. For Bethany is interpreted “house of obedience,” to show that all must come to Christ’s baptism through the obedience of faith.

### On when people began to be bound by the command to receive baptism.

The question is when the sacrament of baptism was instituted, from what point onward it was no longer lawful to neglect it, and from what point receiving it became obligatory. There are, indeed, various opinions on this among different writers. Some say that baptism was instituted when Christ, suggesting to Nicodemus, who came to him by night, the manner of the new birth, said: “Unless someone has been born again of water and the Holy Spirit, he cannot see the kingdom of God” (John 3). Others say that the institution of baptism began when Christ, after his resurrection, was about to ascend into heaven and sent his disciples to preach, saying: “Go, teach all nations, baptizing them in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit” (Matthew 28). Some think that the institution of baptism began when John began baptizing in water, preaching that he would baptize in the Spirit (Matthew 3). Others think that it began in Christ’s Passion, when he said: “It is finished” (John 19), because all the sacraments of the Old Testament then reached their end and the New Testament began.

It seems more reasonable, however, to say that baptism was first administered by John, then for some time by Christ or by Christ’s disciples, so that it might be introduced into use gradually and not seem contrary to established custom; and finally that it was instituted universally, when preachers were sent to baptize throughout the whole world.

These three periods, moreover, appear to be distinguishable. At first, before baptism, circumcision alone had established standing, and it was received for justification without baptism. Finally, now, after circumcision, baptism alone has established standing, and it is celebrated for salvation without circumcision. There was, however, an intermediate period when both circumcision and baptism existed together: circumcision first, in order that it might come to an end; the other, namely baptism, in order that it might be confirmed.

For it was necessary that what was destined to end should not be abruptly or precipitately abolished, but should be relinquished gradually and, as it were, with a certain reverence, so that it might be shown to have been good in its own time. Likewise, what was destined to begin should not be immediately elevated to authority, but should be initiated with delay and solemnity, lest it be thought foreign and suddenly introduced from elsewhere. Thus the former were relinquished, not cast away; that is, the latter were instituted, not usurped, so that the authority of the divine plan might everywhere be preserved and human objection removed, lest anyone dare to criticize God’s works.

Although, therefore, in Christ’s Passion, through which all things were completed, the established order of the ancient figures came to an end and the institution of the new sacrament began, nevertheless for some time afterward the new practices were introduced gradually for the sake of custom, while the old were tolerated for a while according to the divine dispensation. Thus both existed during that period: whether before or after the Passion, from the time when the new practices began until the old were later forbidden.

During the intermediate period in which baptism existed with circumcision—from its beginning until Christ’s Passion—circumcision existed with baptism from Christ’s Passion until the time when circumcision itself began to be prohibited. For just as before the Passion circumcision, in its established form, was received as a remedy, yet even then baptism was not neglected without danger to salvation by those to whom it was preached, so after the Passion baptism, although received in its established form for salvation, circumcision nevertheless was not disregarded without danger to salvation by those to whom its termination had not yet been made clear.

But after it was said, “If you are circumcised, Christ will profit you nothing” (Galatians 5), circumcision could no longer be received for salvation, just as previously, after it had been said: “The male whose flesh of his foreskin has not been circumcised—that soul shall perish from his people” (Genesis 17). Circumcision could not be neglected without danger to salvation by those alone to whom it had been enjoined.

Again, just as at the beginning baptism was given by John as the sole sacrament, so that those who did not know the practice of baptism might be instructed, at the end circumcision was, by a dispensation, received by certain believers as the sole sacrament, lest those accustomed to circumcision should be scandalized.

## On the coming and the character of the person of the Judge

“When the Son of Man comes in his glory, and all the angels with him, then all the nations will be gathered before him” (Matthew 25).

(AUGUSTINE.) The Jews also, who will be punished at that judgment because they persisted in wickedness, are included, as it is said elsewhere: “They will look upon him whom they pierced” (John 19).

When good and evil alike are to see the Judge of the living and the dead, the wicked will certainly be unable to see anything except the form in which he is the Son of Man; yet they will see him in the glory in which he will judge and in the humility in which he was judged. Christ will not again be seen upon the cross. As for that form of God in which he is equal to the Father, the ungodly will certainly not see it. For are they not the pure in heart who are blessed because they will see God? (Matthew 5.) Otherwise, if the Son of God, the Judge, were to appear to the ungodly also in the form in which he is equal to the Father, what would be the meaning of his promise to his beloved as something great: “I will love him, and I will show myself to him” (John 14)?

Therefore the Son of Man will judge, yet not by human authority, but by that authority by which he is the Son of God. Thus both statements can be made: the Son of Man will judge, and the Son of Man will not judge. The first is true because he said, “When the Son of Man comes, then all the nations will be gathered before him”; the second is true because he said, “I do not judge” (John 1), and, “I do not seek my own glory; there is one who seeks and judges” (ibid.).

Accordingly, insofar as in the judgment not the form of God but the form of the Son of Man will appear, even the Father will not judge. For in this sense it was said: “The Father judges no one, but has given all judgment to the Son.” But insofar as it was said, “The Father granted the Son to have life in himself” (John 5), it is not meant that the Father will judge no one; rather, because the Father begot the Son as his equal, he will judge with him.

Thus the statement concerns the fact that in the judgment not the form of God but the form of the Son of Man will appear. It is not that the one who gave all judgment to the Son will not judge, since the Son says of him: “There is one who seeks and judges.” Rather, “The Father judges no one, but has given all judgment to the Son” was said as if he had said: No one will see the Father in the judgment of the living and the dead, but all will see the Son, because he is also the Son of Man, so that even the ungodly may see him, since they will see the one whom they pierced.

He therefore gave all judgment to the Son because the Judge will appear in the form of the Son of Man. That form is not the Father’s, nor is it the Son’s form in which he is equal to the Father, but the form in which he is less than the Father, so that he may be visible in the judgment to both the good and the wicked.

When the wicked see the Judge, he will not appear good to them, because they will not rejoice in him in their hearts. Then all the tribes of the earth will mourn—that is, the whole number of the wicked and unbelieving. That vision of the Son of Man will be neither a good for the ungodly, who will be sent into eternal fire, nor the highest good for the righteous. For he will still call them to the kingdom prepared for them from the foundation of the world. Just as he will say to the former, “Go into eternal fire” (Matthew 25), so to the righteous: “Come, blessed of my Father, possess the kingdom prepared for you” (ibid.). And just as the former will go into eternal punishment, so the righteous will go into eternal life.

What, then, is eternal life except that they should know you, he says, the one living God, and Jesus Christ whom you sent (John 17)—but in that glory of which he says to the Father: “The glory which I had with you before the world existed” (ibid.)? Then he will hand over the kingdom to God and the Father, so that the good servant may enter into the joy of his Lord.

## DIVISION OF THE SERMON

Now, dearly beloved, let us strive continually to consider the day of our death, the coming of our Lord Jesus Christ, and his terrible and fearful judgment. For all the wounds of sin no more useful remedies can be found than for each person to consider that hour when he will depart from this world. How could anyone presume to commit serious sins when he believes that at every moment he may depart from this light?

As Scripture also says: “Remember, son, that death will not delay” (Ecclesiasticus 14), and again: “Remember your last things, and you will cease from hatred” (Ecclesiasticus 7). Whoever carefully considers how severe the examination will be before Christ’s tribunal, where each person will receive according to his works, will not be able to find his own sins or crimes pleasing.

When all the nations have been gathered before that dreadful Judge (Matthew 24), what will then become of the unjust, adulterers, drunkards, and robbers? There will be weeping of the eyes and gnashing of teeth when they see the multitude of the saints separated at the King’s right hand and assigned to glory, while the people of sinners are plunged into the depths of Tartarus and confined in their darkness without any hope of mercy or pardon. They will see themselves shut out from the blessed light of the saints, descending into the depths of hell, and the mouth of the pit closing over them, while they undergo eternal punishments and die an everlasting death.

In vain will the sinner ask for mercy from the poor man whom he despised in this life. In vain will he ask that the tip of Lazarus’s finger be placed upon his burning lips to cool them, when he, wretched man, wishes to rejoice in the glory of the righteous and humble poor whom he once saw subjected to the harsh hardships of poverty and bearing the evils of that life in which they die together with life itself, so that they might not deserve to reach those eternal punishments.

Therefore, so that we may not deserve to hear such harsh and terrible words before the tribunal of the eternal Judge, while it is still permitted and, with God’s help, lies within our power, let us examine our consciences. If we recognize that any grave crimes or capital sins not yet cleansed by almsgiving and prayers still rule within us, let us hasten to enter the harbor of repentance, after overcoming the waves of sin, with Christ as our helmsman.

And if we recognize that the little boat of our soul has been broken by the many storms of sin through pride, split by greed, or loosened by lust, let us hasten to repair and restore it through good works. Let us continually strive to empty out the bilge of our vices. Past sins do not harm us if they no longer please us. Just as the righteousness of no righteous person is sufficient if he does not persevere to the end, so the wickedness of no sinner can harm him if, before departing from this body, he flees to the remedies of almsgiving or the medicines of repentance.

But because we cannot know when or at what hour we shall be snatched from this world, let us hasten without any delay or postponement to flee from the left hand to the right. This must be entrusted to health, not to age. Whoever is always uncertain of his life should always be ready with the remedy of salvation. For the one who made us secure by teaching, “On whatever day the sinner turns, all his iniquities will be handed over to oblivion” (Ezekiel 18), also wished us to be cautious, saying: “Do not delay turning to the Lord, and do not defer from day to day” (Ecclesiasticus 5).

But perhaps, when we call everyone generally to repentance, someone thinks to himself: “I am a young man with a wife. How can I cut my hair or assume the habit of religion?” We do not say this, dearly beloved brothers; we do not preach that young men who appear to have wives ought to change their clothing more than their conduct.

What harm does it do a married man if he wishes to turn to good and honorable works, and strives to restore the wounds of his sins to their former health through almsgiving, fasting, and prayers? True conversion is sufficient in itself without a change of clothing. Religious garments without good works will not only be unable to provide a remedy; they will also endure God’s just judgment.

Let us therefore turn to better things while the remedies remain in our power. Here let us extinguish death by dying to sins; here let us acquire life through the merits of life. Through our Lord Jesus Christ, the only-begotten Son of God, who with the unbegotten Father and the Holy Spirit lives and reigns as God forever and ever. Amen.

## ON THE VIGIL OF THE NATIVITY OF THE LORD. According to Matthew

[Col. 0763]

“In that time: When Mary, the mother of Jesus, had been betrothed to Joseph, before they came together, she was found to be with child of the Holy Spirit” (Matthew 1).

When Matthew the Evangelist narrated the birth of our Lord and Savior Jesus Christ—the one who, eternal before the ages as the Son of God, appeared in time as the son of a human being—he led his brief account from Abraham to Joseph, the husband of Mary, and showed all the persons who were begotten and who begot others according to the common order of human generation. Then, when he was about to speak of this birth itself, he revealed how greatly his generation differed from that of the others: the others were born through the customary union of male and female, whereas he was born through a virgin, since he was the Son of God.

Indeed, it was entirely fitting that when God wished to become human for human beings, he should be born from no one other than a virgin; and when a virgin was to give birth, she should bear no son other than one who was God.

“When,” he says, “Mary, the mother of Jesus, had been betrothed to Joseph, before they came together, she was found to be with child of the Holy Spirit.”

The Evangelist Luke sufficiently explains the order and the city in which the conception took place. But since it is clear that this is well known to your holiness, only a few things need to be said concerning what Matthew writes.

First, it must be noted that when he says “before they came together,” by the verb “to come together” he did not mean sexual intercourse itself, but the period of the marriage ceremonies that ordinarily precede it, when the woman who had previously been betrothed begins to be a wife. Thus “before they came together” means before they had properly celebrated the marriage rites. She was found to be with child of the Holy Spirit.

Afterward, in the order already mentioned, they came together when Joseph, at the angel’s command, received his wife. But they did not have intercourse, since it follows: “And he did not know her.”

“She was found to be with child” by no one other than Joseph, who, by marital permission, knew almost everything about his future wife. Therefore he immediately detected her swelling womb with his inquisitive gaze.

It follows:

“Joseph, her husband, being a just man and unwilling to expose her, resolved to dismiss her secretly.”

When Joseph saw that his betrothed had conceived—although he knew well that she had not been touched by any man—he was just and wished to act justly in all things. He therefore considered it best neither to disclose this to others nor to take her as his wife, but secretly to alter the marriage arrangement and allow her to remain in the condition of a betrothed woman, as she was.

For he had also read in Isaiah that a virgin from the house of David would conceive and bear the Lord, and he knew that Mary had descended from that same house. Therefore he did not doubt that this prophecy had been fulfilled in her. He wished to dismiss her secretly so that he would neither take her as his wife nor prevent her, while still betrothed, from giving birth. Yet there would surely have been few who would have judged her to be a virgin rather than a prostitute.

Therefore Joseph’s plan was suddenly changed by a better plan: in order to preserve Mary’s reputation, he would receive her as his wife after celebrating the marriage feast, but guard her chastely forever. For the Lord preferred that some should remain ignorant of the manner of his birth rather than that the chastity of his Mother should be disgraced.

For it follows:

“This is what he was considering when, behold, an angel of the Lord appeared to him, saying: Joseph, son of David, do not fear to take Mary as your wife. For that which has been born in her is of the Holy Spirit. She will bear a son, and you shall call his name Jesus; for he will save his people from their sins.”

These words clearly teach both the manner of his conception and the dignity of his birth: she conceived of the Holy Spirit and was to bear Christ. Although the angel does not call him Christ in an explicit statement, by explaining the etymology of the name Jesus and showing him to be the author of salvation and the Savior of his people, he openly indicates Christ. In this way he tells Joseph what he did not know and completely removes from his mind any thought of touching the Mother of God.

(BEDA.) Nevertheless, Joseph is commanded to receive her as a wife in name alone, by a dispensation of just necessity: so that she would not be stoned by the Jews as an adulteress, and so that, when fleeing into Egypt, she would have the companionship of a male who, through familiar care, would both protect the weakness of a woman and bear witness to her perpetual virginity.

Catholic interpreters also give other reasons why Joseph ought to have received the Mother of God as his wife. Whoever wishes may find them in their respective works.

The Evangelist also adds to the virgin birth an example from prophetic speech, so that the miracle of such great majesty might appear all the more certain because he believed it to have been not only invented by himself but also foretold by the prophet. It is customary for this Evangelist—that is, Matthew—to confirm everything he narrates by prophetic testimonies.

For he wrote his Gospel chiefly for those who believed from among the Jews but, although reborn in Christ, could not yet be detached from the ceremonies of the Law. Therefore he labored to raise them from the carnal understanding of the Law and the Prophets to the spiritual understanding concerning Christ, so that they might receive the mysteries of the Christian faith with greater confidence, recognizing that these were nothing other than what the prophets had foretold.

“Behold,” he says, “the virgin will conceive in her womb and bear a son, and they will call his name Emmanuel,” which is interpreted as “God with us.”

The name of the Savior, whom the prophet calls “God with us,” signifies both natures of his one person. He who was born before the ages from the Father and is God, in the fullness of time became Emmanuel—that is, “God with us”—in his mother’s womb, because he graciously took the weakness of our nature into the unity of his person, when “the Word became flesh and dwelt among us” (John 1). In a wondrous manner he began to be what we are without ceasing to be what he was, assuming our nature without losing what he himself was.

“Joseph rose from sleep and did as the angel of the Lord had commanded him, and he took his wife, and did not know her.”

He took her in the name of a wife for the reasons already stated, and he did not know her in the marital act because of the mysteries he had learned.

If anyone should oppose this interpretation of ours and insist that the blessed Mother of God was never, even after Joseph had celebrated the marriage rites, taken by him under the name of a wife, let him explain this passage of the holy Gospel better himself. Let him also show that among the Jews it was lawful for a man to unite himself carnally with his betrothed. We willingly yield to sound understanding, provided that we do not believe that anything was done concerning the Mother of the Lord that could be disgraced by public opinion.

As for the addition, “until she bore her firstborn son,” let no one understand it as though he knew her after the son had been born, as some perversely suppose. Your fraternity should know that there were heretics who, because it is said, “He did not know her until she had borne a son,” believed that Mary was known by Joseph after the Lord’s birth, and that from this there arose those whom Scripture calls the Lord’s brothers. They also used the designation “firstborn” in support of their error.

May the Lord God avert this blasphemy from the faith of us all, and grant us to understand, with Catholic devotion, that the parents of our Savior were always distinguished by undefiled virginity, and that those whom Scripture, according to its custom, calls the Lord’s brothers were not their children but their relatives.

The Evangelist did not concern himself with saying whether Joseph knew her after the birth of the Son of God because no one would have thought that this required discussion. It was understood that spouses to whom, while they remained in virginal chastity, the birth of the Son of God had been granted by a unique grace could in no way afterward violate the rights of chastity.

It must also be noted that, contrary to the opinion of the heretics, firstborn sons are not only those who are followed by brothers; there are others as well. According to the authority of Scripture, all who first open the womb are called firstborn, whether brothers follow them or no one follows them.

Nevertheless, the Lord can be understood to have been called firstborn for a special reason, in accordance with what John says of him in the Apocalypse: “The faithful witness, the firstborn from the dead, and the ruler of the kings of the earth” (Revelation 1). The Apostle Paul likewise says: “For those whom he foreknew and predestined to be conformed to the image of his Son, so that he might be the firstborn among many brothers” (Romans 8).

He is the firstborn among many brothers because “to all who received him, he gave power to become children of God” (John 1). He is rightly called their firstborn because he surpasses all the adopted children in dignity, including those who preceded the time of his Incarnation by their birth.

They can most truthfully testify with John: “He who comes after us was made before us,” that is, although he was born in the world after us, he deservedly is called the firstborn of all by the right of his virtue.

He may also appropriately be called firstborn in his divine birth, because before he generated any creature by creating it, the Father generated the Son, coeternal with himself. Before the Word of truth generated any adopted children for himself by redeeming them, the Father generated the Word, coeternal with himself.

Therefore the Word himself, the Son of God, namely his power and wisdom, says: “I came forth from the mouth of the Most High, the firstborn before every creature.” He was God born from God, and in the humanity in which he was created he preceded every creature.

“And you shall call his name Jesus,” he says.

Jesus is called in Hebrew, in Latin, *salutaris* or *salvator*, “saving” or “Savior.” It is clear that the giving of this name was most certainly foretold by the prophets. Hence those words sung with great longing for his appearing:

“My soul will rejoice in the Lord and delight in his salvation” (Psalm 34).

And again:

“My soul has languished for your salvation” (Psalm 118).

And elsewhere:

“But I will glory in the Lord; I will rejoice in God my Jesus” (Habakkuk 3).

And especially:

“Save me, O God, by your name” (Psalm 53).

As if he were saying: “Glorify the glory of your name, by which you are called Savior, in saving me.”

Jesus, then, is the name of the Son who was born from the Virgin, as the angel explains, signifying that he himself will save his people from their sins. Whoever saves from sins will also save from the corruptions of mind and body that came upon us because of sins.

Christ, however, is the title of a priest or of royal dignity. For priests and kings under the Law were also called *christi* from *chrisma*, that is, from the anointing with holy oil. They signified the one who, appearing in the world as the true King and High Priest, was anointed with the oil of gladness above his companions.

From this anointing—that is, from the *chrism*—he himself is called Christ, and those who share in that same anointing, namely spiritual grace, are called Christians. By being the Savior, may he save us from sins; by being the High Priest, may he reconcile us to God the Father; and by being the King, may he graciously grant us the kingdom of his Father forever.

## ANOTHER EXPOSITION OF THE SAME PASSAGE

“The generation of Christ was thus” (Matthew 1).

The question is why he did not say “of Jesus Christ,” but only “of Christ,” reserving the fuller expression for what the angel was soon to say.

“Generation”—that is, Christ himself generated in the flesh. It is as though he were saying: “The generation which is Christ was thus,” to be explained in two ways: either with reference to the place in the genealogy already traversed, where he says, “Jacob begot Joseph, the husband of Mary, from whom Jesus was born, who is called Christ. Therefore all the generations from Abraham to David are fourteen generations, and from David to the exile in Babylon fourteen generations, and from the exile in Babylon to Christ fourteen generations. Now the generation of Christ was thus” (ibid.).

The first condition of humanity is that Adam was formed from the earth. The second is that woman was created from the man’s side. The third is that a human being was born from man and woman.

But Christ’s generation was thus: he was born from a woman without a man, conceived through the Holy Spirit himself. The first and second generations fell; the third generated from the fall; in the fourth they found salvation.

“When Mary, the mother of Jesus, had been betrothed to Joseph,” and so forth.

Christ’s generation was thus; that is, this genealogy belongs to Christ in this way: “When she had been betrothed.” For these reasons Christ was born not from an unmarried virgin but from a betrothed woman: so that the genealogy would be reckoned through a man rather than through a woman, according to the custom of Scripture; so that she would not be stoned by the Jews as an adulteress; so that, when fleeing into Egypt, she would have the support of a husband; so that the birth might be hidden from the devil, who would suppose that he was born not from a virgin but from a wife; and so that the undefiled Virgin would not be exposed to disgrace.

For the Lord preferred that some should be uncertain about his own origin rather than that anyone should doubt his mother’s modesty. Otherwise, if the Lord said, “I have not come to abolish the Law but to fulfill it” (Matthew 5), someone might object: “He was born in violation of the Law, since a husband was provided as a witness to the woman’s chastity, who could grieve and avenge the disgrace if he did not acknowledge the mystery.” This was so that Mary would not seem to conceal guilt by means of a lie.

A betrothed woman had no reason to lie, since childbirth is the reward of marriage for women. It was also so that Herod and the Jews would not be given an excuse for saying that they were persecuting one born of adultery; so that continence might be commended to married believers by mutual agreement; and so that it might be shown how the human race could multiply without injury to virginity, provided that it was not subject to transgression.

“Betrothed”—that is, not yet married.

“His mother.” He says “his mother,” not “Joseph’s wife.”

“Mary, [betrothed] to Joseph.” At the very threshold, the names of both are placed in a manner appropriate to the event.

“Before they came together.” This indicates the approaching time of the marriage, not that they would necessarily come together afterward, as Helvidius says.

“She was found”—by no one other than Joseph, who, by marital permission, knew everything about his future wife.

Thus Matthew omitted many things that Luke narrated, saying: “In the sixth month,” he says, “the angel Gabriel was sent by God to a city of Galilee called Nazareth, to a virgin betrothed to a man whose name was Joseph, of the house of David; and the name of the virgin was Mary. And the angel entered and said to her: ‘Hail, full of grace, the Lord is with you,’” and so forth (Luke 1).

Matthew, indeed, carried the genealogy down to the point at which he said: “Joseph, the husband of Mary, from whom Jesus was born, who is called Christ.” Therefore he left the account of the conception, which he had passed over, to be narrated by Luke.

“In the womb.” This is not to be understood as “receiving into the womb,” that is, as though it had been received from elsewhere, but as being present within through the coming of the Holy Spirit. Thus: “A woman will encompass a man” (Jeremiah 31).

“Of the Holy Spirit.”

The question is: if she was found by Joseph to be with child of the Holy Spirit, why did he wish to dismiss her? Because he neither knew everything nor was entirely ignorant. He knew that she was with child, not through carnal intercourse but through spiritual power; but he did not know from whom she had conceived. This was disclosed to him, as to one who did not know, when he was told that the child was of the Holy Spirit. And so forth.

Again, the question is why Matthew anticipated what the angel was soon going to say. He did this out of spiritual fervor, so that the reader’s mind, even in the space of a few lines, might not hesitate, and so that every word might stand “by the mouth of two or three witnesses” (Deuteronomy 18).

“Joseph, her husband.” In Scripture, betrothed women are called wives, and betrothed men are called husbands.

“Being just.” Since those who are conscious of crimes are subject to sin (Romans 1), why is Joseph called just when he was jealous because of the suspected crime? So that his testimony might be commended as trustworthy.

For this reason, many copies add: “When he was a just man,” to show that Joseph was just according to human justice, since in comparison with the justice of God it is counted as nothing.

And therefore it rightly follows:

“Unwilling to expose her.” He not only conceals her, but does not even dare to touch the temple of the Lord’s body. He is rightly called just because he does not violate the temple of justice.

“To expose.” It is as though he were saying: He was unwilling to take as his wife the betrothed woman whom he suspected of being an adulteress, either by exposing her to others or by exposing her to punishment, since he knew that she had not conceived from a man. The word “expose” is more often found in a bad sense than in a good one.

The Greek expression also conveys this meaning not inappropriately—*vapardeir, mathysai* [the printed Greek forms are uncertain]—that is, “to make public,” which means to reveal and make the conception known to everyone.

“Secretly.” So that, if he publicly dismissed his wife, he would not impose upon her the guilt of intercourse with another man, or, if he retained her, make himself liable as though he were conscious of adultery.

“To dismiss”—that is, not to take her as his wife, or to free an innocent woman from the punishment of adultery.

Behold, the heavenly Adam sets something new against the old. The first time, woman was made from man alone, without a mother. The second time, man was born from woman alone, without a carnal father. It was fitting that the new redemption should come from women, from whom the ancient transgression had preceded.

The earthly Adam was formed from uncorrupted earth. The second Adam was formed from the incorrupt and immaculate flesh of the virgin Mary.

[Col. 0769C] “While he was considering these things, behold, an angel of the Lord.” To a good and just man, considering good and just things, a good and just messenger appeared. Therefore “of the Lord” is added to distinguish him from apostate angels. Many think this angel was Gabriel, in accordance with Luke’s trustworthy account—not because he alone is the messenger of every birth, since his name is interpreted as “strength of God,” and the victory of battles has been entrusted to him. Therefore, at the births of John and Christ, who came to conquer the enemy, he is rightly sent. Likewise, when he was considering the Lord, appropriate consolation was provided, just as Christ was shown to the two walking along the road (Luke 24).

“Appeared in a dream.” The expression “appeared” signifies an unusual occurrence. Divine speech is distinguished in two ways: either through angels or through God himself. When it is through God himself, the heart is taught by inward inspiration alone, without words or syllables, because he opens the hearing but is not perceived to possess a sound. Thus the Spirit said to Philip: “Join yourself to that chariot” (Acts 8).

When it is through an angel, this happens in several ways. Sometimes there are words without any image, as when Christ said, “Father, glorify your Son,” and the response immediately followed: “I have glorified him, and I will glorify him again” (John 12), and so forth. Sometimes there are events without words, as when Ezekiel saw the appearance of amber in the midst of fire (Ezekiel 1), signifying through it Christ’s incarnation. Sometimes there are both words and events, as when Adam saw the Lord walking in paradise after midday (Genesis 3), signifying that the light of truth would depart from him.

[Col. 0770A] Sometimes images are shown to the eyes of the heart, as when Jacob saw a ladder let down from heaven (Genesis 28), and Peter saw in an ecstatic state a vessel full of living creatures (Acts 10). Sometimes images are assumed from the air and displayed before bodily eyes, as when Abraham not only saw the angels but also received them into his house and even fed them with heavenly substances (Genesis 18).
