Thus, when the Lord was baptized, a voice sounded, saying: “This is my Son” (Matthew 3).

Sometimes earthly and heavenly things are joined, as when, before Moses on the mountain, fire and a bush were combined (Exodus 3), signifying that he would be the teacher of the people who would receive the flame of the Law and yet not abandon the thorn of sin; or signifying that from that people would come one who would place the fire of divinity upon the thorns of human nature. Sometimes he inspires hidden repentance in human hearts, as Zechariah says: “And the angel who spoke in me said to me” (Zechariah 2).

When it is said that he appeared here to blessed Joseph, he appeared through an image shown to the heart.

“Joseph, son of David.” He speaks with the affection of one who is reassuring, indicating that Joseph was known and familiar, and his name and lineage are identified. From this it appears that Joseph and Mary belonged to the same tribe, in accordance with the command: “Let no one be joined [in marriage] except from his own tribe” (Exodus 26). Here it should be noted that he called him not so much a son of David according to the flesh as according to the spirit, declaring that, as a just man descended from the race of a just man, he had merited this.

“Do not be afraid.” It appears that the reason for the angel’s appearing was that Joseph was afraid to take her, since he feared professing a marriage of such a special kind. Observe that he was not restrained by the fear by which he had been forbidden to take a wife; rather, he was commanded not to dread taking her to his own regret. Fear is first driven out, so that he might hear more willingly what was to be said afterward.

“Your wife.” Scripture commonly calls betrothed women wives. Or Mary is called his wife because she was under the same yoke for bringing up the Savior.

“What, he says, has been born.” He was not conceived from an external seed, but from the Holy Spirit. Here it is explained what Joseph knew and what he did not know. [AUGUSTINE.] Yet the Holy Spirit should not for this reason be regarded as Christ’s father, so that God the Father begot the Word while the Spirit begot the human being. Rather, it was because the city of Christ was completed through the Spirit’s ministry.

“But she will bear a son.” Yet she will give birth without the pain of childbirth, just as he was conceived without the will of sin. Here four uncertainties concerning every person who is born are displayed: “She will bear a son; he will be called Jesus; he will save his people; and you shall call him,” and so forth.

O Joseph, do not contradict the voices of the prophets. It should be noted that, according to Matthew, the child’s name was foretold as being given to Joseph, while according to Luke it was foretold as being given to Mary, because Jesus came for the salvation of both sexes. The etymology of the name Jesus follows when he says: “For he himself will save his people.” Truly, whose people could they be except his own, from sins? This is directed against the Jews, who think that their people would be delivered by Christ from captivities, not from sins. Note that salvation belongs to him, whereas sins belong to us.

## SERMON ON THE BETROTHAL OF SAINT MARY

[Col. 0771A]

“He placed his tabernacle in the sun, and he himself, like a bridegroom coming forth from his chamber” (Psalm 18).

When this Bridegroom became the Word made flesh, he found a bridal chamber in the Virgin’s womb; from there, joined to human nature, he came forth as from a most chaste bed—humble in mercy beneath all, powerful in majesty above all. Human marriage is the sacrament of this union of Christ and the Church. Marriage is defined as the sole consent of those whose union is under discussion. It is also said elsewhere: “Intercourse does not make a marriage, but consent.” Likewise: “The deflowering of virginity does not make a marriage, but the marital agreement.”

[Col. 0771B] From these statements it is clear that the joining of the sexes is not marriage, but the work of marriage, although Pope Leo says: “Since the society of marriage was constituted from the beginning in such a way that it does not exist apart from the joining of the sexes, which contains within itself the sacrament of Christ and the Church, there is no doubt that a woman does not belong to marriage when it is shown that the nuptial mystery was absent in her.”

But unless this is understood appropriately, it appears contrary to Augustine, who asserts that an even more perfect and holier marriage exists between those who, by mutual consent, have resolved always to abstain from such an act. And since some affirm that consent is marriage, the question arises: consent to what is marriage?

Some answer that consent to the joining of the sexes is marriage. But it is objected that a perfect marriage also exists between those who have resolved to abstain from this act forever. Mary too is called Joseph’s wife, although she herself replies to the angel: “How will this happen, since I do not know a man?” (Luke 1). How can I conceive and bear a son, when I have resolved to complete my life in the chastity of virginity?

[Col. 0771C] To this it is further objected: The blessed Virgin did not have the will for this carnal companionship. Why, then, did she consent to be betrothed?

Some respond to the objection as follows: To be betrothed is one thing, and to have intercourse is another; just as marriage is one thing, and its act is another; just as the presbyterate is one thing, and its office is another. A man is a presbyter solely by ordination, even if he never celebrates Mass. A presbyter, therefore, exists by authority, not by action.

Similarly, marriage consists in a power acquired through betrothal and the marital agreement, not in intercourse. And just as someone consents to be ordained a presbyter even though he intends never to celebrate Mass—as is read of certain men—so the blessed Virgin Mary willingly consented to everything that was solemnly to be done concerning her at her betrothal, although she had no intention of ever violating the virginity she had vowed to God.

For just as Abraham was prepared, at God’s command, to sacrifice his son, from whom nevertheless he hoped for the offspring in whom all nations would be blessed, so the most prudent Virgin obeyed God’s command, given through her parents, that she be betrothed. Yet she firmly believed that, by God’s providence, she would be kept untouched by all intercourse with a man, as is shown to have been fulfilled in reality.

Nevertheless, she was truly a wife because of her consent to the marital agreement, not because of consent to carnal union. Marriage, therefore, is the lawful consent concerning the union of two suitable persons—not concerning the union that occurs through intercourse, but concerning the union established in betrothal. From the first fidelity of betrothal they are called spouses.

[AUGUSTINE.] Far be it that the marital bond should be broken between those who have resolved, by mutual consent, to abstain from the use of carnal desire—that is, to remain continent forever! Rather, it will be firmer, because they have entered into sacred agreements that are to be preserved with greater affection and harmony, not through voluntary bodily bonds but through voluntary bonds of the soul.

For the angel did not falsely say: “Joseph, do not be afraid to take Mary your wife.” She is called his wife from the first fidelity of betrothal, although he had not known her through intercourse and would not know her. The marital designation had neither perished nor remained false where there had been and would be no carnal intercourse.

She was a virgin, and for that reason was joined to her husband more holily and wonderfully: she was fruitful without a husband, unequal in offspring but equal in faith. Because of this faithful marriage, both parents of Christ deserved to be called his parents—not only she as his mother, but also he as her husband and his father, both according to the mind, not according to the flesh.

[Col. 0772C] Every good of marriage was fulfilled in those parents of Christ: offspring, fidelity, and sacrament. We recognize the offspring as Jesus himself, God; fidelity, because there was no adultery; and sacrament, because there was no divorce.

But it should be understood that it is not marriage itself, but the good of marriage, that is divided into three parts: fidelity, offspring, and sacrament. The first is the purity of marriage, the second its fruit, and the third its permanence.

In fidelity, the concern is that, because of the marital bond, neither husband nor wife have intercourse with another. In offspring, it is that a living child be received and religiously raised. In the sacrament, it is that the marriage not be separated, and that neither the dismissed husband nor the dismissed wife join another on the pretext of offspring.

This good of marriage—that is, the sacrament—is a sacrament, that is, a sign of a sacred reality: namely, the inseparable union that exists between Christ and the Church. For this reason, each man should have his own wife, not several wives, and each woman her own husband, not several husbands. Their having one body and one spirit are sacraments of Christ and the Church, with which our Lord Jesus Christ himself will join us both now and in the future. He lives and reigns as God throughout all ages of ages. Amen.

## How the statement “He was conceived from the Holy Spirit” is to be understood

Although the Father and the Holy Spirit, together with the Son himself, worked the Son’s incarnation, it is rightly asked why Scripture speaks specifically of his conception from the Holy Spirit. As with the other things said about him, human understanding approaches this matter timidly; but the devotion of faith, venturing further, inquires faithfully according to a pure conscience.

We must therefore ask first how we ought to understand the statement that blessed Mary conceived from the Holy Spirit (Luke 1). We know—and by the most frequent experience of nature we have all learned—that when a woman is said to have conceived from a man, nothing other than this is meant: she received the substance of flesh for generating flesh through the intercourse of flesh.

This substance of flesh, transferred from the man’s flesh through that very intercourse of flesh, becomes one flesh with the woman’s flesh; and what is to be born, truly taking its origin from the substance of both, is generated from him through her. A woman therefore conceives from a man when, through intercourse of flesh, she receives from the man’s flesh the seed for generating flesh. She conceives nothing other than what he is from whom she conceives; and the woman who conceives gives birth to what she conceives.

What, then, shall we say? Did the Holy Spirit pour seed for childbirth from his own substance into the Virgin’s womb? How, then, could a spiritual substance provide the seed of flesh? Or perhaps what was conceived was not seed of flesh, while what was born was flesh. What shall we say? How did Mary conceive from the Holy Spirit? And if she conceived from the Holy Spirit, how was the Holy Spirit not Christ’s father?

All these matters require profound consideration, lest, in a difficult, exceedingly fearful, and obscure matter, human understanding presume something beyond its capacity. We should not doubt these things because they are obscure; nor should we rashly define something merely because it is to be believed.

Let us therefore ask what Mary conceived. Either she did not conceive flesh and did not give birth to flesh, or, if she gave birth to flesh, she conceived flesh. For what she conceived, she gave birth to. But how could what is not flesh provide flesh, or flesh fail to generate flesh?

Let us consider how this perplexing inquiry—or method of investigation—can be understood soundly and appropriately. First, let us observe how the work of nature is completed in conception as it ordinarily and customarily takes place.

Among carnal parents who generate and, through intercourse of flesh, fashion flesh to be born from flesh, nature provides the substance for the offspring from both sides, so that what proceeds from the flesh of both is flesh, although the flesh being formed is derived from the flesh of only one.

Nevertheless, this contribution, which nature, as though paying a debt established by the Creator, supplies for the construction of the human body, is demanded from it without any necessity or compulsion. Nature is inclined to provide it only through love and, so to speak, spontaneous willingness. Nothing except the will alone can extort this debt from nature. But once it has been persuaded by spontaneous willingness, then, from both sides, each willingly and earnestly comes to the other for the completion of the work.

Whatever is violently seized from one who is willing is entirely unsuitable and ineffective for producing such an effect. Love alone, therefore, can persuade nature and in a certain way compel it, while willing, to sow the offspring.

Indeed, in the woman it is the love of the man, and in the man the love of the woman, that ordinarily brings this about: what nature is not sufficient to accomplish in either one alone, each supplies to the other through love, so that what neither could accomplish alone, each can accomplish with the other.

Thus the woman conceives the seed of human offspring, which is sown jointly by the man and the woman. As has already been said, nature effects this in the woman through love of the man, and in the man through love of the woman.

For this reason, the woman is said to conceive from the man alone, although she receives from herself as well as from the man what makes her fertile. And rightly she conceives from the man alone, since what she conceives is taken from the man’s flesh on one side, while on the other it is supplied through the man’s love.

She therefore conceives from the man not only what she receives from the man, but also what she receives from herself through love of the man.

We do not wish to pass over this point because it is said that Mary conceived from the Holy Spirit (Luke 1). Mary therefore conceived from the Holy Spirit—not because she received from the substance of the Holy Spirit the seed of the offspring, but because, through the love and operation of the Holy Spirit, nature supplied from the Virgin’s flesh the substance for the divine offspring.

Because the love of the Holy Spirit burned uniquely in her heart, the power of the Holy Spirit performed wonders in her flesh. Since his love did not admit a companion in her heart, his operation in her flesh had no precedent.

The Virgin therefore conceived only what she received from her own flesh through the love and operation of the Holy Spirit. From this alone, without the mingling of male seed, she also bore her son.

Thus it was not carnal lust that brought about conception in the Virgin: she received neither seed from a man’s flesh nor conceived from her own flesh through love of a man, but conceived through the love and operation of the Holy Spirit.

Nor should the Holy Spirit himself for this reason be called the Father: his love operated in the Virgin’s conception, but he did not give the Virgin the seed of the offspring from his own essence; rather, through his love and power, he supplied to the Virgin herself the substance from her own flesh.

Christ, therefore, was born from the Virgin because he received the substance of flesh from the Virgin’s flesh; and he was conceived from the Holy Spirit because she, remaining a virgin, conceived from her flesh alone, without the mingling of male seed, through the operation and love of the Holy Spirit.

Hence the angel says to the same Virgin who was about to give birth: “The Holy Spirit will come upon you, and the power of the Most High will overshadow you” (Luke 1).

The Holy Spirit came upon the Virgin so that, through his operation, Christ’s flesh might be formed from the Virgin’s flesh; and the power of the Most High overshadowed her so that, while supplying the substance of flesh, she would not be burned by carnal desire.

[Col. 0775A] ## ON THE NATIVITY OF THE LORD, According to Luke

[Col. 0775]

[Col. 0775A] “A decree went out from Caesar Augustus that the whole world should be registered,” and so forth (Luke 2).

[BEDA.] According to the reliability of the histories, Augustus ruled in such great peace for twelve years around the time of the Lord’s birth that, with both foreign and civil wars quieted throughout the world, the prophetic statement appears literally fulfilled: “They shall beat their swords into plowshares and their spears into sickles. Nation shall not lift up sword against nation” (Isaiah 2).

Christ was born in a time of profound peace because “God was in Christ, reconciling the world to himself” (2 Corinthians 5). Thus the peace established by Augustus signified the peace that our Mediator was to establish, both through himself and through his disciples, between God and human beings.

It was also fitting that the disciples should be protected by the formidable shadow of the Roman name wherever they passed to preach. For just as Caesar required a declaration of the census from the whole world, so Christ was to require a declaration of faith throughout the whole world. Hence: “Go into all the world and preach the Gospel to every creature” (Mark 16).

This registration was the first made when Quirinius was governor of Syria. “And all went to be registered, each to his own city.”

It is not called the first registration with respect to the time of Quirinius, for previously most regions of the earth had often been registered. Quirinius, sent by Caesar to administer justice to the nations and destined to become the assessor of their property, came to Syria.

Because Judaea is like the navel of the whole earth, the census is first demanded at the center of the earth, so that from there it might afterward be required as far as the ends of the world. On this occasion Judaea first became subject to tribute for the Romans. Under Augustus as emperor and Quirinius as governor, everyone went to the registration, each returning to his own city to declare the census owed.

So now, with Christ reigning and promising a reward, let us, through the teachers who govern the Church, declare the census of righteousness; let us take up his yoke, which is light, and we shall find rest for our souls (Matthew 11).

A denarius was paid to Caesar; it contained ten coins and was also marked with Caesar’s name. Let us likewise offer our King the Decalogue of the Law, in which we shall find the face of the King—that is, the recognition of his truth.

“Joseph also went up from Galilee, from the city of Nazareth, into Judaea, to the city of David, which is called Bethlehem, because he was of the house and family of David, to register with Mary, his betrothed wife, who was pregnant” (Luke 2).

[GREGORY.] “The Lord wished to be conceived in one place and born in another, so that he might more easily escape the fury of the treacherous Herod. When the Lord was about to be born, the world was registered, because he appeared in the flesh who would register his elect in eternity. In contrast, it is said of the reprobate: ‘Let them be blotted out of the book of the living, and not be written with the righteous’” (Psalm 68).

[Col. 0776A] “And it happened that, while they were there, the days were fulfilled for her to give birth, and she bore her firstborn son.”

[BEDA.] The Lord is rightly born in Bethlehem both because of the judgment of the royal lineage and because of the sacred meaning of the name. Bethlehem is interpreted as “house of bread.”

[GREGORY.] There the living bread that descended from heaven appears in the flesh, nourishing the minds of the elect with inward satisfaction.

[BEDA.] Every day the Lord is conceived in Nazareth and born in Bethlehem, when any believer, having received the flower of the word, makes himself a house of eternal peace.

Every day he is conceived in the minds of believers, as though in a virginal womb, through faith, and is brought forth through baptism. Every day the Church, as the Mother of God, accompanies her teacher, so that, like Mary with Joseph, ascending from the ruin of worldly conduct—which is what Galilee signifies—into the city of Judah, that is, of confession and praise, she pays to the eternal King the census of devotion.

This Church, in imitation of blessed Mary, is betrothed as it were to one person but made fruitful by another: she is joined to the bishop appointed over her, yet is enriched by the power of the Holy Spirit.

Joseph is therefore rightly interpreted as “increased,” indicating that the diligence of a speaking teacher is of no value without the increase of heavenly help.

The Lord, then, was born according to the flesh, and you are born according to the spirit. Since he was born not from the will of the flesh of a man but from the Holy Spirit, he signified the generation that he was certainly going to grant from the Spirit.

“And she wrapped him in swaddling cloths and laid him in a manger, because there was no room for them in the inn.”

There was no room for them in the inn. It was exceedingly difficult to find vacant houses because of the gathering and crowds of Jews whom that registration had collected together at the same time.

[GREGORY.] He who clothes the world in varied ornament is clothed in humble garments, so that we might receive the robe of immortality. His hands and feet are bound in swaddling bands, so that our hands may be directed toward good works and our feet toward the way of peace.

He is laid in a manger so that he might refresh all the faithful—namely, the holy animals—with the grain of his flesh, he who is the bread of angels. He is confined in a narrow manger so that he might enlarge us through the joys of the heavenly kingdom.

The Lord was not born in his parents’ house, to show that, through the humility he assumed, he was born as if in another’s dwelling, not according to power but according to the nature of humanity. For of his power it is written in the prophet: “All flesh is grass” (Isaiah 40). God became human.

He turns our grass into grain, who said of himself: “Unless a grain of wheat, falling into the earth, dies, it remains alone” (John 12). Hence, too, once born, he is laid in a manger.

The mother laid down the child. Joseph, however, did not dare touch him, because he knew that he had not been generated from him.

Whoever you are, poor person, receive consolation. Joseph and Mary, the mother of the Lord, have no male servant, no female servant, no animal; they themselves are both masters and servants. Timid poverty does not dare approach among the rich.

They go to an inn; he is born in a stable who raises the needy from dung. Job sat upon dung and afterward was crowned, and so forth.

“And there were shepherds in that region, keeping watch and guarding the watches of the night over their flock. And behold, an angel of the Lord stood beside them, and the glory of God shone around them.”

[Col. 0777B] When the Lord was born, the shepherds kept watch and guarded their flock, so that it might be shown that the time had come which he himself had once promised, saying: “Behold, I myself will seek out my sheep, and I will visit them as a shepherd visits his flock” (Ezekiel 34).

The flock signifies the people; the night, the world; and the shepherds, the priests who are to provide for souls with vigilant care.

The angel, appearing with such great light as is not found in the entire sequence of the Old Testament, mystically foretold what the Apostle afterward stated openly: “The night has passed, and the day is approaching” (Romans 13).

“And they were afraid with great fear. And the angel said to them: Do not be afraid. For behold, I bring you good news of great joy, which will be for all the people, because today a Savior has been born for you, who is Christ the Lord, in the city of David.”

Eternal joy is announced to the whole people of the faithful, who are to be gathered from all the varieties of the nations. Although it was night, the angel did not say “on this night” but “today,” because he was announcing great joy. Where sad events occur, mention is usually made of night, as in: “You will suffer scandal on this night” (Matthew 26).

“And this will be a sign for you: You will find an infant wrapped in swaddling cloths and lying in a manger.” The sign of salvation for the faithful is the humility of the Savior, which is opposed to the pride through which death came.

“And suddenly there was with the angel a multitude of the heavenly host praising God and saying: Glory to God in the highest, and on earth peace to people of good will.”

With one angel proclaiming the Gospel, the multitude bursts into harmonious praise, both rendering service to God and instructing us that whenever we hear sacred teaching from the mouth of a brother, we should return praise to God in heart, mouth, and deed.

It is called the heavenly host because they served in the army of the angels that he ordered for our protection against evil spirits.

Since God and man were born, peace is sung to human beings and glory to God, who is glorified by the angels for our redemption. Since neither Jews nor gentiles possess peace—for “there is no peace for the wicked, says the Lord” (Isaiah 57)—the phrase is therefore specifically “to people of good will,” namely, those who receive Christ after his birth.

[GREGORY.] [Col. 0778A] Because through sinning we had become strangers, the angels counted us as strangers from God. But because we recognized our King, the angels recognized us as their fellow citizens.

An angel fears being worshiped by human nature, which he beholds in his own King. Hence Lot and Joshua were not forbidden to worship angels. John, however, was forbidden in the Apocalypse: “See that you do not do this,” he says; “for I am your fellow servant and one of your brothers” (Revelation 22).

“And it happened that the angels departed from them into heaven.”

## ALSO ON THE SAME DAY

“The shepherds said to one another: Let us go as far as Bethlehem and see this word that has happened, which the Lord has made and shown to us” (Luke 2).

They did not say, “Let us see the child,” but “the Word,” as though they were saying: “The Word was in the beginning and became flesh” (John 1).

What did the Lord—that is, the Father—and the Word itself, and the Holy Spirit make? They established that he should become incarnate, and thus showed as accomplished what could not be seen in the Godhead.

“And they came hastily and found Mary and Joseph, and the infant lying in the manger. When they saw him, they recognized the word that had been spoken to them about this child.”

Some people seek Christ but do not find him because they seek him lazily. The shepherds found him because they ran with sincere faith.

In the same way, the shepherds of the Church—or indeed any faithful people—drawn by heavenly teaching, enter as though through Bethlehem’s gates and find the Catholic Church as Mary, the company of teachers as Joseph, and the humble advent of the Mediator inserted into the pages of Scripture, as if in a manger.

When they saw the child, they recognized the word that had been spoken; and we, through faith in the Incarnation, shall come to behold the glory of the Word.

It should be noted that the events themselves are sometimes called “words” because they are worthy of being spoken and recounted. Hence in Isaiah: “There was no word”—that is, no event worthy of the name—“which Hezekiah did not show to the Chaldeans” (Isaiah 39).

Similarly, here the shepherds say: “Let us see this Word that has happened,” that is, this event worthy of narration, which the Lord himself made most excellent and signified to us through the angels. But where it says, “They recognized the word that had been spoken,” understand “word” as speech.

[Col. 0778D] “And all who had heard it marveled at the things that had been told them by the shepherds.”

They marvel both at the mystery of the Incarnation and at the shepherds’ great testimony. The shepherds did not know how to give deceptive expression to what they had heard, but proclaimed the words with simple eloquence.

Thus the Lord sent not rhetoricians but fishermen to evangelize. Likewise, in the Old Testament he appointed shepherds as messengers of his dispensation. Therefore the testimony of shepherds must not be despised.

“But Mary kept all these words, pondering them in her heart.”

Mary, no less modest in speech than silent in body, compares the things she had seen happening around her with the things she had read in the Scriptures as destined to happen.

She had read in Isaiah: “Behold, a virgin shall conceive and bear a son” (Isaiah 7). She had read: “The ox knows its owner, and the donkey its master’s manger” (Isaiah 1).

She saw in the manger the Son of God, her Son, her only Son, crying. She saw that she herself, descended from David’s line, had conceived from the Holy Spirit in Nazareth and given birth in Bethlehem—matters whose testimonies she had read in prophecy.

She therefore compares the words of the prophets with the events and finds in everything grounds for faith.

If Mary learned from the shepherds, let us also learn from priests.

“And the shepherds returned, glorifying and praising God for all that they had heard and seen, just as it had been told them.”

They praised God for what they had heard from the angels and glorified him for what they had seen in Bethlehem. In the same way, teachers of spiritual flocks sometimes inspect the camps of the faithful, seeking examples of good conduct, and sometimes return to their pastoral office to teach.

Furthermore, it should be noted why the Son was sent rather than the Father or the Holy Spirit.

The Son was sent, not the Father or the Holy Spirit, because it would have been improper for the Father to be sent by another, since he was not from another. If he were sent by another, he would have to come from the one by whom he was sent and would have that one as a kind of principle. Therefore the Father cannot be sent by another, because he is not from another.

The Son was sent first, since he is from the Father alone; afterward the Holy Spirit was also sent, since he is from the Father and the Son.

The Son came first so that human beings might be liberated. Afterward the Holy Spirit came so that human beings might be blessed. The former freed us from evil; the latter recalled us to good things. The former removed what we were enduring; the latter restored what we had lost.

The natural Son came, sent by the Father, to call those who were to be adopted into the inheritance, and to give his own consent so as to confirm the grace of adoption. For those who were strangers could not be led into the inheritance by the Father without the consent of the Son.

The Father therefore sent on behalf of his children; the Son came on behalf of his brothers. The names “fatherhood” and “sonship” are established in the Father and the Son, so that those who were to be adopted might receive the name “sons,” through him whose name it was and from him from whom he was.

Wisdom came so that the enemy might be conquered by reason and so that she herself might reclaim her dwelling, which wickedness possessed. Since the enemy had conquered through cunning, it was just that he should be conquered not by strength but by prudence, and that he should be cast down in the very thing by which he had raised himself as victor.

The Son of God became the son of man so that he might make the sons of men sons of God, and so that the name “Son” would not pass to another person, resulting in two sons in the Trinity and confusing the distinction of the Trinity.

If the Father had assumed flesh, he himself would be both Father and Son: Father of the Son whom he begot eternally, and Son of the mother from whom he would have been begotten in time.

If the Holy Spirit had assumed flesh, there would be two sons in the Trinity: one Son of the Father without a mother, and another Son of a mother without a father.

Therefore, so that the incommunicable name would not be divided, the Son alone assumed flesh, so that one and the same person would be both the Son of God and the son of man: the Son of God, begotten from the Father according to divinity; and the son of man, born from a mother according to humanity.

## That the Son alone assumed flesh

[Col. 0780A]

## That the Son Alone Assumed Flesh

It remains to be considered why the Son alone assumed flesh. But perhaps some will say: If the works of the Trinity are inseparable, then whatever the Son does, the Father does. But if everything that the Son does the Father also does (John 5), then, if the Son assumed flesh, the Father also assumed flesh, because the Son could not assume flesh without the Father, if he could do nothing without the Father.

Here we must first consider that, when it is said that the Son does everything the Father does, this must plainly be understood of that operation by which God, the Creator and Maker, establishes, governs, and orders his creation. In this operation the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit cannot in any way be separated, because in the one divinity in which and through which they operate, they are one. [Col. 0780B] We distinguish these matters concerning the divine operation for this reason: so that no one may think it necessary to object against what has been said—“Everything that the Father does, the Son also does”—that the Father begets, whereas the Son does not, and that the Son is begotten, whereas the Father is not.

For if the Son were begotten as the Father is, he would be the Father; and if the Father were begotten as the Son is, he would be the Son. Therefore, lest anyone suppose that, because the Son does not beget what the Father does, the Son does not do everything that the Father does, we say that this must be understood of that operation by which he either works upon creation, so that what did not exist begins to exist, or works within creation, so that what has been made continues to exist in what has been made.

For the whole Trinity operates inseparably wherever neither the Father is separated from the Son, nor the Son from the Father, nor the Holy Spirit from both, in the operation. [Col. 0780C] In the work, indeed, operation itself is properly designated. For in what has not been made, God does not make what he is; rather, he simply is. But what has been made has been made by him from whom everything that has been made has been made. Thus, everything that the Father does, the Son likewise does (John 5).

Since, therefore, the assumption of flesh is found within this operation, it is not improperly asked how it belongs to the Son alone and not to the Father. For when it is said that the Son assumed flesh, a work performed by the Son is certainly signified; and if the Father is excluded from that work, then the Father does not perform everything that the Son does.

Or should it perhaps be thought that, because it was not said, “Everything that the Son did, the Father did,” but rather, “Whatever the Father does, the Son also does,” the Son does indeed everything that the Father does, while the Son does certain things that the Father does not? Far from it. Everything that the Father does, the Son does; and everything that the Son does, the Father does, because in that in which they are one in divinity they cannot be separated in operation. [Col. 0780D]

Therefore, everything that the Son does, the Father does, because in the divinity in which the Son is the Father’s, and because he is one with the Father, he does nothing without the Father’s operation. He did certain things in his humanity, according to which he was not the Son of the Father, because he had not received that nature by being born from the Father. Those things are therefore referred to the person of the Son alone because he did them in and according to that nature which he did not share with the Father, but which he alone received uniquely in time as his own. [Col. 0781A]

Nevertheless, everything which he did in divinity he did not do alone for the reason that he was not alone in divinity; yet he did it together with the Father because he was one with the Father.

If, therefore, the Son assumed humanity in divinity, how did the Father, who was one with him in divinity, not do the same in that divinity? Or perhaps, when it is said that the Son assumed flesh, by the force of the relation whereby he is understood to have united it to himself, the same is not said of the Father because, if it were said, something different rather than the same would be understood?

For if it were said, “The Father assumed flesh,” it would likewise be understood that the Father united flesh to himself—which would no longer be the same thing, but something different. For it would be something different if flesh were said to have been united to the Father from what it is when it is said to have been united to the Son. Just as the Father is one person and the Son another, so one thing is said when the Son is said to have become incarnate, and another would be said if the Father were said to have become incarnate. [Col. 0781B]

It follows, then, that if the Son assumed flesh, the Father also assumed flesh, just as it does not follow that, if the Son united flesh to himself, the Father also united flesh to himself. It does, however, follow that, if the Son united flesh to himself, the Father also united that same flesh to the Son, because, while the operation of both is shown to be one, neither is the Son shown to have operated without the Father, nor the Father without the Son.

But if the Father had clothed himself with flesh and the Son had clothed himself with flesh, this would not be the same thing but something different, since in that very act the operation would not be shown to be the same, and the relation would not be demonstrated to have been made toward the same person. [Col. 0781C]

Now, however, the Father also performed the assumption, or union, of flesh, because he clothed the Son with flesh; and the Son performed it because he clothed himself with flesh. There was one union and one operation. The union was one because what was united was united to one person; the operation was one because what was done was done in one person. Three performed the work, but they did not perform three works; they performed one work. What came to be was the work of one, insofar as it was done with respect to that one person, and the work of three, insofar as it was done by them.

It is read in the Book of Judges that Manoah took a wife for his son Samson (Judges 13), yet he did not take a wife for himself, because he took a wife for his son. The son asked his father to take a wife for him, as though he could not do this by himself; yet no one argues by saying: “If the father took a wife for his son, then the father took a wife,” and contends that the father was married because he took a wife for his son. [Col. 0781D]

Why, then, should the Father be said to have become incarnate because he united flesh to his Son, just as the Son himself is said to have become incarnate because he joined flesh to himself? The flesh is the Bride of the Word. The Word took it to himself, and the Father of the Word likewise united it to his Word. The two performed one thing, and in one person there was one operation of the two.

For this reason he says: “Whatever the Father does, the Son likewise does.” “These things,” he says, “the Son likewise does.” What does “these things” mean? Not other things. What does “likewise” mean? Not otherwise. The unity of operation could not have been demonstrated more perfectly: not other things, not otherwise—the same things and in the same manner.

If he operated the same things but did not operate them in the same manner, the operation would not be one, because it would be different. [Col. 0782A] But now he operates both the same things and in the same manner, so that there is nothing either different or otherwise in his operation.

Show me something that the Father does—if indeed it is necessary to ask what he does who does everything. Nevertheless, for the sake of an example, set forth one thing among all the things the Father does. I say that the Son does this very thing. I do not mean that he does something similar, but that he does the very same thing.

When I say, “I do the same thing that you do,” perhaps because I build a house just as you build a house, and your house, which you build, is one house while my house, which I build, is another, I nevertheless say that I do the same thing as you, because what I do is in some respect similar to what you do. But I do not understand it in this way when I say that the Son does this very thing that the Father does. [Col. 0782B]

If, however, I were building a house and you were building the same house together with me, I would say that you were doing the same thing as I. Indeed, it would be more truly one thing, because it would be the very same thing and not another. Yet even then it would not truly be one, because you would be doing one part and I another; you with your tools and I with mine; you with your hands and arms and I with mine. Finally, you would act with your strength and I with mine. It would no longer truly be one, but in another and through other things.

Do I speak in this way when I say that the Son does this very thing that the Father does? Is the Son’s hand therefore one thing and the Father’s another? Is the Son’s arm one thing and the Father’s another? Is the Son’s power one thing and the Father’s another, when the Son himself is the Father’s hand, arm, and power? [Col. 0782C]

Just as what a human being does with his hand is the same as what the human hand does; what a human being does with his arm is the same as what the human arm does; and what a human being does by his strength is the same as what human strength does, so what the Father does is the same as what the Son does, because everything that the Father does, he does through the Son.

If there is one essence, one nature, one strength, and one will, how can there not be one operation? You say, “The Father does these things.” I say: The Father does this very thing; the Son does this very thing; the whole Father and the whole Son do it. The Father’s very doing belongs to the Son.

Do not weigh this as though there were two actions, one greater and one lesser; or perhaps two equal actions of similar weight. It is unity in itself; do not multiply anything. There is one action of two in one, of three, one action, just as there is one divinity. In the one action there are three—not three agents, but one agent—just as in the one divinity there are three, not three gods but one. [Col. 0782D]

The Father, Son, and Holy Spirit are three persons, but they are not three gods, nor three creators, nor three makers, because in that in which they are one they cannot be divided. Therefore, “Whatever the Father does, the Son also does” (John 5). Likewise—what could be more like than unity? How can what cannot be multiplied be divided, or how can what is one withdraw from itself?

Do not, then, be surprised if the assumption of flesh, which is referred to the Son alone, was not performed by the Son alone, but if, together with the Son, the Father and the Holy Spirit also performed it. Nor for that reason should you say that three became incarnate, because three performed the incarnation of one: the unity of nature makes the operation inseparable, and the propriety of the person makes the assumption singular.

## Concerning the Flesh Assumed into Christ

[Col. 0783A]

It is asked how a human being, personally united to the Word, could be assumed without sin from the mass of the human race, which is entirely corrupted and, as it were, leavened by sin in Adam.

The answer is that the Virgin Mary was cleansed from sin before the conception, through faith in Christ’s future death. Indeed, it was fitting that that Virgin should shine with the purity beneath which nothing greater can be understood in relation to God, since God the Father had determined to give her his only Son—whom, begotten from his own heart and equal to himself, he loved as himself—in such a way that he would naturally be one.

He was likewise the common Son of God the Father and of the Virgin, whom the Son himself chose substantially to make his mother, and from whom the Holy Spirit willed and effected that he should be conceived and born—the one from whom he himself proceeded. Therefore the Son of God could be conceived without sin from the most pure Virgin and be born through the human being united to him. [Col. 0783B]

With the exception of the holy Virgin Mary, concerning whom, out of reverence for the Lord, I wish no question whatsoever to be raised when sins are being discussed—for we know that she was granted greater grace for conquering sin in every respect. Hence she was worthy to conceive and bear him who is known to have had no sin (Augustine, *On Nature and Grace*, chapter 36).

With this Virgin excepted, if all the holy men and women could be gathered together, what would they answer except what John says: “If we say that we have no sin, we deceive ourselves” (1 John 1)?

We read: “The grace of the Holy Spirit had filled Mary completely, and divine love had wholly enkindled her, so that there was in her nothing worldly that could violate her affection, but only continual ardor and the intoxication of abundant love” (Augustine). [Col. 0783C] Since every power of the angels is held to be the Spirit of God, and since the Holy Spirit came upon the blessed and glorious Virgin, bearing the whole God who had entered her and was carried in her womb for nine months, we must believe that she merited greater privileges of virtue and received grace praised even by the angels.

Christ received earth from earth, because flesh is from earth; he received flesh from Mary’s flesh, walked here in that flesh, and gave us that very flesh to eat for salvation. The Apostle: “Who was made to him of the seed of David according to the flesh” (Romans 1). [Col. 0783D]

For just as God was born from the substance of the Father before the ages, so the human being was born in time from the substance of his mother. For if that human being personally united to God had been made from nothing, as some assert, or from a race other than Adam’s, human nature, which was wholly in Adam and sinned there, could in no way have made satisfaction to God for its sin, because neither Adam himself nor anyone born from his race would have paid that debt.

And if Christ were alien to the human race that had sinned, his satisfaction would in no way pertain to Adam and those born from him, and he would seem no more able to help them than the devil could.

“ In the Virgin’s womb there was generative blood and feminine fluid. The Word mingled itself with this blood or fluid and made the substance of the blood into congealed flesh. [Col. 0784A] The Holy Spirit came upon it and, by giving life, formed what had been joined together by the Word’s bonding, and distinguished what had been formed” (Augustine).

“The number forty-six years most fittingly corresponds to the perfection of the Lord’s body” (Bede). “The writers on natural things report that the form of the human body is perfected over that many days: during the six days immediately following conception it resembles milk; during the following nine it is converted into blood; then for twelve days it solidifies; during the remaining eighteen it is formed until all the limbs have their complete outlines; and from that point through the remaining time until birth it increases in size.

Six, nine, twelve, and eighteen make forty-five. If we add one to these—that is, the very day on which the body, having been divided into its members, begins to take on growth—we arrive at the same number of days in the construction of the Lord’s body as the number of years we find in the building of the temple” (Augustine). [Col. 0784B]

“Christ was not first conceived in the Virgin’s womb and then did divinity come into the flesh. Rather, as soon as the Word came into the womb (John 1), while the diversity of its proper nature was preserved, it became flesh, and a perfect human being—that is, in the reality of flesh and soul—was born from that flesh to which the Word had been united” (Augustine).

There is also another reason. It was said elsewhere that what is assumed for offspring from a parent has no will of its own, and therefore no sin. It is consequently clear that, in what the Son of God assumed into his own person, no stain of sin could have come from the Virgin. [Col. 0784C]

“The unchangeable Truth, assuming a soul through the spirit and a body through the soul, and assuming the whole human being, freed him from every weakness. For whatever of the human being he did not assume, he did not free. Just as he did not abandon his flesh in the tomb when he died, so in the Virgin’s womb he formed it when he was born.

Thus he died without life departing, just as he suffered without the power of life perishing. Although he left his soul only for a short time and breathed his last, the divinity abandoned neither of the two, from the moment when the Word became flesh” (Augustine).

Some demand that an explanation be given of how God was mingled with a human being so that Christ might become one person, as though they were being asked to explain something that happens every day: how the soul is mingled with the body so that a human being becomes one person. [Col. 0784D]

For just as, in the unity of the person, the soul uses the body so that a human being may exist, so, in the unity of the person, God uses the human being so that Christ may exist. In that person, then, there is a mingling of soul and body; in this person there is a mingling of God and human being—provided that the hearer departs from the ordinary associations of bodies, since two liquids are usually mingled in such a way that neither preserves its own integrity, although even incorporeal light is mingled with material bodies such as air.

The person of a human being is therefore a mingling of soul and body. For when the Word of God is mingled with the soul adhering to the body, it assumes both soul and body at once. The former occurs every day for the procreation of human beings; the latter occurred once for the liberation of human beings.

Nevertheless, the mingling of two incorporeal things ought to have been more easily believed than that of one incorporeal thing with a corporeal thing. For if the soul, by its own nature, does not deceive itself and understands that it is incorporeal, much more is the Word of God incorporeal; and for that reason the mingling of the Word of God and the soul ought to have been more credible than that of soul and body. [Col. 0785A]

## Sermon on the Nativity of the Lord

Because today the Redeemer was born into the world and brought the remedy of eternal salvation, he made the time of his birth known through many notable miracles. Of all these, the first sign of the Lord’s birth was that, at the time when Christ was born, the sole Caesar Augustus, exceptionally peaceful, ruled the whole world (Luke 2): something previously unheard of, that so many peoples and nations could endure one lord. By this rule of Caesar Augustus, there was truly signified the one who was to come in the flesh, who alone rules and governs all things, who alone presides over everything in heaven and on earth. [Col. 0785B]

The second sign was that there was then such peace on earth as had not been heard of in the world up to that time, so that no one throughout the whole world dared to begin a war; rather, all people lived under one tranquil peace and quiet. The prophecy of Isaiah was truly fulfilled: “And they shall beat their swords into ploughshares and their spears into pruning hooks” (Isaiah 2).

That peace signified him who was born in the flesh, who reconciled the human race, who joined angels and human beings in one peace, and who granted to all who preserve true peace the power to become children of God, saying: “Blessed are the peacemakers, for they shall be called children of God” (Matthew 5). Hence also the angels of God, announcing Christ’s birth on this night, sang: “Glory to God in the highest” (Luke 2). [Col. 0785C]

The third sign was that, by Caesar’s permission, everyone—noble or ignoble, free or enslaved, and even those held in captivity—was ordered to return to his own place. Each person was restored to his own inheritance, and each declared that he would pay his tax to Caesar; that tax amounted to a payment of three denarii, which was called a drachma.

What else was signified by these events than that, as long as we are in the world, we are pilgrims away from God, until through the grace of the Lord’s birth we are led back to the joys of paradise and, freed from the ancient enemy, subjected to divine service? The tax which each declared that he would pay to Caesar signifies the faith of the holy Trinity, which our King requires from all who are regarded as bearing the Christian name. [Col. 0785D]

The fourth sign was that Caesar Augustus made all slaves who were fugitives return to their own masters; and those who disregarded this edict and despised their masters he caused to perish in a single day, nearly thirty thousand of them.

In this decree, therefore, it was signified that every human being, setting aside the desires of the world, should return to his heavenly Lord. But whoever neglects this will be subjected, together with the devil and his angels, to eternal damnation.

The fifth sign was a star of new and unusual brilliance, which was seen in the East by the Magi on the same night and at the same hour when Christ was born (Matthew 2). Recognizing from its extraordinary radiance that the King of kings had been born, they came to Jerusalem under the star’s guidance. Then, still led by the same star, they came to Bethlehem on the thirteenth day, and there they adored God with mystical gifts. [Col. 0786A]

This star signified the grace of divine illumination, by which the Lord, born in the flesh, illuminated those who sat in darkness and in the shadow of death.

The sixth sign was a great circle shining with a golden radiance, which gleamed around the sun throughout the entire day on which Christ was born. It signified this: that the true sun of righteousness had been born, who would illuminate by his grace every human being coming into this world (John 1). Concerning him the Psalmist says: “Light has risen in the darkness for the upright in heart; the merciful, compassionate, and righteous Lord” (Psalm 111).

The seventh sign was that throughout the whole day of the Lord’s birth a stream of oil flowed in the city of Rome, pouring forth into the Tiber. Oil signifies mercy; and by this it was shown that on that day was born the one who came by his mercy alone to seek and save what had perished. As Paul says to his disciple Timothy: “The kindness and humanity of our Savior appeared, not because of works of righteousness that we had done, but according to his mercy he saved us” (Titus 3). [Col. 0786B]

By these and countless other signs God wished to make his birth known, so that he might lead us back from the desires of the world to our heavenly homeland. As Paul says: “Be renewed in the spirit of your mind, in righteousness and holiness” (Ephesians 4).

Today the Virgin gave birth to “Christ, a stumbling block indeed to the Jews, but foolishness to the Gentiles” (1 Corinthians 1). The Jews object, on the ground of nature’s impossibility, that a virgin cannot give birth, without considering that it is written in their own Law: “Behold, a virgin shall conceive and bear a son, and his name shall be called Emmanuel,” which is interpreted, “God with us” (Isaiah 7). By this testimony of Isaiah, blessed Mary is declared destined to be made fruitful by childbirth. [Col. 0786C]

For the Lord commanded Moses that rods be brought from each of the tribes. Twelve rods were brought, among which was the rod of Aaron the priest, placed in the tabernacle of testimony. On the following day Aaron’s rod was found to have blossomed, put forth leaves, and borne nuts. He who commanded this rod, deprived of its root and dried of its sap, to put forth leaves made the true Virgin gloriously pregnant.

Concerning this rod Isaiah likewise says: “A rod shall come forth from the root of Jesse, and a flower shall rise from his root” (Isaiah 11). Jesse was the father of King David; from whose seed the rod—that is, the blessed Virgin Mary—proceeded, and she brought forth Christ, the flower of life. [Col. 0786D]

From David, by grace and mercy, God became human, as the same Isaiah says: “He himself will save his people from their sins” (Isaiah 7). Truly he will save his people from their sins, because whoever faithfully believes in Christ will be his co-heir in the kingdom of his Father, “who rescued us from the power of darkness and transferred us into the kingdom of the Son of his love” (Colossians 1).

Similarly, the Lord wished to make his birth known by the testimony spoken by Jeremiah: “This is our God, and no other shall be reckoned beside him, who discovered the whole way of wisdom. After this he appeared on earth and lived among human beings” (Baruch 3). [Col. 0787A]

The Jews again say that Christ has not yet come but is still to come, without considering Daniel, who said: “When the Holy of Holies comes, anointing shall cease” (Daniel 9). If the Jews therefore contend that Christ is still to come, let them show whom they have as their own king from their lineage. If they cannot show him as their Father, let them believe that Christ, who is the Holy of Holies, has come.

Let them also consider what the patriarch Jacob said before Daniel’s time, deprived indeed of bodily sight but full of the spirit of prophecy: “The scepter shall not be taken from Judah, nor a ruler from his thigh, until he comes who is to be sent; and he himself shall be the expectation of the nations” (Genesis 49).

The Lord’s coming is also demonstrated in the deed of Gideon the Israelite. When the children of Israel were doing many evils in the sight of the Lord and therefore had been handed over to Midian and Amalek and were being oppressed most harshly, they cried out to God, asking him for help. [Col. 0787B] The Lord, moved by their cry, appeared to Gideon and said that through him he wished to free the children of Israel from the oppression of Midian and Amalek.

Gideon said to the Lord: “Give me this sign: I shall place a fleece of wool on the threshing floor, and if only the fleece is covered with dew while the ground all around is dry, I shall know that through my hand you will deliver Israel” (Judges 6). When God fulfilled this according to Gideon’s request, he asked again that, with the fleece placed outside, the fleece remain dry. When God likewise fulfilled this, Gideon, encouraged by the sign, joined battle with the Midianites and destroyed a great multitude with a small force. Thus the children of Israel were freed from the harsh oppression they had suffered at the hands of the most cruel Midian and Amalek. [Col. 0787C]

Midian and Amalek, who afflicted the children of Israel severely, signify the ancient enemy who, before the Lord’s coming, oppressed the human race under the yoke of slavery and afflicted it by imposing sinful desires. Gideon signifies Christ, who withdrew the world from the rule of the ancient enemy.

That the Lord’s coming is demonstrated by the fleece is declared by the Psalmist: “He shall come down like rain upon the fleece” (Psalm 71). The Lord shall come down like rain upon the fleece, while the surrounding earth is still dry, when the Lord was still known only to the people of Israel, when from the Jewish race he chose for himself both the mother from whom he would be born and the disciples whom he would send to preach. [Col. 0787D]

The Lord’s coming is compared to the dry fleece and the surrounding watered earth when faith in Christ became known throughout the world, while only the Jewish people, as now, appeared to remain dry and unbelieving.

Let us earnestly consider him, since God, now made human, has fulfilled the things that he promised concerning his coming through the patriarchs and prophets, in deeds and words. If God came into this world to make us citizens of the angels, let us not ourselves be the cause of our destruction by persisting in sinful desires and thus distancing ourselves from God our Savior. Let us put off the old human being and put on the new human being, who was born into the world for the sake of our salvation. [Col. 0788A]

Let us see how great a dignity the Lord’s birth has granted us. Before our Redeemer was born in the flesh, the angels condemned us as strangers to their fellowship, because they knew that by sinning we had lost our heavenly homeland. But after the Redeemer assumed the earth of our flesh, that angelic height did not despise our frailty; and those whom they had previously regarded with contempt they now venerate as companions.

Hence the angels themselves, rejoicing on this night over Christ’s birth and our redemption, sang: “Glory to God in the highest, and on earth peace to people of good will” (Luke 2). Hence Lot (Genesis 19) and Joshua (Judges 5) adored angels, and yet they were not forbidden to adore them. [Col. 0788B] John, however, wished to adore an angel, and the angel restrained him from worshiping him, saying: “See that you do not do it, for I am your fellow servant and one of your brothers” (Revelation 19) (Gregory).

But after the angels behold humanity in God, they fear being worshiped by a human being; nor do they disdain to have a human being as a companion, since they worship the human God above themselves.

Let us therefore obtain our dignity by our conduct. Let no luxury defile us; let no shameful thought accuse us; let malice not gnaw at the mind, envy not consume it, pride not inflate it, and ambition not tear it apart. Since we are to be co-heirs of God and citizens of the angels, let us lead a pure and angelic life.

May he himself deign to grant this—he who became God and human for the sake of our salvation, Jesus Christ our Lord, who with the Father and the Holy Spirit lives and reigns throughout all ages of ages. [Col. 0788C]

## Sermon on the Nativity of the Lord

“The kindness and humanity of our Savior God appeared, not because of works of righteousness that we had done, but according to his mercy he saved us” (Titus 3).

The cunning of the devil’s deceit had acquired the human race for itself, dearest brothers, and had subjected it to its own condition through the sin of the first parent. But the Lord, the just judge, who does not wish to inflict anything unjust even upon his adversary, but wishes to do everything either through mercy or through justice, wished to redeem the human race by grace in such a way that he would not appear to commit injustice against the devil.

Since Satan had acted cunningly against humanity through deceit, the Lord wished to act prudently against Satan on humanity’s behalf through wisdom. The Lord therefore proceeded according to this plan concerning the restoration of humanity: it was necessary that, in order to fight against the devil, one be sent who would neither succumb but would act rationally, and who would handle everything with wisdom. [Col. 0788D]

Adam was a merely human being, and therefore, through human frailty, he succumbed to the devil’s temptations. For that reason a merely human being was not to be sent for our redemption, since, when tempted, he might himself have been able to sin.

But what kind of sin did Adam commit? A sin, certainly, that was greater than the world. For in one crime he committed six criminal offenses, by which he entangled the six ages of his posterity in death. [Col. 0789A]

The first was pride: he wished to be equal to God, and therefore he who had been set over all became the lowest of all.

The second was disobedience: he transgressed the commandment, and therefore everything that had previously been subject to him also became disobedient to him.

The third was avarice: he desired more than had been granted, and therefore he lost everything that had been justly granted.

The fourth was sacrilege: he secretly stole what had been forbidden in a sacred place, as though by theft, and therefore deserved to be excluded from the sanctuary.

The fifth was spiritual fornication. His soul was joined to God. But when, having rejected God, he admitted the devil, he committed adultery, as it were, with a stranger, and therefore lost the friendship of the true bridegroom. [Col. 0789B]

The sixth was homicide, by which he cast himself and the whole human race into death. Hence he immediately died in the inward human being, and lay buried in the tomb of the body.

For this reason he was bound by a double guilt: one by which he despised God and abandoned the work of obedience; the other by which he fell into the pit of death and rendered powerless the work joined to himself.

How, then, was it necessary for him to return? He had to restore the honor he had taken from God and make satisfaction for the sin he had committed. For it is entirely just that one who has taken away another’s property should both restore what was taken and make satisfaction for the injury inflicted.

What did humanity take from God? Everything that he had proposed to accomplish through that race under his care. How was the stolen honor to be restored? [Col. 0789C] By conquering the devil in the manner in which he himself had been conquered by him, and by restoring himself and all those predestined to life in the condition they would have had if they had persevered.

How, moreover, was he to make satisfaction? Because he had committed a sin greater than the world, he ought to pay God something greater than the world. But since he could accomplish neither of these things in any way, he therefore remained in death.

And why did he not perish utterly? Because God’s decree could not be changed. For God had determined to complete the number of the elect from Adam’s race.

What, then? Because he did not pay the honor owed, God took it from him unwillingly when he subjected him to punishments.

To what end, finally, was he to come? Since a fugitive servant had fled with the theft belonging to his lord to a most savage tyrant, the king’s son was sent from the palace into the prison after the exiled servant, so that he might crush the tyrant and restore the fugitive servant, together with his possessions, to the king’s favor. [Col. 0789D]

Why could man not return by himself after the Fall? Because, just as he fell not by himself but after being impelled by another, so it was fitting that, since he could not and yet desired to return by himself, he should rise again with the help of another.

Why did he not send an angel to redeem him? If an angel had redeemed man, then man would also have been that angel’s servant. Man, however, had to be restored in such a way that he would be equal to the angels. There was another obstacle as well: an angel, in his own nature, was incapable of redeeming man. If he became man, he would be still less capable. Nor was an angel to be sent into this battle, since he could have sinned—he who had previously sinned through pride [Col. 0790A].

Why did he not create another man from the earth and send him on behalf of the lost one? If God had created and sent a new man, redemption would not have pertained to Adam’s race. The one who made satisfaction for man had to belong to his race.

Why did he not send a patriarch or prophet? The patriarchs and prophets had been conceived and born in sins, and therefore could not redeem the human race.

Therefore, since an angel ought not to redeem and man could not make satisfaction, the Son of God, through whom all things exist, assumed a complete man so that redemption might also be accomplished through him; and in two natures he became one person. In the nature in which he was God, he conquered the devil, just as the devil had conquered man, and opened heaven to all the predestined and made them equal to the angels—something only God could do [Col. 0790B]. In the nature in which he was man, he paid more than the world for the injury, when he underwent an undeserved death—something only man ought to do.

Why, then, was neither the Father nor the Holy Spirit sent, but only the Son incarnated? If the Father or the Holy Spirit had become incarnate, two sons would be counted in the Trinity: one, the Son of the Virgin, who had become incarnate; the other, the Son of God.

There was another reason. The Son is the likeness of God, while the angel and man had assumed for themselves the likeness of God. Therefore the one to whom the injury had been specially done ought to become incarnate, so that he might mercifully save the one and justly condemn the other.

Why, then, was the Son alone incarnated? Because action against the devil’s cunning had to proceed through his wisdom. The Son is the wisdom and providence of the Father, through whom all things were made and ordered [Col. 0790C]. Since he is providence, he acted prudently and rationally; since he is wisdom, he acted wisely; and since he is God, he could not sin. Therefore the Son was sent.

As providence, he acted rationally; as wisdom, he dealt wisely with all things; as God, he could not sin. It was fitting, however, that just as man had been overcome and taken captive, so man, by overcoming nature, should set man free. Thus it was not God alone who was sent, but God and man: man to fight, God to sustain the one who fought.

There is another reason. There had been great discord between God and man through the old man; concord was brought about through the new Mediator [Col. 0790D]. Since he was a mediator, it was fitting that he should have kinship with both. Therefore, since he was to reconcile man to God, he who stood between the two had to be both God and man.

“Then the kindness and humanity of our Savior God appeared,” and so forth. That is, he was God and man: “not from works of righteousness that we have done, but according to his mercy he saved us” (Titus III).

He rightly says, “appeared”—that is, he willed to be born of the Virgin.

Why, however, was he born of Mary and not of another? Because she was the first in the world to vow virginity. How could he be born without sin from a sinful mass? From the beginning, God separated some who would worship him more intimately from the others; from these the Virgin sprang, as though drawn from a line. Like a dry branch that once produced a flower without moisture, she brought forth the Savior to the world without concupiscence [Col. 0791A].

How did she give birth? Without defilement and without pain. With the door closed, he entered the chamber of the womb and joined human nature to himself; with the door closed, he came forth from the chamber like a bridegroom.

Why was he enclosed in the womb for nine months? So that he might restore to the fellowship of the nine orders of angels the human beings who were enclosed in the miseries of this world or of hell.

At what hour was he born? At midnight, as it is said: “While the night was halfway through its course, your almighty Word came from the royal throne” (Wisdom XVIII).

Why at night? First, because he came hidden; then, so that he might lead those who were in the night of error into the light of truth. Therefore “the kindness and humanity of our Savior God appeared.”

## Division of the Sermon

[Col. 0791B]

The kindness and humanity of our Savior also appeared through seven special miracles: through the exceedingly brilliant star (Matthew II); through the golden or purple circle that shone around the sun; through the fountain of oil that burst forth from the earth; through the great peace that then existed; through the census in which the whole world was registered; through the fact that many refused to pay the Lord’s census and were killed in a single day; and through the fact that a dumb animal spoke.

What, then, do these things signify? The star signified the saints. Thus the brilliant star shone forth because the Holy of Holies had come. The circle shone around the sun because the Sun of righteousness came to illuminate the Church with the gold of his divinity and crown it with the purple of his passion [Col. 0791C]. The fountain of oil flowed from the earth because the fountain of mercy streamed forth from the Virgin. Oil signifies mercy. Great peace came to be because true peace appeared on earth. The world was registered for the census because the human race was marked with chrism for the kingdom above. Those who refused to pay the Lord’s census were killed because those who said, “We do not want this man to reign over us” (Luke XIX) perished. The animal spoke because the people of the Gentiles were converted to the praise of God.

This birth of our Savior also appeared—or was revealed—to the shepherds through angels. For we read in the Gospel that shepherds were in that region, keeping watch and guarding the watches of the night over their flock:

“And behold, an angel of the Lord stood beside them, and the brightness [Col. 0791D] of God shone around them, and they were afraid with great fear. And the angel said to them: Do not be afraid; for behold, I announce to you great joy which will be for all the people, because a Savior has been born for us, who is Christ the Lord, in the city of David, that is, in Bethlehem. And this will be a sign for you: you will find an infant wrapped in swaddling clothes and lying in a manger. And suddenly there was with the angel a multitude of the heavenly army praising and saying: ‘Glory to God in the highest, and on earth peace to people of good will’” (Luke II).

Hearing this, the shepherds came as far as Bethlehem and found things as the angel had told them. The angel rightly announced these things, because the King of angels had been born. The angel appeared with great light [Col. 0792A] because he declared that the Sun of righteousness had risen as a light in the darkness.

It was announced to the shepherds that he had been born who said, “I am the good shepherd” (John X). He appeared to kings through the star because the King and the star had been born. He is called king, as in: “Yet I have been established as king by him over Zion, his holy mountain” (Psalm II). He is also called the star because “a star shall rise from Jacob.”

Therefore he rightly appeared to shepherds and kings, because he himself was king and priest, and was born from royal and priestly seed: from royal seed because he was descended from David; from priestly seed as well, as is proved by the fact that Mary was related to Elizabeth, of whom it is written: “And the wife of Zechariah was from the daughters of Aaron, and her name was Elizabeth” (Luke I).

The messenger is sufficiently worthy of praise because he was both an angel and accompanied by great light. But listen to what he brought: “Behold, I announce to you great joy,” and so forth [Col. 0792B].

Truly, great joy! We were captives, we lay in prison, and in our infirmity the Savior was born; the physician was born. Behold, great joy! Human beings had still more reason to rejoice when the angels also rejoiced and said, “Glory to God in the highest,” and so forth.

Glory was with the angels in the highest: concerning the restoration of the diminished order. They praise God for the restoration of human beings to the number of the angels.

And there is peace for human beings. He announced peace to those who had previously been at discord with God and the angels, but through the Mediator have been reconciled. And because by sinning we were strangers to God, the angels regarded us as strangers to their fellowship [Col. 0792C]. The angels despised human beings before God, since they allowed themselves to be worshiped by them. Thus Lot and Abraham worshiped angels (Genesis XIX), and before Christ’s coming the angels did not forbid it.

But after the Lord was born, when John wished to worship the angels in the Apocalypse, the angel restrained him so that he would not worship him, saying: “See that you do not do it; for I am your fellow servant and one of your brothers” (Revelation XIX).

At first the angels despised human nature as inferior; but after they saw it assumed above them, they feared to see it prostrate before them. They did not disdain the human being as a companion, since they worship the human God above them.

Peace is announced to human beings, but not to all human beings—only to people of good will. It is as though he were saying: Those will be reconciled to God who have the good will to be reconciled. The one who has the will to be reconciled is the one who submits himself to the Creator and does nothing contrary to his will.

It should be noted why he said “of good will” and not “of good action”: good will is sufficient, even when the ability to act is lacking. Thus good will has value without action, whereas good action never exists without good will. He preferred, therefore, to say “of good will,” which is common to all who are saved.

We have shown you, dearest brothers, how the kindness and humanity appeared, and so forth. But the order of that glorious birth must not be passed over in silence. His coming had been foretold long before by many prophets and prefigured in many figures [Col. 0793A].

Isaiah says: “A branch shall go forth from the root of Jesse, and a flower shall rise from his root” (Isaiah XI).

This was first shown in the time of Aaron as a figure. For the Lord commanded Moses to bring rods from each of the tribes. Twelve rods were brought, among them one that belonged to Aaron the priest. Moses therefore placed them in the tabernacle of testimony. The next day Aaron’s rod was found to have produced flowers and leaves and to have borne nuts (Numbers XVII).

Behold how the prophet and the figure correspond. Jesse was the father of David; the root of Jesse is the family of the Jews; the branch is Mary; the flower is her son, upon whom the Holy Spirit descended in the form of a dove.

Likewise Aaron’s rod, which produced nuts without seed, signifies Mary, who without seed gave birth to Christ. In the nut, which signifies the Lord’s body, there are three parts: the husk, the shell, and the kernel. The bitter husk signifies the flesh, which endured the bitterness of the Passion. The shell signifies the bones; the inner kernel, the soul, white with virtues [Col. 0793B].

Since the Lord’s birth had been announced and demonstrated through these and similar signs, the Lord willed to fulfill the promises. Gabriel was therefore sent to the Virgin Mary in Nazareth and announced the Lord’s descent into her womb. It was fitting that Gabriel, who is called the strength of God, should announce the birth of God, who was to fight with strong hand against the prince of the world.

It was also very fitting that Christ, who had been prefigured by the flower mentioned above, should be conceived in Nazareth, whose name is interpreted as “flower” and “shoot.” He had an outstanding forerunner [Col. 0793C], the eminent commander John the Baptist, who recognized God from his mother’s womb.
