He had been announced by that same angel Gabriel and, contrary to the course of nature, was born of a barren woman—Elizabeth, Mary’s relative.

In the sixth [Col. 0794A] month from John’s conception, Christ was conceived. After he had been conceived, Mary went with haste into the hill country, entered the house of Zechariah, and greeted Elizabeth. When Elizabeth heard the greeting, the infant leaped in her womb (Luke I).

John began to be a prophet before he was born. The servant recognized the Lord; the conceived child prophesied of the conceived child; and through the grace of the child the mother was filled with the spirit of prophecy and said: “How has this happened to me, that the mother of my Lord should come to me?” Mary remained there for three months and then returned to her own house (ibid.).

After this, Joseph went to Bethlehem with his pregnant wife. When the days had been fulfilled for her to give birth, she withdrew into a stable, gave birth without pain, and wrapped him in swaddling clothes. Through divine power, Christ was born of the Virgin Mary (Luke II) [Col. 0794B] without the door of the Virgin being opened, because she was a virgin before childbirth, a virgin in childbirth, and a virgin after childbirth.

Concerning this virginal door the Lord said to Ezekiel: “This gate that you see shall remain closed and shall not be opened, and no man shall pass through it, because the Lord God of Israel has entered through it, and it shall remain closed forever” (Ezekiel XLIV).

Great merit, great gift, great grace: a handmaid gave birth to God; a creature to the Creator; a daughter to her parent; a daughter of divinity, the mother of humanity.

We understand two births of the Lord: one divine, the other human—the former without a mother, the latter without a father.

Today, dearest brothers, we celebrate the temporal birth undertaken for our sake; let us rejoice on account of our restoration. Today the sick world received health; today the captive received freedom; today the exile recovered his inheritance. Let us receive today the coming King; let us prepare the dwelling places of our hearts for such an emperor, so that he may deign to receive us into the heavenly Jerusalem [Col. 0794C].

## The Sunday after the Nativity of the Lord

[Col. 0793]

[Col. 0793C] “The father of Jesus and his mother were going along, marveling at what was said about him, and Simeon blessed them” (Luke II).

(BEDA.) Joseph, because he was the foster-father and watched over Mary’s reputation according to popular opinion, is called the Savior’s father.

[Col. 0793D] “And he said to Mary his mother: Behold, this one is appointed for the fall and rising of many in Israel, and as a sign that will be opposed.”

The Lord was appointed for the fall of many because he is the stone of stumbling and the rock of offense—that is, the ruin of those who take offense at the word and do not believe. Concerning them he himself says: “If I had not come and spoken to them, they would not have sin” (John XV).

He was appointed for the rising of many because those who believe in him have risen from sins through him. He was also appointed in his preachers for fall and rising, as the Apostle says: “We are the good fragrance of Christ to God among those who are being saved and among those who are perishing” (II Corinthians II).

Understand “a sign that will be opposed” as the faith of the Lord’s cross, concerning which the Jews said to Paul: “It is known to us concerning this sect that it is opposed everywhere.”

“And your own soul a sword shall pierce”—that is, the sorrow of the Lord’s Passion, because she could not see her Son crucified without the feeling of a mother’s grief, even though she hoped that he would rise again [Col. 0794D].

Until the end of the world, the sword of tribulation pierces the soul of the Church, when the sign of faith is opposed by the wicked and when she sees many fall.

Alternatively:

(ORIGEN.) The Lord was appointed for the fall of vices and the rising of virtues; nor does resurrection occur unless a fall precedes it. Everything that is related about Christ—that he was born of a virgin, that he rose again, that he entered through closed doors—everything, I say, is a sign that is opposed by unbelievers.

(AMBROSE.) “Your own soul a sword shall pierce”—the sword that is the word of God, revealing mysteries to you—“so that the thoughts of many hearts may be revealed.”

(BEDA.) Previously it was uncertain which Jews would receive Christ and which would reject him. But when his birth was heard of, their thoughts were revealed, as Herod and his followers were troubled [Col. 0795A]. Later, when his teaching and power had become widely known, some regarded him as a teacher of truth, while others withdrew from him as from a deceiver.

“And there was Anna, a prophetess, the daughter of Phanuel, of the tribe of Asher. She was advanced in many days and had lived with her husband for seven years from her virginity. She was a widow until eighty-four years of age; she did not depart from the temple, serving God with fastings and prayers night and day.”

According to the historical meaning, Anna is described as worthy both on account of her devout conduct and her venerable age; she bore witness to the Lord.

Mystically, however, she signifies the Church, which in the present is widowed, as it were, by the death of her bridegroom, the Lord. Seven times twelve makes eighty-four. The seven pertain to the course of the world, which revolves through seven days [Col. 0795B]; the twelve pertain to the perfection of apostolic teaching.

Therefore whoever dedicates the whole time of his life to apostolic observances is praised as though he were guarding the thresholds of the heavenly temple for eighty-four years and asking for the Lord’s coming while he remains a pilgrim away from the Lord.

The seven years during which Anna lived with her husband signify the perfection of the time in which the Church was taught while the Lord dwelt in the flesh. Those years are then multiplied by twelve on account of apostolic teaching, and afterward on account of the Church’s governance.

“And arriving at that very hour, she was confessing to the Lord and speaking about him to all who were awaiting the redemption of Israel.”

At the very hour when Simeon received the child, Anna arrived and was confessing—that is, praising—the Lord. To all the faithful who were burdened by the yoke of Herod, a foreigner, and were awaiting liberation, she promised that redemption would soon be accomplished through Christ’s coming.

Not only angels, but every age and sex bore witness to the child who was born. Just as he was anticipated by the faithful of every age, so, when he came, he was proclaimed with the praise of all the saints.

(BEDA.) The fact that Simeon and Anna, both advanced in years, receive and praise Jesus signifies the faithful Synagogue, which after a long expectation of the promises received with unfailing faith the one who had been foretold.

“And when they had fulfilled everything according to the law of the Lord, they returned to Galilee, to their own city Nazareth.”

At this point Luke passed over what he knew Matthew had sufficiently explained: namely, that afterward, so that he would not be found and killed by Herod, the Lord was taken by his parents to Egypt. After Herod’s death, he finally returned to Galilee and began to inhabit his own city, Nazareth.

For evangelists commonly omit certain matters in this way—matters which they have seen related by others or foreseen in the Spirit as to be related by others—so that, through the continuous sequence of their own narrative, they seem to have omitted nothing. Nevertheless, when the attentive reader considers the Scripture of another evangelist, he can discover the place where these matters have been related [Col. 0795D].

“But the child grew and was strengthened, full of wisdom, and the grace of God was in him.”

Understand “growing in body and being strengthened” as referring to human age. Wisdom is the very divinity with which he was full; grace is the union of divinity in one person.

Grace was also given abundantly to that same mediator of God and human beings, the man Jesus Christ, so that from the moment he began to become man he would be perfect both man and God. Human nature does not receive this, that it should be filled with wisdom before the age of twelve. Just as everything about him was wondrous, so his childhood was wondrous, so that he might be filled with the wisdom of God [Col. 0796A].

## Sermon on the Three Silences

“While all things held the middle silence, and so forth” (Wisdom XVIII).

There are three silences. The first is ignorance of one’s sickness; the second, despair of a healer; the third silence is the acceptance of healing.

The first silence occurred when man did not recognize his illness and therefore remained silent, and no remedy was sought. But after the law entered and showed the sick their wounds, the silence was immediately broken, and the sick began at once to seek health.

But because they wished to be healed through the works of the law, where there is no salvation, they could not find what they sought. At last, then, when man considered that no one could be justified through the law, as though exhausted after prolonged cries, he entered the second silence.

He spoke peace and gave [it]; despairing, he ceased again to speak, and grace followed: it offered mercy and promised pardon, and the sick began to run to the physician and, as though with great cries, to demand a remedy through pure faith of heart and true confession of mouth [Col. 0796C].

This is therefore what is now being accomplished in this present life: when man has received health through God’s grace and has been led to the happiness of the immortality that is to come, there will be nothing more for him to ask. Then the third silence follows, which will never end.

Between the first and middle silence many words sounded; between the middle and final silence one word sounds. There were many and various commandments of the law given through Moses. There is one word, one grace of God, which came through Jesus Christ—or rather, which is Jesus Christ.

Moses, the servant of God, uttered many words and many discourses; God the Father sent one Word, one utterance. But Moses’ discourses were not almighty, because they could not accomplish what they commanded. Therefore, finally, when they failed in the promise, they became silent [Col. 0796D].

Then the almighty Word came. He not only spoke, but whatever he said—or rather, whatever he willed—he accomplished. This Word, this utterance, still speaks as long as he works out his promises in his faithful ones. But when he has fulfilled the promises, then he will, as it were, have ceased.

When the promises have been fulfilled, because nothing will be lacking that could be requested, then there will be a blessed and everlasting silence.

“While, therefore, all things held the middle silence.” He rightly says “all things”: not only those who despaired in petition, but also those things which were [contained] in the promise.

“And the night was pursuing its course.”

In sacred Scripture, night is sometimes understood as the devil; sometimes as his shadows, in sinners and wicked people; sometimes as sins; and sometimes as the present life.

Therefore, by night in this passage the turmoil of this mortal life is signified, just as elsewhere the brightness of everlasting life is signified by day. The present life is therefore death, while the future life is day. Let this night have its evening; let that day have its dawn.

The evening of this night also began from the time Adam sinned, until, after receiving the sentence of death, he was driven from paradise into the darkness of this world. The dawn of the following day came from Christ’s resurrection until the end of the world.

This night is a drop. But what is the course of this life? Mortal life is below, in the lower regions, just as immortal life is above. Again, the journey upward is in the heavens.

The middle is the course of the present life: we enter it by being born, traverse it by living, and leave it by dying. Since, therefore, the night was halfway through its course, when death dragged with it to the lower regions all whom it found in the course of the present life, no mortal could ascend to immortal life [Col. 0797B].

Hence we may understand sin by “night.” This night began with original sin and ran on through actual sins. When, after the original transgression, the transgression of the natural law of the first transgression had been followed by the transgression of the written law, and sin had reached its greatest increase, it was as though night were halfway through its course.

But when the true light appeared, this night immediately began to incline downward. It does not, by some alternating change, gradually diminish and prolong its course until the increasing light reaches full day.

Observe, therefore, the supremely ordered plan of the divine dispensation. When every hope of recovering salvation had perished and death was dragging everything downward with it, then the almighty Word was sent to liberate, so that the gift of divine grace might be commended all the more.

“He came,” he says. Who? The Word of the Most High, the Word of God, the Father’s only Son, the King, the Son of the King.

From where, or to where? From the consent of the Father, to celebrate the mystery of the Passion; from equality of majesty to the gallows of the cross; from the royal throne to the workshop of sin; from the light of heaven all the way to the darkness of hell.

But did he therefore lose the kingdom? Certainly not. He liberated those who had been servants of sin and raised them even to reign with him. Perhaps that is why he came from royal thrones: because “in my Father’s house are many dwelling places” (John XIV), and they will reign with him forever when they receive the kingdom prepared from the foundation of the world [Col. 0797D].

## Concerning the Word’s Assumption of Flesh with Punishment without Guilt, and Mortality without Iniquity

The Son of God, although he was the Father’s only-begotten Son, wishing to join brothers to himself, descended to the human race and assumed a man in order to make brothers for himself, not disdaining to receive into the place of brotherhood anyone whom he knew would be obedient to his commands.

Many ask about that flesh which he assumed: how it was cleansed from sin, and how he bore the punishment of sin without sin. We must not conceal the opinion of some concerning how it was cleansed from sin, lest, if it is not explained, what it is should not be understood, and, if it is not understood, what is not the case should be believed.

Some think that the flesh assumed by the Word was guarded from the beginning, and in the first parent—when the whole mass of human nature had been corrupted by sin—kept free from the contagion and corruption of sin. They hold that from that first parent until its assumption by the Word it was brought forward free and clean from every sin, so that it had never been under sin and therefore was not liberated from sin but was free.

They say that this part of human nature ought not to have been under sin, through which human nature itself, wherever it had been subject to sin, was to be liberated from sin.

To prove the same opinion, they also bring forward what the Apostle shows when he asserts that the new priesthood should be preferred to the old. Melchizedek, who bore the type of Christ and the new priesthood, received tithes from Abraham. In that tithe, he also proves that Levi, from whom it is beyond doubt that the ministers of the old priesthood descended, was tithed. Accordingly, the old priesthood, which in Levi gave tithes, must be regarded as inferior, while the new priesthood, which in Melchizedek—the figure of Christ—received tithes, must be regarded as superior and more worthy (Hebrews VII) [Col. 0798B].

Yet we do not say that Christ, who was then according to the flesh likewise in Abraham’s loins as Levi was, was tithed, lest by the same reasoning the new priesthood that is in Christ be proved to have given tithes there.

How, then, they ask, was Levi, who was then according to the flesh in his father’s loins, tithed, while Christ, who was according to the flesh there, was not tithed? They think that no other reason can be found except that Levi’s flesh was there with guilt, whereas Christ’s flesh was not. Therefore what was subject to sin required expiation, while what was clean and free from sin did not require it.

By this reasoning they think they can prove that the flesh assumed by the Word was never subject to sin, but from the beginning—whether in the one from whom it descended or in those through whom it descended—was kept clean from sin, so that it could at some time become a sacrifice for sin.

But the definition of Catholic truth asserts that the Son of God, who was born for sinners and from sinners, assumed from flesh subject to sin a flesh free from sin—and free because it had been liberated.

It was free not because it had never been under sin, but because at some point it ceased to be under sin. When it was assumed, it was cleansed. Through the same grace, human nature was cleansed so that it might be united to the Word of God, free from sin.

Through him the Christian is liberated from sin, so that the Christian may be joined to that same nature in Christ, the head.

Therefore, as blessed Augustine says, let grace appear to us in our head, from whom, according to the measure of each person, it has spread through all his members. Through that grace every Christian becomes a human being from the beginning of his faith, through which grace that man became Christ from his beginning.

He was born from the same Spirit from whom this one is reborn. Through the same Spirit forgiveness of sins is accomplished in us through whom it was accomplished that he had no sin.

Thus it happened through grace [Col. 0799A] that that flesh was cleansed from the sin under which it had been from its origin. Once cleansed, it was assumed free from sin in him who was free from every sin and was to exist in that flesh. In this way neither grace prejudiced the corruption of nature, nor did the corruption of nature impede grace.

“How, then,” they ask, “was Christ not tithed in Abraham’s loins if his flesh was subject to sin?”

It must be understood that although Christ’s flesh, like Levi’s flesh, was still under sin in Abraham’s loins, the sin under which his flesh was did not belong to him. Only that which was to be his in the future was his there.

Therefore Levi had both nature and guilt there, because through the propagation of origin he was going to draw from there both nature and guilt [Col. 0800A].

Since Christ had his nature in Abraham’s loins, but was going to receive only that nature, he plainly did not require an offering, because an offering was not necessary for that which alone was his there. An offering is offered not for nature but for guilt; for if it were not for guilt, nature would not need an offering.

Thus Levi was tithed in Abraham’s loins because he had both nature and guilt there, and was going to receive both nature and guilt from there. Christ, however, was not tithed, because he was going to receive from there nature alone. He did not then have the guilt that was there, although the nature that was to be his had, in its origin, been subject to guilt.

## On the Octave of the Lord

[Col. 0799]

[Col. 0799B] “When the eight days had been completed for the child’s circumcision, his name was called Jesus—the name given by the angel before he was conceived in the womb” (Luke II).

The rite of circumcision took its beginning from Abraham, at the time when he also received an enlargement of his name. In imitation of this, names were given to boys on the day of their circumcision. The same was done in the case of Jesus.

He is rightly circumcised on the eighth day, so that his resurrection, which was to be celebrated on the eighth day, might also be prefigured, as well as the future eighth age of our own. There are six ages in which labor is undertaken for the Lord; the seventh is the age of souls until the time of the resurrection; the eighth is the resurrection, when the glory of perfect circumcision will shine forth and the whole human being will cling to the vision of the Creator (BEDA).

Now whoever looks upon a woman in order to desire her has an uncircumcised sight. Those are uncircumcised in their ears to whom Truth said: “Whoever is from God hears the words of God. This is why you do not hear, because you are not from God” (John VIII).

They are uncircumcised in tongue and hands: “Their mouth has spoken vanity, and their right hand is a right hand of iniquity” (Psalm CXLIII).

They are uncircumcised in taste, whom the prophet rebukes, saying: “Woe to you who are mighty for drinking wine and strong men for mixing drunkenness” (Isaiah V).

They are uncircumcised in smell and touch who, anointed with various fragrances, pursue the embraces of a prostitute who sprinkles her bed with cinnamon.

They are uncircumcised in their feet, concerning whom the Psalmist says: “Destruction and misery are in their ways, and they have not known the way of peace” (Psalm XIII) [Col. 0799D].

But he who came in the likeness of sinful flesh did not reject the remedy by which sinful flesh was cleansed. Rather, he was circumcised and made subject to the law, in order to prove it just and redeem those who were under the law.

Note that in the law circumcision provided the same assistance against the wound of original sin that baptism now provides in the time of grace—not that entry into the kingdom was not yet open to those circumcised, as it is now to the baptized. In fact, baptism alone does not accomplish this; the addition of the Passion does so as well. If it had been added to circumcision, the same thing would have happened there.

[Col. 0800B] It is asked, however, why baptism succeeded circumcision. As blessed Gregory says in the fourth book of his *Commentary on Job*: What the water of baptism accomplishes among us was accomplished among the ancients either by faith alone in the case of infants, by the power of sacrifices in the case of adults, or by the mystery of circumcision in the case of those who came forth from Abraham’s stock.

Solution. It was fitting for the new King to establish a new law and dissolve the enmity between Jews and Gentiles, so that the two peoples might be joined into one and become one people.

Therefore it was necessary to abolish the causes of enmity—namely, the Jewish rites from which the Gentiles recoiled—and to substitute other sacraments that would be shared by both.

For this reason, too, baptism took the place of circumcision, because circumcision was an imperfect sacrament, since it pertained only to males. Baptism, however, is a perfect sacrament, because it is granted without pain to either sex.

Baptism is consecrated uniformly in water because water flowed from Christ’s side, because no liquid is so effective for washing as water, and because it is easily obtained by everyone, so that no one could excuse himself on account of poverty [Col. 0800C].

Note that it is understood in several ways: of baptisms, one is by water alone, such as John’s, which did not grant remission of sins. Another is in fire or the Spirit, with which the apostles were baptized on the day of Pentecost. Hence the saying: “But you will be baptized with the Holy Spirit” (Matt. III). A third is in water and the Spirit, with which the apostles baptized (Acts I). A fourth is in the shedding of blood.

Three visible things are present in baptism—namely, the priest, the person to be baptized, and water—and three invisible things—namely, faith, the soul, and the Holy Spirit. Yet the Lord, as Ambrose says in the first book of *On the Sacraments*, descended into baptism before the Holy Spirit, whereas now the order is reversed, because the Lord did not need to be cleansed by it. For us, however, the power and presence of the Trinity manifested in Christ’s baptism work invisibly in baptism’s visible sacrament.

A sacrament is a visible sign of invisible grace. Thus, when someone is baptized, the outward washing of the body that we see is a sign of the inward washing of the soul, which consists in the remission of sins. Water, too, cleansing outwardly from bodily stains, is a sign of faith cleansing inwardly from sins. The priest washing in water likewise signifies the Spirit remitting sins through faith.

Nevertheless, concerning this sacrament, as with the others, it must be understood that it makes no difference from which minister it is given. The minister ministers; Christ baptizes. Hence the saying: “This is he who baptizes” (Matt. III). Therefore, whether it is administered by clerics or laypeople, or even by women when urgent necessity requires it, it is not repeated. This sacrament, like the sacrament of the altar, is received by some for life and by others for death. Those who approach rightly receive both the reality and the sacrament; those who do so deceitfully receive only the sacrament. [Col. 0801B] Therefore, if they afterward repent, they are not rebaptized.

The form of baptism consists in these words: “In the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit,” or their equivalent. For the Lord, giving a general instruction concerning baptism, commanded: “Go, teach all nations, baptizing them in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit” (Matt. XXVIII).

Baptism derives its power and efficacy from Christ’s death and the shedding of his blood, like the other sacraments, whether before the Law or under the Law. Through it Christ forgives what has been done, helps so that it may not be done again, brings it about that it cannot be done at all, causes the Law to be fulfilled, sets nature free, and prevents sin from exercising dominion.

Let this suffice concerning circumcision and baptism. As for why circumcision was performed on the male member: it was so that no other member might become either weak or shameful when publicly seen, and so that Christ might be signified as coming through chastity. Circumcision was performed in the flesh of the foreskin because concupiscence, through which original sin is propagated, exercises greater dominion in that part. Therefore, where the way of sin is, there the remedy for sin was appropriately signified; and through circumcision of the flesh, circumcision of the mind was signified, by which the soul was cleansed from vices.

There are therefore three circumcisions: one is the sacrament, while two are the reality of that sacrament—namely, circumcision from sin, which occurs daily in the soul, and circumcision from sin and from every punishment of sin, which will occur in the resurrection in soul and body.

Joshua circumcised those who were to enter the promised land with stone knives, because the rock was Christ (I Cor. X), who takes away the sins of the world (John I). [Col. 0801D]

## SERMON ON THE OCTAVE OF THE LORD

Today we celebrate the eighth day of the Lord’s Nativity, on which the child Jesus received from his parents the sacrament of bodily circumcision in the flesh (Luke II). For, as he himself says, he had not come to abolish the Law but to fulfill it (Matt. III). He fulfilled the Law because, from the dregs of its carnal observances, he left behind a spiritual understanding, and because he retained for a time certain hidden mortal precepts that had been relaxed for the Jews on account of their weakness. Moreover, in the Gospel he added to their precepts, and he himself observed the carnal observances until the time of correction. This is why the child was circumcised by his parents on the eighth day. On the fortieth day he was presented by them in the temple with the legally prescribed offerings. As a young man, too, he frequently went to Jerusalem for the feast of the Dedication and the other feasts, as we read in the Gospel, and in no respect rejected the legal sacraments, until, on the holy day of the Supper, after the old Passover had been sacrificed, he renewed and changed the old priesthood, when he presented himself to his disciples as a fellow guest at the banquet.

Therefore, once the priesthood had been transferred, as the Apostle says, it was necessary that the Law also be transferred. This was the time of correction, when the carnal shadows under which Christ had been born and brought up until childhood were to be removed. Hence the Apostle says: “When the fullness of time had come, God sent his Son, born of a woman, made under the Law, etc.” (Gal. IV). For if someone else, a stranger to the Law, had expounded its sacraments to those who knew the Law, who would have listened to him? Thus, in the proper order of teaching, he who first wished to be a hearer before being a teacher first wished to observe it before revealing its sacraments, so that through his life and teaching he might be recognized as the one to whom the Law and the prophets bore witness.

Since we have given certain reasons why the Lord was born under the Law, let us now, as the Lord grants, discuss the sacrament of circumcision that we have at hand. The eighth-day circumcision corresponded to a single sacrament. In Scripture, the eighth is customarily understood as eternity. Just as the cycle of the number seven signifies the revolving movement of temporal things, so the eighth, which follows the seven, appropriately signifies eternity. Octaves are celebrated because they coincide with the first days, just as the first Sunday coincides with another day celebrated according to the same rite. And because subsequent good works return to their beginnings, in a certain sense we observe octaves.

Such misery existed among human beings before Christ’s coming that no one attained the same innocence possessed by the first man before he sinned. Circumcision, which is celebrated on the eighth day, was performed in remembrance of that first innocence: that is, so that the mind might be circumcised from every carnal contamination, as commanded by the very shadow of future realities. Through baptism Christ restored that same innocence to the human race. Therefore, on the eighth day—that is, on Sunday—the resurrection from baptism is celebrated. This is the difference between those who imitate the first innocence of the first human being and those who were in the Old Testament. Although those people were righteous, they were nevertheless detained within the confines of hell before Christ’s coming; these enter the kingdoms of heaven.

And because our Redeemer wishes to bring us to a better state than the one possessed by the first Adam, an eighth day is still awaited, which will be in the resurrection of bodies. The first Adam was so innocent that he could sin if he wished; and we receive innocence through baptism in such a way that we can sin and can also choose not to wish it. But after receiving their bodies, no one will be able, and no one will wish, to sin.

Since octaves were instituted for the purpose of returning to the beginning, we must consider what returns to the first day of the Nativity in the Lord’s octave. On the first day of the Nativity he came forth from the Virgin’s womb and was found in a manger, wrapped in swaddling clothes. Did he perhaps come forth again from the Virgin’s womb on the eighth day, and was he found wrapped in swaddling clothes in a manger, with the events read as having been performed on the first day at the angels’ announcement repeated? Nevertheless, we can discover in what way the eighth day corresponds to the first.

We understand two things in Christ’s Nativity: first, that Christ came to human beings; second, that human beings came to Christ. Concerning this Augustine says in the first book of *On Christian Doctrine*:

“We are not moved toward him, who is present everywhere, by movement through places, but by good purpose and good conduct. We could not do this unless Wisdom itself deigned to accommodate itself even to such great weakness, so that it might provide us with an example of how to live. Yet it did so only in a human being, for we too are human beings. But because we act wisely when we come to it, when it came to us it was thought by proud human beings to have acted foolishly. And because we grow strong when we come to it, when it came to us it was regarded as weak. Since it itself is the homeland, it also made itself the way to the homeland. And although it is everywhere present to the sound and pure inward eye, it deigned to appear to the eyes of those who had a weak and unclean eye. For because the world could not know God through the wisdom of God, it pleased God through the foolishness of preaching to save those who believe (I Cor. I).”

He is therefore said to have come to us not by traversing the distances between places, but by appearing to mortals in mortal flesh. He came there where he was, because he was in this world, and the world was made through him (John I). [Col. 0803C]

### Division

We celebrate Christ’s coming to human beings on the day of the Nativity. We celebrate the coming of human beings to Christ in his octave. For just as, over the span of seven days, we represented Christ’s temporal birth, by which he came among human beings to endure the evils of this exile and to bestow his blessings upon the sick world, so in the present octave we celebrate figuratively that birth of Christ which, together with the humanity he assumed, passed from this world to the Father, because his flesh too was transformed from corruption to incorruption and from mortality to immortality. In his flesh the victory of death has already been swallowed up; and just as we already believe with firm faith that this has been accomplished in him, so we do not doubt, with firm hope, that it will be accomplished in our flesh.

Thus the Apostle says: “If we have been planted together in the likeness of his death, we shall also share in his resurrection” (Rom. VI). But what that likeness of death is, let us hear from him himself: “For we have been planted together with him through baptism into death, so that, just as Christ rose from the dead through the glory of the Father, so we too may walk in newness of life” (ibid.).

This likeness of death is the perfect cleansing from sin; the newness of life is the observance of righteousness. This is the first resurrection of the soul, concerning which John says: “Blessed are those who have a share in the first resurrection” (Rev. XX). Over these the second death—that is, the eternal death—has no power.

This is also the true circumcision, by which we do not strip the skin of the flesh with stone knives, but, conformed to Christ, we put off the old human being—that is, the likeness of the old human being—together with his deeds. Concerning this the Apostle says elsewhere: “For it is not circumcision that is outward, that is, in the flesh, but circumcision of the heart, which is not performed by the letter but by the Spirit” (Eph. II).

That outward circumcision, therefore, is a figure of this inward circumcision. Thus, concerning Abraham, already justified through faith, the Apostle himself says that he received the sign of circumcision as a seal of righteousness (Rom. IV). The circumcision of our octave is also appropriately fitting: circumcision of the flesh takes place in that part of the body through which human mortality is propagated. For true circumcision will be completed in our octave—that is, in the general resurrection—when this corruptible body will put on incorruption and this mortal body immortality.

As circumcision was seen to be fulfilled carnally in that part of the flesh so that its spiritual fulfillment might be signified, so it is not to be performed bodily, in order that, according to the Apostle, “we may not present our members to sin as weapons of iniquity, but as weapons of righteousness to God” (Rom. VI).

Let us therefore circumcise our ears from unlawful hearing, our eyes from unlawful sight, our nostrils from unlawful smell, our mouth from unlawful taste, our heart from unlawful thought, our tongue from unlawful speech, our hands from unlawful touch, and our feet from unlawful movement, lest, according to the prophet, death enter our souls through the windows (Jer. IX). Hence the first martyr says to the Jews who did not guard the senses of their bodies from unlawful things: “Uncircumcised in heart and ears, you always resist the Holy Spirit” (Acts V).

Whenever, therefore, we celebrate this feast with its annual solemnities, let us honor it according to the faith of the events read concerning it. Referring it to the building up of our conduct, let us hold firm faith, sincere charity, and certain hope until, when what is partial has been abolished, we may deserve to attain the perfection promised to us. With these things remaining unshaken, once the house of this habitation has been dissolved, may we have prepared for us an eternal, not handmade dwelling in heaven, through the favor of our Lord. [Col. 0804D]

## ON THE EPIPHANY OF THE LORD

[Col. 0803]

[Col. 0803D] “When Jesus had been born in Bethlehem of Judea, in the days of King Herod, behold, Magi came from the East to Jerusalem, saying: ‘Where is he who has been born king of the Jews?’” (Matt. II.) (Bede.)

The time of Herod also bears witness to the Lord’s coming. For it had been foretold: “The ruler shall not fail from Judah, nor the leader from his thighs, until he comes who is to be sent” (Gen. XLIX). From the time when the fathers came out of Egypt, they were governed by leaders of their own nation until Samuel the prophet, then by kings until the Babylonian captivity. After the return from Babylon, supreme authority was exercised by the high priests until King and high priest Hyrcanus. At that time, through the treachery of Herod—whose father Hyrcanus himself had raised from an ignoble immigrant, that is, from the Idumaean people—the kingdom of Judea was handed over to Herod to govern by the command of Caesar Augustus.

But since Herod has been mentioned here, I shall briefly relate how he reached the summit of the Jewish kingdom. When those descended from the line of Mattathias had held leadership of the kingdom of the Jews for a number of years, power eventually came to a man born from their stock, named Alexander. When he died after some time, he left a wife with two young children, one called Aristobulus and the other Hyrcanus. When they reached adulthood, they began quarreling with one another out of a desire to reign.

At that time there was a certain man named Antipater, strong in bodily power and exceedingly wealthy, born of a certain Herod who was a temple official of Apollo. Hyrcanus summoned him to friendship and alliance against his brother. When Antipater helped him not only with arms but also with his resources, he also taught him to seek the assistance of the Roman commanders, since at that time the Romans surpassed other peoples in fidelity, wisdom, and courage in arranging the affairs of kingdoms.

Since it would be too long to relate everything individually, when Aristobulus was captured by the Romans and led away under guard, leadership of the Jewish kingdom came to Hyrcanus. Remembering the benefit conferred on him by Antipater, he honored him as a friend and ally, to such an extent that he entrusted to him the administration of a part of the Jewish kingdom.

That same Antipater had a wife named Lypide, born of Arab stock, by whom he had two sons, one of whom he named Phasael and the other Herod. When he died, worn out by old age, he left to his son Herod the power he had received from Hyrcanus over the Jews. Herod, having begun to manage vigorously the matters entrusted to him with cunning and caution, married the granddaughter of Hyrcanus, the daughter of Aristobulus. (Bede.)

After some time Hyrcanus was captured in a battle that he had undertaken against the Arabs and was also held in exile. Then Herod first obtained his authority, as it were in his place. But after some time, when Hyrcanus returned to Judea with his ears cut off, Herod pretended to receive him in peace. Later, however, after killing him by treachery, he fraudulently obtained his power. Receiving authority first from Cassius, the Roman commander, and afterward from the emperor himself, he subjected the kingdom of the Jews to himself.

Thus, through this treachery, Herod, the first foreigner, received the kingdom of the Jews under his control. While he was reigning, our Lord Jesus Christ, as foretold by the prophets, was born in Bethlehem of Judea, in the thirty-first year of Caesar Augustus.

He is said to have been born in Bethlehem of Judea because there is another Bethlehem in Galilee. The Magi came from the East—that is, from the regions lying toward the East. They were from the land of the Persians and Chaldeans, where the river Saba is found. Hence the region is called Saba.

“For we saw his star in the East and came to worship him.” This was said for the confusion of the Jews: “We saw his star,” so that they might learn from the Gentiles about Christ’s birth.

(Ambrose.) The Magi were successors of Balaam, who knew the star through his prophecy. He saw the star in the spirit; they saw it with their eyes and believed. Certainly, they would not have worshiped him if they had believed him to be merely a little child.

(Gregory.) An angel appeared to the shepherds when the Lord was born, but a star appeared to the Magi, because the Jews, as people who used reason, ought to be addressed through a rational creature, whereas signs had to be given to the Gentiles as though they lacked reason. And it was fitting that, once the Lord was speaking, the apostles should preach to the Gentiles, while before he spoke, the elements should preach.

The Magi were called eastern kings, either because they were descended from Balaam, who knew much about incantations, or because they deceived Herod by returning to their homeland by another route. Those who think that they can learn something through stars, birds, or any other signs are also called magi.

“When King Herod heard this, he was troubled, and all Jerusalem with him.” (Gregory.) When the King of heaven was born, the king of earth was troubled, because earthly exaltation is confounded when heavenly majesty is revealed. Jerusalem was troubled because it favored Herod, whom it feared, in accordance with Solomon’s saying: “An unjust king has all his ministers as wicked men” (Prov. XXIX).

“And gathering together all the chief priests and scribes of the people, he inquired of them where Christ was to be born. They said to him: ‘In Bethlehem of Judea. For thus it is written through the prophet: And you, Bethlehem, land of Judah, are by no means least among the rulers of Judah. For from you will come forth a ruler who will govern my people Israel.’”

Bethlehem is indeed a very small village, but you are by no means least among the rulers of Judah—that is, in the excellence of the dignity of Judah’s rulers. For the Savior will be born in it. This testimony belongs to the prophet Micah, but the evangelist, according to his custom, takes the prophet’s meaning and changes the words.

“Then Herod secretly summoned the Magi and carefully learned from them the time when the star had appeared to them. And sending them to Bethlehem, he said: ‘Go and inquire carefully about the child, and when you have found him, report to me, so that I too may come and worship him.’”

(Gregory.) Having learned the place and the time, he does not wish to remain ignorant of the child’s identity. Herod signifies hypocrites who say one thing and think another; while they pretend to seek God, they never deserve to find him.

“When they had heard the king, they departed. And behold, the star that they had seen in the East went before them until it came and stood above the place where the child was.”

When the Magi approached Jerusalem, the star disappeared, because whoever approaches hypocrites and heretics loses the light of God. But after departing from them, he recovers the divine light, so that he may believe that Christ was born of a Virgin.

The star that distinguished the Lord did not follow the courses of the heavenly bodies, but, when it came near the house, stood above it—understand, above the place where the child was. This star, as Fulgentius says, had never appeared before it was appointed to go before the Magi; it was then created, and as soon as its service was completed, it ceased to exist.

“When the Magi saw the star, they rejoiced with exceedingly great joy. And entering the house, they found the child with Mary his mother, and falling down they worshiped him.”

“Entering the house,” that is, the lodging mentioned by Luke, they found the child and his mother. Joseph is mentioned in silence because none of the duties pertaining to a foster father is recalled. Or perhaps he was not present, lest an occasion for evil suspicion arise. Falling down both in mind and body, they humbly worship the Word in the flesh.

“And opening their treasures, they offered him gifts: gold, frankincense, and myrrh.”

In the gold understand the king, in the frankincense God, and in the myrrh a mortal. Gold pertains to tribute, frankincense to sacrifice, and myrrh to the burial of the dead, because myrrh is customarily used to preserve bodies from decay.

(Gregory.) You therefore possess in these gifts no small knowledge of sacred things: in the human being, death; in God, resurrection; in the king, judgment. In the gold also understand wisdom, as Solomon says: “A treasure will be desired; it will rest in the mouth of the wise” (Prov. XXI). In the frankincense, understand the power of prayer: “Let my prayer be directed like incense in your sight” (Ps. CXL). In the myrrh, understand the mortification of our flesh. Hence the saying: “My hands dripped with first myrrh” (Song V).

Mystically, the star’s rising, first understood by the Magi, indicates that the Gentiles would soon believe in Christ. For the star signifies, through prophetic speech, the confession of Christ’s birth. Herod signifies the devil, who, having learned of Christ’s birth, persecutes him in his members. The Magi go to him when the Gentiles withdraw from idolatry and reach the house in which Christ is, that is, the Catholic Church. Entering it through faith, they find Christ with Mary his mother. Christ’s mother is understood as the fellowship of the faithful, in which Christ dwells through faith.

Opening their treasures, that is, their knowledge of letters, they offered him threefold gifts: namely, physics, logic, and ethics; or history, allegory, and tropology; or faith in the Holy Trinity.

The names of the three Magi in Hebrew are Appellius, Amerus, and Damascus. Appellius is interpreted as “faithful,” Amerus as “humble,” and Damascus as “merciful.” In Greek they were called Magalach, Galgalach, and Saracin. Malgalach is interpreted as “messenger,” Galgalach as “devoted,” and Saracin as “grace.”

“And having received an answer in a dream not to return to Herod, they went back to their region by another way.”

Desiring with pious affection to know what the divine will commanded, they received an answer—not through an angel, but by divine instruction from the Lord—not to return to Herod.

(Hilary.) In this we are warned to place all salvation and hope in Christ and to abstain from the path of our former life.

(Gregory.) We return by another way to our homeland through obedience, from which we departed through disobedience.

## On the fact that every creature may be called a theophany, and on the three manifestations

A theophany is a divine manifestation. It is the likeness of God in which God appears and is made manifest. If someone calls every creature a theophany, he will not be wrong.

Theophany of power is the greatness of creatures. Theophany of wisdom is the beauty of creatures. Theophany of goodness is the usefulness of creatures. Every creature possesses some likeness to the Lord.

The first likeness of a creature to God is that it exists; the second, that it is one; the third, that everything which exists consists in this, that it is one. But among those things which exist and are one, some arise from one, as naturally simple things; others arise from many, as composite things. Those which exist, are one, and arise from one are more like God, especially if they do not diffuse into many things the unity which they do not assemble from many.

Such are spiritual natures, which approach more closely to the likeness of God, because they do not arise from many, being naturally simple, nor do many things arise from them, because they cannot be matter. In them the Lord placed two things belonging to nature and two belonging to form: life and sense belong to nature; cognition and love belong to form; cognition belongs to life, and love to sense. These two highest things, nearest to God and an expressed image, are the knowledge of truth and the love of virtue.

Moreover, we must consider the three signs by which Christ wished to appear today. When the Creator, dearly beloved brothers, once came secretly into the world, taking the form of a servant for servants, he wished today to show himself to human beings through three signs. Today he was worshiped by the Magi in Bethlehem (Matt. II). Today he was baptized by John in the Jordan (Luke III). Today, at a wedding, he was glorified by changing water into wine (John II).

The first manifestation occurred in the first year of his birth; the second in his thirtieth year; the third in the year following his thirtieth year. By divine arrangement these three manifestations occurred on the same day in different years. But let us now discuss the first.

The Lord wished to reveal his birth to three Magi living in Chaldea by displaying a new star. When, being skilled in the stars, they saw a new star appear, they understood through their knowledge of the art that a new king had been born (Matt. II). But because a certain prophet, Balaam, had foretold among them many years earlier, “A star shall rise out of Jacob, and a man shall arise from Israel” (Num. XXIV), when they saw the wondrous star, incomparable to any other, they believed that the one of whom Balaam had spoken had been born.

By divine inspiration they came to Jerusalem, which was the capital of Judea. They went to Herod and inquired about the child. When they went to Herod, the star disappeared from them. Herod, summoning the scribes, asked where the Messiah who had been promised in the Law was to be born. They said to him: “In Bethlehem.” [Col. 0809A]

Since Herod was a foreigner and unjustly possessed the kingdom of Judea as a gift from the Romans, he considered how he might kill the child, fearing that he would lose the kingdom. He therefore did not dare go with the Magi to seek the child, lest the child’s parents hide him when they heard of the king’s arrival. He therefore instructed the Magi to search carefully for the child, report back to him, and said that he wished to worship him.

The Magi departed, and the star appeared again. They rejoiced and, with it going before them, came to Bethlehem. The star, however, was not fixed in the heavens but hung in the air. It therefore clearly showed the house where the child was. According to the custom of the Persians, they offered gifts appropriate to the sacrament: gold, frankincense, and myrrh, signifying by gold the king, by frankincense God and priest, and by myrrh the mortal. Behold the first manifestation.

In his thirtieth year he came to John, who baptized not for the remission of sins (Luke III), but in preparation for Christ’s baptism, so that gentle people would not recoil from Christ’s baptism. Since water had previously washed bodies, he wished to sanctify it so that it might have power to cleanse souls. Jesus, therefore, free from sin, asked to be baptized in order to sanctify the water and provide human beings with an example.

When he had been baptized, the heavens were opened, and he saw the Spirit descending upon him in the form of a dove, and the Father’s voice was heard: “This is my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased” (ibid.). Behold the second manifestation.

In the following year he was invited to a wedding. The wine ran out; he ordered six jars to be filled with water and changed the water into wine. This was the beginning of the signs. Through these three signs, dearly beloved brothers, Christ manifested himself to the world, and in all of them God appeared. In the first, he was worshiped by the Magi as God. In the second, the Father’s voice asserted him to be the Son of God. In the third, divine power was declared through the first miracle.

This day is therefore called Theophany, which, as was said above, is interpreted as “divine manifestation.” You have heard the truth of the history and have also learned from us the reason for this feast. Let us now see whether some further mystery lies hidden in the matters mentioned above.

### Division

For this reason, brothers, the shining star appeared: it signified that light had risen for the people in darkness, of which it is said, “It was the true light, etc.” (John I). It appeared to the Gentiles because it foretold that the Gentiles would receive the light of faith, according to Isaiah: “The people who walked in darkness have seen a great light, etc.” (Isa. IX).

He wished to be born in Bethlehem because Bethlehem is interpreted as “house of bread.” He was therefore born there, but he suffered death in Jerusalem, which was populous, because he was not seeking the glory of the world. The teacher of humility deigned to be born of poor parents, in a humble place, in a lowly manger; but when he was to die, he chose a populous city, so that, in the sight of so many people who had gathered for the feast, he might undergo death for us with greater disgrace.

When the Magi turned aside to Herod, they lost the star as their guide, because Herod signifies the devil. Whoever turns aside to him, having lost the true light, is blinded; whoever abandons him immediately receives again the true light that he had lost.

The house where the child was signifies the Church. Whoever seeks Christ finds him in the Church; there they worship and honor him.

Once Christ has been found, we learn what we ought to offer as gifts. Myrrh, namely. Myrrh is appropriate for the dead because its bitterness destroys worms. A person approaching the Church must mortify the flesh together with its vices and desires, lest the worms of sins be born. Once the vices have been destroyed, prayer is necessary, signified by frankincense, which obtains forgiveness. Concerning this it is said: “Let my prayer be directed, etc.” (Ps. CXL).

From there follow works of charity, signified by gold. Just as gold surpasses the other metals, so charity excels among the other virtues. It is the fullness of the Law.

These three things are therefore necessary: repentance, signified by myrrh; prayer, signified by frankincense; and charity, signified by gold.

In the second manifestation the sacraments of our salvation were displayed. For by being baptized he wished to show in himself what would be granted to those who are baptized. When someone is regenerated in baptism, the whole Trinity works there. Therefore the whole Trinity was shown where Christ was baptized. The Son was present in Christ, the Spirit in the dove, and the Father revealed himself in the voice.

The Spirit appeared in the dove (Matt. III) because the dove is a bird of great simplicity. Through this bird he wished to signify the innocence that he confers upon those who are regenerated. What the Father said—“This is the Son,” and so forth—signifies that those who are baptized are sons of God, and that those who previously displeased him begin to please him. The opening of the heavens signified that heaven was opened to those who were baptized, whereas previously it had been closed on account of sin.

The wedding at which he manifested himself for the third time signifies the union of Christ and the Church. At that wedding water is changed into wine (John II), when the old Law is converted into the Gospel. The ancient Law is compared to water because it did not inflame those subject to it with the love of God. The Gospel is wine, which through the inspiration of the Spirit makes the faithful fervent in the love of God.

Consecrated by such great and such numerous sacraments, this day, dearly beloved brothers, is in a certain sense greater than the solemnity of the Nativity. For, as Augustine says, the second birth is greater than the first. In this one baptism began, which is the regeneration of souls. In this water became the mother of many peoples. The first birth is carnal; this one is spiritual. Therefore, just as the soul is more worthy than the flesh, so the birth of the soul is more worthy than the birth of the flesh.

In the first birth he entered the world; in the second he entered heaven. How fittingly these three things came together on one day in such an order: the star leading to Christ, the sacrament of baptism, and the changing of water into wine. In this order the instruction of our life also appears. When someone is converted to the faith, the star—that is, the light of faith—leads him to Christ. Then, after he has been instructed in faith concerning Christ, he approaches the sacrament of baptism. Afterwards he drinks and is refreshed by the cup of evangelical teaching. So that he may not fail from thirst on the journey, the drink of preaching is prepared daily for the pilgrim.

Therefore this solemnity, filled with so many mysteries, is to be celebrated with the greatest devotion. Since today you rejoice in our birth, which today takes its beginning in baptism, rejoice today also in the conversion of the Gentiles, whose first fruits came to Christ on this day—namely, the Magi whom he had drawn to himself with gifts.

Why had he drawn these three Magi? Because he wished to draw to himself the three parts of the world—Asia, Africa, and Europe—through faith and works.

But since the fullness of divinity was bodily present in him, and no grace could accrue to him, why was he baptized? So that he might sanctify the waters for our baptism.

Why was he baptized in water? Because water is opposed to fire. Fire is sin: just as anger is in the soul, so concupiscence is in the flesh. In order that the fire might be extinguished, he was baptized in water, and thus sin is destroyed, so that one may not be punished by the fire of eternal torment.

In another respect, water washes away stains, quenches thirst, and restores an image. Likewise, the grace of the Holy Spirit in baptism washes away the stains of sins, quenches the soul’s thirst with the word of God, and restores the image of God lost through guilt.

Now, therefore, let us receive Christ at our tables, baptized today—the one who today also received the Gentiles coming to him. He is clothed in the poor and fed in the poor; for he was poor in the world, he grants the kingdom to the poor, and he loves the poor. For he himself says: “Whatever you did for one of the least of mine, you did for me” (Matt. XXV). If you receive them in this world, they too will receive you in heaven.

Hence the Lord says: “Make friends for yourselves from the mammon of iniquity, etc.” (Luke XVI). And again: “Blessed are the poor in spirit” (Matt. V).

May our Lord Jesus Christ, who for our sake wished to descend into the world, grant us an increase of virtues, so that we may ascend to heavenly things. Amen.

## ANOTHER SERMON ON THE SAME GOSPEL
“Now when Jesus had been born in Bethlehem of Judah in the days of King Herod, etc. (Matt. 2).” What this Gospel text signifies, dearest brothers, I briefly explain to your affection. The fact that three Magi came to the Lord signifies that the three parts of the world—Asia, [Col. 0811D] Africa, and Europe—were to bow their necks beneath the faith of the Holy Trinity. The fact that they came on the thirteenth day announces that through him the three parts of the world received the Decalogue of the Law. Three times four also makes twelve. Apart from the Lord’s birthday, twelve days are counted, because through the twelve apostles the four regions of the world were converted to faith in the Holy Trinity.

The impious king who is troubled by their arrival is the devil, who lies in wait for the faithful on the way of salvation. The star that leads them to Christ is Sacred Scripture, which shows us the way to life. The house in which Christ is found is the Church or the heavenly homeland, where the Lord will be seen in his glory. The gifts that the Magi offer are good works, which the faithful render to God through faith. Gold is offered to him when he is believed to be the king of all and the price of our redemption. [Col. 0812A] Frankincense is sacrificed to him when he is proclaimed God above all and the sacrifice offered to God the Father for us. Myrrh is sacrificed to him when, through his mortality, the rottenness of our vices is declared to have been destroyed. We too offer these three gifts to God if we believe that he reigns everywhere, governs all things as God, and became mortal for us.

The Magi return to their homeland by another path, because it is surely necessary that we who came through pride into the misery of this exile should likewise return to the homeland of paradise through humility. This star was brighter than the sun; therefore, shining even by day, it could not be obscured by the sun, because by its own radiance it surpassed the sun. It also moved in the heavens, not with the other stars in the air near the earth, because it made known that the Creator of the stars [Col. 0812B] had shone upon the earth.

But why, when they saw the star, did the Magi think that the Lord was to be sought in Judaea? This must be briefly explained to you. In their books they had read a saying concerning Christ, written through their prophet Balaam: “A star shall arise from Jacob, and a powerful man shall rise from Israel” (Num. 24). When God was leading his people out of Egypt through Moses, and they had to travel through the land of Midian toward the promised land, King Balak summoned Balaam, a priest of idols, so that he might curse them and turn them away from his kingdom by his curse. Balaam mounted a she-ass and set out toward the king. But an angel of the Lord stood in his way with a fiery sword; moreover, the she-ass spoke and rebuked the prophet.

At last, when, with the angel’s permission, he had reached the king, and the king had led him to the summit [Col. 0812C] of a mountain, he looked upon the camp of the children of Israel, understood that Christ would be born from them, and foretold the following concerning him: “A star shall arise from Jacob, and a man shall rise from Israel, whose strength is like that of a rhinoceros, and he shall subject the whole earth to himself” (ibid.). After he had received money from the king, he gave counsel against that same people: namely, that girls adorned with gold and jewels should go out to meet the approaching people with wine and an idol, and, when the men sought intercourse with them, should first compel them to sacrifice to the idol; thus, having offended God, they would fall by his hand. And so it happened. For the young men, intoxicated with wine, burned with love for the girls and, overcome by lust, sacrificed to the idol Beelphegor; therefore twelve [XXIV] thousand perished. [Col. 0812D] Afterwards the king, together with all his people and his wicked counselor, was pierced through with the sword, and the entire region was devastated by iron and fire.

These events, dearest brothers, preceded us in figure; but they signified our own times. The people led from Egypt through Moses to the promised land are the Christian people, who through Jesus are led from this world to the homeland of eternal glory. The king who opposed them on the way is the devil, who obstructs our path of life in many ways. The priest who rides upon the she-ass is the order of wicked priests, who are governed by the irrational movement of their desires; he is also rebuked by the she-ass, because even the common people reject the life of such men. The prophet falls silent and the she-ass speaks, because, while the clergy are silent, the word of God is often uttered by the unlearned. Indeed, it is said: “Mute dogs unable to bark” (Isa. 56). Because of the consciousness of their wicked life they fall silent before the word of God, and, lest they be reproved for living perversely, they do not utter the barking of preaching. They are opposed by the angel with the flaming sword, because the judgment of eternal fire is proclaimed to them throughout all Scripture.

Balaam climbs the mountain and prophesies about the future, yet, corrupted by money, attacks the people of God, because such men too sometimes attain the heights of knowledge and preach much to the people about the future life, yet by their reprehensible life contradict what they preach. For it is said through the prophet: “I saw on the mountain something like a city building, and behold, the earth had risen above the windows” (Ezek. 40). The city built on the mountain is the Church established in Christ. The priests are the windows through which the light of divine knowledge ought to shine upon those beneath them. But, alas, earth has grown above the windows and does not allow the light to enter, because desire for earthly things blinds the vision of the priests’ minds; and therefore the light of divine knowledge does not at all radiate through them into the Church. [Col. 0813B]

The star that arose and shone from Jacob is Christ, who shone upon the world from the line of Israel. His strength was like that of a unicorn, which crushes everything that opposes it beneath its horn. Concerning this unicorn, the *Physiologus* says that it has this nature: it is a unicorn, a small animal resembling a kid, exceedingly fierce, and it has one singular horn on its head; no hunter can capture it. But they capture it by this stratagem: they lead a virgin girl to the place where it lives and leave her there alone. As soon as it sees her, it leaps into the virgin’s lap and embraces her until it falls asleep; thus it is seized and brought to the king’s palace. Through this rhinoceros Christ is signified, for he subdued the principalities and powers of the world by the horns of the cross and long ago subjected all kingdoms to his rule.

The adorned girls with whom the people commit fornication and are inclined toward idolatry are the pomp and allurements of the world, by which the people are ensnared and subjected to the devil’s worship. Balaam perishes by the sword because the priestly order, the blind guide of the blind, perishes by divine judgment. Finally, the king and his people are exterminated and the region is burned, because in the end the devil, together with all his members, will be condemned, and this world, which they loved as their homeland, will be consumed by flame. [Col. 0813D]

Today also, beloved, Christ is baptized by John in the Jordan after thirty years; heaven is opened to him; the Holy Spirit is remembered as having descended upon him in the form of a dove; and the paternal voice bears witness to the beloved Son (Matt. 3). The Lord, dearest brothers, [Col. 0814A] washed not his own crimes but ours, and consecrated baptism for us by his entrance into it. Heaven is open to him, and the descending Spirit remains upon him, because those who receive baptism in his name will be filled with the Holy Spirit, and if they imitate the simplicity of the dove, they will be exalted with Christ in heaven.

We are also instructed by animals, so that, putting off our former life, we may put on a new one. For it is said concerning serpents that they received their name because they creep by hidden approaches. The *Physiologus* says that serpents have four characteristics. Their first characteristic is that, when they grow old, their eyes become dim; and if one wishes to become new, it abstains from food and fasts for forty days and nights until its skin loosens upon it. It seeks a narrow cleft in a rock, constricts itself violently there, and, having bruised its body, [Col. 0814B] puts off its old age and becomes new again.

Their second characteristic is that, when a serpent comes to drink water at a spring, it does not bring its poison with it but leaves it in its lair, and thus drinks the water. Their third characteristic is that, if a serpent sees a naked man, it is very afraid to approach him; but if it sees him clothed, it does not flee readily. Their fourth characteristic is that, when a man comes and wishes to kill it, it gives its whole body over to punishment but guards its head alone.

Through this serpent, therefore, every sinner is signified who grows old in many crimes. He ought to come as quickly as possible to the rock, Christ; to take the narrow way that leads to life; to be stripped of the old garment of vices; and to be clothed in the new garment of virtues.

[Col. 0814C] Today also, beloved, the Lord, invited to a wedding after the year of his baptism, gladdened the guests when, as the wine failed, he changed six jars of water into wine (John 2). He gives us to drink of this wine as well, when he grants us to understand these things spiritually.

The pagans of old also regarded this day as celebrated, because of the triple triumph that the Romans presented to Caesar Augustus on this day, since, after conquering three kingdoms—Parthia, Egypt, and Media—he had subjected them to the Roman Empire. Nevertheless, the Church considers it solemn for three reasons and jubilantly praises the King of all: namely, because today, through the three Magi, he subjected the three parts of the world to the scepter of his dominion; because he washed away our sins in the Jordan; and because today he transformed the water of the Law into the wine of grace for the spiritual wedding. [Col. 0814D] Submit yourselves to his rule, dearest brothers, with your whole mind and heart; render him his due service at all times, so that after the poverty of this miserable life you may receive from him the riches and glory that the eye has not seen (1 Cor. 2).

## FIRST SUNDAY AFTER THE EPIPHANY

[Col. 0813]

[Col. 0813D] “When Jesus was twelve years old, and they went up to Jerusalem according to the custom of the feast, and when the days were completed, as they were returning, the boy Jesus remained in Jerusalem, and his parents did not know it” (Luke 2).

When he reached the age of twelve, he began to reveal what he owed to his heavenly Father and what he owed to his earthly mother. The age of twelve was a type of the twelve apostles, through whom his divinity and humanity were to be proclaimed throughout the world. The age of twelve was also a type of the twelve degrees of humility in ascent.

The first degree of humility in ascent is always to display humility in heart and body, with one’s gaze fixed upon the ground. The second is to speak few and reasonable words, not in a loud voice. The third is not to be easy or prompt to laughter. The fourth is silence until questioned. The fifth is to hold to what the common rule prescribes. The sixth is to believe and declare oneself lower than everyone. The seventh is to confess that one must consider oneself unworthy and useless for everything. The eighth is confession of sins. The ninth is, in obedience, to embrace patience amid hard and difficult things. The tenth is to submit oneself to everyone in complete obedience. The eleventh is not to love one’s own will. The twelfth is, through fear of the Lord, to guard oneself at every hour from every sin.

The first two of these degrees are to be ascended outside the cloister of the monastery, so that finally, at the third degree, the one who is ascending may be subjected to the superior. Opposed to these twelve degrees in ascent are twelve others belonging to pride in descent.

The first degree of pride in descending is curiosity, when one’s eyes and other senses wander over things that do not concern one. The second is lightness of mind, which is recognized in words indiscreetly cheerful or sorrowful. The third is foolish merriment, recognized by an excessive readiness to laugh. The fourth is boasting, which spreads itself through much talking. The fifth is private singularity: seeking distinction with glory. The sixth is arrogantly believing oneself holier than everyone. The seventh is presumption, thrusting oneself into everything. The eighth is the defense of sins. The ninth is feigned confession, tested through difficult and harsh assignments. The tenth is rebellion against the master and the brothers. The eleventh is freedom to sin. The twelfth is the habit of sinning.

These last two degrees of pride cannot be descended within the cloister. It should also be noted that in the first seven there is contempt for the brothers; in the next four, contempt for the master; and in the remaining two, contempt for God.

But, to return to Christ’s age of twelve, which was a type of these things, rightly in this number twelve the radiance of his perfection begins to be revealed. He remained in Jerusalem without his parents in order to instruct us that he had God as Father before the world existed.

“They supposed, however, that he was in the company, and they came a day’s journey and sought him among their relatives [Col. 0815D] and acquaintances. And when they did not find him, they returned to Jerusalem, seeking him.”

If anyone asks how his parents left him, though he had been nurtured with such care, we answer that it was the custom among the children of Israel, at feast times, whether they were going to Jerusalem or returning from there, for the men and women to travel separately, and for the children to go with either parent. Therefore Mary and Joseph each supposed in turn that Jesus was with the other parent as they returned.

“And it came to pass that after three days they found him in the temple, sitting in the midst of the teachers, listening to them and asking them questions.”

He sat in the midst of the teachers like a fountain of wisdom; but, as an example of humility, he first asks and listens before teaching, so that the little ones may not be ashamed to be taught by their elders, and so that the weak may not dare to teach (Ambrose). After three days he is found in the temple giving judgment, because after three days he who was believed to have died would rise again in triumph after his Passion.

“But all who heard him were astonished at his understanding and his answers. And when they saw him, they were amazed.”

They were all the more astonished at the wisdom of his answers because they saw how few his years were. His tongue revealed divine wisdom, but his age displayed human weakness.

“And his mother said to him: ‘Son, why have you treated us so? Behold, your father and I have been seeking you in sorrow.’ And he said to them: ‘Why were you seeking me? Did you not know that I must be in the things that are my Father’s?’”

He does not rebuke those who seek him as though he were their son; rather, he compels them to raise the eyes of their minds to seek what he owes to the eternal Father. He shows that both the temple and all that belongs to the Father pertain no less to him than to the Father, whose majesty is one.

“And they did not understand the word that he spoke to them. And he went down with them and came to Nazareth, and he was subject to them.”

His parents do not understand what he says about his divinity; nevertheless, he condescends and subjects himself to them in order to fulfill the duty of filial devotion. How greatly, then, ought we to obey God, since God himself obeys human beings.

“And his mother kept all these words in her heart.”

Everything that she learned had been said or done by the Lord or concerning the Lord, whether understood or not understood, the devout mother stored in her memory, so that in due time she might understand everything as it had happened and explain it to those who asked.

“And Jesus advanced in age and grace with God and human beings.”

Wisdom pertains to the soul, age to the body, and grace to the salvation of both. Thus he advanced in age, as it belongs to the flesh to receive increase; and, in proportion as he advanced in age, he revealed more and more to human beings the gifts of grace and wisdom that were in him. This was advancement in wisdom and grace not in himself but in others: with God and human beings, that is, for the honor of God and the salvation of human beings.

In himself, however, he did not advance at all through intervals of time in wisdom or grace, because from the hour of his conception [Col. 0816D] he was full of grace and truth. Note that the doctors commonly affirm that the soul of Christ was united to the Word of God and received as much wisdom and goodness as it was possible for a creature to receive. For in it, as the Apostle says, are all the treasures of wisdom and knowledge; in it all the fullness of divinity dwells (Col. 2). To others the Spirit is given according to measure (Eph. 4), but to Christ, as the evangelist John says, he was given not according to measure (John 3).

Therefore many assert, as Alcuin does in his book *On the Trinity* addressed to Charles, that Christ’s soul has as much knowledge of all things as the divinity has—yet in such a way that the divinity has it from itself and not from another. He is wise by nature, whereas Christ’s soul is wise through grace from the divinity.

Others, however, do not think that any creature capable of receiving can possess the whole of divine knowledge or the whole of divine goodness, any more than it can possess omnipotence. They regard it as incongruous that a creature should, even in this manner, be made equal to the Creator by having from him as much knowledge as the Creator himself possesses.

### Concerning the fact that the Word assumed a rational soul together with flesh, and what that soul was like in wisdom, power, justice, and goodness

There were certain heretics who believed that, together with flesh, the Word had not assumed a rational soul in Christ, but that only flesh had been united to the Word, and that the very divinity of the Word had given life to the flesh in place of a soul. They also believed that the same divinity had withdrawn from the flesh when it died on the cross, and had returned to it when it was raised, in order to give it life and raise it again.

But the catholic faith holds that God assumed everything that belonged to humanity on account of sin. For otherwise he could not have been true man unless he had assumed everything that pertained to the distinctiveness of human nature. Therefore, together with the flesh and in the flesh, he received the rational soul itself, which would govern the flesh, give it sensation for life, reject sin according to free will, and pursue justice.

Through its association with the divinity, it also received this gift: that it did good by spontaneous freedom, yet could not incline toward doing evil through any necessity or weakness whatsoever. For blessed Augustine says: “The only-begotten Son of God was born of the Holy Spirit and the Virgin Mary, not through desire of the flesh but solely through God’s gift.
