Free will was in him, and it was all the more free because it could not serve sin.”

Many questions are raised concerning that rational soul, one of which is whether it possessed knowledge equal to that of the divinity. I discussed this question more extensively in another work entitled *On the Soul of Christ*. Here it is enough to recall only this: just as that soul possessed the full and perfect wisdom of God united to it, so it was fully and perfectly wise from that wisdom and through it; yet it was not equal in nature to wisdom itself, because it is one thing to possess wisdom and another to be wisdom.

From the moment the divinity was joined to humanity, humanity received by grace from the divinity everything that the divinity possessed by nature, so that, according to that ineffable union, everything that belonged to the divinity was present in his humanity as well. Thus we believe that the humanity of the Word, in its rational soul, received from the first moment of its conception, through the ineffable union with the divinity, full and perfect wisdom, power, virtue, and goodness. And we confess that, just as it remained inseparably in the union with the divinity, so it remained unchangeably in the fullness of virtue that came from that union.

For God did not choose to live among human beings as man so that, as though advancing through intervals of time in wisdom or virtue, he might acquire merit and become better than himself. Rather, by the wisdom and goodness that he had always possessed fully and perfectly in his divinity, and that he once and altogether received fully and perfectly in his humanity, he fulfilled the dispensation of human salvation according to his ineffable ordering.

Therefore, what the evangelist says—that Jesus advanced in age, wisdom, and grace—is not understood as though he became better in himself. Rather, the wisdom and grace that he possessed but that remained hidden he continually revealed more and more to human beings, as the order of time required. Thus he advanced among human beings when human beings themselves advanced in knowledge of him. But he advanced before God in this respect: that, while showing himself full of the wisdom and grace of God, he continually moved them more and more to praise God the Father, from whom he testified that these things came.

## EXPOSITION OF THE SAME GOSPEL

[Col. 0818B]

“When Jesus was twelve years old, etc. (Luke 2).” Just as this world serves human beings in two ways—for the support of the flesh and for the instruction of the mind—so the Word made flesh provides both a remedy and an example. It is a remedy in that he was offered for redemption; it is an example in that what he did was performed for imitation. It is a remedy in what was done; it is an example in what he did, in his imitation and likeness.

“I saw the holy city, the new Jerusalem, descending from heaven” (Rev. 21). It descended from heaven and was fashioned upon earth: from heaven came the form, from earth the material. Just as the form of a human being is a human being, so also the form of Christ is Christ. “Put on the Lord Jesus Christ,” the form of Christ, the image of Christ. The image itself is imitation. Therefore he was made an example for you, so that by imitating him you might put him on. He acted bodily; imitate him spiritually.

“And thus we know Christ according to the flesh, but now we no longer know him” (2 Cor. 5). We knew him according to the flesh in his example, but now we no longer know him according to the flesh in imitation. According to the flesh Christ was born in the world; according to the spirit, truth is born in your heart. Christ is born in Judaea from a Virgin, and truth is born in confession from purity.

“Truth has sprung up from the earth, and justice has looked down from heaven” (Ps. 84). When you confess your sins, truth rises from the earth; when God forgives the one who confesses, justice looks down from heaven. Do you wish God to be with you? Confess what you are. When you begin to be truthful, truth will begin to be with you. Say, “I am evil”—a brief word, but true—and truth will make you truthful. If truth is with you, God is with you, because God is truth.

Behold how truth is born in Judaea, that is, in confession. The virgin mother is purity of heart: you believe in your heart what you confess with your mouth. In the confession of sin there is purity without stain. If you do not pretend to be good, you have no wrinkle; if you hate evil, you have no stain (Eph. 5).

Thus truth is conceived in you through desire, born in action, and nourished by devotion, so that it may advance in age through the progress of time, in wisdom through the increase of knowledge, and in grace through the growth of virtue: [Col. 0819A] among human beings, in reputation; before God, in conscience; among human beings, so that it may be known; before God, so that he may be glorified.

He went up to Jerusalem at twelve years of age because, after the perfection of work and the doubled virtue of charity, he advances toward the peace of contemplation. Jesus’ parents return from Jerusalem after a one-day journey because the senses of the flesh nourish inward truth through the practice of good works, but, drawn back by the pleasure of external things, they cannot remain long in inward peace.

One day, one brightness, one joy, one blessing—the blessing that Esau received, though he could not earn a double garment. This is that one day on which the boy could not be without sin for even one day upon the earth, because the senses of the flesh, which as far as they are concerned always desire childish things, love only the brightness of this life and never remain in it without the stain of sin.

For it does not come to that other day of which it is said: “Announce day to day” (Ps. 95), and again: “You shall add days to the days of the king” (Ps. 60). Therefore the journey of one day is made by those who move away from Jerusalem, because the pleasure of present things puts the mind far from contemplation of eternal things.

After three days Jesus is found in the temple, because after the correction of thought, speech, and action, truth is perceived in a clean heart. He is found among teachers and wise men because truth is recognized in the Law and the Prophets, in the Evangelists and Apostles, and in the teachers of the sacred word.

We also read about a journey of three days, during which the children of Israel went into the desert to sacrifice there to the Lord their God (Exod. 3). There is a certain approach of the soul to God and a withdrawal from God: approach to God, withdrawal from God. For one who departs, the journey is through night; for one who returns, the journey is through day. [Col. 0820A] As many nights as one spends departing, so many days one spends returning.

For one departing, the journey of the first night is through pride, by which he abandons God. The journey of the second night is through desire, by which he seeks other things besides God. The journey of the third night is through stubbornness, by which he rests in other things outside God. In pride there is vanity; in desire, pleasure; in stubbornness, consent. Thus he departs through vanity, stops through pleasure, and sits through consent.

Departing from God through pride, he goes to himself in order to rest in himself. Through desire, he descends beneath himself in order to rest in the flesh. Through stubbornness, he is dragged outside himself in order to rest in the flesh through the appearance of visible things and remain in pleasure. First he goes to glory in his own virtue; second, to delight in his vices; third, to console himself in transitory things.

First: “Cursed is the man who trusts in man” (Jer. 17). Second: “Who makes flesh his arm” (ibid.). Third: “Who trusted in the abundance of his riches and prevailed in his vanity” (Ps. 51).

For one returning, the journey of the first day occurs when the soul turns its intention from what is outside it toward what it is itself. The journey of the second day occurs when it is led from what is in another toward what it ought to be. The journey of the third day occurs when it is snatched from the perception of illumination to the source of light.

The first return is from alien things to what is one’s own; the second is from evil things to good things; the third is from the pursuit of virtues to the perception of inward and eternal sweetness. And thus, after three days—that is, after the correction of thought, speech, and action—Jesus, that is, truth, is perceived in the temple, that is, in a pure heart. Likewise, through the teachers of the sacred word, the truth of these three days of the Hebrews’ departure from Egypt is declared to the faithful.

## SECOND SUNDAY AFTER THE THEOPHANY

[Col. 0819]

[Col. 0819C] “A wedding took place at Cana of Galilee, and the mother of Jesus was there. Jesus and his disciples were also invited to the wedding” (John 2).

The Lord wished to commend marriage to his followers as well as by a miracle, so that heretics would not presume to condemn it. Mystically, in accordance with the desire of the fathers who came before, the bridegroom was called to come to the bride, the Church, before the Law and under the Law; and he came in the grace of the Gospel. The disciples too were invited, as ministers at the wedding.

The bridegroom joined this bride to himself in the Virgin’s womb. For the Word is the bridegroom, and human flesh is the bride. The wedding takes place at Cana of Galilee, in the heaven of migration, because those are worthy of Christ who migrate from vices to virtues, from earth to heaven, through the fervor of devotion.

“And when the wine failed, the mother of Jesus said to him: ‘They have no wine.’” As though she were saying: “Give them wine.” The wine fails because the spiritual understanding of the Law had begun to lie hidden beneath the Pharisees’ deceptive interpretation.

“And Jesus said to her: ‘What is there between you and me, woman? My hour has not yet come.’”

What is there in common between you, my mother according to the flesh, and me, the eternal power and wisdom of God, from which the miracle you ask for is to come? My hour will come—that is, the opportune time of the Passion—when, as weakness begins to hang upon the cross, I, whose mother you are, will acknowledge you as mother in the manner of a son, entrusting care of you to a disciple.

After the Gospel had been preached and divine power had been revealed to the world, the hour of the Passion came. It was not an hour of necessity, as the heretics slanderously claim, but of will. Hence the saying: “I have power to lay down my life and to take it up again” (John 10). The author of time is not ruled by the fate of time.

“His mother said to the servants: ‘Whatever he says to you, do it.’ Now there were six stone jars set there for the purification of the Jews, each holding two or three measures.”

The mother, trusting in her son’s devotion toward her, confidently commands the servants to do what she asks. *Hydor* [ὕδωρ] is Greek for “water.” From it the vessel for water is called a *hydria*. He says “for the purification of the Jews” because they frequently washed their hands and vessels. *Metron* [μέτρον] is Greek and means “measure” in Latin. Hence *metreta*, the name of a measure.

“Jesus said to them: ‘Fill the jars with water.’ And they filled them to the brim. And Jesus said to them: ‘Now draw some out and take it to the master of the feast.’ And they carried it.”

The *architriclinus* is the ruler of the *triclinium*, that is, of those reclining in the dining room. They say that the *triclinium* is a hall made with three chambers, or three houses or three rooms constructed with a vaulted roof, in which the diners reclined as though beneath three arches.

“When the master of the feast tasted the water that had become wine, and did not know where it came from—but the servants who had drawn the water knew—the master of the feast called the bridegroom and said to him: ‘Every man first sets out the good wine, and when they have become drunk, then the worse. But you have kept the good wine until now.’ This was the beginning of the signs that Jesus performed at Cana of Galilee, and he manifested his glory.”

Among the many signs that Jesus performed in Cana of Galilee, this was the first; and, by a certain privilege of dignity involving the transformation of the elements, he manifested his glory, that is, his hidden divinity. We marvel at the miracle of water changed into wine, yet do not marvel that every year God works this same thing in the vines, and from a single grain produces many others. And what is greater: he created heaven and earth from nothing and governs them wondrously. Therefore, because human beings, intent on other things, lost their consideration of the Lord’s works, by which they might praise him daily, God reserved for himself certain unusual deeds to perform, so that, as though awakening sleeping people, he might rouse them to worship him through miracles.

Jesus changed water into wine when he filled the insipid mind of carnal people with the flavor of heavenly knowledge. For we were water, that is, senseless, and he made us wine, that is, wise in his faith. Or water is understood as knowledge cleansing hearers from the filth of sins; it is then changed into wine when someone entirely forgets past evils so as not to fall into them, and begins to burn with the love of God, just as wine intoxicates forgetful drinkers and warms them.

Christ changed water into wine when he showed that what seemed carnal in the Law was spiritual, and made the surface of the letter appear full of heavenly power. For Christ, not yet manifested in the prophets, lay hidden like wine in water; but when he opened the disciples’ understanding so that they might understand the Scriptures (Luke XXIV), he himself was the intoxicating wine manifested in the Law and the Prophets. Therefore, while Christ lies hidden in that Scripture beneath its covering—that is, beneath the working of the letter—it tastes like insipid water. But when he removes the veil, it is intoxicating wine.

The six water jars are the six ages, which would run on emptily unless Christ were preached in them. The first age is from Adam to Noah; the second, to Abraham; the third, to David; the fourth, to the Exile; the fifth, to John the Baptist; and the sixth, from that point to the end of the age. Prophecy is like a water jar in each age. Let us see how, according to the letter—insipid water—is changed into wine when it is referred to Christ and to all the nations.

Whatever was prefigured in Adam concerning Christ pertained to all the nations, as in Genesis:

> “A man shall leave his father and mother, cling to his wife, and the two shall be one flesh” (Genesis II).

Christ clung to the Church so that the two might be one flesh. “Leaving his father” meant not appearing to human beings in the form in which he is equal to the Father. He “left his mother” when he passed from the Synagogue to the Church. The Lord could have removed Adam’s rib without pain while Adam was awake (ibid.), but without doubt Christ’s sleep on the cross was signified in this: from his side, as a bride, the sacraments of the Church flowed.

Let us drink the wine of the other water jars. Christ was prefigured in Noah. For this reason all the animals were enclosed in the ark (Genesis VII), so that all the nations to be saved through Christ might be signified. God was not incapable of creating every kind of animal again, but they were saved through wood because we too were to be saved through wood.

In the third water jar Abraham heard:

> “In your seed all the nations shall be blessed” (Genesis XXII).

Who does not see whom his only son prefigured, carrying the wood for the sacrifice to which he was being led to be offered? For the Lord carried his own cross.

In the fourth water jar David says:

> “Arise, O God, judge the earth, for you shall inherit all the nations” (Psalm LXXXI).

It is as though he were told: “You slept, judged by the earth; arise, so that you may judge the earth.”

In the fifth age Daniel saw a stone cut from the mountain without hands, shatter all the kingdoms of the earth, grow, and become a great mountain, so that it filled the whole face of the earth (Daniel II). Of what mountain is this foretold, if not the kingdom of the Jews, from which Christ was born according to the flesh without human work, since there was no marital embrace?

To the sixth age belongs John the Baptist, saying:

> “Do not say, ‘We have Abraham as our father.’ For God is able from these stones to raise up children for Abraham” (Matthew III).

He calls the nations stones, not because of their firmness, but because of the hardness of their stupidity: while they worshiped images, they became like them. Hence the saying:

> “Let those who make them and all who trust in them become like them” (Psalm CXIII).

Again, the six water jars are the perfected hearts of the saints, prepared in these ages to receive the Scriptures of God and set forth as examples to be seen and believed. They are “stone,” that is, strong in Christ the stone.

It is said that they were “according to the purification of the Jews,” because the Law was given only to that Jewish people, whereas grace was made available to all through Christ. It does not say that some held two measures and others three, but “two or three,” so that he himself might designate two as three.

There are therefore two measures in the Scriptures when the Father and the Son are named, while the Spirit, who belongs to the Father and the Son, is understood there as well, as in the passage:

> “You made all things in wisdom” (Psalm CIII),

that is, in the Son. There are three measures when the Holy Spirit is named and the Trinity is understood more explicitly, as in:

> “Baptize them in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit” (Matthew XXVIII).

Alternatively, the two or three measures are all the nations to which the Scriptures pertain: two because of uncircumcision and circumcision, and three because they were dispersed from the three sons of Noah.

[Col. 0823A] The water jars were filled at the Lord’s command, signifying that Scripture comes from him. He could indeed have filled empty jars with wine, since he created everything from nothing; but he preferred to make wine from water, to teach that he did not abolish the Law but fulfilled it, as he had foretold in the Gospel that he would do and teach these things. The jars are filled to the brim because no period was ever empty of saving doctrine.

The master of the feast is understood as the chief expert in Scripture, which contains histories, moral teachings, and allegories. When, therefore, the word of the Gospel is offered to such a person as Nicodemus, or Gamaliel, or his disciple Saul, the wine made from water is served to the master of the feast.

Some understand the water as John’s baptism and the wine as Christ’s Passion. Hence the wine is first brought to the master of the feast—that is, to John himself—who drank the Passion before Christ did.

The master of the feast, that is, the three ranks of those reclining at the wedding, distinguished from one another by height, represents the three orders of the faithful in the Church: the married, the continent, and the teachers. And because it belongs to teachers to prefer the grace of the Gospel to ancient institutions, the master of the feast, after calling the bridegroom, said that the good wine had been kept until then.

When it is said that he did not know where the wine came from, this is to be understood as referring to the many experts in the Law who, according to the letter, were informed of the Gospel by Christ’s disciples—those who had drawn the water by understanding wisely and opening faithfully the ancient Scripture.

“Every man first sets out the good wine” is said literally according to the custom of many people. Mystically, the man—that is, the carnal person—drinks the worse wine after the good, when the mind descends to falsehood. But the spiritual person is daily intoxicated and advances through the visible wine that was previously hidden in the Scriptures.

Maximus, bishop, in a sermon on the Epiphany, which begins as follows:

> “For us, brothers, it has been fulfilled,” he says. “As antiquity faithfully proclaimed to its posterity, today the Savior was worshiped by the Chaldeans. Today he consecrated the streams of the Jordan by the blessing of his own baptism. Today, invited to a wedding, he changed water into wine.”

## ALSO, ON THE SAME GOSPEL

> “Fill the water jars with water” (John II).

Galilee is interpreted as “transmigration.” The present life, therefore, is Galilee, passing from present things to future things. A wedding takes place in Galilee because, in the passage of time, the union of enduring love between the Church and Christ, and between the soul and God, is sanctified.

The six water jars are the six ages of the world. The first is from Adam to Noah; the second, from Noah to Abraham; the third, from Abraham to David; the fourth, from David to the Babylonian Exile; the fifth, from the Babylonian Exile to Christ; and the sixth, from Christ to the end of the age.

In human life, the first is infancy, the second childhood, the third adolescence, the fourth youth, the fifth mature adulthood, and the sixth old age. The first, infancy, is overwhelmed as though by a flood in the slippery stream of forgetfulness, so that it is not seen afterward and leaves no trace of itself. The second, childhood, first emerging from the flood of forgetfulness into awareness, rises through pride and is divided and scattered through desire.

The third is adolescence. First it is circumcised by restraint through discipline; then it is formed by precepts and governed by counsel. The fourth, youth, is already compelled to serve and is subjected to rule, so that through the fear of human beings it may stand apart for God. The fifth, mature adulthood, comes after fear of human beings to the fear of God. The sixth, old age, is drawn onward as though toward the desires of future things.

Thus the human race was first overwhelmed by the Flood; second, exalted in the building of the tower and scattered in the division of languages; third, circumcised in Abraham, formed by precepts in Moses, and governed by counsel under the judges; fourth, subjected to domination under the kings; fifth, obedient to religion under the high priests; and sixth, illumined by true goodness under grace.

[Col. 0824B] These six water jars, whether in the course of the present age or in human life, are all filled with water, because the world is full of judgments:

> “Your judgments are a great abyss” (Psalm XXXV).

God has done many things from the beginning of the age and does not cease to work until its end; likewise, he works concerning a human being from that person’s beginning to the end. All these things are judgments, and nothing happens without a cause.

But as long as a person cannot say, “Your judgments are delightful” (Psalm CXVIII), the water has not yet been changed into wine. When the old wine fails, the jars are filled with water, because when carnal pleasures fail in human life, divine consolations follow. These give less flavor to beginners but become sweeter to those who advance, because the water is changed into wine when the work of God, which at first did not taste good to one who labored, becomes sweet to the mind illumined by spiritual understanding.

Again, the six water jars are the six ages of the world; the water changed into wine signifies that the deeds of earlier times were performed as figures of spiritual realities. In the first age Abel offered a lamb to God, his brother Cain killed him, and afterward the Lord transferred Enoch to heaven. From this jar’s water, wine is drawn for those thirsting for the word of God when this is opened mystically.

Abel, who sacrificed the lamb, is Christ, who offered his body to God the Father for us. Abel was killed by his brother, and Christ was slain by the Jewish people. Enoch was taken from the earth, and Christ, after his Passion, was transferred to heaven.

In the second age Noah, planting a vineyard, became drunk with wine; while sleeping naked, he was mocked by one son and covered with a garment by two. When he awoke, he condemned the mocker to servitude and blessed the others for glory. This water jar is changed when it is understood in this way.

Noah, who planted the vineyard, is Christ, who founded the Church. He is made drunk by the cup of bitter Passion and, mocked and disfigured by a faithless people, is covered by two—that is, the shame of his Passion is honored by faithful Hebrews and Gentiles. Awakening from the sleep of death, he condemns the mocking Jewish people and exalts those who honor him to life.

In the third age Joseph is sold by his brothers out of envy, accused by his mistress because of his chastity, shut up in prison, and, brought out of prison, placed over all Egypt. This jar of sweet water refreshes us with the taste of sweeter wine.

Joseph, who is separated from his brothers, is Christ, who is handed over by his disciple to the Jews; accused by the Synagogue as Joseph was by his mistress; condemned to death and shut in a tomb; and, returning from the abyss, ruling over the whole world.

In the fourth age David defeats Goliath in battle, and Solomon builds the temple in Jerusalem from gold and gems. The sweet wine of this jar’s water is drunk when it is understood in this way.

Goliath is struck down by David, and the devil is conquered by Christ on the cross. The temple in Jerusalem is built by Solomon with gold and gems because the Church, which is the temple of God, is gathered by Christ in heaven from the perfected.

In the fifth age Jesus the priest returns from Babylon with the captives and rebuilds the ruins of the temple in Jerusalem. This water jar intoxicates us with wine when it reveals these deeds as spiritual realities.

Jesus, who returns from Babylon with the captives, is Jesus Christ, the true priest, who, leading captivity back from hell, returns to heaven. The ruin of the temple is repaired by Jesus in Jerusalem, and the ruin of the angelic court is restored through Jesus Christ.

In the sixth age the whole people comes to Jesus, and he, washing them with water, separates the faithful from the unfaithful. Christ also changes the taste of this jar’s water for us into the sweetness of wine. The multitude of the people comes to John, and he separates them in the river, because in the last days the whole people is gathered to Christ and, by him, the faithful are separated from the unfaithful through a river of fire.

This one, dearest friends, you ought to love with your whole mind’s affection: he refreshes your souls with such mysteries, has invited you to his wedding, and will one day intoxicate you with the wine of eternal sweetness.

## THIRD SUNDAY — ACCORDING TO MATTHEW

[Col. 0825]

> “When Jesus had come down from the mountain, great crowds followed him. And behold, a leper came and worshiped him, saying: ‘Lord, if you are willing, you can cleanse me’” (Matthew VIII).

Miracles rightly follow teaching, so that the word may be confirmed through power.

(Bede.) According to Mark, the leper knelt (Mark I), and, as Luke says, “fell on his face” (Luke V). This expresses humility and shame, so that each person may be ashamed of the stains of his life; yet shame does not suppress confession, but he seeks a remedy for the wound directly.

The leper attributes the power of healing to the Lord’s will. He does not doubt like an unbeliever, but, conscious of his own defilement, does not presume to say, “Cleanse me, Lord, and I shall be clean.” By asking to be healed through the Lord’s power, though excluded by the Law, he indicates that grace is above the Law. [Col. 0825C] For just as authority of power is declared in the Lord, so steadfastness of faith is declared in the leper.

> “And Jesus stretched out his hand and touched him, saying: ‘I am willing; be cleansed.’ And immediately his leprosy was cleansed.”

With an expression of mercy he stretched out his hand and touched the leprosy, teaching us through humility not to despise anyone because of a bodily blemish. The Law forbids touching lepers. But this was not forbidden to the one who is Lord of the Law. He therefore touched him—not because he could not heal without touching, but to show that he is not under the Law, indeed that he is Lord of the Law, who does not fear contagion, since he rather frees others from it.

Out of compassion he said, “I am willing,” healing him in the manner in which he had been entreated. When the leper said, “If you are willing, you can cleanse me,” Jesus added by command, “Be cleansed”; in this the power of his majesty is revealed. There is nothing intermediate between God’s work and his command, because the work is present in the command. For he spoke, and they were made.

> “And Jesus said to him: ‘See that you tell no one, but go, show yourself to the priest, and offer the gift that Moses commanded as a testimony to them.’”

There was no need for him to proclaim in words what he displayed in his body. [Col. 0826B] The Lord teaches that our benefits are not to be publicized but concealed, so that we abstain not only from seeking monetary reward but also from seeking praise. Avoiding boastfulness prevents the leprosy from passing to the physician.

Silence is also commanded because it is better to seek salvation through faith that arises spontaneously than to be invited by benefits. The leper is commanded to show himself to the priest so that the priest might understand that he had been healed not by the order of the Law but by God’s grace. He is ordered to offer a sacrifice so that the Lord might show that he did not abolish the Law but fulfilled it, walking according to the Law and healing above the Law.

In the Law it was commanded that those cleansed of leprosy offer gifts to the priests; therefore he sends him humbly to them. These symbolic sacrifices had to be removed before the true sacrifices signified in them could also be confirmed in Christ and in the Church through the testimony of the apostles and the faith of believers.

The offering is made as a testimony to those who see the leper cleansed: either because those who are saved from the leprosy of sins offer themselves to God if they believe, or because, if they do not believe, they will be without excuse.

Or it may be understood this way: the gift that Moses commanded is to be offered to those priests as a testimony, that is, as a sign of spiritual offering, just as the cleansing of leprosy testifies to the cleansing of sin. That gift, I say, is offered not merely as a sign but in reality, so that you yourself, cleansed from the filth of sin, may pass into God’s sacrifice. Moses commanded a testimony whose fulfillment you bear.

The place where the leper was cleansed is not expressly identified, so that it might be shown that not one people of a particular city but peoples of many places were healed. Since the leper typologically signifies the human race weakened by sins, he is rightly described in Luke as full of leprosy (Luke V). For “all have sinned and lack the glory of God” (Romans III).

The stretching out of the Savior’s hand signifies the Incarnation extended for the salvation of human beings. Hence the saying elsewhere:

> “Already you are clean because of the word that I have spoken to you” (John XIII).

Christ himself is the priest forever. All who have been cleansed from the variety of ancient error ought to show themselves to him by confessing that they are his temple, and they ought to offer their bodies to him as a living sacrifice.

> “When he had entered Capernaum, a centurion approached him, begging him and saying: ‘Lord, my servant lies at home paralyzed and is suffering terribly.’”

There is no contradiction in Luke’s saying, “He sent Jewish elders to him, begging” (Luke V), just as we commonly reach someone through a friend. Nevertheless, Matthew’s mystical solution should also be considered carefully, according to what is written in the Psalm:

> “Approach him and be enlightened” (Psalm XXXIII).

Thus the centurion came in faith. It can nevertheless be said that he also came bodily, and entrusted his request to the Jewish elders, as Luke explains, because they were friends of Christ; this is something commonly done before powerful people.

The paralytic lies suffering from a sharp pain, apparently. He describes this in such a way that he both indicates the anguish of his soul and moves Christ to mercy. Now let us learn to show compassion toward servants, as Luke says: the servant would have died if he had not been restored to life through his master’s faith and Christ’s compassion. So too King Hezekiah, to whom the Lord added fifteen years.

> “Jesus said to him: ‘I will come and heal him.’”

He did not wish to go to heal the official’s son, lest he seem to have honored wealth. He consented to go to the servant, lest he be thought to have despised servile status. But on the journey he healed him by his word, lest he be thought to be going because of inability rather than humility.

> “And the centurion answered and said: ‘Lord, I am not worthy that you should enter under my roof; but only say the word, and my servant will be healed. For I too am a man placed under authority, having soldiers under me. I say to this one, “Go,” and he goes; and to another, “Come,” and he comes; and to my servant, “Do this,” and he does it.’”

Because of his awareness as a Gentile, he feared burdening the Lord. The Lord saw the centurion’s faith, humility, and prudence: his faith, because he believed from among the Gentiles; his humility, because he judged himself unworthy for the Lord to enter his house; and his prudence, because he recognized divinity hidden under bodily form.

With this prudence he also said: “I am a man, and I send men, knowing that the Lord is able to send angels.” Hence it follows:

> “When Jesus heard this, he marveled, and said to those following him: ‘Amen, amen, I say to you, I have not found such faith in Israel.’”

That Jesus marveled signifies for us something worthy of wonder, because when such emotions are attributed to God, they are not signs of a disturbed mind but of a teacher instructing. He says of those present, “I have not found such faith in Israel,” not of the patriarchs and prophets—unless perhaps the faith of the Gentiles is being placed before Israel in the person of the centurion.

The centurion’s faith is placed before those present because they had been taught by the admonitions of the Law and the Prophets, whereas he believed spontaneously, without anyone teaching him.

> “I say to you that many will come from the east and the west and recline with Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob in the kingdom of heaven. But the sons of the kingdom will be cast into the outer darkness; there will be weeping and gnashing of teeth.”

Not only does this centurion from the Gentiles rightly believe in God, but many Gentiles will yet come to right faith. Of the nations that will believe he says, “Many will come and rest, happily feasting.” He calls the Jews “sons of the kingdom,” among whom God previously reigned.

The darkness that remains is inner, not outer. That is, it is called “outer” because the one expelled outside by the Lord has left the light. When he says that there will be weeping and gnashing of teeth, he indicates a true resurrection, since weeping belongs to the eyes, and teeth to the bones.

> “And Jesus said to the centurion: ‘Go; and as you have believed, so let it be done for you.’ And the servant was healed in that hour.”

The centurion returned to his house and found the servant who had been ill in good health (Luke VII). The master’s merit assists the servant.

Let us understand that the centurion finally came to the Lord bodily and returned home with those who had been sent, when the Lord said to him, “Go.” Or let it be understood that, just as he approached through messengers, so he returned through messengers.

By divine providence the Jews were sent, so that they might be without excuse if, after seeing the miracle and seeing a Gentile man believe, they themselves did not believe. The elders intercede with the Lord for the centurion, and the saints for us.

The centurion’s soldiers can be understood as the natural virtues that many people bring with them when they come to the Lord. Concerning these virtues, in praise of Cornelius the centurion, it is said:

> “He was a just man who feared God with all his household, giving many alms to the people and always praying to God” (Acts X).

Those who do not use such qualities well are entirely unworthy of God’s visitation.

The centurion represents the elect from the Gentiles, who, as though surrounded by a hundred soldiers, are exalted by the perfection of spiritual virtues and seek for themselves and their own only the joys of eternal salvation. The number one hundred, transferred from the left hand to the heavenly right, signifies life.

Hence Noah’s ark was built over one hundred years; Abraham, at the age of one hundred, received the son of promise; Isaac sowed and in that year found a hundredfold yield; the court of the tabernacle was one hundred cubits long; and in the hundredth Psalm mercy and judgment are sung to the Lord.

## A QUESTION ABOUT THIS: WHETHER GOD’S POWER AND GOD’S WILL ARE EQUAL

[Col. 0828D]

It is asked concerning God’s power whether it is greater than his will. For if God can do more than he wills, his power seems greater than his will. But if his power is greater than his will, something seems unequal in him, and God does not wholly correspond to himself. How, then, is the whole of what he is one, if there is a greater and a lesser in him?

But if willing and being able are the same for him, then his power and his will are the same. If being able and willing are the same for him, then whatever he wills he can do, and whatever he can do he wills.

He wills everything he has made, because the one who does everything voluntarily does nothing against his will. Again, he does everything he wills, because the ability to do all things is present when willing is not absent.

If, therefore, God cannot do more than he wills, and does not will to do more than he does, it is certainly established that he cannot do more than he does. If God can do more than he wills, he can act against his will, do what he does not possess in his will, and his power is contrary to his will.

It consequently seems that, just as he does everything that he can and wills, so everything that he does he can and wills; everything he can do he wills, and everything he wills he can do.

But if it is accepted that God cannot do anything in another way or otherwise than he does, then he acts out of necessity in all things and is bound and constrained by the law of his works, so that the condition of his work rules over him. But it is impious to confess this.

“How, then,” they say, “are willing and being able the same for God, if his power is greater than his will?”

See what they are saying. “According to you,” they say, “God’s power is greater than his will.” Why? Because you say that God can do more than he wills.

Pay attention. If his power must be called greater than his will because he can do many things that he does not will to do, then let his will also be called greater than his power, since he does not do many things that he can do because he does not will to do them. For if power is called greater because it surpasses the will, let the will also be called greater because it restrains the power.

But just as power is not restricted—that is, by the fact that it does nothing without the will—so the will is not surpassed by the fact that it does not extend to everything within the power.

There are three things: disposition, effect, and relation. Will and power in God are therefore one in disposition and effect, but they are not one in relation.

How are these two one in God according to disposition? Because in Christ there is neither will without power nor power without will. Power would be without will if he possessed some power that he did not wish to possess. Again, will would be without power if at some time he willed something not through strength but through weakness.

Since, therefore, power in him is always willing, and will is powerful—because he wills to be able to do everything that he can do, and wills everything that he wills by power—for this reason in Christ there is neither power without will nor will without power.

Likewise, in effect, neither will can in any way be separated from power nor power from will. For whatever God does voluntarily, he does with power. And again, whatever he does with power, he does voluntarily, because everything he does, he does both voluntarily and with power.

Therefore, in every work of his God exercises both will and power. They do not divide themselves in the work, since they cannot be divided in the one who acts.

Thus God’s power and will remain undivided in him according to disposition and, through him, according to effect; but, in relation to what is outside him, they display themselves differently. God is truly said not to will everything he can do, because he can do many things he does not will to do; yet he wills nothing he cannot do.

Therefore, his power is directed toward certain things toward which his will is not directed, while his power is directed toward everything toward which his will is directed. Divine power therefore relates in one respect to things other than the will, because it possesses nothing against the will.

But they say: “If God can do something he does not will to do, then he can do something against his will. If he can do something against his will, he is not omnipotent, since he can be compelled unwillingly and led to what he does not will.”

But see how the argument holds together. They say that if God can do something he does not will to do, then he can do something against his will. He would indeed act against his will if he did what he did not wish to do. But it does not follow that, because he can do something he does not will to do, he can act against his will. For if he did what he can do but does not will, he would then will to do what he did; just as now, because he does not will to do it, he does not do what he could do if he willed.

So foreknowledge and predestination in God, when considered according to relation, are different, although they are one in God. Foreknowledge relates both to evil things and to good things; predestination relates only to good things. He foreknew everything future, but predestined only the elect.

Likewise, when predestination is understood as disposition, it still cannot be made equal, in relation, to foreknowledge, because God’s foreknowledge concerns both what he will do and what he will permit, whereas predestination concerns only what he will do.

For Ambrose says:

> “God predestined the hell of the impious, but he did not predestine the guilt of the impious.”

He predestined what he was going to do; what he was not going to do but was going to permit, he did not predestine but foreknew.

## EXPOSITION ON THE SAME GOSPEL

> “When Jesus had come down from the mountain, great crowds followed him, and so forth” (Matthew VIII).

Because Christ, dearest brothers, wished to dwell among human beings and show the power of his divinity through his deeds and miracles, he instructed our faith through mystical signs.

The Lord had preached to a few disciples on the mountain, and at that time the crowds had not ascended to him. The Lord came down from the mountain, and great crowds followed him.

> “And behold, a leper came and worshiped him, saying: ‘Lord, if you are willing, you can cleanse me.’”

[Col. 0830D] O, how great was the leper’s faith! This leper had heard that it was written concerning God:

> “The Lord has done whatever he wished” (Psalm CXXXIV).

He had also heard that through Elisha the Lord cleansed Naaman, the commander of Syria, when he was washed in the Jordan; and because the Lord does everything by his will alone, he said to him:

> “Lord, if you are willing, you can cleanse me.”

It was not necessary for you to command, but only to will, because power follows your will. Therefore: “If you are willing, you can cleanse me.”

Seeing the faith of the one calling upon him and the will of the one entreating him, the Lord said, in effect: “Since you ask for my will and entreat it, I am willing, I command, I lay on my hand.”

When he says, “I am willing,” he shows that he wills; when he says, “Be cleansed,” he commands. When it is read that he stretched out his hand and touched him, he shows that he applied his hand.

But why did he touch the leper, since he was unclean, when he could cleanse him by his will alone? He wished to expose and blunt our pride. For this reason he did not shrink from handling the leper’s flesh, in order to do good.

Every rich person, every form of pride, recoils from touching the sick and the horrifying ugliness of corruption, disdains seeing it, and does not wish to approach through compassion. But the Lord rebukes this man both by his deed and by his finger.

Behold, the Creator of heaven, the King of angels, descended into the world to touch a leper. It is as though he said: “Behold, I have come in humility to touch the one who seems filthy to you because of your pride. Let what the emperor does not be vile to the servant.”

Solomon says:

> “Whoever despises the poor insults his Maker,”

because he himself made us, and we did not make ourselves. Through such an act the Lord rebukes this attitude. By his word he will rebuke the proud when he says:

> “I was sick, and you did not visit me” (Matthew XXV).

> “And immediately his leprosy was cleansed.”

He performed another miracle in the same Gospel, in which there is a sign of great humility. Immediately after the cleansing of the leper, a centurion came to him and begged him, saying:

> “Lord, my servant lies paralyzed at home and is suffering terribly. And Jesus said to him: ‘I will come and heal him.’ And the centurion answered and said: ‘Lord, I am not worthy that you should enter under my roof; but only say the word, and my servant will be healed’” (Matthew VIII).

This centurion was a Gentile and had many soldiers under his authority. He had no law commanding him to feel compassion for his neighbor, and yet he grieved—not for a son, not for a soldier, but for a servant.

Christian rulers, if they see their servants become ill, despise and disregard them and take no care for them. But this Gentile, who had great concern for his servant, sent Jewish elders to the heavenly physician, asking him to come and heal his servant.

Because he was a Gentile and foreigner, he did not dare approach the Lord bodily, as Luke says, but sent Jewish elders, as though they were household friends who could ask him more confidently. He considered himself unworthy and, not daring to approach through bodily penance, nevertheless approached in faith.

Therefore the Gospel says, “The centurion approached him,” without bodily presence, yet asking in faith through intermediaries.

> “Jesus was going with them. And when he was already not far from the house, the centurion sent his friends to him, saying: ‘Do not trouble yourself, for I am not worthy,’ and so forth” (Luke VII).

He had nevertheless asked him to come, but he was not speaking of bodily arrival; he was speaking of an approach in compassion. He was separated from the Gentiles by idolatry, and he asks the Lord to approach—not through justice but through mercy.

The messengers, however, understood him to be speaking of bodily arrival. Therefore the Jews asked him to come, saying:

> “He is worthy that you should grant this to him. For he loves our nation and himself built our synagogue.”

The Lord said to them: “I will come and heal him.” And he went with them. When the centurion heard that he was coming, he again sent friends, saying: “Do not trouble yourself, for I am not worthy,” and so forth (ibid.).

Observe the words of the faithful Gentile. He reports to him three conditions of his servant, who lies as though paralyzed and is suffering terribly, so that he might demonstrate the anguish of his own soul and move the Lord.

> “My servant,” he says, “lies at home” (Matthew VIII).

If anyone asks why he did not bring him, as those others brought paralytics on their beds, I reply that there is no need to bring before the sight of one who sees everything the person whose power is present everywhere. Therefore he tells him, “The boy lies in the house,” as though he were saying: “There is no need for him to be carried before you.”

Why, then, does the Lord say, “I will come and heal him” (ibid.), when he does not ask for his coming? A certain royal official whose son was ill at Capernaum asked him to come down and heal his son. Jesus said to him, “Go, your son lives” (John IV). [GREGORY.] He was willing to come to the servant who did not ask him to come, but he was unwilling to go down to the king’s son who urged him. Why this, brothers, unless because there is no partiality with God? We honor the rich and hurry to the rich when they are ill; but we shrink from going to the poor. Behold, the King does not delay going to a servant, and hastens to go to a king’s son. Christ was poor and loved the poor, so that he might enrich the poor with his own riches.

The Lord, then, wished to go to the servant, but the centurion sent word to him: “I am not worthy.” Why am I not worthy? Because I am a gentile, a foreigner, a soldier, girded with a sword; shedding blood, I am not worthy to appear before you. This gentile reveres what no Christian soldier does. Though he is unclean, he does not say, “I am not worthy”; rather, rashly, he will offer him a filthy lodging and receive him there. But this man says: “I am not worthy that you should enter under my roof, but only say the word and my boy will be healed.”

Let us compare the leper and the centurion together and see, since the faith of both was great, which of them had the greater faith. The leper says: “If you will, you can cleanse me.” The centurion says: “Only say the word and my boy will be healed.” The former considers the will, the latter the command, more subtly discerning the divine power. But the one who believes that he is powerful through will alone has the greater faith, because he believes not merely in a command but in will alone. Yet the centurion’s faith is great and wondrous.

For he says: “I believe that by your word you can heal.” “For,” he says, “I am merely a human being, and you are God. I am a man who has soldiers under my authority, and you have angels who perform miracles. I say to this one, ‘Go,’ and he goes, and to another, ‘Come,’ and he comes.” If men obey one who is a man, how much more will angels obey you, and all nature, because you can do all things.

Christ marveled at his faith and therefore said to those who followed him: “I have not found such faith in Israel.” For although the Jewish people had seen him through the prophets, they did not recognize him; rather, they said that he performed all his miracles by Beelzebub (Luke XI). Jairus too, a ruler of Israel, when asking God for his daughter, did not say, “Say the word,” but, “Come quickly, before my daughter dies” (Matthew IX). Nicodemus also, a ruler of Israel, hearing of the mystery of faith, said: “How can this happen?” (John III.) Mary and Martha likewise said: “Lord, if you had been here” (John X), as though, being absent, he could not save him. Therefore: “I have not found such faith in Israel.”

He then said: “As you have believed, so let it be done for you.” And the boy was healed in that hour.

Learn, brothers, from these things some example for our life. Jesus descended from the mountain because he descended from heaven. And after he wished to dwell among human beings, the crowds followed him because they imitated his footsteps. Therefore, if anyone is a leper, let him come to him. For leprosy, brothers, signifies serious sins by which our soul is defiled. If, then, someone is truly entangled in that leprosy, let him hasten to the true physician and say: “If you will, you can cleanse me.”

It was commanded in the old law that if anyone were a leper, he should be expelled outside the camp, and, once healed, should show himself to the priest. Likewise, one who is guilty of serious sins ought to be outside the Church and, once healed through the priest, be received into the Church.

The Lord invites us to humility when he desires to visit a servant, so that the poor may not be despised. And because the Lord is honored in the poor, the Lord honored the poor. “Therefore make friends for yourselves from the mammon of iniquity” (Luke XVI).

# THE FOURTH SUNDAY. According to Matthew.

[Column 0833]

“Jesus got into the boat, and his disciples followed him. And behold, a great storm arose on the sea, so that the boat was covered by the waves. But he was in the stern, sleeping on a cushion” (Matthew VIII).

A cushion (*cervical*) means either a little pillow or anything else placed beneath the neck of one reclining to sleep. The boat appeared to be covered and filled by the waves; therefore the disciples were all the more troubled by fear.

“And they came and awakened him, saying: ‘Lord, save us; we are perishing.’ And Jesus said to them: ‘Why are you afraid, you of little faith?’ Then he rose and rebuked the wind and the sea. And he said: ‘Be silent and be still.’ And there was a great calm.”

Although the Evangelists relate this in different words, there is nevertheless one meaning, and all of it could have been said together. He rules the wind and the sea, of whom it is said: “You rule the power of the sea” (Psalm LXXXVIII). He commanded not through the error of heretics, who think all inanimate things are animate, but with the majesty by which they are perceptible to God and imperceptible to us.

We read a type of this sign in Jonah: while the others were in danger, the Lord followed, slept, and was awakened; and by his command and by the mystery of his passion he freed those who awakened him. Thus he deigned to show both natures in his own person, sleeping as a human being and restraining the sea as God.

“Moreover, the men marveled, saying to one another: ‘What sort of man is this, that even the winds and the sea obey him?’”

Those who did not yet know the Savior’s power are rightly called “men,” whether the sailors are meant, or the others who were in the boat, or even the disciples themselves.

Allegorically, the sea signifies the turmoil of this age; the boat signifies the tree of the Passion, by whose help the faithful cross the waves of the world and reach the shore of the heavenly homeland. Elsewhere he discloses the meaning of the disciples’ embarking in the boat with the Lord, saying: “If anyone wishes to come after me, let him deny himself, take up his cross, and follow me.”

While the disciples sail, Christ sleeps, because when the faithful, treading upon the age in hope of perpetual rest and casting behind them, in rivalry, the world’s haughtiness, are striving onward, the time of the Lord’s Passion arrives. Hence Mark declares that this happened in the evening, so that the setting of the true sun might be signified not only by the Lord’s sleep but also by the hour itself.

When he ascended into the stern of the cross to receive the sleep of death, the waves raised by the demonic storms of those who blasphemed surged up. Yet his patience was not disturbed by them; rather, the weakness of the disciples was endangered. The stern, covered with the skins of the dead, shelters the living and keeps back the waves, and is strengthened by wood; these things indicate that the Church is saved by the Lord’s cross and death.

By the cushion understand the body on which the divinity, like a head inclined, reclines. The disciples awaken the Lord lest they perish, because they were seeking the resurrection with their greatest desires. When the Lord rose, he rebuked the wind because he struck down the devil’s pride by destroying his dominion. He made the stormy water cease because he weakened the frenzy of those crying, “If he is the Son of God, let him come down from the cross” (Matthew XXVII).

Those who were afraid while Christ was present are rightly reproved; therefore, after the resurrection, some of them also heard: “O foolish ones and slow of heart to believe all that the prophets have spoken” (Luke XXIV).

Often, as we too sail, the Lord seems to sleep amid the roar of the sea, whenever, amid the very struggles of virtue, the splendor of faith grows dark, the height of hope withers, and the flame of love grows cold because of the increasing assault of unclean spirits, wicked people, or thoughts. But then we must hasten to God, so that he may lead us to tranquility and grant us the harbor of salvation.

# On the Measure of Loving God

The Apostle says: “Owe no one anything, except to love one another. For whoever loves his neighbor has fulfilled the law” (Romans XIII). We must consider more carefully, however, with what measure God and our neighbor ought to be loved.

Scripture reveals to us the measure of loving God when it says: “You shall love the Lord your God with all your heart, with all your mind, and with all your soul” (Deuteronomy VI). It is as though it said: “I do not command you to love only so much, or only your God. Love as much as you can; your ability will be your measure.”

The more you love, the more you possess; and the more you possess, the happier you are. Therefore stretch out and enlarge yourself as much as you can, so that all that is in you may be filled, even if all that is in him cannot be contained. Do not fear that he will fail you if you become too capacious. However much you can, you will never be able to contain as much as he is. If you could, you would be as great as he is. But now you can grow in him; you cannot become equal to him.

Therefore grow and advance. The greater you are in goodness, the better you will be. If you were supreme, you would be best; but since you cannot be supreme, you can be in the Supreme. This is already great for you, and by this you are great: if you are in the Supreme, you are greater in proportion as you are higher. You ascend when you love. You go upward in love, because love leads upward.

As the Apostle says: “I will show you a still more excellent way” (1 Corinthians XII). Therefore ascend while you can. Now is the time for growing and advancing; afterward, when all things have been brought to completion, you will stand at the point you have reached. That will be your summit in him, beyond which you will not pass; but it will not be his summit, so that, if you stand there, you will not find any further place to which you may grow.

Therefore ascend while you can, as much as you can. You can never do too much where you can never contain everything. Love the Lord your God with all your heart, with all your soul, and with all your mind, so that your whole being may be filled from him, even though his fullness cannot be contained by your whole being. He fills you and overflows within himself.

If the vessel does not fail, the oil is sufficient. Your heart is the vessel; his love is the oil. As long as you have a vessel, he does not cease pouring in the oil (2 Kings IV); and afterward, when you no longer have a vessel, he will still have more oil. Therefore do not spare him; receive as much as you can. Love as much as you are able, because he does not fail.

Love with all your heart, with all your soul, and with all your mind—that is, with all your understanding, all your affection, and all your memory. As much as you understand, as much as you comprehend, as much as you are able, so much love. Let everything be filled with knowledge, everything be moved by love, and everything be held in memory. As much as you are enlightened, so much let yourself be moved, so that everything concerning him that comes into your knowledge and memory may be sweet.

If everything is rightly approved, why should everything not be loved? Therefore, as much as he deigns to make himself known to us, so much let him be loved by us. Let us love all that we are able to contain, and as much as we can.

# On the Measure of Loving One’s Neighbor

Scripture says to us concerning love of neighbor: “You shall love your neighbor as yourself” (Leviticus XIX). We certainly fulfill this command when, beyond the good that we desire for ourselves, we also desire it for our neighbor.

In those matters in which we rightly love ourselves—whether concerning the needs of the body or the salvation of the soul—we ought to love our neighbor sincerely and help him as far as we reasonably can.

Some ask whether the words “as yourself” are to be understood only according to likeness or also according to equality. For if we are commanded to love our neighbors as much as ourselves, a difficulty seems to arise, which we cannot explain lightly.

Suppose there are two people, one of whom must necessarily perish. One person is given the choice of which of the two he wishes to choose, since one of them cannot be avoided altogether. If he chooses his own salvation, he loves his neighbor less. If he chooses his neighbor’s salvation, he loves God less than his neighbor, since he wishes to be separated from God for his neighbor’s sake.

Perhaps someone might say that equal love cannot make a choice: that one should want both equally and reject both equally, and that one cannot prefer either to the other in a choice in which both are altogether equal in love. Thus someone might try to avoid the objection.

But what shall we say? If I must love one person as much as myself, then if there are two, three, or four, should I not love them more than myself? Such are the questions human beings pursue, disturbing themselves with their thoughts.

They say: “What is better ought to be loved more.” Let us suppose there are three people, one on this side and two on the other. I say that either this one or those two must perish. Tell me, then, you who love your neighbor as yourself: What do you choose?

“It is better for one to perish than for two, because it is better to save two than one.”

“Therefore,” you say, “I choose more readily that one should perish and two be saved.”

“So you want those two to be saved more than that one. Do you not, then, love more what you choose as preferable?”

“Yes,” you say, “I love it more.”

“See, then, what follows. Earlier you admitted that you love your neighbor as much as yourself—or that, if you do not, you ought to love him so. If, then, you love this one as much as yourself, but love those two more than yourself, you love those two more than yourself. And if you love those two more than yourself, it seems that you love them more than God, for whose sake you wish to be separated from him, so that you may neither possess nor love God: you wish to perish so that they may be saved.”

Perhaps someone might think that Moses had this sort of love, when, opposing the angry God for the salvation of his neighbors, he said: “If you do not forgive them this offense, blot me from the book that you have written” (Exodus XXXII). The Apostle also wishes to be accursed and separated from Christ for the sake of his brothers, so that they may be saved in Christ (Romans IX).

Perhaps someone might even think that this pertains to love of God: that we should love him so greatly that we would rather wish his glory to be increased in others than confined in ourselves. For this reason, we ought to desire our own destruction for the salvation of many, so that many may be saved and we perish, rather than many perish and we be saved.

But consider that the order of love is such that a person should love himself before his neighbor. He is commanded to draw and shape his love of his neighbor from his own love, when it is said: “You shall love your neighbor as yourself.”

For if he loves his neighbor as himself, how does he love his neighbor when he does not love himself? If he loves his neighbor as himself, then he surely wishes and desires for him the good that he wishes for himself. But if he desires that the same thing happen to his neighbor as to himself, how does he desire the salvation of one whose own destruction he wishes?

Therefore he must first love himself rightly, so that afterward he may love his neighbor rightly, according to himself. But if he wishes to destroy himself in order to save his neighbor, his love is not ordered, because a person can give no exchange for his own soul.

God first requires this from you: that you give your soul to him, and then add the other things. If you wish to give anything for this person, it is not accepted unless you give this also. This first, and the rest together with it.

I do not mean merely two, three, or four people: you ought not love even the whole world more than your own soul. For if you love anything more than your soul, you are plainly shown to love that thing more than God, because you love your soul only in him, since you love the good of your soul, which is God.

Therefore first love your soul by loving the good of your soul. Then love your neighbor as yourself, by loving for him the good that you love for yourself. For this is what it means to love him: to love the good for him.

You could love his good even if you did not love him. You could love it for yourself or for someone else, but not for him; and thus you would not love him, even though you loved his good, because you would not love it for him.

You could love his horse, his house and field, his money, his strength, beauty, or wisdom, even though you did not love him, because you would love these things for yourself, not for him. But you could not love the true good for yourself unless you also loved it and desired it for your neighbor.

Scripture therefore distinguished this love according to the love by which a person is good in and for others. First it commanded a human being to love God, intending precisely that he should love himself in God, because to love oneself is nothing other than to love one’s own good, and to love one’s own good is nothing other than to love it for oneself—that is, to wish for and desire it.

Since everyone who loves his own good loves it for himself, and since everyone who loves God loves his own good, it is altogether clear that no one loves God who does not love him for himself; and everyone who loves, loves for himself, because he desires and wishes to possess the one whom he loves.

Again, not everyone who loves another’s good loves the person whose good he loves, because he does not love that good for him. Scripture therefore distinguished for the human mind, according to the distinctions found among human things, what divine things possess inseparably.

It said that, after loving God, a person should love his neighbor—not because he can do the latter without the former, but so that he would not think it possible. First, then, it said that he should love God, and in him it said that he should love for himself, because everyone who loves his own good loves it for himself.

Since not everyone who loves another’s good loves the person whose good he loves, Scripture immediately added love of neighbor after love of God, so that a person might desire for his neighbor, by loving him, what he desires for himself by loving God.

What is a greater good for me must be loved more by me, because it is implanted in me first that I should love my own good—especially that which is the true good—and after that, and according to that, I should love the good of my neighbor. According to myself and after myself, I owe something to him; before myself or against myself, I owe nothing.

Otherwise the saying “You shall love your neighbor as yourself” would not stand if I loved him while hating myself.

Accordingly, there are only two commandments of charity: the first concerning love of God, in which a person truly loves himself; the second concerning love of neighbor, in which he loves his neighbor as himself.

# THE FIFTH SUNDAY AFTER THE EPIPHANY. According to Matthew.

[Column 0837]

Jesus answered and said: “I confess to you, Father, Lord of heaven and earth, because you have hidden these things from the wise and prudent and revealed them to little ones, etc.” (Matthew XI).

Rejoicing in the Holy Spirit over the salvation of the humble to whom he was speaking, he gives thanks and rejoices in the Father because he revealed to the apostles the mysteries of his coming, which the scribes and Pharisees, who seemed wise to themselves, did not know. Hence the preceding statement: “Wisdom has been justified by her children” (ibid.).

Confession does not always signify repentance; sometimes it signifies thanksgiving. [AUGUSTINE.] In saying “Father,” he shows that he was begotten by God, not created, as the heretics say. In saying “Lord,” he identifies the creator of heaven and earth. Beautifully, he opposed to the wise and prudent not the foolish and dull, but the little ones, that he might show that he condemned arrogance, not intellectual acuity.

Humility is the key to knowledge. Concerning it he says elsewhere: “You have taken away the key of knowledge” (Luke XI), that is, the humility of faith in Christ, by which you could have reached recognition of his divinity.

“Yes, Father, because this was pleasing before you.”

The meaning is: “Certainly, Father, you have done these things because this was pleasing before you,” that is, in your sight. From these words we receive examples of humility, so that we may not rashly presume to judge the heavenly counsels concerning the calling of some and the rejection of others.

He did not give the reason; he merely said that it was pleasing to God, showing that what pleased the just one cannot be unjust. Hence, when returning payment to those laboring in the vineyard, he says: “I wish to give this last one as much as I give you” (Matthew XX). In everything arranged by God, the reason is manifest, but the justice of the will is hidden.

“All things have been delivered to me by my Father.”

Therefore I confess to the Father because the Father has delivered all things to me. He does not mean all things concerning the elements, but those who approach the Father through the Son and who previously were rebellious. Concerning all of these he said elsewhere: “Lord, whatever the Father gives me will come to me” (John VI).

Or in this way: [AMBROSE.] When you hear “all things,” you recognize the omnipotent one, not one unlike or degenerate from the Father. But when you hear “delivered,” you confess the Son, to whom all things rightly belong by the nature of one substance—not bestowed as a gift, but possessed by grace.

Note that Christ, insofar as he is human, confesses—that is, gives thanks—to the Father, or rather to the undivided Trinity. Insofar as he himself is the radiance that shone forth from the Father, he offers no thanks above the level of understanding, although he has all things from the Father, because he has them by nature.

“And no one knows the Son except the Father, nor does anyone know the Father except the Son, and the one to whom the Son wills to reveal him.”

Let Eunomius be ashamed, saying that he possesses full knowledge of the Father and the Son. This should not be understood as though the Son could be known by no one except the Father alone. The Father, however, is known not only by the Son but also by those to whom the Son has revealed him. Rather, both clauses must be referred to the words “to whom the Son wills to reveal,” so that we may understand that both are revealed through the Son.

For the Father declares himself through his Word, because he is the light of our mind. [HILARY.] The things delivered to the Son are none other than those that are known only to the Father in him. The things of the Father are known to the Word, the Son, alone; thus, in this secret of mutual knowledge, nothing exists in the Son that is unknowable except what is unknowable in the Father.

Pay attention: when it is said that the Father alone knows the Son, or the Son alone knows the Father, this means only the exclusion of creatures. For the Son is not excluded from knowledge of himself, nor is the Father, who knows himself, excluded; and the Holy Spirit, consubstantial with both, is in no way separated from the full knowledge of either. Hence Paul says: “The Spirit searches all things, even the depths of God” (1 Corinthians II).

“And turning to his disciples, he said: ‘Come to me, all you who labor and are burdened, and I will refresh you.’”

He speaks of the burden of sin, or invites those oppressed by the yoke of the law to the Gospel. In what way is the grace of the Gospel lighter than the law, when in the law adultery is punished, but in the Gospel desire; there homicide, here anger?

In the law actions are required; in the Gospel, the will. Even if a woman does not possess the will, she does not lose her reward: if a virgin is violated against her will, she is received as a virgin according to the Gospel, but according to the law she is rejected as though corrupted.

He says “you who labor” either because of the difficulties of the law or because of the acquisition of riches. “I will refresh you,” that is, I will restore you, promising an eternal kingdom to those relieved of their burdens through the Gospel.

“Take my yoke upon you, and learn from me, because I am gentle and humble in heart, and you will find rest for your souls.”

The yoke is called the Gospel of Christ, joining Jews and gentiles in one faith, so that they may cultivate the soil of their hearts with the plowshare of sacred speech. “Take my yoke upon you,” placing it, as it were, upon the higher part of your mind and honoring it there.

Learn also from my example to be gentle in heart and humble in spirit, lest a serpent lie hidden beneath the appearance of a dove. The humble despise no one; the gentle, continually persevering in gentleness of spirit, injure no one. Thus, through rest of mind, they will at last find everlasting rest for their souls.

“For my yoke is pleasant and my burden is light.”

[HILARY.] What is sweeter than Christ’s yoke? What is lighter than his burden? To become approved, to abstain from crime, to will the good, to refuse the evil, to love everyone, to hate no one, to attain eternal things, not to be captivated by present things, and not to wish to inflict upon another what would be burdensome for oneself to endure.

Although at its narrow beginning the way is constricted, as he says elsewhere, the way that leads to life (Matthew VII), nevertheless in the course of time it is widened by the ineffable sweetness of love. The yoke of faith is pleasant in comparison with the law, because there children are wounded, while here those who are to be saved are washed. The burden of the Gospel is light in comparison with the law, because there adultery is punished by stoning, while here it is cleansed through repentance.

# On Vices and Evil Deeds; Also on Virtues and Good Deeds

“Come to me, all you who labor and are burdened, and I will refresh you” (Matthew XI).

Wearied by labor, weighed down by burdens, and weakened by hunger, come to me. Who come to whom? Prisoners to the door, the sick to the physician, shipwrecked people to the harbor: to the door of light, to the physician of salvation, to the harbor of rest.

Come to the door so that, having gone out, you may see the truth; to the physician so that, once healed, you may recover to health; to the harbor so that, gathered in after labor, you may rest; empty, so that you may be filled with the light of truth; laboring, so that, having obtained rest, you may be helped; burdened with sins, so that you may be relieved of the weight of others.

There are seven capital, or principal, or original vices by which sinners are burdened and weighed down. Scripture calls them capital, principal, or original because they are the head, beginning, and origin of all the others. For all other things arise from these seven vices.

The difference between sins and vices appears to be this: vices are corruptions of the soul, from which, if they are not restrained by reason, sins arise as acts of injustice. When consent is first given to a tempting vice, the act of injustice occurs; this is called sin. Thus vice is the weakness of spiritual corruption, while sin, arising from corruption through consent, is an act of iniquity.

Vice without consent is weakness. Insofar as it is weakness, mercy is owed to it; but insofar as it is restrained from an act of iniquity, it receives reward and a crown. With consent, however, vice becomes guilt: insofar as it is vice, it is evil; insofar as it is voluntary, it is deserving of punishment.

Vice therefore lies in corruption, while sin lies in action. The act of sin is completed by consent alone, even if no outward deed has occurred, because what belongs to iniquity is completed through perverse consent in the will alone, even when the will is forcibly restrained from carrying out what it wishes.

It does everything that belongs to it, and what it does not do beyond that does not belong to it. The fact that it does not do more is not from itself but against itself. Thus the deed is judged to exist in consent alone. The outward action adds to the malice only insofar as it inflames the movement of the will, which is already acting inwardly, toward malice.

Thus vices are the origin of sins, from which works of iniquity are born. As has been said, without consent they incur punishment because they are corruption; with consent they incur guilt because they are voluntary. Insofar as they are original, punishment is exercised in them; insofar as they are voluntary, punishment is owed to them.

They are these: first, pride; second, envy; third, anger; fourth, acedia; fifth, avarice; sixth, gluttony; seventh, lust.

Of these, three strip a person, the fourth scourges the one who has been stripped, the fifth drives out the one who has been scourged, the sixth seduces the one who has been driven out, and the seventh subjects the seduced person to slavery.

Pride takes God away from a person, envy takes away his neighbor, anger takes away himself; acedia scourges the stripped person, avarice drives out the scourged person, gluttony seduces the expelled person, and lust subjects the seduced person to slavery.

The rational soul, in its health, is a solid and whole vessel without any corruption. The vices that enter it spoil and corrupt it in the following ways: through pride it is inflated; through envy it withers; through anger it cracks; through acedia it is broken; through avarice it is scattered; through gluttony it is defiled; through lust it is trampled down and reduced to mud.

Pride is love of one’s own excellence; envy is hatred of another’s happiness; anger is an irrational disturbance of the mind; acedia arises from confusion of mind. Sadness, or weariness, is an immoderate bitterness of spirit by which spiritual joy is extinguished and the mind, through a kind of beginning of despair, is overturned within itself.
