Avarice is an immoderate desire to possess; gluttony is an immoderate desire to eat; lust is an excessive desire to experience pleasure, or a desire for intercourse that boils over beyond measure or against reason.

There are two kinds of pride: one inward and the other outward. Inwardly it is pride; outwardly it is boastfulness. Pride lies in the exaltation of the heart; boastfulness in the display of one’s deeds.

Pride, because it pleases itself, despises the testimony of others; boastfulness, so that it may please itself more, seeks the testimony of others. Therefore boastfulness pretends to gentleness and flattery, while pride shows itself cruel through fear; for pride wishes to be feared, whereas boastfulness wishes to be loved.

Yet both, in what they desire, are proved to glory in themselves disorderly, though in different ways, each finding pleasure in itself. If someone counts pride and boastfulness as one category, he will find seven capital vices, from which all sins—that is, acts of iniquity and works of injustice—arise.

Some sins are called venial, others criminal. Venial sins are those that can scarcely be avoided so that they never occur, and which, when they occur, do not involve much shame or great harm. Criminal sins are those that either cause great harm or bring disgrace, in which either God or one’s neighbor is seriously offended, or the one who commits them is himself defiled.

Such are homicides, adulteries, perjuries, thefts, and similar things that are joined to or contained in these, such as robberies, sacrileges, incest, and other such acts.

Venial sins include slight and passing anger, laughter, and similar things that occur without deliberation on the part of those acting, whether they are rashly brought about through negligence or precipitated through weakness.

But this must be understood inwardly: those who have recovered from such vices and have repented worthily are received by God in seven ways. First, they are received for sponsorship; second, for protection; third, for support; fourth, for reconciliation; fifth, for approval; sixth, for consolation; seventh, for reward.

First, he receives those who will fight against the devil for sponsorship, as though he were pledging himself for them when he trusts in them, just as he undertook the case of blessed Job, as of a combatant, to be defended against the devil.

Some, as though timid and fleeing from the battle in search of rewards, he receives for support, lest they be crushed. Others, rising after a fall, he receives for reconciliation, so that they may be restored. Others, already acting well, he receives through approval, so that they may be rewarded. Others, through good works, he receives for reward, so that they may be glorified. Others, wearied while working, he receives through inward inspiration, so that they may be refreshed and consoled.

# DIVISION

As we said above that vice is one thing and sin, which proceeds from vice, another, so we understand that virtues are one thing and works of righteousness, which arise from them, another.

Virtue is, as it were, the health and integrity of the rational soul; its corruption is called vice. The work of righteousness, however, lies in the movement of the rational mind that proceeds according to the Lord. It rises from the conception of the heart and advances outward until the completion of bodily action.

Many virtues are enumerated in Scripture, but especially those that in the Gospel are arranged, as antidotes or remedies, against the corruption of the seven vices and in the same number: first is humility; second, gentleness; third, composure of mind; fourth, desire for righteousness; fifth, mercy; sixth, purity of heart; seventh, inward peace of mind.

A person lying in sins is sick; the vices are wounds; God is the physician; the gifts of the Holy Spirit are antidotes; the virtues are health; the beatitudes are joys.

Through the gifts of the Holy Spirit, vices are healed; health from vices is the integrity of virtues. The healthy person acts, and the one who acts is rewarded. Thus good works follow virtues, and good works arise from virtues.

Six works of mercy are specially enumerated by the Lord in the Gospel (Matthew XXV), in which the perfection of good works is signified. First is to feed the hungry; second, to give drink to the thirsty; third, to welcome the stranger; fourth, to clothe the naked; fifth, to visit the sick; sixth, to come to the imprisoned and confined.

In these needs every hardship of human life is either comprehended or symbolized. Whoever, for God’s sake, suffers with his neighbor in such needs merits mercy from God in his own necessity.

# THE THIRD SUNDAY IN SEPTUAGESIMA. According to Matthew.

[Column 0843]

[Col. 0843A] “The kingdom of heaven is like a householder who went out early in the morning to hire laborers for his vineyard,” etc. (Matt. 20). The kingdom of heaven—that is, Christ—is compared to a householder who made the first last and the last first. Christ himself, the true householder, caring for the whole human race, continually calls everyone to cultivate the vineyard. When he is not recognized, he is in concealment; but when he is recognized, he goes out to hire laborers, proceeding from concealment into public knowledge. The vineyard is the Church, which, from righteous Abel to the last of the elect, sends forth as many branches as it produces saints. The laborers are preachers, and each one remains steadfast in right faith and obedience to the divine law.

[Col. 0843B] “And having agreed with the laborers for a denarius a day, he sent them into his vineyard.” The agreement was the confirmed promise that they would be restored to the image of God if, by building up the Church, they persevered in the commandments of the Decalogue. The denarius, therefore, which bears the figure of a king—for formerly the king was reckoned by ten coins—plainly signifies both the reward of obedience and the fact that it is given to the laborers on account of observing the Decalogue.

“And going out about the third hour, he saw others standing idle in the marketplace, and he said to them: Go you also into my vineyard, and whatever is just I will give you. And they went.” By the marketplace the world is understood, in which there are calumnies, injuries, disputes, and the difficulties of various business, always full of tumult, and where everything is for sale. Sinners are called dead, [Col. 0843C] not idle. Just as one is called deaf before the Lord who does not hear the things of God but those of the devil, and blind through whose eyes the devil sees rather than God, so whoever lives for the devil is dead to God. A plunderer is not idle but dead. A drunkard and a fornicator are not idle but dead; the one who takes nothing, however, is idle unless he gives from his own possessions to the powerless. Do you wish not to be idle? Take nothing, and give from what is yours for God, so that you may live not for yourself but for God. Do you wish not to be idle? Fast, and give to God what you ought to eat and drink. Do you wish not to be idle? If you are without a wife, do not seek a wife, but practice a life of chastity. If you say, “I cannot abstain,” I show you how to have a wife and still practice a life of chastity: abstain from a menstruating woman and from a pregnant woman; be ashamed to do what animals do not [Col. 0843D] do. Why did the servant who received a mina from his master hear, “Wicked servant” (Matt. 8), and why was he sent to prison? Because he had gained nothing from it. If, then, the one who stood idle in the marketplace will not be unpunished on the day of judgment, what will become of the sinner who loses his mina?

“Again he went out about the sixth and the ninth hour, and did likewise. But about the eleventh hour he went out and found others standing, [Col. 0844A] and said to them: Why do you stand here all day idle? They said to him: Because no one has hired us. He said to them: Go you also into my vineyard.” The first hour signifies Adam, sent into the vineyard, and the remaining patriarchs up to Noah; the third, Noah himself and those who followed him up to Abraham’s circumcision; the sixth, the period from Abraham to Moses, when the law was given; the ninth, Moses and the prophets; the eleventh, the apostles and the people of the Gentiles, who previously stood idle all day, neglecting to labor for salvation throughout the whole time. The law had indeed hired Israel, saying, “Do this and you will live” (Deut. 6; Luke 10), but no one hired the Gentiles. For it was necessary that the Gospel be preached throughout the world and that the Gentiles be saved through the justification of faith.

Alternatively, morning is childhood; the third hour, adolescence advancing upward like the sun; [Col. 0844B] the sixth, youth; the ninth, old age; the eleventh, extreme old age. Accordingly, the laborers of the first hour seem to be Samuel, Jeremiah, and John the Baptist; those of the third, people who began to serve God from puberty; those of the sixth, those who began at mature age; those of the ninth, those who turned toward old age at the decline of life; and those of the eleventh, those in their final old age. Those who remain sluggish until the last age are therefore rightly rebuked for idleness, so that at least at the end they may come to their senses. No one had hired such people, although the ways of life were preached to them, because it belongs to God alone to teach inwardly—the God whom they had not yet obeyed.

“When evening had come, the lord of the vineyard said to his steward”—that is, either the Father says to the Son, or the Son to the Holy Spirit—“Call the laborers and pay them their wage, beginning with the last and ending with the first.” Consider that he pays the wage only in the evening. Therefore, judgment will take place while this present age still endures, for two reasons. First, because the coming blessedness is the reward of righteousness; second, so that sinners may not see blessedness, as the prophet says: “Let the impious be taken away, lest he see the glory of God” (Isa. 26).

“When therefore those who had come about the eleventh hour arrived, they received a denarius each.” Although all the righteous will receive the blessedness of the resurrection, because some will receive it earlier and others later, those are said to receive it first who receive it after only a short time. Thus the last in labor will be first in reward, and the first in labor last in reward. Since that denarius is eternal life, [Col. 0844D] the first will be equal to the last in that reward—Abel and Noah, for example, called at the first or third hour, and the last, who, from the bodily coming of the Lord, hasten forward at the eleventh hour without any delay. They will shine with a diversity of merits, one more and another less; therefore the householder promised to give each whatever would be just. Nevertheless, eternal life will be equal for all, longer for none and shorter for none, because it will have no end.

It is evening for anyone whose life has reached its end. The householder began to pay the denarii to the last, bringing the thief into the rest of paradise before Peter. Although that thief did not come at the eleventh hour by his age, he came late through punishment. Thus those who arrive late are sometimes rewarded before those who were called in childhood but leave their bodies later.

“But when the first came, they thought that they would receive more. Yet they too received a denarius each.” Those called earlier will receive the same Trinity as the Gentiles who have been justified, being conformed to the glory of Christ. When those who had been God’s people from the beginning came first, they thought that the Gentiles, who had previously served idols, would receive less.

[Col. 0845B] “And receiving it, they murmured against the householder, saying: These last have worked one hour, and you have made them equal to us who have borne the burden of the day and the heat.” The ancients, who reached heaven after long periods in hell, receive the denarius as though after a complaint. We, however, receive our reward without complaint, because as soon as we leave the body we receive it without delay. It should be noted that the denarius is not received all at once: the true worshipers of the spiritual vineyard will have a hundredfold in this life, then heaven, and after the judgment a double robe.

Those who receive the denarius do not murmur against the last laborers out of envy of grace, but out of ignorance of the mysteries they murmur against the householder. Their murmuring is therefore a pious inquiry into higher things, of this kind: Why did you delay so long sending the fire of heaven upon the earth and kindling it? Or why did you not reserve us for this time? Or why did the last not have our times with us? Or how is it that the last did not have our times, while we have the last times? Why is an equal reward given for an unequal calling? They complain in many ways such as these.

The burden signifies the work of righteousness; the heat, the desire of the world. This is said because formerly the world prospered for all good people. Thus those who lived then preserved righteousness with greater difficulty, because worldly prosperity is an impediment to the soul. At that time, therefore, the person who could be righteous was greatly good, while the person who did not flee to God was greatly evil, since those of the earlier age saw the world with more adversities. The burden can also be understood as the burdensome commandments of the law; the heat as the burning error of temptations by which evil spirits inflamed the ancients, provoking them to rivalry with the Gentiles.

[Col. 0845D] “But he answered one of them and said: Friend, I do you no wrong. Did you not agree with me for a denarius? Take what is yours and go.”

He is said to have answered one because the occasion for murmuring was equal in all. This friend is understood as the first-formed man and the believers of that time. When he says, “for a denarius,” it is as though he says: You have received the promised wage—that is, my image and likeness. Your reward of merit is not diminished by another’s companionship. [Col. 0846A] What more do you seek? Go; persevere in the righteousness you have obtained.

“I wish to give to this last just as to you. Is it not lawful for me to do what I wish? Or is your eye evil because I am good?” I wish the Gentile people to become your equal and fellow member. Does a judge not have the power either to administer justice or to bestow mercy on whomever he wishes? Therefore take care not to look upon your neighbor with an envious eye because of an occasion supplied by goodness. To me alone, the invisible and immortal King of the ages, be honor and glory forever and ever.

“Thus the last will be first, and the first last.” That is, as has been shown, the last and the first will be made equal. For just as in a crown there is neither beginning nor end, so among the saints, with respect to time, no one in that age is called last and no one first.

“For many are called, but few are chosen.” This does not concern the superior saints but the Gentiles, because many come to the faith and many fill the walls of the Church, but few are brought to the kingdom.

Alternatively, some understand “the first” to mean not only the good but also certain people who began in the vineyard and did not persevere. Out of envy of the last they murmur, like those who, at the beginning of the Church’s birth, set themselves above those called from the Gentiles. Thus, among statements made in common, some refer to the good, such as, “I wish to give you as I give this last.” Other statements concern those who falsely suppose that they will receive the denarius, such as, “And receiving it, they murmured.” Then follows: “Is your eye evil because I am good?”—“The last,” he says, “will be first, and the first last”: the Jews will be turned from the head into the tail, while we will be changed from the tail into the head. Hence Moses says in Deuteronomy: “The stranger who dwells with you will rise above you; he will be the head, and you will be the tail” (Deut. 28). That many of both the last and the first are nevertheless rejected is added in a fearful sentence: “Many are called” to the faith, “but few are chosen” for the kingdom.

SERMON FOR SEPTUAGESIMA

“The torrent will divide the stone of darkness and the shadow of death from the wandering people” (Job 28). The stone is the hardness of the Jews; the darkness is their unbelief. Death is the devil; his shadow is the Gentile people. For just as a shadow conforms to a body, so that people, by imitating the devil, is made like him. The wandering people is the faithful people sighing in the exile of this life. The torrent is the fiery river that proceeds from the face of the Lord, by which the faithful people is separated from the unfaithful at the last judgment.

The torrent will therefore divide the stone of darkness and the shadow of death from the wandering people when the fire of the final judgment separates from the Christian people the Jews, hardened in unbelief, and the Gentiles, conformed to the devil in wickedness, as weeds from wheat; wraps them in the furnace of hell and burns them with unquenchable fire; and receives the people of paradise, no longer exiles, into eternal dwellings.

The faithful people’s wandering in this life was prefigured by the Jewish people, whom Pharaoh had oppressed for a long time with harsh service. Formerly the Hebrew people went down into Egypt when famine afflicted them, but Pharaoh subjected them to cruel slavery. When they cried out to the Lord, he sent Moses to them, who struck Egypt with many plagues and signs and led God’s people through the Red Sea into a land flowing with milk and honey. Egypt here signifies this world, in which the human race wanders from its homeland, paradise, and is brought under the devil’s heavy oppression. When it cries out to God through the righteous, Christ is sent to deliver it; through him the world is shaken by many miracles, and the people are led through the Red Sea—that is, through baptism—back to the homeland of paradise, where milk and honey overflow, meaning an abundance of every good.

This wandering was likewise prefigured by the same people while they remained seventy years in Babylonian captivity. For Nebuchadnezzar, king of Babylon, besieged and destroyed Jerusalem and led the people captive to Babylon. There they lived in sorrow for seventy years; they did not sound the song of joy but hung their instruments upon the willows and sat beside them weeping. When the seventy years were ended, they returned to Jerusalem and celebrated Passover with joy. Afterwards, when their wives and sons came, they had double joy.

All these things, beloved, look toward the present day; all these things prefigured our times. Jerusalem is paradise; Nebuchadnezzar is the devil; Babylon is this world. Nebuchadnezzar led the people captive to Babylon, and the devil deceived the human race into this world, where it hung its instruments upon the willows and, sitting, poured forth tears. Willows readily grow together with the earth and readily become green again when cut. The willows are lovers of the world, who have sent their roots into earthly things, from which transitory goods flow to them according to their desire. Upon these willows the righteous hang their instruments, because they abandon worldly joys. They sit and lament because, in humility, they groan with great sorrow over the destruction of such people.

The instruments can also signify heavenly teaching, which is hung upon the willows when spiritual teaching is withdrawn from worldly people because it is despised by them. The seventy years during which the people were afflicted in Babylon signify seven thousand years, during which the human race wanders in this life. For just as the whole creation was ordered in the first seven days, so this world is believed to extend through seven thousand years. Therefore, if you divide seven thousand years into seventy hundreds of years and take a tenth of a year from each hundred years, you will have seventy years. Further, if from seventy years you take a tenth, making a day correspond to a year, you will count seventy days. These are the days in which the Church does not sound the other song, because it recalls the seventy years of captivity, which prefigure the seven thousand years of our wandering.

This is also why Genesis is now read: in it the human being’s fall from paradise into this world is described. This time is called Septuagesima because from today until the second Saturday after Easter there are seventy days, when the two alleluias are sung. The people returning to Jerusalem rejoice with gladness because the souls of the faithful will then enter into the joy of the Lord. When the world’s term has ended, and they receive their wives and sons—that is, their bodies and works—they will then exult in the true alleluia, because body and soul together will rejoice eternally in glory.

DIVISION

Because today, beloved, we have laid aside the song of joy and taken up the song of sorrow, I wish briefly to recount to you from the books of the Gentiles how you ought to avoid the melody of worldly pleasures, so that you may first resound with the angels in heaven in sweet harmony. Anyone should lift a gem found in mud out of the clay and set it in royal adornment. Thus, if anything useful is found by us in the books of the Gentiles, it is fitting that it be turned toward the edification of the Church, the bride of Christ.

The wise men of the world write that there were three Sirens on an island in the sea and that they sang an exceedingly sweet song in different modes. One sang with her voice, another with a flute, and the third with a lyre. They had women’s faces, but the wings and claws of birds. By the sweetness of their song they halted all passing ships, tore apart sailors overcome by sleep, and sank the ships into the sea.

When a certain Ulysses needed to sail past that place, he ordered himself bound to the ship’s mast, while his companions stopped their ears with wax. Thus he escaped the danger unharmed and sank the Sirens beneath the waves.

These things are mystical, beloved, although written by enemies of Christ. By this sea the world is understood, tossed by continual storms of tribulation. The island is worldly joy, which is interrupted by frequent sorrows, just as the shore is struck by repeated waves. The three Sirens, who by their sweet song charm sailors and turn them to sleep, are the three pleasures that soften human hearts toward vices and lead them into the sleep of death.

The one who sings with a human voice is avarice, which sings such melodies to its hearers: “You must gather many things so that we may spread the fame of your name everywhere, visit the Lord’s sepulcher and other places, restore churches, and assist your poor relatives.” With such a deadly song it soothes the miser’s heart until sleep overcomes him; then it tears his flesh apart. The waves devour the ship, because this wretched man is violently torn away from his vices by sufferings and plunged into eternal flame.

The one who sings with the flute is boastfulness, which utters songs such as these: “You are young and noble; you ought to show yourself distinguished before everyone. You should spare none of your enemies, but kill all whom you are able to overcome; then they will call you a good soldier.” To another it sings: “You ought to go to Jerusalem and give many alms; then you will become famous, and everyone will call you good.” To converts it sings as follows: “You ought often to fast, often to pray, and to sing in a loud voice; then you will hear everyone praise you as holy with one harmonious voice.” It sounds such a song into the empty heart until the abyss of death devours the wretched person, empty of goodness.

The one who produces melody on the lyre is lust, which sings such tunes to its followers: “You are a young man; you may play with whatever girls you wish and correct yourself later in old age. This one shines with notable beauty; that one is powerful in great wealth. If you have her, you will gain great profit, and nevertheless you will be able to save your soul well.” In this way it softens the lustful heart until suddenly the whirlwind of Cocytus overtakes and swallows him in death.

They had women’s faces because nothing so alienates the human mind as the love of women. They had the wings of birds because worldly desire is always unstable. At one moment people desire this or that; at another they crave something else. They also had birds’ claws because those whom they drag toward sins they tear with pains and bring down to the torments of hell.

Ulysses is said to have been wise. He sails past unharmed because the Christian people, truly wise in the ship of the Church, floats upon the sea of this world. The fear of the Lord binds it to the ship’s tree—that is, to the cross of Christ. With wax, meaning Christ’s incarnation, it seals the hearing of its companions so that they may turn their hearts away from vices and desires and seek only heavenly things. The Sirens are submerged because the Christian is fortified by the strength of the Spirit against desires. The people escape the danger unharmed because after victory they reach the joy of the saints.

SERMON ON SEPTUAGESIMA, SEXAGESIMA, AND QUINQUAGESIMA

Beloved, today’s reading admonishes us how to obtain the victory of which we spoke above. For it says: “Do you not know that those who run in the stadium all run, but one receives the prize?” (1 Cor. 9). Among the Greeks it was customary for a prize to be set before the runners, but it was given not to all who ran, only to the one who first arrived.

The kingdom of heaven is set before us as the prize. Holy Scripture urges us to run toward it with all our strength, because it is granted not to all who run by faith, but only to those who persevere in good works to the end.

They had another custom: naked and anointed with oil, they wrestled together, and the victors were crowned with gold and laurel. We, beloved, have been anointed with the oil of chrism; therefore, naked of vices, we must wrestle with the devil, because “our struggle is not against flesh and blood, but against the assault of vices and demons” (Eph. 6). If, therefore, we conquer lust, anger, hatred, or any other vice, we will have a crown of gold and laurel, because we will receive the splendor of eternal brightness in the ever-flourishing paradise.

Why this Sunday is called Septuagesima, the next Sexagesima, and another Quinquagesima must be carefully explained. It is said that Telesphorus, pope of the city of Rome, added a seventh week, which he called Quinquagesima from the sound of the preceding number, namely forty. When righteous men added an eighth week, they likewise called it Sexagesima from the sound of the preceding number—not because there were sixty days until the resurrection. Others, adding a ninth week, called it Septuagesima from the sound of the earlier number. If a tenth were now added, it would receive not the name Decagesima but Octogesima, named from the preceding number.

Let us see what purpose those who added these weeks had. Those who added the seventh intended to remove seven Sundays; thus forty-two remained, which were also celebrated by some. Those who added the eighth intended to remove eight Sundays and eight Thursdays. With these sixteen removed, forty remained, so that they might fast as many days as the Lord did.

Similarly, those who added the ninth intended to remove nine Sundays, as many Thursdays, and as many Saturdays. Sundays were removed because of the resurrection, Thursdays because of the ascension, and Saturdays so that they would not keep the Sabbath with the Jews.

Lent ends on the Lord’s Supper, when the typological Passover was celebrated. Quinquagesima ends on the first day of the week, the very day of the resurrection; Sexagesima on the fourth day of the week, in the middle of the solemnity of Easter; Septuagesima on the seventh day of the week, when the white garments are laid aside.

There are six days between the end of Lent and Quinquagesima; six between Quinquagesima and Sexagesima; and six between Sexagesima and Septuagesima. Six taken three times make eighteen, in which a mystery is found. For the divided double is compared with the simple. By the double is signified our double death; by the simple, the single death of the Lord, by whose single death our double death was condemned. If he had tasted the double death, he would have freed us from none.

Between the end of Lent and Quinquagesima there are two days, and likewise between the others. For three times two make six. In this the preceding division and the preceding mystery are found. Indeed, if you examine the general meaning of the spiritual Scriptures, a mystery is found in everything.

Sunday in Septuagesima

“He went out who sows, to sow his seed,” etc. (Matt. 18). He speaks many things in parables, because if he spoke everything parabolically, his hearers would depart without benefit. A parable is a comparison made under some likeness between things differing in nature.

The sower who went out to sow is understood as the Son of God, who, going out from the bosom of the Father, came into the world to sow among human beings, through himself and through his followers, the word of truth that he had seen with the Father.

“And while he was sowing, some fell beside the road, and it was trampled, and the birds of heaven came and ate it.” Some fell—understand, grains or seeds—beside the road. The road is the mind worn down and dried out by the constant passage of evil thoughts. There the seed perishes in two ways: it is trampled by the passage of carnal thoughts, and demons eat it—that is, they seize and swallow it with a certain pleasure—so that the mind retains no memory of what it neglected to accomplish. Demons are called birds of heaven either because they are of a heavenly and spiritual nature or because they dwell in the air.

“Other seeds fell upon rocky ground, where they did not have much earth. And immediately they sprang up, because they had no depth of earth. When the sun rose, they were scorched, and because they had no root they withered.” The seeds that fall upon rocky ground—that is, upon earth abounding in stones—can indeed germinate quickly, but the root is not fixed because the earth has no depth, no profundity, and therefore dries up in the sun’s heat.

Here the rock signifies the hardness of a stubborn mind, the earth the gentleness of an obedient soul, and the sun the fervor of a persecutor. The seed of the word falls upon rock when the sweetness of promises moves an untamed heart not penetrated by the plow of true faith. There it finds no moisture, as Luke says (Luke 13)—that is, no love of virtue. It immediately springs up only through recollection, not through efficacy, because it has no depth of earth in the profundity of a good heart where it could be firmly established.

When the sun rises—that is, the heat of persecution or of any tribulation—it is scorched, meaning that it comes to dryness, and dries up completely because it has no root of firm desire. The depth of the earth is the uprightness of a mind instructed by heavenly disciplines and tested in temptations.

“Other seeds fell among thorns, and the thorns grew up and choked them.” Other seeds fell among thorns—that is, between thorns. The word of God likewise falls among thorns when it is received by a heart occupied by care and anxiety over riches. Then the riches, understood as thorns, multiply and occupy the mind, so that spiritual fruit cannot advance in it.

“Other seeds fell upon good earth and yielded fruit, some a hundredfold, some sixtyfold, and some thirtyfold.” As there were three varieties in bad earth, so there are three in good earth. One person is good, another better, and another best.

Since the number ten is usually taken for perfection, because the keeping of the law is contained in the ten commandments, the hundred, which arises through the multiplication of ten, is assigned to great perfection. The good earth is made fruitful a hundredfold when the gentle and teachable heart acquires, through love of neighbor, the active life, and through love of God, the contemplative life, and is adorned with the perfection of spiritual virtues.

Because the world’s adornment was completed in the number six, the sixtyfold fruit appropriately signifies the perfection of good action in the fulfillment of the Decalogue. The thirtyfold fruit signifies the fulfillment of the law through faith in the Holy Trinity.

Having said these things, he cried out: “Whoever has ears to hear, let him hear.” Wherever this admonition is inserted, it shows that what is said is mystical and must be sought more attentively: whoever has ears of the heart—that is, understanding of mind—let him hear, meaning that he should understand these words spiritually.

“And his disciples came to him and said: Why do you speak to them in parables? He answered and said to them: Because it has been given to you to know the mysteries of the kingdom of heaven, but to them it has not been given.” The mysteries of the kingdom of heaven will be revealed in the secrets of Scripture to you, who are with me, and to your followers who enter into me through spiritual understanding. “But for those who are outside,” as Mark writes (Mark 4), “everything is in parables.”

By saying “outside,” he means not only those who neither cared to enter the boat nor wished to know the truth, but also all who resemble them, following bodily senses alone and understanding nothing spiritually. Note that, when it is said that everything is done in parables for those who are outside, this suggests that parables exist not only in the Lord’s words but also in his deeds—that is, signs of mystical realities, which the perverse do not penetrate.

He explained everything separately to his disciples. They were worthy to hear the mysteries in the innermost recesses of wisdom, because, after removing the tumult of thoughts, they remained in the solitude of virtues.

“Therefore I speak to them in parables, because seeing they do not see, and hearing they do not hear, neither do they understand; and in them is fulfilled the prophecy of Isaiah, which says (Isa. 6): You will hear with hearing and will not understand; and seeing you will see, and will not see.”

“Seeing they do not see”: that is, those who presume by their own cleverness that they see are deprived of spiritual understanding. “Hearing,” while remaining outside, they do not hear in the heart, which means not understanding. Hence Isaiah: With outward hearing you will hear the preaching of Christ and will not understand; and seeing, you will often see his miracles with outward sight, but you will not see with the eye of the mind.

“The heart of this people has become fat, and they have heard heavily with their ears, and they have closed their eyes, lest they should ever see with their eyes, hear with their ears, understand with their heart, be converted, and I heal them” (ibid.). The heart of the Jews is said to have become fat through an abundance of wickedness. Therefore they received the Lord’s words without gratitude, which was to hear heavily.

They are said to have closed their eyes so that we would not suppose that the fault belonged to nature rather than to the will. Although they were able to think and understand, they turned away the gaze of the mind out of envy, and thus they themselves became the cause of God’s abandoning and blinding them. Hence John: “Therefore they could not believe, because Isaiah said: He has blinded their eyes so that they may not see” (John 12; Isa. 11).

Because Isaiah, in the spirit of one who foreknew all things, foretold the blinding of the Jews, they could not believe—not because they were unable to believe by necessity, so that they would have no fault, but because they were unwilling. They could not believe because, ignorant of God’s righteousness, they wished to establish their own. They are blinded and hardened because, by denying divine help, they are not helped.

That they are said to be unable to believe is as much a fault of the human will as the statement that God cannot deny himself (2 Tim. 2) is praise of the divine will. Since they were unwilling to open their eyes and ears to the truth, they deserved never to see with their eyes, hear with their ears, or understand with their heart; that is, they would neither see nor hear, nor be converted to repentance, nor be healed of their sins so as to receive innocence.

Or it may be understood in this way: Many did not hear the parables because they were blinded, and they were blinded because they had a heart made fat by pride. The blinding and obscurity of the parables became an occasion preventing them from ever—that is, at some time—turning more beneficially through him who is “terrible in his counsels toward the sons of men” (Ps. 65), showing mercy to whom he wishes and justly abandoning whom he wishes (Rom. 9).

It was not because they failed to understand obscure statements that they did not believe in him and then crucified him. After the resurrection, however, terrified by the miracles, they were pierced by remorse for the guilt of a greater crime. Having received pardon, they burned with a greater love.

Of others the Lord says (1 Cor. 14): “I speak to them in other tongues and with other lips”—that is, the manifest teaching of the apostles—“and even so they will not hear me.” Of these, however, he can say: “Even so they will hear me.”

On Septuagesima, Sexagesima, Quinquagesima, and Quadragesima
The number seventy is perfected by the same perfection as the number fifty. For ten times seven make seventy. The number forty has an affinity with sixty, because struggle cannot exist without the perfection of good works, nor perfection without struggle. Fifty likewise has an affinity with seventy, signifying the rest of mind and body. For it is written: “Individual robes were given to the saints, and it was said to them: Rest and endure until the number of your brothers is fulfilled” (Rev. VI). Individual robes were given to those who presently possess rest of mind in hope. But when the number of their brothers has been fulfilled, two robes will be given, because then they will possess rest of mind and body, as it is written: “In their own land they shall possess double” (Deut. XXI).

We observe the period of Septuagesima as a figure of the seventy years during which the children of Israel were afflicted in Babylon. Just as they, before the seventy years had ended, returned in part and were somewhat consoled, so we also, when the seventy days have ended, although we do not completely turn the mourning of repentance into joy—that is, on the day of the Lord’s resurrection, although our Septuagesima extends to the following Saturday—will be consoled. And just as the children of Israel had no complete peace before the seventieth year, so neither shall we, although through baptism or repentance we return to the heavenly Jerusalem, receive complete freedom before the Sabbath, when the souls of the saints receive eternal rest.

Jeremiah shows that the Lord wishes us to cease from the voice of joy as long as we remain in Babylon, saying: “And I will cause the voices of joy and gladness to cease from you” (Jer. VII). Therefore alleluia is not sung among us at that time, nor the sweetest hymn of the angels, “Glory to God in the highest,” since these are heavenly songs. Hence John says in the Apocalypse: “After this I heard, as it were, a loud voice of many trumpets in heaven saying: Alleluia” (Rev. XIX). Instead of alleluia, however, the Tract is sung, which is pleasing to the ears; but alleluia, on account of the honor of the first language, is more splendid.

For the seventy years of captivity, which we have changed into seventy days, fasting was practiced among the Jews. Hence the Lord says through Zechariah: “When you fasted and mourned during these seventy years, did you really fast for me?” (Jas. VII.) The Greeks sanctify the coming week by their fast. Our clergy, on the authority of Pope Telesphorus, who established a fast of seven weeks before Easter, sanctify the third [week] by their own [fast]. Yet the director of the liturgy on the preceding Sunday, which is called Septuagesima, requires a greater change than the one we make. In establishing its liturgy, he announced fasting in tribulation in the first prayer of the Mass, saying: “That we, who are justly afflicted for our sins …” In the Introit he says: “The groans of death surrounded me, the pains of hell” (Ps. XVII). Because of these pains we cannot rejoice and be secure, but must prepare ourselves for battle, as the Apostle says: “Everyone who competes in the contest abstains from everything” (I Cor. IX). According to Ambrose, our struggle is against all those things that the same discipline has taught must be avoided because of the vices. War is coming; let us abstain from those things that hinder our battle. Hence the director of the liturgy seems to wish the period of Septuagesima to be a time of mourning, as the Introit and Gradual indicate.

The number sixty is perfect because it arises from six. Six is perfect because it signifies the perfection of good works. For God worked for six days, and in the sixth age of the world he came, and so forth. It is rightly perfect, because the souls who are perfect in good works are signified by this number. Concerning the peaceful man it is written: “There are sixty queens and eighty concubines, and maidens without number” (Song VI). Those who stand in the perfection of good works are called queens. Those who fall somewhat short of perfection are designated by the name concubines, while those who are only in the faith are called maidens.

In Sexagesima we are surrounded by the greatest tribulations, as though there were no place of escape. We have sold ourselves under sin; within us there is no power to free ourselves. Hence it is said in the first prayer: “O God, who see that we subsist in no strength of our own.” Therefore, as though doubting whether the Lord is with us, in the Introit we say: “Arise; why do you sleep, O Lord?” (Ps. XLIII.) In the Epistle we are strengthened by the Apostle to seek a way of escape from captivity and to despise the masters who hold us for destruction. Indignantly he says concerning those who yield to evils: “You gladly tolerate fools, although you yourselves are wise” (II Cor. XI).

Thus, ascending from tribulation to seek our own Lord, we say: “Let the nations know that your name is God” (II Macc. I). The Tract, “You have shaken,” shows the earth shaken by the conscience of sins. After the earth has been shaken, seed is introduced. In Septuagesima we were rebuked because we stood idle; we were led to cultivate the vineyard. In Sexagesima, however, we cast the seed.

This period extends to the Wednesday in Easter, on which the saints are called to receive the kingdom. We ought to run toward it throughout Sexagesima. For six multiplied by ten completes sixty. The number ten refers to the reward of works, while six refers to their perfection. Therefore, if anyone seeks the reward of works through perfection, he will receive the kingdom that is promised to us on the Wednesday in Easter.

## DIVISION

The number fifty is no less perfect because it arises from seven. Seven times seven make forty-nine. If you add one, they make fifty. The fiftieth year was called the jubilee, that is, the year of remission, in which every possession returned to its original owner, and every slave went out free; neither ox nor donkey worked. If the earth produced anything of its own accord, it was given to the poor.

The period of Quinquagesima stands at the third stage. Previously we doubted whether the Lord was near us; now we hold fast to him and say: “Be for me a protecting God and a place of refuge” (Ps. XXX). We pray to him to be the leader of our army, saying: “You will be my leader and nourish me” (ibid.). We are already on campaign. Hence the Apostle also indicates with what weapons we should be armed: “Now these three remain: faith, hope, and charity” (I Cor. XIII). Concerning them he says in another Epistle: “Taking up the shield of faith in all things” (Eph. VI), and what follows.

God is the triumphant commander of our army. To him it is said: “You are the God who works wonders” (Ps. LXXVI). The Tract, however, commands us to serve the Lord, because he made us—not the one to whom we sold ourselves.

In the sixty we sow; in the fifty we gather fruit. For what did the blind man seek from the Lord except to enjoy light? He sought fruit and found fruit. This moon touches the day of Easter. Just as the number six demonstrates the perfection of good works, so the number fifty signifies all the good works that are completed through the five bodily senses. Five times ten make fifty. If anyone, through outward administration, has fulfilled the ten words of the Law in the Holy Spirit, let him not doubt that he will attain to fellowship in the blessed resurrection celebrated at the Lord’s Easter.

Through the Sabbath we come to the Lord’s day; so also, by fulfilling the Law through the sevenfold Spirit, we come to the resurrection.

There are three stages of the three offices, because we have advanced as far as this point. The first contains the mourning of captives who do not wish to remain under the dominion of vices. The second demonstrates the desire for flight, provided that the Lord is willing to receive them as his own and not reject them from himself. The third discusses the plan of escape, already confident of acceptance. According to the words of the Introit, it obtains good counsel.

We have spoken of three stages of those striving toward battle; similarly, we speak of three articles of triumph: the first, the fourth, and the seventh day of the week. Through these same articles the people of Israel attained complete freedom. The first return took place under Zerubbabel as leader and Jesus the high priest. The second return occurred under Ezra, as Ezra himself records; but the walls of Jerusalem had not yet been rebuilt, and those who had remained behind and had been left from the captivity were in affliction. The third return took place under the same leader, for it is written: “The king had sent commanders of the army and cavalry” (II Esd. II), and shortly afterward: “And I came to Jerusalem, and I was there for three days” (ibid.). Afterwards Nehemiah built the temple.

The number forty likewise signifies the struggle of the Church. It is perfect because it arises from four, which signifies the perfection of the whole creation. In the forty, some part of the battle has been completed. It tells us whom we invoked as our protector during Lent: “He will call upon me, and I will answer him,” and what follows. The Epistle says: “At an acceptable time I heard you”; and in the Responsory: “The angel of the Lord, guard us.” In the Tract: “We are surrounded by the shield of truth.” In the Gospel we advance toward triumph, so that we may say to the enemy: “Go, Satan, into destruction.”

From the Sunday mentioned above until baptism, forty-two days are counted. These correspond to the forty-two encampments of the children of Israel when they went out from the land of Egypt toward the promised land. The first encampment was called Ramesse, that is, “movement” or “thunder”; the second, Soccoth, that is, “tabernacle”; the third, Etham, that is, “strength” or “perfection”; the fourth, Phihahiroth, that is, “mouth of nobles”; the fifth, Mara, that is, “bitterness”; the sixth, Elim, that is, “strong rams”; the seventh, the Red Sea; the eighth, Sin, that is, “bush,” or “hatred,” or “help”; the ninth, Dephcaphah, that is, “striking”; the tenth, Alus, that is, “firmament”; the eleventh, Raphidim, that is, “the dissolution of the strong” or “the relaxation of hands”; the twelfth, Sinai, that is, “reddish”; the thirteenth, the Graves of Lust; the fourteenth, Hazeroth, that is, “bonds” or “discipline”; the fifteenth, Rithmah, that is, “sound” or “juniper”; the sixteenth, Rimmon-parez, that is, “division of the pomegranate”; the seventeenth, Libnah, that is, “brick”; the eighteenth, Rissah, which is translated “bridles”; the nineteenth, Kehelathah, that is, “assembly”; the twentieth, Shepher, that is, “beauty”; the twenty-first, Haradah, that is, “miracle”; the twenty-second, Makheloth, that is, “gathering”; the twenty-third, Tahath, that is, “terror”; the twenty-fourth, Terah, that is, “military service” or “pasture”; the twenty-fifth, Mithkah, that is, “sweetness”; the twenty-sixth, Hashmonah, that is, “haste”; the twenty-seventh, Moseroth, that is, “bond” or “discipline of the age”; the twenty-eighth, Bene-jaakan, that is, “sons of necessity”; the twenty-ninth, Hor-hagidgad, that is, “messenger,” or “girding,” or “slaughter”; the thirtieth, Jotbathah, that is, “goodness”; the thirty-first, Abronah, that is, “passage”; the thirty-second, Ezion-geber, that is, “the wood of a man”; the thirty-third, Sin, which is Kadesh, that is, “holy”; the thirty-fourth, Hor at the mountain; the thirty-fifth, Zalmonah, that is, “little image”; the thirty-sixth, Punon, that is, “all”; the thirty-seventh, Oboth, that is, “image,” or “spirit-mediums”; the thirty-eighth, Iye-abarim, that is, “heap of stones”; the thirty-ninth, Dibon, that is, “strongly”; the fortieth, Almon-diblathaim, that is, “contempt of the fig-cakes”; the forty-first, Abarim in the mountains opposite Nebo, that is, “among the mountains of those crossing over”; Nebo means “conclusion”; and the forty-second, the plains of Moab above the Jordan.

These are the forty-two encampments recorded in the forty-two days. They also correspond to the generations of Christ, with Jeconiah counted twice, and Christ himself. Therefore it is fitting that one advances toward the heavenly homeland by the same number of encampments by which the children of Israel came to the promised land. And fittingly, those who pass over to Christ arrive at him through baptism by the same number by which Christ deigned to come to us.

## SUNDAY IN QUINQUAGESIMA. According to Luke.

[Col. 0855]

“Jesus took his twelve disciples and said to them: ‘Behold, we are going up to Jerusalem, and everything that has been written about the Son of Man will be fulfilled. For he will be handed over to the Gentiles, mocked, scourged, and spat upon. And after they have scourged him, they will kill him, and on the third day he will rise’” (Luke XVIII).

If the apostles, although so often forewarned of the Lord’s death, nevertheless abandoned him when he was seized, how much more would they have been scandalized if they had not been forewarned? Therefore he frequently foretold to them both the punishment of his Passion and the glory of his resurrection, so that when they saw him dying, they would not doubt that he would also rise. This he demonstrated through the predictions of the prophets, for the destruction of the heretics who would arise in the Church.

“And they understood none of these things. This saying was hidden from them, and they did not understand what was being said.”

We read in the Gospel according to John (John XII) that when he said, “If I am lifted up from the earth, I will draw all things to myself,” the crowd replied and said: “We have heard from the Law that the Christ remains forever; how then do you say, ‘The Son of Man must be lifted up’?” What, then, is the reason that the disciples cannot grasp the mystery of the Lord’s Passion, repeated so many times to them, while the Jews, at one statement so obscurely expressed that the evangelist says it requires exposition—“But this,” he says, “he spoke signifying by what death he was going to die”—immediately understand that the exaltation of the cross is meant? It is because the disciples most greatly desired to see his life and could not bear to hear of his death, since they knew him not only as an innocent man but also as true God. They thought that he could in no way die. But when he spoke to them about his Passion, they thought that he was speaking to them in parables.

“And it happened that, as he approached Jericho, a certain blind man was sitting beside the road begging. When he heard the crowd passing by, he asked what this was. They told him that Jesus the Nazarene was passing by.”

What Luke said of one blind man, Matthew said of two, beginning in this way: “As Jesus was going out from Jericho, a great crowd followed him” (Matt. XX). There were many robbers in Jericho, who were accustomed to attack and wound those going down from Jerusalem to Jericho. For this reason the Lord came with his disciples to free the wounded.

“And behold, two blind men, one of whom was Bartimaeus, the son of Timaeus, sitting beside the road, heard that Jesus the Nazarene was passing by and cried out, saying: ‘Lord, have mercy on us, Son of David’” (Matt. XX; Mark X).

Mark’s silence concerning the other blind man is resolved in the same way as the question about the two possessed by a legion of demons in the region of the Gerasenes was resolved. One of the two blind men was evidently especially famous, since he even mentioned his father’s name. Although Luke recounts the event concerning a blind man in exactly the same way, it should nevertheless be understood that he records a similar miracle in the case of the other blind man.

“But the crowd rebuked them so that they would be silent. But they cried out all the more, saying: ‘Lord, have mercy on us, Son of David.’”

Such is the nature of faith: the more it is forbidden, the more it is inflamed. For the power of faith is secure amid dangers.

“And Jesus stood and called them and said: ‘What do you want me to do for you?’ They said to him: ‘Lord, that our eyes may be opened.’”

The Son of David, that is, according to human nature, cannot illuminate the blind; but the Son of God, that is, according to divine nature, can illuminate them. Therefore he asks what they want. Then they no longer said, “Lord, Son of David,” but only: “Lord, that our eyes may be opened.” As long as they said “Son of David,” their healing was suspended; as soon as they said only “Lord,” it was infused. He also asks this in order to stir the heart to prayer, because he wishes us to ask from him what he foreknows he will grant; or he asks for this reason, so that we may believe that no one can be saved except one who confesses.

“Moved with pity, Jesus touched their eyes, and immediately they saw, and they followed him, glorifying God. And all the people, when they saw it, gave praise to God.”

He touched their eyes bodily, not by a word, because they had called him the Son of David; he healed them as God, because they believed. For when Jesus is passing by, he hears the blind; when he stands, he illuminates them, because through his humanity he sympathizes with our blindness, but through the power of his divinity he pours into us the light of grace.

The one who sees and follows Jesus as he passes by is the person who performs the good that he understands by contemplating him. Such a person both advances and kindles others to the praise of God. The people praise God not only for the gift of light that was obtained, but also for the merit of the faith that obtained it. Therefore they praise him not only because he illuminates powerfully and mercifully, but also because he hears the cry of firmly crying faith.

Typically, those who had not yet been able to say, “In your light we shall see light” (Ps. XXXV), are called blind. He says that they were beside the road because they seemed to possess knowledge of the Law, but did not know the way, which is Christ. Some understand these to be the Pharisees and Sadducees; others, the two peoples, one of whom possessed the written Law and the other the natural law. If the blind refer to the Jews, then the crowd is to be understood as the Gentiles; but if they refer to both peoples, the crowd consisted of both peoples.

Alternatively, according to some, the blind signify two peoples from the nations, one from Ham and the other from Japheth. They were blind because the light of the Only-Begotten had not appeared to them. The Gentiles heard of Jesus’ passing, as the apostles announced it through the testimonies of the prophets.

When he had gone out from Jericho—that is, from this world—for Jericho is interpreted as “moon,” through which the decline of our mortality is understood, the Lord, according to Luke, restored light to the blind as he approached Jericho, because before his Passion he preached only to the Jewish people. Going out from Jericho, therefore, he illuminated the blind, because after his resurrection and ascension he first disclosed through the apostles to Jews and Gentiles the mysteries of the eternal Divinity and of the humanity he had assumed.

Mark, who writes that one man was illuminated, refers to the salvation of the Gentiles, whose blindness was the later one. Matthew rightly writes that two were illuminated for the Hebrews, since he knew that knowledge of God would reach the Gentiles. Hence he also reports that a donkey and its colt were brought together to the Lord (Matt. XX), whereas the other three evangelists mention only the donkey, since they were writing for the Church of the Gentiles.

According to Mark, the Lord calls to himself the blind man who is crying out, when he entrusts the word of faith through holy preachers to the people of the Gentiles, who desire knowledge of the truth. They say with the prophet: “Draw near to him, and be enlightened” (Ps. XXXIII). And again: “Rise, you who sleep, and arise from the dead, and Christ will give you light” (Eph. V). By the garment understand possessions and the restraints of the world.

### Bede on Luke

When our Creator approaches Jericho, the blind man returns to the light, because, when the Divinity assumes the weakness of our flesh, the human race receives again the light of eternal brightness that it had lost. The blind man sits beside the road when he begins to believe in the one who says: “I am the way” (John XIV). He begs when he prays. Hence it follows: “And he cried out.”

Those who go before Jesus as he comes and rebuke the blind signify the tumult of carnal vices, which scatter our thoughts and disturb the voices of our hearts in prayer, lest Jesus draw near to illuminate the heart. Often the phantasms of the sins we have committed confront the heart and disturb the soul; but then we must devote ourselves more ardently to the cry of prayer. When phantasms appear, we perceive to some extent that Jesus is passing by; but when we persist vigorously in prayer, then Jesus draws near to us, and the lost light is restored.

## SUNDAY IN QUINQUAGESIMA

[Col. 0859]

“How great is the abundance of your sweetness, O Lord, which you have hidden for those who fear you” (Ps. XXX).

Truly, beloved, great and immense is the abundance of sweetness in which the righteous overflow, enjoying every delight. This sweetness is now hidden from those who fear God, but then it is perfected for those who hope in him, when, in the joy of the Lord, they will see the King of glory face to face in his beauty, and, themselves glorified, will shine like the sun.

To arrive at this glorification, a ladder is erected for us today, by which the faithful reach the summit of heaven. This ladder is charity, through which the humility of the Church strives toward the heights of heaven. The sides of this ladder are the two commandments of love: love of God and love of neighbor. The steps inserted between these sides are the various virtues through which the commandments of charity are fulfilled. Whoever climbs rightly by them will see the face of the Lord—which is charity—in rejoicing.

Fifteen steps are constructed, because heavenly things are sought through the fifteen branches of charity. Hence in the Lord’s temple one ascended to the sanctuary by fifteen steps, because the one climbing this ladder is lifted up to Christ, the sanctuary of the heavenly temple. Fifteen psalms are also entitled “Songs of Ascents,” by which these virtues are taught, through which the blessed ascend to heaven. Fifteen is three times five, because through faith in the Holy Trinity we ought to fulfill works of charity through our five senses.

The first step of this ladder is patience, in which the eternal wisdom of God teaches souls to possess themselves. We secure our footing on this step when we patiently endure injuries and insults for the love of Christ. He himself patiently endured reproaches, scourges, and death for us, and has restored the rewards of enduring glory to those who imitate him.

The second step woven into the ladder is kindness, through which the dignity of angelic fellowship is acquired. We set our foot on this step when we repay evils not with evils but with good, and generously provide our neighbors with what they need, according to our ability. For Christ repaid his crucifiers with good for evil, namely eternal life for his Passion, and grants the same to those who imitate him.

The third step inserted is piety, through which the sweet satisfaction of the citizens above is obtained. On this step the pious mind is exalted as it climbs, but it does not envy the happiness of others. “Through the devil’s envy death entered the world, and those who belong to his party imitate him” (Wis. II).

The fourth step is simplicity, through which the abundance of heavenly joy is entered. We place our foot on this step when we act neither wrongly nor deceitfully; that is, when we subtract nothing from the service of faith and do good not for popular approval but solely for God’s sake.

The fifth step of the ladder is humility, through which angelic exaltation is reached. The mind climbing this step is strengthened if it is not puffed up by the knowledge it has received and remembers that the Lord resists the proud but gives grace to the humble.

The sixth step is contempt for the world, through which the wealth of the heavenly kingdom is acquired. On this step the glorious soul rejoices if it is not ambitious, because “the mighty will suffer mighty torments” (Wis. VI). If the Lord should wish to teach it, “Friend, go up higher” (Luke XIV), it should not refuse to undertake the Lord’s light burden, so that it may benefit its brothers by word and example.

The seventh step is voluntary poverty, for which abundance of glory and riches is received in the house of the Lord. A person fixes his footprints on this step when he does not seek what is useful only to himself, but what is useful to everyone and pertains to the praise of Christ. Such a person should climb joyfully, because God, in his sweetness, has made provision for the poor (Ps. LXVII).

The eighth step is peace, which is the torch of eternal light. On this step the mind is strengthened if it is provoked by no one in word or deed, if the body is subjected to the soul in the service of God, and if the soul, in harmony with the spirit, continually serves the Lord God. Those placed on this step are called blessed, because they will be called sons of God (Matt. V).

The ninth step is called goodness, through which one enters the delight of heavenly life. A person climbs this step when he not only does no evil but does not even think it.

The tenth step is spiritual joy, through which one reaches the fellowship of the angels. A person should rejoice that he has climbed this step if he does not rejoice over iniquity, if he does not rejoice over the ruin of an enemy or over evils that happen to others, but rejoices with the truth (I Cor. XIII)—that is, with everything done to the honor of Christ, who is the truth, the reward of life, and the fullness of all joy.

Hence the tenth step is placed as endurance, through which the eminence of heavenly glory is acquired. The mind begins to climb this step if it endures all the adversities of the world for Christ. Those established on this step are called blessed if they suffer persecution for justice, because they receive the kingdom of God.

The twelfth step is said to be faith, which makes human beings fellow citizens with angels. A person presses his foot upon this step if he faithfully believes everything piously spoken or written about God and eternal life, because it is impossible to please God without faith (Heb. XI).

The thirteenth step is hope, which does not disappoint those awaiting spiritual things. The holy mind raises its feet to this step if it hopes for all good things from the future life.

The fourteenth step is long-suffering, through which equality with the angels is obtained. Anyone climbing this step will grasp it if he bears all God’s promises with equanimity, if he carries the Lord’s burden until he himself comes, shakes the yoke from his neck, makes him cease from labor, and causes him to recline in rest.

The fifteenth and final step is perseverance, through which the green meadows of the delights of paradise are seized. The lofty mind seeking this step should rejoice that it has reached it if it never falls away from the mercy of God, in which it must never despair. “Whoever perseveres to the end will be saved” (Matt. XXIV).

The Lord, who is charity, will bring whoever properly climbs all these steps into the chambers of eternal sweetness. This ladder is erected, beloved, through fear; by fear charity is led to its summit and itself is brought in as a son into the inheritance of the Lord. But fear is cast out as a servant (I John IV).

It must be understood that there are two movements of the heart by which the rational soul is impelled to undertake everything it does. One is fear, the other love. When these two are good, they produce every good. Through fear, evils are avoided; through love, good things are practiced. But when they are evil, they become the cause of every evil. Through fear, one turns away from good; through love, one commits evil deeds. Thus these two are like two gates through which death and life enter. Death enters when they are opened toward evil; life, when they are opened toward good.

## On Fear and Love of God

Fear is an effect of the mind by which it is moved to yield to one superior: through love it approaches, through fear it withdraws. If human beings had remained in justice, they would have submitted willingly to what was better; but now they submit by necessity to what is stronger. This is the punishment of fear, from which it is called servile: the one who previously refused to submit willingly to what was better is now subjected by necessity to what is stronger. Charity certainly casts out this punishment when it makes submission voluntary (I John IV).

The more charity increases, the more the will increases; the more the will increases, the more necessity decreases. With perfect charity, a person loves, voluntarily submitting in reverence to what is better, and does not fear, unwillingly, the punishment of what is stronger.

It is asked how Christ as man possessed the fear of the Lord. It is easy to show how, insofar as he was himself human, he voluntarily submitted to the Father, who was superior to him, and yielded to him in spontaneous reverence, acknowledging him as superior when he said: “The Father is greater than I” (John XIV).

Just as love, although it is naturally one movement of the mind, receives different names according to its different qualities—sometimes being called desire when it is directed toward the world, and charity when it is directed toward God—so fear, although it is naturally one movement of the mind, is signified by different names according to the different movements by which it is possessed or exercised.

Sacred Scripture distinguishes four kinds of fear: servile, worldly, initial, and filial.

Servile fear is abstaining from evil in order to avoid punishment while retaining an evil will.

Worldly fear is abstaining from good in order to avoid punishment while retaining a good will.

Initial fear is, in order to avoid punishment, cutting away not only perverse action but also evil thoughts.

Filial fear is firmly adhering to what is good because one does not wish to lose it.

Of these four, two are evil: servile and worldly; and two are good: initial and filial.

Servile fear dreads the punishment inflicted by human beings. Therefore it is satisfied to cease from an evil deed, because it serves for outward appearance and does not fear the guilt of conscience, wishing to please human beings.

Worldly fear does not seek to please human beings, yet fears displeasing them, and itself pretends to be what it is not. It is as false in denying the truth as it is deceptive in concealing falsehood. Both offend against the truth: one because it timidly denies what is; the other because it perversely keeps silent about what is not.

Initial fear, because it strives to avoid the punishment with which God threatens, sees that it is by no means sufficient merely to restrain oneself from unlawful action. For before the one who examines the heart, it is not enough, as evidence of innocence, that the deed be blameless, unless the very thought of the heart also appears sincere and undefiled before his eyes.

Because this fear dreads displeasing the one who sees everything, it considers it necessary, for perfect innocence before him, to cleanse everything. Therefore it is called initial fear, because under it, through good will, both the beginning and the completion of virtue are attained. Yet it is not perfection, because while one thing is being done and another is intended, the good itself is still not loved for its own sake.

Then charity approaches and enters through this fear. While fear shows what danger we ought to flee, it in a certain way makes us seek and desire protection. It turns the heart toward God, so that one flees from him to him, as it were: while avoiding having him angry, one strives to have him gracious.

This is followed by filial fear, which is born from the charity that succeeds it. To fear God then means nothing other than, having tasted the good in charity, no longer wishing to lose it. This fear does still have something of punishment joined to it while we walk amid uncertainty, and while the condition of this changeable life can still incline in either direction.

But when there is no longer any changeability, there will be no punishment arising from suspicion amid uncertainty. Then fear will exist, in a certain sense, without fear: we shall be certain of our stability, yet shall not cease to offer reverence to the Creator.

## SUNDAY IN QUADRAGESIMA. According to Matthew.

[Col. 0863]

[Col. 0863A] “Jesus was led into the desert to be tempted by the devil, etc.” (Matthew 4). Luke deliberately placed first: “Jesus, full of the Holy Spirit, returned from the Jordan” (Luke 4), so that there would be no doubt by which spirit he was led into the desert according to Matthew, or driven out according to Mark. Without doubt Jesus is not driven into the desert by the power of an evil spirit, but by the will of his own spirit, so that he might lay low his adversary. Indeed, it is fittingly understood, without any question, that he was led into the desert by the Holy Spirit so that his own spirit might lead him to the place where the evil spirit would find him for the purpose of tempting him. Here it is now demonstrated beforehand that, after baptism, we must gird ourselves courageously against the devil, abandoning the allurements of the world and the company of the wicked.

“And when he had fasted forty days and forty nights, afterward he was hungry.” He presented himself to the tempter for forty days and forty nights to indicate that, whether prosperity flatters the faithful—which pertains to the days—or adversity strikes them—which corresponds to the image of night—the adversary is always present, never ceasing to hinder them by tempting them. He became hungry through exhaustion, so that an opportunity for tempting might be granted to the devil and he might be conquered by the man whose death and calamities the devil boasted of. The devil was troubled by the forty-day fast: he knew that for the same number of days the waters of the abyss had been poured out, the promised land had been explored, the Law had been given by God to Moses, and the children of Israel had lived in the wilderness on the bread of angels. But when he sensed that the Lord became hungry after the fast—a thing not read of Moses or Elijah, that they became hungry after their fasts—he approached to tempt him, far removed from any good intention.

There are ten commandments of the Law, and the world is fourfold. This signifies that Christ’s grace has already been spread throughout the world, since he fasted for a period of forty days. During this fast he cried out, as it were: “Abstain from the desires of this age” (1 Peter 2). In eating and drinking after the resurrection he cried out, as it were: “Behold, I am with you always, to the end of the age” (Matthew 28). Hence, although we do not yet glory, nevertheless we are already nourished by hope.

The fast of Lent was appropriately established in connection with the end of the Lord’s Passion. This signifies that we ought to restrain ourselves from friendship with the world, so that we may be able to follow God. In abstinence, moreover, the number forty is observed, because the virtue of the Decalogue is fulfilled through the four books of the Gospel when the Gospel is kept; or because through the Decalogue we are commanded to love God and our neighbor, while the charity of God and neighbor is violated by the movement of the body, which consists of four elements. Thus, the time of penitence appropriately rises to the number forty for the cleansing of sins.

[Col. 0864A] “And the tempter approached and said to him: ‘If you are the Son of God, say that these stones should become loaves of bread.’ But he answered and said: ‘It is written: Man does not live by bread alone, but by every word that proceeds from the mouth of God.’”

At one time the devil believed that his conqueror had come into the world, just as he said through the possessed man: “What have we to do with you, Son of God? Have you come here before the time to torment us?” (Matthew 8). Later, however, he doubted that this was he, because he endured mortal sufferings. “It is written,” said the Lord, because he had proposed to conquer the devil through humility, not through power. The prince of demons was intent on recognizing God’s power in the transformation of stones into loaves, and on mocking, in the man, the endurance of hunger through the pleasure of food. But the Lord, taking his testimony from Deuteronomy, showed that the nourishment of eternity is to be hoped for not in this solitary bread but in the word of God.

Temptation occurs in three ways: suggestion, pleasure, and consent. Christ, however, was tempted by suggestion alone, because the pleasure of sin did not wound his mind. It was not unworthy for him to be tempted who had come to be killed, so that by his temptation he might conquer ours, just as by his death he bore our sins.

“Then the devil took him into the holy city and set him upon the pinnacle of the temple.” It is not surprising that he allowed himself to be taken, led, and set there by the one whose members he had offered himself to be crucified by. This may also be understood as follows: The devil took him—that is, he attacked him by tempting him—and set him upon the pinnacle of the temple. For this reason there was an occasion by which the Lord was led and set there by his own spirit.

A *pinna* or *pinnaculum* is a summit, that is, a height. For the ancients, as is still done in many places, used to make the upper parts of houses or temples flat, [Col. 0864D] so that they could stand there and do whatever they wished. Hence the Lord says to the apostles: “What you hear in the ear, proclaim upon the housetops” (Matthew 10). They called Jerusalem the holy city because there the temple and the worship of God according to the Law of Moses were maintained.

“And he said to him: ‘If you are the Son of God, throw yourself down. For it is written: He has commanded his angels concerning you, and they will lift you up in their hands, lest you perhaps strike your foot against a stone.’”

In all temptations the devil acts in order to discover whether he is the Son of God. But the Lord so moderates his reply that he leaves him uncertain. By saying, “Throw yourself down,” he is shown to be weak: he can persuade, but he cannot cast down. The testimony he introduces is a prophecy not only concerning Christ but also concerning every holy man.

Jerome explains Psalm 90 in this way: “Whoever believes that the two natures of God and man are perfect in the Savior is surrounded by angelic hands and does not strike his foot against the stone—that is, against Christ—who is the stone of stumbling and the rock of offense.”

Augustine says in the same psalm: “The Lord was lifted up in the hands of angels when he was taken up into heaven” (Acts 1), not because he would have fallen if they had not carried him, but because they were serving the King. If you say, ‘Those who carry are better than the one who is carried,’ I will answer: ‘Certainly, beasts of burden are better than human beings.’ The evasive tempter was silent, however, about his own trampling, not adding that the Son of God would walk upon the asp and basilisk and trample upon the lion and dragon.

[Col. 0865B] Then Jesus said to him again: “It is written: ‘You shall not tempt the Lord your God.’” By the true shields of the Scriptures he breaks the devil’s false arrows drawn from the Scriptures—the devil either proposes falsehoods or attempts to persuade people of falsehoods by means of truths. The Lord brought forward testimonies from Deuteronomy in order to display the mysteries contained in the seat of the Law. He was being prompted, as though he were merely human, to test by some sign how much influence he possessed with God. But, as it is written, a human being must not dare to tempt God when he has something he can do in order to escape what ought to be avoided. Hence the saying: “If they persecute you in one city, flee to another” (Matthew 10). But once human prudence has failed, if a person commits himself entirely to divine power, this should not be called temptation. At that point Christ could have left the temple by another means rather than throwing himself down boastfully.

“Again the devil took him onto an exceedingly high mountain, and showed him all the kingdoms of the world and their glory, and said to him: ‘All these things I will give you, if you fall down and worship me.’”

He showed him the kingdoms on a mountain—that is, above a mountain—not because he had enlarged the sight of the one who sees all things, but, as far as he could, he displayed by word and promise the vanity of human pomp, which he loved, presenting it as something splendid and persuading the Lord that he might thereby subject him to himself. It is fitting that Luke records that temporal things were shown in a moment of time, because human powers quickly fall. By saying, “All these things I will give you,” he speaks arrogantly, not because he could give all kingdoms.
