“Falling down, you will worship” is said because, intending to worship the devil, he first fell. Note that all power and the ordering of powers are from the Lord, but the ambition for power is from evil. The power temporarily promised to the devil is therefore not evil; rather, the one who uses power badly in his ambition is evil.

“Then Jesus said to him: ‘Go, Satan. For it is written: You shall worship the Lord your God, and him alone you shall serve.’”

Satan and Peter are not condemned by the same sentence, as some think. To Peter he says, “Get behind me, Satan” (Matthew 16), that is, “Follow me, you who are contrary to my will.” Here “behind me” is not said, so that “Go into the eternal fire” may be understood.

It is written for every human being that he must worship God and serve him alone. In Greek, *latria* (λατρεία) is called that service which belongs exclusively to God, not to a creature. Hence those who offer to idols the sacrifices that are owed to the Lord alone are called *idololatrae*, idol-worshipers. *Dulia* (δουλεία), however, is common service, whether rendered to God or to a human being. Hence a servant is called *servus* in Latin, corresponding to *doulos* (δοῦλος) in Greek. We are therefore commanded to serve one another through charity—this is called *doulia* (δουλεία) in Greek—and to serve the Lord alone, which in Greek is called *latria* (λατρεία).

[Col. 0866A] “And when every temptation had ended, the devil departed from him until an appointed time. He was also among the beasts, and behold, angels approached and ministered to him.”

He says that every temptation had ended because the origins of all vices are contained in these three temptations, as John bears witness when he says: “Everything that is in the world is the desire of the flesh, the desire of the eyes, and the pride of life” (1 John 2). In the evangelical parable as well, people are excluded from the banquet of eternal life by three rejected occupations: “The first said, ‘I have bought a farm,’ etc. Another said, ‘I have bought five yoke of oxen,’ etc. Another said, ‘I have taken a wife’” (Luke 14).

The desire for a wife, like gluttony, pertains to desire of the flesh. The purchase of the farm pertains to avarice and pride. The testing of the five yoke pertains to desire of the eyes, where curiosity and vainglory reside. Daily oppose weapons of defense to the enemy’s threefold missile, so that desire of the flesh may be driven away by fasting, avarice by almsgiving, and boasting by prayers.

The devil overcame the ancient man through gluttony, by means of the fruit he found. He overcame him through vainglory, saying: “You will be like gods” (Genesis 3). He also overcame him through avarice, when he said, “Knowing good and evil” (ibid.). For avarice is rightly called the exaltation of ambition. Thus he also tempted the Lord, [Col. 0866C] but, defeated, withdrew.

David struck down Goliath with three stones from the torrent; Christ struck down the devil with three testimonies from the Law. Which of the temptations was first, which middle, which last, and in what form the tempter approached—whether in his own form or in the appearance of an assumed human being—it is not very important for us to know.

The devil left the Lord until an appointed time, later to attack him openly through the Jews. So also, when he does not prevail in temptation, he withdraws from us until another time. The Lord dwells among the beasts as a human being, and makes use of angelic ministry as God. When we endure the beastly behavior of human beings in the wilderness of holy conduct, we merit the ministry of angels, by whom, once freed from the body, we may be transferred to eternal joys.

SERMON ON DIABOLICAL TEMPTATION AND ON FOUR OTHER TEMPTATIONS

The mind of the just person is struck in this life by many calamitous temptations. Indeed, he also longs to be completely removed from this age, so that he may be free from its hardships and find that fixed security. There is a great difference between the punishments that the just person suffers in the body, as it were, and those which he endures inwardly through the devil’s deception. For he bears more heavily those over which he inwardly grieves than those which he endures outwardly. The latter he can avoid by place and time; the former he can avoid neither by place nor by time.

The devil does not tempt the elect more than God’s will permits. In tempting them, however, he serves the progress of the saints. [Col. 0867A] Even unwillingly, the devil serves the benefit of the saints when he does not deceive them through his temptations but rather instructs them. For the temptations that he arouses for human destruction Christ sometimes turns, with salutary benefit, toward the exercise of virtue.

Although the devil’s snares and cunning spread here and there as they seek someone to devour, they nevertheless do not go beyond divine power, lest they harm as much as they wickedly strive to do. For how could the virtue of the saints have endured so much if heavenly providence did not restrain the wickedness of demons with kindly moderation? Although the devil always desires to inflict temptation upon the just, nevertheless, unless he receives power from God, he cannot in any way obtain what he desires.

The devil’s will is unjust in itself, but, with God’s permission, all power is just. For of himself he unjustly desires to tempt anyone whatever, but God permits those who are to be tempted to be tempted only justly. Hence it is written in the Books of Kings concerning the devil: “An evil spirit from the Lord rushed upon Saul” (1 Kings 18). Here the question is rightly asked: If it is from the Lord, why is it evil? If it is evil, why is it from the Lord? But in two words both God’s just power and the devil’s unjust will are encompassed. The spirit is evil through its utterly wicked will, and that same spirit is from the Lord through the supremely just power it has received.

The devil is not the one who implants vices but rather the one who inflames them. For he does not kindle the fuel of desire anywhere except where he has first seen the pleasure of an evil thought. If he sees that this pleasure is rejected more fully, he undoubtedly departs in confusion. At once the arrows of his desire are broken, they lie there despised, and his torches are extinguished without light.

The servant of God must carefully understand and avoid the enemy’s snares, and must be simple in the innocence of his life in such a way that he is nevertheless prudent in his simplicity. Whoever does not combine prudence with simplicity is, according to the prophet (Hosea 7), “a dove deceived, without a heart.”

He is called a dove because he is simple; but he is without a heart because he is ignorant of prudence. Often Satan’s deceit is exposed to the hearts of the saints when, while pretending to be an angel of light, he is revealed and despised as he attempts to deceive the elect under the appearance of good. Thus God also makes the saints understand the words of deceitful teaching, so that inwardly they may recognize diabolical error and carefully avoid it.

The discernment of the saints must be so great that, endowed with reason, they distinguish between good and evil, lest the devil deceive them under the appearance of good. The saints then judge rightly concerning themselves when God makes them understand the devil’s deceitful temptations.

Many are deceived by the devil and do not know that they have been deceived, as the testimony of the prophet Hosea declares: “Strangers have devoured his strength, and he did not know it” (Hosea 7). By “strangers” are signified wicked spirits, who consume the powers of the mind; but the hearts of the negligent do not understand this.

The devil is defeated as though unarmed when he attempts to corrupt a person through open iniquity. He then advances armed with a word when, through the hope of holiness and virtue, he destroys what is holy, so that the one who is deceived does not perceive his losses but pursues and loves vices as though they were virtues.

In the eyes of the carnal the devil is terrible; in the eyes of the elect his terror is contemptible. He is feared by unbelievers as a lion, but by the strong in faith he is despised as a worm and repelled as soon as he appears for a moment. Whoever does not receive the devil’s suggestions does not pass into his snares. For he is easily repelled in the subsequent actions if his initial pleasures are rejected.

The devil is a slippery serpent. If his head—that is, his first suggestion—is not resisted, he slips wholly into the interior of the heart when it consents. The beginnings of diabolical temptations are fragile. If they are not guarded against but pass through use into habit, they grow exceedingly strong at the end, so that they are overcome either never or only with difficulty.

DIVISION

Although throughout life the devil desires to make a human being transgress, he nevertheless strives to deceive him more intensely at the end. Therefore, even if he is just, a person must never be secure in this life; he must always beware humbly and always fear anxiously lest he fall at the end.

The devil flatters his supporters, but against God’s servants he contrives contrary temptations, following the example of the Lord, who allowed himself to be tested by the devil after his baptism. The devil does not possess all the saints by holding them, but persecutes them by tempting them. Since he does not reign inwardly in them, he fights against them outwardly; having lost the Lord within, he stirs up war without.

The devil rages more fiercely against the one he possesses when he recognizes that he is about to be expelled from him by virtue. For the unclean spirit also then tears more violently at the boy in whom it had dwelt (Matthew 12), when it was forced to leave him at Christ’s command. This deed also relates to the words concerning Job, where, at the end, Behemoth “tightens his tail like a cedar” (Job 40).

The devil presses more strongly with various temptations against those who can benefit others through their usefulness, so that, while they are hindered, they may not accomplish what they are meant to teach. The evil spirits continually attempt to soil again what we desire to cleanse within us.

The saints, however, foresee their snares with prophetic insight, and whatever earthly thing they perceive in themselves they continually drain away through holy works, so that they may be found pure in their inmost parts. By the same seduction by which the first-created human beings were deceived in paradise, human beings are now deceived by the devil. Through many deceptions of vices he mocks the minds of the rejected when he tempts them.

Now he deceives them by promises; now he entices them with transitory things as though they were necessary. Now he suggests that the punishments of hell themselves are light and temporary, so that he may dissolve the hearts of the wretched in desire and lust and lead them with himself to Tartarus.

The arguments of evil temptations and thoughts—the seeds that the devil scatters into human hearts—often seize and entangle the mind on every side, so that, whichever way someone attempts to escape, he cannot get out without danger. For example: if you swear that you will do this, then, if you do it, you sin; but if you do not do it, you are guilty of perjury. In such a serious danger of evil, so that a way of escape may be opened, the lesser evils must rather be chosen in order to avoid the greater.

When the devil wishes to deceive someone, he first considers the nature of each person, and then applies himself from the point at which he sees the person most liable to sin. He tempts people on the side where he observes that, through an active bodily disposition, they can easily be bent toward vices, applying temptation according to the person’s constitution.

Read about Balaam, who, as a figure of the devil, commanded that pernicious snares be set against the people of God from the direction in which he perceived they were most likely to fall (Numbers 23). For water that is conducted somewhere is not sent by another route except where its current directs it.

No one should think himself free of guilt because he suffers it from his own passion; rather, let him fight against what he endures as much as he can. For if one yields to his constitution, he does not resist temptation or vice at all.

Therefore the devil is called in the sacred writings “Behemoth,” that is, “animal,” because he fell from heaven and descended to earth. He is called “Leviathan,” that is, “serpent of the waters,” because he moves about in the changeable sea of this age with his twisting cunning. For this reason he is called a bird, because through pride he is lifted up to high places.

He is rightly called by these three names: because, according to his deserts, he has earned the air as a bird for his prison; as a brute animal he devours the earth; and as a serpent he is hurled about in the sea of this age in insane fluctuation. Because the devil works through his members, he receives names according to them, so that whatever individuals do at his prompting is named as though he himself had done it.

The one whom the devil does not deceive through what makes him an animal—that is, through fleshly lust—he tempts through what makes him a serpent, namely, the malice of desire and of doing harm. But the one whom he does not deceive even in this way, he attacks through what makes him a bird, namely, the ruin of pride. From the place where he prepares his plots, he persists until he finds a way by which to deceive the unwary.

DIVISION

It is one thing for the devil to enter someone’s mind and another for him to dwell there. He enters the hearts of the saints when he insinuates evil suggestions, but he does not dwell in them, because he does not lead them into his own body. Those who are in his body, however, he inhabits, because they are his temple.

Although the devil may steal into the minds of the elect, he does not rest in them as he does in the hearts of the rejected. For the warmth of faith immediately stirs him to leave the elect.

Some whom the devil had already devoured with greedy jaws are again snatched from his mouth by the hidden mercy of divine judgment and restored to salvation. For divine power has often drawn many whom the ancient enemy held sunk in the mire of lust from his jaws through repentance.

How does the prophet say concerning the destruction of the good that the elect are the devil’s food (Habakkuk 1), while elsewhere it is written of him, “He will eat grass like an ox” (Job 40), unless it is because, in God’s eyes, those who appear to human beings to be elect food are grass? Consequently, those who perish from the number of the good are, among human beings, elect, but before God they are grass.

The devil is said to have swallowed someone when he appears to have devoured him through a perfected crime. But the one whom he has not swallowed through the completion of a deed, whom he bites with the enticements of temptations in order to devour him, he still chews, as it were, in his jaw. Hence Paul has a “thorn of the flesh” by which he is humbled, but he does not have the perfection of sin by which he might be swallowed.

The devil’s mouth is his words; his words, however, are hidden inspirations by which, addressing human hearts, he secretly burns them with desires. Some, because of incorrigible iniquity and because they do not correct themselves willingly, are handed over to unclean spirits to be tormented, so that the demons may have bodily power to seize them; afflicted by their terrors, they may be humbled, repent, and be saved.

Thus the Apostle also says, writing to the Corinthians: “Hand such a one over to Satan for the destruction of the flesh, so that the spirit may be saved” (1 Corinthians 5). It is useful for some sinners to be assigned bodily to Satan so that their souls may be saved, in order that, corrected in the present, they may fear the future judgment and thereafter beware of sinning.

Some are assigned to the power of demons for correction; others, rejected, are handed over solely for destruction. Sometimes the devil increases tribulations of the heart against a just person, or stirs up bodily pains. Hence the Apostle says: “A thorn in my flesh was given to me, an angel of Satan, to buffet me” (2 Corinthians 12).

Often the power of demons torments the mind of the just with various painful afflictions, so that at times he is confined even to the narrow limits of despair. Yet for a soul that remains in the love of God, even such anguish contributes to merit.

Whether in mind or in body a just person suffers adversity through the instigation of unclean spirits, he suffers it by God’s permission. If, in humility, he refers this very thing to God’s glory and says, “If we have received good things from the hand of the Lord, why should we not also endure evil?” (Job 1), he is not separated from God but joined to him, however cruelly he may be tormented by anguish.

The just person suffers many adversities in his soul through the instigation of demons, but such temptations cannot cause him to perish from eternal life, because the merciful Lord does not reckon as the condemnation of guilt what he unwillingly bears by permission of his majesty. We sin where we turn aside our desire or will. But where we are forcibly subjected, even if there is no crime or disgraceful act, there is nevertheless misery as though it were a crime or disgraceful act. Yet because he praises God for the misery poured out upon him, he undoubtedly wipes away the crimes committed.

Moreover, it must be observed that there are four temptations of which Psalm 106 speaks: “Give thanks to the Lord.” Its second verse is: “Let those who have been redeemed by the Lord say so. Let them confess to the Lord his mercies and his wonders to the children of men.” This occurs four times, and by that number, with the Lord’s help, as far as we have been able to investigate, four temptations are signified. From these, therefore, each person is rescued by him before whom every knee bows.

The first temptation, then, is that of error and hunger: error, because a person finds himself in ignorance; hunger, because he desires to know the truth and longs to be satisfied by it. When someone has been wearied by this temptation and has cried out to God from his heart, he will reach the way of faith, by which he begins to proceed toward the city of rest. He is led, therefore, to Christ, who says: “I am the way” (John 14).

Therefore, freed from error and hunger and led to the way that is Christ, let him say: “Let them confess to the Lord his mercies and his wonders to the children of men.” This is the first temptation, from which the one who makes progress is freed, with Christ favorable to him.

The second temptation occurs when a person has received the food of truth and has been placed on the way that is Christ. He hears: “Live well, and, as you have received and understood, strive to become better.” But, presuming upon himself, when he attempts to fight against vices, he is overcome because of the pride of his presumption.

Just as the first temptation was that of error and hunger, so the second is the difficulty of doing good. Therefore, burdened by such difficulty, let him cry out to the Lord; for by crying out to him he will be freed from his necessities. He will break the bonds of difficulty and establish his worker in the work of righteousness.

What had been difficult will then begin to become easy for him: namely, to do good and abstain from every evil. What had been difficulty will become ability. The Lord could have granted this without difficulty, but if we possessed it without difficulty, we would not recognize the giver of this good. We would attribute it to our own strength and would not perceive God as the bestower of this grace.

And because human frailty, even if it wishes to do so, cannot by itself bring to completion what has been commanded to it, let it say again with the Psalmist: “Let them confess to the Lord his mercies and his wonders to the children of men.” This is the second temptation: the difficulty of conquering desires.

After these two temptations, a third receives the person—by “the person” I mean one who has already passed through these two. For these two are known to many. Who does not know that he has come from ignorance to the truth, from hunger for wisdom to the word of faith?

The third, however, is weariness of the divine word: weariness of praying, reading, keeping vigil, and the other practices by which one could advance toward what is better. Sometimes it brings such great danger that nothing previously done well makes the person secure; rather, because of his weariness, he fears that he will perish.

Just as the body is destroyed when it rejects bodily food, so the soul is endangered when it rejects spiritual nourishment. Again he cries out to the Lord and is delivered, and then it follows that he gives thanks.

Behold: darkness has been illumined, the difficulties of former habits have been overcome, and weariness of the word of God has been repelled. Such a person is now fit to be advanced to the governance of churches. But the more he is exalted, the more he is endangered.

Then the storm of the sea arises, shaking the Church and disturbing the helmsman. He is endangered, now ascending toward the heavens through hope, now descending to the depths through despair. Again he cries out to the Lord and is delivered, and therefore rightly gives thanks as before.

This is the fourth temptation, [Col. 0872A] which is called danger in the governance of public affairs. Let no one think that this temptation concerns only prelates, because everyone is carried in the ship: those who work and those who are governed. All are endangered together at sea, and all are saved together in the harbor.

These four temptations are set forth in the psalm, understood through the four occurrences of “Let them confess.”

SERMON ON LENT

Beloved, when we were expelled from paradise, it was said to us: “You are dust, and to dust you shall return” (Genesis 3). Therefore, so that we might be able to return, at the beginning of the fast we performed penance in ashes and sackcloth. For we are dust and ashes, and the son of man is a worm and corruption.

And because we strive to return to our homeland, we know that enemies—that is, demons—block the road of salvation for us. Therefore we raise up spiritual weapons, namely prayer, humiliation, and affliction, so that we may be able to fight against the spiritual forces of wickedness and extinguish all the flaming darts of the most wicked enemy.

When on that day we made a procession with crosses, we went out to meet the enemies for battle as though armed. Hence, through the litany, we invoke the saints for our assistance, so that we may be able to fight courageously and triumph in the heavenly court.

In the fourth age of the world Solomon built a temple for the Lord in seven years. After it had been destroyed by the Babylonians, it was rebuilt by Jesus the priest in forty-six years. Solomon is Christ; the temple is the Church. This temple is built by Solomon in seven years because the Church is formed by Christ through the seven gifts of the Holy Spirit.

It is destroyed by the Babylonians because it is overthrown by various vices through demons. But it is rebuilt by Jesus in forty-six years because during these forty-six days the Church is built together into a temple for God.

Thus forty-six days are counted from the beginning of the fast until Easter. The temple of Christ’s body is also built over forty-six years, and the Church is incorporated into it. Mary was twelve years old when she bore Christ. Christ was thirty-four years old when he died and was released from death. These years joined together make forty-six; and there are that many days from the beginning of the fast until Easter, on which day Christ restored the temple of his body, which the assault of the Jews had previously destroyed.

Therefore we begin the fast on Wednesday, because we proclaim that Christ began his fast on Wednesday; we know that he was baptized on Monday, and we desire through fasting to be incorporated into him. We also imitate Solomon, who in the fourth age of the world built a temple as a figure of the Church, in which we now desire to be built together by Christ.

For this reason we fast for these four days from the beginning of the fast, because the Church is gathered from the four regions of the world into the building of the Lord’s temple.

Then we fast for forty days, because through the four Gospels and the ten commandments of the Law this temple is brought to completion in Christ, since he did not come to abolish the Law but to fulfill it.

This Lent is the Christians’ *carrina* [the term is uncertain in the transmitted text]. For we commit many things during the year that pertain to this *carrina*, and therefore the Church has decreed that we fast this forty-day period on their account.

It is also the tithe of our life. For just as we ought to give a tenth from other things, so we ought to give a tenth of our days. The year consists of 360 days. When, excluding Sundays, we abstain for thirty-six days during this forty-day period, we pay, as it were, a tenth of our days.

The Law is also completed through ten commandments; the year revolves through four seasons—spring, summer, autumn, and winter; and the human being is constituted from four elements, namely fire, air, water, and earth. Therefore, since through the four qualities of our body, in the four seasons of the year, we have committed ten offenses against God’s commandments, it is just that during these forty days we should make satisfaction to our God.

We do this around the time of the Lord’s Passion because, if we suffer with him, we shall also reign with him.

We must also know, beloved, why forty days were instituted. When the Lord rescued his people from the yoke of Pharaoh, he led them through the desert for forty years. He rained down upon them the bread of heaven, which possessed every delight; he brought forth water from the rock, which offered the taste of honey and oil; their garments were not worn out by age or stained with dirt; and there was no weak person among their tribes.

At night the angel of the Lord went before them in a pillar of fire and drove away the terror of night from them; by day he protected them in a cloud from the heat of the sun. After forty-two stations they entered the promised land.

If you tithe a day for each year of the forty years, you will count forty days. These are the forty days observed by the Christian people, whom the Lord redeemed from the oppression of the devil. Through the keeping of the ten commandments and the four Gospels, he feeds them from his own body and brings forth blood from his side, as he brought water from the rock.

That rock was struck twice with the rod: namely, the flesh of Christ was fastened to the two pieces of wood of the cross. This drink gives the taste of honey and oil, because with the oil of mercy he heals the wounds of our sins, and with the honey of eternal sweetness he satisfies us.

And if the garments we received in baptism are not worn away by vices or polluted by sins, then at night, in this dark life, the fire of the Holy Spirit goes before us; and on the day of judgment Jesus Christ our Lord will protect us with the cloud of his humanity from the heat of the eternal fire.

SECOND SUNDAY IN LENT. According to Matthew.

[Col. 0873C] “Jesus went out and withdrew into the region of Tyre and Sidon. And behold, a gentile Canaanite woman, by birth a Syro-Phoenician, cried out, saying: ‘Have mercy on me, Lord, Son of David. My daughter is severely tormented by a demon,’ etc.” (Matthew 15).

The Canaanites inhabited the lands in which Judaea is located. They were either destroyed in war, dispersed into neighboring regions, or subjected to servitude as those defeated in status; nevertheless, they continued to bear the name without a homeland of their own.

From that dispersion it happened, among other things, that this Canaanite woman, who was Syro-Phoenician by birth, was descended from Syrians and Phoenicians. She is therefore a gentile; and, if she was mingled with the Jews, she displayed the form of a proselyte. It is rightly thought that she had learned from the Law what she confessed when she acknowledged Christ as Lord and as the Son of David.

In a typological sense, however, she signifies the Church from the gentiles, which pleads for her daughter when it implores the mercy of heavenly compassion for souls that do not yet believe, so that they may be released from the deceits of the devil.

Fittingly, according to Matthew, she had gone out from her own region, and according to Mark she fell at the Lord’s feet (Mark 7), so that from both accounts it may be gathered when those rightly pray for sinners who abandon the former dwelling places of their unbelief and transfer themselves, with devout dedication, into the Church.

“Jesus, however, did not answer her a word. And his disciples came and begged him, saying: ‘Send her away, because she is crying out after us.’” The Canaanite woman, following the Lord as he walked, uttered supplicatory cries and first fell at his feet in the house, as Mark records. The fact that the Lord did not answer her was not due to the arrogance of pride, but lest he appear to contradict himself, since he had said: “Do not go on the road of the Gentiles” (Matt. X). Nor did he wish to give the calumniators an opportunity, reserving the perfect salvation of the Gentiles for the time of the resurrection. The disciples pleaded on behalf of the Canaanite woman, either because they did not know the Lord’s mysteries, or because they were moved by compassion, or because they wished to be rid of her importunity.

“Jesus, answering, said: ‘I was sent only to the sheep that had perished of the house of Israel.’” He said this because he had first been sent to Israel, whom he was soon to abandon for neglecting the Gospel and to pass over to the Gentiles.

“But she came and worshiped him, saying: ‘Lord, help me.’ He said: ‘Let the children first be satisfied. For it is not good to take the children’s bread and throw it to the dogs.’” What he says amounts to this: It will happen that you Gentiles also will attain salvation, but first it is necessary that at least some Jews—who, by virtue of the ancient election, are called the children of God—be refreshed with the bread of heaven, and that only afterward the nourishment of life be supplied to the Gentiles. The Gentiles are called dogs on account of idolatry; devoted to the eating of blood and corpses of the dead, they are said to run mad. O wondrous reversal! Formerly Israel was the child, and we were dogs. Later it was said of him: “Many dogs surrounded me” (Ps. XXI).

“But she said: ‘Yes, Lord; for even the little dogs eat from the crumbs that fall from the table of their masters.’” The meaning is: Certainly, Lord, what you say is true: it is not good to throw the children’s bread to the dogs. But for that reason I do not cease to implore your mercy, which you can fittingly extend to me in the likeness of bread and dogs. For “yes” means “certainly”: even the little dogs eat from the crumbs. Therefore, if I am unworthy to receive an entire loaf from you, at least grant health to my daughter, as a crumb in comparison with the many wonders you have performed.

Mystically, the table is sacred Scripture, which supplies the bread of life. Hence the Church says: “You have prepared a table before me” (Ps. XXII). The crumbs are the inner mysteries of Scripture, by which humble hearts are refreshed, according to the saying: “He satisfies you with the fat of wheat” (Ps. CXLVII). The little dogs therefore do not eat crusts, because the Gentiles, having turned to the faith, seek not the surface of the letter but the spiritual marrow; and they do so beneath the table of their masters, while, humbly subject to the words of sacred eloquence, they submit the service of heart and body in order to fulfill the commandments. Alternatively, the masters of the table may be understood as the composers or interpreters of the Scriptures. And then he said to her:

“‘O woman, great is your faith. Let it be done for you as you wish.’ And her daughter was healed from that hour.” In the person of the Canaanite woman the great faith, great patience, and humility of the Church are proclaimed. She believed that her daughter could be healed; though so often rejected, she endured and persevered in prayer; and in her humility she compared herself not to dogs but to little dogs. Therefore her daughter was freed. Here an example is given of catechizing and baptizing infants, who through the faith and confession of their parents are freed from the devil in baptism. The fact that the Lord heals the centurion’s boy and the Canaanite woman’s daughter without coming to them signifies that the Gentiles, to whom he did not come, are to be saved through bodily repentance by his word.

SERMON ON THE THREE KISSES—OF THE FEET, HANDS, AND MOUTH—and on the Upper and Lower Lip

“Let him kiss me with the kiss of his mouth” (Song I). There are three kisses. We must consider from what they are named, from where they are received, what fruit comes from them, and which persons or merits each one suits. The first is called propitiatory or reconciliatory, the second meritorious or remunerative, and the third divine or contemplative. The first is received at the feet, the second at the hands, and the third at the mouth.

The first reasonably suits penitents and those wishing to return to God’s grace. The Lord’s feet, which are to be kissed, are mercy and judgment: these inspire a person with hope and fear, lest through presumption he neglect repentance by considering mercy alone, according to the saying: “The earth is full of the mercy of the Lord” (Ps. XXXII), and: “His mercies are over all his works” (Ps. CXLIV); or lest, weighing only justice, he harden into despair, according to the saying: “Who knows the power of your anger, and by reason of fear can number your wrath?” (Ps. LXXXIX.) Let him therefore kiss both feet, saying with the prophet: “I will sing mercy and judgment to you, Lord” (Ps. C), and: “All the ways of the Lord are mercy and truth” (Ps. XXIV).

Of these feet it is said: “Your way is in the sea, and your paths are in many waters” (Ps. LXXVI). And elsewhere: “We worshiped in the place where his feet stood” (Ps. CXXXI). With these feet Christ came to us. Hence it is said: “Mercy and truth have met one another” (Ps. LXXXIV). The fruit of this kiss is the remission of sins.

This kiss was attained by David, the adulterer of his fellow citizen, traitor, and murderer, to whom Nathan said: “God has taken away your sin” (III Kings XII). Thus the tax collector kissed God’s feet and returned to his house justified. That most famous Ethiopian woman, Mary Magdalene, happily kissed these footprints; from her Jesus had expelled seven demons, and to her he said: “Your sins are forgiven you” (Luke VII). In her person it is said in the Song: “I am black” through guilt, “but beautiful” through grace (Song I).

In these kisses, and in similar ones in which we have placed grace, the enemies of the Lord are made his footstool.

The Lord’s hands are his generosity and benevolence, in which God surpasses all others, possessing an excellent abundance for everyone and the most liberal willingness to give. Of his benevolence the Apostle says: “Who desires all to be saved” (I Tim. II). Of his generosity the prophet says: “You open your hand and fill every living thing with blessing” (Ps. CXLIV). O healing generosity and liberality! He shines like the sun, sprinkles like dew, and freely irrigates like a spring; he sends rain upon the just and the unjust.

It is not enough to kiss the Lord’s feet by ceasing from evil, unless we also kiss his hands by doing good and meriting favor. Hence the Psalmist says: “Turn away from evil and” then “do good” (Ps. XXXVI). And Isaiah says: “Cease to act perversely” and afterward “learn to do good” (Isa. I).

The order is appropriate: when someone incurs offense against his Lord, he should fall at his feet and weep before the Lord who made him. After receiving the Lord’s grace, he should approach and serve at his hands—offering service to Christ’s ministers—and thus, according to his merits, he will be rewarded, receiving blessing from the Lord and mercy from his saving God. Hence the fruit of this kiss is progress and the bestowal of virtues.

After the two kisses in which there is the forgiveness of crimes and the bestowal of merits, there remains that third and sweet kiss of the mouth, in which the happy soul is granted the joyful contemplation of the divine face. Of this it is said: “Let him kiss me with the kiss of his mouth.”

The mouth of God is the Word, the Son of God. Hence the prophet says: “We provoked his mouth to anger” (Lam. I). Through him he created all things, as it is said: “He spoke, and they were made” (Ps. CXLVIII), and: “God spoke once” (Ps. LXI). He also spoke to us when he opened the secrets of the Father’s heart.

In human affairs nothing is so sweet as love between bridegroom and bride, because through it two become one flesh. Likewise, no union is understood to be so intimate and so close as that of created and uncreated spirit, because there two become one spirit.

Thus the bride, languishing with love, thirsting for the bridegroom, unable to endure her desire, longs for affection—not by command, but by a wish and an ardent yearning. Hence she says: “Let him kiss me with the kiss of his mouth.”

The bride has two lips. The lower lip is the will, which is called appetite, and consent, which we share with animals. The upper lip is reason.

Again, the Bridegroom has two lips. The lower lip is understanding, when understanding is joined to the will, so that it freely understands how to will and desire, and says: Formerly I desired carnal things, but now “my soul has desired to long for your justifications at all times” (Ps. CXVIII). The upper lip of the Bridegroom is wisdom, which reason touches so that it tastes nothing apart from God and can thus preside over and rule its own sensuality. Tasting the sweetness of God from this wisdom, it says with the prophet: “Taste and see that the Lord is sweet” (Ps. XXXIII).

It remains to see which persons in the Church, or which merits in the soul, these individual kisses suit. Job is prostrate at the feet, scraping away filth with a potsherd—that is, the corruption of sin with severe repentance. Esther receives the kiss at the hands: as she enters before the king, a golden scepter—that is, divine clemency and advancement in virtue—is extended to her from the hand of the generous benefactor. Moses attains the kiss of the mouth: he remains with the Lord on the mountain and speaks mouth to mouth. Or it is Mary, who eagerly desires to hear the Word from Jesus’ mouth with attentive ears.

THE THIRD SUNDAY. According to Luke.

[Col. 0877]

“There was Jesus casting out a demon, and it was mute. When he had cast out the demon, the mute man spoke, and the crowds marveled, saying: ‘Has anything like this ever appeared in Israel? Is this perhaps the son of David?’ etc. (Luke XI).” It is as though the faithful crowds were saying: This man is not only the son of David but also the Son of God.

In Greek, “deaf” sounds better than “mute,” but Scripture uses one indifferently for the other. When they had gone out—understand, from this world—they brought to the Lord preachers and the mute man, namely the mute people who had not yet spoken anything about the glory of God because they had had no preachers. This people is understood to have been from the Gentiles. Hence the crowd’s astonishment follows, since they say that nothing like this had ever appeared in Israel—namely, that so many from it had simultaneously been converted to Christianity.

“But the Pharisees were saying: ‘He casts out demons by Beelzebub, the prince of demons.’” While the less educated crowds marveled at the Lord’s deeds, the scribes and Pharisees labored over a sinister interpretation of them, attributing his miracles to Beelzebub, who was the god of Accaron.

Beel is Baal himself. Zebub means “fly.” According to certain faulty copies, the name should be read with the letter l, or d, at the end. But *Beelzebub* is interpreted either as “man of flies” or “having flies,” evidently because of the filth of sacrificial blood; from this most foul rite or name they called the prince of demons.

Note that Ninus, the king and founder of Nineveh, dedicated a statue to his father Bel and established divine honors for it. The Chaldeans adopted the likeness of this image and called it Bel. The Palestinians, adopting it from them, called it Baal. The Moabites called it Beelphegor; but the Jews, worshipers of the one God, called it Beelzebub in mockery of the Gentiles, asserting that the prince of demons dwelt in this image.

“But when he saw their thoughts, he said to them: ‘Every kingdom divided against itself will be laid waste, and a house divided against itself will not stand.’” He answered the thoughts of the Pharisees so that they might at least be compelled to believe.

In the literal sense it is evident that every kingdom that is solid and firm, if divided into parts, is reduced to desolation when its members are punished or destroyed by one another, emptied of inhabitants. The same reasoning applies to a house or city, as Matthew says. Through concord small things grow; through discord the greatest things fall apart. He explains how these words are to be understood spiritually:

“But if Satan is also divided against himself, how will his kingdom stand?” It cannot stand, but comes to an end, because you say that I cast out demons by Beelzebub. Let them choose whichever alternative they wish. If Satan cannot cast out Satan, they say nothing against the Lord. But if he can, let them depart from his kingdom, which, being divided, cannot stand, lest they likewise be involved in its ruin.

“But if I cast out demons by Beelzebub, by whom do your sons cast them out? Therefore they will be your judges.” He means either the sons of the Jews, the exorcists of that people, or the apostles born from their stock. It is as though he said: If you attribute the expulsion of demons in your sons to God, why do you not do the same in my case?

The apostles, who are lowly and contemptible in this world, in whom not malignity but the simplicity of my power is apparent, will be my witnesses that I cast out demons in the Holy Spirit. And they will be your judges concerning what you attribute to me as being performed by Beelzebub.

Alternatively, the exorcists who are your sons and drive demons from the possessed will be your judges—not by their authority, as my disciples are, but by comparison: they attribute the expulsion of demons to God, whereas you attribute it to Beelzebub, the prince of demons.

“Moreover, if I cast out demons by the finger of God, surely the kingdom of God has come upon you.” If I cast out demons by the Spirit of God—and your sons cannot cast them out in any other way—then without doubt the kingdom of God has come upon you. By it the kingdom of the devil is overthrown, and you are overthrown along with it.

The kingdom of God is the power by which the wicked are ruled and separated from the faithful. Or it may be understood in this way: the kingdom of God signifies itself, concerning which he says elsewhere: “The kingdom of God is within you” (Luke XVII), and: “There stands among you one whom you do not know” (John I).

Or it is the kingdom of Scripture, taken away from the Jews and given to us; or the kingdom of heaven, as though he were saying: If I cast out demons by the Spirit of God, know without doubt that access to the heavenly kingdom has been opened to believers.

The finger of God is the one whom the magicians confessed when they performed signs against Moses and Aaron, saying: “This is the finger of God” (Exod. VIII); by this finger the stone tablets were also written on Mount Sinai. He himself wrote who dictated what was to be written.

The hand and arm of God is his Son, and his finger is the Holy Spirit. He is called a finger because of the division of the gifts given through him, each being proper to its recipient, whether human beings or angels. For division is apparent in no members more clearly than in the fingers.

Just as the finger with the hand or arm, and the hand or arm with the body, are one in nature, so the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit are indeed three persons but one substance of divinity.

The fingers of God, in the plural, are understood as the holy prophets, through whom the Holy Spirit, by his inspiration, composed the books of the Law and the prophets. Concerning them it is written in the psalm: “I will see your heavens, the work of your fingers” (Ps. VIII). By “heavens” he mystically signified the books of the Law and the prophets, and by “fingers,” as has been said, the holy prophets.

“Or how can anyone enter a strong man’s house and seize his possessions in which he trusted, unless he first binds the strong man, and then indeed seizes his possessions?” By this evident parable the Lord shows that people are freed from the demon by the power of divinity.

The strong man is the devil; his house is the world, which is set in evil, in which, until the Savior’s coming, he rested as though in a peaceful dominion, without opposition. Hence the Lord says: “The prince of this world is coming, and he has nothing in me” (John XIV). And again: “Now the prince of this world will be cast out” (John XII).

The Lord himself was stronger than him. He took away his weapons—that is, the deceits and tricks of spiritual wickedness—and, by removing his power to seduce the elect, forced him to be restrained. This was to bind the strong man.

The spoils or possessions are the people deceived by him, whom Christ the victor distributes. This is the mark of a triumphant victor: leading captivity captive, he gave gifts to human beings (Eph. IV), appointing some as apostles, others as evangelists, these as prophets, and others as pastors and teachers.

Thus, to plunder the strong man’s house was to gather into the Church those rescued from the devil and to advance them through the distinct ranks of ministries.

The courtyard guarded by the armed strong man is the heart; the armed strong man is malice; the stronger one who comes upon him is wisdom; the weapons are the members.

Wisdom first seizes malice through knowledge, detecting it; afterward it binds it by restraining it from action; then it scourges it, because a perverse effect is struck as though by certain harsh scourges when, through the discipline of training, it is restrained from what it desires. Finally, as though the limbs had been stretched upon a cross, separated from one another, and fastened with nails, it is pierced when the soul is penetrated by the fear of God after its vices have been separated from one another.

When vices are together, they are stronger, since they protect one another—for example, gluttony lust, and display pride. Divide and separate them from one another, and thus nail your flesh with the fear of God, so that malice may die within you.

Do not be surprised that wisdom does to malice what it first endured from malice itself. First malice crucified wisdom; afterward wisdom, prevailing, crucified malice.

“Whoever is not with me is against me, and whoever does not gather with me scatters.” This is consequently referred not to heretics but to the devil, whose works cannot be compared with the works of the Savior. He desires to hold human souls captive, whereas the Lord frees them. He draws them to vices; the Lord calls them back to virtues. How, then, can those whose works are divided be in agreement?

Whoever does not gather—that is, whoever does not gather my sheep with me—scatters them; that is, he disperses them from the assembly of the faithful. Here he indicates that one who does not possess the Holy Spirit and does not gather with him could never gather under his name. He compels us to understand unequivocally that the remission of sins cannot occur anywhere except in Christ’s assembly, which does not scatter.

“When the unclean spirit has gone out from a person, he wanders through dry places, seeking rest, and does not find it.” These words can suitably be understood of any heretic or schismatic, or even of a bad Catholic.

When the unclean spirit has gone out from such a person at the time of baptism, he wanders through waterless places—that is, he circles around the hearts of the faithful, cleansed of the softness of shifting thought. He seeks rest and does not find it, because he cannot inhabit pure minds or rest except in a perverse heart.

Hence the Lord says of him: “He sleeps under the shadow, in the secrecy of the reed and in moist places” (Job LX). By “shadow” he signifies dark consciences; by “the reed,” which is bright on the outside but hollow within, he signifies hypocritical minds; by “moist places,” lascivious and soft ones.

Then he says: “I will return to my house from which I came.” I will return to that person’s conscience, from which I was expelled in baptism, and subject it to me once more in my customary manner.

“And when he comes, he finds it empty, swept, and put in order.” “Empty,” namely, of good works through negligence; “swept” of its former vices through the grace of baptism; and “put in order” with simulated virtues through hypocrisy.

“Then he goes and takes with him seven other spirits more wicked than himself, and entering, they dwell there.” By the seven spirits he designates all vices, which are rightly called more wicked than the devil in comparison with the former inhabitation.

For although the devil is evil and makes people evil, before baptism whatever he seizes afterward—whether through heretical perversity or worldly desire—immediately casts the person down into the depths of every vice. Such a person will not only have the seven vices opposed to the seven spiritual virtues, but through hypocrisy will also pretend to possess those virtues themselves.

“And the last state of that person becomes worse than the first.” It would have been better for him not to know the way of truth than, after knowing it, to turn back. We read that this was especially fulfilled in Judas the traitor and Simon Magus.

What this parable intends is indicated by its conclusion: “So will it be also with this most evil generation.” That is, what I have narrated specifically of one person will happen to the people of this nation.

The unclean spirit went out from the Jews when they received the Law, and he passed over to the Gentiles. But afterward, when he found no place among the unbelieving Gentiles, he returned to the Jews, who were empty of Christ, cleansed—as they thought—by superfluous observances of the Law, and adorned.

To possess them more firmly thereafter, he takes with him the entire host of demons. The Jews therefore act worse now, possessed by a greater number of demons than before, because it was a lesser thing not to believe that Christ would come than, after he had come, not to receive him.

“It happened that, while he was saying these things, a certain woman from the crowd raised her voice and said to him: ‘Blessed is the womb that bore you and the breasts that nursed you,’ etc.” This woman displays great devotion and faith. While the Pharisees were blaspheming the Lord, she confessed his incarnation with such sincerity that she put to shame the unbelief both of penitents and of those who would come afterward.

For if the flesh of the Word of God had been foreign to the flesh of the virgin mother, as many heretics have said, then the one who bore him came without reason, and the breasts that nursed him would have been blessed without reason. Hence the Apostle says against the heretics: “God sent his Son, made from a woman, made under the Law” (Gal. IV).

Nor should we listen to those who think that we should read “born from a woman” rather than “made from a woman.” Otherwise he would not be truly the Son of Man unless he had drawn flesh from his mother.

According to the natural philosophers also, milk for nourishing children and semen for begetting them flow from the same source. Therefore he who could be conceived from the Virgin’s seed could also be nourished by her milk.

This woman represented the Church, which believes that Christ was born as true Lord and true man. Truly blessed is the mother of Christ, who, as someone said:

“Having borne the King as a mother in childbirth,  
who holds heaven and earth through the ages,”

and whose name and empire, embracing all things in an eternal circuit, remain without end. She, possessing the joys of motherhood in a blessed womb together with the honor of virginity, was seen to have neither a first like her nor a successor.

But he said: “Rather, blessed are those who hear the word of God and keep it.” Beautifully, the Savior assented to the woman’s testimony, affirming that not only is his mother blessed, but also all who conceive the Word of God through the hearing of faith and, by guarding good works, give birth to and nourish him in the hearts of others.

By this saying he secretly strikes the Jews, who deny that Christ is the Son of God. The whole perfection of the heavenly life is certainly comprised in these two things: that we hear the word of God and do it.

SERMON ON SIN AND THE CONFESSION OF SIN

Sin is committed in two ways: either through love of desire or through fear, when someone wishes to obtain what he desires or fears incurring what he dreads.

Sin is committed in the heart in four ways, and perpetrated in action in four ways. It is admitted into the heart through the suggestion of demons, the pleasure of the flesh, the consent of the mind, and the defense of self-exaltation. It is committed in action sometimes secretly, sometimes openly, sometimes through habit, and sometimes through despair. In these stages, therefore, one both sins in the heart and perpetrates wickedness in action.

Sin is carried out in three ways: through ignorance, weakness, or deliberate intent; the danger of punishments is divided accordingly.

Eve sinned through ignorance in paradise, as the Apostle says: “The man was not deceived, but the woman was deceived and was in transgression” (I Tim. II). Thus Eve sinned through ignorance, Adam deliberately, because he was not deceived but sinned knowingly and with full awareness. Whoever is deceived into giving consent plainly does not know.

Peter sinned through weakness, because, out of fear of the servant girl who questioned him, he denied Christ. It is worse for someone to sin through weakness than through ignorance, and worse still to sin deliberately rather than through weakness.

The one who sins deliberately does evil with the application and deliberation of the mind; the one who sins through weakness falls into wrongdoing by accident or precipitously.

Those who sin deliberately are more wicked: they not only fail to live well but also, if they can, turn those who live well away from the truth.

Some sin in ignorance, and some knowingly. There are also those who do not wish to know, under the pretext of ignorance, so that they may be considered less culpable. Yet they do not protect themselves; rather, they deceive themselves.

Not knowing simply belongs to ignorance; refusing to know belongs to obstinate pride. For what is it other than a desire to despise God arrogantly, when one refuses to know what God wills?

Therefore no one should excuse himself on the ground of ignorance, because God judges not only those who turn away from knowledge of him but also those who did not know. This is what may be said about sin.

What, however, the teachers think about confession of sin must now also be considered.

They say, then, that there is much wickedness in human beings. No one, when he wishes to do evil, seeks authority. When we tell people to do good and to confess the evils they have committed, they say to us: “Give us authority. What Scripture commands us to confess our sins?”

If Scripture does not command confession of sins, then answer this: Do you possess Scripture that commands people to commit sins? If you do not wish to confess, when you have no authority for confession, why do you wish to remain silent, when you have no authority for silence?

Nevertheless, because you seek authority, accept authority. The ancient Law commands people to confess their sins and sends them to the priests, so that they may confess their sins and receive pardon (Num. V). There, therefore, transgression of the Law is abolished by confession and offering, when the Law was still a shadow; and at that time confession of the crime ought rather to fear punishment than expect mercy.

If this authority is not enough, hear Scripture elsewhere plainly saying: “Whoever conceals his crimes will not be justified” (Prov. XXVIII). What is it to conceal them except to remain silent and refuse to confess?

For those who reveal their crimes through the shamelessness of wicked action do not merit justification but condemnation. Therefore evils must be concealed insofar as this concerns the shamelessness of wicked action, and revealed through the humility of confession.

Do you still wish to know the danger of silence and the benefit of confession? “Because I was silent,” says the Psalmist, “my bones grew old while I cried out all day” (Ps. XXXI). And again: “I made my sin known to you, and I did not conceal my injustice. I said: I will confess my injustice against myself to the Lord; and you forgave the wickedness of my sin” (ibid.).

See and consider: if you are silent about your sins, they grow old; and if you confess, they are forgiven.

But you say: “Behold, I confess my sin, but to God, not to a human being. I follow Scripture. It tells me to confess my sin to God; it does not send me to a human being. In him there is no salvation. Rather, Scripture directs confession to the one from whom it promises forgiveness: ‘I said: I will confess my injustice against myself to the Lord, and you forgave the wickedness of my sin.’”

What does a human being do? Hear what he does. Was it not a human being who said: “Son, your sins are forgiven you” (Matt. IX)? And it is true, because it was a human being who said this. Therefore those who saw him as a human being but did not recognize God murmured among themselves, saying: “Who is this who even forgives sins?” (ibid.)

They knew that it belonged to God to forgive sins, but they did not know that what belonged to God had been received by a human being from God. That human being possessed what he had, insofar as he was human, because he had received it; but insofar as the human being was God, he possessed that same thing and had not received it.

For this reason he once wished to receive in his humanity what he had always possessed in his divinity, so that he might draw near to the human being in what belonged to humanity; and in that very thing which belonged to humanity he might display to the human being what belonged to God.

In what belonged to humanity he was joined more familiarly to the human being; in what belonged to God he worked more powerfully within the human being.

Therefore he said: “But so that you may know that the Son of Man has authority on earth to forgive sins”—then he said to the paralytic: “Rise and walk” (ibid.). He displayed what they could see, so that through it they might believe what they could not see.

For this reason God became human: to present himself as near and familiar to the human being, speaking with him, so that in one and the same person the human being might find his own kind, to whom he could confidently reveal his weakness, and, believing God to be above the human being, might not doubt the remission of his sins received from him.

DIVISION

[Col. 0884A]

So that the grace of this dispensation might be multiplied more abundantly, God, made man, made men—who were merely human—participants in his power, so that they might fulfill his office by receiving the confession of penitents and exercise his power by forgiving the sins of penitents and confessors.

“Receive,” he said, “the Holy Spirit: whose sins you forgive, they are forgiven them; and whose you retain, they are retained” (John XX). Therefore Christ, the human being, gave his disciples—who act in his place on earth—the authority to forgive sins.

But you may say: Why did Christ not likewise give human beings a command to confess their sins, just as he gave the disciples authority to forgive the sins of those who confess?

Hear why. Christ wished you to rise from yourself, so that your confession would not appear to have been extorted or compelled. Therefore he entrusted to his disciples the office that belonged to him, to be carried out by them, so that, after the manner of physicians, they might receive and heal the sick who came to them.

He told the physicians to heal, but he did not tell the sick to come to the physicians to be healed. He wished it to be regarded as certain that the sick would willingly seek health and offer themselves for treatment if they found physicians. Therefore he instructed only the physicians. For a sick person’s illness itself sufficiently admonishes him, and, if he is in pain, there is no need for a command.

Nevertheless, because afterward the physicians found sick people negligent in their treatment, they aroused them to seek health both by their admonition and by drawing them through a command.

“Confess,” says the Apostle James, “your sins to one another, and pray for one another, so that you may be saved” (James V). What does “to one another” mean? One to another—a human being to a human being.

Not merely a human being to God, as that true confessor says: “I said: I will confess my injustice against myself to the Lord,” etc.; “and you forgave the wickedness of my sin”—that is, a human being to a human being for God’s sake.

For the one who humbles himself before a servant for God’s sake does more than the one who humbles himself before God himself. Therefore: “Confess your sins to one another.”

What does “to one another” mean? Not, however, each person to every person, but “to one another”—that is, among you human beings, to human beings: sheep to shepherds, subjects to prelates; those who have sins to those who possess the authority to forgive sins.

It was indeed owed that you, intending to confess, should go to the one who is over you. Now, however, as a dispensation of forgiveness, it is granted that you confess your sins to one another among yourselves.

The one who alone would receive confession would not make confession, because he would have no sins. But those who receive the confession of sins and forgive the sins of those who confess must themselves also confess their own sins, so that their sins may be forgiven when they repent and confess.

Therefore, confess your sins to one another and pray for one another. For what purpose? So that you may be saved: confess so that you may be saved. What does “confess so that you may be saved” mean? It means that you will not be saved unless you confess. Perhaps you did not wish to hear this, you who seek hiding places and conceal your crimes so that you may not be justified. [Col. 0885A] You are displeased by the statement that those who do not wish to confess their sins cannot be saved. Perhaps for this reason you try to twist another saying of the apostle, so that he may be understood to have promised salvation to those who confess, while not denying justification to those who do not confess.

Listen, then. Augustine says: “No one can be justified from sin unless he has confessed before the sin.” Likewise, Bede, in the same Epistle of James from which we cited the testimony above: “Without confession, sins cannot be forgiven.” If this distinction is said to consist in our confessing daily and lesser sins to one another among equals, so that we may be saved through one another’s prayers, let us, moreover, disclose the uncleanness of the more serious leprosy to a priest and take care to be justified according to his judgment.”

See how [Col. 0885B] the testimonies of truth agree. There is also a certain common penance in the Church, which we perform daily for one another; in it, by prayer poured out for one another over daily and lesser sins, we obtain pardon and remission. But the guilt of a more serious offense we disclose to a priest in individual confession, and, according to his counsel, after offering the payment of satisfaction, we obtain forgiveness of the sin.

But you say: If a person cannot be saved unless he confesses his sins, what is the meaning of the statement found in Scripture: “Tears wash away the offense which shame prevents the mouth from confessing”? For sayings of this kind are found, and people seize upon them gladly—not because they grasp the truth in them, but because they wish to defend their wickedness by means of them. For they say: [Col. 0885C] “Why do you bind us? Why do you constrain us? Our deeds are shameful; modesty does not allow us to speak of them; we blush to confess what we have done. Yet we do what we can: we offer a contrite and humbled heart, we grieve over what we have done badly, we pour out tears, and by mortifying the flesh we punish our guilt. Why do you seek words where good works are present? We have Scripture to console us, saying: ‘Tears wash away the offense which shame prevents the mouth from confessing.’ We do not excuse ourselves by wickedness, but spare our modesty. What, therefore, we are ashamed to say to a human being, we say to God, who does not reproach us.”

By such pretexts people seek an excuse for their flesh and attempt to distort the Scriptures, because they themselves are perverse.

## Division

[Col. 0885D]

What does it mean that Scripture says, “Tears wash away the offense which shame prevents the mouth from confessing”? Did it therefore say: “If you are ashamed to confess your sin, let this suffice for you—if you merely weep, even if you do not confess”? Would it not be much better to understand Scripture as wishing to say that tears, poured forth from deep contrition of heart, can also wash away those sins which cannot be openly professed by the mouth without shame and embarrassment?

What, then? If tears wash away shameful sins, must one be silent precisely where divine assistance is most necessary? On the contrary, one must confess all the more there, so that the humility of confession may increase the tears of contrition. Likewise, when it is said to you, “If you are ashamed to tell your sin to a human being, tell it to God, who does not reproach,” this does not mean: “If you are ashamed to tell it to a human being, do not tell it to a human being but tell it to God.” Rather, God’s gentleness is being shown to you: he is so mild and gracious toward all who flee to him that you need not fear any reproach from him, even if your sins are such that you happen to be unable to reveal them to a human being without embarrassment.

In that very matter of which you are ashamed, when you tell it to a human being, you ought not to be ashamed when you tell it to God, because he does not reproach the one who speaks, but pardons the one who confesses. Tell it, then, to a human being, so that you may be healthfully put to shame before him for a time; this shame will afterward bring you glory and provide you confidence, so that you will not fear reproach when you begin to be revealed [Col. 0886B] before God.

Yet perhaps your thought might say: “If it is so serious to reveal sins to a human being, and if we are so ashamed before a human being, what shall we do before the Lord, whose majesty we cannot avoid and whose judgment we cannot escape?” So that, by thinking thus about God, you may not despair of yourself, God’s gentleness toward penitents and confessors is shown to you: he forgives all sins to penitents and does not reproach those who confess.

Understand the statement in this way: “Tell it to God, who does not reproach.” It is as though he were saying: “Even if you are ashamed before a human being, do not be ashamed before God, for the Lord is milder and gentler than a human being, and is patient with the wretched, so that he does not reproach them.” In this sense, then, you are not told not to tell your sins to a human being, but to trust in God’s compassion even regarding those things which are shameful to confess before a human being. (CHRYSOSTOM)

You still object with those tears of Peter which you read about (Matt. II, 6), while you do not read of confession: “Tears wash away the offense which shame prevents the mouth from confessing.” You oppose these tears, therefore, not because you love compunction, but because you flee confession. You say, then, that you read of Peter’s tears but do not read of his satisfaction. You have heard that he wept, but you have not heard what he said.

“Tears wash away the offense which shame prevents the mouth from confessing.” Do you therefore think that this is being said to you: Because Peter is read to have wept but is not read to have confessed, if you weep, you need not confess? Would it not be much better to understand that what is being demonstrated here is this: if tears alone were so effective there, where they did not have the confession of the mouth, how much more effective are they when they are genuine and accompanied by contrition of heart as well as confession of the mouth? This is demonstrated to you when it is added that one must first weep and afterward confess.

Indeed, this pertains to the truth of confession: first you must be pierced with compunction, and afterward confess. For some are as shameless in speaking as they are impudent in doing. Because they do not see the shamefulness of their conduct when acting, they have no embarrassment when speaking. To them the prophet rightly says: “You have acquired the forehead of a prostitute; you did not know how to blush” (Jer. III).

These people sometimes thrust themselves forward to declare their sins without any fear of compunction and without any touch of fear or love of God, merely to fulfill a habit, believing that simply by uttering the words they will be absolved from the debt of their sins. To them it is rightly said: “First one must weep, afterward confess.”

In the confession of sins, a person ought indeed to be ashamed, so that he may humbly acknowledge what he has done, [Col. 0888A] but not to be so ashamed that he remains silent. That sinful woman knew this well: she came to show that she did not wish to conceal her sins (Luke VII), and yet she stood not in front but behind, to demonstrate that she was attentive to the shamefulness of her sin. For this reason it is rightly said: “First one must weep, afterward confess.”

## Sunday in Mid-Lent

[Col. 0887]

[Col. 0887B] “Jesus departed across the Sea of Galilee, which is the Sea of Tiberias” (John VI). When Jesus heard that John the Baptist had been beheaded, he withdrew from his homeland, where he was then staying, in a boat to a deserted place by himself.

“And when the crowds had heard this, they followed him on foot from the cities. And going out, he saw a great crowd, and had compassion on them, and healed their sick.”

It is rightly said that he “withdrew,” not that he “fled,” so that it might be shown that he avoided persecutions more than he feared them. Waiting for the opportune time of his Passion, he avoided allowing the murder of John to be joined to his own murder. Or he withdrew for this reason: to provide us an example of avoiding rashness in voluntarily handing ourselves over. For not everyone perseveres in torments with the same steadfastness with which they offer themselves to be tormented.

[Col. 0887C] By also seeking solitude, he tests whether the crowds will take care to follow him, and he rewards those who have been proved with a worthy recompense. The crowds, however, undertake the journey through the desert not on beasts or vehicles but by the labor of their own feet, and they show their desire for salvation. Again, by receiving the weary, teaching the ignorant, healing the sick, and refreshing the fasting, he makes clear how much he delights in the understanding of believers.

Alternatively: after prophecy had lost its voice among the Jews, he crossed over to the desert of the Church, which had been without a man. The crowds left the cities—that is, their former ways of life and their variety of doctrines. The phrase “going out” signifies that the crowds had the will to go to him but did not have the strength; and therefore the Savior goes out to meet them.

“When evening came, the twelve approached him and said: [Col. 0887D] ‘Dismiss the crowds, so that they may go away into the villages and farms nearby, turn aside there, and find food, because we are here in a deserted place.’ But Jesus said to them: ‘They do not need to go away; give them something to eat yourselves.’”

He urges the apostles toward the breaking of the loaves, so that, when they testify that they do not possess any, the greatness of the sign may become better known. At the same time he suggests that daily we are to be fed through them. For what do Peter and Paul do through their letters except feed our minds with heavenly nourishment?

He refreshes the crowds in the evening because, at the end of the age, when the Sun of Justice set for our sake, we were freed from the long hunger of spiritual famine. Observe the order of the mystery. After the law’s decline, [Col. 0888B] evangelical food begins; but first medicine is applied to wounds through the remission of sins, and afterward the nourishment of the heavenly table is supplied.

It is therefore not necessary for us to seek food in farms and villages—that is, to abandon the bread of life by purchasing, at the price of study and labor, the doctrines of philosophers defended by their own arguments, whose nourishment might delight us. The disciples’ statement that the place is deserted, however, represents the Jews murmuring about the conversion of the Gentiles. Hence Isaiah speaks in their voice: “Behold, the nations are like a drop from a bucket” (Isa. XL). Likewise: “All the nations are as nothing before him” (ibid.).

“Philip answered him: ‘Two hundred denarii worth of bread would not be enough for them, so that each might receive even a little.’ And he says to them: ‘How many loaves do you have?’ One of his disciples, Andrew, the brother of Simon Peter, says to him: ‘There is one boy here who has five barley loaves and two fish. But what are these among so many? Unless perhaps we should go and buy food for all this crowd.’ He said to them: ‘Bring them here to me.’ And he commanded them to make everyone recline in groups upon the green grass. And they reclined in divisions of one hundred and of fifty.”

The Lord had asked Philip, testing him—as John records—from where food could be given to the crowd. For since the people were ignorant regarding the law—for as long as Moses is read, a veil lies upon their hearts—the Lord’s testing therefore demonstrated the disciple’s ignorance. Andrew also speaks with the same simplicity as Philip.

[Col. 0888D] But the Lord shows that he bestows food freely upon the believing people by the same benevolent power by which, freely redeeming them, he heals them. The boy carrying the loaves and fish was one of the disciples, or perhaps someone from the crowd. As for the fact that Philip or Andrew is mentioned individually by John, the other evangelists report that the disciples spoke in the plural, either understanding that one spoke on behalf of the others or using the plural number in place of the singular.

By “groups” understand the various communities of people who had come from different villages, just as soldiers who share quarters in the same tent are commonly called *contubernales*, “tent-companions.”

The five loaves are the five books of Moses, because in the riches of the law there was life, as it were, in bread. For through the law the knowledge of divine eternity, the creation of the world, the course of the passing age, and the true religion of serving God were made known to the human race.

The two fish signify the Psalms and the Prophets, tempering the austere flavor of the law. For they fed the people instructed in God’s law with the sweetness of the new grace promised in the Lord’s incarnation, as though fostering hope for human life through the power of water. Hence, after his Resurrection, the Lord says: “It was necessary that everything written about me in the law of Moses, the Prophets, and the Psalms should be fulfilled” (Luke XXIV).

Here also, by commanding that the loaves and fish be brought to him, he mystically commanded that the meaning of the Old Testament be referred to him. It is fitting, moreover, that the prophetic books concerning our age are represented by creatures of the water, in which the people of the faithful cannot live at all without the waters of baptism.

The loaves were barley loaves, which are the food of peasants, because rougher teachings, as it were, are to be entrusted to unformed hearers. For the animal person does not perceive the things that belong to the Spirit of God. Therefore the Lord, distributing gifts to each according to his due and always urging them toward greater perfection, first refreshes five thousand with five loaves; second, four thousand people with seven loaves; third, he entrusts to his disciples the mystery of his flesh and blood; finally, he grants that they may eat and drink at his table in his kingdom.

Or it may be understood in this way: the loaves were barley loaves because they belonged to the Old Testament. And just as one scarcely reaches the kernel of barley, so the Old Testament is clothed in a covering of carnal things, but it wounds when one reaches what lies within.

[Col. 0889C] The two fish, which gave the bread its sweet flavor, are the two persons of priest and king by whom the people of Israel were governed, so that through them they might receive the direction of counsel. As these two were shaken amid the crowds of the fluctuating age, like fish, yet did not fail, Christ, the true priest and ruler, was represented.

The boy who carried them is that people, childish in understanding and not eating: it carried what was enclosed as a burden, without feeding others.

Again, the five loaves signify Scripture and the examples of the Fathers who lived in the five ages, by which the faithful are daily abundantly refreshed. In the first age, Enoch refreshes us with the bread of writing when he writes that the Lord will come to judgment with thousands of saints. He satisfies us with the bread of example when Scripture records that he pleased God through righteousness and was taken up into paradise.

In the second age, bread is supplied to us through Abraham, when he is said to have discovered the Hebrew letters, to have written down events from the beginning, to have taught astronomy in Egypt, and to have obeyed God in all things.
