In the third age, we are abundantly refreshed through Moses, when through his writings we are instructed by the Ten Commandments, and he himself is described as having been the meekest of all human beings and as having shone forth through many signs.

In the fourth age, David, Solomon, and nearly all the prophets satisfy us with sweet bread, when they instruct us through mystical writings and deeds.

In the fifth age, Ezra satisfies us with bread, when he repeats the law after it had been burned and rebuilds the destroyed Temple.

These loaves are distributed to the crowds when their writings and deeds are mystically expounded to the faithful by teachers. [Col. 0890A] The two fish likewise designate the two persons of king and priest, who alone in the Old Testament were anointed with sacred oil. Christ, however, caught the faithful, hidden like fish in the salt sea of the age, through the apostles, the fishers, in the net of faith; and he caused them all to be anointed with the oil of chrism as kings and priests. The white garment received in baptism designates the priesthood, while the mitre placed upon the head designates the royal diadem.

The text continues:

“But what are these among so many?” As though it were said: “For so many seeking nourishment beyond all bodily sense and every letter, what benefit is there in the old letter?” Because they understood in a carnal manner and rested in carnal hope, to whom the law had promised temporal things, they are commanded to recline upon green grass: “All flesh is grass, and all the glory of man is like the flower of grass” (Isa. XL).

He therefore reclines upon grass who tramples his flesh and crushes its flowers like withering grass, subjecting the pleasures of the age to himself. The different reclining places of the diners signify the different gatherings of the Churches.

Those who recline in groups of fifty do so because, still placed in penance, they receive the hearing of the word. For the number fifty signifies penance and remission. Those who recline in groups of one hundred do so because, through penance, those numbered by fifty ascend to the perfection of the hundredfold number and already sigh only for the desire of eternal life.

“When he had taken the five loaves and the two fish, he looked up to heaven, blessed them, broke them, [Col. 0890C] and distributed them to the disciples; and the disciples distributed them to the crowds. And they all ate and were satisfied. They gathered up the fragments left over, filling twelve baskets. The number of those who ate was about five thousand men, apart from women and children.”

The Lord looked up to heaven, honoring the Father, from whom he himself had confessed that he was, so that those present might understand from whom he had received the effect of such great power and might likewise direct the eyes of their minds there. If the loaves were not broken, they would not feed so great a crowd. So also the law, if it were not opened, would not feed the many whom its exposition feeds.

Each of the apostles fills his basket with the fragments, either so that he may have something from which afterward to provide food to the Gentiles, or so that from the fragments he may demonstrate that the loaves had truly existed.

The five thousand men signify the perfect. The weaker sex and lesser age are unworthy of the number. Hence, whenever priests, Levites, and armies of combatants are described in the Book of Numbers, servants, women, children, and the lowly multitude are omitted.

The Savior does not create new food, but blesses what is present, because, coming in the flesh, he does not preach something else; rather, he shows that the words of prophecy are laden with the mysteries of grace. Hence it follows that he “broke”—that is, he disclosed the closed mysteries of the law and the Prophets.

The loaves are multiplied by being broken, because many books have been produced through the exposition of the law. Breaking them, he distributes them to the disciples; and they, breaking what has already been broken, distribute it to the crowds. For he opened the understanding of the holy teachers so that they might understand the Scriptures, and, having understood them, they faithfully dispensed them to their hearers throughout the whole world.

The disciples take up what remains for the crowds because the mysteries that are not grasped by the unformed are sought out by the perfect. There are fragments which the people could not eat—certain more secret matters of understanding—with which the apostles were filled, as though they were twelve baskets.

The apostles are represented by the baskets, and through the apostles the choirs of teachers who follow are represented: outwardly despised by human beings, but inwardly heaped up with saving food for nourishing the hearts of the humble. For baskets are ordinarily used for servile tasks. But the Lord filled baskets with fragments because, in order to confound what is stronger, he chose the weak things of the world.

The apostles filled twelve baskets with the fragments of those who had eaten when, in the sixth age, they explained the writings of their predecessors through their own teaching. A basket is woven from slender willow branches, and the apostolic order is chosen from a humble stock.

The basket gathers the remains of those who have eaten because it supplies the letter to ordinary people but reserves mystical meanings for the wise.

And because the external human being has five senses, the five thousand men who followed the Lord designate those who in the world knew how to use well the external things they possess. They are rightly fed with five loaves because such people still need to be instructed by legal commandments.

Those who renounce the world completely are the four thousand, and they are fed with seven loaves—that is, they are elevated by evangelical nourishment and taught by spiritual grace.

For this reason, I think, five gilded columns were ordered to be made at the entrance of the tabernacle (Exod. XXXVI), but before the oracle—that is, the Holy of Holies—four were made: beginners are corrected through the law so that they do not sin, while the perfect are admonished through grace so that they may live more devotedly to God.

“Those men, therefore, when they had seen the sign that he had performed, were saying: ‘This is truly the Prophet who is to come into the world.’ When Jesus therefore knew that they were about to come and seize him and make him king, he fled.”

They rightly understood that so great a prophet was to come into the world through proclamations of salvation—that is, into the common awareness of human beings. The disciples and crowds who believed in the Lord thought that he had come in such a way that he would already reign. This is what it means to wish to seize him and make him king: to anticipate his time, which he himself kept hidden until the end of the age. Hence the saying: “It is not yours to know the times or moments” (Acts I).

By fleeing, he gave us an example, so that in the good works we perform we might avoid the reward of human favor; at the same time, he intimates that his greatness cannot be understood.

## Further Material Concerning Fish

Just as we have briefly touched upon certain allegorical meanings of the five evangelical loaves, so it is pleasing to recall some things about fish, since blessed Ambrose says in the *Hexaemeron* that different kinds of fish have different uses.

Some generate eggs; others give birth to living and fully formed young. Those that generate eggs do not weave nests like birds, do not undertake the labor of prolonged incubation, and do not nourish their young with distress to themselves. An egg falls, and the water, as a kind nurse, receives it into the lap of its nature and returns the animal through rapid incubation. For as soon as it is touched by its parent, the living egg falls, and the fish emerges.

How pure and inviolate is its subsequent succession! No individual mingles with another kind: grayling with grayling, sea bass with sea bass. The scorpionfish also preserves the chastity of an unstained union for its own kind. Thus it possesses the chastity of its kind, but it does not possess the poison of its kind. For the scorpionfish does not strike; it restores.

### Concerning the Parrotfish

The parrotfish is said to ruminate among fish, as those report who have either experienced or practiced or studied such matters. Yet even these do not escape violence from those of their own power; subject to the greed of the more powerful, they are everywhere inferior. Every weaker creature lies exposed as prey to it.

Many indeed feed on plants and tiny worms. Yet there are some that devour one another and feed upon their own flesh. Among them the smaller becomes the food of the larger; then the larger itself is attacked by one stronger and becomes the food of another, a predator’s prey. Thus it happens that, when it has devoured another, it is itself devoured by another, and both arrive in a single belly: having been devoured together with their own devourer, they become, in the same viscera, partners in prey and vengeance.

This injury afterward grew among them voluntarily, just as among us it did not begin from nature but from greed. Or, because they were given for human use, they were also made into a sign, so that in them we might see the vices of our own behavior and guard against the examples, lest anyone more powerful attack an inferior, thereby providing an example of injury against himself.

Therefore, whoever harms another prepares a snare for himself, into which he himself will fall. You too are a fish who invade the entrails of another, who plunge the weak into the depths, who pursue a believer even into the abyss. Beware lest, while you pursue him, you yourself fall into the power of someone stronger, and he lead you into alien ambushes while avoiding your own—someone who, before you, awaits your misery, while he had feared his own because you pursued him.

### Concerning the Whale

Whales are sea monsters. If they float upon the waves, you might think them islands in the sea, or very high mountains whose peaks rise toward heaven. They are said to be seen not near the shore or along the coasts but in the depths of the Atlantic Ocean, so that sailors, at the sight of them, may be recalled from the presumption of sailing in those places and may not venture into the secrets of the elements without the terror of supreme death.

The *Physiologus*, however, says of the whale—for this is nevertheless to be believed—that it has two natures. The first is that, when it is hungry, it opens its mouth, and a very great and sweet fragrance comes out of its mouth, so that the smaller fish are delighted by its sweetness and all gather in its mouth. When its mouth has been filled, the fish closes its mouth and swallows them. But large and mature fish do not even approach its mouth.

Its second nature is that it presents itself in the form of an island. Sailors suppose that it is an island. They tie their ships to it, and when it feels that they have kindled a fire upon it for cooking and warming themselves, it plunges into the depths and drags the ships tied to it after itself.

This is the account of the whale’s natural history. Its meaning must now also be added. In strength the Devil (Zabulus) is like a whale, great in body, as the great magicians whom he makes display the minds of all men everywhere. [Col. 0893A] He hungers and thirsts and destroys as many as he can. But he draws the small in faith through the sweetness of his word, for he does not draw men who are firm in faith. Whoever trusts in him sends himself what seems to be a guarantee; then he is carried away to the Stygian regions—how badly he is deceived.

### Concerning the Moray Eel and the Viper

The viper is a most wicked kind of beast and more cunning than every creature of the serpent kind. When it has conceived the desire to mate, the viper seeks a moray-eel familiar to it as a partner, or prepares a new one; then, proceeding to the shore and making its presence known by a hiss, it calls her forth to the conjugal embrace. The invited moray does not stay away, and it shares with the venomous serpent the desired uses of their union.

[Col. 0893B] What does such an account mean except that the dispositions of husbands must be endured? If he is absent, his presence must be awaited, even if he is harsh, deceitful, uncultivated, slippery, or drunken. What is worse than poison, which the moray does not reject in its spouse? When called, it does not stay away, but with diligent affection embraces the serpent’s slipperiness.

He bears your faults and the ease of feminine fickleness, while you, woman, cannot endure your husband. Adam was deceived through Eve (Gen. III), not Eve through Adam. Since the woman called him to guilt, it is just that she should take him as her governor, lest she slip again through feminine fickleness.

But he is rough and uncultivated. Yet he pleased you once. Must a woman choose a husband repeatedly? The horse seeks its mate, loves its companion, and, if another is substituted, does not know how to draw the yoke. It regards the mate of another as unsafe for itself. You reject your own husband, woman, and think he should be changed; and if he leaves for a single day, you suspect him of ruin and immediately, without knowing the cause, pursue the injury of his honor as though you knew it.

The viper seeks the absent one, calls the absent one, and proclaims with a gentle hiss. When it senses its mate approaching, it spits out its venom; having shown reverence to the husband, it blushes with marital grace. You, woman, drive away your husband when he comes from far away, repelling him with insults.

### Concerning the Polypus

The polypus is a fish—that is, a many-footed creature—for it has very many tentacles. This clever creature, desiring the hook, embraces it with its gills, not with a bite; nor does it release it until it has gnawed all around the bait.

When it finds a rock in shallow water along the shore, it attaches itself to it. Then, with its cloudlike ingenuity, it assumes the rock’s color. With its back taking on a similar appearance, it receives, without any suspicion of fraud, many fish that glide toward it while failing to take precautions and supposing it to be a rock. It encloses them in the traps of its stealthy art and catches them within a kind of fold of its flesh.

Thus prey comes of its own accord and is captured by such devices as those used by people who often change their character and employ different arts of harming, testing the minds and senses of individuals. With the continent they preach continence, while in sexual relations they behave as though they had strayed from the pursuit of chastity and plunged into the whirlpools of intemperance. Those who hear or see them trust themselves with unwary ease and therefore fall more quickly, since they do not know how to distinguish; and no precaution is taken against what harms, because the more serious and more harmful wickedness is shadowed by a veil of kindness.

Therefore those who spread the strands and arms of their fraud far and wide, or assume a many-formed appearance, must be avoided. They too are polypuses, possessing many tentacles and the traits of crafty minds, by which they can entangle whatever falls upon the reefs of their fraud.

### Concerning the Crab

Crabs are called, as it were, shell-creatures with legs; they are hostile animals to oysters, for they live on their flesh by a remarkable art. Since it cannot open the oyster’s strong shell, the crab watches for the moment when the oyster opens the doors of its shells. Then the crab secretly throws in pebbles; and, the oyster’s closure being obstructed, it gnaws away its flesh.

Some report that, when ten crabs are tied together with a bundle of basil, all the scorpions in that place will gather at that spot.

There are therefore people who, using the crab’s method, insinuate themselves into another’s affairs, support the weakness of their own strength by a kind of cunning, weave deceit against a brother, and feed upon another’s misfortune.

But be content with what belongs to you, and do not let another’s losses feed you. Simplicity is good food: innocence possesses good things, knows nothing of lying in wait for others, and does not burn with the torch of its own greed. For every profit is, for such a person, a loss of virtues and an ignition of desire.

Therefore poverty is blessed, if it knows how to possess its own goods with truth, and it is to be preferred to all treasures, because “a little with the fear of God is better than great treasures without his fear” (Prov. XV).

Let us therefore use ingenuity to seek grace and preserve salvation, not to deceive another’s innocence. We may use examples from the sea for the advancement of our salvation, not for another’s danger.

### Concerning the Hedgehog

This terrestrial hedgehog, commonly called an *ericius*, if it senses any danger, closes itself within its spines and gathers itself into its armor, so that whoever thinks he can touch it is wounded.

This same hedgehog, foreseeing what is to come, secures two ways for breathing. When it has gathered that the north wind is going to blow, it closes the northern opening; when it knows that the clouds of the sky are being cleared by the south wind, it turns toward the north, so that it may avoid the blasts coming against it and those which would cause harm from the opposite direction.

This concerns the terrestrial hedgehog. Of the sea urchin, however, it is said that it is a small, worthless, and despised creature. It commonly serves sailors as an indicator of an approaching storm or as an announcer of calm. Finally, when it senses a storm of winds beforehand, it seizes a heavy stone and carries it like ballast, dragging it as an anchor so that it will not be tossed about by the waves. Thus it does not free itself by its own strength, but stabilizes and governs itself through another’s weight.

By this sign sailors take it as an indication of coming disturbance and take precautions for themselves, lest an unforeseen storm find them unprepared. Often people see a disturbance in the air and are often deceived, because they usually disperse it without a storm. The hedgehog is not deceived; the hedgehog’s signs never pass it by.

From where does such knowledge come to so small an animal, so that it foretells the future? [Col. 0895A] The more there is nothing in it, the more remarkable is the prudence it possesses. I believe that, through the Lord’s generosity toward all things, it too has received this gift of foreknowledge.

For if God clothes the grass in such a way that we marvel; if he feeds the birds; if he has prepared food for ravens—for their young cry out to God; if he has given women skill in weaving; if he has not left the spider, which hangs its loose webs at doorways with such subtlety and skill, without its share; if he himself gave strength to the horse and removed fear from its neck, so that it might exult in the field, smile as it meets kings, scent war from afar, and be roused by the sound of the trumpet; if he has filled so many irrational creatures and other insensible things—grass and lilies—with the wisdom of his ordering, why do we doubt that he has also placed in the hedgehog this grace of foreknowledge?

For he leaves nothing unexplored and nothing undisclosed. He who feeds all things sees all things; Wisdom fills all things, for it made all things in wisdom.

## Sunday of the Passion

[Col. 0895]

[Col. 0895B] “Which of you will convict me of sin?” (John VIII). He does not disdain to demonstrate rationally that he is not a sinner.

“If I speak the truth, why do you not believe me? Whoever is from God hears the words of God. For this reason you do not hear, because you are not from God.”

There are some who do not deign to receive God’s commandments even with the ear of the body; there are some who receive them but do not embrace them with any desire of the mind; and there are some who are pierced by listening gladly, but after their tears return to iniquity. These certainly do not hear the words of God, because they scorn to practice them in their works.

Although all are sons of God by nature, as the parables of the dutiful and prodigal son and of the two sons invited to the vineyard show, nevertheless some are of the devil through vice, because they do not love the words of God. Those who are reborn from God through adoption in generation, however, hear the word of God and keep it.

“Then the Jews answered and said to him: ‘Do we not rightly say that you are a Samaritan and have a demon?’”

The Samaritans had received the Lord when he spoke with the woman at the well, and he had lived among them. The Jews therefore call him a Samaritan, as though he were a sinner, because they regarded the Samaritans as sinners and did not count themselves among them.

“Jesus answered: ‘I do not have a demon, but I honor my Father, and you have dishonored me.’”

Of the two charges brought against him, he denied one. For “Samaritan” is interpreted as “guardian,” and he did not deny that he was a guardian. “He who guards Israel neither slumbers” (Ps. CXX). And “unless the Lord guards the city, he watches in vain who guards it” (Ps. CXXVI).

He did not answer with insulting words, though he could truly have replied: “You have a demon.” But our pride is here put to shame. What is suggested to us by this except that, when we receive false insults from our neighbors, we should also keep silent about their evil words, lest we turn the mystery of our correction into weapons of rage?

“‘I do not seek my own glory; there is one who seeks it and judges.’ I do not seek glory as the hypocrites do, who seek to appear to be what they are not. There is a Father who seeks my glory and judges—that is, distinguishes it from your glory—because you glory according to the world, but I do not; rather, it is the glory that I had with the Father before the world existed, which is distinct from human self-exaltation. [Col. 0896B] According to penal judgment the Father judges no one, but has given all judgment to the Son; according to the judgment of discernment he judges, as in the psalm: ‘Judge me, O God’ (Ps. XLII). The explanation of this judgment follows: ‘And distinguish my cause,’ he says, ‘from an unholy nation’ (ibid.).

Likewise, we understand two kinds of temptation, one of which deceives and the other tests. For it is written: ‘God tempts no one’ (Jas. I). And again it is written: ‘The Lord your God is testing you, to know whether you love him’ (Deut. XIII). ‘To know’ is said in the sense of ‘to make known.’ Job was hidden from himself, but not from God. God admitted the tempter and made him known to Job.

So also there are two kinds of fear: servile fear, when you fear that you may suffer punishment; and chaste fear, when you fear that you may lose righteousness. [Col. 0896C] The one kind is cast out by perfect love (John IV); the other preserves us, remaining before God forever and ever. For even the adulterous woman fears that her husband may come, whereas the chaste woman fears that her husband may depart.

“‘Amen, amen, I say to you: if anyone keeps my word, he will never see death forever.’ By his own example he admonishes us not to cease preaching when the perversity of the wicked increases, because the good become better through insults, while the reprobate become worse through a benefit.

“‘Therefore the Jews said: Now we know that you have a demon. Abraham died, and the prophets, and you say: If anyone keeps my word, he will never taste death forever.’” He speaks of the second death, the death of Gehenna, the death of condemnation with the devil, because neither Abraham nor the prophets are dead. [Col. 0896D] They died and live; these people were living and were dead. To see or taste death is to experience it.

“‘Are you greater than our father Abraham, who died? And the prophets died. Whom do you make yourself?’ Jesus answered: ‘If I glorify myself, my glory is nothing. It is my Father who glorifies me, whom you say is your God, and you have not known him. But I know him. And if I should say that I do not know him, I would be like you, a liar. But I know him, and I keep his word.’”

He spoke the Father’s word as Son; indeed, he himself was the Father’s Word speaking to human beings. If they had known the Father, they would have received his Son, whom the Father’s voice glorified at the baptism, on the mountain, and on other such occasions. Therefore, in answer to their words, “Whom do you make yourself?” he refers his glory to the Father, saying: “If I alone, without the Father, glorify myself, my glory is nothing,” as it is with the hypocrites.

“‘Abraham your father rejoiced that he might see my day; and he saw it and was glad.’” Believing, he rejoiced in hope, so that he might see it through understanding. What he means by “my day” may be uncertain: whether the temporal day of the Lord in the flesh, or the day that knows neither rising nor setting. Abraham saw both.

For when he sent his servant to seek a wife for his son Isaac, he said: “‘Place your hand under my thigh and swear by the God of heaven’” (Gen. [Col. 0897B] XXIV). What does this signify except that it was being indicated that the God of heaven would come in the flesh from Abraham’s lineage? Those who criticize Christ’s flesh criticize what Abraham did. Abraham saw the Lord’s day when, as a figure of the supreme Trinity, he received three angels as guests.

“‘The Jews said to him: You are not yet fifty years old, and have you seen Abraham? Jesus said to them: Amen, amen, I say to you: before Abraham came to be, I am.’” He did not say “I was,” but “I am,” because divinity has no time. He draws them from consideration of the flesh to divinity; but, hard as stones, they think this is blasphemy.

“‘Therefore they took up stones to throw at him. But Jesus hid himself and went out of the temple.’” They sought to overwhelm the one whom they could not understand. But the Lord did not wish to avenge himself, because he had come to suffer. Therefore he hid himself, to give us the example of giving place to anger; or else he did so to show that the truth itself is hidden from those who disdain to follow his words, and that it flees the mind because it does not find a humble one.

Note that the Jews inconsiderately said to the Lord: “You are not yet fifty years old.” Some fabricate a much greater number of years from the Incarnation to the Passion than can be gathered from the histories.

## SERMON ON THE FLESH THAT THE WORD ASSUMED: WHAT IT WAS LIKE WITH RESPECT TO SUFFERABILITY AND FEELINGS

It is necessary to speak about the flesh of the Word, because we believe that from the very conception, through the operation of the Holy Spirit, it was so cleansed that the Word himself assumed it wholly free and immune from every sin. Only the punishment of sin remained, assumed by the will, not by necessity, of the one assuming it, so that while he suffered this in the Savior without guilt, he might free those who, in the process of being saved, had been liable to punishment on account of guilt.

Concerning this punishment of sufferability or mortality, some ask how it was present in the Savior’s flesh. It is easy to know how, as long as that flesh remained in the mass of the human race under original debt, it necessarily endured the punishment of transgression, which was held throughout the whole of humanity. But after it was singularly separated from the whole, so that it was neither in the whole nor shared its cause with the whole, it owed nothing further in punishment, because it had no guilt. Therefore, insofar as it was concerned, it did not owe the endurance of punishment, since it no longer possessed guilt.

The Savior could therefore justly, in his flesh—which he assumed without guilt—not have assumed either the punishment of mortality or the weakness of sufferability; rather, because he was not a sinner and did not need to be tested, he could have put on from his first conception the glory of immortality, not only beyond the condition in which we are mortal, but even beyond that which the first human being possessed before sin. [Col. 0898A]

The first human being, because he was to be tested, had to be such that he could either sin or not sin, so that either alternative would arise from will, not necessity. For there could have been neither merit for obedience nor guilt for disobedience unless both obedience and transgression had been voluntary. Thus, because his will was awaited for either outcome in the testing, the possibility of either outcome was granted to him.

Since, therefore, he possessed the possibility of sinning and not sinning, he had to possess the possibility of dying and not dying. For if he had been necessarily immortal, then even as a transgressor and sinner he could not have died, and consequently disobedience would not have received its due punishment. Nor would the sinner ever have recognized himself as such if, being dead inwardly, he had always lived outwardly.

Likewise, if he had been necessarily mortal, then, even if disobedience had continued, he would have had to die; and he would have been punished unjustly without guilt if he died without sinning. Therefore, because he was to be tested and it was awaited whether he would persist in disobedience, his flesh too was mortal in a certain respect, because he could also not die: by virtue of the fact that he could die, he would die if he sinned; and likewise, by virtue of the fact that he could not die, he would not die if he persevered in obedience. [Col. 0898C]

Christ, however, because he was perfect man from the beginning and was found proven perfect, was not awaited either for perfection or for testing; and therefore, though he had free will, he did not have it in such a way that he could sin. Likewise, insofar as it depended on him, he ought to possess immortality, so that he could not die at all.

Hence it is clear that Christ, as man, was owed from the beginning not only the immortality that the first man possessed before his transgression, but also the immortality that the second man now possesses after the resurrection. Just as, through participation in divinity, he was confirmed in spirit unto truth so that he could not sin, so also, through the merit of virtue, he would be confirmed in the flesh unto incorruption, so that he could not die.

But because sinful flesh could not be freed from the punishment of sin unless the flesh that was without sin suffered the weakness of sufferability and mortality, Christ retained these by power and endured them by will; he did not suffer them by necessity.

As for the experience of suffering in Christ’s flesh, some are found to have thought wrongly, asserting that in all the kinds of suffering displayed in and around it, that flesh received the likeness of suffering and pain but endured no pain or suffering at all. They do not consider how great an absurdity follows from such an assertion.

For how was there true compassion in Christ if there was no true suffering? How will the prophet’s statement stand: “‘Truly he himself bore our weaknesses, and he carried our pains’” (Isa. LIII)? If Christ did not suffer pain on the cross, why did he so earnestly ask that the cup of suffering be taken from him? (Matt. XXVI.) What did that sweating blood mean, bearing witness to the anguish of impending death? What did Christ himself mean when, explaining the weakness in which the flesh feared suffering and the will according to which the spirit was ready, he said: “‘The spirit indeed is willing, but the flesh is weak’” (ibid.)?

Therefore those who deny that there was true suffering in the Savior according to the weakness of the flesh are, insofar as it depends on them, convicted of denying the redemption accomplished through Christ’s suffering.

There are others who, with no less madness, concerning the human feelings in Christ—through which he assumed the truth of nature together with humanity—have not feared to utter things that are not only false but even horrifyingly blasphemous.

Because the Apostle says: “‘We do not have a high priest who cannot sympathize with our weaknesses, but one who was tested in every respect’” (Hebr. IV), they assert that the human disposition in Christ experienced the movements of vices, though without the consent of reason. They say this occurred according to the weakness of desiring, by which we sinners, because of the original corruption in the flesh that we bear, commonly experience—even unwillingly—unlawful appetites, the movements of rising desire, and the pleasure of a tempting vice.

They say, however, that Christ voluntarily endured these movements in his flesh so that, by resisting them as they tempted him, he might emerge victorious; thus, by overcoming the temptation of vices, he would acquire for himself the reward of righteousness and form in himself an example for us, who are placed in temptation, of resisting and conquering. [Col. 0900A]

But far be it from Christian understanding to say or believe that there was ever in the sacred flesh of the spotless Lamb any suggestion of disordered pleasure or unlawful desire. For if we were to say that any root of evil pleasure or disordered movement of desire existed in him, we would plainly deny that he was free from these things from the very beginning.

How, moreover, could he cleanse vice if he carried vice? An inordinate movement arising from the weakness of desire, together with the corruption from which it arises, is not only punishment but also guilt. Yet, because in the baptized it is not counted toward condemnation, it is excused through the grace of new regeneration, as the Apostle says: “‘There is now no condemnation for those who are in Christ Jesus’” (Rom. VIII).

This corruption, through the grace of the sacrament, does not receive the status of not being guilt; rather, it receives the status of not being condemnable. For if it were not guilt at all, it would not need to be excused, since things that are not guilt ought not to be imputed.

Therefore we truly say that Christ assumed, with the taking on of flesh, only that weakness of human nature which is punishment. But we unhesitatingly affirm that he in no way admitted that weakness which is punishment in such a way that it is also guilt.

Nor do we wish to call him victor over vices in such a way that we say he ever carried or experienced the very vices that he conquered. For this reason he consented to be weakened by punishment alone: so that he might first justify those who were sick in both guilt and punishment from guilt, and afterward free them from punishment.

## PALM SUNDAY

[Col. 0899]

“‘When they had drawn near to Jerusalem and had come to Bethphage at the Mount of Olives, then Jesus sent two disciples, saying to them: Go into the village that is opposite you, and immediately you will find a donkey tied, and its colt tied with it, on which no one has ever sat; untie it and bring it to me. And if anyone says anything to you, tell him that the Lord needs them, and immediately he will let them go’” (Matt. XXI).

Bethphage was a little village of priests and bore the type of confession, because its name is interpreted as “house of the mouth.” It is therefore fittingly associated with the location on the Mount of Olives, since the nature of oil is to provide light and comfort in labors and sorrows. For those who confess their sins cling to Christ, who refreshes us with spiritual anointing and the light of knowledge.

And so that the city set upon this mountain might not be hidden, he sends the disciples into the village that is opposite them, so that through them he might penetrate the fortifications of the whole world placed in opposition.

The donkey and the colt signify the Jews and the Gentiles, because of certain similarities. This animal is unclean, and, more than other beasts of burden, stupid, weak, lowly, and burden-bearing. Such were human beings before Christ. They were also bound by the devil and could not escape by their own strength.

For just as a ship, its rudder broken, is driven wherever the storm pushes it, so a human being, having lost the assistance of divine grace through sin, does not do what he wishes but what the devil wishes. And just as a people is initially able to make for itself whatever king it wants, but, once he has been made king, it is no longer in its power to expel him from the kingdom, and thus the people’s will is turned into necessity, so a human being, before sinning, possesses free choice as to whether he wishes to be under the kingdom of the devil.

But once he is subjected to the devil by sinning, he cannot leave his power, because the will has been changed into necessity. This is what sinners commonly say: “We would like to be holy, but we cannot.” They speak truly, but they have no excuse, because at first they were able not to be under the devil’s power, from which no one except God alone can rescue them.

Among the people of the nations, entangled in the bonds of unbelief, no human being had ever sat upon the colt—that is, no teacher had imposed the bridle of correction by which its tongue might be restrained from evil or compelled to go along the way of life. That human being would sit upon it—that is, would rest for its benefit by teaching—if someone corrected and restrained its folly more rationally.

Hence, not without reason, the two disciples are understood as the two orders of preachers sent to Jews and Gentiles. Some, however, understand these two to be Peter and Philip, because they were the first to bring Gentiles to Christ: Philip brought Samaria, as the donkey; Peter brought Cornelius, as the colt of Samaria.

The apostles are called and sent two by two, because love is not found in one alone. Hence it is written: “Woe to the one who is alone” (Eccles. IV). Two bring the Hebrews out of Egypt. Two carry the cluster of grapes from the holy land, so that superiors may always join knowledge to their work. Let them bring forth the two commandments from the two tablets. Let them be washed and wash others in two fountains, carry the Lord’s ark with two poles, and recognize the Lord between the two cherubim, singing in spirit and mind:

“Untie them,” he says, “through teaching and miracles.” As though he were saying: “‘Whatever you loose on earth will be loosed also in heaven’” (Matt. XVIII).

Strangers bind in order to possess; Christ loosens in order to hold.

“‘Immediately the Lord will let them go,’” namely, the Lord who, by the right of creation, desires every creature to be devoted to his service. First human beings are called through the teaching and miracles of the apostles; then the Lord leaves them to their own choice, so that they may either remain in the faith to which they were called or return to their former customs: the Jews to their general superstitions, and the Gentiles to their foul practices.

For the fact that we have been called is God’s work. But that we live worthily of our calling is likewise God’s work. And this is what he says: “He will let them go”—not to the devil, but to their own choice.

“‘The disciples went and did as Jesus commanded them. But as they were untying the colt, its masters said to them: Why are you untying the colt? They said: Because the Lord needs it. And they let them go. And they brought the colt to Jesus, and, throwing their garments over the colt, they made him sit upon it.’”

Mark writes that the colt was found tied outside before a doorway at a crossroads (Mark XI). The door is the one who says: “‘I am the door of the sheep; if anyone enters through me, he will be saved and will find pasture’” (John X). The people of the Gentiles lacked these pastures while they stood outside the door, bound at the crossroads.

It rightly stood at a crossroads, because it did not hold to one road of faith but followed uncertain paths in error. The one who doubted between death and life stood at a crossroads in the freedom of choice.

The Lord had many masters, because, being driven about by various errors through many doctrines, it served as many demons as it served vices. Yet they could not claim dominion over it as their own: they had been made masters not by nature but by guilt. Therefore, when the Lord is named, one is recognized. For although there are many gods and many lords, generally there is nevertheless one God and one Lord.

Those who opposed the untying of the colt fall silent when they hear the Lord’s name. The teachers of error who resisted Christ’s teachers defended their darkness only until, with miracles bearing witness, God’s power shone forth.

Thus the free people of believers, who bear God in their hearts, is brought to him. The apostles’ garments are the divine commandments and special grace, by which the shame of our flesh is covered. Formerly these peoples were naked, but now, through the apostles’ prayers, they have Christ as their rider, so that sin may not reign in wanton flesh, but righteousness, peace, and joy in the Holy Spirit.

“‘Now all this took place so that what was spoken through the prophet might be fulfilled: Say to the daughter of Zion: Behold, your king is coming to you, gentle, sitting upon a colt, the foal of a donkey under the yoke.’”

This is written in the prophet Zechariah, from whose meaning Matthew and John depart in no way, even if they set down different words. Since it is Jerusalem itself, he calls the good people in that blind nation “the daughter of Zion.”

“Say to her,” you preachers, “so that she may not fear but, rejoicing, recognize her king,” the one who rules minds and leads them to the kingdom of heaven, lest she say with the reprobate: “‘We have no king but Caesar’” (John XIX).

He came gently—not sitting in a golden chariot shining with purple, nor upon a horse that loves discord, but upon a beast friendly to peace. According to the literal sense, the Lord does not appear to have sat upon both animals during the short journey; rather, it is more fitting that he used the colt for sitting while the donkey was led free.

Mystically, however, he sat in humility upon both peoples under his dominion, with Peter and Paul sent to them. Since the wanton and untamed Gentile people believed through the example of the faithful from the Synagogue, which had drawn the yoke of the law, it is rightly said that the colt was the son of a donkey under the yoke.

Consider that just as this kind of beast, when it goes astray, goes astray through simplicity and not through harshness, so the people from both nations who believed in Christ sinned before Christ not through malice but through ignorance.

“‘As he went, many spread their garments on the road; others cut branches from the trees and spread them on the road.’”

See that the apostles placed their garments upon the beast, while the others placed theirs beneath the feet of the beast. Christians are spread out and adorned beneath the commandments of the apostles; but they trample the commandments of the law—that is, circumcision and the other Jewish customs.

The garments of the crowd are therefore the commandments of the law, spread on the road—that is, trampled by Christians in Christ. The crowd that spread its garments on the road consists of believers from the circumcision who, seeing and recognizing Christ, cast down upon the ground the glory they had from the law, humbling themselves and saying with the Apostle:

“Whatever gains I had, these I have counted as loss because of Christ, and I consider them refuse, so that I may gain Christ” (Philipp. III).

Those who cut branches from the trees are believing and learned teachers who, receiving examples from the prophets as though from trees, spread branches before the Gentile people on the road—that is, in Christ—so that they might enter the sanctuary of God without stumbling.

Or it may be understood in this way: the Savior, sitting upon the beast, travels toward Jerusalem not only when he leads the soul of each believer, as its ruler, to the peace of inward vision, but also when he provides universally for holy Church and kindles her desire for the peace above.

The feet of the beast are the last ones whom the Apostle appointed for judgment. Although they are not the back upon which God sat, they are nevertheless instructed together with the soldiers by John.

Many spread their garments on the road because the army of martyrs gives its bodies as coverings for souls, laying them down for the Lord so that they may make a path of right living for the elect who follow. Finally, they spread their garments on the road who discipline their bodies so as to prepare a way for the Lord to the mind, or to provide good examples for those who follow.

They cut leaves or branches from the trees who pluck the judgments or examples of the Fathers and, with humble preaching, lay them down on God’s road before the mind of the hearer who is coming.

“The righteous will flourish like the palm” (Ps. XCI): narrow at the roots, broad in flowers and fruits, because they are the good fragrance of Christ and spread the way of God’s commandments through their good reputation.

“‘When he was already approaching the descent of the Mount of Olives, all the crowds of those descending began rejoicing and praising the Lord with a loud voice.’”

The Lord descended from the Mount of Olives—that is, humbled himself to the weakness of our flesh, although he was in the form of God. The crowds descend with him—that is, they humble themselves under the hand of the one who is merciful, so that they may be exalted by him.

“‘The crowds that went before and those that followed cried out, saying: Hosanna to the Son of David; blessed is he who comes, the king in the name of the Lord. Peace in heaven and glory in the highest.’”

“Blessed is the kingdom of our father David that comes. Hosanna in the highest.”

The prophets go before; the apostles follow. “Deep calls to deep” (Ps. XLI), that is, one law calls to another. The Jewish people went before; the Gentiles followed.

Faithful people cry out to the Son of David: “Hosanna,” which in Latin is said to mean “salvation,” because they believe that the Son of David, the Son of God, is one Son who saves earthly beings, so that the righteous may be built into the place of the fallen angels.

They also confess that he is blessed who comes in the name of the Lord—that is, in the name of his Father—because the Son receives his name from the Father, and the Father from the Son.

The blessing that takes place in God is confession alone and praise of the good things granted by him. The blessing that takes place from God in us is fulfilled when we are filled with his benefits.

What the faithful of former times believed would come, we believe has come. In his praise heavenly and earthly things sing together. At his birth the heavenly powers sang: “Glory to God in the highest, and on earth peace to human beings.” Now, with the ruler of the world triumphing, mortals return the praise due to him, saying: “Peace in heaven and glory in the highest.”

The crowds, refreshed by the five loaves and two fish, had wished to seize Jesus and make him king, but he fled to the mountain. Now, however, he does not restrain the voices of those who sing that the kingdom of David is to be restored in him. In this he aptly teaches that he was king of an eternal empire in heaven, not merely on earth, and that he would attain it through contempt of death, the glory of the resurrection, and the triumph of the ascension.

For this reason, after the resurrection, he said to the disciples: “‘All authority in heaven and on earth has been given to me’” (Matt. XXVIII).

The praise of the crowd agrees with the voice of Gabriel, who said to the Lord’s mother: “‘He will be great and will be called the Son of the Most High, and the Lord God will give him the throne of David his father, and he will reign over the house of Jacob forever’” (Luke I).

They therefore rightly cry out: “‘Hosanna in the highest,’ that is, ‘Save us in the heavenly realms,’ where every knee will bow to him—of those in heaven, on earth, and under the earth” (Philipp. II).

It should be noted that *hosanna* is a Hebrew compound word made from something corrupted and something complete. “Save” or “make safe” is said among them as *hosi*, while *anna* is the interjection of one entreating.

Thus, in Psalm CXVII, where the Seventy Translators rendered, “O Lord, save me,” it is written in Hebrew: “Anna adonai, hosi anna.” Our translator Jerome, elucidating it more carefully, rendered it: “‘I beseech you, Lord; save, I beseech you.’”

The phrase “O Lord” through the interjection of one entreating means the same as “I beseech you, Lord” through the very word of entreaty. Therefore *hosanna* means “Save, I beseech you,” with the vowel that ends the preceding word omitted when it is fully pronounced as *hosi*.

This is what metricians call *synaloepha* when scanning verses, although, when scanning, they pass over a written letter. In the word *hosanna*, however, the letter is not written; it is wholly omitted while the meaning intended by the speakers remains intact.

## ON PALM SUNDAY

[Col. 0903]

“‘Tell the daughter of Zion: Behold, your King comes to you gently, sitting upon a donkey and a colt, the foal of a beast under the yoke’” (Zech. IX).

The heavenly King, dearest brothers, through the prophet Zechariah commands you to rejoice at his coming. The Lord comes for reconciliation, he who had been estranged from you because of the sin of your first parent.

Before he came, he sent ambassadors—prophets and patriarchs—saying to them: “‘Tell the daughter of Zion,’” that is, announce it to my Church. He calls her the daughter of Zion because she ought to be the daughter of contemplation and delight.

For Zion is interpreted as “contemplation”; she must guard herself against spiritual enemies. But he adds what he means: “‘Behold, your king comes.’”

The Lord had withdrawn from the human race through sin, although he had been near to those living rationally. But he who had withdrawn because of our injustice came through his mercy.

“Through the mercies of our God, the dawn from on high has visited us” (Luke I). “He inclined the heavens and came down, and darkness was beneath his feet” (Ps. XVII).

“He inclined the heavens”—that is, he humbled heavenly things, namely, the Godhead, and even the angels, through the compassion he showed in the restoration of the human race. And he himself descended by uniting human nature to himself.

The angels were inclined when, approaching God, they ministered to him. But although he was humble and shared our frailty, darkness—that is, the blindness of worldly people—was beneath his feet, that is, fully subjected to him.

And when a strong soldier had come to battle, “he placed his tent in the sun” (Ps. XVIII). Christ’s tent is understood as that in which he fought for God the Father. He placed it—that is, established it—in the sun, namely, in the Virgin, who was “beautiful as the moon, chosen as the sun.”

She was the moon because she illuminated the darkness of night; the sun because, more than others, she alone burned with the warmth of the Holy Spirit.

Having therefore prepared his tent, “coming forth from his chamber like a bridegroom” (ibid.), he became the Church’s bridegroom through the union of the flesh. Coming forth, I say, from his chamber—that is, from the virginal womb—he “rejoiced like a giant,” that is, like a strong and unconquerable man, to run the course of his military service.

He came to wage war against the ruler of this world, saying: “‘Now the ruler of this world will be cast out’” (John XII), namely, from the minds of human beings in which he had previously reigned.

He chose a few poor people to be with him, as the Apostle says: “‘He chose the foolish things of the world to confound the wise, and the weak things of the world to confound the strong’” (I Cor. I).

For what were Peter and Andrew except foolish and lowly? And yet, from those few, one fell—that is, Judas, who betrayed him.

Judas was greedy and a thief, and, having the money box, carried what was put into it (John XII). [Col. 0905B] When he saw Mary pour costly ointment over the Lord’s head, he said: “Why this waste? For this could have been sold for much and given to the poor” (Matt. XXVI).

And so he went to the chief priests in order to betray him. Unhappy Judas! He thought that he was suffering loss through the pouring out of the ointment, and he wished to compensate for it with the price of his teacher.

But because the Lord, in supreme mercy, wished to rebuke the erring disciple, he said: “‘The one who dips his hand with me in the dish is the one who will betray me’” (ibid.), so that, knowing that the Lord recognized his thoughts, he might repent.

While the others were drawing back their hands, Judas, in the shamelessness with which he was about to betray the Lord, put his hand into the dish with the Teacher, so that by his boldness he might feign a good conscience.

When the Lord said: “‘One of you will betray me’” (ibid.), and the others said: “‘Is it I, Lord?’” (ibid.), Judas said: “‘Is it I, Rabbi?’” (ibid.).

They called him “Lord,” but Judas called him “Teacher,” because he wanted to lessen the sin he had conceived through the word he used, “Teacher.” For it seemed a lesser thing to betray a teacher than to betray the Lord.

But the Lord overcame him through patience, because he endured him. Although he knew him to be a betrayer, he nevertheless did not refuse to wash his feet.

The Lord was therefore handed over to the Jews and suffered outside the gate, so that he might sanctify the people through his blood: “‘Let us therefore go out to him outside the camp, bearing his reproach’” (Hebr. XIII).

We must therefore remember how great a reproach the Lord suffered for us. When he was being led to a shameful death, he was cast outside the city as vile and contemptible, and he carried his cross and was crucified among thieves at the place of Calvary, where criminals were beheaded.

Although the Jews did these things with evil intent, the merciful Lord, through a great dispensation, wished these three things to occur. He wished not only to give human beings redemption through this kind of death, but also to shape our life by it.

He did not wish to be crucified rather than stoned or punished by some other kind of penalty without reason. Rather, he teaches that something must be understood by his expulsion and crucifixion, when the Apostle says: “‘Let us go out to him outside the camp,’” and so forth.

Let us therefore see how we ought to go out, from which camp, and what reproach we ought to bear.

As long as we are in this mortal body, we are away from the Lord. For we are in these bodies as though in a camp, fighting against a spiritual enemy.

But we must not take pleasure in these camps—that is, in the flesh—for, as the Apostle says: “‘We are debtors not to the flesh, to live according to the flesh. For if you live according to the flesh, you will die’” (Rom. VIII).

We must therefore leave these camps, so that we may not be subjected to the dominion of the flesh. It must serve, not rule. Hence the Apostle says: “‘I discipline my body and bring it into servitude’” (I Cor. IX), or “subject it,” so that it may serve the soul.

This departure is what the Lord says in the Gospel: “‘Whoever wishes to come after me, let him deny himself,’” and so forth (Matt. XVI).

We must deny within ourselves not what God made there, but what we ourselves make. Whatever good we have is from God; whatever evil we have is from human beings. Therefore, “the one who was stealing must steal no longer.”

You have heard what it means to go out beyond the camp; now let us see what it means to bear the reproach of Christ. This is the same as what is said in that Gospel passage: “And let him take up his cross” (ibid.). What does it mean to take up the Lord’s cross? The Lord wished to choose this kind of torment so that from it we might take an example or pattern for our life. For just as one who has been crucified cannot direct his limbs toward any actions, so we must crucify the old man with our vices and desires, so that neither foot, nor hand, nor any other limb may be able to carry out or devise any deceit. Let us therefore take up this cross and crucify our vices within ourselves.

Now, then, let us go out, brothers, to meet Christ with palm branches—that is, with victories won over the devil and his resources—and with the flowers of the virtues. Let one offer the flower of love, which is the principal root of all the virtues. Concerning it Gregory says: “Just as many branches of a tree proceed from a single root, so many virtues are generated from a single charity.”

Let another offer the flower of virginity and the lily of chastity. This is the virtue that commended John, whom Jesus loved, because he was chosen by the Lord as a virgin; the Lord himself praises him in the Apocalypse: “These are they who have not been defiled with women,” etc. (Apoc. XIV).

Let another be adorned with the flower of humility, imitating him who says: “Learn from me, because I am meek and humble of heart” (Matt. XI). Let the flower of mercy adorn another, because “blessed are the merciful, for they shall obtain mercy.” Let another hold the branch of repentance, because “blessed are those who have done penance,” etc. Let another burn the incense of prayers, saying: “Let my prayer be directed,” etc. (Ps. CXL). Let another feed the poor person in Christ, remembering the Gospel saying: “Whatever you did for one of the least of mine,” etc. (Matt. XXV).

And let no one approach the Lord so empty-handed that all may deserve to be made equal, and that he who sits above may deign to lead and guide them to the palms of Jerusalem. Thus, when the Lord entered the city with the crowds, a crowd of children and the whole populace rushed out to meet him with palm branches and received the King of glory with hymns. Entering the temple amid them, he drove out with whips those who were buying and selling doves there, and foretold that the temple of his body would be destroyed but rebuilt after three days. In the temple, therefore, he performed many signs and daily taught the crowds heavenly things.

But because this day is celebrated throughout the universal Church, after the example of that people, with palms and flowers, it is called Palm Sunday. On Wednesday he is handed over by Judas; on Thursday bread and wine are consecrated for us as his body and blood; on Friday he is crucified for the salvation of all; on Saturday he rested in the tomb; on Sunday, rising from the dead, he gave life and joy to all who hope in him.

## On the Lord’s Supper. According to John.

[Col. 0907]

[Col. 0907B] “Before the feast of Passover, Jesus, knowing that his hour had come to pass from this world to the Father, having loved his own who were in the world, loved them to the end” (John XII).

Passover is called a passing-over because the Lord passed through Egypt, striking its firstborn and freeing the children of Israel, and because the children of Israel passed over that night from Egyptian slavery. This signifies that the Lord would pass from this world to the Father, and that his faithful would pass from temporal things to heavenly ones.

“He loved his own to the end,” that is, in himself. “For Christ,” says the Apostle, “is the end of the law” (Rom. X)—the end toward which we may go happily, not the place where we may perish unhappily. Or, “to the end” means “unto death”: not that Christ’s love was ended by death, but that he loved to such an extent that his love led him even to death. [Col. 0907C] In this he gave an example, so that all might remain in God’s truth to the end.

“He rises from supper and lays aside his garments. And when he had taken a towel, he girded himself. Then he poured water into a basin and began to wash the disciples’ feet and to wipe them with the towel with which he was girded.”

In his great humility he did not disdain to wash the feet even of the one whose hands he already foresaw engaged in the crime. What wonder is it that he laid aside his garments, when, though he was in the form of God, he emptied himself? (Phil. II.) What wonder is it that he girded himself with a towel, when, taking the form of a servant, he was found in appearance as a man? (ibid.) What wonder is it that he poured water into a basin with which to wash the disciples’ feet, when he poured out blood upon the earth to cleanse the uncleanness of sins? What [Col. 0907D] wonder is it that with the towel with which he was girded he wiped the feet he had washed, when with the flesh in which he was clothed he strengthened the footsteps of the evangelists?

He came, therefore, to Simon Peter, and Peter said to him: “Lord, are you washing my feet?” It must not be understood that he came to Peter after having approached some others; rather, he began the washing with him. Thus the first of the apostles is terrified that God should wash a human being’s feet.

“Jesus answered and said to him: What I am doing you do not know now, but you shall know afterward. Peter said to him: [Col. 0908B] You shall never wash my feet”—that is, you shall never wash them. Just as a humble person is ready to serve, so a servant serves by refusing to accept service.

Jesus answered him: “If I do not wash you, you shall have no part with me.” He says “you” with reference only to the feet. Whoever is not washed through baptism and the confession of repentance has no part with Jesus.

Simon Peter said to him: “Lord, not only my feet, but also my hands and my head.” Terrified by the Lord’s response concerning the danger to his salvation, he offers his whole self to be washed, troubled by love and fear.

Jesus said to him: “He who has been washed needs only to wash his feet; he is entirely clean.” This is to be understood as “except for his feet.” The whole person is washed in baptism, but when one afterward lives amid human affairs, human affections—without which one does not live—are like feet, because if we say that we have no sin, we deceive ourselves (1 John I). Therefore he who daily intercedes for us washes our feet daily. Hence we also say every day: “Forgive us our debts” (Matt. VI). And in the Song of Songs: “I have washed my feet; how shall I defile them?” (Song V).

Let those who, when love of human praise steals upon them, strive to please people, fear to defile their feet. It should be noted that Peter went astray so that we might not go astray when he offered his whole self to God to be washed. God corrected him, showing that one who has been baptized once must not be baptized again.

“And you are clean, but not all.” For he knew who would betray him. Therefore he said: “You are not all clean.” After he had washed their feet, he took his garments. And when he had reclined again, he said to them: “Do you know what I have done for you?”

He wishes to disclose what he had said to Peter: “You shall know afterward.” Mystically, the supper at which the Lord reclined with the disciples signifies the entire period during which he dwelt bodily in the Church, feeding all the faithful with the nourishment of saving speech and the sweetness of miracles, while he himself was fed by the faith and love of those who listened.

He rose from supper and laid aside his garments when he laid down the members of his body upon the cross. He girded himself with a towel when he surrounded his members with the exercise of suffering. For affliction in the Passion is represented precisely by the towel, which is made through labor of many kinds.

“He poured water into a basin,” etc. When he died upon the cross, he poured water together with blood from his side, by which he deigns to cleanse and sanctify believers.

After he had washed their feet, he took his garments; and, reclining again, he disclosed to them the mystery of the washing, because after consecrating for us, through his suffering on the cross, the bath of remission, he took up limbs that were already immortal and, after the resurrection, explained to them the benefit of his Passion.

“You call me Teacher and Lord, and you speak rightly, for so I am. If, then, I, the Lord and Teacher, have washed your feet, you also ought to wash one another’s feet.”

This must be fulfilled both in the literal and in the mystical sense. Literally, we must serve one another through charity, not only by washing our brothers’ feet but also by helping them in all their needs. Mystically, just as he forgives our sins when we repent, so we must forgive our brothers. And just as he washed us from sins by interceding with the Father for us, so we must pray for our brothers.

“For I have given you an example, so that just as I have done for you, you also may do.”

This means that when you did not allow your feet to be washed, you were asking about what you did not know; the Lord permitted you afterward to know this. It is customary among many people that, when they receive one another as guests, they wash one another’s feet. Where this custom is absent among holy people, they perform it in their hearts; but it is better that what Christ did should be done with the hands. In this we are admonished that, having confessed our offenses to one another, we should pray for one another, just as Christ intercedes for us.

## Sermon on the Lord’s Supper

“Our Lord Jesus Christ, on the night when he was betrayed, took bread, and giving thanks, broke it and said: Take and eat; this is my body, which will be given for you. Do this in remembrance of me. Likewise also the cup, after he had supped, saying: This cup is the new testament in my blood. Do this, whenever you drink it, in remembrance of me. For whenever you eat this bread and drink this cup, you proclaim the Lord’s death until he comes” (1 Cor. XI).

As the moment of the Lord’s Passion approached, dearly beloved brothers, when he was already almost at the point of being handed over, the Lord—who had previously maintained the legal observances and sacrifices, all of which had been figures of Christ’s incarnation and Passion—wished, when the reality arrived, to destroy the shadow. The lamb sacrificed under the ancient law, together with the other victims, prefigured the true Lamb who was to be sacrificed on the cross.

He therefore wished to eat and sacrifice the figurative lamb and to preserve the shadow of the future reality until the sacrifice of the true Lamb took place. Thus, before the time of his Passion, he wished to celebrate the old Passover with his disciples and eat the lamb; then he brought the old figures to an end. After the supper of the lamb, therefore, having ended the old Passover, he established the new Passover and distributed his body and blood to the disciples. For if he had first given his body and then the lamb, it would not have appeared that he had brought the old Passover to an end on account of the new.

Thus he took bread, blessed it, and gave it to them; afterward, the cup. It must be understood that the whole of human nature had been corrupted in soul and body. Therefore, since God came to free both, it was fitting that both should be united to him, so that the soul might appropriately be freed through the soul and the body through the body.

[Col. 0910B] For this reason, also, we place bread and wine upon the altar to represent both, so that through the bread, which has become the body and has been worthily received by us, we may believe that our body will eventually be conformed to Christ’s body in immortality and incorruptibility. [Note: [Col. 0909D] On Consecration, distinction II, “Panis”; IV Sentences, distinction II, chapters “Sub Alia” and “Sed quare.”] Likewise, through the wine changed into blood and similarly received by us, we believe that our souls become conformed to Christ’s soul in this world, while we live, and in glory, when we rise again.

And since Christ’s soul was to be represented by something corporeal, just as his body is represented through bread, nothing among all his creatures was found by which it could be represented more nearly than by blood, which is said to be the seat of the soul itself. But because it seemed horrifying to human nature to take blood, wine was therefore [Col. 0910C] appointed in place of blood to signify the soul.

Yet it must not be understood that in the blood we receive the soul alone and not the body, or that in receiving the blood we receive the whole soul but not the whole body. Although we receive the body and blood separately, we nevertheless receive Christ not twice but once. This custom of receiving them separately arose in the Church from the fact that Christ gave them separately to the disciples at supper, so that by this they might understand that they ought to be conformed to Christ’s soul and body.

Thus God feeds the faithful soul with a threefold nourishment: through the word, through the sacrament, and through the Spirit. When he refreshes us through his words and sacraments, he sets before us a honeycomb to eat; but when he refreshes us inwardly through his Spirit, he pours out honey for us to taste. [Note: [Col. 0909D] On Consecration, distinction II, “In the cup,” and IV Sentences, distinction II, chapter “Qua de consecr.”]

It should also be noted that water is placed in the sacrament together with wine so that the water which flowed from Christ’s side together with blood may be represented. This water signifies the people, or baptism, in which the people are cleansed through the outpouring of Christ’s blood.

There should be no doubt that through the sacred words of the priest’s blessing the bread is changed into the Lord’s body, so that the substance of the bread does not remain; yet the color and taste of bread remain, and under one [Note: [Col. 0910D] On Consecration, distinction III, chapter “Nos”] species the true substance of Christ’s body lies hidden. For if it appeared in the quality in which it truly exists, the human mind would shrink from taking a living human being.

Hence, when the Lord said: “Unless you eat the flesh of the Son of Man and drink his blood,” etc. (John VI), certain people, hearing these words, went away backward, recoiling and thinking that he was commanding them to eat him under the form that appeared to them.

A Christian must therefore necessarily believe that, through the hands of any priest—indeed, of anyone who possesses only the order of priesthood, whether good or evil—the Lord’s body can equally be consecrated through the effective words of blessing, and that the Holy Spirit is present in that consecration.

This offering of Christ’s body is repeated daily, as Augustine testifies, [Note: [Col. 0911D] On Consecration, distinction II, “Utrum” and chapter “Iteratur,” and IV Sentences, distinction XII, “Institutum”] although Christ suffered once, because we fall daily into sins, without which mortal weakness cannot live.

In the form of bread, the invisible one descended from heaven, and he wished the union of the body in the head to be signified in the form of bread, as the Apostle says: “There is one bread; we, though many, are one body, all who share in the one bread” (1 Cor. X). For just as one bread is made from different grains, so from different members we become one body of Christ through the union of hope, faith, and charity.

Therefore, whoever wishes his member to be united in this way to Christ’s body through the heavenly bread should share it with the others. For God broke the bread and gave it to them because he wished what is one to be shared by all, saying: Receive it through conformity, and eat the sacrament itself. “Do this in remembrance of me” (Matt. XXVI).

By receiving the body and blood, let us retain the memory of the Passion, so that, just as he died for us, we may also die for him, if necessary. The same applies to the cup, which he called the New Testament—that is, the new promise—because through that blood he promised not only temporal things but also eternal ones.

This remembrance must be made until he comes—that is, until the end of the age, when he will come for judgment. But consider what follows: “Whoever eats the bread or drinks the cup of the Lord unworthily will be guilty of the Lord’s body.” Let a person examine himself, and so let him eat of that bread and drink of the cup” (1 Cor. XI).

One is unworthy if entangled in a grave sin, or if one remains willing to commit grave sins. “Let him examine himself” not by comparison with others, but by himself alone, considering what sort of person he is, because “whoever eats and drinks unworthily eats and drinks judgment upon himself” (ibid.)—that is, he eats condemnation.

Therefore many among you are weak: the Lord punishes them in this life with fevers and other illnesses because they have received his body unworthily. And, what is worse, many fall asleep unto death, as we still see: after Easter, mortality often approaches.

## Another Sermon on the Lord’s Supper

Brothers, this day that we celebrate today is great and exalted, and no day throughout the whole year is greater. [Col. 0912A] Today the Lord supped with his disciples (Matt. XXVI). Today he gave them his body and blood. Today glory is not sung to the Father and the Son. Today oil for three offices is consecrated in three forms. Today the Lord’s body is reserved until tomorrow; it is also received in commemoration of Christ’s nourishment. Today the brothers’ feet and the floors of the church are washed. Today the altars are stripped until Holy Saturday. Today penitents come for absolution; and the mystery performed today is observed throughout the whole year, but today it is fulfilled and today it begins. Today that reality is effected which, if neglected, is not recovered throughout the year.

Therefore this day is great, consecrated to the Lord, and full of joy and exultation. For three continuous days—that is, Thursday, Friday, and Saturday—we celebrate the Lord’s three-day burial. Accordingly, in order to be joined to the humility of his burial, we lay aside our exalted things: the glory to the Father and the Son, the ringing of the bells, and other things of this kind.

We join Thursday to Friday and Saturday in order to complete the three days because the night of Sunday, which the Lord consecrated by his resurrection and which belongs to the beginning of the following Sunday, is celebrated with great glory.

On this same day oil is also consecrated for three offices: oil for the sick; oil for the newly converted; and chrism, by which people are confirmed after baptism and by which baptism itself is consecrated, through which people are saved. [Note: [Col. 0912D] On Consecration, distinction III, “Litteris,” and IV Sentences, distinction XXIII, chapter 1.]

God can, however, heal the sick without oil, sanctify his own, and drive away demons; he can bestow spiritual oil without bodily oil. But because of the animal-minded, visible things are enacted so that invisible things may be grasped more easily.

If someone should say, “If he can, why is the rite of consecrating oil observed with such devotion?” the answer is: Could not the righteous of old please God without circumcision? They certainly could. But after they were commanded to be circumcised, unless they were circumcised they were held bound by the chains of sin, as Augustine testifies to Seleucius.

The apostles used this practice—that is, oil—for the restoration of the sick; apostolic men used it in the marking of the newly converted. Hence the Gospel says of the apostles: “And they anointed many sick people with oil, and they were healed” [Col. 0912D] (Mark VI).

Bede likewise says: “It is clear that the apostles themselves handed down to the holy Church the custom that the possessed and any other sick people should be anointed with oil blessed by the bishop.”

Concerning the oil poured over the newly converted, we do not read anything of this kind, but we retain the apostolic custom and authority that we have received from the Roman Church. For the practice of God’s apostle and the institutions of our predecessors are to be held as law, as Augustine testifies to the priest Casulanus.

Oil for the sick is consecrated during the very office of consecrating the Lord’s body and blood, before the words are said: “Through whom, Lord, you always create all these good things.” The final prayer of the consecration of the Lord’s body [Col. 0913A] is made from the vow of penitents, concerning whom it is said: “A sacrifice to God is a troubled spirit” (Ps. L). Appropriately, oil for penitents is consecrated in the place where their sacrifice is offered to God.

The consecration of chrism is called principal because through its anointing the principal Spirit is given. It is consecrated in the place where we customarily give peace to one another; this is the work of the Lord’s grace, so that peace and concord may reign among us. For, as Isidore says: “The olive tree is the distinguished tree of peace.”

The exorcism of the oil follows. As Isidore says: “Exorcism,” in Greek, in Latin “conjuration,” or a word of rebuke, is directed against the devil so that he may depart. He concludes in this way: “Through our Lord Jesus Christ, who is to come.” The catechumens are anointed with it [Col. 0913B] so that through this anointing the devil may not be able to return.

We must consider what the Holy Spirit accomplishes in each case. The exorcism of the oil commands the devil to depart from the catechumen, who is still reckoned among the dead because he has not yet been baptized. The anointing with chrism sanctifies one already made alive from the dead. Oil for the sick provides healing to the wounded.

On that same day the Lord’s body is reserved until the following day. For on Good Friday the Lord’s body is not consecrated. It is necessary, therefore, that those who wish to receive communion have a sacrifice from the preceding day. There are people who wish to receive the Eucharist every day. [Note: [Col. 0913D] On Consecration, distinction II, “Quotidie,” and IV Sentences, distinction XII, chapter “Institutum”] For, according to Augustine, neither is blameworthy, including the one who, out of reverence, does not dare to omit it on any day.

Then one proceeds to the meal, from which the day is called the Lord’s Supper. Hence Isidore says: “The Lord’s Supper is so called because on that day the Savior celebrated Passover with his disciples.”

I saw a certain religious man take some food first on that day, then wash the feet of pilgrims, and so proceed to the table. Following the example of our Lord, on that day we wash not only the brothers’ feet but also the floors of the church, to adorn them for the Paschal festival.

The Roman order prescribes that from Thursday until Holy Saturday the altars should be bare. This signifies nothing else, I think, except the flight of the apostles. The altar coverings are Christ’s garments, concerning which it was said: “And they all left him and fled” (Matt. XXVI).

On that very day sinners who, because of their sins and crimes, had been cast out from the embrace of the holy Church return to Mother Church, wherever they may be, after completing their penance and at the command of the bishop or priest; and with great joy and gladness they return to the remission of sins.
