In all these things we recognize that the present day is especially consecrated to the remission of sins. For we do not think that these things happen by chance on the present Thursday.

In the meantime, let us little scholars say what seems to us to be the reason that the Lord wished to wash feet on this very day, after whose example we wash feet and other things. This washing signifies the remission of sins. Therefore penitents also return on the same day to the hands of the priests. And why is oil consecrated on the same day? Christ, anointed with the oil of gladness, came to us at the end of the fifth age in order to make us sharers in his kingdom. Hence this anointing is prepared on Thursday.

Thus a certain form of anointing was conveyed from the Lord’s birth—according to Isaiah and the Gospel, in the form of a dove—until baptism, although from the beginning, from the time when the human being began to exist, we believe that spiritual anointing has remained in Jesus.

It does not conflict with this reasoning that oil is consecrated on Thursday and that the anointing is preserved until our baptism. The law did not remove sins but punished them. On Thursday Christ brought the old law to an end, as Bede relates in his commentary on Luke, and absolved sins.

The same thing is expressed in the first prayer of the Mass, when the priest says: “Thus, with the error of the old order removed from us, may he grant us the grace of his resurrection.”

He also brings oil with which his companions are to be anointed, concerning whom Peter says: “You are a chosen race, a royal priesthood” (1 Pet. II).

Therefore, since all these things bring such great joy to today, and since, as we know and often see, there is such great joy on earth over the absolution and repentance of a sinner, we must believe much more that there is joy and gladness in heaven before God and his angels, as he himself says—the one who established both the day and the human being: “There is joy in heaven before the angels of God over one sinner who repents” (Luke XV).

## On the Separation of Soul and Body in Christ

Some have thought that at death the divinity withdrew from Christ the man, and that the death of the man was nothing other than the separation of divinity from the flesh. They find certain words in which this appears to have been said, and, when they find writings of this sort, they cling to them without reaching the spirit.

Blessed Ambrose appears to say something of this kind in his Exposition of that psalm which the Lord himself showed had been written about him in his Passion: “My God, my God, why have you forsaken me?” (Ps. XXI).

On this passage Ambrose says the following: [Note: [Col. 0914D] I Sentences, distinction XXI, chapter 1.] “The man, about to die through the separation of divinity, cries out,” along with certain other statements brought forward as though to prove the point: namely, that God is life, and where life was, death could not be; therefore, unless life had first withdrawn, death could not have come.

For it is written that “Jesus, crying out with a loud voice, said: My God, my God, why have you forsaken me?” (Matt. XXVII). The man cries out that he has been forsaken by the Lord, complains that God has withdrawn from him, and seems to say that he is about to die because God has withdrawn from him. Therefore it says that the man cries out, about to die through the separation of divinity.

But consider what is being said. If the matter concerns that separation of divinity for which Christ the man cried out on the cross, then it had certainly already taken place. He does not protest that he is about to be forsaken, but that he has already been forsaken, saying: “My God, why have you forsaken me?”

If, therefore, the matter concerns that separation of divinity, God had already withdrawn when the man hanging on the cross cried out that he had been forsaken by God. Yet Christ was still living in the flesh when God had thus withdrawn from him.

Let them answer, then: If death could not exist unless life had first departed, how could life remain after life had departed? For God had already withdrawn in this way, and Christ still hung alive upon the cross while he complained that he had been forsaken.

If, therefore, in this withdrawal of God and this separation of divinity they say that the union of person which existed between divinity and humanity was dissolved, there was a period when Christ was still a living man and was not God. But who could say this? Who, agreeing with sound faith, would not shrink from attributing to God that he abandoned the man he had assumed, accompanying him indeed to the point of death, yet abandoning him at death, when, with greater danger already threatening, greater help was necessary?

Why, then, does he reproach hired servants so severely because, when the wolf comes, they abandon the sheep they ought to guard by fleeing, if he himself, when the wolf came, abandoned that one sheep—the Lamb, the Son of the Virgin, the offspring of the sheep—which he had undertaken not only to guard but also to glorify?

The sheep, previously secure in the shepherd, did not fear when the wolf came, saying: “The prince of this world is coming, and he has nothing in me” (John XIV).

But now, complaining and lamenting that he has been abandoned by the shepherd, he cries: “Why have you forsaken me?”

He was man alone, and God was not; and now God was not man, because God had already withdrawn from the man; [Col. 0915C] nor was the man God, because, still hanging alive on the cross and forsaken by God, he was not.

Therefore divinity had withdrawn from the man not only at death but before death, when the man was still man and mourned that God had withdrawn from him and, consequently, as these people say, mourned that he was not God.

Who could say this? How, then, they ask, are we to understand that Christ cries out that he has been forsaken by God, and that Scripture affirms that the man cried out, about to die through the separation of divinity, if God had not withdrawn from the man?

What then? Could divinity not have abandoned humanity in one respect—namely, insofar as it did not defend it for a time against the power of its enemies—and yet not have abandoned it in another respect—namely, insofar as it did not then withdraw from it through the presence of its majesty?

He abandoned him, but did not abandon her. He abandoned him to them, but did not abandon him to himself. He abandoned him because he did not provide assistance; yet he did not abandon him because he did not withdraw his presence. He withdrew protection but did not separate the union. He separated himself outwardly, so that he would not be present for defense against the enemies; but he did not separate himself inwardly, so that he would be absent from her in the union of person. Thus he abandoned him so as not to help; but he did not abandon him so as to withdraw.

I am traveling along the road; you travel with me, and we walk together. I am secure, as though I had my friend with me. My enemy comes and, rushing upon me while I am unarmed and unable to resist, covers me with wounds. You see me being struck, yet you are not moved; you endure it patiently and stand beside me as though you cared nothing about my wounds, and I say: “Why have you forsaken me?” (Matt. XXVII).

You still stand beside me, and I complain that you have withdrawn from me. You are near in place but far in assistance. You were near when you showed yourself present in love; you became far away when, while I was placed in danger, you withdrew yourself from compassion.

Thus humanity cried out in the Passion that it had been abandoned by divinity, because divinity had handed it over to the power of its enemies to be crucified, as it is written: “You would have no power over me unless it had been given you from above” (John XIX).

Yet because he endured this death not for his own iniquity but for our redemption, while hanging on the cross he asks why he has been abandoned—not as though murmuring against God because of the punishment, but demonstrating to us his innocence in punishment and seeking the reason for what he did not know as sin.

## On Holy Easter Day. According to Mark.

[Col. 0915]

[Col. 0915D] “Mary Magdalene, Mary the mother of James, and Salome bought spices so that, when they came, they might anoint Jesus” (Mark XVI).

It is written in the Gospel of Luke that “returning from the tomb, they prepared spices and ointments. And on the Sabbath they rested according to the commandment” (Luke XXIII).

The Jews had a commandment that the silence of the Sabbath should be observed from evening to evening—that is, from sunset to sunset. The women did this: after seeing the Lord’s burial, they bought spices on Good Friday before sunset, or on the Sabbath after sunset, and prepared the spices so that in the morning they might anoint the Lord’s body.

When, therefore, the faithful remember the Lord’s burial, they prepare spices, as it were, if they turn themselves toward the works in which Christ delights. On the Sabbath they remain silent, intending after the Sabbath to come with the women to the Lord, because, once the preparation of the present life has ended, they rejoice to await the day of resurrection in rest, and then to offer Christ spiritual actions fragrant as spices.

On the sixth day the human being was made; on the Sabbath God rested (Gen. I). Therefore on the sixth day Jesus dies for humanity. Hence he also said: “It is finished” (John XIX)—that is, on the sixth day the work for the redemption of the world was completed, and on the Sabbath he rested in the tomb.

So we too ought to suffer for the Lord in this sixth age, and in the seventh, which belongs to the dead, rest in hidden peace until the eighth age of resurrection comes. The seventh day is not said to have had an evening, because in that age the rest of souls is not consumed by any sorrow but is increased by the joy of the future resurrection.

“On the evening of the Sabbath, as the first day of the Sabbath was dawning, while it was still dark, Mary Magdalene, the other Mary, and Salome came to the tomb, carrying the spices they had prepared.”

By “evening” he designates the night, understanding the whole from a part. Evening is the beginning of night. Therefore he does not say “which dawns” in the masculine, but “which dawns” in the feminine, making the grammatical relation refer to the night, which ends at the dawn of the Lord’s day.

The reason why he is understood to have called that night by this name is that, once the Sabbath had passed, they were already permitted from evening onward to prepare and bring the spices. The Ordainer of times rose during the final part of that night.

What else does it mean for the Son of God to rise again except to revive—that is, to return from death to life? On this night, through the mystery of the Lord’s resurrection, the order of times was changed. Formerly, most appropriately, night followed day (Gen. I), because humanity, having fallen from the light of paradise through sin, descended into the darkness and hardships of this age. Now, most appropriately, day follows night, because through faith in the resurrection, by Christ’s gift, we are led back from the darkness of sin and the shadow of death to the light of life.

It remains, therefore, that when it is said that the Lord was three days and three nights in the heart of the earth, just as Jonah was in the belly of the sea-monster (Matt. XII), we should understand it according to this manner of speaking, in which the whole is understood from a part: namely, through the final part of Good Friday, on which the Lord was buried, the entire day together with its already past night; through the following night, the Sabbath as the third whole day.

“The first day of the Sabbath,” or “one of the Sabbaths,” or “of the Sabbaths,” is to be understood as the Lord’s day, because every week is divided into the Sabbath and the first, second, third, fourth, fifth, and sixth day of the Sabbath. The week itself was also sometimes called “the Sabbath” by virtue of the preeminence of the Sabbath, as in the passage: “I fast twice in the Sabbath” (Luke XVIII)—that is, twice in the week.

“After the sun had risen, they said to one another: ‘Who will roll away the stone for us from the entrance of the tomb? For it was very large.’” After the sun had risen—that is, when the sky had already begun to grow bright in the eastern part, which does not happen except through the nearness of the rising sun. For that brightness is what is commonly called dawn. The fact that the women came very early indicates their great eagerness to find the Lord. Mystically, however, an example is given to us: once the darkness of our vices has been dispelled, we should approach the Lord’s body. For the tomb signifies the Lord’s altar, on which the mysteries of his flesh and blood are celebrated. The spices that the women carry signify the fragrance of virtues and the sweetness of prayers, with which we ought to approach the altar.

It is read that these women were as follows: one Mary was the sister of Lazarus; another was Mary, the mother of James, later bishop of Jerusalem; and the third was Mary, the sister of the Lord’s mother and the wife of Salome. These three came to the tomb with precious ointments, with which they wished to anoint the Lord so that he would not be corrupted by worms. But when they saw the angel, they were thrown into great terror; nevertheless, the angel gently consoled them. It follows:

“And behold, there was a great earthquake. For an angel of the Lord descended from heaven. And he came and rolled away the stone.” The angel rolled away the stone not to open a door for the Lord as he was about to emerge, but to provide evidence that he had emerged. He who had come forth from a closed womb as a mortal, having now become immortal, could emerge from the tomb—and he did. The fact that a great earthquake occurred when the Lord rose, just as one had occurred when he died, signifies that earthly hearts, cast down from heavenly hope, must be shaken by faith in his passion and resurrection toward repentance, and, moved by a salutary fear, must be raised to everlasting life. The rolling away of the stone signifies that the mysteries formerly covered by the veil of the letter have been disclosed. For the Law was written on stone; when its covering was removed, the glory of the resurrection was revealed.

“And looking up, they saw that the stone had been rolled away from the tomb, and the angel sitting upon it. His appearance was like lightning, and his clothing like snow.” Because God is both terrifying to sinners and gentle to the righteous, the angel is rightly shown in this way: by his appearance he both terrifies the reprobate and soothes the devout. In lightning there is the terror of fear; in snow, the consolation of whiteness. The whiteness of the angelic garment announced the joys of our festival. For the Lord’s resurrection both restored us to immortal life and, restoring the number of the angels, repaired the losses of the heavenly homeland.

He was sitting, indicating that he was reigning—he who at the Nativity, by standing, had signified that he would wage war. He was sitting upon the stone by which the tomb had been closed, to teach that the bars of hell had been overcome. As Mark specifies, he was sitting on the right (Mark XVI), that is, on the southern side of that place where the Lord’s body had lain. For the Lord’s body, lying on its back, had its head toward the west and its right side toward the south. What, then, is signified by the left except the present life? And what by the right except everlasting life? Hence the words: “His left hand is under my head, and his right hand shall embrace me” (Song II). Since our Redeemer had already passed beyond the corruption of the present life, the angel rightly sat on the right, because he had come to announce his perpetual life. God therefore placed the left—that is, the prosperity of the present life—as though beneath the head of the Church; she presses it down by the intention of supreme love. But God’s right hand embraces her, because she is held with complete devotion beneath his eternal blessedness.

“But from fear of him the guards were terrified and became like dead men. And the angel answered and said to the women: ‘Do not be afraid. For I know that you seek Jesus who was crucified. He is not here, for he has risen, as he said. Come and see the place where the Lord was laid.’” It is as though he were saying: “If you do not believe the word, believe the empty tomb.” The angel does not console the guards, but the women. “Let fear,” he says, “persist in the unbeliever; but you, because you seek Jesus, hear that he has risen.” Let those be afraid who do not love the coming of the heavenly citizens; let those tremble who, weighed down by carnal desires, despair of being able to attain their company. But why are you afraid, when you see your fellow citizens?

“He is not here” is said with respect to the presence of his flesh, although he is never absent through the presence of his majesty. The bitter root of the cross has vanished; the flower of life has burst forth with its fruits—that is, he who lay in death has risen in glory. The dead body of Jesus is not found, but the living one is proclaimed in the Gospel; for although we have known him according to the flesh, nevertheless now we know him no longer (II Cor. V).

“And it happened, while they were bewildered in mind about this, that behold, two men stood beside them in shining garments.”

The angels announce the glory of the triumphant one not only by their words but also by their shining clothing. The women see angels because those minds behold the heavenly citizens which advance toward God with the spices of holy desires. They were bewildered in mind because they were both astonished that the great stone had been rolled away and grieved that the body had not been found.

It is said that the Lord’s tomb was a round chamber, cut out of the underlying rock, according to Matthew and Mark, and of such height that a man standing inside could scarcely touch the roof with an outstretched hand. It had an entrance on the eastern side, upon which that great stone had been placed. In the northern part of this tomb was the sepulcher itself—that is, the place of the Lord’s body—which had been made from the same rock. It was seven feet long and rose three palms higher than the rest of the pavement. This place was open not from above but along the southern side, through its entire length, and through it the body was brought in. The color of this tomb and burial chamber is said to have been a mixture of red and white.

Thus this new tomb of the Lord can signify Mary’s virginal womb; and the large stone placed at its entrance can show that it could not have been opened without the help of many [the text has “of many tombs”]. Just as no one before him and no one after him was conceived in Mary’s womb, so no one before and no one after him was buried in this tomb. It should also be understood that, just as angels are read to have stood beside the Savior’s tomb, so they should be believed to have stood beside the mysteries of the Lord’s body at the time of consecration. Hence the Apostle instructs women to be veiled in church because of the angels (I Cor. XI).

“But while they were afraid and bowed their faces toward the ground, they said to them: ‘Why do you seek the living among the dead? He is not here, but has risen. Remember how he spoke to you when he was still in Galilee, saying: It is necessary for the Son of Man to be delivered into the hands of sinful men, and to be crucified, and to rise on the third day.’”

What he said could not fail to happen, and it is established that, among the disciples and the women who followed him, the Lord foretold that he would rise. Why, then, do they seek among the dead—that is, in the tomb, which is the proper place of the dead—the one who has already risen?

Following the example of the women, whenever we enter a church, we should enter with complete humility. We bow our faces toward the ground before the sight of the angels when, contemplating the joys of heaven, we remember that we are ashes, as blessed Abraham says: “I will speak to my Lord, although I am dust and ashes” (Gen. XVIII). Notice that the holy women are not said to have fallen to the ground, but to have bowed their faces; hence ecclesiastical custom has established that, either in memory of the Lord’s resurrection or in hope of our own, on all Sundays and throughout the entire period of fifty days we pray not on bent knees but with our faces inclined toward the ground.

It is not without reason that the Lord lay in the tomb for one day and two nights, because he joined the light of his single death to the darkness of our double death. For he himself accepted death in the flesh alone, and released our two deaths, of flesh and spirit.

“And going quickly, tell his disciples: ‘He has risen from the dead. And behold, he goes before you into Galilee. There you will see him. Behold, I have told you.’” The women are told to announce to the apostles the life that has risen, because death had been announced through a woman. Mark, however, says: “Go, tell his disciples and Peter” (Mark XVI).

It must be asked why Peter is designated by name. If the angel had not expressly named him, because he had denied the Master he would not have dared to come among the disciples. Peter is therefore called by name so that he would not despair because of his denial. In this matter we should consider why the Lord permitted the man whom he had decided to place above the whole Church to fear a servant girl’s voice. We understand that this happened through a great dispensation of mercy, so that the one who was to become the supreme shepherd of the Church might learn through his own fault how he ought to show mercy to others.

He therefore first showed himself to him and then placed him above the others, so that from his own weakness he might recognize how mercifully he should bear with the weaknesses of others.

“Galilee” is interpreted to mean “a migration.” The Redeemer had already migrated from passion to resurrection, from death to life, from punishment to glory, and from corruption to incorruption. The Lord is seen by the disciples in Galilee after the resurrection because we shall see the glory of his resurrection afterward, if we now migrate from vices to the heights of virtues.

Or it may be understood in this way: “He goes before them into Galilee,” that is, into the rolling-place of the nations, where previously there had been error and slipperiness, and where they did not set their footprints with a firm step.

Moreover, the statements of Jerome against Helvidius should be considered, based on the testimonies of the four Evangelists, concerning the three sisters who were daughters of Anna, the mother of blessed Mary. Saint Mary, the mother of the Lord; Mary, the mother of James of Alphaeus and Joseph; and Mary, the mother of the sons of Zebedee (Mark XVI)—namely, James the Greater and John the Evangelist—were three sisters.

Mary, the mother of the Lord, was the daughter of Joachim and Anna. After Joachim’s death, Cleophas, Joseph’s brother, took the same Anna as his wife and fathered by her a daughter whom he named Mary. Cleophas and Anna gave this Mary to a certain man named Alphaeus; from him was born James the Lesser, who was also called the Lord’s brother, and he is called James of Alphaeus after his father.

Cleophas betrothed his stepdaughter—that is, Saint Mary, the virgin mother of the Lord—to his brother Joseph, who was the most faithful guardian of her virginity, her companion, and her foster father. After Cleophas died, a certain Salome took Anna herself and fathered by her a third daughter, also named Mary. Zebedee took her as his wife, and she bore him James and John.

Thus it should be understood: “Mary of James,” with “mother” understood; and “Salome,” with “daughter” understood. Anna therefore had three husbands: Joachim, Cleophas, and Salome.

SERMON ON THE RESURRECTION OF THE LORD

Although the other festivals, in commemorating events that have taken place, affect the minds of the faithful with spiritual joy, in Christ’s resurrection both hearts and bodies rejoice in a similar manner. For when Christ rose, our inner self was raised together with him from the death of sin, and the hope of the resurrection of our outer self was confirmed by the sign of baptism. Both therefore rightly rejoice, because both are raised together with Christ: the inner self in reality, namely from the corruption of sin; the outer self in hope, namely of the future resurrection.

But it must be considered whether Christ, whose resurrection we celebrate with joy, was passible or mortal. Passion or death is the punishment of sin, but he lived without sin. By nature, therefore, he was impassible and immortal; yet according to his power he willed to be both passible and mortal. He therefore died in obedience to the Father, as it is said: “He became obedient to the Father unto death” (Philipp. II).

It must also be asked whether the Father demanded death from him. Certainly not. Why, then, did the Jews kill him? Because by living he held unwaveringly to righteousness and by teaching to truth. Humanity owed this obedience to divinity, and God demands it from every rational creature.

But how was it just before God that he should give the best one for the wicked? Because the worst one had led the simple human being astray; it was therefore just that the best one should become a hostage for him, so that he might overcome the worst one and restore the innocent person to his former freedom.

Christ’s death was effective for exhausting all sins. Indeed, it transcended them infinitely. This is proved as follows. Suppose Christ were standing before you, and you knew him to be the Lord of majesty, and someone said: “Kill this man, or the whole world will perish.” Would you kill him in order to save the world? Certainly not. Why? Because his life would appear far more worthy than countless worlds, and you would seem to commit such a crime that an innumerable number of worlds could not atone for it. Therefore, just as his life was more worthy than infinite worlds, so his death was far more precious than innumerable worlds; and for this reason it was sufficient for the redemption of all.

For how many hours was he dead? Forty. Why? So that he might bring to life the four parts that had died in the Decalogue of the Law.

Who crucified him? Because he willed to die for Jews and Gentiles, the Jews plotted his death, while the pagans crucified him.

Christ therefore had lain in the tomb for two nights and one day. The two nights signify our two deaths, one of the body and the other of the soul. The day signifies his death, which was the light of our deaths. He removed one of these deaths and left the other to the elect for their exercise; when he comes again, he will destroy it.

His soul, however, had passed after death into the heavenly paradise, as he had said to the thief: “Today, I tell you, you will be with me in paradise” (Luke XXIII). At midnight on the resurrection—the hour at which the angel devastated Egypt—Christ descended into hell and despoiled it. At this point it should be noted how many hells there are.

There are therefore two hells: one above and one below. The upper hell is the weak part of this world, which is full of punishments. Here there is an excess of heat, great cold, thirst, hunger, and various bodily pains, as well as torments of the spirit, namely fear and shame. Of these it is said: “Bring my soul out of prison” (Psalm CXLI)—that is, “my life out of hell.”

The lower place is spiritual, where there is unquenchable fire. Of it is said: “You rescued my soul from the lower hell” (Psalm XXIX); it is said to be beneath the earth. And just as the bodies of sinners are covered by the earth, so the souls of sinners are buried beneath the earth in hell, as it is said of the rich man: “He was buried in hell” (Luke XVI).

Nine particular punishments are said to exist there. The first is fire, kindled once in such a way that, even if the whole sea flowed into it, it would not be extinguished. It also surpasses this material fire, just as a painted fire is surpassed by an actual one. It burns but gives no light.

The second punishment is intolerable cold. It is said that if a fiery mountain were cast into it, it would be turned into ice. Of these two it is said: “Weeping and gnashing of teeth” (Matt. VIII).

The third is immortal worms—that is, serpents and dragons, terrifying in appearance and hissing. They live in the flame as fish live in water.

The fourth is incomparable stench.

The fifth is the lashes of those who strike, like hammers striking iron.

The sixth is tangible darkness, as it is said: “A land of darkness, where there is no order, but everlasting horror dwells” (Job X).

The seventh is the confusion of sinners, by which everything there is exposed to everyone, and they cannot hide themselves.

The eighth is the dreadful sight of demons and dragons, whom they see striking sparks of fire, together with the pitiable cries of those who weep and those who mock.

The ninth is the fiery bonds by which each of their limbs is bound.

Why do they suffer so many miseries? Because they neglected the fellowship of the nine orders; they will justly deserve to be subjected to nine torments.

And because here they burned with the fire of desires, they will justly burn there in fire. Because here they lacked the wedding garment—that is, charity—they will deservedly gnash their teeth there in the cold. For they are said outwardly to glow with fire and inwardly to freeze like ice in winter, as it is said: “They pass from the waters of snow to excessive heat” (Job XXIV).

And because envy and hatred consumed them here like worms, worms will deservedly bite them there. Those who here delighted sweetly in the stench of lust will justly be tormented there with the terrible stench of decay.

Because they refused to accept discipline here and did not deserve to be scourged together with human beings, they will therefore be beaten there without cessation by thongs, as it is said: “Judgments are prepared for blasphemers, and striking hammers for the bodies of fools.”

Because they loved the darkness of vices here and did not wish to come to Christ, the light, they will therefore be darkened there by horrible darkness, as it is said: “They shall never see.”

Because here they disdained to confess the sins they were not ashamed to commit, they will therefore be perpetually shamed there, naked and exposed before all. Because here they scorned to see and hear good things, they will justly be filled there with a terrifying sight and a pitiable sound. And because here they had become dispersed through their individual vices, they will justly be bound there by chains through their individual limbs.

“They desire to die, and death will flee from them” (Rev. IX). Indeed, their heads are submerged downward, their backs turned toward one another, their feet raised upward, and they are stretched out in every direction. Alas that a human being was ever born who is punished by such a penalty.

Those who are members of the devil—the proud, the envious, the deceitful, the envious [repeated in the text], the gluttonous, the drunken, the lustful, murderers, the cruel, thieves, plunderers, robbers, the unclean, the greedy, adulterers, fornicators, liars, perjurers, blasphemers, sorcerers, slanderers, the quarrelsome—those who have been held in these sins will go into the punishments described above, never to return.

In those punishments the righteous will also see the wicked, so that they may rejoice more greatly that they escaped them. Before the judgment, the wicked will see the good in glory, so that they may grieve more greatly that they neglected it. After the judgment, the good will always see the wicked in punishment, but the wicked will never again see the good.

When the good see the wicked being tormented in this way, they do not grieve on that account. Even if a father sees his son in punishment, or a son his father; a mother her daughter, or a daughter her mother; a husband his wife, or a wife her husband—not only do they not grieve, but it is as pleasurable for them to see this as it is for us when we see fish playing in a pool, as it is said: “The righteous will rejoice when he sees the vengeance upon sinners” (Psalm XXXVII).

Although they see them in punishment, they nevertheless do not pray for them. For they would think contrary to God if they prayed for the damned. They are so united to God that God’s judgments please them in every respect; therefore they will also rejoice in those judgments.

This is what concerns the lower hell. Now we must consider the upper hell.

DIVISION

In which hell were the righteous before Christ’s coming? In the upper one, in a certain place adjoining the lower, where they could see one another. Although those who were there lacked punishment, it seemed to them that they were in hell, since they were separated from the kingdom. To those who were in the lower hell, however, the upper place seemed a refreshment of paradise; hence the rich man asked Lazarus to let a drop fall upon him (Luke XVI).

They had there a certain punishment, namely some darkness, as it is said: “Upon those dwelling in the region and shadow of death, light has arisen” (Isa. IX). Some of them were also in certain punishments.

It must also be considered whether the souls of the righteous recognize one another in that life. The souls of the righteous know all the righteous, by both name and lineage and their merits, as though they had always been with them. They also know all the wicked, to such an extent that they know for what merit each one is there.

The wicked likewise know the wicked and the good whom they see, to such an extent that they even know their names, as in the case of the rich man, Abraham, and Lazarus.

There the souls also pray for their loved ones in this way: the righteous pray for those whom they loved in the Lord, or for those who will invoke them, so that they may be preserved from evil and freed from the temptations of the world; and, if they are in error, so that they may be corrected and joined to them more quickly. Their desire is their order. Whatever they desire, they will receive without doubt.

For them, to pray also means to present either the body’s suffering or the good deeds performed for Christ. Nevertheless, they pray for nothing except what God himself has determined to do. Otherwise they would pray in vain.

Augustine likewise says to Hesychius:

“Many raise the question whether the souls of the saints hear the prayers of those who beseech them; and, when they are invoked to intercede, whether the wishes of those who ask reach their knowledge. It is difficult for a human being to judge about this. For how can our knowledge be certain about those whose knowledge concerning us we can neither grasp nor investigate? This alone is certain: the souls of the saints, established in the secret of divine contemplation, know of the things that take place outside only as much as is evidently useful either for their joy or for our assistance.”

Do they possess complete joy? Certainly not. (Gregory.) For just as those who have been invited to a banquet rejoice in their own reception but are anxious about absent friends, and rejoice more when all have gathered together, so the souls of the righteous now rejoice in their own glory but are anxious about our absence. When they have received their bodies and all have gathered together as one, then they will possess complete joy.

The souls of the righteous also know everything that happens here. Those who are in punishments, however, do not know except what angels or saints report to them. Those who are in hell do not know more about what happens here than the living know about what happens there.

Just as the prophets formerly knew certain things that others did not know, though not everything, so certain souls among the wicked know things that others do not know, though not everything. These things are either revealed to them by God or announced to them by the dying who come there.

Can they appear whenever they wish and to whomever they wish? The souls of the saints appear when they wish and to whomever they wish, whether to those who are awake or to those who are asleep. Those who are in punishments do not appear unless the angels permit it, either so that they may pray for their liberation or so that, having been liberated, they may announce their joy to their friends.

Those who are in hell can appear to no one. If they sometimes seem to appear, whether in dreams or to those who are awake, it is believed that they themselves are not present, but demons appear in their form. They also transform themselves into angels of light in order to deceive.

If something genuine does happen, it occurs on account of someone’s merit, as when the soul of a thief appeared to Saint Martin where he had destroyed an altar; or for the sake of admonition, as when the soul of Pope Benedict appeared in the form of a monster whose head and tail were those of a donkey and whose middle was that of a bear.

In what form do they appear? In human form, having assumed a body from the air.

Regarding the immortality of the soul, blessed Augustine also says:

“The soul of a human being is immortal according to a certain movement of its own, though not in every respect as God is, of whom it is said that he alone possesses immortality” (I Tim. VI). For Holy Scripture recalls many deaths of the soul. Hence the statement: “Let the dead bury their own dead” (Matt. VIII).

It dies by being alienated from the life of God, although it does not entirely cease to live in its own nature. It is therefore found to be mortal for some reason, yet it is also reasonably called immortal.

The soul is not a part of God. For if it were, it would be altogether unchangeable and incorruptible. If it were the same as God, it would neither decline toward what is worse nor advance toward what is better, nor would it begin to possess anything within itself that it had not possessed before, insofar as its own affections are concerned.

Thus far blessed Augustine.

Cassiodorus says as follows:

“God alone is immortal in a unique sense, just, powerful, good, and holy in a unique sense, because although these or similar qualities are said to exist in human beings or angels, none of them reaches the height of his revered power. God alone is omnipotent, for whom being is the same as understanding, being able the same as living, and willing the same as doing. And rightly so, since all things that are truly good do not come to him in order to be improved by him, but proceed from him.

“Therefore this soul, which we have mentioned, is not to be understood as a part of God, because it is changeable; nor as a part of the angels, because it is joined to flesh; nor as being made from air, water, or earth, nor from those things that are joined together by mutual combination, but as simple, distinct by its own nature and from other spirits.

“It is therefore established that in this world the soul changes with a stable yet changeable will, and is capable both of losing and of receiving good things. It does not remain fixed by a single rigidity of its will, but changes itself through manifold alterations, even contrary to its own intention.

“Now it must be understood how this immortal soul is perceived to live. After the loss of this world, it lives in itself, not by breathing air as the body does, but through the equal mobility attributed to it—pure, subtle, swift, rapid, eternal. It sees, hears, touches, and is more powerful in its other senses. It no longer understands through separate parts of itself, but knows everything spiritually as a whole.”

Let this suffice concerning the soul.

DIVISION

The Lord came to the upper hell by being born, in order to free those oppressed by the devil; he descended to the lower hell by dying, in order to redeem captives from the tyrant, as it is said: “Saying to those who are bound: ‘Come out’; and to those who are in darkness: ‘Be revealed’” (Isa. XLIX).

He calls those who were in punishments “the bound”; the others he calls “those in darkness.” At the hour when the angel devastated Egypt, and at the hour when he will free his elect from this world at the judgment—that is, at midnight, the hour of the resurrection—Christ despoiled hell. Returning from there in triumph, he placed those snatched from it in paradise, and he visited the body in the tomb, which he had raised from the dead.

Some think that from the hour of his death until the hour of his resurrection he was in hell with the elect, and that he departed from there with them and rose. Why did he not rise immediately after his death? The reason was that no one might say that he had not died, but had merely fallen into stupor amid the torments. If he had risen after a long time, there would have been doubt whether it was really he. Why, then, did he rise so quickly? So that he might console more quickly those who were grieving over his death.

Why on the first day of the week? So that on the day on which he had created the world he might renew it. Why on the third day after the passion? So that he might raise up those who had died in sins during the three periods—before the Law, under the Law, and under grace—and so that we, who fall through deeds, words, and thoughts, might rise through faith in the Holy Trinity.

Christ therefore rose from the dead on the third day so that he might be an example to us of the future resurrection, which will occur when the last trumpet sounds (I Cor. XV).

What is the last trumpet? When the Lord gave the Law on the mountain, the sound of a trumpet was heard. In the same way, angels appointed for this purpose, taking bodies and trumpets made from air, will thunder the terrible judgment of God over the world with the sound of a trumpet, as it is said: “For the trumpet will sound” (I Cor. XV), and again: “Their memory has perished with a sound” (Psalm IX).

With a loud voice he cries to the dead: “Rise,” as it is said: “At midnight there was a cry” (Matt. XXV). At this voice all the dead, good and evil, rise in the twinkling of an eye—that is, as quickly as one can open one’s eye—or rather, with their eyes opened, they see the light.

What is the first resurrection? Just as there are two deaths, so there are two resurrections: one of souls and the other of bodies. When a person sins, the soul dies, because it is abandoned by life—that is, by God—and is buried in the body as in a tomb. But when, through repentance, it returns to the life of the Lord, it rises as though from death.

The other resurrection will be that of bodies. On what day? On Easter Day, at the hour when Christ rose.

Will anyone then be in the world? It will be as full of human beings as it is today, with people engaged in the same activities as today. Some will be plowing, some sailing, some building, and some doing one thing or another.

What will happen to them? When the righteous rise, they will immediately be snatched by the angels into the air to meet Christ (I Cor. XV), and in that very rapture they will die and come to life again. The reprobate, however, will die from the terror itself, and immediately come to life again. This is what it means to judge the living and the dead.

Will those who died in their mothers’ wombs rise? All who received the vital spirit will rise. At what age or measure? At the age and measure at which they were, or would have been if they had not died beforehand.

Sometimes a wolf devours a human being, and the human flesh becomes part of the wolf’s flesh; then a bear devours the wolf, and a lion the bear. How, then, does the human being rise with them? Whatever was human flesh will rise; whatever belonged to the beasts will remain with them. For he who knew how to create all things from nothing knows well how to separate them.

Thus, whether they are devoured limb by limb by beasts, fish, or birds, all will be restored in the resurrection, so that not even a hair of them will perish (Luke XII).

If cut hair and nails return to their place, will they not be deformed? This should not be understood to mean that they will return to their former place. Rather, just as a potter who knows that a vessel has been made may break it and make another from the same clay, without considering whether the first part was a handle or a base, so God the Maker will reform from the same material another body very similar to this one, free from every deformity and weakness and possessing complete integrity and beauty. Nevertheless, God could also restore each individual limb fittingly to its own place.

Those who here had two heads or several limbs, or who lacked some parts, or who were fat or thin—will they rise in that condition? Those who here had two heads will rise as two bodies, so that each soul may have its own body, with nothing indecent or deformed attached to it, and with all its limbs sound, complete, and filled with every beauty.

What is thought concerning aborted children? Insofar as the substance is semen, it will rise in the father; insofar as it is the mother’s blood, it will rise in the mother.

What sort of bodies will they have? Immortal and incorruptible, shining like translucent glass. The reprobate will likewise have immortal bodies, though they will suffer without end. Their bodies will also be incorruptible in this respect: although they will be afflicted by every punishment, they will not be consumed. Just as the bodies of the righteous will be immortal, incorruptible, and shining, so those of the reprobate will be immortal, incorruptible, and dark.

These two resurrections—of souls and of bodies—Christ commended to us through his own resurrection.

Where did he remain during the forty days after the resurrection? This is questioned. It is believed that he remained in the earthly paradise with Elijah and Enoch and with those who had risen with him—those who are said to have been raised, such as Lazarus.

The outstanding Christian teacher Chrysostom says that although the tombs had been opened at Christ’s death (Matt. XXVII), the dead did not rise from them until after the Lord had risen, so that he might be “the firstborn from the dead” (Rom. VIII). No immortal person rose before Christ; rather, all died again, as Lazarus did. Those who rose with Christ, however, rose immortal and, when he ascended, ascended with him.

What form did Christ have after the resurrection? Seven times brighter than the sun.

In what form did his own people see him? In the form in which they had been accustomed to see him before.

Did he appear clothed? He had assumed garments made from air; when he ascended, they vanished into the air.

How many times did he appear? Twelve times, and eight times on the first day:

First, to Joseph of Arimathea, in the prison into which he had been placed because he had buried him, as the Scripture of Nicodemus declares;

second, to his mother, as Sedulius makes clear;

third, to Mary Magdalene, as Mark asserts;

fourth, to the two returning from the tomb, as Matthew relates;

fifth, to James, as Paul bears witness—he who had vowed on the sixth day not to eat until he saw Christ alive;

sixth, also to Peter, as Luke acknowledges, who, because of his denial, had withdrawn from the others and remained in tears;

seventh, to the two on the road to Emmaus, as Luke again relates;

eighth, in the evening, with all the doors closed, as John describes;

ninth, on the eighth day, when Thomas touched him;

tenth, by the Sea of Tiberias;

eleventh, on the mountain of Galilee;

twelfth, to the eleven disciples reclining at table.

These are the joys of our feast, which Christ has bestowed upon us through his resurrection. Thus (sic), if we wish to celebrate the true Passover, let us always preserve in life and conduct what we signify through the mysteries of things and times. For this reason we celebrate the holy Passover in white garments for seven days, so that we may deserve always to possess bodily purity and the joy of the resurrection. Hence it is said through Wisdom: “At all times let your garments be white, and let oil never fail from your head (Eccles. IX).” This means: Let purity never be absent from the body, nor spiritual joy from the heart. The same thing was signified when the Jewish people, after eating the lamb, fed for seven days on unleavened bread. The Apostle interprets this in relation to its reality: “Cleanse out the old leaven, etc. (I Cor. V).” As if he said: In order that you may be fit to celebrate the true Passover and eat the flesh of the true and spotless Lamb, cleanse out the old leaven, etc. “Remove the old sin, so that you may be a new dough” (ibid.), that is, recover the newness of life which you received in the laver of baptism.

For when a people comes to the faith and is catechized, it is, as it were, ground. And just as the diversity of grains is forced through the mill into unity, so the diversity of peoples is joined through instruction into a kind of unity. Yet conversion has not happened at that point. Water is added, and bread is made, as the Apostle says elsewhere: “We are one bread, one body in Christ, all who eat of his bread and drink from his cup” (I Cor. X).

Just as circumcision, insofar as the effect of the remission of sins was concerned, once stood in place of baptism, while the Red Sea presented the likeness and figure of that same baptism, so the Paschal lamb—whose flesh was eaten by the people and whose blood marked the doorposts of the houses (Exod. XII)—preceded in figure the sacrament of Christ’s body. But after the truth came, the sign was removed: for there was no longer a future reality to be signified, but one that was present and could be received. The figure nevertheless remained as long as the reality had not yet come; and what was later to be fulfilled in truth was first presented in likeness.

Egypt is the world; the destroyer is the devil; the Lamb is Christ; the lamb’s blood is Christ’s Passion; the house of souls is the body; the house of thoughts is the heart. We stain these with blood through faith in the Passion; we stain those with blood through imitation of the Passion, setting the sign of the cross within and without against the hostile powers. Finally, we eat the lamb’s flesh when, receiving his true body in the sacrament, we are incorporated into Christ through faith and love.

Elsewhere: Whatever is eaten is incorporated. When Christ’s flesh is eaten, it is not the one who is eaten but the one who eats who is incorporated into him whom he eats. Therefore Christ wished to be eaten by us in order to incorporate us into himself. This is the sacrament of Christ’s body, and the reality of the sacrament of Christ’s body. Whoever eats and is incorporated possesses both the sacrament and the reality of the sacrament. Whoever eats but is not incorporated possesses the sacrament but does not possess the reality of the sacrament. Thus whoever is incorporated, even if he does not happen to eat, possesses the reality of the sacrament, although he does not possess the sacrament. Whoever receives possesses the sacrament. Whoever believes and loves possesses the reality of the sacrament. It is therefore better for the person who believes and loves, even if he cannot receive and eat, than for the person who receives and eats but does not believe or love—or, if he believes, does not love.

## MONDAY OF EASTER. According to Luke

[Col. 0929]

“Two of Jesus’ disciples were going that same day to a village which was sixty stadia from Jerusalem, named Emmaus. And they were speaking with one another about all the things that had happened” (Luke XXIV).

Greek writers relate that the giant Hercules ran one hundred and twenty-five paces in a single breath. When these had been completed and the distance had been measured, he called such a distance a stadion. A stadion is an eighth of a mile; sixty stadia make seven and a half miles. Taken together, they amount to three and three-fourths leagues. Thus sixty stadia signify seven thousand five hundred paces. This distance of the journey aptly corresponds to those who, certain about the Savior’s death and burial but uncertain about his resurrection, walked along. For who can doubt that the resurrection, which took place after the seventh day of the week, is contained in the number eight? The disciples, therefore, who walked along speaking about the Lord completed the sixth mile of their journey’s beginning, because they grieved that he, who had lived without reproach, had reached death, which he endured on the sixth day of the Sabbath. They also completed the seventh, because they did not doubt that he had rested in the tomb. But they did not complete the eighth, because they did not perfectly believe in the glory of the resurrection.

Emmaus is the notable city of Nicopolis in Palestine. After the conquest of Judaea under the emperor Marcus Aurelius Antoninus, it was restored, and with its status it changed its name.

“And it came to pass, while they were talking and questioning one another, that he drew near and went with them. But their eyes were held, so that they should not recognize him.” Understand *fabularentur*—“they were talking”—as meaning “they were speaking.” *Quaererent* means that they were inquiring into the Scriptures concerning Christ. As they spoke about him, the Lord drew near and accompanied them, both to kindle faith in the resurrection in their minds and to fulfill what he had promised to do: “Where two or three are gathered in my name, there am I in the midst of them” (Matt. XVIII).

He did indeed appear, but he did not show them a form by which they could recognize him. Just as they loved him inwardly and yet doubted, so he was present outwardly among them but did not reveal who he was. Thus, to those speaking about him he displayed his presence, but from those who doubted he withheld the appearance by which he might be recognized.

Hence Augustine says to Bishop Paulinus, in that letter entitled *On the Very Prosperous Arrival of Our Brother and Fellow Presbyter*: “Your inquiry commonly moves many people: how it was that after the resurrection the Lord was both recognized and not recognized by certain men and women. The first question usually raised is whether something happened in his body, or rather in their eyes, whereby he could not be recognized. For it is written: ‘Their eyes were held, so that they should not recognize him.’ Elsewhere it is plainly said: ‘He appeared to them in another form’ (Mark XVI).”

But why does it not disturb us that before the Passion, at the Transfiguration, his face shone like the sun, while after the resurrection it disturbs us somewhat that his features were changed so that he could not be recognized? And why should it not likewise be accepted that he then restored his former complexion, and after the resurrection his former features? Those three disciples before whose eyes he was transfigured on the mountain would not have recognized him if he had come to them from elsewhere in such a form. If someone saw a young man whom he had seen only as an infant, he would certainly not recognize him. Can the Lord’s power not quickly change his features, when the passage of years can do the same through the slow process of human aging?

“And he said to them: ‘What are these words that you are discussing with one another as you walk and are sad?’ And one of them, whose name was Cleophas, answering, said to him: ‘Are you the only stranger in Jerusalem, and have you not known the things that have happened there in these days?’ To them he said: ‘What things?’ And they said: ‘Concerning Jesus of Nazareth, who was a man, a prophet mighty in deed and word before God and all the people; and how our chief priests and rulers delivered him to condemnation to death and crucified him. But we hoped that he was the one who would redeem Israel.’”

Cleophas’s companion was called Amaon, according to Ambrose in his commentary on Luke. They think him a stranger because they do not recognize him. And truly he was a stranger to them: through the glory of the resurrection he already stood far away from their weakness, and, because their faith did not yet know of his resurrection, he remained an outsider to them. They confess him to be a prophet, and a great one, but they are silent about his being the Son of God—either because they did not yet perfectly believe this, or because, even if they believed it, they feared that he might be delivered into the hands of the Jews, not knowing with whom they were speaking.

In a certain sense they also rebuke themselves for having hoped for redemption in one whom they had seen dead and did not expect to rise again. Above all, they grieved that one whom they knew to be innocent had been killed without guilt, and for this reason they walked along sadly.

“And now, besides all this, today is the third day since these things happened. But some women of our company have terrified us: they came before dawn to the tomb, and, not finding his body, returned saying that they had even seen visions of angels, who say that he is alive. Some of our company went to the tomb and found it just as the women had said; but him they did not find.”

From this sequence of the narrative, observe that the women first saw visions of angels; then Peter and John ran to the tomb. The men were therefore terrified by the women’s report of the vision, and the failure to find the body caused them more grief than the announced resurrection gave them joy.

“And he said to them: ‘O foolish ones, and slow of heart to believe all that the prophets have spoken. Was it not necessary that Christ should suffer these things and so enter into his glory? And beginning with Moses and all the prophets, he interpreted to them in all the Scriptures the things concerning himself.’”

Here we are confronted by a twofold necessity for humbling ourselves: we have neither been instructed in the Scriptures as much as we ought, nor have we been as attentive as we should be to fulfilling what we know. For if Moses and the prophets spoke about Christ and foretold that he would enter into glory through suffering, how can someone pride himself on being a Christian who neither investigates the Scriptures insofar as they concern Christ nor desires to attain through sufferings the glory he wishes to possess with Christ?

“And they drew near to the village to which they were going, and he pretended that he was going farther. And they urged him, saying: ‘Stay with us, Lord, for it is toward evening, and the day is now declining.’ And he entered in with them.”

The Lord opened to those two men the mysteries of the sacred Scriptures that concerned him; yet because he was still a stranger to faith in their hearts, he pretended that he was going farther. For we call *fingere*—“to fashion”—*componere*. Hence we call those who fashion clay *figuli*, potters. The simple Truth did nothing through duplicity; rather, he presented himself to them in bodily form as he was in their minds. They were being tested: whether they would love this man, whom they did not yet love as God, at least as a stranger. And because those with whom the Truth walked could not be strangers to charity, they invited him to lodging as a stranger—indeed, they compelled him. From this it follows that strangers are not only to be invited but also drawn into lodging.

“And it came to pass, while he reclined with them, that he took bread, blessed it, broke it, and handed it to them. And their eyes were opened, and they recognized him; and he vanished from their sight.”

They recognize in the breaking of the bread the God whom they had not recognized in the exposition of the Scriptures. They were not enlightened by hearing, but by doing, because it is written: “It is not the hearers of the law who are righteous before God, but the doers” (Rom. II). Whoever therefore wishes to understand what he has heard should hasten to fulfill in action what he has already understood.

The appearance of weakness is withdrawn from bodily eyes, so that the glory of the resurrection may begin to appear to their minds. Hence it follows:

“And they said to one another: ‘Was not our heart burning within us while he spoke to us on the way and opened the Scriptures to us?’”

From hearing the Lord’s words, their heart, previously cold with the torpor of unbelief and fear, was kindled by the fire of the Holy Spirit, so that it burned with heavenly desire and stretched itself toward believing the truth. A person is instructed by as many commandments as though he were set aflame by that many torches.

Nevertheless, they did not recognize him until the breaking of the bread. Certainly this happened because of the mystery: a likeness of him was shown to them which they would not recognize except in the breaking of the bread, lest anyone think that he had recognized Christ if he is not a participant in his body—which is the Church. The Apostle commends the Church’s unity in the sacrament of the bread, saying: “We, though many, are one bread, one body” (I Cor. X). Then we truly recognize him when, through the Church’s sacrament, we faithfully understand that he died and rose again for us.

It is not incongruous to understand that this impediment in their eyes came from Satan, so that Jesus would not be recognized. Yet Christ’s promise was made effective up to the bread, so that we may now understand the enemy’s impediment to be removed when, in the Church, we rightly understand the mystery of the sacrament of the Lord’s body and blood.

“And rising at that same hour, they returned to Jerusalem; and they found the eleven gathered together, and those who were with them, saying: ‘The Lord has truly risen and has appeared to Simon.’ And they recounted what had happened on the way, and how they had recognized him in the breaking of the bread. But they did not believe them.”

It should be noted that some who were there did not believe those two men; but those to whom the Lord had already appeared certainly did believe them. Just as among the women he was first seen by Mary Magdalene, so among the men he was first seen by Peter. Although the Evangelist does not say when or where this happened, he does not conceal that it did happen.

## TUESDAY. According to Luke

[Col. 0931]

“Jesus stood in the midst of his disciples and said to them: ‘Peace be with you. It is I; do not be afraid’” (Luke XXIV).

The mass of the body, in which divinity was present, was not hindered by closed doors. And it is doubtless to be understood that Thomas had gone out from there before the Lord appeared to the others.

“But they, disturbed and terrified, thought that they were seeing a spirit.”

The Apostles believed—but were they not disturbed? First, because the opinion of the few is excluded by the judgment of the greater number; and finally, because Peter, even if he believed that the Lord had risen, could have been disturbed by the fact that the Lord had suddenly entered among them bodily although the doors were closed. They therefore thought that they were seeing a spirit, not flesh, because they did not believe either that true flesh could rise from the tomb on the third day or that the risen Lord could enter to them through closed doors.

“And he said to them: ‘Why are you troubled, and why do thoughts arise in your hearts?’”

Those thoughts did not descend from above but arose from the depths of the heart, like evil grass from the earth. “I demand the faith that I planted in you; I condemn what has sprung up from you. If there is no truth in the resurrection, the fruit of the Passion is lost.”

“‘See my hands and my feet, that it is I myself. Touch and see, for a spirit does not have flesh and bones as you see me have.’ And when he had said this, he showed them his hands and feet and side.”

The traces of the wounds were preserved to heal the hearts of those who doubted. Through many proofs he therefore persuades them of the resurrection, presenting himself to be seen by their eyes and handled by their hands. In showing bones and flesh to be touched, he signifies the state of his resurrection and of ours: the body will be subtle through the effect of spiritual power, yet tangible through the truth of its nature.

Hence blessed Job says: “And again I shall be clothed with my skin, and in my flesh I shall see God” (Job XIX). It should also be known that, just as the Lord deigned to disclose to his disciples the places of the nails and the lance, so on the day of judgment he will show both those same marks of his Passion and the cross itself, in order to confound the unbelief of the proud.

For many reasons he wished the scars to remain on his body. The first was to establish the disciples’ faith in the resurrection; the second, that, interceding for us with the Father, he might always show what kind of death he endured for humanity; the third, to renew his mercy toward us through such signs; the fourth, that on the day of judgment he might show the faithless how justly they ought to be condemned to eternal fires.

If some very brave soldier, at the command of his king, killed an enemy for the safety of his people, having received many wounds, and brought back the enemy’s spoils to his people after defeating him, and a physician asked him whether he wished to be healed so that no traces of the wounds would appear, or rather so that the scars would remain without any disfigurement, he would answer that he wished to be healed in such a way that the marks of his triumph would remain, if this could be done without bodily disfigurement. The Lord acted precisely so. He did not preserve the scars because he lacked the power to heal, but so that he might carry forever the triumph of his victory.

“While they still did not believe and were marveling for joy, he said to them: ‘Do you have anything here to eat?’ And they offered him a piece of broiled fish and a honeycomb. And when he had eaten before them, taking what remained, he gave it to them.”

This should be piously understood: after the Lord’s resurrection, the foods he consumed provided him no assistance for nourishment. Rather, just as water placed upon fire is consumed, so what he ate was immediately taken up by his spiritual power. Certainly, just as he had no need of food after the resurrection, neither shall we; yet he wished to show a real life, not an imaginary one.

The thirsty earth absorbs water in one way, while a burning ray of sunlight dries it in another. The former absorbs out of need; the latter dries by power.

The broiled fish signifies the Mediator, who deigned to lie hidden in the waters of the human race, wished to be caught in the snare of death, and to be broiled through the tribulation of the Passion. But the fish that was broiled in the Passion became a honeycomb in the resurrection. The honeycomb is honey in wax—that is, the sweetness of divinity in humanity. He wished to join the honeycomb to the broiled fish as his food, because he receives into his body for eternal rest those who, while they experience tribulations here, do not depart from the love of inward sweetness. Those who are broiled here for God like fish will there be filled with true sweetness like honeycomb.

“And he said to them: ‘These are the words that I spoke to you while I was still with you: that everything written about me in the law of Moses, the prophets, and the psalms must be fulfilled.’”

“While I was still with you”—understand, “in mortal flesh”—“I spoke these words, namely, that what was written about me must be fulfilled.” See how the Lord removed every ambiguity. He appeared, he was touched, he ate, and he set forth and explained the Scriptures. Then he opened their understanding so that they might understand the Scriptures.

“And he said to them: ‘Thus it is written, and thus it was necessary for Christ to suffer and to rise from the dead on the third day, and for repentance and the remission of sins to be preached in his name among all nations, beginning from Jerusalem.’”

Having commended the reality of his body, he commends the unity of the Church. He wishes repentance and the remission of sins to be preached among all nations, so that those who were to preach would begin from Jerusalem—not preaching only to the Jews, but extending the preaching also to the errors of the nations.

“‘You are witnesses of these things, and I send the promise of my Father upon you.’”

You who have seen and heard are witnesses of the things that must be preached. So that you may be sufficient for bearing witness, I will send you the promise of my Father—that is, the grace of the Holy Spirit.

## SUNDAY WITHIN THE OCTAVE OF EASTER. According to Luke

[Col. 0933]

“When it was evening on that day, the first day of the week, and the doors were closed where the disciples were gathered, because of fear of the Jews, Jesus came and stood in their midst” (John XX).

What is surprising if, with the doors closed, he entered after his resurrection, now destined to live forever, when, coming to die, he emerged without opening the Virgin’s womb? But because the faith of those looking upon that body, which could be seen, was doubtful, he immediately showed them his hands and side. He offered flesh to be touched, although he had entered through closed doors. The nail had fixed his hands, and the lance had opened his side; there the traces of the wounds were preserved to heal the hearts of those who doubted.

In this event he displayed two marvels that, according to human reasoning, are strongly contrary to each other: after his resurrection he showed his body to be both incorruptible and tangible. For what is touched must also be subject to corruption, and what is not corruptible cannot be touched. Yet in a marvelous and immeasurable way our Redeemer displayed an incorruptible body after the resurrection and one that could nevertheless be touched: by showing it incorruptible, he invited us to the reward; by offering it to be touched, he formed us in faith. He therefore demonstrated himself to be both incorruptible and tangible, so that he might show that after the resurrection his body possessed the same nature but another glory.

“And he said to them: ‘Peace be with you.’”

He offered peace who came for the sake of peace. And to those to whom he had previously said, “I leave you peace; my peace I give you” (John XIV), he now says, “Peace be with you,” because the angels preached peace to the world at Christ’s birth.

“And when he had said this, he showed them his hands and side. The disciples therefore rejoiced when they saw the Lord. He said to them again: ‘Peace be with you.’”

Repetition is confirmation. For he gives peace upon peace, as he promised through the prophet. Or he repeats it in order to show that the things in heaven and on earth have been reconciled through his blood.

“As the Father sent me, so I send you.”

As God the Father sent God, so I, a human being, send human beings. The Father, loving the Son, sent him to suffer; and the Lord, loving the Apostles, sent them not to the joy of the world but to suffering.

The Son’s being sent by the Father can also be understood according to his divine nature. For the Son is sent by the Father in the same manner in which he is generated. If “sending” were to be understood only as incarnation, the Holy Spirit could in no way be said to be sent, since he was not incarnated. But his sending is his procession from the Father and the Son. Thus, just as the Spirit is said to be sent because he proceeds, so the Son is said to be sent because he is generated.

“When he had said this, he breathed on them and said: ‘Receive the Holy Spirit. Whose sins you forgive are forgiven them, and whose you retain are retained.’”

By breathing on them, he signified that the Holy Spirit is not the Spirit of the Father alone but also his own. The Church’s charity, which is given in our hearts through the Holy Spirit, forgives the sins of those who share in it, but retains the sins of those who do not share in it. Therefore, after saying, “Receive the Holy Spirit,” he immediately spoke of the remission and retention of sins.

The Spirit is given on earth so that the neighbor may be loved; from heaven, so that God may be loved. And just as there is one charity and two commandments, so there is one Spirit and two gifts.

The Holy Spirit was already present in the minds of the disciples for the sake of faith, but not so manifestly as after the resurrection. Hence the saying: “The Spirit had not yet been given, because Jesus had not yet been glorified” (John VII). Hence also it is said through Moses: “They sucked honey from the rock, and oil from the hard rock” (Deut. XXXII). Nothing of this sort is found according to the historical sense if the entire sequence of the Old Testament is reviewed. But because, according to Paul, the rock was Christ, they sucked honey from the rock who saw the Redeemer’s miracles. They sucked oil from the hard rock who, after his resurrection, deserved to be anointed by the outpouring of the Holy Spirit. The weak rock gave honey while he was still mortal; the true rock poured forth oil when, after the resurrection, he was incapable of suffering.

“But Thomas, one of the twelve, who is called Didymus, was not with them when Jesus came. The other disciples therefore said to him: ‘We have seen the Lord.’ But he said to them: ‘Unless I see in his hands the mark of the nails, and put my finger into the place of the nails, and put my hand into his side, I will not believe.’”

This happened not by chance but through divine dispensation: that disciple was absent then, but afterward he would doubt, touch, and, touching, believe. Thomas’s unbelief benefited us for faith more than the faith of the believers, because, as he is led to faith by touching, our mind is made firm in faith.

“And after eight days his disciples were again inside, and Thomas was with them. Jesus came, with the doors closed, stood in their midst, and said: ‘Peace be with you.’ Then he said to Thomas: ‘Put your finger here, and see my hands; bring your hand and put it into my side; and do not be unbelieving but believing.’”

The Lord’s body entered to the disciples through closed doors, just as at his birth he came forth from the Virgin’s closed womb. Nor is it surprising that, destined to live forever, he entered to the disciples, when, destined to die, he came forth from the Virgin’s closed womb.

The Lord displayed two marvels that, according to human reasoning, are strongly contrary to each other: after the resurrection he showed his body to be incorruptible and tangible. For what is touched must be subject to corruption, and what is not corruptible cannot be touched. But in a marvelous way our Redeemer appeared incorruptible by showing himself, so that he might invite us to the reward, and presented himself as tangible, so that he might form us in faith. A divine act is not very marvelous if it can be grasped or proved by reason. This is the power of reason appropriate to the merits of faith.

“Thomas answered and said to him: ‘My Lord and my God.’”

He saw and touched a human being, and confessed the God whom he neither saw nor touched. Jesus said to him: “Because you have seen me, you have believed.” He saw one thing and believed another: he saw a human being and confessed God.

He did not say “because you have touched,” but “because you have seen,” since sight is in a certain way a general sense. For the other four senses are commonly named through it, as when we say: “Hear and see how well it sounds”; “Smell and see how fragrant it is”; “Taste and see how good it tastes”; “Touch and see how warm it is.” Hence here too the Lord says:

“Put your finger here and see my hands”—that is, touch and see. Thomas therefore saw merely by looking, or also by touching. For it can be said that the disciple did not dare at that time to touch the Lord. It is not written, “Thomas touched,” but that he saw and believed.

“Blessed are those who have not seen and have believed.”

He commends the faith of the nations, but he uses verbs in the past tense because, in his predestination, he already knew as accomplished what was still future. It should be understood that the one who truly believes is the one who completes faith through works. Of those who retain faith in name only, Paul says: “They profess that they know God, but by their works they deny him” (Titus I). And James says: “Faith without works is dead” (James II).

“Jesus performed many other signs in the sight of his disciples, which are not written in this book. But these are written so that you may believe that Jesus is the Christ, the Son of God, and that, believing, you may have life in his name.”

The Evangelist places this as though it were the end of the book, in order to commend greatly the sacrament of the narrative that follows, giving it, in a certain sense, a more eminent place.

## SERMON FOR THE OCTAVE OF EASTER

There are three days of invisible light, by which the course of spiritual life is inwardly illumined. The first day is fear; the second day is truth; the third day is charity. The first day has power as its sun; the second has wisdom as its sun; the third has goodness as its sun. Power pertains to the Father, wisdom to the Son, and goodness to the Holy Spirit.

Some days are ours outwardly; others are ours inwardly. Our outward days pass even when we do not wish them to. But the inward days, if we wish, can remain forever.

Behold, there are three days: the day of fear, which reveals evil; the day of truth, which removes evil; and the day of charity, which restores the good. The day of truth illumines the day of fear; the day of charity illumines both the day of fear and the day of truth, until charity has been perfected, all truth has been perfectly revealed, and fear of punishment has passed into reverential fear.

The prophet Hosea spoke of these days, saying: “He will revive us after two days; on the third day he will raise us up” (Hos. VI). For we have heard and rejoiced in how our Lord Jesus Christ, through the humanity he had assumed, revived and raised us up in himself by rising from the dead on the third day.

But it is most fitting that we repay his benefit and, just as we rose in him when he rose on the third day, so we too, rising for him and through him on the third day, should cause him to rise in us. We must not doubt that he himself wishes us to repay to him what he first wished to bestow upon us.

Therefore, just as he wished to possess three days in order to accomplish our salvation in and through himself, so he gave us three days in order that we might accomplish our salvation in ourselves through him.

These three days are also signified by that bird called the phoenix. Concerning it, the physiologist says that when it has completed ten years of life, it enters the trees of Lebanon and fills both its wings with various spices from that wood. Making a nest from different perfumes, it gathers a very great heap of branches, placing it beneath the nest; then, approaching the air, it draws the sun’s fire with it and sets the branches alight.
