It enters its nest in the month of March and burns itself. On the first day the ash is changed into a worm; on the second day into a bird; on the third day into its former state.

Thus this phoenix, which after a long life of ten years is consumed by fire into ash, then changed into a worm, and finally restored to its former state, signifies the one of whom the Prophet says: “I am a worm and not a man” (Ps. XXI).

Why the Lord of all creation wished to compare himself to a little worm in his Passion and burial can first be attributed to humility, which is the greatest virtue of the saints. Thus holy Moses professes before God that he is an irrational animal, and David often calls himself a flea. But I think it should rather be understood that a worm is born without any external admixture of another body, from earth alone and pure; hence he is compared with the Lord because the Savior himself was born from Mary alone and pure.

We also read in the books of Moses that worms were produced from manna (Exod. XVI). The comparison is plainly worthy and fitting. For a worm is born from manna, and the Lord Christ is produced from the Virgin. Indeed, I would say that Mary herself was manna, because she is delicate, radiant, sweet, and a virgin. As though descending from heaven, she poured forth for all the Church’s vessels a food sweeter than honey.

That food was Christ, who in the Passion was so boiled down by reproaches that he was reduced, as it were, to a worm.

But let us return now to the history of the bird. If five hundred are multiplied by ten, they make five thousand. There were five thousand years from Adam to Christ. During this long period, when almost the whole world was perishing through Adam’s transgression, Christ was born from the Virgin. Gathering various spices with his two wings—that is, love of God and love of neighbor—he made from them in human hearts a nest, as it were, a little dwelling.

When he placed beneath it a burden [probably *sarcinam*]—that is, the dry or biting unbelief of the Jews—which he stirred up against himself through the riches of the righteousness he had performed, they blazed up into such great wickedness that, on the sixth day of the week in the month of March, they consumed him by the fire of the Passion and changed him, as it were, into ash when they crucified him for the salvation of the world.

Then he was placed in the tomb and, like a worm in the earth, was hidden in the sepulcher on the second day. On the third day, however, just as the phoenix is renewed into its former state, so Christ was raised from mortality to immortality.

Alternatively: the phoenix is said to be red, and he is Christ of whom it is said: “Who is this who comes from Edom, with garments dyed from Bozrah?” (Isa. LXIII). Edom, which means “red,” was the name given to Esau because of the red stew with which he was fed by his brother Jacob. From him the region of Idumaea received its name; in it the city of Bozrah was the capital of the kingdom. Job reigned there, and by his affliction prefigured Christ’s Passion.

Christ comes from Edom when, having suffered at the hands of the nations, his flesh reddened with blood. His garment is dyed in Bozrah when, in Jerusalem, which was the capital of the kingdom, his garment is sprinkled with blood.

Here, like the phoenix, he gathered the fragrant branches of trees into a nest when he filled Jerusalem with the writings of the prophets. He is burned by those same branches when, according to the sayings of the prophets, he is consumed in Jerusalem by the fire of the Passion. The bird is restored on the third day because Christ is raised by the Father on the third day.

What took place in Christ was not only a remedy but also a sacrament. It was therefore necessary that it be visibly enacted outwardly, so that it might signify what had to take place invisibly within us. His outward days were our days; his inward days must be sought. Thus we have three inward days, by which our soul is illumined. Death belongs to the first day, burial to the second, and resurrection to the third.

Therefore, in these three days three further medicinal encampments are also signified. They are a health-giving antidote against long-standing diseases, and a heavenly balm against Lazarus of four days. Those who are going to sacrifice to the Lord will undertake these. This journey was commanded to the children of Israel when they were to go and sacrifice to the Lord, as they were being brought out of Egypt [Col. 0939C]. This world must be abandoned, not in place but in spirit—not by advancing with one’s steps, but by advancing through one’s actions.

The priest mentions these three encampments when he prays for himself and for the people, saying: “Mindful of your divine passion, as well as of your glorious resurrection from the dead and ascension into heaven.” Indeed, Christ consecrated the leadership of this religion—our head—through the three days of his death, resurrection, and ascension.

The passion, crucifixion, and burial constitute one encampment. For just as Christ wished to be bound, crucified, and to rest for three days, so we must restrain our senses—which are children without a pedagogue, a horse running without driver or bridle—from their old habit, and make them entirely unmoving, insensible, and dead upon the nails of justice on the cross of repentance, so that we may be crucified to the world within ourselves. Many are crucified to the world, but the world is not crucified to them: such people are despised by the world, yet they themselves love the world. They are dead to the world, but the world is not dead to them. Paul was regarded as the refuse of the world and cared nothing for the world. Hence he says: “The world has been crucified to me, and I to the world” (Gal. VI).

Whoever is thus crucified with Christ is buried with Christ, so that he may keep a spiritual Sabbath-rest. This is the holy rest that the Lord commanded to be observed. This is the first encampment, namely, turning away from evil [Col. 0940B].

The sorrow of the Lord’s passion was followed by the glory and joy of the resurrection. May we also rise with him, so that we may “walk in newness of life” (Rom. VI). This is the second encampment, that is, doing good.

The third encampment is to ascend with the Lord, so that where the head has gone before, the members may follow, seeking and contemplating the things that are above. The righteous undertakes this encampment when, contemplating heavenly things, he expresses another Paul or another Martin, saying: “I desire to depart and to be with Christ” (Phil. I). This is “and dwell for ever and ever” (Ps. XXXVI).

If you pass through these encampments that David recalls in this verse—“Turn away from evil and do good, and dwell for ever and ever” (ibid.)—you offer sacrifice to the Lord, who asks nothing else from you but yourself, and who gave nothing else but himself for you.

Alternatively, these three encampments are three stages of progress. The first is to abandon the habit of sinning. This stage he grants, not greatly fearing for his own party. The second is to abandon the sinful act itself; Pharaoh grants this, but unwillingly and in fear. The third, most difficult stage remains: he must also be forced to drive out the very thing that is the affectionate remembrance of sin. If we progress through this encampment despite our adversary, we will reduce him and all his army to nothing.

## FIRST SUNDAY AFTER THE OCTAVE OF EASTER

[Col. 0939]

[Col. 0939D] “I am the good shepherd. The good shepherd gives his life for his sheep” (John X). He is not good accidentally but essentially, and he adds the form of goodness that we should imitate when he says: “The good shepherd gives his life for his sheep.” He did what he instructed; he demonstrated what he commanded. He laid down his life so that in our sanctuary he might transform his body and blood, and satisfy the sheep he had redeemed with the nourishment of his flesh.

The first duty is mercifully to expend our external goods for the sheep; the final one, if necessary, is to die for them. Hence John says in his Epistle: “As Christ laid down his life for us, so we ought to lay down ours for the brothers” (1 John III). This is the shepherd’s distinctive duty, in contrast with the hired hand or the thief.

All who preside over the Church are sons and shepherds. If they are shepherds, how can there be one shepherd, unless they are all members of one shepherd, whose own sheep they are?

“The hired hand, however, and he who is not the shepherd, whose own the sheep are not, sees the wolf coming, leaves the sheep, and flees; and the wolf snatches and scatters the sheep. The hired hand flees because he is a hired hand and has no concern for the sheep.”

Any ecclesiastical superior who seeks temporal advantages rather than the things that belong to Christ is a hired hand. Of such people the Lord says: “Truly I tell you, they have received their reward” (Matt. VI).

Hired hands, however, are necessary, because through them the voice of Christ is heard. Listen to the Lord as he points out the hired hands.

“The scribes,” he says, “and the Pharisees have sat on Moses’ seat. Therefore do whatever they tell you, but do not do what they do” (Matt. XXIII). What else did he say than: Hear the shepherd’s voice through the hired hands? No hired hand has dared to say to Christ’s people: Seek your own interests, not those of Jesus Christ. He harms, therefore, by the evil he does, not by the good he says.

Pick the grape; beware the thorn. Sometimes a grapevine is planted among thorns, and the thorn bears fruit not its own when a vine rests upon thorns. Moses’ seat was a vine; the Pharisees’ conduct was a thorn; true teaching through evil men was a vine among a hedge, and the grape was among the thorns. Choose carefully, lest [Col. 0941B] while seeking the fruit you tear your hand [uncertain: “the world”?], and while hearing someone say good things you imitate the one doing evil.

“Do what they say; choose the grapes. But do not do what they do; beware the thorns.”

Hear the Apostle speaking of the hired hands: “What then? Only that in every way, whether by pretext or in truth, Christ is proclaimed?” (Phil. I). The truth—that is, Christ—is proclaimed by hired hands through pretext, but by sons in truth. Sons patiently await an eternal inheritance; hired hands eagerly desire a temporal wage.

A hired hand, therefore, is one who occupies the shepherd’s position but does not seek the profit of souls, because he thirsts for earthly advantages and rejoices in the honor of leadership. Whether he is a hired hand, however, cannot be properly discerned until the wolf approaches; the wolf reveals with what intention the flock is guarded by each person.

The wolf comes when some unjust and predatory person oppresses the faithful. The one who seemed to be a shepherd, but was not, flees—not by changing his location, but by withdrawing his support. He is silent and dares not resist injustice. Of him the prophet says: “You did not go up to the breach, nor build a wall for the house of Israel, to stand in battle on the day of the Lord” (Ezek. XIII).

To go up to the breach is to oppose the wicked with free and reasoned judgment. To build a wall and stand in battle on the day of the Lord for the house of Israel is to defend the faithful by the authority of justice against the injustice of the wicked.

The malignant spirit is also a wolf, tearing minds rather than bodies and continually prowling around the folds of the faithful. Of him it is said: “And he scatters the sheep.” He scatters them when he draws one into lust, inflames another with greed, raises another into pride; he spurs this one with envy and trips that one with deceit. Thus the devil dissipates the flock when he kills the faithful through temptations.

The hired hand, seeing the wolf, flees because he is a hired hand and does not love Christ in the sheep, but only their milk and wool. He does not dare freely rebuke the sinner, nor excommunicate one who should be excommunicated, lest he lose the advantage of human friendship or incur the annoyance of human relationships.

He flees because he is silent; he is silent because he is afraid. Flight of spirit is fear: he fears losing the person he loves. In body he stands, but in spirit he flees.

This was not done by the one who said: “Although I am absent in body, I am with you in spirit” (Col. II). Shepherds, therefore, do not flee for themselves if they withdraw before persecution, as the Apostle himself was lowered in a basket over the wall. He commended the sheep to the shepherd seated in heaven through his prayers, while preserving himself for their benefit by fleeing, as he says in another place: “To remain in the flesh is necessary for your sake” (Phil. I).

For they had all heard from him: “If they persecute you in one city, flee to another” (Matt. X). In the hired hand, then, it is not bodily flight that is condemned, but flight of mind, and the fact that he seeks his own interests rather than those of Jesus Christ.

“I am the good shepherd, and I know my own and my own know me.” “I know my own” means “I love them,” and “my own love me.”

Among the good are the door, the doorkeeper, the shepherd, and the sheep. Among the evil are thieves, robbers, the hired hand, and the wolf.

The Lord says that he is both the door and the shepherd. But if we consider their proper characteristics, Christ is neither shepherd nor door; by analogy, however, he is shepherd, door, and sheep. For he was led like a sheep to be sacrificed. He is the door in the head, and the shepherd in the body.

He said to Peter: “Feed my sheep” (John XXI), as if he were saying: “What will you give me, since you love me? Give me this: if you love me, feed my sheep.”

Enter through the door; for whoever climbs in from another side is a thief and a robber. In these persons you will find those whom you should love, tolerate, and avoid. The shepherd is to be loved, the hired hand tolerated, and the robber avoided. The hired hand enters canonically and teaches the truth, although with a wrong intention. The thief enters wrongly and teaches falsehood; therefore he is an outsider.

“As the Father knows me, and I know the Father.” That the Son knows the Father through himself, and that no one sees God except through the Son, is clear from this chapter and from his canonical writings.

“And I lay down my life for the sheep.” This is the proof of love for the Father and for the sheep. Thus Peter, confessing his love three times, is commanded to feed the sheep and to die for them.

Hold fast to this: Christ is Word, soul, and flesh. There were heretics called Apollinarists who dared to teach that Christ was nothing but the Word and flesh without a soul.

“And I have other sheep that are not of this fold. I must bring them also, and they will hear my voice; and there will be one fold and one shepherd.” The one fold is unity in Christ. Hence Paul says: “He is our peace, who made both one” (Eph. II).

The words “of this fold” refer to those in Israel who were destined to be saved, concerning whom the Lord said: “I was sent only to the sheep that have perished from the house of Israel” (Matt. XV). He said this because he did not manifest his bodily presence except to that people. He did not go to the Gentiles, but sent his own apostles, in whom he himself spoke.

## SERMON ON SHEPHERDS, HIRED HANDS, AND SUBJECTS

“A good shepherd lays down his life for his sheep” (John X). Just as a shepherd keeps constant watch when he is accustomed to guard sheep against wild beasts, so the priest of God must be solicitous over Christ’s flock [Col. 0943A], lest the enemy devastate it, lest the persecutor attack it, or lest the greed of any powerful person disturb the lives of the poor.

Wicked shepherds have no care for the sheep. Rather, as we read in the Gospel about hired hands, they see the wolf coming and flee. They flee when they remain silent before the powerful and are afraid to resist the wicked.

Superiors must know that if they ever commit wrongdoing, they are worthy of as many deaths as the examples of perdition they transmit to their subjects. Therefore they must guard themselves from fault with all the greater caution, since through the wrongs they commit they do not die alone.

Those who are subject must be admonished, lest they be punished more severely if they cannot be found free from fault, at least in themselves. Those who are superiors must be admonished, lest they be judged for the errors of their subjects, even if they find themselves already secure regarding themselves.

The former should live with greater vigilance concerning themselves in proportion as they are not burdened with responsibility for others. The latter should fulfill the concerns of others in such a way that they do not cease to attend to their own concerns, and should burn with zeal for their personal care in such a way that they do not grow sluggish in guarding those entrusted to them.

To the person who is idle with respect to himself it is said: “Go to the ant, you sluggard; consider its ways and learn wisdom” (Prov. VI). But the superior is terrifyingly admonished when it is said: “My son, if you have become surety for your friend, you have pledged your hand to a stranger, you have been ensnared by the words of your mouth, and captured by your own speech” (ibid.).

To become surety for a friend is to accept another soul at the peril of one’s own conduct. [Col. 0943C] (GREGORY.) Therefore he is also bound to a stranger, because his mind is tied to a care of concern that previously had been absent. He is ensnared by the words of his mouth and captured by his own speech because, when he is compelled to say good things to those entrusted to him, he must first keep what he has said himself.

He is thus ensnared by the words of his mouth when, as reason demands, he is constrained not to relax his life into anything other than what he admonishes. Hence before the strict Judge he is compelled to fulfill in works as much as he is known to have commanded others by his voice.

There the exhortation immediately follows appropriately: “Do therefore what I say, my son, and free yourself, because you have fallen into the hand of your neighbor. Run, hasten; rouse your friend. Do not give sleep to your eyes, nor slumber to your eyelids” (ibid.).

Whoever is placed before others as an example for living is admonished not only to keep awake himself but also to rouse his friend. It is not enough for him to watch by living well if he does not also separate the person over whom he presides from the torpor of sin.

It is rightly said: “Do not give sleep to your eyes, nor let your eyelids slumber.” To give sleep to the eyes is, when vigilance has ceased, to neglect entirely the care of one’s subjects. The eyelids slumber when our thoughts, pressed down by sluggishness, conceal the things they know should be rebuked in those under their authority.

To sleep fully is to be unaware of the actions of those entrusted to one and not to correct them. But not to sleep, rather to slumber, is to know the things that should indeed be rebuked, yet not to correct them with fitting reprimands because of weariness of mind.

By slumbering, the eye is gradually led to complete sleep. For when the person in charge frequently fails to cut away the evil he recognizes, he eventually reaches, through the merit of his negligence, the point at which he does not even perceive what is being done wrongly by his subjects.

Those who preside must therefore be admonished to strive, through devoted vigilance, to become heavenly creatures, having wakeful eyes within and all around.

(GREGORY.) The heavenly creatures are described as full of eyes all around and within (Ezek. V). It is fitting, therefore, that all who preside should have eyes within and all around, so that they may strive to please the inner Judge in themselves and, by offering examples of life outwardly, detect what must be corrected in others.

Subjects must be admonished not rashly to judge the life of their superiors if they happen to see them doing something blameworthy, lest, from the very point at which they rightly rebuke evil, they plunge into deeper things through the impulse of pride.

They must be admonished that, when they consider the faults of their superiors, they should not become more audacious against them. Rather, even if they judge that some works of their superiors are very wrong, they should do so in such a way that, constrained by divine fear, they do not refuse to bear beneath them the yoke of reverence.

We can show this more clearly if we bring David’s deed into the discussion. Saul the persecutor had entered a cave to relieve himself, and David was there with his men (1 Sam. XXIV), having already endured the evils of Saul’s persecution for so long.

When his men urged him to strike Saul, he restrained them with his answer, because they ought not to lay a hand upon the Lord’s anointed. Nevertheless, he rose secretly and cut off the edge of Saul’s cloak.

What is signified by Saul except wicked rulers? And what by David except good subjects?

Saul’s relieving his bowels signifies wicked superiors—hired hands—extending the evil conceived in their hearts into deeds of foul odor, and displaying through outward actions the harmful thoughts they have harbored within.

David did not wish to strike him because devout minds among subjects, refraining from every plague of slander, do not strike the life of their superiors with the sword of the tongue, even when they rebuke imperfection.

If at times, because of weakness, they can scarcely restrain themselves from speaking of certain extreme and outward faults of their superiors, yet do so humbly, they cut the edge of the cloak silently. That is, they detract at least harmlessly and secretly from the dignity placed over them, as though staining the robe of the king set above them.

Yet afterward they return to themselves and rebuke themselves most severely for having torn even the slightest word. Hence it is rightly written there: “After this David’s heart struck him because he had cut off the edge of Saul’s cloak” (ibid.).

The deeds of superiors are not to be struck with the sword of the mouth, even when they are rightly judged worthy of correction. If the tongue should at any time slip against them, even in the smallest matter [uncertain: “if the tongue slips”], the heart must be weighed down by the affliction of repentance, so that it may return to itself and, having offended against the authority placed over it, may dread the judgment against itself of the one by whom that authority was placed above it.

For when we offend against our superiors, we oppose the ordinance of the one who placed them over us. Hence Moses, when he learned that the people were complaining against him and Aaron, said: “What are we? Your murmuring is not against us, but against the Lord” (Exod. XVI).

## SECOND SUNDAY AFTER THE OCTAVE OF EASTER  
### According to John

[Col. 0945]

[Col. 0945A] “A little while, and you will no longer see me; and again a little while, and you will see me, because I am going to the Father. Then some of his disciples said to one another: ‘What is this that he says to us: A little while, and you will not see me, and again a little while, and you will see me, and because I am going to the Father?’ They were saying: ‘What is this that he says, A little while? We do not know what he is saying’” (John XVI).

This disturbed them because he had said “a little while.” But afterward it became clear. For shortly afterward he suffered, and they did not see him; then again shortly afterward he rose, and they saw him.

Or it may be understood this way: For a short time they did not see him while he rested in the tomb, and again for a short time they saw him when he appeared to them for forty days after the resurrection.

He says, “You will see me for a little while because I am going to the Father,” because, laying aside mortality, he was bringing human nature into heaven. But when he says, “And you will no longer see me,” this must be understood as his earlier statement: “Concerning righteousness, because I am going to the Father, and you will no longer see me” (ibid.), namely, that they would no longer see him as mortal.

“Jesus knew that they wanted to ask him, and he said: ‘Are you asking one another about this, because I said, A little while, and you will not see me, and again a little while, and you will see me? Truly, truly, I tell you, you will weep and lament, but the world will rejoice. You will be sorrowful, but your sorrow will turn into joy.’”

They were sorrowful over the Lord’s death, but soon rejoiced over his resurrection. Here “the world” signifies his enemies, by whom Christ was killed.

“When a woman gives birth, she has sorrow because her hour has come; but when she has given birth to the child, she no longer remembers the distress because of the joy that a human being has been born into the world.”

Childbirth is compared with joy, especially when not a girl but a boy is born. The joy is Christ himself, concerning whom the Apostle says: “Christ, having risen from the dead, will never die again” (Rom. VI).

“And you indeed have sorrow now, but I will see you again, and your heart will rejoice; and no one will take your joy from you.”

The Lord explains the example he gave concerning the woman. The apostles had sorrow when the Lord suffered, but after the glory of the resurrection had been accomplished, they rejoiced at seeing the Lord.

Their joy was not taken from them. Even though afterward they suffered persecutions and torments for Christ’s name, they were kindled by hope of the resurrection and of seeing him, and gladly endured every adversity—or rather, they considered it joy when they fell into various trials.

When he says, “I will see you again, and your heart will rejoice,” this can be understood as follows: “I will rescue you from your adversaries, crown you as victors, and prove that I have always seen you struggling.”

“And on that day you will ask me nothing.” On the day of eternal vision you will neither ask nor question, because then there will be complete knowledge and sufficiency. The word translated as “to ask” signifies not only “to request” but also “to question,” and the Greek word from which this was translated has a form that can be understood in both ways. It is therefore ambiguous.

These words may also be explained as though, in the disciples, the Lord were addressing the universal Church, as when he says: “Behold, I am with you always, to the end of the age” (Matt. XXVIII).

“A little while, and you will no longer see me” refers to the fact that he is going to the Father. By going to the Father, he will withdraw bodily visibility so that the Church may believe fruitfully. “And again a little while, and you will see me”—with eternal vision. Understand “a little while,” according to this interpretation, as the period of this fleeting age.

“You will lament,” he says, because all good people lament amid the hardships of this life, while lovers of the world rejoice.

We call the holy Church a woman because of the fruitfulness of good works and because she never ceases to give birth to spiritual children for the Lord. She likewise never ceases to be exercised by the temptations of the world as long as she persists in the advancement of spiritual virtues.

But when, having conquered the contest of labors, she reaches the palm of victory, she no longer remembers the preceding distress because of the joy of the reward received. “The sufferings of this present time are not worthy to be compared with the future glory” (Rom. VIII), when we shall be like God and “shall see him as he is” (1 John III), as the Apostle says in his Epistle.

Now the Church gives birth with groaning (Rom. VIII); then she will give birth with rejoicing. And for that reason the child is male, because all the duties of action are directed toward the fruit of contemplation.

Just as a woman rejoices when a human being has been born into this world, so the Church is filled with exultation when a people has been born into future life. For this birth she labors greatly and groans in the present, suffering as though in childbirth.

No one should find it strange if someone who has departed from this life is called “born.” Just as someone is said to be born when he emerges from his mother’s womb, so one may also be called born when, released from the bonds of the flesh, he is raised into eternal light.

Hence ecclesiastical custom has prevailed whereby we call the days of Christ’s martyrs and confessors, on which they passed from this world, their “birthdays,” and their solemn celebrations not funerals but birthdays.

It follows:

[Col. 0947A] “You indeed have sorrow.” The whole Church, through the labors and anxieties of this life, strives toward the eternal rewards of heavenly joys, because, as the Apostle says, “through many tribulations we must enter the kingdom of God” (Acts XIV).

When the Lord says again, “I will see you,” he promises a second coming, in which he will see the whole Church in order to reward her completely. And because in the fullness of that joy we will not ask in the present manner, we should pray that we may reach it.

## SERMON ON THE VISION OF GOD

If you ask whether God can be seen, I answer: He can. If you ask how I know, I answer: Because it is written in the most truthful Scripture: “Blessed are the pure in heart, for they shall see God” (Matt. V), and other such passages.

If you ask how he can be called invisible if he can be seen, I answer that he is invisible by nature. Yet he is seen whenever and however he wills. For many have seen him not as he is, but in whatever form he was pleased to appear to them.

What, then, is meant by the same authority’s statement: “No one has ever seen God” (John IV)? And, explaining this more fully and plainly: “No one,” it says, “has ever seen God, nor can see him” (1 John IV).

How, then, did Abraham, Isaac, Jacob, Job, Moses, Micah, Isaiah, and all the others see God, concerning whom the most truthful Scripture testifies that no human being has ever seen God and cannot see him?

This is a great question: how is it not contradictory that so many of the ancients saw God if no one has ever seen God, because no human being has seen him or can see him?

Ambrose says that it certainly cannot be denied that the Father, or the Son, or indeed the Holy Spirit—if there is a vision of the Holy Spirit—may be seen [the printed text may instead mean “may appear”] in whatever form the will has chosen, not one fashioned by nature.

For we also understand the Spirit to have been seen in the form of a dove. Thus no one has ever seen God because no one has looked upon or comprehended with mind or eyes that fullness of divinity which dwells in God.

Hence Moses said to God, with whom he spoke face to face as a friend with a friend: “If I have found favor before you, show me yourself” (Exod. XXXIV).

What, then? Was he not himself? If he were not himself, Moses would not have said to him, “Show me yourself,” but “Show me God.” And yet, if Moses were looking upon his nature and substance, he would much less have said, “Show me yourself.”

He was therefore present in the form in which he had wished to appear. But he was not appearing in his proper nature, which Moses desired to see. That nature is promised to the saints in the other life.

Hence what was answered to Moses is true: “No one can see the face of God and live” (Exod. XXXIII)—that is, no one living in this present life can see him as he is. For many saw him, but they saw what the will chose, not what nature fashioned.

If you ask how the wicked Cain saw him when he was questioned and judged by him concerning his crime, or how the devil himself saw him when he came with the angels to stand before him, or how the “pure in heart” see God, I answer that it does not follow that those who sometimes hear voices produced by God also see God.

For they did not see him when he said to the Son: “I have glorified, and I will glorify again” (John XII).

Nevertheless, it should not be surprising if at times even the impure in heart see God in a form produced by his will, while his invisible nature remains hidden and unchangeable in itself.

If you ask whether he can at some time be seen as he is, I answer that this was promised to the sons, concerning whom it was said: “We know that when he appears, we shall be like him, because we shall see him as he is” (1 John III).

The question is not how God is seen—not in the form in which he wished to appear to certain people in this world—but how he is seen in that kingdom where his sons will see him as he is. Then their desire will be satisfied with good things.

The unworthy will not see God, concerning whom it was said: “Let the impious be taken away, so that he may not see the glory of God.” To them it will also be said: “Go into the eternal fire that has been prepared for the devil and his angels” (Matt. XXV).

God promised that he would show himself to those who love him as one God with the Father—not as he was seen in this world in bodily form by the good and the wicked.

For in the future judgment he will come in the same manner as he was seen going into heaven, that is, in the same form of the Son of Man. They will see that same form to whom he will say: “I was hungry, and you did not give me food” (ibid.), and the Jews will see the one whom they pierced (Rev. I).

They will not see that form of God in which he did not regard equality with God as something to be seized (Phil. II). On that day those will see God who see him as he is.

They will not see him for the reason that in this life they were poor in spirit, or meek, or mourning, and so forth, but because they are pure in heart.

He is seen by the pure in heart who is seen neither in a place nor with bodily eyes, neither represented by sight nor grasped by touch, neither heard through speech nor perceived by movement.

## THIRD SUNDAY  
### According to John

[Col. 0947]

[Col. 0947D] “I am going to him who sent me, and none of you asks me, ‘Where are you going?’” (John XVI.) He signifies that he will go so openly that there would be no need to ask where he was going. They will see him ascending in a cloud, certain of his glory—those who, before the predicted passion, had asked: “Lord, where are you going?”

[Col. 0949A] “But because I have said these things to you, sorrow has filled your heart.” Human affection was saddened because carnal affection—or carnal sight—was being left desolate.

“But I tell you the truth: it is to your advantage that I go away. For if I do not go away, the Paraclete will not come to you; but if I go, I will send him to you.”

If I do not withdraw the tender foods with which I have nourished you, you will not hunger for solid food. If you remain carnally attached to what is carnal, you will not be capable of the Spirit.

The meaning is: You cannot fully receive the Spirit as long as I am bodily with you. Hence the one who had received the Spirit says: “Even if we once knew Christ according to the flesh, now we no longer know him in that way” (2 Cor. V).

“And when he comes, he will convict the world concerning sin, righteousness, and judgment.”

(AUGUSTINE.) This means that, once fear has been driven away, he will give you the freedom to convict. The works of the Trinity are inseparable, but the persons are mentioned individually, so that both unity and Trinity may be understood without confusion.

“Concerning sin, because they do not believe in me; concerning righteousness, because I am going to the Father, and you will no longer see me.”

If a righteous person is at some time convicted of sin, he is convicted not concerning righteousness. Hence it is written: “There is no righteous person on earth who does good and never sins” (Eccl. VII). Likewise: “Do not become excessively righteous” (ibid.).

The righteousness of the wise is not signified here, but the pride of one who presumes. For whoever makes himself excessively righteous becomes unjust through that very excess.

A person makes himself excessively righteous when he says that he has no sin, or when he thinks that he becomes righteous not by God’s grace but by his own will.

The world is therefore convicted concerning sin because it does not believe in Christ; it is convicted concerning the righteousness of certain believers, for the comparison of the faithful is a reproach to the unfaithful.

The meaning is: Your righteousness, by which the world is convicted, will be that I am going to the Father and you will no longer see me, because you will believe in the one whom you will not see.

When you see me, you will see me not humble as I am now, but exalted; not mortal, but eternal; not judged, but judging. By this faith of yours the Holy Spirit will likewise convict unbelievers concerning righteousness.

The same point is made in the second book *On the Baptism of Infants*. What is this righteousness by which, when they did not see him, the world was convicted, except the righteousness by which the righteous person lives from faith, and by which we, not looking at the things that are seen but at those that are unseen, await the hope of righteousness?

“But concerning judgment, because the ruler of this world has already been judged.”

The ruler of the world is the devil, concerning whom he says elsewhere: “The ruler of this world is coming, and he has nothing in me” (John XIV).

“World” is understood both in a good and in a bad sense. For just as a tree is full of leaves and fruits, and a threshing floor of chaff and grain, so the world is full of faithful and unfaithful people.

The devil has been judged—that is, he has been destined for the judgment of eternal fire. The world is convicted concerning judgment when it is judged together with its ruler.

Let people therefore believe, so that they may not be convicted. Let them pass into the number of the faithful, so that they may not be convicted concerning the righteousness of those whom, though justified, they do not imitate. Let them beware the future judgment, so that they may not be judged with the ruler of the world.

It is clear that when the Son of God was in the world he convicted the world—that is, the followers of the world—concerning the sin of their unbelief, concerning righteousness because they were unwilling to imitate him, and concerning judgment because they followed the devil, who had already been judged and condemned.

But it is not without reason that he says the Spirit will do the same when he comes. For through the Spirit’s inspiration the minds of the disciples were to be strengthened, so that they would not fear to convict the world, which was raging against them.

The devil was judged by the Lord when the Lord himself cast out demons and gave the disciples power to trample upon every power of the enemy.

“I still have many things to say to you, but you cannot bear them now.”

This is not contrary to what he said above: “I have made known to you everything I have heard from my Father” (John XV). It is similar to the prophetic statement: “He who made the things that are to come.”

“When the Spirit of truth comes, he will teach you all truth.”

Some manuscripts read: “He will lead you into all truth.” Hence the words: “Lead me, Lord, in your way, and I shall walk in your truth” (Ps. LXXXV).

I do not think that this truth can be completed in the present life. Hence the Apostle says: “Now I know in part, but then I shall know fully, even as I have been fully known” (1 Cor. XIII). For what human being has an understanding of the Trinity like the angels?

It is asked whether spiritual people possess something in their teaching that they conceal from the carnal and tell only to the spiritual. If we say no, Paul’s statement to the Corinthians is obstructed: “I could not speak to you as spiritual people, but as carnal” (1 Cor. III).

If we say that they do possess such things, there is a danger that under this pretext they may teach wicked things in secret.

Once this has been understood in advance—that spiritual and carnal people each grasp the things they hear together according to their capacity, the former as solid food and the latter as nourishment of milk—the necessity is understood as follows: some secrets of doctrine are to be withheld from the faithful who are children and spoken separately to the more intelligent.

For what the Apostle says should be understood in this way: “You could not grasp what I was saying as spiritual people, but as carnal.” Hence he says to the Hebrews: “You have come to need milk, not solid food” (Heb. V).

It follows that spiritual people should not conceal these things entirely from the carnal, because of the Catholic faith, which must be preached to everyone. Yet they should not desire this in such a way that, wishing to bring it to understanding, they turn their speech into weariness for those capable of receiving it.

Christ himself, as a human being, is called the pure milk of children. When he is rightly understood by spiritual people, he is found to be solid food and the Lord of angels.

Therefore children must not be given milk in such a way that they never understand God, nor should they be weaned in such a way that they abandon the human Christ.

“ For he will not speak from himself, but whatever he hears he will speak.” The Son and the Holy Spirit are equal to the Father. But what difference there is between proceeding and being born would take a long time to discuss and would be rash to define, since, whatever the mind may grasp concerning it [Col. 0951A], it is nevertheless exceedingly difficult for the tongue to explain—no matter how great the teacher or how attentive the hearer. The meaning is: “He will not speak from himself,” because he is not from himself. Therefore he will hear from the one from whom he proceeds. For him, hearing means knowing; and knowing means being. Let no one be troubled because the verb is placed in the future tense, since, in what is eternal, a verb of any tense may be used without falsehood. For although that nature is immutable, and in reality it neither was nor will be, but only is—hence the words, “I am who I am, and he who is has sent me to you” (Exod. III)—nevertheless, because of the mutability of time in which our own mutability exists, we truthfully say that it was, is, and will be.

“And he will announce to you the things that are to come” [Col. 0951B]. Many possessed the spirit of prophecy; but since some heal the sick, raise the dead, and command demons, yet do not know future things, this may be understood in the following way: when the Spirit comes, he announces what is to come by recalling heavenly joys to memory.

“He will glorify me, because he will receive from what is mine, and will announce it to you.” It is as though he said: God will do all these things through the Spirit, that is, through his goodness. He will glorify me by taking away your fear and giving you a more ardent love. What they themselves were going to do in the Holy Spirit, he said that this same Spirit would do, as in the words: “For it is not you who speak, but the Spirit of your Father who speaks in you” (Matt. X) [Col. 0951C].

The Greek word *doxasse* (δοξάσει), the Latin translators have rendered, one of them, as “he will glorify.” For *doxa*, from which *doxasse* is derived, is interpreted both as “brightness” and as “glory.” And because glory makes people bright and brightness makes them glorious, what is signified by both words is the same.

Glory is frequent report concerning someone, accompanied by praise. Such glory did not confer anything great upon Christ himself, but upon the world. For a good person’s being praised benefits not the one praised, but those who praise. False glory is threefold: in things, in people, and in both. In things, a person is deceived when he believes that what is evil is true. The same applies to people. It is in both when a vice is thought to be a virtue and the person praised on that account does not possess what is attributed to him, whether he is good or evil. To give one’s possessions to actors is a monstrous vice, not a virtue. And you know how frequent praise of such people is, as in the words: “The sinner is praised in the desires of his soul” (Ps. IX). Those who praise such people are not deceived about the people, but about the things: what they believe to be good is evil. The vicious themselves are just as they are seen to be.

Those who praise hypocrites are not deceived about things, but about people. Those, however, who praise men believed to free their country by magical arts are deceived in both respects.

True glory does not make the just person blessed; nevertheless, there is glory because they love what is just. True glory is in the Catholic Church. Hence the Prophet says: “Be exalted above the heavens, and your glory above all the earth” (Ps. LVI).

“From what is mine,” says the Son, the Spirit has received, because the Holy Spirit has received from the Father what the Son received from him [Col. 0952A]. The Holy Spirit received from the Father by proceeding; the Son, by being born. The Father was born from no one and proceeded from no one.

And just as the Father begot the Son—life, namely, from life—so he gave him life to proceed from him, just as he himself proceeds from him. Truth is born from the Father; love proceeds from both for the sanctification of creation. Wisdom is born from the Father; benevolence proceeds from both toward creation. Counsel is born from the Father; the benefit of love proceeds from both toward creation. The Word is born from the Father; the gift of goodness comes forth from both. From the Father shone eternal splendor; from both proceeded the affection of good will.

Although, therefore, the whole Trinity is Spirit, that is, incorporeal nature, the Holy Spirit is called Spirit in a special sense, as the breath or breathing of the Father and the Son. For the Holy Spirit is breathed forth by the Father and the Son for sanctification; nor does he come without the Father and the Son, because the Trinity is undivided. The Spirit proceeds eternally from the Father and the Son for the distribution of gifts; he proceeds, is breathed forth, and is sent in time through the infusion of graces. This inspiration, this temporal procession, or mission, occurs daily, as different gifts are bestowed upon different people each day.

“All things whatsoever the Father has are mine.” The meaning is: The very being of the Father is in me, and I am from him; thus the Father is the Father of the Son, and the Son is the Son of the Father.

“Therefore I said that he will receive from what is mine, and will announce it to you” [Col. 0952C]. I said this because the Holy Spirit proceeds from the same one from whom I was begotten, so that he might not be thought inferior to me or born from me, as I am from the Father.

# SERMON ON THE THREE DAYS OF THE PASSION, RESURRECTION, AND ASCENSION

The distinguished psalmist David, commemorating the three days—namely, the Passion, the Resurrection, and the Ascension—says in the Psalms: “I have become like a pelican of the wilderness; I have become like a night-raven in a dwelling. I kept vigil, and I became like a solitary sparrow on the roof” (Ps. CI).

The pelican is an Egyptian bird that seeks deserted places, dwelling especially on the deserted banks of the river Nile. When this bird wishes to handle its young more tenderly, it kills them with its beak; afterward it mourns over them, and wounds itself so severely with its wings and beak that on the third day it pours out blood. As soon as the young are sprinkled with it, they come back to life.

This is not inappropriate to our Lord Jesus Christ, who is the bird of the wilderness because he alone was born from a Virgin, conceived alone without sexual pleasure, and born without pain. He killed his young—that is, human beings made by him—with his just judgment, and mourned over them because he wished to become weak for their sake. After the Law, that is, in the time of grace, which is like the third day in relation to the time before the Law and under the Law, he poured out his blood on the cross and gave them life.

And just as Christ had become like the pelican of the wilderness, so also he had become like the night-raven dwelling in a habitation [Col. 0953A]. The night-raven is a bird that flies in darkness. A habitation, however, is a ruined building in which only the walls remain. Christ is compared to the night-raven when, after the cross, he is placed in the habitation of the tomb and is taught to dwell there for several hours.

Then, on the third day, he kept vigil and became like a solitary sparrow on the roof, because, after he had slept in the Passion and then risen from death, he became like a sparrow flying away—that is, ascending into heaven—where he sits as a solitary one on the roof, namely, in heaven, at the right hand of the Father.

These are the three days by which the soul is illuminated. The first day, however, is fear; the second is truth; the third is love. The day of fear is the day of power, which belongs to the Father; the day of truth is the day of wisdom, that is, of the Son; the day of love is the day of goodness, that is, the day of the Holy Spirit [Col. 0953B].

The day of the Father, the day of the Son, and the day of the Holy Spirit are one day in the brightness of divinity. But in the illumination of our mind the Father has, as it were, one day, the Son another, and the Holy Spirit another—not because it should in any way be believed that the Trinity, whose nature is inseparable, can be separated in its activity, but so that the distinction of the persons may be understood through the distinction of their works.

When, therefore, God’s power, considered in wonder, awakens our heart, it is the day of the Father. When God’s wisdom, perceived through recognition of the truth, illuminates our heart, it is the day of the Son [Col. 0953C]. When God’s goodness, attended to in love, inflames our heart, it is the day of the Holy Spirit.

Power terrifies, wisdom illuminates, and goodness gives joy. On the day of power we die through fear; on the day of wisdom we are buried through contemplation of the truth, away from the clamor of the world; on the day of goodness we rise again, made alive through love and desire for eternal goods.

Accordingly, on the day of power, Christ died on the sixth day; on the seventh day he lay in the tomb; on the eighth day he rose like a lion. It is said of this lion that he sleeps with his eyes open and erases his tracks with his tail, so that he cannot be found by hunters. Thus the Lord Jesus, the lion from the tribe of Judah, slept and underwent the sleep of death in his humanity, but kept vigil in his divinity. He concealed the mystery of our restoration in the flesh in such a way that it could not be tracked by demons during the persecutions [Col. 0953D].

It is also said that a lioness gives birth to her cubs dead, and that on the third day they rise at the sound of their roaring father. Thus Christ, who lay dead in the tomb for three days, rose on the third day. He was awakened by the voice of the Father, as the distinguished patriarch Jacob once foretold concerning him: “Judah will sleep like a lion’s cub; who will awaken him? You have gone down to the prey, my son. He will wash his robe in wine, and his cloak in the blood of the grape” (Gen. XLIX).

The Lord from the tribe of Judah slept like a lion’s cub when he lay hidden in the tomb for three days; the Father raised him on the third day [Col. 0954A]. He went down to the prey when, descending to the lower regions, he bound the strong one and plundered his spoils. He washed his robe in wine when his body was drenched in blood. He washed his cloak in the blood of the grape when he sanctified the Church with the oil of chrism.

There is also another beast called the crocodile, twenty feet in length. At times it remains in the water, but at night it stays on land; it attacks passers-by, tears them apart, and devours them; in the open sun it lies sleeping with its mouth open.

Who, then, is signified by the crocodile except the devil, who, before Christ’s coming, moved among the hearts of the Gentiles, but now dwells in the arid minds of the Jews? It devours passers-by because before Christ’s Passion it was dragging all who died to Tartarus [Col. 0954B]. Yet even now, with its mouth open, it longs to swallow the streams of the Jordan, because in its greed it hastens to devour even those who have been baptized.

There is also another beast, called the *enidrus*, covered with spines like a hedgehog. Wrapping itself in mud, it enters the open mouth of the crocodile and is immediately swallowed by it. It pierces all its entrails with its spines, and, after the beast has been killed, it returns alive.

The spiny little animal is Christ’s flesh, afflicted by our miseries. It wraps itself in mud when it submits to the reproaches of death. It enters the beast’s mouth when it is swallowed by the insatiable underworld. But it tears out the beast’s entrails and emerges victorious, because Christ despoils hell and, rising from death with the others, returns victorious to the stars.

And just as the dead Lazarus rose, many bodies also rose in order to display the Lord rising; then the tombs were opened. But they did not rise before the Lord rose, so that he might be the firstborn from the dead. “They entered the holy city” (Matt. XXVII). By “the holy city” he meant either the heavenly Jerusalem, in which they were seen, or the earthly city, which had previously been holy because of the temple and the Holy of Holies, and in distinction from the other cities in which idols were worshiped. They appeared to many, namely, to those who were deemed worthy to see them.

(REMIGIUS.) These are believed to have ascended with the Lord when he ascended, only together with their bodies.

Therefore, as was said above, just as Christ died on the sixth day, the day of power, lay in the tomb on the seventh day, and rose on the eighth day [Col. 0954D], so likewise, first, let power on its day kill us outwardly through fear of carnal desires; then let wisdom on its day bury us inwardly in the hidden place of contemplation; finally, let goodness on its day cause us, made alive through desire for divine love, to rise up. For the sixth day belongs to labor, the seventh to rest, and the eighth to resurrection. May our Lord Jesus Christ mercifully grant this to us—he who died for us, yet lives and reigns as God forever, and so forth.

# FOURTH SUNDAY. According to John

[Col. 0955]

“Amen, amen, I say to you: If you ask the Father for anything in my name, he will give it to you” (John XVI). Whatever is asked against salvation is not asked in the name of the Savior. When he says “in my name,” he does not wish this to be understood as referring to the gift, but to the meaning of the sound. Thus the person who thinks wrongly about Christ does not ask in his name, even if he utters his name; but whoever, thinking rightly about him, asks for eternal salvation or for something pertaining to it, receives it, because he ought to receive it. Nor are certain things denied to him; they are merely postponed so that they may be given at the appropriate time.”

“Until now you have asked nothing in my name. Ask, and you will receive, so that your joy may be full.” Whatever else is asked for apart from the blessed life, or from what pertains to it, is nothing in comparison with so great a thing [Col. 0955B]. The words “Until now you have asked nothing in my name” may be understood in two ways: either because you have not known my name as it ought to be known, or because whatever else you have asked must be counted as nothing in comparison with so great a thing, which you ought to have asked for.

He then explains how they can ask for complete joy: he will make spiritual beings of them from the animal beings that they are, so that, after rejecting bodily images, they may cling to the light with the purity of a sincere mind.

“I have spoken these things to you in proverbs.” The animal person thinks carnally, not spiritually, about whatever he hears concerning God’s nature. Therefore, what he hears concerning the incorporeal substance of God is proverbs to him—not because he regards them as proverbs, but because he thinks as those who hear proverbs and do not understand them [Col. 0955C]. The spiritual person, however, asks in his name because he understands that he is of the same substance as the Father. Spiritual people drive away vanity and fabrications like troublesome flies, and, through their inward vision, recognize the incorporeal—however imperfectly.

“The hour is coming when I will no longer speak to you in proverbs, but will announce the Father openly.” He clearly signifies the hour in which he was going to give them the grace of the Holy Spirit. We may also understand the hour he promises as referring to the future life, in which he will announce the Father openly to the elect, that is, he will show them the Father.

There the elect truly ask in his name when they intercede because of our weakness, so that we may reach the portion of their salvation. It is rightly said “on that day,” because there are no dark shadows of affliction there, but everlasting light.

The spirits of the elect in that heavenly city may also ask on their own behalf, because they desire the time of the universal judgment to come, so that they may also receive the blessedness of their bodies. Hence John says: “I saw beneath the altar of God the souls of those who had been killed because of the word of God and because of the testimony that they held, and they cried out with a loud voice: ‘How long, Lord, holy and true, will you not judge and avenge our blood upon those who dwell on the earth?’” (Rev. VI) [Col. 0956A]. Immediately afterward it says: “And a white robe was given to each of them, and they were told to rest for a little while longer, until the number of their fellow servants and brothers should be completed” (ibid.).

The souls now have individual robes, since they enjoy their own blessedness alone; then they will receive two robes, when, after the number of their brothers has been completed at the end, they rejoice in receiving immortal bodies as well.

“On that day you will ask in my name. And I do not say to you that I will ask the Father on your behalf.” He says this because of the divinity consubstantial with the Father, in which the Father and the Son hear those who ask together and grant what is asked together—something visible only to spiritual eyes [Col. 0956B].

But when he says to Peter, “I have prayed for you, that your faith may not fail” (Luke XXII), and when John says of him, “We have an advocate with the Father, Jesus Christ” (I John II), this refers to his humanity.

Or it may be understood in this way: “I will not ask on your behalf,” because I will rather fulfill what I have hitherto asked. How did he ask? Because he had not yet ascended. For if he had not ascended, no certainty of ascending would have remained. But now, with his humanity seated at the right hand of the Father, it is both the certainty and the pledge that we too will ascend.

Hence Jerome, in his Epistle to the Romans: The Arians are accustomed to raise the objection that the one who is interceded with is greater than the one who intercedes. To them it must be replied that God does not suffer forgetfulness, so that he must continually be reminded on behalf of those whom he has chosen. Rather, he is said to intercede for them (Rom. VIII) in that he continually shows and offers to the Father the man whom he assumed, as our pledge, like a true and eternal high priest [Col. 0956C].

“For the Father himself loves you, because you have loved me and believed that I came forth from God.” The Father loves us because we love the Son, when, through the love given by the Spirit, we receive from the Father and the Son the ability to love the Father and the Son, just as he himself loves them with the Father and the Son. The one who loves first causes us to love.

“I came forth from the Father and came into the world; again I leave the world and go to the Father.” He came forth from the Father because he is from him; and, having assumed flesh, he came visibly into the world, yet without abandoning the Father. He left the world through bodily departure, not through the governance of his presence [Col. 0956D]. He goes to the Father because he brought his humanity to the invisible realities of the Father’s majesty. He left the world because he withdrew from the sight of those who love the world what they had seen. He returns to the Father because he taught his lovers to believe that he is equal to the Father.

“His disciples say to him: ‘Behold, now you are speaking openly, and you are saying no proverb. Now we know that you know all things, and you do not need anyone to question you. By this we believe that you came forth from God.’” They thought that he was speaking openly because they could not grasp his mysteries. They plainly show that the Lord was speaking about things they were pleased to hear and wished to ask about. Hence they believed him to be God [Col. 0957A]. For knowing the secrets of our thoughts is a clear sign of divinity.

# On the order of the resurrection, and how and what sort of bodies rise

The prophet Isaiah says: “The dead will rise, and those who were in the tombs will rise” (Isa. XXVI). Hence the Apostle says: “The Lord himself will descend from heaven with a command, with the voice of an archangel, and with the trumpet of God; and the dead who are in Christ will rise first. Then we who are alive, who remain, will be caught up together with them in the clouds to meet Christ in the air, and so we will always be with the Lord” (II Thess. IV).

These apostolic words most clearly show that the resurrection of the dead will take place when Christ comes to judge the living and the dead. But it is often asked whether those whom Christ will find alive at his coming—their persons and those who were then living with him being represented by the Apostle—will never die at all, or whether, at the very moment when they are caught up in the clouds with those who rise to meet Christ in the air, they will pass from mortal bodies to immortality through death with marvelous speed.

If, therefore, we believe that the saints who will be found alive when Christ comes and who will be caught up to meet him will, in that same rapture, depart from their mortal bodies and immediately return to the same bodies made immortal, we will find no difficulty in the Apostle’s words [Col. 0957C], whether where he says, “What you sow will not be made alive unless it first dies” (I Cor. XV), or where he says, “We will all rise, or we will all sleep” (ibid.). For they too will not be made alive through immortality unless, however briefly, they first die. Accordingly, they will not be excluded from the resurrection, since a very brief—though not nonexistent—sleep precedes it.

How, however, the statement “God will judge the living and the dead” is to be understood must be considered. The words “he will judge the living and the dead” are understood in two ways: either by “living” we understand those whom his coming will find here not yet dead, but still living in this flesh, and by “dead” those who have departed from the body before he comes or will depart; or we understand “living” as the righteous and “dead” as the unrighteous, in the sense that the righteous will judge and the unrighteous will be judged [Col. 0957D].

Some despair that the resurrection of bodies can take place, considering that the spirit is separated from the flesh, the flesh decays, decay is reduced to dust, and dust is dissolved among the elements, so that it is no longer visible to human eyes. When they look upon dry bones, they doubt that these can again be clothed with flesh and become green with life. Yet those who do not hold the faith in the resurrection through obedience ought certainly to have held it through reason.

For what does the world imitate daily in the elements except our resurrection? At every moment temporal light itself seems to die, when the darkness of night comes upon it and removes what had been visible; and it seems to rise again each day when the light that had been taken away and suppressed from the eyes is restored during the night [Col. 0958A].

We also see, through the succession of time, shrubs lose the greenness of their leaves and cease to produce fruit. And behold, when the wood suddenly seems to dry up, as though resurrection were approaching, we see leaves burst forth, fruits swell, and the entire tree be clothed anew in revived beauty.

But behold, I hear of resurrection; nevertheless I seek the effect of that resurrection. I believe that I will rise again, but I wish to hear how. For I need to know whether I shall rise in some other subtle or perhaps airy body, or in the body in which I remain. But if I rise in an airy body, I will no longer be the one who rises. For how is there a true resurrection if the flesh cannot truly be flesh? Plain reason therefore suggests that, if it is not true flesh, the resurrection certainly will not be true. Nor can it rightly be called resurrection when what has fallen does not rise.

Hence our Redeemer, when the disciples doubted his resurrection, showed them his hands and his side. He offered bones and flesh to be touched, saying: “Touch and see, because a spirit does not have flesh and bones, as you see me have” (Luke XXII).

Now, concerning the resurrection of the flesh—not like that of certain people who came back to life and then died again, but into eternal life, like the resurrection of Christ himself—I do not find that I can discuss how it is possible or satisfy all the questions that are usually raised about it [Col. 0958C]. Nevertheless, no Christian ought in any way to doubt that the flesh of all who have been born, are being born, or have died and will die, will rise again.

The first question that arises concerns aborted fetuses. They have already been born in the wombs of their mothers, but not yet born in such a way that they can already be born again. If we say that those who have already been formed will rise again, either position that is stated can be tolerated. But who would not more readily suppose that unformed abortions perish, like seeds that have not been conceived? Yet who would dare deny—or, if he does not dare affirm, how could he deny—that the resurrection will bring about the completion of whatever form was lacking, so that there will be a perfection that would have come with time? In this way, what has come with time will not be corrupted, and nature will neither be deprived of what suitable and appropriate days would have brought nor disfigured by what adverse and contrary days would have brought. Rather, what was not yet complete will be completed, just as what had not yet been corrupted will be restored.

The question of aborted fetuses and monsters—whether they rise again and what sort of resurrection they have—is regularly examined with the greatest care among the most learned, and can be debated. Whether this can be discovered by human beings I do not know: when does a human being begin to live in the womb? Is there some hidden life that does not yet manifest itself through the movements of a living being? For it seems exceedingly shameless to deny that the offspring lived when they are cut apart limb by limb and expelled from the wombs of pregnant women, lest, if they remain there after their death, they also kill the mother [Col. 0959A].

From the moment a human being begins to live, he can certainly already die. But once dead, wherever death could have occurred to him, I cannot see how he would not belong to the resurrection of the dead.

Nor should monsters that are born and live, however quickly they may die, either be denied resurrection or be believed to rise in a mutilated condition; rather, they will rise with their nature corrected and restored. Far be it from us to think that the two-membered person who was recently born in the East, concerning whom, beloved brothers, those who saw him gave an account and the blessed presbyter Jerome left a written record, should rise as one double human being rather than as two human beings—the state that would have occurred if twins had been born!

Likewise, the other cases in which individual births are called monsters because they possess something more or less than they should, through some excessive deformity, will by the resurrection be restored to the shape of human nature, so that each soul receives its own body, with no parts joined together—even whatever parts had been born joined together—but with each person separately carrying his own limbs, by which the integrity of the human body will be completed.

Earthly matter, from which the flesh of mortals is created, does not perish for God. However it may be dissolved into dust or ash, scattered into whatever breezes and airs, changed into any other substance, or turned into the elements themselves; however it may become food for any animals or human beings and be transformed into flesh, it returns in an instant to the soul that first animated it, so that a human being might be made and grow [Col. 0959B].

# On the manner of the resurrection

The restorer of all the limbs, as Augustine says in *The City of God*, promises that they will be restored in an instant and return in greatness, not only from the earth but also from the innermost recesses of the other elements, into which the scattered corpses have withdrawn (the text reads *promittitur*).

That earthly matter itself which, when the soul departs, becomes a corpse will not be restored in the resurrection in such a way that whatever has dispersed and been changed into the various species and forms of other things must return to the very bodily parts in which it was previously located, even though it returns to the body from which it dispersed.

Otherwise, if what repeated hair-cutting removed must return as hair, and what repeated clipping removed must return as fingernails, an excessive and indecent deformity would arise for those who consider the matter—and for that reason do not believe in the resurrection of the flesh [Col. 0959D].

But if a statue made of any malleable metal were melted in fire, crushed into dust, or mixed into a mass, and an artisan wished to restore it from the quantity of that material, it would make no difference to its integrity which particle of the material was returned to which limb of the statue, provided that the whole substance from which it had been formed were restored.

So God, the marvelous and ineffable artisan, will restore our flesh from the whole substance of which it had consisted, with marvelous and ineffable speed. It will not affect the integrity of the thing whether hairs return as hairs, or fingernails as fingernails, or whether whatever of them had perished is changed into flesh and restored to other parts of the body [Col. 0960A]. The providence of the artisan will ensure that nothing indecent occurs.

Nor does it follow that the individual resurrected will have different stature because the living had different stature, or that the thin will rise with the same thinness, or the fat with the same fatness. But if it is part of the Creator’s plan that each person’s individual character and recognizable likeness be preserved in his form, while all the other bodily goods are restored equally to everyone, the material will be proportioned in each person in such a way that nothing of it perishes and that he himself supplies whatever anyone lacked—he who was able to create whatever he wished from nothing.

If, however, there will be a rational inequality in the bodies of those who rise, it will be like the voices through which a song is completed. What is done with the material of the body will make the human being fit for the company of angels and introduce nothing unsuitable to their perceptions [Col. 0960B]. Nothing indecorous will be there; whatever will be, will be fitting, because it would not be destined to be if it were not fitting.

An example of the foregoing: if a human artisan can make a statue that he had made deformed for some reason stand and restore it to great beauty, so that none of its substance perishes but only its deformity, and if something in its former shape projected improperly, lacked the value appropriate to symmetry, and could not be cut away or separated from the whole from which he had made it, but had to be scattered and mixed throughout the whole in such a way that it neither produced ugliness nor diminished the quantity—what should we think of the Omnipotent?

Augustine likewise, in *The City of God*: That infants will not rise in the same stature in which they died. What, then, shall we say about infants, except that they will rise in the smallness of body in which they died, but what would have come to them later through time they will receive on that day through the marvelous and exceedingly swift work of God [Col. 0960C]?

For where the Lord says, “Not a hair of your head will perish” (Luke XXI), this means that what existed will not be lacking; it does not deny that what was lacking will be added. What was lacking in a dead infant was the full size of his body. For perfection is lacking to an infant—namely, the perfection of bodily magnitude—which, once it has been added, cannot become greater in stature.

All possess this measure of perfection, in that they are conceived and born with it; but they possess it in principle, not in bulk. Thus all the limbs are already present secretly in the seed, even though after birth some things are still lacking, such as teeth or anything of that kind [Col. 0960D]. Within the principle implanted in each body’s material, what is not yet present—or rather, what is hidden—already seems, so to speak, to have been shaped; with the passage of time it will come, or rather it will appear.

Accordingly, in this principle the infant is already short or tall, according to whether he will become tall or short. It follows that each person will receive the measure he had in youth, even if he died an old man, or the measure he would have had if he had died earlier, if he died before reaching it. Thus the bodies of the dead will rise neither beyond nor below the form of youth, but in the age and strength to which we know Christ himself attained.

The most learned men of this world have defined youth as extending to approximately thirty years. Once that period has ended, a person no longer advances toward the decline of more burdensome and old age. For this reason the Apostle is said not to have spoken of the measure of the body or the measure of stature, but “the measure of the fullness of the age of Christ” (Eph. IV) [Col. 0961A].

The Apostle’s further statement, “predestined to be conformed to the image of the Son of God” (Rom. VIII), may be understood in this way: just as he became like us in mortality, so we will become like him in immortality. Thus, in these words, we are informed in what form bodies will rise. Just as that measure, so also this conformity is to be understood not in terms of size, but of age.

Therefore all will rise with bodies great in stature, such as they were or would have been in the age of youth. But if anyone insists that each person will rise in precisely the bodily condition in which he died, one should not engage in a laborious struggle of contradiction with him [Col. 0961B].

Augustine likewise, in the *Enchiridion*: Whether the bodies of the reprobate rise with their defects. Whoever is not freed through the one Mediator between God and human beings from that mass of perdition which came into being through the first human being will indeed rise, each with his own body, but in order to be punished with the devil and his angels.

Whether, moreover, they rise with the defects and deformities of their bodies—those who carried deformed and defective limbs in them—why labor to investigate? We should not be troubled by the uncertain condition or beauty of those whose damnation will be certain and eternal [Col. 0962A].

Nor should it trouble us how their body will be incorruptible if it can suffer pain, or how it will be corruptible if it cannot. For there is no true life except where life is lived in happiness, nor true salvation except where there is incorruption; salvation is not corrupted by any pain. But where the unhappy person is not permitted to die, and, so to speak, death itself does not die, and where perpetual pain does not destroy but afflicts, where corruption itself continues and does not end—this is called the second death in the holy Scriptures.

The first death, by which the soul is compelled to leave its body, and the second, by which the soul is not permitted to leave its punitive body, would not have happened to human beings if no one had sinned. The mildest punishment of all will certainly be that of those who, apart from the sin they inherited originally, added no further sin; and among the others who added sins, each person will have a damnation that is more tolerable in proportion to the lesser iniquity he had here.”

# AT THE ROGATION DAYS. According to Luke

[Col. 0961]

[Col. 0961C] “Which of you will have a friend and go to him at midnight and say to him, ‘Friend, lend me three loaves, because a friend of mine has come to me from the road, and I have nothing to set before him’? And the one inside replies, ‘Do not trouble me. The door is already shut, and my children are with me in bed. I cannot get up and give you anything.’ And if he persists in knocking, I tell you, even if he will not rise and give him anything because he is his friend, yet because of his persistence he will rise and give him as many as he needs (Luke 11).”

Some make a question there at the words, “I cannot get up and give you anything”; but the whole passage may also be read under a single verse in this way: Which man is “if one of you has a friend, etc., and if the one inside replies, ‘Do not trouble me,’ [Col. 0961D] etc., and if he persists in knocking, etc.,” except the Savior, who not only taught the form of prayer but also its persistence and repeated practice, even to the likeness of shamelessness? He used an example by contrast, as with that judge who neither feared God nor respected human beings, yet, overcome by weariness, avenged the widow (Luke 18).

A friend comes from the road—from the evils of this present life—not finding the truth by which he may become blessed. He comes to you, a Christian, and says, “Give me an explanation, and I will become a Christian.” He asks you about something you perhaps do not know, and you have nothing with which to refresh the hungry person; but when you wish to teach, you are compelled to learn. Where will you learn except in the Lord’s books? But perhaps what he asks you is obscurely set forth in the books, and you are not permitted to question Paul or Peter, because that household is already resting with its Lord. Midnight is profound ignorance.

For that reason the hungry friend who presses you is not to be abandoned; rather, you must knock at the very Lord with whom the household, having received its rest, abides.
