If he delays giving, he nevertheless wills to give; but he wishes you to desire more greatly what has been delayed, lest what is given quickly become cheap. When you have reached an understanding of the Trinity, you have three loaves with which to feed the wandering friend. Nothing is better than that God give you himself.

Or it may be understood in this way: The friend who comes from the road is our mind, which withdraws from us as often as it wanders outside after earthly desires. It returns, however, and longs to be refreshed by heavenly nourishment when, having returned to itself, it begins to meditate on things above and spiritual. Concerning this friend, the petitioner fittingly adds that he has nothing to set before him, because he has followed worldly things so far that he has neither nourishment from the divine word for himself nor any for another who asks him.

And because he cannot obtain instruction either from himself or from another except through God’s grace, he must earnestly implore from God, in the night of tribulation, three loaves—that is, an understanding of the Trinity by which the labors of the present life may be consoled. The friend’s door is the understanding of the divine word, which is closed to everyone who does not understand until it is opened to him. Hence the Apostle prays that it may be opened to him for proclaiming the mystery of Christ (Colossians 4).

“Do not trouble me.” It is as though God were saying: “If you wish to receive what you can, do not trouble me any longer. Do not, as you have done until now, [Col. 0963A] put me after worldly things. Return to me, and I will return to you. Ask as you ought, and I will give you more than you hope for.”

“I cannot get up”—that is, “I cannot help you through righteousness unless you ask through right faith.” God’s rising is his assistance. Although the Lord does not give to the one who asks by helping him immediately merely because he is his friend—that is, because he is his creature—he is nevertheless not to be understood as denying mercy, but as delaying it for a more welcome reception and to impress the necessity of asking upon him. Hence it follows: “Yet because of his persistence”—that is, because of the urgency of his petition—“he will help him and give him what he needs.” God wishes to be asked faithfully for what he has appointed to distribute to those who ask.

[Col. 0963B] “And I say to you: Ask, and it will be given to you; seek, and you will find; knock, and it will be opened to you.” It is as though someone were to say: “Why do you forbid us to give holy things to dogs when we still know nothing?” Therefore he urges those whom he had previously forbidden to ask for bodily things to ask for spiritual things.

Asking pertains to obtaining the health and strength of the soul, so that we may be able to fulfill what is commanded. Seeking pertains to finding the truth; knocking, to possessing it. To make these three things clear, let us suppose that someone cannot walk because his feet are diseased. First, therefore, he must be healed, and asking pertains to this. But what good is it to be able to walk if he does not know the way? He will not reach where he wishes to go; seeking pertains to this. If, however, he finds the place where he wishes to dwell closed, it will do him no good to have walked and arrived unless it is opened for him; knocking pertains to this.

“For whoever asks receives, and whoever seeks finds, and to whoever knocks it will be opened.” According to the parable of the petitioning friend, perseverance is necessary so that we may receive what we ask for in prayer with faith, find what we seek by living rightly in hope, and have opened for us that at which we knock in love. The reason it is apparent that something is not given to someone is that it is not asked for rightly.

Let us therefore ask and knock at the door of Christ, concerning which it is said: “This is the Lord’s gate; the righteous will enter through it” (Psalm 117). When we have entered, may the hidden treasures in Christ be opened to us, in whom all knowledge is found.

“Or which of you is the man who, if his son asks him for bread, will give him a stone? Or if he asks for a fish, will give him a serpent? Or if he asks for an egg, will give him a scorpion?” He provides confidence in asking and explains what should be asked for, moving from lesser things to greater, just as above with the birds of heaven and the lilies.

[Col. 0963D] “Therefore, if you, though evil, know how to give good gifts to your children, how much more will your Father who is in heaven give good things to those who ask him?” He calls evil those who love the world, whose gifts must be called good according to their own judgment. Or all the things God made are naturally good.

“If we, then, though evil, know how to give what is asked of us, how much more God.” He called the apostles evil, or he spoke of the human race under the person of the apostles, by comparison with divine clemency. What Luke says, “he will give the good Spirit,” in place of Matthew’s “he will give good things” (Matthew 7), shows that the Holy Spirit is the distributor of all spiritual goods.

(AUGUSTINE.) Mystically, bread is understood as love, because of its necessity to appetite: without it, all the other things are nothing, just as without bread the table is poor. Its opposite is hardness of heart, which he compared to a stone.

The fish is faith in invisible things. For just as a fish is born, lives, and is nourished beneath the covering of the waters, so faith in God is invisibly generated in the heart, consecrated by the invisible grace of the Spirit through the waters of baptism, nourished by the invisible aid of divine protection so that it may not fail, and works well with the invisible expectation of rewards. Since faith is also surrounded and buffeted by the waves of this world without being broken, it is rightly [Col. 0964B] compared to a fish. Its opposite is the serpent, on account of the poisons of unbelief, which it also sowed in the first human being through evil persuasion.

Hope is compared to an egg: it has not yet reached the thing itself, just as an egg is not yet a chick, but through incubation it is expected. Its opposite is the scorpion, whose poisoned sting is feared from behind, just as the opposite of hope is to look backward when hope is extended toward the good things ahead.

## SERMON FOR THE ROGATION DAYS

“The eyes of the Lord are upon the righteous, and his ears are attentive to their prayers” (Psalm 33). Those who turn away from evil avoid fornications, adulteries, perjuries, thefts, false testimonies, and similar things. Those who do good give to God what is his and to human beings what is theirs. These are the righteous: upon them the eyes of God’s mercy look, and his ears are attentive to their prayers, because before they call upon him he will say to them, “Here I am.”

“But the face of the Lord is against those who do evil” (ibid.). For what purpose? “To destroy their memory from the earth” (ibid.). Therefore let the righteous rejoice that God looks upon them and hears them, and let them advance toward better things. But those like me—that is, those stinking with crimes—should abandon their sins, flee to the protection of prayer, and know that they too will be heard.

Our prayers are hindered in three ways, so that they are not heard by God. Whoever prays that he may take vengeance on his enemies is not heard; rather, his prayer is turned into sin (Psalm 108). Whoever retains hatred in his heart and does not forgive the one who has sinned against him—God will not hear him when he prays. Whoever commits criminal sins and persists in them with delight pours out prayers in vain, because God does not hear sinners (John 9).

Hence it is said through the prophet: “God’s ears are not burdened so that he cannot hear, but your sins stand in the way, preventing him from hearing you.” Again, the same prophet says: “Because of our sins, Lord, you have placed a cloud before yourself, so that prayer may not pass through” (Lamentations 3).

Sin is heavy like lead, and therefore it drags a person into the depths of the abyss. For just as a wheel is sent down from a mountain and rolls through a precipice to the bottom of a valley, so the soul that willingly abandons God and plunges into iniquity will never remain at the bottom of its fall, but always slips farther into worse things. The sin which repentance does not quickly wash away immediately draws another after it by its own weight, and it falls from sin into sin until it reaches the depth of evils; from there it plunges into the pit of eternal death. Over its mouth a stone of condemnation is placed, and it is not promised release until it has paid the last quarter.

Therefore, beloved, ask God with devoted prayers “that the deep may not swallow you up, nor the pit close its mouth over you” (Psalm 68). “Flee the desires of the world and the flesh, which are the service of demons; seek the Lord, and your soul will live” (ibid.).

The prophet saw a woman sitting in a jar and floating upon the sea, weighed down by a mass of lead. And behold, two winged women lifted the jar with the woman and carried it to the land of Babylon (Zechariah 5). The turbulent sea is this world, stormy with adversities. The woman floating in the jar is our soul, which presides over the body and labors amid the dangers of the world. A mass of lead weighs her down, because grave iniquity burdens our soul.

The two women who lift the jar with the woman are two vices—namely, pride and lust—which soften our soul and body toward unlawful things. Pride raises the soul into exaltation; lust, on the other hand, sinks the flesh into impurity. As soon as the spirit is lifted up in pride, the flesh immediately sinks into lust.

They are described as winged because those who follow them become unstable. They carry the jar with the woman to the land of Babylon, which is called “confusion,” because they clothe those who consent to them in a double confusion: here, they are put to shame in the body before human beings, and in the future they are punished in the soul with eternal confusion, as it is said: “They will be clothed with double confusion, as with a cloak” (Psalm 108).

Therefore, beloved, curse pride and lust, delight yourselves in the Lord, and he will give you the desires of your heart (Psalm 36).

## DIVISION

Because you have gathered here today, you ought to listen attentively to the word of God. The Lord himself says: “A certain man went out to sow his seed. And while he was sowing, some fell beside the road and was trampled and devoured by birds; some sprang up upon rock and, when it had grown, withered because it had no moisture. Some fell among thorns and was choked by the thorns. Some fell on good soil and produced fruit, some thirtyfold, some sixtyfold, and some a hundredfold” (Matthew 13).

The one who sows the seed is the priest who preaches the word of God; the field in which the seed is scattered is your hearts, in which the word of God is cast. The seed cast along the road, trampled by passersby, and devoured by birds signifies those who receive the word of God but, occupied with worldly affairs and earthly desires, trample it, so to speak, and demons remove it from their memory; they produce no fruit of piety.

The seed falling upon rock and withering there signifies the hard-hearted, who, although they sometimes hear the word of God eagerly, nevertheless persist in wickedness. Since they have no moisture from heavenly grace, the word of God in them must wither. The seed that thorns choke signifies those whose riches, pleasures, and anxieties of life harden their ears against the word of God.

But what falls on good soil and bears fruit is the multitude of the faithful, who obeying the word of God labor in good works. Married people produce thirtyfold fruit when they perfect faith in the holy Trinity through the Decalogue of the Law. Those who practice continence produce sixtyfold when they strive to fulfill these things both in action and spiritually. Virgins produce a hundredfold when they strive perfectly to please God in body and spirit.

Beloved, you ought to hear briefly why it was decreed that crosses be carried on these days. It is reported that the earth dried up through drought, while human beings and animals wasted away through disease. Moreover, the ferocity of bears, wolves, and other beasts devastated very many people; their multitude entered cities and villages indiscriminately and tore apart even little children in their cradles.

At that time Mamertus was governing the Church of Vienne. He summoned the people and urged them to fast for three days, pray, and carry crosses, so that God’s mercy—which had freed the Ninevites from destruction through a three-day fast—might assist his people in their present affliction. When this had been done, the plague was calmed, and joy and abundance of goods were granted to those who had been afflicted. It is read that the day called the Major Litany was instituted for this reason.

The Tiber rose higher than usual and, entering Rome, occupied its largest districts. It destroyed churches and overturned many buildings together with their inhabitants. Through its channel an enormous dragon, with a great multitude of serpents, entered the sea; together with all of them, it was drowned there. Washed onto the shore, they corrupted the air with their rottenness and brought a severe pestilence upon the human race.

Arrows were seen coming from heaven; when they struck the groins of human beings, those struck died immediately. First Pope Pelagius died; then almost the entire Roman people were consumed by sudden death. Gregory was therefore raised up as bishop, and he urged the people to fast, carry crosses, and pray. When they performed these things devoutly, the plague ceased and the people rejoiced in God’s peace.

Hence it was established that the same day should be observed annually in the church with the celebration of fasts and litanies, so that God might protect us and our animals from pestilence. And because at this season it often happens through the harshness of the weather that the seeds which have been sown may perish, to the detriment of our use, it was decreed that these days should be observed according to the same rite, namely with fasts and litanies, so that the fruits of the whole year might be kept safe for us from every misfortune.

And so that the merciful Lord might give us confidence in obtaining what we ask, he urges us to devote ourselves to prayer. For he says: “If someone asks a friend for loaves at midnight, so that he may set them before his friend who has come from the road, and if he does not give them to him because of their friendship, he will nevertheless provide them because of the persistence of the one asking” (Luke 11).

This friend is God, who loved us and handed over his Only-Begotten for us. From him we ask for bread at midnight when, in tribulation, we seek his help. [Col. 0967A] And if he delays assisting us because of our sins, nevertheless, if we persevere, he grants us his mercy.

Without a doubt, let us recognize that we are heard if we ask with urgent prayer, seek with attentive mind, and knock with tears. For whoever asks his father for bread will in no way be given a stone. Whoever demands a fish from his father will certainly not receive a serpent. And if he asks for an egg, will he ever be given a scorpion?

By bread, which strengthens the human heart, love is signified, through which a person is strengthened in virtues. By the fish, which is nourished by the beating of the waves, faith is understood, which is brought to growth through the storms of persecution. By the egg, from which a chick is expected, hope is indicated, through which future blessedness is hoped for.

The stone signifies hardness of heart; the poisonous serpent, wickedness; and the scorpion, which strikes with its tail, the vengeance of sins. Whoever therefore asks God for love will never be hardened by him in evil; whoever asks faith from him will in no way be permitted to remain in wickedness. Whoever asks him for hope will by no means be subjected to punishment.

Bread may also signify the crops that now rise in the grass; the egg may signify the offspring of animals; and the fish may indicate whatever already exists by which each person is nourished. For these things your devotion ought to pour out prayers to the Lord, so that here he may protect us from hailstones as hard as stone, from the serpent of pestilence, and from the scorpion of storms.

## DIVISION

[Col. 0967C] Beloved, we have many examples showing how much the persistent prayer of a righteous person avails (James 5). When the people of five cities had provoked God’s anger against themselves through horrifying crimes, Abraham asked God to spare them if he found ten righteous people among them. The Lord said that if he found ten righteous people in those five kingdoms, he would forgive all the others among them and would not destroy the places.

But because only one righteous person was found, he alone was rescued. The Pentapolis, together with its people, was destroyed by fire and sulfur, while the wife of the righteous man, who accompanied him only bodily but remained in mind with the Sodomites, was changed into a pillar of salt (Genesis 19).

From this it is understood that the dwelling of the righteous is the support of the wicked in this life, since through their prayers the latter are spared longer by the divine hand, so that their wickedness may not suddenly be plunged into destruction as it deserves. But when the righteous are taken away, the wicked are immediately carried off to punishments. Thus Sodom perished after Lot had gone out from it.

When the people of God were led out of Egypt through Moses, they were attacked by enemies on the way with weapons. Moses, however, prayed on the mountain with his hands extended, and Israel overcame its enemies. But when Moses lowered his hands, Amalek prevailed (Exodus 17). From this it is clear that the people accomplished more through prayer than through weapons. By praying, Moses obtained the victory that the people could not gain by fighting.

Similarly, Samuel drove away enemies by prayers whom the army could not repel by weapons. In ancient times the people were turned away from the Law and the worship of God and converted to idolatry. When Elijah could not correct them by preaching, he closed heaven against them for three years and six months by prayer (James 5).

When rain was withheld from heaven, the thirsty earth languished, withered, and threatened its cultivators with the dangers of famine. Under the pressure of hunger, the people were compelled to return to the worship of the living and true God. When Elijah prayed, the earth was drenched with abundant rain, and when the people were converted, the abundance of goods was restored. Behold: through the prayer of one person, heaven is closed against the entire people, and through his prayer it is opened again.

At another time, because of human sins, fields dried up through drought, and the hearts of many wasted away in fear of famine. While these people were fasting and carrying crosses with litanies, one of the fathers came upon them and asked the cause of their affliction. When they replied that it was the drought, he said, “Why do you not pray?” They answered that they had labored greatly in prayer but had obtained little. He said, “If you asked attentively, you would certainly receive what you asked for.”

Standing before everyone, he extended his hands in prayer, and as soon as he spoke the first words of the prayer, rain fell, and the earth supplied the farmers with the fruit that had long been denied them.

There was also a certain monk who was constant in prayer. One of the demons was sent by the emperor Julian to obtain a certain response; but through the prayers of that man he was held in one place for twenty days and then returned to the emperor empty-handed.

When Julian asked the reason for the delay, he replied: “I both delayed and returned with the task unfinished. For when I had to pass by that monk, I was hindered by his prayers. While I waited, in case he might perhaps finish praying and allow me to pass, he did not finish his prayers. Since I could go no farther, I returned empty-handed.”

Julian threatened him with punishment, but not long afterward he was killed in war and entered eternal punishment. Consider, I beg you, beloved, how far this man’s prayer extended. Certainly, the devil can fly through the air, penetrate the earth, and even cross the sea. But this man’s prayer, stretching upward to heaven, prevented his passage through the air; extending downward to Tartarus, prevented him from passing through; reaching the boundaries of the world on either side, it allowed the fugitive spirit to pass by the renegade human being on neither side.

Indeed, this man sometimes refreshed his body with food and occasionally with sleep; but the entire attention of his heart continually rose so toward God that every action of his was prayer.

## DIVISION

Beloved, all the righteous from the beginning of the world who merited the kingdoms of blessed life obtained them by praying in this way. All the righteous are said to have devoted themselves to prayer, and therefore they now enjoy with complete joy what they prayed for.

Let us, then, frequently devote ourselves to prayer, so that we may be able to attain complete joy with them. Let us ask everything in the name of Jesus if we wish our prayers to be heard. We ask the Father in the name of Jesus when we ask only for things beneficial to the soul and necessary for the body.

When we pray, we ought to distrust our own merits and rely upon his mercy, because he said: “Truly I tell you, whatever you ask for in prayer, believe that you will receive it, and it will be done for you. If two of you agree about anything whatever that they ask, it will be done for them by my Father” (Matthew 18).

Therefore, be united in prayer; lift your hearts with your hands to God; pray for all the living and the dead, and for those who are in any affliction. If you pray for the whole Church, as for your mother, the whole Church prays for you, as for her children.

But if you pray for the dead, you free yourselves: if they are in joy, they pray that you may come to them more quickly; if they are in punishment, they ask that you may never come there.

Finally, whoever prays converses with the Lord, and therefore it is necessary that whoever asks faithfully should obtain what he asks. And since he himself says, “Where two or three are gathered in my name, there I am in the midst of them” (Matthew 18), how much more should he be believed to be present today among so great a multitude gathered in his name to ask the intercession of the saints?

Since, therefore, the giver of all good things is in the midst of you who are gathered in his name, invoke him with devout prayers; knock with tears and almsgiving, so that he may grant you everything necessary for body and soul and rescue you from your necessities.

Although there are many necessities, there are nevertheless five principal ones, and unless they are removed by remedies, people are endangered by death through them. A person eats out of necessity, because if he does not eat, he dies of hunger. He drinks out of necessity, because if he does not drink, he dies of thirst. He digests out of necessity, because if he does not do so, he dies of constipation. The body is refreshed by sleep out of necessity, because if it neglects sleep, it fails through weariness. A person is clothed out of necessity, because if he neglects clothing, he is destroyed by cold and heat.

For this reason all our labor is directed toward helping ourselves in these necessities. “Seek first,” he says, “the kingdom of God and his righteousness, and all these things will be added to you” (Matthew 6).

And do not be excessively anxious about earthly things or concerned about what is fleeting, because a human being will inherit worms, beasts, and serpents. Ask God, however, to rescue you from these necessities and transfer you to that place where you will not need them: where they will hunger no more and thirst no more; where souls rest from their labors; where they are free and see that he is God, in whose vision the angelic choirs are refreshed.

We have been taught to ask this from him: “Ask,” he says, “and you will receive, so that your joy may be complete” (John 16).

All the joy of this world is deceptive and full of sorrow. If someone rejoices in a beautiful wife, he becomes sad when death intervenes. If he delights in dear children, he is saddened when they are afflicted by illness or taken away by death. If he rejoices in property or money, he mourns when they are lost through some misfortune.

But that is the true and complete joy that all the faithful should desire with all their wishes: the joy in which they are established above all their goods in the joy of the Lord, perpetually delight in the brightness of eternal vision, possess the glory of all the angels, and receive the fellowship of all the saints. This joy will never be taken away from them throughout eternity.

For this reason a woman now has sorrow when she gives birth, but when she has given birth to the child, she no longer remembers her anguish because of the joy that a human being has been born into the world (John 16). This woman is the Church, which now labors in sorrow so that she may give birth to a faithful people for Christ. But when, after the resurrection, she has given birth to eternal life, she will no longer remember the anguish of this life, because of the unspeakable joy that will then be given in fullness to all her children: for then the righteous will shine like the sun and will be equal to the angels.

Beloved, when a cross is carried before us, we follow it. Let us likewise follow the example of Christ crucified, so that through the triumph of the victorious cross we may deserve to reach those joys that eye has not seen and ear has not heard (1 Corinthians 2).

## ON THE ASCENSION OF THE LORD. According to Mark.

[Col. 0969]

[Col. 0969D] “As the eleven disciples were reclining at table, Jesus appeared to them and reproached their unbelief and hardness of heart, because they had not believed those who had seen him after he had risen” (Mark 16).

The eleven disciples, as Matthew writes, went into Galilee, to the mountain where Jesus had appointed them. When they saw him, they worshiped him; but some doubted (Matthew 28). He appeared on a mountain to signify that the assumed body had already been raised above all earthly things.

But why did he specifically predict that he would go before them into Galilee and be seen there, when he was seen neither there alone nor there first? Because Galilee is said to mean “transmigration” or “revelation,” and both interpretations look toward one end. It signifies that just as Christ came from death to life, so his followers will transmigrate from death to life and, contemplating him in the manifestation of his divinity, will praise him without end.

The interpretation “revelation” is also fitting, by which we reveal our way to him in whatever manner and follow his footsteps; contemplating the glory of the Lord, we are transformed into the same image.

Some, however, doubted because Luke says: “But being troubled and terrified, they thought they were seeing a spirit” (Luke 24). Mark, however, says: “He reproached their unbelief and hardness of heart, because they had not believed those who had seen him after he had risen.”

He rebuked the disciples when he was about to leave them bodily, so that the words he spoke when returning might remain impressed more firmly in the hearts of those who heard them. He reproaches unbelief and hardness of heart so that belief may take its place and the heart of stone become a heart of flesh full of love.

Hence it is that companies of martyrs willingly desire the death of this world, because [Col. 0971A] they wish, through temporal destruction, to live forever: a most blessed transmigration from this world into eternity.

“And he said to them: Go into all the world and preach the Gospel to every creature.” “To every creature” is not said with reference to insensible or brute animals. Rather, by the name “every creature” the human being is signified, having existence with stones, life with trees, sensation with animals, understanding with angels, and consisting of hot and cold, moist and dry, because the human being is a lesser world.

Since, therefore, a human being possesses something of every creature, the Gospel is preached to every creature when it is preached to the human being, for whose sake all things were created and to whom all things are in some way similar.

Or by “every creature” the nations of the Gentiles may be designated. Earlier it had been said: “Do not go into the way of the Gentiles” (Matthew 10). When the Truth sends the disciples to preach, he scatters the grains of seed throughout the world and sends a few into the seedbed, so that from our faith he may receive the harvests of many fields. It follows:

“Whoever believes and is baptized will be saved; whoever does not believe will be condemned.” What shall we say here about little children, who because of their age are not yet able to believe? There is no question concerning adults. Therefore, in the Church, little children believe through others, just as through others they draw the sins that are forgiven them in baptism.

“And these signs will accompany those who believe: In my name they will cast out demons; they will speak in new tongues; they will pick up serpents; and if they drink anything deadly, it will not harm them. They will lay hands on the sick, and they will be well.”

Are we not believers because we do not perform these signs? These things were necessary at the beginning of the Church, so that the faith of believers might be nourished by miracles. When we plant shrubs, we pour water on them for as long as necessary, until they become strong in the earth. Hence Paul says: “Tongues are a sign not for believers but for unbelievers” (1 Corinthians 14).

Nevertheless, the holy Church performs spiritually every day what it then performed bodily through the apostles. Priests, by the grace of exorcism, lay hands on believers and cast out demons; and the faithful, abandoning worldly words, sound forth the praises of their Creator, which is to speak in new tongues.

When, moreover, through good exhortations they remove wickedness from the hearts of others, they pick up serpents. And when they hear deadly suggestions but are not drawn into evil action, they drink something deadly, but it does not harm them. When they strengthen the life of the sick in faith by the example of their own conduct, they lay hands on the sick. Therefore the greater the miracles are, the greater they are because through them not bodies but souls are raised up.

“And the Lord Jesus, after he had spoken to them, blessed them, and departed from them, and was taken up into heaven, and sat at the right hand of God.” Because our Redeemer now judges all things and will one day come as judge, Mark describes him as sitting; but Stephen saw him standing, and he had him as his helper (Acts 7). Sitting belongs to one who judges; standing belongs to one who fights or helps.

“But they went forth and preached everywhere, while God worked with them and confirmed the word through the signs that followed.” Obedience accompanies the command, and signs accompany obedience.

We read that Elijah was taken up into heaven (2 Kings 2), but one heaven is the aerial heaven and another is the ethereal heaven. The former is near the earth, because birds fly through it. Therefore Elijah was taken up into the aerial heaven, so that he might suddenly be brought to some hidden region of the earth, where he might live until the end of his life, then return from there and die. He did not escape death but postponed it.

Our Redeemer, however, did not postpone death but conquered it, and by ascending he revealed the glory of the resurrection. Elijah ascended in a chariot because he was a mere human being in need of assistance; for those aids were made and displayed through angels. Our Redeemer, however, is not read to have been lifted up by either a chariot or angels, but by his own power.

Enoch, too, being transferred to the aerial heaven, signified the Lord’s ascension, just as Joseph signified his being sold. The Lord therefore had witnesses of his ascension: one before the Law and another under the Law.

The order in both elevations is distinguished by certain stages of increase. Enoch is remembered as transferred, Elijah as carried upward, so that afterward the one would come who, neither transferred nor carried upward, would penetrate the ethereal heaven by his own power.

Consider, then, how the purity of holiness increased, as is clearly shown in the servants and in the Lord. Enoch was transferred; he was conceived through intercourse and fathered through intercourse, for he had a wife and children. Elijah was snatched up; he was conceived through intercourse but did not father children through intercourse, for he had neither wife nor children. The Lord was taken up, neither fathering through intercourse nor conceived through intercourse.

## SERMON ON THE ASCENSION OF THE LORD

Today, beloved brothers, is the joyful feast of the Lord’s Ascension. Today the captivity of the human race has been destroyed; today Christ’s second victory has been completed; today his triumphal banners are raised, and Tartarus, with its prince, grieves over its plunder. The heavenly army rejoices at the restoration of its loss.

Today that flesh which was raised from the earth has been placed at the Father’s right hand, because it has been set above every creature, and every principality and power has bowed before it.

Today, therefore, the new way of which the Apostle speaks (Hebrews 10) has been inaugurated, because through Christ’s flesh the entrance to heaven has been opened—a way through which no flesh had previously passed.

Today the opening of the book has also been accomplished, a book that no one could open except the Lamb who was slain (Revelation 5), when his mysteries were revealed together with the things concerning Christ that are found in the Law and the Prophets.

Today, too, the dispensation of his humanity has been completed and brought to fulfillment. The Almighty first descended so that he might become a participant in our nature; finally he ascended so that he might make us participants in his glory. He descended to exalt us; he ascended to make us ascend with him.

But it must be considered why he did not send the Holy Spirit to the apostles immediately after the Ascension, [Col. 0973A] but only after ten days (Acts 2). There were certainly three reasons: first, so that the apostles might prepare themselves by fasts and prayers to be fit for his coming; second, because those who fulfilled the Ten Commandments would receive the Holy Spirit; third, because, on the fiftieth day after the Resurrection, just as the people of God received the law of fear on the fiftieth day after their liberation from Egypt, so the people of the faithful, after their liberation from the world, would receive the law of love on the fiftieth day. In the jubilee also—that is, in the fiftieth year—the people recovered their lost freedom and inheritance; and on this day the Christian people recovered their lost freedom and the inheritance of paradise.

Christ therefore now possesses complete joy; in a certain sense he possesses it, and in a certain sense he does not. With respect to his own person, he possesses it most fully; with respect to his body, which is the Church, he does not yet possess it at all. For he is still blasphemed by the Jews, mocked by the nations, torn apart by heretics, attacked by wicked Christians, and despised by priests devoted to lust and therefore publicly anathematized. In his members also he suffers daily. When he has gathered all these things to himself, then he will possess complete joy.

But how is the Church his body, and the elect his members? Just as the body clings to the head and is governed by it, so the Church is joined to him through the sacrament of Christ’s body—indeed, it becomes one with him—and all the righteous, each in his own order, are governed by him as members by their head. The eyes of this head are the prophets, who foresaw future things; the holy [Col. 0973C] apostles, who led others from the way of error to the light of righteousness, are the ears. The obedient are its ears; the discerning are its nostrils. The phlegm expelled through the nostrils is the heretics, who are blown out from the head of Christ by the judgment of the discerning. The mouth is the holy teachers; the teeth are the interpreters of Sacred Scripture; the hands are the defenders of the Church; the feet are the husbandmen who feed the Church.

Moreover, the excrement expelled from the belly is the unclean and lustful ministers of the altar, and other criminals within the Church who burden the belly of Mother Church; through the expulsion of death, demons devour them like pigs. Therefore, since in the Lord’s Ascension we have been clothed with his bodily presence, let us hasten with our whole attention toward the vision of him eternally.

## DIVISION

[Col. 0973D] Foreseeing the Lord’s Ascension, the prophet Habakkuk says: “The sun was lifted up, and the moon stood in its order” (Hab. 5). For while the Lord remained in the world with his disciples, the apostles, trusting in the Lord’s presence, did not aspire to heavenly things. But after the Lord had withdrawn himself from their eyes and ascended into heaven—where the Lord had ascended—the soldiers longed to ascend, eagerly desiring it. For this is our custom: the household desires to follow the king who goes before it. Hence the Church says in the Song of Songs: “Draw me after you” (Song 1). She desired to be drawn after the ascending King once she had been deprived of the consolation of his presence.

Therefore the sun was lifted up—the sun that enlightens every person coming into this [Col. 0974A] world (John 1)—to heavenly things, because through his Ascension the moon stood in its order. The moon signifies the Church, because, just as the moon receives light from the sun, so the Church’s weakness is illumined by Christ; and just as the moon sometimes suffers an eclipse, so the Church suffers amid worldly affairs. But this moon, after Christ’s Ascension, stood in its order. It stood because it grew through preaching, because it burned with eagerness to endure tribulations. Then Peter, who had succumbed to the voice of a maidservant at the door, did not withdraw at the voice of Nero resisting him.

This Ascension is one of the Lord’s leaps of which Solomon speaks in the Song of Songs: “Behold, he will come leaping upon the mountains and bounding over the hills” (Song 2). He came leaping who, in coming for our redemption, made certain leaps from heaven: coming into the Virgin’s womb, from the womb to the manger, from the manger to the cross, from the cross to the tomb, and from the tomb returning to heaven. Hence the Prophet says: “He rejoiced like a giant,” and so forth (Ps. 18). Elsewhere he indicated this rejoicing: “He will drink from the torrent on the way” (Ps. 109). In the world there was a torrent of death flowing down from the sin of our first parent. He drank from it on the way because he tasted death in passing; and therefore he lifted up his head, because what he had placed in the tomb by dying, he raised above the angels by rising again.

After the Resurrection he raised human nature above the angels, although previously it had been lower than the angels. Hence it is written: “You made him a little lower than the angels” (Ps. 8). For as long as he was capable of suffering and mortal, he was lower than the angelic nature, which is immortal. But after God the Father crowned him with the glory of the Resurrection and the honor of immortality, he who had previously been lower was made higher than the angels.

When, therefore, the angels saw human nature exalted above the angelic nature, they—who had previously allowed themselves to be worshiped by human beings—afterward feared being worshiped by the human race so exalted. Abraham worshiped an angel when he saw three, and worshiped one of them, and the angel did not forbid him (Gen. 18). John wished to worship an angel after the Resurrection, but the angel did not permit it (Rev. 19). Previously they despised the human being whom they saw exiled because of his sin; they honored the human nature which they saw exalted above themselves.

They knew indeed that, before sin, the human being had been made for the restoration of the angelic legion that had fallen, but they did not know of his redemption through the Son. At the beginning of the world God made a certain angel outstanding among the others, exceedingly beautiful and wise. Concerning him the Prophet later says: “You were the seal of likeness to God, full of wisdom and perfect in beauty; you were in the delights of the paradise of God” (Ezek. 28). For in him there was a more subtle nature and the image of the sons of God. This is suggested when it is said: “Every precious stone was your covering” (ibid.), because that first angel was adorned and covered with the nine orders, being placed over all the angelic ranks and brighter in comparison with them.

But, having been turned toward pride, in his excessive brilliance he said: “I will ascend into heaven; I will place my throne toward the north, and I will be like the Most High” (Isa. 14). Other angels consented to him; when they wished to become like God and to be unlike the angels, they became lower. Thus that first angel and his companions fell from heaven, while the other good spirits remained; and it is believed that some fell from each of the nine orders of angels. Thus, when there had been eight orders, a tenth was made from the ninth, which perished; and the human race was made to fill their place.

If humanity had not sinned, all would have been saved, and they would have been like the angels and immortal. For if Adam had not sinned in paradise, he would have lived on the fruit of the trees and generated children without lust, while each person would nevertheless have remained on earth until the appointed time.

But how would they have generated children if they had remained in paradise? Just as one hand joins another, so they would have joined without lust; and just as the eye raises itself in order to see, so that sensible member would have performed its function without pleasure. Thus they would have given birth without pain and without defilement.

Would the infant have been as weak and speechless as now? As soon as it was born, it would have walked and spoken clearly; and it would have employed the trees placed there against each individual defect. At the time appointed by God, it would have eaten from the tree of life and afterward remained in one unchanging condition.

They were to remain in paradise until the number of the angels who had fallen was completed, and until the number of the elect that would have been fulfilled if the angels had not fallen was complete. But how could paradise contain them all? Just as now one generation passes away through death—that is, by dying—and another generation arrives through life—that is, by being born—so then the parents would have been taken up into a better condition. The children, at a predetermined time, believed to be around thirty years after eating from the tree of life, would have yielded their place to their descendants; and finally all would have been made equal to the angels in heaven together and transferred alive into heaven.

But when humanity sinned, death entered the world; immortality perished, and ascent into heaven perished. Yet God, in his supreme mercy, redeemed the human being by becoming human. Through his death he destroyed our death; through his Resurrection he recovered immortality; through his Ascension he made an entrance into heaven for us; and the Lordly man himself filled the place of the highest angel. Other human beings, lower than he, restored the fall of the lower orders.

Thus Christ, even according to his humanity, is above all creatures. Hence the Psalmist says: “You have subjected all things beneath his feet” (Ps. 8). But God is greater and higher than that human being; and the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit are so according to divinity. Hence the Apostle says: “Then the Son himself will also be subject to him who subjected all things to him” (1 Cor. 15).

Among other human beings, some will be higher than others according to their merits, being placed with others. Hence the Gospel says: “In my Father’s house are many dwelling places” (John 14). And elsewhere: “They will all be equal to the angels” (Luke 20).

If you ask how many will be saved, or how many souls will reach heaven, hear Augustine: [Col. 0976B] “As many angels as remained there, so great a multitude of human beings is believed to ascend there; and individuals will be associated with the individual orders of angels, according to how God distinguishes them in merits, as it is written in the Prophet: ‘He established the boundaries of the nations according to the number of the sons of God’ (Deut. 32).

“This, therefore, is that day, dearest brothers, on which the fall of the angels was restored, on which the army of angels rejoiced in the fellowship of human beings. This is that festival which is the source of all other festivals, without which the benefit of them all would perish. For if there were no ascent into heaven, the Nativity would be empty, the Passion fruitless, and the Resurrection useless.

“This is such a great festival that in the time of Pope Sylvester it was celebrated in honor of the Ascension on Thursday every week, as solemnly as Sunday is now celebrated in memory of the Resurrection. Let us rejoice with the angels, who today met the royal Son ascending to the Father with great joy. For they said: ‘Who is this King of glory?’ (Ps. 23). Others accompanying the Lord answered: ‘The Lord strong and mighty, the Lord mighty in battle’ (ibid.); and truly he proved to be the King’s Son.

“But what benefit is there in the liberation of our companions unless we become their companions? Let us labor, dearest ones, so that, just as we have been redeemed by the same blood, so we may be rewarded with the same reward of the Ascension, through our Lord Jesus Christ himself.”

## SUNDAY AFTER THE ASCENSION. According to John.

[Col. 0975]

[Col. 0975D] “When the Paraclete comes, whom I will send to you from the Father, the Spirit of truth who proceeds from the Father, he will bear witness concerning me” (John 15). The Holy Spirit came on the day of Pentecost upon one hundred and twenty people gathered together, among whom were all the apostles. When they spoke in tongues, many of those present, astonished by so great a miracle and cut to the heart as they listened to Peter, were converted and received forgiveness.

Seeing this, the Lord was speaking as though he were saying: “They hated me, but the Paraclete will bear such witness concerning me that [Col. 0976D] he will cause many of them to believe in me.” The Holy Spirit came willingly, just as the Son sends him from the Father and refers him to the Father—both because he himself is from the Father and because the Spirit proceeds from both.

Thus it was said through the Prophet concerning the Son: “I fill heaven and earth” (Jer. 23). Where was he sent except where he already was? If he was sent from the Father, where could he be without his wisdom, “which reaches from end to end” (Wis. 8)? But neither could he be anywhere without his Spirit. Therefore the Holy Spirit too was sent where he already was. Hence the Psalmist says: “Where shall I go from your Spirit, and where shall I flee from your presence?” (Ps. 138). The Father is nowhere read to have been sent.

It is customary to ask why the Spirit appeared in fire; why in fire and tongues together; why he is sometimes shown in a dove and sometimes in fire; and why he appeared over the Son of God in the form of a dove, but over the disciples in fire. Let us consider these four questions.

The Spirit is shown in fire because the Apostle says: “Our God is a consuming fire” (Heb. 12). This is true, because through this fire the rust of sins is consumed. Concerning this fire Truth says: “I have come to cast fire upon the earth, and what do I desire except that it burn?” (Luke 12; Acts 2). By “earth” he means earthly hearts, which, by piling up lowly things, are trampled underfoot by evil spirits.

He was shown in fiery tongues because the tongue corresponds to the word, and the Word, who is the Son of God, is one substance with the Holy Spirit. Or he appeared in tongues because, just as a word proceeds through the tongue, so whoever is touched by the Holy Spirit confesses the Only-Begotten of God. Or he appeared in fiery tongues because those whom he fills he makes ardent and eloquent; for those who preach by loving God set the hearts of their hearers aflame.

He is sometimes shown in a dove and sometimes in fire because those whom he fills he makes both simple and ardent. Neither simplicity without zeal nor zeal without simplicity pleases God. Hence Truth says: “Be wise as serpents and simple as doves” (Matt. 10). Paul explains the serpent’s wisdom by saying: “Do not become children in your understanding” (1 Cor. 14). Concerning the dove’s simplicity he also says: “Be children in malice” (ibid.).

He appeared in the Lord through a dove and in the disciples through fire because the just Judge did not wish to strike sinners, but to correct them gently. Those who are merely human beings, and therefore sinners, had to be set spiritually on fire against themselves and saved through repentance.

“And you also will bear witness, because you have been with me from the beginning” (John 13)—that is, from the beginning of my preaching. Love, poured into your hearts through the Holy Spirit, will give you confidence to speak. Peter did not yet possess this when he denied the Lord. The Holy Spirit will bear witness in your hearts, and you in your voices, so that what was spoken may be fulfilled: “Their sound has gone out into all the earth” (Ps. 18).

“I have spoken these things to you so that you may not be scandalized. They will put you out of the synagogues” (John [Col. 0977D] 16). He expresses what they were going to suffer. He makes clear that the Jews would not receive him and would therefore expel those who preached about him. But he foretold the Spirit who would strengthen them, so that this would not be a stumbling block to them, because “there is great peace for those who love your law”—which is love itself.

“But the hour is coming when everyone who kills you will think that he is offering service to God” (ibid.). It is as though he were saying: “They will put you outside the synagogues, but do not fear solitude. Separated from their assembly, you will gather so many in my name that, fearing that their temple and law may be destroyed, they will kill you, thinking that they are doing well.” Behold what the Apostle says: “They have zeal for God, but not according to knowledge” (Rom. 10).

“And they will do these things to you [Col. 0978A] because they have known neither the Father nor me. But I have told you these things so that, when their hour comes, you may remember that I told you” (John 16). I foretold this so that the unforeseen might not disturb those who were ignorant—namely, so that what has been anticipated might be endured patiently when the dark hour of the wicked arrives.

## On the ten descents of Christ and the eight ascents of the soul

In the Fourth Book of Kings it is written that, when King Hezekiah was sick even unto death, the prophet Isaiah entered to him and told him from the Lord that he would be healed. He said to him: “What will be the sign that the Lord will heal me?” Isaiah answered him: “This will be the sign from the Lord: Do you want the shadow to advance ten lines, or to return ten steps?” And Hezekiah said: [Col. 0978B] “I want it to return and go backward ten steps on the sundial” (2 Kings 20; Isa. 38). And so it happened.

What Hezekiah requested as a sign of the salvation to be granted to him—namely, that the sun should move backward ten lines of the sundial, which it had already traversed—signifies the ten orders of time through which Christ, the sun of righteousness, descended as though through the shadow of the law, and made certain leaps through which he ascended again after the Resurrection.

The first step of his descent was from God into an angel, because he himself was the Angel of great counsel; the second step of his descent was from an angel into the patriarchs; the third, in the giving of the law; the fourth, in Joshua son of Nun, so that he might lead the people into the promised land; the fifth, in the judges, because through them he judged and ruled that people; the sixth, in the kings of the Jews, because he himself reigned in them; the seventh, in the prophets, because through them he was announced; the eighth, in the high priests, because he is the supreme priest of the Father; the ninth, into a human being; the tenth, into the Passion.

Through these ten steps, as through the shadow of the ancient law, Christ descended to humanity, and illumined the entire shadow of the law with the ray of truth, revealing obscure things, opening what was closed, and uncovering everything concealed.

Finally, just as Christ descended to human beings by these ten steps, so Christ, through his holy human beings, taught them to ascend to God by eight steps. For Ezekiel, speaking of the building situated on the mountain, says: “Its ascent was by eight steps” (Ezek. 40). Peter likewise counts eight steps of virtue: faith, virtue, knowledge, abstinence, patience, godliness, brotherly love, and charity. By these, fleeing the corruption of worldly desire, we must ascend to the heavenly kingdom, as from the valley of tears to the place of souls—that is, paradise.

Thus he says: Fleeing the corruption of the desire that is in the world, so that you may not be corrupted by desire, make every effort, so that all your care may be directed toward God alone; and in the hidden place of the heart do not be weak or dissolute. “Minister virtue in true faith”: in a servile and humble manner, show your brothers the steadfastness of good conduct, which must be joined to faith, lest faith be dead without works, and so that you may strengthen others by your example in good conduct.

In virtue, add knowledge—that is, learn to do good through good conduct, with hope in eternal things rather than temporal ones. In knowledge, add abstinence. Once you have learned to do good, immediately abstain from evil in hope of eternal life, both in thought and in deed, lest knowledge of heavenly things depart in vain if it does not restrain someone from the allurements of the age.

In abstinence, add patience, so that the person who restrains himself from the world’s pleasures may endure its adversities. In patience, add godliness, so that toward those whom you endure you may be piously solicitous. In godliness, add brotherly love, so that you may perform works of godliness toward adversaries for no other reason than brotherly affection: pray for them, so that those whom your teaching or admonitions have not converted may be converted.

In brotherly love, add charity—namely, the charity of God—which is rightly joined to brotherly love, because neither is God loved without one’s neighbor, nor one’s neighbor without God. For whoever does not love God does not love his neighbor as himself, because he does not love himself either. He is impious and unjust. Whoever loves iniquity plainly does not love, but hates his own soul.

Let us therefore love one another as Christ loves us. For the sake of possessing God, let us do whatever else he commands, so that by his help we may ascend to him through these eight ascents.

Meanwhile, it must be considered how earthly bodies can remain in heaven.

## Again, how earthly bodies can remain in heaven

Some people say that it is necessary for the natural weight of earthly bodies either to hold them on earth or to force them toward the earth; and therefore they cannot exist in heaven. Those first human beings were in an earth that was wooded and fruitful, which received the name paradise.

And he argues from the weights of the elements. (Augustine.) How, then, did they learn from the teacher Plato that the two greatest and outermost bodies of the world are joined and connected by the two middle elements, air and water? Thus, they say, earth is first from here upward; water is second, above the earth; air is third, above the water; and heaven is fourth, above the air. An earthly body cannot exist in heaven. For the elements are balanced by their own weights so that they may maintain their order.

Behold by what arguments human weakness, possessed by vanity, contradicts the omnipotence of God. What, then, are so many earthly bodies doing in the air, when air is third from the earth? Unless perhaps the one who, through the lightness of feathers and wings, granted birds—earthly bodies—the ability to be carried through the air could not grant human bodies, once made immortal, the power to dwell even in heaven.

For although, as we are accustomed to perceive when carrying burdens, the greater the quantity, the greater the weight, the soul carries the members of its flesh more lightly when they are robust in health than when they are thin in sickness. And although a healthy and strong person is heavier for others who carry him than someone weak and sickly, he himself is more agile in moving and carrying his own body when he has greater mass in good health than when, in disease or hunger, he possesses very little strength.

Even in the possession of earthly bodies, although they are still corruptible and mortal, it is not the weight of quantity but the measure of its constitution that matters. And who can express how great the difference is between the present condition—which we call health—and the future condition of immortality?

Let philosophers therefore not argue against us on the basis of the weights of bodies. The order from here upward is indeed: earth first, water second, air third, heaven fourth, so that above all these is the nature of souls. Aristotle too said that the soul is the fourth body, while Plato said it was no body at all. If it were the fourth, it would certainly be above the others; but since it is no body, it surpasses them all the more.

What, then, is something more subtle than all else doing in an earthly body? What is something lighter than all else doing in this weight? What is something swifter than all else doing in this sluggishness? Can it really be that, by the merit of this exceedingly excellent nature, it cannot be brought about that its body be lifted into heaven? And if the nature of earthly bodies can now draw wings downward, will the soul at some time also be unable to lift earthly bodies upward?

Finally, if the order of the elements is arranged so that, according to Plato, the two extremes—fire and earth—are joined by the two middle elements, air and water, and if heaven also occupies the place of the highest, then these things are like the foundation of the lowest world, and therefore earth cannot exist in heaven.

Why, then, is there fire in the earth? According to this reasoning, these two elements ought to have been in their proper places—earth at the bottom and fire at the top—so that, just as they say that what belongs at the bottom cannot be at the top, neither could what belongs at the top be at the bottom. Therefore, just as they think that no particle of earth either is or will be in heaven, so we ought to have seen no particle of fire in the earth.

Yet now fire is found not only on the earth but even beneath the earth. For the summits of mountains belch it forth; and we see that fire is both present in the earth for human uses and born from the earth. At times it is also produced from wood and stones, which are unquestionably earthly bodies.

Why, then, do they want us to believe that the nature of earthly bodies will at some time become incorruptible and suitable for heaven, just as corruptible fire is now suitable for these earthly regions? Nothing in their assertions from the weights and order of the elements gives them grounds for prescribing to the omnipotent God that he cannot make our bodies such that they may also dwell in heaven.

## ON THE HOLY DAY OF PENTECOST. According to John.

[Col. 0979]

[Col. 0979D] “If anyone loves me, he will keep my word, and my Father will love him, and we will come to him and make our dwelling with him. Whoever does not love me does not keep my words” (John 14).

Judas, who said to the Lord, “Lord, what has happened, that you will reveal yourself to us and not to the world?” (ibid.), is not that Iscariot, but the one whose Epistle is read among the canonical Scriptures. And the Lord answered him: “If anyone loves me,” and so forth, in order to show him that through love the holy people are distinguished from the unholy.

For charity makes people of one mind in the house in which the Father and the Son make their dwelling, since they also grant that very love. In eternal glory, therefore, there will be both vision and dwelling—not transitory but eternal—and this will be the manifestation about which Judas had asked.

God comes to the human being when the human being comes to God. The human being comes by believing, obeying, devoutly living, and receiving; God comes by helping, enlightening, and filling. Nevertheless, he comes into the hearts of some but does not make his dwelling there, because through compunction they perceive God’s regard, but they fail through temptation.

“And the word which you have heard is not mine, but the Father’s who sent me.” The Son is not inferior to the Father, and he is not from himself. Nor is this contrary to what he said: “Whoever does not love me does not keep my words” (John 14). Perhaps he uses the plural “words” because of some distinction. Here, however, he says that the word is the Father’s Word, which was in the beginning.

“I have spoken these things to you while remaining with you.” While I still remain with you in bodily presence, which will soon be taken from you, I have spoken of the spiritual dwelling. That dwelling makes the liberated blessed forever; this one visits those who are to be liberated in time.

“But the Paraclete, the Holy Spirit, whom the Father will send in my name, he will teach you everything and suggest to you everything that I have said to you.” “In my name”—that is, in knowledge of me: the Father will send the Spirit to those who confess me. Or thus: “He will send him in my name,” that is, for my glorification in those who love me. Or “in my name,” that is, in the name of the Godhead, because I, the Father, and the Holy Spirit are one God.

Where the Holy Spirit teaches, the Father and the Son teach. But because there is a Trinity, it was necessary for the individual persons to be indicated separately. “Paraclete” is interpreted as “advocate,” because he makes those whom he fills into people who pray successfully. Hence Paul says: “The Spirit himself pleads for us with inexpressible groanings” (Rom. 8). He does not plead as an inferior, but inflames us to plead.

The same Spirit is also called “Comforter,” because, while he prepares a way for the penitent, he lifts the mind from sadness. Why does he say “suggest,” since suggesting ordinarily seems to belong to an inferior? Because “to suggest” sometimes means “to supply,” as here—not that he brings knowledge into us from below, but from what is hidden.

Augustine does not have “he will suggest to you everything,” but “he will remind you of everything.” And he explains it in this way: “We must understand that the most salutary admonitions, which we are commanded not to forget, belong to grace, because the Spirit reminds us of them.”

“I leave you peace; I give you my peace. Not as the world gives do I give to you.” As I am going to the Father, I leave peace to those who follow; to those who arrive, I give it. [Col. 0982A] This is what we read in the Prophet: “Peace upon peace.”

He leaves us peace in this age, by which we may conquer the enemy and love one another. He will give us his peace in the future, when we shall reign without an enemy and without dissension. He leaves us peace so that we may not judge concerning hidden things. He will give us his peace when he reveals the thoughts of the heart.

He is our peace, who made both one (Eph. 2). But why did he not add “my,” saying “I leave,” as he does where he says “I give”? What if he wished his peace to be understood as the kind he himself described, in which there is no opposition, while the peace he left us is without sin? Hence we say: “Forgive us our debts” (Matt. 6).

This peace is therefore not yet complete, by which, according to the inner person, we delight in the law of God, but we see another law in our members fighting against the law of our mind (Rom. 7). We also have peace when we love one another; but that peace too is not complete, because we do not see one another’s thoughts, and we form opinions about one another concerning certain things that are not in us—either for the better or for the worse.

Nor am I unaware that this may be understood as a repetition, so that “my” is understood earlier. But the world—that is, people who love the world—give one another peace for this reason: so that, without strife, they may enjoy not God but the world. And when they give peace to the righteous so that they will not persecute them, it is not true peace, because their hearts are divided.

“Let not your heart be troubled, nor let it be afraid. You have heard that I said to you: I am going away, and I will come to you.” [Col. 0982C] Because I give peace, so that you may keep your hearts above, do not be troubled by what I said: “I am going away,” as though, in the shepherd’s absence, a wolf might attack the flock. And although I go away from you bodily as a human being, I remain present by what I am as God.

The Arians object to us that the Son of God is a creature, on the basis of Solomon’s words: “The Lord created me at the beginning of his ways, before he made the earth” (Prov. 8). But this was said concerning his humanity: “He created me at the beginning of his ways,” that is, so that he might reveal the beginnings of his ways and works through the Gospel. What follows pertains to his divinity: “He established me before the age” (ibid.). What does “before all times he begot me” mean?

They also say: Why do you not deny that the flesh is a creature, when you worship it together with the divinity? Because it is so united to the divinity that the Son of God is both God and human being. Finally, if you separate the human being from God, I would never serve him. If someone found a royal purple robe or diadem, would he worship it? But when a king has put them on, whoever despises worshiping them together with the king incurs the danger of death. Therefore, if anyone refuses to worship the flesh united to the Godhead, he will suffer the punishment of eternal death.

“If you loved me, you would certainly rejoice because I am going to the Father, because the Father is greater than I.” According to the form of a servant, Christ the child was also lower than his parents. “You would rejoice,” he says, because human nature ought to rejoice, since it is raised to the right hand of the Father—a destiny which the others likewise hope for.

[Col. 0983A] “And now I have told you before it happens, so that when it has happened you may believe.” He foretold that he would go to the Father, and after his death they were going to see him alive and ascending to the Father. When they saw this, they would believe that he was the Son of God, since he was able to do it. For faith concerns things that are believed and not seen.

They were going to believe, I say, that he was the Son of God—not with a new faith, since they had believed this previously, but with an increased and strengthened faith, because when he was saying these things their faith was small, and when he died it was almost nonexistent.

“I will no longer speak much with you. For the prince of this world is coming, and he has nothing in me.” The prince of sinners is coming, having received permission from God, in order to hand me over to the hands of the Jews; and I will follow willingly, since he has nothing in me that belongs to him. The Lord did not wish to possess anything that he would lose. He came poor, so that the devil would have nothing to take away.

The prince of this world is the devil; “the world” means lovers of the world. Hence it is written: “Whoever wishes to be a friend of this age is made an enemy of God” (Jas. 4).

“But so that the world may know that I love the Father, and that I do just as the Father commanded me.” He added this as though someone were saying to him: “Why are you dying, if you have no sin?” Because the Father commanded it.

It should certainly be noted that the Father handed over the Son, the Son handed over himself, the disciple handed over his teacher, the devil handed over the Savior, and the Jews handed over their king to the nations and to the cross. Behold one common deed, but utterly different intentions.

## SERMON ON THE DAY OF PENTECOST.

[Col. 0983C] “By the word of the Lord the heavens were established, and by the breath of his mouth all their host” (Ps. 32). Through the Son, who is the Word of God, not only the heavens but also all things were created from nothing; and, lest they be dissolved into nothingness, they were established by that same Word, while by the breath of his mouth all their host was adorned. The angels too are called heavens, because, when others fell, they were established in love through the Word of God and adorned with every virtue through his Spirit. Hence it is written: “The Spirit of God adorned the heavens” (Job 26), because he adorned both these heavens with stars and the angels with virtues.

Through the Son, then, the angelic spirits are created, but through the Holy Spirit they are given life. Through the Son, the substance of light shone forth; but through the Holy Spirit its splendor radiated. Through the Son, the firmament is formed; but through the Holy Spirit it is turned with swift rotation. Through the Son, the sun, moon, and stars are set over the times; but through the Holy Spirit they are polished with the brightness of light. Through the Son, the rivers are poured forth; but through the Holy Spirit they receive their flowing course. Through the Son, the earth is formed; but through the Holy Spirit it is adorned with fruits and flowers. Through the Son, the various animals are produced; but through the Holy Spirit they are endowed with vital existence, and through him birds are supported in flight, fish in swimming, and beasts, reptiles, and creeping things in their movement.

Through the Son, the human being is fashioned in the image of God; but through the Holy Spirit he is given life in his soul. The Holy Spirit inspires different talents; he also grants different crafts. Through the Holy Spirit the varieties of languages were given; through him, from the hidden treasures of wisdom, the manifold streams of the Scriptures were brought forth. Through the Holy Spirit the patriarchs represented beforehand in figures the Christ and the Church that were to come; through him the prophets spoke and announced these same things beforehand in the Scriptures. Through him the apostles were strengthened and preached in the world the things that had taken place; through him teachers, inspired, expounded the Scriptures.

Through the Son, the human being, redeemed, is freed from death; but through the Holy Spirit he is regenerated to life in baptism. Through the Holy Spirit sins are forgiven; through him souls are raised from the death of their crimes. Through the Holy Spirit many, having renounced the world, have led a religious life; through him very many have shone with signs and wonders. Through the Holy Spirit even today many are converted to a better life; through him very many are caught up in mind to heavenly things.

Through the Son comes the resurrection of the dead; through the Holy Spirit comes their transformation. Through the Son the world is judged; through the Holy Spirit each of the two parties is justly rewarded. Through the Son God the Father will create a new heaven and a new earth; but the Holy Spirit will renew all things into a better condition. Heaven, indeed, will through him be clothed with the sun’s splendor; through him the sun will be clothed with sevenfold light; through him the moon will shine with the sun’s brightness; through him the earth will bloom with the loveliness of paradise.

Then the Son will make those who have been transferred from their labor recline at table, and, passing among them, will serve them, because, returning from judgment, he will make the elect rest in different dwellings according to their different merits, and will show them the glory of his divinity face to face. The Holy Spirit, however, will grant them to shine like the full radiance of the sun in complete joy and to know the Trinity perfectly in unity.

## Division

This feast of the Holy Spirit is celebrated for seven days, because he is honored in seven gifts, as was foretold through the prophet: “The spirit of wisdom and understanding, the spirit of counsel and fortitude; the spirit of knowledge and piety, the spirit of the fear of the Lord” (Isa. 11). These are the seven women who seized one man (Isa. 4), because the seven gifts of the Holy Spirit possessed only Christ bodily.

All who fear God will ascend by means of the heavenly gifts of this Spirit. Through him, indeed, fear is granted, and it is divided in two. For there is servile fear and there is filial fear. A servant fears the Lord lest he condemn him; a son fears the Father lest he disinherit him. (Augustine.) “The adulteress fears her husband lest he come; the chaste wife fears lest he depart.”

When the Holy Spirit, who is love, has taken possession of the mind, he will cast out servile fear; but “the fear of the Lord endures for ever and ever.” For then one will no longer fear Gehenna as a servant of sin, because one seeks to commit no sin. As a son, however, one will cleave to God through delight in virtues and will therefore possess his inheritance.

Let us obtain from his grace by praying that, as servants, we may fear the Lord our God by turning away from evil, lest he someday subject us, through contempt for his commandments, to punishments—or rather punish us as enemies rebellious against him with eternal torments. Let us ask him that, like the children of Israel, we may truly revere him as a father, by doing good, so that we may be co-heirs of his Son and enjoy the Father’s presence.

After fear, the Spirit gives piety, so that a human being may serve his Maker devotedly and bestow upon his neighbor whatever good he is able to provide. Then he inspires knowledge, so that a person may know what must be done and what must be avoided. After this, fortitude is given by him, so that a person is not bent toward vices either by flattering enticements or by adversity. Next, he supplies counsel to reason, so that one chooses what is useful and rejects what is harmful. After this, he grants understanding, so that the soul may understand eternal things through visible ones. Then he inspires wisdom, so that the rational creature may despise mutable creation, love its Creator, who is the immutable good, and taste in the Holy Spirit Christ, the sole fountain of wisdom.

Those who flourish in these virtues through the sevenfold Spirit will receive through him seven gifts in the body and seven gifts in the soul, when they possess a double portion in their own land, shining like the sun in body and being equal to the angels in soul.

From him whose beauty the sun and moon admire, they will be illumined in body seven times more brightly than the sun. For Christ, through the Holy Spirit, will refashion “the body of our lowliness, conformed to the body of his glory” (Phil. 3). And since the body will be spiritual, he whose word runs swiftly (Ps. 147) will clothe it with such speed that, as quickly as sight now reaches heaven or thought reaches the world’s extremity through its agility, so swiftly then the body will be carried there through its mobility.

By him who is the strength of all, it will also be strengthened with such power that it could easily overturn the mass of mountains with its foot. By him, too, who was “free among the dead” (Ps. 87), they will possess such gracious freedom that every solid creature will be penetrable to them.

In the vision of him the angels overflow with great sweetness; all the saints abound in the greatest delights. From him they enjoy every abundance of pleasure, while they are established in the joy of their Lord above all their goods. There they will see the King of glory as he is, in his beauty, the one upon whom they desire to gaze; there they will see the glory of all the angels and saints, and behold all their own members shining brightly within and without; there they will continually hear the organs of the saints and the harmonies of the angels resounding; there they will be refreshed by the most sweet fragrance of cinnamon and balsam, feast exultantly in the sight of God, and delight in gladness; they will be intoxicated by the abundance of God’s house and drink from his torrent of pleasure (Ps. 35).

By him who is the salvation of all, they will be made so firm in health that, just as the sun’s ray now suffers no division, so then they will suffer no bodily affliction. By him who is eternal life, they will be so confirmed in longevity that they will never be released into death for eternity.

These are the seven goods they will have in the body through the seven gifts of the Holy Spirit. They will have just as many in the soul, where they will rejoice perpetually in the Lord’s goods. For the fountain of wisdom itself will flow into them so abundantly that it will grant them knowledge of all things. An ineffable friendship joins them together, because they are loved by God as sons and by the angels as brothers. Incomparable harmony cements them together, because neither God nor any of the saints is at variance with their will. They are exalted by immeasurable power, because they rule over the new heaven and the new earth. They are raised up by indescribable honor, because they are revered by God himself and by all the angels. They possess the greatest security, because no one will ever take these things from them. They will have complete joy in them without end; they will rejoice forever that all their friends whom they love enjoy the same goods.

These are the gifts that Christ, ascending on high, gave to human beings—those whom he led captive from the devil and from death, and whom, victorious and glorious, he brought into the starry dwellings.

## Division

[Col. 0986B]
