While they were placed on earth, the Lord bestowed his gifts on them, granting through the charisms of the Holy Spirit that they should shine with signs and new languages. But those who are found empty of the seven gifts of the Holy Spirit will be tortured with as many punishments as these others enjoy goods.

These things were formerly prefigured in the Law; they were foretold through the prophets. From the legal candlestick proceed seven lamps (Exod. 15), because from Christ the seven gifts of the Holy Spirit come forth to the Church. These are the seven pillars by which the house of Wisdom is supported (Prov. 9), because the Church, which is the house of God, is marked by the seven gifts of the Holy Spirit. These are the seven eyes that the prophet sees in one stone (Zech. 3), because Christ, the rock, gave the faithful the seven gifts of the Holy Spirit for the illumination of souls.

These are the horns of the Lamb slain for us (Rev. 5), by which he will break the seven heads of the red dragon on behalf of believers. Hence the same Holy Spirit is also said to have descended upon the baptized Lord in the form of a dove, on account of the seven characteristics that are said to exist in a dove.

The dove nests in a rock, because the Holy Spirit dwells bodily in Christ. It nourishes alien nestlings, when it brings back through repentance those who have gone astray and are alienated from the kingdom of God. It chooses pure grains, because it separates the good from the evil, as grain from chaff. It lacks gall, because it empties those whom it possesses of malice. It does not wound with its beak, because one filled with the Holy Spirit does not plot against a neighbor. It dwells beside streams, because the Holy Spirit dwells in the wise. It flies in a flock, because the Holy Spirit gives his gifts to those gathered in the Lord’s name.

Hence the prophet says: “Behold, how good and how pleasant it is for brothers to dwell together in unity! It is like oil on the head, running down upon the beard, the beard of Aaron, running down upon the edge of his garment; it is like the dew of Hermon, which descends upon Mount Zion” (Ps. 132).

The brothers dwelt together in unity, of one mind and with joy, when the multitude of believers had one heart and one soul. Therefore the oil descended from the head onto Aaron’s beard, because from the head of all—that is, from God—the Holy Spirit, who is spiritual anointing, came upon the apostles.

By Aaron, whose name is said to mean “mountain of strength,” Christ is understood, through whom the faithful stand strong against vices and go upward from virtue to virtue. His beard was the apostles, since they clung to him who is the Father’s mouth as a beard clings to the mouth. The oil flowed from the beard onto the garment, when the Holy Spirit poured himself into believers through the laying on of the apostles’ hands.

The dew of Hermon—which signifies “anathema”—descended upon Mount Zion, which is called “watchtower,” when heavenly grace came from the Synagogue to the Church. Mount Hermon is situated beside the Jordan, where the Lord was baptized. Thus the dew of Hermon is the Holy Spirit, who came upon the Lord in baptism at that mountain and who today descends upon believers on Mount Zion, where Jerusalem is situated.

How this happened, Scripture has recounted to us today. When fifty days had passed from Christ’s resurrection, and the disciples, as he had often commanded them while ascending, were staying together in Jerusalem, suddenly a great sound like that of a powerful wind came and filled the entire house where they were sitting. Fiery tongues appeared to them, and, inflamed by them, they began to speak of God’s mighty works in the languages of all nations.

Because the feast was approaching, Jews from every nation of the whole world had gathered in Jerusalem, since each year they celebrated Pentecost on account of the Law received at that time. When they heard this, they came together, and each one, astonished, heard from their mouths the language in which he had been born.

Peter addressed them, saying that these things had been foretold through the prophets and fulfilled by Jesus, whom they had crucified. Moved to repentance, about three thousand people were baptized, and they too were filled with the Holy Spirit like the others.

On the following day, when Peter and John had healed a lame man through the Holy Spirit, five thousand were baptized. All of these were enriched by the Holy Spirit; they drank in trembling the blood of Christ that they had earlier poured out in fury, and very many poured out their own blood for him.

After receiving the Holy Spirit, the apostles remained in Jerusalem for twelve years, as he directed. They jointly discussed what they were to teach throughout the world; in the surrounding regions they taught Jews and Gentiles, and through signs and wonders they converted many to the faith. All received the Holy Spirit through the laying on of the apostles’ hands and performed God’s mighty works in new languages.

Through the Holy Spirit the apostles restored light to the blind, opened the ears of the deaf, loosed the tongues of the mute, raised the lame to walking, cleansed lepers, drove demons from the possessed, and raised the dead. Moreover, some of them restored the weak to health through staffs or garments, and even through their own shadow.

After this, the Twelve spread throughout the whole world, filled with the sevenfold gift of the Holy Spirit. Through the number seven, the twelve completed their ministry, bringing the four parts of the world to the faith of the Holy Trinity. For three and four, which make seven, make twelve.

As good fishers, they drew fish formerly predestined for life from the sea of the world to the shore of life in the net of faith, through signs and miracles; and, following Christ’s example, as leaders going before them, they laid down their own lives for the sheep entrusted to them.

After God created all things in the beginning in six days, he sanctified the seventh, because, resting in it, he ceased from his work. Thus those who strive to work through the gifts of the Holy Spirit during the six ages of the world will rest from every labor through him in the seventh. So too we labor for six days in the week and are free from labor on the seventh, because now through the sevenfold Spirit we devote ourselves to good works, while in the future we shall happily rest from every work through him. There we shall be free from labor and shall see God as he is.

## Division

In the Flood, the dove, bringing back an olive branch, announced peace to those shut inside (Gen. 8), because the Holy Spirit, through the anointing of chrism, will restore the peace lost by souls enclosed in flesh.

He is also called the finger of God’s right hand, because, just as the hand works through the fingers, so Christ, who is the Father’s right hand, works all things through the divisions of the Holy Spirit’s graces. Hence the magicians who could not withstand Moses said that this was the finger of God (Exod. 8), since they clearly saw signs being performed through the Holy Spirit.

By this finger the Law was written on two tablets, because through the Holy Spirit love was ordered in two commandments. By this finger the Lord casts out demons, because the works of the Son and of the Holy Spirit are inseparable.

Formerly the human race used only one language. But seventy-two giants were building a tower against God; therefore, offended, he confused their languages, so that no one understood the language of another, and thus he scattered them throughout the world. Today the Holy Spirit has gathered them all into the unity of faith through the varieties of languages.

The Hebrew people, freed from Egyptian slavery on the paschal night through the paschal lamb and led across the Red Sea, arrived at Mount Sinai on the fiftieth day. Smoke and fire filled it, and from the midst of the fire the Lord gave them the law of fear written on tablets.

Thus the Christian people, rescued from the devil’s oppression on the paschal night through Christ, the Paschal Lamb, and carried through baptism as through the Red Sea, received on the fiftieth day—that is, today—the law of love in fire. The Lord commanded them to write it in their hearts, so that thereafter they might do willingly, out of love for God, what previously they had done under compulsion from fear.

The Law also contained a command that the fiftieth year should be called the jubilee, that is, the year of remission; that the entire year should be free from servile labor; and that lost inheritance should be restored to its rightful heirs. Through this, the Holy Spirit wished to prefigure the time in which he taught his people to be free from servile labor, that is, from sin, and restored to them their lost inheritance of paradise.

(Gregory.) The Holy Spirit is remembered as having been given to these people when he was given once on earth and once from heaven. The Spirit is given on earth so that the neighbor may be loved; the Spirit is given from heaven so that God may be loved. For “whoever loves God will keep his word” (John 14). “My Father will love him, and we will come to him, and we will make our dwelling with him.”

Therefore, dearest brothers, let us love God by keeping his commandments, so that he may love us, as we prepare a dwelling for him within us. Let us wipe away the filth of sins from the lodging of our heart through repentance and confession; let us wash away its stains with tears; let us strive to adorn it with the flowers of good works, so that the Holy Spirit may be shown to be coming and preparing a worthy dwelling for himself in us.

The Spirit also descended upon the Lord in the form of a dove, because he showed him to be free from sins. But he came upon the disciples in fire, because, consuming sins in them, he erased the record of sin. Hence fire went before the children of Israel and pointed out to them the road to their homeland, because the fire of the Holy Spirit goes before them and shows through the Scriptures the way to the homeland of paradise.

Therefore baptism is now celebrated, because through the Holy Spirit original sin is forgiven. Therefore we also observe fasts on these days, because through the Holy Spirit we hope to receive forgiveness. Whoever blasphemes against the Holy Spirit will not be forgiven, neither in this age nor in the age to come. Through the Holy Spirit forgiveness of sins is granted. Whoever despairs of pardon blasphemes against the Holy Spirit and commits an unforgivable sin.

Just as the Nativity of the Lord is celebrated, dearest brothers, so this feast also ought to be solemn for all the faithful, because just as in that feast God, coming in the flesh, visited human beings, so in this one God, coming in fire, purified human beings from sins and bestowed many charisms upon them.

These feasts are venerable to angels and human beings alike, because they are celebrated in honor of our God. Indeed, at the Lord’s Nativity, the Lord of majesty rose from his throne of glory, put on the weapons of war, and went into exile to fight on our behalf.

But Good Friday was the day of battle and victory, when the Lord, strong and mighty in battle, conquered the prince of the world, the devil, with his attendants, and powerfully gained the victory. The day of the Lord’s resurrection was the day on which, after the battle had been completed, he ravaged the tyrant’s kingdom and gathered to himself the captivity that he had captured.

The day of the Ascension is the day on which the Lord of hosts returned in noble procession and triumphed, and, received by a multitude of angels, exalted our flesh above the heavens. Today’s day, however, is the day on which he distributed spoils to his soldiers, when he bestowed various gifts of the Holy Spirit upon the faithful.

One day still remains: the day on which he will lead forth his bride from this Babylon, when on the last day he will establish the Church in the heavenly Jerusalem. Indeed, the Holy Spirit foretold these days throughout the whole Psalter. Moreover, the Law and all the prophets exulted in these things with harmonious voice.

Therefore, dearest brothers, let us now appear before his sight in righteousness, so that, when his glory appears, we may be able to be satisfied at his wedding feast, to behold the goodness of his chosen ones, to rejoice in the gladness of his people, and to delight in the fullness of all goods (Ps. 105)—“things which eye has not seen and ear has not heard” (1 Cor. 2).

## Monday. According to John

[Col. 0989]

[Col. 0989C] “For God so loved the world that he gave his only-begotten Son, so that everyone who believes in him might not perish but have eternal life” (John 3).

He reveals the cause of human salvation, namely, the love of God the Father, from whom all restoration or establishment comes through his Son in the Holy Spirit. He says the same thing concerning the Son of God that he said above concerning the Son of Man: believers are to attain salvation through him, so that by the one through whom we were created in divinity, we might likewise be restored in humanity.

“For God did not send his Son into the world to judge the world, but so that the world might be saved through him.”

The Savior came to save, not to judge—that is, to condemn. But if a person is judged, he brought it upon himself, because he did not believe.

“Whoever believes in him is not judged; but whoever does not believe has already been judged, because he does not believe in the name of the only-begotten Son of God.”

The judgment has not yet appeared, but it has already taken place. “For the Lord knows those who are his” (2 Tim. 2). He knows who will remain for the crown and who for the flame. In his ark he knows the wheat, he knows the chaff, he knows the crop, he knows the weeds.

Let us not listen to those who deny that a day of judgment will come on the basis of this passage. They say: If the one who believes will not come into judgment, and the one who does not believe has already been judged, where are those whom the Lord will judge on the day of judgment?

The past tense is not understood here as having been used in place of the future. Rather, when it says “has been judged,” it means “has been condemned” in God’s foreknowledge, since he knows what awaits those who do not believe. And when it says, “will not come to judgment,” it is to be understood in this way: “will not come to condemnation.”

“This is the judgment: that light has come into the world, and people loved darkness more than light, for their works were evil. For everyone who does evil hates the light and does not come to the light, so that his works may not be reproved.”

He calls judgment eternal condemnation, which consists in not knowing God, just as eternal life consists in knowing him. Because the light has come—that is, the Word in the flesh—and arouses and warns human beings to recognize their own evils, in which all are involved, those who hate the light that admonishes them are judged. They drive it away so that their evils may not be reproved: impiety, unbelief, hatred of eternal light, and unwillingness to look upon it, but a desire to remain in the darkness of sins.

Certainly, everyone who is intent on evil and works it with love for that evil hates the light, because it exposes evils. Thus he does not come to the light in order to be joined to it, but drives it away so that the evils he loves may not be reproved.

“But whoever does the truth comes to the light, so that his works may be manifested, because they have been done in God.”

Because the beginning of good is the accusation of evil, he does the truth—that is, the things commanded by truth. Whoever, warned by the light, accuses his own evils does the truth, so that both this accusation of his and the other good things he has done may be shown to have been accomplished through divine illumination.

Therefore, whoever wishes to come to the light should abstain not only from great sins, but also make a true confession of lesser sins, since many small sins, if neglected, bring death. For small drops fill a river, and small grains of sand, if there are many, sink a ship. Neglected bilge water does the same as an onrushing wave. Water enters gradually through the bilge, but by entering for a long time without being drained it sinks the ship.

And because God scourges sinners in this age for their correction, bear with the father who disciplines, lest you experience the judge who punishes.

## Tuesday. According to John

[Col. 0991]

[Col. 0991B] “Amen, amen, I say to you: whoever does not enter the sheepfold through the gate, but climbs in by another way, is a thief and a robber” (John 10).

Because the Pharisees boasted that they could see—which they indeed could have done if they had been Christ’s sheep—the Lord, on account of their arrogance, set forth this comparison. He thus shows that neither wisdom, nor observance of the Law, nor any good life is of value except through him.

Whether a Jew, a Pharisee, a Gentile, or even a philosopher teaches a good life, or a heretic teaches under the name of Christ, if he does not preach in Christ, all such people, without him, seize and kill. The sheepfold is the Church. Whoever wishes to enter it should enter through Christ, seeking Christ’s glory, not his own.

Christ is the humble gate. Therefore let the one who enters humble himself, lest, climbing over the wall while exalting himself, he fall. He climbs in by another way who does not enter for Christ’s sake—either because he does not think rightly about him or because he seeks not his glory but his own.

A thief, then, is one who enters wrongly and calls what belongs to another his own—that is, makes God’s sheep his own. He is a robber because he kills what he has stolen, when, through a bad example or perverse teaching, the sheep hear his voice. Yet in this, when the voice of God’s Word sounds, those predestined for life hear it in obedience.

It should be noted that not everyone who enters through the gate is a shepherd, because the sheep also enter. Nevertheless, the unity of the whole Church feeds daily through word and example. Christ is the gatekeeper, who opens himself; or Scripture, which leads to Christ; or the Holy Spirit, who leads to all truth.

“And he calls his own sheep by name and leads them out. And when he has brought out his own sheep, he goes before them, and the sheep follow him, because they know his voice.”

He calls the sheep by name when he says to his disciples: “Rejoice, because your names are written in heaven” (Luke 10). Hence elsewhere: “The Lord knows those who are his” (2 Tim. 2).

He leads them out from here to eternal life; he sends them forth by freeing them from the bonds of sins, and he goes before them by rising from the dead. In another sense, he leads the sheep out of darkness into the light of teaching, and, going before them after they have been brought out as from Egypt, he goes like a pillar of cloud and fire, showing by his example what he taught.

The sheep follow him wherever he goes by persevering to the end. For those who either through blindness do not know the end of right living or, through self-inflation, despise it should not be called people who live well.

“But they will not follow a stranger; rather, they will flee from him, because they do not know the voice of strangers.” Jesus told them this proverb, but they did not understand what he was saying to them.

They are shown to be blind with regard to the good. There is a difference between them and us before we understand these words: we knock, and it will be opened to us; they do not.

“Then Jesus said to them again: Amen, amen, I say to you: I am the gate of the sheep.”

Just as the Son knows the Father through himself, while we know the Father through him, so he enters the sheepfold—that is, the hearts of the sheep—through himself, and we enter through him.

The eye of the flesh cannot see itself, though it sees other things; but the intellect understands both itself and other things. Thus Christ enters both to himself, to you, and to the Father through himself.

For through the word other things are said that are not the Word, as well as the Word itself. There are many shepherds, such as good bishops; but no one is the gate except Christ. In the Apocalypse the saints are called not the gate but gates, through which one reaches the gate.

“All who came were thieves and robbers, but the sheep did not hear them.” Those who came were not those who had been sent. Hence the prophet says: “They came, and I did not send them” (Jer. 23). In those who come there is the presumption of rashness; in those who are sent there is the obedience of service.

Or it may be understood in this way: all who came, namely, apart from me, were thieves and robbers. Heralds of truth did not come apart from him who is the truth, because they believed that he would come in the same way as we believe in him who has come. The times have changed, not the faith.

One canon of Scripture is that statements are not always referred to the whole, but to the greater part, as in: “All have turned aside; together they have become useless” (Ps. 13). Similarly here: “All who came before me were thieves and robbers.” And Paul says to the Corinthians: “I have become all things to all, so that I might save all” (1 Cor. 9). And to the Philippians: “For all seek their own interests, not those of Jesus Christ” (Phil. 2). So too the Father’s words to the Son: “All that is mine is yours” (Luke 15).

It should be understood that not all who heard the shepherd’s voice were sheep, as Judas was not. Under a sheep’s skin, hearing the shepherd, he was a wolf lying in wait for the shepherd. Some of those who crucified Christ did not hear, yet they were sheep. Concerning them the Lord says: “When you have lifted up the Son of Man, then you will know that I am he” (John 8).

Someone resolves this as follows: “When they did not hear, they were still wolves; but when they became sheep, they heard.” This can be said in some fashion. But through Ezekiel the Lord, rebuking the shepherds, says of all: “You did not bring back the wandering one” (Ezek. 34). He calls the wandering one both a wanderer and a sheep. If it was wandering when it was a sheep, undoubtedly it was hearing not the voice of the shepherd but that of the thief and robber.

But the Lord says: “All who came apart from me are thieves and robbers, but the sheep did not hear them.” Therefore, according to God’s foreknowledge, by which he sees who are his, many sheep are outside and many wolves are inside.

Many who blaspheme Christ, yet will believe in him, are sheep outside, but still follow a stranger’s voice. Likewise, many inside praise him but will blaspheme; nevertheless, as long as they think rightly, they hear Christ’s voice.

There is, however, a certain chief voice of the shepherd, in which the sheep do not hear strangers and in which those who are not sheep do not hear Christ. What voice is that? “Whoever perseveres to the end will be saved” (Matt. 10). One who belongs to him does not neglect this voice; a stranger does not hear it. For whoever is predestined and foreknown for life, even if he goes astray for a time, eventually returns and perseveres.

“I am the gate. If anyone enters through me, he will be saved; he will enter and go out, and will find pasture.”

The Teacher of truth exercises them through obscure things and feeds them through manifest things. Anyone who is not false, entering the Catholic Church through the clarity of God’s wisdom, will be saved by persevering; and previously he was already in the sheepfold of divine predestination.

He will enter within by thinking rightly, according to the holy Apostle, who says that Christ dwells through faith in our hearts (Eph. 3). He will go out by acting outwardly, according to the Psalmist: “A person goes forth to his work” (Ps. 103).

Alternatively, he will enter by believing and go out by acting, to battle against heretics. Further, he will enter the Church so that here he may live by faith, because “the righteous person lives by faith” (Heb. 10). And he will also go out through the gate of faith in Christ from this life, so that he may live eternally.

When he adds, “I came so that they may have life,” he seems to say that those entering may have life, and those going out may have it more abundantly. Therefore understand the pasture as the everlasting joys of paradise and the present face of God, who, when seen without interruption, satisfies the mind forever with the food of life.

“The thief comes only to steal, slaughter, and destroy. I came so that they may have life, and have it more abundantly.”

The thief comes to steal by claiming another’s property as his own; to slaughter by drawing one away from the faith; and to destroy by consigning one to eternal condemnation.

## Sunday within the Octave of Pentecost. According to John

[Col. 0993]

[Col. 0993C] “There was a man from the Pharisees, named Nicodemus, a ruler of the Jews. He came to Jesus by night and said to him: Rabbi, we know that you have come from God as a teacher. For no one can perform these signs that you perform unless God is with him” (John 3).

Nicodemus came to Jesus by night either because, being one of the rulers, he feared offending the people, or because, though he was a teacher in Israel, he was ashamed to learn openly.

Night therefore signifies the letter of the Law, or ignorance of heart, or fear. Nicodemus, one of those who had believed through signs, is a figure of catechumens. For although they believe, they nevertheless reach baptism through a certain night of the sacraments, where they pass from the trackless darkness to the path of heavenly light, being reborn.

If the figure of baptism was so powerful that those baptized through Moses in cloud and sea were brought to manna, will not one who receives true baptism be able to attain the same destination? What is manna?

“I am,” he says, “the living bread that came down from heaven.”

Jesus answered and said to him: “Amen, amen, I say to you: unless someone is born again, he cannot see the kingdom of God”—that is, he cannot know me, who am the kingdom of the Father, who am the vision of Truth.

Because Nicodemus had prudently recognized the manifest signs, he deserved to be taught more fully about the second birth and the other mysteries of faith.

“Nicodemus said to him: ‘How can a man be born when he is old? Can he enter his mother’s womb a second time and be born?’” The Spirit speaks to him, but he himself understands his own flesh, not Christ’s, like those who supposed that the Lord could cook and eat it after it had been cut up, like a lamb, when the Lord said: “Unless someone eats my flesh and drinks my blood, he will not have life in himself” (John 6), and immediately afterward they withdrew and no longer followed him. But the Lord explained this to those who remained, saying: “What I have said is spirit and life. For the spirit gives life, but the flesh profits nothing” (ibid.), so that they would not understand carnally what he had said.

Thus Nicodemus did not yet know the parents who beget unto life. One generation is carnal, the other spiritual. It must be understood that, just as the womb cannot be entered again, so neither can baptism be repeated. Whoever is born from the Catholic Church is born as from Sarah; whoever is born from heresy, as from the slave woman (Genesis 21; Psalm 4).

Observe why the Lord says: “I am the God of Abraham, and of Isaac, and of Jacob” (Exodus 3), as though Noah, who preceded them, and Moses, who came afterward, were not holy patriarchs. In these patriarchs we find free women and slave women; all of this is a figure, as the Apostle says: “These things happened to them in a figurative way” (1 Corinthians 10). And likewise: “They were written for our sake, upon whom the ends of the ages have come” (ibid.).

In the generations of free women and slave women there are four kinds of people, in whom the pattern of the whole of Christianity is completed. We understand the slave women as the wicked and the free women as the good. Thus either free women bear good children, as Sarah bore Isaac; or both wicked and good, as Rebecca bore Esau and Jacob; or the wicked bear the wicked, as Hagar bore Ishmael; or the wicked bear both good and wicked, as Jacob’s slave women did.

In accordance with this likeness, either the good baptize the good, as Ananias baptized Paul; or the wicked, as Philip baptized Simon Magus; or the wicked baptize both good and wicked, as certain preachers whom the Apostle says were accustomed to announce the Gospel not chastely. He tolerated them within Christian fellowship, saying: “What then? So long as Christ is proclaimed in every way, whether by pretext or in truth, I rejoice in this” (Philippians 1). He did not rejoice in their wickedness, but because Christ was truly being preached. If such men baptized people like themselves, then the wicked baptized the wicked. But if they baptized people such as the Lord admonishes when he says, “Do what they say, but do not do what they do” (Matthew 23), then the wicked baptized the good.

Therefore, just as among Jacob’s sons it did not harm those born from slave women that they should possess the promised land equally with their brothers, but the father’s seed prevailed, so whoever is baptized by the wicked, although born from the wicked, nevertheless, because he is born from the seed of the Word of God, which is represented in Jacob, will possess the inheritance with his brothers if he wishes to be good.

Therefore, whether a schismatic or any criminal person baptizes in confession of the Holy Trinity, he cannot be baptized again by Catholics, lest the confession or invocation of so great a name appear to be annulled. And in the womb of the Church there is a great struggle between the good and the wicked, just as Jacob and Esau struggled (Genesis 15), and the wicked always persecute the good, as Ishmael did Isaac.

For this reason Sarah said to Abraham: “Cast out the slave woman and her son” (Genesis 21), because she saw him mocking in play—not because Ishmael was playing with her son. Hence the Apostle says: “Just as then the one born according to the flesh persecuted the one born according to the spirit, so it is now” (Galatians 4). Those born according to the flesh are lovers of the world; those born according to the spirit are lovers of Christ. Therefore those who deceive us by mocking us persecute us even more, saying: “Come, come, be baptized; here you have true baptism.”

Ishmael was not disinherited because he was born from a slave woman, but because he was proud. For if he had been disinherited for that reason, Jacob’s sons would not have been admitted to the inheritance. And when Sarah afflicted the slave woman Hagar, this is not called persecution but correction. Hence the angel also says to her as she fled: “Return, and humble yourself under the hand of your mistress” (Genesis 16). In the same way, good rulers rightly afflict heretics and all who are harmful to the Church with exile and other legal punishments.

[Col. 0996A] “Jesus answered: ‘Amen, amen, I say to you, unless someone is born again from water and the Spirit, he cannot enter the kingdom of God.’” The meaning is: Whoever refuses to be born again will not have life, because he has not been born from water and the Spirit—that is, from faith and love.

How is water the sacrament of faith? By the name “water,” faith is understood. The Spirit, however, pours love into our hearts. Thus infants, when through baptism they are united to the Church, are born unto life from the faith and love of the saints, by whose bond the Church is joined to God, through the visible sacrament of water and the Holy Spirit. But whoever ends life having neglected this good will be excluded forever from the kingdom of God.

Those who die for the confession of Christ without having received the laver of regeneration nevertheless receive the benefit of forgiveness of sins as fully as if they had been washed in the sacred font of baptism. For the one who said, “Unless someone is born again from water and the Spirit, he will not enter the kingdom of heaven,” made an exception for these people in another statement, where he says no less generally: “Whoever confesses me before men, I also will confess him before my Father” (Luke 12).

Indeed, the blood and water that came forth when Christ’s side was struck by the wound jointly presented the type of martyrdom and baptism by which one goes to heaven. Therefore, if the moment of death excludes from the sacrament of baptism those who are rooted in faith in Christ and in sincere love, it is clear that they are not excluded from salvation. They are martyrs before God if, with a pure heart, they were prepared for martyrdom and were baptized in fire or in the Spirit, according to what the Lord said to the apostles: “But you will be baptized with the Holy Spirit not many days from now” (Acts 1).

Hence Ambrose says concerning Valentinian: “I grieve in my womb, to use a prophetic example, because I lost the one whom I had been about to regenerate.” Yet he did not receive the grace he had asked for.

Augustine, in Book 4 of *On Baptism*: “Considering the thief to whom it was said, ‘Today you will be with me in paradise,’ I find that not only suffering for the name of Christ can supply what is lacking from baptism, but also faith and the conversion of the heart, if perhaps the celebration of the mystery of baptism cannot be attended to amid the urgency of circumstances.”

Therefore, whatever force the visible sacrament of baptism possesses, the Apostle’s statement—“With the heart one believes unto righteousness, but with the mouth confession is made unto salvation” (Romans 10)—is invisibly fulfilled when the mystery of baptism is excluded not by contempt for religion but by the urgency of necessity.

It must be understood that Augustine did not retract this judgment, as some falsely suppose. Rather, he retracted what he had said in the example: that the thief had not been baptized, since it is uncertain whether he had been baptized or not. Therefore, when he says elsewhere, “We do not believe that a catechumen, even if he dies in good works, has life, unless he was a martyr,” these and similar statements are directed against those who despise the sacraments of baptism.

[Col. 0996D] “What is born from the flesh is flesh, and what is born from the Spirit is spirit.” He distinguishes spiritual birth from carnal birth. From the Holy Spirit our spirit—that is, our soul—is born in God when, through grace, which is understood as the Holy Spirit, sins are forgiven it, so that it does not incur the punishment of condemnation on that account. For it is not the flesh but the soul that can be punished.”

“Do not marvel that I said to you: You must be born again. The Spirit breathes where it wills, and you hear its voice, but you do not know where it comes from or where it goes.” So it is with everyone who is born from the Spirit. The Spirit has power to bestow the grace of forgiveness on whomever it wills, and you hear its bodily voice when it speaks through holy preachers, according to the saying: “For it is not you who speak, but the Spirit of your Father who speaks in you” (Matthew 10).

Nevertheless, you do not know whether that voice comes to certain people through understanding—that is, for what reason, with the same Spirit acting, some who are perhaps less instructed understand that voice—and where it goes, that is, in what manner it departs from others who repent, passing away from them without understanding. In this way that birth which is from the Spirit takes place, while you do not know how the Spirit brings it about invisibly, where it itself performs nothing bodily.

Therefore, do not marvel at this—namely, what is accomplished by the Spirit in that generation—if you do not know it. Or alternatively: The Spirit has the power to illumine the heart of whomever it wishes. And if, while you are repenting, it should fill someone for a time, you hear the voice of that person’s spirit, but you do not know where it comes from or where it goes—that is, how it entered his heart or how it departed again. For its nature is invisible.

Thus the person who is being born again begins invisibly through the action of the Spirit to be what he was not, so that the unbeliever does not know where he comes from or where he goes: in what grace he comes into the adoption of the children of God, and in what way he goes into possession of the heavenly kingdom. Because these things are unknown to the carnal person, he asks again.

“Nicodemus answered and said to him: ‘How can these things happen?’ Jesus answered and said to him: ‘You are a teacher in Israel, and you do not know these things?’” Why did the Lord seem to insult the teacher? He wanted him to be born from the Spirit, which cannot happen except to the humble. But Nicodemus was puffed up and seemed important to himself because he was a teacher of the Jews.

“Amen, amen, I say to you: We speak what we know, and we testify to what we have seen, but you do not accept our testimony.” If they had been born from the Spirit as humble people, they would have believed what the Lord testifies, together with the prophets and apostles, to the world outside, concerning what is seen in the hidden things of God.

The Evangelist John has the custom of doubling “Amen” in confirmation of divine words, attending to what the Lord says: “Let your speech be: Yes, yes,” that is, do not say anything with duplicity, but utter with your mouth what you say and believe it in your heart. Thus “Amen, amen” is as though he were saying: He doubles it—that is, he proclaims the truth both of the mouth and of the heart.

“If I have told you earthly things and you do not believe, how will you believe if I tell you heavenly things?” The meaning is: If you do not believe, nor even understand, that I can raise up the temple cast down by you—which is an earthly thing—how will you believe that human beings can be regenerated through the Spirit?

Yet by reproving him, he invites him and instructs him further concerning his own divine and human birth, his passion, ascension, and many other matters. Hence it follows:

“No one has ascended into heaven except the one who descended from heaven, the Son of Man who is in heaven.” “No one has ascended”—that is, no one causes another to ascend—to the eminence of the heavenly life except the one who descended from there by humbling himself, namely the Son of God, who is the Word of the Father, assuming our weakness, according to which he is said to be less than the Father.

He descended, I say, by becoming the Son of Man, yet he is in heaven—that is, in the equality with the Father that he possessed previously. For in assuming what he was not, he did not lose what he was.

Alternatively: God did not consider his divinity unworthy of the name “Son of Man,” just as he deemed his flesh worthy of the name “Son of God,” lest he be said to be, as it were, two Christs. Thus, according to the distinction between divinity and weakness, the Son of God remained in heaven, while the Son of Man remained on earth. But through the unity of the person—who is one Christ in two natures—the Son of God also walked on earth; and that same person, the Son of Man, is said to have descended from heaven and to have been in heaven before the passion.

The meaning, therefore, is: No one ascends into heaven except Christ in his body, which is the Church. For this reason he descended: so that those who were to ascend through him might be one with him in heaven. The Lord ascended; the body, however, did not ascend but was lifted into heaven by the one who ascended.

For if someone descends, for example, naked from a mountain, and when he ascends he puts on a garment, we rightly say, “No one ascended except the one who descended.” We do not consider the garment that he carried up with him, but say that only the person who was clothed ascended.

“And just as Moses lifted up the serpent in the desert, so must the Son of Man be lifted up, so that everyone who believes in him may not perish but have eternal life.”

The people of God, wearied in the wilderness by the long labor, murmured against the Lord and Moses. Therefore the Lord sent fiery serpents among them. When Moses had prayed, the Lord commanded him to make a bronze serpent and to have those struck by the wounds look at it, so that they might live.

What are the biting serpents? Sins. What is the serpent that was lifted up? The Lord dead on the cross, who is represented by the image of a serpent, because death came through the serpent. Therefore those who look upon him in faith are freed from the wounds of the fiery serpents—that is, from the incitements of vices, which prick the soul unto death.

## What baptism is, and why the sacrament of baptism was instituted

Some ask what baptism is and why the sacrament of baptism was instituted. Baptism, therefore, is water sanctified by the Word of God for the washing away of crimes. (Augustine.)

Water alone can be an element; it cannot be a sacrament until the word is added to the element, so that it becomes a sacrament.

[Col. 0999A] It is asked why the sacrament of baptism was instituted, and why circumcision—which is thought to have been established in its place—was removed or changed when baptism succeeded it. For if sins were formerly forgiven through circumcision, just as now through baptism, what need was there for circumcision itself to be changed when the sacrament of baptism succeeded it? Why is it believed that what was received accomplished less, while what was neglected is affirmed to have caused no less harm?

For just as it is now said through the Gospel, “Unless someone is born again from water and the Holy Spirit, he will not enter the kingdom of God” (John 3), so formerly it was said through the Law: “The male whose flesh of the foreskin has not been circumcised—that person shall perish from his people” (Genesis 17). Unless perhaps the distinction is that the one who is not baptized is said to be excluded from the kingdom of God, whereas the one who is not circumcised is remembered as destined to perish.

Who would not understand that baptism confers something more than circumcision for this reason: circumcision, once received, could free only from perdition, whereas baptism can also lead the reborn to glory? For those ancient Fathers who had received the justification of the sacrament of circumcision were indeed preserved from perdition, but they were not led to the glory of the kingdom until the one came who, extinguishing the fiery sword with his blood, reopened the way to paradise and, going before all who believed in him, first opened the gate of the heavenly kingdom.

But it must be understood that no one has ever been saved from the beginning except by being baptized in some manner. Some were baptized, like Abel, in the shedding of blood; many figuratively, like Noah, in the outpouring of the flood; many by a sign, like Abraham and his descendants; many in the Holy Spirit, like Christians in the immersion of water.

Baptism confers more in this respect: those who have been reborn and depart from this life it sends immediately to the kingdom. Yet this is granted through the power of the blood poured out, which sanctifies the water itself.

Therefore, if someone wishes to say that circumcision was changed into baptism so that baptism might accomplish what circumcision could not, it may perhaps be answered appropriately that the additional benefit found in baptism does not come from baptism itself, but is fulfilled through the passion of Christ, which sanctifies baptism. Circumcision itself could have done the same if Christ’s passion had been joined to it for the cooperation of sanctification.

For in baptism, insofar as this concerns the power of baptism, forgiveness of your sins is received just as in circumcision, because, as has been said, the opening of the way to the heavenly homeland after justification is granted through Christ’s cross.

The forgiveness of sins is indicated by the teachers as being possible in twelve ways.

The first forgiveness is that by which we are baptized in water, according to the saying: “Unless someone is born again from water and the Holy Spirit, he cannot see the kingdom of God” (John 3).

The second is the affection of love, as in the saying: “Her many sins are forgiven, because she loved much” (Luke 7).

The third is the fruit of almsgiving, according to this: “Just as water extinguishes fire, so almsgiving extinguishes sin” (Ecclesiasticus 3).

The fourth is the pouring out of tears, the Lord saying: “Because he wept in my sight and walked sorrowfully before me, I will not bring evil in those days” (1 Kings 21).

The fifth is confession of crimes, as the Psalmist says: “I said, ‘I will confess my injustices to the Lord,’ and you forgave the wickedness of my sin” (Psalm 31).

The sixth is affliction of heart and body, as the Apostle consoles us: “I handed such a man over to Satan, so that his spirit might be saved on the day of the Lord” (1 Corinthians 5).

The seventh is amendment of conduct—that is, renunciation of sins—as the Gospel bears witness: “You have become well; do not sin any longer, lest something worse happen to you” (John 5).

The eighth is the intercession of the saints. Hence the saying: “If anyone is sick, let him bring in the presbyters of the Church, and let them pray over him. For the continual prayer of a righteous person is very powerful” (James 5).

The ninth is mercy and the merit of faith; hence this: “Blessed are the merciful, for they shall obtain mercy” (Matthew 5).

The tenth is conversion and the salvation of others, as James confirms: “Whoever turns a sinner back from the error of his way will save his soul from death,” and so forth (James 5). Yet it is better for you to be weak and lead a solitary life than to perish with many.

The eleventh is our indulgence and forgiveness, permitted by Christ the Truth, who says: “Forgive, and you will be forgiven” (Luke 6).

The twelfth is the passion of the martyrs, the only hope of salvation, and the forgiveness granted to the crucified thief, the Lord saying: “Amen, amen, I say to you, today you will be with me in paradise” (Luke 23).

[Col. 1000C] It is therefore clear that all the sacraments are signs of a certain spiritual grace that is given through them. Moreover, as the course of time progresses, the signs of spiritual graces ought always to be formed so as to become increasingly evident and to be explained more fully, so that knowledge of the truth might grow together with the effect of salvation.

Thus, under the law of nature, the first sacraments were given: tithes, sacrifices, and offerings. In the tithe, the forgiveness of sins was signified; in sacrifices, the mortification of the flesh; and in offerings, the presentation of a gift through a work.

But this signification was obscure in the sacrament of the tithe, where a person offered part of what he possessed and retained part, so that in this way he might attribute to himself what was imperfection and defect, while imputing to God what pertained to goodness.

The nine parts retained signified this, because the number nine is a sign of imperfection, falling short of the perfect number ten. But because the sign of correction in the tithe was obscure, circumcision was given, so that the power of justification might be demonstrated more clearly. The man was commanded to remove from his flesh not something superfluous, but the sign of what was superfluous in man, so that through this he might recognize that the guilt which nature drew through that bodily member was cleansed by grace through the sacrament of circumcision.

But because circumcision can cut away only the outward enormities, and cannot cleanse the inward filth of pollution, the laver of water came after circumcision, cleansing everything, so that perfect righteousness might be prefigured.

Again, because the cleansing of the former people, who served under fear, was laborious, the sacrament of circumcision in the flesh, which involves pain, was given to them. But for the new people, who serve through will and love, the sacrament of justification in the laver of water, which has a pleasant purification, was appointed.

[Col. 1001] THE FIRST PART ENDS.

THE ABBREVIATED EXPOSITIONS OF THE SUNDAY GOSPELS, BOOK 2 OF THE EXCERPTS, BEGIN.

THE CHAPTERS OF BOOK 2 OF THE EXCERPTS FROM THE FATHERS OF LORD WERNER, ABBOT, BEGIN, FROM THE FIRST SUNDAY AFTER THE OCTAVE OF PENTECOST UNTIL THE ADVENT OF THE LORD.

[Col. 1001A]

I. A twofold exposition of the Gospel: “There was a certain rich man.” And concerning the partridge bird. Then another sermon on the punishments of souls. Also on the places of punishment. Also, a sermon on the rich man and the poor man.

II. A twofold exposition of the Gospel: “A certain man made a great supper.” Also, a sermon on the Lord’s body divided into four parts. On the sacrament of Christ’s body and blood. When the sacrament of Christ’s body and blood was instituted. Whether he delivered his mortal or immortal body. Whether it was Christ’s body that Judas received through the dipped morsel. That the sacrament of the altar is both a figure, insofar as concerns the appearance of bread and wine, and the reality, insofar as concerns the truth of Christ’s body. That there are three things in the sacrament of the altar: the appearance of bread and wine, the truth of Christ’s body, and spiritual grace. Why he instituted the sacrament of his body and blood under the appearance of bread and wine. How the change of bread and wine into Christ’s body is to be understood. That when Christ’s body appears to be divided, it is divided only according to appearance; in itself it remains whole, and just as the whole is in each part, so in the separated places there is one and the same body. What those three portions signify that are made from Christ’s body in the sacrament of the altar. That the things which appear unworthy in Christ’s body occur only according to appearance. What happens to Christ’s body, and to the body and bodily presence of Christ, after the sacrament has been received.

III. An exposition of the Gospel: “Tax collectors were drawing near to Jesus.” Also, a sermon on the fall of the first man, and the question: if he did not possess perseverance, how was he without fault? Also concerning what grace he received and many other causes; on repentance and envy.

IV. An exposition of the Gospel: “Be merciful.” Also, a sermon on the alternation of mercy and truth, accusing and defending one another on either side. On lovers of mercy. On hypocrites.

V. An exposition of the Gospel: “When the crowds pressed in.” Also, a sermon on the Church. Also, on the same subject: on ecclesiastical teachers, their teaching and examples; on those who teach well and live badly; on angry teachers; on proud teachers; on the discernment of teaching; and on the silence of teachers.

VI. An exposition of the Gospel: “Amen, I say to you, unless it abounds.” Also, a sermon on anger and on the nature of the torments of Gehenna. Also, on Gehenna: that the bodily fire of Gehenna will torment not only the body but also the spirit; that the fire of Gehenna will shine upon some but not upon others; and that the fire of Gehenna was created from the beginning. Also, on gifts.

VII. A twofold exposition of the Gospel: “I have compassion on the crowd.” Also, a sermon on five periods of seven years. Also, on seven petitions against seven vices. Also, on petitions appropriate to the present life and those appropriate to the future life.

VIII. An exposition of the Gospel: “Beware of false prophets.” Also, a sermon on lying. Also, on false prophets. Also, on good and evil; and another sermon on the same subject.

IX. An exposition of the Gospel: “A certain rich man had a steward.” Also, a sermon on four debtors. Also, on mercy.

X. A twofold exposition of the Gospel: “When the Lord drew near to Jerusalem, seeing it.” Also, a sermon on Elijah and Jezebel. Also, on the words of Wisdom: “Come over to me, all.”

XI. A twofold exposition of the Gospel: “Two men went up into the temple.” Also, a sermon on David’s words: “He established ascents in his heart”; and on three ascents and descents. Also, on boasting and compunction.

XII. A twofold exposition of the Gospel: “Jesus went out from the region of Tyre.” Also, a sermon on priests, the six ages of the world, and the sacraments of baptism divided into two parts.

XIII. A twofold exposition of the Gospel: “Blessed are the eyes that see what you see.” Also, a sermon on the words: “Go forth, daughters of Zion.” And on three visions of Christ. Also, another sermon on the aforesaid words: “Go forth.” Also, on the words of Saint Augustine, by which some rashly assert that the righteous in the future kingdom of God will see God with bodily eyes. Also, how Saint Augustine presents and explains the statements of Saint Ambrose on the same question. Also, the opinions of Cassiodorus and Jerome concerning the future vision of God.

XIV. An exposition of the Gospel: “As Jesus went to Jerusalem, he passed through.” Also, a sermon on the seven kinds of leprosy. Also, a moral interpretation concerning Naaman the Syrian and the seven washings in the Jordan.

XV. An exposition of the Gospel: “No one can serve two masters.” Also, a sermon: The comparison of God with the devil concerning the right of God and man. Also, on the two masters and the two cities, and so forth. Also, examples from birds: the swallow, the crow, the eagle, the coot, the turtledove, the vulture, bees, the nightingale, the owl, the bat, and the rooster. Also, examples from herbs: lilies, the olive, wormwood, hellebore, aconite, and others.

XVI. An exposition of the Gospel: “Jesus went into the city of Nain.” Also, a sermon on the dying; and a sermon on the departure of souls divided into two parts. Also, on death: what death is, and the three kinds of death. Also, on the origin of the soul.

XVII. An exposition of the Gospel: “When Jesus entered a house.” Also, a sermon on avarice. Also, on two kinds of humility, and on the humility of those who read the Scriptures. Also, on the commendation of humility and an attack upon pride, and on two kinds of pride.

XVIII. An exposition of the Gospel: “The Sadducees came to Jesus.” Also, a sermon on love divided into two parts. Also, on the soul: why it is called soul; on the designation of the mind; on the designation of the understanding; on the designation of the spirit; and on the definition of the soul.

XIX. An exposition of the Gospel: “Jesus went up into a boat and crossed over.” Also, a sermon on faith: what faith is, what knowledge of faith is, and on three degrees of each. Also, on the forgiveness of sins, and whether priests, who are human beings, can forgive sins—a sermon divided into three parts.

XX. A twofold exposition of the Gospel: “Jesus was speaking with his disciples in parables.” Also, a sermon on the sacrament of marriage; on the origin of marriage and the reason for its institution; and on the twofold institution of marriage.

XXI. An exposition of the Gospel: “There was a certain royal official.” Also, a sermon on God’s scourges and the twofold striking. Also, on the weakness of the flesh and on enduring divine correction.

XXII. A twofold exposition of the Gospel: “The kingdom of heaven is like a king who made.” Also, a sermon on the forgiveness of sins divided into two parts.

XXIII. An exposition of the Gospel: “When he had lifted up”—reserved for the middle of Lent. Also, two sermons belonging to the same Sunday. Also, sermons on the five degrees of discipline by which the righteous are exercised in this life; on the five states of the mutability of this life; and on the five virtues of the soul.

XXIV. An exposition of the Gospel for the Dedication of a church: “Jesus entered and was passing through.” Also, sermons for the Dedication of a Church:

The first concerns the things visibly performed in it, and then their mystery, which is divided into two parts.

The second concerns the same subject, and the three silences, together with other ecclesiastical mysteries.

The third concerns the same subject, and the seven columns of Wisdom, together with many other mysteries of the Church, divided into two parts.

The fourth concerns the same subject, the mystery of Adam’s sleep, the openings in the rock, the table of the Presence-Bread, and many other significations.

The fifth concerns the same subject and Ezekiel’s vision, where he had been taken up by the Spirit and led onto a mountain; the twelve gems; and the meaning of ecclesiastical things, divided into two parts.

The sixth concerns the same subject, and the three dedications of Solomon, Jesus the priest, and Judas Maccabeus, together with their mysteries, divided into two parts.

The seventh sermon properly concerns the dedication of the altar. In it are noted the various degrees of those who are in the active and contemplative life, the two altars of holocaust and incense, their anointing, and many other highly useful matters. This sermon is also divided into two parts.

[Col. 1003] THE CHAPTERS OF BOOK 2 END.

## FIRST SUNDAY AFTER THE OCTAVE OF PENTECOST

According to Luke.

[Col. 1003A] “There was a certain rich man, and he was clothed in purple and fine linen, and he feasted splendidly every day,” and so forth (Luke 16).

In riches, the desire of the eyes is signified; in expensive clothing, the pride of life; in splendid feasting, the desire of the flesh. Therefore this rich man, as though unknown to God, is not identified by name.

What kind of greed is this, when even the beasts have a limit? They snatch only when they are hungry; but when they feel full, they spare their prey. The avarice of the rich is insatiable: it always snatches and is never satisfied. It fears neither God nor respects man. It spares neither father, recognizes no mother, obeys no brother, and keeps faith with no friend. It oppresses the widow and seizes the property of the orphan.

What madness it is to acquire gold and lose heaven! Yet this man is not reproved for having taken what belonged to another, but for not having given what belonged to him, although in the Law it is not stinginess but robbery that is condemned.

Sea shells, cut around with iron, emit purple tears with which wool is dyed, from which purple cloth is woven. Byssus is a kind of very white and very soft linen, which the Greeks call *papaten*.

“And there was a certain beggar named Lazarus, who lay at his gate, full of sores, desiring to be filled with the crumbs that fell from the rich man’s table, and no one gave him any. But dogs also came and licked his sores.”

He could neither drive the dogs away from himself nor find a visitor who would drive them away. Observe that when parables do not supply proper names, and the Lord, by approving the humility of this poor man, gives him a name, this is not a parable but an account of an actual event.

The rich man, fastidious and disgusted, recoils from the beggar’s sores, lest amid his costly banquets and perfumed guests he have to endure the stench of sores being licked by dogs. Since the poor man lay before his gate, the rich man’s failure to pity him, though he saw him, adds a heap to his condemnation. Conversely, the poor man is tested daily by seeing the rich man. For the greater testing of the poor man, poverty and sickness afflict him together with the sight of the rich man’s abundance and the absence of any consolation offered to him.

Therefore we must beware of despising the poor, even if we see things in them that are blameworthy, because perhaps those whom weakness of character wounds are healed by the medicine of poverty.

[Col. 1005B] “And it happened that the beggar died and was carried by the angels into Abraham’s bosom. But the rich man also died and was buried in hell.”

Abraham’s bosom is the rest of blessed poor people; the burial of the proud and merciless in hell is the depth of punishments. Hence Gregory, in Book 12 of *Job*: “We do not say that the souls of the righteous descended into hell to be held in places of punishment, but that they rested in the higher places.”

The same author, Book 13: Job calls the weariness with which the righteous desired to see the Savior “darkness,” when he says: “In the darkness I have made my bed” (Job 17).

The same, in Book 8: “Just as a cloud is consumed and passes away, so the one who descends to the underworld will not ascend” (Job 7). It is as though Job were speaking openly, saying: The one who runs toward destruction in pride fails as he rushes upward. If guilt once drags him into punishment, mercy does not afterward restore him to pardon.

“Then, lifting up his eyes while he was in torments, he saw Abraham from far away, and Lazarus in his bosom.”

Since Abraham is called our father according to faith, Abraham’s bosom was the assembly of believers awaiting their deliverer, to which Lazarus, made rich from a beggar, was conveyed by the ministry of angels. But the unbelievers, placed according to the variety of their faults in different dwellings at the bottom of punishments, see the faithful above them resting at a distance, because they cannot reach that place by merit.

“And crying out, he said: ‘Father Abraham, have mercy on me and send Lazarus to dip the tip of his finger in water and cool my tongue, because I am tormented in this flame.’”

Just as the Divinity is figuratively said, by metaphor, to have eyes, a tongue, fingers, and other human limbs, so too are separated souls spoken of in these terms. The rich man therefore asks that his tongue be cooled—that is, that the punishment he deserved with his tongue be eased. Since talkativeness usually abounds at banquets, the rich man is said to burn grievously through his tongue.

He therefore desires to be touched by the tip of the finger—that is, to be refreshed even at the very end by the action of the righteous—and thus to receive merciful assistance through the water of God’s grace.

«And Abraham said to him: Son, remember that you received good things during your lifetime, and Lazarus likewise bad things. But now he is being comforted, while you are being tormented.» He is tormented before the judgment, because for the pleasure-loving person to be deprived of delights is punishment [Col. 1006A]. Abraham and the other faithful fathers do not at all strive to free from torments, according to the flesh, those whom they perceive to have deviated from the faith. Perhaps this rich man possessed some good that the happiness of his passing life rewarded, and Lazarus some evil that the fire of his poverty purged. Or he received gifts in this respect because he considered his joy to be passing happiness. The just, however, even if they possess good things in this world, because they burn with holy desires for eternal things, regard the things that are present as hardly good at all.

«And in all these things a great chasm has been fixed between us and you, so that those who wish to cross from here to you cannot, nor can anyone cross from there to here.» Chaos—or *chaus*, as the older manuscripts have it—signifies a permanent dissimilarity between the wills of the good and the wicked, because merits cannot be changed after death [Col. 1006B]. There is no doubt that the reprobate would wish to cross over from their punishments, just as they still desire to attain the lot of the blessed. But the crossing-over of the just is to go in mind, through mercy, to those placed in torment and to wish to free them. They cannot do so, however, because although the souls of the just possess mercy in accordance with the goodness of their nature, they are so firmly constrained by the righteousness of their Author that no compassion moves them toward the reprobate. Alternatively: the just wish to cross over—that is, many think that the just wish to cross over especially to rescue from punishments those to whom they were joined with greater affection in this life.

«And he said: I ask you, therefore, father, to send him to my father’s house. For I have five brothers there [Col. 1006C], so that he may testify to them, lest they too come to this place of torment.» Once hope for himself has been taken away from the man who is burning, his mind turns back to his relatives, because punishment sometimes teaches the mind of the reprobate, though uselessly, to love—so that they may then love their own even spiritually, although, while they loved sins, they did not love even themselves. Thus the rich man is made to retain, as punishment, both knowledge of the poor man whom he despised and remembrance of the brothers whom he left behind. The good know the good, the wicked the wicked, the good the wicked, and the wicked the good. In this knowledge, the reward of both parties increases, so that the good rejoice all the more because they see those whom they loved rejoicing with them, while the wicked, when they are tormented together with those whom they loved in this world [Col. 1006D], are consumed not only by their own punishment but also by that of the others. Something still more wondrous occurs among the elect: they recognize not only those whom they knew here, but, as though seen and known, they recognize good people whom they had never seen.

«And Abraham said to him: They have Moses and the prophets; let them listen to them. But he said: No, father Abraham; but if someone goes to them from the dead, they will repent.» This rich man begins to be a teacher too late, when he no longer has time either to learn or to teach. And because he had despised the words of God, he supposes that his followers cannot hear them.

«But he said to him: If they do not listen to Moses and the prophets, neither will they believe if someone rises from the dead.» Those who despise the words of the Law refuse to believe even one who has been raised [Col. 1007A]. This rich man signifies the Jewish people, who possessed the worship of life outwardly and used the delights of the Law they had received to no purpose. Lazarus, full of sores, is the Gentile people, who, when converted to God, confess their sins and, as though through broken skin, expel outwardly the poison that had been hidden within. Lazarus desired the crumbs of the rich man, and no one gave them to him, because proud Israel despised the Gentile people. While Israel swelled with pride over the teaching of the Law as over possessions received, words flowed from him concerning knowledge like crumbs falling from a table. In sacred discourse, dogs are ordinarily understood as preachers, who, when they instruct those confessing their sins, touch the wound of the mind, as it were, with their tongue. And when, by speaking, they rebuke people for their sins, they bring them back to salvation, just as dogs treat wounds by touching them with the tongue [Col. 1007B]. Hence Lazarus is appropriately interpreted as “helped,” because those Gentiles are helped who cure their wounds through correction by the tongue. The licking of the dogs’ tongues may also signify flatterers, who lick wounds when they magnify our evils with depraved approval.

Abraham’s bosom signifies the repose of heaven, in which those coming from east and west recline with Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob; but the children of the kingdom, clothed in purple and fine linen, will be cast outside. The unbelieving people held the Law in their mouths but scorned to keep it in their deeds, and for this reason they will burn more intensely. The rich man, begging for a drop of water in the next life, says that he has five brothers, because the Jewish people, already condemned in large part, know that their followers have been left on earth, devoted either to the five books of Moses understood carnally or to the five bodily senses [Col. 1007C]. Just as an innumerable multitude of saints is understood through the five virgins and the one hundred fifty-three fish, so in the five brothers of the rich man a multitude of many thousands of the Jewish people is understood—those whom he grieves do not rise to spiritual understanding. He therefore wishes Lazarus, or another of the faithful, to be sent to them; but they will not believe him if they do not listen to Moses and the prophets. The Lord rose from the dead, but the Jewish people, because they did not believe Moses, scorned to believe the Lord. And because they refused to understand Moses’ words spiritually, they did not reach the one whom Moses had foretold. Hence the Truth says: «If you believed Moses, you would surely believe me also» (John 5).

### An exposition on the same subject

[Col. 1007D] «Many say: Who will show us good things?» (Psalm 4.) Truly, beloved, many desire to hear the words of God, but, alas, there are few who will speak them; indeed, what is more grievous, most people, while they neither wish nor know how to proclaim the word of life, persecute those who speak or do good things. They abhor the truth of Christ to such an extent that they disdain even to hear anyone speak about him. And because the word of life torments them—that is, Christ, the Word of God—it separates them from his kingdom as darkness is separated from light. And when they are excluded from the kingdom of God, they must in every respect be shut up with the devil, the author of envy, in the prison of Tartarus.

If there were no Scripture, today’s Gospel alone would suffice the faithful as an example of life. For the Lord relates that a certain man abounded in great riches [Col. 1008A], feasted sumptuously every day, and denied poor Lazarus, who was also covered with sores, the crumbs falling from his table. When he died, he was handed over to hell. Lazarus, however, was placed in Abraham’s bosom. Thus, when the rich man saw himself grievously tormented by the flames and Lazarus rejoicing in Abraham’s embrace, he begged Abraham with a great wail to send Lazarus to drip a drop of water from his little finger and cool his burning tongue. But because here he had denied the beggar a crumb of bread, there the beggar himself did not deserve a drop of water. After he had despaired of himself, he prayed for the salvation of his brothers. Abraham indicated that they possessed the writings of Moses and the prophets, and affirmed that if they did not believe them, they would not believe the dead either, even if they went to them (Luke 16).

This man is implied to have been a king, since he is mentioned as clothed in purple [Col. 1008B], because in former times only kings used purple. But since “king” is derived from ruling, and he himself was subject to the vices of sin, he is called not a king but a man, because he served only gluttony and lust, like an irrational animal. His name is not given, because he is not written with the just in the book of the living. Lazarus, however, is called poor because his name was found written in heaven.

The rich man is read to have been buried in hell because hell is said to be beneath the earth, and whoever is plunged there is covered by the earth, just as a body is covered with dust when it is buried in a tomb. Abraham’s bosom was a place of rest free from punishments, in which the assembly of the saints awaited Christ. Before Christ’s coming, all descended into hell. And if Abraham was with Lazarus among the dead [Col. 1008C], the question arises how the rich man, lifting up his eyes, saw them from afar (ibid.). Two hells are mentioned: the lower and the upper. The lower was where the souls of the reprobate were tormented; the upper was where the elect awaited Christ. Of the lower it is written: «You have rescued my soul from the lowest hell» (Psalm 85); of the upper: «Bring my soul out of hell to confess your name» (Psalm 141).

In the lower hell there are said to be nine particular punishments: unquenchable fire; the incomparable horror of cold; immortal worms; unbearable stench; striking hammers; tangible darkness; the confusion of sins; the sight of demons; the hearing of those who mock; and fiery bonds for each of the limbs [Col. 1008D]. The upper hell, however, was the farthest region of the earth, a place near hell but separated from its punishments, where the just could be seen by the wicked who were in the lower hell.

Some doubt whether souls recognize one another in that life. But since the rich man recognized Abraham, whom he had never seen before, it is clear that the wicked recognize the good there. Since Abraham also recognized the rich man there, whom he had never seen before, it is evident that the good likewise recognize the wicked there.

Again, it is asked whether the souls of the just understand anything about the living, or whether the souls of the wicked perceive anything concerning the living. But since Abraham says, «You received good things during your lifetime, and Lazarus bad things,» it is clear that good people observe the deeds of the living, especially since they immediately come to the aid of those who invoke them [Col. 1009A]. Since the rich man pours out prayers for his brothers who live wickedly, it is clear that the damned know certain things, though not everything, about the living.

Before the judgment, the reprobate see the elect in joy, so that they may grieve more deeply because they neglected to attain it; and the elect see the reprobate in punishment, so that they may rejoice more fully because, with the help of God’s grace, they escaped it. After the judgment, the good will always see the wicked; the wicked, however, will never see the good.

It should be noted that the one in whose every limb the fire was burning specifically asks for relief for his tongue (Luke 16). This makes it understood that each person will suffer greater torments in that limb in which he practiced sin more extensively. And because here he had surrendered himself to gluttony and continually served loquacity, it is rightly said that he is tormented more in his tongue, which he had always let loose in empty talk [Col. 1009B].

It should also be noted that he is nowhere said to have taken anything from anyone, but only to have failed to give what belonged to him. And if, brothers, the one who gives away none of his possessions is punished with so great a penalty, what should we think about those who are always ready to seize what belongs to others? Scripture says of those who eat idly: «The furrows will cry out against them» (Job 31); of thieves and plunderers: «The earth will be turned for them into burning pitch and sulfur» (Isaiah 34).

This rich man did some good things for human praise and received a good reward for them in temporal goods; Lazarus, however, had committed certain evils, which he paid for here through bodily suffering.

**(Gregory.)** Consider, I beg you, beloved, how strict the judgments of God are. Behold: he asks for a drop of water who gave no crumbs of bread [Col. 1009C]. And because he denied the crumbs, he did not obtain the drop. Therefore, my lords, you to whom God has granted the riches of this age, beware lest riches possess you as servants and drag you empty of true riches to Tartarus. Possess your riches by distributing them to the needy, and acquire true riches through these deceptive ones. It is not evil to possess riches, but it is very serious to turn them to wicked use.

David, Hezekiah, and Josiah, for example, as kings, and others like them, possessed many riches, but through them acquired imperishable riches for themselves. Cyrus, Antiochus, and men like them were rich in possessions because they turned them to pride and luxury. And because here they had their kingdom in place of heaven, when they died they found nothing in their hands [Col. 1009D], but with that rich man they will grieve in eternal poverty.

Of such people it is said: «It is easier for a camel to pass through the eye of a needle than for a rich man to enter the kingdom of heaven» (Matthew 19). The Lord tells of a certain man who had acquired very many riches. He demolished his barns, built larger ones, gathered all his goods there, and said to his soul that it should feast and rejoice because he would live for many years and spend joyful days in these goods and pleasures. That same night the wretched man died, leaving his riches to others; carrying only his sins with him, he entered Tartarus (Luke 12). What did riches profit this man, who neglected to acquire eternal things through them?

People are divided into four classes. Some are rich and are saved, such as Abraham and Job; some are rich and are condemned, such as Cenchres, Pharaoh, and Nebuchadnezzar [Col. 1010A]; some are poor and will be enriched, such as Lazarus and the monks; and some, such as Judas and other fraudulent people, are handed over to eternal miseries.

The rich man who was clothed in purple and fine linen is also the Jewish people, who gloried in the kingdom and priesthood of the Law. Through purple, the kingdom is signified; through fine linen, the priesthood. He feasted splendidly every day when, in outward worship, he was fattened on the dishes of the Law and the prophets.

The poor man prefigures the Gentile people, who were wounded by the sores of sins. He did not receive the crumbs falling from the table because he did not hear even the smallest sentence from sacred Scripture. The dogs came and licked his sores because the apostles, God’s dogs, instructed him abundantly in the Law of God and closed the sores of sins with the medicine of repentance [Col. 1010B].

The poor man is carried into Abraham’s bosom, while the rich man is buried in hell, because «many faithful will come from east and west and recline with Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob in the kingdom of heaven; but the children of the kingdom,» namely, the faithless Jews, «will be cast into the outer darkness» (Matthew 8), because they did not believe Moses, the prophets, or Christ rising from the dead.

Even now the wars of kings and their victories are read, so that through them we may be instructed to wage war against sins and become victors over vices. It is read that a certain man had two wives, one fertile and the other barren, and finally the barren one bore Samuel (1 Kings 5). He removed Eli from the priesthood, deposed Saul from the kingdom, and raised David by anointing him with oil and granting him the scepter [Col. 1010C]. David struck down the strong Goliath with a sling and a stone, cut off his head with his own sword, and, after overcoming many enemies, prepared for the Lord an outstanding tabernacle. His son Solomon built a temple renowned throughout the whole world and gave peace to all nations.

The man who joined two wives to himself is God, who betrothed the Synagogue and the Church to himself. Of these, the Synagogue was fertile, because it generated the Jewish people for carnal ceremonies; but the Church, long barren, generated a son—the Christian people—for spiritual observances. This son—the Christian people—rejected Eli from the priesthood and Saul from the kingdom, because it alienates the unbelieving Jewish people from Christ’s priesthood and the Gentile people who persecute the faithful from the kingdom of God [Col. 1010D]. David—that is, the true and desirable Christ—has long been worshiped as king, anointed by the Father with the oil of gladness above his companions.
