He struck down the strong Goliath with a sling (1 Kings 7), when by his humanity he shattered the strong devil. The sling was Christ’s humanity, encircled and whirled about by sufferings. The stone that pierced Goliath’s forehead was his divinity, which pierced the jaw of Leviathan. Moreover, he cut off his head with a sword when, through kings and philosophers—his weapons—converted to the faith, he weakened the devil’s power and drove him away from idolatry.

This David waged many wars when he trained his soldiers, the apostles and martyrs, to fight against Jews, pagans, and heretics. Having struck down the enemies, he made a tabernacle for the Lord. In the warfare of this king, beloved [Col. 1011A], let us fight against vices with the weapons of virtues, so that, crowned with the reward of life, we may triumph in the heavenly kingdom. For human life upon earth is warfare, and its days are like those of a hired laborer. A soldier fights for a benefit; a hired laborer works for an annual reward. So let us, beloved, fight for the benefit of the eternal King and labor intensely for the reward of everlasting life.

David bore the type of Christ, who lived among human beings and fought against enemies for his bride, the Church. Solomon expressed the figure of Christ already reigning in the glory of the Father and triumphing with the saints in perpetual peace. Thus, when the enemies have been defeated as David defeated them, Christ will, just as Solomon built the temple, at the final judgment gather the heavenly Jerusalem from angels and human beings, building it as a city after the enemies have been condemned.

There is a bird called the partridge that broods eggs stolen from another bird. After the chicks hatch, they return to their mother when they hear her voice. God the Father placed the first two human beings in the nest of paradise like two eggs. The devil, the destroyer of souls, stole and brooded them, teaching them every wickedness after they had been seduced away from God. When they came out of the shell, they returned to their mother, when, having come out of the garment of sin, they returned to their mother—that is, to Christ, the wisdom of God.

## Sermon on the punishments of souls

Some think that souls cannot be tormented by bodily punishments except through bodies and while remaining in bodies. Therefore they believe that souls stripped from their bodies endure no other punishments except those inflicted by conscience accusing them within [Col. 1011C]. But the most truthful authority of sacred discourse and the testimony of Catholic truth prove that souls are even now tormented by corporeal and material fire, before receiving their bodies. For if fire is said to have been prepared for demons, who are corporeal spirits, what is surprising if souls stripped from their bodies are tormented by corporeal fire?

“But how,” they ask, “can souls without bodies suffer from corporeal things?” Let us answer: We do not know how this can happen. Is it therefore not true because we do not know how it happens? Yet what is surprising if souls suffer outside bodies? If they are harmed when they are struck while clothed in bodies, why should they not be harmed when they are struck after being stripped of them? If they can be affected when between them and that by which they are affected there is something intermediate through which they are affected, is it not entirely probable that they should be affected much more when they are joined immediately to that by which they are affected?

Nevertheless, we must not inquire into all these matters in such a way as to attempt always to examine by our own reasoning what we are commanded to believe. Holy Scripture, the teacher of our faith, tells us this: Whatever more we seek, let us accept; let us not contradict it.

Blessed Gregory says that they burn in the very thing in which they see themselves burning. What do you think this means—that souls burn in the very thing in which they see their own burning? In bodily matters this is not so: whoever sees a fire does not thereby feel its heat. What, then, is that vision of the soul which feels everything it sees—or, if not everything, at least what it sees for punishment [Col. 1012A]?

Is it because the soul’s sense, when it goes forth through the body, perceives in different ways because it perceives through different instruments? For this reason it does not perceive certain things situated at a distance through bodily sense, because the instrument of bodily sense is not sufficient for perceiving them. Sense fails wherever the instrument is no longer sufficient. Therefore those senses that possess large and adequate instruments have greater power in perceiving. The eye sees what is far away; touch, however, can feel only what is immediately joined to it. If the instrument of touch were as perceptive as that of sight, touch would perceive things at a distance just as sight does.

What follows, then? Where there will be no diversity of instruments, why should every sense not be equal, so that seeing is there when there is touching, and touching when there is suffering? This, however, is to be understood only of those souls that can be affected by torments because, when they depart from here, they carry with them the capacity to suffer, having been corrupted by vices.

Since we have said that the soul can be affected by sense at a distance, we therefore place something like spatial intervals between bodily punishments and the soul itself, because the soul, which by its nature is not extended by any dimension, is proved to be present wherever it is present by sense, and to be present there through itself. Since there is no place in the soul itself, there is no place between it and a place.

Yet, because none of these matters can be investigated by human reasoning, as has been said, let us strengthen our minds in what unwavering faith proves: sinful souls that did not correct their guilt in this life suffer punishment after this life. Although we may not understand how that punishment is sensed by them, if it is just, why should they sense it any less merely because we do not understand it? For it makes no difference from what things they suffer, but how much they suffer, since the force of pain lies not in the instrument of torment but in the sensation of the one suffering.

What would it profit if the external material of tortures were absent, yet the pain of those suffering were for that reason no less? Why do you fear fire and flame, unless because you fear being burned? If wounds and blows did not hurt, who would fear weapons or missiles? See, then, that all these things from which pain can arise are feared only because of pain. Remove the sensation of pain, and there is nothing to fear [Col. 1012D].

God could therefore have given souls a sensation of pain even without material elements for their torment. But it is fitting that they be punished in the things in which they sinned: first without bodies, just as they perversely delighted in them; afterward in bodies, just as they acted wickedly through bodies.

## Sermon on the places of punishments

Just as God prepared bodily punishments for the torment of sinners, so he also distinguished bodily places for those bodily punishments. Since his external works ought to be not only instruments but also demonstrations of what he works invisibly, he therefore distinguished, by bodily places, both the torments of the wicked and the joys of the just.

Hell is therefore called *infernus* because it is below. For just as, according to the body, all lower things are heavier if they retain the order of their weight, so according to the spirit all lower things are sadder. Hence the origin of the name “hell” is also said to be explained in the Greek language from the fact that it possesses nothing pleasant. Just as the heart of an animal is in its middle, so hell is said to be in the middle of the earth.

Hell is the place of torments, while heaven is the place of joys. The place of torments is rightly below and the place of joys above, because guilt presses downward and justice lifts upward. The greatest torments have their place at the bottom; the greatest joys at the top. Intermediate good and evil are mixed in the middle—that is, in this world.

The lower hell is said to be a place at the bottom of the earth, prepared for the punishments of the damned [Col. 1013B]. Yet it is by no means certain in which part of it it is situated—that is, whether within its hollow or externally in some region surrounding it—although it appears more probable that it is placed beneath the earth, like a prison or a dark workhouse.

In this hell, unquenchable fire is prepared from the beginning of the world for the demons to be eternally tormented, a fire that requires no fuel in order to burn forever. In this fire, wicked human beings will also suffer eternal punishment with the demons, because while they were placed in this life they consented to sin with them. The souls of criminals, having departed from their bodies, are thought to be immediately thrust into this hell.

Conversely, the souls of the perfect and the just, and of those who depart from this life purified, are believed to be led without delay to heaven, where Jesus Christ, according to his humanity, sits in glory at the right hand of the Father. Thus it is written: «Wherever the body is, there the eagles will be gathered» (Matthew 24).

There is another punishment after death called purgatorial punishment. In it those who departed from this life with certain faults, but nevertheless as just persons destined for life, are tormented for a time in order to be purified. No place has been definitively assigned to them, except that it has often been shown, through many examples and revelations of souls placed in such punishment, that it is not exercised in this world.

Perhaps it will be more probable to believe that each person suffers punishment especially in those places in which he committed his guilt, as has often been demonstrated by many proofs. If there are other places of these punishments, however, they cannot easily be identified.

Blessed Augustine shows in the Epistle of Peter that the apostate angels, having fallen, were thrust into such depths until their final condemnation on the day of judgment. For what Peter calls the prison of the darkness of hell (2 Peter 2), Paul is believed to have called “darkness,” saying: «the rulers of these darknesses, the spiritual forces of wickedness in the heavenly places» (Ephesians 6).

We understand this prison, or these darknesses, to be this air. Hence they are also called aerial powers. In it the evil spirits are now bound in one respect before the day of the final judgment, insofar as they are constrained by the knowledge of their future condemnation, yet in another respect they are free, insofar as they are permitted, according to the moderation of divine dispensation, to devote themselves to tempting human beings, having been released for the time being from the greatest torments of Gehenna [Col. 1014A].

Concerning hell, where that eternal fire has been prepared for those to be tormented, blessed Gregory testifies in the *Book of Dialogues* that it is more probable to judge—as we have said—that it is beneath the earth, because Scripture says that no one was found in heaven, on earth, or under the earth who could open the sealed book.

It may reasonably be asked whether the souls of the damned—those who, because of a certain measure of wicked living, were less evil than the impious and most criminal—are immediately carried from their bodies to the places of hell [Col. 1014B], or whether, according to a hidden dispensation, they are temporarily kept in certain other punitive places and held back from the heavier torments of Gehenna. Thus, just as the good who are detained with faults in certain abodes do not immediately ascend to the joys of heaven, so too the less evil, although destined for damnation, may be held in certain lighter punishments assigned according to the measure of their faults and not immediately descend to the torments of hell.

There is no doubt concerning the perfectly good: when they depart, they pass immediately to joys. Similarly, there is no doubt concerning the very evil: when they depart from here, they descend without delay to the torments of hell. It is also certain concerning the good who are not perfect that they are now temporarily held back from the joys to come by certain punishments, until they are completely purified [Col. 1014C].

Concerning the imperfect, or the less evil, it is not certain where they now are, until, at the time of the universal resurrection, having received their bodies, they descend to those torments in which they will always be. For if they are said to be held back from those torments because they are less evil, one might, by the same reasoning, believe that they are not held back because they are destined for damnation. What purpose would delay serve where amendment and purification cannot occur? Yet because this matter is entirely hidden, it must by no means be rashly determined.

Let this suffice concerning the places of punishments and the punishments of souls.

## Sermon on the rich man and the poor man

It should be known that a Christian ought not to abound in riches but should always acknowledge himself to be poor. And if he possesses riches, he should know that they are not true riches, so that he may desire others. For whoever desires false riches does not seek the true. They are deceptive because they cannot remain with us for long. They are deceptive because they do not drive away the poverty of the mind. Only divine riches are true, because they make us rich in virtues.

Whoever seeks true riches is still poor, and rightly says: «I am poor and sorrowful» (Psalm 68). Again, the person who is poor and full of wickedness—what does he abound in? He is said to abound because he is displeased that he is poor, and justice itself seems to abound in his heart against the justice of God.

Earthly things are not true riches but beggary, because the more they abound, the more poverty increases, and greed enlarges the desire of the one who possesses them [Col. 1015A].

“The love of money grows as money itself grows.” (Juvenal, *Satire* 14, line 139.)

Concerning these riches it is written: «They will not profit on the day of vengeance, but justice will deliver from death» (Proverbs 11). And elsewhere: «Whoever hastens to become rich will not be innocent» (Proverbs 28).

The one to whom nothing is lacking is very rich. Whoever desires nothing lacks nothing. Therefore a certain wise man said:

“Who is rich? He who desires nothing. Who is poor? The greedy man.”

«Why, then, are these riches sought? No one wants to be rich except in order to become inflated among those with whom he lives, so that he may appear superior to them. The Lord questions the rich and the poor in the heart, not in the chest and the house. Let him possess many financial resources: if he is not exalted by them, he is poor. Let him possess nothing, yet desire and become inflated: God counts him among the rich and the reprobate. Hence the Lord says: It is easier for a camel to pass through the eye of a needle than for a rich man—that is, one who loves riches, even if he does not possess them—to enter the kingdom of God» (Matthew 19).

«For those who want to become rich fall into temptation and the devil’s snare» [Col. 1016A], and so forth (1 Timothy 6). «For the desire for money is the root of all evils» (ibid.), not gold or silver. Hence Solomon said: «He who loves riches will receive no fruit from them» (Ecclesiastes 5).

Therefore the Apostle immediately adds (1 Timothy 6): «But you, man of God, flee these things; pursue justice,» by giving each person what belongs to him; «piety,» by having compassion; «faith,» by not believing that the world is more than God; «love,» by loving God; «patience,» by enduring adversity; «gentleness,» by being harsh toward no one, but gentle. Have these qualities within you. For others, «fight the good fight of faith,» continually and with discernment; and for these things «take hold of eternal life»—that is, seek only that reward.

The greedy person loses all these things and possesses their opposites, because he loves to have more than is fitting [Col. 1016B]. For the faithful person, the whole world is a wealth of riches. Hear Paul: «As having nothing, yet possessing everything» (2 Corinthians 6). And he who provides us—not the rich of this age—with all things abundantly for enjoyment.

Whoever therefore wishes to be rich should not cling to a part, and he will possess the whole. Let him cling to the one who created the whole and who possesses the riches of which it is said: «The ransom of a man’s soul is his riches» (Proverbs 13). Whoever does not possess these is poor and cannot endure threats.

## The Second Sunday after Pentecost. According to Luke.

[Col. 1015]

[Col. 1015C] «A certain man made a great supper and invited many,» and so forth (Luke 14).

Almighty God, at the beginning of the world’s restoration, created two rational creatures—the angelic and the human—in order that they might know him and praise him perpetually. But because a large part of the angelic nature fell through the guilt of pride, it immediately became envious of human nature, led it into the fall of sin, and deprived it of the delights of paradise. Concerning this deprivation, the Lord’s parable says:

> “A certain man made a great supper and invited many.” Spiritually, this man is to be understood as God, of whom it is written: “He is a man, and who can know him?” And again: “A man was born in her, and the Most High himself founded her” (Ps. 86 [LXXXVI]) [Col. 1015D]. He is called a man on account of his humanity, because in his most gracious generosity he daily displays his grace to the human race. He made a great supper because he prepared unfailing satisfaction in eternal sweetness for elect souls. He invited many: first, by preaching to the Jews through himself; afterward, by calling the people of the nations to faith through the preaching of the apostles from the four regions of the world.

It should be noted, however, that calling takes place in three ways. The first mode of calling is from God; the second, through a human being; the third, through necessity. It is from God whenever divine inspiration, infused into our heart, sometimes even awakens us from sleep to desire eternal life and salvation, and urges us through most salutary compunction to follow God and cling to his commandments, just as we read that Abraham was called by the divine voice. For thus he said to him: “Go out from your land and from your kindred” (Gen. 12). In this same way Antony was summoned. For when he heard in church the Gospel saying, “Whoever does not hate father and mother” (Luke 14), and so forth, and also: “If you wish to be perfect, go, sell everything, give to the poor, and you will have treasure in heaven; and come, follow me” (Matt. 19), he immediately renounced everything and followed Christ, provoked by no exhortation or instruction.

The second mode of calling is when either by the examples of the saints or by admonitions we are inflamed with the desire for salvation. In this manner the children of Israel were freed from the affliction of Egypt through Moses [Col. 1016D]. The third occurs when temptations suddenly assail us—temptations that threaten the dangers of death, strike us through the loss and confiscation of possessions, or pierce us through the death of loved ones—and compel us, at least unwillingly, to hasten to the God whom, amid worldly prosperity, we had scorned to follow. Many examples of this are obvious in themselves.

Through this calling many are called, but few come, because many enter the Church through faith, but few are saved through action. And lest people have ignorance as an excuse, he sent his servant at supper time to tell those who had been invited to come. This servant, who is sent to invite others, signifies the order of preachers. While they announce the divine word within the Church, they call very many, as it were, to the supper [Col. 1017A]. For divine clemency was not content merely to prepare eternal delights for us; it also announced their sweetness to us through servants who had been sent.

The time of supper is the end of the age, that is, the time of which Paul says: “We are those upon whom the ends of the ages have come” (1 Cor. 10). Although among the ancients it was customary to eat only once a day, and this meal was called both lunch and supper, nevertheless, according to our customary speech, supper remains after lunch, while after supper no meal remains. Thus this supper not incongruously signifies the day of judgment, or that eternal banquet, to which those who are found worthy to arrive will hunger and thirst no more. Therefore we ought to hasten all the more eagerly to this supper [Col. 1017B], since we know that after it we shall find no other. For, to remove any distaste, he added, saying:

> “Because everything is ready.”

Everything indeed was ready because that singular Lamb had been slain, in whose preparation everything had gone before. Or everything was ready because no example of virtue necessary for our imitation has failed to be displayed in the deeds of the saints. We have already heard of Abel’s innocence, Abraham’s obedience, Isaac’s constancy, Jacob’s endurance, Joseph’s chastity, Moses’ gentleness, David’s mercy, and Job’s patience; and we have seen the Lord’s end.

> “And they all began together to make excuses.”

Those who did not wish to come make excuses, and so shut themselves out from the eternal banquet, which God freely offers to those who desire it, without being asked. All who love earthly things more than heavenly things make excuses, even if they say that they are striving toward heavenly things.

> “The first said to him: ‘I have bought a farm, and I must go out and see it. I ask you to hold me excused.’”

The farm signifies earthly property, which some purchase for themselves with great labor, or even at the cost of faith, either through pride or for the sake of bodily substance. He went out to see it because, abandoning inward contemplation, he thinks only about outward things.

> “And another said: ‘I have bought five yokes of oxen, and I am going to test them. Hold me excused.’”

The five senses of the body are rightly called five yokes because they are doubled in each sex [Col. 1017D]. Since these senses know only outward things and not inward ones, curiosity is rightly signified through them. Curiosity is a great vice: while it investigates the life of one’s neighbor, it leads the mind outward, postponing its own inner concerns.

It should be noted that when they say, “I ask you to hold me excused,” humility sounds in their voice; while, when they scorn to come, pride appears in their action. Thus the sinner who says, “Pray for me, a sinner,” but does not wish to abandon sin, suggests humility while remaining in pride.

> “And another said: ‘I have taken a wife, and therefore I cannot come.’”

In the wife, carnal pleasure is understood—not because marriage is not good for the propagation of offspring, but because some seek in a wife not the fruitfulness of children but the desires of pleasure. Marriage, therefore, is not condemned if integrity is called to a greater honor.

Likewise, in the purchased farm domination is indicated, and pride is chastised. The first man wished to dominate because he did not wish to have a lord. What is domination except rejoicing in one’s own power?

The five yokes belong to the senses: three are apparent, for there are two eyes, two ears, and two nostrils. In taste also there are two instruments, the tongue and the palate. The pleasure of the flesh, which pertains to touch, is doubled more secretly, for it is both external and internal. They are called yokes of oxen because earthly things are acquired through these senses, and oxen turn over the earth. There are also people who are unwilling to believe anything except what they perceive through their senses. The wife pertains to carnal pleasure, which impedes many.

[Col. 1018B]

> “Then the master of the household, becoming angry, said to his servant.”

Just as a king is said to become angry when he exercises vengeance upon sinners, so almighty God will appear angry with those whom he punishes for their sins.

> “And he said to his servant: ‘Go out quickly into the streets and lanes of the city, and bring in the poor, the weak, the blind, and the lame.’”

As there are as many varieties of conduct in this world as there are ways leading to the devil—the general road of perdition—so he says: “Go out to the ends of the roads,” as he says in another Gospel (Matt. 22), so that people of every condition may be called to faith. The grace of God is powerful enough to correct any barbarians in mind: it changed the heart of Nebuchadnezzar to a bestial disposition and again restored it to a human disposition.

He therefore sends them into the streets, lanes, and cities, inviting the poor, the weak, the blind, and the lame, so that no distinction of place or person may be made among those coming to the faith of Christ. For he shows that bodily weakness excludes no one from the kingdom of God, and that the person lacking the enticement to sin sins more rarely and is converted to God more quickly because he has nothing in the world in which to take pleasure.

Alternatively: the poor, weak, blind, and lame are called the Gentiles in comparison with the Jews, who ought to be rich, strong, enlightened, and upright through the law and the prophets—but falsely presume themselves to be so. He sends them into the streets when he calls sinners from the broader roads to the narrow way of life. He sends them into the lanes when he invites those whom the poverty of temporal goods calls. He sends them into the cities when he calls those who distinguish cultivated things from uncultivated things, who had learned to keep the law of nature through a suburban way of life.

[Col. 1018D]

> “And the servant said: ‘Lord, it has been done as you commanded, and there is still room.’ And the master said to the servant: ‘Go out into the roads and hedges, and compel them to enter, so that my house may be filled. For I tell you that none of those men who were invited shall taste my supper.’”

God’s house must be filled with the number of the predestined. But proud sinners, because they refused to come when invited, have irrecoverably excluded themselves. The Lord calls through himself, through angels, through patriarchs, through apostles, through miracles, and through scourges. Let no one scorn to come, lest, while invited, he make excuses and, when he wishes to enter, be unable to do so.

From the streets and lanes have come humbled sinners from the nations [Col. 1019A]; let heretics also come from the hedges. For those who build hedges seek divisions. Let them be dragged from the hedges and torn away from the thorns.

They do not wish to be compelled. “Let us enter,” they say, “by our own will.” The Lord did not command this, for he says: “Compel them to enter.” Let necessity be found outside; let willingness be born within. Thus the roads and hedges are understood as erroneous sects and heresies.

It is therefore clear that some are called and scorn to come; others are called and come; and others are compelled to enter. Those are called and scorn to come who receive the gift of understanding but do not follow that same understanding in their deeds. Those are called and come who perfect the grace of understanding they have received by putting it into practice. Those are compelled to enter whom the Church punishes temporally because they have turned backward after putting their hand to the plow.

## ANOTHER EXPOSITION OF THE SAME GOSPEL

> “Blessed are those who are invited to the marriage supper of the Lamb!” (Rev. 19.) The Gospel reports, beloved, that a certain man made a great supper and invited many. When everything was ready, he sent his servant to call those who had been invited. And they all began to make excuses. One said that he had bought a farm and was going to see it; another that he had acquired five yokes of oxen; another that he had taken a wife and therefore could not come. When he heard this, the master ordered the servant to go out into the streets and lanes and bring in the poor, the weak, the blind, and the lame. And when there was still room, he commanded the servant to compel those from the roads and hedges to enter, swearing that none of those who had been invited would taste his supper (Luke 14) [Col. 1019C].

The man who prepared a great supper and invited many is God, who became man for us and invited all nations to the food of the eternal banquet. He sent his servant to call people to the banquet when he sent Moses, through the law, to transform the people toward life.

But all make excuses for themselves from the supper, because they plainly refuse to appear at God’s banquet. For the first said that he had bought a farm and was going to see it. The Jewish people, as though buying a farm, acquired the promised land through carnal observances. He went out to see it when he left Egypt to possess it.

He also bought five yokes when he received twice five, yoked together by a twofold love, by which he ought to have cultivated the Lord’s field like an ox. But he went to test them when he strove to observe them only for earthly purposes.

He also took a wife because he joined the law to a carnal understanding, and therefore withdrew himself from God’s banquet.

The one who bought the farm also signifies the order of the Jewish rulers, who divided the land among the people and afterward gained the fortified places. The one who bought the five yokes of oxen signifies the subject people, who were bound by the yoke of the law into subjection. The one who took a wife signifies the Levitical order, to which the law was specially joined as a wife.

Since each of these is occupied with earthly business, they make excuses for themselves from God’s banquet. Therefore the master of the household commands the servant to go out into the streets and lanes of the city and bring in the poor and the weak.

The servant who is now sent signifies the order of the prophets. The city signifies Jerusalem, in which the ark of the covenant was revered and in which the temple stood, where sacrifices were offered by everyone. Its streets were the Israelites, who had spread themselves broadly through the twelve tribes. Its lanes were the Jews, who had confined themselves within the narrow limits of the two tribes.

Thus the prophets brought people in from the streets and lanes when they corrected the Israelites and Jews from their error through writings and words. These people were poor because they lacked virtues. They were weak because they languished under vices. They were blind because they did not see the meaning of the law. They were lame because, abandoning the worship of God, they turned aside after idols.

After these had been brought in, there was still room, and the Lord commanded the servant to go out into the roads and hedges and compel people to enter. The servant who is compelled to bring people in from the roads and hedges signifies the order of the apostles, who gathered many from the sects and rites of the Gentiles into the house of God [Col. 1020B].

The roads are the various sects of the philosophers; the hedges are the various rites of the pagans. People entered from these places under compulsion when the nations, rejecting idolatry through the signs and wonders of the apostles, believed in the true God. For the proconsul Paul entered under compulsion when the apostle Paul blinded a magician before him. Constantine entered under compulsion when Sylvester cured him of leprosy in baptism.

Therefore, when the nations have been brought in, they will dine with the Lord; but the Jews, unwilling to enter, will not taste the Lord’s supper.

And you, beloved, have been invited to God’s supper. See to it that, entangled in some business or hindered by someone’s friendship, you do not make yourselves excused from it. For we are servants of the great master of the household, sent by him; we invite you to the food of eternal satisfaction [Col. 1020C]. Therefore hasten all to enter the marriage of the Lamb before the door is closed, so that afterward it may never be opened to those who knock and desire to enter.

The Lord says: “If your right eye causes you to stumble, tear it out and throw it away from you. And if your foot causes you to stumble, cut it off and throw it away from you. It is better for you to enter life one-eyed, or weak, or lame, than to be thrown into Gehenna with two eyes, or two hands, or two feet, ‘where the fire is not extinguished and their worm does not die’” (Mark 9).

It should be noted that the Savior identifies three things: the eye, the hand, and the feet. Through these, the wretched are held back from God’s banquet, because either superiors, relatives, or subjects delay us from the Lord’s supper; these members signify them.

The eye that leads us is the priest, who directs us from the darkness of the world to the light of life. It is therefore called the right eye because it strives to lead us from the left to the right. If this eye attempts to lead us away from God’s way through heretical teaching and bring us into error, or to hold us back from God’s supper through a wicked example, it must be cast out from its assigned office as a useless member.

The right hand, through which we work, is a father, mother, wife, or any dearest friend, through whom we are helped in all things. If these in any way call us back from the banquet, let the zeal of God cut them away from us and cast them far from our constant service.

The foot by which we are carried is any subordinate, through whom we are supported in the necessities of life [Col. 1021A]. If this person in any way hinders us from God’s supper, he must be torn away from us and excluded far from our intimacy. It is much better to be saved without such people than to be consigned to everlasting fire with them. For whoever is the friend of such people is made an enemy of God, and whoever pleases these people is rejected by God in shame.

The person who bought the farm is one who serves only earthly profits and therefore withdraws from God’s supper. The person who bought the five yokes and went to test them is one who turns the five bodily senses, yoked in pairs, toward investigating the actions of others and turns aside from God’s banquet.

Hence it is written that Dinah, Jacob’s daughter, went out to see the women of the region and was violated by Shechem, the ruler of the city (Gen. 34). Let your fraternity, I ask, consider how grave a vice curiosity is [Col. 1021B]. Behold, the daughter of the great patriarch, while pursuing curiosity, is violated by a pagan man, and the city with all its people is destroyed by sword and flame.

Dinah is violated after going out when any soul, scrutinizing the actions of others with curiosity, is joined to the devil. The city with its people will be devastated by fire because the body of the curious person will be tormented in eternal fire together with evil deeds.

The person who took a wife is one who strives only to satisfy the burning of lust. And because he stains the wedding garment, he does not approach the Lord’s supper at all.

Since these people make excuses from God’s banquet, the poor and weak are called from the streets and lanes. The streets are broad public roads along which crimes are committed openly and through power; the lanes are narrow paths on which those who secretly persist in wickedness labor.

The poor are those who acknowledge themselves empty of good works. The weak are those who see that they have languished in the Lord’s commandments. The blind are those who have closed the eyes of their hearts to the light of truth. The lame are those who have not walked in the Lord’s ways.

But all these, when called to God’s banquet, come, as they approach the food of eternal sweetness after being corrected through the teaching of the righteous by repentance.

Moreover, many are compelled to enter from the roads and hedges when, forced by various errors and by the very difficulty of the world, they are converted to piety. Let all these feast in the sight of God and delight in joy, because there is greater joy among the angels of God over one sinner who repents than over ninety-nine righteous persons who do not need repentance (Matt. 18) [Col. 1021D].

To this banquet, beloved, let us all run of our own free will with all our efforts, where we shall never hunger or thirst, but shall rejoice eternally with the angels.

## SERMON ON THE BODY OF THE LORD

> “A certain man made a great supper,” and so forth (Luke 14).

This rich man therefore set a table for this supper—that is, an altar—on which he placed three things: bread, wine, and flesh. Christ himself is therefore the bread of angels. Because man sinned in it in paradise, wine was added, that is, the austerity of the law. But because hard and solid bread is difficult to eat, and because wine kills little children, flesh was added, when the Word became flesh and dwelt among us (John 1).

Thus hard and solid bread was changed into flesh, and austere wine into milk. These three—bread, wine, and flesh—are the sacrament of Christ’s body and blood: one of those things in which salvation principally consists, and unique among all things, because all sanctification comes from it.

For this sacrifice, offered once for the salvation of the world, gave power to all the sacraments that preceded and followed it, so that they might sanctify through it and save all who were to be saved through it.

The Lord Jesus Christ himself instituted the sacrament of his body and blood when, after the supper of the old Passover, he transformed bread and wine into his body and blood by divine power, distributed them to the apostles to receive, and commanded them afterward to do the same in remembrance of him (Luke 22).

[Col. 1022B]

Some people customarily ask what sort of body the Lord Jesus Christ gave to his disciples—that is, whether it was passible or impassible, mortal or immortal, and other matters belonging to this question. In matters of this kind, as in others, I have professed that divine secrets should be revered rather than investigated.

I think this is sufficient for the simplicity of faith: to say that he gave such a body as he wished; and, again, that he himself knows what sort of body he gave. He gave such a body as he wished because he was omnipotent and could do everything he wished. He himself knows what sort he gave because he was wisdom and could not be ignorant of what it was.

For this reason the matter is more lightly resolved, and perhaps more safely remains within itself, when it is not said, “He gave a mortal body,” lest one seem to speak against the dignity of the sacrament, nor is it said, “He gave an immortal body,” lest one be thought to believe against the truth that Christ’s body was mortal before the resurrection.

For this reason it may perhaps be better not to presume to define either one, although we nevertheless believe that it was one or the other. Thus let it not be said, “It was this” or “It was that,” although it is believed that it was one of them.

If one must be named, I approach the matter, without prejudice to the truth, with profound understanding, so that he may be said to have given it as impassible and immortal insofar as this pertains to the sanctification of the sacrament.

If anyone thinks it should be objected that before the resurrection the Lord Jesus Christ bore a mortal body, we also unquestionably confess that the Lord Jesus was mortal according to the humanity he assumed [Col. 1022D], because if we did not believe him to have been mortal, we would deny that he died.

Human nature in Christ was therefore mortal, but by will, not by necessity. Since, through grace, it had been joined to the Word of God in the unity of the person, cleansed from every sin, it was freed from every necessity and debt of death, so that it owed nothing to death, since it possessed nothing of sin.

Nevertheless, he willingly endured mortality, through which he wished to endure death, because if he had not endured mortality, he could not have died at all. Thus he willingly bore mortality until he tasted death and thereby laid aside mortality.

Since he was mortal by will, not by necessity, within the property of that mortality, according to what reason and the order of time required, before he stripped it off completely through death, he laid it aside in part whenever he wished, and again took it up whenever he wished. By this he demonstrated that, insofar as he endured it, he was not subject to it by necessity: for, according to his power, insofar as he wished not to have it, he could not have endured it at all.

It is read in the Gospel (Luke 4) that when the Lord Jesus Christ was preaching the word of life and inviting mortals and those destined to die to life, his jealous enemies, unable to defeat him by reason, wished to destroy him by fury. Thus, as though he had nothing further that was mortal, they laid hands on Jesus and led him to the brow of the mountain in order to throw him down there.

When he was not to be led away, he patiently allowed himself to be held; but when he was to be thrown down, he went powerfully through the midst of them. He was held as long as he wished, and he was not held as long as he wished.

As much as he wished, and whenever he wished, he admitted the nature of mortality. But as long as he wished to endure it, and whenever he wished, he removed that same mortality from himself by his own power.

> “Passing through the midst of them, he went away” (ibid.).

Do you suppose that Christ wrestled himself from the hands of his enemies when he was held by them, so that, passing freely through their midst, he might depart? Then only the strength of the body, and not the power of the deity, would be praised in this. But this is not fitting. Rather, he displayed himself as he wished, admitting to himself, from what he willingly bore, as much as he wished.

If therefore Christ, according to the arrangement of divine providence, laid aside for a time and in part the nature of mortality before stripping it off to live forever, and again assumed it when the time required, is it surprising if he is said at some time, for a cause and according to the reason of the time, to have laid it aside entirely in some respect, while nevertheless he was still destined to suffer in it when the time required?

If, then, it could happen that he himself carried himself in his hands and distributed himself to his disciples to eat without corruption, and yet that the one who gave and the one who was given, the one who carried and the one who was carried, were the same, what is surprising if it is said that in what he gave he was mortal, while in what was given he was immortal, and yet that the one who gave as mortal and the one who was given as immortal were not two but one and the same?

For how could the immortal one not give, when he was received invisibly and eaten incorruptibly? He was received invisibly, I mean with regard to the proper form of his body, not with regard to the appearance of his sacrament. He was received invisibly because, in what was received, what he himself was could not be seen: Christ was received, and only the appearance of bread and wine was seen.

Therefore I say that he was received invisibly, and what he was could not be seen. If, then, in what he gave, what he himself was could be seen, while in what was given, what he was could not be seen; and if, in what he gave, he was held and crucified, while in what was given, he was broken and not divided, eaten and not corrupted, why are you surprised if he is said to have been mortal in what he gave, while he is proclaimed to have been immortal and impassible in what was given?

Let these things be said only in this manner, so that no one is prejudiced concerning what lies hidden in him.

## DIVISION OF THE SERMON

It should be believed that it was the true body of Christ which he offered to his betrayer through the morsel dipped in liquid. “When he had dipped the bread,” he says, “Jesus gave it to Judas Simon Iscariot.”

But, as blessed Augustine says, Judas did not then receive Christ’s body, as some think who read carelessly. It must be understood that he had already distributed the sacrament of his body and blood to everyone, and Judas was among them, as Saint Luke relates most clearly.

Afterward the point was reached at which, according to John’s account [Col. 1024B], he very plainly identified his betrayer by the dipped and extended morsel, perhaps signifying his deceit through the dipping of the bread. For not everything that is dipped is washed; some things are dipped so that they may be stained.

If this dipping signifies some good, condemnation nevertheless followed it—not undeservedly—for he was ungrateful to that good. These, in fact, are blessed Augustine’s words concerning the question whether Judas received Christ’s body in the morsel.

Nevertheless, because the Lord gave his betrayer a dipped morsel in order to identify him, custom has it that the faithful do not receive Christ’s body dipped in liquid.

There are also some who have thought that certain passages of Scripture could be used to support their error, saying that in the sacrament of the altar the truth of Christ’s body and blood is not present, but only its image, appearance, and figure. They say this because Scripture sometimes calls what is received in the Eucharist of the altar its image or appearance—what will be received in participation in Christ Jesus.

They would not have fallen completely into this snare of error if they had either received God’s sacraments with upright and humble faith or handled the Scriptures with suitable understanding. But because they put their own judgment above faith in God’s sacraments, they scorn to maintain a sound mode of interpretation in the sacred Scriptures.

The result is that the word of truth causes them to become even more confused, when, not rightly understood, it supplies error through truth. This, however, is not the fault of Scripture, but the blindness of readers who do not understand; it is not confusion in God’s holy things, but the perversity of presumptuous people.

Here some have perniciously erred by preferring ambiguities to so many clear statements and unequivocal assertions, choosing falsehood rather than truth in these matters—not because something great was said there, but because they believed this to be great.

What then? Is the sacrament of the altar not true because it is a figure? Then neither is Christ’s death true, because it is a figure; nor is Christ’s resurrection true, because it is a figure.

For the Apostle plainly declares Christ’s death and resurrection to be a figure, image, likeness, sacrament, and example, saying: “Christ suffered for us, leaving you an example, so that you might follow his footsteps” (1 Pet. 2) [Col. 1025A].

Therefore Christ’s death was an example, so that we might die to sin; and the resurrection was an example, so that we might live for righteousness. Was it therefore not true? Then Christ did not truly die, and he did not truly rise, if his death or resurrection was not true. Far be it from us! For it is written of him: “Truly he himself bore our infirmities, and he carried our pains” (Isa. 53).

Christ’s death was therefore true, and yet it was an example; Christ’s resurrection was true, and yet it was an example. Why, then, cannot the sacrament of the altar be both a likeness and a truth?

It is a likeness in one respect and a truth in another. For although there is one sacrament, three distinct things are set forth in it: the visible appearance, the truth of the body, and the power of spiritual grace.

The visible appearance that is seen visibly is one thing; the truth of the body and blood, which is believed invisibly under the visible appearance, is another; and the spiritual grace, which is imparted invisibly and spiritually together with the body and blood, is another.

What we see is the appearance of bread and wine. What we believe under that appearance is the true body and true blood of Jesus Christ, which hung upon the cross and flowed from his side (John 19).

We believe that these are signified through bread and wine; nevertheless, we believe that the true body and true blood are consecrated under the appearance of bread and wine. The visible appearance is the sacrament of the true body and true blood, while the body and blood are the sacrament of spiritual glory.

Just as the appearance is seen there, while the thing or substance whose appearance it is is not believed to be there, so the thing itself is believed to be truly and substantially present there, although its appearance is not seen.

The appearance of bread and wine is seen, while the substance of bread and wine is not believed. The substance of Christ’s body and blood is believed, although its appearance is not seen.

What is seen according to appearance is the sacrament and image of what is believed according to the truth of the body. What is believed according to the truth of the body is the sacrament of what is imparted according to spiritual grace.

The sacrament of the altar, therefore, and the divine Eucharist in the Word, body, and blood of our Lord Jesus Christ, is an image according to the appearance of bread and wine by which it is seen, and it is a reality according to the truth of its substance, in which it is believed and received there.

Again, what we now receive visibly according to the sacramental appearance and bodily according to the truth of Christ’s flesh and blood is Christ on the altar. It is a sacrament and image of that same Christ whom we must receive invisibly and spiritually in the heart according to the infusion of grace and participation in the Holy Spirit.

Therefore the most divine Eucharist, which is handled on the altar visibly and bodily according to the appearance of bread and wine and according to the truth of Christ’s body, is the sacrament, sign, and image of the invisible and spiritual participation in Jesus [Col. 1026A], which is accomplished inwardly in the heart through faith and love.

## DIVISION

The Wisdom of God, which manifests itself through visible things, wished to show that his body and blood are the food and nourishment of souls. For this reason he set forth the assumed flesh as food, so that through the food of the flesh he might invite us to taste divinity.

But lest human weakness again recoil from contact with flesh in the act of receiving it, he veiled it under the appearance of the customary and principal food and offered it to be received in this way, so that the senses might be comforted in one respect and faith built up in another.

The senses are comforted in one respect when they perceive only what is ordinary and customary. Faith, however, is built up in another, when, through what it sees, it recognizes what that which it does not see is like.

The appearance of bread and wine is therefore offered so that we may be taught that complete and perfect nourishment consists in receiving Christ’s body and blood from the divinity of Christ. Complete nourishment is food and drink; and the principal substance of food and drink is bread and wine.

The appearance drawn from the principal substance of nourishment is therefore offered so that it may be received in it and so that through it the truth of Christ’s body and blood may be signified, as he himself testifies, saying: “My flesh is truly food, and my blood is truly drink” (John 6) [Col. 1026B].

Yet because the reception of the body and blood alone, without spiritual effect, does not confer salvation, the same Savior himself makes this clear when he says: “The flesh profits nothing; it is the spirit that gives life” (ibid.).

The power and fullness of spiritual nourishment, which exists in Christ’s body and blood, is signified through the appearance of bread and wine; but in the reception of it, the infusion of inward and eternal nourishment is accomplished.

Thus, although the three are one there, in the first the sign of the second is found, in the second the cause of the third, and in the third the power of the second and the truth of the first, these three are one, and they are one sacrament.

It is therefore clear when the reception of the most divine Eucharist is the sacrament and image of participation in Jesus: what we visibly receive as his sacrament is a sign that we ought to be spiritually united to him.

The Eucharist itself—that is, good grace—the most divine sacred sacrifice itself, is so called because it makes divine and grants participation in divinity to those who worthily partake of it; and because it is both sign and truth, in it Christ’s flesh is received under the appearance of bread, and through the flesh worthily received, the reception, participation, and fellowship of his divinity also are bestowed.

For this reason it is called most divine and most holy, sanctifying and making holy all holy things.

Through the word of sanctification, the true substance of bread and the true substance of wine are changed into the true body and blood of Christ, while only the appearance of bread and wine remains, and substance passes into substance. This change itself, however, must be understood not according to union but according to transition: for one essence does not become an addition to another essence, so that through what is added the thing to which it is added becomes greater; rather, there is a transition, so that what is added becomes one with that to which it is added [Col. 1027A].

Nor do we say that Christ’s body is consecrated in the bread in such a way that it receives its existence as Christ’s body from the bread, nor as though a new body were suddenly made from a changed substance; rather, the substance is changed into that true body itself. Nor has the substance of bread and wine been reduced to nothing because it has ceased to be what it was; rather, it has been changed, because it has begun to be something else that it was not. Yet what has begun to be something else did not receive its existence from the fact that it was bread. The wording here is textually unclear: “but it received its being from it, because it was previously bread; but it received its being from it when it ceased to be what it was.”

We have distinguished this more explicitly on account of those who make their own reasoning prejudicial to faith and, proceeding according to their own judgment, try to assert either that it is only what is seen, or that it is such as it is believed to be. That is, because only the appearance of bread and the appearance of wine are seen, they claim that only the substance of bread and wine is present there [Col. 1027B]; or, because the substance of Christ’s body and blood is believed possibly to be present there, they suppose that the appearance and qualities of bread and wine that are seen can remain—as though an appearance could not appear without the substance belonging to it, or a substance could lie hidden without its form appearing.

## DIVISION

When portions are seen in the holy altar, it must not be supposed that Christ has been divided or separated from himself, or that his body has been torn apart as though into limbs. He himself remains whole and is neither divided nor partitioned in himself. But it was necessary that what pertained to the mystical meaning be presented to you according to appearance.

The three portions, therefore, that are made on the altar from Christ’s body have a mystical meaning. For the body of Christ is the universal Church [Col. 1027C], namely, the head together with its members, and in this body there are found, as it were, three parts from which the whole body consists.

One part is the head itself. For the head is both head and likewise a part of the body. Thus the head itself is one part of the body. Another part of the body consists in those members who have already departed and are with the head itself, as the head is, just as it is written: “Wherever the body is, there the eagles will be gathered” (Matthew XXIV). Those, therefore, who have already departed this life, whose bodies rest in the tombs while their souls are with Christ, are the second part of the body. These two parts are, as it were, together: the head, namely, and this other part of the body.

Therefore, two portions are reserved separately on the altar outside the chalice, as though outside the Passion, because the head itself has already risen from death immortal and impassible, never again to die or suffer. Likewise, those who have departed this life, the saints, already rejoice and are glad with their own head, themselves awaiting the resurrection of their flesh; they now feel neither pain nor suffering. These two portions are together outside the chalice and outside the Passion, because in them former things have passed away [Col. 1027D].

The third portion is placed in the chalice, signifying those who still live in suffering until they too depart this life and pass over to their head, where they will neither die nor suffer any longer.

In these mysteries, therefore, an outward appearance is shown to you [Col. 1028A], by which your senses may be instructed, while inwardly the body nevertheless preserves its incorruption, in which its unity is not divided. One portion is seen, and it appears to be merely a portion, although the whole is there. Another portion is seen, and it appears to be another portion, yet it is the same whole. And if a third portion is seen, it is likewise the same thing and the whole.

The whole is here and the whole is there: it is no less in the portion than in the whole, nor greater in the whole than in the portion. However many portions you make, the whole is in each one. Do not be astonished. This is God’s work.

If one person can be in different places, why should the whole not also be present in each portion? Both are astonishing. But something is not therefore false because it is astonishing. Indeed, it is true because it is astonishing; and yet it is not so astonishing, because it is God’s work. It is not astonishing if the wondrous one performs wondrous things [Col. 1028B].

“How,” you ask, “can one body be in different places at the same time?” It is here, it is there, and it is wholly in both places, and in many places. Do not be astonished at this either. He who made place made the body, and made place in the body and the body in place. He who made one body exist in one place made it as he wished; and if he had wished, he could have made it otherwise. Indeed, when he wishes, he acts otherwise, and it is always as he himself wishes.

But because he made it so that one body would be in one place, you have seen what was made and know nothing except what you have seen made. Therefore you are astonished when you see or hear something different from what you have been accustomed to seeing and hearing. He, however, is not astonished when he does something different from what he has been accustomed to do, because when he did that, he also knew that he could have done otherwise, if he had wished [Col. 1028C].

Therefore, whenever you begin to wonder and your thought perhaps says to you, “How can this be here?”, consider the one who made it, and whatever it may be will cease to be astonishing. And even if it does not cease to be astonishing, it will not be incredible. If the almighty maker of all things is considered, nothing that exists will be impossible.

If it should happen at some time, as it commonly does, that you see something take place in this sacrament that seems less than it ought to be, do not recoil: only the appearance that is visible has this effect. It displays the appearance to you; it preserves the reality for itself. It presents to your senses the likeness of bodily food, so that your senses may be instructed in every respect. It preserves for its body the reality of an inviolable and immortal nature, so that it may not be corrupted in its own nature.

If it departed in any respect from the likeness, it would not be a true sacrament; it would lose itself there and remove the place of faith, and it would no longer be believed even if it were seen. This ought not to happen. Therefore, so far as we are concerned, it preserves in every respect the likeness of corruptible food, and yet, so far as it is concerned, it does not lose the reality of the inviolable body.

It appears to be consumed, yet it remains incorrupt. It appears either to be affected or stained, yet it remains inviolate. It allows these things to happen around it, so that our senses may perceive nothing foreign; but it does not receive them into itself, so that its incorruptible nature may not lose its purity.

So great is the dignity and purity of Christ’s body that it cannot be affected by any corruption or stained by filth. Therefore, if you ever see this happening, do not fear for it, but be concerned for yourself. It cannot be harmed; you can be harmed, since you can believe wrongly [Col. 1029A].

But perhaps your thought says to you again: “What happens to Christ’s body after it has been received and eaten?” Such are human thoughts that they scarcely wish to rest, especially concerning matters that ought not to be investigated.

Your heart therefore says to you: “What happened to Christ’s body after I received and ate it?” Hear, then, about Christ’s bodily presence. Do you seek it? Seek it in heaven. There Christ, seated at the right hand of the Father, wished to be with you for a time, when and for as long as was necessary. For a time he presented his bodily presence to you, in order to rouse you to the spiritual presence.

Therefore he came to you bodily and presented his presence to you, so that through it the spiritual presence might be found, which will not be taken away. Thus, through the flesh once assumed, he formerly came into the world and, according to his bodily presence, dwelt among human beings for a time, in order to rouse them to seek and find the spiritual presence.

Afterward, when the dispensation according to his bodily presence had been completed, he withdrew, and according to his spiritual presence he remained. For, to show that he was not departing through his spiritual presence, when he was preparing to withdraw his bodily presence, he said: “Behold, I am with you all the days, until the consummation of the age” (Matthew XXVIII).

Thus, in his sacrament, he comes to you temporally and is bodily with you, so that through bodily [presence] you may be roused to seek the spiritual and helped to find it. When you hold his sacrament in your hands [Col. 1029C], he is bodily with you. When you receive it with your mouth, he is bodily with you. When you eat and when you taste [Col. 1030A], he is bodily with you. Finally, in sight, touch, and taste, he is bodily with you.

As long as the senses are affected bodily, his bodily presence is not withdrawn. But after the bodily senses cease to perceive, bodily presence is no longer to be sought; rather, the spiritual presence is to be retained. The dispensation has been completed through the sacramental act; Christ remains within and passes from the mouth to the heart.

It is better for you that he enter your mind than your belly. This food is for the soul, not for the body. Do not seek in Christ the ordinary properties of bodily food. He comes to you to be eaten, not to be consumed. He comes to be tasted, not to be incorporated.

Augustine hears a voice from heaven, because this could not have been said or answered to him concerning earthly things: “I am the food of the mature. Grow, and you will eat me—not so that you may change me into yourself, as you do the food of your flesh, but so that you may be changed into me.”

Therefore distinguish wisely what in the Lord’s sacrament has been adapted to the senses and what has been accommodated to the spirit. And, as usually happens, if after the reception has been completed you sense something in so great a matter, here too the appearance serves the proper operation of the senses, so that the likeness may everywhere be preserved in its reality.

For if the likeness failed in any respect—namely, in what must be presented to the senses—then without doubt it would not be a sacrament, but the thing itself would be exposed and manifested by an evident miracle. This is not fitting as long as there remains a place for faith.

After this, therefore, if you seek Christ’s bodily presence, seek it in heaven. Seek him where he was previously, before he began to be bodily with you through his sacrament, and from where he did not depart when he came to you [Col. 1030C].

## THIRD SUNDAY. According to Luke.

[Col. 1029]

[Col. 1029C] “Tax collectors and sinners were drawing near to Jesus in order to hear him. And the scribes and Pharisees were grumbling, saying: ‘This man receives sinners and eats with them’” (Luke XV).

**Gregory.** Tax collectors and sinners, drawing near to hear the word of God, were received not only for conversation but also for eating [Col. 1029D]. When the Pharisees saw this, they were indignant, because true righteousness has compassion, whereas false righteousness has disdain—although the righteous also customarily become rightly indignant with sinners.

But one thing proceeds from the haughtiness of pride, and another from zeal for righteousness. Yet because they were ill—so ill that they did not know themselves to be ill, in order that they might recognize what they were—the heavenly physician heals them with gentle remedies, presents a kindly example, and presses upon their hearts the swelling of the wound. For he says:

“Which one of you, having a hundred sheep, if he loses one of them, does not leave the ninety-nine in the wilderness and go after the one that was lost? And if it happens that he finds it, he places it on his shoulders rejoicing, and, coming home, calls together his friends and neighbors [Col. 1030C], saying to them: ‘Rejoice with me, because I have found my sheep that had been lost.’”

Because the number one hundred is perfect, the Lord had a hundred sheep after he created angels and human beings. But one sheep was lost when the human being sinned. He left the ninety-nine when, though rich, he emptied himself—the shepherd whose hundredth portion we all are [Col. 1030D]. The ninety-nine were on the mountains, that is, in the heavenly places, or in the wilderness, because the company of angels remained in heaven.

Why, however, is heaven called a wilderness, unless because “wilderness” means a deserted or abandoned place? Heaven was deserted by the human being when he sinned.

The Lord placed him upon his shoulders because, assuming human nature, he bore our sins. Christ’s shoulders are the arms of the cross. There I laid down my sins; upon the neck of that noble instrument of execution I found rest.

When the sheep was found, he returned home, because, having restored the human being, he entered heaven. The angels are his friends because they steadfastly keep his will. They are likewise his neighbors because they enjoy the radiance of his vision.

It should be noted that he does not say, “Rejoice with the sheep,” but “with me,” because our life is his joy.

“Truly I say to you, there will be greater joy over it than over the ninety-nine that did not go astray and have no need of repentance.”

Although the shepherd undoubtedly loves the ninety-nine much more than the single hundredth sheep, nevertheless, by leaving the others unmentioned, he shows in many ways that he rejoices over the restoration. Thus also the Savior of the human race rejoices more—that is, he shows by more and greater arguments that he rejoices—over this than over the steadfastness of the angels. Or he rejoices more in this sense: he makes us rejoice more because of it.

“Thus it is not the will of your Father who is in heaven that one of these little ones should perish.” Just as it is not the shepherd’s will that one sheep perish, so it is not the Father’s will—that is, the Father does not wish—that one little one should perish.

“Or what woman, having ten drachmas, if she loses one drachma, does not light a lamp, turn the house upside down, and search carefully until she finds it? And when she has found it, she calls together her friends and neighbors, saying: ‘Rejoice with me, because I have found the drachma that I had lost’” [Col. 1031B].

**Gregory.** A drachma is a number of a definite quantity bearing the image of a king. The woman, therefore—that is, the wisdom of God—had ten drachmas when the tenth, the human being, was added to the nine orders of angels, so that the number of the elect might be completed.

The woman lost a drachma when the human being, who had been created in the image of God, sinned. But the woman lit a lamp because the Lord’s wisdom appeared in the flesh. The lamp is light in an earthen vessel, that is, divinity in the flesh.

Concerning the earthen vessel of his body, Wisdom herself says: “My strength has dried up like a potsherd” (Psalm XXI) [Col. 1031C]. The earthen vessel is hardened in fire, and its strength dried up when, through the tribulation of the Passion, he strengthened the flesh he had assumed for the glory of the resurrection.

When the lamp was lit—that is, when the flesh was glorified through divinity—the house was swept, because the human conscience was thrown into confusion by consideration of its guilt. Thus the drachma is found, because the likeness of the Creator is restored in the human being.

She calls her friends and neighbors the angelic powers, which are as close to the Father’s wisdom as they contemplate it more intimately.

**Gregory.** She calls her neighbors together when, through the display of grace bestowed upon human beings, she inflames them more intensely with love for herself.

“Thus, I say to you, there will be joy in heaven over one sinner who repents [Col. 1031D], more than over ninety-nine righteous persons who have no need of repentance.”

Often those who know that they are weighed down by no great burden of sins remain sluggish in performing good works, secure because they have not committed more serious evils. Conversely, those who remember that they have done unlawful things are sometimes pierced by the pain itself and burn with love for God.

There is therefore greater joy in heaven over a sinner who is converted than over a righteous person who remains standing. For even a commander in battle loves more the soldier who, after fleeing, returns and presses the enemy fiercely than the one who never turned his back and never accomplished anything bravely.

The fact that the angels, being rational beings, rejoice over a human being reconciled to them kindles us to uprightness, so that we may do what pleases those whose protection we ought both to seek and whose offense we ought to fear.

In the third parable concerning the reception of sinners, the Lord demonstrates not only his own joy and that of his own people, but also rebukes the grumbling of those who are envious [Col. 1032A].

## SERMON ON THE FALL OF THE FIRST HUMAN BEING AND THE QUESTION: If he did not have perseverance, how was he without fault?

Truth proclaims concerning the first human being, Adam, that he sinned and became a deserter of the good. Hence a question arises: when he deserted the good, did he not have perseverance? But if he had not had perseverance, how was he without fault?

The answer to this question is easy: he did not have perseverance because he did not persevere in the good in which he was without fault. For he began to have fault from the moment he fell. And if he began to have it, then before he had begun he was certainly without fault.

It is one thing not to have fault; it is another not to remain in that goodness in which there is no fault.

We must also consider what answer we should give to those who say: “If he had perseverance in the uprightness in which he was created without fault, then surely he persevered in it; and if he persevered, then he certainly did not sin, nor did he desert his own uprightness or God.”

But, as we have already said, truth proclaims that he sinned and became a deserter of the good. Therefore he did not have perseverance in that good. And if he did not have it, then he certainly did not receive it. For how could he both have received perseverance and not have persevered?

Further, if he did not have it because he did not receive it, then he sinned by not persevering—he who did not receive perseverance. For it cannot be said that he did not receive it because he had not been separated by the abundance of grace from the mass of perdition. That mass of perdition did not yet exist before he sinned [Col. 1032C].

We therefore most beneficially confess that God, because he created all things good, foresaw and knew that evils would arise from good things, and ordained that it belongs to his most omnipotent goodness to do good even from evils. He ordered the life of angels and human beings so that he might first show what their free choice could do, and afterward what the benefit of his grace and the judgment of his justice could do.

Finally, certain angels, rejecting through free choice the goodness of God by which they had been blessed, could not escape his judgment. The others stood firm in truth through free choice and were made certain that they would never fall.

The devil and his angels, although they had been blessed before they fell, did not know that they would fall into misery. And if they had stood firm through free choice, this would have been added to them: that, through the great abundance of God’s love given by the Holy Spirit, they could no longer fall.

But because they did not know their future misery, they enjoyed a lesser blessedness, though still without fault. For if they had known their future fall and eternal punishment, they could not have been blessed, since fear of so great an evil would already have made them miserable.

All the angels, however, were created equal. But when some fell through pride, the others remained joined to the Lord in pious obedience, receiving the certainty of their stability, which those others never had [Col. 1033A].

**Augustine.** These angels who fell are called demons. They are aerial beings because they possess the nature of airy bodies. For this reason they are not dissolved by death, because in them the element that is more suited to acting than to suffering prevails; beneath them are two elements, water and earth, and above them is one, the starry fire.

The elements are distributed into two for suffering—moisture and earth—and two for acting—air and fire. But if those transgressors bore heavenly bodies before they transgressed, it is not astonishing if these were changed through punishment into an airy quality, so that they might now suffer something from fire, that is, from the element of the higher nature.

They have been permitted to occupy the upper and purer spaces of the air, but also these dark regions, which, according to their kind, are like a prison for them until the time of judgment [Col. 1033B].

Thus, just as the angels were created with free choice, so God made the human being with free choice. Although ignorant of his own fall, he was nevertheless blessed because he understood that it was within his power neither to die nor to become miserable.

But because through free choice he deserted God, by God’s just judgment he was condemned together with his entire race, which was still contained in him and sinned wholly with him.

## On the grace received by the first human being, and on several other matters

The first human being received such grace that, if he had wished to remain in it, he would never have become evil; and without it, even with free choice, he could not have been good. Yet he did have the power, through free choice, to desert that grace; he did not, however, have the grace by which he would not wish to become evil.

If the human being had not deserted this assistance through free choice, he would always have been good; but he deserted it, and he was deserted. He was not deserted so that he might desert; rather, he deserted so that he might be deserted.

For with regard to his evil, his will comes first; but with regard to his good, God’s will comes first—whether in making what did not yet exist, or in remaking what had perished. He deserted God by pleasing himself.

The nature of assistance must be distinguished. One kind is that without which something does not happen; another is that by which something happens. We cannot live without food, yet food does not make us live. Thus food is an assistance without which something does not happen, but not an assistance by which we come to live [Col. 1033D].

Blessedness, however, when given to a human being, is an assistance not only without which something does not happen, but also by which what is given comes about. For if blessedness is given to a human being, he immediately becomes blessed; and if it is not given, he will never be blessed.

The first human being therefore received the assistance of perseverance—not an assistance by which he would persevere, but one without which he could not persevere through free choice.

To the saints now such an assistance of perseverance is given that perseverance itself is bestowed—not merely so that without this gift they cannot be persevering, but also so that through this gift they can be nothing other than persevering.

For he not only said, “Without me you can do nothing” (John XV) [Col. 1034A]; he also said: “You did not choose me, but I chose you, and appointed you to go and bear fruit, and that your fruit should remain” (ibid.). By these words he showed that he had given them not only righteousness but also perseverance.

There are two functions of medicine: one by which illness is healed, another by which health is preserved. In accordance with the former it is said: “Save me, Lord, according to your mercy” (Psalm VI). In accordance with the latter it is said: “Judge me, Lord, according to my righteousness” (Psalm VII). And again: “My righteous help is from the Lord, who saves the upright in heart” (ibid.).

Both save. The former transfers a person from illness to health; the latter preserves him in health itself. Thus in the former there is merciful help, because the sinner who still desires to be justified has no merit; in the latter there is just help, because it is granted to one who is already just.

If the Lord provides medicine by which we who are ill may be healed, how much more does he provide medicine by which we who are healthy may be preserved and, already healed, may not be corrupted? For if, while we were still sinners, Christ died for us, how much more, now that we have been justified, shall we be saved from wrath through him? (Romans V.)

The first freedom of the will was therefore the ability not to sin; the final freedom is the inability to sin. Likewise, the first power of perseverance was the ability to desert the good.
