Now through Christ it is granted not only that there be that without which we cannot remain—even if we wish to—but also that it be of such a kind and such greatness that we do wish to remain.

In receiving and steadfastly holding the good, what comes to be in us is not only the ability to do what we wish, but also the willing of what we are able to do. This was not present in the first human being. One of these was present in him; the other was not.

He did not need grace in order to receive the good, because he had not yet lost it. But in order to remain in it, he needed the assistance of grace, without which he could not do so at all. He had received the ability, if he wished, but he did not have the will by which he would do what he could. For if he had had that will, he would have persevered.

He could also have persevered if he had wished. He came to wish otherwise through free choice. His will was so free that he could wish either good or evil. He had assistance—not assistance by which he would come to will, but assistance in which he could remain if he wished, and without which he could not steadfastly hold the good that he wished.

But because he did not wish to remain, the fault was his; and the merit would have been his if he had wished to remain [Col. 1034D].

The first grace was that by which a human being has righteousness if he wishes. The second can do more: by it, a person also comes to wish, and to wish so greatly and to love with such ardor that, when the will of the flesh desires what is contrary, he overcomes it by the will of the spirit.

For God does not give assistance of the same kind as he gave to the first human being—assistance without which a person could not persevere if he wished. Rather, in these people he works the will itself, so that, since a person will not persevere unless he both can and wishes to do so, the possibility and the will to persevere may be given to him.

The human will is kindled by the Holy Spirit to such a degree that it can because it so wills, and wills in this way because God works in it the will.

Thus the human will, weak and feeble in what is still a small measure of goodness, perseveres and does not fail through any adversity by the power of God, whereas the first human will, strong and sound in a greater good, did not persevere—although [the printed text is defective: “not of the future help of God”], without which he could not have persevered if he had wished, and although no opposing law yet fought in his members or earthly habitation weighed down his understanding [Col. 1035A].

## On repentance

Because in what has preceded we have indicated certain matters concerning the fall of the first human being, it remains for us to speak also about repentance.

One kind of repentance is exterior, another interior. Exterior repentance consists in affliction of the flesh; interior repentance consists in contrition of the heart. Through exterior repentance, the guilt of an evil deed is chastised; through interior repentance, the evil guilt of the will is corrected.

The measure of correction must be weighed according to the magnitude of the offense. “Produce,” he says, “fruits worthy of repentance.”

For the fruit of repentance is one thing, and repentance itself another. Just as a tree is one thing and its fruit another, so repentance is one thing and its fruit another.

Repentance is sorrow for the past, when you grieve that you have done what is evil. When, therefore, you disapprove and condemn your evils, you have repentance. But when, through the satisfaction that follows, you both punish and correct your evils, you have the fruit of repentance.

If what you have done displeases you, you practice repentance. If you pursue and punish what you have done, you produce the fruit of repentance.

Repentance is disapproval of an act; the fruit of repentance is correction of the offense.

But because the measure of correction must be weighed according to the measure of the offense, it is necessary to produce fruits worthy of repentance [Col. 1035C]. If the affliction involved in correction is less than the pleasure involved in the guilt, the fruit of repentance is not worthy.

But you say to me: “How can I know when my repentance is adequate?”

Because you cannot know this here, you must always repent. You can make satisfaction; you cannot do too much. It is better for you to do more than less.

Therefore be concerned, strive, work, and devote yourself so that guilt may have an end, but devotion no end.

Nevertheless, so that the sinful conscience may at some time be consoled, a limit and measure of exterior repentance has been established, so that, once it has been completed, you may begin to have perfect confidence and, with a certain secure assurance, trust in the hope of divine mercy for the pardon and remission of sins—and trust all the more truly insofar as you have completed the repentance imposed upon you more sincerely [Col. 1035D].

But perhaps you answer in silent thought: “How can I be certain of pardon on account of repentance and satisfaction imposed by a human being, even if I complete it diligently, when the person to whom I confess my sins often either does not know through ignorance or does not consider through negligence what satisfaction he ought to impose upon me according to the measure and magnitude of my offense?”

I answer you briefly: if a human being does not know, God knows. You, however, do what is commanded you; be obedient in what you are ordered to do. Let God see your devotion, even if the human being does not proportion your affliction adequately.

You cannot perish if you are found to be devoted [Col. 1036A].

“But I am deceived,” you say, “when I think that I have made satisfaction, although I have not. He ordered me to do only so much and did not command me to do more. Behold, I have completed everything, yet I have not made satisfaction. I go to God as though secure, thinking that I have made satisfaction to him, although I am still held liable because I have not made satisfaction.

“Why, then,” you ask, “has it happened that I do not have such a priest as would tell me, ‘This is what you must do’?”

Hear why. This has happened because of your sins. You deserved to have a bad priest because of them; and, if you were strictly judged, you deserved even here to have no priest at all.

For Scripture says: “He makes a hypocrite reign because of the sins of the people” (Job XIV). And it says: “I will make your tongue cling to the roof of your mouth, and you will not be like a man who rebukes, because he is a Lord who provokes” (Ezekiel III) [Col. 1036B].

For, to make you understand that this was caused by wickedness, consider where your devotion was. If you had possessed perfect devotion, then even without anyone admonishing you, you would nevertheless have been able to cease from sin.

But now your sluggishness and negligence sought an occasion for a torturer, not for a corrector. God saw this and gave you according to your heart, so that you would not find what you were unwilling to seek and receive.

Yet I do not say that you should despair, even if this happens—namely, that the person who outwardly applies medicine to the wounds of sinners provides something insufficient. Often what is done less fully outwardly works more effectively inwardly.

There can be great devotion in a small work. A human being looks at the face, but God looks into the heart.

And, to say less, it is a great thing if in this life you can begin, even if you do not make progress [Col. 1036C]. For after death also there is said to be a certain purifying fire, where those who began here but did not complete their work are purified and cleansed.

But those who were unwilling even to begin in this life cannot complete it there. To those who are granted to begin their correction here, even if they are not granted to complete it, the perfection of correction is reserved there.

Nevertheless, it is altogether safer for you to strive both to begin and to complete the work here, so that nothing remains for you there either to do or to suffer. It is difficult even briefly to experience those torments. Therefore it is altogether safer for you to begin and complete here what you ought to do.

But if you cannot complete it here, do not despair if you have nevertheless begun: “You will be saved, but only as through fire” (1 Corinthians III). It will burn until what you carry as a criminal burden has been consumed [Col. 1036D]. But you will be saved, because the foundation of God’s love has remained in you.

## ON ENVY
The envy of another’s good punishes its own author. For from the very thing by which the good person advances, the wicked person wastes away. People who live perversely rejoice at the falls of the good, but are confounded by their upright deeds and perseverance in goodness. The envious person is a member of the devil, through whose envy death entered the world; and so too the proud person is a member of the devil, concerning whom it is written: “He sees every lofty thing, and he is king over all the sons of pride” (Job XLI).

There is no virtue that does not have the evil of envy opposing it. Only misery is free from envy, because no one envies the miserable person, toward whom, in truth, not envy but mercy alone is shown. Many neither wish to imitate the good nor cease wasting away in envious spite at the good’s progress. Consequently, they are not corrected from their evil but become worse through envy, and, insofar as they can, attempt to corrupt the good from their upright pursuit.

When the good see the wicked prospering, they should not be scandalized, but should think carefully about what end the wicked will have. Every envious person does to another’s virtues what Satan did to blessed Job (Job I). For when Job, overwhelmed with prosperity, was afflicted with adversity, the devil believed that he could overthrow him in one respect; but Job’s merits were increased, and from this the more convincing proofs of his patience shone forth.

Thus the envious seek an entrance for evil reputation, by which they may stain the life of the good, just as the Sodomites sought a door through which they might enter Lot’s house in order to harm it. Yet, blinded by the error of their blindness, they saw the walls but did not find the door (Gen. XIX). In the same way, the envious, seeing virtues as though they were a wall, conceal them, but search out vices by which they may burn the conscience of the good.

The diabolical evil of envy, begotten chiefly from pride and vainglory and sometimes increased through avarice, causes the human heart to waste away and become mortally diseased because of the temporal or spiritual goods of its neighbor. Thus it is said: “Nothing is more just than envy: it first gnaws at its own author, torturing the mind.” By this envy savage tyrants have discovered no greater torment. The envious person wishes to harm another by inflicting or contriving evils against him, either personally or through others, by disparaging him or his deeds, whether good or bad, and even by distorting them.

Envy utterly drives out the love of neighbor, whose sweetness of will it strives to uproot or infect completely with the bitter gall of malice. Through that love we ought to regard our neighbors’ good or evil as our own and rejoice or grieve with them, together with the above-mentioned vices—namely, pride and vainglory. For without these others, envy cannot exist at all.

Envy therefore extinguishes the love by which the good is loved—a good that we can all possess, and each of us possess wholly. Yet no one possesses this unless he completely abandons the sort of desire that is the mother of envy. For whatever we desire in this world, we undoubtedly envy in our neighbors. It seems that what another attains is lacking to us. And because envy is always at odds with goodwill, as soon as goodwill seizes the mind, envy departs.

We love our neighbors as ourselves if we love them not for any advantage of our own, nor for benefits hoped for or received, but solely because they share in our nature or in divine grace—or so that they may come to share in it.

# THE FOURTH SUNDAY. According to Luke.

[Col. 1037]

[Col. 1037C] “Be merciful, just as your Father is merciful” (Luke VI). God’s nature is impassible. Just as he is jealous without any envy, angry without any disturbance, and repents without any correction of his own perversity, so he is patient without any passion and has mercy without any pain. “Therefore be perfect, as your heavenly Father is perfect” (Matt. V, 28). The word “as” indicates likeness, not equality of measure. The meaning, then, is this: Be perfect insofar as you can, so that you may be able to benefit even your enemies; it is evident that God does this.

“Do not judge, so that you may not be judged. For with the judgment with which you judge, you will be judged. Do not condemn, so that you may not be condemned.” He entirely forbids us to judge doubtful matters and to condemn the suspected as though they were guilty. Let us therefore interpret doubtful matters for the better, because we are permitted to judge only manifest things, such as adultery, blasphemies, thefts, drunkenness, and similar offenses. Concerning doubtful matters it is written: “Do not judge before the time, until the Lord comes and brings to light the hidden things of darkness” (I Cor. IV).

There are two circumstances in which we must beware of rash judgment: when it is uncertain with what intention things are done that may be done well or badly, or when it is uncertain what sort of person someone who now appears bad or good will eventually be. If we have judged rashly, will God therefore judge us rashly? Certainly not! But it must be understood that the rashness by which you punish another must necessarily punish you. Hence he says elsewhere: “Whoever strikes with the sword shall perish by the sword” (Luke XXII)—namely, by the sword of the sin that he commits with an iron sword.

“Forgive, and you will be forgiven; give, and it will be given to you.” Forgive injuries and give benefits, so that your sins may be forgiven and eternal life given to you.

“They will give into your bosom a good measure, pressed down, shaken together, and overflowing.” This is like what is said elsewhere: “So that they may receive you into eternal dwellings” (Luke XVI). Those to whom you give alms will give—that is, they will be the cause why the Lord gives into your bosom, that is, into great security, a good measure, namely eternal life; a measure filled up, that is, bestowed with all the saints; shaken together with the angels, that is, joined to them; and overflowing, that is, abounding beyond our merit. The bosom is understood as security because we are very secure about what we store in our bosom. Or by “bosom” understand the conscience or the assembly of the saints.

“And with the measure with which you measure, it will be measured back to you.” This can be understood generally of everything we do in mind, hand, and tongue, because God will repay each person according to his works.

“Why do you see the speck in your brother’s eye, but do not see the beam in your own eye? Or how can you say to your brother: ‘Let me remove the speck from your eye,’ while behold, there is a beam in your eye?” If someone sins through anger, you should not rebuke him out of hatred. The difference between anger and hatred is as great as that between a speck and a beam. Hatred is anger grown old.

“Hypocrite, first remove the beam from your own eye, and then you will see to remove the speck from your brother’s eye.” That is, first drive hatred away from yourself—from your intention and from your heart—so that, once the beam of mortal sin has been removed from the light of your mind, you may be able by example rather than by words to teach the removal of lesser sins, which are signified by the speck.

When necessity compels us to rebuke someone, let us first consider whether we have ever possessed such a vice; and if we have never possessed it, let us consider that we could have possessed it. For we are human beings. Hence comes the saying of the wise man: “I think nothing human foreign to me.” But if we have possessed it, let the memory of our common weakness touch us, so that mercy rather than hatred precedes the rebuke.

If we have the same vice as the person we wish to rebuke, let us not rebuke him, but let us groan together with him, and invite him not to obey us but to seek healing together with us. Many, already overtaken by crimes, undertake to accuse everyone out of hatred or envy, and wish to appear as advisers, censuring and condemning lesser sins in their brothers without any example of correcting themselves.

## Concerning the dispute between mercy and truth, each accusing and defending itself in turn

God was above, and the human being below. Truth was in heaven with God the judge, while mercy was on earth with the human being being judged. For where would mercy be if it were not with the miserable person? It had perhaps descended without truth’s knowledge, although truth knew that mercy was coming to the human being and feared her arrival.

Mercy therefore descended first, lest, if truth came beforehand, she herself should afterward find no access to the human being. Then, when the appointed time had arrived, truth was taken up and God descended, so that he might settle the account with the human being.

When mercy saw this, not ignorant of the divine plan, she went to meet him, wishing to soften God and bring him back appeased. Seeing truth advancing with an unyielding countenance, she first met her and begged her to halt her step and not hurry too much until mercy herself had poured out her prayer to the Lord.

There, then, mercy and truth met one another. Mercy then laid a complaint before God in a gentle accusation, saying that she took it badly that she had not been called as a companion and advocate for this affair, especially since God had never been accustomed to undertake any journey here without both companions.

For since it is written, “All the ways of the Lord are mercy and truth” (Ps. XXXIV), how could the Lord God, content with truth alone, fail to call mercy—especially since Scripture everywhere declares that mercy should be not only equal but prior? For it is not written, “Truth and mercy,” but “Mercy and truth are all the ways of the Lord.” Why, then, was she who ought to have been first now last—and, what burdens her more, why did she approach without being summoned to accompany truth?

Truth replied that on this journey mercy could neither be nor ought to be her companion, because a plan contrary to her will had been arranged, and therefore mercy herself could not be present in its execution. Moreover, she had not gone out with him. Truth added that mercy ought rather to give an account of why she had not been present when the Lord departed, and that her absence had grieved the Lord Jesus so much that he had been compelled to undertake the journey with only one companion.

Mercy replied that she had departed neither with evil intention nor while occupied with an evil work, but rather to care for the honor and welfare of her Lord. She sought not to destroy and ruin him, as truth did, but to save him. Truth, however, ought first to be marked out and accused, since she wished the Lord’s servants and ministers to be killed, so that, once all had gone away, she would allow none to be raised up or recalled through any indulgence.

Truth replied that it was not fitting for a good and just Lord to have wicked and unjust servants. Mercy said that the Lord ought not to be without ministers. Truth affirmed that wicked people deservedly ought to be condemned. Mercy replied that they ought to be recalled, even by voluntary compassion, so that they might become good. Truth said that God ought not to spare the wicked at all. Mercy said: “If God spared no one, he would never have the good.” Truth said that she neither wished nor could endure so many human crimes. Mercy replied that the Lord’s grace was more than sufficient for forgiving. Truth said: “Let each person receive according to what he has done in the body.” Mercy said: “Let every human being turn more fully toward the Lord and live.”

When they had thus met one another and desired to incline God’s will in different directions, God saw that such diverse judgments could not proceed to fulfillment together and said: “It is written: ‘God loves mercy and truth’ (Ps. LXXXIII).” Therefore he wishes both always to be present to him. And since it is said again of God, “His place has been made in peace” (Ps. LXXV), he cannot endure them when they are at odds. But there can be no harmony where the will is so different. Truth wishes everything to be reckoned; mercy wishes everything to be forgiven. These things cannot happen together.

Therefore I, who am a lover of peace, must not be compelled to abandon your fellowship; rather, you must strive on both sides to incline your wills toward one agreement.

Truth replied that she would be less praiseworthy if anything were left unpunished. Mercy said that she would be less lovable if everything were not released through gratuitous compassion. Then God asked whether, if both were willing, they would place their wills in his judgment and agree without contradiction to whatever he discerned from them.

When both granted this insofar as it could be done, without diminishing their name or dignity, God said that it seemed just to him that the human being’s sin should be punished in part because of truth and forgiven in part because of mercy.

When both agreed to this, truth added that it was just that, just as mercy had previously been with the human being while truth remained in heaven, so now truth should remain on earth with the human being, while mercy should ascend to heaven with God.

“For it is written,” she said, “‘Mercy and truth shall go before your face’ (Ps. LXXXVIII).” Therefore, if mercy went before while truth remained, it is just that now mercy should remain and truth go before.

Then mercy asked truth to remember their common agreement—not to contrive anything further against the human being beyond what had been granted—and she ascended with the Lord.

Truth, however, entering the human heart, found there every evil and everything deserving punishment, and began to cry out from the earth, accusing the human being. Mercy did not cease praying in heaven, entreating the Lord for the human being.

The human being on earth, provoked by truth, confessed that he had sinned; and God in heaven, moved by mercy, had pity on the one who confessed. The human being made confession with his mouth for his own salvation, while mercy by her prayers compelled the Lord to justify the human being.

Truth arose from the earth through the human being’s confession, and justice, looking down from heaven, was sent to the earth through God’s mercy. Truth said that the one who had first done evil should first be punished; mercy said that the one who had been justified afterward should be saved, because by confessing his evil he had done good.

Through truth he was accused, and through mercy he was justified because of truth, since truth arose from the earth and justice looked down from heaven.

Because mercy was therefore with God on behalf of the human being, while justice and truth were with the human being from God, peace now existed between God and the human being on account of justice. Justice ascended from the human being to God, asking for peace; and peace descended from God to the human being, embracing and kissing justice.

Then justice said to peace: “Is it enough for the best of beings merely to forgive evils, unless he also strives to bestow good things? He has released sins through forgiveness; now let him grant the gifts of virtues through grace.”

Peace replied and said: “The Lord will give goodness, and our earth will give its fruit” (Ps. LXXXIV). “But meanwhile, justice shall walk before him and place his footsteps on the way” (ibid.).

When justice heard this, she ran ahead and returned to the human being, so that she would not depart from him until the Lord placed his footsteps on the way and came.

## Concerning the lovers of mercy

They grievously sin against God who use the riches granted by God not for salutary purposes but for wicked uses. They do not know how to distribute them to the poor; they despise aiding the oppressed; and thus they increase their offenses precisely where they ought to have redeemed them.

The sole good possessed by the ownership of present things is that it may refresh the life of the miserable. For this reason worldly profit is a temptation, and in the future it will bring punishments all the greater in proportion as the riches themselves are greater. “The powerful will suffer powerful torments” (Wis. VI).

By preserving all earthly things we lose them; by giving them generously we preserve them. Earthly inheritance perishes; what has been distributed remains. For we cannot remain long with our possessions: either we abandon them when we die, or they abandon us while we live through the diversity of their uses.

Some perish through worldly possessions, which they seize too greedily. Others are saved while, in the beauty of these things, they admire and praise the most beautiful providence of the Creator, or while through works of mercy they earn heavenly goods from them.

Mercy receives its name from sharing in another’s misery. No one can be merciful toward another so long as, by living wickedly, he is not merciful toward himself. For to whom is the person who is wicked toward himself good?

No crimes can be redeemed by alms if a person persists in sins. The fruit of almsgiving grants forgiveness only when one ceases from the practice of crimes. It is true that all sins are cleansed by works of mercy, but only if the person who exercises mercy now takes care not to sin.

Otherwise, there is no forgiveness for offenses when mercy proceeds in such a way that sins follow it. It is not almsgiving when it is given more for the sake of glory than out of regard for mercy. For according to the intention with which each person gives, so he receives from God.

Whoever here seeks present praise for a good work loses hope and will not receive the glory of the reward in the future. When the poor person is fed for the sake of boasting, the very work of mercy is turned into sin.

The works of almsgiving extinguish sins and perfect a person for the kingdom of the future age to such an extent that the heavenly Judge, coming for the future judgment, will say to those standing on his right: “I was hungry, and you gave me food; I was thirsty, and you gave me drink; I was a stranger, and you welcomed me; I was naked, and you clothed me” (Matt. XXV).

He rightly promises them also, saying: “Come, blessed of my Father, receive the kingdom prepared for you” (ibid.). But to those who are not followed by any preceding deeds of almsgiving, the voice of the eternal Judge says: “I was hungry, and you did not give me food, etc.” (ibid.). To them he rightly says: “Depart from me, accursed, into the eternal fire prepared for the devil and his angels” (ibid.).

Therefore, not only does the person who bestows a benefit on the hungry, thirsty, or naked give alms—or who gives anything else to one in need—but the person who loves an enemy, who offers the grieving the affection of compassion and consolation, or who provides counsel in any necessity, undoubtedly gives alms.

The benefit of discipline or instruction is also almsgiving, and it is more excellent than bodily almsgiving. Whoever asks despite not being in need, while pretending to be needy, should nevertheless be pitied with the whole heart. Even if he perhaps presents a false appearance of need, the person who gives simply does not lose the fruit of righteousness.

However needy anyone may be, no one can plead poverty as an excuse for not giving to one in need, since by the Savior’s command we are even instructed to offer a cup of cold water to one in need. For if we have nothing else, let us give that very thing kindly, and we shall certainly not lose our reward.

But if we are able to give more and, by pretending poverty, give less, we deceive not the needy but God, from whom we cannot hide our conscience.

There are two kinds of almsgiving: one bodily, to give the needy whatever you can; the other spiritual, to forgive the person by whom you have been injured. The first should be given to the miserable, the second to the wicked. There will therefore always be something you can give, even if not money—whether health or grace.

Almsgiving must not be offered with delay, lest the reward already bestowed perish through accompanying sadness. It is given well when it is offered with gladness of mind. Hence the Apostle says: “God loves a cheerful giver” (II Cor. IX).

We must therefore fear that the poor person either receives what is offered with weariness or, having been entirely neglected, departs mourning and sad.

To make alms from another’s stolen goods is not an act of compassion but the profit of a crime. Hence Solomon says: “Whoever offers a sacrifice from the plunder of the poor is like one who sacrifices a son in the presence of his father” (Eccli. XXXIV).

For whoever takes unjustly never distributes justly, nor does he rightly offer another what he wickedly extorts from someone else. It is a great crime to hand over the property of the poor to the rich, to acquire the favor of the powerful from the resources of the needy, to take water from parched earth, and to irrigate rivers that have no need of it.

Sometimes the generosity of the rich is proclaimed and poured out not for usefulness but for self-exaltation. They are compared with hypocrites, who teach not for the edification of their hearers but to enlarge the heap of their own glory.

Excessive outpouring of generosity is blameworthy. For the person who keeps measure is miserly toward no one, but a generous steward toward everyone; he ought not to be wasteful but discerning. He ought to give as much as is fitting, so that by preserving measure he may suffice for many.

## Concerning hypocrites

The hypocrite has the words of the saints but not their life. Those whom he has begotten through the speech of teaching he does not nourish by his example but abandons, because those whom he builds up by words he destroys by his life and conduct.

Hypocrites are called pretenders. They do not seek to be righteous but only desire to appear righteous. They do evil and profess good. Through display they appear good, but through their deeds they are evil.

All other vices may be committed by simple people; simulation and hypocrisy are committed only by those who are wickedly clever—those who are able by cunning to conceal vices under the appearance of virtues and to put forward a sanctity that is not real.

The saints not only do not desire glory beyond what is proper to them; they also avoid appearing to be what they have deserved to become. Hypocrites, however, secretly practicing their malice, clothe themselves before the eyes of human beings in a kind of sanctity of innocence so that they may be revered.

To them the divine voice rightly says: “Woe to you, hypocrites, because you have become like whitewashed tombs, which outwardly indeed appear beautiful to people, but inwardly are full of the bones of the dead” (Matt. XXIII). “So you also outwardly appear righteous to people, but inwardly you are full of avarice and iniquity.”

Hypocrites are condemned in two ways: either for hidden iniquity or for open pretense. They are condemned in the first respect because they are wicked, and in the second because they display what they are not.

Hypocrites do not always remain hidden. Although at the beginning they may not be exposed, before their life ends it is nevertheless revealed how falsely they have lived. Everything sincere endures, but what is feigned cannot be lasting.

The salvation of those who still have some taste for earthly things is not to be despaired of, so long as they are able to do even in secret what may justify them. These people are better than hypocrites in that they are evil openly and good secretly. Hypocrites, however, are evil secretly and openly display themselves as good.

The righteous person is forbidden to rebuke a hypocrite, lest the person corrected become worse, as Solomon says: “Do not rebuke a scoffer, lest he hate you” (Prov. IX).

It must also be understood that vices, not people, are to be hated. Those who waste away in hatred of a brother and harbor destructive hatred against others should be mourned with tears. For those who separate themselves from love separate themselves from the kingdom of God.

Just as Mother Church is grievously oppressed by heretical people but nevertheless embraces them with kindly love when they come to her, so each of us must immediately embrace whatever enemies we endure when they return, imitating our mother.

Everyone should be forgiven quickly when he asks for forgiveness. For sins cannot be forgiven the person who does not forgive the debts of the one who sins against him.

God has imposed upon us the form of forgiveness according to the merit of our condition, since he has commanded us to pray: “Forgive us our debts, as we also forgive our debtors” (Matt. VI). God’s judgment is just, and it shows that the sinner is forgiven by him to the extent that each person forgives another who has offended him.

Some, trusting in their own merits, are slow to grant forgiveness to those who offend them. But it does not profit someone to be free from guilt if he is not ready to forgive. Indeed, this itself becomes a great guilt when the offenses of brothers are released too slowly.

Whoever is slow to reconcile his brother is slow to appease God for himself. In vain does he seek to have God propitiated toward him who neglects quickly to appease his neighbor.

# THE FIFTH SUNDAY. According to Luke.

[Col. 1043]

[Col. 1043D] “When the crowds were pressing upon Jesus to hear the word of God, and he was standing beside the lake of Genesareth” [Col. 1044D] (Luke V).

They say that the lake of Genesareth is the same as the Sea of Galilee or the Sea of Tiberias. It is called the Sea of Galilee from the adjoining province, and the Sea of Tiberias from the nearby city. Moreover, *Genesar*, a Greek term, is said to mean, as it were, “drawing air to itself,” from the nature of that lake itself, which frequently raises breezes from its rippling waters.

The water is indeed fresh, but according to the custom of the Hebrew language every gathering of waters, whether fresh or salt, is called a sea. This lake, through which the Jordan flows, extends forty stadia in length and forty in breadth.

Since the present age is signified by the lake or sea, God stands beside the sea after he has entered the stability of perpetual rest, mortality and the passing life having been overcome. The gathering of the crowds of nations rushing together into the faith is a type of those concerning whom it is said: “And all the nations shall flow to him, and many peoples shall go and say: Come, let us ascend to the mountain of the Lord” (Isa. II).

“And he saw two boats standing beside the lake.” The two boats are circumcision and foreskin. Jesus saw them because he knows which people belong to him from both peoples (II Tim. II), and in mercy he brings them forward, as though toward the shore, to the tranquility of the future life.

“But the fishermen had gone down and were washing their nets.” The fishermen are teachers, who bring us, caught in the nets of faith and raised from the depths into the light, to the shore of the land of the living. For the interwoven sayings of preachers are like nets, retaining in faith those whom they catch. Nets are so called because they are, as it were, things that retain. These nets are now let down for a catch and now, after being washed, are folded, because at one time the teacher’s tongue must be exercised and at another he must attend to himself.

“Getting into one boat, which was Simon’s, he asked him to put out a little from the land. And sitting down, he taught the crowds from the boat.”

Simon’s boat is the primitive Church, concerning which Paul says: “He who worked through Peter for the apostleship to the circumcised worked also through me among the Gentiles” (Gal. II). It is called one because “the multitude of believers were of one heart and one soul” (Acts IV). From this boat he taught the crowds, because by the authority of that Church he teaches the nations to this day.

“When he had ceased speaking, he said to Simon: ‘Put out into the deep, and let down your nets for a catch.’”

The fact that he asked Simon to put the boat out a little from the land signifies either that the word should be used moderately with the crowds, lest one enter meanwhile into the depths of the mysteries and the hearers fail to understand, or that preaching should first be carried out in nearby regions, so that “put out into the deep” may refer to more distant nations, to whom preaching would later be directed.

John Chrysostom: “We understand the Church as the boat, the cross as the rudders, Christ as the helmsman, the Father as the pilot at the prow, the Holy Spirit as the wind, grace as the sail, the apostles as the sailors, the prophets as those sailing, the Old Testament and the New as the sea. Let us therefore commit ourselves to the depth of this sea, to seek the pearl hidden in the divine Scriptures.”

“Simon answered and said: ‘Master, having labored throughout the whole night, we caught nothing; but at your word I will let down the net.’”

Unless the Lord enlightens the hearts of the hearers, the teacher labors in the night. Unless discussions are let down through heavenly grace, the preacher casts out words in vain, because faith does not arise from the wisdom of speech but from a divine gift.

Alternatively: “Master, we labored throughout the whole night,” and so forth. Saint Peter, laboring throughout the whole night in fishing, caught nothing; but at the word of the Lord he let down the net and enclosed a multitude of fish.

Thus, when we preach while darkened by vices and sins, we labor uselessly as though in the night, and therefore catch nothing. We pour out words in vain because the word of God does not catch the person who has a taste only for earthly things.

At the word of the Lord we let down the net when we administer the word of life to a people hungry for righteousness. We enclose a multitude when we bring many, caught in the net of speech, from the whirlpool of sins to the shore of repentance.

Hence Scripture says: “Speak a word to an ear that hears” (Eccli. XXV). The voice of the speaker resounds in vain where the mind of the hearer has turned away. It follows:

“When they had done this, they enclosed a great multitude of fish. But their net was breaking.”

The net was breaking because now so many reprobates enter into the confession of the faith together with the elect that the Church is torn by heresies. The net is broken, but the fish does not escape, because the Lord preserves his own even amid the scandals of persecutors.

“And they signaled to their companions who were in the other boat to come and help them.”

The other boat is the Church from the Gentiles, because not as many from Judaea will believe as have been predestined to life. The net is broken in the Church of the circumcision because Judas the traitor and Simon Magus, those most wicked fish, and Ananias and Sapphira, along with many others, went away backward before Barnabas and Paul had been set apart for the apostleship of the Gentiles.

“And they came and filled both boats, so that they were almost sinking.”

This filling increases until the end of the age. They are sinking—that is, they are being pressed by submersion. For they were not submerged but endangered. Hence the Apostle says: “In the last days there will be dangerous times, and people will be lovers of themselves” (II Tim. III).

The sinking of the boats, therefore, is the falling back of people into the world—people whom Peter, still placed in weakness, displays in these words:

“When Simon Peter saw this, he fell down at Jesus’ knees, saying: ‘Depart from me, for I am a sinful man, Lord.’ For astonishment had seized him and all who were with him at the catch of fish that they had taken. Likewise also James and John, the sons of Zebedee, who were Simon’s companions.”

Carnal people in the Church, by their conduct and actions, in a certain sense repel from themselves the governance of spiritual people, in whom Christ’s person is especially evident—not with the tongue but by their behavior and deeds. They fear that they cannot endure their governance, and yet they honor them greatly, although they differ from them in conduct and deeds.

Peter signified honor by falling at the Lord’s feet; he signified dissimilar conduct by saying: “Depart from me, for I am a sinful man.” Nevertheless, the Lord did not depart from him. This signifies that spiritual men ought not to be disturbed by the sins of the crowds so as to abandon their ecclesiastical office.

“And he said to Simon: ‘Do not be afraid. From now on you will be catching human beings.’”

Carnal people must be strengthened by spiritual people, so that, fearing because of the consciousness of their guilt and astonished at the innocence of others, they may not fear to undertake the path of holiness.

What follows—“From now on you will be catching human beings”—refers specifically to Peter. The Lord explains to him that the catching of fish signified through him the catching of human beings.

“And his disciples believed in him. And when they had brought the boats to land, leaving everything, they followed him.”

Those who have striven to love nothing in this age have left many things behind. Those who abandoned the desires of possession have left many things behind. Through these things we are taught to follow Christ and not to be held back by the concerns of secular life or by the habits of our ancestral home.

Note that, after seeing the miracle of the catch of fish, those who were called, believing more firmly, followed Jesus to remain with him—not only with their nets but after leaving everything.

They brought the boats to land for this reason: although they would not afterward return to their own affairs, the boats might be preserved more securely for use until they passed into someone else’s possession. For it was fitting that the apostles, whom God appointed throughout the whole world as the model of true religion, should despise the world neither proudly nor without caution. We read that philosophers did this.

For Crates of Thebes, as Jerome says in his letter to Jovinianus, after throwing a considerable weight of gold into the sea, said: “Away with you, evil desires! I will drown you, lest I myself be drowned by you.”

# SERMON ON THE CHURCH
Christ and the Church, signified by these evangelical boats, constitute one body. Christ, therefore, is the head, while the body is the Church. For just as there is in the head the life and growth of the whole body, so in Christ there is the life and sustenance of the Church. If it wishes to conform itself to the head and serve it, then, according to the diversity of persons and functions, it will become one with him forever.

The eyes of this body, which ought to provide for its lower members, are the bishops. They are called not only eyes but also shepherds and subjects, not merely by the name of members but with reference to these offices. There is a great difference between a shepherd and a sheep, between a prelate and a subject. The one governs; the other is governed. The one feeds; the other is fed. And just as the shepherd presides over the sheep by the dignity of his creation, because he is rational and upright, directed toward heaven, while sheep bend down to feed, so bishops ought to be called rational and discerning in comparison with their subjects.

They ought to have a dog, a rope with which to restrain it, a staff with which to ward off both the wolf and, if necessary, the dog as well; also a rod for governing the sheep, who cannot endure the staff, and a bag in which to carry their bread. In the Church of God there are plunderers, namely wolves, against whom a dog is necessary—that is, the barking of harsh correction and the threat [Col. 1048A] of imposing the material sword if the spiritual one is insufficient. Yet this dog must be held by a rope, lest it run about violently, because delays must be granted and summonses issued according to the nature of the deed and the dignity of the person. The wolves must be driven away by the staff of excommunication.

If, again, the dog fails to render what is owed to the love of God, the benefit of one’s neighbor, and justice, by giving himself over to love or hatred, the staff must be used; that is, one must not spare oneself, because the just person is first his own accuser (Prov. XVIII). The sheep—that is, the simple—must be touched with the rod of gentle correction, lest they go astray. In his bag he ought to have the bread of the word of God stored away, so that he may be ready to give an account to everyone who asks.

The nostrils are the archdeacons, who, with shrewd discernment, ought to smell out the life of their subjects and report it to the bishop. [Col. 1048B] The ears are the deacons, who ought to hear judgments, so that they may judge according to what they have heard. Hence: “What I hear—not what I hate, not what I love.”

The mouth and tongue are the priests, deacons, and preachers of the word of God. They ought to be such, but now everything has been turned upside down and perverted. The eyes are not upright; rather, they incline toward gifts, hatred, and affection. In them is fulfilled what is said: “Darkness was over the face of the abyss” (Gen. I). In them is the face of Lazarus bound with a shroud. In them are the eyes of the apostles weighed down by sleep. In them is Saul, with scales over his eyes. The nostrils have lost their sense of smell, judging good to be evil and the reverse. They protect those whom they wish and oppress those whom they wish. The ears pervert judgments; the mouth and tongue are silent.

[Col. 1048C] The breast, back, arms, and hands of the Church are the soldiers. In the breast is the heart, in which there is courage. These men ought courageously to defend the ministers of the Church. The back is suited to carrying burdens, the arms to lifting them, and the hands to handling them. They ought diligently to carry, raise, and handle ecclesiastical burdens.

But all these things have been turned upside down. How wicked are the hands that darken and tear out the very eyes which they ought to wipe; that cut off the noses which they ought to cleanse; that amputate the ears which they ought to purify; that close the mouth which they ought to serve! Such is the life of clerics, who quarrel at banquets and engage in disputes over trifles.

The belly, however, which because of its weakness is regarded as lowly and is merely the receptacle of food and the nourisher of the body, digests [Col. 1048D] food and supplies vital juices to the upper and lower members. It represents the monks and hermits, whom the world despises and whom the hands—that is, the soldiers—oppress. They receive the food of spiritual doctrine; they are the support of the Church, signified by Moses praying on the mountain, by Samuel keeping watch in the temple, and by Elijah dwelling in the desert. They supply spiritual juices to the upper and lower members. To them applies the saying, “The human race lives by a few,” because if they did not exist, the world would perish either by lightning or by the opening of the earth.

The feet, which carry the whole body, are the peasants, from whose labor all those mentioned above live. The hands—that is, the soldiers—persecute them by plunder, sword, and fire; they cast them into prison, assign them to chains, and compel them to pay ransoms. [Col. 1049A] Such is the concatenation of the Church, if it wishes to be united with its head.

## Again, on the Church

The holy Church is the body of Christ, brought to life and united by one Spirit, and sanctified by one faith. Each individual believer exists as a member of this body; all are one body because of the one Spirit and one faith.

Just as in the human body each member has its own distinct function, and yet no member performs only for itself what it alone performs, so in the body the gifts of grace are distributed, and yet each person does not possess solely for himself even what he alone possesses. Only the eyes see, yet they do not see merely for themselves but for the whole body. Only the ears hear, yet they do not hear merely for themselves [Col. 1049B] but for the whole body. Only the feet walk, yet they do not walk merely for themselves but for the whole body. In this way, each member alone possesses something within itself, but does not possess it solely for itself, so that, according to the administration of the best giver and wisest distributor, each thing belongs to all and all things belong to each.

Therefore, whoever has deserved to receive a gift of God’s grace should know that what he has does not belong to him alone, even if he alone possesses it. By this likeness the holy Church—that is, the whole company of the faithful—is called the body of Christ because it has received the Spirit of Christ. Its participation is indicated in the name when it is called Christian from Christ. This name therefore signifies members participating in the Spirit of Christ: just as one who is anointed is named from the Anointed One, so one who is from Christ is called Christian.

Christ, indeed, was anointed at that time with the oil of gladness, which he received in fullness beyond all his companions, and which he poured forth from himself, as head, upon all his companions, as members, according to their participation (Ps. XLIV). It is like the ointment on the head that descends from the head onto the beard and then flows down to the hem (Ps. CXXXII), that is, to the edge of the garment, so that it might flow over the whole and give life to the whole.

When, therefore, you become a Christian, you become a member of Christ, a member of Christ’s body participating in the Spirit of Christ. What, then, is the Church if not the multitude of the faithful, the whole company of Christians?

This whole body embraces two orders, laity and clergy, like the two sides of a single body. The laity are, as it were, on the left, because they serve the necessities of the present life. I do not mean “on the left” in the sense in which those will be placed on the left to whom it will be said: “Go, you accursed, into the eternal fire” (Matt. XXV). Far be it from me to presume to place good laypeople there! For those who are good, whether lay or clerical, will not be there; and those who are evil, whether lay or clerical, will be there.

I do not therefore place Christian laypeople who are truly Christians on that left, but on the left of which it is said: “In his right hand is length of days; in his left are riches and glory” (Prov. III). Whoever is on the left in the body belongs to the body, and this is good, although it is not the best. Christian laypeople, therefore, inasmuch as they deal with earthly things and the necessities of earthly life, are the left side of Christ’s body. The clergy, however, because they administer what pertains to spiritual life, are, as it were, the right side of Christ’s body. The whole body of Christ, which is the universal Church, consists of these two parts.

“Layperson” is interpreted as “of the people.” In Greek, *laos* means “people” in Latin. Hence also *basileos* means “king,” and it is thought to be formed as though from *basilāos*, that is, “support of the people.”

“Cleric” is derived from the Greek *cleros*, which, when interpreted, means “lot”: either because he has been chosen by lot by God for God’s service, or because God himself is his lot, and because the cleric ought to have no other portion on earth than God and the things that pertain to God’s portion. He is appointed to be supported by tithes and offerings that are offered to God.

[Col. 1050B] Faithful Christian laypeople are permitted to possess earthly things, while the clergy are entrusted only with spiritual matters. So formerly, in that earlier people, the rest of the multitude, who prefigured the laity, received portions in the inheritance, while the tribe of Levi alone, which represented the clergy, was fed by tithes, offerings, and sacrificial victims.

The Church has a twofold beauty: one which it attains here by living well, and another by which it will be glorified there after tribulation. Because of Christ, the Church undergoes a twofold tribulation: either that which it endured from pagans in its martyrs, or that which it endures from heretics in divided controversies. By God’s grace it overcomes both, partly by enduring and partly by resisting.

The holy Catholic Church patiently tolerates those who live badly within it, but rejects those who believe badly. Against the obstinacy of pagans and heretics, the holy Church devotes itself with the utmost care to wisdom and patience. Wisdom is exercised when it is tested by words; patience is exercised when it is tested by swords.

Through the occasion of heretical perversity, the Church was enlarged in its doctrines. Previously it flourished in simple faith alone. On account of heretics, therefore, teachers in the faith multiplied, and through the sharpness of heresies the teachers of the Church grew. For the assertion of truth is manifested more clearly when some disagreement has become evident.

The holy Church is called Catholic because it is universally spread throughout the whole world. The churches of heretics are confined to parts of the world; this Church, however, is extended and spread throughout the entire globe. Heresies are found operating either in some corner of the world or among a single people, whereas the Catholic Church, just as it extends through the whole world, is likewise constituted by the fellowship of all peoples.

Who are heretics except those who, abandoning the Church of God, have chosen private associations? Of them the Lord says: “My people have committed two evils: they have abandoned me, the fountain of living water, and have dug for themselves cisterns that cannot hold water” (Jer. II).

The cause for which heresy arises is the exercise of faith. The force through which it arises is the obscurity of the divine Scriptures, in which heretics, blinded by darkness, understand something other than what is actually the case. Nor can heresies truly exist, because by the very fact that they exist as heresies, they no longer are. By thinking wrongly they acquire no substance; heretics tend toward nothingness. With immense zeal they learn their falsehoods, and with grievous labor they struggle not to come to the unity of the Church.

Of them the prophet aptly says: “They have taught their tongue to speak falsehood, and they have labored to act wickedly” (Jer. IX), since heretics tear one another apart when they lead one another into their own sects. Yet they clash among themselves in such a way that they fight against the Church with an equal spirit of error; although divided among themselves, they are united in opposition to the Church.

To those who, because heresies are so powerful, seem to think that they possess the truth, this answer should be given: Are diseases to be preferred to health merely because they often occupy the world so generally that they leave only a small place for health?

## On ecclesiastical teachers, their doctrine, and their examples

An ecclesiastical teacher ought to shine both in doctrine and in life. Doctrine without life makes him arrogant; life without doctrine makes him useless. The priest’s preaching must be confirmed by his works, so that what he teaches in word may be instructed by example. For that doctrine is true which is followed by a way of life. Nothing is more disgraceful than for someone to neglect fulfilling in practice the good that he preaches. Preaching is delivered usefully when it is effectively fulfilled.

Every teacher ought to devote himself both to good action and to good preaching. Neither one without the other makes a person perfect; rather, the just person must first act well, so that afterward he may be able to teach well.

Just as a coin is examined for its metal, weight, and shape, so in every ecclesiastical teacher one must consider what he follows, what he teaches, and how he lives. The quality of the metal signifies doctrine; the shape, resemblance to the fathers; the weight, humility. Whoever differs from these three will be not metal but earth.

Sometimes, through the fault of the teacher, the doctrine itself, though true, becomes worthless; and whoever does not live as he teaches makes the truth he preaches contemptible. The tongue of teachers who teach well but live badly is a crooked bow, and therefore they shoot arrows as though from a distorted bow, while they quickly pierce their own perverse life with the bow of the tongue.

Whoever teaches well and lives badly benefits those who live well by what he says; but by living badly he kills himself. If a priest acts with the utmost dignity, as befits a priest, his ministry is useful both to himself and to others. But if he lives unworthily, he is useful to others by speaking while killing himself by living badly. Thus what is dead in him belongs to him personally; what lives in him is, because of this, the sacred ministry belonging to another.

Whoever teaches well and lives badly resembles a candle, which displays goodness to others and provides light, but consumes and extinguishes itself in its own evils. Whoever teaches well and lives badly seems to join good to evil, mix light with darkness, and exchange truth for falsehood.

Irascible teachers, through the madness of anger, turn the discipline of correction into brutality, and from the very source by which they could have corrected their subjects they instead wound them. An angry superior therefore avenges faults without measure, because his heart, scattered among worldly concerns, is not gathered into love of the one God. A mind loosened among many things is not bound by the chain of charity; once badly loosened, it moves badly on every occasion.

A good ruler is one who maintains discipline in humility and, through discipline, does not fall into pride. Haughty shepherds oppress their flocks tyrannically rather than govern them, because they demand from their subjects not God’s glory but their own. Many are not humble but arrogant in the word of doctrine, and they announce the very truths they preach not from a zeal for correction but from the fault of self-exaltation.

Many teach not with the intention of building up but from the swelling of pride; they are not wise so as to benefit others, but strive to teach so as to appear wise. The corrupt judgment of arrogant priests leads them to imitate the saints in the severity of discipline while neglecting to follow them in the affection of charity. They desire to appear rigid through strictness, but cannot display the form of humility, so that they may seem more terrifying than gentle.

Proud teachers know how to wound rather than correct, as Solomon testifies when he says: “In the mouth of a fool is the rod of pride” (Prov. XIV), because they strike harshly when rebuking and do not know how to show humble compassion. The person who takes up the task of curing the faults of another’s sin does this well when he acts from love of heart and humble conscience. But whoever rebukes the offender with a proud or hateful spirit does not correct him but strikes him. Whatever a bold or indignant spirit utters is the fury of the rebuker, not the love of the corrector.

## Division

The same doctrine is not to be applied to everyone; rather, the exhortation of words must vary according to the character of the persons. Some are corrected by a harsh rebuke, others by a gentle exhortation. Just as skilled physicians treat various bodily diseases with different medicines, so that the remedy varies according to the variety of wounds, so the teacher of the Church applies to each person the appropriate remedy of doctrine and announces what is fitting for each according to the development of age and profession.

Not everything that is hidden ought to be disclosed to everyone. There are many who cannot understand it. If such matters are revealed to them indiscriminately, they immediately either disparage or neglect them. The first virtue of prudence is therefore to assess the person whom one ought to teach.

To uneducated or carnal peoples, plain and common matters should be preached, not the highest and most difficult things, lest they be overwhelmed by the immensity of doctrine rather than instructed. To carnal minds it is fitting to preach neither matters too lofty concerning heavenly things nor merely earthly things, but moderately, as their faults and character require them to be taught.

When a raven sees that its young are white, it feeds them no food but merely watches them until they become black with their father’s color, and then it restores them with frequent feeding. So the zealous teacher of the Church, unless he sees those whom he has taught growing through penitential confession into his own likeness and, having laid aside worldly brightness, putting on the garment of lamentation in remembrance of sin, does not yet disclose to them the deeper mysteries of spiritual understanding, as they are still outward—that is, carnal—people. Otherwise, while they fail to grasp what they hear, they may begin to despise the heavenly commandments more than to venerate them.

One must act differently toward those entrusted to our governance when they offend, and differently toward those who have not been entrusted to us. Those who are just must be venerated; if they offend, they should be corrected, where appropriate, solely out of charity, but not with the severity used toward those entrusted to us for governance.

The elders of the people should be taught first, so that those below them may more easily be taught through them. A teacher shows good judgment when he begins with praise of those whom he wishes to correct by salutary rebuke, as the Apostle does with the Corinthians (I Cor. I): he begins with praise but proceeds to rebuke. Yet among the Corinthians there were people deserving both praise and rebuke. He, however, speaks indiscriminately and equally to all, so that both seem appropriate to everyone.

Because of the people’s evil merit, the word of preaching is taken away. Because of the listener’s good merit, speech is granted to the teacher. It lies in God’s power to give the word of doctrine to whomever he wishes or to take it away, and this happens either on account of the merit of the speaker or that of the hearer. Thus sometimes the teacher’s speech is removed because of the people’s fault, and sometimes it is granted because of the hearer’s good merits.

For the good person teaches what is good and the evil person what is evil; nevertheless, this occurs according to the merit of the peoples. Not all times are suitable for teaching, according to Solomon’s saying: “A time to be silent and a time to speak” (Eccl. V). Not indeed because of fear, but through discernment, on account of the corrupting wickedness of evil people, the elect must sometimes refrain from teaching.

Sometimes teachers of the Church, burning with the warmth of charity, fall silent in their teaching because there is no one to hear, as the prophet testifies: “The cities of the south are shut, and there is no one to open them” (Jer. XIII). [Col. 1054B] Whoever receives the office of teaching should sometimes remain silent about his neighbor’s deeds. If he conceals what he can immediately correct, it is true that he shares in another’s error. Many holy teachers, because of the obstinacy of the wicked and because they cannot correct the unrighteous, decide to remain silent before them. But unable to endure the heat of the spirit by which they are moved, they again rush into rebuking the impious—

## Sixth Sunday. According to Matthew

[Col. 1053]

[Col. 1053C] “Amen I say to you, unless your righteousness exceeds that of the scribes and Pharisees, you will not enter the kingdom of heaven, and so forth” (Matt. V).

This is as though he said: Strive to fulfill and teach the commandments. For I, whose words do not change, say to you that unless you surpass the injustices of the scribes and Pharisees, who are regarded as more righteous because of their new traditions, you will not reign in heaven.

Note that since justice is the virtue that renders to each person what belongs to him, justice has many parts, whose combination makes a person just: religion, by which we render to God what belongs to him; piety, which pays to parents what belongs to them; likewise the virtue that renders to superiors and inferiors what belongs to them; and also the virtue that gives the poor what belongs to them. All these, I say, are referred to justice as its integral parts.

“You have heard that it was said to the ancients: You shall not kill. Whoever kills will be liable to judgment. But I say to you that everyone who is angry with his brother will be liable to judgment.”

With a beautiful opening he began to exceed the work of the Law, not abolish it. For he reveals that the movement of the soul toward harming one’s brother is counted as homicide, whereas previously people did not consider homicide to be anything except the destruction of the human body.

The meaning is this: under the judgment of the Law of Moses, whoever kills in deed is guilty; but I say to you that under the judgment of the heavenly law which I teach, everyone who is angry with his brother is guilty.

In some manuscripts *without cause* is added, but it should be deleted, because anger is entirely removed and because we are commanded to love our enemies. If it happens that we become angry, we should be angry not with our brother but with sin, as the Psalmist says: “Be angry” (Ps. IV)—namely, with sin. Hence what follows: “Do not sin” (ibid.).

It must be noted, however, that divine judgment is twofold: one by which people are judged here, and another in the future. They are judged here so that they may not be judged there. Therefore, for some, temporal punishment here is beneficial for purification; for others, condemnation begins here, and there their final destruction is expected.

At the judgment the reprobate will see Christ’s humanity, in which he was judged, so that they may grieve; but they will not see his divinity, lest they rejoice. For those to whom divinity is revealed are certainly shown it for joy. According to the diversity of consciences, Christ will appear gentle in judgment to the elect and terrifying to the reprobate. For each person will have such a judge as the conscience he brings with him, so that, while Christ remains in his own tranquility, he appears terrifying only to those whom conscience accuses of evil.

There are two divisions or orders of people at the judgment: the elect and the reprobate. These are nevertheless divided into four groups. One is the order of the perfect, who judge with the Lord; another is the order of those who are judged. Both, however, will reign with Christ.

Similarly, the order of the reprobate is divided into two, since those who are evil within the Church will be judged and condemned. The first order, consisting of those who are judged and perish, is opposed to that order of the good in which there are those who are judged and reign. The second order, consisting of those who are not judged and perish, is opposed to the order of the perfect, in which there are those who are not judged and reign. The third order, consisting of those who are judged and reign, is contrary to the order in which there are those who are judged and perish. The fourth order, consisting of those who are not judged and reign, is opposed to that contrary order in which there are those who are not judged and perish.

The wicked person is punished by a twofold sentence: either here, according to his merits, he is struck with blindness of mind so that he does not see the truth, or at the end he will be condemned so as to pay the penalties he deserves.

“Whoever says to his brother, ‘Raca,’ will be liable to the council. Whoever says, ‘Fool,’ will be liable to the fire of Gehenna.”

*Raca* is properly a word of the Hebrews. *Raca* is said to mean *kenos*, that is, “empty” or “vacant”; in our common insult we might call such a person “brainless.” Whoever therefore calls his brother empty, who is full of the Spirit [Col. 1055B]—so the text has it—becomes liable to the council and judgment of the saints, destined to pay the penalty for an insult against the Holy Spirit.

*Raca* is an interjection expressing the feeling of an indignant person. I heard this from a certain Hebrew. When I asked him about it, he said that it was a sound signifying nothing but expressing the movement of an indignant mind.

Our brother is the one who believes in Christ. Whoever says “Fool” to one who believes in God is impious in religion. Therefore, whoever utters such a curse against one whom God calls “salt,” or against one “weakened by the fault of a stupefied understanding” (the printed text is grammatically corrupt), will become food for eternal fire unless he makes satisfaction for it.

The righteousness of the Pharisees is that one should not kill; the righteousness of those who will enter the kingdom of heaven is that one should not become angry. Whoever does not kill is not immediately great or fit for the kingdom of heaven, but he nevertheless ascends a certain step. He will be perfected if he does not become angry.

It is lighter to become angry with one’s brother than to say “Raca,” and lighter to say “Raca” than “Fool.” In the first case there is anger alone; afterward there are two things, anger and a voice of indignation; afterward there are three, anger, voice, and a definite expression.

“Judgment” applies to anger, in which an opportunity for defense is still granted. There is a distinction between judgment and justice in that justice differs from judgment. Judgment can be perverse, which is unjust; justice, however, cannot be evil or unjust.

In the council, the matter is no longer dealt with together with the accused himself, but the judges confer among themselves about the punishment. The name “council” (*concilium*) is drawn from Roman custom. At the time when cases were heard, everyone assembled together and deliberated with a common purpose. Hence *concilium* is said to derive from a common purpose, as though from *consilium*. For the eyebrows are *cilia*. Hence also *considium*, *consilium*, with the *d* passing into the letter *l*.

In Gehenna there is certain condemnation. Thus different dwelling places are indicated in eternal condemnation according to the measure of sin.

Note that although becoming angry with one’s brother is less serious than insulting him, God very often kindles anger so that it assumes both the name and guilt of homicide. Hence John says: “Whoever hates his brother is a murderer” (I John III).

*Raca* is an interjection signifying the movement of an indignant mind. But because interjections are not easily transferred into another language, both the Greek and the Latin translator were compelled to retain the Hebrew word itself.

The name “Gehenna” is not found in the earlier books, but is first used by the Savior to designate the torments of hell. It is therefore derived from the name of a place made horrible and foul by the slaughter of people killed there. It is called *gehenna*, that is, the Valley of the Sons of Hinnom, and it signifies future punishments.

In this valley there was a grove consecrated to the idol Baal, to whom Israel in its madness sacrificed and burned its sons to demons. This place itself is beside Jerusalem, at the foot of Mount Moriah, where the Siloam flows. The Book of Kings, Chronicles, and Jeremiah describe this at the greatest length. God threatens that he will fill the place itself with the corpses of the dead, so that it will no longer be called Topheth and Baal, but *Poyandrum*, that is, “mound of the dead.”

Since whoever says “Fool” to his brother will be liable to the fire of Gehenna, reconciliation must therefore be sought with the injured brother. This is what follows:

“If therefore you offer your gift at the altar, and there remember that your brother has something against you, leave your gift there before the altar, go first to be reconciled with your brother, and then come and offer your gift.”

It is absurd to think that, if such a thing has happened, one must seek a brother who is overseas. We are therefore compelled to have recourse to spiritual matters, so that “Go first to be reconciled with your brother” may be understood without absurdity.

We are the temple; the altar is inner faith. When, therefore, we wish to offer prayer to the Lord in our heart, if we have injured our brother in some way, we must proceed to reconciliation not with bodily feet but with movements of the soul. [Col. 1056C] If he is present, he must be restored to favor by asking forgiveness, if you have first done this here before God.

## On anger

Anger is, in every respect, frenzied in many ways. Born from pride and envy, it now burns inwardly, now bursts forth into word or deed, and now, having grown old, turns into hatred. It disturbs and perverts every judgment and reasoning of the mind. Among other evils, it produces impatience, shouting, quarrels, insults, disputes, indignation, curses, and often many injuries to one’s neighbor, bloodshed, and homicide.

Against it, charity, humility, and patience themselves demand not only that we love friends and those who do us good, or those who do us no harm, but also that we love our persecutors and our very enemies, pour out kindly prayers for them, and repay their evil with good. They set before themselves the Lord, who commanded these things and did these things toward his enemies.

He demonstrated not only that we ought to do this, but also that, judging the evils we suffer because of our sins and merits to be less than they deserve, we should apply a ready and willing mind to endure even greater losses, troubles, and injuries for our purification or testing; and that, of our own will, we should even bestow some good upon our persecutors, as the Lord commands: “Whoever strikes you on your right cheek, offer him the other also” (Matt. V).

And again: “Whoever takes your tunic, give him your cloak also. And whoever compels you for a thousand paces, go with him another two [thousand]” (ibid.).

They also demand that, knowing “the sufferings of this present time are not worthy to be compared with the future glory that will be revealed in us” (Rom. VIII), we should not merely endure them with equanimity, but also glory in tribulations in hope of a more certain reward, and rejoice rather than become angry or grieve.

They teach, moreover, that everything must be despised in order to avoid anger, and everything endured in order to preserve the tranquility of love and peace. Just as the enemy, by stirring up bile, separates those who are still carnal because of earthly possessions, [Note: [Col. 1057D] So in the original.] so among spiritual people he produces discord because of differences in understanding.

Hence Solomon: “Hatred stirs up strife, but friendship protects all who do not contend” (Prov. X).

“Therefore the servant of God must not quarrel, but be gentle toward all, correcting with moderation those who resist the truth” (II Tim. II).

He should therefore avoid foolish and undisciplined questions in which there is no progress in knowledge, knowing that they generate quarrels rather than edification. But he should not cease correcting those who err, if at some time God grants them knowledge of the truth and they recover from the snares of the devil, by whom they are held captive to fulfill his will (ibid.).

It is not only unfitting for us to become angry with anyone; we should also overcome those who have been stirred to anger by their own fault through our gentleness, according to the saying: “Do not be overcome by evil, but overcome evil with good.”

By such remedies, whoever has been cured of anger will escape what the Lord says in the Gospel: “Whoever is angry with his brother will be liable to the fire of Gehenna” (Matt. V).

[Col. 1057C] What sort of torments those of Gehenna are seems worthy of inquiry. For it is very worthy of investigation whether only fire is imposed upon the torments of the condemned, because truth mentions fire alone when it says: “Go, you accursed, into the eternal fire which has been prepared for the devil and his angels” (Matt. XXV).

Since in this life penalties and torments arise not only from fire but also from the other elements, why should the punishments of the condemned there not likewise consist in other elements as well as in fire? Concerning the torments of the wicked it is written: “They pass from the cold of the snows to the heat of the fires” (Job XXIV). And again elsewhere: “Their worm will not die, and their fire will not be extinguished” (Isa. LXVI).

[Col. 1057D] If someone wishes to refer the worm merely to the remorse of a sinful conscience, and considers the fire to be bodily but the worm either not bodily or spiritual, what is the meaning of what is written elsewhere: “The vengeance of the flesh of the wicked is fire and worm” (Eccli. VII)?

If bodily fire is believed on the grounds that it is the vengeance of the flesh, why is the worm not likewise called bodily, since it is mentioned as prepared for vengeance upon the flesh? Because of such matters, one cannot lightly define a single interpretation.

Nevertheless, if someone says that the vengeance of the wicked flesh will come through worm and fire because the wicked person, having cursed the flesh, will be tormented in the flesh by fire and in the spirit by the worm of conscience, he will understand correctly: the worm will not die in the eternal torment of conscience, and the fire will not be extinguished in the flesh.

But how are we to interpret the cold of the snows and the heat of the fires, to which the wicked are said to pass alternately for torment? Or should this perhaps be understood only of that punishment by which they are now tormented in spirit before the day of the final judgment, so that through a variety of torments they pass to that one supreme punishment in which they will remain, not only without end but also without variation?

The final punishment of the condemned is reasonably believed to be greater than all other punishments; likewise, because it is sharper than all the rest and more intensely tormenting, it is not irrationally thought to consist in a single torment. Perhaps it will therefore be single for this reason: so that it may always remain supreme, because whatever were added to it would diminish it.

Some, however, as has been said, held that the punishments of Gehenna were to be understood only spiritually and not bodily, because they found certain statements of Scripture that seemed to assert the same thing.
