They say that Scripture teaches that the substance of those below is spiritual, not bodily, and that, although the gnashing of teeth and weeping (Matt. VIII) ought to be understood spiritually of souls, flames and punishments likewise should be conceived as non-bodily but spiritual. Those who are not rooted in faith fluctuate amid such ambiguities of language.

For what necessity was there to believe that the punishments of Gehenna are spiritual only because the substance of those below is said to be spiritual and not bodily? For who are those below except the evil spirits who have fallen from the highest to the lowest both through guilt and through being thrust down into punishment? Their substance, certainly, is believed even after their guilt to be not bodily but spiritual, because although their will has been changed by wickedness toward something else, their nature nevertheless remained the same even afterward.

The substance of the souls now condemned in the lower regions is likewise rightly declared to be not bodily but spiritual, because, now released from their bodies, they are held there in punishments in a purely spiritual nature. Therefore, what Scripture mentions concerning them in terms of the nature of bodily things is rightly believed to be understood not bodily but spiritually. For if what they are is not body but spirit, then what is in them must be understood as not bodily but spiritual. In this way, therefore, the substance of those below is truly judged to be spiritual and not bodily.

But another statement as well—that if we accept weeping and the gnashing of teeth spiritually, we must also believe the flames of the punishments in them to be not bodily but spiritual—can properly be understood in this sense: if the torments of souls, which are believed to be generated by bodily flames, are not understood to occur in them bodily, that is, through the mediation of bodies.

There are many other things that have either been stated ambiguously or can be stated ambiguously. But the truth of things is one thing, and the variety of words another; nor ought we, because of the abundance of ways of speaking, to depart from the simplicity of belief.

Augustine says in the *Enchiridion* that the period placed between a human being’s death and the final resurrection holds souls in hidden receptacles, according as each is worthy either of rest or of misery. Therefore the receptacles of souls are hidden, and what cannot be known by a human being cannot be defined by a human being.

## Concerning Gehenna

### That the bodily fire of Gehenna will torment not only bodies but also spirits

What sort of fire that fire of Gehenna is to be understood to be, and how incorporeal spirits—or souls released from their bodies—can be tormented by bodily fire, is commended not only by the authority of Christian faith but also by that of sacred Scripture.

What is Gehenna? It is called “a lake of fire and sulphur” (Apoc. XIX). It will be a bodily fire, and it will torment the bodies of condemned human beings and demons: solid bodies in the case of human beings, aerial bodies in the case of demons. Or perhaps it will torment only the bodies of human beings together with their spirits, while demons, possessing spirits without bodies, will undergo punishment through bodily fires without imparting bodily life.

**Augustine.** Why should we not say that, although by wondrous means, nevertheless by true ones, incorporeal spirits too can be afflicted by bodily punishment, since the spirits of human beings, themselves certainly incorporeal, have been able to be confined now in bodily limbs, and then will be able to be indissolubly bound by the bonds of their own bodies? If the incorporeal spirit of a living human being is held within the body, why should the spirit, though incorporeal after death, not also be held by bodily fire?

We say that the spirit is held through fire, so that it is in the torment of fire by seeing and feeling. For it suffers fire precisely by seeing it, and because it sees itself being burned, it is burned. Thus it comes about that a bodily thing burns an incorporeal thing, while invisible burning and pain are drawn from visible fire, so that through bodily fire an incorporeal mind is also tormented by a bodily flame.

And shortly afterward:

When, therefore, Truth declares that the condemned rich man is in fire (Luke XVI), what wise person would deny that the souls of the reprobate are held in fires? That avenging flame has the burning of sins, but it has no light. That fire does not shine for consolation; nevertheless, in order to torment more severely, it shines for some purpose. For the reprobate will also see, with the flame illuminating them, their fellow followers in torment—those for whose love they sinned, since they loved them carnally against the commands of the Creator. Their very sight will afflict them by increasing their damnation.

Just as fire knows how to burn for the consolation of the elect, yet does not know how to burn for punishment, so conversely the flame of Gehenna neither shines for the reprobate as a gift of consolation, yet it shines for punishment, so that in the eyes of the condemned the fire of punishment may glow without any brightness and, for the accumulation of pain, may show how they are tormented by their sins.

The justice of the Omnipotent, foreknowing future things, created the fire of Gehenna from the very beginning of the world: it was to begin to exist once for the punishment of the reprobate, but never to end its burning even without wood. For bodily fire, in order to be fire, requires bodily fuel. When it must be preserved by piled-up wood, it is undoubtedly nourished; it cannot exist unless kindled, nor remain unless fed.

By contrast, although the fire of Gehenna is bodily and burns the reprobate cast into it bodily, it is neither kindled by human labor nor nourished by wood. Rather, once created, it endures unquenchable, needs no kindling, and does not lack heat.

Thus it is rightly said concerning the wicked: “A fire that is not kindled shall devour him” (Job XX). Therefore, lest we come to this fire if we should at some time become angry with a brother, the Lord kindly instructs us in these words: “If you offer your gift at the altar,” and so forth.

But now let us examine the different reasons for gifts. Whoever judges rightly and expects a reward for his judgment commits fraud against the Lord, because he sells for money the justice that he ought to have bestowed freely. Those who judge justly for temporal profit use good things badly. Such people are not moved to the truth by defense of it, but by love of gain. If the hope of money is taken away from them, they immediately withdraw from defending justice.

The acceptance of gifts is a betrayal of truth. Hence it is said of the just man: “He who shakes his hands free from every gift shall dwell on high” (Isa. XXXIII). The rich person quickly corrupts a judge with gifts; but the poor person, since he has nothing to offer, is not only despised when he seeks to be heard but is also oppressed against the truth. Justice is quickly violated by avarice, and the accused fears no guilt that he thinks he can redeem with money. For the love of profit gains greater power over the censor’s mind than equity in judgment.

There are three forms of accepting gifts by which human vanity alters justice: the favor of friendship, the flattery of praise, and the bodily acceptance of a gift. The judge’s mind is more easily perverted by a material gift than by the favor of gratitude and praise.

Human judgment is perverted in four ways: by fear, desire, hatred, and love. By fear, when we are afraid to speak the truth because of someone’s power; by desire, when we are corrupted by the reward of some gift; by hatred, when we strive to oppose anyone; by love, when we seek to favor a friend or relative. By these four causes equity is often violated and innocence often harmed.

So much concerning gifts by which justice is violated. Concerning gifts by which the heart is cleansed, Gregory says:

“The Lord looked upon Abel and upon his gifts; but upon Cain and upon his gifts he did not look” (Gen. III). The gift brought from the hand is not accepted by Almighty God when it is offered by a heart bound in wickedness. The mind that wishes to offer a gift to God must first be cleansed, because everything that is given is evaluated according to the mind of the giver. Therefore every stain of wickedness must be wiped away from our inner person by the cleansing of thought, because the judge’s anger cannot be appeased unless the purity of the offerer is pleasing.

Hence it is written: “The Lord looked upon Abel and upon his gifts, but upon Cain and upon his gifts he did not look.” Sacred Scripture does not say, “He looked upon Abel’s gifts, but did not look upon Cain’s gifts.” Rather, it first says that he looked upon Abel, and then adds, “and upon his gifts”; and again it says that he did not look upon Cain, and then adds, “and upon his gifts.” What is given is accepted from the heart of the giver. Therefore it was not Abel who pleased because of his gifts; rather, the gifts offered pleased because of Abel.

For the Lord is read to have looked first upon the one who gave, and afterward upon what he gave, so that, when we hear the order of this account, we may learn that outward gifts are made acceptable by the inward purity of the heart. The virtue of discernment also teaches the reader what he ought to be in himself when he supplies outward goods not only to God but also to his neighbor.

The Lord urges us to possess this purity of heart and equanimity in reconciliation with a brother when we wish to offer a gift at the altar (Matt. V). Concerning this gift it is also said in the office of the Mass: “These gifts, these offerings.”

We customarily reward those from whom we seek to obtain something. Therefore, in our offering, when we present it to the Lord in purity of heart, we say to him:

“Because we reward you with earthly bread, grant that through it we may obtain heavenly bread. Because we reward you with bodily food, grant that through it we may receive spiritual nourishment. Because we reward you in the substance of bread and wine, grant that through it we may receive the body and blood of Christ.”

## SEVENTH SUNDAY. According to Mark

[Col. 1061]

> “When there was a great crowd with Jesus, he summoned his disciples and said: ‘I have compassion on the crowd, because behold, they have now remained with me for three days and have nothing to eat; and I do not wish to send them away fasting, lest they faint on the way,’ etc.” (Mark VIII.)

Because the error of unbelief held the minds of the insolent, it is written that he left them rather than sent them away. He summons the disciples so that teachers may learn to share their deliberations with their inferiors, or for this reason: so that through their conversation they may understand the greatness of the sign.

The crowd supports the Lord for three days for the healing of the sick, and the elect, in faith in the Trinity, beseech the Lord for the illnesses of themselves or of their own. Or the crowd supports the Lord for three days when the multitude of the faithful, turning away through repentance from the sins it has committed, converts itself to the Lord in deed, speech, and thought.

The Lord does not wish to send them away fasting to their home, lest they faint on the way, because converted sinners plainly faint on the way of the present life if they are sent away in their conscience without the nourishment of holy teaching. Therefore, lest they grow weary on the journey of this pilgrimage, they must be fed with sacred admonition.

The pious statement that proceeded from the mouth of Truth deserves careful consideration. Mark says: “Some of them have come from far away” (Mark VIII). There is one who, having experienced no fraud and no carnal corruption, hastened to the service of Almighty God. He did not come from far away, because through incorruption and innocence he was near.

Another, stained by no impurity and no wickedness, but having experienced only marriage, turns to spiritual service. He too did not come from far away, because he did not stray into unlawful conduct through the use of an allowed union.

Others, however, return to repentance and are converted to the service of Almighty God after sexual sins, others after false testimonies, others after thefts, others after unlawful acts of violence, and others after committing murders. These plainly come to God from far away. For the more each person has strayed in an evil deed, the farther he has withdrawn from Almighty God.

The prodigal son too, who abandoned his father, went away into a far country, where he fed swine, because he nourished vices. Therefore let nourishment also be given to those who come from far away, because converted sinners must be supplied with the food of holy teaching so that they may recover in God the strength they lost in their sins. Often they must be satisfied by teachers with more abundant food of teaching, the more grievous the vices with which they came.

> “And the disciples said to him: ‘From where, then, can we obtain so many loaves in the desert to satisfy so great a crowd?’ Jesus said to them: ‘How many loaves do you have?’ And they said: ‘Seven, and a few small fish.’ And he commanded the crowd to recline upon the ground.”

Heavenly grace’s nourishment is bestowed not upon the idle, nor upon those sitting in the city of the synagogue or in secular dignity, but upon those who seek Christ among deserts. Those who do not disdain are received by Christ and are healed spiritually and, if they are in need, bodily as well.

In a mystical sense, preachers, marveling at the Church’s progress, say: “From where do we have such eloquence that we can suffice for so many thousands of listeners, and such eager ones, in the desert of this world?” But the seven loaves—that is, the seven gifts of the Holy Spirit—suffice for all, joined with apostolic authority as though with the savor of a few fish that refresh us by the example of their life or death.

Those who belong to the seven loaves are commanded no longer to sit upon hay but to press upon the ground. In the New Testament we are commanded to leave even the earth and temporal possessions so that we may be perfect.

> “And taking the seven loaves and the fish, giving thanks, he broke them and gave them to his disciples, and the disciples gave them to the people.”

The Lord gave the loaves to the disciples to distribute spiritual teaching to the crowd.

He broke the loaves, that is, he opened the mysteries—namely, himself, who is the bread of life.

He “gave thanks” to show how much he rejoices in the salvation of human beings, and to form us to give thanks always to God, whether we are refreshed in the flesh or in the soul.

For if the seven loaves, which are not read to have been barley loaves, signify the sevenfold grace of the New Testament, what are we to understand by the small fish except the holy authors of that Scripture, or those whose faith, life, and passions that Scripture contains? Rescued and consecrated from the turbulent waves of this age, they furnished us inward refreshment by the example of their life or death, lest we faint in the course of this world.

> “And they all ate and were satisfied.”

We eat by listening attentively and by contemplating examples; we are satisfied by storing them in memory and putting them into practice. This practice corresponds to the Psalmist’s saying: “The poor shall eat and be satisfied, and they shall praise the Lord who seek him” (Ps. II). The people’s being satisfied while eating signifies that hunger will be driven away from the elect forever, when whoever has received Christ’s food will not hunger.

“And what remained from the fragments they took up: seven baskets full.” The seven baskets that remain are the higher commandments or counsels. The multitude cannot attain to them by observance, but only those who are filled with greater grace. To them it is said: “If you wish to be perfect, go, sell all that you have and give to the poor” (Matt. XIX).

And because baskets are customarily woven from rushes and palm leaves, they are rightly understood as signifying the saints. For the rush grows above water, and the elect place the root of their heart in the very fountain of life, lest they wither away from the love of eternity. The palm adorns the victorious hand, and the elect, victors over the world, retain the memory of eternal recompense in their hearts.

But why are there more than five thousand, and fewer than four thousand? (Matt. XV.) Because four thousand remained with Christ for three days, and therefore received more of the nourishment of heaven.

> “Now those who ate were four thousand men, besides children and women, and he sent them away.”

In the earlier sign there were five thousand, corresponding to the number of loaves, because they were near to the five senses. Those who are nourished by the seven loaves—that is, by the consecrated number—are four thousand. This number is always placed in praise. A square stone is not unstable, and the evangelists are four in number.

Thus the number of those refreshed teaches that they were fed with evangelical foods; at the same time it indicates that an innumerable multitude from the four regions of the world will hasten to the gift of heavenly food.

The typological difference between these two feedings is that in the former the old letter was signified as being full of spiritual grace. Here the grace of the New Testament is shown as being administered to the faithful adorned with four virtues. The first is knowledge of things to be desired and avoided; the second is restraint of desire for those things that delight temporally; the third is firmness against the troubles of the world; the fourth, diffused through all, is love of the Lord and of one’s neighbor.

In both places women and children are excluded. In both the Old and the New Testament they are not admitted to the number, because they do not persist in attaining to a perfect man, either in strength of power or in lightness of mind. Both feedings took place on a mountain, because both Testaments proclaim to us with harmonious voice the height of God’s commandments and the height of that mountain which is the mountain of the house of God at the summit of the mountains.

## Another exposition on the same passage

The Gospel relates that a great crowd supported the Lord for three days, that it lacked food, and that some of them had come from far away. Therefore the Lord, taking pity on them, said that if he sent them away fasting, they would faint on the way. He divided seven loaves with a few small fish among them and sent them away fully satisfied. There were four thousand who ate, and the disciples took up seven baskets from the fragments (Mark VIII).

The crowd that supports the Lord for three days is the people of the faithful who retain the seal of faith in three persons. It has no food when it lacks the word of God. As the body is nourished by bread, so the soul is refreshed by the word of God.

Those who came from far away are those who will return to the Lord after many sins. Those who come from near are the ones who live in holiness from childhood. Those who come from far away are refreshed so that they do not faint on the way, because penitents are fed by the consolation of sacred Scripture lest they despair.

The crowd reclines upon the ground because the people of the faithful regard themselves as dust. The Lord refreshes them with seven loaves when he distributes to them the seven gifts of the Holy Spirit.

With one loaf he satisfies them when he illumines their heart by the spirit of wisdom, so that they may savor divine things. With another loaf he feeds them when, through the spirit of understanding, he opens to them the mysteries of Scripture. With a third loaf he refreshes them when he grants the spirit of counsel, by which they choose what is useful and reject what is harmful. With a fourth loaf he satisfies them when he strengthens them in good things through the spirit of fortitude. With a fifth loaf he restores them when he enlightens them through the spirit of knowledge. With a sixth loaf he revives them when he instructs them through the spirit of piety to pursue justice. With a seventh loaf he confirms their heart when he draws them away from evil through the spirit of the fear of the Lord.

The small fish are added when examples of the faithful are set before them. Four thousand are satisfied because the four regions of the world are called through the four Gospels to the seven gifts of the Holy Spirit.

Seven baskets remained from the fragments because the seven books of the Hagiographa overflow with the seven gifts of the Holy Spirit. From these, teachers still minister refreshment to the faithful, as though from baskets.

The first basket is the book of John, through which the spirit of wisdom brought the greatest wisdom into the Church. The second basket is the Psalter, through which the spirit of understanding opens the Church’s sense, above all, to understand spiritual things. The third basket is Proverbs, through which the spirit of counsel gave the Church many counsels for life. The fourth basket is Ecclesiastes, through which the spirit of fortitude abundantly girded the Church with strength against vices. The fifth basket is the Song of Songs, in which the spirit of knowledge disclosed very great knowledge to the Church. The sixth basket is the book of Wisdom, in which the spirit of piety instructed the Church with supreme piety. The seventh is the book of Ecclesiastes, from which basket the spirit of the fear of the Lord instructed the Church in the fear of the Lord more than in any other book.

From these seven baskets, through the sevenfold Spirit, distinguished teachers—Augustine and Gregory, and many others—have refreshed the holy Church by their expositions, as though to satiety.

The crowd is also fed with a fish when it feeds upon the body of Christ. For he himself is called a fish, as is read in the Gospel. When people demanded the tax from him, his angels rendered devoted service: he commanded Peter to cast a hook into the sea and take from the mouth of the first fish that came up a gold double-drachma, so as to pay the tax for himself and for Peter himself (Matt. XVII).

This fish was Christ, who lay hidden in the waves of this age. He had the double-drachma in his mouth because he brought forth the twofold Law, shining through divine deeds. He was caught by the hook of divine counsel and, in the fire of his Passion, roasted for us as food.

The double-drachma is given as the tax for Christ and Peter when both Laws, or the twofold love, are fulfilled by the faithful for the honor of Christ and the Church.

The people of God are refreshed with seven loaves and instructed by the ten commandments. But the people of Pharaoh are held captive by the seven heads of the dragon—that is, by the seven chief vices—and devastated by ten plagues (Exod. VII).

The first plague occurred when the water was changed into blood. Water is changed into blood when baptism or sacred Scripture is reckoned as sin for those who defile baptism through works of impurity and corrupt sacred Scripture in order to strengthen their own errors.

The second plague occurred when frogs covered the land. The loquacity of frogs is the chatter of poets, through whose fables wretched people are deceived when they follow them in their desires.

The third plague was gnats, which bored into bodies with burning stings. These are heretics, who surround simple minds with harmful arguments, piercing them with their deceit and leading them to the stings of eternal fire.

The fourth plague came through the nuisance of flies. These are importunate people in secular eloquence, who tear one another’s flesh through avarice and attack others with cunning words in order to seize their goods.

The fifth plague is the pestilence that kills animals. This is foul lust, which kills those living irrationally and exposes those putrefied in shamefulness to be torn apart by demons as though by dogs.

In the sixth plague, burning blisters and ulcers appear. The ulcers are the deceitfulness of the malicious; the blisters are the swellings of the proud. These torment the wicked and, by befouling them with their conduct, disfigure them as though with a plague.

The seventh plague consists of hail, fire, and thunder. The thunder is the terror of rulers; the hail and fire are the savagery of robbers. These exterminate the impious when they violently scatter them together with their possessions.

The eighth plague is the caterpillar and the locust. The caterpillars are greedy; the locusts are discordant and leap about in pleasures. By devouring the flowers of trees and the crops, they corrode them, because such people corrupt good desires through evil examples and wicked conversations.

The ninth plague was a palpable darkness and a certain terrifying murmur. These are unbelievers, who do not believe future things, draw others back from the light of faith, and insert themselves into the darkness of eternal death, where there is a terrible murmur—namely, weeping and the gnashing of teeth.

The tenth plague is the extinguishing of the firstborn. The firstborn of Egypt are the rulers of the world and secular dignities, which are destroyed by demons through wars and various means, so that the powerful may suffer powerful torments.

Dearest brothers and sisters, let us strive through good deeds to be freed from these ten plagues, to be satisfied with the seven loaves, to be snatched away from the seven heads of the dragon, and to be instructed by the ten legal commandments. Let us imitate those who went before us and entered the joys of life through many tribulations.

## On the Five Sevens

[Col. 1066B]

There are five groups of seven in sacred Scripture. They should first be distinguished individually; afterward, by comparing each one with the others, it will be pleasing to demonstrate what correspondence they have among themselves.

In the first place are set the seven vices: first pride, second envy, third anger, fourth sadness, fifth avarice, sixth gluttony, and seventh lust. Against these, in the second place, are established the seven petitions contained in the Lord’s Prayer. In the third place come the seven gifts of the Holy Spirit. Then, in the fourth place, the virtues follow: first, poverty of spirit—that is, humility; second, meekness; third, compunction or grief; fourth, hunger for justice or good desire; fifth, mercy; sixth, purity of heart; seventh, peace.

Finally, in the last place, are the seven beatitudes (Matt. V): first, the kingdom of heaven; second, possession of the land of the living; third, consolation; fourth, satisfaction with justice; fifth, mercy; sixth, the vision of God; seventh, adoption as children of God.

Let these be distinguished first in this way: the vices themselves are understood as certain illnesses of the soul or wounds of the inner person; the person himself as a sick man; God as the physician; the gifts of the Holy Spirit as the antidote; the virtues as health; and the beatitudes as the joy of happiness.

There are therefore seven capital vices, from which all evils arise. These are the springs of the abyss of darkness, from which the rivers of Babylon go forth and, led across the whole earth, spread drops of iniquity. Concerning these rivers the Psalmist sang in the person of the faithful people, saying: “By the rivers of Babylon,” and so forth (Ps. CXXXVI).

Let us speak, insofar as we think sufficient for the present purpose, about these seven vices, devastators of the human race, corruptors of the whole integrity of nature, and producers at once of the seeds of every evil.

There are seven of them, and of these the first three strip a person, the fourth scourges the one stripped, the fifth drives out the one scourged, the sixth seduces the one driven out, and the seventh subjects the one seduced.

Pride takes God away from a person; envy takes away his neighbor; anger takes away himself. Sadness scourges the one stripped; avarice drives out the one scourged; gluttony seduces the one driven out; lust subjects the one seduced to slavery.

Now let us return and explain each in order.

Pride is love of one’s own excellence, when the mind loves the good it possesses in isolation—that is, without loving the one from whom it received the good.

O destructive pride, what are you doing? Why do you persuade the stream to separate itself from the spring? Why do you persuade the ray to turn away from the sun? Why, except that, when the stream ceases to be supplied, it may dry up, and when the ray turns away from the one illuminating it, it may become dark? Thus, while each ceases to receive what it does not yet possess, each immediately loses even what it possesses.

You certainly act securely when you teach a person to love the gift apart from the giver. You aim at this: that whoever perversely claims for himself a part of the good given by another may lose the whole good that is in him, and thus may be unable to possess usefully even what he has, because he does not love it in the one from whom he has it.

For just as good truly comes from God, so no good can be usefully possessed outside God. Indeed, through this very fact what is possessed is lost, when it is not loved in and together with the one from whom it is possessed.

For whoever knows only the good he possesses must necessarily love it in himself, so that, when he sees in another the good he does not possess, his imperfection torments him all the more bitterly because he does not love the one in whom all good consists.

For this reason envy always follows pride: whoever does not fix his love where the good is, the more perversely he exalts himself over what is his, the more grievously he is tormented by another’s good. The envy that pride itself produces is therefore assigned as the most just punishment for its own exaltation. Because it refused to love the common good of all, it now rightly wastes away from jealousy of another’s good.

The success of another’s happiness would not burn him if, through love, he possessed the one in whom all good is. Nor would he judge another’s good to be alien to himself if he loved his own good there, where he possessed both his own and the other’s good in the same way.

Now, therefore, as far as he exalts himself against the Creator through pride, so far he falls beneath his neighbor through envy; and as far as he is falsely raised there, so far he is truly cast down here.

Nor can the corruption once begun cease. Immediately after envy has been born from pride, it gives birth to anger from itself, because [the following words are uncertain: *miser avis*]. [Note: Thus in the manuscript: *miser aùis*.] For this reason he is now angry with himself over his own imperfection, because he does not rejoice in another’s good through charity, and therefore even what he possesses begins to displease him when he recognizes in another what he cannot possess.

Thus, although through charity he could have possessed everything in God, he loses through envy and anger even what he was trying to possess outside God through pride. After losing God through pride, he loses his neighbor through envy and himself through anger.

Because, therefore, nothing remains from which he may rejoice after losing everything, the unhappy conscience is battered within itself through sadness; and because it refused to rejoice piously in another’s good, it is tormented by its own evil.

After pride, envy, and anger—which strip a person—sadness immediately follows and scourges the one left naked. Avarice then succeeds it and drives out the one scourged, because, having lost inward joy, it compels him to seek consolation outside.

Next comes gluttony, which seduces the one driven out, because, testing the mind that yearns for outward things, this vice first entices it through its natural appetite toward what is lofty. Finally lust arrives and violently subjects the one seduced to slavery, because, after the flesh has been inflamed by excess, the mind, softened and enervated by the lustful heat that follows, cannot overcome it.

Thus the mind, shamefully subdued, serves condemnation most cruelly; and unless the Savior’s mercy arises to help it, there will no longer be any means by which freedom may be restored to the captive slave.

## On the Seven Petitions

The seven petitions follow, directed against the seven vices. In them we pray that the one who taught us to pray may come to our aid (Matt. VI), and he promised that, when we pray, he would give us the good Spirit to heal our wounds and loosen the yoke of our captivity.

But before we come to their explanation, let us first demonstrate by another comparison what corruption the vices mentioned above produce in us, so that, the more dangerous the illness is shown to be, the more necessary the medicine may be proved.

Through pride, therefore, the heart is inflated; through envy, it withers; through anger, it cracks; through sadness, it is crushed and reduced, as it were, to dust; through avarice, it is scattered; through gluttony, it is infected and, as it were, moistened; through lust, it is trampled and reduced to mud. Thus the wretched person can now say:

> “I am stuck in the mire of the deep, and there is no foothold. I have come into the depths of the sea, and the storm has overwhelmed me” (Ps. LXVIII).

When the mind has been stuck in this mire of the deep and wrapped in the mud of defilement and uncleanness, it cannot be pulled out unless it cries to him and asks his help. Concerning him the Psalmist says:

> “Waiting, I waited for the Lord, and he inclined toward me; and he heard my prayers, and brought me up from the pit of misery and from the mud of filth” (Ps. XXXIX).

Therefore he himself taught us to pray so that all our good might come from him, and so that we might understand that both what we ask for and what we receive when we ask are his gift, not our merit.

The first petition, directed against pride, is the one in which we say to the Lord:

> “Hallowed be your name” (Matt. VI).

For this is what we ask: that he grant us to fear and venerate his name, so that we may be subject through humility to the one against whom we stood rebellious and stubborn through pride.

To this petition is given the gift of the spirit of the fear of the Lord, so that, coming to the heart, it may exercise in it the virtue of humility, which heals the disease of pride, so that humble human beings may reach the kingdom of heaven, which the proud angel lost through arrogance.

The second petition is directed against envy, in which it is said:

> “Your kingdom come.”

The kingdom of God is the salvation of human beings, because God is said to reign in human beings when human beings themselves are subjected to the Lord—now cleaving to him through faith, and afterward cleaving to him through sight.

Whoever therefore asks that the kingdom of God come is plainly seeking the salvation of human beings. By asking for the common salvation of all, he demonstrates that he rejects the vice of jealousy.

To this petition is given the spirit of piety, so that, coming to the heart, it may kindle it toward kindness, so that a person may himself attain the possession of the same eternal inheritance to which he desires others to attain.

The third petition is against anger, in which it is said: “Your will be done, as in heaven so on earth.” For one who says, “Your will be done,” does not wish to contend, but indicates that whatever God’s will may be, whether he dispenses it in himself or in others according to the decision of his gracious purpose, is pleasing to him. To this petition, therefore, the Spirit of knowledge is given, so that, coming into the heart, he may instruct it and pierce it beneficially, so that a person may know that the evil he suffers proceeds from his own fault, while whatever good he may possess comes from the Lord’s mercy. Thus he may learn, whether in the evils he endures or in the goods he does not possess, not to grow angry against the Creator, but to display patience in all things. Accordingly, anger and indignation of mind are most effectively softened through the compunction of heart which, through the Spirit of knowledge working inwardly, arises from humility. Conversely, “folly kills the fool” when, agitated and blinded by the vice of impatience amid adversities, he does not recognize either that he deserved the evil he suffers or that he received the good he possesses through grace. This virtue—namely, compunction or sorrow—is followed by the reward of consolation, so that whoever here willingly afflicts himself before God through lamentation may there deserve to find true joy and gladness.

The fourth petition is against sadness, in which it is said: “Give us this day our daily bread.” For sadness is weariness of spirit accompanied by grief, when the mind, as though somehow wasting away and embittered by its own vice, does not desire inward goods, but is dead in all its vigor and does not brighten with any desire for spiritual nourishment. Therefore, to heal this vice, we ought to implore God’s mercy, so that by his accustomed compassion he may bring the nourishment of inward refreshment to the soul languishing in its weariness, so that what the soul, in its absence, does not know how to desire, it may begin to love when prompted by the taste of his present mercy. To this petition, therefore, the Spirit of fortitude is given, so that he may raise up the failing soul, in order that, having recovered the power of its former vigor, it may regain strength from the weakness of its weariness for the desire of inward love. Thus the Spirit of fortitude creates in the heart a hunger for righteousness, so that, while here it is powerfully kindled by the desire for godliness, there it may receive, as its reward, the full satiety of blessedness.

The fifth petition is against avarice, in which it is said: “Forgive us our debts, as we also forgive our debtors.” For it is just that one should not be anxious in repaying a debt if one has been unwilling to be avaricious in demanding it. And therefore, when the vice of avarice is removed from us by God’s grace, the means by which we ought to be released from our debt is granted to us through the condition of salvation that has been set forth. To this petition, therefore, the Spirit of counsel is given, who teaches us in this world willingly to extend mercy to those who sin against us, so that in the future, when we must render an account for our sins, we may deserve to find mercy.

The sixth petition is against gluttony, in which it is said: “Do not lead us into temptation,” that is, “do not permit us to be led into temptation.” This is the temptation by which the enticement of the flesh often attempts, through natural appetite, to draw us toward excess, and secretly subjects us to pleasure while openly flattering us under the guise of necessity. We are certainly not led into this temptation if we take care to provide the support of nature according to the measure of necessity, while always remembering to restrain appetite from the enticement of pleasure. In order that we may be able to fulfill this, the Spirit of understanding is given to us when we ask for it, so that inward refreshment from the word of God may restrain outward appetite, and so that the mind, strengthened by spiritual food, may be unable to be broken either by bodily want or overcome by the pleasure of the flesh. For this reason the Lord himself, when his tempter fraudulently suggested to him, in his hunger, that he should be refreshed by exterior bread, replied: “Man does not live by bread alone, but by every word of God” (Matt. 4), openly demonstrating that when the mind is inwardly refreshed by that bread, it cares little if, for a time, it suffers hunger of the flesh outwardly.

Against gluttony, therefore, the Spirit of understanding is given. Coming into the heart, he cleanses and purifies it, and, healing that inner eye by the reason of God’s word as though with a kind of eye-salve, makes it so bright and clear that it becomes keen-sighted enough even to contemplate the very radiance of the Godhead. Thus a remedy is set against the vice of gluttony, namely, the Spirit of understanding. From the Spirit of understanding is born purity of heart; and purity of heart earns the vision of God, as it is written: “Blessed are the pure in heart, for they shall see God” (Matt. 5).

The seventh petition is against lust, in which it is said: “Deliver us from evil.” It is surely fitting that a servant should ask for freedom, and therefore the Spirit of wisdom is given to this petition, restoring to the captive the freedom he has lost and enabling him, aided by grace, to escape the yoke of unjust domination, which he could not overcome by his own strength. Wisdom is so called from *savor*—that is, from taste—because when the mind is touched by the taste of inward sweetness, it gathers itself wholly inward through desire and is no longer weakened outwardly and dissolved in the pleasure of the flesh, since it possesses entirely within itself that in which it delights.

Accordingly, inward sweetness is fittingly set against outward pleasure, so that the more the former begins to taste good and please, the more freely and willingly the latter is condemned. At last, when the mind has been pacified within itself, since there is nothing outward that it desires, it rests wholly within through love. Thus the Spirit, wisely touching the heart with his sweetness, both moderates the outward ardor of concupiscence and, when concupiscence has been lulled to sleep, creates peace within, so that, while the whole mind is gathered into inward joy, the human being may be fully and perfectly restored according to the image of God, as it is written: “Blessed are the peacemakers, for they shall be called sons of God” (Matt. 5).

## On the petitions that correspond to the present and future

Therefore, just as the Church is divided into two parts—namely, the triumphant part and the militant part—so this sevenfold number of petitions is divided into four and three. For four correspond to the militant part, while three correspond to the triumphant part. The militant part, as long as it lives, is in a precarious condition; therefore it requires a square form of petitions, which is firm, lest it slip. These four petitions, namely, “Give us this day our daily bread” (Matt. 6), and the others that follow, correspond to the present life, in which they are begun and brought to completion. In this life we are refreshed by the bread of God’s word and by the bread of Christ’s body; but when it has ended, we are refreshed neither by the bread of the Scriptures nor by the bread of Christ’s body in the manner in which we are now refreshed. What we now take with labor, as though it were bread, we shall then receive easily, as though it were drink.

In this life also, while we are as though continually stumbling, we need both to be forgiven and to forgive; but in the future, just as there will be no offense, so there will necessarily be no forgiveness. Here too we are tempted, and we must fear that we may succumb to temptation; there, however, there will be no temptation at all. In the present also innumerable evils arise; enemies are visible and invisible; we cannot be entirely without sins, because “there is always a stain on the moon” (Job 25), and “no living human being shall be justified in God’s sight” (Ps. 142). For he found perversity even in his angels, and “my sword is drunk in heaven” (Isa. 34), and the stars are not clean in his sight. Therefore we need to be delivered from evil. In the future there will be neither any infliction of evil nor any necessary deliverance.

The other three petitions, namely, “Hallowed be your name, your kingdom come, your will be done,” and so forth, correspond to the future life. For although sanctification of mind, the kingdom, and the will of God begin here, they will all reach perfection in the future, where, with soul and body wholly sanctified, we shall reign with Christ and fulfill God’s will. It should be noted, however, that although the three petitions are perfected in the future and are later in temporal order, they are earlier in the prayer—either because of the importance of the triad, in which the mystery of the Trinity shines forth, or because they are more worthy.

Moreover, this sevenfold number of petitions can correspond to the preceding sevenfold number of gifts, virtues, and beatitudes, concerning which the whole Sermon on the Mount was delivered, so that a single gift may be desired through each petition, each gift may produce a single virtue, and each virtue may correspond to a single beatitude.

The petitions, then, are those we mentioned above, namely, “Hallowed be the name,” and so forth. The gifts are: the Spirit of fear, of godliness, of knowledge, of fortitude, of counsel, of understanding, and of wisdom. The virtues are: poverty of spirit, meekness, mourning, hunger and thirst for righteousness, mercy, purity of heart, and peace. The beatitudes are: the kingdom of heaven, possession of the earth, consolation, satisfaction, the attainment of mercy, the vision of God, and being called sons of God.

We must consider how and which petitions ask for which gifts, what those gifts accomplish, and why these things are requested. Let this faithful worshiper, therefore, approach in the virtue of double love, having become heaven and the dwelling-place of God, and say:

“Your name be hallowed.”

As though he were saying: “Give us, Lord, the Spirit of holy fear, who may produce in us poverty of spirit, so that we may set aside all temporal things and attain the sanctification received in baptism, in order that, finally wholly sanctified, we may possess the kingdom of heaven.”

“Your kingdom come”—that is, “Give us also the Spirit of godliness, by which, having become gentle, meek, and humble, we may not be moved by any wickedness against harmful enemies, so that, governing ourselves meanwhile and desiring to be governed by you, we may finally obtain a firm possession in the land of the living.”

“Your will be done, as in heaven and on earth”—that is, “Give us also the Spirit of knowledge, who may teach us to mourn for our own sins with Peter and Mary, and also for those of others, with the Apostle who says: ‘Who is scandalized, and I am not on fire?’ and so forth (2 Cor. 11). Let us mourn also from desire for our homeland, with John, who says: ‘And I wept greatly’ (Rev. 5), and with David, who says: ‘Alas for me, that my sojourn has been prolonged!’ (Ps. 119). May the will of God be perfected in us through this mourning, and may we deserve the consolation promised to those who mourn.”

“Give us this day our daily bread.”

As though it were said: “Give us, Lord, the Spirit of fortitude, by which, strong against all evils, we may be refreshed by the bread of God’s word and by the food of Christ’s body, so that, hungering and thirsting for righteousness, we may finally deserve to be satisfied in blessedness.”

“And forgive us our debts”—that is, “Give us the Spirit of counsel, so that, if we cannot avoid offenses in the present, we may at least have this counsel: that we should be merciful and forgive those who sin, in order that in the future we may attain mercy.”

“And do not lead us into temptation”—that is, “Give us also the Spirit of understanding, by which, surrounded by temptations, we may understand what must be done, and, cleansing our hearts, may see God in some measure, so that in the future we may behold him with full vision.”

“But deliver us from evil”—that is, “Give us also the Spirit of wisdom, by which we may be delivered from every evil, so that in the ark of the heart both the tamed and the untamed animals may rest together, and, with perverse impulses calmed and the image of the Father restored, we may deserve both to be and to be called sons of God.”

Let what has been said thus far about the correspondence of the petitions, gifts, virtues, and beatitudes suffice: some of these ask for things—namely, the petitions; others are asked for so that they may accomplish something—namely, the gifts; others are enacted as virtues; and others bring things to perfection as beatitudes.

## THE EIGHTH SUNDAY. According to Matthew

[Col. 1073]

[Col. 1073A] “Beware of false prophets, who come to you in sheep’s clothing, but inwardly are ravenous wolves. You will know them by their fruits” (Matt. 7). Because only a few find the narrow way, he exposes the fraud of those who pretend to seek it. “Beware”—that is, take care. This can be understood of all hypocrites, but especially of heretics who seize the souls’ fruits. Hence they are compared to wolves. Heretics must be avoided above all, since they promise a knowledge of the truth that they do not possess.

Sheep’s clothing consists of the agreeable words of the innocent and the other signs of religion. Sheep ought not, however, therefore to hate their clothing, because wolves often conceal themselves in it, wearing one thing in order to deceive and seizing another in order to plunder. But when the temptation of temporal advantage or the time of persecution comes, what they are is revealed. Their fruits are their evil works.

“Do they gather grapes from thorns, or figs from thistles?” The wise will not gather grapes from thorns—that is, sweet words from heretics, who are called thorns and thistles because they wound souls through the flattering quality of their words. A thistle is a kind of prickly plant. “Neither do they gather fruit from thorns, nor do they gather grapes from a bramble” (Luke 6). Thorns and brambles are the cares of the world and the prickings of vices, concerning which it was said to the sinner: “Your land shall bring forth thorns and thistles for you” (Gen. 3).

The fig and the grape, however, signify the sweetness of a new manner of life, for which Christ hungers in us, and the fervor of love which gladdens the human heart. Hence it is written: “The fig tree has put forth its early figs, and the vines in blossom have given their fragrance” (Song 2). A fig is not gathered from thorns, nor a grape from a bramble, because a mind still weighed down by the habit of the old human being can pretend, but cannot bear the fruit of the new human being. If at times the deeds or words of evil people benefit the good, it is not the evil people who accomplish this, but God’s plan, which works through them.

“Thus every good tree bears good fruits, but the bad tree bears bad fruits. A good tree cannot bear bad fruits, nor can a bad tree bear good fruits.” Just as it is true that figs are not gathered from thistles, so it is true that a good tree bears good fruits. The good or bad tree is the human being—not according to nature, which was created good by God in all things, but according to a good or bad will. The fruits are works, which cannot be good when the will is bad, nor bad when the will is good.

Thus the good tree—that is, the good person—does not bear bad fruits as long as he is good; and the bad tree—that is, the bad person—remains in the fruits of sin as long as he does not turn to repentance. Snow cannot be hot. For when it begins to be hot, we no longer call it snow but water. It can therefore be changed, but not heated. Likewise, the person who was bad can become not bad, but it cannot happen that the bad person does good. Even if he is sometimes useful, he himself does not accomplish this; it comes about through divine providence.

The fact that the Pharisees were heard with benefit did not belong to them, but to God. Concerning them the prophet says: “You sow wheat, but you reap thorns” (Jer. 12). Their hearers, therefore, were not gathering grapes from thorns; rather, through the thorns they were gathering them from the vine. If someone drew a grape to himself through a thorny hedge, that grape would not belong to the thorns but to the vine.

“A good person brings forth good things from the good treasure of his heart, and an evil person brings forth evil things from the evil treasure. For out of the abundance of the heart the mouth speaks.” The treasure of the heart is the same as the root of the tree, and what is brought forth from the heart is the same as the fruit of the tree.

Whoever, therefore, stores in his heart the treasure of patience and pours forth the excellent fruits of this perfect love loves his enemy, does good to the one who hates him, and blesses the one who curses him. He gives his own possessions to everyone who asks and patiently corrects the one who errs. But the person who does not preserve such a treasure in his heart hates his friend, does harm to the one who loves him, and curses the one who blesses him. Thus neither can the devil do good works, nor can Christ do evil ones.

By the speech of the mouth the Lord signifies everything that is brought forth from the heart in deed or thought. For it is customary in the Scriptures to put words for things, as when Isaiah says concerning Hezekiah: “There was no word that he did not show them” (Isa. 39). He revealed, of course, the secrets of things, not of words.

“Every tree”—that is, every person, whether king, prince, old man, or young man—will be spared by none, but every tree “that does not bear good fruit will be cut down” by the angels who cut it down, “and thrown into the eternal fire.” If the one who does not bear good fruit must be separated from the just, like goats from lambs, and thrown into the fire at the command: “Go, accursed ones, into the eternal fire” (Matt. 25), what will become of the one who does whatever evil he can? Since a bad tree cannot bear good fruits, “by their fruits”—that is, the fruits of the false prophets—“you will know them” to be false.

“Not everyone who says to me, ‘Lord, Lord,’ will enter the kingdom, but the one who does the will of my Father who is in heaven will enter the kingdom of heaven.” Just as false prophets, on account of the doctrine of righteousness, must be avoided because they possess the hope of a good life, so too must those be avoided who, conversely, possess sound faith and doctrine but live shamefully. Both are necessary, so that the work may be confirmed by the word and the word by works. “Why do you call me, ‘Lord, Lord,’ and do not do what I say?” (Luke 6). As though he were saying in other words: “Why do you display the leaves of right confession when you show no good fruits?”

Hence the Apostle, distinguishing the perfect disciple from the hypocrite, said: “I will come to you and learn not the speech of those who are puffed up, but their power” (1 Cor. 4). Properly, then, the one who says “Lord, Lord” is the one who proclaims the will through the sound of his voice, in accordance with what the Apostle says: “No one can say, ‘Lord Jesus,’ except in the Holy Spirit” (1 Cor. 12). For truly to say “Lord Jesus” is to believe in the heart, confess with the mouth, and attest through works. To deny one without the other is denial.

Again: “Not everyone who says to me, ‘Lord, Lord,’” and so forth. “The kingdom of God is not in speech but in power” (1 Cor. 4). What you say—“Lord, Lord”—does not help you unless you serve the Lord in fear, unless you eagerly fulfill his commandments, unless you do his entire will, unless you abstain from every impurity and lay aside all iniquity. You cry out for nothing, you shout for nothing, you raise your voice, saying “Lord, Lord,” calling him as a witness to your disobedience by naming him Lord, while neither fearing him as Lord nor serving him with trembling.

Not everyone who calls me Lord without action, using only his mouth, will enter the kingdom of heaven, but the one who performs works worthy of my name and fulfills a way of life worthy of my sanctification will enter.

## On lying

A lie is a false signification accompanied by the intention to deceive. There is not, however, a false signification where, although one thing is signified through another, what is signified is nevertheless true if it is rightly understood. (Augustine.)

There is, however, a certain kind of lying to which everyone agrees, concerning which it must be investigated whether it may ever be useful to utter some falsehood with the intention of deceiving. Those who hold this view bring forward testimony in support of their position, recalling that Sarah, when she had laughed, denied to the angels that she had laughed (Gen. 18); that Jacob, questioned by his father, replied that he was Esau, his elder son (Gen. 27); and that the Egyptian midwives, so that the Hebrew infants would not be killed at birth, lied, with God himself approving and rewarding them (Exod. 1). Choosing many examples of this kind, they recall the lies of people whom they would not dare to blame, and thus one might admit that a lie can sometimes be not only undeserving of reproach but even worthy of praise.

They add something further, by which they seek to press not only those devoted to the divine books but all human beings and common sense, saying: “If someone takes refuge with you and could be saved from death by your lie, will you not lie? If a sick person asks something which it is not beneficial for him to know, and by your failure to answer he could be afflicted more severely, would you dare either to tell the truth to the person’s destruction or to remain silent rather than assist his health by an honest and compassionate lie?” By such arguments as these they think they press their case most forcefully, so that, if the need for giving advice demands it, we may sometimes lie.

Against them, those who hold that one must never lie in this way argue much more forcefully, using divine authority first, since it is written in the very Decalogue: “You shall not bear false witness” (Exod. 20). By this expression every lie is embraced. For whoever utters anything bears witness to what is in his mind. But lest anyone argue that not every lie should be called false testimony, what will he say to what is written: “The mouth that lies kills the soul”? (Wis. 1.) And lest anyone suppose that this can be understood except of certain liars, let him read elsewhere: “You will destroy all who speak lies” (Ps. 5). Indeed, the Lord himself says with his own mouth: “Let your speech be, ‘Yes, yes; No, no’; anything beyond this is from evil” (Matt. 5). From these and other arguments of the same kind it is proved that it is not permissible to lie in any circumstance.

There are eight kinds of lying. The first, therefore, is the capital lie, which must be avoided by far, because it occurs in the teaching of religion and godliness. No one ought to be brought to this lie under any condition, because it is a great crime and the first kind of detestable lie.

The second is a lie which benefits no one and harms someone, because no injury ought to be inflicted; in this kind one must not lie.

The third is one that benefits one person in such a way that it harms another, even if it does not harm him with bodily impurity. In this kind, no one is to be assisted at another’s expense.

The fourth is produced solely by the desire to lie and deceive. It is a pure lie, because the desire to lie is vicious in itself.

The fifth is produced by the desire to please, through attractive speech. In this kind also one must not lie; for if the truth itself is not to be uttered for the sake of pleasing people, how much less should a lie be uttered for its own sake, since a lie, precisely as a lie, is shameful.

After all these have been entirely avoided and rejected, is there a sixth kind—the kind that harms no one and benefits someone who is asking? Yet even in this kind one must not lie, because the truth of testimony must not rightly be corrupted even for someone’s temporal advantage or safety. No one should be led to eternal salvation by the assistance of a lie; one must not be converted to good morals by the evil morals of those who convert. Since salvation must be worked for that person, he himself must also, once converted, work for others. Thus he is converted not to good but to evil morals when he is offered, as something to imitate after his conversion, what was done for him in converting him.

The seventh is the kind that harms no one and benefits someone, except when a judge asks the question. Even in this kind one must not lie. No one’s temporal advantage or safety should be preferred to the completion of faith, not even if someone is so badly disturbed by our good deeds that he thereby becomes worse in mind and farther removed from godliness. Therefore good deeds must be performed, since we must hold especially to this: that we ought to call and invite those whom we love as ourselves. With the strongest courage we must drink in that apostolic saying: “To some we are the aroma of life unto life; to others, the aroma of death unto death” (2 Cor. 2). And who is sufficient for this?

The eighth kind is that which harms no one and serves the purpose of protecting someone from bodily impurity, at least in the manner mentioned above. Even in this kind there must be no lying, because among good things there is chastity of mind and purity of body, while among evil things what we do is greater than what we permit to be done.

In these eight kinds, therefore, a person sins less when he lies the closer he rises toward the eighth, and sins more the closer he rises toward the first. Whoever thinks that there is some kind of lying that is not sin will shamefully deceive himself, imagining that he is an honorable deceiver of others.

Liars make it so that even those who speak the truth are not believed. For a great deal of falsehood often makes a person suspect even when he speaks the truth. The one who is going to speak falsely often promises many true things, so that, having first acquired trust, he may make his hearers credulous toward his remaining lies. Many things seem true to people that are false, and therefore they speak not from God but from their own lie.

Sometimes falsehood is joined to truthful speech, and the one who invents false things often begins with the truth. Truths are frequently concealed under a coating of the honey of words, and the deceiver pretends to the truth for as long as necessary to deceive by deception. Sometimes it is worse to plan a lie than to speak one. For occasionally someone, being unwary, is accustomed to utter a lie through haste; but he cannot plan one except through deliberate effort. Thus the one who lies deliberately is considered more guilty than the one who lies merely through haste.

Every lie must be avoided with the utmost care, although sometimes a certain kind of lie may be a lighter fault if someone lies for the salvation of others. But because it is written: “The mouth that lies kills the soul” (Wis. 1), and “You will destroy those who speak lies” (Ps. 5), even this kind of lie perfect men avoid with the greatest care, so that neither the vices of anyone are defended through their deception nor they harm their own souls while striving to benefit another’s flesh, although we readily believe that this very kind of sin is easily forgiven. For if any fault is cleansed by a subsequent reward, how much more easily is this one wiped away when the reward itself accompanies it.

People lie and invent many things for the praise of others. Thus it happens that they perish by lying and lead those whom they praise to the ruin of empty glory. Just as the person who is conscious of his own uprightness does not fear another’s insult, so the one who is praised by another ought not to attend to the error of another’s praise, but each person should seek the testimony of his own conscience, which is more present to him than the one who praises him. “Let each person test his own work,” as the Apostle says (Gal. 6), “and then each person will have glory in himself,” secretly in his own conscience, not openly on another’s tongue.

Perfect men, founded on a deep root, may indeed be bent somewhat by the blast of praise and blame, as though by the force of winds, but they are not utterly thrown down; instead, they immediately return to themselves through the firmness of their root. A good mind is overcome by neither rewards nor terrors for evil; for the wicked mingle terror with flatteries, either to deceive someone by enticements or to break him by terrors.

## On false prophets

To err is nothing other than to regard as true what is false, or to hold what is uncertain as certain and what is certain as uncertain, whether the thing be false or true. Hence heretics or false prophets are called pseudoprophets, because they do not understand the Scriptures with sound judgment but lead them toward the error of a perverse understanding. Nor do they subject themselves to the meaning of the Scriptures; instead, they perversely drag them toward their own error.

Teachers of error—namely, heretics—bind their hearers by arguments of deceit through perverse persuasions in such a way that they entangle them as in a labyrinth from which they cannot escape. Such is the craftiness of heretics that they mix false things with true and bad things with good, often inserting the poison of error into salutary matters, so that they may more easily persuade people of the perversity of their corrupt doctrine under the appearance of truth.

Heretics frequently write their own statements under the name of Catholic teachers, so that they may be believed when read without suspicion. Sometimes they insert their blasphemies by hidden deceit into the books of our authors and corrupt true doctrine by adulterating it, either adding what is impious or removing what is pious. What is read must be carefully considered and tested with a cautious understanding, so that, in accordance with the Apostle’s admonitions, we may hold fast to what is right (1 Thess. 5) and reject what is contrary to the truth. In this way we may be instructed by good things and remain unharmed by evil ones.

Let us now see what John says about such prophets in his Apocalypse. He says: “I saw three unclean spirits like frogs come out of the mouth of the dragon, and out of the mouth of the beast, and out of the mouth of the false prophet” (Rev. 16). What is the dragon, and what are the beast and the false prophet? They are the devil together with his entire body. Yet, because of the prominence of particular persons and powers, he mentions those who possess greater power within that body of evil: the dragon, that is, the devil; the beast, the Antichrist; and the false prophet, that is, the teachers of that same Antichrist together with the peoples subject to them.

From the mouth of all these there proceed three spirits, which are nothing other than one spirit. Such is the unity of wickedness among all demons that, although they are many in power and malice, they are nevertheless reduced to one through agreement. They attack human beings with the same power and malice, although in different ways. Hence one is called a lying spirit, another a spirit of fornication, and a third an unclean spirit.

He is rightly called an unclean spirit because he has been soiled by grave sins and does not cease to defile others. The unclean spirits themselves are also called the dragon, the beast, and the false prophet, because the devil and all the wicked are one head and members. Frogs are said to have come out of their mouth because, just as such animals trouble human beings by making noise and wallowing in mud, so the ministers of the Antichrist, wallowing in the mud of sins, persecute God’s elect against Christ and disturb them by their chatter—that is, by heresy and blasphemy.

The demons themselves, through those whom they will inhabit, will perform signs, either true ones by God’s permission or false ones by which the reprobate may be deceived, just as the magicians once did, who seemed to raise human beings from the dead, as Simon did in Nero’s presence. Therefore the seven trumpets, of which another passage in the Apocalypse speaks, will sound over them for their destruction. For it says: “I saw seven angels standing before the presence of the Lord, and seven trumpets were given to them” (Rev. 8).

The Church, often commended by the number seven, is entrusted with the office of preaching. The first trumpet of this preaching signifies the destruction of the impious in fire and hail; the second trumpet signifies the devil expelled from the Church and setting the sea of the world ablaze more fiercely; the third signifies heretics falling away from the Church and corrupting the rivers of Holy Scripture; the fourth signifies the decline of false brothers in the darkening of the stars; the fifth signifies the greater infestation of heretics who precede the time of the Antichrist; the sixth signifies the Antichrist’s open war, together with his followers, against the Church. The seventh trumpet sounds the day of judgment, when the Lord will repay his own and destroy those who corrupted the earth.

Therefore heretics, who corrupt the rivers of Holy Scripture and over whom the trumpet of ecclesiastical condemnation sounds, cannot obtain forgiveness except through the Catholic Church. Likewise, Job’s friends could not appease God for themselves by their own means unless Job had offered sacrifice for them (Job 42). The good works performed by heretics, and their righteousness, benefit them nothing, as the Lord testifies through Jeremiah [Isaiah]: “Because you have forgotten me, behold, I will announce your righteousness, and your works will not benefit you” (Isa. 5).

Although heretics may fulfill the Law or the Prophets, nevertheless, because they are not Catholics, God is not in their assemblies, as the Lord himself testifies: “Though Moses and Samuel stood before me, my soul is not toward this people. Cast them out from my presence, and let them go forth” (Jer. 15). Through Moses and Samuel, understand the Law and the Prophets. Although heretics may strive to fulfill them in their works, because of the impiety of their error they are nevertheless cast away from God’s face and separated from the assemblies of the just.

The pagan and the heretic are separated from the just: the former because he was never with God’s people, the latter because he withdrew from God’s people. Both, having departed from Christ, belong to the body of the devil. Those who pass from idolatry to Judaism or heresy fulfill the prophet’s saying: “They slip from evil to evil” (Jer. 9). They have not known the Lord, because they have passed from the error of unbelief into another error.

Everyone whose doctrine one follows is called that doctrine’s son. Thus, through the prophet, the Lord says that Israel has an Amorite for father and a Hittite for mother (Ezek. 16)—not by birth, of course, but by imitation. Conversely, those who keep God’s commandments are called sons of God. Hence we too cry out to God not by nature but by adoption, saying: “Our Father, who are in heaven” (Matt. 6). People can be called someone’s children not only by birth but also by imitation. Thus the Jews are sons of Abraham according to the flesh, but according to their manner of life they are called sons of the devil. Accordingly, those are the seed of Abraham who imitate his faith, not those who were generated from his flesh.

Some also derive both the name and the guilt of an author from the error of that author, so that a person is designated by the name of the one whose error he follows. Thus it is said to the churches of Pergamum and Thyatira: “You have and hold the doctrine of Balaam and Jezebel” (Rev. 2). The Apocalypse therefore says that they possess the doctrine of Balaam and Jezebel because of imitation, not because of their bodily presence.

## SERMON ON GOOD AND EVIL
God performs good works by his own goodness alone, because he himself creates the will together with free choice and gives it the justice through which it acts. But he performs evil only through human guilt, because he would not perform such acts if a human being did not will to perform them. Thus, in good things God possesses both the fact that they are good by essence and the fact that they are good by justice; in evil things, however, he possesses only the fact that they are good by essence, not that they are evil through the absence of the justice that is owed—for that absence is not something.

A human being, on the other hand, possesses in good things the fact that they are not evil, because, although able to abandon justice and do evil, he did not abandon it but preserved it through free choice, with grace giving and accompanying him. In evil things he possesses only the fact that they are evil, because he does them solely by his own—that is, unjust—will.

Injustice, however, is altogether nothing, like blindness. For blindness is nothing other than the absence of sight where sight ought to be; and it is no more in the eye where sight ought to be than in a piece of wood where sight ought not to be. Injustice is not some such thing [Col. 1080C] by which the soul is infected and corrupted, as the body is by poison, and which itself produces something, as seems to happen when an evil person performs evil works. For just as, when an untamed beast breaks its bonds and rages while running about, and when a ship, after its helmsman has abandoned the tiller, wanders and is carried by the winds into every danger, we say that the absence of a chain or of a tiller causes this—not because their absence is something or does anything, but because, if they were present, they would prevent the beast from raging or the ship from perishing—so also, when an evil person rages and is driven into every danger of his soul, which consists in evil works, we cry out that injustice is at work here. This is not because injustice is any essence or does anything, but because the will, to which all the voluntary movements of the whole human being are subject, being without justice—without which a person uses his will, driven by various appetites—hurls itself and everything subject to it into manifold evils, lightly, without restraint, and without a guide; and justice, if it were present, would prevent all this from happening.

From these considerations, then, it is easily understood that injustice has no essence, although common usage calls the affections and acts of an unjust will—in themselves, something—“injustice.” By the same reasoning we understand that evil is nothing. For evil is nothing other than the absence of a due good. No essence, however much it may be called evil, is nothing; nor is being evil something for it. For being evil is nothing other than the absence from an essence of the good that it ought to possess. Therefore, being evil is not something for any essence.

Let this be said about evil, which is always nothing. For just as there are two goods—namely, justice and advantage—so there are two evils opposed to them, namely injustice and disadvantage. This disadvantage is sometimes nothing, as blindness, and sometimes something, as pain and sadness. But when this evil is something, we do not deny that God makes it, since “he is the one who makes peace and creates evil” (Isa. 45). Likewise: “There is no evil in the city that the Lord does not make” (Amos 3). For he creates disadvantages by which he disciplines and purifies the just and punishes the unjust.

That evil, however, which is called injustice, is never something; nor is being unjust something for anything. Or the phrases “creating evil” and “making good” may be understood in this way: to create is to arrange and adapt something. Hence it is said, “Consuls are created,” that is, they are appointed and prepared for this purpose, so that afterward they may be formed and become consuls. God therefore creates evil—that is, sin—when he adapts and orders someone in such a way that he possesses the power to sin. This happens when, through free choice, he gives that person the power and aptitude to live well, but does not give the actual inclination—that is, living well—just as he makes a blind person by giving him the power of sight while denying him the actual faculty, namely sight or vision.

But he makes good—that is, he forms a just person—to whom he grants not only the power of justice but justice itself, namely the form of that power. Hence it is said: “He spoke, and they were made; he commanded, and they were created” (Ps. 32). We command those who are far away; we speak to those who are near. Now nothing is far away except what is unlike something, and what is like is near. But what is more unlike the supreme essence, that is, God, than what is nothing? What is more like than what not only exists but has also been formed?

God therefore commanded those things that did not yet exist and were, indeed, far from him, and they were created—that is, adapted and arranged so as to receive their forms. But he spoke to those things that had already been created and had, indeed, drawn near to him through their power to receive form, and they were made—that is, formed. That God makes all things—that is, forms them—is proved by the fact that he creates all things. For whoever gives created things their beginning also brings them to completion.

### Again, on Good and Evil

[Col. 1081D] Although good and evil are contrary, and contraries cannot exist simultaneously in the same thing, evil and good not only can exist together, but evil cannot exist at all without goods, nor can it exist except in goods. For if good did not exist, evil could not exist either—not only because evil would have nowhere to subsist, but also because it would have no source from which to arise. Evil, that is, the corruption of nature—the destruction of good—or the diminution of good would have no existence unless there were something good to be corrupted. For evil, that is, corruption, always deprives a nature of some good, whatever that good may be. It diminishes its form, measure, or order, just as the vices of souls are privations and diseases of natural goods, and illnesses and wounds deprive bodies of health.

These three—order, measure, and form—are universal goods in things made by God, whether in spirit or in body. For everything made by God displays within itself a certain unity, as well as form and order. Whatever possesses these things is one thing, such as the natures of bodies and the capacities of souls; it is shaped by some form, such as the figures or qualities of bodies and the teachings or arts of souls; and it seeks or maintains some order, such as the weights or arrangements of bodies and the loves and pleasures of souls.

Where these three are great, the natures are great; where they are small, the natures are small; where they are absent, there is no nature. Evil, that is, the corruption or loss of natural measure, form, or order, if it removes every measure, form, and order, will leave no nature at all. Hence whatever can be corrupted is itself also some good; for corruption cannot harm it except by taking away or diminishing its good.

Evil, when well ordered and placed in its proper position, also displays goods more eminently, so that they please more and are more worthy of praise when compared with evils.
