And just as the opposition of contraries to contraries gives beauty to speech, so, through a kind of eloquence not of words but of things, the beauty of the world is set forth by the opposition of contraries; and the order of the ages is adorned, like a most beautiful poem, even by certain antitheses. Hence it is written: “Good is set against evil, and life against death, as the sinner against the godly. And so contemplate all the works of the Most High: two by two, one against one” (Ecclus. 33).

But evils arose from goods, that is, from the free choice of the will. Nor does this contradict the Lord’s saying: “A good tree cannot produce evil fruit” (Matt. 7). This means that a good will cannot produce evil works: a tree remains evil in its fruits of sin only so long as it has not turned to repentance, and a good tree does not produce evil fruits so long as it perseveres in the pursuit of goodness. Yet from the good nature of a human being a will can arise that is both good and evil.

Evil, however, can never exist where there is no good. Hence a remarkable conclusion follows: because every nature is good, when a corrupt nature is called evil, it seems that nothing else is being said. For example, a bad person is called evil, although he is a good [nature]; that is, the human being is nature and is good, while the vice is evil. Yet evil is not good, nor good evil. Thus a bad person is nothing other than a good thing that is evil. The human being is good; wrongdoing is evil.

That prophetic saying must therefore be avoided: “Woe to those who call evil good and good evil” (Isa. 5). For they blame God’s work, which is the human being, and praise the human being’s vice, which is iniquity. Every nature, even if it is corrupt, is good insofar as it is nature and evil insofar as it is corrupt. A sentient nature, even when it suffers, is better than a stone, which cannot suffer; and a rational nature, even when wretched, is superior to one devoid of reason or sensation.

Therefore accursed are those who curse the devil, blaspheming in him the work of God because of the devil’s evil. The first evil, that is, the first privation of good in a rational nature and the cause of evils, was the mutable will of a good being, turning away from the immutable good. The beginning of an evil will could be nothing other than pride, that is, love of one’s own excellence. “The beginning of every sin is pride” (Ecclus. 10).

Then, even against their will, ignorance of things to be done and desire for harmful things entered in; and error and pain followed as their companions. When these two evils are perceived as impending, the movement of the fleeing soul is called fear. But when desire attains what it covets, joy is stirred up. From these sources of disease every misery flows.

## NINTH SUNDAY  
### According to Luke

[Col. 1083]

[Col. 1083B] “There was a certain rich man who had a steward. And he was accused before him of having squandered his possessions,” etc. (Luke 16.)

Now the Lord speaks to the avaricious and proud Pharisees; now he speaks to the disciples while those others are listening, so that they may come to their senses. Properly speaking, a steward is a governor and guardian of an estate, and he derives his name from estate. Here, however, he is used for an administrator, that is, a dispenser, who administers the whole household. For administrator signifies one who dispenses both money and grain and everything that the master possesses.

The steward, then, is one to whom God has entrusted certain sums of money for distribution. He squanders them when he gathers them wrongly or when he does not spend them well.

“And he called him and said to him: ‘What is this that I hear about you? Give an account of your stewardship, for you will no longer be able to be steward.’” God calls when he instills fear of eternal condemnation. A person gives an account when, reflecting that his stewardship will end with this life, he considers acquiring friends rather than gathering riches.

“But the steward said within himself: ‘What shall I do, since my master is taking the stewardship away from me? I cannot dig; I am ashamed to beg. I know what I shall do, so that, when I am removed from the stewardship, they may receive me into their houses.’”

Once the stewardship has been taken away, we cannot dig, because after this life we are not permitted to seek the fruit of a good way of life with the spade of devoted remorse. To beg is a matter of shame, in the manner in which the foolish virgins will beg. The houses of the saints, to whom during the time of this stewardship we have shown mercy, are the heavenly dwellings in the Father’s house.

“Therefore, summoning each of his master’s debtors, he said to the first: ‘How much do you owe my master?’ He replied: ‘A hundred measures of oil.’ He said to him: ‘Take your bond and write fifty.’ Then he said to another: ‘And you, how much do you owe?’ He replied: ‘A hundred measures of wheat.’ He said to him: ‘Take your written account and write eighty.’”

“Take your written account”—understand, the account in which you had written the debt. A bond is whatever provides security against injury, so that justice may be maintained. *Kados* [κάδος] in Greek is an amphora containing three urns; *koros* [κόρος], however, is equivalent to thirty bushels.

The fact that half is remitted to one debtor and one fifth to another, taken simply, teaches that anyone who relieves the need of any poor person among the saints, whether by a half or by a fifth, is to be rewarded with a definite recompense for his mercy.

Or let it be understood in this way: Since the Jews say that tithes must be given to priests and Levites, let us, surpassing their justice with the justice of Christ, give half of our possessions, as Zacchaeus did—not only from the fruits but from all his possessions. Or certainly let us double their tithes by giving fifths to the Church.

“And the Lord praised the unjust steward, because he had acted prudently, for the sons of this age are more prudent in their generation than the sons of light.” Each person is called the son of the one whose works he performs. Hence the good are sons of eternal light, while the wicked are sons of the age, that is, of darkness. Concerning them Solomon [Isaiah] says: “Woe to you who are wise in your own eyes and prudent in your own sight” (Isa. 5).

In this steward we must not take as an example the making of fraud against his master or the giving of alms from fraud; sometimes, however, examples are drawn from opposites. The same is true of the unjust judge; hence Luke speaks of him in chapter 18.

If, then, the Lord, having suffered loss, praises the steward’s prudence—not because he acted fraudulently against him, but because he acted prudently for his own benefit—how much more will Christ, who can suffer no loss and is inclined to clemency, praise his disciples if they are merciful in obedience to his command?

Hence it follows: “And I say to you: Make friends for yourselves from the mammon of iniquity, so that, when you fail, they may receive you into eternal dwellings.” *Mammon* means riches in the language of the Syrians, and “of iniquity” has been added because they have been gathered through iniquity. Hence the familiar saying: “A rich person is either unjust or the heir of an unjust person.”

He therefore teaches us to make friends from riches gained through iniquity—not just any poor people, but those who could receive us into the heavenly dwellings. Or in this way: Let us make friends from unjust mammon, so that by giving to the poor we may acquire for ourselves the favor of the angels and of the other saints.

Some people, misunderstanding this, seize upon it as though they were managing their possessions well, but they are burdened rather than helped. “The sacrifices of the impious are abominable.” Hence Solomon also says: “Whoever offers a sacrifice from the substance of the poor is as though he were sacrificing a son in the presence of his father” (Ecclus. 34).

“He who is faithful in what is least is faithful also in what is greater; and he who is unjust in what is little is unjust also in what is greater.”

A person is faithful in what is least when he has the inward compassion and works of mercy, giving alms and loving his neighbors. He is faithful in what is greater when he clings wholly to the Creator and desires to become one spirit with him. For whoever does not love his brother, whom he sees, and does not have pity on the needy, how does he love God, whom he does not see? And how will he give himself to God?

Theophilus of Antioch, who joined together the sayings of the four evangelists into a single work, said the following about this parable in his commentaries:

“A rich man who has a steward or administrator is almighty God, whose steward was Paul, who learned the law of God from Gamaliel. When he began to persecute Christians and to squander the pride of his master, he was corrected by the Lord, hearing: ‘It is hard for you to kick against the goad’ (Acts 9).

“And he said in his heart: ‘What shall I do, since I was a teacher and steward, but now I am compelled to be a disciple and laborer? I cannot dig’—that is, the commandments of the law, which rested upon the earth, have been destroyed. ‘I am ashamed to beg’—for, having been a teacher of the Jews, I would now have to begin begging the teaching of salvation from Ananias.

“I shall therefore act so that the Christians may receive me when I have been expelled from my stewardship. And he began to say to those who had previously lived under the law and believed in such a way that they thought they would be justified by the law, that the law had been abolished, that the prophets had passed away, and that the things formerly counted as gain were to be regarded as refuse.

“Accordingly, he called two of the many debtors. The first, who owed a hundred measures of oil, represented those gathered from the nations who needed God’s mercy. From the number one hundred, which is full and perfect, he had fifty written down, a number belonging especially to penitents in accordance with the jubilee year, and to that parable in the seventy-fourth homily, in which five hundred denarii are forgiven to one debtor and fifty to another.

“Then he called the second, namely the Jewish people, who had been nourished by the wheat of God’s commandments. They owed the number one hundred, and he compelled them to make eighty out of one hundred—that is, to believe in the resurrection of the Lord, which took place on the eighth day. Eighty is completed from eight decades, so that they might pass from the Sabbath to the first day after the Sabbath.

“For this reason the Lord declares that he acted well: he had changed from the austerity of the law to the clemency of the Gospel. But if you ask why he is called a steward who offered well but did not divide well—believing in the Father but persecuting the Son, possessing almighty God but denying the Holy Spirit—Paul was therefore more prudent in transgressing the law than the former sons of light, who, living in the law, betrayed Christ, who is the true light of God the Father.

“If people are received into eternal dwellings by means of mammon of iniquity that has been well administered, how much more will the divine word, in which there is no iniquity and which was entrusted to the apostles, raise good stewards into heaven?”

“Therefore, whoever is faithful in what is least—that is, in bodily things—will also be faithful in what is greater, that is, in spiritual things. But whoever is unjust in what is little, refusing to give his brothers for their use what God created for everyone, will also be unjust in distributing spiritual money, dividing the Lord’s teaching according not to need but to persons.

“To be faithful in what is least is a great thing. For just as the principle of roundness—that all lines drawn from the central point to the circumference should be equal—is the same in a large disk as in a small figure, so, when small things are handled justly, the greatness of justice is not diminished.”

### On the Four Debtors

There are four debtors: God, the spirit, the flesh, and the world.

God owes the spirit the illumination of knowledge of the truth and the kindling of love for virtue. The spirit owes God the duty of being instructed by him in everything that must be done and of acting according to him. The spirit owes the flesh the duty of restraining it from evil and exercising it in good. The flesh owes the spirit service in doing good and moderation in seeking advantage. The flesh owes the world the duty of taking from its abundance what necessity requires and exercising what virtue requires. The world owes the flesh support in necessity and encouragement in discipline.

But the spirit does not pay what it owes the Creator, because, lifted up by pride, it scorns seeking from him the knowledge of truth, or, bound by sloth, it disdains to exercise in practice the understanding it has received. Therefore the Creator himself justly denies the spirit what is owed to it: he neither illumines it for knowing the truth nor inflames it to love the good. For inwardly he casts the proud away from knowledge of the truth, while outwardly he afflicts the slothful in their works.

Again, because the same spirit does not pay what it owes the flesh—namely, to restrain it from evil or exercise it in good—it comes about that the flesh itself, by God’s just dispensation, does not provide the spirit with what it owes it: service in doing good or moderation in seeking advantage.

Likewise, because the flesh, released through the spirit’s negligence, does not pay what it owes the world but turns its abundance toward the luxury of pleasure and does not secure its service for the exercise of virtue, the world too, by a just recompense, increases the misery of the spirit, breaking the flesh through adversities and dissolving it through prosperity.

Since the spirit alone is the author of this discord, it is necessary that it also be the first to return to peace and arrange the rest afterward into peace. For if it strives both to display the subjection owed to the Creator and to exercise just rule over the flesh, perfect and consummated justice follows, and, justice having been restored, concord and perfect peace are also restored.

For just as through its injustice the peace and concord of all things are dissolved, so through its justice all things are reconciled. Yet the spirit could lose the justice it possessed; once lost, it cannot recover it by itself. For ignorance deceives it, preventing it from paying what it owes the Creator, while desire impedes it from paying what it owes the flesh. And even if it should begin, partly illumined, to recognize the truth, and, partly strengthened, to accomplish the good, it still cannot attain what is perfect. Rather, as it is written, it begins to hunger and thirst for the justice it has tasted in part, but, without attaining its fullness, it does not reach satiety.

### On Mercy

“I shall sing the mercies of the Lord forever,” says the Psalmist (Ps. 88). I shall sing them in myself and make the Lord’s mercies worthy of song to others—mercies, I say, that will remain forever. He uses “mercies” in the plural because as many as have received mercy—that is, have been restored through mercy—so many are the mercies.

He says “forever” in order to show by this that just as anger through Adam was temporary, so mercy granted through Christ is eternal. Therefore, good Jesus, “from generation to generation I shall announce your truth with my mouth” (ibid.). “From generation to generation,” I say, I shall sing your mercies and announce your truth, not my falsehood, with my mouth now in harmony with my heart, because I announce what is yours.

Let my members therefore serve my Lord. I shall speak, but I shall speak what is yours, because I shall announce your truth. For if I do not serve, I am not a servant; and if I speak my own words, I am a liar.

Therefore, for me to speak and to speak what is yours are two distinct things: one is mine, the other yours—your truth, my mouth. And therefore I shall announce your truth with my mouth, the truth that reaches from generation to generation, that is, forever, just as mercy does.

Let us see what mercies he sings and what truth he announces. “For you have said: ‘Mercy shall be built forever; your truth shall be prepared in the heavens’” (ibid.). Therefore I shall confidently sing your mercies and announce your truth, because you, who neither deceive nor are deceived, have said—that is, permitted—mercy and truth to be so ordered in your plan.

Mercy, that is, future restoration, shall be built through grace; that is, it shall be brought to completion, reaching forever. This means: “I build in such a way that I do not destroy.” And indeed it will be so, because in those who have been restored through mercy, having been made heaven, heaven will be prepared—that is, it will be displayed to others so that they do not despair but hope that your truth, that is, the fulfillment of your promises, will plainly appear in them.

For in one there will be knowledge of languages, in another the grace of healings, in others the discernment of spirits, and the other spiritual gifts, just as you promised. When others see this, they will not despair of the fulfillment of your promises, because you have filled with good things the desire of those who, restored through mercy, have been made heaven.

Therefore whoever has been restored through mercy and thereby made heaven, that person the merciful Lord will crown after filling him with his good things. He will crown him in this way: by leading him to that good which is the highest of all goods.

It is therefore not in those goods that, wherever you turn, what has kindled desire becomes worthless once possessed. When I do not have something, I desire it; but once I have it, I despise it. “And through those goods with which you have filled my desire, my youth shall be renewed like the youth of an eagle” (Ps. 102).

Because of old age, the eagle’s upper beak grows over the lower to such an extent that it can neither open its mouth nor nourish itself, and thus it perishes from lack of food. In such distress it seeks a sharp stone and repeatedly strikes its enlarged beak against it until it can nourish itself. Then it recovers both the brightness of its feathers and the vigor of its strength.

Thus our soul was not capable of being refreshed by that bread on which the angels feed, because our mouth was held closed by old age. But a rock was given to us, that is, Christ; when old age had been worn away against it, our mouth, opened by newness, was made fit to eat that bread of angels, of which he said: “I am the living bread that came down from heaven” (John 6).

This bread is eaten here by the soul of each person who has been renewed. Then we shall be fully refreshed by it, when we are changed into an angelic condition, and he himself will be all things in all (1 Cor. 15).

Meanwhile, what happens in this pilgrimage? Certainly we are not abandoned, because the Lord is the one who performs mercies—but only for those who perform mercies. “Blessed are the merciful, for they shall obtain mercy” (Matt. 5).

What measure of mercy does he require? This: “Love your enemy, and give to everyone who asks you.” Yet what is said seems to conflict with this: “Do not receive the wicked” (Ecclus. 12); and with the saying: “Let almsgiving remain in your hand until you find a just person to whom you may give it.”

But the Lord wishes you to show mercy even to the wicked, not as wicked. An unjust person comes before you; in him there is a human being, the work of God, while his wickedness is the work of the human being. Give to God’s work, without considering the human work—that is, do not approve the fact that he is wicked. For if you receive an unjust person in the name of his injustice, you will receive the reward of an unjust person; just as one who receives a righteous person in the name of his righteousness will receive the reward of a righteous person (Matt. 10).

But someone, accepting mercy perversely and excessively, says: “Shall I not correct a lustful son or a wicked servant?” Let him know that the Lord’s rule does not condemn these actions when they are performed; rather, it condemns them if they are not performed. You ought to correct all who are subject to your correction. But if those connected with you inflict an injury upon you, endure it patiently. For just as he will be merciful if you have shown mercy, so he will also see that whatever you suffer for the sake of justice does not remain unavenged.

Truly the Lord is one who performs mercies, because he is compassionate and merciful: merciful in feeling, compassionate in action, because from every direction he calls us to conversion and from every direction to repentance, as the Apostle says: “Do you not know the riches of God’s grace? Do you not know that God’s patience leads you to repentance?” (Rom. 2).

He calls us through the benefits of creation; he calls us through spiritual gifts. Thus he is compassionate and merciful. But he must be understood as merciful in such a way that he is also seen to be just. For just as he is now merciful, so at the end he will be true. Therefore we must fear lest at last we experience him as just because we now despise him as kind.

Indeed, the compassionate Lord is patient and greatly merciful. He is patient because he does not immediately punish our sins but seeks good works through patience. For if he punished the sinner, whom would he have as his praiser? Yet he does not desire delight in a raven’s voice, but confession in the mourning of a dove.

He is greatly merciful because he rewards in us not our merits but his gifts. “The Lord, then, is compassionate and merciful, patient and greatly merciful” (Ps. 102).

He made his ways known to Moses—namely, mercy and judgment—through which he himself comes to us and we come to him. By Moses all the perfect are to be understood, but Moses is mentioned especially because through him he gave the law, and in the giving of that law there is a great mystery.

For the law was given for this purpose: so that, as sin increased, the proud might be humbled; once humbled, they might confess; once confessed, they might be healed. He made these hidden ways of his known to Moses, through whom the law was given, and through the law “the offense abounded, so that grace might abound all the more.”

Nor did God do this cruelly, but beneficially. Many people neither feel their condition nor seek a physician. The disease increases, the suffering grows, the physician is sought, and the sick person is healed. See how mercy pertains to the law.

You may understand judgment by contrast, namely, as pertaining to those who do not attend to this. He made his ways known not only to Moses and to others but also to the children of Israel—that is, to all the lesser ones who now see God by faith and will at last see him in appearance.

He made his intentions known. His will is that we recognize our manifold misery, seek medicine, and thus that he not remain angry forever. He offers this for our consolation. We should not strive only to escape future anger but also to lay aside the present anger, of which the Apostle says: “For we too were once by nature children of wrath” (Eph. 2).

Therefore, to console us, he says that he will not be angry forever. Already, through hope, we have escaped the anger in which we still remain—that is, the punishments of sin—and in the end we shall escape it completely. And just as he will not be angry forever, so he will not threaten forever.

For this present anger is a threat of eternal anger. From that anger may the Lord Jesus Christ mercifully deign to set us free. He lives and reigns as God.

## TENTH SUNDAY

[Col. 1089]

[Col. 1089B] “When the Lord drew near to Jerusalem, seeing the city he wept over it, saying: ‘If you had known—even you—and indeed on this your day—the things that are for your peace! But now they are hidden from your eyes. For days will come upon you, and your enemies will surround you with a rampart and hem you in on every side; they will throw you and your children within you to the ground,’” and so forth. [Col. 1089C] (Luke XIX).

Read the wording in this way: “If you had known that days will come upon you, and your enemies will surround you,” and so forth; you should understand “even you would weep.” But because now you do not know what is impending, you rejoice while giving yourself to the flesh and its pleasures. Indeed, “on this your day”—that is, in this brightness of your prosperity, which is temporal peace for you—you should understand “you would weep,” if you had known the evils that were about to come upon you; but now they are hidden from the eyes of your heart.

Alternatively, from the beginning of the passage one verse may be read continuously up to “which are for your peace,” in this manner: “He wept, saying: ‘If you had known—even you with me’”—understand, “the ruin that is impending”—“you would weep. Indeed, this is certainly also on this your day, which is for your peace”—understand, “you would weep.” “But now they are hidden” would then be another [Col. 1089D] verse extending to the end of the passage.

“And they will not leave in you one stone upon another, because you did not recognize the time of your visitation.”

We know that the overthrow of Jerusalem was carried out by the Roman commanders Vespasian and Titus. The very later migration of the city to the place now built outside the gate where the Lord was crucified bears witness that the former Jerusalem was utterly destroyed. This was the reason for its destruction: it did not recognize the Lord when he visited it. Hence the prophetic saying: “The kite in the sky knows its appointed time; the turtledove, the swallow, and the stork have observed the time of their coming, but my people have not known the judgment of the Lord” (Jer. VIII).

The turtledove is a kind of bird, and does not know how to love what is empty. For once married to one husband, it always departs together with him. Night and day she remains joined to him. No one sees her without her husband. But if she is widowed and deprived of him, she does not marry another mate thereafter; she flies alone, sits alone, and, as though holding her mate in her heart, remains chaste while awaiting him. So every faithful soul, made blessed through a marital covenant—for Christ is her husband—when he fills her breast with himself, lives well and always clings to him. She seeks no alien mate. However Orcus may have taken him, believing that he survives in the heavens, she looks from there for that same one to come, so that he may judge the whole microcosm.

[Col. 1090C] The swallow likewise is a bird, and it gives birth only once. So too my Savior was born once, carried once in the womb, crucified once, and rose from the dead once. One God, one faith, one baptism.

Storks are so called from the sound with which they rattle, almost *cicaniae*. They say that this sound belongs more to the mouth than to the voice, because they make it by striking their bills. These heralds of spring, companions in society, enemies of snakes, cross the seas in flight and proceed in gathered formation to Asia. Crows lead them, going before them, and [Col. 1090D] they themselves follow them like an army against hostile birds. Their devotion toward their young is extraordinary. For they tend their offspring in the nests with such diligent care that, through their constant brooding, their feathers fall out. For as much time as they devote to raising their offspring, they themselves are likewise fed by their young. This signifies morally clemency and compassion.

Thus the Lord wept once over the city when he announced that it would perish; but every day in the Church, through his elect, he mourns the reprobate, who do not know why they are mourned, because, according to Solomon, “they rejoice when they have done evil and exult in wicked things” (Prov. II). If they foresaw their damnation, they would mourn themselves together with the tears of the elect.

Thus the perverse soul has its own day, rejoicing in what is temporary. [Col. 1091A] The things that are present are for its peace, because while it rejoices in temporal possessions, while it is lifted up by honors, while it is dissolved in the pleasure of the flesh, and while it is frightened by no fear of future punishment, it has peace in its own day; but on the final day it will have the grave scandal of damnation.

The enemies are the evil spirits who beset the soul as it leaves the body, although, while it is in the flesh, they nurture it with deceptive pleasures. They surround it with a rampart because, bringing back before its eyes the wicked deeds it has committed, they hem it in for fellowship with their own damnation. They hem it in on every side when they repeat to it not only its evil deeds but also the sins of its speech. Then the soul is thrown to the ground through knowledge of its guilt, when the flesh is reduced to dust. Then its children fall into death [Col. 1091B] when the unlawful thoughts proceeding from it are scattered in the final punishment, as it is written: “On that day all their thoughts will perish” (Ps. CXLV).

“Stone upon stone” means a hard thought upon a hard thought. God visits the perverse soul every day by commandment, sometimes by punishment, sometimes by a miracle, so that the one who does not know may hear; either, pierced by sorrow, he may return, or, overcome by benefits, may blush at the evil he has done.

Moreover, it should be noted that we have within us a certain spiritual nature in which likenesses of bodily things are formed. First, when we touch some body with bodily sense. Second, when we think of absent bodies already known. Third, when we contemplate bodies that we do not know, but whose existence we nevertheless do not doubt. [Col. 1091C] Fourth, when by our own decision or conjecture we think of things that do not exist, or whose existence is unknown. Fifth, when various forms of likenesses of bodily things move about in the mind without our either doing or willing this. Sixth, when we are about to act bodily and arrange the very things we are going to do. Seventh, when, already in the act—whether we are speaking or doing something—all the bodily movements that are to be performed are preceded within the spirit by their likenesses. Eighth, when dreams are seen by sleepers, signifying either nothing or something. Ninth, when, as bodily health is disturbed internally in the pathways of sensation, the spirit so mingles images of bodies with genuine bodies that they can scarcely, or not at all, be distinguished, or when they arise signifying something or without any significance. [Col. 1091D] Tenth, when some illness or bodily pain becomes wholly dominant and blocks within the pathways by which the soul was exercised in sensing through the flesh, and the mind’s attention, having been diverted from sleep, strives more deeply: images of bodily things arise or are displayed, either signifying something or appearing without any significance. Eleventh, when there is no bodily cause, but some spirit takes up and carries away the soul to see such likenesses of bodies, mixing bodily visions with it while it likewise uses bodily senses. Twelfth, when, with the spirit taking it up, the soul is separated from and turned away from every bodily sense, [Col. 1092A] so that it is held only by likenesses of bodies in spiritual vision; I do not know whether in that state anything without significance can be seen.

This spiritual nature, therefore, in which not bodies but likenesses of bodies are represented, has visions of a lower kind than that light of mind and understanding by which these lower things are judged and those things are perceived which are neither bodies nor bear forms resembling bodies, such as the mind itself.

## Another exposition on the same subject

“ The roads of Zion mourn because there is no one who comes to the solemn assembly” (Lam. I).

Zion, which means “watchtower,” is the Church, which will behold the King of glory in her beauty. The roads of this city are understood as the lives and teachings of the saints, through whom the faithful are led to the walls of the heavenly [Col. 1092B] city. These roads mourn because few come to the solemn assembly, since the righteous grieve deeply that few attend the celebration of the Lord’s sacrament. For those who here estrange themselves from the festival of the Church are certainly excluded in the future from the solemn assembly of the angels.

Hence we read today that, seeing the city of Jerusalem, the Lord wept and foretold that it would be besieged and surrounded by enemies and destroyed, together with all its children (Luke XIX). This city over which God weeps is every soul that does not mourn its crimes. Enemies will surround it when, as death approaches, throngs of demons will besiege it. They dig a rampart around it when, bringing its past evils before its eyes, they lead it into the pit of despair. They hem it in on every side when, with horrible expression and gesture, they compel it to go forth to punishment. They throw it to the ground when they kill the body through death. They slaughter its children when, leading it to Tartarus, they torture it in punishment for its evil deeds. They leave no stone upon stone because they will leave no hard thought of the heart unpunished.

All this happens because it does not recognize the time of its visitation. The soul is visited when it is chastised by God along with human beings. But it does not recognize the visitation because it refuses to accept discipline.

The Lord casts out of his temple those who sell and buy because, by the scourge of repentance, he expels from converts those who sell their sins to the devil and buy punishments.

The overthrow of Jerusalem prefigured this, and it happened in the following way. Jerusalem’s visitation was the incarnation of Christ. “The dawn from on high” visited it when, in its midst, he preached the kingdom of heaven and enlightened it with signs and miracles. But it did not recognize the time of its visitation, since it refused to believe that he was the God promised by the Law and the prophets. Moreover, because it feared losing earthly glory, it crucified the King of glory and therefore lost heavenly glory.

He spread out the wings of the cross and desired to gather them beneath the shadow of his wings of mercy, just as a hen protects her chicks beneath her wings from a kite. But they spurned the Lord with their heel, refused to listen to him calling them, and, when he extended his hands behind them, turned their backs toward his face.

But God, patient and very merciful, who transplanted a vine from [Col. 1093A] Egypt and entrusted it to cultivators—whose prophets, sent to them, they treated with contempt and killed, and, in addition, killed his only Son after casting him out of the vineyard—gave them forty-two years for repentance, so that they might obtain forgiveness for their guilt. But they abused the time of grace in their pride and continually provoked God by increasing their guilt. Therefore God’s anger rose against them and destroyed them.

For after they rejected the wise prophets and scribes whom he had sent to them, and moreover stoned some, killed others with various punishments, and drove still others from their borders, the Lord of vengeance, the Lord, remembered that he must require their blood. The blood of Christ and of all the righteous came upon them and upon their children—the blood they had shed from the blood of Abel until they killed Christ’s apostles.

And because they offended the Father and the Son, the father Vespasian and the son Titus avenged this. The boar from the forest exterminated the vineyard of the supreme householder, which they had turned into a vineyard of Sodom and from which they had drunk the wine of Gomorrah, and a solitary wild beast devoured it (Ps. LXXIX). The forest was the Gentile world, from which Vespasian led forth an army like a boar and exterminated the vineyard, namely Judea, with sword and fire. The solitary wild beast was Titus, who devoured Jerusalem through a long siege.

But before the city was overthrown, throughout that entire year a star appeared to hang over it like a sword. A heifer brought to the sacrifices also gave birth to a lamb, and for forty continuous nights fiery armies were seen in [Col. 1093C] the air. The temple doors opened of their own accord at midnight, and when the inside shone with a great light voices of this kind were heard: “Let us depart from these dwellings.”

Thus, forty-two years having passed after the Lord’s Passion, Vespasian and Titus, Roman commanders, entered Judea with a very large army and devastated the entire region with fire. The people had gathered in Jerusalem from all the cities for the Passover festival. The army besieged them at Passover, just as they had crucified the Lord on the day of Passover.

Accordingly, in fulfillment of the Lord’s words, the city was surrounded by a rampart, with siege engines constructed on every side, and was vigorously attacked by its enemies. But it was also [Col. 1093D] defended with the utmost force by its citizens. Since, however, they did not have the Lord God as a shield of protection, they fell into the hands of the enemy.

Some were consumed by famine, others by wasting disease; some were cruelly slaughtered by their own fellow citizens, and some were suffocated by the stench of the dead. For the worst among them prowled around the city like dogs, snatching food from the hands of women and even from the mouths of infants. They tortured with impious steel the citizens lying in the streets and drawing their last breath from hunger; and although they wanted to die, they did not kill them outright but tormented the wretched with wounds.

After they had consumed as food the asses, horses, and other animals forbidden as food, the mothers themselves slaughtered their children to eat them. Hence, when a great outcry arose in [Col. 1094A] the city, the soldiers abandoned the defenses, but the enemies broke through the walls on every side. They invaded the city by force, handed everything over to devouring flames, put the entire population to death by various punishments, and destroyed all the towers, the temple itself, and the surrounding wall from their foundations. After everything had been overthrown, it is said that in the place where the city had formerly stood they drove a plow and scattered salt as seed.

During this siege, it is recorded that 1,100,000 perished from hunger; as many were killed by the sword; an equal number were sold into captivity; and three hundred were crucified in vengeance for the Lord’s death. It is also reported that thirty were sold for a denarius, just as they had handed over the Lord for thirty [Col. 1094B] denarii. Thus, dearly beloved, the Lord repaid sevenfold into the bosom of those who shed the blood of the saints (Ps. LXXVIII).

Thus the house was left deserted—the house they themselves had made a den of thieves. Thus the Romans took away both their place and their nation.

Behold, beloved, you have heard of the captivity of the Jews. We must beware of captivity by demons. That event was written for our correction, lest the camp of the evil enemy surround us unawares. Indeed, so that we might be free from captivity, the Son of the supreme King was given as a hostage for our redemption.

And so that this might be firmly impressed upon our memory, Christ’s bread is formed in the shape of a denarius, because he was certainly handed over into the hands of the impious for thirty denarii. [Col. 1094C] He is the true denarius, which will be given as the reward of all the righteous who labor in the vineyard until evening.

This captivity preceded us in figure, as Holy Scripture tells us. When Elijah was carried into heaven in a fiery chariot, and Elisha, having divided the Jordan with Elijah’s mantle, was returning to Jericho, he went up from there to Bethel, and boys mocked him. They cried: “Go up, baldhead! Go up, baldhead!” (4 Kings I). When he cursed them, two bears came out of the forest and tore forty-two boys to pieces.

Elijah was a figure of Christ. Christ went up to Bethel when he proceeded from Jerusalem to the cross. The boys mocked him, crying, “Go up, baldhead,” when the Jews, with childish understanding, mocked the Lord who had been scourged for us, shorn, and crucified at the place of Calvary. Among the ancients it was customary for those about to be crucified first to be scourged and shorn. This may also be observed in Holy Scripture: “The sword,” it says, “shall devour the flesh of the slain from the blood and from the captivity of the enemies with shorn heads” (Deut. XXXVI). Captives who were sold were also shorn.

This seems to be expressed by our tonsure, since we are reckoned to bear the figure of Christ. The boys are cursed by Elisha when the curse of Christ’s blood is brought upon us and upon our children, the Jews. The two bears coming out of the forest and tearing apart forty-two boys signify that after forty-two years two emperors from the Gentiles emerged and cruelly strangled the Jews with weapons.

Therefore, dearly beloved, let us strive [Col. 1095A] to escape the hands of our enemies, to escape the captivity of our souls, to come to our true King, and to obtain true freedom.

## On Elijah and Jezebel

“Elijah was afraid of Jezebel and fled from the presence of the promiscuous woman. Rising, he went wherever his will led him, and came to Beersheba of Judah. There he left his servant and went into the wilderness, a day’s journey” (3 Kings XIX).

First, the foundations of the historical account must be laid, so that afterward, as it were, oil of morality may be drawn from the wall or rock of history.

Jezebel is interpreted as “a flow of blood” and signifies carnal desire, which kills the prophets—that is, those who see. Hence it is said: “Where is the house of the seer?” (1 Kings IX), that is, of the prophet. For this desire extinguishes prophets and wise men when they submit themselves to pleasure—very alluring indeed, but most shameful and pernicious—and to similar vices, concerning which it is written: “Their flow is like the flow of horses” (Ezek. XXIII).

(Gregory.) Therefore Elijah—that is, any solitary person whom the Sun of righteousness has illuminated—fearing for himself because of her region, fled to Beersheba, which is interpreted as “the seventh well,” namely the Church overflowing with the sevenfold grace of the Holy Spirit. Judah means “confession,” or “the well of satiety,” because the Church has doctrinal commandments and streams sufficient for satisfaction, in which, as someone says, a lamb can walk and an elephant swim. From there elementary and milky teaching is offered to beginners, but solid food to the perfect.

[Col. 1095C] He left his servant there—that is, childish actions and sins by which children stumble—and proceeded wherever his will led him. This signifies the deliberation of anyone who wishes to redeem his sins, so that he may undertake this way of life. At last he goes into the wilderness, that is, he abandons the world: a day’s journey.

There are three journeys or stages (Exod. III) undertaken by those who are going to sacrifice to the Lord, because everything we offer to the Lord must be done in the name of the Holy Trinity. The first stage is to begin, the second to act, and the third to complete or persevere. Or the first is to turn away from evil, the second to do good, and the third to dwell or remain forever and ever. Thus of the first it is said: “Cease to act perversely” (Isa. I), and “Let the one who stole steal no longer” (Eph. IV). Of the second: “Learn to do good” (Isa. I), and “Put on the new man” (Eph. IV). The third stage is to bring the good to completion, concerning which it is said: “He has set ascents in his heart” (Ps. LXXXIII), and in the Song of Songs: “Who is this who comes up through the wilderness?” (Song III).

Of these three days it is said in the Gospel: “Ask and you will receive; seek and you will find; knock and it will be opened to you” (Matt. VII). Elijah, who bears the form of the penitent, proceeded only one stage. Hence he also sat down as though meditating.

It should be noted that there are three recollections of sin. The first affects and delights, and is evil. The second irritates and is called piercing or compunctional [Col. 1096A]; it is useful. The third is glorious and belongs to the perfect.

An affective, that is, an affecting, recollection of sin occurs when a person is moved by the desire and pleasure of sinning, when he thinks back to the pots of Egyptian meat—how deliciously and pleasantly he lived—and to how difficult the journey is that he has undertaken or is about to undertake.

A piercing or compunctional recollection occurs when he remembers how filthily and wantonly he lived—not in order to return to his former ways, but so that he may worthily mourn them and always set them before himself. Hence it is said: “My sin is always before me” (Ps. L). This is like someone who is pruning a field: he cuts back the shrubs, but does not remove them from the field; rather, he places them and spreads them over the field and burns them, so that the field may be more suitable for bearing and producing fruit, according to the saying: “My heart grew hot within me, and in my meditation the fire burned” (Ps. XXXVIII).

[Col. 1096B] The third recollection of sin is glorious. It occurs when a person, reflecting on who he was and by what grace he was freed from the pit of misery and the filth of mud, gives thanks to God, saying: “Not to us, Lord, not to us, but to your name give glory” (Ps. CXIII). With the Israelites, freed from Egyptian slavery, he joyfully sings: “Let us sing to the Lord, for he has been gloriously exalted” (Exod. XV); and with Zechariah: “Blessed is the Lord God of Israel, because he has visited and made redemption for his people” (Luke I).

Elijah, therefore, had proceeded a day’s journey, recalling the past with compunction, and sat beneath a juniper tree (3 Kings [Col. 1096C] XIX), which is a low, thorny shrub signifying the compunction and bitterness of repentance. From weariness and sadness he fell asleep, because the person who is disgusted with his former life ought to become insensible to the world and, as it were, dead.

Hence Elijah also said: “It is enough for me, Lord; take my life” (ibid.), that is, my animal life. Whoever sleeps in this way is awakened by the Angel of great counsel, who says: “Rise from the dead, and Christ will illuminate you” (Eph. V). Hence it is written: “Behold, an angel of the Lord touched him, saying: ‘Rise and eat’” (3 Kings XIX).

This touch is of the soul, not of the body; of the spirit, not of the flesh; of reason, not of sensuality; of the inner person, not of the outer. This angel awakened the sleeping disciples, saying: “Why are you sleeping? Could you not watch with me for one hour?” (Luke XXII).

And behold, at his head there was a cake baked under the ashes and a vessel of water. “At his head” refers to the head of the inner person, that is, the mind. The cake baked under the ashes, which must be blown clean and wiped, signifies the austerity of food by which penitents live. Of it David says: “I ate ashes like bread” (Ps. CI). The vessel of water signifies tearful compunction, which is water that washes and refreshes.

The measure of this compunction is signified by the vessel, because the measure of punishment will correspond to the measure of guilt, as it is said: “You will give us drink in tears, by measure” (Ps. LXXIX), and “My eyes poured forth streams of water” (Ps. CXVIII).

[Col. 1097A] He ate and drank, therefore, and again fell asleep—that is, in peace and the quiet tranquility of mind. The angel of the Lord returned again, touched him, and said to him: “Rise” (3 Kings X), that is, lift yourself up to heavenly things. He also said to the disciples: “Sleep now and rest; it is enough” (Mark XIV).

“Eat,” that is, take a foretaste and taste the inward sweetness. What they ate is not specified, because the taste of that sweetness is unspeakable, indeed inconceivable. It can be acquired, but it cannot be measured.

A great journey remains for him, namely charity, which is present at the table, so greatly that it inclined God toward this valley of tears, so that he might empty himself. Great is the perfection that exalted a human being even to the right hand of God. Whoever walks this road without stumbling may say: “We passed through fire” (Ps. LXV), [Col. 1097B] which consumes solid things, constricts them, and makes them split apart—that is, adversities—and through water, which softens—that is, prosperity.

It should be noted that bread is spoken of in three ways. There is purgatorial bread with bitterness, which beginners eat; this is signified by the cake baked under the ashes with which Elijah was refreshed. There is consolatory bread with sweetness, concerning which it is said: “According to the multitude of my sorrows in my heart, your consolations have gladdened my soul” (Ps. XCXIII). This is eaten by those who are progressing, which is signified by Elijah eating again. There is solitary bread with strength: this is strong and perfect charity, in whose strength he walked for forty days and forty nights—that is, through the fulfillment of the Ten Commandments and the four Gospels—to the mountain of God, Horeb.

Horeb signifies solitude, or a person turned toward the monastic life or the desert, according to the saying: “Who will give me wings like a dove? I will fly away and rest” (Ps. LIV).

## On the words of Wisdom: “Come over to me”

“Come over to me, all you who desire me, and be filled with my generations,” says Wisdom (Ecclus. XXIV).

This is a faithful and exhortatory saying, to be received with eager devotion. There are two great roads, far apart from one another. One separates from and leads astray from God; the other calls back and leads again to God. Along the former, lovers of the world stroll and, wandering along byways, stray widely. Along the latter, with Christ as guide and companion, despisers of the age pass happily from the mud of Egypt into the rest and promised [Col. 1097D] land of the living.

There are also two kinds of desire: one blameworthy, the other praiseworthy. The blameworthy desire is that which plunges us into secular and carnal longings. The praiseworthy kind is twofold. One proceeds from the privilege of nature; the other from the gift of grace.

Natural desire is that by which each person loves and seeks something, although all pursue the same end by different paths: some through riches, some through honors, some through magnificence and the greatness of a name, and some through pleasures, as Boethius says. But they are deceived and wander. This affection is a foreign love that smells goodness from afar but does not contemplate its sweetness up close. It is the good of nature, not the restoration of grace.

The other desire, which grace confers, seeks true and eternal goods as well, when the faithful person, having trampled all transient things underfoot, sighs for God alone, thirsts for him, hungers for him, and thinks of him.

One must therefore pass from love of temporal things to love of eternal things, just as Moses passed over when he saw the bush burning without being consumed (Exod. V). At first he was astonished, having previously experienced another fire—namely, the love of his Ethiopian woman; that is, he had previously been burning with the heat of desire, which clouds those who love it. But when he saw that the bush burned without being consumed, he said: “I will pass over and see this great vision” (ibid.), and thus he passed over to the fire of divine love.

This passage cannot occur except by the grace of God. According to its effects, grace is said to be threefold. The first initiates, so that we may be called and be the beginning of his creation; the second advances, so that we may be justified; the third brings to completion, so that we may be glorified. The first is called good pleasure, the second merit, and the third reward.

Of the first it is said: “From his fullness we have all received” (John I); of the other two: “Grace for grace” (ibid.), that is, for the merit of temporal service, the reward of eternal glory.

Blessed is this passage by which one passes over to wisdom. Whoever has begun to pass over in this way must take the greatest care not to look back like Lot’s wife; having already put his hand to the plow, he must beware of returning to shipwreck, from which he escaped naked; or to the fire from which he came out half-burned; or to the robbers by whom he was left half-dead and from whom the merciful Samaritan brought him back; lest, as a soldier of Christ, having already seized heaven, he be called back from the very entrance like a dog to its vomit or a pig to its wallow.

[Col. 1098C] “Come over to me, all you who desire me, and be filled with my generations.”

There are three generations: carnal, secular, and spiritual.

The carnal generation is what a person generates from himself, namely unclean and vulgar deeds, and the rest—things that are the fruit of a bad tree.

The secular generation consists in the acquisition of estates, the height of power, and the extension of one’s name, as it is said: “They called their names in their lands” (Ps. XLVIII). These generations, as Origen says, do not arise from Israelite nobility. They are the devil’s snares, nets for the Christian soul, and engines of the adversary, which batter the walls of the virtues.

The spiritual generation is that of which the Apostle says: “The fruit of the Spirit is charity, peace, joy in the Holy Spirit, and so forth” (Gal. V). [Col. 1098D] These are the fruits of a good tree. By this seed we inherit the land of the living.

These are our males, whom the surviving Pharaoh still strives to destroy to this day, afflicting us with mud—that is, unclean works—and straw—that is, the lightness of thoughts, by which we are carried about as though by the wind. Hence the Psalmist laments, saying: “How long shall I lay plans in my soul, sorrow in my heart by day?” (Ps. XII).

“Come over,” he says. Two things make walls between us and God: excessive love of ourselves and vain love of the world. Concerning this wall the Prophet says: “In my God I will leap over a wall” (Ps. XVII).

This wall can be leapt over in the present, but it cannot be utterly destroyed. Sin is destroyed in three ways: so that it does not reign, so that it does not exist, or so that it cannot exist. That it may not reign can occur here while sin itself remains. Hence the Apostle says: “Let not sin reign in your mortal body” (Rom. VI). The other two—that it may not exist and that it may not be able to exist—will occur in the future.

## ELEVENTH SUNDAY. According to Luke

[Col. 1099]

[Col. 1099A] “The Lord Jesus said to certain people who trusted in themselves as though they were righteous and despised others this parable: ‘Two men went up into the temple to pray, one a Pharisee and the other a publican,’ and so forth (Luke XVIII).”

They went up, he says, because the ascent to the temple consisted of fifteen steps. He carefully demonstrates that one must not glory in works, but trust humbly in grace. The publican belongs to the humility of the Church; the Pharisee to the wickedness of pride.

“The Pharisee, standing, prayed this within himself: ‘God, I thank you that I am not like the rest of humanity: robbers, unjust, adulterers, or even like this publican.’”

There are four forms in which every swelling of the arrogant is displayed. First, when they suppose that they possess good from themselves. Second, when, if they believe it was given from above, they believe it was given to them on account of their merits. Third, when they boast of possessing what they do not possess. Fourth, when, despising others, they wish to appear uniquely to possess what they do possess—as did this Pharisee.

Hence he departed from the temple without a good deed, because he boastfully set himself above the publican.

“‘I fast twice on the Sabbath; I give tithes of all that I possess.’”

Ezekiel says that the living creatures shown to him were full of eyes (Ezek. I), because the action of the saints ought to be watchful in every direction. But we often, while attending to some matters, neglect others. The Pharisee had an eye toward abstinence and toward mercy, but he had none toward guarding humility. And what good is it to guard a city if one opening is left through which the enemy may enter?

“And the publican, standing far off, did not dare even to lift his eyes toward heaven, but beat his breast, saying: ‘God, be merciful to me, a sinner.’”

“I tell you, this man went down to his house justified rather than the other”—that is, in comparison with him, or more than he—because the Pharisee was justified before himself on account of works, while the publican was justified before God through faith.

Standing far off and not lifting his eyes are signs of humility, which God sees from near at hand. This man presses down his conscience but lifts up hope. He beats his breast, demanding punishments from himself so that God may spare him. He confesses so that God may forgive. God overlooks what this man acknowledges.

But what is “beating the breast” except exposing what lies hidden in the breast, and, by evident beating, chastising the concealed sin?

Typically, the Pharisee is the people of the Jews, who exalt their merits on the basis of the justifications of the Law and withdraw in pride. The publican, however, is the Gentile, who, having humbly confessed his sins, draws near to God and is exalted.

“For everyone who exalts himself will be humbled, and the one who humbles himself will be exalted.”

This can rightly be understood both of the two peoples mentioned above and of every proud or humble person, just as can that other saying that we read elsewhere: “Before destruction the heart is exalted, and before glory it is humbled” (Prov. XVI).

Therefore, from the words of the proud Pharisee, by which he deserved to be humbled, we can conversely take a pattern of humility by which we may be exalted. Just as he, considering the vices of worse people and his own virtues, was lifted up to ruin, so may we, considering not only our own laziness [Col. 1100B] but also the virtues of those who are better, be humbled toward glory, so that each person may earnestly and submissively entreat these things within himself:

“Almighty God, have mercy on your suppliant, because I am not like the countless servants of yours who are exalted by contempt for the world, glorious through the merit of righteousness, or radiant with angelic praise for chastity; nor am I like the many among them who, after public crimes, deserved through repentance to become devoted to you.

“Even if I do anything good by the gift of your grace, I do not know with what intention I do it, or with what severity you will judge me in your presence.”

But we must not pass over what is meant by the statement that Solomon built a temple for the honor of the Lord, to which one ascended by fifteen steps. This is not without a mystery.

That temple prefigured the temple that the Lord builds in the heavenly Jerusalem from living stones, to which one ascends, as it were, by fifteen steps. The number fifteen consists of seven and eight. The number seven signifies earthly things, which revolve according to the number seven. By despising and rejecting these, one ascends to the Lord’s temple through the number eight, that is, through heavenly things, which are acquired through the eight beatitudes.

Alternatively, since there are seven deadly vices, they can be understood through the number seven. Everyone who wishes to ascend to the Lord’s temple must despise them, just as he must ascend through the eight beatitudes, which are understood by the number eight.

## Exposition on the same subject
“Blessed is the man to whom the Lord has not reckoned sin [Col. 1100D] (Psalm 31).” Whoever here washes away his sins with tears and redeems them by almsgiving, to him the Lord will not reckon them in the future, because he himself has condemned them here by punishing them. But whoever does not consider what he has already done, but what he may still do, provokes God’s vengeance, because “whoever loves iniquity hates his own soul” (Psalm 10). And whoever hates his own soul certainly hates God; his iniquity will be found hateful.

There are many who are filthy with sins yet consider themselves righteous and condemn others as sinners. In today’s Gospel the Lord restrains their obstinacy, while raising those despised by them to the hope of pardon. For he relates that two men went up to the temple in Jerusalem to pray: one was a Pharisee, that is, a cleric of the Jews, and the other a publican (Luke 18) [Col. 1101A]. The Pharisee, approaching the altar and raising his hands and eyes toward heaven, gave thanks to God that he was unlike other men, who were robbers, unjust, and adulterers—such as that publican standing behind him—and that he fasted twice a week and gave tithes of all his possessions.

But the publican hid in a certain corner and did not dare to raise his eyes toward heaven. He merely struck his breast and asked that God be propitious to him. Then the Lord says that the man confessing his sins went down justified, whereas the man boasting of his deeds went away rejected, because “everyone who exalts himself will be humbled, and whoever humbles himself will be exalted.”

Therefore, dearly beloved, when you gather for prayer, you must not boast of your good deeds or condemn others, but accuse yourselves and regard all others as righteous. [Col. 1101B] Humble your souls in the sight of God, invoke him with mouth and heart, and he will deliver you on the day of tribulation and exalt you over your enemies. Restrain your tongue from evil and your lips from deceit, because each person will be justified by his words and condemned by his words.

Whoever prays as the Lord taught will be heard by the Lord; but whoever prays otherwise, his prayer will become sin. Ask for the necessities of life and eternal joys, and the Father will give you both. Many pray and do not obtain what they ask, but their prayer will be accursed, because they turn their ear away from the cry of the poor.

“For not everyone who says to him, ‘Lord, Lord,’ will enter the kingdom of heaven, but the one who does the will of his Father will enter the kingdom of heaven” (Matthew 7). The will [Col. 1101C] of the Father is that we forgive those who sin against us and give assistance from our possessions to those in need. Through these petitions we shall obtain the desires of our hearts; through these we shall enter the kingdom of heaven.

By the two men who are said to have gone up to the temple, two peoples are understood: namely, the Jewish people and the Gentile people. The Pharisee who approached the altar is the Jewish people, which possessed the sanctuary and the ark. In the temple he recounts his merits, because in the world he boasts of observing the law. He was not like the rest of humanity, because by circumcision he was distinguished from the peoples of the nations.

The Gentiles were robbers, because they seized the Lord’s goods almost by force, since they did not render him the service owed for the benefits bestowed upon them. [Col. 1101D] They had been unjust, since, rejecting the Creator, they worshiped the creature. They were adulterers, since, abandoning God their true bridegroom, they defiled themselves with demons.

The Jews, too, were robbers, because they appropriated to themselves the merits of the righteous. For it is robbery to wish to possess the praise of a righteous person while refusing to imitate the righteous person’s holiness. Hence it is written: “He did not regard it as robbery to be equal with God” (Philippians 2). When the first man wished to rob this equality, he fell from blessedness.

They had been unjust, since they rendered neither what was due to God nor what was due to humanity. They had been adulterers, since, casting aside the law, their noble bride, they polluted themselves with idolatry.

By the week the whole of time is understood, since it revolves through seven days. He fasts twice in the week who avoids evil in deed and in intention. [Col. 1102A] He gives tithes of everything he possesses who fulfills the law’s Decalogue through the ten senses of the body. For five doubled makes ten, as with two eyes, two ears, and so forth.

But the Jews practiced evil in deed and in desire, transgressing God’s commands with all their senses. The publican who stood at a distance is the Gentile people, which was far from the worship of the Lord. He did not raise his eyes toward heaven because he yearned only for earthly things. He struck his breast while mourning his error through repentance. And because he humbled himself through confession, God exalted him through pardon.

And so let us also, dearly beloved, stand at a distance, judging ourselves unworthy of the Lord’s sacraments and of the company of the saints. Let us not raise our eyes toward heaven, considering ourselves unworthy of heaven. Let us beat our breasts, [Col. 1102B] punishing our offenses with tears. Let us fall prostrate before God and weep before the Lord who made us, so that he himself may turn our mourning into joy and, tearing apart the sackcloth of sadness, clothe us with gladness.

Let us not be robbers, because the rapacious will not possess the kingdom of God (1 Corinthians 6). Let us not covet anyone’s property, nor ascribe to ourselves praise that our merits do not deserve, because those who do these things will be companions of robbers. Let us not be unjust, because the wicked will not obtain the kingdom of God. Let us love God and provide what is necessary to our neighbors.

Let us not be adulterers, because God will judge fornicators and adulterers. Let us preserve the true faith and turn aside toward no heresy, because this is called spiritual fornication, and God will destroy everyone who fornicates away from him.

Let us fast twice in the week, namely on the fourth and sixth days [Wednesday and Friday], because if the Pharisee did this, we ought to do it all the more. And if we do not abstain from food, let us restrain our hearts from evil desire and our hands from wrongful action. Let us give God tithes of all our possessions, because if the Jew did this, the Christian ought to do it all the more.

Not only, dearly beloved, do the sacred writings lead us to eternal life, but the writings of the Gentiles also instruct us; among them certain things ought to be brought forward for edification. And so that no one may be scandalized by this, let it be demonstrated by sacred authority.

The children of Israel plundered the Egyptians, taking gold, silver, gems, and precious garments (Exodus 5), which [Col. 1102D] afterward they offered as gifts to God for the construction of the tabernacle. When they themselves departed from Egypt, all the temples of the idols collapsed.

Those who abandon this world and transfer themselves to a holy way of life depart from Egypt and journey toward the promised land. Then the shrines are destroyed, because those who had been temples of vices are demolished with respect to their sins. They begin already to be God’s dwelling place, and therefore the evil spirit will no longer be able to retain a place to dwell in them.

They plunder the Egyptians when they transform secular studies into spiritual practice. They offer these things for making the tabernacle when they bring philosophical arguments forward for the edification of the Church. They offer the Egyptians’ gold when they adorn spiritual discipline with secular wisdom. [Col. 1103A] They offer the Egyptians’ silver when they turn secular eloquence to the usefulness of the Church. They give their gems when they recount well-expressed opinions for the exhortation of their neighbors. They offer their garments when they report examples from the Gentiles for their brothers’ imitation.

For in a great house not only golden and silver vessels but also iron and earthen vessels are necessary (2 Timothy 2). The great house is the Church. The golden and silver vessels are the volumes of sacred authority. The iron and earthen vessels are secular writings, necessary for external matters. For just as gold shines through iron, so sacred Scripture shines through secular disciplines.

It is also handed down that those who returned from captivity rebuilt God’s temple with the money they had acquired in Babylon. [Col. 1103B] Captives are held among the Babylonians who, straying from the Catholic faith, are held among heretics, or who, apostatizing from a holy purpose, are held among secular people in captivity to demons.

If, by God’s favor, they return to Jerusalem—that is, to Mother Church—and bring forward for the edification of their neighbors what they have learned outside, they certainly build a temple for God with the money they earned among the Babylonians.

The law also prescribes that if a people besieged a city and someone saw a beautiful girl among the enemy, he was to cut her nails and hair; afterward he was to take her as his wife (Deuteronomy 21). We besiege a city when we attack some heresy or error through the writings or disputation of the Gentiles. We see a beautiful girl among them [Col. 1103C] when we find among them some well-expressed opinion. We ought to cut off her nails and hair and thus join her to ourselves, because we must reject what is superfluous and contrary to the faith, but weave into our books for the instruction of the faithful what has been well said and is not at all contrary to our faith.

Philosophers therefore write that a woman is fastened to a wheel and continually carried around, her head now raised on high, now plunged below. This revolving wheel is the glory of this world, which is continually carried around. The woman fastened to the wheel is fortune interwoven with glory. Her head is sometimes carried upward and sometimes downward, because many are repeatedly exalted by power and riches and are also often humbled by poverty and miseries.

They also say that a certain condemned man in the underworld was stretched apart by the spokes of a wheel; this wheel was carried without interruption from the height of a mountain down into the depths of a valley, and, returning again to the heights, slipped down once more. They further relate that someone there rolled a stone up to the top of a mountain, and that the weight of the stone drove the man rolling it headlong from the mountain’s summit; then the wretched man rolled the stone up again.

They relate further that a vulture devoured someone’s liver there, and that, once consumed, it grew again. Since wise reasoning composed these stories, your Love ought to understand what they mean.

The man who is hurled from the mountain’s height into the depths amid the wheel’s whirling is the one who is spun headlong from the height of power or riches into the depth of the abyss. The one who rolls a stone up the mountain, which immediately rolls back down, is the person who [Col. 1104A] obtains offices or whatever else he desires with great difficulty, and through those very things is plunged into the depths of hell.

The person whose liver the vulture eats and which is said to grow green again is the one whose heart’s lust feeds the vulture, and in whom, once desire has been satisfied, foul lust is born again. For desire resides in the liver, while the vulture loves the corpses of the dead.

Concerning this plague they also say that Medusa, of outstanding beauty, incited many to love her, and that she transformed into stones all who looked at her. Perseus protected himself from her face with a crystal shield and killed her with a curved sword.

This woman is lust, which pretends to be beautiful throughout the human breast. But she changes those who gaze at her into stones, because through love she hardens the hearts of the lustful. Perseus protects himself from her with a crystal shield [Col. 1104B] because the strong man, gazing intently at the mirror of the virtues, turns his heart’s face away from her sight. He kills her with a curved sword because, through fear of eternal fire, he cuts her away from himself.

Hence it is read that one of the Fathers brought up a little son in the desert, whom lust assaulted when he had grown up. The father ordered him to withdraw into the desert and devote himself alone to fasting and prayer for forty days.

When twenty days had been completed, he saw a dreadful and exceedingly foul naked woman rushing upon him. Unable to endure her stench, he began to drive her away. But she said: “Why, then, do you shrink from me now, when you burn with such love for me? For I am the image of lust, which appears sweet in human hearts. And unless you had obeyed your father, you, like the others, would have been thrown down by me.”

He therefore gave thanks to God [Col. 1104C] who had rescued him from the spirit of fornication. Many other examples lead us toward the paths of life.

It is read that one of the Fathers, going out, saw an Ethiopian in a forest cutting wood and attempting to lift what he had tied together. Since the bundle appeared heavy, the Ethiopian loosened it and increased the burden. And when it had then become even more burdensome, he added to it and made it impossible to carry. As he tried to lift it, he was crushed by its weight.

Moving on, the Father saw someone pouring water into a vessel, but the water ran out below because the vessel had no bottom. He went farther, and behold, two men were approaching the gate of a city carrying a piece of wood crosswise before them. Neither wished to yield to the other, and both remained outside.

The Ethiopian who increases the burden of the wood is the person who continually heaps up the weight of his sins. [Col. 1104D] Although scarcely enough time remains to correct what has been done in the past, the wretched man never ceases adding more recent sins, until, falling into despair, he no longer earns repentance but is pressed down into death by the mass of his crimes.

The one who pours water into a vessel without a bottom is the person who performs almsgiving or some other good deed but loses it through uncleanness or other vices. Hence it is written: “He gathered money and put it into a pierced bag” (Haggai 1). He gathers money into a pierced bag who indeed performs good deeds but pollutes them through wicked actions.

Those who carried the wood crosswise are those who bear the heavy yoke of pride. Since they refuse to yield to one another, they will not be able to enter the gate of the heavenly city. [Col. 1105A] But those who place the Lord’s easy yoke upon their necks and lift his light burden will enter the gate of the city above.

Toward this city, dearly beloved, let us sigh with our whole heart and hasten with all our strength, so that we may escape the bottomless pit and be able to sacrifice an offering of praise to the Lord in the courts of Jerusalem—where “eye has not seen” (1 Corinthians 2).

## On David’s words: “Ascents in his heart”

“He arranged ascents in his heart, etc.” (Psalm 83).

A person incurs three descending steps of ruin. The first is presumption in one’s own will; the second is the abuse of carnal allurements; the third is the deceitful pursuit of temporal things. By the same road on which he descended, he must ascend, retracing his steps; but in reverse order, so that the first step of ascent is renouncing worldly things; the second, mortifying the flesh; the third, casting aside one’s own will. These are the three stages by which we return to Christ.

Hence Moses says: “We shall go a three days’ journey into the desert to sacrifice to the Lord” (Exodus 3). But those renouncing the world and returning to Christ must make a pure and faithful confession. Hence the Apostle says: “This saying is faithful and worthy of all acceptance: Christ Jesus came into this world to save sinners” (1 Timothy 1).

One sinner confesses his sins with a faithful heart and faithful speech. Of him it is said: “Blessed are those whose iniquities have been forgiven” (Psalm 31). There are others who excuse themselves. Of them the Lord says through the prophet: “I rained upon one city, but upon another I did not rain” (Amos 4). [Col. 1105C] That is: I watered the devoted soul, piercing it through the word of instruction, but left the hard and obstinate soul in sin.

Others confess part of their sins. Of these, the part they confess is watered by words of instruction or confession, while the unconfessed part remains unwatered.

God commanded the children of Israel, when they entered the promised land, to kill all their enemies (Joshua 26). “If any remain,” he said, “they will be to you like nails in your eyes and like spears in your sides or ribs” (Numbers 33).

Through confession, as you depart from Egypt—that is, from the world—you enter the promised land, that is, the heavenly homeland. If we kill every vice without exception, whatever remains will be for us like nails in our eyes and [Col. 1105D] like spears in our ribs. This means obstacles to good intention or torment in the conscience, so that through these even the strong works of the virtues are scattered, by which our weaker inner parts, like those beneath the ribs, are covered and protected.

But it is necessary to know by what road and with what provisions we must travel. We must therefore pass through Jericho, that is, through the decline of this life. For Jericho is interpreted as “moon.” And just as the moon is sometimes seen hollow and sometimes full, so here some are poor and others rich.

This mystical Jericho is fortified with seven walls (Joshua 6). The first is pride, sloth, and the other vices joined to them; the second is envy; the third, anger; the fourth, sadness; the fifth, avarice—each together with the vices and sins associated with it. These are the vices of the soul; the remaining two belong to the body: gluttony and lust.

All these things are commanded to be put to death by those who wish to enter and reach the promised land. No one will enter unless he passes through Jericho by entering through the place opposite to him, because once pride has been destroyed, humility becomes the entrance. Charity is opposed to envy, patience to anger, chastity to lust, generosity to avarice, and abstinence to gluttony.

This, then, is the road by which we journey toward the heavenly homeland. The provision for the journey is the body and blood of the Lord. Whoever lacks this does not reach the appointed place, or rather departs farther from it.

But because some beg for what is not given to them, Solomon says: “Because of the cold the lazy man did not wish to plow; therefore he will beg in summer, and nothing will be given to him” (Proverbs 20). This means: Because of this world, every reprobate person refused to exercise himself in good deeds; therefore, in the brightness of the last day, he will beg for the alms of eternal salvation, and it will not be given to him.
