Winter signifies the present world, where, because iniquity abounds, charity grows cold (Matthew 24). Summer, however, signifies the day of judgment, when the harvest of perpetual salvation will be given to the elect as to good laborers from their cultivation.

## On Boasting

Boasting must be avoided both in words and in deeds. Yet the ruin of wishing to please oneself more than God and to obtain praise from human beings must be mourned. It is empty and full of error for the mind to desire fame and devote effort to acquiring earthly praise.

Look carefully at yourself, O man, and claim nothing for yourself that is in you apart from sin. [Col. 1106C] He does not turn aside to the right who attributes the good he does not to himself but to God; nor does he turn toward the left who does not presume upon divine indulgence as permission to sin.

This is what the Prophet says: “This is the way; walk in it, neither to the right nor to the left” (Isaiah 30). It is true that nature expects to delight in praises, but this is right only if each person is praised in God, not in himself. As it is written: “In the Lord my soul shall be praised” (Psalm 33).

Often, while despising empty glory, a person falls into another kind of exaltation, when he boasts in himself because he has despised human praise. Some are granted the ability to do good but do not possess the fruit of their good work, because they themselves take it away through their pursuit of human boasting. Those who love the favors of empty glory should always look upon their own foulness and grieve that they have lost the good work they performed for the sake of human display.

The lover of empty glory never ceases doing whatever may win him continual praise, and then a perverse desire increases the strength of his vanity. The beginning of a good work ought not too quickly to become public and known to others, lest, when the beginning of the good is exposed to human eyes, the beginning of holiness lose its power to attain perfection. Before the time of ripeness, flowering crops quickly perish, and seeds likewise become useless.

Through the desire for display, the virtues of the saints are subjected to the dominion of unclean spirits. Thus King Hezekiah disclosed his riches to the Chaldeans through boasting and consequently heard through the prophet that they would perish [Col. 1107A], signifying that when God’s servant discloses his virtues through the pursuit of empty glory, he loses them and immediately makes demons masters of his works, just as Hezekiah through his display made the Chaldeans masters of his possessions (Isaiah 39).

The best discernment is that our works should be known for the purpose of hearing God glorified, yet concealed to avoid human praise. The person who should make public the good things he does is one so firmly grounded in perfect humility that no exaltation now touches him. But whoever understands that he is still assailed by love of praise should do his good deeds in secret, lest he lose what he has done.

Sometimes holy men, while wishing to correct their mutability completely, are touched by the swelling of their own exaltation because they are conscious of their actions; but they are cleansed from the evil of this seizure by the compunction of humility. Holy men sometimes instruct those who listen to them, yet they guard themselves with profound reflection, lest, while raising others from earthly concerns, they themselves sink into the pursuit of earthly praise.

Some relapse into vices through careless boasting of their virtues; others, while frequently lamenting the assault of vices, recover more strongly from their weakness through humility. Often it is useful for the arrogant to be abandoned by God, so that, conscious of their weakness, they may return to humility and become humble after their fall.

Some, through a false opinion born of arrogance, consider themselves perfect when they are not, because their imperfection becomes known when temptations arise. The closer someone becomes to the truth, the farther away from it he should consider himself to be. [Col. 1107C] This is humility, which joins a person to God.

Otherwise, boasting divides the eyes with which God can be seen. Just as the eye’s sharpness is weakened when it looks directly at a ray of the sun, so the person who searches for excessively lofty things is dulled in his attention to the truth. Just as an eagle plunges from on high toward its food, so a person descends from the height of a good way of life toward lower things through carnal desire.

## On Compunction

Compunction of heart is humility of mind accompanied by tears, arising from remembrance of sin and fear of judgment. For those who have been converted, that is the perfect affection of compunction which rejects from itself every affection for carnal desires and fixes its purpose, with the whole effort of the mind, upon contemplation of God.

There are two forms of compunction by which the soul of every elect person is moved for God’s sake: either when it considers the evil of its deeds, or when it sighs with desire for eternal [Col. 1108A] life.

There are four qualities of feeling by which the mind is healthfully pierced with compunction: remembrance of past crimes; recollection of future punishments; consideration of its pilgrimage throughout the length of this life; and desire for the heavenly homeland, so that it may reach it as quickly as possible.

Whenever a sinner is pierced by the memory of his sins into lamentation, let God’s servant know that he is being visited by God’s presence when he inwardly blushes at what he remembers having lost and, by repenting, already punishes himself by his own judgment. For Peter wept when Christ looked upon him.

Hence the Psalmist says: “He looked, and the earth was shaken and trembled” (Psalm 17). The steps of God are in the heart of the inner person, where good desires arise so that they may trample down evil. [Col. 1108B] Whenever these things occur in a person’s heart, it must be understood that God is then present to the human heart through grace.

Therefore a person ought to sharpen himself more intensely toward compunction when he feels God working inwardly. To what heights the mind of the righteous person is carried away by true compunction, and how it returns weakened. One who has already tasted something of the greatness of the light can know it.

There are some who do not become accusers of themselves through true compunction of heart; rather, they declare themselves sinners only so that, through the feigned humility of confession, they may find a place among the holy. Each righteous person begins to be righteous from the moment he becomes his own accuser.

Many confess themselves to be sinners against themselves, yet do not withdraw themselves from sin. A great part of righteousness is for a person to know himself, because he is small and, once he recognizes his weakness, submits more humbly to divine power. The righteous person judges himself well in this life, lest he be judged by God with everlasting condemnation.

Each person passes judgment upon himself when, through worthy repentance, he condemns his evil deeds. The bitterness of repentance makes the soul examine both its own deeds more subtly and, in tears, recall the gifts of God that it despised.

Nothing is worse than recognizing one’s fault without mourning it. Every sinner ought to have a twofold weeping in repentance: either because through negligence he failed to do good, or because through presumption he committed evil. He did not do what he ought to have done, and he did what he ought not to have done.

That person performs repentance worthily who mourns his guilt with legitimate satisfaction, namely by despising the things he did while mourning them.

## THE TWELFTH SUNDAY. According to Mark.

[Col. 1107]

[Col. 1107D] “Jesus went out from the territory of Tyre and came through Sidon to the Sea of Galilee, which is between the territories of the Decapolis, etc.” (Mark 7).

The Decapolis is a region of ten cities beyond the Jordan toward the east, around Hippo, Pella, and Gadara, opposite Galilee. [Col. 1108D] Therefore, when it is said that the Lord came to the Sea of Galilee between the territories of the Decapolis, this does not mean that he entered the territories of the Decapolis themselves. For he is not said to have sailed across the sea, but rather to have come as far as the sea and to have reached the place itself that looks toward the territories of the Decapolis, situated far away across the sea. “Between” means “opposite.” Or, it may mean Galilee, which is between the territories of the Decapolis.

“And they bring him a deaf and mute man, and they begged him to lay his hand upon him. And taking him aside from the crowd, he put his fingers into his ears, and, spitting, touched his tongue. And looking up to heaven, he groaned and said to him, ‘Ephphatha,’ which means ‘Be opened.’ And immediately his ears were opened, and the bond of his tongue was released, and he spoke correctly.”

The deaf and mute person is one who opens neither his ears nor his mouth to hear God’s words and proclaim them. The first door of salvation is to lead the sick man away from the crowd. This happens when the Lord, taking hold of a mind weakened by sins, calls it away from its accustomed ways and urges it [Col. 1109B] toward his commands.

He puts his fingers into the ears when, through the gifts of the Holy Spirit, he opens the ears of the heart to understanding. The Lord touches the sick man’s tongue after spitting when he instructs the mouths of catechumens for the confession of faith. For spittle is the taste of wisdom. Hence the saying: “I came forth from the mouth of the Most High” (Sirach 24).

The Lord looked up to heaven to teach that from there one must seek speech for the mute, hearing for the deaf, and healing for all the sick. He groaned to give us an example of groaning both for ourselves and for our neighbors. “Ephphatha” properly pertains to the ears; hence it is followed by: “And immediately his ears were opened.”

Here both natures of the Redeemer are indicated. He looked up to heaven as a human being; he heals as God. Whoever is healed in this way can rightly say: “Lord, open my lips, and my mouth will proclaim your praise” (Psalm 50).

### Another interpretation

The human race, as though it were one person afflicted with various plagues, is blinded in the first-created man while seeing; becomes deaf while hearing; is made to blow its nose while smelling; becomes mute while speaking; becomes crippled in the hand while raising it; is bent over while being raised upright; becomes dropsical while desiring; becomes lame while advancing; is covered with leprosy while being stripped naked; is filled with a demon while desiring divinity; and dies by death while boldly making excuses.

The patriarchs and prophets, desiring the Incarnation, beg that the hand of mercy be laid upon them. Whoever deserves to be healed is always led away from turbulent thoughts, disordered deeds, and incoherent speech, as though from the crowd.

The fingers put into the ears are the words of the Holy Spirit, of whom it is said: “This is the finger of God” (Exodus 8), and: “The heavens are the work of your fingers” (Psalm 8).

The spittle descending from the head is wisdom from the Father, which releases the lips of the human race so that it may say: “I believe in God the Father,” and so forth. “Looking up to heaven, he groaned”—that is, he taught us to groan and to raise the treasure of our heart toward heaven, after the heart has been cleansed from the frivolous joy of the flesh by compunction, as it is said: “I roared from the groaning of my heart” (Psalm 37).

The ears are opened to hymns, songs, and psalms. The tongue is released so that it may pour forth a good word, which neither threats nor words can restrain. Hence Paul says: “I am bound, but the word of God is not bound” (2 Timothy 2).

“And he commanded them to tell no one. But the more he commanded them, the more they proclaimed it, and they were astonished all the more, saying: ‘He has done all things well; he makes the deaf hear and the mute speak.’”

He taught that one should not glory in miracles but in the cross and humiliation. For humility precedes glory. The order of the words is: “The more he commanded them, the more they proclaimed it.” A city set upon a mountain, being visible from every side, cannot be hidden (Matthew 5).

He therefore knew—he who knows all things before they happen—that they would proclaim it more, but by commanding them he wished to show the sluggish how much more diligently and frequently those to whom it is commanded to preach ought to preach, since those who were forbidden to speak could not keep silent.

## Gregory’s Exposition on the Same Passage

GREGORY: “We have heard the words of God. If we do them, then we speak them rightly to our neighbors, when we have first done them ourselves.”

Mark the Evangelist confirms this well when, narrating the Lord’s miracle, he says: “They bring him a deaf and mute man, and they begged him to lay his hand upon him” (Mark 7). He indicates the order of the healing when he adds: “He put his fingers into his ears, and, spitting, touched his tongue; and looking up to heaven, he groaned and said to him, ‘Ephphatha,’ which means ‘Be opened’; and immediately his ears were opened and the bond of his tongue was released, and he spoke correctly” (ibid.).

What does it mean that God, the Creator of all things, when he wished to heal the deaf and mute man, put his fingers into his ears and, spitting, touched his tongue? What are the Redeemer’s fingers except the gifts of the Holy Spirit? Hence, when he had cast out a demon in another place, he said: “If I cast out demons by the finger of God, surely the kingdom of God has come upon you” (Luke 11). For this reason another Evangelist is described as saying: “If I cast out demons by the Spirit of God, then the kingdom of God has come upon you” (Matthew 12). From these two passages it is gathered that the Holy Spirit is called the finger of God.

Therefore, to put his fingers into the ears is, through the gifts of the Holy Spirit, to open the deaf person’s mind to hearing. But what does it mean that, spitting, he touched his tongue? The saliva received from the Redeemer’s mouth is wisdom expressed in divine speech. For saliva flows from the head into the mouth. When wisdom, which is the Redeemer himself, touches our tongue, it immediately forms it for the words of preaching.

He who looked up to heaven and groaned did not himself need a groan, since he was the one who granted what was requested; rather, he taught us to groan to God who presides over heaven, so that our ears might be opened through the good gifts of the Spirit and our tongue might be released through the saliva of his mouth—that is, through knowledge of divine speech—for the words of preaching.

Immediately he says to him, “Ephphatha, that is, ‘Be opened,’” “and immediately his ears were opened, and the bond of his tongue was released.” Here it must be noted that “Be opened” was said because his ears were closed. But once the ears of someone’s heart have been opened to obedience, without doubt the bond of his tongue is also subsequently released, so that he may speak to others about the good things he has done and that they too should do.

Hence it is rightly added: “And he spoke correctly.” For the person speaks correctly who has first done through obedience what, by speaking, he urges others also to do.

### Another interpretation

That deaf and mute man represented the human race when the Lord passed through the territories of the Decapolis in order to heal him. The Decapolis is a region of ten cities and signifies the law of the Ten Commandments. The Lord passes through the Decapolis when he chose to be born under the Decalogue of the law.

They bring the deaf and mute man to him when preachers convert the human race to the faith. It was deaf because it did not wish to hear God’s commandments; it was mute because it remained silent in praise of the Creator. The Lord restored its hearing when he opened its understanding to comprehend the Scriptures.”

## On Priests and the Six Ages of the World
The people called to the faith had to be instructed through visible sacraments, so that through the presentation of visible things they might come to understand invisible realities. The Lord’s priests, who administer this sacrament, must know the manner and order of the sacraments, and the truth of the things signified. Otherwise they are merely stewards of mysteries (1 Cor. 4), like blind guides of the blind, deriving from them only as much benefit as the beasts of burden that carry bread for the use of others, although divine grace does not abandon [Col. 1111C] the sacrament that, through them, is administered for the salvation of others. Let the ministers of the Lord’s sacraments therefore take heed: every day the Church of Christ is gathered from the nations, and through the operation of these same sacraments a people of possession is assembled, whose head is Christ. It is generated through faith, nourished into a perfect man through charity, strengthened in that same faith and charity by the hope of eternity, and, through the ministry of all the saints, directed toward this end: that it may understand the Church of God as a house founded upon faith, built up like walls firmly joined together through love of God and neighbor, and raised to its full height by the accumulation of the most glorious hope of eternity. [Col. 1111D]

Although this body of Christ followed the customary order of birth in being born after the birth of its head, nevertheless, because it would follow the birth of this head in unity, certain members of the body preceded it—namely, the patriarchs and prophets, and many righteous people who, through numerous signs and proclamations, foretold the birth of the head and of the body that would follow. This was well prefigured in Jacob, who bore the type of the interior people: hastening toward birth, he extended his hand and grasped the heel of his elder brother (Gen. 25). By this act he signified that, after the earlier people—whose type Esau represented (Rom. 9)—had been rejected, a younger people, namely the Christian people, would be born and would possess the blessing of God the Father as an eternal inheritance. The sacraments of that Father are, in fact, our lessons: through them that people, like a little child, was nourished with milk and occupied with the worship of the one true God, [Col. 1112A] not wandering after false or alien gods.

Hence, from the beginning of the world, in every age the sacraments of Christ and of the Church were celebrated. Through them that people was nourished, and the manner of our redemption was intimated. In the first age, Adam was fashioned from the earth, his mother, without an earthly father, by God on the sixth day in the image of God (Gen. 1); and in the last age of the world, Christ was born of an earthly mother without an earthly father, and humanity was restored by God to that same image. In harmony with this event, in the same age Eve was formed from the side of Adam, who was a figure of the one to come; and the Church was fashioned through the blood flowing from Christ’s side together with the water of sanctification.

In the second age of the world, the same Church was prefigured through the eight souls who were saved [Col. 1112B] from the overwhelming of the Flood, that is, through those delivered by the ark. In hope of the eighth [day], that is, the resurrection, the Church is delivered through the waters of baptism from the overwhelming abundance of temptations, not without the aid of the saving wood.

Finally, in the third age, the people of God were delivered from Egyptian slavery. They crossed the Red Sea; the sea gave way when struck by Moses’ rod and provided a path for the people of God. The enemies pursued them from behind and were submerged, and here again the sanctification received through baptism by means of the saving wood was represented. For the Red Sea is red, and baptism, consecrated by Christ’s blood, is also red. The enemies pursuing from behind die, because past and present sins are blotted out through baptism.

Then, in the fourth age, in that earthly Jerusalem which is eternal, the kingdom of David shone forth, prefiguring the kingdom of Christ and of the Church. From David’s seed Christ himself was born, reigning spiritually in his Church and, after the passage of time, gloriously crowning it when it obeys him. [Col. 1112C]

This is why those who are to be baptized on Holy Saturday are brought to the Church in the fourth week of Lenten observance, which supplies us with the weapons of self-restraint, and on the Wednesday of the fourth week, to be catechized and exorcized. There they will hear and be instructed about how they are to fight against spiritual wickedness. Nevertheless, their baptism is postponed until Easter Saturday, since the Church observes that those who are called to the contest in the present life are baptized in hope of future rest.

Just as those who are going to fight against visible enemies are not chosen before [Col. 1112D] the fourth age, that is, before youth, so those who are going to fight in this age are made stronger to repel invisible enemies. Thus, chosen for Christian warfare under the figure of this number, let them exercise the Christian name manfully and, in order to deserve to be crowned, let them not withdraw from the battle line.

After the times of the kingdom of Israel, in the fifth age, when Babylon began to take the aforesaid people captive because of its perversity, that same people migrated to Babylon. The one that had voluntarily served confusion served the king of Babylon, whose name is interpreted as “confusion,” unwillingly. After seventy years, through Christ working by means of Cyrus, that people returned, as Isaac first and afterward Jeremiah had foretold.

This aptly pertains to the condition of the Church, which, after the end of this world—whose course is measured by the number seven, the days of the week—has returned to the heavenly Jerusalem after the many hardships it has suffered or will suffer under the kings of this spiritual Babylon, and will no longer serve any confusion. Hence the Apostle says: “The creation was subjected to vanity, not willingly but because of him who subjected it, in hope, because the creation itself will be liberated from the slavery of corruption into the freedom of the glory of the children of God” (Rom. 8). [Col. 1113A]

Throughout all these ages there were righteous men, members of the future Church; and in each age there were appropriate sacraments, like nourishment for the people. Many things could be recited about them, were we not striving for brevity.

Finally, in the sixth age Christ was born of a Virgin, just as the first-formed man was fashioned from virgin earth on the sixth day. Christ is the end of the law, and the truth and fullness of all that had preceded him in the shadows of the sacraments. In the fullness of time, as has been said, Christ was born, grew, and reached manhood. In the thirtieth year of his life, as the evangelists relate, he was baptized by John—not because he needed baptism, but because his life was a discipline of conduct for Christians.

Then he chose the apostles, preached the Gospel, and was crucified, giving us an example of humility and patience. On the third day he rose again, strengthening his members in the hope of their own resurrection. About to ascend to heaven, he instructed his disciples concerning what they should do, saying: “Go, teach all nations; preach to every creature. Whoever believes and is baptized will be saved” (Mark 16). [Col. 1113B]

In these few words we are taught about the priests of the Lord, the successors and vicars of the apostles, of whom it is said: “Instead of your fathers, sons have been born to you” (Ps. 44): how they should catechize inexperienced peoples who still bear the image of the earthly man, and how they should transform them through the washing of water in the word into newness and conformity to Christ. This was done in the times of the apostles and martyrs, who proclaimed the Gospel among Jews and Gentiles, to those who understood its rightful claims and to all persons capable of receiving the word of God. [Col. 1113C]

## DIVISION

After the Church had spread and been gathered among the nations, and no one of mature faith was found among the faithful who was not himself faithful, provision was made for their children as well, lest they leave this life before reaching the age of reason and remain strangers to fellowship with Christ. A remedy of salvation was therefore also provided for them in the form of sacraments or faith, for children to be catechized, exorcized, initiated, and finally baptized. [Col. 1113D]

In these matters the Church hears on behalf of the child and answers the questions asked until the child reaches the age of understanding and can himself comprehend the sacraments of faith, charity, and hope that have been imposed upon him. Concerning these sacraments—what they signify—we have decided to say something, insofar as the Lord may choose to inspire your charity, so that you may understand the power of the sacraments yourselves and strive to teach your hearers.

It must first be noted how the child who is to be baptized is conceived in the womb of Mother Church, and by what nourishment he is fed in that same womb until the birth of the new man. There are three things by which the one to be baptized is conceived until he is clothed with newness: catechism, exorcism, and prayers. [Col. 1114A]

The one who is called to the faith is catechized so that he may be moved by his own exercise of free will toward that to which he is called. He is exorcized so that the devil’s wicked power may be driven away from him. Prayer is added on his behalf so that grace may go before and follow him, granting strength to free will and keeping the deception of the evil spirit far away.

First, therefore, the one to be baptized is marked with the sign of the cross on the forehead, breast, eyes, ears, and mouth. By its power the devil has been conquered and Christ exalted. Hence Habakkuk says: “His horns are in his hands; there his strength is hidden” (Hab. 3).

By this sign, then, the senses of the entire body are fortified. Through its power all our sacraments are completed and all the devil’s fabrications are frustrated. Thus, when the firstborn of Egypt were destroyed, the Hebrew people were saved after marking the doorposts of their houses with the blood of the paschal lamb, in a figure of the Lord’s Passion; but the Egyptian people, who lacked this sign, were grievously struck in their firstborn. [Col. 1114B]

Likewise, in Ezekiel, Jerusalem is promised deliverance from the impending disaster if it is marked with a sign representing the cross, the sign of those who groan and lament—that is, of penitents.

Afterward blessed salt is placed in the child’s mouth, so that, seasoned with the figurative salt of wisdom, he may be rid of the stench of iniquity and no longer decay through the worms of vices, but may be preserved incorrupt for receiving Christ’s grace; so that he may no longer become foolish through the loss of wisdom’s seasoning, nor look back like Lot’s wife. [Col. 1114C]

Afterward the evil spirit is exsufflated outward. These sacred mysteries signify that it is not the child who is exorcized and exsufflated, but the one under whose power are those who are born under sin and have not yet been reborn through holy baptism, although they have already been conceived through the sign of the cross in the womb of Mother Church.

All the gifts of priestly ministry are received through the figure of the cross. All the sacraments that have been and are enacted through exorcisms, prayers, and breathings are, as it were, food that refreshes the children in the womb, so that Mother Church may present them to Christ, joyful after being reborn through the water of salvation.

Afterward his ears and nostrils are touched with saliva. Saliva descends from the head into the mouth, signifying heavenly wisdom. Through its touch the ears of the heart are opened to understand the word of God, and the nostrils are opened to repel the stench of harmful thoughts and pleasures. [Col. 1114D]

Hence blessed Ambrose says in the book *On the Sacraments*: “What we have performed is indeed an opening, because the sacraments are of opening, when he touched his ears and nostrils. This signifies what our Lord Jesus Christ does in the Gospel, when a deaf and mute man was brought to him: he touched his mouth and ears, his ears because he was deaf, his mouth because he was mute, and said, ‘Ephphatha,’ which means ‘Be opened.’”

Then the priest comes to the font, and the font is consecrated in the name of the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit. If the water of salvation is consecrated by these words, baptism is not received in a worse manner from either a good or an evil person. Hence Augustine says in the third book of *On Baptism Alone*: “The water over which the name of God is invoked is neither profane nor adulterous, even if it is invoked by profane or adulterous persons, because neither the creature itself nor the name itself is adulterous.” [Col. 1115A]

The creed is also delivered to those who hear of the new life. It was arranged through the twelve apostles and comprised in an equal number of statements.

Finally, the priest asks the child at baptism: “Do you renounce Satan and all his works, and all his pomps?”—so that he may first reject error and draw near to the truth, and may be able, according to the Apostle, to put off the old man with his deeds, namely his former way of life, renouncing impiety and worldly desires (Eph. 4). The child answers through the mouths of those carrying him: “I renounce.” [Col. 1115B]

Hence Augustine says in *Against Julian*, book 4: “Whoever denies that children renounce and believe through the mouths of those carrying them should also deny that they receive baptism, because they struggle in the hands of those carrying them.”

Likewise, in the book *On Penance*: “The faith of those by whom children are presented benefits them for consecration and the remission of original sin, so that whatever stains of offenses they contracted through those from whom they were born may also be cleansed through the questioning and response of others.”

After the renunciation, the catechumen is anointed with sacred oil on the breast, as though to fortify him against the invisible enemy, lest that enemy persuade him to impure and harmful desires. He is also anointed between the shoulders, where there is strength for carrying a burden, so that he may receive strength to bear the burden of the day and the heat, like a good athlete. [Col. 1115C]

Next he is asked whether he believes in God the almighty Father, and in Jesus Christ, his only Son, our Lord, and in the Holy Spirit—one God in Trinity and triune in unity—whether he confesses that there is one holy Catholic Church, and whether he believes in the remission of sins and eternal life.

If he professes that he believes all these things, the old man already begins to die in him, the man who was created according to God in righteousness and the holiness of truth (ibid.). By renouncing the former possessor, and persuaded by charity, he now wishes to pass into the right of the legitimate possessor, in whom he already professes that he believes and from whom he expects eternal rewards. [Col. 1115D]

The old leaven has already been purged, but the new dough has not yet been made, for the washing of the holy font follows (1 Cor. 5). Under the response to the threefold questioning, the catechumen is washed from the stains of oldness by a threefold immersion, and, clothed with the new man, is buried with the Lord’s three-day burial.

Hence the Apostle says: “For we were buried with him through baptism into death, so that, just as Christ was raised from the dead through the glory of the Father, so we too might walk in newness of life. For if we have been united with the likeness of his death, we shall likewise be united with that of his resurrection” (Rom. 6). [Col. 1116A]

For this reason blessed Ambrose also says in the book *On the Sacraments*: “You were asked: ‘Do you believe in God the almighty Father?’ You said: ‘I believe,’ and you were immersed—that is, you were buried. Again you were asked: ‘Do you also believe in Jesus Christ the Lord, born and having suffered?’ You said: ‘I believe,’ and you were immersed—that is, you were buried with Christ. Whoever is buried with Christ will rise with Christ. A third time you were asked: ‘Do you also believe in the Holy Spirit?’ You said: ‘I believe,’ and you were immersed a third time, so that the threefold confession might destroy the manifold fall of thought, speech, and action.”

The cleansing of holy baptism, celebrated in the likeness of Christ’s death, was prefigured by the water of sprinkling in the old law. Through it the one who had touched a dead body was cleansed so that he might return to the camp. It was mixed with the ashes of a red heifer burned outside the camp, together with hyssop, scarlet, and cedar. [Col. 1116B]

That heifer, being female, signifies the frailty—that is, the passibility—of Christ’s flesh; it was red because of the shedding of blood. It was also cast outside the camp, signifying that the Lord too was led outside the city to suffer. The fact that the tabernacle and all the vessels of the tabernacle were sprinkled seven times with the blood of that same heifer signifies the complete cleansing that Christ’s blood effected both within and without. The soul consists of a threefold power, while the body is composed of the combination of the four elements; both were cleansed through the shedding of Christ’s blood. [Col. 1116C]

The fact that the flesh, hide, and dung of that same heifer were burned signified that all the humility and disgrace of the Passion were transformed into the glory of the resurrection. Fire aptly signifies this, since it always strives upward and transforms into itself what it consumes.

The fact that hyssop is mixed with this sprinkling signifies that sins are cleansed through faith in Christ’s death. Hence the Apostle says: “Cleansing their hearts by faith” (Eph. 5). Hyssop signifies faith because, although it is a lowly herb, it clings firmly to the rock.

Scarlet is also added to this cleansing; by its fiery color it signifies charity, without which whatever faith accomplishes is dead. Cedar too assists this cleansing. It is called an incorruptible tree and takes root on lofty mountains; therefore it signifies the hope of incorruption and heavenly glory. [Col. 1116D]

Through the combination of all these things the water of sprinkling is consecrated. The one who had touched a dead body was cleansed, as has been said, because the one who is defiled by dead works—that is, by original sins—is liberated through holy baptism. He is baptized in faith in Christ’s death and resurrection, with the pledge of charity and hope.

## THE THIRTEENTH SUNDAY. According to Luke.

[Col. 1115]

[Col. 1115D] “Blessed are the eyes that see what you see. For I tell you that many kings and prophets desired to see what you see and did not see it, and to hear what you hear and did not hear it” (Luke 13).” [Col. 1116D–1117A]

He calls blessed those eyes that recognize the sacraments of Christ. Prophets and righteous men, such as Isaiah and Abraham, saw in an enigma and not in direct vision. Abraham rejoiced that he might see Christ’s day; he saw it and was glad. Isaiah and the other prophets saw the glory of the Lord; hence they were also called seers. But they saw in an enigma, not in the present reality, as did the apostles, who had no need to be instructed through angels by various kinds of visions.

Luke calls them kings, while Matthew calls them righteous (Matt. 13), because those who know how to govern the movements of their temptations and preside over them rather than succumb to them are great kings. [Col. 1117A]

Note that the grace and knowledge of Christ’s sacraments were less in the prophets than in the apostles, who, especially after receiving the Holy Spirit, also enlightened the world. Nevertheless, some of the prophets, at times caught up above the human level, contemplated without an enigma through intellectual vision, as did the Apostle (2 Cor. 12).

Hence the Lord says in the book of Numbers: “If there should be among you a prophet of the Lord, I will appear to him in a vision, or I will speak to him in a dream. But my servant Moses is not such. I speak to him mouth to mouth, not openly, not through enigmas and figures; he sees the Lord” (Num. 12). [Col. 1117B]

It follows: “And behold, a certain lawyer stood up, testing him and saying: ‘Teacher, what must I do to possess eternal life?’ The Pharisees, seeing that he had silenced the Sadducees, gathered together. And one of the scribes, a teacher of the law, approached him, testing him, and saying: ‘Teacher, which is the great commandment in the law?’” [Col. 1117C]

Although the Pharisees and Sadducees were opposed to one another, they agreed with one mind in testing the Lord. We read that Herod and Pilate did the same in the Lord’s death. Since the Pharisees had often been refuted, malice and envy nourished their shamelessness. Thus, stripped of truth, they armed themselves with numbers, saying among themselves: “Let us all speak through one man, so that if he is defeated he may appear confounded.”

He calls him “Teacher,” although he does not wish to be his disciple. The most simple-minded questioner and most malicious plotter asks about the great commandment, although he observes not even the smallest one. The person who has fulfilled the lesser commandment ought to ask about the greater justice. [Col. 1117D]

“Jesus said to him: ‘The first commandment of all is: Hear, Israel, the Lord your God is one God. And you shall love the Lord your God with all your heart, and with all your soul, and with all your mind, and with all your strength. This is the first and greatest commandment. The second is like it: You shall love your neighbor as yourself. On these two commandments depend the whole law and the prophets.’”

The first and greatest commandment is to love the one God above all things, and we must place this before everything else as the unique foundation of piety. Therefore he did not say “You shall know,” but “You shall love,” because knowing the one God is almost proper to human nature, whereas loving him belongs to a devout and upright heart.

A similar commandment concerns love of neighbor, because the human being is the image of God. Love of God is the source of love of neighbor, and love of neighbor is the acknowledgment of love of God. [Col. 1118A]

The love of God is expressed in three things, so that nothing may remain in a human being that is not subjected to divine love. When it is said, “Love God with all your heart,” he commanded that all thoughts be directed to God. When it is said, “with all your soul,” he ordered all the soul’s affections to be referred to God. When he added, “with all your mind,” he indicated that all human reasoning, by which we understand and distinguish things, must be occupied with divine matters. When he says, “with all your strength,” he enjoins the goodness of perseverance.

There are likewise two things to be observed regarding love of neighbor: that the neighbor be cherished through the giving of benefits and harmed by no malice. This means: “What you do not wish to be done to you, do not do to others” (Tob. 4); and: “Whatever you wish people to do to you, do the same to them” (Matt. 7). [Col. 1118B]

Although the commandments are therefore diverse—by some we rightly desire what ought to be sought, and by others we rightly guard against what ought to be avoided—they are nevertheless one at the root of charity, because we must fulfill them in the love of God and neighbor. It is therefore rightly said that the law and the prophets are referred to the two commandments of charity, because the entire Decalogue and the admonitions of the prophets find their end there.

“The scribe said to him: ‘Well said, Teacher; you have spoken the truth, because there is one God and no other besides him, and he must be loved with all the heart, all the understanding, all the soul, and all the strength; and to love one’s neighbor as oneself is greater than all burnt offerings and sacrifices.’” [Col. 1118C]

From this response the scribe shows that there had often been a serious dispute among scribes and Pharisees concerning which was the greatest commandment: some praising victims and sacrifices, while others preferred works of faith and love, since many of the fathers before the law had pleased God through faith alone—faith that works through love (Gal. 5)—without any custom of victims and sacrifices, whereas no one had pleased him through sacrifices without faith and love.

We call the great and first commandment so in respect of dignity. Otherwise, the usefulness of God’s commandments is one, and they are so mutually connected that one cannot exist without the other. Thus we say that a foundation is better, although neither a foundation can exist without a building nor a building without a foundation. The foundation is therefore not more useful than the building, but more worthy, just as the head is more worthy than the members. [Col. 1118D]

[Col. 1119A] “When Jesus saw that he had answered wisely, he said to him: ‘You are not far from the kingdom of God. You have answered rightly; do this and you will live.’”

Since our salvation consists in knowledge of the truth and love of virtue, the Sadducees are far from the kingdom of God, because they neither know what ought to be known nor love what ought to be loved. This proud tempter, however, was less far outside the kingdom, because through knowledge he had already assented to evangelical perfection. He would be in the kingdom of God if his knowledge of the truth and love of the good were increased, so that he might receive Christ both as God and as neighbor.

[Col. 1119A] “But he, wishing to justify himself, said to Jesus: ‘And who is my neighbor?’”

No one is nearer to a human being than God, who knows what is within and without and can care for everything. But every unbeliever or tempter has neither God nor a human being as his neighbor.

The lawyer, seeking to win the favor of the crowd, so that he might be acclaimed for having answered wisely, asks the Lord what he should do. But because he desires to justify himself, the Lord tempered his answer by speaking to him in a parable, so that everyone who shows mercy might be understood as a neighbor, and especially that the Son of God, who became our neighbor through his humanity, might be designated.

“Jesus took up the word and said: ‘A certain man was going down from Jerusalem to Jericho, and he fell among robbers.’” [Col. 1119B]

This man is understood as Adam; Jerusalem is the heavenly city, from whose blessedness he fell into this mortal life. Jericho, which is interpreted as “moon,” aptly signifies uncertainty through varied changes. By the robbers understand the devil and his angels; he would not have fallen among them unless he had first swelled with vices. For true is the saying: “Before destruction the heart is exalted” (Prov. 16).

“They also stripped him and, after inflicting wounds on him, went away, leaving him half-dead.”

They stripped him of the glory of immortality and the garment of innocence. The wounds are the sins by which the integrity of human nature was violated. They went away, not by ceasing in any measure from their ambushes, but by concealing the frauds of those same ambushes. They left him half-dead because they were unable to destroy his reason. Insofar as a human being can understand and know God, he lives; but insofar as he wastes away through sins, disfigured by a deadly wound, he lies as though dead. [Col. 1119C]

“It happened that a certain priest was going down the same road, and when he saw him, he passed by. Likewise, a Levite, when he was near the place and saw him, passed by.”

The priest and Levite who passed by the wounded man signify the priesthood and ministry of the Old Testament, in which the wounds of the sick world could be displayed but not healed. For the Apostle says: “It was impossible for sins to be taken away by the blood of calves, lambs, and goats” (Heb. 10).

Thus the priest of God, when the law descended into the world through Moses, brought no healing to the human being. So too the descent of the Levite, who displays the type of the prophets, heals no one; but when he reproves sins, he passes by, because he does not bestow pardon. [Col. 1119D]

“But a certain Samaritan, making a journey, came near him, and when he saw him, he was moved with compassion.”

The Samaritan, whose name is interpreted as “guardian,” signifies the Lord. Against these robbers the Prophet thus entreats him: “Guard me from the snare that they have set for me, and from the scandals of those who work iniquity” (Ps. 140).

The Lord himself, having become human, undertook the journey of the present life and came near the wounded man, made close to us by compassion and near through the bestowal of mercy. The law, however, had not mercy, but judgment and vengeance.

[Col. 1120A] “And drawing near, he bound up his wounds, pouring in oil and wine.”

He restrained the sins he found in human beings by reproving them, promising the hope of pardon to the penitent and instilling the terror of punishment in the sinner. He therefore binds up the wounds when he commands: “Repent” (Matt. 3). He pours in oil when he adds: “The kingdom of heaven will draw near” (ibid.). He also pours in wine when he says: “Every tree that does not bear good fruit will be cut down and thrown into the fire” (ibid.).

Or, he binds up the wounds in baptism and pours in oil and wine, that is, the chrism of the Holy Spirit and the cup of his Passion.

“And placing him on his own beast, he led him to an inn and took care of him.”

His beast is his flesh, in which he bore our sins upon the wood and, according to another parable, carried the wandering sheep back to the flock. To be placed upon the beast therefore means to believe in Christ’s incarnation and to be protected by his mysteries from the enemy’s attack. [Col. 1120B]

The inn is the present Church, where travelers are refreshed in hope as they return to eternal life. By the name “inn” he pointedly intimates the miseries and stenches of this life, lest a human being rejoice in this exile as though it were his homeland. He took care of him so that, once the sick man had been brought into the Church, he would not abandon the commandments he had received.

“On the next day he brought out two denarii, gave them to the innkeeper, and said: ‘Take care of him, and whatever more you spend, I, when I return, will repay you.’”

The next day is after the Lord’s resurrection, which shines more brightly than the preceding time. The two denarii are the two Testaments, in which the name and image of the eternal King are contained. [Col. 1120C]

The innkeeper is the company of the disciples, to whom he opened the understanding so that, through the Holy Spirit, they might understand the Scriptures.

The innkeeper spends more than he received in the two denarii when Paul says: “I have no commandment of the Lord concerning virgins, but I give counsel” (1 Cor. 7). Likewise, he spends more when he says: “The Lord ordained that those who proclaim the Gospel should live from the Gospel; but we have not used this authority, so as not to burden any of you” (1 Cor. 9; 2 Thess. 3).

The debtor who returns will repay what he promised when the Lord says in judgment: “Because you have been faithful over a little, I will set you over much. Enter into the kingdom of your Lord” (Matt. 25).

[Col. 1120D] “Which of these three seems to you to have been neighbor to the man who fell among the robbers?” He said: “The one who showed mercy to him.” And he said to him: “Go, and you also do likewise.”

No one is more our neighbor than the one who healed our wounds, than the head is to the members—

Let us love him, therefore, as God and Lord; let us love him as our neighbor; and let us love all who imitate Christ.

What he says, “You also do likewise,” means this: whatever you are able to do to relieve your neighbor’s need, whether bodily or spiritual, perform it devotedly, so that you may show yourself to be a neighbor. Mercy rightly makes a neighbor, because it accords with nature. For nothing is more according to nature than to help one’s fellow creature.

## Another exposition on the same passage

[Col. 1121A] “Blessed is the man who has not gone in the counsel of the ungodly” (Ps. 1).

Adam was an unhappy man, who, through the counsel of the ungodly, went from his homeland, paradise, and led all his descendants into this exile. Nor did he stand in the way of sinners, because he remained established in sins. He sat in the chair of pestilence, because he taught others sins through evil examples.

Christ, however, was the blessed man who, by the counsel of the Father, went from the court of heaven into prison after the lost servant. He did not go in the counsel of the ungodly when the devil showed him all the kingdoms of the world and their glory and persuaded him to worship him (Matt. 4). He did not stand in the way of sinners, because he committed no sin. He did not sit in the chair of pestilence, because he taught evil neither by word nor by deed.

And therefore, just as that unhappy man drew all his carnal children into death, so this blessed man led all his spiritual children back into life. [Col. 1121B]

For, as he himself relates in the Gospel, a certain man went down from Jerusalem to Jericho. Robbers fell upon him, wounded him, stripped him, and went away. A priest traveling along the same road saw him half-dead and passed by. Likewise, a Levite making the journey passed by when he saw him. But a Samaritan traveling along the same road had pity on the wretched man; after binding his wounds, he treated them with wine and oil, placed him on his beast, and brought him to an inn. On the next day he brought two denarii to the innkeeper, asked him to care for the man, and promised that, on his return, he would repay him whatever more he had spent from his own resources (Luke 10).

The man went down from Jerusalem to Jericho when our first parent came down from the joys of paradise into the decline of death. For Jericho, which means “moon,” signifies the decline of our mortality. He fell among robbers because a crowd of demons immediately surrounded him in his exile. They also stripped him because they deprived him not only of the delights of paradise but also of the garment of immortality. They inflicted wounds because they imposed sins upon him. They left him half-dead because they left him dead in soul but surrounded in body by God’s mysteries. [Col. 1121C]

The priest went down along the same road when the order of the patriarchs likewise extended into mortality. He passed by the wounded man because he was unable to bring aid to the human race, while grieving that he too had been gravely wounded by sins.

The Levite likewise traveled along the same road, because the prophetic order also proceeded along the path of death. He passed by the wounded man because he could not bring help to the lost human being, while lamenting that he too had been wounded by sins. [Col. 1121D]

The half-dead man, however, is cared for by the Samaritan, because the deceived human being is healed through Christ. Samaria was the capital city of the Israelite kingdom. Its captives had been carried away to Nineveh for idolatry, and Gentiles had been settled there. The Jews so detested their association with them that they applied the name to those whom they wished to curse. Hence, while cursing him, they also called the Lord a Samaritan. For he himself was the true Samaritan—meaning “guardian”—because through him the human race is guarded.

He made this journey when he came from heaven into this world. He saw the traveler wounded because he beheld humanity surrounded by sins and miseries [Col. 1122A]. Compassion moved him concerning the man because he experienced all his pains for him; and, drawing near, he bound his wounds when, proclaiming eternal life, he preached that he should cease from sins. He tightened the wounds with the two parts of the bandage when he restrained sins through two kinds of fear. Servile fear prevents people from sinning through fear of punishments; filial and holy fear, however, urges them toward good works.

He drew down the lower part of the bandage when he instilled the fear of Gehenna into human hearts. “Their worm,” he says, “does not die, and the fire is not extinguished” (Mark IX). He drew up the upper part when he instructed them in the fear belonging to good endeavor: “The children of the kingdom,” he says, “will be cast into the outer darkness; there will be weeping and gnashing of teeth” (Matthew VIII).

He poured in wine and oil when he taught repentance and forgiveness [Col. 1122B]. For through wine decayed things are cleansed; through oil, wounds that are fomented are healed. He poured in wine when he said: “Repent” (Matthew III). He added oil when he continued: “For the kingdom of heaven will draw near” (ibid.).

He placed him on his beast when he bore sins in his own body upon the wood of the cross. He led him into the inn when he joined him to the heavenly Church. The inn where animals are gathered during the night is the present Church, in which the righteous are lodged amid the darkness of this life, until the day of eternity breathes upon them and the shadows of mortality are inclined.

On the next day he brought out two denarii. One day was the day of death, the other the day of life. The day of death began with Adam, in whom all die; the day of life began with Christ, in whom all will be made alive. Before Christ’s resurrection, all human beings were advancing toward death [Col. 1122C]; after his resurrection, all the faithful were rising toward life.

On the next day, therefore, he brought out two denarii when, after his resurrection, he taught that the two Testaments are fulfilled through the two commandments of charity. He gave the denarii to the innkeeper when he entrusted the order of teachers with the task of teaching the laws of life. He commanded that the sick man be cared for because he ordered the human race to be saved from sins.

The stench of the sick man compels him to leave the inn because the adversity of this world urges the righteous to seek heavenly things. Two denarii are also given to the innkeeper when teachers are exalted by knowledge of the Scriptures and by secular honor.

“If they expend anything beyond this,” he will repay it when he returns, because, if they exemplify in their works the good things they preach to the peoples [Col. 1122D], when the true Samaritan returns for judgment and brings the formerly wounded man—then already healed—from the inn into the heavenly palace, he will repay the diligent caregivers with eternal rewards.

## On the words “Go forth, daughters of Zion,” and on the three visions of Christ

“Go forth, daughters of Zion, and see King Solomon in the diadem with which his mother crowned him” (Song of Songs III).

This exhortation is offered through the Holy Spirit to the delicate and the weak. Those are delicate who wish to prosper in Egypt and Babylon. Because of their weakness they are called by the female designation “daughters,” since they are not yet perfected enough to be honored by the name “sons.” Of the perfected it is said: “The illustrious sons of Zion” [Col. 1123A] (Lamentations IV).

There are therefore three visions of our King: the first in this world, the second at the judgment, and the third in the kingdom.

Of the first it is said: “Many prophets and kings desired to see the things that you see, and did not see them” (Luke X). And also: “Blessed are the eyes that see the things that you see” (ibid.).

Of the second: “All flesh will see the salvation of God” (Luke III).

Of the third: “We shall see him as he is” (1 John III).

The first vision lasts as long as the present life is “today.” In this vision he appeared humble and compassionate, saying: “Come to me, all you who labor” (Matthew XI). He says the same thing to human beings today.

In the second he will appear terrible and just. Hence it is said: “He will judge the peoples with equity” (Psalm XCV).

In the third he will be seen in glory. Hence it is sung: “God is glorious in his saints, wondrous [Col. 1123B] in his majesty.”

In the first vision he was seen by the good and the wicked, but not by all. In the second he will be seen by all, both good and wicked. In the third he will be seen only by the good, because the wicked will not see the essence of the Deity. Hence it is written: “Let the ungodly be taken away, lest he see the glory of God.”

In his first appearance the Lord is the corrector of morals, saying: “Learn from me, because I am gentle and humble in heart” (Matthew XI); and through the prophet: “Turn to me, and you will be saved” (Isaiah XLV).

In the second he is the discerner of merits, saying to the good: “Come, blessed ones” (Matthew XXV), but to the wicked: “Go into the eternal fire” (ibid.).

In the third he will be the distributor of rewards according to the diversity of moral character, because “star differs from star in glory” (1 Corinthians XV). Yet joy will be common to all, even though the glory of each will differ [Col. 1123C]. There will be neither weariness in desire nor disgust in satisfaction, for otherwise the good would not be perfect.

In accordance with these three visions, the same King and our Lord Jesus Christ is mystically called by three names: Solomon, Ecclesiastes, and Jedidiah.

Solomon, that is, “peaceful,” because in the first vision he made peace between God and human beings, and between angels and human beings. Hence the Apostle says: “Making peace not only between the things on earth but also those in heaven” (Colossians I).

Ecclesiastes, that is, “preacher,” because in the second vision of himself he will gather an assembly and the diversity of the nations.

Jedidiah, that is, “beloved,” because in the third the saints will understand how the Son loves the Father and is loved by the Father, when he has handed the kingdom over to God the Father and he himself is “all in all” (1 Corinthians [Col. 1123D] XV).

Furthermore, it should be noted that in the three books entitled *Proverbs of Solomon*, *Ecclesiastes*, and *Song of Songs*, three renunciations are signified.

The first is that by which we despise, bodily, all the riches and resources of the world. The second is that by which we reject our former conduct, vices, and the prior inclinations of soul and flesh. The third is that by which we withdraw our mind from all present and visible things, contemplate only what is future, and desire the things that are invisible.

The Lord also commanded these three things to Abraham when he said: “Go out from your land, from your kindred, and from your father’s house” (Genesis XII).

First he said, “from your land,” meaning from the resources of this world and earthly works. Second, “from your kindred” [Col. 1124A], meaning from the former way of life, morals, and vices that cling to us from our birth and are related to us as though by a certain affinity. Third, “from your father’s house,” meaning from the entire memory of this world that comes before the eyes.

This takes place when, having died with Christ to the elements of this world, we contemplate, according to the Apostle, no longer the things that are seen but those that are not seen. “For the things that are seen are temporal, but the things that are not seen are eternal” (2 Corinthians IV). We depart in heart from this temporal and visible house to that house toward which we continually direct our eyes and minds.

We shall fulfill this when, while walking in the flesh, we begin to serve the Lord not according to the flesh, in accordance with the saying: “But our citizenship is in heaven.”

These three renunciations, as has been said, properly correspond to Solomon’s three books [Col. 1124B]. *Proverbs* applies to the first, by which the desire for carnal things and earthly vices are cut away. *Ecclesiastes* applies to the second, where all that is done under the sun is declared vanity. The *Song of Songs* applies to the third, in which the mind, transcending all visible things, is already joined to the Word of God through contemplation of eternal things.

“For once the earth is overcome, it gives the stars.” Blessed, therefore, is the one who has been able to see the luminous source of goodness. A mind entirely pure from illicit love can accomplish this. Conversely, whoever, overcome, has turned his eyes toward the Tartarean cavern—that is, toward the love of temporal things—loses whatever excellent thing he possesses, since he looks toward the underworld. Whoever is intent upon temporal things loses whatever good he had acquired.

Indeed, alas, near the boundaries of night Orpheus saw his Eurydice, lost her, and died. This is especially grievous when someone wise and eloquent has at some time converted many to righteousness by preaching, but, overcome by his own desire, perishes himself. For when he looks back toward earthly cravings, which he had almost rejected, he loses all the good works he had done, and himself falls from the height of reason to the depths of earthly things.

Hence Orpheus is explained as though from *aurea phonē* [φωνή], that is, “golden voice” or “excellent voice.” His wife is Eurydice, that is, natural desire. Eurydice is said to mean “judgment of the good,” because each person desires whatever he judges to be good, whether it is so or not.

Therefore we must hasten so that, just as in body, when seeking our homeland, we have despised the world’s riches and pleasures, so also in heart, leaving all these things behind, we do not again return in desire to what we abandoned [Col. 1124D].

But it will not profit us to have accepted the first renunciation with the greatest devotion of faith if we do not fulfill the second with the same zeal and ardor. Once we have also attained this, we shall be able to reach the third: having gone out from the house of our first parent, we shall turn the whole gaze of our mind toward heavenly things.

We shall deserve to attain the true perfection of this third renunciation when our mind, dulled by no contagion of fleshly heaviness but polished by the most thorough purifications, has passed beyond every earthly affection and quality through unceasing meditation on divine things and spiritual contemplation to those invisible realities.

## Again on the same subject

[Col. 1125A]

“Go forth, daughters of Zion, so that you may be able to see King Solomon” (Song of Songs III).

Thus it was said to Abraham: “Go out from your land, from your kindred, and from your father’s house” (Genesis XII).

The broad and spacious land is curiosity. While it wanders widely through outward things, the serpent meanwhile enters within: he extends the fruit and steals paradise. Dinah, found outside, is corrupted (Genesis XXXIV). We must go out from this curiosity in order to preserve the mind.

“Kindred” means the pleasure innate in us from our first parent, who wished to live pleasurably without the yoke of obedience. We must go out from this by mortifying the flesh.

Whoever retains his own will has the devil as his father. Since he wished to make himself another beginning, one must go out from his house [Col. 1125B] by laying aside one’s own will. Indeed, to say it in other words, one must flee from the cage, the prison, and the fetters.

The world is called the prison of captives who are to be redeemed. Hell is the prison of captives who are not to be released. The Lord frees us from the worldly prison. Hence it is said: “The Lord gives light to the blind” (Psalm CXLV)—namely, to those whom worldly things blind.

The cage is our flesh, which crushes the soul; but “the Lord raises up those who are crushed” (ibid.). Whoever follows his own will is held in fetters; but the Lord releases those in fetters (ibid.).

“See King Solomon.” Many see the king but not Solomon: they rule and restrain illicit impulses within themselves, yet hate their neighbors. Conversely, many see Solomon but not the king: they preserve peace but do not correct their vices [Col. 1125C]. Those see both king and Solomon who restrain depraved impulses and cease from hatred.

“In the diadem with which his mother crowned him” (Song of Songs III).

There are three diadems of the true Solomon.

The first is the one with which Judea crowned him. It is a diadem of mercy with respect to him, though not with respect to the Jews. It was made of thorns. The thorns signify the sins by which we are pierced. He himself bore them, not by experiencing them but by compassion. Hence the prophet says: “He himself took our infirmities, and he himself bore our sins” (Isaiah LIII).

The second is the fleshly diadem with which Mary, his mother, crowned him, in which he possessed our affections.

The third is the diadem of glory [Col. 1125D] with which his Father crowned him as he sat at his right hand. Hence the Apostle says: “We see Jesus crowned with glory and honor because of the suffering of death” (Hebrews II). And in the Psalm: “You crowned him with glory and honor” (Psalm VIII).

## On the fact that some rashly assert that the righteous will see God with bodily eyes in the future kingdom of God: Augustine’s words

Some promise us—or rather themselves—that human beings will be more blessed than the angels, asserting that they will see God not only because they were created in the image of God, as the blessed angels see God, but also through bodily eyes in a spiritual body.

If this is true, then, since the vision of God is the blessedness of rational creation, just as some will have both a rational and a bodily vision of God, so also they will have more blessedness than the angels [Col. 1126A]. For angels will see God solely because they are rational, in accordance with the fact that they were made in the image of God. But Truth does not promise that human beings will be more worthy than the angels.

Moreover, those who assert that human beings will see God with bodily eyes, in order that so great a matter may be believed by them, produce the blessed Augustine as a witness. He seems to affirm this in the final book of *The City of God*.

After concluding the question he had proposed—whether human beings would see God through the body, as we see the sun, moon, and other bodies, or not—he says:

“Either God will be seen through those eyes in such a way that they possess, in so great an excellence, something resembling the mind, by which [Col. 1126B] an incorporeal nature may also be perceived—something that it is difficult or impossible to demonstrate by any examples or testimonies of the divine Scriptures.”

You hear Augustine saying that it is impossible to demonstrate from the divine Scriptures that God will be seen with bodily eyes in the future, yet you say that he affirms what he himself denies can in any way be proved.

You hear him say that the spiritual body would possess something resembling the mind, by which the invisible God might be perceived, because otherwise God could not be seen through the body unless the image of God—through which alone God can be seen, as Augustine himself testifies—were created in the spiritual body.

But if this were to happen, the body itself would no longer be a body but would become spirit, which it is impious to believe.

Then he adds the other part of the question, or what is easier to understand:

[Col. 1126C] “Either God will be known and conspicuous to us in such a way that he will be seen by each of us in spirit, in each of us; he will be seen by one in another; he will be seen in himself; he will be seen in the new heaven and the new earth (Revelation XII), and in every creature that will then exist; he will also be seen through bodies in every body, wherever the gaze of the eyes of the spiritual body may be directed.”

Observe how he gathers together the entire question, which had two parts, under a disjunction. He did not say, “This is the case,” but said, “Either this or that.” Therefore, although one of the two alternatives is true, he nevertheless affirmed nothing here—following his customary method—except this single point, which he had placed outside the question as his own judgment: that it cannot be demonstrated by any examples or testimonies of Scripture that God’s incorporeal substance is to be seen through the eyes of the body [Col. 1126D].

As for what he said in the latter and disjunctive part of the question—“he will also be seen through bodies in every body, wherever the gaze of the eyes of the spiritual body may be directed”—either this is the same as what he had placed in the earlier part, namely that God will be seen through bodily eyes, in which case the question does not consist of contrary alternatives and is no longer a question or a disjunction; or, if it is different from what he had proposed, so that it is a question as he himself called it and the signs of disjunction retain their force, that is, “either,” then we must examine what he meant by saying, “he will also be seen through bodies in every body,” and so forth.

Clearly, he meant the very thing he had stated above: that we are credibly to see the worldly bodies of the new heaven and the new earth in such a way that, through the bodies we shall bear and which we shall behold wherever we turn our eyes, we shall see with the clearest vision God present everywhere and governing all corporeal things [Col. 1127A].

It is like this: among human beings, when we live together with people who are alive and exercise vital movements, as soon as we look at them we do not merely believe that they are alive—we see it. Yet we cannot see their life apart from their bodies, although through their bodies we perceive the life in them.

Let us first examine the example. Life, which animates the limbs and by which bodies live, is invisible, as Augustine himself says: “It is in no way seen by the eyes of the body, but by those of the heart.” How, then, do we distinguish living bodies from nonliving ones, unless we see bodies and lives simultaneously [Col. 1127B]?

Thus the same teacher asserts that we see human beings who are alive and exercising vital movements. For what is meant by “we see living human beings,” which he immediately explained by adding “and exercising vital movements,” except that we see not life itself but movements produced by life? These movements are the most certain signs of life, but are not life itself.

We commonly say: “I hear him weeping or laughing in the house,” or “I hear him crying out while absent”—that is, by hearing I apprehend his weeping, laughter, or cry, not the person himself.

Similarly, one says: “I see you acting justly, distributing your goods kindly and cheerfully,” although justice, kindness, and cheerfulness themselves are perceived by no one. Rather, one sees their works, which testify that their causes are present, without which those works would not occur [Col. 1127C].

In this way we say that we shall see the invisible God governing all things: in the spiritual body, with the clearest discernment of spiritual eyes, we shall see not his nature itself but the most subtle incorruptibility, glorious immortality, and other distinguishing qualities that God will work in future bodies. This pertains to his governance.

It should be noted, however, that Augustine says “wherever we direct our eyes.” This implies that even then the eyes will not see everywhere, but only where they have been directed. Otherwise he would have added “we shall see corporeal things wherever we turn our eyes” without purpose.

Finally, if by this example he demonstrated that God can be seen with bodily eyes in the future, he contradicts himself, since shortly before he said that this could be demonstrated by no examples. For these two statements are strongly opposed: that the matter cannot be demonstrated by any example, and that it can be demonstrated by this example [Col. 1127D]. If he contradicts himself, he cannot fail to be false as well. For contrary things cannot simultaneously be true.

But far be it from us to presume to say that what Augustine says is false. Therefore he does not contradict himself. It remains, then, that by this example he does not show that God’s substance itself can be seen with bodily eyes, since he asserted that this could be demonstrated by no examples.

What he does show can be seen is nothing other than, as we have said, the clearest indications of his present power, wisdom, and kindness. Through these he will glorify and conform immortal bodies to the glory of the body of our Lord, and renew heaven and earth.

## How Saint Augustine presents and explains Saint Ambrose’s statements on the same question

[Col. 1128A]

Let us examine what the blessed Augustine thought about the claim that God will be seen bodily by the saints in a spiritual body after the resurrection. For, when questioned about this matter by Paulina, a servant of God, he presented and explained the words of the blessed Ambrose, who was discussing this question as follows:

“No one has ever seen God” (John I), because no one has perceived or comprehended with the mind or eyes that fullness of divinity which dwells in God. “Saw” must be referred to both. Finally, when it is added, “the only-begotten Son himself has declared him” (ibid.), the vision of minds rather than of eyes is indicated. A form is seen; power is declared. The former is grasped by the eyes, the latter by the mind [Col. 1128B].

And what wonder is it if, in the present age, the Lord is not seen unless he wills it? Even in the resurrection it is not easy to see God except for those who are pure in heart. Therefore: “Blessed are the pure in heart, for they shall see God” (Matthew V).

How many people had he already proclaimed blessed, and yet he had not promised them the ability to see God. If, therefore, those who are pure in heart will see God, surely no others will see him. For the unworthy will not see God, nor can one who did not wish to see God see him.

The Lord is not seen in a place, but by the pure in heart. He is not sought with bodily eyes, nor circumscribed by sight, nor held by touch, nor heard through speech, nor perceived by his movement. When he is thought absent, he is judged; when he is present, he is not seen.

Finally, not all the apostles saw Christ, and therefore he said: “I have been with you for so long, and you still have not known me” (John XIV) [Col. 1128C].

“If you understand these words, what remains for me to require further, since the question that seemed difficult has already been resolved? Yet the reason why no one has ever seen God remains to be examined. As the disputant whose words we are considering says, no one has perceived or comprehended with the mind or eyes the fullness of his divinity.

“It remains to inquire how the angels see God. For if he does not appear even to them as he is, but, with his nature concealed, appears in whatever form he chooses, then it is even more necessary to ask how we shall see him as he is. For this is promised as the highest reward in the resurrection: that we shall be equal to the angels of God [Col. 1128D]. Accordingly, if they too do not see him as he is, how shall we see him when we have been made equal to them in the resurrection?

“Note that this is directed against those who say that no creature—neither angels nor human beings—will see God in his own substance, but only in certain apparitions.”

But observe what Ambrose says next:

“Finally,” he says, “when it is added, ‘the only-begotten Son himself has declared him,’ the vision of minds rather than eyes is indicated. A form is seen; power is declared. The former is grasped by the eyes, the latter by the mind.”

Since “form” is more customarily used of bodies or of bodily likenesses, he therefore said: “A form is seen; power is declared.”

Accordingly, the Only-Begotten, who is in the bosom of the Father, declared in an ineffable proclamation that the pure and holy rational creature is filled with an ineffable vision of God—a vision we shall attain when we have been made equal to the angels [Col. 1129A]. For perhaps he is now seen by certain angels in the manner in which he will be seen as he is. By us, however, he will then be seen in this way, when we have been made equal to them.

The question now concerns how God is seen—not in the form in which, even in this age, he wished to appear to certain people, since he spoke not only with Abraham and other righteous people but also with Cain, the fratricide, but how he is seen in that kingdom where his children will see him as he is.

Moses burned with this desire. Speaking with God face to face was not enough for him, and he said: “Show yourself to me openly, so that I may see [Col. 1129B] you” (Exodus XXXIII)—as though he were saying what is sung in the Psalm from the same desire: “When your glory shall be revealed” (Psalm XVI).

Speaking of this vision, Ambrose himself, its lover and desirous seeker, also says:

“God is not seen in a place—not as at the oak of Mamre, nor as on Mount Sinai—but by the pure in heart.”

And I shall follow him, knowing what he desires, what he longs for, and what he hopes for.

“God,” he says, “is not sought with bodily eyes,” with which he showed himself to Abraham, Isaac, Jacob, and others in this world; “nor is he circumscribed by sight,” because of what was said: “You shall see my back” (Exodus XXXIII); “nor is he held by touch,” as when he wrestled with Jacob; “nor is he heard through speech,” as he was heard not only by so many saints but even by the devil; “nor is he perceived by movement,” as when he once walked in paradise at evening (Genesis III) [Col. 1129C].

You see how the holy man strives to call our minds away from all the senses of the flesh, so that he may make them fit to see God.

And yet what does such an external planter and waterer accomplish, unless God, who gives the growth, works inwardly? For who, without the assistance of the Spirit of God, could conceive that there is something—and something greater than all that is perceived through the body—which is not seen in a place, is not to be sought with the eyes, is not heard through speech, is not held by touch, and is not perceived by movement, yet is seen by the pure in heart?

He was not speaking of this life when he said these things. For, distinguishing this age—in which God appeared not as he is but in the form in which he wished to appear to those to whom he wished—from the life of the age to come with the clearest distinction, he said:

“And what wonder is it if, in the present age, God is not seen unless he wills it? Even in the resurrection it is not easy to see God except for those who are pure in heart. And therefore: ‘Blessed are the pure in heart, for they shall see God’ (Matthew V)” [Col. 1129D].
