Here he began to speak of that age in which not everyone who rises will see God, but only those who rise to eternal life.

The Lord himself spoke of this life when, though present, he was not seen: “Whoever loves me keeps my commandments, and whoever loves me will be loved by my Father, and I will love him and show myself to him” (John XIV).

And what is eternal life except what he says elsewhere: “This is eternal life, that they may know you, the one true [Col. 1130A] God, and Jesus Christ whom you sent” (John XVII)?

But he promised to show himself to those who love him as one God with the Father—not as he was seen in the body in this age by the good and the wicked. For in that form of God in which he did not regard equality with God as something to be seized (Philippians II), those who see him will see him as he is.

They will not see him merely because they were poor in spirit in this life, or because they were meek, mourned, hungered and thirsted for righteousness, were merciful, were peacemakers, or suffered persecution for righteousness—although all these qualities also belong to those who are pure in heart. They will see him because they are pure in heart.

For this reason, among the other beatitudes, although those who have a pure heart possess all these qualities, the words “they shall see God” are not placed elsewhere but only where it is said: “Blessed are the pure in heart” [Col. 1130B]. For the pure in heart will see him who is not seen in a place, who is not sought with bodily eyes, who is not circumscribed by sight, who is not held by touch, who is not heard through speech, and who is not perceived by movement.

“For no one has ever seen God” (John I), either in this life as he is, or even in the life of the angels as these visible things are seen by bodily vision, because “the only-begotten Son, who is in the bosom of the Father, himself has declared him” (ibid.).

Therefore the statement that he declares him refers not to the vision of bodily eyes but to the vision of minds. The Word is not a sound striking the ears but an image made known to minds, so that there the saying may shine forth in an inward and ineffable light: “Whoever sees me sees the Father also” (John XIV).

Thus Saint Augustine affirms through these words of Saint Ambrose that the question of how God is seen by his children in the age to come has been resolved; and this is true [Col. 1130C].

## DIVISION

The blessed Ambrose most clearly confirms that in the resurrection God is not seen with bodily eyes even by those who will be unworthy of the vision of God, nor is he perceived by any bodily sense, but only by the pure in heart.

Saint Augustine also, in explaining the statements of his beloved Ambrose, asserts that the declaration by which the Word of God makes himself and his Father known to minds pertains not to the vision of bodily eyes but to the vision of minds.

What could be clearer than the statement that the blessed Augustine made shortly beforehand: “No one has ever seen God” (John I), in [Col. 1130D] this life as he is, nor in the life of the angels as these visible things are seen by bodily vision?

Let us hear Augustine further explaining the words of his Ambrose:

“It may cause difficulty how the very substance of God could have been seen by certain people living in this life, in view of the statement: ‘No one can see my face and live’ (Exodus XXXIII). This is possible only because the human mind can, by divine power, be snatched from this life into the angelic life before the death of the flesh, which is common to all.

“Thus was the one snatched away who heard those ineffable words that a human being is not permitted to speak (2 Corinthians XIII). In him there was such a turning away of attention from the senses of this life that, whether he was outside the body—that is, whether, as often happens in a more violent ecstasy, the mind was carried away from this life into that life while the bond of the body remained—or whether he was entirely released from the body, as happens in complete death [Col. 1131A], he said that he did not know.

“Thus both statements are true: ‘No one can see my face and live’ (Exodus XXXIII). For the mind must be withdrawn from this life when it is taken up into the ineffability of that vision.”

Then Augustine continues:

“Consider carefully whether what you proposed to me has been explained, recalling what has been said. If you ask whether God can be seen, I answer: He can. If you ask how I know, I answer: Because it is written in the most truthful Scripture: ‘Blessed are the pure in heart, for they shall see God’ (Matthew V).

“If you ask by what means we shall see him, I answer: By that by which the angels see him, since then we shall be equal to them. For just as these things called visible are seen [Col. 1131B], no one has ever seen God. Nor can he be seen, because he is an invisible nature, just as he is incorruptible. The Apostle placed these together when he said: ‘To the King of the ages, invisible and incorruptible’ (1 Timothy I). For just as he is incorruptible now and will not afterward become corruptible, so he is invisible not only now but forever.

“For he is not seen in a place, but by the pure in heart; nor is he sought with bodily eyes; nor is he circumscribed by sight; nor is he held by touch; nor is he heard through speech; nor is he perceived by movement.

“But the only-begotten Son, who is in the bosom of the Father, declares without sound the nature and substance of the Deity, and therefore invisibly shows it to eyes worthy and capable of so great a vision.

“These are the eyes of which the Apostle says, ‘the eyes of our heart having been enlightened’ (Ephesians I), and of which it is said: ‘Enlighten my eyes, lest I ever sleep in death’ (Psalm XII) [Col. 1131C]. The Lord is spirit. Hence: ‘Whoever clings to the Lord is one spirit’ (1 Corinthians V).”

Therefore whoever can see God invisibly can cling to God incorruptibly. I think there is no longer anything further to ask concerning the question you proposed [Col. 1132A].

These are Augustine’s words. Whoever understands them sees with complete certainty that he will never see God through the eyes of the body. To omit everything else, God is invisible now and forever, just as he is incorruptible now and forever. He is invisible because he cannot be seen with bodily eyes, with which visible things are seen and for that reason are called visible.

The Only-Begotten also declares and invisibly shows the substance of God to the eyes of the heart. We can cling incorruptibly to God, who is spirit, if we can see him invisibly.

**(Cassiodorus.)** In the resurrection we shall be filled with the recognition of divine wisdom. The truest understanding of things will not be infused through burdensome disciplines but will be revealed in the mind’s cultivated light. There the splendor of the mind and the light of understanding will be such for the blessed that they will deserve to behold the Creator himself as he is in his majesty [Col. 1132B].

Accordingly, we are reminded by true books that the purified and improved part of the mind, by divine gift, truly contemplates the Author, whose image it nevertheless bears. Hence, finally, we shall see God from that part from which we believe, and from that part we shall contemplate the supreme, eminent, singular reality—namely, from the part by which we are better.

**(Jerome.)** “Whoever has received the promised Holy Spirit will at the same time receive the pledge of the inheritance; and that inheritance is eternal life. Just as the pledge granted to us is not outside us but within us, so the inheritance itself—that is, the kingdom of God, which is within us—exists inwardly in us.

“For what greater inheritance can there be than to contemplate and [Col. 1132C] see, through perception, the beauty of Wisdom, the Word, truth, light, and the ineffable nature of God himself, and to behold the substance of all things created in the likeness of God?

“This Holy Spirit, who is the pledge of our inheritance, is therefore now given to the saints so that they may be redeemed and joined to God.”

## FOURTEENTH SUNDAY. According to Luke

[Col. 1131]

[Col. 1131D] “As Jesus was going to Jerusalem, he passed through the middle of Samaria and Galilee. And as he entered a certain village, ten lepers met him. They stood at a distance and raised their voices, saying: ‘Jesus, Teacher, have mercy on us’” (Luke XVII).

The lepers are those who, lacking knowledge of the true faith, profess various doctrines of error. They mix true things with false in disorder, displaying, as it were, the different colors of leprosy. Such people must be avoided by the Church, and, kept far away, they must cry out with great effort until, through knowledge of the Teacher, they return to the form of salvation.

“Having seen them, he said: ‘Go, show yourselves to the priests.’ And it happened that, as they went, they were cleansed.”

The Lord is found to have sent only lepers to the priests, because the Jewish priesthood was a figure of the priesthood [Col. 1132D] that now exists in the Church. And whoever has, by God’s grace, been cleansed of heretical perversity, pagan superstition, Jewish faithlessness, or even fraternal schism must come to the Church and show others a true color of faith, similar to theirs. Hence Paul was sent to Ananias (Acts IX), so that he might receive the sacrament of faith and have the true color of faith approved in him—not because the Lord is unable to accomplish everything by himself, but so that the very fellowship of the faithful, by communicating with one another, may confirm one unified appearance of the true color in faith. Cornelius, too, after his prayers had been heard, was ordered to send for Peter, for the sake of confirming unity (Acts X).

“But one of them, when he saw that he had been cleansed, returned, glorifying God with a loud voice. And he fell on his face at his feet, giving thanks. [Col. 1133A] And he was a Samaritan.” The one who returned giving thanks signifies the humility of the unity of the Church. “Samaritan” is interpreted as “guardian.” By this name is signified the one who attributes all his strength to God, according to the Psalmist: “I will keep my strength toward you, because you are God, my protector” (Ps. LVIII).

He falls on his face who is ashamed of the evils he has committed. Concerning the Lord’s persecutors, however, it is written that “they went backward and fell” (John XVIII). He who falls forward sees where he is falling; but he who falls backward does not see. The wicked therefore fall backward, because the heart is exalted before the fall, so that they do not see what follows them. The righteous, however, fall forward, because they are pierced with remorse and humbled.

“But Jesus answered and said: ‘Were not ten cleansed? And where are the nine? Was no one found to return and give glory to God except this foreigner?’ And he said to him: ‘Rise, go, your faith has saved you.’” If faith saved this man, faithlessness destroyed the nine. If one is added to nine, a certain image of unity is completed, producing such a total that the number does not proceed farther unless it returns to one. Thus the nine need the one for a certain unity, whereas the one does not need them for its own unity. Therefore the one who gave thanks signifies those who are within the unity of the Church, while the nine signify those who are outside it.

The Lord asks where they are, because to know is God’s way of choosing, whereas not to know is to reject. When they were cleansed, they came to know God, but they went away backward. Of such people the Apostle says: “Although they knew God, they did not glorify him as God or give thanks” (Rom. IX).

It should be known that one is called the first unity, while ten is the second. The former is attributed to God, because, multiplied in itself, it is neither increased nor diminished; the latter to the Church, because, multiplied in itself, it grows into a hundred. In the ten, which is the unity of the hundred, variety is generated through multiplication. The ten lepers are therefore rightly said to have existed: they were diverse from the faith of the one God. And just as all the faithful can be signified by the ten, on account of their observance of the Ten Commandments, so all the unfaithful can conversely be understood by the same number, on account of their neglect of those commandments.

The one who returned to the Lord, healed, is called a foreigner either because he had previously been alien to the Church, or because he separated himself from the faithlessness of his companions.

Alternatively: The ten lepers were cleansed when the Lord entered the town. The Lord entered the town when, intending to become incarnate, he descended into the Virgin’s womb, the little sanctuary of the Holy Spirit. The ten leprous men were all human beings stained either by transgression of the Ten Commandments or by the infliction of the ten plagues of Egypt (Exod. VII).

It must be understood that these ten plagues are opposed to the Ten Commandments of the Law. The first plague is water changed into blood; the second, frogs; the third, gnats; the fourth, every kind of fly; the fifth, death among the Egyptians’ livestock; the sixth, pustules and swollen blisters on human beings and animals; the seventh, hail upon all the crops except the late ones; the eighth, locusts, which ate what remained; [Col. 1134A] the ninth, three days of darkness; the tenth, the death of all the firstborn.

As we have already said, the Ten Commandments of the Law are opposed to these. The first commandment is: “You shall have no foreign gods. For I am the Lord your God” (Exod. XX). Compare the first commandment with the first plague: understand the one God, from whom all things exist, in the likeness of water, from which all things are generated. Water changed into blood therefore signifies God, whom human beings then changed into blood when they began to believe him corruptible. Hence the Apostle says: “They exchanged the glory of the incorruptible God for the likeness of the image of corruptible man” (Rom. I). An image is corruptible, like blood.

The second commandment is: “You shall not take the name of God in vain” (Exod. XX). He takes the name of God in vain who swears in God’s name but does not believe that he will be punished. Opposed to this commandment are the croaking frogs, signifying deceitful people who resist the truth and establish falsehood by means of God’s name.

The third commandment is: “Remember to sanctify the Sabbath day; you shall do no work on it” (ibid.). This third commandment implies a certain judgment of rest. That rest is peace of mind, or the sanctification of the Sabbath, because there the Spirit of God rests, as he himself says: “Upon whom shall my spirit rest, if not upon the humble, the quiet, and the one who trembles at my words?” (Isa. LXVI). Opposed to this third commandment—that of rest—are the gnats and flies, which signify immense unrest. [Col. 1134C]

The fourth commandment is: “Honor your father and your mother” (Exod. XX). Opposed to this is the fourth plague of Egypt, namely the dog-flies. For it is characteristic of a dog not to recognize its parent, and to display toward its parents the blindness of mind with which dogs are born.

The fifth commandment is: “You shall not commit adultery” (ibid.). Opposed to this commandment is the fifth plague, namely death among the Egyptians’ livestock. To mate and generate offspring is characteristic of animals; to understand by reason is human. Therefore reason, which presides over the lower impulses of the flesh as over its subjects, must not release them indiscriminately, without measure, unlawfully, or at random. For this reason, by the Creator’s ordinance, the nature of animals was given to them so that they are moved toward females only at fixed times. An animal does not restrain itself by reason at other times; rather, its very impulse breaks and renders it sluggish. A human being, however, can therefore always be moved because he can also restrain his impulses.

The sixth commandment is: “You shall not kill” (ibid.). Opposed to this sixth plague are pustules and blisters on every flesh. This signifies that, just as flesh is inflamed toward hatred of one’s neighbor and toward shedding blood, so it will burn with the fire of eternal judgment.

The seventh commandment is: “You shall not steal” (ibid.). Opposed to this commandment is the seventh plague, namely hail upon the crops. This signifies: Whatever you secretly take away from your neighbor, the heavenly Judge will avenge.

The eighth commandment is: “You shall not give false testimony” (ibid.). Opposed to this is the eighth plague, the locusts, a creature harmful with its teeth. This signifies that the deceitful person strives to attack his neighbor by biting and lying. Hence the Apostle says: “If you bite and devour one another, see that you are not consumed by one another” (Gal. V).

The ninth commandment is: “You shall not covet your neighbor’s property” (Exod. XX). Opposed to this is the ninth plague, namely thick darkness. This signifies that the person who meditates on inflicting upon another what he does not want for himself is in darkness and is heading toward eternal darkness.

The tenth commandment is: “You shall not desire your neighbor’s wife” (ibid.), nor his male slave nor his female slave. Opposed to this commandment is the tenth plague, namely the death of the firstborn. This signifies that those who wish to possess the property of others as an inheritance, and desire the momentary death of others, incur eternity.

By these ten plagues, for transgressing the Ten Commandments of the Law, human beings were stained and, as though struck by them, were lepers. They are sent by the Lord to the priests but are cleansed on the way, because when sinners run to the priests to confess their offenses, they immediately receive forgiveness for what they have committed. The one who returned thanks for his healing is the catholic people, which continually gives thanks to God for its salvation.

## On the six kinds of leprosy

“A man in whose flesh and skin a varied color has arisen, without a pustule, or something resembling a shining mark—that is, a plague of leprosy—shall be brought to Aaron the priest or to any one of his sons. When he sees the leprosy on the skin and the hairs changed to a white color, it is leprosy, and he shall be separated at his discretion” (Lev. XIII).

Leprosy, then, is false doctrine. Accordingly, lepers are not inappropriately understood as heretics who, lacking the unity of true faith, profess various doctrines and mix true things with false ones, just as leprosy stains human bodies by varying true and false patches.

We find that the Lawgiver established six kinds of this leprosy in human beings: the first of the head and beard; the second of baldness and receding baldness; the third of flesh and skin; the fourth of skin and body, and of a white scar with redness; the fifth of a sore and a scar; the sixth of a burn (ibid.).

Those who sin against the divinity of the Father, or against Christ himself, who is the Head, bear leprosy on the head. “The head of a man is Christ.” The Jews, Valentinians, Marcionites, and Photinians had this leprosy. All of them bear leprosy in baldness because they defend their error with open perversity.

Those bear leprosy in the beard who think perversely about the apostles and Christ’s saints and falsely attribute any kind of perverse teaching to them. Just as the beard is an ornament, so the apostles and teachers provide an ornament in the body of Christ.

Those have leprosy on the body who disparage the Church, such as the Exariani, who deny the resurrection of the flesh; the Novatians, who condemn marriage and deny forgiveness to repentant sinners; those [the printed group-name is uncertain: *ex calice*] who, among their other errors, do not believe that little children can possess the kingdom of heaven; and the Arians, who forbid an offering to be made for the dead.

He bears leprosy in flesh and skin who attempts to promote carnal or outward things, such as the Cerinthians, who imagine the future resurrection in the pleasure of the flesh, or those who say that sins cannot be counted against people who remain in the faith, even if they live carnally.

He bears leprosy in the scar of a healed sore who, after knowing God, receiving his healing, and receiving the manifestation of the faith he received from Christ, again approaches, in that very scar, some sign of his former error or the faithlessness of an old doctrine.

They bear leprosy in living flesh who hold some false belief about the soul, which is life—for example, those who say that the soul is propagated from the substance of the flesh, and those who think that the soul dies together with the body.

The Manichaeans have leprosy in the scar of a burn. Through the torment of empty abstinence they burn their bodies, and through faithlessness they produce from it not purity but leprosy. Concerning such people the Apostle says: “Some will depart from the faith,” he says, “giving attention to spirits of error and doctrines of demons, speaking falsehood in hypocrisy, and having their conscience seared, forbidding marriage and abstaining from foods that God created” (1 Tim. IV). [Col. 1136B]

But Scripture further adds the colors of leprosies: pale, red, white, livid, black, and flowering (Lev. XIII). Thus, when it speaks of pale leprosy, it denotes a weak and fragile faith of the mind, which, once the color of the blackness of error has been revealed, languishes through its weakness.

When it displays red leprosy, it denotes and burns those infected with the blood of murder. When it speaks of white leprosy, it denotes those who call themselves pure, or those who glory in a false merit. When it mentions white or livid leprosy, it expresses the marks of envy or resentment. [Col. 1136C] When it indicates black leprosy, it condemns a conscience blackened by the furnace and pyre of idolatrous sacrifices. When it speaks of flowering leprosy, extending over the whole body and covering the body’s skin from head to foot, it reveals the crime of avarice. For when they consider a flourishing and pleasant person happy in this world and apparently rich, then the disease of avarice stains every kind of person—like the whole body—with the frequent contagion of that error.

When leprosy is mixed with redness and pallor, it denotes a person who, although weak-minded and deceitful, easily bursts into fury and soon becomes insolently aggressive through his fickleness. Pallor signifies a lying tongue, while redness signifies anger.

There is the leprosy of sin, which is cleansed by offerings of sacrifice—that is, by a contrite and humbled heart. There is also the leprosy of idolatry, which is washed away by the water of baptism. There is the leprosy of heretics, who are commanded to remain outside the camp for seven days of purification, so that they may be cleansed through recognition of the sevenfold Spirit. There is also the leprosy that is brought before the priests’ sight through doctrine.

The sore of leprosy, which cannot be cleansed at all, belongs to those who sin against the Holy Spirit and do not say that the repentant can obtain forgiveness. Concerning them the Truth says: “Whoever has sinned against the Holy Spirit” will not be forgiven, neither in this age nor in the age to come.

As for the command that lepers leave the camp and sit outside until their leprosy is cleansed, this means that heretics ought to be expelled from the Church until they are cleansed of their own error and thus [Col. 1137A] return. Such people are commanded to sit with their garments loosened, their heads uncovered, and their mouths wrapped, while awaiting the cleansing of their leprosy: with their garments loosened, that is, with all their secrets exposed; with their heads uncovered, so that their nakedness may be seen by everyone; with their mouths closed, so that they may no longer teach or speak impiously.

Scripture further added that leprosy can exist in vessels, on the walls of a house, in clothing, and within a boundary wall. Leprosy on the walls of a house denotes the assembly of heretics, which must be cleansed through the priest. Leprosy in small vessels denotes each person’s sin in his own body. Leprosy in houses or clothing denotes what is nourished outside the body or what is committed within the body; yet it also signifies the human soul and the company of the body’s softest senses. The fact that lepers under the Law are sent to the priest is understood to mean that annual sacrifices ought to be offered in the Church for the cleansing of heretics, and that they should thus be reconciled in the unity of the Church. [Col. 1137B]

## Moral exposition on Naaman the Syrian, and his washing on the seventh day in the Jordan

Naaman was commander of the army of the king of Syria, a great and wealthy man, but a leper. He had in his household a certain young maidservant from the land of Israel (2 Kings V). This is the sequence of the story that we have unfolded.

History is a doctrinal threshing-floor in which good interpreters, with the flails of diligence and the winnowing fan of inquiry, separate grain from chaff. Just as honey lies beneath wax and the kernel beneath the shell, so beneath the outer covering of history lies the sweetness of moral teaching. [Col. 1137C]

Naaman is interpreted as “beauty” or “beautiful,” and signifies the rich of this world, who appear powerful and distinguished in their own eyes. Endowed with an abundance of possessions, renowned through the titles of their ancestors, elevated by the eminence of their acquaintances, and possessing literary and forensic knowledge, they are nevertheless lepers through the variety of their crimes.

Multiplied in the fruit of grain, wine, and oil—which constitute the material and opportunity for sin—they are more inclined to vices and more prepared for crimes, freer to commit injury, as it is said: “Their iniquity has come forth as from fatness” (Ps. LXXII).

When, however, the time of mercy and the time of their visitation comes, they have the counsel of a young girl. This girl is divine grace or wisdom, which is a virgin because of its integrity, like that Abishag who warms old men but does not burn young men. [Col. 1137D] This girl is also a maidservant because she is helpful to everyone. Hence it is said: “Wisdom cries aloud in the streets. How long, little ones, will you love childishness?” (Prov. I). And shortly afterward: “I will grant you a good gift” (Prov. IV). And again: “Drink the wine that I have mixed for you” (Prov. IX).

Although this diligent maidservant and girl has neither stain nor wrinkle in herself, she nevertheless serves the wife of the leprous prince. By supplying the inner natural reason of wicked powerful people with the desire for salvation and knowledge, she renders those made discolored by sins distinguished and radiant.

She therefore gives Naaman this advice: “Go to Samaria, to Elisha the prophet, and he will heal you of the leprosy you have” (2 Kings V). Samaria is interpreted as “guard.” Go to Samaria: return to your guard; watch over your actions. When shepherds were watching over their flock, an angelic vision and address took place.

Know yourself. Hence it is said: “Return, transgressors, to your heart” (Isa. XLVI). Dinah, when she wanders away from the prince of the land, is violated. He does not go to Samaria who, shaken away from his own affairs, attends to the business of others.

At the girl’s advice he went to Elisha and knocked at the door of his house (2 Kings V). Elisha is interpreted as “salvation of the Lord.” This is Jesus, the Savior of the world, who saved his people from their sins (Matt. I). Concerning him the Prophet says: “Your salvation, O God, has received me” (Ps. LXVIII). And he himself says of himself: “I am the salvation of the people” (Ps. XXXIV).

His house is the holy Scriptures, or the Church, or religious persons, in whom he dwells by grace. The door is repentance, through which we enter to him and he to us. Hence it is said: “While you are still speaking, I will say, ‘Here I am’” (Isa. LII); and: “Return to me, and I will return to you” (Zech. I).

We have turned away from him, and he has turned away from us. Let us return to him, and he will return to us.

Elisha, sitting in his chair, sent his servant to him with these words: “Go, descend into the Jordan, wash seven times, and you will be cleansed” (2 Kings V).

Our Elisha, taken bodily from us, sits at the right hand of the Father, in those things that are superior. He does not now appear bodily, but he sends his servant. This servant is the understanding or pure reason, made in the image of God. He is the servant who alone escaped from the slaughter of the sons and daughters, so that he might report to Job.

Or this servant is the Holy Spirit, because he makes us little children in malice and children in simplicity. Or in Holy Scripture the term *puer* (“servant” or “child”) is used on account of purity of speech and chaste utterances.

This servant therefore says: “Descend from Syria”—that is, from exaltation. Syria is indeed interpreted as “lofty”—“into the Jordan,” that is, into conformity with Christ, which is humility.

The title of the devil is pride; the title of Christ is humility. For Christ proposed himself as a student of this discipline among teachers, saying: “I do not send you to the prophecies of the prophets or to riddles, but ‘learn from me, because I am gentle and humble in heart’” (Matt. XI). I set myself before you as a mirror.

Outward humility is of little value unless inward humility is present—namely, true obedience. It requires these three things of you: humility must sit in the heart, patience must be preserved in the mouth, and perseverance must be maintained in action.

The words themselves also correspond: “Descend into the Jordan.” Jordan is interpreted as “descent.” This is one reason why the Lord specially chose this river, so that he might be baptized in it.

“Wash seven times,” that is, perfectly.

Naaman became angry and answered: “Are not Abana and Pharpar, the rivers of Damascus, better than all the waters of Israel, so that I may wash in them and be cleansed?” (2 Kings V).

Damascus is interpreted as “drinking blood.” This is the world, which delightfully intoxicates us with the bloody cup of sin for our eternal death.

Pharpar is said to mean “mole,” that deformed and blind animal that inhabits underground hiding places and caves as its dwelling, and burrows beneath gardens and sown fields. It signifies the appetite for earthly things of those who have set their eyes on turning toward the earth. This is also the bent woman whom the Lord straightened.

Abana is interpreted as “its stones of the side.”

By this the foremost people are signified, whether of the Church or of this world. Of the Church, according to the statement: “The stones of the sanctuary are scattered at the head of every street” (Lam. IV); of the world, according to that same prophet’s statement against Babylon: “Take the stones out of the way” (Jer. L), since those who reject the form of humility seek honors.

They respond daily to us when we tell them to despise visible things: “Is it not better to possess riches, feast lavishly and delicately, sleep softly, walk about as we please, and take pleasure in honors [Col. 1139B] than to spend our days in afflictions?” This is to say: “Are not Abana and Pharpar better than all the waters of Israel?”

His companions and those at his side said to him: “If the prophet had told you to do some great thing, surely you ought to have done it; how much more when he has said to you, ‘Wash and you will be cleansed’” (2 Kings V).

Our companions at our side are the angels given to us for protection, and religious men who say: “Even if what is commanded were beyond your ability, you ought to do it.” They set before us Peter’s cross, Paul’s sword, Vincent’s rack, and Lawrence’s gridiron.

Our own camel also passed through the eye of a needle—that is, Christ passed through the narrowness of suffering. If we look upon these things, then even if a great deed is commanded of us, we must not refuse, because “the sufferings of this present time are not worthy of the future glory” (Rom. VIII).

And if it is a great thing, God gave me to myself in the first creation; in regeneration he returned me to myself; he even gave himself for me. What great thing shall I do for such a gift, for so great a price, expended for me? “What shall I repay the Lord for all that he has repaid me?” (Ps. CXV).

“I shall die,” the Prophet said; for this is “I shall take the cup of salvation” (ibid.).

At their counsel he descended and washed himself seven times in the Jordan (2 Kings V). There are seven washings or cleansings: one washing outside the body, one washing around the body, one washing in the body, two in the tongue, and two in the mind.

The washing outside the body is the renunciation of riches and possessions, which are said to be outside because they neither cling to the body nor belong to its substance.

The second washing, around the body, is contempt for costly clothing. For if it were not sinful to use costly clothing, the Apostle would not say: “Not in costly clothing” (1 Tim. II). Likewise, if it were not praiseworthy to use inexpensive clothing, we would not have so many testimonies and commendations of Christ concerning John and Elijah, who used inexpensive clothing.

Jacob also says: “If the Lord my God gives me bread to eat and clothing with which to cover myself” (Gen. XXVIII). He did not say, “with which I may grow proud,” but “with which to cover my nakedness.”

The third washing, in the body, is the mortification of the members and the discipline of the body. Hence Paul says: “I discipline my body and bring it into servitude” (1 Cor. IX). This flesh is Hagar, contradicting her mistress. Concerning her Ambrose says: “She rightly suffered injury, since she had assumed insolence.”

Our flesh is a wanton animal, a vicious she-ass; but it must be disciplined so that it may obey its mistress.

The two washings in the tongue are: to avoid a boastful word in prosperity, whenever God grants prosperity in bodily or spiritual matters; and to avoid a word of impatience in adversity.

He who is justly punished and is impatient is the companion of the thief hanging on the Lord’s left. He who is unjustly punished and bears it patiently is Christ’s companion. He who is both justly punished and patient is like the thief on the right, who said: “We are receiving what is worthy of our deeds” (Luke XXIII).

The two washings in the mind are the renunciation of one’s own will and the non-presumptuous defense of one’s own counsels.

The will must be renounced, so that one who has outward silence in prosperity and adversity may not retain his own will inwardly and thus become conformed to the devil. For just as God willed himself to be the one origin of all things, so the person who retains his own will and does not submit it to God establishes, as it were, another origin of wills.

One must not presume upon one’s own counsel. Some people add the authority of Scripture to silence others and establish their own opinion.

These seven washings were present in Christ. The washing outside the body: although he was rich, he became poor for us. The washing around the body: he was born, placed in a manger, and wrapped in swaddling clothes. The washing in the body: he fasted and spent the night in prayer.

He did not offend in his tongue through prosperity, because when they wanted to make him king, he fled. He did not offend in adversity, because, like a sheep before its shearer, he was silent.

He had the washing in his heart because he did not come to do his own will but the Father’s, and he placed the divine counsel before Peter’s counsel when Peter said: “Far be it from you, Lord; this shall certainly not happen to you” (Matt. XVI).

Again, when Joseph and his mother said: “Son, why have you treated us so?” he answered: “Did you not know that I must be in the things that belong to my Father?” (Luke II), and yet he followed them and was subject to them (ibid.).

“And his flesh became like the flesh of a child” (2 Kings V), that is, in conformity with Christ. This is the child of whom it is said: “A child is born for us” (Isa. IX).

Adam lost condition, innocence, and immortality. This child restored these three things to us. This is Naaman’s sevenfold washing in the Jordan.

## THE FIFTEENTH SUNDAY. According to Matthew

[Col. 1139]

[Col. 1139D] “No one can serve two masters. For either he will hate the one and love the other, or he will support the one and despise the other” (Matt. VI). You cannot serve God and Mammon; that is, service to the different wills of masters is incompatible. *Mammon* is called “riches” in Syriac and is named *divitiae* in Latin.

Let the greedy man hear this. He did not say, “the one who has riches,” but “the one who serves”—that is, the one who guards them as a servant and does not distribute them as a master. Among the Hebrews, *mammon* means “riches”; in Punic, *mammon* means “profit.”

He who serves Mammon serves the devil, who is called by the Lord “the prince of this world” (John XIV).

“And he will love the other,” that is, God. For who loves the devil? Yet someone tolerates him, just as a person in a great household may, because of his own greed, endure harsh servitude joined to another’s maidservant, even if he does not love the maidservant’s master.

“And he will despise the other.” Who can hate God? Yet someone despises him—that is, does not fear him—when he presumes excessively upon his mercy. Hence the saying: “My son, do not add sin upon sin and say, ‘The mercy of God is great’” (Sir. V).

Luke has “will cling to” (Luke XIII), where Matthew says “will support.” Both expressions refer to the devil, whom those who acquire riches wickedly will support by clinging to him.

“Therefore I say to you: Do not be anxious about your soul, what you will eat, nor about your body, what you will wear.” This is to be understood of bodily food and clothing, because we must always be anxious about spiritual things. Labor must be undertaken, but anxiety must be removed. With regard to bodily things, some add: “nor what you will drink.”

“Is not the soul more than food, and the body more than clothing?” The sense is: He who has provided greater things will provide lesser ones as well. For the sake of this life he placed the soul, according to the saying: “He who loves his soul will lose it” (John XII).

“Look at the birds of the air, for they neither sow nor reap nor gather into barns, and your heavenly Father feeds them. Are you not worth much more than they?” This is to be understood literally, because the Lord clearly urges us to abandon all care for present things and teaches us to be attentive only in hope of the future. A rational creature, to whom eternity is promised, is worth more than an irrational one.

“Much more,” that is, you are of far greater worth than the birds of the aerial heavens. [Col. 1141D]

“Which of you, by thinking, can add one cubit to his stature?” If, then, you cannot do even what is least, why are you anxious about the rest? Leave to him the care of clothing the body, whose care brought it into being.

“Consider the lilies of the field, how they grow. They do not labor or spin.” An allegory is therefore not to be sought here, any more than in the birds; rather, an argument from lesser things is made toward greater things.

“But I say to you that not even Solomon in all his glory was clothed like one of these.” What purple of kings, what design of weavers, can be compared with flowers? The color itself is called the covering of flowers, as when it is said: “Redness covers this one.”

“If, then, God so clothes the grass, which is here today and tomorrow is thrown into the oven, how much more will he clothe you, people of little faith?” God clothes—that is, adorns—the grass, meaning the herbs, with beautiful color and good fragrance. When it has dried, it will be thrown into the oven, that is, into a heap having the appearance of an oven.

Little faith is that which is not certain even about the smallest things and does not yet hope for eternal things.

“Therefore do not be anxious, saying: ‘What shall we eat?’ or ‘What shall we drink?’ or ‘With what shall we be clothed?’ For the nations seek all these things. Your Father knows that you need all these things. But seek first the kingdom of God and his righteousness, and all these things will be added to you.”

The nations have no concern for the future; they always seek present things. It belongs to sons to seek the kingdom of God. All these things will be added through the Father’s grace even to those who do not seek them, so that no grace may be lacking to them either in the present or in the future.

Nevertheless, if present things are taken away, it is for testing; if they are given, it is for thanksgiving. All these things work together for good. The heavenly physician knows what he must give us for consolation and what he must take away for exercise. A person does not withhold food from his animal without reason.

When he said, “Seek first the kingdom of God,” he signified that temporal things are to be sought afterward, not in time but in rank: the former as good, the latter as necessary—but necessary on account of that good.

He plainly [Col. 1142C] showed that temporal things must not be desired in such a way that we ought to do good for their sake, although they are necessary. Whatever we do, we are instructed to do for the sake of the kingdom of God. We ought not to evangelize so that we may eat, but to eat so that we may evangelize; for whatever is sought for the sake of something else is inferior to that for whose sake it is sought.

Not everyone ministers for the salvation of the Church; some do so for the sake of temporal things, or for both. But it was said above: “No one can serve two masters.” Therefore we must work good solely for the sake of the kingdom of God, and in this work we must not contemplate a reward of temporal things, either alone or together with the kingdom of God.

Under the name of all these temporal things he placed the Christian, saying:

“Do not be anxious about tomorrow.” For “tomorrow” is not said except with reference to time. Therefore do not be anxious about the morrow. Tomorrow will be anxious for itself.

“Sufficient for the day is its own evil.” He allows us to be anxious about present things, not future ones. Hence the Apostle says: “Laboring night and day with our own hands, so that we might not burden any of you” (1 Thess. II).

In Scripture, “tomorrow” signifies future time, as Jacob says: “Tomorrow my righteousness will answer for me” (Gen. XXX). By “day” are understood the people whose day it is, as the Apostle says: “Redeeming the time, because the days are evil” (Col. IV).

The sense therefore is: The people of tomorrow—that is, of future time—will be anxious for themselves. But you should be anxious about yourself in the present.

“Anxious” in the foregoing passages signifies distress; here it signifies providence, which the future will bring with it, so that when it is necessary to take up some temporal thing, it will be present, because God knows what we need.

He calls the care of present things “evil” because it is punitive and pertains to the mortality we deserved by sinning. It is burdensome enough in itself; let us not add to it the care of future things.

At this point we must be extremely careful not to judge, when we see a servant of God making provision so that necessary things may not be lacking either to himself or to those entrusted to him, that he is acting against the Lord’s commands.

The Lord himself was even willing to have a money box with money in it, so that no one might take scandal at this matter. [Col. 1143B] Paul also appears to have thought about tomorrow when he says: “Concerning the collections, do as I directed” (1 Cor. XVI).

The whole of this command is therefore reduced to this rule: even in providing these things, we should think of the kingdom of God; but in the evil of the kingdom of God, we should not think of these things. Thus labor and provision are not condemned, but the care that chokes the mind.

## The comparison of God and the devil concerning the right of God and of man
God, intending to redeem the world through a human being, came into the world and found the devil ruling over the whole world. God, visiting the world through a human being, came to what was his own, and the human being, not loving the world through God, had nowhere to lay his head. God as a human being ruled the elements in this world, and the human being, God, said that he did not possess a kingdom of this world. Thus, in one respect everything belonged wholly to God, and in another respect everything belonged wholly to the devil. Everything was God’s that he himself had made; everything was the devil’s that he himself possessed. God had created the world in the beginning, and the devil had possessed the world from the beginning.

Thus a contest arose with God, and a contest arose with the devil. God said that he ought to receive back what was his; the devil said that he ought not to suffer accusation in what was his own. God said that after so long a patience he ought rightly to be honored by satisfaction; the devil said that after so long a neglect he ought not to be deprived of his possession. God said that the devil had fraudulently taken away what belonged to another and had held it by force; the devil said that God had neither objected when the devil took it away nor ever reclaimed it while the devil held it. God said that, if he wished, he could use his power to recover what was his; the devil said that he ought not to abuse his power against justice. God said that it was not just to allow what he had created in goodness to perish; the devil said that it was unjust to restore what had perished voluntarily. God said that he wished to show mercy through his own kindness; the devil said that he knew himself to be suffering loss through another’s power. God said that it was just that those repenting of sin should be received into salvation; the devil said that it was not just that those persisting in sin should be compelled to salvation. God said that he had come not to compel those who were willing, but to help those who were willing; the devil said that, for the time being, he would patiently endure losing those who were willing, if he retained those who were unwilling. God said that he would not lay a hand on what belonged to another if what was his own were restored; the devil said that he was ready to return what belonged to another, provided that what was his own were not taken away. God said that he could turn no one away from mercy; the devil said that, if he lost everyone, he could not bear it patiently. God said that he urged them to withdraw entirely from what belonged to another; the devil said that he requested that, at least out of respect for his former dominion, some rest should not be denied him in part. God said that, since he had previously chosen the better things, he would afterward grant him the inferior ones; the devil said that, since he could not have the right of choice, he would at least exercise the right of division. God said that by the privilege of dominion he claimed power over both portions; the devil said that, since he could no longer claim more, he asked for nothing by right, but only by permission. God [Col. 1144B] said that he would permit only as much as could satisfy even the hunger of the greedy; the devil said that he would not accept so little that he did not desire more, if it could be done.

After these words, God ordered measuring cords to be stretched out for the division. He found green and well-watered places in the deepest valleys—smaller in extent but greater in value—and ordered these to be set aside for one portion. But the deserted and dry places among the crags and high mountains—broad and open to the view, large in extent but cheap in value—he ordered to be assigned to the other portion.

Then he commanded the devil to appear. And he said to him as he stood there: “Lest you be able to accuse me either of the violence of a judge or of the greed of a giver, whatever your eye sees, I will give you.”

Then the devil, who regards everything lofty and is unable to look upon what is low, raised his eyes and gazed at the high mountains, the projecting rocks in the crags, and the open deserts. Rejoicing as though almost everything had been ceded to him, he despised what God had chosen. Rebuking him and mocking the blindness of his arrogance, God said to him: “The measuring lines have fallen for me in splendid places” (Psalm 15). “You praise what you see, and I praise what I see. You are below, and therefore nothing but high and projecting things are visible to your eyes; I contemplate from above what loveliness the lowly things possess, for my inheritance is splendid to me.”

## On the Two Lords, the Two Cities, and Various Other Matters

There are two cities, Jerusalem and Babylon, and two peoples: the lovers of God, citizens of Jerusalem, and the lovers of the world, citizens of Babylon; and there are two kings: Christ, king of Jerusalem, and the devil, king of Babylon.

Between these two cities and two peoples, and between the two kings, there is continual war, discord, and conflict, and each marks his soldiers: Christ marks his, and the devil his, so that each may recognize his own king, be recognized by him, and follow him. Jerusalem is a city in heaven, whereas Babylon is below on earth; likewise Christ is above, and the devil below. Christ’s soldiers follow their king, and the devil’s soldiers follow their king.

Christ set before us three examples of the way that we ought to follow him; similarly, the devil proposed three things by which those who follow him are hurled headlong after him. The road to Christ, because it leads upward, is steep and narrow, and long in its ascent; the road to the devil, because it leads downward, is broad, short, and easy toward the depths and the precipice.

Therefore Christ left the example of poverty, so that, relieved of the burden of earthly things, we might ascend lightly by the steep way; the example of humility, so that, becoming small, we might pass without difficulty through the narrow way; and the example of patience, so that we might not fail along the long ascent.

He gave the example of poverty when he said: “Foxes have dens, and the birds of the air have nests, but the Son of Man has nowhere to lay his head” (Luke 9). He gave the example of humility when he said: “Learn from me, because I am gentle and humble of heart” (Matthew 11). He gave the example of patience when, being struck, he did not strike back, and when he was beaten in mockery, he endured it. He gave the example of poverty because he did not wish to possess riches in this world; the example of humility because he despised glory; and the example of patience because he endured evils.

When he was praised, he did not rejoice; when he was cursed, he was not saddened; when he was oppressed, he was not broken. Someone said to him: “Good Teacher.” And he replied: “Why do you call me good?” (Mark 10.) Behold humility. Others said: “You have a demon.” And he said: “I do not have a demon, but I honor my Father” (John 8). Behold patience. And when the people sought him in order to make him king, he fled, leaving us an example of humility, and despised glory. There are many examples pertaining to these matters.

The first virtue, then, is poverty, so that we may cast away what weighs us down and in which there is an occasion for sin. And because poverty is despised, humility follows, by which even lowliness itself is loved for the Lord’s sake. And because, in turn, one who is lowly is injured without respect, patience is necessary after humility, when all adversities are endured bravely for God’s sake. Poverty makes one light and unencumbered; humility makes one small; patience makes one strong and robust.

Conversely, the devil first burdens his own with the weight of riches, in love and anxiety, so that they may fall downward; secondly, he inflates them through pride, so that they may walk on the broad way; thirdly, he breaks them through impatience, so that they may quickly fail.

These two peoples built two cities from their beginning: Babylon began with Cain, and Jerusalem with Abel.

For the first human being begot two sons, the beginning and sign of division. That mass of human nature, which in the first human being had initially been created entirely for glory, was afterward, through transgression, entirely consigned to punishment, so that it might be shown that mercy and truth had already begun to be divided into vessels of mercy and vessels of wrath. The firstborn of the earth was rejected, just as the firstborn of heaven had fallen—if indeed he was firstborn who was not begotten. For it was said of him: “He is the beginning of the ways of God” (Job 40).

The first things were rejected, to show that the end is better than the beginning. What was made in the beginning was indeed made good by God, but it was good in its beginning; what was to be made at the end was to be good in its making and good in its completion. For this reason also, in the very creation of things, he first made matter and afterward added form (Genesis 1), to show that likewise in rational nature what was first had first been made to exist, but afterward the beautiful and well-formed state was to exist; and something better was to be added, so that it would not glory excessively in having first received what was good, but would hasten instead toward what it was later to receive as better.

But the firstborn loved the first things, so as to lose the last; and therefore he was rejected, both in heaven and on earth. The one, cast down from heaven to earth, overthrew the human being through envy; the other, rejected on earth, killed his brother out of jealousy, because his brother’s life was burdensome to him, and therefore he hastened toward his death. His wicked conscience was tormented, seeing each day the life of the just man bearing witness against him; and the just man was, as it were, burdensome for him to behold, since his own wickedness was condemned by that man’s repentance. Therefore he hastened to remove him from their midst, lest he should see, to his own confusion, the one whom he had refused to see for his own correction and amendment, perhaps thinking that afterward God would not be the avenger of iniquity if no just man remained as a witness to the truth.

Thus Cain, the murderer of his brother, laid the foundations of Babylon, while Abel, murdered and by his blood, consecrated the beginnings of Jerusalem on earth. Thus Ishmael, the firstborn, was rejected, while Isaac was chosen; Esau too was rejected from the portion of the inheritance and the gift of blessing, while Jacob was loved and raised up; and when Eliab the firstborn was rejected, David, the younger, was elevated to the height of kingship.

The devil’s soldiers have always fought in fury, while Christ’s soldiers have conquered through patience, following their king in love of poverty and devotion to humility, and reaching him through patience.

## Examples from Various Kinds of Birds

Because the present Gospel mentions birds and herbs, we have thought it right to insert some material concerning them into this work for moral instruction.

Blessed Ambrose says in the *Hexameron* concerning the swallow:

“The swallow is small in body, but exceptionally dutiful and lofty in affection. Though lacking all resources, it builds nests more precious than gold, because it builds wisely.” For the nest of wisdom is more precious than gold.

What is wiser than that it should enjoy the wandering freedom of flight while entrusting its little ones and their shelter to human dwellings, where no one may attack its offspring? It is also beautiful that, from their first emergence, it accustoms its young to human society and provides them with greater safety from the attacks of hostile birds.

There is also this remarkable feature: with what skill it constructs its houses without any helper, as though trained in an art. It gathers straw in its beak and smears it with mud, so that it can glue the pieces together. But because it cannot carry mud with its feet, it wets the tips of its feathers with water, so that dust may easily adhere to them and become mud. With this it gradually gathers bits of straw or tiny twigs and makes them stick together.

By this method it constructs the whole structure of its nest, so that, as though on a pavement floor, its young may move about within their dwelling without injury, and no foot may be thrust through the little openings in the woven structure, nor may cold penetrate the tender bodies.

This work of industry is nearly common to many birds. But the following is unique, displaying extraordinary care, prudent understanding, and notable knowledge, together with a certain expertise in medicine: if any of its young should be covered with blindness or injured in the eyes, it possesses a means of healing by which it can restore their sight when their vision has been interrupted.

Let no one, then, complain of poverty because he has left his own houses empty of money. The swallow is poorer, yet, though lacking bronze, it abounds in industry. It builds without expenditure, raises roofs, and takes nothing from the need of its neighbor. It is not compelled by poverty to harm another, nor does it despair in the grave weakness of its children.

We, however, are afflicted by poverty, and need drives many people into shameful conduct. In our desire for profit we turn our ingenuity toward frauds, and in the gravest illnesses we abandon hope; improvident and sluggish, we lie prostrate, although we ought to hope more greatly in divine mercy when human resources have failed.

## On the Crow

Let human beings learn to love their children from the custom and devotion of crows. Even when flying, they diligently and anxiously accompany their young, lest the tender ones fail; they bring them food and do not abandon the duties of feeding them for a very long time.

## On Hawks

Hawks are said to show harsh cruelty toward their own offspring. When they notice them attempting the beginnings of flight, they cast them out of their nests and immediately drive them away; if they linger, they repel and beat them with their wings, compelling them to dare what they fear. Afterward they provide them with no gift of nourishment.

Thus they take care that the young do not become sluggish, that they are not softened by luxury, that they do not wither in idleness, that they do not learn to await food more than to seek it, and that they do not lay aside the vigor of their nature. They interrupt the work of feeding in order to compel them to venture into the practice of seizing prey.

## On the Eagle

The eagle is frequently mentioned as disowning its young, but this is not true of both young: some have thought that it kills one of two offspring because it is displeased by the doubling of the food required. But this is not easily believed, especially since Moses gave this bird such testimony of devotion toward its young when he said:

“As an eagle protects its nest, and sits over its young, spreads its wings, takes them up, and carries them upon its shoulders, so the Lord alone guided them” (Deuteronomy 32).

How, then, could it spread its wings if it had killed one of them? Therefore I do not think that it becomes cruel through reluctance to feed, but through examination and judgment. It is always said to test those it has begotten, lest, among all birds, the royal dignity of its kind should be disfigured by the deformity of degenerate offspring.

Accordingly, it is said to expose its young to the rays of the sun and to suspend the little ones in midair by its loving talon. If one, struck by the sunlight, preserves an undaunted sharpness of sight and looks without blinking, that one is approved because it has demonstrated the truth of its nature by the steadfastness of an unclouded gaze. But if, dazzled by the sun’s ray, it turns away its eyes, it is rejected as degenerate and unworthy of such a parent, and is not considered worthy of being reared because it was unworthy of being received.

Thus the eagle does not condemn it through the harshness of nature, but through the integrity of its judgment. It does not disown it as its own, but refuses it as another’s.

## On the Fene or Coot

The bird called *fene* in Greek takes up the eaglet which the eagle has either accepted or rejected, joins it to its own offspring, and, mixing it among its young, feeds and raises it with the same maternal diligence and equal provision of nourishment as its own.

Thus the fene feeds the offspring of another, whereas we cast away our own with merciless cruelty. If the eagle casts one away, it does not cast it away as its own; it refuses to recognize it as degenerate. We, which is worse, disown those whom we recognize as our own.

## On Turtledoves

God infused turtledoves with this affection and gave them this virtue of continence: the one who alone is able to prescribe what all should follow. The turtledove is not inflamed by the flower of youth, nor is it tempted by the allure of opportunity. The turtledove does not know how to make the first bond void, because it knows how to preserve chastity after the first marriage has been contracted.

The rest concerning the turtledove is found in the Gospel: “When the Lord saw the city, he wept over it” (Luke 19).

## On the Vulture

Vultures are said not to indulge in intercourse, nor to unite in the customary manner of marriage and marital coupling; thus they are conceived without any seed of males and give birth without union, and those born from them continue to a great age of long life, so that the course of their lives extends even to one hundred years, and the end of their brief span does not easily overtake them.

What do those who are accustomed to mock our mysteries say when they hear that a virgin gave birth and consider the birth of an unmarried woman, whose modesty had not been violated by any association with a man, impossible? What is considered impossible in the Mother of God is not denied to be possible in vultures. Another gives birth without a male, and no one refutes it; but because Mary, betrothed to a man, gave birth, they make her modesty a matter of dispute.

Do we not perceive that the Lord had first set forth many examples from nature itself by which he might prove the beauty and establish the truth of the incarnation he assumed?

## On Bees: How They Live

[Col. 1148D]

Bees alone, among all kinds of living creatures, have offspring held in common by all. All inhabit one dwelling; all are enclosed within the boundary of one homeland. Their labor is common to all; their food, work, use, and product are common; their flight is common.

What more need be said? Their generation is common to all, and so too is the integrity of their virgin bodies. Birth also is common to all, since they neither unite in intercourse nor dissolve into lust, nor are their births shaken by pains. Suddenly they send forth a very great swarm of offspring, gathering their young from leaves and herbs with their mouths.

They themselves appoint their king; they themselves create their peoples. Although placed under a king, they are nevertheless free. They possess the prerogative of judgment and the devotion of loyalty, since they love him as though appointed by themselves and honor him with such careful scrutiny.

A king distinguished by the insignia of nature is formed among the bees, excelling in the greatness and beauty of his body, and—what is most important in a king—in gentleness of character. For although he has a sting, he does not use it to take revenge. There are laws of nature, not written in letters but impressed upon character: those who possess the greatest power are more restrained in punishing.

Those bees, moreover, which have not obeyed the king’s laws punish themselves with a repentant condemnation, dying from the wound of their own sting. None dares to leave the dwellings, or go out to seek pasture, unless the king has first gone out and claimed the leadership of the flight.

Their procession is through fragrant fields: where the garden breathes out its flowers, where the stream flees through the grass, where the riverbanks are lovely. There is the joyful play of youth, the exercise of the open field, and the release from cares. The work itself is sweet, made from flowers and sweet herbs. The foundations of the hive are first laid. For what else is a honeycomb but a kind of fortress? Finally, the bees’ nectar is protected by these enclosures.

All compete in their duties. Some keep watch while seeking food; others provide anxious protection for the fortresses; others investigate future rains and observe the courses of the clouds. Some seem to fashion wax from flowers; others gather with their mouths the dew poured upon the flowers.

No one plots against another’s labors or seeks life through plunder—and would that it did not have to fear the plots of plunderers! Yet they possess their own stings and pour poisons among the honey. If provoked, they even give up their lives in the wound, fired by the heat of vengeance.

Thus, in the valleys among the fortresses, that moisture of dew is poured out. Gradually, with the passage of time, it is thickened into honey. At first liquid, it begins, through the coagulation and fragrance of the flowers’ wax, to produce sweetness in honey. This honey is useful not only for pleasure but also for health: it sweetens the throat and heals wounds; it also pours medicine into internal ulcers.

Thus, although weak in strength, the bee is powerful in the vigor of wisdom and the love of virtue. Finally, they defend their king with the greatest protection. While their king is safe, they do not know how to change their judgment or bend their mind; when he is lost, they abandon the fidelity of their guarding duty and themselves plunder their honey, when the one who held the leadership of their task has been killed.

Thus, while other birds scarcely produce single offspring in a year, bees create two broods and surpass the others with double fertility.

Justly Scripture praises the bee as a good worker, saying: “Go to the bee and see how industrious she is.” Consider also how honorable is the work whose labor kings and ordinary people alike take for their health! You hear what the prophet says. He sends you, in any case, to follow the example of that little bee and imitate her work, because it is desirable and renowned among all.

## On the Nightingale

The nightingale is a bird that keeps watch throughout the night. While it warms its eggs in a kind of hollow and lap formed by its body, it consoles the sleepless labor of the long night with the sweetness of its song. It seems to me that its chief purpose is to animate the eggs it warms into offspring no less through sweet melodies than through the warmth of its body.

A poor but chaste woman imitates it. Drawing a millstone with her arm for the work of grinding, she ensures that food will not be lacking for her little ones. By singing at night she softens the sorrow of poverty; and although she cannot imitate the sweetness of the nightingale, she nevertheless imitates it in the diligence of her devotion.

## On the Owl

The owl, with its large, gray eyes, does not feel the horror of the darkness of night. The darker the night becomes, the more freely, contrary to the custom of other birds, it exercises unhindered flight. But when day has arisen and the splendor of the sun has spread around it, its sight becomes dull, as though it were wandering in certain darkness.

By this characteristic it declares that there are some who, although they have eyes with which to see, do not habitually see; the function of their sight is enveloped in darkness. The wise men of this world possess eyes but do not see. In the light they perceive nothing; they walk in darkness while investigating the dark matters of demons. They believe that they see the heights of heaven, describing the world by measurement, calculating the extent of the air itself, and pursuing other things of this kind: dull toward eternal realities, and, as though knowing everything, sharp only toward vanities.

## On the Bat

The bat, an ignoble animal, received its name from evening. It is both winged and four-footed, and it uses teeth—things that you would not usually find in other birds. Like quadrupeds, it gives birth not to eggs but to living young; it flies through the air in the manner of birds, but it is accustomed to emerge at evening twilight.

It flies not by the force of feathers but supported by the oarage of its membrane, by which it is suspended and carried about, as though by the flight of feathers, and is given motion. This lowly animal also has the feature that its members cling to one another and hang from some place almost like a cluster of grapes. If any one at the end loosens its hold, they all come apart. This occurs through a certain service of charity, which is rarely found of this kind among human beings.

## On the Cock

The cock’s crow is sweet at night, and not only sweet but useful. Like a good housemate, it both wakes the sleeper and warns the watchful, and consoles the traveler, proclaiming the passage of the night through its melodious signal.

When it crows, the robber abandons his ambushes. At its crow, Lucifer himself, awakened, rises and illuminates the sky. When it crows, the frightened sailor lays aside his sorrow, and every storm, stirred up by frequent evening blasts, gradually becomes calm.

At its crow, the devout person leaps up to pray and renews the duty of reading. Finally, when it crowed, Peter himself, the rock of the Church, washed away the guilt that he had incurred by denying before the cock crowed.

At its crow hope returns to everyone; the affliction of the sick is relieved; the pain of wounds is diminished; the heat of fevers is moderated; faith returns to those who have fallen; Jesus looks upon those who are wavering and corrects those who have gone astray.

Finally, he looked upon Peter, [Col. 1151A] and immediately his error departed, his denial was driven away, and confession followed. Look upon us also, Lord Jesus, so that we too may acknowledge our own errors, release our guilt through holy tears, and deserve forgiveness of sins.

Let these things said about birds suffice. We shall now indicate something that ought to be considered concerning herbs.

## Examples from Herbs

Blessed Ambrose admonishes us in the *Hexameron* to consider the lilies of the field: how great is the whiteness of their leaves, and how the leaves, packed closely together, seem to rise from bottom to top so as to express the shape of cups, with a kind of gold shining within. Yet, enclosed all around by the surrounding wall of the flower, this inner splendor is exposed to no injury.

If someone plucks this flower and loosens it into its leaves, what hand of so great an artificer could restore the form of the lily? Who is so great an imitator of nature that he would dare to repair this flower, concerning which the Lord gave such testimony that he said: “Not even Solomon in all his glory was clothed like one of these” (Matthew 6)?

The richest and wisest king is judged inferior. And how great is the beauty of this flower!

Why should I enumerate the health-giving juices of herbs? Why the remedies of shrubs and leaves? A sick deer chews little branches of olive and becomes well; leaves of olive, gnawed by locusts, also free them from illness. Bramble leaves laid upon a serpent kill it. If you cook wormwood with oil and anoint yourself with it, gnats do not touch you.

But perhaps some may say: “What then? Along with useful things, deadly and harmful things are also produced. Along with wheat comes darnel, which is found to be harmful among foods of life and, unless it is detected beforehand, customarily injures health. Among other nourishment for life, hellebore is also found; aconites too often deceive and mislead the gatherer.”

But this is as though you were to criticize the earth because not all human beings are good. Rather, accept the greater point: not all angels in heaven are good. Is it therefore right, in matters that are useful, to set aside the Creator’s grace and confess that, because of certain harmful foods, the Creator’s providence is defective—as though everything ought to have been created for the sake of appetite, or as though the things that divine indulgence supplies to our stomach were scanty?

The foods assigned to us are defined and known to all, foods that produce both pleasure and bodily health. But each of the things generated from the earth has a particular purpose, which in its proper share completes the fullness of the whole creation. Some things are born for food, others for another use. Nothing is without purpose; the earth produces nothing empty.

What you think useless is useful to others; indeed, it is often useful to you yourself in another way. What does not aid as food supplies medicine, and often the very things that are harmful to you provide harmless nourishment either to birds or to wild animals.

Finally, starlings eat hemlock; it does not deceive them, because through the constitution of their bodies they turn the poison of the deadly sap into something harmless. For its sap has a cooling force, and they forestall it through rapid digestion by leading it through fine pores to the place of the heart, before it can assail the vital organs.

Those experienced in such matters say that hellebore is food for quails, because by a certain natural balance of their bodies they avoid the force of harmful nourishment. Indeed, if by the method of medicine something is often adjusted for the health of the human body, although it seems contrary to it, how much more does what is turned by a physician’s hand toward health benefit the particular nature of food?

Sleep is also frequently induced by mandrake when the sick are afflicted by the distress of wakefulness. Why should I speak of opium? Its effect has become known to us through daily experience, and we know how the gravest pains of the internal organs are often soothed by it.

Nor is it overlooked that the frenzies of lust have often withered through hemlock, and that old disorders of the sick body have been dissolved by hellebore. There is therefore not only no reproach of the Creator in these things, but an increase of thanksgiving. What you thought had been generated for danger works for your health as a remedy. What is dangerous is avoided through providence, and what promotes health is not brought about by human contrivance.

Have sheep and goats learned to avoid what is harmful to them? Even by smell alone, through a kind of natural mystery, although they lack reason, they recognize a means of escaping danger and preserving health, and they distinguish harmful things from beneficial ones. Thus, when they have sensed weapons armed with poison, they are often said to seek familiar herbs and apply them as a remedy to their wounds. Their food is medicine: you may see the arrows spring back from the wound and flee, and the poisons not spread.

Finally, to deer food is poison. The snake flees the deer but kills the lion. The dragon binds the elephant, whose collapse becomes the death of the victor. Therefore the two fight with the utmost force: the dragon so that it may bind the elephant’s foot, where the fall of the defeated cannot harm it; the elephant so that it may not be caught by its hindmost foot or in a narrow passage, where it could neither turn itself around and crush the dragon with a heavy step nor obtain the help of the elephant following behind.

Therefore, if irrational animals know by which herbs they may heal themselves or by which aids they may obtain assistance, how can a human being not know, in whom rational understanding is innate? For this reason examples are given to us from irrational things, so that through them we may arrive at rationality.

# THE SIXTEENTH SUNDAY. According to Luke

[Col. 1151]

[Col. 1151D] “Jesus went into a city called Nain. And his disciples and a great crowd went with him. When he approached the gate of the city, behold, a dead man was being carried out, the only son of his mother. And she was a widow, and a large crowd from the city was with her” (Luke 7).

Nain is a city of Galilee. The dead man, who is carried outside the gate before many people, signifies one who sins criminally and makes his sin known to many through words and deeds, as though through the gates of his city.

He is rightly called the only son of his mother, because although Mother Church has many sons, both good and bad, the wicked are regarded as one person insofar as wickedness is concerned, just as the good are regarded as one person according to goodness. Every chosen person, when instructed in the faith, is a son; when instructing others, he is a mother. Hence Paul says: “My little children, for whom I am again in labor” (Galatians 4).

When, therefore, the good strive unanimously to recall the wicked, the good are called the mother and the wicked the only son.

The gate of the city through which the dead man is carried out is one of the senses by which a person falls into sin. The one who sees opens an entrance to desire; the one who lends his ear to idle or shameful things opens an entrance through hearing; the one who lends his tongue to quarrels opens another; and whoever does not guard the remaining senses opens for himself entrances to death.

Everyone who remembers that the Church was redeemed by the death of her bridegroom should recognize that she is a widow. Many witnessed this miracle, so that many might become praisers of God.

“When the Lord saw her, he was moved with compassion for her and said to her: ‘Do not weep.’” The Evangelist beautifully testifies that the Lord was first moved with compassion for the mother and then raised her son, so that in one act he might show us an example of the piety we ought to imitate, and in the other establish faith in a piety worthy of wonder.

“And he came near and touched the bier. And those who carried it stood still.” The bier on which the dead man was carried is the falsely secure conscience of the despairing sinner. Those who carry him to be buried are either impure desires that drag human beings into destruction or the poisonous flatteries of those who entice, which bury sinners as though under a mound of earth.

When the Lord touches the bier, the bearers of the funeral stand still, because the conscience, touched by fear of heavenly judgment, returns to itself, restraining carnal pleasures and unjust praisers.

“And he said: ‘Young man, I say to you, arise.’ And the one who had been dead sat up and began to speak. And he gave him to his mother.”
