The one who had been dead sits up when the sinner comes back to life through inward compunction. He begins to speak when he shows that he is returning to true life. He is returned to his mother when, through priestly judgment, he is joined to the communion of the Church.

“Fear seized them all, and they glorified God, saying: ‘A great prophet has arisen among us, and God has visited his people.’”

They all glorified him—that is, they praised God—because the heavier the fall, the more welcome is the mercy of the one who raises the fallen, and the more certain is the hope of salvation for those who repent.

God visited his people when he once determined that his Word should become incarnate and when, by sending the Holy Spirit into our hearts each day, he raises us up.

[Col. 1154A] “And this report about him went out throughout all Judea and throughout the whole surrounding region”—that is, throughout the entire region around Judea.

Allegorically, it was the approach of Jesus to the gate of the city: the Word made flesh led the Gentile people through the gates of faith into the heavenly Jerusalem.

Behold, the younger Jewish people, dead through unbelief, are carried out, because Mother Church, possessing nothing in this world as her own, mourns with devoted affection among the many crowds of peoples surrounding her and strives to recall them to life. She obtains this meanwhile in the conversion of a few Jews, and finally in their fullness.

The place where the body is carried is the human being; the bearers are evil habits, which drag him toward death. But Jesus touches the bier when he raises fragile human nature upon the cross. Or the bier of the dead man is touched by God—that is, through the wood of the cross—because the human being perished through the wood of paradise.

The bearers of the dead are the four elements, whose disorder is an incentive to sin in the human being. The bearers stand still because they are no longer able, as before, to drag him toward death.

Jesus’ speaking is the infusion of admonitions of salvation, by which the weakened person is raised to life through good works and thus returned to his mother. Everyone is afraid because many are corrected by the example of one.

## On the Dying and on the Departure of Souls
Scripture says: “Blessed are the dead who die in the Lord” (Apoc. XIV). Those die in the Lord who, though dying in the flesh, are nevertheless found to be living in the Lord. What does “in the Lord” mean? In faith, hope, and charity. For through these one lives in that life [Col. 1154C] in which one lives in the Lord. There is one kind of life by which the body lives from the soul, and another kind by which the soul lives from God. At present, through faith, hope, and charity; afterward, in place of faith and hope, through contemplation, while love remains.

Therefore the soul cannot be harmed if the body loses its life, when the soul itself, persisting in faith, hope, and charity, does not lose its life. Let no one therefore say to me: “Those who have little faith, little hope, and little charity are not saved.” I do not measure them. Let them grow as much as they wish. The greater they are, the better. Yet I do not dare condemn them, however small they may be. From the moment they have been born of God, they are children of God. Do you suppose that God will save the great children and condemn the small ones? Scripture says to me: “Your eyes saw my imperfect state, and in your book all shall be written” (Ps. CXXXVIII). If all, then—the great and the small—what does “your eyes saw” mean? They approved them. What does “they are written in the book” mean? They will be saved. Therefore the imperfect too will be saved. For those who are imperfect are nevertheless something, and they are someone; they are included in the number and are written down. Those who are nothing are no one; those who have nothing cannot be written down or counted.

Therefore, “to everyone who has, it shall be given, and he shall abound” (Matt. XV). To everyone who has merit, a reward shall be given. He did not say, “A reward shall be given to one who has great merit, but shall not be given to one who has little merit”; rather, he says, “to everyone who has, it shall be given, and he shall abound.” Therefore even the one who has little merit, once he has received the reward, will have enough, although he will not have as much as the one who has great merit. The only one excluded from receiving the reward is the one who has no merit at all. Therefore all who die in the Lord are blessed, because after the merit of virtue they attain the reward of blessedness.

Many inquire about the departure of souls. Yet many things may be asked—if, indeed, everything that can be asked ought to be asked. People ask about the departure of souls: how they leave the heart, where they go after departing, and, when they have reached the place to which they go, what they find, receive, or endure. But all these things ought rather to be feared than investigated. They have been hidden for this reason: not that they should be sought or discovered, [Col. 1155B] but that they should be feared. For who can be secure when proceeding into uncertainty?

This one thing, however, ought not to be uncertain: an evil death cannot follow a good life. For death is not evil except when it is followed by evil. Whoever therefore wishes to die well should live well, since what comes after death is arranged in accordance with, and repaid according to, what precedes it in life before death. Until death there is merit; after death, reward. Death is the middle point: in it the Lord’s day begins, and man’s day comes to an end. In his own day man is left to himself, so that he may do what he wishes; but in the Lord’s day man is no longer in his own power, but in the power of the One to whom he has come to be rewarded. Therefore it belongs to man to strive to order well only what has been entrusted to him; but what has not been entrusted to him, but promised to him, he should leave to the judgment of the One by whom it must be fulfilled.

Many inquire about the departure of souls—how souls leave their bodies: whether, that is, they go out in such a way that they leave essentially and locally, beginning to exist outside, as though expelled; or whether their departure consists only in withdrawing from the bodies’ animation, and, as it were, gathering themselves inwardly, ceasing to nourish the bodies so that they subsist in themselves.

For example, when this bodily breath is breathed out, it leaves the body and begins to exist essentially and locally outside the body, whereas previously it had been essentially and locally contained within the body. But when the bark of a tree begins to dry, moisture leaves it and is drawn inward; it does not go out so as to exist externally, but remains within what is inside—whether in the wood or in the pith—so that it is no longer in the bark itself. It completely leaves the bark, so that it is not in the bark, but it does not pour out externally as though outside; rather, it leaves as if gathered inward. If that moisture should again emerge from its interior so as to spread once more into the bark, the bark becomes green again, because the moisture within it is its life.

Thus they ask about the soul when it leaves the body: whether leaving consists only in withdrawing into itself from the body’s animation, so that it is already no longer in the body because it has ceased to animate the body. In this respect it appears already to be, in a certain manner, outside every body: subsisting by itself alone, it is not poured out for the animation of the body. When it is not in a body, it is not in a place, because place exists only in a body. When it is outside the body, it is also outside place. There is no place between it and the body, and it is equally distant from every body, because there is no body between it and the body. If there is no body between it and the body, it is plainly established that there is no place between it and any body, because there is no place where there is no body.

How, then, is it outside every body with respect to place, while being equally near to every body? If, being outside one body, it were nearer to one body and farther from another, there would necessarily be space between it and the body. If there were space, there would be place; if there were place, there would be body. But if there were body between it and every body, then body would be outside every body—which cannot happen.

Therefore it has been said that the soul neither withdraws from body by means of body, nor approaches body by means of body. And so it is not moved locally in order to withdraw from the body, which is in a place; nor is it moved locally in order to approach the body, which is in a place. For between every place and that which is in no place there is no place.

For this reason, they think it has been said that a created spirit is indeed moved in time, because it is capable of change, but is not moved locally: it is not moved locally when withdrawing from the body, which is in a place, nor when approaching the body, which is in a place. For it is not moved when it withdraws from a place, nor is it again moved locally when it approaches a place.

Even when the soul, situated in the body, moves the body locally, it is nevertheless not itself moved locally. If it is considered to be moved locally for the reason that it is in a body which is moved locally, why should wisdom not likewise be said to be moved locally because it is in a body which is moved locally? For if it is said that wisdom is in the heart through the soul itself, and the soul itself is said to move locally through the locally moved body, why should wisdom—which is in the soul—not also be said to move locally through the soul when the soul is moved locally? But if this reasoning does not prove that wisdom is moved locally, even though it is in the soul, why should the soul be said to move locally, although it is in the body that is seen to move locally?

By this sort of consideration he proves that a spirit is not moved locally, although it is in a body that moves locally; yet it is moved temporally, because, being subject to succession, it changes from one thing into another. But we ought not to be excessively curious about hidden matters, lest we presume more than we are capable of knowing. He alone who made the spirit knows what path it takes. We neither know how it comes nor comprehend how it departs.

When this bodily breath is drawn in, it enters bodily; when it is breathed out, it departs bodily and locally. But the nature of the spirit is one thing, and that of the body another. When the soul was first given to the man, God breathed into his face the breath of life (Gen. II). Who can say how God breathed the soul into the body to animate it—whether he introduced it from outside the creature in order to animate it, or made it there where he placed it and commanded the animation created within to emerge, so that the breathing was nothing other than the animation itself?

If, then, it is unknown how the soul is breathed in, how can it be known in what manner it is breathed out? God breathes in; man breathes out. God sends; man sends back, because the soul is sent when it approaches and is sent back when it departs. We know this one thing: when the soul departs, the body dies, and the separation of the soul is the death of the body. It is enough for us to know that it departs. To investigate how it departs is to inquire beyond what is necessary.

**DIVISION**

By many examples we have learned that, at the departure of souls, angels—evil or good—are present, dragging them according to their merits either to punishment [Col. 1157B] or leading them to rest. We also sometimes know precisely, while souls are still placed in the body and before their departure, many things that will happen to them, whether through the response of inward conscience or through revelations made outwardly. We know as well that souls, sometimes carried away and then restored to their bodies, have narrated visions and revelations shown to them concerning the torments of the impious or the joys of the righteous. Yet in these accounts they have reported nothing except either bodily things or things resembling bodily ones: winds, flames, bridges, ships, houses, groves, meadows, flowers, black and white men, and other things such as are commonly seen and possessed in this world, either loved for delight or feared as torment. Likewise, they have said that, once separated from their bodies, they were dragged by their hands, led by their feet, suspended by the neck, scourged, hurled down, and subjected to other experiences of this kind—all of which can belong only to a bodily nature.

If we believe that all these things exist there visibly and bodily, then, in addition to other absurdities that are recognized, we must also confess that souls, even when separated from their bodies, are themselves bodies, compacted and distinguished according to the likeness of bodies by means of limbs.

I must not keep silent about something I heard concerning this matter. A brother of reliable testimony told me that he had heard from his abbot—who affirmed it truthfully—that when the abbot was once traveling, as is customary, to visit certain brothers living at a distance, he received lodging at a certain place. There he learned that something had occurred a few days earlier, an event then famous among all the inhabitants of that place.

A pilgrim, traveling to Saint James for the sake of prayer, lodged in that same place. At night, as is customary for travelers, he rose before dawn. Leaving the village, he reached a forest nearby. There, by chance—as often happens—he became separated from his traveling companions at a turn in the road and began to go astray.

When he had gone some distance, he encountered a man of venerable appearance and bearing. Asked by him who he was, where he came from, and where he was going, he explained his name, homeland, and the purpose of his journey. The other declared that he was Saint James, toward whom the pilgrim was traveling; he said that he already knew everything about him and had now come to meet him as though willingly and graciously. He praised his devotion, commended his good intention, and said that a great reward was being prepared for him with the saint, and that his recompense was already near.

After many words had passed between them on various matters, the stranger finally described the misery and sufferings of this life, whatever their kind or extent. He explained how quickly everything loved in this world passes away, and likewise how everything feared or grieved over passes without delay. Through this and similar rational persuasion, he gradually instilled contempt for life in the mind of the man, who suspected nothing sinister, and removed his fear of death.

Finally, he said that nothing would benefit the man of virtue more than to hasten his departure from this life; and, if no other way were available, to assail death bravely with his own hand and not allow himself to be held long in these sufferings, since he had no doubt that joy was prepared for him.

What more need be said? Deceived, he assented to the fraudulent persuasion and, having plunged in the blade, cut his own throat. His companions searched for him for a long time along the byways. At last they found him dead and carried the lifeless corpse back to the village from which they had departed. Because the host with whom he had stayed that night appeared probably to be aware of the crime, they demanded that he be punished on the basis of a false accusation.

When he saw that his innocence was being endangered without cause and implored, with the inward devotion of his heart, that divine help be present to him, suddenly the man who had died rose up. Explaining what had happened before all who stood there in astonishment, he acquitted the innocent host.

He reported that he had been led to torments by an evil angel, who had persuaded him to kill himself. But while he was being led away, a man with a radiant face had encountered those who were proceeding—he said that this man was Saint James—and had rescued him, taken him up into heaven to the Judge’s throne, and there obtained through prayers that he might be restored to life. He affirmed that there he had seen many thousands of angels.

When asked about their condition and appearance, however, he said that there was nothing in this world resembling them by which he could express the quality he had seen in them—unless perhaps fire or light, though even these were very far from being similar. He said that there was indeed sorrow, but that what he had seen could in no way be expressed.

We have wished to record this so that it may not seem strange if, for the demonstration of spiritual realities, certain signs resembling bodies are presented to souls after they have departed from their bodies. Unless such things are seen by souls stripped of the body, in such forms and through such forms, those who return to their bodies and live within them, knowing only bodily things, could never speak of them.

Although souls stripped of their bodies may see those things in another manner there, they cannot nevertheless narrate them to us in another manner. Those things would always remain hidden, and there would be nothing that could be said about them by those who return, unless they were shown to those who depart and see them according to these forms.

Whether souls that depart from this world and do not return see or experience those things in this manner is altogether uncertain. It nevertheless seems more probable that the things which, while they live in bodies, are impressed upon them through the pleasure of visible things and bodily imaginings are what they suffer as torments there, apart from their bodies. For they do not entirely escape bodily suffering when they depart enveloped and entangled in bodily imaginings impressed upon them by their habitual indulgence in wrongful pleasures.

But those who, while remaining here, strive to cleanse and strip themselves of such pleasures and fantasies of thought do not afterward, once they have departed from their bodies, experience punishment and torment in them. In this respect they are, in a certain manner, incapable of suffering, because they carry nothing with them that deserves punishment.

**On death, what death is, and the three kinds of death**

Death is so called because it is bitter, or because it is named from the bite of the first man. For when the first parent of the human race touched the forbidden tree through disobedience, by that bite he incurred death (Gen. III). Hence death itself is also named from the bite.

There are three kinds of death: bitter, premature, and natural. The death of infants is bitter; that of the young is premature; that of the old is natural.

There are likewise three kinds of death. One is the death of sin, of which it is written: “The soul that sins shall itself die” (Ezek. XVIII). Another is mystical death, when someone dies to sin and lives to God, of which the Apostle says: “We have been buried with Christ through baptism into his death” (Rom. VI). The third is the death by which we complete the course of this life and fulfill its charge—that is, the separation of soul and body.

We therefore observe that one death is evil, if we die because of sins; another death is good, by which the one who has died is justified from sin. The third death is intermediate: it appears good to the righteous, yet is feared by most people. Although it releases everyone, it pleases few. But this is not a fault of death; it is a fault of our weakness, because we are captivated by the pleasure and delight of this life and tremble to complete its course, in which there is more bitterness than pleasure.

Did not holy and wise men, who lamented the long duration of this pilgrimage, desire to be dissolved and considered it better to be with Christ? And because they thought daily about death, believing that they were, as it were, about to depart from this world, there is no doubt that this daily meditation on death killed every vice in them.

To avoid all the weapons of combat, and indeed to suppress every movement of all desires and sins, no shield seems stronger to me than meditation on death and the terror of the final examination.

For one must consider how, when the sinful soul begins to be released from the bonds of the flesh, it is shaken by bitter terror and torn by how many goading stings of conscience. It recalls the forbidden things it committed; it sees the commandments it neglected and disdained to fulfill. It grieves that it received the time granted for repentance in vain; it weeps because the fixed moment of strict retribution is inevitably approaching.

It strives to remain, but is compelled to go. It wishes to recover what it has lost, but is not heard. Looking behind it, it counts the entire course of its past life as though it were one very brief step of a journey. It directs its eyes before it and discovers the expanses of infinite eternity.

It therefore weeps because, within so brief a span, it could have acquired the joy of all the ages. It also laments that, for the pleasure of so brief an enticement, it has lost the indescribable sweetness of perpetual delight. It is ashamed because, for the sake of that substance liable to worms, it neglected the one that was destined for the choirs of angels.

Now it raises the rays of its mind, and, when it contemplates the glory of immortal riches, it is confounded to have lost them through the poverty of this life. When it turns its eyes downward to the valley and foul darkness of this world, while above it marvels at the splendor of eternal light, it clearly discovers that what it loved was night and darkness.

If only it could have merited renewed time for repentance! What a hard course of life it would undertake! What promises, great and numerous, it would make! With how many bonds of devotion it would bind itself!

Meanwhile, as its dimming eyes waste away, its breast palpitates, its hoarse throat gasps, its teeth gradually blacken and draw together a kind of rust, its face grows pale, and all its limbs stiffen.

While these services, then, precede a person as death approaches, all his deeds and words are present together. His thoughts too are no longer absent, and all these things bear bitter witness against their author. Everything is heaped before the eyes of the one who rejects it, and what he refuses to behold he attends to under compulsion and unwillingly.

Moreover, on one side there is a dreadful crowd of demons, and on the other angelic power. In the one who stands between them it is clearly discerned to which side possession ought justly to be assigned. For if the signs of piety are seen in him, he is soothed by the gentleness of the angels’ invitation and summoned to depart by the sweetness of harmonious melody. But if the blackness of his merits and the squalor of his foulness assign him to the left side, he is immediately shaken by intolerable terror, disturbed by the violence of a sudden attack, assailed headlong, and violently torn from the prison of his wretched flesh, so that he is already dragged in bitterness toward eternal punishments.

After departure from the body, who could explain how many armed ranks of wicked spirits lie in ambush, how many roaring bands equipped with deadly weapons block the way, and how, packed together like armies in battle formation, they attack the soul so that it cannot pass freely?

To turn these things frequently over in one’s heart—what is it other than to reject the flattering enticements of this life, renounce the world, suppress the unlawful movements of the flesh, and steadfastly preserve the single purpose of attaining perfection? To these one must also add the terror of the final judgment, so that through its bitterness the false sweetness of this world may be despised.

These considerations are effective for avoiding the troubles of the devil’s battle; we rise up if we wisely reflect upon the danger of the final necessity. If that sudden and terrible coming of Christ is properly weighed, what will there be in the world in which the human mind, even in its folly, can delight?

That day is the day toward which the entire purpose of the preceding ages and their whole culmination are gathered, and to which all the volumes of Sacred Scripture minister. Concerning it blessed Peter says, to shake the hearts of his hearers with fitting terror:

“‘The day of the Lord will come like a thief; on it the heavens will pass away with great force, while the elements will be dissolved by the heat of fire. Since all these things are to be dissolved, what sort of people ought you to be in holy conduct and piety, awaiting and hastening toward the coming of the day of our Lord Jesus Christ, through which the burning heavens will be dissolved?’” (2 Pet. III).

**On the origin of the soul**

We read in the account of creation that, as soon as the body had been formed from the mud of the earth, the Lord immediately breathed into it, and Adam became a living soul (Gen. II). “He breathed” is said in order to express the dignity of the work, so that it might be recognized that something extraordinary had been brought forth by his mouth.

Otherwise, this breathing signifies that which is command and decree. For how can he breathe who neither expels a spirit nor possesses a mouth, which is something bodily? Following this view, some have said that, as soon as human seed has been coagulated into a living substance, souls are immediately created and given to bodies, distinct and perfect.

Skilled practitioners of medicine, however, say that the human and mortal creature receives a soul on the fortieth day, when it begins to move in its mother’s womb. But where God makes souls, I do not know. I know this: for God to make something is nothing other than his will and command.

Saint Augustine, writing through Orosius and Paulinus to blessed Jerome, says the following: “Therefore, not to make this long, you certainly hold this view: that even now God makes individual souls for individual human beings as they are born.”

Lest the objection be raised that God completed all creatures on the sixth day and rested on the seventh (ibid.), bring forward the testimony of the Gospel: “My Father is working until now” (John V). When God therefore creates new souls, each for each person, it is not said that he is doing for each one born something he did not do before.

For on the sixth day he had already made man in his own image (Gen. I), which is understood to have been done with respect to the rational soul. He does this now as well, not instituting what did not exist, but multiplying what did exist. Thus it is true both that he rested from instituting things that did not exist, and that he continues to work until now—not only by governing what he made, but also by creating in greater number not something he had not yet created, but something he had already created.

If it is asked why he made souls for those whom he knew would soon die, we can answer that through this the sins of their parents are either exposed or punished.

Moreover, it must be understood that souls are bound by original sin and cannot be freed from it except through the grace of our Lord Jesus Christ. Hence blessed Augustine says:

“I am also certain that the soul fell into sin through no fault of God, no necessity imposed by God or by itself, but through its own will; and that it cannot be freed from this body of death either by the power of its own will, as though that were sufficient for it, or by the death of the body, but only by the grace of God through Jesus Christ our Lord. Nor is there any soul at all in the human race for whom the ‘Mediator between God and human beings, the man Christ Jesus’ is not necessary for liberation” (1 Tim. II).

“Whatever soul, without the grace of the Mediator and his sacrament—that is, baptism—departs from the body at any age of the body will go into future punishment and will receive its body for punishment at the final judgment. But if, after human generation, which took place from Adam, it is regenerated in Christ, it will belong to Christ’s fellowship and will have rest after the death of the body, and will receive its body for glory.”

These are the things I hold most firmly concerning the soul.

**(CASSIODORUS.)** This, however, must be believed truthfully and firmly: that God creates souls and, by some hidden method, most justly imputes to them the liability in which they are held through the sin of the first man.

[Col. 1162B] But since the course of our discussion has brought us to this point, so that we have said that souls are universally guilty through the transmission of sin, it is fitting to bring forward the soul of the Lord Christ, lest anyone, perverted by a slanderous intention, think that it was bound by a similar condition.

Let us therefore hear the origin of that soul, which was prophesied concerning holy Mary, ever Virgin, by a worthy herald:

“The Holy Spirit will come upon you, and the power of the Most High will overshadow you. Therefore the holy one who will be born from you shall be called the Son of God” (Luke I).

Who, I ask, could believe that in the majesty of this birth there was either the guilt of original sin or any profane offense of the flesh? Without sin, beyond doubt, he came who was going to absolve the sins of all.

Conceived within the Virgin by a mystical inspiration, with no human intercourse whatsoever, he drew nothing from Adam, because he was conceived and born without concupiscence—he who came so that Adam’s evil might be conquered. Hence it was said to his mother: “You will conceive God through the ear, and you will give birth to a human being.”

The first man transmitted destruction to his descendants; Christ the Lord, coming, bestowed the kingdoms of heaven upon believers. Through him he restores the lost condition, just as through the other the merit had been lost. Born in glory and living without blemish, what could he have drawn from the one whom he came to destroy through an opposing action?

A holy life answered a holy origin. He who was born without sin was overcome by no stain of the world. He assumed a true human being, not its vices; he rejected what the first-formed man had done wrong, and assumed the utterly pure human being whom he created—not assuming sin, but assuming sinful flesh without any injury of pollution.

Concerning this God and human being, destroyer of sin, one of the Fathers says:

“He was brought forth from his mother’s womb in such a way that fertility gave birth while virginity remained; nevertheless, his flesh was not of a nature different from ours. For no soul was breathed into him at the beginning in a manner different from that of other human beings, so as to make him excel through a difference of generation, but through the sublimity of virtue.”

From these words we understand that Christ’s soul is of the same nature as our souls. But while our souls are infected both by original sin and by actual sin, we firmly believe and hold that his soul was free from every sin.

**THE SEVENTEENTH SUNDAY. According to Luke**

[Col. 1163]

[Col. 1163A] “When Jesus entered the house of a certain ruler of the Pharisees on the Sabbath to eat bread, they were watching him. And behold, there was a certain man with dropsy before him” (Luke XIV).

The disease of dropsy takes its name from watery fluid; for in Greek, *hydōr* [ὕδωρ] means “water.” It is a subcutaneous disease arising from an ailment of the bladder, accompanied by swelling and foul breathing. It is characteristic of the dropsical person that the more he abounds in disordered fluid, the more he thirsts.

He is therefore rightly compared with the one whom an overflowing stream of carnal pleasures weighs down. He is also compared with the avaricious rich man, who, the more abundant he is in riches that he does not use well, the more ardently he desires other riches.

“And Jesus answered and said to the lawyers and Pharisees: ‘Is it lawful to heal on the Sabbath?’ But they remained silent.” They rightly remained silent, since they saw that whatever they said would be turned against them. If it is lawful to heal, why do they object if he has violated the Sabbath? If it is not lawful, why do they care for their animals?

“He said, saying”—this is a construction like “Waiting, I waited” (Ps. XXXIX), signifying the perseverance of the speaker until he fulfills what he intends.

“But he took him, healed him, and dismissed him. And answering them, he said: ‘Which of you, if his donkey or ox falls into a well, will not immediately draw it out on the Sabbath?’ And they could not answer him concerning this.”

He heals the dropsical man before the Pharisees and then immediately argues against avarice, so that through the man’s bodily illness the illness of their minds might be represented, and so that they might learn to be healed spiritually through the example of bodily healing.

He appropriately compares the dropsical man with an animal that has fallen into a well. For he suffers from fluid. The ox and the donkey signify the wise and the dull, or the ox signifies the people worn down under the yoke of the Law, while the donkey signifies the Gentile people, untamed by any reason, like a stupid and brutish animal. The Savior draws us out of the well of concupiscence, for all have sinned.

“He also told those who had been invited a parable, observing how they chose the first places at table, saying to them: ‘When you are invited to a wedding, do not recline in the first place, lest someone more honored than you be invited by him, and he who invited both you and him come [Col. 1163D] and say to you: Give this man your place. And then you begin, with shame, to occupy the last place.’”

Observing how they strive after the first places at table—or, in his teaching, observing how they ought to choose places at table in the Church—he teaches humility not only before God but also before human beings.

And because the Evangelist calls this admonition a parable, we must consider what it signifies. The wedding is the union of Christ and the Church. Hence Matthew says: “The kingdom of heaven has become like a king who made a wedding for his son” (Matt. XXII).

Anyone invited to this wedding—that is, joined to the members of the Church—should not recline in the first place; that is, he should not exalt himself by boasting of his merits as though he were higher than the rest. Let him strive to be clothed in the wedding garment, to shine with the splendor of virtues, but with humility.

He gives place to the more honored guest when, recognizing better things in others, he considers whatever he had thought lofty in his own works to be small, and humbles himself with the Prophet, saying: “I am poor and in labors from my youth; I have been exalted, but I have been humbled and troubled” (Ps. LXXXVII). Rightly does the penitent hold the last place in the Church with shame when he exalts himself above others more than he exalts God.

[Col. 1164B] “But when you are invited, go and recline in the last place, so that when he who invited you comes, he may say to you: ‘Friend, move up higher.’ Then you will have glory before those reclining with you.”

“The greater you are, humble yourself in all things,” saying with the Psalmist: “I have been humbled to the uttermost” (Ps. CVII). The Lord, coming to judgment or to his daily visitation of the Church, commands the one whom he finds humbling himself most to ascend.

Hence the saying: “Whoever humbles himself like a little child is greater in the kingdom of heaven” (Matt. XVIII). Beautifully it says, “Then you will have glory,” lest you now wish to receive in full what is reserved for the end. Hence Solomon says: “An inheritance to which one hastens at the beginning will lack blessing at the end” (Prov. XX).

In this life as well, the humble person is exalted in the Church in order to obtain greater gifts of the Holy Spirit.

“For everyone who exalts himself will be humbled, and whoever humbles himself will be exalted.” Whoever carelessly lifts himself up on account of his merits will be humbled by the Lord, even if not before human beings; and whoever prudently humbles himself because of his good works will be exalted by him.

**On avarice and its remedy**
Avarice, wearing down and assailing the human race in many unspeakable ways, and itself in a certain manner deriving its origin from pride, entices the human mind to love and covet only external and visible goods, and to regard them as the highest things, devoting his mind and labors to acquiring, multiplying, and preserving them through various anxieties. For it causes some to burn so fiercely with desire for them that they do not fear acquiring or reclaiming them even through crime, and do not shrink from waging wars, committing murders, robberies, acts of violence, plundering, sacrilege, theft, false witness, perjury, fraud, lies, lawsuits, quarrels, oppression of their own dependents or of any inferiors, acts of inhumanity, deception of their superiors, and other such practices pertaining to the injury of their neighbor or contempt of God.

[Col. 1164D]

Others, whom it cannot lead into such crimes, it nevertheless makes greedy and insatiable for shameful profit. It urges them to multiply their possessions through interest and usury, to labor continually at unfair commercial dealings, and to devote all their care, labor, and attention—even their very life—to the hope and desire of increasing their household wealth, as though they could do so without injuring their neighbor and therefore almost without sin.

Others, who resist its persuasion even in this respect, it does not yet abandon. It suggests that they should excessively love the possessions which they have received honorably and without sin as gifts of God, by inheritance, or through someone’s generosity—even though they do not desire to multiply or increase them through any sin—and that they should place their hope, pleasure, and consolation in enjoying them; or that they should grieve and suffer over their loss or diminution more than is reasonable; or that, when storing them away or reserving them for the future, they should become excessively tenacious, careful, and sparing guardians, refusing to distribute them to needy neighbors according to their ability; or that, under the appearance of frugality and thrift, and in fear of waste, they should spare resources granted for the necessary use both of themselves and of their neighbors as though they were sacred and untouchable; or, certainly, fearing future want more than necessary against the Lord’s command, and anxiously and excessively thinking about tomorrow—that is, the time to come (Matt. 6)—they should appear unbelieving or distrustful of his promises, by which he has promised what is necessary.

[Col. 1165A]

It also impels those who seem to have followed the Lord’s counsel by renouncing everything they possess to retain part of it while renouncing imperfectly; or, after renouncing things completely, to desire them again through a mad apostasy; or, at any rate, to long for more than they had previously possessed. It leads others to seek enrichment in wealth for themselves under the pretext of having abandoned the world, under the appearance of religion, through the opportunity provided by ecclesiastical office, through the administration of many affairs or the distribution of alms, or through some building intended for pious worship.

Finally, greed and pride are so completely one evil that no proud person can be found without greed, nor any greedy person without pride. For if I cannot commit any sin unless I consent to my pleasure—which is characteristic of greed—and despise God’s commandments—which is the evil of pride—how could every sin not proceed from greed, which is “the root of all evils” (1 Tim. 6), and from pride, which is called “the beginning of every sin” (Ecclus. 10)? If greed is love of any illicit thing, or love of possessing more than is proper, no sin is committed without greed. What, indeed, is more avaricious than someone for whom God is not enough, and who desires more than the universal good?

[Col. 1165D]

Against this madness, armed with these and similar cunning devices, charity, mercy, generosity, kindness, contempt for riches, and voluntary poverty prepare to defend the human mind. By demonstrating the vanity and uncertainty of all present things, as well as the brevity and uncertainty of our own life; by declaring the moderation required by nature, which asks for little and is content, according to the Apostle, with food and clothing alone (1 Tim. 6); they readily lead pious minds away from incurring, for the sake of some worthless, trivial, or superfluous thing, a grave, certain, and damnable crime or sin, and thus becoming transgressors of the divine commandments, justly condemned.

Moreover, when they have shown how foolish it is to squander in vain the intention, cares, studies, services, and labors by which—even with less expenditure—we could have earned eternal glory and the riches of everlasting life, in the empty hope of a perishable and smoky thing, then surely, if we are wise, we shall strive and serve less for these vanishing trifles than for enduring goods, especially since the Lord himself says: “You cannot serve God and Mammon” (Luke 16), and Scripture again says: “Whoever loves money will not harvest fruit from it” (Eccl. 5). Again: “There is nothing more wicked than the miser, and nothing more unjust than loving money” (Ecclus. 10); and since “the greedy and rapacious will not possess the kingdom of God” (1 Cor. 6); and: “Woe to you who are rich, for you have your consolation” (Luke 6)!

[Col. 1166A]

And when, with these admonitions impressed upon us, we hold firmly in our hearts that whatever goods have been lent to us by God in the present life as though on interest, we did not receive in order to hide them away greedily, but to distribute faithfully whatever is surplus to our necessary uses among our needy neighbors, and to strive thereby to serve the Lord himself—surely, just as he commanded, we should regard the needs of our neighbors as our own, so that, as faithful stewards of the common Lord’s gifts, we may help them as we are able. In doing so, we return to them what is theirs by debt rather than give them what is ours. For if we do not do this, we shall be subjected by divine judgment to just punishment, not as prudent preservers of our own possessions, but as unjust defrauders and violent robbers of another’s property.

These same virtues also teach that vices which emerge under the appearance of virtues are more destructive and farther removed from remedies than those which openly arise from carnal pleasure. For the latter, like illnesses exposed openly and made manifest, are both reproved directly and healed.

[Col. 1166C]

It is exceedingly ridiculous that some, after the first fervor of renunciation by which they abandoned their household possessions, great wealth, and the wickedness of the world, become so zealously attached to things which, in their condition, cannot altogether be dispensed with—although they are small and worthless—that their care for these things surpasses their former possession of all their resources.

Their contempt for greater riches will profit them very little, because they have transferred to small and insignificant things the attachment by which those greater riches ought to be despised. By retaining, with regard to cheaper materials, the vice of greed and avarice which they cannot exercise toward precious objects, they show that they have not cut off their former possession but merely exchanged it. For they remain attached by the same desire as before through excessive and devoted care of a little basket, a small sack, a book, and other similar things, however worthless.

[Col. 1166D]

They guard and defend these objects with such intense rivalry that they are not ashamed to become agitated against a brother on their account and—even more shamefully—to quarrel. In this also they reveal the avarice of their heart: either they take greater pains to possess things that they need to use than the others do, or, exceeding the proper measure of care, they guard certain things more jealously and attentively and defend them from being handled by others, even though they ought to be common to all the brothers.

It is as though only the difference between metals, and not the very passion of greed, were blameworthy; as though it were wrong to become angry over great things but guiltless to do the same over worthless ones; and as though we had rejected more precious materials for no other reason than to learn more easily to despise inferior ones.

[Col. 1167A]

For what difference does it make whether someone exercises the disturbance of greed toward great and magnificent wealth or toward cheaper objects, except that he must be judged more blameworthy when, having despised the greatest things, he becomes bound to the lowest? Therefore this renunciation does not attain perfection of heart: although he bears the status of a poor man, he has not cast off the will of a rich man.

## On Two Kinds of Humility

There are two kinds of humility: the first directed toward oneself, the second toward others. Humility toward oneself is that by which a person thinks little of himself; humility toward others is that by which a person commends their good qualities without envy or spite. Through the first humility one does not desire to preside; through the second one does not disdain to be subject.

[Col. 1167C]

Humility makes a person not conceal what is hidden in himself; piety makes him not presume to judge what is hidden in another. Humility makes a person not excuse his own faults; piety makes him not aggravate the faults of another. Likewise, humility makes one judge truthfully what lies hidden within oneself; piety makes one incline toward the better interpretation of what is not evident in others.

This is why holy men judge themselves with such strictness and think that everyone else ought rightly to be preferred to them. They see both what is manifest and what is hidden in themselves, but in others they see only what is manifest. Since they do not presume to judge the hidden faults of others except insofar as piety, giving its warning, leads them to consider something good, they see more evils in themselves—where they see both manifest and hidden things—than they see in others, where they see only what is manifest.

[Col. 1167D]

For even when they sometimes discern certain hidden faults in others from manifest evidence, they judge their own faults strictly according to truth; but they do not presume to judge those of others according to anything but piety, that is, by making excuses for them. Hence they consider themselves inferior to everyone, and it is sweet to them to think this, since they can aggravate their own faults and lessen those of others.

Yet we must also note what kind of humility readers of Scripture ought to have. Humility is the beginning of liberating discipline. Although it has many lessons, three are especially relevant to the reader: first, not to regard any knowledge or writing as worthless; second, not to be ashamed to learn from anyone; third, after acquiring knowledge, not to despise others.

Many are deceived by wanting to appear wise before the proper time. They break out into such a swelling of pride that they begin to pretend to be what they are not and to be ashamed of what they are; and so they move farther from wisdom, desiring not to be wise but to be thought wise.

[Col. 1168A]

Many of this sort formerly existed. Although they still needed the first elements of learning, they deigned to attend only to the highest matters, thinking that they became great merely by reading the writings or hearing the words of great and wise men. “We have seen them,” they say; “we have read from them; they often used to speak with us; those eminent and famous men knew us.”

Would that no one knew me, and that I knew everything! You boast of having seen Plato, but you did not understand him. I suppose that henceforth you will think it beneath you to listen to me. I am not Plato, nor did I deserve to see Plato. It is enough for you that you drank from the very fountain of philosophy. But would that you still thirsted! After golden cups, a king drinks from an earthen vessel. Why are you ashamed? You listened to Plato; listen also to Chrysippus. A proverb says:

> What you do not know, perhaps a little donkey knows.

No one has been granted knowledge of everything, nor is there anyone who has not received some particular gift from nature. A prudent reader therefore listens willingly to everyone, reads everything, and despises neither anyone’s writing, person, nor teaching. He seeks from everyone, without distinction, what he sees that he lacks; he considers not how much he knows, but how much he does not know.

[Col. 1168C]

Hence they attribute to Plato this saying: “I would rather learn another’s things modestly than thrust my own forward foolishly.” Why are you ashamed to learn, while you are not ashamed to be ignorant? That shame is the greater. Or why do you pursue the highest things while you lie at the bottom? Consider instead what your strength is able to bear. The person who proceeds in an orderly manner advances most appropriately. Some, while trying to make a great leap, fall into a precipice.

Therefore do not hurry too much. In this way you will reach wisdom more quickly. Learn willingly from everyone what you do not know, because humility can make common to you what nature has made proper to each person. You will be wiser than everyone if you are willing to learn from everyone. Those who receive from everyone are richer than everyone.

[Col. 1168D]

Finally, do not regard any knowledge as worthless, because all knowledge is good. If you have the opportunity, do not despise any writing—or at least reading it. If you gain nothing, you lose nothing, especially since, in my judgment, there is no writing that does not propose something worth seeking, provided that its contents are treated in a suitable place and order. Each work also contains something distinctive that a diligent searcher of words may not have found elsewhere; the rarer it is, the more gratefully he should gather it.

Nothing, however, is so good that a single reading exhausts it. If you cannot read everything, read what is more useful; and even if you can read everything, the same effort should not be spent on everything. Some things should be read so that they are not unknown; others so that they are not unheard of, because sometimes we think more highly of what we have not heard, and a thing whose fruit is recognized is more easily evaluated.

[Col. 1169A]

Now you can see how necessary this humility is for you: not to despise any knowledge and to learn willingly from everyone. Likewise, it is useful for you, once you have begun to know something, not to despise others. This vice of swelling pride affects some because they inspect their own knowledge too carefully; and when they have come to think themselves something, they suppose that those whom they do not know neither are nor could have become such people.

From this too arises the boiling over of certain triflers who, boasting I know not from where, accuse the earlier fathers of simplicity and believe that wisdom was born with them and will die with them. They say that divine utterances have a simple manner of speech, so that there is no need to listen to teachers in them, since anyone can adequately penetrate the secrets of truth by his own natural ability.

They wrinkle their brows and twist their nose and lip at readers of divinity, and do not understand that they insult the one whose words they proclaim to be simple in beautiful expression but senseless in their perverse interpretation.

It is not my intention to imitate such people. A good reader ought to be humble and gentle, wholly free from empty cares and the enticements of pleasures, diligent and assiduous, so that he may learn willingly from everyone; never presumptuous about his own knowledge; fleeing the authors of perverse doctrines as though they were poisons; learning to examine a matter at length before judging it; seeking not to appear learned but to be learned; delighting in understood sayings of the wise; and always striving to hold them before his eyes like a mirror of his own face.

[Col. 1169C]

If some things that are more obscure happen not to admit his understanding, he should not immediately break out into condemnation, thinking that nothing is good except what he himself has been able to understand. This is the humility proper to the discipline of readers.

## On the Praise of Humility and an Attack on Pride

O splendid humility, which the majesty of the Almighty embraces! O blessed humility, which a gracious divinity does not disdain to visit, heal, and glorify! O prudent humility, which despises your own excellence and magnifies the Lord alone by the judgment of the soul, rejoicing in his saving joy of spirit!

While you despise yourself, God regards you in heaven and on earth. While you confess yourself to be dust and ashes, you are divinely exalted above your enemies. In the present you make a good conscience peaceful amid biting anxieties; in the future you make it secure from threatening punishments.

Your rival, pride, cast the devil down into hell from the heights [perhaps *superis*] and drove Adam from paradise into exile; you brought the thief into paradise, and prostitutes and tax collectors into the kingdom of heaven. Pride strives above itself and falls beneath itself; you, so that you may be well founded, dig down into the depths; so that you may see God himself, you are raised up into the temple of God.

[Col. 1169D]

Pride makes itself like the Most High—or rather, it raises itself above everything that is called or worshiped as God—and is cast out from every dignity and will exist no longer. You declare yourself poor and a worm, and are raised from the dung heap and placed with the princes of heaven.

Pride praises its own goods, and they perish; you accuse your own evils, and they vanish. Pride wishes to be sufficient for itself and cannot fail; you rely solely on the grace of God, and in the Lord you can do all things. Since pride is what it is—that is, pride—it cannot fail to be what it is, for it cannot submit to any superior, not even to God. But because you are what you are—that is, humility—you submit yourself, despised, to everyone, even the lowest.

Pride sees everything lofty; you, because you do nothing through contention in order to be preferred to others, nor through empty glory, act in humility, each person truly reckoning others superior to himself, since another may possess something hidden by which he is superior and more worthy before God. This is because they do not each consider what belongs to themselves, but what is good in others.

[Col. 1170A]

Pride wounds what is healthy and corrupts what is whole; you heal the wounded and restore the corrupted. Pride is disgusted by things common and customary, even when they are great; it exalts what is rare and singular, even when it is worthless. You rejoice in all good things as God’s gifts, and seek not your own profit but that of others.

Pride arms and elevates itself with other virtues; it is conquered and extinguished by you alone. You desire divine praise; pride desires human praise. You glory in the testimony of conscience; pride in the empty chatter of the tongue. You honor the heart; pride the body. You adorn the soul; pride the face. You please God; pride the devil. You are the slayer of vices; pride is the slayer of virtues. You build Jerusalem; pride builds Babylon.

You teach the soul to possess, stored away in its treasures, whatever it endeavors outside; pride seeks, with the earth sunk down, that which has passed beyond the starry heaven. You are the fountain, growth, and end of the virtues; pride begins, increases, and perfects every evil.

[Col. 1170B]

Pride blasphemes God’s works and, as though wiser than God, alters them as though they could be better than God’s works. But you, knowing that nothing contrary to wisdom belongs to God’s justice, that nothing perverse adheres to omnipotence, and that nothing can resist it, therefore judge everything that exists to be God’s most beautiful, best, and most perfect work. You say: “All the works of the Lord are great and sought out according to all his desires” (Ps. 110).

Therefore you bless, praise, and exalt exceedingly all the works of the Lord. And just as there are two kinds of you by which you are recognized, so there are also two kinds of that other quality by which it too is recognized. There are therefore two kinds of elation: one within, through pride of mind; the other outwardly, through the swelling of arrogance. Pride is within; boastfulness is outward.

[Col. 1170C]

One kind of pride is that by which the mind swells when considering itself; another is that by which it despises others in comparison with itself. Similarly, outward boastfulness has one form by which a person pretends to be agreeable in displaying himself, and another by which he shows himself cruel and terrifying. In the first he strives to please; in the second he disdains to please.

From the first kind of pride, in which a person pleases himself, there first arises the kind of boastfulness in which he desires to please others. From the second kind of pride, in which he despises others, arises the second kind of boastfulness, by which he strives to show himself not lovable to others but fearsome.

## THE EIGHTEENTH SUNDAY. According to Matthew

[Col. 1171]

[Col. 1171A]

“Then the Sadducees approached Jesus, and one of them questioned him, testing him: ‘Teacher, which is the great commandment in the law?’” and so forth (Matt. 22).

Understand “first of all” as referring not to order but to dignity—that is, “the greatest of all,” or “the first,” because before all things each of us ought to establish it in the innermost heart as the unique foundation of piety. Therefore the first and greatest commandment of all is knowledge and confession of the divine unity together with the carrying out of good works. Good action, moreover, is accomplished through love of God and neighbor. The Apostle commends this briefly in other words, saying: “For in Christ Jesus neither circumcision has any power, nor uncircumcision, but faith working through love” (Gal. 5).

[Col. 1171B]

He shows through this response that a serious dispute had often arisen among the scribes and Pharisees concerning which commandment was first or greatest in the divine law. Some praised sacrifices and offerings, while others, with greater authority, preferred the works of faith and love, since many of the fathers before the law had pleased God solely through faith working through love, without the practice of all the victims and sacrifices, and had held the highest place with him. No one, however, is ever found to have pleased God through holocausts and sacrifices alone, without faith and love. The scribe declared that he too held this opinion.

“Jesus said to him: ‘You shall love the Lord your God with all your heart, and with all your soul, and with all your mind. This is the greatest and first commandment. The second is like it: You shall love your neighbor as yourself. On these two commandments depend the whole law and the prophets.’”

Charity securely possesses the whole greatness and breadth of the divine utterances, by which we love the Lord and our neighbor. For the one heavenly Teacher teaches us and says: “You shall love the Lord your God with all your heart,” and so forth (Augustine).

[Col. 1171C]

If, therefore, you do not have time to search through all the sacred pages, to unfold everything in the volume of discourses as it is rolled out, or to penetrate all the secrets of Scripture, hold fast to charity, on which everything depends. Thus you will hold fast, because you have learned in this way; you will also hold fast what you have not yet learned. For if you know charity, you know something on which even that which you may happen not to know depends; and in the very matters in which you do not understand the Scriptures, charity is evident.

Charity therefore holds both what is clear and what is hidden in the divine discourses. Whoever holds charity in his conduct possesses that of which the Lord will make a shortened utterance upon the earth.

“While the Pharisees were gathered together, Jesus questioned them, saying: ‘What do you think about the Christ? Whose son is he?’ They said to him: ‘David’s.’ He said to them: ‘How then does David in the Book of Psalms call him Lord, saying: “The Lord said to my Lord: Sit at my right hand, until I place your enemies as a footstool for your feet”?’”

[Col. 1171D]

For the Lord to say “Lord” to his Lord is to beget a Son equal to himself. “My Lord,” David says, not insofar as Christ was born from him, but insofar as he has always existed from the Father. The fact that the enemies are subjected by the Father, whether willingly or unwillingly, signifies not the Son’s weakness but the unity of nature, by which one acts in the other. For the Son also subjects the enemies to the Father, because he glorifies the Father on earth.

Thus Jesus’ question benefits us against the Jews. The Jews, however, fabricate many frivolous arguments, asserting that Psalm 109 was written in the person of Eliezer, Abraham’s servant, returning from the slaughter of the five kings: “Sit at my right hand.” But the psalm’s subsequent verses do not agree with this interpretation. The objection is therefore properly directed against them, not because they confess that Christ, whom they acknowledge as destined to come, is David’s son, but because they believe him to be merely a human being and not the Son of God.

[Col. 1172A]

“If, therefore, David calls him Lord in the Spirit, how is he his son? And no one was able to answer him a word, nor did anyone dare from that day onward to question him further.”

Because they are refuted in argument, they no longer question him but openly hand him over, once seized, to Roman authority. Hence it is clear that the poisons of envy can be overcome, but that it is difficult for them to become quiet.

## On Charity

[Col. 1172C]

Holy Scripture commends to us a twofold charity: charity toward God and charity toward our neighbor. Charity toward God means loving him in such a way that we rejoice in him; charity toward our neighbor means loving him in such a way that we rejoice not in him but with him in God. That is, we love God for his own sake, but our neighbor for God’s sake.

God is to be loved for his own sake because he is our good; our neighbor is to be loved for God’s sake because, together with him, our good is in God. Let us love God so that we may come to him and rejoice in Christ; let us love this person so that we may run together with him and arrive together with him. Let us love God as joy, our neighbor as a companion in joy; God as rest, our neighbor as a sharer in rest.

What is it to love God? It is to desire to possess him. What is it to love God for his own sake? It is to love him so that you may possess him. What is it to love one’s neighbor for God’s sake? It is to love him because he possesses God.

[Col. 1172D]

Just as we love a person because of justice—that is, because he possesses justice—and just as we love a person because of wisdom—that is, because he possesses wisdom—so we love a person because of God, that is, because he possesses God. Or, if perhaps he does not yet possess him, we love him because he will possess him, as though he already did.

Thus we love for God’s sake a person whom we certainly would not love for God’s sake if we did not love God, just as when I love a person because of wisdom, I love him because I love wisdom itself; I certainly would not love that person if I did not love the wisdom itself for which I love him.

So when I love my neighbor for God’s sake, I love him because I love God. I certainly would not love him if I did not love God, for whose sake I love him. Thus, if I love rightly, I also love what is good. For I do not love rightly unless I love what is good, and I love the good that I love for no other reason than its goodness.

How is this done? A friend in God, an enemy for God’s sake. What is it to love a friend in God? It is to love him because he possesses God—not for his wealth, not for his strength, not for his beauty, but for his justice, holiness, and goodness.

[Col. 1173A]

Those qualities, although they come from God, can be loved apart from God; and often, when they are loved, they turn away and corrupt the mind that loves them, so that it does not love God. Therefore a person should be praised for these things because, when they are given, they are given by God and are his gifts. But one should not love one’s neighbor in these qualities, because they are not his virtue. Nor do such things make a person good, even if he possesses them abundantly; nor does their absence make him evil.

Goodness makes a person good, justice makes a person just, and truth makes a person truthful. When these qualities are present, God is present, because God is goodness, justice, and truth. Therefore a person is to be loved in goodness, justice, and truth; and when he is loved in these qualities, he is loved in God, because God is goodness, justice, and truth.

[Col. 1173B]

If, therefore, we love rightly, we love what is good, and we are good. Nothing makes us good except good love and love of what is good. If we are good, however, we have no friends except the good and no enemies except the wicked, because if we are good, we love nothing except what is good and hate nothing apart from what is evil.

If we have good friends and wicked enemies, we ought to love our friends in their goodness—that is, in God—because they are good. But since we cannot love our enemies in their goodness, because they are not good, we ought to love them only so that they may have goodness and become good. In all these cases, it is goodness alone that is loved, since nothing is loved except for goodness.

[Col. 1173C]

Likewise, when God is loved, he is loved for his own sake, because he comes from no other, nor is there anything other than himself that is loved in him. But when our neighbor is loved, he is not loved for his own sake but for God’s sake: one as a friend who possesses God, the other as an enemy so that he may possess God.

In all these cases, it is God alone who is loved, because what is loved in the one is nothing other than God, because God exists in him; and what is loved in the other is that God may exist in him.

Therefore, when God is loved and when our neighbor is loved, God is loved. Why, then, does Scripture say: “So that you may love both God and your neighbor” (Matt. 22)? If you love God in God and love God in your neighbor, and love nothing else in your neighbor except what you love in God, why are there two commandments of charity?

[Col. 1173D]

If God is loved in both places, one thing is fulfilled in both, and there would have been no need for the commandment to be doubled concerning one work. It would have been enough to say: Love the Lord your God; for everything is contained in this. Whoever truly loves the Lord loves everywhere. If he is truly loved, he is loved wherever he is found: in himself and in one’s neighbor, inwardly and outwardly, above and below, far and near.

If honey is sweet, the honeycomb is sweet as well. If you love honey, you also love the honeycomb, the receptacle of honey. But when honey is loved, it is loved because it is sweetness itself. When the honeycomb is loved, it is loved because sweetness is in it. Honey is loved for its own sake; the honeycomb is loved for the sake of honey.

[Col. 1174A]

And if perhaps you see a honeycomb without honey, you see the receptacles where honey ought to have been, and you grieve that they are empty. They do not please you because they are dry, and you desire that the honey you love be there; and if it comes, you love the honeycomb more.

So love your God, because he is sweetness itself, and goodness and truth. Love your neighbor because he is a receptacle of sweetness and truth. If you find in him what he ought to have—sweetness, goodness, and truth—love those qualities in him and love him for their sake.

But if you find him empty of his proper goods, grieve because you see an empty receptacle, and desire that they come to him and enter into him, so that he may become good, possessing his proper goods, without which he cannot be good.

## Division

Love God because he is goodness; love your neighbor because he is good through goodness, or, if he is not good, so that he may become one who can be good. Those who can no longer become good are not to be loved, because they are not neighbors but alien, distant, and estranged.

“Do not give your honor to strangers,” he says, “nor your years to the cruel, lest strangers be filled with your strength and your labors be in another’s house” (Prov. 5).

[Col. 1174B]

These, then, are the alien and estranged, excessively distant and removed, for whom no return to goodness remains: namely, demons and wicked human beings condemned together with demons. They are no longer to be loved by us because they have fallen irrecoverably from that good for whose sake everyone who is rightly loved is loved.

Nowhere does Scripture tell us to love demons, nor those human beings who have already been condemned together with demons. They are not neighbors but have become distant and alien to us. We, however, ought to love our neighbors, not aliens—that is, human beings, not demons—and those human beings who have either not departed from goodness or can return through the freedom of their will.

Those who, even if they have departed, can still return are not altogether far away. These are the neighbors whom we ought to love: in God, if they have departed; or for God’s sake, if they can return. When we love them, we either love God in them, if they are good, or love and desire goodness for them, since they can become what they are not—that is, good.

[Col. 1174C]

For this reason, then, there are two commandments of charity: charity toward God and charity toward one’s neighbor. Through charity toward God, you love goodness itself; through charity toward your neighbor, you do not begrudge your neighbor the good that you love.

You could love something and not love it for your neighbor; you could wish to possess something and yet not wish your neighbor to possess it. But you could not do this with God. For you could not love God unless you also loved your neighbor, since God cannot be loved together with envy and hatred.

Nevertheless, because you could do this in other matters—wish for something and not wish it for your neighbor—it has been distinguished so that you may understand that both things must be done by you, although you cannot do one without the other. Although they exist together, the love of God and of one’s neighbor are nevertheless two things. They therefore ought not to have been confused in the commandment, even though they cannot be separated in action.

There are therefore two commandments of charity: one by which we are commanded to love God; the other by which we are ordered to love our neighbor.

[Col. 1174D]

But you say: Why were three commandments of charity not given, so that a person might similarly love himself, just as he is commanded to love God and his neighbor?

Consider that it would have been superfluous to command what a person was naturally inclined to do so strongly that he could not or would not abandon it even if he were forbidden. It was therefore not necessary to command a person to love himself; rather, it was more necessary to fear and guard against his loving himself excessively.

This was indeed implanted in nature: a person could not hate himself. Thus no one has hated his own flesh. He inseparably loves the benefit that has been implanted in him by nature, and he always detests and flees what is opposed to it.

## On the Soul: Why It Is So Called; On the Name *animus*; On the Name “Mind”; and On the Name “Spirit”

[Col. 1175C]

The soul has been granted by God the innate [sic] capacity to penetrate the secrets of things and, once they have been penetrated, to disclose them through itself to the living. Hence it is considered foolish for us to be ignorant of that through which we know more things, as though it were alien to us. First, therefore, let it be explained whose soul it properly is and why it is so called.

Properly, then, the soul is said to belong to human beings, and not to animals, because the life of animals is known to consist solely in blood. Since the soul is immortal, it is rightly called *anima*, as though *anaema* [Greek: ἄναιμα], that is, “far removed from blood,” since after the body’s death its substance is evidently complete. Some say that it is called *anima* because it animates and gives life to the substance of its body. It is called *animus* because its extremely swift thought wanders with rapid movement like the wind, which arises from the soul’s appetite, stirred according to the quality of its desire.

It is called *mens* (“mind”) from *mene* [Greek: μήνη], that is, “moon,” because although it is changed by varied alternation, it nevertheless restores itself to what it was through a kind of complete renewal.

*Spiritus* (“spirit”) is also used in three ways. It is properly and truly called spirit when it needs nothing, while it itself is needed by all creatures; it breathes into whatever it wills, distributes all things as it wills, fills the universe, is wholly present in the whole, immovable in place, eternal in will, and singly powerful over all things that are highest. We also call spirit a subtle substance invisible to us, an immortal creature, useful and effective to the extent granted to it. [Col. 1176A] Third, we call spirit that which is emitted and received throughout the whole body, through which the life of mortals is sustained; it never takes rest but is renewed by continual movement.

It must therefore be understood that *animus* and *mens* are not properly called the soul. This is Cassiodorus.

Isidore, however, says as follows: “There is one soul which, while it contemplates, is spirit; while it perceives, is sense; while it understands wisely, is mind; while it understands, is intellect; while it discerns, is reason; while it assents, is will; while it remembers, is memory; while it gives vitality to the limbs, is soul.”

Therefore, according to the agreement of authoritative teachers, the human soul is a spiritual substance created by God, specifically the life-giver of its own body; it is rational and immortal, but capable of turning toward good or evil. [Col. 1176B] It is produced like an egg from which a bird is to be born, in which the pleasing variety of the future bird’s feathers is contained.

Moreover, no prudent person is unaware that souls are made or have been made by God, since whatever exists is either Creator or creature. No creature, therefore, can be a creative substance, because, in order to subsist itself, it needs God, and it cannot give another the subsistence which it has received only for itself. It remains, then, that we must most truly confess that the soul was created by the Godhead, which alone can create mortal and immortal things. For it is clearly written in Solomon: “And the dust will return to the earth as it was, and the spirit will return to him who gave it” (Ecclesiasticus XII). And elsewhere: “I have made every breath.”

What we called “the life-giver of its own body” is said for this reason: as soon as it has been given by an ineffable ordinance, [Col. 1176C] it loves its prison, loves that because of which it cannot be free, is intensely affected by its pains, and fears destruction although it cannot die. Thus it is so trembling at the collapse of its body that you might believe it, which by nature cannot perish, more ready to endure extreme suffering. Although it does not in any way feed upon bodily things, when such things are taken away it is nevertheless consumed by the deepest grief, desiring not what is naturally suited to itself but what, once joined to the limbs, will be beneficial.

The life of the body, therefore, is the presence of the soul received into it, while its death is proved to be the soul’s departure. Thus we say that it is day when the sun gives light; when the sun has departed, it is called night. The body therefore lives by the soul’s protection, and from the soul it is proved to receive the power by which it can move itself. [Col. 1176D]

It extends throughout the whole body which it animates, not by local diffusion but by a certain vital tension. For it is wholly present at once in all its parts, neither lesser in lesser parts nor greater in greater ones, but more intensely present in some places, less intensely in others; it is wholly in all and wholly in each. Although it does not perceive throughout the entire body, it perceives as a whole. For when something touches a tiny point in living flesh, even if that place is not the whole body but is scarcely visible in the body, the whole soul is nevertheless not unaware of it. Nor does what is perceived travel through all the parts of the body; it is perceived only where it occurs. How, then, does it immediately reach the whole, unless because it is wholly present where the sensation occurs? And although it is wholly there, it does not abandon the other parts. For those parts live by its presence where nothing of this kind has happened. If it did happen, and if both things happened simultaneously, the whole soul would likewise be simultaneously aware of both.

Consequently, it could not be wholly present simultaneously in all and in each of the parts of its body if it were diffused through them in the way we see bodies spread through spaces: their smaller parts occupy smaller areas and their larger parts larger areas. The soul has, in a certain way, the capacity to grasp thoughts and to express them through the flexible movement of the tongue. Placed in the body, it sees many things; without going outside itself, it looks upon various things around it. It seems to be extended everywhere, yet no division of the soul is shown to occur. It is known to move, to rise, and to fluctuate; and, as though running through a great space within itself, it wanders through itself.

It does not go out to causes, but through its own processes presents to itself what it observes by its thought: at one time what it has seen with bodily eyes, at another what it has conceived through the imaginative faculty. [Col. 1178A] Sound and complete reasoning therefore acknowledges this substance to be spiritual, because, although we know that all bodily things are contained within three dimensions—length, breadth, and depth—nothing of this kind is found in the soul.
