Furthermore, although the soul is joined to the body and weighed down by its mass, it carefully examines its opinions about things, thinks deeply about heavenly matters, investigates natural things through subtle inquiry, and desires to know lofty things about its very Creator. If it were bodily, it would certainly neither perceive nor see spiritual things through its thoughts.

## NINETEENTH SUNDAY. According to Matthew.

[Col. 1177]

[Col. 1177B] “Jesus went up into a boat, crossed over, and came into his own city” (Matthew IX).

Christ, always intending to calm the wave of the world for the Church, crosses over in the Church’s boat so that he may lead those who believe in him to the heavenly homeland by a peaceful voyage. Mark says that the Lord healed the paralytic in Capernaum (Mark II), while Matthew says, “in his own city.” The question would be more difficult to resolve if Matthew had named Nazareth. Now, then, who would doubt that Capernaum was the Lord’s city—a city which he had made his own not by being born there but by illuminating it with miracles? In comparison with foreign regions, any town of Galilee could rightly be called the Lord’s city, and especially Capernaum, which so excelled in Galilee that it was regarded as a kind of metropolis.

[Col. 1177C] “And behold, four men were carrying on a bed a man who was paralyzed, and they sought to bring him in and place him before Jesus. Since they could not find by which way they might bring him in because of the crowd, they went up onto the roof and lowered him through the tiles, with his bed, into the midst before Jesus. When he saw their faith, he said: ‘Take courage, son; your sins are forgiven you.’”

He called the paralytic whom he healed “son” not because of the man’s own faith—for he lacked understanding—but because of the faith of those who brought him, and for that reason said that his sins had been forgiven. Consider how much personal faith is worth, if the faith of others was worth so much. Therefore, whoever is weighed down by sin should bring in the Church to pray for him.

Here it is indicated that many bodily weaknesses occur because of sins. Perhaps for this reason sins are forgiven first, so that when the causes of weakness have been removed, health may be restored. Hence this paralytic is called “a man,” as though a sinner, in Luke (Luke V); and to another paralytic at the pool it is said: “Behold, you have been made well; now sin no more, lest something worse happen to you” (John V).

There are five different causes for which we are afflicted in this life by bodily hardships. Either the righteous are burdened with bodily illness in order that their merits may be increased through patience, as in the case of Job, Tobias, and the martyrs; or for the preservation of virtues, so that they may not become proud, as in the case of Paul, who says: “Lest the greatness of the revelations should exalt me, a thorn in my flesh was given to me, an angel of Satan, to buffet me” (II Corinthians XII); or for the correction of sins, as when Mary, Aaron’s sister, was struck with leprosy in the wilderness because of her rash words, and as perhaps happened with this paralytic; or for the glory of God who saves, either through himself or through his servants, as with the man born blind, who had not sinned, nor had his parents, but so that the works of God might be manifested in him (John IX); or for the beginning of eternal condemnation, which is proper to the reprobate, as in the case of Antiochus and Herod, who by the misery of their afflictions showed what they would suffer forever in Gehenna. To them the prophet’s saying applies: “Crush us with a double crushing” (Jeremiah XVII).

[Col. 1178C] “And the scribes and Pharisees began to think, saying: ‘Who is this who speaks blasphemies? Who can forgive sins except God alone?’”

The scribes speak truly, because only he can forgive who also forgives through those to whom he has granted the power of forgiving. They thought that the Lord was blaspheming by arrogating to himself what belongs to God; but by revealing their thoughts, and by a visible sign—which shows that healing is equal to divine power, just as forgiveness of sins is—he judges that he is God.

[Col. 1178D] “And when Jesus had perceived their thoughts, he answered and said to them: ‘Why are you thinking evil in your hearts? Which is easier, to say, “Your sins are forgiven,” or to say, “Rise and walk”? But so that you may know that the Son of Man has authority on earth to forgive sins,’ he then said to the paralytic: ‘I say to you: Rise, take up your bed, and go to your house.’”

Only the one who forgave knew whether the paralytic’s sins had been forgiven. But rising and walking was evident to all who saw it. A visible sign is therefore made so that the invisible may be proved. “Take up your bed,” so that what had been a testimony to illness might become proof of health.

[Col. 1179A] “But so that you may know,” and so forth, up to “he said to the paralytic”: these are the evangelist’s words, as though he were saying to the readers of the Gospel: They were murmuring about what he had said, “Your sins are forgiven”; but I tell you that he said to the paralytic, “Rise,” so that by his healing you may know that the Son of Man both then had and now has the authority to forgive sins.

Alternatively, Christ’s words may be understood in this way: You are thinking that I cannot forgive sins; but so that you may know that the Son of Man—that is, I—can do this, he says, that is, the Son of Man himself says to the paralytic: “Rise.”

[Col. 1179B] “And immediately he rose before them, took up the bed on which he had lain, and went to his house, glorifying God. And they were all filled with fear, saying that they had seen extraordinary things that day. And they glorified God, who had given such authority to human beings.”

God’s great power is displayed when salvation is accomplished at his command without delay. Therefore those who were present, rightly abandoning their blasphemies in astonishment, turn to praising such majesty. They would not have feared if they had rightly believed and loved perfectly.

The healing of the paralytic signifies the salvation of the soul that longs for Christ after the inertia of carnal enticement. At first the soul needs ministers to bring it to Christ—that is, teachers who suggest the hope of intercession. According to Mark, there were four bearers, either because the power of the preachers is strengthened by the four evangelists, or because confidence of mind is raised by four virtues in order to obtain healing. Of these it is said in praise of eternal Wisdom: “She teaches sobriety and wisdom, justice and virtue” (Wisdom VIII). Some call these prudence, fortitude, temperance, justice, and virtue.

When they desire to offer the paralytic to Christ, the crowd obstructs them, because often, after the body’s lethargy, the soul desires to be renewed by heavenly grace but is held back by its former sinful habit. Often, amid prayers and pleasant conversation with the crowd, the crowd of thoughts obstructs the mind’s vision so that Christ is not seen.

Then the roof of the house in which Christ teaches must be climbed—that is, the sublimity of Sacred Scripture must be sought, and the law of the Lord must be meditated upon day and night. When the roof has been opened, the sick man is lowered before Jesus, because once the mysteries of Scripture have been opened, one reaches knowledge of Christ. Jesus’ house is described as covered with tiles because beneath the humble covering of letters, if someone opens it, the power of spiritual grace is found.

The fact that the man is lowered with his bed signifies that Christ must be known by a person who is still established in this flesh. To rise from the bed is for the soul to withdraw itself from carnal desires. He therefore says: Rise from the torpor of negligence, and raise up the body in whose desires you lay into the exercises of good works; thus enter the house of eternal habitation. Alternatively, to go into the house means to return to the inner guardianship of oneself, so as not to sin again.

## What faith is, what the knowledge of faith is, and the three stages of each

[Col. 1180A]

Before we begin to examine what pertains to faith, we must consider what faith itself is. The Apostle defines faith as follows: “Faith is the substance of things hoped for, the proof of things not seen” (Hebrews II).

Any thing is apprehended among us either through actual presence, namely when present things are grasped by the senses; or through the intellect, when absent things—or even nonexistent things in their likeness and imagination—are grasped; or through experience, when things that are within us are perceived by us, such as joy, sadness, love, and fear. These things subsist in us and are perceived by us. But the invisible things of God are apprehended by none of these methods; they are believed by us alone. [Col. 1180B] They are not present to us through actual perception, nor can they be grasped in any likeness, nor are they apprehended in the way that those things within us are perceived by us.

They therefore subsist in us through faith alone, and their subsistence is the faith by which they are believed to exist, although what they are cannot be comprehended. Thus they subsist in us through faith alone and are proved by us through faith alone; we can have no other proof except that we believe them by that faith through which we do not comprehend them by reason.

The description of faith does not show what faith does; nor is it defined there what faith is. The definition of faith, however, is this: Faith is a certain voluntary certainty concerning absent things, situated above opinion and below knowledge.

It must be understood that the knowledge of faith is one thing and faith another. When a speech is delivered to the ears of many, all understand equally what is said, but they do not all believe equally. All possess knowledge of what has been said, but not all possess faith.

The knowledge of faith can exist without any faith at all; faith, however, cannot exist without any knowledge. Many believe without possessing knowledge of everything they believe, because they believe those who believe and know, while they themselves do not know everything they believe; rather, those to whom they give their belief know it.

Such is the faith of the simple in the Church: by believing and adhering to those who are more perfect, they are saved, as it is written: “The oxen were plowing, and the donkeys were feeding beside them” (Job I). These people believe more fully in the faith of the perfect; by believing, they know less of it within themselves.

Faith grows in two ways: through devotion or steadfastness, and through knowledge. The growth of faith through devotion proceeds through three stages. The first stage is acquiescence; the second arises from fear; the third stage is certainty.

Corresponding to these three stages, there are three kinds of people who follow the faith. There is one kind of person in the holy Church for whom believing means only not contradicting the faith. They live as they were born to live—not loving but approving what they were born into. If they had been born into something else, they would not be believers. They hold the faith by custom of life, not by love.

There is another kind of person who considers more attentively that the state of human life is uncertain, and therefore begins in a certain way to waver in faith. They see many people turned away from and alienated from the faith; nevertheless, led by devotion to the faith, they choose between two uncertainties what they have learned from Catholic teaching. For these people peace is necessary and tribulation dangerous, lest, when endangered, they become deniers.

There is yet another kind of person who is certain and confirmed in his faith. God has confirmed such people either through external miracles or has taught them through inner inspiration. They are not overturned by tribulation but are exercised by it.

It must also be understood that, just as there are three stages by which faith grows, so there are three stages by which the knowledge of faith grows. The first stage of the knowledge of faith, below which faith could never descend, is to believe that God exists and to await him as savior and rewarder. This knowledge of faith could suffice for the salvation of simple people before the Lord’s incarnation: they believed in God and awaited the Savior, although they did not know the manner or time of their salvation.

There are only two things in a human being: nature and guilt. The Creator relates to nature, and the Savior to guilt.

Under the written Law, knowledge increased when the person of the Redeemer began to be discussed openly, the Savior began to be promised through the Law, and after the promise began to be awaited. Under grace, knowledge increased still further, when the Savior himself was manifested not merely as a human being, as many had previously thought, but also as true God; and when the manner of redemption itself was shown to consist not in the height of earthly power but in the Savior’s death.

## On the remission of sins, and whether priests can forgive sins

Some people have tried to attribute the power of forgiving sins to God alone in such a way that they absolutely refuse to allow human beings any participation in it. To support this assertion they cite the cleansing of the leper, whom the Lord first restored to health by himself, and then sent to the priests—not so that his cleansing might be completed through their power, but merely so that it might be confirmed by their testimony (Luke V).

In the same way, in the present Church they say that the ministry of priests has no greater power than to be certain signs: namely, that the person who has first been absolved inwardly by the Lord through contrition of heart is afterwards shown in confession to have been absolved by them.

They wish to prove that sins are forgiven through contrition of heart alone, even before oral confession, by the prophetic testimony: “At whatever hour the sinner shall groan, he shall be saved” (Ezekiel XVIII); and elsewhere: “While you are still speaking, I will say, ‘Behold, here I am’” (Isaiah LXV). The Psalmist also says: “I said, ‘I will confess my iniquity against myself to the Lord,’ and you forgave the wickedness of my sin” (Psalm XXXI).

Oral confession is nevertheless necessary after contrition of heart because, if someone neglects to confess the same sins even after obtaining forgiveness, he will be guilty as a despiser of divine institution. Although he is not held guilty on account of the sins that have already been forgiven, he will nevertheless be guilty on account of contempt. Or perhaps the sins themselves return to the contumacious person, although they had previously been forgiven when he was humbled through remorse.

By this reasoning, people prove that priests have no power at all to forgive sins, but that this power belongs to God alone. So also, in the Gospel, the Jews murmured against the Lord because he said to the paralytic, “Your sins are forgiven,” and declared that God alone could forgive sins (Matthew IX).

But perhaps those who say this about the absolution of sins do not carefully consider how anyone is bound by sin. A sinner is bound in two ways: he is bound by hardness of mind, and he is bound by the debt of future condemnation.

As long as God’s grace remains with a person, he is free and prepared for good works. But when God’s grace is withdrawn because of sin, the mind is immediately bound inwardly by its own hardness. This hardness or blindness of mind is the inner darkness in which a person is held bound in the present because of his sin; and unless he is freed from it in this life, he is afterwards cast, with hands and feet bound, into the outer darkness.

But because no one could rise by his own power after the fall of sin, unless divine mercy, freely going before him, raised him up, it is therefore necessary that God, when we are to be brought to life for repentance, should by mercy alone, without any preceding merits of ours, restore the grace which he had justly withdrawn from us sinners. Thus the grace that comes may awaken our heart from the torpor of unbelief and from the death of sin.

In this way, those who, through grace alone working first, are pierced with repentance and freed from the bonds of torpor may, through that same grace cooperating afterwards, deserve to be freed as penitents from the debt of condemnation.

This was well signified in the raising of Lazarus. The Lord himself first freed him inwardly from the bond of death and gave him life; then, when he commanded him to be unbound, he caused him to be released outwardly through the ministry of the apostles (John XI).

So now in the holy Church, by his grace alone, he inwardly gives life to those dead through sins, kindles them to repentance, and commands those who have been given life to come forth through confession. Then, through the ministry of priests, he absolves those who confess from the outward bond, that is, from the debt of condemnation.

The debt of condemnation is rightly called an outward bond, because whoever has not deserved to be freed in this life from the inner darkness is immediately consigned to the outer darkness, which he was not worthy to escape.

“But,” they say, “you are acting wrongly toward the priest of the Lord by attributing to him the power of forgiving sins, which belongs to God alone” (Mark II).

I do not make priests gods. The divine word, which cannot lie, calls priests gods: “You shall not revile the gods, nor curse the ruler of your people” (Exodus XXII). These people, contrary to the commandment of the Law, revile gods because they wish to take away from priests the power divinely bestowed upon them.

Nor, in truth, do I attribute the power of forgiving sins to priests. He attributes divine power to human beings who makes gods from human beings. Yet just as God is God from himself, so he can also, whenever he wills, forgive sins by himself without human cooperation.

But those who are not gods from themselves cannot forgive sins unless the one from whom they have what they are works in them and through them, and cooperates with them. God alone is good; yet it does not follow that those who serve the Lord are not also good. God alone performs miracles (Psalm LXXI); yet it is said of a righteous person: “For he performed miracles in his life” (Ecclesiasticus XXXI).

So also God alone forgives sins, even when priests forgive them from him and through him. For he himself does in a human being what the human being does through him. Nor should one say that a human being does nothing there because God does it through him. Rather, he does it much better and much more truly precisely because God does it through him.

Hence he says to Peter, the chief of the apostles: “I will give you the keys of the kingdom of heaven. Whatever you bind on earth will be bound also in heaven, and whatever you loose on earth will be loosed also in heaven” (Matthew XVI).

He did not say, “Whatever you loose”—that is, as they claim, “whatever you show to have been loosed”—“will have been loosed”; rather, he said, “will be loosed,” because the sentence of heaven does not precede Peter’s sentence but follows it.

And lest you think that this was granted to Peter alone, hear what he says to all the apostles, and therefore to all the successors of the apostles and those who act in the place of the apostles: “Receive,” he says, “the Holy Spirit. Whose sins you forgive, they are forgiven; and whose sins you retain, they are retained” (John XX).

Where does he say, “If you show that they have been forgiven, they will have been forgiven”? He never says this. Rather, he says: “If you do it, it will be done.”

Let them therefore hear and understand: “Whose sins you forgive, they are forgiven.” Before this was said to them, they had first been told: “Receive the Holy Spirit” (ibid.), so that what was being given would not be thought contemptible, or what those who received it did would be considered to proceed from human power.

It is therefore no wonder that human beings can forgive sins, because, in order to do this, they receive power not from themselves but from divine power. For God’s giving this to human beings means nothing other than that God does this through human beings.

As for what they object concerning the cleansing of the leper, it contributes nothing to their objection. For if a sinner is to be believed absolved before confession because the leper was cleansed before being shown to the priests, then by the same reasoning a sinner, after contrition, should not go to a priest to mourn his sin but to display his righteousness, since the leper too was sent to the priests not to receive health but to display it. The Christian faith utterly rejects this conclusion.

Therefore, if the miracle performed by the Lord is presented to priests not out of reverence for their office but as an insult, what else is produced than contempt for the new priesthood in spiritual healing?

## DIVISION

[Col. 1184A]

It must also be noted that it says: “At whatever hour the sinner shall groan, he shall be saved” (Ezekiel XVIII). I think this was said especially of those who spend their entire lives in sins, repent at the end, and abandon their sins only when they can no longer have time in this life to make satisfaction.

They are told this so that they may not despair in any way of forgiveness: even then, if they truly repent, they can obtain mercy. “At whatever hour” means even at the end, even at the moment of necessity. If the sinner groans—that is, if he turns with complete contrition of heart—he will be saved, namely, from eternal condemnation.

It is as though it were said in other words: Whenever in the present life a sinner truly repents, he will not perish in the future life.

If someone argues that the phrase “he will be saved” was not said of the salvation granted in the future but rather of that which is bestowed in the present through the absolution of sins, we are nevertheless not required to say that the sinner is absolved from his entire debt immediately upon beginning to groan, before he has obtained the whole remedy that God established for obtaining forgiveness.

This remedy is that he should repent in his heart and confess his sin with his mouth. When he has done this, he will no longer be a debtor liable to condemnation, even if satisfaction still remains for him to perform on account of his sin.

If perhaps a sinner truly repents but, because the moment of necessity intervenes, cannot come to confession, I confidently declare that the supreme Priest completes in him what the mortal priest could not. Before God it is already accomplished: the person truly wished to do what he was unable to complete, because necessity prevented confession, not contempt for it.

Therefore, if the saying “At whatever hour the sinner shall groan, he will be saved” is understood of present salvation, it must be understood as though it said: The sinner’s salvation begins when he truly groans over his offenses; yet that salvation is fully completed when he also confesses with his mouth what caused him to groan.

Likewise, the saying, “While you are still speaking, I will say, ‘Behold, here I am’” (Isaiah LXV), can suitably be understood in this way: God is present in mercy to pierce the heart with repentance; then he is present to grant forgiveness of sins to the one who confesses.

[Col. 1184D]

Finally, concerning the objection drawn from the Psalm—“I said, ‘I will confess my iniquity against myself to the Lord,’ and you forgave the wickedness of my sin” (Psalm XXXI)—Saint Gregory asserted that this refers only to the guilt of thought, in these words:

“Often the merciful God washes away the sins of the heart more quickly because he does not allow them to pass into deeds. Hence the Psalmist rightly says: ‘I said, “I will confess my iniquity against myself to the Lord”; and you forgave the wickedness of my sin.’ A little later he shows how easy forgiveness is in this matter: while he still permits himself to ask, he obtains what he permitted himself to ask. Thus, because the guilt had not proceeded as far as action, repentance did not proceed as far as punishment; rather, the distress conceived in thought cleansed the mind which iniquity conceived in thought alone had defiled.”

If someone wishes to understand this of any sin whatsoever, he should nevertheless know that sin is one thing and the wickedness of sin another. The wickedness of sin is most correctly understood as the hardness of heart itself. This is first dissolved in repentance, so that afterwards, in confession, the sin itself—that is, the debt of condemnation—may be absolved.

But whether the foregoing authorities are explained in this way or in any other, we most truly confess that the priests of God in the Church possess the power of binding and loosing. This power is not merely signified through some unusual manner of speaking; it is truly granted by God to those to whom it was said: “Whose sins you forgive, they are forgiven; and whose sins you retain, they are retained” (John XX).

But perhaps someone will object that priests bind many in the Church who are not bound before God, and likewise absolve many who remain bound before God. They often bind the innocent and absolve those who remain guilty; thus the statement “Whose sins you forgive, they will be forgiven, and whose sins you retain, they will be retained” would not be true.

It must be understood, however, that Sacred Scripture often speaks about something in such a way that it seems to predict what will result from it, while expressing its power more than its outcome. It shows not what must happen but what can happen.

For example, Scripture says in one place: “Whoever believes and is baptized will be saved” (Mark XVI). Yet we know that many believers receive baptism but later, because their sins demand it, are rejected and do not attain eternal salvation.

Likewise, in another place: “Whoever eats my flesh and drinks my blood has eternal life, and will not come into judgment, but passes from death to life” (John VI). Yet Paul says: “Whoever presumes to eat the Lord’s body and drink the cup unworthily eats and drinks judgment upon himself” (I Corinthians XI).

Everywhere, therefore, the power of the sacraments is expressed, not to indicate that all who partake of them will be saved, but that they can be saved through them. It is as though it were said: Such is the power of baptism that whoever receives it faithfully and devoutly can attain eternal salvation through it.

Likewise, such is the power in the reception of my body and blood that whoever receives it worthily can obtain eternal life through it.

In the same way, I think this saying should be understood: “Whose sins you forgive, they are forgiven; and whose sins you retain, they are retained.” It is as though it were said more explicitly: I grant you such power in binding and loosing sins that whoever deserves to be bound by you cannot be loosed before me, and whoever deserves to be loosed by you is no longer bound before me.

Let people hear and understand what protection God grants sinners and what judgment he prepares in turn. Perhaps they do not yet dare to appeal to God. They have priests acting in God’s place, with whom they can meanwhile conduct their case without danger. Let them love their intercessors and fear their judges.

## DIVISION
The question is raised by some people: why does God need to seek human collaborators for forgiving human sins, as though he were unable by himself to accomplish whatever he willed? But we must know with complete certainty that, in the absolution of sins, human cooperation in no way assists God. He nevertheless makes a human being his collaborator because in this way the sinner’s salvation is more suitably accomplished.

For what are sins except certain wounds? And what is repentance except medicine? We know, moreover, that in healing wounds of the flesh, unless an appropriate remedy is applied to the pain, the result of healing by no means follows. Since, therefore, every sin is committed through pride, it is necessary that every repentance be formed through humility, so that obedience may break disobedience and the devotion of humility suppress the swelling of arrogance.

It is therefore highly appropriate that we who, by sinning, were defiant toward God should, by repenting, also be suppliants before God’s servants; and that the human being who did not need a mediator in order to preserve God’s grace should now be able to recover it only through a human mediator. This too is most beneficial for the sinner: that he learn how far he has withdrawn from God by sinning. When he returns to God with difficulty through repentance, he is thereafter made more cautious, since the way to pardon is opened to the penitent only through serious labor.

Let the sinner therefore groan and sigh; let him fear and tremble anxiously on account of his sin; let him run about solicitously seeking helpers and intercessors. Let the human being who refused humbly to stand before the Creator now humbly prostrate himself before a human being, so that by this very act he may in a certain way cry out to God and say:

“See, Lord, consider and observe what I am doing. I know, Lord, and I confess that my proud refusal to submit to you was damnable; but now, for your sake, may this devotion of prostrating myself before a human being not be contemptible to you, I beg. Great is what I took away, and not insignificant is what I am giving back.”

O how gentle and delightful is the mercy of our God! He himself works all our good within us and, like a father playing with his children, does everything in such a way that he seems to do almost nothing.

Look: the repentant sinner is pierced with compunction; he groans, sighs, and weeps; he confesses his guilt, asks pardon, and implores mercy. All this is believed to come, as it were, from the human being. But who, I ask, does this except the one who presides within and moves the human heart to do it?

I ask that it not be burdensome if I set forth a brief example of this matter:

A certain father expelled a defiant son with great fury, so that, afflicted in this way, he might learn to humble himself. But when the son persisted in his defiance, the father, through a carefully devised arrangement, sent the mother to him. She came not as one sent by the father, but as though moved by maternal affection alone, and with feminine gentleness soothed the obstinate son and bent the defiant one toward humility. She told him that his father was exceedingly angry, nevertheless promised that she would intervene, assured him of pardon, offered him salutary advice, urged him to seek intercessors, and said that his father could be appeased only by great entreaties. Yet she declared that she would undertake the matter herself and promised to bring the whole affair to a good conclusion.

Consider, I ask, whether our situation is not handled in just this way. God the Father, as though angry, expelled the sinful son, although perhaps he was never angry with him in the purpose of his good will. But because human weakness cannot rise by itself from its fall, marvelous grace is sent into the sinner’s heart, and a priest is sought as intercessor, so that God, who had not been angry, may be appeased.

What shall I say? “Who is wise and will understand these things, and will keep the mercies of the Lord?” (Psalm 106).

Was what happened done in vain because God was not changed from angry to propitious, since he is never not propitious toward his own? Far from it! But it is necessary that this happen in this way, because otherwise the guilt of the deserved crime cannot be expiated. It is necessary that this happen in this way because God commands that even what he desires to give be requested from him. It is necessary that this happen in this way because, although in God there was no anger toward us in accordance with his purpose, anger nevertheless remained in us in accordance with our guilt. When this is removed through due satisfaction, so to speak, it is not God who is reconciled to the human being, but the human being who is reconciled to God.

## THE TWENTIETH SUNDAY. According to Matthew

[Column 1187]

> “Jesus was speaking with his disciples in parables, saying: ‘The kingdom of heaven has become like a king who made a wedding feast for his son,’” and so forth (Matthew 22).

They hear in parables what they did not deserve to hear openly. Although the Lord knew the will of those raging against him, he nevertheless rebuked them.

This king is God the Father, who made a wedding feast for his son when he joined him to human nature in the Virgin’s womb. This union arose from two natures, not from two persons. It may be stated more clearly: the wedding is the union of Christ and the Church, gathered both from the Jews and from the Gentiles. The bridal chamber of this Bridegroom was the Virgin’s womb.

The congregation of the righteous is called the kingdom of heaven because heavenly powers reign within it. It resembles God the Father in this respect: just as he joined the Church to his Son, so that congregation joins to the Church of the faithful, through the sacraments of faith, the children whom it begets for God through the word of preaching.

> “And he invited many, and at the hour of supper he sent his servants to call those who had been invited to the wedding, and they did not wish to come.”

Luke describes under the designation “supper” (Luke 14) what Matthew says was “dinner,” since among the ancients dinner was taken daily at the ninth hour and was called supper. Dinner, or supper, is the teaching of righteousness and the divine words.

Manna, which prefigured the word, was called manna in the wilderness (Exodus 16) because in Hebrew it means “What is this?”—so that whenever we hear the word, its very name may remind us to ask: “What is this that we are hearing?” And just as, after chewing food, we send it down into the stomach, so a word that has been properly considered ought to be entrusted to memory as to a stomach.

The invitation occurred when the Lord said to Abraham:

> “Go out from your land and from your kindred, and come into the land that I will show you, and I will give it to you and to your offspring” (Genesis 13).

What land? The eastern land, flowing with milk and honey. This is not literally true of the land of Judaea. It never flowed with milk and honey. Rather, it is the rational land that Christ assumed, from whose incarnation milk and honey proceeded.

Milk means the working of miracles, by which the inexperienced are nourished like children; honey means the eloquence of teaching, as the Prophet says:

> “How sweet are your words to my throat, more than honey and the honeycomb to my mouth” (Psalm 118).

It was therefore rightly said to Abraham, “Go out from your land and from your kindred”: one must understand that whoever wishes to be saved must go out from Judaism and from circumcision. Not only Jews, but no human being can eat God’s milk and honey unless he leaves his land and his kindred, as in the saying:

> “Unless someone leaves father and mother, and so forth, he cannot be my disciple” (Luke 14).

Likewise:

> “Whoever wishes to be my disciple, let him deny himself” (Luke 9).

A person leaves his kindred not by despising it, but by loving God more than his parents. He leaves his land when he does not follow the pleasure of his flesh.

This banquet began to be prepared from the time of Moses, when the law was given. The banquet was adorned with various forms of righteousness just as a royal dinner is decorated with various foods. From that same time the inviters went forth—that is, the prophets.

> “Again he sent other servants, saying: ‘Tell those who have been invited: Behold, I have prepared my dinner; my bulls and fattened animals have been slaughtered, and everything is ready. Come to the wedding.’”

The first servants were the prophets who foretold the incarnation; the second are the apostles, who assert what has happened. Hence the dinner is said here to be prepared: that is, the mystery of the incarnation has been completed, and entrance into the kingdom, which had previously been closed, has been opened.

The slaughtered bulls and fattened animals are understood as the saints who were killed. All the prophets, and Christ, were killed so that this spiritual tabernacle might be firmly established. For just as people did not eat the inner parts of the lamb—that is, Christ’s words—until he had been killed, but preached the Gospels after his death, so the inner parts—that is, the words—of the prophets were not received until after they had been killed.

If they had received Isaiah’s words, they would never have sawn him apart; but after he was killed, the Jews began to mourn him. Just as the inner parts of no living animal are eaten, so no one received the words of the living prophets.

The fattened animals are those filled with the grace of God. He did not say “bulls and fattened animals” because the bulls were fattened, but because not all the fattened animals were bulls. Some were prophets only; others were both prophets and priests, such as Jeremiah and Ezekiel. Thus by “fattened animals” he means the prophets alone, because they were filled with the Holy Spirit; by “bulls,” those who were both prophets and priests. For just as bulls are leaders of the herd, so priests are rulers of the people.

Alternatively: the bulls are the Fathers of the Old Testament, who, by the permission of the law, struck back at their enemies as though with the horns of their strength. The fattened animals signify the Fathers of the New Testament, bearing evangelical commandments and, through the grace of the eternal richness they received, fattened and lifted on the wings of holy contemplation to higher things; thus we call birds fattened animals, from the word meaning “to nourish.”

Notice that in the first invitation nothing is said about bulls and fattened animals, but in the second invitation it is, because when we are unwilling to hear his words, God adds examples.

“Everything,” he says, “is ready,” because whatever is sought for salvation has already been fulfilled in the Scriptures. The ignorant person will find there what he ought to learn; the defiant and sinful person will find there the scourges of the future judgment. All kinds of food, for both the small and the great, are found in the Scriptures.

> “But they disregarded it and went away, one to his own farm, another to his business.”

He did not say, “They acted wickedly,” but “They disregarded it,” because not all Jews crucified Christ or consented to his death.

Every human activity is of two kinds: either a farm or a business. By the farm is understood every earthly work, whether in a field, a vineyard, ironwork, or anything accomplished by the labor of the hands. Whatever we obtain through the labor of our hands, but also through other profits—such as remaining in positions of honor, serving in the army, or engaging in commerce—is all called business.

Thus in two words he included every human activity, whether honorable, such as cultivation of the farm—for Solomon says, “Do not hate agricultural work” (Ecclesiasticus 7)—or dishonorable, such as the business of office, military service, or commerce. Previously the Jews possessed none of these things.

But perhaps you say: “Is cultivating a farm a sin, because it is an impediment?” Cultivating a farm is not a sin; you make it a sin by preferring it to God.

Or understand it this way: the farm is this world, around which lovers of the world are occupied; the business is the preaching of the law and the administration of the Temple, which the greedy priests and the other ministers of the Temple regard as a business.

It follows:

> “But the others seized his servants, treated them with contempt, and killed them.”

He says nothing about his own death, because he had spoken of it in the preceding parable; here he shows the death of his disciples, whom the Jews killed after his ascension.

> “But when the king saw it, he was angry, and sent his armies, destroyed those murderers, and burned their city.”

Those who killed the king’s servants are charged with a great crime. When the time of vengeance arrives, the man is no longer mentioned, and only the king is named.

By “armies” he means either evil angels or the Romans under Vespasian and Titus. Through them he destroyed the Jews and burned the treacherous city.

Or understand it this way: by “armies” he means the holy angels through whom he will exercise judgment. He will destroy the persecutors and burn the city—that is, the flesh in which they had dwelt with their souls—in Gehenna.

> “Then he said to his servants: ‘The wedding is indeed ready, but those who had been invited were not worthy. Go therefore to the outlets of the roads, and invite to the wedding everyone whom you find.’”

If in sacred Scripture we understand roads as actions, we understand the outlets of the roads as the failures of actions, because those whom no prosperity accompanies in earthly activities usually come easily to the Lord.

> “And his servants went out into the roads and gathered everyone whom they found, both bad and good, and the wedding feast was filled with those reclining at table.”

By “bad and good” it is openly shown that the Church is signified by the wedding. It now receives people without distinction, but later separates them at the departure. The wicked are mingled with the good, because the sword of the soul is never brought to the refinement of a sharp edge unless it has been scraped by the file of another’s depravity. The good must tolerate the wicked, just as in Noah’s ark there were various kinds of animals, and in the granary there are grains together with chaff.

> “But the king entered to see those reclining at table. And he saw there a man not dressed in a wedding garment, and he said to him: ‘Friend, how did you enter here without having a wedding garment?’”

The king—that is, God—entered, not because he is not everywhere, but because he is said to be present wherever he wishes to look; where he does not wish to look, he is said to be absent.

He entered “to see,” that is, to make the merits of each person visible. Here he speaks of the future through past tenses.

The day of inspection is the day of judgment, when he will visit Christians who recline at the table of the Scriptures—that is, who rest there—and are filled with heavenly teachings.

Understand the wedding garment as the Lord’s commandments. If, therefore, at the time of judgment someone is found wearing, under the name of Christian, the cast-off garments of the old person, he will hear:

> “Friend, how did you enter here?”

He calls him “friend” because he had been invited.

Further: the wedding garment is charity, which every baptized person ought to possess. It is contained in two commandments, namely love of God and of one’s neighbor, just as a garment is woven from two pieces of wood, an upper and a lower one.

“Friend,” he says, as though he were openly saying: “Friend, and not friend: friend through faith, but not friend through conduct.”

But he was speechless. Here we conceal our deeds and hide our hearts. But on that day, when the sun and moon and the whole world stand against us as testimony to our sins, and even if everything else is silent, our thoughts themselves and our deeds in particular will stand before our eyes before God, as the Apostle says:

> “Their thoughts accusing or even defending one another on the day when the Lord will judge the hidden things of human beings through Jesus Christ” (Romans 2).

> “Then the king said to the attendants: ‘Bind his hands and feet and cast him into the outer darkness, where there will be weeping and the gnashing of teeth.’”

Understand the bound hands and feet, the weeping of the eyes, and the gnashing of the teeth either as confirming the truth of the resurrection, or certainly as signifying that the hands and feet are bound so that they may cease from evil works and from running to shed blood.

What is now voluntarily bound in vice will then be bound in punishment through suffering. In the weeping of the eyes and the gnashing of the teeth, the magnitude of the torments is shown metaphorically through bodily limbs.

The outer darkness is the final darkness, that is, the eternal night of condemnation, because the inner darkness is blindness of heart. By the rejection of one wicked person, the whole body of the wicked is expressed, and a general sentence is imposed.

> “For many are called, but few are chosen.”

What he says amounts to this: not merely one of those who were called was cast out from the wedding, but this must be understood of many. We now partake of the feasts of the divine word, but on the day of judgment the king will enter and distinguish us.

Alternatively: because he did not say, “The king entered to reward,” but “to see,” it may be suspected that this should not perhaps be understood of the vengeance of judgment. For he did not say, “Cast him into the lower darkness,” that is, into the lower regions of hell. Hence elsewhere:

> “And you rescued my soul from the lowest hell” (Psalm 85).

Rather, he said “outer.” According to this interpretation, therefore, the day of inspection is the day of testing, when he deigns to test his Church in order to see who has faith and works.

Whenever he tests the Church, he enters it to see who are worthy of the heavenly wedding. If he then finds someone unworthy, he questions him. Since human simplicity has difficulty recognizing the deceitfulness of a simulated mind, God alone finds this person unworthy of the wedding assembly.

The wedding garment is true faith. Hence the Apostle says:

> “Strip off the old person with his deeds, and put on the new person, who has been created according to God in the righteousness and holiness of truth” (Colossians 3).

“Righteousness” pertains to a good conversion; “the holiness of truth” pertains to true faith.

The questioning takes place in the thoughts of the impious person, as though he were saying: “Why did you become a Christian? Your works are not those of a Christian.”

This is what happens when God sees that someone has nothing to answer to his conscience: he hands him over to spirits of deception. For he repays evil through evil ministers. They bind his hands—that is, his works of uprightness—and his feet—that is, the movements of the soul by which it proceeds, not from place to place, but from evil to good and from good to evil—so that in this way he may fall into the snare of perdition.

And so he is cast into the outer darkness, whether of the Gentiles, the Jews, or the heretics. Perhaps the darkness of the Gentiles who despise a truth they have not heard is nearer; the darkness of the Jews who did not believe is more exterior; and the darkness of the heretics who learned the truth is most exterior.

Now they are cast into the outer darkness; afterward they will suffer weeping and the gnashing of teeth.

## Explanation of the Same Passage

> “Blessed are those who hear the word of God and keep it!” (Luke 11).

Many, beloved, do not even wish to hear the word of God with the bodily ear. Most do hear it with the ear, but are not blessed at all because they do not love it in practice. Those who hear it with attentive ears, keep it with focused hearts, and strive to fulfill it through devoted works are blessed, because they will rejoice eternally with the word of God.

The same Word reports today in the Gospel that a certain king made a wedding feast for his son. He sent his servants to call those who had been invited, but they did not wish to come. Again he sent others, commanding them to say to those who had been invited that the dinner was prepared, the bulls and fattened animals had been slaughtered, and everything was ready.

But they, disregarding the invitation, went away, one to his farm and another to his business. Others seized the servants, treated them with contempt, and killed them. The king destroyed these people after sending his armies and burned their city. Then he sent servants to the outlets of the roads and ordered everyone they found to be summoned.

After the wedding feast of those reclining at table had been filled, the king entered and saw that a certain man did not have a garment suitable for the wedding guests. He ordered him to be thrown, with hands and feet bound, into the outer darkness, where there would be weeping and the gnashing of teeth. He also said that many are called but few are chosen (Matthew 22).

The king who made the wedding feast for his son is God the Father, who joined the Church as a bride to his Son Jesus Christ. The bridal chamber of this wedding was the womb of the holy Virgin.

The servants who called those who had been invited were the prophets, who foretold to the Jews through the patriarchs that Christ would become incarnate. Those who did not wish to come were the people who did not believe the prophets.

The servants sent a second time were the apostles, who throughout Judaea preached that Christ had become incarnate for us. The prepared dinner was the fattened calf—that is, the body already offered for us.

The fierce bulls were tyrants who subdued all the kingdoms of the world. The fattened birds were philosophers, who, by investigating everything, flew in their minds as far as the stars of heaven.

These were slain when the wisdom of God had trampled the necks of the proud and lofty, had chosen humble and poor parents, rejected the wisdom of the prudent, and appointed ignorant and simple people to preach.

Everything was ready because all that pertains to salvation had been proclaimed. Scripture had been opened to everyone, and baptism and repentance were accessible to all.

But they, neglecting salvation, did not wish to come to the Lord’s wedding. Instead, one went to his farm and another to his business, because they thirsted only for earthly profits and therefore could not love heavenly things.

The others treated the king’s servants with contempt and killed them, because the Pharisees and chief priests afflicted the apostles with imprisonment, chains, and beatings; they killed some of them and drove others from their territories with insults.

> “But the king destroyed those murderers after sending his armies and burned their city,”

when, at God’s command, Roman rulers entered Judaea with their armies, killed the murderous Jews through various punishments, and burned the city of Jerusalem with fire.

Then the servants are directed to the outlets of the roads and commanded to call everyone, because, when the Jews refuse to come to God’s wedding, the apostles go out onto the road of the Gentiles and invite idolaters to God’s feasts.

They gathered good and bad because they brought many reprobates to faith together with the elect. The wedding feast of those reclining at table is filled when the number of the elect is completed.

The king will enter to see those reclining at table when he comes to judgment to distinguish all according to their merits, as it is written:

> “The Lord will come to judgment with every despised person,”

that is, he will judge the most despised person in this world as carefully as the one most outstanding in every glory.

The man who is not dressed in a wedding garment is cast outside because the one lacking love of God will not be admitted to the wedding of him who is charity. The wedding garment is charity, through which eternal glory is attained.

There the hands and feet of sinners will be bound with the cords of sins, just as here they are fettered by wicked works. The limbs that are loosened here for evil will there be constricted for punishment.

Those who now delightfully suffer inner darkness are cast into outer darkness. There will be weeping and the gnashing of teeth because they will pass from waters of snow to excessive heat (Job 24). From the smoke of fire they suffer weeping, and from excessive cold they suffer the gnashing of teeth.

> “For many are called, but few are chosen,”

because many are called to faith, but only the elect are saved.

There are two callings, one outward and the other inward. Through the outward calling, many were called to faith by the apostles and preachers; through the inward calling, a few were drawn through the Son to the Father.

Through the outward calling, many fish clung to the net of faith, but the electors later cast them out; through the inward calling, a few remained hidden, and these they chose for the vessels.

At present the reprobate are mixed with the elect like chaff with grain. But when Christ comes with the winnowing fan, the chaff will be shaken out and handed over to unquenchable fire, while the grain will be gathered into God’s granary.

And we, dearly beloved, have been called with many to God’s wedding. Let us strive through good works to be chosen with the few. Dinner is prepared for us every day when sacred Scripture, together with the body of Christ, is set before us.

Bulls were slaughtered for this banquet because the apostles, the bulls of the Lord’s herd, fell dead for the invitation to these feasts. Fattened birds were also slaughtered for this banquet because all who, flying upward in mind toward heavenly things, were struck down for the sake of these feasts, were offered in sacrifice.

The bulls were also persecutors, who winnowed the faithful with the horns of cruelty, but were already deprived of strength when Christ came.

The flying creatures were heretics, who in a certain way flew to lofty things when they set their mouths in heaven and spoke wickedness against God on high; but they were defeated and destroyed by Catholics.

And because all these things have been subdued through Christ’s power, everything has been prepared for our salvation. Therefore, let us not, on account of any business, fail to hasten with all speed to God’s feasts. God’s banquet is the joy of everlasting life. Whoever strives to fulfill God’s commandments runs toward it.

We who were called to the wedding from the outlets of the roads are already reclining at table, because we have come together from various errors to the Lord’s sacraments. Therefore, dearly beloved, let us shine in the wedding garment, loving God above all things and our neighbors as ourselves.

If the king, when he enters, does not find someone wearing this garment, he will order him to be bound and cast from the banquet into the infernal darkness. The cities of those by whom the servants sent are insulted and killed are burned when those people themselves are destroyed, because they are permitted to be destroyed by demons—demons by whom preachers are afflicted here with insults and whose bodies are finally burned in unquenchable fire.

King Solomon wove a sweet epithalamium for this wedding when, through the Spirit, he sang the Song of Songs in praise of the Bridegroom and the Bride.

The son of the king of Jerusalem betrothed to himself the daughter of the king of Babylon, accepted her, and handed her over to be instructed and adorned under the care of a guardian. He himself went away to prepare the banquet, since, returning again with immense equipment and the greatest splendor, he would bring her, installed, with him into the bridal chamber for the wedding. He would lead her adorners into the palace, but hand her corrupters over to the punishment of prison.

The king of Jerusalem is God, whose son is Christ. The king of Babylon is the devil. The Gentile world was his daughter, since it was devoted to idolatry.

Christ betrothed her to himself from the Father when, shedding his blood for her, he triumphed over the devil on the cross. He handed her over to a guardian when he entrusted her to the order of teachers to be instructed in the divine law and adorned with the jewels of the virtues.

He himself went away to prepare the banquet, because he ascended into heaven to prepare a suitable place for her in his Father’s house through its many dwelling places.

He will return with the army of all the angels, rescue her from the exile of her Babylonian pilgrimage, and introduce her amid the greatest rejoicing into the glorious Jerusalem of his Father.

Then her adorners will enter together, because those who have instructed the Church here through writings or words and adorned her with good examples will then shine with her like the sun at the wedding of the Lamb.

But the persecutors who tore her apart and inflicted violence upon her, and the heretics and schismatics who corrupted her, will then be cast into the lake of fire and sulfur and burn forever.

So that we may not be deprived of this banquet, the Lord instructs us through various teachings. For he tells how someone had a fig tree in his vineyard and, coming for three years, found no fruit on it; and, so that it might not occupy the ground any longer, he ordered it to be cut down (Luke 13).

The barren fig tree in the vineyard was the Synagogue, fruitless under the law. The Lord sought fruit from it for three years because, before the law, through the patriarchs; under the law, through the prophets; and under grace, through the apostles, he urged it toward the fruit of good works.

But because it had withered through unbelief and occupied the ground fruitlessly, he placed the axe of his judgment at its root when he cut it down by the sword of the Romans.

The barren fig tree in the vineyard is also any person in the Church who lacks good works. The fruit of three years is sought from him when the work of faith in the Trinity is required. Unless he is quickly dug around through confession and manure of repentance is applied, he will be cut down by death and cast into the fire of Gehenna.

This too was prefigured by the woman who was bent over but mercifully healed by the Lord (the same passage).

The woman bent toward the ground was the Synagogue, bowed beneath the weight of the law. She is raised by the Lord when the multitude converted from the Jews is rescued from the burden of the law through grace.

The woman bent over for eighteen years is also every soul weakened under both laws. The number ten pertains to the Old Testament because of the Decalogue of the law; the number eight pertains to the New Testament because of the eighth day of the Lord’s resurrection.

Thus the woman is bent over for eighteen years when the soul is weighed down by transgression of both laws; but she is lifted by the Lord to salvation when his grace saves her through repentance.

Through the poor, dearly beloved, we ought to reach God’s banquet. For the Lord commanded that we not invite the rich or powerful to our dinner, from whom we will receive repayment here, but that we summon the poor, the weak, the lame, and the blind to our banquet, from whom we hope for no repayment.

If we do this, we will be blessed, because when we fail, they will receive us into eternal dwellings.

## On the Sacrament of Marriage, and on the Origin of Marriage, the Reason for Its Institution, and the Twofold Institution of Marriage
Although all the sacraments took their beginning after sin and on account of sin, the sacrament of marriage or wedlock alone is read as having been instituted even before sin—not, however, as a remedy, but as a duty. In marriage, the following must first be considered and distinguished: its origin and institution, together with their manner and causes; and its variation according to time, place, and rite.

God is the author of marriage. For he himself established that marriage should exist when he made woman as a helper for man, for the propagation of the human race. Adam also, recognizing in the spirit for what purpose the woman had been made, said when she had been brought to him: “This now is bone of my bones, and flesh of my flesh. For this reason a man shall leave his father and his mother and cling to his wife, and they shall be two in one flesh” (Genesis 2). Christ likewise consecrated the wedding at Cana of Galilee, not only by his bodily presence but also by the display of a miracle (John 2). In all these things it is shown that marriage is from God [Col. 1196A] and that it is good.

The institution of marriage is twofold. One occurred before sin, as a duty; the other after sin, as a remedy. The first was so that nature might multiply; the second so that nature might be relieved and vice restrained.

The first institution established marriage in a covenant of love, so that in it there might be the sacrament of that fellowship which exists in the spirit between God and the soul. But it established the duty of marriage in the joining of flesh, so that in it there might be the sacrament of that fellowship which was to exist in the flesh between Christ and the Church.

The second institution confirmed marriage in a covenant of love, so that through its goods what was weakness and fault in the joining of flesh might be excused. But it permitted the duty of marriage in the joining of flesh [Col. 1196B] so that, besides the multiplication of the race, the weakness of those who beget might be accommodated (Ephesians 5).

The Apostle hints at why the sacrament of marriage was instituted when he shows that the man is the image of God and, consequently, that the woman in some manner bears the type of the rational soul. God himself, the institutor and arranger of marriage, shows why the duty of marriage was first instituted when he says: “Increase and multiply, and fill the earth” (Genesis 1).

The blessed Augustine testifies in these words that the duty of marriage—that is, the joining of flesh—was instituted before sin not as a remedy for weakness but for the multiplication of offspring, whereas after sin that same act was granted as a remedy for weakness:

“The weakness of either sex, inclining toward the ruin of disgrace, is received within the upright honor of marriage, so that what would be a duty for the healthy may be a remedy for the sick.”

Again, that marriage itself is one thing and the sacrament of another thing, while the duty of marriage is something else and the sacrament of another thing, Augustine himself testifies in his book *On the Good of Marriage*, saying:

“In marriage something good seems to exist not only for the propagation of children but also for the natural fellowship of the two sexes. Otherwise marriage would not be spoken of among the aged, even if they had lost their children or had never begotten them. For although the ardor of the flesh has withered in them, the order of love nevertheless remains vigorous.”

Again: “In marriage the knowledge of the sacrament is more valuable than the fertility of the womb.” [Col. 1196D] (AUGUSTINE.)

“Therefore, some who do not understand what has been said—that a woman with whom it is known that there has been no sexual intercourse cannot belong to the sacrament of Christ and the Church—think that the sacrament of marriage cannot exist where carnal union has not occurred. They do not know that the duty of marriage, in the joining of flesh, signifies that union which was made between Christ and the Church through the taking on of flesh; and therefore they think that where carnal intercourse has not occurred there can be no sacrament of Christ and the Church.

“Yet where carnal intercourse has not occurred, marriage can nevertheless be true, and the true sacrament of marriage can exist even if carnal intercourse has not followed. Indeed, it is all the more true and holy in proportion as it contains nothing of which chastity should be ashamed, but rather something in which chastity may glory. For marriage itself is a sacrament, just as the duty of marriage itself is recognized to be a sacrament.

“But marriage, as has been said, is the sacrament of that fellowship which exists in the spirit between God and the soul. The duty of marriage, however, is the sacrament of that fellowship which exists in the flesh between Christ and the Church. It is written, he says: ‘The two shall be one flesh’ (Genesis 2). And if they are one flesh, they are no longer two but one flesh. This is the sacrament of which the Apostle says: ‘A great mystery in Christ and in the Church’ (Ephesians 5).

“A woman with whom it is known that there has been no carnal intercourse cannot belong to this sacrament. She can, however, belong to another sacrament—not the great one in Christ and the Church, but the greater one in God and the soul. For what of this? If what exists in the flesh is great, is what exists in the spirit not much greater?

“‘The flesh,’ he says, ‘profits nothing; it is the spirit that gives life’ (John 6). If, therefore, what exists in the flesh is great, what exists in the spirit is surely greater, provided that Scripture rightly calls God the bridegroom and the rational soul the bride.

“There is, certainly, something between God and his soul, of which that which exists in marriage between male and female is a sacrament and image; and perhaps, to state it more explicitly, it is that very fellowship which is outwardly preserved in marriage by the covenant of the marriage bond. The sacrament—and the reality of the sacrament itself—is the mutual love of souls, which is guarded between them by the bond of marital fellowship and covenant.

“And this same love, by which male and female are united in soul within the holiness of marriage, is itself a sacrament and sign of that love by which God is joined inwardly to the rational soul through the infusion of his grace and participation in his Spirit.

“Thus the joining of flesh, which before sin was the duty of marriage and after sin was granted in the same marriage as a remedy, is added to marriage in both cases in such a way that it exists with marriage, not that marriage arises from it. For even before it, marriage is true, and it can be holy without it: then, indeed, if it were absent, less fruitful; now, however, if it is absent, more sincere.

“That after sin the joining of flesh is admitted in marriage is chiefly a matter of indulgence and compassion, lest the vice of desire, which took root in human flesh after sin, should flow more disgracefully into every excess if it could nowhere be lawfully received.”

## THE TWENTY-FIRST SUNDAY. According to John.

[Col. 1197]

[Col. 1197C] “‘There was a certain royal official whose son was ill at Capernaum. When he heard that Jesus had come from Judea into Galilee, he went to him and asked him to come down and heal his son, for he was beginning to die. Jesus therefore said to him: “Unless you see signs and wonders, you do not believe,” and so forth (John 4).’

“The royal official believed that Jesus was the Savior from whom he sought salvation; but at the end he doubted, in that he asked for his power to be exercised. Thus the Lord, recognizing the heart of the doubter, reproved his doubt, saying: ‘Unless you see signs and wonders, you do not believe.’

“Prodigies are things that foretell something. The word *prodigium* is said as though it were *prodicium*, that is, something that speaks beforehand: it signifies something future. Those things that were then happening foretold those that are now taking place. Every prodigy is a sign [Col. 1197D], but the converse is not true, because a sign may concern the past, the present, or the future, whereas a prodigy concerns only the future.

“A sign concerning the present was the Lord’s changing water into wine, thereby indicating his glory, just as a circle presently signifies wine for sale. A sign concerning the past is the imprint of feet appearing in snow.

“‘The royal official said to him: “Lord, come down before my son dies.” Jesus said to him: “Go, your son lives.”’ He showed that he is not absent where he is invited, healing by command alone.

“Thus, in the fact that he did not disdain to go to the centurion’s servant when he disdained to go to the royal official’s son (Luke 7), our pride is rebuked, because among human beings we honor not the nature by which they were made in the image of God, but honors and riches.

“Observe the distinction. This royal official wanted the Lord to come down to his house; the centurion declared himself unworthy. Here, condescension was granted to arrogance; there, it was granted to humility—as though the Lord were saying to this man: ‘Do not weary me: you want my power in your house; by a word I can heal your son.’ The foreign centurion believed that I could do this by a word; you do not believe unless you see signs and wonders.”

“‘The man believed the word that Jesus said to him and went away. As he was going down, his servants met him and announced that his son was alive. He therefore asked them at what hour he had improved. They told him: “Yesterday, at the seventh hour, the fever left him.” The father therefore knew that it was at that hour when Jesus had said to him: “Go, your son lives”; and he himself and his whole household believed.’

“The man began to believe that the Lord, though bodily absent, could heal just as though he were present, and thus he obtained salvation for his son. He did not, therefore, distrust God’s mercy by asking the servants about the hour; rather, he desired that the divine power should become known to many through the servants’ testimony. Or he asked so that he might know whether the healing had happened by chance, because perhaps he did not yet believe perfectly.

“In the figure of the sevenfold Holy Spirit, in whom all salvation consists, the fever left him at the seventh hour. This royal official, who was slow to believe, represents the Jews, who came to faith with difficulty—like Thomas when he heard: ‘Come, put your hand here; and do not be unbelieving, but believing’ (John 20).

## On the scourges of God and the twofold striking

The subtlety of divine wisdom searches consciences inwardly as a witness, and outwardly inflicts punishments, so that the prophet’s testimony may be true: God himself is both witness and judge.

God’s mercy is ordered: first, here, he corrects a person from sins through scourges, and afterward frees him from eternal punishment. The chosen person of God is worn down by the pains of this life so that he may gain a more perfect future life.

God by no means spares the offender: he either strikes the sinner with a temporal scourge for purification, or leaves him to be punished by eternal judgment, or the person himself punishes through repentance what he has committed wrongly. Hence it is said that God does not spare the offender.

Temporal scourges lead the just toward eternal joys. Therefore the just ought to rejoice in punishments, and the wicked to fear amid prosperity. God withholds neither mercy nor justice from the just or the reprobate. He judges the good here through affliction and rewards them there through mercy; he rewards the wicked here through temporal clemency and punishes them there through eternal justice.

In this life God spares the wicked, yet does not spare the elect. In that life he will spare the elect, but will not spare the unrighteous. The security of the wicked in this life is dangerous, while the suffering of the good is tranquil. After death the unrighteous will be led away to torment, but the just will sleep secure after their labor.

This must be understood not only of bodily sufferings but also of spiritual ones, so that each person may hope to be rewarded at the end in proportion to the scourges he endures in body or mind.

Often, by the hidden judgment of God, the reprobate remain in this world outside the scourges of correction. Although they seem to have committed many damnable deeds, they are nevertheless despised by God and struck by no blow of amendment. The one whom God loves is corrected more severely, as the prophet Amos says: “You alone have I known among all the nations of the earth; therefore I will visit all your iniquities upon you” (Amos 3). “For whom God loves he corrects: he scourges every son whom he receives” (Hebrews 13).

It is very necessary for the just person to be tested by vices and beaten by the scourge in this life, so that, while he is assailed by vices, he may not become proud of his virtues; and while he is worn down by pain of mind or flesh, he may be withdrawn from love of the world.

The just must be tested, but by the trial of affliction, not by the trial of lust. In this life God deals harshly with his elect so that, while they are struck by the stronger goads of the scourge, no pleasures of the present life may delight them, but they may continually desire the heavenly homeland, where certain rest is awaited.

The elect are tested through the adversity of this life so that, according to Peter, judgment may begin from the household of God (1 Peter 4), while in this life God chastises his elect with the scourge of judgment.

The divine striking is twofold: one is for good, by which we are struck in the flesh so that we may be corrected; the other is by which we are wounded in conscience and love, so that we may love God more ardently.

God looks in a twofold manner, either toward forgiveness or toward vengeance: toward forgiveness, as in the case of Peter; toward vengeance, as when he testifies that he will descend to see the deeds of the people of Sodom.

God strikes those whom he wills in three ways: the reprobate for condemnation, the elect whom he sees going astray for purification, and the just for testing.

In the first manner Egypt was struck for condemnation; in the second, poor Lazarus for purification; in the third, Job was struck for testing.

A person is often scourged by God before sin, lest he become evil, as Paul did, who endured the goads of the flesh at the instigation of an angel of Satan (2 Corinthians 12). He is also scourged after sin so that he may be corrected, as in the case of the Apostle who was handed over to Satan for the destruction of the flesh, so that the spirit might be saved (1 Corinthians 5).

Yet the person who does not know why he is beaten does not justly murmur. For God often scourges the just precisely so that they may not fall by becoming proud of their justice.

In this life God is all the more intent on sparing insofar as he chastens more by delay; yet he corrects some by striking. Of these he says: “I reprove and chastise those whom I love” (Hebrews 12).

He punishes others by striking them, when he sees them sinning incorrigibly. He strikes them no longer under discipline as a father strikes sons, but with strict condemnation as enemies and adversaries. Of these he says: “I have struck you with the scourge of an enemy, with cruel chastisement” (Jeremiah 30). And again: “Why do you cry out over your wound? Your pain is incurable” (ibid.).

Therefore let everyone hasten and fear lest his life be struck together with his guilt. For the scourge then washes away guilt when it changes one’s life. The scourge does not expiate the sins of one whose conduct it does not change.

Every divine striking is either a purification of the present life or the beginning of the punishment to come. For in some people the scourges begin in this life and continue in eternal punishment. Hence the Lord says through Moses: “A fire has kindled in my anger, and it shall burn down to the depths below” (Deuteronomy 32).

Some are accustomed to say: “God does not judge twice for the same thing” (Nahum 1:9, according to the Septuagint). Yet they do not consider what is written elsewhere: “Jesus, having delivered the people from the land, afterward destroyed those who did not believe” (Jude 5).

Although one guilt is not struck twice, one striking by scourges nevertheless becomes the beginning of subsequent torments. Hence it is written in the Psalm: “Let them be clothed with their confusion as with a double garment” (Psalm 108). For *diplois* is a double garment, which figuratively is worn by those who are condemned both to temporal and to eternal punishment.

Thus Jeremiah says: “Ruin upon ruin” (Jeremiah 4), that is, a twofold condemnation, both in this age and in the age to come. And elsewhere the same prophet says: “Crush them with a double crushing” (Jeremiah 17), that is, with a twofold punishment, present and future.

For some, by the secret judgment of God, things are bad here and good there, namely so that, while they are chastised and corrected here, they may be freed from eternal condemnation. For others, things are good here and bad there, as happened to the man who was conspicuous here for the splendor of his power but after death was handed over to the fires of Gehenna for torment.

For still others, things are bad both here and there, because they refuse to be corrected; their scourging begins in this life, and they are condemned in eternal punishment. It is certain that some sink so deeply into despair that they cannot be corrected even by scourges. Of them it is said through the prophet: “In vain I struck your children; they did not accept correction” (Jeremiah 2).

Often the just person mourns and does not know whether he is suffering scourges in repentance for all his sins or only for one. He does not know what guilt it is for which he has deserved to suffer such punishments, and because of this very uncertainty he is especially grieved. Although scourges absolve the just from sins, he is still troubled by fear of vengeance, lest the blows that press upon him be insufficient to cleanse his offenses.

Therefore, while he suffers the punishment of repentance and fears the future, he receives, in a certain way, as the prophet says, a double recompense for his sins.

## On the weakness of the flesh and endurance of divine correction

It is clear that there are some people of the same kind who do not know how to be corrected unless they see others being scourged. They therefore improve by comparison with the wicked, fearing that what they see destroying others may also happen to them.

When God sees that some are unwilling to be corrected by their own choice, he touches them with the goads of adversity. Foreseeing that others may be capable of committing many sins, he scourges them with bodily weakness for their salvation, so that it is more beneficial for them to be broken by illnesses unto salvation than to remain healthy unto condemnation.

God’s visitation is not always understood as good, nor always as evil. It is understood as good in the words: “Visit us with your salvation” (Psalm 105); but as evil according to this: “At the time of their visitation they shall perish” (Jeremiah 10).

Illnesses come upon bodies for three reasons: because of sin, because of testing, and because of bodily excess or passion. Human medicine can nevertheless help with this last cause; for the others, only the divine compassion of mercy can help.

For those who are stronger and healthy, it is beneficial to become ill and not sin, lest, through the vigor of health, they defile themselves with unlawful desires of greed and lust and so sin.

The hardness that weighs upon the mind but is not perceived is usefully punished in the flesh, so that it may be felt and, once understood, corrected. For wounds of the flesh are felt more quickly than wounds of the soul; therefore those who go astray are corrected more quickly through scourges of the flesh.
