This is indicated by the scales of unbelief on Paul’s eyes (Acts 9). When these were punished by the rebuke affecting his bodily eyes, the hardness of his mind was immediately dissolved.

There is a harmful health that leads a person to disobedience. There is also a health-giving illness that, through divine correction, breaks the hardness of the mind.

The sickness of the soul—that is, the sickness of sins—is harmful. Concerning it the Apostle says: “Who is weak, and I am not burning?” (2 Corinthians 11). But the same Apostle approves bodily weakness as beneficial when he says: “When I am weak, then I am stronger” (2 Corinthians 12).

A sinful person ought not to murmur against God’s scourges, because he is corrected especially through the very thing by which he is chastised. Each person bears more lightly what he suffers if he examines his own evils, for which just recompense is inflicted upon him.

Let the one who suffers evil learn not to murmur, even if he does not know why he suffers evil, and therefore supposes that he suffers justly because he is being judged by the one whose judgments are never unjust.

The person who endures scourges and murmurs against God accuses the justice of the judge. But the person who recognizes that he suffers what he endures from a just judge—even if he does not know the reason for his suffering—is justified by this: he accuses himself and praises God’s justice.

Since the just person provides examples to others through prosperous circumstances, he must also be touched by adversity, so that his patience may be proved and those who recognized his moderation in prosperity may once again take from him examples of courage.

The person who is tormented by passions of the soul while the adversary lies in wait should not therefore believe that he is separated from Christ because he suffers such things. Rather, he should consider himself more acceptable to God if, while suffering these things, he praises God instead of accusing him.

By divine judgment the mind of the just is stirred by various trials of suffering for great benefit. If he gives thanks to God for them and reckons that he deserves to suffer such things because of his own guilt, what comes to him from suffering will be counted as virtue, because he acknowledges divine knowledge and understands his own guilt.

## THE TWENTY-SECOND SUNDAY. According to Matthew.

[Col. 1201]

[Col. 1201D] “‘The kingdom of heaven is like a king who was a man and wished to settle accounts with his servants’ (Matthew 18).”

It is customary among the Syrians, and especially among the Palestinians, to join parables to all their speech, so that what cannot be grasped through a simple command may be grasped through a comparison.

Understand the kingdom of heaven as Christ. He is compared to an earthly king in order to show that one ought to grant forgiveness without limit to repentant fellow servants, since through the grace of the Gospel he has freely bestowed upon us forgiveness of absolutely all sins—not on account of our merit but by his gift.

“‘When he began to settle accounts, one was brought to him who owed ten thousand talents. Since he had nothing with which to repay, the lord ordered him to be sold, together with his wife and children and everything he had, and repayment to be made.’”

Christ, examiner of merits, now settles accounts with his servants through the Scriptures. The one who owed ten thousand talents was destined to render an account for innumerable sins or crimes. Since he had neither the strength nor the grace by which he could make satisfaction, he perceived in the Scriptures that God commands such people to be sold and handed over to eternal fire, together with wife and children—that is, together with folly and evil thoughts.

But he promises to glorify the just together with wife and children—that is, with wisdom and good thoughts. The price of the one who is sold is understood as the punishment of the condemned.

“‘That servant fell down and begged him, saying: “Have patience with me, and I will repay you everything.”’”

Humbled by fear of Gehenna, he says: “Spare me, Lord; and I, believing and repenting, will cover the multitude of my sins with love.”

But we must note how the name *servus* (“servant” or “slave”) was first introduced into the Latin language. Wars brought this about. When one person had been defeated by another under the law of war and could have been killed, because he had then been preserved alive he was nevertheless called a *servus*.

“‘Moved with compassion, the lord of that servant released him and forgave him the debt.’”

The sinner who begs receives the gift of ten thousand talents—that is, forgiveness of his committed sins—when he takes up the healing that God instituted for this purpose. This occurs if he receives the washing of baptism without pretense, or if afterward he devoutly receives the baptism of repentance. Thus released from the bonds of present fear, he goes forth in hope of salvation.

“‘But when that servant had gone out, he found one of his fellow servants who owed him a hundred denarii, and [Col. 1203C] seizing him, he began to choke him, saying: “Pay what you owe.”’”

The debtor of a hundred denarii was one who, because of some offenses committed against a brother, is known to have burned with a desire for vengeance.

“‘His fellow servant therefore fell down and begged him, saying: “Have patience with me, and I will repay you everything.”’”

That is: “I will correct what I have done wrong through the counsel or judgment of the Church.”

“‘But he was unwilling. He went away and had him put into prison until he should repay the debt.’”

He was unwilling to examine himself, so as to act mercifully in the spirit of gentleness. Instead, he withdrew from the good grace he had received and sent his fellow servant into the prison of terrible tribulation, perhaps so that he might thereby pay the debt of sin and leave nothing more serious to be avenged in the future.

Thus, according to the Apostle, it happened that the sorrow was swallowed up and the one who hated his brother perished by exceeding the limits of justice (2 Corinthians 2). Concerning this excess it is written: “There is a just person who perishes in his justice” (Ecclesiastes 7).

“‘When his fellow servants saw what had happened, they were very sorrowful. They came and reported to their lord everything that had been done.’”

Spiritual people, who judge all things, are saddened when they see such things and report them to the Lord for correction, imploring his help.

“‘Then his lord summoned him and said to him: “Wicked servant, I forgave you all that debt because you begged me. Should you not therefore have had mercy on your fellow servant, as I also had mercy on you?” And his lord, being angry, handed him over to the torturers until he should repay the whole debt.’”

This summons takes place inwardly in conscience, namely when someone falls into despair. God, in whom there is no change or shadow of alteration (James 1), is nevertheless said at one time to show mercy because he bestows works of mercy, and at another to be angry because in just judgment he hands a person over to infernal ministers for perpetual punishment.

“‘So also my heavenly Father will do to you, if each of you does not forgive his brother from your hearts.’”

It is clear that if we do not forgive from the heart what is committed against us, that debt which we rejoiced had been forgiven us through repentance is again demanded.

Those who are double-minded and unstable in all their ways will therefore rightly pay the whole debt; the exclusion expressed in the parable strikes them particularly. For while they live fictitiously in the Church, they neither love their neighbor with sincere affection nor do anything purely for the sake of God alone.

Thus, what God had forgiven them when they asked—namely, when they had been granted communion in the sacraments—they vainly rejoice has been forgiven them, although their pretense prevented them from receiving true forgiveness. The debt is demanded again, although they may regard it as having been forgiven through repentance.

Prayers, fasts, almsgiving, and similar acts, though they are remedies for sins when those seeking the highest good undertake them directly, are turned by the fictitious, through the wandering instability of their minds, into the security of false hope and the nourishment of sin. Hence it is written: “Let his prayer become sin” (Psalm 108).

Many also criminally fall away from the complete forgiveness of sins and attachment to inward grace that they had first received, as Peter and David did—although they rose again stronger.

“For if the just person falls, he will not be dashed to pieces,” because the Lord, who snatches the just person away lest wickedness change his mind, places his hand beneath the one who is falling (Psalm 36), so that the person who falls through weakness of the flesh may rise again through repentance.

Who, then, would dare to say of those who have been so taken up into grace that God permits each one to fall all the way to condemnation? Nevertheless, if some happen to be condemned, some say, according to the parable, that sins previously forgiven return, even though they have been punished temporarily by the judgment of the Church, so that they may be punished eternally.

For just as justice erases sins committed, so succeeding injustice destroys justice; once justice has been condemned, no remedy remains against the former sins. For the Lord says through the prophet: “On whatever day the just person sins, all his righteousnesses will be forgotten” (Ezekiel 18).

Where perseverance in love has not existed, therefore, no repentance is sufficient. Hence the one freed from sins is told: “Go, and do not sin any more” (John 8).

Secular laws also, because of certain acts of ingratitude, recall those who have been manumitted to their former slavery.

The prophet’s statement is brought forward against this: “A second tribulation will not arise” (Nahum 1), or, according to another translation: “God will not judge twice for the same thing.”

But, as they say, it is not twofold—rather, it is one tribulation and one punishment—when the person who was not sufficiently punished here is punished afterward.

It is also not unreasonable to think that the former desires for sin have returned, according to the parable in which the unclean spirit takes seven other spirits more wicked than itself and says: “I will return to my house from which I came” (Luke 11).

For although a sinner appears in the act of committing one grave sin, he must be understood to possess many others in intention, just as the just person has many more virtues in intention than in action.

Others, however, think that a person is not to be punished again for those sins for which he made satisfaction to God through repentance, even if afterward he commits similar or more serious sins. The sinner does indeed become as he was before and becomes more guilty because of his ingratitude for the mercy shown to him.

They therefore say that the whole debt to be repaid is not the debt that had already been forgiven, but rather the mercy he ought to have shown to others because he had received mercy. Hence it is said elsewhere: “With whatever measure you measure, it shall be measured back to you” (Matthew 7).

The parable, then, is as though it said: If you do not wish to show mercy to others as the Lord showed mercy to you, forgiving sins, the heavenly Father will demand this debt from you.

They therefore consider it a statement made for the sake of terror when commentators commonly assert that what had been forgiven through repentance is demanded again. Now let us examine more carefully the forgiveness of sins.

## ON THE FORGIVENESS OF SINS

In the reconciliation of the sinner to God, three things must be considered: contrition of heart, confession of the mouth, and satisfaction through works.

For Scripture commands us to rend our hearts and our garments, to confess our sins to one another, and to produce worthy fruits of repentance.

It must be noted that many grieve over their sins not because their sins displease them for God’s sake, but because of the punishment. Such sorrow or lamentation is therefore not contrition of heart unto salvation, but consternation of mind unto condemnation. The wicked will grieve in this way in the future.

Some also repent of having sinned solely because of the shamefulness of sin, according to the philosopher’s statement: “If I knew that the gods would forgive and that human beings would not know, I would not sin.”

But contrition of heart is fruitful when someone grieves over the sin by which he has offended God and is troubled because his iniquity displeases him through love of justice.

Hence it is written: “At the hour when the sinner groans, he will be saved” (Ezekiel 18). Since nothing is late or absent for God, the sooner someone truly repents, the sooner the one who is present forgives.

Thus David says: “I said: I will confess my injustice against myself to the Lord, and you forgave the wickedness of my sin” (Psalm 31).

That is: “I resolved in my heart and firmly determined to condemn what I had committed by despising God, accusing myself for God’s sake.” Hence also: “The just person is first of all his own accuser” (Proverbs 18).

For God to forgive sin means to release the eternal punishment owed for it by the bestowal of present grace.

This takes place in infants when the washing of baptism is received. It also takes place in adulterers when the blindness of the mind is dissolved through compunction.

For this reason the teachers of sacred eloquence wrote that original sin passes away in guilt through baptism but remains in action: namely, the dissolution of the body and the numerous multitude of temporal deficiencies.

This is of great value because “all virtue is perfected in weakness” (2 Corinthians 12), and also so that no one might seek the grace of baptism for the sake of the happiness of the present life, and thus neither possess that grace worthily nor attain to eternal life.

In the same way, when the eternal punishment of actual sin has been released through the enlivening of the mind, temporal punishment is left behind, so that what was committed through the soul’s unlawful delight or even through carnal pleasure may be worthily cleansed by the bitterness of satisfaction while a person still has the opportunity, lest he be punished more strictly by God in the future.

For no evil passes without punishment.

[Col. 1206B] Confession was therefore fittingly instituted so that the one who had departed from God while placed under his own authority might return with humility and devotion when placed under another’s authority. For this reason God instituted the priest, or his vicar, almost as a physician, to whom the wounds of sins might be exposed for healing, so that the sinner might receive the medicine of satisfaction not from himself but from another, for the sake of greater humility. The sacraments are, as it were, certain plasters.

Thus it happens that one who was previously contrite and humbled is strengthened in confession; and often a sinner, brought before the priest solely by fear or by the custom of the Church, is truly moved to compunction through the priestly office and departs filled with charity. Some do not then return from the heart, but nevertheless the form of penance that they undertake gradually nourishes [Col. 1206C] charity with humility in them. Likewise, for many who come to their senses, baptism is beneficial even though they approached it only deceitfully.

The canons accordingly leave the length of time for performing penance to the judgment of an understanding priest, because with God the measure of sorrow has greater value than the measure of time, and mortification of vices more than abstinence from food. For this reason they command that periods of penance be shortened according to the faith and conduct of the penitents, and they judge that they should be prolonged because of negligence. Nevertheless, particular forms of penance have been imposed for certain offenses; by these the other offenses are to be assessed, since through the same forms it is easy to estimate the punishment and censure of the canons.

[Col. 1206D] It must nevertheless be understood that the longer someone persists in sins, the longer penance must be performed for him. Since, therefore, the temporal punishment of sin is prolonged or shortened at the priest’s discretion, many understand the following to have been said about it: “Whose sins you forgive are forgiven them, and whose you retain, they are retained” (John XX). For the punishment of sin is called “sin,” according to the principle by which the name of the cause is transferred to the effect.

From what has been said, then, it is clear that through the ministry of priests God forgives some people both sin and the punishment of sin, while to others he forgives only the temporal punishment, because he had already loosed them from the darkness of sin and the bondage of Gehenna. He demonstrated this through Lazarus. He came, called him, and brought him back to life when called; and after he had been restored to life he said to him, “Come out,” and he said of him to his disciples: “Unbind him and let him go” (John XI).

In the same way he comes to the sinner and calls him through an inward inspiration. When the death of sin departs, the sinner is restored to life; and once restored to life, Christ tells him to come out, that is, to show himself to the priests through confession. Concerning him, he says to the priests, “Unbind him,” that is, call him back to the Church, “and let him go,” that is, let him associate and remain with the other faithful.

## DIVISION

God forgives sins from himself and through himself whenever he wishes. Thus he says through the prophet: “I, the Lord, alone blot out iniquity and the sins of the people” (Isaiah XLV). Hence Ambrose says: “He alone forgives sins who alone died for sins. Priests [Col. 1207B] are nevertheless sometimes said to forgive sins, not from themselves, but from the grace working in them and through them, according to the judgment not of them but of God.

“This is like the saying, ‘You alone are he who performs wonders’ (Psalm LXXI),” although many human beings have performed wonders, but not from themselves as God does. Likewise: “No one is good except God alone” (Mark XVI), because he is good from himself. And many human beings are good, “but not in the way God is.”

No one, therefore, except God can save another. He would indeed do so if he forgave sins from himself. That no one except ourselves can condemn us is also shown by the words: “My soul is always in my hands” (Psalm CXVIII).

It should be noted that if someone who wishes to confess cannot do so when the moment of necessity is imminent, the invisible priest does not disdain to supply for him what the visible priest would have administered if he had been present. Concerning him Ecclesiasticus says: “Behold the great priest” (Ecclesiasticus XLV). And the Apostle says: “Many became priests, because they were prevented by death from remaining; but this one remains forever, possessing an everlasting priesthood” (Hebrews VII).

If someone does not confess out of contempt or negligence, it is clear that he does not possess true contrition of heart; and because he refuses to confess that sin, neglecting the institutions of the Church, he is proved to deserve eternal punishment for it.

Leo and Ambrose, and Maximus concerning the sacraments, say: “I read of Peter’s tears; I do not find his confession.” Peter’s tears, therefore, blot out the sins which shame prevents him from confessing.

[Col. 1207D] It must nevertheless be understood that the institution of confession had not yet been promulgated in the primitive Church; or perhaps Peter did confess, although Scripture does not report it, just as we are compelled to believe that the apostles were baptized, though we do not read when or how this happened.

Some, however, think that Peter, by a prudent dispensation, kept silent about confessing his denial. If the others, who were still weak, had known that this chief architect of the Church alone had fallen so gravely, they would have been greatly scandalized against him. Thus, by a salutary dispensation, he concealed that concerning which his conscience would testify against him, so that he would not therefore be punished eternally. If he had disclosed it to someone, it could not have remained concealed; and if it had become known, the Church would have been scandalized by it. [Col. 1208A] If, however, he had done this for his own sake, namely, so that he would not become infamous and contemptible in the eyes of others, it would have been damnable pride.

It is therefore clear from what has been said above that penance is a remedy for a wound and the hope of salvation. The word itself is taken from the punishment by which the soul is tormented and the flesh mortified, and penance is called *poenitentia*, as though it were “punishment.” Those who perform penance grow their hair and beard to show the abundance of crimes by which the sinner is burdened. The haircloth they wear signifies remembrance of sins, on account of the goats that will stand on the left. The fact that sinners are sprinkled with ashes shows that they are ashes and will return to dust.

The tears of penitents are reckoned by God in place of baptism. The lament of penance is twofold: either we mourn what we have done wrongly, or we mourn that we have not done what we ought to have done. The one truly performs penance who neither neglects to repent of past sins nor commits sins for which he must repent.

But whoever pours out tears without ceasing and nevertheless does not cease to sin has lamentation but not cleansing. For while he despises the forgiveness that he could have obtained by weeping, he deprives his tears of purity and makes those very tears filthy in the sight of God.

Those who cut away certain vices from the desire of their heart while persisting gravely in others love fewer evils than before; but unless they love the lesser evil, they do not become less evil. For sometimes the affection for evil in a single crime is so great [Col. 1208C] that it alienates one from the Lord more than many crimes do.

This, however, is certain: while someone lies dead in one sin, he cannot be watered and restored to life by another so as to be wholly wiped away; sometimes, nevertheless, he is rained upon for a diminution of punishment, according to the prophet’s words: “The Lord rained upon one city and did not rain upon another” (Amos IV).

When people’s sins are public, their penance should also be public, for the period determined by the bishop. Their reconciliation likewise ought to take place publicly through the bishop, or through priests, but only by order of the bishops, as the canons of the African council testify.

Concerning this solemn penance, Augustine says to Macedonius that one must understand the following statement: “There is no place for a second penance.” Although, therefore, it was wisely and beneficially arranged that the place of this most humble penance should be granted only once in the Church, lest it become less medicinal or less useful to the sick—for it is more salutary the less contemptible it is—who would nevertheless dare say to God: “Why do you again spare this person, who, after his first penance, once more binds himself in the snares of iniquity?”

Who would dare say that what the Apostle says does not apply to such people: “Do you not know that the patience of God leads you to repentance?” (Romans II). Or that the following does not apply to them: “Blessed are all who trust in him” (Psalm II), and: “Act courageously, and let your heart be strengthened, all you who hope in the Lord” (Psalm III).

But when someone’s sins are hidden and have been revealed voluntarily in confession to the priest or bishop alone, the penance should also be hidden, lest the weak in the Church be scandalized when they see the punishments of those whose causes they entirely fail to understand. It must also be understood that Satan similarly ensnares people through excessive harshness, so that sinners perish by despair, just as he ensnares them through excessive leniency in correction. Hence Solomon says: “Do not turn aside to the right or to the left” (Proverbs IV).

## Explanation of the Gospel: “The kingdom of heaven is like”

“Blessed are those who keep judgment and practice justice at all times” (Psalm CV).

There are two judgments. One is exercised here through the judges who are Christ’s vicars; the other is displayed at the end of time through Christ, who was appointed by the Lord as judge of the living and the dead. Judgment is to distinguish the good from the evil and to repay good things to the good and evil things to the evil. Thus Christ will separate the good from the evil at the judgment and will repay joys to the righteous and punishments to the ungodly.

Those who love the worshipers of the Lord and reject those who despise the Lord keep judgment. To observe judgment also means to inflict upon oneself punishments worthy of one’s evil deeds. Those who afflict themselves for their sins with vigils, fasts, and other pious labors are blessed, because they will not undergo eternal judgment with the ungodly.

There are also two kinds of justice: one natural, namely divine; the other customary, namely human. Natural justice is to serve God and obey one’s parents. Customary justice is to observe laws and the statutes of prelates and to live in concord with one’s fellow citizens. Blessed, therefore, are those who practice justice at all times, [Col. 1209C] because from the justice of the Father, through Christ, they receive the just rewards of life.

Today’s Gospel urges us toward the judgment of justice. For it says that a certain king settled accounts with his servants, and one was brought before him who owed ten thousand talents. Since he had nothing with which to repay, the master ordered that he, his wife, his children, and all his possessions be sold. Falling down, he begged for mercy, and the master, taking pity on him, forgave him everything.

But after he had gone out, a debtor owing one hundred denarii met him. Seizing him, he strangled him, violently pressing him to repay the debt. That man also fell down and begged for mercy, but it did him no good. For he handed the wretched man over to prison until he should pay the debt.

When the master heard this, he summoned the wicked servant, rebuked him harshly, handed him over to the torturers, and ordered that the entire debt be exacted from him. What he signified by these words the Lord made known in conclusion: “So also my heavenly Father will do to you, if you do not forgive people from your hearts” (Matthew XVIII).

Dearest, these things are greatly to be feared and continually retained in memory. The king who settled accounts with his servants is Christ, who brings all human beings into judgment for their deeds. The debtor of ten thousand talents is every transgressor of the Ten Commandments. The debtor of one hundred denarii is the slanderer of his neighbors.

If, then, we wish God to forgive us grave offenses, let us forgive our neighbors their lesser offenses. Everything people do to us is indeed slight, because it quickly passes; but what we do against God is very grave, because it plunges us into destruction.

For this reason the heavenly teacher instructed us to make an agreement with the judge: we should ask that our debts be forgiven us just as we forgive our debtors (Matthew VI). And when Peter asked how often a brother’s sin should be forgiven—whether up to seven times—the Lord answered, “Not up to seven times, but up to seventy times seven” (Matthew XVI), that is, four hundred and ninety times; this means that we should forgive whatever offense is committed against us.

Scripture also says: “A person harbors anger against another person and seeks mercy from God” (Ecclesiasticus XXVIII). Therefore, whoever does not forgive a person who sins against him is never forgiven by God when he sins against God; indeed, what he believes was forgiven him through penance is exacted from him in torments.

But you say: “I cannot forgive the one who injures me, nor love the one by whom I suffer slander.”

O friend, what has the person you seek to kill done to you?

“He killed my friend,” you reply.

And what does the killing of a person have to do with you? We are all servants of one Lord, the King of all, who as a just judge will avenge every human injury. Therefore, whoever kills a person sins not against you but against the one whose servant he has killed. If you seek vengeance for this, you will be guilty twice: first, because you killed your fellow servant; second, because you deprived your master of his judgment.

If, then, you avenge a homicide by deed or counsel, you will certainly be condemned with the murderer, because “whoever hates his brother is a murderer, and he does not have a share in eternal life” (John III).

But, good man, why do you wish to mutilate the limbs of one whom the Son of the supreme Emperor wishes to reign with him?

“He took my goods,” you say.

What goods?

“Gold,” you say, “or silver, or a horse, or something of that kind.”

O man, did you not come naked into this world and bring none of these things with you? There is no doubt that you will also depart naked from the world and leave everything here. All these things came from the earth and will return again to the earth. You possess nothing here as your own; everything is another’s: “The earth is the Lord’s and its fullness” (Psalm XXIII).

He granted you a portion of his goods for as long as it pleased him. When he no longer wished you to have them, he ordered another to take them. As long as he wished, he gave Job his goods; when it pleased him again, he took them away and gave them to the devil. Hence Job himself says: “The Lord gave, the Lord has taken away” (Job I). He did not say, “The devil took them away,” because the Lord alone had power over them.

Since, then, you are a worm and corruption, do not wrong God by taking vengeance on your neighbor.

But you, dear friend, why do you wish to beat him or deprive him of his possessions?

“He spoke evil to me,” you say.

O senseless man! What is a word except wind? Once it has flown from the mouth, it immediately vanishes into the air. The one who spoke evil did not harm you but himself, because whoever speaks even foolishly will be guilty of the fire of Gehenna (Matthew V).

But if you live badly, what will someone else’s blessing profit you? And if you live well, what will someone else’s curse harm you? It is therefore wretched to increase the misery of these wretched people through vengeance, when in their misery they themselves have provoked God’s anger.

For God will condemn murderers, subject robbers to punishments, and separate the accursed from eternal blessing. Therefore, everything committed against us must be forgiven; everything committed against God must be punished by the prelates. Let us punish with suitable penance the sins that we ourselves commit against God. Those subject to us who have sinned against God’s law let us correct not cruelly but mercifully, so that we may save their souls, because “judgment is without mercy for the one who has not shown mercy” (James II). But whatever they have committed against us in word or deed, let us forgive, and we shall receive joy and gladness.

Now let your affection hear how justly God punishes sinners and how mercifully he protects those who call upon him. [Col. 1211B] He himself is the merciful Father of the good and the powerful Lord of the wicked.

King David took the wife of Uriah the commander and also had Uriah killed through a stratagem. In vengeance for this, the Lord put to death the child born of the adultery and stirred up against David his son Absalom, whom he especially loved. Absalom publicly violated his father’s wives and, in addition, deprived him of his kingdom. After David had thus been chastised, God restored him to the kingdom; but he delivered his parricidal son to a shameful death.

David, however, repented and was further consoled when Solomon, his son by the same woman, was placed upon the throne of the kingdom.

It is also written that King Cambyses, wishing to reign alone, ordered Holofernes, commander of the army, to subjugate all the kingdoms of the world to him. Holofernes went out with a powerful force, shattered all the fortified cities around him, and finally reached Judaea, where he besieged Bethulia.

The people of God feared that he would destroy Jerusalem as he had the other cities, and they called upon God with fasts and supplications. He is the protector of all who hope in him, and they asked him to oppose the shield of his protection to their enemies.

The inhabitants of Bethulia had run out of food, and the army had cut off their aqueduct. When they were already failing, the leaders consoled them and promised them the Lord’s help.

In that same city there was a devout widow named Judith. After a three-day fast she put on all her ornaments and descended to the camp of Holofernes (Judith VII). When he saw her, he was immediately captivated by her beauty and prepared a wedding with splendid ceremonial display.

At night, when everyone had been overcome by sleep through excessive wine, Judith arose, invoked God, drew the sword hanging beside the bed, cut off the drunken commander’s head, and returned as quickly as possible to her own people with the head. After summoning the entire people, she displayed the head and urged them to praise God, who had granted them liberation and victory together.

When they recovered their courage, they worshiped God and celebrated his praises with great joy. On the following day they went out from the city, on Judith’s advice, amid great tumult, and attacked the enemy. When the enemy found their lord decapitated, they were struck with overwhelming fear and all turned to flight. The Bethulians pursued them, struck down many thousands here and there, and drove the rest away in great disgrace. Returning, they gathered immense booty, came to Jerusalem, and offered victims to God, who had redeemed his people through a woman and changed their sorrow into joy.

Thus God scattered the proud and protected the humble by exalting them. The fact that this widow conquered the tyrant signifies that the flesh of Christ conquered the devil.

It is also written that King Ahasuerus held a great banquet for all the princes and peoples of his kingdom and ordered Queen Vashti, wearing her crown, to be brought in among the feasts (Esther I). When she refused to enter, the king deprived her of the kingdom and elevated Esther to the royal scepter in her place.

After this the king exalted a certain Haman over the kingdom and subjected all the princes to him. When everyone began to bend the knee to him, Mordecai, the queen’s uncle, refused to worship him. Therefore, Haman, angered, resolved to have Mordecai and all his descendants put to death. With the king’s seal he decreed that all the Jews throughout the territories of Ahasuerus’s kingdom should be exterminated, and he erected a tall gallows on which he wished to hang Mordecai.

Meanwhile, two men sought to kill the king. When they were exposed by Mordecai, the king ordered them to be destroyed. But he ordered Mordecai to be clothed in purple and a crown, led through the city on the royal horse, with Haman and his soldiers going before him and singing his praises.

After this had been done, Mordecai told the queen that Haman had condemned her and all her family to death. She imposed a fast upon the entire people and afflicted herself with them through vigils, fasts, and prayers. When this had been completed, she prepared a banquet, invited the king, and ordered Haman also to be present.

During the feast she begged the king for the life of herself and her people and told him that she and all her people had been condemned by Haman. Filled with fury, the king ordered Haman to be hanged on the same gallows that he himself had prepared for Mordecai. Moreover, he appointed Mordecai as prince in his place; and Mordecai ordered that all Haman’s kindred should perish by hanging.

Thus, by God’s arrangement, the innocent people were delivered and the wicked offspring were justly exterminated. Although this king was a gentile, he represented Christ, the true King of kings, who was born and arose from the root of Jesse.

He held a great banquet for the princes and peoples of his kingdom because he gave his body and Sacred Scripture as food to the apostles, the princes of the world, and to the faithful peoples of the heavenly kingdom.

He summoned Queen Vashti, crowned, to the banquet because he invited the Synagogue, crowned with the law and the prophets, to the heavenly feasts. When she refused to enter, she was deprived of the kingdom and the captive Esther was placed upon her throne, because unbelieving Judaea is cast out of Christ’s kingdom, while the Church from the gentiles, formerly captive to the devil, is led into the king’s chamber as a participant in the heavenly kingdom.

Haman, who is exalted by the king, is the Jewish people, which was exalted by God with kingdom and priesthood and divine worship. He seeks to exterminate the queen’s offspring because the Jewish people seeks to destroy the people of the Church.

Haman, who erected the gallows for Mordecai, signifies the devil, who erected the cross for Christ. He himself is hanged on the same gallows because the devil is seized upon the scaffold of the cross.

The two who conspired against the king are the two unbelieving peoples, Jewish and gentile, who plotted to kill Christ the king. Mordecai accuses them because the Christian people condemns their deeds. They are slain by the king, and these are condemned by Christ.

Mordecai is marked with purple and a crown, and the Christian people is clothed in martyrdom and eternal glory. He is led through the city on the royal horse because the Christian people is honored by teachers throughout the world. The order of preachers is called the horse of Christ the king, upon which he is carried throughout the world.

Haman goes before him with his soldiers and echoes his praises because the Jewish people, together with the gentiles, willingly or unwillingly celebrates the proclamations of the Christian people.

The queen invites the king to the banquet because the Church invites Christ to the solemn rites of her body. She also orders Haman to be present because, through preaching, she offers her feast to the unbelieving people.

Haman, who erects the gallows for Mordecai, [Col. 1214A] is the Antichrist, who imposes the punishment of death upon the faithful people. He is hanged on that same gallows because he too is slain by the punishment of death.

Mordecai is appointed prince by the king because, after the judgment, the faithful people is established over all the goods of the Lord. Haman’s offspring are exterminated because then the generation of the wicked is condemned. The queen’s people is delivered and its sorrow is changed into joy because the generation of the upright will be blessed and will enjoy gladness and exultation.

Now, dearest, let us beseech with our whole heart the mercy of God, who sits upon the throne and judges equity, administering judgment to all who suffer injury. May he separate us on that day from the unbelieving people and associate us with the faithful in his kingdom, where “eye has not seen, nor ear heard” (1 Corinthians II).

## TWENTY-THIRD SUNDAY. According to John.

[Col. 1213]

[Col. 1213B] “When Jesus had lifted up his eyes and seen that a very great multitude was coming to him” (John VI).

Since, according to the ecclesiastical order, this Gospel reading ought to be recited in the middle of Lent, I shall for the present defer its exposition and write another exposition suitable for this Sunday, which is entitled “The Fifth Sunday before the Nativity of the Lord,” for the advancement of the hearers or readers.

Let none of you, dearest, doubt that there are two advents of our Redeemer. We know with certain faith that the first has already preceded us and that the other is still to come. It is worthwhile for your brotherhood to distinguish the two, so that you may know how to hope for mercy from one and fear judgment from the other. In this way your vigilance, placed between hope and fear, may carefully watch both to avoid the evils that will be punished at the judgment and to prepare the good works that will be rewarded by mercy.

At his first advent our Redeemer appeared gentle and humble in the form of our humanity, a true human being among human beings. At the second he will appear exalted and terrible in the glory of his majesty, the God-man above the angels.

At his first advent he was judged on our behalf and endured the curse of the cross, hanging upon the wood of the cross. At the second, when he judges the whole world, he will condemn the ungodly by the manifest power of his Passion.

At his first advent, hidden in the flesh, he was silent like a sheep before its shearer. At the second he will come openly like God and will not remain silent. At the first advent he was silent concerning judgment, but not silent concerning commandment. At the second he will speak like a woman in labor, for as Isaiah says: “He will cry out and shout, and he will prevail against his enemies” (Isaiah XLII).

O bitter voice of the day of the Lord! There the mighty will be afflicted. For as holy David says: “Fire will blaze before him, etc.” (Psalm XLIX). That storm will drive the ungodly far away, because the wicked will be removed so that he may not see the glory of God. And the fire will envelop those who are to be tormented forever, because “their worm does not die, and the fire is not extinguished” (Isaiah LXVI).

The bow in the clouds represents a figure of this judgment. It appears partly blue and partly fiery, so that it may bear witness to both judgments: one already accomplished, when the waters of the Flood were upon the earth; the other still to come, when God will judge the world by fire.

Tremble, brothers, before the terror of so great a judge, so that you may flee from the face of the bow: “He has bent his bow, etc.” (Psalm VII). But for this reason he delays striking you for a little while: so that we may hasten to escape from the face of so great a punishment. “For you have given a sign to those who fear you, etc.” (ibid.). But “beware lest your flight be in winter or on the Sabbath” (Matthew XXIV).

He flees in winter whose charity grows cold and hinders the course of good works. When the Sabbath intervenes—that is, when the end of life arrives—the exercise of good action is cut off from those who delay.

If, then, brothers, you wish to flee from him, flee to him. If you fear the advent of judgment, look toward the advent of mercy. During this week, which is the fifth before the Nativity of the Lord, and during the following week, which will be the fourth before Christmas, begin your preparation for his advent.

This Sunday is called a preparation because from now until the Nativity of the Lord every Christian ought to devote himself to holy good works, so that Christ, when born, may be worthily received.

This fifth week before Christmas is therefore entitled in the ancient books of the offices, and the following week is accordingly designated the fourth. Yet this is not without a mystery concerning our spiritual preparation.

During the fifth week we ought to prepare or begin because of the five ages of the world, in which there were elect people who believed in, hoped for, and loved the Lord’s advent. During the fourth week we prepare because of the four orders of books, namely, the Law, the Psalms, the Prophets, and the beginning of the Gospel.

Although Moses’ book relates that elect men existed in the first, second, and third ages of the world, he wrote the whole account during the period assigned to the giving of the Law.

These two periods—the fifth week and the fourth—also indicate to us a rational preparation, because of the five senses of the human being that are present in our body and the four elements of which our body consists. Now a third interpretation is added: the intellect, which is no less appropriate to the preparation for the Lord’s advent.

We say that there are two orders of the righteous in our Church who devote themselves to preparing to receive the Lord who is to come. One order labors in secular life; the other in the spiritual life.

Concerning the order of secular people we can understand what the reading says in the fifth week before the Nativity of the Lord, that is, today: “Therefore, behold, the days are coming, says the Lord, and they will no longer say: ‘As the Lord lives, who led out and brought back the offspring of the house of Israel from the land of the north’” (Jeremiah XXIII).

The Lord brought the children of Israel from the land of the north when they returned from Babylonia to Judaea. But, in a better sense, the Lord brings our good secular people to Judaea—that is, to true confession—from the confusion of Babylonia, when he frees them from the power of the devil and from his body. This occurs through the baptism possessed by secular, faithful, and spiritual people.

[Col. 1215C] Those who suffer the cold of the north in their minds are members of the devil. Just as the devil in his entirety, that is, in his head, is worse than one of his members, so we have been liberated from the devil’s power more greatly than the children of Israel were from the kings of the Chaldeans.

The Gospel that is read during the aforementioned week speaks of these secular people. For it relates that the Lord fed five thousand men with five loaves (Luke VII). Bede explains this in his exposition of the Gospel according to Luke:

“There were nearly five thousand men, because there are five external senses of the human being. These senses are rightly called men because through them we have very powerful enemies of our soul.”

“And when she was a slave-woman, she compelled her mistress to serve her” (Genesis XVI). What slave-woman was this? Clearly, the flesh, concerning which the Apostle says: “The flesh desires against the spirit, and the spirit against the flesh; for these two are opposed to each other” (Galatians V).

The flesh had corrupted everyone from God. Scarcely could anyone resist its will; indeed, it had sold everyone to Satan. No struggle is more severe than this one, when a person carries his enemy and feeds his enemy; when the one who attacks him comes from his own household; when he does everything good for that enemy, and the enemy repays him with evil.

Such is the flesh: the more it is nourished, the more it exults, and the more it rises up against the soul. For it has five servants, the five bodily senses, by which it leads the soul captive. When someone sins, he is deceived by seeing, drawn in by hearing, enticed by smelling what is illicit, delighted by eating, or engaged in evil actions with his hands.

By these five powers the flesh overcame the first human being, and the human being succumbed, although he had been placed in paradise. But it first attacked the woman as the weaker part.

Hear how the woman sinned through the five bodily senses. She received the devil’s persuasion through her ears and consented when he said such things as these: “On whatever day you eat from it, your eyes will be opened, and you will be like gods, knowing good and evil” (Genesis III).

Behold when the woman succumbed through hearing. Now observe when she was deceived through smell and sight. Scripture says: “The woman saw that the tree was good and pleasant for eating, beautiful to the eyes, and attractive in appearance” (ibid.). When it says “pleasant,” she was captured through smell; when it says “beautiful to the eyes,” she was ensnared through sight.

Two servants still remained, who completed the entire crime: touch and taste. See, then, when through them the flesh completed what it had begun. It is written: “And she took from its fruit and ate” (ibid.). The hand took it; the mouth ate it. Touch served; taste completed the sin.

After the source of all had been overthrown, those servants subsequently subjected the whole world to themselves. The Lord and our Redeemer therefore saw that the flesh was conquering the whole world, because the slave-woman had subjected her mistress to herself (Genesis XVI), and in his mercy he devised a plan to free the world from this captivity.

He therefore put on our enemy, the flesh, so that he might fight against it, crush it, and weaken its servants, so that thereafter they would be unable to resist him and the mistress might govern her servant.

He therefore chose a fitting punishment: the cross, on which he would crucify our enemy and punish our senses. The eyes saw the obscenity of the punishment and those who mocked, and they experienced the darkness of death. The ears heard the most shameful reproaches. The mouth said, “I thirst” (John XIX), and tasted the bitterness of gall and vinegar. The hands were crucified, and the whole flesh suffered there, so that all of it might be subjected to us and obey the soul more fully.

Behold, it lies defeated beneath us; behold, the slave-woman has been scourged. This is why five thousand men followed the Lord: because those who still lived in secular attire rightly learned to make good use of external things, which they possessed through their five senses.

They are rightly fed with five loaves because such people must still be instructed by legal—that is, secular—commandments.

The offices also celebrated in the fourth week before the Nativity of the Lord arouse us, through the four Gospels, to greater perfection. Hence the epistle read in that week says: “Knowing that it is already the hour for us to rise from sleep; for now our salvation is nearer than when we believed” (Rom. XIII).

Concerning these same spiritual persons he says in the book mentioned above (Bede): “For those who renounce the world completely are four thousand, and, refreshed by seven loaves, that is, exalted by evangelical reading and instructed by spiritual grace. To signify this distinction mystically, as I believe, five gilded columns were ordered to be made at the entrance of the tabernacle, but four before the inner sanctuary, that is, the Holy of Holies (Exod. XXXVI), because beginners are chastised through the law, whereas the perfect are admonished through grace to live more devotedly for God. Typologically, through the chant that is renewed in the fourth week before the Nativity of the Lord, we understand the perfection of the minds of the Gentiles. If those who still lament their recent sins in penance are signified by the five weeks, then rightly we understand by the four weeks those who advance with spiritual joy from virtue to virtue. These two orders existed in the Old Testament, and they exist now as well. The renewal of the chant signifies the joy of the elect, who rejoice greatly at the coming of their beloved Lord.

[Col. 1217B] The Apostle Paul also indicates the preparation necessary for us in the aforementioned epistle, which is read in the fourth week before the Nativity of the Lord. ‘The night has passed,’ he says, ‘and the day will draw near. Let us therefore cast off the works of darkness and put on the armor of light. Let us walk honorably as in the day, not in reveling and drunkenness, not in beds and impurities, not in strife and rivalry; but put on our Lord Jesus Christ’ (Rom. XIII).

Thus, just as a subject’s spirit is moved more and more by many and repeated messengers to undertake the care of receiving his superior, so by the renewal of the chant it is moved more and more to attend to our preparation for receiving the Lord. Therefore, eight days before the Nativity of the Lord, the responsories and antiphons are renewed through almost the entire night, so that by this more frequent repetition we may be roused to cleanse away all the refuse of shameful and earthly thoughts, and may prepare a worthy and adorned dwelling—one furnished, namely, with devout thoughts—for the King of kings and Lord of lords.

# THE FIFTH SUNDAY BEFORE THE NATIVITY OF THE LORD

[Col. 1217]

## SERMON

[Col. 1217B]

“Blessed are all who fear the Lord, who walk in his ways” (Ps. II).

To fear God is to turn aside from evil; to walk in his ways is to do good. Those, therefore, who fear God by avoiding sins are blessed, because they escape punishments; and those who walk in his ways by doing good are blessed, because they will enter into the joy of the Lord.

The ways of the Lord are his commandments, which lead human beings to the heavenly homeland: “All the ways of the Lord are mercy and truth” (Ps. XXIV). The ways of the Lord are mercy toward all who walk in them; truth toward all who turn aside from them. Therefore our God is to be feared as Lord by servants and loved as Father by children. Let us flee sins through fear of him and pursue good works through love of him, so that, when we pass from this miserable life, we may escape the life of sorrow and, with his help, attain the blessed life.

There are three lives: one blessed, above us, in which the saints live blessedly with the angels; another characterized by mercy, in which the righteous still sigh and groan here below; and a third, sorrowful, beneath us, in which the spirits of the damned dwell with the demons.

[Col. 1217D] For us, then, established in the middle life, two ways are offered: one leads some to the higher life, while the other leads others to the lower. On the right there is a narrow and confined way, which leads those who walk along it from this miserable life to the loveliness of the blessed life (Matt. VII); on the left, however, a broad and spacious road opens out, leading those who walk upon it to the calamity of the sorrowful life.

The narrow and confined way is to flee the desires of the world and the lust of the flesh, not to return evil for evil, to mortify the body with vigils and fasts, and to labor in prayers and continual praises of God. The broad and spacious way, on the other hand, is to play, eat, drink, fornicate, hunt, oppress enemies, and overflow with the pleasures of the flesh.

The devil taught this way and led the human race to destruction through it. Christ displayed the other by his deeds and words, and through it restored the lost human being to glory. Since the prophets foresaw that the human race would return to its homeland by this one way alone, they all foretold, with one accord, that Christ was the true and certain way, and they all desired to see him.

For Jacob, when dying, said: “I shall await your salvation, O Lord” (Gen. XLIX). Moses also said: “I beg you, Lord, send the one whom you are going to send” (Exod. IV). David likewise says: “Lord, incline your heavens and descend” (Ps. XVII). Isaiah too says: “Would that you would tear open the heavens and descend!” (Isa. LXIV). And rightly they languished with desire for him, since they knew that he was to come.

Before his coming, dark death covered the world and directed everyone toward destruction along the left-hand path. All wandered as though in darkness, because they did not have Christ, the light; and therefore, with blind hearts, they rushed to death by the spacious way on the left. But when Christ, the sun of the sun, appeared in the world—or rather, when the life of the angels presented itself to mortals—black death, terrified, fled and hid itself in the hidden places of Tartarus in confusion, just as the darkness of night is driven away when the sun rises and the world is illumined by its radiance.

[Col. 1218D] Therefore, beloved, since the way of salvation lies open to us through Jesus and the lamp of God’s word shines on both sides of the way, let us abandon the left-hand path with all our heart and take the right-hand path with all our effort, so that we may attain the highest blessedness.

This way is charity, through which one reaches the radiance of supreme blessedness. Fifteen paths extend toward it, leading to the courts of life—namely, patience, kindness, and the others which the Apostle’s subtle exposition enumerates (Gal. V).

Moreover, supreme blessedness draws those who walk in this way toward itself as though by seventeen arms, because through the ten commandments of the law and the seven gifts of the Holy Spirit Christ taught us to enter the gates of life.

The Holy Spirit, through the prophet, explicitly names these seventeen distinctions of blessedness and subtly indicates their individual dignity.

First, he calls blessed those who overcome vices and desires with the shield of faith and meditate day and night on the law of the Lord: “Blessed,” he says, “is the man who has not gone in the counsel of the ungodly, for the Lord knows the way of the righteous” (Ps. I). The first human being, unhappy, consented to evil counsel and dragged all his followers into death. Christ is the blessed man, and he will restore to the joys of the angels all who walk in the way of the righteous through him. Whoever, therefore, does not consent to sins, directing himself toward this blessed man, will be in supreme blessedness, like a tree planted in paradise.

Second, he calls blessed those who rejoice in hope and trust in the Lord, not in themselves. “Blessed,” he says, “are all who trust in him” (Ps. CXXIV), because they will rejoice on his holy mountain, that is, in Christ. Again: “Blessed is the man who hopes in him” (Ps. XXXIII), because he will see good days in heaven. And again: “Blessed is the man whose hope is the name of the Lord” (Ps. XXXIX), because a new song will be placed in his mouth.

Third, he calls blessed those who burn with the love of repentance, because charity covers a multitude of sins (1 Pet. IV), and forgiveness of sins is given through the Holy Spirit, who is charity. “Blessed,” he says, “are those whose iniquities have been forgiven and whose sins have been covered” (Ps. XXXI). Through charity they are forgiven; through good works they are covered. Such a man will be blessed, because the Lord will not reckon his sin against him in judgment. Rejoicing in the Lord with the righteous, he will be glad; with the upright in heart, he will glory.

Fourth, he calls blessed those who worship God purely and desire to become his inheritance: “Blessed,” he says, “is the nation whose God is the Lord, the people whom he chose as his inheritance” (Ps. XXXII). Let them rejoice in the Lord, for praise is fitting for such people. Again: “Blessed is the people whose God is the Lord” (Ps. CXLIII), because they will sing a new song to God when, rescued from the hand of foreign children, they rejoice.

Fifth, he calls blessed those who pursue hospitality, storing up heavenly riches for themselves through the poor. “Blessed,” he says, “is the one who understands concerning the needy and the poor, for on the evil day the Lord will deliver him” (Ps. XL). The evil day is when a person falls into some affliction or into the hands of enemies; from this the Lord will immediately deliver him. The evil day is also the final day, when the Lord, preserving him, will not deliver him into the soul of his enemies but will make him blessed in the land of the living.

Sixth, he calls blessed those chosen from the Lord’s people and taken up to praise him. “Blessed is the one whom you chose and took up; he will dwell in your courts” (Ps. LXIV). Again concerning them: “Blessed are those who dwell in your house; forever and ever they will praise you” (Ps. LXXXIII).

Seventh, he calls blessed those who devote themselves to prayer and continually invoke the Lord’s help: “Blessed is the man whose help is from you” (ibid.). They will go from strength to strength and will see the God of gods in Zion (ibid.), where one day is better than a thousand. Again: “Blessed is the one whose helper is the God of Jacob, whose hope is in the Lord his God, because the Lord will reign with him forever” (Ps. CXLV).

Eighth, he calls blessed those who praise God and contemplate heavenly things. “Blessed,” he says, “is the people who know joyful acclamation” (Ps. LXXXVIII), because they will walk in the light of the Lord’s face and rejoice forever in his name.

Ninth, he calls blessed those who are taught by God and instructed in his law: “Blessed is the man whom you instruct, O Lord, and whom you teach from your law” (Ps. XCIII). The Lord’s consolations will gladden their souls, when, instructed, they shine like the splendor of the firmament and like the stars—those who teach many to righteousness.

Tenth, he declares blessed those who keep just judgment and practice righteousness at all times. “Blessed are those who keep judgment and practice righteousness at all times” (Ps. CV). They are separated from the nations so that they may glory in the praise of God, be chosen to see the goodness of God’s elect, and rejoice in the joy of the holy nation (ibid.).

Eleventh, he sets forth those who fear God as sons fear their father and desire to keep his commandments. “Blessed is the man who fears the Lord; he will greatly desire his commandments” (Ps. CXI). This holy fear remains forever and ever and brings sons into the presence of the eternal Father. Running in this blessedness, they will be remembered eternally and will possess glory and riches in the house of the Lord.

Twelfth, he declares blessed those who are without the stain of sin in the way—that is, in Christ—and who walk in the law of the Lord—that is, in charity. “Blessed are the undefiled in the way, who walk in the law of the Lord” (Ps. CXVIII). Their soul will live forever and will praise the Lord eternally.

Thirteenth, he declares blessed those who search out God’s commandments in order to practice them and seek the Lord with their whole heart. “Blessed are those who search his testimonies and seek him with their whole heart” (ibid.). They will be blessed by the Lord, just as those who turn aside from his commandments are cursed.

Fourteenth, he declares blessed those who fulfill their desire through good things. “Blessed,” he says, “is the one who has fulfilled his desire from them; he will not be confounded when he speaks with his enemies at the gate” (Ps. CXXVI), conquering his enemies, the demons, through humility. The gate is the day of judgment, through which one enters the palace of heaven. At this gate such people will not be confounded by their sins when they speak in triumph with their enemies; rather, they themselves will be the Lord’s inheritance and will have Christ, the fruit of Mary’s womb, as their reward.

Fifteenth, he sets forth those who fear God as servants fear their Lord and walk in his ways. “Blessed are all who fear the Lord, who walk in his ways” (Ps. XXVII). This fear draws a person away from sins and brings charity into the soul. Charity, however, when it enters, casts fear out, because this fear contains punishment. Those who hasten in this blessedness will see the good things of Jerusalem all the days of their life and will possess the peace of Israel, that is, Christ.

“For you will eat the labors of your hands,” that is, whoever makes good works fruitful in the ways of the Lord, “you are blessed, and it will be well with you” (Ps. CXXVII). His wife will be like a flourishing vine (ibid.), that is, his flesh will rejoice with Christ, who is the true vine. His children will be like young olive trees (ibid.), namely, works in the blessing of the saints.

Sixteenth, he declares blessed those who repay Babylon and the daughter of Babylon with the recompense they have inflicted upon us. “Blessed is the one who repays you with the recompense with which you repaid us” (Ps. CXXXVI). The daughter of Babylon is our flesh, the daughter of confusion. It inflicts these evils upon us when it entices us to sin. We repay it with its recompense when we afflict it for the sins committed. Those who do this receive the beginning of joy on the day of Jerusalem.

Seventeenth, he declares blessed those who seize the little ones of the daughter of Babylon and dash them against the rock. “Blessed is the one who will seize and dash your little ones against the rock” (Ps. CXXXVI). The little ones of the daughter of Babylon are the suggestions of carnal pleasure. Those who dash them against the rock are those who reject carnal things because of Christ’s Passion. When they return from Babylon here to Jerusalem, they will sing a hymn from the songs of Zion forever.

Behold how many blessed inheritances those who walk in the way of Christ will possess. And because the prophets understood through the Spirit that Christ would bring so many bridal gifts to the Church, they desired his coming so greatly.

The Church proclaims two comings of Christ: one by which he visited the world in its weakness, and another by which he will judge the fallen world. We extend the remembrance of his coming over four Sundays, because we read that it was announced by four orders: patriarchs, judges, kings, and prophets.

By the patriarchs: Abel offered a lamb; Melchizedek, bread and wine; and Abraham, his own son. By the judges: Joshua, who is also called Jesus, conquered enemies and divided the land among the people; Gideon displayed the fleece upon which dew descended, and he too conquered enemies with jars; and Samson entered a prostitute’s house in Gaza and, through his enemies, ascended the mountain.

By the kings: David felled Goliath; Solomon built the temple; and Josiah celebrated the Passover. By the prophets: Isaiah foretold that he would be born of a virgin; Jeremiah, that he would dwell among human beings; and Daniel, that the Holy of Holies would come.

We also recall his coming through four Sundays, because before the law he was promised to Abraham and the patriarchs; by Moses and the prophets he was foretold; under grace he was revealed by John and the apostles; and he is still to come, manifest to all.

Therefore we now omit the *Gloria in excelsis*, which we will sing at his Nativity, because by being born he brought joy to the world, which previously had sorrow. Enoch and Elijah, going before his coming, will announce that he is to be present in the world, just as the prophets once foretold that he would be born. Through their preaching the Jews will be converted to the faith at the evening of the world and will suffer hunger for the word of God; and, like dogs circling a city—that is, the Church—they will begin to gather the crumbs of God’s words from the table of the Christians.

At that time the Antichrist will reign and disturb the entire world in various ways. He will draw all rulers to himself through money, while he sits in secret with the rich like a lion lying in ambush to deceive. He will deceive the clergy through worldly wisdom when he utters words against the Most High. He will lead religious people astray through signs and wonders, even causing fire to descend from heaven. He will shake the common people with terror when he rages against Christians in a great persecution.

For he will kill Enoch and Elijah and destroy all who resist him by a cruel death. The Lord Jesus will kill him by the breath of his mouth or through the ministry of the archangel Michael, and he himself will then come for judgment. He who first came to be judged will then come to judge. He who first came hidden will then come manifest.

At his coming all human beings will rise and meet him in throngs. For everyone will see him, including those who pierced him (Rev. I). Fire will go before him and consume his enemies round about (Ps. XCVI). Just as once the water of the Flood rose fifteen cubits above all the mountains, so then the fire will rise fifteen cubits above every mountain peak.

Then, with the righteous placed at Christ’s right hand and the wicked at his left, everything that human beings have ever committed in thought, word, or deed will be manifest to all. Each will receive a fitting recompense according to his merits, as the righteous are assigned to joys and the wicked to punishments.

That is why that day is called the day of judgment: then the just Judge, who was unjustly judged, will judge all things justly; he will judge the world in righteousness and the peoples in equity (Ps. IX).

“This day is also called the day of the Lord, because on that day the Lord will repay each person a just wage for his work. Then the devil will be brought bound before human beings and, while all look on, will be hurled into the lake of fire and sulfur. His body—that is, the whole multitude of the wicked—will be cast in with him, and the earth will be changed for them into burning pitch and sulfur forever and ever.

“Then the Church, the bride of Christ, long oppressed here in pilgrimage by the Babylonians, will be led by her Bridegroom out of the Babylonian exile and, amid the great rejoicing of the angels, will be brought into the heavenly city of the Father, Jerusalem. Then the righteous will shine like the sun and will be equal to the angels, and, when all things have been renewed, God will be all in all” (1 Cor. XV).

Therefore, beloved, it is already the hour for us to rise from the sleep of sloth, so that we may be vigilant in good works and joyfully receive Christ when he comes, so that he may conform the body of our humility to the likeness of the body of his glory (Phil. III).

Above is sweetness; below is bitterness; and in this world, which lies between the two, there is a shadowy image. Therefore, may the sweetness of heaven draw us upward and the bitterness of hell drive us onward, so that we may dread the misery of this middle life and receive the glory of the blessed life, full of joy.

Once the world flourished in glory and wealth and was strong in cities and power, yet the righteous despised its adornment, by which they could have shone abundantly. Now the world’s glory has withered; now all the honor of the age has faded away, and we miserable people embrace its dry flower with all our heart. We follow with all our desire what is fleeing from us and mocking us.

And because charity has now grown cold, so that no one’s prayer and no one’s merit supports it, the world, worn out by old age and driven by excessive iniquity, is already collapsing as quickly as possible and crushing all who cling to it in mind.

Now, beloved, let us raise our hearts with our hands to God and anticipate his face in confession, so that, at the approaching feast, he may visit us with his salvation and, when he comes, place us—going out to meet him—in the heavenly palace.

# The Five Degrees of Exercise by Which the Righteous Are Exercised in This Life, and the Five States

There are four things in which the life of the righteous is now exercised and by which, as though by certain steps, it is raised toward future perfection: reading, meditation, prayer, and action. Then a fifth follows, contemplation, in which, as though through the fruit of what precedes, even in this life one receives a foretaste of what the reward of good work will be.

Hence the Psalmist, speaking of God’s judgments and commending them, immediately adds: “In keeping them there is great reward” (Ps. XVIII).

Of these five degrees, the first, reading, belongs to beginners; the highest, contemplation, belongs to the perfect. As for the middle degrees, the more of them a person ascends, the more perfect he will be.

For example: first, reading gives understanding; second, meditation provides counsel; third, prayer asks; fourth, action seeks; fifth, contemplation finds.

If you read and have understanding, and already know what must be done, that is the beginning of good; but it is still not enough for you, and you are not yet perfect. Therefore, climb into the citadel of counsel and meditate on how you may fulfill what you have learned must be done. Many have knowledge, but few know how one ought to know.

Again, since human counsel is weak and ineffective without divine assistance, raise yourself to prayer and ask for his help, without which you can do no good, so that his grace—which illuminated you by going before you—may also, by following after you, direct your feet into the way of peace and bring to completion in good action what as yet exists only in the will.

Then it remains for you to gird yourself for good work, so that, by acting, you may deserve to receive what you ask for in prayer. God wills you to perform the third step, action; you are not compelled, but helped. If you act alone, you accomplish nothing; if God alone acts, you deserve nothing. Therefore, let God work so that you may be able to act, and let you act so that you may deserve something.

Good action is the way by which one travels to life. Whoever runs along this way seeks life. Take courage and act manfully. This way has its reward whenever, wearied by its labors, we are illumined by the grace of heavenly regard, tasting and seeing that the Lord is sweet.

Thus what was said above comes to pass: prayer seeks, contemplation finds. You see, therefore, how perfection meets those who ascend through these degrees, so that one who remains below cannot be perfect.

Our purpose, then, must always be to ascend. But the mutability of our life is so great that we cannot remain in the same state; often we are forced to look back at what has passed, and, lest we lose what we have attained, sometimes we return to what we have left behind.

For example, one who is diligent in action prays that he may not fail. One who devotes himself to prayer meditates on what he ought to pray for, lest he offend even while praying. One who at some point trusts too little in his own counsel consults reading. Thus it happens that, although we always wish to ascend, necessity sometimes compels us to descend—yet in such a way that our purpose consists in the will, not in the necessity. What we ascend is our purpose; what we descend is for the sake of that purpose. The former, therefore, should be primary.

We must now examine how many states of human mutability there are. Human life has five states, through which, because it can never remain long in the same condition, it changes without interruption, either progressing toward better things or failing and declining toward worse. They are: the joy of vanity, the sorrow of confusion, the joy of consolation, the sorrow of exercise, and the joy of happiness.

The joy of vanity is rejoicing over temporal profits. The sorrow of confusion is grieving over temporal losses. The joy of consolation is resting from the assault of vices. The sorrow of exercise is enduring the troubles of temptations. The joy of happiness is tasting the delight of inward sweetness.

Through the joy of vanity the soul is distanced farther from God, because the more eagerly it pours itself out toward external pleasures, the farther it withdraws from him who is within. The sorrow of confusion indeed cuts off bad pleasure, as it were, externally, and compels the soul to return within; yet, precisely because it is drawn back to itself not willingly but somehow under compulsion, it neither abandons the inner self completely nor is truly restored to the integrity of virtue.

The joy of consolation, however, already somehow cherishes and composes the mind inwardly, and persuades it to choose to remain with itself, rather than deign to seek outside what it can possess more truly and securely within. The sorrow of exercise, moreover, excludes from the mind all memory of external love, so that, while it is compelled to attend to its inward sorrow, it scarcely remembers what is pleasurable outside.

Finally, the joy of happiness causes a person even to forget himself, because, while the mind, lifted above itself, longs wholly for the sweetness of heavenly joys, it not only remembers no lowly pleasure, but also, in a certain blessed way, forgets itself.

Thus the joy of vanity scatters the mind; the sorrow of confusion gathers it; the joy of consolation composes it; the sorrow of exercise binds it; and the joy of happiness heals it.

Yet it sometimes happens that the joy of vanity is transformed for some into the joy of consolation; and, conversely, some misuse the joy of consolation because of the joy of vanity. Again, for some the sorrow of confusion is transformed into the sorrow of exercise, while for others the sorrow of exercise is changed into the sorrow of confusion.

To these five states of human mutability, then, let five natural powers of the soul be added.

The first possesses a twofold power and is therefore called “sensitive” in both respects. It gives our understanding the sense by which we recognize incorporeal things through various acts of imagination. It also makes the bodily senses active—sight, hearing, smell, taste, and touch—through which touch we perceive hard and soft, smooth and rough things.

The second is called commanding. It orders the bodily organs to perform the various movements it has determined to accomplish: to move from place to place, to produce sounds, and to bend the limbs.

The third is called principal. When we are withdrawn from every activity and restored to leisure, we consider something more deeply and firmly through the bodily senses at rest. Hence mature people, though not excessively old—for excessive old age diminishes the senses—are judged to have better understanding in their weakness. As the limbs grow old and the bodily senses are softened, they pass for the most part into counsel; and, while the mind is more fully occupied there, it is made stronger through the power of unification.

The fourth is vital: the soul’s natural heat, which, because of its fervor, gives us life and health as we draw in and release the ethereal breezes, so that its heat may be moderated.

The fifth is pleasure, that is, the appetite for good and evil, which the mind desires under the appearance of delight. This appetite is divided into four species.

The first is attractive, drawing from nature what it perceives to be necessary for itself. The second is retentive, holding on to what has been taken in until useful digestion has been produced from it. The third is transformative, converting and transferring what has been received into something else. The fourth is eliminative, which, so that nature may be free, drives away what would harm it.

# AT THE DEDICATION OF A CHURCH  
## According to Luke

[Col. 1225]

[Col. 1225B] “Jesus entered and was passing through Jericho. And behold, there was a man named Zacchaeus. He was the chief of the tax collectors, and he was rich. He was seeking to see who Jesus was, but he could not because of the crowd, since he was small in stature. Running ahead, he climbed a sycamore tree to see him, because he was going to pass that way” (Luke XIX).

Behold the camel, having laid down the burden of its hump, passing through the eye of a needle: that is, the rich tax collector, having abandoned the burden of riches and rejected the revenue of fraud, ascends the narrow gate and confined way that leads to life. And because, through the devotion of faith, he desired to see the Savior, he supplies by climbing the tree what he lacked by nature.

Rightly he receives the blessing of the Lord’s reception, which he did not dare to request but desired.
