Since the crowd is also the ignorant confusion of the multitude, which cannot see the summit of wisdom, rightly he receives the blessing he desires not in the crowd but by passing beyond the uninstructed people.

Zacchaeus, however, is interpreted as “justified” and signifies believers from the Gentiles, weighed down and made insignificant by their involvement in temporal affairs, but sanctified by the Lord. They seek the Savior entering Jericho while they desire to share in the grace of faith that the Savior brought, but the crowd of harmful habitual vices delays them.

Therefore, it is necessary for the small man to rise above the obstacle of the crowd, abandon earthly things, and climb the tree of the cross. *Sycamore* is said to mean “foolish fig,” a tree resembling the mulberry in its leaves but surpassing it in height. Hence it is also called *celsa* by the Latins. The Lord’s cross nourishes believers like a fig tree, but is mocked by unbelievers as foolish.

“For we,” says the Apostle, “preach Christ crucified: to the Jews a stumbling block, but to the Gentiles foolishness; yet to those who are called, Jews and Gentiles alike, Christ the power of God and the wisdom of God” (1 Cor. I).

The small man climbs this tree when any humble person, conscious of his own weakness, cries: “But far be it from me to glory except in the cross of our Lord Jesus Christ” (Gal. VI). He sees the passing Lord when, as far as he can, he attends to heavenly wisdom in the mystery of the cross.

Finally, he was going to pass by there—that is, in the place where the sycamore was, namely, where the Jewish people were, or where the Gentile people were going to believe—in order both to preserve the mystery and to sow grace. For he had come so that he might pass through the Jews to the Gentiles.

“And when he had come to the place, Jesus looked up and saw him.” Already, through the sublimity of faith, he stood out among the fruits of new works, as though at the fruitful height of a tree. Through the heralds of his word, in whom Jesus was present and speaking, he came to the people of the nations, because they were already exalted by faith in his Passion and burned to recognize his divinity as well.

He looks up and sees him because, through faith, he raises up the one lifted from earthly things, and he loves the one who loves him.

[Col. 1226D] “And he said to him: ‘Zacchaeus, hurry and come down, because today I must remain in your house.’ And he hurried down and received him joyfully.”

The invited man invites in turn, because, even if he had not yet heard the voice of the one inviting him, he had heard his affection. Therefore, today he must remain in the house of little Zacchaeus: that is, he must rest, shining with the new grace of light, in the humble heart of the believing nations.

That he is ordered to descend from the sycamore and thus prepare a dwelling for Christ in his house is what the Apostle says: “And if we have known Christ according to the flesh, yet now we know him no longer” (2 Cor. V). “For even if he died through the weakness of the flesh, yet he lives through the power of God” (2 Cor. XIII).

[Col. 1227A] “And when they all saw it, they murmured, saying that he had gone in to a sinful man.”

It is evident that the Jews have always hated, or failed to understand, the salvation of the Gentiles. Hence even the faithful brothers spoke against the leader of the nations: “Why did you enter men who had foreskins and eat with them?” (Acts XI).

“Then Zacchaeus stood and said to Jesus: ‘Behold, Lord, I give half of my possessions to the poor; and if I have defrauded anyone of anything, I restore it fourfold.’”

Zacchaeus stood—that is, persisting in the faith he had received—and showed that he had been completely converted to the Lord. Therefore, if he had defrauded anyone of anything, he restored it fourfold, because the ancient statutes of the Church decreed that one who seized another’s property should not go unpunished but should restore everything with increase.

The laws of the world likewise provide that one who steals another’s property must restore it fourfold to the person from whom he stole it. When Zacchaeus readily promises to distribute half of his possessions to the poor, he also implies that he would not refuse to give the whole.

[Col. 1227B] “Jesus said to him: ‘Today salvation has come to this house, because he too is a son of Abraham.’”

He is called a son of Abraham not because he was begotten from Abraham’s lineage, but because he imitated Abraham’s faith. The salvation that once belonged to the Jews has today shone upon the people of the nations who believe in the Lord.

Hence the Apostle says: “If you belong to Christ, then you are Abraham’s seed” (Gal. III). “For the Son of Man came to seek and save what was lost.” Hence he says elsewhere: “I have not come to call the righteous, but sinners to repentance” (Matt. IX).

## SERMON AT THE DEDICATION OF A CHURCH

[Col. 1227C]

On the sacrament of the dedication of a church, in which all the other sacraments are celebrated, it seems appropriate that we should speak for the benefit of those who do not know these things. The sacraments, then, are evidently of three kinds: some concern salvation, others administration, and others exercise: the first for healing, the second for office, the third for practice. Those that concern administration or preparation are connected with the orders, since the orders themselves are sacraments, as are the things considered in connection with the orders, such as sacred vestments and vessels, and similar objects. All these things, which, as has been said, are considered in connection with the orders themselves, ought not to have been treated separately. All the other sacraments, however, for the preparation and sanctification of which [Col. 1227D] these things were introduced as instruments, require to be treated afterward. And first, as has been said, we shall speak of the dedication of the church as of a first baptism, by which the church itself is in a certain manner baptized first, so that afterward human beings, who are to be regenerated for salvation, may be baptized in it.

For the first sacrament is, as it were, recognized in baptism, through which all the faithful are counted among the members of Christ’s body by the grace of a new birth. Therefore this first matter presents itself for treatment: it is first represented in the dedication of the church, and afterward manifested in the sanctification of the faithful soul. For whatever is visibly expressed here in this house of prayer by way of figure is wholly manifested in the faithful soul through invisible reality. For the reality itself is the temple of God, [Col. 1228A] built through the contemplation of the virtues, like a structure of spiritual stones, where faith lays the foundation. Hope demands the building; charity places the finishing touch.

The Church itself, too, gathered together from a multitude of believers into one, is the house of God constructed from living stones. Christ has been placed there as the cornerstone, joining the two walls—the Jews and the nations—together in one faith. We have therefore first set forth the form of this sacrament, which is displayed in the dedication of a church, so that afterward we may seek the mystical understanding of the faith formed in it. But first let us examine what is invisibly enacted in it.

The bishop first blesses water, mixing into it salt as a type. Then he sprinkles the church itself from outside, going around it three [Col. 1228B] times, while the clergy and people follow. Meanwhile, twelve lights are kindled inside, around the church that is to be dedicated. Each time he comes to the door of the basilica—which, because of the sacramental symbolism, ought to be closed—he strikes its threshold with his pastoral staff, saying: “Lift up your gates, O princes, and be lifted up, you everlasting doors, and the King of glory shall enter” (Psalm 23). The deacon standing inside answers him: “Who is this King of glory?” (ibid.). The bishop replies: “The Lord of hosts, he is the King of glory” (ibid.).

Then, at the third time, when the door has been opened, the bishop enters with the clergy and people for the third time, saying: “Peace to this house” (Luke 10). Then he prostrates himself with the priests, Levites, and clerics for prayer, for [Col. 1228C] the sanctification of the house that is to be dedicated. Afterward, rising from prayer, he does not yet greet the people by saying, “The Lord be with you,” but merely exhorts everyone to pray.

When these things have been completed, he begins at the left-hand eastern corner of the basilica and writes the alphabet across the pavement as far as the right-hand western corner; then from the right-hand eastern corner to the left-hand western corner. After this he ascends to a higher place and, standing before the altar, calls upon God for help, saying: “O God, come to my assistance” (Psalm 69). He completes the verse with “Glory be to the Father,” without “Alleluia.”

After this he blesses water, mixing in salt and ashes, and makes the sign of the cross over it three times. Wine is also added to this mixture. [Col. 1228D] Then he dips his finger into the water and makes a cross on the four horns of the altar. From there he comes before the altar and, going around it, sprinkles it seven times with a sprinkler made of hyssop. Then he goes around the entire church inside three times, sprinkling its walls with the same water, and does this also for the third time.

Meanwhile the psalm “Let God arise” is sung (Psalm 67), with an antiphon. The antiphon “He who dwells in the shelter of the Most High” is also sung (Psalm 90). Meanwhile the bishop himself goes around, passing through the middle of the church and singing: “My house shall be called a house of prayer” (Matthew 21). And again: “I shall declare your name to my brothers: in the midst of the church: I shall praise you” (Psalm 21).

When these things have been performed, the bishop prostrates himself in prayer, praying that all who [Col. 1229A] enter that same house to pray may rejoice that they have been heard. When the purification has been completed, he turns toward the altar and begins the antiphon “I shall go in to the altar of God” (Psalm 42), together with the psalm itself, and pours whatever remains of the purifying water at the base of the altar.

Then he dries the altar itself with a linen cloth, and the bishop brings incense upon it. Afterward he makes a cross in the middle of the altar and, with sanctified oil, makes one at its four corners. Then, around the church, twelve crosses are anointed on the walls by the bishop himself, three represented on each. Afterward they return to the altar, which has been lighted; incense is offered upon it in the form of a cross. Finally, when the consecration has been completed, the altar itself is covered with white veils.

This concerns the visible dedication; but what mystery [Col. 1229B] these things contain must now be considered by us.

## Division

Many profound mysteries lie hidden in all these things. Of them let us touch upon a few, to awaken the memory. The house that is to be dedicated is the soul that is to be sanctified; for water is repentance, washing away the filth of sins. Salt is the divine word, biting through rebuke and seasoning hearts that are insipid. The threefold sprinkling is the threefold immersion by which one is purified through water.

The twelve lights are the apostles, illuminating the Church through the four quarters of the world and carrying the mystery of the cross throughout the world. The bishop is Christ; the staff is power; the threefold striking of the threshold signifies dominion over heaven, earth, and hell. The question of the one enclosed within signifies the ignorance of the people; [Col. 1229C] the opening of the door signifies the removal of sin.

As the bishop enters the church, he invokes the Lord’s peace, because when Christ entered the world he made peace between God and humanity. Prostrate, he prays for the sanctification of the house; and Christ, humbled, prays to the Father for his disciples and for all who would believe, saying: “Father, sanctify them in your name” (John 17).

When he rises from prayer, he does not greet the people, because those who have not yet been sanctified ought not to be applauded, but prayed for. The writing of the alphabet signifies the simple teaching of faith; the pavement signifies the human heart. The alphabet is written on the pavement because the carnal people are initiated through the first and simplest teaching.

The line drawn from the left eastern corner to the right western corner, and then from the right eastern corner to the left western [Col. 1229D] corner, expresses the form of the cross, because it is impressed upon the minds of human beings through faith in evangelical preaching. And because faith was first among the Jews and afterward passed to the nations, and again at the end, when the fullness of the nations has entered, all Israel will be saved, these two lines, joined together in the figure of the cross, signify the gathering of both peoples.

This is what Jacob did when, blessing Joseph’s sons, he expressed the form of the cross with his crossed hands, placing his right hand upon Ephraim’s head and his left upon Manasseh’s (Genesis 48), because, with the earlier people rejected, the younger was placed on the right.

The *cambuca*, or pastoral staff, which Scripture is represented by, signifies the mystery of the teachers, through whose labor and preaching the conversion of the nations has taken place and that [Col. 1230A] of the Jews is to be completed. The fact that he stands before the altar and calls upon God for help signifies those who, through knowledge of the precepts of faith, gird themselves for good works and for struggle against invisible enemies; and because they rely less upon their own strength, they ask that divine assistance be present to them. Since the labor of those who struggle is expressed in this, as though amid sighs and groans, “Alleluia” is not yet named.

After this the water is blessed with salt and ashes, with wine mixed into the water. The water is the people; the salt, teaching; the ashes, remembrance of Christ’s passion; the wine mixed with water, the body that is God and human. Wine signifies divinity, water mortality. Thus the people are sanctified by the teaching of faith and by remembrance of Christ’s passion, united to their head, who is God and human.

After this the church [Col. 1230B] is sprinkled inside with sanctified water, so that the sanctified soul may be shown both inwardly and outwardly. The sprinkler of hyssop signifies Christ’s humility, by which the sprinkled holy Church is cleansed.

The bishop goes around the altar, sprinkling the whole church, as though purifying everyone and caring for all, making himself available to all through word and example. For this reason he also completes the work with prayer, praying that those who ask righteous things there may be heard, because the work of a human being without divine assistance can exist, but cannot be fruitful.

Finally, when the purification has been completed, the bishop turns toward the altar and pours at its base what remains of the purifying water, as though entrusting to God whatever remains beyond his own strength [Col. 1230C] in the perfection of the mystery. Then the altar is dried with a linen cloth. The altar is Christ, upon whom we offer the gift of our devotion to the Father. The linen cloth is his flesh, brought through the blows of the passion to the brightness of incorruption.

The incense signifies the prayers of the saints; the oil signifies the grace of the Holy Spirit, whose fullness went before in the head. From there the participation flowed down to the members. For this reason twelve crosses are anointed with chrism on the walls from the consecrated altar, because spiritual grace descended from Christ upon the apostles, so that they might preach the mystery of the cross through the four quarters of the world with faith in the Trinity.

The white veil with which the altar is covered after the consecration signifies the glory of incorruption, with which Christ’s humanity was clothed after mortality had been consumed through the passion, [Col. 1230D] as it is written: “You tore off my sackcloth and clothed me with gladness” (Psalm 29).

## Sermon on the Dedication

“May the infusion of the Holy Spirit, Lord, cleanse our hearts, and may he make them fruitful through the inward sprinkling of his dew” (Mass prayer).

“Break new ground for yourselves, and do not sow upon thorns” (Jeremiah 4). The Lord says in the Gospel: “No one puts new wine into old wineskins; otherwise the wineskins burst, the wine is spilled, and the wineskins perish. But new wine must be put into new wineskins, and both are preserved” (Matthew 9).

Some wine causes a person to break forth into tears; at other times it also makes the human heart glad. New wine is the word of God, which continually brings new joy to a righteous person. The old wineskins, however, are carnal minds [Col. 1231A], which by their evil conscience deserve the losses of the soul.

Therefore we must say from our inmost hearts: “Create in me a clean heart, O God” (Psalm 51). But if you have been converted and have acquired a right heart through the Lord’s commandments, this will immediately be fulfilled in you: “Turn the wicked, and they will not be wicked.” And when our hearts finally become new, they will retain the new wine.

“His foundations are in the holy mountains; the Lord loves the gates of Zion above all the tents of Jacob” (Psalm 86). The foundations of the Church are the holy prophets, the twelve holy apostles, and also the holy teaching brought forth from their mouths.

The holy gates of the Church, which are [Col. 1231B] dearer to almighty God than all the things prefigured in the Old Testament, are holy virtues joined with good works—namely, holy faith, hope, and charity, and also holy baptism. Those who have sinned after baptism should hasten to these gates of salvation: true repentance, pure confession, and steadfast abstinence from sins.

Over this house, therefore, we plead today with almighty God that whatever good any human being asks of the Lord here, he may deserve to obtain. Today, too, the holy angels visit here their fellow citizens, toward whom they were formerly indignant, and the body of Jesus is received. Hence it is written: “Their angels always see the face of my Father” (Matthew 18).

Here, then, the holy angels ascend and descend today with great joy, approaching the soul [Col. 1231C] when it has been present in all the things it had loved through the flesh. When this soul has rested from external cares in its thoughts and has been, as it were, awake in heart in the contemplation of God, the holy angels undoubtedly meet it rejoicing.

But when the human mind has been struck by the heavy frailty of the body, it is darkened as if in a cloud, which has disturbed the brightness of perpetual light in it. And when, again, at the time of temptation, it falls back into its former thoughts and repeats the astonishing movements of the body, our fellow citizens flee from us, and the angels in heaven are ashamed of our excesses in their ranks.

Therefore, dearest ones, acquire for yourselves the spirit of counsel, so that you may conduct your case in such a way as to please God, possess the friendship of the angels, and hold the hereditary [Col. 1231D] right of the children of God.

Dearest ones, behold: you are standing in the house of the heavenly King. Here he calls his bride—namely, the soul of each person, which he bought with his own blood—and says:

“Rise, my beloved; shake off the dust of the old sin in which you lay asleep. Prepare a temple for me in your heart, because I wish to dwell in it if you abandon your sins. After all your abominations, return to me, and I will return to you.” (Augustine.)

Now, dearest ones, those who recognize themselves as children of the Church rightly celebrate the festivals of the Church. The holy Church is your mother. And if you are also children of the Church, you will rightly celebrate the festivals of its dedication.

Therefore, “Establish the solemn day in dense foliage, even to the horns of the altar” (Psalm 117). Today, then, discuss with one another [Col. 1232A] wherever you have gathered in the name of the Lord, so that you may come more blessedly to the final day of resurrection.

Finally, take care in your gatherings, from hour to hour and from day to day, to go as far as the horns of the altar. This altar is Christ himself, who on the cross offered the price of his sacred blood for us. “The horns are in his hands” (Habakkuk 3): they signify the nails with which his hands were pierced upon the cross.

Let us therefore strive daily, through prayers, fasts, chastity, and other good works, toward the goodness of God, so that when the end of life comes, if we cannot hang upon the cross in its entirety, at least we may be found hanging from one nail of the consecrated cross.

Of this altar God himself had said: “You shall make an altar of earth for me” (Exodus 20). This altar is the divine man, raised from the Virgin Mary and [Col. 1232B] descended from a royal lineage.

Therefore, “When all things were in the midst of silence, and night was making its way in its course, your almighty Word, Lord, came from the royal thrones” (Wisdom 18).

There had been two silences in the world, in such a way that scarcely anything concerning God was heard among the human race. There will also be another silence in eternal rest, where all tumult and worldly unrest are silent, and where they will have ineffable joy among the glittering and beautiful stones of paradise. This is the third silence.

The first silence was before the Law, lasting three thousand one hundred years. The second silence was after the Law and before grace; this was the middle silence. In the first silence they did not at all recognize either the sins they had committed or the prolonged death that was bearing down upon them; [Col. 1232C] rather, they were silent.

But when the Law was given through Moses and sins were revealed, sinners sought salvation, and the prophets broke the silence by proclaiming that the Savior would be born of the Virgin Mary. When they had cried out for nine hundred years, desiring the Lord’s advent, Christ came. Hence everything that was on earth became silent, because Christ had arrived.

For this is the silence in which, when Christ was born, everything that had been born happily cried out: “Have mercy, Lord, have mercy.” When the middle silence was broken in this way, peace, rest, mercy, and forgiveness of sins were bestowed upon the human race through Christ.

This Word of God still addresses the world: “Learn from me, because I am gentle and humble in heart” (Matthew 11). [Col. 1232D] But when mortals have attained blessedness, they will no longer have to cry out or pray; they will be silent and rest from the many groaning cries by which they had clamored that heaven be opened to them, according to the saying: “You tore off my sackcloth and clothed me with gladness” (Psalm 29).

In that middle silence, as was stated above, the almighty Word came from the royal thrones. Who? The Word of God, the Son of God, the King, the Son of the King. From where? From the council of his Father. To what place? To the gallows of the holy cross: from the royal seat to the workshop of mortal sin, from the brightness of heaven to the darkness of hell.

And for this reason he came from “royal thrones,” not from one royal throne, because those who have sought heavenly things with labor will each receive the crown of life, each possessing individual crowns and reigning with his Father in the kingdom [Col. 1233A] he prepared for those who love him from the beginning of the world, as it says there: “But to all who received him he gave power to become children of God, to those who believe in his name” (John 1).

If they are his children, it will also follow that they are kings. And if they are kings, it follows that each possesses a royal throne and each has his own kingdom. An earthly king, having many sons, can raise only one of them to imperial power; but the King of kings, however many sons he may have, grants each one a crown in his own kingdom.

This promise is not ours but Christ’s, who said to his heavenly Father: “I pray not only for these, but also for those who will believe in me through their word, that all may be one, as you, Father, are in me and I in you, that they too may be one in us, and that the world [Col. 1233B] may believe that you sent me” (John 17).

Hence: “Do not love the world, nor the things that are in the world” (1 John 2).

For Ecclesiastes said: “Vanity of vanities, and all is vanity” (Ecclesiastes 2). Everything that is in the world is nevertheless corruptible and vain. Yet this too is written: “God saw everything that he had made, and it was very good” (Genesis 1).

If they are good, then from where comes their vanity? Heaven, earth, the sun, the moon, the noble stars, the splendid face of Moses—all these came forth from the good Creator, and for that reason they are good. Yet if they are compared with God, they are nothing; and in comparison with God they will be much less than the tiny flame of a candle compared with the whole magnitude of the sun.

“All the rivers run into the sea, and the sea is not filled. To the place from which the rivers flow, there they return, [Col. 1233C] so that they may flow again.” Paul also touches upon this same point almost in these words: “For the form of this world is passing away” (1 Corinthians 7).

The same thing happens to us wretched people, who are made from earth and return again to earth. But those who will rise from the earth afterward are now born more blessed and will be much happier.

Dearest ones, let us at some time be reborn for labor, like a bird for flight. When we were born, we immediately heard from ourselves “A, a, a”; but not long afterward, because of the bitterness of death, that same “A, a, a” is repeated. However beautiful the flesh may have been, it will nevertheless become a corpse, and afterward dust.

Therefore note what Job says: “The fewness of my days is coming to an end shortly; release me, Lord, so that I may mourn my sorrow a little, before I go to a land dark and covered with the shadow of death” (Job 10).

Who, then, remembers those [Col. 1233D] who existed long before us? In the same way, after a hundred years or earlier, we too are forgotten. But may the First and the Last remember us. To him let our conversion be directed with our whole heart, and to him let our dedication be transferred, so that the things arranged in this temple may be transformed in us ourselves.

For it is written: “The temple of the Lord, the temple of the Lord, the temple of the Lord is holy” (Jeremiah 7). Paul also indicates this in these words: “The temple of God is holy, and you are that temple” (1 Corinthians 3).

Now, therefore, you must consider what the cemetery that is before the temple signifies; what the door signifies; what the threshold signifies; what the posts signify; what the door with all these parts signifies; what the walls signify; [Col. 1234A] what the cornerstones signify; what the pavement signifies; what the windows signify; what the altar signifies; and what the bells signify.

The cemetery signifies the rest we have on earth after death until the day of the universal resurrection, when we enter that homeland. Hence it is written: “We shall go rejoicing into the house of the Lord” (Psalm 121).

The threshold, where we first enter the temple, signifies the Old Law. The posts signify apostolic teaching and the Gospel. The doorposts, or what is above the threshold and contains both sides, signify the grace of the Holy Spirit. The door as a whole, together with the parts mentioned, signifies the Catholic faith, through which we enter the Church.

The walls, in which one stone is placed upon another, signify that each of us should bear [Col. 1234B] the burden of another, as it is written: “Bear one another’s burdens, etc.” (Galatians 6).

The cornerstones are the gifts of the Holy Spirit, which contain within the eternal temple the two classes of human beings, namely Jews and nations.

The pavement, worn by the feet of all who enter the church, signifies humility, as Christ himself says: “Whoever exalts himself will be humbled” (Matthew 18).

The high window signifies our five senses, which we ought to carry so high above the earth that we may be able to receive the heavenly light, and so that the ancient thief, namely the devil, may be utterly unable to break into them.

The altar is God himself, whom we ought to possess in our steadfast heart. Of it is written: “Jacob raised a stone as a pillar, pouring oil upon it” (Genesis 28).

The bells signify our daily [Col. 1234C] calling into the Church, as in the saying: “Walk while you have the light” (John 12). And again: “Turn to me with all your heart” (Joel 2). And further: “I do not desire the death of a sinner” (Ezekiel 18). Also: “Repent, for the kingdom of heaven will draw near” (Matthew 3).

May the Holy Spirit, dearest ones, graciously grant you this calling, so that you may understand it in such a way that all of you together may reach the hall that receives no stain. May he himself grant this to you, who, having died for you, lives and reigns as God forever and ever. Amen.

## Again, on the Dedication

As your holiness, my brothers and lords, [Col. 1234D] knows very well, today we celebrate the festival of the dedication of the temple, in which the stone was either blessed or anointed, and in which the divine sacrifices are consecrated for us.

When we celebrate these festivals, let us pay careful attention, so that we may strive with all our strength to ensure that what is visibly worshiped in temples made by human hands may also be invisibly completed in us. For although the temples we see constructed from wood and stones are holy, the temples of our heart and body are nevertheless holier before God.

Temples made from wood and stones are assembled through human ingenuity; but the temples of our bodies and hearts are fashioned by a heavenly hand. Concerning this building—namely, the spiritual house—the wise Solomon says: “Wisdom built herself a house; she hewed out her seven pillars” (Proverbs 9).

This house, which [Col. 1235A] Wisdom built for herself, is required of us not only to be dedicated but also to be built inwardly by us. For the present is the time for building it in us, not for dedicating it. The dedication of a house cannot and ought not to take place when its construction is begun or when its middle portion is being built, but rather when it is completed.

Hence there is a great difference between building and dedication. They differ in place, in time, in the quality of the things, and in the quality of the persons.

They differ in place because this house must be built on earth but dedicated in heaven. They differ in time because it must be built in time—that is, in this life—but it will be dedicated in eternity, that is, in the other life. They differ in the quality of the things because the building must now take place in the thing itself, namely in our heart and body; but before this [Col. 1235B] building is complete, dedication can exist only in hope.

For example, while we build this spiritual house in ourselves through sacred virtues, we must meanwhile hope that it will also be dedicated in eternal blessedness.

This building must be carried out through Wisdom, who built herself a house, hewed out seven pillars, set a table, sacrificed victims, mixed wine, and sent maidservants to invite people to the feast.

Wisdom, dearest ones, who built herself a house, is Christ, the power of God and the wisdom of God, who founded the Church from living and elect persons, so that he might dwell in it. To support this house she hewed out seven pillars, because she polished with every kind of wisdom and knowledge [Col. 1235C] the seven books called *hagiographa*, that is, sacred Scripture. Through their teaching the structure of the whole Church is supported toward heavenly things, just as some machine is balanced in the air upon columns.

The first pillar, therefore, is the book of John’s Apocalypse; the second, the book of Psalms; the third, the book of Proverbs; the fourth, Ecclesiastes; the fifth, the Song of Songs; the sixth, the Book of Wisdom; the seventh, Ecclesiasticus.

These seven pillars placed beneath the house of God were afterward painted and made illustrious by noble painters—Gregory, Augustine, and others, and still others who loved the beauty of the house of God—through their exposition, as it were through splendid painting.

In such a house Wisdom set a table when she taught the faithful sacred Scripture everywhere. This table is supported by four feet, because sacred Scripture is understood in four ways. The first foot is history, when [Col. 1235D] it is taken as the letter narrates it. The second is allegory, when one thing is said but another is understood. The third is morality, when conduct is instructed through what is read. The fourth is anagogy, that is, the higher sense, when heavenly and eternal things are taught.

Upon this table different people served different dishes and satisfied the guests with various interpretations as with various courses. Moses, when he recounted the creation of the world, the ordering of paradise, the inundation of the Flood, Abraham’s obedience, Joseph’s chastity, the liberation of the children of Israel, their journey through the Red Sea and the wilderness, the manna raining down for them from heaven, and the water flowing from the rock, brought to those feasting, as it were, sweet dishes of various kinds.

David and the other prophets, when they sweetly narrated the sweetness of the heavenly [Col. 1236A] homeland, offered the diners, as it were, sweet cups.

In this house she sacrificed victims when he sacrificed his body to God the Father for the human race. “She mixed wine” (Proverbs 9) when he poured out his blood for our redemption. In some places wine is mixed with water because of its strength; therefore he says, “she mixed wine,” because from Christ’s side there flowed water mixed with blood.

To invite people to these feasts he sent not servants but maidservants, because he sent not noblemen but apostles—rustic men, namely fishermen—to invite the peoples to the heavenly banquet.

The building of this house must also take place through justice, that is, through holy virtues, which are bestowed upon us from divine grace. Its dedication, however, will be in [Col. 1236B] heavenly glory, when the works of the virtues have been completed.

There is a great difference in the quality of the persons who build and dedicate this house, because a human being cooperates with God in its building, but God alone will act in its dedication. Now, therefore, we must see how a human being cooperates with God in the building, and thus understand how God acts in the dedication.

The Lord Christ is the power of God and the wisdom of God. Christ is called the power and wisdom of God—that is, the Anointed One—because the Holy Spirit came upon him and anointed him, giving him the gifts of all graces beyond measure, above all other human beings, whom that same Holy Spirit had filled.

From this anointing, or from this abundance of all graces, he is pleased to anoint us, and through [Col. 1236C] our anointing to build his house in us. Although this house is his, and although he builds it in order to inhabit it, we also dwell with him in it; indeed, he is not in need of it, but we alone are in need.

Therefore, from the grace alone with which he overflows, and from the anointing of the Holy Spirit by which he was anointed by God above all mortals, he wishes to anoint his house in us—that is, to dedicate it. Since he himself is power, he can also build it as he wishes.

Although these three things—willing, knowing, and being able—cooperate with one another in the building of God’s house, nevertheless there is one house that Power builds for itself, another that Christ, that is, the Anointed One, builds for himself, and another that Wisdom [Col. 1236D] builds for herself.

The house that Power builds for itself in us and through us is first in time and is called the house of power or charity, because power is in charity. The house that Christ, that is, anointing, builds for himself is second and is called the house of anointing or delight, because the anointing by which a person is delighted is found in delight.

The house that Wisdom builds for herself is third and is called the house of wisdom or contemplation, because wisdom is in contemplation.

When these three houses are built in one heart, they are joined there as if into one house, so that there is, in a certain way, one and three houses: namely, the house of the one God and of the holy Trinity, Father, Son, and Holy Spirit.

When this house is built in us, it is not built without us. For we must be God’s fellow workers [Col. 1237A] in building his house in us. It must be built by persons such as Solomon was, who built the house of God (1 Kings 6).

Solomon is interpreted as “peaceful.” Truly peaceful was the one who came to us to build a house in us, so that he might be the tabernacle of God with human beings and dwell with them—that is, among them—and dwell in them—that is, within them.

With them, because he was found in human form (Philippians 2); within them, because he did not regard equality with God as something to be seized (ibid.).

Who, then, is this builder and inhabitant of the heavenly house of God? Certainly it is Wisdom the builder, that is, God and the Son of God. When, in the form of God, he had built a house in heaven—that is, in the angels—he took the form of a servant so that he might build a house, namely [Col. 1237B] the Church, for himself also on earth, that is, in human beings.

This builder of both houses is the true Solomon, who makes peaceful all things, whether those in heaven or those on earth (Colossians 1). Those who wish to cooperate with this Solomon in constructing the house of God—namely, the ministers of the Church—ought to be peaceful in their own measure.

## Division

The house that King Solomon built was first made of squared stones; second, he covered the house inside with cedar wood, fastening sheets of gold with golden nails, and made what was like a golden house within the cedar one (1 Kings 6). He placed the outer part in stone, the interior in cedar, and the innermost part in gold. While it was being built, neither hammer nor ax was [Col. 1237C] heard there (ibid.).

The first house, that is, the first part of the house, first presents itself to us as something to be built from squared stones. This squareness is both God’s and ours: it is God’s because it is from God; it is ours because it is in us. It was expressed by God and impressed by him upon us.

This squareness—that is, a firm and stable form—is found in Christ’s divinity and in Christ’s humanity; it is also found in angels and in human beings.

In divinity there is this squared form by which divinity itself freely came to the human being, freely disfigured by vices: wisdom came to the foolish, charity to the enemy, justice to the unjust, so that, once formed according to itself, it might finally glorify him in itself.

In humanity there is the squared form by which the Son of God came in the [Col. 1237D] flesh and afterward conformed to himself in the flesh, that is, in humanity, those whom he had previously conformed to himself in spirit or soul, so that those who bore the image of the earthly one, namely Adam, might also bear the image of the heavenly one, namely Christ.

In the angels, the squared form is the firm and stable form by which they perpetually stand before God and serve him day and night.

In human beings, the squared form is that by which Christ became for human beings redemption, sanctification, justice, and wisdom (1 Corinthians 1).

He became redemption when he gave himself as the price for us through the sacrament of his passion and death. He became sanctification when through him we were sanctified for the remission of sins through the sacrament of baptism. Christ became justice for us when through him the gifts of the Holy Spirit were bestowed upon us through the sacrament of confirmation. [Col. 1238A] He also became wisdom through contemplation, in a certain present recompense of merits, through the sacrament of the altar.

Behold how the living stones are squared and formed—that is, made firm and established—by Christ and in Christ.

But these living stones must here be struck and polished by the hammer and ax—that is, by fear of eternal fire, fear of purgatorial fire, or the threat of the sufferings of the present life—so that they may be cut away from their wicked actions and placed into the structure of the heavenly house.

This first house is called the house of virtue and love, because it is built by love of God and of one’s neighbor, together with the other virtues. After the outer stone house comes the cedar house, which is called the house of anointing, or of delight, or of joy. Whoever enters this second house has first experienced in the former house that the yoke of Christ is easy and his burden light (Matt. 11), through perfect love of God and of one’s neighbor. The less he loves the world, the more he delights in Christ; turning away from carnal joy, he rejoices in the Holy Spirit. Such joys in the second house are cedar wood, because just as there was great hardness and harshness in acquiring, exercising, and perfecting the virtues during the construction of the first house, so here there is only softness and gentleness—that is, only sweetness and gladness. And just as cedars are lofty in height and incorruptible by nature, so the person who delights in the good, rejoices in the Holy Spirit, lifts his heart upward, and keeps it unharmed by the rottenness of vices is like a cedar.

After the first and second houses—that is, the stone and cedar houses—comes the third, namely the golden house. This was fastened with golden plates to the cedar wood by golden nails. This house is called the house of contemplation and truth. Contemplation of truth is gold. If anything false has been mixed with that truth, the gold is impure; but contemplation of truth without any admixture of falsehood is pure gold.

What is contemplation of truth? It is contemplation of the Creator. And what is contemplation of the Creator? Contemplation of the Creator is contemplation of the highest good, apart from participation in which nothing that is called good by name is truly good. This highest good is contemplated by the pure in heart. Having passed through the stone house—that is, through love of God and of one’s neighbor, and through the exercise of the virtues—and having entered the cedar house, namely spiritual joy, such a person reaches the golden house, that is, purity of heart.

There he contemplates the wisdom and truth present in bodily creation, in accordance with which it was said that everything God had made was very good (Gen. 1). The pure in heart also contemplate wisdom and truth in that spiritual creation of which it was said that it was made in the image and likeness of God (ibid.). They likewise contemplate truth and wisdom in the highest good itself, namely God the Creator, by whom spiritual creation—that is, the inner human being—was created, justified, and made blessed.

The golden plates of the house signify contemplation of God in the spiritual life. The golden nails by which the golden plates had been fastened signify certain delights with which a person is pleased when he is engaged in contemplation. The fastening of the nails signifies a greater delight in the virtues, which every spiritual person who has led the contemplative life will possess.

Since, then, these three houses are built within us, we ourselves become entirely the house of God. Our body becomes the house of God because of the first; our spirit because of the second; our mind because of the third. This spiritual house—that is, the temple of the Church of God—was built by Solomon over seven years, because throughout the whole period of this age, which unfolds through eight days, its structure is continually increased. In the eighth year Solomon dedicated this same house to the Lord and provided all the children of Israel with a most celebrated and splendid festival of dedication.

That dedication clearly signifies the coming festival of the universal resurrection. For when the number of the elect has been completed at the end of the world, the solemnity of the long-desired immortality will immediately follow. After the common resurrection has taken place, all who belong to the kingdom of the peaceful King, namely the true Solomon, will enter with him into the eternal joys of the heavenly homeland. May our Lord Jesus Christ introduce us all together into that homeland of perpetual vision—he who lives and reigns in the unity of the Holy Spirit throughout all ages of ages. Amen.

## SERMON ON THE DEDICATION

“Christ loved the Church and gave himself for her, in order to sanctify her, cleansing her with the washing of water in the word of life, so that he himself might present to himself a glorious Church, not having spot or wrinkle, but that she might be holy and without blemish” (Eph. 5).

Listen, dearest brothers, to the apostle Paul, the messenger of our exaltation and the herald of our dignity. Listen to how great and what kind of love joined Christ to the Church; how great a grace he has displayed toward you through his mercy. For he says: “Christ loved the Church”—through gratuitous goodness, not through any succession of merits, because he loved us first.

But hear how greatly he loved her: “He gave himself for her,” and for her redemption. He did not send a prophet, an angel, or an archangel; rather, as the good shepherd, he laid down his life for his sheep (John 10), so that by humbling himself he might invite us to his humility. For he humbled himself even unto death, and so forth (Phil. 2)—that is, unto the death of a criminal. Therefore he first gave himself up, in order afterward to sanctify her, cleansing her with the washing of baptismal water. The water of baptism could receive no power unless, through the shedding of blood, the water were sanctified for the work of purification.

Thus the Church is said to have been born from Christ’s side. This mystery was prefigured from the beginning of the world in Adam. For the Lord cast a sleep upon Adam, took one of his ribs, and made a woman (Gen. 2). Adam’s sleep signifies Christ’s death. While he hung upon the cross, blood and water flowed from his side. These two sacraments are the origin of the Church.

Noah likewise, when he was making the ark during the flood, constructed an entrance in its side (Gen. 6), because the ark—that is, the Church—received from Christ’s side the door of faith and salvation. Hence the Lord says in the Song of Songs: “Rise, my beloved, and come, my dove, in the clefts of the rock” (Song 2). Rise from the corruption of vices, and come through good works, resting in the clefts of the rock. The clefts of the rock are Christ’s wounds; he is the rock, that is, the firmness of the Church. Hence the Apostle says: “The rock was Christ” (1 Cor. 10).

Therefore the Apostle first stated that God gave himself up, and afterward added, “in order to sanctify her with the washing” of baptism. He continues: “In the word of life,” because, after we have been redeemed and baptized, the word—that is, the necessary commandments of the Lord, which are life—has been given to us, since “man does not live by bread alone, but by every word of the Lord” (Matt. 4).

For this reason the table of the bread of the Presence was placed at the entrance of the tabernacle, and upon it were twelve loaves (Lev. 24), because those entering the Church need the nourishment of teaching and the table of the divine Scriptures, in which the sayings of the twelve apostles are contained, represented by the twelve loaves.

Therefore he sanctified her “so that he might present to himself a glorious Church,” through immortality, “not having spot,” namely of grave sin, “nor wrinkle,” namely of any resentment, “but holy,” through the virtues, “and without blemish,” free from vices. The Lord wishes to dwell in a clean hall adorned with the beauty of virtues. Hence the Psalmist says: “Lord, I have loved the beauty of your house” (Ps. 25). And elsewhere David says to the Church: “The king will desire your beauty” (Ps. 44).

For this Church, so loved and betrothed to the Lord, God established a bridal chamber and a house in which she might delight with her Bridegroom through the teaching of preaching, and in which, when she has fallen, she might be reconciled through confession and repentance.

This place, dearest brothers, where you have now assembled, is called a church or basilica. “Church” means “assembly,” because here everyone is summoned together, signifying that all, united in the same faith and love, become one body. It is called a basilica because it is a royal house: *basileus* is the Greek word for “king,” since this is the dwelling place of the true King.

The very structure of the building moves you to remember the ordering of your life. For in the construction of this material church there are various members that seem to signify something in us. This church has a head, a tower with bells, supporting columns, windows, a door, two walls, and individual stones joined together with mortar; all these things mystically signify something in us.

The head signifies Christ, who is the head of the Church, as the Apostle says; in him the treasure of divine mysteries is hidden (Col. 2). The head is lower than the body because Christ humbled himself, taking the flesh of a servant (Phil. 2) from God, and became lower than the angels according to his humanity. As long as he was lower than the angels, he was made subject to suffering; but after the resurrection he was raised above the angels.

David signifies both conditions when he says: “You made him a little lower than the angels” (Ps. 8), because human nature, being subject to suffering, corruption, and death, was lower than the angelic nature. But after the resurrection, “because you crowned him with the honor of immortality and set him over the works of your hands” (ibid.), that is, over angels and human beings, who are properly regarded as the works of God because of their dignity, since they are rational, as though God had created them with his own hands.

The tower is confession and repentance, to which captives have recourse. The cymbals are the priests, who are heralds of the Church and invite people to confession. Hence Isaiah admonishes: “Cry out, do not cease; raise your voice like a trumpet” (Isa. 58). And again: “You shall hear words from my mouth, and you shall announce them to them from me” (Ezek. 37).

The columns of the Church are preachers, who support the house of God by their preaching. They are silver, because they shine through the word of preaching. Silver is a bright and resonant metal. Thus silver signifies bright and resonant eloquence, as David says: “The sayings of the Lord are pure sayings,” and so forth (Ps. 12).

The windows signify the divine Scriptures, through which the sun of justice—that is, Christ—shines upon us, although in the present we do not see him openly. Hence the Apostle says: “Now we see through a mirror in an enigma” (1 Cor. 13), that is, in obscurity. Therefore the Church says in the Song of Songs: “My beloved looks upon me through the windows” (Song 2), that is, through revealed sayings.

The door is faith, because through it people enter the Church. The two walls are the two peoples, namely the Jewish and the gentile peoples, from whose conversion the Church was constituted. The individual stones are the individual faithful, who are joined together by the mortar of peace. Hence the Apostle says: “Preserve the unity of the Spirit in the bond of peace” (Eph. 4).

Therefore this place is useful not only for the celebration of sacred rites, but is also exceedingly useful for edification.

Moreover, this place is highly venerable because there the body and blood of the Lord are sanctified for our salvation. There children are baptized; there sinners are reconciled; there souls are nourished. Hence it is written: “My house shall be called a house of prayer” (Matt. 21). David promised what should be done in it: “I will enter into your house,” and so forth (Ps. 65).

It is so venerable that, when the Lord entered Jerusalem, he always went to the temple, giving us an example that whenever we enter cities we should first seek out the church. Hence the Gospel says: “When Jesus had entered Jerusalem, he entered the temple” (Matt. 21), and dedicated his house to the service of prayer. He drove out those selling and buying in the temple, saying: “My house,” and so forth (ibid.).

Because of this accusation he was seized and crucified by the Jews. When the Jews saw that he possessed such great power that he had driven them from the temple with a cord, they rose up against him. Therefore through David he said: “Zeal for your house has consumed me” (Ps. 69)—that is, love for my Church, which I defended, has consumed me and became the cause of my death.

But through his children, through his members, the devil assails the Church in every way. He even stirs up to their death the children of the Church whom she has begotten and nourished. Hence the mother asks, saying in the Song of Songs: “The sons of my mother fought against me” (Song 1); and elsewhere: “I nourished and exalted children,” and so forth (Isa. 1).

What greater contempt, what greater violation, what greater insolence is there than to lie in wait for the holy ministers of the Church in a holy place, in the hall of God, in the holy temple? Concerning such people the Apostle cries out: “Whoever violates the temple of God, God will destroy him” (1 Cor. 3).

## SERMON AT THE DEDICATION

That the festival of this day, namely the dedication of the holy temple, was foreseen and foretold long before it occurred by the prophet Ezekiel through the Holy Spirit is made clear by his own words. For in the final vision of his book he says that, taken up and led by the Spirit, he was brought to a very high mountain, and a building resembling a city facing south was shown to him.

There was a man standing at the gate, having an appearance like bronze, and in his hand something like a measuring reed. He spoke to him, saying: “See and understand” (Ezek. 40).

Elsewhere the same Ezekiel speaks of the consecration of the tabernacle under the figure of a Jewish woman, saying: “I washed you with water, anointed you with oil, clothed you in garments of various colors, and behold, you became mine” (Ezek. 16).

You know, beloved, that mountains are made of earth; yet by their height they rise above the earth. By them are signified those who, like living stones, are to be placed in the building of God. Although such people share in the condition of others because of the weakness of the flesh, they surpass others in the height of holiness. Concerning them the prophet David says: “I lifted up my eyes to the mountains” (Ps. 120).

They are also rightly compared to living stones, because just as stones are first squared and polished through many blows, so that at last they may be fitted into a building without noise or sound, so the saints in this life are crushed by many tribulations and smoothed by various persecutions, as though by hammers, so that they may be worthy to be placed without delay or hesitation in the building of the eternal house.

All this was prefigured in the construction of Solomon’s temple, in which no sound of hammer or axe was heard (1 Kings 6).

Since the prophet says that he was taken up to a very high mountain, he showed that by this mountain we should understand not the saints but Jesus Christ, the mediator between God and human beings. Concerning him another prophet says: “In the last days the mountain of the house of the Lord shall be prepared on the summit of the mountains, and it shall be raised above the hills” (Isa. 2), that is, so that it may be the head and summit of the other mountains.

Although he became a participant in our humanity, he surpasses all the saints in the eminence of his deity. To this mountain the prophet was brought—that is, he was established and confirmed in the faith of Christ. This faith is the sacrament of the Church, concerning which the Apostle says: “No one can lay another foundation apart from that which has been laid, which is Jesus Christ” (1 Cor. 3).

Isaiah says of the same foundation: “He will deliver us after two days” (Isa. 34). And again he himself says: “He bore our sicknesses and carried our sorrows” (Isa. 53). Concerning this foundation he says to Peter: “You are Peter, and upon this rock I will build my Church” (Matt. 16)—that is, upon this faith which you have confessed I will build my Church. For he had confessed him to be God and human being. Without this foundation no one will be able to reach the building mentioned above.

Relying upon this foundation and filled with the Holy Spirit, the prophet saw a building resembling a city facing south. It should be understood that the south and the north are contrary winds and locations, differing in opposite qualities. The north wind is cold and signifies the devil, who inhabits only the minds of wicked people frozen by cold. He is aptly signified by the north, because he himself said: “I will set my throne in the north” (Isa. 14).

The south wind, however, is warm and signifies the Holy Spirit. Hence it is said: “Rise, north wind, and come, south wind; blow through my garden, and let its spices flow” (Song 4). “Rise, north wind”—that is, withdraw, devil; “and come, south wind”—that is, Holy Spirit. The Bridegroom’s garden is the Church, which advances through the power of the Holy Spirit toward an increase of virtues.

Therefore it is rightly said that the city faces south, that is, appears to the Holy Spirit, because the entire structure of the heavenly building is held together and governed by his protection and power.

Concerning the order of the building, it should be understood that just as in a material structure there are three kinds of stones, so there are also three kinds in the spiritual building. Some stones there merely bear; some are merely borne; and some both bear and are borne.

Those that merely bear are the first ones in the Church, such as the apostles and prophets, who were not borne by others. Those that are merely borne, like the last ones, will be blessed. Those that both bear and are borne are the teachers and preachers of the present age.

It should also be noted that the merits of these three orders of the elect are distinguished by the twelve gems described in the twelve foundations of the heavenly city (Rev. 21).

The first stone is jasper, green in color, which displays the freshness of faith. Those who conquer vices and demons with the shield of faith will be in this building flourishing like jasper.

The second is sapphire, of an airy color, by which hope in heavenly things is signified. Those who rejoice in hope will shine in this building like sapphire.

The third is chalcedony, which has the appearance of fire, glowing faintly in the open air amid cloudiness and giving off radiance. It signifies those who conceal their good works because of popular approval but burn inwardly with fraternal love. They will shine in this building like chalcedony.

The fourth is emerald, which is placed above them. Its greenness surpasses that of grass and leaves, signifying those who through the fullness of faith perform signs and wonders. They will flash in this building like emerald.

The fifth follows, sardonyx, marked by three colors—black, white, and red. It signifies those who become black through humility, white through chastity, and red through charity, because they patiently endure adversity from their neighbors. Such people shine in the heavenly building like sardonyx.

The sixth is sardius, blood-red in color. It signifies the martyrs, who will radiate in this building like sardius.

The seventh is chrysolite, golden in color and sparkling like a furnace. It signifies those who burn with wisdom and sparkle with varied teachings. They will glow in this building like chrysolite.

The eighth is added: beryl, which is like the sun in clear water. It signifies those who, with pure minds, devote themselves to spiritual things. They will shine in this building like beryl.

The ninth is written as topaz, brilliant in various colors, especially gold and bronze. It signifies those who in the contemplative life gleam with wisdom, desire heavenly things with all their heart, and flourish through good works. They will flash in the ethereal building like topaz.

The tenth is chrysoprase, green and golden in color, emitting golden flames and small purple marks. It signifies those who are green with faith and fervent with charity, sending forth the flames of wisdom’s teachings and the small marks of good examples. They will shine in this building like chrysoprase.

The eleventh is hyacinth, blue in color: beautiful in calm weather, dark in stormy weather. It signifies those endowed with discernment, who change their conduct without fault according to the quality of the time. They will gleam in this building like hyacinth.

The twelfth is amethyst, purple and violet in color, interwoven with golden points. It signifies those who despise the world, die with Christ, and flourish through good actions. They will shine resplendently in the heavenly building like amethyst.

These are the twelve gems in which, as has been said, the merits of the elect are distinguished.

## DIVISION

The man whom Ezekiel saw when the building resembling a city was shown to him, standing at the gate and having an appearance like bronze (Ezek. 40), signifies Christ, who was firm against prosperity and adversity alike. He is said to stand at the gate. Hence the Song of Songs says: “He himself stands behind our wall, looking through the windows, gazing through the lattice” (Song 2).

Two natures are demonstrated in Christ. Just as the one standing at the gate is partly visible and partly concealed, so Christ appeared visibly to the world according to one nature and remained invisible in his majesty according to the other.

“And he had an appearance like bronze.” Bronze is highly resonant and durable by nature. So Christ’s preaching and teaching were resonant when he gathered Jews and gentiles into one. They are everlasting and enduring, as he himself testifies: “Heaven and earth will pass away, but my words will not pass away” (Matt. 24).

“And in his hand was a measuring reed” (Ezek. 40). The reed signifies Scripture, because in ancient times writing was done with a reed. Scripture is rightly called a measure, because by its commandments it is known how much each person is progressing or failing.

This measure is said to be in Christ’s hand, that is, in his activity, because the teacher’s speech labors outwardly in vain unless the grace of the Holy Spirit enlightens the mind inwardly.

Isaiah speaks of this reed when speaking of the Church: “The greenery of the reed and the rush will arise in it” (Isa. 35). The greenery of the reed signifies the light of the Scriptures; the greenery of the rush, which grows in water, signifies the grace of the Holy Spirit, which is given to the baptized in water.

“And he spoke to him, saying: ‘See and understand’” (Ezek. 40). This signifies that one cannot arrive at knowledge of this building except through inward sight and spiritual understanding.

As we said above, the same Ezekiel speaks in this way of the consecration of the tabernacle or church: “I washed you with water, anointed you with oil, clothed you in garments of various colors, and behold, you became mine” (Ezek. 9). It is clear that all these things are done by bishops in these buildings made by human hands. Yet all of it is done for our sake, because we are the temple of God. Hence it is said: “The temple of God is holy, and you are that temple” (1 Cor. 3).

Whatever is done in buildings made by human hands by bishops who consecrate them must all be done in the temples of our souls by us, as we prepare ourselves to be a temple for God.

Therefore now, beloved, we must consider the construction of the temple of God, that is, this house of prayer whose solemn festival of dedication we celebrate today. This house is formed according to the condition of the Church. Hence it is called a church, which means an assembly, because in it the people are summoned together to worship and pray to the one true God.

It is joined together by four walls, and the Church is consolidated by the four Gospels. It has a sanctuary in which the clergy stand, and an outer chamber in which the people stand. The Church likewise has the contemplative life, in which spiritual people dwell, and the active life, in which secular people are established.

The contemplative life is to abandon all earthly things for the love of God, seek only heavenly things, pray constantly, read often, and continually praise God with hymns and songs. The active life is to lead a chaste life with one’s spouse, raise children in the fear of God, refresh the poor with food and drink, visit the sick and widows, and, for the love of one’s neighbor, help as far as one can all who are suffering need.

In the sanctuary there is an altar containing the relics of the saints. This is Christ in the Church, in whose contemplation the minds of the blessed rest, and before whom the righteous rejoice, feast, and delight in gladness (Ps. 68).

The windows by which this house is illuminated are the teachers, through whom heavenly light enters the Church. The painted ceiling with which this Lord’s church is adorned is the lives and examples of the saints, which every devout person in the Church imitates. The unceasing light by which it is illuminated is the grace of the Holy Spirit, by which the Church is continually irradiated.

The cross of Christ is fixed here and adored, and Christ’s Passion is venerated by all Christians. We follow wherever the cross is carried, because we must follow Christ’s footsteps if we wish to come to the heavenly temple. The towers are the prelates of the Church, and their bells are their preaching.

From this house he drove out those selling and buying doves (Matt. 21). The doves are spiritual gifts. Therefore all who buy or sell churches, orders, or any spiritual gift are expelled from this temple with Simon Magus and cast into the eternal fire.

All these things, beloved, concern us. Everything has been made as an example for us. We are the temple of God, dedicated as a dwelling place for God, as it is written: “You are the temple of God” (2 Cor. 6). And again: “I will dwell in them, says the Lord, and they will be my people, and I will be their God. I will also be their father, and they will be my sons and daughters” (Exod. 25).

O how blessed is the person in whom God dwells! For just as this house is constructed from four walls, so the temple of our body is composed of four elements. And just as this house is first sprinkled with blessed water at its dedication and then consecrated with chrism, so our body is first washed with the water of baptism and then anointed with holy chrism.

Certain basilicas are built in the form of a cross, and our body is also fashioned in the form of a cross. The sanctuary of this temple is our mind, which handles spiritual things. The outer chamber is the soul, which through the bodily senses administers what is necessary for life.

The altar upon which sacrifices are offered is our heart, in which pure thoughts and clean prayers are kindled before God. The tower is our head; the bell is the tongue, with which we ought to call our neighbors to heavenly things. In this house the windows are our eyes, while the paintings are good works. The light of the lamp is the light of knowledge.

Therefore, just as the person who violates this temple commits sacrilege, so whoever violates the temple of God with any impurity or criminal sin will be destroyed and condemned by God.

When this house is blessed inwardly, it is sprinkled with ash, salt, wine, water, hyssop, and savin. Ash signifies repentance; salt, wisdom; wine, spiritual understanding; water, care for one’s neighbors.

We sprinkle our house with ash if we wash away past evils through repentance. We sprinkle it with salt if we savor only heavenly things. We sprinkle it with wine if we intoxicate ourselves with spiritual things. We mix in water if we do not neglect care for our neighbors. We sprinkle it with hyssop and savin, which are bitter herbs, if through fasts and vigils—bitter practices—we mortify vices within ourselves.

## On the Three Dedications

The dedication of the temple was held in great honor before the coming of Christ. Accordingly, three dedications of the temple are reported as having been celebrated before the Lord’s incarnation, with the greatest devotion of the Jewish people.

The first dedication was made by Solomon in autumn; the middle one by Zerubbabel and the priest Joshua in spring; and the last by Judas Maccabaeus in winter. In this last dedication, in particular, it is read that a decree was established that the same dedication should be commemorated every year with solemn rites.

Accordingly, it is demonstrated from the Gospel reading that this solemnity continued to be observed until the time of the Lord’s incarnation. For the evangelist John says: “The feast of the Dedication took place in Jerusalem, and it was winter, and Jesus was walking in Solomon’s portico” (John 10).

This was the reason for the second and third dedications. Solomon completed the work of the temple that he had built for the Lord in seven years; but in the eighth year, on the tenth day of the seventh month, which we call October, he dedicated it with great glory (1 Kings 8).

That day had previously also been established as solemn by the Law, so that on it the whole tabernacle was to be purified every year with greater sacrifices.

Finally, after 430 years, the Chaldeans burned this temple and, after destroying the city of Jerusalem, led the people of Israel captive to Babylon. When they were sent back to their homeland after seventy years, during the reign of the Persians, the temple was rebuilt over forty-six years. The work was completed on the third day of the twelfth month, which we call March, and it was dedicated in spring.

The most energetic leaders of the people presided over this work, as we said: Zerubbabel, of royal descent, and Joshua the high priest. The prophets Haggai and Zechariah also assisted them and strengthened the hearts of the people against the ambushes of the enemies who were obstructing the work (1 Esdras 3, 5).

Therefore, after approximately 356 years, the most wicked king of the Greeks, Antiochus, captured Jerusalem by treachery and profaned the same temple with the filth of idols. He removed and smashed the golden altar of the Lord, the table of the bread of the Presence, the lampstand of the light, and the other golden vessels of the temple that he could find. He also set up an image of Jupiter in the temple and forced the people by torture to sacrifice to idols.

But Judas Maccabaeus, being of priestly descent, gathered an army of the righteous, took up arms against the commanders of Antiochus, expelled them from Judea, and brought an end to the most savage persecution. He cleansed the temple of the images of idols, made new altars and the other vessels and ornaments, replaced them in the temple, and dedicated them together with the temple, which he had purified and renewed, on the twenty-fifth day of the ninth month, namely December. That it belonged to winter is beyond doubt.

He established a decree, as we said, that every year the day of the *encaenia*, that is, of the renewal and dedication of the temple, should be celebrated with festive devotion (1 Macc. 4).

All these events, dearest brothers, which took place under the ancient Law are figures of the new Law and have been preserved in memory for your sake.

Solomon, therefore, who built the house of the Lord in Jerusalem over seven years, dedicated it to the Lord in the eighth year, together with the children of Israel. On that day Solomon held a celebrated festival, and all Israel was with him in a great multitude.

The king prayed to the Lord, saying: “Hear, Lord, the prayer that your servant prays in this place, so that you may hear the prayer of your people Israel. Whatever they pray for in this place, when you hear it, be merciful. But if they sin against you—for there is no human being who does not sin—and, having done penance, they pray to you, you will be merciful to your people, because they have sinned against you” (1 Kings 8).

And the Lord said to him: “I have heard your prayer, which you entreated before me” (1 Kings 9).

The temple of the Lord built in ancient times was a type of ecclesiastical temples, and its dedication was an example of our dedication. If the house of the Lord was called the place where victims and sacrifices were offered, how much more should our house of prayer be called the place where the sacraments of his flesh and blood are celebrated?

And if the Lord promised that in that house he would hear the prayer of his people, how much more will our prayers be received in this one, where the true worshipers and those who commemorate the Lord’s Passion are present?

And if so great a festival was celebrated at the dedication of that temple, which was shadow-like and typical, how much joy do you think ought to be expressed at the consecration of our mother?

That it is said to have been built over seven years and dedicated in the eighth is clearly understood to have happened because of a great mystery.

This temple of Solomon, which he made for the Lord in Jerusalem over seven years from hewn and squared stones, had the form of the Mosaic tabernacle. For Moses had made the tabernacle in the wilderness and divided it into two parts.

In the first tabernacle there were a golden lampstand, a table, and the presentation of the loaves; these were called the holy things. A veil hung there, behind which was the second tabernacle, which was called the Holy of Holies.

In it there was a golden censer and an ark made of precious wood and the purest gold. In the ark was a golden urn containing manna, Aaron’s rod that had blossomed, and the tablets of the covenant. Above these was the mercy seat, above which were two angels called cherubim.

In the first tabernacle the priests sacrificed daily; in the second, once a year, the high priest sacrificed a red heifer for the whole people (Heb. 9).

Moses dedicated this tabernacle with the greatest reverence and established an annual festival for the people to celebrate. The Most High sanctified his own tabernacle when, sending the Holy Spirit, he cleansed the Church from sins and gave it many spiritual gifts and knowledge of every language.

Following this pattern of the tabernacle, Solomon, as has been said, built the temple.

## DIVISION
The Temple that was built by Solomon at Jerusalem over seven years [Col. 1248D] is the Church, which is established in heaven by the true peaceful one, Christ, through the seven gifts of the Holy Spirit. It is constructed from stones, cedars, and gold (3 Kings 8), because the heavenly building is raised from three orders: the married, the continent, and the contemplative. The stones selected for this structure are cut by repentance. Moreover, they are squared by the four virtues—namely, prudence, fortitude, justice, and temperance—and prepared for this building.

In the eighth year of the temple’s construction, the festival of its dedication took place, because after the period of this life—which is carried out in seven days and signified by seven years—there follows the supreme festival of the heavenly Jerusalem, which will be celebrated in the eighth year, that is, in the future resurrection. And just as [Col. 1249A] the ancient festival prefigured the feast of our dedication, so our dedication is a type of the supreme and eternal festival, in which we should keep the memory of the future resurrection in mind. These are the three dedications: the first, Solomon’s; the second, our festival; the third, the future resurrection.

That temple, burned by enemies but rebuilt again through the Lord’s mercy and reconstructed over forty-six years (1 Esdras 3), refers especially to the significance of the Lord’s body, which he assumed from the Virgin. For just as the temple was built over forty-six years, so the Lord’s body was raised to life on the third day, from which the aforesaid number derives.

It is said, indeed, that the human body is formed in the differentiation of its members on the forty-sixth day after the beginning of conception [Col. 1249B]. Thus, with that same number of years, the temple was also rebuilt by Jesus the priest, who leads the people out of Babylonian captivity. This Jesus is the true great priest, Jesus, who leads the Christian people back from diabolical captivity. He rebuilds the temple because through human beings he restores the ruin in heaven. He labored on the work of this temple for forty-six years because all who fulfill the ten commandments of the Law through the four Gospels and the six works of mercy advance toward this heavenly building.

But the fact that the same temple, defiled by idolaters yet cleansed, dedicated, and adorned with golden crowns by Judas Maccabaeus (1 Maccabees 4), signifies the Church’s varying circumstances: now she is oppressed by persecutions, [Col. 1249C] now she is liberated from persecutions; and in that liberation, as though in a peaceful dedication, she serves the Lord in tranquil submission. Behold the second dedication.

The festival of the third dedication will take place when, at the end of the world, the number of the elect has been completed, and after the general resurrection of all there follows the festival of eternal immortality. Immediately, all who belong to the kingdom of the true peaceful king, namely Solomon, will enter with him into the joys of the heavenly homeland. Behold the third dedication.

But since we have touched briefly upon certain matters concerning the mystery of the dedication, let us now consider the manner of that same festival. Since it would be lengthy to enumerate everything done in the consecration, let us briefly explain one of those things [Col. 1249D], so that through the others as well the cleansing of the interior of our temple may be understood.

Salt and ash, water and wine are mixed for sprinkling the doors of the church; they are sprinkled with hyssop. These things would not be observed with such care if they contributed nothing useful. Let there therefore be salt in us—that is, the sharpness of repentance—which consumes the rottenness of sins and preserves the integrity of virtues uncorrupted.
