Yet this salt is not sufficient unless ash is added: that is, the memory of our earthly condition or the recollection of sins. Hence the Psalmist says: “My sin is always against me” (Psalm 50). And again: “The remnants of thought”—that is, of sins—“will keep a feast for you” (Psalm 75). This ash moves the water of tears.

For you there are these three things: namely, the salt of repentance, [Col. 1250A] the ash of remembrance of our condition and sins. Spiritual wine will not be lacking either; by it the sons of men will be intoxicated from the abundance of God’s house (Psalm 35), so that they desire nothing apart from him and say: “What have I in heaven, and besides you what did I desire upon earth?” (Psalm 72). All these things must be sprinkled with the hyssop of humility. For whoever gathers virtues without humility carries them like dust into the wind.

For this consecration of the Church, that is, of our mother, all her sons, that is, the faithful, ought to assemble, rejoice, and congratulate their mother on her sanctification. But since her sons come from many regions and hasten to their mother with much labor, they ought not to depart from so great a festival without reward. For the holy Fathers have established that at the dedication of a holy church there should be remission of sins [Col. 1250B], so that, although at other times the cleansing of offenses takes place in it through baptism, at its festival they may rather experience the help of their mother through prayers.

But although, dearest brothers, remission is owed to you because of your labor and your rejoicing in this solemnity, you must nevertheless know that not every sin is forgiven you here, but only those of which you have confessed and for which you have performed worthy penance; for such sins you may obtain indulgence. For if someone wishes the guilt of his sins to be forgiven him, if he wishes his wounds to be healed, he must not conceal them from the physician. First the sinner must acknowledge the guilt of his sins, then show it, and afterward apply medicine to himself. First let him say: “For I acknowledge my iniquity”; then let him add: “I have made my offense known to you” [Col. 1250C]; finally let him say: “Have mercy on me, Lord, for I am weak” (Psalms 6; 50). By such confession or penance, the sinner earns the forgiveness of sins.

Now therefore, brothers, reflect and learn in this sacrament of dedication how great a reverence is owed to the sanctuary of your mother. Here sins are washed away in the water of baptism; here the sacraments of the Lord’s body and blood are consecrated; here prayers are poured out to the Lord; here confessions are made; here reconciliations take place. This is the house of God; this is the gate of heaven. Through it one ascends to the heavenly Jerusalem, which is our free mother. Cleanse your stains in it, so that, purified, you may be able to reach the royal wedding feast, with our Lord Jesus Christ granting and aiding you [Col. 1250D]. He lives and reigns as God with the Father and the Holy Spirit, forever and ever. Amen.

## SERMON TO BE DELIVERED SPECIFICALLY AT THE DEDICATION OF AN ALTAR

The sacred and venerable tradition of the ancient religion has established that altars should be built and consecrated to the Lord. Abraham, Moses himself, the lawgiver, and other holy men by their example and authority left this practice to be observed throughout all our generations.

This dedication of the altar was prefigured in the time of Jacob, son of Isaac. For when, having left his father, he was fleeing from his brother Esau and going to Laban to seek a wife, he took on the way one of the stones lying on the ground [Col. 1251A], placed it beneath his head, and slept in that place. In a dream he saw a ladder erected up to heaven, with angels ascending and descending. When he arose, he took the stone and set it up as a memorial, pouring oil over it; and he made an altar to the Lord, saying: “There is nothing else here but the house of God and the gate of heaven” (Genesis 28).

Behold, this ancient man, without the Law and without Scriptures, sanctified an altar to God and called it the house of the Lord, because through the Holy Spirit he foresaw that the dwelling of God would be there. All these things were figures of what was to come. Jacob, who, having left his father, went to Laban to seek a wife, signifies Jesus Christ, who, as though leaving the Father, abandoned heaven, assumed the flesh of our corruption, and then, leaving those parents from whom he had assumed flesh [Col. 1251B]—that is, the Jews—and leaving his homeland, went from Judaea to the Gentiles to take a bride, namely, the Church.

On this journey Jacob fell asleep, because Christ, on the journey of the present life, endured death upon the altar of the cross. The stone that Jacob placed beneath his head on the journey signifies Christ’s humanity, which is subject to divinity; God is truly believed to be Christ’s head. The ladder erected to heaven is the way and ascent of degrees and virtues. One ascends by various steps—that is, to the heavenly life. Some climb toward the heights through lawful marriage; others in widowhood; others in virginity; others, amid the tumult of the world, by fighting against the world and against the devil. Still others, rejecting the world’s clamor and conquering the spiritual enemy, have ascended by so many steps to heavenly things in the active life [Col. 1251C].

There are also steps in contemplation, by which monks or hermits rise to the heights. They have stripped off the world; they have despised themselves in humble clothing; by pursuing obedience, they have shown love. Thus three virtues especially reign in them, and by three steps of virtue—love, humility, and obedience—they transcend toward heavenly things. Brotherly love is shown in living together; humility is demonstrated in the lowliness of their clothing; obedience is declared in willing service, when they submit to the will of their brothers. By these various steps of virtue, heaven is entered in both the active and contemplative life.

The angels whom Jacob had seen ascending and descending are also holy preachers, announcing God’s word to us [Col. 1251D]. They are said to ascend when they preach higher things, and to descend when they preach humbler things: higher things, such as “In the beginning was the Word” (John 1); humbler things, such as when we preach the one who was crucified.

Jacob also called the stone that he had placed beneath his head the house of God and the gate of heaven. This stone, that is, Christ, was called the house of God because he himself was the dwelling place of the Holy Spirit, and in him the fullness of divinity dwelt.

The builders, that is, the Jews who followed the traditions of the Fathers, rejected this stone, or this altar—that is, Christ. Human beings began to build a wall against God out of sins. Its foundations were laid by our first parents through disobedience, but their descendants built many crimes upon this foundation and separated themselves by this wall from God and from the angels [Col. 1252A].

The Jews, as builders of this wall, rejected Christ, the precious stone, because they did not mix any stains of original sin into the mortar of this wall. Hence “he became for them a stone of stumbling and a rock of scandal” (1 Peter 2). The Church stands well founded and firmly established upon this stone.

Christ is also the altar, because in him and through him spiritual and bodily offerings are presented to God the Father. Through him as mediator and gracious intercessor, God the Father grants us present and future goods. This altar, that is, Christ, was spiritually anointed with the legal unguents with which altars were formerly anointed, as well as with the unguents with which ecclesiastical altars are anointed.

The unguent by which the ancient altar was consecrated and prepared consisted of five kinds of spices: myrrh, cinnamon, calamus, cassia, and olive oil [Col. 1252B]. Let us now consider the properties of each kind.

Some say that *smyrna* is the resin of calamus; others, that it is the resin of myrrh, and suitable for use among pigments. Cinnamon is so called because its bark is rounded and slender like a reed. It is found in India and Ethiopia as a short shrub, though two cubits high, darkish or ash-colored, with extremely thin branches. Whatever grows thick is considered worthless when broken, but it emits a visible breath like mist or dust.

Aromatic calamus is likewise named from its resemblance to ordinary reed. It grows in India, is jointed in many places, tawny, and fragrant with a sweet aroma when broken; it can be split into many parts. In taste it resembles cassia, with a slight, biting sharpness.

[Col. 1252C] Cassia also grows in Arabia. It is a branch with a sturdy bark and purple leaves like those of pepper. It has the virtue of cinnamon and resembles it, but is more powerful in effect.

Oil is named from the olive tree, for the olive is the tree from which oil is derived. Oil pressed from white olives is called *spanum*; that pressed from tawny and not yet ripe olives is called green oil; that from overly ripe olives is called ordinary oil. Of these, for the uses of life, the first is *spanum*, the second green, and the third ordinary. Oil to which nothing has been added is called pure.

With this unguent of the five kinds of spice a priest, king, or prophet was anointed and made such. For the consecration of an ecclesiastical altar, two substances are also used: frankincense and oil. Frankincense is a huge, branching tree of Arabia, with very smooth bark, which pours forth aromatic sap [Col. 1252D].

This preparation of seven substances with which altars were anointed signified the anointing of the Holy Spirit, by which the king himself was anointed. And what is the anointing of the Holy Spirit? It is, namely, his seven gifts. What, then, are the gifts of the Holy Spirit? The gift, or anointing, of the Holy Spirit is fear, piety, knowledge, fortitude, counsel, understanding, and wisdom (Isaiah 11).

By this anointing this altar—therefore Christ—was anointed, and consequently became priest, king, and prophet. Prophet, according to the Mosaic saying: “God will raise up for you a prophet; you shall listen to him as to me” [Col. 1253A] (Deuteronomy 18). Priest, according to the saying: “You are a priest forever according to the order of Melchizedek.” And just as it belongs to priests to offer incense, so Christ, who is more precious than all incense, offered himself to God the Father for us as an acceptable sacrifice, a fragrant offering.

Christ is also king, because, anointed with spiritual oil, he was King of kings and Lord of lords. For he rules and preserves Peter’s little ship, that is, his Church, so that it does not perish amid the storms of this age. Concerning this anointing of this king and priest, David testified, saying: “Therefore God, your God, has anointed you with the oil of gladness” (Psalm 44).

When Jacob had anointed this stone, that is, Christ, and in this way foretold the house of God, he added: “And it shall be called the gate of heaven” [Col. 1253B] (Genesis 28). Christ is called the gate of heaven because he is the door of paradise, as in the saying: “I am the door” (John 10).

The gate of heaven is faith, and baptism is at the gate of heaven; for those who have fallen after baptism, it is repentance, confession, and satisfaction. Through these gates of heaven—faith and baptism, repentance and confession—entrance into the heavenly kingdom is opened to believers and penitents.

Having explained these things allegorically about the stone and the gate, that is, about Christ, you must carefully consider how two altars also exist within us.

## DIVISION

Two altars are recorded as having formerly been constructed: one in the Mosaic tabernacle, called the altar of burnt offering; the other in Solomon’s temple, called the altar of incense.

The altar of burnt offering was constructed [Col. 1253C] from imperishable setim wood. It was five cubits wide, five cubits long, and three cubits high, and it was covered with bronze (Exodus 38). This altar had four corners, and from them four horns projected. It was empty and hollow, so that there might be ample space for receiving both wood and sacrifices. This altar had a bronze grating in the form of a net, so that through its numerous openings the fire placed beneath could freely penetrate to consume the victims.

The altar of burnt offering, constructed from incorruptible wood, signifies the hearts of the elect, in which the practice of good works is offered to the Lord as consecrated sacrifices. The hearts of the elect ought to be so incorruptible that they are worthy to receive the Holy Spirit as their inhabitant.

This altar is described as having five cubits in length and width. What, then, are the length and width of the altar except the five senses of our body? Or what is the length of the altar except the perfection of patience? And what is its width except the perfection of love, by which those who show themselves patient in all things are consecrated to the Lord?

This altar was three cubits high because through these three things—faith, hope, and love—the mind of the elect rises toward the love of God.

This altar was also covered with bronze, because just as bronze remains incorruptible for a long time, so the virtues of the faithful endure firmly in them to the end. It also had four horns projecting from its four corners. The four horns of the altar are the sides of the holy cross: height, depth, length, and width [Col. 1254A].

By these four sides of the cross—height, that is, hope; depth, that is, faith; length, that is, perseverance in patience; and width, that is, love—the altar of the holy Church, namely, the hearts of the faithful throughout the whole world, is fortified on every side. For horns are the defenses of virtues.

This altar was empty and hollow, so that there might be ample space for receiving both wood and sacrifices. Whoever desires to be the Lord’s altar has emptied himself of every worldly contamination, so that the wood of heavenly words and the victim of virtues may have ample room in him, and so that he may receive the flame of the Holy Spirit by which the ecclesiastical sacrifices—that is, the Lord’s body and blood—are consecrated. For unless he empties out what is beneath him [Col. 1254B], he will not deserve to receive what is above him.

This altar had a bronze grating in the form of a net, so that through its numerous openings the fire placed beneath could freely penetrate to consume the victims. It is necessary for God’s elect to open their hearts to divine grace and, as though many doors had been opened, to pray earnestly that through each good work they begin—like each separate piece of a victim—his grace may deign to enlighten them and kindle them toward his love.

These things concern the altar of burnt offering, that is, our body, in which good works are offered to the Lord.

Now let us consider the altar of incense, which was placed in Solomon’s temple (1 Kings 7). This altar was golden and made for burning incense. For just as the elect are signified by the altar of burnt offering—those who crucified themselves with their vices and desires and did not walk according to the desires of the flesh, but, as though sacrificing themselves to the Lord, dedicated all the senses of their body to his will through the fire of the Holy Spirit—so those who, with greater perfection of mind, have entirely extinguished the enticements of the flesh and offer the Lord only the vows of their prayers, subjecting their flesh and overcoming all the allurements of the flesh, are rightly compared to the altar of incense. They live a heavenly life on earth, not living carnally in the flesh.

The more this altar of incense excelled in the brilliance of its metal, the smaller it was in size.

For the holier they are, the fewer they are. Thus the length and width of the quadrangular altar rightly signify patience and love [Col. 1254D], because the souls of the perfect, joined together by interlocking virtues, strive to love their brothers as much as they are able to bear with them, and to bear with them as much as they love them.

It was two cubits high because they hope to receive a twofold reward in the heights, for their souls and bodies. The horns projecting from it signify the preeminence of faith and virtues. They project from it because the elect do not display their works superficially before the eyes of men, but exercise them with steadfast devotion in the deepest root of the heart.

It is clothed in gold because all the perfect shine with the light of inward wisdom. The grating of this altar, which was prepared in its midst to receive the incense, is gilded when the inner person shines with the grace of faith in Christ [Col. 1255A]. The walls are gilded when that same grace of divine love is extended outward through good works. The horns are gilded when the confidence of the strength of the righteous flashes with the radiance of inward light.

When these things have been properly arranged in our mind, we undoubtedly offer to our Lord Jesus Christ sacrifices of prayer that please God and breathe out fragrance beyond every powder of spices [Col. 1256A]. He lives and reigns as God with the Father and the Holy Spirit, forever and ever. Amen.

[Col. 1255] Here ends the *Book of Extracts from the Fathers*, printed at Basel in the year of the Lord 1494.

IN THE YEAR OF THE LORD 1100–1110 [lacuna] — SAINT ROBERT, FIRST ABBOT OF MOLESME AND FOUNDER OF THE CISTERCIAN ORDER

[Col. 1255]

## PRELIMINARY COMMENTARY ON THE LIFE OF SAINT ROBERT

(*Acta Sanctorum* of the Bollandists, April, volume III, 29th day, p. 662.)

### § I. Reforms of the Benedictine Order, Robert’s Beginnings, and the Foundation of Molesme

[Col. 1255B]

1. When the celebrated order of the holy patriarch Benedict, already four centuries old, had suffered in Gaul some loss of its ancestral discipline—through an uncertain evil, certainly through the very antiquity of time, which ordinarily brings destruction even to the firmest institutions—God graciously provided men distinguished for holiness and zeal, who would gradually reform corrupted morals according to the laws and rigor of the original institution.

The first to undertake so holy and useful a task was Blessed Berno, in the year of the Lord 910. After founding the monastery of Cluny in the Mâconnais, on the River Graune, he became the first Father, so to speak, of the new order that took its name from it. How useful he was in restoring the ancient institution to the Benedictine order was shown by the many monasteries, excellently organized and spread from Cluny, as well as by the many holy men and ecclesiastical princes who proceeded from it [Col. 1255C].

Following him at the beginning of the eleventh century was Blessed Bernard of Tiron. With equal success, though with less extensive progress, he introduced the reform into the diocese of Chartres. Yet no reform was more celebrated than that which Cîteaux, founded under the auspices of Saint Robert, first embraced. For that reform, spreading extraordinarily far, was not confined to France alone—although within France it established La Ferté, Pontigny, Clairvaux, and Morimond, the most extensive monasteries that Cîteaux calls its daughters—but soon spread throughout Europe and renewed Italy, Spain, Germany, Poland, and England.

The Sanmarthani authors state that it once numbered more than 1,800 monasteries of men and more than 1,400 of women. On consulting Charles de Visch’s *Cistercian Library*, approximately a thousand are found still existing in our own age [Col. 1256B]. It is therefore unsurprising that several supreme pontiffs and other distinguished men of the Church spoke so lavishly in praise of Cîteaux and the order propagated from it.

2. Henriquez collects in his *Apparatus to the Cistercian Menologium* the splendid encomia by which these men praised the institution. Among them is the following passage by Clement I:

“The Cistercian Order,” he says, “is a spring watering gardens, irrigating the other religious communities and orders and bubbling forth salutary examples into them. It is a pleasant spring, varied with virtues; renowned for the purity of its cleanliness; open in piety; unfailing in holiness. By its merits it deserved to grow so greatly that, surpassing the name of a spring, it is considered a river, whose praiseworthy advance from virtue to virtue, as it proceeds to see the God of gods in Zion, gladdens the unity of the universal Church. In that Church, having attained through the evidence of its merits the splendor of bright light, it shines like the morning star in the midst of the fog of this world [Col. 1256C]. Sending forth brilliant rays like the sun, it overflows like an aqueduct proceeding from paradise into many waters, irrigating with streams of grace the garden of its plantations—the assemblies of monks whom it has produced—and intoxicating the offspring of its birth with the wine of spiritual joy.

“This sacred religious order, at the outset of its institution almost deserted and impassable, since it had as yet been undertaken by only a few cultivators, eventually extended its branches like a terebinth [Col. 1256D], bearing the fruit of honor and dignity; it put forth shoots and produced generations and descendants. Therefore, rejoicing and exulting, it now celebrates and praises its happiness, and exults [Col. 1257A] in the great multitude of the distinguished—though once, as though contemptible, it lay hidden in the desert.”

This is what the pontiff says. The following passage, though shorter, has not been included: it is from letter 96 of Richard, archbishop of Canterbury and legate of the apostolic see:

“O desirable encampments! O venerable congregation! O Cîteaux, how great is your house! How fruitful in sons! How magnificent in tongues! How glorious among peoples!”

Nor has the following passage from Peter of Celle, letter 14 of book VII, been included. He says:

“That hen of Molesme, full of feathers and well fledged—how many and how excellent were the offspring she produced from her womb when the Cistercian community sprang from her in its original stock! My God! From that single egg, what an innumerable multitude of monks and lay brothers covered the face of the earth like sand! With what radiant brilliance did it reform and illumine the skin of the world, blackened by the infection of negligent living!” [Col. 1257B]

3. The sower of this abundant spiritual harvest, Saint Robert, was a Frenchman, by homeland either a Champenois or a Norman. He was born around the year of the Lord 1017 to Theodoric and Ermegard, both noble in wealth and birth. He was transferred from secular to monastic life in the fifteenth year of his age.

He began his novitiate in a monastery of the Order of Saint Benedict not far from the city of Troyes in Champagne. It is called Saint Peter’s Cell of Troyes, and by other names as well: the Monastery of the German Island, Saint Peter of Celle, New Cell, Old Cell, and Cell of Bobinus; in the older French tongue it is now called *Monstier la Celle de Troyes*. We discussed its foundation, laid by Saint Frodobert under Chlodovech II and Chlothar III, in the Life of that same Saint Frodobert on 8 January [Col. 1257C].

After the customary trials of the ascetic life, Robert was enrolled in the order and thereafter cultivated virtue and holiness so diligently that, by the unanimous will and consent of the monastery, he was appointed prior. At that time he was more an exemplar of morals than when he had lived as an ordinary monk.

From there he transferred to the monastery of Tonnerre, situated in the diocese of Langres and dedicated to Saint Michael. It took its name from the town to which it belonged, Tonnerre. Here the monks elected him abbot—Sanmarthani place him third in order after Dodon and Elfred—and he held this office for some time.

When he discovered that regular discipline had so completely collapsed there that, however hard he tried, he was unable to restore it [Col. 1257D], he laid aside his dignity and returned as an ordinary monk to Celle. Later, at the monastery of Saint Aigulf, he temporarily acted as prior in place of its abbot, until he began to establish Molesme.

4. The beginnings of this monastery arose from the former forest of Colan, which was inhabited by a certain priest living as a solitary and situated near the town of Tonnerre. First two brothers joined him, seeking to expiate the crime of mutual slaughter that they had conceived; then four others, who loved the same way of life, joined them as companions. For some time each practiced virtue privately, bound by no common rules.

A little later, however, a certain common manner and form of life was adopted, chiefly that of the Benedictines, which at that time was most widespread throughout Gaul [Col. 1258A]. Therefore, so that they might have both knowledge of that institution and a suitable master, they requested Saint Robert from the neighboring monastery of Tonnerre, whose reputation for holiness was already renowned, as their abbot.

The monks, however, strongly opposed this, because their morals were corrupt and they therefore feared the restoration of the ancient discipline nearby. For the time being the petitioners were refused, but they did not entirely abandon hope of eventually obtaining Robert. When Saint Robert, leaving the people of Tonnerre because of their moral corruption, returned to Celle and served as prior at the monastery of Saint Aigulf on behalf of their abbot, they went to Rome and earnestly petitioned the pontiff to authorize them to take one of the monks of the neighboring Benedictine order as their master in a new and regular life, choosing the man whom they considered most suitable for this purpose [Col. 1258B].

When this was granted, Saint Robert was requested again and, because the pontiff’s authority had been brought to bear, was easily obtained from the abbot of Celle. Accordingly, appointed superior and master of the seven hermits in the forest of Colan, he began to form their morals according to the regular institution of Saint Benedict and gradually to increase the number of his disciples.

Manriquez, in the *Annals of the Cistercians*, states that Blessed Alberic was among them:

“Alberic,” he says, “having been admitted to the habit, consecrated its beginnings. Whether, compared with him [Robert], he was holier or more learned is uncertain; compared with others, both are certain. He was instructed not only in the divine writings but also in human letters. The *Exordium* calls him a man sufficiently learned in divine and human letters, a lover of the Rule and of the brothers [Col. 1258C]. He exchanged all the hopes conceived in the world for that poor condition. The holy Father had other disciples while he remained at Colan, but the direction of affairs lay almost entirely with this man.”

5. Since the origin of the new congregation of regulars had been so happy and auspicious, it promised daily greater progress and future growth for what had been begun. When Saint Robert realized that the forest of Colan was not sufficiently suitable for these developments, he departed in search of a more convenient site for the new monks. Leaving the forest and surveying the surrounding region, he came upon one called Molesme.

Judging it suitable for the greater undertakings he had in mind, he assigned it to his companions as the site for the monastery that was to be built. Its foundation was begun in the year of the Lord 1075, on 20 December; retaining the name of the forest in which it stood, it was called Molesme, and later became a celebrated ascetic community enlarged by many estates [Col. 1258D].

Caesarius praises it in book I of the *Miracles* in these words:

“In the episcopate of Langres there is situated a monastery called Molesme, most renowned in reputation, distinguished in religion, ennobled by illustrious men, rich in possessions, and renowned for virtues.”

Ordericus likewise mentions its beginnings in book VIII of his *History*:

“In Burgundy there is a place called Molesme. There, in the time of Philip, king of the Franks, the venerable abbot Robert founded a monastery; and, with the grace of the Holy Spirit inspiring him, gathered disciples of great religious devotion. With the zeal of virtue, he courteously instructed them in holy poverty according to the practice of other monasteries” [Col. 1259A].

After the monastery of Molesme had been founded in this way, Saint Robert, as was fitting, presided over it first with the authority of an abbot. Public records of donations preserved by the Sanmarthani authors, and the charter of Daimbert, archbishop of Sens, preserved by Camuzat in the *Storehouse of Sacred Antiquities of the Diocese of Troyes*, bear witness to this.

According to Manriquez, Blessed Stephen, on his return from the thresholds of the Apostles, received the monastic habit there. He later became the third abbot of the Cistercians and was commemorated by us on 17 April.

6. The first life and virtue of the monks of Molesme were so illustrious that princes and other prominent men of the surrounding region requested monks from among them to establish new monasteries on their estates. Thus, through the agency of Saint Robert, an ascetic community was founded in the fortress of Vallis-Coloris [Col. 1259B].

Concerning this, the following charter is preserved among the Sanmarthani authors in volume IV of *Gallia Christiana*:

“In the name of the holy and undivided Trinity. Since the fame of the monastery of Molesme, of most sweet fragrance, spread its scent far and wide, many men devoted to religion bestowed benefits and requested monks from the aforesaid place to build monasteries on their own lands and possessions.

“When this request for holiness reached the ears of the aged Joffridus, a most noble prince and most faithful servant of the holy Church, he likewise requested and obtained monks from Lord Robert, the first abbot of that place, a man adorned with morals, proven by the manner of his life, illumined by the radiance of virtues, and distinguished by humility, patience, justice, fortitude, temperance, and prudence.

“These monks built a monastery in the fortress called Vallis-Coloris [Col. 1259C], and there led a life of holy conduct,” and so forth.

Thus the charter.

7. Nevertheless, within a short time the discipline of Molisme’s holy beginnings was corrupted, becoming more lax because of an excessive abundance of temporal goods. This was followed by such a gradual corruption of morals that, however much Saint Robert strove by example and admonition, they could not be recalled to their former integrity. Since a remedy seemed hopeless, he abandoned those whom he had founded and went to Aurum, a monastery near Molisme, where he was first received as an ordinary monk and then as abbot, and continued to shine forth as a torch of holy life.

Manriquez relates that, after Saint Robert’s departure, the care of the monastery remained with Alberic [Col. 1259D], who, while Robert was abbot, had previously held the office of prior, though he was scarcely successful in the altered circumstances, since the monks flogged him and threw him into prison because he demanded discipline. While Brito maintains that this injury was inflicted not after Saint Robert’s departure, and not upon Alberic but upon Stephen, Manriquez corrects him in these words:

> “The Portuguese Brito is therefore mistaken when he changes the time; more seriously, when he changes the persons. He takes these laurels away from Father Alberic in order to crown Stephen with them; and—what you may find surprising—in a speech either actually delivered or fabricated, in which Robert is said to have rebuked the transgressors under this theme: ‘We have cared for Babylon, but it was not healed; let us abandon it.’ In the *Little Exordium of Cîteaux*, written by our earliest Fathers [Col. 1260A], who learned the matter with their own eyes, I read that it was not Stephen but Alberic who, on account of this affair—namely, the reform of the monks of Molisme—had endured many reproaches, imprisonment, and beatings.”

This is what he says. He adds that Alberic’s and Stephen’s withdrawal into the solitude of Unicus must likewise be assigned to this period:

> “When Robert the Father was absent, as he says, the result was that they could and wished to leave Molisme without anyone else’s permission—perhaps even, having received blows, they were virtually compelled to do so—whereas at no other time would they have departed from the place, whether with permission obtained from the Father or without having asked for it.”

Ado—or whoever else wrote the *Life* to be given below—suppresses the imprisonment and beatings; indeed, he even suppresses the heart of the assailants hardened in evil (this concession being made to his Molisme brethren [Col. 1260B]) and attributes their departure to a desire for a stricter and more salutary life:

> “There were among them,” he says, “four stronger men, Alberic and Stephen, together with two others, who, after the rudiments of cenobitic discipline, longed for the solitary struggle of the desert. Accordingly, they left the monastery of Molisme and came to a certain place called Unicus,” etc.

## § II. The Beginnings of the Monastery and Order of Cîteaux, and Saint Robert’s Transfer to It

8. Deprived of such men, the monks of Molisme soon grew weary of their bereavement and, having thereafter become better sons, asked the supreme pontiff to restore to them the Father whom they had lost. With his consent, and after he had entrusted the matter to the bishop of Langres so that he might order the absent monks to return, Saint Robert, their Father, was the first to return, having left Aurum; then the other two, Alberic and Stephen, leaving the forest of Unicus, returned as well.

Ado conceals Alberic’s and Stephen’s return, asserting that, after leaving the forest of Unicus, they immediately began to found Cîteaux. That this is far from the truth is evident from the Cistercian History that we shall immediately present, and may also be inferred from Ado’s own statement that they “received a sentence of excommunication from the venerable man Joseran, bishop of Langres, unless they returned to Molisme.” For it cannot be believed that holy men incurred so great a crime of obstinacy, and so severe a penalty, that they preferred not to return to Molisme—especially since they would find there their Father, Saint Robert, and their brothers’ willing dispositions toward correction [Col. 1260D].

Their return was certainly most beneficial to the affairs of Molisme, since it provided the occasion for the foundation of Cîteaux and of the order subsequently named from it. The following passage, drawn from Manriquez, concerns these events:

> “When all had therefore been restored to Molisme, and one flock had again been formed from them all under Robert as shepherd, they began more fervently to restore discipline. Since some were striving with every effort, while others were frightened by their recent fall and dared not resist, the way to drive out vices was easier. Many things appeared to have been changed for the better, even among those whom the habit of sinning had made impatient of correction; and the more arduous observances were allowed by dispensation in consideration of their former habits. Most points of the Rule were observed to the letter. Anyone who compared the present state with the former [Col. 1261A] might judge that enough, and more than enough, had been accomplished; but to the holy men whatever was not the highest seemed insignificant, and the road already traveled affected them less than the road that remained.”

A little later he adds:

> “Stephen, the chief figure in this undertaking, called indulgences transgressions and dispensations sins. First he urged Alberic and certain others, and then Father Robert, to abolish dispensations, if this could be done while remaining at Molisme; otherwise, to migrate elsewhere.”

This is Manriquez’s account.

9. We now append a much older and more precise account of the entire undertaking at Cîteaux, from Book I of the *Selected History* of the order that subsequently spread from it. It once existed in manuscript in our college at Embrun. It is as follows:

> “These servants of God, few in number but powerfully inflamed by that fire which the Lord Jesus sent upon the earth and wished to burn intensely [Col. 1261B], were listening in the chapter to the daily readings of the Rule. When they perceived that the Rule commanded one thing while the customs of the order maintained another, they were deeply saddened. They saw that they and the other monks had promised by solemn profession to observe the Rule of Blessed Father Benedict, but were in no way living according to its institutions.
>
> “At first, therefore, they often spoke privately among themselves, lamenting their transgression, and carefully considered how they might find a remedy for so great an evil. But when the matter had later become public, the others, who were carnal and could not say with the prophet [Col. 1261C], ‘He sent fire from on high into my bones and instructed me’ (*Lamentations* 1:13), began to mock the servants of God and, by every means available, to harass them so that they would abandon so holy a purpose.
>
> “But those who were led by the Spirit of God, and were therefore free, disregarding their malevolent attacks, turned to God with all the exertion of their minds and earnestly begged that the Lord’s mercy might deign to direct them to such a place where they could fulfill the vows of their lips, which they had confirmed according to the Rule but had not kept.
>
> “Then, considering the Apostle’s warning that not every spirit should be believed (1 John 4:1), and recalling that the Rule—which they desired by every means to observe perfectly—commands that one who presumes to do anything without the abbot’s permission should be corrected [Col. 1261D], they humbly approached their abbot. They presented their complaint about the transgression of the Rule, disclosed their fervent desire to fulfill their vow, and earnestly begged that, with his help and counsel, they might accomplish what they had conceived in their minds under the inspiration of the Holy Spirit.
>
> “By God’s prompting, the abbot was at that moment moved to compunction. He praised the servants of God’s purpose and firmly promised not only to offer them his counsel and assistance, but also to become their inseparable companion in so holy an undertaking. When those humble brothers heard this, they were greatly strengthened in spirit. Then for the first time they understood that the word had truly gone forth from the Lord, and that they had not followed the dreams of their hearts in such a desire, but the right hand of the living God [Col. 1262A], working powerfully within them.”

10. Thus these great-hearted men, destined to become leaders and standard-bearers of innumerable soldiers of Christ, desiring not so much novel things as great things that would benefit the whole world, repeatedly deliberated among themselves about how they might bring their desire to completion in a fitting manner. After prudent reflection, they wisely recognized that they could not presume to change their place or order without the consent of the Apostolic See.

At that time the venerable Hugh, archbishop of Lyon, a man worthy of reverence for his religion, prudence, and authority, was papal legate in the regions of Gaul. The abbot mentioned above and the brothers who were burning with a desire to renew monastic religion [Col. 1262B] approached him. They humbly disclosed the fervor and desires of their hearts. They complained that the customs of the order differed too greatly from the Rule that they had professed; for that reason, with sorrow, they openly confessed that they had knowingly incurred the crime of perjury.

They further declared that they wished to order their lives anew, in their entirety, according to the institutions of the Rule of their holy Father Benedict. They earnestly requested that the legate, with apostolic authority, extend to them the strength of his assistance so that they might carry this out more freely.

The lord legate, being prudent and discerning, carefully considered their arguments and pronounced that they were moved by a praiseworthy impulse. Gladly favoring their spiritual vows, he encouraged them by the following letter to complete, with complete freedom, what they had conceived with pious intent [Col. 1262C].

11. “Hugh, bishop of Lyon and legate of the Apostolic See, to Robert, abbot of Molisme, and to the brothers who, with him, desire to serve God according to the Rule of Saint Benedict.

> “Let this be known to all who rejoice in the advancement of holy mother Church. You and certain of your sons, the brothers of the monastery of Molisme, appeared before us at Lyon and declared that you wished thereafter to adhere more strictly and perfectly to the Rule of the most blessed Benedict, which up to that time you had observed lukewarmly and negligently in the same monastery.
>
> “Since it is evident that this cannot be fulfilled in the aforesaid place because of the many obstacles, we have judged it useful, providing for the welfare of both parties—that is, of those who depart and of those who remain there [Col. 1262D]—that you withdraw to another place which divine generosity shall designate for you, and that there you serve the Lord more profitably and peacefully.
>
> “Therefore, when you were present—namely, Robert the abbot, and also the brothers Alberic, Odo, John, Stephen, Laetald, and Peter, as well as all those whom you shall decide, by regular process and common counsel, to associate with yourselves—we both advised you to preserve this holy purpose and command you to persevere in it; and by apostolic authority, through the impression of our seal, we confirm it permanently.”

This diploma of the papal legate, by which Saint Robert and his companions are granted authority to found the Cistercian order, is also reported by Miraeus in the *Chronicle of that Order* [Col. 1263A]. He attests that, contrary to the account given in the *Life*, Blessed Alberic and Stephen returned from the solitude of Unicus to Molisme before this permission was requested and before all migrated together to Cîteaux. They did not found Cîteaux without Saint Robert, who was both administrator and director of the entire undertaking, although the *Great Exordium* records that Stephen was the first proposer of the project in these words:

> “Afterward, when the idea of renewing religion had been raised in that house, Stephen himself, first among the foremost, labored with the most fervent zeal and insisted by every means that the place and order of Cîteaux should be established. By God’s subsequent ordinance, he was destined to become its shepherd and teacher.”

12. After obtaining from the papal legate permission to renew religious life [Col. 1263B], Cîteaux, then a dense forest of Burgundy, seemed suitable. Before Saint Robert migrated from Molisme with his companions, he is said to have sent Blessed Stephen to Odo, duke of Burgundy, with a letter. We give below a copy of it, produced by Brito from a certain manuscript of the monastery of Alcobaça. The duke Odo of Burgundy’s reply to this letter, written in response, is also preserved in the same manuscript.

13. After this, Saint Robert left Molisme and transferred to Cîteaux. The author of the Cistercian manuscript History mentioned above continues by recounting the sequence of the migration:

> “After these events,” he says, “the aforesaid abbot and his companions, relying upon such and so great an authority, returned to Molisme. From that community of brothers they chose companions who rejected the allurements of a more relaxed life [Col. 1263C] and were ready, with willing hearts, to cling purely and simply to the purity and simplicity of the sacred Rule. Thus, among those who had appeared before the legate at Lyon and those who were summoned from the monastery, there were twenty-one monks.
>
> “Desiring a more perfect life and to observe literally the Rule of their holy Father Benedict, they entered the narrow and constricted way. In the year 1098 from the Lord’s Incarnation, therefore, Lord Robert, abbot of the monastery of Molisme founded in the diocese of Langres, and with him the brothers whose hearts God had touched, preferring to be wearied by labors for God with their beloved Father Benedict rather than be enervated by the comforts of this life, left Molisme [Col. 1263D]. They proceeded joyfully to the place which, by God’s grace, they had already foreseen as suitable for their purpose: the desert called Cîteaux.
>
> “That place lay in the diocese of Chalon and, because of the density of its woods and thorns, was at that time unaccustomed to human access; it was inhabited only by wild animals. When the men of God came to this place of horror and vast solitude, they understood that it was all the more suitable for the religion which they had long before conceived in their minds and for which they had come there, the more contemptible and inaccessible it was to secular people. Having cut down and cleared away the dense woods and thorns, they began to build a monastery there, with the permission of the bishop of Chalon and the consent of the person to whom the place itself belonged.
>
> “In that same year which we mentioned above [Col. 1264A], on the twelfth day before the Kalends of April, the solemn feast day of the most holy Benedict—which a doubled joy had then made especially festive because Palm Sunday had fallen on that very day—the house of Cîteaux began, amid rejoicing angels and demons wasting away. Through these men, wholly freed for Christian philosophy, the religious life of the entire Cistercian order likewise took its beginning.”

These statements agree with what Caesarius recorded about the foundation of Cîteaux in his *History* during the immediately following century. The following verses, inscribed on the façade of the Cistercian church [Col. 1264B], likewise give the year of the order’s foundation and of its first monastery:

> In the year one thousand, one hundred, less twice one,  
> Under Pope Urban and Philip, king of the Gauls,  
> With Odo as duke of Burgundy, giving the foundations,  
> Under Father Robert the Cistercian order began,  
> Producing very many monasteries throughout the world,  
> Thus destined to remain long through the holy name of Jesus.

14. Cîteaux is situated about five leagues from Dijon, in the diocese of Chalon and the duchy of Burgundy. It is now a very large monastery, enriched by many estates. Some derive its name from *cisternae*, “cisterns”; others from *cistels*, a French word meaning marsh reeds.

The estate belonged to Raynard, viscount of Beaune, and his wife Hodierna; consequently, their authorization was necessary for construction. They yielded it very willingly and consecrated their generosity toward the servants of God to posterity in perpetual charters [Col. 1264C]. Henriquez reports the following charter in the *Menologium* under 21 March:

> “Let it be known to all Christians, present and future, that Raynald, viscount of Beaune, and his wife, named Hodierna, and their sons Hugh, Humbert, and Raynard, together with their father-in-law Raymund, for the remission of their sins and those of their ancestors, granted to Lord Robert and the brothers who with him desired to observe the Rule of Saint Benedict more strictly and perfectly than they had observed it up to that time, from their estate, which had anciently been called Cîteaux, as much as would be necessary for themselves and their successors, servants of God, to construct a monastery and its buildings, to plow the land, and indeed for every necessary use.” [Col. 1264D] etc.

15. Odo, duke of Burgundy, also greatly enlarged Cîteaux. He added the estates that had been reserved and excepted by the viscount of Beaune, and built the first house for the new inhabitants.

The previously described charters relate the matter as follows:

> “From the remainder of that land, which Raynard then wished to retain, Odo, duke of Burgundy, with his concession and at his pleasure, made the following exchange and agreement with him for the use of those same monks: in return for that land, Raynard himself and his heirs after him were to receive twenty solidi each year at the castle of Beaune. Moreover, in the same exchange, the duke granted to him and his sons as many vineyards as they might plant and cultivate in the territory of Beaune, on their own demesne.” [Col. 1265A]

Later, the Cistercian manuscript History of our college at Embrun continues as follows:

> “Furthermore, the archbishop, legate of the Apostolic See, through whose blessing, command, and authority so great a good had received a firm foundation, considering the poverty of the servants of God, and because in the barren place they had occupied they could neither subsist nor construct buildings at all unless they were supported by the assistance of some powerful person, wrote to the illustrious prince Odo, then duke of Burgundy. He asked and advised him to foster and support the poor of Christ, who possessed zeal for the glory of God and for the monastic order, and to provide for their needs according to the magnificence of his princely rank.
>
> “The lord Odo, duke of Burgundy, consenting to this request and counsel, and delighted by the fervor and devotion of those brothers, completed entirely at his own expense the wooden monastery which they had begun in their poverty. For a long time he provided them there with everything necessary, and abundantly assisted them with lands and livestock.” [Col. 1265B]

16. Manriquez is the only author of that period to maintain that the place was divinely shown to those who were about to begin the new order. He infers this from the words of the *Great Exordium* quoted shortly before:

> “Leaving Molisme, they proceeded joyfully to the place which, by God’s grace, they had already foreseen as suitable for their purpose—that is, the desert called Cîteaux.”

They dedicated the church to the holy Mother of God [Col. 1265C], following a custom later extended to all the other monasteries of the order. Hence this distinguished testimony of Blessed Humbert, master general of the Order of Preachers, in his sermons:

> “This order holds the Blessed Virgin in such great reverence that all its churches are consecrated in her honor. For this reason the monks themselves in their churches are, as it were, always before the Blessed Virgin and her Son.”

Gregory X similarly says:

> “The Cistercian order, devoted to divine service and distinguished among the other religious orders by its singular devotion to the glorious Virgin from its very foundation.”

17. Manriquez writes that, before Saint Robert left Molisme, he delivered a solemn address to those who remained there [Col. 1265D]. They followed him as he departed with tears, and courteously and lovingly supplied utensils for the buildings of the new monastery, especially those pertaining to divine worship.

Finally, he appointed Gaufred, also called Goffred by others, in his place:

> “A man,” he says, “composed in character and also instructed in sacred disciplines, who could suitably fulfill the duties of abbot if he were capable of making others like himself.”

At Cîteaux, Saint Robert was appointed first abbot by Walter, bishop of Chalon, with the authority of the papal legate. The Cistercian manuscript History says:

> “At that time the abbot who had arrived received from the bishop of Chalon, in whose diocese the place itself lay, the pastoral staff together with the care of souls, by command of the aforesaid legate. He regularly caused the monks who had come with him to establish stability in that same place, so that the church, fortified by both divine and human favor and strengthened also by apostolic authority, arose to be organized as an abbey according to the Rule of Saint Benedict.” [Col. 1266A]

The *Little Cistercian Exordium*, of the greatest authority because it was written by the first Fathers of Cîteaux, recounts the same matter in nearly identical words. This is also confirmed by the letter of the bishop of Chalon to the bishop of Langres, which we shall give shortly, and by the Cistercian Calendar published at Dijon, in which Blessed Alberic is mentioned as the second abbot of Cîteaux.

It is therefore now beyond dispute that Saint Robert presided as the first abbot of Cîteaux. We had left the matter undecided in the *Life of Blessed Alberic* under 26 January and postponed it to this place [Col. 1266B].

## § III. Saint Robert’s Recall and Return from Cîteaux to Molisme; His Age, Sacred Cult, and the Writers of His Life

18. Nevertheless, after a short time Saint Robert had to resign his office among the Cistercians and return to Molisme, since his Molisme brethren again appealed to Urban II for his restoration. “Not long afterward,” continues the Cistercian manuscript History,

> “when this period of time had elapsed, the monks of Molisme, with the permission of their abbot Gaufrid, who had succeeded Robert, sent messengers to the Roman court. They insistently petitioned the lord Pope Urban that the aforesaid abbot Robert should be ecclesiastically restored to his former place, that is, to the monastery of Molisme. Overcome by their insistence, the lord pope instructed his venerable legate, Hugh, to see whether the same abbot could return, and that the monks who loved the desert might remain in peace.” [Col. 1266C]

The *Little Exordium* reports the same matter, with some alteration of phrasing. It also contains the following letter of Urban to Hugh, archbishop of Lyon, concerning Saint Robert’s recall:

> “Urban, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his venerable brother Hugh, bishop and vicar of the Apostolic See, greetings and apostolic blessing.
>
> “We have received a great outcry in council from the brothers of Molisme, who are urgently demanding the return of their abbot. For they said that religion had been overturned in their community and that, because of the absence of that abbot, they were hated by princes and by their other neighbors.
>
> “Finally compelled by our brothers, we command your affection by these present writings, informing you that it is pleasing to us that, if possible, that abbot be brought back from the desert to the monastery. But if you cannot accomplish this, take care that both those who love the desert may rest in peace and those who are in the monastery may serve regular discipline.” [Col. 1266D]

19. Once Hugh had read this letter, nothing was more urgent to him than to carry out the pontiff’s commands. Manriquez writes that a provincial council was convened by him at Lyon at Petra Incisa concerning this matter. At least, he wrote the following letter to the bishop of Langres, preserved in both versions of the *Exordium*:

> “Hugh, servant of the Church of Lyon, to his most beloved brother Robert, bishop of the church of Langres [Col. 1267A], greetings. Concerning the matter of the Church of Molisme . . .”

See this letter in the section on Hugh of Lyon above, col. 523 of this volume.

20–21. How Hugh’s letter achieved its effect is related by both versions of the *Exordium*:

> “That abbot approved and carried out all these things, releasing the Cistercians from the obedience which they had promised him, whether at that place or at Molisme. The lord Walter, bishop of Chalon, likewise released the abbot from responsibility for that church, and thus he returned, with certain monks accompanying him.”

Walter’s letter to the bishop of Langres is also preserved in the *Little Exordium*:

> “To his most beloved brother and fellow bishop Robert, bishop of Langres, Gauter, servant of the Church of Chalon, greetings.
>
> “Let it be known to you that we have released brother Robert, to whom we had entrusted that abbey situated in our diocese and called New Monastery, from the profession which he made to the Church of Chalon and from the obedience which he promised us, in accordance with the decision of the lord archbishop.
>
> “He himself has released those monks who had decided to remain in the aforesaid New Monastery from the obedience which they had promised him and from their profession. Therefore do not hesitate henceforth to receive him and treat him honorably. Farewell.” [Col. 1267B]

From this the manifest error of the author of the *Life* becomes clear. He says that, after Saint Robert’s return to the monks of Molisme, he continued to preside with the authority of abbot both at Molisme and at Cîteaux; and that, because he could not be present at Cîteaux, he first appointed Blessed Alberic as his vicar and, when Alberic died two years later, appointed Blessed Stephen in his place.

The reader can see from the *Little Exordium* that this is contrary to the facts. Its tenth chapter says:

> “When the Cistercian church was therefore deprived of its shepherd, it assembled and, by a regular election, promoted a certain brother named Alberic as its abbot.” [Col. 1267C]

22. After Saint Robert returned to Molisme with only two monks, he nevertheless did not erase the Cistercians from his heart. Chrysostom Henriquez, in the *Fascicle of the Saints of the Order*, states that he addressed frequent letters to them and transcribes one of them from Brito’s *Chronicle*. (See below.)

[Col. 1267D] 23. The writers do not agree about the year of Saint Robert’s death. In his notes under 29 April, Baronius, following the *Chronicle of Sigebert*, assigns his death to the year 1098. Fitero, in his notes on the *Little Exordium*, adds one year, and Manriquez, in his *Annals*, adds two. But they are proved to be mistaken by the donation charters, which Saint Robert signed: at Camuzat, in the *Antiquities of the Church of Troyes*, in the year of the Lord 1104; and at Sanmarthani, in the records of Molisme, in 1105.

The San-Marthani date his life’s end to 1110; Camuzat, together with Jonghelinus and Claudius Robertus in the *Gallia Christiana*, date it to 1111. Whatever the case may be, his life did not extend beyond the year 1112, since it is certain from the evidence cited by the San-Marthani at the place mentioned that Guido was presiding at Molisme in that year.

Nor is there sufficient agreement about the day on which he died [Col. 1268A]. Surius, in his *Life*, and Bernard Brito, in his Cistercian *Chronicle*, give 29 April. But that is the day of the feast’s translation. Therefore the Cistercians, following the instruction of their rubrics, while celebrating Saint Robert’s feast on that day, are ordered to omit from the hymn *Jesu, corona celsior*, which the Church sings for confessors, the verse *Anni recurso tempore*, together with the three following verses.

The rubrics say:

> “The following verse is not said on the feasts of Saints Remigius, Julian, and Robert, on the translation of Saint Benedict, or on the feasts of any confessors whenever they are transferred to another day.”

An old verse composed on this subject agrees [Col. 1268B]:

> At the translations of Remigius, Robert, and Julian, the *Anni recurso* verse is not sung.

Before it was transferred, Saint Robert’s feast occupied 17 April, that is, according to the constitution of the Cistercian chapter:

> “Let the feast of Blessed Robert, the first abbot of Cîteaux, be celebrated on the fifteenth day before the Kalends of May,” etc.

The regular canons of the monastery of Böddeken in the diocese of Paderborn followed this constitution. When they intended to inscribe in their notable codex, folio 178, the *Life* transmitted from John Gamans, they began it as follows:

> “Here begins the prologue to the *Life of Blessed Robert*, the first abbot of Molisme and also of Cîteaux, whose feast is celebrated on the fifteenth day before the Kalends of May.”

According to Fitero, on that same day the verse that was later omitted after the feast was transferred was ordinarily sung. Hence we rightly infer [Col. 1268C] that the earlier feast coincided with the day of his death and, accordingly, that Saint Robert died on 17 April, or the fifteenth day before the Kalends of May, as the author of the *Life* states in the Böddeken manuscript.

In the manuscript additions of certain Carthusians of Brussels to Usuard, under 21 March, the Translation of Saint Robert the abbot is noted. If this is the Robert of Molisme, one may suspect that it commemorates a later translation, perhaps carried out about a century or somewhat more before that time.

24. He was enrolled among the blessed in the year 1222 by Pope Honorius III, who permitted the monks of Molisme “to venerate him as a saint in their church and faithfully implore his intercession before the Lord [Col. 1268D].” In his *Annals* under that year, Manriquez maintains that he was enrolled among the saints not long after the beatification, or at the beginning of the following year, and that the pope issued documents to this effect.

It is certain that in that same year the Cistercian general chapter decreed:

> “Let the feast of Saint Robert, the first abbot of Cîteaux, be celebrated on the fifteenth day before the Kalends of May, with twelve lessons, as for Blessed Jerome; and with one Mass, as for Saint Benedict.”

His name is found in various ecclesiastical calendars: in those of Saussay, Menard, and Wion; in the Roman Martyrology; in the Cistercian *Menologium* of Chrysostom Henriquez under 29 April; and also in the same author under 21 March, on which day he says that he read of his death in the calendars published at Salamanca and Dijon.

In the Dijon calendar, under that day, we read:

> “The Cistercian order began successfully under Abbot Robert in the year 1098. Robert himself fell asleep in the Lord on that same day, which is also sacred to Saint Benedict, our holy Father, in the year 1108.” [Col. 1269A]

As the Sanmarthani state, Guido, the first abbot of Molisme after him, wrote his *Life*. In the twelfth century, nearly one hundred years after Saint Robert’s death, an anonymous monk of Molisme wrote another, at the command, as he says in his preface, of “the most reverend lord Ado, abbot of Molisme.” The Sanmarthani teach that this Ado died in 1197 and call him Odo.

> “I have concealed my name,” he says, “lest perhaps among the uninstructed the work itself should be devalued if the name of a sinner appeared at the very beginning of the work.”

Although he professed an exclusive concern for truth [Col. 1269B], I do not doubt that he also put that concern into practice. Nevertheless, it must be admitted that he was sometimes led away from the truth because he trusted his Molisme brethren too much; out of rivalry against the Cistercians, they considerably obscured the truth of the history.

Our own John Grothusius, of pious memory, was the first to perceive this when, at Embrun in our college, he found in 1638 a manuscript Cistercian history and compared it both with what he had read in the works of Saint Bernard and Peter the Venerable and with the *Life* published by Surius.

Surius, having received a copy of a Utrecht manuscript of the church of Saint Salvator—which is also in our possession [Col. 1270A]—did not have the prologue, since it is lacking there. He also altered the style in several places and, whenever he found words made more concise, rendered them in that form.

We give the *Life* complete and unaltered from the frequently mentioned Böddeken codex. Whatever is less sound and was written from a disposition less favorable to the Cistercians, we have either already corrected in this preliminary commentary or shall warn against it below in the annotations.

Thirty years after Ado’s death, under another Ado or Odo, proceedings were undertaken to obtain canonization, and were completed as we have said. Documents concerning this matter are preserved, inserted by Philippe Labbe in volume I of the *Bibliotheca manuscriptorum*; they are to be transcribed here. Toward the end they mention a *Life* to be presented to the pope by the procurators of the monks of Molisme [Col. 1270B]. It can scarcely be doubted that this is the very *Life* that we are publishing.

Among more recent writers, Simon Martin of the Order of Minims wrote the *Life* in French in *Flowers of Solitude*; Bernard de Brito wrote it in Portuguese in the first part of his Cistercian *Chronicle*; Manriquez wrote it in Latin in the *Annals* of that order; and Chrysostom Henriquez in the *Fascicle of the Saints*. It also appears in the *Legend of the Saints*, printed at Leuven in 1485, and in the Utrecht manuscripts of Saint Salvator, but in a more abbreviated form.

[Col. 1269]

# THE LIFE OF SAINT ROBERT

By an anonymous monk of Molisme under Abbot Ado in the twelfth century, recovered from the Böddeken manuscript by John Gamans, S.J., and compared with the Utrecht manuscripts and with Surius.

## PROLOGUE

[Col. 1269C]

1. Since the way into the holy places has been opened by Jesus, the great Priest, who entered them once for all by his own blood, I consider it worthwhile to describe the lives and conduct of those who, imitating our Savior insofar as human frailty allowed, stood bravely amid the storms of the present life in the contest of battle, glorifying and bearing Christ the Lord in their bodies, and remaining most steadfastly until the end of life in their purpose of holiness. These are the ones of whom Scripture says: “The path of the just, like shining light, grows and advances until the perfect day” (Prov. 4). These are the stars whom the Supreme Pontiff has established in the firmament of the Church; their radiance drives away the darkness of human ignorance and shows the harbor of salvation to those laboring upon this great and spacious sea. Among them the venerable man, Blessed Robert, first abbot of the Church of Molesme, shone with particular brilliance. His purified holiness is rightly proclaimed the more glorious because scarcely anyone is found in our days who fears God.

I have undertaken to write his life, not relying upon my own talent or knowledge, but rather placing my hope of progress and the completion of the work begun in him who makes the tongues of infants eloquent and who, to rebuke the madness of the prophet, once granted human speech to a dumb animal. To this was added the command of the most reverend lord Ado, abbot of Molesme, together with the persistent and devout request of the brethren of that place; and I consider it wholly wrong to deny them anything. Therefore, lest I should appear empty-handed before the Lord, although I am not of such virtue or merit that I could serve as an example to others, I have nevertheless taken care that it should not remain entirely unknown to them who, on account of his deserved holiness, was given to the holy Church for its adornment.

Whoever, therefore, approaches this work as a reader, I ask you not to seek the writer’s name here, because, fleeing human glory and seeking to be praised by God alone, I have concealed my name in this work—also lest the work itself perhaps be cheapened among the unlearned if the name of a sinner appeared at its very beginning. If I have said anything less elegantly or less appropriately, I humbly ask the reader’s pardon. I admonish all to whom this writing comes not to demand from me verbal finery, because truth, sufficient and beautiful in itself, does not seek to be colored by verbal cosmetics, nor painted with the rouge of the harlot Jezebel. Finally, let them hear the Teacher of the nations, and the disciple of Truth himself, saying that “the kingdom of God is not in speech but rather in power” (1 Cor. 4).

## Chapter One. Saint Robert’s birth, the beginning of his religious life, and certain offices of authority

2. Blessed Robert, therefore, born in the region of Champagne [Note: Manrique wrote that he came from Normandy, a province adjoining Champagne.], shone forth like a beautiful flower of the field. His beauty was pleasing to those who looked upon the uprightness of his conduct, and the fragrance of his holy reputation, spread far and wide, invited many to imitate him. I rightly think that I have compared this holy man to a flower, because Scripture says of the saints: “They shall flourish from the city like the grass of the earth” (Ps. 71).

Moreover, since nobility is a kind of praise proceeding from the merits of one’s parents, we shall show from whom this blessed man derived his origin. His father was called Theoderic, and his mother Ermegardis. Both were distinguished according to the dignity of the world, but before God they were most distinguished by the uprightness of their conduct. They used the abundance of possessions with which they were endowed in temporal things in such a way that they appeared rather to be stewards of the supreme Head of the Household than owners of earthly property. Knowing that the one who shows mercy to the poor lends to the Lord, they wiped away the dust of earthly life by pious almsgiving. Indeed, because, though placed in the flesh, they did not live according to the flesh, they dwelt in heaven by thought and desire and adorned their crowns with works of virtue, as with the glory of precious stones.

I have said this in order to show how holy was the root from which this saint sprang for us, like a shoot of the tree of life. But since we have mentioned his parents, we shall briefly explain how the Holy Spirit went before this holy man with the blessing of sweetness while he was still enclosed in his mother’s womb. For the glorious Virgin Mary, Mother of God, appeared in a dream to his pregnant mother, holding a golden ring in her hand, and said to her: “O Ermegardis, I wish the son whom you carry in your womb to be betrothed to me with this ring.” After leaving the sleeping woman with these words, the blessed Virgin disappeared. When she awoke from sleep, she began to turn the vision over in her mind. The blessed Mother of God then appeared to the woman a second time, just as the Lord is once said to have appeared again to Samuel in order to confirm his promise.

3. When the appointed days had passed, the woman gave birth to a son [Note: Surius adds, calling him Robert.], whom, after weaning, she handed over to be instructed in letters. There he advanced beyond all his contemporaries and drew from the fountains of the Savior with a pure heart, so that later he might pour forth among the peoples the grace of salvation.

When he was fifteen years old, avoiding worldly corruption, he resolved to consecrate himself wholly to the Lord. Therefore, offering the flower of his most pleasing youth to God, he received the religious habit at Saint Peter of Celle [Note: This monastery, in the suburb of Troyes, was discussed above.]. There, devoting himself to fasts and prayers by night and day, he rendered acceptable service to God, subjecting the flesh to the spirit and the spirit to the Creator.

When the time came for God to be glorified in his servant and for the lamp that had been hidden beneath a bushel to be placed upon a lampstand to illuminate the Church, he in whose hand are human hearts inspired the brothers of that house to choose God’s man Robert as their prior. It was fitting that he who, guided by grace, had learned through long practice to govern his own life should become the judge and governor of others.

At that time there was a certain hermit hidden far away in the depths of the woods [Note: This wood was called Colan, near Tonnerre, and is mentioned below in no. 8.]. He desired to serve God all the more freely because he did so in greater seclusion. By constant fasting he mortified his flesh, and by persistent prayer he strengthened his spirit. The Lord looked upon his humility, and through him, not without a great miracle, the multitude of those serving the Lord increased.

4. For two knights, brothers according to the flesh but not sharing the same sentiments according to the spirit, devoted to the pursuit of empty glory, sought out the detestable fairs that the common people call tournaments, to display their strength. As they traveled through the wood where the hermit mentioned above lived a solitary life, they began secretly to consider killing one another. Miserably wasting away under the poison of envy, they thought to themselves that, if one of them died, the survivor would succeed to the dead man’s possessions.

But almighty God, who knew that they would soon become vessels of mercy, did not allow them to be tempted beyond what they could bear. Rather, he made a way of escape along with the temptation, so that they would not carry into effect the wickedness they had conceived. God’s providence permitted them to be harassed by so unjust a temptation in order that, when they later advanced in virtue, they would not arrogantly attribute to themselves what they possessed, but would rather ascribe it to the one by whose mercy they had been delivered.

When they had completed the business for which they had gone—conducting themselves in it with sufficient boldness according to the customs of that people, so much so that they carried away the reward of human praise from all who had been present—they returned home. With prosperous steps they reached the place where they had secretly considered killing one another. There, as though warned by the place itself—or rather, pierced by divine inspiration—they began to abhor the wickedness they had contemplated and to be troubled within themselves by the crime they had conceived.

Calling to mind that the hut of the hermit mentioned above was nearby, they unanimously directed their journey to his little dwelling. By confession they vomited out the poisonous venom that had lain hidden in their hearts, and, expelling their impurity, prepared within themselves a pleasing dwelling for God. Finally, rebuked by the man of God for the wickedness they had contemplated, they withdrew from him instructed by saving admonitions. His fiery speech, like a torch, aroused heavenly desires in their minds, utterly uprooting from them the ambition for earthly rank and creating within them the fuel of virtue no less pleasantly than beneficially.

5. When they had reached the place where one had previously thought of attacking the other, they began to speak with one another. One of them said: “What, dearest brother, were you thinking here yesterday as we passed by?” When he had revealed the thought of his heart to his brother, the other replied: “I too was thinking of precisely the same thing.”

Immediately, pierced in heart, they returned to the man of God. Rejecting the pomp of the world and trampling down its pride, they began to live spiritually with him and humbly to bow their necks to bear the gentle yoke of Christ’s heart. Who, then, would doubt that their conversion should be ascribed to the merits of Blessed Robert? Under his direction, as the following account will teach, they were to be instructed in the disciplines of the Rule.

God, however, who consoles the humble, added to their number and multiplied his servants, so that within a short time they reached the number seven. This number represents the sevenfold grace of the Holy Spirit, whom we know to have worked the salvation of many through his servant Blessed Robert. That same Spirit prepared these seven men as seven columns of a spiritual building. Through them the monastic order began to revive, and, having sent down its root, to produce spiritual fruit from the moisture of grace, so that, when it was thought to have been entirely consumed, it might once more sprout in the fragrance of grace and put forth foliage, as when it was first planted.

6. Meanwhile Blessed Robert, sufficiently renowned for holiness and grace with God and human beings, was elected abbot by the monks of Saint Michael of Tonnerre [Note: Tonnerre, commonly called Tonnerre, not far from the Armançon River, where construction of the monastery had begun in 980.].

Since the hermits mentioned above had no one to instruct them in the disciplines of the Rule, when they heard the holy man’s reputation they arranged for two of their brothers to be sent to him. When they reached the place where the man of the Lord was diligently rendering service to God, they found the superior of that house in the audience chamber. Once he had learned their purpose and the reason for their journey, they scarcely obtained from him, despite many entreaties, permission to be led to the man of God’s private quarters.

Wounded by the sword of envy, the superior thought that something of his own would be lost if the Lord ordained anything worthy of praise through his servant for the advancement of others. Accordingly, he persuaded the brothers of that house, as well as the abbot’s companions, not to consent to the request of the brothers who had come to ask that the man of God preside over them.

Nevertheless, Blessed Robert, rejoicing in their request and just desires, would have fulfilled their wish had the brothers of Tonnerre not unanimously opposed it. He sent them back to their own place instructed by saving admonitions, accompanied by prayers, and strengthened by blessings. He established them especially in hope, promising that, as soon as the Lord granted him the opportunity, he would fill them with joy by his presence.

It is pleasant here to contemplate briefly God’s dispensation. Although their purpose was holy and their desire just, it was nevertheless postponed so that it might be broadened and increased; and when they obtained what they had sought, they might hold it more dearly and observe it more carefully.

## Chapter Two. The monasteries of Molesme and Cîteaux founded

7. The man of the Lord, always thinking not about the things of the world but about those of the Lord, saw that the brothers of that place were turning away from the path of righteousness. He feared that an evil companion might rub his own rust against the bright and simple man and disfigure the beautiful face of his soul, since character is usually shaped by one’s companions. He therefore returned to the cloister of Celle, from which he had departed.

There, Leah—who is said to be laborious—having been set aside for a time, he enjoyed the embraces of his beloved and long-desired Rachel, joyfully drawing from the fountains of the Savior what he would later offer to the faithful for their salvation.

But because a city set upon a mountain cannot remain hidden, Blessed Robert, firmly rooted and established upon the mountain of Christ, was again chosen to feed the humble flock of Christ when the prior of Saint Aigulf died [Note: Saint Aigulf, abbot of Lérins and martyr, is commemorated on 3 September. A priory under his name existed near the monastery of Celle and was subject to the abbot of Celle.]. By the unanimous vote and equal desire of the brothers, he became prior in that same house.

The hermits mentioned above, inflamed with love for the heavenly life, continually saw the man of God advancing in God and becoming better than himself. After deliberation, they sent two of their brothers to the Apostolic See, so that by their petitions they might obtain from the Supreme Pontiff that God’s man, Blessed Robert, should become father and pastor of Christ’s little flock.
