They knew that it would be wicked to contradict the Supreme Pontiff or rashly resist his commands.

The Supreme Pontiff [Note: This appears to have been Alexander III, who reigned from 1159 to 1181.], hearing their purpose, rejoiced greatly. He graciously granted their request and sent them back home rejoicing, strengthened by the apostolic blessing. By apostolic letters he instructed and commanded the abbot of Celle [Note: I believe this was Guarinus, identified by the Sammarthani under the year 1050; Bernard, his successor, was elected in 1071.] that he should give them as abbot whichever of the brothers they chose.

When the abbot of Celle learned what the Supreme Pontiff had commanded him, he granted Blessed Robert to those who requested him—sad and grieving, indeed, but not daring to oppose the apostolic commands. He saw that their consolation would be tribulation for himself and his own, because a cedar column, firm and indeed incorruptible, would be taken away from his house.

Blessed Robert, however, devoutly accepted the care of the pastoral office, seeing that his labor would not be fruitless, since the unity of the flock, rejecting earthly things and seeking heavenly ones, obeyed his saving admonitions. Thus he was again joined to Leah—that is, to the active life—in order to beget spiritual children. According to the inner person, he served the Lord in a spirit of humility; according to the outer person, he fulfilled his ministry with great vigor.

8. In the place now called Colan, those serving the Lord endured hunger and thirst, cold and nakedness, fasting and praying, bearing patiently the burden and heat of the day. They sowed in tears so that, together, they might bring back sheaves of righteousness to the Lord’s granary with rejoicing.

But since the sight of a fellow laborer is a consolation in toil, God, who regards the desires of the humble, added to their number and multiplied his servants, so that in a short time they became thirteen and, insofar as it lay within them, corresponded with the apostles in both uprightness of conduct and number.

The man of the Lord Robert, desiring a place suited to them, left guardians there, took the brothers, and withdrew to a certain wood called Molesme. There they labored with their own hands, cutting branches from the trees and constructing dwellings from them in which they could rest. They also completed an oratory in the same manner, in which they frequently offered the Lord saving offerings and the sacrifice of a contrite spirit. Since they had no bread with which to restore their bodies after prolonged labor, they used only vegetables.

It happened that the bishop of Troyes [Note: Everard of Avesnes, bishop of Troyes from 1172 to 1190.] was traveling through that wood, where the men of God were serving the Lord in the greatest poverty and humility, and arrived at that place at the hour of refreshment with a large company of companions.

The men of God received them devoutly, but were in a way ashamed because they had nothing to set before them. The bishop, greatly edified and moved by their humility and poverty, took his leave and departed.

As time passed, and they had no means by which even a little sustenance could be provided for the brothers, they sought refuge in Blessed Robert’s counsel. He, who had never made gold his strength nor said to refined gold, “My confidence” (Job 31), taught them to place their hope in the Lord God, knowing that God would not allow the soul of the righteous to remain longer afflicted by hunger.

Although they had no money, he nevertheless sent them to Troyes to purchase provisions, following the prophet’s counsel literally: “And you who have no silver, come, hurry, buy and eat” (Isa. 55).

When they entered the city of Troyes barefoot, word about them immediately reached the bishop. Having them brought before him, he received them with great devotion and showed, by the kindness he displayed toward the servants of God, the love he bore toward God. Finally, clothing them in new religious garments, he sent them back to their brothers with a wagon loaded with cloth and bread.

Greatly strengthened by this blessing, the brothers learned to be patient amid adversity. Indeed, from that day onward there was never a lack of someone to provide them with what they needed, both in food and in clothing.

9. While they persevered most steadfastly in the service of God, many came to them, fleeing the world and casting off its burden, to submit their necks to the Lord’s gentle yoke. Others sent them necessities from distant regions, so that, by supplying the necessities of the present life to the just, they might receive the reward of the just.

But because an abundance of possessions often brings poverty of character, when they began to abound in temporal things, they began to grow empty in spiritual things, so that their wickedness seemed to emerge as though from fatness.

Blessed Robert, however, did not set his heart upon the wealth that flowed in. Rather, he tried more and more to advance in God and to live justly, piously, and soberly according to the institutions of Saint Benedict. Seeing this, the sons of Belial rose up savagely against the man of God, provoking him to bitterness and tormenting the soul of the righteous by wicked deeds.

Nor should it trouble you, reader, that wickedness claimed a place in that holy congregation, since pride—which, born in heaven, recalls heavenly minds to their original home—may invade them, and that which is accustomed to appear in magnificence, linen, and purple may lie hidden in ashes and sackcloth. Finally, as Scripture testifies, we have learned that “one day the sons of God came to stand before the Lord, and Satan was also among them” (Job 1). Thus, from the beginning, there has never been lacking in the Church a righteous person who advanced and a wicked person who tested him.

10. Seeing that he was making no progress in correcting them, and that, having set aside observance of the Rule, each one was walking according to the perversity of his own heart, the man of God decided to leave them, lest, while seeking spiritual profit from them in vain, he should cause harm to his own soul.

When discord arose among them, he withdrew from them and came to a place called Aurum [Note: Manrique calls Aurum a monastery near Molesme. We have found no other indication of it from which anything can be learned about the site or the place’s former or subsequent condition.]. He had heard that brothers lived there, serving the Lord in a spirit of humility.

When he arrived, they received him devoutly. He lived among them for some time, laboring with his own hands so that he might have something to give to those suffering want. Persisting without interruption in vigils and prayers, he served the Lord tirelessly. Although he excelled all in holiness, serving everyone, he considered himself the least of all.

Not long afterward they elected him abbot. He took care to preside over them with complete moderation, caring for the sick and encouraging the healthy—not as one dominating those in the clergy, but becoming wholeheartedly a model for the flock.

11. The men of Molesme, however, repented that they had offended the man of God and had, in a way, expelled him through disobedience. They anxiously lamented their ruin both in conduct and in possessions. In their downfall they learned by experience that, through the merits of Blessed Robert, the Lord had granted them an abundance even of temporal goods.

They therefore adopted a plan for their salvation and approached the Supreme Pontiff. Relying upon his authority, they recalled the man of God to Molesme. There, constantly devoted to fasts and prayers, he imitated God’s zeal among his subjects, so that within a short time he restored observance of monastic discipline among them.

Among them were four men stronger in spirit: Alberic [Note: Alberic is commemorated on 26 January and Stephen on 17 April, when we published the life of each. The other two are named by Orderic Vitalis, cited shortly below: John and Hilbod.], Stephen, and two others, who, after the beginnings of cloistered discipline, longed for the solitary contest of the desert.

They therefore left the monastery of Molesme and came to a place called Vinicus [Note: Manrique writes Unicum; the Utrecht manuscript reads Vivificum. There is no trace anywhere of either name.]. After they had lived there for some time, the venerable Jocerannus [Note: Jocerannus, or Gaucerannus, bishop of Langres, held office approximately from 1114 to 1127. There is therefore a serious error in the name, if not also in the matter itself. No other episcopate can be identified into which this action could fall except that of Rainard, consecrated around 1065 and subscribing the Council of Saintes in 1080, or that of his successor Robert the Burgundian, predecessor of Jocerannus. Since the Cistercians say nothing of such coercion, and since the writer here is so mistaken, we fear that the entire episode may have been fabricated, and that none of them came to live at Cîteaux except with their abbot Robert.] the bishop of Langres, at the insistence of the men of Molesme, imposed a sentence of excommunication upon them unless they returned. [Note: From this we inferred—something also supported by other evidence—that the saints mentioned above returned from Vinicus to Molesme and did not go directly to Cîteaux.]

Thus compelled to leave the place, they came to a certain forest called Cîteaux by the inhabitants. There they built an oratory in honor of the Blessed Virgin Mary, Mother of God. From that time forward they could be recalled from their purpose neither by threats nor by entreaties. Burning with the Spirit, they served the Lord tirelessly day and night.

When Blessed Robert heard of their holy manner of life, he took with him twenty-two brothers and went to them, wishing to share in and assist their holy purpose. They received him with the greatest devotion, and for some time he presided over them with fatherly care, establishing their life and conduct according to the Rule and presenting himself as a model and example of religious observance and uprightness.

12. The men of Molesme, however, distressed at being deprived of so great a pastor, approached the Supreme Pontiff [Note: This was Pope Urban II, who presided from 1088 to 1090.], so that the man of the Lord, Blessed Robert, might be compelled to return to the Church of Molesme, which he had previously founded.

When the Supreme Pontiff heard that the new foundation of Cîteaux had been firmly rooted in Christ, he rejoiced greatly, having learned that its members excelled in every uprightness of conduct and that, formed by the example of Blessed Robert, they observed the Rule of Saint Benedict with greater fervor.

Seeing that destruction threatened the men of Molesme if they were deprived of the presence of the man of God, he wrote to the bishop of Chalon [Note: The bishop of Chalon mentioned above in no. 21, whom the Sammarthani call Walterius; he held office from 1080 to 1115.], instructing him that, after appointing another abbot for the Cistercians, he should compel Blessed Robert to return to Molesme.

When he learned this, Blessed Robert, knowing that “obedience is better than sacrifice” (1 Sam. 15), and that “to refuse to obey is like the sin of idolatry” (ibid.), arranged there what pertained to observing the new institution. He placed over them as abbot a man worthy of God, named Alberic, who had been one of the first monks of the Church of Molesme [Note: It was shown above, on the contrary, that after Saint Robert’s departure he had been elected by the brothers.]. Thus, after everything had been beneficially ordered, he returned to the monastery of Molesme, which he himself had founded in honor of Blessed Mary.

After Alberic died two years later [Note: Rather, after ten years. Orderic Vitalis explicitly says so in Book 8, speaking of Saint Robert’s return to Molesme: “He chose Alberic, a man of great religion, as his vicar for the work of Cîteaux, and appointed him abbot of Cîteaux over John and Hilbod of Arras and twenty-two other brothers. He lived there in great poverty for ten years and gloriously served God with his companions.” Orderic flourished and wrote around the year 1120 as a monk of Saint-Évroult in the diocese of Lisieux. He must therefore have obtained this information from the men of Molesme themselves, the earliest writers on their foundation. They were deceived only in this one respect: they said that Saint Robert retained some authority over the Cistercians when he returned to Molesme. The contrary has been demonstrated from the letters of the apostolic legate and of Walter, bishop of Chalon. Indeed, the author of this life himself indicates shortly before that the pope had instructed the bishop of Chalon to appoint another abbot of Cîteaux.], Stephen was appointed abbot of the Cistercians by Blessed Robert [Note: It is uncertain whether Robert lived so long. It is certain that he had no jurisdiction over the Cistercians, although I would not deny that they could have been guided by his counsel in both elections. Alberic died, and Stephen, then absent, was elected prior in 1109. The aforementioned Orderic writes of him that he was “English by birth, a man of great religion and wisdom,” and that he held office “for more than twenty-four years, distinguished gloriously by teaching and holy works.” He resigned the government in 1133 and died the following year, as has been shown in its proper place.].

Thus, as the founder of that new foundation, and since the ordering of both monasteries—Molesme and Cîteaux—belonged to his authority, he returned to Molesme with two monks. The Cistercians mourned his departure, while the men of Molesme rejoiced at his return.

A very large crowd of dignitaries and common people from the town of Bar [Note: Bar on the Seine—for this is distinguished by the addition from the other Bar on the Aube—lies two leagues from Molesme, at the mouth of a small river flowing into the Seine, upon which the monastery stands.] came out to meet him. They received him with great rejoicing and divine praises.

He entered the place prepared for him by God with his little flock—or rather, Christ’s flock—that is, the community of Molesme. Magnifying with complete gladness of mind the divine Providence that ordered all things, he cherished the flock entrusted to him with fatherly affection, instructing them in the disciplines of the Rule. Indeed, he became an embodiment of the Rule for them, living among them according to the Rule.

## Chapter Three. The death and burial of Saint Robert, and certain miracles at his funeral

12*. How the holy man departed from the prison of the flesh, and by what signs the Lord also glorified his precious death in his sight, I am pleased to reveal more fully to your charity.

After Blessed Robert had served the Lord through many contests of labor, worn out by profound weariness with the present life, he ardently desired to be released and to be with Christ (Phil. 1). God heard his desire and revealed to him the hour of his departure many days beforehand, just as he himself had earnestly wished. Knowing that it was approaching, he announced it to the brothers.

Held for some time by bodily illness, he increased the merits of his graces through the virtue of patience. He gloried in his infirmities and prepared within himself a worthy dwelling for the power of Christ.

In the eighty-third year of his age, on the fifteenth day before the Kalends of May [Note: Surius, thinking that an error had crept into the numbers, was himself mistaken when he corrected it to “the third day before the Kalends.”], he returned his body to the earth and sent his spirit to God, whose service he had followed without weariness—the earth weeping and heaven rejoicing.

His sons, namely the monks of Molesme, whose entire joy and consolation had been in him, wept most bitterly and attended with ardent devotion to the funeral rites of their revered Father. Although they had no doubt at all about the heavenly recompense of his merits or about the benefits that would be conferred upon them through his merits and intercessions, they were nevertheless deeply distressed that their Father’s presence had been taken from them in this life.

And because, while still on earth, he had proved by righteous works that he was a son of light, God revealed at his passing how great was his merit before him.

13. For at the first twilight of night, above the dwelling in which the lifeless body of Blessed Robert lay, two exceedingly bright arches of different colors appeared. Expanding to the breadth of a great street, they seemed to extend toward the four regions of the earth. One stretched from north to south, while the other extended from north to west.

At the summit, where the two arches joined, a bright light shone forth in the likeness of the circle of the moon. Extending upward, it completely excluded the darkness of night from that place.

Within this light a radiant cross appeared. At first it was small, but gradually it grew large. Around it were innumerable circles of various colors, and within each one there arose a small radiant cross, each growing wondrously together with its circle. When they had spread everywhere across the firmament, they wondrously illuminated the entire site of Molesme, so that by evident signs it appeared that the blessed man, who had received the sleep of death with devotion in that same place, was a son of light.

There can be no doubt that the light with its crosses was sent from heaven to manifest the merit of his holiness, so that it might be understood that the saint of God, fleeing the works of darkness, had crucified his flesh with its vices and desires. The crosses appeared in greater number so that it might clearly be revealed that many would become his imitators, just as he himself had been an imitator of Christ.

What shall I say about the arches except that they were signs of the covenant between God and humanity, between the creature and the Creator? To touch briefly upon something from ancient history, when the Lord had smelled the fragrance of sweetness from the offerings of the holy patriarch Noah (Gen. 8), he said: “I will place my bow in the clouds of heaven, and I will remember my covenant which I made with you” (Gen. 9).

I seem not inappropriately to have applied this testimony of Holy Scripture, although it should rather be referred to the mystery. For the spirit of the holy man departing to God was like a tasting of the sacrifice, and like a taste of the sweetest fragrance.

And since no one doubts that the world stands through the merits of the saints, it must be believed without hesitation that the holy man, already freed from the flesh, obtains forgiveness of sins for those devoted to him and more frequently secures for them the gifts of grace [Note: The entire following passage is found in Surius at the end of the Life.].

14. To impress his holiness more deeply upon human minds, the Creator of all also worked healing among the sick who were devoutly attending the holy man’s funeral; the following account, with the Lord’s help, will make this clear. Two men, fervent in faith, approached the place where the holy man’s body, emptied of its life-giving spirit, lay. After they had been allowed to be placed beneath his bier and touch his shroud, they immediately recovered their former health and turned the mourning of the sorrowful brothers into solemn rejoicing over the miracle performed through God’s servant.

And just as the power of the prophet Elisha was once made known to the king of Syria through a captive girl, so God also wished his servant to become known among the Franks through a woman. The countess of Nevers [Note: This was perhaps the wife of William III, who held the title of this county, situated between Burgundy and the Loire and now converted into a duchy, from about 1100 to 1148, when, aged and converted among the Carthusians, he died; his wife's name is unknown. Unless perhaps the miracle happened later to Countess Ida, wife of William IV, named in a certain charter of Pontigny dated 1156.], while staying in a certain town with a large company of girls and soldiers, possessed a golden clasp at her neck, precious both for the material of its gold and for the engraving of its stones. On one occasion, wishing to display its beauty and value, she removed it from her neck and held it in her hands, handing it to others to carry. As they admired the beauty of the clasp and passed it from one to another to examine, they began conversing about other matters and forgot the clasp they were holding.

The countess then put her hand to her neck and, discovering that it had been unfastened, anxiously began asking to whom she had given the clasp. When each person was questioned separately and said that he or she did not have it, the noble lady became increasingly troubled in mind. There was a great quantity of straw in the place, and she ordered it to be winnowed. Lighting a lamp, she searched and turned the entire house upside down. But when she could not find what she was seeking, a young girl in her service approached her and firmly insisted that, if she faithfully implored blessed Robert, the saint would certainly return her clasp.

The countess faithfully followed this advice and ordered a candle to be lit in honor of blessed Robert the abbot. When this had been done, the clasp was immediately found before a great multitude of people, lying in her lap. Men and women gathered, glorifying God for so great a miracle and proclaiming him wonderful in blessed Robert, his servant. This miracle became so famous that anyone in the whole region who lost anything did not hesitate to seek the help of the man of God, and thus recovered without delay what had previously been lost. Nor is it surprising that the holy man received from the Lord a special grace for restoring lost things, since he is a lamp burning and shining in the house of the Lord, so that whoever approaches him may be enlightened, and through him the lost drachma may be restored [or, according to the manuscript: “be found”; otherwise, “be restored”].

15. When, as customary, the funeral rites had been completed around the blessed man’s body, that most holy body was reverently entrusted to burial by the neighboring abbots and other venerable persons gathered for this purpose, and was honorably buried in the church of the Blessed Virgin, which he himself had founded in her honor.

But almighty God, to demonstrate that his servant blessed Robert continued to live after laying aside the flesh, adorned him with the glory of many miracles. The same holy man, to show that he continued to care for his sons even after his bodily presence had been withdrawn from their eyes, often used to awaken the sacristan when they were negligent in God’s service or had risen late for Matins, rebuking the negligent and encouraging the devout toward better conduct.

We have passed briefly over these matters concerning the life and character of the blessed man in a rough style, taking care to satisfy the devout without burdening the fastidious with an abundance of words. Let no one suppose, however, that all the memorials of his holiness could have been written down. Rather, let it be known that what happened to me is what commonly happens to inept poets: when they undertake material exceeding their powers, crushed beneath its magnitude, they do not complete what they began. Thus not only the Jews but also the Christians of our own time seek signs, although holiness does not consist in the display of miracles, but rather in the practice of virtue. To satisfy both groups, we shall briefly touch upon a few of the many works the Lord performed through him.

16. After the holy man had passed by a blessed departure to Christ, the reputation of his virtues began to spread far and wide, and the Lord was near to those invoking the holy man’s name. The blessed Mother of God, who had betrothed the man of God to herself while he was still enclosed within the narrow confines of his mother’s womb, does not cease to share with her servant the grace that she uniquely received from the Lord.

From the day of blessed Robert’s death, miracles therefore began to occur frequently in the church of Molesme, which that holy man had built in honor of the same Virgin, to whom he had devoted himself entirely from his earliest years and had served with special devotion. As the grace of divine providence proclaimed throughout the whole earth the miracles that almighty God had deigned to perform in the church of Molesme through the prayers of his Mother and the merits of blessed Robert, crowds began to flow there from every nation.

17. A certain poor woman, suffering from the falling sickness, decided to come to the church of Molesme to seek help from the Mother of the Lord and blessed Robert, her servant. Taking with her two little children—one hanging at her breast, while the other, with feeble steps, followed his mother’s footprints—she continued on the journey she had undertaken.

As the day was already declining, she came to the monastery of Quincy [Note: In the diocese of Langres there is the monastery of Quincy, commonly called Quincy, founded in 1133 and belonging to the Cistercian order. It is distinct from Quinciacum, a very ancient monastery among the Poitevins, commonly called Quincay.], begging the monks for lodging. But because their rule does not admit women within their boundaries, the wretched woman was compelled to leave and spend the night in the woods. By chance she found a hearth; rekindling it from the smoldering ashes, she remained there with her two little children.

At midnight a wolf arrived. While the woman sat on one side of the fire, the cruel beast lay down on the other. Seeing this, the woman impressed the sign of the cross upon her forehead and most devoutly commended herself and her children to God, the Blessed Virgin Mary, and blessed Robert.

Meanwhile illness seized her, and while her lifeless body trembled, the wolf—as though it had deliberately been waiting—seized the younger child and fled. When the plague of illness subsided, the woman, as though rising from the dead, searched between her arms for the infant whom she had shortly before been holding and whom she knew she had not otherwise released. She rejoiced to be freed from her illness, but a grief perhaps more cruel replaced it: questioning her older son, she learned the utterly lamentable fate of the younger.

What could the wretched woman do? She did not know where to turn. No one could express the force of so great a grief unless, taking on a mother’s heart, that person had learned through experience how to suffer it. Yet amid her cries these words were repeatedly spoken:

> “Return, return the deposit, Blessed Mary; return the deposit, Father of Molesme.”

A wondrous thing! As she repeated these words and repeatedly called upon Blessed Mary and holy Robert, intensifying the force of her grief, behold, the beast, forgetting its ferocity—for it is characteristic of it not to spare but to devour—came out of the forest with a gentle mouth, carrying the child, and returned him unharmed to his mother. Her subsequent joy consumed her sorrow. She completed the journey she had begun and related the whole sequence of events in the presence of many people. The marks of the teeth could also be seen on the child’s back, a more intimate confirmation of what had happened.

18. How much the Son of God works in the church of Molesme to proclaim the merits of his Mother and of blessed Robert is evident from what has already been said and is made clear by what follows. In a village called Novallavies [Note: Surius has “Novallames.” Neither spelling is satisfactory; it is not easy to discover the true form by conjecture, since the maps show no nearby place whose name resembles it. The Utrecht manuscript omits the name.], a certain man, occupied with business outside the home together with his wife, had left only a little child sleeping in a cradle in their locked house.

Meanwhile fire, finding material for its consumption, gradually grew and began to show itself outside. When the flame was already raging across the surface of the roof, people ran to help avert the disaster, but in vain, for the conflagration, spreading everywhere, prevented access [Note: Our copy lacks this word; we have supplied it from Surius.]. At last the parents arrived prematurely, and repeatedly calling the child’s name, they beat their breasts and tore their hair. Their love for their child, made more violently acute by the danger, felt no awareness of the house’s burning.

Whenever the force of grief allowed the mother to draw breath, she repeated these words:

> “To you I commend my son; be his shield against the face of the devouring fire all around, Lady of Molesme, fountain of mercy.”

At last the parents approached, praying that they might at least find ashes and embers of the child’s body. Who would not marvel? Let those who hear attend, and let the whole world wonder and be astonished at the novelty of so great a miracle. They found the little child smiling among the coals. Although the cradle and its cloths had been reduced to ashes, the fire did not know how to rage against the child alone.

Behold: if anyone wishes to express the likeness and compare the present with the past, in praise of his Mother and to proclaim the merits of saint Robert, the Son of God deigned to renew the ancient miracle of Babylon. For this fourth child could be numbered with those three boys, if only the flames had spared the cloths.

When the child had been brought by his parents and presented to the church, many people gathered, praising the Lord. At their urging, lest the event be removed from memory, it was entrusted to the faithful custody of written record.

## CHAPTER IV. Various illnesses healed; a blind man enlightened; a paralyzed woman raised; women possessed by demons delivered

19. If I should attempt to write down everything the Lord performs through his servant, I could not keep up with the task, since time would abandon me before material did. Every day in the church of Molesme the Savior’s mercy is present to those who implore the help of blessed Robert: through his intervening merits, the blind receive sight at his tomb, the weak recover the use of their legs, the sick are healed, and evil spirits, unable to endure his presence, are driven from the bodies they possess.

To prevent this from appearing incredible to anyone, we have taken care to transmit at least a few examples from the many for the knowledge of posterity. Although tongues are a sign not for believers but for unbelievers, nevertheless, because even in our own times it is necessary for withered and sick faith to be watered, let us now gird ourselves to fulfill what we promised [Note: Surius here follows with what we have already had above, in chapter 3, no. 14. The rest is absent from his text.].

A certain nobleman from the regions of Lorraine, rich indeed in earthly possessions but poor in salvation, burdened by a long life and the affliction of illness, had lost the light of his eyes. Desiring his own healing, he had visited many holy places to seek remedies for his health, but could not obtain what he sought. For the saints, rejoicing that blessed Robert had been joined to their company, were reserving for his merits the novelty of so great a miracle, so that through a nobleman his name might become known even among foreign peoples.

This man then set out for Saint James with a crowd of sons and servants, seeking pardon for his sins. As he continued along his intended route [Note: The direct route from Lorraine ran through Champagne, Burgundy, and Aquitaine. The sworn witnesses to the miracles concerning the blind man and the crippled woman are given below, no. 27.], he heard of the miracles by which the Lord was proclaiming the holiness of his servant Robert. The men accompanying him advised and earnestly urged him to place his hope in the Lord God and approach the tomb of the man of God with devotion.

He accepted their exhortations and kept an all-night vigil at the tomb of the man of God. Hearing a very large crowd praising God in his saint and giving thanks for recovered health through his merits, he was troubled in spirit, confessing his sins and washing away the stains of his former life with streams of tears.

After he had remained there for a week with his entire company without being heard, he cried out to the Lord. Then, again urged by his children and household, he prepared to leave. They took him by the hands and led him as far as the church door. When he realized that he was at the entrance of the church, the man, full of devotion and fervent in faith, turned his face toward the tomb, weeping and lamenting, and frequently calling upon the saint’s name.

What more need be said? While he lay prostrate on the ground, wetting his face with tears and praying God not to regard his sins but, through the merits of blessed Robert, to show mercy to the petitioner, suddenly membranes like little skins burst from his eyes and descended over his face. Feeling this, he placed his hand there; and when he wiped his eyes and marveled that his sight had been restored, he rejoiced. He who had previously wept from grief now began to weep from joy, showing everyone who was trying to lead him away that the brightness of his sight had been restored.

Those present, praising God for so great and unexpected a miracle, returned to the church, giving thanks to God and honoring the man of God’s tomb with gifts. Then they departed joyfully and eagerly completed the pilgrimage they had begun.

20. To confirm this miracle more fully, another occurred, perhaps no less remarkable. As they went on their way, rejoicing and greatly strengthened by God’s favor, they happened to enter a city called Tudela [Note: We have corrected the form, although our copy reads “Cudella.” It is the city of Tutela on the river Ebro, a convenient stopping-place for those traveling from Gaul to Galicia, not far from Calahorra.].

They were received with considerable honor as guests by a powerful man. While they were speaking together as friends, the noble pilgrim attributed God’s mercy to the merits of blessed Robert. Hearing what had happened, their host sighed deeply and said:

> “Behold, my wife is deprived of all use of her limbs from the waist downward and cannot move from her place unless she is carried by the hands of servants or maids. Nor is this wound recent; indeed, seventeen years have already passed since this happened to her. Nevertheless, if that saint whom you mention possesses such great merit, I trust in the Lord that my wife will be restored to health through his prayers.”

The pilgrim recounted not only what he had experienced himself but also what he had seen happen to others through the merits of blessed Robert. He encouraged his host as much as he could to seek God’s favors. The man accepted his words and effectively persuaded his wife to do the same.

When the darkness of night had passed and the Phoebean lamp had illuminated the earth with its rays, the faithful husband placed his wife on a litter and, with a large retinue, entered Gaul. He did not bring his labor to an end until he reached the place where the body of the blessed man had been reverently buried.

21. When they had come to a certain heap of stones called Mons-Gaudii-Dei, intending to seek the help of blessed Robert, she was immediately lifted down by her servants. She prostrated herself on the ground and, wholly dissolved in tears, most devoutly implored that her health be restored.

A multitude of sick, blind, deaf, and paralyzed people, returning joyfully to their homes through the man of God’s power, stopped there with the woman after she had been taken from the litter. Joining their prayers to hers, and recounting what they had experienced in themselves and had seen or heard in others, they inflamed her mind to ask more earnestly.

Without delay, the tendons of her thighs, which the long illness had contracted, gradually began to stretch, and her bones recovered their proper strength. The woman, sensing God’s power working in her, slowly rose and sprang to her feet without anyone’s help. Giving thanks to God and blessed Robert, she caused all who were present suddenly to open their mouths in praise of God and blessed Robert, and a voice of rejoicing was heard far away.

When her husband asked her to climb back onto the litter so that she might proceed to the church, she refused to comply. Instead, she walked and leaped ahead of the others, praising God, so that in her the prophecy of Isaiah appeared literally to have been fulfilled:

> “Then the lame man shall leap like a stag, and the tongue of the mute shall be opened” (Isaiah 35).

For she who had previously been unable to move now went ahead of the others; and she whose mouth previously could not open from shame now poured herself out entirely in the praises of God.

She came to the church where the body of the man of God lay buried, almost two miles from the place where the woman had been healed. There she gave thanks to God and blessed Robert, not doubting that through his merits she had been freed from the illness by which she had been held.

Prostrating herself on the ground before the saint’s tomb and most devoutly kissing the earth in which his body lay, she gave all who were present an opportunity to proclaim God’s marvelous work in his saint. After completing her prayer and honoring the tomb of the man of God with many gifts, they returned home with joy, leaving behind the litter on which she had been carried as testimony to her deliverance. So that this miracle would not remain unknown even to posterity, that same litter hung for a long time before the doors of the basilica.

22. The miracles performed at the invocation of this saint reveal how much power he received from the Lord to drive out unclean spirits. To pass over other cases, a certain woman entered the church of Molesme to pray and was standing before the altar when, by the hidden judgment of God, she was seized by a demon and miserably tormented.

On the advice of an elderly monk who was present, the woman’s husband, who had come with her, bound her to the tomb of blessed Robert. The wretched woman raged so cruelly that she tried to bite everyone who wished to approach. At last, after being admonished by her husband, she called upon the name of blessed Robert, saying:

> “Saint Robert, pray to the Blessed Virgin that she herself may obtain my deliverance from her Son.”

At these words the woman was immediately freed before everyone’s eyes and gave thanks to God.

Another woman from a village called Baignous [Note: Commonly Baigneux-les-Juifs, that is, Balniola Judaeorum, a town of Burgundy near the Seine. It is so identified in P. Duval’s French alphabetical gazetteer and appears to be the same place that is written without the additional designation as Bagnaux in the map of the duchy of Burgundy, one league from Molesme, by the stream that empties into the Seine below the previously mentioned Bar.], after giving birth in her bedroom, was, by some judgment of God, driven insane. She struck and killed her husband Evonga. Bound with ropes and brought to the church of Molesme, she was freed from the demon as soon as she was able to touch the tomb of the holy man and thereafter suffered nothing of the kind.

When she came to herself and saw that she was bound with ropes, she began to wonder. Then, recognizing the crime she had committed, she began to weep for a twofold reason: on the one hand, bitterly lamenting her sin; on the other, giving thanks to God for her deliverance.

The power of Christ does not cease to perform these and similar works through the merits of blessed Robert, to the praise and glory of his name, to whom, with the Father and the Holy Spirit, be honor and glory for ever and ever. Amen.

23. I think it not unfitting to repeat what has been omitted and to note in a few words how moderate in severity toward his subjects and how generous toward the poor blessed Robert was.

One day two clerics found the man of God outside the church doors and began insistently asking him for food. Since the man of God overflowed entirely with compassion and wished to relieve their poverty, he immediately ordered one of the brothers, whose duty it was to serve the tables, to be summoned. When he ordered him to give something to the needy, he received the reply that there were absolutely no loaves in the monastery.

“Then from where,” said the saint, “will the brothers eat today?”

“I do not know,” he replied.

Before long the hour arrived when the brothers, after completing the customary solemnities of the Masses, were preparing to approach the tables. When the holy man heard the sound of the bell, as was customary at that hour, he asked the steward where he had obtained the loaves that he was to set before the brothers at their meal.

“I,” he replied, “had saved a few, making arrangements so that food would not be lacking for the brothers at the hour of the meal.”

Then the man of God, inflamed with zeal, growled and became indignant that the flock entrusted to him should contain the weeds of disobedience and the tares of distrust. He entered the refectory, took the loaves set upon the table in a basket, and threw them down from a nearby hillock of the church into the water that flowed beneath it [Note: Michael Antonius Baudrand, who recently published a geographical lexicon based on Ferrari’s work, enlarged by half, says in his entry on Molesme that it lies on the river Leigne, which one might call in Latin Lenia or Linea. Here, however, this stream flows into the Seine above Bar.], unwilling that the fault of disobedience should be found among the sons of God.

But God, looking down from on high upon his zeal, had already inspired certain devout women from Châtillon [Note: Châtillon is a town on the Seine, three leagues east of Molesme.] to bring loaves for the brothers’ meal. For when God’s man blessed Robert returned from there, he found three wagons loaded with bread at the monastery gate; the women just mentioned had brought them from Châtillon for the brothers’ meal.

Then the man of God summoned the brothers and publicly rebuked the distrustful and disobedient brother, while encouraging all the brothers with salutary admonitions to trust in God’s mercy in times of need.

[Note: This entire paragraph appears in Surius after our number 11.]

## THE CANONIZATION PROCESS

[Col. 1287]

24. This canonization process, together with the origins of the Cistercian order, is found in volume I of the *Bibliotheca manuscripta*, edited by Philippe Labbe. In the year 1221, the Cistercians gathered for a general chapter and there decreed that intercessions should be made and petitions offered to Pope Honorius III, asking him to enroll Robert in the catalogue of the saints.

The people of Molesme likewise applied themselves to the matter, seeking honors for their common Father’s merits. By joining their letters and envoys, both groups persuaded the pope that, judging the request equitable, he should appoint, before granting Saint Robert public worship, certain suitable and reliable men to investigate his holiness of life and learn about his miracles, as is the custom of the Church.

These were Hugh II, bishop of Langres; Valentine Girondus or Giraldus, promoted to this office from the abbacy of Molesme and later of Cluny; and Roland, abbot of Cluny. To them the pope sent the following letter concerning the investigation:

> “Honorius, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to our venerable brothers the bishops of Langres and Valentine, and to our beloved son the abbot of Cluny in the diocese of Mâcon: greeting and apostolic blessing.
>
> “We rejoice in the Lord and delight in his praises because, as the beloved sons, all the abbots of the Cistercian order gathered in general chapter, as well as the abbot of the community of Molesme, have informed us in their letters, Robert, of blessed memory—who was the first abbot of the monastery of Molesme and first laid the foundation of the Cistercian order, which, by the favor of divine grace, grew into a holy temple in the Lord—while living religiously, shone with such a grace of merits that the Lord then worked many great miracles through him and, even after his blessed death, deigns to work greater ones at his tomb, to display his holiness. Thus the glory of miracles indicates to us that he whom the virtue of his conduct honored on the way is honored in his homeland.
>
> “Therefore those same men have earnestly petitioned us that, since it is clearer than daylight that he reigns in the order of confessors in the Church triumphant, we should also enroll him in the catalogue of the saints in the Church militant. But since in so great a matter one must proceed only with the utmost seriousness, placing full confidence in the faith and discretion that you possess in the Lord, we command your discretion by apostolic letter to make a careful inquiry both into the life and into the miracles of the aforesaid saint and faithfully inform us by your letters of the truth you discover, so that, sufficiently instructed by your report, we may proceed thereafter as we see should be done according to God. If not all of you can take part in carrying this out, let two of you nevertheless perform it.
>
> “Given at the Lateran, on the eighth day before the Kalends of February, in the fifth year of our pontificate.”

25. Concerning the investigation just mentioned—which the two bishops conducted at Molesme while the abbot of Cluny was prevented by other business—Manriquez writes that, since Saint Robert had been taken from the living a hundred years earlier and none of his contemporaries survived who could testify about the miracles performed by him while alive, the investigators were content with the written history of his life and miracles and sent it to Honorius, together with the following letter, which contains the canonization process.

The author of the Life he himself calls Odo, perpetuating an error once begun, although this was the name of the abbot at whose command it was written, not the name of its author. The letter itself is as follows:

> “To the most holy Father and lord Honorius, by the grace of God supreme and universal pontiff of the holy and apostolic see, H., by the same grace bishop of Langres, and G., bishop of Valence: greeting with the kiss of your feet and due reverential service.
>
> “We received your Holiness’s mandate in the following form: ‘Honorius, bishop, etc.’ By the authority of this mandate, therefore, we personally came to the place—our colleague the abbot of Cluny having entrusted his duties to us, the bishop of Valence—and received witnesses, whose depositions we ordered to be written down word for word as follows.
>
> “Odo, abbot of Molesme, gave sworn testimony that, when he was a child in secular dress, he saw a certain woman blind from birth who had a daughter, as the mother herself firmly asserted. He brought the woman to the tomb of the venerable Father Robert, the subject of this inquiry, and when she kept vigil there one night with her mother, she received her sight. The same abbot was present at this event and saw it.
>
> “The same abbot also saw, at the time of the dedication of the church of Molesme, after he had received the monastic habit and the priestly order, that when the tombs were being removed from the church out of reverence for the dedication, and they had come to the tomb of the same venerable Father, a certain woman, at the movement of the tomb, anointed her own eyes with earth and received her sight there.”

26. “Another woman, eating some of the same earth, recovered her speech, although she had been mute for three years, as both she and her husband firmly asserted. Later, before two years had passed from the present examination of the witnesses, a certain cow was wounded by a wolf. When its owner, a woman, perceived this, she sprinkled the wound with holy water; immediately an unceasing and violent trembling seized her head and arm. Returning that same day to the aforesaid tomb, she was immediately cured and completely healed. Odo himself saw this at that time, already established as abbot in the same church.

“He also saw a certain monk named Ragnerius, who had become insane, bound to the tomb of the same venerable Father and there recovering his health through divine grace.

“William the priest, under oath, testified concerning the woman who received her sight at the time of the dedication exactly as the abbot had. He said that he had often heard about the woman who recovered her speech, but had not seen her. Concerning the woman who suffered trembling of the head and arm, he testified as the abbot had.

“He also saw a certain woman who had worked on a feast day and therefore, as is believed, had been struck in the hand that same day. Her hand became so useless that it was despaired of ever being healed. But through divine mercy and the saint’s merits, when she approached his tomb, she was immediately healed.

“He also saw a certain insane person healed there.

“Alberic, a monk and priest, under oath, testified concerning the miracles performed at the dedication as the abbot had; concerning the woman who recovered the health of her hand, as William had.”

27. “James, a monk and priest, under oath, testified that a certain blood brother of his, while still a boy, was so severely injured in the head that his eye had been torn from its proper place and hung down from his face. At James’s insistence he was carried to the frequently mentioned tomb, and immediately, through divine mercy, he was healed; the eye returned to its proper place without any injury. The monk James himself saw all this concerning his brother.

“Concerning the other two miracles performed at the dedication, he testified as the others had. The same James also saw a certain woman brought from distant regions who had long been crippled. As soon as she saw the monastery in which the venerable abbot rests, to whom she had vowed herself in hope of recovering her health, she was cured and completely healed.

“Milo, a layman, under oath, testified concerning the eye that had been torn out and restored as James had; concerning the miracles performed at the dedication and concerning the woman who suffered trembling of the head and arm, as the abbot and the others had.

“Bartholomew, a monk and priest, under oath, testified concerning the two miracles performed at the dedication and the woman struck in the hand as the others had.”

28. “Hugh, a priest and monk, under oath, testified that he saw a certain blind citizen of Metz coming out of devotion and in hope of recovering his sight to the frequently mentioned tomb. When he came to it, he recovered his sight and saw scales visibly falling away from his eyes.

“Proceeding from there more quickly toward Saint James, he lodged on the way in the house of a certain woman who lay crippled in bed. But at his advice, she had herself carried to the saint’s tomb and was healed. This is the woman about whom the monk and priest James speaks above. James agrees with Hugh, but only by hearsay.

“William, a monk and priest, under oath, testified that he saw a certain cleric who had long been crippled healed at the same tomb; and concerning the two women at the dedication, as the others had.

“Licelinus, a monk and priest, under oath, testified concerning the two miracles at the dedication as the others had.

“Martin, under oath, testified concerning the miracles performed at the dedication and concerning the woman who had been healed of the injury to her hand as the others had.

“Haymo, a monk and priest, under oath, testified that he saw a certain insane man healed there.

“Master Simon, a priest, under oath, testified concerning the miracles performed at the dedication as the others had, adding that a certain layman at Molesme mocked the venerable Father with insults and ridiculed his miracles. As he was leaving, he was killed the following day within the boundaries of the same village by two soldiers. James also testified that he had seen this.

“Master Simon also saw a certain layman who had been crippled for eleven years healed at the frequently mentioned tomb.”

29. “Fulco and James, monks and priests, having sworn, stated that one day, when they were beside the aforesaid tomb and were showing reverence to the holy man by bowing their heads, a certain monk stood with them and, in their presence and hearing, burst forth abusively in these words: ‘Why do you bow your heads to him? Know for certain that he was never [Col. 1291D] a saint.’ Indeed, a certain very deformed peasant, striking the tomb with his foot, shouted similar things. Immediately a swelling seized that foot and rose throughout his entire body, so that within a fortnight, weighed down by that illness, he breathed his last.

“A countless multitude of those healed from madness and fevers cried out before us and firmly asserted that they had been cured. Thus the common opinion of the entire region concerning these matters became so widespread that it greatly enhances the tenor of the testimonies themselves. These events are said to have occurred in our own times, as was expressed above. From the time of his death, whose date is not remembered, countless miracles are reported; so that the entire neighborhood has no doubt that, through his miracles, [Col. 1292A] he has been made the equal of those listed among the saints. Moreover, his life will be presented in writing to Your Holiness by messengers of the Church of Molesme; it sufficiently shows that he excelled in many merits. But what we have heard, having investigated it faithfully with the utmost diligence, we explain to Your Blessedness in this present written document, so that Your Holy Fatherhood may see what ought to be done in such matters.”

30. Thus far the bishops’ letter to the pontiff, and the investigation concerning Saint Robert’s sanctity and miracles. Concerning these matters, several abbots in the vicinity also sent their testimony in writing to Honorius, in the following words:

“To the Most Holy Father and universal lord, Honorius, by divine providence pontiff of the holy apostolic see: the abbots of Saint Benignus of Dijon, Saint Stephen of Reims, [Col. 1292B] Saint Michael of Tonnerre, and Saint Martin of Melun, of the diocese of Langres, offer greetings with the kissing of his feet and the service owed in due reverence.

“Since the Church of Molesme and those churches in which we have the responsibility of ministering are close to one another, indeed so near that scarcely, or not at all, does anything important occur in one of them that swift rumor does not quickly carry to the others, we have judged it fitting at this present juncture to bear witness to the truth concerning the life of our holy father Robert, first abbot of the Church of Molesme and founder of the Cistercian order—a life that shone forth, worthy of veneration, through innumerable virtues—and concerning the miracles that, through the operation of divine mercy, occur daily at his tomb.

[Col. 1292C]

“For continually the voice of the people of the entire region cries in our ears that a very great multitude of the crippled, the blind, the mute, and others afflicted with various illnesses, who daily stream to the tomb of the said saint in the church at Molesme, after offering prayer and invoking the saint’s name, appear to return safely to their homes, restored to their former health.

“Therefore, inflamed by the miracles of this saint, we humbly and devoutly beseech Your Most Holy Fatherhood, insofar as we are able, that you decree that the aforesaid Saint Robert—whom God has wonderfully magnified in our lands among His elect, through merits shining forth in miracles—be canonized and added to the roll of the saints.”

Thus the abbots.

[Col. 1292D]

31. After reading this letter and the testimonies mentioned above, Honorius, while desiring certain additional evidence before decreeing that Saint Robert receive universal veneration throughout the Church and before declaring him a saint, meanwhile granted the people of Molesme permission to venerate him and to celebrate an office in his honor, but only in that church in which his sacred bones were buried. Concerning this matter, the pontiff’s document is as follows:

“Honorius, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved sons, the abbot and convent of Molesme: greetings and apostolic blessing.

“Formerly, through your letters and messengers, you earnestly petitioned us, supported by the testimonies and intercessions of many, that we should inscribe among the saints the blessed Robert of holy memory, whose body, resting in your [Col. 1293A] church, shone forth through many great miracles. But, lest we appear to act with any levity in so important a matter, we ordered an investigation, through our venerable brothers the bishops of Langres and Valence, both into his life and into his miracles, since, for someone to be regarded as a saint in the Church militant, it is necessary that merits of the true faith—which works through love—precede, together with final perseverance, and that clear miracles follow as well; neither of these, without the other, is fully sufficient as evidence of sanctity. For some perform their works so that they may be seen by human beings; and sometimes Satan’s angel, disguising himself as an angel of light, frequently deceives people, as we read concerning Pharaoh’s magicians. [Col. 1293B]

“When the aforesaid investigators had fully reported the truth to us concerning these matters, [Col. 1294A] although they informed us of certain miracles that he had performed after his death, they did not, however, provide full assurance concerning those he is said to have performed during his life. Therefore, lest we appear entirely to disregard your petitions, we grant you permission to venerate him as a saint in your church and confidently to implore his intercessions with God.

“Given at the Lateran, on the sixth day before the Ides of January, in the sixth year of our pontificate.”

Manriquez says that he took this letter from the Vatican; he adds that, in this same year or at the beginning of the following one, after what had been lacking in the first investigation had been supplied, Saint Robert was enrolled absolutely among the saints, and that it was decreed in the general chapter of the Cistercian family that his feast, on the fifteenth day before the Kalends of May, should be celebrated more solemnly throughout the world with an office of twelve readings [Col. 1294B] throughout the world.

[Col. 1293]

# THE LETTERS OF SAINT ROBERT

## FIRST LETTER. TO DUKE ODO

[Col. 1293B]

To the most illustrious Duke Odo: Robert, abbot of the Church of Molesme, and those who with him desire the service of the Lord, greetings and happiness.

[Col. 1293C] Recognizing the piety and grace granted to you by the Lord, we do not wish to undertake anything new without the approval of Your Highness, although it is an ancient, not a new, practice to run toward the attainment of virtue. Therefore, know that, with the agreement of certain of our companions, who have been granted the grace of knowing themselves, we have resolved, in accordance with the precepts of the most holy Rule, to live in true poverty and sincerity of conscience.

“And because we have not been able to bring the others to the same view, we have decided to leave both them and their governance, and to withdraw into the wilderness with those who wish to follow our footsteps—or rather, those of our holy father Benedict. Since we have so often experienced your disposition toward us, and since we must now experience it against the storms rising up against us, we have informed you of everything, praying the Lord and Father of mercies to preserve you and your household unharmed. Amen.”

## SECOND LETTER. ODO’S LETTER TO ROBERT

[Col. 1293D] Odo, duke of Burgundy, and so forth, to the venerable Father Robert, abbot of Molesme, and to the others who with him are one in the Lord: eternal peace in the eternal God.

Your letter of sincerity was brought to us by the hand of the most modest man, Stephen, your companion. Having read it, we approve both your intention and your undertaking. Do what the Spirit commands; I will not fail you. Rather, from the provincial bishops—and, if necessary, from the Roman see—I will obtain whatever you desire. Choose the place of your solitude, and pray constantly to the Lord for me. May the Lord preserve your sincerity and increase your pure intention.

## THIRD LETTER. TO THE CISTERCIAN BROTHERS

[Col. 1294C]

To the brothers who are ascending the mountain of perfection in the hills of Cîteaux: Robert, formerly their companion, now sunk in the valley of miseries, wishes them the palm after their ascent and remembrance of himself as he ascends.

If the tongue could take the place of the pen, tears that of ink, and the heart that of paper, perhaps the pen would have moved your ears, the ink your eyes, and the paper your affections; and all of them together, together with you all, would have moved you toward compassion.

“For after I did not cling to you, my tongue clung to my jaws; when my eyes no longer saw you, even the light of my eyes was no longer with me. While my heart was torn away from you—if it could ever have been torn away from you—it became like melting wax in the midst of my belly. Yet although this tearing away separated me from you, it did not thereby separate any of you; for those whom the charity of Jesus Christ joins together, the distances of the earth divide in vain.

“Let Molesme possess the presence of my body, bound by the laws of obedience, provided that Cîteaux possesses the desire of my soul. The Most High, whose secrets are inscrutable, has arranged this: that, although I am drawn in different directions, neither may my soul be distracted through bodily association, nor may my body, thus separated, [not] enjoy such a holy way of life. [Col. 1294D] Pour forth prayers for the soul dwelling with you; the body, whose soul you possess—as possessors of its best part—greets you in the Lord.”
